column1: Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's complete style evolution
column2: © Evan Agostini Fashion From freshly-crowned Miss World to 17 years of Cannes Film Festival, we chart all the changes in Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s sartorial journey Often referred to as one of the most beautiful women in the world, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan has long held a prime position under the spotlight since the very inception of her career. She made global news by winning the Miss World title in 1994. Till date, those who grew up in the ’90s will never forget the image of Rai [Bachchan], ecstatic, holding her blue crown. Following which, the actor has over forty Bollywood, international and regional movies under her belt. And the superstar’s 17-year-long association with Cannes Film Festival comes with headline-making sartorial choices every year. Hits, misses, and some iconic looks, we track Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s memorable fashion moments. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan started off with a few modelling stints but made her big silver screen debut in Iruvar (1997). Through her career she has starred in notable films like Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam (1999), Taal (1999), Mohabbatein (2000), Devdas (2002), Bride & Prejudice (2004), Dhoom 2 (2006), Guru (2007), Jodhaa Akbar (2008), The Pink Panther 2 (2009), Raavan and Guzaarish in 2010. The star took a break from acting only to return to the big screen with films like Sarbjit (2016), Ae Dil Hai Mushkil (2016) and Fanney Khan (2018). It’s no surprise that each time Rai Bachchan steps out, fashion lovers take note of the actor’s choice. No stranger to the international red carpets, the star has been a regular at Cannes favouring slinky cocktail dresses, trailing gowns and saris. For her debut appearance, the actor chose saris in bold colours (cue the 2003 Neeta Lulla number) and then moved on to luxe satin and beaded gowns. In 2007, the newly-wed posed on the red carpet with husband Abhishek Bachchan which made headlines. Over the years, she has supported Indian designers like Sabyasachi and Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla. Her other notable sartorial choices have been looks by designer labels Elie Saab, Gucci, Oscar de la Renta, Armani Privé, Ralph & Russo. Her ice blue, full-skirted number by Michael Cinco seen at Cannes 2017 was one of the most sought-after looks. Back home, she prefers traditional choices of elaborate anarkalis and lehengas for family functions, Diwali parties and award shows. Lately, Rai Bachchan has been colour-coordinating with her daughter Aaradhya—most notably in pink dresses at the latter’s birthday party in two years ago and at this year’s Cannes Film Festival in bright yellow. If you are keeping track of the staples in Rai Bachchan’s wardrobe, you’ll find long Indian jackets over anarkalis, skinny pants + blazer combos at the airport, and bold lehengas for weddings. However, when Rai Bachchan does decide to make a statement, she ensures the world takes note. As her stylist Aastha Sharma spoke in a recent interview, “Aishwarya has her own personality, she has been an icon for years, she is always appropriately dressed so it's very easy for me as a stylist. Back home, she favours Indian designers, on the red carpet, we go all out because she is representing a brand and herself—it's almost a form of art.” Scroll ahead for our gallery of Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s most memorable looks. column1: 11 times celebrities proved that ruffled saris are this season's favourite wedding outfit
column2: © Instagram.com/mira.kapoor Fashion From Deepika Padukone and to Katrina Kaif to Kriti Sanon, everyone is crushing on this style of six yard drape. What about you? Timeless saris to hold a special place in every woman's Indian ethnic wardrobe, and are often one of the first sartorial picks for any occasion. But take a peek into the closets of India's best dressed women, and you'll notice that there's a new, playful avatar of the six yard drape that seems to quickly be gaining in popularity. Fuss-free and modern, the ruffled sari ensures maximum impact with minimum effort. Don't go thinking that ruffled saris all come in the same silhouette. While some feature OTT details on just the pallu, others add a touch of ruffle along their entire hemline, and then there are those which come with theatrical ruffled blouses too. Here's a look at how some of your favourite stars are wearing this fun festive look. Still on the fence about working prints for a festive occasion? Allow Alia Bhatt and Kriti Sanon to inspire you to take the plunge. While the former wore a printed green Sabyasachi sari with a ruffled border for the designer’s 20-year celebration, the latter promoted Arjun Patiala in a floral red drape by Arpita Mehta that featured a playful ruffled border, a signature of the designer’s aesthetic. Those looking to create a statement with bold hues can turn to Deepika Padukone and Sonakshi Sinha for ideas. Earlier this year, Padukone was seen embracing a bold acid yellow hue with a ruffled sari that she teamed with a pussy bow blouse, whereas Sinha went all out with a red drape. Mira Rajput Kapoor has been quick to give this trend a test run. For Anil Kapoor’s Diwali party, she topped trending charts in her pastel blue Jade By Monica and Karishma ruffled sari, which she draped over a bejewelled blouse. Just weeks later, the mom-of-two attended Arjun Kothari's pre-wedding celebration at the Ambani residence in another sari look that championed romantic ruffles. This time around, Rajput Kapoor chose a dusky rose Manish Malhotra sari with tiny ruffles along its border, and paired it with a halter blouse doused in large tissue ruffles. Mira Rajput Kapoor Given that the coming months are only going to get chillier, Katrina Kaif's ruffled sari is one you must check out. The actor topped her ivory Anamika Khanna sari at Thugs of Hindostan promotions with a full-length, sleeveless, sequinned jacket. And then there was Shilpa Shetty Kundra, who's never shied away from trying not-so-basic versions of the humble sari. While the star has stepped out in ruffled saris on more than just a few occasions, her sheer, sculpted Amit Aggarwal deserves a special mention for its unconventional cut. Worn with a halter blouse, this pre-stitched number replaced traditional pleats with cascading ruffles instead, to create a party-ready hybrid that's bound to stand out in a crowd. Need more inspiration for the wedding season? Here are some of our favourite ruffled saris of late. column1: 5 Nigerian designers you need to know now
column2: © Manny Jefferson Fashion A dancer who puts movement at the centre of his design practice; a former pharmacist making contemporary clothes from traditional textiles; and a passionate advocate for the environment – Vogue meets five talents showcasing their latest work at GT Bank Fashion Weekend in Lagos Starting in October through the holiday season, the Nigerian megacity of Lagos is home to a succession of cultural happenings, from West Africa’s largest art fair, Art X, to international festivals devoted to poetry, literature, music and fashion – most recently GT Bank Fashion Weekend (9 and 10 November). Now in its fourth iteration, this free public event sees Lagosians engage with industry leaders and designers from across Africa and around the world through fashion shows, a curated market place and a series of masterclasses. Speakers this year included fashion and buying director at Matchesfashion.com, Natalie Kingham, designer Roksanda Ilinčić, Sir John – the makeup artist behind some of Beyoncé’s most memorable looks, and top model Adesuwa Aighewi. Showcasing their latest collections on the runway, meanwhile, were New York-based collective Three As Four, recently launched South African brand Viviers, Ghanaian Studio 189, Imane Ayissi of Cameroon and Nigeria’s own Ituen Basi. Taking time out from the packed GT Bank Fashion Weekend schedule, we met with five Lagos-based designers to discuss some of their most exciting works. © Manny Jefferson © Manny Jefferson The designs of Tzar Studios – the brand Ian Audifferen started in 2013, a year after graduating with a degree in microbiology from the University of Lagos – really have to be seen up close to be fully appreciated. “I think fabric is the most important element of design,” says the 29 year old. “I’ve started playing more with pattern and texture to give my clothes added depth and introduce an element of fun.” What started as a line of shirts has quickly evolved into ready-to-wear for both men and women. For his AW19 collection, Audifferen reinterpreted traditional modes of dress from Yoruba culture in a silk rayon blend; shortening the iro (a wrap skirt) and fastening the buba (a loose fitting blouse) at the neck with a giant safety pin, some also have a tulle yoke or pocket for “added depth”. His “half-half” shirts, meanwhile, are cut from two contrasting ankara fabrics. © Manny Jefferson © Manny Jefferson Mfon Ogbonna’s three-year-old brand, Idma-Nof, is something of a second act for the 40-year-old designer. After working as a pharmacist for a few years, she decided to realise the garments she had been sketching on medical journals, and hung up her white coat to retrain in fashion design. She studied in the US, Paris and London, where she took a course in womenswear and print at Central Saint Martins. “These different experiences have very much formed the person and designer I am today,” she says. “The precision and structure from my career as a pharmacist definitely feed into my work, but at the same time I’m a bit of a wild child.” If there’s a look that encapsulates that sentiment, it’s a neatly tailored coat and trousers from Ogbonna’s AW19 collection, cut from a densely patterned, woven jacquard – fringe bursting from the seams. For SS20, the designer is focusing her gaze on locally produced textiles, such as asa oke, silk printed with her own designs, which are inspired by photographs of Nigerian masquerades by Phyllis Galembo. © Manny Jefferson © Manny Jefferson In 2012, five years after establishing her womenswear label NKWO, Nkwo Onwuka decided to rebrand with a focus on sustainability and artisanal textiles. Her SS20 collection, Be Us Be Them, is so called because: “Humans are destroying the environment. I think we have to go back to where our ancestors are from, look at how they lived in harmony with nature and learn some lessons from them.” With every design, Onwuka minimises waste wherever possible. Think jackets made from upcycled denim jeans; off-cut asa oke threads, woven into a fringe trim and inserted along shirt plackets; ruched strips of Nigerian cotton, dyed with natural indigo and arranged on a dress in formations that pay homage to the body paint worn by the Koro people of Ethiopia’s Omo Valley (“a tribe that continue to live in harmony with nature”); and tiles of white fabric embroidered onto a net tunic – a monochromatic mosaic intended to resemble solar panels. “In Africa we really need to harness the power of the sun to its full capacity to make cleaner energy,” Onwuka adds. “We aren’t doing that right now.” © Manny Jefferson It’s almost 15 years since Lanre da Silva Ajayi founded her eponymous brand, making her a pioneer of Nigeria’s fashion industry along with the likes of Tiffany Amber and Lisa Folawiyo. So what’s changed in that time? “Nigerians are embracing clothes by Nigerian designers more than ever before,” she explains. “Previously we would have looked to European and American designers if we wanted to go to a wedding or special event.” Occasionwear and made-to-measure remain the dominant market in Nigeria; and da Silva Ajayi’s unapologetically decadent style satisfies both those demands. Her The Modern Day Antoinette (SS20) show was no exception, with an abundance of gowns in shocking pink silk, gold lame and yellow tulle – a two-piece suit and mini dress with voluminous cape sleeves cut from olive green organza made a particularly strong statement. “I want to make clothes that empower and flatter women,” says da Silva Ajayi. “The idea that a woman can put on a dress and feel completely transformed is not something I take for granted – Marie Antoinette really took it to the next level and so this season I wanted to create a contemporary interpretation of her style.” © Manny Jefferson Self taught designer Paolo Sisiano has an innate sense of movement when it comes to cutting and draping fabric. Before creating his brand Sisiano in 2013, he studied contemporary dance with Lagos-based troupe ‘Spirit of David’. “I would make my own costumes to dance in,” he remembers. “The transition into fashion was seamless. I want my clothes to be dreamy and romantic, so when you wear them you feel like you are escaping reality to live a fantasy.” Sisiano’s SS20 collection is made entirely from hand-dyed cotton in earthy and pastel tones, with a marble effect that creates the illusion of fabric cascading from the body. However, his ethereal aesthetic is bolstered with an ambitious business plan – on 15 December he will move studios, from the historical area of Yaba to the burgeoning commercial centre of Lekki, where he also plans to open a store. column1: Jennifer Lopez closes out an epic year as the new face of Coach
column2: © 2019 Benjamin Rosser/BFA, Courtesy of Coach Fashion The actor and singer has just been announced as the new face of the brand If there is anyone currently proving that life only gets better with age, it’s Jennifer Lopez. Not only has this year marked something of a career renaissance for the actor and popstar thanks to her part in Hustlers, but she also closed Versace’s spring/summer 2020 presentation in the plunging jungle-print dress that became legendary when she wore it to the 2000 Grammy Awards. Now, the multi-award winning singer has been named as the global face of Coach. So far, we’ve been given a taste of her spring/summer 2020 campaign with a single shot of her wearing a belted trench, silk scarf and chain-strap leather bag. “I’m so excited for this collaboration with Coach,” J-Lo said in a statement. “It is a timeless brand that I’ve always been a fan of and the upcoming collection really speaks to my personal style – an uptown downtown mix.” The appointment marks a new direction for the New York-based brand. Over the years, the label has worked with celebrities including Selena Gomez, Michael B Jordan, and Ariana Grande’s dog for its campaigns. Earlier this year, Coach named Yara Shahidi among its famous fans, as the Grown-ish star was chosen to feature in the brand's autumn/winter 2019 promotional imagery. Of course, Lopez has shared her excitement on Instagram, writing: “Thank you, Coach! Exciting things coming soon!” This article previously appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Ekaya is now in Mumbai: Here's everything we know
column2: Fashion Vogue gets in conversation with the CEO, Palak Shah about Ekaya’s arrival in the city Walk into an Ekaya Benaras store and you're instantly mesmerised by the sheer brilliance of colour on offer and an inimitable sense of culture and heritage. With three such boutiques in the country—Delhi, Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, an expansive e-commerce platform and sub-brand Ekaya Thaan, CEO and co-founder Palak Shah is still looking forward to more. Right now, she’s most excited about bringing her textile brand to Mumbai, a project that has been in the making for a while she tells Vogue. The enormous space will house signature collections and classics, including suits, ready-to-wear ensembles, bridal saris, bridal lehengas and pieces from our collaborations. There’s also a custom-made textile origami installation on display, and a section dedicated to gifting.  Ahead of the opening on November 21, we get into the details of the Shah’s latest project and find out everything about the new store. Kala Ghoda’s historical and cultural landscape is a natural home for us, for Ekaya represents some truly iconic, ever-evolving chapters in the narrative of one of the world’s oldest living cities. We want our consumers in Mumbai to cherish their Ekaya pieces forever. It’s natural for heirloom textiles to be of sentimental value, especially in the context of the wedding and festive season but we would love for people to form their own personal connection with our story.  There was an inimitable splendour to textile art and craft in by-gone times, when they were placed on the high pedestal they deserve, not just on occasion, but everyday. We have tried to bring that back to life, with inventiveness and a ‘tactile’ approach to suit the modern context, but also with due respect for the delicacy of every piece. Signature collections and classics will be displayed all through the 3,000 sq. ft. premises, including suits, ready-to-wear ensembles, bridal saris, bridal lehengas and pieces from our collaborations with various design houses. A tissue silk chandelier by origami artist Ankon Mitra is reminiscent of a swirling lehenga. It conveys the message that handloom luxury is full of life and profound, but with also a touch of easy elegance and playfulness. There is a section specifically dedicated to gifting because we understand how personal an activity this can be; and that it requires time, emotional energy, as well as the space and freedom to make the perfect decision.  Yes, certainly. Thaan is my special labour of love, it represents the heart and soul of the brand. Right now it’s like a small shop-in-shop and it will progressively grow and develop in the future.  All the lehengas! There’s a particular Rangkat one that’s my absolute favourite—it maintains the depth and intrigue of its traditional essence; at the same time there’s something invigorating about the vibrant pink and purple silk. Scroll ahead for a glimpse inside the store. Ekaya Banaras, Ador House, First floor, 6-K Dubash Marg, Kala Ghoda, Mumbai. column1: Block your dates for the Vogue Trunk Show in Pune
column2: © Errikos Andreou Fashion From carefully curated festive wear and heirloom-worthy jewels and wedding experts, the Vogue Trunk Show in Pune promises every ingredient to host a fairy tale wedding or a celebration Once you've locked your wedding dates and venue, the next step is figuring out the outfits and jewellery for your special day. Whether you have an exact vision when it comes to your bridal dress or rather have the experts help you with their on-the-front-lines perspective, putting together that ‘Gram-worthy trousseau can be a daunting task. From store-hopping to the sea of available options, the entire wedding shopping experience can be overwhelming even for the most seasoned shoppers. But it does not have to be. To give you a leg up on your search, Vogue India presents the Vogue Trunk Show in Pune. Slated for Friday and Saturday, 22-23 November, 2019, Vogue India will host the first Pune edition of this luxury wedding and festive exhibition at The Ritz-Carlton, Pune hotel. Located in Yerawada’s business district, this newly launched five-star property boasts of 198 well-appointed rooms and 35 suites, an array of eateries and every luxury amenity for guests to enjoy. The two-day event will gather some of the most renowned experts from the Indian wedding circuit under one roof. Whether you’re looking for a lighter-than-air lehenga for your BFF’s destination wedding or desire heirloom-worthy jewellery for your special day, the Vogue Trunk Show is poised to be a one-stop-shop for not just brides- and grooms-to-be, but wedding hoppers too. For the Pune Vogue Trunk Show, we have handpicked noted designers including Shantanu & Nikhil, Shyamal & Bhumika, and Jade by Monica and Karishma who will be couturiers showcasing their latest collections at the show. If you favour saris versus lehengas, the edits by Shakun Sarees and Anshikaa Jain are sure to catch your attention. Or look forward to getting your hands on gorgeous shawls from Ahujasons. For all your jewellery needs, pick from traditional and contemporary collections by Anjali Bhimrajika X Mehta & Sons, Moksh - Fine Unseen Jewels, Goenka India and Raj Mahtani Couture Jewels. Kapoor Watch Co. will present a range of beautiful watches for men and women along with gifting options by some of the finest watchmakers from around the world. For those who want to raise the bar of their special occasions, turn to the experts at Diageo at the Vogue Trunk Show in Pune. Best known for their bespoke solutions, the brand has championed the art of creating a buzz at celebratory events. column1: 13 times Priyanka Chopra and Sabyasachi proved to be a match made in heaven
column2: © APH Images Fashion From picking a custom-made Sabyasachi lehenga for her wedding to stepping out in styles from his latest collections, scroll down to check out the best of Priyanka Chopra in Sabyasachi When Priyanka Chopra walked down the stairs of the Umaid Bhawan Palace in a deep red Sabyasachi wedding lehenga, it was a moment in time. The coming together of such powerful forces, leaders in their own right, created an impact unlike any other. Ever since then, the duo have been inseparable. Those who followed her larger-than-life wedding celebrations know that the star literally broke the internet with her wardrobe choices. Her bridal trousseau was a line-up of perfectly curated traditional six yards and lehengas that were nothing short of spectacular. Priyanka Chopra's custom-made wedding lehenga took 110 embroiderers from Kolkata a total of 3,720 hours to create the hand-cut organza flowers, French knots in silk floss and layers of thread work that embellished the ensemble. And for her New Delhi reception, she stunned everyone in a regal floral Benarasi lehenga set, embellished with Sabyasachi’s signature borders and a snug corset blouse that was tucked into the lehenga to create the lengthening illusion of a floor-length anarkali gown. Chopra may love her smart pantsuits and slinky dresses, but when it comes to ethnic wear, the star never misses a chance to step out in a Sabyasachi. No matter the occasion, Chopra has proven that Sabyasachi’s six yard drapes are her go-to's. For starters, she chose an embroidered green floral sari for one of her first public appearances post her wedding, and also went with not one, but two Sabyasachi saris while promoting her film The Sky Is Pink: a printed floral number and an ivory and red polka-dotted drape. While his ornate saris and lehengas hold a special spot in her wardrobe, Chopra has also been seen experimenting with Sabyasachi silhouettes recently, picking pieces that are very different from his signature work. Case in point: the sheer polka dotted maxi dress + a matching cape from Sabyasachi Mukherjee’s 20th anniversary show, Kashgaar Bazaar, she picked for a casual night out with Nick Jonas.  And to top it all, of course, was Priyanka Chopra's Vogue India September 2019 cover, which saw the actor walking the streets of NYC in one statement-making Sabyasachi look after another. column1: Meet the ‘doctors of fashion’: a rare glimpse inside the Met’s Costume Institute laboratory
column2: © Shaniqwa Jarvis Fashion The annual Met Gala is the most glamorous event in the fashion calendar. But all year round at the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute in New York, a team of experts diligently conserve its collection of 33,000 fashion items, some dating back to the 15th century. Towering headpieces. Flocks of feathers. Walking hamburgers. The Costume Institute at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art is a visual feast that never disappoints. But behind the scenes, the Costume Institute’s work is significantly more serious. Tucked below street level is a well-lit, climate-controlled, state-of-the-art conservation laboratory. There, a highly skilled team of specialists diligently toil to preserve some of the world’s most fascinating works of art, which just happen to be clothing. Sarah Scaturro, head conservator at the Costume Institute, is energetic and friendly. She towers in her red-suede Salvatore Ferragamo platform sandals, and is the first to relieve laboratory visitors of their ballpoint pens in favour of less-threatening pencils. It’s a relief, actually; who wants to be guilty of disfiguring an Edwardian wedding gown or a Renaissance tunic? © Shaniqwa Jarvis Scaturro’s first responsibility is safety, after all. A lifelong seamstress, she found her way into conservation while studying pattern drafting and tailoring at New York’s Fashion Institute of Technology. With a background in history and an ease with the necessary chemistry, Scaturro found a conservation programme to be a natural fit. She relishes the challenges of a field that achieves the impossible: the preservation of objects that were, for the most part, never meant to last. Alongside her co-workers, Scaturro cares for a collection of 33,000 objects dating from the 15th century to the present day. The team assesses, repairs, preserves and prepares this massive catalogue for exhibition, but its work is far more complicated than a day at the dry cleaners. History, ethics, philosophy and science all influence a conservator’s decision making — it can be surprisingly complex. “By investigating fashion, we can learn a lot about the human condition,” Scaturro notes. Her influence on these objects, so laden with stories, begins with a conservator’s code to “do no harm”. Repairs may be made, of course, but each is undertaken with the original designer’s intentions in mind. © Shaniqwa Jarvis Like therapists, conservators are allies. And Scaturro is the first to admit they aren’t afraid to anthropomorphise. Ballgowns and breeches can have good days and bad, so the conservation team “empowers [each] object to be its best self”. As the Costume Institute prepares for its forthcoming exhibition, In Pursuit of Fashion: The Sandy Schreier Collection, the laboratory’s ‘patients’ lie obediently still. The show will reveal highlights from the collection of Schreier, a fashion historian and collector whose childhood passion for beautiful clothes and silver-screen Hollywood glamour grew into an unparalleled treasure trove of significant clothing. From early-Edwardian gowns to mid-century day ensembles, Schreier’s knockouts (165 promised gifts to the museum) comprise a gorgeous group of fashion’s very best ideas, while broadening the definition of ‘collector’ beyond paintings and sculptures. With this exhibition, the Met further establishes itself as a champion of fashion as fine art. © Shaniqwa Jarvis The lab is abuzz with quiet diligence as garments for the Schreier show and pieces in the permanent collection are conserved to the highest standards. There is no one-size-fits-all approach — as Scaturro says of her conservation assessments, “The only right answer is, ‘It depends!’” — so each receives a tailored treatment. Painstaking stitches are applied with a hair’s-width silk thread; there, sequins are individually flipped back into position. And, like the names on the gala guest list, each ‘patient’ is more fascinating than the last. © Shaniqwa Jarvis Once an eyelash-batting ingénue, now more delicate than ever, this cream-coloured silk gown — promised gift of Schreier — was designed by Callot Soeurs, an early 20th-century French house famed for its lacework and quintessentially feminine aesthetic. Conservator Melina Plottu applied “laid and couched stitching” to a small tear near the hem with surgical needles, a meticulous process that required an hour per inch. At the same time, a row of ornamentation down the front of the dress was manipulated back into shape under glass blocks after receiving a light mist of precisely targeted cool ultrasonic vapour. © Shaniqwa Jarvis This mysterious garment’s imposing and questionable history is a reminder that fashion can leave us with a haunting sense of lived experience long after the wearer is gone. Valuable even at the time it was created, this velvet jerkin has likely been reworked — as Scaturro notes, “Very few things come into our collection 100 per cent unaltered.” Atypically, it does not open at the front. This, combined with its relatively small size, may mean it was worn by a woman. In preparation for an exhibition in another department at the museum, conservator Elizabeth Shaeffer uncovered more of the jerkin’s story, beginning with a microscopic analysis of its cut velvet pattern. By distinguishing between worn patches and places where the velvet was intentionally “voided”, or flat, Schaefer has rediscovered the fabric’s original pattern. With each layer of new information, the stately piece reveals its story. © Shaniqwa Jarvis This group of bold, Pop Art-style toppers look like extras from Austin Powers and an MC Hammer video, respectively. Despite their relative youth, they are some of the most vulnerable ‘patients’ under Scaturro’s care, and she is crafting a new set of protocols to preserve them. Since the mid-20th century, designers have been drawn to shiny, fake-leather materials such as Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) and Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU). While these fabrics are nearly indistinguishable, they require distinct storage environments to survive. Stored at the wrong temperature or humidity level, they can crack, stick, flake and fade. With no way to distinguish PVC from TPU by sight, the museum’s scientists use a complex technological assessment called Fourier-Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, which sends waves of energy to the surface of the object and maps the resulting spectra for comparison to reference samples. In the meantime, each component is loosely enveloped in silicone-coated paper for protection. “Nothing sticks to this,” says Scaturro. Within these billowing white paper sleeves, the Mugler jacket’s “inherent vice”, or self-destructive properties, are curbed. If only it were so easy for humans. © Shaniqwa Jarvis Matchy-matchy, mid-century propriety is taken to the limit in this bold print Christian Dior ensemble worn by American socialite Elizabeth Firestone and is a promised gift of Schreier. Dior’s atelier graciously accommodated his client’s passion for prints, crafting entire ensembles in the fabric of her choosing. In this case, it’s a brushy floral in blue and white, and includes a demure hat and petite pumps. Firestone’s lavish wardrobe was meticulously kept and then preserved by Schreier, and the ensemble is in exquisite condition aside from discoloration due to ageing glue in the shoes. Fortunately, there are back-ups: Firestone always ordered six identical pairs for each outfit, to allow for the toe scuffs that resulted from her husband’s notoriously clumsy dancing. © Shaniqwa Jarvis © Shaniqwa Jarvis 7 ways Yves Saint Laurent changed the fashion world Maria Grazia Chiuri shares the botanical inspiration behind her Dior SS20 collection Met Gala 2020: Everything you need to know What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why Jonathan Cohen prefers to call his brand "responsible", not "sustainable"
column2: © GoRunway.com Fashion Can you work with a friend, create an impact with your label and run an environmentally-conscious practice? One designer shows you how to nail the dream CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund 2019 finalist Jonathan Cohen has been running his eponymous label with partner Sarah Leff for the last eight years. Cohen doesn’t think he’s made it big, despite the brand’s obvious commercial and critical success. “Every season, I feel that I start from the beginning again. It might sound masochistic, but it is what keeps me excited and ideas fresh. I do not think I will ever feel like I have ‘made it’,” he says. Occasionally political, always responsible, the designer has made a mark with his work that reflects the zeitgeist. Vogue got in conversation with the designer on what it takes to create a modern brand with a global appeal. Sarah and myself have known each other since we were freshmen in college. We always talked about starting a company together; we just knew it was meant to be. While our roles our technically split between design and business, we are constantly in conversation about both with one another. It’s not only amazing to see the brand grow, but also watching each other grow within our positions. Spring 2020 © GoRunway.com I think it’s important to have this conversation in general, in and out of fashion. Growing up, I had all these labels put on me by my peers: “Mexican, American, Jewish, gay…”. Sometimes it was fascinating, and sometimes, I was bullied for something I myself didn’t fully understand at such a young age. It made me uncomfortable and quite frankly, scared. As I have grown, I embrace these aspects of myself that were seen as “different”, and it’s impossible for that not to reflect in my work. It may rub people the wrong way, but I am OK with that. It is in the end what makes it individual. And that essentially is what the brand is about, embracing who you are. We work with a great partner named Piece and Co that works with many groups across the world. We developed a special batik print with a group in India on organic cotton. The results were beautiful. It is actually one of my favourite looks from the show. I thought the dye gave it a denim-looking feel, which I loved. We never like to say we are a “sustainable” brand. I think that can be slightly misleading and create unrealistic expectations. But we are striving to be responsible in how we design and produce. We wanted to take ownership of the waste we are creating in our process and find creative ways to re-use it without sending it to a landfill. While we were always conscious of who was making our clothes and how they were being made, we wanted to take that same practice into how are textiles were being created. This meant investigating our resources and being mindful of how each fabric is being produced. I love what I do and couldn’t see myself doing anything else, that’s really what it comes down to. I am constantly inspired and challenged, and that is very fulfilling to me. I love seeing people in the clothes and when I hear the stories and memories they have created with the pieces in their lives, that’s really what keeps me going. Spring 2020 © GoRunway.com Sarah and I are very much in sync, and are always having dialogue back and forth until we both find a resolution that makes sense for both of us. We are lucky to have amazing mentors who have been instrumental within the industry and our growth. However, at the end of the day, you have to follow your gut and your own beliefs. In the end you have to answer to yourself and be proud of the decisions you have made. I always think to myself: “Will I regret going in this direction in ten years?”. column1: What actually happens to your clothes when you recycle them?
column2: © Getty Fashion Once you’ve dropped off your donations at recycling points, your clothes embark on a long, complex journey to either be sold or used for fabric. Here, Vogue finds out what really happens to your cast-offs and unpacks the process of creating reusable textiles It’s never been easier to recycle your unwanted clothes, it would seem. Major retailers including H&M, Zara and Adidas now have handy drop-off points and trade-in projects in their stores, allowing you to easily take back your used garments—often in return for a voucher or discount on your next purchase. But what actually happens to your clothes when you recycle them? “The majority of textiles we collect (50 to 60 per cent) are sorted for re-wear,” Giorgina Waltier, sustainability manager for H&M UK and Ireland, tells Vogue. “Around 35 to 45 per cent is recycled [and] becomes products for other industries, or made into new textile fibres.” H&M © H&M The remainder of the garments, which cannot be reused or recycled, become “combustibles for energy production”. H&M, who has partnered with clothing collection company I:CO to ensure as many of its clothes are reused and recycled as possible, guarantees that none of the garments taken back will end up in landfill. Globally though, only 20 per cent of clothing waste is collected for reuse and recycling, while the majority ends up in landfill or is incinerated, according to a 2017 report by Global Fashion Agenda and The Boston Consulting Group—showing the need for improvement when it comes to addressing the environmental impact of our cast-offs. “There’s too much unwanted clothing out in the world,” says Elizabeth L Cline, fashion journalist and author of The Conscious Closet: The Revolutionary Guide to Looking Good While Doing Good (Plume, 2019). “It is overwhelming [the] systems in place [that are trying to] deal with it.” Once you’ve decluttered your wardrobe and have made the necessary drop-offs to your local charity shops or recycling points, so begins the complex journey of your unwanted clothes. According to a 2017 report by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, 70 per cent of garments collected across the US and Europe are in good enough condition to be reused. Around 20 per cent of these reusable clothes are sold domestically, while the remainder is sold to textile merchants who sort and ship them to countries such as Uganda, Kenya, Hungary and Pakistan. Once they’ve reached overseas, only 70 per cent of this clothing is actually reused, while the rest is recycled into lower-value products—such as insulation material or cleaning cloths—or sent to landfill or incineration. Workers at a French recycling centre © Getty However, importers of secondhand clothing are becoming overwhelmed by the sheer volume of garments being sent to them. The OR Foundation—a US-based non-profit that aims to better Ghana’s secondhand clothing problem, where 30,000 tonnes arrive in its capital, Accra, every year—found that 40 per cent of what the country receives goes straight into landfill. “Countries are concerned about taking used clothing because they want to protect their own primary industries,” says Keith James, special advisor at environmental action group, Wrap. “The challenge is really growing the market for recycling; creating a new demand for recycled fibres.” Mechanical recycling, which involves the shredding of the garments, often leads to a reduction in the quality of the material. In order for the recycled fabric to be turned back into clothing again, the fibres must be mixed with virgin material. “One of the issues with shredding is the fibres get shorter,” explains James. “And there’s a limited number of times that you can recycle clothing [again] in that way.” London second hand marketplace © Getty Garments are sorted by fibre and colour for recycling, but clothing made from blended fibres such as polycotton (a mixture of cotton and polyester) presents another major challenge. Along with dyed fabrics and other contaminants, the different materials in these garments cannot be separated so the majority of this textile waste goes to landfill or incinerators. Second hand clothes to be sent to wholesalers © Getty “Mixtures [of different fibres] are problematic for [current] recycling processes,” says Johannes Bogren, president of Södra Cell Bioproducts. “A polyester-cotton blend is a blend on the yarn level and extremely hard to separate.” Luckily, various chemical recycling techniques are being developed to cope with blended textiles. Last month, Swedish forestry company Södra, which supplies wood pulp for the textiles industry, announced a new technology that will allow poly blends to be recycled at scale (although it only accepts white poly cotton at present). Sodra pulp mill in Mörrum © Sodra The cotton is reused in its cellulose product, which is turned into materials such as viscose and lyocell, while the polyester is currently used for energy. “This is the first step, to show that the technology is available,” says Bogren. “We can close the loop, so to speak.” In the meantime though, it’s better to take time to consider what you’re buying in the first place, and where it will end up when you’re finished with it—rather than relying on the fact it’ll be recycled. “A lot of our clothes are going into landfills; it's a massive global problem,” Cline adds. “We, as consumers, have a lot of control over whether or not we are contributing to textile waste.” 8 organisations that are making recycling easy in India Ever wondered what happens to your clothes after you throw them away? column1: Cleavage or bare back? Bollywood celebrities have picked a clear winner this party season

column1: Documentary film 'Martin Margiela: In His Own Words' tells Martin Margiela’s story, his way
column2: © GoRunway.com Fashion “He won’t work as a fashion designer anymore in his life—probably,” Holzemer told Vogue during an interview on the day of the film’s world premiere “Have you said everything you wanted to say in fashion?” “No.” That is the promise dangling at the end of Reiner Holzemer’s new documentary, Martin Margiela: In His Own Words, which premiered at the Doc NYC film festival last week. After 90-ish minutes of exposition from Margiela himself, who remains so elusive only his hands were filmed, Holzemer abruptly asks if fashion’s most celebrated genius is really, truly, undeniably done with it all. No. And then the screen cuts to black. Any hopes of Margiela’s return to fashion will have to be sidelined for now, however. “He won’t work as a fashion designer anymore in his life—probably,” Holzemer told Vogue during an interview on the day of the film’s world premiere. “But you never know. We all love that the movie ends with this. It gives you a nice smile in the end, which is important.” Holzemer’s film is not so much about where Martin Margiela is in 2019—the designer speaks of painting and sculpting, though those pursuits are not shown in the documentary—or what he might do in 2020, but about the 20 years from 1989 to 2009 during which Margiela operated his eponymous label. As a portrait of a finite body of work—the two decades of Martin Margiela runway shows—Holzemer’s film operates as a circle: It begins with Margiela’s Spring 2009 20th-anniversary show, his final one, then waltzes through a chronology of his life and career with the help of talking head interviews with Olivier Saillard, Carla Sozzani, Stella Ishii, Pierre Rougier, Cathy Horyn, and more of his models, collaborators, friends, and critics, before finishing back at Margiela’s swan song. That format allows for deep dives into the designer’s key collections and career points. It helps that the documentary was made alongside the preparation and installation of the Palais Galliera’s 2018 exhibit, Margiela / Galliera, 1989-2009. For 42 days, Holzemer, sometimes alone, sometimes with a skeleton crew, would visit the museum or Margiela’s studio and get the designer talking. “Which garments are important, which do you think we have to include in the movie?” Holzemer says he asked Margiela as they began filming. There were 110 items in the exhibit, and he made a list of 90 for the film. Ultimately, they settled on around 70 crucial pieces, which are presented with voiceovers by the designer. These range from his cork necklaces—which we see Margiela making with his own hands as the film starts—through his doll collection of 1994 and his stockman collection of 1997. “I’m very grateful that he opened up and he trusted me so much. It was not always easy for him,” Holzemer says. The hits are all here: The Spring 1990 show staged in a playground (“The most magical show of my career”), his time as creative director of Hermès (“For me, luxury is the perfect balance between quality and comfort and if I could go farther I would add timelessness”), the Spring 2007 show that worked to establish new Margiela codes (“I wanted to be different, new, without rejecting my fans…. It felt like a new beginning.”) As the movie seeks to illustrate, Margiela did almost everything that is on trend in contemporary fashion first: He had street cast shows, he popularized the long, lean lines of the ’90s, he made a reissue collection for his 10th show, he pushed and pushed and pushed the creative bounds of what a fashion show was and what a fashion brand could look be. “I hope that, first of all, his name and the work stays alive, that people discover how influential he was, how much of what we see today on the catwalks is sometimes copied one-to-one—I don’t need to mention the names, I’m not an expert of that,” Holzemer says. “I think if the world knows where the Margiela influence comes from, that would make me very happy.” Of course, what Margiela also did first was what he did last: Leave fashion for good. “I was not made to cope with that system as well as Jean Paul Gaultier,” says Margiela, who was Gaultier’s assistant before launching his own label. “Jean Paul always said, ‘Martin you’re too serious,’ and it’s true […] I am probably too serious for that world.” Margiela’s departure is a story that has become familiar within fashion’s creative industries: the struggle to translate a personal passion into a corporate consumer product. It’s here that the film touches a nerve, but instead of prodding it, it lets the audience read between the lines. The sale of Maison Martin Margiela to Renzo Rosso’s Only the Brave group, the departure of Margiela’s partner Jenny Meirens, and Margiela’s own absence are covered without too much emotionality, although fashion insiders will be able to interpret Margiela’s careful language about the reason for his departure: “At the end, I became, in a certain way, an artistic director in my company and that bothered me because I am a designer […] I am not a creative director who directs his assistants.” The irony of Holzemer’s delicate portrait of an artist in absence is that it was Margiela’s replacement who inspired the director to take an interest in fashion as a subject. (Holzemer worked on films about photographers before taking up fashion with the documentary Dries about Dries Van Noten in 2017.) “Why I wanted to make a fashion movie was the Galliano story,” Holzemer says, referencing the public meltdown that got John Galliano fired from his position at Christian Dior. After entering rehab, Galliano was named the artistic director of Maison Margiela in 2015. “I read a big article about the pressure fashion designers are under. I was really touched by that article. It was a bad thing that Galliano did, but in that article it explained that some of the designers take drugs to survive. Alexander McQueen killed himself. That was the thing that caused my sensitivity for the profession, for the world, for the industry. […] How do I say it? I work hard too, but the fashion designers work so hard under such pressure wherever that pressure comes from, sometimes it’s big companies, sometimes it’s yourself. That it’s really a challenge to remain in that business for so long and to survive in that business in a healthy way.” Holzemer indicates that he knows there is a lot of pain here for Martin Margiela—but he won’t say anything about it, nor does much of that tension make it to the screen. “You don’t see that in the movie. Often I was looking at his face, the camera was on the wall, it was only listening, and I thought, It would be so strong if I could show your face now. I still have it in my memory. It was often very touching. The story was always surprising because you could not read it. He told it for the first time: How he felt after the first show, how he felt after 10 years, and how he felt in the end. Nobody knew that before.” Even with these small, tender moments of Margiela’s vulnerability that reveal the glimmer of a sensitive, caring, gentle man, this documentary doesn't go beyond affirming many of the myths already made about Martin Margiela. Yes, there are incredible glimpses into his childhood in Genk, Belgium, and his sketchbooks—with every year of the designer’s life saved by his mother, Léa Bouchet—but the final film still works behind layers of abstraction. It is mostly about the exhibit, it is without its star’s visage, and even the voice over of Margiela’s lyrical Franco-Belgian intonation is slightly engineered to cloak the reality of what Martin Margiela actually sounds like. In Dries, one of the most compelling moments is one that seems almost incidental: Van Noten and his partner, Patrick Vangheluwe, silently snipping flowers from their garden and arranging them throughout their house, not a word spoken, not a nod exchanged. “You can talk a lot about perfectionism or obsession but there you see it, you feel it, and it says it all,” Holzemer says of that scene. Martin Margiela: In His Own Words never gets to that show-don’t-tell moment because so much of the story has to be told in voiceover or in interview segments. To adequately show the brilliance of Martin in the year 2019—30 years after his seismic start and a decade after that anniversary show that proved to be his last—something really unexpected would have to happen in the film. For the most part, it doesn’t. But maybe it’s best that the curtain stays drawn a little longer. By protecting Margiela from the cold gaze of a camera, Holzemer allows us superfans to keep our fashion-world hero alive, no flaws, no tensions, no negativity; only these memories and the knowledge that the heart behind the Margiela universe is still beating. Toward the end of the film, Holzemer shows the opening of the Galliera exhibit, long lines shivering in Paris’s March cold. Inside, Vogue editors gasp at the installation, Raf Simons gestures at a mannequin, Rick Owens contemplates in admiration. The legend of Martin Margiela lives on. And then there’s always the promise of his return…. column1: These celebrity pictures prove that the '90s red carpet is the ultimate fashion throwback
column2: © Getty Fashion As @90sanxiety peaks, let’s look to the decade that saw the likes of Keanu Reeves, Drew Barrymore, Lisa Bonet and Leonardo DiCaprio own the red carpet in effortlessly cool style Red carpet dressing today evokes high glamour, drama and Fashion with a capital F. It is the work of a team: designers, brands, stylists, publicists, assistants, hair and makeup, nails... days of prep. But that hasn’t always been the case. Long before Instagram, the glam squad and even pre-dating Fashion Police-style shows, there was the Nineties—a free-for-all fashion frenzy. While the red carpet dates back to 458 BC and the trilogy of Greek tragedies The Oresteia, not to mention its other (pre-Hollywood) historical connotations with royalty, dignitaries and politicians, it was still a shadow of its current self in the Nineties. For a start, there were no transactions or power plays between stars and fashion houses (although Giorgio Armani had begun courting actors, it wasn’t yet an established practice). Joan Rivers’s now infamous line, “Who are you wearing?” didn’t enter the mainstream until 1995. Broadly speaking, the Nineties was a simpler, more relaxed time for red carpet fashion. Celebrities often selected their own outfits, making personal style statements. See Drew Barrymore’s cream cardigan and distressed denim pairing at the Guilty By Suspicion premiere; Leonardo DiCaprio’s rained-on ensemble at the Benny & Joon debut; Lisa Bonet’s coolest bohemian mum look, with a young Zoë Kravitz at a 1996 premiere; and River Phoenix’s woolly jumper at the Oscars lunch. Each is a testament to their taste, a laissez-faire approach to fashion that speaks of individuality, comfort and ease. On that note, there are also some serious handbags—not minimalist purses, decorative clutches or micro bags, but functional hold-alls that the likes of Kate Moss, Christy Turlington and J-Lo all used to carry their essentials in on the red carpet. (They also carried their coats, and often invites, too.) Shoes were similarly functional, no box-fresh trainers or designer sneakers here. Instead, Keanu Reeves rocked up (on his motorcycle) in well-worn high tops, while Winona Ryder and Gwyneth Paltrow favoured Chuck Taylors. As the nostalgic resurgence of these images continues to fill our social feeds (looking at you, @90sanxiety), Vogue pays tribute to the icons of that relaxed, rebellious and effortlessly cool Nineties red carpet. column1: Kate Middleton accessorised her latest outfit with a Rs 2,400 Zara headband
column2: © Getty Fashion The duchess wore the headband to the Festival of Remembrance Over the weekend, the Kate Middleton stepped out, along with a number of the royal family members—including her husband, Prince William, The Queen, Prince Harry, and Meghan Markle—for a series of Remembrance Day events ahead of the official date of November 11, when those who died on duty in the First World War are remembered. The duchess’s wardrobe is always carefully considered and for the Festival of Remembrance held at the Royal Albert Hall on Saturday evening, an event which Town & Country reports featured musical performances from celebrities like Jeff Goldblum and James Blunt, Middleton’s ensemble was true to thoughtful form but with an affordable, on-trend, high street twist. © Instagram/theroyalfamily For the annual event—which the Royal British Legion website reports this year marked the 75th anniversary of the battles of 1944 and “the friendship of the British, Commonwealth and Allied armies who fought them,” along with the 100th anniversary of the GCHQ (a British intelligence and security organisation)—the duchess opted for an elegant-yet-muted look of a navy boat-neck long-sleeved midi dress paired with black tights and Jimmy Choo black velvet heels, as identified by What Kate Wore. For her accessories, the duchess wore a brooch featuring a trio of poppies—the symbol of remembrance—along with diamond and pearl earrings and notably, a black padded jewelled headband, which has been identified as a UK£17.99 (approximately Rs 2,400) accessory from high street label, Zara. Hair accessories, particularly headbands, have been the must-have accessory of 2019, spotted on the runways (think: Prada’s iconic take in their spring/summer 2019 collection) and on the head of celebrities and street style stars the globe over. Middleton—whose style is endlessly copied and coveted—has taken the accessory of the season and given it a royal seal of approval, and an affordable one at that. The duchess’s glossy brunette locks were held perfectly in place by the Zara headband, and when paired with the black and navy palette of her outfit, respectfully let the poppy brooch shine. The duchess and her sister-in-law, Meghan Markle, then stepped out on Sunday morning for the Remembrance Day Sunday ceremony at The Cenotaph in London, wearing matching black looks. Middleton wore a military-style coat dress reportedly from Alexander McQueen (the same design house behind her wedding dress) with a matching black hat and an intricate hairstyle. The duchess wore another brooch featuring a poppy, What Kate Wore notes this piece is the “Codebreakers Brooch from the Royal British Legion”. Markle too wore black, opting for a belted black coat WWD reports is from Stella McCartney, who also featured in Markle’s wedding wardrobe, as the designer of her reception dress. Interestingly, both Alexander McQueen and Stella McCartney are British labels and played important fashion roles in their respective wearers weddings, a point that seems respectful on a day that commemorates the British armed forces. column1: 23 incredibly cool ways to wear a trench coat now
column2: © Jonathan Daniel Pryce Fashion From tonal layering to the new oversized proportions, here’s how the street style set are wearing the heritage classic this season There are not many fashion staples that Instagram’s most powerful influencers can claim to share with David Bowie, Meryl Streep and Marilyn Monroe—except, that is, for the trench coat. The archetypal heritage wardrobe hero is currently leading AW19’s pared-back mood with a resolutely practical edge. Here’s how to wear the trench coat this season. The trench coat has always been synonymous with the phrase “wardrobe classic”, thanks to its ageless, seasonless and genderless track record (which dates back to Scotland in the 1820s, and encompasses WWI, Hollywood and Burberry). Today, it’s also symbolic of fashion’s burgeoning eco-awareness, in that a good trench coat should last for life. Which is why we hope we’re going to see just as many trench coats at fashion month AW20 as we have on the front rows over the past two seasons. In the course of an average day at Paris Fashion Week SS20, you were likely to spot everyone from super stylist Suzanne Koller, to models Pia Ekman and Leka Dereviankina, to influencer Chloé Harrouche wearing an oversized trench while sprinting between shows. The labels to note? A tweak on the traditional silhouette comes into play with Burberry’s Chelsea coat, which uses the same gabardine fabric that Thomas Burberry patented back in 1879; while JW Anderson’s reversioned classic comes complete with plaid cuffs and lapels. Khaite and Tibi score points for the tonal colour palette, while Versace, Paco Rabanne and Balenciaga do minimalist lines and futuristic, glossy patent. Koller wears hers belted, paired with fine gold jewellery, tonal slacks and Nike Air Force 1s. Attico co-founder Gilda Ambrosio lifts the mood with a fluffy boa; while French influencer Camille Charrière wears hers with white jeans, an enormous Bottega Veneta handbag and mock croc boots. And let’s not forget Reese Blutstein, who winter-proofs a delicate white dress with knee-high combat boots and a slouchy trench. © Jonathan Daniel Pryce © Jonathan Daniel Pryce © Jonathan Daniel Pryce © Jonathan Daniel Pryce © Jonathan Daniel Pryce © Jonathan Daniel Pryce © Hong Sungoh © Getty © Getty © Getty © Getty © Getty © Getty © Getty © Jonathan Daniel Pryce © Getty © Hong Sungoh © Getty © Getty © Getty © Getty © Getty © Getty The enduring appeal of the trench coat, and how to wear it now Deepika Padukone’s new trench coat came with the most unusual sleeves The best street style looks seen at Taipei Fashion Week SS20 Beauty What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Think skinny jeans are out? Let these Bollywood celebrities change your mind
column2: © Viral Bhayani Fashion While roomier versions may have replaced skinny jeans in mainstream popularity, they are still an important part of present-day wardrobes. We bring you celebrity inspiration on styling your favourite pair Remember the turn of this decade when your wardrobe was only brimming with skinny jeans in every colour? They were what all the cool girls in the college cafeteria were test driving before they became the ubiquitous uniform for the next few years to come. Over the years, variants inspired by your mom and boyfriend may have dethroned skinny jeans from their top drawer status, but don’t write them off as has-beens. This once-popular denim style still possesses the power to hug you in all the right places, enhancing your derrière and elongating your frame. And an army of Bollywood celebrities will back this claim. After all, skinny jeans are their ultimate off-duty go-to—whether it’s to catch flights or run errands. The combination of skinny blue jeans and a white top get an unanimous vote among Bollywood’s best dressed set. For a more laid-back look, there is Deepika Padukone, who wears hers with a logo tee, leather jacket, sneakers and enviable cool girl flair. Tara Sutaria, on the other hand, presents lessons in dressing the style up—you too can wear your skinny jeans with a white bandeau and matching blazer, or an off-shoulder crop top to create party-ready looks that don’t try too hard. Shraddha Kapoor’s pairing of a Victorian sleeved shirt is perfect for a movie date, while Karisma Kapoor’s tucked-in printed blouse and loafers mix will provide comfort on a day you’re checking off that to-do list. Kareena Kapoor Khan makes a case for a well-tailored statement white shirt and black skinny jeans combination, while Sara Ali Khan prefers to introduce a measure of youthfulness by styling hers with a printed asymmetrical tunic-inspired top. Meanwhile, Soha Ali Khan likes to keeps things classic, teaming her skinny jeans with a ruffled off-shoulder top and heels for a night out with her husband, Kunal Kemmu. Skinny jeans and airport looks are clearly Bollywood-approved too, particularly when the #OOTD calls for knee-high boots to kickstart those sweater weather holidays. Karisma Kapoor wore boots and jeans with a black full-sleeved logo T-shirt, and Ananya Panday styled hers with a black turtleneck. Anushka Sharma, the ultimate purveyor of ‘keeping it chill’ looks, extends her style philosophy to her skinny jeans too—wearing a white pair with a black crop and denim jacket for supersized comfort. Want to take your skinnies for a night on the town? Follow Disha Patani’s lead and team a snug leather corset with snugger jeans and a wide statement belt for after-hours glam. column2: © Instagram.com/sonamkapoor Fashion From pocket-sized handbags to meticulously carved numbers, Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s roster of bags is anything but boring When it comes to matters of style, there is no denying that Sonam Kapoor Ahuja is a straight-A student. Down the years, her discerning eye has championed classic numbers and uncovered hidden gems alike, and her accessories wardrobe is no different. From logomania-approved Fendi numbers to ethnic potli bags, the 34-year-old delights in rewriting the rulebook. Here are the styles that she’s loving right now. Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s love affair with micro bags is nowhere close to done, as dinky numbers continue to find favour in her closet regularly. During the day, you’ll find her adding a bright pop of colour to a white outfit with a blue box bag by S’uvimol to a monochromatic pantsuit with a statement red L’Afshar bag. On the red carpet, she favours boxy silhouettes—at a recent cocktail night in the city, she picked a sharply tailored Ralph Lauren tuxedo suit and a mini trunk bag. Unafraid to veer into matchy-matchy territory, she also boldly coordinated her oxblood leather culottes with a matching bag from Manu Atelier. On those days when she’s looking to make heads turn, she relies on classics. A sultry Emilia Wickstead bodycon dress, classic choker and high-shine Judith Liber sling clutch offered just the right amount of oomph for a night out. And despite her status as Bollywood’s reigning queen of style, Kapoor Ahuja has a talent for marrying form with function. Fuss-free belt bags command frequent cameos in her wardrobe, usually combined with her love for head-to-toe solid colours. Indeed, at an awards ceremony earlier this year, the star took to the red carpet in a blush pink Fenty suit, cinched at the waist with a coordinated bag. Out and about for the promotions of her last release, The Zoya Factor, the star chose to go hands-free again by carrying a Ulyana Sergeenko belt bag over an all-red co-ord set. Flip over to the ethnic side of her closet, and you’ll find that her love for unconventional silhouettes reigns supreme. In keeping with the fuss-free memo, she paired a floral Vedika M lehenga with a backless blouse and attached belt bag at the waist. Known for reinventing the classic six yards, her newest iteration of the traditional sari came in the form of a Masaba Gupta sari with vintage florals and a not-so-basic blouse. She cinched the look together with a healthy helping of oxidised jewellery by Silver Streak, and an unconventional carved metal bag from the same label. For the recent Diwali celebrations at Anil Kapoor’s house, she spun the colour wheel in favour of a yellow gold handbag against the canvas of her multi-hued Anamika Khanna ensemble. column1: 5 emerging fashion brands that should be on your radar right now
column2: © Instagram.com/wearpoochki Fashion Whether you’re stuck in a sartorial rut or simply looking to update your wardrobe, there are a plethora of up-and-coming designers who can help you give your repertoire a fresh spin. Vogue spotlights the Indian labels you need keep an eye out for right now Launched in 2018, the brand aims to bring Indian simplicity to the spotlight by reviving age-old crafts from across the country with each collection. “What I aspire to do with Torani is to bring tradition and culture to the forefront in the most nuanced and subtle manner. The idea is to create classics that last you way beyond a season, and evoke a personal love affair with the garment that tells your own story,” Karan Torani, founder, Torani told Vogue. Handwoven chanderi and hand-painted chintz on mulmul (that is sourced from Telangana) have been a constant in the brand’s collections since it’s inception. Their other offerings include floral kurtas, saris and sharara sets that are perfect for any occasion. Launched in 2015, Poochki is a concept store in New Delhi that not only houses a design studio with a keen interest in reviving Indian handcrafts— specifically, hand-block printing—but also has a restaurant in its space. “Poochki Shop & Eat is a concept store serving hand-tossed artisanal pizzas in a quiet quaint corner of Shahpurjat Village, New Delhi,” said Ishanee Mukherjee, founder, Poochki. The homegrown brand is majorly inspired by fauna, and most of their ensembles feature hand-drawn illustrations are carved into wooden blocks, and then hand-printed onto carefully chosen textiles. “With mutual love for plants and animals alike, and co-founder Anirudh [Chawla]’s hospitality credentials, expanding into an alfresco garden eatery was always part of the picture,” Mukherjee tells us about the decision to host an eatery in the studio premises. Founded in 2019, Itrh focuses on creating Indian ethnic wear with age-old crafts including kalamkari, madhubani, chikankari, and gota weaving. With boldly hued kurtas and sharara sets featuring gota work and zardozi, it’s no surprise the brand is quickly becoming a favourite among the fashion set. “As a brand, we always celebrate the rich opulence of Indian crafts. With every collection, our main attempt is and would always be to not only revive age-old skills, but also to dignify and preserve this heritage,” says Ridhi Bansal Varma, founder, Itrh. “Our design philosophy is deeply rooted in the exuberance and the graceful glamour of our illustrious past. We want our brand to be a timeless homage to our enriching history and phenomenal craftsmanship,” she adds. Hitting the right cords between modern and contemporary, Beau Monde’s evening bags and clutches are carefully handcrafted for every occasion, be it a cocktail party or a wedding ceremony. “Beau Monde’s USP is its ‘affordable luxury’ factor. It is edgy, quirky, fashionable and so versatile that one just doesn’t want to miss it. It is a statement accessory. The designs are contemporary, and can be paired with both western and traditional looks,” says Kanika Chawla, founder, Beau Monde. Based in New Delhi, Raffughar is inspired by the famous darners of Kashmir. The brand started with producing Namda rugs and pashmina stoles in 2013, and has now moved on to creating jackets, coats and dresses featuring intricate embroideries. “The intention is to revive the traditional and natural processes of craft-making in the contemporary global market scenario,” explains Wajahat Rather, founder, Raffughar. column1: Met Gala 2020: Everything you need to know
column2:
© Getty Fashion From the hosts of the evening to the all-important theme, Vogue delivers the definitive guide to fashion’s favourite red carpet event of the year The first Monday in May, is probably the most (and only) awaited Monday of the year. On the fashion calendar, it marks the opening ceremony of the annual fundraising gala for the benefit of the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute in New York City. Although it was established in 1948, the gala has now become an important part of popular culture since the Vogue editor-in-chief Anna Wintour took over as chairperson in 1995. Vogue answers all your questions about the biggest night in the industry that will mark 150 years of The Met. The Met Gala takes place every year before the opening of the annual spring fashion exhibit at   Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute to public. It is attended by some of the biggest Hollywood stars, names in fashion and influential people from all over the world. The night is an important fundraiser for the Costume Institute. The event consistently raises eight-figure sums; 2019’s edition raised a record $15 million. The “Oscars of fashion” night includes a themed red carpet, formal dinner and first view of the annual fashion spring exhibit. Some of the notable themes in the past include The House of Chanel (2005), Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty (2011), China: Through the Looking Glass (2015), Heavenly Bodies: Fashion and the Catholic Imagination (2018) and earlier this year was Camp: Notes on Fashion. With Wintour as chair, there are co-chairs and honorary chairs every year that have included designers, models and actors from all over the world. 2020 marks the milestone 150th anniversary of the museum so a fitting theme around time has been announced. “About Time: Fashion and Duration” will showcase notable works from the museum's century-and-a-half archives with a common disruptive timeline. Andrew Bolton, curator of the Costume Institute found the inspiration in the 1992 Sally Potter film Orlando, which was based on the time-traveling Virginia Woolf novel of the same name. “This exhibition will consider the ephemeral nature of fashion, employing flashbacks and fast-forwards to reveal how it can be both linear and cyclical,” added Max Hollein, director of the Met. Along with Anna Wintour, Oscar-winning actors Meryl Streep and Emma Stone, Louis Vuitton creative director Nicolas Ghesquière, and Broadway actor and composer Lin-Manuel Miranda will co-chair the gala. Monday May 4. Red carpet arrivals expected to begin around 7 pm EDT, 5:30 am India time on May 5. The gala is always hosted at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City’s Upper East Side. The guest list is only revealed on the eve of the event, previous attendees have included everyone from Princess Diana in 1995, iconic signers Cher, Beyoncé and Lady Gaga to Hollywood actors Sarah Jessica Parker, Gwyneth Paltrow and Nicole Kidman. Designers often arrive accompanied by their muses – Marc Jacobs and Kate Moss; Nicolas Ghesquière and Emma Stone; Riccardo Tisci and Madonna; Brandon Maxwell and Lady Gaga. The Gala takes place on the opening night of the annual fashion exhibit and serves as an important annual fundraiser for the benefit of the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute [which is the only curatorial department at the museum that needs to finance its own activities] in New York City. Although it was established in 1948, the gala has now become an important part of popular culture since the Vogue editor-in-chief Anna Wintour became chairperson in 1995. The “Oscars of fashion” night includes a themed red carpet, formal dinner and first view of the annual fashion spring exhibit. Additionally, the red carpet showcase is the perfect opportunity for designers to present their creativity and push new boundaries in fashion and costume on a global platform. Bollywood's own Priyanka Chopra has attended the fashion benefit three years in a row since 2017, where she made the first public appearance with her now-husband Nick Jonas. It was her custom-made Ralph Lauren trench coat that made headlines worldwide. Deepika Padukone made her Met Gala debut earlier this year in a Zac Posen Barbie-inspired gown [for the surreal theme "Camp: Notes on Fashion", and Isha Ambani also walked the red carpet this year in a lilac Prabal Gurung gown. Stay tuned on Vogue's social media for updated news and images from the event. If you’re on the guest list, not a dime. But for those who don’t get an invite but are lucky enough to secure a chance of attending, ticket prices are around  Rs 21,00,000 each, with tables costing about over one crore rupees. The event hosts approximately 600 attendees. Following the red carpet moments that are covered worldwide, guests get a first look inside the exhibition before taking their seats for dinner and drinks.
The occasional performance: in 2015, Rihanna took to the stage; in 2016, Nas and the Weeknd; in 2017 Katy Perry and Migos took a turn; in 2018 Madonna made a special appearance; in 2019 Cher delighted guests with a surprise performance. The next headline-making event is the after-party that takes place every year after the dinner and performances. Until the much-awaited event takes place, here's a recap of what the best red carpet moments from the Met Gala over the years. column1: 3 designers tell you everything you need to know about wearing fine jewellery every day
column2: © Instagram.com/begumkhan Fashion From the designs and combinations of materials you should opt for to styling and maintenance tips,  we got the experts to answer all your questions on everyday jewellery Gone are the days when workwear meant boring, day dressing was kept simple, and glitter was reserved for the nighttime. Accessories can come in handy to transform your looks, and there’s plenty of options to choose between too, from whimsical motifs to traditional craftsmanship. We rounded up three unique brands that have redefined the way you look at staples, and asked their designers for their top tips on wearing and maintaining everyday jewellery. It’s been over fifteen years since designer Puja Shah set up her bespoke jewellery design studio. Soon after, she also launched her first boutique store in Gujarat, naming her brand, Aurus. Shah’s creative vision has been very clear since its inception—modern design juxtaposed with traditional craftsmanship. This year, she also introduced an extension of her parent brand, Moi, a prêt line of handcrafted fine jewellery. Moi serves a wide variety of ready-to-wear pieces like delicate stackable rings that curve usually around your fingers, their signature pearl tassel necklaces in gold and silver, and diamond-encrusted evil eye bracelets. On maintaining everyday jewellery, Shah says, “My personal care routine for all my jewellery [pieces] is to wrap them in a muslin cloth and store them in lined silk pouches. For daily use, especially the pieces you leave by the bed, I think it’s best to keep them away from perfume and other liquids,” she told Vogue. Turtles, beetles, bees and roosters—these are just some of the species you’ll find in Begum Khan’s jewellery repertoire. Begüm Kiroglu grew up surrounded by rare artefacts and objects from the Turkish empire that were collected by her family. Then, she went on to study Chinese culture and art in Shanghai. So it’s only fitting that Khan’s design inspiration comes from whimsical, unconventional things. Certainly not for the faint-hearted, her pieces are crafted in Istanbul, and can easily be considered as unique collectibles. In her collections, you’ll find Zirconia-encrusted motifs across chunky necklaces, oversized earrings, rings, brooches and headgear. “I love wearing matte gems like pearls, lapis, turquoise and corals in the day. Adding a splash of colour to a white shirt, jeans, loafer is always fun—it’s my day time uniform,” the designer tells Vogue. She also recommends picking crystals with a hint of gold for everyday wear. “They go with every outfit. Crystal is neutral enough to meld in to day look but also brilliant to make an entry at night!” The label enjoys a global presence, and its crowd-favourites include party earrings (animals with golden balls attached) and the Pharaoh cuff. It was Ananya Malhotra’s family-owned fashion business that exposed her to creativity before she discovered the art of jewellery. After completing her Bachelor’s Degree at Central Saint Martins, London, in 2010, Malhotra collaborated on projects with institutions like the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Barbican, and brands like Swarovski and Amrapali. For the now Miami-based designer, her Indian heritage and global travels serve as the starting point for her line of contemporary fine jewellery. In her latest collection, titled Mogra, the designer has favoured white diamonds and mother of pearls for their modern finish, and included them in geometric designs. Ear jackets and miniature clip-on earrings are Malhotra’s go-tos, and she recommends them for work-to-dinner outings. About the materials you should choose for everyday jewellery, Malhotra says, “Pick gold, as it does not tarnish, rust or corrode, and keeps its lustre too. Diamonds are one of the hardest substances and one can never go wrong with them. Sapphires and rubies are also very hardy gemstones. You want to stay away from delicate emeralds and pearls.” Lust list: 8 cocktail rings to take you through the upcoming festive season Black-tie dress code: The Vogue guide The slouchy coat is the It-piece of the season.
