column1: John Galliano Extends His Contract at Maison Margiela
column2: © Photo: Filippo Fior / Gorunway.com Fashion After five years as creative director of Maison Margiela, John Galliano has extended his contract. The news was announced this morning in a release from Renzo Rosso’s Only The Brave, the conglomerate that owns Maison Margiela. “I am super excited for this new chapter and grateful to Renzo for his belief in me and the vision for Maison Margiela,” said Galliano. The exact length of his extension is unclear, but it is expected to be at least several years. Galliano joined Maison Margiela in 2014, taking over the brand’s menswear, womenswear, and accessories and creating its Artisanal couture collection. Under his tenure, revenues have doubled, according to the brand, with accessories making up 60% of the label’s total profits. “Five years ago I believed that John was the only person who could take this house in his hands, and I am even more convinced of this today,” said Rosso in a statement. “John’s undisputed talent is only matched by his understanding of today’s generations, their way of thinking, their struggles, their dreams. And he is doing exactly what this Maison always did at its best: disrupt, innovate, and inspire.” When Galliano arrived as creative director, his first task was rebranding. Not only did he swiftly clip the brand’s name to Maison Margiela—leaving out “Martin,” the name of the brand’s illusive founder—but he also worked to reestablish himself as one of fashion’s great couturiers, coming back from a rehabilitation period that followed his dismissal from Christian Dior for racist and anti-Semitic remarks. Galliano’s return to the runways was an all-red couture collection shown in London that put his craftsmanship and flair for deconstruction on display. What followed since has been a blurring of gender lines, appraisal of historicism, and focus on remodeling tropes of fashion from the staid British trench to the strict nuns habit. Expect all this and more from Galliano at Margiela in the future. This article previously appeared on Vogue.com Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Jonathan Daniel Pryce Fashion Smart, secondhand shoppers have a head start on autumn’s favourite outerwear trend, which is lifted straight out of Hollywood’s Brat Pack style playbook Here’s why the leather blazer trend that Gwyneth Paltrow and Winona Ryder wore (arm in arm) during nights out in the 1990s is resonating with a generation who doesn’t want to buy a brand-new coat this autumn. Who would have thought that the deftly casual outfit that Winona Ryder pulled together in August 1991 for The Commitments Hollywood premiere would still be inspiring fashion moves almost three decades later? Her look — a thigh-grazing leather blazer, a washed-out Tom Waits T-shirt and straight-leg Levi’s — is a key reference point for autumn/winter 2019 because it champions the insouciant sex appeal that comes with a commitment to greener, secondhand fashion. Today, we’re focusing specifically on the vintage 1990s leather blazer: the trophy piece for a generation who aren’t into the faux rock’n’roll connotations of the biker jacket, but prefer to take their leathers a little more streamlined (and with a lot less hardware). Your office’s 25-year-old social media editor who moonlights as a Depop secondhand fashion mogul, American fashion influencer twins Reese and Molly Blutstein (also known as @double3xposure and @accidentalinfluencer respectively) and New York-based power stylist Gabriella Karefa-Johnson (@gabriellak_j). The Blutsteins’ leather-look on day eight of Paris Fashion Week is particularly mood board-able as it shows how something as simple as a pair of black tights (or Marine Serre bodycon) can freshen up an autumnal silhouette. Black opaque tights are, incidentally, enjoying a renaissance of their own thanks to Chanel’s SS20 runway, where the early 2000s look of tights and mini shorts returned in spades. Elsewhere, Karefa-Johnson’s blazer underscores a perfectly composed print clash, while gothfluencer Courtney Trop (@alwaysjudging) showcases her Prada outerwear with coordinating shorts, tread-sole shoes and a slick of red lipstick. column1: 9 things to know about The Queen's dressmaker Angela Kelly
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Queen’s closest member of staff sure has a lot of hats to wear—and by the sounds of it, just as many to design While intimate royal details around the British royal family rarely penetrate the walls of Buckingham Palace—not to mention the undoubtedly iron-clad non-disclosure agreements each and every palace attendant are likely to sign—interesting tidbits tend to find a way through the palace gates every now and again. However, in a brief but big break from the traditional silence, one of the Palace’s principal members of staff is set to release somewhat of a tell-all story about the royal family’s most notable member: Queen Elizabeth II. British dressmaker, milliner, chief dresser and long-time aid of The Queen, Angela Kelly, has received the extremely rare blessing of the royal to publish a book, titled The Other Side of the Coin: The Queen, the Dresser and the Wardrobe, which will cover not only regal fashion, but also her professional and personal relationship with the monarch. But before you sit down to read her book—which is officially on sale from October 29—or listen to its audio book extension, which is narrated by Kelly herself, allow us to give you a compendium of context around the dresser, her life and her extensive career in conjunction with the monarch. For nine things to know about Angela Kelly, scroll on. Unlike many figures in The Queen's life, Kelly’s upbringing was in no way affluent, the parallels between hers and the royal’s family lives are very few and far between. Born in Liverpool to a crane driver and nurse, Kelly was brought up in council housing and is said to have never lost her Scouse accent, according to the Express UK. Kelly didn't begin her career as a dresser, having instead assumed the role as a housekeeper, the occupation she held when she first met The Queen. Working as a housekeeper to the British ambassador to Germany, Sir Christopher Mallaby, Kelly crossed paths with the royal for the first time in 1992, when she and Prince Philip paid a visit to the ambassador during an official visit to Berlin in October that year. According to the Express UK, Kelly found herself in conversation with the monarch, telling her that she was planning to return home. As luck would have it, it only took Kelly a few months of being back in Britain to be offered the role of one of The Queen’s dressers. Following her appointment as one of The Queen’s dressers in 1993, it took only a few years for the royal to recognise Kelly’s unique talents, promoting her to senior dresser just three years later, as reported by the publication. The dresser's arrival at Buckingham Palace coincided with the death of Bobo MacDonald, who had been responsible for both dressing and styling The Queen since her youth. According to the Telegraph UK, Kelly’s role hasn’t solely entailed dressing The Queen for quite some time. In fact, her official title is Personal Assistant, Adviser and Curator to Her Majesty the Queen (Jewellery, Insignias and Wardrobe), one which she has held since 2001. Not only does her lengthy job description reflect The Queen’s increasing reliance on Kelly to run her day-to-day life, but it also marks the appointment of the royal’s first ever personal assistant. “I just want everything to be right for The Queen—to make life easier for her because she is so busy,” Kelly told the publication. “My job is to ensure that when The Queen meets people she looks right.” According to the UK publication, Kelly has not only dressed The Queen, but has also designed a number of looks for the monarch. Having initially created garments with the aid of designer Alison Pordum, the pair uniting in 2002 to launch the label Kelly & Pordum, Kelly herself has been designing clothing for The Queen since the departure of Pordum from the dress team in 2009. Kelly’s recent memorable creations include the buttermilk yellow look Queen Elizabeth II wore to her grandson, Prince William's, 2011 nuptials to Kate Middleton, designing not only the garment she wore, but also her tonally-matched headwear. Kelly also designed the ivory boucle dress with silk ribbon accents the monarch wore to attend her 2012 Diamond Jubilee river pageant, as well as the powder blue coat and hat combination The Queen wore to the wedding of Princess Eugenie in October 2018. Most recently, The Queen wore a white embellished gown designed by Kelly to the 65th State Opening of Parliament earlier this month. Having worked with Queen Elizabeth II for the past 26 years in close proximity, she’s become one the few people permitted to lay hands on the monarch. Kelly has become incredibly close to the monarch, with staff at the Palace noting that when the pair are alone, they often hear their joint laughter echoing through the hallways. “I would never overstep the mark and I remain in awe of The Queen. But she has allowed me to become closer to her over the years,” Kelly expressed in an interview with the Telegraph UK, going on to express just how much fun the pair have together: “I do worry about her and care about her. But we also have a lot of fun together. The Queen has a wicked sense of humour and is a great mimic. She can do all accents—including mine.” Hilarity-ensuring situations aside, Kelly has spoken about the trust The Queen bestows upon her in the past. “I don't know why The Queen seems fond of me—because I don't give her an easy time!” she said. “I do think she values my opinion, but she is the one who is in control. She always makes the final decision.” Kelly and the monarch’s conversations reportedly often drift away from formality, with topics including their own grandchildren, accessories and cosmetics regularly featuring in their chatter: “We are two typical women. We discuss clothes, make-up, jewellery. We say, 'Would this piece of jewellery look nice with that outfit?', and things like that.” In 2006, The Queen appointed Kelly as a member of the Royal Victorian Order, and six years later, she was then promoted to Lieutenant of the same order, in honour of her long-time personal service to the monarch. While many have thought of the royal christening robe as a garment that’s been in rotation over the last two centuries, the piece which is worn today by infant royals at their christenings, is actually a replica. Following its retirement in 2004, after Queen Elizabeth deemed the Victorian garment too fragile for future use, Kelly was tasked with creating an exact copy of the garment, which has been worn by 62 different babies since its creation in the 1800s. Former embroiderer to Queen Victoria, Janet Sutherland, was originally commissioned by the royal herself to make the robe for the christening of her eldest daughter, Victoria, back in 1841, the piece crafted from fine white Spitalfields silk with a handmade Honiton lace overlay, and designed to resemble Queen Victoria’s wedding dress. Since its recreation, Kelly’s christening gown has been worn by Prince George and his younger siblings, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis, as well as the daughters of Zara and Mike Tindall, Mia and Lena. Peter and Autumn Phillips's daughters, Savannah and Isla, have also worn the gown, along with James, Viscount Severn, the son of the Earl and Countess of Wessex. In addition to being tasked with recreating the heritage royal christening robe, Kelly’s styling services have been extended to the wider royal family in the past. The royal dresser styled royal siblings Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie back in 2011 for the wedding of their cousin, Zara Phillips to then-footballer Mike Tindall. Kelly selected a tonal turquoise ensemble for the former, and an earth-toned outfit for the latter. Kelly also joined the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge on the royal tour of Australia in April 2014, aiding the duchess in not only in selecting her attire, but also her accompanying jewels, including a diamond and ruby brooch shaped like a hibiscus flower, and The Cambridge Emeralds. As rare as it is to gain permission to publish a single authorised book about Queen Elizabeth II, Kelly’s soon-to-be-released book won’t actually be her first work which focusses on the monarch. Back in 2012, Kelly published a book titled Dressing the Queen: The Jubilee Wardrobe, which reads exactly as the title suggests and details the careful planning and preparation of The Queen’s wardrobe in the lead-up to her Diamond Jubilee celebrations in 2012. column1: How to choose the best hair accessories for your wedding celebrations
column2: © Instagram.com/ranveersingh Fashion Vogue reaches out to an expert to discover the best bridal hair accessories you can consider for your big day, including the celeb-approved maang tikka and more Your wedding day is the day to play it safe with your sartorial choices. But you can and should add an element of surprise to your look, just to give it a special touch. While every overarching bridal repertoire is likely to centre on that dream lehenga with jewellery to match, we are shining the spotlight on the adornments that decorate your mane. Hair accessories are not just perfect to tie up your tresses, but they have also come out of their costume avatar. Some of the top bridal jewellers in the country have also approved the trend, and now craft hair accessories using precious metals and gemstones. To get more insight on the best hair accessories for the modern-day bride, we spoke to Rohan Narang, managing director of Hazoorilal Legacy. Excerpts below. Among the wide roster of bridal hair accessories, a passa, matha patti, maang tikka, bodla, hair brooch and tiara are the usual suspects for an Indian wedding. Diamond barrettes and semi-precious stone or pearl encrusted headbands have also made a comeback in a big way. We’ve also had requests for a Punjabi paranda in gold and a jade bangara, as well as jada billalu for South Indian brides. Diamond encrusted hair clips and brooches look beautiful underneath a veil. Delicately embellished tiaras with elaborate gowns also make an ideal choice for an engagement or a reception. The vintage appeal of passas, maang tikkas and matha pattis goes well with traditional bridal ensembles too. For a mehandi, brides can opt for lighter neckpieces and stud earrings. I suggest pairing them with an oversized maang tikka or a passa. Alternately, a traditional matha patti can look great with a pair of statement earrings. Delicate diamond tiaras can be teamed with solitaire diamond studs and a string of solitaire diamonds around the neck. With a slew of celebrity weddings last year, there was no dearth of inspiration with regards to the traditional bridal looks. Elaborate matha pattis in polki, pearls and semi-precious stones was a trend that took off in a big way and is still prevalent. Try picking the outfit first. The colour you choose determines whether the jewellery should be in gold, diamond or polki, as well as the style (choker, guluband or a rani haar) [you should pick], depending on the design of the dress. Don’t be afraid to go a little OTT and opt for oversized statement pieces like large maang tikkas, matha pattis or cocktail rings; the bigger the better. You can easily customise them later and use them as versatile separates. Lastly, although social media works great as a reference point, don’t be too influenced by it. Follow your instincts and personal style. Want to wear a matha patti on your wedding day? column1: Gucci's Marco Bizzarri and Renée Tirado on the brand’s new diversity initiative
column2: © Courtesy of Gucci Fashion As Gucci celebrates its Multicultural Design Fellowship Program, which will see 11 international students join its design team in March 2020 as part of its diversity and awareness initiative, Vogue sat down with the CEO and global head of diversity, equity and inclusion to find out what the move means for one of fashion’s most profitable brands Gucci’s Multicultural Design Fellowship Program (GMDFP) award ceremony. Five students were selected by each school and accompanied by a representative on a three-day trip to Italy, where they visited Gucci’s ateliers in Florence and design studios in Rome. Their portfolios were judged by the brand’s design team, who selected 11 finalists — one more than originally planned — who will join Gucci for a 12-month fellowship in March 2020. The GMDFP, which aims to increase opportunities for underrepresented talents and create a more diverse and inclusive workplace, is the first programme overseen by Renée Tirado — a lawyer and former chief diversity and inclusion officer at Major League Baseball (MLB) — who was appointed as Gucci’s global head of diversity, equity and inclusion in July 2019. On the same day as the ceremony, Gucci revealed it surpassed sales expectations with a rise of 10.7 per cent to €2.37 billion (ahead of consensus analyst expectations of 8 and 10 per cent), but 2019 hasn’t all been plain sailing. In February, the company came under fire for producing a balaclava sweater that evoked blackface; shortly after, CEO Marco Bizzarri announced GMDFP as part of a four-pillar initiative focusing on diversity and awareness. Gucci apologised, pulling the design from stores and in March, Bizzarri launched the Gucci Changemakers Scholarship, which will see the brand distribute $1.5 million over four years across two scholars’ programmes. The entire initiative will now be steered by Tirado with the support of the Gucci Changemakers Council, which counts Dapper Dan, Naomi Campbell and Will.i.am among its members. Following the award ceremony, Vogue sat down with Bizzarri and Tirado to learn more about the GMDFP, discuss their next steps to making Gucci more inclusive and find out what the word ‘diversity’ means to them. Renée Tirado [RT]: “The aim was for the students to connect with Gucci and see the brand through Alessandro’s eyes, which is why we decided to host the event in his hometown of Rome — it’s instrumental to his creative vision. For some, it was the first time travelling outside of their home country, so to see the Colosseum and St Peter's Basilica, and have this aesthetic influence on their designs, whether it be for Gucci or their own personal work — it’s beyond experiential.” Marco Bizzarri [MB]: “I’ve been focused on the organisation of the global Multicultural Design Fellowship Program, such as deciding which geographic locations and schools we wanted to work with. When the fellows arrived in Italy, I looked at their portfolios out of interest, but I felt that the winners should be decided on by the design team because that’s who they’ll be exchanging with — it’s not my place to pose an aesthetic on them.” RT: “There are a lot of fashion programmes, so it was important for the tuition to be to a high standard; we sought recommendations from our Changemakers Council. Gucci’s global talent acquisition partner Noemi [Mauri], who works closely with Alessandro’s design team, was largely responsible for bringing this unique group of people together from around the world. On the first day of the trip when the students were introduced to the Gucci team, she got the loudest round of applause.” RT: “To have this global perspective collectively and hear the voices of this generation’s views on the world has been really inspiring. The writer Sinéad Burke has been advising us [on] how we can make Gucci more diverse and inclusive for people with different abilities. A student from [Fashion Institute of Technology] FIT in New York spoke really eloquently about this. Hearing first-hand experiences such as these are essential to developing our strategy.” MB: “There have been so many takeaways. The important thing is to always be open-minded and not pretend to know everything. I think that is why Gucci is continuing to evolve in terms of aesthetic and approach to business — we will always welcome people who think differently from us. No matter how successful you are, or how rich you are, you need to stay true to yourself and explore new paths.” RT: “When I graduated from law school and joined the workforce it was a very homogenous, predominantly male environment and there weren’t people devoted to making companies more diverse and inclusive. As a woman of colour who got her degree from Rutgers University School of Law — not Harvard or Yale like many of my peers who came from more privileged socio-economic backgrounds — I felt isolated and alienated. Of course, individual employees have to work hard to create a positive working environment and better themselves, but corporations need to do everything they can to support that growth. If I had a mentor in law, maybe I would have stuck with it as a career, but then everything happens for a reason and my personal experience has ultimately led me to where I want to be. “I want to make sure that future generations are in an environment that breeds success; work is hard enough as it is. So much of this job is about negotiation and communication, and my background in law has reinforced those abilities.” MB: “Renée looks at things in 360; she can interact with people on every level and that’s essential for this role because it cannot exist alone. It has to feed into every element of this business, which in Gucci’s case is 19,000-people strong. We want to cultivate a workforce with a strong cultural awareness by recruiting from all over the world and creating mobility for employees so they can freely move from one region to another.“ MB: “We have around 150 designers working for Gucci in Rome and we not only need to make sure the 11 fellows are fully integrated, but that they are also supported outside of the studio because it’s a big culture change for them. Hopefully some of them will stay on indefinitely. This is an authentic initiative, it isn’t a marketing activity. RT: “We have a lot of work to do between now and when the fellows come back in the first quarter of next year. There will be some homework involved for the students to make sure they feel prepared to experience a professional environment and we will track their progress and the work they do in the meantime. Internally, we need to ensure all the fellows are fully integrated when they arrive, whether that is overcoming language barriers or catering to people with different abilities. It’s Gucci’s first global [diversity, equity and inclusion] initiative, and you don’t see this type of investment and commitment from global companies in any industry. There’s no pre-existing model to follow so we are making our own and I’m proud to be a part of it. “Beyond the global Multicultural Design Fellowship Program, we are going to be very thoughtful when it comes to new openings in the company. It’s obviously important that diversity in all its forms — from race and languages to socioeconomic and educational background — is reflected in the candidates, but that too goes for the interview panel.” RT: “To me, diversity is people: their perspectives, their values, their experiences, their culture, their language. Everything that makes a person, makes them diverse.” Gucci’s Multicultural Design Fellowship Program (GMDFP) award ceremony © Courtsey of Gucci Alessandro Michele, Renee Tirado and Marco Bizzarri © Courtesy of Gucci Gucci spring/summer 2020 © Getty Also read: Gucci just made the sunglasses chain summer 2020’s most-wanted travel accessory What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Alber Elbaz is back! Here's what we know so far about his new deal with luxury conglomerate Richemont
column2: © Getty Fashion After his abrupt departure from Lanvin in 2015, Alber Elbaz has been sorely missed in the fashion industry. Save for a couple of collaborations and some speaking engagements here and there, he’s been keeping a low profile—until today. Hours ago news broke that the beloved designer is forming a joint venture with Richemont, the Swiss luxury conglomerate that owns Chloé, Yoox Net-a-Porter group, Cartier, and Van Cleef & Arpels, among other brands. Known as AZ Fashion it will be “an innovative and dynamic startup, meant to turn dreams into reality,” according to a release. “Upon hearing Alber Elbaz describe his vision for fashion and the projects it inspires in him, I was again struck by his creativity and insight,” Richemont chairman Johann Rupert stated. “His talent and inventiveness, with his sensitivity towards women and their well-being, will be of great value to our group and its maisons. We warmly welcome Alber to Richemont and look forward to an exciting partnership.” Elbaz added: “I am very happy to partner with Richemont and establish my ‘dream factory,’ which will focus on developing solutions for women of our times. I am extremely excited to collaborate with good people, talented and smart individuals, and look forward to also having a lot of fun with this new adventure.” Given his experience at Lanvin (he was pushed out of his role as artistic director by the label’s owner, Shaw-Lan Wang), it’s fair to assume that one of his dreams is to rewrite the rules of a luxury fashion brand. At the FGI Night of Stars Awards back in 2015, where he received the Superstar Award just weeks before his dismissal, Elbaz lamented how the fashion industry was turning designers into “image-makers.” The following year he gave a lecture at Parsons and discussed the struggle to balance creativity with the demands of a modern business: “I see those CEOs have to manage all of us. And you know what? If we would have a better communication, a better dialogue, with us and the management, that would be the only time when we could make beautiful fashion and a beautiful team. I think that if we inject a little bit more love into fashion and less fear—because today I feel it’s more about fear and less love—we would have a beautiful reason to wake up every morning.” Here’s hoping that’s the case with AZ Fashion. Of course, what’s exciting us most is Elbaz’s promise to develop “solutions for women of our times.” At Lanvin he made women feel beautiful, confident, and, importantly, happy (maybe this is an occasion to bring out those love and happy necklaces again). What so many women have repeated about his clothes is how they felt fresh, yet utterly timeless. In an essay on Elbaz’s legacy, Vogue’s Sarah Mower wrote: “Skimming back through Alber’s Lanvin collections, I am struck by how much he has innovated, how much he owned, and how relevant his clothes still are through time…. When all’s said and done, that timeless hot-yet-elegant relevance is Alber Elbaz’s permanent calling card.” Watch this space for more news on AZ Fashion; it’s still TBD when and how it will be revealed. column1: Exclusive: The International Woolmark Prize 2020 announces its 10 finalists
column2: © Woolmark Fashion Selected from 300 entries, across nearly 50 countries, the best of the world’s emerging fashion talent has been shortlisted — and sustainability is at the forefront of both the nominees’ and judges’ minds. Vogue meets the 10 finalists of the historic prize, previously won by Karl Lagerfeld and Yves Saint Laurent, which will be awarded in London, in February 2020 A-Cold-Wall*, Blindness, Bode and Richard Malone are among the 10 finalists shortlisted for the International Woolmark Prize 2020, one of the world’s most prestigious emerging talent programmes. Selected from more than 300 entries, across nearly 50 countries, the nominees follow in the footsteps of previous recipients including Karl Lagerfeld, Yves Saint Laurent and Giorgio Armani. Most notably for 2020, nominees will not be separated into menswear and womenswear categories. Instead, there will be one winner who will receive AU$200,000 (₹97,10,000), won by British unisex label Edward Crutchley and New York-based husband-and-wife duo Colovos respectively in 2019. The winner of the Innovation Award will also be announced — again, won by Edward Crutchley last time around — who will take home AU$100,000 (₹4,85,507). 2020 marks the first time that all collections must be ‘fully traceable’ to highlight the importance of transparency in the fashion supply chain. The finalists were selected by the International Woolmark Prize’s advisory council, which includes Vogue.com’s chief critic Sarah Mower, Vogue Germany’s editor-in-chief Christiane Arp, Vogue Italia’s deputy editor-in-chief Sara Sozzani Maino and Vogue Australia’s fashion director Christine Centenera. Each of the 10 finalists will present their collection of six Merino-wool looks to a separate judging panel in London, in February 2020. “It is always difficult to choose [the finalists] when you have such a diverse array of designers,” says Eco-Age founder and creative director Livia Firth, who is also on the prize’s advisory council. “I [wanted] to make sure we could showcase all sorts of talents to look at what fashion could look like in the future.” Here, Vogue meets the International Woolmark Prize 2020 finalists: © Woolmark Since launching menswear brand A-Cold-Wall* in 2015, British designer Samuel Ross has gone from strength to strength, collaborating with Nike, Diesel Red Tag and Converse. Now, he is keen to up his green credentials. “Sustainability is an ethos we’ve been filtering into our practice over the past year,” says Ross. “[I want to] expand my knowledge and use of wool as a whole. My approach will be based on reinvention and performance, reconstituting the expectancies of the fibre.” © Woolmark Founded by Seoul-based duo KyuYong Shin and JiSun Park in 2016, Blindess has made its mark with its genderless designs. The pair now hope to push their design talents further by taking part in the International Woolmark Prize. “We wanted to challenge and develop ourselves with new experiences,” they explain. “Brands have a responsibility of using natural resources for the right purpose.” © Woolmark Known for her unique, handcrafted designs made from upcycled vintage fabrics, American designer Emily Adams Bode has been a trailblazer in sustainable fashion since launching her eponymous brand in 2016. “Our collections are 40 per cent made from antique materials; a large percentage [are] made from wool circa 1890 to 1940s,” she says, explaining how the brand is incorporating new but natural materials as it scales up. “I’m excited to include newer and more innovative ways of using wool in my capsule collection.” © Woolmark Since launching menswear brand Botter in 2017, Dutch designers Rushemy Botter and Lisi Herrebrugh have had a meteoric rise, with the pair appointed creative directors at Nina Ricci in 2018. For them, wool is a core part of their blueprint. “Our storytelling about our Caribbean roots is paired with us exploring the way men interpret formalwear and how we can push the boundaries in shape and fluidity,” they say. “We’ve been working with wool since we first started; we love its different aspects [and] that it can be used to create shape.” © Woolmark Chinese-born, London-based menswear designer Feng Chen Wang — who started her brand in 2015 — is an emerging name known for her structured unisex designs. “The [International] Woolmark Prize is a great opportunity to communicate and educate audiences on the beauty and value of my Chinese cultural heritage,” she explains. “[It’s] a global platform that is dedicated to innovation and sustainability.” © Woolmark Berlin-based label GmbH, launched by Serhat Işik and Benjamin Alexander Huseby in 2016, emerged from the city’s underground club scene. The brand, which encompasses both menswear and womenswear, is currently in the process of switching from synthetic to natural materials. “We have been using wool as part of [that] programme,” they explain. “One of the biggest hurdles is cost, and convincing customers that the extra price is worth it.” © Woolmark Balmain-alumni Ludovic de Saint Sernin’s SS20 collection — called ‘Wet’n’Wild’ — certainly made waves at Paris Fashion Week in June. But you might not have noticed some of the knitwear on show, namely its towel look, which went viral on social media. “[The] towel is an expertly crafted virgin Merino wool piece,” says the Belgium-born designer who launched his brand in 2017. “It’s a fun and sexy way to work with wool that people wouldn’t expect.” Again, responsible sourcing is key for de Saint Sernin: “The yarns are sourced in Italy from the best mills and that way we can trace where they come from.” © Woolmark New York-based designer Matthew Adams Dolan has a laid-back aesthetic that has won over fans such as Rihanna, who snapped up one of his denim jackets shortly after he graduated from Parsons in 2014. But despite his A-list fanbase, the designer has been keen to build his brand in a conscious manner. “As a young company, I feel there are certain expectations on our practice,” says Dolan. “That is in sync with how we approach consumption on a broader scale; making responsible decisions, and working ethically and with high quality materials.” © Woolmark Established by brother-and-sister team Dilan and Lezan Lurr in 2017, Swedish-Kurdish menswear brand Namacheko has fast gained acclaim for its reinterpretation of classic pieces, with wool being core to their work. “We have used wool in our collections from the [start],” they explain. “Our approach has been centered around quality and making things that last; [pieces] that can have a second life with many owners.” © Woolmark The Irish designer, who has championed sustainable practices ever since launching his eponymous brand in 2015, carefully sources yarns from the Himalayas, working with local female artisans to weave them into fabrics. “Opening up our supply chain and sharing the journey with customers is extremely important; the reason I have a business today is because of this traceability,” he explains. “[The International Woolmark Prize] was a natural draw for me; it’s mainly the network and the hunger for collaboration that excites me.” The Indian designers competing for the International Woolmark Prize 2018 Designer Ruchika Sachdeva on work and life after the Woolmark Prize Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Obsessed with the '90s? Let these celebrities inspire your Halloween looks
column2: © Shutterstock Fashion From Angelina Jolie’s gothic red carpet appearances, to Drew Barrymore’s beige knit V-neck in Scream—here’s how to repurpose your best vintage pieces this Halloween We can’t pinpoint the exact moment that Halloween became the annual opportunity to demonstrate a knowledge of outlying historical pop culture, but we’d estimate that it was around 2007, with the advent of Tumblr. column1: 5 ways to make sure your next knitwear purchase is eco-friendly
column2: © Vinci Ng/ YanYan Fashion The longevity of wool makes it one of the most environmentally friendly natural fibres around – but then there’s the question of animal welfare and recyclability. Vogue finds out everything you need to know when shopping for sustainable knits As winter sets in, our minds naturally turn towards cosy new knitwear. But after a long summer of climate-crisis headlines, shopping sustainably is top of our agenda, too. “Wool has longevity,” Julie Davies, general manager of innovation and education at The Woolmark Company, tells Vogue. According to a new report by Nielsen for Woolmark, people hold on to their wool garments the longest, compared to other pieces in their wardrobe. “Buying investment pieces is less detrimental for the health of our planet,” Davies says. As a natural and biodegradable fibre, some knits can even have a positive impact on the environment. “Wool sheep can be an integral part of regenerative farming systems,” explains Charlotte Turner, head of sustainable fashion and textiles at Eco-Age. Here, the sustainable fashion experts share five ways to make your next knitwear purchase as eco-friendly as possible. © Courtesy of Carcel It’s best to choose natural fibres that are biodegradable and won’t release harmful microplastics. “Check the labels to know what you’re buying — ideally 100 per cent wool without any synthetic content, as this will affect how the fibre can biodegrade or be recycled,” says Turner.But some wool fibres have a bigger environmental impact than others. “Cashmere is linked to overgrazing and desertification through increased herd sizes as the fibre becomes more popular and widely available,” Turner explains. Alpaca wool — championed by sustainable knitwear brands such as Lauren Manoogian and Carcel — has a much lower impact compared to cashmere. Turner adds: “The animals graze in smaller herd sizes and are also more efficient in terms of the amount of wool they produce. It also comes in a range of beautiful shades so [it] doesn’t necessarily need to be dyed.” © Courtesy of Carcel Look for the Responsible Wool Standard mark — adopted by brands such as Eileen Fisher and Patagonia — on product tags and online, as it ensures the wool comes from animals that are properly cared for. The organisation also prohibits the controversial practice of mulesing: the removal of strips of skin around the backside to prevent the flystrike infection (when parasitic flies lay eggs on damp wool or in open wounds). “There’s a lot of work being done on the traceability of wool to help know exactly where it has come from,” says Turner. “Farmers [are] welcoming audits to share how they are treating the animals, land and water on their properties.” © Courtesy of Everlane Recycled wool has lower carbon emissions. Hong Kong- and New York-based label YanYan uses recycled cashmere, while US brand Everlane has just launched its ReCashmere range, which has half the carbon footprint of its virgin cashmere jumpers. “Our goal is to use as little virgin material as possible, and cashmere is such a big part of our business,” comments Kimberley Smith, head of apparel at Everlane. It doesn’t come without disadvantages, though. Recycled materials often have to be blended with other fibres to improve the quality, making it more difficult to reuse at the end of its life. Everlane’s ReCashmere jumpers are 40 per cent virgin Merino wool. “We would love to do 100 per cent [recycled] cashmere, but it’s [only] just starting to be developed right now,” says Smith, explaining that virgin material also allows the brand to change the colour of its recycled jumpers that aren’t redyed. She adds: “There is technology in development that will take blended fibres, and sort them and recycle them [in the future].” © Vinci Ng/ YanYan When buying a new knit, ask yourself whether you’ll be able to wear it beyond winter. A lighter jumper, which can be layered over other pieces in your wardrobe, can take you right into spring and even summer. “Trans-seasonal garments can be worn for longer, rather than just for certain months,” says Davies. In fact, the new Woolmark study showed that a third of all Merino wool and wool-blend garments are being worn all year round. © Vinci Ng/ YanYan Shopping responsibly is important, but looking after your knitwear once you have it is essential for it to be a truly sustainable purchase. As wool is naturally odour resistant, it won’t require as much washing and therefore, it will last longer. “This can reduce the amount of power, water and detergents used, further reducing wool’s environmental footprint while in use,” Davies adds. “The microfibres it deposits during washing, wearing and disposal naturally break down.” Think twice before throwing a jumper away; any holes can be easily mended, giving it a new lease of life — even if it ends up in someone else’s wardrobe. 7 simple hacks on how to be an ethical consumer Are direct-to-consumer brands the future for sustainable fashion? 17 sustainable buys under 5k to help you commit to slow fashion in 2019 Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The celebrity-approved sunglasses you need in your collection this season
column2: © Instagram.com/deepikapadukone Fashion Can’t settle on a new pair of sunglasses to have and to hold? Take cues from what Bollywood celebrities are wearing nowadays There’s no denying that the right pair of sunglasses can offer a necessary pick-me-up for the dullest of outfits. The no-brainer accessory has the power of making anything you pull out of the closet—whether it’s a casual T-shirt and track pants combination, relaxed pantsuits, or even kurtas—statement-making. The best part? They come in all shapes, sizes and colours, so everyone is sure to find something that works best for their aesthetic. Don’t know how to style them with your outfits? Let Bollywood’s best dressed celebrities show you how it’s done. Deepika Padukone’s arsenal houses everything from oversized bejewelled Elie Saab frames and a tinted square-shaped Dior option to a striking neon pair by Off-White and ’90s-favourite micro sunglasses. In fact, tiny frames have now become a fashion trend that has found its place in most celebrity wardrobes, including Anushka Sharma’s, who wore an oval pair for a flight with husband Virat Kohli. Later on the holiday, she paired gold-rimmed vintage aviators with an orange bikini. Alia Bhatt has a wide collection of sunglasses as well. Her favourites include a frameless hexagonal option and round, bright purple tinted frames. Another great way to experiment with the colour of your sunglasses is by picking a pair featuring a graded tint. column1: Is ‘going viral’ the only way for fashion shows to survive?
column2: © Getty Fashion The cost and carbon footprint of the catwalk plus the saturated schedule and the speed of content consumption mean that to stand above the rest, shows are now competing for the title of ‘most viral’. Here, Vogue asks: are the only fashion shows with a future the ones that become sheer spectacle? The Chanel show falls under the viral fashion shows category in its own right. Karl Lagerfeld’s creations were so sought-after and hotly anticipated each year, that the elaborate runway sets (a tradition continued by his successor, Virginie Viard) were almost unnecessary. This year it was the same, thanks not only to those Parisian roofs, but because the spring/summer 2020 catwalk was the first spring-summer show since the Kaiser passed away. Nevertheless, an unplanned incident is what ended up making headlines: the comedian Marie S'Infiltre crashed the finale and walked a significant section of the runway until the security team realised and tried to remove her. It would have been enough — and indeed it was — for most of the attendees to forget their front-row reviews and immediately post the YouTuber’s entrance, but the epic finale had yet to arrive: it was Gigi Hadid who ended up intercepting and escorting the intruder out. The videos multiplied as much as the pictures, and viewers quickly became split between those siding with the comedian and the ones standing up for Hadid. A perfect example of both the ‘feared’ and the ‘desired’ sides of ‘going viral’, the huge explosion of something that will probably disappear from conversations after a week, even though it managed to reach The New York Times. Taking a look at the viral phenomenon, together with a few more or less similar incidences during the course of this past month, prompts the question: what if the only way fashion shows can survive is by becoming sheer entertainment? Chanel spring/summer 2020 © Getty The debate around whether we still need the shows or not may not be a new one, but the traction that the conversation on sustainability has gained has brought the debate back to the foreground once again, especially after Stockholm decided to cancel their Fashion Week. Francesca Muston, fashion director of the global trend forecasting agency WGSN, described the decision as a “bold and significant” one, thus not only aligning with the imperious (and yes, also viral) Greta Thunberg speech, but also with the actions taken by brands such as Gucci or Burberry in order to offset their emissions, and the agreement reached at the G7 conference by a few fashion moguls. The situation, together with “a new retail phase, more receptive custom production and digital media and online markets developing at full speed — even on a luxury industry level — means that the traditional fashion show schedule is ready to be broken,” argues Muston. An opinion also shared by Anna Wintour, as expressed in her Masterclass lessons: “The idea that everyone must have a fashion show at the same time is completely outdated and it riles me up when I listen to these endless worldwide discussions on the schedule. Why? We work in the fashion industry, which is all about change, and we must lead the way.” A rather unflattering inner perspective, perhaps, but which, nevertheless, still inhabits an irrefutable fact: that the shows are still a communication and viral image tool that many brands want to keep benefitting from. “A fashion show nowadays is nothing but a display of a brand’s wealth and power,” says ManéMané’s designer, Miguel Becer. “They never ceased to be a brand’s collection of samples and an example of that brand’s appeal, but [even more so in the case of the biggest brands], one must say they show the public how mighty a fashion house can be.” Which explains Chanel's humongous sets, or Maria Grazia Chiuri's sustainable garden for Dior, not forgetting the floral structures created by Alex de Betak for Raf Simons when he worked for the same house. Even though the imagery is there, and therefore immediately on online publications, it seems that today’s viral power requires going one step further, one not dissimilar to the performance projected at Louis Vuitton by SOPHIE, the DJ and artist. A step closer to a performance, so that it  looks more like a multidisciplinary show, rather than a simple fashion show. Louis Vuitton spring/summer 2020 © GoRunway One of the best viral fashion show examples we had this season was at Issey Miyake. The brand behind the pleated revolution went for a series of sensory actions that still relied mostly on the visual aspects, but also featured a live speech. Some models were skateboarding, others waved their spring/summer pieces, and one of the most dramatic moments saw models being dressed on the runway by flying robots. Something that feels similar to Dolce & Gabbana’s drones for their AW19 collection or to those robotic arms which sprayed paint over Shalom Harlow at the end of Alexander McQueen’s spring/summer 1999 fashion show; McQueen himself being one of the undisputed masters of fashion show performances. Issey Miyake © Getty McQueen and John Galliano are two exemplary leaders when it comes to theatricality: their  runway shows had more of a narrative than a simple commercial act. The pieces were better interpreted in the context of the show; the message was complete. As Carlota Barrera, menswear fashion designer and winner of Vogue’s Who’s On Next 2019 stresses: “Fashion shows are a way of communicating ideas, perspectives and the creative processes. I don’t believe they are strictly necessary, but they are, without a doubt, spectacles capable of moving the audience in many ways.” Further examples include the battle of Versailles, which officially opened Paris Fashion Week in 1973 or Thierry Mugler’s crowded Zenit Stadium in 1984. It wasn’t just about the set, but also the experience, such as the delicate bubbles at Rick Owens spring/summer 2020 show. Reminiscent of his Mexican roots, the show touched on a childhood in which his mother’s culture (she was seated in the front row) was more than merely present. The delicate play of water and soap could be seen as a childish ending, in contrast with the sharp, geometrical finish of the clothes. Rick Owens spring/summer 2020 © GoRunway Rick Owens spring/summer 2020 © GoRunway It is also easy to include Marc Jacobs in the performance field. Eva Chen, head of fashion partnerships at Instagram notes that the designer “put a marching band playing Smells like teen spirit in his show”. And then there’s Alessandro Michele’s statement in Gucci's spring/summer 2020 show: the allusions to biopolitics, individuality and a curious new sexy via silhouettes and chromatic imagery simplification were presented (at least partially) thanks to a first performative section during which the models wore utilitarian ecru pieces which significantly moved away from the Italian’s usual maximalist language. There were many hints of straightjackets and alienating uniforms, a feeling reinforced by the attitude shown by the models, who remained impassive while the conveyor belt took them from one place to another inside a medical waiting room. Gucci spring/summer 2020 © Getty Sometimes the models’ performance itself is a fundamental factor in making a fashion show go viral. Both Maison Margiela and the famous model Leon Dame, who stormed the catwalk with such an unusual strut that few showgoers were able to put down their smartphones, immortalising the moment on social media. And yes, it was premeditated: “I already had something on my mind, but I worked it out during rehearsals with the show’s movement director Pat Boguslawski the night before,” said the model. Another moment that will go down in history, although not for the same reasons, was when Jennifer Lopez took to the Versace runway in a modern version of that 1990s dress, filling Instagram’s feeds and stories over the following hours. To reference the social network in which the fashion industry seems to have found both a safe space and a constant wake-up call, remains fair game: although drama has existed since fashion shows ceased being intimate presentations and became a part of pop culture, the consequences of readily accessible information seem to have sky-rocketed these memorable moments. In a show schedule where every day includes catwalks by the dozen and trends roll into one another, sensationalism appears to have become mandatory to guarantee not just the fashion show’s survival per se, but also the media representation of the brand that, with any luck, will turn into sales. How are trends made, and why do they keep changing so often? Is mismatched footwear the street style trend you need to watch out for? column1: Good Earth’s Anita Lal traces the rich cultural history of Ajrakh
column2: Fashion Named after the Arabic word for azure and with roots set in Sindhi cultural identity, Vogue explores the details that go into the making of Ajrakh Inspired by the legacy of the various crafts and textiles along the course of the Indus river, Good Earth presented its first independent presentation for their Sustain line. Vogue spoke to Anita Lal, creative director and founder of Good Earth, to understand how the mammoth collection came to life. The Sindhu collection is a journey down the Indus. Just as the culture that inspired it, this collection is a melting pot of a variety of textiles and crafts, both traditional and contemporary, influenced by the sartorial history of the region. The pivotal [element] of the collection is Ajrakh, a time honoured craft of the communities of Kutch, which has been explored in new, contemporary prints and patterns, recreated in different mediums. Besides Ajrakh, Sindhu showcased traditional Mashru from Bhuj along with lighter, cotton silk stripes in bright jewel tones, handwoven in Benaras Bandhini tie-and-dye with highlights of the painstaking rai-dana variety from Bhuj, and the folk Chaand (crescent Moon) motif from Bikaner. Hand-embroideries include zardozi, Punjabi phulkari, suzani, ari, mirrorwork, beadwork, tilla, resham threadwork, Sindhi taanka, Rabari embroideries, folk beading and gota-patti. The hand printing and dyeing techniques include Varq, leheriya, and bandhini. The Sindhu collection is our homage to the unique shared culture of the ancient Indus and the people who lived by it—a tribute to the sea and the land, the Silk Route, the Bedouins and the Banjaras, the nomads, and numerous other civilisations that together enriched India’s culture. It is a celebration of our fascination with ancient trade routes that have been the subject of travellers’ tales. The design team’s inspirations come from the beautiful desert landscape of the Rann of Kutch, and its nomadic, gypsy people, as well as travellers’ accounts of the Silk Route and the transfer of woven cloth, colours and dyes and patterns across these lands—creating textural, layered looks that are firmly rooted in India but at once strongly global. A time honoured craft of the communities of Kutch, with roots stretching from Sindh to Gujarat and Rajasthan, Ajrakh has been passed down through the earliest inhabitants of the ancient Indus Valley Civilisation who, from 3,300 BCE, settled along the basins of the Sindhu River. Traditional Ajrakh is resist-printed, mordanted and dyed in madder and indigo, on both sides of the cloth through a highly complex process comprising almost 30 stages. The presence of Ajrakh fabric from Gujarat in Al-Fostat, near old Cairo in Egypt, speaks of the popularity and the many routes these textiles travelled. The ancient celebrated craft of patterning cloth with block prints and natural dyes, Ajrakh, with its distinctive combination of geometric and floral designs, is a legacy that continues even today, many thousand years later. Additionally, to widen its audience, as part of Sindhu, we also introduce our first-ever menswear line, featuring hand block Ajrakh prints in bold, geometric motifs and silhouettes ranging from jackets, kurtas, dhotis to separates and jumpsuits. The idea of layering is explored vividly in the styling of these garments. Named ‘Azraq’ after the Arabic word for azure, Ajrakh is fundamentally a printed blue cloth that’s central to the Sindhi cultural identity. It is a geometric and abstract red-blue-black-white field of block printed, mordant and resist-dyed textile. With nine to 21 stages of printing and dyeing, Ajrakh is one of the most complex craft techniques in the world. In India, the Ajrakh textile is still printed in the desert region of Kutch and Barmer in Rajasthan by both Hindu and Muslim craftsmen, mostly from the Khatri community. Historically, Ajrakh motifs were inspired by the patterns and colours found in mosques, tombs and other architectural wonders of the lands around the Indus. These craftsmen primarily work with floral or geometric patterns as well as contemporary designs. For it to stay relevant, any ancient craft needs to be revitalised with new design energy. Design intervention of heritage crafts must be done with sensitivity, with a deep understanding of the craft and its tradition so that the artisan who creates it can identify with the new design, and imbue it with their own spirit as well. Although the classic prints of Ajrakh are timeless and continue to delight, we decided to add to its design vocabulary an unusual artwork that was new, contemporary and interesting for the traditional printers of Ajrakh. To represent the movement of ideas and the influence of  East Asia through trade routes, our design team created a valley of flowers juxtaposed with Tibetan Buddhist motifs like clouds, lotuses, dots and fish scales.. We named it Mingora, a region that was an important trading centre on the ancient Silk Route, nestled in the fertile Swat river valley The presence of Ajrakh fabric from Gujarat to Al-Fostat, near old Cairo in Egypt, speaks of the popularity and the many routes these textiles travelled. The universality of this pattern inspired our designers to recreate it in a different medium. Asha, our lead designer, chose to work in silk brocade with the highly skilled weavers in yet another ancient centre of heritage textile crafts, India’s Eternal City of Benares, in numerous tones and shades, and is a recurring theme across the collection. At Good Earth, our endeavour is to continue to champion traditional Indian textiles and crafts, and evolve their design vocabulary to sustain them for the future. Our crafts and craftspeople are the repository of our heritage. My relationship with them is that of great respect and awe, because I am amazed at what they do, whether it be with textiles and how they weave them, the sophistication, technology and level of design, as well as the thought behind it. My endeavour through Sustain is to keep this heritage alive and relevant, and to keep it contemporary so it continues to thrive. That is the path that Sustain will always follow. Sustainability is also about timelessness of garments. All the pieces of Sindhu are created keeping in mind their wearability and versatility across seasons and occasions. When you invest in such pieces, you buy more mindfully and thus, consume less. We want our wearers to understand the larger message behind this collection, and to remind them that they are investing in a piece of history. [We want them] to take a moment to appreciate our rich, inclusive and varied culture, as well as the unbroken tradition of textiles and crafts that continues to thrive even today. We want them to invest in these thoughtfully created pieces as a labour of love. column1: The Bollywood celebrity guide to couple dressing for festive season
column2: © Viral Bhayani Fashion Looking to coordinate your outfit with your partner’s for Diwali? Let celebrity couples like Kareena Kapoor Khan and Saif Ali Khan, and Shahid Kapoor and Mira Rajput Kapoor lead the way If there’s one thing we know about Bollywood’s favourite couples, it’s that they love dressing up together. While they often made a case for coordinated dressing at the airport and the red carpet, it’s their festive looks that have us rummaging around for a book and a pen to take notes. From staying true to their personal styles to serving lessons in navigating the matchy-matchy territories, celebrity couples have long perfected the art of coordinated outfits. Here, we take you behind the scenes to decode how they never fail to make a statement with their showcases. If you don’t have one in your wardrobe already, now is the perfect time to invest in a red sari. Not only is it a classic piece, it also serves your partner with a plethora of options to coordinate their look with yours. Just recently, Nick Jonas wore a beige kurta to complement Priyanka Chopra’s red and gold sari for their first Karva Chauth, while Virat Kohli picked a crisp black number to keep the spotlight on Anushka Sharma’s floral red drape. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan picked a regal red Benarasi sari for Isha Ambani’s wedding last year too, with Abhishek Bachchan accompanying her in an all-black sherwani. column1: Inside Tarun Tahiliani’s exclusive bridal atelier in Mumbai
column2: Fashion The couturier takes you on a tour of his newly launched Mumbai atelier, designed for the discerning brides of today 2019 is the year of new beginnings for Tarun Tahiliani. Having acquired an exclusive address in Kolkata, in addition to his strong presence in Mumbai, New Delhi and Hyderabad, the couturier is now celebrating another first with the launch of an exclusive bridal atelier above his flagship store in Mumbai. Located in Colaba, the new space aims to attend to the needs of modern-day brides in complete privacy as they realise their sartorial dreams for the big day. Taking cues from the waterfront promenade outdoors, the designer has sought to invite the airiness within by imbuing a sense of levity into the structure’s colonial disposition. Brides-to-be, here’s what you can look forward to at the exclusive atelier according to Tarun Tahiliani himself. Often, when clients from Mumbai visited our Couture Studio in Mehrauli, Delhi, they would ask me why I didn’t have something like this in the city. The time had come for a more luxurious experience, one where brides and patrons could have their sartorial needs taken care of in privacy. We now have a dedicated space for couture and bespoke offerings, and a different space for our bridal wear in retail. This is a space we used to utilise a few years ago and now, we have taken it back. It has two beautiful rooms with a large holding space, luxurious fitting rooms and tremendous amounts of privacy. Our classic aesthetic is expressed in the airy elegance of the high ceilings. We have narrow plastered columns and T-jaals on the antique mirror. The essential colour palette is black, beige and charcoal grey, with liberal amounts of mother-of-pearl and beautiful ostler chandeliers from Ancestry, who are known for their classic ostler chandeliers. The furniture is clean, functional and bears our new signature—mother-of-pearl frames that our brides will look into and find themselves reflected with the T-jaal drapes behind. I always like people to see themselves in a very clean setting. This is what struck me the most when I had gone for a couture fitting at Chanel a few years ago. No matter what you were trying on, you saw it in a space that was luxurious and functional enough so you could see every flow. The atelier has been lit by Kanchan Puri-Shetty, and our brief was for the lustre of the clothes to come through—not for dramatic effect, but to see the fit in perfection. Thus, the studio offers different light settings, so the clothes can be seen in the sort of lighting they will be worn in. We did this by superimposing a few modern partition walls, and leaving the bay windows with floating ceilings, which allowed the original architecture to stay. I am not a big fan of false ceilings—for me, the most important ingredient of luxury is the height of the ceilings. Malini Akerkar, who has developed the basic idea, worked with Green Square Turnkey Solutions to give us a wonderful finish and light accessories, so as not to crowd the space. It is really about the clothes, the brides, the couture clients and them being able to marvel at themselves in it. I have always been a fan of pale colours and classic reds, of course. But we have now gone into multicoloured hues, and we also do a lot of skin and peaches in that colour family. I think these sort of colours, along with rose gold, really offset Indian skin [tones]. I am seeing greater sophistication in the modern-day bride. The classic Tarun Tahiliani bride is highly educated, well travelled and is not looking to dress like a costume ball. She is conscious that she wants to reflect her personality as well as her heritage, but not let one overpower the other. The most important thing on her checklist is finding an ensemble that makes her look like a million bucks. However, it is equally important to feel good in the clothes, which is why people are no longer suffering through lehengas that weigh 20-30kgs. The cool brides now want to stay in the outfit till 6am in the morning. In fact, they are very vocal about learning the many different ways of wearing these outfits in the future. As they are confident, it is also necessary for their personality to show through what they are wearing. We hope that our studio will be able to address their needs. The way I look at it, there are only two strong bridal trends, and this is not something that changes from year to year. There is always the very sophisticated pastel with a soft vintage vibe—whether it is the pale pink, blush, shades of gold and, of course, ivory, which is always great on every skin tone. The other decisive trend is the traditional red, emanating from the sindoor that is a symbolic culmination of the marriage. Within the reds, colours have become brighter and more vibrant, as opposed to the dark maroons and burgundies that were on-trend a couple of years back. column1: Gigi Hadid Kaia Gerber and more are taking the cardigan to superstar heights this season
column2: © Getty Fashion The cardigan is autumn’s A-list phenomenon and we’re low-key obsessed We’ll set the scene. Let’s say you’re a pop star with a cool 40-million-strong social media following. Back when ‘hot girl summer’ was a thing, you owned the phrase like you personally coined it and are now looking for ways to stay warm — OK, hot — this winter (minus the defunct Insta-phraseology). Today you’re wearing a humble cardigan. Yes, really. If you’re Dua Lipa, it might even be your boyfriend Anwar Hadid’s slouchy varsity cardi. For autumn/winter 2019, the snuggly button-up knit — beloved of post-punk revivalists everywhere — is now an essential component of the paparazzi-primed outfits worn by the Los Angeles’ teen and twenty something power set, which includes models Kaia Gerber, Bella and Gigi Hadid and Kendall Jenner. Backstage at Prada’s SS20 show, Gerber revealed exclusively to Vogue that her low-maintenance jaw-grazing haircut was directly inspired by Nirvana frontman, Kurt Cobain. Her look that day? An equally low-maintenance lilac cardigan, which candidly referenced the era-defining grunge get-up the rock star wore for the band’s 1993 MTV Unplugged in New York showcase. Gerber isn’t alone in embracing an offbeat, Parma Violets-hued cardigan. The sickly-sweet shade is currently the number one choice for the Hadids and Jenner, and the celebrity style commonalities don’t end there. The way to wear the cardigan now isn’t necessarily chill-proof, but that’s not the point. Start by cutting back on the layers — winter 2019’s cardis are worn with nothing underneath and a pair of faded vintage Levi’s jeans (yes, the ones you’ve had in your wardrobe for the past decade). Case in point: Katie Holmes in a knockout Khaite cashmere bra and cardi co-ords, teamed with perfectly broken-in jeans and a tan. So, why does the knit feel ‘now’? Well, the celeb cardi harks back to the simple girl-next-door look of a 1990s Cameron Diaz, Julia Roberts or Reese Witherspoon — when a strappy top and mohair knit worked for a starry film premiere and a Saturday shopping trip (remember those?). Outings which, back then, came without the tutelage of a celebrity stylist. Fast forward to today and the walk from the hotel to the car has become the new red carpet for some of the world’s most photographed young women. This is where the cardi — worn conspicuously unbuttoned to flash toned abs — comes into its own. The 1990s knit is the apotheosis of ‘candid’ Insta-style, in that it is handpicked from the Pinterest fashion vault precisely because it looks like it hasn’t been styled, but rather thrown on. Sounds simple, right? Here’s your visual recap on how to wear a cardigan now. column1: The story behind Sarah Burton’s favourite Alexander McQueen SS20 dress
column2: © Getty Fashion Alexander McQueen’s spring/summer 2020 show was one of the most beautiful collections of the season, but have you ever wondered how a McQueen dress comes to life? In a Vogue exclusive, creative director Sarah Burton tells us the story behind the dress It was a magical moment at Paris Fashion Week SS20 when Alexander McQueen’s creative director Sarah Burton took her bow alongside the entire McQueen team, after what is now widely recognised as one of the season’s most beautiful collections. The show notes credited the Central Saint Martins’ students whose sketches featured in the collection, too. Set to a score composed by Isobel Waller-Bridge (sister of Fleabag’s Phoebe) and performed by the London Contemporary Orchestra, the enigmatic designer’s choice to share the limelight, as it were, spoke volumes. “I love the idea of people having the time to make things together, the time to meet and talk together, the time to reconnect to the world,” says Burton. An idea she took quite literally, and exquisitely, and look number 10—a round-neck dress with an asymmetric draped skirt in ivory linen, decorated with embroidered dancing girls—best embodies that. Worn by Stella Tennant on the runway, the dress was made from linen crafted in Northern Ireland. The entire McQueen team took part in embroidering the dress, organised and inspired by the Stitch School, which aims to reconnect people to the craft. The designs were the work of a community, too: they were sketched by Central Saint Martins’ MA students during a life-drawing class held at the McQueen flagship earlier this year. Here, Alexander McQueen’s Sarah Burton shares a rare insight into the making of that particular look, and the community spirit behind it. © Courtesy Alexander McQueen When the McQueen flagship store opened on Bond Street in January 2019, the brand hosted a series of educational events, called Unlocking Stories, to celebrate the inaugural exhibition. In an illustration class led by British legend Julie Verhoeven, Central Saint Martins’ MA fashion students sketched the Ophelia dress together (pictured). The result was a continuous, spontaneous sketch of dancing girls that went on to become the foundation and spirit of the dress. With the students’ consent, the final artwork was mapped out and transformed into the pattern that formed the basis of the dress. Here, the illustrations take shape and initial thoughts on embroidery are tested out. © Chloe Le Drezen The illustrations were printed on to linen and stretched over Stitch School looms, installed at the McQueen headquarters in the weeks leading up to the show. The entire team, from HR to IT, was invited to participate in its crafting. © Courtesy Alexander McQueen The McQueen embroidery team were on hand to educate and encourage the wider crew, instructing them in a variety of techniques, including chain stitch, cross stitch, herringbone stitch and French knots. Threads of different thicknesses were used, including a mix of cotton, wool and viscose threads. © Courtesy Alexander McQueen The dancing-girls embroideries developed over a number of days, evolving with each addition. With the use of different techniques and the hands of more than 100 individuals, the end product has a sense of in-built community spirit. © Courtesy Alexander McQueen Once the artisans had completed the linen, 10 separate pattern pieces were cut to create the finished silhouette. © Chloe Le Drezen Intricately constructed miniature paper maquettes—approximately 30 per cent of the original scale—were crafted to perfect the placement of the print against the body. The dolls go on to form part of the McQueen archive. Around 12 metres of ivory Irish linen were used to create the final dress, which itself underwent four separate constructions: one toile fitting and three separate linen versions. It is a process of trial and error, playing with different weights and sheens. The final look was worn by Stella Tennant at the spring/summer 2020 show. © Chloe Le Drezen Why the future of fashion is female All the highlights from Paris Fashion Week spring/summer 2020 Alexander McQueen’s most iconic runway moments Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 10 ways to wear tartan like a celebrity this season
column2: © Viral Bhayani Fashion Throughout fashion history, everyone from royal families and pop culture icons to celebrities have harnessed the power of the iconic print to earn their style stripes. Here, we show you how Bollywood’s A-listers are reprising tartan for 2019 Come autumn season, there are certain patterns your mind is inherently trained to reach out for. The historic tartan is one such prime contender. According to legend, the iconic checkered print dates back to 14th century Scottish Highlands, where wool weavers created these linear patterns as identifiers of the various Scottish clans. It was also around the time that King James V purchased ‘three ells of Heland Tartans’ for his wife, sealing its fate forever. So if tartan denotes interlocking stripes that run in warp and weft, is plaid the same? Pretty much, but the latter refers to a garment featuring the pattern, and originates from the word ‘plaide’, the Gaelic word for a blanket. These days, plaid and tartan are used synonymously for the checkered stripes.   Back in the day, tartan went on to become such a monumental badge for the Highland Gaels that the British government banned the wearing of tartan after the Battle of Culloden in 1746 to suppress rebellious Scottish culture. Later, King George IV’s visit to the Highlands in 1822 was celebrated by a sea of locals dressed in their signature checked kilts, while Queen Victoria embraced the print to furnish Balmoral Castle. Over the years, key members of the royal family—think everyone from Queen Elizabeth II and Lady Diana to Kate Middleton and Meghan Markle—have been spotted in tartan outfits.  So while plaid does represent regality, it’s not without a rebellious alter ego either, as seen in its prominence in the ’70s English punk rock movement and ’90s grunge phase. For his autumn/winter 1996 collection, Alexander McQueen used tartan to denote his Scottish heritage in his controversial ‘Highland Rape’ collection. And McQueen and Sarah Jessica Parker also wore watching plaid to the 2016 MET Gala. But the British brand is not the only one which is known for its signature plaids—Burberry, Vivienne Westwood, Chanel and Ralph Lauren have not been too far behind.  Remember 1995’s favourite Beverly Hills high school princess? Cher and Dionne looking like “total Betty’s” in their plaid skirt suits in Clueless (1995) serve as the most memorable looks in the parade of tartan you can spot in the flick. And then there is Rachel Green looking adorable in a plaid mini and turtleneck sweater with knee-high socks on Friends, giving us a masterclass in acing urban preppy. And who can forget Shah Rukh Khan’s red and green checked shirt as he Senorita-d his way through Switzerland with a doe-eyed Kajol in tow in Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995) or Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s plaid dress and blazer combination in mint tweed in Aisha (2010)? Moving on to the matter at hand—sure, tartan was cool, but is it still relevant circa 2019? Just ask Anushka Sharma. The actor attended this year’s Vogue Women of the Year awards in an I-came-to-play Gucci jumpsuit and blazer in the pattern, toughened with Christian Louboutin boots. And then there is the bevy of Bollywood beauties—Deepika Padukone, Priyanka Chopra and Shraddha Kapoor—who found a unanimous favourite in the classic plaid pantsuit. On the other hand, Janhvi Kapoor has been giving the print a youthful update with her looks—be it in a pink Barbie-ready skirt suit or with lilac trousers, worn with a casual cropped shirt. Serving off-duty tartan inspiration is Ananya Panday, who has been spotted in a grey short suit, styled with a ruched bustier and sneakers, and a strappy mini layered over a plain white T-shirt in recent times. Wondering if the pattern lends itself to print-on-print? column1: 12 looks from Shanghai Fashion Week that confirm street style isn’t dead
column2: © Paul Jeong Fashion The Shanghainese are living proof that fashion subcultures are still flourishing. Here’s what you need to know As the industry takes stock of the SS20 season during October, we’re presented with the perfect opportunity to weed out that illusory phrase ‘fashion month’. As well-trodden as the New York/London/Milan/Paris circuit is, it isn’t the full story. In reality, the SS20 show calendar is far from a four-part tale. Shanghai Fashion Week is well underway (it’s also fashion week in Tokyo and Seoul) and when Vogue dispatched photographer Paul Won Jeong to capture the city’s street style, the results were perhaps not what you’d expect from the world’s most powerful luxury-goods market. “There’s a knack for incorporating Chinese or Asian cultural-esque style clothing in a baggy [or] relaxed fit, but it’s not strictly about luxury labels. It’s about doing something different with what you can access,” explains the 25-year-old, Seoul-based photographer. The generation who congregate in the French Concession, Xintiandi, Nanjing Road and the Pudong area (west of the river) during fashion week share certain style signatures, however. “This season, I saw attendees stacking accessories, whether it was two to three bags overlapping one another or incorporating something completely unrelated like a walkie-talkie with a satchel or a delicate purse,” Jeong adds. This offbeat approach has made the Shanghainese youth living proof that the DIY energy of the street-style subcultures — the ones we got to know secondhand through legendary tomes such as Des Parisiennes by French photographer Pierre Le Gall or Japanese creative director Shoichi Aoki’s FRUiTS fanzines — are still flourishing in 2019. A distinctively individual approach to beauty and detailed 20th-century wardrobe references matter. “A lot of the youth identify with the sneakerhead/goth/grunge/punk subcultures and hip-hop is growing,” Jeong observes. From thrifted Californian surfer shirts, to cheesecloth pinafores (worn with dainty velvet ballet slippers) and a rarefied post-punk take on suiting — here is Vogue’s edit of the 12 best street-style looks at Shanghai Fashion Week SS20. © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong © Paul Jeong What street style taught us about the trends to look forward to this year 15 times Kareena Kapoor Khan showed us how to ace street style Vogue predicts: Fashion month’s 10 biggest street style hits Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast
