column1: How are trends made, and why do they keep changing so often?
column2: © Instagram.com/lakshmilehr Fashion Does a fashion trend first take breath on the runways or through the loving patronage of the A-listers sitting poised in the front row? Or, is there some larger force at play? It would be all too easy to crown green as the defining fashion mood for the year for Bollywood stars. Not just any green, but that iridescent, acid-infused, live wire iteration of the homely botanical colour. Deepika Padukone famously favoured this hue in her Cannes repertoire earlier this year with a voluminous Giambattista Valli number, and later carried it into her airport wardrobe with an oversized Off-White jacket too. Elsewhere, Malaika Arora showcased a fail-safe method to wear the shade while on holiday with a layered blazer and shorts set, while Sonakshi Sinha stepped out in a head-to-toe neon ensemble by Arpita Mehta. More recently, Kareena Kapoor Khan also decisively proved that this colour isn’t going anywhere with her neon Retrofête skirt. While it would be convenient to peg green as the colour du jour, a closer look proves that this trend has been simmering on the slow burner for a while now. Sabyasachi offered a lime green lehenga in his spring/summer 2018 collection, which also went on to find a fan in Alia Bhatt. The young star took the colour to the red carpet in the form of a resplendent lehenga at Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s wedding reception, where it effortlessly stood out in a sea of reds and pastels. Flip further back through the fashion books, and you’ll find this techno hue originally currying favour in the late ’90s grunge phase. The evolution of this colour into mainstream consciousness vouches for the veracity of Laver’s Law of Fashion. Devised by James Laver, a noted fashion theorist and costume historian at the Victoria & Albert Museum, the law prescribes a precise timeline to the life cycle of a trend as it moves from being considered ‘indecent’ and ‘shameless’ up to 10 years before its time, before eventually being called ‘daring’ a year before, and ‘smart’ once it is in current fashion. The trend is then considered ‘dowdy’ and ‘hideous’ five years after its time, only to be referred to as ‘quaint’ and ‘charming’ again a few decades down the line. This law does much to validate fashion’s current fascination with the ’90s. At the recently concluded Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week, Huemn’s collaboration with Pepsi saw the brand’s vintage iconography splashed across easy basics crafted from recycled plastic. Sonam Kapoor Ahuja and Rhea Kapoor's label Rheson has been built on the stilts of late ’90s nostalgia. What’s old is new again, and the sartorial hallmarks of the era—think high-waisted denims, bitsy crop tops and round glasses—have been dutifully reimagined to fit the sartorial mould of the present day. The advent of technology has done plenty to accelerate the retro redux with authentic archives and digital imagery from any given era queued up at the other end of a Google search. The sheer abundance of information we’re inundated with also means that the runway mood now serves as a direct reaction to the world we live in. As the clock ticks on the final countdown to Brexit, the tensile trade agreements and predicted economic slowdown have found expression on the runways. Indeed, the recently concluded London Fashion Week was governed by a defiant sense of buoyancy, with designers opting for pomp and fanfare in the face of economic uncertainty. House of Holland sent print-on-print and disco makeup down the runway, while Simone Rocha generously layered ruffles, lace and pearls for a dramatic production at the freshly restored Alexandra Palace. This omnipresence of information in the digital era can also be credited for giving rise to the ‘see now, buy now’ model. In a bid to service the growing needs of the ever-impatient consumer, brands are slashing lead times to discover the next 'It' thing. Not too long ago, a polka-dotted dress was plucked from Zara’s store racks to achieve social media fame with a devoted fan base of over 26,000 followers on Instagram. The dress’ overnight ubiquity can be credited to the brand’s business model that famously combines social learning with drastically short turnaround times, moving garments from the design floor to racks in as less as two weeks. Taking a page from the international behemoth’s playbook, Trent, the retail arm of Tata Group, is looking to build its own fast fashion empire with everything priced below $15 (approx Rs 100) in India. The brand also plans to routinely shortlist trends spotted on Instagram for a limited-edition run in its stores within 12 days, and further develop it into a full run depending on the response. In the larger ecosystem of macro trends, the race to the finish line is then determined by a brand’s prowess of identifying and reacting to micro trends in time, and a supply chain finely honed to deliver on speed to market. This direct-to-racks model throws the seasonal fashion calendar into further existential crisis, as highly coveted product drops, capsule lines and collaborations with hot-button artists erode the clout of biannual seasonal collections. With technology outpacing the reach of conventional trend forecasting systems, fashion makers are casting their nets wide in a bid to give customers what they want, even before they know that they want it. The next item to stir a need-it-now frenzy in your closet now has a wide array of muses to seek inspiration from—whether it’s a headline in the economic section of the newspaper or the nostalgia-riddled wrapper of your favourite childhood candy. column1: “My bigger task is educating the millennial consumer”: Sabyasachi Mukherjee on his obsession with jewellery
column2: © Marcin Kempski Fashion After celebrating 20 years in the industry this year, the designer opens doors to his first-ever flagship jewellery store. He talks to Vogue about reinventing himself to create a new business He started off as a jeweller before he got into clothing and funded his first line with the money he made selling costume jewellery out of a tiffin box to street vendors in Calcutta. Two decades later in the industry, Sabyasachi Mukherjee has come full circle with his jewellery brand. On wish lists of Indian brides all around the world and as the country’s most sought-after couturier, Mukherjee still feels challenged. As he launches his first stand alone jewellery boutique in Mumbai, he lets us in on why he feels young again with his now two-year-old business. “I think my bigger task is in educating the millennial consumer about jewellery because many of them have grown up not wearing any jewellery at all. So a lot of people look at jewellery as a frivolous expenditure. Yet at the same time, a lot of people in this country look at it as an investment. I look at jewellery as a thing of beauty, more than just investment for women to be able to enjoy it. And I think my job is not only to create relevant products for the market, but also to make the market understand the relevance of these products.” “When I started jewellery, I started feeling young again because I was a little jaded and bored with what I was doing. After some time, the business goes on autopilot, but right now, I am reinventing myself to create a new business. The good thing is that you only learn entrepreneurship lessons once in your lifetime. So you don't make the same mistakes twice. Jewellery is growing at a much faster pace because I do it is a new business.” “We have a different finance team, design team, HR team, and infrastructure team with about 37 people in jewellery, and counting. This is my first standalone in Bombay. It's not going to be a part of the store. It's going to be two floors up, but it's going to be a separate profit centre and a separate store of its own. In Delhi, I have the jewellery inside the bridal section of my store. Even in Calcutta, we'll be adding another floor to push jewellery.” “I have started doing it. There is a custom order that we are doing for somebody. It's close to about Rs 14.6 crores. One family, one of them, and they wanted to do something stunning. Jewellery could start at about Rs 75,000 -  80,000. We even have hoops for Rs 19,000 - 20,000. These are small, intimate pieces, and it could go up to Rs 15 crores. It's very elastic, a lot of it depends on what I want to make. I'm very whimsical about it. I will keep a section that is affordable to everybody for scale. But for me, I never got into jewellery to make money. I have a lot of education in jewellery, I studied jewellery a lot, I’m quite obsessed with jewellery." "I am quite schizophrenic about jewellery. I love minimalism and maximalism. It's the middle part that bothers me. Even if I do simple jewellery, I like layering them or I would do jewellery that is very quiet. And sometimes both of them exist together. I like that push and pull and fusion of opposites because it creates really big stress. And that stress creates a very dynamic energy in desire." The Sabyasachi flagship jewellery store is now open at K Dubash Marg, Ador House, 3rd floor, Kala Ghoda, Mumbai. column1: Are you ready to bring your shapewear out from under your clothes?
column2: © Getty Fashion Once designed to be hidden under clothes to create that coveted hourglass figure, shapewear is now coming out of the closet. Here’s everything you need to know The concept of innerwear as outerwear doesn’t necessarily qualify as radical or new. We’ve seen lace-trimmed camisoles layered under blazers in the boardroom, and plunging necklines with exposed bras at parties. While lingerie has already been invited to take a seat at the main table, a new innerwear staple is also looking to claim its spot in mainstream consciousness now. Shapewear, every celebrity's best-kept secret, is now clocking in additional closet mileage as everyday outerwear—whether you’re headed out for a quick juice run post-gym or a brunch with the girls. Here’s your front-row seat to the revolution unfolding in everyday wardrobes. There’s a reason why Kim Kardashian West clocked in $2 million (approx Rs 1 crore) within minutes of launching her shapewear line, SKIMS, and it extends beyond the cosmic pull she has over our collective wallets and psyche. Down the years, the 38-year-old reality TV star has often candidly documenting her own struggles with finding adequate options. After undergoing extreme measures such as dyeing her own using tea bags, she followed her entrepreneurial calling and launched her own line of shapewear. The record-breaking label offers solutions for every body type, including pieces that can easily work double-duty as outerwear. It won’t require a particular stretch of imagination to see the bandeau bra paired with biker shorts or the cotton plunge bralette layered under a bomber jacket on a lazy Sunday afternoon. These second-skin numbers have been fast currying favour as an off-duty staple with the best dressed names on the style circuit as well. Emily Ratajkoswki was recently spotted in a shapewear romper from her own label, Inamorata. The 28-year-old offered a quick masterclass in the versatility of the sculpted black bodysuit, first pairing it with white sneakers to walk her dog and later dressing up the silhouette with a belt, white boots and an animal print bag. Elsewhere, Kendall Jenner took the traditional unitard silhouette out for a night about town. Spotted stepping out of her hotel during New York Fashion Week, the model took spandex to the streets in her black Atoir romper, paired with strappy Alexander Wang heels and a slicked-back ponytail. The many advancements in shapewear technology, from no-boning fabrics to covert placement of support panels, means that sculpted shapewear now serves as a prime candidate for transition pieces. If you’re looking to make like the Kardashians, pair Commando’s high-waisted faux leather shorts with a basic tank for a day of shopping. Sara Blakely’s brainchild, Spanx, offers a wide roster of silhouettes for outerwear as well—choose from strapless bodysuits or the celebrity-favourite faux leather leggings. Meanwhile, the Meghan Markle-approved label, Heist Studios, has been championing the cause of shapewear as outerwear with a slew of pop-coloured slimming bodysuits, including green ivy and summery sienna iterations that can be easily paired with denims or skirts to become your new weekend uniform. For those special date nights, La Perla wants you to swap your classic LBDs in favour of a figure-enhancing inner with Chantilly lace inserts. Dress it up with your favourite sky-high heels, and you’re good to go. column1: Deepika Padukone and Kareena Kapoor Khan show you how to layer necklaces
column2: © Instagram.com/deepikapadukone Fashion From traditional chokers to modern lariats, here’s a celebrity-approved guide on how to layer your necklaces to create a standout look There’s no such thing as too much jewellery, and one of the most popular trends to take over the fashion landscape stands as proof. Layering your necklaces is not only the simplest way to make a strong sartorial statement, it is ridiculously easy to DIY too. Whether you’re looking to amp up a basic T-shirt or a deep necked evening gown, strategic layers of necklaces will never fail you. Unsure about how to do it right? Let Bollywood’s best dressed celebrities show you the way. Take cues from Kareena Kapoor Khan, who teamed five layers of minimal gold and silver chains featuring diamonds with a white blouse for a recent red carpet event in Mumbai. She had also paired three gold necklaces (two with pendants and one chain design) with an all-denim look in the past. In fact, gold necklaces seem to be a favourite among Bollywood stars when it comes to layering. Deepika Padukone was spotted pairing multiple chunky gold chains with a printed Dior look during Paris Fashion Week. If you don’t want to mix and match, add multiple strings in the same design like Priyanka Chopra did to complete her all-black ensemble during The Sky Is Pink promotions. It is a great way to bring your décolletage into focus with minimal fuss. Or do like Sonam Kapoor Ahuja and throw the rule book out the door, matching everything from mixed metals to your favourite gemstones together in one cohesive look. The trend has taken over international waters too, with A-listers like Gigi Hadid, Rihanna and Kim Kardashian West all giving layered necklaces their stamp of approval. column1: Presenting the winners: Vogue Women Of The Year 2019
column2: © Bikramjit Bose Fashion A list of exceptional people Now in its third edition, Vogue Women Of The Year awards has become synonymous with glamour, excellence and remarkable success. We’ve raised the bar up another notch for 2019, bringing together the most inspiring names from all over the world to tip our hats to their unparalleled talent, and the countless hours they spent perfecting their crafts. From the country’s most successful sportswomen to business leaders, designers, supermodels, Bollywood celebrities and more, meet the winners of Vogue Women Of The Year 2019. © Kreerath Sunittramat Viral YouTube star Lilly Singh is systematically dismantling the all-white world of suits that anchored late-night television. As the NBC newcomer and first Indian-origin female host on broadcast television in America, she has opened the doors for many others who look like her, and brought some much-needed diversity to our TV screens. © Leigh Keily In 2007, Kunal Nayyar’s big break came when he starred as part of an oddball cast of geeks who charmed viewers in The Big Bang Theory—which went on to become the longest-running multi-camera series in television history. While Nayyar’s Raj Koothrappali was a bit of a dorky clown, his intrinsic role in the group and the ability to keep it real set him apart. In 2015, the actor even penned a book titled Yes, My Accent Is Real to talk about how he wasn’t just another Apu in America. After 12 years of relentless work and phenomenal success, he announced to the world his plan to “take a break from social media”. © Getty At just 25 years old, Canadian model Winnie Harlow has already changed the face of fashion. Since she was discovered by Tyra Banks on the 21st series of America’s Next Top Model in 2014—competing under her real name, Chantelle Brown-Young—she’s been central in the move towards a more diverse and inclusive fashion industry. Harlow may not have won the competition, but she didn’t need to. She’s fronted campaigns for the likes of Diesel and MAC Cosmetics, a regular on the catwalk and fashion’s front rows and appeared on dozens of magazine covers, all the while raising awareness about her skin condition, vitiligo (which causes patches of pigmentation loss). It wouldn’t be an exaggeration to say that Huda Kattan is currently the beauty world’s brightest star. She has close to 40 million Instagram followers, clocked 150 million YouTube views and owns a beauty brand with an estimated value of US$1.2 billion. When Kattan started out as a beauty blogger back in 2010, white influencers were the norm, a few African-American names were in the mix, but brown women were totally missing. Kattan has gone on to popularise her own Arabian style of makeup (which resonates strongly with brown women) all over the world—a near-miraculous phenomenon, as traditionally beauty ideals are passed from West to East, not the other way around. © Georges Antoni Our Style Icon of the Year considers style an accessory to life, not the principal driver. A believer in fashion that’s believable (but not basic), Anushka Sharma’s is a covetable wardrobe you’d want to replicate. She’s routinely spotted in a range of athleisure staples and casual wear, and white sneakers are more likely to show up than over-the-knee patent leather boots. “Sometimes we push ourselves to wear extremely uncomfortable clothes. There are clothes meant for a specific reason—they look beautiful on screen but they’re not the most amazing clothes to wear. In my own space I want to be comfortable in what I’m wearing and, most importantly, it has to reflect me,” she reveals. © Bikramjit Bose As a child, Alia Bhatt would dance for her grandparents every Sunday. Her game of choice with her best friend was “actress-actress.” Left to play, she’d conjure an imaginary audience to dance and act for. At 26, this prodigiously talented actor seems to have achieved everything. Gully Boy is on its way to the Oscars, her father is directing her in Sadak 2, and her upcoming feature, Brahmastra is frantically awaited. No wonder she has been crowned our Performer Of The Year this time around. © Signe Vilstrup With her brand new venture into the world of beauty, Katrina Kaif might have just cracked the code to being an unpredictable enigma and yet coming as close to her fans as a superstar can at the same time. Her makeup brand, Kay by Katrina is an unapologetic, honest ode to beauty, and has been two and a half years in the making to speak Kaif’s language. “I want it to portray my philosophy. It definitely does not say, ‘Look like me.’ I want you to have fun with my makeup and let it enhance the favourite parts of you,” she says. © Getty Acting was not part of the game plan for Taapsee Pannu. She had an engineering degree and was preparing for the Common Admission Test (CAT) to apply to business schools. So when did she decide to actually become an actor? She says it was after she completed her debut film, a Tamil feature called Aadukalam (2011). Cut to 2019, Pannu is a well-known face in the Hindi film industry, with blockbusters like Pink and Badla to her credit. Her formula for success? Being slow but steady, and accepting your own reality. Ananya Panday may be just one film old right now, but she has already made a lasting impression in the Hindi film industry. After a prestigious debut in Karan Johar’s Student Of The Year 2 (the first SOTY launched the careers of the likes of Alia Bhatt, Varun Dhawan and Sidharth Malhotra) earlier this year, the 20-year-old actor is now gearing up for her upcoming feature, Pati Patni Our Woh, where she will share screen space with Kartik Aaryan and Bhumi Pednekar. Panday has been ticking off everything that sums up a star’s list—she had signed on as Lakmé’s youngest brand ambassador even before SOTY 2 released, made her runway debut at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2019 for Arpita Mehta and Anushree Reddy’s show, and has now become a regular on best dressed lists. Today, her bag of endorsements also includes denim brand Only and Gillette Venus. © Greg Swales In Ranveer Singh, we have a leading man who takes his work seriously but not himself. Quixotic, intense, angsty and the class clown all rolled into one—here is a man who makes the movies more fun than they have been in a long time. Over the years, he has combined a hyperbolic goofball public persona with a versatile body of work—including Zoya Akhtar’s Gully Boy, India’s official entry to the Oscars this year, and Kabir Khan’s upcoming ’83, which will see him playing the country’s first cricket World Cup-winning captain, Kapil Dev. © Nuno Oliveira Growing up as the son of Mammootty, superstar of the Malayalam film world, Dulquer Salmaan had a vantage point on fame and cinema that few do. But he didn’t really want to act. He was always in awe of his father, so he felt that acting was that one thing he couldn’t do. “My biggest fear was I’d be a humongous failure son of my dad, and that I would lose it all,” he says. Today, Salmaan has some 30 acting awards to his name, and is a consistent name in listicles for the best-dressed and the influential. Clearly he was wrong. © Getty To call Zoya Akhtar unstoppable would be an understatement. Her latest film, Gully Boy, was recently announced as India’s official entry to the Oscars for 2019, and she also produced her first web series, Made In Heaven, for Prime Video earlier this year. Considering her wide range of as a filmmaker—her earlier work includes the likes of Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara (2011) and Dil Dhadakne Do (2015)—it’s not surprising that she’s considered as a fine storyteller and observer of subcultures by critics and audiences alike. Anyone who grew up in the ’90s can attest to the all-pervasive message of Benetton’s ad campaigns: joy, colour, celebration, acceptance, love. Taking the brand’s ideals of multiculturalism, diversity and inclusivity forward is its new artistic director, Jean-Charles de Castelbajac, who has been designing clothes since 1968. The long-time champion of diversity believes that fashion has a responsibility, and that you can say important things with creativity—fashion but with a cause. She was the Vogue India Fashion Fund winner in 2014, the Woolmark International Prize Winner in 2018, and this year at the Vogue Women Of The Year Awards, she’s Designer Of The Year. Ruchika Sachdeva has carved a space for herself in India’s fashion landscape in less than a decade since she founded her label, Bodice, in 2011, dedicated to impeccable construction, menswear tailoring traditions and Indian crafts. Her collections may look deceptively simple, but actually boast of rich, complex textures, a detailed analysis and research of handlooms, and an overarching message of thoughtful design. © Tarun Vishwa An international debut in 2016 at Louis Vuitton catapulted Pooja Mor’s  continental career shift, where part of the perks include being shot by the best photographers in business (Annie Leibovitz, Steven Meisel and the late Peter Lindbergh), a stream of global campaigns and a platform for championing causes. Almost 16 seasons, 68 runways and 76 looks later, Mor has made the world’s runways her stage. © Jarek Pajewski Garima Arora has had quite the year. She became the first female Indian chef to receive a Michelin star for her restaurant Gaa in Bangkok in 2018, and was also awarded Asia’s Best Female Chef 2019 at the World’s 50 Best Restaurants awards. Last month in Mumbai, the 33-year-old chef launched Food Forward India (FFI), a culinary initiative that brings together people at the forefront of the Indian food industry “to re-examine, re-evaluate and reintroduce Indian cuisine to the world”. The cub pharma reporter-turned-chef, who worked with Gordon Ramsay, René Redzepi and Gaggan Anand before opening her restaurant, is applying her journalistic curiosity and chef’s laurels to be the change she wants to see. © Bikramjit Bose In 2013, Heena Sidhu received a phone call that would change her life—she got an opportunity to compete at the World Cup in Munich, Germany. The 30-year-old pistol shooter went on to beat the then world champion with a record score of 203.8, and became the first Indian pistol shooter to win gold at the World Cup. The following year, news emerged that she has made history as the first Indian shooter to hold the World No. 1 title. © Ashish Shah Apart from record-breaking firsts on the track, Dutee Chand is also India’s first openly lesbian athlete. The professional sprinter announced that she was in a same-sex relationship earlier this year, and earned high praise from many quarters, including talk show host Ellen DeGeneres. Just over a month ago, Chand clinched the gold medal in 100 metres at the World University Games in Naples, making her the first-ever Indian woman track and field athlete to do so, clocking 11.32 seconds. Next up on her list? “My ultimate aim is to bring home the gold medal for India in the 2020 Tokyo Olympics,” she reveals. © Kay Sukumar From setting up the 10-acre-large arts village Kaladham in the JSW township in Vijayanagar to starting Art India, the country’s leading magazine for contemporary art, Sangita Jindal is a patron whose engagement with art goes far beyond the act of acquiring. A champion of Indian art for more than a quarter of a century, as the chairperson of JSW Foundation, the non-profit arm of JSW (a colossal steel and energy conglomerate run by husband Sajjan), Sangita proactively promotes heritage as well as contemporary art. © Ankita Chandra It could be refusing to sit on a segregated bus seat, pledging to donate half of their wealth to charity or skipping school to protest. For social entrepreneur Neera Nundy, it was a coming together of her desire to lead and prove herself. As the co-founder of Dasra (an organisation that catalyses India’s strategic philanthropy movement), she has an ambitious goal to transform a billion lives with dignity and equity. She’s a role model of leadership today, proving that it takes vision, a real understanding of one’s skills and a lot of hard work to truly make a difference. © Farhan Hussain A 30-year-old with an annual turnover of over Rs 300 crores, Foodhall founder Avni Biyani has captured the zeitgeist with a food chain that brings trending, premier foods to our pantries. From a starter team of 70 people, Foodhall has now expanded to over 800 employees in the gourmet food space as Biyani gears to open her 10th store in Delhi. The stock, too, has swelled almost double-fold in the eight years since the brand launched in 2011. From introducing India to 2,000 foreign items, they now boast an international stock of over 7,000 items. Biyani is unstoppable. With an app underway, she plans to kick off her digital expansion soon too. There were no case studies, no reference points, no guidelines when Falguni Nayar decided to sell something as tactile as makeup and skincare products online. She noticed how her friends in the States were dependent on shopping on Amazon. She noticed the paucity of a good beauty sale experience in India and combined the two to launch Nykaa in 2012. Today, her empire is worth more than 750 million dollars. column1: Sara Ali Khan: Don’t aim to be someone else’s role model. Be your own
column2: Fashion The actor comes together with Anjali Lama, Dutee Chand and MC Mary Kom to redefine what it means to be a woman in today’s times While some people like to play it safe, others like to take the road less travelled to pave their own path. Such is the case with some of the most impactful women in India, including award-winning athlete Dutee Chand, Bollywood actor Sara Ali Khan, transgender model Anjali Lama and Indian Olympic boxer MC Mary Kom. They have broken the norm in the respective careers, and stood out in the crowd with their talent. Known for her bold personality, Sara Ali Khan isn’t one to shy away from stating her opinion and viewpoints clearly, be it at interviews or at award ceremonies—making her one of the most outspoken actors to grace the big screen in recent times. MC Mary Kom is well-known for breaking stereotypes with her boxing prowess—she’s the only woman to become World Amateur Boxing champion for a record six times. National champion Dutee Chand is the first Indian athlete to publicly come out as a member of the LGBTQ+ community, while transgender model Anjali Lama has made a notable impact on the country’s fashion landscape. These four women, who are also Puma’s brand ambassadors, recently launched the brand’s newest campaign, titled ‘Propah Lady’, which encourages women to write their own rules and redefine the conventional rules of what makes women ‘proper’. We spoke to the stars about the challenges they faced in their careers, and got their advice on how to break through the stereotypes and stand in your own light. There are so many people every day telling you how to eat, sleep, talk every day. But you should believe in who you are. Be honest, confident and cool. The real definition of cool is original and authentic. Spend your time and energy investing in yourself. People are going to ask you [questions like] ‘who’s your role model’, ‘who do you want to be like’, but [remember that] these people are already out there. Be your own role model. [The] aim shouldn’t be [being] someone else’s role model, [it] should be to be able to tell people that there’s no role model. The real role model is standing in front of them every day in the mirror. It’s in your hands to change that role model in [the] mirror, and in her hands to change you. The biggest challenge that people face is accepting who they are. They are afraid to be themselves. They only worry about what people are going to think and say about them. [Just] be yourself and come out of [your] shell. Women have to face a lot of challenges—people tell them what to do, how to behave—and undergo a lot of struggle, but in the end they win. Whatever challenge comes your way, fight it with a lot of courage. Being a woman and a mother, I have faced several challenges that have empowered me to break the rules. I think the biggest challenge is self-doubt and I want all women to overcome it. As Puma gives women a collective voice, I would like to tell all my female fans to never stop believing, [and] never stop fighting the tough fight. [Because] at the end of it, there is supreme satisfaction and happiness. column1: Michael Halpern on the transformative power of clothing
column2: © Mazen Abusrour Fashion Aided with glitter and lamé and fuelled by the nostalgia of his mother’s Studio 54 days, Michael Halpern talks to Vogue about the romantic allure of sequins American-born, London-based designer Michael Halpern has enjoyed commercial and critical acclaim ever since his runway debut in 2017. Having worked with fashion houses like Versace and Oscar de la Renta in the past, Halpern is no stranger to the seduction clothing holds on women. As he launches in Mumbai’s concept luxury store Le Mill, Vogue spoke to the designer about sparkly dresses and their transformative power. I don’t think sexy has anything to do with the clothes. I think it’s about the woman, [her] confidence and how she holds herself, how she treats people, how she lives. That’s what makes a woman sexy. I think for me, it’s so much about how the woman would feel when she puts the clothes on. You [tend to] sit in a certain way, move in a certain way [in some pieces]. You have to be more conscious of what you’re doing, and I love that kind of gracefulness that clothing can bring to you. It’s almost like a character. Even the way a dress sounds when you’re walking—that is what I think about when working on a collection. You can think about it in both ways. The world can be a really scary place sometimes and it can be a way to escape some of those things and not so silently protest feeling a certain way. I think using colour and texture is a way to have that bit of fantasy in your life, and a bit of respite from really scary things. And that’s the way it can be used as a protest, not conforming and not dressing the way that society necessarily tells you to. When it comes to celebration, who doesn’t want to put on a sparkly frock and jump around sometimes? I have a few, but [the] most important is my mother, who was coming of age in the mid-1970s when Studio 54 was in its heydays. I would see pictures of her and her friends going to Studio 54, and listen to them talk about what it was like. Having that contrast of the pictures and how they remember it is always interesting to me. The idea of something growing as time passes excites me. I have this picture of my mom in this great cherry red jumpsuit, and the way she described the night—what she was doing, where they went for dinner and where they went dancing—that’s the really glamorous part. Nostalgia. It’s really fabulous in that way. According to her, the biggest contrast today versus then is that people were a bit freer, more open, more accepting, a bit more wild in a way less controlled, less curated. I like to think about the clothing in that way. Everything doesn’t have to be so 'Instagram perfect'. You can see the beauty and the flaws. And I think that’s really important for me when I’m thinking about the clothes. You should experiment with fashion and colour and texture and sense. I think for us, it’s the dresses. But I also have the customer who loves trousers. That’s our real signifier. I love to see the way people style it, with a big white shirt underneath it or a turtleneck under there with the sneakers. It is really fabulous for me to see how women would interpret it, because that’s the most important thing in fashion—it needs to be authentic to you.  I think it would be really light. We would use a lot of really colourful chiffon and georgette and it would have volume. I’m not trying to make clothes for a bank manager’s job, that’s not my focus. But I think there is a lot you can wear in the day. You don’t have to be so subdued. We’re using a lot of alternative fabrications that still feel really luxe and glam, but don’t necessarily shine. You could do some denim, which will be really fun this coming season. column1: Karl Lagerfeld and Cover Story collaborate for an India-exclusive collection
column2: Fashion The collaboration comes just in time for a seasonal wardrobe refresh. Scroll ahead for a first look Have you ever noticed that the more prolific the personality, the more constant and unchanging their look? Anna Wintour and her always-in-place bob, Alessandro Michele and his biblical beard, the late Karl Lagerfeld and his ubiquitous silver-grey ponytail, sunglasses, suit and glove-covered hands. It’s this iconic Lagerfeld look that found its way on Coca-Cola cans, Faber Castle pencils, and even L’Oreal Paris’ makeup products. When Karl Lagerfeld, the creative director behind Chanel, Fendi and his own eponymous label, collaborated with H&M in 2004 for a first-of-its-kind collision of high street and luxury, he paved a path for several other luxury fashion houses to merge high and low years later. The woman working tirelessly behind the scenes to blur these boundaries was none other than Karl Lagerfeld’s right hand, Caroline LeBar. And on a mid-October day, she is here in Mumbai for the launch of yet another such convergence of two worlds—Karl Lagerfeld for Cover Story. It’s a meeting of minds between Karl Lagerfeld (the brand) and homegrown Indian fashion retail label, Cover Story by Future Style Lab. With 30 stores and several shop-in-shops across 22 Indian cities, Cover Story was a natural choice for the international collaboration. On the eve of its official launch, we caught up with LeBar, who is also the communications head for Karl Lagerfeld, and Manjula Tiwari, CEO, Future Style Lab. Excerpts from the interview below. Manjula Tiwari: We never wanted to lose the essence and signature DNA of the Karl Lagerfeld brand, because that is the whole point of this, but at the same time, we are a brand in India—a successful fast-growing brand in touch with the changing Indian consumers. Our inputs from Cover Story were more to do with the fit or the shapes that Indian consumers are likely to want more—the weather, the fabrics and how it would suit or fit into our lifestyle. So of course, we have the classic black and white, but we also have a touch of pink and very strong red, because Karl loved red. It’s a 90-piece collection that is versatile enough so the Indian woman can adapt and interpret it the way she wants, because that essentially is also what Karl wanted—for people to break the rules and make things their own, while making luxury accessible to many. Caroline LeBar: Karl had very special thoughts about India. As you know, he also did a Bombay-Paris Chanel show in the early aughts. He was very much with us when this collaboration was first ideated and loved it. India is a country of culture, and beyond just expanding our global footprint, it’s also about sharing, opening minds, growing a strong network and breathing a new lease of life into the brand. Caroline LeBar: I still remember when we did the 2004 collaboration with H&M, there was a limited edition sequin jacket that sold out within an hour. Karl was absolutely furious and went to the press and news to say how much he wanted to do something that was really for all people. The Cover Story collection has been made with this memory in mind, and to respect Karl’s wish for being inclusive. We were a digital-first brand, one of the first fashion labels to be present at a tech conference. Once we had tested the waters, we decided to go brick-and-mortar, and now we have 100 stores, and are available in 96 countries through our website. The collaboration is so close to the Karl Lagerfeld DNA. Karl would always say that if he could have invented something, it would be the white shirt. At any given point in the production of shirts, there would be 300 distinct detachable collar choices. This is why there are so many whites in the collection too. He always called himself his own best caricature and it’s the truth. He also used to call himself Charlie Chaplin, someone you could identify from far. You see the silhouette, you know exactly who it is. In fact, eight years ago, at a Halloween party in New York, there were six other Karls! They all dressed up like the real one, who was also there! Manjula Tiwari: In the Indian market, collaborations of this calibre are rare to come by. It’s the whole spirit of doing new things, pioneering and pushing the boundaries that we love at Cover Story. So to think of an Indian-born brand collaborating at that level and making it accessible to more Indian customers has been the most exciting part. The Indian consumer is ready for a collaboration of this kind. I was so surprised that ever since we put out our first Instagram campaign teaser, we’ve had calls, direct messages, and people commenting with positive feedback; customers are sending emails to our store managers. And not only Delhi and Mumbai, we’re getting calls from Baroda, Surat, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru and so on. I think in today's world, consumers are far more aware and connected than we think, and it’s exciting for us to reflect that. Caroline LeBar: I was 19 when I interned with Karl Lagerfeld. I think it was 1985 and he had just done his first collection for Chanel, that was all denim and very very unlike anything ever seen before. That was a huge scandal in France; I remember Le Figaro had it on its cover. I, of course, didn’t know Karl so well at the time, and when you’re a kid you are more traditional and more respecting of rules. I remember thinking that this man was a bit too much. Two months later, I was working for him. There was a point when he was 80 years old and designing between 12 and 14 shows a year, plus all the additional collaborations. So the biggest lesson I learnt from him is to make everything look effortless. He was a very hard worker, pretending he was not getting worked up. It was just not him to bore people with how much effort you put into creating a collection. He liked to pretend that it was as easy as buying a dress or wearing it. I loved this polite side of him… I spent over three decades working with him and he was my mentor. I was educated by Karl. column1: “I want it to be an art orgy”: Rick Owens on his ephemeral Pompidou Centre installation
column2:
© Danielle Levitt Fashion For one night only during FIAC art fair, the fashion designer has carte blanche of Paris’s National Museum of Modern Art. He tells Vogue how he intends to fill the space with his unique, glamour-meets-grunge creative vision For the third consecutive year during the Foire Internationale d’Art Contemporain (FIAC) art fair in Paris — its 46th edition, running from 17 to 20 October — the Pompidou Centre is holding a special event of its own: You x Art x Centre Pompidou. On 17 October, fashion designer Rick Owens will bring his glamour-meets-grunge, or glunge, aesthetic to the fifth floor galleries of the cultural venue — home to the National Museum of Modern Art — with a special performance. Using Rick Owens furniture as the stage, figures from the designer’s creative sphere will respond to the works of art on display before the evening culminates in an after party. Rick Owens © Danielle Levitt Owens follows in the footsteps of Portuguese visual artist Davide Balula, and before him Italian artist and filmmaker Francesco Vezzoli. Both were also granted carte blanche over the museum space; the latter collaborated with the Paris Opera Academy to create an immersive experience for the Pompidou’s 40th anniversary in 2017. Organised by The Friends of the Centre Pompidou, proceeds from the ticketed event will go towards the centuries-old effort to grow the National Museum of Modern Art’s collections. In 2018 alone, 120 works were acquired thanks to the non-profit organisation’s patronage. The museum now boasts the largest collection of modern and contemporary art in Europe. Ahead of the revelry, Owens reveals to Vogue how he intends to exercise his creative freedom. Rick Owens [RO]: “I started with the thought: ‘What is the most radical thing I can do in a space filled with incredible works of art?’ And I concluded it was to bring in my own works of art. So there will be living works of art (people I admire who have devoted themselves to creative expression), standing on works of art (my furniture designs), responding to works of art (the Pompidou’s collection). I want it to be an art orgy in a controlled environment (a museum). “The whole thing is really collaborative. I’m not choreographing the performers or telling them what to do, I’m simply composing them. Then, of course, it’s also a collaboration with my wife Michèle [Lamy], who is nurturing the Rick Owens furniture business. While I have an idea of what I want, it’s her that sees the designs through.” RO: “I think a lot about environment when I’m designing clothes. I love the idea of everything connecting and being authentic; that you wear an outfit that relates to who you are and where you live and how you live — everything complete and resolved. There’s a morality to it which has always interested me.” RO: “Not literally, but like I say, it’s important to me that there is a consistent aesthetic thread through everything that I do in my entire life. My latest collection took inspiration from my Mexican heritage on my mother’s side of the family, which I haven’t explored that much before. I recently went to see an exhibition at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice about Josef and Anni Albers’ travels through Mexico and the country’s influence on their work. They sketched the pyramids and documented Aztec writing systems. It really delighted me because it was a very playful, German interpretation of Mexico — a lens very similar to mine, the opposite of a cliché.” RO: “There’s an installation by [Italian artist] Giuseppe Penone in which all the walls are lined with laurel leaves behind wire mesh. Close to that is a Joseph Beuys installation [called Plight] and the walls are covered with grey wool felt, and, in another room, a floor by Carl Andre [144 Tin Square]. I’ve always thought of that as my fantasy home — a Penone room, a Beuys room, all the floors covered in metal tiles.” RO: “Museums are so compelling to me — they all have a loaded history. Just look at how many works of art have been stolen, or are the subject of controversy, or have been claimed and reclaimed. To me, museums represent the history of the world, wickedness, aspiration, war, greed, conflict and, at the same time, beauty. They’re very salacious places.” RO: “I’ve been influenced by the anthroposophic furniture movement [a school of thought that combines spirituality and materiality for a better humanity] for some time — the clinical composition of organic materials really appeals to me. I've pushed this idea in a more opulent direction by using acres of alabaster and marble. Some of the furniture shapes are so simple — I’ve incorporated antlers into them to give an organic flourish. Antlers represent glory to me — they’re like a crown.” RO: “My houses are very basic usually. All my furniture is made from rustic wood in very simple geometric shapes. I love an extravagant floor; in my Venice house, the floor is made from Sardinian stone, and in my Concordia house, I have travertine throughout. I don’t hang art on the walls; instead, art nouveau sculptures on pedestals are scattered around. A little bit goes a long way with me. Although I’m drawn to modernist art, I like art nouveau for its complete indulgence and sensuality — especially when it’s presented in such an austere space. “I’ve come to realise my homes are pretty autobiographical. I used to be very indulgent and as the years have gone by, I feel more comfortable being controlled. There’s definitely a temptation of collapsing back into indulgence and I think that’s something everyone can relate to. We all think, ‘What if I just let everything go and do whatever the fuck I want?’ at one time or another. There’s something titillating about relinquishing control, but we don’t because we have responsibilities. It’s noble but [tinged] with regret because we feel we would be enjoying things more if we didn’t have to be in control all the time.” --

column1: “It’s a misconception that art is more intellectual than fashion”: Chloe Wise on her biggest solo exhibition to date
column2:
© Courtesy Jacquemus Fashion The Canadian artist recently decamped to Copenhagen to prepare for her current exhibition, And Everything Was True. With her New York show Lineup on the horizon, she discusses her influences, her collaboration with Jacquemus and using fashion as a tool for communication Over the past few months, Montreal-born New York-based artist Chloe Wise’s peripatetic lifestyle led her to call Copenhagen home as she created new work in preparation for her largest solo show to date, And Everything Was True at the Heart Herning Museum of Contemporary Art. The 28-year-old’s portraits parody a consumerist world that she is consciously part of and exercise the classical training she received through her BA in fine art from Montreal’s Concordia University (she graduated with a distinction in 2013). In her piece, Perversely Versatile (2019) Eric Christison — the Canadian choreographic director behind the Gucci SS20 show — and author Martin Kongstad recline against swathes of jewel-toned fabrics; another titled You definitely lied to the right person (2019) depicts American artist and Puppets and Puppets co-founder, Carly Mark, wearing an ironic T-shirt emblazoned with ‘S.P.E.R.M. Society for the Preservation of Equal Rights for Men’. Lactose Tolerance (2017), meanwhile, shows model Lily McMenamy dressed in a voluminous white top, posing with a can of Nestlé condensed milk. These brushes of humour paired with attention to colour, drape and light are among the reasons why Simon Porte Jacquemus tapped Wise to paint his SS19 campaign images. As one exhibition opens, work on another begins. Next, a group show called Lineup that will see her work displayed alongside Matisse and Picasso at the Almine Rech Gallery in New York. Between sittings, Wise delivers words about her influences, collaborating with Jacquemus and using fashion as a tool for communication. Chloe Wise [CW]: “My process changes by virtue of making work all the time, whether that’s looking at people in a certain light or thinking about colours and shadows differently, or reflecting on something I learned at college. Painting is about observing. “Generally, I really thrive in a fast setting like New York and I find I’m always running in a way, constantly creating and never really stopping to take a break. At the same time, I welcome pauses from that. There’s a lot going on in Copenhagen, but there are less distractions and I definitely don’t feel as fearful of missing out on things since being here. With the exhibition [And Everything Was True at Heart Herning Museum of Contemporary Art], I haven’t had the luxury of slowing down, but being in a city that’s calmer, where the air and water is cleaner and you can go swimming in the harbour, it’s made me appreciate patience. “The most bizarre thing is listening to [the US] news, especially if I tune out for a few days and then tune back in. The further you are away from it, the more aware you become of what a circus the political situation is. Seeing what goes on with the Trump administration — the systemic injustices there — and the sensational way in which the media covers it, it’s leading to a culture of normalisation and is [perpetuating a] ‘not my problem’ attitude.” [CW]: “I’ve always loved the way [visual artist] Alice Neel handled paint and the way she depicted people she met in an almost documentarian way at her home, as though they were part of a scrapbook or yearbook. When I was in London [in early 2019], I went to see the Sorolla exhibition at the National Gallery and it really taught me a lot — the way he treated light made me cry and I haven’t been able to stop thinking about it ever since.” [CW]: “I hate the word ‘inspire’ because it’s so overused, but people who have a desire to create excite me, whether that be making music or painting or choreography. It’s often when I’m having a good conversation with someone that I find myself looking at their face noticing that they have interesting features. “It’s not always about painting people who are in my immediate vicinity, either. For one of the group portraits I painted for the [Heart Herning Museum of Contemporary Art] show, people flew into Copenhagen from Paris, London, New York and Los Angeles. Technology enables us to be in constant communication with people around the world and I’m always taking pictures, so sometimes I collage them together to make a group portrait.” [CW]: “While the fashion industry moves at an extremely rapid pace — styles are in for six months then bye, and back they come as retro a few years later (with the exception of fast fashion, of course) — it doesn’t purport to be a deeper philosophical endeavour. It’s aware of its own mortality. “It’s a bizarre misconception that art is a more intellectually apt space for dialogue than fashion because obviously the art world is so market-driven and elitist, and only a select few can communicate using international art speak. Art pretends to be eternal, art purports to be this much deeper expression of the human condition, but it’s just as fleeting and trend-based as fashion at times. “Just look at brands such as Eckhaus Latta, Pyer Moss and Puppets and Puppets — they have an almost community spirit and look to activists, chefs, teachers, artists, musicians to front their campaigns and walk in their shows, as well as models. It’s a sign that fashion is opening up and reaching out for more people to participate and ultimately become more representative.” [CW]: “Simon [Porte Jacquemus] and I met at the bar La Perle in Paris a few years ago. He’s a great dancer and his energy is so contagious. I spend a lot of time in the south of France, and he’s the go-to guide for all the hidden gems on the Riviera — always visiting places such as Santo Sospir [a villa decorated by French poet Jean Cocteau] and Le Corbusier-designed buildings. “I like that he’s not only presenting a historical image of the south of France; it’s a modern interpretation, too. It encompasses the hip-hop scene and tourists with their binoculars and passport holders. There’s this hilarious campy drama to his collections with the giant hats and tiny bags. I always add a layer of humour into my paintings and it’s not obvious they’re made in 2019, so we share that.” [CW]: “Recently, my paintings have been about groups of people cropped in such a way that you focus on individuals. As a viewer there are so many eyes on you, like a stare down, as if to say, ‘What are you looking at?’ — whereas in the past, they have perhaps captured a more voyeuristic moment where the subject seems unaware they are being painted. “I wanted to create that feeling of isolation, but also togetherness that can be found in community — we all know how it feels to be in a room full of people and feel alone — and play on the idea of selfhood. There’s a performative nature to coexisting in a group; the dynamics that play out naturally, or unnaturally, roles that we take on, the roles we think we should take on.” --
Chloe Wise’s solo exhibition And Everything Was True is at Denmark’s Heart Herning Museum of Contemporary Art until 29 March 2020. column1: Is mismatched footwear the street style trend you need to watch out for?
column2: © Instagram.com Fashion From New York to Paris Fashion Week, all signs show that mismatched shoes will be a sure-fire hit this season That memorable fashion faux pas Kareena Kapoor Khan’s Poo made in Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001) is now a legitimate trend. From the streets to the front rows at fashion weeks in New York, London, Milan and Paris, mismatched shoes are being spotted everywhere this season. Even Sarah Jessica Parker came out of SATC retirement to give a Carrie Bradshaw approval on the resurgence of the trend. Designers all over the world also gave the trend their stamp of approval with pre-scrambled offerings (Jacquemus does it best) to make things easier for you. If you want to go down the DIY route, it’s best to stick to wearing different colours of the same shoe on each foot. For example, since neon hues are all the rage at the moment, you can easily channel two trends in one look by pairing a neon shoe with a classic white number. Alternatively, you can style an animal-printed shoe with a basic black version, or go with a classic black and white colour palette. We saw a number of street style stars wearing different styles of shoes in a similar manner. While some opted for strappy heels, others chose mules and ankle-length boots. Bottega Veneta’s woven slides were also a big hit during the fashion month, worn as a mismatched black and white pair. For those who are not shy of a little more experimentation, this trend serves the ideal excuse to take things one step further (pun intended). Go all out by mixing and matching the heels of your shoes—like styling a printed stiletto with a wedged shoe—but make sure that you pick versions featuring similar prints. We even saw a blue knee-length lace-up boot teamed with a grey heel in one look, with the gingham print on both shoes bringing a common element. Another option would be to choose a pair of shoes that already comes with different heel designs. Need some inspiration for the months to come? column1: How sustainable is organic cotton, really?
column2: Fashion It isn’t completely eco-friendly, but organic cotton uses 91 per cent less water than regular cotton and it produces fewer greenhouse gas emissions. Vogue unpacks the confusion around organic cotton and asks environmental experts about how we can all shop more sustainably By now, we all know that cotton can be seriously damaging to the environment. According to the WWF, it takes 2,700 litres of water to produce the cotton needed to make just one T-shirt. However, organic cotton — generally produced without synthetic chemicals, such as fertilisers and pesticides — is a different story altogether. The Soil Association says it uses only 243 litres by comparison. As a result, an increasing number of fashion brands, from Stella McCartney to H&M, are championing the natural fibre. But how sustainable is an organic-cotton T-shirt? It’s a simple question without a straightforward answer. Yes, there is the water consumption to think about, but carbon emissions, transportation methods and packaging along the supply chain must be considered, too. And crucially, what happens to the garment when you’re finished with it? “It’s not perfect — nothing’s perfect,” comments Liesl Truscott, Textile Exchange’s director of Europe and materials strategy, about the production of organic cotton. “And scale is still a challenge.” In fact, less than one per cent of all cotton produced is currently organic, meaning there is huge potential for improvement when it comes to how we make the fibre. Here, Vogue speaks to environmental experts about how sustainable organic cotton really is, and how we can all make our shopping habits a little more eco-friendly. According to a 2017 report by the Textiles Exchange, organic cotton uses 91 per cent less ‘blue’ water (from groundwater and surface-water bodies, such as freshwater lakes and rivers) than conventional cotton. Irrigation in cotton field in Spain © Getty “The majority of organic cotton [is grown on] small-scale farms, which tend to be rainfed rather than irrigated,” explains Truscott, “and because you’re not using synthetic pesticides and fertilisers, you don’t need to use as much water.” Organic cotton doesn’t involve genetically modified crops, which generally require more water, while pesticide-free soil also makes the process more water-efficient. In fact, 95 per cent of the water used to grow organic cotton is green water (rainwater and water stored in the soil). It has been argued that the opposite is true: that because organic cotton tends to produce a lower yield compared to conventional cotton crops, it actually requires more water. “The argument is that organic is less efficient per hectare,” comments Christine Altenbuchner, senior lecturer at Vienna’s University of Natural Resources and Life Science, of the often-cited Cotton Inc report. “However, you have to consider [that] organic farmers grow other crops in their fields.” © Getty Growing organic cotton, rather than conventional cotton, also reduces levels of water pollution by 98 per cent, according to a 2011 report by the Water Footprint, as synthetic chemicals such as pesticides and fertilisers aren’t used. According to the Textile Exchange, organic cotton creates 46 per cent fewer greenhouse gas emissions than conventional cotton simply by not using nitrous dioxide-releasing fertilisers and pesticides, and using fewer mechanised farming practices. By virtue of being fertiliser- and pesticide-free, the soil also acts as a ‘carbon sink’, absorbing CO2 from the atmosphere. Harvested cotton on pile on dirt outdoors, Benin, Africa © Getty Scaling up can be a problem, though. A 2015 report found that when done on a large scale, organic cotton farming can actually produce more greenhouse gases than conventional farming. There are also the emissions created when the raw cotton is spun, woven and dyed in the process of turning it into the garment you’re wearing. While cotton can be recycled — and technically speaking, when untreated, cotton is biodegradable — the technology still needs to be improved. “When you mechanically recycle something, you tend to shorten the fibre lengths, which means the quality is not so good,” explains Truscott. “Cotton can go into what’s called a ‘chemical recycling stream’ and that will break it down into its cellulose; you come [away] with a viscose-type product. But there’s not much of this [happening] yet.” Hand holding Cotton for sale, Gujarat, India © Getty 1 2 3 Sorry, but not all cotton is eco-friendly. column1: Are eco-runners the next big sneaker trend?
column2: © Adidas Fashion Sustainable sneakers are nothing new, but do you know the carbon footprint of your running shoes? And are they the next ‘It’ shoe? Vogue unpacks the challenges of making high-performance trainers that have low environmental impact Remember when trainers were reserved for the gym? It’s a distant memory now given you can wear them everywhere and with everything, be it a tailored suit or a summer dress—but still, there was a time. Today, sneakers have become a currency of their own: minimal Stan Smiths evoke Old Céline elegance; Nike Flyknits show off technical nous; Balenciaga’s Triple S and Nicolas Ghesquière’s Archlight are peak dad/ugly trainer. Then they went sustainable, made eco-conscious from recycled materials with consideration of the environment: there’s the fashion set’s (and Meghan Markle’s) preferred Vejas; Reformation’s latest launch with New Balance; Ecoalf’s #becausethereisnoplanetb designs; Stella McCartney’s Ocean Legends, a partnership with Parley  for the Oceans, which takes ocean plastic and reuses it; and Everlane and Allbirds, which use sugarcane and recycled plastics for their sneakers. And, thankfully, when it comes to casual, everyday trainers, there are many, many more. But what about gym trainers? How eco-friendly are performance running shoes? The reality is, not very. In fact, sneakers have one of the heaviest carbon footprints of anything we wear. A study conducted by MIT found a typical pair of running shoes generates approximately 13.6 kilograms of CO2 emissions. “Unusually high,” comments Randolph Kirchain, one of the co-authors of the research, for a product that does not use electricity or require power-driving components. The bulk of emissions come from manufacturing, which is unsurprising considering the production processes and materials involved. VEJA Condor © VEJA “The typical running shoe is completely made of plastic,” Veja co-founder Sébastien Kopp tells Vogue. “And what is plastic? 99 per cent petroleum.” Petroleum-derived plastics include polyester, thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA). “Our society’s dependence on plastic and oil is an ecological and social disaster,” he adds. Although we know these materials are a calamity, the truth is that they are cheap and practical. Add fibres and you have a flexible but durable upper; pump with tiny air pockets and you have bouncy, foam cushioning; mould correctly and you have structure and stability. Flexibility, strength and durability—all essential for a high-performance shoe. But change is on the horizon. Vivobarefoot Primus Lite Bio II © Vivobarefoo Big brands (such as Adidas and Nike) and niche labels (Vivo Barefoot, for example) are trying to reduce their carbon footprint in different ways, be it through manufacturing processes or material innovations. “I think only by understanding that the current system isn’t sustainable can you really think about designing the future of it,” says Noel Kinder, chief sustainability officer at Nike. The sportswear giant’s Flyknit technology has, it claims, prevented 3.5 million pounds of waste from reaching landfill. “Using recycled polyester made from plastic bottles for core yarns, it is knit to size, which creates 60 per cent less scrap waste than when making a traditional shoe upper,” says Kinder. Earlier this year, Adidas launched Futurecraft.Loop—“a transformative approach to designing performance shoes that are made to be remade from the outset, by using one material type and no glue,” says Amanda Verbeck, the brand’s manager of footwear development. “Plastic is usually not recycled, nor are plastic products ‘made to be remade’. That is the breakthrough of Futurecraft.Loop,” she explains. VEJA Condor © VEJA VEJA Condor © VEJA Veja entered the race with the Condor last month, which it dubs “the world’s first post-petroleum running shoe”. That label might suggest to some that it is plastic-free, but even Veja, with its sustainability credentials, didn’t quite get there. “We half succeeded,” says Kopp, “because we created a 53 per cent bio-based running shoe. But this is OK for the first one!” The French-Brazilian brand is used to criticism, he adds. “It was the same when we launched Veja in 2005. Everybody was saying, ‘Fair trade and organic trainers? What for? Who cares?’ It is the same today, our performance runner is not perfect, but we are on the road.” That is a sentiment shared by minimalist (essentially barefoot) running shoe company Vivobarefoot. “Our ultimate goal is complete circularity,” says design director Asher Clark, talking about the Primus Lite II Bio, the brand’s most innovative shoe to date, made from over 30 per cent natural, plant-based materials including corn, natural rubber and algae foam. “It is not perfect, it still contains significant non-plant-based products, but it’s a step in the right direction.” “Sustainable materials, circularity and style will go hand-in-hand,” says Kinder, hinting at exciting launches Nike has to coincide with the 2020 Olympics. “In May, we published Circularity: Guiding the Future of Design as a call to action for the fashion industry — and ourselves.” Considering that 24.3 billion pairs of shoes were produced worldwide in 2014 alone, according to The Good Shopping Guide, it is clear that immediate action is essential, not optional. Adidas Futurecraft Loop © Adidas Eric Liedtke unveiling the Adidas Futurecraft Loop in New York © Adidas Adidas Futurecraft Loop © Adidas “Each company seems to be tackling one of the problems, but not the whole caboodle,” says Sophie Hellyer, a professional surfer who turned activist after witnessing firsthand the tangible effects of plastic pollution. Hellyer was among the creatives invited to New York to trial the first Adidas Futurecraft.Loop (a decision not taken lightly: Hellyer limits her travel as much as possible and otherwise offsets her air miles). “It kind of depressed me going to the launch,” says the straight-talking Brit. “They're solving the problem with the problem. ‘We have too many plastic shoes, what should we do? Make more plastic shoes!’ That just doesn't seem logical. If they had started the project creating a closed loop and had used materials that weren't plastic, I'd be really impressed.” “But,” she adds, “the fact that these big companies give a shit and are investing money in these innovative ideas is something to be hopeful about. I will still wear and support them because I know they are working on it. If we just carry on business as usual, then we're going to run out of things to make shoes with anyway.” Vogue’s fashion encyclopaedia: The 180-year history of trainers 6 sustainable Indian active wear labels you need to know about Are direct-to-consumer brands the future for sustainable fashion? column1: Lust list: 9 statement watches that will help you round off any outfit
column2: Fashion Whether you’re dressing up for a casual outing or a formal dinner, a statement watch is the perfect add-on for every type of look While chunky dials or sparkling straps may be the first things to come to mind when you think about statement watches, not all timepieces need bling. The classic leather strap + round dial combination, as seen in ‘Pilot’s Watch Chronograph Spitfire’ watch by IWC Schaffhausen or Audemars Piguet’s ‘CODE 11.59 Selfwinding’ watch, is made for your workwear wardrobe. Want to add a pop of colour to your brunch look? Turn to Chopard’s diamond-encrusted bright blue piece or Richard Mille’s blazing orange number, which features an eye-catching rectangle dial. For parties and festive gatherings, shiny metals and diamonds are must-haves. Rolex’s ‘Oyster Perpetual Cosmograph Daytona’ watch comes in a classic black and gold colour scheme to complement any outfit, and Cartier’s ‘Panthere de Cartier Manchette’ qualifies as jewellery that will never go unnoticed. Pair them with casual denim-on-denim looks or formal dresses, these pieces will serve as the ideal finishing touches to almost any sartorial combination you come up with. column1: Prabal Gurung and Aurora James Discuss the Humanity of Fashion
column2: Fashion Designers Prabal Gurung and Aurora James talk to Vogue’s Virginia Smith about bringing a positive change through clothes Fashion might seem like nothing but glamour—all runway shows, stiletto heels, and fabulous gowns. But as designers Prabal Gurung and Aurora James told Vogue’s Virginia Smith at the Forces of Fashion conference, making clothes can also be a force for good. Both designers—Gurung at his eponymous label and James at Brother Vellies—partner with artisans around the world, allowing them to build strong relationships with the people who make their garments and accessories. For James, her business grew out of the time she spent with South African artisans who make traditional footwear. Gurung, meanwhile, has worked with cashmere producers in his native Nepal to ensure his products are made in sustainable ways and in factories that employ fair working practices. It is a testament to both designers’ skill that working responsibly and ethically has done nothing but bolster their creative output. Here, some highlights from their insightful discussion that covered everything from how fashion can support workers’ rights to why consumers should pay a premium for consciously made goods. James started her business working with artisans in South Africa and has since expanded her production to nearly a dozen countries. “A lot of it, in the beginning, was on the ground, and I still do that now and then. We have a lot of partner organizations that will refer people to us; the United Nations, for example, are the ones that brought us into Ethiopia. With our workshop in Mexico, it was actually one of our assistants who was born and raised in Mexico who found both of our workshops for making the cowboy boots and the huaraches. So it can really be all sorts of different ways, but it’s about vetting them and making sure they are working in ways that make sense for us.” After admitting that he came to the United States to meet Oprah—with a joking laugh—Gurung talked about how, after seeing his collection on the cover of a magazine in 2011, he made the choice to do more than just make clothes. With his siblings, he established the Shikshya Foundation in Nepal that provides education to underprivileged children and will soon start educating incarcerated women. “In eight years we’ve been able to impact over 50,000 lives,” Gurung told the audience. “The reason I wanted to do it was that fashion is great, and that’s my first love, and I love doing all of that. But it can’t just be about that; it has to be more than that. The Instagram followers and the platforms that we all have, it can’t just be for my selfies, you know? It would have to be for something else. I want to give back.” After toying with the idea of opening her own factories in the early stages of her business, James had a realization: “The best person to run a workshop in this community is someone that’s from this community and knows this community from top to bottom. It was really about finding those groups of people and finding people who care deeply, deeply about what they’re doing and then just saying, ‘What workload can you handle?’” Today she produces Brother Vellies in nine countries—South Africa, Kenya, Morocco, Ethiopia, Burkina Faso, Mali, Bali, Italy, and Mexico. She checks in on the factories daily on What’s App and Line. What’s more, she is finely aware of the human cost of making her products, and she works to ensure that her suppliers are not stretched beyond their limits. “If you can only make 35 bags—guess what?—we’re only making 35 bags, because if we push it beyond that, that’s when things start getting compromised. Setting those boundaries as a designer also has a lot to do with luxury.” After sharing statistics about black female entrepreneurs, including that only .5% of companies have a female African American CEO and that only 37 black women have raised more than $1,00,000 from venture capitalists, James noted that those opportunities only grow smaller when you are as vocal about causes as she is. “When you speak out about things, people don’t like that either,” she began. “There’s a lot of money that has come off the table for me by advocating for Planned Parenthood. It’s really amazing to get an award at the Congressional Black Caucus from Planned Parenthood, but at the same time, you know you might have just lost your retailers in Texas.” “That is so true,” Gurung added. “And it’s not always direct and obvious. A lot of times, it hits you in weird ways down the road,” James continued. “I think the biggest way to change is a seat at the decision-making table,” Gurung said of how the backlash could be prevented in the future. “It has to be 50% or more minorities. There’s no doubt about it.” “Vintage is always my default,” James told an audience member who asked about the high price of sustainably made fashion. “I would also say we need to reframe and think differently about how we assemble our wardrobes and talk about personal style. Because I only have a limited amount of closet space, I want to make sure if I bring something into my life, it’s going to stay in my life for an incredibly long time, and it’s going to be woven into the intuitive style DNA that I already have. When I think about things, I think about it literally as a cost for wear.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.com. Are our collective efforts towards sustainable fashion enough? column1: Hailey Bieber’s 'Wifey' necklace is a special gift from Justin
column2: © Photo: Getty Images Fashion They’ve taken their couple’s style to the next level. Few couples have a more distinctive sense of style than Hailey and Justin Bieber. While the model sports the latest trends and emerging labels, her husband gives off a sleazy-chic vibe, with loads of sportswear, pieces from his own skater label Drew House, and the occasional pair of Crocs. But now they are taking their mutual love of fashion to a whole new level: designing custom accessories for each other. This weekend, Justin took to Instagram to share a special necklace he created for his wife. “I made her necklace,” he wrote, sharing an image of Hailey in a DIY’d two-tone necklace, finished with yellow and brown beads. (Underneath it, she also proudly wore a “Wifey” necklace—it’s unclear if he made that one, too.) Friends and fans went wild for the design in the comments section, with one user dubbing him, “Justin the Jeweler.” His piece did seamlessly blend in with her other refined jewelry, including the gold Jennifer Fisher hoops that she never takes off. Now the only question is whether the model will return the favor and take a stab at creating a piece of jewelry for her husband?
