column1: Dulquer Salmaan on growing up a star kid and working in Bollywood
column2: © Photographed by Nuno Oliveira. Styled by Priyanka Kapadia Fashion Preternaturally talented, the suave Dulquer Salmaan is Malayalam cinema’s young scion and Bollywood’s latest crush It’s late afternoon on a Sunday and we are at Dulquer Salmaan’s unassuming villa in an upmarket Kochi suburb. I am seated facing the actor on one of two sofas in a mini majlis-like setting inside an antechamber by the entrance, strategically placed so visitors need not enter the heart of the building. Today, Dulquer the fashionable is off-duty. Dressed in an olive-green T-shirt, jeans and a pair of spectacles, the 33-year-old actor looks like a guy you would swap notes with if you missed a lecture. His signature mop, the crown that has been the inspiration for armies of lookalikes, is long and spirited, often falling over his face. Dulquer seems a lot like the chill characters he’s portrayed in his films, though obviously beneath the easygoing front this is an ambitious, hardworking, top-rung actor. “In our business, it’s easy to have a fabulous Friday but you’re only as good as the last Friday. Knowing that drives you.” Growing up as the son of Mammootty, superstar of the Malayalam film world, Dulquer had a vantage point on fame and cinema that few do. His parents chose to raise him and his sister in Chennai, where he studied at Sishya School, largely with kids from business families. “I grew up thinking things could go wrong any moment,” he says. “My mom would always say this is like a lottery, we don’t know how long it will last. Dad’s career could go up or down, and we’ve had phases where he had a year of bad films. So, I’ve never felt wealthy.” He says this very earnestly, like he’s talking about a middle-class dad working at a chaebol. Since his friends were studying business, Dulquer did, too. When he returned to Chennai from Purdue University, he was only sure about one thing: he didn’t want to act. Entrepreneur Ashika Korula, who runs an educational-recreational events company in Kerala, an old friend of Dulquer, recalls that he often talked about directing but was dead against acting. “His father was his benchmark,” she says. “He was always in awe of him, so acting was that one thing he felt he couldn’t do.” Dulquer says he selects work very carefully, focusing on the story and his position in the context of the plot. That sometimes means accepting scripts headlined by co-stars, as was the case in the Telugu film Mahanati (2018) and last month’s The Zoya Factor. “The movie is the hero… The moment I think of myself as bigger than the film, I will lose direction.” But what’s it like to work outside the comfort of the Malayalam industry? “With Hindi, the scale, obviously,” he says. “Because it’s much bigger. But it’s also funny because beyond the main people (the director, co-star, producer), the rest of the unit usually has no idea who I am. Like they don’t think I am an actor of any consequence, so I’m often getting bumped around. I’m like, ‘Bhai, don’t whack me, I’m the hero.’ It’s humbling.” He’s had other learnings, too. “The entire technical crew on my Hindi film was women, which was great. I hope we get to see a much larger representation of women in the Malayalam industry, too,” he says. Perhaps Dulquer could make such changes himself soon, because he is also a producer now. Dulquer married early; at age 25, he wed architecture graduate Amaal Sufiya right around the time he made his film debut. The couple has a two-year-old daughter, Maryam, the real star of his Instagram feed. On other days, his 3.7 million followers lap up his styled shoots and promotions. Perhaps the only Malayali actor to have been on GQ’s Best Dressed List, Dulquer is unmissable on the red carpet. I remind him he once wore a burgundy tuxedo jacket, the most fashionable piece I’ve seen on a Malayali star. He recalls the ensemble worn to receive his 2013 Outstanding Debut award. “It was a combination of Tom Ford and Armani. I must have spent a third of the money I got for the film on that outfit. But it’s important. People are there to see you, and you have to respect them enough to make the effort,” he says. column1: All the pictures that will take you inside Karisma Kapoor’s shoe wardrobe
column2: © Instagram.com/therealkarismakapoor/ Fashion Featuring travel-friendly white sneakers, red carpet-ready strappy shoes and statement juttis for festive season, Karisma Kapoor’s shoe collection is well-stocked for every occasion As a card-carrying member of the minimalist club, Karisma Kapoor believes in editing her jewellery down to one piece before stepping out. It isn’t hard to know what’s gaining dominance in her accessories wardrobe instead—whether she’s on holiday with her girl posse or striding down the red carpet, the star has a discerning eye for statement footwear. Now living her best life in her 40s, you’ll find Kapoor tempering the sweet nostalgia of timeless classics with contemporary flavour in her shoe collection. Those looking for pointers on how to work sneakers for every event on the calendar needn’t look further than Kapoor for inspiration. The sporty vibe has taken hold of the Bollywood star, who can be found pairing her go-to white kicks with everything from shirtdresses to silk kurta sets. For long haul flights, she swears by the classic troika of quirky slogan tees, denims and white sneakers. A girls’ night out, meanwhile, calls for animal printed midi dresses and pristine white sneakers. Flip over to the ethnic side of her wardrobe, and you’ll find her cheekily styling this athleisure staple with brocades and lush silks alike. The scorching heat of the summer called for a deftly draped Antar-Agni ensemble, with a sporty pair adding dimension to the monochrome look. At a recent event in Chennai, she opted for a white button-down and palazzo pants from Payal Khandwala, and looked to sneakers to add the perfect finishing touch. Make no mistake though, sneakers aren’t the only silhouette to have found favour in her ethnic closet. Traditional juttis remain one of her favourite go-tos for the many festive outings on her social calendar. For the recently concluded festivities of Ganesh Chaturthi, she opted for a white kurta set featuring multi-coloured threadwork from Surily G. Coordinated juttis from Fizzy Goblet placed the seal on the delicate romanticism of the outfit. Durga Puja also had her reaching out for eye-catching metallic juttis, worn with a regal Benarasi anarkali set by Ekaya. While comfort takes precedence in her on-the-go wardrobe, the red carpet is her ode to all things feminine. Under the marquee lights, you’ll find her parading exquisite designs from leading couturiers around the globe, usually with a pair of ankle strap heels playing peekaboo under the floaty hems. The intricately beaded magenta Zara Umrigar gown was teamed with classic nude heels, while the scene-stealing Tony Ward Couture number was aptly worn with embellished stilettos. column1: Mahesh Babu on learning from failure, growing up with a star father, and the secret to a happy marriage
column2: © Photographed by Nuno Oliveira. Styled by Anaita Shroff Adajania Fashion Balancing celebrity with humility and professional with the personal, Mahesh Babu is the reigning star of Telugu cinema whose appeal transcends generations In the movie-mad land of the Telugus, where stars are demigods and fandom a religion, Mahesh Babu is undoubtedly the chosen one from his generation. His fame is already the stuff of legend, and his success and failure at the box office makes and breaks the Telugu industry as a whole. It’s surprising then to see the superstar stroll in sans entourage at the Vogue shoot. A noiseless professional, he comes armed with his boy-next-door charm and works with the crew, posing with ease and being a team player from start to end. Stardom aside, at home he is simply Mahesh—the son of Krishna, husband to Namrata and father of Gautham and Sitara. “I haven’t seen a more disciplined and dedicated person. He doesn’t settle for less. And he can balance work-life very well,” says his actor-wife, who also doubles up as his manager. But unlike the cocksure, infallible characters he plays, the Mahesh at work swings between glorious success and bitter failure. As he talks about his journey so far, the 44-year-old (who doesn’t look a day over 25) confesses, “Failure is a hidden treasure. I learn from them. I analyse it. But the initial pain is hard. Namrata helps me through that.” Ask Mahesh about his illustrious trajectory, and he’d have to turn back the clock to how it all began—at the age of four, almost by default, thanks to his father Krishna, a star from an earlier era in the Telugu film industry. Mahesh recalls how his family summered regularly in Ooty, where his father would film songs for the six or seven movies he starred in each year. On one of these visits, his father asked him to play a role in Needa (1979). The four-year-old jumped at the opportunity and the film went on to become a hit. Mahesh proved to be a natural, and soon all holidays came with a dose of histrionics. “Every summer I would do a film in those two months. My only training was the way my father made those films with me when I was a child star. It couldn’t have been done more beautifully.” In 1999, Mahesh transitioned from child star to his debut as the romantic lead in Raja Kumarudu, which won him the State Nandi Award for Best Male Debut and the affection of an audience that cut across generations and bestowed upon him the title “Prince of Tollywood.” But what followed was not so easy: “It was a record-setting launch, but my next few films failed.” Until he nabbed the supernatural drama Murari in 2001: “It was a family film with a plot that was completely new. That was the first time that people thought I could act. Then failure again until Okkadu (2003), which, to be honest, is what made me a star.” What’s unique is even after a 20-year-long career, his public image remains clean and free of scandal. He’s seen as the “good Telugu boy” grounded in family life rather than being caught up in the trappings of fame. On Instagram, fans see a doting dad to his teenage son and seven-year-old daughter, and a loving husband to his wife. Their chemistry is unmissable on set, where Namrata discusses his look with the stylists and he follows her lead. “Namrata and I have been married for 14 years. We understand each other well. And we let each other be. That’s the most important secret to a successful marriage. Space. And of course, children—they ground you. I have to credit my dad for teaching me that. When he came home to us, he wasn’t a star.” Read the complete interview in Vogue India’s October 2019 issue that hits stands on October 7, 2019. column1: Satoshi Kondo talks Vogue through his joyful debut for Issey Miyake SS20
column2: © Getty Fashion “The joy that can be found in this ritual of getting dressed every day, of finding an outfit that can make you happy for the whole day — that’s what inspires me.” Issey Miyake’s new head designer, Satoshi Kondo, on creating clothes for every body and the optimism of the Japanese brand Even the Japanese organization expert Marie Kondo would struggle to find a look that didn’t spark joy in the debut collection presented by Satoshi Kondo (no relation) for Issey Miyake during Paris Fashion Week SS20. Featuring coats made from parachute material that billowed with air resistance as models glided around the showspace (Le Centquatre; a multipurpose cultural centre in the 19th arrondissement) on electric skateboards; lampshade like sculptures that descended from the ceiling and morphed into dresses; and bias-cut silk jersey creations that oscillated around dancers’ bodies – it was as though Miyake’s words, “designing is an act of discovery”, were woven into their very fabric. Over the course of the past half a century, Miyake has designed clothes that honour what is known in Japanese as ma, or the space between two entities (in Miyake’s case the body and garment). The result: timeless designs that suit any shape, as Miyake says “making clothes that everyone can wear means making clothes for people who live with us, our contemporaries – ordinary people.” Kondo has been part of Miyake's story now for 13 years, having worked as a designer for the brand’s Pleats Please and Homme Plissé lines. In his first sit down interview since assuming the role of head designer at Issey Miyake (taking over from Yoshiyuki Miyamae, who is working on a new, soon-to-be-announced project with the brand) the 35-year-old discusses his ideas behind the collection and Miyake’s fine philosophy of melding tradition and innovation. Satoshi Kondo: “I was born in Kyoto [Japan], and I had a pretty normal Japanese upbringing. From a young age, I was constantly drawing. My mother is a qualified sewing teacher — she always made her own clothes, so that definitely had an influence on me. “Even before I joined Issey Miyake in 2007, from my days as a student at Ueda College of Fashion in Osaka, I was moved by Mr Miyake’s method of streamlining garment production through the A-POC system [a production process using long tubes of knitted cloth, which can be cut without any wastage] and its reduction of waste fabric. “While I love fashion and the industry as a whole, what drew me to design is this very Japanese idea of clothing the body. Every morning, like most people, I wake up, take a shower and stand in front of my wardrobe and think: ‘Well, what shall I wear today?’ The joy that can be found in this ritual of getting dressed every day, of finding an outfit that can make you happy for the whole day — that’s what inspires me. I want to create collections that emulate that joy.” SK: “The traditional runway format is fine, but I wanted the presentation to reflect the theme of the collection; to show this image of people getting together, getting dressed and being really joyful. In order to express that idea, I worked with our show director [and choreographer] Daniel Ezralow to find an unconventional approach to the fashion show. I started with sketching the designs and everything grew from that.” SK: “With Issey Miyake, there is always an idea of progression by adding pieces of clothing. So we start with the basics and these colours should be subtle, muted even. Then we add layers, primary colours, which graduate into a wider variety of more vibrant hues. There’s not a conscious decision about what colours to use or eliminate, nor is it a response to anything specific happening in the world right now. The process is organic — I like to think of the collection as a bud blossoming into a flower.” SK on ‘draw and connect’: “This is my first womenswear collection for Issey Miyake, so I had this idea of returning to the basics and fundamentals, and a notion of being naked in a literal and abstract sense. The first seven looks are essentially blank canvases intended to represent the diversity of skin tones. I chose a jersey fabric that stretches, but also drapes over the contours of the body really beautifully. “From here, we move into a series of printed garments. The motif was designed by our in-house team and depicts two people embracing — a primitive gesture of warmth. There is another print consisting of abstract depictions of internal organs, with the idea of communicating our inner energies and, again, warmth.” SK on ‘overlap and dye’: “Throughout the collection, I have combined tradition and innovation. For example, we used a method of embroidery known as sashiko — this literally means ‘little stabs’ and dates back to the Edo period [1615 to 1868] — on a trouser and skirt suit in this section. It’s a running stitch that was originally used to reinforce worn-out clothing but here, if you look closely, you can see that it spells out ‘Issey Miyake’ in tiny letters. “The pattern on the dress and coat, meanwhile, is achieved using a resist-dyeing technique called itajime. First, we pleat the fabric by hand to get the nice, crisp folds, and then clamp it between two boards before submerging it in dye. This way, the dye only touches the folds and the colour graduates to white at the centre of each pleat.” SK on ‘swing and extend’: “I wanted all of these pieces to feel light and airy. The coats catch the air like parachutes, so the models rode electric skateboards in the show to demonstrate this. All of the fringing in these garments has been made using the A-POC system. The most time-consuming part of this process is creating different computer programmes for each design. It’s still probably the most efficient and sustainable way to create clothes because you don’t need a sewing machine and it minimises waste.” SK on ‘move and bounce’: “This series really speaks for itself and the joy is found in the movement of the clothes. We gave the dresses their bounce with a technique used in the Pleats Please line. We used straight machine-pleating working horizontally across the fabric; after that, we hand-pleated the fabric in concentric circles. Combined, these [two types of] pleats give the fabric the effect of a spring. Again, subconsciously, it brings together the ideas of tradition and innovation.” SK: “I oversee the collection as a whole, but we work as a team with a specialist in every field, from print to knitting. Mr Miyake is still heavily involved in the whole process and I regularly show him the collection at different stages of production. He will give his critique, but he maintains that I should be myself and express what I want to express. If you are brave and confident with your designs, he says, then people will feel confident wearing them — our clothes should always make people feel confident and proud. “One of the first pieces in the collection I designed is an overcoat with a blue print — the one with the couple embracing [on it] — and when you open it up, you can see it is made from a square piece of cloth draped over the body. Mr Miyake always starts his designs with a square piece of cloth, which uses clean, minimal cutting and sewing — that concept has never changed. We always try to incorporate traditional techniques into our designs and combine this with Mr Miyake’s attitude of always moving forward and not turning back. Always striving to create something better, something more advanced.” Satoshi Kondo © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Getty © Getty © Getty All the highlights from Paris Fashion Week spring/summer 2020 “I want the audience to see true fantasy, not always reality”: Thom Browne on his SS20 women’s collection Japanese clothing giant Uniqlo will be launching in India this October What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Alia Bhatt's best street style looks
column2: © Viral Bhayani Fashion From see-through sneakers to head-to-toe neon looks, Alia Bhatt’s off-duty wardrobe is a study in statement-making staples Between hectic shoot schedules and social commitments, it is a foregone conclusion that Alia Bhatt has many demands on her time. The peppy 26-year-old responds to the vagaries of her daily schedule with a thoughtfully curated wardrobe of comfort-first staples that deliver an impact. From on-trend prints to interesting cut-out details and innovative silhouettes, it is easy to get behind her memo for non-boring wardrobe staples when off the clock. Bhatt’s formula for delivering a winning look every single time is grounded in her love for unexpected colours. The next time you’re at the airport, just cast an eye for standout hues and you’ll likely locate the young star. After a month-long shoot in Benares, she returned to the city in a blazer, T-shirt and cropped trousers combination by Topshop, entirely doused in the on-trend shade of neon green. Conventional tracksuits have also been given the 2019 update with her millennial purple pick from adidas Originals. The star punctuated the solid colour with a statement mustard handbag by Anya Hindmarch and white-framed sunnies. On days when she’s looking to play with colours, tie-dye comes to her rescue. When she stepped out for a meeting in Mumbai, the Coachella-favourite print added a pop of colour to the rain-drenched cityscape, rounded off with pair of ivory trousers and pink slides. The fuss-free memo carried forward to movie night as well, and for the screening of Arjun Kapoor’s India’s Most Wanted, she opted for summery stripes with an ankle-grazing shirtdress by Silvia Tcherassi. The buoyant pink and red stripes were echoed by her choice of footwear—strappy heels in yellow and white stripes. While she has a discerning eye for colours, Bhatt isn’t one to say no to the power of pristine white either. For another meeting in the city, she opted for head-to-toe white outfit comprising a sweatshirt, matching trousers and chunky sneakers. While hopping on a flight recently, she was spotted in a roomy midi dress from Lovebirds and statement-making clear sneakers. Flip over to the ethnic side of her wardrobe, and you’ll spot her affinity for shararas. Not one to relegate this festive staple for the red carpet and weddings, her lexicon of ethnic casuals plays host to relaxed co-ord sets, light cottons and romantic colours. Among the many looks you’ll want to bookmark is the lightweight blue floral sharara set, accentuated with light chikankari work on the bodice. On those days when you’re running late, the star advises having a floral cotton kurta and metallic juttis at the ready as a fail-safe backup. column1: Costume designer Maja Meschede on dressing Helen Mirren as Catherine the Great
column2:
© Hal Shinnie/HBO Fashion As Helen Mirren returns to regality as Catherine II in the latest royal drama to rival The Crown, Vogue speaks to costume designer Maja Meschede about creating hand-embellished 33lb gowns and putting male actors in corsets Much like its storyline, the costumes of HBO and Sky’s new four-part mini-series Catherine the Great are nothing short of epic. More than 60 were created especially for Dame Helen Mirren in her titular role, who is no stranger to royal characters after winning an Oscar, Emmy and Tony for her portrayals of Elizabeth I and II. Helen Mirren © Hal Shinnie/HBO Some dresses weighed up to 33lb each and consisted of an under-cage, two petticoats, two corsets and an over-robe. Heavily embroidered almost entirely by hand in gold and silver thread, each look was crafted from luxurious brocades and velvets sourced from Rome, Venice and Milan. And behind their majesty is costume designer Maja Meschede, who has also worked on Maleficent and The Duchess.
The story of Catherine the Great — formerly known as Catherine II — is one of scandal, intrigue and power. As Russia’s longest-ruling female leader from 1762 to 1796, she came to power after overthrowing her husband, Peter III. She’s credited with revitalising the country and turning it into one of the great powers of Europe — the period under her rule is known as the ‘Golden Age of Russia’. “There was a lot written in history that she was a sex addict and she had so many lovers, but she actually didn’t,” Meschede tells Vogue. “We wanted to portray her as a strong woman; a very intelligent woman.” Jason Clarke © Hal Shine/HBO When creating the costumes, historical accuracy was of supreme importance for Meschede, who read a number of biographies on Catherine II, Peter III, and his predecessor and aunt, Elizabeth I. Though, that’s not to say a few modern tricks weren’t employed for ease. “We tried to make everything as light as possible,” says Meschede, “but all these fashions were very heavy. Helen never complained. She said, ‘This helps me to walk straight and I feel like I’m Catherine.’ We had a few tricks [to make things a little easier] — the bottom corset had a little zip so Helen could actually do it herself. We used safety pins, double-sided tape and zips, too.” The series spans Catherine’s later life and her blossoming romance with military leader Grigory Potemkin, played by Jason Clarke (Pet Sematary, Everest). At the start, Meschede relied on a softer colour palette, augmented with pearls and gold to show Catherine’s more feminine side. As the story moves on, the empress’s clothing becomes darker to reflect her deteriorating mental health. “We worked a lot with the colour to portray that while she was successful as an empress, there was also a lot of sadness [in her life],” explains Meschede. Helen Mirren © Robert Vigalsky/HBO Meschede had her job cut out for her. Beyond dressing Mirren and Clarke, there were the other principal actors to think about: lady-in-waiting Countess Bruce played by Gina McKee (Bodyguard, Notting Hill) plus an array of armies (Catherine’s imperial guard, the Prussians, the Ottomans, Cossacks and Crimean Tatars, to name a few). While principal actors all had bespoke costumes created, Meschede and her team borrowed some costumes from Italy for the crowds of extras. Meschede’s biggest highlight, though? The Metamorphoses ball in the first episode, a true-to-life historical event started by Peter III’s aunt and predecessor, Elizabeth I, where guests were expected to dress as the opposite sex. Meschede made a sumptuous gentleman’s outfit for Mirren, and dozens of gowns and corsets for the male actors. “Historically, [the courtiers] took it really seriously,” she says. “Men didn’t just borrow their wife’s clothes, which would have been very ill-fitting. They had them made especially [for the ball] and wore wigs and makeup. The two days we were filming, we had so much fun. For men, it’s very interesting to experience wearing a corset. They all had the same reaction: ‘Poor women, how could they wear these their whole lives?’” For both Meschede and Mirren, it was important to represent a historic figure like Catherine as complex and human. “Catherine the Great was one of the most powerful women ever,” concludes Meschede. “She was leading one of the most successful armies. But at the same time, [she was] a very sensitive woman. We wanted to bring that soft side across.” © Hal Shinnie/HBO © Hal Shinnie/HBO © Hal Shinnie/HBO © Hal Shinnie/HBO © Hal Shinnie/HBO © Robert Vigalsky/HBO © Robert Vigalsky/HBO © Hal Shinnie/HBO © Hal Shinnie/HBO The Crown season 3 on Netflix: Get to know the 9 new faces starring in the new season This book traces the evolution of Bollywood costumes with a 100 illustrations The British royal family actually get The Crown spoilers before each season is aired Beauty Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Look of the week: Angelina Jolie is bringing glamour back with this fringed gown
column2: Fashion While attending a screening in Japan, Angelina Jolie channeled old world glamour in a a silver fringed Ralph & Russo couture gown. Scroll down to find out how she aced the look. Angelina Jolie is ready to cut loose. When it comes to style, the Maleficent: Mistress of Evil star can do gothic drama like no one else—does anyone look better in a black dress?—but lately she’s gravitating toward more playful pieces. In a silver fringed Ralph & Russo couture gown, Jolie thrilled crowds at Tokyo’s Roppongi Hills arena by posing for photos and signing autographs while looking like an old-school movie star. The glamorous look, which also nodded to the flapper era thanks to its movement and beaded construction, was an unexpected choice for Jolie. Never one to go for unnecessary embellishment, she prefers to keep things simple even when she’s in the spotlight. The 180-shift towards a bold metallic gown brimming with texture added another layer to her ever-evolving style and made for a dazzling reveal when she emerged on the arena's stage. column1: Is streetwear finally having its moment in Indian fashion?
column2: © Instagram.com/jaywalking.in Fashion With a streetwear-only showcase at Lakmé Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019, homegrown labels and an audience that’s listening, it’s safe to say that streetwear is having a triumphant rise in India The black, one-size-kinda-fits-all Zara leggings were so ridiculously popular in 2014 that you couldn’t walk a mile without the glint of its shiny zips hitting you in the eye. In Delhi, they were seen everywhere—in metro compartments, across university campuses and in corporate offices. On-trend at the time, this pair of sleek, stretchy cigarette pants with a highwaisted band and close to no functionality demonstrated the all-too-common desire to blend in, to look like each other, and consequently, look like we belong. And yet, the average consumer was beginning to see that something was brewing, that the traditional ideas of dressing up were being disrupted. The 'ugly sneaker' made desirable by Balenciaga or Vetements' now-iconic DHL sweatshirt were early indicators that fashion was unbuttoning its collar and rolling up its sleeves. The future was street. When it comes to couture and craftsmanship, Indian designers are in a league of their own. Tapping into the zeitgeist? Not so much. Today, however, there's a brewing subculture of woke millennials that are writing or recognising local rap artists, buying local and aware of what they put on and step out. Addressing their needs is the rising roster of homegrown streetwear which, luckily, is a concept that goes far beyond low-waisted baggy jeans, hoodies and slogan T-shirts to accommodate the diversity of Indian identity. More importantly? It allows consumers the opportunity to bravely reinvent their own sensibilities, find what they like, and think about their choices without worrying about judgement or fear of standing out. In fact, it was from this desire that Jaywalking, Mumbai-based Jay Ajay Ajalal’s streetwear label, was born. “I was tired with the whole fashion scene, with everyone looking exactly the same after Zara and other high street labels came to India. Everyone’s Instagram [feeds] looked the same. I wanted to make something that I liked and, for once, not do something to please a particular audience.” And yet, audiences loved it. They cheered for the first-time Lakmé Fashion Week designer who, along with three other fresh, young brands—Six5Six Street, BISKIT and Gundi Studios—sent irreverent styles down the runway this August. They broke out in mini-dance while still at their seats, as these four labels broke fashion's fourth wall and spoke directly to every audience member present. This show itself was a landmark—this was the first time that the itinerary included a streetwear-only show that, given its resounding success, looks set to become a regular feature at fashion weeks in India. Vogue spoke to the founders of these labels to understand what makes streetwear in India so delicious in 2019. “The cool thing about streetwear is that it can be anything,” says co-founder of BISKIT, Harsha Biswajit. The artist from Chennai—who started the unisex label as one part of a larger multi-disciplinary studio exploring the boundaries between fashion, art, photography and design with his sister, Shruti Biswajit—explains that the juxtaposition of two distinct aesthetics, design choices or ideas is simply a new iteration of street. In fact, this style of clothing traces its origins to the ’1990s surf-and-skate culture of California, and slowly grew to accommodate aspects of Japanese street fashion, elements of hip-hop, punk and sportswear. Today, the fluidity of this style allows designers like Shruti and Harsha Biswajit to work in influences of their diasporic identity—they were born in India and studied in Brooklyn—into the distinct BBISKIT-style of clothing. “Having grown up with stories of NASA, we questioned why we had limited knowledge of India’s space program and wanted to use LFW as an opportunity to explore this story,” Harsha shares. As a result, their first collection takes inspiration from India’s recent propulsion into the frontier of the space race as a starting point to explore the concept of space. It uses various elements from India’s space history to build a visual narrative spanning across a series of classic silhouettes and multi-functional bags combining hidden and functional elements with concept-based based prints. Their show at Lakmé Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019 consequently opened with six models wearing the BISKIT Limited Edition ‘RS’ Spacesuit, which is inspired by the one that astronaut Rakesh Sharma (the first Indian to go into space) wore on his 1984 mission. For Delhi-based siblings Avni and Ambar Aneja, who are the co-founders of Six5Six Sport and Six5Six Street, “streetwear is art and streetwear is protest.” Through their immensely wearable collections—including sheer-sleeved bomber jackets, neon green shrugs, and multi-utility and paperbag pants—they use textual references and millennial slang to speak about the things they feel are relevant. And if you look at their entire body of work (which has been created in the short span of one year), the conversation has escalated in meaningful, nuanced ways. “Our first drop was called ‘The Global Traveller’ and dealt with everything happening around the world with respect to the refugee crisis. Our second drop, ‘Humanity in the Digital Age’, focused on our dependance on screens and fascination with technology.” The collection they presented at Lakmé Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019, ‘WE2.0’ felt like an extension of both these themes, exploring the possibility of the rebirth of humanity as a whole, with technology taking over our current world. Jaywalking’s Ajalal, on the other hand, looks at streetwear as an ice-breaker, a facilitator of conversation and exchange of ideas. “If you’re into streetwear, you have friends everywhere. For instance, if I spot someone wearing a really nice pair of sneakers, I will go up to them and talk to them about it,” he says. If you scroll through Jaywalking’s Instagram feed, you’ll only find images of models from the neck down, posing in front of extraordinarily mundane settings and objects, like the plastic garden chair almost all of us have at home. This was a conscious choice, Ajalal claims, since he wanted his products to look like anyone could own them. “I don’t use faces because I want people to imagine themselves in it. Even the models are not really professional models; they are random people, One of them is an accountant, [and] one of them is the guy who cleans my studio, no joke,” he reveals. The epitome of ‘no filter’ on Instagram, his account is an extension of his personality with lots of cuss words and 18+ content. “Maybe it’s something people appreciate,” he muses, “because street has no filter.” The most exciting thing about the emergence of Indian streetwear brands is that audiences can now buy from a label that resonates not just with their aesthetic sensibilities, but also their political ideologies, their philosophical tendencies or even their hobbies and interests. Popular culture after all, Harsha Biswajit says, is a key ingredient of streetwear. So who is BISKIT reaching out? “We are constantly trying to push our own creative boundaries through creative collaboration, experimentation, and forward thinking, and anyone inspired by our message would be our ideal consumer,” he explains. Meanwhile, the Aneja siblings’ brand of conversational, colourful, wearable, aspirational yet affordable clothing is for anyone who can relate to the catchy phrases that underscore the brand’s beliefs and feels at home in Six5Six Street. Going forward, Biswajit notes that Biskit would like to expand the idea of what streetwear can be. “There is a certain understanding or visual language of what streetwear is, which comes from its original roots in Western sub-culture, but like anything else, when it is taken out of context, it suddenly becomes open to interpretation. Since it’s still a relatively emerging market in India, there is an opportunity for us to form our own vision of what that can be,” he says. Meanwhile, the Anejas are taking Six5Six Street international and will be showcasing at SOLE DXB in Dubai later this year to represent one slice of the country’s streetwear identity. “The market is going to explode and be flooded by lots of streetwear brands now that streetwear is no longer underground, which means that audiences won’t have to buy brands from outside of the country. And we’re happy to be part of the first few to ride the wave,” Avni says. column1: Adidas by Stella McCartney debuts a sports mastectomy bra in honor of breast cancer awareness month
column2: Fashion In honor of the start of Breast Cancer Awareness Month, McCartney will release an Adidas by Stella McCartney mastectomy sports bra for post-op women.  Take a look below. In 1998, Stella McCartney lost her mother Linda to breast cancer. Since then, the designer has passionately advocated for education and awareness surrounding the disease. Beginning in 2014, she also started a yearly Breast Cancer Awareness Campaign through her namesake label. Tomorrow, in honor of the start of Breast Cancer Awareness Month, McCartney will release an Adidas by Stella McCartney mastectomy sports bra for post-op women. One of the first of its kind in the market and the very first for Adidas, the bra was designed in partnership with Monica Harrington, a lingerie stylist and consultant who works with teens, post-natal women, transgender women, and women who have had mastectomy surgery. The sports bra shape was designed to avoid the usual scarring areas around the breasts and comes with a front zipper so that the wearer doesn’t need to uncomfortably stretch their arms up to slip it on. The straps can also be adjusted according to swelling size, and there are hidden pockets sewn inside for prostheses. Starring in the campaign for the Adidas by Stella McCartney release is British boxer and breast cancer survivor Michele Aboro. “With this post-mastectomy sports bra, I really want to encourage women to take care of their health through wellness and self-care,” McCartney says. “This bra allows us to support recovering patients through the next phase of their journey and hopefully give them the confidence to get back into training.” She adds, “It also has a cool and modern look that will help motivate the wearer as well as assure them that they are not the odd one out in the gym.” Thanks to brands like Savage x Fenty by Rihanna, whose epic, empowering Spring 2020 show and performance was one of the most talked about this fashion month, ideas about body-positivity and inclusivity are finally at the forefront of the conversation around underwear. Now, McCartney and Adidas are pushing the needle even further in this direction with a bra that is targeted specifically towards survivors who are also athletes. column1: The cost of Meghan Markle's Africa tour wardrobe will surprise you
column2: © Instagram/sussexroyal Fashion The message behind the royal’s wardrobe, and its price tag, read loud and clear. As the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s royal tour to southern Africa wraps up, we’re not at all shy to admit the amount of brain power exerted and hours spent debriefing about the royal pair’s last fortnight. We’ve melted over the sweetest of memorable moments—this particular tour providing many thanks to baby Archie’s first public appearance since his first photocall at just days old—and, naturally, we closely monitored each and every one of Meghan Markle’s fashion choices. Scanning through the outfits the duchess has stepped out in since the commencement of the recent tour, her royal wardrobe decisions have spoken volumes about her royal tour intentions. The duchess's sartorial style paired with her first moments of African soil—which saw Markle side-stepping the traditional red carpet welcome that comes as custom with each royal tour—communicating that she indeed meant business when it came to the tour. According to a report by Vanity Fair, Markle’s low-key and modest approach to royal tour dressing this time around could not be more different to the tact she took when preparing her looks for the 2018 royal tour of Australia, New Zealand, Tonga and Fiji. As stated by the publication, Markle spent just over £4,000 (approximately AU$7,314) for her African royal tour wardrobe, a tiny fraction of the estimated £118,000 (approximately AU$216,000) spent on her tour wardrobe the previous year. However, as was pointed out, this cost cut is likely due to the lack of formal engagements, such as state dinners, within their schedule, therefore negating the need for black tie attire. Markle also saw her number of scheduled appearances drastically reduced in comparison to her last royal tour so that she could spend much of her time looking after her five-month-old son, Archie, further explaining the reduction in her royal tour wardrobe budget. Setting her fashion intentions from day one, the duchess’s first royal tour appearance reiterated her focus on important causes over sartorial flair, stepping out in a $126 printed wrap dress by Malawi-based designer, Mayamiko. Markle’s outfits then continued to be a study in relaxed royal dressing and fashion diplomacy, a long-held royal custom. The duchess wore pieces from affordable e-tailer, Everlane, recycled many of her outfits debuted during the 2018 royal tour, wore a number of denim items, and continued to include pieces from local African designers within each of her looks. Markle's comparatively low-key dressing allowed the causes highlighted at each of her engagements to take focus. Even when she dressed her son, Archie, for the family’s meeting with Archbishop Desmond Tutu at the headquarters of the Desmond & Leah Tutu Legacy Foundation, the duchess looked to the high street for her son’s outfit, selecting a blue and white pinstripe jumpsuit from H&M for the iconic moment, and choosing a Club Monaco dress in a similar colourway for herself. According to Vanity Fair, Markle’s private secretary, Samantha Cohen, is said to have had a hand in the duchess’s toned-down royal wardrobe, likely aiding her in creating a series of looks that included pieces from reasonably-priced brands—including Sam Edelman, Mother, Madewell and Banana Republic. As one of the Palace’s most experienced aids, the publication pins Cohen as Markle’s secret wardrobe weapon, and her decisions reportedly saw senior royals, including The Queen, pleased with the duchess’s fresh approach to tour dressing. “I expect The Queen will be pleased to see that Meghan has been taking a leaf out of her book, wearing outfits more than once and taking the advice of trusted aides like Sam,” a royal source told the publication. column1: “I don’t work in fashion, I work in style”: Giambattista Valli on his collaboration with H&M
column2:
© Giovanni Corabi Fashion Ahead of the Italian designer’s collaboration launch with the Swedish high-street store in November, Vogue gives you an exclusive preview of his designs, from leopard-print jogging pants to rhinestone-embellished hoodies When it was announced in May that Giambattista Valli would be the next H&M collaborator, it was clear he was going to do things differently. At a photocall at the amFAR Gala during the Cannes Film Festival, Valli appeared alongside his muses – including Kendall Jenner, Chris Lee, Chiara Ferragni and Ross Lynch dressed in Giambattista Valli x H&M, a limited-edition drop of which was made available in selected stores and online two days later, selling out in minutes. “I couldn’t believe so many people worldwide knew the brand,” he tells Vogue when we meet in Rome for an exclusive preview of the collection ahead of the full drop in November. “H&M wanted the enthusiasm of the first collaboration with Karl [Lagerfeld], so I wanted to revolutionise it from the beginning.” After honing his skills with couturier Roberto Capucci, Valli went on to work for Fendi and then Emanuel Ungaro, before launching his eponymous brand in 2005, gaining couture status in 2011. Since then, the likes of Rihanna, Ariana Grande and Emma Stone have sent paparazzi into a frenzy in his effervescent red-carpet dresses. Now the 53-year-old is bringing a touch of that unadulterated glamour to the high street. Valli is such a mainstay of Paris’s show schedules you could be forgiven for forgetting he is in fact Roman. “I come from Rome, I grew up here,” he says. “The city has a very strong DNA, a kind of eccentricity, effortlessness and timeless feel. It’s part of the story of the house.” The H&M campaign stars Ferragni, Jenner and Lee, and was photographed Mert and Marcus in a private garden in Rome and at the Galleria Doria Pamphilj, which boasts one of the world’s most enviable art collections comprising works by Caravaggio, Raphael and Velázquez. “I wanted to show this girl who now lives in LA, Shanghai or Berlin and comes home to Rome with a group of friends, they’re staying at a palazzo and getting ready for a party,” he says of the unashamedly decadent concept behind the campaign. “I’m not a designer who dresses someone to go to work — my community is very jetset. I love this idea of people being comfortable moving from one country to another; one culture to another.” Hoodies embellished with rhinestone floral motifs, elaborate necklaces embroidered into the collar of marl sweatshirts, a leather bomber with a shearling collar — there’s a familiar air of a princess-gone-rogue in these contrasts between refinement and athleticism. With the exception of perhaps six statement party gowns — one a riot of vermillion tulle, the others a botanist’s dream (embroidered, with appliqué flowers or in pleated floral-print fabric) – the collection’s versatile separates and dresses are easily assimilated into a wardrobe. “I don’t work in fashion, I work more in style,” says Valli. “I want to give people the support they need to style clothes their own way and be comfortable; fashion can be too dictated by a ‘look’. When I design, I leave space for people to fill with their personality.” After the limited-edition drop in May, Valli delighted in scrolling through Instagram to see how customers interpreted the clothes. “I love it when people feel in balance with themselves, it's the most elegant thing,” he says. “I hate it when luxury houses make people feel they need to buy something, or else you aren’t cool. What I want to do in fashion is inspire people. ” Valli describes his first foray into menswear as “very autobiographical”. A classic Levi’s jean jacket he wore as a child was the starting point for a denim coat with military detailing and faux sheepskin lining. Meanwhile, a portrait by an unknown Flemish artist that hangs in Valli’s Paris home was adapted into a print that features on a raincoat, scarf and duffle bag. “The menswear is for a man who goes into a woman's wardrobe and gets dressed up — somebody who likes more androgynous clothes — normally it’s the other way around, so I thought it would be nice to do something different,” he says. “I like to remove the etiquette surrounding he and she, and think about creativity and freedom. I thought about who the Valli girl surrounds herself with. There is a fluidity, with the women wearing one of the men’s jackets. Everybody’s free to interpret it their own way.” Acting as a thread of continuity with the old Dutch masters are rococo embroideries that slalom down the legs of trousers and the opening of a military tailcoat, as well as imitation pearls studded along the neckline of a black sweatshirt. “It’s funny,” he says, “pearls look so bourgeois on a little black dress. But when they’re on a man’s black sweater, they become outrageous. I always wear a string of pearls, it’s my lucky charm. I can be standing next to someone covered in tattoos and piercings, but people will look at my pearls.” Then there’s the leopard print, which until now Valli admits was “a very couture idea” to him, so he upended this notion and has used the pattern on jogging pants and T-shirts. Just because the clothes aren’t haute couture, Valli insists they are no less considered: “Yes, the designs are in a different fabric to what I normally use and will be sold at different prices, but everything has a meaning, down to the most simple sweatshirt.” He gestures towards the model Oslo Grace who is dressed in bleached jeans, flowery socks, creepers and a marshmallow-pink hoodie. The ‘love’ motif, emblazoned on socks, a handbag and men’s T-shirts, is how Valli closes his letters, while the lip belt buckle and bag clasp are modelled on his own mouth. “The collection is an a,b,c of what I’ve done up until now,” says the designer. “I’m couture, I’m ready-to-wear, a mix of everything. I want people to be able to wear one of my couture jackets over jeans. I like the idea of H&M in front of a Caravaggio.” This desire to create clothes that won’t dilute the DNA of a brand without beating personal style into submission is a quest for authenticity, as Valli concludes: “I don’t want Giambattista Valli x H&M to be a parody. I’m a perfectionist; I want the collection to be totally faithful and honest to the customer.” --

Where we’ve seen it:Louis Vuitton, Paco Rabanne, Altuzarra What you need to know:Nicolas Ghesquière’s soulful Louis Vuitton SS20 show ended Paris Fashion Week with a standing ovation. The creative director’s signature mix of Seventies tailoring and electrifying futuristic detail hit a euphoric note – think mesmeric print blouses in acid hues and trim trouser suiting. It’s a timeless fashion agenda for the start of a new decade, where a saturated colour palette and pop florals (as seen at Paco Rabanne) are set to unleash an uncompromisingly optimistic outlook. Givenchy © Gorunway.com Lanvin © Gorunway.com Loewe © Gorunway.com Where we’ve seen it:Givenchy, Lanvin, Loewe, Mugler What you need to know:The trend for visible underpinnings has seen a wave of early Nineties bodycon returning to the Paris catwalks. If you missed new Mugler creative director Casey Cadwallader’s epic SS20 show, here’s your rundown. The American designer’s architectural eye (which brought us Bella Hadid in a buttock-revealing bodystocking) has set the gold standard in knife-sharp tailoring for spring, while also making flounce feel modern. Most important of all is Cadwallader’s unifying message on body-confidence. Cue the theatre of a ruched skirt and matching bolero paired, simply, with a black bralet. Meaning that shorter skirts come into fashion during times of economic certainty; and that as stocks plummet, trends for longer skirting take hold. Perhaps in 2020, Taylor’s theory ought to become the ‘frill index’ – the scale of the fluttering peplums and enormous ruffles that took to the Paris catwalks at Valentino, Balenciaga and Chanel, could mean more than first meets the eye. Clare Waight Keller’s SS20 collection at Givenchy delivered a wishlist of refined classics, which also boast durability – her sumptuous, leather looks included. The way to wear it now? column1: All the highlights from Paris Fashion Week spring/summer 2020
column2: © Jamie Stoker Fashion From the stunning shows on the runway to gatecrashers being escorted off stage by supermodels, here’s everything that went down at Paris Fashion Week this season Rainy Paris, sunny Paris, place with the best cafes Paris, city blocked by protestors Paris—every corner in the City of Lights has a new story tell, but especially so during Paris Fashion Week. As the spring/summer 2020 edition wraps up at the tail end of yet another European summer, Vogue looks back at the highlights from the season. While storied luxury houses often draw in the crowd with their big budget productions, extensive promotions and celebrity front rows, this season, PFW made room for younger labels with promising talent. Rok Hwang’s Rokh, which won the LVMH prize last year, presented a collection that drew from his childhood in Texas. Hwang’s brand often labours on the insecurities one has growing up and how they find their way into adulthood. Using a mix of made-to-look vintage fabrics and deliberately deconstructed tailoring, Rokh’s line-up left something interesting behind that will make for a good story to watch unfold over the years. © Jamie Stoker During her time at Dior, Maria Grazia Chiuri has explored themes of feminism and the lack of representation of female artists in the art world. This season, Chiuri focused on raising awareness around climate change. Fashion is the second largest polluting industry in the world and talk about sustainability is as important from the point of view of businesses sustaining as it is about being conscientious. Set in the Longchamp Racecourse, Chiuri worked with Parisian collective Coloco to ensure all of the trees used in the set would find homes around Paris. © Jamie Stoker Marine Serre, another label that hits the right notes of cool and conscious made an impact with presentation this season, offering guests a terrifying perspective of our post-apocalyptical futures. Serre’s production uses 50 per cent upcycled materials and sources the rest from local French mills. Stella McCartney, whose efforts towards building a sustainable company were both early and sophisticated, showcased the Opera Garnier. While the walls of the of the setting were projected with videos of animals, models walked out in signature McCartney tailoring, odd colour pairings—an optimistic view of what conscious fashion could look like. Thom Browne’s presentation for the season went deep into French history, and the iconic Marie Antoinette served as an inspiration for this season. Whimsical soundtrack, larger-than-life wigs and the Thom-fication of costume history from bustles to heeled shoes and parasols—the New York-based designer never fails to put on a show that’s nothing short of mesmerising. What’s equally exciting? People watching the community that attend his presentations. Valentino’s Pierpaolo Piccioli hasn’t failed to charm both the critics and the fans since he heralded the Italian luxury label by himself. Merging couture and ready-to-wear, the summer wardrobe at Valentino went from shirt-inspired gowns to bold prints, floaty chiffon maxi dresses, maribou flounces and ethereal tulle dresses. It’s hard to walk away from a show like this one and not set your dreams on at least one of the looks. Highlighting the evolving definition of beauty, L’Oréal Paris brought under one roof women from all over the world for an inclusive showcase during Paris Fashion Week. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, the global brand ambassador, walked the runway for the show, and was joined onstage by Dame Helen Mirren, Doutzen Kroes, Andie MacDowell and Eva Longoria, who came with her toddler, among others. Sarah Burton’s connect with Alexander McQueen the brand and the man finds its way not into just the storytelling of a collection, but its very inception. This season, Burton not only upcycled fabric from previous seasons but also reinvented some of the brand’s most iconic look over the years. The staff at Alexander McQueen was invited to hand-embroider two dresses and when Burton took the bow, everyone walked with her. Following Karl Lagerfeld’s tradition, Virginie Viard transformed the Grand Palais into a long runway of Parisian rooftops. Chanel’s aesthetic focuses on the classic—tweed jackets, long coats, denim and more. The highlight of the show was a runway crasher who was escorted off the stage by none other than Gigi Hadid. Nicolas Ghesquière is known for travelling in time with his work, and for Louis Vuitton’s spring  2020 collection the designer headed back to Belle Époque-era Paris. From sleeves featuring puff sleeves to the proto-psychedelic swirls of a green jacquard coat, the line-up saw multiple references from the era this season. “I want the audience to see true fantasy, not always reality”: Thom Browne on his SS20 women’s collection “That wasn’t just a fashion show—it was a show.” Maison Margiela’s movement director on that Leon Dame walk “She’s fresh, raw and quite a tomboy”: Meet the new face who opened at Givenchy Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 8 labels championing khadi that can inspire your next buy
column2: © Instagram.com/1111clothing/ Fashion This Gandhi Jayanti, here are the labels that are spinning the wheel in favour of a more sustainable future If the word ‘khadi’ conjures up visuals of coarse kurtas and stiff Nehru jackets, you have grade school history to thank. Championed as the forerunner of the freedom movement, the humble fabric has come a long way in the consequent decades, making the transition from basic to bespoke under the watchful vigil of the country’s top labels—including Sabyasachi, Ritu Kumar, Anavila, Rajesh Pratap Singh and Abraham & Thakore, among others. The former stated in an Instagram post, “As a bridal designer, I keep thinking, ‘What’s next?’, and I keep coming back to khadi. For me, it is the equivalent of wellness, and nothing can be more luxurious than that. When I look back at the last 20 years, my khadi bridal lehengas are what I’m most proud of. Some of my most discerning customers globally have chosen to wear khadi lehengas for their wedding. Almost all of them are not on Instagram. Pity!” However, on the eve of Mahatma Gandhi’s 150th birth anniversary, there is much to be celebrated. The Gandhian fabric has found fresh iteration in the hands of the young guard, with contemporary silhouettes, innovative painting techniques and fresh colour stories bestowing the handspun textile with a modern facelift. Here, we list the labels that are reviving our love affair with the handloom. Since his debut on the Gen Next runway at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016, Gaurav Khanijo’s eponymous label has been anchored by a duality of purpose: providing a glimpse into the future of Indian fashion with fabrics that hark back to the country’s roots. Think contemporary cuts and sharp tailoring delivered against the canvas of khadi. This season, the designer teamed up with the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) to fete 150 years of Mahatma Gandhi. His vision for the future of the freedom fabric? Breezy shirts and sharply cut jumpsuits crafted from 500-count khadi linen. Seeking support from handwoven khadi blankets called ‘khes’, the designer served up everything from stone-washed denim trousers to shawl jackets with equal ease. With a retail footprint that spans multiple countries, from India to Canada, Korea and Japan, 11.11 is primed to deliver India’s sartorial legacy on the international stage with its 100 per cent khadi cotton offering. With an eye on creating meaningful links between farmers, weavers and the apparel industry, the label’s seed-to-stitch ethos is manifested in the completely handcrafted line-up of easy separates and fluid silhouettes. On the Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2019 runway, natural yarn-dyed khadi took centre stage in hues of chambray and indigo. The line-up saw khadi cotton further accentuated with traditional crafts like bandhani, mud resist prints, kalamkari and shibori. Translating into the Sanskrit alphabet ‘a’, the label places handwoven textiles as the starting point of the design process. As a trained weaver, Gaurav Jai Gupta’s experiments with the loom have earned recognition on the international fashion scene, with successful collaborations with Jimmy Choo and Heminstone Paris, among others, as well as a spot in the research archives of the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. The designer’s autumn/winter 2018 offering, titled ‘Irreverence’, championed luxurious urban separates handwoven from a unique blend of wool and khadi in a wide spectrum of charcoal blacks and natural indigos. Functional fashion finds modern form under designer Pallavi Dhyani’s eye. As the creative force behind THREE, her sartorial lexicon comprises of comfort-first separates meant to be layered, with neutral tones bringing forth her minimalist manifesto. Her focus on high utility fabrics found a winning candidate in khadi on the Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2019 runway. The designer gave the homespun fabric her own spin with a colour palette that progressed from greys and whites to deep blues, punctuated by short, sharp bursts of fuchsia. Dhyani’s favour for androgynous silhouettes offered fresh iteration to the age-old fabric—it wouldn’t be hard to picture the unstructured trench coats and midi kurtas in your everyday closet. Among the many laurels that Péro’s Aneeth Arora claims as her own, she is also credited with extending the longevity of the handcrafted movement beyond just the buzzword du jour. The self-professed ‘Indian-ness’ of her textile process means that every garment created under her label passes from the hands of one indigenous craftsman to the other, with khadi being sourced directly from its weavers in West Bengal. The handspun fabric is then fashioned into a wide range of comfort-first separates, including fuss-free midi dresses and reversible jackets. Designer Yadvi Agarwal’s take on Impressionist art is forged with a deep-rooted love for textiles. Today, the label’s uniquely hand-painted lineup is visible proof of the art-meets-fashion ideology, crafted against the base of khadi. The handspun fabric is given a modern-day facelift with layers of hand-painting using blocks and found objects, including crumpled newspaper balls and sticks. The designer’s Impressionist dresses have already found a fan in noted fashion critic and Vogue International Editor, Suzy Menkes. Designer Santanu Das’ exploration of his culture led to the birth of the label, with inspiration from within the doors of his mother’s wardrobe. The back-to-roots philosophy took literal meaning as the designer shifted his base from New York to his homeland, where his journey through the small villages of West Bengal acquainted him with the virtues of the handloom. Today, 100 per cent khadi cotton finds regular favour in his collections, doused in his sartorial signature of hand-dyed indigo. The year was 1984, and Ahmedabad-based textile designer Asha Sarabhai had launched her label ‘Raag’ under the Miyake Design Studio (MDS) in Tokyo. Over the following decades, the label went on to find a place in upmarket stores in Tokyo as well as the archives of Victoria & Albert Museum, earning her the title of the grand dame of Indian textiles. Fast forward to 2016, and her nephew Ajay Mayor had brought the widely-exported label to India under the digital platform, Beej. The retail offering seeks cues from Raag’s DNA and long-standing relationships with handloom weavers to offer breathable basics that age well over time. Interestingly, the connection to khadi dates further back in the pages of history—the Sarabhais are said to be among the wealthy textile clans to have supported Gandhi’s peaceful resistance to the British with the adoption of the homespun fabric during the freedom movement. As India’s second Woolmark Prize-winning designer, Ruchika Sachdeva has leveraged her stellar credentials to give traditional textiles a contemporary makeover. The result includes highly covetable pieces designed for the modern Indian femme that fall in line with the label’s organic ethos. Khadi-panelled cotton shirts, loose trousers and light layering find a place in her line-up, with zero wastage followed through the entire process. The designer, who has often likened khadi to a visual metaphor for India, will be working in a blend of the handspun fabric and silk for her showcase at Paris Fashion Week spring/summer 2020. column1: History of the trouser suit: how a once divisive fashion statement became a wardrobe staple
column2: © Getty Fashion From Hollywood’s Marlene Dietrich, Katharine Hepburn and Greta Garbo to today’s female politicians, the trouser – or pant – suit has built a strong, often political, reputation from the 1930s to now. Here’s Vogue’s definitive guide to the history of the power-dressing two-piece Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, tailored suits were the norm for upper and middle-class women – although quite specifically, a skirt with a matching, fitted jacket. When women began wearing trousers in elite circles in the 1930s, and more generally in the 1960s, the term ‘trouser suit’ — or ‘pant suit’ in the US — was born (to differentiate from the skirted style). This, however, caused controversy. Marlene Dietrich © Getty One of American Vogue’s earliest trouser-suit images is from a September 1933 feature, Riviera Days and Nights, which saw Hollywood actress Marlene Dietrich in a summer trouser suit. Dietrich and others, such as Katharine Hepburn and Greta Garbo, raised eyebrows for boldly wearing these suits in public. Wearing trousers was controversial, but much less so than the whole suit; until the 1950s, women could be arrested while wearing them for “impersonating a man”. During the second world war, some women wore trousers and overalls when working in more practical or dangerous jobs. Still, women had to wait until the 1960s for the trouser suit to gain broader public support. A full-page image by photographer Horst P. Horst from American Vogue’s March 1964 issue ran alongside an article called “Norell’s prophetic trouser suit”. The magazine called the look “the be-all, end-all travelling costume” and the “essence of what pants have become today […] pure fashion, correction easy, contemporary.” In 1966, Yves Saint Laurent introduced Le Smoking, an elegant trouser suit for evening wear. At the time, the style was still controversial enough for American socialite Nan Kempner to be turned away from a fashionable New York restaurant for daring to wear her suit instead of a dress or skirt (rumour has it she took the trousers off and wore the blazer as a very short dress). An issue of Life magazine from 1968 reveals just how divisive the fashion was: in the front pages, a male columnist lamented that Yves Saint Laurent’s trouser suits were contributing to the “destruction” of gender norms, while at the back of the magazine, a woman is quoted as saying that “a well-cut pant suit is most appropriate for city-wear”. And as for those restaurants that refused trouser-wearing women entry, the woman comments: “I would rather change my restaurant than my clothes.” Diane Keaton © Getty In the 1970s, polyester trouser suits and platform shoes were the preferred uniform of the liberated career woman. Yet, the style was still considered to be risky, and women who wore such ensembles often had to deflect criticism from their male colleagues or bosses. Historian Daniel Delis Hill notes that trouser suits were not simply the women’s version of the men’s equivalent (cut from dark or pinstriped worsted cloth). Instead, women’s trouser suits came in vivid colours, textures and weaves, with the jackets sometimes cut into tunic-like shapes. Diane Keaton’s vest-and-tie-wearing character in 1977’s Annie Hall, as well as her public appearances in trouser suits, helped popularise the style even more. Wearing trouser suits continued to be provocative throughout the 1980s and 1990s. While Pat Nixon, wife of President Robert Nixon, was photographed in trouser suits in 1972 (the first sitting first lady to have done so), it wasn’t until 1993 that women were allowed to wear trousers on the US Senate floor. The rule was unofficial, but enforced by the Senate doorkeepers, despite the fact that trousers had been accepted at federal agencies since the 1970s. Carol Moseley Braun © Getty That year, freshman senator Carol Moseley-Braun wore her favourite trouser suit to the Chamber, unaware of the unwritten rule and igniting the ‘pant suit revolution’. Soon after, the doorkeepers received new orders explicitly stating that women could wear “coordinated pantsuit (slacks and matching blazer, no stirrup pants)”. Rihanna in John Galliano © Getty Gwendoline Christie at Emmy's 2019 © Getty In the early 2000s, the trouser suit garnered a fusty and conservative image, despite its radical history — but mid-decade, the look made a strong comeback. Designers such as Bottega Veneta and Chanel sent stylish trouser suits down the runway for autumn/winter 2015, while Rihanna wore an oversized black version by John Galliano at Maison Margiela to the Grammy Awards that same year. © Getty In 2016, 2.9 million supporters joined the Hillary Clinton Facebook group ‘Pant suit Nation’ to champion her style and follow her presidential campaign; Angela Merkel and Theresa May also adopted trouser suits as part of their political imagery. Elie Saab spring 2019 © Gorunway.com Many women now wear trouser suits to cast their ballots for female politicians, in a nod to the suit’s feminist history. In 2019, dozens of US Congresswomen wore white (many of them trouser suits) during the State of the Union address — a joint sartorial message of solidarity to the earlier female suffrage movement and a way to show support for women’s issues. Meanwhile, designers such as Elie Saab and Alberta Ferretti sent trouser suits down the runways during Spring 2019 Couture. column1: Bengaluru gets its first destination for Indian textiles and luxury designer wear
column2: Fashion The House of Angadi’s founder, CEO and design head K Radharaman, takes us inside his soon-to-be-launched multi-designer retail space, Angadi Heritage With the 150th birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi around the corner, khadi is back in the focus—but it is just the tip of the handloom conversation surrounding the massive Indian textile iceberg. The many layers to this conversation ranges from government policies to sustainable craft clusters, and to the marketability of textiles and craft in today’s rather precarious retail market. And one can’t help but wonder that in an environment where most brick-and-mortar fashion players are struggling—be it luxury giant Barney’s or the latest high street casualty, Forever 21, who have both filed for bankruptcy recently—is the physical fashion retail space headed towards a slow extinction, or is there a new formula waiting to be cracked? The so far understated and rather quiet Bengaluru-based The House of Angadi, which traces its genesis from a 600-year-long textile legacy, is confident with their answer, at least when it comes to Indian luxury. In a line, it rests on the soon-to-be-launched Angadi Heritage, a sprawling 18,000sqft space geared towards becoming India’s premier multi-designer destination for Indian textiles and handcrafted luxury. “I inherited a legacy, I didn’t inherit a business,” says K Radharaman, the founder, CEO and design head of The House of Angadi. You might recall him as the designer behind the red and gold saris worn by Deepika Padukone at her headline- and hashtag-breaking wedding. Apart from the accidental celebrity endorsement, Radharaman is quite the unicorn in the Indian fashion market. He hails from a family that traces its roots back to the Padmasaliya weavers of Warangal, he graduated with an engineering degree from Cornell University and went on to work as a textile designer with leading international brands including Ralph Lauren to Louis Vuitton. He returned to India and founded The House of Angadi in 2001, launched the design label ADVAYA, even as he conceptualised and successfully created the first-ever linen blended Kanjeevaram or Khadi Kanjeevaram, which further cemented his reputation as one of the country’s leading textile designers. He is a weaver, textile designer, apparel designer, entrepreneur and legacy heir, all rolled into one. K Radharaman And now he’s ready to claim his spotlight with the launch of his latest store, Angadi Heritage. But what makes this new multi-designer store a game-changer? “Handloom products are generally perceived as a commodity in India, unlike the West where handcrafted products are considered luxury. While this perception is slowly changing, our aim is to celebrate this legacy in a majestic space that showcases the finest products India has to offer, in a manner that befits their stature,” explains Radharaman. While bringing heritage luxury into a contemporary lexicon, is the thread that runs through, to understand how it all comes together you need to break down Radharaman’s one-line mission statement. Let’s begin with the majestic space—the exterior façade and structure is created by architect Brinda Somaya, inspired by Bengaluru’s architectural landmark Vidhan Saudha. From repurposed heritage furniture to an ikat-inspired light installation by Klove Studio, the interiors are designed by Abha Narain Lambah, who seamlessly combines traditional accents with India’s textile aesthetic. From the Chettinad-inspired courtyard that greets you as you walk into this palatial store to the open terrace that drinks in sprawling views of the city, this store is designed to make you feel at home even as you’re enveloped by a delicate grandeur. Talking about the terrace, it is currently home to an exhibit showcasing a tiny sampling of the exhaustive archive of Kanjeevarams and textiles preserved across generations of Radharaman’s family—from Kadhua in a Benarasi silk handwoven georgette to the world’s first-ever Khadi Kanjeevaram. Rumour has it that a private museum in Thanjavur, showcasing The House Of Angadi’s exhaustive textile archive, might be on the cards too. Next comes the collection itself—the almost completely handcrafted collection here is curated from designers across India. “Leather accessories by Nappa Dori; personal care from Pure Earth; fragrances by The Perfume Library; apparel labels such as Anavila, Urvashi Kaur, 11.11, Injiri, Rimzim Dadu, Akaaro; menswear by Suket Dhir and Rajesh Pratap Singh; as well as children’s wear by Love The World Today share space with The House of Angadi’s own in-house ready to wear and sari labels.” From ready-to-wear to bridal saris, there’s an understated elegance to the collection found here, for customers who enjoy the subtleties of master craftsmanship, the purity of finely woven textiles and an evolved design aesthetic. The price points also deserve a mention—they are definitely more affordable than what you might find in most multi-designer stores in Delhi and Mumbai. Add to that a deeply engaged staff, who can trace motifs back to heritage archives and the source of almost every fabric, and you’re gently coaxed into a contemporary Indian vision for slow luxury that openly embraces heritage and legacy. While we’re a long way away from knowing if Angadi Heritage will prove to be the answer to Indian luxury’s ailing retail woes, we’re definitely recommending a visit to Bengaluru’s latest luxury destination. column1: Should the fashion industry be rewarded for being greener? Yes, says Stella McCartney
column2:
© Jamie Stoker Fashion Stella McCartney reveals why incentivising the fashion industry could enhance the future health of our planet When British fashion designer Stella McCartney sat down with journalists in the imposing marble stairwell of Paris’s Palais Garnier, on the eve of her SS20 show, she put a question to her audience. “We’ve seen millions of people marching [for the environment] this week, but not many people in the fashion industry posted those pictures and I was surprised. How can they be encouraged to make it fashionable?”
In the days following 16-year-old Greta Thunberg’s impassioned speech at the United Nations climate summit, concerns as to whether climate change is not being taken seriously enough by the industry have left an indelible mark this fashion month. Designers using their SS20 platform to draw attention to the cause have included Maria Grazia Chiuri at Dior—who partnered with innovative urban planting collective Coloco to surround her catwalk with 164 native European trees, which they planned to replant after the show.
“We know that we’re part of the problem, but we’re trying to think of what we can do through our business to actually make things better,” explains Clare Bergkamp, Stella McCartney’s innovation and sustainability director.
Primarily, this means new technology—the result of years of research at Stella McCartney Ltd—which has propelled the brand into an advanced position on sustainability, enabling it to share its lessons learned with the industry at large. This includes work with Bolt Threads, a San Francisco based biotechnology company that produces fibres engineered from spider silks and MyloTM, a leather based on mycelium mushrooms.
Stella McCartney doesn’t claim to have the solution to the environmental crisis, but she does offer prescient advice to both consumers and her peers in the fashion community. Stella McCartney [SM]: “Giving up meat is the no-brainer. It’s scary, we’re all terrified and we don’t want to feel guilty or bad. We also need to understand the impact of leather and the animal glues that are used in fashion; next time you go to buy a bag or a pair of shoes, just ask yourself if you really need it.” SM: “I was privileged, I grew up on an organic farm and I saw the seasons. My parents were vegetarians, they were change agents—I took that way of looking at the world into my work, to create a product which is still sexy, desirable and luxurious, that isn’t landfill. The people who want to work in the fashion industry now (and it will be even more so in five or 15 years time) want to work in a company that has ethics, and that goes for every business. They want to work in a place that has good moral grounding. What I do everyday in my place of work is to try for better practice in the fashion industry.” SM: “I’m trying to encourage people to be more mindful about what we consume. Rayon (also known as viscose) comes from wood pulp. This year alone up to 150 million trees have been cut down to create viscose. It’s one of the most widely used fabrics in the fashion industry. I’ve spent three years of my life trying to find a solution, so we get all of our viscose pulp from a sustainable forest in Sweden. This is the knowledge that I want to bring to my industry. We need to give people the information so they have a more informed way of purchasing and have a better way of buying.” SM: “[Designers] need to be incentivised. I’ve been doing this my whole career, but I get penalised when I take a non-leather goods into the United States, I get taxed up to 30 per cent more because it’s not made out of leather. We need to give people a reward for doing things better.” © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker Stella McCartney: “Working with and looking at technology gives me hope” Are our collective efforts towards sustainable fashion enough? 5 ways the fashion industry can achieve a greener future Fashion Culture & Living Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast
