column1: “She’s fresh, raw and quite a tomboy”: Meet the new face who opened at Givenchy
column2: © Getty Fashion Vogue speaks to Givenchy’s Clare Waight Keller and casting director Piergiorgio Del Moro about the French house’s SS20 woman, embodied by Norwegian model Silje Lorentzen “I actually looked at them today,” says Silje Lorentzen of the candid polaroids she sent her mother agency Team Models four years ago, “It was so funny.” Now she’s backstage at Givenchy, not just walking in her first ever show, but opening Clare Waight Keller’s SS20 collection, and leading the finale. “I still have to pinch myself,” says the 23-year-old Norwegian model, “I feel very lucky to be here.” Working with renowned casting director Piergiorgio Del Moro, who was also behind the line-up at Versace, Victoria Beckham, Tom Ford and Michael Kors this season, Clare Waight Keller singled out Lorentzen straight away. “She has this very raw beauty,” the artistic director tells Vogue backstage at her Paris Fashion Week show. “The thing that really caught my eye was this idea of absolute purity in her face. The fact that she has these sort of slight freckly cheeks, this freshness: very modern, quite intellectual. But at the same time, just a sophistication to the way she looks.” Del Moro remembers seeing Lorentzen on the first day of pre-castings and thinking she would be great for the French maison. “Without saying anything, when she came into the room, [Clare] immediately said her face was incredible: ‘She looks like an actress!’,” he recalls. “[Clare] is fascinated by faces where you can see confidence and maturity at the same time. She knows what she likes, so it is very clear what I have to deliver.” © Jamie Stoker Givenchy’s SS20 woman is “fresh, raw and she’s quite a tomboy,” explains Waight Keller. Note the crisp tailoring, upcycled Nineties denim, hothouse florals, scarf necklines and balloon sleeves on the runway. Represented by MP Management in Paris and Team Models in Norway, Lorentzen is as surprising as she is striking. Originally from Tønsberg in southern Norway, the former professional show jumper and pre-med student (who once planned on a future in plastic surgery) now lives in Oslo, where she is pursuing modelling full time. The necessary qualities to succeed in today’s industry? “Confidence, persistence and caring about what you do,” says Del Moro. “You can be the most beautiful woman, but if you don't care about what you're doing, you're not listening, growing and evolving your career, you probably won't go anywhere.” With Givenchy under her belt, it is safe to say Lorentzen will go far. © Jamie Stoker The man behind Givenchy AW19 couture’s hairstyle shows us how to recreate it Is the fashion industry truly inclusive? 5 models weigh in Models around the world who are breaking the stereotype of perfection What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Are It Bras the new It Bags for spring 2020?
column2: © Instagram/khaite_ny Fashion Without a doubt, exposed bras have not only been topping celebrity wardrobes but also been making statements throughout the entirety of fashion month. Scroll down to check out how It all started with Katie Holmes hailing a cab. To summarise (because it’s certainly been analysed enough since it happened during the last week of August) the actor was spotted wearing a cashmere bra and matching cardigan by Khaite that immediately went viral. The bra was the kicker—a $520 (approximately Rs 36,840) piece of effortless, painfully cool lingerie that sold out within hours of the photo making the rounds online. Post Holmes, exposed bras have also been making statements throughout the entirety of fashion month. Street stylers have been spotted wearing sleek, simple bras with high-waist skirts and trousers, and the Hadid sisters, who have long been fans of wearing their underthings on the outside, have sported bras with blazers and layered over tanks. On the runways, the bra has become a staple item in many of the top collections, from the bejewelled pieces at Tom Ford and Dior to the more traditional designs worn freely underneath unbuttoned dresses at Chloé and with a pretty, lacy skirt and boots at Loewe. The former Dawson’s Creek star and her style rebirth aside, it is curious that bras seem to be the most-coveted items for spring 2020, especially considering the fact that thus far during fashion month, there’s yet to be a standout bag or shoe that everyone is vying for. The idea of an It bag, and possibly an It shoe, has been waning in popularity for some time now. Novelty is king in this arena: giant platform Crocs, minuscule top handles that fit nothing, and, as was the case yesterday, the release of Virgil Abloh’s newest Off-White bag, which was designed to be “intentionally unfunctional,” due to the fact that it comes with several large holes cut through the middle. That being said, there are heritage brands crafting gorgeous carryalls and footwear that are meant to be invested in, but at a time when It bags and It shoes are becoming slightly obsolete in the grand scheme of things, is the designer bra the penultimate wardrobe item for next season? The trend, though nothing at all new in fashion, also speaks to a certain kind of highly empowered woman right now, one who will wear a black lace balconette under a tailored blazer, à la Gigi Hadid, and head to a meeting. Whoever is lusting after these new designer bras—be she America’s sweetheart who got chic-a-fied or the stylish fashion devotee looking to up the ante on her executive realness—has a lot to choose from. There may be an alluring bag or shoe here and there, but this season, the most seductive, singular accessory is the designer bra worn with pride while hailing a cab, running to and from shows, or walking a runway. column1: “I want the audience to see true fantasy, not always reality”: Thom Browne on his SS20 women’s collection
column2: © Jamie Stoker Fashion Vogue speaks to New York-based, Paris-showing master tailor Thom Browne about creating pieces that make people think and break from “the seriousness” of fashion Following a decampment to show on the Paris women’s schedule two years ago, designer Thom Browne staged something of a homecoming this New York Fashion Week on the streets of the city’s Midtown district. Called The Officepeople, the flashmob-esque occurrence announced the arrival of Browne’s womenswear line to luxury department store Bergdorf Goodman and saw models—male and female—seemingly going about a casual workday lunch break. They walked in two military-precise lines, identically dressed in pleated skirts and blazers, with slick hair to match. While Browne lives in NYC, he’s currently back in Paris for Fashion Week. Working out of his Avenue Montaigne studio, he fits a far more fantastical creation on a model: her hips have been extruded almost a metre to her right and left to create a silhouette that pays homage to panniers—the hooped architecture of formal French dress from the 18th century—the starting point of his spring/summer 2020 collection. Browne’s pieces, though imbued with fantasy, are entirely wearable. The full, tweed skirts—propped up by said panniers for the show—collapse into plush, easy-to-wear forms in the showroom. Sheer organza shirting and taffeta boxers are layered with coated seersucker corseting and opaque skirting. The classic white Oxford T-shirt is reinforced with boning and corsetry lacing at the back; and jackets with pleated backs, inspired by robes à la polonaises, trail in the wake of the wearer to reveal semi-transparent panelling. Reveal and conceal, play and polish—everything goes in the house of Thom Browne. Here, the designer talks Vogue through his vision for the latest collection and the transformative power of fashion shows. Thom Browne [TB]: The collection is based on my interpretation of 18th century dress, focussing on panniers and robes à la polonaise and playing with them in ways that [bring them into] my world, infusing them with American, preppy sportswear. Proportion [is] very important, taking something classic and turning it to something maybe newer or not so understandable. And that was the reason for the panniers, because I thought the proportions of a pannier are so ridiculous! TB: I do work in the old fashion way from head to toe, everything is designed per look, so you’ll see that all the fabrications are specifically developed for each. The collections start from very classic ideas, this time in fabrication—seersucker. I think the heavy use of seersucker screams American sportswear. Even the tweeds have a lot of seersucker woven through and I love fraying them, making them not so precious. The work that goes into the fraying is not as simple as keeping it undone, it’s actually sewn into the fray. So it is a finishing detail that looks very random and haphazard, but [is in fact] completely intentional. TB: For womenswear, it’s the fourth season and for menswear, I’ve been [showing] here for 10 years—and I love being here. There is more pressure; I’m very competitive. I think being here, you want to make sure everything is worthy of being in Paris, so we all challenge ourselves. As conceptual as I want to be, I also want to make sure the quality of what people see is at the highest level and I think Paris really appreciates that. But then Paris also appreciates the idea of telling a story [with] a true concept behind [it], not just commercial clothes. For me, I want the audience to see true fantasy and not always reality, especially in the 30 or 40 ideas that [I present]. I want them to see things differently. TB: I concentrate on tailoring, something that can be very banal and not so interesting, so I like to show it in ways people haven’t seen it before, to make it that much more interesting every season. There has to be something that breaks the seriousness [of fashion]. TB: The shows are supposed to make people think and I want people to have an experience. Sometimes people don't realise there’s a lot more reality behind what they see in the shows. [For this collection] I would like people to understand that you take this pannier out and it’s amazing how [the garment] drapes—it can be worn without the pannier as well. © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker How New York Fashion Week became the first of the Big 4 This batch of Gen Next designers is ready to take on Lakmé Fashion Week New designer launches that need to be on your radar this month Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Instagram/sonamkapoor Fashion Traditional juttis, suede boots, the latest sneaker drop—there's no shoe type that Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s shoe collection doesn't have. Her recent promotional run for The Zoya Factor gave Kapoor Ahuja the chance to dive into her wardrobe for her ethnic best. The star welcomed fall with the earthy hues of an embroidered Good Earth suit, paired with a coordinated potli and juttis by Bhumika Grover. This versatile staple has earned a spot in her vacation wardrobe as well—the star was spotted in a bohemian pick from Sabyasachi’s Kashgaar Bazaar collection, paired with multi-hued juttis, on her summery getaway in London earlier this year. Unafraid of veering into matchy-matchy territory, she opted for head-to-toe red by teaming her Gulabo by Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla ensemble with coordinated juttis by Pastels and Pop. Needless to say, the head-to-toe colour trend finds regular favour in her wardrobe. For her annual stroll down the French Riviera, Kapoor Ahuja stepped out in a canary yellow ruffled number by Ashi Studio, paired with matching heels. On days when she is looking to break the monotony of monochrome, she finds reprieve with some clever tone-on-tone dressing. Out and about for media interviews for her upcoming release, the star boldly paired oxblood leather culottes and a button-down top by Petar Petrov with thigh-high suede boots. Given that her husband is a self-professed sneakerhead and the owner of an indie sneaker label, it stands to reason that the first impression that Kapoor Ahuja made on her sneakerhead husband was heavily influenced by her choice of footwear. She recalled in an interview with Vogue, “I was apparently wearing the worst sneakers he had ever seen. I keep telling him that he fell in love with me despite my bad sneaker game.” Fast forward to a few years later, and we believe that Ahuja won’t have cause for complaint—his wife can be found pairing her favourite kicks with everything from culottes and palazzo pants to printed separates and cotton kurtas at the airport. At an award show earlier this year, the star swapped her usual ballgowns in favour of blush pink Fenty separates, and traded her signature heels for a pair of Air Jordan sneakers. And while the latest sneaker drops are part of routine dinner table conversation, Kapoor Ahuja has an eternal love affair with boots—thigh-high numbers from Stuart Weitzman being her weapon of choice. The star has been spotted styling hers with technicolour Anamika Khanna separates and patterned trench coats alike. Her penchant for creative sari drapes had her reinventing the wheel with a jumpsuit sari of her own invention for Rheson, teamed with chunky platform boots for maximum impact. column1: Christian Lacroix makes an enchanting return to fashion with Dries Van Noten
column2: © Gorunway Fashion From the bold fuchsia and orange palette to the feathers, leopard and zebra print, Lacroix’s extravagant evening wear was fused with Van Noten’s easy silhouettes for a collection that bore all the tropes of the 1980s, but felt contemporary What fashion dreams are made of: Dries Van Noten has collaborated with Christian Lacroix on his spring/summer 2020 collection. Eagle-eyed editors first took note of the Belgian designer’s show invitation: block lettering scrawled across a plain white card. Handwriting similar to the legendary couturier’s presented a major clue. As Paris Fashion Week attendees took their seats they found a single red rose waiting for them, a hint at what a partnership between Van Noten and master of 1980s drama Lacroix—whose own house closed in 2009—might bring. And then came the colour, ornate embellishment and volume that Lacroix built his name on—the trademarks he subsequently transferred to stage costumes after side-stepping from the industry. From the bold fuchsia and orange palette to the feathers, leopard and zebra print, Lacroix’s extravagant eveningwear was fused with Van Noten’s easy silhouettes for a collection that bore all the tropes of the 1980s, but felt contemporary. © Gorunway “Today’s world and the political, economical and environmental climate can be divisive exclusionary and drab, meagre in a way,” read a message from Van Noten shared online. “This left me thirsting for all that would be maximalist, optimistic, flamboyant, inclusive and enchantingly extravagant. There is a place for powerful opulence, exaggeration and fun and I need that energy.” © Gorunway He went on to share that his research into the whimsical Paris couture scene in the 1980s and 1990s—a period that was marked by Lacroix’s artistic vision—was how he formed a personal relationship with the designer. “It became a natural wish that I would love to work with him on this collection,” he continued. “That wish came true.” As the two creatives took a bow next to a model wearing a fabulous confection sprouting luscious cream plumage, there was no doubt they were flying high. © Gorunway This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk The best street style from Paris Couture Week autumn/winter 2019 “We are migrants. column1: These are the It-girl labels that are currently having a fashion moment
column2: © Getty Fashion From Priyanka Chopra’s favourite brand By Far to Eva Chen’s Georgian label N-DUO, these contemporary fashion labels need to be on your radar Whether it is Eva Chen’s balloon sleeved midi dress by Georgian label N-DUO, Selena Gomez’s checkered mini dress from Staud or By Far’s patent leather mules, which Priyanka Chopra recently wore in Miami, it’s clear—contemporary fashion labels are having a major moment. Not only are their designs eclectic (anything from minimalist to oversized tailoring, to androgyny to vintage-inspired designs), the quality is top-notch while their prices are relatively pocket-friendly. With the approval of celebrities and It-girls globally, these labels need to be on your radar now. Based out of Tblisi, Georgia, this label is quite the favourite amongst the influencers. Be it Copenhagen Fashion Week or New York Fashion Week, you will definitely see a street style star snapped wearing one of their effortless, puffed sleeved silhouettes. Co-creative directors Natuka Karkashadze and Anum Bashir’s designs beautifully combine androgyny with exaggerated shapes—yet the clothes are feminine and timeless. Their ‘Dance Through The Meadows’ dress is definitely on our wish list—with its vintage appeal and flirty silhouette, it is sure to get you through the rest of the season in style. Bella Hadid © Getty Launched in 2016 in Bulgaria by Valentina Bezuhanova, Sabina Gyosheva and Denitsa Bumbarova, this accessories brand has come a long way in just three years. Their ’90s inspired low-heeled mules and sling back pumps transition easily from day to night, and have graced the feet of supermodels and fashion editors alike. Their minimalist and cool handbags, like the Amber and Rachel, have found love in the arms of Bella Hadid too. Crafted from deadstock Italian leather, By Far’s products are sustainable, luxurious and affordable all in one. Meghan Markle with Prince Harry © Getty Whether it’s Meghan Markle’s belted maxi dress, which she recently wore on her royal visit to South Africa, or that Large Moon bag Kendall Jenner was spotted with during fashion week, if there’s one label that’s all over Instagram, it’s Staud. The brainchild of Sarah Staudinger and partner George Augusto, the California-based brand is anything but trend-based. Their vintage-style dresses, especially the maxis, can transcend seasons to always stay in style. And their quirky bags, with their unique shapes and timeless appeal, have quickly made it to the It-bags list as well. How can we forget the $375 (approx Rs 25,000) Moreau bag that had the fashion flock in a frenzy last year? Launched by a mother-daughter duo (Marie and Nathalie Dewet) on Instagram in 2017, the label is known for its handcrafted blouses (from their home in France) in luxurious fabrics and flirty silhouettes. And over the last year, these artisanal blouses have gained popularity and have been seen on major influencers like Leandra Medine. They have a weekly e-shop on their website, where you can order the clothes. Alternatively, you can also purchase from Net-a-Porter. Since this is slow fashion, pieces are limited, but oh so worth it. Australian-born Innika Choo’s eponymous Bali-based label makes the most beautiful boho chic clothes. Yet another Instagram success story, her free spirited designs, especially the signature hand-smocked detailing, have gained a cult following. From billowy maxi dresses to voluminous two tiered tops, the clothes are reminiscent of an endless summer. Entirely handmade, they are produced in limited quantities, making each piece truly special. Meet Khaite, the brand responsible for Katie Holmes’ famous cashmere bralette, which sold out within the hour it was seen on Instagram last month. The founder of the label, Catherine Holsetin, has reimagined American sportswear to give it a contemporary spin. From pieces to be cherished forever like hand-knitted cashmere sweaters to Instagrammable yet classic jeans to luxurious trench coats with silk linings, Khaite’s separates have become a staple in many women’s closets around the world. column1: “That wasn’t just a fashion show—it was a show.” Maison Margiela’s movement director on that Leon Dame walk
column2: © Getty Fashion Vogue speaks to Pat Boguslawski, the man behind the walk that everyone’s talking about at Paris Fashion Week, to find out how he makes his moves Model Leon Dame’s severe and seductive strut at Maison Margiela was to Paris Fashion Week what Jennifer Lopez’s jungle dress was to Milan: a viral moment of unbridled fashion joy. And behind the walk that everyone’s talking about is movement director, Pat Boguslawski. “That wasn’t just a fashion show,” Boguslawski tells Vogue from Paris, “it was a show.” The fact that Dame’s stride stole said show came as no surprise to Boguslawski. “I started laughing when John [Galliano] selected him to close because I knew it would be a thing, but I wasn’t expecting this,” he says of the viral sensation. “Seeing this kind of feedback is amazing and makes me so happy.” Boguslawski is a man of many talents: a dancer-turned-model-turned-actor (and all before turning 30), the industry innovator is represented by global creative talent agency, Streeters. As a movement director, Boguslawski is able to fuse all of his passions into one unique role. He’s worked with FKA Twigs, Victoria Beckham, Tilda Swinton and Kim Kardashian; orchestrated runway performances at Tomo Koizumi and Maison Margiela (seven shows to date); and coordinated the flow for Tommy Hilfiger, Off-White, Versace, Issey Miyake, Fendi and Hugo Boss campaigns. And yet, his role remains something of an enigma. Here, Vogue speaks to Boguslawski to find out how he makes his moves. As a movement director, I’m not making steps or crafting a choreography. I’m not showing people exactly how [a routine] has to go. I’m basically inspiring people, showing them different options and ideas, creating stories that help them move better. I’m creating a mood and moving around with [the talent]. A choreographer would normally come on set with prepared choreography. I’m giving more freedom to the people I work with to get the best out of them. By accident, really. It was a very natural process. The first time I did it was in 2013; I was modelling for [Alexander] McQueen and we were in rehearsals. Sarah [Burton, creative director] came over and asked me to show the models how to walk. I was pretty shocked—I thought she had the wrong person, but she told me she’d been watching me and she could see that I understood the collection, was listening to the music and walking to the beat. That’s when I first thought, ‘This could be interesting’. Working with John [Galliano at Maison Margiela] is amazing because I grew up watching his shows and admiring him so much. And models’ walks and fashion shows had become very simple, very ‘street style’ and every day. So it was the perfect time to start working with Margiela to create movement on the runway and make people feel free. A model for Maison Margiela womenswear spring/summer 2020 © Getty No two days are the same. I don’t have a settled schedule. I can be at fittings or on set, or on location. There’s a lot of travel involved, and I try to look after myself—I go to the gym, I do yoga, I swim—and spend a lot of time researching ideas and meeting with different people, friends, family. It can be hectic. It is a relatively new term, so people often don’t understand it at all. They will say, ‘Oh, you’re a choreographer?’ or ‘Oh, you’re a director.’ Sometimes it’s easier to just say yes rather than always explaining the difference. I’m basically in the middle of the model, the art director, the makeup, the music—I make everyone click. “We are migrants. column1: Julien Dossena talks us through his “psychedelic” Paco Rabanne SS20 collection
column2: © Jamie Stoker Fashion “Mens and womenswear should be almost interchangeable and equally radical.” – Creative director Julien Dossena stages a modern unisex revival of Paco Rabanne’s signature ‘Pacotilles’ chainmail at Paris Fashion Week Having been at the helm of Paco Rabanne for five years now, Julien Dossena is suitably in the swing of things at the Parisian fashion house, which was founded in the latter half of the 1960s. The 37-year-old creative director has drawn elements of what the brand is most famous for—dresses made from ‘les Pacotilles’ (tiles of plastic, metal and other materials, joined together using metal hoops) favoured by the likes of Françoise Hardy—and made them his own by quite literally collaging with a multitude of disparate references. “I wanted to explore things that I hadn't explored before,” he explains. “I thought, I’m going to experiment. This summer has been pretty interesting for me; it was spent having fun enjoying my work.” © Jamie Stoker Ahead of the show, Dossena takes Vogue on a trip through the psychedelic prints, naive landscapes and style-defining decades that came together for the Paco Rabanne SS20 collection. Julien Dossena [JC]: This season I wanted the mood of the collection to be optimistic, dreamy, a little psychedelic even, with a feeling of escape. I worked with really bold primary colours, and motifs likes sunsets and red hearts. JC: For some years now, I’ve worked with a print designer who I studied with at La Cambre in Brussels. Print and fabric is always my starting point and it’s a huge part of my design process. I’ve taken a lot of references this season and mixed them up like a collage. I’ve really had fun with that—it goes beyond the prints. There is a Western influence with the jeans and button-down shirts, but it’s given a touch of Pop with embroideries of birds and hearts. Then there’s a 1970s bohemian aesthetic, with medieval sleeves and capes—you can imagine Joni Mitchell in some of these looks; as well as some 1990s gothic dresses printed with roses, bringing romance back into the story. For another contrast, we have a very simple look: a knitted rainbow sweater and beige trousers that were inspired by a photo I saw of David Bowie. All of this feeds into the accessories too, there are a pair of men’s boots with a naive landscape appliqued onto them in coloured leather, and shoes with rainbows and heart motifs. JC: When I arrived at Paco Rabanne, I really wanted to work with the core values of the brand. For me, it stands for radical and conceptual design; and at the same time it’s about body consciousness and sexuality. The house is pretty unique in the landscape of fashion and, because Paco was creating many of his own materials, there are endless possibilities. You can create something out of metal, of course, but also wood, sequins, leather… anything. This season, I wanted to create some flower prints in a really post-modern way, so we played with the scale to create the effect of collage. On one of the looks, for example, I’ve appliqued velvet daisies onto a viscose base. Then I’ve replicated that print onto the chainmail that Paco Rabanne is famous for, I think that’s new; it’s not something I’ve seen in the archives. So it’s about creating these elements of unexpected contrast and harmony between materials. JC: When you think about when Paco Rabanne established his brand [in 1966], and you put it in context – surrounded by Parisian couture houses; where the models would walk up and down in a show with one hand in their pocket and a number in the other—he really changed all that. He thought: I’m going to put a woman of colour on the runway; play Pierre Boulez at my fashion show and stage it in a modern industrial set; send sculptural metallic dresses down the runway, because that’s what a utopia looks like. Françoise Hardy and the likes of Jane Birkin, of course, were a huge inspiration for Paco Rabanne. A woman singing on French TV in the 1960s and 1970s, with a modernist set, with different coloured lights flashing; that’s the kind of character I play into. JC: I collaborated with the graphic designer Peter Saville on some of the T-shirt prints again this season—we’ve been working together for over three years now. The designs act as an introduction to Paco Rabanne menswear. One, worn by a woman in the show, is based on a gay zine from the 1970s. It has an image of the back of a marble bust of a man, and the zine typeface Male Tales scrawled over the top. Another T-shirt has colours fading in and out, Peter felt it was a really dreamy collection, so he made an ironic statement by printing the word Realists over the top. Then there’s a red T-shirt called Unresolved, with the idea to blur the boundaries between genders. I didn’t want the menswear to hold back in any way. Some of the print designs and fabrications are present in both the men’s and women's clothes. For example: the print on a men’s shirt—large, multicoloured polka dots that fade out around the edges, like markings on the carpet of a 1970s nightclub—is used on a men’s chainmail shirt and a woman's skirt. There are embroideries, trousers made out of metallic leather—the mens and womenswear should be almost interchangeable and equally radical. © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker “We are migrants. column1: Bruno Sialelli invites you to dream big for Lanvin’s SS20 Slumberland collection
column2: © Jamie Stoker Fashion “I’m part of a pivotal generation that didn’t really grow up with digital technology, where boredom pushed you to be creative.” Vogue meets Bruno Sialelli in Paris to talk about how the freedom to indulge in fantasy has inspired his second collection for the French fashion house In 1897, Jeanne Lanvin gave birth to her first child, Marguerite, and motherhood marked a turning point in the Parisian milliner’s career. She fashioned beautiful clothes for her daughter in luxurious fabrics and before long Marguerite had a wardrobe that was the envy of all her friends. Seeing an opportunity to expand her business beyond hats, Lanvin established a childrenswear department a little over a decade later, in 1908. Within her lifetime, Lanvin would add lines in womenswear, menswear and homeware, establishing what evolved into one of the first lifestyle brands. It’s this uninhibited imagination and pioneering vision that was the starting point for Lanvin creative director Bruno Sialelli’s SS20 collection—his second for the house. “The collection is called Slumberland, because it's about this idea of being free to dream,” explains the 31-year-old designer, who was appointed in January this year, following a stint as design director of menswear at Loewe. “It’s quite fantastical, a bit unreal.” Lanvin is overdue some fantasy – following Alber Elbaz’s departure in 2015, the 130-year-old French house is now on it’s fourth creative director in four years. Vogue meets Sialelli before the Paris Fashion Week show to hear about his plan to bring Jeanne Lanvin’s energy and imagination back to the brand. Bruno Sialleli [BS]: It’s obviously still a very fresh role for me and I’m a very instinctive person, so I guess it will be easier to explain why we make certain decisions and not others further down the line. What was important for me was to find something in the house’s DNA that mirrored my own personality. I think a lot of people have this idea that Lanvin has a very rigid philosophy, but it’s not the case at all. The archive is a never-ending story and since Jeanne there have been so many interpretations by the various designers who worked for the house, from Jules-François Crahay [head designer, 1963-1983] to [director of menswear, 2004-2018] Lucas Ossendrijver and [creative director, 2001-2015] Alber Elbaz, so there is room for a lot of possibilities. It’s not a house like Chanel with its tweed, or a brand famous for its Matelassé bag; it’s more about emotions and what I most identify with most is that mood of childhood reminiscence. [BS]: When I came to Lanvin I investigated the history of the house and at the beginning she was just creating these beautiful clothes for her daughter that were really appealing to other girls. It was a strong part of the archive that hadn’t really been explored by designers since. There’s a very human story there and it’s a little bit kooky; it really touched me emotionally. I’m 31, so I’m part of a pivotal generation that didn’t really grow up with digital technology, where boredom pushed you to be creative. I feel nostalgic and have this very romantic idea about childhood; the crafts, the books I’d read and games I’d play. It’s something I’ve incorporated into the show set this season. I’m presenting the collection in the garden of the [Musée du] Quai Branly and have put in a screen to block out the sound of traffic, so it’s even more peaceful than usual. The audience will listen to music through headphones, so they’re in a music bubble, like the audiobooks I’d listen to as a child. [BS]: As part of my research I spent a lot of time looking in comic book stores and galleries and I was reminded of this story called Little Nemo in Slumberland that was published in the New York Tribune at the start of the 20th century. It's about a little boy who, when he falls asleep, has surreal dreams and at the end, he always wakes up in his room. We were allowed to use the comic as a print, so we played with the scale and used it on different fabrics, such as silk and lurex – we also did a plisse version. Like I say, the collection is called Slumberland, so I made military parkas cut from striped material reminiscent of bed sheets, and a big cocoon coat stuffed with goose feathers that could have been made from a duvet. There is another story that I'm very, very happy with. After going through the archive I found out that Jeanne was a big traveller. She went alone to countries like Egypt and sourced fabrics and embellishments there, like mukesh. Mukesh is a very rare [embroidery] technique now – we finally found a collective of about 25 women in India who are skilled in it – and we’ve used it to make a motif we call ‘the bathers’ on five grecian draped dresses, which took over 15,000 hours to complete. I love it because the [patterns] are essentially star-shaped studs; there’s no continuous thread, so the fabric can move freely. The motif itself is developed from a pair of balloon trousers that I found in an antique shop, designed by Crahay for Lanvin – a 20-year, bohemian period [for the fashion house] that is often overlooked. [BS]: Again, inspired by Jeanne’s trips to Egypt, some of the shoes are modelled on a pair of gold sandals belonging to an Egyptian queen that are part of The Met’s collection. The metal handle of one of the handbags, in the shape of a wild cat, is a nod to the handle of a fire iron that Jeanne’s designed in collaboration with a furniture designer called Armand-Albert Rateau. Together they designed the interior of her apartment and the Daunou theatre in Paris, among other things. [BS]: It’s not a statement about gender fluidity. Jeanne was the first Parisian designer to launch a made-to-measure clothing line for men [in 1926]. It’s just the way I think things should be done, and I think it’s how Jeanne would have done it. © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker Deepika Padukone attends Dior’s SS20 show in Paris in a printed maxi dress “We are migrants. column1: Did you know washing clothes could release microplastics into the ocean?
column2: © Shutterstock Fashion Microplastics are creeping into the deepest, darkest crevices of our oceans, and your laundry routine could do with an eco-friendly update in 2019. You only need to visit Mumbai’s beaches after Ganpati Visarjan to note the level of ocean pollution we all partake in—many of us already have pictures of the shores overflowing with litter and broken idols on our camera rolls. Every monsoon, the sea spits up tonnes of garbage along the city’s Marine Drive road, sending what was dumped in back out. Apart from visible pollution, the scary thing is that there are also innumerable tiny microplastics floating in what appear as some of the cleanest seas on our planet. These are consumed by all types of marine life including fish, prawns, sea birds and even whales. Most of the plastic in the ocean is actually in the form of these broken down shreds, which are full of toxins and less than five millimetres in length, and not whole items like cups and straws. They’ve permeated the deepest parts of the ocean all the way into the Mariana Trench, and have also been found in the bodies of fishes living in deep seas. Anyone who consumes seafood is effectively consuming these fibres as well, which means that microplastics are effectively working their way up our food chain. One of the biggest sources of microplastics is textile fibres. These enter our seas when we wash synthetic clothing in washing machines. Today, 63 per cent of the all the clothing purchased on Earth is made of synthetic fabric or a synthetic fabric blend. When washed, these textiles not only leach microplastics into the environment, but also absorb high concentrations of poisonous substances from the water around them. Unlike lint in the dryer, there is no filter installed in washing machines to catch the microplastics shedding into our water systems. Each wash load can release more than 7,00,000 microplastic fibres, and while some of these get caught in our sewage systems, others are making their way into the ocean. If we think of how many people wash their clothes daily across the world, the figures quickly get dizzying. While various companies across the world are researching textiles that shed less, as well as filters that will help your washing machine catch microfibres before they reach the ocean, no conclusive research has determined the way forward. However, here are a few things you can do to make your own contribution of microplastics smaller. The simple solution to this problem would be to buy natural fabrics instead of synthetic. But cotton comes its own production issues, like consumption of huge amounts of water. Meanwhile, organic clothing is often a luxury and not accessible to everybody. We must change our consumption habits and buy less so we’re able to invest in versatile, environmentally sustainable clothing, and use those pieces for longer. Addressing our consumption patterns not only solves this particular problem, but can positively impact a lot of environmental issues. There are also a lot of exciting developments in the world of textiles; fabrics are being made out of food waste, which could also be a potential solution to microplastics issue. Educate yourself so you can make wiser purchases. Since the microplastics are leaching into the environment through washing, re-evaluate how often you need to wash clothes. Not everything needs to go into the wash at the end of every day. Bras can be washed after four wears, T-shirts after two, leggings after three and you can wait seven to ten wears for a pair of jeans. Air your clothing out in the sun to be able to wear it multiple times before washing. How you wash your clothes can have quite impact on the amount of microplastics being shed. Research shows that front load washing machines shed less fibres than top load ones, so keep that in mind for whenever you are shopping for your next washing machine. Always wash when you have a full load as it causes less friction between the clothes and thus leads to lesser shedding. Wash at lower temperatures for the same reason. Line dry instead of tumble dry when possible. If you must use a dryer, set it at a low speed to create less friction. The Guppyfriend is a mesh bag made out of polymide 6.6, that catches microplastics inside your washing machine. Consumers are meant to put their synthetic clothing into the Guppyfriend bag and then wash it per usual. Afterwards, you need to empty out the wet clothing, take out the microplastics attached to the hems of the bag and dispose properly. It also reduces shedding by a whopping 86 per cent. While the website doesn’t ship to India yet, try and get your hands on it whenever you travel or alternatively request a friend to pick it up whenever they’re in Europe. Another option is the Kickstarter product, Cora Ball—the laundry ball catches the microfibres leaching out of synthetic clothes inside the washing machine itself. Cora acts like natural coral; it moves around the washing machine allowing water to flow while catching the microplastics in its stalks. After the wash, you have to remove the fuzz from the Cora ball and dispose it in your bin. The ball itself is made from recycled plastic and is fully recyclable. Apart from these actionable points, it is also important to talk about microplastics in the ocean because the problem is not getting the attention it deserves. Making noise about the impact of our fashion choices is another thing you can do to help save our planet while we still have the chance to do so. 5 ways to fix fashion’s biggest pollution problem: dyes Sorry, but not all cotton is eco-friendly. column1: Exclusive: Scott Schuman’s latest book is a tribute to India
column2: © Scott Schuman Fashion The celebrated photographer gives Vogue a first look into the pages of his newest book, The Sartorialist: India, which is a narrative on the country’s unique diversity as captured through his lens I first discovered photographer Scott Schuman’s blog, The Sartorialist, in 2009 as a fashion student researching a project on street style. It quickly became a daily fixture on my browsing history. I eagerly awaited every post, not just for the fashion inspiration but also for the personalised anecdotes Schuman shared with every picture—these coloured them with character much like an accessory would. In his 14-year career as photojournalist and street style documentarian with an anthropological eye and understanding of design, Schuman has certainly earned his stripes—a cult following, a career that spans continents, and a roster of A-list clients including the likes of Burberry, Levi’s, Tiffany & Co and DKNY among others. Last month, Schuman took to Instagram to announce his latest book, The Sartorialist: India. “I’m beyond excited to finally share the cover of my new book (…) Big cities, rural villages, fashion weeks, wrestling, music festivals, and simple street life are all a part of this book that I hope, in some small way, captures the exciting diversity and evolution of this wonderful country,” he wrote in the caption. For Schuman, this anthology is a tribute to his decade-long fascination with the country—a ‘passage to India’, as he refers to it in the opening pages of his book. Vogue India had the chance to preview ahead of its official launch in early October, and life came full circle as I dialled the New York-based photographer to discuss his latest project. Excerpts from the interview below. Scott Schuman: The reason was purely selfish—I like visiting the country! Before my first trip in 2008, I expected to see a typical India. But what I experienced was so different from anything I had seen in books and magazines. You can’t go to India once and say you’ve seen it all. You have to keep going back. And as I learnt more, my curiosity was piqued, and the idea for the book took shape in 2014. I wasn’t consciously shooting for it back then, but of the 300 pages, only about ten images have been seen before. India is changing quickly, and I wanted to capture this diversity before it became another typical world power. I wanted the book to be unlike any other I had seen on India; a representation of the country I saw. So it has traditional, old-school India alongside modern India. There was man I shot in the middle of a flower market on the edge of Kolkata. It was early in the morning and he had a sprinkling of glitter on his face. When I asked him the reason, he simply said, “Rave,” with a sly smile. I was not expecting that. There is no one India; you can’t box it. And the goal was to show this diversity. I don’t try to teach with the book; it’s not an encyclopedia on everything there is to know about the country. I just put myself in a lot of different situations, and shot the things that moved me and were beautiful to my eyes. I’ve been shooting in Peru, China and Africa too, so I wasn’t nervous about getting good shots in rural India. Though language can be a barrier, I’m very good at non-verbal communication. And once your subjects see your sincerity, it all becomes very seamless. The hardest part was finding good guides who were willing take me off the beaten path. I wanted to visit farms and flower markets, and they were so disappointed that I did not want to go to the regular tourist haunts and temples. Visual charisma. Their personalities could be big or small, gregarious or reticent, but there’s always something about them. The man on the cover, for example. I took that picture in the middle of nowhere on the outskirts of Jaipur. The hair, the sunglasses, the cigarette… he was sitting exactly like that when I walked by. He wasn’t surprised when I took his picture; it was almost like he was expecting it. Some guys are just cool guys, you can’t explain it. People tend to gush over the colours when it comes Indian fashion, but that’s so cliché! I feel you find all elements that are integral to design here—fabrics, colours, patterns and proportions. I came across a group of men wearing mismatched plaid (Madras checks) in Mumbai’s Crawford market—whether it was deliberate or not, the end result was very cool. In Rayagada, I photographed a woman wearing her sari in a regional drape. I know it was more functional, but the fall in the front was almost couture-like. My favourite thing about returning is never knowing what you’re going to find next. When you think you finally understand what you are seeing, another layer is revealed. With every answer, a new question is created, and by the time you’ve convinced yourself this will be the last trip, you’re already secretly dreaming of where you will explore next—the middle belt, which I haven’t seen much of, in my case! column1: “There can be no compromise on desirability”: Marine Serre on her upcycled SS20 collection
column2: © Jamie Stoker Fashion Vogue meets the French designer at her studio in Paris, to talk about why upcycling is integral to her ethos, why age is irrelevant and why beautiful design conquers all At the beginning of summer, Marine Serre moved into a new studio in Paris’s 19th arrondissement, which is quickly evolving into a hub for the city’s creative community. Not only did the move bring things full circle for the 27-year-old designer – in February 2018 she held her first show on the ground floor of the same building; the year after she picked up the LVMH Prize for Young Designers – it provided her with much needed additional space to expand her upcycling workshop. Serre’s eponymous brand is divided into three coloured lines: red (red-carpet couture looks), gold (artisanal daywear including tailoring) and white (easy, everyday garments). There was a fourth, the green line devoted to upcycled garments, but she phased it out, or rather absorbed it into all other areas. This season, 50 per cent of the whole collection is upcycled. “We have around 35 full-time staff now and the biggest team works on the development and production of upcycled pieces,” Serre says. “It requires a lot of people, time and space.” On a mannequin nearby is an elegant black tweed coat adorned with over 250 antique brooches; hanging on the rack next to it is a crochet top with elliptical seams cut from a tablecloth. Ahead of her SS20 show, Serre gives Vogue an insight into the latest collection. Obviously a lot of time goes into the sourcing of the materials, then we clean them, take them apart and design within the constraints of the material available. It’s an artisanal process, not as straightforward as going to find a roll of fabric or working with a print you’ve designed yourself. You’re almost working backwards, deciding what you don’t want in a collection rather than what you do; you have to be flexible. By comparison, the final stage, stitching together the pieces, is the quickest part. I have a full-time member of staff who works solely on sourcing materials. So I’ll give her a theme and she’ll go out and find a supplier or we’ll go together. It requires a lot of searching, a lot of time and a lot of people, and we rely a lot on word of mouth. For example, the driftwood for the jewellery came from a friend of my mum who goes beachcombing. Sometimes we’ll find things online or at markets, but the important thing is every element has to be traceable. I’ll travel to meet suppliers, but not usually further than France, Belgium, Germany or Spain because we require such large quantities. All jersey is made using recycled thread, but we don’t need to talk about that – it just makes sense. One design that we keep returning to since the second collection is the djellaba made from six upcycled scarves. You really have to use your imagination when you’re sourcing the scarves – these were all brownish in colour when we found them; pretty ugly and not something that you’d want to wear. The original prints are unique, so we combine designs that compliment one another and in this instance we dyed them red using natural dyes. We make sure that the edges of the scarves meet perfectly when we sew them together and work around any defects in the material. The back of the dress is closed with an upcycled chain so everything down to the trim is considered. This season we layered a pullover made from deadstock towels over the djellaba; I like to keep features that hint to the material’s previous life, so we kept the fringing and border or the towel. I’ve styled it with a pair of leather trousers – also made from deadstock – which I covered with a repeat print of the Marine Serre crescent moon logo using a UV technique to give an embossed effect. Every look is tailored to the model wearing it in the show. We start the casting very early in the season. Out of around 45 models, more than 20 work with me on a recurring basis. I've been working with Amalia [Vairelli], for example, for three seasons now, and this time she is walking with her son. There is a strong feeling of family in this presentation; Marie Sophie Wilson will walk with her son and daughter too. Character is very important to me, age on the other hand is irrelevant. From my childhood: I grew up in a village of about five houses in Corrèze [south-west France] surrounded by forest and nature. I like the term Marée Noire because it has different meanings depending on where you are from, it could be interpreted as black sea or black tide, which sound quite romantic, but of course there are darker connotations, too. It makes people think. While it’s important to me to produce things as sustainably as possible, I don’t want it to be the [sole] identity of the brand – there can be no compromise on desirability. The designs have to be beautiful otherwise what’s the point. Last season we started making upcycled jewellery. That was a real test because jewellery holds a lot of meaning and I thought people might find it strange to wear pieces from materials that aren’t precious in a traditional sense. It proved popular and so this season we have scaled up the number of designs. There are different variations of shamanic-style necklaces made from upcycled chains with charms – raw and painted driftwood, pieces of oxidised aluminium drinks cans, shells – and corresponding bracelets and hoop earrings, plus hair clips made from imitation pearl clip-on earrings like your grandma would wear. I like the bricolage effect, so it looks like the wearer has made it themselves. We inform our clients that every piece is unique and there may be subtle differences, but the composition is always consistent. Like I say, upcycling is an artisanal process making it difficult to scale-up output to tens-of-thousands, but we’ll take on that challenge when it comes. © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker Ever wondered what happens to your clothes after you throw them away? column1: Maria Grazia Chiuri shares the botanical inspiration behind her Dior SS20 collection
column2: © Jamie Stoker Fashion “A garden is something you make for the future, it literally brings oxygen into our lives. Creativity should be responsible – the environment affects everyone.” Maria Grazia Chiuri tells Vogue why SS20 at Dior is all about nature – from the arboretum show set, to the feminist energy of Catherine Dior It’s no secret that Christian Dior was enchanted by gardens. They informed everything from the silhouette of his iconic New Look in 1947 – the shape of an inverted flower – to the toile de Jouy pattern depicting flora and fauna that adorned the walls of his original store at 30 Avenue Montaigne in Paris. For her SS20 collection, Dior artistic director Maria Grazia Chiuri drew inspiration from the heritage of the French fashion house and the garden, but not in the way that you might expect. Instead of thinking in terms of ornament and decoration, she instead looked to Christian’s younger sister, Catherine – a member of the French Resistance who was interned in a German concentration camp during the second world war, and later became a gardener. Every gardener, from Catherine Dior to Vita Sackville-West, is known to have been fond of a hat, and in keeping with tradition they play a central, albeit suitably utilitarian role for Dior this season. “Gardeners need hats to protect them from the sun,” explains British milliner Stephen Jones, who created a bucket-style design for the collection. “The [hats for Dior this season are] made using grasses from Switzerland, Italy, the Philippines and France, so it’s like the United Nations in a straw hat,” he continues, echoing French botanist Gilles Clément’s description of the world as a “planetary garden”. Ahead of Dior’s SS20 show, Chiuri sat down with Vogue to talk botanical theories and research – plus her collaboration with an urban planning collective – which all inspired this season. Maria Grazia Chiuri [MGC]: Straight after the war, Catherine worked as a gardener and sold flowers in the market at Les Halles in Paris before moving to the south of France, where she lived with her father. When Christian bought Château de la Colle Noire near Grasse [widely considered the perfume capital of the world] his sister Catherine came here to plant fragrant flower beds of roses, jasmine and lavender. To have been such an active member of the Resistance and to then work in the garden, establishing her own business – this was not common at the time. Everyone knows the perfume Miss Dior, but not everyone knows the woman who inspired it. I decided to use this show to celebrate Catherine because I really believe that she was a truly modern woman. MGC: Christian and Catherine Dior’s mother, Madeleine, cultivated a beautiful garden at their family home in Granville, even though the weather there and its location overlooking the sea doesn’t lend itself to growing flowers. [Christian later wrote in his autobiography Dior by Dior that his life and style owed almost everything to the house and garden.] After the horrors of the second world war, I think they were both in search of beauty – Christian found it in couture and Catherine found in flowers and plants. MGC: The message in this collection is the idea of taking care of everyone, of the world we live in, just as Catherine Dior and other women in history took care of their gardens. All modern ideas of feminism talk about humans and nature and bringing these two worlds closer together again. MGC: Sébastien and I collaborated on another ballet this summer called Utopia, which was presented at the Origen Festival in Switzerland. The work was based on Monte Verità [the hill of truth] a very special place overlooking Lake Maggiore, close to the Italian border. At the beginning of the 20th century, a community of artists and thinkers [psychoanalyst Carl Jung, dancer Isadora Duncan, painter Paul Klee and novelist Hermann Hesse, to name a few] came here to create new work, but also be more in contact with nature. © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker © Jamie Stoker Watch the Dior spring/summer 2020 show live with Deepika Padukone Gucci just made the sunglasses chain summer 2020’s most-wanted travel accessory Watch the Bottega Veneta spring/summer 2020 show live Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Behind the scenes at the 2019 Paris Opera Ballet gala with Chanel
column2: © Lara Giliberto Fashion Vogue goes backstage at the opening night of the Paris Opera Ballet gala, to capture the dancers – dressed in reams of tulle, adorned with floral-inspired gossamer silk organza by Chanel – as they prepare to take flight The history of the relationship between the house of Chanel and dance is a long and bountiful one. In 1913, its founder Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel by chance saw a performance of Igor Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring, choreographed by Vaslav Nijinsky, the principal dancer of Ballets Russes. An introduction to the Polish pianist and patron of the arts, Misia Sert four years later would help galvanise Coco’s connection to the world of dance. One day, over lunch with Serts and Sergei Diaghilev – the founder of Ballets Russes – she learned of his struggle to find financial backing to revive The Rite of Spring, and decided to help. In December 1920, the production finally returned to the stage in Paris. It was not only Coco’s first act of patronage, but the first of many collaborations with the Ballets Russes. She created costumes for Le Train Bleu (1924), Apollon Musagète (1929) and, a decade after Diaghilev’s death, Bacchanale (1939) in partnership with artist Salvador Dalí. The contemporary designs, much like her fashion, focused on comfort and freedom of movement and were unlike anything the formal world of ballet had ever seen. Throughout his tenure as creative director of Chanel, the late Karl Lagerfeld upheld this tradition. He created the costumes for two ballets by the German choreographer Uwe Scholz (1986 and 1987); designed the outfit for Elena Glurdjidze in a 2009 production of Swan Lake – which took over 100 hours of craftsmanship; and, in 2016, at the request of the then director of the Paris Opera Ballet Benjamin Millepied, he dressed the Brahms-Schönberg Quartet ballet. On Friday 20 September, the legacy of Chanel and dance continued when, for the second consecutive year, the house created costumes for the annual Paris Opera Ballet gala. Under the direction of Virginie Viard, each of the six principal dancers performing Serge Lifar’s Variations wore a dress that embodied a flower. Rose, lily, tulip, wisteria, cornflower and violet were reimagined in gossamer silk organza by the House of Lemarié (part of Chanel’s Métiers d’Art), adorning the dancers’ bodices and frothy tulle skirts. “It’s a challenge for a couture house to create costumes for ballet dancers because we have so many requirements,” etoile Léonore Baulac says of the feat performed by Chanel. “A robe that has a lot of layers may be beautiful, but we have to twirl and jump, so it has to be as light as possible.” The opening night comprised classical as well as contemporary works by the likes of William Forsythe, with a score by James Blake and Rafael Bonachela’s Ab [Intra]. column1: Exclusive: First look at Shyamal & Bhumika’s Hyderabad store
column2: Fashion Here’s all you need to know about the designer couple’s first-ever store in south India Over the course of the past two decades, Shyamal & Bhumika’s couture identity has been constructed on a solid bedrock of old-meets-new. The designer duo has made a deep-dive into India’s sartorial legacy for inspiration, usually served against the canvas of their contemporary sensibilities. Today, the label enjoys an audience in the cultural hotspots of the country, with a retail footprint that boasts of flagship stores in Ahmedabad, New Delhi and Mumbai. The couture couple will now be looking at conquering the southern frontier with the launch of their first outpost in Hyderabad. Situated in the elite precinct of Banjara Hills, the flagship store is sprawled luxuriously over 5,000 square feet. In keeping with the design signature of the label’s existing stores around the country, the new space seeks inspiration from the havelis of Ahmedabad—a city close to the couple’s heart as it served as the birthplace of their label. Upon walking into the luxuriously anointed space, you’ll be greeted with the designers’ runway-ready lineup of womenswear and menswear, standing in resplendent glory against the intricate wall carvings envisioned by the duo. For the designers, the choice of Hyderabad for their first southern outpost was surprisingly simple. “The city is rich in culture and heritage, and people value handcraft which is synonymous with our brand. Our store is located in Banjara Hills, which serves as Hyderabad's leading luxury and lifestyle space. The market is also accessible to other cities in the south, making it one of the prime locations,” says Shodhan. The new space will play host to the label’s recent collections, including Memoirs of a Maharani and The Renaissance Muse. “The former is inspired by the sartorial splendour of the 17th- century royal courts, and focuses on a variety of rare embroideries like marodi, zardozi, aari, as well as beautiful floral vines embroidered in metal thread along the necklines and beautifully embroidered jaals. The Renaissance Muse collection, on the other hand, draws from the iconic period of Renaissance where art, architecture, music and couture were reborn from the medieval ages to relay a modern aesthetic. Intricate details reflecting the era have been showcased using the age-old craft of zardozi,” says the designer. column1: “We are migrants. That’s our philosophy in general, the line between representation and presence”: Telfar opens Paris Fashion Week SS20
column2: © Lara Giliberto Fashion The rule-breaking, New York-based designer Telfar Clemens and the brand’s artistic director and partner Babak Radboy talk to Vogue about crossing the Atlantic to create clothes that defy expectations On Friday 6 September, during New York Fashion Week, Telfar Clemens screened a trailer of a film he has been working on, The World Isn’t Everything, providing audiences with a glimpse of his SS20 collection. In collaboration with and starring a growing circle of creatives – from playwright Jeremy O. Harris and artists Juliana Huxtable and Petra Collins, to musicians Butch Dawson and Steve Lacy – the extended version served as the backdrop (along with live DJ sets and sound art) for the Telfar show, which opened Paris Fashion Week. “It’s not like we are leaving New York, the film is helping us be in a lot of different places,” the 34-year-old designer tells Vogue when we meet him and Telfar artistic director and partner, Babak Radboy, ahead of the show. “We don't really identify with any one place; we're not even at home in America.” Having a presence in two cities in one season, and once again defying the traditional runway format, is just another way Telfar is instigating change in the industry. As the designer points out, in establishing a black-owned, non-gendered fashion project in New York in 2005, he achieved what was widely considered impossible. Here, Clemens and Radboy trace the steps that brought Telfar across the Atlantic to the French capital for SS20. Telfar Clemens (TC): I’ve been wanting to do a show here since around 2008; Paris is the world’s fashion capital. And when it comes to sales, you can meet with the buyers the day after the show rather than wait weeks until they come to New York. As we found out, no one has ever shown on the schedule in two [of the Big Four] cities in one season before, because the FHCM [Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode] doesn’t allow it; we want to change that one day. For now, we’re treating the New York film screening as a kind of on schedule preview, while in Paris we’re showing off-schedule, but with the blessing of the FHCM. It’s like we are taking the Telfar show on tour. Babak Radboy (BR): We started producing in Italy for the first time this season, so we’re travelling back and forth from New York all the time. When you’re standing in line for customs you see almost every kind of person and every type of clothing. We made a list of the items we saw time and time again, and then set about abstracting them. There’s a whole T-shirt dress category, for example; pants that are half denim jeans, half track pants; a top that looks like a Metallica T-shirt, but it’s cut like a sleeveless 1920s wrap top; denim jeans that graduate into fishnet stockings; and slacks with a Budweiser printed cotton insert [the second consecutive season Telfar has collaborated with the American lager brand] that look like sagging pants with a pair of boxers. Producing in Italy and showing in Paris brought up different ideas and migration is part of that. But we don’t want to talk about advocacy for migrants, we want to explode the concept – we are migrants. That’s the Telfar philosophy in general, the line between representation and presence. TC: For Telfar. Not Sergio Tacchini or Michael Kors, it’s a T and a C! The idea behind Telfar is to take clothes that you can’t live without and make them our own. I wanted a pair of classic Seventies-style running shorts all summer, but didn’t want to have to carry a bag, so I made a pair with pockets built into the track stripes for a wallet, keys and phone. There are slacks made the same way. It’s about deconstructing existing garments, adding or subtracting, and then putting them back together. We’ve taken the thigh-hole jean – a signature cut for us – and adapted it for jogging pants. Our classic six-pocket pants (two front pockets; two back pockets and two pouches on the front belt loops) is in a denim-khaki combo for SS20. We also have a new shoe design done in collaboration with Converse; I call them “mandles” – the bridge is open but all those other parts of the foot you want to keep covered are covered. BR: Telfar shows are like a collective, they’re never transactional – we don’t pay artists to be a part of it or to wear our clothes. Jeremy O. Harris wrote most of the dialogue and he fed Ashton Sanders the lines through an earpiece; when you see Sanders speaking in the film he’s hearing and then speaking those words for the first time. At the show, we wanted this level of surprise and risk to play out in real time rather than it be a pre-planned brand statement. We don’t even know what will happen – it’s more exciting for the audience and it’s more exciting for us. We asked the DJ Crystallmess to live score the film and the British sound artist Klein to do vocals. Before we even knew what Petra Collins was going to wear in the show, it just so happens that she appears in the running order at the same time the part of the film she directed comes on the screen. TC: The whole film is an ongoing development. As Babak says, we don't want to control everything that happens. Now we’re hanging out in Europe and we’re documenting what happens as we go. We’d pretty much finished the collection in June in time for the menswear shows, then we did an open call to anyone who wanted to wear our clothes in a music video or TV interview and asked them to give us footage – that’s how the likes of Petra and Steve Lacy got involved. This kind of layering – like how Instagram works – is present in our clothes too, especially the T-shirt prints featuring last season’s campaign imagery and models who regularly walk in our shows, like Johan Galaxy. I don’t think you need to know that much about how it all came together; that’s the kind of work I want to create. Even if we’re not from the same background you can appreciate it and relate to it. © Lara Giliberto © Lara Giliberto © Lara Giliberto © Lara Giliberto © Lara Giliberto Naomi Campbell: “Models of colour are not a trend, we are here to stay” What does the journey of a million refugees look like?
