column1: A brief history of London Fashion Week
column2: © Shutterstock Fashion The youngest of the Big Four fashion weeks, London has produced a cornucopia of fearless fashion minds in its short 35 years. This is how it all began... Each of the “Big Four” fashion capitals exudes a very particular mood, from Milan’s extravagance and sex appeal to Paris’s refined craftsmanship. And when it comes to London, it’s all about fearless imagination, with designers who specialise in tongue-in-cheek rebellion, outrageous displays and the blurring of the lines between art and commerce. Or so the common narrative goes. Of course, none of these cities—which host innumerable designers during their twice-yearly fashion week stints—fit neatly into the categories ascribed to them; the reality is much more sprawling. However, there does seem to be something playful and daring about London’s fashion history. From the Swinging Sixties, typified by Mary Quant, Ossie Clark and Barbara Hulanicki’s Biba, through to Vivienne Westwood’s punk provocations and Alexander McQueen’s dark and dramatic visions, London has a long legacy of producing extraordinary design. It also has the youngest fashion week among its style city brethren, only officially starting some 35 years ago. Models at a 1962 London Fashion Week show © Shutterstock Various people have laid claim to setting the groundwork for LFW, including fashion PR Percy Savage. A gregarious figure who’d previously helped elevate the profiles of Lanvin and Yves Saint Laurent in Paris before moving to London in 1974, the Australian-born Savage staged his first London show, “The New Wave”, at The Ritz, which he soon followed with the “London Collections”,  featuring designers such as Zandra Rhodes and Bruce Oldfield, with Princess Margaret and Bianca Jagger front row. However, it was in the following decade that London Fashion Week as we know it today was born, with the creation of the British Fashion Council (BFC) in 1983, followed by the first official London Fashion Week in 1984. That same year saw the inaugural Designer of the Year award. The accolade was won by Katharine Hamnett, who later caused a stir during her infamous meeting with Margaret Thatcher when she wore a T-shirt emblazoned with the anti-nuclear message “58% Don’t Want Pershing”.  Hamnett got the result she wanted with Thatcher apparently squawking like a chicken and photographers capturing the moment. Former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher greets designer Katharine Hamnett © Press Association Images The first location for LFW was a car park. The Commonwealth Institute’s car park in Kensington, to be precise. Over the rest of the 1980s both this venue and Kensington Olympia would host designers from Ghost, to Betty Jackson, to Jasper Conran, to a young John Galliano (Kate Moss making her catwalk debut aged 15 at his 1989 show). London’s fashion scene at that time was hugely influenced by clubs, counterculture and forward-thinking design. Cult labels like BodyMap, with its distinctive shapes and use of diverse models, paved the way for much-needed changes in the industry, which even today some brands have been slow to instate. The establishment, however, embraced the scene, with Princess Diana holding a reception for various designers at Lancaster House in 1985, and often wearing British designers both at home and abroad. Helena Christensen walks for John Galliano, 1989 © Denis Jones Princess Diana with the Minister of State for Industry at a reception at Lancaster House, held for London Fashion Week © Keystone The 1990s proved to be a tricky decade for London Fashion Week. Economic downturn and waning interest saw the event reduced to a small number of designers showing at The Ritz in 1992. However, it was also a time that facilitated the emergence of names including Alexander McQueen and Stella McCartney, who put on their first shows in 1992 and 1995 respectively. For the latter, hers was unlike any normal graduate collection, with McCartney enlisting supermodel friends Kate Moss, Yasmin Le Bon and Naomi Campbell to walk for her. Kate Moss walking for Stella Mccartney © Shutterstock Shalom Harlow sprayed with paint by robots during the finale of the Alexander McQueen Spring 1999 show © Guy Marineau In 1993 Campbell also featured in a particularly memorable LFW moment when she took to the catwalk topless for Philip Treacy. It was the same year that, across the Channel, she tumbled over in British export Vivienne Westwood’s vertiginous blue platforms. 1993 also saw the establishment of the BFC’s NEWGEN scheme, supporting and nurturing emerging designers. Then in 1994 it was time for another venue change, with most of the shows moving to the grounds of the Natural History Museum. And even though London lost some of its key talent—McQueen heading off to New York in the late 1990s and various others headhunted by French design houses in the early 2000s—plenty more brands flourished, including Matthew Williamson, John Rocha and Julien Macdonald, who was one of several designers to capitalise on the public’s love of the Spice Girls by sending Mel B sashaying down his catwalk in glittering pink in 1999. Mel B of The Spice Girls walks for Julien MacDonald © Dave Benett With the arrival of a new millennium, Hussein Chalayan—already well-loved for his avant-garde approach to cladding the body—put on a show in which the background furniture was transformed into wearable attire. It culminated in the incredible sight of a model stepping into the centre of a coffee table that then concertinaed up into a triangular skirt. And, like those concentric rings of wood expanding upwards, the following decade marked an expansive and exciting time for new designers. From Christopher Kane’s neon-bright debut and Gareth Pugh’s gothic, angular garments to a whole host of other new names including Jonathan Saunders, Erdem Moralioglu, Mary Katrantzou and Roksanda Ilincic, London’s upcoming generation of talented garment makers secured its reputation afresh. Hussein Chalayan autumn/winter 2000 © Alastair Grant Christopher Kane spring/summer 2007 © Rune Hellestad And to top it all, in 2009 heritage brand Burberry returned from Milan to home soil, live-streaming its show to an eager online audience the following February. Other designers returning to London in 2009 included Matthew Williamson, Paul Smith and Luella, and it was also the first year that Somerset House hosted LFW, with shows among its handsome buildings and heels clacking over its courtyard cobbles. The move coincided with the rise of street style, with a handful of roving photographers quickly becoming an ever-expanding gaggle over the following years. LFW has had two more venue changes since then: first a short stint at another car park, this time in Soho’s Brewer Street, before settling at The Store Studios on The Strand. However, in line with other fashion capitals, in recent years more and more shows have taken place off-site, with venues ranging from Tate Modern to the Royal Courts of Justice, to custom sites like Burberry’s Makers House in 2016. And London’s prodigious talent continues to flourish, with Molly Goddard’s tulle and shirring, Matty Bovan’s imaginative flights and Wales Bonner’s intelligent tailoring among the current crop of designers making sure LFW remains a fresh experience every year. column1: Everything you need to know about the Indian craft of gota patti
column2: Fashion From its history to the techniques used, designer duo Sukriti and Aakriti Grover dish out all the details on this traditional handcraft While most believe that gota patti is the forte of Rajasthan alone, some also claim that it is, in fact, a form of Pakistani embroidery that originated in Punjab before spreading in popularity to neighbouring states. The handcraft is actually centuries-old, and was traditionally the domain of the royal family and members of the court. Today, it’s a must-have in festive and bridal wardrobes. Sukriti and Aakriti Grover’s namesake label champions this age-old craft, infusing it with a modern spirit without diluting its timeless appeal in their collections. We called upon the designers’ expertise to discuss what makes gota patti so unique. Excerpts from the interview below. Gota is basically gold and silver lace from Lucknow. This metallic lace is made up of metal-coated weft yarn, while the warp yarn includes ribbons of fibres like cotton and polyester. Small pieces of zari are stitched onto the fabric, with edges sewn down to create patterns. The zari threads are usually real silver, gold-plated or an imitation made with a copper base, and gilded with gold or silver colour. Gota ribbons are woven with a wrap of flattened gold and silver wire, and a weft of silk or cotton thread. This is then used as trims on a variety of textiles. Apart from traditional Indian wear, gota patti can also be found on turbans, rakhis, torans, home decor and juttis. Gota patti was only worn by royal families in the earlier times, but it has become much more commonplace today. This can be credited to the switch from gold and silver to gilt and lurex, as well as mass production of gota by electrically powered swivel looms in Surat and Ajmer.  Surface texturing and embroidery enhances the value of traditional textiles. Worn by Mughal and Rajput royalty of yore, gota patti is unique for its colour and intricacy of technique. As part of a bridal trousseau, an authentic gota piece can easily become an heirloom down the line. Gota patti is mainly used on lightweight fabrics like chiffon, georgette, tussar silks and crepes. The different forms of gota patti include seekhi, phool, bijiya, mothda, bakhandi and lappa, among others. Seekhi gota is categorised by a silver and gold ribbon of gota used as a lace trim, while phool gota spotlights gota circles that are pleated on the ensemble. The crafting of Gota patti is a time-consuming procedure. After tracing designs on paper, setting it on wooden frames, outlining the design on the fabric the  gota patti is attached with a back stitch, and finally securing it with a wooden hammer. Takaayi, which is the process of stitching the leaves to the base fabric, is the most tedious of all the steps. The time taken often depends on how elaborate the outfit is—a heavy bridal ensemble can take up to a week, while a seekhi work sharara can be made in half a day as well. Taking a closer look at the nomenclature, the ‘patti’ refers to the most important part of motif, the leaf. Gota patti involves folding tapes into pattis (or leaves), which are basically rhomboid units. These are organised into butas or a jaal to create a motif, which is later sewn on the fabrics. Popular motifs include peacocks, sparrows, paisleys, floral and geometrical patterns, human figures, palanquins, elephants and horses. In the gota tukdi technique, the gota is first cut into various shapes—gamla (flower pot), kairi (mango) or champak (flower)—and then appliquéd on the base fabric, adorned with embroideries like zari and zardozi. We use gota threads and stripes that are updated to appeal to a millennial dresser, and mix authentic old-world gota embroidery with modern silhouettes and colours to bring a balance of the old and new. We were also one of the first labels to combine this Rajasthan-based craftsmanship with Mughal silhouettes like shararas and ghararas. Our artisans are spread all over the country, including the hubs of Lucknow and Rajasthan. With the mechanisation of gota patti, hand embroidery has taken a hit, and that is the biggest woe for craftsmen today. Moreover, with younger generations of weaver families pursuing different careers, the craft also faces the threat of extinction. column1: Vogue meets New York Fashion Week’s next-gen star, Maryam Nassir Zadeh
column2: © Jamie Stoker Fashion Soulful fashion with a meaningful storyline has become a potent signature for Iranian-American designer Maryam Nassir Zadeh. Ahead of her New York Fashion Week show, she speaks to Vogue about the close-to-home inspiration behind her latest collection, and why we’ll all be channeling the MNZ brand of “mermaid chic” for SS20 With an emphasis on handpicked fashion that has a story to tell, it’s little surprise that New York-based designer Maryam Nassir Zadeh’s New York Fashion Week show is a firm favourite for Vogue editors in need of seasonal inspiration with soul. For SS20, she turns her attention to the sea, with a collection that tunes in to the power of nature and returns to a sense of home. Rather than models, Nassir Zadeh casts friends to wear her designs, a theme that’s more important than ever this season. “I want to go back to my roots,” she says, “with my muses being my biggest inspiration.” Here, Vogue speaks to the designer about her inspirations, ahead of her NYFW show. “For this season, the inspiration was taken from the sea and home and family. We took a lot of direct inspiration from the sea—plants, shells, seagrass and various iridescent, metallic and translucent textures. A little bit less obviously inspired by the sea are the woven surfaces, marbled textures, patchwork with nets, lace and foil, which is something new for the work. The mood of the collection is drapey, fluid silhouettes. I always do a combination of something feminine with something more masculine and clean, so there will be soft shapes and asymmetry with graphic bodycon. I was really excited about the Seventies safari theme of autumn, so I’m carrying that on a bit, but I’m going to fuse it with chic mermaids.” “For the jewellery aspect of the collection, I worked very closely with glass master Gennaro Pepe, taking direct reference from the Mediterranean Posidonia plant, which only exists on the seabeds of Ibiza and Formentera—two places that I have a lot of connection to, I’ve been going there since I was a kid. The name Posidonia is derived from Greek mythology and is inspired by Poseidon, the god of the sea. It’s one of the largest organisms in the world and [one hectare of Posidonia] produces five times more oxygen than a hectare of the Amazon rainforest. When the water is clear, you can tell that the Posidonia is healthy, because it can’t grow when it’s not clean. Gennaro himself is based in Formentera and he packs my jewellery with dried Posidonia plants.” “My summer wasn’t really planned, but it feels like it was very personal to the collection in an unconscious way. I didn’t spend as much time in New York as I’m starting to realise that there are other places that have become home to me. I spent a bit of time in LA, which has always been the epitome of home to me, but I was also in and out of Paris a lot this summer, where I now have a base. From there, I went to the South, exploring Cassis and Marseille. For the last part of summer I travelled to Formentera and Mallorca, where I return to the same homes each year as part of a summer pilgrimage.” “How I love to dress is often handpicked. I take a lot of inspiration from vintage clothing and things where you can feel the soul of the pieces. That also goes for the people that I pick for the casting that wear my clothes; and the references to the sea for this collection. The overall message [of my brand] is minimal dressing and effortless, handpicked layers, with style and quality and an authentic story – the things that you adorn yourself with, but that really have a story to tell which is coming from a deeper place.” “I really felt strongly about the casting for this season because the theme is home and community and family. I want to go back to my roots, with my muses being my biggest inspiration. For the last few seasons we were testing the waters of having more of the collection shown on models, to see how the pieces would respond, and it was a little bit heart-breaking for me because the whole point of why I love doing shows is that I love seeing real people in the clothes. My friends helped me to get started and they’ve always been a part of it—they were sprinkled throughout the last few seasons, but this season there’s going to be a stronger emphasis on my MNZ family, the people that have always been there and a handful of the newer people in my life. “I’m super proud that I’m going to have one of my favourite stylists in the show. Her name is Delphine Danhier, she was my first stylist and really helped defined the MNZ style. I love her so dearly as a person, I’m so excited to have her. I also have another newer friend that I’m very inspired by, Lily Gavin. She’s a fine artist and also an actress, one of her features, Giants Being Lonely, just debuted at the Venice Film Festival. I feel lucky that my friends will take part.” “There is an undercurrent of things moving and changing. ALL-IN, an underground studio and magazine will be holding their show in my store on Tuesday 10 September. The line is called Bror August and I feel like their work is some of the most original and exciting I’ve ever seen, I really believe in them. August Vestbø, the designer, uses found vintage garments, collaging them into one-of-a-kind pieces that look like paintings. It feels refined, but very artful. column1: Alia Bhatt, Sonam Kapoor Ahuja will inspire you to invest in anarkalis this festive season
column2: © Viral Bhayani Fashion From heavily embroidered numbers to printed versions, here’s how your favourite celebrities are wearing their anarkalis Along with lehengas, saris and sharara sets, anarkalis make for a non-negotiable part of most Indian festive wardrobes. The ethnic staple features a flared tunic style silhouette that is not only easy to manage, but can also be dressed up or down depending on the occasion. Whether you’re looking for an outfit for a wintery Diwali party of a summertime mehandi ceremony, anarkalis can help you make a statement no matter where you take them, all while keeping your hands free as you enjoy the celebrations. Celebrities have already proved the versatility of the anarkali, wearing them for everything from red carpet events to promotional outings. Alia Bhatt was spotted in not one, but two anarkalis during her Kalank promotions—an elegant off-white and gold anarkali by Masaba Gupta, and a deep purple set by Anamika Khanna, embroidered with delicate birds and flowers in shades of gold, pale green and powder pink. Karisma Kapoor gave her vote to an ivory anarkali by Varun Bahl Couture, serving the ideal inspiration for those who prefer muted hues, Janhvi Kapoor took an ivory and gold anarkali by Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla to the annual Umang Mumbai Police Show, and Sonam Kapoor Ahuja gave a nod to a high-necked all-red number featuring metallic details by Masaba. If you’re looking for something more dressed down, printed anarkalis will be best bet. Kriti Sanon took printed Anita Dongre anarkali in yellow to her Arjun Patiala promotions, and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan wore a red and black printed number by Rohit Bal for an event. Love florals? Aditi Rao Hydari’s black Nachiket Barve, featuring pink flowers all over, may just be the one for you. column1: The best street style at New York Fashion Week SS20
column2: © Jonathan Daniel Pryce Fashion As fashion month kicks off, New York’s showgoers are getting the last mileage out of this summer’s hero pieces: think silk pyjamas, cotton dresses and barely there sandals. Vogue photographer Jonathan Daniel Pryce captures the best street-style moments After a summer of style inspiration from Copenhagen and Oslo fashion weeks, international street-stylers are getting ready for the Big Four spring/summer 2020 shows in New York, London, Milan and Paris. As ever, New York Fashion Week SS20 (6 to 11 September) leads the way, but this season’s schedule sees a revamp spearheaded by Tom Ford as he begins his duties as chairman of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA), after replacing Diane von Furstenberg in June. A shorter week and changed-up time slots have made way for a whole host of NYFW unmissable moments: Vaquera, CDLM/Creatures of The Wind and Section 8 will present a joint show. Tom Ford, Ralph Lauren and Tommy Hilfiger (who returns in partnership with Euphoria star Zendaya) have brand-new spots on the calendar. And some serious anniversaries are being celebrated: Vera Wang marks 30 years after a two-year hiatus, while Becca McCharen-Tran of Chromat and Prabal Gurung commemorate a decade each. Navigating the new order will be editors and influencers from around the globe. As summer’s warm weather continues in New York City, we can expect that Scandi staple—the mellow cotton dress—to make a significant appearance, as will painterly silk pyjamas, architectural trench coats, supersized chain necklaces and barely there sandals. column1: Meghan Markle attended US Open in a denim dress worth Rs 9,000 (and it's already sold out)
column2: © Getty Fashion The Duchess watched Serena Williams in the US Open in an affordable denim dress, and even went for a public yoga class, channelling her pre-duchess days It’s easy to forget that Meghan Markle had a completely different life before she married Prince Harry and became the Duchess of Sussex. But, on occasion, the Duchess reminds us that she was, in fact, just a regular girl from California living a typical Cali-girl life filled with yoga, denim and trying to land a steady acting job. However, over the weekend, the Duchess returned to her Californian roots in more ways than one. People reports on Friday morning the Duchess left her husband, Prince Harry, and four-month-old son, Archie, at home and caught a commercial flight from London to New York to watch her good friend Serena Williams play in the US Open tennis final. © Getty Images Hopping a plane for a weekend trip to support a friend is exactly the type of move we could see pre-Duchess, Cali-girl Markle pulling. And, once she arrived she continued the trend of reverting to a lifestyle and wardrobe typical of her previous life. In a separate People article, after touching down in New York on Friday, Markle reportedly headed out to a public yoga class at Modo Yoga, a hot yoga studio in the West Village. Markle’s love of yoga is well-known, her mum, Doria Ragland, is a qualified yoga instructor and the Duchess has been vocal about her passion for the practice—a practice synonymous with the mindful, wellness-focussed Californian lifestyle. In fact, in a 2015 interview when asked how she stays in shape, the former Suits actress said yoga’s her “thing”. “My mom is an instructor, and I started doing mommy-and me yoga with her when I was seven. I was very resistant as a kid, but she [Ragland] said ‘Flower, you will find your practice—just give it time.’ In college, I started doing it more regularly.” However, since becoming a Duchess, Markle’s days of attending public yoga studios seemed a distant memory. Until she touched down on home soil that is. According to People, the class she joined was very full, with around 60 other people, and even though her appearance apparently surprised a number of the other participants, it wasn’t a surprise to the studio. “She has been going to Modo Yoga for years and tries to do so whenever she is in New York,” a source reportedly told the publication, adding that it was “the perfect remedy for jet-lag.” After her restorative yoga class, the Duchess then supported her friend, tennis champion Serena Williams at the US Open tennis final on Saturday, stepping out in a classic Californian-style wardrobe item: a denim dress from US label J Crew. The Duchess paired the dress with a AU$276 cardigan coat also from J.Crew and a necklace from Los Angeles jewellery brand Mini Mini Jewels reportedly featuring ‘M’ and ‘H’ initials, in a sweet nod to her husband Prince Harry. Refinery29 notes the AU$187 (approx Rs 9,200) denim J Crew dress is already sold out. According to The Sun the dress sold out on J Crew’s website in every single size a mere 12 hours after Markle was spotted wearing it—no doubt as a result of Markle’s powerful influence on fashion, the so-called ‘Meghan Markle effect’. The jacket is still available on the site, should you wish to purchase at least part of Saturday’s look. Yoga and denim dresses aside, it appears the call of California is so strong Meghan Markle and Prince Harry might be considering buying a place there. Vanity Fair reports there’s speculation the couple are thinking of purchasing a second home in California—their main residence is Frogmore Cottage in Windsor—and have “associates… checking out homes for the Sussexes in the Pacific Coast Highway area [of California], as well as around Pasadena.” After all, you can take the girl out of California, but you can’t take the California out of the girl. column1: Kaia Gerber recreated her mother, Cindy Crawford’s iconic ’90s look for her 18th birthday
column2: © Splash News Fashion Like mother, like daughter Kaia Gerber isn’t just any 18-year-old. Nor did she celebrate her birthday like your average 18-year-old would. Last night the model, who turned 18 earlier this week, rang in her born day with an epic fashion moment at the Edition Hotel in New York City. Gerber wore a custom Atelier Versace mini leather zip-slit skirt, a belt with the House’s Medusa buckle, and a bustier with straps criss-crossing across the chest. She finished off the head-turning look with a pair of gladiator heels that laced up to the knee. She was seen arm-in-arm with her friend actor Tommy Dorfman who was every bit the fashion partner-in-crime in his red knit shift dress and knee socks. © Splash News If Gerber’s bold look is giving you a major case of deja vu, it’s for good reason. The outfit is based on Versace’s Fall 1992 collection—almost a decade before Gerber born! It was titled “Miss S&M,” riffing on fetish wear, and featured a megawatt lineup of gorgeous supermodels. (Pieces from the collection were reissued for Versace spring 2018.) And while Gerber’s mother Cindy Crawford did not walk the Fall 1992 show, she did indeed wear a Versace bondage look to the MTV Awards in 1992. Talk about two peas in a very chic pod. column2: Fashion The runway will feature the TommyXZendaya collection, co-designed by Tommy Hilfiger and Zendaya After presenting a successful collection in Paris, Tommy Hilfiger and Zendaya are now set to showcase their fall 2019 collection at New York Fashion Week. The designer first collaborated with the actor and Tommy Hilfiger brand ambassador in spring 2019, and the two now be debuting the TommyxZendaya fall 2019 collection in an experiential ‘see now, buy now’ event at Harlem’s historic Apollo Theatre in New York today to celebrate inclusion, diversity and empowerment. The new collection takes inspiration from the marquee performers who have graced the Apollo stage over the years, including the likes of Aretha Franklin, Ella Fitzgerald, Patti LaBelle and The Supremes. The evening will also witness a cinematic ’70s Harlem twist, bringing Zendaya’s confident sense of style and optimistic spirit to audiences on site and virtually around the world. The new pieces will be available to shop across an ecosystem of channels in more than 70 countries, including Tommy.com, select stores and Instagram. column1: 13 best looks from Deepika Padukone’s Indian wear wardrobe
column2: Fashion From elegant Sabyasachi lehengas to heritage weaves, Deepika Padukone serves up an easy study in classics She can work them showstopper gowns and voluminous trains, but Deepika Padukone holds a special spot in her heart (and wardrobe) for the classic sari. Credit it to all the period roles she’s essayed on the big screen if you will, but there’s no denying that a part of the Mastani magic lives on in the twirl of her lehengas, and is visible in her stiffly pinned pallus, which speak of the oft-forgotten elegance of a bygone era. With the festive season around the corner, have a quick peek at the winning ensembles that Deepika Padukone has favoured in her ethnic wardrobe. As a bride, Padukone played with proportions, serving classic Kanjeevaram saris and exaggerated sari pallus with equal ease. Carrying a token of the festivities with her, the star channelled the power of bridal reds for the upcoming weddings on her social calendar. Case in point: the head-to-toe red sari Padukone was spotted in at Isha Ambani’s pre-wedding bash. Her go-to trick for standing out from the crowd? An eye for unconventional silhouettes—her Fabiiana pick featured an unusual pleated pallu, layered over a halter neck blouse and multi-tiered necklace. The hue continued to pull favour in her wedding wardrobe—the main wedding ceremony saw her juxtaposing the puritanical white of her sari with a full-sleeved blouse in siren red. For Priyanka Chopra and Nick Jonas’ Mumbai reception, she gave in to the allure of a classic lehenga, and found a winner in a showstopping black and gold number by Sabyasachi. She accessorised the look with a statement emerald choker and the suave Ranveer Singh on her arm, dressed in all-black as well. Those looking for ways to work coordinated couple style without entering matchy territory, take notes. Given the choice between a lehenga and a sari for a red carpet event, the stunner turns to the seven yards in a wide array of the country’s most prized weaves. For an award show earlier this year, she tapped into the power of tone-on-tone dressing with a chikankari sari by Rahul Mishra, teamed with a beaten gold blouse. Another social event saw her walking arm-in-arm with Singh to greet the paps in a silk brocade sari from Raw Mango. Drawing support from the label’s classic aesthetic, she wore the high-necked blouse with a gold choker and traditional floral bun. While Padukone has an unerring eye for timeless classics, when she does decide to experiment, she isn’t afraid to go all the way. For a recent conference on the future of fashion, she left the power suits behind at home and stepped onstage in a voluminous Sabyasachi sari in cheery hues of pineapple yellow. A closer look at the details lends further power to the sunshine colour palette—the pussy-bow collar of the blouse is complemented with billowing sleeves, while the sleek bun is rounded out with shoulder-grazing chandelier earrings and oversized Elie Saab frames. column1: 15 looks that define Priyanka Chopra’s signature style
column2: © Intagram.com/stylebyami Fashion From vintage Roberto Cavalli separates to the unconventional skort silhouette, you can never accuse Priyanka Chopra of playing it safe Whether on the red carpet or catching the red-eye, sitting down with leading women for a power conference or playing fangirl in the crowd for her onstage husband, Priyanka Chopra’s style is avidly watched on both sides of the globe. She can pull out a Mad Hatter-inspired maximalist look just as easily as she can work some 1970s-approved bell bottoms. With the streets of New York serving as her own personal runway, here’s what goes into concocting Chopra’s signature style. It is a universally accepted truth that a wedding is a woman’s biggest sartorial stage, and for her special day, Chopra went for the jackpot with a pristine white Ralph Lauren creation embellished with over 11,000 Swarovski crystals. The ensemble also included a strapless column gown underneath, detailed with over two million mother-of-pearl sequins. As the (literal) crowning glory, the star opted for a tulle veil that clocked in at 75 feet long, mandating an entourage of its own. For the Indian ceremony, she chose a red Sabyasachi lehenga, detailed with hand-cut organza flowers, French knots in silk floss and layers of threadwork. Her go-to stylist, Ami Patel, recalls, “The thing I love most about Priyanka is that she always puts me up for challenges—there’s always little time or something that needs to be done in two days. Needless to say, the biggest challenge she put me through is her wedding. One day, she casually messaged me the date of her wedding. I got really excited at first, and then I realised that it was going to a literal race against time to prep for the entire wedding in one and a half month. The entire process involved a lot of hard work, but putting together all the amazing couture looks in less than two months is one of the most satisfying things I’ve ever done.” When attending weddings as a guest, Chopra often looks towards saris, whether she’s opting for a sheer pink Sabyasachi drape for Sophie Turner and Joe Jonas’ lavish celebrations in France, or a high-shine silver number for a wedding in Mumbai. The Baywatch actor is no stranger to statement-making ensembles when off-the-clock either. Patel attributes her sartorial success to her refusal of playing favourites in her wardrobe. “Priyanka always moves with the times; she doesn’t stick to silhouettes or pieces that she was fond of a few years ago. She simply doesn’t have any favourites; she’s always up for experimenting, and I love how she puts thought into the event she’s attending and the outfit she’s wearing. In her off-duty wardrobe, you’ll likely find easy tops, cool jeans and interesting separates that she just throws together and makes it look effortless. Her inputs on how a certain piece should be worn means that I always take back something with me,” she reveals. At her recent birthday blow-out in Miami, the star of the moment could be seen cruising on a yacht in her latest find—envy-inducing printed separates, courtesy Roberto Cavalli’s archives from spring 2006. Coordinated sets occupy major real estate in her date night wardrobe as well. The actor showed up to support her husband on the sets of his next movie in a sheer polka-dotted maxi dress and matching cape from Sabyasachi, the bandhini print a subtle nod to her roots. If you were to bump into her at the airport, you’d likely find her in head-to-toe florals, while a shopping sesh with Turner calls for summery co-ords. Her love for edgy silhouettes means that it’s no secret she’s campaigning to make skorts a thing, and the half-short, half-skirt silhouette pulled in another appearance in her recent pick from Los Angeles-based label, Dakota Jinx. When she isn’t living the good life with the extended Jonas family, she can be found pursuing her manifesto for making formals fun again. In Chopra’s handbook, the 2019 update to this menswear staple includes silhouettes that are slouchy but never stuffy; businesslike but with playful proportions. The star looks to unconventional styling choices to lend support to her new vision for formals—the annual BeautyCon LA 2019 had her updating the classic pantsuit with a daring sheer blouse, detailed with a pussy-bow collar. Taking this structured silhouette out of the boardroom, she was spotted on a recent date night in a double-breasted blazer dress and PVC mules. Chopra’s discerning eye for non-boring OOTDs is usually served in a roster of statement hues, another crucial cornerstone of her sartorial domination. At a recent event for Bumble, she stepped out in a head-turning tangerine midi dress with sleek cape sleeves from Alex Perry. The conversation-starting hue earned a spot in her off-duty wardrobe as well, and the star was snapped on the streets of New York in a sunset-hued dress from Hellessy. column1: 11 contemporary saris for when your want to give your Benarasi collection a break
column2: Fashion From pre-draped saris to those that are worn with dhotis or jackets, these modern takes on the sari are nothing like you already own From watching our mothers drape their saris when we were children, to finally wearing your own for your high school farewell, saris hold an irreplaceable spot in most Indian women’s memories. But come adulthood, some of us find tying the six yard drape too troublesome, and reserve our sari collection for OTT festive occasions. What if we told you that you could enjoy the elegance of a sari without spending the entire day managing your pleats? Contemporary saris serve as the ideal solution—these often come pre-draped, thus allowing you to bring your favourite ethnic silhouette out from the back of your wardrobe without too much effort. Whether you are looking for something for your best friend’s cocktail or just need something for an upcoming Diwali party, there is a variety of pre-draped iterations on offer—choose between dhoti-style saris, sari dresses, sari gowns and more. Ahead, we list out our favourites to help you make a choice. If you want to make a statement at a friend’s wedding ceremony, go with Amit Aggarwal’s silver sari gown, or Tarun Tahiliani’s head-to-toe red number. You can also look towards Ridhi Mehra’s beige sari if your sartorial sensibilities lean more towards minimalism. Prefer something more out-of-the-box? Rimzim Dadu’s black sari comes with a futuristic molten steel-wire sculpted pallu in purple, Gaurav Gupta’s navy blue drape is paired with an unusual netted blouse, and both Masaba’s bright pink sari and Nikasha’s floral number feature dhoti-style bottoms. column1: What to expect at London Fashion Week this September
column2: © Jamie Stoker Fashion Public shows from Henry Holland and Self-Portrait, protests by Extinction Rebellion, and the ones you definitely don't want to miss: Victoria Beckham and Burberry. This is Vogue’s guide to LFW SS20 London Fashion Week is in a state of flux. As the Brexit deadline of 31 October looms, the British Fashion Council (BFC) warned that a no-deal could cost the fashion industry up to £900 million, threatening both the UK economy and consumers alike. In an official statement released in January, the BFC said: “We cannot emphasise strongly enough that a no-deal Brexit is a scenario that should be avoided at all costs.” The uncertainty of Britain’s political landscape isn’t the only big change for LFW SS20. This season also marks the first time that you can buy tickets to a select number of shows at London Fashion Week, with the aim of bringing the public and designers closer together. “It is a natural evolution of the format for this event,” explains Caroline Rush, CEO of the BFC. “The rise of digital and social media requires more transparency, authenticity and a new type of storytelling; what we’ve seen over the past few years is an increasing appetite for the public to go behind the scenes. By introducing public-facing shows to London Fashion Week, we want designers to reach new audiences.” Elsewhere, climate campaign group Extinction Rebellion will stage disruptive events, targeting LFW shows from 13 to 17 September and culminating in a funeral procession, which they’re calling London Fashion Week: Rest in Peace. “The UN Secretary General says we have until the end of 2020 to change course,” activist Sara Arnold told Vogue. “The fashion industry is completely out of sync with the crisis that we’re in, and if fashion week goes on next season, it’s going beyond that deadline.” Bobby Abley © Tristan Fewings/BFC Here, Vogue rounds up what to expect from London Fashion Week this season: Alexa Chung will show her current AW19 collection in public-facing runway shows at 10am, 1pm and 4pm on 14 September, while Henry Holland and Self-Portrait will show theirs at 10am, 12:30pm and 3pm on 15 September. Tickets start at £135, going up to £245 for a front-row seat, and include access to the BFC discoveryLAB art installation, the Designer Exhibition and industry-led panel discussions. While these are the first runway shows to open to the public, Anya Hindmarch has hosted public-facing immersive installations at LFW before, including her Instagram-friendly Chubby Clouds in AW19. This season, she returns with the Postbox Maze inside Brewer Street Car Park, Soho, designed to coincide with the launch of her new postbox bag. The event will take place from 13 to 16 September, and tickets are £12.50. Rendering of Postbox Maze © Postbox Maze Victoria Beckham (2pm, September 16)—who’s going from strength-to-strength since celebrating her 10th anniversary last year—and Burberry (5pm, September 16)—now in its third season under Riccardo Tisci—remain the two powerhouses on the schedule, drawing the global press to London. However, a number of LFW stalwarts are notably absent this season. Mary Katrantzou is showing at the Temple of Poseidon in Sounion, Athens, in October, and Peter Pilotto has moved his show to Milan. Skipping proceedings entirely are Ashley Williams and Asai. Meanwhile, Grace Wales Bonner and Eudon Choi have foregone shows in favour of private appointments, and Bethany Williams, who won the Queen Elizabeth II Award at LFW in February, showed during the June menswear shows earlier this year. © Jamie Stoker Korean brand YCH—known for its relaxed tailoring and feminine dresses—is making its London debut as part of the BFC’s partnership with Seoul Fashion Week (9am, September 17), while Jeremy Scott-alumni Bobby Abley is also showing at LFW for the first time (3pm, September 17). Also joining the official line-up for the first time are tailoring brand Eftychia (1:30pm, September 13), knitwear designer Apujan (8:30pm, September 16) and cult jewellery label Alighieri (8:30pm, September 13). YCH autumn/winter 2019 © Daniele Oberrauch Victoria Beckham’s hotly anticipated beauty brand, Victoria Beckham Beauty, will launch during LFW, while US designer and royal favourite Gabriela Hearst is celebrating the opening of her first London store with a party (8:30pm, September 13). Fashion photographer Tim Walker’s new Wonderful Things exhibition at the V&A, which opens on September 21, will also be fêted (7:30pm, September 17). Tim Walker Climate change rightly remains high on the agenda. The BFC is hosting a Positive Fashion Designer exhibition for the first time and will spotlight names including Ancuta Sarca and Duran Lantink, who are promoting sustainable practices. “It’s really important that we, the consumers, become more conscious of the vulnerability of our planet and the consequences of our actions on the wellness of the next generation,” Sarca told Vogue in July. Extinction Rebellion © Dan Kitwood Away from the catwalk, campaign group Extinction Rebellion, which formed a series of human blockades during LFW in February, is planning another round of protests this season. Highlighting the impact the fashion industry has on the environment, the group will host a funeral procession and a die-in outside 180 Strand, the home of LFW. column1: Clare Waight Keller and 2019 LVMH Prize winner Thebe Magugu in conversation with Vogue
column2: Fashion “I love the way he talks about his community, the women in his life and the details he notices about how they dress.” – Givenchy artistic director Clare Waight Keller sits down with 2019 LVMH Prize winner Thebe Magugu to talk about what being a designer means today On Wednesday 4 September, Johannesburg-based designer Thebe Magugu became the first African designer to be awarded the LVMH Prize. The 26-year-old was presented the accolade—which comes with a €300,000 grant and one-year mentorship—by Nicolas Ghesquière’s muse, Oscar-winning Swedish actress Alicia Vikander. The newly renamed Karl Lagerfeld Prize (formerly the LVMH Special Prize) went to Hed Mayner (aged 33) of Jordan. Following the event, Vogue sat down with Givenchy artistic director and LVMH Prize jury member Clare Waight Keller and Magugu to hear how the day unfolded and talk about what it means to be  a designer in 2019. What stood out about the finalists this year, Thebe in particular? Clare Waight Keller (CWK): “The finalists were fascinating this year because everybody had a very heartfelt story or an honourable cause. One [Bethany Williams] has a charitable message, several designers [Kunihiko Morinaga of Anrealage, Emily Bode, Phipps by Spencer Phipps, Williams too] were focusing on sustainability. That was the overarching theme that came across, everyone is so conscious about the environment. I think all of us on the jury, it’s something that's on our mind, but for so many of this generation, it's at the core of what they believe in, and how they start their companies. We definitely learned a lot from hearing their stories. “Thebe has such a clear idea of what he wants to achieve. I love the way he talks about his community, the women in his life and the details he notices about how they dress. He gives his clothes stories, and incorporates technology too. There’s a really creative force in South Africa that we don’t hear enough about and it really felt like he could benefit from the prize.” Thebe Magugu (TM): “There is no shortage of talent in South Africa, but the system—distribution and so on—fails us; that’s the reason you don’t hear more about designers from the continent as a whole. On a personal level, the area of Johannesburg I’m currently based in is quite dangerous, so I can’t really take people there to show them my work. Sometimes I'll be watching SHOWStudio and hear gunshots outside and I think ‘wow, my world is split’.” TM: “My mission as a designer is to have a global brand based out of Johannesburg. Rather than have a grand show, I’m going to focus on the structure of my business, so in the future I can do bigger things. I want to get a studio, finally, because I’ve been working out of my home, and hire some more people because, as I was telling Clare and the jury, up until this point, everything has been on my head except the sewing. I’ve had to do the accounting, draft patterns, cut fabric—you have to be so resourceful. Making ends meet—making something out of nothing—takes a lot of energy. Now I feel like am able to breathe for the first time since I started my brand.” CWK: “They have to be able to talk passionately about fashion, it’s amazing how many people there are in the industry without a thorough understanding of how it all works. I think the ability to tell stories through clothes and come up with interesting concepts is a big part of what designers do. Now everyone wants more depth, there’s more emotion in fashion than there’s ever been, so it’s very important to be able to communicate that.” LVMH has renamed its Special Prize for young designers the Karl Lagerfeld Prize in honour of the late designer. What are your favourite memories of him? CWK: “There were so many lovely moments with Karl. We first met around 2011 when I joined Chloé—he had of course been there as the creative head [twice, 1964-1974 and 1992-1997]. Even though he had been in the industry for a long time, he loved fashion so much, he had this way of talking about it as though it was new and fresh to him. He loved discovering new designers, so it was interesting being with him at the prize because he always had a lot to say about each of the candidates.” CWK: “I don't think anyone can function without social media anymore; it's such an integral part of everything we do. Whether you’re a singer, actress or designer it’s about getting to know your audience. As I was saying before, emotion is so much more important now, and what I like about the way Ariana Grande [the current face of Givenchy] communicates herself [via her digital platforms] is the way she is completely upfront about the way she is feeling—she’ll cry, she’ll tell you she’s had a hard day, she writes about it all.” TM: “I'm working with a company called Verizon, who are friends of mine, to create chips that are inserted into all my labels. When you download my app and scan the label, you can get all the information you need about that garment, from the lookbook images, to details about the fabrication, to the retailer who sold it, as well as the story behind the collection. I felt sad because there is so much work that goes into what I do that no one knows about. This technology will change that.” South African designer Thebe Magugu wins the 2019 LVMH Prize Clare Waight Keller unveils the spirit of haute couture at Givenchy Celebrities and muses gather to pay tribute to Karl Lagerfeld in Paris Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: After a three-year sabbatical, JJ Valaya is set to make a comeback with a new couture collection
column2: Fashion The designer’s new line, Tabriz, is inspired by the riches of Persia From Adele to Abhishek Bachchan, creative folk are no longer afraid to take sabbaticals to work on themselves and come out better at the end of it. Designer JJ Valaya is an excellent case in point among Indian couturiers. In 2016, he was attending some fashion shows in Delhi and came away highly uninspired. Despite being passionate couturier and revelling in his craft, he was no longer excited by creative evolution of couture. Instead, he was disappointed in what he felt was the then-prevalent attitude of trying too hard to keep up with the Joneses. The excitement he had felt at the beginning of his career, by stumbling upon new treasures like beads in the bazaar, the block printer in the gully, rich textiles and breathtaking handwork, had dimmed. “I had to face a harsh reality that after 25 years, I was bored of what I was seeing and quite honestly, of what I was doing as well,” says Valaya. “However, a quick hiatus, it turns out, is a wonderfully honest companion. It made me realise even more how intense my love affair with couture truly was. For me, couture is not just crafting clothing. It is a deeper emotion, an experience and a luxury; one that has the ability to alter how people feel about themselves. But it is also about being honest to oneself,” he adds. His latest couture collection is an expression of this love affair. Inspired by a mystical Persia from the 16th to 19th century, the collection—titled Tabriz after the one-time capital of the grand empire—is an ode to arts and crafts of that region and has three distinct lines each revolving around a specific theme. The first of the three lines comprising this collection is called Farsh, and draws inspiration from Persian hunting design carpets as well the Art Deco period. Think flowing ethereal garments in hues of midnight blue, teal and a golden mustard embellished with age-old crafts like metalwork, gota patti and vibrant threadwork. The second line is aptly named Naqshband, which means master craftsman. It channels the royal splendour through a floral pattern created in metallic threads and beads accentuated by delicately glittering borders, antiquated crystals and pearls. You’ll find silks, velvets and tulles in rich red tones and sage green hues in this line. And the third, Khayyam, has nomadic origins in Persia’s royal tent makers and channels their tribal aesthetic. Techniques like antique mirrorwork, rough cotton yarn and unusual appliqué are blended with signature Valaya prints. The palette for this line sticks to black, grey, and burgundy, and comes together to form a montage of raw yet refined elegance. Valaya is not new to spinning stories that are larger than life. The brand’s decades old tag line, The Royal Nomad, still rings true amidst the finery of the upcoming show. The execution, however, ushers in a regal simplicity that will resonate with modern, luxury consumers. So now when someone asks JJ Valaya, “What’s going to be new?”, he simply smiles back and says, “Me.” JJ Valaya Everything you need to know about the ancient craft of mirror work 14 couture moments that went down in fashion history What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Priyanka Chopra in Vogue's September Issue: “Buying a home and having a baby are on my to-do list”
column2: Fashion The global phenomenon has achieved more fame, more fortune, and things can only get bigger and brighter from here. As Priyanka Chopra settles into the role of Mrs Jonas, she tells Vogue India how she’s ready to live her best life Priyanka Chopra Jonas needs some help with her mangalsutra. She’s in the middle of a traffic-stopping photo shoot in Brooklyn, when Vogue’s guest editor and celebrated designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee steps in to give her a hand. He untangles the sacred necklace at a zebra crossing. We are in Park Slope, a leafy residential neighbourhood with rows of brick houses, indie cafés and the typical bustle of New York life—strollers, skateboards and the odd garbage truck. “Sabya, should I have Diana walk down the street with me?” she asks the designer, who is curating the shots. He smiles with approval. Diana is Chopra’s chihuahua-terrier named after the late Princess of Wales. “Diana is my princess,” she says proudly. “She was adopted and lives a grand life now.” And grand it is—the pup sleeps in between the actor and her pop star husband of almost a year, Nick Jonas. “I keep moving her to the side, but she keeps coming back to the middle. She’s so cute, you can’t help it.” A passerby recognises her and hovers by the set. “Can I have a picture with you and my baby?” he asks, nervously pointing to his stroller. Chopra Jonas smiles, stops what she’s doing and takes the baby in her arms. If you follow the actor on Instagram you’ll know that she’s always on the go. “My mother used to say you only have stamps on your passport but you haven’t seen anything,” she says. “So I’m trying to change that.” It’s a wrap for the shoot and our cover girl slips into something comfortable—a black breezy bandhini cape from Mukherjee’s 20th-anniversary show. I ride back to Manhattan with her as Diana settles onto her lap. “For me home is wherever I’m happy, as long as I have the people I love around me.” Her next stop is Los Angeles, a city she sees as a longterm option for her and Jonas. “I have homes in Mumbai and New York, which are very vertical cities. LA is more horizontal,” she says, tempted with the idea of a pool and backyard. The ocean and weather remind her of Mumbai, too. “Buying a home and having a baby are on my to-do list.” The Friday evening traffic across the bridge is slow but we catch a glimpse of Manhattan’s skyline as we pass a billboard of HBO’s Big Little Lies. “I still haven’t seen the second season yet, have you?” she asks. Her days off are saved for television and she’s been binge-watching The Office. “I just love the straight-faced comedy and really admire Mindy Kaling as a writer.” It was while she was developing ideas for her production company, Purple Pebble Pictures, that she decided to give Kaling a call and meet up for lunch. Two hours and two movie ideas later, the duo were well on their way to working together. In April their pitch for a wedding comedy was picked up by Universal Pictures. Kaling will co-star with Chopra Jonas and co-write with Dan Goor (of Brooklyn Nine-Nine and Parks And Recreation fame). “The story basically came from my wedding, where a bunch of Americans were exposed to this grandiose palace—the food, the family, the culture, the clothes and the comedy that comes with it,” she says. She is also proud to add that it’s an all-South Asian star cast, a minority she hopes to see more of in global pop culture. “I think people look at India differently because of Priyanka Chopra. It was stereotypically a land of elephants and snake charmers. She brings a freshness to this and we all feel a strong sense of admiration for her,” shares Mukherjee of his muse today. This year she’s reached No 19 on Instagram’s Rich List (beating Serena Williams and Bella Hadid), created content for her own YouTube channel, and is now writing her memoir. “If you say no, I’ll find someone who will say yes. I’m just that person. If I believe in it, I give my damn best and make it happen.” “Everything that I am today or am doing in America, I learnt in India. I’m just showing a perspective of it,” she muses as our car weaves through the crowded streets of Chinatown. Chopra Jonas started her film career after she was crowned Miss India and Miss World back in 2000. She was a nervous 18-year-old working with big names like Akshay Kumar and Salman Khan. “I didn’t know anything or anyone. I was yelled at by directors, I was thrown into movies, I was thrown out of movies.” On her dad’s advice—“the more you talk, the less you will listen and the less you will learn”—she shut up and listened. “I taught myself confidence. I learnt it’s what you do after failure that makes you a success.” “The space I’m in today is the most content I’ve been in a very long time, and I’m not scared to admit it,” she says. Her twenties were more anxious, she admits, but for her thirties she wants to focus on being more present. “I don’t want to be stuck running on a hamster wheel,” she stresses. She is now careful to carve out time for her personal life, swapping hotel room service for dinner and drinks with the crew. The sun is setting just as we arrive at her destination in the Lower East Side, where the Jonas Brothers are shooting a new music video. “Aren’t you tired?” I ask. “Nick loves it when I come by,” she shrugs happily. She scoops up Diana and adjusts her leash before the paparazzi spot her. Once again, she stops traffic, crossing the road in a whirlwind of polka dots. She’s about to meet her husband after a long day of work and there’s no place else she’d rather be. column1: The fashion world remembers Peter Lindbergh
column2: © Jim Rakete Fashion “Peter was an extraordinary artist—a visionary who could capture the true essence of a person in a single frame”. Here, those who knew him share with Vogue their personal tributes to the extraordinary talent of Peter Lindbergh Peter Lindbergh passed away peacefully during the night of Tuesday, September 3, leaving behind a formidable legacy. A true master of his medium, Lindbergh forever changed both the course of fashion photography and the artistic representation of women. For the female collaborators who became the subjects of his work over the past four decades, Lindbergh was an empathic friend, cherished for capturing their truth. The timeless beauty of Lindbergh’s images are a credit to the kindness he bestowed on those who stepped in front of his lens. Here, those who knew him share with Vogue their personal tributes to the extraordinary talent of Peter Lindbergh. Kate Winslet photographed for Vogue Italia © Peter Lindbergh (courtesy Peter Lindbergh, Paris) “I know I am not alone in weeping tears of genuine heartbreak that this world has lost one of the greatest spirits ever to have graced us with his magnificent presence. Peter was a friend to everyone. He was loved deeply and sincerely by us all. He somehow made everyone feel as though the relationship they had with him was unique. He really had that magic. He had time for everyone. He would always ask how my family were, no matter how recently I had seen him, he would ask again! He was invested in the people he photographed in a way that made us all feel appreciated and noticed, for who we truly are on the inside. He hated makeup! He only photographed the truth, and he had the courage to preserve it. Because he was fascinated by the truth. He adored and celebrated women. His kindness cannot be compared. His energy was the definition of effervescent. “Nobody could come close to his extraordinary photography. Peter was truly a lovely lovely man. There was just nobody like him. Nobody. My thoughts go out to his family who have lost a beautiful gigantic heart." “Peter and I had an instant connection and friendship. I will always remember our time together with great pride and happiness to have experienced a true master like him. He was kind, gentle, and encouraging. It was an honour to have met and worked with him and this is a great loss to our creative community and the world. Rest in peace, sweet legend.” “Peter was an extraordinary artist—a visionary who would capture the true essence of a person in a single frame. A remarkable and rare talent, but more than that, a truly warm and generous man. A shoot with him was never work, but simply joyful, and knowing you were in the care of a true master. I will miss him greatly.” “Peter grew up not that far from me in Germany. We understood each other immediately. His contrast photography, black-and-white pictures often reminded me of the Ruhrpott area. He was an amazing family man, always positive and gentle. Never played games—he was straightforward and honest. He loved women and made everyone look beautiful. I will miss him.” “Peter has taken pictures of me since I was 16 years old. He has been part of my career since the absolute beginning. I have always thought of Peter as family. I felt protected in his company and absolutely adored those stunning black and white images that expressed women’s strength through their eyes. He was capable of capturing people’s soul [in an image].” “I remember shooting with Peter in Paris January of last year. He was one of the first people who I believe truly saw who I was beneath everything. He made me feel so comfortable, and I will forever cherish the confidence he gave me to be myself. Peter was a light in everyone’s life, and I am just one of the lucky people who he shined on.” Cindy Crawford photographed for Vogue Italia © Peter Lindbergh (courtesy Peter Lindbergh, Paris) “Peter was one of those photographers that when I saw his work with Christy [Turlington] or Linda [Evangelista] it would make me envious that I hadn't been photographed... I'd be like, well, why didn't I get that shoot...?! It was because of the way that Peter captured women. It wasn't about the hair or the clothes—all that fell away—it was about the woman wearing the clothes. “I think his real love of women showed in the way that he photographed; he wasn't looking for flawless perfection, he saw the beauty in you. I loved the cover for British Vogue with Christy, Linda and I, and Tatjana and Naomi. It was so iconic in many ways. As was the motorcycle series for American Vogue, when we were wearing biker hats and big, silly, leather jackets. Peter offered a very pared down, modern way to see women coming out of the 1980s, he launched that idea of beauty for the 1990s. “One of my favourite pictures I did with him was in Miami; I was wearing just black pants and a black shirt, sitting on the beach. But it's that gorgeous black-and-white lighting. It's real, but it's a beautified real. There's no other photographer that's even kind of like Peter Linderbegh. His work is identifiable and if you want to get a Lindbergh picture then for sure you needed to get Lindbergh to do it. He understood lighting in a different way. He loved a cloudy day. He also knew how to bring light into a subject's eyes. “On a shoot, Peter never sped through the day or rushed you through lunch. He'd wander in when you were in hair and makeup, later you would sit down and you'd eat together and have a proper catch up. It was the best type of photoshoot. He talked about his kids and would show you pictures, and as much as he showed himself as a full person, not just a photographer, he also wanted to know you as a full person too. “I don't think anyone can talk about Peter without talking about his personality. He was like a big teddy bear. You felt safe; you were in the best hands possible and I remember feeling really comfortable. He wasn't looking for the facade of beauty; he not only saw inner beauty, but he was able to photograph that. And if I knew how he did, I would do it myself! That was his magic. “The last time I shot with him was with my husband and kids. Although Kaia was just starting out and my husband doesn't like to be in front of a camera, I just knew that Peter would make it such a great day for all of us. And I am so thankful to have those images now. It was my Christmas card that year! A Peter Lindbergh family portrait! It was amazing. “Before Kaia works with a photographer, I've always encouraged her to look at their images so she can at least try and speak the same language during a shoot. When you look at enough Lindbergh pictures you understand that there is a soulfulness. [Before Kaia shot with him the first time] I would have told her not to worry, that he's a sweetheart, that you'll look amazing, but real—you will look like you. Peter made you look like the best version of yourself.” Fashion Mode Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: German fashion photographer Peter Lindbergh’s most iconic Vogue covers
column2: Fashion From Anna Wintour’s first American Vogue, to that iconic 1990 supers portrait for British Vogue, we take a look back at the late Peter Lindbergh's most standout covers over the years Peter Lindbergh officially entered the Vogue fold back in 1988, when Anna Wintour asked him to shoot her first cover for American Vogue’s November issue, starring Israeli model Michaela Bercu. Two years later, he went on to shoot the iconic January 1990 cover of British Vogue, which propelled Linda Evangelista, Tatjana Patitz, Naomi Campbell, Christy Turlington and Cindy Crawford to supermodel status. Since then, countless covers have followed, with the prolific photographer shooting for Vogue titles across the world over four decades. This year alone, Lindbergh shot Penélope Cruz and Rosalía for Vogue Spain’s April and July issues; Gigi Hadid for the March issue of Vogue Arabia; and models Luna Bijl, Birgit Kos and Vittoria Ceretti for Vogue Germany’s tribute to Karl Lagerfeld in July. He was also selected to shoot the cover of British Vogue’s September issue, guest-edited by the Duchess of Sussex and starring 15 forces for change, including climate activist Greta Thunberg and New Zealand’s prime minister Jacinda Ardern. Following the news of Lindbergh’s death on September 3, 2019, we take a look back at his most iconic Vogue covers of all time. column1: How Alia Bhatt, Deepika Padukone and more are acing the thigh-high slit
column2: © Viral Bhayani Fashion A favourite fashion move with celebrities right now, the leg reveal is a great way to make a statement, whether on the red carpet or off. Read on for lessons from Bollywood's best Turns out, grabbing attention on a night out isn’t always about short hemlines or bold colours—sometimes, less is more. Enter the sexy slit: the peekaboo detail that instantly adds a sultry spin to any look by giving just a hint leg or thigh without being overtly flashy. A slinky number with a slit is a fail-safe recipe for a head-turning look—just look to Deepika Padukone, Kareena Kapoor Khan and Karisma Kapoor for proof. Scroll ahead to take inspiration from their style. Whether it was Deepika Padukone’s black and white gown at Cannes Film Festival 2019 or Priyanka Chopra’s headline-making gown at the Met Gala 2019, it's safe to say that slits were a hit at the international red carpets. While former wore a white gown by Peter Dundas that showed off her legs till her knees, latter took the trend a step further in a custom Dior that featured a bolder slit. But it's not just the big red carpet events you can spot this trend at. Take a closer peek at Kiara Advani and Sonakshi Sinha’s recent looks for example—while Advani wore a dress that came with a thigh-high slit by designer Prabal Gurung for Kabir Singh’s success party, Singh embraced a floral maxi number for a day out in Mumbai. Even Malaika Arora is a big fan. Be it the bright yellow gown by Los Angeles-based designer Iris Serban or the white Toni Maticevski skirt she wore on the sets of Dance India Dance, the actor never misses a chance to show off her toned legs. Other takers of the trend include the Kapoor sisters, who are often seen favouring gowns featuring thigh-high slit. Convinced to try the trend? column1: South African designer Thebe Magugu wins the 2019 LVMH Prize
column2: © Getty Fashion Other notable awardees include Tel Aviv–based designer Hed Mayner, who claimed the first-ever Karl Lagerfeld Prize Thebe Magugu, the South African designer based in Johannesburg, has won this year’s LVMH Prize. The award comes with 3,00,000 Euro (approx Rs 2.3 crore) and a year’s worth of mentoring from the group. Alicia Vikander, a face of Louis Vuitton, presented Magugu with the honour. “The talent in this room is quite simply stupefying, and the finalists represent the future of fashion.” For two weeks now, those who follow fashion’s up-and-comers have been quietly snapping up pieces by LVMH Prize finalists on 24S, the e-commerce site of France’s Le Bon Marché department store, allowing the first-time finalists to get a head start on such an international showcase. This is why, at the 24S fête hosted at Lapérouse last night, Thebe Magugu felt validated just seeing the DJ wearing his blouse (she wasn’t the only one, either). It was pretty enjoyable stuff for a first trip to Paris—plus the Johannesburg-based womenswear designer just turned 26 last Sunday, making him the youngest of this year’s finalists in addition to being the first talent from Africa to land in the finals. “It’s a lot of firsts,” Magugu allowed, noting that while he had long followed the Prize on Instagram, he almost put off his application until next year. “As a creative you’re always questioning yourself, but people around me told me there was no harm trying. I went into it like a child, and got the chance to speak to my design heroes like Clare Waight Keller and Nicolas Ghesquière. So no matter the outcome, I already felt like I’d won so many things.” Nodding to his trophy, he added, “This is like the cherry on top.” Said Delphine Arnault, the executive vice president of Louis Vuitton and the founder of the LVMH Prize, “The creativity of his designs is great—the colours, the cuts, it’s very feminine. We saw the talent, and we also saw the challenges—in export for example. It’s great to find talent with a huge potential.” This year, more than 1,700 candidatures flowed in from 100 countries. In addition to his 3,00,000 Euro winnings, Magugu will receive one year of business mentoring from LVMH. But that doesn’t mean he will be uprooting himself to Paris—quite the contrary. “My overarching mission as a designer is to showcase a contemporary South Africa,” he said. “So many people have stale ideas of what that means and I really want to change that. There are so many creatives doing incredible work in South Africa. I’m looking forward to traveling but I really want to stay there because it feeds my own creativity.” In another fashion milestone, the Tel Aviv–based designer Hed Mayner claimed the first-ever Karl Lagerfeld Prize—1,50,000 Euro (approx Rs 1.2 crore) plus a year of mentoring—for his crossover-friendly menswear. “It feels like an illusion, a bit,” Mayner offered. “This support means less isolation, so the team can focus on creativity.” Lagerfeld’s absence loomed large inside the Fondation Louis Vuitton. “Karl was really part of the Prize since day one; he put all of his energy, goodwill, and kindness into it,” noted Arnault. “He would always show up to see everyone’s work and encourage them even if he had his own show two days later. He would make jokes on the jury and he had huge culture, he knew all the references. We miss him a lot. Fashion misses him a lot. The Prize won’t be the same without him.” Three fashion students were also recognised with winnings of 10,000 Euro (approx Rs 8 lakh) each and internships in LVMH houses: Alice Paris, a graduate of the Accademia Costume and Moda in Rome; Daisy Yu, a graduate of Central Saint Martins; and Juliette Tréhorel, of the Atelier Chardon Savard will spend the next year working at Givenchy, Louis Vuitton, and Christian Dior, respectively. column1: Peter Lindbergh, a much-loved member of the Vogue family, has passed away at the age of 74
column2: © Getty Fashion The renowned German photographer, who rose to fame in the late 1980s and was best known for his cinematic portraits and iconic Vogue covers, has died at the age of 74 A true visionary, and a much-loved member of the Vogue family, German photographer Peter Lindbergh has sadly died at the age of 74. The news was confirmed by his agent directly with Vogue and announced on his Instagram page: “It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Peter Lindbergh on September 3rd 2019, at the age of 74. He is survived by his wife Petra, his first wife Astrid, his four sons Benjamin, Jérémy, Simon, Joseph and seven grandchildren. He leaves a big void.” Lindbergh was born in Leszno, Poland, and raised in Duisburg, Germany, before moving to Paris, France in 1978, when he began working internationally for Vogue. Known for his cinematic portraits, he rose to fame during the late 1980s, when he photographed a group of rising models—set to become supers—in white shirts for American Vogue in 1988. His shoot for British Vogue in 1990, featuring Naomi Campbell, Cindy Crawford, Linda Evangelista, Tatjana Patitz and Christy Turlington, has become one of the most iconic Vogue covers of all time. This year alone, he’s photographed covers for Vogue Spain, Vogue Germany, Vogue Arabia and L’Uomo Vogue; and most recently he shot British Vogue’s September issue, guest edited by the Duchess of Sussex. The photographer was famed for never retouching his images—ensuring the magazines he worked with signed contracts to agree to this. Sharing his non-negotiable stance on letting his subjects be freely portrayed, without conforming to societal pressures, Lindbergh wrote in his 2015 book, Images of Women II (Schirmer Mosel): “If photographers are responsible for creating or reflecting an image of women in society, then, I must say, there is only one way for the future, and this is to define women as strong and independent. This should be the responsibility of photographers today: to free women, and finally everyone, from the terror of youth and perfection.” Fashion Mode How To © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The top 10 trends the FROW will be wearing at fashion month
column2: © Søren Jepsen Fashion From vegan leather trousers to architectural trench coats, here’s what the industry’s best dressed will be seen in this September Power down your suit blazer with slouchy jeans, invest in a pair of vegan leather trousers and summon your trench coat out of storage. Fashion month kicks off with NYFW on September 6, 2019, and this is your insider guide to what the front row will be wearing. A modern, show-stopping FROW look is a four-part act. This September, our bets are on fashion editors sporting supersized chain necklaces (think JW Anderson’s oversized choker), textured knit, roomy faux leather pants (we love the Mitsu style by Nanushka) and barely-there sandals (by–it probably goes without saying–Bottega Veneta). Extra points for the zero-fuss elegance of a sculptural handbag. © Søren Jepsen While prim shirtwaisters and balloon-sleeve dresses owned last season, the mood has loosened up for September. Come autumn, the fresh cotton shirt dress is going up-tempo thanks to futuristic accessories (including meticulously sourced, vintage running sneakers). © Getty Images Mute the #EndOfSummer social media outpouring; there are some perks to entering the new season. Plaid checks are the preserve of autumn and there’s a back-to-school quality about those reassuringly neat gridlines. A quick tip from the FROW? Buck tradition with boxy silhouettes and lightweight fabrics. © Søren Jepsen Summer 2019 saw our feeds dominated by CHA-NEL emblazoned mules, and co-ordinated crop tops and miniskirts. And the not-so-surprising news is, our collective love of Karl Lagerfeld’s nostalgic logomania isn’t going anywhere. Our in-depth celebrity wardrobe analysis indicates that the Chanel belt will continue to be the most covetable accessory for the FROW, paired with baggy jeans and an hourglass blazer. © Getty Images There’s a lot we’d like to borrow from Vogue Ukraine fashion director Julie Pelipas’ infinitely desirable minimalist wardrobe, but right now we are focusing on the razor-front vest. For Pelipas, sporting a tank top is about nonchalance; she wears her Alaïa vest backwards, accentuating her shoulders and inspiring her legions of followers to do the same. © Getty Images Heads up: you’re still going to be hearing a lot of talk about trench coats this season. In fact, you’ll probably hear more on the trench coat than ever before, as fashion editors get their hands on JW Anderson and Bottega Veneta’s iterations of the classic heritage cover-up. Google Meryl Streep and Audrey Hepburn for a cheat sheet on the FROW’s secrets for styling the trench now. It looks best when worn as a dress, with a pair of knee-high boots or clashing leather mules. © Getty Images There’s a lot of fashion happening in this photo, but today we’re going to focus on the winged-collar shirt and oversized blazer worn by Spanish influencer María Bernad (centre). On the bottom half, Bernad is wearing ultra-casual jeans. On the top half, she’s neatly suited. The beauty of this look lies in the blend of two entirely contrasting moods, something we’re expecting to see a lot during fashion month. As the saying goes, get you a girl that can do both. © Getty Images The mini dress (seen here on stylist Lotta Volkova) has been relegated to the sidelines during the past few years, with even Hedi Slimane moving away from abbreviated hemlines in favour of the bourgeois midi skirt. Well, not this season. The FROW’s go-to modest day dresses are facing new competition from the devil-may-care attitude of the retro party dress. As Volkova’s fit-and-flare Miu Miu style suggests, the time has come to return to a mood of rebellious fun. © Getty Images The forward-thinking Scandi style set have their sights on a retiree chic wardrobe for autumn. Their new season mindset sees empowered under-35s putting comfort first, flipping the condescension once attached to OAP fashion on its head. On the FROW this month, look out for a series of silken grandmother-esque headscarves worn in honour of the recently freed A$AP Rocky; and ergonomic footwear labels in step with luxe sneaker brands. © Getty Images Fashion month officially kicks off with NYFW on September 6, where fashion editors will be getting extra style mileage out of their favourite vintage summer dresses, before the weather cools off. The added bonus? Lightweight dresses mean no checked-in luggage, which is something of a badge of honour among the FROW who a) have phobias of airlines losing their bags, and b) seek to avoid any association with the cliché of the laden-down shopaholic fashion editor. © Getty Images The enduring appeal of the trench coat, and how to wear it now A Chanel loyalist pays her tribute to the late Karl Lagerfeld 14 designers whose fashion is out of this world, literally What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast
