column1: Gaurav Gupta launches a jewellery line to celebrate 15 years in the industry
column2: Fashion Gaurav Gupta Occasions Fine Jewellery stays true to the brand’s ethos of nature-inspired designs with architectural construction Gaurav Gupta is in the middle of client consultations when we reach his flagship store in Mumbai’s Kala Ghoda—he is busy customising wedding outfits for an entire family, even as a steady stream of couples continue to trickle in for face time with him. The Delhi-based designer is in the city for the launch of his couture 2019 collection, ‘Undercurrent’, which was first showcased at FDCI India Couture Week last month. “The language of the brand has evolved so much, and we are now viewing couture through a more refined lens. It’s an achievement to be able to convey that in a simplistic way, without compromising on the scientific construction we are associated with. So the entire collection is confident and celebratory,” Gupta tells us as we settle down in the store housing his sari gowns and pantsuits. The collection is monumental for many reasons—it not only celebrates 15 years of his eponymous label, but also extends his existing menswear line into couture, and marks the launch of his first-ever jewellery brand. So what prompted Gupta to venture into fine jewellery? “On seeing pictures of my brides from their wedding events, I often felt they would get everything—the hair, the makeup, even the decor—right. But the jewellery just wouldn’t complement the outfit, often lacking a keen aesthetic,” explains Gupta. Thus was born Gaurav Gupta Occasions Fine Jewellery (in partnership with Occasions Fine Jewellery), to create an authentic jewellery brand with a strong philosophy and design process. “From our clothes and our stores to the entire Gaurav Gupta experience, I’m obsessive about design and attention to detail. The same extends to this jewellery line too,” Gupta says. Staying true to the brand’s signature ethos, the jewellery is also deeply rooted in elements from nature. The 50-piece launch collection is centred around distinct capsuled themes, and uses high-quality diamonds and precious stones hand-made in a specially-crafted white gold mould. Considering Gupta’s preference for necklaces that sit on the nape of the neck over long haars, the showstopper piece—the Liberation necklace from the ‘Feather Collection’—has been designed in the shape of interwoven wings to mimic a bird taking flight. Painstakingly crafted using 8,000 rose-cut and full-cut diamonds, it took over eight months to create. “Normally artistic jewellery is very stiff. But these pieces are lightweight and flexible. They allow movement. It is very technically engineered fine jewellery,” adds Gupta. The line also includes the ‘Forest collection’, featuring ear cuffs fashioned after exotic creepers and vines, and the ‘Infinity Collection’, which uses special-shaped diamonds, of which the sculpted statement rings are a highlight. “The entire collection is trousseau and event-friendly. You can wear it for your wedding, and then also to a gala in Monaco, a Diwali party, or a wedding reception,” says Gupta. “It’s elaborate in design, but not necessarily in size. Luckily, people are finally looking at investment in jewellery as an investment in design, and not just in diamonds.” Gupta also reveals that September 2019 will see the launch of his first-ever stores in Kolkata and Hyderabad, a series of pop-ups across the country, and ongoing auxiliary projects. After an indiction of having carved a niche in the occasion wear industry, Gupta is now looking ahead to create “a new timeless”, and not just in fashion. It’s about cultivating a design voice and an elevated lifestyle. “Our patrons have evolved and boast well-curated tastes. They are fiercely individualistic and know exactly what they want,” he says. With this in mind, Gupta believes that an old-school approach to couture is redundant. “Couture need not go out in huge boxes anymore. Be it clothes, jewellery or beyond, design needs to user-friendly, travel-friendly and packing-friendly. Which is why we will always champion present-day relevant solutions that are innovative yet wearable,” he concludes. column1: Kanye West interviews Kim Kardashian West for the very first time for Vogue
column2: © Txema Yeste Fashion In her first one-on-one interview with her husband, the reality TV star opens up about fame, family life and constantly being underestimated In a true (and rare) first for Kim Kardashian West, the media mogul, entrepreneur and mother-of-four is interviewed by her husband, Kanye West, for Vogue Arabia. Starring across all three covers of Vogue Arabia’s September issue, Kardashian West is art directed and styled by Thierry Mugler, who famously redefined the female silhouette in the 1980s with his wasp-waisted, body-con dresses. The reality TV star and law student is photographed by Txema Yeste in the Los Angeles desert, wearing outfits by both Mugler archive and autumn/winter 2019 looks from Casey Cadwallader’s Mugler. © Txema Yeste Though this marks her first Vogue Arabia cover, Kardashian West has worked with Mugler before. Most recently, the French fashion designer created her wet-look, crystal-embellished dress for the 2019 Met Gala. “I love working with Kim,” says Mugler. “She is cool and brilliant. When Vogue Arabia asked me to take part, I was thrilled to have the opportunity to portray Kim in a new vision.” “The shoot and interview reveal a side to Kim that many have never seen before,” explains Vogue Arabia editor-in-chief Manuel Arnaut. In what Arnaut calls a “real and raw” interview, Kardashian West opens up to her husband of five years—Grammy award-winning artist-turned-fashion designer Kanye West—about fame, family life and constantly being underestimated. © Txema Yeste “There is a misconception that I don’t actually have to study and that I’ve bought my way into getting a law degree—that’s absolutely not true… Being underestimated and over-delivering is my vibe,” Kim Kardashian West says. When Kanye asks about her views on whether or not fame is addictive, she replies: “I do agree that fame can be addictive, and it took me a long time to recognise how lost you can become when you put too much focus on it. People often ask me, ‘Money or fame?’ My focus has always been on success, and with success comes money. I’m at this place now where I am not concerned anymore about fame, but if you would have asked me this question 10 years ago, I probably would have said that fame and money were of equal importance. My focus has shifted a lot.” © Txema Yeste Kanye goes on to ask which of her Kardashian/Jenner sisters Kim feels closest to. "It changes, just like friends or relationships go in and out,” she replies. “I think this year has been a really strong Kim and Khloé year. I’m obviously close with Kendall and Kylie too, but I’ve spent so much more time on this Earth with Kourtney and Khloé—16 and 17 years longer with them. We have more history, have been through so much together, and we have more friends in common. Kourtney and I will always be really close, but this year, Khloé and I really bonded,” she reveals. © Txema Yeste Vogue Arabia’s September issue also features exclusive access to the wedding of Elie Saab Jr and Christina Mourad, Sheikha Latifah Al Maktoum’s 2020 Summer Olympic dreams, and the Haute Couture debut of Nicolas Jebran. column1: All the highlights from Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2019
column2: © Sagar Ahuja/Vogue Fashion As the curtain goes down on another season of Lakmé Fashion Week, Vogue recaps key trends and the most special moments from the five-day long event in Mumbai On the occasion of Sustainable Fashion Day at Lakme Fashion Week winter/festive’19, the Union Minister for Textiles, Smriti Zubin Irani, launched Project SU:RE, which stands for Sustainable Revolution. An initiative by the CMAI (the largest apparel industry association) and IMG Reliance, Project SU:RE brought together 16 of the biggest brands to sign a charter that outlined a sustainable way forward for India’s fashion industry, and underscored the need to commit to greener, cleaner practices. Addressing the gathering, the Textiles Minister said, “As a proud Indian, I stand here today to witness history. I would like to tell the United Nations that this has become possible due to the initiative of the industry, IMG Reliance and Lakmé Fashion Week. We are celebrating the 150th birth anniversary year of Mahatma Gandhi, who asked us to be the change you wish to see in the world. The sustainability resolution being adopted today is reflective of that very thought of the Mahatma.” The industry impact of this resolution is quite monumental; the combined value of the 16 signatories, which iclude Raymond, Bestseller, Trends, Future Group and Shopper’s Stop, is estimated to be close to Rs 30,000 crores. Both Amit Aggarwal and Abraham & Thakore fashioned their collections from new-age, sustainable synthetics. While Aggarwal used R|Elan™ FreeFlow fabric (made from recycled PET bottles) to bring his collection of structured evening wear to life, Abraham & Thakore launched LENZING™ ECOVERO™, a sustainable viscose brand on Sustainable Fashion Day. The Street Feat showcase comprised runway shows by four young, homegrown labels—Six5Six Street, Gundi Studio, Biskit and Jaywalking—that interpreted street style in their own irreverent, individualistic ways. Co-founded by Delhi-based siblings, Avni and Ambar Aneja, Six5Six Street’s ‘WE 2.0’ was a sartorial interpretation of the world we currently live in and where we’re possibly headed. The line comprised cropped denim jackets, T-shirts, flared jeans and boxy jackets. A clever use of accents—holographic prints, statement pockets, colour blocking, slogans and contrast patches—and a talent for storytelling are Six5Six Street’s strongest suits. Biskit’s line of unisex clothing, ‘Spaced Out’, conceptualised by Shruti and Harsha Biswajit, is characterised by clean lines, neutral colours and statement accessories. The collection featured jumpsuits, oversized T-shirts, overalls and streetwear sets. One of the coolest pieces in Biskit’s collection was the signature black, detachable duffel bag that also triples up as a tote and a sling bag. Jay Ajay Jajal’s bold use of neon, neoprene and ornamentation popped on the runway as his brand, Jaywalking, made its fashion week debut. The founder of this gender-neutral label sent graphic T-shirts, track suits, slim denim jeans and hoodies down the runway on day one at Lakmé Fashion Week. Rapper Rajakumari transformed the ramp into a stage for Gundi Studios showcase, personifying the designer, Natasha Sumant’s muse—the outspoken, bold and confident South Asian woman who refuses to conform. The Studio at Lakmé Fashion Week this year was imagined as a space for experimentation and performance art. Poochki, The Pot Plant, Circular Design Challenger winner, I Was A Sari, and Ka-Sha were among the brands that presented their collections as interactive exhibits that were high on drama and creativity. Student of the Year 2 co-stars, Ananya Panday and Tara Sutaria, also made their LFW debuts together. While Panday walked the ramp for both Arpita Mehta and Anushree Reddy, Sutaria closed the Label Ritu Kumar show. Arjun Kapoor turned showstopper for designer Kunal Rawal, and Jahaan Kapoor (Maheep and Sanjay Kapoor’s son) also made his runway debut by walking for Rawal’s ‘Confluence’. Made in Heaven actor, Sobhita Dhulipalia walked for Bloni, Salita Nanda and SWGT, while Gully Boy’s Vijay Verma rocked an all-black churidar-kurta for Tisa. column1: Smriti Zubin Irani on sustainability, Lakmé Fashion Week and her favourite designers
column2: © Abhishek Bali Fashion In an exclusive interview with Vogue, the Union Minister of Textiles spoke about the roadmap for the country’s textile industry and what the fashion industry should be focusing on At the recently concluded Lakmé Fashion Week in Mumbai, the Union Minister of Textiles, Smriti Zubin Irani, launched Project SU.RE in association with the Clothing Manufacturers Association of India (CMAI); the United Nations in India; and IMG Reliance, organisers of LFW. It’s a significant step towards propagating sustainability practices in a sector that is one of the biggest employment generators in the country, with signatories including CMAI members like Future Group, Shopper’s Stop, Aditya Birla Retail, Arvind Brands, Lifestyle, Max, Raymond, House of Anita Dongre, W, Biba, Westside, Levi’s, Bestsellers and Trends, among others. Under the five-point “Sustainable Resolution”, the signatories pledged the following: Develop a complete understanding of the environmental impact of the garments being currently produced by the brand; develop a sustainable sourcing policy for consistently prioritising and utilising certified raw materials that have a positive impact on the environment; make the right decisions about how, where, and what we source across the value chain by selecting sustainable and renewable materials and processes and ensuring their traceability; communicate our sustainability initiatives effectively to consumers and media through our online and physical stores, product tags/labelling, social media, advertising campaigns and events; through these actions shift a significant percentage of the supply chain to a sustainable chain by the year 2025, addressing critical global issues such as climate change, contributing to the UN Sustainable Development Goals, and building a world that is safe for the future generations, as an acceptance of a responsibility we all share. Ahead of the announcement of Project SU.RE, Irani delineated the roadmap for the Ministry of Textiles in her second stint at the helm of the Ministry, and the need of the hour. Excerpts below. I think till now sustainability has largely remained a buzzword for those who could afford high fashion. The project is between the Ministry of Textiles, IMG Reliance and the CMAI, which has over 25,000-30,000 members who are retailers in the textile trade. The three of us coming together on one platform is indicative of the fact that sustainable fashion is not only a need but also a responsibility. And I’m glad that as minister I see two ends of the industry coming together—one what we call “high fashion,” and the other that retails not as fashion per se but as need-based garments. So the fact that need-based apparel and high fashion can have minds meet, and that the issue on which they can converge is sustainability, is something for us in the Ministry to celebrate. That is an idea we would like to explore, especially given our branding promise in conjunction with the Ministry of Commerce. For instance, in handcraft the community of artisans and exporters got together and created a certification for responsibly accrued wood, called Vriksh. Under the India Handloom Brand (IHB) that the Prime Minister launched, we not only help register design patterns and weaves but also organic materials and dyes. So that is an area we are looking at expanding… I watched a lot of Saaksha & Kinni on Instagram and had told the LFW team that I would like to visit some stalls. I think a lot of hope is generated when we see young designers experiment with heritage ideas. For instance, [if you see] the kind of work that Maku has done with jamdani, one would never imagine that he would be selling in 20 concept stores in Japan. Now that is the kind of impact we’ve seen with young designers, who possibly don’t get a lot of attention but are quietly bringing about a revolution. I think the conscientiousness of a designer [makes a difference]. Anavila is quiet and under the radar but the kind of revolution she’s brought about in the lives of her weavers and economically empowered them… These are stories that need to be told more and more. And for me as a woman it’s a feeling of great pride that a lady from Mumbai would go all the way to West Bengal, find those weavers, and not just run away with their designs but sit and make their lives better and worry about whether they get enough access to healthcare or if they have electricity in their homes… For a designer to invest not only in design but also the lives of the workers is something that much can be learnt from. We have entered the first phase of MoUs with 18 states. We’re also entering into MoUs with industry across the country. Our endeavour is to ensure 10 lakh citizens are skilled in the textile trade, especially to enhance productivity. Given that today opportunities are immense we can meet the targets not only in terms of business but also aspiration, where we skill more and more of our population in the needs of the textile manufacturing industry. From cotton to jute to handcrafts and handlooms to technical textiles, there isn’t one segment of textiles that has been kept out of the skilling process, and we are happy that we see a collaborative attempt between states, who are in the race to get more and more investments, and the industry, which had identified this skill gap and was looking forward to the government hand-holding and supporting such an initiative. We have expanded the bandwidth of NIFT with regard to the services it can provide to the textile community. The entire curriculum of NIFT has now been reinvigorated. The previous chairperson, Rajesh V Shah, and former Director General of NIFT, Sarada G Muraleedharan, have done much to bring about this change in curriculum. Apart from that, NIFT, in collaboration with the Ministry of Textiles, is focusing on trend-forecasting, which was a gap in Indian fashion and the Indian textile market. NIFT is also looking at design-based intervention in the handcraft segment, and we’re also involving NIFT in a lot of archival processes. We want our students to get a multitude of options with regard to the industry, where they are not only proficient in apparel manufacturing but if the students so desire they have other opportunities within the business, so they can oscillate from apparel manufacturing to design innovation and technology to handcraft. Recently we had Shahi Exports set up a Chair at NIFT—the first ever such chair set up by an apparel export house—which shows that not only is NIFT working closely with the Ministry, but also that now the industry is stepping up to ensure it can contribute to enhancing the educational experiences of students. We in the Ministry are also looking at segments of textiles that were not focus areas before. For instance, we have an area of technical textiles wherein the misnomer that textile is only about fashion is something that we wanted to address. And today technical textiles are very much a part of our space programme, the medical needs of our country, our sporting needs, and building needs. The Prime Minister started a special initiative to enhance the capacities of our technical textile trade. For the first time in the history of our country we had HSN (Harmonized System of Nomenclature) codes devised for 207 items in the technical textile business, and the impact was that we saw our negative trade balance improve by 50 per cent, which is a big achievement in this sunrise sector. So not only are we facilitating technical textiles from the perspective of giving subsidies, we are also ensuring that the quality standards that the industry across the world aspires to achieve is something that we can set domestically. I think irrespective of the headwind, we are facing competition from least developed countries that enjoy a competitive tax advantage against us in the international market. Today the apparel industry has seen a steady CAGR (compound annual growth rate) of two per cent. This is irrespective of the headwind, and irrespective of the global slowdown. The government has also provided a special package of Rs 6,000 crore. As per our Textile Commissioner’s office, we’ve had investments worth Rs 13,000 crore come in. It’s only in the past four to five years that we’ve had such major initiatives undertaken. We will see exponential growth, but we are competing with countries that have a tax advantage with the FTAs given that they enjoy LDC status and we don’t because we’re on our way to becoming one of the most powerful economies in the world. One of the biggest challenges that we have is that in countries like Vietnam the labour force is skilled at Level 5, while our current skill capacity is at Level 1. So, we have a huge gap as far as our skilling history goes. The second aspect, which is not a challenge but an opportunity, is that our creative heritage has not been unleashed. At this year’s LFW, for instance, I believe Padmaja used colours produced from temple waste. Now these kinds of sustainable initiatives are something that the world looks forward to as a niche product. Our challenge is the branding and positioning. For instance, we have a cotton called Shankar 6 cotton; if you look at the staple length and the quality, this is a better quality of cotton than even Egyptian cotton. But because it doesn’t get branded or positioned as such in the international market, not many are aware of it. So our intention is to collaborate with the Ministry of Commerce to ensure that we do the branding of such Indian initiatives. The third part is how we have more and more weaving communities come together and become producer unions. Ultimately, if in the handmade segment we want our weavers to flourish and prosper, they need to get the gains of their hard work directly instead of being the last in the value chain where the money’s worth percolates and is diminished. Our endeavour now in the industry is to also encourage weaving communities to come together as producing unions and link them to finance and credit. column1: Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2019: All the Bollywood showstoppers
column2: © Sagar Ahuja/Vogue Fashion From Katrina Kaif’s wedding-ready lehenga to Kareena Kapoor Khan’s glamorous black gown, catch up on all the looks you may have missed from the star-studded week Lakmé Fashion Week isn’t complete without the slew of Bollywood showstoppers that show up to support their favourite designers and model the season’s best looks, and 2019’s winter/festive edition was no different. The shows were held in Mumbai between August 21 and August 25, and celebrities took to the ramp in everything from jaw-dropping gowns to elegant lehengas that are perfect for the festive season. Here’s a quick recap on everything you may have missed. Manish Malhotra’s show kickstarted the week-long event, with Katrina Kaif playing showstopper for his newest collection in black lehenga with intricate gold embroidery. Many of Malhotra’s famous friends showed up to sit front row as well, including Karan Johar, Karisma Kapoor and Khushi Kapoor. Ananya Panday also made her runway debut in not one, but two wedding-ready outfits. She first walked the ramp in an embellished ivory Anushree Reddy creation, and then wearing a hot pink lehenga set by Arpita Mehta. Shibani Dandekar walked the runway twice over the period of five days—first with her beau Farhan Akhtar for Payal Singhal’s show, and then solo for Bandana Narula. Shabana Azmi also made graceful appearance as showstopper for Kaveri, and Kangana Ranaut did a little dance on stage at Disha Patil’s show. Kareena Kapoor Khan maintained her tradition of closing Lakmé Fashion Week, walking the runway for Gauri and Nainika’s finale show this season in a strapless black gown with net details. “It is always iconic to be a part of it. There is always that slight nervousness. With Gauri and Nainika, their entire collection is about flow; we’re talking about freedom. That is going to be the whole look,” she told Vogue India before the show started. On the other hand, Tara Sutaria, who walked the runway for Ritu Kumar, wore a mini black embroidered dress, styled with over-the-knee boots. Disha Patani wore a glittery dress with a slit and plunging neckline, while Malaika Arora had all eyes on her as she donned a red bralette and skirt set for DiyaRajvvir. Arjun Kapoor walked the ramp for his friend Kunal Rawal, alongside his cousin and Sanjay Kapoor’s son, Jahaan Kapoor. Ayushmann Khurrana joined Disha Patani to close the show for for ace designers Rohit Gandhi and Rahul Khanna, who returned to the Lakmé Fashion Week after a 15-year hiatus. Designer Amit Aggarwal showcased his collection with cricketer Hardik Pandya and actor Lisa Haydon as showstoppers for the evening, both wearing purple designs. column1: Everything you need to know about the blazer
column2: © Instagram.com/malaikaaroraofficial Fashion For centuries, the double-breasted jacket has been a unisex classic, but—with origins rumoured from the sports field to the high seas; and a first appearance in Vogue in 1893—what’s the history of the blazer? The blazer is traditionally a thigh-length, double-breasted jacket, tailored in either black or navy lightweight flannel. The brass buttons on the sleeves reflect the garment’s origins in late 19th-century British boating and cricketing culture. A middle child, the blazer is positioned between the formal suit jacket and the casual sports jacket. Worn without matching pants, the blazer is looser and less structured around the shoulder and chest than the suit jacket. Cricketers Andrew Sandham (left) and A Ducat in their team blazers © E. Bacon/Topical Press Agency/Getty The garment has several origin stories. One traces it to the red “blazers”, or bright sporting jackets, worn by the boating team of St John’s College, Cambridge in the 1820s. Another pinpoints the year 1837, when the captain of the HMS Blazer dressed his crew in navy-blue, double-breasted jackets, complete with distinguished Royal Navy brass buttons, in order to welcome Queen Victoria on-board the ship. Or the jacket may have acquired its name from the “blazes”, or stripes, of country club jackets in the 1870s. In any case, the term outgrew its original intention, moving from the water to the shore and beyond the sports club. Colourways expanded similarly, beyond black and navy, with the modern blazer today sold in a wide variety of colours and fabrics. The Henley Regatta at Henley-on-Thames on the River Thames, circa 1955 © Slim Aarons/Getty The blazer made its first Vogue appearance in June 1893: “Now that the boating season has begun, dressmakers and tailors are busy making up fetching yachting costumes,” the reporter wrote. “The smartest I have seen are those which have perfectly plain skirts with the Eton jacket or the long blazer, the revers of which flare tremendously and are faced with white.” Around the turn of the century, the blazer was a staple of the New Woman’s wardrobe, worn with a shirtwaist and a tailored skirt. As sporting activities became accepted for women, leisurewear became more casual, and the blazer was abandoned for sweaters or cardigans. The blazer had its first major revival in the 1950s when British students altered their school blazers to make them stylish. In Mods: The New Religion by Paul Anderson, former followers recount their style inspiration. “Around this period I got a three-chrome, button blazer,” recalls Mickey Modern from London. “It became fashionable to have your initials in Roman characters on the breast pocket.” Lloyd Johnson from Hastings remembers that one of his friends had his mother shorten his school blazer to “look like a bum freezer”, while his friend “took off his tie and turned his collar up”. Some 20 years later, Giorgio Armani ushered the garment back into fashion, presenting his first collection of unstructured men’s blazers in 1975. Unlined and un-ironed, the jacket was less formal than a suit jacket, but still professional. Armani’s blazers could be worn like a sweater or a jacket, casual but sophisticated. The “King of the Blazer” was anointed when Richard Gere wore Armani in the 1980 hit American Gigolo. The blazer had finally garnered sex appeal. Richard Gere in 'American Gigolo' (1980) © Glasshouse Images/Shutterstock Around the late 2000s, colourful blazers were adopted as a fashion trend by women. Made popular during Christophe Decarnin’s tenure at Balmain between 2006 and 2011, the blazer became a statement piece to layer over an evening dress. In the past few years, it has even made an appearance as the dress itself—cut to the top of the thigh, the blazer-dress is but the latest rendition of this classic wardrobe staple. column1: Best dressed this week: Kareena Kapoor Khan and Shraddha Kapoor
column2: © Viral Bhayani Fashion From the best outfits from Lakmé Fashion Week’s front row to the perfect off-duty model look from Gigi Hadid, Vogue rounds up the best dressed celebrities this week With the opening show for Lakmé Fashion Week being held earlier this week, the city was bound to turn into a runway. The budding FRow regular Khushi Kapoor chose to go monotone in a champagne asymmetrical tiered skirt and bralette set by Manish Malhotra, finished with a polki choker for a subtle punch of colour. Karisma Kapoor made a sparkling case for the black sari at the show, adding a risqué spin to the drape with a halter blouse. But just a few days later, her sister, Kareena Kapoor Khan, flaunted her preference for the LBD. Accessorised with her new chop, the black tie-dye knotted Nupur Kanoi dress is ideal for a laid-back yet luxe evening look. Shraddha Kapoor, on the other hand, decided to do cocktail hour glam in a sequinned halter dress from Thym, styled with neutral heels and next-to-none accessories. Céline Dion gave tie-dye her stamp of approval in a white and blue two-piece suit by Stella McCartney. No longer just a hipster favourite, she proved that you can take this trend mainstream, say for Sunday brunch or hitting the shops, with the right choice of colours. Gigi Hadid schooled us in off-duty model cool, and in a manner that only she can pull off, married the season’s reigning trends—black bike shorts, graphic tee and structured white blazer. Our biggest takeaway: sneakers with back-to-school above-the-ankle socks? Yes, please! column1: Sonakshi Sinha’s Indian wear wardrobe: The best kurtas, anarkalis and more
column2: © Instagram.com/aslisona Fashion From printed kurta sharara sets to sequinned saris and anarkalis, Sonakshi Sinha’s Indian wear choices are as diverse as they are experimental. We take a peek inside her closet for the best looks Sonakshi Sinha’s sartorial choices are as varied as her choice of roles, and she doesn’t shy away from modern silhouettes and vibrant colours either. Her ethnic wardrobe in particular houses many options in every kind of Indian wear, be it kurtas, saris, lehengas and even co-ord sets. Scroll ahead to take a peek inside. Sinha tends to oscillate between lightweight, printed kurtas and embellished numbers. Those Anita Dongre floral printed kurta and palazzo sets she wore during Kalank’s promotions fit well under the first category. For the latter, the Arpita Mehta blood red embellished kurta and flared sharara set and the happy yellow Sukriti & Aakriti number serve as good examples. Fully embroidered and printed anarkalis in floor-sweeping lengths come second in Sinha’s ethnic wear preferences. The A-line silhouette effortlessly flatters Sinha’s form, and is sometimes accompanied with a matching dupatta. Our favourite? The embellished maroon anarkali by Falguni Shane Peacock. From sheer saris to handwoven picks, Sinha’s repertoire includes a delightful variety of the six yard staple as well. There’s the sheer, embellished Manish Malhotra sari that she wore with a strappy blouse, the Arpita Mehta red sari featuring ruffles, and Ekaya Banaras’ handwoven kora silk sari that showcased Sinha’s prowess at styling conventional saris. Coming to modern drapes, the actor has given her nod of approval to Anamika Khanna’s pant-style sari, as well as Nupur Kanoi’s sari, which bore resemblance to a gown. The wedding-ready lehenga makes sporadic appearances in Sinha’s wardrobe, worn only for festive occasions or special promotional events. Whether it’s that bright yellow, printed floral set by Anita Dongre, or the black number by Arpita Mehta, featuring a blouse with lace-up details, the actor has often made a case for pairing the traditional lehenga with a jacket to make it more off-the-moment. Zara Umrigar’s embellished lehenga and blouse set in a muted mint hue is another hit that brides-to-be need to check out. You only need to scroll through Sinha’s Instagram feed to note her affinity for unconventional co-ord sets in ethnic wear. We’ve seen dhotis worn with loose kurtas, crop tops and high-waisted palazzos styled with majestic capes and jackets, and dhoti pants and blouses layered with jackets. Bold and contemporary in equal measure, a co-ord set is a clear winner for when you’ve got a reception coming up. 24 pictures that take you inside Sonakshi Sinha’s wardrobe Sonakshi Sinha’s complete style evolution 5 steps to Sonakshi Sinha’s easy glossy eyes and lips Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Decoding Kareena Kapoor Khan and Saif Ali Khan’s couple style
column2: © Instagram.com/tanghavri Fashion From date nights to airport runs, Kareena Kapoor Khan and Saif Ali Khan know how to get their couple looks right Kareena Kapoor Khan and Saif Ali Khan’s relationship has been a major point of interest for Bollywood fans for years now. From falling in love on the sets of Tashan (2008) to Saif getting Kareena’s name tattooed on his arm in 2009, to their intimate wedding celebrations in 2012 and the birth of their son, Taimur Ali Khan, in 2016, this celebrity couple has been making headlines since the very beginning. No strangers to the limelight, their style in public is, at once, easygoing and impactful. In their daily wardrobe, you will find outfits that are always polished and on-point, but still comfortable. For the airport, Kareena Kapoor Khan sticks to her usual roster of logo sweatshirts, T-shirts, classic jeans and the occasional breezy kurta, while Saif Ali Khan opts for casual shirts, T-shirts and denim jeans (sometimes, with a baseball cap). The couple regularly hosts parties at their home for their close friends, but prefer a laid-back approach to dressing for them as well. On the red carpet, the royal couple is seen in their dressy best, with statement-making gowns and pantsuits winning Kareena's vote, while Saif picks smart suits in black and white. But it’s their Indian wear showcases that make the most impact. The couple usually tries to stay away from the matchy-matchy territory, but they do break the rule every once in a while with traditional ensembles—specially for weddings. For example, Kareena wore a white Anita Dongre lehenga for Isha Ambani and Anand Piramal’s wedding, and Saif complemented her in a matching sherwani. And for Sonam Kapoor Ahuja and Anand Ahuja’s wedding ceremony, the couple matched their looks with their son—Kareena wore a pink lehenga, Saif picked a white kurta, and little Taimur was dressed in a pink and white kurta set. column1: Have trouble finding shoes your size? This fashion label is trying to change the game
column2: © Instagram.com/universalstandard Fashion Universal Standard is bringing size inclusivity to footwear Universal Standard began with an ambitious goal: change the way fashion thinks about size. Since launching in 2015, the direct to consumer line has led the pack when it comes to inclusivity, offering its customers an unprecedented 00 to 40 range—not to mention a groundbreaking collaboration with Rodarte which dropped in April of this year. Now founders Alexandra Waldman and Polina Veksler have set their sights on a new challenge: footwear. A year in the making, the line’s first boots made their debut. Black leather with block heels and metallic trim, both styles are appealing; dubbed the Lisbon, the knee-high version comes with a built-in legging and calls to mind on-trend shoes such as Balenciaga’s knife heels. Their Porto ankle sock bootie, on the other hand, echoes a classic Chelsea boot. "What we’re about is access for all women who love and appreciate fashion,” shared Waldman on the phone from the brand's New York headquarters. “[We are] Making shoes or boots that everyone or a vast majority of women can get into.” Offered from size 6 to 13, the boots go beyond most footwear lines, the majority of which top out at 11. Their pliable fabric also addresses the differences in calf width that can make shoe-shopping arduous. Water-resistant, anti-microbial, and able to retain its form-fitting shape no matter how the wearer customises it, the material that makes up the knit portion of each shoe pairs seamlessly with leather. “I thought the design would be a beautiful way to feature any leg that wanted to fit into it,” says Waldman. “We paid a lot of attention to the fabrications and experimented with different variations. You have to see different kinds of leather and how they translate.” Comfort was key. The stacked heels, insoles, and metallic details all received a thorough examination before the boots were ready for production. “We knew we had something we liked from a style and design perspective, but we also really wanted to give it a proper wear test,” says Waldman, who put each pair through the wringer. “Once your foot is bent, does it create that huge crease? How does all of this work in terms of wear-ability?” A self-described “huge fan” of shoes, Waldman has an expansive collection and admits to letting her “selfish gene” have some input into the design process. “I just want to have an amazingly comfortable, super fashionable heel that gives you a bit of height and looks stylish,” she says. With the shoes online today, she hopes her audience gets the chance to make Universal Standard’s latest creation their own. “We don’t want anyone to change to be closer to our style. We want them to be themselves and make these pieces a reflection of who they are.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.com Your summer wardrobe is incomplete without these shoes The biggest fashion takeaways from street style at fashion month The shoe style everyone from Alia Bhatt to Ananya Panday is wearing now Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 8 kurtas with gota patti work that need to be in your festive wear wardrobe
column2: Fashion Our edit of the best kurta sets that are as sparkly as they are elegant Ganesh Chaturthi marks the beginning of India’s festive season, which starts in September and goes on till February, concluding with the country’s most colourful festival, Holi. Considering this, there could not be a better time to stock up on your ethnic wear essentials than right now. Kurtas have always been a winning choice for this season, but if you’re looking for an on-trend upgrade, you may want to swap the heavily embroidered numbers with kurtas featuring gota patti work. The lightweight option is ideal for the current humid weathers, and will help you add a touch of shine to your look too. If you’ve  been inclined towards pink, Aditi Somani’s kurta is sure to find a fan in you. Prefer sharara sets in pastel shades? column1: 5 new ways to wear the power suit this season
column2: © Jonathan Daniel Pryce Fashion From boxy blazers to bold prints, here are five tailoring trends—inspired by street style—to redefine your smart-casual remit ‘Power suiting’ has a new meaning for AW19. Forget any stiff, corporate connotations; laid-back silhouettes and voluminous luxe blazers (paired with wide-leg trousers and fluid skirts) are leading the way now, thanks to the likes of Greek designer Eftychia Karamolegkou. Shortlisted for the LVMH Prize, Karamolegkou’s eponymous label, Eftychia, is garnering attention for its versatile, understated tailoring that redefines comfortwear. “I think comfort is key,” she tells Vogue. “My pieces have a loose-fit to give that relaxed feeling.” So, how can you bring that relaxed feel to your back-to-work wardrobe? Look to the street style set, and their five favourite tailoring trends for AW19. © Jonathan Daniel Pryce The neutral tones that have dominated the past few seasons are here to stay, particularly when it comes to tailoring. And a cream suit isn’t as intimidating as it sounds. See Rejina Pyo for a soft draped version and Acne Studios for a boxy take. Note on footwear: the Nineties-style mules you shopped on Depop way back in January work perfectly for this look. © Jonathan Daniel Pryce If the miniskirt suit had a moment last year, for AW19 it’s all about a longer hemline. Namecheck: Hedi Slimane’s Celine reboot, where a bourgeois Seventies mood was the order of the day; Gabriela Hearst’s pleated Wesley skirt; and easy-to-wear midis via Eftychia. © Søren Jepsen Copenhagen Fashion Week had us sold on orange suiting (reference Georgian brand Janashia’s sleek two-piece), as well as bringing forest green into the mix. When it comes to the colour of your new suit, remember that it’s not always about black, navy and grey. © Jonathan Daniel Pryce The AW19 runways at Givenchy, Maison Margiela and Balenciaga all made a case for the power-suit signature: sculpted shoulders. Mytheresa fashion buying director, Tiffany Hsu has been setting the street style trend, while Rihanna’s debut Fenty collection offered a wealth of structured inspiration—expect to see it across the front rows come September’s fashion shows. © Søren Jepsen Danish-British brand Brøgger’s printed suits have become a street style mainstay, due to their power to turn every photographer’s lens. Closet peacocks should also look to Stine Goya’s AW19 orange-and-pink gingham suit, and Charles Jeffrey Loverboy’s colourful plaid two-pieces. 5 swimsuits that prove the one-piece has won summer 2019 How to give grunge a 2019 update The enduring power (and surprisingly dark symbolism) of red shoes Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Vogue’s fashion encyclopaedia: The history of the bra
column2: © Getty Fashion Vogue traces the fashion history of the bra, from its free-the-corset beginnings in the Victorian age, to the feminist bra burning of the 1960s, to 21st century Victoria’s Secret Angels Fabric has been used for centuries to hold up women’s breasts. The “bikini girl” mosaic from the Villa Romana del Casale in Sicily, dated to the 4th century AD, shows a series of young women wearing supportive fabric bandeau tops while engaged in sporting activities. But the modern “bra” as we know it today—made up of two cups, a chest bandeau and shoulder straps, the word shortened from the French term brassière—is a descendent of the 19th-century dress reform movement. The bikini girl mosaic © Alamy Reacting against the constrictive corsets of the 1850s, doctors and feminists began to champion lighter “breast supporters” that would enable women to digest better and breathe with ease. Prototypes of the first bras were manufactured and marketed in England, America, Germany and France from the 1850s until around the 1920s. During this early period, the bra was still very much a novelty item. The fashionable S-shape figure of the belle époque was more easily acquired through the use of corsets and girdles (which slimmed the waist) than through a bra. But the silhouette shifted during and after the First World War; as the chest was de-emphasised, the bra became better suited to this new look, which was predominantly worn by a young social elite. Lingerie for women in the Auxiliary Territorial Service © Getty In the 1930s, the bra began to acquire many of the features it still has today: letter sizing for cups, eye-and-hook fastenings and adjustable straps. Improvements in textile elasticity, colours, patterns and style options helped popularise it among women aged 17 and above. The bra’s appearance in Hollywood movies—those pointy busts flaunted by popular sex symbols—and major marketing pushes by department stores helped launch the style into the upper-class mainstream. Marilyn Monroe © Getty Historians Jane Farrell-Beck and Colleen Gau, authors of Uplift: the Bra in America, write that American servicewomen were issued bras as part of their uniform during the Second World War and it soon became standard wear for middle-class working women. Jane Russell’s torpedo-shaped bra gave the garment its most recognisable silhouette throughout the 1950s and advertisements show that it was still typically worn with a girdle. The introduction of the “training bra” during this period expanded the consumer market to younger teenagers. By the 1960s and 1970s, girdles had been dropped and the bra’s connotations changed. Comfort and function were prioritised over movie-star glamour and sexiness. Some feminists saw in the bra an example of female subjugation to the male gaze and made a statement of removing the garment altogether—an iconic image from a protest against the Miss America beauty pageant in 1968 sparked the myth of so-called “bra-burning feminists”. However, a vast majority of women still wore one out of comfort, need and personal choice. Elasticised knitted bras, introduced in the 1970s and 1980s for athletes, began to be preferred by some women over underwired models. The bra with sex appeal returned in the 1990s and 2000s, largely driven by that “Hello Boys” Wonderbra campaign starring Czech supermodel Eva Herzigova; plus the Victoria’s Secret Angels. The lingerie brand’s first fashion show was held at New York’s Plaza Hotel in 1995, and in 1999 the event was webcast. Teased during that year’s Superbowl commercial break, the online show was watched by 2 million people online. By 2001, the event was being aired on network television—12 million viewers tuned in for the first broadcast. Companies such as Frederick’s of Hollywood and Agent Provocateur, and performers such as Dita Von Teese, capitalised on the bra’s erotic connotations. They helped the boudoir mentality become mainstream, paving the way for the success of erotica such as Fifty Shades of Grey. Designers during this period also played with the aesthetic of the bra as outerwear. PLAYTEX advert from 1994 for their Wonderbra with Czech model Eva Herzigova © Alamy Gianni Versace spring/summer 1992 © Getty In the ensuing two decades, the bra has been produced in every variation possible—strapless, backless, cup-less, with and without pads or wires, rigid, stretchy—and it is no longer so shocking to see women wearing one as fashionable outerwear (the SS18 shows saw Loewe, Louis Vuitton and Maison Margiela, to name a few, set the bras on top trend). The shape the bra creates has changed from conical, to push-up, to natural, but the foundational garment has retained its basic structure for over a century now—and unless a new, radical alternative is invented, it seems as if the bra is here to stay. column1: How to give grunge a 2019 update
column2: Fashion Grown up punk inspiration from the runway As Marc Jacobs famously said, “Grunge is a hippied romantic version of punk”. If you grew up in the 1980s and were listening to Alice in Chains, Nirvana, Kurt Cobain and Pearl Jam you were most likely a grunge-head. Today this 80’s trend has made a glorious comeback in all our wardrobes in an obvious but simultaneously subtle way. Remember the uncoordinated, deliberately careless look that was the marker of this cool-kids subset? Faded, torn jeans, flannel shirts, black combat-style boots—it was a mood that came across in wardrobes of co-counter-culturists all over. Paco Rabanne autumn/winter 2019 © GoRunway In 2019, grunge has an all-new avatar. It’s the kind of look you can take to work with plaid in light colours, all while retaining its OG edge. Accessorise with a cropped leather jacket, combat boots, retro jewellery or even a baker boy hat. Katana Earrings, Misho The runways showed us how to do grunge for 2019. If you don’t want to go all the way, build accents into your wardrobe. A chunky chain necklace, a mulberry lip, tough boots with a pretty day dress. Call it the modern version of Marc Jacobs’ original Spring collection for Perry Ellis in 1993. Leaders in the ring this fall are Calvin Klein, Anna Sui, Versace, Dolce & Gabbana and Armani, who prove that grunge can lend itself to a more sophisticated state. Closer to home, Nitin Bal Chauhan and Siddhartha Tytler gave a lesson or two on doing slick leather, micro sunglasses and dark make-up. column1: 13 trench coats to help you get your Matrix vibe back on
column2: © Getty Fashion The return of this fan-favourite silhouette proves that ’00s fashion is definitely back, and here to stay Gird your loins and throw on your really, really long coats. The Matrix is being reloaded, again, for the fourth time. Yesterday, it was announced that director Lana Wachowski would be filming what is being referred to as The Matrix 4, with production set to start in 2020 and original cast members Keanu Reeves and Carrie-Anne Moss onboard to star as Neo and Trinity, respectively. (Fun fact: It is currently the 20-year anniversary of the first release of The Matrix.) So what does this all mean for your wardrobe? Well, Matrix style—originally conceived by costume designer Kym Barrett—has been having something of an extended moment in streetwear and on runways over the past few seasons, particularly in the form of those teeny tiny sunglasses that delicately balance on the slopes of celebrity noses. There’s also the sci-fi film’s ankle-grazing leather trench coats, which Kendall Jenner and Bella Hadid nodded to during Fashion Week. To celebrate this completely unexpected news, consider adding some of those sweeping silhouettes to your own wardrobe this fall. For the traditionalist, Georgian label Situationist offers a rich incarnation. For a twist of sheen, Topshop has a belted vinyl design. But given the movie changed how action films looked when it premiered in 1999, you could remix the concept entirely with a faux snake-effect trench by Georgia Alice or a butterscotch piece from A.W.A.K.E. In other words, while the long conversation about whether the real world is really real ensues, make the long trench a reality. column1: How Bollywood celebrities are styling their sports bra for their gym routines
column2:
© Viral Bhayani Fashion From racer-back sports bras to pullover styles, Vogue looks at what Kareena Kapoor Khan, Janhvi Kapoor, Malaika Arora and more are wearing for their workouts Whether you’re an athlete, a gym junkie or a beginner looking to kick-start your fitness journey, a sports bra is an essential in every woman’s workout wardrobe. Not only does a well-fitted sports bra offer some much-needed support to your torso, it also prevents injuries during rigorous physical activities.
Depending on the activity you’re participating in, you can choose between three impact levels: low, medium and high. While low-impact is ideal for easier activities involving slow movements (think yoga and Pilates), the medium-impact works for slightly more energetic workouts, like brisk walking and cycling. If you’re into running, boxing, dancing, functional training or playing sports, the high-impact sports bra is for you. Other styles like the racer-back or criss-cross back provide firmer support for high-intensity workouts, if that’s what your fitness routine calls for. Considering that Kareena Kapoor Khan and Malaika Arora are avid lovers of yoga and Pilates, you’ll mostly spot them in compression sports bras that are best suited for low- and medium-impact activities. These are pullover styles that are non-padded or underwired, and may include an elasticised bottom. Take a closer look at Arora’s collection and you’ll see her switch between low-impact bras (the décolletage-baring strappy styles) and medium ones (the high-neck sports bras). Deepika Padukone prefers well-fitted, full coverage options that offer a lot of support, whereas Janhvi Kapoor is more experimental with her choices—22-year-old Kapoor opts for strappy numbers and halter-neck styles in a vibrant colour palette, or picks numbers featuring cut-outs in the front. Meanwhile, Shraddha Kapoor’s dance classes require that she wears high-impact sports bras, and you’ll often see her layer them a cropped tank top for double coverage. This layering was recently seen on Janhvi Kapoor as well—she paired her strappy purple sports bra with a cropped cami top in a neon green hue, and a pair of black shorts. Other ways to layer include adding a jacket—take cues from Kapoor’s cropped mesh option, Disha Patani’s cropped full-sleeved throw on, Kapoor Khan’s sporty sleeveless jacket and Arora’s full-sleeved jacket. If you’re conscious about working out in a sports bra, you can opt for easy cover-ups like these light layers. column1: From Kareena-Karisma to Kendall-Kylie: 5 celebrity siblings who are nailing sister style
column2: © Instagram.com/therealkarismakapoor Fashion Matching your style with your sister's is not as basic as wearing the same thing anymore. Here's how your favourite celebrity sisters are getting it right If you grew up with a sister, your earliest memories of fashion likely involved matching (not necessarily fashionable) outfits picked out by your parents. Your favourite celebrity siblings are no different either, but years down the line, they're putting a grown-up spin to twinning, in looks that complement, though not necessarily coordinate with, each other’s. If you’re looking to up your sister-style game from matchy outfits, these celebrity sisters prove that the family that slays sartorial looks together, stays together. From cosy Sunday brunches at the It-spots in town to themed birthday getaways abroad, the Kapoor sisters know how to steal the spotlight. While Kapoor’s preferences run towards classics, Kapoor Khan extends her favour to statement, high-impact pieces. Her older sister seconds the sentiment. “I like sophisticated, chic kind of looks and she likes vibrant colours and very bright, flowy things. We give each other tips, we share clothes, we share shopping ideas, what we should get and what we should do. It is really nice to have that bond. In a strange way, we are so connected yet so diverse in our taste,” she once revealed in an interview with a leading daily. Further proof to that end can be found in the images from an exclusive party in London, which had both sisters twinning in black. However, it was their signature beauty choices that set their looks apart—while Karisma Kapoor opted for a statement red lippie, Kareena Kapoor Khan went with her signature nude lips and winged eyeliner. It’s safe to say that the Arora sisters share plenty of things, including a packed social calendar. And even a five-year age gap can’t come in the way of their intuitive sibling bond. Case in point: a recent family dinner, which saw the sisters accidentally twinning their outfits. If you’re looking to veer away from matchy-matchy territory, take notes from their styling choices. While Malaika Arora chose a fitted, cropped white tee and skinny jeans, Amrita Arora Ladak elevated the basic white-and-denim duet by opting for bootcut denims with a thigh-high slit and a fuss-free crop top. With a shared love for all things fashion embedded into their DNA, it seems only fitting that Rhea Kapoor plays stylist to her sister Sonam Kapoor Ahuja, who she’s candidly dubbed as a ‘dress up kind of girl’. On the roster for a girls’ night out? A double-breasted Tibi pantsuit with jhumkas for Kapoor Ahuja, and sharply tailored trousers and a trench coat for her style twin. What about a day out in London, you ask? The Kapoor sisters would like you to place all bets on glamorous vintage prints. With their sartorial sensibilities cosmically aligned, the duo rolled the dice on retail fashion in 2017 and launched their own line, Rheson, to invite their loyal following into their world of style. Because two style superstars are better than one. Born one year apart, Gigi and Bella Hadid aren’t your usual twinning-is-winning sisters—the two supermodels’ individual aesthetics are as incredible as they are distinctive. The former’s wardrobe is dotted with fresh off-the-runway picks, while Bella has a discerning eye for indie picks. Together, the yin-and-yang of their style sensibilities is perfectly encapsulated in their off-duty choices. If you were to run into them in the streets of Paris during fashion week, you’d find them championing neon hues—while one sister picked a graphic leather jacket from Prada, the other opted for a glazed pink blazer that scored high on shine and impact. Cinching the looks together, the duo opted for coordinated black turtlenecks and pulled-back buns. With the Kardashians for family, it can be said that it was kismet for Kylie and Kendall Jenner to follow in the footsteps of their well-heeled older siblings. One is now a business mogul at the helm of a billion-dollar cosmetics company, while the other is the darling of the runway. Needless to say, the two have come a long way from giving each other impromptu haircuts, and have outlived the matchy-matchy vagaries of tweendom to emerge as individual style icons in their own right. Today, their idea of coordinated fashion comes in the form of statement couture on the most-watched red carpets of the world. Leaving her beau Travis Scott on the sidelines, Kylie Jenner made an entrance with her sister instead at the Met Gala this year. Culling inspiration from the evil stepsisters of Cinderella, the duo dished out an extra helping of feathers—with a little help from Versace, of course. column1: If you really care about the planet, you should be rethinking how you buy jeans
column2: © Bikramjit Bose Fashion As ubiquitous as they are in our wardrobes, denim jeans may not be the most environmentally-friendly option if you're thinking of switching to a greener wardrobe Blue jeans are one of the single, most long-lasting fashion trends that have been loved for over a century. They’re ubiquitous in wardrobes across the world, and have ardent fans in everyone from American teenagers to Indian grandmothers. Denim is the single biggest textile type sold in the world—a whopping 1.25 billion pairs of jeans were sold in 2017 alone. Fashion editorials and advertising also deem it essential to stay on top of denim trends. In 2019, the newest cuts and colours include asymmetrical, wide leg, patchwork, pastel and ombre jeans. So it’s safe to say most denim-lovers can easily be tempted into buying one more pair that makes them feel great. But before you shop your next distressed jeans, do evaluate the stress they’re causing the environment, especially since most of the bulk denim production happens in Asia. The production processes for jeans have a significant impact on our continent, populations, as well as the workers involved in creating them. To get a better understanding of this product and how it is meant to be used, we need to look at its history and cultural significance. In 1853, a Bavarian immigrant named Levi Strauss imported denim (an indigo-dyed twill with a diagonal weave) to San Francisco when the gold rush was at its peak. Back then, men were toiling in mines and working as labourers, so conventional trousers didn’t last long in those settings. Strauss collaborated with a tailor called Jacob David to make sturdy work wear trousers with further fortification of copper rivets on the pockets and fly, and in 1873, they patented these blue jeans. The fabric was originally named ‘serge de Nîmes’ after the French town it was produced in, and eventually came to be called denim. Essential details like zippers and belt loops were added much later in the 20th century. The garment did start out as sturdy work gear, but Hollywood made jeans extremely popular among the masses. Eternal cowboy John Wayne wore blue jeans as early as the ’20s, but it was really in the ’50s, when teen idols like Marlon Brando and James Dean rocked blue jeans, that they came to be associated with a rebellious, anti-establishment attitude. The youth began to go crazy for them. In the ’60s and ’70s, jeans were a symbol for counterculture, worn by rock stars, hippies and anti-war protestors. While Vogue first gave denim its stamp of approval in the ’30s, they only showed up on the runway in 1976 at a Calvin Klein show. Today, high fashion giants like Burberry and Gucci have embraced jeans as part of their luxury collections. Interestingly, as they’ve become a fashion product, consumers seem to have lost sight of the fact that jeans were meant for longevity. The average American woman owns seven pairs of jeans. While that may not seem excessive, it’s worthwhile and eye-opening to evaluate the life cycle of a pair of jeans from fibre to wardrobe. The environmental impact of jeans is so staggering that it’s been the subject of recent documentary, titled Riverblue, which records the toxic chemicals and immense amounts of water it takes to produce a single pair of jeans. The movie depicts how waste from these factories is polluting rivers, ecosystems and impacting local communities in China, India and Bangladesh. Directed by David McIlvride and Roger Williams, Riverblue has already won 13 awards globally, including Best Documentary at Raindance in London. Watch it here. To properly understand what all goes into creating a pair of jeans, we need to start with its raw materials. Denim is produced by weaving an indigo-dyed cotton warp with white weft yarn; it is usually 98 per cent cotton and two per cent elastane. This is problematic, because the cotton crop also relies heavily on pesticides and water—every single pair uses up to 2,000 gallons (20 bathtubs full) of the precious resource. Although organic cotton uses no synthetic chemicals, it represents less than one per cent of total production, which is 25 million tonnes per annum. Then comes the production that involves spinning, dyeing, weaving and manufacturing, all of which uses an incredible amount of energy. According to Vice, 50 thousand tonnes of synthetic indigo dye are produced annually, and 95 per cent of this is used by denim manufacturers, with the run-off polluting nearby rivers. What more, the specific colour and texture of jeans, especially the extremely popular distressed look, are a result of chemically intensive and high water usage treatments that are not only bad for the planet, but also the factory workers. Greenpeace also found heavy metal residue in the river water near the top denim-producing towns in Asia. Using one pair of jeans causes a minimum of 32.5kg of CO2 emissions. Attitude Organic has termed this heavy carbon footprint “jeans pollution”. The story, however, doesn’t end with the production cycle. The average consumer purchased 60 per cent more clothing in 2014 as compared to 2000, but kept each garment for only half as long. It is estimated that one garbage truck of wasted clothing is burned or sent to landfills every second. Our throwaway fashion habits are costing the planet dearly. Since jeans have such a heavy carbon footprint and cotton is extremely difficult to recycle into new clothing, it’s imperative that we use our favourite pairs for a long time. After all, if miners could wear theirs for years, surely we can make ours last beyond a few fashion seasons. How long your jeans last in your wardrobe depends on how you care for them. Try spot cleaning stains and airing out your denims, and wait at least five to six wears (if not more) before a full-fledged wash. Internet hacks also include popping them in a freezer or oven to freshen them up. You can justify washing your jeans when they start to smell. Ideally, turn them inside out and soak then in cold water with very little detergent, and line dry away from the sun to prolong their life. The good news is that now that are various labels and companies innovating with technology to make jeans eco-friendly. In India, the label Korra uses organic cotton to make raw selvedge jeans that last a long time. All their fits are custom tailored, and each pair is sown by a single tailor. They have a six-month guarantee against manufacturing defects, and the label also offers one-and-two-year care plans. Overseas, Spanish company Jeanologica has developed lasers, light and air to give jeans a distressed look, instead of relying on chemicals and water. They work with brands like Levi Strauss, H&M, Uniqlo and Marks & Spencer, among others. Various other labels are also coming up with creative solutions, like MUD jeans, which allow customers to rent a pair. Levis uses recycled polyester fibres, and Freitag makes fully compostable jeans out of linen and hemp. It pays to contemplate your choices before purchasing another pair of these thirsty threads. Denim lovers, make your jeans last for as long as you can. The planet is counting on you. Earthy, boxy, boring: Do sustainable clothes have a standard look? column1: Designer Anavila Misra reveals the intricate process of weaving a linen sari
column2:
Fashion Known for her handwoven linen saris, designer Anavila Misra talks to Vogue on working with the weave, how she is modernising it, and the challenges she’s faced in doing so There’s a good reason why linen textiles happen to be one of the oldest in the world. The fabric—derived from the fibres of the flax plant—is extremely strong, absorbent and keeps skin cool in hot and humid weathers. Such was its exclusivity that linen was even used as a form of currency in ancient Egypt. And though it was laborious to manufacture (the flax thread is not elastic, which makes it difficult to weave into a cloth without breaking the threads), it didn’t stop the weavers in those times to weave the fabric from hand spun yarns, creating a fine texture. Today, the textile is used for a wide range of products, from bed sheets and table cloths to clothes, including saris. © shivammisraa Since the inception of her label in 2011, designer Anavila Misra has been championing linen saris for the modern-day woman. Lightweight and comfortable with minimal design, Misra’s offerings disrupted the six yard drape that was conventionally heavily laden with embroidery. Over the years, she has worked towards modernising the weave, and today, Misra works with around 200 weavers who are based out of Phulia, West Bengal. Ahead, the designer chats with Vogue about the labour-intensive weave, how long it takes to create a linen sari, and the cons of working with linen on the loom. At the onset of my journey as a designer for menswear brands, I was exposed to linen textiles. The raw luxury of this yarn stayed with me, and was a natural choice when I started creating my own design aesthetic. Using linen to weave a sari was an idea that came through this experience, and it has now created a whole new category in saris. I mostly work with linen because of its natural properties, comfort and raw elegance. Since the very inception of the brand, we have been working on creating a modern language in saris using linen. Starting with the very basic plain weave, we have worked on different textures in linen itself, blended a variety of yarns with linen, created blocks and experimented with hand block printing on linen textile. The blend of zari and linen has also created a beautiful luxury textile.
  I love to work with plaids, stripes, all-over textures, cording, hand block printing and Khatwa. Delicate motifs of flowers and birds find their way into our jamdani saris. From pre-loom process to the final sari off the loom, the process takes anywhere from 15 to 60 days, depending on the weave, texture and design. Our weavers for the linen sari are mostly based out of Phulia region in West Bengal. We work with approximately 200 weavers now. Apart from this, we also work with printers in Gujarat, batik artisans in Bengal and Khatwa artisans in Jharkhand. What are some of the challenges you faced while weaving linen? Linen is a tough yarn to weave on the loom—it breaks easily during weaving. This was our initial challenge while weaving a linen sari. Also, linen has a low elastic recovery, which is why it gets crumpled easily. Hence, we had to relook the loom set-up completely to weave a sari. Also for the initial year, it took some time for the weaving cluster to adjust to the new yarn for weaving, and get familiar with how it works on the loom. column1: Oversized scrunchies are the latest ’90s hair trend to make a comeback
column2: © Instagram.com/jenatkinhair Fashion They may have been previously villainised as a relic of the past, but today, the easy-to-wear hair accessories can be spotted everywhere you turn The ’90s are well and truly back, and you only need to look at current fashion and beauty trend charts for proof. Following the resurgence of lip gloss, barrettes and claw clips, the next hair trend to bring the ’90s back to your repertoire is oversized scrunchies. It’s almost become an off-duty signature for models, most popularly seen on Kendall Jenner, Hailey Bieber and Gigi and Bella Hadid, who often tie their hair up with a colourful, well-cushioned scrunchie. Apart from just being a fun trend to try, fabric-coated scrunchies are also better to maintain a hairstyle—the softer material doesn’t leave dents in the hair like traditional hair ties do. It also has actual benefits for the health of the hair; the weaker elastic does not pull at the roots, thus minimising tension. Even undoing the hairstyle is easier, since you don’t have to twist or tug the scrunchie off. This effect is doubled if the fabric used is silk or satin, which can hold hair up without causing any frizz or flyaways. Plus, the cushioning means that ponytails don’t have to be pulled super tight, preventing the headache you’ve come to expect with a tight hairdo. Whether you're looking to add flair to a traditional top knot, trying a half-up hairstyle, hiding second day hair or attempting to maintain a blow-out, a scrunchie is your best bet.
