column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan's stylist Tanya Ghavri reveals the star's shopping habits
column2: © ViralBhayani}}} Fashion Whether she’s heading home from Pilates or boarding a flight in pyjamas, Kareena Kapoor Khan is always on top of her fashion A-game. The actor’s personal stylist, Tanya Ghavri, gives us a sneak peek into her style, her fashion obsessions, and the websites she bookmarks for all her shopping There are celebrities who step into the industry topping best-dressed lists, there are those who hone their skills to win the title, and then there is Kareena Kapoor Khan. The 38-year-old actor creates a fashion flurry every time she steps out—whether she’s grabbing lunch with her girls in Bandra or picnicking with the family in London’s Hyde Park. “Kareena is not shouting she’s fashionable from the rooftops. She just is. And that’s what makes her so stylish,” concurs her personal stylist of seven years, Tanya Ghavri. Case in point? The now ubiquitous pap-loved gym looks, which the actor pretty much invented with her post-pregnancy workout wardrobe. “She had no intention to actually do so. It’s all unplanned. There’s no strategy or gimmick behind it. What she wears becomes a rage. Kareena’s not doing it for the ’gram or trying to cultivate an image. She’s just being herself,” says Ghavri. Kapoor Khan has always enjoyed a prime spot on the style icon pedestal owing to the sheer wattage of their inherent star power. Ahead, Ghavri gets candid with Vogue about the actor’s fashion inclinations, revealing everything from her sworn favourites to her fail-safe looks. Read on for the insider intel. “Kareena’s aesthetic has always been ‘less is more’—she’s a jeans and T-shirt girl at heart. She’ll have fun with her looks but never compromise on comfort for the sake of fashion. She’s experimental, but also has a strong understanding of what works for her, so there’s always a balance. “Kareena also likes to stay up to date with fashion news—she keeps track of her favourite brands on Instagram and is clued-in on new launches on LuisaViaRoma, Farfetch, Matches Fashion and Net-A-Porter. Her interest has only grown over time.” “No ballgowns for her. No body-hugging silhouettes, ruffles or busy textures either. Kareena favours structure and clean silhouettes, so column gowns always work well. As do block colours. Think [designs by] Armani, Prabal Gurung and Ashish N Soni.” “Kareena is the only celebrity I know who isn’t styled for the airport. It’s not the kind of thing she will break a sweat over. She has an amazing wardrobe, so she’ll just pull something from it based on her mood that day—unless it’s Indian wear, which I help her curate.” “I often say to Kareena that the only parties you really attend are the ones in your house. Kareena and Saif host friends at their home a lot, and she prefers easier looks for such intimate affairs. So she’ll choose from a shift, skater or wrap dress, but with, for example, a shorter hemline or sequins for some glam. Or she’ll simply go with jeans and a smart shirt.” “When the paps are around, she’ll be in something elegant. If you’re looking for someone who’s overdressed to grab attention, it’s not going to be Kareena. You’ll find her in a midi dress, tailored pants or a boyfriend blazer. With minimal precious jewellery, often from her own collection. She’s not so big on costume jewellery.” © Viral Bhayani “It has to comfortable Indian wear, predominantly mul and khadi kurtas topped off with mojris or kolhapuris. She’s obsessed with Good Earth. Kotwara by Meera and Muzaffar Ali, Simar Dugal and Punit Balana are some of the other brands that work for the occasion.” “London is Kareena’s favourite city, so she does a lot of her shopping there. She loves wearing her new buys on vacation. Again, these are styles that are comfortable from AM to PM, nothing unnecessarily avant-garde—so jeans and sweatshirts with leather or bomber jackets. And sneakers, which she loves collecting!” “She’ll skip the gown and opt for a cocktail dress, pantsuit or a skirt and blouse set instead. Kareena loves her separates and neutrals. You’ll rarely find her in a jumpsuit or playsuit—she feels they are unflattering on her.” “Shoes are her big obsession—Gianvito Rossi, Manolo Blahnik, Gucci, Saint Laurent; you name it, and Kareena owns the brand. She prefers investment buys when it comes to her heels and sneakers. Ditto with her bags, which are mostly travel-friendly totes and day bags.” “Kareena swears by Ralph Lauren. She also loves Saint Laurent, Gucci, Proenza Schouler and Rag & Bone, Sandro and Maje. But she mixes these with high street finds from Zara, H&M and Mango, or boutique finds from her travels.” Kareena Kapoor Khan: I think all my friends want to raid my wardrobe Kareena Kapoor Khan’s guide to acing vacation style Kareena Kapoor Khan’s guide to wearing a sari for any occasion What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The most memorable fashion moments from Stranger Things season 3
column2: Fashion Everyone’s outfits were on fleek this season, but some will go down in TV history. Scroll ahead for our favourites Warning: Spoilers for Stranger Things season 3 ahead Another season of Stranger Things has come and gone (assuming, of course, that you did the only acceptable thing and binge-watched season 3 the weekend that it was released), leaving a Hopper-shaped hole in our hearts. You see, bad-boy-turned-superbad, Billy Hargrove was not the only casualty; the gruff Chief of Police made the ultimate sacrifice to save Hawkins from yet another icky monster from the Upside Down, leaving El in the care of his best friend, Joyce Byers. It was hard, guys. The silver lining, however, was that mid-credit scene, which teased a possible return of The Hop. And the fashion, of course. Season 3 had, by far, the greatest Stranger Things fashion moments (five, to be precise). Ahead, we’re counting them down. Right from the day that the season 3 trailer dropped, fans of the ’80s-inspired sci-fi series knew that Hawkins’ newly-opened Starcourt Mall would be taking centre-stage. But it was only in episode two that we learned just how crucial it was. Not just the battlefield where El & co would take down the Mind Flayer in the finale, it was also the site of El’s iconic makeover. Dressed in hospital nightgowns and Hopper’s hand-me-downs for a large part of season one and two, El is introduced to the world of JC Penney and The Gap by her new BFF, Max Hargrove. And their mysteriously-financed mall crawl is possibly one of our favourite things about the new season. El bought not one, not two, but three new outfits, and there was a clear favourite. The black printed romper that she paired with Reebok CL Leather sneakers and white socks sent fans into a tizzy. The Stranger Things Eleven Short Sleeve Romper was briefly available to shop at Target, but the website says that it is currently out-of-stock. It was a relief to see Hopper swap out his uniform for a, wait for it, Hawaiian shirt! When Hopper asks Joyce out to a totally casual dinner ‘as friends’, he settles on a pastel Hawaiian shirt that, costume designer Amy Parris says, was inspired by Tom Selleck’s style in Magnum, P.I. Wrangler jeans, a light beige blazer, a brief moment of indecision with regards to topsider or boat shoes, and the comfort of his work boots later, Hopper is the epitome of cool-dad style. And the Internet agrees. A personal favourite of the writer, El put together quite the outfit from her newly-acquired wardrobe in episode 6. Costume designer Amy Parris styled her in a pair black, high-waisted pleated jeans together with a black and yellow aztec print shirt and a canvas beige belt. The overall effect of watching her float in and out of Billy's memories in this outfit, stark against the black of his mind, was quite dramatic. Developed as part of another Stranger Things collaboration, this outfit was available at Levi’s but (yep, you guessed it) isn’t in stock anymore. Mike’s mom, or Mrs Wheeler, really brought her A-game to the Hawkins’ community pool. While every swimsuit we saw her in was evocative of ’80s fashion, there was one that left a greater impact than all the others. In episode 1, she is seen wearing a high-cut (like, super high-cut) two-tone blue and pink swimsuit that screams throwback. Not all heroes wear capes; sometimes they wear bright blue suspenders, high-waist denim jeans, a printed black button-up and a yellow scrunchie. Like El did in episode 4, The Sauna Test, when the gang decides to find out (once and for all) if Billy has, in fact, been flayed. El wears her shoulder-length hair half-up, half-down and completes the look with a pair of white sneakers. As comfortable as it is chic, the outfit is perfect for a day when you know you’re going to be running around, trying to save the world. column1: Exclusive: Inside Shantanu & Nikhil’s autumn/winter 2019 couture collection
column2: Fashion From voluminous ball gowns to dramatic lehengas, the designer duo’s latest line encapsulates the best of both worlds Wondering what a modern-day princess would dress like? Designer duo Shantanu & Nikhil are presenting their sartorial opinion in their new couture collection, which is entirely dedicated to her. Titled ‘Raj-Kumari’, the autumn/winter 2019 showcase portrays the juxtaposition that broadly makes up the personalities of today’s millennials—they’re playful yet composed, dainty yet bold. “They don’t shy away from voicing their beliefs, and if need be, fight for it,” explains Shantanu Mehra, co-founder of the eponymous label. Nikhil Mehra of Shantanu & Nikhil While bold hues of black, red and gold dominated last season’s collection, the designers have looked towards wedding-ready shades of bright pink, yellow, green and blue this time around. “The collection is a representation of the soul of India, with a contemporary blend of electric, radiant and vibrant hues,” says Nikhil Mehra. Overall, the collection builds on Shantanu & Nikhil’s anti-trend philosophy, which ensures that brides and grooms focus more on their individuality and less on trends—a belief that is strongly resonated through dramatic silhouettes and exaggerated neo-drapes. “From voluminous ball gowns, intricately designed new-age lehengas and anarkali gowns to an eclectic menswear collection featuring muted textures and embroidery, this collection’s narrative encapsulates the spirit of vintage India, blended with the excitement of modern India,” says Nikhil. Expect a variety of rich fabrics like silk jersey, raw silk, luxurious brocades and silk organza in the autumn/winter 2019 range. The motifs take on the ancient form of storytelling through the tales of Panchatantra to depict a harmonious array of flora and fauna. You’ll also spot the designers’ signature techniques of tone-on-tone textures and metallic appliques on the garments. column1: 12 models who are championing a brighter future for women through their activism
column2: © Mara Desypris Fashion From diversity and inclusivity to women’s rights and mental health, these powerful women are breaking the stereotype attached to their modelling careers Back in the day, models were expected to be attractive, skinny, tall and taciturn—their opinions, beliefs and issues held almost no weightage when compared to their sharp looks. In the ’90s, we were graced with a glimmer of hope when supermodels like Naomi Campbell, Cindy Crawford and Christy Turlington raised their voices against the use of fur in Peta’s “I'd rather go naked than wear fur” campaign, which sparked a huge debate in the fashion industry. And last month, the British Fashion Council announced that Campbell will be honoured with the prestigious Fashion Icon award at The Fashion Awards 2019 this year, for championing female empowerment and diversity. To commemorate her achievement, Vogue takes a look at twelve powerful voices who have lent their support to the issues rampant in the modelling industry, from biased casting practices to climate change. Trans model Anjali Lama has broken countless gender barriers in the modelling industry. Despite facing rejection on many occasions, Lama finally had a breakthrough at Lakmé Fashion Week, which heralded her as the first transgender model to walk on the runway. Lama has openly spoken about the difficulties faced by a transgender model, and strongly advocates the inclusion of the LGBTQ+ community in India’s fashion industry. While Indian models are crossing over into international boundaries and setting new milestones, the industry in India is still stuck revolving around its unrealistic beauty standards. Fair skin is given as much preference as possible over dusky or dark skin. Model Nidhi Sunil, who has first-hand faced the issue of being discriminated over her skin colour, openly talks about how she fails to understand the term “dusky”—that’s used too often  in India. Nitika Chopra was diagnosed with a debilitating case of psoriasis at a young age of 10 years, and when she was 19, psoriatic arthritis took over most of her joints, leaving her in severe pain. Today, Chopra has no qualms about sharing her chronic illness journey and its learnings with fellow women through her Instagram page Chronic Official. When she’s not being a muse to Sabyasachi Mukherjee, supermodel Kanishtha Dhankhar is busy raising awareness about the growing concerns of single-use plastic and its detrimental effects on the environment. Self-care begins at home, and if you’re not sure how to begin, look no further than Adwoa Aboah’s Gurls Talk. Founded by Aboah, the website is an online community for young women to share and discuss issues such as depression, addiction, relationships, sexuality and mental health. The platform has become a safe zone for many, as you will note by the number of honest, moving letters penned by girls from all around the world. One scroll through Cameron Russell’s Instagram account will provide insight into all the social, political and environmental issues she cares about—whether it is spreading awareness about climate change, or advocating ethical working conditions and fair wages for garment workers. Her TED Talk from 2013 helped garner her attention for her causes—the ten-minute video talks about everything from how she won “a genetic lottery” for her looks to the prevalent lack of diversity in the fashion industry. Yet another TED speaker, Leomie Anderson is the founder of LAPP, a blog that supports women’s issues, including relationships, sex, mental health and more. In addition to the blog, Anderson also launched LAPP The Brand, a clothing label that aims to empower women and promote body positivity through its feminist messaging. In 2012, model Lauren Wasser suffered from a case of tampon-related toxic shock syndrome (TSS) that left her without her right leg and left toes. Six years later, Wasser had her left leg amputated because of continuing complications. This episode prompted the model to turn into an educator and spread awareness about the dangers and risks of TSS. Today, she also represents the physically impaired in the fashion industry. Body image is a prevalent issue amassing concern in the fashion industry, and no model—neither thin or plus-size—is spared from it. To help other women accept themselves for who they are and celebrate themselves, models Charli Howard and Clémentine Desseaux started All Womxn Project, a photo series of diverse, non-retouched campaigns that are empowering and positive in equal measure. Ebonee Davis has safely established that her career is not limited to modelling in the fashion industry. She wrote an impassioned open letter in 2016 that called out the fashion industry’s biased casting practices, and even struck a conversation on the existing issues of diversity during her TED Talk in 2017, highlighting her experiences as a black model. Another model to raise her voice against environmental issues—especially those caused by the use of plastic—is Arizona Muse. The model also shares a keen interest in sustainability—right from what fabrics to use to how to shop ethically. column1: The Indian kids brand Meghan Markle chose for baby Archie's first public appearance
column2: © Getty Fashion Duchess of Sussex Meghan Markle’s love for feel-good Indian fabrics seems to be a deciding factor in her choice of baby essentials as well After Prince Harry and Meghan Markle first introduced their son, Archie Harrison Mountbatten-Windsor, to the world in May, the youngest member of the British royal family made his first public appearance at the King Power Royal Charity Polo Day on July 10. Cradled in his mother’s arms, baby Archie looked comfortable in his white onesie—but it was the baby blanket that Markle later threw over him that caught our attention. The cotton dohar was crafted by Indian label Malabar Baby, and features beautiful block prints, all done by hand. © Getty Founder and managing director of Malabar Baby, Anjali Harjani-Hardasani, had no idea that the dohar had been purchased by a member of the royal family. “I was in Italy when I found out and I feel truly honoured. It’s great that Meghan Markle is advocating feel-good Indian fabrics,” says Harjani-Hardasani. “What baby Archie is swaddled in is a receiving blanket—it’s extremely lightweight and snug, is made out of cotton voile and can be easily packed into a bag. Erawan Cotton Dohar, Malabar Baby © Getty No wonder Meghan took it with her for the outdoor family event. As it turns out, Archie isn’t the only celebrity baby to be associated with Malabar Baby. Closer to home, Shahid Kapoor and Mira Rajput Kapoor also bought the label’s handmade play mat for their daughter, Misha. The brand is relatively new—it launched just two and a half years ago, when Harjani-Hardasani noticed a paucity of essentials for her then-newborn baby. Over 70 per cent of the label’s products are made in India, using quality fabrics like GOTS (Global Organic Textile Standard) approved natural cotton, organic muslin and even bamboo. “Bamboo has anti-fungal properties which ensure that babies don’t get rashes. It’s also a very breathable fabric and is hypoallergenic. We’ve used it in our line of towels too,” says Harjani-Hardasani, further stressing on the label’s strict policy of sourcing sustainable and natural fabrics. “Apart from block prints, our products also incorporate water colour art work, for which we work with artists from around the world,” she says. column1: Alber Elbaz gives us a first look at his new collaboration with Tod’s
column2: © Tods.com Fashion “When you come to Paris, where I live, there are so many roads for pedestrians only. So maybe shoes are the new cars,” the designer said about how he imagined this project After accepting an invitation from Tod’s chairman Diego Della Valle to visit “just for pasta, not for work,” designer Alber Elbaz discovered something wonderful. “Behind the concrete wall of their headquarters, I met a beautiful group of artists and artisans,” he remembers. “They were working hard with their hands and their hearts. The beauty was to see that Tod’s is one big family.” Elbaz would eventually sign on to design a capsule collection for the Italian heritage brand, which debuts today in Paris. It will officially launch online and in stores on July 15 under the umbrella of the collaborative Tod’s Factory project. He’s calling it Tod’s Happy Moments by Alber Elbaz, happy being the feeling you get while wearing Tod’s classic driving shoes in various scenarios. “I thought, What would be the right shoe to make you run to your office so that you are never late?” the designer says. “So I thought, Happy not to be late! As we know, Anna [Wintour] always likes to be on time. She was actually on my mind.” Also on his mind were happy, bright metallic bags and T-shirts, which also form part of the collection and feature Elbaz’s cheery signature sketches. But mainly, the shoes were the starting point for Elbaz—he’s incorporated more colour, the Tod’s logo, and a platform sole in these new iterations. © Tods.com “Talking about driving shoes,” Elbaz says, “when you come to Paris, where I live, there are a lot of roads that are saturated because now, there are so many roads for pedestrians only.” He adds, “So maybe shoes are the new cars—that’s how I imagined this project. I also wanted to change the shoe’s sole without changing the soul of Tod’s.” Elbaz clearly had fun with this project, which is his first for a major European fashion house since he left his position as creative director at Lanvin in 2015. He says that it’s difficult for him to choose a favourite piece from this collection, just as “asking a mother who is her favourite kid is always a hard one. I think it’s really about the sneaker,” Elbaz explains when asked about the core product in the capsule. “The sneaker is the right product for today because it’s a world of rapidity and it liberates women. That’s probably why sneakers are becoming the new It bag.” He adds, “I tried with this collaboration to create an Instagram moment and to create a buzz, but it was more about finding the mix between the ideas and the desires of people right now. column1: Princess Diana’s workout sweater just sold at auction for Rs 3.6 million
column2: © Getty Fashion That’s one pricey piece of activewear Well, you blew it. Unless you are the “collector in California who wishes to remain anonymous,” you did not manage to outbid everyone else in order to acquire Princess Diana's old Virgin Atlantic sweatshirt. The athleisure in question was a gift from Virgin Atlantic’s founder Richard Branson to Princess Diana, and then a gift from Princess Diana to her trainer, Jenni Rivett, over two decades ago—a kind of gym clothes pay-it-forward. Rivett put it up for auction, promising to put proceeds to “help a Malawian family based in South Africa.” The auction house, RR Auction, announced that it went for $53,532 (Rs 36,70,569). The piece was special not just because Princess Diana wore it, but because she used it. “I remember one of her strategies was that she was going to wear the same Virgin Active sweatshirt every single session,” Rivett told Yahoo’s The Royal Box recently. Many paparazzi-plagued celebrities have borrowed this strategy since, like English actor Richard Madden, who recently admitted to The New York Times, “I wear the same clothes days in a row, because if it looks like the same day, they can’t run the pictures. There’s only so many photos you can have of me with a green juice walking down the street.” Or a royal in a ratty old sweatshirt walking down the street. Princess Diana has lessons to teach yet. column1: This accessory is quickly becoming World Cup winner Megan Rapinoe’s signature
column2: © Getty Fashion As it turns out, the US women’s national football team co-captain has a penchant for giant sunglasses All hail the pink-haired woman who said, “I’m not going to the fucking White House.” Today, millions around the world watched as Megan Rapinoe rode with her equally badass US women’s national football teammates in New York City, which held a ticker-tape parade to celebrate their historic World Cup win. As they traveled up Broadway to City Hall, the team danced and chanted and sipped (chugged?) Champagne wearing their “World Champions” T-shirts. Co-captain Rapinoe was also wearing a giant pair of bright red sunglasses that not only made her stand out on the float, but bumped her swag up another notch, if that were even possible. For her speech, she changed into another pair of bottle-cap frames to speak powerfully about how “it’s our responsibility to make this world a better place.” Rapinoe has been loudly and proudly outspoken about the fight for equal pay and LGBTQ+ rights both on and off the field. In the last month, she’s become an idol for young feminists and a role model for little girls who have big dreams of playing in the World Cup. She is more than an athlete: she’s a symbol of hope and strength against the backdrop of the current administration’s attitude and backward policies toward women. As such, Rapinoe is developing a signature look in this new spotlight, one that recalls RBG’s dissent collars and Nancy Pelosi’s shades and fiery red Max Mara coat. Rapinoe’s statement sunglasses—which she not only wore to the parade today (twice) but also to visit Good Morning America yesterday and to several events in the days beforehand—grant her some extra edge. And while Rapinoe certainly doesn’t need any accessories or clothing to make her appear even cooler, the sunglasses do give off an attitude and swagger worthy of a new icon, holding a golden trophy in her hands. Next up: a trip to Washington, DC, to discuss equal pay with lawmakers. column1: Why "recommerce" is the next big thing in fashion
column2: © Signe Vilstrup Fashion Renting and shopping for pre-owned fashion is one way to close the loop and reduce the hazardous impact fashion has on the environment. Ahead, Vogue deep dives into the rise of the borrowed closet There’s no denying that there’s an emotional aspect to dressing up. It's easy to dismiss a garment as just an object, but the label might dictate how expensive or inexpensive it was, the person who wore it will not just remember it for the price; it will be more about how she felt in it. Did she meet someone special when she took it out, or did the party that she was at turn into one the most special nights ever? Did she wear it to her first day at the job she always wanted? These are the things that make an outfit special. But will someone else’s bag of emotions find room in your closet? Vintage clothing is for the nostalgic, romantic kind yes, but it’s also for the conscious consumers. You can’t have a conversation about sustainability in fashion without bringing up the resale market. With options for everything from buying pre-owned luxury to renting wardrobes, this is far from the scavenging you’re expecting, in that typically quaint store stocked with garments smelling of mothballs. We’re talking archival pieces that will hold a place of pride in your closet. Pre-owned Versace at Farfetch There's a growing sales model that now supports this movement: Recommerce or reverse commerce refers to the process of selling pre-owned products to consumers who are willing to repair, if necessary, and reuse, recycle and resell them. Renting clothing for special occasions is a concept you might already be familiar with. Maybe you don’t want to spend a small fortune on an outfit that will see less than 10 wears in its lifetime, and there’s no reason you should feel that pressure. The fashion industry is adding toll on the environment through its careless means of production, but the onus also lies with the consumer. The best way to be sustainable is to stop creating more waste, and not buying that extra item of clothing is ultimately a good choice.  Rent the Runway is a popular choice among many fashion lovers in the United States. With subscription packages ranging across varying costs, a member can borrow anywhere from four to unlimited products from the website in a month. If you love what you borrowed and wish to make it your own, you can simply buy it. Along with offering free shipping, Rent the Runway also uses responsible, non-hazardous dry cleaning, and encourages reuse of plastic bags in which the dry-cleaned clothes are sent. Vestaire Collective, The RealReal and Farfetch are big names in the luxury resale market. Equipped with an army of experts who authenticate products, a grading system indicative of the wear a garment or accessory has seen, and options to both buy and sell luxury, these websites are almost making shopping current season seem passé. Circularity is important for the millennial consumer and brands who want to survive the market in a time when the fashion economy is being called out for the damage it causes the planet. Taking the greener route is the only smart move to make. The Real Real, which began out as a start-up, went public late in May this year. Prior to that, the company raised no less than $350 million (~Rs 24 billion) in funding. Luxury e-commerce retailer Farfetch has also stepped up its game, extending its offering of luxury fashion to include pre-owned pieces that go under the tag ‘Positively Conscious’ on the website. Vogue spoke to Celenie Seidel, senior womenswear editor at Farfetch, about what gives the platform a competitive edge over the others. Pre-owned Versace at Farfetch Farfetch partners with an incredible group of boutiques and brands. We do not have physical stock of the products we sell, but instead enable the exchange between these boutiques and brands to customers globally. Farfetch has always had a strong and varied offering of special vintage and pre-owned pieces. We have been able to curate such a wide range of pieces by working with specialists from amazing boutiques across the world, such as D.A.N.G.E.L.O in Italy and Amore in Japan. Pre-owned Versace at Farfetch Our specialist partners are truly experts in their fields, and they validate the product and set the price. Proprietary Farfetch technology enables them to upload stock onto the site, once it has been photographed by our team of experts in one of our four global photography studios. Pre-owned Versace at Farfetch Our customers are fashion lovers. They know the pieces they are looking for, and sometimes come to Farfetch for specialist pieces. Consumers are becoming more comfortable with the online resale market now, thanks to improved trust and verification processes and the ability to offer a range of options across the market. A lot of our consumers have also taken part in the resale market by selling their pieces or buying pre-loved fashion. Pre-owned Walter Van Beirendonck at Farfetch Farfetch offers an amazing and varied range of vintage pieces onsite. With our boutique partners, we’ve curated a few specialist archive collections that we’ve received really great feedback on from our customers. For example, a celebration of some of Rei Kawakubo’s most iconic Comme des Garçons pieces to coincide with the Met Gala exhibition in 2017; over 500 pieces of original Gianni Versace, which we launched for sale last year; and our recently launched collection of Walter Van Beirendonck archive pieces. column1: Ralph & Russo gets a $50 million investment from La Perla
column2: © Instagram.com/badgalriri Fashion Worth almost Rs 3.5 billion, this investment will help the brand bring its relatable couture to a younger audience British couture house Ralph & Russo, which became a household name when Meghan Markle wore the brand for her engagement portraits with Prince Harry in 2017, has received $50 million (£40 million) from La Perla Fashion Investment B.V. The new partner has taken a non-controlling minority share in the 2010-born label, which became the first British guest member of the Chambre Syndicale de la Haute Couture for more than a century in 2014. “This strategic investment signifies an important step in allowing Ralph & Russo and our team to realise our long-term growth plans whilst keeping the brand privately owned and managed,” said chief executive Michael Russo, who founded the company with creative director Tamara Ralph. The business move marks a new chapter for the Mayfair brand. After building up a high-profile fan base that includes Sonam Kapoor Ahuja, Rihanna, Zendaya Jennifer Lopez and Gwyneth Paltrow, its frothy, fantastical couture and newer ready-to-wear line began to attract a younger following. “In the past two seasons we’ve seen a huge growth from 18-25-year-olds,” Ralph told Vogue after the autumn/winter 2019 couture show. “They’re actually buying pieces as separates, putting a skirt with a T-shirt and wearing it with sneakers… It shows the evolution of [couture].” Pascal Perrier, La Perla Global Management (UK) Limited chief executive, who will join Ralph & Russo’s board of directors, praised the couple for doing “a phenomenal job at creating one of the world’s top luxury fashion brands in a short space of time”. Russo, in turn, said he was looking forward to putting Perrier’s expertise (he has formerly held executive positions at the Burberry Group and the Gucci Group) to use, as well as the financial aid. For a label that knows its audience, La Perla’s backing is an opportunity to grow its relatable couture and high-fashion into something that reaches the masses—not solely on Instagram. column1: Stella McCartney’s new capsule collection is inspired by The Beatles
column2: © StellaMccartney.com Fashion “It’s emotional, authentic and, politically, it has never felt more relevant,” the designer said about her new collection When Paul McCartney hosted a family screening of Yellow Submarine, the 1968 fantasy film inspired by the music of The Beatles, it wasn’t just his grandchildren who were in awe of the psychedelic trip down Abbey Road. McCartney’s daughter, the activist designer Stella, was blown away. “It affected me in a way I just wasn’t expecting,” McCartney tells Vogue. She found herself removed from her familial ties and inspired as a creative to channel the trippy colours, comedy, lyrics and spirit of togetherness into a capsule collection, aptly entitled “All Together Now”. “It’s shockingly modern to me that these four young guys from Liverpool were championing themes of unity and solidarity,” she continues. “This idea of connecting people has never been more relevant.” The riotous palette, prints and process continue the narrative McCartney told through her autumn/winter 2019 collection, inspired by the Northern Soul scene of the late 1960s. “I wanted to take the Stella McCartney woman—and the heritage ingrained in me—and pump the whole thing up,” she smiles of the childlike state of wonderment she adopted during the design process. The “Lucy In The Sky With Diamonds” scene in the film, for example, informed dresses with whimsical circus-esque prints; a fur-free jacquard coat pays homage to the band’s marching uniforms, and pop-art portraits of the musicians are realised as patches and motifs on bold womenswear, menswear and kids wear, which McCartney hopes her customers will wear fluidly. The lyric-driven pieces, such as knitwear and jersey printed with the phrase “All Together Now” in multiple languages, or the separates bearing the words “all you need is love” and “love, love, love”, elaborate on McCartney’s thought process. “There’s so much paraphernalia from The Beatles already on the market,” she says. “The band says no to 99.9 per cent of collaborations, so I wanted to take the lightness of heart into a collection that speaks to yesterday and today—not just replicate their iconography.” The fact her father agreed is a huge compliment for her. “I started thinking about fashion design from a young age because I was interested in the psychological connection between how you feel and what you wear,” McCartney elaborates. Central to this is the social responsibility McCartney has instilled in her vegetarian brand. “I’m not perfect, by any means, but I’m trying very hard to create a different business model for fashion,” she affirms. “I don’t want to participate in the mass murder of animals and the environmental destruction this creates, outside of the overwhelming waste in the industry.” As well as organic cottons and yarns used in the capsule, McCartney focused on upcycling vintage patches and fabrics to use. “Designing in a timeless way is key to sustainable fashion, and this is a collectable collaboration you won’t want to throw away.” Nor, she hopes, will you cast aside the message of togetherness. “It’s emotional, authentic and, politically, it has never felt more relevant.” The “All Together Now” collection, which is priced from £235 (Rs 20,000) to £4,550 (~Rs 4 lakh), is available at Stellamccartney.com and select stores worldwide. column1: Kim Kardashian West reveals how painful it was to get into her Met Gala dress
column2: © Instagram.com/kimkardashian Fashion “I have never felt pain like that in my life,” the entrepreneur shared in a recent interview As a beauty entrepreneur, law student, reality TV star and mother-of-four, Kim Kardashian West, has never been one to shy away from any type of challenge, particularly in the name of beauty or fashion. Often that daring, entrepreneurial attitude has worked out, such as when the 38-year-old decided to launch a beauty brand despite not having any on-the-ground experience in the cosmetics industry. Kardashian West’s beauty brand, KKW Beauty, launched to huge success, quickly earning its place in the beauty hall of fame as one of the most sought-after beauty brands in the world. But, other times that same attitude hasn’t resulted in quite the same successful outcome and a recent fashion choice left the mother-of-four in physical pain and reminded us all why this outdated piece of clothing is best left in the fashion archives. Speaking to the Wall Street Journal about her upcoming as-yet-unnamed shapewear line—which has been shrouded in controversy after Kardashian West announced the line would be called Kimono and then had to retract the name—the Keeping Up with the Kardashians star revealed the anatomy-defying waist-cinching Thierry Mugler dress she wore to this year’s Met Gala took a very painful physical toll on her. “I never felt pain like that my life,” the 38-year-old told the Wall Street Journal of wearing the Mugler dress to the Met Gala. “I’ll have to show you pictures of the aftermath when I took it off—the indentations on my back and my stomach.” The beauty entrepreneur further made a point of saying that although there was talk that she had had ribs removed to fit into the dress, this was not the case. “I don’t even know if that’s possible [to remove ribs],” Kardashian West noted. Instead, her impossibly tiny waist was reportedly achieved through a Mister Pearl corset worn under the dress. Not only did the corset and dress cause external physical marks, it also reportedly required her to take “breathing lessons” so she wouldn’t pass out from lack of oxygen while wearing such a tight garment. The Cut reports the reality star shared the detail about the breathing lessons in an Instagram post from May, reportedly saying Mister Pearl, the corset-maker, schooled her in breathing while wearing a corset. Kardashian West’s confession is a timely reminder why the corset is no longer in fashion. Wearing something that restricts lung capacity and causes pain is taking the old adage of “suffering for fashion” to an extreme, unhealthy place that has no currency in the current fashion conversation; pairing comfort and style is the new order of the day. column1: This Indian cashmere brand just launched their new collection in London
column2: Fashion Janavi India unveiled the first palette from its unique ‘Paintbox’ collective with an exclusive event at The Ritz London. Here’s why you need to know about it From its humble beginnings in 1998 (launched from Jyotika Jhalani’s son's room), Janavi India has clearly come a long way. Today, the brand is taking the ‘make in India’ label to global spotlight with their ethical cashmere collectibles, retailing at the world’s shopping meccas—like Bergdorf Goodman and Lane Crawford. Their luxe cashmere shawls and stoles celebrate their founder’s Kashmiri origin, while also championing Indian craftsmanship. To mark Janavi India’s 21st anniversary, Jhalani revisits her childhood and fondness for painting with a one-of-its-kind collective—The Janavi India Paintbox. A thematic representation of the colours of life inspired by 12 destinations close to her heart, each palette narrates a chapter of the designer’s own journey here. The big unveil of the first palette was held at the same location it was inspired at: The Ritz London. The likes of Nina Campbell, Tikka Shatrujit Singh, Feroze Gujral and Kate Baxter were in attendance at the traditional English high tea celebration hosted by Fizzy Barclay. “The Paintbox is a celebration of what Janavi India’s real signature is: unusual colour stories. Fizzy is one of my closest friends, and we host an exhibition at her hotel every year. So, there was no better way to launch this collection,” says founder and creative director Jhalani. The collection borrows from an archive of over 50,000 designs as well as the setting, and is replete with hues mimicking the soft edges of clotted cream, the subtle pinks of smoked salmon and the mellow sheen of marmalade, punctuated with ivory tones. These are further enhanced with hand painting, delicate lace and resham threadwork on the shawls. The 11 other palettes—each with its designated set of shawls and stoles—also touch on Jhalani’s life while taking you around the world—a desert thali in Jaisalmer, the still lakes of Srinagar, the grandeur of St Petersburg, the energy of New York, the Ladurée macaroons of Paris, and the serenity of the Tuscan sky in Florence among other cities like Hong Kong, Bhutan, Philippines, Shanghai and Mauritius. 6 women of Indian origin who are carving out their own design niche Exploring the Indian block print’s rich cultural history With a 50-year-long legacy behind her, Ritu Kumar is “nowhere near done” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This sustainable fashion brand features clothes made by Indian prisoners
column2: Fashion Designer Abhishek Dutta’s new label Parole is created by both male and female inmates of Kolkata’s prisons. Here’s everything you need to know about the brand ahead of its launch With the aim to empower Indian prisoners to attain an honest living, designer Abhishek Dutta is launching Parole, a sustainable clothing brand that has been produced by both male and female inmates of Indian prisons. The label, which unveils its first collection on July 30, has been in the making for the last two years. “This project came from the West Bengal Correctional Home, when their DG and IG Arun Kumar Gupta approached [me] to train the inmates in designer cloth stitching and making,” reveals the Kolkata-based designer. Prison inmates in Parole “This initially started with 40 inmates at the Presidency Central Correctional Home, and has now expanded to include the Alipore Women’s Correctional Home as well, wherein women also got engaged in the same,” Dutta says. “The brand Parole originated from here because these inmates have now mastered the skills, and are making a living during the period of their conviction. It gives them a fresh start to [earn] a better livelihood once they are released,” he adds. Most of the life convicts are involved in the project, but it’s a constant method of training and involving new inmates as the older ones get released. The best part is that most of the fabrics in this collection are handwoven, and even the packaging uses recycled material—making it an all-round sustainable brand. “The fabrics used are mostly cotton and linen, denim and jamdani blends,” says Dutta. The collection, which is based on four themes—Denimactic, Powerholic, Infusion and Printarazzi—features Western wear as well as Indo-Western wear. Expect waistcoats, lapel jackets, bandis, kurtas and bandgalas in the menswear range, and jumpsuits, shift dresses, jackets, draped kurtas and more in the womenswear line. Both will soon retail at multi-brand outlets and leading online portals. Dutta is also pioneering the way for non-discrimination by using the inmates as the face of the brand. “This is a movement of reformation, where the inmates are truly altering their life choices and taking up an honest profession,” he concludes. Earthy, boxy, boring: Do sustainable clothes have a standard look? Are our collective efforts towards sustainable fashion enough? Are direct-to-consumer brands the future for sustainable fashion? "I dreamt about a woman with nonchalant elegance,” Viard said of her graceful 1930s silhouettes. The result? A perfectly peaceful moment that skilfully reminded viewers of the “calm procured by reading”, the collection notes revealed. A cue for showgoers to put the phone down momentarily? Mais oui! Valentino autumn/winter 2019 © Shutterstock Pierpaolo Piccioli has many masterstrokes. His Autumn 2019 Valentino couture show was not only an ode to texture play (sequins, feathers and yarn) or scenic prints (in homage to paintings of Diana Vreeland) but the benchmark for diverse casting. “The only way to make couture alive today is to embrace different women’s identities and cultures,” Piccioli told American Vogue’s Nicole Phelps during a private collection preview. The finale look—a handmade dress constructed of feathers and stainless steel, which took four months to create—was made in collaboration with American kinetic sculptor Anthony Howe. Consider the bar on performative fashion officially raised. It was here that he declared his couture intention to be “impulsive and anarchic”, and sure enough the iconoclastic designer scored a critical success with a collection that showcased his unmistakable talent for transforming the everyday (in this instance, men’s trousers) into fantasy couture. column1: Vogue’s fashion encyclopaedia: The pencil skirt
column2: © Prasad Naik Fashion Associated with sex symbols and power women alike, the pencil skirt has many guises—and rather surprising origins. Vogue recaps its history The pencil skirt has long been an evocative garment—stirring admiration and frustration in equal measure, its history one of femme fatales, bookish authors and movie stars. Its origins are said to lie in one rather curious incident in 1908 when Mrs Edith Hart O Berg became the first American woman to fly as a passenger in an aeroplane, tying a stretch of rope around her ankles to save the fabric of her skirt from billowing in flight. This allegedly inspired the trend for hobble skirts—though French couturier Paul Poiret claimed he’d devised the design independently. Whichever way, the ensuing taste for skirts tapering sharply around the shins, forcing wearers to move in short, rapid steps, was rapacious—and mercilessly mocked. Satirical cartoons took potshots at the vanity of prioritising appearance above movement, while special hobble skirt-friendly carriages were added to streetcars in New York and LA. The trend was brief, dispensed with in favour of easy motion and much shorter hemlines. Marilyn Monroe in Some Like it Hot © Getty The pencil skirt as we recognise it today first entered the world several decades later in 1954, when Christian Dior’s H-line collection introduced another new shape for the modern woman. Named after the way its silhouette resembled a capital ‘H’, complete with straight lines and a slight emphasis on the waist, it had the advantage of both lengthening the wearer’s legs and placing greater attention on the hips. It also offered something tighter and more streamlined for those tired of the New Look’s excess fabric and frou-frou prettiness. Of course, Dior can't fully claim credit. The skirt’s precedents can be seen in the boxier shapes of the 1940s, typified by Lauren Bacall in To Have and Have Not, as well as in the work of other contemporary designers—especially Cristóbal Balenciaga, who cut clothes directly onto the contours of the body rather than relying on padding or crinolines. James Stewart and Grace Kelly on the set of Rear Window © Getty The pencil skirt became a defining garment of the 1950s and early 1960s. It could be luxuriously smart, as seen in lime green on Grace Kelly in Rear Window. It could exude sex appeal, as demonstrated by Sophia Loren who paired it with strappy tops and tightly tailored jackets. It could be chic in black on Audrey Hepburn. For Marilyn Monroe, perhaps the most famous wearer of the pencil skirt, it came to define an entire aesthetic: one predicated on a particularly voluptuous projection of femininity, complete with tight sweaters, crisp white shirts and an overarching emphasis on her hourglass figure. Like the hobble-skirt, it required a very particular way of walking—see Monroe’s famous wiggle epitomised in Some Like It Hot, her wide-eyed character Sugar Kane sashaying provocatively in the skin-tight skirt. Director Billy Wilder with Audrey Hepburn © Getty When it comes to movement, the pencil skirt’s restrictions on gait and emphasis on particular points of the body are often associated with conscious displays of sex appeal (no wonder that Rizzo in Grease and Joan in Mad Men wear them) and empowered women (think Joan Collins in Dynasty). It can also be either erotic or camp (or both) in its nods to fetishwear when rendered in fabrics like leather and latex—think Dita Von Teese or Aquaria’s shiny red entrance look on RuPaul’s Drag Race. Arguably, the pencil skirt is also the forerunner to and participant in the 2000s and 2010s’ interest in bodycon—typified by the Kardashian clan’s propensity for clinging fabrics and form-hugging designs. Dita Von Teese © Getty In contrast, however, the pencil skirt also came to be thought of as a very practical garment in the 1950s and 1960s: a smart working uniform for women, especially with a little pleat at the back to help motion. It’s a garment that’s still a crucial part of the office wardrobe for many today, often favoured by those with roles in public office, as seen on Meghan Markle and Michelle Obama. Under those circumstances it embodies a particular kind of neutral chic, the kind reflected recently on the catwalk by designers such as Victoria Beckham and Rejina Pyo. Michelle Obama © Getty Sensual or serious, undone or polished, beloved or rebuked, worn by everyone from teenage girls in the 1950s determined to defy their parents to modern-day drag queens, it’s clear the pencil skirt isn’t a straightforward piece. Enmeshed as it is in questions of movement, appearance and gender (see Art School’s AW19 gender-neutral pink pencil skirt), no doubt it will continue to inspire designers, one rather small step at a time. column1: Your favourite fashion trends from the 2000s are ruling the charts in 2019
column2: Fashion Noughties nostalgia reigns supreme in 2019, with sartorial hallmarks that were championed by celebrities like Paris Hilton, Britney Spears during the decade Everything old is new again, or so the adage goes. The cyclical nature of trends means that you don’t require a time machine to travel back in time. Chances are, your favourite souvenirs from adolescence have made a comeback under the watchful eye of Instagram’s cool crowd. While chokers and bell bottoms have been enjoying their moment in their spotlight, post-Y2K staples are now making their presence known on the style scene. It’s time to dig through the wardrobe for your choicest teenage relics, because these are the trends that have been branded cool again by the powers that be. Baby tank tops, over-the-loop belts and navel-baring denims—Christina Aguilera prize-winning formula has been given the 2019 treatment with slouchy fits and rolled-up hems edging hip-hugging skinnies out the door. Yes, fashion is celebrating the midriff again, and low-rise denims are poised on the cusp of a mainstream comeback with the best dressed set on social media dropping their waists to a nostalgia-inducing level. Slashing cleanly across toned navels, the nonironic resurgence of this trend has seen itsy-bitsy tanks swapped in favour of cropped button-down shirts and knotted blouses. If you aren’t ready to hop on the peekaboo thong trend yet, why thank you, layer yours under a tailored blazer for a sophisticated take on your teenaged go-to. Some say that this après-dark staple is coming back, others argue that it never really left. After triangle top halters and tube tops, the time is nigh for Paris Hilton’s sartorial signature to reign again, with dressy tops that make heads turn across a crowded bar, but don’t feel too restrictive on the cab ride back home. The go-to candidate for last-minute plans, these fuss-free numbers make a strong case for leaving complicated zippers and jumpsuits behind. Invite spaghetti straps and peplum along, and you have a true-blue Y2K party on your hands. For an adult take on this teenage favourite, pair yours with mid-rise denims or flowy culottes, and opt for of-the-moment animal prints and metallics—the former comes approved by street style icon Kendall Jenner. It should come as zero surprise that low-rise denims booked a berth for two on the throwback express, and invited chain belts along to the party. One thing that all style savants will agree upon is that accessories maketh the outfit. And for the fuss-free route to everyday chic, tiered chain belts stand as prompt service. Back in 2003, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan took hers to the beach with an asymmetrical dress and open-toed flats. Today, you can look to vintage gold numbers to elevate everyday gingham and plaid, or take the trend with you into the fall by draping one over an oversized sweater dress. If you’re feeling the retro love, loop yours through a high-waisted pair of denims and wriggle into a tiny puff-sleeved crop top. © Getty This schoolgirl staple is having a coming-of-age moment on the style scene, and now serves as an easy way to humble-brag about all the hours you’ve been clocking in at the gym. You won’t have to look too far for inspiration on styling these bite-sized staples—the noughties saw Kareena Kapoor Khan opting for embroidered numbers in Mujhse Dosti Karoge! (2002). Elsewhere, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan gave the silhouette her own party-ready update by pairing it with a blingy bodysuit in Dhoom 2 (2006). While flirty hemlines make for a no-brainer during the summer, you can leverage it for fall fashion with over-the-knee boots, or by layering it under an A-line jacket. When you’re ready to break free from the everyday grind, pair distressed cut-offs with a slogan tee and your go-to Converse shoes for an impromptu road trip. column1: These fashion brands are making a strong move to combat climate change
column2: © Instagram.com/ralphlauren Fashion While Prada recently announced that it plans to launch virgin nylon by 2021, Burberry is setting emission goals in an attempt to become carbon neutral. Ahead, Vogue lists all the luxury brands that have recently committed to becoming more environmentally conscious Sustainability has become a big business in the fashion industry, with greenwashing—claims that make a company look more eco-friendly than it actually is—becoming an actual threat. According to Global Fashion Agenda’s 2018 report, brands stand a strong chance to improve financially if they make investments towards incorporating sustainable materials. Whether brands are thinking about profitability or the environment as they make changes to mitigate their carbon impact is secondary—the fact is that it’s a long-term goal every business needs to seriously consider. Policymakers in the United States are also showing their support by advocating the Green New Deal, an initiative that aims to address climate change and economic inequality. Even the European Trade Policy saw a more climate-oriented approach courtesy French president Emmanuel Macron and Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg. While achieving a business that is hundred per cent sustainable still seems like a far-fetched reality, Vogue looks at the fashion brands that have recently announced plans that will help them inch closer to that fabled dream. Last month, the Italian luxury group announced that it would be launching a range of nylon bags made using ocean plastics, fishing nets and textile fibre waste. The ‘Re-Nylon’ capsule collection will feature six styles including the belt bag, the shoulder bag and a backpack. What’s more, Prada hopes that the 7,00,000 metres of nylon it uses annually, will all be recycled by 2021. Considering the brand is known for its nylon bags, which go back to the ’80s, it’s a huge move for them to go environment-friendly with one of their iconic offerings. Another brand that made headlines last month was Burberry, which now plans to cut down on their greenhouse gas emissions in an attempt to become carbon neutral in their energy use by 2022. This move comes after the British luxury house made a formal statement last year that they would not be destroying their unsold stock, which was worth millions. Following suit is the French luxury house Chanel, who recently invested in a green chemistry company called Evolved By Nature, an American start-up that specialises in the silk industry and uses environmentally-conscious production techniques. The idea is for Chanel to adopt a more sustainable approach—like using the company’s Activated Silk™ invention, which can be used to create innovative textiles that don’t harm the environment. Kering, the French luxury conglomerate that owns brands like Gucci, Saint Laurent and Bottega Veneta, celebrated World Environment Day by launching a new digital platform dedicated to its Environmental Profit and Loss (EP&L) account which allows access to information about the business and its relationship with natural resources. On the same day, Gucci also launched its version of EP&L on Gucci Equilibrium that details its sustainability progress as well as its goal to ensure that hundred per cent of its raw materials are traceable to source by 2025. To commemorate Earth Day, Ralph Lauren introduced the Earth Polo, a classic take on the American brand’s iconic polo shirt, made entirely from hundred per cent recycled plastic (precisely, twelve) bottles. The brand has also committed to converting their virgin poly-fibre to recycled poly-fibre by 2025, while also removing 170 million bottles from the environment by the same year. In March, PVH Corp’s chairman and chief executive Emanuel Chirico revealed their goal to reduce emissions across their supply chain by 30 per cent by 2030. It’s evident that PVH, which owns brands like Tommy Hilfiger and Calvin Klein, is taking its sustainability commitments seriously—they first set emissions reduction targets all of two years ago. The popular American denim label is well aware about how much water is required to make one pair of jeans (around 7,600 litres, in case you were wondering). To combat the same, Levi’s introduced Water<Less® techniques which use far less water than traditional methods. By 2020, Levi’s aims for 80 per cent of its products to be made using these innovations (right now, it’s more than 40 per cent). Are our collective efforts towards sustainable fashion enough? column1: 8 things to know about Valentino’s autumn/winter 2019 couture show
column2: © Getty Fashion In another breathtaking distillation of artisanal skill, the Valentino autumn/winter 2019 haute couture show was big on diversity, imagination and emotion. Here's everything you need to know about Pierpaolo Piccioli's masterclass in gasp-worthy gowns © GoRunway Models wore headdresses comprising thousands of curiously spun yarns, bedecked with pom poms and tassels in a manner that, Vogue’s critic Anders Christian Madesen observed, “felt Berber” but also “a little Sámi.” At other points in a jaw-droppingly diverse collection, the yarns took the place of feathers. As Piccioli told Madsen in a preview: “I love this idea of all people: a combination of identities. It’s not place-specific. It’s not about ethnic. It’s about roots and identities, but I love the embrace of different cultures together. It’s about humans.” © GoRunway “A fantasy of flowers” was how Piccioli described some of his more mind-bending floral creations. These were not any species with which a green-fingered couture client would be familiar: Piccioli plumbed the depths of his imagination to come up with blooms that looked almost extra-terrestrial. Think Elizabeth Taylor blasting into outer space hand in hand with David Bowie and you're on the right track... © GoRunway The 75-year-old variously sang along to the Aretha Franklin soundtrack (‘You make me feel like a natural woman’), smiled at the audience and chatted to some FROW-ers, all while sashaying her way through the gilded rooms of Hôtel de Rothschild in a Kelly green exemplar. Fittingly, she was met with spontaneous ripples of applause so enthusiastic that one could chart her progress through the rooms by the decibel level. © GoRunway Is it just us, or does this dress resemble an exquisitely iced tray of Mr Kipling fondant fancies? Piccioli played with his colour palette, as always, mixing frothy lime with patrician purple, cerise with dove grey, salmon pink with sulky red, but it was the head-to-toe shots of colour—turquoise, emerald, marigold—that enthralled. © GoRunway In a show that was made for Instagram—and we mean that in the best possible way—it was fitting that the glitter- and feather-chocked makeup looks also came in filter form, so that guests could try the dramatic eyelashes that might eventually accompany their couture purchases themselves. As for the jewellery, clients had to be content to merely ogle: earrings were shoulder-grazing and pleasingly eccentric. © Getty Consider this a worthy 2019 addition to one of Vogue’s favourite tumblrs, Awesome People Hanging Out Together, as well as the perfect trio of candidates for the fashion team’s front row game of choice: “Couture clients: what do they talk about?” When Celine met Christian met KST—how’s that for small talk? © Getty How to offset the enchanting decadence of utterly exotic gowns? A simple single-soled sandal, with one clear strap and a bow at the ankle, was enough to complete myriad show-stopping looks. © Getty Following Piccioli’s documentation of the Valentino seamstresses on his Instagram feed, captioned with quotes from the Portuguese communist writer José Saramago, the designer brought his Roman team out onto the catwalk for a finale bow. Many were crying, and all made a beeline for the founder of the house, Valentino Garavani, who was sitting front row (next to Naomi Campbell, no less) and was subsequently showered in kisses. “I don’t like people that just work with me, I like people that share with me [in] the dream,” Piccioli has said, of his atelier. column1: Priyanka Chopra gets candid about her Dior experience at Paris Couture Week
column2: © Getty Fashion “It had so many interesting textures and uniquely structured pieces that I really connected with,” Chopra said about the brand’s autumn/winter 2019 couture collection Priyanka Chopra understands couture. Made to measure pieces have been a key part of the actress’s wardrobe since the beginning of her career, and she’s developed a knowledge and appreciation for the artistry behind each look. Front and centre during the Paris collections, Chopra took in Dior’s Fall 2019 event at the brand’s Avenue Montaigne flagship with her husband Nick Jonas. Enthralled by the spectacle of designer Maria Grazia Chiuri’s architecture and philosophy-inspired creations, Chopra couldn’t help but be impressed. “There is such an elevated sophistication not only in the clothing, but in the concepts and creative of the presentations themselves,” she shared post-show. “It was cool to see how [Dior] drew inspirations from elements of nature—fire, air, water—and the feminist artist Penny Slinger.” © Instagram.com/priyankachopra Known for her expansive wardrobe and ability to pull off difficult trends, Chopra lets her feelings guide her style choices, especially when she’s in the City of Light. “My fashion is as moody as I am, and any time I’m in Paris, I tend to gravitate toward super simple and feminine pieces,” she said. “I loved the colour of the dress I wore to the show, and the elegance of its simplicity. It was perfect and made me feel beautiful—at the end of the day, that’s what it’s all about.” The pieces on the runway proved equally inspiring, particularly the jet black separates and dramatic ball gowns detailed with sequins and dégradé mesh. “This Dior collection had so many interesting textures and uniquely structured pieces that I really connected with,” Chopra said. © Instagram.com/priyankachopra The fashion may have been thrilling, but no trip to Paris would be complete without a little relaxation. Chopra’s favourite way to unwind? Enjoying the city’s café culture and indulging in a bit of people watching during after a long summer day. “It’s crazy that it doesn’t start getting dark until 10pm,” she said. “I love sitting at a hotel lounge or cafe with friends and family watching the world go by!” © Instagram.com/priyankachopra This article was originally published on Vogue.com Deconstructing Dior’s AW19 with Maria Grazia Chiuri Dior Cruise 2020: How the new look of iconic Bar jacket came to be Riccardo Tisci on the new Burberry: “I want to make it more democratic” Fashion People Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The pioneering feminist artist behind the gold doll’s house at Dior's couture show
column2: © Penny Slinger Fashion For Dior’s autumn/winter 2019 Haute Couture show, Maria Grazia Chiuri reached out to the 1960s feminist surrealist Penny Slinger, and the result was magic. Vogue talks to the artist about exploring sexuality, feminine power and the female body Penny Slinger has a history with houses. In the early 1970s, the artist responsible for giving Dior’s recent couture show an occult edge, made surreal sculptures out of doll’s houses and used an abandoned country mansion as the backdrop for haunting collage works. Born in London in 1947, Slinger studied at Chelsea College of Arts at the end of the 1960s, when nearby King’s Road was the epicentre of the Swinging Sixties. Bold, clever and unabashed, even as a student Slinger was making strikingly original work using the tools of an earlier generation of male surrealists to explore the feminine. Penny Slinger © Penny Slinger In her Wedding Cake series, made in 1973, Slinger dressed in bridal white as a three-tier gateau, offering herself to be sliced into: a critical take on the packaging of women’s bodies for men’s desires. A striking beauty who modelled for Thea Porter, Slinger made a political point of posing naked for men’s magazines in which she talked about her work, confusing the idea that a beautiful woman in a state of undress was just an object to be looked at. Slinger’s concept for Dior nods to her great work An Exorcism (1977). Seven years in the making, its experimental—and often sexually explicit—collages are set within the spectral, crumbling grandeur of Lilford Hall, a Jacobean pile in Northamptonshire, UK. Using posed photographs of herself, her girlfriend Suzanka Fraey and her ex-boyfriend, the filmmaker Peter Whitehead, Slinger used the building as a metaphor for the psyche, later describing the process as one of self-psychoanalysis. Who Turns Her Back, a collage from An Exorcism © Penny Slinger Slinger went on to explore the liberated body more fully in the unabashedly erotic collages of Mountain Ecstasy, currently on show at London’s Richard Saltoun Gallery. By the late 1970s, she’d stepped away from the art world to pursue her fascination with tantra, co-authoring the bestselling work of erotic scholarship Sexual Secrets. To a new generation of feminist curators Slinger’s works of the 1960s and 1970s still feel fearless and fresh, exploring ideas around sexuality, feminine power and the female body. Following the release of Penny Slinger: Out Of The Shadows—a film exploring her early career, in cinemas now—we talk to the artist about fate, the feminine and constructing a fantasy for Dior. © Getty “Maria Grazia Chiuri reached out to me to collaborate with her as she had seen An Exorcism, my series of photo collages from the 1970s, in which I used an English mansion house as the setting for my surreal scenarios. I envisioned an artistic alchemy which would bring the four elements of nature into the building and create an immersive experience as they overtook every wall, ceiling and floor throughout the salons and the stairway, revealing the muse of the building: the many faces of the feminine that have inhabited and inspired this place throughout its evolution. It’s a celebration of the clients, friends and seamstresses who have made the story of the maison. A huge tree was fabricated that inhabited the stairwell like a gigantic tree of life, and photographs from my worldwide travels adorned every surface with textures of fire, water, air and earth embodied as trees, rocks and crystals. Four life-size sculptures were created to embody guardians at the portal, an alchemical goddess and a caryatid. It was an expansive experience to work with Maria Grazia and her creative team to manifest my largest collage ever. For the last look on the runway, I designed a wearable doll’s house, manifested impeccably by Maria Grazia's atelier at Dior. This was a model of the building, covered in 24-carat gold leaf—the embodied gold of the alchemical journey—which opened to reveal the body of the woman within.” “I was using the toolkit of surrealism, which allowed you to find archetypal symbols from the subconscious and unconscious realms, and then put them together in these new formulas. I very much had the intention of wanting to describe the inner workings of the feminine. I'm a woman, and I felt that it was an area that had been very neglected. The female image and form was prevalent in the history of art, and woman used as a muse, but not actually delving into what's happening under the surface, what's in the dreams and fantasies of women, what is really there underneath the skin, rather than just in the manifestation of that skin. My language evolved out of that: trying to find things that captured a state of consciousness, an atmosphere, a dream, a longing.” Mouths and masks, 16mm film © Penny Slinger “Before I went to a convent I thought it was going to be fantastic: a mystical order of sisterhood. When I got there the nuns were so mean, so bitter, twisted and uptight. I was nine, coming on ten; I was beginning to sense my body awakening. Other girls I knew had started getting breasts. I was very interested in all of this, and yet there it was something you shouldn't have anything to do with; you must completely set all that aside. It goes together with all these ideas of original sin. I was always very curious; I wanted to find out about my body and its feelings. When I was young I had all kinds of experimentations with my sexuality and sensuality. By the time I was 16 and the pill came into being, this was a great freedom that we hadn't had before then. I was very keen to experiment and experience all that I could through this vehicle that I felt had been so shut down. Now we had an opportunity to be much more liberated and open, and find out what it was all about. These ideas of the body as dirty, shameful and sinful have so robbed us of our potential to fully experience life with all our senses. All this apparatus that we’re given to have joy, to have bliss, shouldn't be taken away from us by cults of shame and taboo. This is the path of the feminine that we're hopefully now embracing: full embodiment, which is the full acceptance of the material, of all that we are, being as sacred as the spirit.” “I found myself in a very shattered state of being because of my breakup with Peter Whitehead, which was a very major relationship for me, at the same time as the disintegration of the Women's Theatre Group. I found myself feeling that I'd lost, in a way, both masculine and feminine sides of myself, and I thought, 'Why is this? What's happening to me? How can I heal this rift?' I felt I had to examine all the factors that had brought me to this situation: why you feel dependent on the man, what's going on? The old derelict mansion house is the seat of power, representing a lot of the Western heritage of masculine power, and yet it was derelict. I used all the rooms, all the aspects of the self, of the psyche, that I felt I needed to explore. All the skeletons were brought out of the cupboard so that I could examine them in the light of day. I was exorcising them by really looking at them and not having them hold me in fear or subjugation. I wanted to get deep because I believed that if I was experiencing this, it must be something common to other people; other people may not have identical experiences, but they have things that are in parallel to this. We all have the dark night of the soul some time or other, and here I was trying to find the lights in the darkness that would guide me through to the other side, to be reborn to my true self and understand what was mine and what was the projections of others and the society that I grew up in. If I can go through this game of detection, find the clues, follow them and come out the other side, then I can make landmarks along the way that will be helpful for other people.” The Larval Worm © Penny Slinger “I like to think of it as spontaneously arising reality: those things that happen outside of control but are guided by who you are. All the heroes and heroines in my life have been much more anti-rational in a sense, and allowed things to happen in the moment. I think you prepare yourself to have that allowance and find a space that it can manifest. This is the thing I love about collage: you have that element of chance encounter. I don't think I could call myself a surrealist if I didn't have that inclination to just be in the moment and see what happens. It allows for more openness in life, and for things to happen that are outside the norm (and I've always tried to live outside the norm!). I have also trusted my intuition: I've followed my heart and my inclination for better or for worse. Sometimes it's led me to some rather tricky areas, but in the end I wouldn't swap it for any other approach to life. You do your best at all times and then you cast your fate to the wind in order to see what providence will offer you. I have always lived my life like that.” Penny Slinger: Tantric Transformations is at London’s Richard Saltoun Gallery until August 24 Penny Slinger © Getty Tantric Transformations © Ben Westoby © Getty Dior Couture gives the smoky eye a modern update Dior’s 2020 Cruise collection: Vogue speaks to Maria Grazia Chiuri Watch the Dior spring/summer 2019 show live now Culture & Living Culture & Living Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan, Priyanka Chopra show you how to wear a cut-out gown
column2: © Instagram.com/tanghavri Fashion From Kareena Kapoor Khan’s strategically cut-out gown to Priyanka Chopra's one-shouldered red number, celebrities are giving a clear green signal to outfits that subtly flaunt small flashes of skin When your profession takes you to red carpets as often as the celebrities, you need a wardrobe that is filled with statement-making sartorial choices. Bollywood and Hollywood A-listers are no strangers to risqué fashion choices on the red carpet, and they’re only getting bolder in recent times. Forget plunging necklines and backless numbers—gowns with slits, slashes and strategically placed geometric cut-outs have found themselves carved into just about every celebrity couture closet. The trick to owning the look? Swapping over-the-top numbers with low-key ones, and going easy on the embellishments and accessories. Everyone from Kareena Kapoor Khan to Priyanka Chopra, Gigi Hadid, Kendall Jenner and Kim Kardashian West has already given the trend their own spin, leaving us with all the lessons we could ever need to ace cut-out gowns. When not in highly embellished gowns or acres of tulle, celebrities are opting for gowns featuring geometric cut-outs. Kareena Kapoor Khan is not one to shy away from a revealing ensemble—so long as it’s done tastefully. Her yellow Prabal Gurung gown came with cut-outs at the waist, while her green Tadashi Shoji number featured minimal cut-out detailing at the shoulders and the bodice.  Kriti Sanon showed off her toned abs with an interestingly cut-out gown by Shivan & Narresh. For those who are looking for a subtler way to wear cut-out gowns, Priyanka Chopra’s red Jason Wu gown may just serve as the answer—the cut-out detailing were placed on a safe zone in this one: at the shoulder.  Kim Kardashian West, Bella Hadid and Kendall Jenner also gave their vote of approval this style. While Hadid wore an embellished black Moschino number to Met Gala 2019, Kim Kardashian West sported a vintage Mugler gown that well, only she could. Kendall Jenner took a daring Rami Kadi number—with a cut-out bodice and the highest thigh slit we’ve ever seen—to this year’s post-Oscars party.
