column1: From farm to atelier: the making of Viktor & Rolf’s AW19 Couture collection
column2: © Anton Gottlob Fashion The Dutch duo have left the meme dresses of last year behind and teamed up with textile artist Claudy Jongstra, along with her biodynamic farm and heritage sheep, to craft a collection that puts a positive spin on sustainability “F* this, I'm going to Paris,” proclaims the first of three tulle couture dresses that greet us at Viktor & Rolf's brand new atelier in the western harbour area of Amsterdam. These are, of course, the gowns from last season that became Insta-hits thanks to their meme-able remarks and bright fabrication. The hype, however, didn’t go to Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren’s heads. “There's always a next season,” says Horsting matter-of-factly. “It is business as usual, but that means starting from scratch, doing something new.” Snoeren adds: “We wanted to focus on trying to get to the meaning of things.” © Anton Gottlob This season, they've taken starting from scratch to heart, teaming up with Dutch artist and textile designer Claudy Jongstra. “We really admire her,” says Snoeren, reeling off a list of Jongstra's skills and projects: her felt artwork, for which the wool is provided by her herd of indigenous and rare Drenthe Heath sheep; her social projects, helping local children with art; her biodynamic dye garden and self-sufficient farm; her scientific exploration of natural dyes. The list goes on. “The entire production process is taken into her own hands,” explains Horsting. “We have wanted to do something with her for a long time, so we were already in touch. This season it all just came together." Although the collaboration is new, the theme is a recurring one for the Dutch duo: sustainability. “We were thinking about how important it is to take positive action,” says Horsting. “There is a general feeling of doom about the environment and society, but with this collection we wanted to make a positive statement; being active about it and actually doing something.” © Anton Gottlob The collection is split into two parts: a series of dark coats, sculpted from Jongstra's felt, and a colourful set of dresses and skirt-and-top combinations. These are made from a fabric crafted by the couturiers using vintage garments, pulled apart and appliquéd back together for a bright take on felt via needlepoint rather than wool. “The idea is to take off your black coat and reveal a positive message underneath,” explains Snoeren. Here and there, the dark fabric bleeds into red or blue, all marks of Jongstra’s mastery of her craft and the designer’s appreciation of it. “The aesthetic of the entire collection is one of handicrafts, of manual labour; we wanted it to feel like it's been done by hand,” explains Horsting. Embroidery rings of various shapes and sizes also frame the elaborate needlework. “The mood,” notes Snoeren, “is slightly pagan, too, because we are working with embroideries of the moon and the sun and butterflies and owls—a feeling of earth mother.” © Anton Gottlob The coats—sharp, theatrical silhouettes—are all burgundy black, a natural dye which Jongstra, together with the University of Amsterdam and the Rijksmuseum, has spent the last year rediscovering, decoding recipes that date back to the 15th and 16th centuries. She’s an artist by trade but with the mind of a scientist, passionate about tapping into the heritage that she refers to as “our legacy” and “our global DNA”. In her idyllic studio in Friesland, an hour and a half away from the Dutch capital, the facilities—labs, raw ingredients and greenhouse—host these historic re-enactments. But it is her 15 years of practical experience that are most valuable. “It has taken 20,000 hours in knowledge to achieve this,” she says, of recreating the natural dye. And that’s before you consider the time required to grow and age the ingredients, getting the wool from the sheep, dying it all, creating the felt and assembling it into the catwalk-ready designs. © Anton Gottlob “She’s not ironic or cynical,” the designers observe of the artist, who has worked with everyone from John Galliano at Maison Margiela to Google. The pair have changed out of Nikes and jeans into full tuxedos, adding their signature surreal spin to proceedings. Between posing with three of Jongstra’s freshly shorn sheep and admiring the biodiversity of her garden, we visit the farmhouse where the wool is being hand-carded, spun into cotton candy-like bundles, blended with natural linens (merino wool, in this instance), layered and transformed into felt. The process is laborious, but worth it. Four weeks away from the show and Jongstra and her team are working at full pelt to complete the fabric order. “So much fabric we have to make!” she smiles. “It looks really like theatre. It's very spectacular, the tactility and the sensory qualities [of the fabric]. It is about valuing the quality of craft, valuing the quality of this legacy of knowledge... It makes you understand why it's important to show that on a certain platform.” © Anton Gottlob There may be no tulle or snappy one-liners in this collection, nor will they instantly explode all over Instagram as the previous season did—but all things considered, they really should. © Anton Gottlob © Anton Gottlob © Anton Gottlob © Anton Gottlob © Anton Gottlob © Anton Gottlob © Anton Gottlob © Anton Gottlob © Anton Gottlob The 9 biggest talking points from couture spring/summer 2019 Watch Dior’s autumn/winter 2020 couture show live here 14 couture moments that went down in fashion history What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: From American dynasty to Parisian couture: Vogue speaks to designer August Getty
column2: © Amy Harrity Fashion At the age of just 25, August Getty is already a firm A-list favourite, dressing the likes of Jennifer Lopez, Rachel McAdams and Miranda Kerr. Here, he discusses redefining the Getty family dynasty, the future of couture and gives Vogue a preview of his latest collection “I’ve always said the best place for my clothes is the bedroom floor,” says August Getty in his Los Angeles studio—a sprawling, white space in Los Angeles’s Culver City, complete with neon branding above a glass-walled atelier. “I want the woman to have the same feeling in my clothes as she does out of them: that strength, that bravery, the beauty, the glamour.” Model Natalia Getty, Ariadne Getty and designer August Getty attend the August Getty Atelier dinner in Beverly Hills, California © Getty It’s quite the cavalier attitude to have towards one’s couture; perhaps an indication of the fact that Getty has grown up surrounded by finery as standard. The 25-year-old great-grandson of oil baron Jean Paul Getty—who was, at a time, considered the wealthiest living American in recorded history—August has a lineage of glamorous women from which to draw inspiration. From 1960s supermodel Talitha Getty (his grandfather, John Paul Getty II’s second wife) his sister, Nats Getty, a model-designer and LGBTQ+ rights activist whose collections are designed and realised in an adjacent atelier on the same lot. Not to mention the Hollywood elite he counts as friends. The Getty family has captured the intrigue of many over the years, more recently director Ridley Scott, whose film All The Money In The World (2017) was based on the 1973 kidnapping of John Paul Getty III, as was Danny Boyle’s television series Trust (2018). However, ask August Getty whether he feels the weight of this hefty ancestry, and he shrugs. “Not at all. It’s all I’ve ever known. The person that’s born climbing a coconut tree isn’t afraid of falling out of a coconut tree. I hope!” To focus solely on the designer’s past, however, would be to miss an auspicious present—namely his couture presentation for the Paris shows in the Salon d’Été at the Ritz today, which he’s completing when Vogue visits the atelier. Getty began his self-taught fashion career in ready-to-wear, first showing at New York Fashion Week aged just 19. A high-octane, Hollywood-inspired collaboration with artist David LaChapelle followed, as well as a more sedate presentation in Paris, where the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode spotted him. This January, he was invited to debut as a guest designer on the couture runways, presenting a salon-style show, also at the Ritz, where models in sculptural, meticulously embellished looks lounged around a white grand piano; old-world glamour personified. Ariadne Getty © Getty For all the elegant women in his orbit, there is one who has held his attention since he was three: “My mother is everything to me,” he says. “She has all these beautiful gowns and shoes”—despite being a self-confessed tomboy, Ariadne Getty is an avid collector of fashion, favouring Luisa Beccaria, Roland Mouret, Alexander McQueen and Stella McCartney suiting. “We were in the middle of nowhere in England and I’d just create this woman and imagine her in these gowns,” he continues. “Running through the fields, the gardens, the house and from there [my ‘#GettyGirl’] kind of developed.” Sara Sampaio © Getty Indeed, there is a glamour to his aesthetic that is perfect for the red carpet crowd. Jennifer Lopez was an early adopter. Soon after, in 2016, Rachel McAdams accepted the Oscar for Best Picture alongside the cast of Spotlight in an August Getty Atelier emerald silk gown with a plunging T-back. Miranda Kerr attended a Golden Globe 2017 after-party in a strapless ivory dress, complete with thigh-high split, by the designer. While both Sara Sampaio and Zendaya favoured his signature ‘cupcake’ style—the former wore a crystal-beaded version for May 2019’s MET Gala, and the latter wore a custom leather creation at June 2018’s MTV Movie & TV Awards. Rachel McAdams © Getty For this season, Getty explains, his muse took a turn. “The storyline behind the ‘#GettyGirl’ was completely different, much darker,” he offers. “Apparently I’m one of the only couturiers who uses green, which is considered unlucky in Paris. But if someone tells me something is unlucky, I’m not going to take it out of the collection, I’ll add 18 more looks. I’ve already got the OK to show, I’m going to fucking show!” he laughs. In hushed tones amongst his 25-strong atelier team, he explains that the collection is believed to be haunted. “There’s this house in Venice, for inspiration, and everyone who buys this house dies mysteriously. We had a picture up of it and the whole time, people in the studio were getting hurt, pictures were falling off the walls, racks would fall down—only for this collection.” His second couture collection is shaping up to be more grown up, too, with an almost Lynchian sensibility that danger is lurking. There’s the aforementioned oxidised copper green, jet black velvet trains crawling with Swarovski crystal spiders, fishnet and a bodice inspired by a fountain Getty saw in a Paris cemetery, which will be finished in hand-painted, hard leather that stands on its own, as though inhabited by a ghost. “It starts with the phantasmagoria, the movie trailer in my head, and then it will be an intrinsic effort to watch certain movies,” says Getty, who turned to 1920s German expressionist films such as Metropolis, Nosferatu and The Cabinet of Doctor Caligari for inspiration. “I’ve seen such a different designer emerge since he has changed to the couture calendar,” notes his mother, Ariadne, who’s the CEO of both August Getty Atelier and Strike Oil, Nats Getty’s streetwear brand. It was ‘Mama G’, as August’s friends refer to her, that first noted her son’s flair for fashion design when he started designing gowns for forks using serviettes as a toddler. Soon he moved on to Barbies, cutting up his mother’s shoe bags for material. “I started buying shoes I wasn’t going to wear, for the shoe bags,” says Ariadne. “I would walk into a store, Harvey Nichols, wherever, and I’d see someone trying on shoes from a box with a green shoe bag and I’d say, ‘Those!’” These days, she’s just as proud of her son’s creations, and is wearing one of his bell-sleeved leather jackets to meet Vogue. “I have jackets from pretty much every season. I love them,” she says. Zendaya © Getty When asked about August’s relationship to the dynasty’s past and its future ahead, Ariadne elucidates. “I haven’t said this ever before but, when the children were little, I had the last name of Williams [from her first marriage to actor Justin Williams]. So there was no ‘Getty’ anywhere,” she says. “When we would drive to Marina del Rey and go through ‘Getty Circle’, I wouldn’t say anything. I wanted them to grow up with their own complete identities, without the weight of the name and I’m really happy I did that. I always knew he was going to create something very special and meaningful over a long period of time and be referenced in the future through his designs. He’s created his own dynasty, which I love. Obviously, the name is there, but he’s on his own track.” For now, that track leads to Paris and the couture schedule. But what’s next? “I know that there will be a time when I need to cross the pond and [move] to Paris. The most rewarding part of my career is doing couture and hopefully, down the road, to do Haute Couture,” August says, adding: “Dior was one of the youngest to do Haute Couture and he was 42, so I’m taking my time.” © Amy Harrity © Amy Harrity © Amy Harrity © Amy Harrity © Amy Harrity © Amy Harrity © www.amyharrity.com Dior Couture gives the smoky eye a modern update Vogue decodes the Chanel makeup look straight from the couture runway Watch Dior’s autumn/winter 2020 couture show live here Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Can you spot the Britney Spears reference in Miley Cyrus’ new music video?
column2: © Instagram.com/mileycyrus Fashion The video for Miley Cyrus’ new song, ‘Mother’s Daughter’ focuses on the current wave of anti-abortion laws that is sweeping across the US In classic Miley Cyrus fashion, there’s a lot going on in her new music video. The ‘Mother’s Daughter’ visual dropped today just at the close of Pride month, and it seemingly centred on the rollback of reproductive rights that women have recently experienced in the United States. Cyrus sings “Don’t fuck with my freedom” and there are title cards that declare, “Virginity is a social construct.” There are also breastfeeding babies, skateboarder Lacey Baker wearing a T-shirt with the words “they/them” embroidered on it, and model Aaron Philip dressed in a shimmering, crystal mesh crop top. And while these cameos and political statements make up the bulk of the clip, it’s the red latex suit that Cyrus wears at the start of the video that’s particularly eye-catching, albeit for a different reason: it’s a clear reference to the cherry red skintight jumpsuit that Britney Spears famously wore in her ‘Oops!… I Did It Again’ music video from 2000. Cyrus’, however, has a bit more teeth (there’s a vagina dentata part of the suit that you can only really see up close). Britney Spears It’s not the only memorable fashion moment in the clip—there’s also a surprisingly sweet mother-daughter scene, where Cyrus and her mother wear matching Chanel tweeds—but it’s one that clearly shows that while Cyrus is clearly concerned with our deeply troubling present, she’s just as well-versed in her pop music fashion history, too. column1: Céline Dion, 51, is killing it with her leg reveals at Paris Couture Week
column2: © Instagram.com/sydneylopez Fashion From a no-pants look to mini dresses, Céline Dion's couture week wardrobe proves that age is just a number Naturally, Céline Dion has whipped through a dizzying lineup of extraordinary fashion moments at Paris Couture this week. And while each elaborate confection is more awe-inspiring than the next, her latest look—debuted ahead of the Alexandre Vauthier show this afternoon—caused heads to swivel even more than usual. At first blush, Dion’s off-the-shoulder ivory gown appeared to cover the lower half of her frame with its extreme draping. But when she lifted her billowy sleeves to the side, the frock’s mini-skirted hemline—and her impossibly toned legs—were revealed to stunning effect. The secret behind her sculpted limbs? column1: Designer Rahul Mishra showcases couture in Paris for the first time
column2: Fashion With an 18-piece collection inspired by growth, Mishra gets in an exclusive conversation with Vogue about his vision for couture this season Fall 2019 couture marks Rahul Mishra’s entry into the world of international couture with a showcase during Paris Fashion Week. The designer, who presents regularly on the couture schedule in India, is excited. To many, couture is a final destination—the marker at the end of a journey, an approval from a higher authority on the artistry exhibited by their label. But for Mishra, it is a special part of being a creator because of the freedom of expression it affords him. “It is the evolution of my work,” says the designer, whose design process is more stream of consciousness than a rigid method. His collection, Metropolis 1, explores the concept of growth—cityscapes and overgrown trees are the running leitmotifs for the season. Mishra has taken his signature 3D embroidery to the next level, making it lighter than ever to layer hundreds of buildings in one lightweight frock, and place flowers and leaves with a density to exact the sound of rustling leaves. The 18-piece collection will see a follow-up next season. “Most couture houses have their forte, what is mine?” is the question Mishra is trying to explore. The cultural petri dish that Paris is draws at his spirit to explore new facets of his creativity. “Paris is what I do to satisfy my creative hunger, it enriches your soul,” he concludes. column1: New designer launches that need to be on your radar this month
column2: Fashion These designers are breaking away from bi-annual fashion weeks and launching curated capsule collections on Instagram. Vogue rounds up the latest that you should know about Anjali Patel Mehta's Verandah has launched its resort and swim 2020 collection that has been designed keeping the environment in mind—each piece has been crafted with fabrics made from Econyl yarn that uses fishing nets as well as textile and carpet waste. "Our palette for the season is vibrant, with corals, yellows, blues and motif prints on white that include coral, marine leaf and stripes indicative of the symmetry in nature. Our signature hand embroideries, stark neutrals in woven fabrics including sustainable, vegan options and upcycled denim are part of this holiday-ready collection," shares Patel Mehta. The brand that launched reversible saris and the Little Sari is now introducing a new range of handwoven silk saris. Titled ‘Mira’, Payal Khandwala’s collection features the six yard staple in bold hues and stripes to help you breeze you through the upcoming festive season. The creative minds behind The Olio Stories, Sneha Saksena and Aashna Singh, have recently launched Olio Jewels—a line of earrings, necklaces, hair accessories and more that promise to serve as ‘modern heirlooms’ in your closet. Made from brass, the jewellery is plated in 18-carat gold, and uses gemstones like amethyst, carnelian and turquoise. “Inspired by our grandfather’s coin collection, we created pieces with antique coins that span many eras—from Athena’s coins dating back to 420 BC and Jahangir’s Zodiac coins circa 1569 to modern day paisas,” says Singh. Keeping functionality in mind, the designers have also created special reversible pieces that allow you to play around with them. Arpita Mehta, who routinely showcases at Lakmé Fashion Week, decided to experiment with the launch of a new capsule collection, ‘Neocap’, to tap into the burgeoning neon trend. “I have always had a strange fondness for neon colours, but refrained from incorporating it in my designs,” says Mehta. The capsule line features a flamboyant colour palette that is balanced out with on-trend styles, like the neon green cape, bustier and pants that Sonakshi Sinha was recently spotted in. Got a destination wedding coming up? Look towards Pittie’s ‘The Mogra Muse’, a line of handcrafted jewellery featuring statement bridal pieces. Think ear cuffs, necklaces, rings and cuffs, all inspired by the mogra flower. The Limone dress Krésha Bajaj’s limited edition prêt collection, ‘Tesoro’, is inspired by her recent travels in Italy, and each ensemble points to a particular place. “The Limone dress was created thinking about the lemon stands in Sorrento, while the Capri set with its blue print was designed keeping the Temptation room at Ill Riccio Capri Palace in mind,” the designer shares. Even the colour palette hugely borrows inspiration from the picturesque country. “The blues have been inspired by the sea and the skies from the Amalfi coast, while the reds represent the sea cliff houses.” Expect a mix of easy-to-wear pieces like capes, trench coats, play suits and midi dresses. If you love the trend of layering necklaces, check out Misho by Suhani Parekh’s latest collection that reinterprets historic chains by giving it a contemporary spin. Pair them with hoop earrings to give your outfit an interesting twist. column1: Haute couture 2.0: How the high art of fashion is moving with the times
column2: © Stephane Cardinale - Corbis Fashion Haute couture has entered a new era, with a governing body—Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode—that’s switched up its style to bridge the gap between heritage and contemporary design. Vogue speaks to those in the know, including Dior’s Maria Grazia Chiuri, about the inner workings of this highest echelon of fashion There are few things grander in fashion than haute couture. With a miniscule client base (approximately 4,000 worldwide) and an exclusive allocation of industry tickets for runway presentations, the practice can seem entirely fanciful and out of reach. In truth, the art of couture is a tightly controlled, invite-only application, governed by Paris’s Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode (FHCM) with widespread influence on the fashion industry at large. Founded in 1868, the FHCM preserves the exacting standards of French fashion culture by presiding over Paris Women’s and Men’s Fashion Weeks, as well as endorsing and nurturing designers who exhibit a quality of craftsmanship that meets the level required to show on the official Haute Couture schedule. Vogue speaks to key figures within the organisation—as well as Dior’s artistic director Maria Grazia Chiuri, a major player on the couture scene—about the inner workings of this enigmatic French institution. Christian Dior © Victor Boyko The Fédération has approximately 100 members and comprises three Chambres Syndicales, or central bodies (Haute Couture, Women’s Fashion and Men’s Fashion). FHCM president Ralph Toledano works alongside the board of directors—Pietro Beccari (Christian Dior), Delphine Bellini (Schiaparelli), Riccardo Bellini (Maison Margiela), Philippe Fortunato (Givenchy), Bruno Pavlovsky (Chanel) and Sophie Waintraub (Jean-Paul Gaultier)—to approve members. Christian Dior © Francois Guillot Once approved, the fashion house will be supported in strategic, communication, marketing, and economic, technological, cultural and even political possibilities—and Haute Couture members also gain a position on the official couture schedule. As of January 2019, the couture members include Adeline André, Alexandre Vauthier, Alexis Mabille, Chanel, Christian Dior, Franck Sorbier, Giambattista Valli, Givenchy, Jean Paul Gaultier, Julien Fournié, Maison Margiela, Maison Rabih Kayrouz, Maurizio Galante, Schiaparelli and Stéphane Rolland. Since the advent of ready-to-wear at the start of the 20th century, haute couture’s relevance has been slowly diminishing. The demanding guidelines and labour-intensive practices (today, one Giambattista Valli couture gown can take approximately 240 hours and 6,000 metres of fabric to create) render it inaccessible to anyone outside of the 0.001 per cent target audience. Guided by the FHCM, haute couture has evolved to be an Insta-friendly showcase of craftsmanship and creative grandeur, an ode to what can be achieved by the industry’s foremost designers and artisans, its creations providing a trickle-down effect of inspiration on ready-to-wear and fast-fashion collections. Ralph Toledano © Victor Boyko “Haute couture is a spearhead in terms of creation, a fantastic laboratory for research, both in terms of craftsmanship and design innovation,” explains Toledano. “Haute couture is a land of free expression for designers, as well as an image builder for brands.” Maria Grazia Chiuri © Peter White Dior’s Maria Grazia Chiuri continues: “Creatively, FHCM is an incredible support because it is capable of coordinating a very rich and diversified body without getting involved in the vision of each house. I began working with FHCM while I was creative director at Valentino, although I wasn’t in such close contact as I am now. Since being at Dior, I’m frequently in touch with FHCM and the collaboration has been fundamental in my understanding of how French fashion works and performs, what its cultural and political appeal is and how they are brought forward.” She adds: “Support for fashion culture here is extraordinary: something other countries should really look at in order to think about their own policies, and the weight and significance they give fashion as an essential part of focusing on national identity.” Much mythology exists around the strict rules and regulations required of haute couture houses by the FHCM. ‘Haute couture’ is a legally protected term first set in 1945 and a label can only be awarded (or withdrawn through failure to meet the requisite regulations, outlined below) by a commission appointed by the Ministry of Industry. Chanel © Luc Braquet In order to be eligible for haute couture status, members must create made-to-order garments in an atelier of at least 15 full-time staff, as well as 20 full-time technical workers in one of their ateliers. Collections must be presented with a minimum of 50 original designs, including day and evening looks, presented to the public in January and July and created for private clients, with each piece requiring more than one fitting. Guest members are invited each season, and if a brand is invited four times in a row, it becomes eligible to be a member. Chanel © Luc Braquet There are those who challenge the institution—see Chiuri’s AW18/19 collection for Christian Dior, with its precision internal structure and finishings realised in comparatively humble silhouette—however, she did have the support of the FHCM. “I dedicated the [collection] to the contemporary sense of couture, trying to start a conversation between different key concepts based on its definition,” Chiuri explains. “I moved it into difficult territory. My message was linked to the fact that rules—strict, yes, but necessary—must help to stimulate creativity and find solutions and new paths more than simply standardise.” When founded, the FHCM was known as the Chambre Syndicale de la Couture or des Confectionneurs et des Tailleurs pour Dame (clothing manufacturers and tailors for women). Following a few (equally wordy) iterations, the name was changed to today’s slightly sleeker Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode in June 2017. Giambattista Valli © Luc Braquet Up against the digital revolution and a new, younger audience, the FHCM has had to remain agile to keep the heritage practice of couture relevant. “Whereas haute couture was usually reserved for older women, we have witnessed an interesting phenomenon of generational change and millennials are now intelligently included,” says Toledano. “Millennials in search of constant expertise add vitality to the subject [of couture, while] new technologies are a formidable ally to develop crafts and materials—[it’s] a ‘new’ haute couture for this new generation,” he continues. “Houses’ websites are fuelled by formats adapted for [and by] millennials: inspirations are shared directly by the designers, imagery is vibrant rather than formal, [they] film visits of ateliers, share cultural experiences with creative communities, tutorial films. An educational chapter has been opened in a very respectful way.” Elie Saab © Luc Braquet To ensure the next generation of couture clients remains connected, the FHCM pays close attention to societal trends, technological advances, digital platforms and their links with fashion and creativity. “In a turbulent world such as ours, it is very important for our audience to rely on points of reference in which it believes, pillars on which it can count, institutions capable of building bridges between heritage and the contemporary, and to anticipate the upcoming world. This is the way the FHCM sees its role,” explains executive president of the FHCM, Pascal Morand. Elie Saab © Jamie Stoker In recent years, the FHCM has spearheaded changes, including: the merger of the École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne with the Institut Français de la Mode; opening up higher education opportunities in couture; and establishing selection committees for womenswear and menswear via representatives from brands, buyers and journalists to promote objectivity and transparency throughout the membership process. When it comes to the design and development process, Chiuri sees the FHCM’s dialogue with industry pioneers as an opportunity for growth and expansion. “FHCM encourages interest and attention into what’s going on outside of France, to find ways of including technologies from other cultures and manufacturing traditions, [integrating them with] French [couture] production.” Giambattista Valli © Jamie Stoker “The FHCM closely monitors the Fourth Industrial Revolution and its impact,” says Morand. “It is always a question of balancing in an optimal way low-tech (intelligence of the hand), mid-tech (mechanisation) and high-tech (digital revolution/robotics). We also work on the way innovation can support the move toward sustainable development.” Morand explains that the FHCM works with members, as well as tech companies and academic experts, to ensure a constant dialogue between couture and the digital revolution. “Technology and innovation must support design and creativity, and never alter them, in any circumstance.” Valentino © Pascal Le Segretain Viktor & Rolf © Victor Boyko Schiaparelli © Stephane Cardinale - Corbis Christian Dior © Jamie Stoker 14 couture moments that went down in fashion history The 9 biggest talking points from couture spring/summer 2019 Couture is far from dead—and it’s making a comeback Beauty Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why couture is at the cutting-edge of sustainable fashion
column2: © Getty Fashion Free from the need to mass-produce, couture designers are taking the lead in reimagining fashion for a sustainable future. Vogue talks to Ronald van der Kemp, Iris van Herpen and Xuan-Thu Nguyen about their eco-conscious visions Couture is the antithesis of ready-to-wear: one-off pieces rather than mass-produced; timeless rather than trend-led. Arguably, this makes it inherently more sustainable. “We only do two collections a year [instead of] six,” Ronald van der Kemp tells Vogue. “Couture pieces are collectibles, pieces of art; they’re timeless.” Fellow designer Iris van Herpen adds: “You're not creating in the hope that somebody will wear it; you're creating [on] demand.” Iris van Herpen spring/summer 2019 couture © Getty Van der Kemp and van Herpen are among the crew of couturiers looking to build on these ideas and disrupt the rest of the fashion industry through their sustainable practices. “There [is] so much waste in fashion, so much damage to the environment,” says van der Kemp. Instead of sourcing new fabrics, he fashions his creations out of materials that already exist. “I work with leftovers from other [brands], or vintage pieces,” he explains. Iris van Herpen spring/summer 2019 couture © Getty The Dutch designer says it’s important that he’s not in the Paris fashion bubble. Both he and van Herpen are based in Amsterdam, along with compatriots Viktor & Rolf—who have also made sustainability one of their key focuses. “It was a conscious decision for me to work from Amsterdam because I wanted to do it my own way,” van der Kemp says. “In Paris, I would feel pressure to go with the system; being based here gives me another perspective.” Ronald van der Kemp spring/summer 2019 couture © GoRunway However, he still hopes to impact the industry from the outside. “I want to work with bigger companies and their leftovers [to] produce clothes; to find solutions for their waste problem—instead of burning [it].” Van der Kemp thinks that other fashion brands could take a cue from the pace of couture: “I think we should [all] slow down instead of producing so many clothes.” Ronald van der Kemp spring/summer 2019 couture © GoRunway Xuan Xuan-Thu Nguyen, founder of Paris-based Xuan, is also using her couture experience to explore new ways of creating fashion, launching a new line of upcycled pieces called 1/Off. “We’re working with vintage items and giving them a new lease of life,” she says. Like van der Kemp,  re-using existing materials is already intrinsic to her design ethos; 90 per cent of Xuan’s AW19 collection is crafted from deadstock fabric. “We shouldn’t just throw materials away,” Nguyen says. “It’s still beautiful so why not use it?” Xuan Meanwhile, van Herpen has a different approach, working with architects and scientists to develop new, more eco-conscious fabrics. “Within couture, there is time and space to develop materials,” she says, admitting that creating completely sustainable textiles is not without its challenges. “Some of these materials do not contain any chemicals, for example, but it does mean they have [less] durability.” For her AW19 collection, van Herpen has looked at how a single garment can take on multiple forms. Together with American wind sculptor Anthony Howe, she’s created a kinetic dress that changes shape as it moves down the runway. “The wind activates it,” she explains. “It's a really delicate construction, made from [fabric] joined around a steel core on various levels, creating a four-dimensional piece.” She’s also evolved her SS19 “glitch fabric” with architect and long-time collaborator Philip Beesley. “We've combined it with a traditional technique of Japanese ink printing, so when you look at it, you don't know if you're looking at an existing material or at something almost digital.” The possibility of octopus skin-like textiles (which have the capacity to change colour and shape) particularly excites van Herpen. “It’s [still] further in the future, but [it] creates a lot of possibilities for fashion,” she says. “You [could] change the design and colours; customise it. That creates less need for a lot of clothes; it becomes a whole different philosophy of owning.” Van Herpen hopes her work will eventually make waves across the rest of the fashion industry. “This is couture; you will not see this in a store next week, but [it’s] the principle behind it. [I have] big hopes that we will be able to change the way we think about materials, and the way we produce.” Are our collective efforts towards sustainable fashion enough? column1: Vicky Kaushal on his love for acting: "I was a shy kid, but I felt very liberated on stage"
column2: © Tarun Vishwa Fashion From restrained performances to mainstream conviction, he’s the thinking person’s actor and a star in his own right. And as he readies to play Aurangzeb and Udham Singh, Vicky Kaushal is committed to having his best year in cinema yet, all with a singlehanded devotion to entertainment Seven years ago, Vicky Kaushal clutched firmly onto his backpack as he waited for a train at one of Mumbai’s busiest local stations, Dadar. It was late, the station and trains were relatively empty, but Kaushal’s grip was resolute; he was carrying precious cargo, after all. Inside his bag was his first pay cheque—1,500 for working backstage at a Rage Productions play. Kaushal felt so privileged, he decided to treat himself to a seat on the train as opposed to his usual hanging out of the carriage (“for the breeze,” he explains). Fast forward to May 2019, Kaushal has just returned from New York, where he celebrated his 31st birthday. At the café of a Mumbai five-star hotel, he is interrupted thrice in 45 minutes—one wants a selfie, another wants to congratulate him on his performances, and the third bunch tells him how much they love seeing him on screen and what a formidable talent he is. He is gracious with each, first apologising for halting our interview, then obliging a couple who risk missing their flight for an opportunity to get a Vicky Kaushal selfie. Dressed in jeans and a black T-shirt, Kaushal looks like the boy-next-door, except he’s six feet tall and currently sporting scar tissue on his right cheekbone, a result of an accident on the sets of an upcoming film. His face embodies the remnants of the character behind his latest success—the rugged Major Vihaan Singh Shergill from Uri: The Surgical Strike. For Kaushal, 2019 opened on a bang with Uri, a film about a covert operation the Indian Army led against militants in Kashmir in 2016, which entered the 200-crore club, making the already-popular actor a legit star. Next, he portrays Aurangzeb in what’s pegged to be Karan Johar’s magnum opus, Takht; freedom fighter Udham Singh in Shoojit Sircar’s next; and even stars in a horror flick called Bhoot, whose poster looks promisingly spooky. The range of characters he plays in the next 12 months is a good indication of the sheer talent Kaushal exhibits on screen. He’s been a critical and box-office success ever since Masaan (2015) displayed his stoic and restrained form of acting to the world, but it is films like Raman Raghav 2.0 (2016), Love Per Square Foot (2018), Raazi (2018), Lust Stories (2018) and Manmarziyaan (2018) that have further honed his ability to occupy different stories with an infectious conviction. Whether it is caste politics or a woman’s right to pleasure—Kaushal’s characters have had us rooting for his cause because he reasoned it out so simply. This is what makes him the affable ‘thinking person’s actor’, one who moves effortlessly through popular mainstream cinema as he does within the platforms of indie-toned films. “I never really get labels or tags,” he says. “Cinema is always evolving and changing according to the evolution of the audience. I used to think that alternative films were those where people don’t get any money for making them, or are for new filmmakers and unknown actors… festival films. Maybe it’s just that they’re not popular films, but as an actor all that matters to me is whether it’s a good film or a bad film.” Thanks to streaming services like Netflix, Amazon, Hotstar and Voot, the nature of the entertainment industry is changing. They have opened up opportunities to create content for a niche audience without the strain of box-office success weighing them down. Easy access to world-class content also means that homegrown content now has serious competition for eyeballs—which is great news for writers, directors and actors from the subcontinent, who want to tell stories that look beyond the climax to a big fat Punjabi wedding. Kaushal understands the arena and timing well. “Masaan came out when films like The Lunchbox (2013) did well. There was an audience for these smaller budget films, and the timing was great,” he says. In Masaan, which pegged Kaushal as the debut of the year, he plays an ordinary man determined to fight caste divides. In Lust Stories, he tries his best to understand why a woman might need to pleasure herself for the sake of it; and in Uri, he leads a troop of soldiers on a successful surgical strike. These aren’t just “message-driven” films but ones that leave the audience with a kernel of a thought. “When I watch a film and it stays with me, whether it’s a character or a situation, and when I find myself thinking about it or talking to myself about it or to my friends, that’s when I know I’ve been entertained,” says Kaushal. It’s a simple approach but says a lot about what makes Kaushal a nuanced actor—he has the ability to spot a great story. “I always read a script at one go, as if I were the audience,” he says. It’s the first thing he looks for—has he been entertained? Step two is when he looks at his character, and just how far out of his comfort zone it can take him. “I should feel that I don’t know if I’ll be able to do it,” he adds. This cautious, weigh-the-pros-and-cons-that-matter approach has served Kaushal well, ever since he decided to quit engineering to pursue acting. “Don’t get me wrong, I love engineering. I don’t know what my kids will do, but I’m going to make them do engineering—three months full masti, then study hard for one month and pass your exams. They can do whatever they want after that,” he says. For him, it was a chance visit to an MNC that crashed Kaushal’s engineering dreams: “I didn’t know what I wanted to do, but I knew I definitely did not want to do that.” Some intense introspection led him to consider acting. “I was always active on stage. I was a shy kid, but I felt very liberated on stage. I’d think, ‘Arre yaar, platform mil gaya to do something.’ Whatever I couldn’t do here, I could do there.” Read the complete interview in Vogue India’s July 2019 issue that hits stands on July 5, 2019. column1: Aditya Roy Kapur: “I love being on set. I’m the happiest there”
column2: © Tarun Vishwa Fashion The guy next door (if only he were this good-looking) with an unpretentious disposition and eyes to the stars, Aditya Roy Kapur is the reluctant actor who chooses craft over celebrity. In a candid interview with Vogue, he talks about success, failure and all things in between “I incrementally got famous” is how VJ turned actor Aditya Roy Kapur cautiously describes his star status after the release of the 2013 blockbuster Aashiqui 2. Till then, the TV personality and ensemble film actor was fairly ‘well known’ but it was the success of this tear fest that took him from being able to ‘vagabond’ on the streets of Mumbai to losing his anonymity. Over a decade into show business, he speaks of the privileges of his fame in a restrained manner—and in no time it’s clear that he’s a working actor who is here for the craft and not just the celebrity. He breezes into our shoot, his movie star looks making it obvious as to why he first made it to the silver screen. A thorough professional, he remains calm through the frenzy, glugging black coffee to battle post-work exhaustion when we sit down for our interview. As he recounts his fairly tumultuous movie career and talks candidly about his struggles, citing roles as “jobs” and professing an earnest desire to “stay employed” as his goal, it’s his disarmingly Everyman persona and surprising self-awareness that make him stand out from the crowd of all those other perfectly built leading men of Bollywood. “I started doing films because the opportunity presented itself; I didn’t actively go seeking it. Being a VJ is like being a heightened version of yourself, and it was a great experience but when acting happened I found it more rewarding because you get a chance to do different things—and you have an excuse for behaving the way you do,” he says. “Aashiqui 2 made its mark on me, and I felt like I had to be the character all the time, but now I’ve found a way of slipping in and out. Funnily enough, even though it’s been 10 years, I feel like there’s a lot that I haven’t experimented with and I have a long way to go.” Success and star-struck fans notwithstanding, Roy Kapur has been picky with roles, turning to older brothers Siddharth (producer) and Kunaal Roy Kapur (actor/director) for advice on occasion, and steering clear of projects that didn’t excite him, even if it meant two years between releases and a year-long sabbatical (“I did other things”). “I think I said no too much,” he laughs. “I feel like if you’re going to do something for six months and you’re giving your everything to it, you have to be convinced. Having said that, I love being on set. I’m the happiest there,” he says. His measured modus operandi is to take it as it goes—work with interesting filmmakers and subjects and not be too cautious or planned about the results. It seems to have worked, as he has enough in his kitty—Sadak 2, Malang and Anurag Basu’s next. As we chat about his film trajectory and his fixed goals (or lack thereof), it’s clear he’s here to stay but Roy Kapur is in no hurry or pressing for fame. For now, he is sure he doesn’t have the “head for production” and he’s merely toyed with the idea of direction. “The more I work, the more I realise how tough directing a film is. There’s a lot I need to understand about making films before I could direct one.” Read the complete interview in Vogue India’s July 2019 issue that hits stands on July 5, 2019. column1: Decoding your favourite Bollywood celebrities' vacation wardrobes
column2: © Instagram.com/anushkasharma Fashion Kareena Kapoor Khan and sister Karisma Kapoor are vacationing in London, Sonam Kapoor Ahuja just got back from her Japan holiday, and Alia Bhatt recently returned from New York—making this the perfect time to break down their holiday styles If you find packing to be the most demanding part of your holiday planning, take solace in the fact that you’re not alone. How many pairs of shoes are enough? Should you pack that dress or not? If you don’t want to repeat your outfits on an upcoming vacation, you need a cheat sheet on what to pack and what to leave out of the suitcase. And who better to serve it than your favourite celebrities? From Kareena Kapoor Khan to Priyanka Chopra, Vogue rounds up what Bollywood’s leading ladies are carrying in their luggage this year. AKA the essentials you’ll be building your travel wardrobe on, which is also where most of us get stuck. Jeans? Track pants? Both? If you know your vacation involves a lot of sightseeing and exploring on foot, it makes sense to pack comfortable clothing that will take you from dusk till dawn. Take your cues from Anushka Sharma’s vacation picks. The actor’s trips to Belgium and Australia this year saw her in basic T-shirts, denim jackets, ripped jeans, sneakers, backpacks and even baseball caps. Kareena Kapoor Khan’s current London trip is equally heavy on nonchalant clothing too. Some of her recent showcases include a sweatshirt + jeans combination, paired with sneakers and a sling bag; and a simple white T-shirt worn with a trench coat, boyfriend jeans and sneakers. Alia Bhatt’s New York trip (the actor just came back to India last week) was big on athleisure—relaxed outfits teamed with sneakers held top priority—while Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s Japan trip saw an infusion of classic white shirts and loose trousers. Whether it’s a date with your beau or a night out with your girlfriends, leading Bollywood celebrities believe maxi dresses and elegant gowns can see you through it all. Both Malaika Arora and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan rely on dreamy maxi dresses in solid colours, styled with statement necklaces. And sisters Kareena Kapoor Khan and Karisma Kapoor trust in the power of black, though shimmer makes an appearance through dresses and sequinned blazers. Gowns with high slits (look towards Kapoor Khan’s royal blue number) also make an appearance. Coming to footwear, high heels win all votes. If you’re heading to the beach, your outfits have to resonate your holiday’s relaxed vibe. We’re thinking floral printed dresses (courtesy Priyanka Chopra’s Miami holiday), lace dresses (like the one Sonam Kapoor Ahuja wore to the Uluwatu beach in Bali), vibrant bikinis or monokinis (check out Malaika Arora, Katrina Kaif’s picks), lightweight cover-ups, oversized sunglasses, straw hats and comfortable flats like ballerinas, loafers and flip-flops. Travelling to a city where the temperatures are likely to be sub-zero? Take notes from Priyanka Chopra, who prefers to stay covered up in puffer jackets, beanies, boots (did you see her recent silver pair?). Kareena Kapoor Khan also likes puffer jackets—she once picked a sunshine yellow number and styled it white jeans. Parineeti Chopra, on the other hand, likes to add a feminine touch to her winter wear—check out the plaid skirt she styled with her feather jacket. Also in her suitcase: turtlenecks, sweaters, track pants, bright mufflers, woollen dresses, stockings, beanies and socks. Which celebrity’s style will you take with you for your next vacation? column1: From Ancient Greece to Prada SS19: The history of the headband
column2: © Getty Fashion Since ancient times the accessory has evoked sporting prowess, regal ambitions, hard work and louche lounging, as well as eternally nostalgic style on the catwalk. Vogue traces the history of the headband As the models emerged on Prada’s SS19 catwalk, their padded headbands immediately made an impact. Worn with every look, in designs from pearly shell pink to black studded leather, Miuccia Prada’s luxurious creations kick-started the resurgence of this age-old accessory. Alice in Wonderland © Alamy In many ways, the headband is less a singular item, more a whole genus of accessories. It can be padded à la Prada or a classic Alice band, so named after Lewis Carroll’s eponymous character (followed by Disney’s 1951 film, which further cemented the girl who tumbled into another world’s status as a memorable headband wearer). It’s incarnation as a wrap or a scarf has a history as long as it is complex, ranging from specific faith-based and cultural uses to Gloria Swanson lounging around in silks. It can also be something elaborate, closer to a fascinator or headpiece. No surprise then that the reference points are so immediately wide-ranging. Headbands and their attendant variants have been around for centuries. Mesopotamian fillets kept hair in place, while Greek laurel wreaths were rooted in mythology; both were images of intellectual or physical prowess. Then there’s medieval diadems and the ever-eternal flower crown, beloved of ancient civilisations and Coachella attendees alike. Portrait of actor Louise Brooks © Getty In the 20th century the headband moved through plenty of iterations, too. In the 1920s it was worn by a new generation of women determined to do away with past sartorial restrictions. Ideal for accentuating fashionably cropped hair, silent film stars Clara Bow and Louise Brooks were both fans. It’s a detail of the decade that’s stuck ever since: any Great Gatsby-themed party is incomplete without a sea of feathers bobbing from spangled headbands. © Getty Come the 1930s, Coco Chanel made the headband look effortless, styled with belted white trousers; while the 1940s saw it take on a more practical guise for women in the Second World War. This functional headband not only changed the position of women in the professional sphere, but also the role of clothing in a society where, for a while, fabric rationing and workplace requirements called for pragmatism. Most famously worn by Rosie the Riveter in her poster proclaiming “We Can Do It!”, the red polka-dot bandana—described in another ad as “Water repellent. Washable. Dust proof.”—formed part of the uniform of Women Ordnance Workers. Audrey Hepburn holding her pet fawn © Getty Post-war the headband returned to its decorative roots. It could reliably be found atop a beehive or adding a final touch to an immaculate New Look-inspired get-up. Brigitte Bardot wore them frequently; most famously in Le Mépris, her wide navy scarf accompanied by stripes and thick eyeliner. Grace Kelly always looked polished in hers. For Audrey Hepburn, headbands came with bows (and sometimes accompanied by her baby deer Pippin). Jackie O wore one in hot pink during a trip to India. Sharon Tate’s flower child garb was completed by headbands worn low across the forehead. American singer and actress Diana Ross, 1973 © Getty Tipping towards the loose lines and easy glamour of the 1970s, Diana Ross plumped for glitz and velvet, while Bianca Jagger favoured opulent headwraps and metallics for her Studio 54 nights out. The 1970s also saw the return of the headband in a sports context—the legacy of 1920s tennis player Suzanne Lenglen continued in Björn Borg’s famous striped terry-cloth styles. Off court, the rise of fitness videos in the 1980s inspired some memorable looks from the likes of Olivia Newton-John and Cher, a brightly coloured headband proving the perfect counterpart to spandex and leg warmers. Hillary Clinton attends White House event © Getty In the 1990s and 2000s, the Alice band returned to the fore. Hillary Clinton wore them frequently; while on screen, the preppy all-American won out—from Alicia Silverstone in Clueless to Selma Blair in Legally Blonde, and the ultimate queen of headbands and venomous remarks, Leighton Meester as Gossip Girl’s Blair Waldorf. Princess Diana in a David Emanuel dress © Getty With this legacy, the headband now occupies an interesting position: running the gamut between carefree afternoons on the beach to political rallies and heady, after-dark occasions. It’s been the domain of coquettish flappers and machinating students, wannabe princesses and neon-bright fitness queens, boiler suit-clad workers and perfectly manicured women. And it will forever evoke Princess Diana, repurposing an emerald and diamond choker as a jewelled headband during a tour of Australia in 1985. Today, the headband suggests a certain kind of cool too: the minimalism of Dior’s SS19 sleek bands over even sleeker hair, or the eclectic (and, crucially, Instagrammable) appeal of fur and pearls crowning braids à la Shrimps AW19. In the hands of Simone Rocha, with her inclusion of sparkling headbands for both SS19 and AW19, they’ve become something delectable. These are a new type of headband altogether. One that taps into the current taste for late 1990s/early 2000s’ rhinestone-and-barrette-edged nostalgia, while also offering the pure childish pleasure of donning a toy tiara, a glimpse of gems or satin nestled atop a head held high. Whether worn by ambitious girls or royalty, the headband is the ultimate chameleon, which will no doubt retain its allure for years to come. © Sophie Glover American actor Sharon Tate (1943-1969) wearing a pink top and headband © Getty Suzanne Lenglen jumping to hit a ball © Getty Tennis star Bjorn Borg during the WCT Challenge Cup 1978 © Getty Whitney Houston sings national anthem at Super Bowl XXV © Getty Cher © Getty Alicia Silverstone, Brittany Murphy and Stacey Dash in Clueless © Shutterstock David Beckham © Getty Jackie Kennedy arriving at Jaipur airport during her tour of India © Getty Pandora was the first mortal woman according to the Greek poet Hesiod © Getty Dior Cruise 2020: How the new look of iconic Bar jacket came to be Why some of the world’s leading fashion designers love beige Dior’s 2020 Cruise collection: Vogue speaks to Maria Grazia Chiuri What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy is the ultimate Nineties style icon
column2: © Getty Fashion From naked sandals to headbands, white shirts to slip dresses, the Calvin Klein publicist and wife of John F Kennedy Jr predicted every new trend back in the early 1990s—and has proven an enduring muse for designers since. Vogue shortlists seven ways to channel her classic look, now Fashion’s nostalgia for the 1990s shows no signs of waning, bringing with it a renewed appreciation for the era’s biggest style icons—and none were more prolific than Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy. The impeccably dressed Calvin Klein executive first entered the public eye when she began dating John F Kennedy Jr in 1994. Two years later, the pair married on the remote island of Cumberland in Georgia. The bride wore a silk gown by Narciso Rodriguez and beaded Manolo Blahnik sandals, a look splashed across newspapers around the world. In the years that followed, it was her effortlessly cool street style that stole the show. Fresh-faced and tousled-haired, she became a byword for turn-of-the-century minimalism and established the modern-day fashion editors’ uniform: sleek, understated separates that never go out of style. Though Bessette-Kennedy’s life has been overshadowed by her tragic death in a plane crash in 1999, her fashion legacy lives on. She has featured on designers’ mood boards for the past two decades, and in recent months the industry’s fascination has only intensified. Ports 1961’s AW19 collection took inspiration from her clean lines and subdued colour palettes, Alexander Wang cited her as a beauty muse and Maryam Nassir Zadeh has taken cues from her season after season. To emulate her look, Vogue picks seven staples to stock up on now. Newlyweds John F Kennedy Jr and Carolyn Bessette walk along Varick street © Getty As seen at: Sonia Rykiel; Rejina Pyo; The Row; ATP Atelier This season’s must-have shoe was a favourite of Bessette-Kennedy’s: the thin-strapped, minimal mid-heel, as seen on the runway at Sonia Rykiel and Rejina Pyo. For dressier options look to The Row, while commuter-friendly flat iterations can be found at ATP Atelier, Emme Parsons and Ancient Greek Sandals. Worn with cropped jeans and a tank, they spell insouciant ease. Carolyn Bessette, wife of John Kennedy © Getty As seen at: Prada; Simone Rocha; Alexandre de Paris; Lele Sadoughi Silk-satin headgear might be back at Prada, but Bessette-Kennedy was an early advocate, regularly pairing a broad tortoise-shell Alice band with oval shades and a white T-shirt. Structured styles abound at Simone Rocha, Alexandre de Paris and Lele Sadoughi, proving that the prim, childhood staple can translate to the streets of New York, the boardroom and beyond. Carolyn Bessettee at Whitney Museum of American Art Annual Fundraising Gala © Getty As seen at: Jacquemus When it came to elevating classic pieces, few could compete with Bessette-Kennedy. For a black-tie gala at the Whitney Museum of American Art, she transformed a white shirt into an evening wear essential, unbuttoning it to the breastbone, rolling up the sleeves and adding a floor-skimming tiered skirt. Accessorised with black sandals and a gold beaded bag, it was the epitome of uptown glamour without compromising on her pared-back aesthetic. For summer soirées, channel the look in a plunging Jacquemus white shirt and Molly Goddard’s ruffled navy skirt. John Kennedy and his wife Carolyn in New York © Getty As seen at: Paco Rabanne; Alberta Ferretti; Refine Bias-cut slips formed the backbone of Bessette-Kennedy’s wardrobe, from her Narciso Rodriguez wedding gown to black minidresses worn during blistering summers in the city and ribbed grey styles hidden under cover-ups for cooler days. With a slip dress revival on the catwalk at Paco Rabanne and Alberta Ferretti, new brands are eager to meet the growing demand. Try London-based label Refine, which offers mid-length slips in black, white and dark chocolate, fittingly named “The Carolyn”. For true devotees, there are even headbands to match. John F Kennedy Jr and bride Carolyn Bessette Kennedy stand in front of their apartment in Tribecca © Getty As seen at: Burberry Once dismissed as an unwearable combination, Bessette-Kennedy was a long-time champion of beige and black in all its forms: a pale fawn pencil skirt with a black knit and brown boots; a black T-shirt with camel-hued trousers and loafers; dark caramel cords with a black turtleneck. For a fresh-off-the-runway version, look no further than Burberry, where Riccardo Tisci’s debut collection for the house ran the gamut from heritage trenches to coffee-coloured skirt suits. John F Kennedy Jr and Carolyn Bessette © Getty As seen at: Emilia Wickstead; Tom Ford Much like her mother-in-law Jacqueline Kennedy, who covered her hair with loosely tied silk scarves while holidaying in Capri, Bessette-Kennedy had a penchant for block-colour bandanas. Paired with denim, a tank and a longline blazer, it’s the ultimate in modern Riviera chic. For pretty pastel shades head to Emilia Wickstead, while Tom Ford makes a case for classic black. Carolyn Bessette in New York © Getty As seen at: Rouje; Reformation; Réalisation Par Bessette-Kennedy knew how to turn up the volume on a floaty summer frock: just add stilettos, bed-head hair and a black patent Prada bag for an off-duty look that’s equal parts polished and effortlessly cool. Hunt down the perfect floral midi dress at Rouje, Reformation or Réalisation Par, and combine with shiny accessories that lend a subversive edge. column1: Kenzo names Felipe Oliveira Baptista as its new creative director
column2: © GoRunway Fashion After serving as Lacoste’s creative director for eight years, Baptista will now take over the responsibilities at the French luxury house Just six days after Carol Lim and Humberto Leon presented their final collection as co-creative directors of Kenzo, the brand’s owner, LVMH, has named their successor. Felipe Oliveira Baptista will be Kenzo’s new creative director, taking over on July 1. Oliveira Baptista comes to Kenzo from Lacoste, where he was creative director from 2010 to 2018. “What made us choose Felipe above other candidates is the fact that he has a global artistic approach,” Kenzo’s CEO Sylie Colin told WWD. “He has a 360-degree creative vision and will oversee artistic direction globally, dealing both with collections and communication.” During his time at Lacoste, Oliveira Baptista turned the tennis brand into a runway mainstay, bringing a freewheeling sportiness and environmentalism to his collections. Bucket hats, anoraks, and bold graphics were the tentpoles of his final collections at Lacoste, as was a Supreme collaboration revealed in 2018. Born in Portugal and based in Paris, Oliveira Baptista also ran an eponymous line from 2003 to 2013, which won the Hyères prize in 2003 and the ANDAM Prize in 2003 and 2005. column1: 21 pictures that will take you inside Sophie Turner’s wardrobe
column2: © Getty Fashion From stunning gowns and dresses to athleisure separates and even embellished lehengas, the Game of Thrones actor proves that she can pull any kind of look with equal ease Sophie Turner rose to fame as Sansa Stark in HBO’s Game of Thrones, and there’s been no looking back for the actor ever since. Sister-in-law to Priyanka Chopra, the 23-year-old actor has had a rollercoaster of a year with GoT coming to an end and her impromptu wedding to long-time beau Joe Jonas. Turner knows exactly how to work a red carpet, is hilarious and endearing on social media, and has a wardrobe everybody wants in on. Ahead, we take a look at her style game. From coordinating pared-down athleisure separates with husband Joe Jonas to stepping out in head-turning numbers, Turner’s sartorial meter oscillates between extremes. Her go-to staples for a winning red carpet look include statement-making gowns and embellished dresses, while her off-duty wardrobe is filled with fitted silhouettes, power sneakers and mirrored aviators. A brand ambassador for Louis Vuitton, Sophie Turner is unmissable wherever she goes, but she outdid herself at Priyanka Chopra and Nick Jonas’s wedding in India—going all out in the most stunning kurtas and lehengas. The Game of Thrones star picked a green lehenga by Anita Dongre for Chopra’s mehandi ceremony, while a red and gold Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla lehenga featuring gold embroidery won her vote for the sangeet. On the red carpet, Turner can usually be seen in miniskirts, metallic gowns, pantsuits and jumpsuits. And if she’s looking to shake things up, she likes picking looks that stand out in a crowd—like her Louis Vuitton number for the 2019 Met Gala. LBDs have also long been a mainstay in Turner’s repertoire. (Remember the short black Mugler dress she wore while promoting X-Men: Dark Phoenix?) When it comes to her off-duty looks, Turner’s wardrobe is high on relaxed track pants, sweatshirts, dresses, and shorts + blazer combos. While she prefers towering heels for red carpet events, casual outings mostly have her sticking to her extensive sneaker collection. column1: What does it take to create a chikankari lehenga fit for royalty?
column2: © Instagram.com/abujanisandeepkhosla Fashion Designer duo Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla tell Vogue about the rich and nuanced heritage of Lucknowi chikankari, how the craft has evolved over the years, and what it will take to keep its legacy alive Understated yet luxurious, chikankari embroidery's timeless elegance has earned it many ardent fans. A-listers like the Bachchan family and Madonna have embraced the craft, which can be adapted to look equally at home in a bridal trousseau or the red carpet. Vogue spoke to Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla, the designer duo that is known to use it heavily in their couture, about the Persian origins and technical intricacies of chikankari, its evolution through the decades, and their own attempt to make this ancient embroidery relevant in the 21st century. Abu Jani: “Chikankari, the delicate, traditionally white-on-white embroidery, was originally done by hand on Muslin cloth. There are several theories associated with its origin in India. The most plausible one is that it came from Persia, brought to the Mughal courts in India by Persian nobles. It was patronised by Nur Jahan, the wife of Mughal emperor, Jehangir, who ruled in the 17th century. Eventually, it became a favourite among Mughal nobility.” Sandeep Khosla: “In the 18th century, the court of Oudh shifted to the city of Lucknow and the then Nawab Wazir, Asaf Ud-Daula, was a lover of luxury and the arts. So a variety of scholars, poets and craftsman like jewellers, painters and embroiderers flourished in his reign. It is during this same period that chikankari (which was virtually unknown until the mid-19th century) started gaining popularity all over the country. Over the years, it has been patronised by Lucknowi nobility and today, there are thousands of artisans practising the chikan craft in the villages around Lucknow.” AJ: “Chikankari embroidery is a [thing of] pristine beauty. It is delicate shadow work that is refined and impossibly elegant, but also time-consuming process and laborious to produce. First, we design the pieces in-house and accordingly structure and cut the fabric. Once cut, the cloth is block printed with motifs that are used as patterns for embroidery. They also help to demarcate the areas for different stitches. This is done by expert printers using blocks of sal and sheesham wood, which are difficult to carve but highly durable. “Then, our highly-skilled female embroiderers work on the fabric under the guidance of teachers like Parveen Abbasi. Three or four women handle each cloth, with each one focusing on a different stitch. There are three main types of chikan stitches—the flat stitch, the embossed stitch and the jaali stitch. These are further subdivided into more than 20 specific stitch techniques. Bakhya is a stitch worked with six strands on the wrong side of the fabric to create shadow work for the leaves and petals. Hool often forms the centre of a flower. It is created by punching a hole into the fabric with a needle and holding it with small stitches all around, using one single thread. Hatkati is row of jaali pulled together, and is often used for the spine of the leaves, to encircle flower heads or edge the fabric. Jaali consists of various pulled stitches worked from the back of the cloth using a fine strong thread. And they are many types too, such as Siddhaur, Bangla and Madrasi. Pechni is a major stitch usually used for trailing stems. It is worked with six strands on the right side of the fabric and progresses along a design without continually finishing off threads. Murri is also a prominent feature of chikan and used to create small embossed leaves and petals. Finally, Phanda is a small knot similar to (and usually mistaken for) a French knot. “Post embroidery, the fabric needs to be washed for several days until it is ready for stitching. It is then transported to our workshop in Mumbai, where it transforms into shararas and saris and dupattas. The time taken for each garment depends on the complexity and intricacy of the work. Our saris typically take up to six months to craft. A bridal lehenga involves more than a year of work, because everything is handcrafted and that takes both precision and time.” SK: “Originally, chikankari was only done on muslin cloth featuring motifs in the Mughal tradition. These were mainly nature-inspired such as creepers and flowers like the rose, jasmine and lotus. There were also paisleys and jaali work inspired by stunning Mughal architecture. However, in the 1980s, synthetic textiles and cotton became the canvas, and chikankari was far removed from its noble provenance. Crude embroidery and simplistic patterns were the norm. It had become mass and casual wear. “In 1992, Abu and I visited Lucknow and decided to restore and reinvent the ancient techniques of chikankari. We worked with our aunt, Sita Sondhi, and friend, Shahnaz Kidwai, to restore chikan to its former glory. It took two years of intensive training, research and development before we could create our first collection. The process started with existing artisans (typically older ladies) who we re-trained for the complex stitches. They passed on the techniques and skill to younger women. We sourced vintage blocks for printing exquisite, multiple patterns and then had to train our artisans to embroider these fine stitches. Instead of cotton, we used luxury fabrics such as georgette, chiffon and organza to create chikankari ensembles. “Those early days were a huge learning curve and full of experimentation. Each garment would take six months to complete because of the refined nature of the embroidery and patterns. But the fruits of our labour paid off and the first collection itself was completely sold out. Our customers knew the value of what we were attempting to recreate.” AJ: “We are now in our 27th year of working with chikan and from the beginning, it has been our mission to elevate chikan to couture, red carpet and bridal wear. Our first chikan bride was Shweta Bachchan Nanda in 1997. As artists and designers, it has always been our goal to see the old with brand new eyes, to reimagine beauty and raise it to unimaginable standards of finesse and style. “To have taken chikan from a casual, mass market category and made it haute couture is something we take great pride in. We’ve also kept it on the high fashion map for two and a half decades. It is now an embroidery coveted by India’s most discerning fashionistas, celebrities and actors as the pièce de résistance ensemble for their most important events. For her wedding reception last year, Deepika Padukone chose to wear and ivory and gold chikankari ensemble created by us. It was brought to life using intricate, tone-on-tone thread embroidery along with sequins, Swarovski crystals and gold zardozi embroidery. We are constantly striving to refine and hone our expression using new embellishments and silhouettes, with extremely detailed embroideries and motifs. We’ve even created western gown silhouettes incorporating chikan embroidery in our “Chamki Chikan” collection. They are the glamorous, bodycon avatars of the traditional embroidery.” SK: “Chikankari is a craft that is very much current and simultaneously, eternal. We have over 200 female artisans in Lucknow. Each one of them is an absolute mistress of her craft, and we’ve invested in their training, ensured substantial remuneration and quality work environments. They are central to the creation of our masterpieces, and we ensure that they know that. If you want to save a dying a craft, treat artisans like artists and not labour. It will always remain our passion to ensure chikankari flourishes, for our own sake as well as the sake of our craftswomen.” 9 chikankari kurtas that are perfect for the summer Exploring the Indian block print’s rich cultural history The chikankari lehengas your summer wedding wardrobe needs right now Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This batch of Gen Next designers is ready to take on Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: Fashion Lakmé Fashion Week’s celebrated Gen Next Designer Programme has handpicked six designers who will be showcasing their debut collections at the upcoming winter/festive edition. Here’s everything you need to know about their work Being selected for the Gen Next Designer Programme is every aspiring Indian designer’s dream come true. After all, the initiative has introduced us to some of the country’s best designers—think Rahul Mishra, Masaba Gupta, Aneeth Arora of Péro and Nachiket Barve. For this year’s edition, six names have been carefully chosen from a pool of 400 designers to make their debuts at the upcoming Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2019. Vogue chatted with the lucky six to gain an insight into what we can expect from their collections. Inspired by his keen interest in architecture and aboriginal native Australian art, New Delhi-based Sahib Bhatia’s winter/festive 2019 line brings forth a range of trench coats, jackets, blazers and more that uses embroidery and surface techniques. “Since it’s a winter collection, a lot of cotton and woollen blends have been used to ensure the pieces are sturdy. There will be a lot of layering and hints of traditional Japanese fashion can be seen as well,” says Bhatia. Gaurav Singh’s winning collection drew inspiration from ‘Kadali-Patram’. “It’s the Sanskrit name of a banana leaf that is considered sacred,” the designer explains. His winter/festive collection acknowledges the architectural dynamics of the banana leaves through innovative tailoring, complete with unexpected drapes. “The unprocessed side of a material (especially khadi) that comes with a rough texture has been the driving force for Kadali-Patram,” he says. Expect dresses, jacket dresses, tops and skirts in handwoven khadi, and techniques of draping, layering and boning. Henri Matisse, the famous 20th-century French artist, draftsman and collagist, served as the starting point of Ankita Srivastava’s collection. The prints you will see on the Edwardian-inspired silhouettes are inspired by the cut-out and hand drawing technique used by Matisse in the late 1940s. “They are hand sketched and then translated on the fabric using screen printing,” says Srivastava. Coming to the fabrics, the designer made sure to use sustainable and eco-friendly options like handloom cotton khadi, handloom cotton and silk Chanderi. “We’ve introduced a new fabric called CUPRO as well, which is also known as vegan silk and is made from the waste of cotton,” she says. Wide pants, variations of puffed sleeves and vintage silk shirts with saris make up her winter/festive 2019 collection. “As a day dreamer myself, I scripted a short story of ‘Noie’, a young girl who breaks into a cloudy sphere of dreams and fables. Our winter/festive collection is a reflection of this make-believe story wherein the designs are, in fact, the transition between dreams and reality,” explains Aggarwal. The two themes are juxtaposed into details, textiles and silhouettes. Fabrics like linen, linen silk, silk organza, jute and 100 per cent cotton are used to create clothes that are subdued yet eye-catching, with bold shoulders and flowy hemlines taking centre stage. Manjushree Saikia’s ‘Dawn to Reality’ explores timeless silhouettes that come in handmade textiles. “In a world that’s shackled by the compulsion to rise in progressive environments, this line honours the efforts made by artisans,” says Saikia. Fabrics like tea-dyed mulberry, eri and muga silk from Assam are incorporated to craft tailored silhouettes that resonate historical significance. Stanzin Palmo’s collection pays homage to the flora of Ladakh, with apricot blossoms and sea buckthorn being translated onto the garments using digital art and embroidery. “The silhouettes incorporated in the line borrow inspiration from the traditional Ladakhi dress, right from its shape to the way it gathers. I have used Ladakh handmade pashmina, Ladakh’s textile (Nambu) wool, silk, cotton linen and rayon,” says Palmo.
