column1: American designer and heiress Gloria Vanderbilt dies, age 95
column2: © Alamy Fashion One of America’s last aristocrats, the fashion designer, artist, author and heiress Gloria Vanderbilt has died, aged 95. Here, Vogue looks back at her life Gloria Vanderbilt, American fashion designer, artist, author and heiress, died on Monday 17 June, aged 95. Vanderbilt had cancer. She is survived by her sons, CNN anchor and journalist Anderson Cooper—who confirmed her death, saying she was the “coolest and most modern” person he knew—Leopold Stokowski and Christopher Stokowski. Throughout her life, Vanderbilt operated at the nexus of American society—first as an heiress who was the subject of a fraught and highly-publicised custody battle, and later through her myriad career ventures, social life and four marriages. A regular on the international best-dressed list, in 1968 LIFE magazine called her “an up-to-date and very feminine version of the many-faceted Renaissance man” on account of her work as a “poet, actress, literary critic and artist”. But it was in the late 1970s, with the launch of her eponymous denim line in collaboration with Murjani, that Vanderbilt experienced her greatest financial and critical success. Launched in 1977, it generated $300 million in sales within three years, outselling Calvin Klein in 1979 by 20 per cent. “She's tried to do many, many things for many, many years,” reflected her friend Diane von Furstenberg in 1979. “The thing that you least associated her with—jeans—worked.” This was in part a marketing triumph, with sales supported by what The New York Times called “the most extensive television campaign ever waged by an apparel company and a blitzkrieg of print advertising and promotional tours”. In later life, she continued to exhibit as an artist and wrote several books, including an erotic novel released in 2009, which The New York Times argued “may be the steamiest book ever written by an octogenarian”. Born in 1924, Vanderbilt made headlines from birth. The great-great-granddaughter of Cornelius Vanderbilt, who by the time of his death in 1877 had amassed an enormous $100 million fortune, Vanderbilt’s father passed away when she was an infant, thus leaving her in the care of her mother. It was a difficult childhood, with her mother largely absent and embroiled in a frenetic European social life with her twin sister Thelma, who was the mistress of the future King Edward VIII. “She was always off, exquisitely dressed, going down the hallway with a man,” Vanderbilt later observed. Her mother’s behaviour eventually resulted in a very public custody battle instigated by her paternal aunt, Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, who founded the New York museum bearing her last name. Due to the salacious details of the case, Vanderbilt became a subject of national fascination, termed a “poor little rich girl” by the press. “I just never read anything about myself,” she later said in 1982. “I started that as a child because of the kind of publicity I had. And, not reading these things, well, that has enabled me to survive.” It was the aunt who eventually won, with Vanderbilt dispatched to live on her Long Island estate and only see her mother at weekends. The challenging nature of this arrangement meant that at 17 she fell into marriage with agent and rumoured mobster Pat DiCicco after an affair with his boss, Howard Hughes. “What can one say about a first marriage, except that it’s wonderful?” she told reporters at the time—though her comment about it being her first was prophetic. Vanderbilt later called the union a “desperate measure” adding that DiCicco was violent towards her. After four years, she divorced DiCicco in 1945 when, aged 21, she was finally able to access her trust fund. In the same year she remarried, this time to conductor Leopold Stokowski, who was 40 years her senior. The union lasted 10 years and produced two sons. It was Stokowski who reportedly encouraged her artistic pursuits and she went on to study at The Art Students League of New York, staging her first solo exhibition in 1952. In 1968, her designs were licensed by Hallmark to appear on their cards and stationery. In 1953 she turned to acting, receiving training from Sanford Meisner and appearing on Broadway in 1955, and on television thereafter. In 1955, she also published a collection of Love Poems and divorced Stokowski, briefly dating Frank Sinatra and Marlon Brando before marrying director Sidney Lumet. The two were married for seven years before divorcing in 1963, when she married writer Wyatt Emory Cooper. It was this final union in which she was most happy and the two remained married until Cooper’s death in 1978. The marriage also produced two sons, with the elder, Carter, tragically committing suicide at 23 in front of his mother, by jumping off the terrace of her 14th floor apartment. She remained close with her younger son, Anderson, until her death. Throughout her life and marriages, Vanderbilt captivated the attention of the fashion press. “She has that Bacchanalian look the Vanderbilts all had,” said Diana Vreeland, who first featured her in the pages of Harper’s Bazaar in 1939 aged 15. She later appeared in Vogue, photographed by Richard Avedon, with whom she built a particularly strong relationship. “The reflection Dick gave back to me made me believe in myself,” she later said. “The shoots marked the pivotal moment when I knew then at least I could trust myself and that I was free. I was free and unafraid. I fought Stokowski for custody, and Sidney told me, Gloria you won where your mother failed.” In 1968, LIFE magazine said she had “spearheaded and developed a style of dressing which she calls ‘putting bits and pieces together’”, instead of wearing one head-to-toe look. Her feats as a decorator—she said she was allergic to professionals—were captured by Horst P. Horst for Vogue, and her status as a girl-about-town was cemented by a close relationship with Truman Capote, who was rumoured to have used Vanderbilt as inspiration for the character of Holly Golightly in Breakfast at Tiffany’s. Though the two later fell out, he aptly summed up her appeal: “Gloria’s attraction was that she had the beauty of an actress with the pedigree of an heiress and the attitude of an artist.” Not all her business ventures were successful: a 1976 ready-to-wear collection failed to take off, while the decline of her jean business in the 1980s coincided with a money troubles brought on by the fraudulent management of her estate by her lawyer and psychiatrist. Vanderbilt successfully sued the pair, but she never received the money she was owed, and as a New York Magazine article noted, “She spent it as fast as she could make it.” Her son Anderson Cooper later said, “My mom is a survivor, but has none of the toughness that term often implies. She has strength, great stores of it, but she has refused to develop a layer of thick skin to protect herself.” Confirming the news of her passing, Cooper concluded, “Love is what she believed in more than anything. Gloria Vanderbilt died as she lived: on her own terms.” Portrait of Gloria Vanderbilt as a baby © Getty Mr. and Mrs. Reginald Vanderbilt posing with their daughter © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt and her aunt Gertrud Vanderbilt - Whitney in Long Island In 1934 © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt on horseback in 1937 © Getty Goria Vanderbilt back form Cuba in 1939 © Getty Gloria Vanderbuilt and her mother Gloria Morgan Vanderbilt © Getty Pasquale DiCicco and Gloria Vanderbilt © Bettmann Gloria Vanderbuilt Barnum & Baile circus in USA © REX Vanderbilt On CBS Radio © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt in Künstlerin, USA © Getty Gloria Jr. Vanderbilt © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt and Frank Sinatra walking together © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt holding her boys Stanislas and Christopher © Alamy Gloria and Sidney's Wedding © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt swimming © Getty Gloria and her sons in New York © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt for Vogue in 1975 © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt for Vogue in 1961 © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt jeans © Getty Gloria Vanderbilt and Wyatt Cooper © Shutterstock How ’80s acid-wash denim is making a comeback in 2019 Vogue encyclopaedia: The history of denim jeans Heads up, you may start seeing these strange jeans everywhere soon Wellness Culture & Living Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: It took designer Prabal Gurung over 400 hours to create his first lehenga
column2: © Nick Tucker Fashion "Anjuli was set on wearing a traditional lehenga with a personal twist. I thought it would be special to embroider special memories and signifiers of her and Charlie’s relationship into the panels of the skirt," Prabal Gurung takes us through the details that made this bridal lehenga special For the New York-based couturier, designing his first bridal lehenga was a true labour of friendship and love. Vogue got him and the bride, Anjuli Nanda Diamond, to tell us more about the ensemble Since I launched my business ten years ago, Jennifer and Nell Diamond have been loyal supporters, advocates and most importantly, friends. They are both incredible, strong, resilient, and witty women who so inspire me. I got introduced to Anjuli as she was marrying Jennifer’s son, Nell’s brother Charlie, so the collaboration all came together quite organically. Anjuli wanted to infuse her Indian roots into the wedding ceremony and reception and I felt an immediate spiritual connection to her and this idea. It was a marriage between Anjuli and Charlie, yes, but this process also felt like the perfect creative marriage between Anjuli and I. © Nick Tucker Anjuli was set on wearing a traditional lehenga with a personal twist. I thought it would be special to embroider special memories and signifiers of her and Charlie’s relationship into the panels of the skirt. Each panel on the skirt was hand-embroidered with special places and symbols in their relationship—where they met, their dog, and a visual to pay homage to Anjuli’s late mother. It was such a personal work of art. © Nick Tucker Red is one of my absolute favourite colours. I find nothing more striking than a strong and beautiful woman dressed in all of her glory. It’s become a bit of a brand signature. Anjuli was also set on the idea of red to honour her mother, as red was the colour her mother wore to her wedding. We used gold hand embroidery to finish the look. The result was a hand-embroidered raw silk blouse and skirt with bullions, sequins and crystal zardozi work. We spent over 400 hours hand creating her lehenga. Anjuli Nanda Diamond in Prabal Gurung © Nick Tucker I’d love to! We do offer lehengas and saris as part of our bespoke Atelier Prabal Gurung line, but I’d love to expand and grow that portion of our business throughout India when we can find the right partner. © Nick Tucker “I’ve always been a huge fan of Prabal’s work and value his deep connection to India, where my father is from. He’s also a close friend of my now-husband Charlie’s family. Early on in the planning process, I mentioned that we were planning to have a Hindu ceremony. He was thrilled with the idea and immediately offered to design my bridal lehenga. From the beginning, I knew that I wanted the lehenga to be red, in honour of my late mother who wore red for her marriage to my father. One of my absolute favourite elements was the eight customised panels of the skirt. It was the talk of the wedding! Everyone wanted to get up close and see the incredible detail of the embroidery. Each panel had a framed motif that was symbolic and personal, including Claridge’s (where Charlie and I got engaged), our favourite bar in the West Village (Greenwich Treehouse), our favourite places (Nantucket, London), our dog (Duchess), even the view from our apartment overlooking the Hudson River! One panel that was extremely special to me was in commemoration of my mother, Patricia, whose birthday was July 14—Bastille Day. Prabal and his team creatively incorporated this fact by including an Eiffel Tower with fireworks. I was incredibly touched to have her included in such a poetic manner. It was a wonderful way to celebrate her memory and have her with me throughout the big day.” © Nick Tucker Recreate Janhvi Kapoor’s white lehenga look from Dhadak’s title track Alia Bhatt, Kareena Kapoor Khan and more stars who love black lehengas 11 printed lehenga choli sets your festive wardrobe needs right now What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Designer Naina Jain talks about the labour intensive craft of bandhini
column2: Fashion Kolkata-based designer Naina Jain talks about the craft of bandhini, the technique that goes into creating it, and its significance in the world of Indian textiles Derived from the Sanskrit word ‘banda’, meaning ‘to tie’, bandhini is an intricate form of tie-dye indigenous to Gujarat, Rajasthan and parts of Uttar Pradesh. The centuries-old craft has retained its immense popularity over the years, and has seen a decided comeback in the form of contemporary Indian wear this year. Kolkata-based designer Naina Jain has been a particular champion of the art with her heirloom #EvergreenBandhanis. She givesVogue a behind-the-scenes look into the making of an authentic bandhini textile. The earliest evidence of bandhini can be traced back to the Indus Valley civilisation. It can also be seen in the paintings at Ajanta Caves (dating back to 1st and 2nd centuries BC), and are mentioned as a part of the royal marriage in Bānabhatta’s Harshacharita back in 7th century AD too. Though the technique of tie-dye originated in China, it was slowly adapted to the western part of the Indian subcontinent, and Gujarat and Rajasthan became the centres for its development. Bandhini is a resist-dying technique where the fabric is plucked with fingernails and tied with a cotton thread forming a figurative design. This is later dyed into the desired colour. Eventually, the resisted areas are opened to unveil the finished pattern. The fabric is first dyed in the desired bandhini dot colour, and then tied into the desired pattern. The fabric is usually folded in half to make the process easier. This also results in a mirror image of the pattern. True masterpieces are those that are tied without any folds. This means that each bandhini dot is tied single-handedly. The most common colours for bandhani dots are yellow, white and red. Fine dots and high precision make a bandhini creation more valuable. Usually, it is easier to attain fine bandhini on a thinner fabric as compared to a thicker one, but there are master craftsmen who specialise in the latter too. Depending on the design of the final product, a bandhini pattern can either be called shikari, chandrakhani or gharchola, which are all related to how the knots are tied. A bandhini sari can take anywhere between four months to a year to weave, depending on the number of hands working on it. Some take over a year with a single hand creating it. This makes the piece all the more unique, as all the bandhini dots are similar in size. The bandhini sari is worn with great pride and care, and passed down several generations as heirloom treasures. It is a timeless handcrafted piece, and is often attached to special moments in one’s life like a wedding or the birth of a child; adding even more significance. Figurative patterns such as elephants, parrots, peacocks, dancing humans, flowers, diamond-shaped barfis and mango-inspired keris are common motifs. A bandhini sari is a must-have in a bride’s wedding trousseau, especially as a dupatta for her pheras. The bandhini piece that a bride or groom’s uncle traditionally presents her with is referred to as a chunnari. A white bandhini, called the panetar, is often the choice of Gujarati brides. It is believed that a red bandhini sari brings good luck to a bride-to-be. Bandhini pieces presented to a new mother are called odhanas. Gharchola bandhini saris are popular in the Gujarati and Jain community for festive celebrations. Our association with bandhini goes back a long way. What started as a store for bandhej pieces in 1997 has now created a niche in bandhani and beyond, making it more wearable and accessible in styles that will appeal to women of all ages. We’ve not only combined bandhani with hand embroideries from across India, but also married it with craft techniques such as Kota weaving, chikankari and Paithani—giving bandhani a never-seen-before update. We also experiment with bandhani on fabrics such as organza, which is again an uncommon practice. Our weavers are based in Kota, Rajasthan and Beneras, while our bandhini artisans are from Kutch, Gujarat. Their challenges are many. The power loom sector is slowly taking over the handloom industry. We are also now seeing motifs that were typical to the handloom sector being easily copied by the power loom sector at cheaper price points. In Kota this crossover by a craftsmen is considered to be a serious offence—if a weaver chooses to shift his practice to replicate designs using mechanised forms, he is socially disregarded from the community. The industry is also facing threats due to poor payment and long turnover periods, which has led to a downfall in the number of artisans creating bandhini. Our long-standing endeavour has also been to support the handloom sector and ensure artisans are paid in accordance to the intensive work they put in. We also prefer to deal directly with the artisans to eliminate unwanted middlemen and promote systems of fair payment. column1: Let’s hear it for the return of the non-fashion flip-flop
column2: Fashion From Havaianas to Etro, everyone does flip-flops. Scroll through a few good ones to complete your summer look. The flip-flop has come a long way from being the post-pedicure footwear of nail salons and the lazy shoe of beach boardwalks. This past week, outside of the men’s shows in Milan, French journalist turned Instagram sensation Sophie Fontanel, known for her quirky mirror selfies, put her flops to the pavement. While en route to the Fendi show in a quintessential French look that included an Yves Saint Laurent vintage shirt, Céline skirt, Louis Vuitton sunglasses, and Dior tote bag, she sported an incongruous pair of Brazilian-made . “I used to wear [them] when I was a child, and I kept this habit,” she explained in an email. “Ava Gardner, Ali MacGraw, Carolyn Bessette used to wear them, and nowadays Sofia Coppola wears them. Since it’s the simplest shoe ever, it enters into the category of a white T-shirt and a pair of jeans. I like it.” Her pair had personality too: They were white with a sky blue strap. (To make the look all the more French, Fontanel opted to go laissez-faire with unpolished toes.) Even resident Vogue street-style photographer Phil Oh noticed the down-to-earth pair and Insta Storied Fontanel’s look with the note ”best shoes” in all caps. Bien sûr. Etro spring/summer 2019 © Vogue Runway It’s not only the streets where modest flip-flops have been having a rubbery resurgence. Look to the Spring 2019 runways: Acne Studios showed an array of neutral-colored pairs, while Etro added a creative twist, churning their incarnations out with a decorated thong strap. The sandals have made their way into the Vogue offices as well. Market editor Anny Choi swears by a pair of plain black flip-flops. “I wear them with loose jeans and a vintage blouse for a night out in Montauk or dress them up in my tailored mom shorts and a button-down,” says Choi. “They aren’t so bratty. They make you look cool without actually trying.” Her sole qualm? “I do worry that bouncers might not ‘get’ the look.” Acne Studios spring/summer 2019 © Vogue Runway The best way to balance the flip-flop’s inherent casualness is to make sure the rest of the outfit is dressed up. Take a note from Fontanel: “It is fantastic with a long dress,” she writes. “The more elegant you are dressed, the more efficient it is.” Better yet? A pair of her Havaianas will only set you back $18. Here, shop the best pairs to wear everywhere from the pavement to the playa. column1: Humberto Leon and Carol Lim leave Kenzo after eight years
column2: © GoRunway Fashion The co-creative directors will be turning their attention to Opening Ceremony, the store and brand the pair founded in 2002 After eight years at Kenzo, co–creative directors Humberto Leon and Carol Lim are stepping down. The announcement was made by LVMH in Paris this morning, with the conglomerate confirming that the duo’s spring 2020 show, scheduled for June 23, will be their last. “After eight incredibly special years at Kenzo, we are passing the torch of that historic brand with great pride,” said Leon and Lim in a release. “We are thankful to our wonderful Kenzo team and the LVMH group for the opportunity to take forward [founder Kenzo] Takada’s groundbreaking legacy. We are excited to bring so many rich experiences and memories from our time at Kenzo to new frontiers.” The rationale for their departure is the reacquisition of all shares of Opening Ceremony, the store and brand the pair founded in 2002, from Berkshire Partners, which had held a minority stake in the OC business. “With full control of the company we are focused on growing our company even further,” Leon and Lim said. When Lim and Leon joined Kenzo in 2011, they resurrected the label’s tiger graphics to great commercial success and continued to mine Takada’s archives in a sub-brand called Kenzo La Collection Memento. The pair also collaborated with H&M and introduced biannual film projects directed by the likes of Gregg Araki and Carrie Brownstein. Kenzo’s 2016 fragrance campaign, directed by Spike Jonze and starring Margaret Qualley dancing around a hotel, was a viral sensation that also scored the duo an award at Cannes Lions. Priced more competitively than LVMH’s other luxury brands, Kenzo has become a mainstay on shop floors—whether it will remain so depends on who steps in as creative director. According to LVMH, Kenzo’s next “creative step” will be announced soon; whether that is a new design lead or a new commercial direction is unclear for now. column1: Why terming every label that makes tracksuits "streetwear" is lazy
column2: © Getty Fashion The description “streetwear” has become ubiquitous in fashion parlance in recent years, but as designers including Kerby Jean-Raymond of Pyer Moss and Nasir Mazhar start to take issue with the term, it’s time, says writer Micha Frazer-Carroll, that we all reflect on its loaded connotations When you’re a writer covering someone else’s work, the more guidance the artist can give you, the better. But when Pyer Moss designer Kerby Jean-Raymond tweeted a piece of simple advice in November, it marked a revelation. “To all the writers newly covering Pyer Moss, thank you and welcome,” the Haitian-American designer wrote. “Please refrain from calling us a streetwear company. It’s lazy and singular, we are more, you are more.” Pyer Moss © Hunter and Gatti In three short sentences, Jean-Raymond reignited a conversation about the term that hinges on one simple truth: the involvement of people of colour (either designers or models) is ultimately not the determining factor of whether something is “streetwear”. The always-shifting category, which grew out of skate, surf and hip-hop subcultures, has historically done what it says on the tin – represented the way that those resisting the fashion mainstream have worn comfortable, everyday garments outside in the real world. Nasir Mazhar © Getty Nasir Mazhar, who has designed pieces for Lady Gaga, was the first to launch a thousand think pieces on the racial dynamics of the term, pointing out the racially coded way the word is deployed by fashion writers in 2016. The milliner-turned-clothing-designer told journalist Ted Stansfield: “The minute people see black or non-white models and casual silhouettes, they think it’s streetwear.” Nasir Mazhar spring/summer 2017 © Getty When it comes to what is essentially lazy racial profiling, fashion writers should do better. But in some cases, the haste to eschew the label seems worth interrogating, too. Beyond simply being incorrectly deployed, the word “streetwear” has been described as tacky, basic and degrading by many – but why? Fashion designers have also often positioned streetwear as the antithesis to luxury fashion, but does this have to be the case? Nasir Mazhar autumn/winter 2016 © Getty When Mazhar elaborated on his gripe with the word, saying those that use similar terms “have to be like no, this isn’t fashion, this is something else. Fashion isn’t this, fashion isn’t tracksuits, fashion isn’t mixed ethnicities, fashion’s not about that really. So they have to be able to name it something else… Givenchy sells trackies and sweaters and T-shirts, but Givenchy would die if they called it streetwear!” Louis Vuitton autumn/winter 2017 © Getty Although designers like Mazhar are entitled to label their work as they see fit, maybe this description of streetwear is where part of the problem lies. While fashion big guns may well take issue with the term, perhaps the negative connotations surrounding streetwear are also underpinned by a kind of racially charged elitism. Why must streetwear, a style closely associated with people of colour, be a dirty word at all? Although the subculture has historically been positioned as anti-fashion, as it has moved into the mainstream, rigid adherence to this idea has posed paradoxical problems, like what to call Louis Vuitton’s 2017 Supreme collaboration. Louis Vuitton autumn/winter 2017 © Getty It’s worth considering the role appropriation plays in the problem of understanding streetwear in the mainstream. Ana Andjelic of luxury fashion consultancy Havas LuxHub told Complex magazine in 2017: “It’s all about cultural appropriation, but in a very flattened form. It’s like, ‘I’m going to take references, mix them and make them my own, but I don’t have any appreciation for the street to really understand that it’s an actual mixture of music, of street artists, of the local interesting people who reflect global culture.’ It’s very fashionable to be street.” I’ve seen truth in this myself; at my university, Cambridge, club nights were peppered with puffer jackets, thick gold hoops and cargo pants – visible zips lining every garment. This may be surprising considering the fact the university’s demographic is far removed from the style’s roots; in 2017, 81 per cent of Cambridge offers went to students in the top two socioeconomic groups in the country. But there are ways to do streetwear in the mainstream without outright appropriation and exploitation. The popularisation of streetwear should be seen as appropriationist when designers and consumers don’t pay due respect and, where appropriate, money to the style’s roots, but some designers are undoubtedly doing this right; like Kim Jones, menswear artistic director at Dior, who has openly proclaimed that the style is a source of inspiration for his designs, but also takes issue with the term. The politics of streetwear are ultimately complex – especially when the category is in many ways broad and nebulous. While it would be welcome to see more designers showing warmth towards the word, this is impossible in a climate where streetwear is either appropriated or doubles as a euphemism for “not fashion” or “not white”. No one can change the meaning of “streetwear” overnight, repackaging it as something that all designers suddenly want to be associated with. But it seems the industry’s relationship with the word is due a makeover – and one that pays respect to its origins. The style encompasses and represents exciting, evolving, dynamic and subversive cross sections within fashion – and while we should be critical of the ways it can be weaponised against people of colour, “streetwear” doesn’t have to be a dirty word. Micha Frazer-Carroll is a freelance journalist and first person and opinions editor at gal-dem. column1: In pictures: Kareena Kapoor Khan’s most stylish onscreen moments
column2: Fashion From Poo’s It girl wardrobe in Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham... to the ‘Chammak Challo’ sari immortalised at the Madame Tussauds wax museum, Vogue traces Kareena Kapoor Khan’s most talked-about onscreen outfits Barely one year old in Bollywood, and Kareena Kapoor Khan was flexing her sartorial muscles with everything from faux fur stoles to trend-setting mismatched heels as Poo in Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham... (2001). The runaway success of her wardrobe choices likely set the tone for her onscreen career, from the patiala-clad Geet of Jab We Met (2007) to the sultry red sari from ‘Chammak Challo’ that inspired a corresponding makeover for her wax statue at London’s Madame Tussauds. Unapologetic in her choices and unafraid to step away from the revolving door of fashion fads, it is perhaps this refusal to adhere to trends that serves as the rich breeding ground for setting new ones. Here, we dial the clock back to her most memorable onscreen looks over her two-decade-long career in Bollywood. It has been over 17 years since Poo crunched society’s internalised misogyny under the heel of her patent leather stilettos. However, the most definitive proof of her dominion over our fashion narrative can be found in the fact that her sartorial choices continue to live on two decades down the line—eagle-eyed netizens were quick to spot the K3G reference when Kylie Jenner shared a photo wearing all-red leather separates on Snapchat. She can play the archetypal glamazon in her sleep, but Kapoor Khan is no stranger to girl-next-door roles. Further proof of her relatability can be found in the patiala pants and long T-shirt that she wore in the movie’s memorable train journey—a combination that you’ve definitely thrown together yourself on a lazy Saturday afternoon. No stranger to making headlines, Kapoor Khan ushered in a new era in onscreen fashion when she debuted her headline-making size zero body, clad in a lime green bikini. She then proceeded to flaunt her washboard abs in a pair of golden shorts over a shimmery swimsuit, while her toned pins had their time in the spotlight in a flirty mini skirt and metallic bustier. While the backless poster dominated the headlines, the true fashion renaissance can be found in the ‘Shukran Allah’ track that had Kapoor Khan adapting to the wintry climes of Delhi as a university professor, with a wardrobe to go with it. Mojiris, scarves and oxidised jewellery sourced from local markets were called upon to complement the birth of a new trend in ethnic fashion—churidars worn under midi skirts. Bollywood can rightfully be credited with a never-ending love affair with flimsy chiffon saris, and Kapoor Khan isn’t immune to the allure of a slinky number. The soulful backdrop of the ‘Teri Meri Kahaani’ track had her opting for fluid numbers in a diverse palette of colours, ranging from angelic white to canary yellow. Life can be strange when you’ve got a video game protagonist masquerading as your dead husband, but when the going gets tough, Kapoor Khan finds solace in a head-turning OOTD. A sheer red sari, worn sans pallu and accessorised with a rustic kamarbandh and nath, for Akon’s ‘Chammak Challo’ gave Bollywood’s sartorial archives a new iconic outfit to list down. Billed at a whopping 1.2 crores, the costume wardrobe for the movie played host to 130 bespoke pieces designed by couturier Manish Malhotra. Touted as the designer’s most ambitious project for a single actress, the fruits of his labour can be found in the visuals—like that sheer black sari draped with a sash-style hot pink pallu for ‘Halkat Jawani’. The titular walk down the aisle for this veere’s wedding earned a spot on every bride-to-be’s moodboard, with a vintage Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla lehenga and baby’s breath dupatta doing the honours. While the kitschy lehenga from ‘Bhangra Ta Sajda’ serves as another winner, you’ll want to bookmark the lace-trimmed bodysuit and latex skirt from ‘Tareefan’ for the après-party. column1: Iris van Herpen on maximalism, outer space and making clothes that transcend the current definition of fashion
column2: © Getty Fashion “I approach fashion as a tool to open an unspoken dialogue between our insides and our outsides, that circulates our deepest desires, moods, and our most personal expressions,” says the Dutch designer, in conversation with Vogue Spend a few minutes on Iris van Herpen’s Instagram feed and you will be mesmerised by the quantum of effort that goes into creating something as basic as the fabric of a dress. The craftsmanship is evident when it’s spotted on a red carpet or in an editorial offering. Even before social media took over our lives (Instagram was only founded in 2010), the world had its sights set on the Dutch prodigy since her debut, in 2008. With a vision unlike anything you’ve seen before, and aided by cutting-edge technology, van Herpen’s work extends beyond the realm of the blue planet. Vogue got in conversation with visionary on her extraordinary approach to design. I wouldn’t call myself a maximalist, my home is actually very minimalistic. [There’s] almost nothing there, just some plants and the bare essentials. I like emptiness. But for my designs, both the labels of maximalist and minimalist don’t fit. In my designs I look beyond today’s definitions of a garment, and I approach fashion as a tool to open an unspoken dialogue between our insides and our outsides, that circulates our deepest desires, moods, and our most personal expressions. [But] on the level of personal and emotional impact, I do search for the max. So many! One look that comes to mind is the skeleton dress from my Capriole collection—which is inspired by the parachute jumping I do sometimes. The dress visualises the inside of the body outside, and depicts what I feel when I jump and free fall for one-and-a-half minute. The dress is fully 3D-printed, and making it was a huge challenge as the texture is so complex and delicate. It was also very difficult to get all the proportions right and make [the garment] fit well. We 3D scanned a model that we work with for the show, and that helped to get the fit right down to the millimetre. After it was printed, it had to be hand-finished and hand-stitched to make it wearable. It took us three months to make it, and though they weren’t easy, they were worth it. To me, the skeleton dress represents freedom and imperfection, and in between those, beauty can be found. I have practiced classical ballet from a very young age, until I went to the art academy. In these years of dancing, I studied the transformation of movement and the ‘evolution’ of shape. Today, I still use my dance background to explore how I can sculpt the female form. My work is like a diary. Through my collections, I learn about the world around me as much as I learn about myself—what is actually important to me, what shapes me as a woman, why I’m alive, what has meaning for me, what I hope to do for the world. These are not things I can just sit down and think about. It doesn’t work like that for me. It has to come out through action, through the materials I choose and through the textures and shapes. I’ve always tried to keep that naturalness in there. When I start a collection, the easiest thing would be to think about what I want to make and then start making it, because it’s the most effective way of producing. But when you start working that way, everything comes from memory. I don’t want my collections to come from logic or my memories; I want them to express me, here and now. My intuitive and unconscious design process is my most powerful tool. That relates to dance again—if have to consciously think of each movement when you dance, you would always be too late. When I look around me, I consider what I can’t see as much as what I can see, and that transformative focus creates freedom in my work. I constantly search to new forms of delicate craftsmanship and innovation. I go back to forgotten craftsmanship and the love for handwork, but at the same time I'm embedding new technologies and collaborations with artists, architects and scientists. Some are like extensions of my atelier, and they take me out of my own bubble of knowledge and experience, creating a kind of collective intelligence. I intentionally stretch the edges of my medium. I think this type of collaboration, and the sharing of expertise among specialists in diverse disciplines, can re-shape fashion. Blending fashion, architecture, science and biology opens up infinite possibilities, and it can help fashion advance in ways previously unimaginable. The art of fashion, this delicate place where innovation and craft are perfected to the finest possible level, is creating new terrains for collaboration with other disciplines, and those will shape what fashion will look like tomorrow. By combining traditional craftsmanship with innovative technologies, the atelier is exploring uncharted territory to create a more sustainable future for fashion. My triangle of inspiration is nature, art and science. I find beauty in contrasts; contrasts at the intersection between precision and chaos, art and science, and the artificial and the organic. In my collections I often try to visualise the invisible, trying to find the forces behind the forms in nature. I also constantly look at the patterns of nature and civilisation, chaos and order, that are blending into infinite hybrids. column1: Leggings, Bermuda shorts, and everything else you'll be wearing in 2020
column2: Fashion The influential international cruise shows are underway, but what are we going to be wearing this time next year? Here, we list out seven essential takeaways from the Resort 2020 collections (so far) The Resort 2020 collections are shaping up to be a celebration of vintage heroines and attuned femininity. From the return of retro-inspired suede to the staying power of the Bermuda short, here’s what we know (so far) about next year’s incoming fashion mood. Jil Sander Resort 2020 As seen at: Prada, Chanel, Jil Sander When it comes to tailoring, we’re witnessing a shift away from fashion’s seemingly-endless appetite for die-hard minimalism. The new mood in suiting has swung in a more practical direction, with pockets signalling ready-to-wear’s new ready-for-anything ethos. Expect to see Prada, Chanel and Jil Sander’s refined take on military references leading the way. Your muse? Lauren Hutton, naturally. And model Anna Ewers, with her hands buried in the pockets of Bottega Veneta’s glossy forest-green trench for the label’s Resort 2020 lookbook. Fendi Resort 2020 As seen at: Valentino, Fendi, Prada, Jeremy Scott Imagine Pepto Bismol pink (the de-facto hue of Millennial marketing tools), but with a hint of subversion. The squeaky clean shade is undergoing a makeover for next year thanks to Valentino, Fendi and Prada, where acres of silk and pleated taffeta are dismissing the ‘basic’ tagline that has haunted the mood-lifting tone over the past few years. This is a story with both glamorous and grungy ends. Plot twist: Jeremy Scott’s suburban prom queen wears a slasher movie rendition of the ephemeral pink gown. Burberry Resort 2020 As seen at: Burberry, Oscar de la Renta, Givenchy While practical pockets and gymnastic body-con are set to have a moment next spring, there’s also a revival of monochromatic gowns (seen at Burberry, Oscar de la Renta and Givenchy) that riff off old Hollywood silhouettes. If it seems like the runway is giving mixed signals on modernity, take a closer look. There are bare-faced models defying outmoded red carpet tropes with a powerfully physical approach to modelling and a unanimously stripped back approach. The sun has set on the condescension of the word ‘starlet’ and the stock character of the ‘ingenue’, and the very public uniform of the world’s most recognisable women is readied for action come 2020. Louis Vuitton Resort 2020 © GoRunway As seen at: Bottega Veneta, Louis Vuitton, Chanel, Simon Miller This season’s roomy longline shorts—the sort that once populated yacht clubs in the 1980s—are here to stay. Credit to Daniel Lee at Bottega Veneta for resuscitating the look with the house’s deftly chic SS19 collection. Whether you wear yours with a bustier, knitted twin-set or skater tee (seen at Louis Vuitton, Chanel and Simon Miller respectively), Bermudas are all about versatility, something that we can definitely get on board with. Balmain Resort 2020 As seen at: Chloé, Balmain, Chanel Here’s your headstart on a fuss-free summer. Instagram’s favourite no-trousers look has come of age with Chloé, Balmain and Chanel offering up the shirt dress as next year’s warm weather style shortcut. Wear yours belted or layered beneath a lightweight jacket, powered up with an ankle boot or paired with a zero-hassle sandal. Alberta Ferretti Resort 2020 © GoRunway As seen at: Jil Sander, Alberta Ferretti, Prada If there ever was a moment to channel a 1970s Jackie Kennedy, it’s now. From Jil Sander’s directional shift dress, to Alberta Ferretti’s loungey co-ords, or Prada’s clean take on the trench, it pays to switch out the denim outerwear for a more tactile approach. Accessories-wise, Bottega Veneta’s suede clutch is destined to be the new cult choice for 2020. Givenchy Resort 2020 As seen at: Givenchy, Chanel, Gucci When Givenchy and Chanel showcase the redeeming qualities of leggings, we take note. In theory, the structured-jacket-plus-running-tights could be the workwear dress code we’ve been waiting for. Or maybe it’s more about the full hosiery look seen on the runway at Gucci’s cruise show in Rome, where the tights themselves took centre stage. Ignore the niggling voice that’s saying no, you shouldn’t, you couldn't. Because, yes, you should and you absolutely can. column1: Tracing the rich history of Kerala’s traditional white and gold kasavu saris
column2: Fashion Designer Sreejith Jeevan tells us everything there is to know about Kerala’s iconic cotton saris, from its royal origins to the reasons behind its minimalist aesthetic In a country full of myriad patterns and bold colours, Kerala’s traditional kasavu sari stands out for its elegance and visual restraint. But beneath its simple appearance lies a cultural legacy and unique aesthetic. Worn by the Malayali community to temples, wedding and funerals alike, today, this age-old woven craft is in need of a design intervention. Vogue spoke to Sreejith Jeevan, founder and designer of clothing label ROUKA, to understand the intricacies of the kasavu weaves. The term kasavu actually refers to the zari used in the border of the Kerala sari and not the sari itself. It is the name of a material used in the manufacturing process. Thus, when kasavu becomes a part of the mundu (dhoti), it’s called a kasavu mundu. Kerala kasavu embellished sari with zari border, Ajio In Kerala, traditional attire like saris, mundus (which are sarongs worn by men) and settu mundus (a two-piece sarong sari) are generally called kaithari, translating to handloom. And the identity of the sari generally comes from the cluster they are associated with. Kerala has three clusters that have been given a Geographical Indication (GI) tag by the Indian government, and all of them make what are widely known as kasavu saris, as well as the white Kerala saris that swap the kasavu border with a coloured iteration (called kara). These three famous clusters are Balaramapuram, Chendamangalam and Kuthampully. The Balaramapuram cluster is based near Trivandrum and the artisans here are from the Shaliar clan. They were originally from Tamil Nadu and were brought down to Kerala by the Travancore royal family. Balaramapuram is famous for its use of pure zari (silver thread plated in gold), and very fine thread counts like 120s. The second cluster called Chendamangalam is famous for saris and mundus that are normally woven using half-fine zari and 80s-100s thread counts, but without too many motifs. They had the patronage of an aristocratic family called Paliam. Finally, the Kuthampully cluster also makes white saris with zari, but includes patterned and jacquard borders featuring human figure motifs. The artisan community here is called Devanga, and they were brought down by the king of Kochi. Traditionally, there was actually no concept of a sari at all in Kerala. Instead there was the mundu. Everyone wore a mundu from the waist downwards, and there was no upper garment for men or women, neither was required to cover their upper body. On the contrary, in a lot of places women were not allowed to cover their upper bodies, and had to pay a tax to do so. However, post-colonisation, women started wearing an angavastra (similar to a shawl) on their upper body and thus the mundu transformed into the two-piece settu mundu. People wear one mundu at the waist, and the other one as a sort of half-sari. The single-piece sari evolved much later, which then led to the popularity of a blouse. This was the first stitched garment they wore. The production time totally depends on the count. A plain sari with just a border and stripe on the end piece will take three to five days. But if it features motifs, it’ll take much more than that. When there are extremely elaborate motifs (such as those on a wedding sari), it can take up to a month because it is all done by hand wefting. The pricing also varies accordingly. If you purchase from a cluster, you can get a basic cotton sari for 3,000 rupees (which, in my opinion, is very underpriced), but with the zari it can go up to one and half lakh rupees—depending on how much gold and labour has gone into it. A weaver works at the loom The yarn must have been hand-spun traditionally, but these days they use mill-made yarn (hand-spun is both expensive and difficult to mass produce). They put this yarn through a long pre-weaving process, and especially at Chendamangalam, it is this process that got them the GI tag. Once they get the yarn, it is soaked in water for seven or eight days, and stamped on every day (the artisans do this with their feet) while it’s soaking, to get the dirt and starch out and make sure it is completely soft. The yarn is taken out after a week, and part of it is dyed (if required). Then, they make the warp and stretch the yarn. But according to tradition, this stretching has to be done between four and seven in the morning—the temperature and atmosphere during those hours was considered apt for this process. Technically, the yarn has to be stretched in an open area, but these days it’s difficult to find that kind of space. Before the warp is put on the loom, the artisans re-starch it in the morning and allow it to dry. Then they starch it once more and brush with a comb made out of coconut fibre. It is dried until 7.00am and then put on the loom. This stretched yarn is clean and absorbent, and the starch is added so it doesn’t break on the loom. Beyond this, there is really no post weaving process. They just take it off the loom and put it on the shelf. The Kerala sari and mundus are very minimalistic because they’re predominantly white with a plain weave on the body. The only design element these garments have is the border, which is the selvedge—it has a rib weave to add a more solid look to the gold or colour. Patterning is minimal and happens sometimes with weft inlay or using jacquards. However, it is this very simplicity that makes Kerala saris and handlooms so special. They have an extremely minimal approach to design. The difference between what you wear to a wedding (a sari with a two-inch gold border) and what you wear to a funeral (a sari with a half-inch coloured border) is simply in the colour and thickness of the border. Basically, when you add gold, it becomes a luxury product. Golden stripe kasavu sari, Kuthampully Handlooms Back in the day, patterning was almost considered a crime, and minimalism was the best form of refinement. Only the royalty and the rich aristocrats wore the kasavu sari, while commoners wore colour. However, even the royals wore a coloured border at home and would wear a kasavu only when they went to an event. The aesthetic was as subtle as that. I’ll give you a personal example. My cousin is getting married so my aunt gifted my grandfather a settu mundu with a one-inch border. My grandfather looked at it and said, “Oh this is too gaudy, I only wear borders that are 0.25 inches. I’m too shy to wear all of this.” However, as time has passed, people are finding the kasavu sari too minimal and subtle, so there are a lot of motifs being used now. The traditional motif is like a little flag at the end of the stripe called the chutti. Besides this, they also do very small extra-weft motifs (sort of like hand inlay) at one corner of the garment. As maximalist style is becoming mainstream (and people are getting bored of the same concept) we’re seeing even more motifs. Artisans weave trees and peacock motifs with extra wefts or jacquards, but these are all very recent additions. In terms of the colour scheme, there really is no definite answer for why all the saris are white. One argument is that there’s so much green and colour in Kerala that people chose to wear neutral. Another technical reasoning says that since Kerala gets so much rain, the dyeing process was difficult. A third school of thought links the white to the predominant gold culture here. Since a lot of the adornment came from jewellery, the fabric didn’t need to be patterned. I have used the kasavu fabric to create clothes in Indo-western silhouettes. I did a show at Lakmé Fashion Week in 2015, where we got the same kasavu sari fabric woven by a cluster and used it to make my apparel line called Rouka. Rouka at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2015 © Sagar Ahuja/Vogue In the early days, I did experience an interesting incident. I met a weaver in Thiruvananthapuram and suggested to him that we re-work the plain fabric and see how we can maybe add checks or stripes to it. This made him completely furious. “I only make things for elite!” he said. It hadn’t struck me until then that patterned cloth is not considered elite—which is interesting, now that I think about it. Even today, you’re not allowed to enter a temple wearing Madras checks because they’re considered casual. But I hadn’t thought about it like that before. Last year, the Chendamangalam cluster was badly affected by the floods that took place in Kerala, and they lost a lot of their looms in Kochi. What was worse was that the water had entered the stock room, and 40 lakhs worth of stock could have gotten stained. So we launched a social media campaign to help sell their stock on an urgent basis. The campaign went viral with celebrities like Kalki Koechlin and Tillotama Shome reposting our message. I realised the true power of social media when all the stock sold out in two weeks, and people even came forward to help set up the looms—they were all up and running by December. After that, we did a pop-up called The Wardrobe timed to the Kochi Biennale, where four local designers used kasavu saris to make clothing. I’m now working with another cluster near Chendamangalam called the Cherai society. We are looking at how we can do a different take on the Kerala sari and quirk it up using traditional techniques and fun motifs. You can buy the same Kerala sari anywhere, so why not try some design intervention? Most of the weaving clusters in Kerala work through co-operatives that work in their village. This is great because the system becomes fair-trade by nature. All the weavers are literate and part of the co-operative; there are fixed wages and bonuses and nobody gets exploited. However, that does mean that the fabric is more expensive. I’ve heard designers say things like ‘Kerala cotton is expensive, and we can easily get something similar but cheaper like a muslin from Bengal’. One way to circumvent this is to market the product to an affluent customer, but this has not happened yet. Marketing efforts have been lacking when it comes to Kerala’s handlooms. Another serious issue is that all the clusters are basically making the same product, and not much has changed in terms of design. The product still exists in its traditional form and there’s not been a different take on it. As a result, the sales are seasonal and all the clusters are competing for the same market on occasions like Onam or Vishu. The government gives a 30 per cent rebate then, so customers also wait till festive season because they get a discount. A serious design intervention is required to get out of this rut. The third issue is that because kasavu weaving is talked about as a dying industry, there’s no young blood coming into it. It sounds strange but one good thing that happened with the floods and the social media campaign that went viral was that there was suddenly a lot of awareness about the different weaving clusters all over India. We were joking about how the floods is when Chendamangalam got its Benares moment! Everyone wanted to wear one for charity and I got 300 emails in a single day. But charity cannot be sustained and demand has to be nurtured. Once someone has worn the kasavu, they will know how elegant and comfortable it is, especially for Indian summers. Foreigners who buy them come back and tell me that they’ve used the saris as table linen and curtains. So it could also translate into other products, but none of this is happening yet. They are proud of it, but like I said, it still is festive wear for most people. It is part of a bride’s trousseau, and they’re likely to already have in their wardrobes. There’s a lot of appreciation, but they also need a reason to buy more. As somebody who is from Kerala and lived in different places, it is something I’ll always carry with me. column1: Indian designers show their support for wildlife at The Animal Ball 2019

The proceeds from the ball will go to the Elephant Family and their efforts to support harmony between the human population and wildlife. column1: Exclusive: What to expect from the Shivan & Narresh x KOOVS collection
column2: Fashion The designer duo’s first non-swimwear collection paves the way for an athleisure-inspired curation of bombers, hoodies and more, all splashed with their signature prints For the longest time, the world of Indian swimwear was in something of a flux, lacking a definitive voice to steer the way onto the global fashion map. But the tides changed once luxury label Shivan & Narresh made its way into the market, bringing along a merry mosaic of prints and textures in memorable silhouettes, like the bikini sari and trikini—the former even found a fan in global icon Kim Kardashian West. Having expanded their sartorial lexicon to include wedding design, the designers are now marking another first by exploring the world of athleisure for their upcoming collaboration with fashion e-tailer, KOOVS. As the first collection without any resort or swimwear, the label is seeking inspiration from the tropics to express their language of sporty chic. The cool hues of sky blue, desert rose, red dahlia and mauve come together on a palette of Insta-worthy prints that will take the guessing game out of what to pack for your next weekend getaway. “The entire collection is super social media-friendly, and it photographs beautifully. We know our millennial audience; we know they love to click pictures when they travel. So we knew that we had to make sure the clothes look as good as they do when they are heading on a holiday,” says Narresh Kukreja, one half of the  duo. Slated to launch on June 20, the designer gives you an all-access low-down on what to look out for. Shivan and Narresh x Koovs The idea is to be disruptive, not only in terms of reaching out to a much wider and younger demographic, but also by delving into a set of different categories that we don’t usually work with, including streetwear and athleisure in addition to cocktail dressing. We’re attempting to reach out to a much younger audience with a capsule collection for a limited period of time, so they can get it at rates that are accessible to them within their preferred category of athleisure. The world of sportswear and athleisure, at best, does colour-blocking or fluorescent accents here and there. This one comes at the back of a print-driven collection which is very Shivan & Narresh, but you’ll be seeing it in a much younger avatar than the glamorous women we are used to dressing. We’ve done four different prints—Summer Night, Sweet Magnolia, Rose Magnolia and Lush Vineyard—with a sporty vibe, as athleisure is the heart of this collection. These prints are served in diverse silhouettes such as bombers, tank tops, jackets and footwear like espadrilles. The line-up is divided 50:50 between menswear and womenswear, and we’ve worked on blurring the lines by keeping the offerings gender neutral—the jackets and bombers can be worn by women as much as men. Shivan and Narresh x Koovs The brief that we discussed for this collaboration was very simple—work to our strengths. KOOVS felt that the signature print we were to design for the collection would be our biggest asset, while they would leverage their vast reach to deliver it to their design-savvy young audience—marrying the two was the solution we were looking at. This is why you will not see any resort or swimwear but instead, silhouettes that are sporty and within our universe of maximalism and print. The designs are very holiday-friendly and functional enough to be worn both on vacations and in the cityscape. For a tropical getaway, I would recommend the Rose Magnolia print for the day and the Summer Night print with a black base for the night. The elements of these prints are very tropical in nature, but the black, sweet rose and bubblegum pink serve as a great transition from daywear to evening wear. You can then pick your silhouette depending on where you’re travelling. If you are headed to a beachy destination, we have some fabulous bodysuits. Or if you are planning to visit a colder place in the hills, we have joggers and bombers, woollen dresses and gender-neutral hoodies. Shivan and Narresh x Koovs The pieces are best paired with sporty shoes or block heels and wedges if you are looking for that elevation. Pack a few oversized jackets, and ensure that you keep the vibe as sporty as possible. In terms of sunglasses, I am currently a fan of frames that are smaller than the shape of your face, whether it’s oval or round or square. column1: Behind-the-scenes exclusive of SS20 with Craig Green
column2: © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN Fashion The three-time winner of the British Fashion Council’s Menswear Designer award gives Vogue an insight into his latest collection via his personal Polaroid pictures Craig Green is feeling positive, and his SS20 show—a true London Fashion Week Men’s highlight – showed that in colour-soaked abundance. His references ranged from Mexican papel picado (Easter flags)—“so throwaway, but also about resurrection and hope”; to mirrors—“I always think of mirrors as possibilities, but also the idea of scrutinising yourself”; Egyptian death rituals—“being put into a tomb, all the way through your life, you’re never that protected!”; and using skin as a material. And true to form, Green effortlessly weaves them all together, this season in a palette of cobalt blue, powdery pink and vibrant orange. “The aim is to make it look effortless,” he laughs. “Sometimes you don't know how they are going to go together, but we are hopeful that they will kind of counterbalance each other, all meld into one.” They definitely do. The show also revealed his highly-anticipated athletic collab: Adidas Originals by Craig Green. An array of textured, colourful footwear, with nubby soles and contrasting hues, colour-matched each runway look. He shows Vogue his Polaroids—a passion project turned official brand archive, taken on a restored Polaroid camera that he was gifted two years ago. Angelos Tsourapas, Green’s partner and the brand’s business manager, started using it to document the campaigns and collections, creating an authentic visual record to refer back to. And it’s been kept under wraps until now. “There's something beautiful about having a Polaroid rather than a digital image,” says Green. “You can't edit it and it feels like it’s very much a real snapshot of what is happening at that time.” Here, the three-time winner of the British Fashion Council’s Menswear Designer award shares his personal Polaroids with Vogue. © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “There's a lot of analysing and trying and testing [that goes on when a collection is coming together]. Change is part of the process. A certain object, topic or material taken out of context can kind of mean anything, it just depends on what your point of view is. Things can mean everything to everyone, but also nothing at the same time.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “This is actually plumbing pipe. My dad is a plumber, so I’ve always grown up around it. I found that you can melt them with a heat gun and mould them into different shapes quite easily. They were meant to look like bones, or skeletons, but they also start to look kind of like a wind chime, and symbols or hieroglyphics, even though they’re not specific. But they're almost like children's toys as well, or weird instruments... There’s a beauty in how simple they are.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “This is the first season for Adidas Originals by Craig Green. We worked on a few different stories for this season. Pictured here are what we called ‘the ghost trainers’ in the studio, because they are taken from archive Adidas shoes and overlaid, so it looks like a ghost on top of a ghost. Another pair of shoes we called ‘lizard skin’ shoes, and then there’s the black, moulded, more minimal shoes, too.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “We're quite a ‘making’ studio. Everyone in the team is quite hands-on and can switch their skill-set across different things. For example, our accounts manager is amazing at embroidery, she’s a knitwear graduate. So, days before the show, she'll be working on embroideries rather than accounts. We all wear many hats.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “I think something that linked everything in the collection was what happens next: what happens when you die? I like that the idea doesn’t have to be morbid; it all depends on your viewpoint. The imagery on the Mexican-inspired pieces—hanging on the rail here—is quite childish, but also about resurrection and celebration.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “Three days to go to the show, we’re picking out looks for the show, piecing it all together.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “We kept calling these dream suits… like something you’d wear to dream, or that you would keep under your bed. But it also looks like you are wearing someone else’s skin, because of all the hands and the feet. Originally they were inspired by lots of different anatomical drawing from different cultures around the world. In a lot of the drawings I saw, muscles started to resemble flowers, which I thought was interesting. So depending on your mind, it can be one or the other.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “The shapes of these looks were almost meant to look like—it’s a bit morbid—but like death shrouds... Bedsheets or tablecloth that had holes and openings in them that you could slot your body in and out of. There was something beautiful about that; about the folding and packing away of the body, which goes back to the embalming of the body and those Egyptian references.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “In the run-up to the show, time sort of disappears. This is one of those moments. I'm thinking: ‘Can we stop the clock for a few hours? Can we gain a few more hours?’ But at some point you stop worrying and become laser-focused on getting things done, piece by piece.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “The night before the show, we’re still making modifications. Now everything is so constructed, almost, in imagery. I think there's something nice about a Polaroid image that is just authentic and true.” © Courtesy of: CRAIG GREEN “Inspired by Mexican Easter flags, these looks are made from ripstop [nylon], a material traditionally used for boat sails, so they are quite hard wearing, which is interesting: it’s a sail that doesn’t work because it has holes in it. And the Mexican flags are very delicate and single use, so I like [the juxtaposition] too. But they also look a bit like a recycling bag, slotted over someone’s head. That can be positive and, in another way, child-like too.” This London-based designer’s new collection will feature Indian textiles These Indian designers showcased at London Fashion Week How powerful are designer collaborations?
