column1: Is the fashion industry truly inclusive? 5 models weigh in
column2: © Greg Swales Fashion Models Radhika Nair, Halima Aden, Luc Bruyère, Stav Strashko and Robyn Lawley talk to Vogue about the inclusive fashion future they’d like to see Fashion has long had a problem with inclusivity. While the industry is becoming more global, with a greater focus on international markets, models of colour continue to represent a small percentage of those in campaigns, editorials and on the runway. The Fashion Spot’s most recent runway diversity report found that just 38.8 per cent of models cast in New York, London, Milan and Paris were non-white. Meanwhile, diversity in all its other forms—including the participation of older, plus-size, transgender and non-binary models, as well as those with disabilities—is still rare. Plus-size models accounted for just 0.69 per cent of those who walked the runways last season, while only 0.77 per cent were openly transgender women and non-binary models. Although there have been moves towards inclusivity over the last few years (the autumn winter 2015 runways, for instance, were 80 per cent white), much more remains to be done. Below, Vogue asks five runway regulars how the industry can become truly inclusive. Radhika Nair, Vogue India September 2018 issue © Greg Swales Radhika Nair, with her mop of dark curls and handsome looks, bagged herself a Balenciaga exclusive in 2016 and has had a stream of top jobs since. Henry Mackintosh Thomas, the man behind the famous scouting, told Vogue, “Designers today are interested in characters with a look and attitude. They want to dress these characters and their stories. Radhika, and girls like her, represent this and a youth culture that’s more accepting of the way people are.” “I started modelling at the age of 19 because my dad said he wouldn’t pay me any more pocket money. But I’m South Indian, and my parents had different expectations from me, so I went on to study economics and got a job in finance. Later, I was scouted in Bengaluru and moved to Mumbai to pursue full-time modelling. “Fashion’s come a long way in representation, but we still have a way to go. Sometimes for a show they forget to look at you as a person and focus on your colour instead. You hear things like “enough brown girls” or “enough white girls”. But I do know I have a responsibility to those girls who haven’t seen a South Indian with their skin tone being called beautiful in mainstream media. I want these girls to understand that I’m being myself and that’s what diversity is. It’s not just about race and colour but about individuality. There’s also diversity in the way we accept our flaws. I have scars on my face that I never want airbrushed in shoots. It’s a small disfiguration, but that’s all right.” Halima Aden © IMG Born in Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya, Halima Aden moved to the US at the age of six. She made her New York Fashion Week debut in 2017 at Yeezy and has walked for everyone from Max Mara to Alberta Ferretti. Aden is the first hijab-wearing model to appear on the cover of British Vogue and Vogue Arabia, the first to wear a hijab and burkini in Sports Illustrated Swimsuit and has her own hijab line, Halima x Modanisa. “I started modelling two and a half years ago, and it was a learning experience for everybody involved. Most people had never worked with a hijab-wearing model, who dresses more modestly and has wardrobe restrictions. Early on, I used to bring an entire suitcase full of hijabs, scarves, turbans and turtlenecks to shoots so that stylists would have more options. I did whatever I could to help and it’s always been very collaborative. It’s funny because there are always hairstylists on set and they don’t have much to do—they love me because they can just have fun, enjoy the shoot and not worry about doing my hair. “I have to give the industry a lot of credit because I’ve seen so much growth in a short time. It’s been amazing to see more models in campaigns and on the runway proudly wearing hijabs, and I think my agency IMG really paved the way by signing me and taking that risk. The people I work with are also really considerate. They make sure I have my own private dressing space and they let me go and pray, and then come back to set and shoot. While I’m fasting during Ramadan, they make sure my nails don’t get painted and use fake nails instead [because nail polish must be removed before ablution as it doesn’t allow water to touch the nails which makes the ablution invalid]. When it comes to inclusivity more broadly, the most important thing is that we continue having this conversation and invite models to contribute to the industry in other ways too. I started out as a model, but now I have Halima x Modanisa, my own 47-piece hijab line that includes pre-tied turbans. It’s so great when models can do more, have a voice and talk about important things. I think that’s the next step for fashion.” Luc Bruyere © Jonathan Daniel Pryce A model, actor, dancer and visual artist, the multi-talented Luc Bruyère was born without his left arm. He has gone on to redefine traditional standards of beauty, appearing in presentations for Kenzo, campaigns for Nike and performing at the historic Paris Opera. “After graduating from art school in Brussels, I arrived in Paris at the age of 18. At the time, I was studying theatre and acting, and I couldn’t even imagine being a model—especially without my left arm. But then I met Humberto Leon and he cast me in a show for Kenzo. In the presentation, I stood completely naked on a pedestal like a piece of art, my body painted with a marble effect. It was then that I understood that I could become an example for others, the sort of example I never had growing up. After that, Citizen K magazine offered me my first cover. Since then, I have danced with Marie-Agnès Gillot and soon I’ll be directing my first film. “It can be difficult to find your place within the fashion industry. There were many agencies who didn’t want to represent me because they thought I was too different. The mission for fashion now should be to promote self-acceptance and embrace our differences. The role of casting directors is important because they can give us access to designers and CEOs. There are also lots of young designers bringing diversity to their shows, but I want to see more of that from bigger brands. At the moment, I see diversity in editorials and campaigns, not so much on the runway, but some brands are doing it right—I love the casting at Vivienne Westwood and Gucci, for instance. Going forward, I think fashion needs to look back at the 1980s and 1990s. That was a time when being a model meant breaking the rules and having a personality—just think of Naomi Campbell and Kate Moss. I think we need to get audacious again. The industry needs to create new icons and celebrate diversity. I’m still considered an exception and I don’t want to be an exception anymore.” Stav Strashko © One Management Trans model Stav Strashko has walked the runway for Marc Jacobs and Coach, been a muse to Proenza Schouler’s Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, and broken boundaries across industries. In 2018, she starred in the film Flawless*, for which she became the first transgender woman in the history of Israeli cinema to be nominated for the Ophir Award for Best Actress.* “When I first started modelling, the Israeli fashion industry had a hard time casting androgynous models. As a result, most of my early career was spent working for European and Asian markets, even though it wasn’t much easier there either. I’ve been modelling for ten years now and I walk for many top designers, but the thing that is closest to my heart is my leading role in the Israeli film Flawless. I was nominated for the Best Actress prize in the Israeli equivalent of the Academy Awards, and I was the first transgender woman ever to be nominated in that category. That made me very proud and I felt closer to my country. “Fashion is changing the way it looks at gender. It’s already come a long way in the past few years, and that has made a huge community of people feel less isolated. We need to understand that the industry can have an impact on the way our society views certain things. When it comes to casting, we need to seek out as many people as possible from diverse social backgrounds and different cultures, and make sure their voices are being heard. I think this benefits brands and consumers. It allows companies to reach out to more people and means that customers can identify with the brands they are buying into. Street casting is also becoming more and more popular, and I think it makes fashion more accessible. Perfection is boring—people just want to see what’s real.” Robyn Lawley © MiLK Management & Muse Model Management The Australian model is an advocate for body positivity, having been one of the first women above sample size to appear in the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit issue. She has been vocal about the need for change and last year started a petition calling for Victoria’s Secret to be more diverse and inclusive of body shapes and sizes on its runways. “When I started out in the industry over ten years ago, you didn’t really see curvy girls on the catwalk. For me back then, it was all about editorial and trying to snag one shot in one magazine. Otherwise, curvier models were mainly doing catalogue. When you’re 18 or 19 and seeing other girls do cool stuff that you can’t do because of your size, it’s very strange. It took years, but slowly photographers wanted to shoot us. They didn’t see why the industry should be so segregated, but often they wouldn’t actually have the right clothes for us. Half the time you’d wear what you could fit into or it would be open from the back or you had to be in lingerie. Sports Illustrated was huge for me. MJ Day, the editor of Sports Illustrated Swimsuit, has been trying to push for more representation for years. She’s curvy herself! And look at what they’re doing now with Tyra Banks back on the cover at 45 and Halima Aden wearing a hijab and burkini. “To this day, there seems to be a ridiculous ideal and I don’t know who’s dictating it. With Victoria’s Secret, I spoke out because I was tired of seeing the same body type over and over again. I knew [Victoria’s Secret executive] Ed Razek was notorious for commenting on women’s bodies. He said no one wants to see plus-size or trans models, and he’s wrong. He’s eating his words now because the show isn’t returning to network TV. Going forward, it’ll have to get with the times otherwise it’ll be obsolete. It’s so funny when we say ‘curvy’ because we just mean normal compared to the very slim and young bodies we’re used to seeing in fashion. It’s empowering to see curvier girls walk in shows, and if it doesn’t happen it’s just because people are scared—scared their decisions won’t be well received, that people won’t buy their clothes or that they’ll be judged somehow. Designers are our last hope and they need to be the ones to change the game. Some designers see us as mannequins and they just want to get their designs on the runway, but at fittings there are seamstresses. After designing my own swimwear line, I realised that you can make samples in any size very easily. To me, that part of the argument is null and void.” With input from Akanksha Kamath 9 ways the fashion industry embraced inclusivity in 2018 Models around the world who are breaking the stereotype of perfection Pierpaolo Piccioli: “Fashion should be about inclusivity rather than exclusivity” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Meghan Markle’s new diamond ring from Prince Harry has a very special meaning
column2: © Getty Fashion The Duchess of Sussex debuted a sparkling new ring when she stepped out for her first post-pregnancy appearance this past weekend The Duchess of Sussex paused her maternity leave last weekend in order to join the royal family’s celebrations of Queen Elizabeth II’s birthday. The entire family were out for Trooping the Colour, which commemorates the official birthday of the British sovereign. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex joined the Duchess of Cambridge and the Duchess of Cornwall for a carriage ride as part of the Trooping the Colour parade, before appearing with the royal family on the balcony of Buckingham Palace. It was during the carriage procession that the Duchess of Sussex took off her navy gloves to reveal a new piece of jewellery. While previously the duchess wore two rings—her engagement ring and wedding band—she is now wearing a third, sparkling diamond ring. A closer inspection proves the ring to be a silver pavé-set band, meaning it’s totally covered with diamonds. Given it’s being worn with both her engagement and wedding band, it appears to be an eternity ring, which symbolises commitment. You can see the ring up close in the picture posted by a fan account below. People has confirmed the ring was indeed a gift from Prince Harry, though it’s not known whether it was gifted to the duchess on the birth of their son, as a “push present”, or on the occasion of their first wedding anniversary. People is saying it is the latter. Either way, it is most definitely a symbol of the couple’s eternal love, which makes this ring one very special piece of jewellery. This was the Duchess of Sussex’s first public appearance since the couple debuted baby Archie at Windsor Castle last month. The new mother wore all-navy Givenchy for the occasion, removing her elegant coat while on the balcony of Buckingham Palace to reveal a matching dress that featured white accents on the shoulder. The couple were joined by the rest of the royal family for the annual celebrations, which has a rich history going back more than 250 years. It originated from when royal palace guards would assemble to “troop” colours—meaning they would show off a regiment’s colour by way of brightly colour flags, which could be seen above any action during battle. In 1748 it was also declared the official birthday of the British sovereign, meaning that regardless of a king or queen’s date of birth, their birthday is officially celebrated during the Trooping the Colour weekend. In modern times, the parade showcases soldiers, horses and musicians who display their military capabilities to the royal family in the centre of London, which concludes with a 41-gun salute. The royal family then congregate on the balcony of Buckingham Palace to watch the Royal Air Force flypast display—hence why we see so many pictures of the family looking up into the air. This year’s Trooping the Colour also marked Prince Louis’s debut at the event, though baby Archie seems to have been just a bit too young—we can expect him to make his debut next year. Prince Louis was seen perfecting his royal wave from the safe arms of his mother, the Duchess of Cambridge. Although Markle joined the family this weekend, she is not officially back from maternity leave yet, so make the most of these pictures as we don’t know when we’ll see her next! column1: Meet 3 of Hedi Slimane's favourite artists
column2:
Fashion Celine’s new band of artists—Elaine Cameron-Weir, James Balmforth and Oscar Tuazon—talk to Vogue about their creative influences, and latest works commissioned by the French fashion house’s creative director Hedi Slimane When Hedi Slimane took the mantle at Celine last year he told Le Figaro that it meant starting “a new chapter” with the 74-year-old French fashion house. “We arrive then with our own stories, our own culture, a personal semantic that is different from the ones of houses in which we create,” he continued. “We have to be ourselves, without any stance, against all odds.” Now remember, Slimane is as much a photographer as a fashion designer. He has taken residency at the Kunst-Werke Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin and exhibits with Almine Rech gallery, who represent the likes of Richard Prince and Jeff Koons—two of the world’s most expensive living artists—as well as fashion’s favourite portrait painter Chloe Wise. It’s natural, then, that art would play a central role in his vision for Celine. In February, the brand announced that British artist James Balmforth had been commissioned to create an original artwork for the Celine’s Madison Avenue store, as part of a new architectural concept that will be implemented worldwide. Several more artist partnerships have been announced since, including Elaine Cameron-Weir and Oscar Tuazon for the Tokyo and Paris stores respectively. Vogue met the trio to learn more about their practice, their lives in and out of the studio and what motivates them. The 34-year-old Canadian sculptor grew up in rural Alberta before moving to the buzzing metropolis of New York to gain her MFA from NYU's prestigious Steinhardt School. Her work, which in part explores humans’ growing disassociation from the natural world, has been exhibited internationally, including two recent solo shows at the Dortmunder Kunstverein in Germany (2018) and New York’s New Museum (2017). Elaine Cameron-Weir © Isabel Asha Penzlien “When I was 19, after my first year studying drawing at the Alberta College of Art and Design, I rode a Greyhound bus for 72 hours to Northern Ontario where I had a forestry job for the summer planting trees. I slept in a tent and planted every day with a minimum quota of 2,000 trees per shift. You got paid per tree so it was like a weird tree Olympics—the more you planted the more money you made. At the end of the summer, I caught the train to New York on a whim. It was the first time I had been to the city and that was pretty much when I decided I wanted to live there.” Snake 8, 2017 © Elaine Cameron Weir as part of a solo exhibition titled 'viscera has
questions about itself' at the New Museum, New York “After I finished my undergraduate degree, I relocated to New York at the age of 23 to do my MFA in Studio Art at NYU. I hadn’t been to a city like New York before my first trip there, but I wasn’t overwhelmed, rather amazed by the high energy and fast pace of everything. Although I grew up in a small town, I was never interested in staying, it just felt more natural for me to be in a place where there's more going on, more people around, more diversity and opportunities to seek an audience for what I do.” “When I was asked to do this project, the space wasn’t yet complete, but I knew what size the piece needed to be (nine metres) and that it would be installed near a spiral staircase, so I wanted to make something that worked with that. Snake X is a continuation of a sculpture series I started in 2016 only bigger. It’s made from enamelled copper scales arranged over a chain-metal screen so that it resembles a snakeskin. I had been thinking a lot about the cyclical nature of things and how snakes are used to symbolise that, whether in Biblical allegories like Adam and Eve or the ouroboros in  various ancient iconographies, which show a serpent eating its own tail as a metaphor for eternal return. Snake X, 2019 © Celine “I find it interesting when humans refer to the natural world as though we as a species are separate from it or in some way outside of its jurisdiction. I consider these types of disassociation through sensory knowledge of material. And obviously all materials have their origins in natural resources, some of them have just gone through a series of processes designed by humans. I’m interested in how we define what is synthetic versus what is deemed natural, what is elemental or true versus what’s created.” Elaine Cameron-Weir has a solo show opening at New York’s JTT Gallery in September. Describing himself as a “frustrated engineer”, the 39-year-old, London-based artist uses daring industrial techniques to create his colossal sculptures—pushing materials like concrete and steel to the limit. A graduate of the esteemed Chelsea College of Arts, Balmforth’s work has been exhibited at the Royal Academy of Arts and Tate Britain, and he is represented by pioneering South London gallerist Hannah Barry. James Balmforth © Nick Seaton “I try not to take anything as a given. As a student at the Chelsea College of Arts I would reinterpret what my lecturers were saying; I think jumbling information leads to forming new wholes. It’s the same when it comes to books, cinema and music. At the moment I’m reading Intelligence and Spirit by Reza Negarestani and Mark Wilson’s Physics Avoidance—I always read several books at once so I can cross-pollinate the ideas explored in them. The film essays Sans Soleil (Chris Marker) and Dial H-I-S-T-O-R-Y (Johan Grimonprez) are among my favourites because they allow you to draw your own conclusions. In my studio I tend to listen to music without any lyrics as it’s less distracting—my song of the moment is Morphine by Boy Harsher. Collectively these stimuli contribute to developing ideas and exploring new processes.“ Boundary Interface, 2018 © James Balmforth “It's a challenge being an artist in a major city like London because the cost of living is very high, especially when you are a sculptor—you need space. At times I have considered moving to the countryside or elsewhere in England, but I need the creative energy of London and the connections that can be made here given its status as an art capital. I’m based in Peckham where I help do maintenance for a non-profit organisation in exchange for workspace, it’s good to have an arrangement that is mutually beneficial.” Cass thermic lancing process © Barney Hindle © Cass Sculpture Foundation “I’m something of a frustrated engineer—through my work I employ industrial techniques and mechanisms to expose materials to extreme conditions such as pressure and heat. One tool I’ve used a lot lately is a thermic lance. It’s like a torch and can burn concrete and steel at a temperature of 7,000 degrees, and is usually used for demolition work. It’s really quite terrifying and I have to wear protective leather clothes to use it and breathing apparatus because it can create metal vapours and you don’t want to be inhaling those. As you can imagine, you ideally need to use it in an open and unpopulated space—and it’s good to see the finished sculptures displayed in an open setting too. One such place is Contemporary Sculpture Fulmer in Buckinghamshire outside London where some of my work is currently on display. They’re set among beautiful private gardens originally laid in the late 19th century by Sir Harry Legge, a personal aide-de-camp to Queen Victoria—she used to plant trees there.” Surface Response (Stack), 2019 © Celine “Surface Response (Stack) is a continuation of a series I started in 2016. It’s an eight-and-a-half-feet-tall tower of four stainless steel cubes positioned on top of one another. One face of each cube has been worked on with a thermic lance—the chemical reaction that takes place is essentially hyper accelerated rusting, an oxidation of the iron within the steel. The resulting material is darkened and has a bubbly texture like dried lava. This residue is known as slag and considered waste product in industry. I like the idea of giving it purpose and value.” James Balmforth’s work is on permanent display at Contemporary Sculpture Fulmer. Out of his Los Angeles studio—itself part of a work of art entitled Zome Alloy (2015), a nod to Steve Baer’s Zome House—the 43-year-old Seattle native investigates the relationship between art, architecture and environmental sustainability using wood, concrete, glass and steel to create installations that encourage a sense of community. Currently the subject of three major solo exhibitions at the Aspen Art Museum, Michigan State University and Bellevue Arts Museum near Seattle, Tuazon has also shown at the Venice Biennale and major fairs such as Art Basel and Frieze. Oscar Tuazon © Nuage Lepage “Hedi and I met in 2011 when he invited me to be part of his exhibition Fragments Americana at the Almine Rech Gallery in Brussels. We were living parallel lives between LA and Paris and were aware of one another’s work. He was exhibiting an anthology of his photography and I contributed three sculptures. We spent the best part of a week installing the show, working together and thinking together and have stayed in touch ever since.” Oscar Tuazon-Mobile Floor, 2019 © Celine “Fashion and artist collaborations can be fraught with danger because of the power imbalance, with the brand dictating what the artist can and can’t do. What excites me most about this project is that Hedi gave me carte blanche. Travel has informed the work I’ve been producing lately with shipping containers and other transportation infrastructures. Mobile Floor is a site-specific installation for Celine made from steel, fir and oak wood, concrete, aluminium and paint in the form of a shipping container floor. When you come to a shop you are there to touch and experience the clothes, so I wanted to create something that invites physical engagement.” Oscar Tuazon © Nuage Lepage “In 2016 I went to the Dakota Access Pipeline protests at the Standing Rock Indian Reservation and this sparked my interest in water systems. I’m currently showing one of my Water School projects at the Eli and Edythe Broad Art Museum, Michigan State University. The installation, a large glass façade filled with water, is inspired by the engineer and inventor Steve Baer, who created the Zome Home (1972), one of the earliest examples of passive solar architecture. During the day, the building collects and stores the sun’s energy in drums of water installed in large, bay windows, which then provide heat during the night.” Oscar Tuazon: Water School © Oscar Tuazon; Courtesy of the artist, Luhring Augustine, New York, Galerie Chantal Crousel, Paris, and Eva Presenhuber, Zürich, New York “I think making connections between creativity and the natural world is really important—architecture and design have the power to help alleviate the pressure we are putting on the environment. My Water School project comprises a series of public talks and arts programming to address water, land rights and other socio-environmental issues. Typically artists work in isolation but it’s been really exciting to work with people and create a sense of community and expand beyond the conventional art space. My current solo show, Collaborator at the Bellevue Arts Museum near Seattle, features work made in collaboration with at least 15 people. Among them is the architect Antoine Rocca who worked with me on two concrete fire pits—the second is on display at my other solo show at the Aspen Art Museum right now. The idea is to bring people together around the warmth of the fire.” How Hedi Slimane’s Celine has immortalised Phoebe Philo Hedi Slimane: “It’s important to have a clear and distinct voice” Hedi Slimane named artistic, creative and image director of Céline Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This pop-up is bringing Sri Lanka’s emerging fashion scene to Mumbai
column2: Fashion A collaboration between two concept stores, Annika Fernando’s PR Sri Lanka and Samyukta Nair’s Clove, has eight young Sri Lankan designers coming down to the city. Here’s everything you need to know about it In her quest for curating a wardrobe that reflects her global mindset, the modern Indian connoisseur is often on the lookout for inimitable fashion labels beyond local shores. Annika Fernando’s store, PR Sri Lanka, is one such go-to for this style set on their visits to Colombo. And now, Fernando is bringing a slice of the island nation’s design aesthetic to Mumbai with a month-long collaborative edit at Samyukta Nair’s concept store, Clove. It was Fernando and Nair’s common endeavour to promote design, fashion and culture through their respective ventures that served as the foundation for their friendship. And considering the recent attacks, their latest collaboration comes at a sensitive time too. “We have a similar vision that focuses on supporting emerging talent in our countries. This edit, in particular, aims at promoting fresh talent of a country in time of suffering, and supporting its culture and people. The designs are quintessentially Sri Lankan, but seamlessly extend to the Indian market as well,” explains Nair. ‘Heart of Sri Lanka’ will feature everyday staples, easy separates and jewellery by eight young Sri Lankan designers, many of which enjoy prominence in Fernando’s own wardrobe. “I represent so many labels. Their signature pieces are now my go-to staples. I live in MAUS’ organic comfort wear. My other must-haves include Sonali Dharmawardena statement skirts, KT Brown pants and dresses, Anuk kimonos, and KÛR summer dresses,” says the aesthete. “I mostly wear Sri Lankan and Indian designers. It feels relevant,” she adds, before naming Rajesh Pratap Singh, Bodice, Olivia Dar, Aish, D’Ascoli and Verandah as her favourite Indian labels. Dress, Kûr Dress, Anuk Fernando’s store has provided a platform to several under-the-radar brands from her home country. And over the years, she realised that these designs appealed to PR Sri Lanka’s Indian patrons too. “I like designers who are authentic and have a strong identity. I already know that Sri Lanka’s pared-down island style appeals to Indians, so we curated a well-thought-out selection to complement the unique aesthetic of Clove as well as the weather in Mumbai.” Scroll ahead for some of the designers featured at the pop-up. column1: Big Little Lies season 2: The clues in the costumes to look out for
column2: © HBO Fashion As the hit HBO show returns for its much-anticipated second season, Emmy-winning costume designer Alix Friedberg gives Vogue a preview of the biggest style moments and the clues to look out for Alix Friedberg is no stranger to murder mysteries. The costume designer behind HBO hits True Detective and Sharp Objects, won an Emmy in 2017 for her work on the first season of Big Little Lies. The TV adaptation of Liane Moriarty’s bestselling novel became a global phenomenon—winning four Golden Globes, turning the Californian coastal town of Monterey into a holiday hotspot and sparking serious real estate envy. It also spawned countless articles about Big Little Lies style tribes, a testament to Friedberg’s impeccable work when dressing the show’s five leads: preppy perfectionist Madeline (Reese Witherspoon), elegant Celeste (Nicole Kidman), high-powered CEO Renata (Laura Dern), boho Bonnie (Zoë Kravitz) and casual Jane (Shailene Woodley). But when returning for the second season, how could she improve upon perfection? For Friedberg, the answer was simple: if season one was about establishing the characters and their distinctive looks, season two is about watching them unravel. “We’ve already nailed down each woman’s silhouette and colour palette,” she tells Vogue, “but this season, a lot has changed. Some characters aren’t coping well with what happened and others are rising above it. We tried to reflect their emotional journeys through their costumes.” This plays out most noticeably with Celeste, the former lawyer and mother-of-two who is still reckoning with the death of her abusive husband, Perry. The Monterey Five © HBO “Celeste’s look has always been about luxurious fabrics and classic design,” says Friedberg, of her season one neutral separates by Chloé, Max Mara and The Row, carefully hiding her bruises beneath turtleneck sweaters and cosy scarves. Now, free from the trauma of her marriage, she feels conflicted and guilty. The first episode of season two, titled What Have They Done?, marks a departure from Celeste’s polished aesthetic. “She’s grappling with grief,” explains the designer. “She’s not as effortless as she looked in season one and her survival mechanism has kicked in.” While high-end outerwear remains a crucial part of her wardrobe, season two also sees Celeste donning T-shirts and soft knits. “You can sometimes see her wearing Perry’s old T-shirts and sweatshirts—things she can still smell him on—and that’s another expression of her grief,” adds Friedberg. © HBO Also struggling to deal with Perry’s death is Bonnie, the free-spirited yoga instructor, who feels wholly responsible for the incident. Incorporating flowy kaftans, slinky workout gear, turquoise jewellery and barely-there slip dresses, Bonnie’s wardrobe was one of the sartorial highlights of season one. “Her vibe is bohemian, printed and light,” says Friedberg, referencing brands like Anthropologie and Free People. “But she’s really darkened this season and taken on the burden of Perry’s passing.” In place of her usual loosely draped robes and vintage maxi dresses, Bonnie’s look becomes more protective as she hides herself in argyle jumpers and figure-swamping blazers. © HBO © HBO The opposite is true for Jane. “In the earliest episodes, she was feeling self-conscious about her body, wore deliberately shapeless clothes and just wanted to be invisible,” explains the designer. “This season, she’s got the light back in her eyes. She has a new job at the Monterey Bay Aquarium, she’s moved closer to the ocean and she’s adopted this vintage, Californian, surfer vibe. It’s still a lot of recycled, sustainable and vintage clothes, but you see more of her skin and her shape. There’s a newfound sense of confidence.” © HBO Two characters certainly not lacking in confidence are Madeline and Renata. In season two, both deal with personal crises by amplifying their style. Stay-at-home mother Madeline has a new job as a real estate agent and is hiding the true cause of Perry’s death as well as an affair with her community theatre director Joseph. “She loves bold colours, prints and feminine silhouettes,” says Friedberg. “That perfectly put together Madeline look is a mask for what’s happening in her personal life. Her marriage is crumbling and her daughter is making poor choices.” The designer relied on many of the same brands she gravitated to in season one—Dolce & Gabbana, Red Valentino, Zara—and added accents including a Prada bag in a signature shade of sugary pink. “Madeline mixes high and low end,” she adds. “It doesn’t need to be at Renata’s level of fashion.” © HBO The latter’s wardrobe is easily the most glamorous of the group, comprised of Stella McCartney jumpsuits and Azzedine Alaïa dresses. “I’ve definitely cranked it up with Renata,” says Friedberg, referring to the season two scene where the CEO wears a floor-length gown for a photoshoot in her own home. “She’s always been structured and rigid, but now she’s even more over the top. She relies on her clothes to make her feel more powerful.” This intensifies later in the season when that power comes under threat. “She’s worked so hard to be as wealthy as she is,” adds the designer. “So, when she’s in trouble, Renata clings desperately to her possessions. She’s strong and stoic but later on, there’s a sense of desperation in the way that she’s dressing.” Meryl Streep © HBO While costuming the Monterey Five is second nature to Friedberg, season two presented a unique challenge: dressing new addition Meryl Streep in the role of Mary Louise, Perry’s mother who arrives in Monterey to solve the mystery of his death. “It’s been one of the highlights of my career,” says the designer of working with Streep. “When it came to dressing Mary Louise, the thought process was that she’s dealing with her own grief and it manifests in her clothing. She has a uniform and it’s very prim, very tailored, very expensive—soft Belgian loafers, shirts made in France, an Hermès scarf. They’re beautiful pieces, but quite colourless because she doesn’t want to draw attention to herself. And that beige coat she wears? It’s almost detective-like.” © HBO © HBO Mary Louise is on the hunt for clues about the night that Perry died—the night of Otter Bay’s Elvis and Audrey-themed fundraiser which garnered the show’s most memorable costumes to date. Is there anything new that could rival those ensembles in season two? “There’s an episode where Renata throws a disco-themed party,” says Friedberg, alluding to a scene that briefly appears in the trailer. “She and her daughter have matching costumes and they look amazing—it’s so Renata and so much fun. That’s my favourite and definitely one to look forward to.” An Indian actor may join the Big Little Lies cast for its second season What to stream on Netflix, Prime Video, and Hotstar in June What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Then and now: Karan Johar’s complete style evolution
column2: © Picasa Fashion From all-black basics in 2011 to championing fashion’s favourite designers in 2019, Karan Johar’s sartorial sensibilities have gone through a 180 degree shift. Here's how his wardrobe has transformed over the years Karan Johar first made his directorial debut back in 1998 with Kuch Kuch Hota Hai—a widely successful venture that propelled him head-on into India’s film industry. Then came Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham... (2001), Kal Ho Naa Ho (2003), and Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna (2006), that, among other works, cemented his status as a director who knows how to to deliver a box office hit. Being a Bollywood insider (he is late film producer Yash Johar’s son, and iconic director/producer Yash Chopra’s nephew) had its benefits too—Johar went on to kickstart his very own talk show Koffee with Karan in 2004, which concluded its sixth season this year. He also has a radio show called Calling Karan, and outside the entertainment industry, a fine jewellery brand called Tyaani, which he launched in 2017. Johar confesses that he has always had a love-hate relationship with his clothes. “My sartorial choices have almost always been dependent on my waistline—which has fluctuated more than the weather in England,” he says in Vogue India’s June 2019 issue. “I was large for a very large section of my life, and my body didn’t support my sartorial ambitions. I would wear ill-fitted black suits so I could camouflage under the layers.” Johar’s red carpet appearances between 2011 and 2017 serve as proof—he mostly opted for all-black tuxedos back then. Fast forward to today, and the director and producer has transitioned into a self-proclaimed maximalist. From bold prints—floral, leopard and even the runway-approved tie-dye—to statement accessories (think metallic platform sneakers, bejewelled loafers, shiny brogues, oversized glasses and a lust-worthy collection of bags), Johar’s given every trend a try. “With age and maturity came a sense of abandon that has allowed me to live without any fear of repercussions—even when my mother tells me my distressed Balenciaga jacket looks like someone snipped it with scissors while I was asleep or when my two-year-olds eye my look with judgement,” he says. In Johar's own words, “My style today settles somewhere between Ranveer Singh’s flamboyance and Saif Ali Khan’s subtlety.” Take a look at Karan Johar’s maximalist approach to fashion—with several moments of nonchalance, of course—here. column1: 15 pictures that will take you inside Diljit Dosanjh’s wardrobe
column2: © Marcin Tyszka Fashion From neon Balenciaga track jackets to limited-edition Dapper Dan pieces, here’s decoding Diljit Dosanjh’s inimitable style The only thing that rivals Diljit Dosanjh’s love for a certain blonde by the name of Kylie Jenner, is his love for labels. In the three years since he made his debut in Bollywood with Udta Punjab, the singer-turned-actor’s signature style has become daring and is no small way fuelled by his love for all things Gucci. From fresh-off-the-runway looks to the latest Yeezy drops, his maximalist manifesto has him setting his sights beyond the conventional. “Yeh India mein woh cheezein bhejengey jo do mahine pehle khatam ho chuki hai… I love London. I simply take a mahak of how interestingly the clothes have been styled by people in fashion and do my own thing. Main same nahi karta; woh copy-paste ho jata hai,” he told Vogue. Today, his has earned him the attention of other fashion icons on the scene as well. In a recent episode of No Filter Neha 3, Karan Johar commiserated, “I think we’re both crazy shoppers and we invariably land up wearing the same clothes because we love the same brands. I’m also an online shopper, so I go through this process of buying these things and wearing them on an occasion. But Diljit buys and wears it immediately and puts up an image. So, we had this faux fur jacket and I was saving it for my big photo opportunity time when I was travelling to Europe, and suddenly the night before I take that flight, I see the image uploaded by Diljit. I called Nikita, my stylist, and I’m like, ‘I’m shattered, I’m broken and I’m totally like, Channa Mereya right now because I wanted to wear this jacket.’ I was so upset, it broke my heart.” As he graces the cover of Vogue June in head-to-toe Gucci alongside the leading forces of fashion, here’s taking a closer look at his more-is-more aesthetic. Loud-and-proud neon hues jostle for space with oversized silhouettes in his wardrobe, and his flair for drama isn’t just restricted to the stage—a casual event during the day could call for anything from a printed Hawaiian shirt from Balenciaga to a hooded bomber jacket from the cult-favourite label, Vetements. Usually a fan of standout hues, on those days when he’s looking to indulge his quieter side, he takes his whites with embroidered Bart Simpson motifs from Off-White. A self-professed fan of Virgil Abloh’s unconventional approach to street style, his discerning eye has also found a winner in the indie design collective, Ader Error, that is touted as South Korea’s answer to Vetements. The star-studded lineup in his wardrobe is rivalled by his sneaker collection, featuring iconic names such as Gucci x Dapper Dan and multiple Air Jordans. Undaunted by the spectre of public opinion, he took the ugly sneakers trend for a spin by picking up a chunky pair of Balenciaga Triple S kicks. When he’s looking to make heads turn, he calls upon statement high tops from Maison Margiela to cement his status as a street style icon. When in front of the spotlight, Dosanjh’s take-no-prisoners style has him opting for maximalist silhouettes in a palette of traffic-stopping hues. The singer notably took to the stage in a colour-blocked Balenciaga track jacket, while his chevron Gucci jacket remains another favourite with fans. The crowning glory in his wardrobe, however, is reserved for the Gucci-Dapper Dan Hercules necklace, embossed with a sculpted mask and polished to a vintage gold finish. Further notes on the versatility of the statement piece can be found on his Instagram, where he accessorised it with first, a Versace silk pyjama suit and later, a suede sweatshirt from the Harlem designer’s limited-edition collection. column1: Scouting for India 2019—Vogue Talents x FAD is back in Mumbai
column2: © JDS STUDIO 19 Fashion The winner will be given the opportunity to showcase their collection at the Vogue Talents event hosted during Milan Fashion Week in September 2019 After a successful debut last year, Vogue Talents  and FAD International Academy is back with its second edition of Scouting For India 2019. Aimed at talented Indian designers, the global project scouts for emerging names who can be the next big thing in fashion. Last year’s edition was won by Shyma Shetty and Pranav Mishra of Huemn, who then showcased their spring/summer 2019 collection at Milan Fashion Week. This year, the selected designers will be presenting their work to a jury that includes some of the most talented people in the fashion industry—Vogue India’s fashion director, Anaita Shroff Adajania; Vogue Italia’s deputy editor in chief, Sara Sozzani Maino; Mickey Boardman, editor of Paper Magazine; designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee; sustainability activist, Bandana Tewari and Shivang Dhruva, founder and director of FAD International Academy. "I do a lot of scouting throughout the year and I see many designers from different nationalities. I think to consider a brand promising right now when the market is full, it's very important to have their own vision. New designers should have a message and basically, be able to communicate it to the market. I also think it's very important to consider sustainability for emerging designers, who start their own brand. They need to think about a sustainable and responsible way of creating fashion," said Sara Sozzani Maino, Vogue Italia’s deputy editor in chief. "I think the strength of Indian designers is their deep link to tradition in their background. It is very interesting to see the evolution of the designers we have selected in these past two years. Although their strength lies in their tradition, they have adapted to the international market and trends by travelling or by being curious. The designers can see how the market is changing and just form it in a modern way. The strength of these emerging countries lies in their use of traditions in a modern way while designing clothes," said Sozzani Maino. Stressing on the importance of communication for a young brand, the editor added, "I feel that the lack of Indian designers in the global market right now is because most of them are based out of India and hence do not get a lot of visibility in the international scene. This is why we decided to do this event with FAD International Academy.  So when designers ask me what I can do to be seen more, I tell them that where you live no longer matters, if you are true talents, you can be seen, no matter what. It’s a matter of how you communicate, so I always suggest that they invest time and obviously a little money into the communication." The event, to be held at Mumbai’s Soho House, will see a list of participating designers that includes Kanelle by Kanika Jain, Kanika Goyal by Kanika, Rara Avis by Sonal Verma, Two Point Two by Anvita, Helena Bajaj Larsen by Helena, The Pot Plant by Resham Karmchandani, Ode To Odd by Shreya & Priyal and Chola by Sohaya. column1: Sobhita Dhulipala talks about her success on the internet and the road ahead
column2: © The House Of Pixels Fashion From indulging in introspection of Shakespeare’s Hamlet to gardening for digital detox, the actor takes us through her life journey, on and off-camera It’s a good time to be alive—the internet happened, and digital streaming took over the real world with binge-worthy content across a plethora of web platforms. As a result of this new ecosystem, great talent has come into spotlight—one in particular is the 27-year-old Sobhita Dhulipala. 2019 has been a good year for the actor who played the lead in Amazon Prime Original Made in Heaven. Created by Zoya Akhtar and Reema Kagti, the web-series had Dhulipala play Tara Khanna, a wedding planner who marries rich and moves through the complexities presented in her life. Her nuanced portrayal of a layered character that is flawed, yet vulnerable (and relatable in some ways) is what got her the recognition she rightfully deserves. With movies like Raman Raghav 2.0 (her debut film in 2016), Chef, Kaalakaandi and most recently a Telugu spy thriller (Goodachari) under her belt, Dhulipala’s career graph represents a striking evolution that has taken place in a short period of time. While she took the pageant route, unbeknownst of the outcome (and winning Miss India title in 2013), it wasn’t until her first audition that she realised where her true strengths lie. Perhaps the reason why she makes a fitting addition to the newly acclaimed treasure chest of actors is because she chooses to present herself as a blank canvas, ready to immerse herself in the now—an attribute that could be credited to her upbringing in Vishakhapatnam, completely detached from films. While most actors grow up consuming films for meals, Dhulipala’s childhood was more about the written word and less about cinema. A quick scroll through her Instagram handle will tell you that she has appeared in numerous editorials in the last few months, partakes in frequently mirror selfies, and is open about her personal life, sharing photos of her boyfriend, Pranav Misra—one-half of the fashion label Huemn. She is self-aware and intelligent—coupled with a great jawline, Dhulipala has the makings of a disruptor, irrespective of the content medium she opts for. A few days after ringing in her 27th birthday in her hometown, the actor gets in conversation with Vogue, excerpts below: When I signed on Made in Heaven in May/June 2017, the digital medium wasn’t what it is today. It was the start of something potent and I feel uninhibited in attempting new things. The fact that Made in Heaven was being made by people of such distinct merit naturally made it easy for me to hop on-board. Besides, an actor emotes, irrespective of the medium. I auditioned for it not knowing too many details, I got called back for a look test a month and a half later where I met Zoya and Nitya [Mehra]. Their keenness towards me, coupled with the simple fact that every person involved was of such great merit catalysed the process of decision making. I may have drawn from a lifetime of being very sensitive and stubbornly following instincts and impulses. I’m not as unapologetic as Tara but we do share a great, common friend—fortitude. Playing complex characters has made me even more empathetic. To have a protagonist who is flawed and displays strength despite crises breaks so many stereotypes. The burden of being perfect for others is replaced with a drive to make the most of opportunities—something that is as possible as positive. It is immensely character building. Anurag Kashyap has a very strong sense of self both as an individual and as an artist. I’m fortunate to have been influenced by brave people. As an actor, there isn’t much of a difference really. Newness and creativity often go hand-in-hand. I’m fascinated to see how our developing country will be shaped by this new wave of information generation and entertainment. I took the pageant path without knowing where I wanted to go next. All experiences and the lack of them, make us who we are. Acting has deepened my sensitivity. I feel comparatively freer from the need to please or belong and I understand better. I subscribe to experimenting, to taking chances. [Post Made in Heaven] all welcomes have become much warmer and I’m very grateful for the kindness. But I’m not easily rocked by highs or lows, I think. I am in a place where I’m able to have a balanced conversation, like equals across the table. It’s essential and encouraging. I am grateful for this life and am very moved by little joys. I have been financially independent since the age of 20. I learnt things through trial and error, I’m an accountable person and am not easily carried away in these matters, my disciplined roots keep me grounded perhaps. Everyone must be emotionally, physically and financially self-sufficient since during or after college I believe. Irrespective of gender. It’s indispensable. How can one be woke when they’re lazy? “I have a developed a passion for painting and gardening of late. The internet is an abyss, I’m wary about obsessing with it. I indulge in a lot of reading, occasional writing and travelling to the countryside or quiet beaches whenever I can.” “Get yourself the right heroes. Read. And at some point in your journey, make sense of Hamlet’s soliloquy (to be, or not to be).” “Gucci, The Row, Huemn, Raw mango and vintage YSL are some of my favourites.” “Sitara, produced by Ronnie Screwvala, Bard of blood by Red Chillies for Netflix, The Body by Viacom, Azure with Emraan Hashmi and Rishi Kapoor; Moothon by Geetu Mohandas with Nivin Pauly—these are up for release. And three new projects that I can’t yet speak of but am very excited about!” Serial wedding-hoppers, Prime Video’s Made In Heaven is just for you Sobhita Dhulipala’s latest hairstyle is ideal for summer nights out Decoding Made in Heaven’s wedding-ready costumes What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Lust list: 9 most promising wedding bands for every bride-to-be
column2: Fashion From classic bands to engraved ones, Vogue curates an envy-inducing list of wedding bands every bride-to-be needs to check out Getting married this summer but not sure how to find the perfect wedding band? column1: Gaurav Gupta on being bullied for his sexuality, and how fashion gave him a voice
column2: © Shutterstock Fashion To mark Pride Month, Vogue spoke to Gaurav Gupta about his experience of growing up gay in India in the early ’90s, the challenges he faced in choosing a career he loved, and how his struggles shape his work today I still remember the first time I draped a sari on a mannequin back in college, it was like unfolding a different chapter. But my love for fashion actually evolved from an organic love for art. Art was an outlet for me; I had taken up sculpture in the eighth and ninth grade. I was in awe of the art of making sculptures, and I still am. My love for design has witnessed its fair share of trials, like confronting my parents about my passion, and saying no to their aspirations for me. One of my most memorable report cards was in sixth grade, when I actually flunked with a C in Maths and Science, but got an A+ in Art. For the most part though, I was a straight-A student—securing 90 percentile in 12th grade—and like many other Indian parents, mine expected me to follow a business-centric academic path to eventually join the expanding iron and steel family business. I remember my dad telling me when I was filling out the forms for the NIFT entrance exam that if I were to not get through it, I would have to tread on the path chosen for me by them. Honestly, all I ever wanted to do was act on the voice inside of me—a fledgling, curious need to explore and express. In all of this, I was also dealing with the aggression that came with growing up a homosexual boy in the ’90s. I’m okay talking about my sexuality openly now, but when I was younger, people didn’t even know what being gay was. People would say things like “he’s ‘a’ gay”. In mainstream movies, the gay character was often silly and teased—that was the stereotype. I was really bullied in school; I went through torture, but that is a part of my strength today. I think my family didn’t even realise that I was gay till later. I was out to my brothers, but I came out to my parents after being in London. In between, I'd keep telling them that there are all kinds of people; that when they come to London, I would show them the gay bars or sex shops around. After being at Central Saint Martins and just generally living in London, seeing so many different kinds of people and having a whole life where being gay is normal, I became comfortable with it. When I came back [to India], I decided that there were no two ways about it—that this is how I look and this is who I am, and if somebody wanted me to talk about it, I would definitely respond. Whenever there were LGBTQIA+ marches, I was there. Now that I look around me, I would say things have eased down a bit, especially after the verdict on the decriminalisation of Section 377 last year. I remember tears rolling down my eyes when I heard about it. It was a relief knowing that people can now express and love however and whomever they want to without having any fear of criminal repercussions at the back of their minds; it was a very surreal moment. So many more boys and girls in the world would suffer less, and why should they suffer? Why should they be teased for who they are? While the law now protects the community, the cultural shift has a long way to go, but at least there’s an awareness about being gay. It’s very important to have a Karan Johar (who is helping normalise homosexuality in popular culture) or a Keshav Suri (who fought tirelessly for the 377 verdict), and a lot of people who are in fashion and are confident, successful, and open. We have many more milestones to cross, but for now, we will savour and cherish the fact that we have emerged victorious. As fate would have it, my love for fashion was so unflinching that it ended up drowning the hushed tones of shame and disbelief from my relatives. Not only did I go on to receive awards and accolades for my work and talent, I was at ease with my honest self in that creative universe, around like-minded peers. This, ultimately, made my parents believe in what I always had my heart set on, and what I was capable of. And the rest is history. column1: Vogue meets Chloé’s Natacha Ramsay-Levi to talk Resort 2020 in Shanghai
column2: © Hui Li at Art+Yard / M+A Group Fashion The creative director on why China’s cultural metropolis is the perfect setting for Chloé’s first runway show outside of France Chloé’s creative director Natacha Ramsay-Levi is sitting behind an improvised desk in a cavernous industrial room in Shanghai’s waterside Long Museum. On the concrete bund below, freight ships pass by a handful of skateboarders practising tricks in the shadow of the ruins of the city’s coal stores, out of the midday sun. The space, like Ramsay-Levi herself, is calm. It has been her centre of operations since Saturday, when she arrived from Paris ahead of the brand’s Resort 2020 show on 5 June. The occasion marks the first time the house has staged a runway show outside of France and Chloé’s arrival on the global pre-collection circuit. If the pressure is on, it doesn’t show. Neither the impending collection reveal, or the relentless 31-degree heat are altering the designer’s characteristically unphased demeanour. There’s no thrum of mood-rousing music from the temporary backstage dressing area, no trace of late night coffee orders, or iPhone din. She isn’t jet-lagged—gently shrugging off the notion with a smile, “I’m pretty easy with that”—and like the local Shanghainese, her covered-up dress code—black kick-flares, a soft-line navy blazer and silk shirt—is notably intact. As is her signature kohl-rimmed eye makeup. Natacha Ramsay-Levi © Hui Li at Art+Yard / M+A Group At 39 years old, Natacha Ramsay-Levi oversees 82 Chloé boutiques worldwide and four collections annually. The house has evolved in the two years since she joined from Louis Vuitton (where she was Nicolas Ghesquière’s creative director of womenswear), adopting a harder edged bohemianism, with an awareness that the Chloé girl is “not always the blonde. Let’s move out from there,” she says. There’s also a new sense of robust practicality to match the house’s peripatetic spirit. Motherhood and work are concurrent modes, which the designer shifts between—something she credits for “giving balance” in her life. “I talk a lot with my studio team about how you feel in the clothes and maternity gives you much more awareness in that sense—even something as simple as ‘Do I have enough pockets?’” she jokes.   Her own approach at Chloé has also evolved. “In the beginning, I had a vision of Chloé that was very broad, but I think now people want something very precise from Chloé—the flou.” In explanation, she steps towards a large board displaying the running order of the final show looks. “Here, I have tried to do something new for me. You still have the very boyish attitude and tailoring, but I think there is much more delicate femininity in this collection.” The pieces themselves are rich in nuanced references to Chinese culture, from the opening look—a quilted jacket that pays homage to the padded motorcycle covers Shanghainese women use during winter—to silk pyjama silhouettes. The collection also sees the return of two Art Deco Chloé logos, resurrected from the house archive, that nod to the city’s skyline: one was discovered on a 1970s suitcase and the other created by Stella McCartney for the invitation to her debut Chloé show. Today, it’s rendered in jacquard on a pair of tailored trousers. “I’ve had my eye on it for a while, but it never felt quite right to bring back, until now,” Ramsay-Levi says, her Parisian accent strong. The unexpected entry? Acid brights. “Voila! You know, last winter I did a collection that was all about blue, white and red, very simple. For this show, I wanted fun colours.” The C bag likewise appears in juicier new shades, championing the energy of China’s modern street style heroes, whose “super gothic style” and signature chokers offer a fresh, inspirational kind of “toughness”. “Coming to Shanghai, I found a very modern city, but still you have all the layers from history—the Belle Epoque, Art Deco, and Communist era. The collection reflects this,” explains Ramsay-Levi. Formerly a history student, the designer has a long-time obsession with Chinese cinema (specifically, the work of director Jia Zhangke)—as she talks animatedly, a 12 ft moodboard of Chinese film references on the opposite wall sets a fitting backdrop. It’s this interest that has informed the research visits to Shanghai’s fabric markets and outlying villages, which play an integral role in her designs, both past and present, and prompted her decision to show in Shanghai. In January, she returned to Shanghai once again, to “listen to the mood”. She spent time observing the full scale of the city, from the super-chic to the everyday, ultimately deciding to show at the Long Museum because “the river is always present in Jia Zhangke’s films”. The art house references are something Ramsay-Levi has a skill for shaping into work that’s resolutely democratic with pop culture momentum, as her predecessors at Chloé did too. “You don’t need to know a lot about fashion to understand a Chloé show,” she says, extending another enormous smile as we walk back across the gallery to the outdoor terraces, where a production crew are busy installing the runway. The light streams through the Art Deco logos that decorate the floor-to-ceiling windows, casting soft-focus ‘C’ shadows. “Gaby [Aghion] was an intellectual, but she was super edgy,” she says of the industrious Chloé founder. “With Karl [Lagerfeld], the house was very outrageous—super sexy and very funny. The thing with Chloé is that it’s always about something that’s very positive.” Meet the Indian artist behind Chloé’s folklore-inspired collection Rithika Merchant’s work explores the commonality between cultures Re-booting Chloé for the woman of 2018 Weddings Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Alia Bhatt’s guide to wearing kurtas for all occasions
column2: © Viral Bhayani Fashion From wedding-ready sets by Sabyasachi to cotton versions that can be worn on the daily, Alia Bhatt’s wardrobe has a versatile collection of kurtas. Here's a look at how she makes the staple work for every occasion Alia Bhatt’s sartorial choices are just as versatile as her movie roles. One look through Bhatt’s wardrobe, and you'll agree that one of her favourite silhouettes is the humble kurta. Whether she's promoting a film (her most recent include Kalank and Raazi), heading out for a movie date, or simply going to the salon, the actor loves wearing the Indian staple, and seems to have collected a wide range of styles, cuts and colours over the years. Bhatt is often seen in designer kurtas, and some labels she keeps coming back to include Sabyasachi Mukherjee, Anita Dongre and Manish Malhotra. Need some inspiration before you stock your own closet with some kurtas? Scroll down to take a closer look at Alia Bhatt's collection. A few weeks back, Bhatt joined Varun Dhawan at Kalank promotions in a black kurta and sharara set by Anita Dongre, which wouldn't look out of place at your BFF's engagement party. column1: Kylie Jenner’s favourite micro bags are worth their impracticality
column2: © Backgrid Fashion From Jenner to Bella Hadid, Lilian Afshar seems to have become the preferred accessory designer for a wide roster of It-girls Despite all protests about impracticality, celebrities and style enthusiasts remain hooked on purses that barely fit a lipstick. No one has embraced the style quite like Kylie Jenner. An accessories addict with a closet full of Hermès at her disposal, Jenner and stylist, Jill Jacobs prefer the teensiest versions they can get their hands on. Case in point: when heading out to dinner yesterday in Los Angeles, Jenner paired her slinky blue minidress with a Lucite clutch from Dubai-based brand L’Afshar. Crystal clear and no bigger than an iPhone, it added a touch of sparkle to Jenner’s evening out look. British-born Iranian designer Lilian Afshar’s accessories have become a staple within Jenner’s wardrobe, but due to their diminutive size, you may have missed them. The petite clutches in marble, lucite, or croc-embossed leather don’t distract from the reality star’s runway pieces; instead, they blend seamlessly with whatever she chooses to wear. Back in April when she headed out for date night with partner Travis Scott, the boxy white Ida bag paired perfectly with her cream maxi-dress. On New Year’s Eve, she chose a transparent pagoda purse. On Instagram, where Jenner is apt to upload multiple outfits per day, the bags pop up regularly in selfies, Stories, and even snapshots with her famous siblings. Jenner isn’t the only celebrity who has been drawn in. During Paris Fashion Week, Bella Hadid paired the label’s clear Grace clutch with layers of logo-print Fendi, while Emily Ratajkowski carried a black version of the Ida to the Met Gala after-parties earlier this month. column1: 6 sustainable Indian active wear labels you need to know about
column2: © Instagram.com/satvaliving Fashion This World Environment Day, turn to eco-friendly athletic gear by Indian brands to do your bit for the planet you call home With delayed monsoon predictions, it appears we’ll need to hold on to the rain excuse to not work out a little longer this year. Whether you choose to fly with Anshuka’s aerial yoga or sweat it out at the SOHFIT bootcamp, your workout attire can make the experience a whole lot more cool and comfortable. As sustainability slowly becomes a part of mainstream fashion conversations, the athletic industry is also catching up. Certified organic cotton is making waves for its ability to let your skin breathe, and recycled plastic bottles are being converted to yarn to make polyester and weather-resistant fabrics. A slew of indie labels producing eco-friendly active wear in India have cropped up in recent years. From human working conditions and conscious fabrics to eco-friendly production practices, these clothing start-ups are gentle on people as well as the planet. Scroll ahead for a detailed low-down. One of the biggest players in the sustainable active wear category, Satva got first got famous for its sturdy and comfortable organic cotton leggings. The brand partners with Suminter India Organics®, an environmental and socially conscious organic cotton production corporation in India for its raw materials, and together the two companies also educate and support development of rural farming communities in India. The cotton cultivation is done with organic, non-GMO, non-treated seeds, and no chemicals (including harmful dyes) are used for producing of their apparel. The cherry on top is that the clothing does not compromise on style either—their latest colour block collection stands as proof. Satvaliving.com Nirali Mehta and Jeenie Madan are childhood friends who were looking for a change in their careers. The girls took a design course together and decided to venture into a sustainable athletic wear start-up. They source their textiles from Chetna Organic, a factory that adheres to fair trade practices, and use eco-friendly dyes to make durable and allergy-free clothing for men and women. Their geometric collection is subtle yet stylish, and is definitely worth checking out. Make sure to add a headband to your order upon checkout, as all profits from headgear go towards helping farmers’ families. Stretchery.in Founded by Milind Soman and Darshan M, this active wear label specifically caters to Indian sensibilities and body types. Accordingly, their product range includes performance kurtis, harem pants, copper water bottles, yoga mats and incense. All their production happens in fair trade facilities using raw materials like organic cotton, banana fibre, wild grass, coconuts, recycled polyester etc. Deivee’s philosophy is to make the world a healthier and happier place using yoga and active living. So they also have a program where their NGO partner, Grow Trees, plants a tree in Chantamani, Karnataka, for every purchased Deivee Tree T-shirt. Deivee.com Soul Space’s line of apparel are fair trade and GOTS (Global Organic Textile Standard) certified, which is the leading textile processing standard for organic fibres. The cotton they use is grown with less water and energy, and also maintains soil fertility. There’s a wide range of tops, jackets, shorts, bras, vests, underwear for both men and women, but their funky printed leggings deserve a special mention—they will definitely make you stand out in your exercise studio. Mysoulspace.in Perfect for the modern yogis and yoginis, Proyog blends Indian styles with comfort to make dhoti-shorts, wrap tops, infinity scarves with built-in pockets and more. They’ve done extensive R&D on textiles and developed a trademarked HYPERBREATH™ fabric, which is organic, super soft and moisture wicking. Their core-spun organic cotton has better stretch and recovery than regular cotton elastane and is also 100 per cent opaque. Don’t forget to check out their yoga props either—the Bengal mat is both biodegradable and anti-microbial. Proyog.com Mumbai-based sustainable fashion house Pause has collaborated with celebrity trainer Sohrab Khushrushahi to create a range of light, breathable jerseys in edgy silhouettes like crop tops and muscle tees. Founders Neha Modi and Neha Tham chose a blend of organic cotton yarn and a biodegradable fibre called TENCEL™, which is primarily made from pure eucalyptus cellulose grown on land not suitable for agriculture, for their wares. The fabrics are dyed with natural colours and processed at a certified mill with a water recovery plant. And the neon accents and catchy quotes make this jersey a bootcamp staple. Interestingly, it’s not just niche labels that are making strides in sustainable workout wear. Even the bigger sportswear brands are taking note of contemporary consumption trends and releasing recycled collections. Adidas has collaborated with an organisation called Parley for the Oceans to create high performance footwear and clothing from marine plastic waste; they are hosting a run and beach clean-up on June 8 in honour of World Ocean Day. Earlier this year, Nike also made headlines by dressing India’s national cricket teams in jerseys made out of recycled polyester. (These are also available to purchase in select stores across India.) And Columbia Sportswear uses 21 recycled plastic bottles to make its OutDry Ex Eco Jacket entirely out of dye-free, recycled fabric. The garment is breathable, waterproof and perfect for outdoor physical activities. 5 great homegrown fitness labels that will make you want to work out 8 Indian sportswear labels for every fitness enthusiast How do you make sure that the fashion you’re buying is sustainable?
