column1: Score! 4 streetwear designers reinvent Nike’s football jersey for women
column2: © Nike Fashion As we gear up for the Women’s World Cup 2019, Ambush’s Yoon Ahn, Koché’s Christelle Kocher, MadeMe’s Erin Magee and Marine Serre reveal their favourite designs from their capsule collaboration with Nike What does fashion’s take on the football jersey look like? Ambush’s Yoon Ahn, Koché’s Christelle Kocher, MadeMe’s Erin Magee and Marine Serre have all put their designer spin on the functional garment, in collaboration with Nike. Rather than dressing it up, these streetstyle stalwarts—enlisted by Nike to design lifestyle collections to coincide with the Women’s World Cup 2019 (June 7 to July 7)—have gone back to the drawing board and paid tribute to the unifying power of sport. “We take pride in standing up for our values and empowering women to have an equal opportunity in sport,” says Rosemary St. Clair, VP and GM of Nike Women. “[Nike has] over 40 years of championing the world’s largest community of female athletes—like Joan Benoit Samuelson, Serena Williams and Caster Semenya—on and off the field of play. Today, we are more committed than ever to use our brand as a catalyst—celebrating athletes, supporting sports and building the best product for her.” Here, Vogue speaks to each of the four fashion designers about their concepts behind the collection, their favourite pieces and the power of sport. © Nike “I wanted to create a universal piece for everyone to celebrate in,” says the Korean-American designer of her take on the jersey-turned-coat, teamed with a bra top, sported by Japanese footballer Risa Shimizu. “I was inspired by the happi coat—a traditional Japanese, straight-sleeved coat, usually worn to festivals,” says Ahn. “Although we are celebrating the World Cup and the incredible female players, I believe it is just as important for the fans, for everyone—old, young, women and men.” As well as highlighting the importance of diversity and culture, there’s a secret message in the jersey, too. “My Nike x AMBUSH® jersey has an inner pride message that reads: ‘Make each game your masterpiece.’  That’s exactly how I feel.” © Nike The LVMH Prize-winner’s signature half-moon print comes together with the Nike swoosh, forming the base of her capsule favourite: a jersey-turned-dress, teamed with a printed bodysuit. “I loved the idea of a garment that is adapted to the body that it dresses,” says the French designer. “So I concentrated on the natural shape of a woman’s body, allowing enough space for movement.” © Nike Modelled by Adwoa Aboah, the bodysuit is screen printed using reflective ink, marrying form and function. “It is aesthetically a feat; and answers the functional demands of running in the dark or among traffic,” Serre explains. “I really like to do things like that—reusing archetypical references, in this case of sports garments, like reflective print, the tracksuit running archive and the construction in this piece – and then really transform and reorient the way they are approached.” © Nike Kocher’s dress and matching bra, crafted using the sportswear brand’s technical fabrics, are firm favourites thanks to their ease and energy. “I created this dress by reconstructing the soccer jersey around the female body, adding some very feminine elements, like lace, to sporty codes,” says the Paris-based designer. © Nike “The idea was to give the feeling of movement and positive energy,” she adds of the design, worn by French footballer Marie-Antoinette Katoto. “It is a dress that can be worn by a girl who plays, dances or moves in the city.” © Nike Working with the United States women's national soccer team (USWNT) crest was central to New York-based Magee’s design. “My first thought was I wanted this jersey to be sport first, fashion second. It’s meant to celebrate the incredible, victorious history of the USWNT, by drawing attention to the woman namesake of the iconic sportswear company itself: Nike, goddess of victory.” © Nike As seen on American footballer Mallory Pugh, the jersey is based on the pitch-ready silhouette we all know and recognise, while Nike’s Classic Swoosh bra provided further inspiration, with both pieces crafted from Nike’s signature Dri-FIT technology. “This is a jersey that can be worn on and off the field; it’s true to sport and function. And it is the first time MadeMe has ever designed piece that can be worn at the highest level of play.” 8 Indian sportswear labels for every fitness enthusiast Buy workout gear like a fitness junkie—here are all the tips you need The perfect sports bra does exist, ladies What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Aeance: Is this the most sustainable brand yet?
column2: © Aeance Fashion As Aeance’s third collection—created by renowned industrial designer Konstantin Grcic—lands in stores, Vogue meets the founders of the functional brand challenging every fashion standard In a landscape of fast fashion and logomania, Aeance stands apart. The minimalist brand is the embodiment of both style and substance; clothing designed to meet the demands—and values—of modern life. Doing more with less, essentially. “We started with our own needs,” Arendt van Deyk, one half of the duo behind the German label tells Vogue. “We wanted timeless, high-quality clothing—like Jil Sander or The Row—but in a more functional way—breathable, waterproof.” And sustainable, too: 96 per cent of its textiles are recycled, natural, biodegradable or bio-based. Set up just four years ago by van Deyk and Nadine-Isabelle Baier, Aeance goes against the fashion grain in a number of ways. Firstly, it eschews the traditional fashion calendar in favour of a non-seasonal approach, launching collections only when they are ready. “It is a difficult concept for retailers to grasp,” comments Baier. “The fashion industry is, in general, so [stuck] in its old cycles.” © Aeance Secondly, collections are concise. The latest, Collection 03, only has nine pieces. “We’re going back in time to when clothes were made to last, hence the timeless quality to our designs,” offers Baier. Thirdly, it is a fashion brand without a designer. The duo have previously tapped designers Hien Le and Steven Tai to translate their ethos into functional designs. “For the third collection, we decided to give it a new approach,” says van Deyk. Enter celebrated industrial designer Konstantin Grcic. His tailored and streamlined pieces—in a sober colour scheme of black, blue, grey, red and mauve—sit seamlessly with Aeance’s previous two lines. “The idea is that you can build on what you have,” says Baier. “We’re not trying to break through the cycle by constantly creating something new; we’re adding and improving,” © Aeance In a final act of rebellion, the pair deplore fashion trends. Athleisure, for instance. “We don't like the term for us… We sometimes call it ‘athletic fashion’. We like Uniqlo’s ‘life wear’, but we’re a more functional version of that,” says van Deyk. “Athleisure is more casual,” adds Baier. “We’re more refined than that.” Each radical point of difference is born of the brand’s mission to be as sustainable as possible. “We think that all companies, new or existing, have to do their very best to reduce their impact on the environment and make their product in the most responsible way,” says van Deyk. The pair’s vision has taken them into groundbreaking territory, working with material developers to find the best solutions possible. “[Though] there is no single perfect solution,” laments Baier, “like most things in life, we’re having to use a mix of solutions to address the problems of the fashion industry. ” © Aeance Jackets are made from super-fine merino wool from New Zealand and a lightweight Japanese stretch fabric made from recycled nylon. Coats are crafted from a breathable and waterproof fabric using chemical-free ecorepel Bio, which imitates plants’ natural protection from water and aqueous dirt. Trousers are produced using fibres extracted from naturally grown beech wood. And the skirts? The fibre technology in them ensures they would biodegrade to organic matter in just five years if buried. Athleisure suddenly looks very basic. column1: Model Toshada Uma talks about finding comfort in her own skin
column2: © Instagram.com/toshadaa Fashion Diagnosed with a condition causing severe hair loss, Toshada Uma found a way to create a unique identity for herself and continue with her dream of becoming a model despite the odds To stand in front of a camera with the aim of leaving a mark in the fashion industry is a daunting task by itself, but when you’re petite and look nothing like the average Super in an editorial spread, holding on to that dream requires some serious determination. I ran into Toshada Uma at the private room of Kitty Su amidst anniversary celebrations, and first thing that I noticed about her was her daring style, and soon, we were talking about changing perceptions, experimenting on the daily and acceptance. Excerpts from our conversation below. The first bald patch was quite small and I thought it would grow back. I was a nine-year-old, it took me a few years to realise that the condition is here to stay and may worsen or get better from time to time. I didn’t care about it too, till my peers started pointing it out. That is when I started loathing the condition and tried growing my hair long—which I'd never done before. Although luckily this phase didn't last too long, since I realised my hair is such a small part of me. There is so much more to me as a person. I focused on being comfortable in my skin and developing my talents instead. Getting dressed and groomed has always something I’ve loved to do; it’s quite ritualistic to me, and there are barely any days when I don’t deck up. The process behind each look can differ—some days I wake up with an entire look in mind, it could be a colour that evokes ideas; some days I’m inspired by specific textures that determine the final aesthetic. I count my privileges—I have a roof over my head, food in my system, people who love me, and work that I enjoy. It’s very confidence invoking. I always loved being in front of the camera and I loved fashion. Modelling happened—my aspirations lay more in being a performer, which I’m also able to browse opportunities for at this point. I would credit the visibility modelling gave me for the same. I was very unsure about how I’d withstand the industry walking into my career as a model. But in my personal experience everything worked better than planned; little did I know about the love I’d be filled with for my work. I really admire Rei Kawakubo. Nothing too wise, just simple things that help me get by—love yourself, pursue your goals and don’t give up. It’s honestly amazing to see the attempts made towards inclusivity across the globe. We’re seeing more diversity than ever before, although it still is under the tags of inclusivity and diversity. I hope for a day where it is just the norm. column1: Rihanna reveals the story behind her latest collection’s imagery
column2: Fashion “We want people to see the parallels between what was then and what this is now, in a modern way.” – Rihanna tells Vogue about how the 1960s Black Is Beautiful movement and its most influential players, photographer Kwame Brathwaite and the Grandassa Models, inspired her latest Fenty fashion collection There was a definite glint in the famous green eyes when Rihanna said, “Every collection will change—you’ll see that to come,” at the launch of the first release of her fashion collection with LVMH in Paris last week. We’ve come to expect surprises from Ms Robyn Rihanna Fenty—CEO and creative director of the Fenty enterprise—but what few knew last week was that she had another move up the super-long sleeves of her white jacket-dress: the reveal of her collection imagery, alongside photographs by Kwame Brathwaite, hero of the Black Is Beautiful movement instigated by African-American creative forces in New York in the 1950s and 1960s. “When I was coming up with the concept for this release, we were just digging and digging and we came up with these images—they made me feel they were relevant to what we are doing right now,” Rihanna tells Vogue. Among the now 81-year-old New York photographer’s archive, she came across a documentary about black female fashion activism in America—a group of young women, known as the Grandassa Models, who got together in the early 1960s in New York. “It was a really strange and powerful parallel,” says Rihanna. “And he gave me permission [to use the imagery], obviously that is a big deal.” Intent on exercising fashion and beauty as a medium of empowerment and change against the dominance of white-centric popular culture, the Grandassa Models organised sell-out shows that reinvented super-elegant, high-style black beauty, African clothing references and natural hair. Critically influential, years before mainstream designers reappropriated and recast these references, the models were backed up by Brathwaite and his older brother, graphic designer Elombe Brath. All of them were integral players in the coming together of musicians, writers and politicians of the Black Power movement. The backstory interweaves Rihanna’s personal Bajan history with wildly re-affirming connections between the past and her present. For starters, there is a close-to-home coincidence, she says: “Kwame Brathwaite is from Barbados! And, his last name is my grandfather’s name, which was my mother’s name before she was a Fenty.” Rihanna points to a 1964 studio portrait of Nomsa Brathwaite in a high headwrap and spectacular below-the-shoulder earrings: “She’s his sister-in-law!” (Nomsa was married to Brath). Another photo of Nomsa shows her smiling in front of a map of Africa in 1968—the time when the political and social movement was reaching out beyond America to support the struggle for liberation in Africa and the Carribean. Another photograph, dated 1968, shows Grandassa Models at the Renaissance Casino Ballroom in Harlem on Garvey Day. In the background, a poster reads “Buy Black”. As soon as she began looking into in, Rihanna wanted to know more—cue more “digging” to turn up the fact, via writer and historian Tanisha C. Ford, that the Grandassa Models designed and made their own clothes. Aside from looking incredible, their radical reclaiming of African inspiration, elegant robes, headwraps and jewellery led to a wave of female entrepreneurship, creating self-owned boutiques and a whole community of black designers, stylists, hairdressers and makeup artists. The through-lines to how Rihanna organises her world as a multi-hyphenate musician/performer/ fashion designer/beauty change-maker are hard to miss. How does she manage her music career alongside her massively successful Fenty Beauty business, the Savage X Fenty lingerie collaboration and now Fenty fashion? She laughs, leaning in: “Well, I work all the time. I visualise Fenty as a hub, bringing in creative people. We travel together, we eat together, we’re always working. That’s how I want to keep it.” In other words, she’s the digital-age, hyper-connected, 21st-century manifestation of exactly the kind of discipline-crossing way of working that Kwame Brathwaite documented. In bringing up his photographs for her legion of followers to discover, she’s re-establishing that connection; giving them the opportunity to be inspired by this progressive, elevated black cultural revolution that happened not so long ago, when music, fashion, beauty, art and politics overlapped, and everyone worked in unison. “And here are the men who started the Black Is Beautiful movement,” Rihanna concludes, pointing to her last choice, a 1961 photograph of six slim-suited collaborators of the African Jazz-Art Society and Studios, set up “to reclaim jazz as the music of contemporary African traditions that should be controlled by black artists,” she explains. Kwame Brathwaite holds his camera at the back; Elombe is seated at a layout desk. So, seeing Brathwaite’s work intermixed with pictures of model Debra Shaw and images of London, does Rihanna want people to discover a political message as they shop her latest Fenty collection? “Well, I don’t know if it’s political so much as embracing the fact that people should be more aware,” she shrugs, smiling. “But definitely, we want people to see the parallels between what was then and what this is now, in a modern way.” Rihanna unveils her ground-breaking Fenty collection in Paris Fenty Fashion: Everything to know about Rihanna’s fashion brand You have already seen Rihanna’s new Fenty collection Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Are you ready to bring your favourite childhood trends back into your wardrobe?
column2: Fashion Remember Mary Janes and babydoll dresses, Disney prints and diamanté hair slides? If you were born in the 1990s, it’s time to indulge your inner child because your cherished childhood favourites have just had an upscale makeover If it’s true that “all grown-ups were once children... but only few of them remember it”, as Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote in The Little Prince, the grown-ups that don’t remember have 2019’s catwalks to jog their memory. From Burberry’s covetable Mary Jane flats to Prada’s retro babydoll revival, grown-up women are re-selecting childhood classics that add a dash of wit. Here are the four mood-lifting fashion retakes to know about now. A model walks the runway wearing Mary Janes at the Burberry spring/summer 2019 show in London © Getty Burberry creative director Riccardo Tisci may be well known for his rave-ready sneakers, but for spring/summer 2019 he turned his attentions to the black, patent Mary Janes which you probably haven’t thought about since you were ten years old. How to wear them now? Switch out the trainers and ditch the ankle socks. London-based French style star Camille Charrière pairs hers with a raw hem miniskirt and Chloé sweater. Linda Tol in a Babydoll dress © Jonathan Daniel Pryce Hit pause on the midi-dress. The itsy-bitsy, 1960s babydoll is back and shrugging off its after-dark rep. Dutch street-style regular Linda Tol offers up a lesson in pulling off the new abbreviated hemline during daylight hours with a winged collar shirt and sober beige sweater layered underneath. Our tip? Pare back the retro mood with a sturdy Chelsea boot. Bows, Paris, spring/summer 2019 © Jonathan Daniel Pryce Remember when you had someone else on hand to brush your hair in the morning and a stash of cherished hair accessories? Well, that time has come around again – for the accessories part at least. Bows, scrunchies and hair slides are back thanks to a new generation of devotees, including German stylist and makeup artist, Stella von Senger, and Ganni girls Courtney Trop and Emma Rosenzweig. Plus, that oversized Prada headband doesn’t seem to be slipping off the fashion radar any time soon. Meanwhile, anyone growing out a fringe has Chanel, Dior and Simone Rocha’s decorative hair slides to make the process painless. Consider these the fastest way to lift your mood and your outfit. Loewe has similarly gone back to the Disney drawing board, putting Dumbo’s cherished stars front and centre of a limited-edition accessories run timed to coincide with Tim Burton’s recent remake of the 1941 classic. column1: What gives Benarasi brocade its timeless appeal?
column2: Fashion Benarasi brocade is a treasured Indian handloom that celebrates history and intricacy in equal measure. Textile designer Kshitij Jalori tells us what goes into the making of these coveted heirlooms Mark Twain once said: “Benares is older than history, older than tradition, older even than legend and looks twice as old as all of them put together.” So it only follows that the weaving heritage from one of the world’s oldest cities is gold as far as handlooms go. Dating back to the 1600s, the craftsmanship of these zari-woven patterned silk brocades as we know them today was a result of a famine in Gujarat. It lead to an influx of silk and brocade weavers in Benares, which was essentially a cotton weaving centre at the time. Textile designer Kshitij Jalori, whose eponymous label approaches Benarasi weaves with a minimalistic and sophisticated mindset, gives us an in-depth 101 on the fabric. Excerpts from the interview below. The fabric is primarily created using a pit loom, where silk warp threads are laid on a frame in a repeat pattern depending upon the size of the jacquard. In the earlier days, a jangla was used instead of the present-day jacquard to create the fine patterning. Depending upon the design, the weft is thrown in a shuttle to form the base of the fabric, while smaller spindles wound with zari are used as extra wefts to form the pattern. Benares is a very special centre for weaving, and the loom and techniques used are some of the most detailed and advanced despite their indigenous nature. Over the centuries, Benares has been exposed to much cultural diversity and has seen the convergence of multiple pilgrim and trade routes. This has introduced a confluence of multiple cultures into its textile. The jangla sari has a dense interlaced pattern—usually floral or konia (betel leaf or paisley motif)—with an intricately patterned border and pallu, while the shikargarh sari is famous for its hunting scenes and animal motifs (mainly tigers, deers, peacocks and parrots). Kimkhwāb features heavy zari work that renders the underlying cloth almost invisible. The word is of Persian origin and loosely translates into ‘a golden dream’. It gained immense popularity during the Mughal rule. Tanchoi is an interesting technique where the base weft itself is used to create a pattern on the fabric. According to ancient folklore, the technique first came to Gujarat from China, before making its way to Benares. Gyasar is woven with Tibetan motifs that are seen in Buddhist monasteries. Mashru and himroo, though not traditionally woven in Benares, are being made here today due to advanced looms—the former uses silk warp and cotton weft with zari patterning and the latter is made only from silk and cotton. Some of the other important Benarasis are the tissue sari, butidar sari, organza sari, nilambari, pitambari and raktambari. Depending on the design and technique, it can take anywhere from 15 days to six months to weave a Benarasi sari. The three primary extra weft techniques used for weaving are kadhwa, phekwa and katarwan. Of these, kadhwa is the most tedious, as every design detail is created using individual zari or resham wound spindles as extra wefts on top of the base fabric. This ensures there are no loose threads on the back of the sari. Having said that, the meticulousness and clarity of a design does not depend on the technique alone. The plotting of the graph for the card cutting of the jacquard as well as the use of urtoo (weave detailing of each shape) has an equally significant role. These typically include betel leaves, paisleys, foliage, shikar scenes, rudraksh and chand motifs. But the design vocabulary is not limited to just these anymore. With the intervention of several designers, you can now find Benarasis in a range of interesting, modern patterns. While the Benarasi sari does not hold cultural significance like a Bagh Phulkari, its opulent nature and the use of pure zari makes it a trousseau must-have. Since the inception of my brand last year, I have witnessed modern Indian brides who now choose to wear Benarasi saris for their wedding instead of a lehenga. When I first started working in Benares, the idea was to create exquisite pieces that glorify the technique. This resulted in a range of Benarasi saris and dupattas which are now available under the Kshitij Jalori CLASSIC label. Cashmere brocade shawls, where pure pashmina yarns are used to form the base fabric for intricate brocades, are also part of this range. The zari used in our CLASSIC range is specially developed and has a very high percentage of real silver with a sprinkle of real gold, all wound on a mustard cotton yarn. This lends it a beautiful metallic sheen. The urtoo technique, where the weaving patterns are created in each shape to maximise the intricacy, is also used extensively. Since my background is in textiles, I constantly innovate with weave structures, design and fabrics to add contemporary flair to them. All the fabrics are especially developed for each collection; kadhwa, phekwa*,* mashru*,* tanchoi and satin tanchoi are some of them. We have worked with satin tissue for my upcoming collection, which also features saris with modernised konia motifs. While the current demand for brocades generates ample work for the artisan community of Benares, this often leads to a shortage in supply or sub-standard quality. Quantity has taken precedence over quality, and as a result the importance of urtoo, and the purity of zari and silk has deteriorated. I employ 50 looms, of which 10-15 are in the heart of Benares, and the rest are in surrounding villages like Cholapur and Ramnagar. While most of our weavers are skilled master craftsmen, we are happy to have young weavers in the mix as well. Encouraging the next generation is what will ultimately keep the craft alive. column1: This Indian textile store and design studio houses up to 1,000 handwoven fabrics
column2: Fashion Palak Shah’s cultural initiative Ekaya Thaan showcases the legacy of India’s textile heritage to the world while doubling as a retail showroom and design studio A rediscovery of roots is very much the mood of the fashion industry right now. And it is the very foundation on which Palak Shah has built her brand as well. The Benaras-born fashion entrepreneur hails from a family that has been preserving the tradition of Benarasi textiles for four generations now. With a 120-year-old legacy in the handloom industry, her love for textiles was honed at a young age. So it was no surprise that Shah launched Ekaya Banaras—a luxury handloom label that reinvents Indian textiles by giving them youthful relevance for the homegrown connoisseur—in 2012 soon after graduating in business management from King’s College London. Even as she endeavoured to change the conversations around indigenous weaves with her modern collections for Ekaya Banaras, she did feel there weren’t enough initiatives to bring India’s rich textile legacy to the world minus the preconceived notions. It was while pursuing her MBA at Babson College in 2016 that a project turned into a business model: Shah realised that there while there was great interest in Indian textiles internationally, what lacked was a bridge to ease its attaining. “A global consumer is not going to buy a sari unless they have an occasion for it. But nothing is stopping them from buying an Indian textile to use the way they want.” Thus, was born Ekaya Thaan in August 2017 to simultaneously function as a textile gallery, design studio and concept store housed within Ekaya Banaras’s flagship stores in New Delhi, Hyderabad and Ahmedabad. “The vision was to create a destination for luxury handloom textile shopping for global enthusiasts who want to take back a little bit of India with them. While Ekaya Thaan stays true to our core ethos of highlighting the mastery behind these handwoven Indian fabrics with our inventive designs, it also broadens the scope of how you can play with them,” adds Shah. With close to 1,000 fabrics to choose from (and new additions every month) Ekaya Thaan is truly is the textile connoisseur’s candy store equivalent. Benarasi weaves are a mainstay, spanning across techniques like kadwa, fekua, cutwork, gyasar and jamdani, made on individual looms at their Benaras atelier housing a team of 8,000 artisans. But handlooms from different parts of the country, such as kanjeevaram or chanderi, are not ignored either. “Our main agenda is to challenge ourselves technically. People are drawn to Ekaya because of our never-seen-before Benarasis, and we want to stay true to that. So we are constantly innovating—you’ll find snakeskin patterned Benarasis and reverse cutwork detailing. We also have a range that recreates chikankari and parsi gara embroidery on Benarasi with the weaving technique,” Shah explains. “Apart from preservation, modernising is an important aspect too. Ekaya Thaan will always have an eclectic undertone.” Handwoven Benarasi mashru silk fabric, Ekaya Sustainability and evolution go hand in hand according to Shah. “We cannot confine our crafts to India alone if we want them to have a longer lifespan. The Benarasi textile should become a part of the global lexicon, where designers from the world break away from traditional ways of using it.” This is where Ekaya Thaan’s design studio comes into play by giving international designers (Missoni and Salvatore Ferragamo are some of the fashion houses they have worked with) easy access to the handloom market; entirely customising the fabric based on the designer’s collection as well as consulting on its usage. Last year, the brand travelled to Paris Haute Couture Week for Fédération Française de la Création Couture Sur Mesure—a collaboration where 15 international designers worked with Ekaya Thaan fabrics to create collections for the French wedding and couture market. Then there are also Ekaya Thaan’s collaborations with Indian labels like Play Clan, Archana Rao, Ashdeen and most recently, Masaba Gupta. Ekaya at Fédération Française de la Création Couture Sur Mesure. Image: Adil Hasan Shah admits to being a sari hoarder, and confesses you’d be hard-pressed to find her in anything but an Ekaya silk drape for festive occasions. However, she prefers to experiment with the styling to bring out the sari’s design. On one day she’ll wrap the pallu around her neck and on another, throw in a belt bag or a denim jacket for added impact. So yes, while Indian textiles and festive occasions are often used in the breath, Shah is also intent on giving them a modern makeover. How so? “We are working on launching more stores in India and internationally. There are also upcoming collections of home décor, stationery and western wear using these fabrics. The focus is on versatility and global appeal without compromising on our heritage and craftsmanship.” Handwoven printed cotton fabric with zari booti, Ekaya This new collaboration uses Indian handloom textiles in French wedding wear The millennial’s guide to understanding handloom Why all eyes in the fashion industry are currently on khadi Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: A ringside view of the 72nd Cannes Film Festival
column2: © Gisela Schober Fashion From the celebrities to the films, this Vogue insider recounts her experience at the prestigious film festival You don’t walk to the famous red carpet at Cannes, I was told as I made my way to my first-ever premiere at the Cannes Film Festival—you must make a dramatic entry, via a chauffeur-driven luxury vehicle and then walk the red carpet. It’s all part of the heady drama of Cannes. The red carpet, I realise, is much smaller in person (and much more crowded) than it seems in pictures, but is still mighty impressive. It gives back as much as you give it—the more love you give it, the more it adores you. While we jumped out of our car and hurried across the carpet, anxious to get out of the rain and settle into our seats to watch Les Plus Belles Annees d'une Vie, Priyanka Chopra and the ever-graceful Helen Mirren took their time, resplendent in couture and jewels by Chopard, a long-standing partner of the festival. A few days later, Brad Pitt and Leonardo Di Caprio cleaned up to debut Quentin Tarantino’s thriller, Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, 25 years after the director debuted Pulp Fiction at the festival. Priyanka Chopra and Nick Jonas on the red carpet at the 72nd Cannes Film Festival © Gisela Schober But while red carpet moments like these dominate our timelines and the world press, it’s the movies that actually take centre stage at the festival, with parties and fashion playing the supporting act. Thousands of films are submitted into the festival each year, with only 50 feature films and 30 short films finally making the cut. Helen Mirren in Chopard © Daniele Venturelli This, the 72nd edition, saw some incredible films debut including Tarantino’s, which received a seven-minute long ovation. Other films like Elton John’s biopic Rocketman, starring Richard Madden and Taron Egerton, which should hit our screens later this summer, generated plenty of buzz, as did The Lighthouse, a black and white thriller starring Robert Pattison and William Defoe. Festival favourite Pedro Almodovar also had a winner in Pain and Glory, as did British filmmaker Ken Loach with Sorry We Missed You. Business also seems to be healthy, with Amazon Studios buying Les Miserables for a tidy sum, and Paramount bought the rights to Down Under Cover, a comedy starring Chris Hemsworth and Tiffany Haddish. With many heavyweights in the running, deciding who to award the Palme D’Or, the festival’s highest prize, which was announced last night, could not have been harder. But this was a Cannes of many firsts—director Bong Joon-ho became the first Korean director to win the top prize at Cannes, for his black comic thriller Parasite. The Grand Prix was awarded to Senegalese director Mati Diop for Atlantique—and in a festival where diversity was keenly discussed, she was the first black woman to have a film in the competition, and she did not disappoint. With any luck, some of these films will make their way to a cinema near you soon. column1: The Spice Girls really, really wanted a grown-up take on girl power for their reunion tour
column2: © Instagram.com/spicegirls Fashion Costume designer Gabriella Slade talks exclusively to Vogue about creating the looks for the Spice World tour, which kicks off in Dublin tonight—seven years after Scary, Sporty, Baby and Ginger last took to the stage together at the 2012 Olympics. Who better to mastermind the looks for a Spice Girls reunion tour than a Spice Girls fan? “I absolutely adored them, they were part of my childhood,” costume designer Gabriella Slade tells Vogue, adding that, like so many children of the '90s, she changed her mind constantly about which Spice was her sartorial spirit animal: Scary, Ginger, Baby, Sporty or Posh. Four months ago Slade, who fondly recalls dressing up as her pop heroines as a young girl, found herself tasked with dressing them for Spice World, the first tour in more than a decade for four out of five of the girls (Victoria Beckham won't be joining), which kicks off tonight at Dublin's Croke Park. And while she's far too diplomatic to single out a favourite fashion moment from the kaleidoscope of leopard print, lycra and little black dresses that was the group's heyday, she admits to being obsessed by plenty of their style signatures—platform boots among them. So can we expect to see a buffalo trainer or two when the lights go up later? Sadly, Slade isn't telling. What she will say is that the costumes she and her team have spent eight weeks creating for the 13-date tour stay true to the “DNA” of the group. “There's a definite honouring of the '90s, but with a contemporary twist,” she says. “I really wanted to bring back a sense of what the Spice Girls were, what they stood for. It's respectful of their legacy... that's what the fans want.” A sketch of the girls' look for their 2000 hit “Holler”, shared exclusively with Vogue ahead of opening night, certainly brings the memories flooding back: the use of leather calls to mind the music video for the group's brief foray into R&B all those years ago, while Mel C's crop top and trainers combo is vintage Sporty. For the group's last tour in 2007, Roberto Cavalli was called upon to create corsets for Victoria Beckham, suits for Mel C, flirty dresses for Emma Bunton and Geri Haliwell and catsuits for Mel B—all in a metallic palette of silver and gold. While Slade won't reveal whether any major fashion designers have been part of the process this time around (although Swarovski has provided “phenomenal” crystal embellishments), she says the focus has been on the different girls' individual aesthetics. “No-one wanted the typical ‘girl band’ look,” she says. With that in mind, each band member will have their own 'House'—made up of a dedicated troop of five dancers—and a House colour. “The dancers' outfits will reflect the DNA of that Spice Girl,” Slade explains. This, it seems, is the closest we'll get to confirmation that Ginger's Union Jack dress could be reinvented for this latest Spice Girls revival, or that Scary's leopard print could prowl the stage once more. “There are multiple looks for the dancers as well as the girls, that was an important part of their vision,“ says Slade, who tells Vogue the group was “very much” involved in the whole process. Ultimately, says Slade, she “wanted the girls to feel empowered by what they're wearing”. Empowered is a word she returns to a lot. “It's a really fun aesthetic for everyone to enjoy, but it respects the fact that they're four different women now, they're coming to this from a different place than when they were first in the charts.” So grown-up looks, but with added girl power. What could be more true to the legacy of Spice than that? column1: How to layer necklaces like a celebrity
column2: © Steve Granitz, Getty Images Fashion From Priyanka Chopra and Deepika Padukone to Gigi Hadid, A-listers all over the world are wearing their necklaces on top of each other. Here, we show you how to do right by the trend Why wear one necklace when you can flaunt five at the same time? Minimal styles are the way to go this summer—we’re talking gold chains with tiny pendants, diamond chokers and silver chains with charms—and they're best worn together if you want to make an impact. If you’re looking for pointers, just look to the celebrities who are effortlessly nailing the trend for notes. From Deepika Padukone’s showcase at this year’s Cannes Film Festival to Gigi Hadid’s Coachella version, inspiration is aplenty. Rule one is to remember that there are no rules—layering your necklaces is all about having fun. Mix and match, and play with lengths and colours to make an effortless statement. On her second day at Cannes, Deepika Padukone put her best foot forward in a white sheer blouse and high-waisted trousers combination, accessorised with two gold necklaces featuring statement pendants—one a pearl, the other a big gold number. Disha Patani went down the same route by layering different lengths and styles of necklaces—chokers included—but only in gold. Notice how the actor skipped earrings? Sonam Kapoor Ahuja has given the trend a try as well—with multiple chokers worn together with a statement neckpiece and a long, thin necklace featuring a big pendant. Rihanna’s take on the trend saw her layer multiple gold necklaces with emerald pendants in varying lengths. And in another instance, she layered her cross necklace with a minimal choker, adding big hoop earrings to complete her look. Gigi Hadid has no qualms about going OTT with the trend. Here, the supermodel plays with minimal gold and azure necklaces, and don’t miss those mismatched earrings either. column1: The evolution of sunglasses
column2: Fashion Gucci ski masks, Prada insect eyes and Dior reflective shades—sunglasses are making a strong statement on the catwalks right now. Here, Vogue looks back at the history of the accessory that’s gone from a supporting to a starring role in fashion Karl Lagerfeld in signature black, Jackie Kennedy in supersized ovals, Audrey Hepburn in Manhattans, Elton John in kooky and outlandish, Tom Hiddleston and Tilda Swinton in Wayfarers in Only Lovers Left Alive—everyone has their own take on wearing sunglasses. And the 1920s-born accessory is as synonymous with celebrity and the silver screen as it is with sunshine. But lately, sunglasses have experienced quite the design overhaul with a presence on the international SS19 catwalks that has seen them go from supporting to starring role. Gucci fall 2019 Sunglasses took on the guise of ski masks at Gucci and Loewe, but were conversely thin with bold framework at Courrèges; Prada opted for insect-like styles, while Balenciaga went playful and oversized, and Dior got very reflective. And at new-look Celine, almost every look was accompanied by a pair of shades to underpin the burgeoning cool factor. “Design has evolved from the traditional offer of basic metal-frame aviators and acetate readers to more statement pieces that express individualism,” says Gary Bott, director of cult frame innovator Gentle Monster. Since launching in 2011, the Korean brand has become known for its experimentation with signature collections, such as the bestselling Flatba, which features the lens mounted on top of the frame, not inside, to create a flat and clean aesthetic. “We experiment, not just with product design but also spatial design,” Bott says, referring to the brand’s penchant for unique retail concepts. Which, as a result, perhaps goes some way in explaining why sunglasses across the board have now become so much more designed and statement-making than ever before. A look ahead to the AW19 collections and this trend shows no signs of abating: sunglasses are morphing into full-on visors at Gucci and retro-slim rectangles at Louis Vuitton, while the latter’s cruise 2020 collection proffers jewel-hued lenses and goggle-aviation shapes, often worn with a helmet-type head cap. The beauty, of course, is that sunglasses quickly and completely transform your appearance. The allure is in the styling, something that strikes a chord in 2019 as we increasingly devote time to what we wear and look like on the digital screen and the social media lens replaces Hollywood’s. It might be no surprise to hear then that for luxury online retailer Net-A-Porter, sunglasses are its third most searched accessory, with Balenciaga leading the way with its super-designed aesthetic, and new brand Anna-Karin Karlsson, with its ostentatious bling, also performing well. The e-tailer has plans to further indulge our optical obsession with the launch of the Insta-friendly Barcelona brand Kaleos (think pronounced, angular and confident shapes that will get you noticed) and will play host to Zimmermann’s first sunglasses line (the brand is currently best known for its swimwear). Historically, the existence of sunglasses can be traced back as far as Roman times when, supposedly, Emperor Nero would watch gladiator sports through an emerald to protect his eyes from the light. Similarly, the Inuit are said to have worn snow goggles crafted from a piece of wood or bone with a small slit at the front to protect themselves from snow blindness. But the actual first pair of dark-lens glasses are thought to have been produced in 1885; while Sam Foster, the founder of the US eyewear maker Foster Grant, started mass-producing the eyewear in 1929. In 1936, Edwin H. Land introduced a polarised version. Each decade since has had its own defining styles—from the cat's-eye of the 1950s to the playful plastics of the 1980s. The hallmark of the 2010s as it draws to a close? Sunglasses that in many ways speak of the entire evolution, or rather revolution, of the eyewear to date. Goggles, visors and masks are among the most throwback and avant-garde styles, while at the opposite end of the spectrum there are tiny, tech-y, sci-fi and futuristic looks. No longer just a cool or practical accessory, sunglasses are now a complex statement of individualistic style and intent. column1: Here’s why the bowling shirt is summer 2019’s most practical purchase
column2: © Getty Fashion Low-maintenance and versatile, the throwback short-sleeved shirt is about to streamline your work wardrobe and your holiday packing The realities of warm weather dressing in the office can be arduous. If you’ve already made the switch to barely-there sandals, you’re probably on first-name terms with your pedicurist. Likewise your dry cleaner, for the delicate beige separates you were encouraged to invest in for spring (sorry). Faced with the prospect of continuous sunshine, not all ideas for refreshing your summer wardrobe are such hard work, however. Where the boxy, short-sleeved shirt is concerned, the challenge of getting dressed in under five minutes in the morning is suddenly not all that unrealistic. The modern update on the old-school bowling shirt is the time-poor woman’s friend, because it offers something that we don’t champion often enough in workwear: laziness. So, who’s doing the new bowling shirts and why are they about to be your favourite fashion shortcut? London-based Korean designer Rejina Pyo’s are made of non-iron, crinkled satin and come in a range of sorbet shades that lift an all-black look. 2019 BFC/Vogue Fashion Fund winner Wales Bonner offers up crisp nylon with an ultra-flattering, silhouette-skimming fit, while New York’s rising star Sandy Liang stocks leopard-print crêpe de Chine. If you’re not in the habit of sloshing juice (ok, Aperol) down your front, you could get away with hanging any/all of the above on the back of the bathroom door for a mild steam, rather than committing to a full wash cycle. Anyhow, you get the gist—this is a minimal maintenance purchase, and if there is ever a season for swerving demanding fashion choices, it’s this summer. As for the styling, there’s (at least) four ways that the bowling shirt makes life a little easier. When worn untucked and paired with lightweight trainers, it takes the office-y edge off the pencil skirt you already own. Which a pussy-bow blouse won’t. Unbuttoned and layered over a midi dress, or ribbed vest and straight-leg jeans, it will double as a lightweight summer jacket. Useful on days when you don’t want the unnecessary weight or warmth of a blazer. If suiting is a non-negotiable, this is your modern departure point from the formality of a regular full-sleeve shirt or the conspicuously dressed-down T-shirt. And, lastly, when you’re out of office, the bowling shirt is too. Chanel teamed its short-sleeved utility shirt with cycling shorts on the SS19 catwalk, and Marni’s polka-dot style or Acne’s linen version work particularly well worn unbuttoned over a swimsuit. Meaning this could be the summer you finally stick within the airline carry-on allowance. Laziness has never looked so good. column1: Paithani saris: Everything you need to about this Maharashtrian wedding staple
column2: Fashion From the year-long weaving process to the nature-inspired motifs, designer Gaurang Shah decodes the favoured weave of Maharashtrian brides, the Paithani sari India’s love affair with handloom spans the course of centuries, with precious weaves preserved and passed down from mother to daughter as a treasured heirloom. Headlining this roster is the Paithani sari. The cultural significance of its kaleidoscopic colour palette is underscored when you factor in the fact that it has been favoured by Maharashtrian brides for centuries. We spoke to textile maestro, Gaurang Shah, about the distinctive ethos that makes the Paithani sari stand out, and the best way to honour this weave in your own wardrobe. The Paithani sari has its origins in antiquity, hailing from the royal dynasties of the medieval town of Paithan near Aurangabad. Named after the town, the sari is believed to have been originally made with the finest silk threads from China and pure zari that was spun locally. This sari signifies years of superfluity and the finesse of Indian handloom, and every piece is characterised with the luxurious and liberal use of gold, as well as floral and bird-inspired motifs. The modern iterations of the sari from Paithan and Yeol are crafted from homegrown silk threads from Bangalore, while the zari is sourced from Surat. To create a genuine Paithani sari, around 500 grams of silk threads and another 250 grams of zari threads are utilised for a regular six-yard piece, while the nine-yard iterations use more raw material and can weigh up to 900 grams. The lustrous weave makes for a joyful intermingling of hues that creates the delicate illusion of shifting colours. The traditional motifs include parrots, peacocks and lotuses; however, during the Peshwa period, the Hans motif, the Ashraffi motif and the Asawalli were equally popular. The pallu usually consists of Muniya, a kind of parrot that is woven in the borders in green, with a whimsical touch of red at the mouth. Some of the other designs found on the pallus include the Panja, a geometrical flower-like motif most often outlined in red, the Barwa, that consists of twelve strands of a ladder and three strands on each side, and the traditional Mor (peacock). Over the years, Paithani has evolved from a cotton base to a silk base. Silk is used in weft designs and in the borders, whereas cotton was used in the body of the fabric. Contemporary versions of the Paithani sari don’t have a touch of cotton. On the design front, besides the intricacy of designs and reviving traditional complex patterns, the big change is that weavers have moved away from the small borders to bigger ones, thus changing the silhouette of the sari that can now accommodate a range of motifs—including those transplanted from other regions, such as the Tree of Life. After years of working with the weavers and plugging all flaws, the contemporary Paithani colour-scape is dazzling, even featuring statement numbers in chocolate brown gold zari weft with sunflowers. The experimental colour palette also makes space for violet warp with gold zari weft and pink roses, as well as navy blue with silver weft. Weaving this fabric has been an inventive journey, and the Calico Museum taught me and my team of weavers a whole new way of exacting finesse from the threads by drawing patterns and mastering the motifs. One particular Paithani collection had us supplying 100 kilos of yarn in the varied colours that were required for the design. Such is the story behind every Jamdani Paithani. Paithani saris are an integral part of Maharashtrian culture. Considered as the queen of saris, it is what the Kanchipuram sari is to the South. Needless to say, it is a must for every Maharashtrian for auspicious occasions, festive moments and weddings. A Paithani weave is like gara embroidery; it leaves no threads hanging. It is all sealed and doesn’t get entangled with accessories, which always makes brides heave a sigh of relief. Over the years, this heritage weave has been given a contemporary update as modern brides find newer ways of embracing their roots. Most brides opt for tucking the pleats on the sides, and draping the remaining yardage around the neck like a dupatta. Other unique ways to style this sari include swapping the conventional blouse in favour of white shirts and jackets, well-cut tank tops or a T-shirt for the pre-wedding ceremonies. If you wish to channel the royal grace of fore, look to Maharani Chimnabai of Baroda’s signature Nauvari drape, usually paired with a long jacket blouse. Brides can also choose to drape the sari like a gown, reminiscent of the style attributed to Suniti Devi, Maharani of Cooch Bihar. The preparation of the loom is an essential factor to guarantee the accuracy of the weave. The timeline to produce the sari depends on the weaver’s measured and unhurried harmonisation of hand, foot, and eye to create a free-flowing, handmade sari. The creation of a Paithani sari can take anything between six months to two years, depending on the intricacy of the design. The body of sari bears no extra weft-forming figures. The figuring weave is obtained by a plain tapestry technique, and the three major types of weaving include the split tapestry weave, interlocking method, and dove-tailing method. A distinctive characteristic of a Paithani is that both sides of the sari look exactly the same. This makes for a valuable way of distinguishing it from the plethora of Paithani saris made on a power loom and other fakes in the market. Look for the popular colours such as reds, yellows, sky blues, magentas, greens, peach-pinks and purples, as well as the traditional motifs—the Narali (coconut) is usually seen on the border along with pankha or fan shapes. If you wish to extend the longevity of your prized possession, spread the fabric in a dry place after every use and let it breathe for a day. You can even choose to routinely do this when you haven’t worn it for a while. Avoid direct sunlight for prolonged periods, but don’t keep your sari closeted away in a dark space either. Once done airing out the fabric, change the folds and place it in a muslin bag or wrap it with cloth before storing it in a wooden chest or dresser. If you’re taking the piece out of your wardrobe after a long time, use a dry iron first and always start ironing from the reverse side first. Weaving this fabric is a continuous learning ground. We have recreated the Bangadi-Mor (bangle-peacock) motif of Paithani. It was an arduous process, and my weaver warned me that it could take up to three years. This pattern had two rows of overlapping one-and-a-half inch bangle patterns between which peacock motifs, measuring at three-quarters of an inch, were sandwiched. When I visited the Calico Museum of Textiles in Ahmedabad, I observed the Mughal motifs on khadi Paithanis, and it mesmerised the textile designer inside me. What I saw was a few floral motifs that appeared circular from a distance but upon a closer look, you’d find delicate petals that were woven in the squares. These little details can be found in our painstakingly crafted Paithanis, making them timeless classics for connoisseurs. Sari shopping in Delhi? column1: Giambattista Valli is coming soon to an H&M near you
column2: Fashion The Swedish retail giant continues its series of annual designer collaborations—this year, it’s couturier Giambattista Valli who will be bringing his tulle-heavy touch to high street Did we see all the tiered tulle there was to see at the Oscars, the Met Gala or even at Cannes this year? Maybe not. Italian couture legend Giambattista Valli, who can’t resist layers, volume, feathers or long, long trails for some good old-school drama, is bringing all of that to a wider audience. H&M’s tradition of collaborating with designers annually is a winning formula. Previous collaborations have included the likes of Lanvin, Maison Martin Margiela, Viktor & Rolf, Stella McCartney, Versace, Moschino, and the first ever with Karl Lagerfeld back in 2004, which started the trend. The collection was revealed at the amfAR Gala in Cannes last evening. Kendall Jenner, Chris Lee (Li Yuchun), Chiara Ferragni, H.E.R., Bianca Brandolini d’Adda and Ross Lynch were present at the launch event. “I am excited about this collaboration: H&M gives me the opportunity to bring my vision of style and my celebration of beauty to a wider audience. The goal is to share my love for beauty and to be able to be part of everyone’s “happy moments", to help create love stories all around the world,” the designer said in the announcement statement by H&M. While the collection will drop on November 7, a limited pre-collection of the Giambattista Valli x H&M collaboration will be available in 12 selected stores around the world and on Hm.com on May 25. column1: Anita Dongre and other Indian voices at the Copenhagen Fashion Summit
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From leading designers to young brands and tech innovations, here are the Indians representing change at one of the most important forums for sustainable fashion “Somewhere we underplay ourselves, and as a country we're very sustainable, but we try to ape the West and have become more materialistic. 30 years ago, we lived so mindfully—for instance we always had steel tiffins and never plastic. We always conserved; we were very mindful about wasting food. We have rich culture that we can imbibe from, there's so much we can still learn from the villages of India,” Anita Dongre mused at the Copenhagen Fashion Summit. If you had to look at the largest fashion brand to come out of India, Anita Dongre would be it. A regular at the Copenhagen Fashion Summit, Dongre is on the international radar for the sheer size of her company. Along with a couture label, she runs two major high street labels, a jewellery brand and Grassroot—a subset dedicated to ethical fashion. The Grassroot story comes from empowering women in rural India by providing them opportunities to earn a livelihood. “As a woman I measure success as a life well-lived, looked after my family and did what I could do for the society and environment, the balance is important. To me it matters; I would feel [like I've had] a life not lived well if I didn't do something impactful, it would bother me a lot.” At her presentation, ‘Taking the Pulse of the Fashion Industry', Dongre spoke about learning from the villages in India and changing the stance in measuring a company's progress. The designer was also at the CEO lunch hosted by the organisers, where industry leaders like François-Henri Pinault were discussing how a change in leadership could solve the various perils we are facing with climate change. “The top 12 CEOs who met agreed that certain sustainable efforts we take initially will cost us money and we cannot let the fear that that competition's cheaper means will outraise me. This fear is never going to let anyone be sustainable, because all sustainable actions will take a certain investment which companies we will have to absorb it.” Anindit Roy Chowdhury was one of the strongest speakers at the summit. As the global development management specialist – gender justice and human rights, C&A Foundation, Chowdhury spoke about the responsibility of governments in safeguarding human rights for underprivileged factory workers. “About 11 per cent of India's export business is from the garment industry and that is humungous. Not once does the government of India say ‘Make In India responsibly', and that's a big one. Don't just say ‘Make In India' for businesses to flourish; make sure the needs of the workers are also met,” he said. Transparency in supply chain management is crucial for any business that is serious about honouring the tenets of a sustainable business. With the aim of collecting data from one brand that has found the right channels to work with and providing it to others who want to take a similar route, TrusTrace, a software founded by Hrishikesh Rajan and Saravanan Parisutham—who were a part of the Innovation Forum at the summit—is dedicated to finding sustainable solutions through blockchain. Those in attendance were encouraged to learn more about the practical solutions growing in the industry to counter the various repercussions of producing fashion. Young designers like Delhi-based Madhurima Singh of label Dhuri were also invited to speak at other events hosted by the summit during the same week. “I was invited to be on a panel discussion on Modern Slavery in the garment industry. In India, this was organised by the Copenhagen Business School. I was amazed to see the Innovation Forum and the solutions they had come up with, whether it was to make the supply chain completely transparent, waterless dyeing techniques, or new options of eco-friendly and bio-based fabrics. And being amidst these groundbreaking ideas I learnt so much and became aware of the practices I could adopt from the very beginning as an upcoming brand. It was such an enriching experience and I definitely came back a more educated and aware brand owner.” Weddings Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Rihanna unveils her ground-breaking Fenty collection in Paris
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From strong-shouldered corseted trouser suits sold with matching bum-bags and men’s cotton shirting, to multi-pocketed oversized jackets in Japanese raw denim, Rihanna’s foray into the world of fashion is as power-packed as you expected it to be It's no secret that Rihanna marches to the beat of her own drum. At the pop-up store in Paris for a walk-through of Fenty, her debut ready-to-wear collection created in partnership with luxury conglomerate LVMH, she postponed the meeting by one hour, which then turned into a further two-hour delay before she eventually arrived more than three hours late. If this were any other designer, editors would be fuming, loudly staging a mass walk-out. Instead, they were happily shopping. When the fashion world's harshest critics begin purchasing straight from the rails, it's a sure sign that Rihanna has another hit on her hands. The collection—two years in the making and priced from 200 Euros (~Rs 15,000) for a white, waist-cinched T-shirt up to around 1,100 Euros (~Rs 85,000) for a reversible parka—is a round-up of the kind of clothes Rihanna wanted to have in her own wardrobe but couldn't find. “I often walk into stores and I'm like, ‘I love this, but I wish it was more like that, or in a different colour or in a different fabric'—and now I get to do it,” she said, dressed in Fenty's tailored white blazer-minidress hybrid. Highlights included strong-shouldered corseted trouser suits sold with matching bum-bags, men's cotton shirting, and multi-pocketed oversized jackets in Japanese raw denim. “I love strong silhouettes, and for women to look confident, that's what I want to achieve with this collection,” she said. The debut extends, too, to accessories, from point-toe strappy sandals in zingy and neutral hues, to statement shield sunglasses, and bold architectural jewellery in polished gold with crystal pave. “I always had a love of fashion and style,” she explained, adding, “I loved everything my mum wore, from her makeup to her clothing...” I ask what her mum's style was like. “Oh, she was bad ass. She wore a lot of oversized stuff but still very feminine, I just wanted to be her.” Of course, this isn't her first foray into fashion. The 31-year-old was creative director of women's collections for Puma, and she has designed lingerie under the Savage x Fenty moniker. But this is her first experience of working in the luxury sector. “We're using the best fabrics I've ever encountered; everything is so well made. We want the best quality and we want to make something that someone can have forever. I know what's gone into the making of every single piece.” She's tried and tested everything herself and says there is big emphasis on fit. “I'm a curvy girl, if I can't wear my stuff then it just won't work. I need to see how it looks on my hips, on my thighs, on my stomach—does it look good on me or only on a fit model? It's important.” She's also re-writing the way things are done at LVMH. Fenty represents the first major fashion brand that the conglomerate has founded from scratch—not to mention comprising the first luxury fashion brand helmed by a black woman. And, by offering this collection as a direct-to-consumer retail model with new pieces arriving on a six to eight week basis, she's also changing up the fashion production schedule. The first instalment goes on sale on Fenty.com on May 29; the next instalment launches at the end of June. “There is no six-month wait, you get it when you see it,” she said. “There's no tease. You see it, love it, and want it and that's because I'm like that, I want things right away—I see designers' new season [products] and I'm like, ‘Look 11, I need that!'” She laughed. “It's frustrating when you can't buy straight away.” The retail strategy is a first for the luxury conglomerate. “I really appreciate that LVMH is flexible enough to allow me to have a different perspective on how I want to release things,” she said adding, “Mr Arnault [Bernard Arnault, chairman and CEO, LVMH] is not an idiot, he's a very smart man and he's open.” She hopes the customers will be open, too. “There is huge diversity in the collection, which you will see as the new pieces come out, because that's my style,” she said. “I'm all over the place, in sweats one day and a dress the next.” She promises streetwear elements but executed in a luxurious way. Likewise, Rihanna hopes that men will shop from the collection, too. (British Vogue's editor-in-chief, Edward Enninful, purchased the reversible brown and black parka for himself.) “I like to wear men's clothes, I don't like to say, ‘It's a man's thing or a woman's thing.' I hope men and women just wear it because they love it.” With everything she's achieved—eight critically acclaimed albums, 14 US No.1 singles, sell-out tours, nine Grammys, and the not so small matter of her ground-breaking, million-dollar Fenty Beauty line (and its 40 shades of foundation which literally turned the cosmetics world on its head)—does she still feel pressure to out-perform, to do better? “I feel pressure in everything, of course. I care to make it the best and present it in the best way, there is pressure every single second, I feel it… not like crumbling pressure,” she laughed, “but fearlessness is a façade.” It's clear Rihanna isn't one to take stock of her successes and she doesn't seem the reflective type. But you get the sense that she acknowledges the gravitas of this partnership with LVMH. Becoming the first black woman to run a major luxury fashion house surely demands a moment of reflection. “Personally, for me as an immigrant moving to America; that's a big journey for me to even get here to Paris. And that's something I celebrate and embrace,” she said. “I just want to make my boss proud,” she said, referring to Arnault. If the number of editors leaving here with Fenty purchases are any kind of signifier, that's already a done deal. Scroll ahead to take a look at some of the pieces from Fenty's new collection. column1: You have already seen Rihanna’s new Fenty collection
column2: © SplashNews Fashion In case you were wondering what the pop icon's debut collection will look like, we'll you've already seen it Rihanna is set to debut her first Fenty collection with LVMH via a pop-up shop in Paris this week, easily the most highly anticipated fashion drop in recent memory. Still, if you’ve been paying close attention, you’ll know that the musician turned mogul has been test-driving her own creations for months now. Just as she began to incorporate Fenty Beauty’s products into her makeup routine long before they hit stores, Rihanna and style director Jahleel Weever have covertly mixing samples into her outfits both for meetings and public appearances. Fans got their first glimpse at Rihanna’s vision for Fenty back in January, when she headed out to 718 Spank’s concert in New York. Clad in an oversized blazer and Balenciaga’s knife boots, she accessorized with a dramatic pair of shield sunglasses that would later be revealed as her own design. The break from the tiny shades trend caught the attention of the paparazzi and devoted Instagram fans alike, who began to speculate on their origin. Since then, nearly every unidentifiable piece within the star’s wardrobe has been rumored to be a part of the label. Now that a sneak peek video of the campaign has been released on Instagram, some of those missing credits seem to be tracing back to Rihanna’s own hand: the corseted chartreuse mini-dress she wore at Fenty Beauty’s London party back in April, the coral suit and matching fanny pack she chose for a business meeting later that same week—pieces that will soon be available for the masses. column1: Prada and Miu Miu become the latest labels to go fur-free
column2: © Rex Features Fashion As of their spring/summer 2020 collections, the Italian luxury group will no longer use real fur Prada is the latest fashion brand to join the fur-free alliance. As of September, (for their spring/summer 2020 collections) the luxury group, which includes Prada and Miu Miu, will no longer use animal fur in its products, though existing stock will continue to be sold. “The Prada Group is committed to innovation and social responsibility, and our fur-free policy is an extension of that engagement,” said Miuccia Prada in an official statement today. “Focusing on innovative materials will allow the company to explore new boundaries of creative design, while meeting the demand for ethical products.” The decision was reached following “positive dialogue” between the luxury group and the Fur Free Alliance, an international coalition of over 40 organisations—including Lega Anti Vivisezione (LAV) and the Humane Society of the United States (HSUS)—advocating for the protection of animals. Joh Vinding, chairman of the Fur Free Alliance, applauded the Milanese group for the move: “The Prada Group now joins a growing list of fur-free brands that are responding to consumers' changing attitudes towards animals.” Fur Free Alliance programme manager Brigit Oele said the pledge shows “that this global movement is gaining momentum fast. It's very unlikely that fur will ever return as an acceptable trend.” Since the beginning of 2017 alone, Burberry, Versace, Gucci, Chanel, Coach, Donna Karan, Michael Kors, Jimmy Choo, Diane von Furstenberg, Columbia Sportswear, Farfetch, Yoox Net-a-Porter, Burlington, Timberland, The North Face, Furla and Bottega Veneta have all gone fur free. As did London Fashion Week. column1: Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s final Cannes 2019 look took 495 hours to create
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We got an exclusive look at what went into the making of Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s white Ralph & Russo tuxedo for Cannes 2019. Scroll ahead to find out The red carpet makes a fine platform for Sonam Kapoor Ahuja to show off her sartorial prowess, and her choices for Cannes 2019 definitely took things up a notch. Yesterday marked Kapoor Ahuja's last day in the French Riviera, and for her final show-stopping outfit, the actor looked towards her favourite London-based designer duo, Ralph & Russo. But instead of picking a voluminous gown or a hybrid version of a lehenga (remember the one she wore last year at Cannes?), the actor surprised everyone by opting for a tailored suit. “When Sonam and I first started talking about this year's Cannes Film Festival, I suggested right from the start that we go for a tuxedo look as I felt it would be very different for the red carpet, and also something Sonam has never done before—at least on the carpet,” says Tamara Ralph, creative director and co-founder at Ralph & Russo. “Once this was determined, I felt something modern, clean, chic—and a bit sexy—would look amazing on her, and so the white tuxedo was born. I was also inspired by a similar piece from our spring/summer 2019 couture collection,” she adds. The most astounding detail? The piece took a total 495 hours to create. “Out of the 495 hours, 115 hours were dedicated to pattern cutting, and the remaining 380 to fittings, sewing and alterations,” Ralph reveals. Dressed in a silk crepe tailleur with a dramatic overskirt, complete with a two-metre long train, Kapoor Ahuja's outfit brought together the best of both worlds. Ralph says, “With the train, I wanted to keep an element of drama and strength—especially with this being the red carpet and the Cannes Film Festival specifically. It transformed the look into a different one altogether—essentially part gown, part tuxedo.” Kapoor Ahuja skipped the shirt inside, instead choosing to accentuate the plunging neckline with a multi-tiered emerald necklace by Chopard that beautifully offset the white tuxedo. The stark white hue of the Cannes veteran's last outfit was a deliberate decision as well. “When we got to the stage of talking colours, we agreed on something very fresh—and what could be more perfect than a crisp white? It's also very much in keeping with the season, and personally, I love Sonam in white,” Ralph says. To round things off, the actor looked to an elegant pair of pointed-toe heels by Jimmy Choo, and a simple beauty look comprising a middle-parted low bun, kohl-lined cat-eyes and nude lips. column1: Inside the Rocketman wardrobe with Taron Egerton
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ahead of the London premiere of Rocketman, the actor tells Vogue about collaborating with Etro on his red-carpet look, getting into character as Elton John, the crucial details to look out for in the film’s costumes and the one item of clothing he will get to keep from the set Taron Egerton is poised for greatness. The 29-year-old star of Robin Hood, Eddie the Eagle and the Kingsman franchise takes on the role of a lifetime this month as Elton John in Rocketman, the long-awaited fantasy musical about the pop icon's life. After a splashy premiere at Cannes, where he walked the red carpet alongside John himself, the duo are now back on home turf for the next leg of the press tour. Ahead of the film's London debut on May 20, Egerton tells Vogue about working with the Italian fashion house Etro to create his red-carpet look, the crucial details to look out for in the film and the one piece of clothing he will get to keep from the set. “I'm wearing a very beautiful Etro suit to the London premiere. It's more muted than Elton's usual style, but it is very Seventies. I'm fairly new to the brand and my stylist Gareth Scourfield and I absolutely love the cut, fabric and colour of the suits it makes. Its aesthetic is incredibly versatile and there's a wonderful balance between stylishness and exuberance.” “When I first dived into the wardrobe for the film, the first thing I noticed was how empowering it all is. Not only do the clothes make you feel taller and more imposing, but they are intensely expressive. The colour palette, the crazy, sequinned, glittery gorgeousness of it all makes you feel ready to take on the world. When you're performing, those costumes feel like suits of armour. They're about peacocking in a way that makes you feel invincible. I think that's part of why Elton developed this really unique sense of style.” “Rocketman begins and ends with Elton going to rehab. In our story, that happens after a missed concert at Madison Square Garden. He marches to rehab in a costume that is designed to be part of his grand entrance on stage. It's orange neoprene, covered in Swarovski crystals, has these two enormous horns, feathered wings and comes with seven-inch platform heels. It's so clever what Julian Day, the costume designer, has done with it because there's this duality between the devilish and the angelic. It's a metaphor for the struggle between the light and the dark, the struggle between a man in the grips of addiction and a man who wants to find himself again. To cap it all, Elton gave me a diamond earring a year ago and it's the first one he bought for himself in the early 1970s. He made a gift of it to me and I asked Julian if he'd mind me wearing it for this scene. He agreed and so it's in the movie!” “For Elton, nothing is too elevated. It's just a question of self-belief and allowing your personality to come out. What he wears is a celebration of colour, texture and sparkle. As time goes on, we're all less constrained by traditional ideas of masculinity and femininity. I think Elton understood that decades before the rest of us.” “There's a denim jacket I wear for the ‘Tiny Dancer' sequence in the movie that takes place in the early 1970s. It's covered in these embroidered patches, it's very rock and roll, very of its time, but it's also pedestrian enough for me to feel like I could wear it myself. I've been campaigning for many months to have it and Julian emailed me recently to tell me that I'll be getting it next week! I promise that you will see me in it before this press tour is over.” View Gallery 9 Photos Inside the Rocketman wardrobe with Taron Egerton Inside Sonam K Ahuja's Ek Ladki Ko Dekha Toh Aisa Laga wardrobe Fashion in film: The best designer and director collaborations Neeta Lulla on recreating Rani Lakshmibai's wardrobe for Manikarnika What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast
