column1: 50 outfits from Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s Cannes wardrobe over the years
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From her earliest Indian ethnic outings to those princess-perfect ballgowns, here’s charting Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's most memorable looks from the Cannes Film Festival so far It's a universal truth that Aishwarya Rai Bachchan shares a special bond with May, the month that marks her annual sashay down one of the most highly-touted red carpets in the world. Delivering surprises and showstopper moments each time, May is her month to lay rest to the tried-and-tested template of classics and see where the day takes her. From conversation-starting lilac lip colours to frosty Disney princess gowns, everything's fair game in her sartorial rulebook. With another edition of Cannes waiting to unfold alongside the charming locale of the French Riviera, we are dialling the clock back to her fashion evolution at Cannes Film Festival over the years. The former Miss World first rubbed shoulders with Hollywood's finest at Cannes when she made her debut in 2002, and opted for a Neeta Lulla sari in a statement yellow to mark the occasion. She looked to the designer again next year, and took to the red carpet in a lehenga with a pink bustier followed by another sari in a striking shade of neon green that wouldn't have looked out of place on spring/summer runways. After opting for a risqué cut-out gown from the designer the following year, her fashion mood board looked westwards for inspiration, eventually finding a winner in a svelte Gucci gown with a plunging neckline for her walk down the red carpet in 2005. Having hit her stride, Rai Bachchan delivered a showstopper moment at the 2006 edition of the film festival in a strapless Elie Saab number with a bejewelled serpentine neckpiece slinking its way around her neck. After tying the knot amidst much fanfare in April 2007, a glowing Rai Bachchan lit up the French Riviera in an elegant Giorgio Armani gown, which she wore on the red carpet alongside husband Abhishek Bachchan. She loved the look enough to reprise it the next summer with another strapless number from the couturier, before pulling a bait-and-switch from the classic neutral palette to the loud-and-proud fuchsia hues of a sweeping Roberto Cavalli gown. Come 2009, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan gave ivories her vote of approval with a form-fitting Cavalli gown that swept gracefully behind in a ruffled train. The next year marked her return to Indian designers, as she made her appearance in an embellished Sabyasachi sari. The year will also be remembered as the beginning of her love affair with Elie Saab, with a muted lavender number claiming love at first sight for the star. She turned to the Lebanese designer again in 2012, her first post-baby Cannes appearance, and her next walk for the festival had her standing out in Gucci. 2014 served as a landmark year for Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, who returned to Cavalli once again. That gilded number was made to be worn with siren red lips and superstar waves, and the actor didn't disappoint. Following on the heels of the red carpet success, she indulged her experimental side with a dramatic Ralph & Russo number next year and another lacy Elie Saab gown, offsetting the emerald green lace with a deep marsala lip colour. And while the internet-breaking lilac pout and floral gown serve as the lasting legacy of her 2016 stint on the red carpet, the star managed to work in her own flavour of classic romanticism in a delicate Elie Saab number and old-Hollywood waves. By 2017, the actor had clocked in 15 years of appearances at the annual film festival, but proved that she hasn't run out of steam just yet with a voluminous Cinderella-esque gown from Dubai-based couturier, Michael Cinco. Before anyone quite had a chance to catch their breath, she strolled down the red carpet in a full-skirted Ralph & Russo creation with Boomerang-approved tiered ruffles. Last year, Rai Bachchan looked to Cinco to help her deliver another showstopper moment, and boldly strode out of her comfort zone by choosing a butterfly-patterned gown with an embellished train that cut a clear path through the swarm of stars, paparazzi and film folk at the event. Ivory may not necessarily be a novel choice in her Cannes repertoire, but she made the second look her own by teaming the structured Rami Kadi gown with a Samurai-esque top knot. Can't wait to see what Aishwarya Rai Bachchan has up her sleeve for 2019? Until we get a first glimpse, scroll through our gallery below to follow her style evolution at Cannes over the years. column1: Virgil Abloh and Kim Jones join Vogue’s Forces of Fashion Summit line-up
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The annual fashion summit is adding more speakers to discuss the industry’s most pertinent issues, from sustainability to inclusivity Today, a few more speakers are joining the roster for the 2019 Vogue Forces of Fashion Summit. Newly appointed chairman of the CFDA Tom Ford, Tory Burch, Wes Gordon of Carolina Herrera, Kerby Jean-Raymond of Pyer Moss, and Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez of Proenza Schouler are all participating, as are Dior Men's artistic director Kim Jones and Off-White and Louis Vuitton menswear designer Virgil Abloh. Vogue editor in chief Anna Wintour will once again serve as the host of the event. Scheduled over two days in New York City, on October 10 and 11, the summit will include not only impactful Q&As but experiential sessions and group discussions. This year's theme focuses on the future of fashion. Designers, entrepreneurs, and cultural influencers will address topics from sustainability to inclusivity in no-holds-barred, everything's-on-the-table conversations. Stay tuned for more announcements, and be sure to keep checking the official Forces of Fashion website for updates. column1: 11 beige kurtas that are just right for the blazing summer heat
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion White kurtas are great, but this summer, it's time to update your wardrobe with some earthy beige options While kurtas in pastels and whites are a firm summer favourite, this season, why not elevate your wardrobe with the quintessential kurta in shades of beige? From minimal versions sans embroidery to embellished numbers, consider this your one-stop guide on how to incorporate beige in your Indian ethnic wear collection. When it comes to kurtas, Indian designers and labels will leave you spoilt for choice. Today, the market presents a myriad of styles to choose from—asymmetrical hemlines, easy breezy A-line silhouettes, floor-sweeping lengths, straight cuts and kalidaar details being some of them. And just because it's beige, doesn't mean it has to be boring: intricate embroidery and vibrant prints help elevate the nude kurta from its basic status. While labels like Ritu Kumar and Vrisa incorporate floral and geometrical prints on their beige kurtas, Devnaagri pays homage to the rich craft of block printing, and Jayanti Reddy uses the antique art of zardozi. Prefer the ‘less is more' aesthetic? Look towards Lajjo C and Good Earth's minimal offerings that are ideal for lazy Sunday brunches. Feel-good fabrics like cotton, silk, linen and chanderi make them perfect for even the sunniest days. column1: What’s it like when your sister is also your style twin?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From sharing their wardrobe to twinning accidentally-on-purpose, these girls have more in common than just genetics One of the many trends that fashion seems to never let go of is twinning, and both the runways and red carpets offer never-ending proof of it. Even before Instagram hijacked the trend with its widely-used hashtag, the Olsen twins were parading it at countless movie premieres in the late '90s and early 2000s. Having evolved from tweens dressed in preppy chic granny gowns to style icons in their ultra-glam avatars, they are probably the OG flagbearers of this trend. While we often take to twinning with our friends on holidays, brunches and wedding occasions, when it comes to our siblings, nailing this style requires minimum effort. Cases in point: Kendall and Kylie Jenner's feathery ensembles for Met Gala 2019 were a glamorous nod to the trend; the Hadid sisters—Gigi and Bella always nail their street style looks in similar silhouettes; and on the home turf, the youngest Kapoor sisters on the circuit, Janhvi and Khushi, are often spotted making statements in outfits borrowed from each other's closet. So is your sister also your style twin? We get into a discussion with four sets of siblings about their style, and how they end up sharing the same taste in fashion and more. “We are two peas in a pod,” says Aakriti who grew up idolising her elder sister, Sukriti. “We've always been super close, even as kids. I think of her as my confidant—not just because we run a business together but also on a personal level, because we understand each other well,” Sukriti sums up their relationship. The girls believe that they share the same sartorial sensibilities, a primary factor that has led them to start a label together. While Sukriti finds it creatively stimulating to work with her sibling, Aakriti banks on her sister's eye for trends and her styling when it comes to their collections. When it comes their personal style, the sisters admit to sharing their clothes since they were kids. “We're the same size, so I pretty much have her wardrobe at my disposal,” says Sukriti, who borrows her sister's formal wear from time to time. The designer duo are biased towards everything made in cotton, and are comfortable wearing breezy, yet chic Indian wear on a daily basis, often getting mistaken as twins. “If we were ever left in a store and made to choose outfits for each other, we would end up picking the same clothes,” says Kaabia when asked about her and her sister's fashion choices. While the two do enjoy coordinated fashion moments, they do factor in their individual personalities—which distinguishes one's style from another. “We've shared our wardrobes for years, until Kaabia got married. Even though we live in different cities now, we still exchange notes on our latest buys and I can't wait to try on her new Zimmermann pieces,” says Sasha. Known for their statement jewellery pieces, the sisters share their affinity for mixing traditional items with sartorial souvenirs picked up during their travels—a philosophy that seamlessly flows into their brand's design aesthetic. As all twins do, Barkha and Bahaar Peshawaria grew up wearing the exact same outfit for every occasion. Their relationship has remained unchanged over the years. “I have always very protective of Barkha, especially back in school,” quips Bahaar, who believes that she shares not just a sartorial connect with her sister, but also a telepathic one. Over time, they have evolved into different personalities, choosing individual careers for themselves, but they share a similar sense of style. “Your wardrobe automatically doubles when you have a twin, but who gets to wear a new outfit first is always up for debate,” says Barkha, who swears by the accessories her sister collects. Their common sartorial sensibilities can be credited to the fact that they grew up watching their mother and elder sister dress up. While they live in different cities, the duo still relies on each other's unbiased opinions and style tips. Often photographed together for fashion editorials and campaigns, the 19-year-olds are now known faces in the industry. “Most people know us as ‘the twins' and we are okay with it because we know that even though we look alike, we are two different individuals—with common tastes on a few things but distinctly different opinions on some,” says Gayle, who tends towards a chicer side of fashion while Deveney chooses to dress in a more relaxed, casual vibe. While their personal tastes are vary slightly, the girls are currently obsessed with a K-pop band that goes by the name Blackpink. “We are really into Korean fashion trends lately, even KPOP boy bands are quite cool,” says Deveney. So what's it like to grow up with a twin? “It can get quite confusing for people, but it's really important for us to be seen as individuals and in some ways, our sense of style helps us create distinct identities,” says Gayle. 3 sets of seriously stylish sisters decode the dynamics of working together These sisters are creating makeup that looks good on every skin colour Inside the Kapoor sisters' birthday lunch with mom Babita Kapoor What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Vogue’s fashion encyclopaedia: The history of the T-shirt
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Have you found your perfect white T? And more to the point, have you thought about what drives that mission? Vogue dives deep into the history of the T-shirt, to find out how and why it’s become such a fashion classic The T-shirt, now unisex and all-purpose, began its life as an undergarment worn by men. In the Middle Ages, T-shaped shirts made of woven cotton or linen provided a layer between the body and the garments worn over top. These shirts were easy to wash and provided a hygienic barrier for the skin. Wearing a clean, laundered shirt showed off a gentleman's wealth. The shape of the shirt—large, rectangular pieces of cloth sewn into a “T” shape with long shirt tails that tucked between the legs—changed in the 19th century when the shirt tails were removed and the body of the shirt slimmed down to a tighter fit. The T-shirt underwent several significant changes in the 19th century. New knitting technology meant that it could be mass-produced in a more form-fitting shape, with added refinements and in a wider range of textiles such as calico, jersey and wool. Hygienists lauded knit-wool, T-shaped undershirts as protection against colds and bodily maladies, and recommended that women wear them instead of corsets. By the late 19th century, British sailors had begun wearing white flannel T-shirts under their woollen uniforms. At the end of the century, the British Royal Navy began allowing their sailors to wear these undershirts when working on deck. The practice of wearing T-shirts as outerwear was quickly adopted by working-class men on the weekends. In 1880, the US Navy included a loose-fitting flannel shirt with a square neck in its uniform; in 1913, it adopted a white, cotton-knit T-shirt as its official underwear. The cotton dried faster than the flannel and was more comfortable. The T-shirt business boomed in the early decades of the 20th century. The P.H. Hanes Knitting Company began producing men's underwear in 1901, while Fruit of the Loom began marketing T-shirts on a large scale in the 1910s. By the 1930s, T-shirts were standard issue for college sportsmen. In 1938, the American retailer Sears, Roebuck and Company began offering white cotton “gob” (slang for sailor) shirts for sale. “It's an undershirt, it's an outershirt” the advertisement stated, reassuring men that they could “wear it as an outershirt for sports and for lounging, or as an undershirt—it's practical, correct, either way”. By the Second World War, the US Army and Navy were issuing white, short-sleeved, cotton T-shirts to their troops. Wartime and post-war imagery of T-shirt-clad soldiers at war helped popularise the association between the T-shirt and heroic masculinity. “You don't need to be a soldier to have your own personal T-shirt,” Sears proclaimed in 1941. By the time that Hollywood's rising method actors began donning white T-shirts to signal their character's rebelliousness—Montgomery Clift in A Place in the Sun (1951), Marlon Brando in The Wild One (1953) and James Dean in Rebel Without a Cause (1955)—the T-shirt officially entered the man's wardrobe as a garment that could be worn on its own outside of the workplace. It would take another 60 years or so for the T-shirt to be accepted as office attire, though. Worn close to the skin and revealing of the body, the T-shirt's inherent sex appeal was first picked up by actresses and singers in the 1960s. By the 1970s, the T-shirt was truly unisex. In 1977, Jacqueline Bisset scandalised American movie goers with her wet, see-through T-shirt in the movie The Deep. As the T-shirt made its move from underwear to outerwear, the garment became a blank slate for messages, whether political, advertorial, graphic or humorous. Technological advances in silk-screen printing in the early 1960s made it easy, fast and inexpensive to print designs onto shirts. By the 1970s, consumers could have personalised, custom-made T-shirts. Businesses soon realised the potential of T-shirts for marketing, as did bands and music management companies. Because of its association with the working class and the subversive nature of wearing an undergarment on the outside, the T-shirt has appealed to generations of musicians, writers, actors and intellectuals. Rappers donned T-shirts in the 1990s, as did pop stars and models. And while the T-shirt can flatten socio-economic standing—inexpensive T-shirts are worn by a wide range of earners—it can also be a clear mark of conspicuous consumption in its designer versions. High-fashion T-shirts have been marketed since the 1950s and the garment has been reinterpreted by many designers since: from Yves Saint Laurent and Dior in the 1970s, to Chanel, Lacoste, Calvin Klein and Polo Ralph Lauren in the 1990s. Giorgio Armani, Helmet Lang and Nicolas Ghesquière wear the T-shirt as a uniform. Today, it's come a long way from its humble beginnings as a utilitarian garment over a century ago; in fact, it's hard to imagine any wardrobe without a T-shirt. column1: The updated salwar guide you need to bookmark this summer
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From floor-sweeping ghararas to the contemporary dhoti salwar, Vogue rounds up all the trending salwar styles that will help elevate your kurta game Of late, there is an evident shift in the modern-day woman's sartorial choices—especially when it comes to Indian ethnic wear. The salwar suit as we know it no longer commands the attention it once did. With a myriad of reinvented salwar styles put forth on the runway by leading Indian designers, the takers for the traditional salwar style are few and far between. From tapered pants to floor-length ghararas, the silhouettes for the salwar have undergone a massive makeover. With experimentation being the bottom line, it's safe to say that if you're looking to amp up your ethnic wardrobe for summer, start with the new-age salwar styles. While promoting Kalank, Alia Bhatt embraced ethnic wear like never before—from billowy ghararas worn with short kurtas to churidars styled with A-line kurtas and even farshi salwars worn with long kurtas, Bhatt presented a strong repertoire of salwar styles, very consciously barring the conventional one. Sara Ali Khan's approach is fairly similar. For her Kedarnath promotions late last year, the actor put her best foot forward in ethnic wear—there was the shimmering Raw Mango brocade kurta paired with cigarette pants and that long Sukriti & Aakriti kalidar kurta worn with a churidar. And, who can forget the bright neon kurta and sharara set she wore by the same designer duo? Meanwhile, Karisma Kapoor has found the perfect balance between conventional and contemporary styles—the actor routinely opts for tapered trousers or cigarette pants that she styles with her kurta. One of her most recent picks: a layered kurta and pant set by Antar-Agni, styled with fuss-free sneakers. Another win in Kapoor's closet: this elegant Anamika Khanna printed front-open long kurta that was teamed with pants. "Out with the old, in with the new" seems to be the motto for leading designers like Tarun Tahiliani, Payal Singhal, Anita Dongre and more, who are reinventing the salwar with interesting iterations like the dhoti-style salwar, slim-fit trousers, loose pants, shararas and cropped palazzos being some of the biggest hits. column1: This is Student of the Year 2 star Ananya Panday 5-minute morning routine
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Student of the Year 2 debutante reveals her go-to hack for styling crop tops, the social media habit she’s trying to break, and her first red carpet memory Don't let Ananya Panday's diminutive silhouette fool you. This petite 20-year-old has been making big waves even before signing her first movie, and now on the cusp of its release, has plenty to cheer about as the newly minted brand ambassador of high street label, ONLY. Just any other modern-day millennial, she religiously consumes her required quota of water for the day from a flashy bottle, even as she sighs and admits that she needs to stop checking Instagram every other minute. In between takes at the campaign shoot, she kicks back on a couch in a fuss-free tank top and unbuttoned dungarees to give us the 411 on her effortless style. Scroll ahead for the details. I am the type of person who can get ready in precisely five minutes, so I obviously just mix and match and wear whatever I am feeling like on that day. I don't like to wear much makeup when I'm off-duty, so I usually just swipe on my Lakmé lip balm, wear a little mascara and I'm ready to head out the door. An oversized T-shirt, a pair of tiny shorts and sneakers. I believe crop tops can be worn with literally anything, but I think it'd be really cool to pair them with track pants. I'm a serial scroller, and whenever I have a minute to spare, you'll find me on my phone scrolling through Instagram. Limiting my time on the platform is something I really need to do, but I'd advise everyone not to overthink it. There's a lot of fluff out there, so just find yourself and be real. I remember going to the screening of Paa with my mom and dad. I was just 11 back then, so I was in this cute top, jeans and a hairband. I remember holding on to my parents' hands as there were all these lights flashing. I was just smiling away, without really knowing what the pictures were for. In the trailer of the movie, you'll see me doing that “princess” dialogue in a military print jacket that I absolutely love. That's my favourite piece from the movie, and I am trying to low-key steal it from the crew. For a Sunday brunch, you'll find me pairing the short denim skirt with a white tee and sneakers; and for a movie night, I'd choose the statement black jacket with fringe. Denim dungarees make for a really comfortable option for a quick dash to the airport, but if I was at a cosy family dinner, you'd find me in an ONLY tank top and sweatpants. column1: Lust list: 8 elegant chokers that are perfect for the modern bride
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From minimal diamond encrusted chokers to dramatic kundan versions, here’s how you can nail your jewellery game at your wedding If there's one accessory that begets attention when worn, it's your neckpiece. A leading trend this summer, the choker promises to be your best friend when it comes to dressing up your wedding wear. And it has also won the approval of leading celebrities like Kareena Kapoor Khan, Alia Bhatt and Janhvi Kapoor, most of whom have opted to wear the neckpiece as a stand-alone accessory sans any other distracting jewellery. Considering the scorching summer heat, it's a given that high-neck ethnic ensembles will be given a miss at wedding functions this season, with the emphasis maintained on low necklines—featuring the perfect canvas to show off your precious jewels. Whether it's a minimal diamond choker or a dramatic kundan number, industry experts believe wearing a choker for a summer wedding is a fail-proof pick. “While chokers have been around for many years, it's a trend that has appeared more recently in wedding wear,” says Josina von dem Bussche-Kessell, global sales director, Fabergé. “The modern day woman is approaching her look as a whole, focusing on how jewellery can balance the entire outfit,” she adds. Investing in a statement neckpiece also removes the requirement of layer multiple ones. “During summers, we don't feel the need to wear a lot of heavy jewellery, and a statement choker cuts out the need to wear multiple necklaces,” explains Kiran Datwani, founder, Gehna Jewellers. “They work beautifully with different necklines and can be easily dressed up or down, according to your style.” Sangeeta Dewan, principal designer, Zoya, adds that wearing a choker brings attention to your face, neck and collarbones. “Chokers are unique because they have a universal appeal and are versatile—they look equally good with western gowns and saris,” she explains. Do your sartorial sensibilities point you in the ‘more is more' direction, or does minimal design cut it for you? For brides, the trend seems to point towards the former. “Simplicity in bridal jewellery is more on the decline with brides opting for bolder, statement styles, and a choker can be an elaborate way of portraying this,” says Bussche-Kessell. If you're a bridesmaid or a guest attending a wedding, you can pick between either styles. But Nishant Tulsiani, co-founder, Anaqa Jewels, recommends keeping things understated. “Beat the heat by keeping the choker light to make a formal yet minimal style statement.” Meanwhile, Zoya's Dewan has a particular style in mind for summer. “Chokers with dangling pearls and stones look gorgeous as they drape the neck,” she concludes. Ahead, Vogue rounds up eight statement chokers that will help you ace your summer wedding look. column1: Sonam Kapoor Ahuja attends Michael Kors’ new store opening in London
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The actor was spotted at the glamorous launch with other A-listers including Kate Moss, Gemma Chan and Jourdan Dunn. Scroll ahead for an exclusive first look inside Michael Kors’ new London store Shopping today can sometimes feel a little cold and impersonal,” sighs Michael Kors. The designer—who told press, “I don't wanna sound like Pollyanna but the reality is, I think fashion's joyous,” after his last show—has channelled his passion for fashion and interior design acumen into his latest London outpost. Kors fell for the Georgian townhouse on Old Bond Street immediately, owing to its charming façade, and set about making it feel like home. “We wanted to achieve a sense of residential ease with a personal touch, like you're relaxing in your own living room, or mine,” Kors tells Vogue ahead of the ribbon cutting. “We all live such busy lives—I think our customers will appreciate being able to step inside and feel a world away from the bustle of the city.” He drew on the “warm modernist” interiors of his cross-coastal homes more than he has done before for his 1,000-plus stores. “I prefer design and decor that is streamlined but still inviting,” he muses. “I have taken the same sensibility and infused it into our store, with a neutral palette, landscape artwork and rich wood, steel and marble finishes throughout.” The first pictures shared exclusively with Vogue emulate the shortbread-hued furniture and treasure-laden shelves in his (latest) holiday home in Florida. His search for serenity—“Getting into nature is important,” he told British Vogue's fashion features editor Ellie Pithers in the March 2018 issue. “Not that I'm hiking and eating granola. But I need to decompress, be in that chilled, barefoot zone”—has followed him across the Atlantic. As well as the “fabulous neutral linen and cream leather touches for glamour”, Kors instructed his team to embrace the history of the building and its features, including the original fireplaces and brass fixtures. “Everything has been customised though, from the hangers to the Eero Saarinen chairs, which we have had reupholstered,” he says keenly. “This is a new store concept for us and I think that it demonstrates how we see luxury today.” Kors believes that the sumptuously peaceful setting in which to indulge will appeal to a London audience, because they will be able to place special orders on evening wear and purchase Bond Street exclusives. He is also positive that the sportswear will fly. “In a big city, our customers are looking for clothes and accessories that make them look and feel great, and that don't slow them down.” As always with Michael Kors, there's something to satisfy everyone in his broad customer base. The difference with the Bond Street store is that he goes beyond to make the Michael Kors proposition personal, too. The launch of the charming new space saw Kors host a number of A-lister names to celebrate, including none other than Sonam Kapoor Ahuja, Kate Moss, Gemma Chan, Jourdan Dunn, Erin O'Connor and more. column1: Louis Vuitton wants to turn your bag into a portable TV
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As part of their resort 2020 show, Louis Vuitton had models carrying bags with functioning canvas video screens on their sides In 1962 Eero Saarinen revolutionised architecture with his TWA Flight Center, an avian—or maybe alien—shape looming over the the outskirts of John F Kennedy (then called Idlewild) airport. Fifty seven years later, Nicolas Ghesquière landed on that secret spot to revolutionise your handbag. Among the Elizabethan-meets-disco ruffs, Blade Runner suiting, and Chrysler Building embellishment, shown as a part of Louis Vuitton's Resort 2020 show were a handful of bags with functioning canvas video screens on their sides. Called the “Canvas of the Future,” LV's latest bags are a prototype, the first of their kind to walk a runway show. The moldable, flexible screens are made of AMOLED technology—the same LED lights found in some smartphones—and allow for a 1920 x 1440 resolution. The goal, according to a press release from Louis Vuitton, is to eventually blur the lines between your smartphone and your sac. For those old enough to remember a time before smartphones, well, they'll note this isn't the first time a TV has appeared on the LV runway. All the way back in October 2007, i.e. the earliest days of the iPhone, Marc Jacobs, Vuitton's artistic director at the time, took his bow at the end of the Spring 2008 show carrying a mini trunk with an LED screen playing Spongebob Squarepants. The reference was punny, coming at the end of Jacobs's inaugural collaboration with Richard Prince, and pointed. Earlier in the season, Jacobs had been accused of plagiarising colour schemes and silhouettes from Comme des Garçons's Rei Kawakubo for his Surrealist eponymous collection shown in New York. “I'm a fan of SpongeBob SquarePants—and for all I know, so is Rei Kawakubo, because that's where our colour came from!” he told Sarah Mower at the time. column1: Style face-off: Ananya Panday vs Tara Sutaria
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion With their debut film Student of the Year 2 slated to hit the silver screen this weekend, these two young actors are working hard to earn their style stripes. We compare their sartorial sensibilities ahead of the big release As the newest kids on the block, it's a given that all eyes are on Ananya Panday and Tara Sutaria right now. Their debut film, high school drama Student of the Year 2, is part deux of the popular Dharma Productions franchise that launched bona fide stars Alia Bhatt, Varun Dhawan and Sidharth Malhotra back in 2012—so one can safely assume that the duo is striving to emerge at the top of this class much like their predecessors. And under the tutelage of Karan Johar, it's a given that their acting prep came accompanied with after-school style lessons. Both the leading ladies have already found their own fashion footing, and feature decidedly distinct style sensibilities. So who's winning that gold? Or will Panday and Sutaria share the metaphorical sartorial trophy? We're reaching for our binoculars to track the race. High school heart breaker—the textbook popular girl who every boy crushes on, and every girl secretly vies to be—just about sums up Sutaria's personal style. While her go-to look is inherently girly-girl, it's also unabashedly traffic-stopping with every outfit underlined with a hint of oomph. And with a wardrobe replete with look-at-me hues like tangerine orange and fluorescent brights, you have a burgeoning style maven who doesn't shy away from the spotlight. Crop tops are a much-favoured constant in her closet—be it a white off-shoulder variant worn with blue jeans or a bandeau top teamed with a matching skirt. Sutaria loves her form-accentuating minis too, and often coordinates her two preferred staples as matching sets. Add to that pink and white pointy-toe heels, and you have an overall repertoire that is the epitome of millennial Barbie. While Panday comes across as the quintessential rich brat in the movie's trailers, her off-screen persona is more Miss Congeniality, post-makeover that is. The Betty to Sutaria's Veronica, she succeeds in bringing glamour to the girl-next-door narrative. More sparkle and less high ponytails and basic jeans, Panday's wardrobe is doused in high shine ensembles that she wears to parties and movie screenings with equal ease. Think rainbow-hued sparkly blouses with matching skirts, a sequin-spangled pencil midi, and a shiny jersey top with denim cut-offs. But she also balances the glitter with relaxed silhouettes like denim boiler suits and oversized jersey dresses. As a '90s kid, her closet is not without age-appropriate elements that give it millennial cool cred—a Bart Simpson print blazer, an army of sneakers and clog heels, and nostalgic polka dots can all be found inside. Panday also demonstrates a definite penchant for short suits (from checks to geometric prints), often worn with crop tops. column1: These pieces of pearl jewellery are nothing like your grandma’s old sets
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Pearls are being redefined for summer, but which jewellery designs should you be investing in? Vogue finds out from the best in the business Pearls are back, and one thing's for certain—they are not your grandma's pearls. It's all about pearl head-to-toe—from jewelled barrettes, mother of pearls dangling from earrings, pearls on denims and pearls on summer sandals. We spoke to the founder and CEO of Moksh, Milan Chokshi, who is doing anything but ordinary things with pearls, to know more about the latest trend. The choice of the star piece in their latest collection of jewellery? Keshi pearls in all shapes and sizes—one of the rarest jewels in the world. Keshi pearls are one of several products we source from Japan. The pearl is nothing but pure nacre; as uncultured pearls, it isn't produced by a mollusk (like an oyster or a snail), there is no nucleus inside, and thus is highly treasured. Because Keshi pearls are made up of pure nacre, there is nothing to stop the reflection of light—making them extraordinarily lustrous. And the colour and lustre remains unchanged even through time. As they are formed without a nucleus, their shapes tend to be more baroque, however the round Keshi that we use is extremely rare. Other shapes include rice, oval, flat and semi-round. The word Keshi is actually Japanese for poppy seed, hence the nickname the ‘Poppy Seed Pearl'. Known as ‘the gifts of the mermaids,' these pearls were worn with pride for centuries by Arabian princesses—their special lustre creates a remarkable radiance when worn on the skin. Pearls sourced from five different countries and multi-coloured gemstones from five others countries makes this a truly global collection. We are planning to launch in the US, India as well the far East. Jackie Kennedy famously said “Pearls are always appropriate.” There will never be a dearth of elegant women who want lustrous beautiful pearls, but there definitely is a finite quantity of natural pearls available. [As] brooches—a very elegant and regal accessory that's making a huge comeback globally. And it complements Indian outfits just as much as western ones. A beautifully crafted pearl brooch is a must-have. Our ‘Emerald Chaandbali' is created after layering multiple components. We used various raw materials, milgrain work along with different types of gemstones, set in one piece. column1: This is how Deepika Padukone pulled off her Met Gala look in 24 hours
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How do you stay calm when you have only 24 hours until the Met Gala 2019 begins, and you haven’t even tried your show-stopping gown? Deepika Padukone shows us how it's done “What's life without a few risks, right?” Deepika Padukone's meaningful question is apt considering the circumstances she was in hours before she walked the pink carpet at Met Gala 2019. The actor touched down in New York just a day prior to the annual event, and headed straight from the airport to Zac Posen's studio for a first look at her intricately embroidered strapless pink gown. “I've been seeing sketches and some ideas, but this is the moment when I see it for the first time,” she revealed to Vogue US in a special pre-Met video that's now on YouTube. “Oh my god. It's incredible, look at that!” Padukone squealed when she caught a first glimpse at the theatrical number with a look of awe on her face. “It's not a dress, it's like art!”. And art it was, when the actor twirled across the studio in the beautifully sculpted creation. “We wanted the whole form [the sculptural outfit] to move with the train. That's a good red carpet dress,” Posen said as he made last-minute adjustments. After finalising her jewellery (and perfecting her spins), Padukone also allowed her fans all over the world into her dressing room on the day of the Met Gala 2019, showing them how much effort and time goes into getting ready for a celebration as big as this one. With less than three hours to go, the actor admitted that her excitement was slowly transforming into nervousness. “There are these beautiful sea urchins that Zac has done—it has a metallic purple, and that was the starting point for the eyes,” Padukone explained as her makeup artist deftly applied shimmering purple eyeshadow on her lids. “This is probably the most adventurous look I've ever tried. The theme for today really allows everyone to have fun, and I've always been open to experimenting.” Camp, the Met Gala's theme, is indeed open to experimentation—and Padukone admitted that her husband Ranveer Singh would have made a great candidate for the pink carpet this year. “He has this crazy sense of dressing. He would be a perfect fit for tonight as he would do hundred per cent justice to the theme. But I'm representing him tonight,” she smiled, while checking out his Instagram feed and his latest post, another outrageously fun OOTD shot. With her dramatic hairdo and bold makeup ready, Padukone spent her last few minutes before leaving her hotel room checking out Lady Gaga's theatrical entrance (“She just pulls it off. Four looks!” she observes). As for her own hyper-Barbie look, “We wanted to keep it super elegant and beautiful, but really hit the nail on the theme camp," hairstylist Gabriel Georgiou tells Vogue India. "Deepika is super daring, and she was ready to go all out for the Met. We created this big hairstyle with a hair piece and padding to create the height and volume, which definitely feels heavy on her head! But we want her to feel comfortable, so obviously that is important and we tweak it to work for her.”   Slipping into her ostentatious gown, Padukone couldn't help but reminisce about her own childhood. “I feel like Barbie,” she laughed, as she perfected her purple lip colour in a light-up portable mirror. “A new trick I've learnt is to use numbing cream on my feet so that they don't hurt from the heels that we have to wear for 5-6 hours at least.” And just like that, in 24 hours, Padukone was ready to hit the red carpet. How does one beat the nerves before walking out to a sea of photographers? Padukone found release in an impromptu dance performance to her own track, 'Deewani Mastani' from Bajirao Mastani. column1: Elle Fanning’s Met Gala muse is 1970s Barbie
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As she hits the Met Gala red carpet, the actress’s stylist Samantha McMillen breaks down her look for Vogue – from the outlandish accessories to her unexpected style muse A front-row regular since her teens, Elle Fanning mastered the red-carpet princess moment long ago—just think of her in lavender tulle Rodarte at the Cannes premiere of The Beguiled or caped Valentino couture at the Berlin International Film Festival. So, when the Met Gala theme calls for all-out glamour via “camp”, what's a girl to do? Turn up the volume, obviously. “Elle's been one of the faces of the Miu Miu campaigns for a while,” explains the actress's stylist Samantha McMillen, who is also behind Brie Larson's best looks. “This year, she's going with Prada and wearing Miu Miu.” The look? A two-piece comprised of a crop top and bell-bottom trousers, offset with some spectacular accessories. Below, McMillen breaks down the outfit for Vogue. Image credit: Getty “Camp is such a fun theme to work on with Mrs Prada. Throughout her career she's executed so many looks that are technically camp, but in this incredibly beautiful, fashionable way. She's great at taking a concept like that and making it universal. At the Met Gala, you always need to take into account the designer who has invited you and then think about how the theme could be melded together with their work.” “We wanted to see what the brand would come up with, but we also took our ideas to them. For instance, Prada and Miu Miu use a lot of oversized charms—whether it be on a keychain or big brooches—and we were inspired by those 1980s necklaces with the kitschy plastic charms that you can take on and off because Elle's mum has been collecting them for years. So we took that concept to Miu Miu and they made big, chunky charm necklaces for us to layer. The charms make them really special. There are ones that say: ‘The Met', ‘Camp' and ‘2019', and smaller ones with flowers, animals and unicorns. There's even a charm that is a cameo of Elle, with a picture of her from the last Met Ball she went to, the one in 2017 where she had the blue Miu Miu gown and vintage tiara. So it's meta and it's camp!” “Because of the necklaces, the rest of the look needed to be rather simple. With the outfit itself, we went for a 1970s Barbie vibe. It's Elle, but to the nth degree—super Barbie-ish and super camp. I also love that salmon pink colour. Elle loves to wear pastels, so we wanted it to be in keeping with the tones she likes, but also to pump it up a bit and be bolder.” “The Met Gala is a lot of fun, but it can be tough depending on the theme. In the past, it didn't matter as much if you went with the theme or not, but that's completely changed in the last six or seven years. Now, people are really hardcore about embracing it. There are so many things you can do with Camp: Notes on Fashion. I think the last time people had this much fun was probably with the Punk: Chaos to Couture theme in 2013. The best part is that it's about the designers. It's their night, so it's fun when they can express themselves through their art and even better when they take guests who really bring those creations to life.” The best celebrity hair and makeup looks from Met Gala 2019 Isha Ambani makes a statement at the Met Gala 2019 in Prabal Gurung You can't miss Natasha Poonawalla's Dundas dress at the Met Gala 2019   Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Cardi B’s Met Gala 2019 gown had 30,000 feathers and a three-metre train
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The award-winning rapper’s custom Thom Browne gown for Met Gala 2019 took 35 people and 2,000 hours of work Last year was Cardi B's first Met Gala, and naturally she made it count. Cardi arrived at the divinely themed Gala in a gem-encrusted Moschino gown fit for a queen, showing off her baby bump in the process. After spending months concealing her pregnancy with belly-obscuring peplums and A-line skirts, Cardi opted for a look that accentuated her maternity curves—plunging neckline, bump-hugging waist, and a daring leg reveal. This year, though, the singer went for something much more reserved. She showed up to the Met Gala red carpet completely covered up, head to toe, in an anatomically accurate, oxblood custom Thom Browne gown that extends outward in concentric circles for about ten feet (three metres). Made from tulle and silk organza and filled with down, the hand-embroidered dress is also decorated with 30,000 burned and dyed coque feathers. It took 35 people more than 2,000 hours to create, and it's finished off with a bugle-bead headpiece that Browne made in collaboration with Stephen Jones. Browne says he was inspired first and foremost by the female form. “I designed this dress for Cardi specifically because she has the ultimate beauty in a woman's body, and that is what the dress is about for me: taking advantage of that beauty,” the designer says. In spite of its full coverage, the dress really does emphasise certain areas—there are yonic embellishments, a heart-shaped cutout on the backside, and ruby nipples. Only Cardi could manage to show no skin yet still draw attention to every single body part. column1: Lady Gaga makes an epic Met Gala entrance in four statement outfits
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Check out the performance that launched a thousand memes Lady Gaga certainly knows camp. column1: Isha Ambani makes a statement at the Met Gala 2019 in Prabal Gurung
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Prabal Gurung was Isha Ambani’s choice of designer for Met Gala 2019. Vogue takes you inside the making of the statement look for the evening Businesswoman and modern-day heiress Isha Ambani is no stranger to the Met Gala. As a supporter of the Fine Arts, Ambani's presence at one of the biggest events hosted to celebrate the legacy of fashion comes as no surprise. Today, she was among the women to be dressed by Prabal Gurung for the Met Gala. Ambani and Gurung collaborated and arrived at a lavender gown keeping in mind the theme for this year's gala, “Camp: Notes on Fashion”, which is a play on Susan Sontag's iconic essay “Notes on ‘Camp'”. The themes for the Met Gala often throw a curveball and make attendees work hard on matching the dress code of The Costume Institute's exhibition for the year. Ambani's look, which comprised of a full-skirted lavender couture gown, didn't disappoint. "We've been working on this together for many months. With the camp theme, we wanted to celebrate the exuberance and essence of who Isha is," Gurung said about coming together with Ambani's red carpet look. "We chose to highlight her spirit through the glamorous silhouette and the intricacies of the hand embroidered feathers and beadwork. In keeping with the theme, we had a vision of Isha in a magical, dreamlike state and looked to the work of Degas' ballet dancers, evoking an ethereal and romantic quality where the power of her femininity is heightened. We took a couture approach and played with the proportion of her skirt." But that's not all. Friend and mentor Priyanka Chopra had a special role to play in the making of Ambani's Met Gala look too. "We worked very closely with Isha through the entire process," Gurung says. "We started conceptualising the look in the winter and began the fitting process a couple of months ago. We had three fittings in India, where we made tweaks to the colour, fabric, and overall fit, and had a final fitting in our New York Atelier on Saturday. Priyanka Chopra stopped by for that one and we all had a collaborative conversation on styling the accessories, hair and makeup to elevate the camp look." Chopra also happens to be part of this year's Benefit Committee, and made an appearance with husband Nick Jonas. This is not the first time Isha Ambani has attended the Met Gala. Back in 2017, she was dressed in a Dior couture number for the “Rei Kawakubo/Comme des Garçons: Art of the In-Between” gala. Still in line with her feminine aesthetic, Ambani's lavender number was a balance of delicate detailing and statement-making volume. Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s guide to wearing anarkalis like a celebrity
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From heavily embroidered anarkalis to subtle everyday options, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s wardrobe has an anarkali for almost every occasion Aishwarya Rai Bachchan is known for many things, but a boring wardrobe is definitely not one of them. Whether she's walking down red carpets or simply attending weddings in the city, she is always dressed to impress, more often than not in anarkalis. Take a closer look at her repertoire over the years, and you'll notice how she has always banked on the traditional silhouette to make an impact. From bright coloured anarkalis to simple white numbers, there's no dearth of options in her closet. If you've been following Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's style, you'd be aware that the actor has a special spot for Manish Malhotra creations. For the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne (IFFM), Rai Bachchan chose a studded white and blue anarkali that's perfect for the minimalists. When the occasion warranted an all-out ensemble, she's often picked highly embellished anarkalis, just like the heavily embroidered variant she wore for her Diwali party. Rai Bachchan also has a flair for white anarkalis. (Remember her ivory high-shine outfit for Anushka Sharma and Virat Kohli's Mumbai reception?) column1: The 10 commandments of camp fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Camp is a subject so complex that the task of defining it would give even Hercules pause. But that’s the theme of the latest Met Gala and accompanying exhibition, “Camp: Notes on Fashion”, which will launch, probably in an eruption of feathers and sequins, on May 6. Here, fashion designer Alejandro Gómez Palomo gives a masterclass on camping up your style To say the Met Gala has always been a bit camp is like saying Diana Ross is quite good at singing. But the exhibition itself is always scholarly and this year's is no exception. Andrew Bolton, curator of the Costume Institute at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, used Susan Sontag's seminal 1964 essay Notes on Camp as a starting point. “[Sontag wrote that] in naïve or pure camp, the essential element is seriousness, a seriousness that fails,” Bolton told Vogue in a recent interview. “People have a definite idea of what camp is, that it's superficial, about gay men and transvestites. And it is that, but it's many other things too.” It can be Princess Diana in the 1980s; Joan Collins in the 1970s; John Waters just about whenever; drag queens and Quentin Crisp; Björk in a swan dress; or Marc Jacobs in any dress. It is a broad church that welcomes nearly all worshipers. One of the things it definitely takes in is the work of Alejandro Gómez Palomo, the 27-year-old designer behind Palomo Spain. Palomo founded his brand in 2015 shortly after graduating from the London College of Fashion, and has shown in Paris, Madrid and New York in the campest of styles ever since. His exuberant, gender-agnostic designs—which have drawn inspiration from a cast ranging from Louis XIV and Ballet Russes' Serge Diaghilev to Virginia Woolf's Orlando—have included raven-feathered dresses, sheer bodysuits trimmed with sequins, periwinkle bouclé jackets paired with knee-high boots, and bunched Bermuda shorts. Modelled by androgynous male models, and favoured by the likes of Beyoncé and Years & Years frontman Olly Alexander, Palomo's work so strongly appealed to Bolton that he included six Palomo Spain looks in “Camp: Notes on Fashion”. Garlanding Palomo in such a way—alongside the likes of Gucci's Alessandro Michele and Dutch couturiers Viktor & Rolf—pushes the designer into the ranks of a bona fide camp icon. But if you'd ever seen one of his shows you'd know this already. Here he delivers his 10 commandments for camping up your personal style. “Think like fashion designer Charles Jeffrey or stylist Luke Jefferson Day or, you know, myself—I'm camp, I dress up. Modern camp is more than being extravagant or, you know, glamorous or dramatic, it is about doing all that in a very natural way, an almost divine way. It is extravagance on its own terms. Extravagance that it is meant to be. Treat every day as if it is your last moment to make an impression.” “Never leave the house without your pearls, wear them at all times,” says Palomo, following the tradition of Britain's late Queen Mother, who wore a three-strand necklace even while visiting bombed-out buildings during the Second World War and summoned servants by means of a Fabergé pearl bell (“my Borgia bell”, as she called it). As Palomo points out, “Pearls need to be looked after, they need the heat of your body or they die—so wear them when cleaning or cooking. They light your face up so nicely, after all. I think it is very good way to put you in a good mood for the whole day.” It certainly worked for Her Majesty, who lived to 101, had five houses and departed this earth with a £7 million overdraft at Coutts Bank. “I have always been drawn to feathers. Everyone has had a feather boa at some point, no? My mother had one when I was growing up, though she never wore it—I have made up for that since. It was so wonderfully ridiculous,” says Palomo. By bringing together the notion of the “wonderfully ridiculous” and feathers, the designer may have in mind the late romantic novelist Dame Barbara Cartland who was deeply imbued with the first and was seldom seen without the latter. She sold two billion copies of her novels and always had some pink plumes about her person. “Feathers,” Palomo says correctly, “are everything.” “Who wants to look simple and minimal!” exclaims Palomo. “I think we get excited about textures and details and all those things.” To understand this commandment in all its full sequined glory, we suggest watching the 1932 film Blonde Venus where the late Marlene Dietrich cavorts around a cabaret stage in a sequined dress trimmed with feathers, two enormous chains of faux, oversized pearls and a blonde wig pierced by two silver Cupid's arrows. “More is more!” says Palomo. Amen to that. “Moire is an old and incredibly excessive, glamorous fabric. It comes in all these wonderful shades and changes with the light,” says Palomo. Created by a finishing technique called calendaring, it gives wool, silk, or sometimes cotton, a watermarked appearance and first came on the scene in the Middle Ages as a facing for dresses. Later it was adopted by those twin icons of camp, Roman Catholic cardinals, who use it for the enormous red silk cloaks they wear at parties, and Russian tsars, who had liked the sash of their orders of chivalry to be in a nice, light-blue moire (see Paul Delaroche's portrait of Peter the Great for inspiration). Palomo advises wearing “moire as frequently as you would wear a pair of jeans. I think it's time for it to make a big comeback.” “Leopard, zebra, python—don't mind the species if you wear animal print: just wear them all together. Ditto with florals—pair a rose-print frock with a daisy-patterned stocking and a broad-brimmed hat decorated with sunflowers. It works with herringbone, houndstooth, pretty much everything. Make it overwhelming. It is perfect, perfect, perfect.” “Christian Lacroix's costume jewellery from the 1980s and 1990s—all those bedazzling gemstones and intricate detailing—is the epitome of over-the-top glamour,” says Palomo. Call it rococo, baroque or just extra, Lacroix was never dull. As he told Vogue's Suzy Menkes in a 2017 interview, “I didn't think about fashion [when I was a couturier]; I thought about theatre.” Quite a camp statement in itself. Palomo agrees: “‘Over the top' elevates the person who is wearing it. These little touches every day makes you feel that bit better, that bit happier.” That great arbiter of such things, Victoria Beckham, had this one covered when she declared on British television, “I can't concentrate in flats!” A sentiment Palomo can get behind. “Ever since I started doing men's heels, I've been wearing them every day of my life. Now I feel ridiculous when I don't wear them. It is this whole other way of elevating yourself. The taller you are, the better you feel,” he declares. Or, as ever-camp Bette Midler said of vertiginous heels, “Give a girl the correct footwear and she can conquer the world.” “Not so long ago everything was about restraint: the little black dress, in particular. Now it's more about putting on your makeup. The more out there, the more drag, the better,” Palomo says. The drag scene, such as we know it, started in the 1950s and 1960s, but it was in the 1980s that the form took on its current guise: using makeup to wholly transform the self. It is a little art form all of its own—and one happily now copyable from one of hundreds of YouTube clips. “So, drag is the new black and before you go out in it, throw a little glitter over your look to make it that little bit extra.” “I think it's important to take liberties daily as a way to express ourselves. Frills are the perfect example of that because they are fundamentally unnecessary. They are that little bit extra, an expression of a person who is not scared of showing who he or she is,” says Paloma. And if it isn't wholly clear how extra they can be, you need only Google “Princess Diana in frills in the 1980s” and you will quickly be assailed by more pie-crust collars and ruffles than you thought could possibly adorn any one 20-something princess. column1: At Rs 81,000, Givenchy’s newest sunglasses are the OTT pair you need
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Givenchy’s crystal-encrusted sunglasses are clearly the most extra way to shade yourself from the sun Sunglasses are one of the most practical investments you can make in regards to your wardrobe. Not only are they designed to shield your eyes from the sun, but they're also an easy way to hide insomnia, jet lag, or protect your anonymity (should you be a celebrity hiding from the paparazzi). Sure, sunglasses are sometimes cast in poppy pastels or encrusted with glitter, but it doesn't mean they're any less practical. Givenchy, however, have taken this notion of practically and married it with frivolity, creating what can only be described as a statement piece of jewellery masquerading as eyewear. Givenchy artistic director Clare Waight Keller has named the accessory the GV Shower—inspired by rain showers and the idea of “nature's perpetual state of transformation”, she says, adding she took inspiration from the notion that “in springtime, ice melts into water”. [#image: /photos/5ce40f8e3bf9b41839b1a817]||| ||| Image: GoRunway One glance at the hundreds of crystals dripping from the frame, and the “shower” reference is clear. The sunglasses originally came about as the Mask shape from the spring/summer '18 collection, but the newly added Shower style features “Swarovski crystals that enhance the frame and spill into a cascade of crystals at the temples,” Waight Keller explains. The crystals will undoubtedly catch not only your eye, but also the eyes of everyone you pass. Also, given the frames are intended to mimic rainfall, they may be a good way to destress via retail therapy if the soothing sounds of a storm help you sleep at night. Now available in Givenchy boutiques around Australia, this piece will set you back a cool $1164 (~Rs 81,000), but that's a small price to pay for such an iconic fashion investment. The lenses are available in clear or tinted options and the nose pads are also adjustable. One thing is certain: if you're looking to make a statement with your accessories in 2019, Givenchy just solved all your problems. This article originally appeared on Vogue.com.au Audrey Hepburn fan? column1: These celebrities prove that beige is definitely not boring
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Alia Bhatt and Priyanka Chopra to Meghan Markle, celebrities are giving a nod to beige this year. Ahead, we give you all the inspiration you need to ace the trend 2009 belonged to beige. Industry heavyweights like Chanel, Valentino and Max Mara brought pastel and nudes to the catwalk. Fashion, known for its revolving doors of trends, is now scrolling through its archives 10 years later to bring back earth-toned colours for 2019. Coco Chanel famously said, “I take refuge in beige because it's natural,” and this spring, designers took refuge in this neutral, versatile and sophisticated shade in both experimental and traditional manners. There were classic trench coats at Burberry, free-movement pleated skirts at Christian Dior, sandy cropped jackets at Fendi, stone-toned suits at Tibi, and tea-stained athleisure by Jil Sander. Shades of oatmeal, toast, cappuccino, sand, biscuit, and the never-ending spectrum of beige, worn head-to-toe, won designers' approval this season. The hue found patrons among the A-lister too, with stars like Priyanka Chopra and Meghan Markle all putting together seriously cool beige looks. As a starting point, beige works as a building block in any wardrobe, and can be worn with almost everything. Chopra, for example, styled beige with sharp contrasting colours, while Sonakshi Sinha opted for a glittering beige sari by Manish Malhotra. For those weary of the head-to-toe look, try off-the-moment colour pairings of beige + neon, beige + animal print and beige + checks. You can lift a khaki jumpsuit with bright orange heels; an oversized coffee coloured trench goes best with snakeskin boots; and a checked shirt can make a beige suit pop. Alternatively, you can also go down the puritan route by wearing a nude shirt under the suit to stay true to the all-over beige look that the street style set are really into this season. column1: 10 pictures that will take you inside Padma Lakshmi’s wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Padma Lakshmi’s signature style is a study in the power of classics. Below, we decode her personal and red carpet style As a celebrity chef, producer, model, TV host and mother, Padma Lakshmi is a proud multitasker of the 21st century. And if her jet-set lifestyle takes a toll on her time, you'll be hard-pressed to find proof of it. Whether she's stepping on the red carpet or lounging by the waves, this modern-day multi-hyphenate exudes her own brand of effortlessness—all while treading over dated notions of age-appropriate dressing. From plunging necklines to daring bikinis, Lakshmi's top sartorial picks serve as a masterclass in dressing your outside to match the inside. Take notes. Now at 48, Lakshmi is living her best life yet, hopping from her work commitments at Top Chef to sun-kissed days by the pool with her daughter As the host of the Emmy-winning show, her work closet eschews the usual line-up of staple workhorses in favour of non-boring silhouettes. The onset of summer had her opting for a strapless midi dress from Veronica Beard, doused in a merry riot of dark florals. The finishing touches came in the form of a double-breasted blazer casually thrown over her shoulders and some delicate pieces of fine jewellery. The hotter months on the calendar also have her opting for season-friendly fabrics—think lace-trimmed Jonathan Simkhai midi dresses in nautical hues and breezy Zara tops in eyelet lace. When off-duty, Lakshmi chooses to make the most of her time with her nine-year-old by the pool, usually sporting a slew of string bikinis in pop colours, ranging from vivid blue to neon yellow. Her love for prints extends to loungewear too, and she can often be found getting ready for events in her signature tropical print wrap. Not one to shy away from drama in her accessory choices, you'll find her wearing everything from wine-hued patent leather boots to faux fur-throws, depending on the occasion. Having made her career in the spotlight, it comes as little surprise that Lakshmi is most comfortable on the red carpet. For the opening night of the Metropolitan Opera, she opted for a glamorous number from Russian fashion house, Yanina Couture, that did justice to her statuesque figure. Her discerning eye for prints means that her recent appearance on The Daily Show with Trevor Noah had her picking a sleek strapless number from Rochas with printed florals, further accessorised with a blue ACLU ribbon to signify her support for individual rights and liberties. And of course, there's the crimson J Mendel number that she took to the 70th Primetime Emmy Awards for the second time, after wearing it to the Vogue Women of the Year Awards in 2017. In a post on Instagram, she stated, “I think we should stop sending the message to young women and girls that we all have these endless closets of couture we're never allowed to wear more than once. The hours that it takes, the artisans' labor and the gorgeous fabrics all deserve to be worn again and treasured.” Scroll through the gallery below to go through Padma Lakshmi's best wardrobe picks. column1: No jewellery on the red carpet? These celebrities are here for it
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Pairing statement ensembles with minimal or no accessories seems to be a ruling trend on red carpets in 2019. Below, we show you how Bollywood and Hollywood celebrities are pulling off the look One of the oldest rules in sartorial books has always propagated wearing statement outfits on the red carpet with fine jewellery pieces, and the winning combination has more often than not been most celebrities' go-to look. This year, however, has shown a new trend on Indian and international red carpets—one that demands simplicity, especially when it comes to accessories. From Alia Bhatt to Lady Gaga, A-listers around the world are opting out of bold neckpieces, bangles, rings and earrings, proving that less is definitely more. The new rule for acing red carpet dressing in 2019 demands making strong sartorial choices that support the minimal accessory trend. Look towards Alia Bhatt's Ralph & Russo ensemble, Karisma Kapoor's Naeem Khan number and Irina Shayk's Atelier Versace outfit for example, each of which made a striking statement through the use of sheer fabrics and sequins sans any accessories. Meanwhile, Janhvi Kapoor, Karlie Kloss and Lady Gaga's red carpet appearances saw them opt for barely-there diamond stud earrings and rings that subtly complemented their sartorial choices. Cate Blanchett's Christopher Kane ensemble came embellished with large stones (reminiscent of the Infinity Stones from Marvel's recently concluded Infinity Saga) that were complemented with matching rings, balanced out with bare ears. Diana Penty's sultry off-shoulder gown by Shriya Som was accessorised with a dainty diamond bracelet, and Deepika Padukone's vivid red Gaurav Gupta gown left no room for complaints either—the star relied on her wedding ring and a pair of gold clip-on earrings to round off her look. column1: Ballgowns and sneakers are a thing (again). Here’s why
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Monday’s Met Gala is set to deliver a stream of enormous red carpet dresses—but is the ballgown about to enter our everyday wardrobes? 2019: the year that the full-circle skirt was adopted into the catwalk repartee of even the most conspicuously low-key designers; and the ballgown became the wardrobe staple you never knew you needed. From Off-White to Y/Project (the Parisian label helmed by Belgian designer Glenn Martens that famously brought you the denim knicker), fashion editors are now unphased when ballgowns appear on the runway in between herringbone-tweed coats, leather suiting and cycling shorts. Modernity and the maxed-out taffeta dress may seem like an unlikely match, but consider Molly Goddard. The British designer has been turning us on to the versatile power of tulle since the launch of her eponymous label back in 2014. Goddard's enormous petticoat dresses have been worn repeatedly by everyone from Rihanna to Jodie Comer and Zawe Ashton, and kickstarted the zero-rules-apply styling approach that sets the new era ballgowns apart from their debutant roots. For proof that the big-dress-plus-sneakers mood that RiRi tapped so well in 2017 hasn't aged, look to Virgil Abloh. The designer's SS19 collection was a Nike mashup that flipped the ballgown's regal tendencies into wearable (and ‘extra') art—flashes of fluro yellow included. As for theories on why the ballgown has returned, the international hemline index, which links longer skirt lengths to economic hardship, doesn't account for sweeping ballgown trains—or their out-of-nowhere return. Could they hint to our collective longing to deliminate more personal space, which body-con athleisure didn't budget for? Perhaps. What we do know is that for AW19, the ballgown revival has been about breaking new ground. Case in point: Japanese designer, Tomo Koizumi, who caught editrix Katie Grand's attention thanks to Instagram and went on to steal the show at New York Fashion Week with a fantastical collection built solely of frothy polyester dresses, to resounding critical acclaim. Even at couture level, the ballgown's natural fashion habit, the old school splendour of a full-skirted silhouette is underpinned by resolutely present-day thinking. Valentino's SS19 couture show was creative director Pierpaolo Piccioli's opportunity to “put black women in the centre,” he told British Vogue, with at least half of the 65 looks worn by models of colour. Need we address the question of how the new ballgowns fair on the street? Well, even your scruffiest sneakers won't dampen the drama—but that's precisely the point. column1: Looking for summer shorts? Take cues from Malaika Arora, Ananya Panday
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion This summer, Bollywood’s best dressed set has been merging style with functionality by opting to wear shorts for their many appearances. Take cues before you head out for your shopping spree here Nothing marks the arrival of summer like the sudden urge to embrace higher hemlines. If we had to pick just one piece of clothing that fits in with this desire, it'd have to be shorts. From structured numbers that flaunt your toned legs perfectly to airy iterations that help you stay cool while also making a statement, they serve the easiest way to follow summer's ‘less-is-more' mantra. The best part is that there's something out there to satisfy every kind of sartorialist—really short shorts, printed versions and even ones with quirky details—but the key, as always, remains in styling them right. From classic denim shorts to playful numbers, celebrities have brought their favoured shorts out from the back of their closets come summer. Recently, Mira Rajput Kapoor proved her alliance to classic denim shorts when she stepped out for a dinner date with husband Shahid Kapoor. And Ananya Panday gave the short suit trend her own spin for an event, styling checkered shorts with a  matching blazer. Malaika Arora wasn't too far behind either, opting for a polka dotted short suit for a day out under the sun. column1: Your guide to the perfect bikini and swimsuit for every occasion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Just like the rest of your outfits, your swimsuits and bikinis also need to cater to the type of event you’re attending. From weekend getaways to poolside weddings and even your own honeymoon, these are the styles you should be looking at The sun's out with a vengeance, and the ensuing heatwave means only one thing—it's swim season, and it shouldn't matter if your bikini bod is still underway. Instagram's favourite It-girls are already posting belfies in their two-pieces—leopard print for Kendall Jenner, tangy orange for Gigi Hadid and textured white for Selena Gomez, in case you were wondering—leading the way for the styles that will soon turn into unanimous summer crushes (besides, Noah Centineo, that is). 2019 is all about animal print, high legs, underwire tops (thank god for the support), textured metallics and belted styles. But swimwear shopping can be daunting even for the most seasoned shopper. It's hard enough to find the most flattering fit, cut and hues; and then you need to factor in the occasion as well. How skimpy is too skimpy for a poolside brunch at a family wedding? What's a viable real girl option for an all-girls' vacation (because let's face it, only a few of us look like runway models)? Vogue's something-for-every-occasion guide answers these burning questions. Low-key R&R at a seaside resort or your best friend's holiday home is probably high on your mind come balmy summer days. If your only POA is flopping on a lounge chair to finish your reading list with a pitcher of mimosas, then a monotone or colour-blocked one-piece with high-cut legs (and mirrored sunglasses to match) is exactly what you need. Your or your main girl's pre-wedding getaway is license to be extra. Turn up the heat in sultry sets—think bandeau and triangle bikini tops in snakeskin or tiger print. For when you're in the mood for something a little less itsy-bitsy, pick a longline bikini top. Don't forget to pack a sparkly metallic high-rise bikini set or a halter monokini (matching, if the crew is feeling extra cheesy) to hit a beach club for sunset drinks. Even though the setting is casual, you're still at a wedding soiree, so you need to dress up a tad more than your average pool day. Ruffled suits are great way to add wedding-appropriate flair to your look, as are one-shoulder maillots with bow detailing. A tasseled kaftan or skirt with statement accessories like wooden bangles and a straw bag are winning additions for photo-ops with your favourite cousins. But you are going to be thrown in the pool at some point, so what's underneath that cover-up is just as important. More cutesy less edgy needs to be your mantra for an occasion like this one. A retro mood in polka dots, perhaps? You can always turn to candy-coloured stripes if you're not feeling too nostalgic. Belted styles, whether as a one-piece monokini or high-waist bikini, are perfect for beach days with the fam. Carrying your little one around too? Dodge the waves with your mini-me by twinning in coordinated print-on-print smocked sets. Set the mercury rising on that first beach date, but leave something to the imagination as well. Centre the look around one bold element, one that you are at ease in. A plunging halter neckline or a bare back will get you the double take you're after. Top off the look with a wide brimmed hat and an oversized white shirt tied up at the waist. Say yes to flirty silhouettes when taking stock of your honeymoon bathing suit inventory. Dare to wear white (with floral accents for a touch of pretty) for a nightcap in your private villa plunge pool, and pick a cut-out one-piece (safe midriff cut-outs or full-centre ones, depending on how bold you're feeling) for a lazy day on the beach. There's nothing like an hour of serious pool time to stay in shape during summer. If swimming is your preferred workout, opt for functional styles that you're comfortable in. Save that ruched off-shoulder suit for another day, and stick to fuss-free maillots instead. A popping neon or a scoop-back will keep this look from becoming too boring.
