column1: What makes the Gujarati patola sari a priceless heirloom?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From the legends surrounding its origin to the time-consuming process that makes it so invaluable, Glasgow-based designer Ayush Kejriwal talks to Vogue about the intricacies involved in making the patola weave The recent revival of Indian weaves has led to a renewed interest in several time-honoured techniques, and Gujarat's famous weave, patola, is high on that list. Considered heirloom buys owing to their one-of-a-kind designs and painstaking weaving technique, an authentic patola is as intricate as it is impactful. Glasgow-based designer Ayush Kejriwal, who is a champion of this timeless weave, gives Vogue a masterclass in everything you wanted to know about it. The name patola is derived from the Sanskrit word ‘pattakulla', and is the plural form of the word patolu. Even though the patola fabric is said to be of Gujarati origin, its earliest mentions can be found in religious texts in South India too. The religious text Narasimha Purana talks about this fabric being worn by women during ceremonies and holy occasions.   Its Gujarati connection, pattakulla, first appeared only after the 11th century. After the decline of the Solanki Empire, the Salvis found a rich trade in Gujarat. Patola saris quickly became a sign of social status among Gujarati women, especially as part of their wedding trousseau. It is believed that 700 silk weavers from the Salvi caste of Karnataka and Maharashtra moved to Gujarat in the 12th century to acquire the patronage of the Solanki Rajputs, the ruling class of Gujarat and parts of Rajasthan at that time. There is another story that claims that patola originated 900 years ago, owing to the patronage of king Kumarpala, who made it a symbol of wealth. Initially, his patola supply came from Jalna in Maharashtra. But on learning that the king of Jalna used the patola as bedsheets before selling or gifting them to other aristocrats, he brought 700 patola craftsmen and their families from Maharashtra and Karnataka to Patan in Gujarat. It's said that he then staggered production, and despite the seven-month-long manufacturing time, he received at least one new patola to wear to the temple every day. Patolas are manufactured by the resist-dyeing process using the warp and weft technique. It normally takes three people about four-to-seven months to weave a patola, making it expensive and time-consuming. A sword-shaped stick made out of rosewood, called vi, is used for adjusting the yarns. The first step involves tying of the yarn with cotton threads according to the pattern. Measurements can be as small as 1/100th of an inch. The yarn undergoes multiple cycles of tying and dyeing, following a specific order of colours. Displacement of even a single yarn can disturb the design arrangement and make the entire set redundant. Every colour has a unique place in the design; which needs to be carefully aligned while weaving it. Such intricacy requires extreme precision and patience. A unique feature of the patola loom is that it is tilted to one side, and requires two people to work in tandem on one sari. Depending on the length and intricacy of the pattern, it can also take up to a year to make these pieces. Patolas are generally represented by abstract designs and geometric patterns. Elephants, human figures, kalash, flowers, shikhar, paan and parrots as well as designs inspired by the architecture of Gujarat are popular. The most sought-after designs each have their unique names like nari kunjar bhat (women and elephant patterns), paan bhat (peepul leaf motif) navratna bhat (square-shaped pattersn), voharagaji (inspired by the Vohra community), fulvali bhatt (floral) and rattanchowk bhat (geometric). The complexity and time-intensiveness is what makes patola so valuable. A dizzyingly mathematical process, it involves intensive manual work, fortitude and exactitude. Natural dyes like catechu, cochineal, indigo, turmeric, natural lakh, harde, madder roots, manjistha, ratnajyot, katha, kesudo, pomegranate skin, henna and marigold are used in making them. The fact that they are reversible, their unfading bright colours, and their rich history add to the uniqueness. Ikat is a type of textile produced in modern-day Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. It's a common name for the yarn, technique and the fabric. Generally speaking, it is a technique that involves resist-dyeing. Bundles of yarn are tightly wrapped together and then dyed as many times as is required to create the desired pattern. This dyeing process is different because the yarns are dyed before being woven into cloth. In most of the other resist-dyeing techniques, like batik for example, it is the final cloth and not the yarn, that's dyed. Once the yarns have been suitably dyed and dried, the weaver lines them up on the loom to form the pattern. The design takes form as the yarn is woven into cloth. This is an incredibly complicated process, as the weaver has to precisely dye the threads, and place them correctly so it forms the correct pattern when woven. In order to replicate a pattern, the weaver would have to dye the thread in exactly the same place as before, line it up on the loom in exactly the same place, and then weave it exactly the same way. The most complicated type of weaving is double ikat, where both the warp and weft threads are resist-dyed prior to weaving. In single ikat, it is the weft threads that are resist-dyed. The pattern will be formed only as the weaving progresses. This means that the weaver has to constantly centre and readjust the yarns to ensure the pattern is formed correctly.   Patolas are essential in ceremonies of certain communities as they are believed to have magical powers to ward off evil. A popular pattern including a circle of lotus flowers, buds and leaves known as chabardi bhat (basket design), is associated with fertility and is worn for wedding ceremonies in some cultures. In Gujarat, patolas are given to brides as a part of her trousseau. My aim has never been to modernise this age-old craft. It is perfect just the way it is, and I don't intend to mend what's not broken. Instead, I strive to innovate the patterns in a traditional colour palette. The kaligulab patola from my collection is a good example. It has elephants on the border and red roses in the body, which is unusual for a patola sari.     I work with weavers from Patan and Rajkot as I stock both single and double ikat patola saris. It took me some time, but I was able to convince my weaver in Patan to weave single ikat patolas rather than only double ikat, making it more affordable for my patrons. The kaligulab patola is a result of that. Digital printing and mass production of patola-inspired patterns in Surat is heartbreaking. Often, people are unable to appreciate the skill, time and energy that goes into making a patola which justifies its value—they are not expensive, they are priceless. 8 classic Kanjeevaram saris you need to add to your ethnic wardrobe How to wear saris every day: The Bollywood celebrity guide What I've learnt in my struggle to find The Perfect white wedding sari Fashion Fashion What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How Instagram is helping put young designer labels on the map
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Looking for a fashion brand that everyone isn’t wearing yet? Head to Instagram. An incubator for emerging talent, Vogue speaks to a buyer, stylist, branding expert and designer about discovering the next big thing via the feed What do LA-based brand Cult Gaia, London's Rixo and Copenhagen's Ganni have in common? They all found fame—and fortune—thanks to their Instagram profiles. While consumers look to Instagram for styling inspiration and the latest must-haves, there's also a growing trend among fashion's most influential tastemakers—buyers, editors and celebrity stylists included—who are using the app to scout new talent. Japanese designer Tomo Koizumi—whose AW19 show was a standout moment at New York Fashion Week – is a prime example. When he posted one of his frothy rainbow creations on Instagram in January, he didn't expect to catch the attention of stylist and LOVE editor Katie Grand. “[Grand] DM-ed me, and we started chatting,” he tells Vogue. “She said, ‘How about a show?'” Despite having just a month to prepare, Koizumi's show saw the likes of Bella Hadid, Joan Smalls and Karen Elson walking in his colourful designs at the Marc Jacobs store on Madison Avenue; with a finale of Gwendoline Christie in the dramatic gown that Grand initially spotted on Instagram. Koizumi says Grand's support has been big, vastly increasing his international presence. Since New York Fashion Week, his Instagram following has grown by 1,000 per cent—posts last year were getting a few hundred likes, now he's easily attracting several thousand—and he's had considerable interest from fashion editors and buyers around the world. He's already working on future collaborations, too: “It's really exciting. I wasn't thinking about [doing] any retail after the show, but now I am.” Although Koizumi's rapid ascendance is slightly unusual, Net-A-Porter's global buying director, Elizabeth von der Goltz, confirms that Instagram now plays a vital part in buying strategy. “We use it to scout new brands, including Attico, Staud and Alanui [in the last couple of years],” she says. Net-A-Porter's Vanguard initiative, which supports and promotes emerging talent, has discovered several new designers via Instagram, including jewellery label Anne Manns and bag specialist Ratio et Motus. While some brands follow key industry figures in the hope they will get noticed, the buying team tends to come across most organically. Von der Goltz describes a certain thrill in landing on the feed of an unknown designer that aligns with Net-A-Porter: “When you click on a brand's profile and you see they have less than 100 followers, you get that exciting feeling of discovery.” Celebrity stylist Danielle Nachmani agrees: “[Instagram] gives you access to brands you would usually spend so much more time searching, or going to a million appointments to find.” Instead of adopting a specific strategy to find new talent, she says she simply follows accounts she likes. The stylist recently put actress Laura Harrier in a floral dress by Commission, a New York-based label that caught her eye while scrolling. “I saw a skirt in an editorial, and it was tagged with [Commission's profile],” she says. ”I just became obsessed with their feed; I loved their campaign imagery. You want to support [new brands] because you know how much an impact an actress wearing their clothes can have.” Creative director and branding expert Emmanuelle Goutal says emerging designers should have two key focus points: the images shared on their own Instagram and ensuring their pieces are seen on the right people. “The Instagram campaign is very important; and influencers are also great ambassadors for brands,” Goutal says, explaining that influencers increase exposure, and therefore the chances of striking virtual gold. This strategy put Peter Do, an alum of Phoebe Philo's Céline, on Net-A-Porter's radar—the buyers first noticed Do's muse, model Maggie Maurer, wearing his sleek tailoring and pleated midi skirts on Instagram. Outwear brand Ochi did the same when Vogue Ukraine's fashion director Julie Pelipas featured in the label's lookbook. “There are several editors in the industry who are always championing new brands,” von der Goltz explains. “We know and trust Julie's taste so knew this would be an exciting brand if she was backing it.” Ultimately though, it's the designs themselves that do the talking. Koizumi sees his creations as “pure and different”; qualities that he believes sparked Grand's interest. “My pieces are not really commercial,” he continues, “I believe in the power of fantasy [and want] my story to give young designers hope.” View Gallery 14 Photos Instagram is the go-to for new fashion talent Instagram just made shopping on the app easier for its users Jennifer Lopez shares pictures of her proposal on Instagram 10 new beauty and wellness influencers you need to follow on Instagram Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Move over millennial pink, this is how to wear sunset colours
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Celebrities show you why your wardrobe needs more shades like marigold yellow, painterly orange and more We looked at the runways from New York, London, Milan and Paris and came to an undeniable conclusion—it was all yellow. Marigold, canary, lemon with bursts of orange—sunset colours are clearly hot right now. From Chloé's sunset-splattered cross-body bag and Max Mara's tiered look in marigold yellow to Anita Dongre's Tencel lehenga in apricot on home ground—everything points to the saturated colour wheel. These sunnier shades come right in time for summer. Whether you're stepping out for a spring wedding, a beach party, or getting ready to jet-set to warmer tropical climes, these hues will serve you well from dusk to dawn. To make the colour palette your own, take cues from Priyanka Chopra, who stepped out in New York wearing a layered look of egg yolk yellow, and paired her outfit with black boots and a sticker-strewn, logo-laden Gucci tote to take the monotony out of monotone. Gigi Hadid gave the trend her vote of approval too, first in 2018 with a head-to-toe citrus look—a neon-orange polo tee with a blood orange skirt and strappy gold heels—and then on the red carpet, where she was spotted in a floor-grazing marigold jumpsuit fresh off Brandon Maxwell's spring/summer 2019 collection. Closer to home, Alia Bhatt took the saturated shades to traditional wear with an acid yellow Sabyasachi lehenga, and even made a case for florals and yellow being the perfect combination in a wallpaper-patterned dress. And Kiara Advani's glamorous approach saw her don a yellow gown with a thigh-high slit. Scroll through our gallery to find your spirit celebrity and their yellow style. column1: How a century of Bauhaus has influenced fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion To mark the 100th anniversary of Bauhaus, Vogue looks at how the German art movement has inspired fashion designers on the catwalk, including Mary Katrantzou, Roksanda Ilincic and Paul Smith Bauhaus—the German art school known for its use of geometric shapes, sharp lines and pops of colour—may be 100 years old this year, but it remains as current as it was a century ago. From David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust jumpsuit to the Ikea flat-pack furniture in our living rooms, elements of the Bauhaus ethos have worked their way effortlessly into our lives. Beyond an aesthetic movement, it is the Bauhaus's experimentation with colour and geometry that we most readily recognise today. Not least because it has regularly been transposed onto the catwalk. Think of Jonathan Saunders' interlinking shapes and bold lines in his SS05 collection; Roksanda Ilincic's signature use of primary block colour; and Mary Katrantzou‘s incorporation of Bauhaus posters in her AW18 collection. Elsewhere, Hugo Boss's AW15 collection featured checks inspired by the wall hangings of Anni Albers; while Paul Smith has also been drawn to the textile artist's work. “What [the Bauhaus] tried to establish through artists like Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky was this idea of essential forms, and colour relations,” explains Grant Watson, co-curator of Bauhaus Imaginista, a major exhibition marking the 100th anniversary of the art school at Berlin's Haus der Kulturen der Welt. The Bauhaus was also concerned with functionality and simplicity of form. “The early Bauhaus was very expressionist. Later on, it became more of this functional aesthetic, stripping down to a set of essentials,” explains Watson. These clean-line principles inspired some of the most influential fashion designers of the 1960s, including André Courrèges, Mary Quant and the celebrated minimalist Jil Sander. “My roots are in the Bauhaus movement, which applied functional rationality to the design of practical everyday life,” Sander told Vogue's Suzy Menkes in a 2017 interview. “Streamlined beauty, clear structures, reduction to the essential and free movement.” [#image: /photos/5ce3f3183bfc80bf62abbe41]||| ||| Jil Sander spring/summer 2013, Milan Fashion Week The interdisciplinary approach of the Bauhaus, which saw the blurring of boundaries between art, architecture and design, is also one that has been adopted by the fashion world. Hussein Chalayan, for example, is known for merging art and technology, echoing the work of Oskar Schlemmer, a key figure from the Bauhaus theatre workshop, with his dramatic catwalk designs. As Bauhaus turns 100, three top fashion designers tell Vogue how the movement has influenced their work. “Bauhaus has been a huge influence, particularly with colour blocking which I've been using ever since my first show. Artist Josef Albers is always on my mood boards. His use of colour always draws me to him, particularly the way he juxtaposes colours that we don't see could go with each other. It is this experimentation with colour, the pushing the boundaries of what is harmonious and what is not, that I aspire to. “Architect Mies van der Rohe is another one of my great idols. I discovered him as a student and absolutely fell in love with his work. The fluidity of his architecture, the way that he designed houses that were beautiful—very airy on the inside, protective on the outside—these elements exist in my work. At the beginning of my career, I was designing drape dresses made out of fluid fabrics with this type of architecture in my head.” [#image: /photos/5ce3f318ad9a212475b3ea86]||| ||| Paul Smith fall/winter 2015, Paris Fashion Week “I became aware of the Bauhaus when I was growing up in Nottingham. Students from the local art college told me about ‘the Bauhaus'; I thought it was a council estate at first! The beginnings of my career can really be traced back to those conversations. “There's a practicality and functionality to the work [of the Bauhaus] that is very important to what I do. I also love the idea of the creative collective and the collaboration that the Bauhaus celebrated. Working together, sharing ideas and taking inspiration from all the various fields that they covered. “It was my collection for AW15 that most directly took inspiration from the work of artists Josef and Anni Albers. More recently we worked on a small collection inspired by Anni's textiles to coincide with the exhibition that opened in Tate Modern. One of my major considerations was respecting Anni's amazing history of weaving and making sure my designs represented her work in the most sensitive and accurate way possible.” [#image: /photos/5ce3f318b41afb5563a96952]||| ||| Mary Katrantzou fall/winter 2018, London Fashion Week “As a school of thought, Bauhaus epitomises how designers think about design in today's world. I think fashion, as an applied design discipline, has to always find an equilibrium between creativity and commerce; looking at the functionality of design, while communicating something for our times. That is as relevant today as it was then. “For AW18, I was looking at incredible Bauhaus posters and images, and I found Bauhaus-ims in my past work. There was this picture of figures wearing different geometric shapes, which reminded me of silhouettes I've played with in the past, like the lampshade skirts from 2011. In my AW18 collection, Bauhaus represented this purity of form, the pragmatic nature of design and how that directly translated into fashion. Graphically, we looked a lot at Bauhaus posters, the utilisation of geometry, which we translated as knitwear.” View Gallery 17 Photos How a century of Bauhaus has influenced fashion Take a first look at Mary Katrantzou's 10th anniversary collection 14 couture moments that went down in fashion history Culture & Living Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 12 times fashion designers were inspired by superheroes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From comic books to the catwalk, designers love superhero style. Vogue highlights 12 of the best references, including Mugler’s Iron Man-esque armour, McQueen’s Batman masks and Black Panther cameos, and Catwoman and Wonder Woman across the board, as we start to see a more empowered approach to modern costuming The fashion world has long been entranced by comic books. No wonder. They offer up world upon world of city skylines and sinister laboratories, showy costumes and dramatic story arcs, battles raging between good and evil. In fact, in 2008 the MET devoted an exhibition to the potent power of various much-beloved characters, Superheroes: Fashion and Fantasy delineating how designers have been influenced by fantastical figures, dastardly villains and women metamorphosed into (often scantily clad) warriors. It focussed particularly on the relationship between superhero-influenced apparel and physicality—for where better than in the realms of Spiderman, Thor, and Black Widow to explore how a body can transform, and how dress can transform a body? From detectives to monsters to students (see Riverdale's update of the Archie comics), the comic book genre has grown to encompass all sorts of storytelling. And modern day reworks are, thankfully, beginning to reckon with age-old limitations. Contemporary film adaptations of classics, from Gal Gadot as Wonder Woman to the current Captain Marvel starring Brie Larson, have allowed for more nuanced explorations of women—while Sana Amanat in her role as VP at Marvel has been explicit on the need for further diversity among the characters we see on page and screen. Here, we explore fashion's infatuation with comics, from the 1990s to now, taking in heroes, nemeses, a spy and ample explosions along the way… One can't explore comic books without thinking of Mugler's work, with its emphasis on athleticism, excess and often provocative approaches to shape and cut. His famous AW95 armoured suit—revealed from beneath a sweeping cape—was featured in the MET's exhibition, displayed alongside Robert Downey Jr's Iron Man costume. Often described as a designer of high drama, a certain kitsch comic book influence permeated Mugler's catwalks, populated with OTT villains and heroes in iconic moulded bodices, bodysuits featuring flames, starbursts and metal belts, extravagant padding and latex leggings. Where plenty of superhero get-ups seem to be engineered for agility or aerodynamic feats, Mugler's designs take a different approach. One that's battle-clad. (Although, not without controversy in relation to the female body, given that this armour wouldn't be especially effective in protecting the wearer's breasts, stomach, or thighs.) [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e14a30b3b65412a939]||| ||| Image: Rex Features Perhaps one of the most prevailing points of influence on the fashion industry is Wonder Woman. First featured by DC Comics in 1941, this (literally) Amazonian figure with her mythical background and belted bodysuit, has inspired numerous designers—not least, perhaps, because of the backstory to her character's creation, allegedly rooted in the three-way relationship between creator William Marston, his wife Elizabeth Holloway, and his partner Olive Byrne, who also lived with them. An avowed advocate of equal rights, Wonder Woman's proclamations of strength—both physical and political—guided John Galliano's SS01 couture show. Charting a history from subjugation to emancipation, via bespectacled, be-corseted monochromes, 1950s suburban domesticity amplified into billowing gowns embroidered with household items, and some requisite All-American stars and stripes, the collection ended with a (now rather dated looking) imagined return for Wonder Woman to Paradise Island. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e13bfc80e807abbdfb]||| ||| Image: Rex Features The relationship between comic books and fashion is symbiotic: designers draw on comics, and comics (and their film franchises) draw on the catwalks. For 2018's Black Panther, Ruth E. Carter kitted out the characters in various high fashion pieces, including Alexander McQueen. McQueen is particularly apt, given how frequently his work involved subtle nods to the moral complexities and aesthetic modes of heroes and villains alike. AW02 aligned with comic book visuals in Val Garland's makeup, distinctly reminiscent of Batman's winged mask; while Sarah Burton's AW15 collection featured black lacquer masks, created by Pat McGrath to frame models' faces. The mask, of course, is a stalwart sartorial feature for any superhuman figure needing to obscure their day-to-day identity. Other designers have played with the possibilities of concealment and disguise too—see Gucci's AW19 black, turquoise and white spiked masks for a fiercer interpretation. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e10c1a90ca6ec794b0]||| ||| Image: Rex Features Though Spiderman himself might feel a little too much like a fancy dress costume (unless you're Vetements, who've recently been plastering the logo and that instantly identifiable shade of red all over quilted coats, silk scarves and bodycon dresses with built in gloves), his multi-purpose webs have been of more interest to designers. Gaultier has demonstrated a consistent interest in comic book elements (see #7, below), perhaps most literally in his Wonder Woman- and Superman-themed fragrances released in 2017. Long before that though, he turned to Spiderman for his SS03 couture show: a delicate button-sewn web of gold radiating from the hip of a dress, combined with rusty ruched fabric and turquoise gloves to create a look somewhere between arachnid and eclectic showgirl. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e15a354fe66506ecbc]||| ||| Image: Rex Features Gareth Pugh is another designer whose dark, almost gothic, take on silhouettes links to the strangeness and exaggeration of the comic book universe. Look to his AW18's black plastic and fiercely proportioned shoulders, or AW11's metallic chevrons and plentiful capes—diminutive costume designer Edna Mode might have tersely declared “no capes!” in The Incredibles, but fashion does love a garment that swoops down from the shoulders. Also featured in the MET exhibition, the standout look from Pugh's SS07 collection was a shiny all-black outfit that resembled an angular, Tetris-built Batman. With a mirrored headpiece and a vast, spiked structure descending from the model's shoulders, it was a startling, sci-fi re-imagination of an instantly recognisable figure. Batman has proved fruitful for other designers too, notably in The Blonds' AW14 show nodding to a series of the superheroes' nemeses, including The Joker and Poison Ivy. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e03bfc80512cabbdf8]||| ||| Image: Marcio Madeira Catwoman is, well, catnip, to a lot of designers: her leather-clad antics charming plenty, with actors including Eartha Kitt and Halle Berry taking on the role in various on-screen adaptations. Nicolas Ghesquière's tenure at Balenciaga drew on the spirit of this intriguing antiheroine, from his all-black SS98 debut (featuring headpieces that wouldn't have looked out of place in Gotham City) to AW03's thigh-high boots. For SS07, Ghesquière said he'd been inspired by The Terminator's mechanised visions, but there were also looks reminiscent of Selina Kyle, with dark, angular suits and shiny, form-fitting dresses. More literal interpretations—complete with cat ears, cat-suits and cat-everything-else—can be found in Iceberg's furry-coated AW08 collection, Givenchy's AW11 aviator jackets and velvet bodysuits, and Mugler's full-on caped homage for AW96. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e1b41afbc614a968f0]||| ||| Image: Getty Beginning with Lily Cole emerging in a zip-up black leather catsuit complete with bowler hat, briefcase and umbrella, Jean-Paul Gaultier's Hermès AW10 offering paid homage to the character of Emma Peel, played by Diana Rigg, in The Avengers—a British 1960s espionage TV show, also serialised in comic book form. (Entirely separate, it must be noted, from Marvel's US-based superhero team The Avengers.) In her on-screen persona, Peel was best known for sporting a series of glorious catsuits: the ideal garment for sneaking around in, standing assertively and executing some impressively forceful high kicks. Gaultier's emphasis on leather—in blacks, browns, plums and more—made for a memorable collection of office-wear meets fetish gear, from ties to trousers and every modern-day-spy essential, a statement trench coat. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e04a30b3729e12a937]||| ||| Image: Getty Jeremy Scott is a fan of a flashy pop culture reference; designs for both Moschino and his eponymous line have featured everything from Pikachu to McDonald's to The Powerpuff Girls. His AW11 show saw models with pastel-dipped pigtails and neon eyeshadow, clad in stripes and metallics, Coca-Cola-esque logos emblazoned with ‘Enjoy God' and perhaps the two most famous comic book logos: Batman and Superman. The latter's insignia was inverted to become a question mark, appearing first on a tank-top and then on the front of a glittering blue sequinned gown for the finale, with a red cape trailing behind. Elsewhere, the Captain Marvel lightning bolt plunged from necklines, while a blue-and-white starred dress with red shoes suggested Wonder Woman out to dinner. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e23bfc80f357abbdfd]||| ||| Image: Getty Sometimes it's as simple as a single graphic. Tom Ford's 2013 return to the catwalk saw models decked out in lavish leopard prints, elaborate knee-high boots and pink and purple patchwork, alongside some distinctly comic book-inflected motifs. Glamorous long-sleeved evening gowns, sporty bomber jackets and sequinned skirts featured punchy, jewel-hued explosions—the kind beloved of fight scenes and superhero spectacles. Doing what he does best, of course, Ford elevated these explosions to something both tongue-in-cheek and tremendously alluring. Elsewhere, 3.1 Phillip Lim's Pre-Fall 2012 collection saw Kapow!-style sweaters and bags; while Jeremy Scott mixed comics with primary-colour pop art lettering (and a dash of David Bowie) for SS12, and exclaimed ‘Shock' and ‘Power' in neon fonts for SS19. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e2b41afb2b71a968f4]||| ||| Image: Getty The comic book format, comprised of panelled images and text, is largely acknowledged to have taken off with the launch of Superman in America in 1938 (first in Action Comics, then just a few months later with his own self-titled comic)—but plenty of examples laid the foundations, not least the emergence of manga in Japan in the 18th and 19th centuries. It's a heritage Japanese designer Tsumori Chisato drew on for AW15, her own childhood dreams of becoming a manga artist revisited in a playful collection where many of the clothes could, quite literally, be read like a book. Mixing illustration styles and influences, Chisato included Catwoman-esque figures slinking across dresses and tops, and more fun, abstract reference to the colour-palettes and graphics of comics and manga, via bright, oversized coats, flame-patterned tights, elaborate collars and the odd speech bubble. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e23bfc803524abbdff]||| ||| Image: Rex Features Where many have been inspired by the actual costumes of superheroes, others have turned to the drawings themselves. Miuccia Prada has been playing with comic book motifs and ideas for the last few years, from AW18's futuristic neons and Gotham City-style set to the recent Frankenstein graphics in AW19's menswear and womenswear shows. But it was SS18 that saw her most explicit acknowledgement of the power and potential of comics, via collaborations with eight female cartoonists and manga artists—including Trina Robbins, who was the first woman to draw Wonder Woman in the mid-1980s. The collection provided a welcome corrective to the comic-book tendency to objectify and sexualise women's bodies for the male gaze; instead it was a celebration of the rich history and ongoing present of those drawing more inclusively. [#image: /photos/5ce3f2e40c1a9017a3c794b7]||| ||| Image: Rex Features When looking to the future of fashion—one that, with its interest in innovative production and boundary-pushing approaches to the body, doesn't seem too far removed from some of the costuming ideas explored here—Iris van Herpen seems like a natural place to alight. A pioneer of 3D printing and other forward-thinking techniques, her clothes are startling, sculptural and often made for movement. Plenty of offerings from her AW18 couture show, which merged biology and technology, looked fit to clad a modern-day superhero: from dynamic, almost winged, bodysuits to mesmerising gossamer-light organza capes. column1: Lisa Ray on watches, wellness, motherhood and her upcoming memoir
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The multi-hyphenate Lisa Ray reveals her current life mantra, and talks about how writing her memoir, Close to the Bone, was a cathartic process Actor, model, entrepreneur, philanthropist, and now writer—Lisa Ray wears many hats, but each one comes dripping with experience. Through her battle with cancer and an elaborate surrogacy process, the multi-hyphenate has dealt with life's travails in her own way, retaining specks of optimism. Vogue caught up with the star at Rado's recent launch, where the brand showcased timepieces from their ladies collection, to find out more about her upcoming book, Close to the Bone, and her take on motherhood, wellness and of course, watches. Excerpts below. Personally, I look out for watches that are enduring and will make the transition from day to night, or from formal to informal [easily]. I'm a nomad; I'm constantly on the go, and I love a watch that travels and keeps up with me. I don't tend to change my watches a lot; I just wear the same one for a year. So that time piece has to be multi-functioning, it has to be chic, it has to be a statement in itself, and it also has to complement my lifestyle. The Rado Coupole Moon Phase watch is my current favourite from the new collection. It's been 13 years of my association with Rado. It's not been a straightforward journey, but it's safe to say that there is something in my DNA that matches with the label. I love the fact that I could pick up a watch from 10 years ago, and it would still feel fresh and contemporary. All my learnings have led me to write my upcoming book, Close to the Bone, which I've been working on for the last two years. It's not just a memoir; it's my first project as a writer. And honestly, all these labels of being an actor, a model, an entrepreneur, pale in comparison to writing. Writing has always been my first love, and people close to me recognise that. In a way, writing is another form of storytelling, and that's what I have been doing for the last 15 years—whether it was through modelling, or performing in a film or a TV series. Coming to what I've learnt in my journey, I feel that there is beauty in being broken. [This mantra] derives from Kintsugi, the Japanese art of binding cracks in ceramics with gold and making the object more beautiful. I really believe that's the theme of my life today. The memoir takes into account all of my experiences up till my wedding. I hope that I am serving others through my words and candid tone—considering I had to fight very hard to tell my story the way that I wanted to. Writing about my personal journey made me realise that us women have to fight in every moment of life, especially when we need to be heard in a way that is meaningful to us. Finding meaning in every moment and transcending labels is challenging work—and that's what Close to the Bone aims to do. The only tip I have—which also happens to be one I received from someone—is that your babies don't need a perfect mom. They need a happy mom, and what makes me the happiest is their happiness. Who doesn't want happy, well-rounded kids? I don't want to force my children to give in to society's expectations of what a girl should be like. I know it's going to be an interesting journey in bringing up my two girls and I only want to encourage them to be the best versions of themselves. To me, wellness is about finding me time. I really enjoy what I do—I've been facing the camera for around 30 years now—but I have to remind myself to fill up my cup and be still. Wellness comes from within; it's not about finding my cues in the outside world, but instead quietening everything around me so that I can hear that deep voice within which is my inner guide. Finding that stillness inside in the middle of chaos is really essential to me. column1: Decoding Made in Heaven’s wedding-ready costumes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Sobhita Dhulipala’s daring monochromatic look in 431-88 to Aditi Joshi’s journalist vibe in Péro, we break down the costumes seen in Amazon Prime Video’s Made in Heaven When it comes to visual media, fashion plays a vital role in enabling each character to construct, sculpt and express their identities in a way that supports the narrated story. Amazon Prime Video's Made in Heaven created a close association with clothing, but in a way that seamlessly suited the characters' personalities. Costume designer Poornamrita Singh's eye for detail got the wardrobe of the show to act as an enabler, such that it helped construct identities and journeys unique to each individual. The beautiful yet broken grandeur of the big, fat Indian wedding dream translated into the costumes of the series, from the glitz and glamour of each bride to the simplicity of the girl-next-door employee. Made in Heaven had some well-known designer names on board, but what the show got right was respecting each culture and individual without promoting a designer-driven wardrobe. Fashion played an integral role as an intermediary between character and narrative here. As you follow the story of Tara (Sobhita Dhulipala) and Karan (Arjun Mathur), two wedding planners who have the echelons of Delhi's society as regular clients, you'll notice that each of their personalities are authentically translated in the way they dress. We see Tara's journey from a humble beginning, when she wore kurtis and jeans and had unkempt hair, to the top of the society as the wife of a rich businessman, appearing as hard and polished as the diamonds she's seen wearing. From her unapologetic looks, one in a monochrome 431-88 outfit and another in that Shivan & Narresh swimsuit, to her elegant showcases in Raw Mango and Kirran Uttam Ghosh saris, each look defines the world that Tara had entered into. In fact, her wardrobe can also be seen as an overcompensation for the life that she had left behind. The subtle nuances of class division that the show touches upon are brought through with the help of Poornamrita's on-point styling. Karan's humble wardrobe makes him come across as the dependable companion to Tara in her otherwise rocky life. And right in the middle of the glamour that surrounds Indian weddings enters Jazz, an outsider who is trying hard to find acceptance in her workplace. She is seen supporting a simple everyday wardrobe with few outfits thrown in to effectively note her yearning to be part of the world she has stepped into, like the gold sequinned dress we see her wear to a house party. Apart from the lead characters of the series, each bride goes on a journey of her own with her clothing. What was interesting was that rather than following any bridal trends, the show relied on the costume of each bride to reflect her personality and culture, with a myriad display of colour and silhouettes. Actor Amrita Puri is seen as the polished and well-groomed Rajput bride, wearing a wedding lehenga that actually looks like a royal heirloom, and looking like a spitting image of Maharani Gayatri Devi on another occasion, wrapped in a soft chiffon sari with strands of beads around her neck. And Deepti Naval's elegant look as a Raw Mango bride in emerald is a complete contrast to Maanvi Gagroo's dream of shooting her wedding video ‘Bollywood-style'—in a part-bridal and part-badass outfit that featured ripped shorts. The sociopolitical issues that the show touches upon are rendered into the clothing as well, like in Rasika Dugal's on-screen wedding that saw the women in jewel-toned woven saris and the men in bandhgalas—a wardrobe one would typically expect at an influential political wedding—or through Aditi Joshi's journalist vibe in Péro. She transformed into a Sabyasachi bride later in the episode, once she embraced the wealth she is marrying into. Each bride's wardrobe was a delight to the eye, bringing in a riot of colour and style that stands true to Indian weddings. The most radical fashion moment in the entire series was when Tara was shown soaking in her bathtub, dripping in jewels, truly bringing out how complex her character is. The scene was beautifully shot and a huge character-defining moment for Tara, a woman who worked her way up and wasn't one bit afraid to own it—this was the scene that Sobhita Dhulipala's entire character had worked up to, and it came across flawlessly through the extravagant styling. The Made in Heaven wardrobe achieved the gist of the show in a heartbeat, broken and imperfect on the inside, yet keeping up the appearance of being ‘made in heaven'. column1: AK-OK? Anamika Khanna says yes and more
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In a Vogue exclusive, Anamika Khanna talks about her coded communication with her twin sons that led to the genesis of a deeply personal, unfiltered collection It's been a tumultuous year to say the least for Kolkata-based designer Anamika Khanna. An illness, winning the Designer of the Year Award at Vogue Women Of The Year 2018, having her twin sons graduate from university and join the business—high highs and low lows. But Khanna has come out on the other side resilient and more determined than ever to showcase her evolution as a designer, and her unique perspective on India modern that has long captivated her peers and customers. This evening, Khanna launches her AK-OK collection on Instagram, taking viewers into a deeply personal space. It's probably her most intimate collection to date. Khanna speaks exclusively to Vogue about what she was really thinking while designing these clothes. Excerpts below. I am so emotionally invested in this collection. I felt this amazing sense of freedom doing this. You know, I do feel in fashion we are getting bound in shackles, and here it was about strength and courage to find a path that's just yours. AK-OK has already become a talking point, but for me it started with being OK, physically and emotionally. I love this story and would wear every look. More so because it allows me to do my thing, which is something I have always strived towards. It's fashion forward and at the same time draws inspiration from our roots. There are no rules here and I enjoyed doing the scripts most. It's really become a mantra in my life—all my friends now use AK-OK instead now. My twin boys were studying at USC in Los Angeles, and we often had to communicate via phone or email about my health issues. During the height of the 1960s USA Space Program, NASA invented the term A-OK, apparently because the sharp sound of an A could cut through static and space easier. Harnessing the transmission power of the term A-OK and adding personal twist of my initials, A-OK became AK-OK—a code that would travel back and forth between us over 13,000km and four years. Using that mantra as a starting point, I wanted to wear them loud and proud on our clothes. I really am clear that I don't want to box this into a particular age group or genre. It's meant to be made your own, no matter your age, gender, size—make it mad, make it elegant, team it with pieces you already have, use one focal piece; as long as you feel easy about it and not weighed down, that's really the key message. These are feelings too that I've been going through, and having the boys involved brought in that millennial mindset and the energy. It's been the most fun collection I've done to date. It's really brought in a new mindset and a realisation that the world has changed. As a result, we're evolving constantly as well—we are bolder, younger and more experimental. Whew! We have a lot planned including a flagship in Mumbai, menswear (it was about time and with two boys on board, the next step) and an accessories line. I am just so excited for the opportunities that are coming my way. Valuing my personal space and the right kind of energy. I won't allow myself to get trapped in what could be or should be. column1: Instagram just made shopping on the app easier for its users
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Instagram now allows you to shop from brands like Burberry and Dior without ever leaving the social media platform Instagram has launched an online shopping feature that will allow users to easily buy products directly from the social media platform. In short: users will be able to shop with a single tap on their phone. The feature, which launched on March 19 in the US, allows users to buy products from 20 different brands—including Burberry, Dior and Prada, as well as beauty brands KKW Beauty and NARS. The platform plans to roll out the new feature in “the coming months” as it attracts more brands to get on board. With the new checkout feature, shoppers will be able to select and pay for an item, all in one smooth process. “People no longer have to navigate to the browser when they want to buy,” the company said in a statement. “And with their protected payment information in one place, they can shop their favourite brands without needing to log in and enter their information multiple times.” By keeping a note of individuals' payment details—shoppers can use Visa, Mastercard, American Express, PayPal and Discover—on profiles, people no longer need to navigate away from the app to make a purchase on a brand's website. All brands will be charged a “selling fee” when a sale is made on the platform. In recent months the platform has allowed brands to add tags to posts, making it easier for users to find out more information about certain products. More than 130 million users a month have been tapping on posts to look at the products —a considerable increase from 90 million last year. It looks like shopping on Instagram is a welcome addition. column1: Why poetry is back in fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From echoes of Dante’s Inferno on Alexander McQueen and Valentino runways to poems sewn into the very fabric of designs, Vogue examines the rich and creative partnership between poetry and fashion The adjective “poetic” crops up all over the place in fashion show coverage, applied to anything with any kind of sensitivity or technical mastery to it. Though occasionally apt, it often loses any particular clarity of meaning, being easily replaced with its linguistic bedfellows “lyrical” and “romantic”, and applicable to everything from diaphanous dresses and pastels to vaguely studious silhouettes and flamboyant shirts that wouldn't look out of place on Lord Byron or Percy Bysshe Shelley. In more precise ways, though, the relationship between poetry and fashion has proved itself to be a rich one, especially recently, with a number of collections explicitly framed and shaped by the words, work and lives of poets both ancient and contemporary. For his AW19 Valentino offering, Pierpaolo Piccioli collaborated with four contemporary poets (Yrsa Daley-Ward, Mustafa the Poet, Greta Bellamacina and Robert Montgomery), inviting them to contribute words to a series of garments—as well as an accompanying volume titled Valentino On Love. This rising trend has grown in tandem with the increasingly abundant state of poetry. In fact, figures released recently by Nielsen BookScan reveal a 12 per cent rise in poetry sales within the UK, an upward surge driven, mainly, by young women. The news is just as good elsewhere. Last year a report from the NPD Group showed a 21 per cent compound annual growth rate in poetry book sales over the last few years in the US. With the internet providing fresh platforms and visibility for a plethora of voices, and publishing houses championing the sector, the future of verse feels bright. In the fashion world this optimism was perhaps most strongly felt during the AW19 menswear collections. Poetry was, quite literally, everywhere: from Siki Im featuring sections of Pablo Neruda's poem Lost in the Forest on a number of pieces, to Undercover and Valentino collaboratively nodding to Edgar Allan Poe's poetry and prose by way of space-age prints (referencing the conspiracy theory that Poe's startlingly accurate predictions of future events and discoveries could have only been achieved via time travel). At J.M. Weston, Olivier Saillard appeared dressed as a Parisian waiter to describe each shoe on display in verse, while Takahiromiyashita The Soloist added eye-catching patches of poetry to jackets and leather dungarees. At various SS19 shows poetry also reigned supreme. In London, Xu Zhi presented a show infused with the spirit of American poet Emily Dickinson—a series of dramatically tasselled, pale garments alluding to the ongoing mythology around Dickinson's apparent penchant for wearing white. Turkish designer Bora Aksu felt moved by the spirit of poetry too—specifically by the words of Polish-Romani poetess Papusza, otherwise known as Bronisława Wajs. He tells Vogue what specifically resonated within her work. “Gypsy Song Taken From Papusza's Head was the poem that spoke to me most. I really felt her sensitivity—longing for settlement in a nomadic community, the isolation she felt. But also her love for nature. I think her poetry has no filter. It's honest, emotional... Somehow I connected to her and understood her through her poems.” How does one translate a poem like this into wearable clothes though? In the case of Bora Aksu, it meant frills, lace, floral headpieces and plenty of dramatic sleeves, the colour palette running from palest lilacs to opulent reds and oranges. “The SS19 collection is actually a patchwork of episodes from Papusza's life,” Aksu explains. “I took certain parts from her poetry and turned it into colours, trying to reflect her character through layers. Nature was always part of her and her poems, so I designed dresses [that] almost came from nature. The prints and intricate embroidery were a reflection of her sensitivity and complex character.” The dialogue between clothes and poetry isn't a novel one. In the 1920s, textile artist Sonia Delaunay collaborated with a series of Dadaist poets including Tristan Tzara and Joseph Delteil to cover a series of dresses in snippets of their poetry. She called them robes poèmes. None of the resulting works still exist, but illustrations show gorgeous, colour-blocked garments with words snaking across arms and descending down skirts. Other contemporary designers have played with the possibilities of placing actual text on clothes, transforming gowns and T-shirts into serious reading material. Valentino's SS15 couture show was a swirling confection of tulle in various shades of sugared almond, with choice lines from Dante's Inferno gracing a number of gauzy gowns. Meanwhile, over at Alexander McQueen, SS18's menswear show saw fragments of Rudyard Kipling's The Explorer embroidered and printed onto blazers and capes, further embellished with trailing threads. The design house is no stranger to poetry—McQueen's AW96 show was named after Dante and full of appropriately provocative visuals (the Inferno has proved a rather surprisingly popular draw for designers). It's not a one way street when it comes to the well of inspiration either. Poets, in turn, have been drawing on the intricacies of the material world for centuries. From Sappho's “delicate woven cloths” through to Carol Ann Duffy's lavish poem Warming Her Pearls (Duffy, incidentally, edited an anthology in 2004 of fashion-oriented poetry), there's a long and luxurious history of verse centred on the symbolic power of garments. It's something poet Amy Key is especially aware of—her ornate, aching collection Isn't Forever (Bloodaxe) is stitched through with a keen awareness of the thrall and challenges of what we wear. “The language of clothes and fashion gave me access to a different palette of colours and textures—a sumptuousness and a means of augmenting desires I could not possibly fulfil,” she says, when asked about why she's so acutely attuned to dress. “Growing up wearing hand-me-downs and feeling desperately unfashionable, it was revelatory to me when I began to shop in charity shops as a teenager and gained agency over my look. In that way dressing is like making a poem—all those details to make decisions about.” Poet and DJ James Massiah, who's known for his punchy performances exploring love, intimacy and identity, recently collaborated with Grace Wales Bonner for the designer's current Serpentine show A Time for New Dreams. His voice features in the installation alongside Ben Okri's (who also wrote and recited a poem for Bonner's AW19 co-ed collection inspired by the Eighties styling of black intellectuals at Howard University), and he's been involved in events and readings around the exhibition. For one of them, Bonner dressed him in a robe by Erin N Mack “which for me was as much a part of the performance as the reading. I'd have felt differently and perhaps the whole performance would've been perceived differently… had I just been dressed in my black and navy bomber and biker trousers, as opposed to this… garment that uses many of the same materials and stylistic references as the works in the show,” he says. Whether on a catwalk, in a gallery or on a stage, printed on the page or carefully stitched into fabric, the dialogue between poetry and fashion presents plenty of glorious possibilities. Designers pay homage to works that have moved them, whether literally or by way of inventive interpretation. Poets grapple with the intricacies of our sartorial choices. Performances are augmented by careful costuming decisions. Massiah is quick to praise this creative cross-pollination, advocating “finding new ways to connect with other fields and industries, such as fashion, art, film, technology and music, to broaden our reach and heighten our presence within the cultural landscape”. Sometimes, too, it's just a matter of appreciation and being continually, hungrily receptive to what's around us. “All art forms are enriched by other forms of art,” notes Key, “and fashion is no exception.” View Gallery 26 Photos Why poetry is back in fashion After slogan T-shirts, celebrities are turning to ethnic wear with script Not all heroes wear capes, but many Valentino models do Alexander McQueen's most iconic runway moments Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What’s new with denim in India?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Three homegrown labels are making moves with denim in contemporary fashion. Vogue explores their approach to the fabric Indian couturiers seem to have found more ways to express their inspirations through florals than any other design community ever. Finding options for ethnic wear rarely poses a challenge, but to get your hands on a piece of contemporary Indian fashion that blends well with your party wardrobe can be quite a task. Interestingly, the emerging crop of designers that have tapped well into the zeitgeist of the country, have all experimented with denim. Dhruv Kapoor, winner of Vogue India Fashion Fund 2015, looked at taking denim out of the casual context and making it more luxury. “The idea was to explore new washes and to combine something as basic as denim with more expensive materials such as shearling and tigrado fur. This helped us enhance and uplift the ‘basic' approach towards denim,” explains the designer. Kapoor exhibits his work in European countries a few times year, so keeping up with their seasonal cycles is equally important for the homegrown brand. “We are currently working on resort and spring/summer 2020 and denim is still a key fabric for both the forthcoming seasons. For spring 2020, we shall be exploring multiple weights in denim and extending our “jeans” line,” he tells us. At the recently concluded Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week, Huemn, also a winner of Vogue India Fashion Fund (in 2016), showed some key denim pieces for their autumn/winter 2019 lineup. Pranav Misra, one half of the label, started off his career at Orient Craft—one of India's largest garment production units—in their denim washing unit. Interestingly, while developing Huemn's line of denims, Misra worked with Orient Craft to produce the garments. “We are working towards using more environmentally safe washes for jeans with them,” he tells us. While the Indian consumer does not hold back from spending heavily in the bridal category, shopping for a statement piece of denim is not a norm. Though Huemn is steadily pushing for denim in the luxury streetwear category, the response has been slow. “Denim is a fabric that comes in so many weights; the range of products that can be made [with it] is quite wide,” says Misra. For autumn/winter 2019, the brand experimented with leather and rubber patchwork for a graphic look. Diksha Khanna's eponymous label has been working with denim since its debut too. The ripped denim sari that was spotted on the runway won Sonam Kapoor Ahuja's approval. This autumn/winter 2019, she came through again with a collection inspired by the Middle East that was heavy on modest dressing. Khanna opened the season with a patchwork denim and crochet sari, moving into zari denim pantsuits. One can only hope for more experimentation from Khanna. If you look at the landscape of Indian fashion, there is an obvious gap in the market for a denim-only brand. Like Rag & Bone and True Religion, will a homegrown label make a mark in this untapped segment? column1: 7 sari styles for women who can’t drape the six yard staple
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Love wearing a sari but can’t quite perfect the drape? Don’t fret, these styles guarantee the same look minus the effort Whether you consider the sheer elegance of a sari to be its winning factor or its versatility, which makes it appropriate as both day wear and evening wear, the traditional six yard ensemble is undoubtedly a wardrobe staple among women of all ages. Its final look, however, is dependent on how well the sari is draped and pleated. If your amateurish skills still require you to ask your mother or a professional draper for help, you can now look to unique sari iterations to take care of any draping difficulties. “The Indian woman of today has evolved and so has the sari,” Tarun Tahiliani said on a recent Instagram post. “I think pre-constructed saris are in response to the needs of women of today, who have much lesser time to dress, but yet maintain comfort and style. The concept sari is for the modern Indian woman who is aware of traditions, yet strong in her own individual style statement.” Whether it's a sari gown from Tahiliani's latest autumn/winter 2019 collection, Payal Khandwala's redesign of the conventional sari AKA the little sari or even Manish Malhotra's sharara-style sari, these seven saris styles will surely appeal to every modern Indian woman. The hybrid of a sari and a gown, this style is apt for the girl who prefers adding a contemporary touch to her traditional look. An elegant Tarun Tahiliani sari gown or a flattering take on it like Deepika Padukone's Anamika Khanna number, this pre-stitched sari style is easy to wear and comes in a myriad of options. For those of you who want to give your favoured jumpsuit a traditional turn and make it wedding-appropriate, Sonam Kapoor Ahuja and Rhea Kapoor's latest Rheson collection features a version of this Indo-western piece. Love experimenting? Bookmark Mira Rajput Kapoor's daring Shantanu and Nikhil pant-style belted sari for a statement wedding reception look. Swap the strapless blouse with a structured shirt to add a contemporary twist. This sari style replaces the A-line skirt with a sharara or palazzos as the lower half, and comes with an attached pallu draped over it. It's a great alternative to the traditional sari look. Accessorise this one with a statement necklace like Katrina Kaif did, or cinch your waist in with a big belt. If neither sari gowns or pant-style saris work for you, look towards designer Payal Khandwala's little sari. As the name suggests, this sari style is half the size of a sari but still longer than a dupatta. The best bit? You can use it to transform your everyday outfits—a pair of jeans and a shirt; pants and a blouse—into traditional showcases. In an attempt to make saris more feasible for daily wear, designer Rashmi Varma introduced the sari dress, which melds both styles together. Akin to a maxi dress, this variation features a pallu to retain the essence of a six yard drape. Similar to a lehenga set, the lehenga sari comes with a pre-stitched lehenga and an attached dupatta that is draped on top. column1: This fashion stylist is now launching his own clothing label
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion KuGar by Kushal Parmanand and Asgar Munshi is all about resort wear glam for the sophisticated modern woman It all started when fashion stylist Kushal Parmanand wore a self-designed kaftan shirt for a party, and was flooded with requests to make some more by his girlfriends. The idea to launch a label took shape in November last year over a conversation with his friend Asgar Munshi, who has been designing couture and bridal wear for more than a decade now. The duo decided to marry their respective creative flair and technical prowess to launch KuGar—a play on their names as well as a light-hearted ode to the women who inspire them. Parmanand, who has worked with magazines like Seventeen and L'Officiel and publishing houses like Condé Nast India in his 15-year-long career, describes KuGar as “everyday resort glam for the woman who wants to have fun, whether she's headed to a dinner party or a destination wedding. While the aesthetic is grown up, it's for the ones who don't take themselves too seriously.” The duo's close-knit circle of friends (and cheerleaders)—including the likes of Gucci's Maneka Thadani, Atosa's Aparna Badlani, fashion designer Payal Singhal, stylist Nisha Jhangiani, TheLabelLife.com's Preeta Sukhtankar and former GQ India fashion editor Natasha Chib, among others—are the muses for the label. “Each piece has been designed with one woman in mind. Working with a mood board of such diverse sensibilities, personalities, skin tones and body types has allowed us to create an exceedingly versatile collection with something for everyone,” adds Munshi. The brand's maiden summer collection is centred around a colour palette of foliage green and old rose with hints of red, and also features custom floral print. The silhouettes include anti-fit kaftans, column gowns and separates that are not only comfort-driven, but also encourage mixing and matching. column1: Captain Marvel’s costume designer on not giving the hero a sexier outfit
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As Captain Marvel continues to smash box-office records—and gender stereotypes—Vogue speaks to costume designer Sanja Milkovic Hays about her vision for a new dawn of female superheroes Superhero films are on a roll—and none more so than Captain Marvel, which is already one of the highest-grossing film of 2019. Part of the genre's appeal—good vs evil fantasy aside—is the kick-ass costumes; see Ruth E Carter's Oscar-winning Afro-futurist designs in Black Panther, and here, Sanja Milkovic Hays' creations for Marvel's first female-led film. Known for her work on action and sci-fi movies including Star Trek Beyond and the The Fast and the Furious franchise, Hays was thrilled to join the Marvel family for the landmark film. “We want to see women on screen, especially women that are so strong and so powerful. I'm so happy to be part of this,” Hays tells Vogue. Andy Park, Marvel Studios director of visual development, who previously helped shape the looks of Black Widow and the Wasp, created the initial designs for the modern Captain Marvel, the superhero mantle taken on by pilot Carol Danvers (played by Brie Larson) when she acquires special powers. Hays collaborated with Park to bring the costumes to life and transform the concept into functional garments. This contemporary Captain Marvel represents the way female superheroes can, and should, look going forward—embracing their gender without being objectified or overtly sexualised. “Her suit is strong and super-heroic, but still very feminine,” explains Hays. “It was a conscious decision to not just make her a gorgeous, beautiful thing; but instead make her costume part of her attitude. She's a girl with an attitude and rightfully so, she has nothing to prove. It's a very modern concept for a female superhero. Hopefully a lot of young women can relate to that.” Captain Marvel's suit includes elements that could belong to any superhero, regardless of gender. Her iconic masked helmet for example, with its striking mohawk, is typically not something we've seen female superheroes wearing on-screen. She wears sturdy boots, rather than high heels, and there was never any discussion of having her wear a sexier outfit, closer to the comic book depictions, says Hays. Larson wears two different super-suits in the film: a military-inspired blue, red and gold Starforce one-piece, created from synthetic “liquid leather”; and her Captain Marvel suit, made from leather backed with a stretchy fabric and moulded 3D elements. Hays and her team had about eight months to prepare ahead of filming, using life-sized models of the actors to help guide the process. Fitting Larson, however, proved to be a challenge as she got increasingly fit in training for the role, which meant continuous costume adjustments. “She was working out like crazy—I'm so in awe of her,” says Hays. “Her body was changing, as expected, so she was coming in repeatedly for fittings. Over the course of working out she was finding out more and more what her action scenes were going to be, and so we were making sure what we were doing would allow her to do certain things.” The look for alter-ego Carol Danvers is purposefully edgy, too. When she lands on earth and needs street clothes, she grabs baggy jeans, a Nine Inch Nails T-shirt and a flannel shirt, evoking classic Nineties grunge. Of the tee, Hays says she wanted an unassuming but spirited logo, to make a subtle statement: “It had to be period, but it had to be attractive to the audience today. She's a pilot and a tomboy, so what would a young woman like that wear? And she's a big rock‘n'roll girl. So, a combination of rock‘n'roll and grunge was obviously the way to go.” (The band is now selling a special edition Captain Marvel tee on their website.) Beyond the aesthetic, the costumes needed to be functional too. “The hardest part was translating [Park's vision] into a costume that can be worn,” says Hays. “Brie had to be able to do all the action scenes, running and jumping and spinning and fighting—all the crazy stuff you see on-screen. The costumes had to be comfortable enough to move in, but also look perfect when standing still. It's a very, very specific geometry. We were moving things by half an inch here and half an inch there [to get it right].” View Gallery 5 Photos The making of Captain Marvel’s costumes Captain Marvel returns to help save the day in Avengers: Endgame. column1: Gucci is selling intentionally dirty sneakers for almost Rs 60,000
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The ugly sneaker trend continues to thrive on runways, with the Italian luxury brand making the latest addition to a long line of purposely unattractive designer kicks Complete with a bi-colour outsole, green panels of leather, and a terry-cloth trim, Gucci's Screener sneaker is also available in a crystal-embellished edition that you can shop now if you happen to have a spare AU$2,015 lying around. While this isn't the first time we've seen brands including including Balenciaga, Hood By Air and Vetements take the ugly sneaker trend to a whole new level, it is necessary to note that Gucci's take on the old-school trainer retails at a total of AU$1,175. You might find yourself asking why someone would willingly fork over almost $1,200 for dirty shoes? Per US Vogue, Wellesley College assistant professor of psychology Angela Bahns has the answer. “Our research found that having neat and tidy shoes tends to correlate with the person being anxious, conscientious, or politically conservative,” she told the publication. “So the choice to use dirty shoes on the runway might be an effort to portray an image of being calm, not uptight, or politically liberal.” However, while this may in fact be the case, the trend has managed to offend those who find it only serves to contribute to the glorification of poverty. And when Golden Goose's AU$745 edition hit stands in 2018, Twitter also erupted with a slew of memes. “I think peak capitalism is selling shoes characteristic of those who can't afford new ones for $530,” wrote one user at the time. “Are people really out here paying $500 for brand new shoes that look worn out...bc if so I got some fire for you guys for a cheap price of $400,” wrote another. As for how the Gucci's Screener sneaker, which is now available for purchase both in store and online, will be received, only time will tell. column1: 8 indie Indian labels your ethnic wear wardrobe needs
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion These independent brands are redefining ethnic wear with their ‘less is more’ approach to traditional silhouettes like kurtas and saris Think of ethnic wear, and the first natural association is ‘extra'—high-shine embellishments, dramatic silhouettes and an overall ‘more is more' aesthetic. But look beyond the mainstream, and you'll discover a growing tribe of indie labels that have extended their pared-down sensibility and sustainable mindset to traditional silhouettes. We handpick eight such homegrown brands that ought to be on your radar—whether you choose them for an intimate destination wedding or to elevate your everyday repertoire, that's entirely your call. The brand name translates to pure cotton in Hindi, and true to its etymology, thrives on local fabrics and handmade creations. Bohemian at heart, Khara Kapas' shararas, saris and angarakhas, featuring soft colours and light embellishments, are perfect to kick-start the festive season. Think roomy. Think comfortable. Silāi's mostly khadi and cotton creations are all about fuss-free cool, and their festive staples are replete with layered tunics, cropped palazzos and delicately embroidered jackets. You may end up with the most bling-heavy wedding season wardrobe, but your ethnic wear will definitely be exceedingly effortless. Eclectic and bright hand blocked patterns are the mainstay of this brand, which uses natural Indian textiles and works directly with craftsmen at the grassroot level. Jodi wears its ‘made in India' tag proudly but doesn't ignore its contemporary patron either, which is why their silhouettes are high on versatility. Those colour-blocked maxis can translate from brunch to mehandis, and the printed saris are just as apt for a dinner party as they are for a puja. Rooted in Indian heritage, Galang Gabaan takes its cues from the textiles and handicrafts of Odisha to create modern-day must-haves ‘with love', which is what the brand name means in Santhali (a regional language) too. Their fuss-free and easy-to-drape linen saris are made for women who are textile connoisseurs. Tales of Indian mythology inspire Torani's handcrafted clothing, thus every collection is high on nostalgia and old-world influences. The ethnic wear designs are as luxurious as they are individualistic. So what you have are Chanderi saris paired with reversible block print jackets, scalloped farshi pajamas, and handwoven choga jackets worn with crushed skirts—ideal for the woman who wouldn't be caught dead in looks similar to what the crowds are wearing. The label claims to have an ‘awe-inspiringly nonchalant' ideology, much like the personal style of its founder, model-cum-stylist Chandni Sareen. The collections are free-spirited and bohemian, combining ikat with khadi, cotton and denim to create versatile separates that define easy luxe. Wear their crop top and skirt sets for a beach wedding or as separates on days spent out and about town. Brainchild of former Calvin Klein designer Caroline Weller, who is now based in Jaipur, Banjanan is a play on ‘banjaran', giving the brand an inherently gypsy soul. The artisanal label supports the local craft community of Rajasthan's capital city with its vibrant prints and free-flowing silhouettes. These are designs to roam the world in, whether your itinerary includes a pre-wedding brunch in Udaipur or a poolside date in Ubud. Simran Chaudhry of Artisau originally started off making clothes for dolls, which probably explains her emphasis on creating happy clothes. Simple yet not boring, Chaudhry embellishes her roomy palazzos and tunic dresses with soft fabrics and hidden details.
