column1: This is how the LGBTQ+ world is inspiring designers
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Erdem’s full-blown homage to two Victorian cross-dressers, to artist and drag queen Sasha Velour’s SS19 Opening Ceremony takeover—Vogue explores the queer icons that are inspiring fashion right now Opening Ceremony's SS19 show wasn't just a show, it was an extravaganza. Taking place at New York's (Le) Poisson Rouge and curated by renowned drag queen, artist and winner of RuPaul's Drag Race series nine, Sasha Velour, the two-hour affair saw a vast cast of LGBTQ+ performers and models present an elaborate, joyfully executed celebration of queerness. Oh, and some clothes too. “I didn't really grasp the magnitude of what we were doing until I was standing on stage in front of Nicki Minaj, Whoopi Goldberg and Baz Luhrmann, wearing a three-foot tall headpiece dripping in hair, a dress I could barely move in, all while balancing on 11-inch heels and lip-synching to Dionne Warwick!” Velour exclaims. As with so many fashion shows, it was all a whirl of grand ambitions and frantic last-minute assembly. One that, predictably, left people talking for days. It felt like the right time for a show like this—one putting queer people front and centre, both on stage and behind the scenes. “Although this certainly wasn't the first collection to take inspiration from queer styling (or even to star LGBTQ+ or drag models), to my knowledge it is the very first to invite a working drag performer and nightlife producer to design the show from the concept onward,” Velour notes. “It really is such a gift to be present at the table in that sense; to have a role in crafting an evening that represents our voices and tastes alongside our imagery.” The worlds of fashion and queer culture have forever been intertwined. Clothes have long helped shape and articulate identity (as well as restrict it), especially for those whose identities are marginalised or under threat. It's something that this year's Met Gala theme and Costume Institute exhibition, Camp: Notes on Fashion, picks up on, taking Susan Sontag's famed essay of 1964 as its starting point. Camp's roots are firmly anchored in gay culture, with Sontag's 58 fragmented notes outlining an aesthetic and sensibility reliant on pastiche, subversion and high drama. One that, historically, saw expressions of sexuality coded into an intricate series of choices around dress and mannerism. However, camp is expansive. Over time it has been described as everything from a language to a particular way of seeing. Sontag's work is as mercurial as the subject matter; the Costume Institute's head curator Andrew Bolton says, “In all these years we've been talking about camp, still nobody has a definition. They might agree to the fact that it came out of queer culture. They agree that in the modes of expression it's often [incorporating] exaggeration, artifice, ironies. But when it comes to defining it, it's impossible because it's amorphous, it changes so much, it's parasitic.” Among the various strands and meanings of camp, the exhibition explores the relationship between fashion, camp and queer culture in a number of ways. As Bolton observes, “Part of the idea behind the exhibition is to isolate an aesthetic that's become so invisible, and show its roots and its origins.” He also wanted to foreground the political implications. “It's still being used without realising it, and it's interesting because when you talk to young kids about drag queens and gender fluidity, it's not something they think about consciously because it's so integrated into our lives. So part of it is isolating camp in order to talk about it, but also partly to show appreciation for it too.” In doing so, the exhibition also looks to a long lineage of LGBTQ+ icons, from playwright Oscar Wilde to Victorian cross-dressing duo Fanny and Stella. The latter's significance is illustrated via two dresses from Erdem's SS19 collection, where the pair became reference points for a show both dreamy and dramatic. And Erdem isn't the only designer who's been delving into the queer history books recently. SS19 saw an array of acknowledgements of LGBTQ+ figures: from Matty Bovan drawing on Derek Jarman to Gareth Pugh paying his respects to Judy Blame. First though, back to Fanny and Stella. Otherwise known as Frederick Park and Ernest Boulton, the pair became something of a sensation in 1870 when they were arrested after frequenting the theatre in women's garb, as they were regularly known to do, and brought to trial on accusations of sodomy. They were never charged, but the entire affair brought to light not only wide-scale police corruption, but also the establishment's disquiet with—and need to make a moral example of—unabashed, unconventional displays of gender and sexuality. Erdem first discovered their narrative after finding a plaque dedicated to the pair in Bloomsbury, where he and his partner Philip live. “When I started to research their story I was fascinated,” he says. “Fanny and Stella lived at a time when Darwinism was rife and the Republican movement was rising. They were living very much on the fringe of society. They were well-known nightlife characters in London.” Using this as his starting point, Erdem researched the rich history of 19th-century cross-dressing—looking, too, at female performers who donned men's clothes on stage. The results are gorgeous: an appropriately theatrical profusion of lace, lavish prints, black net veils, voluminous skirts, puffed sleeves and bright pink ribbons galore. “For me every season it's less about exactly who the characters were but the trigger that causes you to go there with the collection,” he says. “This was about two women who dressed to be who they fundamentally were.” Elsewhere in London, Bovan turned to Jarman, the mischievous, multitalented, deliciously frank film-maker and writer. Outspoken in his sexuality (and particularly trailblazing in his level of public honesty around his AIDs diagnosis), Jarman's legacy remains a powerful one, both creatively and politically. Bovan first discovered Jarman's films aged 19 after moving to London. “I loved his sense of 'just get on with it'—no lavish budgets, and he collaborated with friends to create something raw and something new. He told a story with film and always had his tongue in his cheek. He knew what he was making was a construct.” Jarman's DIY spirit and anti-establishment ethos comes through strongly in Bovan's collection: from the clash of fabrics and textures—layers of netting erupting from dresses, screen-printed words proclaiming “Infinite Void” sliding across garments—to the cascades of crocheted flowers and bright plastic cable ties. There's an impish exuberance to the clothes and headpieces, many of which wouldn't look out of place at Andrew Logan's Alternative Miss World competition (which, incidentally, Jarman won in 1975, under the moniker Miss Crepe Suzette). Pugh's collection, meanwhile, paid homage to Blame, another gay man who revelled in turning the mundane upside down. The influence of the late designer, artist, stylist and 1980s club maven, with his meticulous eye and taste for elevating everyday objects to unexpected ends, was keenly felt: echoes found in Pugh's outlandish proportions, melodramatic makeup and generally playful approaches to outfitting the body. Across the Channel at Givenchy, Clare Waight Keller was looking towards Annemarie Schwarzenbach: someone else who, to paraphrase Erdem, dressed to reflect exactly who she was. A remarkable Swiss-born journalist, novelist and photographer, she was best known for her extensive travels, androgynous style and numerous affairs with women (plus a face that the novelist Carson McCullers claimed “would haunt me for the rest of my life”). With her short hair and propensity for perfectly tailored menswear, numerous portraits suggest a figure both coolly self-possessed and comfortable with blurring any rigid definitions of masculinity or femininity. Keller translated this into a louche palette of blues, greens, silvers and browns, with plenty of boxy blazers and tailored trousers with room for striding along the way. Other design houses have drawn on queer women and non-binary people in recent years – but in smaller numbers than their male counterparts. Alongside Schwarzenbach, there are the Surrealist artists Leonor Fini and Claude Cahun, both of whom have been referenced by Maria Grazia Chiuri at Dior: Fini's love of costuming lending extra spectacle to SS18's couture show, and Cahun's gender-neutrality (and, perhaps, time spent living on Jersey) informing a series of suits and vaguely nautical touches for pre-fall 2018. Elsewhere, authors Virginia Woolf and Vita Sackville-West—whose exquisite, funny love letters deserve reissuing—have been called upon repeatedly. During Christopher Bailey's tenure at Burberry, Woolf was often cited to conjure up a particular kind of thick cardigan-clad bohemianism—culminating in his SS17 show, hooked on her novel Orlando, the theatrical ruffs and swishing coats riffing on a protagonist who switches gender, loves both men and women, and was very much an adoring tribute to the physicality and temperament of Sackville-West. More recently, Preen's pre-fall 2019 drew on a visit to Sissinghurst Castle, where Sackville-West lived, by way of tartans, checks, lavish drapery and plenty of feather trim. Givenchy aside, it's interesting how many of SS19's explicitly queer-inspired offerings are also inextricably linked with what goes on after dark. Pugh's tribute to Blame culminated in a Vogueing Ball in his honour, in collaboration with Benjamin Milan—a fitting send-off for someone who figured so vividly in London's nightlife. Elsewhere, Ashish's glitz and neon affair could have been lifted from a 1990s rave (and came with a series of messages about inclusivity—ones made especially resonant in the wake of the designer's powerful words the week before on the decriminalisation of homosexuality in India). It's something Erdem is cognisant of too. “I was thinking about what Stella and Fanny would want to wear if they lived near King's Cross during the 1980s and 1990s,” he reflects, “a time where there was this sense of taboo and all the warehouse parties were happening.” I ask Velour about this. Why is nightlife, whether performance or club-oriented, especially important to queer communities? “Often we have no choice but to build our spaces and culture in the dead of night!” she says. “Very few queer people have the freedom to deliver their full queerness during the day. In many cases, making ourselves truly visible can even open up real danger.” In the case of Velour's line of work, it's also a question of economic necessity. “Drag is usually a late-night activity because most kings and queens have day jobs. I used to cover my eyebrows with glue in the bathroom at work, so I wouldn't be late to the gig!” Whether in daylight or after sundown, perhaps what feels especially intriguing about this handful of shows and reference points are the ways in which they've created a particular kind of dialogue with queer culture, both past and present. One running the gamut from crisp shirts to tongue-in-cheek offerings to some of the dazzling costumes soon to be exhibited at the Costume Institute. One unapologetic, celebratory, sly and often very beautiful too. It's a dialogue set to continue into AW19—with Thom Browne's office-inflected show including graphic monochrome prints of sculptor and translator Una Troubridge, the long-term lesbian partner of author Radclyffe Hall. There's still undoubtedly a long way to go, especially when it comes to the role of queer people within the fashion industry—whether behind the scenes or on the catwalk (though it must be noted that Erdem, alongside other designers including Louis Vuitton and Marco Marco, emphasised the presence of trans, androgynous and non-binary models in their shows). But it's an optimistic mood and one that's left Velour hopeful for further visibility. “Queer-run operations, historically situated a bit outside the mainstream, have developed different ways of doing work that are just as valid. Given the opportunity, I think a lot of us would love to share our talents with a wider audience.” View Gallery 20 Photos The queer icons shaping fashion 5 pro-LGBTQ shows you need to watch on Netflix now H&M launches its first ever collection dedicated to the LGBTQ+ community How Barbie's commitment to diversity has changed the game for the brand  What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights: Day 4 of Lotus Makeup India Fashion Week A/W 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Siddartha Tytler’s ’80s inspired collection to the sari show finale, here’s everything that went down on the last day at Lotus Makeup India Fashion Week Lotus Makeup India Fashion week came to an ended with a multi-designer finale—one that paid homage to the six yard drape. The grand finale saw the classic sari interpreted by some of the most noted labels in the industry, including Akaaro, Alpana & Neeraj, Amit Aggarwal, Anamika Khanna, Anavila, Anita Dongre, Bodice, Gaurav Gupta, Little Shilpa, Neeru Kumar, Pankaj & Nidhi, Payal Khandwala, Prashant Verma, Raw Mango, Rimzim Dadu, Rohit Bal, Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna, Tarun Tahiliani, Urvashi Kaur and Wendell Rodricks. The last day also witnessed some young designers on the block including Doh Tak Keh, Tiso Ghari by Badal & Bhumi, Naka clothing by Paras Chawla, Done & Dusted by Disha and SGBG Atelier for the #YoungGuns showcase. Scroll down to catch up everything you missed from Day 4. Young Guns Emerging labels Doh Tak Keh, Tiso Ghari by Badal & Bhumi, Naka clothing by Paras Chawla, Done & Dusted by Disha and SGBG Atelier came together for a showcase that highlighted their strengths. Siddartha Tytler Channelling ‘80s glamour, Siddartha Tytler showcased his autumn/winter 2019 collection titled ‘Shadow' that was inspired by old-world glamour. The lineup saw a mix of bodycon dresses with risqué cutouts, velvet joggers, embellished jackets and sheer shirts. Tytler made use of fabrics such as neoprene, velvet and tulle. Actor Jim Sarbh played the showstopper for his show and walked the ramp in an embellished black jacket. Grand finale Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019 came to a close with some of the biggest names in Indian fashion paying homage to the sari. From more structural sculpted looks by Gaurav Gupta and Rimzim Dadu to conceptual pre-stitched numbers by Suneet Verma, Tarun Tahiliani and Anamika Khanna, the show proved to be the place to source inspiration from. No sari show would be complete without some exceptional weaves, and designers like Akaaro, Payal Khandwala and Urvashi Kaur came through. Keeping things modern with contemporary takes on the sari were labels like Bodice, Prashant Verma and Amit Aggarwal. 21 designers, 50 models all putting their best sari foot forward, what's not to love ? column1: 24 pictures that take you inside Sonakshi Sinha’s wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From lazy girl-approved athleisure to couture gowns, Sonakshi Sinha’s wardrobe plays host to all of them In the nine years she's clocked onscreen since her debut in Dabangg, if there's one thing we've figured about Sonakshi Sinha, it's that she has no time for half-measures. Her unapologetic candour extends to her wardrobe too, which serves up a merry directory of diverse silhouettes. From pared-down athleisure separates to princess-perfect ballgowns, Sinha's sartorial meter runs the gamut between both extremes. If you're looking to take notes from the laid-back glamour of her wardrobe picks, here's a closer look at her staple favourites. Fuss-free silhouettes dominate Sinha's closet when off-duty, with a statement bomber jacket serving as her personal go-to for elevating a basic outfit. Regardless of the temperature outside, crop tops are another frequent feature in her style directory, usually featured with a rotating roster of high-waisted pants, paper bag palazzos and hybrid dhoti pants. For days when you're looking to make a statement, you'll want to take notes from the actor's discerning eye for layering. Long, trailing jackets serve as Sinha's answer to just about every sartorial query in the book, from breaking up the monotony of matchy-matchy separates to amping up a basic tank top. Sonakshi Sinha has been championing bodycon minis and androgynous suits with equal flair on the red carpet, leaving behind a trail of broken fashion myths about body types and silhouettes littered in her wake. Her signature flair for drama usually puts in an appearance in her red carpet picks, whether it is a head-to-toe sequinned Dhruv Kapoor pantsuit or a turtle-necked, form-fitting metallic gown from Yanina. From mesh inserts to lacy bustiers, her experimental streak means that you won't see her wearing one silhouette the same way twice. Flip over to the ethnic side of her wardrobe, and you'll find unconventional styles clocking in major face time—a prominent social wedding in December last year had her opting for a fusion Anamika Khanna sari paired with gold pants, while the recent Ambani bash called for a sheer champagne-hued sari from Manish Malhotra. column1: Alexander McQueen’s most iconic runway moments
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion To mark what would have been the designer’s 50th birthday, Vogue revisits his most memorable runway moments—from a ring of fire and rain on the catwalk to spray-painting robots and a hologram of Kate Moss Alexander McQueen was a visionary. Over the course of his 18-year career, the designer's presentations for both his eponymous label and Givenchy, where he served as creative director from 1996 to 2001, were the stuff of legend: 10 minutes of pure theatre that enthralled audiences with their audacity and conceptual brilliance. The recipient of four British Designer of the Year awards, as well as a CBE, and now heralded as a genius, it's easy to forget that McQueen's creations were divisive from the offset. His 1992 graduate collection, entitled “Jack the Ripper Stalks His Victims”, included a coat printed with thorns and locks of McQueen's own hair sewn into the garments. It set the tone for the shows that followed: “Taxi Driver” paid homage to Martin Scorsese's troubled protagonist Travis Bickle; “Highland Rape” was a commentary on England's violation of Scotland; and “The Hunger” showcased transparent bustiers filled with worms. For “Dante” in 1996, a skeleton was seated front row, while the 1997 show “It's a Jungle Out There” saw a car catching fire, albeit accidentally. McQueen's shock tactics weren't always a hit with his sponsors. The designer's spring/summer 1998 show, partly financed by American Express, was originally titled “The Golden Shower” before the company demanded the name be changed. McQueen conceded, calling it “Untitled”, but that didn't stop him sending models down a runway made of water-filled tanks while rain poured from above and spotlights bathed them in a suggestive yellow glow. For “Joan” later that year, his exploration of the elements moved from water to fire with a show that ended with a masked model being surrounded by a ring of fire. Meanwhile, 1999's “No. 13” was the collection that cemented McQueen's reputation as the ultimate showman. It not only featured Paralympian Aimee Mullins wearing prosthetic legs carved from elm wood, but ended with two robots spray-painting a dress worn by supermodel Shalom Harlow. The latter went on to become one of the most memorable catwalk finales in fashion history. But the designer wasn't done yet. Over the next decade, showgoers were treated to a presentation with a sinister merry-go-round, a human game of chess, a vision of an underwater world post-climate change and a ghostly hologram of Kate Moss. On what would have been the designer's 50th birthday, Vogue pays tribute to his incredible work and revisits 20 of McQueen's unforgettable runway moments. column1: Highlights from Day 3 of Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week A/W 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Pankaj & Nidhi’s party-ready collection to Namrata Joshipura’s edgy ensembles, catch up on everything you missed from Day 3 of Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019 Day 3 of Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019 saw a mix of several different aesthetics. While designer Vineet Bahl presented a print-heavy, desert-inspired collection featuring, both Pankaj & Nidhi and Namrata Joshipura went for embellishment and shimmer this season. Missed all the excitement from yesterday? Scroll ahead for a quick recap of all the top moments from Day 3. Vineet Bahl's autumn/winter 2019 collection titled ‘Safari Soirée' championed print-on-print. Colours of the desert dominated his collection, which came in a palette of orange, white, yellow and scarlet. But that's not all. Along with layering, Bahl's latest offering also featured nautical elements for a fun twist. Pankaj & Nidhi's autumn/winter 2019 showcase highlighted the brand's forté—surface embellishment. The collection was inspired by the duo's recent visit to the Rijksmuseum museum in Amsterdam, Netherlands. From fringe detailing to quilting, the designers explored a host of techniques to create yet another unique evening wear collection. The line-up was a mix of sequinned dresses, skirts, jackets and ruffled blouses, that came decorated with floral origami-like geometric patterns on rich taffeta, silk velvets and organza. [#image: /photos/5ce3f3e3b41afb61e5a96af8]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue Day 3 of Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019 came to a close with Namrata Joshipura's show. The designer, who's best known for her party-ready creations, presented a collection that was as eye-catching as it was wearable. Think embroidered cocktail-appropriate skirts, sparkling pantsuits and festive gowns in a palette of charcoal, dark blues, black and deep purples, with a pop or two of scarlet thrown in to the mix. And what better way to give the line a fun spin than with unexpected accessories liek baseball caps and belt bags? column1: Bhumi Pednekar’s complete style transformation
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From vibrant floral skirts to slinky party dresses, Bhumi Pednekar’s sartorial choices showcase inspiration for distinctly different body types Bhumi Pednekar first came into the limelight with Dum Laga Ke Haisha in 2015, a movie that put her in the headlines for more than her acting chops—her debut role demanded she play an overweight bride, for which she had to gain 12 kilos. Once the initial buzz around her weight gain and subsequent loss died down and she was seen in other features—Toilet: Ek Prem Katha (2017), Lust Stories (2018), Sonchiriya (2019)—it was clear that Pednekar was a talent to be reckoned with, with a few sartorial tricks up her sleeve, too. Right from the beginning of her career, Pednekar seems to have possessed an innate sense that has helped her pick outfits that flatter her body. Whether it was a crop top and high-waisted A-line skirt combination that brought attention to her midriff or a free-flowing maxi dress, Pednekar's outfits have often been met with an appreciative nod. Her personal style veers more towards casual and functional dressing with the likes of skirts, blouses, jeans, tops, dresses and ethnic wear making up the majority of her wardrobe—things we would easily find in our own closets. As the years progressed, so did Bhumi Pednekar's taste in fashion. But it was only in 2019 that we saw an actual round-about in her picks—monochrome dressing became a common theme, designer handbags served as statement accessories, and black became a go-to hue for day wear and evening wear alike. Her beauty look also transitioned from muted and understated to bold and sharp—red lips, heavy-duty eye makeup and sharp contouring. column1: How Deepika Padukone does movie star casual
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Since the beginning of her career, Deepika Padukone’s wardrobe has featured both casual and statement-worthy pieces alike. Here, we tell you how to get three of her looks No one does glamour like Deepika Padukone, the Bollywood leading lady known for her incredibly elegant wardrobe and box-office hits. Since the beginning of her career, the April Vogue cover star has used fashion as her means of self-expression, switching from breathtaking saris by Indian designers like Sabyasachi Mukherjee to sumptuous couture from Zuhair Murad. Together with husband, Ranveer Singh, she is also part of one of the world's most stylish couples, but her love of fashion extends far beyond those oft photographed opulent gowns. Yes, Padukone and her stylist Shaleena Nathani pull out one dramatic look after another on Instagram and at events like the Met Gala and Cannes Film Festival, but there's room for casual clothes in her impressive wardrobe, too. Padukone doesn't need a special occasion to make a statement, and her more laid-back looks showcase an international movie star's take on everyday dress. To breeze through the airport in Mumbai last week, a Valentino T-shirt paired with a black leather jacket made for a simply chic outfit. Likewise, a trip from Bangalore in November required a Philo-era Céline striped top and Burberry bag. Even a brunch date calls for a little something. Out in London yesterday with Singh and fellow Bollywood star Varun Dhawan, Padukone gave the paparazzi an athleisure moment in a tangerine Nike sweatsuit. Effortless—and the perfect contrast to Singh's head-to-toe Gucci logo print—it was one of her most relaxed outfits to date. Naturally, Padukone couldn't resist adding a little luxury. column1: Two real women debate the practicality of the cycling shorts trend
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion When it comes to the cycling shorts trend, are you a yay or a nay? Two women, with two wildly differing opinions, help you decide Disclaimer: My age, size and fashion predilection have nothing to do with my views on the following trend. There are two vivid images that front my imagination when I am forced to think of cycling shorts—one of the late Princess Di leaving the gym. And Lance Armstrong during Tour de France. Playing a lead role in both, the shorts then represented function over fashion. Comfort, not style. When they were conceived in the '70s, these sweat-wicking, stretchy shorts were made with the specific purpose of making it easier for cyclists to prevent chafing and bunching. Which is precisely why, when two decades later, these distant cousins of the legging family have started invading my Instagram timeline, often tagged gladly as the #OOTD, I am compelled to ask aloud: What went wrong here? Do we live in times where anything goes as fashion? Can balance be restored in the sartorial cosmos? All our years of getting oriented to good style and great fashion teach us that clothes are personality-markers. They give away so much about your life, your mood and what you want the world to know about you. So, when you show up at work in a belted white shirt with cycling shorts underneath, what are you saying? That you forgot to change one half of your gym gear? That if you are happy to wear your cycling shorts to work, you would be just as open to wear that shirt to the gym? Or that you are just confused about what makes for good style anymore? Then there is that added problem of accessorising. Too Candy Crush and you risk looking like Kimmy Gibbler's doppelgänger from Full House. Too much and you risk looking like you are about to break out any moment into Salt-N-Pepa's ‘Push It'. Good news is, it's not too late to save your style. If you have yet to buy one, thank your fashion police, you have been absolved. And if you have succumbed to the pressure and own a pair, introduce them to your tees, sneakers, tracks, hoodies...you know. Verdict: Cute in a gym if you must. Completely un-cute IRL. Remember the first time you realised the fanny pack was making a serious fashion comeback? And good ol' mom jeans? Let's not forget the hard-hitting dad sneakers. Cycling shorts are the next '90s mega trend to be back in the spotlight. And if it isn't love at first sight, that's okay. Just don't be a hater. This little number is as comfortable as leggings (people run marathons and climb mountains in these) and as flattering as a miniskirt (think of all that leg it has to offer). All you need to do is pair it with your favorite XXL top. Sounds easy enough? Well, it is. It also helps that science is on our side. Never before has the cycling short been more flattering. Suctioning waistband with built-in tummy control? Yes, please. Spandex slimming silhouette? Bring it on. Butt contouring? Don't mind if we do. Please note that Princess Diana was slaying this trend way before any of these sneaky tricks existed. These days our feeds are dominated by Kim K, who prefers her variety by her husband's label Yeezy, and sister Khloé, who makes her own version at Good American. Even the Hadid sisters are getting in on the action. I am no Hadid by any means, especially after baby number two and stubborn postpartum weight. But I've realised it's all about proportion for me. If I want to wear a potato sack to cover my flaws on the top half of my body, so be it, but for the bottom half I've got to give them something to talk about. And if I want to make it look more sexy, less spin class, I bring out a structured blazer and heels. Cropped tops work too, but are preferred with toned abs and a thigh gap, neither of which are applicable currently. For now, as a mom of two, I'm going to stay in the athleisure space, channelling my inner aerobics instructor without bothering to set foot in the gym. So sceptics, move aside; this waist-slimming, butt-perking slinky short is a keeper. If it's good enough for a princess, it's good enough for you. column1: Highlights from Day 2 at Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Huemn and Samant Chauhan to Suneet Varma, catch up on all the leading shows you missed from Day 2 at Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019 As an unlikely mid-March rain poured in New Delhi, complete with cloudy skies and chilly winds, the runways at Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019 countered the gloom with shiny couture courtesy Suneet Varma, an existential commentary by Huemn and dreams of safari escapes at Samant Chauhan. Read on for everything you missed from Day 2. Backstage, Shyma Shetty, one half of Huemn, said, “We're inspired by Kashmir again this season. Only this time it's the other side—the youth of Kashmir and their raw energy against the beautiful but conflict-ridden landscape they live in.” And while '90s sneaker culture came to the fore along with the label's signature athleisure in their collaboration with Reebok's ‘Alter the Icons' collection, what really hung in the air was Pranav Misra and Shetty's voice-over in the background asking all the real questions: “Why are we here? What are we going to do? What are we here for?” Questions they called our generation's focus. Questions that we must ask because isn't that after all the essence of being human (or Huemn)? The social commentary continued with Chauhan's show, but this time we were transported to somewhere in Africa. As the models walked down a dried-grass lined runway in lofty whites, there was a semblance of summer in the autumn/winter collection. The show notes read: “Chauhan garbs his woman in layers, capturing the myriad hues of her existence, the conflicts and harmony, the distortions and the truth weaved in detailed embroidery in jewel tones and shades of pink, orange, rust and burgundy on whites and ivories.” The last show for the day and also the most upbeat of the day, Suneet Varma's bridal couture collection, in association with Nirakara Jewels, was all kinds of happy and shiny. From foot-tapping music to paillette-covered lehengas, ruffled and bedazzled saris and even evening gowns, there was never a dull moment. In his signature style, Varma ended the show with a siren red lehenga with an exaggerated veil. And just when you thought it was over, the designer presented a bold black lehenga skirt hybrid with a crystal bodice. Black for the bride, you ask? Why not. column1: 3 Middle Eastern designers you need to watch out for in 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Sonam Kapoor Ahuja to Kendall Jenner, every celebrity has these Middle Eastern designers on their speed dial Middle Eastern designers have always been known for their love of glamour and drama—and it is for this reason that so many designers from this region have ruled on the red carpet, especially during awards season. Reem Acra, Elie Saab, Zuhair Murad and more recently, Georges Chakra and Ashi Studio have become regulars, and are now the go-to designers for many international celebrities. Indian stars like Sonam Kapoor Ahuja, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, Priyanka Chopra and Malaika Arora are also regularly spotted in dresses by these designers. At the Oscars ceremony last month, there were a few new names from this region that made an impact. Scroll ahead for the designers you need to watch out for in 2019 from the Middle East. Hannah Beachler, who took home the Oscar for Best Production Design for her work on Black Panther, had turned to Dubai-based Rami Al Ali for her dress. The Syrian, Dubai-based designer has been known for his couture gowns for many years, and is a favourite among the fashion set in Dubai. He is most popular for his love of handmade details like beading and appliqués, and also his fit. While the crimson sculptural Flamenco-inspired dress Beachler chose for this year clearly made an impression, this is not the first time Ali has seen his work on the Oscars red carpet—Helen Mirren has previously worn one of his dresses to the awards ceremony too. When it came to Beachler's dress (which came from the designer's spring/summer 2019 couture collection), asymmetrical details, ruffles and a high slit ensured that it does not go unnoticed. Beachler (the first African American to win an Oscar in this category) completed the look with a gold chain draped on her face in an ode to Black Panther. The Lebanese designer has previously dressed Jennifer Lopez and Sonam Kapoor Ahuja and now, thanks to the shimmering black dress that Kendall Jenner wore to the Vanity Fair Oscars after-party, will go down in history as the designer who took the slit to a whole new level. With bead and fringe details on the hips and a deep keyhole neckline, Rami Kadi's dress, which had been shown at Paris during couture week, left very little to the imagination. And even if you thought its hip high slits were too much, it did make a statement. On Jenner, who is known to be daring, the ensemble allowed the supermodel to push the envelope on how much skin one can show on the red carpet. The Kuwait-based label made the dazzling pink jumpsuit that Kylie Jenner wore for her 21st birthday last year. And in India, both Kajol and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan have worn Labourjoisie dresses to events in recent times. If there's one thing that's been made clear from these celebrity appearances, it's that Lebanese designer Antoine Salameh, the name behind the label, definitely likes to create dresses that make heads turn. Labourjoisie was also sighted at the Vanity Fair Oscars after-party this year on actor Shay Mitchell, who opted for an emerald green off-shoulder gown by the label, featuring slits, feather details and a belt around the waist. column1: Highlights from Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Designers pledging for children’s rights, denim saris, anniversaries and more from Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019 Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2019 started out on a tepid note. The schedule is peppered with a handful of strong names, attendance seems to be dwindling and the perspective of a fashion week being a space for buyers and press to interact with talent is lost. The first day saw designers taking a pledge with Nobel Peace Prize winner Kailash Satyarthi, a child rights activist who is fighting for underage labour to have a chance at a childhood. Unfortunately, garment production units regularly employ children below the legal age as cheap labour sources, and Satyarthi is dedicated to put an end to it. Designers like Rahul Mishra, Namrata Joshipura, Varun Bahl and Pankaj & Nidhi were present for the ceremony. Diksha Khanna's ripped denim sari, worn by the likes of Sonam Kapoor Ahuja, quickly won fashion's favour. The designer returned to the autumn/winter 2019 runway with another collection that championed denim—there were a few denim saris in the line-up, use of crochet, draped silhouettes in white and shimmering pantsuits. Inspired by the Middle East, the collection hit the spot for modest dressing. [#image: /photos/5ce3f45e5a354fef4f06ef79]||| ||| Diksha Khanna. Image: Sagar Ahuja Suket Dhir likes to work at his own pace. For his latest showcase, which also happens to be his first runway show ever, the Woolmark Prize award winner played to his strengths. Some of the prints paired with brocades took as long as two years to perfect. Dhir's brand is a product of experimentation fuelled by whims and understating design as a functional part of everyday life, and not something that needs to be romanticised. His show, ‘He for She' adapted men's tailoring for women. Dhir cited his wife Svetlana to be the source of inspiration behind this direction. [#image: /photos/5ce3f45fc2f95c13235d6400]||| ||| Suket Dhir. Image: Sagar Ahuja Look closely at his work and you will see screen printed brocades, bomber jackets embroidered with Morse code branding—his cheeky approach to logomania and playful landscapes. Dhir fell into garment design after trying his hand at several vocations—it seemed to have paid off really well. As an emerging brand, he is still working on systems and processes and organising his business, but his approach remains organic. “I am a social person, I have created this label by building relationships. If it clicks inside, then the rest will iron itself out,” he tells us. Rahul Mishra, the first Indian designer to win the International Woolmark Prize, closed the day by showcasing his body of work for the last decade. His wife Divya Bhatt Mishra, who has been working by side since the inception of the label, styled pieces from various seasons to put together a seamless timeline. From decoding the patterns on the wings of a butterfly to tessellation and pointillism, Mishra's 10 year journey in fashion has showcased his eye for detail, and was a testament to the timelessness of his work. Queen's ‘I Want To Break Free' played for the last walk—Mishra's promise to himself to find a new design language for his future work. column1: Samantha Akkineni reveals her favourite new fashion trend
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Louis Vuitton is coming to Hyderabad on March 14 and 15 to host its spring/summer 2019 salon, and has collaborated with the famed South Indian actor for it 2018 was a momentous year for Louis Vuitton in India—the luxury brand launched its ready-to-wear line, expanded its flagship Delhi store and created a capsule collection of an India exclusive bag. And now, Louis Vuitton is coming to Taj Krishna in Hyderabad on March 14 and 15 to host a salon that will feature their spring/summer 2019 collection as well as their signature luggage pieces (Horizon's and Keepall's), trunks (like the Coffret Montres and Coffret Treso) and handbags (the Dauphine bag, the stylish Egg bag and the Toupie, among others). Creations from the men's creative director Virgil Abloh's first show will also be on offer here. What's more, the French label has collaborated with South Indian star Samantha Akkineni. Vogue caught up with the star to chat about her love for all things Louis Vuitton and her new collaboration. Excerpts below. When I was young, I really wanted to buy myself a bag from Louis Vuitton. So I went for something that was the most affordable—a wallet. It cost me around Rs 30,000; I remember it was a big day for me. Fast forward to ten years later—that wallet is my absolute favourite and I still use it. I love the new Horizon luggage collection. I would really want one for my travels. And the Petite Malle handbag, which is one of their most classic pieces, is another favourite too. It's a statement bag that goes with everything. Last but not the least, I think the brand's jewellery is a must-have for every girl. I especially liked the monogram earrings, which are unlike anything I've ever seen before. I really liked one of the looks I wore—the head-to-toe monogram outfit, complete with a complementing bag—that matched my personal style as I'm loving the logomania trend. column1: 13 celebrity-approved statement chokers to bookmark for wedding season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Alia Bhatt to Kareena Kapoor Khan, Bollywood celebrities are proving that a dramatic neckpiece is a non-negotiable part of your wedding wardrobe Indian weddings have always demanded ostentation—a traditional bridal look is often considered incomplete without jhumkas, a necklace, a nath, a matha patti and a haath phool. But if you're not the bride, one strong focal point is often all that is needed, and the choker serves this purpose perfectly well. If you're readying your wardrobe for the upcoming wedding season, take cues from Bollywood's leading ladies to do it right. Akash Ambani and Shloka Mehta's recently-concluded wedding brought quite a few celebrities to the red carpet, and most were spotted styling a single piece of jewellery—a statement choker—with their ethnic wear. While Alia Bhatt paired a beautiful choker by Sabyasachi Jewellery with her festive yellow lehenga set, Kareena Kapoor Khan went in for one with blue stones by Anjali Bhimrajka Fine Jewels to complement her pastel lehenga. In terms of accessories, both stars carried potli bags that accentuated their looks. It helped that Bhatt and Khan's blouses featured deep necklines for the statement choker to stand out, but the versatility of this jewellery type allows you to wear it with a modest blouse with a high neckline as well (look towards Kangana Ranaut's beige gota patti sari, which she styled with a heavy pearl and ruby choker, for an example). The best way to maximise the impact of this piece is to definitely skip larger earrings that will take attention away from your choker. If required, you may add a pair of minimal diamond earrings à la Natasha Poonawalla, who wore a simple pair with her elegant choker. Whether it's a sari, a lehenga set or even a contemporary crop top, pants and cape look, a statement choker is all you need to sail through the upcoming wedding season. column1: After slogan T-shirts, celebrities are turning to ethnic wear with script
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Sonam Kapoor Ahuja to Karisma Kapoor, Bollywood celebrities are favouring customised ensembles with typography. Here’s why we think it could make an interesting addition to your wardrobe Let's face it—floral and geometrical motifs are undisputedly the most common designs you will find on ethnic wear. Their intricate patterns and the exquisite embroidery techniques they are made with make them universally loved. Typography, however, serves the purpose of sending out a message in a way that floral and geometrical motifs cannot. While slogans on everyday wear like T-shirts, sweatshirts, denims and even jackets have been trending for a while, it's refreshing to see words feature on the somewhat unlikely canvas of Indian traditional wear. Take it from Karisma Kapoor, who recently wore a typography-printed sari by Satya Paul that spelt out ‘mirchi' written in Hindi. “A typography print sari is quite contemporary as it tells a story; suppose you're travelling abroad, everyone can see our language written on this piece of clothing, and it's a novel concept,” Karisma Kapoor told Vogue in an interview. Most recently, it was Nita Ambani's lehenga choli set by Sabyasachi that she wore to her son Akash Ambani's wedding with Shloka Mehta that was embroidered with “Shubharambh” in Hindi—which translates to “A good beginning”. Deepika Padukone's red dupatta by Sabyasachi that she draped over her head during her Sindhi wedding ceremony is another instance—the actor had the Sanskrit quote“Sada Saubhagyavati Bhava” embroidered in gold on the border of her dupatta, which translates to “May you always be lucky as a married woman.” However, it was Sonam Kapoor Ahuja's House of Masaba sari that she wore during her Ek Ladki Ko Dekha Toh Aisa Laga promotional tour that truly reflected the potential of the typography trend. The mellow yellow sari featured lettering in Tamil that translated to “Sonam, Masaba and Ek Ladki Ko Dekha Toh Aisa Laga”. For those of you who love personalised ensembles, bookmark this look for sartorial inspiration. Yet another typography-printed look Kapoor Ahuja as well as her sister Rhea Kapoor wore was by designer Anamika Khanna, which featured their names along with a significant phrase, “Everything is AK-OK” that the trio used among themselves. While Kapoor Ahuja wore a bright pink lehenga choli set complete with a dupatta that came printed with the phrase, her sister wore a sari that was printed with the same words. Whether it's a phrase embroidered onto your lehenga choli set or a single meaningful word printed on your sari, this look promises to add a personalised touch to your ensemble. column1: How MasterG is encouraging female participation in the fashion world
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion MasterG, a training program launched by Gayatri Jolly, is transforming the role of women in fashion production. Learn more about it here It was when Gayatri Jolly made the switch from business to fashion that she finally felt at home. “This is where I belong,” she realised on day one of her fashion degree program at the Parsons School of Design in New York. That feeling of contentment—of home—is what drives her work, and what led to her founding an all-female training program/factory called Master G upon her return to India. “What my design education did for me, that's what I want Master G to do for the girls,” says Jolly over the phone from her home in New Delhi. “It fundamentally changed me. I had so many mental blocks about how I was supposed to live my life, despite my access and exposure. And I began to think: so what's happening to women who don't even have that exposure?” Design is a male-dominated industry in India, led by “masterjis” who have been conditioned to believe that women are incapable of skills like pattern-making. A lack of confidence in women's abilities, the absence of a support structure that offers them anything beyond marriage and motherhood, and the denied access to education, has led to generations of Indian women being held back from achieving any real independence. Enter Master G. Launched by Jolly in 2015, the training program equips women and young girls with the design skills required to hold a job and earn a decent wage in safe and respectful working conditions. “It can change the way these women think,” says Jolly. “Design is a tool for breaking mental patterns; it's not just a physical skill but changes the way you think. It has helped these women go home and begin to question why things are the way they are.” Image: Andrew Bowe In the three years since Master G's launch, the factory has worked with labels like Doodlage and NorBlack NorWhite for their production needs, and is now lending its workforce to its own in-house label, Heimat. “It closed the loop,” says Jolly of this recent move. “It's a market-driven approach instead of something charity-driven. Charity doesn't last. You give something today and it's gone tomorrow.” Now, as Heimat launches its first collection, we catch up with Jolly to learn more about the brand and the factory behind it. To scale up MasterG training programs and reach women digitally, we're launching digital training modules—kind of like Coursera in regional languages. We're executing the program through NGO partners who roll it out in the community with posters and banners, and we go from home to home to convince families to send their girls to us. Around the time when admissions begin, I have to drink 20 cups of really sweet chai every day. At the end of the program, girls either apply for jobs (with designers or export houses), start shops with one or two machines in their community, or become teachers and start a centre of their own. Some girls go on to teach at other centres too. They learn how to use smartphones as an educational tool so they can navigate the industry; they even post their garments on Instagram and sell them online. It's a German word that means belonging, the feeling of home. You meet a really old friend after a long time for coffee—that feeling of home. You can create that ‘heimat' wherever you go when you have that highest potential inside of you. Heimat is a word that came to me in 2007 when I was in college and it stuck with me. I'm obsessed with the idea of what home means. It's something I thought about a lot when volunteering with women at NGOs in Delhi's slums, who didn't have a home that was a nurturing environment. I was debating this for a long time. Having our own brand gives us the validation to be trainers in the field. If I'm selling in the industry and people are paying for the product, it shows that we're not teaching in a vacuum. We're walking the walk, not just preaching. If we can be a profitable brand, that means this is a working model for the industry. And when they see that this is a running business... that's the only way to fundamentally disrupt the existing system. It's functional, comfortable and fairly minimal, although there's some embroidery—the garments are embroidered with an aerial view of the topography of the slums where these girls come from, and the colours are also inspired by the architecture of where these girls live. The bright blue we call ‘tirpal blue' comes from the plastic of Dharavi. ‘Asbestos grey' is named for the asbestos sheets covering their roofs. Washed brick, moss green, jamun—all these colours are picked up from their living habitat. I spent so many years in the slums. There's a beauty in the haphazardness of their homes that's so striking that I had to base the first collection on that. Image: Andrew Bowe One thing I learned is that there's this blanket belief that ‘ladkiyan pattern nahi bana sakti.' It's the way khandaani darzis work—daughters don't feature in that tradition. It's fathers and sons. Masterji is the person who cuts patterns, and nowhere in India was that being done by women. It's a systemic thing, a mental block. It has little to do with the actual skill, and more with how women are viewed by their families. There's nothing so complicated that women can't do it. It's being done in our factory—they learn pattern-making and sewing and technical design here. It's been phenomenal. The kind of transformation I've seen in these girls is a constant inspiration. They are girls who have the toughest circumstances, who come to work and know they can make a better life for themselves. Every day I go to work and there's a new girl, a new story, a new milestone. This is why I jump out of bed each day. It makes it all worth it. Scroll through the gallery below to take a look at some of Heimat's latest offerings. column1: Are direct-to-consumer brands the future for sustainable fashion?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Made-to-order, zero waste and trendless luxury are the touchstones for a new wave of designers hoping to turn the tide away from fast fashion towards a more sustainable approach. Vogue speaks to Bionda Castana, Misha Nonoo and Olivia Rose The Label to find out how they’re making eco-commerce work When cult shoe brand Bionda Castana re-launched last November after a two-year hiatus, its founders felt they needed a new business model. “We wanted to take a more sustainable approach to fashion,” designer Jennifer Portman explains. “Customers are becoming more conscious in how they spend their money; they want to know that it's ethical, that the product is being made somewhere people get a fair wage.” Portman and co-founder Natalia Barbieri, who split from their investors in 2016, decided a direct-to-consumer approach was the best way to achieve this. The London-based brand, first founded in 2007, uses leftover fabric in its archive to create four, limited-edition designs each month, which customers pre-order. The result? Zero waste. “We make to demand, so the collections don't end up in landfill,” explains Barbieri. Every month, customers only have a five-day window to purchase the collection, which—along with the amount of fabric available—limits the run of each design. Bionda Castana has managed to streamline its production process at its factory in Milan, meaning it only takes three weeks for orders to be fulfilled. “[Customers] really don't mind the wait for a luxury pair of shoes handmade in Italy,” Portman says. “We support artisan manufacturers; I think that means a lot to them.” Once the materials from the archive have been used up, the brand will turn to unused fabrics from other fashion houses in order to maintain its zero-waste policy. Along with its sustainable approach, the focus for the shoe brand – whose celebrity fans  include Kate Bosworth, Alexa Chung and Olivia Palermo—is offering “trendless luxury”, with current designs drawn from their archive. Old favourites, including the Lana, are back in refreshing new prints and starting at a lower price point of £375 thanks to the new direct-to-consumer model. “We can use the silhouettes we've had for so long and bring them back to life,” Barbieri explains. “It's not fast fashion; it doesn't always have to be about new designs.” Trendless fashion is also central to the ethos of Misha Nonoo, who switched to a direct-to-consumer model in 2016. Her New York-based brand—whose fans include Nonoo's long-time friend, the Duchess of Sussex—allows customers to “simplify [their] wardrobe and fill it with timeless staples”, the designer tells Vogue. This is encapsulated by The Easy 8 collection, consisting of eight wardrobe basics—ranging from the Husband shirt, famously worn by Markle, to a black blazer dress—that can be styled to create 22 different looks. Nonoo explains how her brand, like Bionda Castana, makes its products (starting from around £55) on demand, not only because it is more sustainable, but also because it is good for business. “It makes a world of a difference to our bottom line because we don't have excess inventory at the end of each season,” she says. “We're reducing overheads for the company and drastically reducing resource consumption and environmental impact.” Her designs are made in a Hong Kong factory—which employs both ethical and sustainable practices, including recycling programmes—within just five days of an order being placed. The label's made-to-order approach has allowed it to stand out from its competitors, Nonoo says, as it is still “fairly rare among non-luxury brands”. She continues, “Our combined philosophy and product offering attracts the kind of consumer who is willing to wait those few extra days to receive the piece that will give them years of use.” A direct-to-consumer strategy also allows new talent to get their designs out there. British designer Olivia Rose Havelock, who launched Olivia Rose The Label in 2017, saw her business grow rapidly after her puffed sleeved blouses and dresses (priced from £45) proved to be an Instagram hit. “Handmade brands are starting to get noticed now,” the designer tells Vogue. “I started making everything from the beginning, and that's how I've kept it.” Working in this way also allows Havelock to tailor each design to her customers' measurements. “Direct-to-consumer is better for customers if they want something specifically for them,” she says. However, the designer admits it will be difficult to scale up her brand, considering she currently spends four to five hours hand-making each piece herself. “That's something I'm working on now; I'm trying to decide whether I'm going to be wholesale in the future,” explains Havelock. The challenges of moving towards a more sustainable model is one the fashion industry is facing as a whole, alongside shoppers who are becoming increasingly aware of the environmental impact of their spending habits. “Consumers have an exceptional power to shift demand away from fast-fashion retailers,” Nonoo comments. “The tide is slowly but surely starting to turn.” At the moment, however, independent brands adopting a direct-to-consumer, made-to-order strategy are leading the way. “It's a far more modern approach,” says Barbieri. “We're producing really beautiful things while being conscious about it. We're creating a better earth.” View Gallery 15 Photos Are direct-to-consumer brands the future for sustainable fashion? column1: What you can learn about wearing a sari from Deepika Padukone
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We’ve compiled all the notes you should be taking from Deepika Padukone’s repertoire of red carpet sari hits. Read and take notes She may love glamorous couture gowns just as much as the next celebrity, but when it comes to harnessing the allure of the traditional sari, Deepika Padukone is a girl after our own heart. From Sabyasachi classics to indigenous weaves, her bridal trousseau was headlined by a breathtaking line-up of the traditional six yards that you know will make for treasured heirlooms to pass down the generations. If you're looking to tap into the old school nonchalance of her sari wardrobe, here are the key factors you need to keep in mind. A connoisseur of classics, heritage silks and pure Kanjeevaram weaves dominate Deepika Padukone's ethnic wardrobe. Her timeless grace finds expression in stiffly starched pallus, which are pinned with precision against a rotating roster of high-necked blouses. For her grand wedding with Ranveer Singh in November last year, the 33-year-old donned a pure gold zari Kanjeevaram brocade silk sari from Angadi Galleria, gifted by her mother. Back on home ground, she continued to pay homage to her roots with another pure zari Kanjeevaram sari in a palette of gold and soft neutrals. Clearly not one to shy away from drama, Padukone's Mumbai reception had her opting for a hand-embroidered ivory chikankari sari by Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla, paired with a gorgeous dupatta that the actor pulled over her head. Back at her social commitments post her marathon nuptials, the newly-wed proved that she has more than one trick up her sleeve with a contemporary ruffled sari from Faabiiana, and a halter-necked blouse to go with. Padukone's sartorial rulebook is headlined by her love for classic silhouettes, and her lexicon of couture saris is usually complemented with full-sleeved, high-necked blouses that speak of an oft-forgotten, old world glamour. For the grand Ambani wedding last year, she played with contrasts—her ivory jamdani sari came with a scarlet embroidered blouse, coordinated perfectly with her chooda. Not loathe to experimenting with silhouettes, 2018's TIME 100 Gala saw her rubbing shoulders with the international glitterati in a bespoke Anamika Khanna sari, worn with a ruffled blouse and cape for maximum effect. Just when you think you've seen it all, Sabyasachi's risqué bikini blouse and belted sari proved that there is no silhouette she can't master. Remember what you've always been told about not wearing high necklines with chokers or other neckpieces? The rules don't apply when you are a style icon of international calibre. Throwing convention out of the window, Padukone has been accessorising her designer threads with gusto. Her penchant for modest blouses is styling them with head-turning chokers, with emeralds being her gemstone of choice for adding a dash of colour to a neutral palette. When it comes to earrings, you'll find her veering between extremes—delicate tear drop studs or statement chaandbalis, nothing in between. A self-professed normcore enthusiast, Padukone's preferred shorthand for whipping out a red carpet success with a beauty look involves two simple variables—a slicked-back bun and a to-die-for red matte. In a bid to flaunt those embellished blouses, the star frequents centre-parted updos with high shine. Looking to repeat an ensemble twice? Padukone doesn't shy away from it either. The Padmaavat star wore the Benarasi weave gifted to her by Rekha on two separate occasions by simply adding statement smoky eyes to the mix the second time round. column1: Want an engagement ring customised with your love story?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Jewellery designer Zameer Kassam has designed pieces for stalwarts like Lupita Nyong’o, Ashley Judd and Constance Wu as well as brides around the world. The common thread between them all? Every creation is customised based on the patron’s life story A second-generation jeweller, Zameer Kassam recalls helping out at his parents' jewellery store in Vancouver, Canada, since the age of 14. Even so, he wasn't keen to pursue it as a career, and went on to work at MTV India and McKinsey & Company New York during his early 20s. It was only while pursuing his MBA at Harvard Business School that he began flirting with the idea of returning to the world of fine jewels. An introduction by a friend led to an internship at De Beers in London in 2007, that then secured him the position of head of classics and bridal at the brand. His eponymous label was officially launched in 2011. What started as an engagement ring for a friend in 2009 has since then, catapulted into Kassam's creations being worn by the likes of Ashley Judd and Lupita Nyong'o. He also customised jewellery for the premiere of Crazy Rich Asians for Constance Wu, Michelle Yeoh and Ming-Na Wen, and tailor-made jewellery suites for the wedding of Nigerian presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar's son. Vogue India caught the New York-based designer in an exclusive one-on-one during his recent visit to Mumbai. Lupita has always been vocal about representation and gender equality, and we wanted to use jewellery as a tool to tell her story. The black and white ring features prongs inspired by the Wakanda Forever pose from Black Panther, and there are 14 diamonds on each side to celebrate her historic 2014 Oscar win for 12 Years A Slave. The stones culminate in the words ‘your dreams are valid', which is her message to girls around the world. From the time I worked at my family jewellery store, I've been interested in people's stories more than any other aspect of business. So it had to be at the core of what I do. My clients are primarily men, who want to gift their partners a significant piece of jewellery. The first step is a clear set of recommendations to maximise beauty and value. The second step is the discovery, where I dive deep into the high-level details of the relationship and the couple's milestone moments. Finally, storytelling takes over as we sketch and work on stones and settings. The final piece is all hand-made in New York. So it literally goes from his heart to her fingers. Photographs and messages fade away. But jewellery will outlast us all, and continue to tell the story of their love. My first ring was for my friend Simon's girlfriend Pooja, who had been my classmate at business school. I did not want to make something generic. So when Simon told me about their journey and what made him decide to propose, I used it all in the ring—the inside of the band had the gemstones in the colours of Portuguese flag, as Simon realised that he wanted to marry Pooja after their vacation in Portugal. The prongs were inspired by a temple in India, where Pooja's family is from. Another client wanted to pay tribute to his girlfriend's grandmother, who was a nun at a Catholic church in Helsinki. Since there were very few photographs of the inside of this church, I flew to Finland, and sat in the pews to sketch the moulding, which we then carved on the sides of the ring. There has been a seismic shift in the way people think about jewellery. Millennials are tired of legacy brands. They want something personal, special and meaningful. They have also become conscious of the etymology of the stones they are buying and the impact it has on the craft people involved. Make it personal. You will never regret infusing your personality into the design. Have fun with accessories and coloured stones, but for jewellery that represents major moments in your life, go classic. Yellow gold is making a comeback, and I'd opt for a paler shade so the look is not too dated. Pale rose gold is another favourite. Emerald-cut solitaires are the most popular right now. I'm deeply invested in where the diamonds I use come from. There has been a lot of talk about blood diamonds, especially since 2006. My parents are from Dar es Salaam in Tanzania, and most diamonds come from Botswana. I knew that if I worked in the jewellery industry, I would have to stand behind every aspect of it responsibly. I spent my second year of business school in Botswana understanding what goes on at these mines. We sought to understand how we could create more value for the people of the country, and I feel we can make positive social impact with thoughtful public-private partnerships. Forevermark has launched ethically sourced branded diamonds that come from the mine in Botswana where I worked. So Zameer Kassam Fine Jewelry has partnered with Forevermark to use these diamonds as often as I can. column1: Pernia Qureshi: “I never thought I was building a fashion empire”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Creative director of Pernia’s Pop Up Shop and founder of Pernia Qureshi Brands, Pernia Qureshi is moving at breakneck speed Pernia Qureshi may be the name behind multiple labels—there's Pernia's Pop Up Shop; the eponymous fashion line; the newly-launched Pernia Qureshi Brands—but behind it all is one woman manning the reins. Qureshi's journey as a fashion entrepreneur started in 2012 when she launched the luxury e-commerce portal Perniaspopupshop.com. After successfully expanding it across different avenues—there's a brick-and-mortar store now and a dedicated app too—Qureshi sold a majority of its stake. And now, the newly-launched Pernia Qureshi Brands has her undivided attention. Vogue spoke to the multi-hyphenate to gain insight into her journey so far and map her plans for her ever-growing business. Excerpts below. “My journey as a fashion entrepreneur began soon after I designed the costumes of my first film, Aisha. During the making of Aisha, I became well versed with the fashion industry in India and realised there is a lot of talent. Once the film released, I wanted to start something of my own. I am a classical dancer and needed a flexible schedule so I could fit in daily rehearsals. It was then that I realised there was a big gap in the Indian market for a luxury online multi-designer boutique. I quickly hired consultants for advice and put my fashion relationships to use. “Pernia's Pop Up Shop started with 10-12 designers on the site. I wanted to start modest and let the business grow slowly as we got sales. I never thought I was building a fashion empire. My thought process was targeted towards build something good, sustainable and useful. I wanted to pay attention to details, so we took one day at a time.” “There were many learnings along the way since we were the first movers in this segment—we didn't have the luxury of following a set model. I tried to go with my instinct and logic, and allowed myself to make mistakes because they are the best lessons. One of my biggest learnings has been that building a dedicated team and learning how to manage people are the most important aspects of owning a business. Also, your attitude has a lot to do with how well your business grows. In the worst of times, I just kept going.” “A great team and a strong back-end lead to Pernia's Pop Up Shop becoming an established business. I still stay connected, especially for approvals and supervision, as Pernia's Pop Up Shop's creative director. I have been in the luxury e-commerce space for seven years now, and what I've learnt about clients from different parts of India and the world is invaluable. Pernia Qureshi Brands is a product of those learnings.  I am involved in every detail: design, production, shoots, the website, marketing and sales. The idea was to learn from my experience at in e-com and create in-house brands that cater to the needs of the clientele. [#image: /photos/5ce3f510c2f95c0b405d64e0]||| ||| Pernia Qureshi's eponymous label “Currently, we have four clothing labels that appeal to various kinds of women. My eponymous label Pernia Qureshi revolves around my personal style, and offers a range of modern, feminine and well-designed outfits. Amaira, our easy Indian and fusion wear label, features simple silhouettes at great prices. Umrao Couture is dedicated to the sophisticated woman; every garment is a piece of art with intricate hand embroidery. We also have a kids wear line and costume jewellery as well.” [#image: /photos/5ce3f5100db22dcc7881a0b1]||| ||| The Peacock set from Qureshi's Polki Box jewellery line “Sketch to Reality is a feature that is exclusive to Perniaqureshibrands.com. It is the first augmented reality shopping service where the client can fully customise their outfit. The website has simple steps wherein our dedicated designers take the client step-by-step from choosing the budget, fabrics, embroidery and silhouette to finally create their dream outfit. In Delhi and NCR, we also offer clients a home visit by our in-house designers.” “A big focus of ours for the future is to make our labels sustainable and evolve Pernia Qureshi Brands into an ethical and socially conscious platform. We already work with Janhit Sewa Sansthan, an NGO in my hometown Rampur, that helps us with embroidery for our label Amaira. This centre teaches various skills like embroidery to under-privileged girls and empowers them to earn a financial livelihood. We are also looking into incorporating organic fabrics in our collections and eventually having a complete line of clothing made using hundred per cent organic materials.” [#image: /photos/5ce3f511b41afb0e87a96c9c]||| ||| An embroidered ensemble made in association with NGO Janhit Sewa Sansthan Pernia Qureshi's online Pop-Up Shop makes its brick-and-mortar debut Careers in fashion: Pernia Qureshi on how to make clothes that sell online Now you can shop on the go from Pernia's Pop Up Shop What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Gigi Hadid’s new sunglasses collection has something for everyone
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Gigi Hadid x Vogue Eyewear’s third collection is about to drop. Here’s everything you need to know about it It's a rainy day in Manhattan and swarms of paparazzi and selfie-seeking fans have already gotten word that Gigi Hadid is visiting the Luxottica office this morning. The 23-year-old supermodel is here in a neon orange tuxedo to show off her third stint at eyewear designs, and the crowds are desperate for the first peek. With 46 million Instagram followers, numerous magazine covers to her name, and a runway slot at every major fashion show around the world, Gigi Hadid clearly lives a busy life, but that hasn't stopped her from pursuing her other interests—including working on a third collection with Vogue Eyewear, a partnership that first began in 2017. The latest pieces are a dedication to her life in New York, with styles like ‘High Line' inspired by Manhattan architecture, and ‘Lafayette', paying homage to her home address. “There's something here for every personality,” she explains as she tries on a dramatic cat eye frame in the mirror. The supermodel's a pro at this now—she has collaborated with Tommy Hilfiger and Reebok in the past, and has even gone behind the lens to shoot a Versus campaign. Vogue gets the low-down on her latest collection as Hadid tries on each pair. Do you remember your first pair? My first pair were by Barbie; they were pink plastic—I have a picture of me wearing them in the back of a car. I definitely own a lot of sunglasses, and I joke that because I try on clothes all day, when I go shopping I don't want to try on any more clothes. Glasses is easy for me; that's probably why I have a lot. I have a strange emotional connection with sunglasses. They are my shield. They make me feel more confident to go out and face the world even when I don't want to put makeup on. Everyone needs that confidence sometimes. I am taking more chances. I trust myself more. Even though there may be shapes people won't love, I am not scared. I am excited. I'm confident to try new shapes, textures and colourways without holding back. I feel connected to all the pieces—they are my babies. I love sculpting, painting and drawing. My dad is an architect and my mom is an interior designer, so I was always surrounded by creativity while growing up. They taught me about putting love and focus into something and following your gut and intuition. With Vogue Eyewear, I enjoy the design process—sketching, touching the pieces, trying them on and re-sketching. Yes, and one called ‘Yola' after my mom, too. When I showed my sister the collection, I told her I would name one after her and she chose her favourite. They are how I see Bella—effortless, powerful, glamorous, beautiful. And [the sunglasses] look good with a great lip on. To give you a closer peek at Gigi Hadid's new eyewear collection, we asked her to describe some of the designs, and where she thinks they work best. Scroll ahead for the details. “These sporty goggles are great for when you need full coverage, like [when you're] running to the market or the airport. They also have a ski feel. While designing, I really wanted the shield to curve and wrap around the face. Each pair has a different tricolour lens to it too.” “It's the cross street I live on right now, so it's very New York with a lot of style. These glasses are a more refined version of the cat eye we had done previously, so it's much more of an everyday shape. You can keep these in your bag and throw them on whenever. The colours are pretty neutral too—except for the red lenses.” “These have a crafty, costume element to them, with little Swarovski crystals on the sides. They feel like big square vintage glasses that had their lenses cut off to look more 2019.” “Opticals have been really popular for us. I would wear these for dinner in the East Village.” “This is my ‘if I were a space captain' pair. They are for people who want to make a statement, so I want them to feel powerful. Zoom has a double meaning here—zoom in terms of speed and being on the run, or zoom like a camera lens to see the world.” What to expect from the next chapter of Gigi Hadid x Tommy Hilfiger How to get Gigi Hadid's retro chignon and dramatic cat eye How to wear neon, according to Alia Bhatt, Bella Hadid and more What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

From micro florals and larger blooms to modern gothic motifs and artful abstractions, there are ample prints to choose from—and they have all found a special spot in celebrity wardrobes of as well. column1: 10 outfits that define Anushka Sharma’s signature style
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From her statement-making pink Sabyasachi wedding lehenga to her unconventional ways of sporting denim, Anushka Sharma is clearly a pro at marrying comfort with style Vogue India's March 2019 cover girl Anushka Sharma is a bona fide trendsetter, and much of this can be credited to how unapologetic and uncompromising she is in preserving her authenticity. While she can pull off glamorous red carpet looks with flair on any given day (cue the lilac beaded and feathered Falguni Shane Peacock gown she wore to Deepika Padukone and Ranveer Singh's reception), she has often spoken about her penchant for comfortable looks and her bias towards clothes with pockets. Scroll ahead to take a look at 10 outfits that perfectly define Anushka Sharma sartorial voice. One of Anushka Sharma's most iconic looks remains her wedding outfit—a baby pink custom-made Sabyasachi lehenga that has not only taken over bridal Pinterest boards ever since she debuted it, but has also paved the way for brides to experiment with colours beyond the conventional red. Another closet favourite is denim, but almost always with an interesting update. Pulling off a Canadian tuxedo is no mean feat; more so when cold-shoulders and frayed hems are involved. But Sharma achieves this effortlessly in her Dhruv Kapoor belted denim trench and trouser set. Matching separates are another go-to for the star, making for some of her most noteworthy looks. The head-to-toe Cinq à Sept ruffled separates she was recently seen in? It takes enviable confidence to pull off a look as overwhelming as that. The trick, it would seem, is to avoid accessories and jewellery that will fight a traffic-stopping colour for attention. Another applaud-worthy addition to the actor's repertoire are the Raw Mango separates she wore to the Sui Dhaaga trailer launch—brocade pants with a boxy crop top—that provide ample inspiration to translate your heritage weaves to a western setting.
