column1: Why you need to consider renting designer clothes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion With fast fashion wreaking havoc on the environment, runway trends begging to be bought and an overflowing wardrobe to contend with, clothing rental websites may just be your best bet. Vogue lists the leading names in the fashion rental business that offer everything from designer lehengas and saris to gowns and more Being a fashion insider can sometimes take from you more than it gives. Not only does it require you to stay up-to-date with the latest runway trends, it also demands an unending supply of resources (time, money and space). While investing in classics—like the must-have LBD, a crisp white shirt, a pair of blue jeans, a black pantsuit—as well as pre-owned clothes à la vintage fashion is a smart move, you don't want your wardrobe to miss out on the OOTDs that are dominating your Instagram feed. This is where the concept of renting clothes comes in. Barring your hesitation to wear pre-worn clothes and give up on your regular shopping routine, the benefits of renting clothes are actually worth noting. Scroll ahead to find out why you need to consider renting clothes in the first place, and where you can do it from—we've listed out all the clothing rental websites you should try. Shopping may be your form of cardio, but how often have you bought something you've barely ever worn since the purchase? Renting clothes allows you to spend less money acquiring outfits you really don't need, while also saving precious time and energy that you would have otherwise spent scouring through shops. What's more, renting clothes instead of buying them equates to making more space in your already overflowing closet too. Sounds like a win-win. In case you weren't aware, the fashion industry is one of the world's major polluting industries, with fast fashion to blame. Renting clothes can help counter the negative effects of this by ensuring garments are reused and repurposed, thus encouraging a circular economy which will reduce the waste that ends up in landfill. Ellen MacArthur Foundation reports that if you double the number of times you wear a garment, its environmental footprint is decreased by 44 per cent. But in the age of Instagram, where you're posting what you wear on a daily basis, repeating outfits for important events can be embarrassing to some. Renting clothes can curb both issues—decrease the environmental footprint of your clothes, plus provide you with new designs. The idea of renting clothes is gaining momentum in the US, UK, Australia and China, with leading fashion rental companies like Le Tote, Girl Meets Dress, Rent the Runway, Glam Corner and YCloset offering designer clothing as well as everyday wear on a monthly subscription basis. Closer to home, we've seen a sudden spike in the number of fashion websites that offer rental services. Up for renting garments or buying pre-owned designer wear? Our list below features exactly where you can find it. If you're looking to rent designer clothing at affordable prices, Stage3 has got you covered. Whether it's a Sabyasachi Mukherjee sari (Rs 7,500) or a Shantanu & Nikhil gown (Rs 6,000), Stage3 lets you rent designer outfits for three to six days with easy returns. Stage3.com Investing in pre-owned vintage luxury items is another eco-friendly option for conscious consumers. Take your pick from leading luxury labels like Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Chanel and Prada on Luxépolis, an online portal that lets you buy and sell premium products. Luxepolis.com Have a pre-wedding shoot planned but still figuring out the outfit? Flyrobe's diverse range promises to provide a myriad of options—from designer lehenga sets and anarkalis to gowns and sari gowns, rent your outfit according to the occasion for four complete days. Flyrobe.com If you're not shopping occasion-wise and are on the lookout for a statement piece to amp up your look, head to The Clothing Rental. Apart from traditional ethnic wear, the website also offers tops, dresses, jackets, trench coats, jewellery, handbags and footwear. Theclothingrental.com Rent At Tali is another platform that has a wide range of contemporary clothing and accessories to choose from. Designers like Dhruv Kapoor, Hemant and Nandita, Jade Couture and Misho are some whose clothes are available on rent here. Rentattali.com Love wearing celebrity-approved outfits or accessories? The Style Ease offers styles that have previously been seen on stars like Jacqueline Fernandez, Shraddha Kapoor and Malaika Arora. Choose from ethnic wear, Indo western styles and designer accessories. Thestylease.com From bridal designer lehenga sets to Indian outfits featuring a Western touch, choose your ensemble and keep it for three, five, seven or 10 days. column1: 30 pictures that will take you right inside Gauri Khan’s wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From designer ethnic wear and athleisure-inspired ensembles to contemporary styles, Gauri Khan’s wardrobe is clearly a vibrant mix One would expect an interior designer to be well-versed with sartorial knowledge, and Gauri Khan doesn't disappoint. While she may only grace the red carpet at select occasions, a quick scroll through her Instagram profile will prove that when she does, she's decked in couture. It's evident that Khan knows what works best for her, and can expertly oscillate between traditional Indian wear and a myriad of contemporary styles like pantsuits and gowns. Though her go-to colours are mostly warm and muted, her silhouettes swing between sharp and structured (think tailored blazers and pantsuits) as well as relaxed and comfortable (we're looking at easy-breezy dresses and oversized T-shirt and jeans combinations). Bohemian prints are sometimes favoured, as are exaggerated sleeves. Her experimental taste allows her to mix and match—we've seen her team sneakers with both a dainty dress and a crop top, shirt and track pants combination. Khan's not one for statement jewellery; you will seldom find her in ostentatious necklaces or earrings that scream for attention. Her approach is more timeless, and her jewellery (a watch or a ring that she sometimes wears) is chosen with care. Footwear, on the other hand, is a different ball game altogether. Given her love for designer shoes, Khan's shoe wardrobe houses every style—right from Christian Louboutin studded pumps to Adidas Originals sneakers. The same goes for her choice in handbags—there's the staple Goyard tote she often carries, and she has many designer clutches stocked for red carpet events. column1: Sabyasachi’s latest collection will be on every summer bride’s wishlist
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From fuss-free caftans and togas to organdy saris and THAT red lehenga Priyanka Chopra wore to her Hindu nuptials, Sabyasachi Mukherjee's spring/summer 2019 collection is set to dominate wedding mood boards this season The release of Sabyasachi Mukherjee's spring/summer '19 collection on Instagram feels familiar, yet different. Having clocked in two decades in the industry, the whisper of his legacy informs his signature opulent fare in his newest offering, titled ‘Fiza'. Crafting couture out of flimsy organdy and adding chintz florals to menswear, the couturier continues to surprise. With the promise of summer beckoning around the corner, the designer serves up the frivolity of the season with fuss-free silhouettes in unassuming organdy. The colour palette moves from earthy neutrals—that you'll want to bookmark for the next mehandi on your social calendar—to sorbet hues, and builds up to a climax with the showstopper rouge lehenga that Priyanka Chopra favoured for her Udaipur nuptials. Bearing in mind the demands of the season, the designer's lexicon of summery silhouettes includes twirl-friendly togas and caftans, as well as hand-crushed saris punctuated with stately baroque embroidery. And for brides who want nothing less than a fairytale wedding, the designer also offers a western-style veil apart from the rectangular dupatta—also last spotted on Chopra. The opulence of the ensembles is underscored by heritage jewellery, with motifs such as hand-carved peacocks sculpted out of 22-karat gold. Expect uncut diamonds, sapphires and Colombian emeralds to dominate your jewellery kit for the season. While keeping up with convention, the couturier's flair for whimsy stays alive with his choice of fabric for wedding lehengas—the humble khadi. “As a bridal designer, I keep thinking, ‘What's next?', and I keep coming back to khadi. For me, it is the equivalent of wellness, and nothing can be more luxurious than that. When I look back at the last 20 years, my khadi bridal lehengas are what I am most proud of. Combined with Indian jewellery and flowers, they create a very potent and timeless image. Some of my most discerning customers globally have chosen to wear khadi lehengas for their wedding. Almost all of them are not on Instagram. Pity!” he quips. Scroll through the gallery below to bookmark your favourite looks from designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee's spring/summer '19 collection. column1: Rahul Mishra’s moving collection for fall 2019 draws from his childhood
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From seeking inspiration in an abandoned space to carving a spot for Indian designers in an international space, Rahul Mishra explains the thought and creative process behind his latest offering at Paris Fashion Week Some create from a robust sense of structure, others with a moving sense of colour. Rahul Mishra is a creator who operates on emotion. If you had to look at his body of work, it would inadvertently be tangled with nostalgia. This season, he looked through a poetic lens at the house he grew up playing in as a child. “I come from a village called Malhousie, in Uttar Pradesh. Look it up; even Google won't be able to help you,” he jokes. The abandoned house of his youth might be run down, but instead of harping on the decay, Mishra noticed something else. “The house was taken over by nature and it was beautiful to see all these weeds and animals as the new residents of a place so rich with memories for me,” he describes the exact point where inspiration crept for the making of the new collection. Divya Bhatt Mishra, Rahul's partner and confidant, swiftly arrived at the scene with a select team to capture the essence of the space and to be able to translate it into something tangible. The lineup is a coming together of two main aspects—the architecture of the house and school uniforms of childhood are represented with graphic textile, and the wilderness of nature done in signature Rahul Mishra applique. “Everything is made by hand and really no two garments are alike,” he explains. While the base for some of the looks is a basic worsted fabric made from Merino wool, nearly 80 per cent of the graphic textile is handwoven used using khadi yarns, while the sheer fabrics are made in Maheshwar, Madhya Pradesh. Mishra, who comes from a educational background in Physics, really stumbled upon design as solution rather than art. His purpose comes from trying to create something that will benefit both the maker and the person commissioning it. He is an ardent proponent of growing the handloom sector in India as well as using reverse migration as a business model to not uproot his artisans from their hometowns. “For me it's about participation and how inclusive we can make the whole process of creation. It's not just about what is made at the end but also how it is made,” Mishra says. As a designer, Mishra is conscious not to be written off as one dimensional. “We wanted to bring a modern touch to the heritage textiles and craftsmanship I use,” he says. For the first time, Mishra also made use of a darker colour palette moving from moody greys to blacks. In terms of styling, one saw sheer dresses worn over trousers, evening dresses and a lot of tailoring. Rahul Mishra completes 10 seasons of showcasing at Paris Fashion Week with this show since his big International Woolmark Prize win in 2014. As a young father, Mishra was hesitant to be away from his daughter for a long period of time due to the demands of a show of this scale, but with talks with the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode about presenting couture in the works, consistency was critical. The designer also has the ambitious plan of opening a retail space in Paris. “It's becoming increasingly difficult for departmental stores to do justice to smaller brands, so the future lies in taking charge of the narrative,” he says. Mishra's process is unorthodox but rooted in tradition; it's unlikely you will see anything resembling his work on the lineup. “I can very easily use the most luxurious fabrics and feathers to create something similar to product that's already available in the market but what would be the point of that?” Just as much as there is room for Rahul Mishra's clothes in an international competitive space, there's hope for a woman who understands them. column1: Priyanka Chopra: “My personal style has changed quite dramatically”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Priyanka Chopra, who was in the country this week for Ralph Lauren’s first store launch in New Delhi, discusses her love for the American brand and her personal style Ralph Lauren has been a long-standing favourite with Indians for several years now, and actor Priyanka Chopra is definitely among those leading this pack of patrons. Following her first major appearance in the brand at the MET Gala in 2017 (in that now-iconic trench coat look), she went on to sport the label on several occasions. And her wedding ceremony in December 2018, where Chopra became one of the only three brides to be dressed by Ralph Lauren himself in the last 50 years, clearly topped this list. Chopra was in attendance at the American heritage brand's India debut (in partnership with Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail Limited), as they opened doors to their first luxury store in New Delhi's Chanakya Mall, styled in the Randall evening dress from Ralph Lauren's spring/summer 2019 collection, with a gold patent leather minaudière by the same label. Spread over two floors, the store is home to the world of Ralph Lauren, and stocks Purple Label and Ralph Lauren Collection alongside classic Polo Ralph Lauren. On the occasion, Chopra speaks to Vogue about her fondness for the brand and the evolution of her personal style. The 2017 MET Gala was an event of many firsts. When my stylist, Christina Ehrlich, and the Ralph Lauren atelier suggested the idea of the trench look, I was immediately convinced. I believe Ralph celebrates a woman who is strong and independent, but doesn't need to prove it in any way—she dresses for herself, and this is an emotion I relate to. Ralph Lauren is a classic brand that exudes effortless, timeless style. But most importantly, it stands for and celebrates family. I think the reason people world over connect with Ralph Lauren is because no matter our differences, we all believe in this too. I think a Ralph Lauren suit is the most feminine armour a woman can put on—it will make you feel like you can take on anything. I'm also a huge fan of the evening wear, with its elegant details and graceful silhouettes. From the spring/summer 2019 collection, I am really digging the vibe of the pristine white admiral jacket, paired with those billowing, wide-legged pants. I think my personal style has changed quite dramatically. I experiment far more now than I did before. I have also come to enjoy the process much more. Over the years, I've realised that I have to be true to me, whatever the trends might be. It takes an army! I manage with the help of a great team of stylists, makeup artists and hairstylists. A team that understands your aesthetic definitely makes the process much more fluid. My go-to staples would be a midi dress in a classic silhouette with a pretty pair of pumps. Recently, I have also fallen in love with mini bags and smaller sunglasses. Whilst I often stick to more tailored shapes, I do have fun experimenting with exciting and quirky accessories. column1: Ever wondered what happens to your clothes after you throw them away?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue spoke with designers and brands who are paving the way for recycled and upcycled fashion in India to understand what happens to your clothes once you throw them away As voracious consumers of fashion, we're quick in purchasing clothes that catch our fancy, and equally swift in discarding them. But have we ever given a thought to where those clothes are ending up? The staggering statistics of the quantity of clothes that end up in landfills is not news—in fact, what is new information is that landfills are brimming with so much urban waste that by 2050, India is reportedly going to need a landfill that's the size of its capital, New Delhi (as claimed by a joint report by Assocham and accounting firm PwC). The telling numbers and warning signs cannot be ignored anymore by consumers and companies alike. Which is why, designers and brands are stepping forward now more than ever to intervene. Kriti Tula is one such name, whose contemporary label Doodlage is upcycling factory waste into innovative designs. “In a linear fashion model, it's estimated that 73 per cent of all our clothes end up in landfill for various reasons like the lack of collection systems and ineffective redistribution. There are no large-scale solutions available to recycle blended yarns at the moment,” explains Tula. “In India, the end of the line for our garments is limited to charity, which eventually fill up local landfills,” she states. Ironically, instead of recycling the fabrics and textiles that are over-loading India's landfills, we are importing huge quantities of second-hand clothing from countries all over the world including the US and the UK, all of which are ending up in Haryana's Panipat area. “When we dispose our clothes, they either end up in landfills or are sold again. However, now there are many recycling mills where second-hand clothing and fabrics from all over the world are segregated, torn apart to remove buttons, zippers and labels, and then treated to be re-purposed and used as yarn. This yarn is used to create inexpensive blankets and carpets that are sold at rock-bottom prices,” explains designer Amit Aggarwal, who works with waste material to design his couture collections. How does Tula hope to make a difference with her ethical label? “We have spent a lot of time understanding fabric waste in the fashion industry—both post-consumer and post-production—and the current solutions available,” says Tula. “At Doodlage, we approach circularity holistically. Our raw material is factory waste. Scraps are patched together to create collections in ethical spaces, with fair wages given to artisans. For fabrics that are too small to be patched together, we create textures that are used to make bags and home accessories. The last stage is recycling to make paper for stationery products,” says Tula. Doodlage's products also come packed in bio plastics that are 100 per cent biodegradable, with the final packaging layer being a reusable fabric tote bag made from their own leftovers. What goes around comes around, especially in fashion. Ask Swedish multinational retail company H&M, who launched the Garment Collection Program in 2013, a global initiative wherein consumers are encouraged to bring in their old clothes in lieu of a 15 per cent discount voucher. “95 per cent of clothes that get thrown away could be re-worn, reused or recycled,” says Dhatri Bhatt, spokesperson at H&M. “The Garment Collection Program offers an easy solution for our customers to leave their old, unwanted clothing and home textiles (of any brand, in any condition) at the recycling box at any H&M store.” What is astounding to note is the amount of textiles H&M collected. “The equivalent of 89 million T-shirts were collected in 2017,” reveals Bhatt. The initiative is evidently successful, and to make the most of it, H&M made it their short term goal to minimise (and avoid, as much as possible) the waste that goes to landfill. So what actually happens to the textiles after the customers discard them in the recycling boxes? “The clothes are then segregated into three categories: Re-wear (clothes that can be worn again are marketed worldwide as second-hand); Reuse (old clothes and textiles that are no longer suitable to wear are converted into other products, such as cleaning cloths); Recycle (textiles that can't be reused get a new chance as textile fibres or are used to manufacture products such as damping and insulating materials for the auto industry),” explains Bhatt. The brand also launched a Conscious Collection in 2018, which was made using environmentally smarter materials and came marked with a green hang tag. For Aggarwal, his entire creative process is initiated with a central recycled material around which he develops his collection. “I enjoy the material play that goes into the making of our clothes, as well as the various textures which are developed through materials that aren't a regular find in the market,” he says. The concept of recycling brings us to its relatively greener cousin, upcycling. “Upcycling does not break down the properties of the fabric into fibre to change it into another material. Therefore, it is less resource intensive [than recycling],” explains Tula, whose label Doodlage works with both upcycling and recycling, but focuses more on the former. Aggarwal, on the other hand, understands the benefits of both, and has adopted them as a practice in his design process. “Waste materials are picked up from various industries as leftovers. For us, it is a sustainable and aesthetic choice that we make when utilising such materials,” he explains. The unique aspect, though, is how the couturier combines the recycled materials with heritage vintage fabrics like Benarasi, Patola and phulkari textiles, and reinvents them into modern garments. “We live in a world where a product's life cycle can be extended through responsible design ethics, but sustainability is a process and has to be a part of you before you implement it into a collection,” says Aggarwal. Tula agrees. “Sustainability cannot be achieved by simply introducing a new fabric in a short collection. It has to be rooted in the DNA of the brand and communicated with this entirety to the consumer,” she adds. Whether our clothes are recycled into new textiles or upcycled into contemporary designs, it's crucial that we choose biodegradable and 100 per cent environmentally friendly fabrics, like organic cotton, hemp, jute and silk, in the long term. And H&M is striving to achieve this exact same outcome. “By 2020, the H&M group aims to source 100 per cent sustainable cotton, and by 2030, we're looking at 100 per cent recycled or other sustainably sourced materials. Today, 35 per cent of all materials we use in our products are recycled or sustainably sourced,” says Bhatt. “Having a circular approach to how products are made and used is important—with the goal being to only use recycled/sustainably sourced materials and renewable energy in all our direct operation—all the while decreasing the dependence on virgin resources, chemicals, energy, water and minimising the amount of materials that end up as waste,” explains Bhatt. The answer may lie in adopting a slow lifestyle that respects the value of clothes and maximises its longevity. Additionally, it's important for brands and designers to provide easier options for consumers to recycle. “We are working to raise funds to build post-consumer waste management in India,” says Tula. “This will allow consumers to send back to us garments that can be recycled, upcycled or resold, depending on the garment itself.” Other options include making a note of swap websites and reselling portals that can help extend the life of each garment by 20-30 years. “We need to create more alternatives to fast fashion, and make them accessible and affordable to allow consumers to make a switch. It all starts with raising more awareness about the impact of fashion,” concludes Tula. column1: Luxury leather label Nappa Dori set to open its flagship store in London
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Gautam Sinha, founder and creative director of Nappa Dori, speaks to Vogue about the new store, its prime location in Central London, and the label’s new offerings If you're a connoisseur of handcrafted leather products, you would be familiar with Gautam Sinha's luxury label, Nappa Dori. From an expansive range of luggage and bags to minimally designed stationery and accessories, the Delhi-based design house has long established itself as a brand that celebrates India's rich heritage and artisanal craftsmanship. Now, Nappa Dori is going global as it extends its reach with a flagship store at the heart of London, opening in late April 2019. “Right from the start, the brand's ethos has borrowed inspiration from the British. So it was apt for Nappa Dori to open its doors in London, [which is also] considered a key city in the world,” Sinha tells Vogue, adding that this plan took a year and a half to materialise. “The store is located at Seven Dials, a prime location in Central London that is known for its cafes and boutiques, and Nappa Dori will fit right in,” Sinha adds. The store will also be home to Café Dori, where one can help themselves to small eats and a cup of Mumbai's famous cutting chai—all in all creating a space that emphasises on traditional Indian influences. The store is spread over two floors, and the brand's DNA is notably present throughout the interiors. “Since the label gravitates towards the nostalgia and romance of India, the store includes mood boards that showcase the brand's values. There is also an atelier in the basement that will show how the products are made,” says Sinha. While London is known to have an eclectic vibe and is the birthplace of the dandy aesthetic, it does have a market for a more sophisticated aesthetic. Considering this, who will Nappa Dori be targeting its products to? “A bit of both audiences,” says Sinha. “The products have a dapper and young vibe, infused with simplicity and sophistication to match the aspirations of modern day aesthetes. If we wanted to specifically target the hipster crowd, we would have looked at a store in Shoreditch, not Central London.” For its new store, Nappa Dori will be introducing a collection of London-inspired tote bags. “The label's offerings cater to an international palette. We will make some tweaks in colour, but apart from that, the range of products will remain the same,” Sinha concludes. column1: Vogue previews Paco Rabanne’s AW19 collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion If last season the Paco Rabanne woman was exploring far-flung destinations in tie-dye, this season she’s ready to go out and strike a pose. Vogue meets creative director Julien Dossena to talk about the resurgence of voguing, the transformative power of fashion and why his sequinned dresses are set to take over the night It's an unseasonably hot day in February when Vogue meets Paco Rabanne's creative director Julien Dossena ahead of the autumn/winter 2019 show. Upstairs in the Rue François 1er studio—through a brilliant white lobby where a diverse cast of models await their fittings—Dossena, who is responsible for the label's modern reboot, is stationed behind a large glass desk to oversee proceedings. Dutch model and member of the new-era Paco Rabanne clan, Rianne van Rompaey, enters wearing a strapless tiger-print sequined gown layered over an Art Deco-print sports jersey, strands of gold threaded through her auburn hair catching the light as it pours through the panel windows. Parisian power stylist Marie-Amélie Sauvé is stationed close by, on hand to direct the young design team who swoop in to adjust van Rompaey's hemline and waistband, a half-centimetre here and there. Before the model heads back to the screened-off changing area, she pauses for the photograph that will identify her look backstage at the show. The heels of her oxblood cowboy boots sink ever so slightly into a carpet that Dossena says is just like one you'd find in LA's Beverly Hills or Sunset Tower hotels—a feature he will replicate on his runway this season. “I was looking at a lot of David Lynch movies. It's not decadent, but it's old-school Hollywood,” he explains of the new eveningwear-focussed collection. The shadowy opulence of Lynch's masterpiece Mulholland Drive also served as inspiration for the Art Deco chandeliers that will hang above the Paco Rabanne catwalk. If last season the Paco Rabanne woman was enjoying a leave of absence, soaking up the charms of a far-flung destination in tie-dye emblazoned with the words “lose yourself”, this season she is prepped to venture out into the night. “We all love the coolness of casuals, but the core of fashion for me is really trying to give people the possibility of clothes,” Dossena explains—and it's this transformative power of clothing, giving you the freedom to become whoever you choose, that has inspired the latest collection. His intuitive understanding of fashion's ability to transport its wearer to another realm references everything from Paris' dandy culture, to the non-stop tabloid coverage of royal style and the modern resurgence of New York's legendary vogue balls. There are long hemlines, cropped shorter at the front for a modern take on an heirloom gown, and shoulder-grazing diamante earrings that hint at the treasures of a drag artist's jewellery box. “I was looking at vogueing to build a character that gives you freedom and more personal expression,” Dossena says, citing documentaries such as 2018's Pose and 1990's Paris is Burning as references. “These films show gay, transgender, black American kids that were, in the 1980s, on the edge of society—who were so precise about what power fashion can give them.” It's no coincidence that the French capital is currently experiencing a vogueing revival, spearheaded by local artists including musician Kiddy Smile, who launched his new album One Trick Pony at the end of last year with a ballroom fete. As Dossena puts it, it's in these spaces that we are able to “live [our] inner self and show it to the world”. For Dossena, the elemental chainmail that features so heavily in Paco Rabanne's legacy helps tell a new story in 2019, offering a declaration that in cities across the world our nightlife is not disappearing. That clothes can be uplifting and “touch every side of society”, he explains. Whether the idiosyncratic chainmail or “plasticy pop” spirit—as the designer fondly refers to it—Paco Rabanne's archive celebrates something at once tender and primal that hasn't dated since those electrifying designs of the 1960s. These new carpet-skimming dresses and acres of sequins ask to be taken out and, in modern party vernacular, snapped under iPhone flashlights. As the sun sets on Dossena's acclaimed SS19 collection, a new night-time tale begins for AW19. “I was really interested in uplifting people,” he says as we part. Words that resonate as Chinese model Liu Wen, fresh out of her fitting, catches us on the way out to express the joy of test-running her catwalk look. Hanging on the mood board in the background, the sequinned skirt she will wear glitters, refracting the light. Just imagine the damage it could do on the dance floor. column1: Everything you need to know about Rihanna’s new fashion house
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion New details have emerged When news broke that Rihanna was reportedly launching her own luxury fashion house alongside LVMH, we questioned whether the development was just too good to be true. However, as new findings supporting the venture emerge, it would seem it's not. While we're yet to uncover just what Rihanna plans to offer us via the launch of a new label, given the success that both Fenty Beauty and Savage X Fenty have seen, we have no doubt she'll once again fill another gap in the industry's market. Said to be coined Project Loud Fashion—supposedly a nod to her 2010 album, Loud—Business of Fashion is reporting that the label will see to the “conception, fabrication, distribution, commerce, importation and exportation” of products ranging from womenswear, menswear, childrenswear, footwear and eyewear, to leather goods, sportswear, “goods linked to lifestyle”, high-tech products, office supplies, home decor and garden products. According to WWD, Rihanna has enlisted Jean-Baptiste Voisin, LVMH's chief strategy officer, to assume the role of Project Loud Fashion's president. In addition, LVMH has been said to have also already pulled multiple employees from Louis Vuitton and Celine that are now set to join the new label, with the address listed as 24-32 Rue Jean Goujon in Paris, the same address as the LVMH Fashion Group. Via a series of financial findings acquired by French accounting firm Ledouble, Business of Fashion has confirmed that through her company Denim UK Holdings, Rihanna will be a 49.99 percent shareholder. As such, the multi-hyphenate has reportedly already invested over AU$47 million into her new label, while LVMH has contributed a little over that same figure. As we await an official release date, further details regarding the venture and confirmation of the products Project Loud Fashion will offer, we've already begun picturing just what an armchair, iPhone case, and collection of office supplies designed by the singer will look like. Hint: we're guessing quite unlike any other. column1: Chanel announces Virginie Viard and Eric Pfrunder as co-creative directors
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The clarification around Karl Lagerfeld’s replacement comes a week after his death Chanel has named Virginie Viard and Eric Pfrunder as co-creative directors of the house, following Karl Lagerfeld's death last week. Lagerfeld passed away aged 85 in Paris, with the news being announced on February 19, 2019, and then confirmed by Chanel. At the time, the historic French house stated that Virginie Viard, the director of Chanel's fashion creation studios and a close collaborator of Lagerfeld, had been “entrusted” with the “creative work for the collections” but did not confirm her role. According to Business of Fashion, Chanel has now clarified studio chief Virginie Viard will indeed be stepping into a creative director role, alongside image director Eric Pfrunder, who is also a longtime associate of Lagerfeld. As per Business of Fashion, Viard's title is artistic director of fashion collection, while Pfrunder has been appointed artistic director of fashion image, making them co-creative directors of the house. Lagerfeld had a lifetime contract with Chanel and held a 36-year tenure there before passing away last week. Viard joined Lagerfeld at the label in 1987, only four years after the iconic creative director and although she went to Chloé for a short time, it was also under Lagerfeld's lead. Meanwhile, Pfrunder has also been at the house for three decades. Alain Wertheimer, co-owner of Chanel, “confirms his confidence in the team that worked with Karl Lagerfeld for over 30 years,” a statement from the brand said, according to Business of Fashion. column1: Indian designers Kulsum Shadab Wahab and Dhruv Kapoor win big in Milan
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designers bagged both first and second places at the Fashion Hub Market prize, making it a proud moment for the country As we get into Paris Fashion Week, a notable highlight from Milan Fashion Week was when Ara Lumiere by Kulsum Shadab Wahab and Dhruv Kapoor won the Fashion Hub Market prize by Camera Moda della Moda Italiana and The Best Shops (a non-profit Italian chamber of buyers), bringing home not one, but two wins from the fashion capital. Ara Lumiere's intricate head scarves are made by acid attack survivors and the social angle was part of the pull for the label's win. Carlo Capasa, president of Camera Moda took to Instagram to congratulate the label's first-place win: "Congratulations to @ara_lumiere, awarded by @cameramoda and @thebestshops.it at the #FashionHubMarket. The art of perseverance woven into perfection by Acid Attack Survivors. Ara Lumiere is a head couture brand propelled by Kulsum Shadab Wahab at Hothur Foundation. This organisation utilises funds raised in the sales of these pieces to support survivors of acid attack. #fashion #socialresponsability #mfw.” Reeling from the excitement of the prize, Shadab Wahab told us, “With this win we will be able to stock at all the best shops in Italy. This is huge for a label like ours and it can't get much bigger than this. This kind of visibility and acceptability in society for our acid attack survivors is important and it is so great that they got an international platform.” Also competing for the prize were 12 brands from countries like Seoul, Paris, China, Ukraine and Romania. We sat down with another India participant, Dhruv Kapoor (former Vogue India Fashion Fund winner) and in second place at the Fashion Hub Market, to know more. Edited excerpts below. Fashion Hub Market is an initiative by Camera Moda (The Fashion Council of Milan, similar to what FDCI is in India) where they invite emerging brands to present their collections mostly scouted by Sara Maino (Vogue Italia) and Paola Arosio (head of new talents at Camera Moda). This was the second season for us here, and this year they introduced the Camera Buyer Prize. The prize was offered by Best Shops, which is an organisation that includes 107 members and 450 fashion concept stores in Italy. What will follow after the prize is many meetings in the following week, and opportunities to stock at some of these stores where they buy the fall/winter 2019 collection and promote it through social channels, specially curated window displays, etc. It has come at the perfect time; just when we are strategising our expansion into the EU. Considering that Italy is a major fashion capital, it is good PR for the brand and [can provide] great business and visibility. The label incorporates a mix of my education in Italy (at Istituto Marangoni) where I fell in love with the minimal Italian aesthetic and the extravagance of India (prints, colours and hand crafted embroideries). This combination totally works for us and shall definitely help us grow at a much faster rate. Always. International recognition has been on our agenda since day one. However, India still generates 70 per cent of our total business. Yes! [Italy] is very close to my heart. And with some knowledge of the language, it's always a pleasure to come back to the city where I learnt it all. I have always dreamt of days like this and opportunities like these, and finally it's taking shape. Couldn't ask for more at this point. The prize had a buyer's choice tag to it. It fits in seamlessly. Reworking the classics with embellishments and a burst of colour and print patchwork make the product more refreshing. The price points are very competitive, which worked in our favour. We are trying to tap into every possible aspect in both directions—at home and away. The collection is now on its way to Paris and will be displayed at a reputed showroom throughout Paris Fashion Week, after which it will come back to India to be presented at India Fashion Week. We are excited to hear the feedback and general response towards the product. As for me, I'm moving onto the next season: spring/summer 2020. column1: What I’ve learnt in my struggle to find The Perfect white wedding sari
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion There a few things you must keep in mind if a white sari will be your garment of choice on your wedding day. After many store visits, trials and hours spent on Pinterest, this is what I've learnt so far I am all of six months away from my wedding and the one question I can't seem to escape is, “What are you wearing for the big day?” Being the type of person that I am, I have been working on a Pinterest board for my wedding way before there was an actual person in my life to wed. One would assume I have everything figured out, but that's far from the case. Like fervent koi fish swimming upstream against the current of societal norms, I want to wear white for the kalyanam (the Malayali wedding ceremony). The codes of colour are strict for Indian weddings and unless you hail from a community where brides do traditionally wear white, it can be considered pretty inauspicious a choice. Having successfully found a loophole in the system—Malayali brides are known to wear Kasavu saris, white has been approved by my Maharashtrian family rather grudgingly. But the conundrum doesn't end there. For the last four years, I have sat through at least 90 per cent of the major fashion shows that took place in the country. If I had to imagine what my temporal lobe would look like, I am certain like my image library would be filled with endless runway looks. None of this helps when I have to make the daunting decision of picking just one sari for a pretty important event in my life. Do I pick a weave or go with something sexier? Are you supposed to look sexy on your wedding day? Will threadwork look too weak amidst a sea of bright Kanjeevarams? Will the lighting make my outfit appear washed out? Besides my need to text someone every 30 minutes, scrolling through Instagram feeds of designers and recent brides has contributed to the budding carpal tunnel syndrome in my right hand. This is not an exaggeration—I now wear a wrist brace (in generic grey) to recover from the damage of this search. In conclusion, here are a few of my top pointers if you plan to wear white to your wedding. Now, I don't mean you ape their look to the T, but rather focus on the elements that made their outfit memorable. How do you wear white in the day versus at night? Which kind of makeup look will complement it well? Whether it's the Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla drape Deepika Padukone wore to her wedding reception or the equally demure all-white look by Rahul Mishra she wore more recently, it's important that you pay attention to the small details. If you go with a handwoven silk or a cotton jamdani sari, pair your look with some stunning vintage jewellery. If you opt for a sheer, embellished number, pick your jewellery to match the colour of the embellishment. Since you're in the desaturated side of the colour box, work a design element to your advantage. It could be an impressive mathapatti, a veil, or a cape that makes your look extra special. Finally, if you need a break to the all-white look, pick saris that have a hint of colour in the border. You can alternatively choose off-white or a very pale hint of pink for the base. If your bridesmaids play a crucial role in the ceremony, request a pastel colour palette from your main girls to ensure visual harmony in the photographs—the only other real reason to get married. column1: This label is why your feed will soon be filled with spa robe dresses
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Barbara Potts happened upon the inspiration for the new Saks Potts collection while on holiday at Switzerland’s 7132 Hotel. Think: logo pedicure sandals, quilted towelling handbags and hooded dresses that riff off the classic spa robe. Vogue meets the Danish designers in Paris for an exclusive preview and a lesson in sartorial serenity In just five years, Danish brand Saks Potts has established itself as the darling of Paris Fashion Week's competitive showroom circuit, and counts Cardi B, Selena Gomez and North West among its fan base. Its Copenhagen-based founders Catherine Saks (26) and Barbara Potts (25), who met in kindergarten aged six, are still spinning from the runaway success of the Foxy—a clean take on the classic Russian princess coat launched in 2017 as part of Collection 6, in a series of social media-friendly shades. It struck a chord with Instagram's global network of influential female creatives, as did the label's philosophy: “We see ourselves as a fashion brand with a focus on outerwear and we wanted to make a cool feminine coat in a style that you could also wear with sneakers,” Potts explains. The emphasis on outerwear in Saks Potts' business plan is no accident. “Growing up in Copenhagen you learn that the most important investment in a woman's wardrobe is a coat, as the weather is chilly most of the year. We wanted to make colourful outerwear that really stands out.” In the beginning, they produced just one coat shape in four different colours and, encouraged by friends, sought out a handful of local Danish boutiques who stocked a few of the early prototypes. Everything changed in 2015 when the designers received a message from Sarah Andelman, founder and creative director of Paris' now-shuttered cult concept store, Colette. Andelman bought up the collection, with the big retailers in the US, UK and Seoul quickly following suit. Today, the self-described “niche label” relies on small-batch store drops, which mean that the Foxy is never not sold out. “Every time we restock, it's sold out the day after. Right now it's also sold out,” Potts explains. Their collections, which are individually themed and numbered in a departure from traditional autumn/winter or spring/summer tagging, now include ready-to-wear pieces, swimwear and bags, which are also frequently sold out. With demand so high, it's perhaps unsurprising that the label's industrious founders have their sights set on a restful spa theme for their 11th collection. Potts' inspiration arrived while on holiday at 7132 Hotel in Vals, Switzerland, with her boyfriend in October 2018. Just days earlier, Cardi B had stepped out in Paris wearing the brand's Foxy lime green jacket for the first time. Their homegrown brand “was exploding”, Potts explains, speaking to Vogue ahead of unveiling their Spa collection at Ladda, a light-filled massage space in Paris' 10th Arrondissement that's a locals-only secret. “We were hiking in the mountains during the day and relaxing in the spa during the evening,” she says of the 48 hours spent in Alpine paradise. The calming effect of Peter Zumthor's quartz-stone architecture together with the spiritual lure of healing thermal waters stayed with Potts back in Copenhagen, where the pair who design everything together (Saks oversees production, while Potts takes care of PR and marketing) got to work on spa-themed designs. The final inspiration, Paolo Sorrentino's 2015 film Youth—also set in a Swiss spa—translates to a de-stressing colour palette: a serene uniform of supple jackets and separates in beige and black that you could wear anywhere. This evolved collection is ready-to-wear for the baths, the boardroom and beyond. The pieces naturally come imbued with a dash of Scandinavian wit too, think: logo pedicure sandals, quilted towelling bags emblazoned with yin-yang symbols and hooded dresses that riff off the classic spa robe. For the presentation in Paris on Tuesday 26 February, Egyptian-Canadian artist Nadia Gohar, who is on board as guest creative director, has created towel-animal sculptures, while Danish photographer Casper Sejersen is shooting the campaign on Argentine model and filmmaker Clara Cullen. The famed neon Saks Potts colours that make your Instagram grid pop are still there (just like the bright nail varnishes you find on the spa shelf), but the overall impression—including Potts' own favourite pieces from the collection (the plush beige down jacket and jumpsuit)—is resoundingly calming. Potts tells Vogue, this is “the opposite of Collection 10”, which was the subject of ardent celebrity pick-up—in case you missed it, North West sported a custom-made mini version of the poison green shimmer look (with matching hair scrunchie). Selena Gomez' stylist Stella Greenspan pulled the same look for the singer's appearance in the 'Taki Taki' music video alongside megastar, Cardi B, who broke the internet all over again by stepping out in a one-of-a-kind Saks Potts patent leather lilac coat. The closest we got to peering in the group chat between team Cardi and team Saks Potts was a quintessentially cool Scandinavian response-plus-smile from Potts. “We suggest something and she comes back with her thoughts. But, you know, it's Cardi B! She wants something super eye-catching.” The race to pick up Collection 11 will begin at the end of April when a limited-edition drop of spa-themed merch will hit the Saks Potts online store in time for your summer holiday, followed by lightweight RTW pieces (including swimwear) in June, with the outerwear arriving in stores in August. Prepare yourself for another shopping frenzy, set a calendar reminder and stake out your piece of Saks Potts serenity. Just don't say we didn't warn you. column1: Vogue chronicles the closets of five women who wear their values
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From a love for lived-in fashion to loyalty to the loom, these sartorialists are making a statement on the impact of choice with their clothes [#image: /photos/5ce41357ce1c69f8630f936a]||| ||| Image: Indra Joshi/Vogue “A common misconception about modest dressing is just because you're covered up your thinking is orthodox and backward,” says blogger Summiyya Shah of a correlation she'd like to see challenged. For the 29-year- old, who cites Halima Aden (the first hijab-wearing model to appear on the cover of British Vogue) and Blake Lively in her suited avatar as her pin-ups, modesty is more than just a buzzword. “I come from a conservative background and I've dressed this way for as long as I can remember but that has never curbed my enthusiasm for fashion,” she adds. When it comes to her career choice (Shah is co-founder of millennial-minded blog House of Misu), the decision to not show skin has come with roadblocks but none that couldn't be overcome with a few modest modifications—clever layering, she says, is key. “I've lost count of the number of times I've paired a crop top or a camisole dress with a shirt.” With modest-friendly labels making their way into the industry, the country's couturiers, too, are willing to cater to the demand. When Shah tied the knot, she was dressed by designers spanning Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla and Gaurav Gupta. “They knew I had to be covered but that didn't take away from anything. They took it as a challenge.” —Neharika Manjani [#image: /photos/5ce4135889be362ccb7ce113]||| ||| Image: Indra Joshi/Vogue “I recently acquired an Emmanuelle Khanh jacket from Berlin. Very '70s, something you would imagine Freddie Mercury wearing!” says Divya Saini, stylist and owner of lived-in fashion label Bodements. Two years ago, Saini chose to stop shopping cheap and cheerful fast fashion; a prerogative that resulted in Bodements, where she curates well-loved vintage from monolithic labels like Burberry, Jean Paul Gaultier and Saint Laurent. “I have an affinity for fashion steeped in history, like YSL's legacy of introducing menswear codes in womenswear,” says the vintage collector who realised bringing back little treasures from her travels through Europe could grow into a business endeavour. So far, it's been a series of successful pop-ups in Mumbai, Delhi and Paris. But has India really warmed up to the idea of pre-owned fashion? “Buying pre-loved and worn-in clothes can make some uncomfortable. For me, though, promoting a more ethical fashion industry and dressing accordingly is not just exciting, it's rewarding.” As someone who references the past through her closet, for the shoot she handpicks a snake-print polo layered under a psychedelic patterned suit and scuffed cowboy boots that tell a story of their previous wearers. I inquire about their origins and promptly comes her reply, “I can never tell you! An important lesson I've learnt as a vintage professional is to never reveal my sources!” —Akanksha Kamath [#image: /photos/5ce41358cc50be50bb13d62f]||| ||| Image: Indra Joshi/Vogue Dubbed India's Ellen DeGeneres for her man style and pithy comic timing, Vasu Primlani has always worn the pants—on the job or at home. “My father served in World War II, and he raised me like a soldier. I was to sit up straight, follow discipline, and perform the traditional role of a man around the house.” Four decades later, it's an upbringing that has filtered into her wardrobe. Her steely disposition matches her perfectly ironed pantsuits, while her wit complements a growing collection of quirky bow-ties. Not one to borrow from the boys but rather reach out for the racks in the men's section, Primlani admits to a style that comes with no frills attached. “I'm training for the Ironman at least 1.5 hours every day, 2-4 hours on Saturday and 4-8 hours on Sunday. So, I'm almost always in sportswear,” she says, citing functional shoe label Keen as her favourite in footwear. On occasions when she has been presented with awards like the Nari Shakti by the President of India, she turns to traditional saris. “I love gamcha saris in earthy tones and vegetable dyes.” Following an impactful 17-year stint as an environmentalist in America, Primlani found her voice in stand-up comedy, where she calls out social issues. Her loudest and most clear message yet—her choice of a gender bending closet. “In India, society conforms a tad excessively to what men and women can and cannot do.” —Akanksha Kamath [#image: /photos/5ce41358cc50bea81a13d631]||| ||| Image: MKT Other than a fondness for folk music, what binds the Nagaland-born Tetseo sisters—a cross-generational quartet made of mother-of-two Azi, content curator Mercy, fashion blogger Kuvelü and medical student Alüne—together is their loyalty to designer Aneeth Arora's label, Péro. Arora's allure lies in her ahead-of-time aesthetic, they explain. “She is always thinking up the most colourful ways of reinterpreting weaves, colours and prints. Her clothes are so much fun, not to mention always a conversation starter. There is a story to every piece,” says Azi. Today, the label not only dominates their personal but also their professional wardrobes; Arora has on more occasions than one customised pieces for their performances. “The designs are sustainable, ethical and true to traditions. They are earthy yet contemporary,” says Mercy of Péro's philosophy, one that is mirrored in their mantra as musicians. “We as folk artists are truly proud of our culture. We celebrate simplicity in every way possible while staying true to traditions. We try to make our music more relatable and contemporary, appealing to both young and old, local and foreign,” adds Alüne. Like the proverbial travelling pants, the sisters' favourite Péro purchases routinely swap hands. “We share regularly. Some of our favourites are the shirt dresses, wool sweaters, reversible coats and dresses, pyjamas, the embroidered bolero jackets and of course the customised wool tops embroidered with our names and a Péro heart,” says Kuvelü.—Neharika Manjani [#image: /photos/5ce41357b803114ea68f4f01]||| ||| Image: Indra Joshi/Vogue You might recognise Kaur from the Vogue.com video, meandering through the lanes of Delhi's Shahpur Jat, sourcing fabrics, hand-dyeing them with local artisans and conjuring up designs that she then wears herself. Welcome to a day in the life of Prabhleen Kaur, design head at NorBlack NorWhite. “I don't wear labels. It's usually me rummaging through my collection of indigenous textiles—handloom cottons and silks from the regional markets of Chennai, Kolkata and Karnataka—to construct new silhouettes,” says Kaur, who grew up in Punjab, where, with limited access to designer labels, she started creating pieces of her own with locally available textiles and make-do resources. “Handwoven fabrics stuck around for me during this time, like a steady relationship,” she adds. As a 28-year-old, Kaur makes a strong case for a return to craft. “The notion that handloom is dull and boring isn't true. On the contrary, Indian textiles have never been shy of bright, stirring prints. And there are no rules—you can use them in an athletic bomber jacket, or an elegant wrap kimono. You make the call.” For Kaur, the texture of a natural loom-made fabric (with slubs and everything) trumps any mill- or machine-made fabric. “Climate and cultural symbolism all affect the nature of handmade textiles. It's what renders them unique. What fun is it wearing something whose life cycle you can't trace?”—Akanksha Kamath These Indian women left careers in other spheres for the love of fashion Why the Indian industry has its sights set on street The enduring appeal of the trench coat, and how to wear it now There's a new vintage store in Mumbai and it's a must-visit People Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The enduring appeal of the trench coat, and how to wear it now
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion An enviable array of macs once again dominated street style and catwalks—JW Anderson, Burberry and Simone Rocha—at London Fashion Week. Could this wardrobe evergreen be the piece to kick-start a sustainable approach to shopping? You've probably spotted influencer and creative director of Social Zoo, Pernille Teisbaek, a self-confessed “sucker for a good trench”, wearing one of her beige Celine or Nili Lotan Topher coats as part of the tonal looks that populate her Instagram grid. Teisbaek leads by example. Along with her trench-coat-wearing peers—Leandra Medine, Gilda Ambrosio and Linda Tol—the Danish creative director dominates the international street style circuit, where the mac is now an evergreen staple, worn year round no matter the city or the weather. Ever synonymous with British style, the mac can also be regarded as the unofficial uniform of London Fashion Week—it led the charge again at this season's AW19 shows, the perfect antidote to unpredictable downpours. But then, the power to weatherproof in style is the reason the trench coat exists. Rewind to 1879 when Thomas Burberry invented the water-repellent gabardine fabric, paving the way for the prototype of an army officer's raincoat that Burberry submitted to the United Kingdom War Office in 1901. The gabardine proved so effective at fending off the damp that it was worn by explorer Ernest Shackleton on his 1907 expedition to Antarctica and used to create the tents that sheltered his crew. Nowadays, minus the death-defying polar adventures, hardy gabardine trench coats offer the kind of one-step dressing solution that editors love. The trench is versatile: swerving the formality of angular blazers on days when a more casual note is needed, and ingeniously replacing dresses for evening occasions during fashion month, when there's no time for a costume change beyond the addition of a second-skin knee boot (in place of trainers) and pearl-drop earrings. Away from the street style paparazzi, the trench also offers everyday practicality. “I'll often style my trench with either a camel chunky knit, boots and suit pants for a tonal look or over a suit jacket, jeans and sneakers underneath for a day in the office or to take my kids to the playground,” Teisbaek explains. This time-saving, wear-anywhere power of the trench is now backed by modern design acumen, with fresh renditions appearing on the AW19 catwalks at Burberry, Gabriela Hearst and The Row. Elsewhere there was a slick patent version (at Simone Rocha), revitalised heritage checks (JW Anderson), architectural sleeves (Ports 1961) and leather panelling (Proenza Schouler), so there's guaranteed to be a style to suit any taste. View Gallery 7 Photos The enduring appeal of the trench coat and how to wear it now How we wear our trenchcoats has also evolved. London-based Korean designer Rejina Pyo has a knack for playing down decadent pieces—like her eye-catching new season silver lamé dress—with a glossed leather or coated fabric trench coat. It's this focus on versatility that offers her the freedom “to reinterpret them as dresses, or flip between masculine and feminine looks", which for a new generation of women who wear their trench with logo tights or sweatpants, means that it continues to hold appeal as one of fashion's enduring rites of passage. And at a time when we're reevaluating just how sustainable our wardrobes really are, the lure of investing in a remixed heritage classic that's engineered to last a lifetime is all the more appealing. Here's how to wear a trench coat now: [#image: /photos/5ce411ee3bf9b463c9b1a88c]||| ||| Image: Jonathan Daniel Pryce Instagram's Eva Chen splits her transeasonal fashion month wardrobe between starched trench coats by Monse and Sies Marjan. The secret to the appeal of the latter's cotton canvas style is the doubled-up design that riffs on the runways' love of layering. If wearing two trench coats together feels too conceptual, try the trend with an unbuttoned men's shirt. [#image: /photos/5ce411eeb40d263f41d6a9be]||| ||| Image: Jonathan Daniel Pryce Note how the coat, shoes and tee all stay within a small spin of the colour wheel—the easiest way to crack spring 2019's obsession with beige is to wrap up in a mac (and put an end to concerns about what underwear could work with semi-sheer cream trousers). [#image: /photos/5ce411ee9cc0c072eef9b489]||| ||| Image: Jonathan Daniel Pryce Riccardo Tisci's clever ‘chopped and spliced' use of the house check at Burberry is inspiring shoppers to seek out vintage Burberry trench coats that can be flipped inside out to expose those cult gridlines. [#image: /photos/5ce411efb803118d868f4ddb]||| ||| Image: Jonathan Daniel Pryce The fastest way to refine your transeasonal wardrobe? Shop your trench coat one size up, allowing extra fabric to fold back the collar and cuffs, and the option to cinch in at the waist with a contrasting belt if (like most of us) you aren't runway model height. [#image: /photos/5ce411ef4a30b3feb912b1d8]||| ||| Image: Jonathan Daniel Pryce If the gabardine trench feels too old-fashioned, a glossy vinyl retake offers a modern edge without losing any of the versatility. Opt for a butterscotch shade (as worn here by Net-A-Porter's global buying director Elizabeth von der Goltz) over the punkish mood of liquorice black vinyl. 5 fashion trends from New York Fashion Week you need to know about London Fashion Week AW19: The biggest fashion trends on the runway Vogue predicts: Fashion month's 10 biggest street style hits Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Deconstructing Dior’s AW19 with Maria Grazia Chiuri
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue meets the artistic director of Dior, Maria Grazia Chiuri, ahead of her AW19 show in Paris, to talk about the British Teddy Girls-inspired collection, collaborating with Italian artist Bianca Pucciarelli Menna (Tomaso Binga), and creating a “global conversation around femininity” Maria Grazia Chiuri is in a reflective mood when she meets Vogue at Christian Dior's design headquarters in Paris, ahead of their AW19 show. The artistic director of the French fashion house, now aged 55, first met Karl Lagerfeld when she was a 25-year-old designer at Fendi, and news of his passing has led her to contemplate her role in the fashion world. “He was the original creative director, the first to work under another house name like Chanel and Fendi,” she says. “You have to reflect the history of a brand when you are designing for somewhere like Dior, people on the outside recognise the code, and the most important code of Dior is the Fifties silhouette.” But this season, Chiuri didn't want to rely solely on the nipped waists and voluminous skirts of Dior's iconic New Look. She is excited by the “completely new point of view” that curator Oriole Cullen has brought to the Christian Dior: Designer of Dreams exhibition at London's Victoria and Albert Museum (until 14 July). The show centres on Mr Dior's anglophile leanings—not only did he famously dress Princess Margaret, he had a penchant for Savile Row suits, enjoyed starting the day with a traditional English breakfast and, in his own words, loved “English traditions, English politeness, English architecture”. And so, Chiuri started looking for her own new point of view for Dior's AW19 collection. [#image: /photos/5ce4132dce1c691c240f934b]||| ||| Image: Jamie Stoker “You never know where inspiration is going to come from when you work in fashion,” says Chiuri. For this season's boxy blazers in leather, denim and corduroy we have Stephen Jones to thank. About six months ago, the British milliner—who has been creating headpieces for the house of Dior since 1996—brought Chiuri a photograph taken by his friend's father, the late film director Ken Russell. In the 1950s, before directing films like the Oscar-winning Women in Love (1969), and The Who's rock opera Tommy (1975), Russell spent time documenting the Teddy Girls and Boys of London on his Rolleicord camera. The photograph that Jones gave to Chiuri was of 14-year-old Jean Rayner, who befriended Russell and introduced him to this post-war subculture. “She had attitude by the truckload,” Russell told the Guardian in 2010. “They were tough, these kids… they knew their worth. They just wore what they wore.” The Teddy Girls created an arresting visual identity by styling Edwardian drape coats—an aristocratic hallmark—with American rock-and-roll-inspired fashion, such as rolled-up jeans and flat shoes. They exemplify, Chiuri says, everything that fascinates her about British style: “It speaks about tradition, but at the same time it really breaks the rules.” When Chiuri joined Dior in July 2016—the first woman creative director in the house's 73-year history—she took the opportunity to rethink her approach to design. “I was very naive when I started working in fashion, it was all about self-expression back then,” she says. “Now, I see it as my job to deliver a positive message to society. I really believe that we are responsible for the next generation.” At Dior, Chiuri has instilled that message via her collaborators—choosing photographer Brigitte Lacombe to shoot the campaigns and commissioning women artists from around the world to redesign the Dior Lady bag. Her objective, she says, is to create a “global conversation around femininity”. For her SS17 collection, Chiuri printed the title of Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's essays, We Should All Be Feminists on white T-shirts; and for AW19, she has once again emblazoned the cotton basic with feminist directives, this time with the cover art of Sisterhood Is Global, the international women's movement anthology by American author Robin Morgan. “It's a promotion for the book,” she adds. “I want Dior to be about collaborating with other women to support one another's point of view.” “When you collaborate with another artist you have to give them freedom to express themselves,” says Chiuri. For AW19, she asked 88-year-old Italian artist Bianca Pucciarelli Menna to create the set. “I met her to speak out the project and then left her to it,” Chiuri continues. Menna is better known by her male alter ego Tomaso Binga, which she adopted in order to penetrate the misogynistic art world in the 1960s, before revealing her true identity as a form of protest during the feminist movement of the 1970s. Building on two bodies of work from the latter decade—Living Writing and Alfabetiere Murale—Menna photographed herself naked in poses that resemble letters. These prints have been arranged around the interior of the Musée Rodin in Paris, where the Dior show is taking place, so the letters spell out one of Menna's poems. “Words are a very important source of inspiration to me,” says Chiuri. “Books aren't like a film where everything is defined, when you read, you dream.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Spotify is finally in India, and it’s about to change your Instagram stories
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s everything you need to know about the launch of the music streaming giant, Spotify, in India, and how it will upgrade your life There is a new entrant to the ever-growing digital streaming market in India— Spotify, the world's largest music streaming service, has finally made it to the country. The music streaming app, available on Android, iOS, desktop and tablet, has been one of the most anticipated launches and is focusing on English and Hindi music, as well as Punjabi, Tamil and Telugu music in India. Like in other nations, Spotify says it will offer personalised, local-flavoured playlists to Indian listeners. But avid Instagrammers have another reason to be happy: with the app finally in India, Spotify users will be able to share music on their stories (and listen to the music shared by Instagrammers across the globe—a facility that was so far not available in India. As it is globally, Spotify offers a free version supported by advertisements. With a premium version, the customers will get one-month free trial. The subscription starts at competitive price of Rs 119 per month (as opposed to $9.99 in the US); users can also choose from daily and weekly plans. What gives Spotify an edge over current music streaming services in the Indian market? According to music aficionados, the recommendation and artist suggestions features are better than any other apps in the market, and so is the user experience, making it easier to discover new music of your taste. It offers a web player, which is not available on Apple Music. And the fact that it does offer a free version means that you can share a song with any of your friends who have that app, again, not available if you are an Apple Music user. And if you're really into pop, Spotify has a featured series called Secret Genius, which has songwriters talk about their top hits. The launch in India comes amid a continued battle with Warner Music over licensing fees. Spotify was able to secure direct licensing agreements with Sony Music and Universal for the Indian market, but couldn't come to an agreement with Warner. Instead, the music service is relying on statutory licensing for the use of music from Warner's catalogue. Culture & Living Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why the Indian industry has its sights set on street
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From a want for wearability to a rebellion of sorts Scroll through your Instagram feed on any given day and you'll stumble upon the latest iteration of the sneaker, bum bag or sweatshirt, not from your average sportswear or high-street label but from the most storied fashion houses. Whether it's Balenciaga's bestselling bazar bag that cues memories of a tote typically spotted in Thai markets or Louis Vuitton's Archlight sneakers which come with a $1000 price tag, it's safe to say the boundaries between street culture and luxury have been blurred. The Indian fashion industry too isn't immune to this phenomenon. For a while now, street staples have surfaced on the runway courtesy of a young, iconoclastic crop of talent and found favour in the wardrobes of countless celebrities. With a little help from the stars and the designers fronting the movement, Vogue studies the state of street in the country. The Kardashian Jenners and Hadids have long been supporters of street but closer to home too, there doesn't seem to be a shortage of celebrities championing the style. While bomber jackets from fashion heavyweights like Fendi are a building block of Alia Bhatt's wardrobe, Ananya Panday's favourite finishing touches come in the form of Louboutin sneakers and an Off-White crossbody. It doesn't stop at members of Gen-Z, Kareena Kapoor Khan has stocked up on everything from sneakers to sweatshirts from It-label Gucci and Ranveer Singh, has on more occasions than one, been spotted in logo-laden track suits.   Delhi-based designer Dhruv Kapoor, whose collections frequently feature high-shine bombers and track bottoms, credits the influx of street influences to a want for a more wearable wardrobe. “As formality enters a void, utility takes over. Each designer is giving us variants of the same thing in their language. In the end, these silhouettes are easy and have a higher repeat value.” On the same page is Shyma Shetty, one half of the duo behind Huemn, a label with its roots steeped in streetwear. “Investing in fresh fashion only for occasion-wear is at an all-time low. We want wardrobes that we can take from work to evening and comfort is essential to this,” she says. For Shetty, this also represents a rebellion of sorts. “Doing something traditionally ‘unacceptable' has always been what sets the trend for tomorrow. Fashion today celebrates the individual and your sartorial choices can be absolutely fearless as long as you're convinced”. But what sets streetwear apart from athleisure? And more importantly, what justifies the hefty price tags that accompany luxury streetwear? While the latter can attributed to buying a sense of exclusivity and belonging, the former is about mastering a mix. “There is an overlap between street and athleisure but for me, street is a dressed-up version of it. It's about mixing easy with statement, while retaining functionality.” A certain coming together is also key for the former Vogue India Fashion Fund finalist Kanika Goyal—whether it's pairing phulkari with boxy basics or collaborating with another designer. "Streetwear is all about eluding traditional categorisations through collaborations and mergers. You see a couture brand making baseball caps, something that we never saw in the past. It's a space to explore your creativity and not be bound by the traditionally set norms," she says. Speaking of mergers, it's hard not to touch upon a boundary-blurring piece of news from last year. Off-White's Virgil Abloh was anointed artistic director of Louis Vuitton's menswear and charged with the task of making the house more millennial-minded by bringing to it a sense of street. But while hallowed houses are keen to inject a dose of cool, can the same be said for the future of fashion in India? 2018 also saw the appointment of Nimish Shah (the name behind decade-old label Shift) as creative director of streetwear brand Bhaane. “I am a one tune trumpet. Shift will rub off on Bhaane but I am very mindful of this. Bhaane has evolved to become wholesome but the spirit stays street, my aesthetic just brings more finesse,” says Shah. With young designers having set their sights high on the streetwear-inspired aesthetic, will it change the look of our wardrobes significantly in the next couple of years? column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In a skimpy gold mesh top with a long black Saint Laurent skirt that hit right below the navel, the actress instantly stole the spotlight There are several surefire ways to cause a stir on the red carpet. A thigh-high slit is bound to get people talking (just ask Angelina Jolie). As for the guys, wearing a harness over your traditional tux is as attention-grabbing as it gets these days. There were also three eye-catching rings all set in platinum and covered in diamonds. In other words, her look gave new meaning to the idea of a golden fashion moment.
