column1: The expert guide to renting designer fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Could the future of sustainable fashion lie in the rental economy? Vogue speaks to experts about how you can upgrade your wardrobe by borrowing, not buying Whether it's a vintage Dior gown or a million-dollar Tiffany necklace, celebrities are well-accustomed to borrowing designer pieces to wear on the red carpet—especially during awards season. But for the everyday consumer, renting premium fashion remains a relatively untapped area that is far from mainstream. This, however, is about to change. Thanks to the influx of fashion rental sites across the world—from the US-based Rent The Runway, to Girl Meets Dress in the UK and Rent At Tali in India—the rental economy is growing, with the industry set to be worth $1.9billion by the end of 2023. One of the major factors driving change is the increasing global concern surrounding sustainability; a circular economy has been widely recognised as a legitimate solution. “People are becoming more aware of their environmental footprint; these days none of us want to be wasteful,” Girl Meets Dress co-founder Anna Bance tells Vogue. “50 per cent of fast fashion pieces are discarded within a year and as responsible shoppers we are under pressure to close this loop.” The rise of Instagram and influencer culture that feeds the need for more variety in people's wardrobes has contributed to the boom in rental businesses too. For those who want the best of both, sustainable fashion updates if you will, renting is the perfect solution. Merri Smith, co-founder of peer-to-peer app Tulerie observes that “with social media, people are photographing their entire lives now, you don't want to wear things over and over”. But instead of buying something new, “why not borrow it?” she asks. Luxury brands are also beginning to tap into the potential of the rental market. In fact, Rent The Runway recently teamed up with Derek Lam, Jason Wu and Prabal Gurung to unveil their first exclusive capsule collections. “As the scale of our business has grown, [designers] have realised [the fashion rental market is] healthy; that it's not hurting their regular business,” says Rent The Runway's senior buying director James Newell. With the industry on the rise, Vogue gets the inside track on renting premium fashion. You should think of renting as a way to upgrade your current wardrobe, says Smith, who founded Tulerie with business partner Violet Gross after finding they were increasingly borrowing from friends. “70 per cent of your wardrobe is the pieces you're wearing over and over. We want people to look at enhancing that,” she explains. By renting pieces to supplement your core wardrobe, you can also afford to invest in more expensive staple items that would normally be out of your reach. As you're not committing to a single piece, you can experiment outside of your style comfort zone when renting—including when it comes to new brands. “Be willing to take risks! This is your chance to take rational decision-making out of your fashion choices,” Newell, from Rent The Runway, advises. “Swap out clothes regularly, try new trends and borrow for parts of your life you didn't anticipate at the start of your journey.”   If you've got a big event coming up, it's important to think ahead—as popular dresses can often get booked up. “There is no rule about how far in advance of the event you should order. The sooner the better. We get dresses booked for weeks, months ahead,” Bance, from Girl Meets Dress, advises. The boom in the rental fashion market is in part due to more relaxed dress codes in the office, making workwear a key focus area. “15 to 20 years ago, a woman could wear the same anonymous suit as her male counterparts, or invest in a couple of chic dresses and get by with that,” Newell says. “Now there is such a tremendous demand to have varied looks. [Renting] offers a nice solution.” The online communities that exist around fashion rental sites are a valuable resource. 60 per cent of Rent The Runway customers leave reviews on items they've borrowed; and Tulerie, which sees users borrowing from each other, has also found their members wanting to share tips. “People want to talk, they want advice on how to style something,” Smith explains. “We are trying to create this network of women, who are bonding over [a] shared interest of clothing.” 4 experts answer all your questions on shopping for vintage clothing 17 sustainable buys under 5k to help you commit to slow fashion in 2019 What to keep in mind when shopping for vintage designer wear Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Celebrities who have dared to defy red carpet fashion rules
column2: © Scott Gries Fashion From Lady Gaga’s meat dress to Jennifer Lopez’s dangerously low Versace, Vogue looks back at stars who have defied the red carpet fashion rules over the years Award shows are, for all intents and purposes, a stage—where fashion fantasy plays out, where talent is celebrated, and more recently, a moment to take a stand. Last year, for example, Los Angeles and London's award ceremonies stood in solidarity with the #MeToo movement with an all-black dress code. But statements come in different shapes and styles—and cuts and colours, too. Over the years, the red carpet has hosted its fair share of renegades, subverting the sartorial rules at the time. Unforgettable looks from the archive include Bjork's swan dress, which dominated headlines at the 2001 Oscars. Not content with rejecting the traditional sweeping gowns, the Icelandic singer took things even further when she stopped to ‘lay an egg' on the red carpet. Bjork at Oscars 2001 © Getty Lady Gaga caused quite the stir at the 2010 MTV Video Music Awards when she arrived in a dress made entirely out of raw meat. Although many took it to be a statement in support of animal rights, the star revealed she wanted her jaw-dropping outfit to show that “if we don't stand up for what we believe in... we're going to have as much rights as the meat on our bones.” Lady Gaga at 2010 MTV VMAs © Getty Others who have thrown the rule book out of the window include Cher, who defied all red carpet convention by baring her midriff at the 1986 Oscars. The singer—who said she didn't want to look like a “housewife in an evening gown”—ensured she commanded attention in her Showgirl-inspired two-piece and dramatic feathered headdress by legendary fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie, despite not being nominated for an award for her role in Mask. Cher at Oscars 1986 © Getty While showing off flesh on the red carpet is much more common these days, Elizabeth Hurley managed to secure her place in fashion history in 1994, wearing that plunging Versace dress held together by huge gold safety pins at the premiere of Four Weddings and A Funeral. Featuring a daring thigh-high split and slashed sides, is still often referenced today, over two decades later. Liz Hurley with Hugh Grant © Getty Another often discussed power move is Julia Roberts' feminist statement at the 1999 London premiere of Notting Hill—when she showed off her armpit hair in a glitzy red sequinned dress. Though years later she admitted it was unwittingly done, having not taken her sleeve length into account when waving to fans. Speaking to Busy Philpps on her E! Talk-show last November, Roberts clarified: “It wasn't so much a statement as it's just part of the statement I make as a human on the planet for myself.” Julia Roberts © Getty More recently however, actor Ezra Miller has pushed the boundaries of men's red carpet style—which typically consists of a tailored suit and bow tie—donning a black Moncler x Pierpaolo Piccioli puffer gown with a dark lipstick to match at the Paris premiere of Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes Of Grindelwald last November. column1: Lingerie you should buy this Valentine’s Day, based on your zodiac sign
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Baby dolls, classic lace pieces, or a camisole set? Find out what kind of lingerie your zodiac sign should invest in this Valentine's Day It's that time of the year again! Come February, romantics all over the world start conjuring dreamy Valentine's Day plans and exciting ways to treat their better halves. And while sweet trinkets and candlelit dinners are always welcome, nothing makes Valentine's Day as fun as a special after-hours treat. Whether you're heading for a quick getaway with your S.O. this V-Day or just staying home to enjoy some alone time, it's not a bad idea to spruce things up with some innovative inner wear. But should you go for sexy bondage-inspired lingerie, a feminine babydoll or something a little sporty? Let your zodiac sign help you make your choice. [#image: /photos/5ce4166bc8a4687d4df24e5e]||| ||| Logo bra and boy shorts, Pink Has Aries ever shied away from the spotlight? That's right, she hasn't, and she definitely shouldn't on Valentine's Day. Your vibe has always been bold, and nothing can do your energetic self justice like a printed lingerie set. Since you're a fitness fan, there's no harm in giving your inner wear a sporty spin for your special evening. Try boy shorts in an unexpected print like camouflage. [#image: /photos/5ce4166bb8031159568f52df]||| ||| Lace and satin underwired bra and briefs, Stella McCartney You've always been drawn to beautiful things Taurus, and quality is one factor you'll never compromise on. Instead of going OTT this season, go with what you're naturally drawn to. A classic lace lingerie set is right up your alley. Try a siren red balconette bra for the perfect balance between sexy and sweet. [#image: /photos/5ce4166b89be360e567ce4f1]||| ||| High-neck underwire bra and panties, Victoria's Secret There's nothing Gemini won't try atleast once, and Valentine's Day is a great opportunity to experiment a little. Opt for a colour you wouldn't usually wear (and by that we mean skip the predictable pinks and reds), and play with not-so-basic silhouettes. How about an interesting high-neck bra in an unexpected shade of mint green? [#image: /photos/5ce4166c4a30b39e5412b6bc]||| ||| Satin slip dress, Dolce & Gabbana If there's one zodiac sign that's all about passion, Cancer, it's you. End your Valentine's Day on a sweet note with a slinky slip instead of a racy lingerie set. We recommend a sprightly version covered in blooms, which should appeal to your hyper-romantic nature. Bonus points: You can always use it as a layer over your favourite set. Leo, luxurious things have always caught your eye, and striking colours and patterns seem to be your favourites. Make sure you stand out this Valentine's Day by picking something few others would: a wild animal print or even dramatic baroque patterns. If there's one person who can carry this off, it's you. [#image: /photos/5ce4166c1dc2679133c76e7d]||| ||| Silk-charmeuse camisole and pyjama shorts, Morgan Lane You're a perfectionist Virgo, and comfort is key when it comes to you. Why not go down the path no one else does on Valentine's Day and opt for a fuss-free camisole set? Equal parts casual and cute, this one's great for a romantic Netflix and chill session with your S.O. [#image: /photos/5ce4166c89be3623fc7ce4fb]||| ||| Triangle bra, thong and dress, ID Sarrieri Lace, satin and a hint of velvet... when it comes to lingerie Libra, you like your fabrics plush, but you know not to ever go overboard. Opt for something that harmoniously brings all your favourite elements together, and layer up with a semi-sheer cover up for your special Valentine's Day night. [#image: /photos/5ce4166c1dc267711cc76e7f]||| ||| Stretch-tulle and lace bodysuit, Spanx You're as seductive as they come Scorpio, and it's rare for you to have an uneventful Valentine's Day. Go all-out this year with a bodysuit in a deep jewel tone and match it with a dramatic eye mask. We already know you'll be picking something daring. [#image: /photos/5ce4166e4a30b3b86e12b6c6]||| ||| Bra, suspenders and briefs, Agent Provocateur Sagittarius is a free spirit, and your love for adventure always has you ready to take risks. This Valentine's Day, it's a good idea to invest in something you've never worn before. Try a bondage-inspired bra and panty set with suspenders. If black is too obvious for you, why not try a striking shade of purple instead? [#image: /photos/5ce4166e3bf9b4d905b1ad52]||| ||| Lace bra and thong, Coco De Mer You may be all about work sometimes, Capricorn, but when it comes to matters of the heart, you're a traditionalist all the way. Add a string of pearls to complete the look. [#image: /photos/5ce4166e1dc267e5c2c76e84]||| ||| Stretch-tulle underwired bra and briefs, La Perla You're a trendsetter, Aquarius, but why not throw caution to the wind and tone things down this Valentine's Day? column1: Jewellery connoisseurs, you can’t miss this trunk show in Mumbai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Delhi-based jewellery designer Hanut Singh returns to Mumbai for his annual trunk show at Maithili Ahluwalia’s store, Bungalow Eight. Get all the details now He's a jewellery designer whose patrons include the likes of Beyoncé, Rihanna, Christian Louboutin, Mary-Kate Olsen and Amber Heard. She's a curator whose Mumbai boutique is a go-to for one-of-a-kind brands. Together, Hanut Singh and Maithili Ahluwalia come together each year to host an annual trunk show that is a must-visit for the city's discerning jewellery lovers. Singh and Ahluwaila's association dates back to 2004, when Ahluwaila's Bungalow Eight was an interior-focused store and Singh had newly launched his eponymous jewellery label. “The trunk show with Hanut was our first-ever fashion pop-up and the collection completely sold out,” recalls Ahluwaila. “What I love about his work is the unpredictability. You never know what is coming next. Hanut is always on the hunt for new materials and explores them in dynamic ways. His work is flowing, evolving and reaching new heights, always. Even after all these years, he has managed to keep the brand inaccessible, and people wait to see him.” Singh, who is a descendant of the Kapurthala royal family of India, developed a keen appreciation and understanding of jewellery early in life. His cosmopolitan creations are as timeless as they are bold, and the designer is adept at weaving together ancient Indian and European inspirations and techniques. “I always put my best foot forward for my Mumbai shows with Maithili because she gets my essence and we have great synchronicity. The women are receptive to my work, have great flair and know their minds, which I love. This year, I am presenting a new collection of primarily earrings, which is a distillation of the highest order of my own growth in my profession. I am upping the ante big time,” adds Singh. The designer has worked with 17th century carved emeralds and opals in painterly pavé work and ombré tones, featuring architectural, linear and deco influences. column1: The most interesting designer saris spotted at Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Anita Dongre’s romantic floral printed saris to Shivan & Narresh’s fringed numbers, check out our edit of the best saris from the summer/resort 2019 edition of Lakmé Fashion Week Whether it's handwoven or hand-embroidered, a sari not only makes for a quintessential piece of clothing in every woman's wardrobe, but can also double up as an heirloom that is passed down from mother to daughter. Vogue spotted all varieties and hybrids possible of the much-adored six-yard staple at Lakmé Fashion Week's summer/resort 2019, right from saris made out of sustainable Tencel fibres to trouser-style iterations. While florals for spring may not be groundbreaking, the way they were used on saris this season brought a fresh spin to the popular motif. Designer Anita Dongre presented an eco-friendly collection comprising lightweight saris in vibrant prints, and Rohit Bal turned to the darker side of the colour palette with floral printed saris in black, one of which came layered with a rose-embroidered cape. Varun Bahl introduced his prêt line that incorporated prints created out of a five-petal flower sketch, as seen on his white sari featuring blue and yellow floral prints. Anushree Reddy's dark blue number featured coral pink and green flowers intricately embroidered on the border. Handloom saris shared equal limelight on the runway—designers Sailesh Singhania, Parvathi Dasari, Anka and Latha showcased traditional weaves that are sure to serve as a classic piece in every millennial's ethnic wardrobe—and ruffle tiered saris got their moment too, lending a feminine touch with their dreamy hues of candy floss pink (showcased by Shehlaa by Shehla Khan) and mellow yellow (spotted at Anushree Reddy). Details like tassels and pearls worked as decorations on saris as well, as seen at Payal Singhal and Shivan & Narresh respectively. Accessories like belts added a contemporary touch to saris, and designers like Punit Balana, Shantanu & Nikhil, Shivan & Narresh and Anka used everything from printed belts to studded belts to update the look. Meanwhile, sari blouses saw myriad options: structured shirts at Jajaabor, statement sleeve blouses at Payal Singhal, bandhgala-inspired crop tops with military influences at Shantanu & Nikhil and strappy embellished ones at Sukriti & Aakriti made an impact. Anavila's embellishment-free saris in bright natural colours and dyes caught our attention for lazy summer brunches, and Shantanu & Nikhil showcased a contemporary range for girls who always struggle with draping issues—a trouser-style sari. column1: Inside Meghan Markle’s wardrobe: The Duchess’ favoured sustainable labels
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Veja to Gabriela Hearst, Meghan Markle has championed a host of sustainable brands since becoming a full-fledged member of the royal family. Here, Vogue rounds up seven of the eco-conscious labels she’s sported thus far If there's one message Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, is sending out with her wardrobe, it's the importance of sustainable fashion. The royal has regularly supported eco-conscious brands since marrying Prince Harry last year, including: Stella McCartney, who has long been known for her ethical approach to fashion; Gabriela Hearst, whose eponymous label combines luxury with a low environmental impact; and lesser-known designers such as Outland Denim, Rothy's and Kimai. Here, Vogue takes a look at the sustainable brands the actress and activist has worn since becoming a fully-fledged member of the royal family. [#image: /photos/5ce415643bf9b4729bb1ac14]||| ||| Meghan Markle on a visit to Sussex. Image: Rex Features Meghan Markle is one of Gabriela Hearst's most famous fans, first sporting the emerald Demi satin tote during a visit to Sussex last October. She opted for the Nina bag (not for the first time) during a visit to Birkenhead this January, which happily coincided with the week that Hearst launched an exclusive collection with Matches Fashion, and LVMH announced a minority investment in the brand. Founded in 2015, Hearst's whole ethos is about producing “luxury with a conscience”—with leather only cut to supply demand, a priority of using sustainable materials and reducing waste and plastic in the brand's design processes. [#image: /photos/5ce41566b40d267db9d6ad5d]||| ||| Prince Harry and Meghan Markle in Sydney during the Invictus Games Sydney 2018. Image: Getty French trainer brand Veja has achieved cult status since launching in 2004, with its mission to offer consumers full transparency when it comes to its supply chain. The Duchess of Sussex wore the brand's Esplar trainers, named after a Brazilian NGO that supports cotton farmers, while watching a sailing event during the Invictus Games in Sydney in October 2018. [#image: /photos/5ce415641dc26715f5c76d1b]||| ||| Meghan Markle and Prince Harry at Dubbo Airport, Australia. Image: Getty The so-called “Meghan-effect” came into full force after the Duchess wore Outland Denim's high-rise Harriet jeans not just once, but five times, during her first overseas tour last year. The Australian brand—which uses ethically sourced materials and employs women in Cambodia who are at risk of falling into poverty—revealed it was able to hire 46 more seamstresses after sales grew by 640 per cent following the royal endorsement. [#image: /photos/5ce415651dc267310ec76d1f]||| ||| Meghan Markle in London. Image: Getty Lab-grown diamonds are changing the face of the jewellery industry, offering a more sustainable alternative to traditionally-mined stones. And the Duchess is an early adopter, wearing British brand Kimai's now sold-out Felicity earrings—featuring synthetic diamonds set in ethically-sourced gold—while visiting the Smart Works charity in London in January 2019. [#image: /photos/5ce415661dc2673745c76d21]||| ||| Prince Harry and Meghan Markle in New Zealand. Image: Getty Keen to support local designers during her first royal tour, the Markle wore a white tuxedo dress by sustainable New Zealand-based brand Maggie Marilyn at a reception in Wellington. Founded by young designer Maggie Hewitt in 2016, the brand makes a point of manufacturing all its clothes in factories in New Zealand, paying workers a living wage, and using environmentally-friendly fabrics. [#image: /photos/5ce41564b8031175738f5170]||| ||| Prince Harry and Meghan Markle at South Melbourne Beach. Image: Getty Rarely seen without her towering stilettos, the Duchess made an eco-friendly statement by wearing a pair of flats by Rothy's, established in 2016, while visiting a Melbourne beach in October 2018. The upper layer of the Point flat is made entirely from recycled plastic bottles, while the insoles are made from foam that's been re-fashioned from old shoes. [#image: /photos/5ce415641dc2676556c76d1d]||| ||| Meghan Markle in Birkenhead. Image: Getty The Duchess of Sussex showcased the gold-plated Wide Ripple Bracelet by up-and-coming British brand Bar Jewellery—which uses recycled metal for its pieces—while visiting Birkenhead in January 2019. Founded by designer Sophie Mckay (who previously worked for luxury brands including Tom Ford and Versace), Bar's ethos focuses on ethical and sustainable practices and the collection is handcrafted in London. column1: Isha Ambani Piramal: “I grew up very much a tomboy”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue India's February 2019 cover girl, Isha Ambani Piramal, talks about childhood, close friends and other connections It's safe to say that we have all been curious about the life inside Antilia. From parvenus to blue bloods, the country's collective obsession with Ambanis has built up intrigue that often spurs into gossip. But what was it like for growing up in India's richest household? “Very, very normal,” insists Isha Ambani Piramal, as she takes us back to her favourite memories from her childhood—school, friends and what they taught her. Isha Ambani Piramal: I was the only girl with four boys at home. It was Akash, Anant, Anmol, Anshul and me. So by default, I had to be naughty to survive. If I tried to be anything else, I wouldn't be included in all their games and fun. I grew up very much a tomboy. At home, there was no gender bias. I was never told that because you're a girl, you can't do this or that. IAP:  While growing up, I never felt different from my peers and classmates. I think there are very few people who have tried to be friends with me because of fame or prominence. When I was studying and working abroad, I was pretty much anonymous. It would be naive to say that I've never come across such sycophants, but I always try and see the good in another person and assume their best intent. I haven't come across a “yes” person, who agrees to everything I say. At Jio, we are treated as any other manager working at Reliance—if you are not doing your job well, somebody else will take your job and do it. It's not like you are the only person who will do your job. And we are held accountable for what we do. But we are very normal. It may sound weird to some people, but I do believe that we are ordinary in the sense that we live like everyone else—my family, our relationships—we are very close, grounded, and our relationship is based on love. My parents have had the same friends since I was born. And it's the same with Akash, Anant and I. Of course, we have some new friends, but our core group has pretty much remained the same. In that sense we've been very lucky to be surrounded by real people who tell you the tough things in life if they have to. IAP: PC, I've known forever. But she is more like an elder sister to me. We actually got closer when we were both living away from home in the US. We again share a very real relationship—we see each other in real-life settings and not in like glamorous ones; we have real conversations. She's a really strong mentor and role model [to me]. IA: Akash has the largest heart ever. He changed his wedding dates for me. He got engaged to Shloka before Anand and me, but he was like, “I'll get married afterwards, you take my wedding dates.” He's like one of the most—I don't think there's a word for it in English—“dayalu” humans in this world. He's empathetic, gracious and gentle, just like Shloka. In fact, Shloka's sister, Diya [Mehta Jatia] and I were in the same class in Sunflower and then in JB [Petit]. We have been best friends for over 25 years. Then when I moved to Ambani, I skipped a grade and went to Shloka's class. So I've been like a third sister to them. I was thrilled with the engagement news. Shloka's always been part of the family for us. IA: My siblings love him (Anand). He is hysterical and always has everyone in splits! One thing that he always tells me that I did not practice in my life earlier, is spirituality. He quotes the Bhagwat Gita often. Through him I have learnt that in life, nothing can substitute good thoughts and good deeds. Akash and Anant look upon him as an older statesman of the family. IA: Not really. I have a private account on Instagram because there's no need for me to have a public account. I'm not an influencer and it's not something that I want to be. I don't want to be known for the number of followers I have. I use social media for fun—scrolling through Instagram is a huge source of entertainment for me! column1: Highlights: Day 5 at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Ranveer Singh’s impromptu rap performance to Kareena Kapoor Khan playing showstopper for Shantanu & Nikhil finale show, here’s everything that went down on the last day at Lakmé Fashion Week Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 came to a dramatic close with designers Shantanu and Nikhil Mehra presenting their collection with Kareena Kapoor Khan as showstopper. [#image: /photos/5ce4153ab80311df878f513f]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Punit Balana at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce4153acc50be55a413d82f]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Misfit Panda at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce4153a3bf9b4062ab1abe3]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Neha Agarwal at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Punit Balana's summer/resort 2019 collection ‘Maya' championed eco-friendly techniques like block printing, as seen on showstopper Karisma Kapoor's anarkali, which came with two dupattas. While Soha Ali Khan closed the show for Agarwal in an off-white front-open gown and palazzo set, Misfit Panda put the spotlight on badminton player PV Sindhu, who wore a hybrid of sneakers and gladiators in a metallic pink hue. While Shehlaa by Shehla Khan's collection was inspired by the 1980s and incorporated shoulder pads, bold embroidery accents and sheer fabrics, Shriya Som's carefree ensembles featured elements of raffia in a tribute to the free-spirited woman of today. column1: Fendi brings back their iconic bag with this collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The storied Italian fashion house has relaunched their iconic Baguette with a fresh video campaign, but that’s not all that’s new with the bag Will the iconic Fendi baguette ever rest in peace? We don't think so. Proving fashion's obsession with making everything old new again, the Italian luxury brand recently relaunched their iconic design with the cutest video series yet. Titled the #BaguetteFriendsForever series, this video campaign centres around female friendships and is shot in various metropolitan cities including Shanghai, Hong Kong and New York. The third video to be released is shot in New York and features a group girls discussing the latest It-Bag that one of them sighted at a Fendi store. To make up for the brief moment of indecision, they return to the store to make the purchase—only to be met with disappointment; the arm candy already has a new owner. Distraught, they run to locate the bag and are deeply surprised to meet the woman who inherited their treasure. None other than Sarah Jessica Parker turns around to remind the girls, “It's not a bag, it's a Baguette!” Fendi's spring/summer 2019 collection saw new and refreshing versions of the classic bag that is perfect for the girls who love staying on trend. From being associated with Sarah Jessica Parker  to finding a cult following in the likes of Kate Moss and Sienna Miller, the bag has been a favourite ever since it was launched in 1997 by Silvia Venturini Fendi. In 2019, the classic bag is being made available in a new oversized design, in addition to the mini versions. The new pieces are crafted from multiple range of materials including the new eye-catching soft FF logo embossed leather in pastel colours. If you're a diehard fan of the '90s, Fendi's new edition of the baguette bag is a definite must-have. Wear it with your LBD for a night out in the town or simply style it with your all-white look to grab all the attention. Scroll through our gallery to take a look at the making of the pieces, and the times Sarah Jessica Parker was spotted carrying a Baguette. column1: Fashion politics: why conscious dressing feels relevant for now
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion #MeToo and Time’s Up have made us think harder about what we’re wearing – who are we dressing for, and why? Vogue investigates whether a new era in fashion marks the end of sexed-up style When the miniskirt launched in the 1960s, it was deemed one of the greatest fashion revolutions of the past century. Based on a traditional tunic worn by the ancient Greeks and Romans, it set a new agenda, breaking free from the constrictive, voluminous skirts and nipped-in waists of the 1950s. Of course, exposing the female thigh after all this time made it controversial and divisive, too—but the miniskirt came to be known as an emblem of London's new “youthquake” and an enduring symbol of women's liberation. Fast forward nearly 60 years and the miniskirt continues to divide opinion – but 2019 is a very different landscape. In fact, minis were met with such widespread disapproval by critics at Hedi Slimane's debut SS19 Celine show, it raised the question of whether certain items and aesthetics are now off limits for designers. Slimane responded to the furore, asking: “Does this mean women are no longer free to wear miniskirts if they wish?” and whether the reception of the collection was due to the difference in style between himself and his predecessor, Phoebe Philo. Where Philo's Céline (with the equally divisive accent) had always been about minimal, covered-up, everywoman designs—architectural yet wearable, and often involving an ugly-chic shoe—Slimane's debut brought back the short and sexy silhouettes he'd made his signature while at Yves Saint Laurent. It wasn't just the switch from Philo's aesthetic that sparked debate. Post #MeToo and Time's Up, we know fashion has power—remember the all-black outfits at the 2018 Golden Globes—but fashion needs context, too. Maria Grazia Chiuri's autumn/winter 2018 Dior show also focused heavily on miniskirts—but hers were inspired by a striking archive image of women protesting outside a Dior shop because there weren't enough miniskirts inside, and the whole collection, titled “I am woman”, was intended as a celebration of female empowerment. Indeed, Philo's aesthetic was changing mindsets long before any public movements. “I started my career being known for my ‘sexy' styling, so that has definitely changed," says fashion stylist Katie Mossman, who pinpoints the Philo years as the starting point for her shift in attitude. While she admits that “the oversized-trouser-and-sneaker-wearing editor" look, as she describes it, took some time to get used to, it was a fresh aesthetic that meant women could be "powerful and chic as well, [and] no longer dressing for a man". “The black looks at the Golden Globes had a big impact,” London-based stylist Elizabeth Saltzman told Vogue last December. “I take my job seriously. Every look has to be considered," she says, referring to a need to think about the wider picture before agreeing on a look with the client—hers include Saoirse Ronan and Gwyneth Paltrow. Mossman is inclined to agree: “I think there is a certain cautionary feeling in the air after the #MeToo movement.” The great thing about fashion is that it's always got a historical reference point. When Dior unveiled its New Look in 1947, its end-of-austerity escapism changed the way women dressed until the miniskirt came along. But Dior's vision wasn't welcomed with open arms by those who had enjoyed the simple cuts and shorter lengths that wartime had necessitated. The New Look's signatures—corseted waists and long, splayed skirts constructed from yards and yards of fabric—felt like a backward step, and were vehemently opposed by, among others, the Little Below The Knee Club, which formed in Dallas in 1947 to protest against just this. Another product of post-war society, the flapper dress, also split opinion—it could by turns be associated with young and giddy debs who spent their time dancing the Charleston, or with liberating women's attire and putting it on a more equal footing with men's. Compared to what had come before it, the short, dropped-waist flapper dress, and the androgynous figure it favoured, felt modern and more masculine. It would be frowned upon by some and embraced by others for both these reasons. “I feel like #MeToo and other sensitive movements have definitely caused people to step back and think more about what they do and wear,” concludes Mossman, who says it's always something she considers when styling a shoot or dressing a celebrity. “If it's a short dress, it's long sleeves or high neck; one or the other.” Ultimately, rather than declaring certain clothes off limits, it's more important to be comfortable in what you're wearing—dressing consciously is perhaps the most relevant fashion statement for 2019. column1: All the Bollywood showstoppers from Lakmé Fashion Week S/R 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Kareena Kapoor Khan and Ranveer Singh to Janhvi Kapoor, Kangana Ranaut and Tabu, see which Bollywood stars walked at Lakmé Fashion Week S/R 2019 Lakmé Fashion Week isn't just a much-followed event because of the many designers and fashion enthusiasts it brings together. Each time it comes around, Lakmé Fashion Week also lights runways up with a slew of celebrity showstoppers dressed in the season's most exciting look, and 2019's summer/resort edition was no different. Held in Mumbai between January 29 and February 3, Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 was brimming with Bollywood showstoppers dressed in everything from wedding-ready lehengas to weekend-appropriate dresses and elegant evening wear too. Here's a look at everything you missed. If you thought India's wedding season was over, Lakmé Fashion Week's celebrity showstoppers will have you thinking otherwise. This season, fashion week had some of Bollywood's biggest stars closing shows in extravagant wedding-ready ensembles. While Janhvi Kapoor joined uncle Anil Kapoor at Raghavendra Rathore's show in a sultry all-black jacket + lehenga combo, Karisma Kapoor walked for Punit Balana in a flowy anarkali and Kangana Ranaut transformed into the ultimate summer bride for Anushree Reddy in that feminine peach lehenga. Other stars whose festive looks topped trending charts: Lisa Haydon, Aditi Rao Hydari and Soha Ali Khan Pataudi. Along with Indian ethnic ensembles, Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 also featured several Western evening looks that you need to check out if you've got a thing for gowns. On January 29, Gaurav Gupta kicked off the season with Karan Johar and Tabu, who made a rare appearance in a dramatic powder blue gown and just days later, Malaika Arora played showstopper for Manoj Agarrwal in a gown in the same palette. One of the biggest presentations of the season was Shantanu & Nikhil's closing show, which featured Kareena Kapoor Khan as showstopper. This time around, the actor brought Lakmé Fashion Week to a close in a slinky black gown with criss-crossing leather panels on the bodice. The latest season of Lakmé Fashion Week didn't just feature some of Bollywood's biggest female stars; it included a handful of the Indian film industry's favourite men too. While Anil Kapoor danced down the runway (and was joined by front-rower Ranveer Singh) at Raghavendra Rathore's show, Singh celebrated his upcoming film Gully Boy with a special show on Day 5, for which he was spotted rapping on the runway. Aditya Roy Kapur went head-to-toe black at Kunal Rawal's showcase and Karan Johar turned showstopper not once, but twice this time. After walking the ramp with Tabu for Gaurav Gupta, the Bollywood director was also seen joining Bhumi Pednekar and Isabelle Kaif at Shehla Khan's show. Missed what all your other favourite Bollywood stars wore on the runway this time? Catch up now. column1: Highlights: Day 4 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Day 4 at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 was busier and buzzier thanks to all the conversation-starter moments the runway served up Bodice by Ruchika Sachdeva bent towards realism with a casting that spanned from songstress Rachel Verghese and DJ Zokhuma aka Arman Menzies to actors Kalki Koechlin and Jim Sarah, while the day's finale, Raghavendra Rathore pulled out all the stops with Janhvi Kapoor, Anil Kapoor and a dancing Ranveer Singh in the audience at his show. Here are all the moments you probably missed from the latest showcases at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019. [#image: /photos/5ce418c045074a4152905b41]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Saaksha & Kinni at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Part of a larger Diamond Producers Association sponsored ‘The Real Cut' show, which included Rara Avis and Verandah, Saaksha & Kinni's showcase came accessorised with sleek jewellery by AS Motiwala, Om Jewellers and others. The label, known for its use of geometric prints and patterns (recently worn by Frieda Pinto) on lady-of-leisure kaftans, had a lineup featuring sheer jackets, pants and skirts. A star layered piece: checks on checks on checks—all in sheer organza. [#image: /photos/5ce418c04a30b32ac712b96e]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Rara Avis at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Verma's collection was a lesson in getting clever with colour. Featuring camel, fawn and tan, the all-beige palette of her safari-inspired collection introduced textures as a way to tackle tricky monotone. And then there were the denim shorts with cowri shell detailing, perfect for summer days spent at the beach, plus poplin ecru dresses with doodles in rainbow colours. Perhaps not an intentional move, but could this be a little way to inject Pride on the runway? We may have missed the parades happening all around the city, but we did find ways to spot the spirit of one love wherever we could. [#image: /photos/5ce418c14a30b3d9b012b970]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Nikhil Thampi at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Nikhil Thampi made his return to Lakmé Fashion Week with none other than supermodel Carol Gracias in tow. Now 40, Gracias walked long and lithe down the ramp in a cleverly cut rust dress. With ‘Semi Colon', Nikhil Thampi took to a new territory for cuts that travelled low along the neck and back, while slits ventured higher up the thigh. The Dynasty-inspired strong shoulders and tuxedo dresses were an ode to '80s maximalism—think Bianca Jagger at Studio 54. When a model glided down the ramp in a side-slit dress with nothing but semi colons holding the fabric in place, we were reminded of that iconic Liz Hurley safety pin dress that has gone down in history, and possibly made it to Nikhil Thampi's mood board as well. column1: Highlights: Day 3 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Anavila’s collection inspired by slow fashion and slow living to Kanika Goyal’s sarcastic play on the current consumerist culture, catch up on everything you missed from day 3 of Lakmé Fashion Week Mumbai's Jio Garden is abuzz with designers, influencers and fashion insiders alike, and day 3 was the busiest so far. Some shows were a carry forward from Sustainable Fashion Day and incorporated a similar ideology in their collections—like Sweta Tantia's Tahweave, whose collection revived the age-old craft of ikat, and Anavila Misra's Anavila, who used 100 per cent natural colours and dyes. Other shows, like Essé by Sahib & Sunayana and Kanika Goyal, came with a powerful message. Scroll ahead for all the highlights from day 3 of Lakmé Fashion Week. [#image: /photos/5ce417a24a30b3691c12b80d]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Essé at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a145074a09fa905a20]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Essé at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a245074a6c27905a22]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Essé at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Starting off day 3 were designers Sahib and Sunayana whose label Essé asked the audience a valid question: Why so offended? Cropped jackets worn with bralettes and wide-leg cargo pants, dresses with statement sleeves, crop tops with skirts, won full marks on the sartorial scale for their contemporariness. [#image: /photos/5ce417a2c8a4686145f24f71]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Tahweave at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a2cc50be452d13da8e]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Tahweave at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a23b32c358c5d99b13]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Tahweave at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Sweta Tantia of Tahweave took inspiration from the French architecture of the 17th century and gave it an Indian spin with the use of ikat. The collection featured easy-breezy dresses with overlays in summery shades of yellows, corals, pinks and blues, making it an ideal pick for a relaxed summer day. [#image: /photos/5ce417a23b32c32c23d99b14]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Kanika Goyal at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a33bf9b45b1cb1ae6a]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Kanika Goyal at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a489be3622197ce60f]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Kanika Goyal at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Kanika Goyal's ‘Plastic Fantastic' overtly conveyed a powerful message—in this world that's overloaded with information and is led by consumerism, it is possible to feel that you are enough. Goyal, through her use of bold hues and maximal aesthetic, made the audience sit up and take notice as models walked down the runway wearing dresses with sheer layers and checked pantsuits with slogans like “Sensor Is Tripped”, “Don't Cash Feelings”. [#image: /photos/5ce417a489be363a947ce60e]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; SVA by Sonam and Paras Modi at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a4b80311571a8f53ec]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; SVA by Sonam and Paras Modi at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a545074ac916905a24]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; SVA by Sonam and Paras Modi at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 The afternoon moved on to showcase festive ethnic wear, and Sonam and Paras Modi made a strong case for pastels at their summer/resort 2019 show. From lehengas styled with denim jackets to organza layers paired with printed denim shararas, ‘Tara' lent a boho touch to festive dressing for summer. Brides-to-be, are you taking notes? [#image: /photos/5ce417a5cc50be8e8113da90]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Payal Singhal at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a4b40d26f4f5d6aff5]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Payal Singhal at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a5b40d26c6d8d6aff8]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Payal Singhal at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 For her summer/resort 2019 collection ‘Qo'shilish', Payal Singhal traced the Silk Route, right from Samarkand in Uzbekistan to Benaras in India, to create a definitive renaissance-meets-Mughal art look. The line introduced new silhouettes like the Nizami sharara, short lean kurtas, saris and renaissance tops in fabrics like velvet, crepe, silk, organza and more, in a colour palette that revolved around moss green, periwinkle blue, dusty rose and sandstone. [#image: /photos/5ce417a5c8a468de29f24f73]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Eka at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a5b40d2609b4d6aff9]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Eka at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a59cc0c01a93f9ba8d]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Eka at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Rina Singh of Eka's collection described summer in the best possible way—breezy blouses, relaxed dresses, delicate layers in fabrics like sheer and lace, in a colour palette dedicated to pastels, made up the range. What's more, models and influencers alike walked the runway for Singh to pay homage to the real women of India. [#image: /photos/5ce417a73b32c33827d99b18]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Anavila at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a74a30b3c59412b817]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Anavila at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce417a6b80311fe368f53ef]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Anavila at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Closing day 3 of Lakmé Fashion Week was designer Anavila Misra, whose summer/resort 2019 collection took inspiration from the culture and diversity of the Sa Pa tribes of Vietnam. The handwoven and handcrafted line featured saris and relaxed dresses in natural yarns like cotton, linen and silk with techniques like pleating, cording and embroidery. The colours and dyes were 100 per cent natural, making the collection eco-friendly and good for the planet. column1: The Valentine’s Day outfit to shop for based on your zodiac sign
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Let astrology (and our handy guide) decide your look this Valentine’s Day With Valentine's Day approaching soon, it gives you yet another reason to get your hands on some envy-inducing wardrobe must-haves. Whether you're a true believer of astrology and horoscopes or just someone who reads them for fun, it's interesting to see if your stars align with your wardrobe choices. On this Valentine's Day invest in some stunning dresses, blouses, skirts and pantsuits—but do it with the blessings of your zodiac. Scroll ahead to find out what your vibe should be on your V-Day date night. Crop Top, Miu Miu; Palazzo, Palomo Spain Without a doubt, your creative sensibilities and bold decision making skills makes you the chameleon of the fashion world. While you like sticking to your signature style, you also want to add a touch of glamour to your look every time. Style Miu Miu's black leather top with a pair of burgundy velvet palazzos by Palomo Spain to channel your love for athleisure on Valentine's Day. Top, Carine Gilson; Skirt, Gucci; Earrings, Gas Bijoux Taurus, when it comes to your sartorial choices, you always value quality over quantity, and prefer easy breezy ensembles to complex statement-making numbers. Invest in soft fabrics from your trusted brands to integrate comfort with your appreciation for the finer things. Throw a silk camisole over a pair of printed silk trousers by Gucci to add a fun twist to your date night look, and top it off with golden hoop earrings by Gas Bijoux. Jumpsuit, Norma Kamali; Earrings, Mignonne Gavigan You are not the one to shy away from experimenting in the sartorial department. In fact, you don't even like tying yourself down to a signature style. This Valentine's Day, dress yourself in Norma Kamali's metallic jumpsuit featuring kimono sleeves and a deep neckline, and complete your outfit with chunky earrings by Mignonne Gavigan and a pretty red pout. [#image: /photos/5ce416c789be36178d7ce544]||| ||| Dress, Self Portrait; Earrings, Irene Neuwirth It's safe to say that Cancer, you're a hopeless romantic who pretty much wears your heart on your sleeves. Having said that, your wardrobe is also reflective of your mind, and so, you like favouring feminine outfits with interesting prints and cut-out details. For your Valentine's Day celebrations, accessorise Self-Portrait's one-shoulder polka dotted dress with gold heart-shaped earrings by Irene Neuwirth. [#image: /photos/5ce416c7b803115fed8f5328]||| ||| Blazer and flared pants: Hebe Studio, Earrings, Oscar De La Renta Admit it Leo, you love attention. From brightly-hued dresses to outfits featuring cut-outs, your wardrobe has no dearth of bold ensembles. Instead of taking the done-and-dusted dress route, go with a powder pink fitted blazer and a pair of flared pants, both by Hebe Studio, and add a sultry spin by skipping the under shirt. Top it off with crystal hoops by Oscar de la Renta. [#image: /photos/5ce416c71dc2670f20c76ed4]||| ||| Dress, Versace; Heels, Valentino You are a perfectionist by nature and that's also true for your wardrobe. From black dresses to white T-shirt and jeans combinations, your love for tried-an-tested outfits is known. As you plan your look for this Valentine's Day, upgrade your wardrobe with a sleeveless silk dress by Versace, and add a pop of colour with a pair of Rockstud heels by Valentino. [#image: /photos/5ce416c7b40d2681bed6af16]||| ||| Top, Sacai; Skirt: MSGM As a Libra, you love striking the balance in all spheres of life—be it your work, wardrobe or relationships. When it comes to your sartorial picks, you prefer to invest in refined separates. Consider Sacai's lace top, worn over MSGM's vinyl pleated skirt for your date night look. [#image: /photos/5ce416c7b40d26c564d6af18]||| ||| Dress: Brandon Maxwell; Heels: Giuseppe Zanotti Pulling off bold and magnetic looks is a cakewalk for you, Scorpio. Your style choices tend to be both powerful and sexy while still being very low-maintenance. Opt for a statement-making one-shoulder dress by Brandon Maxwell, featuring a thigh-high slit that will instantly add a sexy spin to your wardrobe for your date night outfit, and elevate it with glittery pump heels by Giuseppe Zanotti. [#image: /photos/5ce416c93b32c35a8cd99a81]||| ||| Top: Derek Lam 10 Crosby; Pants: Alice + Olivia Sagittarius, experimentation is your middle name when it comes to your fashion choices. Considering you love adventure, comfort is an element you dare not miss out on in your wardrobe, but you don't shy away from bright hues too. Pair a dark shade with a lighter one to stand out in the crowd—a combination of a pink Derek Lam blouse and wide legged pants by Alice + Olivia will serve as a good option for Valentine's Day. [#image: /photos/5ce416c8b803118fb18f532a]||| ||| Top: Orseund Iris; Skirt: Diane Von Furstenberg Elegant choices and Capricorn go hand-in-hand—and this fact extends to the Capricorn wardrobe too, which mostly comprise of pieces that are ideal for work-to-drinks plans. This Valentine's Day, invest in a pleated skirt by Diane Von Furstenberg and wear it with Orseund Iris' blouse featuring balloon sleeves. column1: Decoding Kriti Sanon’s Indian girl-next-door look from Luka Chuppi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion After giving stellar performances in Raabta (2017), Bareilly Ki Barfi (2017) and Stree (2018), the actor will now be seen in Luka Chuppi opposite Kartik Aaryan. Here, we decode her look from the film In case you didn't know it yet, Kriti Sanon and Kartik Aaryan's next film, Luka Chuppi, released its trailer last week, and ever since, sartorialists everywhere have been taking note of Sanon's ethnic look in the movie. Slotted to hit the silver screen in 2019, the feature is a romantic comedy showcasing the plot of a live-in gone wrong, and is sure to be an interesting watch. Sanon's effortless Indian ethnic wardrobe matches the quirkiness of the film's story and her feisty role as a journalist, and features a host of bright cotton salwar suits and kurtas with block print dupattas. Also Read: Kriti Sanon's bright pink lehenga could be your next bridesmaid look Kriti Sanon plays the role of Rashmi, a small-town girl who graduates from Delhi. Sukriti Grover, stylist to Bollywood stars, who also designed Sanon's look for the film, says, “It's like a small-town-meets-big-city-fashion. It involved creating an ethnic wardrobe in a conservative, yet chic and contemporary manner.” This resulted in the perfect blend of what Grover calls ‘The Ethno-Cool' wardrobe, comprising a variety of trendy silhouettes including custom made anarkalis, shararas and palazzos with sartorial combinations like kurtas and jeans. We won't be surprised if you want to get Kriti Sanon's Luka Chuppi look for yourself. In fact, we've already predicted this, and got Vogue India's senior fashion editor Priyanka Kapadia to list down five easy way to incorporate the actor's style. Here's what she had to say. “It's high time we bust the myth of stereotyping kurtas to typical Indianness. Now, you can elevate the staple to a whole new level by either experimenting with the varied silhouettes—from dramatically flared to shirt-like—by belting it, or by layering it with unique jewellery,” says Priyanka Kapadia, senior fashion editor. Pick newer silhouettes: Choose from flared, skater, shirt-style versions instead of the usual A-line or straight cut kurta. Pair them with dhoti pants, palazzos, or even your everyday denims. Clash prints: Wear a floral kurta with a pair of striped pants. Print-on-print is a fun trend to experiment with. Buy separates that you can mix and match, but make sure you don't go all out. Keep your outfit coordinated. Choose brighter colours: When it comes to colours, pinks, greens and yellows are the biggest trends this season, but you can go for muted shades too. If you want to wear brighter hues, choose for a monochromatic head-to-toe look, like a bright pink kurta with pink dupatta and pants. Accessorise to accentuate: Pair your kurtas with delicate silver jewellery, tribal jewellery, or even the ever-popular circular hoop earrings. You can even style them with baubles, chaandbalis or colourful tassels. For the footwear, give slides, mules or platforms a shot. Bag it right: While the jhola aka the cloth bag is a definite no-no, you can always opt for the good ol' (leather) sling bag. Give it a twist with different geometry and shapes. I would recommend the on-trend circular bamboo bags from Cult Gaia. We've put together a curated edit of the best options to shop for to cop Kriti Sanon's Luka Chuppi look. column1: Ashley Graham on body confidence, diets and modelling advice
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion While in Dubai for a store launch, the body positive model talks about her experiences in the modelling industry, and doles out her advice to women everywhere This week, size-inclusive Italian luxury fashion label Marina Rinaldi opened their first store in Dubai, and it was only apt that body positivity activist and model Ashley Graham, who has been designing capsule collections for the label, inaugurate the store at The Dubai Mall. Apart from being a popular plus-size model who recently walked the runway for Prabal Gurung, she's the author of the book, A New Model: What Confidence, Beauty and Power Really Look Like, and also owns her own lingerie line, Addition Elle—but she's clearly not done delving into newer territories yet. She revealed she will be doing something in the bridal space soon, and also spoke about her experiences in the industry, why she does not believe in diets, and how concealer is her go-to beauty product. Scroll ahead to find out what she had to say. “Firstly, remember that you are not alone—so many women feel like that. Affirmations have helped me get out of that rut. It might feel weird to stand in front of the mirror and say “I am bold, I am brilliant”, but everything you say has an impact, even what say about yourself. Use words; your words have power. For me, it is important to tell my story about the issues I have had with food, with my family and with dating. You always help someone else when you tell your story. It is also nice to have that confidante; friends are important.” “For me, it's a question of balance. There are some weeks I am really good and some I am not. It is a question of how I feel and not about rules and regulations. I have been on every diet. There were times when people in the industry told me to lose weight. I realised that when you say, 'Screw you, I am going to be me,' then the same people turn around and say, 'We like you the way you are'. No one has ownership over my body but me.” “Don't do it! Seriously, breaking into modelling is not easy no matter what size you are. Being rich, famous or feeling pretty should not be the reasons—all three happen by luck. What you need is perseverance. I still get told no all the time; it is just part of how it works. Find your niche, look at what is missing—like I realised there was a need for women with curves in the industry, so I went and spearheaded it.” “Until recently, there were no girls with curves in beauty campaigns, and now I have a Revlon contract. It is unbelievable that I am the first girl of my generation to have a beauty contract. Lipstick does not have a size. The beauty industry is changing to become more inclusive [not just with size, but] between race, size, religion and gender too. That is what beauty should be—a representation of who you are. When it comes to beauty, I am a minimalist. A good concealer is must, and I just love Revlon's Candid concealer as it does not go into your fine lines. On my eyebrows I use a hair gel. I just love skincare and no matter what you must wash your face at night.” “As every curvy girl will know, finding luxury clothes that work is just hard. When you think of luxury brands and extended sizes, there is only Marina Rinaldi. I wanted it to be fresh and young so I started with denim. Plus as a curvy girl, I had this inner hatred of trying jeans on—nothing really works, either the knee is wrong place or the inner leg is too tight.” “That women should use their boldness and brilliance to change the world. Women should always know they are worthy.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights: Sustainable Fashion Day at Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From upcycling label I Was A Sari’s collection, which won India’s first sustainability award in fashion, to Anita Dongre’s collaboration with Tencel for her ready-to-wear lineup, Vogue recaps the best fashion shows from Day 2 at Lakmé Fashion Week This year, Day 2 at Lakmé Fashion Week (popularly known as Sustainable Fashion Day) celebrated India's rich heritage of textile crafts and brought attention to the unsung artisans and women weavers who toil away at looms relentlessly to create one-of-a-kind garments. The summer/resort 2019 edition saw collections that were a collaborative effort—take Ujjawal Dubey's Antar-Agni collection for example, which was designed for Raymond, or designer Anita Dongre's lineup that was entirely crafted using Tencel fibres. Scroll ahead for everything you missed from Day 2 at Lakmé Fashion Week. Sustainable Fashion Day kicked off with the Circular Design Challenge, an initiative by Reliance Industries Ltd's R|Elan, Lakmé Fashion Week and the United Nations, that aimed to bring light on the sheer amount of garments that end up in a landfill. In order to increase the garments' longevity, eight talented designers were chosen out of a pool of 900 registrations to showcase collections made using waste fabrics. A panel of six judges—including Bandana Tewari, Rahul Mishra and Neha Dhupia—announced I Was A Sari by Stefano Funari as the winner of the award, a brand that upcycles pre-loved saris into garments and accessories. Funari took home a cash prize of Rs 20 lakhs. [#image: /photos/5ce4181789be36ee667ce6a2]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Antar-Agni at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce418174a30b3388712b89b]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Anita Dongre Grassroot at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Let's begin with statistics, as divulged by Gaurav Mahajan, president-apparel, Raymond group. India has around five million weavers who can weave 1.2 billion metres of fabric. This translates to 500 million garments that can cater to 70-100 billion consumers. But the catch here is that this ideal scenario is not going to be possible without design intervention and corporate funding. That's where ‘Weaving Partnerships for Change' by the UNDP in India and IMG Reliance comes in. The show featured two collections—Raymond x Antar-Agni and Anita Dongre Grassroot—that were facilitated by GoCoop (a marketplace for weavers), who employed women weavers in Assam to create the handwoven garments. [#image: /photos/5ce4181745074a8839905a98]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Doodlage at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce418179cc0c088f4f9bb06]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Door of Maai at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce4181745074a12f9905a9b]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; Rossbelle at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 [#image: /photos/5ce41818b8031106ba8f546c]||| ||| Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue; The Woolmark Company x Péro at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 Aneeth Arora of Péro transformed the runway into a hip Parisian street with skateboarders, hip hop dancers and graffiti artists who joined the models. The collection paid homage to the Bhuttico Weavers Co-operative Society—one of the oldest in Kullu—who worked on creating the handmade Merino wool garments. Showcasing a fully sustainable collection made out of Tencel fibres, Anita Dongre's ready-to-wear lineup transported the audience to a balmy summer day spent in a garden with colourful flowers in bloom. From lightweight saris to skirt and crop top sets—all in happy hues and vibrant floral prints—the eco-friendly collection is sure to inspire your festive wardrobe this season. column1: Freida Pinto talks about the future for Hollywood post-#MeToo
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion She meditates, drinks lemon tea and has a Kondo-esque clutter cleanse every few months—but don't be fooled into thinking Freida Pinto is just another LA star now. Vogue speaks to the Indian actor about why she's rejecting "exotic princess" roles; her latest film Love Sonia, which tackles sex-trafficking; and Hollywood in a post-#MeToo era By the time Freida Pinto and I collect our lemon ginger teas from a coffee shop in the leafy Hancock Park neighbourhood of Los Angeles, the table we had been eyeing outside has been taken. Pinto turns to me and says, “Let's go,” then dashes across Larchmont Boulevard and slips into a nearby cafe, hoping no one will notice that we BYO'd. “I have breakfast here every other morning. It should be fine,” she says with that megawatt smile. It's hard to imagine anyone ever says no to her. “But they might just kick us out who knows. I never take anything for granted anymore.” After her breakout role in Danny Boyle's multi-Oscar-winning Slumdog Millionaire, Pinto has quietly scored part after part, working with the most celebrated directors in cinema today (Julian Schnabel, Michael Winterbottom and Terrance Malik to name a few), starring alongside the likes of Christian Bale, Cate Blanchett and Willem Dafoe. But despite the subsequent flood of work, things weren't as sunny as they seemed. “When Slumdog happened it was just like high, high, high,” she says stretching her hand into the sky. “At some point it had to come down, right? Sometimes when the start is higher, the fall is greater.” Pinto explains that, with very little work in her late twenties, this was one of the most difficult times in her career. She partly attributes the hiatus to the lack of compelling roles to be had. “I was feeling degraded by the offers that were coming in. ‘Is this what you think I'm capable of?',” she remembers asking herself, and by extension, the powers that be in Hollywood. “I indulged in a lot of anxious thoughts and going down a rabbit hole of ‘I should have chosen those roles.'” I ask if she means the “exotic princess” roles she had spoken about in a previous interview? She replies, “Yeah. And I've done them. Once is enough. After a while I said, ‘I don't want to do this shit anymore, I'm not growing in my career.'” What began as an eye-opening, first-hand experience of the cruel realities of Hollywood—namely the lack of multi-dimensional parts for women, especially women of colour—ended up being a crucial time for self-growth. These days, at 34, Pinto has admittedly become a California convert and seems to have comfortably settled into her groove. “When I moved to Los Angeles from London in 2011, I wasn't happy about it,” she remembers. “Although I hated the first two years, now I miss this city when I'm gone.” She's found a small group of friends, including her roommate, Preeti Desai (former Miss Great Britain), who she fondly refers to as her “wife”. Each morning, Pinto practices meditation and chanting, she's into cleanses (she is currently abstaining from red meat), and speaks of the benefits of a simple, pared-back lifestyle (she cleans out her closet four times a year giving away anything that she deems not totally “essential”). Naturally, she also has a yoga guru in Silver Lake. She insists, though, that her practice has nothing to do with Los Angeles and everything to do with the 2014 film Desert Dancer, when she worked with choreographer Erin Elliott. “Erin asked me if I had ever done yoga and I said, ‘Oh no no no, don't try to get me to do yoga. You freakin' Angelenos are all quacks. I come from the country of yoga! I do not need a white person to teach me yoga.' But I was so wrong,” she says looking down as if still sorry. “I discovered my body for the first time. I discovered where I hold my sorrow and happiness. It opened me up emotionally.” When we meet, Pinto has just returned from a 48-day trip to India and Nepal. It's the longest she's spent in India since she left for London in 2008. Officially she was there to promote her new Netflix film, Mowgli—playing Messua, Mowgli's mother, after taking the initiative to call the director Andy Serkis (who she worked with on Planet of the Apes) to actively ask for a role. Unofficially she was tour guide to her boyfriend, adventure photographer Cory Tran, who joined her in Mumbai to see where she grew up and meet her mum, dad and sister for the first time. Apparently it went quite well, “Though I don't think he was prepared for the level of spice,” she laughs. An upside to never having done a Bollywood film means that Pinto can move around her home country relatively incognito. And Tran isn't phased, or particularly enamoured with the celebrity world either: “He doesn't give a f***,” she says, “and I loooove that about him.” This January, Pinto stars in Love Sonia (released in India in September 2018)—a Hindi film shot between Mumbai, Hong Kong and Los Angeles, which she knew from the get-go was one of those once-in-a-career kind of stories that needed to be told. Inspired by real events, writer, director and activist Tabrez Noorani pulls back the veil on the sex trafficking industry, with the story of a young Indian girl in search of her sister who disappears in Mumbai's red-light district. Pinto and Noorani first met on the set of Slumdog in 2007 (he was a line producer), which is when he asked her to read an early draft of the Love Sonia script. Pinto was both disturbed by what she read and immediately drawn to the character of Rashmi, a 30-something sex worker, with a schizophrenic-like demeanour, damaged from years of abuse. “I had just finished playing Latika in Slumdog and I was like, ‘This was too much sunshine,'” explains Pinto of the motivation to do something darker, edgier. “I came alive when I read this part. I got into the mindset of jealousy, the fear of not being the one on top anymore, not being the preferred one. She [Rashmi] wants to be the special one.” Ten years later, Pinto's predilection towards Rashmi and the urge to do something “wild” and “transformational” remained. In Love Sonia, she is almost unrecognisable—her teeth stained yellow to simulate years of beedi smoking; wearing spandex floral short shorts, a blue crop top and a purple sash tied around her hip (Pinto chose the costume herself). The film was particularly timely, says Pinto, considering the climate post-#MeToo. “There has to be accountability whether it's [the sex trafficking industry] or the #MeToo movement. People think they can do whatever they want because, guess what? They can,” she says with frustration, referencing the sexual assault allegation waged by Stanford professor Christine Blasey Ford against the ultimately successful Supreme Court nominee Judge Brett Kavanaugh in September 2018. “There was a strong enough testimonial from Dr Ford, but it still did not stop someone from holding a very powerful position on the Supreme Court. At the end of the day, it's this mindset that refuses to change.” “I feel the sense of unity and strength in numbers is so key,” she continues. “The #MeToo movement got a little angry at one point, but I don't have a problem with anger. There is nothing wrong with expressing anger, it's healthy.” So, what makes Pinto angry? “It's infuriating when girls are not believed. There will always be certain races in this world who will be believed less [than others],” she adds.“They [casting agents, producers and the other cogs that make the wheels of Hollywood turn] will never say something to your face. When you're smart enough, you understand what they mean when they say, ‘Oh you didn't get the part because you were too young,' then they cast someone waaaay younger,” she says. “I also don't spend too much energy blaming or feeling sorry for myself that the colour of my skin might have been the deciding factor in getting a certain role. It's beneath me, I don't want to talk about it and make it real. I want to go out there and get what I deserve. And that has never been taken away from me.” A turning point came after reading the script for Guerilla (her involvement was announced in 2016, and the first episode aired in April 2017) on a flight to Miami. Inspired by the British Black Panther movement and set in the politically charged London of the 1970s, the mini-series was written and directed by John Ridley and co-starred Idris Elba. Pinto auditioned for over two months before landing the part of Jas Mitra. “Rather than being in the biggest blockbuster movie that wins all the Oscars, it is more important to me to tell the right stories.” Next up for Pinto is Only, a post-apocalyptic love story co-starring Leslie Odom Jr; and another hotly anticipated project with 12 Years A Slave screenwriter John Ridley called Needle in a Timestack, alongside Orlando Bloom. The latter is slated to premiere at the South by Southwest film festival in Austin, Texas in March, which couldn't be more convenient as Pinto announces that she and Tran are going to start splitting their time between Los Angeles and a home they recently acquired in Austin. Tran grew up in Dallas, but spent his twenties in Austin and it's where he made his “friend family”. The move will be yet another chance for Pinto to reinvent herself, she jokes, “I'll be a brisket-making mama.” And you almost believe her.
