column1: “I was the first martyr in fashion because I talked about race”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion When Pyer Moss founder Kerby Jean-Raymond made the catwalk a platform for political activism four years ago, it nearly cost him his label and his sanity. But now his brand of socially conscious fashion is paying dividends. Vogue meets the designer in his Manhattan studio In 2015, Pyer Moss founder Kerby Jean-Raymond made a decision that almost destroyed his fledgling fashion label. In the wake of the death of two black men, Eric Garner and Michael Brown, at the hands of American law enforcement officers, thousands were marching on New York to protest against police racism and brutality. Jean-Raymond, who founded his brand in 2013 after stints working with Kay Unger and Marchesa, felt compelled to respond. So, with next to zero budget, he produced a short film addressing the ongoing crisis and screened it before his spring/summer 2016 show at New York Fashion Week. Washington Post critic Robin Givhan, who appeared as an interview subject in the film, wrote an article about the project, propelling the little-known Pyer Moss (pronounced Pierre Moss) into the spotlight. But the immediate, material impact on Jean-Raymond's label was far from positive. His show venue pulled out. A European stockist dropped his line. And that was only the beginning. “Within 36 hours, six of my biggest accounts dropped me,” he remembers. “The remaining ones were sub-$20,000 season accounts—not enough to keep our lights on. So I'm at this point where I'm about to lose my company, I've pissed off investors and I'm getting death threats from white supremacist groups.” The 12-minute film was built from a series of interviews with prominent black Americans, including Usher and the artist Kehinde Wiley, addressing the issue of racism in policing. It also featured conversations with family members of black men who had been killed by police officers, including Garner's daughter, Emerald. The clothes, his first foray into womenswear, were deafeningly quiet—casual tailoring, biker jackets, crisp fencing shirts, kimono-style coats and tracksuits in black, white, olive and grey; spray-painted live by the graffiti artist Gregory Siff and treated with a simulated blood-spatter effect, as though not to distract from what had preceded it. Until this point, Jean-Raymond had largely refrained from political statements because he was “scared of the space”, ie, the fashion industry. “It was very Anglo, elitist, prejudiced,” he explains when Vogue Business meets him in his compact but meticulously organised studio in midtown Manhattan. “I didn't feel like there was a place for me in fashion, so I never spoke up.” Now Jean-Raymond was speaking up, and he was being admonished for it. “I was the first martyr in fashion because I talked about race,” he says. On top of these struggles, he also became embroiled in a protracted legal battle. In early 2016, his investors wanted to pull out of the business and served Jean-Raymond with a lawsuit that accused him of a litany of transgressions including trademark infringement and unfair competition. Under the shadow of these new legal proceedings, which dragged on into 2017, Jean-Raymond became depressed. He had panic and anxiety attacks. Worst of all, he now had to deal with all of this in public. “People were recognising me now on the train—I was broke and famous, and it was really scary.” Just when Jean-Raymond was about to walk away from it all, he received a call from Erykah Badu—a fan of the label—encouraging him to persevere. “Kerby is putting an important message out there,” the multi Grammy Award-winning artist told Vogue via a telephone call. “It doesn't matter whether his clothes make you feel happy, angry, guilty or sad—whether you agree with what he's saying or not—he is creating a movement beyond the world of fashion.” Using money from personal orders (which included professional basketball players Dwyane Wade, Carmelo Anthony and Amar'e Stoudemire), he set a date for another show. Staged in February 2016, the collection addressed the weighty theme of mental health. Garments were printed with darkly satirical statements and emotive quotes like, “You don't have any friends in LA” and “My demons won today I'm sorry”. The latter was the final Facebook post of Black Lives Matter activist MarShawn McCarrel, who'd committed suicide less than 10 days before. Social commentary on the catwalk became Jean-Raymond's signature. His Spring/Summer 2017 show made a touchpoint of money, linking white-collar criminals like Bernie Madoff to his own legal drama. Autumn/winter 2018 took inspiration from 19th-century African-American cowboys, and for his spring/summer 2019 show last September Jean-Raymond enlisted artist Derrick Adams to create 10 new works to be incorporated into the designs, presented entirely on men and women of colour. The show opened with a couture-quality dress, embellished with thousands of tiny caviar beads which came together to depict a black man tenderly cradling a baby. “[The collection] focuses on the black family. What does it mean to be black? What does black normalcy look like? What does black mundane life look like?” he explains. “When black people are spoken about in the media it's always in a really sensationalised way. Either you're really extraordinary or you're really bad and terrible—either way, you're a statistic. I wanted to fill in the blanks.” The show was warmly received and widely regarded as one of the highlights of New York Fashion Week. American Vogue fashion director Virginia Smith called it the “most memorable, goosebumps-inducing moment of the season”, while The Cut's Cathy Horyn wrote that “Jean-Raymond's gift is for responding to things right in front of him, and then making simple, wearable clothes with a spark of wit.” Two months later, Jean-Raymond won the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund for emerging American design talent. CFDA CEO Steven Kolb tells Vogue that Pyer Moss stood out for the clarity of its vision and Jean-Raymond's consistency in conveying a strong message. The label received recognition in the form of celebrity fans, too. Michelle Obama wore a suit from his AW18 collection in an appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. From a critical perspective, Pyer Moss had reached new heights. But critical acclaim does not necessarily equal commercial stability. As recently as the autumn/winter 2017 collection, Pyer Moss was still facing closure, so its founder sought a solution in the form of a corporate patron, striking an agreement with Reebok that offered Jean-Raymond a multi-year deal with complete creative control. Jean-Raymond's experience in the wake of his SS16 show is a case study in the dangers a small business faces when it becomes explicitly politically engaged. For a young, upscale fashion brand that drives neither high production nor sales volumes, margins are thin at the best of times. Any unexpected challenges can be cataclysmic. For Pyer Moss, they nearly meant closure. The political climate has changed significantly, though, in the years since Jean-Raymond's pivotal SS16 show. Brands are aligning more closely with their customers' social and political views—often with financial benefits. Nike's campaign with athlete and activist Colin Kaepernick added $6 billion to its market cap. Reebok's decision to embrace Pyer Moss as a collaborator also speaks to this shift. The Reebok money has enabled the designer to buy out his former partners and pay off his debts. And with $400,000 in prize money from the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund, Jean-Raymond is now focussed on building a sustainable business and will skip New York Fashion Week this February. “I've got to be realistic—our cachet is still growing, there's a lot of people who know the brand now, but how many of them are true customers?” he says. “If I'm going to expand the business, it has to be because the demand has exceeded the supply—it's not there yet.” First published on Voguebusiness.com Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Denim jumpsuits: The trend that won’t go away
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Gwen Stefani to Bella Hadid and Kendall Jenner, the denim jumpsuit is loved by celebrities and fashion insiders alike. Vogue rounds up some of the best, for the ultimate one-piece inspiration The denim jumpsuit epitomises effortless chic; a one-piece that you can simply throw on before leaving the house. So it's no surprise that it has become a staple on the street style scene, with stars including Gwen Stefani and Bella Hadid championing the trend over the years. In fact, the jumpsuit's roots lie far from fashion world. First created by Florentine artist and designer Thayat in 1919, it was functional style created with skydivers and parachuters in mind. Denim overalls became increasingly popular as a durable garment for workers during the first half of the 20th century, including the women manning the factories during World War I and II. Recall the WWII ‘We Can Do It!' poster of Rosie the Riveter with her headscarf, flexed bicep and rolled-up-sleeve jumpsuit? Since then, the denim one-piece has been reimagined on the catwalk by the likes of Celine, Louis Vuitton and Christian Dior, ranging from laid-back utility pieces to more fitted Seventies-inspired styles. On the streets, A-listers and fashion insiders alike regularly step out in the wardrobe staple, with Ganni's AW18 pink version being a recent favourite. Here, Vogue rounds up some of the best denim jumpsuits, as seen on the stars, both A-list and street style, over the years. column1: Exclusive: Isha Ambani Piramal on work, legacy and life after marriage
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion She’s born to privilege with a silver-spooned childhood and a fabled last name. But this modern-day heiress is determined to create her own legacy. Girl-to-watch Isha Ambani Piramal talks to Vogue India about work, life and the future, and why, for her, India is at the heart of it all A modern-day heiress, it is easy to judge her, assume you know her and label her without ever meeting her. As the daughter of business mogul Mukesh Ambani, she must be wellborn, entitled, maybe even a bit of a brat who is far removed from reality. But the truth couldn't be further, as I find out when I meet Isha Ambani Piramal, director, Reliance Retail and Reliance JIO Infocomm Limited, in the most natural of her habitats—her workplace. As expected of a modern-day heiress, Isha is razor-sharp, ambitious and adept at talking business, but it's when you talk of anything else that she throws you off completely. You then meet a 27-year-old—part giggly, part naïve, she's disarmingly honest at all times. She's an extremely private person who is responsibly trying to navigate her life through the public lens. A delicious dichotomy of contrasts, she makes me want to know who the real Isha Ambani Piramal is. Over the next two hours we catch up on all the things that make her world go around. Excerpts from our conversation. Isha Ambani Piramal: The wedding went off beautifully. Like any other bride, I had my share of bridal jitters but getting married at home made it very special and I had the time of my life celebrating my most memorable moments with all the people I love. IAP: During the wedding my mom was CEO and I was chairperson. She and dad did all the hard work. Thankfully, we ended up liking the same things, so that made it a breeze. I didn't go to a single wedding meeting. I was never someone who dreamt of how my wedding would be, yet it was wonderful in more ways than I can imagine. It was a very emotional affair for everyone in my family. I was emotional too but everyone around me would cry all the time. I only cried at my bidaai because I felt some peer pressure as everyone else was crying, especially my parents. IAP: The surprising truth is that though my parents were exceptionally busy, they were really hands-on. I was born in 1991, right after Liberalisation, which was a real inflection point for the Indian economy—it was the first time that Indian companies could dream of global scale. I saw my father work very hard to chase that dream and build Reliance into the organisation that it is today. And though he worked long hours, he was always there when we needed him. At home, we were raised to have the same value system that our parents grew up with. They made sure we understood the value of money, hard work and humility. My parents had us after seven years of marriage—my twin Akash and I were IVF babies. When my mother finally had us she wanted to be a full-time mum initially. Later, she went back to work when we were five, but she was still a tiger mom. I remember, whenever mom and I had fights, we'd call dad to resolve the issue. My mom was way stricter. If we wanted to bunk school, dad would be like “It's no big deal” but mom would ensure we ate on time, studied hard and got our playtime as well. My grandparents (paternal and maternal) and my maasi played a huge role in bringing us up. IAP: Reliance Arts Foundation's aim and mission is to showcase the best of Indian art to the world and bring global art to India. Our collaborations with the Met and the Art Institute of Chicago have allowed us to take Indian art to an international audience. Eventually, we want to evolve into a full programme that strengthens the art platform in India. Spanning artists, young or old, modern or traditional, our aim is to ensure they thrive and flourish. My dream is to create a museum in Mumbai and bring shows from all over the world to India. I'm inspired by Dasha Zhukova's work with the Garage Museum in Moscow as well as the Mori Museum in Tokyo. Their curatorial skills creatively open up spaces for citizens to access, participate and engage in art. Art is a way of recording the history, culture and times. It's as important to preserve art of our times as it is to preserve art of the generations before us. IAP: I am very passionate about education. DAIS for me is more than a place of work, it's a place I love. I absolutely love kids. Even at Stanford, I taught two-year-olds. Being able to mould their thinking at an early age is what I found fulfilling. Schools have such a profound and lasting impact on young minds. I don't think any student ever forgets a good teacher, and that is why I see education as a huge opportunity to shape the next generation. It is one of the strongest agents of positive change. IAP: As much as I want to believe that women can have it all, I know that my mom gave it all up to raise us. But once we grew up, I also saw her balance work and home perfectly. Watching her play all these different roles—from full-time mom to businesswoman—I learnt how important each facet is in a woman's life and how one needs to define what “having it all” means during these different stages. I feel very passionately about gender equality and equal participation in the work force because growing up I was made to believe that I could do whatever my brothers could do, as well if not better. So as a working woman, I believe that companies must create an environment that fosters equal participation. At Jio, we have programmes for women that allow them to form communities and support each other. But what would really give me satisfaction is when I know that no matter which meeting I enter, engineering or design, there will be an equal number of women in the room. IAP: I can't stop at one! (laughs). I love his amazing sense of humour and his spirituality. IAP: He hates attending events, I enjoy them. I really enjoyed our wedding, but it was not exactly his idea of fun (laughs). He's more spiritual than I am. But we are also very similar. We are both very family-oriented, and we both love food. I remember in one of the speeches that my father gave at my wedding, he listed ten reasons why he liked Anand. It was hilarious, and dad concluded by saying that these are probably the same ten things that he would also use to describe himself. And it's true; in many ways Anand reminds me of my father. IAP: Last night, we had dinner, and then from 11pm to 3am Anand had a meeting in his office. So, I don't think his life has changed, and neither has mine. At this stage, work is a priority for both of us. And luckily, our parents understand that. Fortunately, the family I was born into and the family I married into have the same work ethic—every member of both families knows the importance of work. IAP: At work, I love wearing Indian clothes... cotton kurtas with block prints. I think it's one of the greatest things about being Indian—our clothes! I used to hate dressing up in business formals during my time in America. It was a nightmare to get into a blazer. It works well for slim bodies, but how do you wear a pencil skirt if you have a curvy body? Off work, I like wearing international and Indian designers—Valentino, Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla, Dolce & Gabbana, Manish Malhotra, Celine and Sabyasachi are some of my favourites. I love when a garment fits just right, and that's not easy. For my comfort picks, I switch between my salwar kameez, Lululemon sweats and cosy sweaters. IAP: The branding and marketing of Jio—I had the most fun doing it. When we launched in 2015, India ranked 155 on the mobile broadband consumption index, but today, post-Jio, India ranks number 1. IAP: I will feel proud if someone says: “She furthered her parents' legacy.” And of course, if Reliance can be one of the top 10 companies of the world, that would be a dream come true. column1: The new restaurants you must visit if you’re in Dubai this week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Along with being the most popular shopping hub in the world, Dubai is also known for the its vast culinary scene. But it can be difficult to meander through the options, specially if you can’t keep track of all the new entrants Dubai leaves you spoilt for choice when it comes to food, but that stands true for everything else the city offers too. Whether its international favourites like La Petite Maison and Zuma, or home-grown restaurants that have now become globally known dining destinations such as 3 Fils or La Serre, you could eat every meal at a different place in Dubai, and if you pick well, you would never be disappointed. Scroll ahead for our curated list of the new must-visit eateries in Dubai to find out where you need to go. Mediterranean Food has always been very popular in Dubai, but off late there has been a serious focus on Greek food. Characterised by grilled meats, simple yet scrumptious fish preparations and an array of fresh vegetables and salads, Greek cuisine is certainly having a moment in the Middle East. Opa stands out as it combines classic Hellenic techniques with a contemporary Mediterranean touch. Though it is located in the busy downtown Dubai hotel, The Fairmont, its interiors, featuring white-washed walls with blue accents, transport you instantly to island living. What's makes this place interesting is their approach to flatware—the breaking of plates is a well-known Greek tradition, that Opa actually embraces! What can be more stress busting than a great meal accompanied by the smashing of dishes and some Zorba dancing in the background? Address: 1st Level, Fairmont Dubai, Sheikh Zayed Road, Dubai; Tel: (04)3570557 If you have not visited Dubai Opera yet, you simply must—this modern day opera house is a true architectural landmark, and their programming is truly diverse and innovative. Now, a new restaurant has opened just a stone's throw away from the space that is all about soul food. Called Kizmet, a word that means destiny or fate in 14 different languages, this eatery offers a unique, creative menu encompassing dishes that are made to be shared, including smoked duck pizza with goat cheese, and chilli and the lamb shoulder with eggplant and tahini. Considering the comfort food-focused fare, it is definitely not the place to go to if you are watching those calories. End your meal with their fabulous Tres Lecher Cake—a traditional sponge cake with coconut foam and yuzu sorbet—which speaks to Kizmet's cooking philosophy: combining classic good food with new-age fusion techniques. The space comes complete with a co-working space and a library bar, so you can literally spend the whole day here. Address: Dubai Opera District, Dubai; Tel: (04)3388717 A trip to Dubai is incomplete without a good Lebanese meal—from fast food to fine dining, there is something for every occasion and budget when it comes to this cuisine. While the original Babel opened in Lebanon's Dbayeh, a coastal Mediterranean town that is known for its neighbourhood eateries, Dubai's Babel is located at La Mer, a new beachside development. A licensed restaurant specialising in seafood, it allows you to pick your own catch from the ice bar and offers a delicious mezze. The terrace is a perfect place for an intimate dinner or a leisurely lunch, and you can finish your dining experience with a shisha or one of their many desserts too. Address: S30, La Mer South, Jumeirah Beach, Jumeirah 1, Dubai; Tel: (04)4190220 This family-friendly restaurant was launched by one of the most celebrated chefs in this city—Izu Ani, who is known his flair with French food, and has previously worked at La Petite Maison and La Serre. The Nigerian British chef started this restaurant as a tribute to his wife, Carine, and you can tell every dish is cooked with love here. Located at the Emirates Golf Club, the space features a light, airy vibe due to its chic interiors and terrace setting (with a great view!), and has a bistro-style approach to its food. They are known to serve the best burrata in town, their spice lamb comes saddled with parsnip puree to indulge your tastebuds, and their desserts are the sorts that'll make it hard for you to pick just one. column1: Justin Bieber just launched his clothing line Drew House
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The millennial kid’s answer to casual wear, with a Bieber twist Justin Bieber has already had a busy 2019 and January isn't even over. Bieber has been hard at work planning his wedding to Hailey Bieber (née Baldwin), though when the nuptials actually take place is cause for great debate, especially considering the pair have moved the rumoured date a handful of times. Now though, Bieber has launched his clothing line, Drew House, the millennial kid's answer to casual wear, with a Bieber twist. “Drew house is a place where you can be yourself. blah blah blah blahsdbksjdfhl wear like you don't care. come chill. k. bye,” the brand attests on its website, alongside moody pictures of 20-somethings in the brand's pieces. So what is the Drew House aesthetic? Think skater boy corduroy, pops of yellow, red and mustard sitting alongside what will no doubt become the brand's main signifier, a yellow smiley face whose smile has been replaced by the word Drew. Why Drew? No, Bieber doesn't have an affinity for Drew Barrymore but instead the singer has decided to trademark his middle name. According to Fashionista, Bieber trademarked “Drew,” “The House of Drew” and “La Maison Drew”, in early 2018. The Biebers have of course already been spotted out and about in Drew House, with the couple donning sweat shirts and slippers by the brand. Justin Bieber even showed off a range of pricey looking Drew House necklaces that seem to be laced with diamonds. Drew House does ship its ethically-made-in-the-USA wares to Australia and even goes so far as to describe to potential buyers where and when the clothes would be suitable to wear. For example, the Chaz Corduroy Shorts are “kinda like the chaz pants, but ya know...shorter. great for sitting in bean bag chairs and couches.” Or there's the Chaz Corduroy Pants which are “perfect for doing the kinds of things you'd normally do while wearing pants.” Aside from these helpful styling tips, Drew House also bestows upon its customer weird facts while the peruse certain items, highlights include: “There is an official wizard of new Zealand”, “Polar bears can eat as many as 86 penguins in a single sitting”, “7% of American adults believe that chocolate milk comes from brown cows” and “you can't hum while holding your nose closed.” Why are these facts included? No one knows but it's safe to say it's Justin Bieber's world and we're just along for the ride. column1: Tabu, Karan Johar walk for Gaurav Gupta’s showcase at Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The opening show for Lakmé Fashion Week saw Gaurav Gupta’s latest couture collection titled ‘The (Un)folding’ at The Royal Opera House, Mumbai A venue like The Royal Opera House demands a performance, and Gaurav Gupta delivered on the theatrics with his opening show for this season of Lakmé Fashion Week. Titled ‘The (Un)folding', the presentation saw Gupta's mix of cocktail couture, lehenga gown hybrids and edgy clubwear in his signature sculpted silhouettes. The Central Saint Martins grad, who once spelt his label backwards, marks 15 years in the industry this year. Over time, Gupta's aesthetics have evolved to a sweet spot where commercial viability and drama sing in sweet harmony, but Gupta likes to maintain his crazy, retain the joy and exuberance of unapologetically enjoying good fashion. As the lights dimmed and the curtains parted, poet Navkirat Sodhi stood covered in yards of fabric and was slowly hoisted upwards until she was suspended in air in what seemed like the tallest dress of all. Images of doves were projected on her dress, which also covered a part of the curving staircase behind her. Setting the theatrical tone of the evening, Sodhi recited live verse, talking about “killing pain with couture”, capturing the essence of Gupta's creative spirit. Tabu opened the show in a floral embellished gown and was followed by in models structured couture, some glimmering in silks and embellishments, others highlighting the beauty of chikankari and brocade. The lineup of pale blues, whites, greys and blacks also saw a mix of menswear. Karan Johar closed the show for the designer in an extravagantly embellished red jacket covered in studs and beading. Gupta is a connoisseur of lines; he owns them in a manner no contemporary of his can. From the curving twists of the models updos, to the boned ruffles on gowns, even the way Sodhi's dress intersected the curving staircase, Gupta draws dizzying maps that invite you to be a part of his couture fantasy. He might be selling cocktail wear, but he also sells dreams of another world—defiant and free of constraints, always entertaining. column1: Alia Bhatt’s complete style transformation
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Student Of The Year to Gully Boy, Alia Bhatt’s career has only grown from strength to strength. And her wardrobe is clearly not falling behind either To say that Alia Bhatt grew up in Bollywood not be an understatement. The daughter of actor/producer Soni Razdan and filmmaker Mahesh Bhatt was first seen in as a child actor in Sangharsh (1999). But it was her big Bollywood debut in Student Of The Year that truly put Bhatt on the map. From ingénue to one of best actors in the industry, the star's rise in the last few years has been meteoric. Much like her evolving craft, Bhatt's wardrobe has changed since she first appeared in public eye. Alia Bhatt starred alongside Sidharth Malhotra and Varun Dhawan in Karan Johar's coming-of-age film Student of the Year (2012), after which she's taken on a variety of challenging roles in films like Highway (2014), Udta Punjab (2016) and Dear Zindagi (2016). But, that's not to say that she doesn't opt for movies with a more mainstream appeal—her filmography includes projects like 2 States (2014), Humpty Sharma Ki Dulhania (2014), Shaandaar (2015) and Kapoor & Sons (2016). In recent times, the star gave a laudable performance in Raazi (2018), and is currently working on her upcoming features, namely Brahmāstra (2019), Kalank (2019) and Gully Boy (2019). 2013 saw Bhatt sport young styles, with maxis, palazzos and neon blazers ruling her wardrobe during the promotional runs of her first film. Among her biggest style moments that year were wearing Dior at the Vogue Beauty Awards, and donning a Manish Malhotra lehenga at the Filmfare Awards. The actor's style took a turn upwards in the coming year: the lines got cleaner, the accessories were more muted. Her minimalist look at the launch of Miss Vogue in 2015 had her looking more grown-up than ever before. In 2016, Bhatt was partial to feminine dresses, whether she was out promoting films or attending red carpet events. Pussy bow details, bold stripes or florals, dresses were Bhatt's style staple for the year. With the rise in popularity of athleisure, coupled with Bhatt's enthusiasm for a healthy lifestyle, led to the star being spotted often in sports luxe in early 2017. She is clearly partial to denim, and is often seen in a fitted, ripped pair of jeans out in the city. Over the last few months, Bhatt has become even more refined with her style. Between Indian ethnic wear, red carpet couture and airport looks featuring bum bags, she has certainly come a long way. While Bhatt's sense of style veers towards the classic, it is not without a willingness to experiment. In fact, from safe red-carpet choices to slouchy, edgy separates, Alia Bhatt's sartorial sensibilities have only become more confident with time. Always erring on the side of caution, the star is not one to stray too far from her personal style for the sake of fashion either. Her go-to designer labels include Manish Malhotra, Prabal Gurung, Masaba and Raw Mango. Scroll through our gallery to take a closer look at Alia Bhatt's complete style evolution. column1: Condé Nast International launches Vogue Business
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All you need to know about the new title Introducing Vogue Business, a new digital-only B2B title offering analysis of the fashion, beauty and luxury industries. Rooted in facts and data, the Condé Nast International project—which began as a newsletter—will look at trends; the impact of broader global market dynamics, from climate change to geopolitics; cultural patterns and shifts that impact retail and vice versa; and how technological and scientific advancements shape the ways products are produced, marketed and sold. “In a consolidating media landscape, the launch of a new global title is a rare thing,” says Wolfgang Blau, president of Condé Nast International. “No one else in the world employs more fashion journalists in more places than we do. Our global network of journalists, digital editors and researchers are immersed in the relevant trends on all inhabited continents, giving the team of Vogue Business access to an unparalleled depth of knowledge, from local design trends to changes in manufacturing, training, technology and distribution.” Edited by Lauren Indvik, who will lead an independent editorial team in London, Vogue Business will operate as a wholly separate entity to Vogue, but tap into Condé Nast International's network of brands, including Vogue, GQ, Glamour and Wired, as well as drawing on insights from 29 markets in order to fill the gap in the market for industry decision-makers. “We take a new global, visual and data-driven approach to journalism,” adds Indvik. “Our journalism is designed for maximum impact and accessibility, making it easy to understand key ideas at a glance, and to enable fashion leaders to make the decisions that will grow and future-proof their businesses and careers.” Voguebusiness.com Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The Ministry of Textiles’ latest move aims to boost the handloom sector
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Government of India has signed MOUs with renowned textile companies to further the use of handlooms in production Last evening marked a huge victory for India's handloom industry—leading retail giants came together to join hands with the Government of India to boost the development of the handloom sector. This major commitment will require the private sector to directly source from handloom clusters, thereby improving the economic opportunities for weavers and artisans as well as ensuring that age-old crafts don't die. Textile companies Arvind True Blue Limited, Raymond Ltd, Welspun India Limited, Titan Co Ltd and Reliance Retail Limited signed agreements with the Office of Development Commissioner (Handlooms), Ministry of Textiles and textile companies, Weavers' Service Centres to work with textile clusters identified by the Government to ensure a sustainable development of the handloom sector. The announcement was made by Smriti Zubin Irani, Minister of Textiles, and the legendary cricketer Sachin Tendulkar yesterday at the Artisan Speak event organised by the Ministry of Textiles, in partnership with IMG Reliance. Set against the backdrop of the historic Elephanta Caves, India's leading fashion designers got together to showcase the prowess of Indian textiles—Rahul Mishra and Meera Muzaffar Ali put the spotlight on chikankari; Payal Khandwala took to Benarasi brocades; Gaurang incorporated Kanjeevaram silks; Karisma Shahani Khan used Kota doria/Chanderi textiles; Padmaja utilised Maheshwari textiles; Abraham & Thakore showed hand-block prints on handloom cotton among others. The high point of these textiles was the fact that they were all drawn from various regions of India. And to ensure that this legacy is preserved, the Government has patented exclusive crafts with GI (Geographical Indication) with around 168 handlooms and handicraft products registered under it. This collaboration with the private sector will thus encourage the use of such textiles while strengthening the supply chain capacity of grassroot stakeholders. column1: New designer stores in South Mumbai perfect for a weekend shopping spree
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion While designer Kunal Rawal has opened a second outpost in the city, Nisha Mehta launched her first-ever flagship store. Here, we list out the four new store openings in South Mumbai that you need to know about Whether you're searching for a designer ensemble to wear to your best friend's wedding or a luxurious decor to match your home's aesthetic, these four new stores will be your one-stop shop for everything fashion. But that's not the best part—these four designer outposts are all located in South Mumbai, making your shopping spree devoid of any major traffic delays. (If you drive a car in Mumbai, you know how important this is.) From Kunal Rawal's lavish outpost in Kala Ghoda to Ogaan's multi-designer offering in the same location, Vogue brings you the four new stores that deserve to be on your must-visit list. Muse, a luxury gifting store, is architect and designer Nisha Mehta's first flagship store in South Mumbai's Kemps Corner. “Muse is a mid-century modern space that is styled in a stark monochromatic look with colour accents, a signature to my architectural roots,” says Mehta. The decor takes after the 1940s heritage building in which the store is located—think big stone arched windows, ebony walls, mirrors. There are also some European influences, like the cobalt blue door nestled in a white archway, that takes inspiration from the buildings of Santorini, Greece. “We have four different collections in fine jewellery, and a collection of home products that feature everything from puja sets to dining accessories,” adds Mehta. Address: Muse, 7/11 Mohammedbhoy Mansion, next to Crossword Bookstore, Kemps Corner, Mumbai After a spacious store in Juhu, designer Kunal Rawal has now expanded his territory to the other side of Mumbai with a flagship store at Kala Ghoda's iconic Rhythm House. Designed by architect Rooshad Shroff—who also designed Sonam Kapoor Ahuja's first home in London—the space reflects Rawal's love for vintage and modern design. Elements like grey walls, teakwood flooring, modern brass fittings, high ceilings, motorised racks, metal tables with armour line detailing and French knots can be seen throughout the store. Getting married this year? Drop by the Kala Ghoda store with your fiancé to check out Rawal's new signature collection of festive wear. Address: 59, 1st Floor, National Indian, Building 2 Of Kalaghoda Building, Dr, VB Gandhi Marg, Fort, Mumbai One of the country's oldest multi-designer fashion boutiques, Ogaan recently opened doors to a new flagship store in Kala Ghoda, Mumbai. Spread over two floors, the space houses some of country's leading designers including Péro, Eká, Bodice, Dhruv Kapoor, Payal Khandwala, Shivan & Narresh and others, as well as accessories from Misho and Deepa Gurnani. Address: 6/8, Navbharat House Military Square Lane Burjorji, S Bharucha Marg, Kala Ghoda, Fort, Mumbai Singer-turned-entrepreneur, Kanika Kapoor, has launched her very own fashion label titled House of Chikankari in Fort, Mumbai. The brand aims to create the best chikankari products and, in addition to their elegant anarkalis and kurtas, offers a custom-made service to cater to your sartorial needs. “Some traditions are inherited and some are created by chance. 25 years ago, when my mother started her charity to support the local women's craft in making chikankari, she unknowingly started a tradition that I am now hoping to take on—a tradition to uplift, illuminate and encourage the less fortunate women from my hometown, Lucknow,” says Kanika Kapoor. column1: Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019: What we’re looking forward to
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Anita Dongre’s sustainable collection created using Tencel fibres to Shantanu & Nikhil’s couture collection for the finale, this is your ultimate guide to navigating this edition of Lakmé Fashion Week If there's one element of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 that we're excited about, it's the innumerable collaborations that are taking place with a focus on sustainability and handloom—Anita Dongre has combined forces with Tencel; Rohit Bal will showcase a collection made by the Kashmiri women working at Usha Silai; Reebok will launch a new menswear line with Ruchika Sachdeva's Bodice; and The Woolmark Company joins hands with Aneeth Arora's Péro. A few weeks ago, Vogue also announced the eight designers who had been shortlisted for the Circular Design Challenge, India's first sustainability award. On the second day of fashion week, which is known as sustainable fashion day, the winner shall be announced. Topping it all off is Shantanu and Nikhil Mehra's couture collection, to be showcased at the finale. Scroll ahead for everything we're looking forward to from Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019. Kicking off the five-day spectacle is designer Gaurav Gupta, who will be presenting ‘The (Un)folding' at Mumbai's iconic The Royal Opera House today. Handwoven fabrics like Benarasi brocades take centre stage through fluid-structural constructed dresses, pantsuits, sari gowns and evening wear in pastel shades (including a festive yellow that makes its debut). Along with zardozi, 3D flowers in organza and georgette, the designer will also be making use of chikankari embroidery for the first time. In a showcase that celebrates the fusion of fashion and art, Bobo Calcutta by Ayushman Mitra will present a minimal collection in monochrome tones. Titled ‘Blackout/Whitewash', Mitra says that the line is an artistic representation of suppression and the forceful silencing of creative voices who use art as a tool of socio-political protest. Expect voluminous garments with the label's signature prints, hand embroideries and embellishments on digital prints, developed from Bobo's paintings that depict scenes of contemporary revolutions. The designer returns to Lakmé Fashion Week after four years with a new label—Varun Bahl Prêt. Here, you will find easy, ready-to-wear separates like kurtas, dresses, cardigans, culottes and trousers that retain the designer's signature floral aesthetic—in fact, the entire collection has been created through one simple sketch of a five-petal flower. The colours? A fully pastel palette, of course. The Delhi-based designer duo is back at Lakmé Fashion Week, this time with 'The Art of Latte', a resort 2019 collection designed for the free-spirited woman who is also an avid traveller. With an intent to glamourise your holiday wardrobe, the range focuses on powerful floral prints and vibrant solids in shades of reds, pinks, nudes and browns. Fabrics like chiffon, crepe de chine, silk taffeta, organza and micro crepe lend a luxurious feel to their high-low dresses, and other ensembles featuring floor-sweeping trains, breezy wrap-arounds and more. Rohit Bal's summer/resort 2019 line is all about championing sustainability and empowering women. The designer has joined hands with sustainable fashion label Usha Silai to birth ‘Guldastah', a collection that has been exquisitely embroidered by female Kashmiri artisans. Fabrics like organic fabrics, cotton silk blends, Chanderi, silk organza, silk and velvet come decorated with techniques like thread embroidery, gold wire and zardozi, in floral motifs reminiscent of Kashmir. All profits earned from these garments will be given back to these women artisans to help empower them financially. The renowned Australian wool company has joined forces with Aneeth Arora's Péro for the very first time to showcase a handwoven collection made with Merino wool. “The Woolmark Company approached us for this collaboration,” says Arora. “We worked closely with Bhuttico—one of the oldest co-operative weaving society in Kullu—to revive traditional geometric patterns of pattu (shawls draped by women) in monochrome colours with tone-on-tone textures in blue, khaki and off-white,” adds Arora, who incorporates dresses as well as jackets with pattus in this collection. For her summer/resort 2019 collection, designer Anita Dongre has collaborated with Tencel to create ‘A Summer Reverie'—a line of lightweight lehengas, maxi dresses, jumpsuits, crop tops and skirts in fresh floral colours of yellow, apricot, sea foam, blue, pink and blush. The specialty of these pieces is that the Tencel fibres are hand spun along with silk and satin, and then woven into fine blends. [#image: /photos/5ce41772b80311278a8f53c9]||| ||| Image: Dhiraj Singh for UNDP India Antar-Agni by Ujjawal Dubey has associated with Raymond for his summer/resort 2019 show ‘Balance', to create a capsule collection that promotes sustainable development from northeast India. Each garment has been created by artisans in Assam, who have used weaving techniques to work with fibres like cotton, eri, tussar and muga silk in neutral colours of ivory and grey with accents of green and citrine. In a world that's ruled by consumerism and drowning in information, Kanika Goyal's summer/resort 2019 collection will make you sit up and take notice. Whether it's the use of bold colours or iridescent hues, unexpected pairings with sheer overlays and loud prints, or the overall maximal aesthetic, Goyal's ‘Plastic Fantastic' line aims to break the vicious cycle of this consumerist culture through outfits that promote self-love, emotional well-being and kindness. In her summer/resort 2019 collection ‘Qo'shilish', Payal Singhal explores the journey of Indian art and its cultural influences to create a renaissance-meets-Mughal-inspired look, which incorporates ancient artistry techniques. The designer also introduces new silhouettes like the Nizami sharara, short lean kurtas, contemporary saris and renaissance tops in her signature fabrics of crepe, velvet, silk, organza, brocade, tissue and georgette. Taking inspiration from the culture and diversity of the Sa Pa tribes of Vietnam, Anavila Misra puts together an entirely handwoven and handcrafted collection that pays homage to the craft techniques practiced by the local women. Techniques like pleating, cording, embroidery and hand batik have been incorporated on natural yarns such as cotton, linen and silk. However, what makes this collection unique is the use of 100 per cent natural colours and dyes, which Misra worked closely on with clusters in West Bengal, Bhuj in India and Sa Pa in Vietnam. Rina Singh's Eka will showcase their ‘Post cards from summer' collection, which is synonymous of all things summer.  The fabrics see the use of sheer and lace, while the colour palette is dedicated to pastels. The range features easy-breezy blouses, relaxed dresses, delicate layers and fragile under-layers, all reminiscent of a dreamy summer afternoon. The best part is their collaboration with Lupin Life's Corcal, which aims to pay homage to the real women of India who will be walking the runway for Eka—each one having been chosen through an online audition. Bringing sustainability to gym wear is designer Narendra Kumar's collaboration with Alcis Sports by Roshan Baid. The collection is entirely made out of recycled polyester sourced from PET bottles, and incorporates latest technologies like dry-tech, anti-odour and anti-static. The collection features T-shirts, joggers, bombers, blazers, layered jackets and leggings in prints inspired by Indian textiles and Indian art. This time round, designers Shivan & Narresh take inspiration from two tribal art forms of two different states—Bengal's Kalighat Pattachitra art and Andhra Pradhesh's Tholu Bommalata leather puppetry, which are juxtaposed together in the ‘Patu Series'. The range introduces six new prints—Panthera, Sunderbans, Iconorosh, Fagun, Urvi and Deccan—that are set against colours like indigo, slate and wheat, among others, making the outfits an ideal match for a holiday or a destination wedding. Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice is all set to launch her menswear collection, Bodice Man, at this edition of Lakmé Fashion Week. Sachdeva carries forward her signature sleek lines and attention to detail in the menswear range including both corporate suits and streetwear styles. The summer/resort 2019 collection will also show her usual womenswear line, crafted using India's indigenous textiles and artisanal techniques. The Jodhpur-based designer's collection for Lakmé Fashion Week 2019 celebrates the reinvented bandhgala, both for men and women. Designed in silk and natural yarn, Raghavendra Rathore's collection uses intricate embroideries on a colour palette of dark neutral tones like blue, black, ivory and grey. While the womenswear range of bandhgalas reflects muted opulence, the menswear collection incorporates bolder and modern masculine lines. For their Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 collection, Bhavana Pandey, Dolly Sidhwani and Nandita Mahtani of Love Gen take inspiration from Ranveer Singh and Alia Bhatt's upcoming feature, Gully Boy and puts together ‘Gully Gen'—a collection that's an ode to hip-hop and its influences on street culture. Expect the Gully Boy cast, complete with rappers, to walk the runway clad in menswear jackets, hoodies and T-shirts adorned with statement slogans from the film. Closing Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2019 is designer duo Shantanu and Nikhil Mehra, whose couture collection ‘Recruit' highlights the evolution of the millennial Indian woman. Prepare yourselves for avant-garde silhouettes with structured shoulders and exaggerated drapes in vibrant shades of black, gold and red, with the accessories seeing a mix of medallions, silk tassels and gold embroidery. column1: You will want to buy everything from this new luxury kids wear label
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The luxury baby and kids wear line is a collaboration between designer Elodie Le Derf, Antonia Achache and Jérémie Sabbagh of Suzette and Kitchen Garden It was when French designer Elodie Le Derf, who has been living in Mumbai since 2013, found herself pregnant that she came face to face with the city's dearth of luxury kids wear. “I found myself getting frustrated with the options on offer, and my local and expat friends echoed similar sentiments. The designer in me identified a business opportunity, and three years later, we are ready to open doors to the first Born store,” she explains, talking about the launch of her new kids label in collaboration with Antonia Achache and Jérémie Sabbagh from Suzette and Kitchen Garden. Born is a high-end baby and kids wear label (for new borns to age eight) that boasts an unmistakable French style, but is made in India from start to finish. Le Derf, an erstwhile bridal couture designer, brings her Parisian sensibilities to the creations (which are equal parts comfortable and romantic) while highlighting her love for Indian hand embroidery. “The first impression is inherently French because of the colours and finishing, but the brand narrates my love story with India. I have worked with the same craftsmen I have been associated with for 15 years (for my bridal wear) for Born as well.” Le Derf's modern approach to Indian handcrafts gives her designs their distinctive flair—she has played with khadi and designed patterns using block prints. The maiden collection, ‘India Song', is composed of delicate embroideries and romantic floral prints inspired by the flower fields of Kashmir, Mughal art and Indian fauna on light cotton voile and soft linens. Choose from baby essentials, rompers, bodysuits, T-shirts, bottoms and dresses in soft pastel tones. “We also plan to introduce matching mother-daughter outfits, textiles and blankets in a few months,” adds the designer. Le Derf has partnered with friends Achache and Sabbagh to bring the Born universe to life. The couple not only encouraged the designer to launch her label, but also invested in the venture, with Achache assuming the role of interior designer too. “I have worked on the interiors of our restaurants, and came on board to translate Elodie's vision into the store. We have recreated a typical Haussmannian French apartment in shades of nude, grey and celadon, localised with furniture and accessories sourced from vintage markets in Mumbai. The wallpapers feature prints from the collection. The store aesthetic combines all the elements of the brand manifesto, which are, Born wild and free, Born kind, Born Parisian and Born in India,” elaborates Achache. The flagship Born store in Bandra's Pali Hill neighbourhood is divided into two levels, and recreates a kid's playroom (with accoutrements like a blackboard, rocking horse, dollhouse and books) so that the children feel right at home, leaving their parents free to browse. “The Born experience is inclusive of not just the mothers but the kids as well. Even our launch shoot features our and our friends' children. We turned the shoot into one huge play date, and this is the very spirit that spills over to our collections as well,” concludes Le Derf. column1: The new red carpet style rules for 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From buzz cuts to tattoos and the rise of upscale specs, these are the nine reasons why red carpet dressing just got interesting In recent years, the red carpet has become a forum for protest as well as a space where new fashion and beauty trends are forged. With a rise in stars who don't want to be associated with the prevailing cultural conformity associated with ‘dressing up', there now aren't any red carpet fashion don'ts. Instead, the awards circuit has become an important space for Hollywood's leading women to do: to speak out and address issues that can no longer be silenced—be that challenging notions of female sexuality and self-acceptance or revealing their own journey. Here, Vogue explores the style rules (and tricks of the trade) fit for a generation of stars who are using red carpet appearances to create new conversations. [#image: /photos/5ce4164e4a30b32d4312b6a5]||| ||| Image: Getty In the wake of 2018's #MeToo movement, which saw many stars wearing head-to-toe black at awards shows in solidarity with women worldwide, 2019's red carpets are ablaze with colour to mark the dawn of a new era in Hollywood. Marigold, fuchsia and gleaming metallics are now just as likely to appear at the Oscars on February 24, as a classic burgundy, white or black. The time has come to put the naked dress on hold (who, after all can top the Swarovski-crystal-encrusted Adam Selman gown that Rihanna wore to the CFDA Fashion Awards in 2014?). Dramatic taffeta ball gowns that offer escapism from current political turbulence are reigning supreme, thanks to the heavenly red carpet coupling that is Lady Gaga and Valentino (her train had to be aided by two assistants on the Golden Globes 2019 red carpet). Look to intricate beading, fringing and feathers (we're fawning over Alexander McQueen and Miu Miu) to rouse drama without any big reveal. If it's okay for Oprah, Dakota Fanning and Meryl Streep to forgo contact lenses and make upscale specs a thing on the red carpet and podium, it's okay for us too. Colour coordination helps: Fanning matches her pastel dress to whisper-light acetate frames; while Oprah syncs emboldened cat-eye specs with an off-shoulder black gown. [#image: /photos/5ce4164e4a30b3ca1d12b69f]||| ||| Image: Getty When it comes to jewellery, big isn't always better. “Many women feel that they need to wear a big necklace in order to be glamorous,” Emily Blunt's red carpet stylist Jessica Paster explains over lunch in LA, her voice lowering to a whisper: “You can always tell if those aren't real diamonds.” The rule to remember? Subtle earrings never fail to elevate a dress—a delicate stud or drop pearl earring (the sort that Zoë Kravitz wears so well) paired with a strikingly bare décolletage will do the job without any of the fuss. [#image: /photos/5ce4164e4a30b30d4912b6a2]||| ||| Image: Rex Features While a dramatic red-carpet transformation scores points on social media (yes, we're thinking back to Gaga—again—at the Venice Film Festival wearing yet another pulse-racing pink-feathered Valentino couture gown) there's a lot to be said for the Hollywood stalwarts who stay true to their everyday selves and avoid the gown altogether. Take Judy Greer in an oversized tux (complete with bow tie), Jane Birkin in a relaxed suit or Gigi and Bella working low-key tailoring (sneakers included)—if you wouldn't be caught dead in ankle-grazing silk, it's time to define your own dress code. [#image: /photos/5ce4164e9cc0c00fa2f9b941]||| ||| Image: Getty The stories about A-list actresses being sewn into their dresses are real. This approach isn't for everyone (obviously), but there is a lesson to be learnt: Your best friend is and always should be your tailor. That simple black gown you wore four years ago (pre-break-up/pre-baby) is still just as good as the day you bought it, subject to a slight tweak or tuck in the hands of an expert. Look to Amandla Stenberg at the Critics' Choice Awards 2019 wearing this season's backless silhouette for fresh inspiration. Rather than panic buy for the big occasion, set aside a few weeks to go back through your wardrobe to pull classics that can be altered to meet a modern mood.   The big night is fast approaching and you're panicking about visible underwear/an unflattering neckline/finding the right footwear—shelve the stress, we've all been there. For the moments when simplicity feels powerful (or the confidence needed to push the fashion envelope fails you), there's always a long-sleeve body-skimming column gown—see Nicole Kidman at this year's Golden Globes ceremony. The additional perk? This silhouette can conceal an optional full-body Spanx catsuit. [#image: /photos/5ce4164e89be3601747ce4d9]||| ||| Image: Getty Once upon a time it was a red carpet faux pas to bare piercings or tattoos, let alone a shaven head. But a lot has changed since Angelina Jolie attended the Original Sin premiere in 2001, revealing her ‘Billy Bob' tattoo as part of a look considered risqué at the time. Today's starlets, just like Jolie, aren't about conforming. Which means that the red carpet buzz cuts proudly sported by Kate Hudson, Cara Delevingne and Charlize Theron, or nipple piercings (Kendall Jenner and Bella Hadid) are setting the new norm. [#image: /photos/5ce4164f89be3636427ce4db]||| ||| Image: Getty We'll let you into the secret that every Hollywood celebrity stylist bestows upon their A-list clients who opt for vertiginous heels on the red carpet. Stash a mini Haute Heels foot spray in your handbag and apply to the soles of your feet every two-to-four hours. Consider the tingle a sign that it's working. column1: Anita Dongre’s spring/summer 2019 showcase will use eco-friendly fabric
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Created in collaboration with Tencel, Anita Dongre’s latest collection not only doubles as a capsule closet for destination weddings, but also serves a fresh spin on conscious clothing If there's one thing veteran designer Anita Dongre has mastered, it's the makings of a memorable collection. Case in point: Dongre's latest line-up, A Summer Reverie. Created in collaboration with Tencel, the collection not only doubles as a capsule closet for destination weddings, but also serves a fresh spin on conscious clothing, quite literally. The airy, lightweight silhouettes in a happy palette of blush, sea foam and sunshine yellow were all created using Tencel's biodegradable fibres. As she gears up to unveil her spring/summer 2019 collection at Lakmé Fashion Week, Vogue sits down with the designer to talk about everything from the star silhouettes to the one myth about sustainable fashion she'd like to shelve. This is a ready-to-wear collection that features feminine and relaxed outfits, much like my personal style. It's colourful, but at the same time, very minimalistic. I've taken inspiration from nature, summer flowers in particular, and the show will be held at a beautiful venue where our aim is to re-create a summer garden—the perfect backdrop for the collection. You'll find light lehengas, maxi dresses, jumpsuits and crop tops with skirts, while the menswear line consists of kurtas and bundis with happy colourful prints. Delicate hues dominate the shade card made of yellow, apricot, sea foam, surf blue, onion pink and blush. There are also playful summer prints in green, marigold yellow, misty blue, champagne pink and lavender that perfectly embody exquisite flowers in all their bloom. The starting point of the collection was Tencel's cellulosic fibres, which come from renewable raw material and are manufactured using an environmentally responsible production process. Composed of natural material, these fibres are biodegradable and compostable, and can fully revert back to nature. These are used with silk to produce fine summer blends. When you love creating garments, new fabrics are like exciting adventures. The entire process of working with Tencel was exciting as we were breaking stereotypes by merging couture with sustainability. Many people are of the opinion that sustainable clothing can't be fashionable. That is not the case. The two go hand in hand. Sustainability is a way of life and fashion is a part of that. It's all about practices that respect the planet. The fashion industry is still young in India. We need to learn from the problems and issues the West is facing, like how to dispose garments, how to recycle them and how to produce responsibly. Sustainability is the need of the hour and India too has to learn, understand and make the necessary changes in how we produce and dispose on a war footing. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How modest dressing found its way into mainstream fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Style that was once perceived as old-fashioned or mousy has gained respect and understanding in mainstream fashion. Vogue explores the impact of modesty If the short length of a hemline is not a barometer by which to judge a person's character, then covering up should not equate to regressiveness either. If showing one's skin is a choice that needs to be respected, then the opposite of that stands equally true. 2017 was the year we saw more crop tops, miniskirts and even the first hint of the return of the low rise, but it also brought another trend to the forefront: modesty. Stemming from the sartorial needs of women from various religions and faiths—and even just preferences—modest fashion gained recognition in the narrative of contemporary fashion. Despite (often unjustly) being branded as transient, fashion is a reflection of society, and in the era of respecting individual choices, modest fashion has left the fringes of the lexicon of style and moved up, front and centre. One prominent sign of change was the acceptance of Halima Aden's hijab on the runway. The poster girl for modest style, Aden was a part the Yeezy Season 5 show. “Halima Aden stood out amongst a diverse group of her model peers in a long faux fur coat and her own hijab (in 20 years of watching runway shows, that was a first),” Nicole Phelps, director, Vogue Runway, recounted in her review of the presentation. In the same year, The Modist, a luxury e-commerce destination dedicated to progressive modest dressing, came into being. Abayas, hijabs, headscarves were no longer exotic or foreign, and accepted as part of personal style. International luxury retailers who have seen the rising opportunity in business have already started investing in this promising vertical too. Farfetch will be curating a selection of pieces from The Modist on its own portal, and Net-a-Porter has a selection of on-trend edit of clothes from luxury labels tagged under ‘modest' as well. Despite its origins as a way of dressing for women in Muslim countries, modest fashion has evolved into a global phenomenon now. Take for instance the work of Batsheva Hay, whose exaggerated conservative aesthetic has won critical approval with celebrities and fashion retailers. Hay, a follower of Orthodox Judaism, is dedicated to modernising elements of clothing that signify restraint and repression, and making them into something of an armour for those whose fashion choices are not just about following Instagram trends. Simply put, Hay is making modest fashion cool, and more about making a statement. Of course, the concept of modest fashion does not restrict itself to items of clothing that have a religious significance. Now, even those who simply choose to cover up for the sake of own comfort can find a wider range of fashion to suit their preferences. Brands like The Row, Ganni and Etro naturally fall into this category, given their patterns and cuts that favour high necklines, longer hems and relaxed fits. Without trading faith for fashion or vice versa, modest dressing has found its own unique charm, exuding a quiet confidence. The impact of standing one's ground has birthed a new dimension of style. Intrigued with the concept? Look out for Vogue India's February 2019 issue, which will talk about the impact of choice on modest fashion. column1: 6 lessons to learn from Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s Indian wear closet
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We take a peek inside Sonam Kapoor Ahuja’s wardrobe and bring you six tricks that will help you ace an ethnic look that’s fashion-approved for 2019 Actor Sonam Kapoor Ahuja is a bona fide trendsetter. Much has been said about her game-changing fashion sensibility and approach to personal styling (in collaboration with her stylist sister, Rhea Kapoor), and with good reason. Kapoor Ahuja loves her anarkalis as much as she loves her anti-fit dresses, and is the choicest muse of many an Indian designer. It's no surprise then, that she often has first dibs on yet-to-be-launched collections from top labels, ranging from Anamika Khanna to Good Earth Couture. Not only has the actor championed Indian wear, she also creates looks worth emulating every time she steps out in traditional finery. We zoom into her ethnic repertoire to bring you lessons that will help you curate your wedding season wardrobe with equal flair. Modern Indian silhouettes are all good, but have you ever worn an heirloom sharara to stand out in a crowd of dhoti pants? Kapoor Ahuja's Good Earth sharara set, which she wore for a friend's wedding, recently exuded serious yesteryear maharani vibes. Living coral may be Pantone's colour for 2019, but there is something about a classic ivory Indian look that personifies ultimate grace. Case in point: this Rohit Bal floor-length anarkali jacket set Kapoor Ahuja wore, accentuated with just the right hint of gold. A statement piece of jewellery, such as the actor's head harness, helps in modernising looks such as these. Embroidered lehengas are passé—2019 features a catchphrase and your name (rendering all pick-up lines useless). Simply ask the trio of tastemakers that are the Kapoor sisters and Anamika Khanna. It's not just Audrey Hepburn who believes in pink. Kapoor Ahuja doesn't shy away from adding a conspicuous hit of this look-at-me hue to her traditional wardrobe either—be it dramatic pink-on-pink anarkali sets or more pared-down kurta sets. Contemporary blouses should be the modern woman's go-to arsenal when it comes to reinventing a traditional silhouette—this can be anything from a sari you wear as a newlywed, to a lehenga you're yearning to repeat. When in doubt, just wear a sari—Kapoor Ahuja sure does. The actor has sported this ageless drape everywhere from the red carpet to promotional events, making a strong case for its versatility and aptness for every occasion. column1: Gauri Khan reveals the first piece of jewellery Shah Rukh bought her
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion On the reopening of Zoya - A Tata Product’s flagship store in New Delhi, Gauri Khan talks to Vogue about her favourite piece from their collection, the jewellery she's passing on to daughter Suhana, and her first ever gift from husband Shah Rukh Khan Zoya, the diamond boutique from the House of Tata has finally reopened its flagship store in South Extension, New Delhi. Yesterday, the brand celebrated the occasion by hosting an evening of cocktails and a fashion showcase in collaboration with Monisha Jaising. The models were dressed in gowns and dresses styled with Zoya's 6299 Hollywood Blvd collection, which draws inspiration from three iconic Hollywood eras and “Whispers from the Valley”, which captures the poetic beauty of Kashmir and picturesque icons of the land. The 4,600sqmt space is designed like a minimal fine art gallery and its no-fuss interior will surely appeal to the taste of the determined shopper. The ground floor of the three storied store features a stunning champagne and rose gold chandelier of blown-glass drops, and will be housing the brand's new collections including 6299 Hollywood Blvd, Whispers from the Valley, Musee Du Luxe and Pezzo D'Arte, while the second floor will showcase Zoya's collection of high value jewellery. What's more, the customers will also be guided by a personal jewellery expert to give them the detailed insight about the products. The launch was also attended by interior designer Gauri Khan, who walked in wearing a statement blue tanzanite and diamond necklace from the label's latest 6299 Hollywood Blvd collection, worn with a black Monika Jaisingh gown. Vogue chatted with Gauri Khan at the event about her favourite jewellery pieces and more. It's a beautiful store and every product is artistic, beautifully crafted, with a story to tell. I liked the store's minimalistic layout and the fact that it is uncluttered, and navigation is well-planned with a serene colour palette. You can spend time appreciating the beauty of every piece individually. I like the matrix necklace from “6299 Hollywood Blvd”, their new Hollywood-inspired collection, which has beautifully cut tanzanite and diamonds set in white gold. The design is simple, and it's impeccably crafted with minute details. A gold wedding band. My mother's polki set, the one that she had worn for her wedding. It is very special to my heart, so I would like Suhana to have it. Suhana and Aryan are now at university and AbRam is in school, so there's more time for design-related work. For me, it's all about balancing your priorities. I would have been an artist, because I studied art and history in school and college. So I think something connected to art. Creating something and then seeing it come to life, I'd say. Starting from scratch and seeing the smile on a client's face when it all comes together in the end, it's a lovely feeling. To keep growing and doing well, staying open to inspiration and making beautiful spaces. I think it's important to keep moving forward so that the soul can grow. column1: Earthy, boxy, boring: Do sustainable clothes have a standard look?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion For long, sustainable fashion has been typecast as 'dull'. How are labels working at breaking that mould? A week ago, when Vogue India's fashion and e-commerce editor, Rujuta Vaidya, approached me about writing a story on the predicable aesthetics of sustainable fashion, I was intrigued to say the least. And my first thought was: does conscious fashion fit a specific mould? Close your eyes and imagine an item of sustainable clothing. What do you see? The picture that came to my mind was that of a loose-fitting dress in cream, made out of handwoven fabric with the tiniest touch of hand embroidery at the edges. I was honestly surprised at my own stereotypical perceptions of sustainable fashion, even though I know I have seen cases that have showcased very unique elements. While I acknowledge there are exceptions, a fair amount of slow fashion is restricted to a neutral or earthy colour palette (white, beige, indigo, black, salmon pink), has loose or boxy cuts and follows a distinctly minimal aesthetic. I spent some time digging deeper into this phenomenon and asking conscious designers, sustainable bloggers and upcycled clothing makers if they also thought this was true. I did find some who agreed with the idea in principal, while others upheld a different opinion. “Sadly, apparel produced by sustainable clothing labels in India does look similar,” says Shivangini Parihar, creative director at The Summer House, a slow fashion label. “Most of us have similar aesthetics but I do think that this is changing.” On the other hand, Vincent Declety, founder of Ahmedabad-based Indigenous Industries, a company that produces sustainable clothing for international brands like Galleries Lafayette in France and Matter Prints in Singapore, disagrees that new-age sustainable clothing fits into a certain mould. “This may have been the case 10 years ago, but today you can find sustainable fashion in all styles. For instance, we produce sports shorts for a label using recycled polyester, but you cannot tell that the item has been conceived with sustainability in mind just by looking at it.” Despite these inconsistencies in expert opinion, a few key factors did come up repeatedly in my conversations, which can provide some explanation about the consistent look of conscious clothing. By its very definition, slow fashion is the opposite of fast fashion. Instead of dropping by Zara and H&M every week to pick up trendy items like animal print slacks and off-shoulder dresses, the idea is to buy fewer, quality pieces that you will want to wear for a long time. This is probably why neutral-coloured, simple basics become the clothing of choice among sustainability patrons—they're versatile, timeless and will be treasured in your wardrobe for much longer than any others. This also explains the tendency for so many sustainable clothing labels to create simple, white, black and beige clothing. “While slow fashion celebrates every process and minute elements involved in making an item, fast fashion hangs onto introducing more and more pieces with total disregard to the process,” explains Bengaluru- and Atlanta-based responsible fashion blogger, Swati Dixit. “I do agree that there are some restrictions when it comes to fabrics, colours and designs being adopted by sustainable brands. But I find the whole idea of ‘trendy' clothing very subjective. If you ask me, I find a basic white shirt and a pair of denims very stylish and classic. I'd rather opt for a style that's comfortable, timeless and resonating with my personality, than something that's ‘trendy' and poorly made.” How many of you have heard of the 10X10 challenge on Instagram? Lee Vosburg, founder of sustainable fashion blog Style Bee, started this viral social experiment, where users pick a capsule collection of 10 clothing and footwear items from their own wardrobe and use only those for 10 days (they are, however, allowed to accessorise with additional hats, bags and jewellery). The rules of the challenge force people to take a deep, hard look at their style choices and consumerist tendencies. You can be rest assured that a lot of those capsule wardrobes will feature neutral-coloured basics within them. Another obvious difference between fast and slow fashion is the use of responsibly-produced, natural fabrics like cotton, silk and wool, which have no give as opposed to lycra and polyester, which have in-built elasticity. This naturally speaks to the tendency of conscious clothing being roomy or boxy, instead of having fitted and cinched silhouettes. Besides this, one also needs to consider if the sustainable fabric is handwoven or factory-produced, because the width of a handwoven fabric will only be as long as the weaver's arms. Thus, if a designer wants to support India's traditional weaver communities while still creating inclusive sizing in their collections, he or she has to find creative ways of designing clothing with a cut or joint running through the centre. Ironically, this could create more similarities in the way garments are cut and tailored. One of the most harmful by-products of producing apparel is the chemical dyes that get released into the environment. The counter solution employed by multiple conscious clothing labels is to use vegetable dyes instead which are made of natural ingredients and aren't harmful to the planet. This plays into the specific colour palette usually seen in slow fashion clothing. “Natural dyes won't come in flashy or neon shades,” says Declety. “You'll get a warm colour palette to work with. It's not possible to do micro prints (less than 1mm) with natural dyes, which is a big drawback.” Most importantly, in a single collection, it's usually too expensive to produce more than four or five different colours, so you have to work with a limited shades, or costs escalate. Thus, you'll notice that many sustainable fashion labels tend to have numerous styles, but a limited amount of print and colour options—and those too in earthy tones of mustard, beige, indigo, etc. So does that mean you need to quash your inner Lady Gaga if you are a sustainable fashion consumer? Not necessarily. “India eventually is not a minimal country,” says Parihar. “While we may appreciate minimalism, and there will always be a niche crowd that always stays true to it, the fact is that we love our colours, we love our flamboyance. Who are we without that? We had a lot of whites when we first started The Summer House label, but today we have consciously introduced colours and prints using azo-free dyes. At the end, it is a business, and to dream really big in India, you need to cater to people's style.” Another fascinating aspect is the role technology is going to play in creating new raw materials and building eco-friendly production processes—and this could completely transform the look of sustainable fashion. Salvatore Ferragamo, for one, made news for using fabric being made out of waste orange and peels from the juice pressing industry in his creations. “There are a lot of new age fabrics being developed from food waste,” says Declety, who's at the forefront of sustainable fashion technology in India. “There's pineapple leather, which is a great replacement for the real thing; bean fibre is making a lot of noise—it's made out of the leftovers from tofu and soy sauce. Even in Tamil Nadu and Kerala there are people experimenting with indigenous plants like bowstring hemp to make new fibres.” Buying vintage or pre-worn clothing is another way to be shop consciously without compromising on your own style. “I love investing in pre-loved vintage pieces—the nostalgia and mystery around their journey is too interesting to resist,” says Dixit. “If you can shop from an already existing pile, it not only takes off a notable amount of burden on the environment, it also adds an element of individuality to your wardrobe. Also, vintage pieces are of far superior quality than their shoddily-made fast fashion counterparts.” Don't know where to find sustainable fashion? I Was A Sari is a non-profit organisation that uses pre-loved saris to make accessories, beachwear and more. In Mumbai, the No Borders shop in Khotachiwadi, Girgaon, has a great collection of vintage clothing including Hermès scarves and vintage denim jackets upcycled by Péro. Sustainable clothing may veer towards beige-toned basics, but those with a will, will always find a way of expressing their personal style without compromising on ethics.
