column1: What work looks like when you are Sonam K Ahuja
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue follows Sonam K Ahuja to Geneva, where she’s attending the IWC Schaffhausen event, to give you an inside glimpse of the inner working of the world of horology Ever wondered what a day in the life of Sonam K Ahuja looks like? From her morning coffee recipe to her arm candy situation, we follow the IWC Schaffhausen brand ambassador to Geneva, where she's attending the ultimate watch trade show, Salon International de la Haute Horlogerie (SIHH), and a star-studded gala with Bradley Cooper, Rosamund Pike and Dev Patel—better known as her ‘IWC Family'. Sonam K Ahuja shares two pages out of her calendar with us. 1pm: I've been spending a lot of time in London with my husband [Anand Ahuja] lately, so I fly in from there to Geneva Airport. 3pm: I check into the Mandarin Oriental and get straight into bed for a power nap—I've been working all morning. 5pm: I pick a black Ralph & Russo outfit from their new ready-to-wear collection for the IWC Schaffhausen opening dinner at La Reserve. I accessorise with Amrapali jewels and my favourite ‘IWC Da Vinci 36mm Moonphase' watch with brown leather strap. I wear this watch almost all the time like a piece of jewellery—on flights and in my films too. It's an old-school classic design with a whimsical touch. That's why it works with everything. 7pm: Dinner is served! The risotto is yummy and there is fondue too. I catch up with Karolina Kurkova as we have a lot of common friends. I also meet Hend Sabri, and my IWC Schaffhausen team from around the world. 10pm: I head back to the hotel—it's bedtime for me. 6.30am: I wake up and work out. I do cardio, followed by yoga and some stretching. 8am: Breakfast today is a Gruyère cheese omelette with strawberries and avocado. I like my morning coffee in a very specific way: two shots of espresso with coconut oil, lots of dark chocolate and a dollop of heavy cream—no sugar. 9am: I get ready for the day in a purple Calvin Klein suit I got this summer, [wearing it] over a Prada bow shirt my sister and I found in Austria. For accessories, I go for black Rag & Bone booties, pearl earrings and a full gold ‘IWC Da Vinci Automatic 36mm' watch with a diamond bezel. For a tall person I have really tiny limbs, so I've realised that 36mm is the best dial size for me. I don't usually go much larger than that. 10am: I get to work—I'm currently working on a new collection for Rheson with Rhea, and I speak to Nimish [Shah] for Bhane. My husband is in Portland right now, so I'm overlooking things for him. 3pm: I head to Palexpo, the exhibition hall where the SIHH watch fair is taking place. I go to the IWC Schaffhausen booth to see the new timepieces, and to check out the Spitfire plane from 1943, which the brand will be sponsoring for its journey around the world. I'm also looking for a new pocket watch for Anand; I recently got him an ‘IWC Big Pilots Boutique Rodeo Drive Edition' watch because he's fascinated by the movement and technical side of watchmaking, much more so than fancy cars! 5pm: I'm getting ready for tonight's gala. I'm wearing a pink dress by Mark Bumgarner, diamond stud earrings and a ‘IWC Portofino Automatic 37mm' watch in red gold with diamonds and lilac Santoni leather strap. 8pm: I'm at the gala and Kaleo is performing. I'm a big fan! They also fly the Spitfire plane right on the stage. 9am: Before I leave Geneva, I always pick up chocolate from Sprungli and Laderlach. Cheese too, usually brie—I was vegan for a while so I try to eat and buy rennet-free vegetarian cheese. This was a short trip to Geneva, so I didn't get a chance to go to my favourite restaurant, Izumi at the Four Seasons, or my favourite vintage store in town, where I once found a black YSL gown for a very reasonable price. It'll have to wait till next time. For now, I'm off to Los Angeles. Fashion Fashion How To © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: It’s confirmed: Low-rise jeans are making a comeback
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion After nearly two decades, this Noughties-favourite trend is now making its way back to both the runways and into our wardrobes Rewind back to the early 2000s, and you'll instantly recall a time when most celebrities—from Paris Hilton and Britney Spears to Christina Aguilera—showcased their washboard abs in dangerously low low-rise jeans. And soon it wasn't just the A-listers—from teenagers to fashion-forward mothers, everyone had a trusty pair in their wardrobes. The trend made appearances at red carpet events, as expected, but also featured in popular music videos featuring Jennifer Lopez, Beyoncé, Pink and Britney Spears and of course Poo in Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham—usually paired with equally risqué crop tops. Come 2019, low-rise jeans are climbing back up on the charts, and according to trend forecasters, they will be back in full power by the coming spring season. Those who are still unsure of the resurrection of the frequently-dreaded style possibly just missed the signs on both Instagram and the runways. Levi's officially added low-rise styles to its 2019 offerings, New York-based label Linder NYC showcased it in their spring/summer 2018 collection, and brands like ALYX, Alexander McQueen, Roberto Cavalli and Balenciaga served hip-grazing designs on their ramps too. And if the runways weren't enough proof, take a look at the number of the celebrities that have come to this style's rescue (again!). Early signs of the resurgence could be seen in the wardrobes of  Emily Ratajkowski, Lily Aldridge and Rihanna in 2017. And Bella Hadid, who never misses a single trend, was spotted out and about in a pair of low-slung jeans, worn with a cropped shirt to give a peek at her perfectly toned mid-riff. Scroll through our gallery to spot all the times celebrities donned low-slung jeans like pros. column1: Jean-Charles de Castelbajac joins United Colors of Benetton as artistic director
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The fashion designer, known for his whimsical approach and love for colours, is sure to inject quirk in the Italian brand’s future collections. Veteran designer Jean-Charles de Castelbajac has always blurred the boundaries between fashion and art. His most memorable creation, worn by Madonna and Lauren Hutton back in 1989, was a snuggly winter coat made with precisely 39 teddy bears. Two decades later, Lady Gaga was heralding his muppet-inspired fashion via a green Kermit the Frog jacket. And now, it's time for Italian label United Colors of Benetton to get a makeover as Castelbajac takes the helm as its artistic director. Benetton, renowned for being a trailblazer for promoting diversity and inclusivity, has always embraced equal representation, whether it is through their choice of strong colours used in the collections or the bold political statements communicated through their campaigns. The brand has also been open to collaborations, like the designer collection co-curated with Stella Jean back in 2016, which showcases their ability to stay ahead of the curve. Castelbajac has already started prepping for his first Benetton collection, which (according to his latest Instagram posts) aims to bring to light Benetton's rich heritage. What we're looking forward for the most, though, is for Castelbajac's quirky yet stylish aesthetics in Benetton's clothing that can be channelled into everyday wear. The artistic director, who launched his first brand in collaboration with his mother in 1968, has been a big proponent of art—whether it was his street art-inspired collections or his collaborations with artists like Andy Warhol. Needless to say, his first collection for Benetton will be infused with art and bright colours. “United Colors of Benetton and I have always had a similar take on fashion, characterised by the passion for knitwear and the love of pop and rainbow colours,” the designer says. column1: Couture is far from dead—and it’s making a comeback
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Beyond aspirational, the alluringly closed-doors world of haute couture is having a moment, with Balmain returning to the hallowed world and rumours Celine will soon follow. But why now? Vogue investigates the booming business of exclusivity “When people say couture is dead… perhaps for them, but not for us.” So said Karl Lagerfeld, just after he'd overseen the outing of 68 entirely handcrafted looks at the spring/summer 2018 Chanel haute couture show. Recorded by Andrew Rossi for the Netflix documentary 7 Days Out—which goes behind the scenes at major live events in fashion, sports, space and food—the designer's comment plainly contested the idea that high-fashion fantasy is dead. Indeed, the idea that couture is on the wane positively flies in the face of 2019, with big brands promising a renewed focus on the rarefied craft of creating clothing for the individual, not the mass market. Balmain, under the helm of the spirited and dynamic designer Olivier Rousteing, is returning to the couture calendar for the first time in 16 years; Hedi Slimane, now creative director at Celine, plans to expand into the category as part of his new vision for the label; and, more than ever before, young ready-to-wear labels—including Mary Katrantzou, Richard Quinn and Marine Serre—are exploring the notion of “ready-to-wear couture”. “Haute couture is a growing market; fashion houses keep increasing their sales in this activity and the clientele is expanding, diversifying,” explains Ralph Toledano, president of both the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode and Chambre Syndicale de la Haute Couture, the body in charge of all couture output. “Haute couture has always been, and remains, a land of free expression for designers, a land where creativity meets tradition with innovation.” New technologies, he says, are helping to push boundaries and possibilities when it comes to couture, with innovative materials, techniques and approaches piquing the interest of previously untested audiences—including millennials. And where once the realm of such a world might have been considered old guard, reserved only for red carpets and grandiose weddings, suddenly couture feels in touch—and it's striking a pertinent chord when it comes to our emotional needs as consumers. “There is more of an interest [in couture] because today everything [else] is trying to get us into the same mass-market culture,” says Parisian couturier Alexis Mabille, noting especially a desire for individuality and authenticity. He cites the importance of the unique relationship between the house and the customer, and the magic of a made-to-measure experience—which stands out as a true luxury in a sea of all too similar style right now. “Sensoriality is also key,” agrees Toledano. “As long as there are people looking for the exceptional, there will be haute couture.” Couture is making its mark within ready-to-wear, too. “It has become even more noticeable that brands are looking to expand their ready-to-wear couture offering,” observes Elizabeth von der Goltz, global buying director at Net-A-Porter, which has been growing this eveningwear category substantially, increasing it by over 50 per cent this year compared to last. “We're seeing even more demand from our EIPs (Extremely Important People), who are looking for exquisite pieces to make a real entrance at their events.” Alexandre Vauthier and Ralph & Russo (both of which do ready-to-wear and couture), she notes, have become favourites. Indeed, the effect was strong among the spring/summer 2019 collections—runways were awash with feathers, voluminous shapes and the intricate embellishment so indicative of couture. “It's what we're calling ‘modern couture',” says von der Goltz. Matchesfashion.com, too, is focusing on “demi-couture” for the new season—something that was very much in action at Mary Katrantzou's 10th anniversary show this past London Fashion Week. The designer, famed for her exquisite “lampshade” skirts and “perfume bottle” dresses, went big on couture-like techniques for her collection, with around 90 per cent of the looks revealing an incredible level of detail and craftsmanship. Katrantzou is no stranger to this approach; outside of ready-to-wear, she often works with private clients designing bespoke pieces for celebrities including Beyoncé and Cate Blanchett. Couture's extension beyond the salons of select maisons can be traced back to 1997, when the status of “guest member” was created by the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode. Guest member status granted new, less traditional and non-French names a place on the schedule of this highly closed-doors, invitation-only industry (haute couture follows strict rules about who can show and when, and what qualifies as “couture”). Exploration of new techniques followed; aesthetics began to diversify and move away from traditional high-society styles. Then came business strategy. In 2014, both Jean Paul Gaultier and Viktor & Rolf decided to close their ready-to-wear operations and focus on couture and fragrance—and neither brand is any the worse off for doing so. Jean Paul Gaultier makes a profit, going up each year. And arguably Viktor & Rolf's conceptual-art sensibility makes more sense in the creative forum of couture than it does within the commercial constraints of ready-to-wear. “The magic of haute couture is the fact that almost everything is possible,” says Mabille. “It is a secret world, all created for one special individual.” It is an alluring proposition—one still so exclusive that very few of us will ever get to experience it. As hair stylist Sam McKnight observes in 7 Days Out, “These clothes are something that the vast majority of people in the world will never see close up, they'll never touch, they'll never be in the same room as. It's so aspirational that it's breathtaking.” Upholding artisan traditions in a fresh, modern way? Little wonder couture has found its groove in the era of Instagram. column1: Arsenal footballer Héctor Bellerín gives us his top 10 style tips
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Arsenal and Spain defender is reinventing flash footballer style, one Craig Green jacket at a time. Ahead of the men’s fashion shows across Europe, he shares his tips for avoiding a sartorial own goal On the pitch, 23-year-old footballer, Héctor Bellerín—who plays for Arsenal and Spain's national team—is known for his pace and performance. But elsewhere, he is fast gaining a reputation for his keen eye for fashion. Here, ahead of January's menswear shows in London, Paris, Florence and Milan—where Bellerín is likely to be in the FROW—he shares his top 10 style tips with Vogue. “If you are familiar with the football world you will know that the professional footballer's style philosophy is: ‘If it looks expensive, or has a big logo demonstrating that it cost me a lot, then yeah, I'll have it.' If it ends up looking good, even better. In terms of my teammates, I've been seeing a lot of Gucci tracksuits with the double G pattern all over them, tons of skinny ripped jeans and what feels like every single pair of sparkly or studded Louboutin high tops ever made. Jokes aside, though, I think the younger generation is way more clued up on fashion. They know a lot about brands and they always try to look good, which wasn't always the case—so, it's a start!” “Right now, the coolest thing in my wardrobe is a grey, see-through Margiela trench coat in PVC. It's such a cool piece—not the easiest to wear, but if you put it together right, it looks so good.” “For me, London-based designer Samuel Ross at A Cold Wall* is one to get excited about, but there is so much talent in the UK right now. I personally love the clothes and message behind Liam Hodges and Paria Farzaneh, and I always look forward to seeing Christopher Raeburn's collection—I've been to his studio and I love the philosophy behind his brand. At this season's London Collections: Men (LC:M) I'm hoping to make it to Cottweiler; but I also want to go to the menswear shows in Milan and Paris, neither of which I have done before. I'm excited for the experience.” “Even though we just entered 2019, for some people, a man wearing a bag doesn't really make sense. That said, I've been carrying bags a lot lately and I love the practical element, as well as the fact that it's one more item you can play around with. I think it's good not to always look at trends and instead, follow your instincts regarding what looks best on you.” “You may have seen a picture of me watching my team from the stands in December wearing a Burberry scarf, a trench coat and tiny-lens sunglasses. It seems to have caused a major stir amongst football fans—they're not used to seeing football players dressing outside of the box or just trying different things. Some people are claiming micro-sunglasses are over, but I love a Matrix kind of vibe worn with a trench coat.” “The thing I love most about winter is the layering opportunities—and the coats. The more clothes you can put on, the more you can express yourself. I love an oversized cardigan that you can just throw on over an outfit to add character. I've also got my hands on some very cool coats and jackets this year: a yellow Kenzo duffel is one of my favourites, as well as a Raf Simons for Calvin Klein red puffer.” “In winter I usually wear something on my head, whether it's a beanie, a bucket or a hood. The weather is always changing in London and I only ever really feel safe going out if I've got one of them with me. That, and my Burberry trench coat for when it rains. I like wearing classic pieces and then pairing them with something that doesn't really make sense.” “In January of last year I wore silk pyjamas with Gucci loafers for a show at LC:M—that was a big thing in the dressing room. A couple of days after I wore that outfit, there were pictures of me in it pasted all over my locker. But every time I dress up there is always something to say. If my teammates laugh at me, it's fine, because most of the time it means I'm doing something right.” “I love white trainers, whatever the occasion. I like how they can take the seriousness out of an outfit. Obviously keeping them box-fresh is a bit more tricky, especially with London weather and being someone who likes to walk a lot. But I have a whole tool kit to make sure they shine every time I wear them. My favourites at the moment are a pair of white Velcro Acne Studios trainers, but even a pair of classic white Pumas work for me. “My style is always evolving and I'm still in a phase where I like to change it up. Since it got cold this winter, for instance, I've been wearing a lot of baggy jeans and trousers with Nineties hip-hop vibes, but now I've decided that I want to wear more fitted stuff. The elements that usually stay the same with me are the accessories: my rings, my hats, my earrings—they are what define my style.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Anita Dongre’s latest bridal line is stunning, and only features 15 pieces
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Anita Dongre has released a capsule collection of one-of-a-kind bridal wear hand-painted with Pichhwai art, and if you want one, you may have to make a run for it Rajasthan's rich traditions and its time-honoured craft legacy have been the foundation of Anita Dongre's bridal couture label since its very inception. And now, the designer pays yet another ode to her everlasting inspiration by the way of her latest bridal couture capsule collection, based on the art of Pichhwai. An ancient art form that originated in Nathdwara, Pichhwai paintings are intricate pictorial portrayals inspired by Lord Krishna. Dongre's collection, which comprises 15 hand painted limited edition pieces, mirrors the same design aesthetic and attention to detail. This painstakingly created line has been in the work for two years now. “Two years ago, when I was in Rajasthan for a shoot, I encountered Lekhrajji, who was painting the walls of City Palace, Jaipur. I was intrigued and inspired by the intricacy of his work and his flawless brushstrokes. We chatted about his craft, and during this time, he also mentioned how inconsistent work was. My creativity is fuelled not just by design, but also by the revival of Indian crafts. I immediately knew that I wanted to give this art another form of life. So I invited Lekhrajji to our design headquarters in Mumbai, and that's how the Pichhwai collection came to life,” reveals the designer. Scroll through our gallery to take a look at the collection. column1: Curvy girls can wear anything they like, and these pictures are proof
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Why does your body shape have to dictate what you wear? Vogue asks three women with hourglass physiques to bust the myths    The trend: Ruffles and volume [#image: /photos/5ce41b513aeed651b0bcd8bf]||| ||| Image: Sushant Chhabria I'm not a fearful dresser. I enjoy both fashion and my body. Rules are meant to be broken. If everyone subscribed to rules, we wouldn't have new fashion at all. Carry it with confidence. That's the trick to wearing anything. Make sure it makes you happy and that it's  comfortable and occasion appropriate. Oversized silhouettes are a huge trend right now. Zendaya, Erykah Badu, Rihanna and the Olsens are nailing volume. I would wear unexpected shoes with this look—tall leopard print Christian Louboutin pumps, Loewe hybrid heels or cool sneakers. I've collected many statement pieces over the years. My Huemn sweatshirt with ‘DON'T TRY' in leather letters always turns heads. The expert: “The volume and ruffles have to be in control—they should not drown you. The material has to be right, too. Try not to superficially mask the curves with layers; show skin by highlighting a favourite body part. Eventually, it all comes down to body language.” —Nimish Shah, founder, Shift; creative director, Bhaane The trend: Horizontal stripes [#image: /photos/5ce41b50b803113ec08f58ad]||| ||| Image: Sushant Chhabria I like to highlight my shoulders, neck and décolletage. I'm most conscious of my arms and stomach. I always tend to layer to avoid showing them. I was concerned about all the fabric making me look frumpy. But I feel really great and comfortable. I've been eyeing a lot of striped swimsuits lately. Forever 21 Plus has a really fun yellow and white one that I love. Brigitte Bardot wore stripes best. She was simple and effective. I would carry a small coin bag with this look. Like the Dolce & Gabbana raffia crossbody. I can't stop buying Adidas slides. They are so practical for Mumbai. I am also kind of obsessed with sneakers and want to buy a pair by Golden Goose. The expert: “Opt for an atypical stripe such as a continuous repeat pattern or weave that forms the illusion of a horizontal stripe, rather than the bold linear version. Also try and stick to one key item of clothing, like a dress or jumpsuit. Adding colour is always fun, too!” —Archana Walavalkar, co-founder and creative director, Stylecracker The trend: All-over white [#image: /photos/5ce41b519cc0c04a28f9bf0d]||| ||| Image: Sushant Chhabria I love my collarbones and shoulders. I like to emphasise this when dressing. White has always been my go-to colour. I wear a lot of separates but this is my first time in all-white. This look is versatile and ethereal. It can take me from day to night. I would love to splurge on an Alexander McQueen all-white pantsuit. I'm a jacket-and-trousers person and the sharp suit with wide shoulders is on my wishlist. I always pick up my T-shirts from the men's department for the fit and feel. All Saints makes a great white tee. The expert: “Layer sheer whites or pick performance friendly fabrics like neoprene that glide along your curves for a bodycon silhouette. To trim your frame, ensure the fit is snug and perfect.”—Shivan Bhatiya and Narresh Kukreja, founders, Shivan & Narresh What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 12 designer kurtas for Lohri that will help you stand out in the crowd

column1: This is how much royals spent on their wardrobes in 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The cost of being a modern day royal For some, the dream of being royalty is a reality, and while some are born into their roles of princess or queen, others marry into sovereign families. And while it is a family, albeit a very famous, very influential family, being a royal can be a full-time job too. But what does one wear when meeting and greeting the public, opening hospitals and supporting the troops? It's a job that requires balancing etiquette and long upheld traditions with rigorous schedules and gruelling world tours. In short, it's a complicated feat managing a royal wardrobe and quite an expensive one, too. Looking the part certainly does come with a price tag, at least that's what data pulled from royal clothing watchdog UFO No More tells us, with the site detailing just how much royals from around the world spend on their clothing. So who spent the most in 2018? Well, it should come as no surprise that the newly minted Duchess of Sussex had the highest spend of the year considering she was thrown into royal duties and a royal tour in her first few months of marriage. Plus, there was the need for a whole host of new maternity clothes when it was announced Meghan Markle was expecting her first child. Markle spent almost six times more on clothing than her sister-in-law Kate Middleton last year and this figure, per UFO, does not even include her custom Clare Waight Keller-designed Givenchy wedding dress. Some of the biggest sartorial highlights for Markle in 2018 included a yellow Brandon Maxwell shift, a white Maggie Marilyn tuxedo dress and a navy Dion Lee wrap that the duchess wore in Australia during her first royal tour. Where Markle spends isn't just noteworthy for our wardrobe but it also means big business for the brands she taps—the Markle effect is alive and kicking! Some of the duchess' favourite brands in 2018 included Aquazzura, Jason Wu, Asos, Victoria Beckham and Club Monaco. As for Middleton, brands like Jimmy Choo, Jenny Packham, Jigsaw and Alexander McQueen were standouts in 2018. Other famous royals on the list include Crown Princess Mary of Denmark, Crown Princess Mette-Marit of Norway and Princess Charlene of Monaco. column1: Heads up, you may start seeing these strange jeans everywhere soon
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's why Tattered thong jeans in Japan! Denim with a crotch-to-waist fly by Vetements and Lorod! A jean leg sewn on another jean leg by Yajun! Now, yet another pair of double-take–inducing jeans have surfaced courtesy of Ksenia Schnaider. The Kiev-based designer, who had a buzzy jean moment thanks to her Bella Hadid–approved demi-denims, has one-upped herself with an optically jarring pant: one side is reminiscent of a JNCO and the other side is chicly narrow. They currently retail for $377. Schnaider based the pant on two of her best-selling models, a wide-leg and a pair of high-waisted mom jeans. “My partner Anton Schnaider said that it was too crazy and no one need jeans like this, so I abandoned this idea for a couple of seasons,” she says. “But a few months ago, I realised that at least one person need such kind of jeans—me!” While the creation isn't a complete trompe l'oeil, it's certainly weird and a bit trippy. Plus, surreal fashion has been having a moment. Estonian singer Tommy Cash recently wore digitally warped UGGS á la Y/Project's collaboration with the label, and Balenciaga and Vetements have both been experimenting with altered visuals on their social media accounts. So far, Schnaider has only worn them in her studio, but has gotten some fun reactions from her team, writing, “The jeans can surprise and make people smile,” and adding that she'll bring them to the streets during Paris Men's Fashion Week in January. As for what she'll wear them with? Schnaider will go simple with heels and hoodies or loafers and “boring” sweaters, saying, “They are crazy enough, so I think other items should be all-time classics.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.com Fashion Culture & Living Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Meet the 3 Indian designers who were just honoured with National Awards
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s what they had to say Recognition of an individual's contribution in a sector is a special moment in their career. Recently, the Ministry of Textiles awarded 17 designers and artisans with the ‘Threads of Excellence' award. Rajesh Pratap Singh, Rahul Mishra and Aneeth Arora of Péro were the three Indian designers to receive this honour. Each of these designers have created a name for themselves with the unique narratives and exploration of textiles. Experiencing pride on the occasion, here's what the designers had to say. "It's an honour to be recognised by the government of India, Ministry of Textiles, for the work we have done in taking Indian traditions to the global platform. This will inspire a lot of upcoming designers to continue working with the weavers and craftspeople, which will in turn help keep the heritage of traditional Indian textiles alive." - Aneeth Arora “I felt emotional seeing the national emblem on something that has been conferred to you, it really means a lot to me. column1: 5 fashion trends from 2018 we don’t want to see in 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Au revoir, micro mini sunglasses 2018 has been a great year for fashion. We saw a resurgence of '90s trends (bum bags, flared pants, chokers, band T-shirts), and also stood witness to the birth of new trends (micro bags, head-to-toe animal prints, micro mini sunglasses, neon clothing) that earned instant approval from the fashion fraternity. Such is the fleeting nature of a trend in fashion that as soon as its popularity peeks, the slightest presence of an overdone item instantly puts you off it. As we step into 2019, Vogue recapitulates the trends from 2018 that we do not want to carry forward to the new year. This trend has found patrons in A-listers all over the globe, from Priyanka Chopra Jonas to Kendall Jenner—but we're not convinced. Sure, they will guarantee a statement addition to your outfit, but not every look warrants an exaggerated accessory. These can go straight back to the '90s where they came from. Thank you, next! At first, it was Chanel's see-through collection of PVC boots, jackets, hats, gloves and more that created an uproar; then it was Calvin Klein 205W39NYC's clear coat, Celine's plastic shopping bag, the Off-White x Jimmy Choo plastic pumps and even the Off-White x Rimowa transparent suitcase that caught everyone's attention. Yes, it's true that the fashion industry needs to herald in transparency, but this trend took it too literally. Also, who needs more plastic in the world than there is already? You know that feeling when you've eaten way more of the same item than you should've? It's the same feeling we get when we spot this trend. It only takes one look around the clothing racks at most major shopping centres to notice the (excessive!) number of tops and dresses featuring the familiar cut-outs—resulting in the kind of monotony that appeases nobody. Considering it's the start of a new year, can we all just agree to give the trend a cold shoulder and leave it in the past, where it deserves to be? The sock boot trend came to life when athleisure met sophistication to create a shoe option for evening wear that was equal parts sporty and elegant. Think Balenciaga's knife booties and Vetements' sock boots, which carved a niche of their own. What was once an alternative style that wasn't entirely loved but not quite hated on, is now omnipresent. We are definitely over these. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 5 ways to take mismatched earrings off the runway and into your closet
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How to nail the runway- and celebrity-approved trend One of the oldest rule in the fashion book is that elements of your outfit should match each other—the colour of your top should complement its bottom counterpart, your belt and shoes should never be in different colours, and matching your shoes with your bag can give your look an instant fashion-approved polish too. So when the mismatched earring trend came around, people who went by the rulebook did a double take. But despite its unconventionality, the trend slowly gained attention when designers like Chanel, Dior, Louis Vuitton and more showcased it on the runway. Closer home, we saw designers like Pankaj and Nidhi, Ritu Kumar and Dhruv Kapoor, among others, incorporate the look at their recent fashion week showcases. What's more, celebrities like Sonam K Ahuja, Meghan Markle, and more recently, Amber Heard—who wore a pair of mismatched fringed earrings in gold by Delhi-based designer Hanut Singh at the 76th Golden Globes Awards—have given it their stamp of approval. Interesting and quirky in equal measure, mismatched earrings prove to an easy way to add a talking point to your outfit—if done right, of course. Ahead, we've put together an easy-to-follow guide on how to ace the trend. A smart and noticeable way of highlighting your mismatched earrings is to wear a long earring (hoops, danglers, shoulder dusters—take your pick) on one ear, and a shorter one (like a simple diamond stud) on the other. Look no further than Amber Heard, who is nailing the trend with her latest red carpet showcase. Keep things interesting by pairing earrings in different shapes—hoop earrings with rectangular-shaped ones, square-shaped earrings with triangular ones, round stud earrings with star-shaped numbers... you get the gist. You can also try styling two earrings of the same length in contrasting colours. Think embellished earrings in different metal tones like gold and silver or rose gold and bronze, or even the timeless combination of black and white. Give your outfit an unexpected twist by wearing earrings of different sizes. Take inspiration from Sonam K Ahuja, who paired a mini hoop earring with a large-sized hoop earring, both in gold. Prefer simplicity? Follow the easiest way of nailing the trend by wearing a singular statement earring in one ear. Let designers Payal Pratap, Anupama Dayal and Louis Vuitton show you how to style this. column1: Thinking of a career in fashion? Here’s how to pick the right course
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From the emerging trends in fashion education to what program to pursue, Vogue asks an expert for a fashion student-friendly lowdown Fashion poses many challenges to those wanting to enter the industry—from the dilemma of picking the program that suits your skillset to scoring a valuable internship—especially when you don't have someone to guide you. Vogue chats with Roberto Riccio, group managing director at Istituto Marangoni, to help aspiring fashion students find their way. Excepts from the interview, below. Curiosity—for applied and visual arts—is crucial. Not only should the student be tuned into the fashion landscape, but they must listen to music, attend concerts, visit museums, be interested in cinema and travel a lot. Travelling for a fashion student is one of the most vital elements—it's a great source of inspiration and one is sure to come back loaded with ideas. Students should also be diligent, and have a strict and structured approach to everything they do. Another skill to have is the ability to network—fashion is all about networking and creating contacts from all over the world. It's important that students evaluate their own dreams and expectations, so it helps for them to identify where their passion and talents lie. Fashion schools have workshops during open days, wherein students can drop by with their parents and speak with the teachers to get a taste of what to expect from the course. The introduction of pathways in courses also gives students the liberty to decide what they want to specialise in at a later stage, when they have a more mature approach to fashion. Fashion education changes so fast—there is something new every year. Studying online is a trend, but a video or webinar isn't the best approach to learning. Studying the arts is a more hands-on experience. The best option for a student today would be to attend courses across fashion capitals like London, Milan, Paris, New York and Shanghai. Even if it's a semester spent abroad, it will expand a student's vision and perception of fashion in different countries. This is also a great way to network. India is a hub of crafts and has a rich culture which can be re-thought, re-innovated and re-designed by students. The advantage of pursuing fashion education in India is that the market is booming. The country is the next frontier in fashion, and Indian parents who are skeptical about their children pursuing fashion should know this. However, I've noticed that Indian students in Europe are some of the best, but here, their attitude is very laid-back. Low attendance at school will never help a student make a career in fashion. Another trend I've observed in India is of young designers launching their namesake brands and transforming into entrepreneurs—a skill that's as important as being creative and staying up-to-date with today's trends. One needs to focus on learning about production, marketing, communication, advertising and the life cycle of a product as well. Internships are fundamental, and today, most fashion schools help students get one, which sometimes gets converted into a job. However, every student must remember that it's their responsibility during those three to six months to showcase a professional and hardworking attitude. Firstly, students should choose their school wisely, as the institution plays a big role in securing a job. Secondly, networking is just as essential. Students must also be dedicated, creative, hardworking and prepared to face challenges. The latest developments are related to fashion business. This interdisciplinary area has opened up so many roles, like that of production managers, communication managers, online merchandisers and visual merchandisers, among others. It's not true—fashion pays well. It may be difficult in the beginning, just like any other job, but I foresee India's attitude changing with the development of fashion. column1: Neeta Lulla on recreating Rani Lakshmibai’s wardrobe for Manikarnika
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From the grand outfits to the handcrafted jewellery Ask anyone about the Rani of Jhansi and it's unlikely that you'll ever get a blank stare. Everyone who's familiar with the history of India recognises the queen as a legacy who played a vital role during the Indian Rebellion of 1857. Which is why Neeta Lulla—who has worked on over 300 films—was a natural choice when it came to designing the costumes for Manikarnika, a period drama based on the feisty queen. From the grand nauvari saris that Kangana Ranaut (who plays the Rani of Jhansi) wears to the carefully-crafted jewellery pieces, the designer reveals her journey of working on costumes for Manikarnika. I knew the story of Rani Lakshmibai, so I was aware that her look would be of a warrior queen. But when KV Vijayendra Prasad (the scriptwriter) narrated the script to me, we spoke about the various facets that would play a role in creating her look—especially her nature. She was spontaneous and feisty; she learnt sword fighting at an early age. In the end, we decided on giving her four different looks through her characterisation, and we divided the colour palette according to that. The first part features her decked in pastel tones. When she gets married, you will see her wearing jewel colours that resonate happiness. But when she loses her husband and her child, the colours get toned down—we used khadi and dyed it in pale, warm shades. The fourth part sees her as a warrior, and for that, we've used dark and strong colours like emerald green, deep blood red, jet black and deep blue. We had some pictorial references of the Rani of Jhansi wearing angarkhas with a child tied at the back, but apart from that, there was no evidence. Initially, we did not want to work with strong colours and fabrics, so I did an amalgamation of the nauvari sari with long-sleeved high-neck blouses in vegetable-dyed colours. The saris are nauvari (nine yards, approximately 8 metres) in statement, but they're actually more than 13 metres long. In terms of fabrics, we incorporated a lot of cottons and silks, and textured it out to give a rough finish to the fabric. For silk fabrics, we gave it a fall so that it reflected femininity and strength in equal measure. You will also see a lot of thread work. The purpose of angarkhas and achkans was to showcase her bold personality and the ferocious warrior that she was. We tied up with Amrapali to create designs that were an amalgamation of Maharashtrian jewellery for all the pivotal characters in the film. Then there are some pieces, like the armor jewellery for Kangana, that I have crafted myself. For her warrior look, there's a pearl necklace that she always wears with the achkan. Then throughout the film, there's a piece she wears on the temple of her forehead that we've used for a decorative purpose. There are also round boota earrings that are a favourite. Mostly, we've kept the jewellery restricted to Maharashtrian styles—like the moti haar and the pohe haar. The nauvari sari has to be the grandest garb, but for Kangana's warrior look, it has to be the one in ivory that's on the posters. It features handmade jewellery that I have designed myself. Kangana was very open and receptive to my costumes. She didn't interfere with the design process. The one conversation we had revolved around one nauvari sari she would be wearing for a scene and she asked me what its texture was like, and what the lighting would be. The only challenging fact was that it was a different genre of the period film that I had to create various looks for, while keeping the magnanimity and the sobriety of the outfits evident throughout. column1: Potli bags vs clutch bags: which one will you choose?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The all-important handbag choice There was a time when we justified the six-figure price tags on our designer handbags with the rationale that they would pair well with our Indian wear too. Whether it was at Diwali parties or destination weddings, high-shine Chanels and silken Bottega Veneta knot clutches were often as meticulously paired with lehengas and anarkalis as the jewellery itself. Cut to the present-day festive circuit, and everyone is suddenly all about the potli bag. Nondescript but not ordinary, what the potli lacks in structure and weighty logos, it makes up for in variety. The versions are many: gota work, zardozi embroidery, pearl work, colour blocks, mirror embellishments, or the one you designed with your mum's leftover sari border. Everyone from Kareena Kapoor Khan and Alia Bhatt to Sonam K Ahuja and Athiya Shetty has been spotted in at least one this season, but does this mean you should simply jump onto the bag-wagon? Sure, the potli's shape and size renders it convenient to quickly throw in your house keys, phone and power bank when you're already running late for a function (box clutch connoisseurs will admit they cannot claim the same with a sigh that comes from years of buying bags based on the dimensions of their phone), but does that mean that the potli should now replace all your clutches as the ultimate festive season go-to? Probably not. It doesn't necessarily work for every occasion and outfit in question. The silhouette, for starters, plays an important role. The potli is a fitting accompaniment for utterly traditional looks, but contemporary Indian wear demands bags that feature a more modern touch. Then there is the event you're wearing it for—make potlis your arm candy for soirees like Diwali dinners, wedding pheras or a formal reception, but when ‘Lamberghini' starts blaring through the speakers at a sangeet party, you'll definitely want a mini chain strap bag you can hastily sling across your shoulder as you take over the dance floor. column1: Conscious shoppers can’t miss this designer pop-up at Fort Kochi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Shop for a good cause If you're a patron of sustainable fashion and Indian textiles, we've got good news for you. India's leading designers are now showcasing an exclusive collection of khadi ensembles at One Zero Eight, a pop-up store in the heart of Fort Kochi in Kerala that coincides with Asia's largest art event, Kochi-Muziris Biennale. An initiative of Ramesh Menon's non-profit organisation, SaveTheLoom.org, the collection at One Zero Eight has been curated to pay a tribute to the 700 weavers and spinners whose houses and looms were destroyed during the Kerala floods in August 2018. The pop-up store will run till March 29, 2019. Expect the likes of Abraham & Thakore, Rajesh Pratap Singh, Ujjwal Dubey, Aneeth Arora, Gaurav Jai Gupta, Karishma Sahani Khan, Santanu Das, Poornima Indrajith, Shreya Oza, Anuj Sharma and Swati Kalsi at the concept space, all of whom have specially designed ensembles in khadi for One Zero Eight—proceeds from which will go towards aiding the handloom projects of SaveTheLoom.org. Meanwhile, designers like Adaveita Mathur, Aditi Dhar, Usha Devi Balakrishnan and more will be retailing their lines—with a special focus on handloom and khadi—at the store as well. What's more, the space will also be home to various workshops and dialogues revolving around the handloom industry. The One Zero Eight pop-up shop—designed and executed by Himanshu Shani of 11.11/Eleven Eleven, experiential designer Wasim Khan of Lemon Design, and Ramesh Menon and Alpi Boylla of SaveTheLoom.org—takes place in a 300-year-old heritage Portuguese home-turned-store in Aambal. column1: Mary Poppins is back, and serving up some unlikely style inspiration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As Emily Blunt steps into the shoes of Mary Poppins in the upcoming sequel, designers have been looking to Julie Andrews’ no-nonsense style in the original 1964 film for inspiration. Cue high necklines, lean skirt suits—and lots of sassy, suffragette attitude. It was back in 1964 that Dick Van Dyke, as Bert the chimney sweep in Disney's original film adaptation of PL Travers' Mary Poppins, sang “wind's in the east, mist coming in; like something is brewing, about to begin,” observing all too appropriately that same feeling one gets when a new trend begins to emerge. This season, in a coincidence that's practically perfect in every way, it's Mary Poppins herself. The character is back on our screens this month, in an updated version of the classic musical fantasy: Mary Poppins Returns stars Emily Blunt as the much-loved magical nanny, with Emily Mortimer and Ben Whishaw and as a grown-up Jane and Michael Banks. And Poppins' signature Edwardian style seems to have resonated with designers, too—high collars, puffed sleeves, and lean, buttoned-up suits, as well as a riff on the merry widow hats of the time, have all appeared in the autumn/winter 2018 and spring/summer 2019 catwalk collections. At Erdem and Simone Rocha, those hat brims were dressed and decorated in elaborate beekeeper styles, while at Moschino and Alexandre Vauthier they had an added Eighties appeal, almost a little caricaturesque—which, bold and fanciful with frills and bright colour, was the case with the overall Poppins looks at Marc Jacobs. Meanwhile, swathes of skirt were in motion at Olivier Theyskens; suit ensembles took to the runways of Chanel, Givenchy and Dior; ruffles were seen at Philosophy di Lorenzo Serafini; and John Galliano's show was simply an ode to the Edwardian wardrobe, inspired as it was by the 1900s-set novel Picnic at Hanging Rock. “High necklines; long, narrow skirts; structured, tailored, emphasised shoulders; covered-up bodies, but not dreary or dowdy, plain or safe; hats and shoulders framing a purposeful gaze…” is how costume designer Liz Krause, who has previously assisted on the TV period drama Poldark, as well as films The Great Wall, Thor and the upcoming JoJo Rabbit, describes the look. “Of course, with Andrews' costumes, there's a healthy dose of late Fifties to early Sixties Hollywood in there and Poppins' accessories were transformed with a sprinkling of Disney dust to become colourful, graphically simple and just a little bit cute,” she adds. It's not the first time the character has found herself with fashion pin-up status. Cast your mind back (again) to Marc Jacobs' hit spring/summer 2009 collection: the designer combined the grunge plaid of his Perry Ellis days with the era's S-bend silhouette, complete with sashes and jaunty boaters for a cool new update. This time round, the homage is more literal, which makes sense in the year that celebrates 100 years since the suffragette movement. (A side narrative in the original film is that Winifred, the Banks children's mother, is herself a suffragette—echoed in the style of clothes she and Poppins wear.) And similarly, it makes sense in a year that sees the revival of two major heritage houses, Poiret and Jean Patou, both of which championed comfortable but elegant dressing and, importantly, no corsets, and both of which experienced an interwar heyday (Mary Poppins Returns is set in the 1930s), revolutionising the way women dressed. Which is perhaps why Mary Poppins has indeed returned. Following fashion's most recent mini streetwear and sportswear revolution, something with structure and a sense of occasion, with heritage and a spot of magic, seems right for now. And all reasoning aside, Mary Poppins famously never explains herself—surely the same sentiment stands when it comes to the renewed appeal of her wardrobe. column1: Micro purses: The extreme accessory trend celebrities can’t get enough of
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Approved by Priyanka Chopra Jonas, Bella Hadid and more We have officially entered 2019, and the micro bag trend isn't going anywhere. Occupying the sweet spot between an evening clutch and a utilitarian shoulder sling, these itsy-bitsy—if somewhat impractical—bags have outlived their longevity from mere runway eccentricities to occupy a cosy spot in the coveted closets of the best dressed of showbiz. Slung over the shoulders or held daintily with a three-fingered grip, micro purses have found a fan in a versatile array of wardrobe options. Just ask Priyanka Chopra Jonas, whose street style rulebook has a pint-sized bag for every occasion and every mood—the newly-married diva's inseparable love for micro purses had her stepping out four times in the same week with this matchbox-sized accessory for company. From pairing a nano Jacquemus bag—that clocked in at 4.75 inches—with a peplum top, to teaming an alligator print Stalvey bag with head-to-toe florals, to mixing up her colour-blocked crimson coords with a miniature statement black bag, Chopra has been feeling the love for minimalism. And she wouldn't be the only one, either. Out and about in town during her debut appearance at Cannes, Kangana Ranaut worked a miniature Tod's bag with flair, opting for a boxy silhouette to elevate its value from a glorified coin purse to a functional wardrobe staple. And it isn't hard to see why the cool crew of Bollywood are leaving behind the carry-alls in favour of these dinky bags. If you've ever been lost in the blackhole of your tote, fighting the clock as you scramble for change for your morning latte ritual, these micro bags herald in essential minimalism. When distilled down to the bare basics of MILK (money, ID, lipstick and keys), you might just find yourself re-evaluating the clutter that your handbag ferries around every day. And what better way to opt for a bout of self-introspection than with a tiny bag that wouldn't have looked out of place in your childhood dollhouse? column1: Ralph Lauren reveals more details hidden in Priyanka Chopra’s wedding gown
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You may know the words she had embroidered on to her white wedding dress, but did you know the significant spots they were placed at? 2018 may be over, but the wedding season that brought the year to close is a gift that keeps on giving. Following Priyanka Chopra's dreamy wedding, which had two ceremonies honouring Hindu and Christian traditions, images have been surfacing now and then giving us a peek at what could have happened at the very private event in Jodhpur. As the newly-weds enjoy their honeymoon in Switzerland, a new set of images from the Christian wedding have surfaced, and give a better peek at all the hidden details incorporated in the white wedding dress. Chopra's wedding gown was crafted by the quintessential American label Ralph Lauren—not a common choice for bridal wear, but certainly a serendipitous and an iconic one for the star. In the last 50 years, Ralph Lauren has only dressed three brides, making her dress one for the books. One look at Chopra walking down the aisle in a 75-foot long veil against the picturesque backdrop of the Umaid Bhavan Palace will have you floored. But it's not the grandeur of the setting or the popularity of the wearer that made the dress unique. Some dresses are meant to endure time and Priyanka Chopra's wedding gown is certain to go down in history for that. The silhouette of the white gown was a modest one, featuring a coat-style high neck, long sleeves and a controlled A-line bottom, but the detail gone into it makes it exquisite. According to RL Mag, Ralph Lauren's official internal publication, “At Priyanka's request, eight special words and phrases were incorporated into the embroidery pattern of the coat, including “Hope” and “Compassion,” as well as a Hindu mantra, “Om Namaha Shivay,” and “December 1, 2018,” the date of the ceremony. The placement of the groom's full name, Nicholas Jerry Jonas, at the front of the coat was mirrored on the back by the names of her parents. (A piece of lace from the dress Nick's mother wore at her own wedding was also sewn into the pattern.) “Family” scrolled along the right sleeve, where Priyanka has a wrist tattoo reading “Daddy's Lil Girl…” And, finally, just over her heart, the word “Love” was stitched in ivory thread.” Chopra was always clear that the message she sent out from the wedding celebrations was that of embracing new cultures and celebrating the best of both worlds. Her gown was laboured over by fifteen artisans in who recreated a pattern resembling Chantilly lace with a mix of techniques including pastiche threadwork and tulle applique. 32,000 pearlescent sequins, 5,600 seed beads, and 11,632 Swarovski crystals were sewn into the body of the dress for an understated but overall pearlescent finish. Underneath, the star wore a strapless column covered in sequins to add more shine to her look. “It's about a woman and a moment. Priyanka knows exactly who she is, and so I wanted the dress to reflect, not only her love story and the romance of India, but also her unique sensibility: strong, smart, and beautiful,” said the designer. Needless to say, groom Nick Jonas was also dressed by Ralph Lauren in a custom Purple Label double-breasted tuxedo with a piece of the bride's dress concealed in a part of the lapel right above his heart with the words “My Jaan” embroidered on it. Families of the bride and groom and the bridal party were also dressed in custom Ralph Lauren looks. Take a closer look at the new images of Priyanka Chopra's wedding dress here. column1: 8 ways to edit your wardrobe for 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get a head-start on spring/summer trends with Vogue’s guide to switching up your style Swap Western boots for barely-there sandals, ditch the cold-shoulder cocktail dress for a crochet midi and switch wintry corduroy for acid-washed denim—your head-start on new season fashion begins now. If you navigated 2018's summer party gauntlet in an off-the-shoulder knee-length dress, your occasionwear wardrobe in 2019 will be all about crochet. The hippified staple has smartened up and (according to Altuzarra, Rodarte, Michael Kors and Self Portrait) now has cocktail-hour approval. [#image: /photos/5ce41bedb8031174ca8f5952]||| ||| Image: Indigital When it comes to your weekend look, it's time to stash Prada's earthy corduroys (for the moment), as Eighties style sweeps back into your off-duty wardrobe – with high-waisted, acid-washed denim, reclaimed from the realm of bad taste. column1: 12 times Kate Middleton’s style got us talking in 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Pregnancy, maternity leave and two royal weddings: the Duchess of Cambridge has navigated 2018 in true British style, calling on her most trusted designers including Alexander McQueen, Jenny Packham and Erdem. Vogue charts Kate Middleton's best looks of the year 2018 was a year of change for Kate Middleton, the Duchess of Cambridge, not least in terms of fashion. She started the year as a proud mother to Princess Charlotte and Prince George, expecting her third baby; and welcomed Prince Louis in April. While on maternity, she went on an international royal tour of Sweden and Norway with Prince William. And later in the year, she attended two royal weddings—all in her signature, impeccable style. Dressing a bump is now second nature to the future Queen, who navigated this pregnancy with a far more experimental approach than before, wearing lots of prints and textures. See the Erdem dresses from her Scandinavian royal tour, particularly the blue velvet midi; the blush pink Alexander McQueen gown with diamond-encrusted neckline in Oslo; and the floral Orla Kiely dress from her visit to the National Portrait Gallery in March. After the birth of Prince Louis, she turned to one of her favourite designers – introducing her newborn to the world outside London's Lindo Wing (the maternity ward where the Duchess, and Diana, Princess of Wales before her, has had all of her three babies) in a red Jenny Packham dress with a white collar. She previously wore a dark green gown by the British label to the Baftas in February; and chose a cream polka dot tea dress by Jenny Packham for the women's final at Wimbledon in July. Naturally, there was a slew of standout McQueen pieces: from the fuchsia knee-length dress she wore to Princess Eugenie's wedding, teamed with a matching Philip Treacy hat; to the pale yellow version of an old favourite for Meghan Markle's big day; the off-white number at Prince Louis's christening, paired with a hat-cum-hairband by Jane Taylor; and the powder blue coat-dress at the RAF centenary celebrations. And the pièce de résistance? At a state dinner at Buckingham Palace in October, the Duchess dazzled in an ice-blue McQueen gown with a fitted, ruched bodice, paired with incredible jewels on loan from the Queen, including what's becoming her go-to tiara (previously one of Diana's favourites too), the Lover's Knot, and Queen Alexandra's wedding necklace (first created in 1860 by royal jeweller Garrard). Her Royal Family Order brooch, awarded by the Queen to relatives as a reward for their service, was the perfect finishing touch. Since resuming royal duties later in the year, she returned to her tradition of recycling outfits. The best repeats? Her lilac Emilia Wickstead dress at the Global Ministerial Mental Health Summit in London (first worn in Hamburg last year); the Catherine Walker coat-dress worn to attend a memorial service in Leicester (debuted at a Sunday service in Balmoral in August); the burgundy Paule Ka skirt and blazer on a visit to University College London (worn for royal engagements in 2012 and 2017); and that turquoise Jenny Packham dress (from the British Olympics Gala in 2012), which she wore to attend the Tusk Conservation Awards. That isn't to say she hasn't had great new additions to her royal wardrobe too. Her off-the-shoulder bouclé-tweed Erdem dress, with pearl button embellishments and a raw hem, worn to the Victoria & Albert Museum in London is perhaps the best yet—taken to the next level by adding Erdem's floral drop earrings. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It’s time to take out your sartorial big guns Let's be honest, most of us have been a little afraid of giving the clashing prints trend a go. But as both celebrities and runways have proven, there is more than one way to get the look right. Forget those archaic sartorial rules of balancing your floral skirt with a solid hued number this season, and instead aim for a mash-up—think chevrons, polka dots, stripes, tartans or vivid graphic prints, nothing is off the table. Whether you are planning a day look or just want to give your work wardrobe a ready-for-the-new-year twist, clashing prints will help you get the right kind of attention in a room. The trick to acing print on print with ease? Stick to one colour family, and match a bold print with a simpler version. Also, don't shy away from mixing prints of the same family—wear micro florals with large sized ones or simply merge differently sized gingham pieces together. You can also marry camouflage with micro florals and animal print with wallpaper blooms. Scroll ahead to get your styling lessons on how to wear print-on-print from the stars themselves. From mixing stripes and polka dots to different animal prints together, here's how the best dressed names on the block have embraced print on print and made it their own. If you're in the mood for taking this mix from desk to drinks, take notes from Kareena Kapoor Khan's closet. Given her knack for being sartorially forward, she worked a polka-dotted one shouldered blouse with a striped skirt once, while Priyanka Chopra Jonas, wore separates showcasing similar prints—a micro floral top with a matching skirt featuring larger sized blooms—at an outing in New York. Katrina Kaif was not too far away either. The actor recently went down the experimental route when she paired a checked grey skirt with a full-sleeved floral top in pink. column1: 3 top celebrity stylists on how they mastermind red carpet looks
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ahead of awards season, Vogue decodes the strategy behind a red carpet look and meets the influential stylists rolling out hit after hit Red carpet premieres and film festivals are year-round occurrences, but awards season—the two-month period bookended by the Golden Globes and Oscars—poses a unique challenge. For the actors, directors and writers nominated, it is an assault course of interviews, panel discussions and awards shows that requires a slew of show-stopping looks. This is where celebrity stylists come in—tastemakers who are experts at interpreting dress codes, have a meticulous eye for detail and have the necessary contacts to nab a client's dream dress straight off the runways. “There are so many things to consider,” says Penny Lovell, the LA-based British stylist behind Rose Byrne and Chrissy Metz's red carpet looks. “What designers do you want to work with? Does the client want something custom? Should we adapt an existing dress?” In a world where a star's red carpet season is distilled into an Instagram gallery, how the looks work alongside one another also becomes important. “I'm always thinking about the story,” agrees Jason Bolden, the stylist responsible for Taraji P. Henson and Yara Shahidi's red carpet hits. “It needs to make sense for the client and show their point of view. Sometimes it can be very personal.” With Hollywood still reeling from the seismic impact of #MeToo and Time's Up, stylists must also consider the political context of their work. “The black looks at the Golden Globes had a big impact,” says Elizabeth Saltzman, who dresses Saoirse Ronan and Gwyneth Paltrow. “I take my job seriously. Every look has to be considered. Last month, at the Governors Awards, I put Saoirse in this white Calvin Klein turtleneck dress. The time was right for that dress. You have to think about what was going on in California at the time with the wildfires. Is that a time to wear sequins?” Ahead of awards season, Vogue speaks to Saltzman, Bolden and Lovell to learn about their process, decode their favourite red carpet looks and hear their plans for the coming year. Clients: Saoirse Ronan, Gwyneth Paltrow, Uma Thurman, Gemma Arterton, Phoebe Waller-Bridge and Jodie Comer. On how she became a stylist I have Valentino's Giancarlo Giammetti to thank for that. Gwyneth and I had been friends forever, but Giancarlo was the first to suggest I style her. I was a fashion editor at American Vogue and then Vanity Fair, so I could always get my friends dresses, but I didn't think I could go into styling. So, I sat down with Gwyneth, interviewed her and measured every inch of her body. If I was going to do it, I wanted to do it well. Luckily, it was a great match. On being methodical Styling is like playing chess—you need to think ahead. I like to talk to people and understand what's going on in their world and how they're feeling. Then I think about the designers I want to work with, what colours I'm interested in, and if the dress has been worn before. Finally, we call in or create the dresses and set up a fitting. I don't choose very many because I don't like designers to get false hope in case it doesn't work out. On her editorial approach The story as a whole is very important. When a client is on a press tour that's like working on a magazine for me. It comes from my editorial training—you don't work in magazines for 30 years and not come out thinking like that. There are the front of book looks which are the press looks, the ones for where she's doing smaller Q&As and screenings. Then the next looks are the ones in the well of the magazine where there are a few different stories for night and day. Then the back of the magazine is for her party looks. On dressing Saoirse Ronan for her Lady Bird press tour It was one of my favourites because all the looks during the tour were so strong. The black Versace dress at the Golden Globes blew my mind, as did the Gucci orange and pink dress with those Fernando Jorge earrings. Then we had the Calvin Klein with the pink bow at the Oscars. Saoirse and I rode on a bus from the hotel to the ceremony—she wasn't allowed to sit down because we didn't want oil marks on the bow, and she had to have white gloves on. It was a great moment to share with her. On her plans for this awards season One of my ladies, Sandra Oh, will be hosting the Golden Globes! I'm starting to work with designers on that. I'm also dressing someone for pretty much every event on the calendar. Clients: Yara Shahidi, Sasha Lane, Taraji P. Henson, Ava DuVernay, Ryan Coogler and Zazie Beetz. On getting his start in the fashion industry I grew up in the American Midwest and went to medical school, but it wasn't really my thing. I ended up getting a job in retail, and that led to me launching my own vintage store in New York. My first styling gig came after I got a phone call from my friend Gabrielle Union. She asked me to come down for Art Basel and to bring stuff from my store. I brought some vintage Alaïa and Lanvin dresses, we got press coverage and the rest was history. The calls just started rolling in. On his unconventional methods This might sound a bit wacky, but when I get the events calendar I see which of my clients is attending, note that in my head and in a couple of days I'll wake up with an idea. It's always about the silhouette for me and then I think about the brands who can provide that. Then I start digging into the shows, swipe through the past five seasons and see what I love. I'm really lucky to have clients who completely turn it over to me. I think in the minds of most people, fittings involve 7 rolling racks and 900 pairs of shoes. My fittings consist of 2 to 3 dresses and 5 pairs of shoes, and we have 2 fittings max. On his favourite look Taraji P. Henson at the 2017 Oscars in her custom Alberta Ferretti is one of my favourites. That year was so monumental for her with Hidden Figures, and the look was an homage to Katherine Johnson, who she played in the film. I brought the Alberta Ferretti design team to her, we nipped in the waist, brought the slit up slightly and that was it! On planning out a red carpet season Sometimes the first red carpet look is the biggest and then I scale down. Or I go super easy to begin with and then go really big at the Oscars. It depends on other things too, like does the client have a big movie out this year? For example, Zazie Beetz was doing a press tour for Deadpool 2. She's in that film with a bunch of guys and so I kept it really relaxed and playful: she wore vintage T-shirts with trousers. Then for that very last red carpet, which was the New York premiere, she arrived in this romantic, floral Valentino couture gown. It felt like her fairy tale moment, and it made even more of an impact because her other looks were low key. On his golden rule for red carpet dressing Make sure the look resonates with the client's personal style. If I was out of the picture, is it something they'd have in their wardrobes? Clients: Kristen Wiig, Rose Byrne, Chrissy Metz, Taylor Schilling, Bella Heathcote and Mary Elizabeth Winstead. On her fashion background I used to work with John Frieda and then I did PR for Burberry. When I started styling for myself I worked for The Sunday Telegraph, The Independent and Condé Nast Traveller. After that I moved to New York and met Keira Knightley on a photoshoot. She was young and in need of a stylist for her next press tour and asked me if I would do it. That's how I started out. On the process of planning a look For me it all depends on the client and it's very different each time. Sometimes I get an idea and put images together for it, and sometimes the client has an idea and comes to me. A few years ago, in the days that women didn't wear jumpsuits on the red carpet, Rose Byrne wanted to wear one. She called me and I suggested this Elie Saab couture jumpsuit. I remember Ryan Seacrest on the carpet saying, “Wow! She's wearing trousers!” and Rose saying, “Why is that such a big deal?” I'm very collaborative and the most important thing for me is that my clients are able to go out, feel confident and do their job. On always having enough options Sometimes you'll see something on the runway and you'll know it's right. It can be that simple, or it can be the last dress the client tries on. Obviously, you have to have back-ups too. What if they spill some coffee down the front of it on the way out of the door? It does happen. If I'm not making a custom dress then I'd have quite a few options. I'll always have my favourites, but beyond that I'll have others should they not work out. On the importance of fit I always try to avoid the moments when people are wearing something strapless and they keep having to pull it up. Fit is a massive thing for me and I work with an amazing tailor. No one should have to worry about their dress falling down on the red carpet. We make sure that all those things are taken care of so the client can be carefree. On bold red carpet dressing One of the looks I'm really proud of from this year was Chrissy Metz at the Emmys. We decided to do something very 1950s and strapless that shows off her beautiful décolletage. I worked really closely with the designer to get the shape and colour we wanted. It was specific to her requests and she felt fantastic in it! When someone really feels good in something you can sense it. column1: Need party dressing inspiration? These celebrities will have you covered
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Right in time for NYE With a little help from the fashion folk, here's your party style pinned down in four tribes. Whose team are you on? [#image: /photos/5ce41b9b89be36d0b07ceafb]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/bellahadid We may have spent the first half of the year obsessing over every permutation of plastic but for the party months, satin, in all its sensuousness, is staging a comeback. There's the buttery and bright version that cues memories of Kate Hudson in How To Lose A Guy In 10 Days (Naomi Campbell wore an almost-identical slip dress to the CFDAs after-party). Then there's the Barbie pink, vintage Jean Paul Gaultier rendition spotted on Bella Hadid. And let's not forget the modern update on the material as seen on Queen Bey in ‘Everything is Love', where a glossy Peter Pilotto pantsuit was anointed the new night-out hero. [#image: /photos/5ce41b9ccc50be7e6413df41]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/rosie.huntington It's safe to say the fanny pack has severed its tourist ties and officially made the transition from micro trend to mainstay. No longer belted to the waist but casually strapped across the chest, fashion insiders have been, quite literally, keeping it close to their heart. To make it after-hours-appropriate, trade in nylon for nappa, straps for chains (cue Rosie Huntington-Whiteley's Alexander Wang number) and logos for embellishments—the It bag of the fanny phenomenon, a butterfly-laden Gucci Marmont, has our vote. [#image: /photos/5ce41b9b3aeed62da2bcd90a]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/kimkardashian We've all found ourselves in this all-too-familiar scenario: you've scored the perfect party pants but don't have a top to match. Taking the stress out of styling are co-ords—yes, matching is now on the mandate. The coolest take on conscious coupling comes courtesy the Kar Jenners—Kim matched her ride with a highlighter hued two-piece and Kylie Jenner's #mirrorfie featured a red-hot latex set. For those still loco for logos, Olivia Culpo's Fendi find is the way to go. [#image: /photos/5ce41b9c3bf9b45854b1b2cc]||| ||| Image: Getty So, here's what's been flashing on our feeds: Priyanka Chopra's form-flattering gown as she arrived at Ralph Lauren's 50th anniversary celebrations, Kendall Jenner alongside Bella Hadid in a one-shoulder Alexandre Vauthier dress and blogger Chiara Ferragni's custom made Prada for her rehearsal dinner. What did these looks have in common? They all came covered in crystals of the splashiest kind. Our advice is to not stop at a mere smattering or trimming but go all out—there isn't a trend more optimistic and uplifting to ring in the new year. column1: 10 tiny sling bags that are just enough for your New Year’s Eve essentials
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From beaded multi-coloured bags to fringed versions, we’ve got them all New Year's is just around the corner, which equates to unending party plans and numerous outfit changes. While you may have already shortlisted options for your party dresses, don't forget that the bag you carry deserves equal attention as well. Fact is, your choice of bag can make or break your outfit—and this season, the memo reads ‘the smaller, the better'. What you need is something that's just enough for a lipstick, a phone and some money. In this carefully-curated guide, we've put together the best sling bags that can also double up as clutches (in case you want to ditch the strap). If you go by the philosophy that more is more, settle the compromise you made on the size of your next bag by going down the glitter route, like with Jimmy Choo's sparkly sling bag. Love studs and beaded embellishments? Christian Louboutin's leather sling bag with its signature gold-tone metal studs, or Zara's beaded multi-hued sling bag, may just be the ones for you. Want to try a different silhouette? Give your outfit a twist with the potli-style sling bag from Topshop—its sparkling sequins will surely set your bag apart from the crowd. Or go with Mark Cross' boxy sling back in gold and black for something more structured. If you're looking for a unique, statement-worthy piece, the pink and metallic minaudière by Okhtein is the one that deserves your attention. Its intricately engraved back and front will elevate your outfit, and you can carry it as a wristlet as well to further reduce any sartorial distraction on the dance floor. Alternatively, you can also channel the holographic trend with Balmain's sling bag, or opt for Mango's fringed version, if you prefer a more minimal option. Our edit features a host of sling bags that will not only keep your nights hands-free and be the saving grace of your party outfits for any end of year celebrations, they won't burn in a hole in your pocket either.
