column1: Meghan Markle’s best style highlights of 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue looks back at Meghan Markle’s mega 2018. From the Givenchy moments—including her wedding dress—to a classic McQueen suit, Stella McCartney styles and a Dior debut, here are her fashion highlights this year To say 2018 has been a whirlwind year for the Duchess of Sussex is something of an understatement. She started as Meghan Markle, former actress and fiancée of Prince Harry, and ended as a fully-fledged member of the royal family, with a title of her own and a marathon of a royal tour—16 days across Australia, Fiji, Tonga and New Zealand—under her belt. Not to mention, she's expecting her first child. Along the way there have been many sartorial highlights, and a rather stealthy transformation too. When her engagement to Prince Harry was announced, Markle's wardrobe consisted of a relatable high-low approach, with a steady rotation of British brands and well-chosen Commonwealth labels, plus a few more affordable pieces from high street brands like J Crew in the mix. Her most significant fashion moments? The navy blue Stella McCartney cape-dress for the Queen's 92nd birthday celebrations; the skinny Alexander McQueen suit she wore to attend the Endeavour Fund Awards in February; and the Amanda Wakeley white coat from the Commonwealth Service at Westminster Abbey, Markle's first public appearance with Her Majesty. Bags from Mulberry and Scottish label Strathberry, hats by Stephen Jones and Philip Treacy, and shoes by Manolo Blahnik also featured as her accessories of choice. Then the big day arrived and her style rocketed to decidedly high-high. Her wedding dress, by Clare Waight Keller, was Haute Couture Givenchy—and the start of a very special relationship with the British designer. Since then, the Duchess has turned to Givenchy for many landmark events. Her first Ascot? A My Fair Lady moment. Her first solo appearance with the Queen? You guessed it: a cream cape-dress, belted at the waist. The Duchess has also championed designers from the Commonwealth, including Canadian brands Judith & Charles and Mackage; as well as supporting many ethical fashion brands, such as Reformation, Outland Denim, Veja and Rothy's. Aside from her first public appearance after the wedding—at Prince Charles's 70th birthday celebration, wearing a simple dress by British high-street brand Goat (and those much-discussed tights!)—the newlywed's wardrobe has been almost exclusively designer, often custom-made, blowing the budget with every new outing. Highlights include: Carolina Herrera (both the off-the-shoulder pale pink number at June's Trooping the Colour, and the flared denim summer dress at July's Sentebale Polo Cup); Prada (at the Queen's Young Leaders Awards Ceremony in June); Dior (at the RAF centenary celebrations in July); and Oscar de la Renta (a romantic black tulle gown, with laser-cut bird motifs, worn in Sydney on the Australian leg of her royal tour). We've seen her fashion sense shift, from a more relaxed, minimal and trend-led approach to dressing, to a more feminine and tailored version of herself. And as her style changes during pregnancy, her love of monochrome and block colours is likely to continue. As is her penchant for tailored jackets, shirtdresses (the pleated, olive green Brandon Maxwell in Sydney deserves a shout-out for supreme easy elegance) and, of course, luxury labels. But before we look ahead to next year, Vogue looks back at her best outfits of 2018. View Gallery 18 Photos Meghan Markle’s best style highlights of 2018 Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 52 beautiful Bollywood-approved saris we spotted in 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Designer drapes done right Lehengas, anarkalis and sharara sets will always look good, but no silhouette can beat the timeless elegance of a sari. Over the past year, Bollywood's best dressed women have returned to the six yard staple time and again, proving that the drape is as versatile as it is beautiful. Here's a look back at how Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, Deepika Padukone, Sonam K Ahuja and others wore their saris in 2018. Back in June, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan attended an event at the Ambani residence in a sheer, burnt gold sari that had everyone's attention for its party-ready vibe. As the year progressed, we've seen more than just a few Bollywood ladies spruce up their festive wardrobes with shimmering cocktail saris. While Priyanka Chopra Jonas celebrated Isha Ambani's engagement at Lake Como wearing an embellished nude Manish Malhotra sari, both Gauri Khan and Esha Gupta made things easier with pre-draped saris that are perfect for the woman who likes to keep her hands free on the dance floor. Khan stood out this year in her blush pink Tarun Tahiliani, and Gupta's feather-detailed Falguni Shane Peacock is one every bridesmaid should check out. Bollywood icon Rekha is known for her extensive collection of Kanjeevaram saris, but she's not the only one to favour the handwoven drapes. This year, several Bollywood stars were also spotted in rich weaves, from Kanjeevarams to silk brocades. Post her mother's demise, Janhvi Kapoor collected Sridevi's last National Award in Delhi wearing a pink and ivory sari that belonged to the late icon, and later in the year, Anushka Sharma made a strong case for Chanderi saris in her deep green version. At Sonam K Ahuja's wedding reception, Chanderis won Kangana Ranaut's vote too. As for Rekha, this year's winning look was that gold and white sari, worn with a delicate choker in June. As fashion continues to reinvent itself, so has the traditional Indian sari. During Veere Di Wedding promotions, Sonam K Ahuja pushed the envelope once again with her sartorial choices, promoting the film in a distressed denim sari (worn over a cropped white shirt instead of a blouse) on one occasion. At red carpets, Malaika Arora ditched traditional drapes for a strapless futuristic Amit Aggarwal sari gown, and both Mira Rajput Kapoor and Kriti Sanon skipped on fussy petticoats for trousers under their saris. Pro tip: You can easily give your sari a new-age spin by following in Mira Rajput Kapoor's footsteps and adding a belt over your OOTD. Across ages, occasions and styles, one colour reigned supreme in Bollywood's sari wardrobe this year: white. While Jacqueline Fernandez picked a lacy Manish Malhotra sari earlier this year, Dimple Kapadia went the royal route in her ivory Kanjeevaram drape, and Sara Ali Khan's creamy white Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla sari was another winner. Sisters Kareena Kapoor Khan and Karisma Kapoor proved that a white sari can work just about anywhere (with the former in Manish Malhotra, and the latter in an bohemian Anamika Khanna embroidered with multicoloured threads), and Deepika Padukone even worked a white caped sari during at TIME event in New York. column1: All I want for Christmas: The Dubai edition
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Fill your Christmas stockings with treats from the Middle East This year, I have made my Christmas wishlist a ‘Made in the Middle East' one, as there so many fabulous local designers who have managed to marry this region's love of decadence with an au courant feel of modern restraint. The result is something that has a hint of opulence, but is so elegant that it becomes a timeless investment. This is why, everything I want for Christmas is full of Middle Eastern promise. If you are going to Dubai for the holidays, why not look at something local that speaks of modern Arab design as a stocking filler for your loved ones? Women in this region love their arm candy, and a designer bag is a must in most wardrobes—they seldom leave home without one. The region has a couple of home-grown handbag brands such as Natalie Trad and Sarah's Bag that have made a mark internationally. And Dubai-based Lilian Afshar's brand, L'Afshar, known for their Perspex clutches, is definitely one to watch out for too. The lines of her clutches are very clean, but textured effects such as marble or a “crushed ice” look add a feel of luxury to them. What's more, she can personalise your bag with your birthdate or wedding date too! The brand is popular among celebrities—Kendall Jenner has stepped out in a Lucite bag from L'Afshar on more than one occasion—and the clutches make for the perfect companion to a cocktail dress, or even a cocktail sari. L'Afshar is available on both Moda Operandi and Net-A-Porter, and Afshar recently started a collection of leather bags as well. Stacking rings is so 2018; now it's time to make a statement with the signet ring. Traditionally worn by men, this accessory has become a girl's best friend in recent times. A true signet ring is personalised, and when it comes to personalised jewellery in Dubai, your go-to jeweller has to be Bil Arabi. The brand is all about the use of the Arab alphabet with a contemporary touch. Hailing from Beirut, Nadine Kanso is proud to call Dubai her home and is known as someone who sets the style agenda in the Middle East. Thanks to her love of rings, which she marries with her unique take on androgyny, the signet has always been an important part of her collection. She recently launched a new collection of signet rings that use both enamel and diamonds, and they are beautiful enough to tempt you to get one for every finger. Situated at a studio in the Dubai Design District, Kage is one of the coolest Arab labels to know. A pioneering brand that went low-key for a few years, this one made a comeback with their fall/winter 2016 collection, under the creative directorship of Basma Abu Ghazaleh. Unlike other ‘Made in the Middle East' labels, Basma stays away from embroidery and embellishment—making Kage the go-to label for the more discerning fashion girl. Well-tailored and free spirited, she mixes plaid with floral prints and blazers with Bardot-style dresses. Her fall/winter 2019 collection is eclectic yet elegant, and is currently stocking at stores like Saudi Arabia's Harvey Nichols and Dubai's Etoile. In conclusion, Kage is wearable label that features a street-style feel, and works well for a working girl who still likes to have fun with fashion. Shiffa Beauty is one of Middle East's best-selling luxury skincare brands, and also has a sizeable global presence. Run by Emirati beauty boss, Dr Lamees Hamden, its ‘hero' product is the healing balm, which I use as a night cream in the winter months. The cult clean beauty brand recently introduced an Emerald Clarifying Oil too, inspired by Indian gemmology, which has been tailor-made for oily skin types. With an ingredient list of neem and sage that provide with antibacterial and anti-fungal qualities, the oil promises to balance and purify one's skin. column1: Karisma Kapoor takes you on a tour inside her wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The actor who swears by a minimalist manifesto, lets us in on all the designer labels you’re likely to spot in there (and the shoes she partial to) For as long as I can remember, black has been a constant in my closet. Black is such a chameleonic colour; what changes is my interpretation of the shade. With a little bling, it becomes perfect for a night out. Those who know me know that I'm an introvert and, given a chance, I would skip a club opening for dinner and drinks with my closest crew. An ideal Saturday night is one where the entire Kapoor family comes together at my sister's house, where so many special evenings have transpired. In these casual and intimate moments, my style always remains classic—a pair of well-cut trousers and a blouse (in black, of course) and sometimes a simple silhouette swap, like an off-shoulder top, adds a quick dose of glamour. For me, nothing goes as seamlessly from day to dark like a black top with tassels paired with jeans and ankle boots—it's been my fail-safe formula for lazy brunches that can sometimes turn to long nights. Finding designers that you automatically gravitate towards in a row of clothes is the most liberating feeling. There are only a few that perfectly fall into my comfort zone. There's Stella McCartney, Loewe, Armani (their classic dresses are a mainstay in my wardrobe) and, of course, Balmain. I recently wore a glitter Balmain jacket for a semi-formal evening and all I needed was a pair of second-skin jeans and stilettos to complete the look. My advice to those who stock up on staggering stilettos, like I do, is to invest in comfortable Aquazzura and Saint Laurent shoes. Their heels have seen me through long nights of dancing with Bebo, Mala and Amu. I'm a firm believer in keeping accessories to a minimum—you'll rarely see me wearing earrings. I like sharp looks and sometimes jewellery just isn't required. If I'm wearing a red gown to an event, as someone who likes to edit her jewellery down to one piece, I'll give earrings a miss for a slightly statement necklace. For anything other than the red carpet, my only finishing touch is a statement watch. And more often than not, I'll add a bright lip—a fiery red is always a classic. While dressing up is such a large part of the excitement of going out, in my opinion, beyond the restaurants, the house parties and the late nights that turn into early mornings, happiness is at the centre of enjoying yourself. If you're positive, the party is always in your head, and it doesn't really matter where you go or what you wear. — As told to Akanksha Kamath View Gallery 5 Photos Karisma Kapoor takes you on a tour inside her wardrobe Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 17 times Bollywood celebrities proved the versatility of the denim jacket
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The denim jacket has earned its place as a favourite in celebrity wardrobes, but that’s just one of the reasons why it should make its way to your closet It may see its popularity rise and ebb in phases, but the denim jacket never given up its spot as a wardrobe essential. This year itself saw the outerwear staple on the runways of Chanel and Miu Miu, while designers closer to home—Dhruv Kapoor and Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice—gave it their own new-age spin. Given the myriad ways it can be styled in, it is little wonder that this multi-purpose closet essential is so popular among women from all walks of life. Those charting celebrity style in 2018 may have seen leading Bollywood celebrities like Kareena Kapoor Khan, Sonam K Ahuja and Alia Bhatt all making the denim jacket their go-to layer, no matter the season. Take Kapoor Khan for instance, who sported three different styles (embroidered, oversized and acid washed) on three different occasions (the gym, the airport and a movie screening respectively), proving the piece's versatility. Meanwhile, Ahuja gave the denim-on-denim trend new meaning by pairing her light blue, boxy, cropped jacket over a button-down denim waistcoat, and Anushka Sharma played with colour with hers, picking a vibrant yellow slogan denim jacket by Kanika Goyal x Babbu. Sharma's recent airport look was also equally slick—the star opted for a deconstructed denim trench coat by Dhruv Kapoor, and wore it with a pair of jeans. While Kapoor Khan styled her denim jackets in athleisure-inspired outfits only, Katrina Kaif was more open to experimentation with her sartorial pairings—the actor layered her boyfriend denim jacket over a sequinned, champagne-coloured dress, making a strong case for denim jackets as a worthy addition to your party wear wardrobe. column1: Tarun Tahiliani fondly remembers his eternal muse, Minal Modi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion "She taught me more than anybody else about fashion and quality, and what the essence of luxury was." Minal Modi, 64, wife of former IPL chairman Lalit Modi, lost her battle to cancer last week. To honour her memory, Tarun Tahiliani gets nostalgic about his one true muse, remembering the woman who played an integral part in couturier's life. There were two things that always struck me about Minal: One, how she was always so kind to everybody, and how everybody from the watchman up always loved her, because she always spoke to them with genuine love and kindness as opposed to lot of people who look down at their staff. Two, she had the ability to take things from wherever she went and incorporate it into her life. So food would be served in slabs of mother of pearl, bohemian glass would be used to complement her dinner table, little chatai-ed bowls were used for pills and other things—everything always had to have an aesthetic. It was never about the value. It was the way it was used that gave it power and beauty. And for me, that was the real learning before the age of the brand, where a logo made up often for a lack of quality of style. She also ran a very successful business doing embroideries for the greats in interior decoration, like Alberto Pinto, who taught her, and then she would in turn teach me. She taught me more than anybody else about fashion and quality, and what the essence of luxury was. Not sure when we first met; I think I saw her on a flight. I was fascinated by [the fact that] somebody that tiny [was] being helped with 12-14 suitcases. Subsequently, I met her when her son was born and she came in to get something done for a big lunch that was being held at the Modi residence in Delhi. And slowly as we discovered we had common interests—common heritage and a delicious taste for fine things. We became friends. Like a good wine, it was a slow and steady process that took years to find itself. When Tanya Godrej got married, she came back to me with these wonderful custom-made Manolo Blahniks and said: I've heard you drape, I want to look like I am draped in a turban. And so began another lecture and journey on how the best patterns were cut on the body. Obviously, this is someone who's had couture all her life and didn't subscribe to the Indian idea of couture—which was just very beautiful embroidery—but of things that were being moulded to the body. And so on and on we went; we travelled and saw wonderful exhibits together, we saw the south of France, we were in Thailand... we did amazing trips through Africa and, of course, London and New York. Going over to Juhu was always a visual treat, because she lived cocooned in her own little world of palm trees, fresh motias, candles, and very fresh organic food. [But] there was nothing excessive about her. She achieved the perfect balance, and that's a learning for a lot of us. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The most stylish designer kurtas to stock up on before the New Year
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Just in time for your end-of-year shopping spree No matter what the season is, a classic kurta is the perennial staple your wardrobe needs all year round. Not only is it perfect for traditional events, it is also one of the most fuss-free pieces of clothing, and can be styled in multiple ways to suit any kind of occasion. December is a good time to get your closet ready for anything the new year may have to throw at you. Pick from basic whites, printed kurtas and even embroidered versions to add the convenience of kurtas to your daily wear in 2019. From sheer to patterned, party to minimal, these are the trending kurta styles we are currently eyeing. Yellow has long been hailed as the definitive shade of this season. Those wanting to inject of bolt of colour into their wardrobe can look to Kanelle's side-draped kurta set or Samant Chauhan's embroidered kurta and sharara for a mehandi ceremony. The sartorially brave may be tempted by NorBlack NorWhite's bold checked kurta set for a weekend getaway, while Payal Khandwala's striped number, styled with a pair of flared jeans, will make for a sound option for a day full of errands. Gopi Vaid's embroidered kurta and dhoti set is perfect for those in search of something breezy and bohemian too. But if you're more of a minimalist, throw Bias' oversized kurta over a pair of ripped jeans to channel a cool, laid-back vibe. Come festive season, don't miss out on Abhinav Mishra's kurta and sharara set featuring mirror detailing. Those looking for something bolder can check out Nikasha's pink kurta and tunic set as well. Looking for something to replace your formals for work? Bank upon Anavila's tie-up kurta or go with Simar Dugal's block-print sharara set to tide you through the days you don't feel like dressing up for the office. But the versatility of a kurta is not restricted to workwear and casual wear. Swap your done-and-dusted LBD with Abraham & Thakore disco-ready kurta and salwar pants this party season, to ensure nothing comes in the way of you dancing till dawn. column1: From Meghan Markle to the Queen, how the royals do Christmas Day dressing
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The royal family’s sartorial choices are a source of global fascination year-round, but rarely more so than when they step out together for their Christmas Day church service at Sandringham. Vogue looks back at their most memorable festive outfits to date Last Christmas, the internet went into a collective frenzy following an unprecedented break in royal protocol. Meghan Markle, newly-engaged to Prince Harry, had been invited to attend the Queen's annual Christmas Day church service. Held at St Mary Magdalene near Sandringham House, the event is normally reserved for members of the royal family (the Duchess of Cambridge has only attended since her marriage in 2011), so Markle's presence raised a number of questions. Would the couple disregard protocol in other matters? What were their plans over Christmas? And, what had she chosen to wear on this momentous occasion? The answer to the latter was a Sentaler camel coat, a chestnut-brown Philip Treacy hat, suede Stuart Weitzman boots and a Chloé Pixie bag. No sooner were the items identified, that many of them promptly sold out online. Bojana Sentaler, the designer behind the Toronto-based outerwear label Sentaler, told People that she began receiving orders for the coat from around the world. “Meghan has been a fan of Sentaler for a couple of years now, so I was aware that she owned our coats,” she added. “But it wasn't until that day, at 6am, that I woke up to a tweet of Meghan Markle wearing my coat. It was the best Christmas present I could have ever received!” “‘The Meghan effect” has proven to be as lucrative for brands as “the Kate effect”. On the same day, the Duchess of Cambridge opted for a Miu Miu tartan coat with gold buttons and a black velvet collar. Within 24 hours, it was out of stock online and being advertised on eBay for exorbitant sums. In the past, the Duchess's Christmas Day uniform has consisted of sleek coats, knee-high boots, Lock & Co. hats and delicate Kiki McDonough earrings. She has a penchant for jewel tones and an eye for a high-street bargain: in 2016, she wore a burgundy belted coat from Hobbs that cost just £182. The brand benefited from the association, posting a 14.3 per cent increase in sales over the 13 weeks leading up to New Year's Eve. Also of note are the Queen's Christmas ensembles: brightly-coloured coats, coordinating hats, brooches and her signature pearls. Meanwhile, Prince Philip, William and Harry rely on dark suits and wool coats, rounding off a supremely stylish group. As the royal family prepare to reunite for this year's outing, Vogue looks back at their best Christmas Day outfits to date. column1: Hot pink is the new black, and these celebrities are here for it
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Rihanna to Deepika Padukone, everyone is crushing on this colour Move over Barbie and Elle Woods. There is a new clique of pink purveyors in town, and they are less about sugar, but all about spice. While one can easily find over 30 variations of pink in the Pantone shade card, it's the deep Mexican pink that has recaptured the imagination of this style set. And Priyanka Chopra Jonas' style diaries showcase that she prefers to wear pink from head-to-toe, either as a pantsuit or a silk shirt and trouser set, complete with matching heels—less Barbie clone, more badass boss lady, we think. column1: 3 Indian designers who hit the 10-year milestone recount their journey
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The years aren’t just a measure of time; they encompass effort, evolution and achievement From the sleepy village of Malhausi in India to the runways of London, Paris and Milan, Rahul Mishra's career trajectory has been on an upward swing ever since his breakout collection at the Lakmé Fashion Week in 2006. All through his success over the past decade the 39-year-old designer has stayed true to his roots, showcasing a love for traditional Indian textiles and handmade couture very early on. “Each collection has a narrative inspired by childhood memories,” says Mishra. He tells Vogue how he has evolved through every milestone. [#image: /photos/5ce41e059cc0c012bcf9c2a2]||| ||| Image: Farhan Hussain Who'd have thought that a boy from a remote village in India would become the first non-European to win a scholarship to Istituto Marangoni, the prestigious school of fashion and design based in Milan, Italy? If you knew Rahul Mishra as a child, however, you'd be far from surprised. “I've always wanted to be an artist, but because I was a good student my father was determined I get into IIT and become an engineer. After a confrontation with him on my career choices, I moved out, got a post-graduate degree at the National Institute of Design in Ahmedabad, shifted base to Delhi and never looked back.” Mishra credits his vast knowledge of sustainable fashion to an early exposure to nature and colour as well as the many stories he grew up listening to while living with his grandparents. “The background that I come from actually gave me an edge—I understood the hardships Indian artisans go through, how even with the lack of electricity work goes on,” he says. It was his debut collection created with cotton handloom textiles from Kerala that led to his selection by the Istituto Marangoni and eventually the launch of his eponymous label in 2008. In 2014, Mishra catapulted to international fame when he won the International Woolmark Prize, beating frontrunner Joseph Altuzarra. The international jury spoke about being “impressed by his incredible knowledge of the art of embroidery, by the coherence of his collection and also by his great passion.” Showing at Milan's La Triennale museum, Mishra's winning collection, The Lotus Effect, brought to life fabric with Merino wool yarn and woollen zardozi embroidery by craftsmen in Kolkata on jackets, dresses and trousers. “No one from India had ever won before.” The line also made way for retailers like Harvey Nichols and Saks Fifth Avenue. A year after Mishra won, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London made The Lotus Effect a part of its The Fabric Of India exhibition for three months. “This prize defined who I was as a designer. I began defying stereotypes. Just because I won did not mean I was the best—I had to continue to work hard.” Mishra debuted at Paris Fashion Week in 2014 with The Ferryman's Tale. “Showing here is on the wish list of every fashion student and designer. It was no different for me.” With a poem by Rumi as its inspiration note, the collection got a great reception and soon saw him showing at fashion capitals around the world. “It was a surreal experience—before the show my wife Divya and I visited a temple, and when we finally entered the venue she could not hold back her tears. It was that special for us,” recalls Mishra, “Nine seasons later, the feeling is the same. To showcase your work alongside iconic brands like Chanel, Dior…” After every season in Paris, the designer says he comes back brimming with ideas. “It makes you question your design ethos and review your intellectual property,” says Mishra. Earlier this year, Mishra was back in Paris to showcase his Gossamer collection. “Usually when designers use craft it is either too decadent or bohemian. With this collection, we tried to make the clothes strong and modern,” he explains. Mission accomplished when Suzy Menkes said: “In his nostalgia for the India of his childhood, the designer might seem to be drowning in a romantic view of his country's past. Yet his work with traditional craftsmanship produced fine examples of modern fashion—the apparently simple beginning easier to digest than the more elaborate evening looks. But Rahul Mishra is a rare Indian designer to bring his creativity literally and figuratively away from his homeland.” — By Sheree Gomes Gupta “Our work cannot be vacuous. It needs to be political. It needs to be more proactive, in some cases provocative. As creatives, our work needs to consume us,” says the Kolkata-based designer as he traces his 10-year tenure. [#image: /photos/5ce41e049cc0c06669f9c29e]||| ||| Image: Farhan Hussain Making clothes was not part of my big life plan. I had a background in macro economics and I only pursued fashion as an escape. I never felt a sense of belonging in the schools and universities I studied in, the cities I lived in, and the social circles I placed myself within. It was after I graduated from Central Saint Martins that I strategically chose Kolkata to reside in. The city has afforded me a sense of anonymity; it has kept me away from the epicentre of the industry I engage with and has facilitated the way I currently operate. I stay hidden by choice and use that very choice to interact with the mainstream when required. The early 2000s were an important time for fashion in India, when my generation of clothes-makers all brought something new to the table—there was the exploration of cutting-edge textiles, the questioning of non-sustainable practices and, with designers like myself, the introduction of conscious anti-fit clothing and prints. Print, for me, has always been a form of storytelling. In my spring/summer 2010 collection, I used jail stripes and barcodes to depict concentration camps in Russia. If you ever scanned the barcodes, it would say 1955—the name of my label. Over time the storytelling evolved into a social commentary of sorts. I stopped using prints, because I felt the industry was saturated with them, and turned to extreme silhouettes. I designed a dress called ‘The 80-year-old woman'. Through pattern-cutting techniques, I created a saggy front leading all the way to the knee of the dress. Today, free flowing three-dimensional folds, fabrics travelling in multiple directions, garments oscillating on an imaginary axis and pattern manipulations are all elements still crucial to my craft but what's new is a sense of urgency. I feel like I need to do everything to encapsulate the meaning of our times. When it comes to exhibiting my work, I've looked beyond the runway, be it in the form of a zine or at a gallery. In 2013, I showed at Project 88, a beautiful art gallery in Mumbai, and later at Kolkata's Harrington Street Arts Centre. What prompted me to forgo traditional formats was my residency at Khoj International Artists' Association, where there were no constraints. You could have a book reading or film screening to show your designs. The experience also encouraged me to send out incomplete garments on the runway so I could clearly convey concepts behind my creations. I am extremely fortunate that I have been able to work as a free agent, delve into projects that interest me and, above all, collaborate with creatives who don't necessarily share my personal train of thought but with whom I can create meaningful bodies of work. In the past, I've collaborated with Eina Ahluwalia, a close friend and jewellery artist. I had zero understanding of metal and she took the time and energy to explain how things work. We are now creating a full-fledged collection of jewellery together. I've also partnered with Paul Matter in Delhi. They took me through their workshops and adapted my pattern-cutting methods for metal-cutting to make lights. In the next decade, I look forward to more such meaty collaborations and allies. I also urge the younger generation to be braver. The moment they realise that their creative agency lies within them, it will transform their work. Good design is the only currency they need to employ. That is how it's been for me the last 10 years.” —As told to Neharika Manjani What do a military man, a bohemian artist and fashion-forward poetess have in common? They each laid the foundation for designer Urvashi Kaur's eventual road to fashion. The Delhi-based history graduate, well known for her trans-seasonal, travel-inspired collections and celebration of textiles, walks us down memory lane as she reflects on her 10-year journey in the industry—from her love for new cultures born from living all over the globe as an army chief's daughter, following her painter mum to local weavers' haunts, and summers spent in her writer nani's garage-turned-walk- in-closet (think vintage-style tin almaaris housing a cornucopia of clothing). [#image: /photos/5ce41e04cc50be564113e2d9]||| ||| Image: Ankush Maria [#image: /photos/5ce41e04cc50be013113e2d5]||| ||| Image: Ankush Maria But the road to fashion was more serpentine than straight. While she enjoyed clothes and the drama of dressing up, the professionally trained dancer joined a theatre troupe after college. A serendipitous moment—being chosen to hand-craft costumes for Amir Raza Hussain's interpretation of Andrew Lloyd Webber's Starlight Express—propelled her to view fashion as a veritable career. Following a yearlong apprenticeship with designer Neeta Paul and a stint at ESMOD France, she launched Urvashi Kaur in 2008. [#image: /photos/5ce41e05b8031154588f5c0e]||| ||| Image: Ankush Maria A little-known town in China called Xining, the myriad colours of Fez in Morocco… travel has been a constant muse from the start, finding expression in most of her collections. Says Kaur, “Growing up, I moved around a lot, so had to constantly adapt. I was drawn to different cultures and characters. I love studying people and discovering their stories, the clothes they wear, the materials they use… They all have so much to say. I make it a point to travel to a new place at least once a year. “I recently attended a family wedding in Florence, which is one of my favourite places to visit. And I'm always up for adventure and would love exploring the Far East and South Africa a bit further.” Recognised for her patronage of Indian weaves and use of handmade techniques, Kaur, whose personal favourites include labels like Loewe, Marni, Rick Owens and Maison Margiela, highlights her brand's USP: “I work well with the trans-seasonal aspect and each of my collections is fluid and can transition into different seasons effortlessly. This realisation helped me grow and has now come to be a key feature of the label.” She veers towards handmade pieces because of the emotional connection, “Handcrafted pieces tell a story about the person who made them. They lend pieces of themselves to it, making it personal.” [#image: /photos/5ce41e054a30b3857d12c0a5]||| ||| Image: Ankush Maria Sustainable. Eco-conscious. Gender-fluid. Inclusive. These buzzwords have permeated the fashion industry lately, but for Kaur, who launched a menswear collection and a dynamic, accessible diffusion line (Kapda by Urvashi Kaur) in 2016, her sensibilities have always led her to create conscious clothing with a focus on reviving indigenous crafts and techniques—think batik, shibori and block-printing coming to life through fluid layers and easy separates. Recently, the label was even invited by the government to create and explore indigenous Rajasthani textile treatments with master craftsmen from Rajasthan, and they also work with Sally Holkar's Handloom School, amongst other weavers and organisations. Kaur is also constantly looking ahead—from being a finalist at the Vogue Talents contest of Vogue Italia, showing at Who's Next Paris in 2018 along with gearing up for making inroads into newer markets, this year has been a busy one. Reflecting on her evolution and the current fashion scenario, Kaur says, “I've evolved and learned along the way. Our world is currently going through such a major upheaval— we're slowly going back to methods and ways of living that are in sync with the environment. It is a rediscovery of sorts. And our belief in the co-existence of heritage and accessibility within a contemporary fashion and lifestyle framework has led to a beautiful, explorative journey personally as well as for the label.” — By Chandni Sehgal What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The one print every celebrity is wearing right now
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Are you ready to follow your animal instinct? With throwback revival in full swing, fashion offers a warm welcome to an old favourite—animal prints. Making its way through the plethora of patterns, the 1980s wild trail of animals are currently ruling the fashion game. This time around, it's not just about the classic leopard prints—think snakeskin, zebra, python prints in the boldest hues. From Tod's snakeskin bags, Victoria Beckham's leopard print coats and Diane von Furstenberg's vibrant dresses, the classic animal prints are getting a fresh new perspective. Equal parts dramatic and statement-making, these eye-catching prints promise to help you channel your spirit animal with zestful appeal. Whether you want to wear the print head-to-toe, or prefer to bring the trend in with a singular sartorial element, here's how you can get a head start. Who better than the leading celebrities to inspire you to try it, right? Kareena Kapoor Khan's put her stamp on animal prints when she was spotted in a striking red Vetements' top at a dinner date with friends. Even Priyanka Chopra Jonas was quick to give the trend a test run—be it by braving the New York chill in a cosy leopard-print fluffy Alice + Olivia coat or by opting for a printed cheetah print turtleneck for a flight. And Malaika Arora proved her alliance with that grey and black animal print dress by her own brand, The Label Life. But that's not all. Overseas, Kylie Jenner sported snakeskin boots with a denim jumpsuit, and Kim Kardashian West turned heads with her printed green dress. Scroll ahead to take a closer peek at A-listers donning animal prints. View Gallery 11 Photos The one print every celebrity is wearing right now Considering party season is here, there could not be a better time to kick things up a notch sartorially. Trade your classic LBD with Balmain's leopard print velvet mini dress, or opt for Sara Battaglia's leopard print metallic version to ensure that all eyes stay on you. Alternatively, showcase a daring take on the trend by styling Versace's printed yellow blazer with flared pants, or go all out with Tom Ford's red pants. Kolor's zebra print coat also offers a great way to add animal prints to your winter wardrobe in a not-so-subtle manner. Not a fan of maximalism? Look to Francesco Russo's ankle length boots or Casadei's pump heels to elevate your weekend look. If you always wanted to give animal prints a go, now is the time to do it. column1: 44 coolest celebrity-approved pantsuits we spotted in 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Power dressing on the red carpet A crisp white shirt, a classic black dress, a simple sari... some silhouettes just never go out of style, and a pantsuit is one of them. From brand new Bollywood faces like Janhvi Kapoor to celebrity icons such as Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, the classic has won everyone's vote this year and for good reason. The coordinated blazer and trouser set says ‘business' when worn in a neutral hue, but can just as easily work at a party if you know how to play with your prints and colours. Here's a look at how our favourite Bollywood and Hollywood stars worked the power staple this 2018. Black is a failsafe option, but that doesn't mean one shouldn't have fun with crazy colours. This year, Deepika Padukone threw caution to the wind in her purple Victoria Hayes pantsuit, while Kangana Ranaut took to pretty pastel pinks and blues at the Mumbai airport. Overseas, Tracee Ellis Ross went for a royal blue House of Holland look, Kendall Jenner traded black pantsuits for a canary yellow avatar and Gal Gadot proved you can work a bright bubblegum pink hue pantsuit for red carpet events. Love bold patterns and embellishments? So do Priyanka Chopra Jonas, Malaika Arora and Blake Lively. While Chopra Jonas had everyone doing a double take in her crazy printed Anna Sui, Arora made a strong case for dainty patterned pantsuits and Lively relied on not-so-basic versions of the power staple while promoting her film, A Simple Favor. column1: Meet the woman behind Priyanka Chopra’s best red carpet moments
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Remember the trench coat dress? View Gallery 40 Photos Meet Cristina Ehrlich the woman behind Priyanka Chopra’s style transformation What goes into making a crossover star and style phenomenon? Meet Cristina Ehrlich, the driving force behind Priyanka Chopra's newfound style. The accolade-sweeping stylist is responsible for many a memorable red-carpet moments for stars like Penélope Cruz, Allison Williams, Tina Fey, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, amongst others. From the emoji evoking red dress, to the trailing trench coat dress that launched a hundred memes, Ehrlich's touch has elevated Priyanka Chopra's style from ‘best dressed' to one that warrants conversation. Vogue spoke to the star behind the star. How would you describe Priyanka Chopra's sense of style? She has a lot of creative freedom and likes to play around with wearing different looks. She really gets into every detail of a look, down to the small details like the colour of her nails, to what shoes she is wearing. She is like an artist; you can see she has fun with it and doesn't like to get lost in a crowd. In a way, she is a stylist's dream. She likes to use her voice and fashion to express her different moods. And how would you say you have influenced her style? My take on it is that, when Priyanka came to New York for different roles than she plays in India, she wanted to collaborate with someone who could open her eyes to fashion, more from the American perspective. I have a very European style, so that was a common denominator for us—where she knew I would push her a little but her style would remain true to who she is. She has a very strong sense of style and knows what she likes. Priyanka is a global celebrity who has a strong fan following with the India audience. As a stylist, which audience's taste do you cater to? Working with Priyanka is a complete collaboration. She is my audience and I feel that with her sensibility of fashion with India, she likes to play with different silhouettes and colours. There is something about her that no matter what the look is, there is usually a strong point of view. She isn't someone who puts half a look together. She likes to have a reason behind why or what she is wearing. She is incredibly porous and really loves the collaboration and depending on the day, she likes to do different things—she loves urban street wear, is inspired by music and model off-duty looks. She is very versatile and will try anything from a pair of men's pants to a pyjama look, to a classic bombshell moment. What do think of her style in India? She has a different team in India. We've had some dialogue, but when she goes to India, she works with her team there. To date, I haven't collaborated with them but I think it would be fun and am open to it! I think her style in India has a little more ease and an effortlessness to it that is very whimsical. Typically, when she is there, she is on the run with a very busy schedule. How do you think her style has evolved? Priyanka has a great appreciation for fashion and a strong eye for her personal style and what she likes. She is not interested in playing it safe and likes to dress according to her mood. I think her style is in a constant evolution and will continue to evolve and change because it is a reflection of who she is as a person and what she is feeling at that particular moment. What are the challenges styling Priyanka Chopra? There really aren't any, except that she has a very busy schedule and she is always on the go. I always need to make sure she has everything she needs when she leaves on a press tour or another event and to have enough back-up options for her. What are your favourite looks seen on her? Of course her Met Ball Ralph Lauren trench coat look, the fluorescent purple Costume Nationale turtle-neck dress that she wore on the top of the Empire State Building, the red Jason Wu dress, the Carolina Herrera denim look she wore to a book signing event, the Marc Jacobs long-sleeve lace dress she wore in Berlin, the Michael Kors long gown that we chopped to make it tea-length, the polka-dot Altuzzura dress she wore to a Veuve Clicquot event and the Public School menswear inspired suit-look with the cut out detailing at the shoulders. Tell us about the show-stopping Met Gala trench coat look. We literally had her first fitting 48 hours before the event because she had been travelling out of the country. We had just had a great home run with her gold Ralph Lauren Golden Globes dress, so we knew that we had to go big or go home for the Met Gala. We were talking about ideas with Ralph and we knew that she didn't want to go to the event and not stick out. Her first reaction to the coat-dress was that she was a little nervous about the fabric weight, the sleeves, etc, but once she had her fitting she really got into it. For me, that event was really a testament how beautiful a collaboration can be when the trust is there and the stars are aligned and it all comes together. What were the highlights from your Paris Couture Week trip with Priyanka Chopra? Priyanka was a guest of Mr Armani's. We put her in something a bit less classic Armani when we styled the look with a men's shoe—which we both loved. When you have a woman like Priyanka with a bombshell body, there is an obvious way to dress her—but she was very open to going in a different direction and didn't mind being a little tomboy, which was so fun for us both! What are your rules of red carpet dressing? It is important for me to be able to look back five or ten years from now and feel proud of my work. For me, styling is not about playing off of current trends, it is about collaborating with my clients so together we create the right look for that particular event and that they feel unique and special in what they are wearing. column1: These are the rarest handbags in the world
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How much would you pay for a handbag? As one-of-a-kind, decadent designs are drawing record numbers at auctions around the world, Vogue speaks to London’s Christies, to find out why this fashion category is becoming a lucrative collectors playground We're used to hearing about the history-making sales of sprawling art collections that once belonged to American banking dynasties and French couturiers, within the hallowed walls of Christie's auction house. It's the place to go if you're part of the one per cent that has a cool £342 million to spare on a Leonardo da Vinci or are looking to stock up on the finest bottles of Romanée-Conti. But in London this week it was handbags going under the hammer. Not just any old handbags, though; some of the rarest, most luxurious, most decadent—and most expensive—designs to have ever been made. The Handbags and Accessories sale broke the European record for a bag sold at auction. A 2010 Hermès, matte Birkin 35 with 18k white gold and diamond hardware, went for an eye-watering £236,750, exceeding the estimate by over 60 per cent. It's the third sale of its kind in just over a year from the auction house, which achieved notable success with the previous two in terms of customer growth (31 per cent new buyers: 30 per cent from Asia, 30 per cent from the US and 30 per cent from Europe). Other notable lots from last week's auction include an extremely rare aluminium Explorer Trunk by Louis Vuitton dating back to 1892, when the production of aluminium was so complex it was deemed more expensive than gold (£162,500). And a 2017 custom made Hermès Quelle Idole—a style released in 2000 to celebrate the millennium—which sold for a cool £68,750. According to Rachel Koffsky, who heads up the London department of Christie's International Handbags and Accessories, the market has changed dramatically in the past 10 years. “Out of the recession, we've seen women looking at their handbags as an asset and not just a frivolous accessory,” she observes. “We're seeing this female collector emerge. They're starting to look at these pieces in the same way that perhaps men were traditionally looking at watch collections. There's an awareness in terms of what a collectible handbag means and the value of these pieces on the primary and secondary market.” Bags, Koffsky adds, is one of the only women-centric collection categories, even in jewellery men still make up the majority of bidders. Collecting frenzy has also grown in line with the popularity of Instagram, fan accounts, street style, YouTube closet tours and the re-issue of certain archive designs—such as the Gucci monogram by Alessandro Michele and the Dior saddle bag by Maria Grazia Chiuri. The presence brands have in the handbag and accessories arena can be linked to specific designers; after all the longevity of a creative directorship at a fashion house is often determined by the success of these moneymakers. Louis Vuitton's foray into creating collectible show bags is relatively recent—when Marc Jacobs took the helm of the 19th century trunk makers two decades ago. The designer famously instigated collaborations with artists such as Takashi Murakami, Yayoi Kusama and Richard Prince and his legacy can still be felt. (Last year Louis Vuitton launched its second Masters collection in collaboration with Jeff Koons.) Iconic and obvious It bags aside, a piece could be worth more, or less, than its original retail price depending on what exactly it is. While there is a standard equation to help determine a bag's potential worth, there aren't any hard fast rules. The rarity is absolutely an important factor, as is the condition (graded from one, for new, through to six, for damaged). Then there's the model, age, materials, label, size (there's been a significant trend for small bags at auction lately) and, more subjectively speaking, how keen a bidder you have in the room on the day. “For a collector who's been looking for this [said] bag for 10 years, they'll pay any amount for it,” says Koffsky. The room usually ranges from the first-time buyer, who will walk away wearing the piece she just bought, to the seasoned top buyer, who will treat it like art displayed in specially curated gallery-esque closets. “There's a life cycle to a bag when it comes to limited editions,” says Koffsky. Expect a huge premium on the market to begin with, then give it a year to 18 months and it may experience a dip before it comes back. It might be a celebrity or important influencer that creates the renewed interest. Season to season, the market is prone to fluctuate. And these rare bags are the ultimate anti-fast fashion buy—long-lasting heirloom pieces with a pretty much guaranteed resale value. Koffsky predicts that if you spend £2000 on a piece you can be confident to get that back at resale. The recent news that Chanel will no longer use exotic skins or fur in its designs will surely only serve to increase the value of certain vintage pieces, too. Handbags are also a very personal thing. They hold our secrets, they tell a story. For example, the tiny horseshoe motif you'll find inside an Hermès bag means it was custom-made for the buyer at the time, making it even more collectible. It's because of these special equestrian insignias and heritage, coupled with almost unparalleled quality, that an Hermès has the highest return of any bag in the world. column1: Will the red carpet still be relevant in 2019?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In the era of Time’s Up and #AskHerMore, the red carpet has been dismissed as an outdated institution. But with protests staged at this year’s Golden Globes, Baftas and Cannes Film Festival, it has also proven to be a valuable political platform. Ahead of awards season 2019, Vogue asks what has been achieved, what comes next and if the red carpet can survive Hollywood’s post-Weinstein reckoning “Who are you wearing?” That has been the perennial question on the red carpet for the past two decades, as reporters asked stars about their dresses, beauty routines and exercise regimes. But at the 2018 Golden Globes, the phrase rang hollow. Following the Harvey Weinstein scandal and the launch of Time's Up, more than 300 women in Hollywood had announced their intention to wear black to raise awareness for gender inequality. In response, E! Entertainment, the US network that has long been the home of red carpet reporting, announced they would be changing their signature question to “Why are you wearing black?”. When Ryan Seacrest posed this to Meryl Streep, who was attending with the activist Ai-jen Poo, she replied, “We feel emboldened in this moment to stand together in a thick black line dividing then from now.” Streep was presaging a new era for women in Hollywood, but also the beginning of the end for the red carpet as we know it. Red carpets have a long and illustrious history. The earliest reference to one can be found in ancient Greece, with Aeschylus's 458 BC play Agamemnon showing a red carpet being rolled out for the eponymous king upon his return from the Trojan war. His wife Clytemnestra says, “step down from your chariot, and let not your foot, my lord, touch the earth.” He responds, “I am a mortal, a man; I cannot trample upon these tinted splendours without fear thrown in my path.” Even then, the red carpet was hallowed ground—it had the power to elevate mere mortals into deities. During the Renaissance, red carpets were reserved for throne rooms due to the high cost of scarlet cochineal dyes. One was used in 1821 to welcome US president James Monroe ashore in South Carolina, while in 1902, the New York Central Railroad used them to direct passengers onto their 20th Century Limited train. It wasn't until 1922, at the premiere of Douglas Fairbanks' Robin Hood, that movie stars first walked the red carpet. The Oscars adopted them in 1961, the ceremony was first televised in 1964, and thus the red carpet parade as we recognise it today was born. Footage from the 1964 Oscars shows fans screaming with delight at the arrival of Julie Andrews and Gregory Peck, before the stars are quickly shuffled into the auditorium. It would take another 30 years for interviews, camera crews and live coverage to become de rigueur. At the forefront of this new trend was Joan Rivers, who first hosted E!'s Golden Globes pre-show in 1994. Her acerbic wit was a hit with viewers, particularly at a time when red carpet fashion was becoming more outlandish (Céline Dion wore a backwards Dior tuxedo to the Oscars in 1999; Björk showcased her swan dress in 2001). 1998, the year that Titanic took home the award for Best Picture, was a high-water mark for TV ratings, with the Oscars ceremony garnering 57 million viewers. By this point, Rivers' pre-show was so popular that the network doubled its running time to two hours. Buoyed by this success, E! expanded its roster to include the post-awards special Fashion Police and added a host of new features to its red carpet coverage: the glam-360-cam, the clutch-cam, the stiletto-cam and the mani-cam. The latter, which involved a miniature red carpet on which actresses were asked to flaunt their fingers, provoked a swift backlash. At the 2014 Golden Globes, Elisabeth Moss told E!'s Giuliana Rancic, “There's something I wanted to do last time but didn't”, before giving a middle finger to the mani-cam. Her frustration was echoed by Cate Blanchett at the Screen Actors Guild Awards. When an E! camera scanned her body up and down, she peered into the lens and said, “Do you do that to the guys? What do you think is going to happen down there that's so fascinating?” The following year, Reese Witherspoon, Jennifer Aniston and Julianne Moore all refused to put their fingers in the mani-cam at the SAG Awards. At the 2015 Baftas, Buzzfeed parodied these increasingly ridiculous red carpet interviews by asking men the same questions as women. This included requesting Eddie Redmayne to twirl for the camera, asking a bewildered Michael Keaton if he was wearing Spanx and quizzing Weinstein himself about how long it had taken him to get ready. Public opinion was beginning to sour and E!'s ratings were plummeting. Following the death of Rivers in 2014, Fashion Police went on a five-month-long hiatus before being cancelled in 2017. Seacrest continues to host the pre-Oscars red carpet show, which this year averaged at 1.3 million viewers, a 43 per cent drop from last year. The audience for the Oscars ceremony also hit an all-time low in 2018, at 26.5 million. This decline of the red carpet coincided with an increasingly tense political landscape in the US. Donald Trump's travel ban prompted several attendees of the 2017 Oscars, including Ruth Negga and Karlie Kloss, to wear blue ribbons on the red carpet in support of the American Civil Liberties Union. Meanwhile, Emma Stone had a Planned Parenthood pin fastened to her Givenchy couture gown. Resistance was more overt at the 2017 SAG Awards, where The Big Bang Theory actor Simon Helberg walked the red carpet with a sign that read “Refugees Welcome”. It was with #MeToo and Time's Up, however, that red carpet protests transformed from tacit non-compliance to out-and-out rebellion. A sea of women in black swept the Golden Globes like an unstoppable army, calling out the gender pay gap on the red carpet (Debra Messing criticised E! for failing to pay host Catt Sadler the same as her male co-presenter) and exposing the lack of female directors on the stage (Natalie Portman introduced the category by saying, “here are the all-male nominees”). The Baftas mirrored the all-black dress code, while the Grammys invited stars to wear white roses. But for the 2018 Oscars, Time's Up announced there would be no dress code and no call to arms on the red carpet. Some interpreted this as Hollywood's return to business as usual, but the tectonic plates had already shifted. The red carpet hoop-jumping of previous years no longer felt like a requirement. The morning after the Oscars ceremony, Vanity Fair's Hollywood correspondent Nicole Sperling noted the palpable change. “It felt kind of subdued,” she said, speaking on the magazine's awards season podcast Little Gold Men. “A lot of people skipped the red carpet this year. Jordan Peele skipped it, Sam Rockwell skipped it—they took some photos and were escorted straight into the show. The publicists I spoke to said they just didn't see the value in it anymore. I don't know how this is going to proceed because there is that light, frothy red carpet that people like, but is that something we need? Is that a progressive part of our society?” The women at the Cannes Film Festival certainly didn't think so. In May, jury president Cate Blanchett led a rally on the red carpet arm in arm with 82 women—one for every female-directed film ever to have competed for the festival's top prize in its 71-year history, compared to 1,645 films directed by men. Only one woman, Jane Campion, has ever won. Other injustices were also brought to light: 16 black actresses demonstrated against racism in the French film industry and co-authored a book entitled Black is Not My Job. A minute of silence was held on May 15 in honour of the 60 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces near the border between Gaza and Israel, with actress Manal Issa carrying a sign on the red carpet that read “Stop the attack on Gaza”. At a screening of The Dead and the Others, a film about northern Brazil's indigenous Krahô community, placards demanded better treatment for the country's native people. Among the activism, jury member Kristen Stewart dominated headlines for taking off her Christian Louboutins at the premiere of BlacKkKlansman, defying Cannes' heels-only policy. “There's definitely a distinct dress code,” she told The Hollywood Reporter. “People get very upset if you don't wear heels, but you can't ask people to do that anymore. If you're not asking guys to wear heels and a dress, you can't ask me either.” Far from being empty gestures, the festival's protests enacted policy change. A new charter for gender parity was signed at Cannes and has since been adopted by other leading film festivals including Venice and Toronto. The Cannes red carpet, which had once been Weinstein's hunting ground, was slowly being reclaimed by women. ”I am heartened by the progress we've seen,” says Jennifer Siebel Newsom, founder of The Representation Project, whose #AskHerMore slogan has been gaining ground on the red carpet since its inception in 2014. “We're hearing more questions asked of women beyond what they're wearing, but that said, one important next step is amplifying other critical conversations like those raised by Time's Up. We want to work alongside like-minded organisations with missions towards equal, diverse and gender-balanced representation in Hollywood and beyond.” So, where does that leave us on the eve of 2019? The Toronto Film Festival and Emmy Awards passed largely without incident, though Planned Parenthood pins, ACLU ribbons and “I am a voter” badges nodded to the upcoming US midterms. Critics fear a slowdown at next year's awards season, but that seems unlikely. The Golden Globes will follow the one-year anniversary of Time's Up and once again no women have been nominated in the directing category. The 2019 Women's March falls on 19 January, right between the Critics' Choice Awards and the Producers Guild of America Awards. Just last week, Kevin Hart stepped down as Oscars host three days after being appointed, following controversy over perceived homophobic comments. Hollywood is as politically fraught as ever. For now, the red carpet has survived, but its future depends on its willingness to adapt to changing times. Stylists, for whom it remains a lucrative enterprise, are wary of boycotts but recognise its need to change. “Of course it's important,” says Elizabeth Saltzman, who dresses Saoirse Ronan and Gwyneth Paltrow. “But maybe it's important in a different way. Maybe now we can use the red carpet to show people as they really are. Does it matter? Only as much as we all want it to. Is it the most important business? Well, it's my business so it's damn well important to me. I think there's so much we can do with the red carpet, so let's do it instead of giving up on it.” Will next season's red carpet heed Saltzman's words? We can only wait and see. column1: 6 trends that we’ve spotted in Deepika Padukone’s wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Take a closer look at her sartorial staples Deepika Padukone has made a habit of topping best-dressed lists every time she steps out. Her personal style—a crossover between comfortable, sophisticated and traffic stopping—is the woke-up-like-this variety of effortless. column1: 8 major fashion moments from 2018 that made this year #woke
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From luxury labels going fur-free to more diversity on the runway 2018 has been a rollercoaster of a year, especially for the fashion industry. The year started on a tumultuous note with allegations of sexual misconduct against international photographers and stylists, which brought the wave of Time's Up and #MeToo in the world of fashion. Inclusivity, body positivity, diversity and feminism were other keywords that the industry was buzzing with. India saw its own reckoning with Section 377 being decriminalised, leading to widespread celebrations amongst the LGBTQ+ community. What's more, Vogue India's October 2018 issue, under the theme of Blurred Lines, opened the floor to designers, artists, actors, models, writers and even drag queens, to have a dialogue about gender, geography, codes and disciplines. All in all, 2018 was a woke period that is marked by banished societal norms and opened hearts. Read on to find out all the noteworthy moments from the year that went by. The start of 2018 carried the Time's Up movement with it from last year, which emboldened models to share the skeletons hiding in their closets. Fashion photographers Bruce Weber, Mario Testino, Patrick Demarchelier and stylist Karl Templer were accused of sexual abuse, bullying and coercive behaviour. This conversation started a wildfire in the fashion community that refused to be doused without strong actions being taken against the perpetrators. Revelations of misconduct amongst the models brought rival luxury conglomerates LVMH and Kering to join hands and create a website called Wecareformodels.com. The website combats abuse and aims to empower models with physical and mental wellness tips, all while bringing transparency in the industry. After designers Rahul Mishra and Suket Dhir winning the menswear title for the International Woolmark Prize, it was Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice who made India proud with her momentous win. The designer was presented with the womenswear title from the Australian-based award company, and lauded for her thoughtful design techniques and approach to sustainability.   The autumn/winter 2018 season at New York Fashion Week had designers like Prabal Gurung, Christian Siriano, Carly Cushnie, Chromat and more fully embrace body positivity and inclusivity. Plus-size models Ashley Graham and Candice Huffine were prominent names that walked the runway. Meanwhile, model Mama Cax—who is an amputee—walked for Chromat. Gurung, a self-proclaimed feminist, had models from over 35 countries walk for his show. Closer to home, model Anjali Lama made the transgender community proud by gracing the runway for leading fashion designers like Anita Dongre and Tarun Tahiliani at Lakmé Fashion Week spring/summer 2018. British model, fashion designer and social media influencer, Amena Khan, who became the first hijab model to star in a leading hair-care campaign, modelled in a Sabyasachi sari and jacket, along with a hijab from her head scarf company, Pearl Daisy. This move welcomed diversity and advocated the sari's universal appeal. 2018 saw luxury fashion brands Burberry, Versace and John Galliano join the clan of fur-free designers, and ban pelage from their collections. Chanel followed suit and made a powerful move this December by banning exotic animal skins too—which means you can bid adieu to handbags, shoes and clothes made from the skins of snakes, crocodiles, lizards and more. The Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week SS19's grand finale witnessed 41 leading designers—the likes of Manish Arora, Pankaj and Nidhi, Abraham & Thakore, Dhruv Kapoor and more—come together to create a rainbow collection that paid homage to the Supreme Court's historic verdict on decriminalising homosexuality. The vegan designer, who has been quite vocal about her stance on sustainability, announced a United Nations fashion industry charter to be held this month at the United Nations Climate Change Conference at Poland. This charter aims to combat climate change and encourage the fashion industry to take strong action towards it. Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Isha Ambani’s wedding lehenga had a very special significance
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s what you need to know about the intricately detailed bridal look It's been almost a month since the wedding celebrations of Isha Ambani, daughter of Mukesh and Nita Ambani, kicked off with a dandiya raas night. And just yesterday, the 27-year-old businesswoman finally tied the knot with her childhood friend, Anand Piramal, the scion of industrialist Ajay Piramal, in a bespoke Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla creation. Isha Ambani strayed away from a linear approach when it came to her wedding ensembles, choosing custom creations from leading couturiers in the country. After donning a high-octane Manish Malhotra lehenga for her pre-wedding ceremony, the bride went with a romantic Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla design, which was customised in a touching nod to her love for her mother: Nita Ambani's wedding sari, a 35-year-old heirloom piece, was incorporated in her own bridal lehenga. A ravishing off-white set featuring a trail and kalis with floral motifs was Ambani's pick for the day. Enhanced with intricate red zardozi borders as well as mukaish and nakshi work, the designer duo's signature of infusing Indian craftsmanship with heritage textile was evident in Isha Ambani's bridal number. The lehenga also came with two dupattas—one a tulle version on the shoulder, and an embroidered one with a long, sequinned trail, that the bride draped over her head. One of the biggest weddings of the year without a doubt, the couple's celebrations saw the who's who from across industries (and countries) come down to congratulate and and celebrate the union with them. In case you missed it, the pre-wedding festivities concluded last weekend in Udaipur with the likes of the Beyoncé, Hillary Clinton and almost all B-town celebrities in attendance. Unlike the Udaipur functions, the traditional wedding ceremony was a smaller affair with a guest list of 600 close family and friends, held at the Ambani family home, Antilia in Mumbai. The 27-storied mansion, also touted as one of the most expensive homes in the world, was decked with red flowers and diyas before the ceremonies kicked off. Clearly an Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla patron, Isha Ambani had opted for another creation by the designers—a multi-hued lehenga with intricate mirror work and threadwork—for her dandiya raas night in November. She was also seen sporting an outfit by the veteran couturiers for brother Akash Ambani's engagement to Shloka Mehta earlier this year in July. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Karan Johar puts his stamp of approval on a fine jewellery line
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And no, it won’t burn a hole in your pocket From producing and directing films to hosting a talk show and even authoring his own memoir, you would have thought that Karan Johar has done it all by now. But he's clearly not finished. The multi-hyphenate has now added yet another feather to his cap through Tyaani, an online destination for jewellery lovers. Kickstarted in partnership with renowned jewellers Satyani Fine Jewels, Tyaani offers handcrafted jadau and polki jewellery sets in 22k gold at prices that won't burn a hole in your pocket. “Jadau and polki jewellery are seen as luxury and are associated with traditional jewellery. With Tyaani, we want to take polki out of bridal trousseaus or milestone events and make it accessible for the modern woman as everyday wear,” says Johar, who is curating the pieces for the portal. The lightweight collection sees chaandbalis, embellished chokers, single-beaded necklaces, statement rings, multi-beaded bracelets and even evil eye neckpieces, ensuring that there's a unique piece for every occasion. “Jewellery makes a memorable impression, and women must be unapologetic about their choices. If you're wearing a mini set on a regular work day, carry it with aplomb rather than thinking you're overdressed,” Johar advises. Handcrafted by over 70 trained artisans who work towards the highest levels of craftsmanship, each contemporary design comes with a European Gemological Laboratory certification. What's more, the designers at Tyaani can personalise jewellery to your taste and liking. From minimal polki bracelets costing as low as Rs 18,000 to embellished chaandbalis retailing at Rs 1,20,000, these covetable pieces promise to double up as hand-me-down jewellery for generations to come. “We have developed a proprietary gold rolling technique that lets us create polki jewellery in lighter settings, and using that technology solution makes polki affordable, but retains the charm of traditional handcrafted jadau and polki jewellery,” explains Johar.
