column1: Arianna Huffington and Sonam K Ahuja’s lessons on living more mindfully
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Six tips that will help tackle modern-day stress We live in a world that is incredibly driven and ambitious, and as modern-day busy bees, we're constantly making strides in our life—but truth is, we're left with little time to pause and savour it all. The struggle is real, and combating this stress and burnout epidemic is a cause global media magnate Arianna Huffington has always championed. With her company Thrive Global India, she advocates sustainable, science-based solutions steeped in ancient wisdom to enhance our quality of life. And it now looks like Huffington has found a like-minded ally in actor Sonam K Ahuja. The duo recently engaged in a refreshingly honest discussion on self-belief, our relationship with technology, and the key to leading a more meaningful life. Vogue listened in on the conversation, and came back with takeaways that promised to add value to our lives. Here, we're sharing them with you. Take notes. Ahuja revealed that her husband, Anand Ahuja, has a non-negotiable house rule: no phones are allowed in their bedroom at night. The actor, a self-confessed phone addict, went on to add that her newfound digital-free nightly routine has been a welcome detox. “Not only have my stress levels gone down, but I am also more thoughtful about my replies now, be it to personal messages or on social media,” said Ahuja. The hyper-connected world we live in allows our successes to be celebrated on a global stage, but it also shows no mercy in shining the spotlight on our missteps and failures. The detractors are not just those around us, “but also the obnoxious roommate living in our own heads,” Huffington said. “My second book was rejected by 36 publishers, but that did not deter me. You have to live as though everything is rigged in your favour,” she carried on. Ahuja added: “Constantly seeking validation is not a healthy way to live. You have to centre yourself to believe in your own strengths. Ignoring negativity is a superpower we all have. Let's practise it.” Ahuja recalled a period in her life when she didn't sign on any movie for one-and-a-half years because she could not resonate with the roles coming her way. When she finally went ahead with Raanjhanaa opposite Dhanush, people questioned her choice, but the movie ultimately went on to become a massive success. “Make your own choices. Have an opinion. Never lose the idealism you had as a child. It's the only way to grow from strength to strength, and to empower the coming generations to be progressive.” As women, we are programmed to constantly juggle multiple balls. We often want to be everything to everyone. Huffington noted that, “mothers take the baby out and put the guilt in. We're always trying to live up to impossible standards. But we need to put our own oxygen mask on first before helping others.” Ahuja agreed that the only way to be effective is to put yourself first, and take care of yourself mentally, physically and spiritually. Ahuja grew up with the important learning that when you have a lot, you should build a bigger table and not a higher wall. “Connections and kindness are everything. There should be no place for negative ‘isms' in our lives.” The actor and the entrepreneur are both advocates of surrounding yourself with a community of women who are your biggest cheerleaders. “Put your differences aside and rise with each other. Let's be empathetic and laugh a lot,” Huffington advised. Ahuja recites the Gayatri mantra before going to bed every night, while her husband practises gratitude. The couple has now combined their individual rituals to end the day on a more positive note, “and sleep peacefully!” Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: All the Dubai updates you need to catch up on before the holiday season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Glam game on With festive season around the corner, the holiday spirit has officially hit Dubai. In a week or so the fashion and beauty industry will go into “switch-off” mode, which clearly explains why the past fortnight in the city was so eventful—with holding parties from big labels like Gucci and Tom Ford, and makeup masterclasses from top artists in the world. Here, we give you a look at some of the more off-beat soirees, where you really got an insider's view. When it comes to her glam, makeup maestro Mario Dedivanovic is Kim Kardashian West's go-to. Dedivanovic had travelled to Dubai with the reality television star two years ago, hosting a makeup masterclass that was so oversubscribed, I remember being unable to book a ticket for it. He was back again last week, in his new role as Laura Mercier's brand ambassador, for a more intimate and private event for makeup artists and select media personnels. The event taught attendees some easy-to-use tricks of the trade from one of Hollywood's best makeup artists—all in less than an hour. The Laura Mercier brand has been known for its powders since its launch in the 1990s. And now, they've just launched their Glow Setting Powder—the product comes with a fine textured powder, so even those with oily skin can use it. Dedivanovic applies it over foundation with a puff instead of a brush, because a brush can “ruin” your base. The acclaimed makeup artist shared a number of beauty revelations and tips over the span of the event too. For example, he “hates” liquid lipsticks, and uses a translucent powder over one coat of lipstick before applying another—this layering effect ensuring your lipsticks lasts all day (or all night!). I was especially surprised when Dedivanovic revealed that he never uses foundation under the eye—he applies till just under the eye, and uses a layering concealer system for the area, starting with a dry concealer, a light liquid and then followed by an even lighter liquid. The man who confessed to loving Arab women as they, “always have glam makeup on”, ended the session by taking selfies with everyone present. We all know that Priyanka Chopra chose to wear a custom made column Ralph Lauren dress for her white wedding, but my personal favourite has been always been Oscar de la Renta. The label just introduced some demi couture gowns in their autumn/winter collection—which have been touring and spent a few days in Dubai last week at their flagship store—and the attention to detail is noteworthy to say the least. Oscar de la Renta designers Fernando Garcia and Laura Kim feel that a woman should have some input on the most important (and probably most expensive dress) she will ever buy, which is why the gowns are demi couture, allowing the bride to tweak things as she sees fit. The label behind Amal Clooney's custom designed, fully beaded wedding gown, has always been popular in Dubai for its love of elegant embroidery, and it seems the brand hopes that demi couture will be of special interest to brides not just from Middle East, but also from South Asia and India. The Harmonist is a unique perfume that's attuned to your personal energy. Inspired by ancient Asian philosophies, it encourages one to seek the right balance of yin and yang between the strongest of the five elements—water, wood, fire, earth and metal. Founder Lola Tillyaeva worked with Delhi-born and London-raised Priya Sher—a Feng Shui expert to the likes of Deepak Chopra and Paula Coelho—to create 10 perfumes, plus the newly launched Yin Transformation (which is my personal favourite). The premise to these is simple: a fragrance is matched to you according to your personal Feng Shui element. Sher was in town for the launch of Harmonist, which will now be available at  the Harvey Nichols stall at Mall of The Emirates. While the expert herself will not be at hand at the stall, an app will help you know which perfume is the one for you. Who knew that a fragrance could help you further your career and enhance your personal life, right? Weather-wise, this is best time of the year to visit Dubai, so it's easy to predict that the city will soon be flooded with tourists. Beach days are finally here, which means only one thing now—it's time for a new beach bag. Woven by Wayuu women of Columbia, Soraya Hennessy's newest offering has become the It-bag of the season. The bag features a hammock-style feel because of their weave, and the fashionistas in Dubai love the ones that features slogans such as “Yalla” and “Habibi” on them. Though the brand's founder was born in Venezuela, she has spent a lot of time in Chicago and now lives in Abu Dhabi. Her work has that East meets the West aesthetic, with a dash of Latina thrown in. If you have a beach holiday planned, I'd suggest you look at her designs. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What does it take for a designer jewellery label to reach cult status
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Valery Demure lets us in on the dos, the don’ts and the hard truths Valery Demure's job is the kind that is at once incredibly difficult, yet immensely satisfying. A mentor, a buyer, a PR strategist, the founder of her eponymous agency and an online shopping portal plus a collaborative concept space Objet d'Emotion—she is known name in the luxury jewellery and accessories space for her discerning eye. Having helped with the success of brands like Shourouk, Fernando Jorge, Monique Péan and Noor Fares, there's no contesting that Demure's advice is heavily valued. But it's not just talent she is after—amplifying the reach of a boutique brand is a result of several elements coming together at the same time. We spoke to the opinionated consultant on what it really takes to create a cult favourite jewellery label. It's a mixture of things. What makes an actress unique? What makes a singer unique? It's talent. But talent without discipline and a business mind can also be completely wasted. I think consistency is very important and now more than before, people are less patient. But it requires patience, to go step-by-step; it's not going to happen in a day. There are various ways. One of them is when I notice a designer and I get in touch, which doesn't happen a lot. But usually it's [through] word of mouth. People will tell me, “you should check this designer out” or they contact me. Then we usually ask for marketing material, a look book; we ask what their goals are, do they have a business strategy, are they prepared to work on all of these and not just go in blindly. There are a lot of protocols involved. The product needs to have quality, that's super important. Originality, which is also becoming difficult. An original collection, an original vision—it needs to feel genuine because if it isn't, you know it won't last. We like meeting business-minded designers. If the designer is strictly creative, then he or she needs to have someone in the team who has a clear business vision. It may be the business partner or the co-founder or family. Creativity alone is not enough; it is important, but then the business has to happen. Usually when we reject, it's either not my thing, or I don't get the aesthetic, or I don't love it. I mean, you have to love it, and sometimes they're not ready. Like I said, if they're not business-minded or if they don't have someone with them to organise structure, we know our job's going to be difficult. I think your product alone is not enough. I think you need to have a combination of a good product, a story to tell, to be different, because the market is very saturated. A brand needs to have a genuine story, to have good marketing material because if you don't have good marketing material, how are you going to get the press interested in what you're doing? What helps obviously is to have some cool girls being sort of like patrons or ambassadors of the brand. Above all, what's really important is to be consistent, which is something quite difficult to find. And I think all of it requires patience, which is also not easy. Things like production, delivering on time, are where the problems lie. Retailers are becoming so demanding that it is hard for a young brand to keep up. A lot of brands struggle financially. You get an order for, let's say a hundred thousand pieces, and you have to produce it; it takes time. Assuming it takes two months for production, then delivery and payment can take another five months. You need to be quick to deliver or you are penalised. You have quality issues, you're penalised. If you grow really fast and if you don't have financial support, it's really hard. If you reach a higher level of business, your team expands, you hire people, but if there's a slack, you immediately have to start letting go of people. There are a lot of copycats, brands taking things from here and there; you see so many brands that do a lot of mix and match. It's hard for a designer to sustain because the consumer and retailer's need for newness is a problem. I think ready-to-wear is trickier, because it is very seasonal. Fine jewellery is not seasonal, costume jewellery is probably more seasonal, but I also think you don't have the issue of size with jewellery; with clothing you have that. I think jewellery is trickier because it requires more education. Like in stones, they need to educate the customer more. A dress suits you, it looks good or it doesn't. With jewellery, you need to educate [the customer] on how it's been made, on how it sometimes attaches, or how to style it. We are mentors, we are a little motherly, we do a lot of guidance, advising and mentoring. We have to quite often do therapy, when the designers don't feel very inspired for a season. We have meetings, we look at how they are evolving, we look at their business development, we help them sometimes in styling look books, so we are very hands-on. There is one, that is honesty. I think you have to be honest with designers, that's probably one of my drawbacks. I could have a much bigger business by not being brutally honest. You have to be careful with people's expectations, because a lot of young designers have unrealistic expectations—they think they are going to show two seasons and sell in all the stores around the world. That's not going to happen, unless you're a genius. When you tell them that, they prefer to go to a showroom or press that tells them “yeah, I'm going to make it big for you”; doesn't happen. But we have had massive successes. I think you need to be a lot more strategic, like be in very good points of sale, sell directly, maybe open an online boutique; you can't expect retailers to do everything for you as you used to. It is tough, but it is also exciting for someone with talent. I think in a way, craft is coming back. Many luxury consumers don't just want the brand name anymore, they want beautifully made [products]. I think more and more, the luxury client wants to know about the provenance, the make. column1: Can fast fashion ever be green?
column2:
© Vogue Images Fashion Is H&M’s latest eco-initiative mission impossible? Vogue talks to the fast-fashion brand about their non-profit, which aims to offset the huge impact their industry is having on the environment In two decades, the H&M Group has grown from a medium-sized European retail chain to the second-largest garment company in the world, producing approximately 3 billion items per year to sell across its 4,800 stores. But a recent drop in sales and profits have forced the Swedish giant to face its structural issues, including a production process which led to $4.3 billion of unsold clothes in early 2018. “The old brick-and-mortar [model of] just pump up new stores, push out garments into stores and someone will buy them, is dead,” David , H&M Group's head of production, said at a recent meeting in Hong Kong. He was addressing the winning founders of this year's Global Change Awards, an annual event organised by the H&M Foundation, the non-profit arm of the Swedish company. (Full disclosure: Vogue was a guest of the foundation, who paid for flights and accommodation.) “We have to produce what people want to buy and not hope that they want to buy what we have produced. That model is not sustainable.” Over the last decade, luxury conglomerates and fast-fashion retailers alike have made public commitments to sustainability. According to Anna B Töndevold, strategy manager at Accenture, companies aren't only responding to external pressures—reevaluating and boosting transparency around production processes is necessary “to operate in the long term”. It improves consumer trust, brand value and talent attraction, while reducing risks such as boycotts and litigation over workers' rights. The H&M Group, which includes Cos, & Other Stories and seven other brands, was one of the first fast-fashion companies to implement programmes to reduce its environmental footprint. It launched its first Conscious Collection in Spring 2011, which included materials like organic cotton and recycled polyester, as well as a garment-collecting initiative in 2013. The company has also experimented with combined deliveries, electrical vans and packaging-free delivery in India to curb its e-commerce impact. These efforts have given the Swedish retailer a number four spot in the Fashion Revolution 2018 Transparency Index. “We already know that we are over-consuming the planet, meaning that in 10 years you cannot be successful in this industry if you are dependent on those resources,” says Hanna Hallin, sustainability manager for H&M Group in Greater China. “H&M and Zara are seen as two leaders in sustainability,” Elizabeth Cline, author of Overdressed: The Shockingly High Cost of Cheap Fashion, says. “However, it's not enough to just be less bad than your competition.” If retailers want to effect change, they need to focus on manufacturing, rather than greening stores and logistics. Fibre and fabric production, yarn preparation and dying contributed to 97 per cent of the apparel industry's total global climate impact in 2016.
Retailers, however, rarely own the factories producing their garments. Zara owner Inditex owns around 3 per cent of its manufacturing capacity, while the H&M Group exclusively
works with external suppliers, which number more than 1,000. Companies often point to a lack of factory ownership to justify their limited influence on supply chains, but Rachel Arthur, chief innovation officer at innovation agency TheCurrent, thinks they can do more: “They deal with [these suppliers] in big numbers, so they have the ability to put pressure on them to make these changes happen.” “These multinational companies also have enough scale to lobby governments to implement better regulations,” she adds. Another challenge? Suppliers who want to become more efficient are further deterred by the fashion industry's practice of rapidly moving between countries where production is cheapest. “Much more local management of the supply chain is what is required from all of these brands,” says Matthew Drinkwater, head of innovation agency at London College of Fashion. “It's resource-intensive but there isn't really another choice.” In addition to working more closely with suppliers, Drinkwater urges companies to invest in technologies that could reduce production volume. 3D design, 3D sampling and 3D prototyping can all help cut waste, while artificial intelligence can be used to produce small garment runs for specific stores. These technologies could be implemented almost immediately, but companies need to make the skillset to manage and operate them a priority. Drinkwater believes that the H&M Group, which appointed Linda Leopold as head of AI policy and Cambridge Analytica whistleblower Christopher Wylie as head of research for artificial intelligence this year, is heading in the right direction. Despite its widely publicised commitments on sustainability, the company has no plans to change the factors—production volumes, turnarounds times, low prices—that have helped shaped a throwaway culture that sends 300,000 tonnes of clothes to landfill per year in the UK alone. H&M's Hallin doesn't see an alternative. “We can stop producing the volumes we do [now], but then the 98 per cent [of companies that are] less transparent and less sustainable will just keep making money. We have a role to play going forward—we ought to put others that are not transparent out of business.” This is where the H&M Foundation comes in. Backed by $177 million from the Stefan Persson family (owners of H&M), it wants to do its part to reach the UN's Sustainable Development Goals for 2030. One of its most recently unveiled projects is a hydrothermal recycling system that solves one of garment recycling's biggest obstacles: separating fibre blends. Occupying the space of a small conference room, the Green Machine could boost the amount of recycled material used by the H&M Group, which currently numbers less than 0.5 per cent. Once it reaches industrial capacity, the Foundation hopes it will be adopted by other companies as well. While garment recycling addresses only a small part of the problem, it is a step in the right direction, says Jeffrey Silberman, chair of textile development and marketing at the Fashion Institute of Technology (FIT). “If this becomes one of many operations that can recycle and keep significant amounts of unused fibre and fabric out of landfills and the oceans, it could change the way the industry creates product and manages its lifecycle.” View Gallery 7 Photos H&M Sustainibility – Can fast fashion ever be green? column1: How this influencer turned her Instagram-fame into a global brand
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Following a $15 million investment, Danish influencer-turned-designer Anine Bing’s eponymous label is one to watch for 2019. As she opens her 10th store in London, Vogue speaks to Bing about how she built her brand, balancing work and family life, and what to expect from their upcoming collections Anine Bing was an Instagram hit pretty much straight off the bat. An early adopter when the social platform launched in 2010, the Danish influencer-turned-designer's effortless ability to marry timeless simplicity with a rock 'n' roll edge proved a winning combination. In 2012, she and her husband, Nicolai Nielsen, launched their first collection, consisting of 15 timeless pieces, from their Los Angeles home. Fast-forward six years (and 629,000 Instagram followers), Bing has just secured a $15 million Series A (funding for start-ups) investment, from key investors Index Ventures, Greycroft Partners and Felix Capital. She has opened nine bricks-and-mortar stores, with the 10th opening in Los Angeles's Mayfair this week. The brand has a cult lingerie following—doubling its collection last year to include the under-$200 silk camis and lace bralettes favoured by Kendall Jenner—plus its signature studded boots (as seen on Gigi Hadid). “It's the versatility of each piece that sets the brand apart,” says Elizabeth von der Goltz, global buying director at Net-a-Porter, who has retailed Anine Bing's lingerie since March 2017. “The modern shopper is less defined now—she wants fashion that can be worn day or night. Each of [Bing's] collections has a strong fashion identity whilst being completely wearable for every woman.” Bing's success goes beyond her ability to tap into the modern woman's multifaceted wardrobe of classics plus key seasonal pieces. She adopted a see-now, buy-now model long before Burberry—posting monthly collections to both the brand and Bing's Instagram accounts. If Bing was pictured wearing something, her fans could wear it too. A shorter production lead time, combined with a strong e-commerce, marketing and social media strategy has cemented Anine Bing as a community-driven success. And as the brand approaches its seventh year, Bing stays true to the platform that helped her launch her eponymous label; utilising all of the latest Instagram roll outs, from swipe-to-shop, to shoppable posts. “We were ahead of the curve in that way,” Bing tells Vogue ahead of her London launch, “and with how to promote things and build a brand on Instagram. I think the investors saw that as an innovative way of working and it really appealed to them; they actually approached us.” To top it all off, she still manages her own account. That alone would make for a busy life, more so when coupled with running the business, alongside her husband, and being a mother of two. Her children, Benjamin and Bianca, are five and seven, respectively. “We're still learning and it's really hard,” she says of finding a personal and professional balance. “The key is to love what you do.” The early days were harder still, when Bing and her husband did everything from marketing and design, to customer service and packing orders. But over the past two years the company has tripled its employee base to 60—appointing chief operating officer, Annika Meller; chief financial officer, Paul Courell; and vice president of e-commerce and growth, Jacob Rokeach—and doubled its revenue year-on-year (forecast to do the same in 2019.) Beyond driving international growth and expanding their retail footprint, Bing plans to use the $15 million funding she secured in September to strengthen their denim offering. Jeans, she explains, were a catalyst for launching the brand six years ago: “I had around 100 pairs of jeans, but I couldn't find the right style.” Although it's a challenging category—the perfect wash, the stretch in the fabric, the placement of pockets and fit—she wants to get it right. “There's no better feeling out there than when you find the perfect pair of jeans. You can wear them with a simple white T-shirt and a blazer and feel confident. I want to create more of that feeling for my customers.” What else can we expect? It's all very hush-hush; but if this year is anything to go by, things will not be slowing down anytime soon. In 2018 alone, the brand collaborated with Janessa Leone hats and Scandinavian brand Gina Tricot, launched its children's wear offering with Bing Kids and opened three stores, in New York, London and LA. “Plans tend to move so quickly but we're working on some big things for 2019,” says Bing. That includes at least five new stores worldwide, as well as new (yet-to-be-announced) collaborations, partnerships and product categories. Now that she has taken on kidswear with aplomb, will the future include branching into menswear, Vogue asks? “Not on the agenda for now, but never say never!” View Gallery 7 Photos How this influencer turned her Instagram-fame into a global brand What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: A modern-day mother’s guide to curating her kid’s wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Pallavi Swadi of COO COO lets us in on the tricks Searching for the latest trends to style your child in? Look no further than the designer label COO COO by Pallavi Swadi that's launching its first brick-and-mortar store in Mumbai's Nariman Point. The store will play host to the label's offerings that cater to age groups spanning new borns to 13-year-olds, “The space has been designed to establish a warm and relaxed ambience that underlines the aesthetic of the brand while at the same time providing a space for creative design,” says Swadi. Read on to find out all the colours, fabrics and prints that need to be a part of your child's wardrobe. “As a mother of two, I feel less is more when I dress my child,” says the designer. When it comes to colour and prints, Swadi recommends choosing colours that suit your child's complexion and prints that are not too over-powering. “At COO COO, we use a colour palette of pastels. Girls' clothing incorporates floral prints, and boys' outfits see a lot of nautical prints,” she says. “Keeping in mind India's weather, every parents' first choice of fabric should be cotton. Ensure it is of good quality to allow the fabric to breathe,” advises Swadi. “COO COO uses fabrics like modals, sateen cotton, dobby's, oxfords, chambrays and fil-a-fil cottons for girls and boys. Our Indian collection features Chanderi and muslin cottons,” she says. “Unicorn prints and embroidery are quite the rage these days, as is the up-and-down sequin trend. Acid and ice-wash finishes on shirts for boys are in popular demand too,” says Swadi, who is incorporating these in the label's spring summer 2019 collection. “Our next collection introduces our much-awaited Mommy & Me box-pleat lace dresses in navy, white and mustard; seersucker cold-shoulder tops; ruffled-neckline dresses in red and ruffled tops, just in time for Christmas.” View Gallery 5 Photos COO COO Address: COO COO, 402 Maker Chambers 5, 221, Nariman Point, Mumbai Fashion Fashion Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Gucci kick starts Sole DXB with a bang
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A party like no other It does seem ironic that a city known for its over-the-top glam dress code, is the host for an event like Sole DXB that celebrates all things street. Easily one of the coolest events to take place in the Dubai, the exhibition, which started on Thursday, will continue over the weekend. From fashion and art to hip-hop and basketball, it has become quite the meeting place for stylish sneakerheads from all over the world. And many luxury brands are a permanent part of this youth culture fest, but last night was the first time Gucci, the brand that marries street style and high fashion like none other, collaborated with Sole DXB. Sole DXB is known for its live performances, and we all know Gucci loves its music, so decided to host a pre-opening party. It all started at its eclectically designed three store mega flagship store at The Dubai Mall, which is just a few months old. The store was turned into a nightclub, and there was some serious dancing going on every level of the floor as Dubai-based DJ Karrouhat ensured that that there were standing feet in flagship store till the mall's doors closed. The private party then moved to Sole DXB's venue at Dubai Design District where everything flowed—the drinks, the food and the music (there was a line of DJs playing). column1: Sara Ali Khan’s most notable looks from Kedarnath promotions
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Inside the young debutant’s wardrobe Even before Sara Ali Khan's debut film Kedarnath releases, style watchers have been eyeing her sartorial moves. The film, which features Khan alongside Sushant Singh Rajput and comes with the tag line ‘Love is a pilgrimage', is a love story set against the backdrop of the 2013 Uttarakhand floods that left the state devastated. Kedarnath is slated for release today, but the young debutante has already made headlines with her sartorial choices during its promotional rounds. 25-year-old Sara Ali Khan made sure that every look of hers for the movie's promotional round counted. column1: How Vans is winning with the younger generation of women
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vans went viral with Gen Z a couple of years ago, popular not just for their style, but for comfort and cool collabs. Vogue charts the success of the trainer brand, and discusses why now more than ever, it’s got global girl-power appeal The day Vans went viral with Gen Z was 15 February 2016, when Californian high-schooler Josh Holz tweeted a video of his friend Daniel Lara—a series of Snapchat stories, ending with the line, “Damn Daniel, back at it again with the white Vans.” The inexplicably funny video earned the pair tens of millions of views, a spot on Ellen and a lifetime supply of Vans, which Lara donated to his local children's hospital. Two years later and American teenage girls are the engine behind Vans's growth. In the most recent quarter, year-on-year revenue was up 36 per cent in the US (and 27 per cent globally). According to Piper Jaffray's biannual Taking Stock With Teens survey, it's the fastest-rising brand the firm has ever reviewed, unseating Nike as the most popular footwear label for upper-income females. So how exactly has Vans become what women want? It's all down to clever campaigns, the return of classic Nineties-era sportswear—from the runways to street-style stars—and that elusive quality favoured by Gen Z, “authenticity”. “It's the grassroots brand that everyone loves,” says 19-year-old Jacob Chang, director of trends at Jüv Consulting, a US consulting outfit run by teens. Vans's collaborations with the likes of Nintendo, Disney, Marvel and Nasa have also hit “that sweet spot of nostalgia and passion that Generation Z lives for”, Chang adds. According to Ayako Homma, senior analyst at Euromonitor International, American teens today are less brand loyal than previous generations, valuing comfort, quality and value over a name. If they do wear logos, they prefer Fila, Tommy Hilfiger, Champion and other Nineties-era streetwear labels, she explains. Vans' roots in Nineties' skater culture, emphasis on comfort and $50 entry point compliment these trends perfectly. But most importantly, Vans's marketing speaks directly to Gen Z's skater girls. “Some of the stories we're putting out are a little bit more geared to women,” confirms Nick Street, Vans' vice president of global integrated marketing. For International Women's Day this year, the brand launched “Girls Skate India”, a long-form video filmed at Holystoked skatepark in Bangalore, which features Vans athletes Lizzie Armanto and Atita Verghese, and aims to teach, empower and inspire the next generation. The campaign was accompanied by the opening of more than 100 skate clinics around the world to encourage women of all ages to learn the sport. Euromonitor International reports that in the US footwear market, Vans has a 0.8 per cent share versus Nike's 19.7 per cent. But with more live music events and communal skateparks in the pipeline, and the sportswear trend enduring, Vans is unlikely to stay niche for long. column1: Take a walk down memory lane, on Mélange’s 25th anniversary
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue sat down with founder Sangita Kathiwada to reminisce on the store’s many firsts On the 10th richest street in the world, tucked under the lush foliage of Mumbai's Altamount Road, lies Mélange. Inside its cavern-like entrance, the stone-covered walls of the multi-designer store serve as owner and curator Sangita Kathiwada's creative lair. A melting pot of jewellery (on the day of the interview, Kathiwada is wearing a fabric necklace from her upcycled ‘Rescued from the Bin' collection), ready-to-wear and contemporary art, the store fits its moniker. Over the last 25 years, we've come to know the space as a creative hub where designers like Sabyasachi Mukherjee, Anuradha Vakil and Rahul Mishra have kick-started their careers. As Kathiwada readies to look back at the last two and a half decades with a Mumbai x Mélange memories exhibit, it's evident that this intimate store has played a large part in bringing Indian designers to where they are today. Kathiwada reminisces on the firsts. “I look for a certain eccentricity in a designer, and the designers housed at Mélange create out of freedom. I spot the talent and launch them in a gallery-like platform. After that, my job is done. When I met Ramesh Nair, he was just a simple Kerala boy. I looked at him and told him, ‘One day you will be in Paris.' I remember he had an intellectual and quirky, creative method. We were working on a khadi fashion show and he rummaged through long lost archives of national newspapers from the Gandhian and Partition eras. He went directly to the source and came out with garments that had newspaper clippings printed on them. Anuradha Vakil was another such designer that Mélange has exclusively stocked from day one. I admire her absoluteness in creativity. She uses pure silks, pure handwork, pure gold thread. And although we made a conscious decision not to stock bridal couture at the store, Anuradha is the only exception we'll ever make.”   “This business I've chosen thrives on the experience of entering a store, and the touch and feel of trying on clothes. It's a ritual that the Mélange woman cherishes. This is probably why I haven't warmed up to the idea of e-commerce. For me, a garment is not just something you get in a packet. The women who have been coming to Mélange for 25 years, whether it's Tina Ambani, Neerja Birla or Neena Gupta, feel one with the store when they are here. Now more than ever, we are looking to slow down the pace of things. With everything meticulously planned for Instagram, we all look forward to those rare effervescent moments that no camera can catch. With brick and mortar, the setting becomes the backdrop to narrate a designer's story.”   “For our first anniversary show we got the Royal Opera House to open its gates after 30 years. The theme was khadi and designers like Ramesh Nair and Hemant Trevedi made their interpretations of the conscious fabric. We draped the red velvet seats in white khadi and got Rahul Akerkar to cater a regional menu paired with coconut water for the event. Everyone talks about farm-to-fork now and we were doing it all those years ago! From Aishwarya Rai Bachchan (who modelled for the show) to writer Bandana Tewari, we brought together the tastemakers of the time under one roof. For me, fashion is spaces, it's how you walk into a place, how you feel, what you wear and what you see. I chose a fashion show to get my message of returning to our Indian roots across because, of course, fashion has and always will be the most attractive medium.” Scroll through the gallery below for a look at some of the best moments from 25 years of Mélange: View Gallery 13 Photos On Mélange’s 25th anniversary, let’s take a look back at their journey What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Meet Priya Ahluwalia, the winner of the H&M Design Award 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Priya Ahluwalia’s focus on sustainable vintage fabrics and modern Nineties nostalgia has won her the H&M Design Award 2019—the brand’s annual prize for the best graduates around the world. Here, the young British designer chats to Vogue about her fashion inspirations This year's H&M Design Award winner—graduate of London's University of Westminster Priya Ahluwalia—says a lot about the fashion industry's current drive for sustainability. The final took place in Berlin on November 28, a city known for championing youth and innovation, with a panel including Ann-Sofie Johansson, creative advisor at H&M, Vogue Germany editor-in-chief Christiane Arp and stylist Jan-Michael Quammie. Previous winners have included Stefan Cooke (in 2018) and Richard Quinn (in 2017), both graduates of London's Central Saint Martins, known for their fresh forward-thinking approach to technique, silhouettes and materials. And this year has seen design taken to the next level, with a global eco-fashion focus. Priya Ahluwalia convinced the judges mostly because of her sustainable approach, said Johansson—she works exclusively with vintage fabrics and uses second-hand clothing as the basis for her designs. It's an issue that is becoming increasingly important to H&M, and the wider fashion industry, Johansson adds. After graduating with an MA in June, Ahluwalia launched Ahluwalia Studio, and the prize fund of €50,000 will no doubt help in furthering her success. Here, Ahluwalia talks to Vogue about her sustainable vision, her love of menswear, how her dual Nigerian-Indian heritage influences her design and what she's got planned for next year... That came pretty fast, yes. During my bachelor's studies, I started out designing womenswear, but after a menswear project, I realised I liked that a lot better. Yes, exactly! These divisions don't have much to do with how people actually dress and consume fashion anymore. But, certain menswear traditions fascinate me, the sequence of designing and tailoring pieces. And there are interesting rules that have evolved over time. For example, the patch on sportswear is always on the left side—traditionally you want it to sit over your heart, because you love your team so much. This kind of symbolism has brought me to menswear. And I love sportswear from past decades. The 1990s, of course. I really love it. I'm 25 now, so of course I'm nostalgic about the 1990s. But I also see great things from the 1980s, I'm discovering all kinds of new things from that era. When I design, I always look at old photographs, especially of my family. The silhouettes they used to wear always give me inspiration. One of my uncles is probably my most important muse—there is a picture of him in a down jacket that I keep thinking about. As a teenager, yes. I started when I was about 16. Finding good vintage wasn't that easy back then, today there are a lot more options. But at least the shops on Brick Lane in East London were still good and not as overpriced as they are today. One of my hacks at that time was to go to the richer areas of London, Richmond for example. People there threw away so much and so many good things, unbelievable! You could buy pieces by Issey Miyake for five pounds! Now, I also do a lot of online research. But actually there's nothing better than finding a good piece of vintage after hours of trawling through the shops. There are huge depots that sort out second-hand clothing and merchants that deal in large quantities of fabric. Sometimes, I need flat fabrics to work with, sometimes I can deconstruct existing pieces. In my next collection, I will largely be using materials made from recycled plastic. Some were more open, some less. But it has always been an advantage that I use a mix of existing garments and old fabrics. I also completely deconstruct and re-manufacture them—I cut them open, change the cuts completely, turn them around to make entirely new pieces. In a way, it just means there is one more task because I have to bring them back to their original fabric state. Many people didn't understand that. That's why they were looking at me quite critically for a long time. But during my master's, the time had come, I was fully supported in doing this. Both. I'm a nostalgic person, but I don't want to live in the past. The word sustainability sometimes scares me. Some people hate it. Maybe I wasn't any different back then, before I really started to deal with the global cycle of garments. Sustainable fashion had such a bad reputation for so long, it immediately made me think of something made of bamboo, which I certainly don't want to wear. At least that's how it's always been among my friends. Right. Now that's changing because there's a lot of sustainably made stuff that people really want to wear. Now sustainability stands for cool, forward-thinking, with the future in mind. This is also important in my use of vintage clothing: that we think ahead. My fashion should not be a #throwback. I just want my audience to love the pieces—regardless of the fact that it is vintage and sustainable. If they think that's good too, great. At the moment, I'm working by seasons and I see the pieces as small capsule collections. There are always some pieces that have the same cut, but are made from different materials, as I only have a limited supply of each fabric. For example, if a store orders 3,000 of my red patchwork trousers, the patches will be different. So each piece is unique. I hope that this will encourage people to keep my pieces forever. Exactly. Many people forget that this is also what sustainability is about. Not only about how something is made, but also how long it is being worn. If someone buys a sweater in a fast-fashion store, but wears it for years and cares for it, then it can also be sustainable. It always depends on the point of view. Fast-fashion companies like H&M are also rethinking—case in point, they chose me as this year's winner! Recently, my main focus has been to find even better and more efficient ways of obtaining materials. But for now, that's going to remain my well-kept trade secret... My mother is Indian and my father Nigerian. I went to Nigeria to visit him and some relatives, he now lives in Lagos again. It is! The cool thing about Nigeria is that everyone there is a fighter, everyone wants to create something, everyone wants to be someone, everything is fast. That's what makes people creative and the city so exciting. It is so good to see that the world understands this now, and that many Nigerian artists also have international success. All these negative clichés about Africa are finally changing, there's not just poverty and war. For me, the way many people dress in Nigeria was also totally inspiring. Especially the people selling clothes there, who wore a compelling mix of second-hand clothes from all over the world—it didn't look like second-hand, though, I only knew because it was something like a T-shirt from a mud-run in England. In conversations with them, I learned that all second-hand clothes have to be bought in African countries and that they are not actually being donated, which is what we think in Europe. I found out that Panipat in India is the place where the most second-hand clothes are being traded worldwide. Exactly, that made sense anyway, because my mother is from India and I hadn't seen my grandmother who lives there for such a long time. What I saw in Panipat was overwhelming and shocking. So much clothing that nobody wanted at first. Once you've seen that, you can't just sit back and do nothing. At least I couldn't. So it became clear to me which way my fashion should go. column1: 6 celebrity brides you need to check out for wedding jewellery inspiration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Priyanka Chopra, Deepika Padukone, Sonam K Ahuja and more It doesn't matter if you've portrayed bejewelled queens like Kashibai or Padmavati on screen. Turns out, when you play the quintessential Indian bride IRL, you cannot escape the allure of decadent wedding jewellery. Whether it was newly-wed Priyanka Chopra's luxurious Umaid Bhawan Palace wedding, Deepika Padukone's Lake Como extravaganza or even Anushka Sharma's marriage last year, each Bollywood bride has proven that statement-worthy wedding jewellery is the way forward. The movie industry's latest bride, Priyanka Chopra's Sabyasachi wedding jewellery for her nuptials with Nick Jonas was an ode to the Mughal era. Crafted with uncut diamonds, emeralds and Japanese cultured pearls in 22 karat gold, it also featured delicate tiny stars in uncut diamonds for a touch of whimsy. While Chopra layered on the pieces for her Hindu ceremony, she kept it simple for her white wedding—accessorising her Ralph Lauren gown only with tear drop-shaped solitaire danglers and her Tiffany & Co. engagement ring. Deepika Padukone, who tied the knot with her long-time beau Ranveer Singh in Lake Como last month, was a picture of unparalleled elegance for both her wedding ceremonies. And while her bespoke Sabyasachi garb had much to do with it, so did her accompanying Pinterest-worthy bridal jewellery. We stalked some Bollywood brides to curate a must-have list of wedding jewellery every Indian bride needs to complete her repertoire. The headpiece is definitely the hero(ine) of bridal looks this year. Sonam K Ahuja made a bold choice with a pearl and gemstone vintage headpiece featuring a statement tikka designed by her mother, Sunita Kapoor. Padukone, on the other hand, opted for an oversized polki maang tikka for her Anand Karaj and a matha patti for her Konkani ceremony, while Soha Ali Khan gave her roots a nod with a maang tikka accompanied by a paasa. Another wedding jewellery trend Bollywood brides have been saying ‘I do' to is layering. Padukone, Ahuja, Khan and Anushka Sharma sported chokers with rani haars to add to the impact. Sharma played up the pastel pink of her bridal lehenga by opting for a combination of polki and tourmalines while Khan added a hint of colour to her gold bridal ensemble and jadau choker with a layered emerald necklace. Stacked bangles—a mix of traditional red choodas punctuated with gold and polki pieces—are then rounded off with dangling kaleeras. Neha Dhupia's uncut diamond earrings or Ahuja's gold and gemstone ones, jhumkis are a unanimous favourite this time around, as are stacked bangles with gold kaleeras. Just take a cue from Padukone's recent repertoire, and put a ring on it (read: every finger), so that you have a bridal look even Beyoncé would approve of. column1: These two trends are giving hope to the laziest girls this party season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Fashion has a plan for when you just can’t Staying up till 4am in a nightclub is not for everyone. While we admire the strength, grit and determination with which some continue to make an effort to dress up for a social event, after the 10th night out, even the most dedicated party hopper will reach some level of saturation. If your mood is to stay in for most of December but your calendar has other plans, there are two whole trends that you can enjoy. Some pleasures in life cannot be measured in the form of material satisfaction—photographic or otherwise. Catching your reflection on a particularly good hair day in store window, toss-dunking a ball of tissue in the paper bin across the room, lying in bed for hours after a shower and doing sweet nothing on a work day happen to be a few. If you're the kind of person who can lie around in her bathrobe, dreaming up empires without moving a muscle, bathleisure, and not athleisure, is the trend that's after your own heart. Bathleisure took the Internet by storm earlier this year, when Rihanna graced the cover of Vogue Paris in a slip dress with a towel atop her head. Inspired by the queen of R&B and authority on living life on your own terms, influencers joined in on the trend and started posting selfies in bathrobes and towels from the comfort of their tubs. Traces of bathleisure, though, can be traced all the way back to Elizabeth Taylor, the OG, whose iconic image in a lavender towel had Kim Kardashian West replicating the moment. The kind of girl who chooses laid-back glamour over perfection is the one who will fall for the trend. She can add yet another manicured square of pixels to her feed, but instead she chooses irreverence. Is a terry robe and wine glass enough to make a fashion statement? It can be if you are Rita Ora and take it to the red carpet with a side of diamonds. The key ingredients in the scenario are, of course, a robe, maybe a headwrap and even a pair of pool slides. But the year of rest and relaxation in trends in not limited to dewy post-shower selfies. Pyjamas have been A-OK to be worn outside the confines of your apartment for a while now. Sleepleisure now takes on an upgraded form—and there are no limitations to the fantastic iterations evolving from the combination of sleepwear and regular items of clothing. We are talking quilted robes casually thrown over a jumpsuit, a lacy slip dress paired with jeans and a leather jacket, or a matching set of pyjamas and a housecoat complete with a sash belt. Draw inspiration from Carrie Bradshaw's New Year's Eve moment in pyjamas, pearls and a warm coat. The enthusiasm for this trend begs the question: does fashion's tryst with laziness have a deeper meaning? Perhaps after one too many events and parties, December is making you want to hit the snooze button more than ever. Or have we harnessed BDE to its highest potential and started to care less about how we project ourselves? If you're too lazy to take a deep-dive into this stream of thought (we understand, it's the end of the year), and are only here to know on how you can get your bathleisure and sleepleisure on, head straight to our shopping gallery below, where the good stuff rests. column1: 10 high-impact fashion trends that ruled 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Your recap on the fashion trends that defined the best-dressed in 2018 It's been a busy 12 months in the world of Vogue. This year, we've witnessed the meteoric rise of Instagram's It-hat (thank you, Jacquemus, for enlivening our feed), gone with the Western mood (as seen at Versace, Calvin Klein and Isabel Marant), invested in a perfectly cut suit and revisited Noughties logomania. Here's your rundown of the catwalk trends that scored top marks in 2018. Models at Loewe, Versace, Gucci and Balmain wore their brands on their sleeves in the name of new-era logomania and we fell for the trend wholesale (as did the rest of social media). The highpoint? New mother Kylie Jenner stepping out in California with her Fendi logo stroller, matching minidress and belt bag all in sync. [#image: /photos/5ce41925b40d26fa6fd6b1a6]||| ||| Christian Dior autumn/winter 2019 show at Paris Fashion Week. Image: Getty Did you back Adam Selman's turn-of-the-Millennium indigo and Dior's retro patchworking? Or did Alberta Ferretti and Miu Miu's acid-washed Eighties jeans top your 2018 wishlist? Yes, this was the year that investment denim came with a Pinterest mood board featuring Britney and Bananarama. The question we asked when browsing for a new pair of jeans: which decade is flavour month? [#image: /photos/5ce41928b8031100c98f55ce]||| ||| Chloe spring/summer 2018 show at Paris Fashion Week. Image: Getty Whether you did a midnight black boxy blazer and oversized slacks or lightened the mood with a pastel-hued silhouette—this year, we all wanted to wear a suit. Be that with sneakers, Nineties mules or barely-there sandals. And we're not about to retire our love of the new rainbow shade suiting anytime soon… 2019 sees just as much emphasis on tailored twosomes in appealing non-corporate colourways. [#image: /photos/5ce4192889be363a767ce7d6]||| ||| Celine spring/summer 2018 show at Paris Fashion Week. Image: Rex Features Louis Vuitton, Off-White, Rodarte and Phoebe Philo's final Céline collection made the case that full-look leather works for daytime, and we were sold. Our dream capsule wardrobe? Max Mara's maxi skirt, Victoria Beckham's crisp shirting and Alexander McQueen's skate-style dresses. [#image: /photos/5ce419284a30b38ce312b9ea]||| ||| Molly Goddard autumn/winter 2019 at London Fashion Week. Image: Getty While the ladylike kitten heel was enjoying a revival, we dived into our late Nineties reference books and got on board with the prim pencil skirt too (which punctuated collections at Dries Van Noten, to Hermès, Miu Miu and Molly Goddard). The office-ready staple was re-pitched as a personality piece; decadent brocade and feather trims became the order of the day. The impact? Our collective return of modesty made Hedi Slimane's return to the runway at Celine (and those slashed-to-here minidresses) all the more shocking. [#image: /photos/5ce419273bf9b44be7b1aff0]||| ||| Isabel Marant autumn/winter 2019 show at Paris Fashion Week. Image: Getty Calvin Klein, Versace and Isabel Marant can lay claim to 2018's obsession with ranch style. There were prairie dresses a plenty on the catwalks, but it was the pieces that put a polished spin on the trend that stole our hearts: Think glossy cowboy boots and Western shirting. This wasn't our first fashion rodeo, but boy did we fall hard for the look. Were you lured by the confident, colourful palette at Marc Jacobs, Marni, Jil Sander and Roksanda? Us too. While this wasn't a year for the sartorially shy, we definitely relished the energy boosting effects of a shot of magenta, canary yellow or azure. [#image: /photos/5ce41929cc50be131d13dc3d]||| ||| Proenza Schouler autumn/winter 2018 show at Paris Fashion Week. Image: Getty Leopard print wasn't a hard sell to the fashion set—street style peacocks and fashion editors know how to capitalise on its eye-catching power during the busy show season. On the catwalk, Tom Ford, Balenciaga, Proenza Schouler and Victoria Beckham were all on hand to build momentum for the kitsch-cum-cool look, with pulse-racing prints designed to be worn head-to-toe. Mary Katrantzou, Marine Serre and Jacquemus were among the designers who overhauled our attitudes to cling this year—delivering second-skin rash vests, grip leggings and cycling shorts. This time, the trend was more to do with body-confidence than a pseudo-wellness gym culture. Caveat: The cycling shorts are sticking around for another season (appearing at Stella McCartney, Chanel and Off-White for spring/summer 2019). [#image: /photos/5ce4192c9cc0c0d9eff9bc56]||| ||| Jacquemus spring/summer 2018 show at Paris Fashion Week. Image: Getty From Gucci's balaclavas to Prada's bucket hats and Jacquemus' supersized sunshades, there was a catwalk hat for every occasion this year. The potential to make a #extra entrance became a reality thanks to these outlandish designs. On the catwalk they came in particularly handy for any model growing out last year's buzz cut. column1: 14 celeb-approved designer saris that are perfect for a cocktail party
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The must-have colours, must-try drapes and must-wear blouses If you were looking to give your trusty lehenga a rest, this wedding season presents the perfect opportunity to bring out the sari—no matter the weave, the drape or the embroidery. Bollywood has laid claim on the evergreen sari as the perfect cocktail outfit, and has served all the inspiration you'd need to give your ethnic wardrobe a modern do-over. From sari gowns to differently-draped versions, this edit features a roundup of all the celebrity OOTDs you need to see to be convinced that it's now time to make the shift. Notebooks at the ready? Here we go. The first style tip to make note of is that this season, vibrant shades of red, tangerine and fuchsia have been moved off the trend meter. ‘The more muted, the merrier', is what's currently ruling the charts. Kareena Kapoor Khan recently wore an ethereal white sari from Bollywood's favourite designer Manish Malhotra, styled with an intricately embellished blouse. And Jacqueline Fernandez followed suit with her Tarun Tahiliani white and gold silk georgette jaali sari, paired with a collared blouse. Don't miss out on Kiara Advani's sequinned beige floral sari by Shehlaa Khan either, which she wore with a bustier. If your personality veers towards the extravagant, we suggest you check out Malaika Arora's electric blue sari gown by Amit Aggarwal, Janhvi Kapoor's yellow Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla number and Kriti Sanon's olive green and silver Manish Malhotra sari. Those looking to create a statement can always look to one of fashion's favourite colours, black, to be their saviour—yes, even for ethnic functions. Rani Mukerji's Sabyasachi sari, Radhika Apte's classic black ensemble by Sunaina Khera and Mira Rajput Kapoor's easy-to-wear Anamika Khanna sari gown all serve as great examples of Indian ensembles in ebony. column1: The best fashion designer and artist collaborations of all time
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion When art and fashion collide, a special kind of creative alchemy happens. From Elsa Schiaparelli’s collaborations with Salvador Dalí to Louis Vuitton’s artistic alliances, Vogue looks back at the best fashion and art collaborations When it comes to fashion's love affair with collaboration, few of its unions sit quite as comfortably as that of leading designers and the art world's most interesting talents. From walking works of art like Yves Saint Laurent's 1965 Modernist collection, which featured his now iconic Piet Mondrian dresses, to complete creative exchanges that become part of a house's DNA (see Kim Jones's Dior menswear), these increasingly symbiotic relationships are fed by an enduring appetite for artfully erudite couture. While many of us consider fashion an art form itself, both industries continue to collaborate to forge deeper creative conversations. Painters, illustrators and photographers have become important contributors to the fashion industry, their input often adding instant value to a collection. The direction is often set by the designer and fuelled by a mutual appreciation of each others' work. Elsa Schiaparelli and Salvador Dalí were friends who shared such an appreciation, one of the earliest examples of the artistic cross-pollination that designers now seek. The Italian couturier's exquisite surrealist evening gown featured a large Dalí-esque lobster painted across the crotch area—an exploration of sexuality. The arrival of Andy Warhol in the 1960s signalled a new breed of cultural icons that reignited fashion's appetite for art. Yves Saint Laurent and Warhol became friends and collaborators—Warhol painted a series of colourful portraits of the designer, while Saint Laurent designed his autumn/winter 1966 Pop Art collection, a sartorial embodiment of the artistic movement. Countless designers have featured Warhol's work in their collections since—including Gianni Versace, Jean-Charles de Castelbajac and Raf Simons—cementing his status as fashion's favourite artist. Beyond Warhol's enduring influence, Raf Simons, Miuccia Prada, Marc Jacobs and Kim Jones have continued to call upon lesser-known artists to enhance their creative process—not just referencing the artwork, but featuring it front and centre. Prada's standout collaboration was with French artist Christophe Chemin for the celebrated autumn/winter 2016 menswear collection. In recent years, Louis Vuitton has been leading the charge in artist collaborations. During his time as creative director, Marc Jacobs helped establish a tradition of partnerships between the French house and global artistic talents. He commissioned Stephen Sprouse to reimagine its monogram print in graffiti form for Vuitton's spring/summer 2001 ready-to-wear collection, and went on to forge a 13-year relationship with Takashi Murakami. The Japanese artist introduced the Multicolore monogram bag in 2003 which quickly became the It bag of the early 2000s. Jacobs was also inspired to work with provocateur Richard Prince for his spring/summer 2008 runway show, which featured models (including Naomi Campbell) dressed as nurses and yet another iteration of the Vuitton cult monogram print. Nicolas Ghesquière, the current creative maestro behind the French label's womenswear lines, has continued to build on this heritage with Vuitton's Masters Series, giving American artist Jeff Koons unprecedented freedom to play with the house's signature canvas. Elsewhere, former Vuitton menswear designer Kim Jones has begun to establish a similar culture of artistic collaboration at Dior Men. Jones teamed up with New York-based contemporary artist Kaws for his debut collection, which saw the artist reimagine the house's signature bee logo for a capsule collection. Kaws also created a giant version of his BFF character made entirely from flowers that formed part of Jones's runway set, as well as becoming part of Dior Men's SS19 campaign imagery. And Jones's latest pre-fall show in Tokyo featured an imposing 12-metre high robot by Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama—the artist also designed a limited-edition bag for the collection. Art has always influenced fashion, but when designers move beyond references and subtle nods and instead work directly with artists, truly extraordinary and original work is created. Such collections—many now cult collectibles—occupy an exciting new space where the two fields meet, standing not only as works of art in their own right, but as fun, highbrow sartorial offerings that allow designers to create beyond the normal realms of fashion. column1: The Marni family launches a brand new label called ‘Plan C’
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And it’s keeping the iconic household’s heritage alive, while breathing new life into Italian fashion When founder Consuelo Castiglioni quit the fashion scene by renouncing her position at Marni, the industry was left anticipating what lay next on the cards for the Italian luxury house. Now, two years on, her daughter Carolina is furthering the family's sartorial repute by helming an exciting new label called ‘Plan C', launched earlier this year. Carolina Castiglioni, who formerly spearheaded special projects at Marni, is mostly known for her unconventional approach to fashion, having constantly reinvented the wheel—after all, it was she who devised the Bauhaus-inspired theatrical piece ‘Looking for Marni' to launch the brand's eyewear line, as well as the globetrotting flower market that was part of Marni's 20th anniversary celebrations. As the creative director of Plan C, Castiglioni has integrated much of her eccentric and playful personality into her label's DNA, reflected clearly in its luxe knitwear, ready-to-wear and accessories collections, including handbags adorned with drawings made by her four-year-old. From billowy parkas and masculine shirts to voluminous dresses and shorts slathered with sequins, Carolina evidently strives to break free from the hackneyed mechanisation of Italian fashion, and to create something that speaks of art, androgyny and a greater sense of newness. The collections here function on a bi-annual model (Castiglioni does not intend to present them on the runway yet) and what with their exaggerated forms, sculptural silhouettes and a bright colour palette, it is almost impossible to not see glimpses of Marni's unmistakably bold aesthetic woven into them. The brand primarily trades from its central base in Milan, and has already caused ripples with its debut spring/summer 2019 line, which was launched this June. With father and Marni's co-founder Gianni Castiglioni serving as CEO-at-large and brother Giovanni Castiglioni posing as operations director, one can only await the innovations that lie in the pipeline for the renewed Plan C family. column1: Can lab-grown diamonds become a girl’s best friend?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion When it comes to diamonds, rareness and extravagant price tags have always been welcome touchstones, but as technology steals a march on nature, is the ultimate gemstone undergoing a make-under for the modern day? A diamond is just a lump of coal that did well under pressure. But exactly what kind of pressure, and in what conditions, lie at the centre of a debate that has divided and disrupted the sparkling world of fine jewellery. Technology has evolved so rapidly over the past five years, the industry has witnessed a boom in lab-grown diamonds—gemstones that are chemically and aesthetically identical to those found at the bottom of the Earth, yet can be produced in a matter of months. And with a younger, more ethically conscious generation coming of diamond-buying age, many argue that this environmentally-friendly, sustainable method is the best way of providing the world with its favourite gemstone. Synthetic gemstones have been manufactured as far back as the 19th century—but the challenge of creating a decent-sized diamond, however, has long eluded scientists. While lab-made rubies, sapphires and emeralds have gone mainstream, diamonds have retained their cachet as a symbol of rarity, luxury and uniqueness. “Grown diamonds” (a term the Diamond Producers Association initially disputed as misleading, only to be overturned by the US Federal Trade Commission in July, allowing synthetic manufacturers to market their products as “real”) costs, on average, 30 to 40 per cent less than natural diamonds. And as the practice becomes more widespread, that gap will likely widen—with mined diamonds dropping in value to remain competitive. So how do you “grow” diamonds? There are two ways to do it. The first simulates the crushing force of Mother Nature by applying high temperature and high pressure in a microwave chamber to transform carbon into a diamond. The second is akin to 3D printing, where pieces of carbon are layered on a diamond seed in a vacuum chamber. Both processes, it should be noted, are hardly eco-friendly—they require an enormous amount of energy to operate. But the technology is so advanced now that experts require a machine to distinguish between synthetic and mined gems. And whereas once consumers perceived synthetic diamonds to be less authentic and valuable than natural ones, today they are being viewed as an enticing gateway to bigger diamonds at lower prices and, crucially, a guilt-free investment. “A lot of young people are interested in this category of diamonds—they saw the film Blood Diamond and they know about the dark side of mining,” says Jean Pigozzi, one of many multi-millionaires with a stake in Silicon Valley-based Diamond Foundry. One of the biggest producers of synthetic diamonds, its investors include Leonardo DiCaprio, the founders of Facebook and Twitter, and the founding CEO of eBay. “When you go to a jewellery store, 32 people on average have touched the diamond before it reaches you, and those people are not traceable. In the case of lab-grown diamonds, they go straight from the factory to the jeweller,” says Pigozzi. Consumers are equally aware of the environmental impact of diamond mining, and Diamond Foundry is keen to convey its “world positive” ethos. “Currently, we are the only diamond producer that is certified carbon neutral,” says CEO Martin Roscheisen, who points out that his diamonds are manufactured in a hydro-powered plasma reactor. “Mining has a larger environmental footprint than any other human activity. For a single carat of diamond, approximately 250 tonnes of earth have to be dug up, 2,011 ounces of air pollution is released and 143 pounds of carbon dioxide is emitted.” Of course, the most environmentally-friendly way of buying diamonds is not to buy new diamonds, synthetic or natural, at all. Many pre-owned stones are available at both retail and auction level, and most jewellers offer bespoke services to reset and redesign second-hand pieces of jewellery. Many jewellers have made it their USP to rework antique jewellery for a contemporary audience. For the big jewellery houses, however, the shift towards synthetic has proved more problematic. Take historic brand De Beers, which monopolised the diamond market for well over a century and is still the world's largest miner, with exclusive access to Botswana's entire supply chain. Having coined the phrase “a diamond is forever”, for years, De Beers expressed its reluctance to embrace synthetic diamonds, preferring to focus on the image of mined diamonds as rare, eternal and the only option for engagement rings. But this May, the house performed a U-turn with Lightbox, a new range of lab-grown diamonds produced under the De Beers Group umbrella. With a $94 million facility in Oregon, Lightbox aims to produce 500,000 synthetic carats per year by 2020. Lightbox's approach is telling. Targeted at a younger clientele, its campaigns will be lighter in tone and geared towards fashion trends, rather than playing on the emotional gravitas of engagement rings. Prices are $800 per carat; by comparison, a one-carat mined diamond will usually sell for about $8,000. “It's light and fun and decorative,” says chief marketing officer Sally Morrison. “We tell it like it is and we are pursuing completely linear pricing. With natural diamonds, pricing follows a curve based on rarity, which just doesn't make sense for lab-grown products.” Morrison says Lightbox's biggest competitors are costume-jewellery behemoths, such as Swarovski. De Beers is effectively betting on splitting the market—with luxury, complex, mined-gem engagement rings at the top, and lab-made fashion jewellery, mainly solitaires, aimed at millennials, at the bottom. “We hope to become a lighthouse brand for this category,” adds Morrison. “Right now, it's a tiny little team. Notwithstanding the power of our parent company, it's very start-up-y.” For jewellers old and new, lab-grown diamonds remain uncharted territory. On the one hand, it presents a new medium that is chemically the same as mined diamonds, available ethically and at a much more accessible price point. On the other, it could dilute the aura of luxury and rarity that so many jewellers trade on. For Stephen Webster, one of London's leading independent jewellers, it is a point of interest—but only to a certain degree. “The one thing that everyone would agree on is that you don't want to see confusion,” he says. Whereas he uses mined stones for his namesake label, the jeweller has partnered with Atelier Swarovski on a line of fair-trade pieces featuring 14-carat recycled gold, rose quartz and lab-grown pavé diamonds—or “created” diamonds, as Swarovski prefers to call them. “When I was asked by Swarovski to work on this project, I knew I was working on something completely separate to what I do,” says Webster. “The stones that we're using in this collection are intentionally small stones, to add a bit of glitz to a piece. A lot of fashion-forward jewellery is about design, [and] not so much [about] high-value individual stones.” For Webster, working with synthetic diamonds provides an opportunity to speak to a younger audience at a more accessible level. Prices start at £1,290 and go up to £7,490. He agrees that synthetic stones could act as a more democratic platform for fine jewellery, just as diffusion lines or high-street collaborations can for high-end fashion designers. “There's a call for more democracy in fashion and jewellery,” says Webster. “I'm not bursting any illusion about the rarity of what comes out of the ground, which is to do with colour and size and uniqueness. As beautiful as they are, a lab-grown diamond is coming in as an alternative for people to make up their own mind about.” “It will be totally disruptive,” asserts Nadja Swarovski, matriarch of the legendary crystal manufacturer, which began cutting gemstones in 1965. “There's that belief that diamonds and rare and precious, and I think it's also going to be a generational thing. My mother would never buy a created diamond, but my daughters would only buy a created diamond.” For Swarovski, which for years has been associated with crystals, this marks an unprecedented dive into the world of diamonds—and Nadja is keen to add that the Austrian company will also be looking into using natural diamonds, as long as they are ethically sourced. “It's exciting for us to go into the fine jewellery market,” she adds. “I'm not sure how fine jewellers are not embracing created diamonds.” Within the jewellery community—and indeed among luxury consumers—synthetic diamonds just don't have the same ring (for want of a better word) as mined stones. Currently, engagement rings account for almost a third of global diamond jewellery sales, which makes them a substantial contributor to the revenues of jewellery houses. It remains divisive whether consumers could be drawn to synthetic diamonds for such a highly sentimental piece of jewellery. De Beers is adamant that they won't be—yet, in a survey by market research company MVI, the percentage of consumers willing to buy an engagement ring with a lab-grown diamond is steadily increasing, rising from 55 per cent in 2016 to almost 70 per cent in 2018. “With how quickly this industry is growing, it could eclipse mined diamonds by 2030,” says Diamond Foundry's Roscheisen, who adds that the company's production and sales have almost doubled each quarter and it is currently producing more than 100,000 carats per year. If those figures are anything to go by, it may not be long before the esteemed names on Place Vendôme take note. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast
