column1: Power moves and power plays: What made the headlines in fashion in 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Look back at the firings, hirings, moments and mergers that made fashion headlines in 2018 How will you remember 2018? Phoebe Philo fans would say it was an “annus horribilis”, whereas menswear aficionados would argue it was the most transformative year yet. Either way, there were moments—firings, hirings and acquisitions—that definitely dominated the conversation in the industry. Here, we look back at the happenings that shaped 2018. The managerial musical chairs started early in the year with the return of British designer Nathan Jenden to DVF. Taking on the role of chief design officer and vice president, Jenden replaced Jonathan Saunders, who departed from his role at the New York-based brand the month prior. Matters gathered pace when Kim Jones's departure from Louis Vuitton was confirmed, effectively setting off a chain reaction that would shake up menswear over the coming months. But the biggest appointment came on 21 January, when Hedi Slimane was named as Phoebe Philo's successor at Céline—at that point still with an ‘é'. His first big announcement? Adding menswear, couture and fragrance to the LVMH-backed brand. [#image: /photos/5ce4192189be3681657ce7d0]||| ||| Queen Elizabeth II at Richard Quinn's show during London Fashion Week. Image: Getty London Fashion Week got the royal seal of approval when Queen Elizabeth II made a surprise appearance at Richard Quinn's show. Sitting front row with Anna Wintour, Her Majesty presented the rising star with the inaugural Queen Elizabeth II Award for British Design. Earlier that week, Christopher Bailey bid farewell to Burberry, ending his 17-year tenure with a rainbow-bright collection celebrating LGBTQ+ communities—his replacement yet unknown. In the first of a series of major acquisitions, France's oldest surviving couture house Lanvin found new ownership. Chinese conglomerate Fosun did not share any details (or figures) of the transaction, but was said to be injecting €100 million into the struggling brand. Meanwhile, Massimo Giorgetti's MSGM sold a minority stake (32 per cent) to Italian private equity fund Style Capital. [#image: /photos/5ce41921b80311684d8f55c6]||| ||| Hubert de Givenchy with Audrey Hepburn. Image: Getty The fashion world went into mourning when the founder of the couture French maison Givenchy, Hubert de Givenchy, passed away, aged 91. Burberry named Riccardo Tisci as chief creative officer, reuniting him with former Givenchy colleague Marco Gobbetti, who took over as chief executive in October 2017. The menswear musical chairs continued with news of Kris Van Assche's departure from Dior Homme. The French fashion house was swift in naming a replacement: Louis Vuitton's former designer Kim Jones, who was slated to show his first collection in June at the same time as his successor at Louis Vuitton, Off-White founder and streetwear stalwart Virgil Abloh. Following Fosun's investment in Lanvin, the shake-up began. The first to step down was artistic director Olivier Lapidus, eight months after being appointed; Joann Cheng was named interim CEO. In an unprecedented move, Stella McCartney took back full control of her eponymous fashion label, buying back Kering's 50 per cent stake. Berluti parted ways with Haider Ackermann after just three seasons, spurring rumours—which were confirmed days later—that Kris Van Assche would succeed him. The Belgian designer's first collection for the Italian leather goods and menswear brand scheduled for January 2019. While speculation mounted around Hedi Slimane's Celine, it was his landmark $11.5 million settlement against Saint Laurent that garnered more column inches in April. The French court ruled the designer had been underpaid by Kering for his last year of service at Saint Laurent. Givenchy was once again making headlines, but in a royal capacity this time: Meghan Markle married Prince Harry in Haute Couture Givenchy, designed by British designer Clare Waight Keller. French designer Simon Porte Jacquemus decamped the fashion crowd to Marseilles to unveil his very first menswear collection, putting an end to all the #NewJob rumours doing the rounds about about potential roles at Celine or Versace. French contemporary brand Carven filed for bankruptcy. The brand was forced to cancel deliveries of its spring collection, designed by Serge Ruffieux, earlier in the year. The setback is said to have cost the brand several million euros. American designer Kate Spade was found dead in her New York home, aged 55. Quirky yet quintessentially American, Kate Spade's namesake bags became a preppy and peppy rite-of-passage purchase for a generation of women. Tomas Maier's 17-year tenure at Bottega Veneta came to an end, with former Céline, Maison Margiela and Balenciaga alum Daniel Lee named to succeed him. The Italian “stealth wealth” brand skipped the September shows to give the incoming designer time to settle in. Two fiercely independent brands took major investments: the Missonis sold a 41.2 per cent stake in their family business to FSI Mid-Market Growth Equity Fund, and Belgian brand Dries Van Noten was acquired by the Spanish fashion group Puig. Kim Jones's and Virgil Abloh's highly anticipated debuts at their new roles—heading up Dior and Louis Vuitton, respectively—did not disappoint. Jones mined the Dior archive and teamed up with New York-based artist Kaws to create a BFF doll, a ten-foot floral version of which sat at the heart of his show set. Meanwhile, Abloh's Wizard of Oz-themed show was a riot of colour, not least because of the rainbow runway. President Donald Trump's daughter, Ivanka Trump, closed her fashion brand in order to “remain in Washington indefinitely”. The acquisition game continued when Japanese conglomerate Fast Retailing (owner of Uniqlo, Theory and Helmut Lang) took a stake in French brand Lemaire. Christophe Lemaire, who is also head of Uniqlo's Paris R&D Center and designer of the Uniqlo U line, extended his contract with Fast Retailing for a further five years. After facing serious criticism over destroyed samples, Burberry's newly appointed head, Italian-born designer Riccardo Tisci, unveiled his first major overhaul: the logo. Based on a 1908 monogram from the archive, founder Thomas Burberry's initials interlock in white and orange over a honey-coloured background. Following this announcement, the brand confirmed it had stopped destroying product and would go fur-free, as Versace had done earlier in the year and Coach, DVF and Jean Paul Gaultier would pledge later on. Designer duo Rushemy Botter and Lisi Herrebrugh were announced creative directors for Nina Ricci. And yet another independent brand, Thom Browne, was bought up. Zegna Group acquired an 85 per cent stake, and vowed to let the Browne run independently while providing support in the global retail expansion and manufacturing process. Versace's acquisition by Michael Kors caught the industry off guard. Although the rumours had been chronicled for a while, it was the provenance of the buyer that took people by surprise. The $2.1 billion deal left Donatella Versace, sister of Gianni, founder of the house, in charge of overseeing the day-to-day running of the brand. Michael Kors Holdings Limited has since rebranded to Capri Holdings and also owns shoe brand Jimmy Choo. London Fashion Week saw the return of British fashion designer Victoria Beckham after a decade presenting in New York. For the brand anniversary, the former Spice Girl worked together with Juergen Teller to recreate the memorable Marc Jacobs 2008 campaign of her trapped in a shopping bag. Hedi Slimane's first move at the helm of Celine was a contentious one: a new logo which dropped the accent of from the first ‘e' (which many replaced on the street posters in protest) and, effectively, erased all traces of Phoebe Philo. His Paris Fashion Week debut was equally controversial, with many saying his models were too thin and his designs too familiar. In the second Royal Wedding of the year, Princess Eugenie married her long-term partner Jack Brooksbank wearing a Peter Pilotto design. The dress had an emotional reveal as Princess Eugenie decided to opt for a semi-backless option that exposed her scoliosis operation scar, a powerful and inspiring nod to those affected by the illness. Troubled French brand Carven was rescued by Chinese group Icicle. The price tag? €4.2 million with, according to AFP, the promise of a further €8 million in investment. Swiss-born Serge Ruffieux would step down later in November as result of the internal re-evaluation inside the brand. Lacoste named Louise Trotter as creative director, making the Brit the first woman to lead the French sportswear institution since it was founded in 1933. Continuing the shake-up at Lanvin, one of the oldest French houses in operation, menswear creative director Lucas Ossendrijver departed after 14 years in the role, with no successor confirmed as yet. Proenza Schouler's Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez followed in the footsteps of Stella McCartney by buying back control of their label from Castanea Partners through the backing of a private investor. column1: Kim Jones reveals what inspired his Dior Men’s pre-fall 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Dior menswear artistic director, Kim Jones, on why he looks up to Karl Lagerfeld, the real reason behind his artist collaborations and why he isn’t afraid of being considered commercial What would Mr Dior do? A fine question, if ever there was one. And the perfect place to start. Dior's menswear artistic director Kim Jones is between fittings, the day before his pre-fall show in Tokyo, Japan, referencing Mr Dior with the ease and familiarity you'd expect of blood relations. Models take a break on the terrace while trolleys of fruit and nibbles get wheeled down the hallway; trays of jewellery and belts coming and going. It is unseasonably warm in the Japanese capital but the heating remains decidedly on in the hotel, as if to preempt a sudden temperature drop that just doesn't seem to come. Despite the jet lag and looming deadline, the Dior team is excited, working away not to the beat of music, but a crackling extractor that keeps the makeshift (but extremely neat and ordered) photo studio ventilated. “It's been non-stop,” says Jones modestly. Less than 24 hours ago he was celebrating the launch of his (since sold out) summer 2019 capsule collection with Kaws in Tokyo's Isetan Shinjuku department store. But neither jet lag nor the whirlwind year that has been can keep him down. Yesterday's large-scale show marked not only his first pre-fall collection (he was only appointed in March), but also the first pre-fall show undertaken by a menswear artistic director at the historic house. In many ways, it was also the first real glimpse into what Jones' Dior Men will really be. “The brand is brilliant, but it was a little quiet,” explains Jones of the decision to turn pre-fall into a full-blown extravaganza. “[This show was] just to say, ‘Hey, we're really here!' And to show we're doing it with conviction. Tokyo was loved by Mr Dior very much; he referenced Japan a lot, he visited Japan a lot. I love Japan, he loved Japan, it seemed the perfect place to start.” Where his spring/summer 2019 debut was light and romantic—a softer, more elegant departure from the moody, razor-sharp suiting of Kris Van Assche and Hedi Slimane—Jones' pre-fall is “quite tough, actually”, he reflects. “Lot of metallics, the Dior grey and tailoring. It still has that relaxed fit, but it's strong.” The colour palette is (naturally) darker, with Dior grey, midnight blues and subtle pinks. “Mr Dior had a very fixed palette when he worked,” notes Jones in raptures over the Dior archive. The “strict” colour palette isn't the only way Mr Dior has directly inspired the collection: the last tie the couturier was given has sparked a whole suit; the leopard-skin print, too, was taken directly from the archive; the kimonos closing the show are based on Mr Dior's own sketches for his Japanese clients; and, of course, there's the cherry blossom motif. True to style, Jones has taken these Dior classics and reinvented them. The metallic buckles of Matthew Williams of Alyx make a welcome return, giving outerwear a decidedly modern update, as does the Tailleur Oblique, which is designed to wrap the body diagonally with a single button. “As well as outerwear, we've also [added the oblique] onto the bestselling tailoring shapes, which existed pre-me joining Dior. I think is important to tell the customer that these things are still here,” he says, conscious of the need not to alienate Dior devotees. Jones has no qualms with the word “commercial”, a term often derided by designers. Instead, Jones embraces it: “I'm quite happy to be commercial. You have to be nowadays to survive in these big jobs.” The artist collaboration also makes a welcome return. “I'm working with artists because Christian Dior was a gallerist before he was a couturier,” says the designer. “He worked with the leading artists of his time, like Salvador Dalí and Picasso, so I looked to what the modern generation's take on that would be, hence starting with Kaws and now Hajime Sorayama.” The Japanese artist and master of “super-realism” may not be as well known as Yayoi Kusama and Takashi Murakami, but his futuristic point of view proves a fascinating addition to the Dior universe. Aside from the erotic, 12-metre-tall sculpture at the heart of the set (“It's the most beautiful thing ever,” remarks Jones as we watch a clip on his phone, entranced by the giant robot being lit up by strobe laser lights), there's the limited-edition robo-take on the saddle bag, dubbed Sorayama metals, of which only 10 will be made. Sorayama has updated Mr Dior's beloved cherry blossom, and his celebrated feminine forms and T-Rex illustrations have become prints, too. No less impressive are a series of “metalised” pieces. “It is a new technique that hadn't been tried on garments before,” explains Edward Crutchley, Dior's fabric expert and long-term collaborator of Jones'. “The garment is placed in a vacuum chamber, we take out all the air, explode the fabric and atomise it, and then metal is magnetised through the garment.” Beyond artists, Jones' crew of collaborators remains key: milliner Stephen Jones, right-hand woman Lucy Beeden, Alyx's Matthew Williams and jewellery designer Yoon Ahn included. (The last speaks openly of her own admiration and respect for Jones. “You can definitely feel the energy every time you go to the studio,” Ahn tells Vogue ahead of the show.) “I think it's really important to have a team of people who you love around you,” says Jones. “You look at people like Karl Lagerfeld, he's the person that everyone in the industry should look at because his team absolutely loves him, he'll make them laugh, he'll make them work, he'll inspire them... I think that is how things should be.” Notably missing (again) is the streetwear sensibility that Jones became so synonymous with during his Vuitton tenure. “You have to challenge yourself and look at how people are looking at things, how they wear things. For me, it's [about] respecting the house codes and finding new, exciting things to make people want to buy each season. I've got confidence in what I do, but, you know, you never really know… You have to do things with your instinct; trust yourself and take intelligent risks.” Less than nine months in, what has he learned at Dior? “I've realised that clothing is not that fickle. You buy something because it makes you feel good, and I think that's an important thing to do. Especially when the world is so dire. Enjoy the things you can enjoy, and the things that make you feel good about yourself.” Does that mean the autumn/winter show in January will be a feel-good affair? “It's very full-on. It's my favourite collection out yet, and I've done quite a lot.” View Gallery 7 Photos Kim Jones reveals what inspired his Dior Men’s pre-fall 2019 What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 6 ethical jewellery brands that would make the perfect Christmas gifts
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ethical jewellery is the new luxury, with fans from Hollywood to Queen Elizabeth II herself recognising the extra shine in fair-mined gold and traceable diamonds, plus the eco-studios and women artisan collectives behind the designs. Vogue presents the best conscious brands to buy into now When it comes to gifts, jewellery is always top of the list. And as the conversation around sustainable fashion ramps up, the focus is starting to shift away from the usual machine-made, mass-produced pieces. Instead, jewellery designers like Lilian von Trapp—whose Berlin-based brand financially backs an environmental and humanitarian campaign in Uganda—are finding ways to do more than just accessorise. She's among a band of small international jewellers that are raising the bar with ethically-sourced gold, traceable diamonds, female employment collectives and local artists—just a few of their ethically-sound initiatives. Here, Vogue presents six conscious jewellery brands, carving their own unique path in the industry. After art school in London, and a brief stint in New York, jewellery designer Suzzan Atala decided to open her workshop in Mexico City—she says that she was keen to be “part of the social change” in her home country, creating jobs and supporting the local economy. Designing for “empowered women”—Adwoa Aboah is a fan—Atala sources materials for her trinkets from artisan suppliers in Mexico, including Taxco, a town southwest of Mexico City famed for its jewellery and silverwork. Star pieces are the gold vagina necklaces and milagro earrings (flaming heart votives). Instagram: @tuzajewelry; Website: Tuzajewelry.com Lebanese sisters Dima and Tania Nawbar are fourth generation jewellers. Their family's Beirut-based business was founded by their great-great-grandfather in a gold souk in 1881. Establishing their own brand, L'atelier Nawbar, in 2011, the sisters have modernised, both in design—with symbolic rings and Petit Bling (a line of charms for children)—and in policy—increasing the company's female quota to equal that of the male, and training socially disadvantaged and displaced women in handmade techniques, such as intricate beading and stone carving. Although 90 per cent of this work is attainable by machines today, the Nawbars insist on keeping the, often elderly, women artisans in work. Instagram: @lateliernawbar; Website: Lateliernawbar.com Lena Dunham, Leandra Medine and Marion Cotillard were first in line when Joyce Binneboese and Dana Roski—a former model and a fashion stylist—partnered up to present their debut collection of jewellery at Berlin Fashion Week earlier this year. Featuring seashells, freshwater pearls and Swarovski crystals, each piece is handmade by Wald Berlin's “fair trade mums collective”—a group of unemployed mothers and grandmothers, many of whom live in small villages in Germany where jobs are scarce. Instagram: @waldberlin; Website: Wald-berlin.de The buzz surrounding the fine jewellery of Brazilian designer Ana Khouri reached fever pitch when Lady Gaga donned a pair of her earrings on the October 2018 cover of American Vogue. New York-based Khouri—who trained in sculpture in Sao Paulo, before studying at the Gemological Institute of America and Parsons School of Design—works exclusively with fair-mined 18-carat gold and platinum, traceable diamonds and gemstones from Zambia. Winning the Andam Fashion Accessories Prize in 2017, four years after setting up her eponymous label, friends of the brand now include Claire Foy, Charlize Theron and Alicia Vikander. Instagram: @anakhouri; Website: Anakhouri.com A pioneer in compassionate design, Pippa Small has even been recognised by Queen Elizabeth II, who awarded her an MBE in 2013 for services to ethical jewellery production. The London-based jeweller built her brand by collaborating with indigenous and traditional craftspeople the world over, from Afghanistan to Botswana. Working alongside Turquoise Mountain—an arts charity founded by HRH Prince Charles and the former president of Afghanistan Hamid Karzai to revive Afghan crafts banned during the Taliban regime—Small's AW18 Burma collection seeks to create local jobs and promote declining traditional jewellery techniques, which have been integral to Burmese society since 200BC. Instagram: @pippasmalljewellery; Website: Pippasmall.com Best known for pushing perceptions of “precious”, Melissa Joy Manning started her brand in 1997, long before sustainability and ethically-sourced were the buzzwords they are now. Beyond using sustainable materials—including recycled silver and 14-carat gold, and responsibly-sourced stones—her California and New York studios are totally green: using recycled paper, soy ink and energy-efficient heating and cooling processes. They also have a zero-waste policy and carbon offset each shipment. Angelina Jolie, Anne Hathaway and Jessica Alba are fans—as is Net-a-Porter. column1: Why the ‘ugly’ boot is this winter’s most powerful wardrobe statement
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Set aside ugly sneakers, this winter it’s the turn of the ugly boot. In 2018's socio-political climate, the word ‘ugly' feels passé. There are now, thankfully, very few places in the fashion world where ‘ugly' can stick. Naturally, it should never be applied to people, nor to dismiss designs that, at first glance, jar their audience. Footwear is the exception to the rule. From the knee down, ugliness is a byword for youthful relevancy, avant-garde luxury and comfort (as Instagram's obsession with gargantuan trainers has proven). And this season it's the turn of the ugly boot. Why? Well, there are a few obvious perks to the ugly boot. Yes, it's practical: you can walk at pace and potentially slash your Uber dependence. Seldom will it demand expensive visits to the cobbler, because it's too down-to-earth and sturdy for that. Often, it's waterproofed (see Prada and Calvin Klein). And then there are the less obvious perks. Ugly footwear in general is a wardrobe power move, dialing up new-era body confidence to read as sexy precisely because it's not about seduction. It's political. The ugly shoe movement has been in its easy-going stride for well over a decade now, bringing classic Ugg boots (ugly), Crocs (extremely ugly) and FitFlops (ugliest)—with all three succeeding in changing the fashion footprint of this century, overcoming gender, wealth and age barriers, and inspiring various catwalk renditions along the way, which is no mean feat. Notice how 2013's ubiquitous ugly pool slides segued into 2017's ugly sneakers? Today, those have morphed into 2018's ugly boots and this, like it or loathe it, is one trend that's impossible to ignore. Take Chloé's hit hybrid boots, which come with a lug sole and Cuban heel and rubber toecap. Not only do they satisfy our sartorial polyamory for different types of boots with one faithful style, they have helped bring about a shift in gear at the house. Under Natacha Ramsay-Levi's watch, Chloé's characteristic bohemian spirit has gained a new, tougher sensibility. Unlikely as it may seem, these characterful boots work very well with tapered silk trousers (where a spikey kitten heel would be predictable) and those handkerchief hem dresses (served up with muddy-brown opaque tights on the catwalk). It isn't a look for the inhibited, but then again, neither is the Chloé woman's peripatetic spirit. At Dries Van Noten and Rochas, the focus was on the heel of the ugly boot—a gnarled silhouette lending a surrealist twist. Crucially, you can wear them from dawn through to dawn. The notion of 24/7 wearability (which the ugly hybrid boot does so well) isn't anything new for shoppers, but designers are now embracing it too. The boldest iterations on the autumn/winter 2018 catwalks featured oversized rubber toecaps, see Calvin Klein and Phillip Lim, while Prada showcased wellies—proper, old-fashioned baggy wellies. These robust boots are prepped for adventure without losing any of their luxe kudos. Prada's wellies are instantly recognisable thanks to bright white logo—and it's precisely because they are not ‘pretty' that they feel like a classic slice of the brand The same can be said for Christopher Kane's latest foray into the ugly shoe world. As the industry's unofficial ugly shoe champion, Kane has followed up his crush on Crocs with this season's diamanté-encrusted sneaker-boot, a collaboration with orthopedic footwear brand Z-Coil. It comes complete with a shock-absorbent heel for a mashup that defies description. It's too much in nearly every way, but then, that's now the point. When it comes to our feet, exaggeration holds newfound appeal as designers see accessorising as an opportunity to reach fresh extremes, and to exhibit a sense of humour. While we may still be wearing our minimal day dress or a neat pencil skirt day in, day out, our shoes have turned up a notch. Balenciaga's witchy-toed knee boots poke fun at the very notion of prettiness, but aren't they good? Miu Miu's bejewelled booties are a dash too saccharine, but a sickly-sweet indulgence from time to time doesn't hurt, does it? The truth is, what we mean by ‘average' has changed in that there is now no average, no normal. These boots flip attitudes that once separated ‘the ugly' from ‘the beautiful' on their head. Ugliness has, quite rightly, never looked or felt so good. View Gallery 8 Photos How the ‘ugly’ boot ousted the supersized sneaker Fashion Culture & Living Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Here’s everything that’s hot in Dubai this week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion People, collaborations and online shopping With its skyscrapers, trendy bars and restaurants, Dubai is one of the most cosmopolitan cities of the world. And like all other fashion capitals, it is now addressing the question of why fashion needs to include everyone. If you're in Dubai this week, this is everything you need to make space in your black book for. Sinéad Burke, a young Irish activist who has been raising awareness about the lack of inclusivity of people with non-conventional body tyoes in fashion, was recently in Dubai. In case you didn't know it, Dubai Mall celebrated its tenth anniversary and partnered with Vogue Arabia for a ten-day long extravaganza which included a series of master classes and talks. Burke was a part of the Vogue Loves Fashion Avenue panel discussion on diversity in fashion. The day after Sinéad's talk, I was lucky enough to find myself sitting next to her at a dinner. Besides telling me that it's her dream to go to India (one of her favourite films is Bride and Prejudice), Burke had always had a passion for fashion. She started blogging from a little person's take on style, which eventually resulted in her becoming a strong advocate for inclusivity in fashion. A contributing editor for British Vogue and now consulting with brands that voice the needs of women like her, Burke has her hands full. “You know the skirt's length at the back needs to be longer than the front for us, as we tend to carry a lot of weight on our derriere,” she explained, which had everyone at the table talking about how not one of us have the perfect figure that fashion often expects too. There's no doubt we need more Sinéads in the world to be real and critical about the industry, and who still appreciate how beautiful fashion can make a women feel. Last year saw the launch of 11honore.com, a size-inclusive website that works with designers such Zac Posen, Prabal Gurung, Naeem Khan and Dubai's Dima Ayad. Starting with US size 10 and up, the website is dedicated to making fashion accessible to the curvier woman. 11 Honoré just announced they will start deliveries to the region and marked the occasion with a special pop-up shop. The label's Los Angles-based founder, Patrick Henning was also in town. “I am happy to see that this region is finally talking about fashion inclusivity,” he said. “It's such an important issue right now and it was time that the Middle East also became a part of the conversation.” Ashley Graham, Rebel Wilson and Octavia Spencer have all been seen in designs from the website, whose tagline is “The runway, edited. Size ten to twenty”. It is amazing to think there was no luxury fashion website that looked at fashion for the curvier woman (and the figures show in 11Honoré own home country, America, 67 percent of American women wear a size 14 or larger) till last year. In town to launch an 11-piece capsule collection with The Modist, the Dubai-based global luxury fashion website is Austrian designer Petar Petrov's brainchild, who is known for his love of metallic fluid dresses and sharp tailored pantsuits. “You have to remember that Vienna is very opulent city,” says the designer about his decadent designs. He enjoys designing clothes for real women of all ages and all sizes.  His love for lightweight fabrics is what makes his clothing perfect for this region. Sonam K Ahuja recently wore of his maxi dresses recently for a lunch date with her husband too. And if it's statement dressing you need, look at the gold Lurex from this designer's capsule collection with The Modist. Another week means another opening at Dubai Mall's The Fashion Avenue—and here, it is not so easy to have people attend a store launch unless the designer behind the brand is at the event. Maison Assouline has had no problems with its attendance as a collectible book publisher. The concept store houses beautiful books, vintage objects d'art, sculptures, art and tables sourced from the British Library that dates back to the 1900s. Each piece has a story behind it, and everything in the store is available to buy, making it a true lifestyle store. Assouline founder, Prosper Assouline, calls his retail space a “cabinet of curiosities”. You can enjoy its old-world feel and soak in the vintage vibe, as their Swans Bar offers a menu of food and drinks inspired by Maison Assouline's book titles. At the café here, you feel as though you have transported to New York in the 1950s, while its outside terrace enjoys views of the Dubai Fountain. I think I found my new go-to spot at the Dubai Mall. column1: Samant Chauhan and Rohit Kamra have a double store launch
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Two is better than one Adding to South Mumbai's ever-growing list of designer flagship stores is a double launch by Samant Chauhan and Rohit Kamra at the Roosevelt Building. Back in 2011, designer Chauhan stayed at the decadent Taj Palace Hotel and felt an immediate connect to the streets of Colaba; the soul of its architecture struck an instant chord with him. “I could easily relate it to my brand, my work and wished to have a store there since then. My work is inspired by an era rich in art, culture and heritage, and Colaba, for me, signifies the very essence of these qualities, especially in its architecture,” he tells us. Chauhan chose to take up space because of its striking colonial architecture, and decided to honour the heritage of the space while modernising it in his own style. He restored teakwood in its original form, which was gifted by the Maharaja of Mysore. “We have kept the lower border of the wall intact and have scraped it to show the number of paint coatings applied over the years. It teleports you to the colonial era and walks you through the years till the present. Remaining walls have been painted keeping our theme in mind. A small section of the store is dedicated to exposed brick wall, which again tells us the quality and design of bricks used in that era, which are not to be seen anymore,” says Chauhan. Samant has always been inspired by silk, and believed firmly in exploring his native Bhagalpuri silk and its versatile character into his line. “The core offering still remains my simple clean-cut, hand-woven, handmade garments, adorned by embroideries highlighting Indian craftsmanship,” the designer shares. Meanwhile for Kamra, “Colaba is the heart, the epicentre of art, design, and it was very crucial for me to come up with a store in a neighbourhood that has a rich history, and resonates with the ideology of my brand.” All efforts have been made to move away from traditional luxury materials and to use more organic, sustainably sourced elements. The decor offers a mélange of easy luxury, the interiors have been done in reclaimed timber with an eclectic chandelier. His collection offers bespoke services with a range of shirts, half jackets, breeches and bandhgalas, all with a touch of detailing that makes the garment stand out from the vast sea of uniformly dressed men. The idea is to push the envelope on menswear and present coveted embroideries, sculpted cuts in silhouettes, the techniques of ombres, lehariya, marble print and much more in a masculine way. column1: The new collaboration that every fashion girl needs to know about
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Come together Known for his pop art and graffiti strokes, Keith Haring's work is the perfect canvas for designer Stacey Bendet of Alice + Olivia's whimsical aesthetic. The designer, known for her signature personal style, also has a keen eye for art. Past collaborations have included Domingo Zapata, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Donald Robertson. See a pattern emerging? For resort 2019, Bendet realised that the primary pops of colour she was drawn to, reminded her of Haring's statement works. A capsule collection soon came together, featuring his trademark dancing figures and prints in patchwork collages. The pieces include a leather jacket, a reversible bomber, tees, ballgown skirts and accessories, which are available online. “I have always been a fan of Keith Haring's work—the colours and graphics,” says Bendet. “He was also one of the first artists to advance social causes, and I think at this time in our world, it's especially important to support artists who have made a difference.” Scroll ahead to take a look at the pieces from the collaboration. column1: Bye, black dresses! Alia Bhatt’s blue number is a party season favourite
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Take a closer look at it now Alia Bhatt knows that while little black dresses will always be a hit at parties, it's nice to give the classics a break for something new every once in a while. On November 26, the actor stepped out in a pretty blue Prabal Gurung number for Priyanka Chopra and Nick Jonas' pre-wedding bash at Estella, Mumbai, which you have to check out if you're on the hunt for something not-so-basic this party season. Bhatt has been spotted at almost all of Chopra and Jonas' pre-wedding functions so far (she made an appearance at the couple's house party back in August 2018 too), and there was no missing her versatile sartorial choice for this occasion. Take a closer look at her evening ensemble now. [#image: /photos/5ce41857b40d26c6fad6b0cd]||| ||| Image: Viral Bhayani Alia Bhatt has been a fan of Prabal Gurung's creations for years now. To celebrate Priyanka Chopra and Nick Jonas's upcoming wedding, the actor gave predictable party dresses a skip and dropped by their pre-wedding bash in a deep blue number by the Nepalese designer. What made the outfit an exciting pick was its interesting silhouette. The strappy midi dress cinched in at the waist and featured a ruffled wrap-around skirt. Adding an interesting pop of colour to the look were the little multi-hued flowers embroidered all over the dress. Bhatt played up the feminine vibe of her number with a pretty pink lip colour and baby pink Gucci sandals. Instead of matching her pastel pink shoes to her bag, Alia Bhatt opted for a bold red and white box clutch for her night out. Though it may sound like a strange choice, Bhatt's bag perfectly complemented the red threadwork on her dress, and is a great accessory to have this party season. A clutch like Bhatt's is all you need to spruce up even the simplest of outfits, be it an all-black dinner ensemble, a breezy dress, or even a simple shirt and jeans combination. column1: Shloka Birla makes her Le Bal debut in Manish Malhotra couture
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Heavy on the sparkle Many years ago, when Manish Malhotra was still finding his footing as a costume designer turned fashion designer, Yash and Avanti Birla offered to help setup his first-ever retail store. Thus, it only seemed serendipitously right that he dress their daughter, Shloka Birla, for one of the most celebrated debutante balls of all times—Le Bal. “When Avanti asked me to dress Shloka for Le Bal, I was delighted to take up her offer. We go back a long way; it was Yash and Avanti who persuaded me to first open a store in Mumbai. They showed tremendous confidence in me, and as they say, the rest is history,” the designer tells Vogue. Malhotra describes the petite young deb as one with a vivacious personality. “Shloka's look will essay modern glamour with spunk,” he said. After trying on several couture gowns, Malhotra and Birla settled on a custom-made sheer number that was covered in florals. Accentuating the tone-on-tone look was intricate beadwork, which added the element of glamour to her gown. “I was ecstatic at first to hear that it was Manish because he is a dear friend of my mom's, but more than that I think his work speaks for itself, since it's one of the best in the country and has surpassed all expectations,” Birla said about the couturier. The result is every bit as glamorous as intended to be. Prince Jean de Croÿ Solre was Birla's cavalier for the evening. Accompanying her were Princess Ananya Raje Scindia, who wore a Lecoanet Hemant creation and was escorted by Prince Yuvaraj Mahanaryaman Scindia of Gwalior; Aria Mehta, daughter of Payal Mehta, the official jeweller for Le Bal, who chose a Georges Hobeika gown; and True Whitaker, daughter of actor Forest Whitaker, who picked a Gaultier look for the evening. Scroll through our gallery to take a look at the debutantes from Le Bal. column1: Priyanka Chopra’s maxi dress is for every girl who loves busy prints
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Boho dressing done right Just days before her wedding, Priyanka Chopra finally wrapped up her work on upcoming film The Sky Is Pink, and on October 25, flew from Delhi to Mumbai with fiancé Nick Jonas. Given that she's one of the busiest brides you'll come across in the country right now, Chopra touched down in the city wearing the breeziest of travel outfits: a full-sleeved maxi dress covered in a fun floral print. Both comfortable and interesting to look at, her latest showcase makes a fail-safe choice for long flights and hectic days. Check it out now. [#image: /photos/5ce41a08cc50be701013dd3a]||| ||| Image: Viral Bhayani All set to tie the knot between November 28 and December 3, 2018, Priyanka Chopra was spotted walking hand-in-hand with fiancé Nick Jonas at Delhi airport recently, and there was no missing her pre-wedding glow. The bride-to-be, who will soon be seen in a handful of stunning wedding wear, chose to go the fuss-free route for her latest flight in a flowy blue number that brought clashing floral prints together. Standing by her side for the cameras, Nick Jonas too kept his travel look casual in a striped T-shirt, brown jacket and blue trousers. The key to making an outfit like Priyanka Chopra's work is balance. Since her maxi dress brought together so many colours and patterns, the actor kept the rest of her on-flight ensemble simple. Instead of fussy accessories or a statement bag, Chopra went with a simple black handbag that didn't take away attention from her interesting dress. The actor also made sure to keep her beauty look minimal. Freshly blow-dried locks, a bare face and a nude manicure were her picks of the day. column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan’s sparkly strapless gown is not for the faint-hearted
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion High shine content Kareena Kapoor Khan has a knack for owning bold looks. Case in point: yesterday, the Veere Di Wedding actor stole the spotlight in a metallic gown by Mary Katrantzou and silver Charles & Keith heels at the screening of Mowgli: Legend Of the Jungle in Mumbai. The event, which was attended by the likes of Christian Bale, Benedict Cumberbatch, Anil Kapoor, Abhishek Bachchan, Frieda Pinto, Radhika Apte and Madhuri Dixit Nene, saw Kapoor Khan in two ensembles—a black THEIA Couture gown, and that head-turning metallic dress. Scroll ahead to see how you can recreate her look. It's safe to say that Kareena Kapoor Khan has a thing for sequins (remember the red dress she wore for Soha Ali Khan's book launch?). Right in time for the upcoming party season, she picked a strapless gown by Mary Katrantzou that featured all the elements of a winning look. The knotted waist cinched the dress in for a curve-hugging silhouette, while the bare shoulders highlighted her collarbones. And if the drama of the metallic hue wasn't enough, the dress also featured a thigh-high slit at the front. If you have a cocktail party coming up, take a page out of Kapoor Khan's stylebook and pick an all-eyes-on-you sequinned gown just like hers. Metallic heels are a mainstay in most of our shoe wardrobes, and Bollywood is no different. The actor rounded off her bold outfit with a pair of strappy heels by Charles & Keith, and paired it with a dramatic beauty look: dewy makeup, heavily kohled eyes, nude lips and slicked back hair. Whether you need something to amp up your black velvet pantsuit or to take that mini dress to the next level, metallic heels like hers will help you round off any ensemble. column1: Your first look at Varun Bahl’s Mumbai flagship
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Brides-to-be, take note The ever-growing ‘fashion meets art deco' district in South Mumbai is all set to house yet another sprawling showroom showcasing bridal couture in its expanse. Delhi-based Varun Bahl is now neighbours to likes of Ensemble and Shantanu & Nikhil, capturing 3,000sqft of the city prime real estate in Kala Ghoda. Designed to entice modern brides, the space is brightly lit instead of being bogged down by references to ancient India. Bahl has been a leading bridal couturier for the past 17 years. Florals and fresh pastels almost always dominate his meticulously detailed garments. “I'm extremely excited about our first-ever flagship store in Mumbai. It has this beautiful, modern, yet old-world charm. As someone who tries to balance craft, opulence and innovation, I'm hopeful my Mumbai clients will like what I've done,” says the designer. The store has been designed by Huzefa Rangwala and Jasem Pirani of MuseLAB. The two-storied space bears arches at the entrance, while inside, a clever play of mirrors and decorative grills set the ambience. The focus is the conservatory, which highlights the latest collection and acts as an in-store window. If you have a big wedding on the cards anytime soon, you can't miss paying the flagship a visit. column1: Vogue’s red carpet recap: The most impactful moments of 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Oprah’s seismic Golden Globes speech, to the revitalised power of pink and Lady Gaga’s show-stopping feathered gown—these are the nine moments that redefined the red carpet in 2018. [#image: /photos/5ce41a879cc0c0c1edf9be17]||| ||| Image: Getty When Oprah Winfrey took the stage on January 7 at the Golden Globe Awards to receive the Cecil B DeMille Award for her outstanding contributions to the world of entertainment, the world listened up. Wearing a symbolic black Atelier Versace gown in support of the #TimesUp movement, Oprah's acceptance speech reflected her own power to transcend culture, geography, race, religion, politics or workplace and would go on to have a profound effect beyond Hollywood. The words that lingered in hearts around the world: “For too long, women have not been heard or believed if they dared to speak their truth to the power of those men, but their time is up.” Lady Gaga was tipped to garner rapturous reviews for her Hollywood turn in A Star Is Born, but it was her red-carpet appearance at the 75th Venice Film Festival at the end of August which left the fashion crowd enamoured. Her pink feathered Valentino couture gown (showcased on the haute couture winter 2018 runway by Kaia Gerber) was certainly worthy of a standing ovation. [#image: /photos/5ce41a871dc2676328c7733e]||| ||| Image: Getty It's not unusual for Kendall Jenner's every move to face global scrutiny on the internet, but at the 75th annual Golden Globes (where she appeared in a frothy black Giambattista Valli gown) it was her face itself that became the subject of an online conversation, after one of Jenner's fan wrote on Twitter: “Ok but @KendallJenner showing up and strutting her acne while looking like a gorgeous star is what every girl needs to understand.” Kendall's empowered response? “Never let that sh*t [sic] stop you!” [#image: /photos/5ce41a88b40d26001ad6b397]||| ||| Image: Tarana Burke Activist and founder of the #MeToo movement, Tarana Burke's appearance at the 2018 Golden Globes carried a message of unity. “To stand with the members of the #TimesUp campaign who have stood up and spoken out in this groundbreaking historical moment” was a matter of “huge pride”, Burke said in a joint statement released before the ceremony. She was accompanied by actor Michelle Williams on the red carpet. Linked arm-in-arm and both clad in black, Williams described feeling “moved beyond measure to be standing next to [the activist]. I have tears in my eyes and a smile on my face.” [#image: /photos/5ce41a88cc50bef34e13de14]||| ||| Image: Getty Amal Clooney cleverly parted with convention for her fairytale Met Gala 2018 look. The combo—a bustier with cascading floral train and office-proof black trousers (by London-based designer and winner of the inaugural Queen Elizabeth II Award for British Design, Richard Quinn) put a whole new spin on the straight-from-work cocktail wardrobe for women everywhere. [#image: /photos/5ce41a88b803110c8e8f57b8]||| ||| Image: Rex Features 2018 will undoubtedly go down in history as the year when black gowns, worn in support of the #TimesUp and #MeToo movements, ruled the red carpet. There was, however, another shade which began to triumph as the year progressed: fuchsia. An unabashedly feminine hue worn by Tracee Ellis Ross, Zoë Kravitz and Viola Davis. [#image: /photos/5ce41a881dc267cc1cc77342]||| ||| Image: Getty Rapper Cardi B cut through a crowd of episcopal gowns at this year's Met Ball wearing a pearl-encrusted Moschino dress (complete with train and headdress), which was custom-made to accommodate her pregnancy bump. Proof that she nailed the ‘Heavenly Bodies: Fashion and the Catholic Imagination' theme? Within hours of her red carpet arrival, #CardinalB began trending… [#image: /photos/5ce41a8989be363b6b7ce9db]||| ||| Image: Getty Claire Foy may have shrugged off her regal image to appear as Lisbeth Salander in The Girl in the Spider's Web, but at the 75th Venice Film Festival the star of The Crown delivered a red carpet moment worthy of a modern queen. The number in question? A Valentino couture dress that married clashing pops of scarlet and fuchsia in one scene-stealing look. [#image: /photos/5ce41a89b40d266aced6b39d]||| ||| Image: Rex Features Lourdes Leon (daughter of Madonna) isn't about to succumb to outmoded beauty standards. When walking the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund red carpet in New York in November, the 22-year-old wore a sheer dress by rising fashion label, Lunar, which revealed her leg and underarm hair, galvanising her reputation as a Gen Z style icon. column1: First look: Krésha Bajaj’s dreamy new boutique in Bandra
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Consider your wedding wardrobe sorted In the quaint landscape of Bandra, Krésha Bajaj's new outpost bursts through like fresh blooms in spring, with a millennial-approved pink palette and couture concoctions in sorbet hues lining the walls. The green lawn and wooden white lattice outdoors give way to the vintage charm of a French-inspired boutique inside that plays host to the designer's pret wear. “Once a commercial bank, this place has been completely transformed to make for a homely place where young girls can come to browse with their friends and family,” Bajaj says. The couture haven goes beyond the norm to encompass a multi-sensory experience, with strategically placed Jo Malone candles scenting the boutique. The luxury fragrance label had scented Sonam K Ahuja's wedding earlier this year, and you'll find the feminine notes of Peonies and Blush Suede heralding brides-to-be on the quest for their dream lehenga at the outpost. “The bridal boudoir serves as a completely bespoke area, accessible by appointment only, with sunny French windows, velvet drapes and crystal chandeliers from my own travels, put together to resemble the dream walk-in closet from every girl's wildest fantasy,” the young designer smiles. Over a mock fireplace in her cabin, the iconic Love Story Lehenga assumes pride of place in a gilded frame. Even though it's been four years since Bajaj assumed headlines by recreating her love story in intricate embroidery on her bridal lehenga, the bestseller still continues to pull in the crowds. “There isn't a single day that goes by when we aren't requested by patrons to see the lehenga in person, so it made sense to have it framed at the epicentre of all creativity in the boutique. I think what struck a chord with people is that it is truly personalised, and we've now extended the concept to bridal blouses and grooms' sherwanis—we've even created embroidered family trees for expectant mothers at baby showers,” the Mumbai-based designer elaborates. The outpost will also serve as the launchpad for her new collection, ‘Dentelle' which is inspired by her own scuba diving experiences in Indonesia. Expect French lace with braid detailing to take centre stage on her signature frothy creations. “I wanted to create a moment that speaks to fantasy and inspiration—this collection is a celebration of my favourite things, a mix of modern and fun blouses, techniques and ideas I love,” Bajaj explains. And while she is mum on her plans for the future, “Opening a couple of boutiques internationally is on the bucket list definitely,” she adds. column1: Everything you wanted to know about Deepika Padukone’s Kanjeevaram saris
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer behind the traditional drapes reveals the significance of Deepika Padukone’s choice Long before we saw the actual proof, it was clear that Deepika Padukone was going to be a Sabyasachi bride. But one of the key pieces in her wedding wardrobe—the Kanjeevaram sari Padukone wore for her Konkani ceremony—was discovered to be not from the designer's repertoire, but a gift from her mother Ujjala Padukone, that was finished and styled by Sabyasachi Mukherjee for the actor. The source of this contested weave (and the gold one she wore for her Bengaluru reception) was one Angadi Galleria—a heritage store in Bengaluru that has for nearly 600 years been invested in the practise of weaving. The retail store offers a range of saris including Benarasi, jamdani, bandhini, kantha, kalamkari, chikankari, phulia, Kota doria and more. However, their in-house label Advaya, designed by founder K Radharaman, caters to bridal saris, Kanjeevarams, and couture, one-of-a-kind weaves. We got in conversation with Radharaman about the importance of Kanjeevaram saris in South Indian weddings, what makes them unique, and the unexpected fame as a result of dressing a Bollywood celebrity. A Kanjeevaram sari is exemplified by its use of real zari and characteristic design vocabulary. The lustre and luxurious drape make the Kanjeevaram sari a luxurious statement. Most Kanjeevaram saris are made using yarn from silkworms fed with Mulberry leaves. A Kanjeevaram is unique in the fact that most of them (though not all) use heavily plied silk yarn to increase the weight, durability and life of the sari. In most South Indian families, the Kanjeevaram sari is considered an heirloom and one that is meant to last a lifetime. Hence the emphasis on the use of pure zari and heavily plied silk yarn. The ply of the yarn increases the thickness of the yarn. In simple language, this means that the amount of silk used per square inch of the sari is more, and hence makes the sari more luxurious and durable, and worthy of being an heirloom. Our retail brand, Angadi Galleria, houses many different handwoven and handcrafted genres in a curated space, one of which is Advaya, a label designed by me. The essence of Advaya is ‘innovation in handwoven textiles'. We only claim credit for the designs under the Advaya label, such as the one worn by Deepika on her wedding. Every sari has its unique story and signature, which does not alter its inherent identity. The Advaya range consists of many first-of-its-kind designs, such as the first-ever linen-blended Kanjeevaram and the khadi Kanjeevaram, among others. Advaya also consists of an extensive bridal collection with zari brocades in elaborate intricately woven designs. Yes, they have, as are many of the old South Indian families. The Padukones, as is the case with many other celebrity families, chose to maintain a low profile about the impending wedding. But yes, the exclusive Advaya bridal collection was showcased to them for this very purpose. That Deepika came with her mother and selected the saris personally was also a clear indication of the fact. No, the saris that were showcased from a collection of limited edition Advayas as per their requirement. They stated their preference among the saris from the collection to our team at the store. The sari worn for the traditional Konkani ceremony that took place in Lake Como took approximately 45 days and the sari worn at the Bengaluru reception took approximately 60 days to make. The Gandaberunda, a mythical two-headed bird seen on the orange sari, is symbolic of Deepika's home state of Karnataka. The bird is part of Indian legend and folklore and represents prosperity and wisdom, namely material and spiritual wealth. It is a symbol of royalty and heritage and the fact that Deepika wore it for her wedding and chose a Bengaluru-based design label is a matter of pride to her home state. We personally never sought to publicise the saris worn by Deepika as our work, but we are nevertheless delighted to have been rightfully acknowledged as the designers. The Kanjeevaram is an eternal and timeless weave, and is in my opinion, the queen among saris. The Kanjeevarams in times past were largely patronised only by the royalty and elite. In recent times, the genre has not had the spotlight it deserves due the lack of design intervention. The way Deepika wore her saris with pride clearly shows that she is a true style icon and has brought back the necessary media attention to this genre. column1: Shraddha Kapoor makes a case for the white party dress

column1: Clothing label Rūh makes its way to Net-a-Porter
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A religion major with an interest in fashion and technology is looking to provide women with a label that represents their true self. Sonia Trehan tells us more about Rūh The concepts of privacy and anonymity lie at the centre of ready-to-wear brandRūh, which makes sense when the CEO and founder Sonia Trehan declines to have her image featured in this story. Trehan, a New Yorker who lives in Oxford, has a strong background in academia and wishes to inspire women through the medium of fashion and technology. Launched on Net-a-Porter as part of an incubator programme, she sheds light on the collection. I struggled to find a brand that spoke to the part of me that wanted to be intellectually engaged with style. Rūh is a reawakening to the idea that style can be private, an escape from the pressures of digital exposure and social validation. I would like it to be identified with a movement, one where people are stepping away from the exhibitionism of our digital world. There is a backlash to our current always-on-display culture and a return to the nuances of style: what it means to dress for oneself rather than for the world to see. Refined yet conceptual and challenging. Our woman would like her clothes to say something compelling about her. column1: How powerful are designer collaborations?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Louis Vuitton x Supreme to the forthcoming partnership between Burberry x Vivienne Westwood, luxury brands are stirring up a collaboration frenzy. As H&M’s buzzy annual designer collaboration—done this year in partnership with Moschino’s Jeremy Scott—arrives in stores across the globe, Vogue investigates the value of fashion collaborations Buy One, Get One Free isn't the sort of sales incentive you'd expect to find in a luxury fashion boutique. Yet in the last few years, one would be forgiven for thinking there are bargains to be found in the form of two-for-the-price-of-one luxury goods that bear the branding of not one, but two monolithic brands. Fashion—or luxury, rather—has caught the collaboration bug. Look no further than Louis Vuitton and Supreme, which sold out at eight dedicated pop-ups around the world and has rocketed in resale value on platforms such as Grailed and eBay—you can currently buy a red keepall for just under £14,000 on the latter, almost six times the original retail price. Elsewhere, there's also been the unexpected combinations of Fendi and Fila, Polo Ralph Lauren and Palace, JW Anderson and Converse, Burberry and Gosha Rubchinskiy, and Vetements and just about everyone. In February, Moncler launched a dramatic new business structure entirely centred on multiple collaborations with a diverse range of designers, such as Valentino's resident couturier Pierpaolo Piccioli, lauded London designers Simone Rocha and Craig Green, buzzy streetwear label Palm Angels, and cult Japanese designers Hiroshi Fujiwara and Kei Ninomiya. The Italian brand put its 27 per cent jump in revenue in the first half of 2018 down to its Genius project, which has already lived up to its name. Tod's has also launched a similar initiative titled Tod's Factory, a non-seasonal collaboration in the form of a capsule collection, the first of which is designed by Alessandro Dell'Acqua. Next month, Burberry will drop a capsule collection designed by Vivienne Westwood—just in time for a collaboration-friendly Christmas. If it all sounds familiar that's because it is—albeit at a much more accessible level. Limited-edition collaborations are nothing new. In fact, they've always been a mutually beneficial trade-off for catwalk designer and mass-market retailers or sportswear giants. Just look at H&M's ambitious partnerships with just about every monolithic fashion designer—from Karl Lagerfeld and Martin Margiela to Rei Kawakubo and Donatella Versace. This year, the Swedish fashion label's buzzed-about partnership is with Moschino, the Italian fashion house headed up by Jeremy Scott. The collection launched with a star-filled fashion show in New York last month and it hits stores on November 8. “When I got the call about working with H&M and being their designer collaboration for this year, I was excited as I love the idea of bringing my [designs] to the masses,” Scott told Vogue at the show. Indeed, making catwalk fashion available to a wider audience is a central tenet to H&M's approach. Ann-Sofie Johansson, H&M's creative advisor, points out that when the first collaboration (with Karl Lagerfeld no less) was launched, it was expected to be on the rails for weeks, but completely sold out. “The word collaboration is now part of fashion's everyday language,” she says. “With each of the collaborations, the aim is to pinpoint the essence of the brand. It is all about capturing the designers' or the brands' DNA and offering it to the world.” At the height of H&M's collaborations—which have arguably waned over the years, according to media impressions—it was the blue-chip designers who were in feverish demand. In 2018, the tables have turned. Now, it's the cheap-but-cool streetwear and sportswear labels that really matter—and the luxury brands are the ones eager to get in on the action. For younger designers, collaborations with mass-market retailers can be a lifeline. In New York, designers such as Prabal Gurung, Jason Wu and Proenza Schouler have partnered with Target. In London, runway stars Christopher Kane, Ashish, House of Holland, Charles Jeffrey and the now-defunct Meadham Kirchhoff have relied on collaborations with Topshop to bolster business. “We have to keep it interesting and keep the momentum going, and I have to keep challenging myself, otherwise I would still be making ruffled shorts,” Jonathan Anderson said at the launch of JW Anderson's collaboration with Converse. “Sometimes you have to change the fundamentals of what you're into, which takes a lot of energy. You have to question yourself and think of how you keep your brand moving forward.” Anderson has collaborated with several brands including Uniqlo, Sunspel, Topshop, Converse and even Diet Coke, and has acknowledged that collaborating with flagship brands is an essential part of growing a fledgling label. “Converse or Uniqlo serve an incredible purpose to me,” he says. “They are universal and I would love JW Anderson to be that universal, but we don't have that [production] volume.” “Collaborations are not going away soon—they are a much needed marketing tool to assist institutions with cutting through the massive amount of noise which is disseminated through owned, earned, and paid-for media every single day,” says Marc Beckman, CEO of DMA United, an advertising and talent agency that has brokered deals with Target for several designers, as well as deals between Jeremy Scott and Pepsi and the NBA. “North of seven digits is not uncommon now,” adds Beckman, who points out that pre-recession a designer could earn as little as $20,000 to participate in a mass market collaboration. Today, Beckman says that fees continue to increase exponentially. “If properly executed, this can bring [designers] significant brand awareness, exposure to new audiences, and of course, meaningful revenue.” So why are established luxury brands tapping into collaborations right now? As creative directors continue to play musical chairs, coming and going at an unprecedented speed, collaborations provide a sense of security for fashion executives and allow brands to tap into the non-seasonal ‘drops' that have been popularised by streetwear labels, such as Palace and Supreme. Collaborations are no longer just celebrity lines for mass-market retailers or designers creating cheaper facsimiles of their most recognisable designs or looks. Right now, it's about high-low, hype-slow, luxe-street juxtapositions. “Fashion collaborations are one of the levers that brands are using to surprise consumers, get their attention and drive traffic to stores,” explains Luca Solca, head of luxury goods at Exane BNP Paribas. “We are living in an era of abundance, with many brands competing for the consumer wallet. Surprise—with new products, new communication, new stores—is of the essence and that's the main reason behind pop-up stores and collaborations.” It's no coincidence that Off-White, which is known for its relentless collaborations, was named by Lyst as the “hottest brand on the planet” according to the inaugural Lyst Index. Part of the brand's meteoric success, according to Lyst, is Virgil Abloh's collaboration with Nike. However, there's also his hook-ups with Ikea, Rimowa, Levi's, Dr Martens, Byredo, Jimmy Choo, Kith, Moncler, Warby Parker, Umbro and Champion to name a few. What once would have been considered brand dilution for a luxury brand is now seen as brand enrichment. If there was ever any doubt, in March, Abloh was named the new artistic director of menswear at Louis Vuitton, a brand that has a long history of collaborations with artists and designers, and recently experienced blockbuster success with its logo-heavy Supreme collaboration, which sold out at pop-up locations around the world. For the customers who queued and were limited to purchasing only a few items, it all came down to one thing. Well, two things, really. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Can hemp be the textile of the future?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Cherished by ancient civilisations, hemp is a potential game-changer for the fashion industry Consider this. It takes 2,700 litres of water, 0.22 pounds of fertiliser, 0.1 pounds of pesticides and 1.2 pounds of fossil fuels to produce and transport a single cotton T-shirt in India.* That's enough water for one person to drink for two and a half years—and we are a country affected by drought. How long does this T-shirt last in your wardrobe? Now think about the resources required to produce a pair of jeans or a sari. In addition to this, studies on buying patterns reveal that the average consumer bought 60 per cent more clothing from 2000 to 2014, but kept each garment for only half as long. We've all read the depressing statistics about the fashion industry being responsible for colossal levels of waste and damage to our rivers, oceans and atmosphere. It is estimated that a truck full of clothing waste is being burned or landfilled every second! While a many are concerned, the currently available sustainable fashion solutions are heavy on the pocket and require significant personal commitment. This is where hemp fibre steps in. Hemp fibre or industrial hemp is obtained from the outer layer or the bast of the Cannabis sativa plant, which is more popular for producing marijuana or hashish. However, while marijuana contains 20 per cent tetrahydrocannabinol content (THC) which causes the high when smoked, industrial hemp only contains 1 per cent THC. This fibre has some incredible properties: it conducts heat, dyes well, resists mildew, blocks ultraviolet light and has natural anti-bacterial properties. It is used in many industries including paper, biodegradable plastic, construction, health food, chemical clean-ups and fuel. Automobile companies like BMW use hemp fibre to reinforce their door panels for better safety standards. There's even an urban legend that claims the first pair of Levis jeans were made from hemp! Just so you know, hemp isn't a new discovery at all. It was one of the earliest domesticated plants by mankind with roots dating back to the Neolithic age in China. Hemp has had numerous applications in ancient Indian, Chinese and Egyptian civilisations such a food, fibre and medicine. European explorers made sails and ropes out of hemp while Rembrandt and Van Gogh painted on hemp canvases. In fact, the American declaration of independence was drafted on hemp paper. However, during the industrial revolution, the mechanical cotton gin made it more efficient to produce cotton and thus hemp production decreased tremendously, albeit at the cost of the environment. Today, there is a dire environmental crisis on our hands and the production of hemp fibre is a highly sustainable process. It is a carbon negative crop because it actually absorbs CO2 from the air. It can be produced with half the amount of water and land in comparison to cotton has thrice the tensile strength of cotton. It can also be easily blended with other fibres and doesn't strip the soil of nutrients. On the contrary, hemp returns 60-70 per cent of all nutrients back into the soil. So why is hemp clothing not widespread? Prior to the '80s, hemp fibres had a very coarse texture and thus could not be used for apparel. However, in the 1980s, Chinese scientists made a breakthrough and figured out how to remove lignin from hemp fibres without compromising its strength. Today it is similar to linen and can be used to make anything that is made out of cotton. The fabric is porous and thus retains colour and is very breathable. Hemp clothing is highly durable and does not lose its shape easily. The fact that it is anti-bacterial and blocks ultraviolet rays doesn't hurt. Turning to hemp clothing is big step you can take as a conscious consumer and will go a long way in saving our planet's resources. Is hemp the textile of the future? There is a good chance it will be. Labels like Armani, Ralph Lauren and Calvin Klein have already made collections using hemp fabric. Sports brands like Nike and Patagonia use it in their athletic wear. In Mumbai, BOHECO is an organisation that has been working with policy makers, scientists and farmer groups to position India in the exploding cannabis space worldwide. They are doing studies on the wild cannabis that is widespread in North India to standardise low THC seeds that could eventually be used to grow industrial hemp within the country's legal stipulations. BOHECO is involved in a number of exciting projects: they have developed hemp denim in conjunction with Arvind Mills, they are working with IIT Delhi on technology to process hemp fibres from the plant and also have also launched two hemp fabric brands. Label B sells hemp clothing at affordable prices via Boheco.org and is present in 10 boutiques across the country including Creo in Mumbai, People Tree in Goa and Mo Studio in Ahmedabad. Their second, newer label is called Hemp Fabric Lab (Hempfabriclab.com) where they sell this raw material to designers like Arture Design and Sui by Sue Mue. BOHECO is happy to sell this fabric to consumers with no minimum purchase requirements. Thus, you can order just 1 metre of fabric if you wish. “The best part about hemp fabric is that is has the look of linen but the hand feel of cotton, says co-founder Yash P Kotak. “It gets better with every wash and is the strongest natural fibre known to man. We need to be more mindful in the fashion choices we make. Typically plan A is either cotton or polyester and that's why we call our brand B label, which means it's time for plan B.  We urge mindful consumers to look for us: the alternative that is more environmentally supportive. Even making ten percent of your wardrobe sustainable would make a huge difference!” Learn more about ethical practices in fashion with our Sustainability Matters series What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 10 wedding invitation mistakes you should avoid at all costs
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Omitted information, poor syntax, over-ordering and more When planning your very own magnum opus aka your wedding, it's easy to get carried away with every detail; be it the flowers, the bespoke designer lehenga or the chefs being flown in from Italy. But before the ‘I dos' comes the invitation. So it's only understandable that you spend countless hours choosing the calligrapher, scented paper and printed envelope liners. The invite, after all, introduces your impending nuptials to your guest list while also setting the tone for the celebration to follow. But don't get so engrossed in perfecting the colours of the marigold on your cards that you overlook errors that will only reflect too poorly on the couple and their planning entourage. Read on to ensure you're not guilty of committing any of the following. 1 Typos are a bigger eyesore than garish design. I once received an elaborate (and undeniably expensive) invite with especially commissioned artwork and real gold foiling, but the number of spelling mistakes had me reaching for that red marker. Read and re-read every word multiple times or enlist the help of a detail-oriented friend to proofread the copy. Because misspelling your mother-in-law's name would be blasphemy. 2 Less is more when it comes to the actual text. Don't populate the card with a verse from your favourite poet on the same page as the event details. Choose a font that's legible but not colossal. 3 Date, time, venue? Check. But have you ensured that the days of the week and year are correct too? Or that you haven't skipped the time the sangeet begins? Omitting key details of the itinerary is not an option. 4 Indian weddings are a kaleidoscope of varied elements. You may be tempted to add hints from your carnival-themed mehandi, the colours of your reception décor and the lace pattern from your sari pallu to the design. Resist it. Keep it simple and elegant with your wedding emblem and an all-encompassing theme. 5 Partly in English and partly in your native tongue will not do your invite any favours. So when it comes to language, pick a side. 6 Do a thorough count of your guest list so that you don't end up over-ordering. Each member of the family does not require individual invites, so plan accordingly. However, it does help to keep a few spare invitations handy for late additions or just as keepsakes. 7 Gift information is against traditional wedding invitation etiquette, so you're better off without the ‘blessings only' footer that is so common of Indian wedding invitations. 8 Is the entire family invited or only certain members? Address the invitations correctly to avoid any such awkward confusion. Add the appropriate honorific for all your guests too. 9 Even if you already know that your second cousin has another wedding to attend on the same dates as yours, doesn't mean you shouldn't send them an invite at all. The idea behind sending out such meticulously designed cards is to invite your friends and family to share in your joy, even if they can't be present physically. 10 If your guest list has a large number of out-of-towners, refrain from wedding invite accompaniments that are prone to damage in transit. Save the Murano crystalware for hand deliveries. You're better off mailing a box of gourmet teas or tried-and-tested dry fruits instead. Weddings Weddings Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How Gul Panag and Shruti Seth Aslam’s Festivelle is empowering women
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion An event celebrating women trailblazers across disciplines The discourse around female empowerment seems to be ever-transitioning. Of late, a pool of headstrong female voices is coming to the fore, and with movements like #MeToo steadfastly gaining momentum in India, there has never been a better time for events and collectives like Sheroes, We The Women and SheThePeople.TV, which celebrate the strength, courage and power that comes with womanhood. Another such event that seamlessly fits the bill is ‘Festivelle – Boss Lady', a coming together of women across disciplines (think entrepreneurs, influencers, artists and more), which took place at Mumbai's affluent A Club on the evening of November 17. Essentially a ‘crowd-sourced cultural festival', the event was an amalgam of entertainment and interaction, where women from different walks of life drove each other's spirit and intellect over sparkling cocktails and wines. Conceived and curated by television stars Gul Panag and Shruti Seth Aslam, it is no surprise that the event brimmed with the biggest voices of the country—think Red FM's Malishka Mendonsa, Le15 Patisserie's Pooja Dhingra, The Sassy Spoon's Rachel Goenka, SheThePeople.TV's Shaili Chopra, Pooja Makhija, Tara Sharma and the like. The evening started off with women taking rounds introducing themselves and getting to know the others better. What made the do more special is a five-course dinner fused with fine spirits, which made for an intimate setting. Panag briefly outlined the essence and intent of the event by saying, “We want to bring together women who have achieved the unthinkable by making their own rules of success. It is vital to discuss issues that women encounter on a daily basis and to challenge stereotypes that surround a woman's identity. Some of the issues that continue to persist are—how women deal with a largely patriarchal environment, workplace biases, and how to combine motherhood and professional roles and requirements. The event was an open minded discussion where our Boss Ladies shared, how they have dealt with curveballs in the past and addressed such issues. The precursor to any change is dialogue, discussion and debate, and that's what we are doing with Festivelle Boss Lady today.” Scroll through for a look at some of the guests at the event: View Gallery 9 Photos Gul Panag and Shruti Seth Aslam celebrate women with Festivelle – Boss Lady 2018 What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Your first look at FILA x NorBlack NorWhite’s athleisure collaboration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet your new wardrobe staples Having earned their stripes on the national and international circuit—including a special nod of approval from Frida Gianinni, ex-creative director of Gucci, along the way—NorBlack NorWhite is showing no signs of slowing down yet. Mriga Kapadiya and Amrit Kumar, the creative force behind the label, are winding up the year with a unique collaboration with sports giant, Fila. The result? A fusion Indian streetwear collection, featuring voluminous silhouettes serenaded by a riot of colours, that you'll want to get your hands on, stat. As one of the few global brands with decentralised creative control on product customisation in India, the powers-that-be at Fila charted a path directly to NorBlack NorWhite to bring about an intriguing clash of the worlds, juxtaposing the latter's ideals of modern India against the backdrop of global street culture. “We have always unabashedly celebrated textiles, colours and patterns, so applying our aesthetic within the bounds of Fila has helped us push the envelope on our creative capacity, and also led to many firsts—designing shoes and socks has been one of our favourite parts of the process,” Kapadiya reveals. What you can expect from the collaboration is an on-trend update for your athleisure wardrobe—think oversized mesh baseball jerseys, bandhani print sweats and shorts and the classic NorBlack NorWhite patterns on sporty hoodies. And there are more surprises in store in the accessories lineup; “The fanny pack and the socks have also been treated with NorBlack NorWhite's signature bandhani print, and the true showstopper is the iconic Fila Disruptor shoe that has been infused with the signature NorBlack NorWhite prints,” says Abdon Lepcha, creative director, Fila India. “We wanted to apply our love for pattern and colour, while keeping the creations breathable and digestible in the sporty space. We also had a fair amount of fun playing with our colour palette for the classic FILA logo,” Kumar adds. While athleisure has been around for a while now, we are yet to see all that this world has to offer. Lepcha's trend forecast includes, “Relaxed volume, fluidity and comfort. Unicolour track sets will be the key silhouettes in the coming seasons, and the anti-fit movement will continue, tempered with vintage nostalgia.” In keeping with the memo, Kapadiya explains that the collection will come in handy for anyone looking to give their athleisure wardrobe a modern update; “This collection is for anyone who likes to be a little extra, loves patterns and is confident in their skin. Although we love a good matching set, these pieces are pretty bold on their own, and can really be paired with some solid basics to keep the vibe minimal,” she says, while Lepcha advises, “As a finishing touch, accessorise with a fanny pack and quirky socks to strike the right balance between casual and sporty.” View Gallery 3 Photos FILA x NorBlack NorWhite’s athleisure collaboration Fashion Weddings Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast
