column1: Rodarte designers Kate and Laura Mulleavy talk about their new exhibition
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Hitchcock movies to the redwoods of California, Kate and Laura Mulleavy are more akin to artists than designers when it comes to finding inspiration for their Rodarte collections. As a new exhibition of their work opens in Washington, DC, Vogue meets the sisters to talk slow fashion, storytelling and women at the top Walking past the world's most famous political address of 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue on Wednesday morning and the rustling of progress was almost as audible as the autumn leaves underfoot. Democrats may not have flipped as many states from red to blue in the midterm elections as they would have liked, but the record number of women—more specifically liberally minded women of colour—who successfully ran for office was enough to permit just a moment of elation. Their victories made arriving at the National Museum of Women in the Arts (NMWA) in Washington, DC—the only major museum in the world solely dedicated to championing women in the arts—for the preview of the Rodarte exhibition feel even more momentous. Established in 2005 by sisters Kate and Laura Mulleavy, the brand name alone—reinstating the “e” of their mother's name Rodart, which was changed in the US citizenship process when her father emigrated to the US from Mexico—is enough to deliver a powerful message. Spanning the first 13 years of their career, the exhibition is not a retrospective, the designers insist, but an opportunity to reflect on their oeuvre to date in an industry notorious for its relentless pace. “In fashion, we are still in this habit of only looking at the latest collection and deciding straight away whether or not you're into it—it's about instant gratification,” 39-year-old Kate tells Vogue. “That's the nature of our world, but I think taking the time to look at this work collectively shows the larger story of who we are and the fact we have remained independent for 13 years.” She has a point—with hallowed brands such as Versace and Dries Van Noten having sold majority stakes in their businesses this year, the independent designer is a truly rare breed these days. Add to that the woeful statistic that only 14 percent of major brands are helmed by women, and that Rodarte defies many of the profiteering rules of fashion (the label shows two rather than four collections a year, and its pieces are labour-intensive and expensive, taking up to 150 hours to produce with dresses from the autumn/winter 2018 collection retailing at more than $9,500)—and you realise just how exceptional this brand is. Away from the catwalks of the “big four” fashion capitals, Rodarte occupies the entire second floor of NMWA. On entering the space, you are greeted by the painstakingly engineered garments from the Mulleavys' autumn/winter 2009 collection. Hand-marbled leathers and complex knits that fuse mohair, felted wool, and metallic threads into a single dress make the case for fashion that can be classed as art. Taking centre stage in the exhibition are the Odette and Odile tutus worn by Natalie Portman in her Oscar-winning role as Nina Sayers in Darren Aronofsky's film Black Swan—showcasing the sisters' passion for channeling their creativity into costume design. “You know, when I look back, there has always been something in us that wants to create narrative,” explains Laura, who is a year Kate's junior. “If you're watching Alfred Hitchcock films from a young age as we were, you realise how important fashion is in communicating a story.” Alongside the Black Swan, tutus are costumes from the sisters' own debut feature film Woodshock, which premiered at the 2017 Venice Film Festival. It comes as no surprise that the designers have branched out into directing—“I could watch my favourite films without any sound because so much, for me, is communicated through these visual signifiers,” says Kate. The Mulleavys first engaged with costume through their grandmother, who was an opera singer, and their mother, an artist. It was she who instilled in them their love of film—on one occasion encouraging them to take a week off school to finesse their Hitchcock repertoire. Their work has, at times, drawn criticism for artistry at the expense of functionality, but “wearability”, Laura argues, is not a “universal concept”. Kate defines fashion as a “visual language”, a way of expressing one's individuality, and Rodarte provides one way of doing that. The costumes from Woodshock are perhaps the most literal example of how fashion can be used to externalise emotions. The distressed silk slips worn by Kirsten Dunst's character, Theresa, range in their level of “damage”, the lace eroding in places and some designs violently slashed to reflect her character's inner state as she grieves for her mother. Set in California's redwood forests, similar to where the Mulleavys grew up in Santa Cruz, the term “woodshock” describes the sensation of becoming lost and disoriented among the trees. The cinematic quality of Rodarte's designs feeds into the way the exhibition has presented the 94 looks on display. Rather than order them chronologically, Rodarte's guest curator Jill D'Alessandro—curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco—arranged them thematically across eight rooms. In Magical Beautiful Horror, fluorescent tubes spotlight dresses from the autumn/winter 2008 collection; constructed from hand-dyed tulle pin-tucked into sinewy formations, they could be the product of Dr Frankenstein's laboratory. In The Garden, which acts as a grand finale to the show, a yellow column dress from the designers' first catwalk collection stands harmoniously next to pieces from the spring/summer 2018 collection presented during Paris couture week, bringing the visitor full circle. Perpetuating the sisters' longtime love of nature (their father was a botanist who discovered a new species of fungus), gypsophila flowers cascade from the mannequins. Framing the heads like a lion's mane—the work of French hairstylist Odile Gilbert—the flowers have become an almost indelible Rodarte signature. Rodarte is the first fashion exhibition to be held at NMWA in its 30-year history, but on initial visits to the museum, the Mulleavys were empowered by the institution's extensive collection of textiles, which includes works by the late German-American printmaker and master weaver Anni Albers. It's Albers I think of as I speak to the sisters. Contrary to popular reporting, they don't finish one another's sentences; rather, conversation, and their working process as they describe it, passes from one to the other—like a shuttle navigating the warp and weft—ultimately weaving into something bigger and better than their own individual ideas. Albers famously took up weaving at the Bauhaus school because—much to her frustration—it was the only workshop open to female students. A century on, the Mulleavys express similar chagrin towards the reductive vocabulary used to describe their work and that of other women designers and artists. “Women's work shouldn't be talked about with language that's less powerful than our male counterparts; if we change our language, that'll change everything,” says Laura. “Crafty” is a word that she finds particularly problematic; why, she wonders, wouldn't the word “couture-like” be used instead to describe the metallic chantilly lace, appliqué sequin flowers and dramatic Thomas Gainsborough-inspired rococo silhouettes of the spring/summer 2017 pieces on display in Rodarte? “It's not that women aren't out there working, it's that there's a disconnect between the recognition men and women receive for their body for work,” Kate adds, expressing her disappointment that, including Rodarte, only around a fifth of the designers showcased in the Heavenly Bodies exhibition at the MET were female. “I'd like that to change. It's about time.” View Gallery 14 Photos Rodarte: The Art Of Fashion Rodarte is at the National Museum of Women in the Arts in Washington, DC until 10 February 2019 What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Designers are at long last embracing the full spectrum of skin tones, sexuality and gender fluidity—but what about “plus-size” models? Vogue investigates Over last month's spring/summer 2019 show season, of the 2,203 model appearances in 76 major shows, only 49 were “plus-size”. While that is certainly a positive increase from the previous autumn/winter 2018 season, it still means that the majority of women on the street (68 per cent in the US, according to Plunkett Research) are currently being represented by just 2.2 per cent of models on the runway. And, with only seven models above a size 14 landing ad campaigns for AW18—including Paloma Elsesser at 7 For All Mankind—brands are failing to speak to a key, multibillion-dollar sector that is growing by the day. “I've definitely talked about this at length, but in this day and age, brands like Victoria's Secret and stuff need to wake the fuck up,” says curve model Robyn Lawley who recently made headlines when she called for the boycotting of the Victoria's Secret runway show for not including women of size. Lawley, who is a size 12, was the first “plus-size” model to be featured in the pages of Vogue Australia, the first on the cover of Sports Illustrated and, alongside Tara Lynn and Candice Huffine, one of the first to cover Vogue Italia. This month, she staged a We Are All Angels runway show in London, with lingerie models of all sizes wearing the feathered angel wings that have become Victoria's Secret's MO. “They're not really concerned with inclusivity. I'd be very interested to watch the [Victoria's Secret] show if they included someone above a size 10,” she adds, speaking from her home in upstate New York. “I was very impressed with New York Fashion Week. They've proven that it's out there. It's loud, it's proud. It's more than just one plus-size model.” Of course, the term “plus-size” itself is problematic. The average woman in the UK wears a UK size 16; in the States, a size 18—yet in the fashion world, “plus-size” is often used to denote anything upwards of a size 10. “There are truly plus-size people and models out there, but I do not think it's right to call a girl who's UK 12 or 14 plus-size,” says Anna Shillinglaw, a former “straight model” who moved into the “curve” category before establishing her London-based modelling agency, Milk. She uses the term “curve” to describe models on her books between sizes 12 and 18, and denotes 18 and over as plus-size. Milk was one of the first agencies in London to have a model roster representing all sizes, including Tess McMillan, who featured in British Vogue's September 2018 issue. And, though she was pleased with the diversity on New York Fashion Week's spring/summer 2019 runways—“Amazing! Not just size, but ethnicity, gender, everything!”—she was disappointed with the remaining three fashion capitals. While designers who didn't demonstrate diversity were an anomaly in New York, it was business as usual in Europe. London Fashion Week featured a single plus-size model, Raisa Flowers, who walked for a single presentation, Nicholas Kirkwood (who, incidentally, makes shoes, and not the wide-fit variety). Paris had one (Jill Kortleve at Alexander McQueen); Milan, three (Ashley Graham, Lady Kitty Spencer and Lori Harvey at Dolce & Gabbana). “Every season we do a [curve casting send-out], we get compliments from casting agents but nothing seems to materialise,” she says. “And this is happening year in, year out. I don't know what it is, but they're not interested. London is meant to be a fashion capital, but we're missing a beat.” And if what's happening on the high street is anything to go by, Shillinglaw is right. The women's plus-size market is currently the fastest growing apparel market in the US, with analysts predicting it will continue to grow up to $26 billion by 2020 (according to Marketdata). Reports such as this have seen a number of retailers scramble to buy into it. Walmart bought clothing brand Eloquii, which makes clothes exclusively for size 14 and up; Old Navy launched a “Size YES!” campaign, making previously online-only, plus-size collections available in stores; J Crew expanded its sizes for the autumn/winter 2018 season; Nordstrom added size 14 and above across 30 of its stores in the US, introducing mannequins to highlight this; while e-tail giants Amazon, ASOS and Mango have stables of plus-size brands. When it comes to high-end designers, however, there's a school of thinking that suggests sample and runway collections are just too complex to engineer in curve or plus-size. It's an issue Sander Lak of Sies Marjan is familiar with, having cast his own friends and family, including his mum, in his spring/summer 2019 collection at New York Fashion Week. By default, they represented varied and diverse body types. Talking to Vogue from his showroom in Paris, Lak admits that sizing “does become more complicated the lower or higher up you go, because it becomes a completely different design. When it comes to more involved pieces, you literally have to re-drape the whole thing.” As well as the added pressure in terms of time and workload that designing for a spectrum of sizes brings, he continues, it is riskier for emerging brands to offer curve and plus sizes because “the whole industry is built around a certain type of body—so if I make all my samples in a [larger size], it immediately eliminates a lot of possibilities, like getting press, for example”. But while the financial restrictions faced by emerging and independent designers can conceivably make additional sizing difficult, the larger houses are turning over the kind of revenue that could and should facilitate it. Take, for example, Gucci, which began the year with a 49 per cent upturn in sales; Saint Laurent (up 19.7 per cent); and Chanel (11 per cent); they're all doing rather well. And the demand is there for high-end plus sizes, as the rise of brands such as 11 Honoré will testify. The e-tailer collaborates with big names for its collections, including Christian Siriano, Prabal Gurung, Derek Lam and Mary Katrantzou, to name a few—leaving less room for excuses from the mainstream luxury sector as to why more sizes aren't being catered for. “There are so many pieces of the puzzle, but if it's a priority for you, you'll figure it out,” says Chromat's Becca McCharen-Tran from her New York studio. “Our models have always reflected all the people in our community, behind the scenes and on the runway.” To wit, she has long used street-casting, celebrating diversity in all its forms for her Chromat presentations and campaigns. In fact, her inclusive approach saw Chromat top TheFashionSpot.com's list as one of the most size diverse of the spring/summer 2019 season, followed by Rihanna's Savage x Fenty show. “Sample sizes are not preordained industry standards, it's the choice of the designer,” she says. “Whether you choose to [produce samples] in a (US size) 2, 8 or 12, that's up to you. It's important to me and I make that choice, allowing more people into that world to see their body in a high-fashion context. It's worth the challenges.” She would know, having done the leg work. In a bid to better understand the idiosyncrasies of body shapes and prepare for the launch of a size range that runs through to XXXL, the designer hosted a four-day, open-door sizing initiative, fitting over 500 women across all sizes. “[The prejudice against plus-size] is definitely changing and I'm excited about that. I think one reason for this is social media. I don't need to wait for the approval of the old guard. People are claiming these spaces for themselves and that's beautiful.” It's a sentiment echoed by international curve model, writer and activist Jessica Vander Leahy, who launched her women's platform Project Womankind in 2015 to push unapologetic body love and more visible diversity following her experiences in the industry. Living between NYC and her native Australia, Vander Leahy's followers are vocal. “This is why Instagram is amazing; [users are] crying out for diversity,” she explains. “Fashion at its base is an expression of the world as it is; it really is art. And it's not fair to actively leave out people who are wanting to feel represented in that expression.” So, while this season has paved the possibility of a more racially diverse and gender-fluid runway, there is still a long way to go for body-size diversity—and even further for representation of models with disabilities, and those over 50; a total blind spot in fashion right now. One of the more hopeful anecdotes comes from New York-based plus-size model Mercy Rose Watson, whose portfolio includes Levi's campaigns and editorial with photographers David Sims and Catherine Servel. She recalls a brief exchange at the school gates with her teenage niece and her school friends, who were super-excited to be meeting a model. “Not a ‘plus-size model',” Watson recounts. “Just a model.” View Gallery 14 Photos Plus size models Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Deepika Padukone picks a demure Sabyasachi lehenga for the Sindhi wedding
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Have you seen a prettier bride? Now that the pictures of Deepika Padukone and Ranveer Singh's intimate wedding ceremony in Lake Como are out, let the detailed investigation into their looks begin. Padukone is an exclusive Sabyasachi bride (no surprises there), picking a bridal lehenga by the designer for the Anand Karaj ceremony held earlier today. Meanwhile, dapper groom Ranveer Singh was seen next to his bride in a sherwani. Deepika Padukone opted for a decadent red Sabyasachi lehenga, complete with an embroidered veil that bore an incantation, of which ‘Sada Saubhagyavati Bhava' was visible on the border in Devnagri (which roughly translates to ‘may you always stay married'). And Singh complemented her in a vermillion brocade sherwani, also by designer Sabyasachi. The duo have played a couple on-screen on several occasions but their chemistry at the ceremony, from what we can see in the pictures, was a sight. Padukone accessories her lehenga with a maang tikka, traditional kalire, a statement nose ring and several rings, but it wasn't just the bride who went big with the baubles–Singh wore strings of large rubies, and a jadau necklace too. For her Konkani wedding ceremony the day before, the actor chose a gold Kanchipuram silk sari  by Sabyasachi Mukherjee again, while Singh picked a white and gold kurta dhoti set. Both weddings took place at the picturesque Villa del Balbianello. Padukone rarely has an off-day in the sartorial department, and as a bride, she managed to stay true to her aesthetic without going overboard with the finery. With her ensemble, Sabyasachi Mukherjee crafted a look that will be referenced for years to come. Scroll onwards for the pictures. column1: Why you can’t miss the Vogue Wedding Trunk Show coming to your city
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It is as grand and glamorous as you would imagine it to be Many (if not most) would agree that the Vogue Wedding Show is one of the most celebrated wedding exhibitions the country has to offer. Keeping in mind the overwhelming footfall the event has garnered over the last six years—with a consumer attendance from over 70 cities—Vogue India has now launched a sparkling new extension to the event—the Vogue Wedding Trunk Shows. Targeted towards customers across metropolitan and semi-metropolitan cities over the course of the year ahead, the first edit of the event is slated to happen at Hyderabad, the City of Nizams, and will act as a one-stop destination catering to every facet of wedding planning. At its very heart lies the motive to help a bride curate a well-heeled wedding, where a coterie of services spanning trousseau, bridal wear, gifting, jewellery, menswear and wedding consultancy come together under one roof, with leading brands like Tarun Tahiliani, Shantanu & Nikhil, Jade by Monica and Karishma, Ekaya, Dolly J, Palam Silks, Birdhichand Ghanshyamdas Jaipur, Khanna Jewellers, Rare Heritage, Rose, Forevermark, Kapoor Watch & Co., Ahujasons, The Good Life Company (TGL CO.) and many more vying for attention. The Hyderabad edition of the Vogue Wedding Trunk Show sees brands like Forevermark, Diageo and Taj Krishna Hyderabad as sponsor partners, and will be inaugurated by GVK's Pinky Reddy, who also happens to be the national president of the FICCI Ladies Organisation (FLO). “I am delighted to support Vogue in this exciting new format of Vogue Wedding Trunk Shows. It is exciting that they chose Hyderabad for the first one. I have also supported the annual Vogue Wedding Show that takes place in Delhi since its inception in 2013. I look forward to seeing the selection of brands Vogue brings to Hyderabad,” remarks Reddy. Among the many takeaways is a fashion showcase presenting designer wear and jewellery from participating brands during the show, along with an elaborate line-up of masterclasses across fashion, beauty, nutrition and wedding photography. Insightful and immersive, these sessions are spearheaded by Vogue India's fashion coordinator and stylist Priyanka Parkash, and several industry experts namely Anu Kaushik, Dr Geeta Fazalbhoy, Dr Vishakha Shivdasani, Diageo's Zachary Abbott and Asmani Subramanian, along with prominent photographers Joseph Radhik and Joshua Karthik. column1: Where to buy pure Kanchipuram silk saris for your wedding wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Nothing but the best will do If your adolescent self didn't lose her heart to the stiff regality of the traditional Kanchipuram weave, whether on the big screen or in your mother's treasured wedding heirloom archives, you may want to reconsider your childhood. When it comes to silk saris, you can never have one too many, but the clear bestseller is the timeless allure of the Kanchipuram sari—an eternal wardrobe staple that officially marks your transition into adulthood. Famed for the contrasting borders, the archetypal Kanchipuram silk sari also goes under the moniker of Kanjivaram sari in common everyday parlance. Needless to say, this sari owes its name to the town of Kanchipuram where it originates from, close to Chennai in Tamil Nadu. Crafted out of the highest quality of pure silk, the true moneymaker here is the intricate border that can feature everything from elaborate florals to temple designs, and even exquisitely detailed depictions of paintings. The zari threads used to bring this artwork to life are said to contain a government-mandated amount of pure silver and gold, ensuring you a timeless investment for your ethnic wardrobe. With the wedding season officially upon us, the time is nigh to work the vintage charm of this A-lister approved classic. While Rekha has turned this precious weave into her own signature, the younger crew isn't shying away from the magnificence of the Kanchipuram silk sari either. Fashion maven Sonam K Ahuja's wedding reception called for some unconventional sartorial choices, and in a sea of backless cholis and frothy tulle lehengas, Kangana Ranaut made heads turn in a Kanchipuram silk sari from Gaurang Shah in an earthy colour palette. And while Deepika Padukone knows how to work a red carpet in elaborate couture concoctions, the promotions run of Padmaavat saw her in a cherry pink silk number with a sleeveless blouse. If you've been looking to add this wardrobe staple to your wedding lineup, we've rounded up the best places to start shopping. While an original silk sari can cost you anything in the ballpark of one lakh and above, the weavers' cooperatives in this locality retail via small shops that provide with reasonable options. Look out for the Silk Mark to verify the authenticity of your purchase, and you're golden. If you are looking for maximum value for your money, head to the heart of the Kanchipuram silk sari's place of origin. AS Babu Sah is easily among the biggest merchants in the town, and have dressed generations of brides in their regal silk threads. Address: 85 Gandhi Road, Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu As one of the leading silk merchants in the country, the sartorial durability of their creations will provide you some relief when it comes to the after-care of your precious investment, allowing for ease of hand-washing at home for days when you don't have the time to make a detour to the dry cleaners'. Address: No 87, Gandhi Road, Opposite GRT Regency Hotel, Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu One of the first few stores to head the organised retail movement in South India, the centuries' old legacy of the Angadi family is visible in the artful pallus and pure silks that grace the roster of their designs Address: 23, Sankey Road, Sadashivnagar, Bengaluru, Karnataka If you can't make it to the original hinterland, the vivid colours and masterful artistry that epitomise the Kanchipuram silk sari can found in this Mumbai haven too, which imports its creations directly from the handlooms of its origin town. Address: 13, Bhimdiwala Building, L N Road, (Central Railway), Matunga East, Mumbai Scroll onwards to have a look at how Bollywood celebrities aced Kanchipuram silk saris. column1: Your winter look is incomplete without these boots
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Start shopping already! As we venture from fall to winter, one thing gets made clearer every day—your shoe closet could definitely use an upgrade. Whether you are planning to visit a colder country or need something for everyday use in the city, the time to cast your trusted flats away in lieu for a stunning pair of boots is finally here. With countless options to pick from, there is something for everyone's need and style. Black is a mainstay in most of our wardrobes, and makes for a sensible shoe colour choice as well, considering the versatility of the hue. If you're looking for a pair to elevate a casual look, pick between Raid's ankle-length number—featuring metallic chains and studs—or Jessica Simpson's leather calf-lengths. Not found anything to help you get on the clear shoes bandwagon yet? Look to Zara's version to add a cool twist to your denim-on-denim look. You don't need to limit yourself to neutrals either. Let your inner shoeholic out and style a little black dress with Topshop's sequinned boots to really make a statement (and stay safe from the winter chill), or wear Versace's printed boots with a short blazer dress to proclaim your sartorial loyalty to Marylin Monroe. Investing in a pair of Dolce & Gabbana's rose-jacquard over-the-knee boots will also help you add something noteworthy, yet subtle, to your winter shoe closet. And if you have a knack for logo-mania, Gucci's knee-high boots will be absolutely perfect for you. Scroll through our gallery for the perfect edit of boots for you to try right now. column1: 5 trends that Priyanka Chopra never stopped wearing
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How does she look this good in everything! Is there anything Priyanka Chopra can't do? As if being a triple threat actor-singer-producer wasn't enough, the multi-hyphenate star has now added entrepreneur to her glowing resume (which also includes merits like being a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador and a Padma Shri awardee) after investing in Bumble. Half measures are not Chopra's MO, so whatever she does, she does in style. Naturally, that includes her fashion game. With a global career that straddles film industries in India and America, Priyanka Chopra and her team of stylists have done a fine job of cultivating a signature repertoire that's polished, individualistic and on-point. We round up the trends that always seem to be on the actor's radar. Considering the all-round boss lady that she is, pantsuits are a fitting uniform for Priyanka Chopra as she sets about on her mission of world domination. And if her Instagram captions are anything to go by, it's how she prefers to ‘make Monday her b***h'. Bold prints for celebratory flair, checks for long flights, all-white for a laid-back vibe or head-to-toe red for a traffic-stopping statement, Chopra demonstrates that there's a pantsuit for every mood and occasion. column1: Is the lehenga sari what you need for the upcoming wedding season?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The hybrid that will rule Wardrobe planning for the wedding season can be daunting, especially if you're a serial wedding attendee. After all, there are only so many times you can revamp, say, your saris, while still keeping every final look fresh. Your way out of a sartorial rut? Saying yes to a plethora of silhouettes. After the revival of interest in the sari, it is the lehenga sari that is now inching its way into the spotlight. The crossover silhouette combines the flare of a lehenga with the elegance of a sari to give birth to a style that is equal parts comfortable and stylish. Moreover, it's a fitting initiation into wearing more cumbersome traditional styles for first-timers. Often pre-stitched or pre-draped, the lehenga sari is extremely easy to wear. Considering that it's high on comfort, and doesn't need you to spend an hour (or more) perfecting the pleats, your destination wedding wardrobe will be thankful for its addition. In fact you can do with the pleats altogether and play around with the drape for an ingenious impact. If you plan to take over the dance floor at an upcoming sangeet, make this fuss-free style your plus-one, or wear it to your best friend's pheras so that your outfit doesn't come in the way of fulfilling your bridesmaid duties. column1: In Dubai this week? This is what you should be doing
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Piercings, art and more Over the past few weeks, Dubai and Abu Dhabi have been buzzing with excitement. The cities have played host a variety of celebrities like supermodels Joan Smalls, Liv Tyler and designers Prabal Gurung, Stella McCartney and Michael Halpern, and also been the venue for Cartier's big blowout bash, where Lebanese-born English singer MIKA came to perform as well. This week however, the focus moved from glamour to design as the fourth edition of Dubai Design Week and Abu Dhabi Art commenced. Additionally, renowned architect Mohit Gujral is also one of the speakers at Downtown Design. Marquee brands like Herman Miller, Frato, Baxter are a part of this too, but look out for Dubai-based design incubator Tashkeel, as they unveil the new range of the Tanween design programme, providing emerging UAE-based designers with the opportunity to develop, produce and retail a range of limited-edition pieces made with materials sourced and manufactured in the UAE. Sharjah-based 1971 Design Space will present contemporary Arabian pop-up majlis designed by Alia Mazrooei (a well-known name in design here, who has also shown at Milan Design Fair). Her inspiration comes from the shapes found in the deserts of the UAE. It is the blend of East and West that makes Dubai Design Week special in the international art and design calendar, and every year it's just getting bigger and bigger. This time, there is special showcase for limited edition pieces called Downtown Editions too. Downtown Dubai's fair director Rue Kothari says, “This debut showcase for limited edition design will bring together designers from around the world with our largest ever curation of talent from across the Middle East.” You can also download the Dubai Design Week app, which was launched this year, to make finding your way around this region largest design fair more manageable—as it can be confusing. Having relocated to the Middle East a few years back, I've happened to come across so-called ‘influencers' and ‘bloggers' by a dime a dozen. Amongst a sea of them is Anum Bashir, founder of the blog Desert Mannequin, which is truly a breath of fresh air. This half-Indian and half-Pakistani creative consultant believes that “clothes are best served with a side of intellect.” With a website that boasts of thousands of visits a month and a dedicated Instagram following of over 60,000 followers, her alternative and eclectic take on style has ensured that she enjoys a cult following. Bashir comes to Dubai via New York and Doha, where she worked in the art world for almost six years. An influencer who advocates repeating an outfit, Bashir is also a style contributor at ManRepeller.com. More recently, Bashir launched her DM Dinner series—a carefully curated dinner concept which boasts partnerships between handpicked brands and Bashir herself, within an event setting celebrating the two with some of UAE's finest and most interesting women. Her most recent collaboration was with David Webb, the New York-based jewellery house that used to be a favourite among iconic celebrities of the yesteryear, like Elizabeth Taylor and Estée Lauder. The luxury extension at Dubai Mall is truly a fashion girl's idea of heaven—home to 150 flagship stores, including the largest Miu Miu store in the world, as well as a three-storey Gucci shop which includes their decor collection. And now, lots of niche and speciality brands are opening up here too, including one by fine jewellery designer and celebrity piercing expert Maria Tash. The store will open this week and be the Middle East's first luxury piercing destination in a permanent location—featuring four custom piercing rooms and a VIP lounge. It will also be the brand's second freestanding location, after the global flagship located in New York City. Maria Tash is widely regarded as the pioneer of the modern movement around designing and curating elegant fine jewellery for piercings, and is influenced by both Indian and Pakistani cultures in her designs. She started in 1993 with a piercing shop in New York, and believes you should “just say no” to piercing guns. In town to launch a special capsule collection with MatchesFashion.com was Michael Halpern, the 30-year-old designer known for his sequinned multi-coloured dresses, has become one of biggest names in fashion to watch out for. His label, Halpern, will be available in Mumbai's luxury fashion store, Le Mill, soon. He hopes to make a trip to India in the recent future too, considering he hasn't been here yet. With both colour and shine being in his label's DNA, he knows it will be a country that will inspire him. Popularly known as the designer who makes Studio 54-inspired party dresses, he also attempts to make a socio-cultural statement with his designs—like all good fashion should. Says Halpern, “For me fashion acts as an escape. My dresses are a contrast to the dreary and sad times we live in. Serious fashion can also be fun and exciting.” Along with having one of the best attended shows at London Fashion Week, Halpern has also won the British Emerging Talent Womenswear award for his label at the 2017 British Fashion Awards. He has also worked for Versace and Oscar de le Renta prior, and made London his home (he's originally from New York) after attending Central St Martins. Fashion's current shine specialist is all about clothes that empower a woman by being fun, flamboyant and fabulous. “My dresses give women a special feeling,” he says. column1: These Indian boutiques are taking sustainability offline
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Treat it as your guide to guilt-free shopping Now more than ever, sustainable fashion has been an enterprise many—from designers and writers to environmentalists and critics—have been poring over. India has been steadily emerging as one of the many nations advocating fair trade, organic and cruelty-free clothing. Cases in point: the bevy of e-commerce websites selling only sustainable labels, eco-fashion weeks, sustainable fashion markets and most importantly, designers championing the cause of green fashion—think Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice, Nimish Shah of Shift and Rahul Mishra, among many others. However, for the most part, sustainable fashion remains largely inaccessible to the layperson, what with price points that are considerably higher than its fast fashion counterparts and the increasing ambiguity around what it really means. While it may now be possible to buy from ethical labels online, a sizeable chunk of consumers still believes in the essence of the good ol' brick-and-mortar. An interesting breed of boutiques prove that you no longer have to scour for sustainable clothing online or bury yourself in seemingly endless suggestions on where to buy it first-hand. Homegrown, coveted and close to the heart, we give you a lowdown on some of the country's solely-ethical retail spaces, which are adding a newfound dimension to India's eco fashion scene. [#image: /photos/5ce41a6a4a30b358f012bba0]||| ||| Images:Instagram.com/livetoile Toile is touted to be Mumbai's first eco-friendly multi-designer boutique, and is home to labels like Doodlage, Naushad Ali, Mati and Amrich, among others. With a minimalistic aesthetic at its core, the boutique stocks up on a variety of breezy, layered and upcycled ensembles. Address: Ground Floor, Plot 764, 5th Road, Khar West, Mumbai [#image: /photos/5ce41a694a30b3479c12bb9d]||| ||| Images: Instagram.com/saahraofficial From decomposable hangers and plastic-free packaging to electronic invoices, this boutique incorporates sustainability in its entirety. However, what makes the store stand out is its focus on sustainable fashion and luxury, resulting in a unique blend of contemporary labels like Anavila, Akaaro, Chola, 11.11/eleven eleven and more. Saahra has also launched the ‘Conscious Effort' edition, a collective of events promoting sustainable living through various media platforms. Address: C-16, Hotel Surya, New Friends Colony, New Delhi [#image: /photos/5ce41a6a1dc2677e37c7730a]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/aambalclothing In a 300-year-old Portuguese house in the heart of Fort Kochi lies Aambal, a quaint, eco-clothing store. Here, everything from billowy maxi dresses (in vibrant block, ikat and kalamkari prints) to structured trousers crafted from organic cotton and jute co-exist with a smattering of yoga mats, home decor items and cruelty-free cosmetics. Address: Napier Street, Fort Kochi [#image: /photos/5ce41a6a4a30b3643912bba2]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/mysoulspace.in SoulSpace already had a strong online presence through its website and major e-commerce portals when, earlier this year, they extended their presence offline by throwing open the doors to its first-ever retail outlet in Pune. Specialising in organic athleisure, yoga wear and basics, the fair trade label believes in spirituality and cognitive development as much as it does in transparent fashion. With its clothing certified by the General Organic Textile Standard (GOTS), the brand is also empowering farmers along the way. Address: Phoenix Market City, F4, Viman Nagar Road, Pune [#image: /photos/5ce41a6b9cc0c022b6f9bdf3]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/bykaveri Housed in a bright and airy studio, this brand is big on breathable, free-flowing attires crafted from handwoven cottons and linens which defy trends, seasons and sizes. Once here, visitors can expect to find an interesting interplay of saris, drapes and even accessories made from scrap metal. Address: 29, Kasturi Rangan Road, Poes Garden, Chennai [#image: /photos/5ce41a6b1dc267d657c7730c]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/sienna_store There is an increasing need to bridge the gap between the consumer and the maker of any given product, and Sienna harbours this very aim at its heart. Here, handcrafted kaftans, gamchas, saris and shift dresses adorn rustic brick walls, along with artisanal jewellery, ceramics and terracotta pottery. You can also pop into its quaint cafe for a steaming espresso or wholesome salads. Address: 49/1 Hindustan Park, Kolkata [#image: /photos/5ce41a6b89be3685d87ce9ac]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/theopentrunk This sprawling space vouches for organic clothing, sheltering labels like House of Three and Amita Gupta Sustainable, and is also the exclusive address of another such sustainable label called House of Primes. Along with boasting a roster of garments like chanderi wrap skirts, handwoven linens and naturally-dyed khadi overcoats, the studio also houses a host of other Indian designers selling couture. column1: Do fashion and politics belong together?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Interesting bedfellows When Melania Trump wore a jacket emblazoned with ‘I Really Don't Care, Do U?' to a migrant shelter, her choice of clothing was obviously derided globally. It was a tone-deaf move but also served as a reminder that fashion is very much an integral part of the political conversation. London-based designer Ashish Gupta is a man who has never shied away from making a statement about current affairs. He tells Vogue why fashion and politics have always made interesting bedfellows. “I have always used sequins as a kind of rebellion against the blandness of everyday life. In recent times, I think they are a rebellion against the dark times we live in. I call it “ fighting gloom with glitter.” I think everyone has a responsibility to make a change or at least raise awareness. Ironically, I think the most interesting art and fashion comes in troubled times like these. It forces us to be more resilient and brave in what we choose to say and how we say it. When the referendum happened in the UK and there was a vote for Brexit, it made me question how I felt about living in the UK. That season I decided to celebrate my Indian roots, to say that I am an immigrant in that country, and I am proud of my heritage, and it's fine to be both those things. I hate it when people say, “We are a tolerant society.” I don't want to be “tolerated”—like bad weather. It's like saying, “You're not welcome but we will put up with you.” When the shock of the 2016 US elections had died down a little, I had to say something about toxic Trump. “MORE GLITTER, LESS TWITTER” was one of my favourite slogans that season. Fashion and politics have always made interesting bedfellows. The strongest politicians always distil their style into a uniform. A uniform means less distraction, stronger message. I always admired Indira Gandhi's style. She famously made the sari a symbol of Swadesh—always sophisticated, starched and neatly draped into a silhouette that was no-nonsense and strong, just like her politics. She accessorised minimally with a man's wristwatch. It was a clever understated code signalling briskness, efficiency and strength. On foreign trips, she would mix a slightly glitzier version of her trademark sari with a trench or a fur—creating a brilliant sartorial treaty. An East-meets-West gesture way before fashion started mixing it up. In 2016 Hillary Clinton's style gave rise to the ‘Pantsuit Nation' movement. People still stereotype women, especially in positions of power, and it made me wonder if it was her way of saying she could be ‘one of the boys'. In her book, she wrote, “I ... thought it would be good to do what male politicians do and wear more or less the same thing every day,” and that she looked “different from the men but also familiar.” Trump, on the other hand, wears badly tailored suits. The hair is an unruly straw-coloured nest. His ties, scotch-taped into place, always seem to hang too low. Fran Lebowitz said: “Trump is a poor person's idea of a rich person. They see him. They think, ‘If I were rich, I'd have a fabulous tie like that. Why are my ties not made of 400 acres of polyester?' It all makes him look angry, sloven, sloppy.” As in fashion, so in life?” View Gallery 8 Photos Fashion + politics Fashion Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show 2018: All the runway photos
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion See what the 2018 Victoria’s Secret Angels and models wore on the runway in New York Wings, glitter and Angels: that was the order of the day on the 2018 Victoria's Secret Fashion Show runway in New York City on November 8 (November 9 for us in India). All your favourite runway regulars were there, including Kendall Jenner, Gigi Hadid, Bella Hadid, Georgia Fowler, Kelly Gale and Shanina Shaik, clad in pretty, slightly complicated lingerie and a number of wings. The Angels too were out in full force with Taylor Hill, Sara Sampaio, Jasmine Tookes and Romee Strijd (who wore the sought-after Shooting Star Swarovski look) flitting, stomping and almost flying down the coveted runway. Let's not forget we also saw the return of Candice Swanepoel and Behati Prinsloo who both welcomed their second children earlier in 2018. Most significantly though, Adriana Lima took her final bow after a 19-year reign and three Fantasy Bras as the longest-serving Angel in history—an emotional moment for the model and her fans. New kids on the block, Australians Alannah Walton, Subah Koj and Duckie Thot as well as Winnie Harlow (who made history as the first model with vitiligo to walk the VS Fashion Show), Kelsey Merritt (the first Filipino model to walk in the show), Sadie Newman and Yasmin Wijnaldum all made very Victoria's Secret debuts in their respective lingerie looks. It was also a big year for returning models with Barbara Palvin (whose boyfriend Dylan Sprouse was in the audience for moral support) back after a five-year hiatus and Toni Garrn making a comeback after a four-year break—both of whom made this year a triumphant one and proved they always deserve a spot in the line-up. Of course, the runway really belonged to Angel Elsa Hosk who was the lucky model chosen this year to wear the USD$1 million Dream Angels Fantasy Bra. The blonde bombshell didn't let us down and pranced down the runway with all the vim and vigour an Angel needs to pull off the biggest look of the night. Other highlights included this year's designer collaboration with British-based Mary Katrantzou, which resulted in a number of bold, bright and pretty-patterned looks roaming down the runway, all the other 2018 themes (Downtown Angels, Pink, Celestial Angels, Golden Girls, Royal Glam and Flights of Fantasy) and the musical performances from Bebe Rexha, The Chainsmokers, Halsey, Kelsea Ballerini, Rita Ora, Shawn Mendes and The Struts. column1: Stella McCartney: “Working with and looking at technology gives me hope”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Through our New Horizons series, we’re taking you on a whirlwind—and impossibly stylish!—world tour. But don’t bother packing your passport. This odyssey is all thanks to the globally minded designers who simply refuse to see borders Stella McCartney has always been a tree climber. Hers was an English-countryside childhood spent riding horses and shimmying up giant oaks. “I grew up being aware of the seasons and the planet's power and immensity,” she says. And as McCartney learned more about the harm caused by fashion manufacturing, she began to approach all aspects of her burgeoning namesake line ethically. From its very beginnings in 2001, it has been leather-, fur-, and feather-free—a fearless and peerless stance in the early aughts, one motivated by her personal choices as a committed, lifelong vegetarian. Climate change, of course, knows no borders. At some point, McCartney's sustainable way of doing business will of necessity be the only way of doing business in a world of shrinking natural resources. But the designer, now 47, proved herself a pioneer all over again when she announced a collaboration with Bolt Threads, the Bay-area biotechnology company that engineers new fibres based on proteins found in nature—in this case, silk made from yeast rather than worms. Even more radical than laboratory-made silk: McCartney's habit of telling her customers who come looking for sustainability advice to rent clothes or to buy vintage or secondhand (she's partnered with the high-end resale site TheRealReal on a first-of-its-kind recommerce project). Going against the grain, in fact, is precisely how McCartney has carved out her unique and—since buying the 50 per cent share of her company that had been owned by the luxury giant Kering—newly independent space in the fashion sphere. “I know you can have a healthy business model in this industry that isn't using leather, isn't using PVCs, isn't using fur; that tries to use solar panels or wind power in stores around the world. Working with and looking at technology gives me some hope,” she says. “How do you have children if you don't have some kind of hope?” McCartney has two boys and two girls—tree climbers, all of them—and she recently spoke to her younger daughter's class. “I talked about fashion, and I tried to keep it exciting and glamorous—which it is. But then I started talking about the Loop shoe”—an in-house innovation that makes glue, which is typically made from animal or fish bones, unnecessary. Let's just say she got their attention. “When you're young, you have different expectations of how to treat our fellow creatures and how to respect the planet,” McCartney says. “It's their future we're talking about. Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 3 Victoria’s Secret models talk about the need for diversity on the runway
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ahead of their debuts at the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show 2018, Vogue meets Winnie Harlow, Duckie Thot and Kelsey Merritt to talk about the need for more representation on the runway It all started with an Instagram post. On September 7, a few days after the final castings took place for the Victoria's Secret Fashion Show 2018, model Kelsey Merritt took to social media to announce that she had earned her wings. In the soon-to-be viral photo, she also revealed that she would be the first Filipino woman in the history of the lingerie brand to walk in its annual extravaganza. The news revived an ongoing discussion about diversity on the Victoria's Secret runway. In 2017, Teen Vogue reported that the show's model lineup was the most diverse yet, with almost 50 per cent of those walking coming from Black, Asian or Hispanic backgrounds. This figure was around 30 per cent in 2016 and even lower (25 per cent) in 2015. The comparative surge in representation at last year's show was also partly a result of its location in Shanghai. As the brand's first-ever presentation in Asia, it featured a record number of Chinese models—eight—a number unlikely to be matched this year. Limitations in the casting at Victoria's Secret are symptomatic of an industry-wide failure to ensure consistent representation on the runway regardless of seasonal whims. The Fashion Spot's latest diversity report notes that while the spring/summer 2019 shows were the most racially diverse of all time, only 36.1 per cent of models were people of colour. It also highlights the continuing lack of plus-size, older, transgender and non-binary models on the international catwalks—a problem mirrored at Victoria's Secret. In 2017, Ashley Graham called out the company for never having included a plus-size model in their shows, while earlier this year Leyna Bloom campaigned unsuccessfully to become the first transgender woman to be cast. The Victoria's Secret Fashion Show is still the most-watched fashion event of the year, so diversity on this global stage is crucial. The brand has a long way to go in order to become fully inclusive, but among the newcomers in this year's show are several models of colour who have been outspoken about the need for greater representation, from runway regulars such as Winnie Harlow and Duckie Thot to rising stars like Merritt. Ahead of this year's show, Vogue speaks to them about the importance of inclusivity and asks what still needs to be done to promote diversity in the fashion industry. “You do realise you're going to be the answer to a trivia question now!” 2018 has special significance for 22-year-old Kelsey Merritt. It will mark both her Victoria's Secret debut and her first time walking on a catwalk outside of her home country. “I was born in a small town called Pampanga near Manila,” she tells Vogue. “I started modelling there at 15 and at 17, the director of Wilhelmina International scouted me on Instagram. I waited until I finished university and then moved to New York when I was 21.” After three years with Wilhelmina, Merritt started shooting campaigns with Victoria's Secret. “It was great to work with the brand, but that doesn't guarantee that you'll walk in the show,” she explains. Before Merritt, Janine Tugonon made history in 2016 as the lingerie brand's first Filipino spokesperson but failed to be cast in the show. “I always watched the shows growing up and we all knew that a Filipino girl had never walked in it,” says Merritt. “That had been my goal for a while, but I never thought it would happen. It's hard for models from the Philippines to make it in New York in general. When I started working here, I only knew four other girls from my country.” Merritt admits that this lack of representation made her feel uncertain about her place in the industry. “I grew up thinking that Western models were superior to me,” she says. “When I started working, they always booked better jobs and I never thought I'd be good enough to compete with them. The truth is, when it comes to diversity, there really isn't a lot in this industry.” This was something she describes feeling even more acutely during her casting for Victoria's Secret. “There are only about 15 slots for newcomers. You really have to fight for your place, and as a woman of colour you have to work even harder.” After the three-day casting and an anxious wait, she found out she had made it onto the lineup. “I was so excited. Victoria's Secret changes the lives of the models who walk in the show. I was talking to a friend about it and he said, ‘Kelsey, you're the first Filipino to be walking in it. You do realise you're going to be the answer to a trivia question now!' But the fact that we are being included means that times really are changing.” If a commercial juggernaut like Victoria's Secret can push for more diversity, Merritt hopes other brands will follow. “Everyone should be more inclusive, and now there's no excuse. There's a huge public demand for it.” According to Merritt, the best way to encourage representation in the industry is to convince companies that it is profitable to use models who reflect a brand's diverse consumer base. “Victoria's Secret is massive in the Philippines. There's a huge market out there, people love their products and there's a big viewership for the show too. So for one of us to be in it sends a great message to my country. It shows that success on this scale is achievable for us. For a long time, I didn't think it was.” “The Victoria's Secret runway needs to be representative of reality” When Winnie Harlow didn't make the lineup after trying out for the Victoria's Secret Fashion Show last year, she was disappointed to say the least. “Ever since I first took an interest in modelling, Victoria's Secret has been the top goal on my career bucket list,” she reveals to Vogue. So, when the 24-year-old Toronto native returned to castings this year, she was feeling the pressure. “I actually broke down in the car and needed my driver to take me around the block twice so I could get myself together before I walked in. I had my trainer on the phone and he helped calm me down. When I did go in, my nerves turned into excitement.” A few days later she learned that she had been cast in the show. Harlow will be the first model with vitiligo, a condition that causes pigmentation loss in skin, to walk the runway at Victoria's Secret. While she has spoken about being bullied at school and struggling to enter the modelling industry due to her condition, it has since made her one of the most recognisable faces in fashion. After appearing on America's Next Top Model in 2014, she walked for several international brands including Fendi, Coach, Marc Jacobs and Julien Macdonald. She has cameoed in Beyoncé's visual album Lemonade, participated in the Women in the World Summit and given a TEDxTeen Talk entitled “My Story Is Painted on my Body” that garnered over a million views on YouTube. This year, Tommy Hilfiger announced that Harlow would be his new global brand ambassador alongside Hailey Baldwin. Considering her success, why does being cast in the Victoria's Secret Show still feel so significant? “It's special for me because it's so incredibly coveted,” says Harlow. “This show is different because of the unique focus on the talent. For most fashion shows, the focus is on the clothes, and even though the designs on the Victoria's Secret runway are incredible, the emphasis is on the models.” The casting process has been gruelling, but she admits that it has added to her sense of achievement. “The brand selects the cast very carefully and behind all the glitz and glamour there's a lot of hard work and dedication. Every girl in the show spends a lot of time making sure she looks and feels her absolute best. It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.” Despite Victoria's Secret's history of featuring black models such as Naomi Campbell and Tyra Banks on some of its earliest runways, Harlow believes the brand can do more to embrace diversity in all its forms. “The show has a global impact and so it's important that Victoria's Secret makes sure the runway is representative of reality. We live in a diverse world with beautiful women of all shapes, sizes and ethnicities. It's great that the brand is making efforts to show this on the runway and the industry as a whole is becoming more inclusive, but there's always room for improvement. It's important that we continue to make sure representation is not just a trend, but a standard.” “Have we made enough progress? Not necessarily” For 23-year-old Duckie Thot, the rise to fashion superstardom has been swift. Born and raised in Melbourne, the daughter of South Sudanese refugees, she first came to prominence after finishing third on Australia's Next Top Model in 2013. Editorials for Paper and Black Magazine followed, until a chance encounter with Kanye West sent her career into overdrive. After meeting the rapper at a casting in New York, she stormed the runway at Yeezy's spring/summer 2017 show and was introduced to Pat McGrath in the process. This led to Thot being featured in the makeup artist's “In the Mirror” video series, which went viral on social media. Since then, the model has gone on to walk for Balmain, Moschino and Oscar de la Renta. Rihanna is a fan, having cast Thot in the autumn/winter 2017 Fenty x Puma show and chosen her as one of the faces of Fenty Beauty. Last year, she starred in the Alice in Wonderland-themed Pirelli calendar shot by Tim Walker, and this September was named the newest ambassador for L'Oréal Paris. “The Victoria's Secret Show somehow feels different because of how difficult it is to be a part of,” Thot tells Vogue. “I didn't get it the first year I auditioned and had to work really hard over the last year to get to this point. It's been challenging, but it makes being a part of the show even more special and rewarding.” Thot has long been vocal about the need for more diversity in fashion, particularly in Australia where she initially found difficulty booking jobs. She believes that the problem extends far beyond the question of casting, having spoken openly about the fact that many makeup artists on shoots still don't carry her foundation shade or know how to style natural hair. “The industry has definitely made strides in terms of representation recently,” she admits. “And I'm so glad to be a part of this change. Have we made enough progress? Not necessarily. We can still do more and I'm certainly up to the task of creating more opportunities for those who have been underrepresented.” She hopes her appearance on the Victoria's Secret runway will be a watershed moment for other models of colour. “Diversity is important because beauty and fashion are such integral parts of culture, and the runway should represent what's actually happening in the world. If the representation isn't there in the shows and marketing, it can be problematic in making marginalised communities feel like they don't belong. Setting an inclusive standard helps younger girls realise their own potential and visualise themselves in similar spaces. Seeing models of colour in previous shows had a similar effect on me. I want to do the same for other young women.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What makes fashion today global, democratic, empowering, and essential
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion US Vogue’s creative digital director, Sally Singer, pens down what fashion means to her in the present day The present moment is a time in which the style industry is ubiquitous in the culture worldwide to an unprecedented degree. Everywhere you turn, every narrative you bump up against, you find clothes are part of the story—on television, in print, on-site and on social media. ‘Beyoncé is first to perform in Riccardo Tisci's Burberry' is one headline I encounter this morning, as I grab my coffee and settle down to write; meanwhile, Paul Manafort's ridiculously lavish ostrich jacket (he of the Mueller investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 US presidential election) is still the talk of the television pundits. And did Meghan Markle really just wear Club Monaco pleats to Prince Harry's pal's wedding? It is now entirely normal that clothes are integral to the conversation in everything, from political discourse to dinner table gossip, and no one bats an eye when even a child can spot a Gucci loafer from ten paces. For someone like myself, an obsessive and professional style watcher, it is exhilarating and perhaps a tad exhausting. How does my day at Vogue.com begin? There are the pictures to pore over from parties (frocks!) and airports (bags!) and city streets the world over (jeans! boots!). There is the user-generated footage to edit from micro-influencers who live everywhere from North Dakota to Nairobi. There are the original celebrity videos in need of notes and polish. There are the dancers on Youtube I need to check out, the ladies with floor-length extensions in Chicago I need to know more about, the 19-year-old photographers on Instagram who follow a skate world but not one I have ever seen before. There is the slate of candidates for elective office who we cover exhaustively and whose style is part of their promise. And then there are the pop stars, who are now designers and want to be directors as well if we can only find the right casting of, say, gorgeous octogenarian swimmers. Then there are the collections, the pre-collections, the capsule collections, the collaborations, limited-edition collections, that endless stream of clothes and more clothes, some of which are genius, some less so, but all in need of conscious consideration. And then there are the geniuses behind those clothes, the creators themselves, who fuel and shape this giddy barrage of self-expression. They, too, require attention and support. Fashion, for me, is global, democratic, empowering and essential: it is the fundamental element that sends us out into the world to be our best selves in whatever form we choose to do so. Twenty years ago, when fashion shows were attended by the lucky few and the information gleaned from them highly guarded and dispensed gingerly, I still wanted to find the intersection between the runway and the street; it never made sense to me to see fashion in isolation. Even at the haute couture shows, where one really can appreciate the creations of an atelier on their own terms, free from the burden of utility or scaleable commerce, I still look on at the most elaborate and (possibly) impractical looks by Pierpaolo Piccioli at Valentino, say, or Maria Grazia Chiuri for Dior and think, I want to see someone in that walking down my street. I want the world to look at that marvellous and original thing. I don't care to see fashion in a museum: life is too short and the burden of our times too great. We need glamour in every form. We need beauty. And we need change—at least in my country—which necessarily involves the shock of the new, which is the essence of great style. When people say that fashion is not political, I say consider the sea of knitted pink hats that greeted our new president on his inaugural weekend. Remember last year's Golden Globe Awards and Oscars, and the rightness and chicness of those black dresses worn to affirm solidarity with Time's Up! For the first time in many a year on the red carpet actresses did not answer questions about their clothes and jewels; they discussed the issues and their work. Their dresses spoke for them. Isn't it cool when fashion can be part of the conversation without anyone having to say a word? Culture & Living Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Bollywood’s newest love affair? High-waisted jeans
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Something for everyone Whether you take your denim skinny or with some '70s-inspired flare, you've likely got your favourite styles bookmarked in a silhouette that goes all the way above your natural waist. There's no two ways about it any longer—high-waisted jeans are here, and they are here to stay out. The reasons behind why they are edging out their low-rise brethren are many and varied, but the most probable one is perhaps the fact that this universally flattering style has found a fan in celebrities, street style icons and everyday women alike. Those in need for proof need look no further than Deepika Padukone's wardrobe for her stint at Cannes earlier this year. The leggy diva packed her favourite denims alongside all the trailing gowns, and was spotted maxing the value of a basic white tee tucked into a pair of crisp high-rise jeans, before swapping out the former for a white tank and the bedhead waves for a poker straight hairdo. If you've been looking for some more dramatic pairings, take notes from Anushka Sharma, who has been championing the cause of denim-on-denim in recent times. Not one to have too much of a good thing, the promotional slew for Sui Dhaaga had her teaming a deconstructed denim top from her eponymous label, Nush, with a pair of bell bottoms. She revisited this winning combination again this month with a ruffled top tucked into belted jeans. As the mercury slowly dips to herald the onset of winter, everyone's favourite globetrotter Priyanka Chopra is keeping her wardrobe prepared for all possibilities with some handy layering; the Baywatch star recently stepped out in a brown overcoat, offsetting the earthiness of the colour palette with a pair of white denims with an unconventional button fly. If you'd like to humble brag about your washboard abs, Athiya Shetty's weapon of choice is a cropped jumper, while Alia Bhatt makes a strong case for a half-tucked slogan tee to nail off-duty chic. Scroll onwards for our edit of all the times Bollywood celebrities aced high-waisted jeans. View Gallery 11 Photos All the times Bolloywood celebrities aced high-waisted jeans To avoid clocking in endless miles between the trial room and the racks, it pays to take some time out before shopping to make note of what works for your specific body type. If you're on the petite side, skinny jeans are your best friend, as they will accentuate the smallest part of your waist and add an illusion of longer legs. Steer clear of the boxiness of mom jeans, as there's a good chance they will end up overwhelming your small frame. On the other hand, if you've got curves and you'd like to flaunt ‘em, bootcuts, wide-legged and bell bottoms all work, since they create that much-touted hourglass figure while also flattering your legs. To create a streamlined silhouette, pair it with a fitted blouse or a breezy crop top. Despite the flared hem, keep a vigilant eye on the fit while trying on your options in the trial room; gaping waistbands and drooping butts are a universal no-no, regardless of the style you're opting for. column1: Marine Serre: “If you keep doing things the same way, nothing will change”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Through our New Horizons series, we’re taking you on a whirlwind—and impossibly stylish!—world tour. But don’t bother packing your passport. This odyssey is all thanks to the globally minded designers who simply refuse to see borders It's a broiling hot July day in Paris, and the fan valiantly whirring away to cool down Marine Serre's studio has its work cut out for it. Yet Serre doesn't seem unduly bothered. Her five-foot-nothing frame is clad in a billowing dress, and she's sipping water from a tumbler not much bigger than a shot glass. But then, heat is something that she has had to get used to lately. While this 26-year-old Marseilles native has only been in business for about a year, she now has 15 employees, 70 retailers, one LVMH prize, and three collections to her name. “A year ago I was in school and couldn't even pay for my apartment,” she says. “But I'm not scared, because I have nothing to lose.” Serre's runway debut this past February upended clichéd notions of beauty and power by the way she slyly shot her looks through with political and sexual commentary: riotously patterned vintage scarves upcycled into dresses; sick, slick, fetish-y PVC coats; head-covering bodysuits dotted with her crescent-moon logo, a look equal parts high-performance athleticism and modest observance. Each of them was imbued with Serre's exacting, fearless attitude—“One-metre-fifty, but a will of steel” is how Karl Lagerfeld once described her. “I think we need to be a little aggressive in a way because things are so stuck,” she says. “If you keep doing things the same way, nothing will change.” Those scarf dresses are a case in point. Serre had to work hard to persuade her factories to make them, given their technical complexities, and she relished the David and Goliath aspect of it. “The biggest challenge for a young designer now is learning to take care of yourself so you can be sharper,” she says, “because we have to be as quick as the big houses.” When she sold those dresses, though, she didn't make a whole song and dance about the upcycling. “I don't want to confuse Marine Serre with a brand that wants to make money doing green stuff,” she says. “Everyone should be caring about that already because otherwise, fashion is going to die anyway.” It's that stance—pragmatic in its progressiveness—that underscores Serre's approach to everything she does. She's of a generation that grew up with the world always at its fingertips thanks to technology. Social media's periscope into far-flung destinations—not to mention her own peripatetic moves from Marseilles to Brussels and now Paris—has allowed her to honour cultural differences while celebrating what's common to all of us. She recently took a work tour of Asia, and while she was struck by the rush of the new, it was the universality of life that captivated her. Likewise, Serre has been thrilled by how her moon leitmotif has traversed from continent to continent, each time interpreted—and appreciated—differently. “I think it's quite symbolic with what is happening today,” she says. “There shouldn't be boundaries when we're making fashion.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Virgil Abloh: “Race, religion, gender tend to disappear in a global community”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Through our New Horizons series, we’re taking you on a whirlwind—and impossibly stylish!—world tour. But don’t bother packing your passport. This odyssey is all thanks to the globally minded designers who simply refuse to see borders “We're in a time where this wash of humanity is truly in influencing—upstream—what fashion will become,” says Virgil Abloh. The indefatigable multitasker is the designer behind his own label, Off-White, as well as the new head of menswear at Louis Vuitton; a footwear collaborator with Nike; a furniture collaborator with Ikea; an artistic collaborator with Takashi Murakami; a formally trained architect; an in-demand DJ; and the subject of an upcoming exhibition about his own work at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Chicago. Abloh, 38, is silhouetted by a citrine-yellow French summer sun on a recent Monday afternoon, not long after the polychrome storm of his debut at Louis Vuitton, which featured a rainbow-painted catwalk meant to broadcast an international message of inclusivity and show notes with an infographic of the widespread birthplaces of his cast. Though his intention is nothing less than a reset of a company that's been around since 1854, he's kickstarting it with an entire world of inspiration—the exact opposite of a blank slate. And this is the thing about Abloh: He travels so extensively for his many jobs that there's a kind of horizon-surpassing, border-blind eye to so much of what he creates. Off-White, the label he founded independently, “gives me the freedom to chronicle what's happening—and a large part of Off-White is the dialogue I've had between being from Rockford, Illinois, and spending time in Europe.” Those disparate settings are evinced in the vast range that Abloh builds into Off-White's lineups: For autumn, we see everything from a gauzy ombré tulle dress (very modern Victoriana) to an all-black, action-hero-slick catsuit (very, well...modern American). How, then, does someone who routinely spans the world with evidently limitless energy collect his thoughts to track, channel and reflect the forever-transforming world? “It's like I'm walking down different streets all at the same time, seeing, smelling and breathing diversity, and realising that things you grow up with—race, religion, gender or anything else—tend to disappear once you're embedded in a global community.” As for what fuels Abloh's engine, particularly when it comes to Off-White: “Young people in every city that I go to are loving life and actively participating in it. I am shocked at how open-minded young people of different cultures are compared to the presiding older generations. Australia, Tokyo, downtown Los Angeles: It's the same community, bound by youth. And that gives me great hope.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Looking for an anarkali? Take inspiration from these Bollywood celebrities
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Right in time for the festive season The mark of a wholesome traditional wear wardrobe is variety. The renewed interest in the sari is at an all-time high, lehengas are a wedding season staple, and modern variations of Indian silhouettes are trendy additions to any wardrobe. As you're building a personal collection of MVPs this festive season, don't forget to add the trusty anarkali to the mix. The flared tunic style silhouette is easy to dress up or down, and is capable of holding you in good stead at events ranging from a Diwali poker party to a sangeet. A favourite with Bollywood's style set, we train the spotlight on some of their most memorable designer anarkalis to bring you inspiration just in time for Diwali From pastel anarkalis to intricately embellished numbers, there is one for every occasion. Alia Bhatt is a sworn patron. From a sunny yellow embroidered number for her friend's mehandi to a halter neckline for an au courant update, the actor makes a strong case for its versatility. Looking to wear the silhouette for a Diwali party? Choose a billowy floral print anarkali like Jacqueline Fernandez or an angarakha-style creation as seen on Athiya Shetty. Go easy on the embroidery but extra with the jewellery. Anushka Sharma, Kareena Kapoor Khan and Gauri Khan are in favour of floor-length anarkalis for the wedding season, as they are equal parts comfortable and statement-making. Complete this look with statement earrings as you sport it for an engagement or reception party. Janhvi Kapoor's ivory anarkali with multi-coloured embroidery, on the other hand, is an ideal choice for daytime pheras. column1: Riccardo Tisci: “Breaking down borders has always been important to me”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Through our New Horizons series, we’re taking you on a whirlwind—and impossibly stylish!—world tour. But don’t bother packing your passport. This odyssey is all thanks to the globally minded designers who simply refuse to see borders “It's great to be back in London again!” says Riccardo Tisci. “There's been such an incredible evolution since I studied at Central Saint Martins nearly 20 years ago—I really feel the change. But one thing that always remains in this city is its diverse energy and incredible spirit. It's what I loved so much as a student, and it's something that's so important in my work now at Burberry.” Tisci could hardly be a better standard-bearer for the creative free flow of talent, ideas, and trade that is fashion's modus operandi: an Italian, tutored in British-style individualism, who honed his couture skills in Paris at the top of a luxury house (Givenchy, which he helmed from 2005 to 2017) and is now chief creative officer of the biggest British brand of all. He fits no mould except his own. “I consider myself very nomadic,” Tisci says. “I have been so lucky and lived in so many places, making a big family of friends and relatives along the way.” In a time when identity politics have become embedded in 21st-century consciousness, the fact that Tisci chose the image of a unicorn to accompany him for his Vogue portrait reverberates with resonances. Unicorns are symbols in both international pop culture and medieval British history—while a unicorn emoji might summon notions of a wondrous and sensitive person to a Gen Z-er, to a British person it reads as the mythic beast on the lion-and-unicorn royal coat of arms of the United Kingdom, a synonym for goodness and integrity that must be defended in the world. It was also—according to Tisci's archival research—engraved on the Burberry family silver, presumably after the working-class owners had risen to wealth on the manufacture of check-lined trench coats. Is this a picture meant to speak across generations? That would be totally Tisci—and not just because he has a long track record of ranging between haute couture and luxe streetwear. “Openness and breaking down borders have always been very important to me,” says the quiet revolutionary whose actions—in deeds, not words—made him a pioneer in dissolving the white, young, thin, heteronormative homogeneity of fashion and an opener of doors to every shade of gender and colour in his time at Givenchy. “I am proud and very fortunate to have been able to champion progressive, strong and for- ward-thinking people,” Tisci says with a shrug. “This has always felt instinctive for me, and it seems that it is becoming more and more natural and normal for the whole industry now, too.” It's a way of thinking, working and living that fits right into the multicultural, LGBTQI-friendly ideals of the capital city, where Mayor Sadiq Khan's #LondonIsOpen campaign has been waving a defiantly celebratory flag since the Brexit referendum in 2016. Tisci, of course, is one of thousands of Europeans contributing to the culture of modern British dynamism—albeit the one most visible in projecting it on the global stage. “It feels very natural for me to be bringing the house's British heritage and style to people around the world,” he says.
