column1: The two new cool designer collaborations you need to watch out for
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Right in time for the festive season It's almost Diwali, and this time around, there are two new cool collaborations out there to answer all your gifting and wardrobe conundrums. One gives the humble shawl a luxurious update, courtesy Janavi x AJSK, while the other comes as an antidote to heavy festive wear. Think light as air bandhani jackets and wrap kurtas in signature Anushka Khanna style. Read on to know where to find them. Janavi x AJSK Sure, you can send over a platter of sweets and candles to near and dear ones for the festive season, but to really make your gift memorable—read: not long forgotten in the confines of a cupboard—opt for a cosy cashmere shawl by Janavi x AJSK. To curate a sensory overload, multiple eras and cultures from around the world collide on the shawls in the form of iconic motifs like exotic birds, Art Deco florals and elephants from the Mughal era. The designers have painted a perfect picture of glory days past using silk thread embroidery in gold and silver on a pastel palette, with a melange of craftwork like zardosi, sequins, crystals and bugle beads. “These shawls are meant to drape a dreamer—someone who appreciates fine design and craftsmanship. They can go from a soiree or a cocktail to a wedding reception or black tie. They can be draped as scarves or as wraps. This collection takes the perceived staidness out of cashmere and makes it out of the box, deeply delicious, glamorous for every woman,” say Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla of their creative method and partnership with Jyotika Jhalani of Janavi. ANUSHKA KHANNA @ CLOVE What do you get when Samyukta Nair, the multi-hyphenate behind the coolest store in Colaba, Clove, and designer Anushka Khanna, who is known for her easy-breezy contemporary Indian separates, come together for the festive season? A 12-piece capsule collection to help build your Diwali wardrobe. And just in case you miss it in time for Diwali, the edit continues in store until late December, so you can gear up for all the weddings pencilled in your calendar. Nair, who transforms the one-stop postcode for home, fashion and jewellery to match the flavour of the month, tells us the reason for partnering with Khanna this season. “Anushka's aesthetic of meeting Indian heritage with a global perspective is what really drew me to her work. Her love for colour and prints creates a perfect balance without being too overpowering and holds true to what we value at Clove.” And for those who need a helping hand with finding jewellery to match, Nair's curation serves up one statement jewellery piece for each languid Anushka Khanna look. Of her own creative method, Khanna says, “The collection is really about being effortless and easy. These clothes go beyond just festive wear; these are pieces you could wear anywhere in the world, for pretty much any occasion.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How Demna Gvasalia channels his experience with war through fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Through our New Horizons series, we’re taking you on a whirlwind—and impossibly stylish!—world tour. But don’t bother packing your passport. This odyssey is all thanks to the globally minded designers who simply refuse to see borders “This stars-and-stripes jacket which represents the States is my favourite—because American culture is what I loved when I was growing up.” The night before his Vetements show in July, Demna Gvasalia paused to pull out a patchworked-leather bomber, then turned it around and pointed to the slogan on the back. “What I like is that it says AMERICA, but in Russian.” No one in the designer fashion world understands more about the human cost of what happens when neighbours fight over borders than Gvasalia, who was 12 years old when he and his younger brother (now his business partner) Guram had to flee their home during the brutal civil war that overtook Sukhumi, Georgia, in 1993. “Everybody today talks about war, refugees,” he says, “and I am like, yes—I know exactly what that means.” One of the dresses in the spring show was made from a single square of off-kiltered white cotton, a memory of the bedsheets the family grabbed as they fled to bomb shelters before eventually trekking across mountains under sniper fire. (Seen down the long barrel of history, Georgia's problems then were only a dress rehearsal for the violent displacement of peoples across the Middle East, Europe, and sub-Saharan Africa, which are the continual horrors on our screens now.) In his formative years, Gvasalia moved to Odessa (which is part of Ukraine but has recently been in conflict with Russia) and Düsseldorf, Germany, eventually studying fashion at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, Belgium. Now he works in Paris—since 2015, as creative director of Balenciaga—and Zurich, where he chose to settle with the Vetements team last year. Since he took up residence in clean, calm, safely neutral Switzerland—well away from any of fashion's main drags—Gvasalia has increasingly channelled his past traumas into positive creative energy. National flags have been popping up in his work—in Balenciaga resort prints, on Vetements parkas—but on an equal footing with the international rainbow symbol for acceptance and love. A fake snow-boarder's mountain was installed as the set for the fall Balenciaga show, and on its crests and crevasses were multicoloured graffiti—spray-painted, Gvasalia claimed, with words he and his team had been throwing around in the studio. Among the smiley faces and Balenciaga logos, two slogans jumped out: BE AWARE and NO BORDERS. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Hedi Slimane: “It’s important to have a clear and distinct voice”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Through our series New Horizons, we’re taking you on a whirlwind—and impossibly stylish!—world tour. But don’t bother packing your passport. This odyssey is all thanks to the globally minded designers who simply refuse to see borders In April 2016, Hedi Slimane revealed that, after a rollicking four-year tenure marked by his compulsive and convulsive rewriting of the house's most revered codes, he was leaving Saint Laurent. Then, in January of this year, the news broke that Slimane was heading to Celine to replace the departed Phoebe Philo—another seismic jolt to the system, one amplified by the briefest of statements (Slimane has long been a man of few words but many actions) outlining that in addition to women's collections there would also be, for the first time, a Celine collection for men, as well as haute couture in due course—or his version of it, at least. Though these two events both occurred within 24 months, given the hyper speed at which everything turns these days you might as well count the time elapsed in light-years. The political and cultural metamorphoses—and all that reordering of hierarchies and taste and beauty—that have touched us all have left Slimane eager to return to the fray. “Current evolutions make me want to focus, commit and engage even more,” he says. “There is, besides, a really inspiring generation coming out.” This is quintessential Slimane: a headlong rush into newness powered by the youthful energy fomenting in the world. “It's quite liberating to see how new aesthetics can transcend preconceived ideas and conventions,” he adds. “It is important not to fall for generic or fake postures of progress, but rather to question a status quo, to have a clear and distinct voice.” And what of Slimane's voice, one of the most clear and distinctive out there: How has his time away altered its timbre? For one thing, Los Angeles, whose sonic and aesthetic landscapes helped shape his vision for Saint Laurent, is being reevaluated. “There is clearly a change, a certain edge that feels disturbing,” he says of his adopted hometown. “I'm always attached to the idea of California, but recently less so to the city of Los Angeles. I don't feel comfortable with the evolution over the last few years—too many people have moved in; we have seen entire neighbourhoods destroyed by speculation and developers. Something untouched, mysterious and magical has gone.” Instead, this serial nomad, who has also lived in Berlin and London, is gazing back to France. “Clearly, the political shift has changed the dynamics of the city and the country in general,” Slimane says. “It has definitely moved my focus toward Paris.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Gosha Rubchinskiy: “An artist should not be a spokesperson for a culture”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Through our New Horizons series, we’re taking you on a whirlwind—and impossibly stylish!—world tour. But don’t bother packing your passport. This odyssey is all thanks to the globally minded designers who simply refuse to see borders Moscow-born Gosha Rubchinskiy, 34, surprised the fashion world earlier this year by announcing the end—at least in its seasonal capacity—of his namesake line. His many ardent fans, though, needn't worry—he's got plenty in the pipeline: In July, Rubchinskiy opened a skate shop in Moscow, Oktyabr, named after a Russian skate team, and he's further developing his skate line, Paccbet (pronounced rassviet—it means “sunrise” in Russian), launched with skateboarder Tolia Titaev. Rubchinskiy made major waves with his label, founded in 2008 and later backed by Comme des Garçons, which delivered a singularly cool viewpoint of Russian youth culture to a global audience. His homeland-as-aesthetic muse—Cyrillic writing, tracksuits, clubwear influenced by late-Soviet-era underground parties—depicted Russia as a vibrant place with a community of people who share contemporary values and lifestyles (an especially welcome message given that, in the US at least, recent Russia-related headlines told a rather different story). “I am happy that voices in Russia from the fashion and artistic world may be becoming more recognised elsewhere,” says the designer. “I don't think any artist should be a spokesperson for a culture. I just want to express what I want to express—to be free.” For his final three collections, Rubchinskiy staged runway shows in three different cities: Kalinin- grad (where he unveiled a collaboration with Adidas in advance of this summer's World Cup); St Petersburg (where a collaboration with Burberry dropped); and Yekaterinburg. That last collection had the most interesting international touch of all: tops and scarves with the connected flags of the US, Russia and Japan, all unveiled in the same place where the Kremlin's nuclear briefcase from the Cold War is on display. While the designer's next big move is still under wraps, Rubchinskiy's start-stop-start-again business model is true to a major trend of today's fashion system, where niches are exploding and limited product drops rule the retail game. “If you aren't thinking globally,” he says, “your thinking is out of date. The world is a small place.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Met Gala 2019: Everything you need to know, from the theme to the guests
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue delivers the definitive guide to the most sartorially significant red carpet event of the year You've seen Rihanna make an entrance in a sweeping gown on the famed steps; it's where Priyanka Chopra met her fiancée Nick Jonas—the Met Gala is where the magic happens. On the first Monday in May, the best in the world of fashion and film congregate to celebrate the opening of the Costume Institute's annual fashion exhibition. The dress code for the evening is in tandem with the theme of the exhibition. Often referred to as the Oscars of fashion, the gala presided over by American Vogue editor-in-chief Anna Wintour since 1995, has become an annual celebration of fashion featuring some of the world's biggest stars. More than a party, it's a fundraiser for the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute, timed to mark the grand opening of the Costume Institute's annual fashion exhibition. 2018's exhibition was the Costume Institute's most-visited ever, and one of the top three most-visited exhibits in the history of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The event consistently raises eight-figure sums, 2017's edition raised a record $13.5 million. This year, the museum announced its major Costume Institute exhibition for 2019: “Camp: Notes on Fashion.” The theme is a play on Susan Sontag's 1964 essay “Notes on ‘Camp'”, where she defined it as an aesthetic (“The essence of Camp is its love of the unnatural: of artifice and exaggeration,” she wrote) and outlined its primary characteristics. The exhibition therefore will be devoted to how these elements—which include irony, humour, parody, pastiche, artifice, theatricality and exaggeration—are expressed in fashion. Andrew Bolton, Wendy Yu Curator in Charge of The Costume Institute on the theme: “Fashion is the most overt and enduring conduit of the camp aesthetic. Effectively illustrating Sontag's Notes on ‘Camp', the exhibition will advance creative and critical dialogue about the ongoing and ever-evolving impact of camp on fashion.” Camp fashion can be mistaken as bad fashion, however, it's the thought behind it that personifies the object to be more. Whether it's Gucci mixing highbrow and seemingly low brow tastes or Balenciaga's exaggeration, camp as an aesthetic is very relevant to our current times. Sontag wrote, “Camp sees everything in quotation marks. It's not a lamp, but a “lamp”; not a woman, but a “woman”. To perceive Camp in objects and persons is to understand Being-as-Playing-a-Role. It is the farthest extension, in sensibility, of the metaphor of life as theatre.” The exhibition will feature approx 175 objects, including fashion, sculptures and paintings, dating from the 17th century to the present. Spanning Versailles and the royal courts of Louis XIV and Louis XV to the figure of the dandy and the queer subcultures of Europe and America in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Designers featured will include: Cristóbal Balenciaga, Thom Browne, Jean-Charles de Castelbajac, John Galliano, Jean Paul Gaultier, Guccio Gucci, Demna Gvasalia, Marc Jacobs, Stephen Jones, Christian Lacroix, Karl Lagerfeld, Alessandro Michele, Franco Moschino, Thierry Mugler, Norman Norell, Marjan Pejoski, Paul Poiret, Miuccia Prada, Richard Quinn, Christian Francis Roth, Yves Saint Laurent, Elsa Schiaparelli, Jeremy Scott, Viktor & Rolf, Anna Sui, Philip Treacy, Versace, Vivienne Westwood, and Charles Frederick Worth. In earlier years, the Costume Institute has explored the relationship between faith and fashion (Heavenly Bodies: Fashion and the Catholic Imagination), the role of technology in fashion (Manus x Machina: Fashion In An Age Of Technology) and paid tribute to avant-garde designer Rei Kawakubo (Rei Kawakubo/Comme des Garçons: Art of the In-Between). The evening's co-chairs will be Lady Gaga, Alessandro Michele, Harry Styles, Serena Williams, and Anna Wintour. The Met Gala will take place on May 6. Red carpet arrivals expected to begin around 7pm EDT, [4:30am on May 7, IST]. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City's Upper East Side is where the event takes place. An army of nearly 200 photographers expected on the red carpet to capture attendees as they arrive. Guest list is only revealed on the eve of the event, previous attendees have included everyone from Beyoncé and her sister Solange to rap supergroup Migos and actress Priyanka Chopra. Designers often arrive accompanied by their muses—Marc Jacobs and Kate Moss; Nicolas Ghesquière and Game of Thrones actress Sophie Turner; Riccardo Tisci and Madonna. The dress code for the evening coincides with the theme of the exhibition, which will be, “Camp: Notes on Fashion.” Expect celebrities accompanied by designers to turn up in the most extravagant creations that best interpret the theme. Stay tuned for live red carpet updates on Vogue India's Instagram page and the complete coverage of the evening on the website. The Met Gala is the most important source of funds for the Costume Institute, which is the only curatorial department at the museum that needs to finance its own activities. The red carpet serves as the perfect opportunity for designers to showcase their creations on a global platform. If you're one of the lucky ones to be invited then you can enter for free. But for those who don't get an invite but are lucky enough to secure a chance of attending, ticket prices are around 30,000 USD each, with tables costing about 2,75,000 USD. column1: Will we ever tire of white shoes? Bollywood celebrities say “no”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The stars just can’t seem to get enough of this trend Of all the fashion staples that have taken up permanent residence in the limelight, you'd be forgiven for having a soft spot for the classic white sneakers. Unlike other flighty trends, you don't need to twist yourself into a pretzel to fit into them, and this lazy girl favourite comes approved by both celebrities and the who's-who of the world of fashion. And what more can a girl ask for, other than knowing that her wardrobe shares a common staple with everyone from Kareena Kapoor Khan to Kim Kardashian Khan? For a wardrobe item that's been around for the better part of the last two centuries, white shoes are only just getting warmed up. Join us as we flip back through the pages of history to fan our collective obsession over this fuss-free favourite. Given their timeless versatility, the bragging rights of the humble white shoes include the ability to reinvent themselves every time you pair them with something new. The possibilities are endless, and you'd be forgiven for thinking that we are only just scratching at the surface. However, the seeds for the era of comfortable luxury were sown way back in the 1800s when tennis shoes began peaking off the court as well—the British Navy greenlighted this wardrobe staple as regulation footwear on ships, and eventually the rich patrons who boarded these cruises found a winner in the low-top sneakers for playing sports. The name ‘sneakers' itself caught on as the rubber soles didn't make a sound while moving, as opposed to the hard-soled leather shoes that weren't quite as ideal for sneaking up on people, so to speak. The onset of the Olympics tournament forever changed the course of history for white shoes; from being an aristocratic favourite, they now found themselves in the spotlight of the international arena in the form of no-nonsense white canvas shoes. It was, however, in the 1960s when French tennis player Robert Haillet finally one-upped the stakes by introducing the world to leather tops that were durable, supple and provided a firmer grip on the field. As the demand for white sneakers boomed, the major players of the footwear got hooked on the ready market for athletic shoes. The rest, as they say, is history. Does fashion influence the masses, or do the masses lay down a trail of breadcrumbs for the designers to follow? Throwing down the gauntlet on this ongoing debate about the cyclical nature of runway trends, the powers-that-be at fashion weeks have been giving their own spin on this everyday wardrobe basic. Cue the sudden influx of dad sneakers that have been edging out mommy jeans from trend charts, from Balenciaga's Triple S collection that paid homage to this everyday staple with a pre-scuffed design, to Louis Vuitton's ‘Archlight' that pairs a chunky silhouette with an exaggerated arch. And the world of couture isn't the only one fighting the good fight. Flip through the pages of history, and you'll likely find a pair of pristine white shoes beaming back at you through the most iconic moments in time. The Nike Cortez hit the spotlight with the 1972 Munich Olympics as one of the earliest long distance running shoes, and attained immortality in the 1994 comedy, Forrest Gump. On the other side of the stable, the Adidas Stan Smiths achieved cult status by leveraging the popularity of its namesake former world number one American tennis player. It was Gucci's traditional white leather shoes with the signature stripes that finally earned this everyday staple the seal of approval from the world of luxury fashion. Given their illustrious history in the limelight, white sneakers may not necessarily be a new addition to the sartorial scene, but that doesn't stop Bollywood's best from finding innovative pairings to style them with. Rhea Kapoor kept it real at sister Sonam K Ahuja's mehandi ceremony by teaming them with her Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla ensemble—all the better for dancing the night away—while, on the other end of the spectrum, Kangana Ranaut nailed the memo on high-low dressing by pairing a Topshop pantsuit with Gucci kicks. Shoes comfortable enough to run in, yet classy enough to give the paps something to write home about as you stride across the airport with your Insta-famous toddler in tow—Kareena Kapoor Khan has the market covered with her signature white kicks, which she wears with everything from slogan tees to military jackets. And the love for no-muss, no-fuss sneakers is clearly infectious, because Karisma Kapoor was also spotted twinning with her sister in comfy sneakers as the duo traipsed around London on a holiday. column1: 72 times Bollywood stars inspired us with their airport looks in 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Plus, a peek into each celebrity’s on-the-go wardrobe Gone are the days when Bollywood's jet-setters flew out of Mumbai in whatever they could get their hands on first. Today, every Indian celebrity has a travel wardrobe that's been curated to perfection. While some have signature on-flight looks that they've mastered over the years, others are game to trying something new each time they head out to board a plane. And no matter where (or when) they're flying, the stars' airport looks manage to take over social media pages within minutes. If you haven't figured out your own trademark travel look yet, let the likes of Deepika Padukone, Priyanka Chopra and Kareena Kapoor Khan inspire you. No on-flight look is a winner unless it's comfortable, and the Kapoor sisters have figured that out. While Kareena Kapoor Khan can most often be seen catching flights in cosy Gucci jumpers and relaxed (but vibrant) shirts, older sister Karisma Kapoor likes to fly around the globe in relaxed versions of the classic white T-shirt. For Bollywood debutante Janhvi Kapoor, kurtas in soothing pastel shades are an absolute on-the-go favourite, but roomy maxis and jeans are winners in her book too. While most celebrity fliers tend to stick with their tried-and-tested looks, there's a special category of Bollywood stars who enjoy going over and above the norm with their on-flight ensembles. Kangana Ranaut, the original trendsetter of Mumbai's terminals, jumps from khadi saris and Péro kurtas to ladylike dresses and not-so-basic pantsuits without breaking a sweat, while Deepika Padukone's travel closet includes everything from maxi gowns to pleather pants. Though Katrina Kaif tends to play it safe with her daily wardrobe, she's not afraid to experiment at the airport with slogan tees and eye-catching shirts. Colours, prints and embellishments are always fun, but everyone can agree that neutral shades and fail-safe silhouettes are much more practical picks for long flights. It's rare to see Aishwarya Rai Bachchan fly in anything but top-to-toe black ensembles, and Anushka Sharma often boards planes in white kurtas (remember that star-print Sabyasachi version she wore right after her wedding?). Constantly jumping between Mumbai and New York, Priyanka Chopra has now put together a travel wardrobe that will never let her down. The actor swears by her coordinated sets and roomy tote bags. If you're the kind of traveller who tends to get cold on flights, you're not alone. Alia Bhatt's wardrobe now includes a line-up of warm, yet interesting outerwear (think biker jackets, neon dusters and floral blazers), and Sonam K Ahuja's look has graduated to include several not-so-basic layered ensembles. Her picks include quirky Rheson pullovers and billowing coats. Another actor who never boards a flight without a jacket in hand is Jacqueline Fernandez. Blazers to bombers, she's got them all. Sneakers? Check. Tracks? Check. Jerseys? Check. When it comes to on-the-go ensembles, few do athleisure with as much dedication as Parineeti Chopra, Athiya Shetty and Sonakshi Sinha. One of Chopra's most-loved sporty separates includes a pair of navy blue Adidas track pants, while Shetty prefers ebony tracks that match with just about anything. Of the three, Sinha's the one to follow if you like crazy colours—there's no forgetting the time the actor walked into Mumbai's departures terminal in that UFO-patterned red tracksuit. Breezy dresses aren't just for brunch—they're for extended flights too. For Dia Mirza and Kriti Sanon, midis are almost always winners for long days of travel. Over the past year, we've seen Mirza in countless cotton numbers, and Sanon seems to enjoy sportier picks, often styled with belt bags to give her outfits a millennial-approved update. Another Bollywood lady who's got a great collection of flight-ready dresses: Shraddha Kapoor. One of her best from this year included a patterned khaki number by Nimish Shah. column1: Fashion history 101: The biker jacket’s best celebrity moments
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A rebel classic that transcends style tribes, the biker jacket has been inextricably cool since Irving Schott created the original Perfecto in 1928. Vogue looks back at its most memorable outings on everyone from Marlon Brando to Kate Moss and Deepika Padukone Nothing says laid-back cool quite like a biker jacket—it's hard to find a fashion icon who hasn't capitalised on its cult appeal. Like so many of our most beloved wardrobe staples, the biker has practical beginnings. Before it become synonymous with punks and pop idols, Irving Schott's original 1928 Perfecto motorcycle jacket was intended to be a more functional outerwear option for the Harley-Davidson-riding gangs of New York. Schott's ingenious redesign included an asymmetrical front closure to allow for easier movement and extra layers of insulation, a belted waist for a secure fit and zippers rather than buttons—all of which remain integral elements of the biker in its truest form today. The jacket's connotations of roguish cool made it a natural choice for decades of rebel spirits to come. From on-screen outlaws like Marlon Brando in The Wild One (1953) to the 1960s rockers raging against the mods and 1970s proto-punks such as the Ramones and Debbie Harry, the leather jacket has become an iconic symbol of rock 'n' roll, adopted by everyone from Madonna and George Michael to Rihanna. The fashion world was a little slower to join the party—Yves Saint Laurent's 1960 alligator interpretation for Christian Dior is reported to have been controversial among the senior figures in the house. However, Jean Paul Gaultier, Nicolas Ghesquière, Alexander Wang and Hedi Slimane have since helped to establish the biker jacket as a cult buy that is eternally in vogue. On the streets, the style continues to reign as one of fashion's favourite pieces, regularly worn by models, fashion editors and influencers. It sits pride of place in the off-duty wardrobes of Cindy Crawford (1990s and today), Kate Moss and Deepika Padukone, demonstrating its enduring, effortlessly cool appeal. Whether you choose to wear a classic, cropped or customised take on the biker, its ability to transcend style means it remains fashion's easiest ride. column1: Angela Missoni’s guide to finding your place in the fashion industry
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion “Curiosity is where all creativity begins” 2018 celebrates 65 years of Missoni, and 21 years of Angela Missoni at the helm. Her first few collections with their fitted silhouettes, deep necklines and slick ad campaigns immediately gave Missoni a sexy, bold edge, plunging the knit brand into the heart of the naughties. In 2017, a parade of pink pussy hats took over the Missoni runway—a celebration of female solidarity in honour of the Women's March that was taking place at the same time. Over the years, Angela Missoni has continued to build on the legacy her parents began while fearlessly ushering it into the present. She's managed to not only stay in tune with the zeitgeist, but also with her own aesthetic and vision as a businesswoman. In 2018, the Missonis sold 41.2 per cent stake of their company to a private equity firm, but retained full creative control and the majority stake, even as her daughter Margherita Missoni was appointed creative director of M Missoni—they found a way to navigate through and thrive in a difficult industry and a tricky market. From Angela Missoni, one of the leaders of the fashion industry, here's a step-by-step guide to finding your place here. First of all, go to design or fashion school. If you love fashion, that's great, you now have to figure out which of the hundreds of jobs in the industry, is for you. If you figure that out you can do very well and be very satisfied. Not everybody is a designer. You need to figure out what your talent is and follow that (styling, merchandising, writing, etc) and for this industry to run we need all of this. And, no matter what, just try to follow your passion. Use your time at school to learn how to work as a team; when you start working (even if it's your own thing), you will realise that you cannot build anything alone. So if you're good with working as a team, your professionalism will be very well recognised. And that will help your creativity and you will get to be part of beautiful projects. You cannot judge fashion if you know only the last three collections or the last five years. You have to start from the beginning, and trace the evolution of fashion right from the start. There's a lot of things that can inspire you, not just the works of other designers. You should know who's doing what and why, and who is referencing whom. You admire a designer, figure out who they admire and so on. Knowledge and information are very empowering. When I was teaching at a fashion school in Milan, the first thing I would ask the students to do was to take pictures of anything and everything that intrigued them for a week and present it to the class. They had to show me their work, their world, their interests—I wanted to see how curious they were. Because, curiosity is where all creativity begins. If you have the chance to get into a studio, go for it immediately—this is when you truly start learning. School doesn't prepare you for the many chances and realities of the real thing. Experience is everything. It is a very stressful job, so you need to have the physical and mental capability to deal with the levels of stress. You're putting out work every six months (and with fast fashion, capsule collections etc, even sooner); you are judged every six months. Think of the great sportswomen and men—it's never physical capacity alone, it's mental capability that makes someone a winner. My parents have been revolutionary; they invented something that is rare and unique to them. And they taught me my biggest lesson—to be yourself, and do your own thing; and finally, to never be a follower. To find your own voice, you first have to know yourself. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Cultural and religious reasons may have birthed covered-up fashion, but today the aesthetic has gone to a whole new stylish place, turning the heads of a young generation of cosmopolitan, social media-savvy consumers. Vogue investigates the multi-billion-dollar modest market Batsheva Hay was itching for a project. So, on her birthday two years ago, the Manhattan-based former lawyer decided that she'd gift herself a dress of her own design. “I was like, ‘OK, if I can really customise, then let me just add a different type of sleeve and a different type of shoulder,'” she recalls of her creation, a vintage cotton dress that quickly morphed into an elaborate piece of whimsy. Buoyed by her success—it was, she notes, “cheaper than shopping at Barneys”—she made more. Soon, strangers were stopping her in the subway, curious about her old-fashioned frocks and the matching dresses she stitched for her daughter. One website, an edgy Instagram account and several orders from Japan later, her Orthodox-friendly label Batsheva now shows at New York Fashion Week and was recently stocked by global e-commerce retailer MatchesFashion.com. Batsheva's skyrocketing success signals the way in which modest fashion—once a niche market—has entered mainstream consciousness. No longer dismissed as the dowdy domain of religious folk, this multibillion-dollar industry is being driven by a young and cosmopolitan consumer who demands coverage in accordance with her faith but refuses to skimp on style. It's also been embraced by those who simply prefer an aesthetic that doesn't cater to the male gaze. Even Hollywood stars are dabbling—at the Venice Film Festival, Tilda Swinton wore Haider Ackermann on two occasions, each time sporting a long-sleeved, ankle-swishing silhouette with a ruffled neck that brushed her jawline. “I know some people will think modest fashion is regressive and telling a woman to cover themselves, but I actually feel like the women it appeals to want to wear stuff that's fun and don't have to worry about being a sex object for a man,” says Hay about her designs. As the movement has gained momentum, it's revealed the economic clout of those driving it. Hay's brand caters to a secondary tier of religious women—namely Orthodox Jews and Christians—as well as secular shoppers interested in pieces that can be appreciated for their style and craft. But it's a new generation of Muslim consumers that has emerged as the demographic heavyweights, their modest-fashion spend accounting for $44 billion of the $1.9 trillion global Muslim market. “What's nice about this space is that you've got a loyal audience because they've committed to it for a higher reason,” says Alia Khan, founder and chairwoman of the Dubai-based Islamic Fashion Design Council. “They're not doing it to impress anyone, so there's no passing fancy, there's no fad involved in this. They're first and foremost doing this because of their values and belief set, which are going to stay with them for life.” Hay's own journey from Jewish secularism to observance began when she started dating her now-husband, fashion photographer Alexei Hay, who had already embarked on his own foray into Orthodox Judaism. Together, they began to observe Shabbat and keep a kosher household, deftly straddling two worlds: New York's highly secular fashion scene and a new, spiritual realm of “super intense” Friday-night dinners with her husband's rabbi and his 14 children. Inspired by outfits she spies at religious weddings, Hay designs her collections with tzniut—the Hebrew word for modesty applied to Jewish women's rules of dress—in mind. The dresses might look better next to a 19th-century covered wagon, but they sport the high necklines, low hemlines and long sleeves required by Orthodox Judaism. “Honestly, I'm designing for myself,” Hay says with a shrug, pointing out that a childhood diet of thrift-store finds and Laura Ashley bed sheets has translated into an ultra-feminine aesthetic that favours puffed shoulders, extravagantly ruffled collars, candy-coloured taffeta and loud floral prints. “The majority of it really is totally modest, but it doesn't freak me out if there are one or two things that aren't.” For Khan, this proliferation of new styling is proof of the industry's burgeoning innovation. She explains that Muslim women worldwide tend to follow the same Islamic principles of propriety—full sleeves, ankle length, no cleavage, no sheer fabrics—but it's their variance in interpretation and execution that proves exciting. An Iranian woman in Tehran might favour a loosely draped headscarf matched to her trousers and jacket; her counterparts in the Gulf often have a fondness for flowing abayas that fuse Western influences with Eastern style. Even within one country, such as Saudi Arabia, there can be regional variations in the style of abaya sported. Far from being a monolith demographic, the Muslim consumer is as diverse in her needs as any other consumer group. The success of brands rests on their ability to recognise and cater to that. “What we're seeing now is that the boundaries are disappearing and there are no rules as long as the general expectation of modesty is met by the consumer's demand,” Khan says. “The rest of it is really a great playground for these designers to come up with some fabulous, disruptive ideas.” In a study into the behavioural habits of modest fashion consumers, Romana Mirza, a senior researcher at the Islamic Fashion Design Council, found them to be “savvy” shoppers with established and thoughtful opinions on brands. “The modest fashion consumer shops luxury, mainstream and modest fashion brands to fulfil their demand in this space,” she says. But despite their population size and spending power, they still feel desperately underserved by both bricks-and-mortar stores and online retailers. International brands, urges Mirza, must listen to this “insightful, articulate and attentive consumer”—after all, it's their needs that will continue to take the driving seat in shaping this market. In recent years, Western brands have made tentative attempts to court them. Every season, high-street retailer Mango releases modest-friendly collections of tunics, kaftans and maxi-dresses, and late last year, Nike announced the release of a high-performance hijab. In April, Net-A-Porter promoted capsule collections designed specifically for Ramadan by brands including Oscar de la Renta and Jenny Packham; the website also includes ‘modest' as a category within its clothing menu, filtering all womenswear that fits the bill aesthetically, regardless of whether it was designed expressly for the modest market. A shift towards inclusion can also be seen with the advent of hijabi supermodels like Ikram Abdi Omar, who walked the catwalk for Molly Goddard at London Fashion Week, and Somali-American model Halima Aden, whose runway shows have included Max Mara, Alberta Ferretti, and Kanye West's Yeezy label. This May, Aden made headlines as the first hijab-wearing supermodel to pose on the cover of British Vogue. In 2017, Algerian financier Ghizlan Guenez decided to launch luxury e-commerce site The Modist after noticing the dearth of options for modest-minded women like herself. She was convinced of the business's viability—while considered a niche offering, The Modist's nondenominational approach means it appeals to women across different faiths, age groups, sizes and cultures. “It doesn't matter to us what the reason for dressing modestly is. All we care about is offering women fashion and functionality in an elevated experience,” she says. “Our woman is bold in her fashion choices and we love that because it smashes all stereotypes around modesty and it being dull and boring,” continues Guenez, as she scrolls through the site's current curation of more than 180 brands, including avant-garde favourites such as Haider Ackermann. Guenez—who grew up surrounded by modestly dressed women—is particular about catering to their needs. Sleeve lengths and fabric opacity are all taken into consideration. Sometimes her team will work with designers to customise pieces specifically for the modest dresser, like an exclusive party-wear capsule collection by Petar Petrov that launches in November to correspond with the festive season. “Ultimately, we want every woman globally who struggles with dressing modestly to see us as her go-to platform,” she says. Yet despite the recent publicity surrounding modest fashion, to claim it as a new trend would be to overlook the many women who have clothed themselves like this for millennia. “The truth of it is that modest fashion has been around since the beginning of time,” says Khan, exasperated at the notion that covering up is anything new. And it's not that the number of modest dressers has increased so much as that we're finally noticing it. So what's changed? The intersection between a rapidly growing and remarkably youthful Muslim population of consumers (their global median age, in 2015, was 24) and social-media technology has enabled a wave of influencers, designers and consumers to broadcast their lifestyle to a like-minded audience. “I think platforms like Instagram and Facebook have enabled a dialogue to take place among women who may not have had that chance in the past and it has enabled their voices to be heard,” says Guenez. “A modest dresser in Indonesia is now able to connect with a modest dresser in New York and see how much they share in common in terms of their fashion and lifestyle choices, and with that comes a movement that started on these platforms and is translating to other aspects of life.” While social media has thrust modest fashion into the international limelight, the way these platforms are being utilised is often accompanied with a raised eyebrow. Susan Sabet, an influential Egyptian fashion magazine publisher and founder of Cairo's Fashion Nights (a seasonal city-wide shopping event), recently joined the executive committee of Fashion Trust Arabia, an annual prize initiative that will nurture regional design talent. Sabet has witnessed first-hand the powerful impact of social media for emerging designers: it gains them a fanbase which, in turn, convinces retailers to stock them. But as she points out, many in conservative Middle Eastern Islamic societies see an inherent contradiction between the religious symbolism of modest clothing and the propriety of influencers who model their outfits to a mass following. “The Koran states that [believers] should lower their gaze and be modest,” she says. “When you have a lot of social media influencers who are basically posing on social media with millions of followers, and are not lowering their gaze, a lot of people see this as a bit controversial. This has people saying, ‘Is this right? Is this really a modest person at the end of the day?'” One such tastemaker is Ascia, a Kuwaiti-American Instagram star whose 2.4 million followers enjoy her propensity for streetwear-infused style, neatly wrapped turbans and shoulder-skimming statement earrings. She launched her account in 2012, frustrated by the lack of women who “looked like her” online. As Instagram ascended, so did her visibility. Now Ascia heads up an empire—including a Korean-inspired beauty line and a range of baby slings—that has been built on a willingness to share her deeply personal approach to blending fashion and faith. As such, she is highly attuned to the religious and cultural sensitivities that come with a public platform. Although Muslim, she is careful to avoid referring to herself as a hijabi in deference to the stricter dress codes observed by other women. Instead, she prefers to identify under the broader “modest space” umbrella. “My brand has evolved with my transition and my own understandings of where I'm at with my relationship with God and where I'm at with my relationship with my dress sense and my own body,” she explains. Some days, that means Ascia wakes up with a hankering for longer hemlines; other days she's comfortable in a pair of jeans and an oversized top. Her own varying approach to fashion mirrors the vast—and vastly overlooked—possibilities of modest dressing. “For so many years, we've been written off,” she says. “No one catered to our dress sense, no one thought about us as an entity.” Slowly, with the increased presence of women like her in the media, she sees that attitude changing. “Just fit us in, make space at the table. That's really what we want.” View Gallery 20 Photos Once a niche segment, modest fashion is now bringing in the big bucks Fashion Fashion Wellness © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This new store in Bengaluru highlights Mewar’s dabu work
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We have all the details for you Reviving traditional Indian crafts is the mood of the moment, but it's something designer Alka Sharma has been passionate about ever since she graduated from the Indian Institute of Crafts and Design, Jaipur with a specialisation in textile studies in 2003. After spending the next few years laying a strong foundation, she launched Aavaran in 2011. The label takes Mewar's dabu mud-resist, hand-dyed and hand block prints and makes them contemporary with its signature range of clothing, home furnishings and accessories. The Udaipur-based brand now forays out its home state with a 1,000sqft store in Bengaluru's heritage art deco building, Ambara, overlooking the picturesque Ulsoor Lake. “I launched Aavaran not just to sustain and revive this traditional textile craft but also to provide economic empowerment to the indigenous craftsmen of the region. We give this heritage craft a modern spin with our intricate dabu printing, use of handwoven fabrics, and indigo and natural dye-based collections. All our patterns and motifs are extremely well-researched,” explains Sharma. The Bengaluru store will house silk and cotton saris, kurtas, dupattas, menswear and kidswear. Patrons can also shop for Aavaran's popular bed linen, tableware, cushion covers, quilts and kitchen accessories. The brand's zero waste policy has led to the creation of a special range of décor accents like durries, coin bags, quilts, poltis, jewellery, juttis and gift items, that Sharma points out have become extremely sought-after. Also on offer will be Aavaran's festive collection ‘Neem e Jaal', their very first embroidered line. “We have also developed a range called Ayurvastra, which is steeped in Ayurvedic teachings on medicines, health and healing. We use organic cotton treated with a precise combination of herbs and oil to promote health and help cure ailments. It's just what one needs to relieve their body of stress in today's fast-paced times,” signs off Sharma. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In a sea of people dressed in cocktail attire, Kiran’s uniform left a unique mark on all who attended the event At the Vogue Women Of The Year 2018, Usha Kiran was awarded with the ‘Young Achiever Of The Year' award for her exemplary work—Kiran, at 28, is the youngest female CRPF officer to be a part of COBRA, and is currently serving the volatile region of Bastar in Chhattisgarh. When Janhvi Kapoor and Ishaan Khattar presented the award to Usha Kiran, it was met with  thundering applause. “This award I would like to say this is not just to Usha Kiran, it's for every soldier, every force personal who are literally putting in their blood and sweat to maintain peace and harmony in the country,” said the officer on receiving the award. “And thank you CRPF because this wouldn't be a reality without you. Thank you, Vogue India, once again for recognising the efforts of the uniform.” Host Karan Johar promptly acknowledged Kiran's attire and commented saying, “That's probably the best red carpet look of all-time.” Clothing can be seen as an extension of one's personality, their aesthetic or as a means by which to convey a stronger message. However, when it comes to the armed forced, the uniform is not merely an equalising dress code, it is a sign of pride, of one's achievements and significant of their duty for the country. In a sea of people dressed in cocktail attire, Kiran's uniform left a unique mark. column1: How much do you know about Karl Lagerfeld’s journey?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The original boundary-breaking fashion designer tells all Karl Lagerfeld might be the original boundary-breaking fashion designer. Raised in bourgeois comfort in Hamburg, he set off for Paris and Pierre Balmain's studio when he was a teenager and his work caught the attention of the couturier. Soon bored at Balmain, he left to become the head designer at the staid house of Jean Patou, but he was soon bored there, too, and, disillusioned with the world of haute couture, left for Rome to study his favourite composer, Bellini. In 1965, however, he met the quintet of formidable Fendi sisters: By his own estimate, he has since travelled to Rome 800 times. In 1982, Alain Wertheimer hired Lagerfeld to revamp Chanel. “When I came to Chanel, I said to Mr Wertheimer, ‘Let's make a pact, like Faust with the Devil,'” Lagerfeld says. “But we don't know who is the Devil and who is Faust.” In 1992, when the supremely erudite Rosamond Bernier went to call on Lagerfeld, she noted that the designer owned seven houses in four countries, each furnished with museum-quality antiques, state-of-the-art contemporary commissions, and a quarter of a million books. Now he lives with his beloved cat, Choupette, surrounded by the tools of his work and food for his mind. “I have so much to do that I'm not so much for travelling anymore,” Lagerfeld says. “For Chanel alone I do 10 collections, and I do it all myself, all the sketches.” Those Chanel projects include showcasing the Métiers d'Art collections around the world, drawing attention to the skills of the great fashion fournisseurs that Chanel has acquired to ensure their survival—among them the embroidery house of Lesage, the feather-and-flower establishment of Lemarié, shoemakers Massaro and milliner Maison Michel—and initiating the trend for exotic destination presentations. After forays to Mumbai, Salzburg, Dubai, Seoul, Havana, Singapore and Linlithgow, in Scotland, Lagerfeld staged a triumphant homecoming in Hamburg last year. Savagely unsentimental, relentlessly un-nostalgic, he remains, in his ninth decade, fuelled by his insatiable curiosity and a passion for the present and the future. “I have a strong survival instinct,” he says. column1: Which designer will Priyanka Chopra pick for her wedding looks?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We’re popping the big question Considering her multi-hyphenate status, you can safely expect Priyanka Chopra and Nick Jonas' upcoming nuptials to take over your social media feed with speculation, for the foreseeable future. Over the course of the past one year, the duo made headlines almost every other day with new developments of their then-budding relationship, and almost broke Instagram with images of a beautiful (and completely unexpected) roka ceremony in Mumbai. Most recently, Chopra and Jonas were spotted scouting wedding locations in the rustic locale of Jodhpur. Even as we await word on the final wedding date, rumours are flying fast about which designer will be the chosen one for the Quantico actor's grand wedding. Given her track record of bringing the internet to a grinding halt with her fashion outings (her Zuhair Murad gown at Academy Awards 2016 was Google's most-searched outfit), it stands to reason that the superstar will be choosing her bridal designer with care. With the entire roster of Indian and international designers at her fingertips, here are the ones that are most likely to make the cut. Chopra's roka ceremony had her stepping out in a crisp canary anarkali suit with gota work by the designer duo, and she even sported one of their showstopper red saris at the big Ambani engagement last year—which was also the very first event that the actor attended with Jonas as a couple. Not one to play it safe, her unique vision of OTT elegance is sure to be catered to by the couturiers who pride themselves on their larger-than-life silhouettes and ornate embroideries. Chopra and Malhotra have served up countless winning looks over the years, most recently at Isha Ambani's engagement which saw her and beau, Jonas, in couture ensembles by the designer. Malhotra understands decadent glamour like few others in the country do, and knows just how to deliver a jaw-dropping look—and possibly another prime spot on Google's most searched list. If Anushka Sharma's all-Sabyasachi nuptials weren't proof enough of the fact that the couturier is Bollywood's favourite for bridal wear, maybe this will convince you—rumours say that Deepika Padukone is likely to wear her go-to designer for the big day as well. Chopra also has a relationship with Sabyasachi that goes way back, and the Baywatch actor has taken his ensembles with her to international events as well. Third time could definitely be the charm, with the couturier's luxe creations thriving in their natural habitat—the palatial panorama of Rajasthan. The 34-year-old may have gone traditional with her choice of venue, but does that mean it is too late to rule out a white wedding? Given that the actor famously teamed up with Ralph Lauren for an internet-breaking trench coat-gown at the Met Gala 2017, it's clear that she knows exactly where to look to find a winning number for her big day—in case she chooses to walk down the aisle instead of to the mandap. They have history together, of the red carpet dominance kind. Chopra followed up her viral Zuhair Murad outing at the Academy Awards 2016 with a structured geometric number the next year from British faves, Tamara Ralph and Michael Russo. The designer duo know their way around frothy couture concoctions, and make a no-brainer choice for a highly-touted celebrity shindig. From Miranda Kerr to Chiara Ferragni, the couture house has dressed some of the most iconic brides, and Chopra's name would be a fitting addition to the club—especially considering the waves that they made together when she wore a princess-perfect sequinned number to her close friend Meghan Markle's royal wedding reception. column1: Your guide to looking beyond diamond jewellery for your next cocktail do
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Leave your solitaires behind for a dash of emeralds and rubies Let's face it; we are all at a loss when it comes to picking the right jewellery for an evening of fun cocktails and dancing. You've picked out the perfect dress or sari for the evening, but you have no idea how to accessorise your look with jewellery. Some of us tend to opt for an easy way out of this dilemma with diamonds. Whether you're prepping for a big fat Indian sangeet, your best friend's birthday celebration, a business mixer or are just looking for an excuse to flaunt your latest designer number, we've put together a guide to urge you to skip the basic sparklers for jewellery pieces that feature brighter hues. Want to catch eyeballs when you raise your glass of champagne for a toast? Replace the tennis bracelet that you wear for every occasion with a studded emerald cuff from Diacolor, or a subtle ruby bracelet by Jet Gems set with Gemfields Mozambican rubies. For a high-octane cocktail sangeet or a Diwali party, ditch your traditional diamonds for a livelier set of chandelier earrings like the Fabergé chandelier emerald earrings. And considering solitaire rings can often look very conventional, you can give them a miss by opting for a heritage emerald ring to create a signature style. Choosing the right earrings can often be tricky affair. Skip your favourite diamond studs and go for a ruby encrusted pair of floral studs instead to add a pop of colour to your cocktail look. For a glamorous evening, amp your outfit up with a set of danglers in emeralds or rubies in geometrical shapes to accentuate your face structure. Love circular or oval-shaped earrings? The Federica Rettore emerald and gold danglers will make you stand out in the party crowd. And if you're biased towards the tear-drop shape, you can accessorise with a pair of statement teardrop earrings by Rosentiques, set in a deep shape of emeralds—these go with both traditional as well as contemporary choices of clothing. column1: Maria Grazia Chiuri talks about femininity at Jade’s 10-year celebration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And reveals what she loves about India The fact that Maria Grazia Chiuri, artistic director Dior is in India, is all over Instagram. Chiuri is in the country for numerous reasons, but her presence at Jade's 10-year celebrations last night speaks of her two-decade long friendship with the founders of the brand. Legend has it Chiuri has been working with Chanakya, the export house owned by the family since her days at Fendi. Thrilled to be a part of the celebrations with founders and sisters-in-law Karishma Swali and Monica Shah, the artistic director of Dior talked about the importance of women supporting women. The evening started with a walk through of 100 archival pieces from Shah and Swali's private collection, showcasing exemplary craftsmanship from different decades. From Chinese silk tapestries to hand-beaded bags from France, the archive highlighted skill and visual details from different parts of the world. After cocktails, guests were ushered to the show area to witness the unveiling of Jade's special edit titled ‘Oneness'. After a stunning dance performance by Padma Shri awardee Astad Deboo, models walked out in Jade's vision of contemporary couture. Intricately embroidered tulle skirts paired with dainty blouses, gowns and lehengas dominated the runway. Jacqueline Fernandez brought the show to a close, and prominent personalities like Ananya Birla, Roohi and Chetan Jaikishan, Gayatri Rangachari Shah, Farah Oomerbhoy, Chhaya Momaya and Sangita Jindal were amongst those seen at the show. Before the spectacle, Vogue got in conversation with Maria Grazia Chiuri about the language of colours in India, the importance of female leadership and what she will take back from this trip. Excerpts below. Oh, I really love their archive because while it speaks about the past, I think that they are aspiring to make something for the future. I am very fascinated by them. I met them when I was very young and we very happy to work with them because they spoke very good Italian. You can tell my English is not so good, and so it was easy to start working with them and to make something together. This was many many, many, many, many years ago. We were all kids in some way. It was the perfect coming together of my creativity and their incredible passion for this kind of work. Oh, I am really happy to be here. I really love India. I love there is a huge tradition of craftsmanship, which is also very close with my past, because in some way even in Italy we value tradition. I really appreciate that. I am so lucky to work with such a huge brand like Dior, which has a huge tradition in craftsmanship and couture, and so I think all this is very important to me because it is my passion. I think India is a country with many contradictions, but at the same you can see that all the contradictions can live together. I think fashion has to think about that. You also have to leave a good message for the future, and that it is possible to live also with many contradictions. I think it's important to support other women [and] to care about other women. I am very proud to be here to support them. I think it is very important to speak about what is it to be a woman, [and] the idea of a sisterhood in some way is really important to me. I really love the work that they have started in India, where it is a male dominated ambience. So, in some way I think we are so lucky—me, Karishma and Monica—that we can give something back to the community. We talk about a new femininity. Dior is a feminine brand and it is important to speak about that. Too much. I would like to make many things, but I would have to decide the priority. The important thing for me is the colour, because I think here is a colourful world and sometimes, we forget the power of colour because we live so fast, especially in Europe. Here, you will see that the colour gives you good energy. It is a language of colour and so probably I want to test that in the future. I think Dior is a worldwide brand, so it is very important that our language is really global. I think we have to be proud about our heritage. We are in any case a French brand, but at the same time we speak with words from all worlds, so we have to be global too. column1: Vogue Wedding Studio spotlights bridal trends at the Hyatt Regency, Delhi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How to shop for your big day When it comes to Indian bridal couture, designer Tarun Tahiliani has carved an exceptional niche for himself, what with his pieces finding favour with brides, grooms and wedding-goers across the spectrum. Considering this, Vogue India's senior fashion editor Priyanka Kapadia helmed a sartorial session together with Tarun Tahiliani and Kotawala Jewellers for the Vogue Wedding Studio this year, where she used some of the designer's prized pieces to shine the spotlight on the most-coveted trends of the fast-approaching wedding season. The immersive event took place at The Mansion at Hyatt Regency Delhi, and had a special wedding menu created for it too. Guests were treated to delicacies such as Peking Duck, Penne All'Arrabbiata and Chaap Taazdar. The open show kitchens offer diners a theatrical experience, where they can watch their meal being prepared by skilful chefs. Modelled around the concept of a decadent house, the space features the Oval Room and Regency Ballroom on the ground level, living rooms on the second level and an outdoor garden. The idea was to offer guests an experience combining innovative food and beverage concepts at the venue. The Oval Room at The Mansion is Delhi's first event space featuring dramatic show kitchens. So what are the bridal trends you need to know about this season? Scroll on to find out. Kapadia brought the newest wedding must-have to the fore—the ‘hero blouse'. “Bejewelled, embellished and simply beautiful, the hero blouse is getting all the attention this season,” she said. If you're wondering why, it's most likely because this one can be effortlessly paired with a breezy, lightweight lehenga, thus putting an end to the plight of the countless brides who simply cannot bear the weight of a heavy ethnic number. Don't know how to accessorise the piece? Kapadia is of the opinion that with a blouse like this one, layered necklaces work quite well. No bridal ensemble is ever complete without a hint of red in it, a colour which remains on top of bridal trends whether styled traditionally, or peppered with new-age elements. “Wear it from head-to-toe for a contemporary finish, and experiment with different types of jewellery for a more customised look,” explains Kapadia. The floral print is held dear by most brides we know, and this season, it has been reinterpreted in 3D. A pastel palette forms the perfect backdrop for these intricate floral details, which have taken over bigger motifs this time around. The icy blue hue, which has been hailed as the colour of the season, found a place in Kapadia's list. “Icy blue is a refreshing break from the usual peach and pastel pink shades. Tone-on-tone embroidery gives it a fresh spin, whereas diamonds or stones of a similar hue lend it maximum impact,” she elaborates. Also in store was counsel for the oftentimes-ignored groom. Kapadia proclaimed salmon pink—paired with pale neutrals—as the perfect pick for daytime weddings. For a vintage appeal, a mix of different fabrics, accessories and muted embellishments can be put to use. But what about all the other wedding ceremonies you have to dress up for? The sangeet and the receptions, and everything that is organised for when the sun goes down? For the after-hours, Kapadia explains that it is all about playing with fabrics and silhouettes. Think black and burgundy paired with brocades and velvets. Catch up on everything that happened at the glamorous event now. column1: Here’s what you can expect from Gaurav Gupta’s new flagship in Delhi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Flying mannequins, an in-house museum and sculptures that serve as clothing racks—at Gaurav Gupta’s new store in the capital, no fantasy is too far-fetched At a time when fashion is steadily making its way to our fingertips, how do you keep the brick-and-mortar experience exciting? For Gaurav Gupta, the answer lies in a 5,000sqft atelier that alludes to an iconic Charles Dickens adaptation and on occasion doubles up as a venue for opera performances. “It's not a store but a surreal maze that celebrates architecture, sculpture and beauty. I live in a different world in my head and I wanted to share that with everyone,” says Gupta of the fitting home to his avant-garde designs. The designer gives Vogue a glimpse of what's in store. “Metal swan gates lead you to a dreamy space, reminiscent of my favourite scenes in Great Expectations (1998). From the garden to the Romanesque cobbled fountain, I've recreated what I loved most. At the entrance is an age-old Siris tree encased in glass.” “Expect magic, fantasy and Surrealism in each of the five rooms. While the Prism room is made of mirrors with light bouncing off all sides, the Sculpt room is a mini museum for our iconic sculptural garments collected over the last decade or so. Also on offer is a space dedicated to couture and customisation.” “At any given time, there'll be at least 1,000m of organza in the store.” “Currently, there are nearly 23 racks and 220 hangers. Each rack is a metal sculpture, and the mannequins take various forms—flying, dancing or sitting.” “The walls come adorned with mini mural sculptures inspired by elements that have long defined my work. Think flying angels, wings, fantasy creatures, birds and trees.” “The space was created with Studio Lotus. The conceptualisation alone took over two months.” “All plastic used is bio-degradable fruit plastic. column1: Looking for something to inspire your next jewellery buy? Give art a try
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We looked at some of the most iconic paintings in the world to amp up your festive wardrobe Paintings often hold an iconic position in art, culture and history. So much so that they have, time and again, also inspired statement jewellery designs. From regal portraits that have aristocratic women decked in pearls and precious stones to a much more abstract version by Austrian symbolist painter, Gustav Klimt, jewellery pieces have made their presence felt in oil-on-canvas through various art movements. The ornamental baroque style, in particular, is also highly influential in merging the two art forms of painting and jewellery-making. Ever thought of channelling a renaissance woman's elegant taste in jewels? Or taking cues from details in modernist paintings? Scroll on for our picks of the best jewellery designs to help you recreate the grace that is a norm in paintings. This portrait of the Dutch Countess, Anna Illyeshazy from 1840, is a lesson in the art of stacking your bracelets. Take cues from this one to recreate your own totem pole of arm candy. You can also mix your heirloom cuffs with the modern, embellished bangles to get the same effect. Buy now: Bracelet, Rewind Vintage Affairs Buy now: Bangle, Christian Dior Vintage Buy now: Bangle, Chanel Vintage Chokers are always an excellent way to draw attention to your face and accentuate your neck at the same time. Let Gustav Klimt's biblical painting of Judith serve an inspiration for your next collar necklace, which will make for a great accessory option for the upcoming Diwali festivities. Buy now: Choker, Rebecca De Ravenel Earring fact 101—chandbaalis can be a 24/7 look. A minimalist can always team it up with a classic collared shirt or a day dress, and you can never go wrong with pairing them with your ethnic best for a Diwali card party or a wedding. Still not convinced? Mexican surrealist Frida Kahlo's portrait by Robert Montenegro is proof that earrings of this design are timeless pieces. Buy now: Earrings, Jaipur Gems It is a well-known fact that a pearl necklace is oblivious to trend cycles. From the era of modern renaissance to now, they're extensively seen on aristocratic portraits across various cultures and countries. If a pearl necklace with a renaissance pendant serves your aesthetic, you can recreate the looks keeping Pieter de Kempeneer's ‘Portrait of A Lady' in mind—layered with a few other long chains in gold. Or let Johannes Vermeer's masterpiece, ‘Girl with A Pearl Earring', serve as an inspiration for keeping it simple, yet elegant with a pair of single pearl (or faux pearl) earrings. Buy now: Earrings, Simone Rocha Highly ornamental, the Rococo or late-baroque style is easiest to adopt—especially if you are looking to wear a single piece of design with a contemporary twist. Spanish painter Vicente Lopez's oil-on-canvas details the bracelet to perfection, and offers jewellery inspiration for women across all ages. Don't shy away from wearing your mother's navratna bracelet to get this look. And if you want to keep it casual, you can always go for a signature Roxanne Assoulin design. column1: Here’s why you should ditch the bridal lehenga for a designer sari
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We asked four couturiers to weigh in Today, the modern Indian bride is ploughing deeper into her roots while curating her bridal repertoire, and that's a big win for the sari. The time-honoured quintessential Indian drape is a classic pick you can't go wrong with, but it's often overshadowed by the ubiquitous popularity of lehengas, especially when it comes to brides. But changing times also lead to a change in sartorial preferences. The sari is no longer an afterthought reserved just for the trousseau or that one-off pre-wedding function—it is now a strong contender for key wedding day looks. Take Anushka Sharma and Sagarika Ghatge for instance. Both chose red Sabyasachi saris for their reception and civil ceremony respectively. While the addition of the designer sari as a bridal wear option for one of the many ceremonies of a wedding celebration is great, what about the pheras? Can you wear a designer sari for your walk around the ceremonial fire too? Vogue asks the experts. Latha Puttanna feels that nothing quite beats the elegance and grandeur of a traditional wedding sari. “While lehengas, dhotis and other experimental silhouettes are on-trend, the sari is a classic. It will never go out of style.” She advises brides to factor in their personality and comfort when making the final choice. “I recommend pinning the pallu to the shoulder, and finishing the ensemble with a kamarbandh to hold everything in place and allow easy mobility. The traditional Maharashtrian drape is also very slimming and comfortable,” she adds. Naina Jain advocates getting inventive with the drape as well. The double pallu drape is her favourite. “Drape two saris together on an underskirt for a look that's not just heavy, but also the perfect blend of traditional and modern.” Gaurang Shah, on the other hand, would have brides play with the hues of their sari. Bridal red is no longer the only acceptable choice for brides. Pastel pink, beige, pistachio green, lilac, sea blue, and deeper tones of wine red, bottle green and peacock blue are Shah's top picks. Benarasi and Kanjeevaram weaves, as well as organza saris with a mix of silver and gold zari work, are styles the bride just cannot go wrong in. “Traditions have changed over time, but the grace of a sari remains unchallenged even today. Every state has its own draping style and weave. Choose the style where your heart and roots belong.” Saris are a fitting outfit for the plethora of pre-wedding events that lead up to a wedding as well. A dramatic ruffled version with a cape for the welcome dinner or an exquisite hand-me-down from your grandmother for a puja, the options are many and varied. Gaurav Jai Gupta of Akaaro too feels that saris lend themselves to every function on the Indian wedding calendar, as long as the bride ensures that its visual appeal complements the event in question. For instance, a graphic metallic sari is the ideal choice for the vibe of a cocktail party. The sari's traditional core, coupled with its flexibility to be draped in versatile ways, makes it Shah's go-to suggestion for brides for their various events. “You can mould it to accentuate your personality and body type with ease. Among my favourites is Maharani Chimnabai of Baroda's signature nauvari drape. I suggest wearing it with a long jacket blouse. You can also drape your sari like a gown, reminiscent of the style attributed to Suniti Devi, Maharani of Cooch Behar.” Puttanna feels that the blouse is the easiest way to update the sari based on the event. “Pair your traditional sari with something modern, such as a monochrome crop top or a bold off-shoulder blouse. You can even repurpose your old sari into a lehenga, an evening gown, or a statement dupatta to wear with anakalis and kurtas after your wedding.” Jain advises brides to combine their saris with lehengas for their festivities to add drama to their repertoire, and also because both can be used as separates down the line too. Use the sari as a statement-making dupatta in weaves inspired by West Bengal, Maharashtra and Gujarat. column1: Take a walk inside Rahul Mishra’s spanking new Mumbai flagship
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From couture to ready-to-wear, all under one roof Rahul Mishra is one of those rare homegrown names who is as relevant in India as he is overseas. Fresh after showcasing at Lotus Make-up India Fashion Week and Paris Fashion Week, the designer is showing no signs of slowing down. The latest from him? Mishra has opened the doors to his new flagship store in Mumbai's plush Kala Ghoda district. Nestled among other high-end designer stores like ASAL by Abu Sandeep, Ritu Kumar and Gaurav Gupta, is Mishra's vision in brick and mortar. “It has always been my dream to open a flagship store in Kala Ghoda. When I worked with Animesh Nayak of Open Sky Architects on the project, we wanted to create a space that carried the vibe of Kala Ghoda into our store,” said the designer. Sure enough, in an ostensibly austere setup, the designer has displayed his finest work. “The idea was to create a grey cemented cuboid with accents of copper and wood, to give a very vintage feel of something that is old yet very precious,” Mishra explains. But it's not all concrete and clean lines—the designer has introduced a sense of lightness to the store by way of plants and natural light. Inspired by the lanes of Kala Ghoda, the store has corners that the designer wants the shoppers to discover as they browse through his work. The store introduces customers to Mishra's signature couture collections, moving into lighter Indian ethnic wear and then onto ready-to-wear. “We wanted to explore the room structure, which is typically old-Mumbai style, and enhance it, while still retaining the original aesthetic by creating a loft ceiling. The minimalism and work-in-progress feeling of the grey cement texturing which runs from floor to wall, makes it almost like an art gallery, canvas-like space for our clothes where every garment is able to stand out as its own art piece,” he concludes.
