column1: Decoding the Metropolitan Museum of Art Costume Institute’s next theme
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The famed fashion institute presents “Camp: Notes on Fashion” for its spring 2019 exhibition This is the moment of the great unveiling: The Metropolitan Museum of Art Costume Institute's spring 2019 exhibition will be “Camp: Notes on Fashion” (May 9 through September 8, 2019). Andrew Bolton, Wendy Yu Curator in Charge of the Costume Institute, has framed the exhibition around Susan Sontag's seminal 1964 essay “Notes on ‘Camp,' ” which posited different ways in which the concept could be construed. Bolton explains that he found Sontag's writings—in a nutshell, she argued that camp is the “love of the unnatural: of artifice and exaggeration... style at the expense of content... the triumph of the epicene style”—so timely with what we are going through culturally and politically that, “I felt it would have a lot of cultural resonance.” Sontag found camp, for instance, in Busby Berkeley movies and in the he-man actor Victor Mature, in Mae West and General de Gaulle, in Swan Lake, Flash Gordon comics, Caravaggio, chinoiserie, and the entirety of the Art Nouveau movement. “Camp taste has an affinity for certain arts rather than others,” she noted. “Clothes, furniture, all the elements of visual decor, for instance, make up a large part of Camp.” Camp, as Bolton notes, “has become increasingly more mainstream in its pluralities—political camp, queer camp, Pop camp, the conflation of high and low, the idea that there is no such thing as originality.” Camp, he continues, has been described as style without content. “But I think you've got to be incredibly sophisticated to understand camp—look at Yves Saint Laurent and Marc Jacobs.” The exhibition, which will be presented in the Met Fifth Avenue's Iris and B. Gerald Cantor Exhibition Hall, is made possible by Gucci. For Gucci's creative director Alessandro Michele, Sontag's essay “perfectly expresses what camp truly means to me: the unique ability of combining high art and pop culture.” No one growing up on a diet of Italian television and pop stars such as Mina, Patty Pravo and Raffaella Carrà in the 1980s could be a stranger to the concept of camp, which Bolton also points out embraces elements that include “irony, humour, parody, pastiche, artifice, theatricality, excess, extravagance, nostalgia, and exaggeration”—all of which can, by turns, be discovered in Michele's playful Gucci oeuvre. As the Metropolitan's director Max Hollein notes, “camp's disruptive nature and subversion of modern aesthetic values has often been trivialised, but this exhibition will reveal its profound influence on both high art and popular culture.” Bolton has traced the word itself back to the French verb se camper, meaning to strike an exaggerated pose, and its origins in the flamboyant posturing of the French court under Louis XIV. The Sun King himself consolidated his power by compelling the French nobility to abandon their country strongholds and to gather at Versailles, the glittering showplace that he had built a suitable distance from Paris, where the elaborate protocol and demands of dress forced them to squander vast sums literally to keep up appearances. The king ordered elaborate court ballets that required complex costuming, and established complex faux military camp cities made from canvas in which he and his courtiers paraded in yet more lavish ensembles. At Versailles, everything was pose and performance. Louis XIV's effeminate brother Philippe I, duc d'Orléans, meanwhile, who was deliberately raised in such a way that he would never prove a threat to his brother's rule (as many testosterone-charged siblings had been in France's belligerent history), was in many ways the paradigm of camp. A dance manual of the period records the king's stately dance steps as well as his brother's own extravagantly bold movements. Monsieur, as Philippe was formally known, was obsessed with clothing and jewellery, besotted with his pretty male favourites, and disinterested in his second wife, the plain-looking, plain-speaking German-born Princess Elizabeth Charlotte, Madame Palatine (known as Liselotte), who has thankfully left us her unvarnished memoirs of court life and the “flibbertigibbet” to whom she was married. Monsieur managed to sire several children, with the aid, as his wife drolly noted, of “rosaries and holy medals draped in the appropriate places to perform the necessary act.” Bolton is including a Roman sculpture of a young Hercules from the museum's collection in his exhibition to illustrate the beau ideal of the classical pose—contrapposto, hand on hip—that became the default aristocratic stance in Versailles, as practiced by the king himself in a 1701 swagger portrait by Hyacinthe Rigaud that depicts him in his magnificently camp coronation robes, his calves set off by white silk stockings and his white shoes with high red heels. (Bolton will include a rare extant pair of these shoes, from the collection of Boston's Museum of Fine Arts, in the exhibition). Aristocratic Italians, meanwhile, adopted the idea of sprezzatura, or studied nonchalance, that became the attitude favoured by the influential taste-making dandies of early-19th-century England. For Bolton, the first mention of camp appears to have been in a letter dated 1869, sent by Lord Arthur Clinton to his lover Frederick Park, a cross-dresser known as Fanny. “My campish undertakings are not at present meeting with the success they deserve,” Lord Clinton notes. “Whatever I do seems to get me into hot water.” Fanny and his partner in cross-dressing, Ernest Bolton (known as Stella), were indeed sent to the courts for gross indecency but ultimately cleared of wrongdoing, to the delight of the crowds. Their story—documented in Neil McKenna's riveting 2013 book Fanny and Stella—inspired Erdem Moralioglu so much that he based his recent Spring 2019 collection on them, including trans beauties in his runway casting. Oscar Wilde built his career on camp posturing. His epigrams, for instance —“One should either be a work of art, or wear a work of art”—are the essence of camp. But after his terrible fall from grace (beautifully documented in Rupert Everett's new movie The Happy Prince), these attitudes were rendered suspect and forced underground. A 1909 book of Victorian slang explicitly describes camp as “actions and gestures of exaggerated emphasis used chiefly by persons of exceptional want of character.” The word gained currency in the early-20th-century worlds of fashion and the marginalised queer world at a time when homosexuality was a criminal offence and subtle signals and a coded slang language called Polari were all discreet signifiers of queerness, along with such sartorial details as a green carnation in a buttonhole, brown suede shoes, overly tight clothing, and—wait for it, Mr President—a red tie. Later in the 20th century, Andy Warhol, the ultimate camp Pop icon, co-opted Sontag's essays for his 1965 movie Camp, (he even screen-tested the writer), and the Stonewall riots of 1969 ushered in a newly open embrace of camp in fashion and culture. For Bolton, one key aspect of camp is the idea of “failed seriousness—not consciously trying to be camp.” He cites Charles James's elaborately constructed ball gowns and the work of the very serious Spanish couturier Cristobal Balenciaga, particularly his game-changing 1957 Baby Doll dress, as well as an evening dress worn by the museum's benefactor Jayne Wrightsman in 1966 sewn with tendrils of pink ostrich feathers that flutter in movement. The cochairs for the Gala on Monday, May 6, will be Lady Gaga, Alessandro Michele, Harry Styles, Serena Williams, and Anna Wintour. But what to wear? Dietrich and Garland were camp, as are Cher and Elton John, and Bolton mentions the idea of “surplus—when things are too much” as a keynote of camp. “A bow that's too big,” he says, “too many feathers, too many sequins.” For Bolton, Virgil Abloh's little black dress printed with the legend “little black dress” in quotation marks is camp, and follows in the camp tradition of such designers as Franco Moschino (and Jeremy Scott for Moschino), Jean Paul Gaultier, Jean-Charles de Castelbajac, John Galliano and Thom Browne. New-generation designers like London's Molly Goddard, Richard Quinn and Matty Bovan; Madrid's Palomo Spain; and New York's Vaquera and Gypsy Sport's Rio Uribe also trade in camp ideas. Bolton is on a roll. “Chanel was camp as a person but her clothes weren't camp,” he explains, “whereas Schiaparelli was camp as a person and so were her clothes. You end up seeing camp everywhere!” View Gallery 8 Photos The Metropolitan Museum of Art Costume Institute Presents “Camp: Notes on Fashion” for Its Spring 2019 Exhibition The 2019 Met Gala will take place on Monday, May 6, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. column1: 10 places you can head to for customised designer lehengas

From designer ateliers to neighbourhood tailors, customising (more than) a few ensembles during the course of your life is a norm in the country, rather than the exception. It could have been the lehenga you wore to the very first wedding you attended as a toddler, or that elaborate anarkali you conceptualised from scratch with your favourite designer—getting your clothes designed for any special occasions can easily be denoted as a cultural tradition here. Now while there is no denying the charm of wearing fresh off-the-runway styles, the merits of customising your traditional wear are aplenty too—especially when it comes to the lehenga. A festive season MVP, the lehenga is as appropriate for a Diwali cards party as it is for your brother's sangeet ceremony. And if you're invested in curating a wardrobe that's in tune with your personality, a mannequin-ready look may not always work for you. You may want to switch up the colours, tone down the embroidery or change the blouse to accentuate your body type. Luckily, off-the-rack is not the only way to go. We round up some of the coolest designers on the block who will save the day with a timely stitch. column1: Deepika Padukone’s top styling tips for every occasion on your calendar
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We got the style icon to give away her trade secrets When it comes to Deepika Padukone and best-dressed lists, the norm is pretty set in stone—the lady makes for a dramatic picture on the red carpet, but it is those effortless everyday basics that truly spell her vibe. “My wardrobe is dominated by tons of denims and whites,” she confesses with a quick flash of her million-dollar smile, as she settles in her vanity van after a long day of posing for the lens in All About You's autumn/winter '18 collection with Myntra. Dressed in a head-to-toe mustard ensemble, with that signature slicked-back hair look she is partial to, Padukone, indeed, has plenty on the cards this season to grin about. “Feminine dressing has been a constant from the time we started. We are building on that in a festive light this time round, so you are going to see a lot of mustard and blush,” she says, before adding, “Winter wear has always been a strong point for the label, and our current lineup has some beautiful tweed jackets and stripes. We also always [have] a lot of takers for prints, but the real beauty is in the detailing—with understated frills on the sleeves or that little ruche on a skirt that makes you pause.” While the label has clocked in three years, the Padmaavat star still looks forward to the creative brainstorm that precedes each collection. “The period between when we conceptualise to the time we hit the market is eight months, so we have to be omniscient with our moodboard to ensure that we keep the brand's aesthetic and philosophy in mind, but also strike the right balance with predicting what is going to be in fashion eight months down the line—from the silhouettes to the all-important colour palette. We then have a second round of shortlisted designs that I approve myself, and once we have [the] sign-off on a sample, we go into production,” she elaborates. And while the actor makes everyday dressing look unfailingly easy, we got her to let us sneak a peek at her styling cheatsheet to help you with your morning wardrobe dilemmas. Here's her top dressing advice for that perfect OOTD, no matter the occasion. There's no going wrong with a nice shirt and a pair of staple jeans—fitted, high-waisted or loose. Take your pick depending on your personal style, but remember to pair with a crisp shirt. A couple of easy swaps will see you through. If you are wearing a blouse and trousers, you exchange the latter for a skirt. Or if you are wearing a shirt and trousers, you throw on a statement jacket. You can't go wrong with flirty dressing, with a hint of effortless glam. Even if it is just a staple LBD, you can pair it with the right shoes or an accessory that gives it that little pop. Our All About You dresses always have a fun element, either in the form of a low back or a slit, to keep that flirty vibe alive. My advice is to always turn to a classic, whether it is a crisp white shirt, a classic LBD or even an Indian outfit with a flattering silhouette. When you don't have the time to think and prepare something special, turn to that one classic outfit in your wardrobe that never lets you down. There are enough styling expectations and demands on us girls through the week, whether it is at office or a night out, so opt for something that goes with the mood of a Sunday and allows your skin to breathe. As easy, flirty dress is a no-brainer for setting a lounge-y vibe. Beauty What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Guess who Victoria’s Secret is collaborating with next?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Her designs have been worn by the likes of Rihanna and Cate Blanchett Last year, lingerie giant Victoria's Secret tapped French designer and Kardashian-favourite Olivier Rousteing of Balmain to create runway looks for its annual show—remember the shimmer-smothered bralettes that took over your Instagram feeds? This year, for its second high fashion collaboration, the label has teamed up with London-based, Greek-born designer Mary Katrantzou, who is also commonly known as the ‘queen of prints'. The Central Saint Martins graduate, who recently hit the 10-year milestone, has found quite the celebrity fan following for her dizzying prints, bold use of colours and structured silhouettes—the likes of Keira Knightley, Rihanna, Kerry Washington and Cate Blanchett have all been spotted in her creations till date. With a little help from the Victoria's Secret team (the show's creative director Sophia Neophitou-Apostolou, executive producer Monica Mitro and the Angels all gave their inputs), Katrantzou has created a capsule collection of lingerie that will be revealed at the show in New York this November. While more details are awaited, the event will also feature 18 fresh faces, including Duckie Thot, Sadie Newman and Winnie Harlow. Stay tuned to this space for the updates. The collection will be available online and in Victoria's Secret stores What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights from Day 4 of Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A quick recap From Shivan & Narresh's Gond art inspired separates to a decadent Rainbow-themed grand finale, the last day of the four-day-long Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week had the strongest lineup of all days. These are the standout shows you need to know about. With the focus on blurring lines and abolishing predefined gender roles in our society, designer Dhruv Kapoor presented a collection titled ‘New-Butch' for spring/summer 2019. While the collection mainly comprised of printed dresses, sequinned skirts and suits, trench coats and fluid separates, it also featured a strong influence of the '80s, with bold floral prints in bright yellows, oranges and blues. Whatever the season, Shivan & Narresh's is one of the most anticipated shows on the schedule. Drawing inspiration from the Gond Art of the Koi tribes, the designer duo presented a collection featuring six new prints this time, which they conceptualised with a Gond artist. There was a mix of influences here, from the designer's childhood in Madhya Pradesh to the the spice markets of Istanbul and even Spain. Catering to destination brides, this collection came packed with embellished dresses, decadent lehengas, printed saris and relaxed swimwear, and bore classic holiday essentials for men too—swim trunks, shorts, robes and trousers. For the season finale, 41 designers came together to present the Rainbow Show in support of the abolishment of Section 377. The stage was set, and hits by Madonna and George Michael had the audience tapping their feat as models showcased each designer's interpretation of the universal colours of Pride. From Manish Malhora's stunning sari, Rajesh Pratap Singh's colourful number to Gaurav Gupta's reiteration of the sari, each and every designer presented a garment that showcased their support for the LGBTQIA+ community. The large set of models also included individuals who identified as a wide spectrum of genders. Watch the highlights in the video. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Can the clothes you wear also heal your mind and body?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A new wave of fashion is weaving healing properties into the very fabric of the designs. From Victoria Beckham’s ‘crystal alchemy’ and Viktor & Rolf’s ‘colour magic’ to Ayurvedic dyes and shoes that ‘earth’ you to the planet, Vogue checks out the medicinal possibilities on offer “What a strange power there is in clothing,” Nobel Prize-winning writer Isaac Bashevis Singer once mused. It's true, isn't it? We all know the transformative abilities of a precision-tailored trouser suit to straighten the posture, a nipped-in waist or a flippy hem to make you feel feminine, or your favourite heels (the ones you can actually walk in) to put a runway-worthy spring in your step. In short, we know fashion can give us a good dose of self-confidence—but increasing numbers of designers are also looking more closely than ever at what lies within those threads. From materials that tap into your spiritual side to fabrics using tech to improve how they interact with your skin—and their impact on the planet—Vogue meets the designers blazing a trail in this innovative fashion field. [#image: /photos/5ce429d64a30b308db12d161]||| ||| Emma Watson at the The Museum of Modern Art Film Benefit in Kitx. Image: Getty For Kitx, a sustainably focused Australian label founded by Kit Willow Podgornik (and favoured by eco-chic actor Emma Watson), conscious, ‘healing' fashion is something we can literally wear on our sleeve. The designer uses ancient Ayurvedic recipes from southern India to dye her fabrics, infusing her garments with antibacterial properties. For the resort 2019 collection, which she showed in Paris in October, the designer worked with independent Indian dye house The Colours of Nature, based outside Tamil Nadu. It was her second time working with the initiative. “They recovered this old recipe book of dyeing; our beige is from jackfruit, yellow is from marigold, and our red is from a plant [called] rubia cordifolia. I love the idea of going back to nature—and using it to create colours with ancient practices is such a beautiful thing.” And if you haven't experienced a Kitx creation yet, don't imagine it's all kaftans and harem pants; instead, think  precision tailoring and luxe evening wear, in hues with a depth of colour, richness and rawness that sets this label apart. [#image: /photos/5ce429d5b40d268f13d6c7c6]||| ||| Bode spring/summer 2019 It's a similar story for Emily Bode—the CFDA 2018 Fashion Fund finalist whose eponymous menswear label counts Childish Gambino's Donald Glover among its fans. “I was working with a factory in India and was coincidentally introduced to a venture that creates textiles with ‘medicinal' qualities,” the designer explains from her New York HQ. She describes the indigo yarn she's used, which is hand-dyed with “basil, neem and turmeric. The fabric is aromatic and is said to help with respiratory issues [and] congestion, and [to be] anti-fungal and anti-diabetic. Some of the fabrics are more heavily scented—you can still smell the basil”. [#image: /photos/5ce429d5b40d268be9d6c7c8]||| ||| Cara Marie Piazza Also based in New York is natural dyer and textile designer Cara Marie Piazza, who has lent her “sartorial healing” abilities to labels including Eckhaus Latta and Loup Charmant. “The feeling of wearing something dyed with flowers can be beautiful and soothing,” she explains. “By wearing clothing that was naturally dyed and imbued with plants that have herbal and healing benefits, we can ‘absorb' the essences of these plants through our skin. I work with a lot of plants that [have been] used as medicine. Black walnut is antimicrobial and antiseptic, and is also a form of bug repellent while indigo roots have [traditionally] been prepared as medicine used for infections such as the common cold.” [#image: /photos/5ce429d6f55c27629da27595]||| ||| The Row, Miranda Kerr for KORA Organics and Victoria Beckham autumn/winter 2018. For the spiritually leaning, crystals have proved to be something of a buzz material of late. The Olsen twins handed out healing crystals to attendees at their fall/winter 2019 collection; each millilitre of Miranda Kerr's KORA Organics skincare products is passed through a rose quartz filtration process to “cleanse” them and “harness the crystals' powers of self-love”; and Victoria Beckham's pre-fall 2018 collection was scattered with jasper, tiger's eye, white howlite, sodalite and yellow calcite; some garments were even constructed with secret pockets for the crystals. [#image: /photos/5ce429d7b40d26774ed6c7cc]||| ||| Astara For Los Angeles-based footwear designer Mariah Lyons and her brand Astara, venturing into “wearable wellness” was a natural progression. A former dancer, she worked as a stylist and press agent for Burberry and Jimmy Choo, but found the change from the dynamism of dance to a more static office role took a noticeable toll on her body. Autoimmune issues such as joint pain led her to begin researching and soon she came upon the theory of Schumann resonances, which finds that humans separated from the Earth's electromagnetic fields and the natural healing quality they produce begin to develop ailments. The condition is experienced by astronauts in space and led Nasa to develop a way to simulate the Earth's vibrations to curb “space sickness”. “We used to be outdoors and in communion with nature, but now we're inundated by WiFi and radiation all day long,” says Lyons, a self-described “intuitive healer, herbalist and crystal alchemista”. To that end, the soles of the shoes in her collections are fitted with metal tag technology that resonates at the same vibration as the Earth's magnetic field—7.83 hertz. Lyon describes the in-shoe experience as feeling like you're barefoot in the sand or grass. “Each shoe has a different crystal on it—black onyx, clear quartz, rose quartz—and I'm doing a blue apatite for resort. Every crystal has its own frequency and vibration, which helps people connect even more deeply to the Earth.” For Viktor & Rolf's spring/summer 2018 haute couture collection, the healing properties of colour were the starting point. “A lush colour palette resulted in an emotive and healing visual experience,” the designers tell Vogue. “This season we also launched our jewellery line featuring stones with ‘healing' properties. For us, [an intense colour palette] always ties into a visual meditation.” [#image: /photos/5ce429d69cc0c057a2f9d2eb]||| ||| Organic Basics Other brands are focusing on the tech benefits of materials that naturally protect against nasties. Denmark's Organic Basics innovated SilverTech technology—a fabric woven with fine silver threads which has antibacterial and antimicrobial properties—“to change the way people think about the clothes they put right next to their bodies”, says co-founder Mads Rasmussen. “When we first started making underwear we discovered that two thirds of the environmental impact of our clothing was actually created by doing laundry. We'd been hearing about the odour-controlling effect of silver so we decided to weave it into our GOTS [Global Organic Textile Standard] organic cotton basics line to make them stay fresher for longer. More recently, we've started making recycled nylon activewear treated with a Bluesign®-approved [i.e. sustainable] recycled silver.” The upshot is that you can wear your bacteria-killing underwear for longer (yes really) without needing to put them through an environmentally unfriendly hot cycle. For the future, tech labs and initiatives are already working on fabrics that purify the air around them, measure the wearer's heartbeat, stop radiation from being absorbed and are infused with disinfectant abilities for the skin. It's no secret that when we feel our best, we look it—and this is feel-good fashion at its finest. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights from Day 3 of Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s what you missed https://youtu.be/Z_aoEmTBxsU Runways covered in trees, an abundance of polka dots and modern separates laced with nostalgia—Day 3 at Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week took us deeper into the mindset of some of our favourite labels. Payal Pratap's brand of clothing is one that is relatable to most women—not heavy on the trends, but with silhouettes that flatter most body types. This season, the designer's collection ‘The Sound of Silence' drew inspiration from the quiet that emanates deep from the heart of the forest from dawn to dusk. While Pratap primarily focused on various shades of green, there were also hints of pink, mustard and blues in the lineup. The sustainable collection was replete with motifs of leaves woven into fabrics and florals carefully crafted out of ribbon embroidery. Day dresses, cropped wide-legged trousers and jackets dominated the designer's offering for spring/summer 2019. Amrita Khanna and Gursi Singh of Lovebirds are on a mission to refine the Lovebirds aesthetic to their perfection. While the lineup for spring/summer 2019 featured the signature pleated trousers, long kurta-esque tops layered with cropped bottoms and a host of drop-waisted dresses, this season the designers brought in subtle changes by introducing sheer organza and silk fabrics as well, adding more definition to the cuts. “It's absolutely modern, contemporary, urban clothing for very modern women,” said Singh. Rahul Mishra returned to main schedule of India Fashion Week after nearly five years and was feeling emotional about his show titled ‘Gossamer'. At first glance, Mishra's collection might be categorised under easy, modern day separates, but if you look closely, you know the designer has worked upon the garments with great detail and care. From using handwoven Maheshwari and jamdani textiles to labouring over each piece with intricate chikankari and daraz work to mimic impressionist brushstrokes, Mishra's eye for detail is hard to match up to. “It somehow reflects my most intimate and intuitive memories,” he summed up about the collection. column1: Highlights from Day 2 of Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion More is more https://youtu.be/YMeRNaiAC7c On the second day of Lotus India Make-Up India Fashion Week, it seemed as though designers longing for a bit of drama on the runway had disregarded the season they were showcasing at, and jumped for the flair and drama of couture. Gauri & Nainika's label is synonymous with extravagant gowns. This time around, the designer duo doubled up the level of sparkle on the runway by way of metallic fabrics and sequins. In terms of silhouettes, frothy frocks cut at midi length were tailored to the taste of a younger audience, while acres of tulle and oversized ruffles articulated the designers' love for all things glamourous. On the other hand, Prashant Verma is in a state of flux, in finding his one true creative outlet. Designer, singer and actor, he has been wearing a few hats over the course of the past few seasons. His spring/summer 2019 collection, which was centred around the cathartic emotion of letting go, was ironically crafted in layers and layers of fabric. Varma's influences for the collection ranged from the couture houses of the past to Maria Callas and the West Side Story. The designer also spoke about his obsession with a kind of nostalgia for the future that comes bearing something familiar. column1: 23 times Bollywood celebrities proved the versatility of kurtas
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Kareena Kapoor Khan to Alia Bhatt, these leading ladies swear by the comfortable everyday basic Basic kurtas are for daywear what the eternal classic LBD is for a night out—never underdressed, but never OTT either. Low maintenance yet form-flattering, the classic kurta serves as an essential rite of passage by doing everything you need it to do on those days when you just can't even. And Bollywood celebrities seem to wholeheartedly agree too. While your favourite style icons may prefer dramatic long trains on the red carpet, cut to their off-duty wardrobe and you'll find everyone from fashion maven Sonam K Ahuja to debutante Janhvi Kapoor favouring comfort above all else. But that doesn't mean they take a complete hall pass from sartorial flair on their days off. Bollywood's best dressed names have made a home for themselves in the intersection between fuss-free and fashionable, with casual kurtas in the driver's seat. On a scale of 1 to 10, from basic all-white to head-turning twirls, there's a celeb-approved choice for everyone out there. If you like your kurtas breathable enough to feel like second skin, do like Deepika Padukone, who was recently spotted at the airport rocking a the Indian ethnic staple, sans the bells and whistles. Kangana Ranaut added this no-fail staple to her airport wardrobe as well, in the form of an all-white ensemble, with red lips and a tangerine handbag to go with it. And it isn't just the established names on the block that are showing their approval for this wardrobe basic. Debutante Janhvi Kapoor has been living double life of sorts; the style chameleon is just as home on the red carpet in elaborate couture concoctions as she is in a basic, no-frills kurta when off from work. Firmly edging out the rulebook, the vivacious 21-year-old is unafraid to be herself in the front of the paps with a slew of long kurtas paired with tailored pants that prove that there does exist a wonderland between style and comfort. Pastels are another winner when it comes to off-duty kurtas, with Kareena Kapoor Khan giving her Gucci threads a rest in favour of a subtly embroidered number as she jetted back into town from one of her work trips. And everyone's favourite millennial, Alia Bhatt, can be spotted working different hues in the form of coordinated separates with relaxed silhouettes often too. Even Sonam K Ahuja bowed down to the power of pink with an empire-line Péro kurta with white leggings. If you are looking at dialling things up a notch, these fuss-free staples can also serve you well during the upcoming wedding season. Anushka Sharma is only too happy to work flowy kurtas from Sabyasachi on the way to the airport, but when the occasion calls for it, you can easily tempt her with embellished separates too. The promotional spree of Namaste England had Parineeti Chopra pairing a fitted silk kurta with brocade pants from Raw Mango, while Kapoor Khan swapped her abs-baring separates in favour of an ivory Tarun Tahiliani kurta and dhoti pants for her Veere Di Wedding promotions—perfect for the bridesmaid on duty. column1: Highlights from Day 1 of Lotus Make-Up India Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Lost fish, landscapes of Kashmir and beautiful florals https://youtu.be/Fs3TZ4nZp-Q October in New Delhi is serving up the perfect weather for the viewing of the spring/summer 2019 shows this season. With the mercury set at a broiling 33 degrees, the audience would have gladly swapped the clothes on their backs with those on the runway. Rimzim Dadu, for one, is the kind of designer whose brand of creativity stems from her love for detail and the perfection of her craft. This season, Dadu highlighted her signature cord work while drawing inspiration from techniques of lace-making and stencils. One coral jacket, made of just the outlines of floral motifs crafted in the shape of a jacket, took nearly 400 hours to come to life. Pranav Mishra and Shyma Shetty of label Huemn are back from their Vogue Talents showcase in Milan, and have been working with photographers Mark Hanauer and Azaan Shah for their latest lineup. The designers emphasised on recreating Shah's landscapes of Kashmir in hand embroidery from images shot by these photographers. Huemn always been known for capturing the energy of the youth, and took a more mature approach with their athleisure and street fashion-influenced line of clothing this season. Aneeth Arora's brand Péro is all about storytelling. This season, she retold a modern classic of finding a fish lost in the sea, however in her version, the aquatic being was named Péro instead of Nemo. The audience sat by the poolside sipping on fresh coconut drinks as a band played Caribbean folk music, and some sand lined the snaking ramp on which models danced rather than walked. Péro's easy yet meticulously detailed separates came in sunny yellows, seaweed greens and soft teal blues this time around—the idea was to find the little fish lost in the mix of gingham, stripes and florals. But Arora's presentations are rarely done with finding just one hidden detail. The designer launched ‘Found Péro' this season, which is a sub brand from the house that curates local Indian crafts. The wicker baskets for the press kits were created by local craftsmen in Manipur, while the crisps inside came from an organic food brand called C. Green. Models wore Havaianas and Birkenstocks customised by Péro, and the paper headgear of corals and fishes were handcrafted by Italian paper sculptor, Carlos Urgese. The talk outside of the shows is, however, not limited to the picturesque life by the sea. The depleting quality of air in Delhi is also furious with the angry smoke of India's recent #MeToo movement. Will more names come up this week? Will the fashion week cultivate more than discussions on the evolution of aesthetics? Answers will be found, but only with time. Till then, make sure you don't miss out on everything that happened on Day 1 at Lotus Make-up India Fashion Week by checking out our video above. column1: What are the trends fashion buyers are backing for spring/summer 2019?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Fresh from a month of shows and globetrotting, the world’s most influential luxury stores reveal what they’re stocking in store for spring To buyers, the spring/summer 2019 collections were refreshingly feminine. Suits were softened, slip dresses entered the mix, dusty pastels and candy colours took centre stage. Two of autumn/winter's key trends—jumpsuits and animal prints—were reworked for the season ahead. There was a sense of inclusivity and empowerment, too, in the form of bold shoulders and easy, flat shoes. Buyers were understandably excited by new ideas from heritage houses, like Givenchy, Burberry and Oscar de la Renta, while buzzy up-and-comers, such as Alessandra Rich, Molly Goddard and Partow, added intrigue to the mix. Here, eight of the world's most influential buyers divulge what they're stocking in store for spring. Natalie Kingham, fashion buying director, London Top SS19 trends: Inclusivity, functionality, flat shoes Favourite SS19 collections: Valentino, Prada, Molly Goddard, Haider Ackermann, Marine Serre Kingham's take: “In a social climate that is striving for inclusivity, designers are being more conscious about the women who will ultimately wear their clothes. Anything done for design sake doesn't feel modern. Valentino and Haider Ackerman were standouts for this—the collections looked to embrace the varying and busy lifestyles of women and the need to dress for a number of different occasions and purposes in a day. We are seeing a strong move towards flat shoes even with unexpected pieces, such as gowns. Marine Serre did this particularly well, showing a range of dresses from evening gowns to bold minis and her signature scarf dresses with neoprene flats and trainers, while Haider Ackermann paired even the more glamorous pieces of the collection with heavy flat boots. What woman doesn't want a bit of stability as she dances the night away?” Kristen Cole, president and CCO, Dallas, Texas Top SS19 trends: Volume, pink, softer suits Favourite SS19 collections: Balenciaga, The Row, Sacai, Gabriela Hearst, Adam Lippes, Partow, Rochas, Plan C, Rosie Assoulin, Sies Marjan Cole's take: “Volume ruled. The Row, which always performs for us, showed volume in the most chic and luxurious floor-length dresses. Demna Gvasalia's voluminous wrap coats and dresses for Balenciaga were high impact. Our client loves drama and Rodarte's colourful showstoppers will do well for our event dressing. This season, pink is the new black. The colour was everywhere as the new neutral, especially at Adam Lippes, Rochas, Plan C, Rosie Assoulin and Partow. Gabriela Hearst's pink suit with strapping detail feels sculpted, yet relaxed. Designers are making suits distinctly for women, not residual men's silhouettes—a softer, more relaxed take. Sies Marjan delivered a suit with a whimsical print and lovely colours. Y/Project's off-the-shoulder suit with ostrich feathers provides drama, but still in a suit. Rosie Assoulin's little checked number with the cropped pant is so perfect for professional women running around town in a pair of trainers. I'll be wearing it.” Deena Khourshid, senior buyer, Dubai Top SS19 trends: Animal print, suits, gingham Favourite SS19 collections: Calvin Klein, Victoria Beckham, Oscar de la Renta, Isabel Marant Khourshid's take: “Our customer is bold and fashion-forward. Leopard and zebra prints are still going strong from shirts and dresses to shoes and accessories. Victoria Beckham celebrated her ten-year anniversary with a strong, feminine collection based on her design evolution over the past decade. Oscar de la Renta's spring/summer 2019 collection was Moroccan-inspired and filled with stunning prints and fringes, which is something our customers always look for in the summer. We are always used to Isabel Marant's collection being bohemian-inspired, however this season, it was all about the disco girl with stunning lamé pieces.” Maria Milano, head of womenswear, London Top SS19 trends: Slip dresses, dusty pastels, Victoriana Favourite SS19 collections: Peter Pilotto, Valentino, Burberry, Dior, Alessandra Rich Milano's take: “Our customer definitely prefers to wear dresses, especially in the summer. Slip dresses are versatile and can be dressed up or down and layered easily. White does extremely well with our customer base across ready-to-wear, outerwear and even accessories, so yes to white dresses—especially in guipure lace and cotton eyelet. Pastel shades are less sugary and more dusty for spring 2019: think antique rose, pistachio and lemon—feminine, but not saccharine. The Victoriana trend of ruffles was prevalent especially in London and looked really romantic on long dresses. The Peter Pilotto collections keep getting better and better, and the pastel colour palette and lurex accents make this the ultimate summery collection. Riccardo Tisci's take on Burberry hit the spot. We particularly liked the corset trenches and how he transformed the iconic check into a stripe. Dior's collection was like couture and the new iterations of the saddle bag and book tote are beyond covetable. Valentino was a masterful collection by Pierpaolo Piccioli, who issued a supremely feminine yet effortless lineup. Gowns with pockets: yes! Gorgeous flats: yes! More raffia bags: yes! A well-deserved standing ovation.” Brigitte Chartrand, womenswear buying manager, Montreal Top SS19 trends: Femininity, lingerie-inspired, tie-dye Favourite SS19 collections: Calvin Klein 205W39NYC, Kwaidan Editions, Loewe, Stella McCartney, Chloé Chartrand's take: “Overall there was an increased level of femininity in the spring/summer 2019 collections, with designers using materials like chiffon, silk and georgette and with slinky, lingerie-inspired silhouettes like at Stella McCartney. I loved how tie-dye was used in unexpected ways. Raf Simons incorporated it in his wetsuit looks for Calvin Klein 205W39 NYC and Marine Serre used a pastel tie-dye in her tracksuits and dresses. Designers also embraced prints, but the florals stood out for me. Kwaidan Editions and Chloé showed large, bold and flowery prints in unexpected colours. Loewe had a great mix of textures and a lot of beautiful dresses.”   Ken Downing, senior vice president and fashion director, Dallas, Texas Top SS19 trends: Biker shorts, romanticism, power shoulders, candy colours Favourite SS19 collections: Chanel, Stella McCartney, Dries Van Noten, Saint Laurent, Givenchy, Alexander McQueen Downing's take: “Biker shorts bring newness to our customer's wardrobe and they show off her great legs. Overt romanticism speaks to her feminine spirit and her love of pretty things in her wardrobe. The takeaway anorak is for the girl on the go. Every conversation begins with colour: saturated shades of joyous candy colours brighten a spring wardrobe and will put a smile on the customer's face. We love the obsession with the 1980s on every runway. The power shoulder puts confidence edge and excitement into our ladies' closets.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Justin Timberlake and Levi’s have a surprise for denim fans
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The pop singer turns designer 37-year-old Justin Timberlake has sold over 32 million albums, and has ten Grammys, four Emmys and nine Billboard Music Awards to his credit till date. And now, he has added yet another achievement to his already admirable career graph—the pop star just debuted his collaboration with storied denim brand, Levi's, for an all-new men's collection titled Levi's x Justin Timberlake ‘Fresh Leaves'. Inspired by Timberlake's obvious love for music, ‘Fresh Leaves' presents a modern take on iconic Levi's pieces, and derives from the concept of the singer making his own mark and offering a fresh spin on classic, timeless pieces to leave behind for the next generation. He worked closely with the design team at Levi's to create the exclusive collection, during design and listening sessions at the brand's San Francisco Eureka Innovation Lab, the Levi's Archives and their showroom in Los Angeles, called the Haus of Strauss. The result? A 20-piece menswear collection grounded in the most iconic fits through the lens of the unexpected and modern. Fans will always remember Timberlake walking the 2001 American Music Awards red carpet with Britney Spears, both dressed in matching all denim outfits. His preference to Canadian tuxedos has also been noted over the years—so it was only time for Timberlake to rewrite history in the world of denim, just as he did in the global music industry. “Clothes are as important to a musician's creative process and performance as the music itself. This Levi's collection is my attempt to share some of my experiences with fans,” said Timberlake. The capsule collection is the ultimate fall set, and introduces the best of the Levi's icons, all rooted in quality craftsmanship and premium fabrics. It offers hints of modern streetwear and plays with proportions, offering longer and oversized lengths, and adding hoods on truckers and shirts. It also features a rendition of the iconic 501 jeans called the 501 Slim Taper, which is inspired by how the singer wears his pair. Timberlake first partnered with Levi's when he was asked to customise the Levi's Trucker Jacket for its 50th anniversary last year, when the brand got icons from all over the world to come up their own versions of the iconic piece. The partnership evolved as Levi's also celebrated the launch of his tour by creating eight pieces (truckers and flannel shirts) for his pop-up in New York, and then helped outfit him with custom pieces for the tour itself. column1: This new fashion line caters to your every basic wear need
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Details this way The wine director at her family's The Leela Group, vegan and raw food entrepreneur with Amai, Vogue's contributing editor, and now designer with Aligne, Aishwarya Nair Matthew tells us about her latest project that launches at Design One in Mumbai today. Aligne was birthed from a place of spiritual calm. Having a true love affair with fashion, it was just natural to use my knowledge of what I liked and create something new and simple with fresh perspective. With Aligne, the focus is the working woman, and we look into how to adhere to her basic wants for fashion and a holistic lifestyle with our blog. What I found missing was a brand that can seamlessly transition from work to play, and from season to season, at an accessible price point. Our key area of expertise is elevated essentials. This came about from drawing influence from my personal journey of being a hotelier with an intensive travel schedule. I wanted to build a brand that looked at how we feel—with the clothes we wear, but also look at how we think. Conscious consumption is our goal, and this in essence comes from the mind. We have pledged to talk about our spiritual journey through all our branding, and are looking to develop a lifestyle house that dwells into beauty and inner well-being products. Very much like my vegan brand Amai, Aligne is a labour of love. Both the brands have a strong, manifested philosophy that I hold sacred. While Amai dwells into food and natural consumption, Aligne looks at an external reality of getting dressed. After our clothing collection launch, our next endeavour will be with crystals—and thereafter we are developing essences to elevate one's mood too. After our launch at Design One in October, we will launch our web portal featuring the entire collection. This is also when we will unveil our, which that features issues that are close to and inspire the working women. Scroll onwards for a quick peek at the collection. column1: Shantanu & Nikhil’s big international plans for modern Indian couture
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From London to Lithuania It has been a busy year for Shantanu and Nikhil Mehra, the two-pronged creative force behind the eponymous couture label. The month of September saw them flying over to London—at the behest of the Indian Ambassador to the United Kingdom, YK Sinha—to put together a special showcase for the city's crème de la crème. “Saatchi Gallery is renowned for bringing the best of art, culture and music together to London. It was not only an honour, but a privilege for us to have represented what modern Indian couture stands for today through our autumn/winter 2018 couture collection, ‘Independence'. Showcasing Indian textiles and couture there made us feel proud for changing the pre-constructed notions about the Indian fashion industry,” recalls Shantanu. Labelled the ‘future Louis Vuitton of India' by Eastern Eye, this wouldn't be the label's first tryst with the European fashion scene. Last year's autumn/winter 2017 collection found an audience in Lithuania, courtesy the Indian Consulate. “‘The Regiment' represented vintage India with military sensibilities, thereby bringing our anti-trend brand philosophy to prominence in the Western world. Moving beyond wedding ensembles, this side of Indian couture had not been seen by Europe, and ‘The Regiment' led to the onset of our label's influence there,” he elaborates. The couturiers were quick to pick up on the preconceived notions attached to Indian couture, and were glad to shatter some of them. “The Indian fashion landscape is seen through the lens of tradition, and is perceived by what Indian brides and grooms wear. However, recent digital developments on social media and opportunities like the ones we were given are beginning to spark a change in the preconceived notions about Indian couture. Connoisseurs of fashion in Europe have thus far only witnessed the handcrafted and embroidered aspect of Indian fashion, and we were glad to be able to showcase the sartorial finesse, use of voluminous drapes and minimalism as a signature of our legacy,” Shantanu adds. As boundaries shrink and the world grows smaller, the couturier acknowledges that to be globally scalable, independent labels need to focus beyond the clothes themselves, to what they represent. The designer explains, “Couture is no longer merely a space for innovation in clothes; it is now a medium for experiences and storytelling. Consumers do not want to invest in clothes for occasions but rather, want to relive experiences and witness different feelings through couture creations. Playing upon a sense of familiarity with neo-grandeur is the path that has aided in our success, and we have found that honest innovation curated with expertise and minimalism is accepted worldwide.” From a business standpoint, he won't deny the impact that the international shows have had on their brand footprint across the world. “Social media is a very powerful tool and, through our digital prominence, our brand followers have now begun to adopt the indie-chic philosophy internationally. We now have international clients who hail from varied parts of the world, and are enamoured by our take on anti-trend, minimalistic couture. It is heartening to know that our S&N family is only increasing from strength to strength,” Shantanu says. Post the showcase at The Saatchi Gallery in London, the designer duo tapped into the Middle-Eastern market with the launch of an exclusive S&N experiential retail space at Robinsons, Dubai Festival Mall. Closer home, the unveiling of a flagship store is on the cards by the end of this month. “The Shantanu & Nikhil flagship store in Bandra has been constructed as a luxurious, state-of-the-art space where consumers can be inducted into the S&N #IndiaStory. Our take on couture is based on telling stories of the past amidst the glorious modernity of the present, and you'll find that replicated in our latest venture,” he promises. column1: What to expect at Lotus Make-up India Fashion Week spring/summer 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s a teaser of what you can look forward to from the lineup As they say, it's always fashion week somewhere. While the rest of the world may have put their feet up after New York, London, Paris and Milan, for us back home in India, the season is just kicking off at Lotus Make-up India Fashion Week. With one day to go, we've packed our bags (fashion week survival kit of sturdy sneakers and portable chargers intact), and gotten ready to make our way to the capital, where we'll greet some old faces—both those who are regulars to fashion week (Pero's finally a fixture on the official schedule), and those who are marking their return this season—and some new ones too. From an offsite show to a presentation and even a rainbow show, here are our picks of all the showcases to look forward to in the coming week. Scroll on to see seven designers reveal their collections to Vogue, and give us an insider's view to what inspired them this season. “My fascination for textures, material and re-engineering fabrics continue this season as I try to explore the relationship between positive and negative space. The collection draws inspiration from age old techniques of lace-making and stencilling in handmade chiffon, metallic cords and metal wires. The presentation aims to explore an intersection between fashion, art and technology through a collaboration with multi-disciplinary artist, Harshvardhan Kadam and creative tech studio, Digital Jalebi.” “Through the collection and the experience of the show, we want to project a change in the teaching system, where men are taught empathy at a young age by disregarding the traditional masculine values labeled as “Butch”. The starting point for each collection is always conversations, discussions and the society that we live in. This one was about blurring lines and abolishing the predefined gender roles in our society. There is also a strong influence of '80s and pop colours from the '60s.” “The collection explores an all-black uniform for both men and women. There is intricate metal work on constructed garments and matte and gloss textures dividing the body in unusual patterns. We are moving away from prêt and presenting a 14-piece red carpet-ready collection from the couture line, where luxurious satin and twisted crepe are used.” “We are playing with volume, circular form and asymmetry, but for this season, updating it with satin-organza and even block printing on handwoven cottons, linens and silks.” “This is one of my most intimate collections as it is inspired by memories from my childhood, as well as the ones with my daughter, Aarna. When I play with her, I am reminded of my own childhood, and of my mother, who used to wear the patchwork Maheshwari sarees. I am reminded also of my house, where daraz curtains would hang and our wooden table covered in coloured lace cloth. These memories are mirrored in my collection. It also marks the first time I've experimented with pure white textures—in the past I have always worked with crème or ecru.” “The Koi Series captures the finer nuances of Gond art from Madhya Pradesh and coalesces it with colour inspiration from the spice markets of Istanbul, both of which were discovered by us on our recent travels. This collection is a way to marry the Indian art form with fashion and make it relevant for the globetrotting millennials. It is reflective of the non-conformism of the generation today, always on the lookout for innovative cultures and experiences.” “The spring/summer 2019 collection is influenced by the cultural and socio-economic ambience of conflict-ridden Kashmir and the hope and pride in its growing youth. Its stark contrasts of what has passed and what is to come forms the backbone of our narrative. Images by renowned photographers Mark Hanauer and Azaan Shah have been played with and converted into print and mixed media textures. An assortment of intricate handwork techniques have been used to add unexpected detail to individual garments. column1: Aishwarya Rai Bachchan walks for Manish Malhotra’s show in Doha
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Did you miss Aaradhya Bachchan’s matching look? Fab Entertainment's Fashion Weekend International came to a close with a glamorous presentation by Manish Malhotra at the Mondrian Doha, Qatar. As was announced previously, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, a longtime friend of the designer, took centre stage as a ballroom full of people waited with bathed breath to watch her walk down the runway. Despite the long wait before the show could begin, a line of Qatari women sat exuding a quiet strength in the front row. While continuing to dress modestly in their hijabs, their handbags, shoes and diamonds peeked through to reveal not only their purchasing power, but also their hankering for designer fashion. The Indian population in Qatar is nearly twice as much as the local, making it a unique showcasing ground for Indian fashion; a piece of information that was gathered from the Indian Ambassador for the State of Qatar, P Kumaran and his wife Ritu Kumaran. Shows of this magnitude are rare, but a treasured spectacle. Qataris enjoy one of the highest per capita incomes in the world, making it even more interesting for homegrown couture labels who are looking to find space in the Arab country. Manish Malhotra's lineup, ‘Zween', was also tailored to the taste of the new audience. Amidst his signature voluminous lehengas and sheer floral blouses, were even more ostentatious pieces—a feat that's not easy to pull off without compromising on one's aesthetic. From mirror work to diamond shaped paillettes and a lavish use of feathers, the designer upped the ante with his already extravagant couture. Malhotra also made sure he included separates like long jackets, embroidered kaftans and shararas that are more commonly worn in the Middle East. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan brought the show to a close in an ombré pink gown that ended in dramatic ruffles. Aaradhya Bachchan, who sat front row with her maternal grandmother, wore a matching number and blew kisses to her mother as she made her walk back. Sophie Choudry, Azaan Sami, Hamza Abbasi and several diplomats were present to witness the spectacle. A trunk show will have Malhotra receiving VIP guests by appointment, following the show. column1: Everything that went down at fashion month this season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All the major moments, both on and off the runways Whether you're right there, front and centre, taking it all in from the front row at a fashion show, or behind your phone screens, with eyes on Tom Ford in New York and Prada in Milan—fashion month is an all-inclusive and all-immersive time. But, whether you're there or not, with over four shows a day and all that street style streaming in, some of the finer details can miss your attention. Celine's é-dropping, Gucci's packet-full-of-herbs invite and even Anna Wintour's doppelgängers outside a show venue in Milan, this season was not without its talking points. While they say, the real show happens outside the show venue (where models meet half way through hair and make-up and the runway's trickle down trends come into their own on street style stars), we can't ignore all the seminal catwalk moments that will shape the season to come. Be it the age-agnostic movement among designers (Dolce & Gabbana made a strong case for octogenarians in the season's best) or Gigi Hadid's magical bridal moment at Moschino and Marine Serre's ‘hardcore couture'—here's everything that made the month a headlining one. First the accent was dropped. Then the interview came out. And finally the invite arrived. Hedi Slimane's Celine was going to be a club-kid central collection, even before it showed. The signs were all there. The invite with images of iconic Parisien night clubs, shot by Slimane, showed that his heart was in a sultrier place. Whoever did get their hands on the photo book invite—keep it safe. One of the designer's older books is now reselling at a whopping $4,000(!) Just as New York Fashion Week wrapped up, our social media feeds were taken over by a glamorous dinner party hosted by fashion's first family—the Hadids. Kitted out in the week's best—from Gigi in a spangled Marc Jacobs pant suit to Bella in Rodarte and brother Anwar in Pyer Moss—this is one dinner party no one should miss. Let's talk about the sets. Wouldn't you like to know what went into building Chanel's set, which transformed the Grand Palais into a beachside (with actual water indoors)? And if you thought that was extra, there's always Balenciaga's digitised tunnel catwalk with phrases like “Presence is key. Now is the answer.” dancing in the dark as the models came out—all in all, a sensory overload. Just going to leave this little Gucci packet-of-herbs invite on your screen to enjoy. What's better than one fashion state head? Four of them. Meet the Anna Wintour look-alikes—sharp bob and sunglasses intact. Jeremy Scott created the perfect Princess-bride moment at Milan Fashion Week, starring Gigi Hadid. If you aren't thrilled just looking at this picture, spot the smiles on the front row. It's not the first time Maye Musk made a strong case for silver foxes as fashion's new supermodels. Designers Sachin & Babi presented their fall/winter 2018 collection on Musk, and Rahul Mishra had her sitting front row. The overarching theme at the spring 2019 shows was age-agnostic—designers obsessed with youth culture and millennial minds, fashioned their clothes on bodies that have lived the test of time. column1: Alexander McQueen SS19: The making of a dress
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion British designer Sarah Burton reveals how a vintage wedding gown inspired her hauntingly beautiful spring/summer 2019 collection and how she’s marrying enigmatic elegance with signature Alexander McQueen power Sarah Burton's spring/summer 2019 collection for Alexander McQueen was an ode to womanhood and its milestones, rituals and rites of passage: “Birth, sisterhood, betrothal, marriage and mourning,” explains the British designer. The final show of the penultimate day of Paris Fashion Week, Burton's creations were set against a rocky landscape of giant boulders, partially plastered with worn posters, with white gravel underfoot crunching under the models' every step. True to style, the collection was at once fierce and delicate, deftly employing the house's characteristic sharp tailoring and haunting elegance to dramatic effect. This season, pagan references, Victorian silhouettes and dense floral embroideries and prints came together in a provocative, but empowering way, highlighting both the strength of women and the importance of vulnerability and emotion. Take the leather pieces—such as the opening look, inspired by a blacksmith's apron—which were matched with knitted lace dresses: hard and soft in perfect matrimony. Here, Burton shares a rare insight into of one of her favourite looks of the season and reveals the couture levels of craftsmanship that went into it. A vintage wedding dress sourced from a London antique fair was key to the collection's narrative. The show notes referenced the idea of long-forgotten treasures—kept in a trousseau, folded with pressed flowers—and heirlooms—clothing embedded with memories and meaning. The dress, thought to date back to the turn of the century, and was crafted from shredded silk paper taffeta, tulle and lace, delicately ruched and trimmed with Honiton lace. Burton was inspired by the work of British photographer Julia Margaret Cameron. The Victorian artist's portraits of women featured on the SS19 mood board, while her atmospheric techniques inspired the approach and design of the Ophelia print which became the basis of the fabric. To create the Ophelia print, the vintage wedding dress was scanned and overlaid with individual photographs of wild peonies and rambling roses. That image was then digitally engineered, placing special emphasis on symmetry, before being printed onto silk taffeta. The print is so detailed that before the dress takes shape, intricately constructed miniature paper dolls are created. Approximately 30 per cent of the original scale, these mini-maquettes are designed to perfect the trompe l'oeil effect of the print on the bodice, pleats and dress edge. The paper dolls form part of the McQueen archive, too. Some 20 meters of silk taffeta was printed for this one dress, with around 30 individual panels and singular pieces of patterns carefully engineered to perfectly fit the design. Taking up to three months, the fitting process is exacting work. The intricate creative process begins in London, where silk print trials are pinned and fitted perfectly to the dress toile. Then engineered printed silk taffeta panels are cut, hand sewn and fitted in the Paris atelier ahead of the show. The silk taffeta corset dress with poet sleeves, portrait neckline and full skirt with side pleating takes to the runway. column1: H&M launches a special collection for Breast Cancer Awareness Month
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion This is why it’s worth your attention If you've found your feeds painted pink with jewellery, sneakers and even stationery from a slew of labels ever since October 1 rolled by, we're not surprised—October is, after all, globally known as Breast Cancer Awareness Month. And this year, Swedish fashion giant H&M has decided to show its support to the cause by going down a more personal route. Launched earlier this week, the label's capsule collection of bras, Close to My Heart, is inspired by an employee and a breast cancer survivor's futile hunt for affordable, stylish and functional lingerie. Staple styles like sports bras with front closures, bralettes and soft-cup bras in neutral tones, with fabrics spanning from lace to micro-fibre, make up the line, which is designed for women who have undergone a single or double mastectomy. While the bras may not seem out of the ordinary at first glance, they come with special features. Starting at 32A and going up to 38D, they offer more coverage and have pockets made out of mesh to support the prostheses. What's more? All the proceeds from the sale of the collection, which will also be available online, go to the American Cancer Society (ACS). Through the month of October, H&M will work with ACS to raise $125,000 for causes spanning research, up-to-date cancer information and education, along with access to cancer screenings and follow-up care. column1: All the outfits a bride needs for the days leading up to her wedding
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And no, we are not talking about your trousseau So much focus is laid on finding the perfect wedding lehenga that we forget that it is only the tip of the proverbial iceberg otherwise known as a bride's shopping list. Sure, the outfit you say ‘I do' in will always be a cherished wardrobe treasure, but that doesn't mean the remainder of your wedding repertoire should be playing second fiddle. The adjectives attributed to the big fat Indian wedding are apt for a reason. Whether the soon-to-wed couple signed up for the whirlwind of celebrations whole-heartedly or not, their calendar is almost instantly populated with a dizzying number of parties, dinners and ceremonies to toast their nuptials. And while being the centre of this revelry is positively giddying, it also comes attached with the stress-inducing question of ‘what do I wear?' Your outfit for a pre-wedding puja will be abundantly different from what a dinner party in your honour calls for. The dichotomy of this exercise can sometimes make the otherwise pleasurable task of shopping somewhat painful. But before you send out an SOS to your bestie (who probably has her own wardrobe for your wedding to stress about), read through Vogue's guide for a low-down on all the must-have pre-wedding ensembles you need to stock up on. If there is one thing Indian weddings are not short on, it's the myriad number of customs. Each accompanied by a ceremony to boot. Rest assured that your walk from the roka to the mandap would be brimming with several such occasions. So where does one begin, as far as the wardrobe is concerned? By investing in a few fail-safe classics. Handwoven saris and kurta sets are a safe starting point. Benarasi, Paithani, Patola, bandhani and gara work saris can work for functions with a traditional bent. Versatile metallic blouses can be easily paired with a variety of these drapes. Lucknowi, mukaish, gota or even printed kurta sets, anarkalis and shararas will be handy additions to your pre-wedding wardrobe as well. You can easily wear one to a sindhara lunch hosted by your mother-in-law. Sonam K Ahuja chose an embroidered pastel sharara set for her at-home mehandi ceremony and a fuss-free printed sari to run her bridal errands in style. On the other hand, Anushka Sharma went dupatta-free for her mehandi ceremony in Tuscany, choosing a bright Sabyasachi lehenga with a modest floral blouse. Pre-wedding parties are the perfect platform to take those new-age Indian silhouettes for a spin. Draped trousers with lavish capes, dhoti pants with intricate jackets and cocktail saris with contemporary blouses (paired with statement jewellery, of course) will always hit bull's eye. Wear an ivory belted ruffled sari with emerald jewellery for your welcome lunch or a peplum jacket with flared pants for a dinner thrown by your favourite aunt. Each event on your wedding invite also warrants an outfit that will be one for the ages (no pressure). The mehandi gives you room to combine modern elements with traditional silhouettes. So choose a Patola lehenga with a crop top or silk shirt and ditch the dupatta. Or better yet, team your ruffled sharara with a bustier, cape and heirloom jewellery. The sangeet often boasts a more elaborate dress code. A lehenga, more often than not, does the trick. Take the liberty to switch up the same ol' blouse with a ruffled version, or choose pearl and Swarovski work over zardozi embroidery. But also be deliberately savvy in your selection of these outfits. They should be versatile enough to be worn long after your wedding. Extra props for looks that can be easily deconstructed to be used as separates. Check out our edit of the best Indian ethnic designer wear to add to your pre-wedding wardrobe now. View Gallery 8 Photos Outfits for weddings- Indian Is your fiancé's best friend hosting a boozy pre-wedding party as a lead-up to the wedding? Or is a bachelorette trip to Greece on the horizon? A set of western silhouettes will be an imperative part of your pre-wedding sartorial selection, for events that don't require a traditional dress code. And truth be told, there are no rules. Wear a whimsical tulle dress to a garden bridal shower hosted by your coterie, or turn up to a cocktail dinner in a fierce pantsuit with a diamond necklace gifted by your in-laws. Take stock of your final set of parties before the ring, and hit the stores (or the atelier of your go-to designer) accordingly. An all-purpose selection of dresses will never be amiss. Priyanka Chopra chose a blush sheath dress for her roka after-party, while Isha Ambani wore a nude embellished gown for her engagement in Lake Como. Be it sequinned bodycons or dainty lace midis; include only those styles that you're comfortable in. After all, you don't want to spend the better part of your ‘one month to go' brunch adjusting the plunging neckline of your floaty maxi dress. Throw in a few jumpsuits to the mix as well. Cape sleeves, strapless or tuxedo-inspired, this one-piece staple is as apt for your last dinner as a singleton as it is for a pre-wedding dinner with your co-workers. Wardrobe planning for a destination bachelorette requires meticulous attention as well. While the location will have a big say, debauchery will most likely be the order of this celebration. Glamorous blouses, tailored trousers, trendy playsuits, coordinated sets and versatile dresses will see you through. Throw in some swimwear to flaunt the results of those killer workouts, while you're at it too. There will be no overcoming the impulse to splurge on a few avant-garde pieces. Don't fight it. But make more space for functional outfits that can be carried over to your life as a missus, starting with the honeymoon. column1: How to pull off brown this wedding season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Welcome this earthy shade into your Indian ethnic wardrobe While we won't deny you your pick of florals for spring, with the wedding season upon us, the time to make friends with moodier shades has officially arrived. Your flirty pastels will serve you well for those beach weddings next summer, but the festive season calls for some unconventional hues for the bridesmaid and her troupe—and brown emerges as a likely contender, having curried favour with A-listers like Anushka Sharma, Katrina Kaif and Sara Ali Khan. So how does one adapt this statement colour without upstaging the bride? Allow the best in the biz to lead the way. If you thought your options were restricted to pastels and reds for the wedding season ahead, you might want to rethink your choices—Anushka Sharma boldly went where few brides have gone before, and opted for a belted Sabyasachi lehenga in a regal shade of vintage brown for her wedding reception in Mumbai. Doubling down on her vote of approval for this unconventional colour, she was spotted at a recent event in a muted brown sari from the couturier, juxtaposed with an intricately detailed hazar-buti blouse in a deeper hue. And she isn't the only one either. Katrina Kaif's recent stint as a showstopper for Manish Malhotra had her ditching the crowd favourites in favour of a deep brown lehenga, paired with a twirl-ready cape jacket. If you are on the fence about carrying off strong earthy tones, you can take notes from Sara Ali Khan, who took the colour for a spin in a corset and lehenga with dove grey undertones. View Gallery 5 Photos Brown for weddings- Celebrities While your favourite A-listers have given a sartorial thumbs up to this colour, the runway has been inviting the darker hues of the spectrum as well. column1: How Hedi Slimane’s Celine has immortalised Phoebe Philo
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion There was more than just an accent missing Some called it a horror show, others deemed the casting tone-deaf—the outcry against Hedi Slimane's debut collection for Celine was palpable, complete with long, articulate angry messages on Instagram. Fresh after the Ford-Kavannaugh hearings, an air of resentfulness and doom surrounded Slimane's Paris La Nuit showcase. Now, while some might argue that the events took place in different parts of the world, to the global community tuned in online, the two followed one after the other. The 96-piece collection of womenswear and menswear bore the French designer's distinct stamp—short sparkly dresses, skinny suits and fascinators. So evident was Slimane's signature that visual comparisons were drawn between his previous work at Saint Laurent, and it's truly impossible to tell it apart. A few days shy of the show, a rare interview with the designer surfaced in which the Slimane bluntly put forth his vision for the cool-girls-club French label. “At Celine, the weight of the past is not as strong as at Dior or Saint Laurent. We can break free of it more easily,” he told Le Figaro. Translation, Phoebe Philo's legacy, which was built on a real understanding of what women can aspire to be through her clothing, meant little to him. The designer-fashion house game of musical chairs is simultaneously entertaining and often times pointless. Not every new appointment is a success and debut shows are rarely unanimously loved by consumers and critics at once. That Slimane's show didn't earn the respect of either could have passed with tepid show reviews, but what the audience felt in this case can only be described as a betrayal of sorts. Apart from Slimane at Celine, another new appointment that was being closely watched this fashion month was Riccardo Tisci at Burberry, but the reactions to their debut shows could not have been more different. Tisci, despite his aesthetic rooted in sensuous, tortured couture, tailoring, and an insider's viewpoint on street culture, made an instant connect with Burberry's posh audience. But Slimane, who also enjoys the approval of the after-hours party set, was ripped apart for doing the exact opposite. While there is no mandate that dictates a creative director should ease into their appointment by continuing in the same vein as their predecessors, connecting the past with the future is a responsibility that is expected of them. Tisci's too made a brave move with a redesign of the logo to create noise about his appointment, but it was his approach that made the transformation a welcome one. Enlisting the help of English art director and graphic designer Peter Saville, Tisci crafted a monogram using the initials of the house's founder Thomas Burberry. Despite being an Italian who spent his professional career in France, Riccardo Tisci's appointment at a British heritage brand was a successful one. On the other hand, Slimane, a Frenchman obsessed with the surfer communities of California with a taste for rock 'n' roll, already rubbed the audience off the wrong way by taking the accent off Celine. Such behaviour is hardly a surprise coming from the designer, who got rid of the ‘Yves' from the iconic house of Yves Saint Laurent when he was appointed creative director six years ago in 2012. It's important to speak of the women who influenced Philo's formative years, for their impact can be seen in her work too. The student of OBE Louise Wilson, the late design director and lecturer at Central Saint Martins London, who also cut her teeth at Stella McCartney's Chloé previously, exited the LVMH-owned French brand Céline in 2017, where she had held the position of creative director for 10 years. To her credit, Louise Wilson has raised some of the most influential names in the industry, including Alexander McQueen, Jonathan Saunders and Christopher Kane. Stella McCartney had exited Chloé in 2001 to create her sustainable fashion label, which is now known for its unique feminine, sophisticated charm. And when Philo took over the reins at Chloé, she moved away from McCartney's rock 'n' roll inspired lineup to a more edited, practical one too. When it came to Céline, Philo's own work was of a feminist at heart. The clothes were created for the intellectual woman who didn't feel the need to join the trend bandwagon. She wasn't dressing up to impress anyone other than herself and the choice to turn on the sex appeal was up to her. For a mid-sized luxury brand, the Céline show was always deemed important on the schedule, and Philo ran a tight ship with limited invites to her shows and even more limited press interactions. Simply put, Slimane's work does speak to the Philophile. A part of the resentment towards him comes from a lack of acknowledgement for his predecessor. The second wave of anger, is due to the fact that he isn't contributing anything new to the industry. Slimane could draw from a hundred references that inspire his photography, but instead he chooses the lazy ‘sex sells' formula, regurgitating clothes that have already existed previously. He uses the excuse of not ‘being weighed down with the past' to wipe out Philo's work and, ironically, do what he has always done. After John Galliano's disgraced exit from the house of Dior, the British-Spanish designer was given a second chance at a career at Maison Margiela. Breaking free of his own legacy at Dior, Galliano took on the challenge to create something simply unique that's neither old Maison Martin Margiela, nor Dior or John Galliano, but instead, a true reflection of his understanding of the brand's narrative. Slimane's Celine will sell just like his work at Saint Laurent, which also showed a surge in profits. But the larger question at hand is, how long will a giant like LVMH rely on a ‘star' designer to helm the design of the future? After all, the likes of Alessandro Michele, Maria Grazia Chiuri, even Natacha Ramsay-Levi, rose from the ateliers of luxury houses and created unique work when given the chance to showcase a fresh perspective. And as for Phoebe Philo, there hasn't been a moment when the designer was missed more. The frankly woke fashion audience has no room for Slimane's myopic vision. In his attempt to erase Philo's legacy, he has only brought her into conversation more than ever before. Here's a look at some of Philo's best work at Céline.
