column1: Here’s why it’s time to bring the scarf print back into your wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get with this vintage-inspired trend When Richard Quinn, winner of the first ever Queen Elizabeth II Award for British Design, showcased his fall/winter 2018 collection in London, it was all anyone could talk about. Quinn's show was attended by none other than the Queen herself, who sat next to fashion royalty Anna Wintour—a front row image that made it to every fashion enthusiast's social media feed. Quinn's riot of prints—florals, polka, animals—all clashed in unholy harmony, but not without acknowledging the Queen's love for scarves. Held together in a dress, fashioned into trousers or simply worn as headscarves, it was a telling of the season ahead. Iconic Italian fashion house Versace can be credited as being the starting point of the obsession with scarf prints. The '90s era Versace, under the helm of the late founder Gianni Versace, created the house's signature by fashioning second-skin trousers and shirts in the house's instantly recognisable logos and colours. Given the current obsession with the decade, it's no surprise that Versace's fall/winter 2018 collection looked into the house's archives to revive the look. Marine Serre, winner of the 2017 LVMH Prize, also took the scarf and showcased a plethora of ways to wear it, apart from its predictable avatars as a headgear or a dress. At Serre's fall/winter 2018 show, the billowing swathes of fabric were draped onto rash guards, styled as earrings and also converted into bags. View Gallery 6 Photos How and why you should be wearing scarf prints now-2 Fashion enthusiasts have been on the trend since it was spotted on the runway during the spring/summer 2019 shows. Swishy printed skirts paired with solid T-shirts or all-over patterned dresses—the vintage-inspired look is having a moment. Would you prefer to invest in a scarf-printed halter top and pair it wide-legged jeans, or pick an archive-print bum bag from Burberry? column1: You can now buy Payal Khandwala’s most-loved pieces online
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer is all set to expand the consumer experience of her label With two stores in Mumbai and New Delhi (at Ogaan), and a recently launched space in Bengaluru, artist-turned-designer Payal Khandwala's latest venture is a debut into the realm of e-commerce. Khandwala's foray into online sales comes with the singular intent of creating an ease in the purchase of her products. “The label has grown at a very gradual pace. Once we realised that we have a growing client base that is unable to travel to our flagship stores, or the multi-designer stores that house our pieces, we made the organic move to e-comm,” said the designer. A new vertical for the brand, you can expect to see a selected range of their most loved pieces that are constantly in demand here—a wide range of handloom saris and their signature pleated classics. These garments do away with size restrictions, making the process of online purchases simple and easy. “Size and fit are crucial when it comes to online purchases. The pleated garments are very size inclusive and the saris bear no size constraints, making the online customer's buying options easier,” the designer explains about her choice of products that will be sold on the website. Known to serve understated elegance, the label's aesthetic lies in reimagining ethnic wear in a contemporary yet minimalistic form. Geometric silhouettes, layered separates, colour blocking and an extensive use of handwoven fabrics—these are the makings of a distinctive Payal Khandwala look, which has given way to a sizeable loyal customer base. With sales spread across cities in India and in parts of England, Singapore, North America and especially Middle East (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar), their focus is now on understanding the diverse range of their customers, and growing by catering to their unique sartorial choices. Khandwala wishes to adapt the label's on-ground service philosophy into their online store by providing the customer with an opportunity to connect with her team of brand representatives via call or social media. It goes without doubt that Khandwala plans to translate her detail-oriented design approach into her interface for the e-shop as well. Payalkhandwala.shop is live now. column1: Just do it: How Virgil Abloh is creating “Nike Couture”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Between the final fittings of his Off-White spring/summer 2019 show, Virgil Abloh talks to Vogue about collaborating with Nike, enlisting an Olympic cast of models for his show and how he’s elevating “athleisure”. You hear him before you see him. From the moment we arrive at the Off-White studio in the north-east of Paris, Virgil Abloh is a bursting with energy. Look away for one second and he's off, in a different corner of the room, talking to another set of people; iPhone forever in his hand, a smile and laugh never far from his face. Split across two levels, the studio is a hive of activity: catering, hair and make-up on the mezzanine level; a makeshift photo studio, the busy atelier and fitting corner filling the warehouse-like space below. Tables run along the sides of the giant white room – one side piled with shoes, accessories on the other. Everywhere there are towering mood boards reclining against tables and rails, neatly titled “Track & Field” – note the ubiquitous Abloh quotation marks. Like the jazz playing in the background, it is an organised chaos; a hundred things happening at the same time with no seeming order but in perfect harmony. It is the day before the Off-White show and final fittings are in full swing. Jourdan Dunn waits patiently; Bella Hadid and Kaia Gerber slip in silently, flurries of action following them the second the studio spots their presence; then the Olympians enter. British sprinter Dina Asher-Smith and track and field star Katarina Johnson-Thompson take the scene in excitedly. Did they ever imagine they would walk at Paris Fashion Week? “That's the first time someone has actually said [it like] that,” says Johnson-Thompson, still somewhat bewildered that this is in fact reality. Joining them on the runway will be high jumpers Vashti Cunningham and Cecilia Yeung, 100m dash champion English Gardner, Colombia's Caterine Ibargüen, Belgium's Nafissatou Thiam and the French runner Rénelle Lamote. Together, they will sport Abloh's latest collaboration with Nike, his Nike Running and Nike Women debut. Of course, it is an evolution from previous projects. Last year saw him reimagine ten models from the brand's sneaker archive, including the classic Air Jordan 1s, Air Max 90s and Air Force 1s. Earlier this year he dressed Serena Williams for the the US Open. This time around he's focusing on the total look. “[I asked myself,] what can I add to something that is seemingly already perfect?” says the creative polymath. Here, the American designer, DJ and music producer talks exclusively to Vogue about merging athletic apparel with fashion (not athleisure), championing women on a global scale and his fuss-free approach to balancing so many different projects at once. “Essentially, it is femininity crashed against athletic apparel and sport. The juxtaposition is how you know something happened; that is the crash. There's textures, there's silhouettes. The shoes for example, I started with a very athletic shoe and crashed it into a very feminine high heel. Take the suiting: there's a biker short, but in tailoring. That's the crash in 3D. The end result is Off-White; it's a metaphor.” “Whenever I'm doing a collection, I'm inspired by the world around us. Not in a flowery way of ‘I saw something out a car window', it is more [about] the social context of womenswear now, women in culture and how they are represented. I also noticed – at least in America, in my social circle – that an active lifestyle is becoming the norm. It is a lifestyle: be healthy, live healthy, eat healthy and work out. So workout apparel donning this name ‘athleisure' to me was not fully embracing fashion as a united idea, so I wanted to merge this athletic apparel with fashion but in a way that it's organic.” “They are totally different. If you could combine the best of athletic wear – its performance, its fabrication, its sensibility – and bend that into fashion, what does performance apparel look like? Or what does fashion look like after it has [gone through] this thought process? That is where a lot of the fabrics and the silhouettes came from. It's ‘Nike couture'.” “In my mind it was natural to have real athletes [in the show]. I do fashion to tell a narrative. In my mind, the muse is the athlete. These Olympic athletes, they train for a living, they live in workout clothes. So I wanted to see what these clothes look like on real women who actually do that. I think it can extend out to the girl who likes to work out and loves athletic wear.” “Working with Nike this time was more apparel-focused; it's more a total look than just focusing on the T-shirt. What I feel like I can add is the flair of relevancy or the lifestyle. Not so much the product itself, but why wear the product or how can the product be intriguing? What would make an athlete feel prideful? Or confident? Like they look their best? I believe that little extra element, which is above and beyond the product, can make someone perform even further - thereby achieving a better result.” “In a weird way, the key is not to think about it. I don't sit and think, ‘Oh, I'm working a lot.' Every idea that comes to mind I execute or I look for outlets to put out ideas. I just do it.” View Gallery 11 Photos Just do it: How Virgil Abloh is creating “Nike Couture” Culture & Living Culture & Living Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What does it take for an Indian designer to go international?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice talks life after the International Woolmark Prize If the past eight months of designer Ruchika Sachdeva's life are anything go by, percolating international markets, from Mumbai to Brooklyn, have been a by-product of winning the International Woolmark Prize earlier this year. From Vogue India's September cover co-star Radhika Nair wearing a pleated silk dress by the designer, to singer ELSZ sporting a pair of billowing trousers of exacting tailoring for her performance in Brooklyn, and just a few days ago, Anushka Sharma stepping out in a milk chocolate dress by her label (and one in navy as well) during the promotion rounds for her upcoming feature, Sui Dhaaga—Bodice's several sightings in just under a month prove that designer Ruchika Sachdeva is omnipresent right now. But it wasn't always like this. Ask any young designer and they'll tell you, to survive the fashion industry, you need a) talent; b) a business head; c) the kind of push that money brings; and a recent but highly important addition—d) charisma for marketing a brand story so unique, it could make the most jaded fashion folk optimistic again. When Sachdeva entered the International Woolmark Prize battle of the brands, she had a, b and d down pat, but lacked the missing ingredient of a financial surge to take her brand to global audiences. The Prize, previously won by Karl Lagerfeld, Yves Saint Laurent and recently Rahul Mishra, has done a lot for Sachdeva, who is still revelling in the aftermath of winning. A new appointment-only studio at Delhi's Green Avenue, stockists in the world's best department stores and 20 per cent new hires later, former Vogue India Fashion Fund winner, Sachdeva spills all. I definitely felt them many times. I would think to myself, “Oh my God, this is difficult”, because the level and quality of work that is presented there is phenomenal. Having said that, I noticed some judges spending time with me and asking a lot of questions during the final presentation in Florence, just before the results were announced. At that point, I felt like, okay, they are interested. There were 25 judges and most of them [were names] I have looked up to for a long time. Sarah Mower, for one, is a champion of new talent, and she says it like it is. So a lot of useful advice came from her in the form of questions. Designer Phillip Lim is so exceptional, and for him to hang around my spot and ask me many questions… you could see that he really appreciated what I was trying to do. I don't think I have ever tried to go out of India, perhaps because I wasn't sure and the judges showing keen interest [in me] kind of gave me that confidence to feel ready. Samantha McCoach of Le Kilt was also in the competition and she is from London, a part of London Fashion Week and was [someone who was already] selling in all the stores I wanted to! In my head, I thought “god, she's already made it." In India, when you see the bigger perspective, it seems like we are really far away. And international press rarely hears about us—so overall, I was up against a lot. I think the attention to detail helped Bodice stand out. In fact, for me it's just the result of overthinking everything, even my clothes, but the judges were fascinated by how I thought about the button of the garment, what was used to coat the button, the thread used in the embroidery, each yarn of the fabric. I wanted to get international exposure, knowing how saturated and competitive it is out there. Having said that, India still remains my most-favoured market, because it's open-minded and welcoming. From the start, I've been very watchful to expand slowly and strategically. I didn't want to spend all the prize money on a big international show, and then feel a little lost afterwards. The main takeaway has been the relationships in the industry. Liya Kebede presented the Prize to me in Florence, and now I just met her in New York, just to say hi and hang out. Developing these relationships from different industries and hearing their feedback makes you keep going on the right path. Another outcome has been launching Bodice Studio, a premier line of the main label. This has been a long-time dream. The line provides me creative freedom, when I wasn't able to do many things in the past due to financial constraints. I can now use exquisite fabrics, intricate techniques and experiment without worrying. For example, saris used to be made out of wool and silver earlier, or silk and silver, and that, over time, changed—and now, everything is made out of polyester. Now, I can use merino wool with steel, and make a fabric out of that, which I could not have dreamed of at a Bodice price point. I have also moved into a bigger studio that is attached to a large glasshouse-like retail space, which will be open to public soon too. The idea was to make an experiential space, because a brand like Bodice goes beyond clothes. We will offer made-to-measure luxury in its true sense—like dry cleaning services to take it one step beyond the regular. We've hired more people to make all this possible as well. We already had a lot of tailors, but I realised that we really required more managerial staff. Now, we have an in-house marketing person, a pattern master and a quality-control guy. The biggest opportunity has been to stock at the most prestigious stores around the globe, which has led to a sustainable business. With this has also come the opportunity to showcase at the right places every season—New York, Paris or London, where we can be seen by the right people. International attention from press has helped increase awareness about the brand, which will eventually lead to people buying the product, and there is not a greater joy than seeing your garment on a real person. What else do you do, really? You have a label, you want to take it outside India, you showcase it at the right places, get to know the right people and hopefully things just go from there. I think one of the biggest pain-points as young designers in this country is having to do everything ourselves. There are, of course pros and cons to it. When you are doing everything yourself, you can really control things and do it exactly the way you want, but to grow from there can be challenging. For how long can you micromanage? I'm learning this as I venture out of my comfort zone. Another cliché that we, as Indians away from home, might slip into is ending up doing an Indo-western fusion aesthetic, almost because it is expected of us. It is important to not be boxed-up by this. It is important to break free from that creative barrier, as much as it is important to be rooted in a certain Indian-ness, because that's what makes us authentic. column1: How the Atelier India project is bringing Indian designers to Dubai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Will their labels find a permanent home in the Emirate? In case you didn't know it, Dubai seems to be witnessing its own mini ‘India Fashion Week', as a host of Indian designers make their way to the fashion-forward emirate. Suneet Varma will soon be coming to town for a private showcase of his couture 2018 collection, which he presented at India Couture Week 2018 in July this year. And Payal Singhal is set to host a trunk show at the multi-brand store, The Rack by Kachins, too, with pieces from her fall/festive 2018 line that she previewed last month at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2018. Indian designers coming to Dubai to host trunk shows and pop-ups is not exactly a novel concept, but now, it is being taken a step further. Robinsons, one of Singapore's most iconic department stores, opened a 200,000sqft space at Dubai Festival City last year, which made them largest department store in the United Arab Emirates. Now, news is that they will dedicate some of this space to Indian fashion. The brand's latest project, ‘Atelier India', will include the work of four Indian designers handpicked by the store, namely Raghavendra Rathore, Rajesh Pratap Singh, Shantanu & Nikhil and Rohit Bal. Adosh Sharma, general manager, Robinsons, who has been working in retail in the Middle East for almost 15 years, says, “There is a lacuna among premium departmental stores in addressing the paradigm shift in the lifestyle of Indian diaspora in the region. The fact is, there is a huge audience for Indian fashion among Indians, Pakistanis and Emiratis.” The exhibition will be in-store from September 27 to October 20, 2018, and has been tailored to appeal to Dubai's diverse market, which includes Arabs, Indian, Pakistanis, as well as the expatriate European community. “Indian designers are a potent force, they are creating waves in the West and it is time to showcase them differently,” Sharma adds. For the opening on Thursday, a runway show is being presented at the InterContinental Hotel in Dubai Festival City, where each designer will showcase ten pieces from their collection. But the clothes for the Atelier India project have been tweaked to keep retail reality in mind. Shantanu & Nikhil's looks are curated from their ‘Independence' collection, shown at New Delhi in July, which featured a more progressive take on fashion by blurring lines between womenswear and menswear. The looks will have the feel of their runway show, but will be a more commercial line that keeps the Middle Eastern women's dressing style in mind—it includes many fluid gowns that are more about cut than embellishment. “The pieces retailing at the Atelier India are toned down for wearability and pricing. But the show pieces can be special-ordered,” explains Rohit Bal of his own curation. His showcase will be from his ‘Guldastan' collection, which was full of references from his home state, Kashmir, and was first presented at India Couture Week 2018. Rajesh Pratap Singh has kept his designs as close to the runway show as possible too, adding shapes that the store suggested would work better for the Middle Eastern sensibilities. His offering will come from his fall/festive 2018 show, which he presented on Sustainable Day at the most recent edition of Lakmé Fashion Week, while Raghavendra Rathore, who is best known for his bandhgalas and his aversion to participating at any fashion weeks, will bring catwalk pieces that are usually revealed to bespoke clients, at this Dubai presentation. While Sharma admits that the concept started as a Diwali promotion, he realised Indian fashion needed a proper showcase in Middle East through his meetings. “We aim to expand base further,” he says. While stores like Harvey Nichols, Bloomingdale's and Wafi Mall's Salam have all flirted with Indian designers, most ‘made in India' labels have found it hard to become part of the organised retail system, which is why they oft choose to take pop-up route. Rohit Bal, for one, has been a part of several flash retail experiences in the city. “The Middle East is a huge market for Indian fashion, and not just with the Indians who live there. There is a similar aesthetic and I have not done as much as I would like to be more active in the Middle East. My label has to be presented and shown properly, and this is what Robinsons is doing with Atelier India. I would say they are testing the waters. They did say if this does well, they will look at working with Indian designers permanently.” The space also gives the participating designers a real chance to understand the market better. Rajesh Pratap Singh says, “I am excited to see how we do in Dubai and see what sells. I would love to spend more time there, but to be honest, internationally it has been all about Paris for us so far.” The timing and curation of this exhibition has made this one special for Nikhil Mehra of Shantanu and Nikhil too. “I think we forget Indian fashion is young and recently there has been a maturity in design,” explains Mehra. “Over time we have learnt how to keep our ethos Indian, yet [keep] our look very global. And I think that is what all the designers who are part of this have in common. Our styles are very different, yet we all work together.” Could Robinsons' Atelier India project prove to be the start of Indian fashion receiving the mainstream distribution that it has been looking for? column1: How to ace the crop top and skirt combination like a Bollywood celebrity
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Name a better duo; we’ll wait There was a time when crop tops were reserved for beach vacays and lazy summer days, but the all-pervasive longevity of this '90s comeback means that you can throw on your favourite itsy-bitsy top in the morning, regardless of what weather it is outdoors. If you've been facing denim ennui though, time to give your favourite ripped pair a rest and allow another worthy candidate to take its place: the humble maxi skirt. Absolutely fuss-free and universally flattering for every body type—can we get an amen? The best-dressed crew of Bollywood clearly agrees; breakout star, Janhvi Kapoor allowed her Dhadak promotions wardrobe to be dominated by basic crop tops and breezy skirts. In keeping with the memo for casual daywear, she picked a slew of monochrome tops and printed skirts from Anamika Khanna and Label Anushree. Gentle braids and dewy, romantic makeup completed the vision of the blushing debutante. Still on the fence about working prints for the festive season? Allow Shraddha Kapoor to lead the way; the Stree actress has been boldly taking on the delicate task of mixing prints with a host of abs-baring crop tops paired with flowy, printed numbers. Her go-to hack for avoiding OTT territory? Pick from the same colour palette; like her AM:PM separates—or if you are up for some adventure, you can look to her co-ordinated crop top and skirt from Nikhil Thampi for inspiration. Those in love with layering can take cues from the fashionista herself; Sonam K Ahuja takes her crop tops and skirts with a coordinated jacket. Fearless in the face of metallics for daywear, she styled her DVF separates with sneakers and a basic black crop top to avoid letting the ensemble overwhelm her. Similarly unafraid to play with head-to-toe colour, an event earlier this year saw her pairing a ruffled Rosie Assoulin crop top and skirt with a jacket in the same hue. If you'd like to dial things up a notch, take notes from the hottest momma on this side of town, Kareena Kapoor Khan. The promotions run of Veere di Wedding saw her stepping out in coordinates from Abraham & Thakore; with her hair tied back, she let her vacay-ready abs take centre stage instead. column1: From sketch to catwalk: The Dior spring/summer 2019 collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In an exclusive interview, creative director Maria Grazia Chiuri discusses dance and deliverance in the modern woman’s wardrobe for Dior’s spring/summer 2019 show “I broke my femur in December and it's taken six months of work [to recover]. That's probably why I'm obsessed with dance,” explains Maria Grazia Chiuri between fittings, the Saturday evening before the Dior show. Though she is fully recovered, the creative director's desire for movement is tangible in her spring/summer 2019 collection, not simply splashed across her mood board, across which twirl dancers Loie Fuller, Pina Bausch and Isadora Duncan, but through liberating Dior's traditional codes. To wit, she removed the corsetry that anchors Dior's gowns and replaced them with gauzy, translucent tank-top shapes and liquid-silk jersey gowns. Her favourite dress, made of no less than 90 metres of blushing nude tulle, highlights a lineup of feather-light fabrics in hand-painted degradé—rose to honey, seafoam greens to blues—so delicate they cling to the touch as much as they float away on a breath: tulle macramé pieces realised in exacted detail; a patchwork-silk scarf dress with double print; silk jersey chiton-style dresses; tie-dyes; bleached denim; and head-spinning micro treatments—a kaleidoscopic feather embellishment is particularly dizzying in its detail. All bolstered, of course, by Grazia Chiuri's alchemic ability when it comes to accessories. This season, the Saddle Bag (which has a perpetual waiting list) is shrunk down to a belt bag and flattened into a pochette as sheer as a crepe. Plexiglass-heeled wedges emulate a ballet dancer's foot in motion and there is an elegant pair of nude sneakers, which—though constructed to be high-performance—are likely to be safeguarded for far more special occasions. Here, the Italian designer talks exclusively to Vogue about her inspiration for the collection—and the Dior woman. “I tried to translate this idea of lightness and freedom. So we have many Dior references, but I took off all the corsets and put inside a tulle lining to maintain the drape. For the first time at Dior, I did dresses in silk jersey—it's very good for modern women to put in their luggage! The shape is really Dior, but in jersey it's completely different. People think that with [the brand] it's about the silhouette—very 1950s—but Dior is not about shapes, it's about femininity. So we found materials to maintain this code in a contemporary but different way.” “The process is not easy. Honestly, in fashion creativity is important, but also discipline. If you don't work [with discipline] it's impossible to maintain or realise this kind of job. So I use intuition and passion, but at the same time discipline. It's very important for me to test new things—such as the silk jersey—it's a new adventure. I think to be in fashion today as a luxury brand you have to maintain your heritage but to ‘renovate' what is iconic for you.” “The inspiration is dance: fashion speaks about the body in the same way dancing does—it's like music, it's a universal language. Last year, we did costumes for the ballet at the Guggenheim, so I asked [choreographer] Sharon Eyal to work with us on a performance for the show. Sometimes we can be too closed in our worlds and I think this kind of collaboration is very important, with a woman especially. “ “Normally with bags you think more of maroquinerie [leather craftsmanship], but in this collection, the kind of craftsmanship we are using is closer to couture. [Some styles] are entirely embroidered and with no leather. The Dior Book Bag done in this way is something new. We are working more closely with the world of couture.” “I think it's very important now that you give women a real wardrobe. Sometimes the idea of a couture brand is too [inaccessible]. I think couture means to take care—and that means to give women different options to empower them for different occasions. I think a couture brand like Dior, with iconic pieces, has to be timeless and propose that with a few pieces you can have a Dior wardrobe.” View Gallery 9 Photos From Sketch To Catwalk: The Dior SS19 Collection Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Nimish Shah’s new gig with Anand and Sonam Ahuja is fashion serendipity
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Are you ready for the new Bhaane? “The conversation started a few weeks ago and it all moved very fast,” Nimish Shah tells us, pleased about his new appointment as the creative director at Bhaane—the cool kids clothing label by entrepreneur Anand S Ahuja. Ever since tying the knot with Sonam K Ahuja, the fashion couple is on a mission to evolve the premium high-street label focused on street culture and normcore aesthetics. First came the launch of the sneaker store Veg Non Veg and Bhaane's outlet in Bandra, Mumbai, and now, the attention is on crafting a defined fashion identity for the label. “Bhaane is an evolving brand with a contemporary vision. Both Nimish and I are aligned in this vision and excited about the opportunities our market has to offer,” said Anand S Ahuja. Shah will be moving to New Delhi to assume his new responsibility while remote-operating his own minimal—on occasion fuelled by whimsy—decade-old fashion label, Shift. Bhaane comes with a dedicated team of professionals that specialise in product development, womenswear and menswear. “Bhaane has a great team of cherry-picked industry professionals that have been doing a great job thus far. The idea is to make a focused noise on what Bhaane means,” Shah tells us. His vision for the label is a 2.0 version of Bhaane, tailored to taste of the millennial customer. “We have seen industry evolve in the last 10 years or so. The consumer is looking for a more conscious product.” To Shah, this means more collaborations with artists, musicians and putting the spotlight on the subculture Bhaane stands for. “It may not always be a direct translation into a product but it could be about enhancing user experience.” In a statement on the new step for the label, Sonam K Ahuja said, “I have always admired Nimish's design and aesthetic and worn his creations frequently over the years. His penchant for cool vintage and finesse in fashion will expand Bhaane's rationale while still exciting our loyalist.” Bhaane will continue to maintain its accessible price points while putting out an evolved product. Showcasing at a fashion week, too, is not entirely outside the realm of possibility. Will the new Bhaane under the helm of Nimish Shah be India's answer to a cult favourite brand? column1: Paris Fashion Week: What to expect from the spring/summer 2019 shows
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ahead of the spring/summer 2019 shows in the French capital, Vogue previews the labels to keep an eye on, from the innovating newcomers to the heritage houses with exciting new stories to tell “People don't take trips, trips take people,” John Steinbeck famously wrote. And the same can be said about this Paris Fashion Week. Each season, the city of love and lights closes a month-long marathon by offering couture and croissants to its drained crowd, and for the spring/summer 2019 shows, which kicked off on September 24, as well as the usual grandiose productions and age-old craftsmanship, show-goers will be presented with an alternative take on Parisienne chic with a raft of inclusive labels, eco-conscious projects and multimedia performances. In an industry as hyperactive as it is hyperconnected, the maisons' revolving doors are turning faster than ever, leading to notable absentees. Since parting ways with Olivier Lapidus after a mere eight months, Lanvin has retracted from the schedule and is to return once a successor has been named. The same decision was made by designer-less Lacoste after ending its eight-year collaboration with Felipe Oliveira Baptista last May, an alliance that spearheaded the current athleisure trend, leaving big shoes to fill. Following the departure of Guillaume Henry, Nina Ricci is also a no-show—but not for long. Its new creative duo, Rushemy Botter and Lisi Herrebrugh, is already working on the pre-fall 2019 collection and aficionados are curious to see how the pair's vision (think cultural mash-ups and kooky upcycling) will be rethought for the house's streamlined elegance. As for Carven and Vanessa Seward, both are taking a sabbatical season while looking for new investors; Undercover is switching from a runway to a presentation format; and ANDAM-winning Avoc is taking time off—a reaction against today's endless acceleration? Launched four years ago by Pierre Kaczmarek, when he was still at high school, and his stylist girlfriend Elena Mottola, Afterhomework makes its official fashion week debut, as does Ottolinger, the Berlin-based label founded by Swiss-born Christa Bosch and Cosima Gadient, which dressed Beyoncé for her On The Run Tour. Other newcomers include Ukrainian designer Anton Belinskiy's eponymous brand, and Natalia Alaverdian's A.W.A.K.E label. Last but not least, tech-meets-craft shoe label BOTH, spotted on the feet of Bella and Gigi Hadid, will expand into a full-blown womenswear collection. Cédric Charlier is also back in the calendar, and L'Oréal, which inaugurated its first runway collection last season on the Champs-Élysées, is expected to produce an equally lavish event. For one season only, Gucci is eschewing Milan for Paris (at legendary club Le Palace, no less) in its third and final homage to France, after a resort show in Arles and a May 68-inspired pre-fall collection. London-based label Marques'Almeida is also returning to Paris after being awarded the LVMH Prize in 2015. After presenting his autumn/winter in New York, Esteban Cortazar—the former head of Ungaro who famously left after Lindsay Lohan was brought into the creative team—is shipping his bold feminine silhouettes back to Paris, while Zadig & Voltaire is paying its hometown a visit for a show that will accompany the launch of its new scent, Girls Can Do Anything. While France is best known for haute couture, its niche labels are attracting serious attention—and investment. From Thom Browne, recently acquired by Ermenegildo Zegna, to Dries Van Noten, bought by the Puig group, these moves follow a David and Goliath-esque trend pioneered by Diesel's purchasing of Margiela in 2003 and LVMH taking shares in JW Anderson in 2013. Fashion is something of a cultural barometer, so it's no surprise that balaclavas, bulletproof vests and army pants (an influence the internet has nicknamed warcore) popped up all over Paris menswear week back in June as terror attacks, police brutality and the migrant crisis continue to make worldwide headlines. And the toughened lines and Amazonian silhouettes in the recent women's collections are no doubt a reaction to the #BalanceTonPorc movement—France's equivalent of #MeToo. See Sacaï's hybrid bomber-military jackets, Loewe's belted black leather coats and Koché's couture cargo pants, as well as Dior's last show, which opened with a jumper emblazoned with the words “C'est non non et non” (It's no, no and no). At a time where (some) creative directors have a wider following than the brand they work for, choosing the right designer is more complex than ever. From streetwear-inspired Kim Jones, fresh at Dior Homme, to über-connected Virgil Abloh's hyped first show for Louis Vuitton menswear, the position now requires a multi-layered, 360-degree vision. A challenge Hedi Slimane has taken on too, as he is about to present his highly anticipated debut collection for Celine. Far from the boyish rock 'n' roll lines he is best known for, the pieces will have to rethink the house's minimalist heritage, fit for the 3.0 age, something he's already made a start on by unveiling a reworked, 1960s-inspired logo (losing the é) days before the show (a buzzy tradition he started at Saint Laurent when he dropped the “Yves”). The French have dozens of word for “rumour”—rumeur, ragot, potins, qu'en dira-t-on, bruit de couloir, ouï-dire to name just a few—which is especially handy when fashion week approaches, as the semaine comes with an incessant flow of whispers. Following a viral article suggesting Vetements' sales were floundering, Demna Gvasalia took to Instagram to deny all gossip. More recently, word on the street had it that Nicolas Ghesquière was leaving Louis Vuitton to launch his own brand. The designer announced the renewal of his contract on his personal platforms. One stereotype that remains true about the French is their undying passion for intellectualism—so trust Paris to organise, right in the middle of a back-to-back schedule, a cycle of fashion conferences hosted by the Fashion Institute of Technology's Valerie Steele at the Palais de Tokyo, in partnership with the prestigious Ecole des Hautes Etudes en Sciences Sociales. Equally highbrow, Guerlain is celebrating its 190th anniversary by curating an exhibition opening on September 19, featuring leading contemporary artists such as Christian Boltanski and Jean-Michel Alberola. And that's not all: consultant Laura Brown is holding a series of talks in which models and journalists will discuss women's empowerment; indie magazine Antidote is launching its next issue (the theme of which is excess) in a talk focusing on the sociology of consumerism; model Regina Demina is presenting a conceptual multimedia performance reflecting on Greek myths; and Unemployed magazine will be revealing a collaborative fanzine it has created with contemporary artist Reto Schmid. Last but not least, surrealist accessories designer Yazbukey will be showcasing her latest creations in the form of a performance centred around gym culture, reflecting on the current fitness craze. While the wider population in France still holds its foie gras dear, in fashion there is a growing appetite for a more eco-conscious stance. Leonard Paris, headed by hip designer Christine Phung, will feature jewellery by Alama on its runway—a sustainable, ethical brand that promotes traditional designs entirely handmade by Maasai women in collaboration with an NGO. The city's first vegan concept store Manifeste011 will host an event with Casa93, a free fashion design school set up in the modest banlieue of Saint-Ouen. A line of fully upcycled clothes designed by the students, will be staged and the sales donated to Moda Nova, an organisation fighting to make design education more inclusive. With so much going against the (gros)grain this season, could the Zoolander era be over? column1: Ever wondered how a modelling agency really works?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Operating largely behind the scenes, model agencies are integral part of the fashion industry machine and are single-handedly responsible for cultivating the careers of their “talent”. Vogue went behind the scenes at Ford Models—the agency behind some of the biggest names in modelling to have emerged in the past 70 years—to find out more about their inner workings During Fashion Week, everyone is visible—the models on the runways, the designers, the army of backstage hair and makeup artists, press, celebrities and influencers; they're all on show 24/7 while the week plays out on Instagram. By contrast, modelling agencies are perhaps the ultimate-behind-the scenes players; their world is a much more closed-doors affair. And as our digitally-driven, socially switched-on era has changed our perception of models in recent years—from their Insta presence to their wellbeing and working conditions—agencies have also been changing with the times... But the curiosity still remains: what do modelling agencies do, exactly? As fashion month kicked off in New York City, Vogue went behind the façade of one of the world's foremost agencies—Ford Models—whose key players gave us an insight into how they operate in 2018. “I don't view the well-being of our models as a corporate initiative,” says CEO Nancy Chen, from her minimalist office in Manhattan's Flatiron District. “It is always part of the management plan to sit down with each individual talent and understand what they need.” Since becoming CEO in 2016, Chen has moved quickly to reposition a company that “had fallen a little out of favour editorially and gotten a little bit commercial... it needed to be restored”. There's no doubt that Ford has tremendous pedigree. Its founder, Eileen Ford, discovered some of the 20th century's most famous faces—Carmen Dell'Orefice in the 1950s; Jean Shrimpton in the 1960s; Jerry Hall in the 1970s; Christie Brinkley and Brooke Shields in the 1980s; and Christy Turlington and Naomi Campbell in the 1990s. But come the 21st century, Ford lost its matriarch—Eileen died aged 92 in 2014—and for a while seemed to be losing its way. Under Chen's direction, the agency is in the midst of an ambitious overhaul, looking to Eileen's founding principles as a way of responding to the landscape of 2018. “She was this grand matriarch who fought for her talent [and] wanted to make sure models were treated as businesswomen, not as props.” Ford was so formidable and so protective that one of Chen's favourite stories is how legendary photographer Richard Avedon “wouldn't dare shoot an extra minute into overtime without calling Eileen first”. Looking after the models' interests, both financial and emotional, was central to Chen's plan. Her first task was to find the right team—people, she says, who work “passionately and [understand that] the mission is bigger than any one of them.” Among them was Christopher Michael—a founding member of the Society Management, the US division of longtime Ford rival Elite World—whom she hired as chief creative officer. Chen's next move was to pare down the “talent” (what they call models) on Ford's roster, so that the team could really focus on quality—and care. There has been a lot of criticism of the modelling industry for allowing exploitive actions to go about unchecked. Last year alone, prominent photographers were accused of sexual harassment; an industry veteran called out casting directors who refused to see models of colour or who used underage models; and, according to one report, a large group of models was allegedly forced to wait in a darkened stairwell for hours while the casting directors went to lunch. Part of Chen's job is to prove she's fully committed to shaping each model's career—whether that means developing their social-media voice or customising a plan for healthy living. “My role is making sure I'm there for them,” says Chen. “And sometimes it's moral support and listening on my couch. I'm the mother hen”. After joining Ford Models in May 2017, Chief Creative Officer Christopher Michael enlisted famed art director Fabien Baron—who had worked with Eileen in the past—to oversee the rebranding of the agency. Another major change Michael spearheaded was to do away with the old-fashioned method of categorising the models by age or body type. “We've abolished that now-antiquated system,” says Michael. Ford no longer employs models under 18 and has begun to enlist non-binary and trans models, signing Asia Kate Dillon and Andreja Pejíc respectively. Michael also wants to focus on “ways to help our talent tell their own stories”, and because of the massive success of the so-called Insta Girls, such as Cara Delevingne and Karlie Kloss, everyone at the agency is invested in building the models' social presence. Michael has also launched two video series, one that documents the models' outside interests—boxing or painting, for example—to share with clients and a second collaborative project with Models.com, where industry leaders discuss important topics occuring in the business, from diversity to bridging the gap between print and digital media. During the frenetic flurry of activity in the lead-up to New York Fashion Week in early September, Michael is like the agency's air-traffic controller. Around the third week of August, Ford sends out its show package—a set of photocards depicting the 21 models they're putting forward for Fashion Week—via courier to casting directors, who work with the designers. Negotiations begin immediately, as casting directors vie to secure their top picks for the shows they're working on and models criss-cross the city to see casting directors, designers and stylists and confirm shows. “Certain brands know what they want, and others who might be known for, say, launching new faces, will be making changes up until the very last minute,” says Michael. Heading up the Ford office in Paris, Alexis Louison works with partners who scout new talent. For him, finding the next “face” is less about look and more about spark. “Today it's about the personality. You must be captivating on social media, so video is much more important than it was five years ago,” he says. While some new models might have a superstar like Karl Lagerfeld fall in love with their look and cast them immediately, others need time to learn to move, to pose, and to see if they even like the work. To avoid throwing them in at the deep end, Louison sends them to so-called development markets, such as Tokyo, or his favourite, Singapore—widely considered to be like a finishing school for runway walkers. They're cities that are safe and have smaller markets open to new faces. “We try to make sure the girls come into the main Fashion Weeks—Paris, London, Milan, and New York—with as much confidence and experience as possible.” For James Wood, who has been working as the manager of the women's talent division for just three months, his job as an agent is to be a point person, handling requests from certain casting directors. Wood got his start while studying fashion and realised he cared more about the models than the clothes. He's learned a lot about the importance of Fashion Week for models at every stage of their career—for newcomers, it's the key to getting noticed, while for more seasoned professionals, it's all about creating a buzz around cameo appearances. “I'm working on how to build these girls into future supermodels,” he says. “There has to be a strategy for the new girls, because overexposure can be a problem, but so can a girl who is falling through the cracks because she's not doing all the top shows.” The industry has a poor reputation for churning out models and then moving on. The answer to that vicious cycle at Ford has been the new, leaner roster—so that they can really get behind each model they represent and ensure they're happy in the job. “[Some] girls will have given it a full year and travelled and made some money and decided they'd like to go to college—fashion isn't for everybody.” (And some new faces might bloom later. Some designers, including Rachel Comey in New York or Simone Rocha in London, have been known to use middle-aged models.) “My job is testament to where the industry is moving,” says Jeffrey Schnabolk, who heads up the nebulous-sounding Brand Management department, which brokers deals with brands and organises event appearances or capsule collections. “This is an industry and career that can have a short shelf life. We don't find it interesting to work with a girl for four years and then send her on her way, so the question is: how do we steer this ship? I work on how to amplify their voices.” The key to giving the models' career longevity, Schnabolk says, is to respect the audience. “They know what's genuine, and what they're not excited about.” Yorkshire-born Fran Summers has just turned 19 and, after being discovered in a Westfield shopping centre, has already appeared in Prada campaigns and on Vogue covers. So, this Fashion Week, she's already busy. Models often have their portfolios (aka “books”) on iPads but she prefers the more tangible version. “I still carry around a physical copy of my book, going between designers' headquarters, showrooms, studios,” she tells Vogue. She runs around town at a frantic pace, trying to go to as many appointments as possible in the few short days leading up to Fashion Week—up to 10 a day. At the casting appointments, she may be asked to demonstrate her runway walk, which she says has been a learning curve. “I didn't have a natural model walk because I never wore heels.” Now that she's more well-known and has got to know designers and stylists, she says the experience of castings is much chattier and more informal. When we meet, she is preparing to open the Tom Ford show, kickstarting a gruelling month of travelling to every fashion capital. On top of the hectic schedule of castings, meetings and fittings, there is no shortage of brand launches and after-parties to attend. She's good at saying no to most of it. At night, she's usually found having a mellow meal out with friends, or back at her hotel, FaceTiming her family and her dogs. “By the time I take the Eurostar home to London from Paris Fashion Week, I'm so tired,” she says. She has a vacation planned for when the madness ends, though: “After [all] this, I'm going to Florida with my sister and brother and we're going to Disneyworld for Halloween.” A fitting end to the frenetic Fantasia of Fashion Month. column1: Here’s why you should buy into this season’s trickiest fashion trend
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From the designers who got it right to the style mavens who braved the scene-stealing trend, have you been inspired to make a neon purchase yet? It's clashing. It's distracting. It reminds you uncomfortably of an awkward time in your life growing up. And though you probably can't quite place when you were first drawn to a loud neon yellow T-shirt, you're likely to remember wearing it lovingly till the hue had faded. The tricky colour way brings mental images of a Club Kid's life with it, lit with after-parties and fuelled by insomnia. It is equal parts exhausting and exciting, but also has a more important premise—while neon has been a highlight in the past, it now offers the promise of the future perfect. For instance, Olivier Rousteing imagined the runway of 2050 at Balmain this season, showcasing models dressed in bodycon dresses with vibrant bursts of neon alongside holographic sequins and space-age silver. While Miuccia Prada liberally splashed on neon on the Prada autumn/winter 2018 lineup to comment on the #TimesUp movement. The Italian label found the perfect metaphor in clothing for being seen, heard and unapologetically bold in cannot-be-missed palliates, tulle overlays and digital prints. And Maryam Nassir Zadeh, who's popular among the cool girl crowd for her aesthetic, which hovers between eclectic and minimalism, offered a paler, faded version of neon green in easy wardrobe separates like tailored trousers and shift dresses. And that's wasn't all—a simple swipe of eyeliner in traffic cone orange on the models made for an audacious yet simple touch of neon, perfect for someone trying to step out of their comfort zone to try the trend. View Gallery 3 Photos Neon fashion designers For an influencer like Kim Kardashian West, neon was a tool to channel her new avatar. From dyeing her hip-grazing mane in pale canary to accentuating her much-talked-about curves in shocking pink, Kardashian West has reinvented herself in a neon-centric wardrobe for the season. And the likes of Chiara Ferragni, Eva Chen and Gigi Hadid have tested the palette too, though without a closet of glow-in-dark clothing. While some influencers have given neon their whole-hearted approvals, others have played the fluorescent card subtly, like Hadid did with her Burberry trench. View Gallery 7 Photos What will you make of the season’s neon trend? Some might argue that neon, much like other shocking trends, is a passing fancy. These are expected to suffer the fate of a limited shelf life, and don't make for outfits that can be easily repeated. After all, how many times will you go to your local watering hole in that perfect garish turtleneck? But if you're still willing to invest in at least one piece that shocks your aesthetic, ensure that you make it count. There's Supriya Lele's twisted cut-out dress in spandex for the party girl in you, while Ashish has given the fluro dress a floral touch with a spangle of sequins too. Want to play it cool with the street style squad? Go with Balenciaga's eye-grabbing slip-on sneaker. And the minimalist can choose Off-White's bustier with just a hint of neon at the edging as well. Still hesitant to take the plunge? Scour your favourite high street stores for easy-on-the-wallet buys to encourage yourself to give the trend a try. column1: How to add the biggest ‘80s trends to your wardrobe today
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Tricky doesn’t even begin to describe the big, bad trends of the ’80s. Whether you’re testing the waters or taking the plunge, here’s a guide to bringing back the decade of excess Amidst the proselytising around what constitutes good taste (and doesn't), the most important point of the existence of fashion gets forgotten—freedom. In the history of fashion, every decade had its fashion moment—the miniskirt of the '60s, '70s bohemia, '90s denim. The 1980s were the decade of everything—of Cher and Brooke Shields, the red-leather danger of ‘Thriller' and the neonoir dystopia of Blade Runner, the dancy-aerobic energy of Jane Fonda and Jennifer Beals, of Madonna and her rugged net and lace, of Jerry Hall and her golden waves and lips like red lacquer, of shoulder pads that could balance planets and gold studs that could rival them. The autumn/winter 2018-19 runways paid the time the tribute it deserved—the neo-Dynasty glamour at Alexandre Vauthier and Tom Ford, the elegance of '80s haute couture at Marc Jacobs, the sequins and neon at Christian Cowan... Want to bring it to your own wardrobe? Here's how. [#image: /photos/5ce428beb8031122768f6a60]||| ||| Saint Laurent. Image: InDigital [#image: /photos/5ce428be4a30b3002b12cf9b]||| ||| Attico. Image: InDigital Where would we be without sequins? Those little disco balls of life and raucousness that we wear and carry everywhere. According to historians, sequins first made an appearance on the tomb of King Tut in Egypt. They were a significant element of the go-all-out aesthetic of the '80s, personified by the likes of Laurence Kazar and Oleg Cassini. Attico, the Milan-based label started by friends and street-style stars Gilda Ambrosio and Giorgia Tordini, is known for infusing everyday pieces with statement accents. Naturally, sequins are key: the sequinned wrap dress in verdigris that looked almost sunlit from A/W 2018-19; the now-iconic rainbow wrap dress from A/W 2017-18... Happy, sexy clothes, but also a little louche. “Among all the embroideries we use, we feel sequins are the perfect balance between elegance and fun, with a strong impact. I mean, which woman doesn't like sequins!” says Ambrosio. If too much shine scares you, Tordini recommends their drawstring sequinned pouches. The rule, she says, is of no rules. “We like it spontaneous, like the woman we have in mind when we design.” — Attico [#image: /photos/5ce428becc50beb58413f127]||| ||| Fausto Puglisi. Image: InDigital While Mary Quant popularised the miniskirt in the 1960s, it was in the '80s that they re-emerged, in glamorised versions of the original silhouette, but most notably in the form of the “rah- rah” skirts that took after cheerleader uniforms. Ever since, there's barely a season or label that doesn't feature some iteration. For Fausto Puglisi and his five-year-old label, the miniskirt has been a recurring silhouette—there were the A-line lampshade skirts of A/W 2018-19, the monochrome lace versions of the Carolyn Bessette Kennedy-inspired S/S 2018 collection... Puglisi explains, “Short is connected to positive vibes, freedom, music. Think of Mary Quant, the British boom, the happiness, the sense of freedom.” For Puglisi it comes down to carriage. “You can be vulgar wearing a long skirt and chic wearing a miniskirt. It's all about beauty, culture and personality... A woman today takes care of her skin and body! Why cover the legs if they are so beautiful? — Fausto Puglisi [#image: /photos/5ce428bfcc50be466713f12b]||| ||| Philipp Plein. Image: InDigital [#image: /photos/5ce428bff55c27be8fa27413]||| |||  Gareth Pugh. Image: InDigital Few subcultures have had as enduring an impact on fashion as '80s punk. Recall the pieces that constituted a means of expression then—leather biker jackets, studs and spikes, plaid flannel, Dr Martens and rock tees and ripped jeans—and you'll know they've somehow worked their way to your wardrobe. This was an era of anarchy, of fashion that was also anti-fashion. For designer Philipp Plein, punk has been a common denominator through his mega production shows. (Early on, he sent quite a clear message with his ‘Plein is Punk' tee.) Few designers are as much at ease with black leather and studs as Plein. In his hands, even pink can be punk, like the bubblegum punk version he sent out for resort 2015. Explaining the centrality of punk in his aesthetic, Plein says, “Music is an important part of my life and inspiration. Punk music and culture had an incredible impact on fashion from the '70s until our days.” It's tricky, he says, if stereotyped but cool if readapted. How does one incorporate punk into everyday wear? “Embellishments and accessories, makeup but also iconic elements of punk inspired fashion, such as tartan, black, fishnet socks and ripped clothing,” he suggests. — Phillip Plein [#image: /photos/5ce428bfb40d26ecf3d6c666]||| ||| Balmain. Image: InDigital [#image: /photos/5ce428bf3bf9b4370eb1c45a]||| |||  Chromat. Image: InDigital [#image: /photos/5ce428c0b8031114348f6a63]||| ||| Christian Cowan. Image: InDigital Jane Fonda's Workout came out in 1982, and that was the end of the world as we know it. There were the belted leotards, the slouchy leg warmers, the opaque tights. If it's cool to wear a pair of bike shorts with a blazer today, somewhere Ms Fonda is responsible. This was athleisure before we knew to call it that. For 23-year-old Cambridge-born designer Christian Cowan, who has found fans in the likes of Cardi B and Lady Gaga, his A/W 2018 show featured a strong exploration of neon athleisure, including ultra-cropped hoodies and plastic trench coats. For Cowan, who's already established a reputation for his flair with paillettes, neon was a continuation. “It is something I had been wanting to do for a while. I always use materials that reflect light, so I thought: Why wait till someone is in the right lighting?” Never pair neon with normal colour tones, he warns, as the neon washes them out and looks mismatched. Can neon be for everybody and everywhere? “Well, neon is certainly ageless—if it makes you happy, then do it! And neon is fit for all occasions if you want to be the star, but the best place is on vacation, especially Miami.” — Christian Cowan What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How fashion houses are reinterpreting their past for the future
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Reinterpreting and repurposing Fashion's newest game: seeing if you can put a date on Miuccia Prada's references. Recent collections have mixed everything from her early minimalist nylon pieces to mid-'90s geek-chic prints. Versace, meanwhile, couldn't be more Versace. Or Gucci more Gucci. Or Chanel more—you get the idea. Fashion's best-known names have been exploring their signatures—the visual cues that define their identity—like never before. The Baroque splendour of the late Gianni Versace's gilded extravagance? These days it's streamlined by his sister, Donatella, into everything from draped and fringed cocktailiana to treadmill-friendly sneakers. The instantly recognisable Chanel double-C logo? Forever reinvented—as a surfboard decal, a laurel wreath—via Karl Lagerfeld's imagination. (Lagerfeld's Chanel remains, after nearly four decades of reinvention, House Zero for the art of self-referencing.) By sampling and remixing the past with the stylistic hallmarks of the present—streetwear, logomania, gender fluidity and athleticism, for starters—these designers and others (Stefano Gabbana and Domenico Dolce; Anthony Vaccarello at Saint Laurent; Kenzo's Carol Lim and Humberto Leon) are making sense of right now. Witness what Demna Gvasalia is doing at Balenciaga: The architectural beauty of Cristóbal Balenciaga has been given a sidewalk slouch in the form of voluminous multilayered parkas that echo the shape of the house's iconic '50s haute couture opera coats. “Putting Balenciaga's aesthetic into a present-day context is a very important challenge,” says Gvasalia, “because the question of brand identity is more relevant than ever.” We live, after all, in an increasingly ephemeral and cacophonous era. When we've already scrolled through Instagram a dozen times since waking up (and when not much of what we've seen has truly stuck), the need for designers to state loudly and clearly who they are, and what they're about, has never been more crucial. Looked at another way, this inventive remixing of what we already know, and love is something we're already doing in our everyday lives: When we hashtag our yesteryears as #tbt and #fbf, why would designers be immune to the same impulse? “There would be no future—or even present, really—without the past for us to draw from,” says Dolce & Gabbana's Stefano Gabbana. Newness in fashion, then, is becoming less about some notion of the never seen- before and more about seeing something familiar in a new and unexpected context. After an era dominated by the invisibility of norm core and the coded insider cool of streetwear, this new go-iconic-or-go-home era is hugely welcome for its exuberance, it's fun, and—weird as it might be to say—its sense of value. The received wisdom was that to get the most out of designer purchases, focus on things that look as understated as possible because they'll last a whole lot longer. But where's the joy in that? Fashion is at its best when it's emotional—when it's what Saint Laurent's Vaccarello calls “an escapist fantasy,” not the closet equivalent of your 401(k). Take Gucci's iconic Flora pattern—a wild garden print rendered in nearly 40 colours, first seen in 1966 on a scarf made for Grace Kelly. Fifty-two years later, Alessandro Michele has taken that same motif, added the New York Yankees logo, and made a pyjama top out of it. By going big and unabashed—not to mention wildly, joyfully unexpected—Michele has breathed new life into much more than just that Flora print; he's gone full-throttle overboard with its iconic red-and-green stripe and the label's double-G logo. Far more than an impulse to flaunt, this new wave of playing with signature style is, deep down, a tug at our hearts. With our culture moving at lightning speed, this reusing and retinkering is both a mooring in the mayhem and an opportunity for creative reinvention. After all—a signature is what makes things official. View Gallery 12 Photos How these fashion brands are reinterpreting their iconic pieces Fashion Culture & Living Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What to keep in mind when shopping for vintage designer wear
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The co-founders of the iconic New York vintage institution share their top tips on bagging pre-loved treasures, just after celebrating their 25th anniversary with a one-off sale at Christie’s “When we began, there wasn't really a true appreciation for vintage,” says Seth Weisser, co-founder of New York's vintage specialist brand, What Goes Around Comes Around. Weisser set up shop in SoHo with his college friend Gerard Maione in 1993, focusing on authentic pieces from top tier brands in pristine condition. After 25 years in the business, they have transformed vintage fashion into a luxury all of its own, and are one of the most trusted destinations for high-end second-hand shopping today—a market which is showing no signs of slowing down. Reuters recently reported that vintage fashion is worth $25 billion in annual revenue, with a predicted yearly growth of 10 per cent—which is more than double that of the primary market's. “The truth is that vintage and pre-owned items are sometimes more exclusive than the actual new products,” says Weisser, adding that some items in their possession could be considered museum pieces. “We are seeing some top Christie's clients across the board—from fine art to interiors—gravitating towards vintage, which is even more celebrated than what they can buy in Barneys,” explains Caitlin Donovan, Christie's head of sales for handbags and accessories. “[Gerard and Seth's] immense understanding has really helped shine a light on this market.” To mark the shop's first quarter century, Christie's held a one-off auction on September 18, where around 220 of What Goes Around Comes Around's collectible pieces—including accessories from the Louis Vuitton by Stephen Sprouse 2001 collection, a Philippe Barland for Chanel surfboard and a series of multicoloured Hermès Kellys and Birkins—went under the hammer. We got in touch with Maione, Weisser and Donovan to find out more about their top vintage shopping tips. The first thing to remember, whether you're looking to make an investment or want a statement piece, is to always let your heart lead you. “Usually what we recommend is for people to go with what they feel really strongly about and what they love,” says Weisser. Sometimes, he says, customers decide to bet on niche brands in the hope that they will accrue value over time. Weisser takes the example of an Ossie Clark dress, bought maybe ten years ago when the brand wasn't particularly sought after, which has probably doubled its value by now. But if you do want your piece to hold investment value, Donovan suggests sticking with premier designer labels, and avoiding ‘It bags' or trend-driven pieces. “Some clients only collect Hermès from the 2000s, others only want vintage Chanel pieces from the 1970s,” she explains. “Each collecting category has its own degree of success.” Both Weisser and Maione agree that buying online can be risky unless it is from dealers you already know, or e-commerce websites connected to a trusted brick-and-mortar store. “I've noticed that in Europe, Vestiaire Collective is a very popular site, but the sellers are just private people putting their stuff up,” explains Maione. “Whether it's on eBay or anywhere else online, you don't have the ability to know how strongly these people are able to protect you.” It's essential to go to a reputable source when you're shopping in-store too. Some stores have a good, word-of-mouth reputation, but don't be afraid to ask questions about the shop, its owner, how it operates and the items you are interested in. “It's always a good sign when shop owners and clerks know about the origin and history of their pieces,” says Weisser. What Goes Around Comes Around prides itself on only trading in pristine items, a conviction that, according to the owners, should be waived only in exceptional situations—ie, when a one-of-a-kind or uber-rare piece that has been discontinued comes along. Some materials, such as leather and denim, will develop a natural patina with age, which is fine. Be wary of comparing prices between items that actually belong to different quality categories, though. “People are doing a lot of price checking online, but they are actually looking at a perfect Grade A bag, compared to something that might be a B-grade,” explains Maione. “They are looking at the pricing and thinking that's a great deal, then realising there are imperfections.” For Weisser, the general rule to follow is that if something seems too good to be true, it probably is. “There's no get-lucky reality,” he says. “People don't make that kind of mistake anymore.” According to Weisser, while some vintage buyers have particularly strong personal styles often associated with a specific era, others are also extremely cognisant of evolving trends, and often become early adopters. In recent years, the What Goes Around Comes Around shop floor has seen the birth of a couple of major trends, such as the return of the Fendi Zucca print and the popularisation of the Japanese sukajan jackets—the souvenir silk bomber jackets from the 1940s and 1950s which have been reworked by Gucci, Saint Laurent and Louis Vuitton. So what's the next big thing? Weisser is wary of giving a definite answer, but the focus seems to have shifted from specific styles to brands. “There's certainly a big demand for 1990s designer fashion, a little bit more statement [than before],” he says. “I've also seen a renewed interest in Gianni Versace, and both Fendi and Dior are very hot right now.” Scroll onwards for a look at Christie's x What Goes Around Comes Around 25th Anniversary auction preview, the sartorial pieces that were on showcase at the auction, and the vintage brand's Soho store. column1: What to expect from Milan Fashion Week spring/summer 2019
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ahead of the spring/summer 2019 shows in Italy’s fashion capital, Vogue previews the labels to keep an eye on—from the innovating newcomers to the heritage houses with exciting new stories to tell Milan is traditionally known for its elaborate productions. Last season, designers scaled up the atmosphere, transporting guests into dystopian realities where drones sent bags down the runway and models were accessorised with severed clones of their own heads. Kaia Gerber and Gigi Hadid walked alongside alien-like models at Moschino; otherworldly references were echoed at Jil Sander; and Prada immersed its audience in a virtual-reality wonderland, towering above the Italian fashion capital. In Milan, the performance is often as revered as the product, and in the age of virulent social media, everyone's mapping out their Instagram moment. But this Fashion Week (September 19-25) has a large void where there is usually an exclamation mark, with Gucci relocating to Paris to complete a three-part homage to France that has played out over the past year (the brand's Cruise 2019 collection was unveiled in Arles, and an ad campaign referenced the Paris protests of 1968). Will the absence of Alessandro Michele's theatrics dim the spotlight? No doubt—but never fear. While the legacy houses have all dialled up the innovation over recent seasons, a new wave of designers is infusing collections with a youthful energy that typically fades after the second stop in London. As if Gucci's absence weren't enough of an anticlimax for Milan,  Bottega Veneta is also bowing out—until autumn/winter 2019, that is, when newly appointed creative director Daniel Lee (a Central Saint Martins graduate, formerly at Céline) makes his debut. Gucci will return in February, CEO Marco Bizzarri has confirmed. In the meantime, perhaps the most unexpected addition to the schedule is sportswear giant Fila. The brand signalled its high-fashion aspirations last season, when Fendi re-appropriated its logo for a limited-edition capsule collection. Attico is one the most enchanting brands to come out of Milan in a long time, and since launching in 2016, it's become an industry favourite (Net-A-Porter, Moda Operandi and Bergdorf Goodman are just a few of its retailers). The vintage-inspired brand marks a return to elegance, with beautiful silhouettes, rich colour and artisanal detail. Designers Gilda Ambrosio and Giorgia Tordini describe it as “sophisticated but fun; luxury but also easy to wear”. Details on the presentation are yet to be revealed, but it's typically shown in a private residence. Other highlights include Philosophy di Lorenzo Serafini and Arthur Arbesser, the latter honed his skills under Giorgio Armani and was shortlisted for the LVMH prize in 2015. Moncler took out the coveted opening spot last season with its Genius project, featuring eight men's and women's collections created by different designers, including Simone Rocha and Valentino's Pierpaolo Piccioli. The outerwear specialist is scheduled on day one again and is slated to follow a similar narrative with a mixed-gender presentation, adding to a trend that has become more prevalent across the industry (including the Versace menswear show in June, where we saw Bella Hadid and Kendall Jenner modelling statement minidresses). Furla will also be presenting both men's and women's collections together for the first time on 20 September. “I think glamour all the time. I wake up in the morning and I'm already thinking glamour.” It's a quote that makes Donatella Versace seem even more charismatic, and a spirit that's informed her collections. This year, the 40th anniversary of Versace, also marks the point at which Donatella has now headed the brand for longer than her brother Gianni had before he died in 1997. The show is scheduled for 8pm on Friday night, and it's sure to be one of the week's most vibrant events. Another quintessentially Italian brand with something to celebrate is Missoni, marking its 65th anniversary. It will be interesting to see what Paul Surridge,  now on his third collection for Roberto Cavalli, will do this season, but if the recent lines are anything to go by, we can expect the routine mix of leopard prints, cut-outs and plunging necklines. Italy's fashion houses are as ingrained in its identity as its historic monuments—many of which have been restored by major Italian brands: the Trevi Fountain by Fendi; the Spanish Steps by Bulgari; Tod's €25 million donation to the Colosseum. The link the industry has to local culture is significant, but younger generations aren't seduced by status alone and recasting the grandeur of the past has been a key focus. Gucci has been a trailblazer in engaging millennials, who gravitate towards inclusive and creative brands. Dolce & Gabbana has also made moves to capture a younger audience, mining YouTube for talent and having young royals, including Lady Kitty Spencer, walk in its millennial-centric ‘secret show'—a supplementary event that has recently become the norm. Alberta Ferretti catered to the revived penchant for retro logomania in February (something we're sure to see more of), paying homage to Italy's national airline with an Alitalia capsule collection. And several long-established names—Prada, Fendi, Versace and Max Mara—mixed archives from the 1980s with aesthetics of the 2018 power woman (big shoulders and bold prints, perfectly attuned to today's visual culture). Mrs Prada has always been known to explore feminist themes, so we'll see how this plays out at the show on 20 September. Regardless, it's sure to be one of the week's headline acts. column1: 5 takeaways from Riccardo Tisci’s Burberry spring/summer 2019 debut
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In case you haven’t been paying attention New contexts are expected to produce the most interesting results. Shake things up a little bit, throw together people in places not seemingly natural cohabiters, and what comes out is more likely to surprise—and in a good way. Riccardo Tisci's appointment at the helm of Burberry, a house as intrinsically British as fish and chips, made the house's spring/summer 2019 show one of the season's most anticipated—an excitement spurred no less by the release of the house's new Peter Saville-designed logo (Burberry London England) and TB monogram (for the initials of founder Thomas Burberry) a few months ago. Monday night's show was the main event, a clever mash of sportswear-inspired softness and the welcome severity of classic tailoring amidst the streetwear explosion elsewhere. There were of course the trench coats, but there were also covetable slip dresses, cow-print skirts, mixed animal prints, multi-way scarfs, curtain fringes, flawless pencil skirts and artsy pockets—134 looks in a co-ed show that spelled out his designs on the label. Here are a few takeaways. Replacing the knotted belt of the classic trench with an elasticated belt, Tisci put the focus on the middle—cue his versions of peekaboo double-waist trousers and dresses, chain-belt bags for evening, and bicycle chain lock belts on the men. …and the peep-toe court shoes, and belt bags and umbrella holders and passport cover necklaces and sunglasses fit for their own Dele challenge. Accessories, those instigators of excitement, assumed centre stage here. …comes in tomato. Look to one silk shirt and the peek of colour on beige court shoes for inspiration.
