column1: Matchesfashion.com moves from e-commerce to a six storey retail space
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You’ve never enjoyed a retail experience like this before We all know fashion is cyclical. It's an industry that loves to dip into its own archives to find inspiration and then give it a fresh, new take. And that is exactly what London's MatchesFashion.com is doing. 31 years ago the first Matches store opened its doors in London's affluent residential area, Wimbledon. Known for its edit of super cool and independent labels, the brand soon opened a second store in the very trendy Marylebone and started to work with the big brands too. In 2006, the brand decided it was time to go e-tail—and today MatchesFashion.com has become every fashion girl's go-to digital destination. It was one of the first brick-and-mortar stores to make that jump into e-commerce. And today, alongside Moda Operandi and Farfetch, it is where every young designer hopes to make its e-tail home. But in an interesting turn of events, it seems like the time has arrived for fashion e-commerce to look to the past to stay on top of the curve. While fashion customers may love the ease and convenience of e-tailing, they miss the touch and feel that physical locations allow you to have with clothes and accessories. “Customers like to connect, to engage,” explains Jess Christie, chief brand officer. That's why when the brand turned 30 last year, they looked at pop-up concepts in New York, Los Angles and Paris. And this system that has not only worked for MatchesFashion.com—Moda Operandi has embraced the concept too, and has a by-appointment showroom in New York and London. The success of the pop-ups prompted MatchesFashion.com to take things one step further, and open a space that takes experiential retail to a entirely new level. Located at 5 Carlos Place in London's Mayfair, a stone's throw from Goyard's and Roland Mouret's flagship stores in London, this five-storied, 7000sq ft, 19th-century heritage townhouse building is very different to any other brick-and-mortar retail destination. Designed by the architect firm P Joseph, it is on the cutting edge of technology (with embedded QR codes all over the house), and all pieces can be delivered to you within 90 minutes, provided you are in London. It's almost like the store provides you with the convenience of online shopping, while also making you feel like you're part of a member's only club. And of course you can pre-reserve pieces through MatchesFashion.com. There are two floors of curated retail space and two floors of personal shopping suites, along with a broadcast hub, from where all events and collaborations held at the space will be broadcasted on their website. “We wanted to look after our existing customers [and] offer them a space which gives them the best,” said Christie. “And at the same time, the Townhouse will allow new customers to discover and understand the world of MatchesFashion.com.” Even the art, curated by the non-profit London based gallery House of Voltaire, is shoppable. MatchesFashion.com is known for working very close with the art world. “It's very much lead by our clients, and art and food is a big part of their lives, and so it needs to be a part of our environment too,” explains Christie. With its chic cafe, tropical garden and a calendar of events that includes a focus on new talent—right now French designer Marine Serre's special capsule collection is on display on the ground floor, in an installation form that celebrates the label love for all things sporty. For the launch week, MatchesFashion.com worked with Prada on an installation that highlighted the 100-plus pieces that had been exclusively designed for the project. The brand says that shopping is about more than just clothes. It's about a lifestyle. “It is an experience in story-telling,” says Christie. It is bringing a personal touch back to fashion—one that is about touch, feel and emotions. “The pace of this very thing has become relentless, and perhaps there is need to slow things down, to remember to enjoy experiences.” This clearly explains why the e-tailer is not only looking to the traditional retail at this point in time, but is also reinventing it to become something more than your regular shopping experience. column1: Fashion’s favourite supermodels of all time—then and now
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Does your answer match that of the industry experts? If you had to pick your favourite runway star, who would it be? We spoke to the movers and shakers in the industry about their ultimate supers of all times. All-time favourite: “Lily Cole, Alek Wek and Naomi Campbell. In the Indian context, I love Madhu Sapre—she is simply gorgeous and her presence is just so large. She was the epitome of supermodels in India.” Current favourite: “I like Radhika Nair and find her really interesting—she represents the diversified, millennial vibe and a new global culture.” All-time favourite: “My favourite model of all time is Kate Moss. I have had so many dreams where I am photographing her; she is on all of my moodboards!” Current favourite: “Imaan Hammam. She's breathtaking, original, has the best walk and is very sexy and powerful!” All-time favourite: “Natalia Vodianova!!” Current favourite: “The gorgeous redhead Natalie Westling.” All-time favourite: “Padma Lakshmi is absolutely timeless in her beauty and inspiring in every way. As a supermodel, TV host, actor, author and a philanthropist who uses her influence for remarkable causes, she plays every role in her life flawlessly. Can she do anything wrong? I highly doubt it!” Current favourite: “Bhumika Arora is a breath of fresh air and a game-changer in every possible way. Just watching her stand out beautifully on the runway is a delight. She's an inspiration for young girls in every part of the country with dreams of modelling.” All-time favourite: “Naomi Campbell for her fierce personality and persistent beauty.” Current favourite: “My darling Nidhi Sunil, for her intelligent sensibilities, natural sporty sex appeal, and wholesome beauty.” All-time favourite: “Rachel Reuben had great style and a very international look. I loved the way she photographed even though she was shorter than the required runway model; she stole the show even on the ramp.” Current favourite: “Diva Dhawan. She is fabulous in front of the camera and brings a certain cool energy which I love.” All-time favourite: “Christy Turlington—she's elegant, stunning and ageless. I believe her dignity, intelligence and grace get better with age. Whether it is her iconic yoga-inspired Vogue cover or her campaign for safe childbirth, she is a sparkling elixir of beauty and brains!” Current favourite: “Gisele Bündchen—though she has been iconic for a couple of decades now, she still tops my charts. I remember seeing her first cover when I was a teenager and there was something amazingly striking and feline about her beauty. She has remained relevant ever since and created some iconic images. I am not a fan of homogenised clones that one sees on catwalks at the international shows. Women who are different, individualistic and combine beauty and brains really stay timeless in my opinion.” All-time favourite: “Then it was Marielou Phillips. She was one of the few Indian girls to conquer the international runways." Current favourite: “Now, it's Kanishtha Dhankar. She is intelligent, bright and kind, and that makes her all kinds of beautiful.” All-time favourite: “Through the journey of my three-decade career, I've worked with the best models in the Indian industry. From the classic beauty Shyamoli Verma to the stunning Mehr Jesia in the '90s, to the golden couple Milind Soman and Madhu Sapre. The early 2000s saw the beautiful and dusky Sheetal Mallar and Dipannita Sharma, who starred in my campaigns and ruled the runways. This last decade has belonged to gorgeous Sonalika Sahay and the majestic Lakshmi Rana.” Current favourite: “From the recent younger lot, I really enjoy working with Archana Akil Kumar. She looks divine in photographs and on the ramp!” All-time favourite: “Archana Akil Kumar. She has walked for us several times at fashion week, and she is always opening or closing for me. Her body language is always on point. The way she carries off our heavy couture outfits is absolutely effortless.” Current favourite: “Namrata Tripathi. She is our muse for the autumn/winter 2018 campaign and she absolutely nails the sensual modern bride. She owns each and every look and moves effortlessly in front of the camera.” [#image: /photos/5ce42747b40d26d4edd6c47c]||| |||  Image: Bikramjit Bose “My favourite model then and now is Lakshmi Menon. All the iconic black and white imagery created by Prabuddha Dasgupta, modern visuals in Le Mill's campaign to the recent Tom Ford catwalk—it all embodies no-border beauty.” “My favourite super model in India then and now is Lakshmi. Somehow the poise, sex appeal and grace she has is something that has become quite rare to find. Lakshmi's recent campaign with Rohit Bal was beyond amazing and she still opens and closes most shows for major designers.” “Lakshmi Menon, then and now...she can bring something strong yet fragile, so effortlessly all in one frame.” What's New Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Richard Quinn on his new collection: “We make things that women want”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ahead of his spring/summer 2019 show at London Fashion Week, the first fashion designer to receive the Queen Elizabeth II Award for British Design from Her Majesty herself, opens up about his business strategy and ambitions for the future “It's simple maths,” says Richard Quinn, sitting at the end of one of the long working tables that fill the ground floor of his south London studio under the railway arches of Peckham. Around us, a group of industrious assistants work on the flower embroideries that will be featured in the brand's upcoming spring/summer 2019 collection on September 18. “You have a show garment, you've got a commercial garment. You've got X amount of stockists who might like two of them—just times it by two on your calculator minus what it has cost you to make it and you'll know if it's worth it.” Quinn's approach to fashion is almost purely pragmatic. Less than a year after graduating from London's Central Saint Martins in 2016, the designer set up a printing facility in his studio. Equipped with state-of-the-art machinery, the enterprise has produced prints for high-end brands and emerging labels from Burberry to Charles Jeffrey LOVERBOY, becoming a solid side revenue stream. Meanwhile, Quinn has eagerly embraced a number of successful commercial collaborations with high-street and luxury retailers, including Liberty, Matches Fashion and H&M, which have upped the brand's popularity beyond the fashion world. After being crowned the recipient of the inaugural Queen Elizabeth II Award for British Design earlier this year—presented by Her Majesty herself—his stockists more than doubled (going from 15 to 45), taking his signature floral garments all around the world. Despite his quick success—Quinn has achieved all this in less than three seasons—he is still a newcomer; not that he is remotely in awe, or surprised by his fast ascent. Nor is he particularly troubled by the possible challenges that lie ahead. Instead, Quinn possesses the kind of confidence that comes from knowing how your business works and focusing on what it needs, down to the last trim of printed silk. He tracks each and every one of his garments, from where the fabric comes from to what the price should be for wholesale as opposed to retail; keeps surplus stock at a minimum with a made-to-order approach; and maintains an open dialogue with stockists and buyers to understand how better to tailor his products to the end consumer. The London-born designer has also been able to capitalise from a combined flush of financial help. In 2016, he received a €50,000 prize for the H&M Design Award, which he invested in his print facility. Since 2017, he has also been supported by NEWGEN, the mentoring and financial initiative for emerging talents sponsored by the British Fashion Council. The grant has proved essential for the label to afford its catwalk shows, among other things, but Quinn strongly believes in working towards self-sufficiency. It's an aim that he sees as achievable and, more to the point, his duty. “I just find it weird that people drop off the face of the earth—what have you been doing? Why don't you have a commercial top?” he says, alluding to the brands that have shown under the scheme for a number of seasons but haven't been able to stand on their own feet afterwards. Quinn is eager to distance himself from the often romanticised image of the designer as creative genius struggling to make sales from an east London squat. It is not only unappealing, he points out, but also factually wrong. For him, being commercially viable doesn't come at the expense of creativity, but is a consequence of applying your creative talent in a 360-degree manner. “If you create a world that is actually desirable, people want to buy into it, whether through a (commercial) collaboration or through a (mainline) piece,” says Quinn. “The notion that things don't sell is just not right.” Madeleine Macey, marketing and communications director of Liberty, credits Quinn with the ability of applying his unique point of view to his work with authenticity, regardless of the project he is working on. “He has a very strong visual language which is totally transferrable,” she says, alluding to the series of accessories—including tote bags, pouches and scarves—that the designer has recently created reinterpreting the department store's classic prints. For his part, Quinn believes that fashion and its spectacle are only relevant when they have a strong point of view. “Gucci suddenly booming, it's because it has a point of view again,” explains the designer. “If you compare the Tom Ford era (at Gucci) to now, they are completely valid but completely separate worlds—but that's why they are so strong, they are both pivotal moments in fashion.” Quinn sees designing a garment as a step further into building the Richard Quinn lifestyle, a universe that people and other brands want to be part of and buy into. It's an all-round curation that includes focusing on the smallest details—like printing the linings knowing that only the wearer will be able to see them—as well as looking after styling, presentation and the overall image of the label. It's the kind of approach that has allowed more established brands to build a core identity strong enough to venture in other streams of revenue—denim, perfume, sportswear lines and collaborations—without sacrificing value. As for his first post-Queen show, the designer is presenting a collection that is less a breaking point than a subversive evolution and amplification of his signature themes. He hints at constricted and expanded silhouettes—think tight waists and big skirts; a more classic direction for fabrics, abandoning foil for moire silk; and regular, instantly recognisable shapes elevated by embroideries. Nodding to his first collection in collaboration with Liberty, Quinn is planning to divide his spring/summer 2019 looks into very defined sections, each group almost resembling a subculture of its own. Most importantly, the designer is aiming for a show that will deliver “high drama” in the hope of creating a chain of anticipation for all the ones to come. “Fashion should be exciting,” he says. “I know how lucky I am to have (NEWGEN support), so I think it's insulting to turn up and just show a collection up and down on a white background.” After the royal boost of last season, Quinn's show will be a highly anticipated one, but the designer remains unfazed, his eyes set on the target. “We make desirable things, make new things, make things that women want.” View Gallery 9 Photos What next for Richard Quinn? Other than being statement-making, both those outfits had one more thing in common—they came from Khosla Jani, a line launched by designers Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla in 2016. “We wanted to challenge ourselves, reinvent our own creativity by breaking into western wear. Lehengas with meticulous mirrorwork may be what first come to mind when you think of the designers, but their signature opulence also feels right at home on contemporary separates. “Our passion for embroideries and embellishment finds new ground in this label as we incorporate intricate hand-crafted detailing onto western silhouettes. Khosla Jani is our imagination run wild,” adds Jani. In two years, the line has acquired a fans in celebrities as varied as Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and Tyra Banks. So who really is the Khosla Jani woman? “First and foremost, her own human. Well-exposed, discerning, with an eager interest in living the good life. An eclectic spirit, a searching soul, a committed traveller to new destinations. Au fait with trends, but never ruled by them,” says Khosla. column1: 5 women across different industries on how to dress for work
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The perfect work outfit is the dream—but how do you match style with function and then add in your own personality? Vogue talks to five women who’ve made their wardrobes work for them Steve Jobs wore a black Issey Miyake turtleneck every day; Barack Obama stuck to a wardrobe of grey or navy suits. A little boring? Perhaps—but the concept of uniform dressing can be a helpful way to approach workwear without losing your individuality. It can even be creative. The idea is to hone the most work-appropriate version of your personal style, developing a streamlined wardrobe of mix-and-match pieces that meet the demands of your job, but still feel like the real you. In her role as global relations VIP client director of Net-a-Porter, Lupe Puerta encounters some serious high-flyers. “A lot of them are women who sit in positions of power—founders of their own businesses, CEOs, managers of huge hedge funds,” she says. Where classic “power dressing” used to be quite formulaic (aping businesswear for men), Puerta has found that women increasingly see their workwear as an opportunity for self-expression. “The women we work with never say ‘I need three jackets this season.' Now they say ‘I love this piece. How can I incorporate it into my working wardrobe?' I would say it's about having your basics but then adding more interesting pieces to create a stronger look.” A busy working lifestyle has practical demands. “We are talking about women who are constantly on the go and travel a lot,” she says. “They spend most of their days in meetings then immediately have to go to a client dinner. One of the things that is very important to them is having transitional pieces that are great from day to night—another is making sure that they have enough separates and products that travel well. Suiting is always important—it offers a lot of variation.” And yet for 2018's working women, suiting can be less conventional, more experimental. “A lot of our customers will buy a great tailored jacket and match it with a patterned skirt or a well-cut pair of trousers, which feels more modern,” says Natalie Kingham, fashion buying director of Matchesfashion.com. “We often think about the younger CEO who doesn't want to dress in a traditional ‘power way', but instead builds shirting into her wardrobe from brands such as Palmer Harding and Jil Sander. Then there are women working in creative industries, who enjoy wearing more informal suiting from brands like Charles Jeffrey and Pallas x Claire Thomson-Jonville.” To provide inspiration for your own uniform style—whatever your industry—Vogue spoke to five highly successful women about how they shop, how they dress and why it works for them. “At the Serpentine, our big focus is being boundary blind, in terms of moving from fashion to architecture to music, and the same thing has to be true of my wardrobe. I'm meeting with corporates, I'm meeting with creatives and it's not in any way a job that's defined by distinct hours in the gallery—it's so often international and so often off-site. “Suits are a staple. I love Racil, Roksanda and also Grace Wales Bonner, who we're incredibly excited to be showing in the gallery next year. I think there's something about the suit that's a wonderful armour, but that also enables you to really move through your day in a way that's chic and comfortable. And you can always trade an Erdem blouse underneath for a T-shirt. “In terms of basics I love Cos, and there are some great separates that you can get in every colour. I love Fite T-shirts and Bodas for everyday underwear. For jewellery I love Rosa de la Cruz. She's got the sparkliest smiley faces. At the same time I wear a beaded bracelet from my eight-year-old daughter.” “My work clothes need to be versatile. I look for neutral colours, items that can easily be mixed and matched with outfits in my closet, and shirts or blazers with fashion details. Unusual buttons, stitches on necklines, hemlines, pleats, high-low details or unique colours—these are all things I look for in my clothes that are subtle but still special. “In terms of uniform dressing, I always have something black on. It makes me feel comfortable, and you can match anything with black. I've also begun to wear more blazers—they look smart and professional, and you can change up the fabrics to make them more interesting. “I wear Blazé Milano, The Row, Theory, Thom Browne and Sacai pleated skirts. When I travel I take all my best basics, so I can mix and match, and two or three iconic pieces, with accessories to elevate my outfit. I don't bring any items that are high maintenance; I only pack outfits that I have worn and styled before, so that it's less of a hassle when I get there.” “I like simple, striking dresses, with a bit of impact either through colour or cut—round necklines, and what I can only describe as ‘swishy' skirts, quite fitted but not tight. Quite often, I have to go from one event to another and am often speaking, so what I wear needs to have a distinctive silhouette. I've learned that well-cut clothes are very empowering. I have a real physical sense of getting dressed to do what I need to do, and I gain confidence from the right—strong but feminine—dress and heels. What works for me isn't for everyone—but part of it being empowering is that it's my own look and it feels like an extension of who I am. “I've definitely evolved my style as I've become more confident. I have a picture of myself from the 1990s in a very masculine ‘power suit', pinstripes and all, and I would never wear anything like that now—I feel much more able to be myself, to be feminine and to wear dresses. I've realised that by emulating men, we [women] hold ourselves back. We have our own style of doing things and what we wear should in no way hide our differences. I know now that a great outfit is one that I don't think about once I'm dressed—I can just get on with the day. “I turn to Roksanda time and again. I have dresses of hers that are several years old and still going strong and always work. I love her use of colour and the mostly simple shapes. I also mix up high street and designer: someone asked me the other day about the dress and coat I was wearing and I realised the combination was Zara and Prada, which sums up my approach. I don't like anything blingy or too top-to-toe.” “Usually when I'm shopping I'm looking for items that I can wear in multiple ways or dress up or down as required. I've come to the conclusion that garments that sit on my natural waist are the most flattering on me; I love a good high-waisted pencil skirt and wide-leg or cropped trouser. Casual cotton jersey dresses or a fitted black polo-neck dress are such a blessing when I'm in a hurry in the morning and don't want to think about coordinating a top and bottom. “I cut off all my hair about a year ago and it's in a tricky stage. Luckily I have a large collection of silk scarves, so I've been wearing them as head wraps. I love it because it instantly polishes your look. “As autumn is around the corner, I'm looking forward to bringing out my silk, button-down blouses from J.Crew and cashmere crew-neck jumpers from N Peal—I wear them with a well-tailored trouser for a polished look. I'm also really looking forward to bringing out my coats again—my favourites are a classic black Burberry trench and a blush-pink, oversized wool coat from Whistles. “I love a good ballet flat, particularly in a nude shade; I wear them from the collection Nubian Skin created last year and they're great for running around in. Now that summer is drawing to a close, I'll be living in ankle boots and Stuart Weitzman knee-high boots with a low heel.” “I don't shop for work clothes, I just shop for clothes. I buy clothes that I like and I combine them in different ways to make them a little bit more restrained or more playful. It's something that I've grown into, maybe because I've become settled with exactly how I want to look rather than how people want me to look. “I wouldn't wear anything that I'm not comfortable in. I like to wear heels for work, but not stilettos; I wear mostly platforms by Vivienne Westwood. Clothes-wise I wear Comme des Garcons, Simone Rocha and Hussein Chalayan. Generally speaking they all play with volume and form—maybe that's my architect side coming in. “I love wearing black, but if I go to places where I'm surrounded by the architecture community, everyone tends to be wearing it and so I gravitate more towards colour. I'm lucky that as a female architect, there's very little protocol for what I should be wearing because there aren't many of us around. I exploit that; since I'm not going to fit in, I'll do what I want. I think that when it comes to other industries, it's for every woman to decide what they want to do. To decide to conform is one's own problem.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Jenny Packham celebrates 30 years in fashion at London Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Duchess of Cambridge-endorsed British brand and red-carpet regular returns to London Fashion Week with a Hollywood-inspired collection. Here, Packham looks back at her career highlights, the benefit of staying niche and her future aspirations It is almost ironic the difference between Jenny Packham the brand and Jenny Packham the person. Her dresses—heavily embroidered and heaving with embellishments—speak of someone who actively seeks out the spotlight. Packham the person? She's far more reserved. Dressed in a pair of black Celine booties, blue jeans, navy shirt and black tailored jacket, she is a far cry from her bedazzled designs. Where her dresses invoke fantasy, drama and a sense of occasion, she is serious, quietly confident and surprisingly calm. It is mere days away from her London Fashion Week presentation—her 30th anniversary no less—and her north London studio echoes her deep serenity. It may be a hive of activity but not a hint of panic or stress hangs in the air.Instead the team of over 40 beaver away conscientiously, The Jackson Five playing on the radio. “I know the 30th is a big landmark, but for me this is just another season,” says the designer matter-of-factly.“I have to create a collection that sells well, and I want to put on [a set that shows] ‘Jenny Packham moving forward into the next decade'.” Fuss-free, as ever. We can't discuss where she is going without first referencing where she's been. Duchess-endorsed and Oscar red carpet-approved, Packham is known for her cascading beadwork, delicate cocktail dresses and universally flattering silhouettes. She's worked with and dressed everyone from Kate Winslet, Angelina Jolie, Kate Hudson and Dita Von Teese to Li Bingbing, Angelababy and Tiffany Tang. Her most important “celebrity client” arguably remains the Duchess of Cambridge. As well as a number of red-carpet events, the Duchess has turned to Packham for all three of her post-partum photocalls, a sign perhaps of the trust between the two women. “I can't talk about that,” says Packham with a wide grin. Can't or won't? Her pride is self-evident regardless. In many ways, the Duchess is Packham's perfect ambassador: traditional, elegant, with just the right amount of contemporary elements to her style without venturing into trend territory. (Simple, flattering silhouettes never go out of style.) “I like to design things that make a statement, that a woman can walk into a room and feel amazing in. It is a bit attention-seeking, I suppose.” Though she refuses to mention the Duchess's many Packham moments among her career milestones, Packham does reference the “high-profile women” she's been fortunate enough to dress. “When we started working with A-list celebrities—Sandra Bullock at the Golden Globes, Angelina Jolie, Kate Winslet—that was really exciting.” “Looking back,” she adds, “it was quite brave of us to go into the luxury end of the market.” She and her partner (in business and life) Matthew Anderson started working together in 1988. “We were very young and learned [everything about building a brand] the hard way, but when you are that age you have the benefit of energy and naivety. Arrogance too.” From the very start, eveningwear has been at the heart of the brand—which they own 100 per cent of to this day, a rare thing in fashion today. While the fashion crowd refuse to be moved by her enduring red-carpet ranking, Packham has made it her strength. “They say when things are really bad people party more.” Niche, it turns out, is good business. Her only regret? “I wish we had opened our shop sooner.” Bricks and mortar it seems is something of an obsession with Packham. The London store opened in 2006, the Beijing flagship in 2018. Shanghai and New York, she hopes, will be next. An interesting move at a time when brands are looking to grow their digital footprint. “We're doing that too,” she hastens to add, “but I don't like the idea of a world without shops.” For spring/summer 2019, Packham is returning to London after 17 seasons in New York. “I was getting a bit tired; it was very chaotic.” She's sticking to her preferred presentation format, foregoing the traditional runway extravaganza. Her muse this season is Jean Harlow, the 1930s American film star and ultimate bad girl in pre-code Hollywood—a brief but exceedingly raunchy time in film before censorship guidelines were introduced. “I didn't realise she was dead by 26,” says Packham of one of the many things that piqued her interest. Harlow's equally tragic and glamorous life is translated into show-stopping dresses, with art deco beading, ostrich feather trimmings and frills aplenty. The Mayfair store will be transformed in tribute, complete with an exhibition of Harlow memorabilia—sunglasses, silk gloves, a Max Factor pressed powder case. The showcase will be open to the public on 17 September. “It's an opportunity for the whole team to participate, something that doesn't happen when you show overseas.” True to style, Packham is making this a celebration of everyone except herself. column1: Victoria Beckham celebrates 10 years with a debut at London Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The former Spice Girl-turned-fashion designer is celebrating a decade in the business with a blockbuster anniversary show on her home turf. Here, Victoria Beckham talks about her casting, the inspiration behind her zany colour scheme and the many ways she plans on celebrating her decade as a designer “Putting Victoria into Victoria Beckham since 2008,” says the British designer in perhaps the most meta moment of London Fashion Week, describing the punchline of her joke in her Juergen Teller campaign. The image—Beckham being swallowed whole by one of her supersized carrier bags—features on the sought-after capsule collection T-shirt, created to mark her tenth anniversary and sold exclusively at her Dover Street and Hong Kong stores as of this weekend. “I think it is important to have a sense of humour, but I do take what I do very seriously.” Making her London Fashion Week debut is cause of nervous excitement for the pop star-turned-fashion designer. “I'm always nervous ahead of a show and I've never done anything at home, but it's good to feel part of LFW. I'm excited.” Rather than taking a nostalgic trip down memory lane, Beckham is rooted firmly in the here and now for spring/summer 2019. “This season is about giving choice to my customer. Does she want a skinny pant or a larger pant? Does she want a short skirt or a midi or long?” The languid shapes—“not body-con, but conscious of the female form”—build on the codes she's developed over the past decade. Her floaty dresses couldn't be further away from her sucky-sucky designs of 2008, but there is a faithful adherence to tailoring and a greater adoption of ease. Fluid tops with delicate lace inlays, lurex skirts, knitted separates and light outerwear navigate that fine line between masculine and feminine. Colour remains important too. This season, she takes inspiration from New York-based British artist Nicola Tyson; her signature brights—cornflower blue, tangerine red and ochre—popping against each other. “It is still very important for me that I try on the clothes, that I use the bags, that I wear the shoes,” she says, dressed head-to-toe in her designs—flat sandals, black tailored trousers, a plain white tee and an oversized camouflage jacket from her resort collection. “As a woman, I want everything to be wearable.” Casting for this show was important, too. “Showing in London this season meant that, more than ever, I wanted to celebrate Britishness. Of course, there are women from around the world in the show—but I'm really excited to have some iconic faces of the British model industry, like Stella Tennant and Edie Campbell, walking this season. Casting has been a different process this time. We started at the beginning of the summer and the show features faces you have seen before like Liya Kebede but also new girls that I am so excited by. But at the end of the day, it is all about her customers. Beckham is hosting a series of events—“activations” as Beckham's team calls them—with them in mind: a private breakfast here, a stint behind the till at her Dover Street flagship there, inviting customers to her actual show. Though undeniably in a celebratory mood, does she feel more scrutiny being back on home turf? “I think I'm always under scrutiny [regardless of where I show]. I always feel it, but I try to ignore that, keep my head down and do the best that I can.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Take a first look at Mary Katrantzou’s 10th anniversary collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue goes behind the scenes with Mary Katrantzou at her north London studio as she puts the finishing touches to her tenth-anniversary collection—a distillation of all that’s gone before, from her perfume-bottle dresses to her headline-grabbing lampshade skirts “Oh wow! Can we inflate it?” asks Mary Katrantzou, spotting a blow-up, see-through bomber jacket filled with dried flowers and beaded butterflies. She's curbed by her colleague—not until the show. It's four days before the Greek designer's ten-year anniversary collection for spring/summer 2019 at London Fashion Week and she's clearly uplifted. “I'm proud that I was never scared of pushing the boundaries of what's considered desirable, what's considered wearable.” When Vogue visits Katrantzou at the north London studio she has gradually monopolised over seven years, she streams cigarette smoke and merry monologues at her patio table, reflecting on ten years in the trade. “Sometimes you try ideas and they fail, and sometimes you don't think they're going to work and they become the most amazing thing of that show,” says the designer, who is renowned for her uniquely embellished dresses and pick-me-up digital prints. “But I've never feared, and I think that sometimes leads you to major disasters and sometimes it leads you to greatness. But most of the time it just leads you to build confidence.” At the start she felt too shy to take her finale bow and had little confidence discussing her work. “I just didn't want to be part of a picture.” From dingy, east London start-up digs (“tiny, concrete floor, mud coming through, jail bars outside”) to the two-floor operation she runs today, the Central Saint Martins graduate has garnered celebrity clientele from Kerry Washington to Kylie Jenner. “Looking back I'm like wow, we've done some amazing things.” The new collection evokes “some of the techniques we've done in the past and silhouettes that we loved”, but spotlights everything Katrantzou has learned along the way. The perfume bottles that were printed onto tunic dresses for autumn/winter 2009 have been remade in metal mesh with crystal embroideries on top. As we speak her design team continues to jigsaw together the colourful crystal mesh dresses inspired by bottles of Eternity, Pleasures and Shalimar that have taken months to make. “They're special because they connect back to my very first collection,” says Katrantzou. The new body of work also draws on her spring/summer 2013 collection that she did on stamps and obsolete banknotes, as well as “things that were maybe not developed fully because the resources were not there or ideas that people loved that we have brought back”. Her reference board is pinned with pictures of Christy Turlington and Kate Moss from the 1990s, pages from vintage editions of Vogue, images of leather bonnets and samples of polka-dot tulle. “It's important to reflect back,” she says. In January she did just that with a 180-piece retrospective held at the Dallas Contemporary. “It gave me a moment to see what the thread was that connects my work and try to bring that into this collection.” She pulled that thread and all sorts of collectibles fell out—perfume bottles, objects of art, stamps and heraldic symbols. “A lot of collections I have done in the past have revolved around the theme of collecting.” And for spring/summer 2019, the “Collection” is titled just that. The Mary Katrantzou collector's club is a varied one. From Cate Blanchett at Cannes Film Festival 2018 wearing a custom-made cloud of crystals  to HRH Princess Beatrice of York in a peacock-plume print dress and Kendall Jenner, who wore a pre-fall 2018 Lichtenstein-inspired shirt with frayed cut-offs. Her most poignant moments have been more personal. “I remember when Colette's [founder] Sarah Andelman sent her first order through. That was amazing because it was my very first season,” she says. Another big moment was winning the Swiss Textiles Award in 2010. “Big because it was my first award and so early in my career, and it was supporting me financially. It gave me confidence.” She won the British Fashion Award for Emerging Talent the following year in 2011. Another benchmark moment was her spring/summer 2011 collection featuring her standout “lampshade” skirts. “I think that was the time that we were really noticed. I remember the shift that happened in my business. We scaled up really, really quickly.” Her label is now near fully inflated.  A birthday bonus arrived earlier this year with a cash injection from Chinese investor Wendy Yu; Katrantzou is now building her brand up in Asia and plans to expand into jewellery... “We've also  tapped into bags and shoes but never really had the infrastructure to do our own range.” For the upcoming show Katrantzou has collaborated with Jimmy Choo on Perspex stilettos with heels filled with fake butterflies. “I've always been interested in interiors too, but I just never have the time. I feel when you're building a brand it takes ten years just to realise who you are!” she says. “But I'm not in any hurry.” View Gallery 20 Photos First look at Mary Katrantzou’s 10th anniversary collection Weddings Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Birdhichand Ghanshyamdas unveils its latest collection, Delhi Durbar
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion An ode to the royal heritage of India At the launch of their new collection, Birdhichand Ghanshyamdas showcased an army of model brides all decked in intricately handcrafted jewellery by the bespoke brand to the finest of Delhi's society, with Sufi folk singer Kutle Khan charming the assembled crowds. The models were dressed in Jayanti Reddy couture, but the jewellery was clearly the star of the show. The Jaipur-based jewellery brand, which was first established in 1950, looked back to India's imperial past to dress the 21st century bride. A tribute to the city's bejewelled past of slow luxury and regal opulence, Delhi Durbar features uncut diamonds and precious stones layered into intricate statement one-of-its-kind pieces of jewellery—but still showcases a modern slant with its overly pastel colour palette. Made for brides who want to embrace tradition and grandeur, the collection ensures that pieces will go on to become modern heirlooms. Sonam K Ahuja was seen at the event, channelling the role of the trendsetting bride yet again. Yash Agarwal, creative director and design head, Birdhichand Ghanshyamdas, Jaipur says, “I am extremely elated that our journey that started with our first store in Jaipur has now reached the national capital. Always taking the road less travelled, we at Birdhichand have always stood as the paragon of innovation and panache in the segment of luxury jewellery brands and will always look forward to. We have graciously received an overwhelming response to the Delhi Durbar collection and we look ahead to serving the Delhi brides in the coming times.” Scroll onwards to take a first look at the new collection. column1: Andreja Pejić: “I had never imagined myself being an LGBT activist”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The androgynous model takes us into her world https://youtu.be/2DY1iJTpzTg Andreja Pejić is a poster girl for diversity in the world of modelling. The Bosnian-born Australian model is recognised as the world's first completely androgynous model, has been outspoken about being a transgender woman and has a unique story that is one known to many. Needless to say, Pejić is a runway favourite and has walked for the likes of Jean Paul Gaultier, Jeremy Scott, Thom Browne, Marc Jacobs and many more. But what's it like to be Andreja Pejić? For starters, she hates mornings but her favourite meal happens to be breakfast. “Tea can save a life,” she jokes. Being over six feet tall and stepping out in towering heels draws some amount of attention, but Pejić has learnt to take in her stride. “Confidence is like a house and you build it brick by brick. I had never imagined myself being an LGBT activist. That does sometimes mean people do, kind of put you in a certain box. But I have chosen to share that,” she says. column1: Why you need to choose a baby pink lehenga for your wedding
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All the inspiration you need Let's just agree that this is an age of renaissance for Indian wedding wear. The modern bride 2.0 is not merely content with following in the footsteps of her predecessors—she wants to pay homage to her traditions, but she also wants to make some of her own. So customs, though revered, are also being given an unapologetic present-day update. Case in point: the growing departure from the customary red that erstwhile brides unanimously wore, and the rise and rise of baby pink for the walk to the mandap. The 2018 bride is individualistic and refined in equal measure—she may want her wedding pictures to break the Internet, but she doesn't want her bridal garb to overpower her. Yes, her wedding day ensemble needs to be ornate, but that does not mean ostentatious in her sartorial dictionary. Baby pinks strike this delicate balance to achieve the tricky feat with flair. Season after season, Tarun Tahiliani has been championing lightweight bridal wear that doesn't hinder the bride from enjoying her own wedding celebration. Blush pink reflects this sensibility, and was one of the key colours in his ‘In Elysium' couture showing too. Tahiliani married the hue with free-flowing lehengas, modern blouses and sophisticated embroideries—as seen on Aditi Rao Hydari, who closed the show for him. Rahul Mishra's take on baby pink at India Couture Week 2018 favoured ombre over monotone—so you had soft pinks seamlessly juxtaposed with saffron and watermelon pink, with accents like cape blouses and nature-inspired embroideries. While Shyamal & Bhumika's line-up had a baby pink lehenga for every occasion, where one could pick between a heavily embroidered lehenga set with a nude dupatta for the engagement or a pink off-shoulder blouse and lehenga for the sangeet. Falguni & Shane Peacock presented variations of this au courant colour as well, that were mixed with steely silver and nude for a pre-wedding function or head-to-toe pink with a feathered hemline for the reception. Baby pink has also been the go-to colour for celebrity brides this year. It all started with Anushka Sharma, who ventured beyond the norm with a blush pink Sabyasachi lehenga for her Tuscan wedding. Then there was Sonam K Ahuja, who wore traditional for her Anand Karaj ceremony, but changed into a dusty rose Anamika Khanna lehenga soon after. Neha Dhupia also chose a minimalistic pink Anita Dongre for her wedding, fittingly complemented with polki jewellery. And the women of the Ambani clan favoured the hue at Akash Ambani and Shloka Mehta's engagement too—Isha Ambani chose an ornate creation by Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla, worn with statement diamond jewellery, while Mehta wore a soft Sabyasachi number with kundan bijouterie. column1: Nikhil Thampi and Hérmosa Design Studio launch a new furniture collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And it’s equal parts stylish and functional Nikhil Thampi's urban, glamorous take on fashion has earned him a spot among celebrities' favourite designers. Now, his latest collaboration with bespoke furniture brand Hérmosa sees him dabbling into the world of home decor as well. The collection, launched earlier this month, is the coming together of Thampi's signature aesthetic and Hérmosa's clean lines—think suede sofa sets bearing the designer's logo in gilded metal work or a centre table that forks out into singular seaters. “Our brand resonates with designs that are strong and powerful with a hint of glamour; which is the vision I see Hérmosa having as well,” says Thampi, illustrating the practicality and minimalism the two brands have in common. For the range, Thampi drew inspiration from his label's existing collection, Quantum, and focused on how to tactfully utilise space—making his latest offering the ideal choice for the ‘millennial homemaker'. “Being from Mumbai, I understand space constraints, so the statement sofa and tables are designed in a manner which caters to the different needs of an urban home,” he explains. From chests and drawers to bar consoles and nesting tables, each piece is strategically fashioned with materials such as charcoal, metal and brass. In many ways, the collaboration has been a great learning experience for the designer, wherein he has delved into the technical aspects of furniture design while also lending it his modernist sartorial streak. “I like to challenge myself at every given opportunity, so there are many more projects to come,” he says, eager to offer his designing prowess to other realms as well. column1: What does circularity mean for sustainable fashion?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A step-by-step breakdown of circular fashion, and why you should care about it If you're not aware by now that fast fashion is damaging the environment, you've been living under a rock. Fashion is one of the major contributors to pollution in our air and oceans, and is also harming the health of those to produce it. According to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation, the textile industry will add 22 million tonnes of microfibers in the ocean by 2050, and will also increase its share of the carbon budget from two per cent to 26 per cent. In essence, we will be eating and breathing our own clothes. According to the World Bank's World Development Indicators, clothing production doubled from 2000 to 2015 but the utilisation of clothing items has significantly decreased, leading to an immense amount of waste. It is estimated that one garbage truck full of clothes is burned or landfilled every second, and that half of all fast fashion production gets disposed of under a single year. This is an immense amount of pressure on our planet's natural resources. To combat the waste and unsustainable nature of the fashion industry, a few visionaries are talking about redesigning the textile industry with a circular vision. Circular fashion was a term first used publicly in 2014 by two people, independent of each other. One was Felix Ockborn, the then environmental sustainability coordinator for H&M in Stockholm. The other was Anna Brismar, one of the world's leading sustainability consultants in the textile industry and the owner of Circularfashion.com. Circular fashion envisions a new future for the industry where clothing and accessories are designed in such a way that they're produced without microfibers and other harmful raw materials. There is an emphasis on quality and longevity of each item of clothing, and a special focus on recycling as well as a biodegradable end. Thus, the life cycle of a fashion item can be broken down into the following elements Design: The design process will bring the concept of a circular economy to fashion. Clothing and accessories will be designed for eco-friendly production using high quality materials to increase their wardrobe life, and will also have a timeless style to appeal to new users. The design will also build in recyclability and biodegradability within the sub components of each item of clothing/accessories, so that they can be reused or composted later. Production: Circular fashion will be produced using high quality materials for a long lifespan, non-toxic and local substances to minimise environmental impact and preferably be biodegradable, so it can be composted at the end. The production methods will use renewable energy, minimise waste generation and any spill will be reused for other production processes. Alternatively, clothing and accessories will be produced with non-toxic, synthetic materials that may be effectively recycled, such as recyclable polyester. Use: Circular fashion will have multiple users through borrowing, renting, redesign and secondhand services, thus extending the life span of fashion items significantly. Reuse: At the end of the product life cycle (if there is an end), the material and subcomponents will be used as raw materials to make new products, or get composted to turn into biological nutrients for microorganisms in the soil. Circular fashion also applies to consumers of fashion. As a user, you need to think about borrowing, swapping, renting or purchasing vintage pieces before buying new items. When you do buy fashion, look for high-quality, timeless fashion which you will use for a long time. Opt for fashion made with organic, non-toxic and recyclable materials, and adopt good washing and repairing practices. Donate or pass items on to friends and family to give them new life, or take them to a recycling centre. H&M, for one, has garment collection boxes at all stores worldwide and even gives you vouchers in return. MUD Jeans is the first circular fashion brand that allows customers to lease jeans and send them back after a year to be recycled into more jeans or sweaters. In India, Aterlier OM + OM Khadi in Goa is a fashion label that invites its customers to bring back any of their products after two years to be re-fashioned, reprinted or re-dyed. In January 2018, the Global Fashion Agenda (GFA) 2020 Circular Fashion Commitment was announced to take tangible steps towards a circular fashion industry. 64 fast fashion companies and luxury designers have signed the agreement including Zara, Asos, H&M, Adidas and Kering—the parent company of Gucci, Saint Laurent and Balenciaga. Each company has set their own environmental targets for 2020 with a total of 143 targets set. Adidas will set up collection centres for used clothing; ASOS will re-train their designers to use the circular fashion philosophy and stop using non-recyclable materials; while H&M will fund research on textile recycling. column1: Why Suhana Khan’s versatile style is worth stealing
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From party dresses to breezy floral lehengas Ever since Suhana Khan made an appearance at the opening of mother Gauri Khan's Mumbai restaurant, Arth in that tangerine bandage dress by Hervé Léger, she has had the spotlight trained on her for her stunning sartorial choices. Needless to say, the 18-year-old has is no stranger to the limelight, and has remained undeterred by both the media scrutiny and the fashion police on social media. Whether she is vacationing in Europe or attending family weddings, Suhana Khan has all grounds covered when it comes to her attire. We took a peek into her closet to help you understand how to update your own better. It seems like white is the obvious choice of colour for most of her looks. The all-white ensemble she chose while on a holiday in Pompei with her family, for one, made headlines all over the country. Khan paired white shorts with a matching lace top for this look, and added some minimal jewellery. Her favour towards all-white separates was evident at Shah Rukh Khan's birthday celebration in Alibaug as well, where she posed with friends in a white Givenchy T-shirt, worn over shorts in a similar hue. Suhana Khan is often seen opting for dresses when it comes to social events. At a recent party in London, she channelled an iconic Paris Hilton look that was reminiscent of the '90s vibe of the socialite's 21st birthday celebrations—Khan sported a glamorous silver dress with a bold red lip here. Another event hosted by mother Gauri Khan—at Cirque le Soilel for Halloween—saw the the young star kid in a full-sleeved gold dress too, proving her favour towards the silhouette. Khan's Indian ethnic wardrobe is envy-worthy to say the least. Did you miss pictures of her attending a wedding in Delhi in various Indian attires—that traditional golden lehenga by Monisha Jaising, another floral outfit in pink and a heavily embroidered wine-red lehenga? It came as no surprise that she can ace ethnic wear for a casual look too. A trip organised by Gauri Khan for Suhana Khan and her school friends saw the star kid posing against the backdrop of the Taj Mahal, dressed in a breezy floral kurta with jeans and silver sneakers. Gauri Khan is often seen in T-shirts and ripped jeans, and it's clear that her teenage daughter has taken some style cues from her. She's frequently spotted in outfits similar to the ones her mother favours. Keep scrolling to peek into Suhana Khan's personal wardrobe through her many, many pictures. column1: London Fashion Week spring/summer 2019: What to expect from the shows
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In a city ruled by emerging designers, September's shows are dominated by news from the establishment London is traditionally known for its young designers, but in recent years the success of the city's fashion week has turned it into a much more dynamic affair. The electric tension between huge power houses and emerging designers makes for an unpredictable week with a schedule you can't really pre-empt. Last season, for instance, Richard Quinn stole the show in more ways than one when the Queen decided to make an unannounced appearance. This September, Quinn and his emerging peer designers are back, but by the looks of it this London Fashion Week could be overtaken by the establishment. Burberry will unveil its revamped image under the artistic direction of Riccardo Tisci. The former Givenchy couturier, who surprised the whole industry when he took over from Christopher Bailey in March, makes his runway debut at the British fashion institution on Monday, September 17 at 5pm. In July, the Italian designer announced a Burberry collaboration with Vivienne Westwood. The capsule collection isn't set to hit stores until December, but the punk nature of that constellation tells us a thing or two about the Great British heritage and punk influences that have captured Tisci's mind during his first few months on London soil. Victoria Beckham is celebrating the 10th anniversary of her brand with a triumphant return to the motherland. While the designer's studio is based in London, Beckham has historically presented her collections in New York where her sleek sense of modernity and power-dressing has been a natural fit. On Sunday, September 16 at 10am, we'll see if the change of scenery will impact her creative approach. Either way, we're in for an emotional—and hopefully nostalgic—ride with the pop idol who became a fashion icon and won over the pickiest industry in the world. Fingers crossed for some Spice Girls on the front row. Alexa Chung makes her runway debut on Saturday, September 15 at 11am. Not as a model but as the creative head of the label she launched in May last year, attaching her evergreen it-girl name to collections that echo her distinct sense of style. Chung's arrival on the London show schedule serves as a reminder of the capacity of this fashion capital. From a mega star like Victoria Beckham to a niche style starlet like Chung, celebrity-fuelled brands co-exist with young dressmakers just out of Central Saint Martins and industry mastodons like Burberry. There's room for everyone. Nicholas Kirkwood takes on the historic challenge of an on-schedule shoe show this season. Marking his return to London from Paris where the British-bred shoe designer has staged smaller presentations in recent years, he is promising an “immersive and experiential" evening on Sunday, September 16 at 5pm, as he told the Business of Fashion in April. “[London is] where my design studio is, where I live and what I'm exposed to for my inspirations, so it makes sense. I'm not going to do it in a traditional runway format. There will be other elements that make it far more of an experience. It's something I will continue to do." Halpern, Matty Bovan and Richard Quinn will fly the flag for the future establishment amongst so many other young and emerging designers responsible for retaining London Fashion Week's reputation as the ultimate breeding ground for new talent. As far as news angles go, September's shows in the British capital may be dominated by the establishment but rest assured: none of them would show in London were it not for its young and experimental backbone. At the end of the day, in this city, it's the kids who run the show. This story originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 20 celebrity couples show you how to step out in style
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Take notes Couples who dress up together, stay together—not that you have to remind Bollywood's lovebirds about that. Without ever setting toe into the matchy-matchy territory, the top celebrity couples of the country have been flexing their sartorial muscles with everything from laid-back street style for date nights to tastefully coordinated ensembles at the many, many celebrity weddings on their calendars this year. From Virushka to Deepveer, here's how your favourite celebrity couples have been faring on the style charts. Image: Viral Bhayani While the jury is still out on the will-they-won't-they debate of their impending nuptials, Padukone and Singh continue to tease their fans with public PDA at the airport. Together, their couple style mirrors the yin-and-yang of their relationship: while Padukone maintains fidelity to laid-back luxury with easy separates from Burberry, Singh remains as incorrigible as ever with his sartorial choices, rocking everything from bowler hats to Gucci fanny packs. Image: Viral Bhayani The intrigue that surrounded the initial stages of their relationship could fuel a five-part Bollywood franchise on its own, but avid fans got some long-awaited validation when the couple stepped out together for the paps. Their chemistry on the Met Gala red carpet last year, and the surprise engagement that followed all the rumours about their coupling in Mumbai led fans into a frenzy. The couple has only been serving up yet more good news with their wardrobe choices lately. Casual dinner dates call for gingham separates and easy basics, but that doesn't mean they're afraid to step up the ante if needed either, with blingy Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla saris and quintessential three-piece suits. Image: Viral Bhayani One, a leading Bollywood actor with a penchant for unconventional couture; the other, a self-professed sneakerhead at the helm of an indie fashion label. Together, the young lovebirds are only too happy to explore uncharted sartorial territory. For her wedding day, the actor opted for a traditional ensemble from Anuradha Vakil and followed it up with a classic Anamika Khanna lehenga, while Ahuja siphoned off some of her fashion acumen by pairing a traditional bandhgala with grey trainers at the reception. Image: Viral Bhayani In a tale worthy of the larger-than-life movies that Sharma stars in, cricket's favourite bad boy fell for the sassy star. Since that grand wedding in Italy, the couple have been creating headlines everywhere they go with a slew of on-point ensembles at the airport. While their preferred modus operandi is laid-back luxe, the duo honours their social commitments in style whenever required too—a recent high-profile dinner had Sharma opting for a breezy anarkali to go with her husband's formal attire. However, it's the couple's off-duty style that makes them resident kings of cool round the clock. Image: Viral Bhayani Throw two A-listers together, and you have the perfect recipe for sartorial success. The gossip mills may have been put to bed with an official confirmation, but all eyes still remain on this new couple, and their outings together. After making their couple debut in a lime green Sabyasachi lehenga and a formal bandhgala at Sonam K Ahuja's Mumbai reception, the two have been blowing off steam with stolen dates in dressed-down outfits, with flowy separates for Bhatt and the occasional monogram tee for Kapoor. Image: Viral Bhayani When you put a former Miss World together with the scion of one of the most powerful families in Bollywood, fireworks are just about expected. Together, the Bachchans have their pick of the top couture labels, and often give the paps something to write home about with coordinated his-and-hers ensembles at the many festive parties and weddings they attend. Image: Viral Bhayani Hailing from two of the most powerful legacies in Bollywood, the Khans sure know how to put on a show. While airport runs are dominated with Gucci merch, red carpets call for bespoke couture from the country's top designers—Sonam K Ahuja's reception saw the couple channelling their potent fashion acumen. While Kapoor Khan opted for an embellished Manish Malhotra sari with an itsy-bitsy blouse that did justice to her washboard abs, Khan stood by her side in a royal bandhgala of his own. Image: Viral Bhayani At the top of the power pyramid in the industry, there's little that the Khans do without their signature flair. Given the demands of their packed social calendar, the couple is most often spotted giving paps their money's worth in head-to-toe couture. Not strangers to making heads turn, the couple showed up at Akash Ambani and Shloka Mehta's pre-engagement party in a Falguni & Shane Peacock outfit and a custom suit that drove the shutterbugs into a frenzy. Image: Viral Bhayani There's nothing that unites a couple together better than a shared love for a sharp, on-point OOTDs. Whether it's a quick dash across the airport or a special date night, this duo knows how to make an entrance with their mirrored sunnies and coordinated sneakers. While Basu throws out the rulebook on age-appropriate dressing with a string of crop tops, cold shoulders and the reddest matte the beauty gods can concoct, Grover remains steadfast to his love for V-necks, accessorised with his signature tats. Image: Viral Bhayani Much like their low-key relationship, the Hyderabadi princess and her businessman beau prefer to channel some chic minimalism when it comes to their selective public appearances. Despite co-owning a production house together, they refuse to let the inherent filminess of their job description take over, allowing easy prints and muted colours to dictate the mood when they have to navigate the cameras instead. Image: Viral Bhayani When you have one of the most iconic names of the Indian film industry on your arm, simple just doesn't cut it. Which is just as well, because Dixit Nene's surgeon husband, Dr Ram Nene isn't afraid to match his superstar wife in the sartorial stakes. The duo's favourite Saturday night haunt is the red carpet, where the actor gives rein to ethereal ensembles from the country's top couturiers, with Nene meeting her halfway with crisp black ties and bandhgalas. Image: Viral Bhayani They may have one of the most conventional love stories out there, but that doesn't mean they play by the book when it comes to their sartorial choices as well. At Sonam K Ahuja's grand wedding reception in May, the duo indulged their love for experimental silhouettes with the missus picking a belted Anamika Khanna ensemble, as her husband stood tall in an asymmetrical pleated kurta. When off the clock, this couple ditches the layers in favour of fluid separates. Image: Viral Bhayani The hush-hush lovebirds may prefer to fly under the radar, but their killer couple style signals otherwise. When not on the job, the duo shares a mutual love for effortless street style, but they are just as comfortable driving the bar a bit further up each time with their red carpet outings. The recent Ambani-Mehta engagement had Patani channelling her millennial magnificence in a rose gold lehenga, while Shroff opted for an understated all-black ensemble by her side. Image: Viral Bhayani Much like their surprise nuptials, Dhupia and Bedi's couple style comes as a breath of fresh air. Those in need of proof need look no further than a recent wedding reception, where we saw the couple play dress up in a regal navy Raw Mango lehenga and a classic Shantanu & Nikhil bandhgala. When out on the town, Dhupia holds on to her street style cred with a host of fuss-free silhouettes, with Bedi serving the perfect foil to her OOTDs in monochrome basics. Image: Viral Bhayani It should come as zero surprise that this overachieving couple brings their collective zest for perfection to the art of dressing as well. A handloom loyalist, Rao tends to the formal events on her social calendar by stepping out in crisp silk saris, pinned with military precision, with Khan complementing her in classic kurtas. When off-duty, they channel their flair for the fuss-free with breathable separates and monochromatic prints. Image: Viral Bhayani This cricket-meets-Bollywood union has been churning out wardrobe hits and headlines in equal measure. While their off-duty style mirrors the effortless ease of their relationship, the couple have definitely received the memo on how to do justice to the red carpet: the recent engagement of the young Ambani heir had Ghatge stepping up to the plate in an embellished sari by Jade and a Bottega Veneta clutch, while Khan channelling his dapper charm in contrasting formals. Image: Viral Bhayani Clocking in close to a decade of being married, we are guessing that the secret sauce to the Kundras' happiness is their shared love for lighting up the red carpet. As Shetty Kundra lives her best life in her 40s in show-stopping couture, her industrialist husband is only too happy to give her company to her red carpet commitments in sharp formals. Off-duty fashion calls for a classic Hermès bag and monogrammed Moschino tees for her, and laid-back staples for him. Image: Viral Bhayani You won't spot this secretive couple out and about together often, but when you do, you'll be able to tell it's them from their signature wardrobe decisions. Ever the Sabyasachi loyalist, Balan has yet to find anything to replace her love for a classic embellished sari. Look to her left, and you'll find the dapper Roy Kapur channelling his love for minimalism in glorious monochrome. Image: Viral Bhayani Just like fine wine, this celluloid couple just gets better with age, and as do their wardrobe choices. While Khanna is game for everything from the nonchalance of a Lavish Alice cape blazer at movie screenings to the timeless elegance of Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla at Sonam K Ahuja's reception, Kumar plays between an off-duty style of T-shirts and jeans, and ethnic looks that complement his wife's, like the contrasting side-buttoned sherwani he wore for the celebrity reception. Image: Viral Bhayani This relationship may have been kept under the wraps enough to have escaped the tabloids for the most bit, but there was no denying the paparazzi at Sonam K Ahuja's wedding reception. The blockbuster kid ditched the usual suspects in favour of a powder blue sherwani, while his date for the night channelled some easy elegance in an embellished pick from her eponymous label. When off-duty, the young (alleged) couple can be spotted in effortless essentials and weather-mandated daywear in the city. column1: From sketch to runway: how Coach’s spring/summer 2019 lineup came about
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Stuart Vevers shares his favourite look from the Coach spring/summer 2019 lineup and discusses the influence of Santa Fe, the importance of New York City and how he is developing an American point of view on craft Ready-to-wear is relatively new territory for Coach, despite the American brand's 77 years in the leather goods business. Since his arrival five years ago, British designer Stuart Vevers has worked tirelessly—and successfully—to forge an identity for the all-American luxury label that is at once preppy and prairie, folksy and brimming with open-road idealism. The key to his success? Building on touchstones from the label's heritage in an authentic way. “The pieces have a real sense of imagination to them too,” the designer tells Vogue ahead of the spring/summer 2019 show. “Coach obviously didn't have ready-to-wear in the '50s and '60s, but [seeing the collections now] you can imagine that ready-to-wear could have a longer tradition. [The designs] feel believable.” One such touchstone Vevers returns to season after season is the leather jacket, fusing it with raw collars, vintage motifs, personalised patchwork and even—as he did in autumn/winter 2018—with supernatural symbols. Here, Vevers shares with us this season's take on the heirloom piece (sleeveless, soft suede) and the anatomy behind one of his favourite looks of the entire collection. “What I like about this look is that it holds together a lot of the key messages of the season. The big ruffled blouse, the prairie skirt, the suede jacket with fringing, the detailing—you can really feel the human hand in the craft behind it all. That concept is something I've been exploring more deeply over the last couple of seasons, trying to find what an American point of view on craft can be, and how that can feel different from the traditional European luxury world.” “My first thought when creating a Coach jacket is that when you come to put it on, you should instantly feel cooler. It is all about attitude. That is often why we give the items a distressed look; we wash the leather or choose materials [that will] have a rugged, deliberately worn finish. There is something about the Coach approach to leather too: it is useful. It is about taking American icons and American archetypes and giving them a less formal approach.” “The most important source of inspiration for me is the people of New York City. This is Coach's home and has been since 1941, so it makes sense that it is the starting and ending point for every single collection. While I've travelled around America and regularly draw inspiration from many parts of the country—this season from Santa Fe [in New Mexico] in particular—the Coach customer dresses in the city, and picks up things on his or her travels… That urban attitude is really important.” “I travelled to Santa Fe and came across all these little villages—sometimes just a few houses—and so many of the buildings, gardens, fences, were made from scavenged materials. That had a big impact on this season overall. It is about assembling and reconstructing the craft and the spirit of the American look; exploring and playing with these salvaged heirlooms and placing them a new context. Often it means we end up playing with elements, things you wouldn't usually see together—a soft suede trainer with a sporty sole, for example—and fusing them to create something new and unexpected.” “The thing that took the longest to resolve was all the embellishment. It is really important to get that balance of finish and fines, without it feeling too precious or too perfect. I think if things are too perfect they don't have that attitude. The washing technique took time, too—particularly the fringe on the jacket. They are deliberately distressed, but you have to have the right balance. Take it too far and it won't look good, but too crisp and perfect and it will lack attitude.” View Gallery 6 Photos Coach’s Stuart Vevers on craft, heirlooms and attitude What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Manish Malhotra is set to release a memoir that you’d want to pre-order
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you need to know Manish Malhotra is easily one of India's, and Bollywood's, most loved designers. The couturier began his career as the costume designer for Rangeela back in 1995, and has dressed everyone from Sridevi, to Kareena Kapoor Khan, Kajol and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, to younger stars such as Alia Bhatt and Janhvi Kapoor through the years. Now, Malhotra is all set to add yet another feather to his cap—that of an author. Rupa Publications just announced the release of a new book by Manish Malhotra, co-written with journalist-author Sonal Kalra. “I finally thought the time was right for me to tell the story of my life. After completing 25 years in the film industry, my life has become entwined with Indian cinema and its constituents. Now after having completed 13 years of my couture label, I feel my journey can inspire those who find fashion as their true calling,'' said Malhotra about his new book. Slated for a 2019 release, the autobiographical account will encapsulate everything about Malhotra's career, right from tracing his forays into modelling to his association with the leading ladies of Bollywood. The book will give answers to the age-old question of why everyone from Rekha to Bollywood newest generation wants to wear the Manish Malhotra brand, and will also take you into the designer's life, where he also recounts his interactions with international celebrities like Michael Jackson and the Princess of Riyadh.
