column1: Do Crocs really deserve the fashion industry’s disapproval?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion What makes it cool to be uncool There are few debates in the world that can spark off polarising views as the humble, undemanding Crocs slipper—is it a sartorial tragedy that has dogged the steps of mainstream fashion down the ages, or is it a meritorious win for substance over style? And right between the two ends of spectrum lies a deep, bottomless chasm, where fashion vitriol locks horns with an all-enduring consumer fanbase. In the interest of context, Crocs aren't the only persona non grata in the cool kids' club either. The many designer renditions of Birkenstock still hold a divisive audience, and the Ugg boots are no closer to claiming a seat at the grown-ups' table. Throwing this gag reflex to ugly shoes in sharp contrast is the fact that the mysterious forces that govern the catwalks have found a sense of humour, and bad taste now makes the billing as good fashion. From luxury makeovers for humble Ikea bags to severed heads as runway accessories, self-aware irony is busy chalking out its boundaries in the hallowed world of couture. Campy kitsch is the new flavour du jour, and cool is the new uncool. With the resurgence of interest in Crocs, which side of the fence should you be standing on? If you haven't quite been able to bring yourself to walk into the roulette wheel of candy floss hues that headline a typical Crocs outpost, or the sartorial backlash has kept you from trying one on for size, here's a look at the facts from a completely blank slate. Leave the memes at the door, and consider the fashion significance of this enduring foam clog without any preconceived notions. A superhero is only as good as his origin story, but fashion's favourite punchline had a surprisingly grounded birth. On a trip across the Caribbean, three friends discovered the virtues of slip-resistant clogs brimming with untapped potential for everyday consumers—the sales pitch wrote itself. After licensing the product from the Canadian company manufacturing the foam footwear as boating shoes, they added the now-iconic straps and holes. Deciding the name was the easy bit: after realising that the top looked like a crocodile snout from the side, the moniker of ‘Crocs' was finalised. And just like that, a legend was born. Upon its unveiling at a local boat show in Florida in 2002, all 200 pairs were sold out, and the black sheep of the fashion fraternity has since gone on to find a home in over 300 million shoe closets around the world. Not one to blindly follow the herd? Allow the visionary genius of Fashion Week mainstays to help you navigate this minefield. Christopher Kane decisively added a high-fashion lustre on this normcore staple when he sent his models down the spring/summer '17 runway wearing gem-encrusted Crocs, sparking shockwaves through the fashion insiders perched prettily in the front row. And he did this at his 10th anniversary show! “I've always been a fan of the iconic Crocs clog. I like that they are perceived by some to be quite ‘ugly' and not at all feminine or designed to flatter,” declared Kane at the release of the collection. Kane isn't the only one to come out swinging in favour of this everyday basic. Balenciaga went where no other couture house had before by putting ‘platform heels' and ‘Crocs' together in the same sentence. Models stomped down the spring/summer '18 catwalk in rainbow-hued, ten-centimetre tall platforms topped off by the signature Crocs design—with an embellished update, of course. While internet cynics wrung their hands in distress, the design quickly sold out before our eyes. And just when you thought that you had seen everything, the label has now dropped stiletto Crocs—that look exactly like what the name suggests. Hot pink foam resin narrows out into a sleek, pointy heel, with kooky charms adding to the sartorial nonchalance. The time for this-can't-be-real has passed. We are now headed into a future where Crocs are a couture staple, and the top-billing designers are just sinking their teeth into this meaty world of possibilities. Not too sure what the real-world future looks like for Crocs, beyond the forgiving canvas of boundary-pushing catwalks? Look to your favourite A-listers for inspiration. Kate Middleton, for one, has no qualms popping on her cherry red pair for a quick stroll outdoors with young Prince George. The result? A 1,500 per cent increase in sales the very next week. The shoe's comeback to grace was further cemented in place by Drew Barrymore, who dropped a viral music video earlier this month serenading this versatile staple. If you're still not ready to make friends with this fluffy foam concoction, consider its multiple benefits. Apart from being orthopedic-approved for your posture, Crocs also aid the circulation of blood, while massaging the arches of your feet as a special bonus. If you're worried about damaging your style cred, keep in mind that the key to not letting your Crocs overwhelm your entire look is to just treat it as any other shoe. Liven up a colour-blocked outfit with this rubber pair in a neutral hue, or dress it down with a basic white workwear shirt and your favourite ripped denims. For your work wardrobe, throw together a pleated accordion skirt, a basic tee and a statement pair of Crocs for an effortless pass to kitschy cool. And once you've worked your way up the comfort charts, look to Christopher Kane's animal-print version to work wonders for breaking the monotony of head-to-toe colour. column1: Can you guess how much it costs to put up a fashion show?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion For new designers wanting to present their vision to the world, a fashion week show is golden. But what are the upfront costs? Vogue gets a breakdown from model fees and venue hire from New York-based designer Christian Siriano Flashy, extravagant and Instagram-ready, fashion week is a daunting event for brands on a tight budget. Producing a show is a highly expensive business, and one that not every label can afford. Vogue speaks to New York-based designer Christian Siriano, who first gained fame as the youngest winner of Project Runway, hot on the heels of his spring/summer 2019 show at Gotham Hall about what a show really costs and why it's worth it. There's a lot of reasons I still do it. My clothes have a lot of movement to them and that is always important to showcase on a bigger scale. I also fill my shows with customers [in the audience], it's why our business has been able to grow season after season, because we have always really supported the women who are shopping. It is hard to see, ‘Oh are we getting anything back?' I think when our investors go through the numbers, it's really hard for them to see actual return. Obviously, there are ways to tell if a collection is more successful than another, but that doesn't necessarily have to do with the show. It has more to do with the timing, or the fabrications we're using or what's happening with the seasons. It's such a big part of branding for the business. Without my shows, I wouldn't have been able to put it out to the world that we're changing the face of fashion and who should be celebrated. It [results] in so many types of business. $40,000-$60,000 for models For a model with a big name and following, add $20,000. $20,000-$50,000 to rent a venue The production company does location scouting and then we take a day and I go to maybe five or ten places and it's pros and cons—what works, what's the price, how many people can we fit? Obviously, that's the challenge of New York because space is limited. $10,000-$40,000 on lighting The price varies depending on what the venue has set up—and sometimes that's not even a lightbulb. $5,000-$10,000 for sound $20,000-$30,000 for production The production company are backstage with their headsets, calling the show, doing the lighting, doing the sound. They do all the unglamorous stuff, but they're very important and they can be very expensive depending on what you're doing.” $5,000-$10,000 for seating “I've had venues where you're on stadium-type seating. That's super expensive to bring in, but it's important because if you have this amazing venue and the fourth row can't see anything, then there's no point.” $20,000-$100,000 on set design “Putting on a show at fashion week is almost like putting on a Broadway show, but you don't get a dress rehearsal. We literally get one shot and you just hope it works out. That's why it's such a crazy thing what we do.” $2,000-$5,000 for catering Including backstage and team dinners the week prior to the show (often sponsored). “I always make sure the catering is amazing because I want everybody to feel good and not feel hangry.” $5,000-$7,000 for car services including last-minute team errands and VIP arrivals. “It can really add up. We're so busy, we'll send interns in cars to run clothes to an actress.” $0 for hair, makeup and nails which are always sponsored—as is the after-party. Total: $125,000-$312,000 plus the cost of producing the runway collection itself. View Gallery 8 Photos Can you guess how much a fashion show costs? Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Lakshmi Menon talks about Indian representation both on and off runways
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And tells us why she quit social media It's early morning and I'm meeting Lakshmi Menon in the lobby of her hotel. It's day two of New York Fashion Week, and she's in town from India for the shows. When I greet her, she's wearing a hoodie, leggings and sunglasses, and her hair is pulled back—an unpretentious appearance that is not unlike the model herself. We go back to her room to talk, and though the sequence of events seem fairly ordinary, the person who stands before me is anything but. Menon, 36, has been modelling for over a decade, booking campaigns with Hermès and Givenchy and walking shows for fashion labels like Chanel and Stella McCartney, to name a few. She's also graced three covers of Vogue India till date, including the very first issue. Between the strength of her work and the relationships she's built with people in the industry, Menon has not only attained supermodel status, she has also achieved an elusive longevity and cachet that few models achieve. But perhaps her greatest victory has been the visibility she's created for Indian models. India's population was almost one-fifth of the world's up until a few years ago, but there was only one top Indian model working in fashion internationally. Menon broke barriers in her industry, and helped open the door for all the Indian-origin models practising their careers overseas today. We settled into chairs at her hotel room's balcony to talk about Indian representation, and why she's not doing four shows a day anymore. Not fashion-wise, it's always meeting up with my friends here, who are pretty much like my family. And fashion-wise, I'm doing a few shows: Tom Ford, Ralph Lauren, Escada. I mean, it's not like the old days where one would end up doing four shows a day. Those days are over for me, I think. I've done it for so long now, it makes sense to do just the crucial, critical shows. Thankfully, I have an agent who's completely on the same platform as I am, so there's no conflict between us. He's one of the classiest men I've met in the business. He's very charming, he's very down to earth, very approachable. He's a nice man. You know, you can actually have a conversation with him. You don't feel that he's detached from the people around him. He's very warm and friendly—that makes a huge difference. More than anything else, it's the people who you work with and the energy that one has that makes a difference in the work that you do. He is very inclusive. He appreciates diversity, which is how it should be. The world is made of different kinds of people, races, ethnicities... and all of that should be celebrated. You can't just isolate one race and say, “This is the only beauty that's around.” That's just unfair. It's important that beauty is represented in all of its forms. When I first broke into the scene here, it was still all white girls. It was Russian, Eastern European, blonde girls that were dominating the shows. And there was constant talk about lack of diversity. When I started, I think Ujjwala [Raut] was the one just before me, and I think she had sort of stopped around that time. When I came in, I was the only [Indian] girl who was working, the one who was visible. After me, there was a whole bunch of other girls who have come in, and I'm very happy for it. It's important. There are a lot of Indians in the industry—perhaps more on the business side of it versus the creative side. Of course, the one person who comes to my mind who has forged his way ahead is Ramesh Nair, who is at Moynat as the creative director of the label. Manish Arora also shows his collection in Paris every season. Then there's Bibhu Mohapatra, Prabal Gurung—he's from Nepal, but it's all in that region: Asia Pacific and Southeast Asia. So to answer your question, yes, I do, and of course there's room for more. I hope there will be more kids who will come out. There's a girl at Central Saint Martins, Supriya [Lele], who just graduated last year and she's doing interesting work. I think there's some young and upcoming talent in the business now too. [The creative field] was not considered to be economically viable [back in the day]. That's the reason why engineering, being a doctor, being a professional was what made sense. At that time, acting [was not an option either], especially for girls, because there was this whole prejudice of women in those fields being exposed to what was considered taboo. But now it's all opening up, because they realise this is a serious industry. The film or fashion industry are all very serious professions. I think that the whole mindset has shifted. There are girls who are doing great stuff. I mean, Priyanka Chopra's made it big here. She's extremely successful in the US. I've given it all a shot. I tried Facebook for a bit. I realised it was not for me. I tried Instagram. Same thing. I mean, I don't like the culture of narcissism and voyeurism. It's very addictive. And the more time you spend on it, the more followers you get, the more likes you get. The more selfies you post, the more followers. It's a weird algorithm. It's an algorithm that feeds into your narcissism. We all have that narcissistic tendency amongst us, but it's about whether you feed that part of you or don't. I chose not to. No. I mean, I did it more out of a curiosity. When I decided to sign out of it, it hasn't [affected work]. I think this is just a fad. I feel like the teenagers now don't really care much for social media. I was reading that in The Guardian the other day. They were saying that [teenagers] prefer to engage in other things like books or sports or music, to develop themselves in different ways versus just social media. I like being home. I was born there, raised there. I spent a considerable amount of time outside of India working, living, [and] I just chose to move back. I find my life there to be a lot more wholesome. Being closer to my family, my close friends...being at home grounds me. I live in Goa now. I moved there a year ago. I live in a house with 10 dogs. It's the absolute opposite of New York City. I have a garden, the air is clean, I like to swim, I'm learning to windsurf, I do yoga, so it's more of a holistic approach to my life there versus being in the rat race constantly. When I'm in New York my usual arrangement with my agent is that I come here for two weeks, I do as much as I can and then I go back home. I think I'm a lot more self-assured. That's something you gain with getting older. It comes with gaining more experience in the business. I'm a lot more confident than what I used to be then, I would imagine. [Back] in those days, I would sort of play it cool, but now I think I've truly just come into my own. Twenties are that decade of really exploring yourself and finding out who you are. I moved out of my parents' home when I was 21; I moved to Paris. And that was the start of my own journey of self-discovery. And I think that's the journey you experience all through your life. This is my thirties, it's a completely different sensation of who I am, of the woman that I am and of being comfortable physically, emotionally, mentally. I think now I'm [now] interested in a more spiritual journey. I think that also kicks in. I would imagine that would be the critical difference. Especially in this business, the minute you get self-conscious, you lose it. It has to be effortless. There has to be a sense of nonchalance, which is what actually makes that person attractive. The minute you know that you are beautiful, and you sort of present yourself like that, I think it's over. You lose that spark, which really makes you who you are. column1: Proenza Schouler return to NYFW with a stripped-back aesthetic
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Designers Lazaro Hernandez and Jack McCollough are marking their departure from Paris with a stripped-back aesthetic that focuses on collaboration and inclusivity September—the month when the cogs of daily routine spring into action again, freshly oiled after the summer recess. It's a time of year the French call la rentrée—‘the return' following their national August hiatus—an expression that carries with it a sense of optimism, aspiration and newness. Having shown their past two collections in the French capital, this autumn sees the return of Proenza Schouler—the endlessly hip American brand founded by partners in life and work Lazaro Hernandez and Jack McCollough—to the New York Fashion Week schedule. Guests at the presentation on Monday would have been surprised by the restraint McCollough and Hernandez, whose loyal fan base includes actors Chloë Sevigny and Kate Bosworth, have demonstrated in their spring/summer 2019 collection. As Vogue discovered on a visit to the designers' studio just days before the show, they are marking their departure from Paris with a stripped-back aesthetic that focuses on collaboration and inclusivity. “The inspiration for this collection was twofold,” explains Hernandez when we meet during fittings. “We are obviously coming back to New York, so we wanted to go back to our roots and really hone in on our city, our experiences here, our universe, our friends and our creative crew.” Those in their universe who took an active role this season include artists Olympia Scarry and Bunny Rogers, who traded the front row for the runway to model looks from the collection, while longtime collaborator Ashley Brokaw (the casting director behind every Prada and Miu Miu campaign in the past six years) enlisted Amber Valletta (who fronted the brand's autumn/winter 2018 campaign) and Gemma Ward—the faces of fashion in the 1990s and 2000s respectively. “It's a big mix of girls, a wide and inclusive net which is very America today,” McCollough adds. The second fold to the inspiration was a desire to move their fabric story in a different direction. During their “Paris chapter”, as the designers refer to it, their work became increasingly focused on French craft, with featherwork, ruffles and lace dominating their spring/summer 2018 collection, and macramé featuring heavily for autumn/winter 2018. “We were pushing the envelope on the technical side of things in response to showing alongside the likes of Dior and Chanel,” says Hernandez. “We didn't want to rely on those tropes anymore, and the creative challenge became to strip it all back.” “It's about humble materials,” McCollough continues as we walk over to look at the styling boards. “The entire collection is made out of cotton and denim; there's tiny bit of leather and embellishment.” The images on the boards show models in deconstructed blazers styled with oversizes, marble-dyed shirts, denim dresses of varying shades with dungaree straps, and baggy leather boots bound at the ankle. Possessing all the serene minimalism of an Agnes Martin painting, these are clothes for the 21st-century pioneer woman. Just as the designers sought out the expertise of craftspeople for their Paris collections, for spring/summer 2019 they worked with denim specialists in Los Angeles to experiment with different wash treatments. “We collaborate with these pockets of unique skill sets around the world on each collection,” says Hernandez. “Using techniques that only these denim specialists know, but getting them to do it in a high-fashion way. They'd never made clothes like these before.” Hernandez and McCollough have now been in the business for the best part of 20 years, having launched Proenza Schouler (the brand name is derived from the maiden names of the two designer's mothers) in 2002. In that time, “we have developed a shorthand, so we can jam it out a lot quicker than we used to,” says McCollough. “Usually it starts off as a conversation between the two of us about what feels right and relevant for this moment—what direction we want to take [the collection in] while still keeping the spirit of the [Proenza] girl.” The duo describe how they then delve into research—“throwing images onto the walls, taking them down, editing them, putting them back up.” After going through several of these research cycles, they abscond to their country home in the Berkshires of Massachusetts, where they spend around 10 days sketching garment designs for up to 12 hours a day. “We riff off one another,” McCollough explains. “I'll draw a detail on a jacket that then Lazaro will put onto a dress, for example.” By the end of that time, they have a stack of sketches, which they edit down until they have a coherent collection. Designs are then allocated to the in-house seamstresses so they can start making toiles (test versions of a garment), which are then fitted to a model until the desired cut and shape is achieved and the final sample is put into production. Their process for spring/summer 2019 has been somewhat different, with the initial conversation opened up to include German artist Isa Genzken, perhaps best known for her sculptures of monumental metal roses and subversive mannequins. Hernandez and McCollough had been fans of her work for some time and finally forged a relationship with the artist during a trip to Berlin in the spring. They describe the spring/summer 2019 collection as less of a collaboration with Genzken and more of a “creative dialogue”. They sent her clothes, which she incorporated into one of her mannequins—on display in the show space. In this way, she has served as something of a muse for them. “We are using each other's work as a starting point to, in turn, create our own work,” says Hernandez. “It's similar to how we work together, in a way.” If there is one thing taking a break from showing in New York every September and February has afforded Hernandez and McCollough, it's time for experimentation. “You don't have to be stationary or locked into a certain way of doing things; you can be a lot more fluid and a lot more free with how you explore ideas,” says Hernandez. “Especially an independent company like ours; we can operate in a more flexible way”. “Who knows,” McCollough adds, laughing. “Maybe next season we'll show in London.” Scroll onwards for a closer look at the new collection. column1: What you need to know about designers Sachin & Babi’s take on inclusivity
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You can sit with us This year, British Vogue made headlines for featuring Hijabi model Halima Aden on its most diverse cover yet, Versace unveiled its longest campaign (a line-up of 54 models across genders and ethnicities) and Egyptian-born American Anok Yai became the first model of colour to open a Prada show in 20 years. Now more than ever, it is clear that inclusivity isn't just a fleeting phase in the fashion industry; it is a movement—one that is rapidly raking in participants from all over the globe. The latest to sign up? New York-based designers Sachin and Babi Ahluwalia. “When we start the design process for any collection, we think about all different skin tones and body types,” explained Babi. “Most pieces from our ready-to-wear line are going to be sized from 0-20 and [will be] available on our website this year. In the past, we have shipped up to size 18.” For spring/summer 2019, the husband-and-wife duo forwent the traditional runway format in favour of a campaign fronted by two models of Indian origin—Ujjwala Raut (a face frequently spotted on the catwalks of Tom Ford and Emanuel Ungaro in the '90s) and Kiran Kandola, who you'll recognise from Tim Walker's famous shoot for i-D. “We arrived in this country 20 years ago when there were not as many people who looked like us in the industry. When we saw Ujjwala walk the Tom Ford show, there was a sense of pride. We wanted to relay that same message in our shoot, as Ujjwala has paved the way for models like Kiran,” adds Babi. Today, the mother to a 13-year-old girl and self-proclaimed yogini, Raut modestly credits her meteoric success to being in the right place at the right time. “There weren't many Indian models when I started out and I used it to my advantage,” she says. For her, the campaign seemed to be the perfect fit for three reasons. “Not only are the duo a delight to work with, but what I really love is that their pieces cater to all ages, are so real, and most importantly are made in India.” As for Kandola, who holds a law degree and enjoys kickboxing in her downtime, the connect with the designers traces back to her roots. “The first thing Sachin asked me was where I was from, and we realised our families' are both from the same city, giving me an even deeper connection to the label. Also, their clothes are colourful and vibrant, which I think [is what] we need in our life right now.” Culture & Living Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Ralph Lauren celebrates 50 years and is launching in India this year
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How do you distill five decades into one night to remember? Ralph Lauren achieved the impossible with an emotional show and dinner “Hello everyone my name is Oprah.” The sentence that summed up the magnitude of the evening. There was Oprah Winfrey giving a toast; a front row that boasted everyone from Blake Lively and Jessica Chastain to Priyanka Chopra and Kanye West; models that spanned from Kaia Gerber and Gigi Hadid to Laxmi Menon and Bhumika Arora; and an incredible venue in the middle of Manhattan—Central Park. This is the American Dream. And no one embodies the idea more than Ralph Lauren, who celebrated 50 years in the business with a spectacular and very emotional night, right in the middle of New York Fashion Week 2018. “A triumphant evening and triumphant show. We salute you Ralph... we are all here because of you and 50 years of you designing our dreams. Your story exalts our collective story. Not just about fashion but represents what's great about America. Your work has told the stories of our lives, the ones we live and the one we aspire to,” said Oprah, to the few hundred guests seated for dinner around the Bethesda fountain. “It's not a retrospective,” Lauren had told us earlier in the day. “It's very much about who we are now,” and the show reflected Ralph Lauren signatures in his expansive style. Unsurprisingly, his show concluded with a rousing standing ovation (not to mention the crowd surging towards him to capture the moment for digital posterity). Polo Ralph Lauren is all set to arrive in India this month, with the designer's eponymous label Ralph Lauren following suit later in the year. “I'm very lucky. If I had to have a dream, this is beyond my dreams. I don't dream this big, but this makes me look big tonight,” the designer concluded before kicking off the dinner. column1: Net-A-Porter launches a new Vanguard program to mentor emerging labels
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's what you need to know When Net-a-Porter launched in the summer of 2000, the pioneering e-commerce site's focus was on the high end. The platform debuted as an online shopping destination for those in search of the latest and greatest from big-name brands like Balenciaga, Saint Laurent, Gucci, Stella McCartney, and Dolce & Gabbana. It was among the first e-comm concepts to successfully translate the luxury fashion market, and ever since the site has grown exponentially. Almost three years after founder Natalie Massenet's departure and a merger with Yoox, Net-a-Porter now looks to a new era on the horizon, with a widely expanded roster of designers that fits into new categories, including streetwear, bridal, contemporary, and sport, among others. Today the brand is launching a new initiative called the Vanguard, which will help move Net-a-Porter further into the future by nurturing emerging labels around the world. The incubator program will be overseen by Net-a-Porter's team of buyers and its retail fashion director, Lisa Aiken. Each fashion season, four new designers will be chosen based on their potential to sell globally online. The Net-a-Porter team across all regions will provide mentorship, which will include sessions that discuss business strategy, buying, social media, and public relations and marketing, all while stocking the brand on the site. As Aiken explains, “The Vanguard is our way of formalising and extending the support we already offer emerging talent. Launching a young brand successfully and with longevity requires so much more than design talent.” Aiken also points out that “in an industry so focused on the new, we want to introduce novelty to our customer in a responsible way that also lends itself to the longevity and self-sustainability of these brands.” With labels like Off-White and Vetements leading the fashion conversation, it is undoubtedly true that fashion's compass is pointed in the direction of the underground and the disruptors. But how to scout labels like that? “The first Vanguard brands were chosen because we believe that they each have a unique design aesthetic that will contribute to the fashion conversation,” Aiken says. “We ultimately choose the brands that we believe have the potential to grow into meaningful businesses with a global resonance.” Here, meet the inaugural Net-a-Porter Vanguard class of 2018. Les Rêveries is a romantic, feminine New York–based label helmed by sisters Wayne Lee and Ai Ly. Before launching their family venture, Lee was a buyer at Barneys New York and had her own label, Wayne, while Ly held design jobs at Donna Karan and RRL Ralph Lauren. Their new line features painterly floral-print dresses in silk and lace with subtle ruffle detailing, as well as logo tees, hoodies and colourful knits. The versatile range of day-to-night dresses is really this label's sweet spot, all inspired by daydreams (hence the name), poems, musical melodies, and the sisters' shared love of the arts. French-Spanish designer Julien Martinez launched his line of woven shoes last year. He uses a traditional Spanish hand-lacing technique to craft his neutral-coloured leather footwear, which is available in styles ranging from mules to ankle boots. As the designer describes his label, “Martinez was born from a tribute to the shoes that my grandmother used to wear. She had a timeless Mediterranean elegance. I really wanted to blend the Spanish inspiration and traditional craftsmanship with Parisian style.” Sonia Trehan launched her brand of sophisticated ready-to-wear, RUH, in 2016. Trehan's focus is on craftsmanship and she works with a family-run factory in Naples, Italy to ensure that every piece is made with care and expert craftsmanship. RUH's small, in-season capsule collections, which drop every six to eight weeks, include refined layering pieces like pleather trench coats, A-line skirts, and oversize collar blouses. The name Gu_de comes from an old Scottish pronunciation of good, and it couldn't be more fitting for this buzzy new brand of bags out of Seoul, South Korea. Designer Ji Hye Koo founded her label of understated, geometric top-handles, cross-bodies, and clutches in 2016 and became an overnight sensation in her home country, where she says her customers were on the hunt for something that blended classic lines with a modern aesthetic. column1: The past, present and future of the Indian fashion industry
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As he celebrates two decades in fashion, Rajesh Pratap Singh, one of the architects of the Indian fashion industry as we know it, asks the important question plaguing the industry today and talks about what he envies about this new generation of talent What was the industry like 20 years ago when I started out? It's a question I get asked a lot. It was smaller, more nascent, but in a lot of ways it was formalised, like we see it now. The first stockist of my line of jackets and shirts was Amaya, a store started by Amrita Singh in Delhi's Santushti Complex, and then Ogaan and Ensemble, where hanging on the racks with me were pieces by Suneet Verma, Ravi Bajaj (the pioneer of Indian fashion, Rohit Khosla, had passed by this time) and the designer whose aesthetic excited me the most—Shahab Durazi. He really went against the grain, and there was a quality to his clothing and strong tailoring that was unlike anything we had seen. His label gave me hope that the Indian market would extend beyond traditional wear and open up to other points of view. It was a different time. As designers, our orientation was to focus on the West. We had a great deal of freedom and we were still finding our feet. We didn't worry about brand DNA or making a mistake. Before I started at NIFT in Delhi, I interned with Abraham & Thakore and Martand (Mapu) Singh. A&T, at that time, didn't even retail in India; their focus was on export. Naturally, when I started out, I followed suit. So my marketing was very different. I looked for feedback from the international audiences. I would ask myself: How do I modernise my Indian references for a global product? What will we do with the Indian skirt, so that for a person wearing it in any other part of the world the core values remain the same? Now of course, the Indian market is more important. In the next few years, I plan to communicate and innovate better. And what excites me is working on new materials, combining high and low tech, and experimenting. The concept for India's fashion week was actually created quite literally on a paper napkin. In 1998, 10 designers were taken by the AEPC garment council to New York, London and Paris, and at the end of the trip we were all sitting in a café with Sumeet Nair. We realised that we needed to have a timetable, and we needed to organise the industry to be able to compete on a global scale. Unfortunately, now fashion weeks worldwide are becoming irrelevant, and in India they have become a spectacle—there's one in literally every town. We need to have one week, we need to have one governing body. It's not about the individual or about a single company; it really is about the industry's future. The state we are in now is a result of limited foresight and we have to make that correction. I'm not a forecaster, but I can say that for Indian fashion to come of age we need to have a strong edit—editing the number of designers, and definitely editing the number of weeks. We need to take a step back and see what is required. When I started out, the feedback was that our clothes were too minimal. But that wasn't even our reference point. It was about showing a kind of purity. It wasn't the popular kitsch and Bollywood representation—I wanted to show a different side of India. At that time, there was a great interest in textiles; that was actually what the Indian industry started out with. Mapu played a definitive role in introducing the art and science of Indian textiles to audiences globally. He inspired a lot of designers and artisans, including me. Both he and Rita Kapur Chisti, who worked closely with him, were incredibly passionate about Indian craft. The movement, sadly, lost steam in the '90s and now it's so fantastic to see that it's coming back strong. It's these aspects that are our strengths; the variables we get to play with as Indian designers. Our cultural context is just too strong, and that will always be our identity. In my generation of designers, we thought twice about things, which isn't the same now. You need to keep evolving—the moment you stop, stagnation sets in. It is incredible, the speed at which this generation of young talent moves. Information travels so quickly now, and I think that's what is needed—communication and the confidence to be irreverent. We need to start focusing if we want to move forward. The ministry of entertainment imposes a tax on us. So are we entertainers for a small lot or are we going to be making a difference? The Indian market is ready. What direction are we taking? That's the question that we, as an industry, need to answer. — As told to Priyanka Khanna Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Punk, pretty, powerful: Why are we still talking about pink?
column2:
© Vogue Images Fashion Ahead of ‘Pink: The History of a Punk, Pretty, Powerful Color’, the Museum at FIT exhibition opening on September 7, Vogue looks at pink’s many shades of meaning, from India’s rebellious Gulabi Gang uniforms to the saccharine outfits of Japanese Lolita fashion “Red is dead, blue is through, green's obscene, brown's taboo. And there is not the slightest excuse for plum or puce… or chartreuse,” declares Maggie Prescott, editor of the fictional Quality magazine. “Think pink!” The opening scene of the 1957 musical Funny Face has come to exemplify the whimsical—or perhaps dictatorial—relationship that fashion is understood to have with colour. Today's colour-pop “yeah!” is condemned to be tomorrow's tired tonal “meh”. While the pronouncement of colour trends from on high by waspish editors may now be an established comic trope—who can forget that cerulean scene from The Devil Wears Prada?—the call to “think pink” had particular significance in the 1950s. After the drab palette imposed by rationing after the Second World War, pink broadcast fun and optimism. Historically used for both men's and women's clothing, in the 1950s and '60s pink's links to femininity were avidly promoted as a “corrective” to mounting gender equality. As Valerie Steele, director of The Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology (FIT) in New York, points out, “Pop psychology encouraged a strong emphasis on distinct gender roles”. The Museum at FIT's upcoming show Pink: The History of a Punk, Pretty, Powerful Color is both celebratory and corrective in its reading of pink in fashion. There are some downright gorgeous clothes: a rose-pink Dior cocktail dress from 1960 with a skirt billowing like a bud about to burst; an Elsa Schiaparelli gown in signature “shocking” pink; a Charles James evening ensemble in palest peach, the bodice spilling open with a bouquet of silk flowers. And yet in the hands of Vivienne Westwood, Rei Kawakubo or Zandra Rhodes, pink can also be punk—a violent riposte to tasteful restraint. In fact as a rebel hue, pink comes into its own. Take the Pussyhat: launched by Jayna Zweiman and Krista Suh to coincide with the global Women's March in 2017, the knitted headgear, made to an open-source design, was created in response to Donald Trump's “grab them by the pussy” boast. It quickly became an international symbol of support and solidarity for women's rights—though just as quickly garnered controversy, too. Amana Fontanella-Khan's 2013 book The Pink Sari Revolution: A Tale of Women and Power in the Badlands of India follows the Gulabi (“pink”) Gang, an all-female vigilante group in Uttar Pradesh led by Sampat Pal Devi, which fights for justice for women. Pink performs eye-catching duties as a uniform: both the Gulabi Gang's saris and the Pussyhat are exercises in assertive visibility. “When my Pink Gang arrives in a village to speak to an abusive husband, everyone comes to watch,” Pal told Fontanella-Khan. “We always attract attention.” While pink has remained popular with peacocking men—rapper Cam'ron in pink mink, preppies popping their polo collars, suited Sapeurs in Congo, Dalston's dandy daddies—it has stuck, since the era of Funny Face, as the colour of cute. On show in “Pink” is a lace-trimmed, shell-toned, frou-frou polka-dot ensemble by the Tokyo-based fashion house Baby, The Stars Shine Bright. Worn by Misako Aoki, Japan's official Kawaii (“cute”) Ambassador in 2010, the Victorian doll-like style of the outfit epitomises Lolita Fashion, a subculture that first emerged from Tokyo's Harajuku district in the late 1970s. The idea of pink-for-a-girl extends far beyond fashion. Artist Portia Munson first exhibited her Pink Project: Table in the New Museum of Contemporary Art's Bad Girls exhibition in 1994. A collection of pink objects—mostly plastic, both found and purchased—that the artist had been accumulating since the 1980s, the work's atmosphere is overwhelmingly girlish. Munson showed an updated version of the work with P.P.O.W. Gallery at Frieze London in 2016: a relentless rosy sea of hairbrushes, accessories and tchotchkes, it exuded a magnetic, irresistible kitsch that remained unmistakably feminine and spread across Instagram like a pink rash demanding calamine lotion. Reeling off a list of names for different shades of the colour—baby pink, ballet-slipper pink, Barbie pink, blush pink, bordello pink, bubblegum pink, candy pink, Champagne pink, tranquilising pink, Tumblr pink, ultra pink, watermelon pink, young-girl pink—Steele points out that even where it's explicitly associated with girls and women, “it can signify very different types of femininity—from sweet and innocent to edgy and erotic”. Centuries before Janelle Monáe praised the intimate “Pynk” to be found “beyond forest and thighs,” the colour has carried sexual associations. In the book published to accompany the exhibition, Steele explores the role that Madame de Pompadour, the mistress of King Louis XV, played in popularising pale pink in the 18th century. In a portrait (1721–64) by François Boucher, the marquise appears in voluptuous deshabille at her dressing table, teasing a brush loaded with rosy blusher between her delicate fingers in a moment of staged intimacy. In Au Bonheur des Dames(1883), Emile Zola described the pale-pink undergarments displayed in a lingerie department “as if a group of pretty girls had undressed, piece by piece, down to the satin nudity of their skin.” The composer Richard Wagner had a fetish for pink satin, lining not only his black garments, but also a room of his home in the material. Pink's association with intimate and fetish apparel was sexually weaponised in the bullet-bra'd stage costumes created by Jean-Paul Gaultier for Madonna's Blond Ambition Tour
in 1990. (As testament to the lasting power of that design, a version appeared, updated by Aquaria with the addition of pink sequinned nipples, in the latest season of RuPaul's Drag Race. The popularisation of pink had geopolitical as well as social origins. The South American paubrasilia tree, with its spectrum of pink dye extracts, became so prized in 16th-century Europe, it gave its name to its country of origin: Brazil. Central America, in turn, is home to an indigenous dye source—cochineal—that has been used to produce scarlet since the 15th century. Derived from insects found on the prickly pear cactus, cochineal became one of the principal exports of colonial Mexico. Following the country's revolution (1910–20), cochineal's associations with indigenous cultures led to a widespread embrace of the intense Mexican pink derived from it. In the era of trend forecasting, today's equivalent of ‘think pink' comes via Pantone's colour of the year announcements: tinted takes on the mood of the moment. In 2016, Pantone suggested a pink/blue combo of Rose Quartz and Serenity to reflect “societal movements toward gender equality and fluidity”. The former was a pale dusty rose, a tone since celebrated (and reviled) as millennial pink and worn widely by men and women alike. The doll manufacturers may be yet to receive the memo, but pink is shifting its girly connotations. Punk, pretty and powerful: who wouldn't want in? column1: Models around the world who are breaking the stereotype of perfection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get acquainted with the icons of today One of the meanings of the word model, according to the Oxford Dictionary, is “A thing used as an example to follow or imitate.” For a long time in the fashion and beauty industries, the gold standard for this thing had the following characteristics: statuesque, with perfect locks of hair, beautifully proportioned eyes, a shapely nose, toned body and blemish-free skin. Often, however, a few personalities have walked in to take the industry by storm, and break the cookie cutter moulds of beauty. Resonating with the themes of inclusivity and diversity, these models have, over time, broken the conventional code and formed new norms, urging the society to accept each other and themselves for their individual differences. Don't believe us? Let us give you a quick run-down. In the 1960s, Lauren Hutton became famous for the gap between her teeth; Grace Jones for sharp, androgynous features; and Twiggy, who was “too small and too thin”, became the face of liberal fashion in the '60s. Soon after, Iman became one of the first black models to strut down the runway, paving way for a new generation of models from different origins to become accepted in the otherwise white-washed industry. Coming closer to recent times, Indian models like Ujjwala Raut and Lakshmi Menon made way for others of Indian origin to eventually become front-runners in the international fashion scene too. And as a result, we can now see Dipti Sharma and Radhika Nair (among other Indian models) walking for labels like Balenciaga, Dolce & Gabbana and Vetements. Along with different ethnicities, uncommon features can also be seen on runways around the world today. Not too long ago, Cara Delevingne broke the conventional norms of beauty with her bushy haired brows. She went on to not just start a trend with them, but also encouraged girls to accept their natural features and celebrate them. Ashley Graham followed suit, shattering the notion that models must be of a certain size and proportion—making her a prominent poster girl for body positivity in the industry. Then there's Adowa Aboah, a British model with a shaved head and freckled face who has not only become famous for her looks, but also because of the causes (mental health, sobriety) she supports. Very recently, a petite, hijab-wearing, Halima Aden became an icon for inclusivity in the industry. Having walked for various labels like Alberta Ferretti and Max Mara already, Aden was even featured on the covers of British Vogue and Allure. She prefers to keep her hijab as it forms a part of her identity, and wears braces on her teeth. There are many other game changers in fashion and beauty who have broken through the glass ceiling of rules that dictates the meaning of beauty, embraced their imperfections and inspired others. Here's a few of them. Famously known for her shaved head, tattoos and that gap-toothed grin, Slick Woods needs no introduction anymore. When Woods is not playing muse to Rihanna's inclusive beauty brand, Fenty, she's walking down the runway for Marc Jacobs, Jeremy Scott and Fendi. Starting her career with Kanye West's Yeezy, the 21-year-old now has a massive following (her Instagram boasts of 600K+ followers) and is often photographed by publications worldwide. [#image: /photos/5ce42800b803114e238f6912]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/slickwoods The half Greek-half British model rose to fame for her unibrowed look. Fiercely kickstarting the #UnibrowMovement on social media, the 20-something model loves her natural brows. While the student and model has widely spoken up about the bullying that she has faced because of her jet black brows, she is quite keen on keeping them as they are until she prefers not to—making this about her personal choice and not about beauty standards that change with trends. [#image: /photos/5ce4280089be3651267cfb2a]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/sophiahadjipanteli The 28-year-old model suffers from a genetic condition called ectodermal dysplasia, which has led to abnormal facial structures. Up until a few years ago, Gaydos hated getting her photo taken, but now, she is one of the faces that challenge societal norms of beauty—regularly appearing in numerous photo shoots. A contestant on America's Next Top Model, Winnie Harlow gained popularity for being a model and spokesperson for vitiligo, a skin condition. Unfettered by the white patches of discolouration on her skin, Harlow has gone on to become one of most photographed faces of fashion and beauty. The 19-year-old, four-feet-something Mumbai-based model has gained popularity on the Indian fashion circuit for her unabashedly beautiful face and bone structure. Suffering from alopecia, a disorder that causes partial or complete absence of hair, Toshada Uma is breaking standard beauty norms in India with her looks. She's also a stylist, blogger and co-founder of a project called Altshop—which sells wigs and other accessories. The world knows about Ashley Graham and how she paved way for curvier models in the industry. However, 36-years-old Katya Zharkove, has been modelling in Russia since she was 14 and is considered the first plus-size model of Russia. Just like Graham, Zharkova is also an advocate for body positivity, giving priority to a woman's choice to be healthy and not succumb to societal standards. Diandra Forrest is a black model with albinism. But that didn't stop her from becoming the face of a beauty brand (Wet n Wild), starring in Beyoncé music video (“Pretty Hurts”) and working for designer labels like Vivienne Westwood and Jean Paul Gaultier. Spotted on the streets of New York by a photographer, she also became the first female model with albinism to be signed by an agency—Elite Models NY. Forrest believes her appearance makes her the symbol of racial unity: a black girl, in the skin of a white person. Latvian model and singer-songwriter, Viktoria Modesta, voluntarily chose to have her leg amputated below the knee to avoid future health complications. She now uses a prosthetic replacement and calls herself a ‘bionic artist' and a ‘futurist'. She's not only an amputee model, but also the world's first amputee pop-star, who uses ‘alternate' prosthetics as a part of her projects. The 60-something model's first modelling gig was at the age of 62 for American Apparel's lingerie collection that bore the tagline, “Sexy has no expiration date”. Ever since, she has walked for Tome and been featured in a number of Diesel campaigns. Considering that the industry scarcely represents ‘advanced' or older models, hers is a breakthrough achievement. Like Maye Musk, who began her modelling career at 69 and Carmen Dell'Orefice, who is the longest working model in the industry, O'Shaughnessy is one of the few carrying the baton for this under-represented category in the modelling industry. Largely known for being featured in the Gucci Bloom campaign with Dakota Johnson and Petra Collins, Hari Nef debuted her runway career with the likes of Hood by Air and Ekhaus Latta. She is also the first widely known transgender model in the world. A graduate from Columbia, she is an actor, model and writer, as well as a spokesperson for the transgender community. Her acceptance and success in the industry has encouraged an influx of other transgender models like Andreja Pejic, Carmen Carrera, Isis King and many more. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 10 eco-friendly wardrobe basics that will breathe new life into your closet
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From khadi T-shirts to organic denim, these sustainable fashion staples are made to last For a long time, whenever I entered a store, my eyes were immediately drawn to ruffled blouses and sequinned skirts. I wanted to buy clothes that simply stood out at a party, no matter what they were made of. But a three-month fashion cleanse started me on a journey of sustainable fashion that irrevocably changed my style to make it what it is today. I can say that I actually grew into my love for the basics. Today, I cherish my jersey tank tops and custom-fit jeans as much as I valued those dramatic dresses. More importantly, I am willing to pay for versatile, high quality basics that will last in my wardrobe for a long time now, unlike statement clothing that loses its value once it's worn in front of certain crowd, and can never be repeated again then. ‘Less is more' is the golden rule of fashion, and no clothing embodies this philosophy as much as sustainable basics. A basic T-shirt, for example, can easily be worn with a pair of distressed shorts at a casual outing, but wear it under a blazer with trousers or a skirt, and it can played off as office attire too. A silky LBD works for family dinners, but add statement earrings to your ensemble, and the same outfit can take you to drinks at the bar after you're done as well. That's the thing about wardrobe basics—they become what you them to be. Here are 10 environmentally friendly sartorial pieces that we curated with the goal of making your wardrobe sustainable and versatile at the same time. Keep scrolling. column1: New York Fashion Week: What to expect from the spring/summer 2019 shows
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion No longer the poor cousin to its European counterparts, New York Fashion Week is having a moment. Vogue brings you the lowdown on which designers to mark your card for New York Fashion Week has always felt like the underdog. It's relatively remote geographically, compared to the London-Milan-Paris circuit. It's criticised for being overly commercial. And a few seasons ago, it seemed to touch a nadir, with some of its most acclaimed brands like Thom Browne, Joseph Altuzarra, Rodarte and Proenza Schouler choosing to show in Paris instead. Today though, its schedule, running from September 6 to 12, looks as robust as ever. With some major brands returning from overseas, others celebrating important anniversaries and a full complement of exciting up-and-comers eager to make a mark, the spring/summer 2019 calendar is New York's most exciting in recent memory. After three seasons of showing in Paris, Proenza Schouler and Rodarte are returning to New York. Neither missed a beat in their time away—though Rodarte skipped a runway show last season—and it would not be surprising if they chose to return with a flourish. In their absence, design duo Eckhaus Latta has quickly established itself as one of the most compelling brands on the NYFW schedule. The Rhode Island School of Design graduates were shortlisted for both the LVMH Prize and ANDAM Fashion Award earlier this year, and in August their first solo exhibition opened at the Whitney Museum of American Art—the institution's first fashion-related show in 21 years. Sander Lak is now five seasons deep at Sies Marjan and his work there has established the label as one of New York's most consistent. With an eye for rich, unique colours and impeccable draping, the show on September 9 is appointment viewing. PriscaVera, the three-year old label designed by Prisca Vera Franchetti, shows off-schedule on September 8. Franchetti's work is boldly sexy with a sense of humour, recalling the flair of Demna Gvasalia's early Vetements collections—minus the kitsch. Kozaburo Akasaka's label Kozaburo will show in New York for the first time on September 10. Akasaka, born and raised in Tokyo before studying at London's Central Saint Martins and completing Parsons' MFA postgraduate degree in NYC, is based in Brooklyn. He won the Special LVMH Prize in 2017, and he designs with an edgy, romantic whimsy that recalls his countryman Takahiro Miyashita's work for Takahiromiyashita The Soloist. Telfar, founded by Queens-born designer Telfar Clemens in 2005, has long been a bright—and under-appreciated—light of New York's fashion scene. His collections—and the way they're positioned and brought to market—are whip-smart and super contemporary. His after-show parties are the stuff of legend, too—ask anyone who ended up partying at White Castle in Times Square after the spring/summer 2016 show at Milk Studios. Telfar received some well-deserved recognition in 2017, winning the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund. Look for Clemens to pump up the volume with his early evening show on September 9. Almost all of the finalists of this year's Fashion Fund are showing this season, too. Of particular note are Matthew Adams Dolan, whose expressionistically exaggerated proportions have made him a favourite of Rihanna's, and Raul Lopez's Luar, which embodies a strong DIY, club kid energy. To mark its 40th anniversary and new direction under the stewardship of former Hunter designer Niall Sloan, German label Escada will stage its first runway show. So too will Longchamp. The 70-year-old French house—known primarily for its handbags—has shown a selection of ready-to-wear by appointment for about a decade, overseen by artistic director (and granddaughter of the brand's founder) Sophie Delafontaine, but now it's looking to make a bigger splash, having also enlisted Kendall Jenner as the face of the brand earlier this year. Perhaps Longchamp has sensed an opportunity to cash in on a consumer base in the throes of legacy brand logomania—we'll see on September 8. Among the American legacy brands, Calvin Klein and Ralph Lauren are the two to watch. At Calvin Klein, on the evening of September 11, look for Raf Simons to continue his exploration of Americana's darkest recesses, while Ralph Lauren's 50th anniversary show on September 7 will surely be a spectacle. As usual, the week will end with a Marc Jacobs show at the Armory on the evening of September 12. column1: 7 street photographers reveal how Bill Cunningham shaped their careers
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As Bill Cunningham’s secret memoir is published, Vogue talks to seven street photographers about how the American maverick who birthed street-style fashion photography influenced their style A familiar face for many New Yorkers and fashion industry insiders—unmistakable in his simple uniform of blue French worker's jacket, white shirt and beige slacks—Bill Cunningham documented decades of street style through his New York Times columns “On the Street” and “Evening Hours”, both launched around 1989. Riding his bike up and down New York to capture the ever-changing fashion of the city, the Bostonian photographer gathered an incredible photographic archive of almost anthropological nature, which has been valued at $1 million. Combining the rawness and immediacy of street photography with the glamour and extravaganza of fashion, Cunningham invented a whole new genre that forerun the rise of street-style blogs. Magazine editors started dressing for him well before the birth of the first Instagram influencers. Many of today's street-style photographers were directly influenced by Cunningham, while others didn't discover his work until later in their careers when it became available to a wider international audience in its digital format and through the 2010 documentary Bill Cunningham New York. Two years after his death, his work, unpretentious demeanour and direct approach to photography—swift and without frills—continues to lead the way. In time with the release of his highly anticipated, posthumous memoir, Fashion Climbing: A Memoir with Photographs, seven street photographers tell Vogue how Cunningham has influenced their work and how his legacy still dominates the field at large. Bill's photography was very spontaneous without any careful premeditation—especially when he photographed the [fashion show] audience. He would bring the camera to his face, snap the shot and lower the camera all in about a second. And he was always smiling—I wonder if this was because he was trying not to make the subjects of his photographs aware. I launched STREET magazine in 1985 because I felt that documenting true fashion was a meaningful act and that there wasn't anyone doing it. Little did I know that Bill had been shooting in New York for all those years. Back then I didn't have any opportunities to see his pictures in Japan. Japan is a fish-consuming nation, so the distinction between wild fish and farmed fish is important—I think the same distinction exists in street-style photography. Generally speaking, “farmed” photography makes for more profitable business, but Bill would only accept the “wild” kind. I first met Bill at a Metro station in Paris. It was the first day of my first season shooting the shows and I had been thinking about Bill all day. As I walked along the platform, I noticed a man wearing a blue coat. I caught up with him, introduced myself and told him how much his work meant to me. Since that first meeting, I bumped into him countless times and I was very touched that he remembered me. I discovered his work for The New York Times in 2008 while studying in the city. Before that, most of the photography I was interested in was glossy, glamorous and untouchable, but he made me look at the people on the street. Bill was always definitive in not publishing unflattering photographs of his subjects and I have followed in his footsteps with this, as well as with the diverse focus of his photography. He taught me that living a life of kindness and humility can still lead to success. During fashion month, I tend to get my coffee at the most obscure, “locals only” bars. The coffee is usually terrible, but I like to keep myself on the ground during these lavish weeks of luxury. In a bar like that, on a side street around Place Vendôme in Paris, I bumped into Bill Cunningham. He was sitting by himself, eating a tuna sandwich. He said he always came to this place between the couture shows to let his eyes rest from all the fashion extravaganza. I understood that we were on the same page—we are part of the fashion world, but we do our best to keep looking at it from an outsider's point of view. He created a genre and he will always be the face of it. I grew up in Poland and his photos were nowhere to be seen, so his work didn't directly influence mine, but I think we had similar inspirations. I photographically “grew up” admiring the works of New York street photographers like Garry Winogrand, William Klein and Joel Meyerowitz—people walking the streets of New York City with their cameras, simply shooting whatever came their way. I think Bill translated their visual language into the fashion world. His photos were always more about what he saw than how he saw it. I met Bill only once, about four years ago in New York. He was unmistakable in his uniform and the economic deftness with which he moved. I didn't speak to him, I just watched him work. My work, and the entire genre of street style, wouldn't exist without him, but Adam Katz Sinding, Scott Schuman and Tommy Ton were my introduction. I studied Bill's work later on and it inspired me to focus on the streets and to take my photos without introduction and posing. Bill created a new genre of photography, so all of our work is his legacy. He brought a very democratic, but equally educated and experienced eye to fashion on the street, a domain that had never been acknowledged before. The first time I saw Bill was at the Jazz Age Lawn Party on Governors Island in New York, probably around 2012. I was just starting out and I tried to give him my business card. He said, “Oh no, I don't do that” in a very nice way and went straight back to shooting because he was so into what he was doing. Bill's work for The New York Times really made him the grandfather of street style. He was like an anthropologist, documenting what people wore throughout the years. It didn't matter who you were, what your background was, if you followed fashion or not. Back then people where just dressing for themselves. I saw Bill once when I went to Paris Fashion Week. He walked right past me. Someone who didn't know who he was would have definitely thought that he was just an ordinary passerby. At the time, he was wearing his usual blue jacket and he looked a bit older than in photos. Bill stayed true to his own style and documented people who took what they wore seriously. He is an example for all street photographers. He respected the art of photography—there was a sort of purity about him. In choosing his subjects he always adhered to his own principles, without being swayed by brands or marketing reasons—this is what has influenced me the most. In the same way, I'm committed to my own photography style and vision when I choose who to photograph. I think it's a way to show respect for the job and I hope I can convey it to my followers. Bill didn't influence me in terms of style. I wanted to get pretty pictures and instead he used to take these really fun snapshots and documentary-style images capturing a wide range of styles. However, I was influenced by his work for The New York Times—I absolutely loved the way he was able to observe details, depict a trend and put the clothes in a cultural context. His passion and dedication is what has influenced me the most, teaching me the importance of learning more about the clothes and why people wear them. He was a very gentle person who kept to himself, but you could tell how much he enjoyed what he was doing. He had such a playful spirit. I was always stunned by how modest Bill was in this business of vanity—I think that's an important lesson to keep, no matter how successful you are. column1: Two of a kind: 9 of most popular model siblings on the fashion circuit
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Sister act It's not rare to see the sibling revelry in the modelling world—after all, the industry thrives on what the right mix of genes serves up. Over the years, we've spotted a number of model sisters featured together on campaigns and editorials all over the world, and with good reason. Here's our list of model siblings who prove that while one is great, two is always better. The Delevingne sisters have been on the fashion circuit for quite some time now. While Cara is known for her bushy brows and strong jaws, Poppy is the one with the soft, romantic face. The sisters are quite close—the two bought a house together and Cara was Poppy's bridesmaid at her wedding. Setting #SisterGoals on Instagram, the Hadid sisters are probably the most popular duo of the lot. Known for setting trends with their street style choices, Gigi and Bella are often seen borrowing from each other's closet. While Gigi keeps it super chic, Bella prefers to give her ensembles a sultry edge. These American teen models became multimillionaires very early in their lives, and are famous for their Vogue spreads. At age 11, Krissy (the younger of the two) began accompanying her sister for shoots and soon started getting photographed alongside her as well—she even walked the ramp with '90s Supers before her untimely death in 1995. Having done a Gap ad campaign together, the Rayder sisters were a bit hit in the late '90s and early 2000s. While elder sister Frankie was the face of Chanel, D&G and Versace, Missy worked extensively for Gaultier, Prada and Moschino. Popular on the Indian runway, the Chatterjee twins are probably few of the most missed models at Indian fashion weeks. The sisters were considered head turners in the early 2000s, and have walked the ramp for a lot of Indian labels including Sabyasachi. Of Norwegian and Tanzanian origin, the 19-year-old twins were discovered on Instagram and are currently among fashion's favourite twins. Frequently photographed by street style photographers in Oslo, the twins have also made an appearance at Beyoncé's Ivy Park campaign. When the OG supermodel introduced us to her half sister, Lottie, the fashion world went into a frenzy over how similar the two looked. Lottie Moss' body of work includes an homage to her elder sister's iconic Calvin Klein campaign, and she is often spotted sitting front row with '90s supermodels. These two been a part of the Indian fashion circuit for more than a decade. While Binal stuck to modelling, Pia went on to become a popular TV host. When your father is rock royalty Mick Jagger, you're bound to step into the spotlight at some point in your life. While Georgia May Jagger has been spotted hanging out with Gucci's Alessandro Michele, Lizzy has done campaigns for likes of Tommy Hilfiger and Mango. The two have also starred together in Sonia Rykiel's campaigns. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: As The Oak Tree shuts doors, founder Priya Nathani pens down a tribute
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Plus, four regular patrons of the iconic Colaba store reminisce about their favourite moments “18 years ago, I opened The Oak Tree with a simple mission: to have a store where women of all ages could come and shop for fun, day and evening wear clothes and accessories. Back in those days, Mumbai lacked any high street retail, and there were certainly no global chains present. The Oak Tree set out to be an accessible fashion store with an eclectic collection of merchandise that people could afford. It was the kind of place into which anyone could wander, whether they were a local or a tourist. I would like to think that there was always something for everyone, reflecting current trends and that too, at a great price. All across India, there are many people who bought their first sparkly tunic, or a black dress or their first Kolhapuri wedges at The Oak Tree. From quirky headbands to evil eye bracelets to really cool clutches to resort travel totes, we carried it all. So many people tell me that the store was a mandatory visit before they travelled on holiday. And everyone brought their friends who visited from out of town to the store. We were on the must-visit shopping list in all the travel guides. The whole ethos of the store was friendly, and personal. For many years, my beloved dog Maggie was a fixture, as she sprawled her maginifcent golden retriever self on the floor. She was The Oak Tree mascot. I still miss her like crazy. Our wonderful sales staff, Sandeep, Abhijit and Jayesh, who have been with me for the past 15 years or more, knew everyone's likes and dislikes. In the pre-mobile phone and Whataspp era, these things counted for something. Well before there were big exhibitions, pop-ups and the Internet, The Oak Tree was a launching pad and platform for many young designers who were just starting out with their lines of either clothing, jewellery or shoes but had no retail outlet in which to show their talent. I always wanted to give an opportunity to young designers who had The Oak Tree sensibility and who complimented our style and vision of easy, breezy chic. It's been wonderful seeing designers who first showed at the shop bloom and become successful! Over the years the store has served its customers well and had become an institution in the city's retail landscape. I am so grateful for all the love and appreciation that we have received over the years. Now it is time for new beginnings and new endeavours.” Vogue spoke with four patrons on everything from their first buy to their favourite memory at The Oak Tree “The first thing I bought at The Oak Tree was a tunic dress in earthy colours from Shalini Shahani. Walking into the space on Colaba Causeway was often like walking into a really hip resort shop in Miami. You know, there are lots of multi-brand stores, but I think what completely stood out with The Oak Tree was, of course, Priya's curation and eye, and how ahead of its time it really was. At a time when everybody was busy buying either formal designerwear, or still trying to grapple and figure their style, there came a store that was vibrant, fun, and sassy. It was where all the cool people seemed to congregate.” – Priya Tanna “Back then in Bombay, there was no other standalone store like The Oak Tree. Some of my earliest buys from there were a few totes, shawls, clutches, resort kurtis and Elizabeth Hurley swim and resortwear. Being at The Oak Tree was quite a personal experience. On some days, I would drop in for a cup of coffee with Priya, or to just sit and chat. While in summers, Maggie, the resident pup, would sit and play at our feet while we chatted and drank endless jugs of nimbu pani. I think these little incidents are what I would miss the most about the place. It has also contributed to the Indian fashion industry to a great extent, having brought western as well as locally-made fashion to the city.” – Roohi Jaikishan “The Oak Tree was a must-visit for all friends and family who would come to Bombay. A gorgeous Shalini Shahani kurta, a pair of coveted Kolhapuris, and a sparkly beach bag were some of my first purchases. A pre-holiday ritual and a one-stop shop of the best in the market, it offered India a pool of fresh designers, with unmatched styles and price points. I deeply admired Priya's eye for style; what I will miss the most about The Oak Tree is its collection of unique pieces, and Christmas shopping for my friends living overseas.” – Samantha Nayar “The Oak Tree used to be my go-to shop for gifts for friends abroad, and to pick up trinkets for my daughter. I bought a bright, printed kurti 17 years ago from the store, which I still have and wear. What I will miss the most about The Oak Tree is being able to make a happy stop to give Priya a hug—it had an amazing, happy vibe which was all ‘Priya'. The Oak Tree brought us tasteful kitsch. It was casual India with a dollop of sophistication. Well-priced and well-curated.” – Haseena Jethmalani Culture & Living Culture & Living Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Slow living devotees will love Verandah’s new outpost in Mumbai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A home away from home In a world teeming with chaos, Verandah by Anjali isn't afraid to press pause and slow down the hamster wheel of fashion. It stands to reason that the label's newest outpost should reform an industrial area into a homely atelier, boldly juxtaposing the corporate humdrum in the heart of Lower Parel's business district. “Keeping in mind the discerning tastes of our clients and the fact that I'm a working mum of two young kids, I wanted to create a cosy space within this office complex that spoke my language and was evocative of the relaxed nature of the label. The space is cosy and inviting, much how I like my home to be,” designer Anjali Patel Mehta says. The brooding split-level industrial unit has since been transformed under Patel's creative supervision to make room for personal mementos from her travels. One by one, the false ceilings and walls came apart to be replaced by glass and exposed i-beams, with airy fabrics that reinforce her dedication to upcycling. “I vowed to stay true to my belief that the old can be rebottled into new, and with a little imagination, the place has come alive with a breezy vibe. The dining table is refurbished with a pine top and seasoned mango wood, complemented with old teak chairs from home. Antique kilims, collected on my travels to Turkey, also find a home here. But one of my favourite pieces in the space would be the ‘bling dhurrie', a handcrafted rug made with hemp and silver gota by a Jaipur-based artist, Elizabeth,” she elaborates. Patel's love for whimsy means that artwork from her young toddlers shares space with exclusive pieces from international art galleries. “As the finishing touch, we added in art by my kids, Alekha and Sumer, alongside prized posters and limited-edition prints from my favourite flea markets and art galleries in Paris, Vietnam, New York and Ceylon of Malewitch, Klee and Kandinsky. A special work is a pen and ink drawing of me by my mum, alongside a much needed Nespresso machine and Netflix for dire babysitting needs!” she divulges. The label's new address will house the main collection this season, as well as limited edition pieces from their main print stories. “Bespoke pieces for clients is something that I still love to do, and this space allows me to slow down and do what I love, apart from scaling up the business. The idea is for clients to come by appointment and get a feel of our entire range of work as opposed to a rack in store,” she adds. And while we have crossed the halfway mark on 2018, Patel is only just getting started. Next on the cards for the label is the resort/spring '19 collection inspired by the designer's 150-year-old family home in Mumbai as a tribute to all things vintage. You are also going to want to watch out for the launch of Verandah Swim, a supplementary line made with recycled polyester and the finest grade Italian fabrics at a sustainable water neutral facility. But above all, Patel hopes that, “Our work grows slowly, organically and sustainably with the fairest and most transparent trade practices, and is worn with love.” View Gallery 9 Photos First look at Verandah’s new outpost in Mumbai Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This shopping event will shine a light on special education in India
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In New York? Mark this on your calendar Any seasoned shopper would have frequented the Intermix stores in New York. For over two decades now, they have served as a one-stop shop for labels both established and emerging. Think the likes of Balmain, Alberta Ferretti, Ulla Johnson and Attico. Now, Intermix has joined forces with Indira Bodani, founder of the Gateway School of Mumbai—a space dedicated to empowering children with learning difficulties. The result? A shopping event that brings into the spotlight the creative efforts of the school's students, while treating those in attendance to the store's carefully curated collection. “This April, we had an art show, which was the coming together of five labels, Monisha Jaising, Vikram Phadnis, Surily DP Goel, SS Homme, Seema Khan, and the children of Gateway. That, I think, was really liked by Intermix and they wanted to celebrate these kids, and at the same time create awareness about special education in India,” says Bodani. Also, on display are the children's collaborative works with Supriya Himatsingka of the Baby Baazaar and home accessories created with Tanya Deol. “They are inviting their regular clients to, of course, come shop, but also see the lovely work done by the kids. What I'm hoping is that maybe some designer or some design home in the US gets interested and we can actually work with them.” The event will be held on Thursday, September 6, from 5pm to 8pm at Intermix Columbus, 210 Columbus Ave Culture & Living What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast
