column1: Crazy about shoes? These 5 Instagram accounts will feed your obsession
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Don’t say you love shoes if you haven’t heard of them If “feet first” is how you like to go in, Instagram has you covered. While #Shoefies, #ShoeGame and #ShoeAddicts acknowledge and drive our narcissism and need for micro-chronicling our lives, the following Instagram accounts show us there are other routes to #ShoeLove. Follow, double tap. Diana Rojas has a knack for turning the season's snazziest/ugliest/coolest kicks into their ceramic versions. A pyramid of Uggs? Of course, it's a thing. Vetements flame-pattern platform boots? She's done a version. Hood By Air double boots, Balenciaga platform Crocs, Gucci platform loafers? Duh. “In the criminal justice system, shoe-based offences are considered especially heinous” is the premise with which Crimes Against Shoemanity begins chronicling crimes of fashion (back pat, back pat). Thought you've seen it all? “Ugly” doesn't even begin to describe the ones that find pride of place here. Follow Belgian footwear designer Mats Rombaut for an off-the-centre take on footwear, all united by a thrust on eco-friendly, sustainable materials like natural fibres, stone and bark. The label's Instagram account is meant to read aloud the brand's sustainable philosophy—read beach sandals fashioned out of seaweed, turnip-heel sandals, brown-paper slides, etc—besides of course the label's more wearable vegan cult sneakers that are stocked by the likes of Comme des Garcons and Saks Fifth Avenue. column1: These female designers are bringing body positivity to swimwear
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Feeling good on the beach or poolside is the first step to looking good. Vogue talks to the swimwear designers who are putting inclusivity front and centre With the Miss America pageant announcing that the swimsuit competition will be retired in June and catcalling being banned in France this month, as Europe's annual August migration to the coast ensues, what does this spell for the swimsuit? Will we see a return to more covered-up styles reflecting a changing world? Yes and no, opines Russian designer Olga Vilshenko, who just debuted her resort line Morye. “Miss America has always had a massive influence on young minds all over the world,” says Vilshenko, who welcomes the acknowledgment that “the beauty of every woman comes primarily from within”. However, she's quick to point out that since its inception, the swimsuit has always been the subject of passionate discussion and debate and, ultimately, women have the right to choose how they want to look on holiday. “Some will feel comfortable when the body is more covered, some will feel comfortable in a tiny bikini, but we must remember that both have the right to choose and both have to be equally respected,” she says. American designer Mara Hoffman agrees. “You can go to the beach nude or totally covered; it's more about validating women in their choices and bodies whatever they may be,” she says. “Body positivity does not mean more or less clothing, it means being aware of your relationship with your body and feeling comfortable in what you choose to do with it and what you choose to wear.” She adds, “Society sexualises women, clothing does not. It's necessary for us to acknowledge and teach that a woman's body is not an object, regardless of what she wears or how she acts.” Here, Vogue takes a look at five female-designed brands reconsidering what the swimsuit might symbolise and say about women today. “I think more women than we think dread beach season, so that's one of the reasons it felt like a natural extension to create flattering, modest swimsuit styles in the brand's signature floral prints,” says Olga Vilshenko of Morye, which means “sea” in Russian. “We put a lot of effort into creating precise scaled prints that will look great on different sizes. My key is to combine minimalistic design with lines that compliment a woman's body.” Vilshenko set out to create solutions for women of all shapes and generations. “I wanted the resort wear to take our customers from the city to the beach, so it's less of a scary transition into their holiday wardrobes,” she says of the collection of suits and coordinating loose, easy-to-wear dresses, which have already amassed a following of Instagram stars including Lucy Williams, Blanca Miró and Maja Wyh. “It's an exciting time right now to be a woman,” says Carly Brown, who created the size-inclusive Australian line, Une Piece, after scouring stores for a sophisticated, well-designed one-piece that didn't oversexualise women. “The last decade has seen the impact social media can have on body image, often not positive, but I believe the last 18 months have seen a resurgence in women readdressing and reconsidering how they feel about their body in a more positive way,” says Brown, who tested her suits—ranging from a zip-up, long-sleeve “Sexie Rashie” to a twist-centre halter—on hundreds of women of all shapes before launching. “There are some amazing role models, champions and brands out there challenging narrow representation of beauty and body type,” says Brown, whose one-pieces are made with UPF50+ Italian Lycra that blocks 98 per cent of UV rays and feature 28 individual pieces, compared to an industry average of eight, to support and cinch in all the right places. “It's important to reinforce the idea that any body is right for the beach, any body is right for a swimsuit,” says Mara Hoffman, who's working to feature women with different bodies across her platforms and to make different types of suits for women who want a variety of styles, colours, coverage, or support levels. In addition to championing body positivity, she's also rethinking her legacy. In 2015, after 15 years in business, she overhauled her manufacturing process, switching to responsibly sourced, organic recycled materials. “We were in the business of making more, more, more and I was becoming increasingly at odds with that mentality,” she explains of the motivation behind such a massive undertaking. “I was becoming aware of how my son would inherit the consequences of my choices today and the long term environmental impact of those choices.” Today, Hoffman's swimwear is made exclusively of either recycled polyester comprised of post-consumer plastic bottles, or recycled nylon made from fishing nets, industrial plastic waste and fabric scraps. “In 2017 alone, our use of ECONYL® diverted 10,797 lbs of waste from landfills, including 2,744 lbs of fishing nets,” says Hoffman, whose fans include Michelle Obama, Gabrielle Union and Issa Rae. Marysia Dobrzanska Reeves welcomes the recent flurry of female-founded swimwear brands. “One needs to understand how it feels to have the female curves and the imperfections that fit models don't have,” says the LA-based, Polish-born surfer, former ballerina and designer of the eponymous line, Marysia. She also views her role as designer as an opportunity to influence the next generation of women. “We need to teach young girls how to think on their own and decide how they want to dress and why,” says the mum of two daughters, who's known for her scalloped-edge swimwear, cut by hand in a couture factory. “In my campaigns, I try to portray a different, more classy young girl who is cool and fashionable all at the same time,” she says of her children's line, Bumby. “Slowly we're becoming more accepting of others and not trying to fit them into some ‘box',” adds Reeves, whose following includes Lupita Nyong'o, Gwyneth Paltrow and January Jones. “There's nothing sexier than a woman who's comfortable in herself, regardless of her size, shape and form,” says Christine Tang, co-founder of Australian label FELLA. The secret to confidence, says Tang, is “owning what you wear because you feel amazing in it”. To that end, she offers a made-to-order service within her online shop. “One of the greatest things we're able to do is create custom-made swimwear, which allows the suit to fit a woman's body almost perfectly to her size and shape,” says Tang, who's sensitive to the apprehension beach season often arouses. “It's the most exposed most women will be to the public eye,” notes Tang. She and co-founder Rosie Iffla are working to make their factory carbon neutral this year, and they strive for sustainability by designing pieces built to last. “I still wear my Lennox and Otis swimsuits from our very first collection six years ago!” says Tang, whose devotees include Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Behati Prinsloo Levine and Georgia Fowler. column1: Here’s why you keep spotting the same names on a designer’s front row
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Often seen side by side at fashion week to support their design house, fashion’s muses travel in packs. Vogue breaks down some of the most well-known and the designers they have followed through the years Ever faithful to their favourite designer, groups of stars often pledge their allegiance early in the game, sitting side by side on the front row from season to season. Take Gucci, for instance. With a roster as eclectic as his collections, Alessandro Michele's “Gucci Gang” now even boasts a theme song (thanks, Lil Pump). From Jared Leto and Dakota Johnson to A$AP Rocky, Florence Welch and Elton John, Michele's front row is glittering with megastars from music and film. The latest addition to the group? Heartthrob Harry Styles, who broke the internet modelling the brand's tailoring collection at a St Albans chip shop in June, following a series of front row appearances for the house and a glittering all-Gucci tour wardrobe. Despite the ongoing creative director swaps, some designers take their celebrity pack with them when they hop from house to house. Take Louis Vuitton's Nicolas Ghesquière and his reported “fashion soulmate” Jennifer Connelly; the two met while Ghesquière was still at Balenciaga when he made the gown she wore to accept her Supporting Actress Oscar in 2002. Their 13-year fashion friendship has seen Connelly become almost synonymous with Ghesquière's hard-edged aesthetic, and she is a front row stalwart alongside fellow brand ambassadors Alicia Vikander, Michelle Williams and Emma Stone. Unlike Connelly, for some stars it's all about the house. Jennifer Lawrence first became a Dior darling during the Raf Simons years, signing the dotted line as brand ambassador in 2012. Since then, Lawrence has appeared at the shows season after season, alongside fellow Dior devotees Robert Pattinson and Natalie Portman. When she took a tumble at the 2013 Oscars while accepting her award? Dior. While she juggled a glass of wine and climbed over seats at the 2018 Oscars? You guessed it. And her allegiance continues: J-Law's most recent Dior gown, worn for the premiere of new film Red Sparrow, took eight people 800 hours to make. And naturally, since the dawn of the new streetwear luxe, there is one gang fashion's coolest scenesters want to be a part of: that of Virgil Abloh's. Rihanna, Kim Kardashian West, Kanye West, Bella Hadid, Hailey Baldwin, Kylie Jenner—the front row of Abloh's Vuitton debut was the most star-studded FROW to date. column1: The rise of the supermodel: Naomi Campbell’s best 1990s moments
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It was the decade that propelled Naomi Campbell from fresh-faced runway darling to bonafide supermodel. Vogue celebrates her most defining—and fabulous—fashion moments of the 1990s Decades on from being part of the "Big Six"—the group of all-conquering supermodels alongside Cindy Crawford, Claudia Schiffer, Linda Evangelista, Christy Turlington and Kate Moss—Naomi Campbell shows no signs of slowing down. Her charitable initiative Fashion For Relief, launched in 2005, has raised millions for a range of causes (this year's proceeds will go to Save the Children and Time's Up); she is a champion of African culture and fashion, most recently with an appearance at Lagos Fashion Week; and has recently ventured into journalism as a contributing editor for British Vogue, interviewing the likes of Apple's Jony Ive and Mayor of London Sadiq Khan. But lest we forget, Campbell will always be first and foremost a supermodel, and the 1990s were her most memorable years. Aged 15, Campbell started her modelling career, adopted and mentored by her ‘papa', the late Azzedine Alaïa, with whom she lived on and off throughout her early career and to whom she credits her success. At the tender age of 18, she walked for the inimitable Yves Saint Laurent in his 1987 haute couture show, wearing a gown made entirely of creamy wafts of fur. The designer famously petitioned to get Campbell her first Vogue Paris cover in 1991. Later that year, Gianni Versace made her the face of his brand, asking her to walk in his iconic autumn/winter 1991 show alongside fellow supers Christy Turlington, Linda Evangelista and Cindy Crawford. The fashion moment was recreated by Donatella Versace in September 2017 to mark the 20th anniversary of Gianni's death. Campbell's life off the catwalk in the 1990s was equally glamorous. From standing beside Nelson Mandela, to raucous nights on the town with best friend Kate Moss, the supermodel was a regular at the hottest parties of the decade; see her laughing with Grace Jones, rubbing shoulders with Madonna or giggling with Dame Vivienne Westwood. column1: A look back at the history of one of fashion’s biggest trends, jumpsuits
column2:
© Vogue Images Fashion The effortlessly cool all-in-one first became a fashion statement in the 1930s—and today it’s a chic wardrobe staple worn by everyone from Solange to Bella Hadid. Vogue looks back at the most memorable jumpsuits of all time There are few pieces in fashion that offer effortless impact like an all-in-one. From its practical beginnings as accidentally chic air force attire, to its domination of the hedonistic dance floors of 1970s disco, to its current status as a street-style staple, the jumpsuit is a classic that designers continue to reimagine. No matter what the mood of the era, its unrivalled ability to make a sartorial statement means it remains the ultimate outfit fix.  It may now be a cult, off-duty piece by day and a cooler alternative to the cocktail dress by night, but before it landed on the runways and red carpets of the world, the jumpsuit served a more practical contingent. Early incarnations came in the form of Italian couturier Elsa Schiaparelli's pocketed bunker suit and Florentine artist Thayat's streamline 1919 take designed to liberate parachuters, skydivers and the era's freethinkers. The simplicity and utility of the one-piece was quickly adopted by other aviators, racing drivers and international air forces and by the Second World War, Vera Maxwell-designed, short-sleeved overalls had become a core part of women's wartime workwear and an emblem of female empowerment. In the decades that followed, Hollywood starlets like Janet Leigh and Katharine Hepburn helped to glamorise figure-elongating, cinched-waisted styles on the silver screen, while Yves Saint Laurent, André Courrèges and Emilio Pucci introduced their own dramatic interpretations to fashionable European society. On stage, Elvis Presley, David Bowie and Cher capitalised on its theatrical potential and on the dance floor, Bianca Jagger and the sybaritic Studio 54 crowd made the jumpsuit an icon of 1970s disco. Sigourney Weaver's khaki military look in Alien, Mel B's unforgettable leopard print one-piece and Britney's infamous red latex catsuit have since helped immortalise its iconic status. The all-in-one continues to evolve both as a cool fashion staple and a standout piece of occasion wear, even bridal wear since Solange Knowles wore a cream, caped iteration at her wedding in 2014. And on the runway, it's still delivering standout moments—see Kaia Gerber in Versace's spring/summer 2018 tribute to the printed body stocking Christy Turlington wore at its spring/summer 1991 show and Alessandro Michele's pistachio-green, belted 1970s Gucci suit—proving that fashion's love affair with this full look shows no sign of slowing. From utilitarian 1950s workwear to street-style set essential, Vogue looks back at the most memorable jumpsuits of all time.  [#gallery: /galleries/5ce428cb3bf9b4aab7b1c46c]||| |||

column1: Why the fashion world needs to commit to an 18+ modelling standard
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion While we can’t rewrite the past, we can commit to a better future Pasha Harulia was fifteen when strangers began reaching out to her on Instagram, asking if she was interested in modelling. She wasn't—but at her mother's urging, she agreed to give it a shot. Weeks after signing with an agency in her native Kiev, the then-sixteen-year-old was en route to Paris, booked for the Balenciaga show. “I didn't even know what Balenciaga was,” says Harulia, who is now nineteen. “People told me it was good.” After Paris came Tokyo, where Harulia shared a models' apartment with several Russian girls, the youngest of whom was thirteen. It was an intense few months, much of the time spent in a van that shuttled the young models to castings. “I had some fun,” she says. “But mostly I was thinking about the money.” Guangzhou, China, was different. Modelling for e-commerce sites, she says she'd sometimes shoot up to 100 looks a day. “It was like, how do you say it—like someone wiped the floor with me,” Harulia recalls. “And then threw me away.” How did we get here? How did the fashion industry become so reliant on the labour of teenagers? What's striking about Harulia's story is how typical it is. Cara Taylor began modelling at fourteen. Imaan Hammam was thirteen when she was spotted near an Amsterdam train station. Andreea Diaconu was an unusually tall eleven-year-old when scouts started circling. These girls are a few of the lucky ones; resilient Harulia signed with blue chip agencies in New York and Paris and walked for Miu Miu in March for the fall 2018 collection, but many of the roommates with whom she shared flats in unfamiliar cities were discarded or burned themselves out—“broken from the inside,” as she puts it. Fashion has long valorised youth. But the churn of “new faces,” as rookie models are known, has become relentless. Vast numbers of them cycle through the industry at hyper speed. “It's not like all these kids are destined to become stars,” notes Angus Munro, a casting director who works with designers including Rick Owens and Isabel Marant. “It's more that the business model has become, let's throw a bunch of spaghetti at the wall, and maybe one noodle sticks and books the Prada show.” No one designed the system to work this way. But can we change it? Early this year, in the wake of #MeToo revelations, Condé Nast International, the publisher of this and many other magazines, issued a new global vendor code of conduct. Responding to stories about models both male and female being inappropriately touched, pressured for sexual favours, and even assaulted, Condé Nast established provisions aimed to ensure that all its editorial shoots are safe working spaces—harassment-free zones with private dressing rooms and allowances for model approval of both poses and clothing. Another set of provisions addresses the age of models: In recognition of the unique vulnerability of minors thrown into a career where they have little control and where abuse has been all too commonplace, the vendor code of conduct stipulates that no model under the age of eighteen will be photographed for editorial (unless he or she is the subject of an article, in which case the model will be both chaperoned and styled in an age-appropriate manner). This is partly the result of an internal reckoning. Vogue, along with a number of other publications, has played a role in making it routine for children—since that's what they are—to be dressed and marketed as glamorous adults. When Brooke Shields, then fourteen, graced the February 1980 cover of Vogue, she was an outlier. Since then, models in their mid-teens have appeared in many of our fashion editorials. No more: It's not right for us, it's not right for our readers, and it's not right for the young models competing to appear in these pages. While we can't rewrite the past, we can commit to a better future. Will the rest of the fashion industry follow suit? The Council of Fashion Designers of America is on board: As its president and CEO, Steven Kolb, explains, the CFDA has witnessed positive changes since establishing a sixteen-plus standard on the runway eleven years ago. “The brave men and women who have come forward to talk about a culture of sexual harassment in certain parts of the fashion industry have made us reevaluate,” he says. “Young models are still developing. There can be a lack of the confidence, strength, experience and maturity it takes to deal with the pressures of this work. The CFDA supports the recommendation of raising the minimum age—we want young models to have the time to come into their own so they feel safe and in charge in the workplace.” A small ask, you might think. How hard can it be to commit to working with models old enough to vote? Consider Naomi Campbell. The ne plus ultra of supermodels, Campbell was just shy of sixteen when she launched her career in the mid-1980s, when there were but a handful of twice-yearly fashion shows—a model could stay in school if she wished. Agencies signed very few names and invested in their long-term success by being selective with their bookings. Thus Naomi and her peers were sought-after. They developed close working relationships with designers, who would rigorously fit the variety of looks handpicked for them to wear on the runway. “It used to be, the fittings would take forever,” remembers David Bonnouvrier, co-founder and CEO of DNA Model Management in New York. “Now the girls are cast to fit the dress.” “It's a numbers game,” agrees Chris Gay, co-CEO of Elite World Group; it includes The Society Management, which represents Kendall Jenner, among others. “Brands want 40, 50 girls in a show, leaving less opportunity for designers to spend time with each talent. There's no time for long fittings. But you know who fits those tiny samples?” Gay shakes his head ruefully. “Teenagers—girls who haven't finished growing yet.” Starting this month, DNA Models and The Society Management will no longer be submitting new models under the age of eighteen for show consideration in North America. (For DNA Models, one exception is models who previously participated in Fashion Week and are under eighteen.) Bonnouvrier and Gay are hopeful that other agencies here and abroad will join them—and that designers and casting directors will embrace the change as well. “Let's get back to believing in models and developing them,” Bonnouvrier says. “Let's get back to a model being a muse and not a coat hanger.” If you want to understand why very young models became the runway norm, you have to look at the evolution Gay and Bonnouvrier have observed—from show samples' being fitted to variously proportioned young women to young women's being matched to size 0 samples. And to understand why the fix isn't as simple as, say, cutting larger samples, you have to tease out the other factors at play, from the rise of the internet to the fall of the Iron Curtain. It's a systemic problem. Its causes are diffuse. Around the time Naomi Campbell locked arms with fellow supers Linda Evangelista, Christy Turlington, and Cindy Crawford to sing along to George Michael's “Freedom! '90” on Versace's runway, tectonic social and political changes were afoot. Sir Tim Berners-Lee had just built the first World Wide Web browser; NAFTA negotiations had commenced, jump-starting globalisation; celebrities were beginning to displace models on the covers of fashion magazines; and the breakup of the Soviet Union had left millions of people scrambling for a foothold in the emerging New World Order. The desperate poverty throughout the Eastern Bloc, as the fashion industry would soon delight in discovering, meant there was a seemingly endless supply of tall, high-cheekboned, often undernourished girls who saw modelling as their ticket out of chaos. “That was a turning point,” admits Angela Missoni of the influx of models from Eastern Europe and the former Soviet republics. “You know, the fashion sketch—it was always about elongation, exaggeration of the silhouette. Suddenly there were all these girls who looked like the sketches. If I think back,” she says, “that's probably when the sample size dropped. It wasn't that we wanted to make them smaller—it was just that the girls showing up at castings were smaller. So we adapted.” Sample sizes weren't the only thing that shrank: Paychecks did, too. In economic terms, models from the East—and later, Brazil—flooded the market. Designers no longer needed to shell out thousands of dollars to the women walking in their shows, so instead of hiring a few to quick-change in and out of several looks, it became standard to cast dozens, who would each wear one. That suited stylists: As veteran casting director James Scully notes, when celebrities came to dominate magazine covers, “shows became the primary creative outlet for models; that's when you see the emergence of the super­stylist. The girls became more interchangeable, and the show was all about the proposition, the big look.” The catwalk's uniform army was born. Their ranks served another purpose. With Condé Nast's launch of Style.com (now Vogue Runway) in 2000 and the advent of runway images posted to the internet, designers found themselves speaking directly to consumers. This was a sea change. Previously, shows were for editors and buyers, whose job it was to interpret designers' ideas. Now those ideas needed to be communicated directly. A strong, singular look—reiterated many times—got the point across. Shows became more “editorial,” in the industry vernacular, the styling punchier and the clothes more ornate. The aim was to underline the uniqueness of a brand at a moment when great numbers of them were hopping on the fashion-show bandwagon. And why wouldn't they? With the market globalised and runway models to be had on the cheap, what better way to stake a claim on potential shoppers' attention than by staging an advertising campaign that would be broadcast, via the internet, instantly and worldwide? “First it was more shows; now it's shows all the time,” says Ashley Brokaw, the casting director for brands including Prada and Chloé. “If I look at my calendar, there are three months out of the year where I don't have a fashion show, but I'm casting all year. It's become a supply-and-demand issue: Everyone needs bodies—more girls, more boys. Agents and scouts have to supply those bodies to meet their clients' demands,” she continues. “It's not like the old days, when Linda and Christy and Naomi could do everything.” Countless teens daydream about becoming models. It's an appealing fantasy: Someone plucks you out of the crowd at Coachella, tells you you're gorgeous, asks if you've ever modelled before, et voilà: Goodbye, teenage angst; hello, jet-setting around the globe with your new squad of cool, beautiful friends. Jeff and Mary Clarke are the kinds of people who discover girls at summer music festivals. The proprietors of St. Louis-based Mother Model Management, the Clarkes talent-spotted future stars Karlie Kloss and Grace Hartzel. And they've dispelled a lot of teenage fantasies. “This is a tough business,” says Mary. “We're very up front about that with our models. We tell them there are no guarantees—you're going to face a lot of rejection and a lot of criticism, and you have to know how to deal with that and not let it crush you.” “And that,” adds Jeff, “is why the development process is key.” The Clarkes do more than scout: They're “mother agents.” Mother agencies train models and break them into the industry's primary markets of New York and Paris. Of course, this isn't the only way models enter the business. Competitions like Elite Model Look are another pipeline, and these days models can be plucked from Instagram by scouts from all over the world, who pitch them straight to casting directors. When the Clarkes develop a new face like Mallory Veith, seventeen, one of their most promising signees, they bring her to their home studio to do test shoots with trusted photographers. They teach her how to pose, how to walk, and nudge her into paid work—booking, say, shoots in St Louis, a few hours from the small city where Mallory lives. Then they'll advance her to larger cities. Over the past year, Veith spent a month each in Tokyo, Los Angeles, and Mexico City, experiences she describes as like “getting to go to college early.” She's made friends on those trips, ones who make up for the friends she's lost touch with since deciding to finish her studies online. “Mallory's an old soul,” explains her actual mother, Krista Veith. “She was over the gossip and drama of high school by the end of her freshman year.” Mallory believes she's ready to try her luck in New York; the Clarkes agree. And Krista takes comfort in the fact that when Mallory embarks on her first round of show castings, Jeff and Mary will be there for her. But not all mother agents are so, well, motherly. As casting director Munro notes, “There's no book of ethics” for agents. Some are good; some are unscrupulous; some don't believe they have any particular duty of care when it comes to the young models on whom their paychecks depend. Andreea Diaconu recalls, for instance, that when she developed a painful dental abscess in London early in her career, her former agent “couldn't even be bothered to get an ibuprofen.” “I am beyond grateful for everything this job has given me,” says Diaconu, now 27. “Yes, I missed out on languid summer days with friends. I went from being one of the best students in my class to barely passing my math exams. But I traveled, I learned languages, and now I've been accepted to Columbia University—and I'm pretty sure no scholarship in Bucharest would have brought me there.” That said, Diaconu's early experiences in the fashion industry illustrate its perils for young models. “When I was fourteen, I'd have photographers asking me to go topless. There would be 20-hour days, taking green tea pills for stamina. Once, when I was about sixteen,” she says, “I had a booker tell me I had to socialise and go to clubs. It still makes me uncomfortable when I see models dressed as exotic parrots, hanging out at bottle service.” Diaconu tossed the drugs and drinks she was handed on those nights out. Other teen models aren't as savvy—nor should we expect them to be. “Look, it's not just girls,” says Jeff Clarke. “There's a boy from Racine, Wisconsin, we're working with. He's never had a job. I mean, just think about all the changes you go through between the ages of sixteen and eighteen, all the first-time experiences you have. There's no way this kid's first job should be working as a model in New York. That's completely overwhelming.” “These are children trying to understand and fit into an adult world,” observes Maria Bruce, LMHC, a New York-based licensed psychotherapist who specialises in working with high-achieving adolescents and adults, including athletes, dancers, and actors. Bruce says that the models she's counselled struggle to navigate the mixed signals they get on the job. “They're told to ‘grow up' if they complain that they're tired,” she says, “and yet in other ways they're already treated as grown-ups.” This confusion, she says, leads teen models to feel too uncertain of their own authority to say no when they encounter dicey situations. Some muster the courage to speak up; most shut down. “The teenage brain is sensitive to overload,” Bruce explains. “And some of the possible psychological consequences of dealing with these stressors include low self-esteem, obsessive-compulsive disorders, anxiety, and depression.” Issues with body image form their own special subcategory of model ailment. Despite efforts throughout the fashion industry to address the problem, eating disorders such as anorexia remain pervasive. Models are most vulnerable, Bruce notes, as they cross the threshold out of puberty and find that size 0 samples no longer fit. It's a moment Karen Elson remembers well. “I was a late bloomer, and at the same time went on birth control to control my acne,” recalls Elson, the flame-haired beauty who led the wave of idiosyncratic faces that crested in the late 1990s. “They say it's a myth that you gain weight, but my breasts got bigger, my hips got bigger. I'd hear comments. One of my reps told me he'd give me $20 for every pound I lost.” In 1998, the same year she was honoured at the VH1/Vogue Fashion Awards as Model of the Year, nineteen year-old Elson turned up at Milan Fashion Week ten pounds heavier than usual. Elson recalls that she was canceled from a major show and wound up sitting out the rest of the season. “Somehow that leaked to the press,” she says with a sigh. “It was on the news—that I was too fat to walk in Milan. I mean... that's just wrong.” Myriad young models are flushed out of the industry when their adult curves emerge. Others continue to work but don't do shows. Imaan Hammam is one of fashion's current superstars, and she has the kind of healthy, toned body many women aspire to—but says she exceeds what some say is the regulation 34-inch hip and so is rarely spotted on a catwalk. “So many times I'd do fittings for shows and then they'd cut me at the last minute,” she says. “I tried to work out, eat healthy—but at a certain point, I had to say, Enough. This is who I am.” The epic finale of Versace's spring 2018 show featured Claudia Schiffer, Carla Bruni, Helena Christensen, Campbell, and Crawford—women whose ages hover around 50 and who began their careers before the cult of extreme thinness took hold. Their return to the catwalk served as a riposte to the idea that high fashion only looks good on gaunt teens. “Sometimes I look at shows and think, Who are we talking to?” comments Chris Gay. “These clothes are for adults—grown women. Are we trying to project an image they can relate to, or are we, as an industry, just entertaining ourselves here?” Attitudes are starting to shift at some established European houses: When Natacha Ramsay-Levi debuted her first collection at Chloé last year, she caused a minor stir by opening her show with model Sophie Koella. The nineteen-year-old was willowy, to be sure, but she also boasted noticeable curves. “Sophie's the perfect natural beauty, which is the whole idea of Chloé,” Ramsay-Levi says. “But with her proportions, you have to build the clothes for her. You can do that with a few looks, but you don't have time to do that with 50. So I don't know—maybe we need smaller shows. Maybe we need to create space in the show calendar so that designers have time to do proper fittings.” Ramsay-Levi makes an essential point: Unless and until the underlying dynamics of the fashion-show economy change, the conditions they've created will remain in place. Modelling will go on being a commodity business, with one new face easily replaced by the next. There will be exceptions, of course—Gigi, Kendall—but as Gay notes, “You can't make policy around the exception.” The eighteen-plus runway initiative has the opposite aim: Jam the gears of the machine so it's forced to rebuild itself. Women's fashion—at least the part where models are concerned—is at a fork in the road. Go one way, casting director Munro says, and we'll wind up looking like men's fashion—a place, in his view, where “models have generally been treated as disposable.” The other path is lit by the “personality” models—women with large social media followings who are staking a claim on the runway not by fitting a size but by being themselves. Their distinctiveness gives them power. It also allows fashion to reenter the business of vaulting stars into the celebrity firmament. Balmain designer Olivier Rousteing has been at the forefront of fashion casting with an eye toward pop culture, and he attributes much of his success at the house to the fact that, as he puts it, “women can recognise themselves in the Balmain vision. The women on the runway have to be there for a reason—and the reason is that they're relevant to the women looking at the show. Fashion isn't about ‘reality,' ” Rousteing adds, “but its dreams have to come from reality. That's the only way it can be modern.” Virgil Abloh extends that logic. Seeing reality, for the Off-White and Louis Vuitton menswear designer, is about seeing humanity. A self-described fashion outsider who worked as an architect, a gallery owner, and then as Kanye West's creative director before embarking on a career in design, Abloh says he was struck, when he started casting his shows in 2015, by the “namelessness” of models. No other aspect of his creative life worked that way. “Anyone I collaborate with, I want to have a conversation,” Abloh explains. “What are your dreams? What do you have to say? The way I see it, the people on my runway should be people first, models second. I want artists, musicians, charismatic characters in my shows. And that's why it's important to diversify this industry. Not just in terms of black, white, brown, but in terms of point of view. When you have people with new ideas working in the atelier, and in upper management, that's when you're going to see the old codes break down.” The generational shift Abloh alludes to is already under way. Millennials are demanding a culture of openness from brands, and so the trend is toward a runway that welcomes all colours, creeds, ages and shapes. Streetwise labels such as Hood by Air and Vetements ignited fashion's street-casting movement, and many other brands have followed suit, exalting the individuality of models by casting from their own communities for their shows and campaigns. New codes are materialising. They're updating behind the scenes, too. New York-based Model Alliance recently announced its Respect Program, an initiative to create industry-wide standards for models' working conditions. Expanding on the principles outlined in the Condé Nast International vendor code of conduct, it also includes complaint and enforcement mechanisms to assure those standards are upheld. The aim, says Model Alliance founder and executive director (and model) Sara Ziff, is to dignify models as workers, people doing a job, who have basic needs and who deserve basic rights and protections. This may seem obvious until you consider the tenuous employment status of so many models, who often work for free or for “trade”—for goods from the brands that hire them. “We need to inject a labor consciousness into fashion,” says Ziff. “Models are not the people you picture when you think of workers' rights, but the fact is we are doing a job and deserve to be treated fairly—just like anyone else who works for a living.” “The age of models is just one component of a big conversation,” agrees Stella McCartney. “If you have a business that employs people, you have to be mindful of their conditions of employment—period. There's no reason fashion should think it's above that.” McCartney goes further. Viewing the fashion industry through the lens of sustainability, she sees it as one piece of a very large puzzle. “We live in a disposable culture,” she says. “With so much on offer, what's even desirable anymore? Something new is always coming through: new models, new clothes, new TV shows, new stuff of all kinds. How do we hit the pause button?” A shift to using models eighteen and older on the runway won't solve every problem for models or for fashion or for the world that's helped mould the industry into its current shape. Promising teens will continue to be signed, no doubt, but agencies will need to invest more time and resources in their models' development, particularly as they adapt to the demands of video and social media. “That's changing the game,” says Chris Gay, who points out that the qualities these new modelling platforms reward are ones that tend to come with maturity. “A model needs to be dynamic, someone you want to have a conversation with.” The ability to communicate, Gay likes to say, is the new hip size. “What's great about the eighteen-plus initiative is that it's going to make everyone take stock, look at the big picture, and say, ‘You know what? We could do this better. Or that better,' ” says Mother Model Management's Mary Clarke. “What I'd like to see is a fashion world that the women I know here in St Louis can look to for inspiration.” Karlie Kloss believes that world is emerging even as we speak. “I'm optimistic about this industry,” she says, “because everything I'm seeing points toward more inclusivity and more opportunities for models to have their own voice. “When I started modelling at fifteen, maybe I was mature for my age—but still, I was fifteen,” she says. “Over the ten years I've been in the industry, I've changed—my body's developed, as any woman's does, and my mind has developed, too.” And that, Kloss says, makes her a better model than she was in her teens. “It's not about fitting a bill; it's about what you bring to the table, what kind of image you project to the world. It's not just being seen—it's being heard.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.com What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: A look through Princess Margaret’s royally rebellious style
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion This month would have marked Princess Margaret’s 88th birthday. On the occasion, Vogue takes a look back at the royal’s most stylish moments Princess Margaret may have found a new generation of fans thanks to Vanessa Kirby's passionate portrayal in The Crown, but the original royal rebel was raising the sartorial standard and tearing up the royal rule book practically from birth, over 80 years ago. Born on August 21 1930 to King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, Princess Margaret was four years younger than her sister, Elizabeth, who would go on to become Queen Elizabeth II in 1952. Whereas Elizabeth's role meant she had to support British designers and dress diplomatically, Margaret was afforded greater sartorial freedom. Perennially glamorous, she was frequently dressed by Norman Hartnell, the celebrated British couturier, and an avid follower of Dior—in 1958, she hosted the presentation of Dior's winter collection, overseen by a young Saint Laurent, at Blenheim Palace. She referred to the Dior dress she wore for her 21st birthday portrait as “her favourite dress of all time”—though the evening gown she wore for her 26th, a pink-tulle, sequin and flower-embroidered number captured by Cecil Beaton, can't have been far behind on her list. Margaret's eye for style—and penchant for parties in particular—made her very popular with the press. Her marriage to Antony Armstrong-Jones, a non-aristocratic fashion photographer in 1960, caused quite the furore. A portrait he took of the princess—not unlike the risqué image imagined in The Crown—was particularly controversial. Wearing nothing but a diamond necklace and a pearl earring, Margaret looks over her naked shoulder straight into the camera. They divorced in 1978. From her cloud-of-tulle Hartnell designs to full-skirted Dior cocktail dresses and truly outstanding jewels, take a look back at Princess Margaret's most memorable fashion moments. column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan closes Monisha Jaising’s finale for Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Watch it here now  After nearly eight years of her association with Lakmé, Kareena Kapoor Khan took the opportunity this fashion week to announce the launch of her own makeup line with the brand. Aptly titled ‘Shades of a Diva', the range draws from the different moods of the style icon herself. As is tradition, the grand finale for Lakmé Fashion Week takes its theme from Lakmé's biggest launch of the season. And Monisha Jaising, who is synonymous with cocktail couture and resort, was perhaps the perfect fit to materialise this idea on the runway. Jaising has the ability to pull a crowd with ease. For her show this season, her collaborator for MXS and friend Shweta Bachchan Nanda, sat with Karan Johar and Sussanne Roshan, while Manish Malhotra arrived with his close friend Sophie Chowdry, and Alanna, Deanne and Ahaan Panday were spotted dressed up in finery in the front row. The show started with a stellar performance by the dancers of the globally acclaimed circus troupe, Cirque Du Soleil, which is set to arrive in India later this year. Jaising's lineup went from short cocktail dresses and beaded gowns to sari hybrids and taffeta gowns in solid hues. Kareena Kapoor Khan closed the show in an iridescent pleated number. Another designer offering that caught our eye on the last day of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2018 was that by Label Ritu Kumar. Dedicated to fulfilling the needs of the well-travelled, urban fashion lover, they focused on taking inspiration from various tribal cultures this season, and adapting the visual references for the current times. column1: Day 4 at Lakmé Fashion Week: Kangana Ranaut and Jacqueline Fernandez
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s what you need to know  Day 4 at Lakmé Fashion Week saw collaborations between brands and designers being translated on the runway. Kangana Ranaut walked for Pankaj & Nidhi's latest show. The designers tried to interpret the amalgamation of fashion and technology with their collection ‘After Dark', which was presented by Nokia. “What I like about Pankaj and Nidhi is that their clothes [are] for real and not just the ramp,” said Ranaut. The lineup of dresses, fringed capes and trousers worn with high-low tops is perfect for the party season later in the year. On the other hand, Payal Singhal's offering for Lakmé Salon's show-stopping bride was mix of bohemian and vintage influences. The collection was titled ‘Mu'asir', which means modern contemporary in Persian. Singhal's collection was alternative when compared to what's available in the contemporary space of bridal fashion. The motifs took their form from Turkish rugs, medallions and trees. Instead of emphasising on full looks, the designer also aimed to created separates that could be worn with other pieces from the collection. Dsigner Ashish N Soni had Jacqueline Fernandez walking down the ramp for his latest showcase. Presented by Tresemmé, the theme behind the show was that of ‘Metamorphosis'. The designer's lineup focused on tailoring, and went from constructed shift dresses to suits and structured gowns. Models walked the runway in an alarming variety of hairstyles that drove the point of metamorphosis home. “I like it because it's not fussy, but still very glamorous,” Fernandez said of the collection. column1: Janhvi Kapoor, Karisma Kapoor and more from Day 3 at Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s what you missed If there's a fashion week that is made for showstoppers, it would have to be Lakmé Fashion Week. Day 3 saw some strong shows on the runway, which were further highlighted by the celebrities walking down the ramp for their favoured designers. Among the designer offerings for the day was Arpita Mehta's collection, ‘La Fleur', which was created for the wedding hopper. Keeping the fabrics and construction breezy with strategically placed embellishments, Mehta's lineup was for the wedding guest who needs a wardrobe that can go from poolside mehendi to an after-party seamlessly. Karisma Kapoor walked the runway for the designer in a sheer black ruffled sari, complete with an embroidered cape that wouldn't look out of place at a cocktail. While Janhvi Kapoor closed the show at R|Elan presents Nachiket Barve. The collection, inspired by millennial maharanis, was designed keeping the globe-trotting wedding guest in mind. Barve used a combination of sheer fabrics and embellishments to keep the collection light yet occasion-wear friendly. Nimish Shah of Shift went his minimal route and created a collection inspired by vamps from '90s movies, with Seema from Maine Pyaar Kiya featuring on his moodboard. The collection drew from both film costumes and '90s nostalgia. On the other hand, Amit Aggarwal debuted menswear with a futuristic collection this season. Both Shahid Kapoor and Disha Patani walked the runway for the designer, bringing Day 3 to a close. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why can’t women with big feet get feminine shoes?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Model and journalist Jess Cole lives in Converse and Dr Martens. Why? Because she’s a size 42. Here, she argues that the fashion industry needs to stop excluding women with large feet One of my earliest memories is being told by a close family member that I would be too heavy-footed to be a ballerina. I tried tap dancing, but the constant stomping only made me more fixated on how big my feet were compared to the more petite girls in my class. I would wear three pairs of socks to bed and tie my toes together with string in the hope of making them smaller. Anything so I could squeeze into those dainty pink ballet pumps, the symbol of femininity. As a young woman, finding size 43 shoes for school, prom and parties was a nightmare, and an ex-boyfriend mocking my “dragon feet” didn't make me feel any less abnormal. Now, as a model, my feet continue to be a constant source of scrutiny. I've had jobs cancelled because my shoe size is larger than the usual size 40 samples, and on one occasion I forced my feet into shoes that were so small I had to be wheeled around set because it was too painful to walk. Thankfully my immediate colleagues are aware that, logically, tall women (I'm 181cm) have long feet. On shoots I have found only a few brands—Céline, Saint Laurent and Prada—that seem to recognise that women with big feet don't want to wear men's shoes and trainers all the time. We, too (shock, horror) want to be chic. Outside of work, my clothes rotate around a pair of Converse, Dr Martens and posh loafers that only fit when I bend the backs down. The New York College of Podiatric Medicine confirms what I already know, too—its patients have admitted that although they wear trainers on a daily basis, on more polished occasions they will cram their feet into heels. Formal shoes are an essential part of working and social life, so for women who don't fit into them, practically the only thing they can do is buy too-tight shoes out of desperation. Moving through the world with pinched toes and bunions is a constant reminder that our place within society remains collateral with the pain of conforming to beauty ideals. Oppression, as writer and social activist Bell Hooks once wrote, is the absence of choices. Since the 1970s, women's feet have grown at least two sizes bigger. This is down to genetics and richer diets, meaning we are growing bigger and living longer, with our feet spreading as we age. There is so much cultural stigma surrounding women with big feet, these stats can only signpost a much larger truth. According to research by the clothing brand Long Tall Sally, 40 percent of us haven't measured our feet in the past decade. The reality is women's feet are longer and wider then we would all like to think and admit. Women with small feet have epitomised femininity across various cultures. In traditional China, foot binding was a popular method used to break women's feet into the desired three-inch golden lotus. Achieving this incapacitated their movement, but gave them marriageable status which, ironically, improved their social mobility. Although the practice has died out, its legacy continues to resonate today. Just look at Cinderella, whose dainty feet are the only ones to fit into the glass slippers; that story has its origins in 9th-century China. Jaehee Jung, a professor of fashion psychology, says that despite “lesser gender boundaries for social functions and privileges”, shoe size remains a symbol of the “physical characteristics that are associated with gender differences”. These ideals masquerade throughout contemporary culture as shoes empowering women: Dorothy's red shoes transformed her from farm girl to heroine in The Wizard of Oz, Sharon Stone's white stilettos dominate the male gaze in Basic Instinct and Carrie Bradshaw's success was footed by her Manolo Blahniks. The repetition of this imagery normalises an association of shoes with successful, sexy and strong women, and marginalises women whose shoes never fit. So much ideology is tied up within footwear for women that if a woman enters a store and is told her size does not exist, she is also being denied her female identity. When cultural ideologies pressure women into believing that they do not physically fit into the norms reinforced by retailers, they feel they must violently alter themselves to have a social standing. On a daily basis at the New York College of Podiatric Medicine, Dr Marie-Christine Bergeron and Dr Matrona Giakoumis see the extent to which women deform their feet by wearing footwear that is too small. “Conditions like hammertoes (flexible or contracted toes, which are often painful), blisters, wounds, bleeding under the toenails and even losing toenails” are common issues caused by wearing shoes that don't fit properly. Despite these toe-curling issues, the doctors report that “it does not stop women torturing themselves to fit into the ideal mould dictated by society.” The sociocultural pressure placed on women to buy ill-fitting shoes comes down to shoe manufacturers not accommodating a broader range of shoe widths and sizes. “Footwear production is generally very technical and is an art,” says Christina O' Shea, who is a footwear buyer for Long Tall Sally. “For every size of shoe, a bespoke ‘last' (a three-dimensional foot-shaped mould on which each shoe is made) needs to be created—which is expensive.” A lot of brands seem unwilling to take the economic risk of creating larger shoe sizes for women, because for so long women have bought ill-fitting shoes and accepted the pain. This is counterintuitive—like clothing diversity, the only way to normalise all female feet is to have adequate representation in stores. Again, it is mostly online that all women's sizes are being catered for. Net-A-Porter has identified “a significant increase in shoe sizes above an UK size 7 since last year,” recognising the lucrative opportunity of larger sizes, which are already reaching “particularly high sell-throughs”. Long Tall Sally has consistently catered for women with larger feet and ASOS offers wide fits and half-sizes. Although this is promising, our needs as women must to be visible outside the digital sphere—we exist in the physical world, and our presence should be accounted for. It is also not enough to have a couple of boutique stores offering larger sizes—there has to be space made in stores and society to give women of all economic backgrounds the freedom to buy well-fitting shoes. It is only then that we can step beyond the sizing standards that minimise what we are, and what we can and want to be. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Watch: The biggest highlights from Day 2 of Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Rajkummar Rao walked the runway for Rajesh Pratap Singh, while Rina Singh of Ekà showcased a new direction with her latest collection The second day of Lakmé Fashion Week is always dedicated to the cause of sustainability. Amongst the lineup of shows that made up Day 2 at the fashion week, the two that stood out the most were Rajesh Pratap Singh and Ekà. Rajesh Pratap Singh worked with the plant-based fibre Tencel for the second season in a row this season. This time, he used the fibre to create fabric that featured prints, brocade and Chanderi weaves. The collection, titled ‘Welcome to the Jungle' was inspired by a brocade created by Pratap Singh a few years ago, which bore the same name. The designer experimented with Indian ethnic silhouettes, largely drawing from Rajasthani poshaks and dance costumes. Rajkummar Rao walked the runway for the designer. “He is very unconventional,” said the actor of Pratap Singh before the show. “He keeps things very simple, minimal, but his eye for detailing is something I have huge respect for and I could just connect with it because in my work, I try to keep those things in mind too.” Rina Singh of Ekà, on the other hand, is a champion of slow living, and unlike the other designers you can count on seeing at every fashion week, she doesn't always follow the format. But on the occasion she does, she tries to do her best to go beyond what comes to her naturally. This season, Singh experimented with colours—a territory hitherto unexplored for the designer, who's usually known to play around with nudes and neutrals. Taking a leap of faith, she worked with bold reds, warm yellows and sprightly greens in different opacities of fabric. The designer also used checks, stripes, chintz prints, handwoven linen, khadi and Sujani embroidery in the lineup. Diaphanous frocks, luxe pyjama sets and sheer trenches were seen on the runway. Singh explained that she had been observing her clientele at Ekà and drawing from each one's mannerisms and particular way of styling, which influenced her moodboard this season. To put it simply, it's time for a new Ekà wardrobe. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2018 Day 1: All the debuts
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We take you inside the best shows As is tradition, the first show at any Lakmé Fashion Week is all about putting fresh talent on the map. Day 1 began with the Gen Next presentation which brought forward names like AUR by Ajay Kumar Singh, Anurag Gupta, Jajaabor by Kanika Sachdev, SWGT by Shweta Gupta and Yavï by Yadvi Agarwal. You can read all about their individual collections here. Abraham & Thakore, who celebrated 25 years in the industry recently, showcased in Mumbai for the very first time with their collection ‘Cocktails & Samosas'. The label has always emphasised on textile research, and this time around too, they used specially woven brocades, lightweight tussar and sequins to create an overall burnt gold colour palette for the collection of evening wear. “It's cocktail dressing with a desi twist,” David Abraham explained. Bar jackets worn with trousers, saris, lungis and even lehengas made it to the lineup, which were both luxuriously festive, yet restrained in the sense of not having gone overboard with the combination of these elements. Good Earth, the homegrown luxury label that offers lifestyle accessories and sustainable clothing, ventured into couture for the first time this season. Showcasing at Lakmé Fashion Week was yet another first for the brand, and they did so with an offsite presentation at the Good Earth flagship in Mumbai. Their collection, titled ‘The Miniaturist', drew similarities between the intricacies of crafting gota with the effort a miniaturist takes to create a detailed painting. Starting with a tableau-style demonstration that educated the viewer on the finer points of gota, the presentation then went on to include the models coming out to perform small skits, recreating scenes of the past in the couture line. There was the begum with her box of paan, a bevy of girls doing their hair and snacking on grapes, and a single girl dancing in the moonlight. With musicians performing the score live, the team at Good Earth worked on bringing the idyllic moods of miniature paintings alive. Deepshikha Khanna, head of apparel, Good Earth, told us that the idea was to stick to their brand aesthetic first. “When you think of gota, you think of Rajasthan and all these bright colours which is really beautiful, but when you see Good Earth, we're so quiet in everything we do. So we thought of our strong aesthetic and decided that the only way to do a craft that is so easily available, is through the Good Earth eyes. We decided to change the colour palette, so now it's all really lovely and pastel. When the first samples came out, they were so intricate, and so the miniature art form became something that we related this to,” she explained. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 12 breezy kurtas that are perfect for Raksha Bandhan
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And you can buy them all online! Considering Raksha Bandhan is just days away, it's high time that you gear up for the festivities. As you shop for an interesting rakhi to tie on your brother's wrist, don't forget to upgrade your own festive wardrobe as well. Kurtas have been having a major fashion moment of late, and what better occasion to bring fashion and tradition together than this one? Whether you're looking for a vibrant colour-blocked kurta or prefer something more minimal, we've put together some of the stunning numbers available online that need to be on your shopping radar. Florals almost never go out of trend, and they're easy to style too. Channel your inner flower child with Biba's blue floral kurta and wear it with a pair of mom jeans, or simply step inside Nikasha's peach kurta and salwar set. If you feel like experimenting with the colour of the moment—yellow—invest in Global Desi's asymmetrical kurta, or go an extra mile by opting for Ilk's subtle pomp pom number. The trick lies in balancing the proportions. If you want to take the minimal route, choose Vaarha's pastel kurta and sharara set. You can even accessorise your look with silver jhumkas and a pair of juttis to go with your ethnic look. And the best thing about all of these options is that they don't need to catch dust in your wardrobe once Raksha Bandhan is over—the versatility of the garment will allow you to recycle them again and again, for any season and occasion. column1: What to look forward to at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All the designers you should be watching out for The winter/festive 2018 edition of Lakmé Fashion Week kicks off tomorrow, which basically means that your feed will soon be taken over by what will be a week of showstoppers and trendspotting on the runways. Ahead of all the shows, we give you a glimpse at what to expect from the event, and the designers we are keeping an eye out for. The veteran designer duo will be presenting in Mumbai for the very first time, with their collection cheekily titled ‘Cocktails and Samosas'. “Mumbai has a sort of gritty urban glamour for us, which is very attractive. We hope there are elements in this collection that are relevant to this fascinating city,” said David Abraham, one half of the label. Having worked on Martand Singh's series of ‘Vishwakarma' exhibitions, Rakesh Thakore had developed textiles for them, and the results of the learnings will be carried forward in their collection this season. “Besides the brocades developed in Varanasi, the collection uses a lightweight tussar with the addition of viscose to increase softness and drape,” Abraham added. Ujjawala Dubey classifies the nature of his collection as “the sweet spot of rebellion versus tradition”. He continues drawing parallels between contrasts. “It is a celebration of the repetition of the self and the mundane. The self that sometimes is quiet as a shadow and sometimes takes over. The new line is inspired by these human emotions that tend to make us break away and still keep us rooted,” says the regional finalist for Woolmark Prize 2017/18. This will be the first time Dubey will be showcasing a festive lineup. “We have experimented with deconstructed embroideries and have developed an amazing handloom fabric with lycra, zari and cotton.” Good Earth will be debuting at Lakmé Fashion Week with their first ever couture collection, ‘The Miniaturist'. “The idea is to show the beauty of gota in its original form and level of craftsmanship. The collection is a play between the versatility and flexibility of gota, and its reinterpretation in a contemporary context that will resonate with the modern consumer. Miniatures were all about transcendent worlds of imagination and paradise. We have tried to bring this thought to life using the medium of garments—by evoking the same pleasures and domains of wonder. These are the feelings our collection seeks to evoke,” said Anita Lal, founder, Good Earth. Rina Singh of Ekà likes to take a deep dive into her creative processes. This season, Singh looks at hand-spun khadi, hand-woven linen and the Kashmiri embroidery ‘Sojani' for the upcoming season. Singh's clothes are for the woman who enjoys a slower take on life. Stripes and chintz prints will also feature in the collection, which is titled ‘Lived In'. “All printing, manufacturing and finishing happens in our studio factory with a slow production methodology, and using a minimum waste from production philosophy, followed under stringent controls,” she tells us about her ethical processes of creation. Designer Rajesh Pratap Singh will be working with Tencel, a botanical fibre, for the second season in a row. “This collection uses an amalgamation of traditional handloom craft, embroidery, hand block print, ikat, leheriya tie dye, jamdani and traditional brocade jala weaving techniques. It also adapts some of the prints of the iconic William Morris, under an ongoing project. This collection, in effect, experiments with Tencel in a wide variety of genres,” the designer tells us. Pratap Singh will be playing with a full lineup of Indian ethnic silhouettes, which are modern interpretations of traditional costumes from the Mughal era, as well as from the repertoire of dance costumes. Akshat Bansal of Bloni continues to explore gender norms with his collection ‘Neutrios' this season. “It symbolises the wrath of all the atrocities experienced by humans of the world due to biological, cultural and aesthetic differences. This is a slow beginning to our own end and that's what my collection brings forth—an identity that is neither male nor female, but neutral,” he says. The designer has made use of econyl (a fabric crafted from marine plastic waste), organza and tie-and-dye in the collection. If you look at Nimish Shah's Instagram feed, it's a curious mix of his own work and the things that interest him—which includes several vintage throwbacks. Therefore, it comes as little surprise that the inspiration behind his newest collection is “oddly beautiful vamps from the '90s.” Shah is a minimalist by nature, and continues to experiment with shapes and treatments in order to make the vibe effortless. Seema from Maine Pyaar Kiya features on Shah's moodboard for this collection. Kallol Datta prides himself on being a ‘clothes maker', and not a designer. His latest offering, clinically titled ‘Volume 1 Issue 2', “reveal questions that confront him in his pursuance of understanding and skewing forms”. In a way, Datta is unlike any of his contemporaries, focusing on unsavoury bits in a world driven by glamour. “There are notions of navigating, transposing to and inhabiting such space. A definitive loop exists in the works displayed, that originate from a singular concept and form. How does one afford access in a design practice, partially?” He poses a Sphinx-worthy riddle to his audience with his latest collection. Amit Aggarwal will be launching his line of menswear this season. Aggarwal is an experimentalist by nature, and his collection of men's clothing is unlike anything you've seen before; think metallic armour that you can wear to a party, moulded over a body. “The collection effortlessly marries culture with modernity as it restores vintage Phulkari, the traditional Indian metallic embroidery technique. We have restored it by using our signature polymer details and contemporary intricate hand embellishments,” he tells us. Easily the biggest show of the season will be Monisha Jaising's grand finale presentation, featuring a performance by Cirque du Soleil and definite walk down the runway by Kareena Kapoor Khan. Her collection titled ‘Shades of a Diva' is a lineup of 65 looks that a diva can wear everywhere from the pool to a party. “People are bored of greys and navy blues,” she said. “The current mood for the festive season is leaning towards a lot of colour, which is tempered with the eternal allure of sexy black.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Topshop teams up with Halpern for their next designer collaboration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Party-goers are going to fall in love with the 28-piece collection, due to come out in November In December 2017, New York-born, London-based designer, Michael Halpern, won the British emerging talent gong for womenswear at the Fashion Awards. That same evening, Vogue cover star Adwoa Aboah, who was crowned model of the year, wore a glittering Halpern jumpsuit to the prestigious event. With the most influential industry figures in attendance at the most important event on the fashion calendar, the award ceremony certainly cemented the 30-year-old's status as one of the most promising designers on the scene right now. Halpern's ascent has been rapid, graduating from Central Saint Martins in 2016 and debuting his eponymous collection at London Fashion Week in February 2017. Today, the lauded designer, adored for his modern take on '70s glamour and sequins, has been announced as Topshop's latest collaborator. “We are thrilled to collaborate with Michael; especially at such an exciting time in his career,” Anthony Cuthbertson, global design director of Topshop Topman enthused. “Our capsule embodies the disco spirit and signature feminine silhouettes he is renowned for; we can't wait to bring the world of Halpern to Topshop with styles that will no doubt kickstart the partywear season for our customers.” “I think it's fabulous that as a younger brand we're able to work with Topshop, making the type of clothing we do for the main Halpern collection in an accessible way so more people can really feel the glamour,” Michael Halpern added. "I want the whole world to feel as glam as possible, and this type of collaboration is a fantastic way to accomplish that." The 28-piece collection, which will drop in November, will offer a more affordable range of the disco-ready partywear worn by Halpern's celebrity fanbase including Amal Clooney, Lupita Nyong'o, Diane Kruger, Giovanna Battaglia Engelbert and Marion Cotillard. The Topshop x Halpern collection will include neon velvet separates, printed two pieces, sequin-adorned jumpsuits and iridescent camouflage print mini dresses, with prices starting at just £35. The high-street collaboration follows on from a special Halpern capsule collection with Browns which launched earlier this year in February, called “After Midnight”. Timed perfectly in the run-up to the festive season and the influx of Christmas parties, we couldn't think of a more suitable designer to inject some fun into our winter wardrobes. column1: When Kaia Gerber met Karl Lagerfeld: Behind the exciting collaboration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion On the release of the new Karl Lagerfeld x Kaia collection, Kaia Gerber spills the beans on working with her fashion hero “I'm from Malibu, and there's a Californian casual way that people dress here,” explains Kaia Gerber. If you'd heard of the 16-year-old a few years ago, it would have been as the daughter of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber; more recently it's likely to be as a budding supermodel in her own right, who has already opened shows for brands including Chanel and Saint Laurent and covered several Vogues. “Then there's the Parisian look, which is very chic and very pulled-together, but in also a cool and casual way. I think Karl and I really wanted to just bring the two worlds together.” Which Karl is she referring to? Lagerfeld, of course. Gerber has joined forces with the designer on a new capsule collection for his eponymous brand, blending polished fashion tropes—a tux jacket, a studded bag—with elements from her own relaxed, sporty look. “It was just really cool to see the way that those two worlds met. You wouldn't necessarily place them together, but I think it worked out really well.” Lagerfeld and Gerber only met in September 2017, at a fitting for Fendi, but she's long been a fan. “Genuinely, Karl has always been my fashion hero, and having worked with him, he's still my hero. He's such a visionary and he's been in this industry, which is not an easy industry to be in, for such a long time. I love how passionate he is about what he does.” Though she grew up with a mother who'd worked at the heart of fashion, her own exposure to the business was gradual. “I didn't even know modelling was a thing until I was older,” she says. “But we had Herb Ritts, Richard Avedon and Bruce Weber books around my house growing up. I didn't really know what they were or why they were there, but I remember sitting down and going through them and just being mesmerised.” No wonder then that even at the tender age of 16, she was ready for this high-profile design gig. “I always have mood boards going, no matter if I'm working on something or not—I just like having inspiration,” she says. “So when this opportunity came I was like, ‘Oh perfect, I basically already have all my ideas.'” She was surprised and flattered to find that Lagerfeld and his team genuinely wanted her input. “They wanted to know what I thought. I was really excited because it really did feel like a collaboration—we both played a role in the final outcome.” What she brought, perhaps, is a certain practicality; Gerber isn't one for style over substance. “I get dressed before I do anything else,” she says. “Then I'll go downstairs, eat breakfast or whatever I'm doing and make sure that the clothes I wear are functional before I leave the house. That's my biggest thing—I don't want to start going about my day and realise, ‘This is not going to work—I can't walk anywhere.' We brought that thinking into the collection, because I wanted to make sure that people could actually wear these pieces in their everyday life.” Below, she takes Vogue through her favourites. Gerber's twist on the classic leather biker includes a hand-painted, graffiti-style logo across the back. “I've always loved customising my own clothes,” she says. “I would draw on things or cut the sleeves off. With this, I really wanted to make a piece that felt original.” Her father, Rande Gerber, is a rock ‘n' roll inspiration too. “He loves riding motorcycles—I remember him picking me up from kindergarten on a Harley Davidson,” she says, laughing. “I really loved it. He loves music and rock—he would play The Rolling Stones and all these bands, and so I just grew up knowing who these people were, seeing rock stars on stage and being like, ‘This is how everyone should look.'” “This is probably one of my favourite pieces from the whole collection,” says Gerber of what is also the most original garment: a long tux blazer that can be unzipped around the waist to form a cropped jacket and skirt. She has a personal connection to the tuxedo look—she wore one to her prom. “Blazers are a big staple in my wardrobe—I love playing with the idea that they don't have to be formal, so I'll pair them with biker shorts or jeans,” she explains. “I really wanted to make one that you could wear every day but also in different ways—instead of having to buy three different pieces, it's all in one.” You might expect a skyscraper stiletto from a model; from Karl Lagerfeld x Kaia you'll get a functional skate shoe instead. “I grew up in Malibu in this skating and surf culture, so I really wanted to bring that in,” says Gerber. “My childhood would have been nothing without going to the beach and skating around. My brother and I used to bring our skateboards everywhere with us—at dinner with my family we would be wanting to go outside and skateboard.” Off the runway, she says, she's not much of a heels girl: “Definitely in my everyday life I'm a flats person all the way. I want to be comfortable and I want to be able to run around and do whatever.” Gerber travels light: “Chapstick, my phone, my wallet and a portable charger—the biggest lesson I've had to learn is always have a portable charger,” she says. She tends to go hands-free with a crossbody bag, so she and Lagerfeld added one to the collection. “Every handbag Karl does is amazing, so I really took his lead because I wanted to learn. We kept it classic and functional—I didn't want it to be too heavy, because you want to be able to carry it all day.” Millennials are too young to remember it, but older fashion followers will recall Peter Lindbergh's 1991 Wild at Heart shoot for the September 1991 issue of American Vogue. In it, a flock of supermodels posed with motorcycles and leather Harley Davidson baker-boy caps. Among them was a young Crawford. “I actually hadn't seen that shoot before,” admits Gerber, who is often seen wearing similar caps and has designed one with Lagerfeld. “When my mom saw the sample, she was like ‘Oh my god, this reminds me of this shoot that I did,' and she showed it to me. But I've just always loved that style of hat!” Ahead, scroll through for a behind-the-scenes peek at the collaboration: View Gallery 18 Photos When Kaia met Karl: the model reveals a new collaboration What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast
