column1: How to buy bridal jewellery: Your ultimate guide
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Bridal jewellery shopping is not like those whim-driven weekend sprees. Things like engagement rings and weddings sets need careful thought over before you commit to your favourite designs. Our guide is here to help If you think about it, bridal jewellery is about more than just adding the right finishing touches to your wedding celebration outfits—it marks the different stages of your courtship as a bride-to-be as well. First comes the ring, followed by the engagement party, where Indian customs dictate that the groom's family gift the bride her jewellery, and then there's the trousseau shopping. All of this ultimately culminates on the big day, with the future missus sporting jewellery that (more often than not) channels her inner princess. From piling up on the bling to adopting a nuanced sensibility, jewellery choices of the modern Indian bride have come a long way compared to her predecessors. ‘More is more' is no longer the accepted norm, nor is giving your family free rein over what to buy. The millennial bride believes in a more sophisticated and well-informed approach to jewellery shopping, one that values quality and versatility in equal measure. At the same time, the lead-up to your wedding is also probably the only time you will ever go this all-out with jewellery shopping. One of the best ways to walk this thin line is to chalk up a list of essentials that will stand the test of time, balanced with a few of-the-moment pieces. The wedding set is the crowning glory, but jewellery for your pre-wedding events, if designed smartly, can be reused with ease even after the celebrations have drawn to a close. And since your in-laws are bound to gift you a few sets as well, it's advisable to plan well to avoid any overlaps. Whether you already have a Pinterest board filled with your top picks or you're just beginning your research, Vogue brings you some handy tips to guide you through the process. The first order of the day as you assume your role as a bride on a (retail) mission, is the ring on the finger. Your engagement solitaire ring is that one piece of jewellery that will last you a lifetime, and in turn become a family heirloom. So it only follows that it should be an extension of your personality. Considering that diamond rings cost a pretty penny, it's important to know your basics. A classic round-cut is more expensive than fancy shapes like pear and marquise. Asscher-cut diamonds are all about art deco glam, while modern brides are increasingly favouring emerald- and cushion-cut diamond rings. You could choose to have the ring customised in a prong or halo setting, accentuated with either a simple gold band or an intricately carved one depending on your preferences. Certified stones are non-negotiable. A nifty trick is to choose a solitaire that's just shy of the next carat in order to maximise your budget. A trend that is quickly catching on is one of the couple investing in matching wedding bands to solidify their commitment to each other. It's advisable to choose a ring design that complements your engagement ring, so that it can be stacked together. Gold rings (white, yellow or rose—pick your favourite) and platinum rings are timeless favourites. You can go a step further and have your wedding date or hashtag engraved on yours, to always have a memory of your special time on hand. Many brides choose their lehenga first and then follow it up with the jewellery, though it's advisable to do the opposite. Your wedding set will be a hefty investment, so choose timeless over trendy. Think ahead and create a set that will become a cherished family treasure. Diamonds and uncut diamonds are the most popular choice for the pheras. If you're choosing the former, opt for a mix of white and yellow diamonds should your budget permit it. Punctuate the set with precious gemstones like Colombian emeralds, tanzanites, rubies and tourmalines for a hint of colour. The addition of rose-cut diamonds will lend more visual appeal to your diamond necklace as well. Brides with a traditional sensibility tend to favour polki or jadau sets as they give the overall repertoire a royal charm. Don't shy away from sprucing this time-honoured pick with unconventional meenakari work employing hitherto unseen colours like blue and black. You can also elevate it with south sea pearl or coloured stone drops. The trend this year is to tap into your inner princess, so look to customising a complete set including a necklace, earrings, maang tikka or matha patti, bangles and a nath. But elaborate does not mean gimmicky. Avoid looking like you raided the entire store, and keep it refined instead. If you choose a statement matha patti, then stick to a choker instead of two layered necklaces. Similarly, if you're going bold with your nath, then don't go OTT with your earrings too. There is no time like your wedding day to embrace your roots. For instance, if you choose to wear a gold set with your kanjeevaram silk, include pieces like the vanki (armlet), waist belt and jadai (hair ornament) to your gold bridal jewellery sets. The colour of your lehenga and your chosen bridal jewellery should be in sync with each other. For example, pastel lehengas and coloured stones pair beautifully. Both Neha Dhupia and Mira Rajput Kapoor had chosen baby pink lehengas for their respective big days, and while the former wore hers with an elaborate polki choker with emerald drops, Rajput Kapoor sported a navratna necklace for her wedding look. If you decide to go with a traditional red or pink lehenga, choose a polki or diamond set that does not feature an overpowering mix of colours. Balance is everything. Gone are the days when wedding sets simply gathered dust in the bank vault. The goal today is to invest in trousseau pieces that allow for easy wearability. Buy detachable, multi-purpose necklaces that can make a statement at the next family wedding, but can also be broken down for a more laid-back festive dinner party. Reversible and layered necklaces are the epitome of form and function. Instead of one OTT polki necklace for your wedding, break it down to a choker and layered rani haar. Sonam K Ahuja, for one, wore a choker and a guttapusalu necklace on her wedding day, both of which can be easily worn individually too. While heavy necklaces are an important element in a bride's trousseau, so are lighter pieces that can be worn for your pre-wedding events, as well as for a friend's wedding a few months down the line. For her mehandi, Bipasha Basu paired her floral jewellery with a satlada that can be repurposed with everything from a kurta set to a sari with flair. Multi-layered gemstone necklaces like emeralds, rubies and pearls are versatile picks as well, since they can be dressed up or down. You can wear pearl necklace and solitaire studs to a dinner party, and an emerald necklace with chand balis to a sangeet. And you won't regret adding a single-line solitaire necklace to this mix either. Combine these classic must-haves with everyday necklaces too. Pearl and gemstone lariats and station chains are easy to throw over semi-casual looks, traditional and western alike. The modern bride's well-planned strategy should be to buy jewellery that she can wear for her pre-wedding and wedding events, and then inventively re-style post her big day as well. Invest in multiple sets of earrings, as they are the easiest way to amp up any given look. Variety is definitely the spice you should be after. Solitaire tops are a fitting choice for everyday wear, better if they match your engagement ring. Gold temple earrings, polki and pearl chand balis, diamond and gemstone drop earrings, oversized studs and chandelier earrings have you covered for after-hours glam, be it a cocktail party or a destination wedding. Ahuja has been spotted wearing the same polki studs she wore for her at-home mehandi with shirts and dresses post her nuptials too. Matching these earrings with a bracelet where you can, will serve as a smart decision. This combination can easily be worn as a set in itself for occasions that don't necessarily demand a necklace. column1: 5 cool ways Bollywood celebrities are wearing blazers right now
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Style cues from the stars Blazers are no longer resigned to just board meetings and client presentations. If styled right, they can be just the high-value currency you need to give your repertoire a generous dose of cool. From working lunches and paparazzi-approved airport looks to dinner dates and black-tie galas, you'll be hard pressed to find an occasion where a blazer won't work like a charm. Vogue decodes your favourite Bollywood celebrities' looks to show you how you can look every inch the girl boss in one, both in and out of the office. Short suits can be as vacation-friendly as they can be party-ready. Easy to dress up or down, you can wear one with a white shirt like Jacqueline Fernandez for AM to PM chic. Swap the shirt for a logo tee to dress it down even further, perhaps for a day of exploring a new city. If you'd rather be at the other end of the spectrum, then get inspired by Malaika Arora Khan and wear your short suit with a bustier or a crop top for a night out about town. Who needs a gown when you can wear a pantsuit instead? A sworn celebrity favourite, there are many ways to dress up this wardrobe MVP. Deepika Padukone chose a deep purple set with a bare décolletage at Cannes Film Festival this year. Channel her look by donning a pantsuit in an equally striking colour, and style it with minimal jewellery for an after-party. Or do like Sonakshi Sinha and team your blazer with a corset and layered necklaces. If you'd rather give the tailored trousers a skip, then follow Sonam K Ahuja's lead and wear yours with flared palazzos or a maxi skirt instead. Twinsets are already a winning choice, but you can count on a blazer to take them a notch higher. Turn to Priyanka Chopra for a 101—drape yours nonchalantly over your shoulders as you dash from the airport to a client presentation. Go a step ahead and match your heels to the colour of your blazer. Blazers worn with denims are all about off-duty cool. A lesson in laid-back comfort, this is an apt pairing for a late bite or a quick flight out of town. Shilpa Shetty Kundra paired her checkered-and-denim blazer with skinny jeans and a grey tee—an easy last-minute dinner outfit to throw together. While Kareena Kapoor Khan sported a Canadian tuxedo in her oversized boyfriend blazer and cropped denims to play the formal yet cool vibe. Wear yours for a friend's birthday celebration with statement earrings to ace the outfit. One of the easiest ways to give feminine looks an androgynous update, this pairing adds visual interest to your dresses and blazers. Borrow from Karisma Kapoor's stylebook and win print-on-print with this combination, or keep it fail-safe in a printed jumpsuit and solid-coloured blazer like Diana Penty. column1: What to expect from Good Earth’s debut collection at Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We spoke to founder Anita Lal to get a closer glimpse at the luxury brand’s first-ever couture line Good Earth is one of the finest examples of a homegrown luxury label that is India-proud not only in its use of materials, but also the in their language, legacy and aesthetics. The brand believes that the finer things in life need to be savoured, whether it's sipping on a hot cuppa from a picture-perfect teacup or setting the mood with a diffuser that evokes a sense of calm. It's hard to walk into a Good Earth store and not linger around to soak in the soothing atmosphere, curated to promote the idea of slow, mindful living to consumers. Naturally, the brand's clothing lines carry forward the same line of thought. After Sustain, Good Earth's offering of ethically-produced womenswear, the brand will now be debuting a couture collection at the upcoming Lakmé Fashion Week's winter/festive 2018 edition. Drawing parallels between miniature art and fine craftsmanship, the design team at Good Earth has put together a unique lineup of bridal couture highlighting the craft of gota, which is a far cry from the can-can stuffed lehengas that are currently headlining contemporary markets. Vogue spoke with Anita Lal, founder, Good Earth, about their new venture and the reclaiming of gota as an art form. It feels like a natural extension of the brand. When we launched Sustain in 2010, the apparel market was saturated and I felt that no one catered to my preference for pure fabrics and versatile silhouettes. There was a need to create elegant daily clothing for ‘everyday luxury' that celebrated Indian crafts and textiles. Since its inception, the label has mindfully used design intervention to reimagine traditional crafts in a contemporary language, making it relevant for women across all ages and sizes. As Sustain grows, part of the growth initiative is to add categories, which then allows us to work with so many more techniques and fabrics. Since we already address the prêt/ready-to-wear needs of the market, we are now ready to add a couture segment where the objective would be to restore and showcase traditional crafts in a way that they were done in the past. Each of the 27 garments of this collection is of museum quality, and hence will only be available for bespoke orders. With ‘The Miniaturist', the idea is to show the beauty of gota in its original form and level of craftsmanship. The collection is a play between the versatility and flexibility of gota, and its reinterpretation in a contemporary context that will resonate with the modern consumer. While wearability will always be the primary pillar of Sustain, with this collection we also wanted to create wonder and delight for the wearer. While the quality and effort in creation remain the same, what is different in this collection is the painstaking detail of workmanship and use of craft. We have worked with gota for the very first time. The size of gota we have used is really small, around one to two millimetres, and our treatment is subtle and delicate. Traditionally, gota was worn in royal households and by the elite, because it was originally made from gold or silver threads. The motifs used in gota were more traditional—buti and kairi. Gota had utilitarian purposes as well as decorative, and evoked a sense of luxury and beauty at the same time. Over time, gota started being made with synthetic thread, which allowed it to become more quotidian and synthetic fibres became fashion. As the material to build gota ribbon became more affordable, it permeated into a larger fashion aesthetic on textile. The result was a focus on volume, with craft and craftsmen taking a backseat. For us at Good Earth, the real joy was to be able to explore the history and intricacy of the art that is gota. It was when we started working on the collection five to six months ago that we understood the delicacy of work that goes into each gota motif. We have worked with old techniques such as cutting and folding the thread to lend a 3D effect, as well as adding a touch of texture to it with aari, dori and dabka work. We have also used ‘farad', which is printed fabric from Jaipur, to accentuate the gota. The resulting collection brings together classic silhouettes; diaphanous, pure fabrics and whimsical motifs for the modern woman. The highlight of ‘The Miniaturist' are definitely the motifs inspired by ‘gardens and cosmos'—our take on reimagining traditional motifs through the lens of Good Earth. As the name of the collection suggests, conceptually, we were deeply inspired by the miniature painters. A prominent artistic tradition, the genesis of Miniature Art can be traced back to the 11th century, after which it became a genre in itself with the coming of the Mughals. Besides the royal patronage that both Miniature Art and gota enjoyed, there was also similarity in the manner in which royals commissioned specialised ateliers and master craftsmen to create high quality works for imperial households. Miniature paintings were meant to be read up close, with the kind of detailing and small surfaces used in this art form—which evoked a sense of wonder and pleasure. Our designer is like the miniaturist with her imagination and fine detailing on the garments, visible only when seen up close. Miniatures were all about transcendent worlds of imagination and paradise. We have tried to bring this thought to life using the medium of garments—by evoking the same pleasures and domains of wonder. These are the feelings our collection seeks to evoke. She would certainly be a discerning customer with a deep understanding and desire for authenticity in craft. It could be anyone, young or old, who appreciates our aesthetics, which are rooted in culture and tradition. © Vogue Images Fashion We take a look back at the extraordinary woman on her 135th birth anniversary Gabrielle Bonheur “Coco” Chanel or just Coco Chanel, as she is known to the world, brought modernity, simplicity and wearability to lives of women in France and eventually, the world. In a time when Christian Dior was churning out feminine silhouettes (the New Look, post-World War II) with full skirts and cinched waists, Coco Chanel prevailed with her jersey dresses—a sign of the liberated woman who has endured yet another war by actively participating in the society. She is known for introducing the now-classic ‘little black dress', tweed jackets and the unforgettable iconic fragrance, Chanel No 5 as well. It is a well-known fact that she considered five as her lucky number and that's why she chose it as the name of her fragrance. Perhaps, the idea of not giving it a descriptive name to keep the essence of its modernity intact through the years may have passed her mind too. Not only did Chanel do away with corsets and introduce lighter, functional fabrics to her clientele, she also paved way for the liberal woman to step into a modern world—taking great pride in the fact that a woman was designing for her female clients. Over the years, the signature Chanel aesthetic created by the self-confident Leo has stood the test of time. Here's a glimpse at Coco Chanel's life through her pictures. column1: Wedding dresses: Everything you didn’t already know about them
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How, where and what to shop for before your big day To talk about wedding dresses in a country like India is to capture the nation in itself. Everything from the traditions to crafts and regional influences come into play when deciding the attire for a bride on her wedding day. Over time, films, celebrities and the evolving nature of fashion have somewhat homogenised the concept of bridal dressing. But by and large, the northern half of the country celebrates in a more lavish manner than the southern half, and the weather plays a big deciding factor in what a bride chooses to wear on her big day. In the essence of it, a bride's wedding ensemble truly speaks of her personal style, and tone she chooses for her life post nuptials. The market for bridal fashion can be broadly divides into saris, lehengas and gowns. If you're planning to tie the knot yourself, or know someone who will getting hitched soon, our cohesive guide to shopping for wedding dresses will help you make the right sartorial choices for the upcoming celebrations. Not entirely unlike the variations in language and cuisine, wedding dresses vary in almost every state. The weather plays a crucial role in the matter, as does the relevance of colours and symbolism of motifs. Kashmiri brides wear pherans, which are made of pashminas and gold threads. In Gujarat, the bride traditionally changes two saris—a panetar and a gharchola. Punjabi brides traditionally pick lehengas in hues of pink and red, and while the Bengali bride too can choose a completely red ensemble for the main event, her trousseau is never without a traditional red and white sari. In Assam, brides wear a mekhla chadar, while in Orissa, the bride and the groom are decked out in headgear similar to the Bengali bride. In Maharashtra, Paithani saris are a important part of the bridal trousseau. Tamilian and Telugu bridal attire is all about laying the focus on wedding jewellery, and most often, the bride will tie the knot in an elegant silk sari. Further down in Kerala, Malayali brides prefer the white and gold kasavu sari, accessorised with several gold necklaces. Of course, religions play a role in the wedding dress the woman will don on her big day. Muslim brides often choose an ornate sharara set; Parsi brides opt for the traditional lace or gara sari in white; and Christian brides opt for gowns, though, some choose to wear both a sari and a gown on their big day. Despite these nuances, the bridal lehenga has recently emerged a collective favourite. Romanticised by Bollywood and fine-tuned by designers, the lehenga has become a mainstay in a wedding trousseau today. The outfit—comprising of a choli, a full skirt and dupatta that may or may not be worn like a veil—has seen many iterations in its time. Some might choose to go demure without baring much skin, while others may opt for daring cuts—this garment has something for everyone. Bridal lehengas are not limited to the ones worn on the day of the wedding either; several brides also choose the style for their sangeet ceremonies and receptions. In the recent past, Anushka Sharma's blush Sabyasachi lehenga and Sonam K Ahuja's bold red Anuradha Vakil number were well received. Sabyasachi, Manish Malhotra, Tarun Tahiliani, Anita Dongre are amongst the most popular choices for brides. Sabyasachi lehengas come bearing the designer's signature penchant for old world nostalgia. The designer has a dedicated Instagram page for Sabyasachi brides too, where real girls are highlighted in the designer's finest. Tarun Tahiliani's lehengas are for the bride who doesn't want to be weighed down. Tahiliani is an expert of lightness, and offers volume and embellishment without cutting back on the glamour quotient. Manish Malhotra is a celebrity favourite. The designer's second-skin blouses and heavy-on-sequins skirts will undeniably ensure that you are the focus of everyone's attention. And Anita Dongre's designs are for the modern woman who likes monochrome and understated embellishments. While there are many in favour of the lehenga camp, a traditionalist bride will find it difficult to forgo the sari on her wedding day. Benarasi saris are currently trending, and an increasing number of brides are falling for the charm of these decadent drapes. Traditionally worn with an ornate belt to cinch the waistline and accessorised with a veil on some occasions, a brocade sari can make for the perfect look for the pheras. In case of Parsi weddings, brides like to go down the route of a delicately embroidered lace sari, however, the modernist in you might want to opt for a sari-gown hybrid. Wearing an heirloom may be an unconventional choice to some (given that tradition dictates the bride is decked out in brand-new finery), but it's not something that hasn't been done before. Head to your favourite designer and custom create a blouse that elevates the sari. How do you go about making sure you don't blend in with the rest of the crowd that is also in saris? Most cultures assign a specific colour or a drape for the bride that cannot be repeated by the guests in attendance out of respect. But if you're still unsure if you want to give up on the splendour of the lehenga, you can opt for other occasions like a puja, or a smaller ceremony preceding the pheras. Unless you're having a Christian ceremony or a completely bohemian version of a wedding that does not adhere to conventional codes, a wedding gown can seem completely out of question in a bridal trousseau. But the general sequence of events surrounding a wedding have made room for more experimental sartorial choices. A youngster's party or the reception are the perfect occasions to have your modern-day princess moment. If neither of those occasions warrant the cause, plan in advance and choose a theme for your engagement that allows you to go all out in a gown. While the options for couturiers offering lehengas and saris in volume are high, there are those who have cracked the code and perfected the art of crafting gowns for weddings. Gaurav Gupta is your go-to designer whether it is for a sangeet or a party. Amit Agarwal's futuristic looks are a better fit for the bridal party, but if your vibe happens to be experimental, look no further than his sculpted looks that are unlike anything you've seen before. Gauri & Nainika, Shehlaa and Karleo have options for the demure bride as well. Gone are the times when wearing a white gown to your wedding directly translated to a frothy concoction of tulle, a satin bodice bursting at the seams, accompanied by itchy gloves and train that may or may not match the rest of the garment. The new-age bride prefers simpler cuts—think Meghan Markle's understated Givenchy number. The key is to balance the elements and focus on one aspect of your wedding dress, rather than going overboard. If you want to go heavy on embroidery and details, ensure that you go easy on the volume. There's a host of designer bridal gowns available to choose from online, but if you want an Indian couture experience, Sabyasachi has recently launched a collection of bridal gowns with his ‘International Wedding collection' that you should keep your eye on. After choosing the theme of your wedding, it is important to narrow down on a colour scheme for all the events. Your bridesmaids are going to feature in most of your wedding pictures and therefore, picking their dresses is as important as picking your own. While most choose a universally flattering silhouette for all, you can allow your bridesmaids to pick different silhouettes for their individual outfits, and fashion the garment out of the same fabric. If you want to allow for complete freedom, request your bridesmaids to stay within the same colour scheme and choose one element like ruffles or lace to feature in all of their looks. There will be no dearth of parties in the countdown to the big day, and they could be varied in their natures. Just because you are a bride-to-be doesn't mean you need to start going all out with your wardrobe picks already. Exercise moderation and keep an arsenal of Indian ethnic wear and party dresses ready for impromptu invites. Scroll on for our edit of celebrity brides that you can take your inspirations from. column1: Inside Abraham & Thakore’s debut collection for Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Cocktails and Samosas, anyone? It has been more than a quarter of a century since David Abraham and Rakesh Thakore came together to create a label that gave Indian textiles a contemporary perspective. But even after being veterans in the industry a while now, this year will mark the first time Abraham & Thakore showcase at Lakmé Fashion Week in Mumbai. David Abraham dissects the details that have gone into the making of their debut collection, which features quite a quirky title—#CocktailsAndSamosas. Our ever first show was in 2010 in New Delhi. We were keen to bring a collection to Mumbai as we wanted to reach a new audience, and Lakmé Fashion Week provided the appropriate occasion. This collection is mainly evening wear—cocktail dressing with a desi twist, and hence the name. Rakesh worked closely on some of the textiles developed for the ‘Vishwakarma' exhibitions by Martand Singh, which compiled directories of textures and patterns both in weave and print. These elaborate compositions comprised of varied patterns that were set together in a grid-like composition, and served to illustrate the diversity and complexity of skills in Indian textile tradition. We were inspired by this and developed fabrics based on this concept in Varanasi, using silk and two different shades of zari. Some silhouettes are inspired by jamas, chogas and the way the North Eastern garment—the baku—is wrapped around the body. We also looked at lungis and sarongs, which are simple wrap structures, and developed a collection which draws on these traditions, but are re-interpreted for a modern fashion silhouette. Besides the brocades developed in Varanasi, the collection uses a lightweight tussar with the addition of viscose to increase softness and drape. Hand embroidery and sequins create different textures, and negative cut work on layered silks plays with the geometric forms inspired by the weaves. There are elegant evening cover-ups in this collection in the form of kimonos and wraps, as well as capes that can be thrown over simple pieces. There are also simple wrap-and-tie garments that work as sari blouses, as well as dresses. We've followed our beliefs and convictions for 25 years, and refined and reworked our core concepts. We are always excited by the “next” collection and new ideas! Mumbai has a sort of gritty urban glamour for us, which is very attractive. We hope there are elements in this collection that are relevant to this fascinating city. column1: 7 fresh Indian wear trends all brides-to-be need to know about
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Are you taking notes? If one were to chalk up the most defining qualities of the millennial Indian bride, attributes like individualistic, risk-taker, bold and unconventional would top the list. So it only follows that this bride is not out to be a mere clone of her predecessors. She is dressing for more than just that picture-perfect portrait for her 'gram. This bride wants her sartorial repertoire to be a narrative of her personality and sensibility; she wants her ensembles to be as high on comfort as they are on style. That it is no longer just about choosing the heaviest outfit in the store is clear, so what should you be looking to pick up? Vogue trains the spotlight on all the trends you need to screenshot if you're tying the knot this year. While there exists a tribe of brides who couldn't imagine wearing anything but the ceremonial crimson red at their weddings, there is a growing set that is itching to venture beyond. Delicate pastel hues have emerged as a clear winner. With Indian bridal finery being the epitome of ‘more is more', soft shades bring balance to the overall look. Cases in point: Anushka Sharma and Neha Dhupia both wed in baby pink lehengas, while Sonam K Ahuja chose an ivory chikankari lehenga for her mehandi function. The newest bride in town, Shloka Mehta, was seen in the hues of soft pink, dusty rose and dull gold at her multiple engagement parties. At the recently concluded couture shows, Tarun Tahiliani championed powder blue, blush pink and nude, while Rahul Mishra and Gaurav Gupta were all about minty hues. Rose quartz, pink, peach, ivory and gold are top picks for the pheras, and this colour story can easily be extended to the other wedding functions as well—for instance, a pistachio green sari for a puja, misty lilac lehenga with metallic accents for the sangeet and a pale daffodil yellow sharara for the mehandi. After a renaissance in blouses, it's now the dupatta's turn. No longer treated as an afterthought, designers are revamping this drape to add additional visual interest to bridal looks. Sabyasachi's summer collection champions striped, floral and Benarasi dupattas, that are often in contrast to the lehenga. Manish Malhotra's fringed dupattas, particularly for his cocktail lehengas, are akin to stoles that can be looped around the arms, while his pre-stitched dupattas promise hands-free comfort. Tarun Tahiliani's collection was all about weightless gossamer tulle dupattas. Considering the bride in question is mindful of traditions but modern in her outlook, she is not willing to stick to demure looks for every event on her wedding invitation. Second skin blouses, with their strategic sheer panels, give her the perfect opportunity to amp up the sex appeal without being scandalous. Tarun Tahiliani's and Manish Malhotra's sheer detailing on their blouses create the illusion of it being stitched directly on the skin, and are best teamed with high-waist lehengas and barely-there dupattas. Ideally, do away with the necklace and wear these with enormous shoulder dusters. The veil is an important part of the customary bridal attire in India, and is draped over the head during the pheras. This swathe of fabric is what gives the look its final finishing flourish, differentiating the bride from overdressed wedding attendees. A delicate translucent veil works best, and lets your hairdo shine through as well. Keep the veil in the same colour family as your lehenga, going a few tones lighter or darker for additional impact. The wedding is often touted as the bride's very own princess moment. And the 2018 bride is piling on the jewellery to leave no room for doubt. Following in the footsteps of Deepika Padukone in Padmaavat, the trend is heavily in favour of royalty-worthy jewellery for the pheras. This has also led to the resurgence of several time-honoured styles like aad chokers, haslis, stacked gajra pearl bangles, oversized naths, statement matha pattis, temple jewellery and layered polki necklaces. The modern bride wants to look like a sophisticate, not a mannequin. Piling on elements like she raided the latest bridal exhibition in town is not her M.O. She would rather let one aspect of her repertoire shine through—so if the earrings are OTT, she will skip the necklace; if the lehenga is loaded with embroidery, the blouse will be simple. Brides today are heavily involved in the design process. They are not content with the prettiest lehenga on the rack. They would rather customise their trousseau with personalised additions, styled with family heirlooms—this could be her grandmother's hand-me-down Benarasi dupatta teamed with a brand-new lehenga, or her mother's wedding jewellery worn for one of the functions. For instance, Kapoor's at-home mehandi outfit by Anuradha Vakil featured vintage borders that belonged to her mother, as did the maang tikka she wore the next day. column1: Our cheat sheet to the best of Indian fashion from autumn/winter 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The sari gets a makeover, pantsuits rule the party circuit, and floral trench coats break free of cold-weather neutrals If there was any doubt on the state of the sari, the season will banish it. Bringing new fabrication, varied starting points and a play on drapes, designers looked to new iterations. Two worlds—denim and sari—collide for this irreverent expression that Sonam K Ahuja approves of. Carry forward your rebel streak with Diksha Khanna's distressed denim sari. Fit for brunch, art openings and more. Forget your mother's version of the six-yard drape and make room for its sultrier cousin. Resort wear label Shivan & Narresh, which advocates the high-flying, party-hopping lifestyle, brings the pre-draped dhoti sari in their signature skein work. The ultimate weapon in your wedding-season wardrobe is Nikasha's gold sari paired with an asymmetric long blouse that's all about soft power. Inspired by the monsoon and the #MeToo movement, designer Nikasha Tawadey's offering is about celebrating a new era. “If women want to be full of colour and shine, let them own it,” she says. While most of India tends to have one season—uniformly hot—autumn/winter fashion carries the thrill of chic outerwear. Not everyone associates with colour and maximalism. Gaurav Jai Gupta brings quiet elegance back to fashion that's functional if anything. Not only does he vouch for the dress-over-pants look, he also adds to the mix a sleeveless jacket. Doing away with navy and grey for winter, Aneeth Arora injected bright reds and pinks into her collection. For the show, Arora had live hard-candy-making stations by Pappabubble and a capella performers transport the audience to a heartwarming, cosy scene. The resultant trench coats in bold hues and hopeful florals carry some of that energy—one that expels the gloom associated with winter and in its place brings looks worthy of conversation. David Abraham and Rakesh Thakore's trans-seasonal collection #SadakSmart is quite literally inspired by the streets of New Delhi. The mix of cultures and subcultures spotted in the crowds was translated onto the runway. Our vote goes to the chintz trench worn over a sari—prepare to be papped. Has the LBD taken a backseat? Are bandage dresses finally being put to bed? Make way for the new after-hours must-haves. The pantsuit continued its reign. Namrata Joshipura's millennial pink version is the perfect antidote to the LBD. Pair with a diamond choker and towering stilettos for maximum supermodel appeal. Essential for a shrobing selfie is Siddartha Tytler's crimson velvet puffer jacket. Embrace your inner brat and style it with leather trousers or with hot shorts and knee-high boots. Kanika Goyal has a knack for dressing the after-hours crew. “It isn't as simple as wearing clothes, it's about creating a moment,” she explains. Mint green, white and oxblood collide in this preppy-meets-slick dress that also features holographic detailing. Recommended: a pair of glitter socks to carry on the party. Clothes have the power to make a statement. Choose your cause with these designers. Nitin Bal Chauhan brings back a sense of radical activism to the runway with his deliberately incoherent garments. A commentary on displaced refugees world over, Bal Chauhan's collection has a strong message to convey. Kallol Datta's latest collection also touches upon a message—one of inclusivity. His line of modest styles and native wear includes hijabs and chadors in shocking pinks and reds. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Meet the mothers who are balancing both career and home with style
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Moms on the move From an art benefactor to a social media star and an emerging entrepreneur—meet the mothers who are balancing it all while raising the style stakes After years of conducting cancer research and investing in companies in the biotechnology and pharmaceutical space in the US, Sunaina Murthy moved to India to co-found Currentkids.in, a website that encourages children to get acquainted with world affairs. For Murthy, her personal style doubles up as her armour. “It's how I present myself to the world, and it also impacts the way I feel.” Her sensibilities, of course, have changed after the birth of her kids. “Earlier, I wore suits almost every day to the office. Now, whatever I wear needs to be appropriate for meetings, for writing and editing and, above all, dropping to my knees for sticky, sweaty hugs when the kids come home from school. Comfortable footwear is a must. Luckily, trainers are in fashion,” adds Murthy. Rag & Bone pants, 7 For All Mankind skinny jeans, dresses from Alice + Olivia and Maje, T-shirts from Gap and running essentials from Lululemon are a part and parcel of her multifunctional life. —SGG For Biyash Choksey, mother of two girls, staying on top of trends is almost mandatory. “My daughters are always questioning my fashion choices and lack of makeup,” says the industrial engineer from the University of Michigan, adding that she prefers simple lines and neutral colours. Like her friend Sunaina Murthy, the other co-founder of Currentkids.in, Choksey gave up a lucrative career in logistics and strategy consulting in the US to make a change in her home country India. A “manic list maker,” Choksey is often seen in chikan kurtas, James Perse sweatpants, jeans paired with pastel silk blouses and the LBD with Tahitian pearls. “I like discovering new labels, though I do love Helmut Lang, Tibi, Ulla Johnson, Raw Mango and Anjul Bhandari,” she adds. “My mom taught me to appreciate varied aesthetics—double-ikat saris, patolas and kantha work. I owe a lot of my style to her.”—SGG A course in art history at Sotheby's in London and brief stints at Osian's and Bodhi Art Gallery in Mumbai inspired Amin to launch her own studio in her hometown Vadodara. Space Studio was launched in 2010 and with it her wardrobe went from formal work wear to chic casual separates. Today, the mother of two young girls, Naintara (8) and Inaaya (5), has not only provided a platform to over 200 budding artists (Neha Choksi and Hemali Bhuta are some of the names on which she has placed her bets), she also balances her life between [Mumbai](https://www.vogue.in/topics/mumbai/) and Vadodara with commendable ease. Her wardrobe, much like her work schedule, is multifunctional and adaptable. A dress from Idli, Jaipur, a blouse from Danish brand Ganni, a dash of Dolce & Gabbana, some See by Chloé, pearls inherited from her mother, and finger rings snapped up at flea markets and Barneys in Japan—Amin manages to make the eclecticism work. —KD Being a mother of two and raising funds for the treatment of lesser-privileged children can get anyone hot under the collar, but Mehta prefers to play it cool in casual, sporty clothing. Read boyfriend jeans with tees on an average day, or flared denims with a crop top for an evening out—“very laid-back, casual and bohemian. Everything retro is so me.” Her wardrobe comprises geometric pieces from Tibi, boho-chic clothes from Ulla Johnson and timeless dresses from Saloni London. For her retro fix of high-waist trousers and off-the-shoulder blouses she turns to Marissa Webb, Georgia Alice and Paper London. And since she leads an active lifestyle, running, swimming and playing tennis with daughters Kimaya (13) and Advika (9), sportswear from Lululemon and Nike feature heavily, too.—KD Richa Khanduri has led quite an unconventional life. After a 15-year stint in the banking industry, she quit to be with her family as well as give back to society. Now, during her free time, she finds solace in solo trips, “largely with people I don't know. It has been transformational in so many ways,” says Khanduri whose wardrobe mirrors her love for travel. On most days, you'll spot her in eco-friendly clothing sourced from across the world. Staples in her wardrobe include hand-woven linen, mul and khadi outfits (most with Indian accents) and traditional saris from Ekà, Padmaja, Runaway Bicycle, Lovebirds, Anavila, Péro, Ikai and Plantation House. “How I dress depends on my mood. It's sometimes androgynous, sometimes severe, sometimes quirky, but almost always comfortable and local.”—SGG Begani, who handles social media and marketing for her family-run business Begani Jewels, also blogs under Mommyn'lo, where she documents details of adventures with her children. Her kids, Arsh (6) and Aira (2), are only too happy to pose. “I catch up on my work on my phone when they are sleeping or at school. But when I'm spending time with them I don't touch my phone at all, except when I'm taking pictures of them for my blog,” says the Kuwait-born blogger mom. Naturally, her style choices gravitate towards Middle Eastern brands and designers, who, she says, have a certain flair. Apart from trawling through shops like Riva and Choice Moda for her Arabic designer picks, she favours Chanel, Dior, Miss Selfridge, H&M and COS. “I wore COS dresses through my pregnancy and I wear them even today. They're fuss-free and classic,” says Begani. What does she enjoy most about being a mom? “Waking up every morning to see my children's happy, smiley faces.”—KD When her search for a decent mani-pedi experience in Delhi came to naught, Tina decided to take matters in her own hands, literally, and launched 1010 The Nail Spa in 2012. Two years later, she followed it up with The Powder Room, a mobile makeup and hair bar, and ended up balancing two businesses with mommy duties. “The first two years were challenging but it gets easier and the guilt eventually fades once you plan better. Right now, I wouldn't trade being a working mom for anything,” says Talwar. The former Singapore and Dubai resident's schedule may have been chaotic but her well-planned parenting style and minimalist wardrobe are not. Her mother's adage of ‘less is more' has stood her in good stead. “For the day I prefer flowing dresses or a well-cut shirt with trousers, and at night it really depends on where I am going or what I am in the mood for,” she says.—KD You can never have too many whites, believes Akanksha Agarwal, whose style, when sized down, spans separates, traditional and Western, all in this pristine hue. “I am in love with my grandmother's saris in white with gold zari, which she passed down to me,” says the former actor—her last film was Garv (2004) with Salman Khan— and name behind gifting company Exclusively Yours that deals with silverware. The mother of two girls—who returned to India from New York some years ago—has practically lived her whole life in jeans and tops, veering towards designs that are effortless and chic. While she loves shopping in New York and Europe, her favourite labels include Anne Fontaine, Frame, J Brand, Roberto Cavalli, Tom Ford, Self-Portrait and Zimmermann. “I've always believed the simpler you dress, the classier you look,” she adds.—SGG While her blog chronicles an American girl acclimatising to life in Chennai, Acharya admits that her wardrobe, too, has adapted to motherhood and the city's sultry weather. Functional clothing has become important for keeping up with her two physically demanding boys, Jaidev (4) and Raghav (3). “Now, the accent is on being elegant and adding quirky elements instead—a funky drape here, a puffed shoulder there,” says Acharya. And while the Florida girl lives in nipped-at-the-waist knee-length skirts and culottes teamed with scoop-neck T-shirts, she's also loving local designers. Brass Tacks, Nicobar, Aapro, EnEch by Nupur Harwani and Aruni are just some of her favourites.—KD “I remind myself I have the same hours in a day as Beyoncé,” says Danani, an entrepreneur who brought Funky Monkeys, an indoor unstructured play area, to Chennai. Born in Mumbai and raised in Singapore, not only is the mother of three always perfectly put together, she also deftly juggles work and family. Inside her cross-continental closet you'll come upon labels like Delpozo, Valentino and Maison Margiela. While she credits her love for classics to her grandmother and mother, comfort, she says, has become a priority since she had children. Now, Danani is always on the search for separates that transition smoothly from day to night. Think crisp button-downs and trusty denim.—SGG For as long as she can remember, Kayan, a petite entrepreneur who runs a concept design store called The Space At 9/2, has tried to follow her mother's motto: Stay true to yourself, in the way you live and the way you dress. “Simple, androgynous and slightly experimental is how I would describe my style,” she says. An item she wears on rotation? “My husband's shirts from college. I pair them with high-waisted pants and slick shoes.” Currently, her loyalty lies with labels like J Brand, Acne Studios, Bodice, Shift and Anamika Khanna, who incidentally designed her pearl-strewn wedding lehenga, which she's keen to pass on to her daughter.—SGG What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 20 Bollywood celebrity looks that will help you plan your festive wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get your inspiration from the best in the biz While festive season brings a wave of cheer along with it, it also demands a wardrobe full of stop-and-stare ensembles. From Raksha Bandhan to Ganesh Chaturthi, Durga Puja to Diwali, you know your social calendar is going to be brimming with social events in the coming months. Now whether you're planning 0n playing the host or merely attending a festive occasion at a relative's place, the one thing you will decidedly require is a stellar Indian ethnic wardrobe. Don't forget to stick to the dress code of the festivities as you plan your looks. While some occasions may call for kurtas and anarkalis, others will give you a chance to try your mother's vintage saris. An anarkali, for one, will never disappoint, whether you wear it for a Durga Puja at your local pandal or to a close friend's elaborate Diwali party. Choose between heavily embellished numbers or simpler printed versions to channel different vibes. Or do a 360 and go with a sari—it's the perfect pick for Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations at home. If you don't want to deal with hassle of a six yard drape for the entire day, you can always count on a kurta and sharara set. And while most of the festivities may not permit you to step out in a lehenga, there could not be a better time than Diwali to experiment with all the kinds you can get your hands on. Still feeling unsure? Let the celebrities show you how it's done. Saris are always big hit with the stars during festive season. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan made a strong case for a burnt gold drape at Akash Ambani and Shloka Mehta's engagement party, while Jacqueline Fernandez stood out in her off-shoulder blouse at Sonam K Ahuja's mehendi function. Those looking to swap the embellished drapes with something lighter can turn to Alia Bhatt for the ultimate inspiration. And if you are not shy of trying unconventional outfits, invest in a pre-draped sari like Mira Rajput Kapoor's Anamika Khanna ensemble to ensure all eyes stay on you. That's not all, anarkalis are also popular during the festivities. Take style cues from Alia Bhatt and style yourself in a printed twirl-worthy number, instead of opting for the usual embroidered ones. You can also look at elegant kurtas and sharara sets. If lehengas are your personal favourite, try a look like Sonam K Ahuja's white and gold mehendi ensemble. Or take cues from Karisma Kapoor's Sabyasachi outfit, and style a floral lehenga and dupatta with a solid hued blouse while playing the hostess at your Diwali party. ICYMI, white is a huge trend this festive season as well. Swara Bhasker chose a stunning lehenga for Sonam K Ahuja's mehendi function, and Sara Ali Khan donned a white sari for Saudamini Mattu's reception as well. If you want to stay on trend, style your white outfit with chunky jewellery and a pair of metallic heels. column1: 3 Indian women take Anita Dongre’s designs to the streets of New York
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Anita Dongre's new store in SoHo is a coming together of contemporary and traditional Indian fashion, with a living, beating heart at the centre of it all. Vogue gets three Indian women to show how they translate modern Indianwear into their Big Apple lives On an evening in May, visitors to Soho, Manhattan's buzziest shopping district, would have come across the heady fragrance of jasmine blooms and heard the dramatic percussion of tablas. Anita Dongre, arguably India's most successful designer, was throwing open the doors to her brand-new store. The two-storey space is home to several of the house's lines, including bridal and occasion wear, ready-to-wear and jewellery, as well as Grassroot, the Indian contemporary line with a social conscience. [#image: /photos/5ce42ae3cc50be804013f3d0]||| ||| Image: Manasi Sawant Brides of Indian origin living in the US used to travel all the way to India for their trousseaus, making multiple trips to select outfits and conduct fittings. We had several brides at our Indian stores, and the feedback we got from them was partly why it occurred to us that we should have a presence in the US,” says Dongre about this bold move Stateside. With busy careers and an annual holiday allowance that only extends to three weeks, it's understandable, Dongre says, that brides want those precious days to be spent on the wedding and honeymoon instead of schlepping across continents to ensure their choli fits just so. Till Dongre's store opening, brides (and grooms) looking for Indian designer wedding wear had to rely on a couple of stores and websites that offered a random selection from a handful of designers. “Those stores would buy from a few Indian designers but they never carry the latest collections. A buyer can come and buy three or four lehengas from us and put it in a multi-designer store, but it's not the experience that our own store offers,” Dongre says. Apart from bridal looks, the store also offers special-occasion outfits, designer jewellery as well as menswear, taking care of the sartorial needs of the entire wedding party. Customers also include non-Indians marrying into Indian American families or guests attending Indian weddings. While the bridal market was a strong business move, for Dongre, launching Grassroot, her socially conscious line, came from the heart. “Grassroot is really special. There's nothing like it in New York—where you can buy a contemporary piece of clothing that is handcrafted and empowers rural artisans. Today, fashion that works with craft and sustainability has a global platform,” she says. While Grassroot actually made a debut in the US last year with a standalone store in New York, it's now available in this space. The past year, Dongre says, has proved useful to fine-tune details such as sizing. And taking the weather into account, a special New York-only line will make an appearance soon. We celebrate the occasion with three incredible New Yorkers of Indian origin, who easily fit Anita Dongre's modern Indian aesthetic into their cosmopolitan lives. Wearing Grassroot, these women hit the city streets. FOUNDER, EXECUTIVE AND ARTISTIC DIRECTOR, INDO-AMERICAN ARTS COUNCIL [#image: /photos/5ce42ae3b803111f448f6cf3]||| ||| Photograph by Kat Irlin “I am into simplicity and prefer clean lines. I like excitement in my clothes, but in the form of bright colours. When I wear Indian textiles, it's in a tailored Western style. I prefer some of the heavier weaves that can be crafted into jackets. I often have to attend events in the evening after work. On those days I turn to all-black and carry a statement jacket, scarf or piece of jewellery to add on. I slip on a pair of heels and I'm dressed. If I'm organising an event, I tend to opt for Western cuts and silhouettes, as they're easy to change into, run around and work in. I save my Indian outfits like saris for galas or weddings.” ART MARKETING CONSULTANT [#image: /photos/5ce42ae461774d5de35aa2d0]||| ||| Photograph by Kat Irlin “I realise now that I'm in my thirties, my body and tastes have changed so much. I know what makes me feel comfortable and chic. It's not so much about showing skin as it is about classic silhouettes. For special events, I like wearing things that not everyone has worn before. I don't like to look like a cookie-cutter Indian girl. So, I tend to mix and match a lot. I like handwoven textiles over heavily embroidered clothes, with subtle colours and minimal embroidery. I recently acquired a blue jacket from Anita Dongre that was originally paired with a tulle skirt for a bridal look. I wore the same jacket and white trousers for my cousin's mehendi. I now buy Indian clothes that I can also wear in New York, and ones that are relevant to my life here.” FOUNDER, CLASSPASS; ARTISTIC DIRECTOR, SA DANCE COMPANY [#image: /photos/5ce42ae49cc0c01376f9d419]||| ||| Photograph by Kat Irlin “Since I'm into fitness and movement, I like things that are comfortable and have a bit of flow to them. It's not uncommon to come to work in workout wear—I'm often seen in leggings at the office. Another thing I love is tailored touches, pieces like pleated shorts and clothes with textures like ruffles, cut-outs or leather. Black and white with a pop of colour is one of my favourite combinations. I also love the concept of a lehenga and choli; I like playing with that structure—a separate top and skirt is a combination I wear a lot. Indian wear can be heavy at times, so I'm always trying to add subtle Indian touches like prints and jewellery. I design all of the Indian dance costumes for my dance company, and for those I'm always exploring ways to incorporate an Indian as well as an American identity. I get to explore my Indian identity not only through my own clothes but also through dance wear, which is more dramatic.” Styled by Yael Gitai What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What to expect from Monisha Jaising’s grand finale at Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The couturier reveals all the details There's little that designer Monisha Jaising does as well as unabashed glamour. Decadent silhouettes come alive on her moodboard, usually set in a palette of sumptuous metallics and tulle. Considering that the couturier has taken up the baton for the grand finale at the upcoming Lakmé Fashion Week winter/sestive 2018, Vogue caught up with her to sneak a peek at the production that she has planned. “Being the ‘chosen one' is definitely an honour, but it only drives me to work extra hard to do justice to it. I am blessed to be working with Lakmé on this special collection, and I'm very pleased with what I have come up with along with my talented team,” Jaising says about taking the role of finale designer at the week-long fashion extravaganza. Lakmé's beauty statement, ‘Shades of a Diva' served as the point of departure for the collection, as the designer delved into the lifestyle of an archetypal fashion savant for inspiration. “We have come up with a total of 65 shades of a diva, because I am showing 65 garments on the big night. The collection is primarily inspired by a diva's lifestyle, and the spots that she frequents—luncheon with her friends, an exotic destination wedding, lying by the poolside or grooving at a beach club party with the ‘it' crowd. Accordingly, I worked on creating something that she would wear to each of these places. Since a diva is an influencer who people look up to as a trendsetter, she would necessarily look to statement, fashion-forward pieces, which is what our collection is about,” Jaising explains. Expect a dichotomous colour palette that starts from sorbet hues like bleached aqua and sea foam green, and gradually progresses to cherry red, fuchsia pink and Pantone's current darling, ultraviolet. “People are bored of greys and navy blues,” the designer adds. “The current mood for the festive season is leaning towards a lot of colour, which is tempered with the eternal allure of sexy black.” Stay tuned to this space for all the updates on Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2018. column1: Dressing like a Duchess: Meghan Markle’s best royal looks
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Since marrying in Givenchy, the Duchess of Sussex has stepped out in true royal style. To celebrate Meghan Markle's turning 37 this month, Vogue looks back at the Suits actor's standout fashion moments She may have married in Givenchy—and partied in Stella McCartney—but the Duchess of Sussex's arrival was in fact a week later, at Prince Charles's birthday celebrations. Her Flavia silk-crepe pencil dress from British brand Goat—topped with a Philip Treacy dome hat and nude Tamara Mellon pumps, with nude tights—was the first in a parade of sophisticated looks. Pre-wedding she may have been more relaxed and minimal in her choices, but since joining The Firm, she's taken a turn for a more feminine, tailored approach. First came the muted ensembles: the pale pink off-the-shoulder Carolina Herrera number from the Trooping of the Colour, the off-white caped Givenchy style for her first solo royal engagement with HRH The Queen, and a prim, pink custom Prada ensemble for the Queen's Young Leader Awards. (Lest we forget her Ascot debut too; a white Givenchy number and Philip Treacy hat that channeled Audrey Hepburn's My Fair Lady.) Then she broke the colour scheme with a citrus yellow, boat-neck sheath dress by Brandon Maxwell; a palette cleanser, if you will, ahead of a darker slew of sultry shades. She wore olive green Ralph Lauren (with a matching Stephen Jones hat and Manolo Blahnik pumps) to attend Prince Louis's christening, followed by a bespoke navy Dior dress, crescendoing with a forest green Givenchy skirt and top. The next sartorial twist came at Wimbledon, where the Duchess stepped out in Ralph Lauren white wide-leg trousers and a striped button-down shirt. A rather more affordable dress followed: a trench-coat dress from Canadian label Nonie (teamed with nude Dior stilettos and a simple Mulberry clutch) and, most recently, a denim Carolina Herrera wrap dress, paired with a J. column1: Meet the jewellery designer speaking up against unethical gold-mining
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion When Lilian von Trapp inherited her mother’s jewellery collection, she was inspired to launch her own ethical label using recycled gold. She tells Vogue the story of her new-found passion and how her chic, minimal designs are doing—not just looking—good You don't need to know anything about Lilian von Trapp to see the appeal of her jewellery designs. You certainly don't need to know that the Berlin-based designer is running her brand sustainably, and supporting an essential environmental and humanitarian campaign in Uganda, more of which later. Von Trapp's elegant, minimalist pieces in recycled gold are fuss-free classics that speak for themselves – the sort of jewellery you see on smart, interesting, chic women. The actor Emma Watson is among her fans; so is the model Arizona Muse. “In order to create an ethical brand, you have to think of the pieces you create in a sustainable way, so it's not only about fashion or being trendy,” says von Trapp. “It's about creating a piece that a woman would hopefully want to wear for her whole life or even pass on to someone else. That's why when I create the pieces, I'm thinking ‘What can I design that will become someone's uniform, that they don't want to take off, that they can wear from the office to dinner?' The jewellery just becomes part of you really.” It was only in January last year that von Trapp officially launched her label, though it had been a long time coming. “I came to jewellery design through, let's call it destiny,” she says with a laugh. She'd started out studying law and briefly worked in a law firm. “Then my mother passed away and for me that time was really life-changing. I realised that life's too short to do things you're not passionate about.” She left law and found a job in fashion, working as a buyer in a Berlin department store. At home she was sorting through her mother's things and came across her jewellery. “It was not only hers, but also from two grandmothers and great grandmothers, and I really didn't know what to do with it. I didn't want to sell it obviously and I didn't want to keep it in a safe. I thought it was a shame not to wear it, but most of the pieces were not my style—I didn't have an emotional attachment to most of it.” It dawned on von Trapp that she could recycle the pieces to make something she would actually wear and she soon found a goldsmith who agreed to melt them down and create new designs that she had sketched. “I think I did five or six styles, and of course I'd wear them at work and in my personal life. People started asking me ‘Where is this from?' and I realised it was something I could do as a business.” Her pieces, designed in Berlin and manufactured in Pforzheim (known in Germany as “golden town” because of its formidable goldsmithing industry), use recycled gold. (Von Trapp hopes one day to use vintage diamonds in her main line too, but for now the process is so complex she has to restrict stones to her custom-made pieces.) “When I started the brand, I read up on mining and it became clear to me that I would never want to work with newly mined gold,” she says. She was shocked by what she read about how gold is sourced—and the often crippling impact on mining communities. “In the gold pits of Uganda, there isn't only the danger of dying by being crushed,” she says, “the other horrible situation is—and this is why people in Uganda have a low life expectancy—they are handling mercury and cyanide with their bare hands. I've seen mothers my own age or even younger burning mercury without any protection while they have babies on their backs. Of course those toxins go into your organs and they destroy everything from within, and they also go into the groundwater, which contaminates the soil.” It's these revelations that led von Trapp to add a charitable element to her brand: two per cent of her revenue is given to the Earthbeat Foundation, which raises awareness about mining conditions, promotes more ethical methods of mining and develops alternative income sources for workers to give them a route out of the industry. Von Trapp has just come back from a trip to Uganda with the foundation. “We've been planning this project now for a year, focusing on three communities,” she explains. “The people there earn one dollar per day and they work in the mines from 5am to midnight or even later—it's really modern slavery. We talked to them and asked them, ‘Is there anything else you would rather do instead?' And they told us they would like to do farming again because before the gold rush in the 1930s all of their ancestors were farmers—but nowadays they can't farm because the soil is contaminated.” Earthbeat brought in permaculture experts from Kenya, who have worked with the communities to develop a solution: they plant bamboo and vetiver grass, which suck out the toxins from the soil, and can ultimately be harvested and sold. The farmers can then plant further crops like coffee and peanuts, all chosen because they naturally replenish the soil and nurture one another. “Not only can the communities live off this food themselves, but they can sell it and create a new income, and then naturally they will move away from mining because they don't depend on it anymore,” says von Trapp. Back home in Germany, the designer has introduced a limited-edition necklace, “The Bar”, to raise money for the project; 100 per cent of the profits from this piece will go to the Earthbeat Foundation's work in that Ugandan community. More generally, she tries to position her brand as far away as possible from throw-away consumerism. Every design stays in her portfolio and some of them, like her “The Round Ones” hoop earrings, are designed to be attached to other pieces, so that you can update and customise them yourself. “When I'm designing, I think about myself, the women I'm surrounded by, and my mother and grandmother,” she says. “I'm thinking about what they would like and what I like, and I try to create something that can work for a woman at any age. You can wear it and you know that nobody had to suffer in a mine, that everything's recycled, that a part of it goes directly back to the foundation and supports people who are still suffering in mining. I mean, of course we don't need jewellery to live, but it's something that makes us feel good, makes us shine, allows us to honour ourselves or someone else. And then knowing that this piece of jewellery, beyond that, can do something good—it's great.” View Gallery 7 Photos Meet Lilian von Trapp, the jewellery designer speaking up against unethical gold-mining What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Denim Rebooted: 3 brands reinventing denim with sustainability at heart
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The most popular fabric in the world is causing environmental havoc—but no one wants to give up their jeans. Vogue meets three pioneering denim labels who are leading a production revolution that focuses on sustainability without sacrificing style Sturdy and resilient as the material they are made of, denim jeans remain one of the most popular items of clothing worldwide. Last year, according to a global report published by Orbis, the global denim jeans market was valued at $55.6 billion and is predicted to reach $62 billion by the end of 2028. The workwear staple has survived almost 150 years of fashion trends, developing a multitude of styles, dyings, cuts and finishings, while infiltrating the ranks of high-end fashion as exemplified by the latest reinterpretations by Vetements, which contributed to the relaunch of patchwork denim in 2015, and Gucci's hyper-embellished denim jackets and trousers. Denim's unfailing popularity has also been accompanied by a growing awareness of its devastating environmental impact. Thousands of litres of water are used to created a single pair of jeans—according to Levi's, one pair of 501s uses 3,781 litres of water in its full lifecycle. Often, where the textile industry is less supervised, the toxic chemicals used in the colouring and washing—heavy metals including cadmium, chromium, mercury, lead and copper—are directly discharged in rivers creating irreparable damages to the environment. With smaller production numbers and dynamic business structures, emerging denim brands are finding new ways to tackle the issue, combining a made-to-order approach with upcycling and tighter controls on their production chain. Vogue meets three emerging brands leading the change. London College of Fashion alumni Nathalie Ballout launched her eponymous upcycling label in 2016, soon drawing a consistent celebrity following that includes Dua Lipa, Winnie Harlow and Ella Eyre. Attracted by the versatility and ubiquity of the material, the Swedish Lebanese designer started by upcycling all kinds of denim clothing, but from her spring/summer 2018 collection her focus has shifted to old Levi's jeans which she buys in bulk and reworks into voluminous jackets cinched at the waist, frayed boiler suits and skintight pencil skirts. Ballout's production process is laborious and intensive, but clever too. Her made-to-order approach means there is little to no waste in the production process. She and her small team start by deconstructing vintage jeans, cutting up the seams and laying the fabric flat to bleach or dye it before placing the desired pattern.“I'm trying to promote slow fashion and I want people to appreciate what they are buying and the craft that has gone into it,” explains the designer. Ballout has also been experimenting with upcycling other fabrics, including hand-embroidered Swedish linen and tapestries, which will be featured in her denim pieces for her upcoming spring/summer 2019 collection, presented as part of Vogue Talents during Milan Fashion Week. Ksenia Schnaider started to work with denim in 2016, five years after launching her brand with husband and business partner Anton Schnaider. Their big break came with the launch of the “demi-denims”, a reworked denim blend of high-waisted jeans layered over a boot-cut style inspired by her friends' 1990s vintage jeans; they were immediately picked up by Instagram influencers and celebrities, including Bella Hadid. Schnaider describes the style as “amusing and unusual, but really sexy on any body type”. “Clothing used to be something exciting back then,” she explains of her post-Soviet influences, which come through in the exaggerated volumes and severe cuts of her reworked denim, as well as in her references to sportswear. “We want to take that feeling back and translate it to a modern audience.” Today, a third of Schnaider's collections is made from vintage fabrics, upcycling around 6,000 pairs of jeans each year to make the popular demi-denims, and also what they call “denim fur”—blue faux-fur jackets and coats made from the leftover scraps of the demi-denims—and “rainbow denim”, which is made with reworked fabric of different shades of blue. The remaining production is outsourced to partners in Italy, Ukraine and Turkey, but the brand is working towards improving its sustainability footprint. Next up, it will develop a collection of organic and ethical denim in collaboration with Isko, a denim manufacturer based in Turkey which has developed technologies to reduce water waste and the use of chemicals and cotton. When Ségolène Jacmin grew tired of her job in consulting, she asked her twin sister Alexandra to join forces to create a new creative project together. “She was not enthusiastic at all,” says Ségolène. “Then one Christmas, when I had abandoned the idea of doing something together, she arrived with the concept for the brand and all the drawings—that is typical of my sister”. Alexandra, a designer with experience at Jean Paul Gaultier and Maison Margiela, decided to bring innovation and refinement to denim by venturing beyond the ubiquitous jeans and jacket pairing to create a complete wardrobe of dresses, coats, skirts and jumpsuits designed to be timeless in both style and quality. Japanese denim—renowned for its tight, sophisticated weaving and characteristic indigo blue—was the obvious choice for the Jacmin sisters, who source most of their fabric from a supplier in Okayama. The atelier, which has been certified with the STANDARD 100 by OEKO-TEX, a certification that guarantees that the products' harmful substances are below an established limit value, is also fitted with a clean water purification system. According to Ségolène, water samples are checked daily by the city government to ensure they are fit to be discharged in the rivers. To complement their standard collections of timeless and seasonal pieces, the sisters have launched an artisanal collection of hand-made pieces that combine denim with traditional techniques like embroidery and smocking. “Our big values are quality, resistance and finishing—we want to create pieces you can keep your whole life,” explains Ségolène. column1: Can you really wear your wedding lehenga after the big day is over?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Why wear the outfit of a lifetime, only once? The Vogue India team takes from their personal experience to help you bring your wedding lehenga back into your wardrobe Finding the perfect wedding lehenga is no mean feat. Every bride is confronted with some pressing questions: “Is it one of a kind?” “Can I re-wear it?” “And how will I style it after the wedding?” Long story short, more often than not, after the wedding, when you've unpacked from your honeymoon, and returned to normal everyday life, the lehenga is packed away and left to become a memory of the past. To come to the rescue and help brides-to-be, five women in the Vogue office let us in how they would re-style their wedding lehengas back in their closets, and keep them from collecting dust. Image: Artfoto Studios “My lehenga was a custom Manish Malhotra. Since my wedding was just three months ago, I haven't had the chance to wear it again. But I did choose it with the idea that I could style it with something else. It doesn't have sequins or a zari work, making it easy to pair with a plain shirt or a lighter blouse. It is still quite heavy, so I would wait for a family wedding to re-wear it.” “Since I had a destination wedding, I didn't want a lehenga that was over the top or really heavy. My blouse and skirt were one colour and didn't have any big borders. I re-wore it again, eight months after I got married, for a close relative's wedding. I had a slip top made to match the skirt to make the outfit look like a dress. I wore Indian jewellery but no dupatta. It was a completely different look from how I wore it on my wedding day.” “I had a Muslim and Hindu wedding, so I had two different outfits. I haven't had a chance to wear either since then, but I have definitely thought of some ideas for when I do. For my Muslim wedding, I wore a lehenga with a long kurta over it, that can easily be worn with pants. My Hindu wedding lehenga had a long, heavy red dupatta that I want to get made into something.” “My sister, designer Anushka Khanna, customised my wedding lehenga. I take immense pride in the fact that I was her first bridal client, she was just starting out! But on the flipside, my lehenga became a sample! I gave her all the creative power, because who knows you better than your sister? And it turned out exactly how I wanted it to. It really pains me when wedding outfits are not repeated again. In this age of conscious consumerism, it's really imperative that we re-use our clothes more than once. The fact is that an incredible amount of artistry, hand-work and labour goes into every lehenga created, and why should it not be seen more than once? I think every modern bride should re-wear their bridal outfits, whether it's by exchanging the dupatta for a jacket, knotting up a beautiful silk shirt over the skirt, or re-wearing your choli with different saris. It seems almost criminal to let such beautiful creations languish in closets.” Image: Mark Swaroop “The great thing about your wedding lehenga is that it's never going to look the same as on your big day. Even just adding lighter jewellery or draping the dupatta differently changes the look. It's only been six months since my wedding, and I've already had a separate blouse made to wear with my lehenga. Since the skirt was very heavy, I decided to create a plain velvet blouse. I made it very tiny and sexy to make the look more modern. It's such a beautiful lehenga and there are so many ways I can re-wear it. Even ten years from now, if I'm as skinny as I was when I bought it, I would keep it as a part of my wardrobe.” Weddings Fashion Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast
