column1: A brief history of espadrilles: From humble origins to fashion must-have
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A 14th-century peasant shoe, footwear for Republican soldiers during the Spanish Civil War and iconic fashion must-have since the 1940s—Vogue looks back at the history of espadrilles Before we were captivated by Jane Birkin in striped T-shirt, flared denim, wicker basket and woven sandals, French writer and philosopher Simone de Beauvoir was taking her infamous hikes in search of intellectual enlightenment wearing “an old dress and espadrilles” in 1930s Marseille. Around the same time, Coco Chanel was enriching Riviera chic with naval-inspired espadrilles, which she wore to the beach accessorised with strings of pearls and a sailor hat. Meanwhile in Figueres, Spain, surrealist Salvador Dalí was making jute-sole sandals—picked up from his local shop—a part of his signature look. Today, from sea to city, Coco to Karl (Lagerfeld revitalised the shoe on the Chanel spring/summer 2013 runway), the enduring espadrille has travelled well. The once-humble footwear now comes strung with charms, studded with Swarovski crystals and monogrammed with YSL  or interlocking Cs. Creeperstyle or embellished with brocade, its latest reinvention is courtesy of Rihanna, with a Fenty Puma collection featuring rope-sole slides in ‘Sulphur Spring' yellow shades and ‘Drizzle Bay' grey. Espadrilles take their name from the Catalan word espardenya, used to describe the canvas shoe with coiled rope sole and vertical stitching worn by 14th-century peasants in the Spanish Pyrenees. Castañer, a family-run Catalonia espadrille factory founded in 1927, was commissioned to supply footwear to Republican soldiers during the Spanish Civil War, ands has since created luxury espadrilles for Lanvin, Hermès and Christian Louboutin, as well as famously making Yves Saint Laurent's first wedge style in the early 1970s. By the 1940s, the style had already featured on several covers of Vogue and the trend had been picked up by Hollywood. Lauren Bacall wore lace-up espadrilles throughout 1948's film noir Key Largo opposite Humphrey Bogart and donned a wide-strapped style, which she teamed with silk, polka-dot shorts, in The Big Sleep (1946). A decade later, Grace Kelly wore coral-coloured espadrilles in High Society (1956) and paired a simple black style with shirt and shorts in Alfred Hitchcock's To Catch a Thief (1955). The 1960s saw Jeanne Moreau riding her bicycle in a striped Breton top and espadrilles in François Truffaut's Jules et Jim (1962) and Romy Schneider wore hers poolside in La Piscine (1969). At its height, Yves Saint Laurent took the trend exactly two inches higher. Collaborating with the Castañer family—whom he met at a trade show in 1970—together they created the first wedge espadrille, an elaborately woven shoe with gold satin ribbons and gold thread mixed with jute coils. The now-fashionable wedge style was made iconic by Diane Keaton in Play It Again, Sam in 1972 when she teamed a pair of denim-look, rope-sole wedges with grey knee socks and denim shorts. Bianca Jagger took to the natural heeling in the 1970s, boosting their style status. In the late 1980s, Castañer created thigh-high black leather espadrilles for Jean Paul Gaultier. By then espadrilles were a fashion staple. For his spring/summer 2012 show, Valentino launched a decadent flat black leather and lace version; styled with the label's signature studding followed. Chanel upped the jute game in spring summer 2013, reintroducing espadrilles in pastel shades. The trend continues to walk the runways. Last year saw the introduction of Giambattista Valli's “cocktail espadrille”—soft leather flats with black ribbon ankle ties worn with a couture collection of duchess satin silk shift dresses and trailing gowns. And so from Audrey Hepburn in red Breton top and boyish flats in the 1950s to Amal Clooney in towering wedges today, footwear's woven wanderer is a perennial favourite. And with Chanel's summer debut of its Coco Beach line—including espadrilles inspired by Coco's favourite seaside resorts—this hard-working style shows no sign of checking out. column1: How to style traditional silver jewellery like a Bollywood celebrity
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Learn from the best Bollywood's love affair with jewellery is an enduring one, and the celebrity set's choices tend to be a lesson in fail-safe trends to invest in. There was the chandbali phase and the not-so-fleeting obsession with temple jewellery. The current favourite, however, is a departure from this erstwhile preference for gilded bling. Silver jewellery, which was previously bracketed as strictly tribal and boho-friendly, has now taken centre stage. Is it any surprise that Sonam Kapoor-Ahuja has been a champion of the trend long before it became a wardrobe norm? Whether it's her off-duty travel repertoire or promotional appearances, you'll be hard-pressed to find her without her trusty silver baubles. In fact, Kapoor-Ahuja probably packs as many silver pieces when travelling as her husband Anand Ahuja does sneakers. The actor dismisses the myth that silver jewellery is only compatible with traditional wear. Most recently, she paired statement silver shoulder dusters with a Canadian tuxedo and sneakers. Antique silver chokers with off-shoulder dresses, silver necklace and earring sets with maxis and saris, and even layered silver necklaces with anti-fit dresses, the style maven defies conventional codes of ensemble-and-jewellery pairings to curate individualistic looks. Janhvi Kapoor seems to have taken a leaf from her elder sister's stylebook too. The debutante actor has a strong affinity for silver jewellery, and has been seen in styles like balis, danglers and mismatched stacked silver bangles on more than one occasion. Come festive season, take a cue from Aditi Rao Hydari and skip those precious pieces in favour of silver chokers or earrings with hints of colour. Neha Dhupia, on the other hand, would have you juxtapose your silver pieces with jadau and pearls for the best of both worlds. column1: Watch Christian Louboutin sing and dance to Bollywood’s biggest hits
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion What happens when the celebrity-favourite shoe designer with a passion for Bollywood meets songstress Kanika Kapoor? Find out now Christian Louboutin is no stranger to Bollywood. His love for the industry dates back to his childhood, one that was defined by frequent visits to his neighbourhood cinema in Paris. “There was a cinema on my way to school. It used to play musical comedies, Egyptian and Bollywood films. I remember being fascinated by the posters. Aan (1952) and Mother India (1957) were some of the first movies I watched,” says Louboutin. Over the years, Indian films have come to influence his designs in more ways than one. “Bollywood has so much to offer. From the dance to the music and the vibrant colours, there are a lot of elements very dear to my work,” he adds. The French designer whose red-lacquered soles have become a firm favourite with a legion of leading ladies around the world, is also known to find Bollywood music therapeutic while he works. He cites Chaiyya Chaiyya as one of his favourite songs. So, it comes as no surprise when the shoe maven meets singer Kanika Kapoor at his sun-dappled apartment in the heart of Paris, their conversation quickly spirals into a singing session. Watch the duo belt out two of Kapoor's biggest hits, Chittiyan Kalaiyan and Baby Doll (bloopers included). column1: The Meghan Effect: Studying the sartorial power of the new royal
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue looks at how the Duchess’ sartorial style has shifted since joining The Firm, and wonders how it will affect her global fashion influence From the moment Meghan Markle officially stepped out with Prince Harry at the Invictus Games in September 2017, it was clear that she was not a conventional princess in the making. Dressed in torn Mother jeans, a Misha Nonoo “Husband” shirt, tan Everlane tote and tortoise sunglasses by Finlay & Co, she set the tone early on: here was a woman ready to shake things up. The then 36-year-old actor's relaxed garb seemed to break every royal protocol in the book, but more than that, her style sparked a £20,000 spike in the sales of Finlay & Co sunglasses overnight. Thus the Meghan Effect, as it has become known, was born... This should come as no surprise to an audience already well versed in the Kate Effect. According to Newsweek, the Duchess of Cambridge's high-low approach, with her steady rotation of custom McQueen and high-street favourites (Zara, Reiss, Topshop, Hobbs), was said to be worth £1 billion to the British fashion industry in 2012—a Midas touch that has extended to her children's wardrobes, too. Consultancy firm Brand Finance pegged Princess Charlotte's net worth at £5 billion (not bad for a three-year-old)—and estimated that Meghan's wedding day alone would add £1 billion to the UK economy. “We are observing only the beginnings of the Meghan Effect,” notes Brand Finance CEO David Haigh. “It will undoubtedly match or even surpass the Kate Effect in its influence on the fashion industry.” Pre-wedding, Markle appeared to be taking a similar approach to that of her future sister-in-law, showcasing a roster of well-chosen "home turf" pieces that duly flew off the shelves. Recall the sellout, bell-sleeved M&S jumper she wore to visit a Brixton radio station in January; the bag by Edinburgh brand Strathberry, carried at her first official appearance after the engagement announcement (out of stock in 11 minutes flat); or the black Hiut jeans worn in Cardiff, which required the Welsh denim brand to upsize factories in order to fulfil its three-month waiting list. Her influence appeared to operate at all price points (after she wore Jason Wu's £1,415 navy dress in February, Net-A-Porter reported a 600 per cent increase in sales) and was a masterclass in diplomatic dressing, embracing major British names (Burberry, Alexander McQueen, Stella McCartney) and smaller labels from across the Commonwealth, including Canada's Smythe, Line The Label and Greta Constantine. Comparisons have been drawn to Michelle Obama and the Duchess of Cambridge, both celebrated for their ability to fly the flag for home-grown and emerging brands. But whereas the Duchess of Cambridge married just a year after Instagram was invented, the Duchess of Sussex is navigating an uncharted path through public life: she was “on social” before she met Prince Harry and will be conscious of the unprecedented scrutiny enabled by these platforms. Myriad dedicated websites and accounts follow her every sartorial step, including US-based What Meghan Wore (WMW) and Australia's Meghan's Fashion. Both report exponential traffic growth. WMW's average readership “has more than quadrupled since January”, say founders Susan Kelley and Susan Courter, who created the site as a sister to their already successful What Kate Wore. In 2018, we can all get a piece of Markle's “real-life fairy tale”, says Elizabeth Vollman of @Meghansfashion, “but she's also the modern-day version of royalty. She is not afraid to take fashion risks and I think that only makes her more relatable.” Michael Kors similarly noted the way the Duchess of Sussex “definitely brings a modern attitude to royal style” in an interview with British Vogue earlier this year. Vogue contributor and dedicated royal watcher Elizabeth Holmes—whose hilarious So Many Thoughts series shot her to Instagram fame—agrees. “Meghan feels very much like she is one of us, which of course she isn't—she is a well-to-do actress who had a lot of experience in the spotlight before becoming a royal. She is an American who before all of this was an influencer. She readily shared her feelings and her passions online. That's really relatable to a lot of women today.” But what is most intriguing is how Markle's approach has changed since becoming Duchess of Sussex—blowing the budget with every new outing, perhaps with an eye on her Insta-impact. “Before the wedding, she was all about relaxed, minimal, fashion-y pieces—the sartorial version of her favoured messy bun,” notes Holmes. “As the Duchess of Sussex, her looks are much more feminine and more tailored.” With just a few exceptions here and there (such as the J. Crew wicker clutch she carried at the polo in July), Meghan's post-wedding outfits have been exclusively designer, often custom-made. While her more accessible looks have included a £625 trench-coat dress by Canadian brand House of Nonie and the £590 Goat dress she wore to her first post-wedding event, paired with £2,200 Vanessa Tugendhaft earrings (which, by the way, sold out in ten minutes), her new royal wardrobe is more likely to bring out the big guns—Prada, Ralph Lauren, Oscar de la Renta, Carolina Herrera, Dior and, of course, her wedding dress designer, Givenchy. Perfectly polished, it reads more Upper East Side than international; dare we say it, more Melania than Michelle. And while if anything her look appears to have become more conservative, the tabloids have been clamouring to point out when she has flouted royal rules. She's not worn the supposedly obligatory flesh-toned tights on every occasion; she's revealed a penchant for trousers; and she showed a sliver of shoulder at the Trooping of the Colour—apparently something “fashion tradition” dictates is not allowed. (Debrett's, the authority on modern etiquette and publisher of A-Z of Modern Manners is quick to point out that there is no such thing as “an official royal style rulebook” as far as it is aware.) The stylist behind the Duchess of Sussex's wardrobe is among one of the best-kept secrets in the industry. Prime suspect is Jessica Mulroney, Markle's long-time friend (her pageboy twins stole the show at the royal wedding) and the woman behind the wardrobe of Canada's First Lady, Sophie Grégoire Trudeau. Mulroney has been said to “unofficially assist” the new duchess, though she has publicly denied it in the past. House of Nonie designer Nina Kharey may have blown Mulroney's cover when she publicly thanked her on Instagram for the Duchess's appearance in one of her designs in July, implying Mulroney played a rather more active role in creating the look. How the Duchess comes by her clothes is another source of intrigue and mystery. Brands, though thrilled with the association, refuse to comment on the matter, lest their relationship with Kensington Palace be damaged. On repeated occasions, the Palace has noted how the royal family is not allowed to accept freebies, nor do they make a practice of borrowing clothing the way celebrities do for red-carpet events. The Duchess will be paying for her clothing—though, more than likely, at cost rather than full whack (another factor brands keep schtum about). Regardless, we remain a people obsessed. The Duchess of Sussex's wardrobe may have changed from high-low to high-high with limited fallout thus far—but will that last? Or does her increasingly aspirational style make her IRL fairy-tale fantasy all the more alluring? Will she and the Duchess of Cambridge share the role of royal fashionista upon the latter's return from maternity leave? Either way, we'll all be watching closely. column1: Malini Vachani-Akerkar launches her first jewellery collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Inspired by art deco Malini Vachani-Akerkar is well known in hospitality circles as one half of the duo (the other being her husband Rahul Akerkar) behind iconic eateries like Indigo, Indigo Deli and Tote on the Turf. The entrepreneur is taking a hiatus from her culinary conquests for creative pursuits as she unveils her maiden jewellery collection with a preview at Ensemble, Kemps Corner, Mumbai. Vachani-Akerkar's eponymous brand, Malini Akerkar Design, already has her pursuing her passion for painting, interior styling and art deco-inspired semi-precious jewellery in its latest extension. Her penchant for vintage jewellery is a long-standing one, inherited early on from her mother. Her time as a student in London also contributed to this love, as she often scoured flea markets for unique vintage finds. “This was further cemented when, 25 years ago, Rahul (Akerkar) proposed to me with a stunning antique art deco ring that belonged to his German great grandmother,” recalls Vachani-Akerkar. Over the years, Vachani-Akerkar has been collecting art deco furniture, art and fashion with fervour. “But I found myself wanting whenever I hunted for art deco jewellery. So two years ago, I started researching jewellery from the era, which I have now revived with my line,” she explains. The semi-precious range of jewellery is equal parts accessible and affordable, and features earrings, pendants, necklaces, bracelets and rings using semi-precious and hydrothermal gemstones, and high quality Swarovski stones set in silver and white gold alloys. “We lave laid immense focus on the handicraft value and aesthetic sensibility of the pieces. They are timeless heirloom collectibles that can be passed down for generations,” says Vachani-Akerkar. Driving this point home is the campaign featuring three generations of women who have played a part in inspiring the jewellery—Jinx Akerkar (Malini's mother-in-law), Radhika Vachani (her sister), Avantika Akerkar (her sister-in-law), Shaan and Amalia Akerkar (her teenage daughters), and Nida Merchant (her friend). Age and occasion are no bars for the designer. Each piece from her launch collection is bound to resonate with well-travelled multifaceted women, who will be able to style these classic designs for a versatile roster of events ranging from dinner parties to destination weddings. column1: Kangana Ranaut talks about the Indian ethnic look she’s most partial to
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The actor, who is the brand new face of Global Desi, on her favourite picks for the festive season Global Desi's new collection is titled #GypsyHeart, and as the name suggests, channels a bohemian aesthetic. Designed for a free-thinking woman, this line features a unique take on basic ethnic wear, showcasing a mix of dresses, jumpsuits, skirts, tops and jackets in shades of blues and reds, with a touch of pastels. Also on offer are bags, footwear, sunglasses and jewellery that complement the garments. But that's not the only news Global Desi has to share with us. Debuting this line is the new face of the brand, Kangana Ranaut. We chat with the actor to find out everything about her new association with Anita Dongre and Global Desi. It feels amazing, as Global Desi has always been one of my favourite brands. Before becoming the muse of her brand, the first time I met Anita Dongre, I told her to keep certain pieces for me. I am delighted to be a part of this campaign as it is such a lively, young and vibrant brand. It is a privilege to be the face of their new campaign. I think Anita Dongre's philosophy and her interpretation of Indian wear is outstanding. She makes comfortable and elegant ethnic wear accessible for young and independent women like us, who find it difficult to wear Indian clothes in everyday life. There are some versatile pieces in this collection. For example, I have never worn a dhoti sari or a sari-pants hybrid in my entire life. I wore it for the first time and I have to say it is super comfortable. I also love the way Anita gives a personal touch to all her pieces. It's very youthful, independent and vibrant in nature. More than that, they're pieces that you would want to wear every day. From going shopping to attending a meeting, it's perfect for all occasions. You can even do yoga in some of the pieces from the new collection. My favourite festive trend is a lehenga skirt. Usually you can't move around while you are wearing a heavy lehenga, but the lehenga skirt that is a part of their new collection is so fuss-free that you can wear it for any festive occasion, and feel comfortable in it. My personal style is very bohemian in spirit, exactly what Global Desi stands for. It is the perfect representation of today's generation and their wild thoughts. We don't belong to any place but [to] the globe, the entire world. So you can wear this dress and land anywhere in the world and you will be the centre of attraction because of your individuality, [and] at the same time your openness to what the world is today. column1: TheLabelLife.com opens its first brick and mortar store in Mumbai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And there are more in the pipeline When it launched in 2012, homegrown lifestyle brand TheLabelLife.com instantly stood out for its one-of-a-kind concept of collections curated by their celebrity style editors Sussanne Khan, Malaika Arora and Bipasha Basu. Over the past six years, the one stop shop has become the go-to for a handpicked selection of fashion, statement accessories, home decor and limited edition capsule lines. After hosting a series of countrywide pop-ins since 2016 and offering at-home trials to patrons in Mumbai, the brand has now fully committed to an offline presence with their first ever store in Bandra, Mumbai. “When we first started out, the plan was to remain strictly online. But we are a consumer-first brand. It became clear that our shoppers were keen to touch and feel the products before making their purchase. As we scaled, it became important to establish a physical connect, so here we are. column1: How basket bags became 2018’s hottest accessory
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue examines the holiday staple that became a high-fashion item The woven bag may once have been an accessory for the beach or market only, but in 2018, fashion has taken it into every arena. The straw and raffia pieces we're seeing on celebrities and office workers alike this summer are not only holdalls into which you can chuck a bottle of sunscreen or a loaf of bread, but chic, embellished totes, rattan clutches and elaborate cross-body pouches. These bags have evolved from quirky holiday buys to high-fashion investments, with price points to match: Mark Cross's structured wicker bags have leather frames and gold-plated brass hardware, and cost around £1,700, while Gucci's striped raffia beach tote costs £875. The shopping appetite around them has reached fever pitch: according to the global fashion search engine Lyst, searches including the terms “straw”, “raffia” and “wicker” are up 56 per cent year-on-year as we all seek to buy into the trend. Luxury retailer Matchesfashion.com reports that sales have increased, and at Pinterest, there were 573 per cent more saves of woven handbags over the last year than there had been the year before. The art of weaving bags from natural materials—dried grass or bamboo, for example—is millennia-old, with basketry techniques dating back at least to ancient Egypt. It was in the 1950s, though, that the straw tote came to be seen as a stylish item associated with luxurious travel, sold in holiday destinations as a chic souvenir. In London, The Eaton Bag Company purveyed desirable raffia bags and woven trunks, while across the Atlantic, cane bags woven in Nantucket became a vacation status symbol for wealthy Americans. Audrey Hepburn, who lived in Holland and Belgium as a child, often carried a basket. But wicker's most enduring style moment came in the late 1960s and 1970s, when actress and singer Jane Birkin—later associated with the Hermès Birkin—made a picnic basket her signature accessory when she was out and about in Paris, Cannes and London. She didn't know it then, but she was planting the seed for a million Instagram #inspo posts. In 2018, it's not just basic baskets that have caught our imagination. The most popular brands this season are the most imaginative. They include Cult Gaia, whose cage-like bamboo bags have been carried by Jessica Alba and Chrissy Teigen, and Heimat Atlantica, which offers colourful, reed-woven cases with porcelain embellishments. Serpui uses straw in highly saturated hues to make evening clutches, some of which are embroidered with tropical flowers and birds, while Sophie Anderson turns raffia and toquilla straw into spherical cross-body bags and Ulla Johnson's lantern-like Tautou design is currently the most viewed straw bag on Lyst. Major fashion houses have joined the fray too: at Matchesfashion.com, Loewe's relaxed totes were a sell-out in the spring, while Balenciaga's striped Panier has sold steadily. Should you prefer to channel Birkin's dreamy style, Etsy and eBay are full of vintage and second-hand options with a Provençal market vibe—a glamorous European lifestyle is entirely optional. column1: Riccardo Tisci revives historic Burberry logo
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's what has changed   With anticipation mounting ahead of Riccardo Tisci's Burberry debut at London Fashion Week in September, the Italian designer has unveiled his first major overhaul of the British house: the logo. Tisci, who took up the role of chief creative officer in May, revealed the new logo and monogram, which uses founder Thomas Burberry's initials “TB” interlocked in white and orange over a honeyed background, on Instagram. The social posts show a series of emails between himself and British art director and graphic designer Peter Saville, who was commissioned by Raf Simons last year to re-design the Calvin Klein logo. The exchange signified that the logo was inspired by Tisci's archive research and a particular 1908 Thomas Burberry monogram that felt contemporary to him. Saville, who was given four weeks to complete the project, championed red and honey as a strong combination. A conversation between #PeterSaville and #RiccardoTisci A post shared by  Burberry (@burberry) on Aug 2, 2018 at 2:29am PDT The new brand identity will be used on all channels and in all advertising campaigns from today, in a landmark shift since Burberry's last logo change 20 years ago when the "S" dropped from its name. The London Fashion Week showcase will also see Tisci put his new product strategy in place. He will release a limited-edition capsule collection as part of his first ready-to-wear offering in order to build on its see-now-buy-now model, and keep the delivery cycle dynamic and fresh. Burberry's collaboration with Dame Vivienne Westwood will follow in December. This article previously appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why it’s time to reconsider cycling shorts
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The classic piece of sports-cum-streetwear made iconic by Princess Diana in the 1990s is now being worn by everyone from Kim Kardashian West to Bella Hadid. Vogue talks you through this summer’s must-wear trend It may or may not have escaped your notice that shorts are big news this season and none more so than the skin-tight, saddle-ready styles of the late 1980s and early 1990s. Now worn with statement slides or heels for maximum impact, cycling shorts are the versatile, sleek tomboy alternative to feminine skirts and dresses—and they are this summer's new cool-girl staple. While some may yet to be convinced, pedal pushers have been quietly making a comeback ever since Karl Lagerfeld layered skinny tweed and embellished shorts under skirts and dresses in his autumn 2014 Chanel couture show. The trend has since picked up pace with Alexander Wang, Dion Lee, Dolce & Gabbana and Off-White all breathing new life into the forgotten sportswear classic for spring/summer 2018. At Off-White, Naomi Campbell closed the show wearing sporty ivory bike shorts and an asymmetric white jacket in a homage to Princess Diana, who made the look iconic some two decades ago. Elsewhere, cycling shorts were seen at Saint Laurent where Anthony Vaccarello's delicate lace iterations formed part of a catsuit with peplum, taking the shorts into more feminine territory. On the ground, street-style stars such as Kim Kardashian West and Bella Hadid were early adopters—Kardashian West wore her glute-huggers with a ubiquitous strappy heel well before the trend hit the masses. At Cannes Film Festival this year, Hadid's affinity for early noughties styling—think cropped tees and slinky party tops worn with metallic leather shorts—helped make over-the-knee shorts a viable piece of partywear. From striped go-faster Lycra styles worn with oversized shirts to more minimal all-black shorts paired with synched blazers or statement knits, micro-leggings are an easy styling win that just happen to also be extremely comfortable. Still not convinced? Opt for shorts in a slightly longer length (closer to the knee) and experiment by layering a body-con shorts under skirts to reacquaint yourself with the thigh-skimmers before going full-frontal. But whatever style direction you take, cycle shorts are this summer's sleekest wardrobe update. Take your lead from the women already feeling the pedal power, below. column1: We’ve guessed your personality based on the shoes you own
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We see you, chunky sneaker   Your shoe wardrobe can say a lot about you as a person. From the trends you like to pick up on, to the colours you choose and the styles that resonate with you, there's so much to be gleaned from a peek inside the shoe rack of a stranger. Don't believe us? Take a look at your own footwear collection and answer us this: why wouldn't you want to be defined by your shoes. Whether it's the edgy black boot that screams ‘I'm a badass!' to the dainty pumps that bring a serious touch of femininity to your weekday wardrobe, a look at your shoes is like a look inside the inner workings of a soul. Take notes, ladies. You don't shy away from a trend, embracing everything and anything that the shows throw at us. You trawl Pinterest for the perfect outfit and don't get offended when people tell you you're ‘fashion obsessed'. It's not a bad thing, right? You might work in a corporate office but you want everyone to know you subscribe to Vogue. You know there's nothing worse than ruined suede, so your shoe choices reflect an all-weather approach. You know that the best trends are the ones that confuse your parents the most. You've realised there's more to life than heels, and prefer to get ahead of the rest by embracing the kitten heel—which might confuse your boyfriend, but it puts you miles ahead with the fashion set. Potentially a long lost member of the Versace family, you prefer prints over, well, anything else, and take your martinis dirty, thank you very much. [#image: /photos/5ce42e0cb40d26aadad6cd72]||| ||| Image: Getty You're no-nonsense and straight forward, a good planner with an eye for detail—and maybe a Virgo or Pisces? You'd prefer to be out all night and wake up at midday than go to sleep on time, because life's too short for early bedtimes and flat shoes. You know there's nothing better than vintage Vivienne Westwood and a Dior slogan T-shirt is on your birthday list. Just like this niche buy, you're not afraid to make a statement with your footwear or in your life. Watch out, everyone—you mean business. Some may say you have two personalities, naughty and nice, but we disagree: you've just got a lot to offer. column1: Pop icon Madonna talks about being a soccer mom
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Her new life in Lisbon and what she wants her children to be “My son David has wanted to play soccer professionally for years [and] I've been desperate to get him into the best academies with the best coaches...I felt it was a good time [to move and to make] a change. And I wanted to get out of America for a minute – as you know, this is not America's finest hour.” "I've just met lots of really amazing musicians, and I've ended up working with a lot of these musicians on my new record. Lisbon has influenced my music and my work. How could it not? I don't see how I could have gone through that year without being informed by all this input of culture." “Any woman who is a soccer mom could say it kind of requires you to have no life in a way, because things change from week to week and games change from weekend to weekend. It's impossible to make plans, and then you feel like you're not being fair to your other kids, or being fair to me!” “A lot of people say to me, ‘You must really want your son to be a successful soccer player, your oldest daughter [Lourdes] to be a dancer, Rocco to be a painter.' And I always say no, what I want my children to be is loving, compassionate, responsible human beings. That's all I want.” “I don't care what the vehicle is, I just want them to be good human beings that treat other human beings with dignity and respect, regardless of skin colour, religion, gender. This is the most important thing, you know what I mean? If they happen to be the next Picasso or Cristiano Ronaldo, then great, that's just the cherry on the cake.” View Gallery 8 Photos Madonna- Vogue Italia August Issue Text courtesy of Vogue Italia What's New Culture & Living Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Farah Khan Ali is all set to launch her debut lifestyle collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Just in time for gifting season As a jewellery designer whose work is favoured by Bollywood's glitterati, Farah Khan Ali is no stranger to bling—she's leveraged its charm with a subtle touch of femininity in her design narrative from the get go. The launch of the new collection heralds the expansion of her creative domain into Farah Khan World, a luxury lifestyle destination with its sights set on the customised wedding space. “I believe that the need of the moment right now in the world of gifting is designing experiences. With our new offering, we are now looking at designing the entire wedding experience for the bride, covering every detail from the invitations to jewellery essentials for every function as well as the trousseau, hampers and wedding giveaways,” explains the designer. For those looking to play the perfect hostess, Khan Ali has something in mind as well: the collection includes two fine bone china collections comprising of an elaborate range of gilded crockery. column1: Fashion designers are finding new ways to reduce your plastic waste
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Taking sustainable fashion to the next level Are plastic straws the new cigarettes? Maybe that's a little extreme, but in the week or so since Starbucks, American Airlines and the entire city of Seattle announced that they're going straw-free, those little plastic tubes have begun to feel like a dirty habit. (Our own cafeteria here at One World Trade Center has gone strawless, too.) It's serendipitous timing, considering we're at the height of summer—ie, peak cold-brew season. Our Instagram feeds have become an endless scroll of friends showing off their new no-plastic-straw lifestyles, either by drinking their coffee through a reusable (and chic!) copper straw, or by sipping it the old-fashioned way. Ditching your straw is a small victory you can feel good about, and it's greatly heightened awareness of plastic waste in general. Straws are a serious offender because they're single-use (plastic utensils are also a culprit) and according to For a Strawless Ocean, most straws are too lightweight to make it through a mechanical recycling sorter, so they slip through the cracks and contaminate recycling loads or end up in a landfill, where they won't break down. Ultimately, millions of discarded straws and other pieces of plastic end up in the ocean, where they've severely harmed wildlife. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation writes that at this rate, the oceans could contain more plastic than sea life by 2050. Fixing the problem clearly goes way beyond your morning cup. On a big-picture scale, companies need to start using less plastic in general, but what about all of that plastic floating around the ocean? Several designers are addressing it with new technology that's turning ocean plastic into fabric: Adidas and Stella McCartney have partnered with Parley for the Oceans on shoes, clothing and accessories in a special yarn comprised of Parley Ocean Plastic, which is upcycled waste found on the beach. Then there's Girlfriend Collective, an indie athletic brand dedicated to sustainability: each pair of compression leggings repurposes 25 water bottles; its T-shirts are made from 100 percent Cupro, a natural byproduct of the woodcutting industry; and its dyes are eco-friendly. Girlfriend's latest release, the Lite legging, is made with Econyl, a fabric by the Italian company Aquafil comprised of discarded nylon fishing nets found in the ocean. To feel the leggings, you'd never know they were made of trash; they're sleek, stretchy, and super soft—and as a bonus, they're extremely light and moisture-wicking, which makes them ideal for hot days. On the site, the product description cheekily reads: “Lite was made for all those heated workouts like hot yoga, cycling and picking up trash on the beach.” The Lite leggings were a year and a half in the making, so it's something of a coincidence that they're launching in tandem with the straw ban. But they were first and foremost designed as a response to Girlfriend's shoppers asking for thinner, lighter leggings: “We had so many customers who loved the softness, thickness, compression, and support they got from our first leggings, and they wanted a product with the same [qualities] but in a lighter weight,” cofounder Quang Dinh tells Vogue. “From that feedback, we went through the same rigorous product development cycle that we used on our first legging and were finally able to come out with something that we're proud of.” Girlfriend will be introducing bodysuits and sports bras in the Econyl fabric, too. Swimwear designers are also using Econyl and other recycled-plastic materials, including Araks Yeramyan; Tropic of C's Candice Swanepoel; Vitamin A's Amahlia Stevens; and Mara Hoffman, who uses Econyl as well as Repreve. There's a reason these fabrics are mainly popular with athletic and swim brands: They're sleek, techy, and quick-drying, so they're well suited to body-conscious performance pieces, but few designers are testing recycled plastic fabrics in ready-to-wear, too: Maggie Marilyn's Resort 2019 collection included a full, pleated white skirt made from 100 percent recycled plastic water bottles. Similarly, Svilu's Marina Polo and Britt Cosgrove developed a taffeta with post-consumer bottles, which has a silky, semi-stiff finish on their Vestry dress. (Then, of course, there's Stella McCartney, who has been moving the needle in her ready-to-wear line with glue-less sneakers, recycled nylon fibers, and a new, non-PVC material she developed for clear “Lucite” shoes.) Gabriela Hearst is rethinking plastic waste in another way: shipping. She recently swapped out her plastic packaging for compostable Tipa bags, which biodegrade in 24 weeks (as opposed to 500-plus years, which is how long it can take plastic to do the same). That may not be the sexiest talking point, but we can't think of many other designers who are analyzing their impact quite so closely. In a few years, we have a feeling plastic hangers, price tags, and buttons will be next to go. When your wear something by Falguni and Shane, it makes you feel sexy, and I think that's why women love their clothes so much,” she said about the designers. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Festive season inspiration We are firm believers of the fact that there's a sari for each occasion. Whether it is a wedding reception, cocktail, sangeet, puja or even a celebratory dinner that you have pencilled into your little black book, saris make for a compelling wardrobe choice. column1: Inside designer Rahul Mishra’s collection at India Couture Week 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A study of visual history and connections was the driving thought this season Perhaps one of the more surprising things about Rahul Mishra's show was that it was one of the few showcases at India Couture Week 2018 that forwent the use of a showstopper. The scene before the start of the show was idyllic—the designer and his team were set up well ahead of their time slot, the main show area was covered in foliage, the clothes were steamed and the models were completely at ease—if you're a regular at fashion week, you know this is not a regular phenomenon. Backstage, Mishra got into the details of the title of his collection, ‘Maraasim'. “In Urdu, Maraasim means relationships. I tried to look back at connections between the past and present. How what was once considered beautiful still affects us. There was also a thought about how the indoors is connected to the outdoors,” he explained. Mishra is known to go heavy on the research with his work. For this season, the designer deep dived into a study of visual history starting from when the Mughals invaded India. “I thought about this contradictory time in history when the Mughals arrived and the cross-pollination of ideas that took place because of it,” he explains. “They brought in geometry from Persia when we're all about natural forms and the resulting design exploration that it brought about in our structures. Similarly some of the earlier miniature paintings bore a resemblance to Pichwai paintings.” It's clear—a myriad of what remains of the visual cultural history from late 16th and 17th centuries took over Mishra's moodboard for his latest collection. These references translated to stunning garments on the runway that  were meticulously laboured over for five months; some even took nearly 4,000 hours in production. For visual cues, Mishra looked at one piece of architecture in particular—The Tomb of Asif Khan in Lahore, Pakistan, which was commissioned by Emperor Shah Jahan. “The Taj Mahal is the showstopper, so no one looks at this tomb,” he jokes. The story behind how the collection came about may be compelling, but what's most endearing about Mishra's narrative are the clothes themselves. With or without the knowledge of his references, you would still fall for them. The lineup went from soft pastels to ivory and a few pops of colour like sunset orange and bold red. Chanderi, organza, chikankari embroidery, signature 3D appliqué, resham threadwork all sat comfortably next to each other. There was something for everyone here—cocktail dresses, light saris, kurtas worn over lehengas and of course, bridal lehengas. In what was clearly a season of firsts, the designer used Swarovski crystals in the most understated way to add sparkle to his clothing—an addition that Rahul Mishra brides would be happy with. And keeping with the theme of innovation, the designer debuted menswear this season as well. At the close of the show, the names announced were Rahul and Divya Mishra. Other than being the founder and director at Rahul Mishra, Divya, the designer's spouse, has been his aid, confidante and support system since the inception of the label, and he didn't want his wife's work to unnoticed. “She does so much here; we are nothing without her,” he says. Needless to say, the audience clapped even harder out of respect at the show. For a collection about relationships, this truly did make for the most befitting end. column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan walks for Falguni Shane Peacock’s couture 2018 show
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All eyes on the runway To say that the Falguni Shane Peacock show at India Couture Week 2018 was high on shine would be something of an understatement. Aside from the liberal use of crystals on all of the garments, there's was sparkle everywhere—from the argent lids of the models to the glitter on the ramp that inadvertently caused the audience members also to be covered in tiny flecks of shimmer. Models posed on the many crescent moons on the runway, and then there was Kareena Kapoor Khan, the star of the evening. Falguni and Shane Peacock have carved their niche in the market as India's answer to an ultra glamorous, red carpet-worthy label. Sure enough, they have no dearth of admirers internationally: the latest feather in their proverbial cap is a custom created gown for none other than Beyoncé. Last night, the designer duo brought that hard-to-look-away-from quality on the runway. There were no elaborate tales spun around inspiration—it's clear that their USP is to offer the audience what is of the moment and what can provide confidence to the wearer. While gowns dominated the lineup, we saw a few lehengas as well, along with a gown-salwar hybrid that wouldn't be out of place at a wedding. To balance the seasoned use of crystals in every formation and iteration, the designers maintained a restrained colour palette—the pastels were more washed-out water colour hues, the golds were duller and the crimsons, somber. And as is their signature, feather trims lent the perfect touch of exaggeration to nearly all of the looks, while crystal festooned veils and cut gloves added another layer of drama. In a surprising little accent, the models walked the ramp with Apple watches strapped on their wrists. The drama was only amplified when showstopper Kareena Kapoor Khan walked out in a glimmering, champagne-hued lehenga. “No one manages to mix Indian and western like them and I think that's what sets them apart,” she told us about the label after the show. “When I dress up, I look for something that's very high on glamour. When your wear something by Falguni and Shane, it makes you feel sexy, and I think that's why women love their clothes so much.” All said and done, you simply can't deny the hold Falguni Shane Peacock has on maximalist stars, here or anywhere else in the world. column1: 9 ways the fashion industry embraced inclusivity in 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It’s the dawn of a new age There's no denying that, in its long and prominent history, the fashion industry has more often than not represented one standard of beauty. From catwalks to advertising campaigns, brands in days past have typically veered towards models of a typical build, age and ethnicity—but we all know the world is a much richer tapestry. However, in recent years, the industry has been doing more to champion diversity, and 2018 in particular has seen a much more inclusive approach to representation. Here, we've rounded up some of the most noteworthy moments that symbolise how inclusivity has become more of a norm, not a buzzword, this year. The Sudanese-Australian model made history this month, after she became the second-ever model of colour to make a final stroll down the runway at the French maison's fall 2018 show. Akech Bior was handpicked by Karl Lagerfeld as his ‘Chanel bride' of the season, joining the ranks of models selected for the spot in collections past, including Cara Delevingne, Luna Bijl and Alek Wek. The latter was the first model of colour to close Chanel's haute couture show, back in 2004. Eighteen-year-old Akech Bior also opened Chanel's Cruise show earlier this year, though admitted her turn at the Couture display was her “proudest achievement.” “No matter who you are, where you come from or what you have, as long as you have a dream it is achievable,” she wrote on Instagram following the show. “Put in hard work, give it your all, stay dedicated, determined and most importantly, never give up, because you will make that dream a reality at some point.” Another French heritage house closed its fall 2018 Couture show with a model of colour—in this case Indira Scott for Christian Dior. Even more noteworthy was the model's locks, an often unrepresented hairstyle on the catwalk. Scott's dreads were accessorised with wooden beads, the neutral shades playing off the muted, grey-mauve gown. The model later revealed she cried after closing the Dior show, thanking artistic director Maria Grazia Chiuri on Instagram for “believing in her”. The Italian fashion house brought together tens of models for its recently unveiled fall 2018 campaign, which the brand claims is the “longest-ever advertising image”. Among the famous faces that took part were half-Palestinian catwalk stars Bella and Gigi Hadid, Nora Attal and Egyptian-Moroccan model Imaan Hammam, as well as Kaia Gerber, Stella Maxwell and Adut Akech Bior. Using models of colour and women embracing their curls (we're looking at you, Imaan), Versace said the 54-model-strong campaign “symbolised inclusivity, a key value for artistic director Donatella Versace and her vision for the brand”. “The longest Versace line-up is made up of a mega mix of personalities—from supermodels to young new talent in looks that are all about confidence,” the brand added on Instagram. Several labels have made roads in expanding representation in their collections in recent seasons—most notably Tommy Hilfiger and Asos, both of which this year broadened their accessible clothing offerings. Giant e-tailer Asos partnered with BBC reporter Chloe Ball-Hopkins to design a tie-dyed jumpsuit, created especially with wheelchair users in mind (think waterproof, versatile, and with a longer hem at the back). US label Hilfiger also unveiled a disability-friendly line named Tommy Adaptive, which includes a range of pieces crafted with adjustable details and easy-use fastenings. The campaign for the line brought together a diverse range of models, from US Paralympian track star Jeremy Campbell, to motivational speaker Mama Caxx, who has a prosthetic limb. According to The Fashion Spot, Spring 2018's fashion campaigns were the most inclusive to date, with 34 per cent of models used representing women of colour. The report looked at 218 campaigns starring 541 models in total, with the results increasing 1.2 per cent from its fall 2017 report. Models such as Haiti's Aube Jolicoeur and South Sudan's Shanelle Nyasiase were among those who featured prominently in campaigns, the site reported. Indian supermodel Laxmi Menon is a part of COS's autumn/winter 2018 campaign. For July/August 2018, Vogue Arabia enlisted not one, but two voluptuous models for their front cover—Ashley Graham and Paloma Elsesser. The runway stars also documented their journeys to self-love in an accompanying interview, with Graham, the tenth highest-paid model in the world, opening up about how her body-positive message might just be her “destiny.” “My mother told me that when I walked into a room, I would greet every single person—even at three years old,” the model said. “It was more of an emotion that I would give people, and it would leave them feeling good about who they are. I think that's what I'm doing today; letting women know that they are worthy, that they are beautiful, and that they can be happy with who they are in their skin.” Following in Naomi Campbell's footsteps might be an overwhelming prospect for some, but this 19-year-old model took it in her stride. The Egyptian-born American became the first black model to open a Prada show in 20 years when she stepped out onto the Fall 2018 catwalk in February, the first model of colour to do so since Campbell in 1997. “It was an honour and I'm proud that I was the one chosen to open, but this is bigger than me. Me opening for one of the top fashion houses is a statement to the world—especially for black women—that their beauty is something that deserves to be celebrated,” Yai told Vogue UK of the moment. For fall 2018, the Lebanese designer called upon Maria Borges and Cindy Bruna to lead his finale, with the two strutting down the catwalk side by side, wearing complementary gold and silver beaded gowns. After decades of women of colour getting no representation on the runway, seeing two close a show together made a powerful statement. Years after she was released from her contract with the beauty brand for being too old at age 43, Lancôme put the now-65-year-old actor front and centre of its 2018 adverts. The Italian star was first resigned with the cosmetics and skincare label in 2015, but only started appearing in campaign imagery again earlier this year. “They told me they needed somebody younger. The advertising was aspirational, and even though they have clients of many ages, the desire was for youth,” Rossellini told The Cut of being let go. Her 2018 adverts, shot by Peter Lindbergh, are refreshingly unretouched, and just one of several beauty brand adverts in recent years to use models representing the over 60s (think Charlotte Rampling for NARS). “It's wonderful to be back, to be a part of women's emancipation, and I just happen to represent it through Lancôme,” the star told Vanity Fair. column1: Etsy makes its way to India’s untapped community of local entrepreneurs
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion What does this mean for their businesses? Etsy.com is a true-blue hipster's paradise. Whether you're on the lookout for vintage lace, handmade bowls or a unique engagement ring, this online global marketplace can be a treasure trove for all the  knick knacks you didn't even know you needed. It wouldn't be too far off to say that anything Pinterest presents, Etsy can help you manifest. Founded in Brooklyn in 2005, Etsy now generates 3.25 billion dollars in sales. It also offers sellers personal storefronts and with a small fee, allows people from all over the world to showcase their wares on a global platform. If you're an Indian entrepreneur, we've got good news for you. The e-commerce website has now set up a team in New Delhi to bring local businesses to an international audience. This not only offers sellers the opportunity to grow their business, but will help create an authentic marketplace for Indian handicrafts that is easily accessible. Naturally, this shift in the market should also encourage craftsmen to continue their family trades, instead of being forced to choose non-traditional professions to make ends meet. This could also help budding artists and designers to set up their own trades with minimal investment. In order to get the ball rolling, Etsy has planned a series to recruit and assist new sellers online and offline, which includes offering free listings and incentives to all new sellers in India on the platform. column1: Pernia Qureshi’s online Pop-Up Shop makes its brick-and-mortar debut
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Keep your wallets ready When entrepreneur Pernia Qureshi launched her e-commerce store Perniaspopupshop.com in 2012, she ushered in a new chapter in India's fashion retail-scape. Ever since, the one-stop shop has continued to raise the bar, be it by shining the spotlight on promising homegrown designers or by hosting shopping festivals in the metropolises of Mumbai and New Delhi. Now, Qureshi is all set to elevate the brand's offline presence with the launch of their first-ever flagship store, Pernia's Pop-Up Studio, in Mumbai. “This is one of our biggest markets online, so it only made sense to give our customers a physical store experience as well. Mumbai is a fashion-conscious and cosmopolitan city with great potential to reach new patrons,” she says. Located in the suburban district of Juhu, the 1,500sqft space is all about creating a tailored shopping experience that is integrated with their e-store. Shoppers can browse their website via in-store touchscreen kiosks to explore collections beyond the curated mix of industry veterans and upcoming designers housed in the studio. “Most of our collections are trans-seasonal, but the focus is on Indo-western styles with a festive flair this season. In the true spirit of pop-ups, our designer selections will change every week. Dhruv Kapoor, Nishka Lulla, Pernia Qureshi label, Pallavi Jaipur, Pink Peacock Couture, Samant Chauhan and Eurumme are some of the labels one can find here,” adds Qureshi. Pernia's Pop-Up Studio's lounge section will focus on personal styling consultations while Qureshi's top picks of the month are also showcased on a dedicated shelf. column1: Tarun Tahiliani opens India Couture Week 2018 with Aditi Rao Hydari
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All the action you missed from last night Tarun Tahiliani is more than a veteran on his home turf as he arrives on the sets of his couture show in New Delhi; he is something of a presence. With his calm confidence and a keen eye for detail—both byproducts of having spent years perfecting his craft—Tahiliani commands the best from his people without having to say so explicitly. Everything is in order for the opening show of India Couture Week 2018—a rarity when backstage is normally a pandemonium of 40-plus models, choreographers, hair and makeup teams, helpers, jewellers and cameramen, all fighting for room. Last evening, the designer presented his couture line for the year, titled ‘In Elysium'. Homer's understanding of Elysium was that of a paradise, and if you were a bride shopping for a wedding, Tahiliani's lineup would evoke something similar. For some time now, he has been working on making wedding wear that is lighter in weight, in an attempt to ensure that brides are not weighed down during the celebrations. “As I get older,” he says, “I become clearer about what it is to be Indian and modern, which is the basis of my line.” Starting with tones of beige and black, the collection offered occasion wear options for cocktail dressing. Lighter dresses, anarkalis and pre-draped saris dominated the runway, and heavy embroidery was replaced with Swarovski crystals in colour. This season, the designer also employed lace edgings that bore Swarovski crystals, making the garments glimmer under the lights. The fact that blush pink is every bride's go-to colour for the year 2018, no one can deny. Last year, Tahiliani closed his couture show with a lehenga in the hue, with an off-shoulder blouse and a dramatic veil. This season too, saw iterations of that gasp-eliciting look in lighter forms that could be worn by the sister of the bride, or even a more restrained bride herself. Of course, there were options for the client who places value on larger-than-life volume and a sense of theatre in couture. From hand appliquéd tulle lehengas to the kinds that come heavily embroidered in zari, Tahiliani made sure he catered to the expectations of every kind of bride. If one had to place a bet on the styles that would fill up your social media feeds come wedding season, gossamer veils and sheer blouses would rank high. As the show reached its point of culmination, Aditi Rao Hydari walked out in lehenga that encapsulated the mood—in soft pink, dripping in crystals and pearls, with a touch of feathers and an ombré veil, paired with an off-shoulder tulle blouse. Earlier, backstage, Tahiliani had described the tone of the evening as “weightless, finesse and extravagance,” which Rao Hydari seemed to agree with. “It felt ethereal,” she said, to sum up the experience. Couture in India is about creating a timeless moment that stays in the viewers' minds, and is more often equated with bridal wear. In that vein, the show was set against a stunning backdrop—Tahiliani's set resembled a 3D printed skeleton of a palace. Strings of jasmine hung from the ceiling. “Sway your hips, make eye contact,” were the directions being fired by choreographers at the rehearsal. Model Laxmi Rana was made to give a demonstration of the ideal walk to the younger girls, while Noyonika Chatterjee opened a sequence during the show. Such was the combination of her stage presence, the pulsating lights and the sparkle of the clothes that for a moment, you could find yourself transported to a make-believe Elysium. Once the show had ended, Tahiliani celebrated Chatterjee's 30th year in the industry with some ceremonial cake cutting. You have to give it to Tahiliani—it's hard not to enjoy working with him. column1: 6 women of Indian origin who are carving out their own design niche
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From the West Midlands to West Hollywood, from ready-to-wear to layettes—these Indian-origin women are creating distinct identities in design across the world. “Hensely provided me with the independence and experience in a new country where I didn't know anyone in the industry, where I had to find my own expression and individuality,” says Neha Kapur Nayyar, once a Delhi-based model who moved to Los Angeles following her marriage to The Big Bang Theory's Kunal Nayyar. For the former beauty queen, designing was a natural transition. “Aesthetics are important in every individual. Mine are derived from travel, books, art. My style is in a neutral palette, and I enjoy adding an element of surprise.” The label got picked up exclusively by Moda Operandi in its first season itself and has now expanded to more retailers. “The idea of making a tool for the woman who doesn't need assurance, is unapologetically curious, and has a key sense of luxury—that is the intention.” Her influences range from actor Leela Naidu to artist Marina Abramović and interiors expert Ashley Hicks. “Hensely is about the all-encompassing life of a woman,” she explains. Hensely.com 1 It may be only three years old, but childrenswear label Blu & Blue comes from a 35-year denim heritage. For Aaina Jain Malik, her family's clothing business drew her back into the manufacturing fold following stints at Estée Lauder, Jo Malone London and Gap. Late parenthood and, as a result, more disposable income, greater awareness in children and the need for good-quality, functional and fashionable clothing are resulting in a burgeoning childrenswear market, believes Malik. “With Blu and Blue, I'm inspired to do denim right. We are constantly coming up with new ideas, fabrics and design techniques in our collections that are great and comfortable for children,” she says. Bluandblue.com 1 For grandmother Usha Doshi, her role at COS (the sleek, affordable label that Vogue editors love) was meant to be temporary, but 11 years later she's still an important contributor to the label's signature brand of minimalism. My story: “I was born and raised in a small village in Kenya. My first introduction to pattern-cutting was when I studied dressmaking and embroidery at college. At 18, I started my own business, at first making childrenswear and then moving to women's garments. I moved to the UK with my family in 1969 and I spent the early years here focused on raising my children but still working on the side. In 1986, I joined the Royal College of Art and spent over 20 years there as senior technician in the fashion department. I am now a Fellow of the RCA and have been privileged enough to work with some incredible designers during their formative years. I have worked in the design studio at COS since its inception in 2007. It was meant to be a temporary role but now, 11 years later, here I am! I'm passionate about the work I do, in particular the draping techniques that I have championed and feature in my co-authored book Creating With Shapes (2017). ” My book: “Funnily enough, my granddaughters inspired the technique that is featured in the book. I gave them fabric to play with and they cut out basic shapes like squares, triangles and circles. There were no rules or boundaries in the way they played with the fabric. The resulting forms were something I had never seen in my 40 years in the industry: the drapes were dramatic, practical and, most importantly, completely effortless. Thanks to the technical knowledge I've developed over the years, I was able to take this simple idea and create real, functional garments.” My wardrobe: “I like wearing simple designs, good-quality fabrics and clean cuts. When I am not working, I wear Indian styles as well. From COS, every woman should have a well-tailored coat, a comfortable casual shirt, and any item in a high-quality tactile fabric.” “We felt unfulfilled by the way the industry was pushing us to consume in an unthoughtful way. There was a lack of quality mid-range essentials for women,” says Shilpa Shah, one half of the duo behind the San Francisco-based Cuyana, whose philosophy is “of fewer, better”. Shah, who was born to Punjabi parents and raised in Los Angeles, credits her Indian heritage as the foundation of her work. “My love for textiles comes from growing up around the rich fabrics of Indian clothing. We wanted to make materials mean something again.” We asked Shah to tell us more. We are lucky to have created a company with an ethos that is sustainable and timeless. You can have amazing quality and curated design that is still accessible. Through Lean Closet, we've inspired women to rethink their approach to consumption and, in asking them to edit their closets, we've created an opportunity to provide clothing and other items to women in need. Donations made through our non-profit partner HEART have made a huge impact on the lives of many women. Heritage brands like Céline and Levi's as well as newer brands such as Sophie Buhai and Payal Singhal! Cuyana.com 1 The last few seasons, a British-Asian designer has been on the radar of fashion watchers. We sit down with Supriya Lele. “I grew up in the UK, in a small village called Meriden that is in the West Midlands. I then studied at Edinburgh University/Edinburgh College of Art for my BA, and then completed my MA at the Royal College of Art in London. I expressed an interest in art from an early age. I used to draw and paint and make clothes for my dolls. As I grew up, I experimented a lot with how I dressed and expressed myself that way. I studied architecture for just under a year before I switched to fashion—I was also really interested in sculpture. I think the three disciplines cross over a lot. My interest in architecture informs my minimalist aesthetic. My signatures are my use of drape and palette—I like to mix unusual colours. I subvert Indian codes through my work and create a hybrid of the two cultures that represent me: British and Indian. I try to keep things modern and contemporary in the design of the garments and use subtle codes to reflect upon my heritage. I visited India for the first time in a few years to see family and was inspired by the rapid development; how the landscape had changed so quickly. For S/S 2018, I interpreted visuals of Indian building sites as reference points, using printed and plasticised organzas, hot pink silk and blown-out florals, clashing the old and new.” Supriyalele.com 1 For the Chicago-based Monica Royer, the birth of her daughter was a seminal moment in more ways than one. Realising the lack of quality organic childrenswear in the market, Royer (whose brother Andy Dunn founded Bonobos) decided to take matters into her own hands. The result was Monica + Andy, a thoughtful childrenswear label with a strong digital presence and guideshops (as they call them) in Chicago and New York. “For me, after I had my daughter, there was no market that was more important. Her skin was so sensitive that I thought a lot about what went into the clothing that she wore,” says Royer, whose product range spans the spectrum of tulle dresses and homecoming blankets. The real product star, however, are the customised layettes—they take the stress out of baby-gifting and are perfect for new, harried mothers. The next few years are already planned for Royer. “I am excited to grow to more locations. Just opening the doors of our first guideshop was such a powerful experience. I love bringing together a community of moms wherever we are able to go,” she says about the milk-and-cookie bar in Chicago and the Mommy and Me classes they hold in both locations. But like every working mother, she's always trying to achieve that elusive balance. “It takes so much support. My parents live in the same condo building and they are a huge help, as is my husband and my brother. My mom is from Delhi but now most of our close family is in the States. I think you can have it all, but not necessarily all at once.” Monicaandandy.com 1 1 What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What Karisma Kapoor and Shilpa Shetty Kundra wore on 24/07/2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From casual looks to slinky dresses No matter the season, Bollywood's leading ladies love bringing out their festive Indian ethnic wear. column1: 5 ways in which jumpsuits test your commitment to fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The trendy silhouette might lend itself to multiple occasions, but there are some fundamental issues with the jumpsuit that nobody can seem to solve Jumpsuits have the rare ability to be sharp, elegant, occasion-appropriate, feminine and striking all at once. Though you may see them disappearing from trend charts from time to time, jumpsuits and playsuits have never really left the scene—they only keep coming back with bigger and better updates. At the fall/winter 2018 shows, we saw a gorgeous holographic jumpsuit with shoulder pads at Balmain, a powerful tailored silk jumpsuit at Fendi and a formal belted version at Philosophy di Lorenzo. While trends are always fun to try out, some tend to be more difficult to wear than others. Jumpsuits, especially, can make for tricky sartorial beasts to tame—if you've ever spent an entire Saturday night downing drinks and have been dressed in one, you'll know what we mean. We list down all the reasons why the jumpsuit tests the commitment of even the most fashion forward of us. On any given night, most women are well prepared. If it's a strapless dress, we've got our pins, tape and transparent straps to solve any problems that may crop up. If it's a chapped lipped situation, we've got our gloss. But if it's a jumpsuit and you need to use the bathroom, there is no fix. For starters, you need to take your entire outfit off—clearly not an ideal picture of elegance. And nor is it convenient, especially a few drinks down. When you're done, it's possible that you might need help slipping the jumpsuit back on. A stretchy fabric that will go back on as easily as it comes off, may offer some respite. Tall girls know the pain of finding a jumpsuit that does not leave them in an uncomfortable wedgie situation. Since most high street labels offer the single-piece garment in one size, the outfit becomes especially elusive to women with a longer torso. For shorter women, too, a standard piece may hang unattractively at the crotch. Make sure you pick one that works for your body type, otherwise you'll be uncomfortable all night. We're all for body positivity, but this silhouette may not be ideal for diverse body types. It clings to parts of the body that most women want hidden and can be very unflattering—pear shaped women may find themselves struggling with the fit at the hip, while women that are broader on top could become frustrated with the bust or the shape of the shoulders. Finding the perfect jumpsuit can be a bit of a hunt, but if you show some patience and try different fits, you could find ‘the one.' There are alternatives, of course—playsuits work great when you want to show off that narrow waist or those fit calves. But even they won't solve your bathroom woes. Few things can become as problematic as a zipper on a jumpsuit—it's hard to tug all the way up, and could even break on occasion. Zippers also make your outfit third-party dependent—you've got to bring a girlfriend along if you plan to wear a jumpsuit with them; after all, you don't want to have to ask a stranger to zip you up after a trip to the washroom. We'd suggest you wait a couple dates before you decide to unleash the jumpsuit. If you want to keep things mysterious and not go beyond second base, it can be a bit hard because this shape doesn't really allow for mystery. It's all or nothing with the jumpsuit, so choose wisely. A first date should have romance, dim lights, great food and wine and slow kissing, not the plight of you running to the bathroom and fighting to put on your jumpsuit for an indeterminable period. column1: Stormi Jenner’s stroller pushed this brand to the top of the world’s hottest
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A new report shows the global power of the Kardashian-Jenner effect Fendi has leapt into the world's ten hottest brands following months of high-profile love from the Kardashian-Jenners, according to the latest Lyst Index released exclusively to Vogue. In the second quarter of 2018, the Italian fashion house became the eighth most popular brand in the world, moving up from number 17 in the previous quarter. The highly influential Kylie Jenner can surely take some of the credit. In April she shared a picture with her 108 million Instagram followers, in which she wore a vintage Fendi dress and belt bag, and pushed baby Stormi in a pram plastered with the brand's logo. It's not the only celebrity boost that the Karl Lagerfeld-helmed label has enjoyed this year. On the cover for her April single Chun-Li, Nicki Minaj wore a Fendi fur jacket and logo-printed thong, and back in February, Kim Kardashian West shared an image of herself in matching monogrammed sheer tights, blouse and coat, posing for Odda Magazine. No surprise that those iconic Fs were one of this spring's most coveted logos. The Lyst Index, compiled by the global fashion search engine Lyst, is a quarterly ranking of more than five million shoppers a month across 12,000 designers and stores. It's based on a broad analysis of online shopping behaviour, including Google searches, Lyst page views and searches, wishlist saves and purchases. Another key finding? Italian brands are some of the strongest in the world right now, holding five of the ten slots. Versace, in particular, is rising up the ranks—from 21st place in the first quarter of the year to seventh place for April to June. The jump can most likely be traced back to the Catholicism-themed Met Gala in May—Donatella Versace co-hosted the event and the house dressed Gigi Hadid, Kim Kardashian West, Katy Perry, Blake Lively, Gisele Bündchen, Mary J Blige and Cindy Crawford. Brand awareness may also have been boosted by store expansions, a slew of big-name magazine covers featuring the spring/summer 2018 collection (including British Vogue and Vogue Japan), and The Assassination of Gianni Versace: American Crime Story, an unauthorised TV drama that aired earlier this year. Gucci enjoyed a prosperous second quarter too. The label reclaimed the top spot on the list from Balenciaga, which dropped to third place. The index also includes a breakdown of the hottest products of the quarter, and Gucci is winning there as well: the GG logo belt—an influencer favourite that's been worn by Alexa Chung, Lou Doillon and Kendall Jenner—was number one. Also ranking highly were Fila Disruptor sneakers (number two) and Prada's nylon and leather belt bag (number four), while Balenciaga's controversial platform Crocs sneaked in at number ten. The second release of these in June saw them sell out worldwide for a second time. Prada and Nike (the top-ranking sportswear brand) also joined the top ten names of the quarter, while Givenchy enjoyed a rise of two places to fourth position, almost certainly thanks to the Duchess of Sussex's Clare Waight-Keller-designed wedding dress. Valentino, Yeezy, Moncler and Stone Island, however, all dropped out. See the lists in full below.
