column1: How these four women learned to dress for their diverse shapes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It all comes down to confidence Nadine Abdel Aziz wears Dress, Enfold at BySympony; Pants, Loewe; Sandals, Stuart Weitzman; Earrings, Roberto Cavalli. Dima Ayad wears Top, Pants, Layeur at The Modist; Shoes, Stuart Weitzman. Rhea Jacobs wears Top, Pants, Stella McCartney; Belt, Earrings, Marni; Shoes, Fendi. Amna Al Haddad wears Dress, Cédric Charlier at BySymphony; Pants, Emporio Armani; Belt, Givenchy; Shoes, Christian Louboutin. Photographed by Ziga Mihelcic Tall, athletic, voluptuous, petite… bodies come in all shapes and sizes and dressing for them means paying attention to proportion, detail, cut and fit. But one thing is for certain—whatever your build, natural elegance all comes down to confidence. Four diverse women show why what makes you unique can ultimately be your biggest style weapon. Nadine Abdel Aziz, influencer “I am 1.8m tall and have always been skinny; I have a fast metabolism. Growing up I was a non-stop eater, especially when it came to junk food. I'm more health conscious now and work out a few times a week but it's all about balance. Sometimes a steak and salad would do and other times, all the burgers and pizzas in the world are not enough! For me, balance is about being disciplined during the week and ‘cheating' on weekends. “Snug, tailored pieces work for my hourglass body type. Stretchy materials hug my body, while soft fabrics like knits and silk blends gently drape over my curves. I love wearing low necklines, pencil skirts and skinny jeans, especially paired with high heels to add extra length to my legs. I avoid low-rise pants since they make my hips look wider and my legs shorter. There is no such thing as the ‘perfect body.' What makes your body perfect is your perception of it. When we interpret our body image as ideal, that is what you will project and others will perceive it as such as well.” Amna Al Haddad, competitive weightlifter “As a child, I was quite slim but as teenager, I had a love/hate relationship with my body. I've always had wide shoulders and an athletic shape. It was only when I changed my mindset and started to exercise out of love for my body, its longevity and its health, that I felt at home in my own skin. I'm still trying to figure out what clothes work for me. I enjoy wearing maxi dresses, coats and training clothes. A stylist once pointed out that I should wear skirts, so I experiment with that too. Anything square-shaped makes me look bulky and bigger than I am. “Everyone has a different body type, different gene makeup and different hormonal factors that affect weight distribution. We're all on our own journey to discover what works for us—and it's a beautiful experience once you see what your body is capable of and when you take care of it from a place of love. Your cells react to words and thoughts. If you say you want to ‘lose' weight, you're sending a message to your subconscious that you have lost something and want it back. But if you use the word ‘release,' you tell your body that you are letting go of something you no longer need. Find an activity you like and explore what your body can do. You will be amazed by how strong you really are.” Rhea Jacobs, Marc Jacobs Beauty ambassador “I was always insecure about the way I looked. I once jokingly asked my mother what I needed to do to look like a specific cover star and she replied, ‘The world already has one of her. It needs someone who looks like you.' It was like a light went on. I realised that your individuality is your weapon and the moment you start loving yourself, the world will reciprocate. “I'm hourglass petite and love to contrast silhouettes such as a fitted body suit with a sheer, flowing coat with exaggerated sleeves. I also prefer anything high-waisted, symmetrical, or cinched at the waist. Boxy shapes, horizontal prints and midi dresses don't work on me. Women get bombarded with so many images per day that we eventually start believing that that's what the ‘ideal' body looks like. We need to realise that there is no one ‘perfect' body. We define it for ourselves. As long as you are healthy and fit, you must embody your individuality unapologetically. Don't change to fit the fashion, change the fashion to fit you.” Dima Ayad, designer “I'm curvy and tall with broad shoulders; everything is longer than ‘normal.' I think most of us tend to focus on what we don't like about ourselves, as opposed to what we do like. I started embracing myself in my late twenties—and that's when I started thinking about creating my brand. I wanted to tackle the challenge of not finding clothes that fit. I still have days when I want to be a certain size—that never goes away. But I've accepted myself and I love myself. “I like wearing clothes that flatter and accentuate my shape. Midi dresses are my go-to, as are long tops and structured blazers. I avoid wearing A-line dresses or skirts and wider pleats. There needs to be an awakening that there is beauty in every shape and size, you just need to see it. Acceptance of who you are, what you stand for and how you look all contribute to the energy you bring to a room. The world is becoming more inclusive—follow people and brands that inspire and empower. Don't just wear trends because they are in season. Wear what suits you. Black is not the only colour! Experiment with cuts and shapes—you'll be surprised that a style you never thought would work on you, actually does.” Photography: Ziga Mihelcic. Styling: Keanoush Da Rosa. Hair: Blowout & Go. Makeup: Mariam Khairallah, Cheryl Leonard at MAC Cosmetics. Style assistant: Mallory McLane. Producer: Danica Zivkovic This story was originally published in the July/August 2018 issue of Vogue Arabia Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 35 times Jennifer Lopez was the queen of head-turning fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Stage, screen and style icon Jennifer Lopez has a history of head-turning red-carpet looks. As the pop diva turns 49, Vogue looks back at her most memorable fashion moments It was 1997's biopic Selena that arguably catapulted Jennifer Lopez—a former Fly Girl dancer from the Bronx—firmly into the spotlight, flipping her instant fame and fortune. And while the emerging Latino icon soon added Grammy-nominated singer to her expanding repertoire, she was also becoming renowned for her statement wardrobe. J.Lo (as she later become known) may have proclaimed that “love don't cost a thing”, but she knew how to rock a rhinestone like no other: she busted a belly top with bejewelled bandana like any other girl of the late 1990s Juicy generation, but her Hard Candy ring was Harry Winston, and she paired Puff Daddy with Versace palm print. While music events saw J.Lo's jigsaw approach to dressing—queen of cutaway dresses with lots of missing pieces—the Oscars and Met Gala red carpets saw her approach a fairy-tale finish. See her one-shoulder pistachio Valentino gown for the 2003 Academy Awards, for instance, inspired by Jackie Kennedy's dress by the fashion house in 1967. From handkerchief tops and barely-there Versace to thigh-high splits and princess gowns, Vogue looks back at the head-turning, red-carpet style of the American superstar. column1: The return of the chintzy dress
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Chintz is not just for summer. The flamboyant, floral fabric has become a perennial favourite, and continues to flourish for autumn/winter 2018 The busy botanical flowers we're so used to seeing in chintzy home interiors and on soft furnishings have been creeping back into fashion. Naturally, that comes as no surprise during the spring and summer, when petal-infused patterns lend themselves to the standard sartorial fare for weddings and social occasions such as Britain's Royal Ascot and the Chelsea Flower Show. But look around and ahead to autumn/winter 2018, and the chintzy dress is popular once again. “I wanted to use the bright pop colours with a classic print to create depth and something that was quite unpredicted,” says Mulberry creative director Johnny Coca. The designer looked to the eccentricity of British style and the aristocracy for wallpaper-like prints and added to them a layer of clashing colours via the '70s. Alessandro Dell'Acqua at Rochas had a similar take: “A woman who is sophisticated and keeps this cool aesthetic that you find in the chintzy dresses from the Seventies,” is how he described the vibe. “I think floral print is always feminine and brings freshness and a great attitude to a silhouette.” Which is more or less how, back in the 1600s, “chintz” ended up working its way from cushions on to clothes. It had style and status—although it is said it was initially the servants who had taken the initiative to use their upper-class employers' redundant textiles to create linings and garments. It's also how—even though it's the finish of the cotton or calico fabric itself (in a sheeny glaze, usually of starch) that defines whether or not it is chintz—the term has now become widely understood to mean vivid and lush prints of flowers and plants, as these are what was traditionally depicted. The word “chint” means “printed cloth” in India, which is where most of the fabrics originated. Chintz became so popular in the 17th and 18th centuries that apparently there was a ban on wearing it, to protect English linen, wool and silk weavers who were unable to produce it. Fashion and florals have had a long-standing relationship—and it's one the chintzy dress is central to. Laura Ashley, the Welsh design and manufacture company, built its legacy on it. Conceived in 1953 by husband and wife Bernard and Laura Ashley, by the '70s, the brand had become best known for its Edwardian-style dresses printed with floral motifs inspired by 18th and 19th century patterns (Rochas and Mulberry had an air of this aesthetic in their designs this season). In the '80s, Diana, Princess of Wales could often be seen in blooms. It proved to be a heyday for the fabric before the '90s took hold, bringing with it grunge and minimalism. An advertisement by the Swedish furniture brand Ikea back in 1996 marked the fabric's demise when it instructed its customers to “chuck out your chintz!”. As women filled skips with flower-printed sofas and lampshades, the insinuation was that twee, “twirly” prints were old-fashioned and naff-looking. But a handful of designers have kept an eye on the chintzy dress. Erdem Moralioglu has long been infatuated by its regal charms; Demna Gvasalia made it central to his Vetements genesis (the seed was sown with the spring/summer 2015 collection, before autumn/winter 2015 set the agenda for the brands now signature loose, oversize styles), which further took effect at Balenciaga, where he was subsequently appointed artistic director. Alessandro Michele has allowed for more than just a little bit of flora and fauna to flourish at Gucci, and new favourite Richard Quinn has put petal prints at the centre of his designs since graduating from Central Saint Martins in 2016. The winner of the (inaugural) Queen Elizabeth II Award for British Design in February (the Queen attended his show), Quinn's aesthetic is very much one of English country gardens, subverted. It's no surprise to discover that his spring/summer 2018 collection involved a collaboration with London department store Liberty, famed for its own floral archive. His chintzy campaign continued for autumn/winter 2018 via pleats on asymmetric flyaway hems. Why does chintz feel right now, after all this time? “Using an eccentric treatment on a classic base brings modernity,” explains Johnny Coca. He notes, also, the tapestry-like effect of the florals through their colours and textures—there's a sophistication, femininity and glamour. And certainly, at this moment, that's where fashion's focus lies. View Gallery 10 Photos The chintzy dress is back What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Shantanu & Nikhil play with freedom in their latest couture collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Drama meets military-inspired couture Yesterday, on a meandering red carpet ramp running through the pillared and arched backyard of Bikaner House, the capital's cultural hub, Shantanu & Nikhil unveiled their autumn/winter '18 couture collection. Just like their collection last year, “The Regiment”, their latest showcase also had the running theme of  military and revolution-styled dressing. This year, the designer brother duo marched on to present “Independence”. “It's the story of India. Gender is becoming more fluid, women's empowerment is on the rise, and freedom is what we're really after. A lot of us are looking at finding our own independence,” says Nikhil Mehra. Their ideas of India lie somewhere between ideal and aspiration—but in this they seem to have found their signature aesthetic—and they are sticking to it, even as their design vocabulary matures to include newer shapes, silhouettes and finer detailing. Clearly aimed at their growing millennial tribe, designers Shantanu and Nikhil play with ideas of independence, freedom and individuality in dressing. “Gender fluid dressing is a new take on couture and we want to explore this as much as we can.” explains Shantanu Mehra. Their menswear carries on playing with drapes and sees an infusion of caped jackets, while their womenswear explores a range of separates, including unusual pairings such as voluminous gowns worn over tailored pants. Pinstripes, chevron and florals add the right bit of contrast, further subverting ideas of delicate and strong. “There is purush and prakriti, there's male energy and female energy, and we use the values of both energies in our clothing,” adds Nikhil. They seem to have found their niche in the bridal market, not so much by way of bride and groom, but as the go-to for “the friends-of-the-bride and attendees”. It's probably also why they get to play more with their couture—a dark colour palate dominates the collection this year, with purples, greens, blues and blacks, and the season favourite, yellow. And though the garments remain monochromatic, there's a generous play of textures as well, where sculptural skirts meet floaty sari-inspired jackets and capes and leather trims accentuate cascading fabric. They've also managed to slip in a sporty vibe into their military grammar, along with the expected dramatic flair. The designers seem to have made “Independence” their draping and tailoring playground—happily toying with contrasts be it masculine-feminine or vintage-futuristic. “It's all about discovering a lost language for us. And in the past couple of years we were able to decode a new form of couture—which is all about concept and storytelling. It's not just about how a garment looks on a mannequin, we want to relate to couture today, and find bits of ourselves in it,” says Shantanu. column1: A look at some of Selena Gomez’s best off-duty looks of all time
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Though it’s often shrouded in mystery, one thing we do know about Selena Gomez’s private life is that the girl has mastered high-low, off-duty style. On her 26th birthday, Vogue hand-picks the star’s best looks so far Is she, isn't she? Are they, aren't they? The hundreds of millions of fans who follow Selena Gomez's every move are drip fed her off-duty goings on via sporadic and often cryptic Instagram posts, like that Polaroid picture tribute to Justin Bieber on his birthday or the suggestive lyric captions as she gazes wistfully out of a window. But lucky for us, one glimpse we do get into this millennial megastar's day-to-day is her excellent off-duty wardrobe. Gomez manages to oscillate with ease between relaxed streetwear cool and woman-about-town glamour, rocking slouchy two-pieces from Vetements (2016), Miu Miu (2017) and most notably, Derek Rose pyjamas, all paired cleverly with a heeled sandal to take the look from pillow to pavement. Ever an advocate of playful style, Gomez likes to throw on comfortable knits—from Coach's cult dinosaur sweater to oversized Free People—elevated with voluminous midi-skirts, Vetements jeans or more daring leather jogging bottoms by Nicolas Ghesquière at Louis Vuitton, Gomez's long-time, go-to designer. Although, times could be changing. Recently, the starlet has been favouring French fashion darling Simon Porte Jacquemus—a favourite of Kim Kardashian, Emily Ratajkowski and Beyoncé—to dress her in her downtime. His broad-shouldered, form-fitting designs in block colours are giving the star an air of cool sophistication as she settles into her mid-twenties. Her latest off-duty style home run? Gomez revived the band tee overnight after a recent outing in a Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers T-shirt, taken up a notch with a red Céline wrap skirt and Dior slogan slingbacks. A nod to the recent media storm around a certain ex's engagement? Who cares—it's a fashion triumph and speaks to Gomez's impeccable personal style. See Vogue's pick of her best off-duty looks. column1: Lust list: 10 watches that feature stunning craftsmanship
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A piece of art for your wrist Buying a classic well-crafted watch is no less than investing in precious jewellery—they are both equally important when it comes to adding a bit of luxury to your ensemble. While silver and gold watches are mainstays in most of our accessory boxes, the ones with detailed craftsmanship help you bring a flash of drama to your wrist. From ones featuring feather marquetry and intricate stone work to the ones with enamel detailing, its time to add these detailed pieces to your watch collection, in case you haven't already. If you're looking for a way to add some bling to your date-night outfit, look to the ‘Oyster Perpetual Pearlmaster 39mm' watch by Rolex. Want something minimal? Pick the new ‘Tissot PR100 Lady Sport'. Those with a love for all things pink can go with Breguet's ‘Classique Phase de Lune Dame 9085' piece, while those looking for something more artistic can spend their time admiring a Jaquet Drox's ‘Petite Heure Minute Carps' number on their wrist, or invest in a ‘Slim d' Hermès Perspective Cavaliere' by Hermès. column1: Meet the designers behind the latest crop of It bags
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Sculptural shapes, offbeat touches and endless adaptability—Vogue gets a measure of the new bag designers who are starting an under-the-radar accessories revolution Is it a purse? Is it a belt? Or is it a bag? It's all three, thanks to a new breed of contemporary bag brands whose designs are as Instagram-friendly as they are fully functional and magically transformable. One bag can now take on as many incarnations as you like, as labels increasingly cater to our multifaceted lives with multi-option designs. Straps and statement hardware are created with a sleek customisable spirit in mind, which mean it's up to you how you want to wear your bag. “Ever since the launch of Mansur Gavriel's bucket style, which was the first contemporary It Bag, selling out within 24 hours every time it came back on site, we've seen more and more brands offering amazing designs at accessible price points,” says Net-A-Porter's retail fashion director Lisa Aiken. “Customers are now basing their love for a bag on its aesthetic as opposed to the branding. They appreciate an amazing design and are looking for a fun statement piece that's versatile and stylish.” And right now, there are plenty of choices out there. Wandler, Danse Lente, Manu Atelier and Yuzefi are among the labels fashioning a new and successful approach to bag design and, consequently, finding themselves featuring in the top ten best-performing brands in the contemporary bag category for spring/summer 2018 at Net-A-Porter. Aiken notes sales have nearly doubled since the previous season with no signs of slowing down (NAP is actually increasing its buy) and designers are responding accordingly. “It felt like the right time for my designs,” says Elza Wandler, who launched her Wandler label last year with a mix of unexpected dimensions, clean lines and bright flashes of colour. An Amsterdam Fashion Institute graduate, she has already had huge success with the Hortensia and Luna bag styles, both of which feature optional handles. “I think that a bag should give you a sense of empowerment and joy when you use it. A little bit of functionality can't hurt,” she says. Which further accounts for the versatility of the Anna Belt Buckle Bag, which can be worn as a cross-body bag, a waist bag or used as a wallet; and the Lotta Tote, which makes a decorative feature out of the studding that lines the length of its adjustable strap. Aesthetically speaking, it's a combination of these hardware details and eye-catching graphic shapes that feature across the board in the designs of these dynamic brands. Which, no doubt, were inspired by Loewe's Puzzle bag back in 2015, an instantly recognisable sculptural design that perfectly lent itself to the Instagram lens. “Instagram absolutely has a part to play in [these bags'] success,” says Aiken. “It brings a huge level of exposure to a brand and it's not just about fashion. Instagram portrays a lifestyle which customers want to buy into. The idea of having a bag from an under-the-radar brand shows off your fashion credentials.” Note, it's all about design, details, shape and size and less about slogans or logos. The heavy branding and seasonal ostentation of these labels' established designer counterparts are left behind in favour of each brand's own idiosyncratic bells and whistles. And from a consumer point of view, in our increasingly wear-once world, the in-built flexibility of these designs means that you don't need to worry too much about being snapped with the same bag. Because you essentially can't be—a switch of a strap, lengthen of a handle or tuck under the arm will easily solve that. column1: The iconic fashion pieces that made a comeback this season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A blast from the past Fashion is a funny thing—its revolving doors make sure that trends come in as fast as they go out, only to come right back again. For 2018, nostalgia has been the reigning theme. From Versace's tribute show, recreating that iconic moment when the Supers walked down the runway in 1992, to John Galliano's 1999-made Dior Saddle Bag now seen on millennial models like Bella Hadid, Kendall Jenner and Adwoa Aboah on coffee runs and fitting meetings—vintage is on everyone's mind. What is it about this sepia-tinted view of fashion? Never have throwbacks and flashbacks been more exciting. Perhaps, in a time when everything is changing so rapidly, looking back is the only way to move forward. So, how are brands doing vintage again? Prada brought back its iconic fire-wedged heel, while Kim Kardashian West wore Chanel's itsy-bitsy logo bikini from way back when and Viktor & Rolf dug deep into their archives for their 25th anniversary to give us a double take of their seminal blanket dresses. column1: How to style breezy silhouettes for every occasion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From music festivals to workwear Do you find yourself reaching for a pair of jeans and a T-shirt every time you have to step out, just to avoid having to deal with an uncomfortable outfit? We bring you five breezy looks to help you break through your sartorial rut this season. If you've been seeking inspiration for your next music festival, look no further; we've found the perfect outfit to make you stand out in a sea of graphic T-shirts and ripped denim shorts. Pair a bralette with your high-waisted shorts, and pull the look together with a bright, long jacket to add some length to your look. Go all out with your jewellery to accessorise—stack rings, anklets and bracelets, and layer statement necklaces of varying sizes. Swap the breezy dress in favour of a fitted one with big, voluminous sleeves when you head for Sunday brunch. The key is to let one aspect of your outfit do all the talking. For added effect, keep things easy in the accessories department. Strike a balance between tradition and modernity when you dress for work. Pick a kurta that features a long slit on the side—this will elongate the silhouette of your look. Add a pair of perfectly tailored pencil trousers in the same colour scheme to keep things work-appropriate. This season, try experimenting with loud, colourful patterns. The good thing is that you can never layer too many. Stay comfortable yet stylish in mosaic print palazzo pants, paired with a cropped embroidered jacket—perfect for a day spent relaxing at your best friend's house or at the neighbourhood cafe. Want to add a touch of bling? Stack a few silver bangles on your wrist and you're good to go. There's nothing like a printed maxi dress to make you feel like a diva against the scenic backdrop of your next holiday destination. The loose fit and flowy silhouette keeps things relaxed and allows you ample movement. Wear it to a sundowner by the beach or for a busy day of shopping to keep things fashionable on your days off. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The women behind the exquisite threadwork on your Anita Dongre lehenga
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How does one harness a craft without meddling in it? How will local go global? And how does a village in Gujarat figure in all of this? We follow designer Anita Dongre to Bakutra, Gujarat, to find some answers At this very minute, in a cluster of villages in India's west coast, a group of women are probably embroidering pieces that will make their way to showrooms in New York. Not in a dimly-lit airless factory where they are invisible cogs in the global machine that makes the clothes we wear and discard, but at home, practising a craft that comes as naturally to them as, to use a cliché, riding a bike. It's a craft that adorns their clothes and their homes—needlework as comforting as knitting but a lot more intricate and painstaking. The women are part of SEWA (Self-employed Women's Association), and if you're marvelling at the intricate ari work on your friend's Anita Dongre lehenga, thank them. The designer has been working with these women for over three years, commissioning work that adorns her Grassroot and bridalwear lines. On a recent visit to Bakutra, one of the villages on the outskirts of Ahmedabad where SEWA operates, Dongre allows us a peek into an oasis of colour in an arid land. “We purchase the fabric and design everything at our design headquarters in Mumbai. Sometimes we even do a sample swatch. We then send them the design, the full colour printout. And it travels from here to Ahmedabad, Ahmedabad to Radhanpur, Radhanpur to Bakutra. Once it goes to Gauriben's house, she informs the other women. In all, it takes 7-10 days for the piece to reach the artisan. We've now given them phones, so we can track our pieces and the progress made. They're sending us weekly updates right from the village. And then it's the same process for the pieces to come back. Most pieces take anywhere between 25 and 60 days, depending on how intensive the work is. It's a long-drawn-out process. It's truly slow fashion.” “Gauriben lives in Bakutra and is the leader. Women from the surrounding villages come to her, and she then distributes the work. She's feisty, she's spirited... These are amazing women. They lead such a hard life because the conditions are difficult but they're always smiling. I love how they dress, I love their spirit and their attitude. When I first met them I was moved by their passion and their determination to succeed. And that's what pushed me to work with them and succeed in what we had set out to do together.” “They do a lot of stitches but we primarily work with ari, soi and bharatkaam. We, though, use contemporary colours. Grassroot is a luxury brand—it's for a very global consumer and most of what they make is selling in New York—so we use colour combinations that are more relevant and now. The colours on their lehengas are beautiful, but they don't work for our more contemporary designs. You should, however, never touch the craft. We're here to modify the design, not the craft. It has to be a design intervention— you can't do a craft intervention.” “The women were already working with SEWA, but when SEWA came to me the issue they were facing was that their embroidery was no longer relevant. That's how we stepped in. I think we brought in a whole new perspective to their embroidery. We're currently working with 600-700 women, all between the ages of 17 and 70. When we visited them they spoke about how this work has impacted their lives— how the additional income has given them respect in the village with the men, the sarpanch, and how today the men listen to them and, if there is a piece to deliver urgently, the men will even help them out because they see how well they're doing. So it's definitely empowered them and given them confidence. The additional income goes a very long way for them.” “Embroidery is a big part of their lives. They have embroidered panels on the walls. Embroidery, for them, is therapeutic. They love to finish their chores in the morning and sit on their embroidery. Like how one knits. And living off it gives them a sense of pride... I didn't know there were so many stitches. My work there has just begun and there is so much to learn. There are other organisations, too, that are working on teaching the next generation some very difficult stitches that the younger generation doesn't want to practise. So there's more that needs to be done. I've just begun. It's a slow process. I'm still trying to take it further.” View Gallery 9 Photos It takes a village Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Gucci’s latest project captures the nature of time with Martin Parr
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Take a closer look Above all else, storytelling is the key to making a megabrand relatable to a millennial audience. Lucky for Gucci, creative director Alessandro Michele is already in on the secret. Ever since he took the helm at the Italian luxury house, Michele transformed the narrative of the storied brand from high octane glamour to cool and eccentric. Simply put, he elevated the idea of Gucci as a clothing label to an aesthetic that can be translated into a lifestyle. Amongst the many ways in which Michele brought about these changes is by constantly collaborating with different artists. This time, he worked with documentary photographer Martin Parr, who caught Michele's eye with his satirical and anthropological viewpoint to modern life. In-the-moment, humorous and somewhat abrupt, Parr's images evoke a sense of surprise while offering commentary on our everyday goings on. Parr will be lending his discerning eye to Gucci to capture the nature of time—featuring Gucci watches in the specially commissioned Instagram project #TimetoParr. Parr shot his new work against the backdrop of nine different spots where Gucci has previously staged shows or campaign shoots, or simply places that inspired Michele. The documentary photographer has used real, unknown people in #TimetoParr, preserving his love for authenticity. There are images of people performing completely normal actions like washing their hands or feeding a dog, taking a selfie and so on. Each of these makes room for a Gucci watch that's ubiquitously, but unassumingly, part of the frame. Vogue helps you get to know Martin Parr, the man behind the camera, better. Social media has not changed how I work or view people. For me it's [about] having and growing a larger audience for my work; it's now easier to get your messages out. I made photographs of the places and the Gucci watches within these places, being worn and appearing in real situations or laid out in interesting and different ways, again referencing my own work. Gucci allowed me to use my experience by giving me freedom within the brief. This allowed me to widen the parameters and make interesting work. column1: Why Hawaiian shirts are so hot in fashion right now
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The flamboyant island shirt first attracted style setters in the 1930s—and today it’s riding a resurgent new wave on the catwalk The street-style and runway set were clearly in cahoots this season as they both set about putting the Hawaiian shirt back at the forefront of menswear. Characterised by its vibrant and bold, nature-based prints, not since the noughties, when the tropical palms of brands like Quiksilver were so in vogue, have we seen it surf such a fashion wave. Previously, it had been relegated to the rails of vintage stores, pigeonholed for its sartorial comic appeal or simply confined to the memories of old holiday snaps. Not anymore. There was lush foliage from Kim Jones at Louis Vuitton; red-hot deserts from Demna Gvasalia at Balenciaga; hibiscus blooms (studs, leopard print and a whole lot more) at DSquared; Dries Van Noten showed muted and toned-down versions; MSGM's take hung out with California surfers; while Salvatore Ferragamo opted for something seaside-y anchored in the Mediterranean; and Paul Smith combined carp and coral to decorative effect. And that's not even taking into account the showgoers themselves who had already been won over by the shirt's charms. Sitting somewhere in the middle of the menswear style spectrum, with streetwear at one end and the dandy at the other, the Hawaiian shirt is easy to wear, and has as much panache and sophistication as it does personality and casual appeal. Of course, long before its renaissance on the spring/summer 2018 catwalks, and the street-style snaps currently peppering your Instagram feed, the Hawaiian shirt had a whole history of its own: 1 The shirt is largely thought to date back to the 1930s and the rise of American tourism in Hawaii, which only became a US state in 1959. Small tailor shops began to produce prints on their local shirts, generally known as the palaka, often made from native tapa or bark cloth, for this new wave of clientele. The shirts were also worn by Hawaiians for special occasions. 2 Ellery Chun, a Honolulu-based Yale graduate who studied economics, is credited as being the first mass producer of Hawaiian shirts—and the mastermind behind their name. 3 Chun supposedly picked up on the trend after a shirt maker called Musa-Shiya Shoten ran an advert in a 1935 issue of The Honolulu Advertiser for “aloha” shirts with “well-tailored, beautiful designs and radiant colours”. Chun quickly jumped on the idea and registered the aloha trade name in 1936. 4 Prints on Hawaiian shirts were typically a mix of exotic flowers, plants and ocean scenes that fused the cultural influences of Tahiti, Japan and the Philippines. Sometimes considered a bit gaudy, cheap imitations were associated with tourists, while higher up the fashion food chain expensive styles carried significance through their use of colour and storytelling design as an homage to Hawaiian heritage. 1 In 1950, Hawaii-based aloha wear manufacturer Alfred Shaheen started printing his own fabric with designs created by salaried artists, which eschewed overly loud colours and clichés. They took off and it's one of his designs—which now reportedly go for tens of thousands of dollars at auction—that Elvis wore on the cover of Blue Hawaii in 1961. 2 Popular with surfers and beach boys, Hawaiian shirts came to represent downtime weekend dressing, an acceptable casual chic for men. President Harry Truman appeared on the cover of Life magazine in one in 1951, while President Nixon was photographed wearing one in 1960. 1 By the 1980s, their appeal began to dwindle. But where fashion failed them, film and screen did not. The lengthy list of Hawaiian shirt pin-ups includes: Tom Selleck in Magnum, P.I., which ran from 1980 to 1988; Al Pacino in Scarface (1983); Tom Cruise in Cocktail (1988); Christian Slater in True Romance (1993); Brad Pitt in Fight Club (1999); Johnny Depp and Benicio Del Toro in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (1998); Leonardo DiCaprio in Romeo + Juliet (1996)—and even Jim Carrey in Ace Ventura (1994). Intriguingly, in film the shirt came to represent a type of rebellion, salvation, escape and bohemianism among the characters who wore it. 2 A brief spotlight on the style came at the turn of the millennium with surf, skate and snowboard brands like Quiksilver and Billabong enjoying a mainstream heyday. Since then, it's been a little quiet on the aloha shirt front. Until now. As menswear starts to move away from street and sportswear, designers from Milan to Paris are finding inspiration in the colourful shirt, with any former naff-tourist associations now long gone as the Hawaiian shirt takes on trophy shirt status for spring/summer 2018. column1: Cropped trousers are here to solve all your wardrobe woes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The latest trend is to crop it like it’s hot Not many trends are truly versatile enough to be worn at the airport, while running errands, and also on the red carpet, but Bollywood celebrities seem to have found one that works just right, no matter what the occasion. Pantsuits have been reigning over celebrity wardrobes lately, bringing a breath of fresh air to tailored silhouettes, but the separate of the moment is cropped trousers. Given that the weather is all set to rain on our parade over the upcoming few months, this might be the best pair of trousers to wear until the skies are clear again. There are numerous ways in which you can give this trend a go yourself. You could follow in Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's killer Jimmy Choo stilettos, with which she styled a jet black pair of Armani cropped trousers when she attended the Cannes Film Festival earlier this year. If you're looking for a more vibrant ensemble, you can take inspiration from Katrina Kaif and Esha Gupta—both ladies have sported a vivid yellow pair of ankle grazers in two very different silhouettes. Diana Penty put a contemporary spin on her monochromatic airport look, with the hem of her trousers ending inches above her ankle. The beauty of cropped trousers lies in the fact that they can be paired with an array of tops, from office-appropriate button-down shirts, to party-ready crop tops, or even kurtas. Take your look from day to night by simply accessorising your trousers differently: a pair of classic ballet shoes in the day can be swapped for a glossy pair of pumps in the evening. column1: Janhvi Kapoor’s best Indian ethnic looks from Dhadak promotions
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion So much inspiration for the wedding season! Bollywood fans spent the better part of 2017 speculating about when Janhvi Kapoor, daughter of late icon Sridevi and producer Boney Kapoor, would make her Bollywood debut. Rumours of her emergence as a star with Dharma Productions' Student of the Year 2 were rife for months, until Karan Johar finally let the cat out of the bag by revealing the official first look for Dhadak. The film is slated for release on July 20, but the young debutante has already made headlines with her sartorial choices during its promotional rounds. Dhadak's filming may have ended in April, but the last few months have kept Kapoor busier than ever. She's been jetting across the nation for one promotional soiree after another, and keeping in line with her on-screen persona, has been showcasing a range of charming, feminine silhouettes through stunning anarkalis, breezy kurtas and cropped lehengas. She is also following in her mother's footsteps as Manish Malhotra's muse—the 21-year-old has been seen out and about in his creations often. For those seeking inspiration for a fresh Indian ethnic wardrobe for the wedding season this year, there's a lot here to bookmark. Her outfits are anything but basic too; she donned a bohemian look by Anushka Khanna one time, and chose a floral anarkali by Sukriti & Aakriti for another look. While her vibrant Anamika Khanna looks made her stand out against the dull monsoon skies, her glittering Ritika Mirchandani ensembles ensured that all eyes remained on the star as she met fans across the country. And all of them will find a place in your carefully curated OOTDs as you hop from a friend's sangeet to a cousin's mehandi event soon. column1: Mira Rajput Kapoor guide to stocking up a stylish maternity wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Lessons from the chic mom-to-be If the stork is expected to pay you a visit and you want to keep your sartorial credentials intact while you're with child, turn to second time mom-to-be, Mira Rajput Kapoor. Rajput Kapoor delivered her first-born Misha Kapoor in August 2016, and announced her second pregnancy in April this year, and it's safe to say that she's a seasoned expert in dressing impeccably, even through the glowing child-bearing months. Don't expect to see this star wife in frumpy dresses or baggy tops just because she's expecting; she is not one to let pregnancy bring her A-game down. Instead, she makes a strong case for stepping into motherhood without a hair, or sartorial move, out of place. In case you haven't seen her recent OOTDs, the 23-year-old hasn't traded young silhouettes for boring maternity wear. In fact, it has been quite the contrary. From itsy bitsy playsuits and front-tie shirtdresses to ruffled off-shoulder dresses, she proves that no style or hemline is off limits for expecting mothers. And this dictum can be applied to Indian wear as well. Case in point: the au courant Anamika Khanna draped skirt, crop top and belted dupatta set the young mother wore for Sonam K Ahuja's reception. If you're looking to channel her style, ensure that while you keep your wardrobe choices trendy, you keep them comfortable as well—lightweight, breathable fabrics over heavy embellishments and crossbody bags and totes over top handles. Printed dresses and roomy fit-and-flare tops paired with jeans are Rajput Kapoor's go-tos—they accentuate the bump just enough to create a flattering look. She also advocates giving heels a rest during the difficult months and giving in to sneakers, sandals, thong slippers and slides. column1: Bollywood’s leading ladies show you how to make monochrome interesting
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Tone-on-tone dressing is having a moment. See how your favourite Bollywood stars are doing it right Have you ever wondered how Bollywood celebrities always look so put together, whether they're dressed for a long-haul flight or a red-carpet event? The key, if you pay attention, lies in monochromatic dressing. Notice how Priyanka Chopra is frequently spotted wearing a single shade from head to toe, and pairs her attire with various statement accessories for a smooth transition from day to night. Perhaps Malaika Arora's style appeals to you more, in the way that she styles white co-ords with a red handbag to add a pop of colour—further exemplifying why monochromatic outfits are a sure win, while showing us how to carry them off with ease. The essence of monochromatic dressing is pairing separates of one colour, in either similar shades or textures, for a tonal look. Sporting a single hue throughout your outfit is an underrated approach to putting an ensemble together, as these outfits can be accessorised and worn in a multiplicity of ways to suit both your personal style and the occasion. Layering items of one tone but varied textures adds depth and dimension to an outfit, while affording you the freedom to highlight or downplay certain features. In particular, monochromatic ensembles create an uninterrupted line from head to toe, elongating your silhouette to appear sleek even if all you've done is simply roll out of bed in a tracksuit. You don't need a celebrity stylist to guide you towards acing this trend: simply check out some of your favourite stars' OOTDs for inspiration. Follow in Kangana Ranaut's heeled booties or Janhvi Kapoor's trainers by donning a unicoloured tracksuit for an effortlessly comfortable airport look. You can add an ethnic twist to a monochromatic outfit, like Deepika Padukone in her elegant pink anarkali, or Shilpa Shetty Kundra in her stunning emerald sari. You could even make like Swara Bhaskar and limit your accessories, so that your vibrant ensemble can take the spotlight. The increasingly popular minimalist lifestyle has extended to the world of fashion lately, what with capsule wardrobes and similar trends making an impression across the globe. Relieve yourself of decision fatigue, while keeping in mind that simplifying your life doesn't mean you can't spice it up when you need to. Are you due for a closet upgrade? column1: Manish Malhotra on designing for Aishwarya Rai Bachchan in Fanney Khan
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Plus, looks from inside the much-awaited film that you haven't seen before Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and Manish Malhotra's muse-designer relationship has seen years now. Whether in films, runway shows or red-carpet appearances—their partnership is one that has been applauded time and again. This year, the duo has come together yet again for the much-awaited Fanney Khan, which sees Rai Bachchan play the part of a pop sensation—Baby Singh. The film is remake of the 2000 Belgian comedy Everybody's Famous!, and will feature Anil Kapoor and Rajkummar Rao along with the former Miss World. For her character, a globally-adored diva, Rai Bachchan sports fiery red highlights, spangled on-stage costumes and off-duty camo jackets; a look as imaginative as one would expect that of a performer to be. Manish Malhotra, who in his 28th year as a costume designer, has been the brain behind the creation of Rai Bachchan's persona. We spoke to the designer about what into the making of Baby Singh's closet. Baby Singh is a very popular singer. She's got the superstardom of what Aishwarya has in person and she also has the heart—she's soft, she's young and she is warm, and it's very close to Aishwarya's personality. Aishwarya is very warm, she has a lovely laugh, she's intelligent and has maintained her friendships and relationships over many years, so I felt there was a nice parallel there. My mood board had everyone from Beyoncé to Ariana Grande and Selena Gomez. What we took from them was the glitz and glamour but added a touch of reality to it. And if you notice, Aishwarya's costumes have brought that in. I think Aishwarya and I were really keen on getting out the reality aspect of a superstar. People might see her as an achiever or a megastar, but she is also very human. She is in touch with day-to-day fashion like every other girl. So there are lots of jeans, sneakers and a lot of happy, fun clothes as well. We were very keen that we didn't want to do the stereotypical star. Aishwarya wears everything from a camouflage jacket, ripped jeans, big sunglasses and tracksuits to very a simple jeans and shirt look. There is a lot of high street [style], but it's also a lot of high fashion. People see stars as divas, but they are human too and that's what we are trying to portray in the film. She's done up in two of the songs, but it's not unrealistic. You could wear the looks to a crazy party. If you see the other songs, it's all sequins—sequinned blazers, jackets and jumpsuits. Internationally too, sequins are making a huge comeback—the whole '80s influence is evident. I think the hair was more of Aishwarya; she wanted to do like this big hair. When she showed the hair to me, I was like yes, we should go ahead with it. I think she carries it off really well. Aishwarya got in touch with me and spoke to me about this film. I've worked a lot with Aishwarya before—I've known her for many years of course, and she's a very close friend. She's someone I admire for her work ethic. column1: Calvin Klein gets inspired by its own history to launch a sub-label
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Brooke Shields is back Few images in fashion history are as iconic as the 1980 Calvin Klein campaign. This one was shot by late American fashion and portrait photographer Richard Avedon, and featured a young 15-year-old Brooke Shields with a provocative tagline: “What gets between me and my Calvins? Nothing.” Raf Simons' Americana theme at Calvin Klein has clearly continued through the years—the brand is all set to launch a new sub-label showcasing a streetwear and athleisure-inspired line, Calvin Klein Jeans Established 1978. Here, Avedon's iconic image gets translated as an all-over print on everything from a trucker jacket to a denim bucket tote, alongside a crewneck sweatshirt, white tee and even a keychain. There are also patchwork beanies, pouches and boots emblazoned with a label that reclaims the brand's legacy: “CALVIN KLEIN JEANS ESTABLISHED 1978 THE FIRST DESIGNER DENIM ORIGINALLY DESIGNED IN NEW YORK CITY 205 W39TH ST.” No better way to flaunt your loyalty to the emblematic American brand. column1: The making of Beyoncé and Mariah Carey’s couture Cavalli costumes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion For their latest tours, the superstar singers have once again turned to the Italian house for a high-voltage dose of glamour and showmanship. Vogue talks to new Cavalli creative director, Paul Surridge, about creating custom-made designs for Beyoncé and Mariah Carey Beyoncé and Mariah Carey were back in Roberto Cavalli on stage this month—but unlike in 2014 when both divas wore the same embellished black dress, this time they were dressed in custom-made designs by the Italian label's new creative director Paul Surridge. Carey kicked off her Las Vegas residency on July 5 in a couture Cavalli dress, while Beyoncé stepped out on July 6 in Milan in two custom-made creations for the latest leg of her OTR II Tour. “I jumped at the opportunity,” Surridge tells Vogue of the chance to work with the two living icons. Both singers have worn the Italian label on and off the stage throughout their careers, but this was a chance for Surridge to reimagine them in his vision for the “new” Cavalli. “For me, the woman who wears Cavalli wants to be visible and wants to be celebrated,” says the British-born and Saint Martin's-trained designer, who succeeded Peter Dundas at the helm of the Italian house in July 2017. “Both women represent very different things, but fundamentally they are both artists, both passionate and both beautiful women.” Carey's couture white dress, especially commissioned for her Vegas show, was inspired by the heritage zebra print. “She wanted something very traditional,” notes Surridge, passionately describing the painstaking detail—“hand-placed beading, using french sequins, crystals and glass fringes, layered with beautiful marabu and white ostrich feathers at the bottom”—of the garment, which took over 100 dedicated hours of hand sewing to complete. The aim was to evoke a traditional sense of glamour and showmanship. “Mariah's is a voice that I grew up with and this [design] is her in a dress.” Discussions with Beyoncé and her team started when the pre-collection was published on Vogue Runway in May. “Beyoncé and her stylist saw it and got in touch. We started working on renderings and took it from there.” The custom-made outfits were delivered at breakneck speed; a process that would normally take two months from start to finish took less than three weeks. “She's an athlete and a very powerful performer, so we had to take that into consideration,” says Surridge of the design. “She wanted colour, she wanted graphic, she wanted something very visual. But ultimately it had to be practical—it had to stretch, it had to be easy to move in.” As well as easy to get in and out of—“Some costume changes need to happen in as little as 30 seconds,” Surridge notes. Practicality is a familiar concept for the designer, who previously held menswear positions at Burberry, Calvin Klein, Jil Sander and Z Zegna. His tailoring has already proved popular on the red carpet, particularly at Cannes where he dressed Romee Strijd and Isabelle Huppert in sumptuous tuxedos. Which isn't to say he shies away from the decadent and wild dresses Cavalli is renowned for—see Hailey Baldwin's glass-bead and crystal-fringed strapless dress, or Joan Smalls' sheer skirt and long-sleeved bodysuit embroidered with black ostrich feathers. Like the red carpet of Cannes, the stage requires show-stopping impact—and no detail was spared. Beyoncé first outfit—a white bolero and matching romper suit—despite it's 120 hours worth of pavee crystals and metallic sequins mirror effect, was “relatively straightforward”, Surridge says, at least when compared to the second outfit. “The yellow- and black-bead fringe was layered over a printed top, and each fringe had to be hand-matched so that when she moves, the print is seamlessly lined with the beading. That—making the fringe and the underpiece seamless—took a lot more work.” (150 hours for the top alone.) “It is incredible to see something handmade come to life on the biggest superstars in the world,” he says, “Not just for me—the beauty of this work is also in the seamstresses who make them. Design is one thing, but behind these garments is a huge amount of innovation and art form.” View Gallery 12 Photos Roberto Cavalli’s creative director on dressing Beyoncé and Mariah Carey What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Does your blouse really need to match the sari? We settle the debate
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Mix it up or keep it simple? Matching the blouse to the exact shade of the sari had been an accepted sartorial norm for decades—it was how Maharani Gayatri Devi wore her gossamer chiffons and Indira Gandhi, her raw silk and khadi drapes (unless she was in her trademark white cotton blouse, of course). But the coming of age of Indian fashion has shaken up sensibilities. Never before has the timeless sari been viewed through such a radical lens. As designers continue to innovate with modern variations of the six- (or nine-) yard staple, new ways of sporting the classic favourite have emerged too. The blouse now requires as much attention as the sari. Whether you wish to experiment with contemporary blouse silhouettes or keep it old school, Vogue tackles the imminent ‘to match or not to match?' question—should you do like your grandmother and match the colour of your blouse to the sari with microscopic precision? Or should you do a 180 and walk the other way? Or, is there a middle ground that you can choose to partake in instead? Read on for all the answers. Now, we're not saying that matching your blouse to the fabric, colour or embellishment of the sari is passé. After all, Priyanka Chopra championed it with her recent stints in Tarun Tahiliani and Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla, and Madhuri Dixit-Nene, Kangana Ranaut and Shilpa Shetty Kundra have been established patrons of the head-to-toe monotone look as well. We're just saying it's not the only way to go. Sonam K Ahuja, for instance, prefers to mix it up. She paired her light blue floral print Neeru's sari with an oversized violet blouse for one outing, and her monochrome Masaba drape with a pop pink one for another. While Kareena Kapoor Khan plays with colour blocking by pairing her yellow sari with a pink blouse, Deepika Padukone likes to combines the best of both worlds. The actor often teams her saris with blouses that are a shade darker than the former, or plays up a hue in the print of the sari with them. [Celebrities] Sabyasachi Mukherjee punctuates his hand painted floral saris with blouses in contrasting hues for an eclectic mix of colours in his ‘An Endless Summer' collection. Anamika Khanna, on the other hand, prefers blouses in the same colour family, or ones with a clashing print. Anita Dongre and Shyamal & Bhumika are in favour of a neutral route with versatile metallic blouses that easily lend themselves to mixing and matching, and Payal Khandwala's white halter blouse manages this feat with flair too. column1: 26 spectacular outfits to celebrate Abba’s comeback
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It wasn’t just the music that made Abba one of the biggest phenomenons of the 1970s—the Swedish supergroup also knew how to dress big. As the band makes a comeback after 35 years, Vogue looks back at the outfits that made fashion history From the moment they walked into the limelight at the Eurovision song contest in Brighton in 1974, Abba proved they meant business—in music and in style. Swinging on the upbeat notes of “Waterloo” played by their other halves Björn Ulvaeus and Benny Andersson, Agnetha Fältskog and Anni-Frid Lyngstad appeared on stage in full 1970s glamour—Agnetha donning a cobalt blue bomber jacket in velour with matching satin pantaloons and sparkly cap; Anni-Frid wearing a swooshing, floor-sweeping skirt made of white and orange panels topped with a white jacket with large orange cuffs and collar. With one performance they dazzled the public, brought home the title and began their implacable climb to the top of the international music charts. Most of Abba's looks to come were masterminded by Owe Sandström, a Swedish high-school teacher with a knack for fashion design. Under the name Artist Dressing and with his partner Lars Wigenius, he created some of the band's most memorable outfits and the group's tour costumes, including the triumph of spandex in shades of blue, purple and white designed for the 1979 tour, and Agnetha's white jumpsuit with ruffled trousers and sleeves, completed with an emerald green cape rimmed with white feathers for the 1974 European and North American tour. From skinny scarves and embellished double denim to platform shoes and animal prints, Sandström revelled in all the major trends of the decade while stealing references from traditional attire—think Japanese kimonos, flamenco costumes and Swedish folk outfits—to create Abba's signature style. Glamorous, flamboyant and thoroughly enjoyable, even when veering towards kitsch, Abba's sartorial choices didn't cease to amaze their fans off-stage too. They appeared in full gear at London Airport, strolling on the cobbled street of Warsaw in Poland and posing in front of a poster of themselves in Los Angeles. Earlier this year, the band announced a special TV appearance for autumn 2018, followed by a tour in 2019-2020 where they will appear as “Abbatars”, computer-generated versions of their younger selves—and possibly new stunning costumes. In celebration of their long-awaited comeback, Vogue looks back at their best fashion moments from the 1970s. column1: Love La Perla lingerie? The brand’s India CEO has good news for you
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Sapna Shehrawat, the India CEO of the lingerie label, reveals her plan for the brand, and gives us a peek at her personal style “Look how far we've come,” says Sapna Shehrawat, the India CEO of iconic lingerie label La Perla. We're in the country's only La Perla store—they opened doors in August 2016—situated in the capital's glossy DLF Emporio mall, and Shehrawat, dressed simply in a sleek black silk jumpsuit and no jewellery, is quite the picture of restraint. It could be said that the Delhi-based Shehrawat, who visits Milan to do the buy herself, knows the label quite intimately. The York University double major in sociology and mass communication swears complete brand loyalty in her choices (both in inner wear and in taking the pieces out of the boudoir, but more on that later), and easily rattles off all the key facts—currently, apart from luxury inner wear made from the finest lace, silk and micro jersey, La Perla also makes ready-to-wear, all under the creative direction of Julia Haart, who came on board in May 2016. Since then, the brand has seen a revival of corsetry (Ada Masotti, who founded the house in 1954 in Bologna, Italy, started out as a corset-maker) as well as the re-launch of its classic Maison line of intimate and nightwear for women. For Shehrawat, 41, whose own style influences range from Russian fashion media magnate Miroslava Duma to Italian designer Alberta Ferretti, this role is a sartorial dream come true. “What most people are just realising about La Perla is that our pieces work across occasions. Take the Freesia bodysuit, one of our bestsellers—I've worn it with velvet trousers, and even paired it with a sari.” She pairs a classic blue silk camisole from the Maison line with high-waisted skirts or trousers. She's even worn it under a formal pantsuit. “The pieces allow me to experiment with innerwear as outerwear,” she says. Her aesthetic, she says, veers towards the contemporary. “For me, it's all about luxury without compromising on comfort,” she says, describing her style as classic with a touch of bohemia. “Change is constant, and the quick-paced evolution of fashion excites me,” she adds, and cites her preference for Céline's minimal designs as well as her love for the raw energy of Jacquemus' deconstructed tailoring. “My wardrobe essentials are a custom-made blazer (my favourite is one from Blazé Milano), a silk slip from La Perla, and well-fitted white shirts. These styles can dramatically change your look without bulking up your closet.” In fact, her commitment to this more textured minimalism extends to her home as well. Pristine white walls, furniture and floors abound, filled with fresh flowers and candles in every room. “Every couple of months, I like to add colour to the space with artworks I paint in my free time, rugs and pillows from artisans and small brands from across India. It's like having a blank canvas every season,” she says. “This resembles my state of mind when I wake up in the morning and ask myself what I want to wear.” Mostly, though, she answers that question by going for her favourites: “A simple white T-shirt and blue jeans are my everyday staples. I like high-waisted jeans from Frame, and add colour to my outfits through accessories—shoes from Dior, Hermès, Chloé and Saint Laurent, and handbags from Chanel, Céline and Hermès, plus my watches. When in doubt, I gravitate towards black—I have a closet full of it.” In doing so, she creates a practical look that works well, whether she's in India or travelling the world. Her latest acquisitions: Off-White X Jimmy Choo Jane sandals, a La Perla swimsuit, and a multi-purpose gilet from Isabel Marant. And as she moves ahead with her plans for La Perla—kickstarting the label's Indian e-retail platform, Laperla.in, by November or launching male innerwear and expanding the existing shop-at-home service—you can be sure she's doing it in her very own style. column1: Here’s what to expect from Amit Aggarwal at India Couture Week 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The intricacy of crystal formation plays muse for the designer this time around Architecture and structure serve as the driving element for repurposed couture in designer Amit Aggarwal's sartorial realm. As fashion's favourite unconventional darling, the couturier takes great pride in routinely shaking the status quo, whether it is by bringing recycled plastics on the mainstream map or reinterpreting quintessential zari embroidery with avant-garde materials. It should come as little surprise that he has a few tricks hidden up his sleeve for his debut at India Couture Week as well. We got him to let us sneak a peek at his lineup. Our ‘Crystalis' collection is inspired by its namesake. I was especially intrigued by how a certain number of molecules come together to create patterns that are repeated for infinity, and we've worked on emulating this crystallisation process in our lineup through pattern-making, silhouettes and structure. A video on the natural phenomenon of crystal formation struck my fancy, and with that as the starting point, we worked on aligning the rest of the process with our ethos and signature style. The heart of the collection revolves around the intricacies of how a single unit is replicated to form a complex, multifaceted pattern. We've specially handpicked colours that emulate the radiance and translucence of crystals, from rose and amethyst to sapphire, emerald and peridot. Meticulous hand embroidery, angular structures and our signature polymer detailing has been used in conjunction with multiple textile techniques to create dimension and surface texture. Another special highlight is our collaboration with Tanira Sethi on a range of one-of-a-kind cashmere lace textiles woven in France. Much like our showstopper for the collection, the ideal Amit Aggarwal muse finds glamour in her strength. As an independent woman, she understands her heritage and is mature yet individualistic in her tastes. We have always worked on creating a new language of sustainability by understanding how workmanship can be used in coalition with the latest advances in technology. What you'll see in this collection is the age-old techniques of aari and zardozi embroidery, but the fabric underneath has been replaced with something radical. column1: The cool Norwegian jewellery label that celebrities are loving right now
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From signet rings to denim, bee charms to a pave diamond collection, in just five years Norwegian brand Tom Wood has cornered the market in must-have jewellery. Vogue catches up with the label as it launches an exclusive Dover Street Market anniversary celebration In 2013 when Mona Jensen launched Tom Wood, the Scandinavian purveyor of modern signet rings and unisex jewellery, she had an ambitious aim. “It was my hope to start something from Norway with an international focus,” says the designer from Oslo, where she lives with her husband Morten Isachsen, managing director and co-owner of the company, and their two daughters. “[Norwegian brands] are not something we are renowned for—we are more famous for our fish, oil and natural resources.” After 15 years spent advising entrepreneurs as a marketing consultant, working on everything from logo and website design to international campaigns, Jensen felt the need to test the efficacy of her own theories. She saw jewellery as a still largely unexplored field with a significant potential for growth—the “candy” of the accessory world that could become a leader if approached with the appropriate strategy. “I thought it would be interesting to start a label from a branding perspective rather than a design perspective,” says Jensen. The first step was to develop an instantly recognisable identity for the label. Jensen has often described Tom Wood as her male alter ego and, at the beginning, she built the brand image around this whisky-drinking, bike-riding, all-round cool guy character. At the same time, she decided to focus on one single style: the classic signet ring. Reinterpreted in polished sterling silver and natural stones including turquoise, onyx and jasper, the rings have become synonymous with the brand which, despite the masculine influence, was conceived to appeal to a unisex clientele of all ages. Today, Tom Wood has around 200 stockists worldwide and with its expanding range of rings in different materials, shapes and sizes, it has wooed the likes of singers Kendrick Lamar and Miguel, models Caroline de Maigret and Kozue Akimoto, and influencers Pernille Teisbaek and Camille Charrière. With operating margins of over ten per cent and revenue of £3.2 million (up from £2 million in 2016), the brand was recognised as the best performing business in Oslo and the third best performing business in Norway by Dagens Næringsliv, Norway's leading business newspaper. This healthy growth is largely due to a set of rules enforced by her husband, whom Jensen took on board in 2015. As Isachsen, a creative consultant who was marketing manager for Levi Strauss & Co for seven years, explains it, the company doesn't have loan or cash credit, production is strictly dependent on orders and full ownership of the brand is non-negotiable. In addition, the brand has been diversifying its revenue streams adding a ready-to-wear denim line in 2015 and new jewellery styles at different price points, including charms, earrings and necklaces, while reinvesting money and resources in increasing sales and elevating product positioning in all categories. “I believe a brand should be flexible; the market changes, so to be relevant you need to look at it and at the people who buy your product and try to adapt,” says Jensen. If at the beginning it was important to present an unequivocal identity to break into the market and be recognised as the go-to brand for signet rings, now Jensen can indulge in different projects with the certainty of having a solid consumer base at her side. “I'm working on how we can elevate the brand, while also offering smaller items [to someone who] already has a few rings,” says the designer. At the same time, “It's important to challenge [the jewellery] category to become a brand that people also think about when they think about denim,” she says, stressing that it is going from being a jewellery brand to being a complete brand. The ready-to-wear line is now stocked in around 60 per cent of their current retailers and, according to Jensen, has helped to attract new ones. Jensen and Isachsen will celebrate their achievements, and the five-year anniversary of the brand, with a special anniversary collection launching exclusively at Dover Street Market locations worldwide on 14 July. Including six styles of ring in oval, square and octagonal shapes, the collection is the first one to be entirely conceived in pave diamonds and gold, which Jensen has previously used mainly on made-to-measure commissions. It's a confident nod towards high-end jewellery, a move Jensen describes as a “test” to see how the brand could be elevated into the luxury segment, covering a price range similar to that of fellow contemporary labels such as Sophie Bille Brahe and Charlotte Chesnais. But, she clarifies, “Our aim is not to become a luxury brand, but to stay in the commercial segment of the market. The collection is something to honour the brand and Dover Street Market, and to offer our clients something unique.” View Gallery 8 Photos Why jewellery label Tom Wood is the one to watch What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: For every fashion girl who loves sneakers, this is the holy grail
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Anna Wintour-inspired Air Jordans, anyone? Every Vogue editor remembers their first AWOK, the little acronym (short for Anna Wintour Okay) scrawled on each print page by the inimitable editor in chief. It is the ultimate sign of approval in this office and the wider fashion world. Now, it is being applied to a delightful new venture: a limited-edition capsule of Air Jordans as edited by Vogue and inspired by the woman in charge. For the special collaboration, Jordan Brand has reimagined two versions of its iconic sneaker. The Air Jordan 1, available July 21, recasts the retro, high-top shoe in rich red or white leather with a crimson tongue concealed behind a key-ring zip (as worn by Wintour in the video, above). The Air Jordan 3 SE, which drops September 7, nods to her signature Chanel tweed suits and sunglasses—the top is cut from glimmering black or red tweed. Both models have AWOK stamped on the sole. It's a match made in fashion heaven. From Nicolas Ghesquière's sculptural Louis Vuitton Archlights to Demna Gvasalia's infamous Balenciaga Triple S and Speed trainers, sneakers have featured on every other runway for several seasons and show no signs of stopping. Take it from Wintour: There's something in juxtaposing an elegant rose-print dress, say, with a slick set of high-tops. The results are magic—a slam dunk in our book. column1: Forevermark is creating jewellery for the bold, modern woman
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Forevermark’s latest collection is all girl power and subversive trends Think diamonds and you see Marilyn Monroe swearing forever friendship and the material girl cascading through suits in candy pink, or of promises made on bended knees and hidden desserts. These shiny glittering rarest of rare stones have for long captured various stages and kinds of womanhood, along with our wardrobes, hearts and investment portfolios. It's no wonder that the future of jewellery initiates much interest among consumers worldwide. We got in touch with Federica Imperiali, head of new product development at Forevermark, to find out more about it. That's exactly the objective we had in mind; it is how I understand womanhood. Our personalities are complex, we are sure of ourselves and not afraid. We dress to express our personality. We are not following a cliché, but creating new rules instead. One of our big trends for the year is ‘Think Pink', a provocative take on the colour pink which has been associated with women in a typically clichéd girly way. But the way we have approached pink is [actually] the opposite [to that]. I think a pink jacket is as powerful in the boardroom as a blue one. We wanted to bring this into jewellery as well. It is a celebration of a bolder personality, who is confident of what she wants and will do everything to achieve it. It simplifies things, as a woman speaking to women directly is much simpler; rather than pandering to a woman's desire through a man's wallet. It will give us the opportunity to explore more innovation with design. We feel that the woman of today is more open to new things. We are now working to create bolder shapes of diamond jewellery that can be worn on a daily basis catering to work and play, because her lifestyle has changed or is changing. She is owning her space in jewellery. Today, if she sees something on the shelf that she likes, she will buy it. And with agency comes the urge to experiment. So bold patterns, unconventional positioning of diamonds and versatile pieces—it's a great opportunity for any designer. The Forevermark woman is very conscious about what she does, not just for herself but also for the community. She is not only interested in the aesthetic, but also goes beyond the visible. Our promise to you as a brand is that you are making an ethical choice. And with our inscription you can be confident that you are buying a rare, beautiful and responsibly sourced diamond. We are also giving back to the community and environment we operate in. And these are the concerns of women today—we are aware and we want our jewellery to reflect that. As Forevermark, our design DNA is modern and clean, but we are also culturally sensitive. So in terms of shapes and silhouettes, we are influenced and inspired by local traditions constantly—even in terms of creating occasion wear jewellery to match specific needs. But we like to mix the new into the old. We are now working on a second collection with Bibhu Mohapatra, and while we will keep the Indian woman in mind, there is also a universality to our sensibility. And next year, we will propose a trend which will pair two culturally diverse markets together with each one's design sensibilities infusing into the other's—for instance, Japan and India. For me, tradition and modernity go together. There is so much to learn here; all we need is an open mind. column1: All the times the Indian sari has seen itself on international runways
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Re-imagining the traditional six yard staple At their Alta Moda collection showcased at Lake Como in Italy, Dolce & Gabbana dressed Indian model Deepti Sharma in a sari, complete with a headpiece and earrings. The story of how this ensemble came together is quite interesting. The designers apparently took cues from the model herself—they gave her fabric and asked her how she would drape it as a sari. The following look amalgamated as a result of the experiment. Traditionally a single piece of unstitched fabric, the sari has often found itself being reimagined on international runways. Vogue went back to the sartorial archives to find all the moments in fashion when the Indian ethnic drape got a global update. After a trip to India, Alexander McQueen worked on his fall 2008 collection, making brocades, military tailcoats and diamond neckpieces a key part of the show. One of the looks clearly drew inspiration from the traditional Indian sari. The model strutted down in a white gown with a red brocade fabric draped around her—complete with jewellery reminiscent of Indian royals. Another designer whose sensibilities are often drawn from Indian fabrics and prints is Dries van Noten. His spring/summer 2010 collection was inspired by ikat, a print that is widely identified in southeast Asia. Skirts half draped like saris, outerwear with Indian motifs and ikat juxtaposed with other patterns–all done with a signature Dries van Noten flair. In 2011, Hermès launched a collection of saris for the Indian luxury market, inspired by Indian hues and brightly coloured geometric designs. French luxury house Chanel too gave an ode to Indian royalty with their 2012 pre-fall collection. Karl Lagerfeld dressed his models in signature Chanel tweeds, mixed with draped silhouettes and accessories that were reminiscent of Indian jewellery worn by royals. Elie Saab's 2016 couture collection saw pieces inspired by the Indian drape and its opulence. As is his trademark style, the looks featured elegant silhouettes and lace in shades of ivory and blue.
