column1: Stock up on all your summer wardrobe essentials at this Mumbai pop-up
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You can’t miss this Samyukta Nair, the multi-hyphenate behind one of Colaba's hippest shopping grounds, Clove, is all for shining the spotlight on homegrown brands in her curated space. Nair is bringing Bengaluru-based label, The Summer House to Mumbai this weekend. Vogue chatted with her on the nature of the pop-ups at Clove, The Summer House aesthetic, and providing shoppers with an offering that doesn't necessitate maxing out your credit card. What do you try to highlight with the pop-ups at Clove? Celebration of Indian design is integral to our philosophy at Clove. By way of our pop-ups, we wish to create a platform to showcase India's talent at work. Moreover, pop-ups give us the ability to engage with patrons on a personal level and create distinctive experiences that make Clove a dynamic space for them to keep coming back to. What do you like the most about The Summer House? In addition to the co-founders—Shivangini Parihar and Rekha Datla—I most like their ability to combine Indian craft with responsible processes to create modern pieces that can be a part of any woman's wardrobe. The attention to detail in their luxurious yet comfortable clothing celebrates the little things in life and reinforces Clove's ethos of everyday luxury. What aspect of The Summer House's design ideology appeals to your sensibility? I love that The Summer House is an accessible brand to people with taste, and not necessarily just those with the means. Their soft-spoken design sensibility and minimalism is derived from intricate, sometimes complex, processes. They focus on sustainable, responsible methods of designing and manufacturing, and that is something I greatly appreciate. Tell us a little about the collection itself. What can shoppers look forward to? Their new collection, ‘A place called Summer' will debut at the pop-up at Clove. It's an ode to nostalgia, the art of discovery and making the time for oneself. In an array of pastels, the edit features minimal summer dresses, along with shirts and co-ordinates that are made with linen and organic cottons. Having partnered with Sewa Lucknow, a framework of Women's Rights and Sustainable Human Development, the collection also pairs elegant silhouettes with chikankari embroidery to spell a perfect summer romance. column1: Dresses: Decoding the past and present of this trusty closet staple
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet your most versatile sartorial friend You may come across a host of silhouettes claiming to be the ultimate one-piece wardrobe wonder, but there is no disputing the fact that the dress is an easy winner in this never-ending battle. Utilitarian, versatile and all kinds of flattering, it's the minimum-effort-maximum-impact variety of outfit that is the only shining armour a lady needs in times of sartorial distress. Or, during the most important milestones of her life. Think about it, the dress has been a constant through all your rites of passage—the princess-worthy first birthday frock, the tulle prom dress, your first date wrap dress, an elegant graduation sheath, the first-day-at work midi—the list goes on. You may have called your trusty BFF for advice on how to get through said days, but it's the dress that was always the fall-back #OOTD. It's true for you, and was true for generations of women before you. Vogue traces the rise and rise of the perennial popularity of this unquestionable closet MVP. A quick dip into history books is enough to realise that the dress has tweaked itself to mirror the mindset and sensibilities of the times for eons. The ancient Greeks had the toga, while women in 11th-century Europe wore loose dresses that were similar to men's tunics. Empire line dresses were the norm du jour of the 18th century, alongside the three-part dress that included the front-open gown, the skirt and the bodice. The 1860s witnessed the popularity of crinoline-supported dresses, but it was also around this time that the dress started undergoing several modern reforms. By 1910, the Edwardian look made way for sleeker silhouettes, driven by the comfort and practicality demanded by working women of the era. The introduction of the innovation of factory-made clothing in 1910 took the dress mainstream. Ever since, there has been a signature style that has defined every decade, be it the drop waist flapper dress of the Roaring Twenties, the full-skirted cinched dress of the 1950s, the bohemian maxi of the '70s, the power-shoulder party dress of the disco decade or the gauzy slip dress of the '90s. As for the dress' most memorable moments in the spotlight? There are plenty. It doesn't get more iconic than Audrey Hepburn in the little black dress designed by Hubert de Givenchy for Breakfast at Tiffany's. Though it was Coco Chanel who originally created the now-indispensable LBD in the 1920s. Christian Dior New Look from the 1940s and 1950s was game changing while Marilyn Monroe's iconic white ‘subway' dress from the 1955 film The Seven Year Itch continues to be a costume party favourite even today. From Princess Diana's black off-shoulder ‘revenge dress' from 1994 to Kate Middleton's wrap dress—she wore it to announce her engagement in 2010—and Meghan Markle's sheer bodice gown for her official portraits with Prince Harry, the dress has gotten a stamp of approval from the royal family too. View Gallery 5 Photos Dresses: Decoding the past and present of this trusty closet staple The dress has many champions, and continues to be the uniform of choice for present-day celebrities as well. From off-shoulder LBDs and dramatic keyhole cutout sheaths to casually layered slip dresses, Kareena Kapoor Khan prefers to wear her dresses with a siren twist. On the other hand, sister Karisma Kapoor advocates elegance, and is most likely to be seen in classic cuts. Alia Bhatt is a style chameleon when it comes to her choice of dresses, experimenting with everything from one-shoulder ruffled pieces to strapless maxis. View Gallery 28 Photos Dresses: Everything you wanted to know about this closet staple It's true that there is a dress for every occasion, mood and personality. Its various silhouettes are as varied as the number of events it can lend itself effortlessly to. The LBD, of course, is an intrinsic favourite, winning the approval of even Karl Lagerfeld, who famously said: “One is never overdressed or underdressed with a little black dress.” Then there is the equally iconic wrap dress, invented by Diane von Furstenberg in 1974, which is favoured for its innate ability to complement every body type. The star of the nineties (and also of Kate Moss' wardrobe back in the day), the slinky slip dress has been resuscitated by the millennials, who have chosen it over the erstwhile party girl go-to bodycon dress. As comfort increasingly becomes the key principle on which style connoisseurs are now building their wardrobe, styles like the causal maxi, anti-fit boxy dress and athleisure-approved sweatshirt dress are reigning charts. Even so, structured styles like sheath midis and skater dresses continue to enjoy an unwavering patronage. Nothing says ‘I have arrived' quite like an office wardrobe bursting with power dresses. The hardest working garment in the working women's wardrobe, this one is a natural pick for its ability to easily adapt itself to today's on-the-go lifestyle. Don a blazer over a tailored solid-coloured sheath dress for a client presentation and then, trade it for a statement necklace for drinks with your partner after. The shirtdress is another boardroom staple. Choose one with pinstripes and cinch it with a belt for added impact. From catch-ups over salads and smoothies to morning errands, the day dress is capable of fitting itself into every agenda on your to-do list. A ruffled midi in a pleasant print is as brunch-ready as it gets, while a simple shift dress is a practical shopping companion. Picking your kids from school followed by a trip to the grocery store? Pick an oversized cotton dress with stylish flats to maximise comfort. Nothing makes a woman feel as glamorous as a head-turning party dress. It helps that it's a fuss-free option too. The cocktail dress is a legitimate excuse to channel sparkle and decadence, in case you needed one. Whether it's a sequinned drop waist dress, a dramatic neoprene ruffled sheath or a metallic slip dress, choose one that accentuates your curves, leaves an impression, and can becomes the life of the party. column1: Why I, as a mother, refuse to put my baby girl only in frilly frocks
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion So what if, at 10 months of age, the guard aunties at the airport think my ‘son’ is cute? The first time a woman at a mall referred to the two-month-old sleepy infant I was slinging along in a Baby Bjorn as a boy, I stopped to examine the inference. My little girl was dressed in a striped blue onesie and was bereft of any tell-tale bows, earrings and confections. If, like me, you believe that colours don't have genders, you may be right or wrong depending on what persistent stereotypes and biases you consciously or unknowingly cling to. I've grown up with three sisters, and yet, I didn't think for a minute about dressing my daughter in only pastels and poppies. Heck, I'd brought her home from the hospital in a navy-blue jumper with anchors and ships on it. Not because I'd gone in hoping that I was having a boy, but because blue is my favourite colour. To be very honest, Baby A isn't of the delicate features and gamine looks variety, so can't really blame mall aunty for mistaking her for a boy. But when it became a weekly occurrence, I started getting a little annoyed. Blues, yellows, greys, whites, greens and purples are apparently not ‘girly' colours, and stripes and checks are totally unbecoming for babies of the ‘fairer' sex. At seven months, she was commended for “doing ladies shopping with mummy”. Blame factor—yellow T-shirt and blue-and-white striped tights. Now, don't get me wrong. I may be a fashion editor, but I'm not a norm-shattering avant garde dresser. My personal style is, at best (as a designer friend once politely described it), more “functional chic”. But with both my parents being artists, the creative choices I was given and the liberties I took were definitely more than my peers. Ever so often influenced by uniform codes and societal and professional concerns, I have arrived at my personal style after 40 years of ‘phases' and a fair share of stereotypical labelling. No, I'm not angry that people think my girl is a boy, nor am I rushing to pierce her ears to cast all doubts aside. For the record, we absolutely love our bows, baubles and lace, but we also adore our football jerseys, joggers and beanies. I'm just surprised at how deep the sex stereotyping schisms run when it comes to clothing. Browse through the children's section of any store or skim through any kids site and you'll see the segregation—pinks, butterflies, cupcakes and hearts for the girls; boats, cars, bulldozers and dinosaurs for the boys. Boys ostensibly love superheroes and football, and girls adore rainbows and fairies. According to Smithsonianmag.com, historical references point to the fact that today's colour dictate wasn't established until the 1940s, as a result of American preferences that were interpreted by manufacturers and retailers. And in our enthusiasm to ape the West, this gender binary is yet another clothing construct we've embraced and perpetuated. So, thank god for brands like John Lewis—that put dinosaurs on dresses—and River Island, that launched a unisex line for kids last year. Abercrombie & Fitch followed suit with their Everybody Collection earlier this year. Meanwhile, in India, the gender neutrality conversation is still confined to the cognoscenti, fashion week concept notes and the cool street-style kids' corner. It is yet to draw itself out of the realm of conceptual onto the platform of the practical. Social media offers a glimmer of anti-normative hope where hashtags like #AGenerationWithoutGenderBias (started by Chennai girl Deepika K, who's known as @mommyingtales on Instagram) are going viral and mothers and brands are increasingly talking about #GenderNeutralKidsClothes. Elsewhere, misguided parents dress up children as their clones thanks to the Mini-me fad. Adults continue to confuse androgyny with gender-neutral clothing and well-meaning friends continue to gift us pink onesies. So, any chances of an overnight revolution in kids wear, or even a perceptual shift, look rather slim—more like a princess' castle in the air, pun intended. But Baby A and I are hoping to slay the dogma dragon one misguided mall aunty at a time. So what if, at 10 months of age, the CISF guard aunties at the airport think my ‘son' is cute? The offending piece of clothing in this case—a green superhero tee that proclaims, ‘My cape is in the wash'. Maybe my daughter will want to become Wonder Woman someday, or she'll grow up to be a tennis player with a fondness for glitter a la Serena Williams, or think hearts and angels are cool AF. Maybe she will be a Ninja in a salwar kameez (India's original gender-neutral attire, amirite?), or she will do epic things in a pink tutu. Or wear a tuxedo to her prom. I want her to appreciate the freedom of choice, know that she can wear what she wants and ultimately be whoever she wants to be. Till then, each time I debate the gender binary with someone, I will do my best Iggy Pop (for H&M) imitation in my head: “There are no rules in fashion…”. The future will, hopefully, be fluid. column1: This 40-year-old Rolex watch is selling for nearly 4,00,000 Swiss Francs
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The secret is in its rare dial The Rolex ‘Paul Newman' is the megastar of collectible watches. Each time a collectible vintage timepiece is sold, records are broken. This time, Sotheby's will be leading their spring sale of important watches in Geneva with a rare Rolex Daytona ‘Paul Newman' watch that is estimated to fetch between CHF (Swiss Francs) 2,00,000 - 4,00,00. But what is so interesting about a watch that has seen over four decades of wear, for it to fetch such a sum? The timepiece in question was purchased as an 25th wedding anniversary gift by the owner's wife back in 1975 for GBP 134. The childhood sweethearts shared an emotional history of having been together all through his service in the British Army during World War II, as well as in India and in Iraq. The watch has been preserved along with the original paperwork. But the reason behind the piqued interest in this token of love is the rare dial of the watch. The unusual feature of the dial is that it changes colour with age—it has transformed from the original black to a rich brown now. Vintage watch collectors refer to this process as ‘tropical', and are placing a high value on such timepieces, making them extremely covetable in the current market. Aside from the sentimental value of the watch, the investment value of this piece is undeniable. The Sotheby's Important Watches auction will take place on May 13 at the Mandarin Oriental, Geneva. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Jeans will never fail the stars The past weekend has been a busy one for the stars. Scroll on for more. Kareena Kapoor Khan loves her casual ensembles, and manages to make a basic top and jeans combination look new each time she wears it. This weekend, the star showed French fashion house Balmain a whole lot of love, picking its pieces on two occasions. After being spotted at Mumbai's Mehboob studio in a white Balmain tank top featuring a fun slogan—a trend Kapoor Khan seems to never tire of—the actor stopped by Manish Malhotra's house in a black and gold Balmain sweatshirt. How does one make a cosy sweatshirt look party-ready? Kareena Kapoor Khan paired her latest pick with ripped white jeans, shimmering gold Brian Atwood heels and a matching Chanel bag. column1: H&M announces a new collaboration with Moschino
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion That too, through Gigi Hadid’s Instagram profile This morning, H&M confirmed its latest designer collaboration, with Italian fashion brand Moschino. News of the collaboration was first revealed late on Saturday evening at Jeremy Scott's 11th annual party, held at the Coachella music festival. The announcement, which is always one of the most anticipated on the fashion calendar, came via an Instagram live call from Gigi Hadid to the designer. Both were dressed in looks from the Moschino [tv] H&M collaboration, giving a first taste of the playfulness and humour—synonymous with Scott's designs - that we can expect to see in it. “I am so excited about Moschino [tv] H&M,” said Scott today of the announcement. “My life's work has been to connect with people through fashion, and with this collaboration, I'll be able to reach more of my fans than I've ever had the ability to do.” After Scott's long-standing collaboration with Adidas ended in 2017, this partnership will offer fans a chance to snap up his collections again at a more accessible price point. Prices will range from approximately £25 to £300. “There's a silver sequinned parka dress,” Scott told Vogue. “Denim pieces are all twisted into something else. Puffers and jackets are reconfigured into cropped things or double-long things. There's a sportswear-with-evening kind of feeling, like a hockey jersey with a train.” H&M's creative advisor, Ann-Sofie Johansson, said that the partnership is “the perfect collaboration for fashion right now” and mixes “pop, street culture, logos and also glamour.” We told you to stand by — and now we can finally tell you. We're collaborating with fashion's most fun and charismatic brand, @MOSCHINO ❤📺 To be released 8 Nov 2018. — REACT NOW at #HMOSCHINO A post shared by  H&M (@hm) on Apr 15, 2018 at 1:51am PDT “Jeremy Scott is amazing—he knows how to have fun with fashion, and to connect with his fans around the world,” she added. Moschino will follow in the footsteps of the hugely successful 2017 Erdem collaboration, with a collection including womenswear, menswear and accessories. It also joins an impressive history of fashion houses that have collaborated with the high-street brand, since Karl Lagerfeld did it first in 2004, including Balmain, Marni, Kenzo and Versace. The (often star-studded) campaigns and launches each year are as tailored by the respective designers as the collections are. This year is set to be no different, with the campaign said to be a “radically innovative TV concept enmeshing social and traditional media to create a multi-platform takeover—a captivating new “zapping” experience for the digital world.” The Moschino x H&M collection will be available online and in-store from November 8th. column1: I gave up skinny jeans, and I’ve never felt better
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion So much elastane, so little room There's a reason why The Sisterhood Of The Travelling Pants wasn't titled The Sisterhood Of The Travelling Red Shoes, or The Sisterhood Of The Travelling Prom Dress, or The Sisterhood Of The Travelling Polka-Dotted Sunglasses. Few wardrobe relationships endure—and evolve—as much as that between a girl and her pair of blue jeans. You might not remember your first dress, but you'd very clearly recall how your first ‘proper' pair of blue jeans looked and felt—mine was a pair of indigo Levi's bellbottoms that my brother bought for me, baggy and oh-so-cool with those Converse All-Stars I was so into during that phase of my life (and under which the said jeans would keep slipping like a little dustpan). And they came a year after I graduated. Before that were the years of Blue Denim Wilderness. If you grew up in a small town in West Bengal in the '90s, chances are the perfect pair of jeans was something you spotted often—but mostly on the better-travelled others (who also were the proprietors of the cooler double-decker pencil boxes). Yours was always a little too droopy at the back, gaping at the waist like a little fish gasping for air, sagging at the knees as if you spent the whole day digging flowerbeds, wide at the thigh, not tapered (or flared) enough at the hem. The perfect pair of blue jeans was the unicorn of your wardrobe dreams. Then, a denim brand called Ruf n Tuf (of which a young Akshay Kumar was the brand ambassador) came up with a ready-to-stitch denim kit—legs, zipper, rivets, leather label, et al—which you were supposed to give to the local tailor with the instruction booklet that accompanied it. The excitement of owning my very own bespoke jeans, however, was short-lived. Not sure how to punch in the rivets, and not used to the mechanics of stitching five-pocket jeans (and clearly not accustomed to following instructions that could have overcome the two handicaps), he followed the template he had developed for the 50-year-old men that mainly comprised his clientele—high-waisted, pleated, front-creased. They were in dull-grey denim—so 50-year-old with a midlife crisis. You could have pulled them off now. Then, as a skinny teenager with two oiled braids, bad posture and Sreeleathers sandals, not so much. College, the sartorial watershed for many a youngster, brought for me a miracle made of stretch and cotton—skinny jeans. The discovery that one garment could lift and mould and embrace like second skin came with its own sense of freedom. They went with everything from T-shirts to kurtas, and became my de facto travel uniform (this was in the pre-athleisure days). Because they were universally flattering, adopters ranged from college kids to South Delhi aunties. They still do. If getting into them required that one did a Stanky Leg dance, so be it. If at 2pm, in an airless classroom, they made you feel like a cling-film-wrapped tuna sandwich, it was totally worth the effort...till it wasn't. When Levi's re-introduced their iconic 501 CT jeans for women four years ago, it came with the distant interest in owning my one pair of button-fly jeans. Non-stretch, high-waist, boyfriend-fit—they were everything all my previous pairs were not. Even if I bought a size 26, the waist had to be tucked in if I wasn't aiming for a paper bag look. Soon, however, possibilities opened up—the fact that I can wear a men's shirt three sizes larger and tuck it in without looking like I shoplifted potatoes in my pants; the fact that the same pair will look just as good with a tank; the fact that the aforementioned Stanky Leg routine became history; the fact that my non-arthritic knees don't scream every time I sit (8.5 hours everyday); the fact that my day-to-night dressing has become simplified; the fact that I can wear my beloved pointy pumps one day, flip flops another, Stan Smiths one day, and heels if I feel like (never, actually, but I at least know that's an option); the fact that after three washes, all the elastane doesn't turn the pair into a melting Gingerbread Man. We put a lot of trust on ‘flattering' clothes when we are just about coming in to our own with our clothing choices. Now, in my mid-thirties, clothes that just let me be hold a special kind of attraction. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 5 jewellery designers reinventing pearls
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Stripped of its staid connotations, the natural gemstone is experiencing an edgy rebirth. Vogue dives into the world of pearls with five designers responsible for its renaissance The arrival of jewellery designer Camille Miceli at Dior in 2009 signalled a new, more playful approach to pearls (see her punky double-pearl Dior Tribales earrings, which have since become a signature design of the maison). Add to that the rise in popularity of face-framing accessories led by Instagram and fashion brands like Gucci and Céline, as well as independent designers Sophie Bille Brahe, Delfina Delettrez and Gaia Repossi, and you have the perfect backdrop for the resurgence of the pearl. Here, Vogue speaks to five jewellery designers who are at the forefront of their reinvention. Julie Nielsdotter One of the youngest designers championed by online store The Jewellery Room, Julie Nielsdotter launched her eponymous brand in 2015 via Instagram. Since then, she has enchanted a growing number of followers with her pastel pearl creations, like Danish designer Stine Goya, who was so taken with Nielsdotter's jewellery she featured it in her Spring/Summer 2018 runway show. Nielsdotter's creations play with contrasts: in her Pearlstick earrings, bumpy freshwater pearls hang at the end of thin gold bars, while her Sunray Pearl earrings feature perfectly round pearls nestling inside the curves made by undulating gold. “It's really important for me to underline the beauty of the material itself,” explains the designer, who is careful to use gold and gemstones to intensify—never outshine—the beauty of the pearl itself. Mateo After five years designing jewellery for men, in 2014 CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund finalist Matthew ‘Mateo' Harris launched his first collection for women. An ode to modern art, his earring designs feature cultured pearls suspended on Calder-inspired mobiles, while others seemingly float inside diamond-encrusted orbits - a direct reference to Wassily Kandinsky's Floating painting. The self-taught designer hasn't left the classic pearl necklace untouched either. His Not Your Mother's Pearl Collar is a traditional collier, but is only half covered in the round gemstones - the remainder is a sleek, gold ribbon, making it the perfect nine-to-five piece. “We want to make jewellery that women can really, truly wear and pair with their wardrobe every single day,” says the designer. Pernille Lauridsen Pernille Lauridsen's use of pearls is multifarious, and her eclectic taste is expressed through designs that can be graphic and geometrical, or extravagant and imaginative. The Copenhagen-based designer, who set up her eponymous label in 2013, has used pink freshwater pearls as diamonds, setting one on the top of her Portia ring just where a solitaire would be, and created miniature orbiting systems featuring two round pearls of different dimensions, connected by a thin gold bar. With other pieces Lauridsen has created an enticing underwater fairytale universe. Combining Keshi, South Sea and baroque pearls with colourful gemstones, her Waves earrings are all set on undulating silver and gold stems that move as the wearer walks. Lia Di Gregorio Lia Di Gregorio was initially taken by pearls for their clean, spherical shape and neutral colour. “I was influenced by what was happening in fashion at the time, by that wave of conceptualism,” the designer says of her search for a personal design language in the late 1980s. “It was instinctive for me to use a precious object that I viewed as a solid shape—the pearl—and overturn its [usual] position.” The result is Touch, her first collection, which sees pearls playing hide and seek- nestled inside or in between simple gold bands and visible only to the alert observer. In Forme, miniature Akoya pearls almost disappear to complement the graphic shapes of interlocking earrings, while in Nodi, freshwater pearls delicately mingle, strung together with fine gold thread. The designer personally creates all the prototypes and closely follows the work of her Milanese artisans. “It's an old-style operation,” she says. “It's tiring and requires time, but the beauty is that it allows me to have this kind of attention to detail.” Mizuki Mizuki Goltz might be a veteran in the jewellery world—she established her eponymous label in New York in 1996—but her brand continuously evolves with the times. Goltz is known for her unusual pairings (pearls and leather, she's discovered, make excellent bedfellows) and experimentation—pearls in her designs don't stand alone as they usually do, instead she modifies them with gold lacquer and  diamond embellishments. She has also found innovative ways of wearing them—her earcuff design, for example, wedges a pearl in the outer ear. One of her latest innovations is Privé, a capsule collection of one-of-a-kind pieces made from pearls she has collected over the years. Driven by a desire to return to her sculpting background, each piece “starts with the pearl and ends with the pearl”, she says, celebrating the singularity of this gemstone. column1: Bridal jewellery guide: What should a summer bride buy for her trousseau?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Hear from the experts How does a summer bride ensure her jewellery trousseau is in tandem with the mood of the season? Jaipur-based jewellery designer Sunita Shekhawat's signature pastel-hued meenakari jewellery is equal parts steeped in tradition and on trend with the season's favourite pastels. We asked the designer how to make the most of shopping for jewellery for your big day. A bride can choose from a plethora of options. But a maang tika, nose ring and a neckpiece—preferably a Rajputi Aad—are essentials for any bridal trousseau. They accentuate the bride's natural beauty and her wedding attire at the same time and take it to the next level. Since destination weddings are popular this season, brightly coloured meenakari jewellery are the perfect fit, keeping the thematic settings in mind. I would suggest detachable and reversible jewellery pieces—simply because as luxurious and as exquisite as they can be, they are also convenient and can serve different purposes for the modern bride. Unusual colours from nature are key sources of inspiration. Contrary to popular belief, the colour black is really catching up as an unconventional choice for brides. When enhanced with gold, diamonds and polkis, it just stands out and epitomises the balance between modern and traditional. As I mentioned before, black has to be a definite choice—it can be paired with any material and goes well with any mood. Apart from this, I believe white enamel jewellery can also be blended easily with different outfits and colour palettes to create striking looks. Contrasting jewellery is on trend. If you are wearing a light pink, peach, green, lilac or light blue lehenga, then you can opt for jewellery of the same colour family, but go for a darker hue so that it stands out against the lighter outfit. Pair rubies or dark pink stones with a light pink or peach lehenga. For dark green beads, choose a pale green outfit, and with blue stone jewellery, match a pale blue outfit. When opting for a contrast like this, a long necklace combined with a neutral shorter one works best—anything else could cause an overdose of colour. The richness of the craft is incomparable, as the process remains the same as it was 500 years ago. Even today, a meenakari artefact goes through the same assembly line of craftsmen as it used to hundreds of years ago. Certain things should be kept under consideration when choosing the wedding set—like the budget, the wedding occasion, the wedding attire, the skin tone, the face shape, the hairstyle one is going for and above all, think about long term while trying something different. You may love the idea of a braided rose gold ring or a diamond eternity band, but once you get to the store, make sure you try some rings that aren't on your inspiration board. It's easy to go wrong with the layering—you could do too much, or too little, or put the wrong colours or shapes together. You can either go classic with a choker and a long necklace, or go delicate with pearls and golden beads. If you want to go the maximalist route, layer chunky stones and multiple colours, or if you want to go safe, wear coordinated necklaces with similar designs. These days, wearability is being built into signature pieces. The jewellery made for weddings is generally so heavy that it is rarely used after one's wedding ceremony. For this, the best option would be to opt for heavier jewellery pieces with detachable settings that can be used in the future. The pleasure of owning splendour that is yours in every possible manner is incomparable to the grudging and tepid choice made from a limited assortment. By customising your own jewellery set, you don't need to settle for something less than perfect or accept compromises. You will not only enhance your bridal look but also do justice to your vision for the big day. You can ace that flawlessly by having a clear mindset about what you want, and finding the perfect bespoke jewellery designer and stylist, who can work with you to make it a reality. Revamping and including family heirlooms is another classic idea for wedding jewellery. Modifying old classics with a modern touch adds emotional value to your jewellery, and also creates a unique piece only for you, which you can share with your mother or grandmother. column1: Céline Dion’s best street style moments
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Canadian songstress always steps out in style As one of the best-selling artists of all-time—she's a seven-time Grammy winner with record sales of over 220 million copies worldwide—Céline Dion doesn't really need an introduction. But it's not Dion, the music icon we want to talk about this time around. It's Dion, the style icon, who has been having a defining sartorial moment of late. While Dion crooned her way into hearts with her powerful ballads ever since she came onto the scene in the '80s, she was never really a fashion darling. Sure, she made the occasional statement by wearing a white tuxedo backwards, accessorised with a tilted hat like her 1999 Grammys appearance, but her diva status was always a result of her musical genius rather than her wardrobe. Come 2016, the songbird's sartorial sensibility took a complete detour, with Dion reemerging as a couture-loving fashion fiend who wore Off-White and Reem Acra with equal flair. #CélineTakesCouture, the hashtag that has taken over her Instagram page, became her style dictum. Vogue takes a look at the 50-year-old's style renaissance. Was there a defining moment that can be dubbed as the coming out for her second innings on the fashion circuit? Many would point towards her look in a Vetements hoodie with images from the 1997 cult film Titanic—she wore it with jeans and Gucci sandals. It was a tongue-in-cheek statement that only she could have pulled off—and it made people take notice, but Dion had already been painting Paris chic with her Balenciaga dresses, Saint Laurent biker jackets, Fendi coats and Balmain trousers. Dion roped in the expertise of image architect Law Roach in 2016—who was best known for his work with Zendaya back then—to elevate her style. It was a testimony to the life-changing power of fashion, which, according to reports, the singer was harnessing to bring back joy to her life (following the death of her husband and brother earlier the same year). Together, Dion and Roach sealed the former's status as a bona fide style star. She sat front row at Paris Couture Week last year in the season's most coveted looks and made her debut at the Met Gala as well. Safe to say, Dion, the fashion star had arrived. Ever since, Roach has been creating a roster of looks that are as unexpected as they are on point. She's seen in head-to-toe florals by Roberto Cavalli one day and Givenchy leather overalls with a Céline blouse on another. Pinstriped Ellery pantsuits, Dice Kayek tops, Louis Vuitton x Supreme coordinated sets, Rochas python coats and Off-White tracksuits—it's almost impossible to predict what the duo will pull off next. But you can be sure that each look will be more striking than the previous. Don't believe us? Take a look at our slideshow. column1: Save or splurge: The spring 2018 must-haves you can buy online
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Step into the new season in style Even the most carefully put together trans-seasonal wardrobe needs to give into the lure of au courant trends every now and then—especially with the onset of spring, and the fresh promise of a busy social calendar that it brings along. Whether it's for a vacation with the girls, dates by the pool or lazy terrace brunches, we decode the flavours of the season that will hold you in good stead as you saunter your way through the months to follow. Spot a trend with staple potential? Then why not break the bank for it? Or not. Luckily, we've rounded up options no matter which side of the ‘save or splurge' fence you're sitting on. If you're planning to spend the better half of summer in ‘out of office' mode, then you might as well jet-set with a bag that lets you play (anti-)tourist to the hilt. Enter fanny packs aka bum bags aka the it-bag that everyone from Kendall to Rihanna can't get enough of. And when in doubt, just join the Gucci gang. We don't blame you for wanting to resign those skinny jeans to the back of your wardrobe until the unforgiving heat is on its way out. Luckily, the tailored belted trouser is a welcome reprieve—it's versatile enough to work from desk to dinner and merciful enough to allow for utmost comfort. Choose one in the reigning colour of the season, purple, like this Miss Selfridge number. Or ride high with shorts. We're placing our bets on the biker, Bermuda and preppy variety. Speaking of colours, pink and red is the hottest power couple, and its one that you can easily add to your wardrobe in multiple ways—take baby steps with Attico's buckled mules or plunge in with an ASOS swimsuit in the combination. Not your basic Panama hat, spring 2018's straw hat is bold à la Samantha Jones. Jacquemus' La Bomba straw hat is the only way to turn heads as you cover yours. Unless you're looking for a more wallet-friendly option, in which case, Topshop could come to your rescue. Can't get enough of hoop earrings? It's a good thing their must-have status remains intact through the season. Whether you go luxe with Fendi or high street with & Other Stories, you're golden either way. column1: 25 times Deepika Padukone and designer Sabyasachi were a perfect match
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Making sartorial history together Deepika Padukone's love affair with Sabyasachi's designer ensembles is as timeless as the period epics she regularly brings to life on the silver screen. Sure, she loves her high street labels, but when it comes to traditional wear, the statuesque 32-year-old turns to the designer for statement looks, which could easily double up as a showstopper piece at his larger-than-life runway shows. The master couturier, in turn, makes the most of his beautiful canvas and dresses the leggy lass in everything from ornate saris, to breezy separates in his signature florals. Each time the designer drops a new collection on Instagram, we like to believe that Deepika Padukone is right there with us, avidly scrolling through his feed and scoping out the prospects for her next red carpet stint. Together, their history has been a euphoric one, dating back to her newbie days in the industry. With Cocktail (2012), her career hit a turning point, as she lived up to her onscreen persona of fashion-forward Veronica during the movie's promotion spree. After flaunting a modern take on the classic sari in the ‘Second Hand Jawani' track, she followed up with multiple fashion hits from the designer. Scroll through her style evolution over the years, and there's a good chance you'll be able to trace a resounding majority of her looks back to Sabyasachi. Ever the risk-taker, she skipped the memo on dramatic gowns, and stepped on the IIFA 2015 red carpet in a statement metallic sari instead, draped to perfection on her 5'7” form. If it looks familiar, it is because Kim Kardashian West favoured a similar rendition of the number in the pages of our February 2018 issue. As her career graph started including more period dramas, Deepika Padukone turned to the designer more often, to help recreate the old-world royalty of her onscreen roles. The promotions run of Goliyon Ki Rasleela Ram-Leela (2013) and Bajirao Mastani (2015) had her parading a series of jaw-dropping concoctions from the designer—his flair for luxe silhouettes and sumptuous bling in full attendance. In her downtime, she opted for breezy florals to redefine airport chic. While his elaborate saris hold a special place in her heart, flip through her Sabyasachi outings in recent years, and you'll find her asking for more from her clothes. She has been opting for hybrid silhouettes; her recent outfits will make you rethink what you knew about Indian traditional wear. And just when you thought that palazzos were the only way to go, she stepped out in a bodycon kameez and churidar; the stark monochrome palette mirroring her sartorial chutzpah for pushing the envelope. Yes, his decadent lehengas remain her major weakness, but Padukone is just as game for his fur neckpieces—and when she wants to make an impact, a belted sari with a bikini blouse. Pairing a white workwear shirt with a statement embroidered skirt? Oh yes, she can. She largely credits him as one of her all-time favourite designers, and he remains an integral part of the important milestones in her life. When her first Hollywood co-star, Vin Diesel made his way to India, she promptly introduced him to the transformative powers of a Sabyasachi sherwani. A recent felicitation ceremony for her father, Prakash Padukone had her opting for a classic Benarasi weave by the designer. Her recent appearance at an award show saw the Padmaavat star in a black organza sari with a webbed blouse, unlike anything we've seen before. column1: 14 silk camisoles you can buy online now for your summer wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion No better way to beat the heat In the coming months, the temperatures are going to start hovering between exhausting and torturous, and you need to prep your wardrobe for it. Swap your basic T-shirt for a silk camisole to combat the struggles of this season. Whether you're looking to elevate your formal look or give your date night outfit a stylish spin, a breezy silk camisole will do the trick. The simple silhouette continues to be favoured for its easy, versatile aesthetic. Style it with a pair of stone washed jeans under a denim jacket, or tuck it inside a skirt—you don't need to think too hard with this summer staple. Wear H&M's nude silk number with a pencil skirt for a stellar evening look, or take the retro route and invest in Ganni's polka dotted camisole. Flaunt your collar bones in Iro's white number or step inside Prabal Gurung's colour blocked camisole to add some character to your outfit. You can also add some visual interest to your basic white T-shirt by throwing on Anomaly's silky black number on top. And if subtle hues are too low key for your taste, pick a playful striped Diane von Furstenberg camisole, or go with Gucci's floral number. Cushnie et Ochs flirty rani pink silk top paired with a pleated black skirt is the ideal pick for a date night outfit. Amp up your evening look with the way of classic gold hoop earrings and strappy heels. From brightly hued to ones with lacy detailing, scroll through our edit of best silk camisoles to try this summer. column1: Guess which Indian designer Vidya Vox is collaborating with?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion First of its kind If you're one of Vidya Vox's four million subscribers, you'll know that the YouTube sensation's Indian roots and American upbringing come together not only in her viral videos, but also in her personal style. So it's no surprise that Anita Dongre's east-meets-west label Global Desi has tapped the artist to kick start their new music property #VoiceYourStyle—a collaboration with Indian musicians from across the world. Vox's exclusive track, Minnale (Tamil for lightning), shows the label's India-inspired, summer separates finding the perfect backdrop in LA's gritty landscape. Vogue sits down with her to get in on all the details. Tell us about your collaboration with Global Desi. How did it come about? I first discovered Global Desi when I was living in Mumbai, and I've been wearing their pieces for a few years now. The label was also a partner for a couple of my live shows in Mauritius. We've been fans of each other, so the collaboration felt only natural. Take us through the making of the video. What was the most exciting aspect? Shankar [Tucker] and I had an idea for this tune—something dreamy, soulful but upbeat and funky. We were excited about the idea of lightning and thunderstorms, about how they can be beautiful and powerful but also cathartic at the same time; similar to the relationships most of us have experienced in our lives. Once we had the song down, Shankar had the idea of combining the gritty LA scenery and rooftops with neon lighting, which exemplifies the dreamlike feeling. The most exciting aspect was seeing it all come together in the editing process. We couldn't be happier with the way it turned out. What are some of the similarities between music and fashion? Music and fashion, like many other creative endeavours, are deeply personal expressions of creativity. It's so subjective and relative to each person, and there is room for everyone to express their voice through it. I always say fashion is so powerful because you can say so much without speaking even a word. Music is similar to that; you can channel your emotions and experiences and weave that story in a song. How do the pieces from Global Desi fit into your bold wardrobe? Global Desi fits into my wardrobe so well because their clothes bring India-inspired prints to western silhouettes, like a fusion of sorts—much like my music, which combines traditional and contemporary elements. What made LA the right backdrop for the video? LA was perfect for the video because it was all about bringing life, creativity and colour to bold urban landscapes. The grittiness of the rooftops contrast well with the colours of the clothes, and the femininity of the jewellery, while maintaining the energy of the city and the song (through the dance) at the same time. What, according to you, does Global Desi stand for? The label is bold and unapologetic, yet colourful and warm. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How to find the best swimsuit for you in your 20s
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It’s time for the sun and the sand Along comes summer, with its sultry promise of lazy days by the beach doing absolutely nothing, with salt in your hair, sand in your eyes and a break-the-internet worthy Instagram snap to show for it. The latter, of course, calls for a showstopper swimsuit that makes you look good, and feel even better. But if you thought that swimsuit shopping meant a binary choice between coverage or comfort, think again. Inspiration, as always, isn't far away. The petite Disha Patani regularly strikes Instagram gold with her swimwear choices that feature an on-trend rota of mesh pieces, lively silhouettes and itsy-bitsy bottoms. Sonakshi Sinha, on the other hand, refuses to succumb to a monotonous tankini, and instead looks to vibrant prints to liven up her frequent sojourns to the beach. View Gallery 10 Photos How to work swimsuits in your 20s The 20s mean that you have a sartorial clean slate to be whoever you want to be, so dive headfirst into the possibilities. Make the most of your 20s bod by never repeating the same silhouette twice–which shouldn't be tough, because your options are many and varied, from the humble onesie to a head-turning bandeau bikini to criss-cross plunging necklines. When it comes to fabric, eschew the age-old Lycra in favour of on-trend options like crochet and mesh inserts. Now is the time to play up the drama, so say yes to everything from metallic crossbody embellishments to beaded halter necks. Of course, with great swimsuits come great accessorising possibilities, so look to a slogan ‘Do Not Disturb' floppy beach hat to serve as the perfect foil for your OOTD. The world of cover-ups has received a modern update as well, and the candidates for your dash from the pool to the bar include crochet palazzos, sheer kaftans and tie-dye sarongs. Leave the earrings at home, and instead slide on a pair of statement sunglasses to make those heads turn. Not everyone can be comfortable with the amount of bared skin that traditional swimsuits demand, and not everyone should have to be. The crux of body positivity asks for you to be comfortable with your shape, exactly the way it is; you can then take an informed call on what works best for you to play up your assets. Scalloped two-pieces with a bow neckline work wonders for a smaller bust, while a retro high-waisted bottom promises coverage and sartorial savoir-faire, both at once. Geometrical patterns can help tone the figure, and a colour-blocked onesie can shave off a couple of inches from your silhouette, if needed. Find a swimsuit that makes you feel good, rather than trying to align your choices with the latest trends, and you won't find yourself fidgeting all day or longing for the safety of your cover-up. Focus your energies instead on ensuring that your choice of swimwear doesn't leave any room for malfunctions. There's a lot you can't control once you are in the water, so ensure that your suit fits you perfectly—when in doubt, make fast friends with double-sided tape. In the trial room while shopping, give equal importance to function as well as fashion. That plunging neckline on the bikini top may look good on the mannequin, but if you can't move in it without courting disaster, opt for a more fitted neckline that will hug your skin better. column1: Jacqueline Fernandez launches her own active wear brand
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Give your workout wear a ‘Just F’ upgrade Jacqueline Fernandez is on a roll. With multiple brand endorsements, shoots, and a new venture into the food industry with her Sri Lankan based restaurant Kamae Sutra (which launched in December last year), you'd think she already has enough on her plate. But too much to do and too little time never stopped Fernandez from pursuing what she believes in. And the actor is back at it again with the launch of her new feminine active wear brand, Just F. “Just F, as an idea, came to me through my agent and manager, Anirban Das Blah,” says Fernandez. “It was basically about setting up a product that revolved around the world of fitness for women. As a consumer, and as someone who has a passion for fitness, I noticed that I just wasn't able to find the right clothes to work out in the country. We realised that there is a gap in the market for this. That's when we decided to set out on this journey to make sure that whoever you are, and whatever type of woman you are—whatever your size is, how your personality is—you'd be able to find something to work out. And well, that's what Just F is.” Co-created and co-owned by Mojostar and Fernandez, Just F is a move to redefine the space of female active wear in India. Designed for the trendy and free-spirited 20-something girl, the line will cover a range of trends, and will eventually be divided into seven subsections—club-inspired, monochromes, florals, colour blocking, typography, a detailed collection of sports bras, and a core collection, which will be an essentials line. Fernandez tells us more about her journey, and what we can expect from her new brand. “To be honest, I wasn't too keen on the idea when it came to me. I knew that fashion isn't actually my forte; fitness is my forte. And I know that everyone's sort of jumping on this trend, and I didn't really want to follow the herd. But on second thought, it was the fact that we were venturing into something I truly believed in—into athleisure, fitness and lifestyle, which is something that I want to inspire in everyone—that made me realise that this is something I really want to do.” “The name took us a while to get to. The more we sat on it, the more we started thinking about the communication of the brand. And the communication was simple. It was reminding people that guys it's time to start giving an F about your life, and changing it for the better. Here, we are incorporating outfits for that you don't necessarily have to wear only to the gym. You can just make your everyday life more active. As someone who's been involved with fitness for so long, I know the benefits of it. And I know it can just change your life around. And that is exactly what I want to start infusing into people's mentality.” “The Just F girl can be anybody. Fashion for me is a form of art. You can judge it, but you can't completely critique it in a way that claims you're the only one who's right. You have to let people do what they want to do. The Just F collection has a plethora styles that cater to so many different people—personalities, types—because that's what we are. No two people are the same. Everyone has their own taste and their own choices, and you should be able to do and wear what you want to wear, without any judgement.” Check out her interview below Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Meghan Markle’s wedding dress: Meet the 8 designers in the running
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meghan Markle’s wedding dress is the most coveted fashion commission of 2018. But who’s the lucky designer behind the history-making garment? In anticipation, Vogue reviews the most likely contenders As details of the royal wedding come to light—the die-stamped, calligraphed invitations and the lemon and elderflower cake—the biggest question still remains unanswered; who will design Meghan Markle's dress? Once upon a pre-Prince Harry time, Markle opened up about her sartorial preferences. “Classic and simple is the name of the game, perhaps with a modern twist,” she said when Glamour asked her about her personal style in 2016. For a wedding dress, she revealed that she preferred something either “whimsical or subtly romantic.” She praised the bridal works of Delphine Manivet and Christos Costarellos for “their uniqueness and beauty,” and touted Elie Saab and J. Mendel to be “spectacular as well, especially for more structural designs.” For this historic gown, Markle has her pick of the fashion pack, be it a renowned British fashion house or an American label. The names she mentioned two years ago are long shots for her big day, to be sure. But they do give us a clue about the look she might go for; her own post-engagement, pre-wedding appearances do the same as well. Markle tends to go for generously cut jumpers, wide-leg trousers and midi skirts. She clearly prefers neutrals over colour, and oversized separates to tailored dresses. Her minimal, relaxed choices are more fashion-forward than we often see among the royals, and telegraph her California roots. Is she laying the groundwork for a similar vibe on her big day, or are we in for a royal surprise? It goes without saying that the pressure is unbearably high, for this one gown must do many things—be true to Markle, while also being fit for the royal family she is about to join and be appealing enough to be accepted by the throngs watching along at home. The upside for the label, however, is sizeable too—the chance to be world renowned and, one would presume, a considerable uptick in sales. Here is a look at all the likely contenders. The London-based couture label by Australian Tamara Ralph and her partner Michael Russo is considered the frontrunner, so much so that bookies suspended their bets on designer guessing in mid-March—bids re-opened soon after though, upon rumours of other contenders, and they currently stand at 1/3. Founded in 2007, Ralph & Russo was the first British brand to be invited to show on the official schedule at the Paris Haute Couture Week. Markle is a known fan—she wore a striking and unusually contemporary gown from the house for her engagement photos, with a sheer gold-embroidered top and black fringe-tiered skirt. The brand is definitely crème de la crème, with her engagement dress rumoured to have cost £56,000. But Markle may be looking to spread her designer love a bit. Ralph & Russo's designs can be quite revealing, which may not pass muster with the Queen herself. The celebrated British design house, helmed by Sarah Burton, is a favourite with Markle's soon-to-be sister-in-law, Catherine, the Duchess of Cambridge. Catherine selected Alexander McQueen and Burton to create her 2011 wedding gown, which was universally celebrated around the world. “Bride's Dress is a Flawless Success,” read a headline in the New York Times. Burton has dressed the Duchess for countless engagements in the seven years since, but that close relationship could play against McQueen when it comes to the Duchess's future sister-in-law. Who could blame Markle, who is already well aware of Catherine's long shadow, for wanting to stand apart on her big day? The designer, formerly known as Posh Spice, has allegedly struck up a friendship with Markle—a British tabloid reported the two bonded over beauty tips. Beckham and her brood split their time between London and Los Angeles, giving her and Markle much to talk about (along with their world-famous gentlemen). This commission would be a stretch for Beckham, as she is not known for evening wear. But her minimal and relaxed ready-to-wear collection is every bit Markle's royal vibe. The bride-to-be wore an off-white VB jumper on a recent appearance, prompting bookies to slash the odds. Safer bets are on Beckham designing the second dress of the day, for the much more private reception. The London-based designer has become one of the go-to dressers for the Duchess of Cambridge. Both of the frocks she wore to introduce her children to the world—the blue and white polka dot dress for Prince George's arrival, and the yellow floral ensemble for Princess Charlotte's debut—were Packham designs. She has also turned to the designer for formal state dinners and red carpet occasions in the past, including the BAFTAs. Packham's independent label is known for its old-school glamour and its bridal offerings (shown regularly at the New York Bridal Fashion Week), and would make a nice sartorial shout-out to Markle's home country. Erdem Moralıoğlu is a beloved figure on the British fashion scene and, more recently, a favourite of the Duchess of Cambridge, who wore two of his designs on her recent Scandinavian royal tour. An expert craftsman with the respect of fashion critics, Moralıoğlu is British by birth, but studied in Toronto—the city Markle called home while filming her television series, Suits. In her 2017 Vanity Fair cover story, Markle referred to Erdem as “a designer I've been wearing for years.” His designs are gorgeous, intricate and otherworldly—but predictably less princess-y than some of the other contenders. This could play in his favour, however, given Markle's sartorial preferences of late. Markle chose an Amanda Wakeley coat and dress for the Commonwealth Day Service—her highest-profile, pre-wedding engagement till date. Wakeley, also British, has an established wedding business and describes her aesthetic as “clean-glam”. The London-based designer has a longstanding rapport with the royals—in the brand's early days, more than 25 years ago, Princess Diana wore an emerald green two-piece skirt suit from Wakeley. While not an obvious choice, she's not to be ruled out just yet. If Markle wants to use her sartorial powers to help out a friend, she could have Nonoo design her dress. The Bahrain-born, London-raised, New York-dwelling Nonoo is friendly with both the bride and groom. It would be a bit of a reach for Nonoo, who is a relatively new designer known for her day wear. And Markle has already given her plenty of exposure. She famously wore Nonoo's oversize white poplin top—a style called ‘the Husband shirt'—when she first appeared with Prince Harry at the Invictus Games last year. Heads may roll if Prince Harry's future wife were to wear a non-British designer on her wedding day, which makes this pick mighty unlikely. But if Markle were to pledge allegiance to her American roots, Oscar de la Renta would provide all the glamour needed to fill St George's Chapel at Windsor Castle. The design house still teems with the stately legacy of de la Renta, who passed away in 2014, and is now infused with the fresh, young energy of Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia (the current design heads who studied under the late de la Renta). It is a long shot, to be sure, but what bride wouldn't want to wear Oscar down the aisle? column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Modern-day fairy tales If you follow Gucci's Instagram handle, you must already know of the label's love for cool underground artists from their feed. From modern interpretations of fairy tales to Ophelia floating on the river and knights in shining armour, texting and in possession of Gucci totes—Monreal's narrative is intriguing to say the very least. Adding a special touch is the packaging, which will feature the artist's work. Monreal worked on a special collection such as this one for Gucci's Gift Giving collection earlier last year. But the artist's first collaboration with Michele was for the #GucciGram project in 2015, the artworks from which were printed on T-shirts for the cruise 2018 collection. And that's not all—Monreal has also created wall art just off Brick Lane in London, inspired by Ignacio Zuloaga y Zabaleta's painting, Portrait of Señora de Garay, and the popular fairy tale, Rapunzel. column1: Kallol Datta on blurring the line between fashion and art
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue chats with the clothes maker as his eponymous label turns 10 Kallol Datta provokes. One look at his decade-old label (Kallol Datta 1955), and you will understand that his design lexicon boasts of an esoteric evolution of cloth with a detailed narrative. Ten years ago, the clothes maker (as he would like to be addressed) began his journey in the Indian fashion scene with his anti-fit clothes. For as long as we can remember, he has promoted his garments as sexless forms, emphasising that the cloth doesn't adapt to the body, the body adapts to the cloth. This remains his design philosophy. So, what has Kallol Datta been upto lately? Going by his social media feed, he has been sauntering around in the streets of London, Paris and Reykjavik—capturing them in colour film. “My friends are quite surprised by the recent influx of colour on my Instagram feed. I'm usually someone who sticks to blacks and whites,” he muses. A subconscious decision perhaps—his rendezvous with colour has trickled into his most recent collection titled ‘2018 Vol. 1'. “Not that I haven't used bright colours before, [but] the main state has always been monochrome with accents of colour. This collection, however, is visually a massive departure from the former,” he insists. The crux of Datta's design process involves dissecting the relations between body and fabrics. For this collection—which commemorates ten years of him as a clothes maker—he has experimented with native wear and reduced it to its contemporary best. As always, his clothes are a brooding reaction to the current zeitgeist (some would say, an extension of his personality). The silhouettes are intricately layered in silk-velvet, crepe and mulmul. The pieces are a sartorial manifestation of his thoughts on seclusion, almost as if they were forming a cocoon; a response to the melancholic state of the world. Once a regular at fashion weeks, Datta has grown to believe in producing one collection a year, stressing on the relevance of intelligent construction and pattern-making process. As someone who has insisted on blurring the line between fashion and art, his previous works demonstrate his beliefs. At Gallery Experimenter last year, he draped brass sculptures in robes of black silk and plastic—a conceptual approach titled ‘Random Access'. His autumn/winter 2013-2014 presentation is also one for the keeps. Shown at Mumbai's Project 88 gallery, he had his signature oversized tunics, but with the words ‘Quirky Print' printed on them—a call-out to the plagiarists. How has Kallol Datta and his brand evolved over the years? “I started off with working on my own—doing everything by myself, for myself. Time has led me to appreciate meaty collaborations (be it with photographers, designers from their respective fields or galleries), to redefine collaborative alliances and to add to my body of work.” Check out a few glimpses of his 2018 Vol. 1 collection, below: View Gallery 3 Photos 10 years of Kallol Datta Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Designer Philipp Plein tells us why age is just a detail
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And how never playing by the rules always worked for him High octane style is German designer's Philipp Plein's mantra. The designer is barely 40 years old, and already has over 120 mono brand stores all over the world. The law-student-turned-furniture-designer, who decided that fashion was his true calling, was a little known for several years. Today, he is a leather jacket must-have, and his rabble-rouser ramp shows at Milan Fashion Week are always one the highlights of the season. Known for his fantastical take on fashion, Plein is no stranger to the celebrity crowd either. In the March 2018 issue of Vogue India, Kim Kardashian West sizzled on the cover in a low cut, high slit black dress with chain detail straps by the designer. Plein was in Dubai recently for opening of his new flagship at The Dubai Mall. We caught up with the firebrand fashion designer then, to ask him more about his enfant terrible reputation. Do you believe you are the bad boy of fashion? I never played by the rules. I have always been different and independent. No loans, no funds—I built this group with just hard work. And since next year marks the 20th anniversary of the brand, I must have done something good. Is the story about a leather jacket with Swarovski skulls being your first dip into fashion, true? It was actually a military parka. I was making furniture at that time and needed something to fill a closet at a design fair. I bought a military parka from a bazaar and added a Swarovski skull at the back—my skull pillow was a bestseller, which is why I chose the motif. Everyone asked me what brand it was from, and if it was for sale. In fact, when the tenth person asked me the same question, I quoted a crazy price of like Euro 2,000. Then, I sold millions of them. At first, the powers that be at Milan Fashion Week did not want you to be on the calendar—does such rejection make you stronger? I am different, and this might annoy the bigger powers in fashion, but I let my success speak for me. I just keep doing what I do and dream bigger every day. Your clothes have such a strong handwriting. Can all women wear your clothes? My designs are for strong independent women. Attitude is key! Is there any age when you should tone it down? You must have heard the saying ‘mutton dressed as lamb'; what makes a woman guilty of this? I believe that everyone should feel confident in their clothes—as long as you aren't disrespectful, age is just a detail. Which is the one moment that you are most proud of? My fashion shows. I like to entertain and to present my collections with big productions, and I'm always very proud of them. column1: 10 times Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and Sabyasachi made a winning pair
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Remember that sari from Cannes? Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee's association is one that leaves little room for error. One of India's most loved designers meets the world's most beautiful woman—what's not to love? While the actor's extensive ethnic wear wardrobe often features Manish Malhotra's romantic creations, her love for Sabyasachi's drapes is no secret to star-watchers. Be it an award show, a movie premiere, or just a day out with her family—Aishwarya Rai Bachchan has a Sabyasachi ensemble for every occasion. The design label's old-world charm featuring high necklines, vintage embroideries, florals and a heavy dash of black perfectly falls in line with the star's personal aesthetic. In an interview, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's stylist, Aastha Sharma revealed, “Aishwarya has her own personality. She has been an icon for years, and is always appropriately dressed, so it's very easy for me as a stylist. I don't have to convince her to do anything—if it's an international red carpet event, we go all out because she is representing a brand and herself—it's almost a form of art. Back home, she favours Indian designers and has more understated sense of style.” For more than a decade now, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan has been spotted favouring knockout gowns while walking the annual red carpet in France. But that's not to say that she's left her roots behind. In 2010, the actor opted for a sheer Sabyasachi sari at the Cannes Film Festival. Paired with a simple black blouse, Rai Bachchan's heavily embellished nude sari made for a stunning red carpet outfit. Again, in 2013, while attending the celebration of a hundred years of Indian cinema at Cannes, she donned a dramatic black-and-gold velvet Sabyasachi sari. When the occasion demanded something subtle, the actor ditched busy numbers for lightweight kurtas and easy drapes. Case in point: the pastel pink kurta she was spotted in at an event in the city. While attending Lalbaug's Ganpati pooja however, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan went all out in a deep red Sabyasachi sari featuring gold border. Most recently, the Ae Dil Hai Mushkil actor stepped out in a golden kurta set and a pink brocade dupatta from the design house for another event. When it's time to go glam, Rai Bachchan is not afraid of choosing high-shine numbers. Last year, for the success party of her movie Sarbjit, she went the traditional route with a Sabyasachi ensemble. The actor chose a beige kurta that was intricately embroidered for the event. But her love for Sabyasachi is not limited to red carpet events. She was recently felicitated with the First Ladies Award by the President of India Ram Nath Kovind, and opted for a Sabyasachi sari for the evening. Even while receiving the award for best actress for Sarbjit at the Lions Gold Awards, Rai Bachchan channelled an all-white look in a cream and gold anarkali set by Sabyasachi. column1: 33 times Deepika Padukone’s gowns made it to the red carpet hall of fame
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Which of these is your favourite? Deepika Padukone and the red carpet are a match made in sartorial heaven. Whether she is channelling an unapologetically sexy vibe or going down the minimal route, the Padmaavat actor knows how to get people talking. In the past couple of years, Padukone has had a taste of global success, which has only made her lust-worthy wardrobe even stronger. Some of her favourite red carpet designers include Ralph & Russo, Gaurav Gupta, Gauri & Nainika and Tommy Hilfiger. From being on Vanity Fair's list of Hollywood's Next Generation to attending the Oscars after-party, the Met Ball and the 70th Cannes Film Festival, the actor never seems to drop the ball. At the 2016 IIFA awards, Padukone made headlines with her black custom-made Swapnil Shinde. While the plunging neckline added to the sex appeal, the extended net trail made for an arresting look. 2017 saw the actor pushing the envelope even further. From attending the xXx: Return of Xander Cage premiere in a sequinned Naeem Khan gown to the dramatic Gauri & Nainika number she wore for Filmfare Glamour and Style Awards, Padukone's arsenal of gowns has only grown stronger. In an interview, Padukone's stylist Elizabeth Saltzman revealed “I think she is open to learning and [is] excited [about it], so there are no demands. We work on everything together. The one thing I do ask of her and every client I work with is complete honesty and feedback, which I think is important.” Describing her personal style, Saltzman added “I think her style is classic with a twist. She can do sportswear really well, but I like that she looks great even in travel clothes. Her personal style is little bit bodycon, a little edgy—not funky-edgy, but interesting.” Padukone has been spotted stepping out in some scene-stealing numbers in 2018 as well. Recently, the actor won the Entertainer of the Year (Female) award at Hello! Hall Of Fame Awards in a white Falguni Shane Peacock outfit and then attended a magazine launch event in a black off-the-shoulder Amit Aggarwal gown. Since singling out one statement look is a particularly tough choice to make with a wardrobe as extensive as hers, we put together an edit of Deepika Padukone's best gowns looks over the years. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Take cues for your summer wardrobe This weekend was an exceptionally busy one for Bollywood celebrities. While Aishwarya Rai Bachchan (dressed in a pink Masaba lehenga) was honoured with the Woman of Substance title in Pune, Rani Mukerji continued to promote Hichki, this time in a summery black and white ensemble, and Riddhima Kapoor Sahni kept her look classic in Delhi wearing midnight blue from head to toe. column1: Designer Neeta Lulla has exciting news for Delhi brides
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Planning a wedding? You cannot miss this Delhi's DLF Emporio, a mall already studded with storied international and Indian brands, adds yet another to its luxurious repertoire this month. House Of Neeta Lulla opens its shutters on April 14, and invites its capital audience into a mesmeric world of drama, royalty and couture—all spread across 2,000sqft. Interior designer Rajeev Achari has filled the space with vintage chandeliers, rich tapestries and Victorian furniture. According to him, the only way to capture “the Neeta Lulla charm” was to make the space “indulgently opulent”. With bridal couture at its centre, the store will showcase Lulla's latest collections, including Legacy Of Qom, Timeless Markanda, Benarasi Charm and Edwardian Vanity—each as unapologetically glamorous as the next. This store is all set to be the one-stop for all fairy tale-loving brides and trousseau hunters. The entire process of conceptualising and setting up the new space has Lulla both thrilled and overwhelmed. “It's like the birth of a new baby,” she says. “[There are] a lot of mixed feelings of excitement, anxiety, stress; but somewhere, this complements the inner creative instinct I possess.” The store also marks the expansion of the brand into the big fat Delhi market. While clients from the city have always been on her roster, the designer revealed that “45 per cent of my clientele hails from Delhi NCR”. This will be her first physical space in the city. Lulla sees this as a stepping stone to her larger plan of expanding her brand across cities all over India, over the next five years. She tells us more about her new space. Why Delhi, why now? Delhi has always been one of my key markets for a flagship store, and our physical presence was much needed. We wanted to secure the right location, and DLF came in at the right time. What is the experience you want to create for shoppers through this new space? We want our clientele to feel unique. Our motto has always been to ‘be your own bride', and it will reflect strongly in the experience. We want our clients to feel beautiful and confident in their own style statements, while we accentuate their core persona through our styling. Victorian grandeur and a palatial aesthetic seems to capture the Neeta Lulla charm. What inspired the decor and feel of the new space? I have always been inspired by cinema, royalty and heritage, and it is something that I feel passionately about. Rajeev Achari designed the space keeping my style in mind. Each element of the space shimmers and glows—the rich metallic textures adding a sense of romance to the ambience, and the heavy embellishment evoking a palatial feeling of royal aesthetic. The hint of rose gold tones on the furniture and frames, coupled with the chandeliers, give a sense of opulence. The frame-within-a-frame aesthetic of the store entrance, on the other hand, gives it the feeling of being a canvas, with all the elements within inspired by an artist's imagination. The space and the clothing complement each other—the antique charm brings out the luxury of the brand, creating the effect of a story in which the store is the stage and her designs, the characters on it. Neeta Lulla at DLF Emporio Mall, 4, Nelson Mandela Road, Vasant Kunj, New Delhi. Tel: 011-46116666, opens on April 14 What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast
