column1: From Nike to Jimmy Choo: Virgil Abloh’s best collaborations to date
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Since its 2013 launch, Virgil Abloh’s label Off-White has become known for its fusion of streetwear and high fashion, as well as its compelling line-up of hype-generating collaborations. As he is named the new men’s wear designer at Louis Vuitton—the heritage brand that itself hit big with its Supreme collab last year—Vogue looks back at the partnerships that Virgil Abloh is best known for Virgil Abloh may have risen to prominence as Kanye West's creative consultant, but through a series of high-profile collaborations and one-off projects, he's become a name in his own right—more so now that he has been appointed as Kim Jones's successor at Louis Vuitton. Through his label Off-White (which he insists is not a clothing line, but “a vehicle to express ideas”), Abloh has redefined the way sportswear is perceived, democratised design and won countless awards—including the Urban Luxe Award at the Fashion Awards last December. Along the way, he's gained a legion of famous fans too, from A$AP Rocky and Kendall Jenner to Naomi Campbell. Nike, Levi's and Jimmy Choo are among his many hype-inducing fashion collabs, but Abloh's multidisciplinary practice has taken the peripatetic polymath further afield. Earlier this month he unveiled his first fragrance, Elevator Music, created with cult Swedish brand Byredo, and he's worked with everyone from breakout rapper Lil Uzi Vert to artist Jenny Holzer. Most recently he teamed up with frequent Louis Vuitton collaborator Takashi Murakami to put on a show at the Gagosian Gallery during London Fashion Week. He's even lent his hand to Ikea's signature Frakta bag, with furniture soon to follow. Not to mention his “personal” “belongings” suitcases for Rimowa. Such an output, he told The New York Times during the weekend, “has been to make a compelling case for me to take on a role such as this,” referring to his appointment as Louis Vuitton's next men's artistic director. The French fashion house has had its fair share of streetwear success too, namely with the sellout collaboration with Supreme. While the fashion world awaits to see what form Abloh's Louis Vuitton collaborations will take, Vogue rounds up the Off-White founder's best collaborations to date. The blockbuster collab with the sportswear brand is perhaps Abloh's most popular. In two separate drops across different cities around the world, Abloh deconstructed 10 of Nike's most iconic trainers—including the Air Jordan 1, the Nike Blazer, the Nike Air Presto, the Nike Air Max 90 and the Nike VaporMax. Some styles had very subtle changes—the placement of the logo overlapping with the sole of the Blazer, for example—where others were more dramatic, exposing the internal functionality of the shoes often hidden in traditional designs. Created for Made & Crafted, Levi's premium line, Abloh's 11-piece collection from 2016 brought the denim brand's working roots into a contemporary setting. The gender-neutral designs included classic 501 jeans and tucker jackets, spliced with clean lines of contrasting white or bright yellow. Abloh and Jimmy Choo's Sandra Choi first bonded over a shared love for Comme des Garçons at New York Fashion Week, but it was their ladylike collaboration that the fashion crowd bought into. Inspired by the style of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, for Off-White's spring/summer 2018 show, their collection proved to be Instabait gold—see the “glass slipper” stilettos wrapped in cling film and quilted, 1980s-issue boots. Last summer, Abloh put his spin on sunnies with American brand Warby Parker. The three frames—all based on the same sleek, black unisex style as a base—were available in three different sizes: small, medium and large. They retailed at only 95 USD and sold out immediately. Inspired by football culture, Abloh's take on the British sportswear brand was quickly adopted by the likes of Bella Hadid and Justin Bieber—both were spotted in the plaid shorts. The flannel shirts were also a huge success too, as was Abloh's take on the classic Coach sneaker, which he reimagined with premium leather, additional stitching and the Off-White logo on the heel. Though the streetwear and sneaker emporium is no stranger to long queues of shoppers, the most buzzed-about drops were 2017's capsule collections with Abloh. The limited-edition collections—“Off-Palette” dropped in March and “Just Global” in October—included his quintessential oversized hoodies, crewneck jumpers and T-shirts, rendered in soft pastels for spring, and in a strict black and light grey palette for winter. Marrying urban style with luxury sensibility, Abloh's collaborated with the Italian ski wear label on a number of capsule collections. “Moncler O” in June 2016 was inspired by the high seas, and was translated to a wardrobe of fisherman yellow puffers, fuzzy hoodies and rubberised parkas. “Black Swan” in February 2017 played with the logos of both labels to create a medley of white stripes and plenty of arrow prints. The iconic Dr. Martens Talib boot got the Off-White treatment for the autumn/winter 2016 show—full leather uppers in midnight black and cobalt blue, matched with colour-coordinated rubber soles and slashes at the ankle. Abloh's signature was applied to two premium Les Boots for retail, too. The black and tan boots came with contrasting laces. "The clothing was created at a 50 per cent capacity,” Abloh told i-D at the time of his collaboration with online retailer Ssense and fashion photographer Pierre Debusschere. “Only after we did the film [with Debusschere] would the 100 per cent identity of the clothing be finished.” Dubbed “Before and After”, the collection started off as a unisex collection of all-white trousers, hoodies and jackets with black diagonal stripes, rendered kaleidoscopic when models jumped on mattresses covered in pigments. column1: Meet the cool crusaders of conscious clothing
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion New do-good labels to add to your shop list Update your know-how of ethical labels with our list of new brands to know. Honest By, Bruno Pieters (Belgium) [#image: /photos/5ce41f249cc0c03a4cf9c47b]||| ||| Bruno Pieters has worked for brands like Christian Lacroix and Martin Margiela, and was the creative director of Hugo, the avant garde line of Hugo Boss. But travelling for two years across India changed everything for him. He made a radical shift in his outlook on life, and through his new line—Honest By—he put his focus on environment, animal welfare and children's causes. Today his label is the world's first 100 per cent transparent company, and a pioneer in price transparency. His minimalistic designs use organic materials and have delicate architectural nuances, making them both superbly modern and sustainable. Honestby.com   Kings Of Indigo, Tony Tonnaer (The Netherlands) [#image: /photos/5ce41f233bf9b43c78b1b7bb]||| ||| Designer Tony Tonnaer makes ‘veggie jeans' from 100 per cent indigo. Since 2013, his collection has expanded to shirts, tops and dresses—all made using natural dyes extracted from the Indigofera plant in India, entirely devoid of chemicals. The label's acronym K.O.I is also the name of a Japanese fish that is a symbol of wisdom and happiness and one of the few fishes that swim against the current. K.O.I is a member of the Fair Wear Foundation, which means the brand practises fair trade, is not mass-produced and instead focuses on small collections of clothes made from organic cotton, recycled jeans and Tencel. The brand is future-focused and is actively innovating and experimenting with materials like hemp and flax (both require very little water, no chemicals, and grow quickly). Kingsofindigo.com  8 Eden Avenue, Jessica Gruner (Germany) [#image: /photos/5ce41f23b803114bd78f5d73]||| ||| The hallmark of this brand is luxurious, Camembert-soft cashmere. Founder Jessica Gruner, who launched the brand in Munich, struck gold—one collection of cashmere came from the same herd of cashmere goats in Mongolia that supplies to Hermès, and her Indian business partner was able to get access to it. Gruner, who worked as product designer for Cerruti, Adidas and Diesel, went solo with dreams of empowering women through design, and now, her scarves are handwoven by the 800-strong workforce of Mukti Datta's cooperative Panchachuli Women Weavers. Add to that the traditional silk ari embroidery, a type of chain stitch associated mostly with India, and you have designs that will be appreciated for generations. 8edenavenue.com  Lemlem, Liya Kebede (USA) [#image: /photos/5ce41f239cc0c05ea4f9c475]||| ||| For this supermodel, actor and WHO Goodwill Ambassador, her hometown of Addis Ababa is the ultimate inspiration for her collection. Liya Kebede's brand LemLem, which means ‘blossom and thrive', focuses on the indigenous skills and handmade textiles of Africa, a tribute to the variety of talent that the continent has to offer. It is, she says, as much about creating timeless pieces as it is about generating jobs in Africa. Her bright-coloured, easy, resort-centric collections come from Rwanda, Ethiopia, Madagascar and Kenya so far, but she intends to bring other African countries into the fold and celebrate the works of exceptional artisans in the entire continent. Her design repertoire is delicious—pinstripes, abstract prints and embroideries adorn clothes that are simple but fun to wear anywhere in the world. Lemlem.com  Living Blue, Mishael Aziz Ahmad (Bangladesh) [#image: /photos/5ce41f24cc50be386413e4bd]||| ||| Mishael Aziz started with a big dream—allow farmers, especially women, in the northern part of Bangladesh to supplement their wages from arduous agricultural work with skills that are intrinsic to that region. First, the area is a very well-known source for the indigo plant; second, it is recognized for quilting and hand-embroidery. Living Blue combines both these assets and makes a collection of kimonos, head wraps and scarves. Many of the workers in Living Blue are landless farmers. Aziz Ahmad leases fallow lands from the government, provides the farmers with indigo seeds and eventually purchases the crop from them. Livingbluebd.com  Learn more about ethical practices in fashion with our Sustainability Matters series Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Lehengas: Everything you ever wanted to know about this wedding staple
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Its history, celebrity patrons and best ways to wear it; all in one neat list Circa 2018, the lehenga is an indispensable staple in every Indian traditional wear wardrobe. In fact, you may be hard-pressed to remember a time when the silhouette did not feature prominently in your festive celebrations—it was probably a part of your first Diwali when you twinned with your excited mum, your school annual day cultural event, your elder sister's wedding, and even your own engagement. And it's not just you—we're talking the collective (sartorial) consciousness of the entire country that continues to be enchanted by the lehenga's timeless appeal, even after all this time. The lehenga is believed to have originated during the Mughal era, largely owing to the dynasty's patronage of exquisite craftsmanship and elaborate finery. From being a noblewoman's attire of choice to a trousseau necessity, it has retained its essence through the years, while also artfully adapting itself to the mindset of the succeeding generations. From cues on how to make the lehenga work for you on various occasions to celebrity inspiration, Vogue puts together the only thorough dossier you need to bookmark. View Gallery 24 Photos Lehengas: Everything you ever wanted to know about this wedding staple – celebrities Be it wedding functions or movie promotions, the lehenga is a unanimous favourite with the Bollywood celeb clan. From traditional weaves to contemporary sets, you will find ample inspiration to resonate with your personal style sensibility. Take Benarasi or brocade lehengas for instance—Kiara Advani advocates giving it a head-turning spin by wearing it with a teeny blouse, Athiya Shetty prefers restraint with the help of a modest peplum blouse, while Neha Dhupia is all about teaming it with a simple high-neck blouse. Take your pick. Style maven Aditi Rao Hydari often turns to the silhouette too, but mixes it up to create fresh looks every single time. You'll see her in a voluminous silk lehenga with an off-shoulder blouse minus the dupatta on one occasion, while on others, she'll wear the skirt with an asymmetrical tunic instead. Bollywood's new guard presents a masterclass in wearing the lehenga with a millennial vibe, befitting your age. Get inspired by Alia Bhatt's corset blouse or Khushi Kapoor's strapless swing blouse for the next wedding you're due to attend. Though you can't go wrong with the tried-and-tested manner of wearing the lehenga set, there may be times when you yearn to give it a more au courant twist. Switching up the blouse is an easy way to achieve this. Skip the traditional choli in favour of its new-age successors like capes, crop tops, floor-length jackets, off-shoulder blouses or cropped boxy shirts. Then go a step ahead and add look-at-me embellishments such as dramatic sleeves, fringed embellishments and sheer bodice detailing. Though Indian in origin, you can style your lehenga right to give it a contemporary update and mirror your global lifestyle. Replace the blouse with a luxurious white silk shirt, cinch it with a belt picked up on your travels and forgo those jhumkas in favour of avant-garde jewellery by international labels. And then, shock some more by rounding off this look with your coveted sneakers instead of the juttis you were expected to wear it with. There is no denying the must-have status hand-embroidered lehengas have in one's personal collection. But it's the impact-generating, versatile disposition of the modern printed lehenga that has made it a go-to for Indian women today. The lehenga is that one sacrosanct silhouette around which an entire bridal wardrobe is generally centred. Even so, this time-honoured tradition has not escaped a present-day makeover. For instance, bridal red is no longer the norm for one's pheras. From pastel hues (Anushka Sharma made a strong case for blush pink with her bridal attire) to ivory, the entire Pantone wheel is yours to choose from. And while the lehenga lends itself to all your wedding functions like a seasoned expert, don't shy away from experimenting with silhouettes based on the event in question. A palazzo-lehenga hybrid is a fitting choice for the mehandi, while ruffles will do the trick for your sangeet. If you consider the wedding season a legitimate excuse to go extra with your wardrobe, then what you need is a bevy of lehengas to catapult into the belle of the baraat. Turn to head-to-toe embroidered ones for a palace wedding, printed sets for beachside ceremonies and heirloom treasures for family celebrations. A friend's wedding is an opportune occasion to give all those trending blouses a go while your brother's wedding is license to steal the spotlight in a more-is-more creation. From inspiration for your best friend's wedding to your own nuptials, scroll through our gallery ahead for some of the most striking designer lehengas spotted on the runway. column1: 14 times Aishwarya Rai Bachchan aced Manish Malhotra’s designer ensembles
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A match made in sartorial heaven Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's love for designer Manish Malhotra is nothing if not obvious. From stunning gowns and tasselled saris to embroidered lehengas, the couturier's extravagant designs and his love for high-octane glamour has made him Bollywood's favoured designer. Malhotra's aesthetic matches perfectly with Rai Bachchan's elegant yet statement-making style. Indian ethnic wear by the designer in particular, is a much-loved addition in Rai Bachchan's wardrobe. Whether it's working an intricate anarkali at a friend's wedding or donning a lehenga set for a media event, the actor has worn it all. When the occasion doesn't warrant ethnic dressing, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan prefers Malhotra's scene stealing gowns. From a grey satin number embellished with floral details to a sleek floor-sweeping ensemble, the actor has been seen in multiple floor grazing dresses over the years. When it comes to dressing up, the former Miss World has been favouring couturier's work since the beginning, be it at international red carpet events, Diwali Pujas or family weddings. "I first met him in 1993,” Aishwarya Rai Bachchan once told Vogue in an interview. “At that time he was just starting out with a little bit of designing around here. He had made the clothes for a commercial of mine, and that's where we first met. I think it's just amazing how he has pursued his passion with absolute conviction and focused direction. I love his work and the dedication he does it with.” While attending Anushka Sharma and Virat Kohli's star studded wedding reception, the Ae Dil Hai Mushkil actor favoured an ivory high-shine lehenga choli by Manish Malhotra. As is the designer's signature, the lehenga was embellished with thread, lace and pearls. The actor paired it with a long choli and a sheer dupatta sporting delicate pearl detailing. Recently, Rai Bachchan channelled a similar look when the actor attended the Smile Train India event in yet another pristine white anarkali. And that's not all. To support her close friend and designer for his special showcase—titled ‘The Gold Story' at the HT Most Stylish Awards—Rai Bachchan chose a midnight blue and mint green lehenga from his collection. Malhotra's work as a costume designer in Bollywood has received considerable applause too. He created stunning outfits for Anushka Sharma's Alizeh and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's Saba in Karan Johar's cinematic emotional rollercoaster, Ae Dil Hai Mushkil. Rai Bachchan played a poet in the movie, and was styled in elegant, sophisticated pieces. In 2015, the veteran designer completed 25 years in the industry. The designer celebrated the milestone moment with an extravagant grand finale at Amazon India Couture Week, with Aishwarya Rai Bachchan returning to the ramp after five years. For the big day, Rai Bachchan played showstopper in a detailed burgundy and gold lehenga set. Before that, the actor was seen walking the ramp for Malhotra in 2010. But it's not just Aishwarya Rai Bachchan who is a fan of Manish Malhotra. The superstar's daughter Aaradhya Bachchan has also been dressed by the ace designer. While hitting the international turf for the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne (IFFM), the mother-daughter duo twinned in custom-made Manish Malhotra ensembles. While the global icon chose a white and pastel blue studded anarkali, the little one was decked up in a white lehenga and choli set. For her sixth birthday, Aaradhya Bachchan celebrated an Enchanted Meadow-themed birthday party in a flouncy pink Manish Malhotra number, embroidered with colourful blooms. column1: The interesting 122-year history of the Louis Vuitton’s monogram
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We tell you all about it Louis Vuitton announced the appointment of  Virgil Abloh as its menswear artistic director. As such, Abloh will become the latest designer to reinterpret Vuitton's 122-year-old logo. Before Alboh there were Nicolas Ghesquière's's runway reworks (Marc Jacobs's before him), Takashi Murakami's Pop-minded collaboration of 2003, Catherine Deneuve's traveling trunks, and Dapper Dan's knock-ups made in his boutique on East 125th Street in Harlem. But of course, how you know the monogram isn't what matters—it's that you know it. The interlocking L and V with floral pattern was designed by Louis Vuitton's son, Georges Vuitton, in 1896 as a way to brand his nascent box and luggage business, and in the 120 years since, it's become one of the most recognisable marks in the world. Within the fashion arena, the LV monogram is having something of a resurgence. Since Ghesquière was named artistic director in 2013, the designer has made a point of incorporating it into his collections in new and novel ways—the floral-shaped heels of his spring 2015 boots are an example of the same. Abloh's predecessor Kim Jones also had his way with the logo, using it in a Supreme collaboration in 2017 and as his sign-off from the maison during his final fall 2018 menswear show. Here, a look back at the storied history of Louis Vuitton's iconic LVs. Let's see where Virgil takes them this June. column1: How to choose a wedding lehenga in your 20s
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion No pressure; it’s only the most crucial OOTD of your life If you thought that finding someone you'd want to spend the rest of your life with was the hard part, welcome to the complicated world of organising the wedding itself. The task of finding the perfect lehenga can seem easy on paper (given that you've may been visualising this day since you were five), but the liberty of having more choices means having to make tougher decisions. Should you go with your mum's heirloom zardozi masterpiece or step out of tradition with an all-out glam number? Should you be sitting with colour swatches to coordinate with your to-be or playing it safe with the trusted red-and-gold staple? While we can't rope in Cinderella's benevolent godmother to drop by with your dream bridal look in tow, we can help make the legwork easy for you. Here's all that you need to know before picking your wedding lehenga. View Gallery 9 Photos Wedding Lehengas in your 20s Your eyesight hasn't suddenly been reprogrammed to think in pastels. It's Anushka Sharma who holds the blame for your avid obsession with fairy tale hues. The 29-year-old actor paid homage to the postcard-perfect backdrop of Tuscany, Italy with a blush pink masterpiece from Sabyasachi. Meanwhile, 25-year-old Alia Bhatt makes the most of having age on her side with a string of fun lehengas with interesting cutouts that do justice to all the hours she clocks in at the gym, and complements them with on-trend hair accessories. The only rules are that there are no rules. The 20s provide a sartorial carte blanche for you to be whoever you want to be. Want that fairy tale wedding with all the bells and whistles? Opt for something dramatic with just the right amount of bling from Manish Malhotra. Looking to paint a more sophisticated picture? Sabyasachi invites you to partake in his world of elegance and ethereal couture. Shyamal & Bhumika know exactly what clicks with the millennial crowd, while Falguni and Shane Peacock are here to help you make an entrance. However, your 20s also probably mean that you are just making your way up the corporate ladder. Budgets will definitely help you from going overboard, but if you ever find yourself in the place where you need to pick between your ideal outfit or an elaborate real jewellery set to go with, go for the lehenga—it definitely deserves to be the star of the show. As your career advances, there will be plenty of chances to invest in real diamonds and jewels, but your wedding day will come just this once. You'll find that costume jewellery or a statement kundan set will work just as well with your lehenga, while still helping you stay on-trend. Or if you are daring enough to push the envelope, take notes from Bhatt, who walked the ramp for Manish Malhotra last year with a high bun and a marked absence of jewellery, letting her statement lehenga do the talking instead. When it comes to your wedding lehenga, everyone has an opinion and a vision for what it should look like. It can be easy to get swept away by all the chatter, but ensure that your final choice remains true to yourself. Your lehenga needs to be an extension of your personality; so if you personally prefer muted colours and neutrals, don't bow in to pressure and opt for a siren red number just because tradition dictates so. Know your options, research well and make an informed choice that will see you through the ages. column1: New label to know: Les Héroïnes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Resolving a bridesmaid’s dress conundrum Who: Founded by Australian born stylist Vanessa Cocchiaro, Les Héroïnes is the answer to the woes of a bridesmaid who doesn't want wear the same, unimaginatively tailored dress or gown as her fellow bridal party members. The French label for occasion-wear offers a curated collection for women across all ages, with individualistic style and taste. What's endearing is that each piece from the label is named after women who are real life heroines—Rosa Parks, Simone de Beauvoir, Maya Angelou and even Cocchiaro's mother, who she pays sartorial homage to with a jacket named after her (Antonietta).  Stemmed from her personal experience as a bridesmaid, the label's vision is to give bridesmaid attires a contemporary touch, so that they can be worn again. “Our heroines are the people who mean something special to us. They are our inspirations, our confidantes, our companions. They're the ones that stand alongside us during our most important moments. For every bride on her wedding day, her bridesmaids are her heroines—a unique group of friends, fellow adventurers and cherished companions chosen to come together to share in this special day,” reads the brand's about section. The brand is also known to be promoting body positivity and is inclusive of all sizes. Signature: A minimal, relaxed aesthetic—ranging from suits to chic cocktail dresses. Key pieces to own: Les Héroïnes' aesthetic is such that their pieces need not be reserved only for weddings. You can recycle the looks for other formal occasions too. column1: These are the best designer blouses to pair with your favourite silk sari
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's how you can revamp the silk sari that you've sported one too many times Investing in luxurious traditional Indian wear can possibly plant one in the centre of a catch-22 situation. You (understandably) want to get maximum wears out of your beautiful new buy; but you don't want the naysayers to go all Regina George on you for “wearing the same silk sari two weddings in a row,” either. The answer lies in reworking your outfit in a way that instantly gives it a fresh appeal. Take your collection of handwoven saris for instance. Your first designer purchase, or time-honoured silks lovingly passed on by your grandmother, are often cherished wardrobe treasures, and nothing should stop you from sporting them at back-to-back festivities. A quick switch of the blouse can easily make the sari as good as new again. Vogue spares you the trouble of styling with a guide on the best blouses to wear with your favourite silk saris. Sari champion Deepika Padukone's repertoire is a masterclass on the styles that work best. Often seen in silk saris by designers like Sabyasachi and Raw Mango, she prefers to go the classic route by pairing them with modest high-neck blouses. But don't write this off as boring. It's the restrained nature of this blouse that adds the appeal to the outfit. You can also give it some sartorial relevance by experimenting with the sleeves or opting for a boxy fit, as opposed to a traditionally cut one. Kangana Ranaut and Anushka Sharma mirror similar aesthetics as Padukone. Have a look at how Bollywood does its saris here. View Gallery 8 Photos The best blouses for your silk sari celebs If you're drawn to a timeless sensibility, then traditional blouses will never disappoint you. Pair them with polki or jadau jewellery, and you have a fail-safe winner on your hands. But this is also the perfect opportunity to marry two different worlds in one look—traditional wear seems to be thriving on this very mood nowadays. And you don't need to go all ‘out with the old, in with the new' to achieve this. Pair your vintage (or brand new) silk sari with a contemporary blouse to give it a present-day update. Fringe, tassel and feather embellishments are one way to do it. Shirt blouses, capes and cinched jackets topped off with a belt promise to work just as well. Don't shy away from doubling that beadwork crop top you picked up on your last holiday as a sari blouse either. While mixing and matching is encouraged, make sure that the ultimate look is complementing, and not confused. Browse through our edit in the gallery below to make your pick. column1: These handbags are just as iconic as the women who inspired them
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Hermès’ iconic Birkin to Mulberry’s Alexa and Coach’s Selena Grace, luxury brands have a long tradition of naming cult handbags after stylish women. Vogue compiles a visual history of the most famous bags, as worn by the muses who inspired them From the Hermès Birkin and Kelly bags to Dior's Lady Dior, the history of cult handbags being named after fashion icons is a storied one. Though, not all bags named after these real-life women were designed with them in mind; some were renamed after the famous faces that carried them. Hermès' Kelly, known as the ‘Sac à Dépêches' for two decades prior, was rebranded after Princess Grace famously used it to shield herself (and her growing baby bump) from the paparazzi in 1956. Likewise, Dior renamed its Chouchou bag in 1996 after the late Princess Diana, who adopted the style as her own upon receiving one from Bernadette Chirac, France's first lady at the time. And who could forget the Jackie O? The Gucci Constance bag, originally created in 1955, was quickly renamed after the American first lady stepped out wearing it. There are cases of famous fashionistas designing eponymous bags too. The Birkin, for instance, was created by Hermès creative director Jean-Louis Dumas and the singer songwriter during a long haul flight in 1981. More modern incarnations of the iconic handbag may have come about less organically, but still to maximum effect. Salvatore Ferragamo threw its hat in the ring in 2009 with the Sofia bag, named after iconic actress Sofia Loren. British brand Mulberry made its name with a string of famous bags named after contemporary It-girls, including 2010's bestseller Alexa (named after Alexa Chung), the Del Rey (named after the “Young and Beautiful” singer) and the Cara (Delevingne). Coach too has followed suit, enlisting singer Selena Gomez to co-design the sellout Selena Grace in 2017. column1: 10 outfits to add to your wedding wardrobe if you want all eyes on you
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Perfect for the one who loves being the centre of attention If you find yourself identifying with all those "gauc is extra, but so am I" memes on the Internet, then chances are you don't cower in the face of extravagance. Most definitely not when your sartorial sensibility is involved. In fact, excess might be the very sentiment around which your entire wardrobe has been built. We're all for minimalism and a pared down aesthetic when the occasion calls for it, but if you're not entering the wedding season guns blazing, then why are you doing it at all? Dial up the flourish, and inject your wedding wardrobe with some fearless tongue-in-chic glamour. There might not be any street-style photographers whose eye (or camera lens) you can catch, but perhaps this individualistic statement will help you make it to the wedding video—and that's not half bad. If ‘more is more, and less is a bore' are keywords rather than buzzwords for you, putting bold looks together is probably second nature to you. If you find yourself stuck, just take a breath and think, “What would Iris do?” That's your starting point. Take outré international trends and wear them with an indigenous take. Print on print at the sangeet? All you need is a Benarasi lehenga paired with a brocade blouse in a clashing print, but with complementing colours. Ruffles, feathers and fringes—whether on your anarkali sleeve or your dupatta hems—are easy ways to get in the maximalist state of mind. Tried-and-tested bold colours and head-to-toe embellishments will always be there to do your bidding, but that's not to say soft hues can't create drama. For instance, a heavily embroidered blush-toned chikankari lehenga or sharara with jewels to match, is as look-at-me as it gets. Since we're talking weddings, it's the jewellery and accessories that will help you pack in that extra punch. You don't need to stop at the chandbalis and matching maang tikka for the fear of being too much. Go ahead and wear the layered necklace as well, if you so please. Instead of neutral-toned bags, pick ones that are statement-makers by themselves. A pearl-work potli or a bejewelled chain-strap bag might be more fitting choices. But bear in mind—OTT doesn't mean gimmicky. Brazen is an inherent attitude, and if you're only jumping onto a bandwagon, you're bound to slip. Maximalism and comfort are not mutually exclusive. Nothing should stop you from wearing sneakers under your heavy lehenga at the baraat, if dancing is the only thing on your mind. column1: A former Voguette’s tips on how to dress like a Parisienne
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Anne Benichou reveals her style secrets I must admit, I have a girl crush on Anne Benichou. There's just something so uniquely stylish about this former Voguette (she worked with the legendary Anna Wintour at the Parisian offices of Vogue Italia and Vogue France for a decade), that it's easy to get drawn in by her French charm. When I met Benichou for a breakfast meeting at the Ritz, Paris (a member of the Leading Hotels Of The World), earlier this year, she was wearing a gorgeous vintage Chanel skirt bought at a flea market with a black top, big statement earrings and Aquazurra suede ankle boots, complemented with a simple black clutch. Minimal makeup and coiffed hair completed her look. Benichou, who was incidentally in charge of the commercialisation of the ‘Temptation' Gallery at the iconic hotel, shares her secret to dressing up like a true Parisian. Sheree Gomes:  So, tell me, what's the starting point of a wardrobe according to you? Anne Benichou: I think accessories are key—they can change the way you look completely. SG: Are you saying you can just wear something black, throw on a pair of jeans and complement it with statement earrings like the ones you are wearing? AB: Absolutely! Mine are from a small boutique in Venice. When I open my closet, I think accessories first and then the rest. SG: What, according to you, are modern day classics? AB: White shirts, perfectly cut jeans, black stilettos and clutches. SG: How much of one's wardrobe should be an investment and how much of it should be set aside for trendy stuff? AB: I would invest in classics (every lady should definitely own the 2.55 Chanel bag). Of course, you should look at what's trending at the moment and be informed of what's in fashion, but in my opinion, classics remain. More importantly, you should create your own style—this is really important. Most people today just follow trends and don't seem to have their own style SG: How important do you think is investment buying? Would you put it right up there? AB: No, not really. My job at Vogue was to pick all the accessories, but not the high-end ones like Chanel, Tod's, Gucci etc. I had to find the right accessories, but not too expensive. You can have fantastic budget pieces mixed with all the new brands. I'm not too much into high-end clothing either—I don't think it's always worth it. SG: What according to you are the rules for layering? Most French women seem to get it right. AB: Yeah, it's a part of the French ladies' vibe—you can recognise them immediately when they enter the lobby. In Paris, we have so many options besides all the high-end and high-street brands. You can go to the flea markets and get the best one-of-a-kind vintage pieces like this Chanel skirt I am wearing. I like going to Les Puces de Saint-ouen, especially on a Sunday. SG: What do you think are the common mistakes women make when dressing up? AB: Mixing too many colours—I think you have to find the right balance. Another big mistake is putting on too much makeup. For the French lady it's really changed, she's now not wearing any makeup and looking very fresh now. Be natural—that would be my advice. SG: What are your tips for buying the right pair of jeans for your body type? AB: I love high-waisted Levi's jeans. The light blue is perfect with sneakers, stilettos or ankle boots. I tend to go to the same shop and buy the same pair of jeans, since they fit so well. If you find a brand that fits you well, stick to it. By all means, experiment with different brands, but at the end of the day go with the tried and tested. SG: What about shoes and jackets? AB: I am an absolute shoe woman. I love Aquazurra—it's one of my favourites. I'm wearing Aquazurra's suede ankle boots today. It's the perfect size—not too high and very comfortable. I need to be super comfortable with my shoes—I love Gianvito Rossi for stilettos and Chanel for ballerinas. SG: What are your favourite high street as well as high-end brands? AB: High street brand & Other Stories is great, and the flea markets, of course. High end—I love Australian fashion designer Alex Perry's style. I'm getting married next October and he's doing my wedding gown. I love wearing one strong piece; in my case it's mainly accessories. You have to have the right eye to pick the right accessory. Even if it's expensive, you can mix it with a simple pair of Levi's jeans, a crisp white shirt and flip-flops. SG: What are your tips for accessorising since accessories are key for you? AB: It has to make you feel pretty you know. And keep it understated. So if you are wearing a statement necklace, then go with smaller earrings. If you have big earrings, then wear nothing else or maybe just one ring. I love watches as well, antique ones. SG: What are this season's must haves? AB: This season I would say Chanel boots, in both silver and gold.  I have the medium size and I love them—the style is fantastic. The Saint Laurent bag is also very cool. I'd like to see what Hedi Slimane will do at Céline. Chloé is also nice—super feminine, elegant, trendy and fresh. SG: Dressing curvy women. How tough is that? AB: It's not that tough anymore. You just need to explore which brands are nice. Max Mara has opened their second line called Max & Co. where you can find beautiful things for curvy women. Curves are beautiful and are a part of being a woman—they should definitely be flaunted. SG: How important is age-appropriate dressing for you? AB: I think especially here, you will see many 50-plus women wearing shorts, skirts and high boots—I really don't think it's appropriate. You need to change your style as you age and accept the changes in your body. Every single age is an experience. Your life is a gift, so one must enjoy every decade of your life in a dignified manner. SG: On a completely different note, did you ever ‘eat' when you worked at Vogue Italia and Vogue France? At Vogue India, lunchtime is one of the most exciting times of the day. AB: Oh yes. I love Indian food—it's one of my favourites. I also love spicy food and I'm almost a vegetarian. But in the midst of relaxation and Easter weekend celebrations, make sure to take a moment out for a visit to No Borders—a vintage shop nestled in designer James Ferreira's 200-year-old bungalow. In the meandering lanes of Khotachi Wadi, an other-worldly lazy colony in Mumbai, the shop curated by multi-hyphenate Kanika Karvinkop is a respite from the fast pace of fashion and city life. No Borders houses vintage pieces from around the world (read: a Dior borrowed-from-the-boys jacket from the '80s and Alexander Wang's black canvas mini dress circa 2000) mixed with current collections by Indian designers like International Woolmark Prize winner Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice, Ekà and Péro by Aneeth Arora. But beyond the hand-me-down luxury staples, Karvinkop has managed to get her hands on collections by up and coming designers from Morocco, Ghana, Peru, Puerto Rico and art by emerging names like Ayqa Khan and Negine Jasmine. An upcoming collaboration for the store will see vintage Ralph Lauren, Dior and Levi's denim jackets upcycled by Péro in a limited edition collection. On her aim behind the store, she says, "No Borders is a concept store that focuses on diversity in fashion, culture and art. I'm always inspired by designers who focus on their country's heritage and use indigenous textiles. I spend a lot of time picking, choosing and curating artists that I like and think fit the ethos of the store. We focus on designers' stories, the people they work with and their backstory." On choosing a 200-year-old bungalow as the location she says, "The space is timeless, much like the clothes that reside in it. It's a complete misfit in the 21th century, but in a good way." For anyone interested in a visceral connection to clothes, head over here for nostalgic garments laden with wearers' stories. column1: Your guide to investing in jewellery when you get your first raise
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's everything you need to know How do you invest in jewellery when you finally get the raise that you deserve? We asked the experts. Caroline Scheufele, co­-president of Chopard gives her inputs on buying jewellery when you get your first raise. “For such an occasion, you're looking for a timeless buy, so something from Chopard's Happy Hearts collection is a great choice. The heart is a motif very dear to me and an important symbol for the label. It's a token of love and a lucky charm and the line interprets it with playful creativity.” For the fine jewellery fresher, Gemfields breaks down the four crucial Cs of gemstones. 1 Colour is defined by hue, saturation and tone. Hue describes the accuracy of the principal colour and the extent to which secondary colours are present. Saturation relates to the vividness, brightness or intensity, sometimes described as the amount of ‘life' in the gem. Tone is the lightness or darkness of a gem or the degree to which white or black appears to have been mixed in with the pure hue of the gem. 2 Clarity describes the extent to which a gemstone contains inclusions and fractures. The fewer the inclusions, the better, as this enhances transparency and brilliance. That said, emeralds are famous for having visible inclusions known as ‘jardins'. These feather-like inclusions give the gem its unique character. 3 Cut is typically divided into faceted gems (gems with geometrically shaped fl at faces) and non-faceted gems (gems with rounded surfaces, generally called cabochons). Value is enhanced when a gemstone is well proportioned, symmetrical, and possesses good lustre. 4.Carat takes its name from the ‘carob' seed, the original unit of measurement for gem traders. Today, a carat is equal to exactly 0.2 grams, meaning there are 5 carats in a gram. Each carat can also be divided into 100 points. View Gallery 4 Photos 1. column1: How to wear lehengas to weddings in your 40s
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Amp up the flare As the lehenga's current reincarnations assume a younger sensibility, it is easy to fall into the trap of believing that they are now best left to the millennials. But the age box you check on forms puts no restrictions on giving this time-honoured Indian wear staple a go for festive occasions. From wedding to festive parties, the lehenga still continues to be a winning choice even as you step into the fourth decade of your life. But how does one balance its modern avatar without entering into teenybopper territory? Vogue is here to guide you. Need a little help to get by? Borrow from the stars who wear it best. Karisma Kapoor prefers to wear the lehenga with her signature dose of elegance—restrained colours, heavy embroidery and minimalistic make-up always seem to do the trick for her. Malaika Arora oscillates between siren and sophisticate—she wears barely-there blouses and kurta and lehenga sets with equal flair. Take a leaf from her book and let your mood dictate your choice. Shilpa Shetty Kundra, on the other hand, could give every 20-something a run for their money with her crop top and lehenga sets. Why add a dupatta when you can flaunt the results of your Pilates class instead? You can add the lehenga's contemporary variations to your wardrobe just as easily as the traditional ones. As long as you wear it with confidence and carefree abandon, you'll always make a memorable impact. But take the occasion into account too. A floor-length jacket and lehenga set might be more appropriate than a cold shoulder cropped blouse for your niece's pheras. A cape or fringed blouse with a voluminous silk skirt, on the other hand, will be a charming choice for a friend's reception party. Your choice of accessories will also go a long way in giving modern lehenga sets the dignity you value in your repertoire. For instance, wear a shirt and printed skirt set with solitaires gifted by your doting husband instead of pairing it with costume jewellery. Kurta and lehenga sets work owing to their restrain, with their versatility serving as an added bonus. You can easily team the same kurta with palazzos and churidaars when you need to wear it more casually. Needless to say, traditional lehenga sets in heritage weaves are a timeless pick. So dig into your own trousseau and pull out that Benarasi set you wore for your roka—it will serve you well even today. column1: Celebrities are beating the heat with the off-shoulder trend
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Drop those sleeves With summer staring us in the face, it is time to let your hair down and shrug those sleeves lower. Sure, a crop top is good for flashing some abs, but the collarbone doesn't judge, or necessitate endless hours in the gym. Skirting around the risqué factor of strapless pieces, off-the-shoulder tops serve up a perfect compromise between style and comfort. Not that you'd have to tell the stylish crew of Bollywood celebrities twice. From quick dashes at the airport to all-out glam, here's how the best dressed names on the block have embraced the cold shoulder trend and made it their own. There's nothing quite like getting the basics right. Elevating a basic jeans and tee day, Shraddha Kapoor opted for a fuss-free embroidered top with blue pants for an enviable day look that requires minimal maintenance. Meanwhile, Disha Patani chose to make the most of her toned, petite physique with easy separates that remain true to her normcore aesthetic. Movie promotions for her upcoming release, Baaghi 2, call for a ruched tube top and plaid pants, while off-duty chic encompasses her love for voluminous silhouettes with an oversized boyfriend shirt reimagined as a crop top to make room for those enviable abs. If you're looking to kick things up a notch, swap out your basic blue jeans in favour of a skirt. Aditi Rao Hydari's flair for all things fusion is visible in her ethnic striped top and embroidered denim mini skirt. If you're in the market for taking this duet from desk to drinks, take notes from Malaika Arora's closet. Never one to say no to sartorial drama, she worked a ruffled off-the-shoulder top with a pencil skirt. The contrast in proportions echoed in the colour palette that moved from stark black to snowy white. Or maybe, you're wondering how to make this classic staple fit the bill for a glamorous night out. Help is on the way from Kangana Ranaut, who makes the most of her assets with structured off-the-shoulder tops that are sculpted to her curves in all the right places. While Bibhu Mohapatra's vision for his geometric off-the-shoulder top came with a textured shirt underneath, Ranaut chose to make the most of her enviable collarbone by letting the dropped sleeves have their moment in the spotlight with an elegant updo. column1: Tarun Tahiliani launches debut jewellery collection for Confluence
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You can now own a work of art from the designer without breaking the bank Designer Tarun Tahiliani has monopolised bridal wardrobe wishlists for long. Now, the master couturier is ready to expand his dominion to our jewellery kits as well. The designer is set to launch his debut collection for Confluence from Swarovski Crystals, a jewellery collective that has featured the likes of Suhani Pittie, Rohit Bal, Gaurav Gupta and Manish Arora, since its inception in 2016. Tahiliani is now channelling his design philosophy into one-of-a-kind bejewelled creations for the brand. Fashion insiders will have you know that the collaboration has been a long time coming, given his illustrious history of working the glittering crystals into his couture creations over the past two decades. Titled ‘Tarakini', the collection interprets the haze of stardust that lights up the sky into a delicate array of jewels featuring hoop, dangler and stud earrings with a selection of maangtikkas—all within a budget-affirming price range of Rs 5,000 to Rs 15,000. The designer's flair for the classic is mirrored in the colour palette that features golds, rubies and emeralds, often accompanied with pearls and vintage Patina Crystals from the brand. As Tahiliani prepares to drop his debut jewellery collection on Jabong, Myntra, Aza and Ogaan on March 29, we got him to take us behind-the-scenes on the journey behind the jewels. How has your journey been with Swarovski over the past two decades? It has been an extremely interesting and engaging road. I was first introduced to the brand by my great friend Isabella Blow, and we collaborated, all the way back in 1995. At that time, Swarovski's crystal components were not available in India and were usually carried into the country by hand. Mixed with our Indian traditional embroideries and other forms of threadwork, I found that, for me, Swarovski crystals had a very particular niche in the fashion world. In addition, they have consistently collaborated with creative minds around the world and pushed the envelope to see where the product can go. Some of my favourites were the installations by Philip Treacy and some very interesting things done for them by Manish Arora. This year, we are also looking forward to collaborating again at our Couture Week show, where we take the usage into totally different realms, combine it with a lot of components and give Indian women a modern twist on the couture that is rooted in our tradition. To me, the excitement comes from mixing and meshing the two worlds, rather than letting them stay mutually independent. What was the inspiration behind your first jewellery collection for Confluence? The inspiration for our debut jewellery collection was basically a lot of Indian baalis in traditional forms and maangtikkas that we wanted to have easier versions of. So, we decided to take easy, wearable pieces and fashion them out of Swarovski crystals. We wanted to do a beautiful blend of East and West, done with the finest crystals in the world. All the principles that we use in design have found their way into this whimsical collection of asymmetrical pieces. How did you decide on the colour palette for the collection? Emerald, ruby and ivory are classic jewel tones. Emerald and rubies are getting rarer and rarer now, and are often heat-treated in the market. So, we said, why don't we give people really fun, vibrant jewel tones through the [Swarovski] stones. We didn't want to go for a very ‘diamond' look, but really use the colours, because Indian women wear colours beautifully. There was an image of Angelina Jolie at the Oscars a few years ago, wearing earrings made out of solid emeralds—just emeralds. That really stuck with me. As a colour palette, using tone-on-tone coloured stones is very beautiful, modern and works with western clothing, which the jewellery is designed to go with. How does the creative process begin when designing jewellery? The creative process, like anything else, begins with a mood board, with ideas or words we want to embody in the collection and, of course, some visual references of medieval things we can't find anymore. Then, we start sketching our own proportions, after which you have to lay the stones down and see how they fit. This is not an actual diamond that can be sewed or cut away. These have to be used in the sizes that they are provided for. Hence, we decided to do a combination of the rest of it. In terms of styling, how do you see women wearing the Confluence pieces? These pieces are great travel pieces, especially for a younger market that may not have access to real jewels all the time. It is also modern to mix real and costume jewellery all the time, as far as you are confident enough to carry it off. This jewellery works well with a lot of our lighter ready-to-wear pieces—it is not something you would wear as a bride, but is great for travel and destination weddings, or parties where people don't want to carry a lot of real jewellery. These pieces are easy, represent India in a funky way and are modern—they are like the first jewelled T-shirt. column1: 50 times designer Sabyasachi dressed Bollywood for the wedding season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Stunning lehengas, timeless saris, and more Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee has been synonymous with Indian bridal couture for a while now. The Kolkata-based designer is known not only for his beautiful bridal creations, but also for being one of Bollywood's favourite designers. A long list, including Deepika Padukone, Priyanka Chopra, Karisma Kapoor, Kangana Ranaut, Rani Mukherjee, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, Kalki Koechlin and Anushka Sharma, has the designer in their wedding wear rotation. With his obvious popularity among Indian brides and grooms, it's no surprise that many of Bollywood's leading ladies including Bipasha Basu, Asin Thottumkal and Anushka Sharma, chose to wear a Sabyasachi outfit to tie the knot. While Bipasha Basu picked a patent red and gold Sabyasachi lehenga, Thottumkal chose a nude look for her big day. Most recently, Anushka Sharma showcased her love for the designer via her wedding pictures, which were all over our Instagram feeds in December 2017. The actor stayed loyal to the designer for all her ceremonial outfits—a blush pink Sabyasachi lehenga for the pheras, a bohemian lehenga for the mehendi, vermilion brocade Sabyasachi sari for the Delhi reception, and a vintage gold lehenga for the Mumbai one. Many other celebrities favour the designer's ensembles frequently—for weddings and Diwali parties to red carpet events and movie screenings. Over the years, some Bollywood stars have embraced Sabyasachi's saris, while others have been spotted acing chikankari kurtas, longline jackets and sharara sets. For Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and Priyanka Chopra, the designer has been a constant in their ethnic wardrobes. While Rai Bachchan is often seen favouring his chikankari kurtas, the Quantico actor is often spotted in his intricate saris. Kangana Ranaut, too, has been an ardent fan of designer's dramatic drapes. The actor has tried everything from Sabyasachi's signature floral saris, to his brocade numbers. But on a list of the staunchest supporters of the couturier, Deepika Padukone would feature among the top few. If an occasion calls for ethnic wear, chances are that Padukone will be in a Sabyasachi sari. From walking the IIFA red carpet to attending a friend's wedding, the actor never shies away from favouring his dramatic ensembles. Most recently, Padukone was seen in a number of looks from the designer during Padmaavat's promotional rounds, and she also picked a traditional Sabyasachi sari for a special occasion—her dad's felicitation with a Lifetime Achievement Award.  View Gallery 50 Photos 50 times Bollywood wore Sabyasachi wedding wear Weddings People Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: These labels are serving up fashion-with-a-cause with a side of fun
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Add to your lust list now Who says giving back or buying-for-a-cause has to be a self-sacrificing act that involves quietude and boring reverence? You can have plenty of fun, buying the kind of things that makes you happy; simultaneously, it can also make people less privileged than you, happier. Here are two witty, sustainability-focused labels that have captured our imagination (and our giggles). Mua Mua Dolls Ludovica Virga met Karl Lagerfeld during a Chanel fashion show in Venice in 2009, and she handed him a Mua Mua doll—a crocheted doll that resembled the designer, created with the help of Balinese artisans. Lagerfeld was so impressed that he commissioned 500 dolls to be sold in the Lagerfeld shops. Virga's humorous and ironic take on fashion now has a universe of dolls—Anna Wintour, Coco Chanel, Franca Sozzani, Lady Gaga, Suzy Menkes, Jay-Z, Beyoncé, and more—which have become prized collectibles. Luisa Via Roma, the eclectic Florentine fashion behemoth, started stocking Mua Mua Dolls in 2010, and today she is available in top fashion concept stores all over the world. Lady Gaga chose her Mua Mua doll to be part of her Barney's Workshop, and it sold out within weeks. While it's the wit and humour that draws her clients, Virga is quite philosophical about her creativity. “A deep soul has a very light mind” she says. But it is the heart-felt story behind the brand that has her fan following increasing by the day. When the tsunami hit Bali in 2004, many artisans were left without work, as tourism dipped sharply following the catastrophe. Virga decided to do her bit to help. She employed mostly women, living in difficult conditions in rural Balinese villages, to craft her Mua Mua dolls. Part of the proceeds of the sale is donated to a school in Sumbawa to support women's education. Just recently, Virga added to her eccentric design repertoire. “We have designed a limited edition collection decorated with sequins that are completely recycled from plastic. It has a bold catch-phrase—No Plastic is Fantastic,” says Virga. Fifty per cent of the profit will be donated to ByeBye Plastic Bag—a non-profit organisation created by two young students in Bali who work relentlessly to educate locals on plastic pollution. “For me, giving back to the communities I work with is a no-brainer. It's a regular engagement that is part and parcel of the fabric of my brand.” Threaded Tales With Threaded Tales, you can wear your heart on your sleeve and have your life embroidered on your jeans. Robin Domeniconi, the founder of this loveable brand, is nothing short of a fashion-therapist, as she embroiders the most memorable moments from your life story on your favourite piece of clothing—an instant boost of happy hormones. All you have to do is fill out a questionnaire that will help her chart your favourite moments in life in little embroidered patches. “I have a team of illustrators. After reviewing the answers to questions from a client, we consider several different things. For example, we consider age, life-stage (we check Instagram and Facebook for likes and interests), and of course, the answers themselves. Then, the client is matched with one of our illustrators, and we work together to interpret the designs that are literally drawn directly on the clothing article that is sent to Haiti for hand-embroidery. Each piece is a one-of-a-kind creation.” Once you send your favourite piece of clothing, your custom-crafted story is ready to go for a walk within eight weeks. But here's the best part—the intricate and delightful embroideries are done by the incredibly talented women of Haiti. Domeniconi was on the board of an organisation called Global Goods Partners, which empowers female artisans around the world. One of the artisan groups she now works with is Haiti Projects, which provides the incredible embroidery skills to her projects. For every piece of personalised clothing, one Haitian child gets free education for a year. This embroidered narrative has the power to educate and enrich the lives of this less privileged than you. “As each pair takes over 100 hours to create, these are not inexpensive—they retail at about $1,250,” says Domeniconi. “However, it was important for us to also make sure that each pair of jeans would pay for one-year of education for a Haitian child, while also paying the artisans 3x fair trade wages.” While there's no doubt that the need for exclusivity, self-expression and a desire to give back is what drives this brand, Domeniconi says that her belief that “there isn't a single person you couldn't learn to love once you've heard their story” is what makes her fashion a journey of passion. column1: New label to know: Dôen
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And why it needs to be on your summer shopping list Who: The brainchild of a California-based collective, Dôen is a label made by women, for women. Co-founded by sisters Margaret Kleveland, CEO and Katherine Kleveland, COO, the all-female collective includes other founding partners as well—a design consultant, a legal advisor, a financial advisor and a content director. The brand was founded with the objective of providing customers with relatable, high-end clothing at approachable price points. “Because of the plateau of the wholesale market, and the rise of direct-to-consumer selling channels, there was a new, accessible space in the market for independent companies, and the possibility to create an elevated product that was well designed, in luxe fabrics, at a price that was still approachable,” Margaret explained in an interview with Vogue.com. The women behind Dôen are also passionate lovers of nature, along with being collectors of vintage clothing and furniture. Their diverse backgrounds come in to play as they take on different roles in the collective. The label also takes pride in using domestic production wherever possible, and selects manufacturers across the globe that follow the same values as them. Dôen's commitment to include more women in the workplace extends overseas as well. Signature: Dôen's vintage-inspired aesthetic is romantic, breezy dresses, vintage-inspired blouses, cozy knits, kids wear and ballerina slippers—all straight out of Joan Didion's California. Seen on: January Jones, Dakota Jonson, Emily Ratajkowski and Sarah Jessica Parker Key pieces to own: Since the Dôen DNA is about carefree, wearable fashion, you'll find that the brand will almost always have something that you can grab and add to your wardrobe. These are the pieces you should be eyeing this summer. View Gallery 5 Photos New label to know: Dôen What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Martin Margiela’s Paris exhibitions celebrate his personal legacy and skill
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The skill and talent of the elusive Martin Margiela, known as the king of the undone and the recycled, is celebrated in two separate Paris exhibitions: the fruits of his Hermès tenure at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs, and a more extensive retrospective filling the Palais Galliera An elegant camel coat is pitted against a white wrap-dress, stained with shocking-pink blotches. The alliance between the noble French house of Hermès and the disruptive Belgian designer Martin Margiela seems an unlikely combination. But in Paris, two separate exhibitions—at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs and the Palais Galliera— are looking at the iconoclast from Antwerp. The decision to show Margiela's work at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs, newly shortened to MAD, was encouraged by Pierre-Alexis Dumas, artistic director of Hermès and president of the museum. “We want to make the museum more exciting and appealing, especially for the new generation,” Dumas said, as he stood amid the crowd of visitors, looking at the ripe fruit of a six-year design relationship between the noble French house and Margiela, from 1997-2003. The iconoclastic designer, who has never shown his face to the fashion world, is known as the king of the undone and the recycled—and a revelation of what lies beneath. His exceptional skills can be seen in Margiela: The Hermès Years, which runs at MAD until September 2, after transferring from the Mode Museum (MoMu) in Antwerp, Belgium. His talents also tell a fascinating fashion story—especially in relation to a simultaneous Paris exhibition at the Palais Galliera, curated by the “invisible” designer himself. At this exhibition, the 20 years of Margiela under his own label are not only displayed, but each procedure is explained by the designer, with the support of the museum and its outgoing curator, Olivier Saillard. An example of the Belgian designer's work are the ‘Tabi' shoe-boots he created with two toes, and an entire collection in 1997, literally built exclusively on his Stockman dressmaker's dummy. At MAD, the most dramatic effect is the colour, that juicy orange of Hermès shown against the white of Margiela, who painted every item in his studio stark white—from floor to ceiling—and even asked his staff to wear white lab coats. But the noble brand and the imaginative designer are not always so far apart. Using the deep ‘V' neckline of the Vareuse—once a French sailor's jacket—the designer's work for Hermès can look streamlined, graceful and well-suited to the women of a certain age, who appear in videos as lively exhibits. Some of Margiela's Hermès pieces look almost like haute couture, for example, coats with a semi-transparent silk cover flowing over fine wool for protection. Other offerings have the bizarre Margiela touch, as in a ‘glove story' using nothing but unmatched pairs to construct a slender dress. In a similar way, the designer used a collection of engagement rings worked in thread to make a silvered gown. Margiela never speaks publicly. But having talked to him at length when the exhibition was first presented at MoMu in 2017, I still had vivid memories of what he said—especially when he told me that he wanted to show work that had languished for years in cold storage at Hermès. “The memory was lost,” he told me, explaining that his two decades of creation, 1989-2009, just missed the smartphone and the internet era. Now that there are two ways to look at the designer's work, at MAD for his Hermès period and at the Palais Galliera for 20 years of his own creations, I have to ask the question: will the real Martin Margiela please stand up? And I am not even starting to think about the fact that John Galliano has now taken over at Maison Margiela, playing with the same issues of plastic, at its most fantastic, and the entire subject of what lies beneath those sheltering clothes. The story of Margiela's Hermès is easy to define. It is about a modern elegance, de-sexualised, with a fresh take on traditional French style. “Fluid is a word we often used—it had to hang off the body,” Margiela told me. And the effect of oversize, which he started around 2000, is evident in his own work. Critics of the time felt that Margiela could and should have grown Hermès faster and further. During his tenure, he took the iconic Hermès' hand-rolled scarf and used that technique to edge blouses and tunics. He also played artfully with logos and identity, creating in 1997 a way of button stitching that produced the subtle ‘H' motif. Yet he never experimented with the famous Hermès patterns on headscarves and neckties, although he played with hand-printing in his own label, extending the patterned effect on legs and arms. Spread over a generous space, the MAD exhibition includes short films of the Martin Margiela shows—including the famous 1990 presentation held on scrubland on the outskirts of Paris, where local kids joined the parade. Only just after he had left his job working for Jean Paul Gaultier in 1987, Margiela already showed symbols of his personal style. Clothes apparently worn inside-out and his early use of transparent plastic were in stark contrast to the glamorous style of the over-the-top 1980s. Margiela was clearly forging his own fashion path—a full seven years before he started designing for Hermès. Kaat Debo, director of MoMu, who was instrumental in the original exhibition, rejoiced in its move to Paris. “I am proud and very thrilled to have this show in Paris, the fashion world's capital,” she said. “It's an honour to have Martin's oeuvre here. I really think he deserves it. And for us at the museum, it is always a joy to travel and see it in a different place and different context.” “But if you really want to understand Martin, you have to see both shows,” Debo continued. “At Galliera, there is an excellent overview of his own brand. And here at MAD, we see how he translates his DNA for another house.” The second exhibition, Margiela/Galliera 1989-2009 (on view at the Palais Galliera through  July 15) is unique—and not because his name is scribbled in ink at the entrance to the grand building. It is rather the words printed on the exhibition pamphlet: “Artistic Director Martin Margiela”, it reads, above the name of Alexandre Samson, the director of Contemporary Collections. In an exceptional collaboration, the Belgian designer was in a position to write his own history—or rather to show how he developed his fashion aesthetic in direct contrast to the extravagant 1980s, when he started his career working with Jean Paul Gaultier. From his early training at the fashion school of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, he used his knowledge to deconstruct garments, revealing the hidden sewing skills behind linings, stitching and shoulder pads. He even had his mother knit an openwork sweater using broom sticks, adapted dolls' clothes to create giant Barbies, and produced oversize clothes so enormous that they were twice the normal shape. “He never used the word ‘recycling'—it was giving life to pieces he liked, and he loved vintage,” Samson said. “We chose the silhouettes together to make the collection he loves.” That included a huge American mannequin from 1936, which Margiela used as the foundation of his oversize collection. Other original moments in the 1990s included the artisanal dress made from four separate 1940s outfits, and for autumn/winter 1994 when he selected five groups of garments to show in shop windows in France, Japan and New York. A later elaboration in the new millennium was to have two trench coats assembled to have four sleeves. Having attended Margiela shows in the weirdest places—one in a ghostly, abandoned underground Paris metro station, where I never managed to open the entrance door, and had to view the clothes afterwards—I have many memories and an understanding of what made the designer so utterly original. Margiela took us to extraordinary venues, from under an ephemeral cover in the wasteland on the outskirts of Paris to a Salvation Army depot. In 1992, the ‘set' was not one, but two divided areas; one where everything was shown in white, the other in black. The passion with which Margiela's followers collected his clothes is shown at the Palais Galliera in reconstructions of the compact apartments of Japanese fans who dedicated their small living spaces to their idol. Looking at the exhibition leaves the impression that Margiela pioneered great things. In 1999, he made an entire collection out of old duvets—anticipating by a decade the fashion for padded puffer coats. His oversize outfits appeared just at the fashion moment devoted to skimpy, body-clinging outfits. Saillard, the former director of the Palais Galliera, was the instigator of the exhibition back in 2017, when, he says, an interest in Margiela had blossomed again because of the work of Demna Gvasalia, another alumnus of the Antwerp school, who led the design team at Maison Margiela before launching anti-fashion brand Vetements and then designing for Balenciaga. “When I met Margiela, the idea was to do an exhibition through an exhibition—showing the clothes from each collection as a personal and fashion retrospective,” Saillard explained, saying that the only designer who had shown the same passion for a museum show was the late Azzedine Alaïa. And from Saillard, a final wise comment, as we looked at Margiela dresses cut horizontally, instead of vertically: “Young people coming here should understand that the problem of creating new fashion is not about a lack of money, but of imagination.” View Gallery 10 Photos Martin Margiela’s double bill in Paris explores his personal legacy and his skill at Hermès Fashion Culture & Living Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 14 times Aishwarya Rai Bachchan aced all-black looks
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Classics to swear by Aishwarya Rai Bachchan never fails to make an impression. Whether she's walking down red carpets in showstopper outfits, going out to dinner with family and friends, or heading out of town, the celebrated beauty is always dressed to the nines, and more often than not, in black. Take a closer look at her sartorial go-tos, and you'll notice how black is Mrs Bachchan's happy colour. Japanese fashion designer Yohji Yamamoto's discourse on the hue can easily explain Rai Bachchan's preference for it. He said, “Black is modest and arrogant at the same time. Black is lazy and easy—but mysterious. But above all black says this: ‘I don't bother you—don't bother me.'” Neatly fits the bill for the lady in question. A fail-safe red carpet pick, it's a colour that has always served the actor well at gala affairs. For instance, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan recently paired a strapless Gauri & Nainika gown with her signature soft curls and a bold pout—a combination that never gets tiresome on her—for a Longines event. She has also mastered the art of extending the cocktail glam vibe associated with black to her traditional wardrobe. Cases in point: the Shahab Durazi lace panel sari, and the Anamika Khanna anarkali she's been spotted in. While the actor's style tethers more in the classic territory, she is always game for giving the LBD an of-the-moment spin. Her Nedret Taciroğlu lace off-shoulder dress, or even her look in Bibhu Mohapatra's cold shoulder version, shows us how to use this closet MVP to enhance a svelte frame, and keep up with the times without trying too hard. When in the mood to unleash your inner drama queen, channel Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's look in Andrew Gn separates, with exaggerated sleeves and a fringed hemline. Black and airport looks? A match made in heaven, if the actor's repertoire is anything to go by. Keep changing it up with trouser and blazer combinations, sweatshirts or trench coats in the solid shade. That's the thing about black—it will mould itself to any occasion, sensibility or mood on your mind. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and her all-black ensembles have proved this time and again over the years.
