column1: A look at Virgil Abloh’s meteoric career graph
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In less than five years—and without any formal fashion design training—Virgil Abloh has gone from debuting his own label to becoming the men’s artistic director at one of the world’s leading fashion houses. Vogue retraces the pivotal career moments that lead the multi-talented creative to Louis Vuitton On Monday, Louis Vuitton sent industry heads spinning when it announced that Virgil Abloh—the Rockford, Illinois-born creative polymath behind Kanye West and Off-White—has been appointed as the men's artistic director, replacing Kim Jones (who started work at Dior Homme the very same morning). Despite the growth and accolades racked up by his own label—Off-White has opened nearly two dozens flagships in the last five years and made the final round of the LVMH Prize in 2015—Abloh is still perceived as a fashion outsider, best known as the creative force behind West and his creative agency, DONDA. His work for Off-White has helped usher, and define, today's streetwear boom, while simultaneously being criticised by his peers for offering nothing truly novel nor innovative. (Abloh's hero, Raf Simons, divisively said last year that Abloh's work was not “original”.) But in fact, Abloh has been working in and around the fashion industry for some time, starting with an internship with Fendi in 2006—where he met then-Fendi CEO Michael Burke, the man who would later hire him at Vuitton. That stint was followed by dozens of high-profile collaborations and one-off projects, as well as a short-lived label called Pyrex Vision; all of which would lay the groundwork for the rapid ascension of Off-White. Abloh has said for years that his chief aim is not to transform Off-White into a major global brand, but to use it as ‘résumé' to land a creative director role at a major luxury fashion house. As the designer finally gets his wish, Vogue revisits the designer/DJ/creative tour de force's fashion career to date. Virgil Abloh is born in Rockford, Illinois, to a couple of Ghanaian immigrants. As a teenager, Abloh was immersed in skate culture, developing musical influences spanning from hip-hop to grunge and rock 'n roll—references that will resurface through his multi-faceted artistic production years later. “My upbringing, being a teenager in the '90s in America watching rap, hip-hop, graffiti, skateboarding—that's where my point of view comes from,” Abloh explained to Hunger in 2017. At around the age of 18, Abloh starts DJ-ing, a past-time that he would transform to an ongoing side career under the name Flat White in the years to come. He enrolled at the University of Wisconsin Madison and gained a bachelor degree in Civil Engineering. Abloh graduates with a Master's degree in Architecture from the Illinois Institute of Technology. According to a 2013 interview with GQ, the young graduate skipped his graduation critique to meet with Kanye West's then manager, John Monopoly, and was hired to design merchandise for the American rapper. Abloh's role soon developed in a full-fledged artistic direction, encompassing global tours, performances and artwork. Abloh joined West in Rome, where they interned for Italian luxury brand Fendi for six months. “I paid them $500 a month!” Michael Burke, Fendi's CEO at the time, recently told The New York Times. “I was really impressed with how they brought a whole new vibe to the studio and were disruptive in the best way. Virgil could create a metaphor and a new vocabulary to describe something as old-school as Fendi. I have been following his career ever since.” The designer collaborated with Kanye West for Pastelle, the graphic streetwear label announced and promoted by the “Life of Pablo” singer, that was never released. Abloh co-founded RSVP Gallery in Chicago, a concept store blurring the lines between art, music, and fashion. The retail space showcases works by artists like Stephen Sprouse, Jeff Koons and Takashi Murakami; carries an eclectic mix of brands including Undercover, Raf Simons, Stone Island and Nike; and hosts design and music launches, including a 2012 collaboration with A$AP Rocky called R$VPA$AP, and the Spring/Summer 2014 “Raf Simons x Sterling Ruby Collection” modelled by Travis Scott. Having no formal fashion education, Abloh made his first independent fashion foray with Pyrex Vision, a one-time small collection described by the designer as “an art piece”. He repurposed old T-shirts, hoodies and flannel shirts from brands including Ralph Lauren and Champion, screen printed logos over them and sold them for as much as $500. Abloh also collaborated with Matthew Williams, Heron Preston and other creatives on the hyper-hyped brand and lifestyle collective Been Trill; he was appointed creative director of Kanye West's creative agency DONDA; and received a Grammy nomination for Best Recording Package for his directional work on Jay-Z and West's album “Watch the Throne”, designed by Riccardo Tisci. In late 2013, Abloh launched his new label, Off-White c/o Virgil Abloh. Based and produced in Milan, the brand is conceptualised as a high-fashion take on streetwear and was instantly snapped up by now-defunct Parisian concept store Colette. "I want to give my point of view and merge street sensibilities in a proper fashion context. I think that if I can merge the two, it'll make something interesting," Abloh told Style.com of the launch. In April, Abloh revealed his first womenswear collection for Off-White, titled “I only smoke when I drink” and featuring the label's signature diagonal stripes and Pyrex Vision-inspired collegiate lettering. In September of the same year, his womenswear line made its fashion week debut in Paris. In March, a little over a year after the launch of Off-White, Abloh was nominated among the finalists for the LVMH Prize. He was the only American designer. In September, the designer held his first womenswear catwalk show during Paris Fashion Week, presenting a collection of 20 looks built on reinterpretations of the classic white t-shirt and denim look. In January, Abloh debuted his first menswear catwalk show in Paris. Titled “Don't cut me off”, the collection was partly inspired by Lucio Fontana's Spatialist art, featuring a series of canvas coats with slashed backs. Invited to Pitti Immagine Uomo 92 as the guest artist of the year, Abloh collaborated with artist Jenny Holzer to set up a crossover between a show and an art installation at Palazzo Pitti in June. Described as “the most important show of my career” by the designer, his spring/summer 2018 menswear presentation tackled political themes including war, immigration and the international refugee crisis. “I wanted to do something that Pitti had never done and give Florence an artwork that was large scale and spoke to the moment. I'm at a place where I can add something to the conversation,” Abloh told W magazine. 2017 was also one of Abloh's most prolific year in terms of collaborations, including the ‘The Ten'—a re-design of Nike's 10 most iconic sneakers that sold out in minutes, the launch of Off-White x Jimmy Choo during his Princess Diana-inspired spring/summer 2018 show, and the announcement of a collaboration with Ikea on a line of affordable furniture for millennials scheduled to hit stores in 2019. On March 26, Virgil Abloh is appointed Louis Vuitton's new men's artistic director, following Kim Jones's departure earlier the same month. Abloh, who has previously referred to Jones as one of his mentors and considers him “the designer that I always wanted in the modern industry, the epitome of high fashion and streetwear,” seems like a natural continuation for the luxury French house. “His sensibility towards luxury and savoir-faire will be instrumental in taking Louis Vuitton's menswear to the future," said Michael Burke, Louis Vuitton's chairman and CEO of Abloh's appointment. The designer will debut his first menswear collection for the brand in June 2018. column1: Lust list: 10 stunning diamond-studded watches you need to buy for yourself
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion These are worth breaking the bank for Rihanna has rapped about them, Elizabeth Taylor swore by them—there's plenty in the realm of pop culture in favour of sparkling diamonds. Other than the ubiquitous tennis bracelets and solitaire earrings, how do you go about adding extra bling on your daily wardrobe? Diamond watches are an easy way to dress up even the most minimal ensemble, and present a new way to go about investment shopping. If you need one for everyday wear, you could choose a timepiece that is discreet enough to be appropriate at your workplace, but decadent enough to add an extra something to that power suit. IWC Schaffhausen's ‘Da Vinci Automatic 36' and Omega's Constellation are great options to put on the daily circulation. For those looking for a hint of the dramatic, Cartier's on-trend ‘Panthère de Cartier' watch or a classic ‘Oyster Perpetual Pearlmaster 39' by Rolex, are worth a look. If you need something more statement-making for a cocktail party, look at the ‘Emerald Cadenas' watch by Van Cleef & Arpels. column1: Sarah Jessica Parker’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion With a successful acting career that spans theatre, film and television, it’s no surprise that the American actress has served as a fashion role model for a whole generation. Ahead of her birthday, Vogue revisits her most memorable looks over the years Sarah Jessica Parker may be best known as Carrie Bradshaw from Sex and the City, but that doesn't mean she lacks a sense of style to call her own. Prior to conquering television, she started her career on Broadway, where she starred in the titular role of Annie, before transitioning into film, appearing in Herbert Ross's Footloose and alongside comedian Steve Martin in Mick Jackson's satirical rom-com L.A. Story. Since then, the New York fashion figure and dedicated mother of three's style choices have been well-documented. During the '90s, Parker frequently appeared on the red carpet in Versace, either wearing one of Gianni's very own glistening Atelier Versace jackets or equally glittery minimal tube dresses, like the one she brought out for the New York City premiere of Roland Emmerich's 1998 remake of Godzilla. More recently, however, the actress has graced the red carpet several times in romantic Alexander McQueen ball gowns, complemented by elaborately ornate headwear, courtesy of Philip Treacy. But it's not all glitz and glamour, all the time, for the Ohio native. Parker is also known for her fashionably understated ensembles, like her head to toe Vivienne Westwood get up from the 2000 Screen Actors Guild Awards—the signature corset top was armed with sleeves that came undone via buttons down the length of the arms. As the Sex and the City star turns 53, revisit her style compendium in pictorial form. View Gallery 50 Photos Style Evolution- Sarah Jessica Parker Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and Kareena Kapoor Khan wore on 26/03/2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Slinky gowns, cosy sweatshirts, and everything in between [#image: /photos/5ce420003bf9b46698b1b8db]||| ||| Kriti Sanon, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and Aaradhya Bachchan, Kareena Kapoor Khan. Image: Viral Bhayani From Katrina Kaif and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan to Alia Bhatt and Kareena Kapoor Khan, Bollywood's favourite faces flaunted their sartorial prowess in several must-see looks yesterday. column1: Why Virgil Abloh’s appointment at Louis Vuitton matters
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As the disruptive designer is made artistic director of the French luxury house’s menswear division, we outline what it means for fashion and culture today As fashion houses go, Louis Vuitton is among the most established—but today, it announced the appointment of fashion's newest phenomena to head its menswear division as artistic director: Virgil Abloh. “Virgil is one of the few designers who truly marries street culture with high fashion—and the first black designer to be given such a position in the gilded halls of LVMH. His appointment is a step in the right direction for diversity, as well as a particularly exciting creative moment for the industry,” British Vogue's Editor-in-chief, Edward Enninful, commented on the move. A 34-year-old Chicago native with no formal fashion training, his brand, Off-White, has had an almost incalculable impact on the industry since its inception in 2014 (its former incarnation, Pyrex Vision, was founded in 2013). His democratic approach to design has opened the doors of luxury to a generation often alienated by its impenetrable veneer. “My motivation is, in part, a bit of angst that comes from feeling like I don't belong—that our generation doesn't belong,” he said in September, at a free-admission panel talk that he hosted with Nike. “I made a conscious decision that I wasn't just going to be a consumer; that at least one of us would appear at the end of a Parisian runway.” Now that he will be appearing on one of the world's most revered catwalks in June, we run down why his appointment matters. It speaks to a new generation Kim Jones' tenure at Louis Vuitton embraced youth culture with remarkable impact. Not only was his Supreme x Louis Vuitton collaboration the most hyped of 2017, but his nuanced understanding of streetwear and branding gave the Parisian powerhouse a thoroughly contemporary cachet. Currently, fashion brands are clamouring to engage a new generation of consumers, and in that sense, Abloh's appointment is surely a savvy move. Sales of his clothing have increased 230% year-on-year at Selfridges—Off-White is one of MatchesFashion.com's best performing brands—modern icons from Beyonce and the Hadids to Drake and ASAP Rocky are proud ambassadors for his designs (and without a lucrative sponsorship contract). What Jones started, Abloh is sure to continue; the two are close friends, and Abloh spent one summer sleeping on Jones' Maida Vale sofa while learning about design. “I find the heritage and creative integrity of the house to be key inspirations. I will look to reference them both while drawing parallels to modern times,” Abloh said in a statement this morning. It will be fascinating to see how Gen-Z buys into this new era of French luxury; if this morning's Instagram feed is anything to go by, it will be powerful. It will merge streetwear with luxury Pyrex Vision, Abloh's first brand, started as a foray into streetwear—hoodies, basketball shirts, slogan T-shirts et al. While its evolved incarnation, Off-White, has developed into tulle ballgowns and tapestried tailoring, that modern sensibility is still at its core. This season, the Off-White woman “grew up riding horses, so has a knowledge of formalwear, but is equally intrigued by going to the gym during the week and figuring out how to wear athleisure in a new way,” he explained backstage. It is this hybrid identity that we expect to see translate into Vuitton's menswear, which will likely position luxury leathers and new-gen sportswear alongside each other. Think of Abloh's most vocal proponents: people like Luka Sabbat who wear cashmere hoodies with the hottest trainers, and queue for Supreme drops with the same fervour they do new-season Balenciaga. Speaking of trainers, Abloh's Nike collaborations have had near riotous reception. Ghesquière has designed the season's hottest turbo footwear; we are sure Abloh's will take it a step further. The industry is making genuine steps towards representation When Abloh started attending Paris Fashion Week in 2009, it was with Kanye West (Abloh worked as his artistic director for years, and the two of them interned at LVMH-owned Fendi together). They were refused entry to half of the shows they tried to attend—two young black men were simply not their target audience. “You don't have to get past someone with a clipboard at a fashion show anymore in order to be a part of the conversation anymore,” Abloh told me earlier this year. “For me, fashion has to be inclusive, and not exclusive.” And his trajectory has certainly dismantled the industry's long-standing barriers to entry. It almost goes without saying that there are only a handful of black fashion designers in an industry renowned for white-washing—and hopefully Abloh's appointment semaphores an era where diversity is celebrated rather than visibly tokenistic. The occasional appointment of a non-white campaign star is simply not enough; change needs to happen behind the scenes of the industry as well as on its runways. “Today you have changed history. The first to ever do it. Young black man in the biggest fashion house in the world. This is a win not only for you, but the culture as a whole,” wrote Sabbat on Twitter. Aptly said. Its collaborations will be hot Kim Jones made a strong case for collaboration at the house (from Supreme to the Chapman brothers, his forays were a resounding success), and Abloh is another master in the field. Last month he launched collaborations with Byredo, Chrome Hearts, Nike; he famously has one with Ikea in the works (ranging from rugs to furniture, it is set to be enormous); he even has his own type of Spirulina water sold at Parisian hipster hotspot Wild & The Moon. “Who wants to be friends with the person who comes to the bar and is like, ‘me, me, me'?” he asked me last year. “The people who are fun to hang out with are normally a collective… and it feels more modern to specifically cite your influences in fashion; like, you're saying, 'this is my squad'.” It remains to be seen who his Vuitton squad will be, but you can rest assured they will be painfully cool. column1: Arpita Mehta expands her label with a prêt and a fusion line
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion She tells us what makes her spring/summer 2018 collection unique Ever since she launched her eponymous label in 2007, Arpita Mehta has had brides (and the entire wedding crew, for that matter) flocking to her for her innate knack of reimagining traditional mirror work for the contemporary Indian woman. The steady patronage of celebrities like Deepika Padukone, Sonam Kapoor, Madhuri Dixit-Nene and Aditi Rao Hydari from the very onset only accelerated Mehta's rising popularity. View Gallery 8 Photos Arpita Mehta expands her label with a prêt and a fusion line Mehta maintains that she designs for a woman who is, “really stylish, chic and doesn't try too hard. She wears everything effortlessly, always carrying it with elegance and poise.” She understands that the millennial sartorialist's enthusiasm for a great outfit extends well beyond weddings. It was this understanding that encouraged the designer to launch her prêt and fusion labels, along with her spring/summer 2018 ‘Enchanted Forest' collection, thus allowing one to add Mehta's inimitable flair to every event on the social calendar. “The entire collection is a translation of my definition of new-age femininity, which is free-spirited, fearless and sensual,” she explains. The prêt range, which currently features 12 pieces, is easygoing with free-flowing, comfortable silhouettes at the centre of every design. “We have kept it rather simple and classic, with styles that will flatter every body type.” The sartorial quotient of the prints-only range is further amplified with the ingenious use of these patterns. From print-on-print kurta pyjama sets for everyday affairs, to cape-and-tulip-skirt sets and ruffled sleeved tunic sets for celebratory occasions, variety is the spice in this case. The fusion line, on the other hand, is experimental with a bohemian soul. The core colour palette is one of melon mint, ivory and ruby red with lemon mint and ivory prints. The pairings are as unconventional as they are versatile. The line features tulip skirts teamed with bralettes and ruffled jackets, as well as the brand's classic palazzos in variations like tiered ruffles and modern shararas. “We've given the slip dress our own spin. Ours can be worn with a cape or a jacket for your best friend's mehandi or as is for a pool party. Each piece is extremely easy to wear.” So how has Mehta retained her original aesthetic while extending her presence in her client's wardrobe? “Embroidery has always been an important part of the brand's DNA. We have retained the mirror work but reinvented it in a different and subtle manner. You will notice a lot of thread embroidery with mix of kaduna and mirrors, ensuring that each piece is a true Arpita Mehta signature,” signs off the stylish designer. column1: Tracing the trend: How to shop for polka dots this summer
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Reimagining fashion’s favourite print Princess Diana at the races, Julia Roberts in Pretty Woman, Dimple Kapadia in Bobby—some fashion moments have an instant recall value. Each of these looks exemplify a timeless quality; pluck them out of their context and imagine the same clothes at a café or a beach holiday in the present day, and they fit right in. This season, fashion offers a warm welcome to an old favourite—the polka dot print. A far cry from its association with Minnie Mouse, designers have looked at polka dots with a fresh new perspective. View Gallery 11 Photos Tracing the trend: How to shop for polka dots this summer Everyone's hot favourite Parisian label Jacquemus, had them on the runway with draped skirts and the signature oversized ‘Bomba' hat. Johanna Ortiz made them perfect for a special night out. Carolina Herrera imagined a more whimsical, look with contrasting play of colours. Dice Kayek ignored the black and white and chose red and blue instead. Jason Wu's version played with different sizes of the dots adding another twist to the trend. Street style photographers were quick to spot the pattern amongst those who attended fashion week. Come summer, polka dots will be everywhere. Be ahead of the game and add a dotted piece to your wardrobe. Try the trend in varying dosages, depending on your proclivity towards polka dots. Starting from the classic midi length dresses to obi belts and caps, there are multiple ways to give a nod to the trend, and you can pick your own. Swimwear, cami tops, skirts and date night dresses—get your hands on the best polka dots for the summer. column1: You can’t miss Nikhil Thampi’s debut fashion films for Belvedere Studio B
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In collaboration with Sidharth Malhotra, Lekha Washington and Lost Stories You know a Nikhil Thampi design when you see one, with its signature detailing and power rush-inducing monochrome palette. Having championed the cause of sleek silhouettes for the better part of this decade, both on and off runways, the designer's next milestone comes in the form of an exciting collaboration with ‘Belvedere Studio B'. The property, which will be launched for the very first time in India, inspired him to put his head together with actor and artist Lekha Washington, and DJ duo Lost Stories, to create two mini fashion films to be curated and presented by Sidharth Malhotra. The films have him experimenting with the genre for the first time. “What I liked most about the project, when I first got the brief, was that they required and pushed me to think out of the box, and get as creative as I wanted to depict the brand through a fashion perspective. We wanted our concept to last beyond just creating an impact for one night; which is why we did not opt for the obvious choice of doing a show, but went a step forward to create a property that would add value to both the brands. We worked in tandem to create fashion films that would prove to be great assets and highlight both brands in a new light,” smiles Thampi. A post shared by  Nikhil Thampi (@nikhilthampi) on Mar 14, 2018 at 6:54am PDT The two fashion films are scheduled to unveil tonight, and while he remains tight-lipped about his designs, he does promise a night of high glamour. “After days of ideating, we narrowed down our concept to revolve around the key components that come together to make this beautiful spirit come alive—rye and water—while seamlessly merging it with my brand's DNA. What you can expect is two fashion-forward mini films, subtly highlighting properties of both brands. We have worked out of our comfort zone to create an unforgettable experience, with a shot of pure, unadulterated, high-glam fashion,” he says. column1: 5 textile innovations set to redesign fashion’s future
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From materials made of algae, fungi and crop waste to dissolvable threads and fabrics that improve the quality of your skin—meet the new crop of game-changing ideas and technologies honoured at this year’s H&M Global Change Award How, in an industry defined by the embrace of the new, do we eliminate waste? How do we turn the fashion industry's current linear model into a circular one? How can we protect or even improve the planet? These are among the questions the H&M Foundation—a non-profit arm of H&M—posed during the Global Change Award summit in Stockholm this week. Ever since its inception in 2015, the Global Change Awards have been announced at a grand award ceremony in Stockholm's City Hall—the same venue where the Nobel Prize is presented, signifying the scale and influence the initiative aspires to have. As with previous winners, this year's final five—selected out of 2,600 entries from 151 countries by a panel of expert judges—are as disruptive as they are inventive, aiming to challenge the fashion industry's current status quo and create positive change on a grass root to global level. View Gallery 13 Photos 5 pioneering fashion innovations to know now On the whole, Hennes & Mauritz AB has had a tough time of late. There have been accusations of racism and cultural misappropriation and, most recently, copyright infringement over the use of a mural by graffiti artist Jason ‘Revok' Williams as a backdrop to their campaign. Add to that disappointing financial results—shares have dropped 44 per cent over the past year, leaving them trading at a 10-year low—and the picture looks rather bleak. “We're obviously not satisfied with our performance,” H&M CEO Karl-Johan Persson tells Vogue. “One part is the market transformation that we all know about, but the other part is that we have not performed up to our own expectations. We made some mistakes, but now we're working to correct them.” Investing heavily in the digital space—improving and expanding the mobile experience—is key, he explains, as is “creating a more inspiring shopping experience.” Beyond the immediate changes to the website and stand alone stores, Persson is also thinking about the future metrics that he believes will play a big role for consumers in the future: “We are working to make sustainability fact-based and consumer-facing, so that when you buy a dress you can see a tag that not only tells you the price and quality, but also [gives you an industry-wide] sustainability score. Then you will see how one company compares to another, one dress to another,” he says. “People have the idea that low prices can't be good, but I want to break that to say we can have great design, good quality and low prices; we can make fashion accessible for everyone. And we can do it in a sustainable way.” The spirit behind Persson's ambitions for H&M and H&M Foundation's aims are echoed by the judging panel, including Vogue India editor at large Bandana Tewari. Wearing a coral pink dress made using a technique developed by one of last year's winners—the Australian scientist collective behind the denim dyeing project—Tewari is clear about the potential at hand. “Scalability and impact [are key when narrowing down the entries],” she explains. “When you come from a country with a billion people, it is all about numbers. And how fast it can be scaled up, how many lives it can impact and how quickly you can get these choices to people.” To help the winners address those specific challenges, the H&M Foundation, in partnership with consultancy firm Accenture and Stockholm's KTH Royal Institute of Technology, run a year-long accelerator programme which provides support and access to key industry leaders for the winners. “We don't see innovation as a competitive edge, but as a collaborative space,” says Erik Bang, H&M Foundation's innovation lead. “The aim is to unlock exponential impact, to do good through the circular economy and have a positive effect. But we can only do that by working together.” Collaboration has been a buzzword of the summit, as former United Nations Deputy Secretary-General Jan Eliasson asserted in his keynote speech: “Nobody can do everything, but everybody can do something.” As well as a coveted spot on the accelerator programme, the five innovations get a share of the €1 million grant—portion sizes are decided by an online public vote. Here are the winning entries set to redesign the future of fashion: Crop-A-Porter This year's first place winner, Crop-A-Porter, uses leftovers from food crop harvests—like oilseed flax, hemp, sugarcane, bananas and pineapples from China, North America and soon Costa Rica—to create its sustainable bio-textiles. Crucially though, they do so by adding value for the communities they work with. “We've created what we call the agraloop,” explains Isaac Nichelson, the CEO of the American-based company. “[This is a] regenerative system that uses plant-based chemistry and plant-based energy to upgrade the fibres whilst enriching the local communities and creating a new economic system.” As the first place winner of the public vote, Crop-A-Porter won the lion's share of the grant (€300,000). The Regenerator “We are looking at the textiles that are already out there and [how to] use them as valuable material resource rather than as waste,“ explains Lisa Schwarz Bour who, coming in second, won €250,000 of prize money. Simply put, they want to render the fabrics already in circulation—including popular mixed fabrics like cotton and polyester blends—into separate and totally reusable fibres. The Regenerator—the first Swedish innovation to claim a spot in the H&M hall of sustainable fame—uses an eco-friendly chemical process to separate blended materials and make two fully usable textile fibres. Algae Apparel The concept of feel-good fashion is nothing new, but clothes that improve the quality of your skin as you wear them? Now that's a revelation! Algae Apparel's bio-fibre can be engineered to release different kinds of antioxidants, vitamins and other nutrients depending on the type of algae used, but perhaps more importantly, tackles issues raised by conventional fabric production, namely the large amounts of water required in the production of cotton, and the pollution caused by textile dyeing. “We aim to be the green engine of the fashion revolution,” explains Renana Kelbs, one half of this father-and-daughter team. Like the other third place winners, Algae Apparel gets €150,000 of the grant money. Smart Stitch The disassembling of garments is so labour intensive that it rarely happens, but Smart Stitch has made the recycling process easier with its special thread, which melts away when exposed to temperatures of 266 degrees. “When making a new product, most of the time you combine different materials to meet different requirements,” the company's founder, Cédric Vanhoeck's explains. “A shoe is a nice example. You need different materials for different parts, but if you take a recyclable sole, and a recyclable top, and stitch them together, you end up with an unrecyclable shoe.” Funghi Fashion Grown from mushroom roots, Funghi Fashion uses 3D-printing technology to make fashion as close to zero-waste as possible. Aside from reducing the amount of water used in the manufacturing process; the need for transporting raw materials from one place to another, and the amount of waste product—the garments have a unique benefit, which the Funghi Fashion's founder Aniela Hoitink points out: “When you are fed up with your T-shirt, you can just bury it.” Vogue India's March 2018 issue is now available on Amazon.in Culture & Living Culture & Living Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Ditch the salwar: Try these celebrity-endorsed alternatives instead
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Bottoms up The humble salwar may have stood the test of time, but that shouldn't stop you from updating your Indian ethnic wear wardrobe with more of-the-moment alternatives to team your kurtas and jackets with. New-age bottoms, whether they're draped skirts or dhoti pants, can inject your look with millennial cred. And that's just one reason to embrace them. The other being, a quick swap of the salwar for trendier trousers will instantly revamp an outfit that has probably been in your wardrobe for ages (without anyone even realising). Vogue narrows down on the styles you should place your bets on this season. View Gallery 16 Photos Ditch the salwar: try these alternatives instead-Celebrity Need a break from lehengas but still want to look extra? A sharara will do your bidding. Go a step ahead and add some flair with embroidery that complements the kurta too. Choose one with a sprinkle of sequins or tiered layers to give your sharara a modern upgrade. The ability to marry comfort with versatility makes the dhoti a universal favourite. Easy to dress up or down, the dhoti can be worn with an off-shoulder cape for a laid-back festive repertoire, or with a heavily embroidered jacket to look wedding-appropriate. You can also use your dhoti for a contemporary take on the sari by wearing it with a crop top, and draping the dupatta like a pallu. A draped skirt is a utilitarian separate to own in your Indian ethnic wear wardrobe—it will complement your hand-embroidered capes just as easily as those sequinned crop tops. Anamika Khanna's pairing of a floor-length jacket with her signature draped skirt is a winning reception look, while an Amoh by Jade skirt with an off-shoulder top is perfect for a mehandi. Want to revamp a simple tunic without losing its easy chic essence? Just replace the churidaar or salwar with roomy palazzos or cropped trousers. Sonam Kapoor's striped palazzo and tunic set is all about fuss-free glam while Anita Dongre's flared kurti and palazzo set is perfect for a destination wedding. column1: Alicia Vikander’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Tracing the star’s wardrobe choices through the years Humanoid robot, artist, Lara Croft—Hollywood actor Alicia Vikander is the master of transformation. The Swedish actor not only made it to the Forbes 30 Under 30 list, and is known for the red carpet style, but has also been nominated for several awards. Vikander entered Hollywood in 2010 with Pure. Ever since, she has featured in films like The Crown Jewels (2011), A Royal Affair (2012), Anna Karenina (2012), The Fifth Estate (2013), Hotel (2013), Son of a Gun (2014), Seventh Son (2014), and Testament of Youth (2014). 2015 was a strong year for the star, where she won critical acclaim for her films, Ex Machina and The Danish Girl. She has also starred in films like Burnt (2015), The Light Between Oceans (2016), Tulip Fever (2017), Euphoria (2017), and Submergence (2017). This year, Vikander was seen in the much-awaited remake of Tomb Raider. There is no doubt Vikander favours dresses in her closet above all else. Always feminine in her sensibilities, the star is known to make elegant wardrobe choices. Vikander's aesthetic ensures that she is noticed in the crowd, without letting her clothing choices be the only impression she makes on the audience. Back in 2012, she was seen on red carpets in monochromatic cocktail gowns with light embellishment that became her signature for the years to come. In the year 2015, Vikander was made the face of Louis Vuitton. Ever since, she's been seen in several custom creations by Nicolas Ghesquière, the creative director of the French house. The addition of leather accents, sequins and latex to her wardrobe made her sartorial choices a lot more interesting. Even then, Vikander is partial to floral midis and monochrome. Here's a closer look at her complete style evolution. View Gallery 41 Photos Style Evolution- Alicia Vikander Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 14 sling bags you’ll always see on your favourite Bollywood celebrities
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Trigger warning for your bag fetish A tote bag may be practical, but there's something so very charming about a dainty sling bag. Through the years, Bollywood's most fashionable celebrities have found themselves eschewing functionality in favour of an itsy-bitsy sling bag. Worn crossbody or delicately slung on one shoulder—what these bags lack in terms of compartment space, they make up for with sheer impact. From Fendi's graphic numbers, to the signature Chanel quilted envelope sling that lets the world know you've arrived, these are the tiny bags that your favourite celebrities are writing out big cheques for. There's nothing like an explosion of colours and graphics to liven up a basic outfit. column1: This new collaboration uses Indian handloom textiles in French wedding wear
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s where you can catch Ekaya’s first international outing When you mix France's unparalleled fashion savoir faire with India's nuanced textile heritage, you know you have a winner on your hands. Committed to reviving its Benarasi legacy, Ekaya has had an illustrious history of collaborations so far, from Abraham & Thakore to Play Clan, and their latest might just be their biggest yet. The label has come together with Fédération Française de la Creation Couture Sur Mesure - Paris to put forth an international exhibition, Consu d'Or, that translates the best of Indian handloom to bespoke French wedding wear. For its premiere international outing, owner Palak Shah chose to reimagine the possibilities of their staple Benarasis. Usually native to stiff saris, the fabric has now been reinvented to serve as the canvas for 14 French designers to create minimalistic French couture. The label's capsule collection features a luxurious palette of ivory-hued fabrics, subtly enhanced with metallic geometric patterns to maximise the potential of traditional handwoven silks and cottons. Their signature brocades share top billing with organza, mashru silks and chikankari hand-embroidery. The designers of the Federation then adapted the textured fabrics into an array of luxurious silhouettes to create a bespoke wedding wear collection that pushes the boundaries of Indian handloom textiles. After an exciting run at the Paris Haute Couture Week in the month of February, the exhibition is now travelling to the label's home turf and will be on display at Bikaner House, New Delhi, on March 24 and 25. column1: The most romantic royal wedding dresses of all time
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion While we wait to see what Meghan Markle and Princess Eugenie will wear on their respective wedding days, Vogue looks back at the most iconic royal bridal looks of all time, from Grace Kelly to the Duchess of Cambridge The word 'iconic' is a tricky one, and is often overused in fashion to describe anything recognisable or quintessential. But if ever the use of the term were justified, it would be to describe royal wedding dresses. After all, who doesn't remember seeing the Duchess of Cambridge step out in her cathedral-length Alexander McQueen dress on April 29, 2011? In fact, the very tradition of wearing white to wed was started by Queen Victoria, who donned the colour for her nuptials to Prince Albert in 1940. Throughout history, many have erred on the side of the traditional. Queen Elizabeth wore a long-sleeved design by Norman Hartnell, embroidered with 10,000 white seed pearls, silver thread and crystals. Princess Margaret followed suit by covering her arms when she wed Antony Armstrong-Jones in 1960 (also in a Hartnell dress). In 1981, Lady Diana Spencer raised the stakes on sleeves with her David and Elizabeth Emanuel-designed dress, which famously featured a dramatic 25-foot train. Queen Letizia of Spain's Manuel Pertegaz-designed dress—a silk robe delicately embroidered with silver thread—married a more conservative approach to covered arms and, indeed, trains. It was still almost 15 feet long! Lately, however, there has been a wave of more contemporary brides, opting for sleek, off-the-shoulder wedding dresses. Charlene Wittstock's column Armani Prive dress; Crown Princess Victoria of Sweden's satin Pär Engsheden design and Princess Madeleine of Sweden's lace-trimmed Valentino are examples of the same. Mary Donaldson's wedding dress—she wed Prince Frederik of Denmark in 2004—also had a daring neckline. Royal weddings are the closest we come to real-life fairytales. In honour of Meghan Markle and Princess Eugene's nuptials later this year, Vogue looks back at the most romantic royal wedding dresses in history. Check them out. column1: A peek at Manish Malhotra’s glittering summer couture 2018 collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A show-stopping lineup Manish Malhotra's unveiling of his summer couture 2018 collection over the weekend was a show of many firsts for the designer. Forgoing the Instagram show format that has become quite the rage with Indian designers today, Malhotra decided to stay true to his characteristic opulent modus operandi, but only took it a notch higher. So what you had was a one-of-its-kind 400ft circular ramp built on the premises of Panchshil Realty's YOO Villas in Pune, which the show was also designed to launch. Then there were his three showstoppers (that is, if you don't count the sweeping riverside location as a showstopper in itself)—Bollywood celebrities Aditi Rao Hydari, Radhika Apte and Nushrat Bharucha, all walking for the designer for the very first time, with Sophie Choudry belting out some tunes to start the show. “This is the first time I am walking for Manish, so it's very special. I always feel that the ramp ends too quickly, but we have a 400ft stage today, and I almost feel like I am running marathon!” gushed Hydari minutes before the show. The 50 models sashayed in a collection inspired by the natural vistas and verdant valleys of Kashmir, with delicate pastel shades, gossamer fabrics and zealous blooms serving as the collection's mainstays. The fresh, modern take on traditional wear was decidedly intent on allowing the serial wedding attendee to have unabashed fun without compromising on look-at-me impact. The silhouettes did not falter in imitating the drama of the ramp and the gurgling fountains it was centred around. Punctuating the glamour of the free-flowing lehengas, saris with trailing pallus, and tulle gowns was the graceful colour palette of light pink, powder blue, mint green and nude. Think very the-fairy-tale-princess'-millennial-alter-ego. The clever use of sheer play on the gowns and blouses, with a helping hand from beads, pearls, fringes, and feather embellishments, teased, and then left you wanting more — perfect for the lady who values an air of mystery over putting it all out there. Malhotra's collaboration with YOO Villas was a coming together of like-minded stalwart design entities. Brainchild of John Hitchcox and Panchshil Realty, this collection of 45 (and counting) swanky residences in a plush parkland in the heart of Pune, have been designed for the city's jet-setting crew by internationally renowned British designer Kelly Hoppen. A larger-than-life show by the well-loved Malhotra was the only fittingly way to give the city's inner circle a taste of this project. “Panchshil Realty and the Manish Malhotra Label speak the same design language. We both stand for modern luxury, an uncompromising eye for detail and reinventing glamour. So the extravagance of YOO Villas was the perfect match for the launch of my equally dramatic Summer Couture 2018 collection,” concluded Malhotra. column1: Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2018: Highlights from Day 4
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Holographic dresses, a pink runway and tech The last day of the short four-day long Amazon India Fashion Week had the strongest lineup of all days. These are the standout shows from the day you need to know about. Kanika Goyal's collaboration with Adidas Originals saw a fast-paced, modern collection catered to the sneaker collecting, phone-obsessed millennials of today. Goyal went with asymmetric skirts, jackets with removable sleeves, skirt-trouser hybrids and fitted dresses with unusual panels slashing through the print this season. The design was inspired by abstract art and the Japanese technique of Kintsugi when imagining the colour palette. Where Goyal makes up for in creating structured formals for evening wear, she loses in the use of outlandish fabrics. Perhaps it's time to let go of leather, fur and plastic to add an element of ‘edge' to each look. One holographic dress in the lineup, however, stood out in as a winner for the maximalist who likes drawing attention in any room she is in. Siddhartha Tytler made a renewed comeback this season with his collection ‘F.U.S.S.'. Tytler's lineup of bomber jackets with oversized sleeves, slick pencil skirts, pantsuits was interesting one which drew from the decades of the '80s and '90s.  Inarguably, the menswear was stronger in comparison than the womenswear with pieces that were more relevant to kind of men that like to look after their bodies. What Tytler could do away with is the hot fix rhinestone embellishments that remind one of the past in a not-so-nostalgic way. Former Miss India, model and actor, Neha Kapur, a friend of the designer, walked out a white pantsuit bringing the show to a close. To talk about a Péro show is never to talk about one aspect of it—Aneeth Arora makes sure your senses are assaulted on all counts even while you're staring at the runway. What's usually a blacked out show area was swathed in pink. Rows of neatly tied up favours sat on them. Backstage, models were glad to be in warm sweaters and flats for once. Arora, whose pre-show jitters usually have her stressed out to the maximum was also in a lighter, easier frame of mind. “People came to associate us with greys and navy blues for winter, and I just wanted to change that perception and go with a bold pink,” she explained. The collection comprised of standard Péro jackets in Scottish tartans in hues of pinks and sudden citrus bursts of orange. There were winter flowers embroidered, 3D applique-d, prints of flowers sewn onto the checks and more. Arora is a perfectionist who sees things through till she can no longer visit a concept with differentiating perspective. The designer also introduced large tote bags this season that many have already set their eyes on. While candy makers from Pappabubble made live hard candy on one side of the ramp, an a capella group provided live soundtrack on the other. Namrata Joshipura's collection ‘Now' was the designer's perspective on the influence of technology in our lives. With artificial intelligence looking more human every day and us increasingly dependent on machines, Joshipura's lineup was about drawing those parallels. The designer's take on the matter was more aesthetic than functional. Party-ready sequinned pantsuits in Tumblr pink, plenty of close-cut pile fabrics in metallic accents cut into trousers, electric blue, gowns made for a futuristic collection. The designer made use of crystal chain that was sewn on tulle to resemble rows of blinking lights. Joshipura's show brought the season to a close. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Péro's all-pink-everything show to Namrata Joshipura's party perfect collection, here’s everything you need to know from the last day of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2018 Pero's autumn/winter '18 show was in a league of its own. Aneeth Arora's collection was inspired by a floral winter. “I just wanted to surprise everyone with shocking pink," she said. The designer swapped her otherwise dark colour palette in favour of vibrant fuchsias and corals. Lending to the mood, the set also had a live counter skillful candy makers from Papabubble. From detailed beadwork to  crochet detailing, Arora's collection also made use of passamanaria or Portuguese lace on the separates. Kanika Goyal's recent collection draws inspiration from Tacheism, and Kintsugi, 'the art of precious scars'. While Tacheism is a French art movement that features spontaneous brushwork, drips and blobs of paint applied straight from the tube, Kintsugi is is the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with lacquer dusted or mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum. The designer stayed true to the brand's signature style of panelling and colour blocking with a playful twist. High shine and abstract lines on skirts, dresses and statement jackets dominated designers collection. For the last show of the season, Namrata Joshipura presented a futuristic maximal collection that was inspired by the increasing use of technology in our lives. This season the designer not only used metallic fabrics but also experimented with crystal chains by sewing them on net. Joshipura focused on evening wear featuring party-ready dresses, embellished gowns, jumpsuits with feather detailing. Acing the art of evening wear, her collection was ruled by a colour palette of electric blues, magentas, greens and pinks. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2018: Highlights from Day 3
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s what you missed From Shivan & Narresh's stunning closing show of the night to  Anju Modi and Gaurav Jai Gupta's showcase,  Day 3 of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2018 was packed with surprises. Here's everything you need to know. For their latest showcase, designers Shikha Grover and Vinita Adhikari of Ilk presented a collection titled ‘#offline'.  In favour of slow living and all things relaxed, the duo used khadi. From the six-yard staple, fuss-free dresses to relaxed separates, they presented a line-up of simple silhouettes in icy blues, teal, marigold and greys. The effortlessly layered separates featuring woven khadi, cord embroidery, polka dots and geometric patterns made for the perfect winter wardrobe. This season, Anju Modi and Gaurav Jai presented a capsule collection in collaboration with Liva. Channeling a modern vibe, Gaurav Jai Gupta recent collection titled 'The Upside Down' used Liva blends to create textures along with digital prints to create contemporary separates. Models walked through the ramp in structured jackets, relaxed trousers, knotted capes and shirtdresses in a monochromatic colour palette with a hint of blue. Anju Modi's collection, titled 'Mystical Forest', was a perfect marriage of flowy fabrics and draped silhouettes. The colour palette varied from yellows, teal green to ruby reds her in the designer's unconventional colour story for autumn/winter 2018. Drawing inspiration from their travels to the Seychelles, designer duo Shivan & Narresh presented their 'Edomer Series' which was inspired by Edo Art. Catering to destination brides, the collection came packed with printed dresses, decadent lehengas, embellished saris and relaxed swimwear separates. Extending their line of accessories, the duo also presented bags, footwear, and printed belts. The lineup saw versions of tropical prints and detailed embellishments that perfectly captured the essence of the holiday. For men, the designers kept it classic with holiday essentials—swim trunks, shorts, robes and trousers. Recreating the most photographed beach, Anse Source D'argent, made for the ideal runway backdrop. column1: Kim Kardashian West’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Back to the start Whether you can keep up with your own life or not, keeping up with the Kardashians is sacrosanct for Generation Z. And as the grande dame of the Kardashian-Jenner clan, our March cover star Kim Kardashian West' life(style) has a far-reaching impact that is undeniable. The stylist-turned-TV-personality shot to fame when the reality TV show centred on her family, Keeping Up with the Kardashians (2007), became a runaway hit. Ever since, the mega star has only been adding more hyphens to her credentials. The OG of today's new breed of ‘break the internet' social media influencers, the mother-of-three is also an entrepreneur and beauty mogul. Whether she's attending Oscar parties in backless Maison Margiela dresses or posing with her sisters in a bodycon dress paired with a fanny pack, her sartorial stints are what several girls' night conversations revolve around. Vogue tracks Kardashian-West's rise to the top of best-dressed lists. Back in the day, Kardashian-West's wardrobe was more look-at-me than who's-that-girl. When not twinning in LV with BFF Paris Hilton, she was often seen in party girl dresses, bold colours and bolder prints, rounded off with six-inch stilettos. Logos and more-is-more accessories were a recurring part of her repertoire. Kardashian-West's style took a visible turn around 2012, as her now-husband Kanye West assumed the role of her unofficial wardrobe advisor—a fact she admits to herself. “Kanye's definitely inspired me to be a little bit more of an individual. I think my style is just evolving and changing and I think it should,” she has been recorded saying. But while her repertoire assumed a more refined aesthetic, she did not shed the sartorial daredevilry she had come to be associated with. Though she took things up a notch by toning it down. Second-skin silhouettes continue to be a constant in Kardashian-West's wardrobe. So she will dress her baby bump in Givenchy lace, sport a Tom Ford for Gucci suit unbuttoned and shirtless and cinch a sheer Roberto Cavalli gown with a leather belt. The look-at-me colours of yore have given way to a more sophisticated colour palette dominated by nudes, greys, black and ivory, with her ensembles often designed (if not custom-made) by her circle of designer friends like Olivier Rousteing, Riccardo Tisci, Valentino Garavani and Alber Elbaz. As a working mom, Kim has now added a generous dose of comfort to her closet as well. Off-duty KKW has embraced luxe athleisure in comfy tracksuits, joggers, and her new favourite, biker shorts, mostly paired with crop tops and oversized jackets. From the girl who couldn't do without her Louboutins to a lady who is now often seen in Adidas Yeezy Boost kicks and flurry sliders, her footwear choices have a taken a step in the fuss-free direction as well. column1: Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2018: Highlights from Day 2
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Watch the video to see what you missed At Day 2 of Amazon India Fashion Week's autumn/winter 2018 edition, standout collections by designers Vineet Bahl, Nikasha and Nitin Bal Chauhan made their way to the runway. Holidays aren't just about relaxing, they also open your eyes to different cultures. Inspired by the art, architecture and costumes he saw on a recent visit to the Middle East, designer Vineet Bahl's collection took form from his ideas on his trip. Titled ‘Quashqai', it pays an ode to the Turkish clan of the same name. In a way to make the motifs and embroideries used in their costumes contemporary, Bahl juxtaposed them on denim culottes, minidresses, jackets, cargo pants and more. The designer balanced florals, leather, velvet, gold embellishments and denim, all in one lineup. Designer Nikasha Tawadey firmly believes that inspiration does not strike oneself at regular intervals. Sometimes it grows inside you and only manifests itself when it is ready to. The cinematic magic of Satyajit Ray's Apu Trilogy was the starting point of her collection ‘Keya', which means a flower blossoming in the monsoon. Tawadey wanted to recreate the glistening sheen on nature after a shower. The #MeToo movement also served as inspiration for the collection, as Oprah Winfrey's speech at the Golden Globes struck a chord with Tawadey. “I wanted the clothes to be languid, free, almost celebrating this new era for women.” Using the monsoon as a metaphor for change, Tawadey's lineup of embellished ethnic separates in bright hues and florals is for the woman of change. Nitin Bal Chauhan has never shied away from the extreme, but his presentation at Amazon India Fashion Week was palatable to the mainstream audience. The lineup saw deconstructed tailoring to create visually interesting tops, checkered dresses and colour blocking. The designer kept his sense of whimsy intact with giant floral and asymmetric headgear. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Bollywood has had a busy day Priyanka Chopra is one busy star. The actor paired her cheery summer outfit with black kitten heels and a handful of minimal gold rings. column1: Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2018: Highlights from Day 1
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Diana Penty, Vaani Kapoor and more To say this season of Amazon India Fashion Week is as compelling as any of its previous one would be inaccurate. With the general dip in the morale of the environment owing from budget cuts, the absence of a finale spectacle and lesser than usual number of known models, the established fashion platform is finding it challenging to meet its own set standards. However, on the first day, Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017, a lineup of established labels kept the crowd immersed. David Abraham and Rakesh Thakore's collection #sadaksmart was as the name suggests, inspired by the sartorial ways of the streets of New Delhi. Abraham & Thakore has long established itself as label that's to do with people, urban needs, social commentary while staying in the prêt space. The designers showcased their trans-seasonal lineup of belted jackets worn over saris, high waist trousers, crop tops, kurtas and lehengas. A shadow of a construction worker, a working millennial, a social worker—the references were self-explanatory. This season, the designer duo also experimented with colour and besides their beloved monochromatic pieces added variations of chintz to the lineup. Prints and applique work came through in soft pinks, oranges and greens. Rajesh Pratap Singh, Payal Pratap, Gaurav Gupta were amongst the designers seen at the show. Shyamal and Bhumika Shodhan of Shyamal & Bhumika paid an ode to the Parisian skies. Dainty lace saris, cocktail dresses, lehengas and more were seen on the runway. Diana Penty sashayed in an embellished skirt worn with a velvet cowl top. More Indian in translation than French, Shyamal & Bhumika's latest collection was obviously appealing to wedding-hopping crowd. For the last show of the day, Gauri & Nainika and Ashish N Soni presented a joint show under the same sponsor. Keeping the lineup unified under monochrome, the two labels went high glam with black tie dressing. Gauri & Nainika's love for large florals, diaphanous pleated tulle, layers of ruffles lent itself to the Bond-themed show. Ashish N Soni went with sharp cuts and pattern play for the dapper models. Vaani Kapoor opened the show in a dramatic white gown by Gauri & Nainika and closed the show in tuxedo by Soni. column1: Ritu Kumar’s learnings in textiles take form of a new exhibition
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Textile revivalist, Ritu Kumar, documents her journeys to the craft centres in South Asia and Europe On one of her trips to Bukhara, designer and textile revivalist Ritu Kumar stumbled upon old family portraits in a photographer's studio. On looking closely at the attire of the subjects, she made an interesting discovery—that the hand-block printing traditions of Uzbekistan and India were startlingly similar. “The photographer has about two dozen black-and-white images, which I buy for 25 dollars. They prove to be the missing link between hand-block printing, ikat and zardozi,” she wrote in her diary. And now these diary entries are being given a three-dimensional form as part of the exhibition, Crossroads: Textile Journeys with Ritu Kumar. Vintage textiles, bought during her travels in Europe, India and the Far East, memorabilia and collages, will be juxtaposed with these snippets to weave together an intimate story of Kumar's discoveries on her quest to revive textile traditions. She is also coming up with a series of publications—part professional memoirs, part musings of an art enthusiast—about the historical regions that she has visited. This is, perhaps, the only known contemporary travelogue authored by a designer in post-Independent India. The first in the series, on Uzbekistan, will be launched during the exhibition, which starts on March 22, and the rest, about centres such as Kashmir, Benaras, Bengal, Bhutan and Burma, Tamil Nadu, Masulipatnam, Goa, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Rajasthan, will be released by the end of the year. “As a researcher, one is constantly looking at historical travelogues for references. However, there is no such reference in the contemporary context. Hers is the first one,” says designer and textile historian, Mayank Mansingh Kaul, who has curated the exhibition. The show gives a tangible form to the connections that she has made between the various traditions from across the world, with the textiles providing a visuality to a deep personal journey. “For instance, the block makers in Uzbekistan had a similar practice to those in Farrukhabad, Uttar Pradesh. The latter, in fact, trace their lineage to Uzbekistan,” says Kaul. The exhibition begins with her entries about Ajanta caves, in which she challenges the theory that the stitched garments came with the Muslims. In these caves, one can see some of the figurines wearing ikat. “She then goes on to make a connection with poetic, non-geometric ikats from Odisha and compares these with the ikat traditions in Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat, which are more geometric,” says Kaul. There are wonderful collages and paintings created by Kumar herself, which bring some of these journeys alive—offering a glimpse of some subtle observations that she made while travelling. For instance, she has juxtaposed the lush mango orchards, seen en route the weaving villages in Benares, onto the city's famous ghats. The decision to put together a series of travelogues and exhibition didn't happen overnight. Rather, it stemmed from the in-depth research on textile traditions done over 30 to 35 years. “Today, there is a great movement of being organically sustainable, within an indigenous framework. But, you need to know how to go about it and who to go to. So, I realised that it was time to pen down chapters on each region—what I did, what I found,” says Kumar. The idea of the travelogues—published as easy reads—is also to make these craft regions accessible to all. When Kumar started her journeys, there was little connectivity, no hotels, Internet or mobile phones. But today, with these facilities available, it is now possible to go to Bhuj and see craftsmen working with bandhini or to visit the ikat practitioners in Odisha. “These publications will guide you on how to go, where to stay, who to meet. They could be used as an educational tool for the younger generation, who should be encouraged to work there,” she says. column1: Meet Samhita Mukhopadhyay, Teen Vogue’s new executive editor
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion On her new role, her Indian roots and her advice for Indian-origin teenagers At the beginning of February, Teen Vogue announced its new executive editor, Samhita Mukhopadhyay. The news came just three months after Radhika Jones was appointed editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair. Both women are the first Indian Americans to hold their respective titles at these prestigious publications, blazing new trails for desis in media and advancing desi representation in general. Mukhopadhyay, 39, was the former senior editorial director of culture and identities at Mic.com, the former executive editor of Feministing.com, and, as we learned, her roots in social justice date back to her years as a teenager. We sat down with Mukhopadhyay at Teen Vogue's headquarters in New York City to discuss her new role, her advice for Indian-origin teenagers, and her relationship with Indian culture. Tell me about your career arc and how you arrived at Teen Vogue. I have a women's studies undergraduate and graduate degree, so I started pretty young in terms of being really invested in women's issues and feminist issues. Even as a teenager I was always calling out my parents on double standards they had for me and my brother, like, “Why does he not have to do work in the kitchen and I have to do work in the kitchen—I'm not doing work in the kitchen!” Probably the most monumental thing in my career was when I started blogging at Feministing in 2005. At the time, I was working as a substitute school teacher and involved in social justice, but not really sure what I wanted to do. So I started blogging on top of working and, basically, through that got my first book deal. And then I spent the next couple of years going between freelance writing and working a lot in digital strategy. I've worked on several jobs that involved taking people's content strategies and figuring out how to really engage people online with them. So it was kind of a natural fit to come to a place like Teen Vogue where they're at the intersection of activism and this growing young population who are very invested in social and political issues, and has done really groundbreaking work on that. But also pivoting in terms of how to really make it impactful in the digital space. What is your vision for, say, six months down the line? What will Teen Vogue look like under your leadership? I'm really committed to and interested in expanding and deepening our political coverage. I think we've done an amazing job in terms of covering a vast array of topics and really claiming our space in that, and gaining some respectability in that space. I'd like to see us elevate more stories of the young people who are leading these initiatives. Right now we're working with several of the survivors from Parkland [Florida]. We published an op-ed from someone who survived last weekend. And really learning that young people trust our brand enough to bring us their stories, and that we'll do a good job with them. So, I hope to see a lot more of that. I'm also really interested in profiling the teens who are now—there are teens running for office across the country and who are getting involved in the political process. Also balancing [content] with, you know, people want to be fashionable, they want to be, like, it's OK to take selfies and look cute in them with your political quotes. I love our style and beauty coverage. I'm so impressed with it, and I want to see us doing more of that. My vision for six months is that we take over the senate and the house [laughs]. You mentioned op-eds. Are there other things you're currently working on that you're excited about? We're working on a series of investigative pieces around gun violence in the country. I think there's many pieces of the debate that are coming out right now that we're not talking about in concrete enough terms… and the issues we're not talking about are, like, toxic masculinity, and being exposed to violent behaviour, and all of these other kind of societal ills that lead to these moments, and so we want to dig into that debate. What is the biggest misconception about teenagers today? That they only care about selfies. That they're vain. And they're always texting and on their phones, which they are, but so are we. People of all ages are on their phone all the time. And that they're not engaged politically. We're now dealing with the youngest group of millennials and, if anything, we're into Gen Z. Millennials are criticised the same way, yet they are out here changing the world. They are some of the most innovative people in the economy; they're leaders in political movements. There's so much exciting stuff happening, and I think the same is true [for teenagers]. Now they're educated and they have social media and they're ready to take on those powers. What are the major issues impacting teens today? I can speak for Teen Vogue readers, I think more so than [all] teens. I was obsessed with New Kids on the Block when I was a teenager. Jordan Knight: I still follow him on Instagram [laughs]. So, obviously, they're very interested in pop culture and love Beyoncé and Rihanna and all of the same things that teens of every generation have always been interested in. But of the things I have noticed is that they're very interested in gender identity. Even working at an office that's a younger office, I'm finding the comfort with gender fluidity and being really cognisant of peoples preferred gender pronouns. These are things that I haven't seen in older work environments. They're very interested in gender expression, gender nonconformity, and trans visibility. I've noticed a lot of interesting cultural appropriation and making sure you're always tracing things to the right root and understanding whether it's appropriate or not to do something. You mentioned Teen Vogue's readership, and not necessarily being able to speak to all teens. How representative is Teen Vogue's readership of teens in general? I think fairly representative. Even just in that we have a sizeable readership and that we have a lot of teens who really look up to the brand as aspirational, which is exciting and really why I came here. But I do think we are very cutting edge; if you look at other teen publications, they don't focus and prioritise politics and social justice in the same way. That's not to say that Teen Vogue readers and our staff don't also love makeup and heels and dresses and all of that—we do. But I do think that because Teen Vogue really prioritising the social justice themes has developed a devout audience for us, but it's a specific audience. What advice do you have for teenagers and, more specifically, desi teenagers? Don't listen to your parents. It will work out OK [laughs]. Yeah, no, my advice to all teenagers is to stay woke. I think there has to be, more than ever, ways for us to stay optimistic, because it can feel very overwhelming how many things we have to worry about right now outside of your day-to-day anxiety of, like, “Is he going to text me back,” which is a real thing. There's climate change, there's Trump in the White House, there's just so many things to be anxious about right now. So finding ways to stay optimistic and to be innovative in a time when things are a little bit chaotic. Because in that chaos there's also possibility, and that's why I'm so inspired by teens, because I do feel like they are so creative amidst all the chaos. Specifically for desi teenagers, I would really like to see some leadership in the South Asian community talking more openly about the relationship between police brutality and black racism, and Asian American exceptionalism and the model minority myth. I'm so disappointed to see how many South Asian actors and actresses and spokespeople are silent on a lot of those issues. I do think that connection really needs to be made, because often I find that as a South Asian woman people will say, “Oh, well, we have a woman of colour spokesperson for this”. “Privilege” is the wrong word—but I have that kind of social acceptability without it being interrogated in terms of like, “What were the privileges that I experienced that are different than if I were black or latino, or came from a poorer community or didn't have access to the same kind of education?” I worry about that. My parents were immigrants and they had to work so hard to get us to school and do all of that; they did internalise this myth that they were somehow better than other minorities. I worry about how that impacts another generation. One of the things I loved about Aziz Ansari's Master of None was his relationship with Lena in it. I talked to one of my dear friends Rashad Robinson [American civil rights spokesperson] and we talked about how black and Indian relationships are never on television, but they are these really important friendships because often you might both be growing up in predominantly white areas where you don't have another person of colour, so your bestie will end up being the other person of colour in that school. Let's talk about your relationship with India. Growing up, you split your time between India and the United States. Can you speak to that and your current-day relationship with Indian culture? I'm Bengali. Like, I'm such a Bengali [laughs]. Whenever I tell people I'm a writer and I'm Bengali they're like, “We're not surprised.” I did spend a lot of time in India as a child. My parents went back and forth a lot. We come from a huge family, so I have over 60 cousins, and a bunch of them actually live in the States now. I have a very complex relationship with Indian culture. Because the core of my work has been gender identity and sexuality, I have not always appreciated what some of the cultural traditions have been. I am aware enough to know that they're not unique to Indian culture, and that's why I'm not like, “You're uniquely more sexist than your white counterparts,” because I think that's a myth. But that said, in my own experience, my father is still upset that I'm not married yet; he doesn't understand it. Or when I go to India they're kind of like, “Oh, you're just the woman-child. We're not interested.” But my brother gets all this attention and all this interest, and that kind of sexism that's really embedded in the culture [is what] I was very critical of. But, I also think it's an ancient culture with a lot of different perspectives, and they have amazing, amazing feminist movements in India. So I came up on South Asian feminists, like Chandra Mohanty and Gayatri Spivak. That allowed me to dig back into my South Asian roots, because I did feel very alienated when I had this very strong gender analysis, but I didn't see other people who looked like me in the feminist movement. So [I tried] finding other ways in; for me it was really black feminism and Indian feminism that brought me back into it to really look at and understand my mother's life or my grandmother's life. And so I feel really proud to be an Indian, and I feel really inspired by what a robust, vast, and complex culture it is, and all the possibilities that are there. Who are some Indians you look up to? I do look up to Mindy [Kaling]. I think she's a really talented joke writer. She broke into an industry that was really hard to break into as a woman, let alone a woman of colour, let alone a dark-skinned woman of colour who's not skinny. I'm really inspired by the Blank Noise project. It's these women who are doing public actions in India where they physically take up space to show that women are allowed to own and have their own physical space. They'll go into a crowded market space—it's like a flash mob, but they just stand still and they won't move, and so you have to walk around them. It's a protest but it's also performance art around owning your own space and owning your own body. It's a response to street harassment and sexual assault. What strides would you like to see the Indian community make in the next few years? I would like to see more [South Asians] being more vocal politically. Not just in terms of solidarity with other ethnic groups, but I would like to see us—and this is both South Asians and Asians—you know, when something like the Muslim ban happens I would like to see the South Asian community come together and say, “No, absolutely not.” Or, God forbid there's another attack on a Sikh temple, for their immediate response to not be, “Oh, but we're not muslims.” Because we need the next sentence. We need to say, “Who cares if we're muslims? None of us should experience this kind of violence.” And I would like to see more visibility. I'm glad Mindy Kaling is out there, but she's just one person. I would like to see more South Asian—women in particular—creators being in charge of their own narratives. column1: Manish Arora and Rahul Mishra talk about meeting the French President
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Inside the Élysée Palace Two Indian designers showing on the main schedule of Paris Fashion Week is no small feat. Every designer in the world has a dream of showcasing on a platform that big; and when it comes true, what more can be done to top it off? Manish Arora has been a regular in the French capital for the last decade while Woolmark Prize winner Rahul Mishra's journey in Paris only started four years ago. But everyone was an equal at the Élysée Palace when President Emmanuel Macron and First Lady Brigitte Macron hosted a sit-down dinner for all the designers who showed at the recently concluded Paris Fashion Week. France is a nation that values the arts, and the business that it brings to the economy is a direct result of the supportive environment it offers to the creative force. In the caption to an Instagram picture he posted after the dinner, Macaron says, "These creative men and women with entrepreneurial spirit come from different places. Some are French, some are not. The thread that binds them: they all chose to come or stay, here in France, and develop fashion companies. This family picture emphasizes the attractiveness of France as the homeland of everyone who wants to create and succeed." The picture almost reminds you of a class photo. But the night wasn't just about photo ops.   Manish Arora, one of the attendees of the dinner, says, "It was quite an honour to represent India among such influential designers. The whole experience was both calm and incredible. It was a great initiative by the President, I have also met Former French President Jacques Chirac many years ago, and now I'm glad that the new president has started this initiative again. It was an amazing feeling to be part of that ballroom and being treated like part of a family."   Rahul Mishra's infectious, wide-eyed account of the evening is relatable to everyone who has ever idolised designer icons. "When we were standing in line to get our IDs checked, I realised I was standing behind Maria Grazia Chiuri and I had a fan boy moment with her. She said she loved New Delhi and wanted to learn more about the work we do here. I also introduced myself to Jean Paul Gaultier and I spoke about how overwhelming the encounter was and he just said, "Hey, this was an experience for everybody."   Mishra also spoke about how the informal tone of the evening made it possible for honest exchanges to happen in the crowd. "Stella McCartney put the great Sir Paul McCartney on a video call with President Macron and the First Lady and that was a big highlight for him from the evening I guess." The honest, giddy smiles seen in the selfies taken from that night are adequate proof that the dinner was a success. He recollects, "We were all taking the group photographs and calling Anna Wintour to pose with us, but she humbly turned us down, 'You guys get a picture clicked I'm not a designer,' she said." Now that President Macron and the First Lady are currently touring the country, they made it a point to meet with the designers again. More on their tour, here.
