column1: Haider Ackermann knows his priorities: clothes before celebrities
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The French designer and Antwerp art academy dropout sits down with Vogue I arrive soaking wet at Haider Ackermann's unmarked studio in the 8th Arrondissement of Paris. The space is well-lit, full of natural light and devoid of any clutter. In the corner, the designer sits by the window posing for portraits, while his team eats lunch at a communal table in the back. As the rain dies down, the sun's rays shine through a door left half-opened, leading to a room full of garment rails and shoes left on tabletops—a glimpse of what he might show come Saturday morning. Today, Ackermann is in many ways part of fashion's fading gentry. He is a highly skilled women's tailor who has shunned logophilia, a visionary who finds inspiration from the streets—as evident in his bestselling velvet sweats and bomber jackets worn by the likes of Kanye West and ASAP Rocky—but one who's been careful not to succumb to the hype of streetwear. Having enrolled at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, where the likes of Ann Demeulemeester and Martin Margiela were educated, Ackermann left without completing his degree, interning with John Galliano at Dior before establishing his own label. It's a rare and impressive thing for a designer to be a fixture at both Paris Fashion Week and its counterpart for men. Earlier in his career, Karl Lagerfeld heralded Ackermann as a talent worthy of succeeding him at Chanel. But these days, his eponymous label is just as well known for its menswear as its womenswear. In 2016, he was appointed creative director of Berluti, the only men's-focussed luxury brand under the LVMH umbrella, and with all the attention surrounding Berluti's renaissance, it might be easy to forget that when Ackermann first arrived onto the scene at the turn of the millennium, it was actually for his womenswear. The earlier collections, of jersey wrap-over dresses, harem pants and immaculately cut tailoring, coloured with a polished palette of blues, blacks and greys, were shown on the Parisian catwalks to critical acclaim. The man, he reminds me, arrived much later. In fact, it would take nearly a decade for the designer to show a menswear collection on the runway, at Pitti Uomo, the Florentine trade show, in June 2010 for spring/summer 2011. “Suddenly, men appeared, because I was wondering, who was the man behind an Ackermann woman?” The Bohemian collection he exhibited at Pitti featured layered silk tops alongside opulent brocades fit for a Silk Road merchant. According to Ackermann, the introduction of men's garments to complement the womenswear was what he describes as a “mental seduction.” He had hoped to give more attitude to the woman through the man by her side. “It was an exercise of style, a trying-out.” But it would only be temporary. “Then we stopped for a few seasons because I was absolutely was not ready for it.” In 2013, however, it would return for good. And the rest, as they say, is history. After so many years in the industry, Ackermann has experienced the evolution of luxury fashion first hand. But never mind the ugly chunky dad shoes or the slouching hoodies repeatedly plastered with a brand's name.“Do you know how many sneakers they're selling in the world? It's insane,” he raises his voice slightly. To this day, Ackermann still sees himself as a purveyor of stories and dreams, not only clothes. “You just have to think about the story you like to tell,” he continues. For his spring/summer 2018 womenswear collection, the designer sent out asymmetrically cut golden blazers that appeared to crumble on one side, like shifting tectonic plates, alongside white jackets cut with red revers like delicious velvet cake. “Commercially, it's another step that falls behind. We are faced with reality enough: the designs that I have made me travel with my mind, and I like that—I think that's luxury.” At his Autumn/Winter 2018 men's show this season, I spotted the likes of R&B star Miguel and Gabriel-Kane - a front row fixture and son of actor Daniel Day-Lewis—sitting by the runway attentively. Although his clothes have been worn by a cast of A-listers over the years, including Tilda Swinton and now Timothée Chalamet, Ackermann assures me he isn't interested in playing the game of celebrities. “One has to be careful because it's uninteresting to read articles where they first talk about celebrities, and then the clothes,” he warns me. “The first row is taking more attention than the clothes on the catwalk nowadays.” It's an epidemic that the designer attributes to social media. Ackermann, like 800 million others around the globe, is on Instagram. So he's aware of the witch hunts and the culture of calling-out that the platform fosters. “I think due to social media, and everything that happens nowadays, everyone has an opinion,” he says. “But one should always have an opinion that is loaded with knowledge and history.” I ask if he's referring to any accounts in particular. “No, I can't,” he replies, laughing. “Nowadays, whether it's in fashion or in general, everyone can throw their garbage out there, accusing anyone and everyone.” He continues: “It's this public scenery, where you burn witches in the fire—I find it too vulgar for words.” For so many of us who have succumbed to the pressures of documenting our waking moments , the constant scrolling through social media has become less entertainment and more of an inevitable chore—a Sisyphean task for the modern individual, the price we pay for living in the 21st century. “My life is so uninteresting to be shared, and I don't see why someone is interested in how I wake up in the morning,” Ackermann says. “That's not my job; my job is to make nice clothes, to search for a type of beauty—if a man or a woman feel attractive in it then I did my job.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: In Paris, Chinese designers are changing attitudes and increasingly in demand
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The presence of Chinese designers in the international fashion arena is growing thanks to a critical mass of talent showing on-schedule in Paris. As storied French fashion house Paul Poiret prepares to relaunch under designer Yiqing Yin, Vogue looks at the growing impact of these brands in fashion’s reigning capital. When South Korean investor Chung Yoo-kyung announced that the legendary couture house Paul Poiret, which fell into obscurity almost a century ago, would relaunch at Paris Fashion Week this season, the designer tasked with its new creative vision wasn't the first name on everyone's lips. Helming her own eponymous label, Yin showed her collections during couture week as one of the 15 fully fledged members of the Chambre Syndicale de la Haute Couture alongside the likes of Dior and Chanel. Since then, she's put her brand on hold to focus exclusively on this new endeavour. Yin is - and Poiret was - a couturier by training, but the newly relaunched brand bearing the latter's name will now focus on ready-to-wear, with offerings in accessories and footwear. It's a move that neatly captures how much the fashion industry has changed since Poiret's heyday during the turn of the 20th century. Although Chinese designers have long shown during Paris Fashion Week - Shiatzy Chen of Taiwan, for instance, made her debut in 2008 - what makes Yin's appointment extraordinary is that there has never been a Parisian maison so deeply entrenched in the history of French fashion with a Chinese designer at the helm. In his prime, Poiret was heralded as the King of Fashion, dominating the Pre-War era: he replaced the once fashionable excesses of Edwardian frills and S-bend silhouettes with fluid draping, vivid colours and longer corsets, pioneering the girlish figure of the early 1900s. Established in 1903, the brand postdates Lanvin but predates Chanel, making it one of the oldest houses in French fashion. Yin joins several Chinese designers of diverse backgrounds on the Paris Fashion Week lineup, including London-based Yang Li, Shanghai-based Uma Wang and Jourden from Hong Kong. “This phenomenon [of Chinese designers showing in Paris] is quite natural and reflects the growing place of China and the constant progress of the Chinese design culture,” Pascal Morand, executive president of the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode, tells Vogue. “Our constant is to detect the greatest talents all over the world, but it is true we see some more Chinese talents both on the menswear and womenswear calendars.” According to Morand, 50 percent of the brands showing during Paris Fashion Week are not French - rather they belong to 20 different nationalities. Beyond the runway, the top Chinese designers who show on the stages of Shanghai and London, including Shushu/Tong and Xiao Li, all have their showrooms in the French capital. The increasing volume of Chinese talent in Paris and elsewhere in Europe can be attributed in part to the evolving perception of Chinese design and manufacturing internationally. “With the growing level of design sophistication and quality, this new generation of Chinese designers has created a new authority in ‘made and created in China,'” says Joanna Gunn, chief brand officer of Lane Crawford. Yang Li, for example, is a purveyor of £2,000 parkas and £1,000 bomber jackets - all made in China by KTC, a premium performance manufacturer that additionally produces for brands like Rapha, the cycling outfitter. “There is an appetite to take risks, and an increasingly global mindset, which informs bolder and more original aesthetics,” Gunn continues. “We found that across visual language and price point, these designers want to stand out, instead of blend in.” Moreover, attitudes towards Chinese design is changing within China itself. “[It's] more and more positive than even five years ago, with progress being made on both creativity and commercial value,” says Tasha Liu, co-founder of Dongliang, the Shanghai-based concept store committed to Chinese designers, and Labelhood, an independent fashion platform that champions Chinese talents. Today, the country accounts for about one-third of global luxury sales, but despite the constant stream of Chinese tourists visiting London's Bond Street or the Champs-Elysées, domestic consumers are becoming increasingly discerning. Beyond Louis Vuitton or Gucci, many are looking for a point of difference in design and style, thus sparking an interest in the new generation. “But showing in Paris alone cannot replace the designer's connections with the market: the product itself, along with the the positioning, price and design, is taking a more important role than where they have shown,” Liu continues. Given the critical mass of Chinese designers in Paris, one might be tempted to draw comparisons to the other East Asian wave that hit the City of Light several decades ago, when the likes of Yohji Yamamoto and Rei Kawakubo first arrived. But such a comparison is only superficial. “The Chinese wave is marked by a double - that is, Western and Eastern - culture of designers, linked with education and experience,” Morand says. “The Japanese wave was more strictly relying upon Japanese culture, while playing with Western codes.” What's even easier is to misguidedly consider all the Chinese designers of Paris, and beyond, under one umbrella despite their aesthetic differences. Wang, for instance, draws from her Chinese heritage, combining Eastern references and Western counterparts, with a focus on developing new innovative materials. For her Spring/Summer 2018 collection, the designer showed fabrics that resembled the patterns of Gustav Klimt's paintings and gowns cut with Chinese collars. Meanwhile, Central Saint Martins drop-out and former Raf Simons intern, Yang Li - who has a penchant for tailoring - regularly turns to music for inspiration. Last season, he sent out an array of all-black looks, comprising double-faced silk coats and biker jackets, as Michael Gira of the band Swans played on stage. Diverging approaches to fashion notwithstanding, the likes of Wang and Li today continue to share the one-dimensional label: Chinese designers. Does the taxonomy of being reduced to their cultural identity bother them? “I think it is normal and makes sense now; never before in the Western world have so many Chinese designers blossomed,” Wang replies.” I believe that in the near future, the Western world will have a deeper understanding of the story and style behind all the Chinese brands. But only time can tell.” View Gallery 9 Photos In Paris, Chinese designers are changing attitudes and increasingly in demand Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Behind Rahul Mishra’s fall 2018 collection for Paris Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Inspirations, musings and more When Rahul Mishra designs a collection, it is bound to reflect his multi-dimensional thought process. From spinning sartorial saagas about the secret tales of ferrymen carrying travellers across water to imagining the colour spectrum from a bee's perspective, Mishra is a maverick who believes in peeling off the exterior layers and getting right into the heart of the matter. This season has been about introspection—of his subconscious and nostalgia carried by the memories that he captured throughout his years of growing, moving and learning. Landscapes have been an ever-changing factor in Mishra's life, who hails from a village in Kanpur. "It's all about what you see through the bars of a window grill—an homage to the transitioning realities, from my childhood recollections of the unending trail of fields to the concrete cluster of a cityscape," he muses. The pink and orange sunset hues mirrored on the glass and metal of the towering skyscrapers, the tessellations produced by a constellation of buildings and patterns recreated through his picturesque memory of linear plains have served as inspirations for his intricate surface techniques. [#image: /photos/5ce4211289be3621817cf286]||| ||| The fierceness of the '80s and early '90s, dazed memories of his mother's brocades, corduroys and sequins are on Mishra's mind this season. "The pieces from this presentation are a personal reminiscence distorted by seminal pop cultural moments of an era that is now blurred by trends of today," he says. A master of surface detailing technique, the presentation for fall 2018 is dedicated to sequins, the holographic trinket synonymous with the sparkle of vicious eighties. There is of course, the ever-present representation of his roots—this time through 'kinkhab', a brocade of the oldest form—woven in silk and gold or silver threads. Summarised in a word? 'Rhizome'. A botanical definition will lead you to believe that it is a continuously growing horizontal underground stalk which puts out lateral shoots and adventitious roots at intervals, but Rahul Mishra will tell you that rhizome just means the longing that stems underneath the eternal flux of your memories, impressions of the past. The Swedish brand's design ideology is aimed at catering to the masses—this season was about painterly prints, party-ready fringes and elevated separates that would make day dressing as a concept a whole lot interesting. After facing backlash over the careless use of a black model with a sweatshirt bearing the slogan “the coolest monkey in the jungle”, the brand has been very careful about being sensitive to other cultures. Despite Japan being the reference point for the collection, the interpretation was kept ‘conceptual' according to Andreas Lowenstam, who heads menswear. "It was so exciting to see our strong statement of print and colour with clean lines inspired by Japanese design. Together with the authentic setting, tableware, decorations and other details, there was a quiet grace that really shone through. We can't wait to see how our customers around the world will be styling their favourite pieces," said Pernilla Wohlfahrt, H&M's design director. Masked musical trio Dancing Strawhatz performed at the show. Cherry blossoms descended from above the ceiling at the finale. All of the looks seen on the runway can be yours now. column1: Riccardo Tisci joins as Burberry’s new chief creative officer
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's what we can expect from the new appointment Christopher Bailey's swan song of a finale show for Burberry was easily the biggest highlight of London Fashion Week just last month. Almost a year ago, Riccardo Tisci, the visionary at Givenchy, stepped down from his role as creative director. Somewhere in the interim, Phoebe Philo exited from Céline. 2017 was a year of talent parting ways with enormous luxury giants whose very image they helped wield through their careers. Observations and speculation form the backdrop against which fashion's musical chairs are played. Many predicted a future for Tisci at Versace—the designer has made his respect for Donatella Versace very clear in the past few years. Meanwhile, Philo moving to Burberry was also part of the guesswork. However, news broke out today laying all speculation to rest; that Riccardo Tisci will be taking over Bailey at Burberry. Tisci's era at Givenchy will be remembered fondly in fashion history. His gothic, romantic aesthetic was championed by critics, fans and celebrities alike. British giant Burberry is known for its "classics reinvented" approach. The two distinctly different ideologies coming together is unexpected to say the least. Tisci, who is seasoned with no less than 12 years at Givenchy, transformed the couture house from one of French elitism to a brand that could produce couture and streetwear with equal ease. In many ways, the move is a smart one for both parties involved. Tisci's creativity supported by the resources at Burberry will only bring about favourable results. Safe to say, hardcore fans of the designer will carry forward their loyalties to Burberry. Not unlike Nicolas Ghesquière's move to Louis Vuitton in 2013, the union could prove to be deeply satisfying one—commercially and creatively.   Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

We already have two stores in Mumbai and our store in Ogaan in New Delhi acts as our flagship, so expanding to Bengaluru seemed like a natural choice,” she told us early in 2018, while setting up her new space. Bengaluru's niche market for designer fashion has already been identified by concept store Cinnamon, and Khandwala thought it best to go with the experts. “The store has been around for so long and it is such a beautiful space. Radhika Poddar is a true tastemaker,” she says. Set inside the courtyard of an old haveli, Khandwala's store will rest inside Cinnamon's premises. "The customer in Bengaluru is very different from the north Indian one. I think culturally, they don't feel the pressure to overspend on clothing so what our store will offer is more of the kurtas, saris, some brocade pieces and a lot of accessories. The edit will be about clothes that can be worn again and not just occasionally,” Khandwala adds. As is the case with every store, the designer has hand-painted a mural—this time of marigolds to add her personal touch to the space. column1: First look at Dior’s autumn/winter 2018 set: a scene of revolution and protest
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Inside the show For her autumn/winter 2018 collection for Christian Dior, Maria Grazia Chiuri is returning to the Musée Rodin, this time with her most striking set design to date: a defiant collage of 3,000 posters. Conceived by set designer and longtime Dior collaborator Alexandre de Betak, the backdrop takes its cue from the collection, which marks the 50th anniversary of the protest that  shook Paris in May 1968. The series of strikes proved to be a turning point in France, igniting a deeper conversation about society and its values. It took 150 people three weeks to build the set: covering the double runway—seats, walls and all - with posters inspired by that anti-authoritarian, urgent and creative spirit of 1968. An expansive mirrored ceiling reflects the cacophony of visuals beneath: fragments of feminist slogans, vintage magazine covers—British and American Vogue included - and archive protest images, patched together like a collage of insurgence, reinvention and strength. Through the commotion, one poster stands out clearly, daring black writing on a white backdrop at the end of the runway: “I AM A WOMAN.” This dramatic backdrop marks a stark departure from previous seasons. When she started, Chiuri's set designs were a comparatively simple affair, providing clean backdrops that allowed the collection to do the talking. Recall Bureau Betak's pared-back wooden runway, flanked with solid oak benches and dove-grey surfaces for spring/summer 2017. Even the mosaic mirrored set of spring/summer 2018, inspired by the sculptor Niki de Saint Phalle, was somewhat soothing in comparison with it's cave-like setting. Her couture and resort collection backdrops—know for their dramatic, awe-inspiring scale—often take a wistful, serene approach; think of the resort show set against the Santa Monica Mountains, or the garden of her couture debut. Not so this season: this is the scene for a revolution. View Gallery 6 Photos Dior set Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 6 things to know about Simon Porte Jacquemus
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Paris Fashion Week's new darling Since the start of the new year, Simon Porte Jacquemus has been teasing his more than 400,000 Instagram followers with hints of a #NewJob. On Monday night he opened Paris Fashion Week with a bang, revealing the details of his new challenge: his own menswear line. The first collection of L'homme Jacquemus did not hit the runway, but will debut in Paris come June, during men's fashion week. Already a firm fashion favourite, the self-taught Jacquemus set up his label in 2009, aged just 19. He's developed a signature that is at once classically Gallic—think Breton stripes and quintessential French motifs—yet surreal, earning him the LVMH Special Prize in 2015—on his second attempt. Aesthetically, Jacquemus treads a neat line between the conceptual and the commercial via twisted and deconstructed shirt dresses, asymmetric blazers and statement blouses. This year, he introduced mini-handbags, helping launch the trend after the creations were spotted on the likes of Rihanna. His poetic approach to presentations, cinematic campaigns and noted Instagram presence have made him a force to be reckoned with. As he announces L'homme Jacquemus, Vogue rounds up six things you may not know about the young designer… Jacquemus' brand pays tribute above all else to his mother's style and spirit. As a child, he made a dress for her out of beige linen, which she wore to take him to school the following day. Her untimely death (she died in a car accident aged only 42) pushed Jacquemus to start his own brand, under her maiden name. She remains a constant source of inspiration for the young designer, too: “I always want to try and create something very innocent,” he told Dazed in 2016. “Jacquemus is not about nightlife and clubbing and things like that, it's more about fruit and vegetables and rolling in the grass.” “Although my parents weren't in church I insisted on having a communion. I wanted to become a priest,” he told Ssense in 2016. “Not because I believed so much in God, but because I was obsessed with the uniform of the priests. I even went so far as to force my family to take me to church every Sunday. After I wanted to be a priest, I wanted to be in the military and after that I wanted to be a lawyer. All because of the uniforms. I love wearing uniforms.” Though briefly enrolled at the École Supérieure des Arts et techniques de la Mode, Jacquemus's true fashion education came from Comme des Garçons. “I've never been to fashion school, but I worked at the Comme des Garçons store in Paris to finance my brand, and I feel it was my school,” he told Marie Claire in 2017. “It taught me about clothes, and how to be sure of who you are, treat your people and approach your customer.” “Fashion is poetry,” he told Interview in 2016. “It's a way to tell a story, to say something in this world, because you always send a message with what you wear. Yet, fashion is also a business. I sell poetry. For me, there is no point in fashion if you don't sell. That is why what you see in my runway shows is what we sell. I like to have that transparency. Now with Instagram and social media, people see a fashion show and they want to buy what they see.” Jacquemus didn't set out to be a minimalist designer: “When I started my brand, minimalism was more a necessity than a plotted concept,” he told Ssense. “I didn't have much money, but I knew I had to make the best that was possible with what I had.” Speaking to Vogue, he described how, after sourcing the fabrics he wanted from marché Saint Pierre he stumbled across a woman who was making curtains. “I asked her to make me a high-waist skirt with no buttons but a zip on the side. I also said no pockets because pockets and buttons are very expensive. So minimalism was not a reference, it was because I had no money.” Jacquemus' Instagram savvy is well-known—he was among the first to post three related images as a means of story-telling and his time-stamped Stories are widely imitated—but his virtual presence extends beyond the visual platform. A true child of the digital age, some of Jacquemus' closest friends and collaborators have come from cyberspace. The influencer Jeanne Damas? They met as teens via Tumblr. Pierre-Ange Carlotti, a photographer born in Corsica, and Fabien Joubert, now the company's commercial director, both corresponded online with Jacquemus for years before meeting. Jacquemus and his boyfriend, filmmaker and photographer Gordon von Steiner, first connected online, too. “For me it's not about being strategic, it's about being spontaneous,” he told AnOther of his Instagram approach. column1: Indian designers mourn the loss of a style icon in Sridevi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Tributes from Manish Malhotra, Tarun Tahiliani, Sabyasachi and more On Sunday morning, the nation woke up to the shocking, sad news of the demise of iconic Bollywood actor, Sridevi. The superstar, all of 54, passed away relatively young due to a cardiac arrest in Dubai. Sridevi, arguably the biggest female superstar of her age, left behind a prolific body of work that will continue to inspire and entertain audiences in the coming years. Although the actor had taken a hiatus from her career in 1997 after her superhit film Judaai, her powerful comeback in 2012 with the critically acclaimed English Vinglish, proved that she could still single-handedly lead a film to box office and critical success. A legendary beauty and a talented dancer, Sridevi had currently become the favourite muse of many of India's top designers. With her admirers still in shock, the design community has expressed their grief at the untimely loss of an icon. "Sridevi and I first met in 1990 when she was already a superstar and I was beginning my career. Working with an icon I always called “Ma'am” was a turning point in my career, as it was the beginning of many associations and a longstanding friendship beyond work. We have seen each other grow professionally and personally—it was amazing to see the roles she blossomed into, her passion for painting, and the doting wife and mother she was. I met Sridevi very recently in Dubai and we just had so much to share. The news that she is no longer with us comes as a shock. I will always cherish the precious memories of a friend who was an iconic superstar. At this point, all my thoughts are with Sridevi's family and I request for privacy as we honour a friend and we grieve her loss."   "Saddened by the untimely demise of India's greatest actor, Sridevi. An epitome of beauty and grace. We would like to express our deepest condolences to the family. May her soul rest in peace."   "We are extremely saddened at the sudden demise of Sridevi. We extend our deepest condolences to her family at their hour of bereavement. May her soul rest in peace."   "Iconic. One word that Sridevi owned and made her own. We mourn her cruel and untimely passing. Our first thoughts go to her beloved daughters who must learn to live without their mother. To her husband. We celebrate a woman who ruled the silver screen, pan India for decades. Who lit it up with one solid gold performance after another. A powerhouse of talent, a muse for millions, style setting, trailblazing diva. A life lived fully and cut so brutally short. As fans of Cinema, as designers and as two men who knew this legend, we will miss you terribly, Sridevi. Fly, Beautiful Soul."     Fashion What's New Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What to expect from the autumn/winter 2018 shows at Paris Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From intriguing designer hashtags and an iconic couture house relaunch Last September, the fashion world was all aflutter in anticipation of a slew of debut collections by designers for the grandes maisons of Paris. Exciting for some, and nerve-wracking for others, spring/summer 2018 signalled a changing of the guard—one that has now settled in (presumably) to their new positions in the upper echelons of the industry, alongside a crop of talents who have decamped from New York to try their luck in the City of Light. Though some think of fashion like a house of cards, the reality is a little more stable—and at this end of fashion month, labels are keenly investing for long-term gain—pouring new foundations, renovating, upscaling and toying with a ‘sea change' in the fashion real estate game. French wunderkind Simon Porte Jacquemus kicks off the show season in Paris with his Monday night slot, the only show on a day when buyers, editors and the rest of the fashion pack are still transiting from Milan. On Wednesday, he unveiled via Instagram that his autumn/winter 2018 show ‘Le Souk' (no prizes to whoever guesses that inspiration) will take place at the Petit Palais which, like last season's Musée Picasso affair, is a serious step-up from his early show locations, which included a local swimming pool and games arcade. His hash-tagging of #newjob has fashion folk gossiping as to what he'll unveil the day of the show, but with rumours of the Céline position clearly misplaced, the jury's out on this one. Could he have been chosen to revive a slumbering fashion house, perhaps? With Hedi Slimane's appointment at Céline, Phoebe Philo's coveted Sunday afternoon spot on the PFW calendar was up for grabs, as the house reshuffles for Slimane's first show in October. Instead, Belgian entrepreneur Anne Chapelle (business partner to both Ann Demeulemeester and Haider Ackermann) seized the time slot for Poiret—the century-old French maison she has revived (thanks to financial backing from Samsung heiress Chung Yoo-Kyung) with Chinese couturier Yiqing Yin at the creative helm. Another newcomer on the schedule is the 2017 LVMH Prize winner Marine Serre. Since quitting her day job at Balenciaga to go solo, her printed body stockings and flouncy, voluminous gowns have been snapped up by the likes of Dover Street Market and Opening Ceremony. Serre will open the first full day of shows on Tuesday morning before big-ticket blockbusters: Dior by Maria Grazia Chiuri in the gardens of the Musée Rodin and—just hours later—Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent. Autumn/winter 2018 is the season of the sophomore, as a trio of designers will each present their second collection at a Parisian house. First up is Natacha Ramsay-Levi at Chloé, who will be moving her second show to an as-of-yet undisclosed location after last season's exclusive outing (60 per cent less seats!) inside the new, contemporary art-filled Maison Chloé. Later that day, Dior alumni Serge Ruffieux's pretty, bohemian new vision for Carven will play out at a middle school in the 15th arrondissement, whilst Clare Waight Keller's Givenchy show returns to the Palais de Justice on Sunday morning. After mixed reports of her first women's and men's ready-to-wear collections last September, Waight Keller made a splash at her first-ever haute couture show in January, leaving the ball in her court for a strong follow-up for the house that Hubert built. Not only have designers been switching houses, but labels have been exploring the geographic limitations of when and where they show their collections. Despite their studios remaining in New York City, a handful of designers have decamped to join the Paris schedule, just as others (like Bottega Veneta and Esteban Cortazar) have been trying their luck with one-time-only fashion shows in the Big Apple. Following buzzy debuts in Paris last October, Thom Browne and Joseph Altuzarra will show once again on the official calendar this week. Also of note, Demna Gvasalia will show both menswear and womenswear at his Balenciaga show on Sunday for the very first time. Runway shows aside, Paris Fashion Week will play host to hundreds of presentations, cocktails, dinners and after-parties that cater to a broad cross-section of the fashion community. Highlights will include the semi-finals of the fifth 2018 LVMH Prize, a competition presided over by a prestigious jury including Nicolas Ghesquière, Marc Jacobs, Clare Waight Keller, Haider Ackermann, Karl Lagerfeld, Maria Grazia Chiuri and Jonathan Anderson. The 21 finalists (which this year include Eckhaus Latta, GmbH, Matthew Adams Dolan and Charles Jeffrey) will be whittled down to eight, with the winner announced in June. Finally, and for those seeking the veritable holy grail of fashion inspiration, the exhibition “Margiela Galliera” opens at the Palais Galliera museum on March 3, its last show before closing mid-July for renovations and the establishment of a permanent collection. The Margiela exhibition—curated by Alexandre Samson and instigated by outgoing director Olivier Saillard—includes more than 130 silhouettes by the seminal Belgian designer, and word has it his personal implication in the project has been considerable. column1: Sonam Kapoor: “I don’t want anyone telling me what I can or cannot wear”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The actor goes candid at United Colors of Benetton's 25th anniversary in India Italian label United Colors of Benetton has been in India for the last 25 years. To celebrate the occasion, Sonam Kapoor visited the brand's flagship store in Bandra. Dressed in a striped dress with a black jacket nonchalantly thrown over her shoulders, Sonam Kapoor looked every bit the style icon she is. Kapoor recalled her earliest memories with the brand, and how it's unique campaigns impacted her as a child. “When I used to go abroad, when I was much younger, I used to see different campaigns, but there were only campaigns with just white people in it. Benetton was the only one which was inclusive, they had people of all colours wearing Benetton clothes. As a young person that made an impression on me—if somebody of colour can wear this so can I.” Speaking of her personal style, Kapoor revealed that she is all about colours these days, especially yellow and fuchsia pink, and hopes to incorporate more vibrant hues into her wardrobe. Kapoor is one of the few Bollywood actors who have aced androgynous style. A firm believer of the movement towards gender-neutral fashion, Kapoor spoke about blurring the lines of fashion, “It's very important because I don't want anyone telling me what I can or cannot wear. I think those days are gone and it's important to understand that you can wear whatever you want.” She went on to add how tuxedos, traditionally a menswear look, always look sexy on women, especially with a red lip. Aside from the basic differences in body structure between men and women, she further remarked, “Of course body shapes differ, but sometimes it doesn't matter what looks good or doesn't look good on you, as long as you feel it's looking good.” Another current fashion movement she is glad about happens to be athleisure, because she loves wearing laid-back, relaxed clothes, so much so that she called a tracksuit her go-to date night outfit! That's why she is a fan of the T-shirts and jeans from Benetton's latest summer collection. However, is there any trend she isn't so happy about? “Tattoo chokers, those plastic ones from the nineties,” she quips, “Although I've been guilty of trying one, with a black lip and spiked hair.” Talking about summer, we asked her which movies remind her of summer. “Aisha and Khoobsurat, they're both summer movies, they released in the summer and they're fun, happy movies—romantic comedies, that are also empowering for women!” Lastly, what does summer mean to her? “The beach! Or, especially because of Indian summer, I like to travel up to the hills.” View Gallery 5 Photos Sonam Kapoor shares her earliest memories about United Colors of Benetton Culture & Living What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Jeremy Scott, a designer built for the Instagram age
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer speaks to Vogue about tuning out the critics Two things that Jeremy Scott was made for? Social media and Moschino. The American designer's 2013 appointment at the Italian heritage label was the ultimate career coup for someone whose creative tendencies lean towards all things feel-good-fun and pop-culture cool. Amidst the quick-fire comings and goings of creative directors during the past few years, from Raf Simons at Dior to Hedi Slimane at Saint Laurent, Scott—a Pratt Institute graduate who came to the role armed with nearly two decades of experience running his own eponymous brand—has stayed put. “I've been having the time of my life,” says the Kansas City-born designer, who describes the fit as “hand in glove”. We're speaking by phone from the Moschino studio in Milan,  where he is putting the final touches on Moschino's autumn/winter 2018 collection. Scott is the incarnation of everything Moschino was under its original founder, Franco Moschino, his own aesthetic so incredibly in-keeping with that irreverence and fashion satire that set the brand apart from its '80s contemporaries at the time. “I never really imagined this [role] until it was offered to me and then I realised... there isn't another person who could do it or do it better,” he says. “I have a respect for Franco and a respect for his legacy and I wanted to do something that would honour that and bring back the lustre to it.” Where Franco did teddy-bear toys on dresses and silverware on suits, Scott continues that trompe l'oeil trope of surrealism. McDonald's, My Little Pony, Barbie and Sponge Bob Square Pants have all played muse; candy wrappers and household objects have been fashioned into ball gowns. He sees the world through an iconographic lens and his clothes, informed by tongue-in-cheek visual puns, embody humour, sexiness, are whimsical and playful yet come with a thought-provoking social streak. While some designers and pundits have bemoaned the impact of Instagram on fashion—arguing that it favours photogenic, bi-dimensional clothes over those with more nuanced artistry—Scott has an automatic affinity for it. “I think I was built for social media and not in the sense that I'm a selfie person,” he says. “Social media now is really about Instagram, it's about a picture that is less than the size of the palm of your hand. What is impactful is not an all-black look. It's about being colourful and bold and my work was already that and has always been that way,” he reflects. “It's kind of like that world has caught up to me.” It's something we'll see in action again on Wednesday evening, as he unveils Moschino's latest collection. The designer was thinking about conspiracy theories—an all-too-timely theme for a designer living in Trump's America. “I've been thinking about conspiracy theories that have existed for a long time, like those surrounding John F. Kennedy and Marilyn Monroe,” he says, adding that there will also be references to Jacqueline Kennedy—and aliens. Could there be more wonderful starting points for a collection? It's classically Scott: suitably outlandish and totally compelling. “My work is always about communication first and foremost. The more understood I can be, the more international it is,” he explains. “You don't have to know about some very obscure German painter from the ‘20s to understand this collection. It's like: Oh! I get it.” Except that sometimes people don't. The critics. Scott has come under fire for his pop-kitsch point of view. “A lot of things I've done people have turned their noses at when I did it, or didn't always give it the proper consideration, and that's fine, that's part of the cross that I bear,” he says. “I don't design my clothes for the critics, it's not for pleasing a diminishing elite in the fashion world; it's for people, I make clothes that real people wear.” And that is the biggest irony of all: while some critics may deem his clothes unsophisticated, absurd, even non-wearable, on the latter front they are very much the opposite, worn by everyone—from Björk, Rihanna, Katy Perry and Kylie Minogue to the legion fans that stand outside his shows each season, pining for a glimpse. While Scott may be modest about his contributions on the design front, when it comes to business, he's proven a real frontier man. He's built a career on cleverly bridging the gap between high and low fashion (cementing him as the ideal man for Moschino) and did the streetwear-infused thing well before his peers. (Indeed, he has been collaborating with Adidas with his own line for over a decade.) Consider, too, the see-now-buy-now phenomenon that gained momentum when Burberry and Ralph Lauren got on board two years ago. Scott was already testing the model as early as 2014, when he made his debut collection for Moschino available to buy immediately afterwards both as the brand's own retail locations and major department stores like Nordstrom—and most of which sold out the next day. He's even proven a trendsetter when it comes to real estate. “Even my friend Hedi [Slimane] will say: ‘You're the pioneer, you came to LA first—Tom [Ford] and I followed you!'” he laughs, the sunshine city having become fashion's favourite new capital in recent years. “I remember Tom asking ‘How are you going to do that? How are you going to work from there? I wish I could do that!' And now look who's doing that!” Where Scott goes, others follow—even if the latter don't always admit it. column1: Post PETA intervention, Anna Dello Russo withdraws fur coats from auction
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Dello Russo has decided to donate the fur pieces due to be auctioned off Anna Dello Russo, the international tastemaker and editor-at-large of Vogue Japan, is taking a stand against fur, donating a number of garments that were due to be auctioned off at Christie's this week to PETA, the animal rights campaign group. The special archive auction, scheduled to take place during Milan Fashion Week on February 24, will see 30 Dello Russo-acquired looks from the last three decades—head-to-toe, including accessories—auctioned off in aid of the Swarovski Foundation Scholarship Program, which provides bursaries to emerging fashion talents at Central Saint Martins. Three fur pieces originally included in the catalogue—a Miu Miu fur stole, an Antonio Berardi embellished jacket and an ermine fur and metal-knit Dolce & Gabbana number—have been withdrawn from the bidding war, and will instead be donated to PETA's fur amnesty programme. When the auction was announced in January, PETA wrote to Dello Russo to implore her to forego fur at the event. The creative consultant wrote back to say that the selection for the auction had already been made, but that she would instead like to donate the pelts to the group's amnesty programme. “Her decision is a sign of the times,” PETA director Elisa Allen tells Vogue, “and we're truly delighted that she's championing this change.” The animal rights group plans to use the coats in high-profile educational displays to highlight the plight of animals killed for their fur, or as bedding for sick and orphaned animals in sanctuaries. "The fashion community is increasingly moving away from fur and so am I," said the street style star, referring to fashion brands like Gucci, Armani and Michael Kors, all of which have recently implemented fur-free policies. "This auction is about passing my heritage on to the next generation, but as someone who cares about animals I no longer feel comfortable passing these fur garments on to others.” What the auction will include is a treasure trove of legendary runway pieces, including Hedi Slimane's heart piece from Saint Laurent's autumn/winter 2016 as well as looks by Nicolas Ghesquière for Balenciaga, Raf Simons for Jil Sander, Tom Ford for Gucci, Riccardo Tisci for Givenchy and a Giorgio Armani suit from 1988 that Dello Russo wore to attend her sister's wedding. Bidding will commence at just €50, but prices are expected to climb much higher than that. A further 150 pieces from Dello Russo's private collection—none of them featuring animal skins—will be put up for sale via Net-A-Porter, alongside a new tome chronicling a series of object that encapsulate her fashion journey, AdR Book: Beyond Fashion, published by Phaidon and art directed by Luca Stoppini. “Anna Dello Russo is one of the most talked-about women in fashion; where she leads, others follow,” says Allen. “We're sure her compassion will inspire yet more style icons to rid their wardrobes of fur garments and send them to PETA so that we can put them to good use through our amnesty programme.” View Gallery 7 Photos Anna Dello Russo withdraws fur coats from Christie’s auction What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Kering to launch an online course on sustainability for young designers
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All the details on the free online course here Sustainability has been a hot topic in fashion for years, but until recently there were few resources available for brands and designers who wanted to be more environmentally savvy. Four years ago, Kering and the London College of Fashion, the prestigious constituent college of the University of the Arts London, partnered to create a series of courses that offered just that. Now they are taking their partnership beyond the classroom with the launch of their first open-access digital course. Launching on April 9, the 18-hour online course, titled “Fashion & Sustainability: Understanding Luxury Fashion in a Changing World”, will provide free and flexible access to both Kering and LCF's experts over a six-week period. “We couldn't be everywhere at once,” Marie-Claire Daveu, chief sustainability officer and head of international institutional affairs at Kering, tells Vogue of the demand her office saw for appearances, speeches and trainings on the subject. As a result, they decided to make the materials of their courses with LCF widely available through a Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). The new platform was presented by François-Henri Pinault, chairman and CEO of Kering, at an event during London Fashion Week, highlighting the opportunity that sustainability and innovation provides not just for the world, but businesses and consumers too. “We believe that to change the business model of the fashion industry to include sustainability you need also to know how to do it,” says Daveu. “With this MOOC we give guidelines and how to manage them, everything from material dimensions and sourcing for luxury fashion, to how to measure your environmental footprint. Everytime we speak about an issue—for example climate change, biodiversity, resource scarcity—we give concrete tools and solutions to determine what, as a young designer, you have to do. So it is theoretical as well as operational.” The course, for which registration is now open, is divided into six modules, presented through videos, podcasts, activities and discussions that participants can undertake at their leisure. Plans for a translations, namely in Chinese, are underway, as well as as an abridged version that all new Kering hires can undertake. “This course is not a revolution, and I'm not saying that after it everything will be perfect,” says Daveu, “but I am convinced that it will concretely change the way designers and the fashion industry can do their job. You can't say that one thing will cause a revolution, but step by step, stone by stone, we will make a change.” View Gallery 4 Photos Kering is launching an online course to educate young designers on sustainability What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee just dropped his new summer collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Brides take notes Sabyasachi Mukherjee's work is easily distinguishable from that of any of his contemporaries. High necklines, vintage embroideries, a sudden burst of florals, a dash of black—Mukerjee's signature take on old world nostalgia has had the country falling for his work since the inception of his label. Having forgone the standard format of runway shows, the designer released his spring/summer 2018 collection on Instagram last night. This season, Mukherjee's offering, 'An Endless Summer', is divided between three themes—florals, bright colours and a lineup of ivory and gold looks inspired by Lutyens' Delhi. To complement all of the garments are Sabyasachi Heritage Jewelry pieces that elevate the edit of occasion wear. Mukherjee's references for the collection range from Alice in Wonderland to Sarojini Naidu. To describe his standpoint on couture, he borrows from a designer whose aesthetic could not further be away from Mukherjee's own. "'Couture is an attitude, not a price point' - Jeremy Scott, Creative Director at Moschino. Confidence gives you a sense of freedom. And I see that reflecting in the choices that brides make today. What is good enough for some to wear in a mehendi, becomes bridal for some. These decisions are not affected by price restrictions, they are merely forward-thinking choices. More and more brides I meet are going forward and embracing a sense of whimsy," he elaborates in one Instagram caption. Personal references are the foundation on which Mukherjee constructs his work. Those in the arts know that the thing that differentiates great work from good work are the emotions that it rides on. Between the high-brow influences of Lutyens' Delhi and Shikargah paintings is a humble memory of visiting a certain circus in his childhood. Therein lies the influence behind the near-lurid colours, stripes and a sense of rhapsodic joy that comes from the smell of turmeric popcorn. Mukherjee takes his stream of thought and coverts into bridal couture that is the stuff dreams are made of. column1: Why Louis Vuitton’s new exhibition is unmissable
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The landmark Time Capsule makes its debut at Chadstone, Australia After travelling across the globe, from Hong Kong, Bangkok and Shanghai to Singapore, Berlin and Dubai, Louis Vuitton's landmark exhibition, Time Capsule, is now headed to Melbourne, Australia. Starting February 24, patrons of Chadstone—The Fashion Capital, a premier fashion and entertainment hub, will be embarking on a journey through time, travelling through 160 years to revisit landmark innovations in design at Louis Vuitton. View Gallery 10 Photos Why Louis Vuitton’s new exhibition is unmissable By juxtaposing rare antique objects with contemporary pieces, the show will highlight the ways in which the luxury house has anticipated the needs and desires of a changing sociocultural landscape. Serving as a visual timeline, of sorts, Time Capsule will take one through such key moments in the story of the brand, divided into six chapters. One will enter the exhibition through the ‘Artisans Room' for a live experience with the Louis Vuitton craftsmen, and move onto ‘The Key to the Codes', which is about those distinctive design features that can be traced to the brand's first trunks.  While ‘Journey Around the World' will serve as a revelation of how Louis Vuitton met the demands created by new advances in transportation, the next segment—‘Elegance in Motion'—will be all about the myriad ways in which the luxury house enabled its patrons to travel in style. Some of the brand's most memorable and emblematic creations will form a part of ‘Icons of the House', and ‘Magic Malle' will offer a story behind the symbol of Louis Vuitton. For the first time, a room dedicated to Louis Vuitton publishing will also be created. Several rare and previously unseen objects will also form part of the exhibition at Chadstone, especially the trunks with close ties with both Australia and New Zealand. For instance, one will get to see a cricket trunk, especially ordered by Australian cricketer Michael Clarke. Handcrafted by a single artisan, the trunk is covered in Louis Vuitton's iconic Damier Graphite canvas. Measuring 140cms in height, the piece features a black leather trimming, chosen by Clarke himself, and is fitted with the brand's signature brass lock and corners. The black lining perfectly complements the trunk's chic exterior. The object is equipped with ample storage space, with special compartments for bats, batting pads, gloves, boots, helmet and the baggy green cap. A unique design feature is the docking station for a portable Bose sound system.  Yet another significant trunk is the one that Louis Vuitton designed to carry the 2015 Webb Ellis Cup, one of the most coveted prizes in rugby in New Zealand. The piece features hand painted flags of the two finalists: Australia and New Zealand. By hosting this exhibition, Chadstone seeks to position itself as more than just a shopping centre. Over the next couple of years, it hopes to deliver unrivalled experiences, similar to this show, thus becoming a fully-integrated dining and leisure hub. Time Capsule can be viewed at Chadstone – The Fashion Capital between February 24 and March 21, 2018 What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet the tiger who has a fashion collection named after him We are nowhere near done with our obsession with animal prints, and it's just as well that designer Anjali Patel Mehta's roving eye picked on a certain majestic animal from the Ranthambore Forest to serve as the muse for her cruise '18 collection. From gutsy prints to hand-sewn sequins in soft, touchable fabrics, the designer serves up her usual whimsy in an earthy palette inspired by the showstopper of the Ranthambore National Park—T91, or the Cowboy Tiger as he is commonly known, caused a stir recently when he wandered out of the forest due to a turf war and escaped a near-death experience on his journey back home. The fearless spirit of the feral cat is echoed in Verandah's new collection that features tiger stripes, luxe beaded kimono jackets and hand-knotted macramé with a dose of upcycled denim reinforcing her commitment to sustainability. Before she jets back to New York, we sat down with Mehta to hear the story behind the collection firsthand. The story begins with my visit to Ranthambore Forest, which served as the inspiration for my summer/resort '18 presentation at Lakmé Fashion Week. I later learned that the tiger, T91 who had inspired the collection had gone missing and was hunted down on foot by a villager from the non-profit organisation, Tiger Watch. The renegade tiger and the magnificent backdrop of the forest ultimately served as the driving point for my cruise '18 collection. The laid-back glamour of the pieces translates into an ideal holiday wardrobe, from beach to safari chic. There's something beautiful about how the worlds of travel and fashion overlap, and the alluring Ranthambore Forest inspired the earthy palette of the collection. The colour story gradually moves towards sandy pinks and blues that were derived from the beautiful backdrop of daylight and dusk against which these majestic animals lounge. As someone who originally wanted to be an architect, I am extremely drawn towards geometric elements, and the key chattri motif has been inspired from the canopy that dots the remnants of the Ranthambore Fort. Through all our collections, we have always worked on ensuring that each garment can serve as a versatile, standalone piece to invite women to work in their creativity in mixing and matching. The sari jacket from our evening edit, for instance, can be worn for a relaxed sundowner or paired with trousers and a crisp white shirt for the day. I have always viewed sustainability as a two-fold responsibility. First, as fashion designers, we need to put back in what we take out. We are a product of the culture we live in, and giving back to the society needs to be hardwired into our DNA. To that end, I have pledged ten per cent of the profits from the global sales of the collection to the Tiger Watch organisation to acknowledge my social responsibility as a designer. Secondly, I believe that sustainability goes much beyond a buzzword and should be prominent in our daily practices at the grass root level, including fair trade practices and reasonable wages for craftsmen to ensure a circular economy that benefits everyone. In the many years since the inception of the label, we have adopted a zero-waste policy across all our workshops. The result being that every last piece of scrap cloth and trimmings is meticulously stored (for three years at a stretch, sometimes) and one piece from each of my runway collection is built purely from these recycled materials—the kimono jacket from my summer/resort '18 collection, for instance. We work on utilising every last part of the production process, and are currently looking for a leather substitute. Our new collection has been accessorised with handmade macramé earrings and jute bags from virgin fibres, patchwork belts from upcycled materials and vegan shoes to promote sustainability of the environment and the livelihood of the communities that live within it. Our country is bursting with artisanal talent, and it all comes down to how you fashion it to benefit everyone. column1: Milan Fashion Week: Your guide to the autumn/winter 2018 season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The third round of womenswear shows kicks off in Milan Just over three years ago, Alessandro Michele remade Gucci in his image almost literally overnight—his first outing for the label, its autumn/winter 2015 menswear collection, was designed in about six days. Since then, his eclectic vision has reestablished Gucci as luxury's pace-setter—and the brightest light of Milan Fashion Week—driving industry-wide trends that trickle down to fast fashion copycats while flying off the shelves. Lallo has since solidified his signatures: a kaleidoscopic, era-collapsing trip unspooling 100-plus looks. The big question rolling into Milan's autumn/winter 2018 shows is: will any of Gucci's peers attempt a similar reinvention? The 93-year-old Fendi hasn't undergone a change in leadership—the long-tenured Karl Lagerfeld is still calling the shots—but its past two collections have shown traces of Michele's influence. This time last year, Lagerfeld began reintroducing Fendi's classic double-F glyph on accessories. In his spring/summer 2018 collection, it crept onto outerwear, too. It's a smart move in today's era of logophilia, as historic houses embrace the logo-centric energy of streetwear, plastering insignias over bomber jackets and parkas. One can easily imagine a Fendi double-F hoodie turning up all over paparazzi and street style snaps. Fendi shows on February 22, and we'll see then what direction Lagerfeld will take the label next. Later that day, Miuccia Prada will unveil her latest collection at the Fondazione Prada, and she, too, has been dipping back into her archives. After she brought back a selection of greatest-hits prints in her most recent men's collection, it's fair to wonder if she'll show something similar for women. It would be somewhat uncharacteristic—Miuccia's always kept her label resolutely future-focused—but there's no doubt that it would be a commercially savvy move. And if there's anyone who could repurpose her own label's past without it tipping over into nostalgia, it's Miuccia. Last September, Donatella Versace made a similar trip back in time, reinterpreting motifs from some of her brother Gianni Versace's most impactful early '90s collections. Of course, the impetus there was more than commercial—Donatella was paying homage to Gianni to mark the 20th anniversary of his murder. Rumours that Donatella would soon name a successor have been swirling for months, and her last show was so emotionally charged that it would have made for a fitting conclusion to her time at the helm. But, a week before the label's February 23 show, she remains creative director—though it's worth noting that Kim Jones, one of the many names linked to Versace over the past few months, is now a free agent, having left his creative directorship of Louis Vuitton menswear in January. Watch this space. Husband-and-wife duo Luke and Lucie Meier's spring/summer 2018 collection, their first as co-creative directors of Jil Sander, was met with lukewarm reviews. Before their appointment, Luke, who also designers under menswear label OAMC, was the head designer of Supreme for nearly a decade, while Lucie worked under Raf Simons at Dior, as well as Marc Jacobs at Louis Vuitton and Nicolas Ghesquière at Balenciaga. All of the elements that made their appointments so enticing were present—studied, utilitarian minimalism, luxe fabric selections, unique colour selections—but they have yet to cohere it into more than the sum of its parts. If the Meiers are able to find their footing, Milan will have another label whose shows are a must-see each season. Milan isn't only about the old guard. While the city may not have the same youthful energy as London or even New York, it does play host to some intriguing up-and-comers. Arthur Arbesser, who shows on February 21, is due for a big break. He was shortlisted for the LVMH Prize in 2015, and has turned out a steady stream of collections that are equal parts erudite and eccentric since. Twins Florence, which shows on February 22, is another young label to watch. Founder Linda Calugi is an architect by training, and it shows in her designs—sumptuous and refined, rendered mostly in deep, muted hues, and reliant on proportion play. They don't reinvent the wheel, but they look ready to be lived in. Here's hoping some more new faces make an impression next week, too. column1: The best graduate collections we’ve seen at London Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A taste of talents yet to come Imagine sending your school work down the runway at London Fashion Week alongside a brand like Burberry. It's the dream of a thousand fashion students who each year descend upon the capital to study. And for the most promising graduates from three of the city's most prestigious courses, it's a reality. While the Central Saint Martins MA—which graduated the likes of Alexander McQueen, and more recently Christopher Kane and Craig Green—has long served as LFW's glimpse into the future, these days, the course is joined by the London College of Fashion MA and newcomers from the Westminster BA. As the fashion circus moves to Milan, Vogue turns the spotlight to five gifted graduates who showed this past week. View Gallery 12 Photos The best graduate collections we saw at London Fashion Week Elise Perrotta Central Saint Martins MA Italian knitwear designer Elise Perrotta, whose sculptural knits were like canvas surfaces dabbed with colour, sought to subvert the feminine stereotypes with her graduate collection. “I think there's still this idea that when women are creative and [skilful] with their hands, they're crafty,” she tells Vogue. “What tools can be more powerful and useful in investigating these stereotypes [than] those that have contributed to their reinforcement?” Using stitching techniques taken from vintage craft magazines and soap felting tutorials, the designer turned old-school granny patterns into impressively knit robes, and felted pencil skirts to resemble hairy furs wrapped around models' legs. It was a rare conceptual exercise that yielded a collection of highly wearable garments. Having completed two seasons at Phoebe English before starting her MA, she continues to work for the London-based designer on textile and knitwear on a freelance basis. But before that, she had collaborated on a knitwear collection with Santoni Shanghai, the Chinese knitting machinery manufacturer. “It really opened my mind technically speaking, working with all the different circular knitwear machinery and trying to find ways of achieving techniques.” As to what she'll do next, the designer likes to keep an open mind. “I feel like I would like to join a brand that I really respect and keep growing and learning within the industry… but let's see what happens!”   Dmitry Gotsfrid London College of Fashion MA Inspired by the golden age of haute couture, graduate Dmitry Gotsfrid turned to the likes of Christian Dior and Cristobal Balenciaga for his thesis collection, titled Femme Fatale x Praying Mantis. “What fascinates me about couture is the inner construction of the garment and quite often I find the interior much more interesting than the exterior.” A translucescent gown in a distinctively Post-War silhouette was sent down the runway, embroidered to give the illusion that the model was being swarmed by an army of insects. As one of the three winners of the Armani x BFC competition last year—which saw students from the city's design schools submit reinterpretations of classic Emporio Armani styles—Gotsfrid was invited to Milan last summer, where he worked at the Armani studios. Working with the team, the designer produced the toile of his award-winning bomber jacket, which would later be sold at the recently renovated Emporio Armani store on Bond Street. He will be returning to Milan to complete a three-month post-graduation internship at Emporio, as part of his prize package.   Manon Planche University of Westminster BA At the University of Westminster BA's show on Friday, shiny metallic bodies with flaming prints descended down the runway like race cars on the track. For her graduate collection, French designer Manon Planche turned to an peculiar source of inspiration: drag racing. The result was an unexpected exploration of the feminine and the hypermasculine. “I was worried about the cliches about drag racing, so I went to see one,” Planche says. Much to her surprise, “it was truly a family event with none of the cliches that I had imagined—the half-naked girls waving flags and what not.” Instead, there were women drivers and teenage girls training as mechanics. The signature grid-like, three-dimensional surface seen on outerwear was a nod to the gear that protect drivers in their accelerating vehicles, created by trapping foam squares under the shiny surfaces. Meanwhile the playful print patterns resembled the paint jobs of the vehicles themselves. Last year, Planche returned to Paris, where she was raised, to work in the accessories division of Louis Vuitton for nine months, developing all the jewellery for the autumn/winter 2017 runway collection. “I got to see the whole process: I did research at the very beginning; developed new handmade techniques to do the jewellery; then I had to produce them. I went to Italy to the factory so I can teach them to other people so they can make the pieces for the show; and after the show, we revised the pieces so they can be sold,” she recalls. As she wraps up her Bachelor's studies, what does the designer hope to do next? “Ideally, I'd like to start my own brand.” Liam Johnson Central Saint Martins MA Kicking off the Central Saint Martins MA show on Friday evening was a conceptual flurry of colours: a red mesh circle that wobbled up and down the opening model's head; a blue version of same material was cut into a gown resembling a mosquito net; a green cube held firmly by the model against her otherwise exposed chest. These were human bodies clothed in garments that transformed them into freakish automatons, as cylinders trapped the models' arms by their sides, while printed powersuits with shoulder pads exaggerated the torso. The penultimate look was a UFO casting a ray onto the ground, beaming the model up into the sky. It was nothing like we've ever seen before. The colourful designs were like the Platonic forms of garments, each abstracted from the physical - devoid any consideration of consumer trends or the fashion cycle. This was the work of graduate Liam Johnson, whose instinctual creations are pure stimuli. Chosen by Sarah Burton as a Sarabande scholar, the designer completed the BA Fashion course also at Central Saint Martins, completing a placement at Maison Margiela under alumnus John Galliano on both the ready-to-wear and artisanal collections. Hailing from South Wales, Johnson's father worked in the garment industry, and he grew up watching underwear being produced—clearly a source of inspiration for the materials used in his show. Jiali Lu London College of Fashion MA Chinese graduate Jiali Lu turned to Jane Austen for her graduate collection, particularly the 1940s film adaptation of the British author's magnum opus Pride and Prejudice in a confrontation of the Postmodern and the Romantic. The designer draped fabrics to create the puffy sleeves in tuxedo jackets, while skirts were twisted in unexpected ways to refresh the silhouettes, and models wore handcrafted wire-frame glasses. Strong tailoring was ubiquitous in the black-and-white lineup, with numerous references to traditional menswear, particularly the male sartorial choices of the Romantic era. Having established her own brand as an undergraduate in China, Lu has yet to intern under another designer. But she's learned plenty from her time as an independent designer, particularly in balancing the creative with the practical, as well as the logistical and commercial sides of the business. But now that she's graduated, does she plan on picking up where she started? “I am going to do some internships first and I want to work with some brands I really love,” Lu says. “I think I still have a lot to learn and practice.” Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Connecting the dots between race, politics, fashion and emotions
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And the progress we have made I read an editorial piece by one of my favourite writers Lauren Sherman in The Business of Fashion couple of days ago—a succinct round-up of the recently concluded New York Fashion Week titled “New York Fashion Week's Got the Blues”. She states that “there are few designers showing here who have a sense of what they stand for or why they need the platform of fashion week. It doesn't have to be that way.” No, it doesn't, indeed. If fashion designers are struggling to focus on what they stand for, I say, look no further than last week's epochal event at the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery —the unveiling of the official portraits of former US President, Barack Obama, by Kehinde Wiley and First Lady Michelle Obama, by Amy Sherald—that reignited our collective dialogue on race, class, power, politics, and what this reinvention of classical portraiture tells us about our contemporary world, including the world of fashion (read about the Smithsonian exhibition here). Baltimore-based artist Amy Sherald's portrait of the first lady, wearing a sweeping Mondrian-like dress inspired by a gown designed by Michelle Smith's spring 2017 Milly collection, had a poignant role to play. Smith told Washington Post that that season, she was inspired by a “desire for equality, equality in human rights, racial equality, LGBTQ equality,” she says. One of the recurring elements in the collection were various forms of lacing and ties; the details were meant to suggest a “feeling of being held back. . . that we're not quite there yet.” Whilst lacing and ties in fashion have played symbolic roles of power and exploitation in varying measures, the couture-like dress made of cotton poplin was the feature that made my mind and heart race. Cotton in American history has been pivotal in the African-American struggle for freedom and equality. This cotton poplin—a no-fuss fabric used by working class folks in America, was as much a symbol for the fight for dignity, as was Khadi, the frugal hand-made, hand-spun cloth from India, eulogised by Gandhi as a symbol of India's Freedom Movement from British colonisation. Cloth has been a tool of protest throughout history. And here, I am not talking about just spraying a slogan on a T-shirt. It is also about the production and distribution of raw materials that became tools of exploitation, a symbol of political and social disenfranchisement. Cotton—the farmlands of which became the battlefields of racial conflict in American history, made "cotton picking" the subject of generations of African-American blues and jazz songs—heart-wrenching musical renditions of the injustices done to them especially between 1920s and 1940s. At the height of the Khadi Movement in India, Gandhi beseeched millions of ordinary Indians—weighed down by heavily-taxed clothes from English mills—to burn the factory-made clothes, and instead, take up the spinning wheel to weave their own. Clothes have played such significant roles in the political narrative of entire nations, it is important to revisit them to remind ourselves that beyond the glare of hi-voltage fashion shows, clothes tell stories of displacement, cultural alienation, appropriation and financial exploitation. At the Smithsonian unveiling, the significance of this particular moment was not lost to Obama—a black woman in a couture-like dress in a museum, run by, and filled with, white people on its walls for aeons. “I'm thinking about young people, particularly…girls of colour who will come to this place and they will look up and they will see an image of someone who looks like them on the wall,” she said. Like works that adorn walls in museums, on our bodies are canvases of our inner toils and tribulations. “What if clothes were not simply reflective of personality, indicative of our banal preference for grey over green, but more deeply imprinted with the ways that human beings have lived: a material record of our experiences and an expression of our ambition?” asks the prolific lecturer Shahidha Bari in her piece “What do clothes say?”. It's time we all asked ourselves the same question. Former president Barack Obama's 7x5 feet portrait was painted by Kehinde Wiley, whose extraordinary oeuvre is painting ordinary black men from the streets, but in the style that mimics Western classical artists. In a Time magazine editorial, writer Maya Rhodan describes the portrait and the setting against which the beloved president is ensconced: “Wiley stripped away the trappings of office in order to depict the former President's life journey. African blue lilies are a nod to Obama's father's home country of Kenya. Chrysanthemums are the official flower of the city of Chicago, where Obama met his wife Michelle and started both his family and political career. Pikake, or Arabian jasmine, thrives in Hawaii, where the President spent much of his youth. These botanicals are a challenge to viewers to grapple with the improbability of Obama's rise. The way the president appears to lean toward the viewer, his collar unbuttoned, exudes a level of openness not seen in some of the other portraits, says Taína Caragol, who curated the Wiley commission for the Portrait Gallery. It's “indicative of the values of his presidency,” she says, “And the notion of a democracy that works from the bottom up instead of from the top down.” Kehinde Wiley's penchant for subtext is extraordinary. And as bold and bright his paintings are, his artistic reflections are nuanced and inquisitorial. In 2012, Sean Kelly Gallery opened an extraordinary exhibition: “An Economy of Grace” by Wiley who collaborated with Ricardo Tisci, creative director of Givenchy at the time (see the exhibition here). Wiley, who usually focused on black African-American men in contemporary wear, but painted them in Baroque, Rococo or other neoclassical western art styles, focused solely on women this time. African-American women. Tisci and he chose paintings from the Louvre (Paris)—poses based on historical portraits of society women by Jacques-Louis David, Thomas Gainsborough and John Singer Sargent, among others. They served as inspiration for a series of portraits of Africa-American women in couture gowns. Wiley asked Tisci to make custom dresses for the sittings. “Couture is a symbol of wealth and excess, and that's what art has been” said Wiley in a 2012 interview with WSJ Magazine. “I think one of the things that must happen in the work is for it to become class conscious.” ‘Grace' portrayed through the gentrified pose, and stance, the opulence of couture dresses—makes one thing as stark as midday sun—the gap of black women in the history of art. Wiley questions this notion of grace through clothes—is “grace” merely a commodity that can be bought or painted? Like royalty, power, nobility—can couture ‘manufacture' a persona? And this is why fashion is important. It is the visual trajectory of our deeper-seated needs and desires as human beings. At the Smithsonian unveiling of the president's portrait, Wiley, overwhelmed to be the first African-American artist to paint the first African-American, president, said, “This is about who we decide to celebrate, it is our humanity, this is our ability to say I matter, I was here”. This momentous occasion allowed him to go beneath the clothes and touch the skin of the wearer. Fashion designers should try that too. Beauty Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: At 30, Rihanna’s red carpet style is still unmatched
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In a league of her own If red carpet appearances were a competitive sport, Rihanna might be the reigning world champion. Aside from being a regular highlight of the Met Gala, the singer/actor/designer/businesswoman has made red carpet appearances to promote her various films, including Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets and Battleship; taken over fashion weeks from New York to Paris as designer of her Fenty line in partnership with the Kering-owned Puma; and launched her own, LVMH-backed cosmetics line. Whether it's in a luxurious handmade Giambattista Valli haute couture gown or power-dressing in her jacquard Dior blazer jacket with a matching skirt and white Dior boots, Rihanna has proven again and again that she can't be rivalled on the red carpet. As a champion of young designers, she loves to mix the best emerging talents with all the historic maisons of Paris—she is evidently a fan of Maria Grazia Chiuri's Dior, but also of London designer Molly Goddard's tulle dresses. From Burberry's classic checks to a nude Adam Selman dress to the most avant-garde looks straight from the Comme des Garçons runway, is there a look that Rihanna can't pull off? Luckily for us, we'll continue to see plenty of Rihanna on the red carpet this year—she's starring in director Gary Ross's Ocean's 8 due in June. As Robyn Rihanna Fenty turns 30, revisit the looks that we'll all still be talking about a decade from now.
