column1: The making of Sonam Kapoor’s wardrobe for Pad Man
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Plus, some unseen pictures of the star from the movie Pad Man, which releases today, finds its inspiration in Arunachalam Muruganantham, whose story also made it to Twinkle Khanna's book, The Legend of Lakshmi Prasad. Khanna also plays producer for the film, which stars her husband Akshay Kumar alongside Sonam Kapoor and Radhika Apte. Needless to say, the movie has created quite a stir even before its release, be it with the #PadManChallenge on Instagram or Twinkle Khanna's meeting with Malala Yousafzai at the Oxford University during the promotions. Sonam Kapoor's deglamourised look to keep in tune with her character has also become another talking point of the film. Conceptualised by stylist and costume designer Theia Tekchandaney, who incidentally also worked with the actress in Neerja, 28 looks were created for Kapoor. Vogue speaks to Tekchandaney about what went on behind-the-scenes in the wardrobe department (also catch some unseen pictures of the actor from the movie in our slideshow below). Sonam's character is a final year management student from Delhi, who graduates through the course of the film. She is also a tabla player. As per the script, these were the two defining characteristics that had to be kept in mind when planning her wardrobe. Other than that, director R Balki left the decision of charting her character's look entirely up to me. Since Sonam's character in Pad Man is working at the grass root level in the movie, there needed to be a hint of conservatism in her ensembles, but we did not want it to be boring. So we chose an in-between path with her ensembles—we turned to Indian fabrics and designs but stayed away from typically traditional outfits like salwar kurtas. She needed to be approachable as per the storyline, so we married comfort with practicality in all her outfits. For instance, we initially put her in sneakers, but realised that the process of taking them off every time she visited the villagers in their homes would become tedious for her character. So we then changed her footwear to basic leather chappals. We worked with a host of designers rooted in an Indian sensibility, and had them custom-make styles they are really strong at. We then mix-and-matched these to create individualistic combinations, so that no look was by one designer head-to-toe. The entire pre-production process took two-and-a-half months. Maku by Shantanu Das and Aneeth Arora of Péro allowed us to dip into their archives to choose the looks that worked best for us. Anavila customised linen kurta shirts with minimal detailing and stoles for the movie while Grassroot by Anita Dongre created shibori stoles and a beautiful chikan kurta. We used Eká's winter collection for the sequence in the Unites States, though the scene did not make the final cut. Sanjay Garg designed an aqua chanderi sari for one of the key scenes in the movie where Akshay Kumar's character visits the UN, accompanied by Sonam. R Balki wanted a visual connect between both the leading ladies (Sonam and Radhika Apte) in the film. Radhika wears a pair of gold jhumkas in the movie, which we adapted in silver for Sonam's character in a slightly bigger size. Sonam made small additions to her look. Giving her characters glasses and a backpack were her ideas. The second time Sonam visits the village, she is wearing an orange Péro kurti that is actually mine. We teamed this with a Vrisa by Rahul n Shikha stole, jeans and a burlap backpack. The scene is very significant, as Sonam comes in and takes the storyline forward. She enters the picture as a ray of hope, and we wanted that metaphorical brightness she brings to translate on screen visually as well. We really thought this look through, and it ultimately came together beautifully. column1: Abraham & Thakore joins hands with Vana for a sustainable future
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Slow living at its best Nestled amongst the sal trees of Dehradun is Vana, an ecological retreat that endorses physical, emotional and spiritual wellbeing through various holistic practices. With mindful living at the heart of its philosophy, before settling on a collaboration, finding those whose ideals match their own was a must. Abraham & Thakore, who celebrated 25 years in the fashion industry this year, are known for their modern take on Indian separates and for honouring the principles of sustainability. The A&T DNA is very strong and the stellar work that have done in the Indian textiles industry, shaping its aesthetics, needs to be taken to a wider audience,” said Veer Singh, founder of Vana who has invested in the Abraham & Thakore label making him the fourth partner in the company (along with David Abraham, Rakesh Thakore and Kevin Nigli). "Vana helps to bring financial capability within a framework to provide operational and management support on leadership so we can achieve our common vision. Underlying all of this is a close friendship and a very high degree of respect and admiration of the work they do – because without that there is nothing to have a dialogue on," he adds. “As A&T and Vana's friendship continued to evolve, we hoped to work on further interesting initiatives together which distilled the essence of both brands. There are many areas of confluence and we are excited to embark on the Vana journey supported with the incredible vision of its founder,” David Abraham, one half of the label adds. column1: Inside Rohit Gandhi and Rahul Khanna’s 20-year-long journey in fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Celebrating two decades of classic glamour Somewhere between the world of geometrical silhouettes engineered with surgical precision and an infinite plateau of statement neutrals, lies the domain of Rohit Gandhi and Rahul Khanna. Largely credited as the country's first prêt menswear designers, they have since taken over womenswear as well, finding loyal fans in the likes of Katrina Kaif and Priyanka Chopra along the way. As the duo clock in two decades in the spotlight, we got Rahul Khanna to take us back to the start when western ready-to-wear looks were something you had to stock up on when you were on holiday abroad. From starting their own boutique to an experimental clientele to showcasing at Tranoi in Paris to expanding their dominion to the European market (do we hear of an international store in Spain on the cards?), here's your ringside view to their sartorial journey. Congratulations on completing this milestone. How are you planning on celebrating? We're marking this milestone with our autumn/winter 2018 show, ‘An Evening Of Reflections'. It will be a special collection inspired by our archives, with designs recreated to fit within the contemporary sphere. Our friends from the film and fashion industry are flying down to be a part of the celebrations. Take us back in time to when you first decided to start your own label with Rohit Gandhi… The year was 1997, Rohit and I had been travelling and were really inspired with the ready-to-wear western wear that we came across. The fashion scene in India was drastically different back then; there was no Zara or H&M back then and people usually travelled abroad to find these silhouettes for their daily wardrobe. We started out with menswear, flooding our racks with the slim fit shirts and tapered blacks that we wanted to wear but weren't available in the market back then, and slowly branched out into womenswear as well. How has it been working with Rohit Gandhi as a partner through the decades? It has been a revelation. Rohit is quirky and funny, and fortunately, our aesthetics align well with each other—we both share an incorrigible love for greys and blacks. Work becomes play when we are together, and over the years, our store has become a meeting point for people. Clients became friends—it helps when you have great coffee flowing! The days have really flown by, but I can see a marked shift from our earlier experimental fare when we first started out to a more commercial approach now as per the demands of the time. What would you say has been your standout moment over the past 20 years? Seeing our creations grace the windows of Selfridges was definitely a huge high. In the early 2000s, we decided to start showcasing internationally at Tranoi in Paris and New York, and received an overwhelming response. It made us realise that staying true to our individuality was the way forward. How would you say the fashion scene has evolved from when you started out two decades ago? The market has definitely opened up. When we started out, the couture scene was dominated with traditional Indian wear; there was no Fashion Week back then and people were largely intimidated by designer stores. For us as a label, Rohit and I served as the designers, managers and accountants all at once, working to service our small yet loyal clientele. In a way we have all grown up together with the models back then—John Abraham, Dino Morea, Bipasha Basu and Deepika Padukone, among others. We believe we drove up the demand for prêt Western wear in the country, and also had a hand in educating the consumers about fabrics and styles. What would your advice be to a designer entering the fashion game now? It is both easy and difficult—social media has definitely been instrumental in increasing exposure for newcomers in the industry, but at the same time, given the sheer volume of competitors fighting for the same share of the market, it is crucial to have a signature, distinctive style of your own to avoid being drowned out. You need to have a clear vision that fulfils a gap within the market, and ensure that you don't follow the tribe. What can we expect from the next 20 years of Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna? Well, at the moment we're actually planning a long overdue holiday! The next milestone for us would be to expand beyond India. We have clients all over the world and would be concentrating on opening stores in new cities and regions—maybe Spain and Dubai. It is the digital age and fashion has never been more relevant, which makes it integral to go with the flow. You can definitely expect some edgy creations using techniques like 3D laser printing and collections that are contemporary and exciting. column1: The real showstopper at Lakme Fashion Week spring/summer 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Thoughtful. Powerful. Forward thinking. The real showstopper at Lakmé Fashion Week was Anamika Khanna’s finale show. Here’s how the designer brought her full fashion game to Bandra fort Last night, under the stars at the mossy Bandra Fort, Kolkata-based designer Anamika Khanna closed this edition of Lakmé Fashion Week. It was a season, more misses than hits, to let's face it, an audience that is quite jaded, but Khanna's finale was a success, both for her clothes and her messaging, showcasing why as a designer, she's really in her own league. View Gallery 4 Photos The real showstopper – Anamika Khanna It's been three years since Khanna's last showcase in the city, and you get the idea, that ensconced in her life in Kolkata, far away from the fashion frenzy, Khanna really deliberated about what she wanted to say. How was she going to break out of her own comfort zone? How could she really jar us all of this creative ennui we are all in? How could she push the boundaries of the boxes Indian fashion has created for itself? “Honestly, I've been feeling fashion fatigue,” she tells me, her voice raspy from exhaustion, this morning. “Fashion in this country, has been put into two boxes—wedding wear and the whole organic, khadi, anti-fit space. There's more to it. And I wanted to make my own statement—to not fall into these boundaries.” For Khanna the statement covered the sublime—from the sensory beat of the drummers she had commissioned, to the powerful, sinewy strength of the dancers, from the dramatic lighting to the dry ice she used to mist (Earth, Wind, Fire anyone?). Before the collection even came out, the stage was set. “The visual of three models wearing that red, with the dancers in the black, it was in my mind's eye—before I even started. It was about collaborating across the disciplines.” And then there was the fashion. In a palette of crème, ecru, red and the blackest black—Anamika's Army came through. Her tribe of strong, powerful women, who are not afraid to in her words, to “do their own thing.” The collection of separates (“Pieces that were versatile, that mixed with anything. Like the millennials, who I looked to, who wear their clothes so lightly, I wanted to push that message.”) had her signature trademarks, but Khanna pushed her consumer appeal to a newer space. “There was deconstruction, but it was softer. We actually had the courage to rip a shirt or pyjamas and let it go out—frayed and disheveled. The fringing was more luxurious, with organza, it was a new technique and we had fun with patchwork.” Yes, there were her signatures—her inventive use of classic drapes, her easy layering, her asymmetrical silhouettes, her riff on the power suit, her indi-coat in all its glory, and in a nod to her front row clientele, a collection of pieces (lehenga, sari et al) that work for their festive needs. But here's what I loved in particular—the fact, that in closing the show, Kareena Kapoor Khan's look was stripped of the fluff. There was no excess, there was no added need for drama. In black, Khan projected, the power of a woman, who is not covered in embellishment, whose comfortable in her own skin. And that was dramatic enough. And herein lies the crux of Khanna's message. column1: Watch: Kareena Kapoor Khan at Anamika Khanna’s Lakmé Absolute Grand Finale
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Catch the biggest highlights from the final day Day 5 at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018 saw some serious star power. Shyamal and Bhumika Shodhan of Shyamal & Bhumika wove fairy tale romance with their collection ‘Wonderland'. The occasion wear label's offering for the season ranged from date-night dresses to gowns, saris and lehengas in a palette of pastels with hints of orange and green thrown in. Kangana Ranaut took centre stage in a champagne ballgown covered in floral embroidery, complete with a chapel veil—did someone say summer wedding? Meanwhile in the evening, the stage for the Lakmé Absolute Grand Finale with Anamika Khanna was set against the facade of the Bandra Fort. In Mumbai, February bears the signs of a retreating weather, with just a slight chill in the air adding to the atmosphere of the outdoor, seaside venue. Fairy lights in the shrubs, minimal thread installations, ambient music and air-kissing—nothing could have prepared one for what was next. Grand finales are all about showcasing the fullest extent of a designer's talent, and last night, Anamika Khanna demonstrated just that. To start with, a group of modernist dancers performed in the waters of the fountain to the beating of drums. One by one, models snaked the course of the stairs at the Fort—defiant, not demure. Khanna's forte lies in her craftsmanship. Without equating embroidery with shine, and crafting her own patterns that can never be duplicated successfully, Khanna is up against herself in setting the bar for alternative Indian wear. To categorise the silhouettes under specific shapes would be a disservice. Irreverence was the common factor in each of the looks that were seen on the non-traditional runway. There were plenty of commercial options for weddings and occasions, but one hardly wears an Anamika Khanna outfit to blend in. First came the beiges, then whites with red embroidery that mimicked brushstrokes, then a few pops of pink moving into deep reds, and finally blacks—the colour palette rose in a crescendo that was highlighted by the dancers, whose movements intensified with each passing look. If the dance started off expressing strife, it went onto describe agony and then turmoil, until they finally saw the bold Anamika Khanna woman in a new light. The designer spoke about taking inspiration from the mindset of the young millennials as a reference point for the collection. On show day, there were obvious tribal influences seen in the collection, including facial jewellery by the designer's sister and jewellery designer Suhani Pittie. Three years ago, Anamika Khanna's Lakmé grand finale was set to happen at the Dr Bhau Daji Lad Mumbai City Museum, but owing to political unrest, was forced to happen at the St Regis Hotel. Last night was a quiet victory in the sense that the designer's work was finally seen in the space it deserved to be. From the ace choreography to the lights and music—it was a perfect example of what can be done in a space that comes with its own history. Karisma Kapoor, Rhea Kapoor, Sunita Kapoor, Masaba Gupta and Isabelle Kaif were seen in the audience. Kareena Kapoor Khan emerged amidst the activity on stage and everything stopped for a moment. In a simple, striking black sari worn with ear cuffs that the star pulled off in her unique charm, she brought the show to a fitting close. column1: 20+ Bollywood looks to help you choose your wedding cocktail gown
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Red carpet-ready You may be the heroine of your life, but your wedding is an once-in-a-lifetime chance to feel like a true superstar. The days leading up to that proverbial walk down the aisle are all about you, and a decadent bridal wardrobe only adds to the charm. While most events of the big fat (or not) Indian wedding shine the spotlight on traditional silhouettes, the cocktail party breaks the streak by allowing for some red carpet-friendly glamour. Let your favourite celebrities play fairy godmother so that you can look like the ultimate belle of the ball… even after the clock strikes 12. Vogue rounds looks worth taking inspiration from. Blush tones and millennial pink should be go-to hues for the romantic bride. Take a cue from Sonam Kapoor and Katrina Kaif, and don't hold back on those fairy tale vibes. Complete the look with diamond jewellery and dewy make-up, topped off with embellished hair accessories as seen on Kareena Kapoor Khan. But if your bridal style is less demure and more daring, then Deepika Padukone and Priyanka Chopra are your sartorial soul sisters. Amp up the drama. Go extra with every aspect of your gown, be it the colour and silhouette or the jewellery you complement the gown with. There is no room for restraint once you jump on this bandwagon. Ruffles, feathers, fringes and tassels are a norm this season, and if they aren't already a part of your sangeet or reception repertoire, give in to them for the cocktail. Rival your wedding cake (because, why not?) with a fluffy ruffled gown à la Alia Bhatt or dial it down a notch with just a hint on your gown sleeves like Athiya Shetty. If it's a night of debauchery that's on the cards, then gowns with feathers and sequins should be the order of the night. Let Diana Penty and Disha Patani lead the way. Feel you've worked too hard on them pins to forgo the only chance of flaunting them during your wedding? Parineeti Chopra gets you (as do we). Follow her lead and choose an embroidered mini with a voluminous train for maximum impact with minimum effort. For brides with a more classic sensibility, monochromatic tones are no-brainers. Channel Mira Rajput Kapoor and opt for a white form-fitting gown with unconventional sheer panels for a touch of playfulness. Emerald earrings will lend your look regal flair. The anti-bride, on the other hand, ought to borrow from Sonam Kapoor's book, and give her gown an androgynous update with a blazer nonchalantly thrown on. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion See what the designers had to say The fourth day of the summer/resort 2018 edition of Lakmé Fashion Week saw standout shows by labels Payal Singhal, Lovebirds and Shantanu & Nikhil. column1: Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018: Day 4 highlights
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s what you missed out on Couldn't make it to day 4 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018? Here's what you missed out on. View Gallery 12 Photos Highlights from day 4 of Lakme Fashion Week spring/summer 2018 The runway came into full bloom with husband-and-wife designer duo Sonam and Paras Modi's spring offering aptly named Dahlia. Attention to detail lay at the heart of the lineup heavy on high-shine embellishments, intricate embroidery and hand-painted floral prints. Models walked the ramp in silhouettes spanning the spectrum from tried-and-true (saris and layered lehengas) to of-the-moment (pleated pants and embellished camisoles). The colour story saw subdued hues like ivory and nude paired with coral and the label's signature blue. Designer Payal Singhal's collection Saira, could easily double up as the serial wedding attendee's capsule closet. For spring/summer, the designer delved deep into the history of Islamic culture and captured it in her creations through decadent finishing touches that came in the form of antique embroidery, filigree and jaali work. Fuss-free, contemporary Indian silhouettes such as dhoti saris, off-the-shoulder blouses and capes proved to be the perfect foil for the age-old techniques employed by Singhal. Midnight blue, rose pink and mint were some of the hues prominent on the shade card. A radiant Aditi Rao Hydari brought the show to a close in a meticulously embroidered lehenga. When visual artist Princess Pea and contemporary label Lovebirds come together, you can be sure to expect a conceptual show to make you uncomfortable and intrigued, all at the same time. #BornofFire was a thought-provoking collection. Innocence came through in playful polka dots, gossamer frocks, sweet bows in the hair, poplin coords with pyjama-like charm but also school-girl perfection. In the stark backdrop of the “What about me if I only think about you?” soundtrack and solemn faces, you felt disturbed and sad at the all-resounding loaded phrase. What about me, if I only think about you? The duo presented a yet another fierce collection. Pleated drapes in ochre served up with slate grey jackets and an army of women in new versions of the sari, corseted and draped over second-skin pants, attached with tribal silver jewellery (from shoes and ankles to jackets and knuckledusters). The highlight: Saif Ali Khan awarding a medal of honour to a fellow female model. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Sonam Kapoor makes a case for modest fashion with this e-commerce platform
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The actor adds another cover to her growing list That Sonam Kapoor is one of India's favourite cover girl's is no new news, (she was Vogue India's cover girls just a few months ago) but now she seems to have become the face of Indian fashion, globally. You may remember she walked the ramp for Ralph & Russo at their couture show in Paris last July, and now she models for Dubai's The Mod, The Modist's editorial offering. The Modist is a Dubai-based luxury fashion destination that has become the Net-a-Porter of modest clothing. Launched just last year, it has a roster of designers that includes Ellery, Mary Katrantzou and Stella Jean, as well as home-grown labels such as Taller Marmo and Dima Ayad. It is all about an elegant, covered up and layered mix-and-match eclectic style that is very much a fashion trend right now. For many women, dressing modest is a personal choice. Says The Modist's creative director Sally Matthews, “We are very fashion forward and also colour is very important to our buyers… We find our clients tend to be working women, and also those who are curvier.” And not surprisingly, the site has found traction in India. The Mod is the site's editorial page, and every purchase from The Modist comes with a print version of the The Mod. Previously having featured Yasmin le Bon, Caroline Issa and Halima Aden, Sonam Kapoor graces the latest cover of the book. This is the first time, though, an Indian has been chosen. Says Matthews, “Sonam has been on our minds since before the site launched. She has such global appeal and an elegant style. We shot in London, and we wanted to celebrate her style.” View Gallery 3 Photos Sonam Kapoor makes a case for modest fashion with this e-commerce platform The Indian film actor has worn Dubai's Michael Cinco as well as Lebanon's Ashi Studio on the red carpet, and for the Cannes Film Festival, Elie Saab is almost her go-to designer. Kapoor herself tends to be a modest dresser, and for The Modist's shoot, she wore Oscar de la Renta and Preen by Thorton Bregazzi, while most of the jewellery is from her own collection. Says Kapoor in her interview for the luxury website, “I feel that you can express yourself without being on show. Being modest about the way you dress, being modest about your work, being modest about who you are... It grounds you. The more you shout, it shows your insecurity. It's important to have a sense of self and a quiet confidence.” And with Sonam Kapoor giving modest dressing her thumbs up, it is just a matter of time before more Indian fashion influencers take on the trend. column1: Watch: Sonakshi Sinha, Kriti Sanon and more at Lakmé Fashion Week S/R 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion What you missed from Day 3 It's the third day of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018, and Bollywood has started making its way to the runways. Monica Shah and Karishma Swali of Amoh by Jade, the pret line by bridal couture label Jade, looked towards the descendants of the mountain God Niyam Raja for inspiration. The tribe's way of living has honoured maintaining the ecological balance and the designer duo kept peace at the back of their minds while working on it. Minimal occasion wear in soft beiges and whites were seen on the runway in organic fabrics. Kalki Koechlin played showstopper. Falguni and Shane Peacock's eponymous label has always dressed the glamorous, partying crowd. This season, forgoing their signature red carpet gowns, the designers debuted their menswear line keeping director Karan Johar in mind as muse. Sonakshi Sinha opened the show in a pantsuit embellished with decals. The lineup of dinner jackets and tuxedos came with metallic fabrics and sequins. Rappers performed as models walked by, and Karan Johar closed the show. Kriti Sanon was the showstopper for Tarun Tahiliani's spring/summer 2018 collection that was inspired by the constellations of the Milky Way. Wedding wear that doesn't weigh down the wearer has been Tahiliani's priority for a while now, and he managed to achieve it yet again with the help of Swarovski crystals. Models walked through glass boxes down the runway to give the impression of angels walking amongst stars. See it all in our video. What's New Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018: Day 3 highlights
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Details this way From Falguni Shane Peacock's first menswear collection to Tarun Tahiliani's celestial lineup, here's what you missed on Day 3 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018. View Gallery 12 Photos Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018: Day 3 highlights If you have a summer wedding on your calendar, Amoh by Jade is your one-stop source. This season, designers Monica Shah and Karishma Swali looked to the descendants of the mountain god, Niyam Raja, for inspiration. The collection saw a slew of easy-fitting silhouettes from dhoti pants and skirts to feather-light jackets in soft, supple fabrics. Think cotton, khadi and fine silk. The primarily ivy-hued palette was accentuated by metallic accents and bright floral embroidery. Kalki Koechlin walked the ramp for the duo in a voluminous beige lehenga. When you think of Falguni and Shane Peacock, floor-grazing, red carpet-worthy gowns instantly spring to mind. This season, the husband-and-wife designer duo brought their love for unabashed glamour (sequins, shine and even fluttering feathers) to their first-ever menswear collection Louche. The show began with Sonakshi Sinha serving up a three-step tutorial on the new after hours attire—Sinha took the ramp in a curve-defining corset, blazer and billowing trousers. Models shortly followed suit wearing generously embellished, tailored separates in a shade card that ran from midnight hues to deep red and even powder pink. A dapper Karan Johar closed the show clad in a high-shine suit. The Woolmark Company and celebrity-favourite designer Manish Malhotra joined forces to present a never-before-seen take on merino wool with a capsule collection of traditional wear made using the natural and biodegradable fibre. To set the tone for the show with a strong focus on sustainability, attendees were treated to a screening of Slowing Down of Fast Fashion by Alex James and a panel discussion moderated by Vogue India's associate fashion features director Priyanka Khanna. After some of the industry's noteworthy names, including International Woolmark Prize winner Ruchika Sachdeva touched upon topics such as the meaning and surprisingly high cost of fast fashion, models took the ramp in Malhotra's wool separates—saris for women and sherwanis and bandhgalas for men. Yami Gautam played showstopper in a statement, tasseled number. When it comes to ending the evening in style, you can always count on Tarun Tahiliani. To showcase the fashion veteran's celestial collection, which took its cues from the Milky Way and constellations, models emerged out of glass boxes and shimmering, crystal-covered silhouettes steadily dotted the runway. This season, central to Tahiliani's lineup was comfort. The designer ditched heavy fabrics for light layers and gossamer garments catering to the easy-going bride. Rising star Kriti Sanon was the perfect showstopper for Tahiliani's fresh spin on bridal wear. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018: Day 2 highlights
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's what you missed The second day of Lakmé Fashion Week has forever been dedicated to the cause of conscious and ethical practices in fashion. Its evolution from Handlooms Day to Sustainable Fashion Day is sign of the week's keeping up with the changing times. Efforts to promote designers who are championing the cause are not only made on the runway, but also seen among the crowd that is seen dressing differently on this day. Starting off with addressing systematic change at a higher level was dialogue between the United Nations and designers from the North East of the country, on driving more business to the North Eastern states without obliterating its fragile ecosystem. Yuri Afanasiev, resident coordinator United Nations in India, spoke about the goal of the UN in India to create supply chains that benefit North Eastern states to improve their quality of life and economy. Given the possible threat of harming local traditions by way of excessive industrialisation, the UN would function as a mediator to help with mobilising communities and local governments. Designers spoke about the challenges they face while producing in the different states of the North East—lack of raw materials, political unrest, the need to implement region specific government schemes to help with grants, were some of issues that were brought up. Designers Sonam Dubal and Aratrik Dev Varman of label Tilla; Sonnie Kath, founder of the Exotic Eco; Orsola De Castro, founder of the Fashion Revolution; were some of the speakers at the talk. Osama Manzar, founder, Digital Empowerment Foundation; and Siva DeviReddy, founder GoCoop demonstrated digitisation at the grass root level to aid weavers. For the first show of the day, designers worked with fabric and crafts for different states. The result was lineup of everyday separates that echoed with tradition. The labels seen at the show were Khumanthem, Daniel Syiem, Jenjum Gadi and Exotic Echo Artisans Society, Tilla by Aratik Dev Varman and Kuzu. Indian footballer Bhaichung Bhutia walked for Kuzu while the Tetseo Sisters, a folk music band from Nagaland performed at the closing. View Gallery 20 Photos Highlights from Day 2 of Lakmé Fashion Week Hemang Aggarwal's designs are the kind of occasion wear done in traditional Indian fabrics that the audience has come to appreciate. His collection, ‘Un-Revive', was about modernising the textiles of Benares, laying the spotlight on the Tanchui and Katarwaan weaving techniques. The designer worked with pastel hues of powder pink and peach with silver and gold accents for a wide range of silhouettes, ranging from dresses to jackets and saris. Textile have always played hero at label Maku. This season, the designer worked with hand-woven silks, cotton, khadi and jamdani weaves for his collection ‘In Transit', which favoured the slow life. Actor Tillotama Shome opened the show with a monologue about missing out on the finer details of life in the fast pace will in present day. The performance was followed by a lineup of relaxed silhouettes that would be perfect to lounge in on a day off. If there is a mainstream vision of a concept, Rajesh Pratap Singh is sure to have an alternative take on it. Sustainable Day's biggest show was by the veteran designer, in association with Tencel—botanical fibres from Lenzing. The designer's only driving thought behind the collection—which he refused to title or name an inspiration for—was to create sustainable clothing that isn't anti-fit, bear an obvious stamp of being handwoven and step away from the palette of beige that is often associated with sustainable clothing in the country. To take this thought forward, Pratap Singh dived right into colour—sorbet pinks, reds, pale blues juxtaposed with brown, white—colour blocking was the obvious trend that came to mind when the models walked down the runway. Aside from using pure Tencel fibre, the designer worked on creating blends of the yarn with silk and steel in various weaves at the label's own research facility. Modern suits, kurtas, dresses made it to the runway. There were no artisans who walked down the runway, the audience wasn't left feeling forcibly sympathetic to the cause of conscious fashion. If sustainability is a course we need to follow, we need solutions from the likes of Rajesh Pratap Singh for clothes that fit right in to the context of urban India. column1: Meet Thaddeus O’Neil, the American designer in love with ikat
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How one consummate surfer boy discovered and fell for the craft As one of the finalists of the esteemed International Woolmark Prize 2013 and the CFDA Vogue Fashion Fund 2015, Thaddeus O'Neil has a lot to show for his time. In the five years since launching his eponymous label in 2013, he has quietly and steadily created a disruptive niche for himself that lovingly redefines the beach and surf culture as luxury playwear with silhouettes that stay true to his nomadic ethos. And if you were to look closely, you'd find the indigenous craft of ikat gracing his artfully laid-back palette. After admiring from afar, the Long Island-born designer finally made his way to the country for an immersive trip in Goa, taking in the cultural cosmos of the beach central. Here's what he is taking back with him. View Gallery 15 Photos Meet Thaddeus O’Neil, the American designer in love with Indian art techniques How was your trip in India? I've been dreaming of India for at least a decade now, so this visit was a long time coming. It's been worth the wait. The vibrant colours, the kind people, the spirit, vitality and natural glamour of the everyday wear of the people on the street has been very inspiring. I am madly in love with India. I have heard such incredible things about Jaipur and Varanasi, but unfortunately I ran out of time since India is so vast. I plan to come back as soon as I can get away from the studio again for a reasonable stretch. What role do you see the vibrant city of Goa playing in your next collection? I was incredibly charmed by Goa during my trip, where the wonderful team at W Goa helped me tap into some talented local creators, from pottery to painters, and introduced me to the rich Portuguese influence that still resonates there. It also didn't hurt that the beaches in Goa are absolutely stunning. The best inspiration always comes as a surprise. I particularly recall the evening I spent watching fishermen carefully detangle and roll their nets in preparation for the next day of fishing. The ocean was aglow and absolutely serene. Their quiet, expert fingers worked the nets that were magnificently faded into pale hues of turquoise, blue and pink. When they were all finally rolled into a mass of net, the layers of the net were haloed with the soft light of late afternoon and had the same luminosity of ikat cloth. I wonder if this perhaps inspired the first ikat weavers? Traditional Indian techniques have made it to your lineup in the past. What drew you to the craft in the first place? First and foremost, I am drawn to generationally refined craft and artisanal practices for obvious reasons, all of which emanate from the touch of the skilled hand. But with ikat specifically, the allure was its peculiarly idiosyncratic appearance, the beautifully rendered forms that almost appear to glow and vibrate from the cloth, like the haze of a hot summer beach. My brand being a luxury take on beach and surf culture, this lively quality of ikat cloth appeals to me very much. How does the Thaddeus O'Neil label work towards preserving artisanal practices? I run a relatively small, independent brand, so in my limited way, I make a very intentional choice to uphold these practices by consistently working with the artisans in a mutually respectful and supportive way. If enough brands do this—not in a superficial way or on a seasonally trend driven whim, taking for themselves what they need to fulfil a given mood board and then moving on, but collection after collection, working with the artisans and developing profound rapport and relationships with them—we can preserve these practices in the long run. How did 'playwear for everybody' evolve to be at the core of your design philosophy? My clothes have always been for men and women. They are fundamentally masculine in their appeal, but there is a certain levity and ease to them that is universal. Likewise, with my design philosophy, I favour enthusiasm over discipline. I am an enthusiastic person, and I have incredibly serious fun designing my clothes. How has your time at the CFDA Incubator Program shaped you as the designer that you are today? From being chosen as a finalist for the Vogue CFDA Fashion Fund to the Incubator initiative for emerging design talent to membership in the Council of Fashion Designers itself, their recognition of my work and vision has been very inspiring and motivates me to keep playing hard. 10 years down the line, Thaddeus O'Neil will probably be... Living near the ocean with his family creating things for his own and others' appreciation and doing all the good he can do in the world. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 5 things to know about John Targon, Marc Jacobs’ latest hire
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get to know the latest designer to join the label This week, Baja East designer John Targon joined Marc Jacobs in a yet-to-be clarified role—the first major hire under new chief executive Eric Marechalle. The appointment comes at turbulent time for the LVMH-owned brand, which announced the closure of its London store in addition to numerous European locations last month. As he enters into the picture, get to know the latest designer to join the brand. Before joining the team at Marc Jacobs, Targon co-founded the New York-based it-label Baja East with Scott Studenberg, which has been showing at New York Fashion Week since 2014 and is today carried at such influential retailers such as Barneys in New York, Maxfield in Los Angeles and Net-a-Porter. As purveyors of a self-proclaimed “loose luxury”, the brand prides itself on an array of easy-to-wear, off-duty pieces: Think slim-legged sweatpants and tie-dyed hoodies, but also proper luxurious cashmere and even swimwear sets, designed for young urban professional types who work by rooftop pools—or perhaps the beach. Even before starting his own brand, the designer amassed a decade's worth of experience in sales. Until 2013, Targon worked as the director of wholesale for menswear at Burberry, following stints at Céline, Condé Nast and Prada. Such experience on the business side of fashion is rare—and makes him an appealing talent in today's challenging retail climate. In 2015, Baja East was named a LVMH Prize finalist alongside the likes of Vetements, Off-White and Marques'Almeida. Although the label did not ultimately take home the €300,000 in prize money, it did secure its status as one of the buzziest shows of New York Fashion Week. Plus, it was a chance to shake hands with Karl Lagerfeld. “We met Karl Lagerfeld,” Studenberg recalled to Out Magazine in 2015, “and when we told him about our ambisex concept, he stopped us right away and said, ‘Everyone has two arms and two legs!' ” Heralded as one of the 10 faces of the next generation of American designers, Targon and Studenberg were nominated for US's most prestigious young designers' prize in 2015, competing in a series of design challenges before a panel of experts including designer Diane von Furstenberg and American Vogue editor Anna Wintour. For a brand founded just half a decade ago, Baja East has managed to accumulate an impressive roster of celebrity fans. A quick scroll through the brand's Instagram feed reveals that Lady Gaga is a #bajabae, as is Winnie Harlow, Miley Cyrus and Karlie Kloss. Pop stars Justine Skye and Demi Lovato have been seen in Targon's creations, as well as models Bella Hadid and Duckie Thot. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Watch: Rajesh Pratap Singh closes Day 2 at Lakmé Fashion Week S/R 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Giving sustainable fashion a new dimension Sustainable fashion in India has been a talking point for the last few years. However, you sit for one too many shows on the day dedicated to its cause and they all start to resemble each other. When designer Rajesh Pratap Singh decided to work on a collection for the closing show of Day 2 at Lakmé Fashion Week, he aimed to work on a line that wasn't anti-fit, worn-in looking, or associated with the colour beige. This season, the designer worked with Tencel—a botanical fibre from the house of Lenzing. Aside from using pure Tencel fibre, the designer worked on creating blends of the yarn with silk and steel in various weaves at the label's own research facility. Modern suits, kurtas, dresses made it to the runway in sorbet pinks, reds, pale blues juxtaposed with brown and lots of whites. The collection was accessorised with Perspex sunglasses and jewellery, and hiking boots. Pratap Singh's idea was to offer a solution to creating sustainable clothing that could be worn in the modern day context and that came through. There were no artisans who walked down the runway, the audience wasn't left feeling forcibly sympathetic to the cause of conscious fashion. Rajesh Pratap Singh wouldn't have it any other way. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From hot pink stilettos to tasselled stunners As any Carrie Bradshaw fan worth her salt would know, the first step to making a good and lasting impression is getting your footwear right. A statement, possibly embellished pair of shoes, can lift even the most basic outfit and even set the mood for the evening. With Valentine's Day just around the corner, it is the perfect time to add a statement shoe (or five) to your wardrobe. For an ultra-feminine vibe, pair Topshop's pale pink heels with a flirty ruffle dress, or channel your inner femme fatale with New Look's risqué black fringed black heels, paired with a classic LBD. If you're the kind that prefers being on the dance floor all night, Zara's pair of pearl-studded flats are just right for you. Seek comfort more than height? Mango's embroidered velvet loafers are perfect for those who want a luxe look without the vertigo. Miss Selfridge's pink embellished stilettos are versatile: pair them with cropped jeans to upgrade them to a night look, and then wear them with a hot pink lehenga for the next wedding on your calendar. Nasty Gal's tie-up version is perfect for a Valentine's Day brunch—a flirty sundress and sunglasses, and you're good to go. For the woman who prefers a minimal vibe, Glamorous' copper tie-ups will be the perfect go-to for every occasion. column1: Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018: Day 1 highlights
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The best shows from fashion week When all the fashion folk flock to a venue, you know it's that time of the year again. Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018 kicked off with its usual promise of new design talent via the longstanding Gen Next show. Only this time, with a collective cult that spotlighted an aesthetic that's fast gaining momentum. Think anti-fit, a muted palette and a return to the handmade and handwoven. Standing out from the crop were labels Mohammad Mazhar and Two Point Two. The former for its Indian summer sensibility featuring khadi cotton and silks, and the latter for an off-kilter, left-of-centre twist on basics. And then, just when our eyes were peeled for another less-is-more collection, out came Bobo Calcutta's paillette covered, pop prints-on-acid peppy take on fashion. View Gallery 18 Photos Highlights from Day 1 Lakmé Fashion Week Spring/Summer 2018 Next stop, Jio Garden's 6 Degree studio (a space for experimental presentations by fashion and textile designers) saw label Half Full Curve make its debut at the week. Former Quirkbox co-creative, Rixi Bhatia teamed up with sister Tinka for a summery collection of dresses and skirts that are perfect for every woman, whether you're a size 2 or 16. Here's to channelling your inner Ashley Graham. Another highlight at the experimental stage was Rara Avis by Sonal Verma. The accessories-first designer showed her growing skills in the ready to wear department with her ‘Koya' collection, reminiscent of middle eastern sand dunes and souk markets. Layered sequins, fringed leather jewellery and bags and maxi dresses with kaftan-like flow made up the showcase, and cacti were strewn around the space for added effect. As evening set in on a hot Mumbai day, Label by Ritu Kumar amped up the glam by several notches. The collection ‘Hip Hop Baroque' was exactly what the name alluded—velour tracksuits, lurex skirts, red velvet pantsuits that were a throwback to '90s glam-leisure. At a prime-time 9pm slot, Anita Dongre closed the first day of Lakmé Fashion Week at an off-site venue. Battery packs and fashion week survival kits intact, the fashion set descended at ITC Grand Central for a terrace garden show. Printed florals on lehenga-skirts that just about grazed ankles, fluffy tulle skirts worn under resham embroidered silk tunics and a star-studded finish by Mira and Shahid Kapoor (the ultimate sweet summer couple), Anita Dongre's ‘Songs of Summer' ended Day 1 on a happy note. column1: What to expect from Shyamal & Bhumika at Lakmé Fashion Week S/R 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Brides and bridesmaids, take note Luscious tulle and luxe fabrics doused in liberal doses of millennial pink and come-hither silhouettes—it comes as little surprise why Shyamal and Bhumika Shodhan, over the course of their two decade-long career in fashion, have become the go-to designers for brides and bridesmaids alike. And their latest stint at the Lakmé Fashion Week runway promises to be no different. Titled ‘Wonderland', the collection lives up to its moniker with an ethereal garden paying homage to the fairy tale-perfect creations being paraded down the runway. We caught up with designer Bhumika Shodhan to sneak a peek at what she has lined up. What can we expect from Shyamal & Bhumika on the Lakmé Fashion Week runway this season? We are creating a magical spectacle for our guests this season. We want everyone to feel like they are a part of a stunning, dreamy landscape. We have a magnificent afternoon planned with some great surprises thrown in and perhaps, a special muse of ours will make an appearance! What served as the key inspiration behind your new runway collection? We have embarked on a marvellous journey that takes us through a metaphorical landscape that brings to life the picture-perfect fairy tale wedding. Through this collection, we want to celebrate—celebrate love, celebrate couture and all the fantasies of the world. You can expect pastel colours with beads strung together on tulle, delicate embroidery with flowing satin and our quintessential saris with our signature cutwork edges. What do we have in store for us with the launch of ‘Wonderland'? With ‘Wonderland', we have tried to create a perfect fusion of enthralling elements in gorgeous hues and intricate embroidery. A thought-provoking collection of luxury prêt has also been introduced for global brides who value the finesse of handcraft above all else. The collection is an interesting take on a fairy tale-perfect backdrop that paints a fine picture of the 'Wonderland' we aim to create. How does the creative process begin when designing a new collection? Our creative process starts with our inspiration, around which we then build our concept. The idea goes in for several rounds of brainstorming on how we can build and develop the thought, bring out the best illustrations, designs, the kind of intricate techniques that need to go into each and every outfit, putting the relevant mood boards together, working together with the design teams and artisans where the design and imagination takes form. We experiment a lot with the embroidery on different materials using colours to fit the concept, sketches based on our inspiration, and only then do we finalise any details on the individual ensembles. Who would you describe as your muse for the collection? Our muse is the adventurous girl of today—confident, elegant and beautiful. She is extremely proud of her roots and her heritage, but adapts to the world outside with a bright and bold attitude. Our showstopper for ‘Wonderland' is the perfect example of this. She exudes confidence, is beautiful and is the perfect example of a Shyamal & Bhumika woman. Flip through the gallery below for an exclusive preview of the collection. column1: Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2018: What happens off the runway
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Keep up with it all The buzziest part of Mumbai currently is Jio Gardens at Mumbai's Bandra Kurla Complex, where Lakmé Fashion Week's summer/resort 2018 edition taking place. Nestled among the high-rises of corporations is the venue buzzing with talent, celebrities and more. While you're probably being updated with the happenings on the runway (check out Vogue India's Instagram story feed to keep up), here's the best from off the runway. Fashion week leads to discoveries of people with unique personal style. Some amount of peacocking is inevitable. How to tell one apart from the other is best left to the trained eye. Day 1 saw the likes of Priyanka Bose, Tillotama Shome amongst others at the venue. Keep up with our street style updates for more. Documentary photographer Trupal Pandya has been photographing tribes from around the world that are facing extinction. The Fashion Institute of Technology graduate showcased some of his work near the main show area. From the Huaronis of the Amazonian Forest to the Headhunters of Nagaland, keep an eye out for his arresting portraits. Designers spoke about the challenges they face while producing in the different states of the North East—lack of raw materials, political unrest, the need to implement region specific government schemes to help with grants were some of issues that were brought up. Designers Sonam Dubal and Aratrik Dev Varman of label Tilla; Sonnie Kath, founder of the Exotic Eco; Orsola De Castro, founder of the Fashion Revolution; were amongst the speakers at the talk. Osama Manzar, founder, Digital Empowerment Foundation and Siva Devireddy, founder GoCoop demonstrated digitisation at the grass root level to aid weavers. The Woolmark Company and celebrity-favourite designer Manish Malhotra joined forces to present a never-before-seen take on merino wool with a capsule collection of traditional wear made using the natural and biodegradable fibre. To set the tone for the show with a strong focus on sustainability, attendees were treated to a screening of Slowing Down of Fast Fashion by Alex James and a panel discussion moderated by Vogue India's associate fashion features director, Priyanka Khanna. After some of the industry's noteworthy names including International Woolmark Prize winner Ruchika Sachdeva touched upon topics such as the meaning and surprisingly high cost of fast fashion, models took the ramp in Malhotra's wool separates; saris for women and sherwanis and bandhgalas for men. Yami Gautam played showstopper in a statement, tasseled number. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Condé Nast International announces Code of Conduct
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In the wake of sexual harassment allegations in Hollywood and more recently in fashion, Condé Nast International has published behavioural guidelines for partners working on Condé Nast shoots. Condé Nast International has issued a new Code of Conduct, effective immediately, to safeguard the dignity and well-being of all who work with its brands. The guidelines, which will be rolled out to partners in all owned and operated markets, stipulate that: All models on set must be 18 years old. Where exceptions need to be made—such as when children are essential a story—they must be accompanied by an agency-provided chaperone. Any shoot requiring nudity, sheer clothing, lingerie, swimwear, animals, simulated drug or alcohol use or sexually suggestive poses must be signed off in advance by the subject. No shoot participant may be under the influence of alcohol or illegal drugs. A private dressing space must be provided to every subject on set. At all other times, subjects should not be left alone with a photographer, makeup artist or any other participant any time during a shoot. Condé Nast U.S. and Condé Nast International began work on the Code—an update to the Model Health Initiative in place since 2012—in October, following a New York Times report outlining decades of sexual harassment allegations against Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein. To develop the guidelines, Condé Nast spoke with more than 150 bookers, publicists, agents, models, stylists, editors and others working across the publishing spectrum. “We are committed to collaborating to find solutions to the problem of sexual harassment in our industry,” says Jonathan Newhouse, chairman and chief executive of Condé Nast International. “By adopting these recommendations all those involved in the creative process will be doing their part to ensure a safe and respectful work environment.” In conjunction with the new guidelines, a committee of senior Condé Nast executives has been established to review any complaints brought forward. Should the committee discover any violations to the Code did occur, the company pledges to immediately terminate its working relationship with the individual in violation, and ensure that all other necessary steps will be taken. Read the Code of Conduct in full below. Condé Nast Code of Conduct: No Harassment or Discrimination Everyone working on projects for Condé Nast should be treated with dignity and respect. All work done for Condé Nast must be performed in a professional manner, free of any form of discrimination or harassment. Any inappropriate conduct toward others, including but not limited to that based on an individual's sex, race, colour, weight, body shape, size, religion, national origin, ancestry, age, marital or domestic-partnership status, disability, sexual orientation, or gender identity or expression, will not be tolerated. We expect that all companies and vendors working with Condé Nast have clearly communicated equal employment opportunity and anti-harassment policies. Condé Nast may request a copy of these policies. Shoot Guidelines Photo and video shoots must be professional environments. Any disrespectful or inappropriate conduct toward others, including but not limited to that based on an individual's sex, race, colour, weight, body shape, size, religion, national origin, ancestry, age, marital or domestic-partnership status, disability, sexual orientation, or gender identity or expression, will not be tolerated. Every shoot performed for Condé Nast must adhere to the following guidelines: · All models must be at least 18 years old. Exceptions will be made for subjects appearing as themselves as part of a profile or news report. In the event a shoot calls for subjects younger than 18, a chaperone must be provided by the agency, and the agency must ensure compliance with any applicable labour laws, including child labour laws. · All work performed during a photo or video shoot must be in compliance with applicable laws and regulations, including but not limited to labour, wage and hour, and immigration laws. · Photo shoot participants may not be under the influence of alcohol or illegal drugs (including unauthorised prescription drugs), and the consumption or use of alcohol and illegal drugs (including the misuse of prescription drugs) on the premises of a shoot is strictly prohibited. · A brief describing any nudity, sheer clothing, lingerie, swimwear, animals, simulated drug or alcohol use or sexually suggestive poses planned to be incorporated in a shoot will be distributed to all concerned parties and must be agreed to in advance by the subject of the images. All attendees at the shoot will be notified of any planned nudity. · A private dressing space must be available to everyone appearing in a shoot. · If sheer clothing is to be included, appropriate undergarments must be provided unless otherwise agreed to in advance by the subject of the images. · Any concerns a subject has regarding the amount of skin exposure of wardrobe must be considered, and no subject should be pressured to expose themselves more than they feel comfortable. · While Condé Nast maintains control over creative and aesthetic decisions, any concerns of a subject's agent or other representative should be given respectful consideration. · We recommend that a model should not be alone with a photographer, makeup artist or other contributor participating in a Condé Nast shoot. · Throughout the shoot, including any related travel, photographers and videographers may not shoot anyone engaged by or through Condé Nast other than as requested by Condé Nast. All participants in a photo or video shoot must act professionally and refrain from harassment of any kind. Unacceptable conduct includes but is not limited to the following: · Sexual advances or propositions. · Any type of sexual activity or contact. · Any suggestion, direct or implied, that submission to or rejection of sexual advances will affect an individual's ability to perform services for the shoot or any other Condé Nast project. · Display of pornographic or obscene material. · Offensive comments regarding a person's sex, race, color, weight, body shape, size, religion, national origin, ancestry, age, disability, sexual orientation, or gender identity or expression, including epithets and slurs. · Physical threats or assaults. Anyone who has concerns about conduct occurring on a photo shoot may contact the Condé Nast contact listed on the call sheet for the shoot that has been provided and/or posted on-set. legal Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What needs to be in your ethnic wear wardrobe in your 50s
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you need to keep the good times rolling The true beauty of traditional wear lies in the fact that it doesn't subscribe to arbitrary age restrictions. You can wear a lehenga with just as much flair in your 50s as you did three decades ago during your crazy 20s. Saris only get better with your age, and your options for daily casuals have been more varied. Dressing your wardrobe in this fifth decade of your life isn't half as intimidating as it sounds in your head, and if you're looking for some quick inspiration to get started, you've come to the right place. View Gallery 9 Photos Ethnic wear in your 50s- Celebrities Over the 50 milestone and showing no signs of slowing down, you'll find Bollywood's fifty crew inundated with powerhouses who like to dress the talk. Couture fiend Sridevi thrives on the red carpet, letting the age-appropriate concerns bite her dust as she glides by in dramatic flowing trains and designer saris, with designer Manish Malhotra feeding her love for all things sparkly. Having returned to India after a sabbatical, Madhuri Dixit-Nene is likewise having the time of her life, having given her wardrobe free reign to include everything from experimental saris to couture gowns. Runway trends aren't off the table for you just because you've crossed the 50 barrier. See a print you love? Go for it, but ensure that you incorporate into your personal palette of style that you know for a fact works for you. Not too confident about outfits that flaunt skin because it might not be deemed appropriate? Opt for interesting cutouts and flirty inserts as a compromise. This is also the perfect time to put all the luxury investments that you have been amassing over the years to use, from your designer clutches to that heirloom sari you've preserved all this while. When you feel comfortable is when you look your most confident, so take a call whether it's worth fidgeting all night just to keep pace with a trend. Instead, allow your hairstyle and jewellery choices to communicate a cohesive look. Heavy jhumkas in your ears are best complemented with a chic updo, while a statement necklace looks better when framed with a wispy bun. Floral hair accessories, especially the traditional gajra, is no longer reserved for the grannies—just ask Sonam Kapoor who routinely turns to this ethnic staple for the many weddings on her social calendar. Allow your traditional wardrobe to meaningfully express your connection to your roots, and you're golden. Looking for new additions to your ethnic wardrobe or maybe just a modern update? Pick from our line-up of all the styles that are making waves right now. column1: Kirsten Dunst confirms her pregnancy in the new Rodarte lookbook
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Check out the fairy tale setup Today, Kirsten Dunst confirmed her pregnancy by posing in the Fall 2018 Rodarte lookbook, titled Women Who Inspire Us. As part of a portrait series posted on Instagram, Dunst wears a romantic floral embroidered tulle gown and cradles her baby bump. Rumors began swirling last December that Dunst was expecting her first child with fiancé Jesse Plemons, and today's news marks just the latest in a series of fashion-centric pregnancy announcements that illustrate a growing trend. The celebrity pregnancy reveal has become something of an art form of late, and often, there's a style component baked right in. Beyoncé announced she was pregnant with twins through a highly stylised photo series in which she wore satin ruffled skivvies. Meanwhile, Serena Williams broke the news by posting a swimsuit selfie that showcased her expectant figure in a sportier setting that befit the tennis star. On the runway and in lookbooks, it's rare to see a pregnant model, but a number of designers have broken with convention. For the spring 2018 show, Eckhaus Latta cast artist Maia Ruth Lee, who strutted out in a snap-front cardigan dress unfastened at the centre to reveal her pregnant belly. Before that, Karl Lagerfeld called on a seven-month pregnant Ashleigh Good to play the Chanel bride of fall 2014 couture. The next year, Dolce & Gabbana muse Bianca Balti walked the Fall 2015 runway while pregnant with her second child; her presence fell right in line with the show's famiglia message, as babies and toddlers accompanied many of the models on the catwalk. Dunst's appearance in Kate and Laura Mulleavy's new lookbook puts a similar high-fashion spin on a major milestone, and one can only hope she will continue to wear the unabashedly pretty designs in the coming months. column1: Tarun Tahiliani’s Lakmé Fashion Week S/S 2018 line is a treat for brides
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get all the details here Veteran couturier Tarun Tahiliani's is easily one of the most anticipated shows of Lakmé Fashion Week. This spring/summer, comfort tops the agenda for Tahiliani. “Since we did our Tarakanna collection, I have been thinking about fashion's role in bridal wear and how it has failed the modern Indian bride because the clothes are very heavy and stiff. So, we set out, in keeping with the global trend of true equality for women, to create clothes that had all the glamour but let women be comfortable and have fun,” says the designer of the collection, which highlights his love for layering and gossamer fabrics. When it comes to delivering the standout, celestial line-up (think everything from Swarovski-laden lehengas to shimmering kurtas inspired by the Milky Way and constellations), Tahiliani's plans are nothing short of grand. “The models will come down in a glass box like they are floating angels amongst stars,” he says. And who better to play showstopper for the fresh take on bridal wear than a young, rising star? “I first noticed Kriti Sanon, re-noticed her rather, last year on the cover of the April issue of Vogue India where she was wearing a piece from Tarun Tahiliani in the South Africa story styled by Anaita [Shroff Adajania]. I then had the good fortune to see Bareilly Ki Barfi and decided she's the new girl for the label. She is the appropriate fit for the modern youthfulness and trans-India cool,” says Tahiliani. column1: Meet the Indian artist behind Chloé’s folklore-inspired collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Mythical forms on romantic silhouettes For her debut collection at Chloé, new creative director Natacha Ramsay-Levi chose to use Barcelona-based Indian artist, Rithika Merchant, to pay ode to painted dresses, drawing from Karl Lagerfeld's work at Chloé. The resulting collection was an eclectic mix of delicately embroidered bodices, romantic paints on crisp cotton and python pieces, souvenirs from Chloé's sartorial past. View Gallery 11 Photos Meet the Indian artist behind Chloé’s folkloric collection Merchant is a Parson's alumni who has showcased in various parts of the world including the United States of America, United Kingdom, Canada, Portugal, India, Singapore, Denmark and Spain. Her work has always been an exploration of myths across civilisations and their culmination in contemporary world. Botanical drawings, organic forms and symbolism form an integral part of her style, which added a subtle element of mysticism to Ramsay-Levi's designs for spring/summer 2018, rendering every dress unique. Alliances between artists and designers are not a new phenomenon. In the '30s, Italian designer Elisa Schiaparelli and Salvador Dali collaborated to create iconic pieces like the 'Lobster Dress' and 'Shoe Hat'. In the '60s, Yves Saint Laurent was inspired by Piet Mondrian's works to create simple, A-line silhouettes that captured the zeitgeist of changing times. This creative entwinement between art and fashion stands stronger than ever, giving artists prominence in pop culture. In recent years, designers like McQueen worked with Damien Hirst to create the seminal skull prints, Marc Jacobs (circa Louis Vuitton) collaborated with Yayoi Kusama to create polka-dots galore. Vogue chats with Rithika Merchant about her recent project: How did the collaboration come through? Totally by chance. Natacha came across my work while going through images on the internet. She really liked my work and said that it fit what she had in mind for the painted dresses. They sent me an email asking if I wanted to come on board for the collection. It was totally out of the blue for me and a very nice surprise! After a few email conversations and a Skype call, I had been briefed on the scope of the project and that was it. They invited me to come to the studio in Paris to work with them on the dresses, and so I spent about two weeks there working with Natacha and the rest of the team to place my drawings on the garments. What is it like to work with Natacha and the Chloé team? I really liked working with Natacha, we got along well! Working with her was a great experience because she is very easy-going but she also knows exactly what she wants. She was very open to creative opinions and inputs from me but also had a clear vision for her team and the debut collection. This made it very simple for me to follow her feedback and work on them throughout the creative process. How are artist-designer collaborations mutually beneficial? This is always a two-way process, however in my case, I perceive it as more visibility for me out of my sphere. Chloé is an established label and to be acknowledged through them widens my scope of visibility as an artist. These collaborations are mutually beneficial as they create an external outlet for artists to showcase their works outside of the art world, and it allows for fashion designers to become a part of the art world as more than just clothing. The spectacle that is created through such a collaboration bridges the minuscule gap that exists between art and fashion. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Grammys 2018: What your favourite celebrities wore
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The night of the white rose Hollywood's war cry against sexual abuse is only becoming more resolute with each passing day. After the Women's March and the all-black red carpet at the Golden Globes Awards, the red carpet at the 60th Annual Grammy Awards too saw a massive show of support for the #TimesUp movement. This time, the symbol used to show resistance against abuse was a white rose, which is symbolic of respect, and pays homage to new beginnings. View Gallery 37 Photos Grammy Awards 2018: Who Wore What While she skipped the red carpet, Beyoncé made her debut mid-show, accompanied by her husband Jay-Z and daughter Blue Ivy, in a custom black gown by Nicolas Jebran that was inspired by the Black Panther movement. Showing off her baby bump, Chrissy Tiegen chose a shimmery Yanina Couture dress while her husband John Legend complemented her in a dapper suit. While Rita Ora took her look up a notch in a velvet Ralph & Russo one-shoulder gown, Cardi B went all-white in an Ashi Studio dress. Others who were seen favouring pantsuit on the red carpet included American rap artist Eve in Naeem Khan, Anna Kendrick in Balmain and Kesha in Nudie's Rodeo Tailors. From TV show host James Corden, to Nick Jonas and members of The Chainsmokers, the men were also seen supporting #TimesUp in tuxedos and white roses. While most of the men wore black, Zayn Malik chose a baby pink suit by Richard James. There to celebrate the year's biggest tracks, videos and names was guest list featuring Kristin Cavallari, Lana Del Rey, Janelle Monae, Cyndi Lauper, Camila Cabello, Ashanti, Hailee Steinfeld, Katie Holmes, Heidi Klum, Miley Cyrus, among others. Scroll through our gallery to see what all the stars wore to the Grammy Awards 2018. column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan on fashion, motherhood and chasing dreams
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet the face of AND's summer 2018 campaign Kareena Kapoor Khan has had a near two-decade-long successful career in Bollywood, embraced motherhood and never dropped the ball, and she makes no bones about any of it. The star, who has worked with Anita Dongre's label AND previously, now joins a league of extraordinary women in the summer 2018 campaign #ANDiRISE. Bharti Gehani, entrepreneur who continued to follow her dreams and overcoming physical trauma, transgender model Anjali Lama, makeup artist Kritika Gill who continues to push the boundaries with her craft, and activist-rapper Sofia Ashraf, all feature alongside the star in the campaign as role models in their own right. View Gallery 4 Photos Kareena Kapoor Khan on fashion, motherhood and chasing your dreams Vogue sat down with Anita Dongre and Kareena Kapoor Khan to chat about the power of women, style and work-life balance. What was the driving force behind the collection? Anita Dongre: The driving force behind this campaign or any other campaign we do is that every woman has the ability to rise. We are showcasing stories of four women who inspire and have risen above all the challenges that life has thrown at them. Kareena you're a friend of the brand. What makes you want to return to AND as their ambassador? Kareena Kapoor Khan: I think the ideas Anita comes up with for each campaign are very relatable to my personality. I think it's a brand that is about confidence, wearability, elegance, the working woman; and like Anita said, it is about rising above yourself which I think is something a lot of people associate with me. I have always tried to rise above the circumstances, which is why there's always been a relatability factor [with the audience]. Speaking about rising above challenges, you got back to work a few months after your son was born. What was the first day back on set like? KKK: Strangely, the first work commitment I took after having my baby was walking for Lakmé Fashion Week for Anita Dongre. Taking to the ramp right after delivery was not something other actors have done, but I just wanted to show to the world that having a child is a joy but you can also continue your work and passion. There are working women around the world who do both and the fact is so can we; somewhere, it just sets an example. AD: I think what Kareena did was truly inspiring. It was just 40 days after she had Taimur; the moment was truly special. A huge focus of AND has been addressing to the needs of working women. Tell us, what are the questions women should be asking in the workplace? AD: Over and above all, equality. Kareena, what did you like most about the collection? KKK: I think the collection has a lot of colour this time: there's greens, indigo blue, florals; and summer is always about all of these elements. How would you describe your personal style? KKK: My style has always been very confident. It's in the very casual, chic zone, not very couture. People relate to me in my jeans and sneakers because you have to keep the practicality of the situation in mind. It's obvious that Taimur is already a bit of a celebrity in that his clothes make news all the time. Do you enjoy dressing him up, shopping for him? KKK: I like dressing him up because I like doing it, not for the paparazzi. I am happy for him to get clicked in his kurta pyjamas also. You have often said that Karisma has influenced you in life, what is the best style lesson you learnt from her? KKK: She is always elegant and put together. I think what I have learnt from her is that you can be casual but there needs to be an air of elegance about it. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This is the one textile exhibition you cannot miss
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Inside 'A Search in Five Directions' Slow. Time. Inquiry. Passion. Respect.  If you feel these words sound somewhat alien in a world obsessed with fast-fashion with stunted ideologies, thoughtless cultural appropriation and disregard for provenance, this exhibition: 'A Search in Five Directions', is a must see, to allow ourselves the opportunity to re-evaluate the cursory cultural values we have succumbed to in our fast lives. View Gallery 5 Photos This is the one textile exhibition you cannot miss This exhibition celebrates Martand Singh's long and loving public contribution to the field of traditional Indian textile, and the profound dialogue about the state of Indian design that ensued, igniting minds and works of top designers and experts in this field. You will find gems that will stir you—a sari from Odisa that has the most exquisite calligraphy across the entire length of the unstitched cloth; another, a unique piece of textile art with a romantic medley of jamdani and kalamkari. “It's called the Kodalikarupur sari, and the combination of the two techniques are extraordinary,” says Rakesh Thakore, prolific designer and one of the curators of the exhibition. This technique had been dead for decades; but Martand Singh went through 100-year-old sources to trace the provenance of this textile and then produced it with craftsmen from Thanjavur. Mapu's life-journey with hand-made textiles resonates with scores of stories like this, full of awe and wonder, but more importantly, stories that reveal his commitment to the authenticity of the people and processes behind the products. The exhibition is an off-shoot of a series of seven textile art and history exhibitions called 'Vishwakarma—Master Weavers' that took place between the years 1981-1991. It was hailed as the pinnacle of Indian textile design, a tribute to unparalleled craft traditions that had remained uncelebrated and obscured by neglect, as the country catapulted into an era of speed and industrialisation. Mapu, the circumspect cultural crusader, worked tirelessly for years to document India's myriad traditional textile techniques—pigment-painting, dye-painting, resist-dyeing, printing and weaving from centres across the country—which are recognised today not only as an ode to the cult of hand-made, but the very antidote to quick consumerism. Mapu, disenchanted by glamorous urban fashion, pledged his solidarity with the bucolic artisans across the country, always reminding the world what they most represented—the magic of hand-made, the imperfections of their hands and their lands, and most of all, the humanity of slow creation. 'A Search in Five Directions' presented by the Devi Art Foundation is on at the National Handicrafts and Handlooms Museum, New Delhi, and will continue until March 31, 2018 Culture & Living Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast
