column1: Here’s how India’s rich textiles were used to create French wedding gowns
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A peek at Ekaya’s first international collaboration What do you get when you merge India's rich aesthetic with the insouciantly chic style of the French? Palak Shah of Ekaya and the Fédération Française de la Création Couture Sur Mesure - Paris have come together to present Indian textiles in a never-before-seen light through a capsule collection of fairytale-worthy wedding gowns. Vogue got Shah to delve into the details of the collaboration that came to life at Paris Haute Couture Week. View Gallery 4 Photos Here’s how India’s rich textiles were used to create French wedding gowns Every year, during haute couture week, the Fédération Française de la Création Couture Sur Mesure - Paris organises an event that celebrates the know-how of its members in partnership with the greatest weavers from across the globe. For 2018, the federation turned to India and Véronique Poles (of Poles Luxe Consulting Pvt Ltd) introduced them to Ekaya's daringly minimal and contemporary take on traditional textiles. The collaboration, Cousu d'Or – Magical Weaving, showcases wedding couture designs, which demonstrate the excellence of Indian craftsmanship. A clever fusion of the past and the present is the best way to describe the capsule collection. Ekaya has carefully curated a selection of ivory-hued, handwoven fabrics including signature brocades along with silks, cotton, georgettes, chiffons, tusser, organza, mashru silks and chikankari hand-embroidery. Metallic fabrics and geometric patterns bring a new urban glamour to the intricately woven silks and cotton. The federation represents some of the most renowned designers and couturiers in the French fashion and seeing these fabrics transform in their hands has been a revelation. The collection truly represents the best of both worlds and redefines the perception about handwoven crafts. While Ekaya brings forward textiles unique in their make and design, the federation and their designers bring a fresh perspective, where they identify new details applying them to a distinct modern silhouette. Ekaya's main goal has always been to challenge the stereotypical designs that are usually made in Benares and expand the vocabulary of the weavers, by daring them to explore unusual motifs and patterns. As for the French, they had never worked with a 45-inch fabric (typical to the Indian handloom industry) before, so trying to make a garment out of that was a little challenging. Moreover, we had to work around the weight of the fabric and the way it draped. The designers discovered and explored the reversible quality in the fabrics, which came as a surprise to us as we had never considered using our fabrics in reverse so beautifully before. As of now the main goal is expansion in India and more reach in the international market through Thaan. We're are also looking towards more interesting collaborations both domestic and global, where we aim to continue introducing handloom fabrics to the world in newer ways. As a brand we want to break the stereotypical ways Indian fabrics are viewed and exhibited abroad by puncturing the rules that are usually placed towards their usage. The exhibition commenced January 22 and will be on till February 25, 2018 at Sofitel Le Faubourg Weddings Weddings Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How do you make sure that the fashion you’re buying is sustainable?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Your ethical shopping guide Now that you know sustainable fashion is something to genuinely care about, it's time to look at the factors that determine a garment being worthy of being tagged as an environment-friendly one. Making the switch from fast fashion to eco fashion is not going to be an overnight transformation, but being an informed shopper will bring you closer to your goal. When a designer label or a store alludes to taking the green path, what is it that they are referring to? Vegetable dyes, organic cotton, linen, organic wool, bamboo fibre and recycled polyester are elements in garments that have a lower impact on the environment. Organic farming is more expensive than the alternative as it eliminates the use of toxic pesticides and short cut methods of production that affect the toxicity of soil. This automatically makes sustainable garments more expensive than others, but the choice to buy less in favour of saving natural resources is a better one. Tip: Read the fine print before shopping. One of the key goals of sustainability to keep ecosystems in place. Sweatshop factories harm lives of workers and negatively affect their future. A design label that follows ethical practices makes sure the workers are being paid fair wages, their families are taken care of, and, if possible, that they are not displaced from their origins. Reverse migration is a system in which designers tie up with NGOs and craft clusters and assign work to artisans in their original homes instead of relocating them to cities where they find it hard to survive given the high cost of living. Another positive outcome of reverse migration is that it keeps traditional crafts and alive and promises authenticity of products. Tip: Be an informed customer and check with the store manager about how clothes are being produced. Circularity is an important word in the lexicon of sustainable fashion. The reason behind the garment industry's increasing contribution to world pollution is putting the textile industry in overdrive. Fast fashion encourages consumers to shop for more than they can consume. Most of these garments end up as landfill and they have rarely been damaged. Upcycling breathes a new life into clothing with minor repairs or fresh outtake on garments like jeans, outerwear, vintage saris amongst others. Tip: Keep an eye out for upcycling workshops or request your favourite designer to rework a garment that you are too fond of to discard. Fast fashion giants operate on being hyper trendy. The idea is to make runway trends available at throwaway prices while maintaining low cost of production. This encourages consumers to shop more than needed and discard clothes as soon as they go out of trend and move on to whatever comes next. This system has led to overconsumption and the resultant waste from it. Another growing movement amongst designers is to disregard the trend cycle in order to make clothes timeless and not bound to seasonal fads. Tip: Ignore the trend of the moment and make the shift to buying classics that will have a longer life in your closet Learn more about ethical practices in fashion with our Sustainability Matters series What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Designer Ulyana Sergeenko is receiving backlash for using the N-word
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion She has since apologized Designer Ulyana Sergeenko is under fire for a note that she sent to influencer Miroslava Duma, a cofounder of Buro 24/7 and The Tot. The note, which was accented with emoji hearts on Mira's Instagram story on Monday night, read, “To my n/*ggas in Paris.” Ulyana, a white Russian designer and socialite, was immediately met with swift and rightful backlash, calling her out for using a racial slur to address her white friend. On Tuesday morning, Ulyana posted an apology on her own Instagram. She wrote, “I woke up this morning with my phone full of insulting messages ‘you deserve the worst in your life,' 'die white trash'…and so on.” She went on to add that she is from East Kazakhstan, her daughter is part Armenian, and “I have never divided people on white or black.” But that's when it starts to get even more dicey. She shares, “Kanye West is one of my favorite musicians, and NP is one of my favorite songs,” continuing, “And yes, we call each other the N word sometimes when we want to believe that we are just as cool as these guys who sing it.” [#image: /photos/5ce42569b40d2622f4d6c200]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/miraduma Her apology continued to offend. Commenters responded in fury, writing, “being white doesn't give you the right to comment about how non whites should feel.” And “This just sounds like you're mad at your friend ‘naively' exposing you rather than being genuinely apologetic over your word choice.” Miroslava Duma has yet to make a statement at all. This isn't the first time Miroslava has been accused of racism. In 2014, she drew ire with a feature on her website Buro 24/7 that portrayed an editor sitting on top of a chair made to resemble a black woman in bondage. column1: What can we expect from Hedi Slimane’s recent appointment at Céline?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue takes a look It could be said that in her decade-long tenure at Céline, Phoebe Philo has brought into the fashion lexicon, a modern elegance. She ushered in a new wave of minimalism, that was softer, but no less confident. This was a woman who made Joan Didion her campaign star, luxe track pants a wardrobe essential, and clothes that worked across generations. Philo's sophisticated pieces (from leather T-shirts to turtlenecks—not to mention those fur slides and Trapeze bags), instantly became street style fodder. In the fashion history books, they are a double whammy—serving the contemporary woman's wardrobe needs, while being inherently timeless. They also came in at a time when fast fashion was dominating the market—though ironically enough, her cuts and designs were always the first source of inspiration for these retailers. So this week's news that Hedi Slimane, the rebel with a cause, the man who looked to LA street culture for his last gig at Saint Laurent, was named, artistic, creative and image director at Céline, came as quite the surprise to many. Slimane's youth culture-driven appeal is quite the departure from Philo's aesthetic. With his love for the Eighties (that distressed denim, those leather jackets, the big-big '80s party dresses), he made the label, the ultimate for millennials. Naturally, his reign at Saint Laurent, was controversial to say the least, beginning with his decision to drop ‘Yves' from the label, his rock and roll styling of a traditional French house, and his designer prices on clothes that were often deemed ‘too accessible'. But what both Slimane and Philo have in common is this—they are both commercially incredibly successful. And at the risk of perpetuating a cliché, what does unite their two very disparate styles is that they are both disrupters. Both Philo and Slimane caused a paradigm shift in their approaches to fashion. Slimane's role will also involve expanding to menswear, fragrance (their last perfume was in 1964), and couture. What he brings to Céline, remains to be seen, but in his classic style, I bet it will cause quite the debate. After all, breaking the mould is something he has down pat. column1: The Bombay Shirt Company finds a home in the city of New York
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's a look at the store View Gallery 3 Photos The Bombay Shirt Company found a home in the city of New York The Bombay Shirt Company, as the name suggests takes pride in its city of origin, Mumbai. Known for their custom-tailored shirts, BSC's offerings are for the corporate crowd, yet anything but generic. BSC originally started out as an online store in 2012, extending to stores in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkatta, New Delhi and Dubai, and now, the label has found a new home. Carrying forward their minimalist urban aesthetic, the Bombay Shirt Company has a new space in SoHo, New York City. Vogue spoke to founder and creative director Akshay Narvekar about the big move. When we launched Bombay Shirt Company, our mission was always to create a global brand. Nothing signals global more than New York City. We have an exciting price/value proposition for the market in the United States. Once we found the correct partners, we were ready to go full steam ahead with the launch. All our stores, be it in India or abroad, are bound together by certain themes—colour palette, the materials used in construction, typography and product selection. However, each store is fit out to suit the neighbourhood that it resides in. Our Kala Ghoda store has a mid-century feel to it given the history of the surrounding area. The New York store has a few more modern touches given that it's in vibrant Soho. So, every store is distinct but yet identifiable as a BSC store. Our products are fairly similar across stores and geographies. However, with New York, we have to cater slightly more to seasonal and weather-related needs. More flannels and warmer brushed fabrics work well especially this time of the year. We hope to double our store count over the next 12 months. column1: The making of Dior’s spring/summer 2018 couture collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue steps into the famed fashion house’s white-washed ateliers to watch it all come together It's 1:45pm on a drizzly Saturday, just 48 hours before Dior will present its spring/summer 2018 haute couture collection to some of the world's most powerful tastemakers on a makeshift runway at the Musée Rodin in Paris. A kilometre and a half away, Maria Grazia Chiuri is sitting in the spacious, mirror-lined ‘fitting room' of Dior headquarters, scrutinising the back of a model in a delicate white dress. With a semi-transparent bodice sculpted in bande en crin and a skirt shaped like a tall water glass spun in feathers, it has all the commanding elegance of a late 19th-century society portrait and yet is unmistakably contemporary. View Gallery 19 Photos Dior couture spring/summer 2018 The collection—Chiuri's third—is a striking departure from her debut show a year ago. Gone are the fairy-like gowns in champagne and pastel; in their place is a graphic, architectural assembly rendered almost exclusively in black and white. (Chiuri has restricted her palette in such a manner before—her A/W 2017 ready-to-wear collection was composed almost entirely in navy.) A sequel of sorts to her spring/summer 2018 ready-to-wear show, which drew on the work of sculptor and former Dior model Niki de Saint Phalle, this collection takes its inspiration from Leonor Fini, the Argentinian-born Surrealist artist whose work and intrepid personal style caught the attention of Christian Dior years before he opened his own fashion house. “I am very fascinated with the idea that before Mr Dior was a couturier, he was a gallerist connected to an incredible artistic moment in Paris,” Chiuri explains. “He was the first gallerist to do an exhibition of Leonor Fini, who was really unconventional at the time, one of the first women artists, really modern, her outfits were really cool. She would say, I don't want to wear a gown to the ball, I want to dance, I want to show myself.” Yet it seems de Saint Phalle is not entirely out of Chiuri's mind: the collection's searing patterns, recurring eye motifs and the bold hand-painting of the dresses have more in common with Saint Phalle's Tarot Garden than Fini's ghostly, sexual paintings. Inheriting a legacy Dior is one of the last great houses of haute couture, keeping alive a tradition of hand-made dressmaking in Paris that dates back to the court of Napoleon III. Today, there are just 14 designers permitted by the French Ministry of Industry to bear the ‘haute couture' label, down from 106 in 1946. They serve a small, yet increasingly global clientele with an appreciation for bespoke fits, fabulous embroidery and feathers applied by hand, and the means to pay the tens—sometimes hundreds—of thousands of euros required to realise them. “I love both [haute couture and pret-a-porter], but couture is a different language for me,” Chiuri says during a break between fittings. She is outfitted in a black turtleneck and high-waisted trousers, her fingers dressed in her favourite heavy Codognato rings, her peroxide chop pulled into a neat, low ponytail. “In couture we speak about timelessness, heritage, tradition, craftsmanship. In pret-a-porter… we speak about now. The audience also is different. In couture you have a small audience that has to understand what you mean by couture, why you buy couture.” Though she must counterbalance its demands with the full and pre-season ready-to-wear collections, Chiuri is in some ways more involved with couture than the man who founded Dior 71 years ago, who preferred to let his designers work with complete freedom from his sketches, only stepping in to make adjustments when the toiles, and later the final dresses, were presented. (Or so he claimed.) Today, collections begin two months in advance with a story and a set of sketches, which are divided among designers in two ateliers: flou, on the fifth floor, for dresses, and tailleur, on the sixth, for tailored garments including suits and coats. The designers, or modelistes, are responsible for the draping and construction, while the detailed handiwork—painting, embroidery, pleating, feather-application, etc—is sent to speciality workshops, many of them, like the famous embroider Lesage and flower and feather-maker Lemarié, older than the couture houses themselves. They are returned to the atelier for final assembly and rounds of fittings, sometimes less than a week before the show. The twice-yearly collections are only a part of what the ateliers do; like tailoring, couture is a service, and the staff spends the better part of the year adapting runway models and working on private commissions. “It's a different way to work,” Chiuri explains. “You give the first sketch, and after in the atelier you see the first shape, you add embroidery. It's step by step; every day you work in couture. It's more about the relationship between the designer and the atelier, the staff and the atelier.” In the ateliers Upstairs on the fifth floor is the flou atelier, composed of three adjoining rooms: two for cutting and sewing, one for pressing. Client mannequins, showcasing the breadth of the female form, line the walls in profile, back to front, above plexiglass cases of pins, rolls of silk ribbon and worn handbags. Sketches for each dress are hung on the wall; each designer keeps a second copy in a three-ring binder. The clean white tables are covered in yard upon yard of the world's richest fabrics. Half-dressed mannequins dot the room, attended by two to three petites mains at a time, each wearing a white smocked monogrammed in Dior grey. Some of them began working at Dior more than 40 years ago, hired by the house's third artistic director, Marc Bohan. The work is slow. There are none of the usual sounds of a workroom for clothes—no steady hum of a sewing machine, no clacking of an embroidery needle. The hemming of skirts and stitching of linings is done entirely with chalk and scissors, needle and thread. Three women bend over a pale pleated skirt decorated in thousands of tiny sequins. They take scissors and tweezers to each one, trimming loose threads, pressing them perfectly flat. In the last of the three rooms, Hongbo Li is bent over a broad table examining the trim of an airy white dress. Those who watched Dior and I, the 2014 documentary on Raf Simons' first haute couture collection for Dior, will remember him as the Chinese designer responsible for the “big dresses”. Outfitted in white leather Alexander McQueen sneakers and army-green cargo trousers, a pincushion strapped to one wrist, he is every bit as modest and charming in person, his hair greyer than when we saw him on the silver screen. Born in Dalian, a large city on China's northeast coast, he came to Paris in 2001 with dreams of working for Dior. “When I studied fashion in Dalian, I already knew Christian Dior and loved him, and thought that if one day I have the chance to move anywhere, Paris would be first.” After taking a degree at the esteemed École de la chambre syndicale de la couture Parisienne, he joined Dior in 2004. Li draped three of the dresses in this collection. The one he is working on presently he describes as “the most difficult” of the lot—though, devoid of surface decoration, it appears to be one of the most simple. Made of 19 uniquely shaped “petals” in semi-sheer double-organza edged in black, it took more than 400 hours to complete. “It's really pure,” he says, explaining that each petal required its own pattern. In the adjoining room, Chantal Birba adjusts the pleats of a sand-coloured organza bodice, its surface decorated in a fine serpentine thread-pattern and thousands of transparent sequins, which were stitched, trimmed and pressed by hand. Birba, who hails from Martinique, wears large rectangular glasses in grey tortoiseshell and a tiny diamond cross at her throat, her hair swathed in a scarf of colorful ankara-print cotton. A former flight attendant for Air France, she started at Dior in 2012, working on Raf Simons's first couture collection. “I spent a month and a half working on only one dress. It was straight, with a bustier, with sparkles like this one. A couple of months later I saw Jennifer Lawrence wearing it,” she recalls with a smile. “Every day I'm grateful I chose to change jobs and work in fashion instead of tourism.” The future of haute couture As Chiuri herself likes to say, haute couture is a dream, a fantasy. To keep the ateliers alive is to keep a legacy of craftsmanship alive, too. But couture is also a business. “For me it is very important that we sell what we show,” says Chiuri. “And not only a specific outfit they ask for. If [clients] choose pieces from the show that is good for me, because that means that in some way I can do something fantastic and dreamy, and at the same time wearable.” And what of the future of couture? Does she believe it will still be in practice 50, 100 years from now? Chiuri says yes, but that it will be “another kind” of couture. “If you think of couture in the traditional way, of course it is only possible with a huge brand. But couture for me is not only that.” She believes its fate rests not only with the big houses, but in the hands of individuals committed to keeping the craft and tradition alive, “working in small ateliers,” perhaps alone, making things one-of-a-kind. “I think that's couture too,” she says. column1: How Meghan Markle’s favourite couturier rose to the top
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet Ralph & Russo’s Tamara Ralph It's safe to say that Ralph & Russo has a finger in just about every fashion pie going. With seven seasons of couture collections under their belt, the Australian duo behind the label launched their first ready-to-wear collection during London Fashion Week last September, while continuing to expand their nascent leather goods and accessories lines. Despite an uncertain global economic climate, they have managed to build a business with an estimated value of more than £100 million—all the more impressive given that many legacy houses no longer turn a profit from their haute couture collections. And they've done it whilst dressing some of the most famous women in the world, including Angelina Jolie, Meghan Markle, Bella Hadid and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan. View Gallery 7 Photos Meet Ralph & Russo’s Tamara Ralph, the couturier who dressed Meghan Markle “[Ralph & Russo] is not couture designed for ‘the art of it' it is, rather, designed to be worn,” observes Helen David, chief merchant of Harrods in London. “They are in a league of their own.” Meeting Tamara Ralph, creative director of Ralph & Russo Four days ahead of her spring/summer 2018 couture show, Tamara Ralph is standing in the private office at her atelier off Sloane Avenue. She's the very definition of “well put together”: dressed in pristine white cashmere joggers and a matching jumper, a trench coat from her ready-to-wear collection resting cooly on her shoulders. Not an eyelash is out of place. Box-fresh trainers, a bright red lip and an immaculate blow-dry complete the look. It's comfortable, but composed, too. One side of her office is covered floor-to-ceiling in sketches, while the other has a table running the length of the room, strewn with fabric swatches, turbans and small net veils. At capacity, the London atelier (the brand has a second one in Paris) holds more than 300 artisans and seamstresses, who work across the couture collection, private client commissions and ready-to-wear. Masseuses work their way around the room, helping relieve sore shoulders and necks bent over delicate embroidery work. Posted signs remind the team just how many days away the show is, but the atmosphere is devoid of tension. Ralph too has a serene aura, greeting me in her office with a smile and an earnest Australian lilt. “It's like a hive, isn't it?” she remarks proudly. Building a couture empire from London When they set up shop in 2007, Ralph and her partner, Michael Russo, had little more than a sewing machine and a single client. What they lacked in resources, they made up in ambition. “Our very first client bought a dress from a sketch I drew,” explains Ralph. “There were no prototypes, no samples, she just bought from my sketch.” Word of mouth soon spread: “One client turned into 10, 10 turned into 100, and turned into what we have now,” she says, noting that the current client count hovers in the  “several” hundreds. They quickly built a reputation for their Old Hollywood silhouettes, love of fine detail and opulent bridal gowns. By 2014 they were sufficiently well-established to merit an invitation to join the Paris couture week schedule, making Ralph & Russo the first British couture label in a century—and Ralph the first Australian designer ever—to gain admission. They are not content to rest on their laurels. In 2018 the pair plan to open 12 boutiques across the US, Asia and the Middle East. They also plan to grow their leather goods line, which they started in 2016, and will soon expand into beauty, fragrance, eyewear and, eventually, menswear. But haute couture was always meant to be to the heart and soul of the brand. Ralph herself comes from a long line of couturiers—four generations' worth of dressing Sydney's socialites—and it is clear that is where her passion lies. The Ralph & Russo woman Ralph & Russo's youngest client is three months old; the oldest is in her late 80s. What unifies this broad spectrum? Other than their obvious wealth—the brand's ready-to-wear ranges in price from £1,000 to £27,000, and couture starts at £50,000—it's their style. “For me [the Ralph & Russo woman] is someone that is very confident,” explains Ralph, “who knows who she is and has a definite feminine side to her. Women have so many sides and angles to them these days, they are not just mothers or working; they are doing both.” They're competitive, too. Ralph claims at least 70 per cent of a collection is sold or reserved before it's even off the runway. “New age purchasing,” as she puts it, means transactions happen in real-time via WhatsApp. And that is just the clients who are at the shows. There are plenty others—princesses, sheikhas and Hollywood starlets—who frequently turn to Ralph for formal occasion dressing. That is something else that unifies this group of women: they are extremely loyal to Ralph & Russo, Ralph claims, buying whole wardrobes each season as opposed to a one-off dress. “When we set up the brand we really asked ourselves what we could do that the other brands, with far longer histories, can't. And that is great customer service,” she offers as as explanation as to what keeps her clients coming back. “We travel to see our clients, we work around them. We make buying couture simple.” By its nature couture is exclusive, but Ralph wants to make it inclusive, too—particularly when it comes to sizing: “It's about making people feel welcome, making someone feel special. Michael has this saying, ‘There's no room for arrogant luxury anymore,' and that is very much part of our ethos.” On Meghan Markle On December 21, the internet paused for a moment when Kensington Palace released the official engagement portraits of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, shot by fashion photographer Alexi Lubomirski. In two of the three pictures, Prince Harry's soon-to-be-wife is wearing a floor-length black dress with a ruffled tulle skirt, its tight, sheer bodice embroidered with gold leaf. No sooner was it identified as a Ralph & Russo design that the rumour mill pegged them as one of the brands likely to receive the much-coveted commission for Markle's wedding dress. Bridal is a big part of its business, after all, though any talk of wedding dresses—royal or otherwise—is promptly diverted by Ralph's publicist. On her upcoming couture collection The spring/summer 2018 haute couture collection is Ralph's eighth. Inspired by her recent travels to Asia, it is rich in traditional decorative details and architectural ruffles informed by the buildings she saw. Two gowns stand out as we talk though the collection: the first is a kimono-inspired number in cream crepe, with hand-painted peonies climbing up the skirt. Studded with 30,000 translucent opals and delicately dotted with 3D organza petals, it took over 400 hours and 10 specialist artisans to complete. The second stand-out is an eggshell-white bridal dress, due to be modelled by a Brazilian influencer with 6.9 million Instagram followers. As we walk around the atelier, five seamstresses are busy at work on it. The ruching on the bodice alone has taken more than 200 hours and four specialists to complete. The skirt is as of yet unadorned, but once complete, will have approximately 3,000 leaves picked out in Swarovski crystals, with 40,000 pearls lending their sheen to the silk thread work. In total, more than 2,000 hours of work will have gone into it. These are dresses that wouldn't be out of place in a museum—nor, dare we say, a royal wedding. The Ralph & Russo spring/summer 2018 show is taking place in Paris on January 22 at 9.30pm (IST) Fashion Wellness Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Hedi Slimane named artistic, creative and image director of Céline
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's what happens next LVMH has announced Hedi Slimane as the new artistic, creative and image director of Céline, putting to an end the rumours of who will replace Phoebe Philo. Slimane will take over the LVMH-owned fashion house—extending the label's offering to include men's fashion, couture and fragrances—as of February 1. His first collection for men and women will debut during Paris Fashion Week next September. Beyond his rock-inspired photography, black suede Chelsea boots and sharp tailoring, Slimane is known in the industry as a preeminent image-maker and trendsetter. He launched and defined Dior Homme in the early 2000s and then went on to reinvent (and rename) the Kering-owned maison of Saint Laurent between 2012 and 2016. “His arrival at Céline reinforces the great ambitions that LVMH has for this Maison,” said Bernard Arnault in the statement confirming Slimane's appointment, praising him as “one of the most talented designers of our time.” Sidney Toledano, who famously recruited Slimane at Dior, added: “Hedi Slimane is an exceptional designer, complete artist and passionate about his work. I am certain that he will bring his renowned creative energy and discipline to lead Céline to ever greater success”. The appointment puts to an end rumours that Slimane would be the next designer to reimagine Chanel and Dior. “I am delighted to join Bernard Arnault in this all-embracing and fascinating mission for Céline,” he said. “I greatly look forward to returning to the exciting world of fashion and the dynamism of the ateliers”. He takes over from Phoebe Philo, who announced she was stepping down as the creative director of the brand last December following a celebrated decade of minimally chic design. column1: 6 fashion brands that champion the cause of veganism
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vegan fashion is more than just a catchphrase Have you heard of pineapple leather? What about bags made from bottle corks? You don't have to be a vegetarian or a PETA supporter to embrace cruelty-free fashion. It was British designer Stella McCartney who set the bar high when she became the first ‘vegetarian' luxury label in 2001. Her no-leather-no-fur-no-feathers products are seriously cool and so beautifully crafted that you'd never know the difference. Here are some other incredible new labels on the rise. View Gallery 6 Photos 6 fashion brands that champion the cause of veganism Matt & Nat Montreal-based Matt & Nat's (Materials and Nature) Indian-origin founder, Inder Bedi, started out in 1995 after finding his options as a vegan very bleak. Sleek, functional and found in muted earthy colour tones, the lining of a Matt & Nat handbag is made with 100 percent recycled plastic bottles: clocked at approximately 21 bottles per bag, and over a whopping three million plastic bottles recycled by 2017. Little details, like the recycled cork label and the price tag that moonlights as a bookmark, make Matt & Nat a charming sustainable experience. Mattandnat.com Gunas Raised between Ludhiana and Pune, Sugandh G Agrawal founded Gunas in New York in 2009 after a nightmarish experience interning at a handbag label that specialised in exotic-skin handbags and shoes. It was after the vegetarian- turned-vegan came face-to-face with raw hide that she decided to start her own line of animal-friendly fashion. Now, Gunas is looking to launch in India. Gunasthebrand.com  Angela Roi Driven by altruism, another New York- based label, Angela Roi, launched in 2013. It uses EPUL (Exquisite Polyurethane Leather) and gold-plated hardware: the poly material is processed multiple times to attain a soft and smooth texture. Angelaroi.com  Grain Closer to home, Grain, started by Avinash Bhalerao, offers bags for him and her, in ahimsa leather. While vegan brands have mastered the art of revamping polyurethane, for those who want the ‘real' thing, ahimsa leather is made by recycling the skin of non-slaughtered dead animals into leather. Part of the process sees Grain working with 30-year-old tanneries. Grainindia.com Rheson In the celebrity realm, Sonam and Rhea Kapoor's label, Rheson, sends a positive message with adordable animal-friendly bags that recently received a PETA Compassionate Business Award. Facebook. com/wearerheson Bourgeois Boheme In London, ex-podiatrist and long-time vegan Alicia Lai started her own footwear label, Bourgeois Boheme, in 2005, where the ethical shoes (designed in London and handcrafted in Portugal) are Vegan Society-trademarked and PETA-approved. column1: Kim Jones, the designer who reinvented Louis Vuitton’s menswear
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion On his departure from the label, here are five things to know about the man The British-born talent's departure from Louis Vuitton – where he brought in blockbuster collaborations with the likes of Supreme – sets into motion another round of fashion musical chairs. Here are five things you may not know about the outgoing designer… Kim Jones, Louis Vuitton's men's artistic director of seven years, will step down from his role this week. “It has been a huge privilege to work with Kim,” said Michael Burke, chairman and chief executive of Louis Vuitton in the statement confirming the designer's departure on Wednesday morning. “His ability to set trends is impeccable and his talent and determination have ensured that Louis Vuitton is firmly placed as the leading brand in luxury menswear today.” View Gallery 6 Photos 5 things to know about Kim Jones, the designer who reinvented Louis Vuitton’s menswear Since joining Vuitton in 2011, Jones ushered in a new fashion identity that pushed the boundaries of the storied luggage brand without alienating existing customers – no simple task – and turned out collection after collection of directional menswear. He pre-empted the mass adoption of streetwear silhouettes and motifs long before “athleisure” became a bonafide trend, and was the creative force behind blockbuster collaborations with Supreme, Fragment Design, and British artists Jake and Dinos Chapman. The fashion world is already eagerly speculating his next move, with creative director vacancies at top fashion houses like Burberry, Céline and Versace yet to be announced. Here are five things you may not know about the British talent... He had a nomadic childhood Born in London in 1979, Jones and his family led a globetrotting lifestyle thanks to his father's work as a hydrogeologist. First came Ecuador, followed by Africa and the Caribbean, instilling in him a deep appreciation for different cultures and travel — two things he often references in his collections. “Growing up in Africa, living with little lizards, snakes and elephants or being chased by baboons — it never really goes away,” he told The New York Times in 2011. After graduating from Central Saint Martins in 2002, he launched his eponymous label, known for its streetwear aesthetic. In 2008 he gave it up to become creative director of Dunhill. Louis Vuitton came calling three years later. He's a collector “I have a collection of more than 500 sneakers in my personal archive,” he told Designboom in 2016. “I keep them all in my house in London, and many in my cupboards in Paris. I have a lot of Jordans, and Huaraches because when they originally came out, I bought them in bulk because I loved them so much.” But beyond trainers, he also has a penchant for vintage fashion, as he told AnOther, with an “exquisitely preserved collection” that includes club kid staples from Vivienne Westwood, Stephen Linard, Rachel Auburn and Modern Classics, as well as Issey Miyake and Jean Paul Gaultier and – Jones's all-time favourite – Christopher Nemeth. John Galliano spotted him early on – and upset him a little, too Ever the auspicious talent, Jones nabbed the attention of  John Galliano while he was still a student. “He bought half my graduate collection,” he told The Guardian. “It was a big deal, I guess, but I didn't realise at the time. I was just upset because I wanted one of the jackets he bought for myself; it was hard to make and I didn't get to keep it." He's happy to put “all his eggs in one basket” Speaking to Drapers on the eve of his appointment at Dunhill London in 2008, Jones said how happy he was to renounce his own label: “This is what I always wanted to do. People don't realise that I never really wanted to have my own label, I just fell into it.” Echoing a similar statement in 2013 with British Vogue, he said: "Why would I want to do my own label when I can do fantastic things here [at Louis Vuitton] and put my spin on things? As a designer, the things you can do at Vuitton are second to none. In LVMH, they are very respectful of the designer, you are a special person in the company. You can't be that naive about the world, you have to get on with stuff." His HR file most likely has him down for shouting — at HR "There's a lot of hierarchy in a lot of houses, and they see a high turnover," he said to Fashionista, speaking about the importance of nurturing staff. "I don't really like to have too much change in the studio. My right hand's been with me for 10 years and she's really, really good. If I'm not there, she knows exactly what I like, and she can say yes or no. We have stagiaires [interns] that come, and if they're really good, I'll go up to the CEO and say 'I want to keep this person, because I know they'll be a valuable member of the team.'" What is more, he fights to ensure they are paid fairly: "When I started, we did four collections a year, and now we do 12. It's a lot. I do expect my team to get paid to do 12 collections, not four. So I will go and shout at people and make sure that HR realises, you know, you can't expect extra work for free. That's just important. Probably if I do have an HR record at work, it would be for shouting at HR, because they do get a call quite often." What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: LVMH expresses interest in an alliance with Baba Ramdev’s Patanjali
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The French conglomerate owns stakes in luxury labels like Dior, Fendi European multinational luxury goods conglomerate, LVMH (Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE) has expressed interest in investing in yoga guru Baba Ramdev's FMCG brand, Patanjali. The luxury goods giant holds stakes in many coveted international brands like Dior, Fendi and Givenchy, to name a few. While it may seem like an odd arrangement at the outset, there lies some logic in the fact that health has become the ultimate luxury to invest in. An acknowledged fashion powerhouse, LVMH intends to up-sell the products that Patanjali produces and could invest $500 million to this end, according to a report in the Economic Times. Seeing Ayurveda brand's meteoric rise as India's fastest growing FMCG company, L Catterton Asia—a private equity firm co-owned by LVMH—has expressed interest in taking it to a global platform. Established as a private limited company in 2006, Patanjali is reported to have hit revenues of Rs 2,000 crore across 4,000 stores in 2015. While the indigenous brand is seeking investors and this move could help their products get a global reach, their business model which is positioned against multinational corporations may prove to be a hurdle in this alliance with LVMH. While Acharya Balkrishna, Patanjali CEO, stated in the Economic Times piece that the company isn't open to selling stakes or equity to foreign MNCs, Ravi Thakran, managing partner at L Catterton has expressed his enthusiasm, saying that they would “love to work with him if we can find a (business) model.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: A peek inside Louis Vuitton’s incredible Parisian flagship boutique
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Architect Peter Marino gives us the details Place Vendome, circa 1854, was home to 18th-century townhouses or hotel particuliers lived in by well-heeled aristocrats and later even future emperor Napoleon III. It was here that a young Louis Vuitton started his boutique 163 years ago, selling sleek luggage essentials. Fast forward to present day and the new Louis Vuitton flagship store stands in place of the townhouses as a historical memoir of where it all began. In a four year restoration project, architect Peter Marino transformed the neo-classical townhouses into a stunning sunlit space, where ready-to-wear, jewellery, watch-making, leather goods, shoes, fragrances and artisanal workshops come alive. We have the details. View Gallery 8 Photos Home Coming What was particularly challenging about this project? The Place Vendome facades were created for Louis XIV and are marvellously Baroque. I thought I would juxtapose a modern aesthetic with everything within the walls and restore the exterior as beautifully and faithfully as possible. To rebuild the inside was a great challenge. The balance between modern and old is what Paris is about and the staircase is a particularly good example of this—it's an 18th-century design in stone contrasted by high tech glass balustrades suspended from stainless steel cables and artwork embedded within the stairs. What have you reinvented in the two hotel particuliers and what have you preserved? We used many 18th-century techniques in our work that reference French history and craftsmanship. We worked with French artisans to fill the store with vintage and modern objects. Every window is different—the glass installed was hand-rolled and the result is natural imperfections typical of an earlier time. But the overall approach was not just to reinstate the two townhouses but to unify the whole space as one new house for Louis Vuitton. We reference various French periods and contrast this with an art-filled, sleek, ultra-modern interior. We call it the Louis Vuitton Maison—The House of Vuitton—as it is intended to make visitors feel at home. What are your favourite elements of the store? The staircase, the skylight courtyard, the World of Travel room and the women's ready-to-wear salon. Is there a dedicated space for art in the Maison Louis Vuitton Vendome? It has 21 pieces by 19 artists that represent six continents. Among them are major commissions by Laurent Grasso, Farhad Moshiri and Annie Morris. Louis Vuitton is very forward-thinking when it comes to the art world and thinks globally. The artwork is selected from artists in Iran (Moshiri), China (Yan Pei-Ming), Germany (Gregor Hildebrandt), South Africa (Kendell Geers), and of course from France: ceramics by Jean Lurcat, photography by Martin d'Orgeval, custom light sculptures by Philippe Anthonioz. Much of the artwork in the store is joyful and positioned to play off the architecture. For me, shopping should be fun and a learning experience, not the dull mechanical pressing of internet buttons. How do you want people to feel when they visit the store? On entering, excited and expectant. On leaving, happy and uplifted. Fashion Fashion What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Roberto Cavalli’s son debuts own brand at Pitti Uomo
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer talks about his label's identity and how he handles comparisons with his father View Gallery 11 Photos Roberto Cavalli’s son debuts own brand at Pitti Uomo On the penultimate day of Pitti Uomo, at a quiet Florentine sculpture workshop just south of the Arno river, Robert Cavalli—son of the Italian designer Roberto Cavalli—presented the debut capsule collection for his brand Triple RRR. Before the guests arrive at the gallery on the raining afternoon, the venue is quiet. With slicked-back black hair, the soft-spoken Cavalli glides through the room with confidence. Framed by Renaissance sculptures and tools of the trade are mannequins dressed in buttonless coats and jackets, crafted from velvet and silk, and trousers cut like joggers from a jacquard fabric featuring pomegranate embroideries. Cavalli is wearing all black, save for his metallic watch and Nike Vapormax sneakers. He sports golden wire-framed glasses and a buttonless jacket reminiscent of a lounge robe from his own collection. Tattooed on his hand is the letter “R”. He soon explains the three Rs of his new brand: Roberto, for his father; Robert, for himself; and the third R, he says with a smile, represents the brand itself. On the day of his big debut, the 24-year-old designer—who has never formally studied fashion—doesn't show the slightest bit of anxiety. After all, with a last name like that, why should he? His father built an empire in the '70s and '80s, dressing the rich and famous, and helped lay the foundation of glamour, glitter and print for late 20th-Century fashion. Choosing to enter a field where his father played such a seminal role invites criticism, and Cavalli, despite being fashion royalty, is aware. Is it easier or harder to make it in the industry, being Roberto's son? “It is what it is,” he says. “I don't know anything else. People ask me, ‘How does it feel?' I don't know. If I lived two different lives, I could tell you. But it is what I am.” The unveiling of his collection coincides with 032c's highly-anticipated show, where former Brioni creative director Justin O'Shea is bartending and the niche Berlin-based fashion magazine's apparel collection is being showcased. But Cavalli's work is aimed at a different crowd. His designs are the kind of clothes you'd wear to a fancy dinner party on an Italian estate; not to a dark Kreuzberg club. Inspired by loungewear, “it's a visitation of the home look, for the street,” he says. Cavalli's garments are luxurious, with the price tags to match: A soothingly soft cashmere coat sells for about 1,800 euros. They are the kind of clothes that would accommodate Cavalli's own lifestyle, frequently documented on Instagram. In one photo, he is smoking shisha in a suit on the beach while wearing a bow tie. In another, he is posing with Natasha Poly, the supermodel who has regularly walked for the brand his father founded. Is this clothing line supposed to be aspirational, too? “I think selling a lifestyle with my clothes, that's an old mindset,” he says. “It's something very beautiful that my parents did—they were selling a lifestyle. But I don't think it's modern. I don't think it's young. I am trying to create a new code of fashion for what I believe to be the next trend.” Cavalli proposes a return from the streetwear trend that has dominated the past half-decade of men's fashion back to the classically sartorial, but with the former's casual standard of comfort. In an age when Balenciaga is sending hoodies down runways while Louis Vuitton is collaborating with Supreme, who the Triple RRR customer, really? “Most of the pieces I did have a vision,” he explains. “A person. My friend—who is Korean or Saudi or Russian... It's very international.” Age is trickier to pin down. “There isn't really an age… [just] a younger generation that wants to be a little bit more sophisticated,” he concludes. column1: Is Gucci’s fine dining a new step in luxury fashion?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Pairing fashion with food The crowds visiting the new ‘Gucci Garden' in Florence explored the shop with its floral and animalistic patterns. They climbed the stairway of the ancient 13th-century palazzo to view past and present archives. And these visitors and customers then spilled over into the kitchen. View Gallery 10 Photos Is Gucci’s fine dining a new step in luxury fashion? The kitchen! had designer Alessandro Michele, Michelin-starred master chef Massimo Bottura and CEO Marco Bizzarri decided to have a bite to eat? No – they were introducing a new concept of luxury. Shop – until you drop in for a first-class meal. Or dine first on a sumptuous scale. “For the moment, it is a one-of-a-kind project,” said Bizzarri, who has been a friend of the chef since their school days and believes that, following the success of Michele's fashion, “Luxury can also be expressed in the idea of eating. ”The restaurant is therefore set at the highest level of quality and price – creating an exceptional experience and one that reflects the fact that in the 21st century, time is one of the greatest luxuries. But could a restaurant expressing the character of each luxury brand really be put on the table? Raffaello Napoleone, CEO of Florence's Pitti Immagine menswear show, says that he sees the link between fashion and food as genuine – especially in Italy. “The Italian way of life is that we like dressing ourselves in the best way possible and we also like to share eating. It's a good choice because at this moment Massimo Bottura is the one reference. Gucci, too, is the fashion reference of the moment. So, it is a wedding of two Italian excellencies.” Bizzarri says, “The future cannot be defined. But my opinion of the industry is that at a certain point, the overlapping between shopping, music, culture, food and beverage will be more and more important. "The executive continues, “The way in which Alessandro thinks and the way the industry is going, the blending of experiences will be more and more important. It will be more natural for us to talk to industries that are already linked to fashion: culture, aesthetics, food and beverage and music, of course.” Since few other countries have turned food into an art form – Japan might be another contender – it is hard to imagine dressing and dining combinations across the world. And although fashion designers have created restaurants – Giorgio Armani and Ralph Lauren among many others – no one has brought the idea to a worldwide level. The Gucci restaurant will certainly bring food for thought to the entire luxury industry, which is in a state of flux. Imagine Birkenstock, defined by practical, orthopaedic footwear, holding at Pitti Uomo a glamorised nature stand that included green leaves, silvered sandals and the company's beauty products. Explaining that the 35 million pieces of Birkenstock footwear were all made in Germany, CEO Oliver Reichert ruminated as to whether his company could be considered as modern luxury. “It's a tough question – because what is luxury?” he said. “I would say that luxury is time – and it is health. Birkenstock is close to these things because we are slow fashion, beyond fashion. We are fashionable with a different angle.” “I think Gucci is on the perfect track,” Reichert continued, “Because I think – and hope – fast fashion is dying very quickly. A Gucci restaurant is a brilliant idea because they give you time. You go to the shop and then they say ‘Hey! Come down, sit here – and their present to you is time.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why transparency is increasingly becoming important in fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion No room for errors If the end of the last year saw the #MeToo uprising, this year started off with the #TimesUp movement. Just halfway through January, we can see that 2018, so far, has been a year of reckoning. Case in point, when the biggest celebrities in Hollywood chose to show solidarity to victims of sexual abuse by dressing in all-black at the Golden Globes. Throughout history, fashion has been wielded as an effective statement in waging wars against injustices, but what about the industry itself? Right after the Globes, more eminent personalities were added to the growing list of sexual predators. This time it was two decorated fashion photographers, in a reveal that sent shockwaves through the fashion world. Transparency, inclusivity and sensitivity might be the direction the industry wishes to head in, but the path to absolution is not an easy one. View Gallery 6 Photos Why transparency is increasingly becoming important in fashion No longer scared Hollywood's watershed moment with the Harvey Weinstein scandal made victims believe in the power of solidarity. Terry Richardson's downfall came soon after, when several models and celebrities came forward with their disturbing experiences of working with the photographer. Most recently, incidences have come to light against Bruce Weber and Mario Testino, both powerful photographers in fashion. The New York Times's inquiry into the matter is replete with stories by models and assistants who speak of unsolicited advances, molestation, but more importantly, inspiring a sentiment that being subject to abuse was a rite of passage. Roman Barett, an ex-assistant of Testino's, mentions in his statement, “He misbehaved in hotel rooms, the backs of cars and on first-class flights. Then things would go back to normal, and that made you feel gaslighted.” Anna Wintour, Vogue editor in chief and Condé Nast artistic director responded to situation with a statement reading, “Even as we stand with victims of abuse and misconduct, we must also hold a mirror up to ourselves—and ask if we are doing our utmost to protect those we work with so that unacceptable conduct never happens on our watch. I believe strongly in the value of remorse and forgiveness, but I take the allegations very seriously, and we at Condé Nast have decided to put our working relationship with both photographers on hold for the foreseeable future.” No room for error Last week, H&M released their kidswear lookbook, featuring a young black boy in a sweatshirt bearing the words "Coolest monkey in the jungle". The picture unsurprisingly caused an outrage, making the Swedish retailer issue an apology for their lack of foresight, in missing the message that the juxtaposition of the model and the controversial hoodie, sent. Rappers The Weeknd and G-Easy severed their contracts with the retailer, and took to social media to announce their stance on the matter. However, it's clear the apology was not enough to soothe the angered audience. The tone-deaf image led to violent protests in South Africa, forcing H&M to temporarily shut stores in the country. What's evident from the incident is that inclusivity and tolerance will not be achieved just by using models of colour, but needs to reflect in the brand's ethos and sensitivity in portraying varied communities, failing which it would be difficult to retain customer bases. Social media vigilantes What started as an insider Instagram account ousting brands for ripping off work from artists and other labels, is now the torchbearer for righting wrongs in the world of fashion. Diet Prada, run by Tony Liu and Lindsey Schuyler, have earned both respect and fear in the fashion community for their ability to spotlight the faltering footsteps of brands. Their razor-sharp commentary on inauthentic designs has gained the support of many, including Naomi Campbell, who openly supports the account. Diet Prada is known to take things to an extreme, with visuals of burning labels, but is also a symbol of the winds of change in the industry. But it's not just uncredited counterfeiting that Diet Prada is going after. After calling out hot favourite labels including Gucci, Dolce & Gabbana, Off-White, Dior and Jeremy Scott for their blunders, in the recent past the account has been outspoken about the lack of sensitivity and sexual abuse in fashion. The account was vocal in condemning Valentino for continuing to use campaign images shot by Terry Richardson as accusations of his sexual misconduct rose to the point where Condé Nast banned the photographer's work from their publications. The account has also pulled up Business Of Fashion's Colin McDowell and Grace Coddington for supporting Bruce Weber. What happens now Harvey Weinstein to Terry Richardson, the one thing common to all these powerful predators is that the nature of their actions was an open secret. Why didn't these revelations happen earlier and who in the system was complicit in keeping it under wraps? Raising awareness about what constitutes as ‘work' and not is not enough. Model Edie Campbell sums up the current atmosphere in a post on Instagram, "We have a problem: We operate within a culture that is too accepting of abuse, in all of its manifestations. Although we may not all, as individuals, have actively contributed to this culture, every time we turn a blind eye, our silence perpetuates that culture. Our inactions make up complicit." As an industry, we all bear the responsibility of ensuring that none working in it feel that being subject to abuse is the price one has to pay to for the sake of a career. column1: This designer’s new line makes a tough statement against sexual assault
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Check out NorBlack NorWhite's collaboration with Dharavi Art Room A few years ago, you could spot pink posters scattered throughout Mumbai, put up by artist Aqui Thami of Dharavi Art Room. These pink posters spoke the uncomfortable truth: carrying the message, "A woman was harassed here", the posters called out places in the city where she and women she knew had experienced harassment. What began as an art movement inspired the designer duo of NorBlack NorWhite to initiate a limited series collaboration with Thami in order to create awareness and spark conversation around gender violence, and the lack of literal and metaphorical safe spaces in our society today. View Gallery 4 Photos This designer’s new line makes a tough statement against sexual assault The collaboration A close friendship between the artist and the designers who have supported the Art Room for years years led to inception of this collaboration a few years ago that has recently come into fruition. With a shared purpose of wanting to create a socially conscious environment that liberates the women of India, they came up with a series of T-shirts and tote bags that carry the message from the posters imprinted on them. "This collaboration allows my work to be in spaces where the posters cannot be, addressing the same issue at its heart and dismantling it,” says Thami. The capsule collection is available on NorBlack NorWhite's website and the sales will be used to support the effort of Dharavi Art Room. This platform is also endorsed by Madame Gandhi, a musician, activist and ambassador for the “Future is Female” movement. 2017 saw the beginning of seminal movements like the Women's March, which sparked the fire against gender inequality and sexual violence worldwide. The year ended with #MeToo, a hashtag that encouraged women to share their experiences of harassment, in an attempt to unshackle themselves from the culture of silence surrounding these injustices. The New Year too, kick-started with an uproar that has manifested itself into the #TimesUp movement, underlined by Oprah Winfrey's speech at the Golden Globes, an empowering anthem to stay with us for the coming years. Since its inception, NorBlack NorWhite has committed to re-defining the stereotypes of contemporary India. “We want to create and promote visual aesthetics that can connect with the youth culture in the country. The spirit of our design philosophy lies in fusion of our Toronto-based roots with the cultural experiences in India,” says Kapadia. "In supporting her, we want to raise the women that speak up and choose to change their narratives from hushed whispers to hot-pink, impossible-to-ignore truths," she concludes. column1: Sanjay Garg new collection gives sari lovers more covetable pieces to own
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Find out more about it There are designers who invent trends with each season and there are designers who like to ruminate on ideas and explore them to their last detail. Raw Mango's Sanjay Garg falls in the latter category. The designer completes his 10th anniversary in the industry this year and just released possibly the only one collection he will be showcasing in 2018. View Gallery 17 Photos Sanjay Garg launches a new collection of sari inspired by the night “If you look at my ‘Vana' collection, it was very pastel, very day, and I thought, why not look at how flora and fauna looks at night? That was the thought behind the Midnight Collection. Things are exactly the same in the dark as they are in light, but you tend to perceive them differently,” he explains his ideology behind the line. At first glance the collection looks like it comprises exclusively of black saris bearing florals, but upon closer inspection, each one has a distinct identity. “You can't really tell colours in the night, which is what I wanted to bring about,” Garg says. There are deep blues, dark greens, charcoal greys, lights greys and black which make the backdrop for the flowers. Silk screen printing was the method used to recreate raat ki rani and dhaturas on the gossamer, hand woven saris. “On the organza saris, some of the print blurs out, like your vision is at night,” he continues. To carry the thought through, the collection was shot in the middle of the night by Ashish Shah. In honour of the launch, Kiran Rao and Gayatri Rangachari Shah co-hosted a dinner for a select crowd with Garg. Anupama Chopra, Prerna Goel, Priyanka Bose, Lisa Ray were seen at the event. From the pavement outside, to the centrepiece of the table, the fragrance of fresh flowers lingered. Scroll through our gallery for more. Fashion Fashion Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Comfort first View Gallery 14 Photos Why sweatshirts are a part of every celebrity wardrobe Gone are the days when the laid-back sweatshirt was a lazy girl staple, shunned by the denizens of chic. Blame it on Vetements or the rise and rise of streetwear-inspired fashion; but the once-modest sweatshirt has now become a star staple every cool girl worth her Instagram brags owns more than a few of. And considering its cred as a tried-and-tested street style winner, it's no surprise that Bollywood's stylish set has warmed up to this cosy cover-up all too quickly. Vogue investigates this sweatshirt invasion of the celebrity wardrobe. Be it a transatlantic flight or a post-shoot smoothie, the sweatshirt brings a dose of casual cool to the most basic of off-duty outfits. How so? Simply take one look at sweatshirt-phile Kareena Kapoor Khan's repertoire. Her selection ranges from Stella McCartney to Gucci, and serves her well whether she's creating a stampede at security check or accompanying her son to a birthday party. While the sweatshirt is a trusty celebrity travel companion, you can think beyond the airport as well. A slogan version with ripped jeans as seen on Kriti Sanon is perfect for a Sunday at the spa while a white-on-white look like Shraddha Kapoor's is what lunch with the girls calls for. Swap the pants with a metallic skirt and you can easily take your oversized fuzzy friend to the bar come Saturday night. Aditi Rao Hydari would approve. Humble as the sweatshirt may be, one needn't remove high fashion from the equation. Be it Katrina Kaif in Moschino, Aishwariya Rai Bachchan in Monisha Jaising or Sridevi in Dolce & Gabbana, normcore is always accompanied with a side of luxe in this style circle. Less I-spent-the-entire-weekend-on-the-couch and more slay-all-day-everyday, if you may. Browse through our slideshow for some celebrity sweatshirt inspiration. column1: Why you need take sustainable fashion seriously in 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Facts that matter ‘Sustainable' an adjective that translates to ‘able to be upheld or defend' is one of the most loosely used terms in fashion. There labels following sustainable practices, eco fashion weeks, CSR projects implemented by brands to clean up their track records and more. But why should you shop consciously? And more importantly, what does it mean when you speak of sustainable fashion, and why should you care? Why is fast fashion bad for the planet? It takes about 6,800 litres of water to grow enough cotton to produce a pair of jeans. Your average high street retailer will sell these between Rs 2,000 and Rs 4,500. The worker who labored over making the pair of jeans makes an approximate of Rs 100 for his work. There are two glaring causes of concern in this model. The first being the excessive use of a natural resource like clean water which will be sparse in the near future. Second is the obvious difference in the money paid to the factory worker versus the money that goes to the large corporation. High street retailers are known to create as many as 24 collections in a year encouraging consumers to buy more than they which results in waste, not to mention the after effects of industrialization. In a nutshell, there's a whole picture hidden behind that pair of jeans that won't sit in your closet for longer than a year. Lives harmed The collapse of the Rana Plaza building in Bangladesh in which 1,138 workers were killed brought to light the plight of workers in garment factories. while some companies took responsibility for their actions, how much has really changed?  Production houses which are often in developing countries like China, Bangladesh and India are forced to keep their costs low in order to attract brands for contracts. This directly impacts worker wages, less than favourable working conditions and little or no support to their families. At the same time, a different picture of what goes on in a factory is painted to the brand reps who visit the facility a few days in a year, leading them to believe that facility is meeting the required standards. Anna Gedda, head of sustainability at H&M explained the complicated logistics of monitoring living wages. “One of the most common questions we are asked is if wages are too low, why don't we just pay the workers more? Unfortunately, the reality is not that simple. The standard factory set up is that workers sit in rows and each of these rows are working on different brands. It can be brands that are at lower or higher price points than us and no matter, they are paid the same and work in the same living conditions. So, if we are tackling fair work wages, it is not possible to pay the workers working on H&M garments more than their colleagues. When we talk about the cost of creating a garment, we negotiate and fix the labour cost and keep that aside from the other costs of the garment production,” says Gedda. Toll on the planet It's often said that the fashion industry is the second most polluting one in the world. However, the facts to prove this statement are scanty. According to Racked.com's inquiry into the subject matter, “the few unproven but legitimate-sounding “facts" get seized upon by well-meaning advocates, wrested out of context, and splashed across the internet, creating a circular feedback loop of bad information.” McKinsey's detailed report on sustainability reveals that, “We estimate that if 80 percent of the population of emerging economies were to achieve the same clothing-consumption levels as the Western world by 2025, and the apparel industry does not become more environmentally efficient, then the environmental footprint of the apparel industry will become much larger.” When a fashion label categorizes of being sustainable, it is in some way trying to overcome these shortcomings of the trade. We will be exploring more about these practices in our series. Learn more about ethical practices in fashion with our Sustainability Matters series. column1: Ruchika Sachdeva and Matthew Miller win International Woolmark Prize
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Find out more about the big win View Gallery 3 Photos Ruchika Sachdeva and Matthew Miller win International Woolmark Prize It's the opening night of the Pitti Uomo in Florence, and a crowd has gathered in the Stazione Leopolda to celebrate the winners of the International Woolmark Prize. Inside the dark exhibition hall, flood lights shine on rows of models displaying the finalists' collections, as industry members, fresh off the plane from London Fashion Week: Men's, talk shop and patiently await the news. Soon, the prize organizers take to the stage to reveal this year's two big winners: Indian womenswear designer Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice and British menswear designer Matthew Miller, each of whom will take home AU$200,000. American menswear brand Dyne is then awarded the inaugural Innovation Award, a prize of AU$100,000. The Woolmark Prize began in 1953 as a platform to showcase emerging fashion talent and to promote the usage of Australian Merino wool, which remains one of the country's chief exports. During its sophomore year, a 21-year-old Karl Lagerfeld and 18-year-old Yves Saint Laurent were each awarded the prize for their innovative use of wool — forever establishing Woolmark as one of the most important contests for young designers. After a hiatus that spanned decades, the Prize was successfully relaunched in 2012. Today, it's more global than ever, spotlighting designers from six territories and over 60 countries, who take part in regional design competitions before a select few ascend to the final round. This year, the jury comprised designer Phillip Lim, Vogue Italia Editor-in-Chief Emanuele Farneti, and models Amber Valletta and Liya Kebede, who spent the day reviewing the final collections in Florence. Tonight's womenswear winner, New Delhi-based Sachdeva, uses her brand to explore her roots, employing indigenous textiles from her native India in innovative ways. A newcomer and graduate of the London College of Fashion, her naturally dyed collection is made up of colourful shirts and dresses fitted with a unique accordion pleating, all produced in collaboration with local Indian artisans. She was inspired by two Indian artists, who, through their usage of colour, developed an visual language to express what the designer calls the “spirit of a newly independent India.” The jury panel was especially impressed with her attention to detail, which saw her produce sustainable buttons using coconut shells. “When I first approached her section without even speaking with her, I looked for the immediacy of the clothes,” says jury member Phillip Lim. “I looked for a collection that was visually well balanced… this is the language we speak. It was instant right away, because it felt romantic, modern, relevant… I can see friends and colleagues in her collection.” Menswear winner Matthew Miller, already a familiar name on the London Fashion Week: Men's schedule, showcased his signature tailoring, which included wearable tuxedos with detachable straps and button fastenings from salvaged marble, as well as waterproof bonded wool. Meanwhile, Innovation Award winner Dyne produced highly technical performance gear, such as “smart” snowboarding outfits fitted with NFC chips. “Obviously, these are emerging designers, and it's important to see how they look at the future, and the way they invest in their supply chain,” comments jury member Livia Firth, creative director of sustainability-focused brand consultancy Eco Age. “I was very impressed how many designers took into accounts issues as zero waste, and dyeing techniques, and how much water was being used in the process of the wool crafting.” After taking home the big prize, what are Sachdeva's plans for the future? “I'm still soaking it in. It's a huge opportunity to show my work on a global stage, because you can do something very beautiful and nobody knows about it,” she says. “What's important is that I can do my work and actually have a platform, where people have access to it.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 5 things to know about DVF’s new creative director, Nathan Jenden
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion He famously didn't know who Diane von Furstenberg was The first designer appointment of the year has been made, and it is a familiar one. Seven years after his departure, Nathan Jenden will be returning to Diane von Furstenberg as its chief design officer and vice president of creative, replacing outgoing creative director Jonathan Saunders. But what is there to know about the British-born talent? Here are five things to may not know about DVF's incoming creative director... View Gallery 7 Photos 5 things to know about DVF’s new creative director, Nathan Jenden Dynasty piqued his interest in fashion “I got into clothes as a teenager from watching Dynasty,” he told the South China Morning Post in 2008. “My parents were also the organisers of Live Aid so when they did Fashion Aid in 1985 [at the Royal Albert Hall] I remember seeing the Armani show and how beautiful it was, especially the long sequined fishtail skirts. From that moment on I knew I wanted to do fashion.” Galliano was one of his first teachers Jenden gave up his place at the prestigious Oxford University in favour of Central Saint Martins. After graduation, the Londoner followed up with a masters at the Royal College of Art,“because I didn't know how to sew when I left Central Saint Martins,” he confessed to Michael Hertz during a Fashion Business Club meeting in 2009. After working with John Galliano, he headed to Paris with Kenzo before departing for New York to become design director of ‘90s cult brand Daryl K. In 2001 he joined Diane von Furstenberg as creative director, where he remained for a decade, departing only to focus on his namesake brand and, most recently, serving as creative director of American mall brand Bebe. He didn't know who Diane von Furstenberg was at first In conversation with Herz, Jenden admitted to not knowing who the designer – famous for marrying a prince, divorcing him, building a fashion empire in her 20s and rebuilding it in her 50s, all while partying with everyone from Salvador Dali to Jade Jagger – was in 2001. "Diane called me, [and] I said to her, 'I don't really know who you are and I haven't really heard of you,'” he recalls saying. “She interviewed me but didn't ask me my name. We went backwards and forwards. “[Then] we [Jenden's wife] went to dinner with her – Blondie and Vanity Fair had thrown the dinner [party] – and I thought that this might be quite good." Despite that, they grew close and are clearly very fond of one another He and von Furstenberg have become great friends since. “It is with joy and pride that I look forward to welcoming Nathan back,” she said in the statement confirming his appointment. Emphasis on the joy. Von Furstenberg and Jenden have a history of exchanging kind words about one another. "He is young and talented, I am old and experienced," she told The Guardian in 2003, a sentiment she repeated with the news of his appointment. “Nathan is an extremely talented and technically skillful designer who also has a great gift at surrounding himself with young, emerging talent.” Jenden likewise is full of praise for von Furstenberg. Speaking to WWD in 2010, he said: “Diane taught me a talent for life, and how to live your life to the fullest, and how to maximise it… and to do it with a smile." Despite his role at DVF, he wanted to make a name for himself Launched in 2006, Jenden's own collection was heavy on the DVF spirit, with bold prints and plenty of party dressing. It was a long time in the making. From his university days, he aspired to build his own brand: “When I finally told Diane that I wanted to do it, she was wary,” he told Drapers in 2007, “but this is something I have always wanted. I realised that I wasn't getting any younger.” Ultimately, she supported him, often spotted cheering him on, front-row center – even after they had parted professionally, and he moved his show from New York to London. Jenden will certainly find the storied American brand changed since he last designed for it. Thankfully, we won't have to wait long to discover his vision: his first collection will be shown next month at New York Fashion Week. Weddings Fashion What's New © 2019 Condé Nast
