column1: Can you wear tube tops in your 30s?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The top names on the style scene sure seem to think so Slip dresses and chokers have both wormed their way back into the wardrobes of the most stylish names on the block, so why should you discriminate against your favourite bandeau top from the ‘90s just because you've crossed the big 30 milestone? Trends come and trends go, but some styles make a return in a better version. And now that the humble tube top has made its way back, you might as well throw all those age-appropriate concerns to the wind and give your once favourite wardrobe staple a modern update. Let's begin? View Gallery 6 Photos Can you wear tube tops in your 30s? – Celebrities How to make it work for you The year may be 2018, but bandeaus have yet to earn billing as office wear. If you're looking to take your favourite tube top for a spin with your work crowd, reserve it for the after-party by switching out your basic white shirt under your blazer in favour of a cropped strapless number. If you aren't entirely sold on the idea of stepping out minus the safety net of straps to secure your crucial bits, layer it under a denim jacket to score instant brownie points for off-duty chic. Those plunging necklines and backless jumpsuits? Not so much of a fashion risk when you throw in a tube top in a trendy print underneath to play peekaboo. Know before you go As with all things strapless, forewarned is forearmed. Take those extra five minutes out in advance to ensure that your choice of innerwear complements your risqué neckline and won't have you fidgeting all day. If in doubt, invest in some double-sided tape, instead of crossing your fingers and hoping that gravity goes easy on you. Likewise, while browsing the racks for one, look for fabrics that stretch with you so that a simple shrug won't result in a fashion faux pas. The low neckline, however, does leave the floor open to creative accessorising, so bring out those statement necklaces. Borrow from the stars When it comes to giving global runways trends their own unique spin, Bollywood's best brigade has always risen to the challenge. Jacqueline Fernandez likes her tube tops however she can get them–whether it's paired with a metallic skirt or under a slogan bomber jacket. Ileana D'Cruz takes her layered with denim jackets for daywear, and under sheer tops for some bling. Likewise, Katrina Kaif layered her printed tube top under a one-shoulder gown at a recent award ceremony. Ready to give the trend a whirl? column1: Remembering the man behind some of Vogue India’s most iconic shoots
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The inimitable Narii View Gallery 9 Photos Remembering the man behind some of Vogue India’s most iconic shoots Production is the trade of unsung heroes. Aside from the more commonly known talents of photographers, stylists, models, actors, hair and make-up are the dedicated team of producers who work behind-the-scenes to hold everything in place. Those who ensure that flowers are dewy fresh for a shot, arrive hours in advance to ensure a smooth shoot day, pour their heart in a project to make a vision come true. One such producer, that Vogue India worked with was Narii whose untimely death on December 29, 2017 came as a shock to all of us. Narii ran Temple Road Productions alongside Bindiya Chhabria—his second in command. The duo were on holiday in Turkey when Narii collapsed and breathed his last. Therein began their last journey together where even complete strangers rushed to help Chhabria with the herculean task of bringing him back. A true man of his word, Narii's passing away comes as a huge blow to those who have had the opportunity to work with him. The Vogue India team remembers the man he was. “I had heard about Narii long before I even met him. One half of the Temple Road Productions team, he, along with Bindiya quietly created magic for us shoot after shoot. When I finally put a face to the name, I found him to be a soft-spoken and warm person who smiled easily and often. His lovely energy and his touch of brilliance will both be missed greatly.” -Priya Tanna, Editor-in-chief “Narii was one of the most dependable people. Anything you asked was always possible. He was always in the shadows, waiting to lend a hand. He created some of the most beautiful sets for our shoots, making a lot of the stories and ideas that were in my mind come alive on the pages of Vogue. His warm smile would make any form of stress go away. Bindiya and Narii were a formidable team and had the perfect balance with each other.” -Anaita Shroff Adajania, Fashion Director “Over the last four years, I worked with Narii on several shoots. He left us too soon. He was one of those producers who was always calm—you never felt stressed around him. He was kind and fair to his crew and us. A Bindya and Narii production was always all pure heart. Narii will be missed.” -Divya Jagwani, Bookings Editor “Narii's effervescent personality and calm attitude made even the most stressful shoots go smoothly. He always had a warm big smile and even warmer heart. He will be sorely missed.” -Priyanka Kapadia, Senior Fashion Editor “Only a few weeks ago, I was in the middle of my shoot and felt like everything was crumbling. And then, Narii arrived on the sets and all the chaos was pushed aside with his calm yet in control personality. That's the kind of person he was—every bit the professional but always with a warm smile and a sense of familiarity. Our shoot sets will never be the same without him.” -Ria Kamat, Fashion Stylist We look back at some of Vogue India's most iconic shoot which would not have been possible without Narii's support. column1: 13 best running shoes that will help you achieve your fitness goals faster
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Jet, set, go View Gallery 13 Photos 13 best running shoes that will help you achieve your fitness goals faster This 2018 as you plan for a newer, better year ahead, fitness goals are sure to have topped the charts. Running is one of the best workouts knows—it's practically cost free, it helps you relieve stress, makes you a happier person and obviously shed some of that famous winter weight. The only thing that counts as an investment when it comes to this form of cardio is buying a pair of a good running shoes. While there are several options to choose from, it's recommended that you don't pick a pair of running shoes just because it's easier on the wallet or because it looks good. Running injuries are very real and it is better to chase your fitness dreams after some thorough research.  1 Cushioning is one of the most important features to bear in mind while buying a pair of running shoes. The high-impact nature of running can damage your joints if the shoes you have on cannot balance your weight. 2 If you plan on running outdoors, be careful about the grip of your shoes—the last thing you want hindering your fit streak is a fall. 3 Size matters, no matter whether you're at your local gym or on a trek. It's ideal to have half a centimeter of free space above your large toe to allow your foot to have free space in your running shoes. From Nike's customisable pair to Adidas's ‘Ultraboost Uncaged' ones, running shoes have never looked this good. Go with something from the Ea7 Emporio Armani range or Y-3 if having designer approval on your gym gear is crucial. Scroll through our edit of the best running shoes to add to your closet in 2018. column1: Neha Dhupia’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We went back to the beginning True to the spirit of the Miss India crown that she bagged at the age of 22, Neha Dhupia is a woman of many talents. Having embarked on a career in Bollywood, she has since diversified and today serves as a judge on the popular Roadies franchise and runs a star-studded podcast, No Filter Neha. When she isn't doing either, she can be found keeping her sartorial cred in place on the red carpet, with her off-duty chic practiced to perfection simultaneously. And they said women couldn't multitask? View Gallery 92 Photos Style evolution of Neha Dhupia After being crowned Miss India in 2002, Dhupia has made the most of her time in showbiz since. She forayed into Bollywood with Qayamat: City Under Threat (2003), and became a mainstay with Julie (2004), Garam Masala (2005) and, more recently, Hindi Medium (2017) and Tumhari Sullu (2017). She made her presence felt on the small screen by booking a berth on the judge's panel of Roadies, while simultaneously trying her hand at the audio industry with her eponymous podcast, No Filter Neha. As she enjoys her best sartorial days in her 30s, here's tracing her fashion journey from the beginning. Style files Counted among the sexiest names in showbiz as a debutante, the leggy lass made the most of her figure with fitted silhouettes. 2011 had her opting for ruched waists and halter necks to flaunt her fabulous collarbone, while 2012 was the year of relaxed silhouettes with flowy palazzo pants and easy separates. Always a fan of the androgynous movement, Dhupia could be regularly found ditching the dreamy gowns on the red carpet in favour of formal pant suits. Not one to shy away from playing into her feminine side either, she favoured plunging necklines and strategic cutouts as well in 2013. Style evolution The years to follow truly cemented her status as a sartorial force to reckon with as she ditched the binary choice between all-out traditional and contemporary, and instead forged her own path with innovative fusion styles. 2015 had her taking to form-flattering separates and smart layering. The good news continued in 2016 as she championed indie labels like Chola and The Meraki Project alongside the Abu Jani and Sandeep Khoslas of her wardrobe. column1: Sonakshi Sinha’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Why we are fans View Gallery 121 Photos Sonakshi Sinha After bursting onto the Bollywood scene with Dabangg in 2010, Sonakshi Sinha's acting career began as a typecast of the traditional Indian woman. But the actor has an independent sense of style that revolves around retro-Bollywood and vintage Hollywood—and sometimes even playful sixties pin-up. In other words, Sinha's found clothes to complement her shape. Film career After winning the Filmfare Award for Best Female Debut, Sinha went on to star in films like Rowdy Rathore (2012), Joker (2012), Dabangg 2 (2012), Himmatwala (2013), Lootera (2013), Once Upon a Time in Mumbai Dobaara! (2013), Bullett Raja (2013), Holiday (2014), Tevar (2015), Naam Hai Akira (2016), Force 2 (2016), Noor (2017) and Ittefaq (2017). She is currently working on projects like Dabangg 3, Shiddat and Crazy Hum. Style files In 2013, the actor played it safe on the red carpet with Indian sari drapes. The traditional red bindi appeared to be her favourite accessory and Sinha toyed with colour as much as she worked with neutral looks in her wardrobe. Fast forward a year and Sinha seemed to have comfortably worked out her own style language with a rigorous fitness routine to back it up. “My body adapts to any kind of workout very quickly, so my trainer makes sure I keep changing it up,” she tells Vogue. The actor sported sleek and classic looks in Nikhil Thampi, experimented with fishtail gowns and spiked headbands from Gauri & Nainika and embraced her curves in waist-cinching gowns and A-line skirts. 2015 has seen Sonakshi in a brave new avatar: the star chopped off her signature mane of glossy locks for a care-free bob with red tips. Since then, we've seen her in Manish Malhotra lehengas and dark gowns, but her red carpet appearances have featured some novel picks too: think grungy jeans and sneakers for a movie screening, that belted Nishka Lulla gown, and her new fashion favourite Huemn. Style evolution “My style has always been casual and simple,” says Sinha. “But losing weight has opened up a whole lot of wardrobe options for me. Clothes fit and fall better on a fitter body. I've always been curvaceous and I take great pride in my curves even today. That's something I don't ever want to lose, so I try and dress accordingly.” In 2016, Sinha became a fan of athleisure, often pairing dresses with white sneakers. Bomber jackets were abundant at airports as were sweatshirts. The star never strayed far from her love of monotone. In the last year, the star favoured Indian designer labels like Manish Malhotra, Masaba, Nupur Kanoi and Anita Dongre amongst others. From commercially appealing choices to edgy designer wear, Sonakshi Sinha style has come a long way. Take a complete look at the star's style in our slideshow. Never one to maintain a straight face while posing for the cameras, the Sri Lankan native has made a name for herself in Bollywood for starring in popular series like Race and Housefull. Fernandez is also a passionate advocate for animal rights. Film career Fernandez debuted on the film scene with Aladin in 2009. Some of her most striking looks from 2011 and 2012 were an ombre lace sari by Gaurav Gupta, a mustard kurta by Anand Kabra and a black sequinned Amit GT gown. column1: 25 times Bollywood celebrities made jeans look not boring in 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Straight from the closets of Alia Bhatt, Sonam Kapoor, Deepika Padukone and more View Gallery 25 Photos All the times Bollywood celebrities made jeans look not boring in 2017 Sure, they can work their haute couture threads and voluminous ballgowns, but at the end of the day, you'll find that the true litmus test of a celebrity lies in how well they elevate everyday basics. And on that end of the bargain, Bollywood's best dressed delivered in 2017. Basic tee and denims? That's so 2016. The humble pair of jeans was given a millennial update this year, featuring everything from sequin-encrusted tropical prints to feather trims. From Anushka Sharma's love for ripped jeans to Alia Bhatt's favourite embellished pair, celebrities have been stepping out in jeans that are nothing the ones you wore growing up. Traditionally reserved for a quick dash to the vanity van and back, denim has slowly worked its way up the ladder in celebrity closets and now demand billing as couture. Metallic embellishments to retro bell bottoms, you'll find celebrities making their denim work as hard as they do. As the year winds to a close, join us in noting down all the many, many non-boring ways to wear this wardrobe staple. Throwback time There are those days when we look at our wardrobes and it's like the '90s never left. The retro mood snuck its way into the denim section of celebrity closets as well, with Deepika Padukone and Athiya Shetty opting for loud-and-proud bell bottoms. Anushka Sharma and Kriti Sanon, meanwhile, went high-waisted with their denim fare. Bling thing When the paparazzi flash goes off, you're going to want something that shines as bright as you do. If you thought that metallics and denims were two words you'd never read together, 2017 was the year of surprises. Take cues from Alia Bhatt who boldly juxtaposed a tartan shirt with sequinned denims from Monisha Jaising. If you like your bling on the less-is-more side, look to Parineeti Chopra who routinely opted for embellished denims in her promotions wardrobe for Meri Pyaari Bindu (2017), first from Monisha Jaising and later from Zara. Slasher flick Regardless of whether you weren't a fan of the distressed denim trend to begin with, 2017 was the year to push your boundaries. Ripped jeans received a nearly-fatal update with busted knees and frayed cutouts. Sharma amped up a basic day look with white jeans ripped all over, while Sanon took her distressed pair to the airport. New mom Kareena Kapoor Khan included hers as a part of her travel uniform. Take a look back at our favourite jeans seen on celebrities this year. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This adorable Missoni backpack was made for globetrotting kids
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It comes fashion heiress-approved View Gallery 2 Photos Why every cool kid will carry this Missoni backpack North West, Blue Ivy Carter, Harper Beckham, Princess Charlotte—it's no longer just the grown-ups making the headlines with their style, and the world has taken note. Designer, influencer and mother-of-two Margherita Maccaponi Missoni, who launched her eponymous childrenswear label a little over two years ago has, just unveiled a limited-edition backpack in collaboration with the Luxury Collection Hotels & Resorts. Vogue got the Italian powerhouse heir to tell us everything about the new accessory, guaranteed to be a hit with tiny tastemakers. Tell us about the backpack and the inspiration behind it. This collaboration was inspired by my recent family vacation with my husband and two sons, Otto and Augusto. We traveled to Portugal for the first time and stayed at Pine Cliffs Hotel, a Luxury Collection Resort. Algarve is known for their colorful fish and actually served as the inspiration for the print of the backpack, and the patterns on the fish were inspired by Portugal's famous hand-painted Azulejo tiles. This is the second time you have collaborated with the Luxury Collection. What sets this collaboration apart? Travelling is one of my biggest passions and I love sharing that with my children. The ability to become immersed in my surroundings is key when I am looking to design something special, and I think what sets this collaboration apart is the designs and inspiration are not only a reflection of my love of travel, but also will always remind me of the incredible memories I have with my family. What was the most exciting aspect of this collaboration? I have two sons, so it was a natural fit for me to design this backpack for them and other children. I truly enjoy designing for them as I want to inspire them to be playful and creative, and to also feel like they have plenty of choices—whether it's what they want to wear in the morning, or what they want to bring along with them in their backpack. I also designed this backpack with the goal to make something that is not only fun for kids, but practical for parents too. It's not easy traveling with little ones! Take us through the features of the bag. What makes it child-friendly? I wanted this backpack to serve as a sense of adventure for children who are always on-the-go. It was important that in addition to style, I also designed this backpack with practicality in mind. That is why I chose to incorporate easily accessible pockets, perfect for storing toys and snacks! I wanted the fabrics of the backpack to be durable and functional, so we chose an easy-to-wash polyester material. This makes it easy for kids to see exactly what's inside and to grab snacks and toys on the go. I also added turquoise stretchable mesh sides which are designed to hold water bottles for long day trips with the family. What's in your backpack? I always travel with a pashmina, eye drops, and lots of magazines. What was your favourite accessory growing up? Always headpieces! As a child I would wear three headbands at a time. What do your two sons like most about the backpack? I think that what they love most is that they get to have their own bag while traveling and can make their own choices with what they want to put in it. So much of being a little kid is having your parents make choices for you, so I think they really enjoy having their own little bag that they can take along and fill with goodies. What are some of your favourite places in Portugal? Algarve is all about the beaches! We spent a lot of our time shore on the shore of Praia da Falésia so the kids could go back and forth from the pool at Pine Cliffs to the beach to play in the sand. We also loved the fresh seafood and Portuguese cuisine at O Pescador, the poolside restaurant at Pine Cliffs where we dined alfresco overlooking the coast. I highly recommend checking out the local food market, Mercado Municipal de Loulé, where I found a lot of tasty snacks to bring to the beach. Make sure to go early in the morning to beat the crowds! What, according to you, are some of the holiday destinations the backpack is likely to be spotted at? From cities to beaches, the backpack is great for any holiday travel with kids as it is perfect for storing snacks, toys, and extra layers to keep warm or swim suits for a spontaneous dip in the water. I will take this with me on all of my travels, including when we visit Puntaldia, Sardinia, where my family has a home. Are there any other collaborations in the pipeline? I am also collaborating with Splendid on an exclusive collection that will be available in March. The backpack is available on Theluxurycollectionstore.com What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Anushka Sharma’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From glitter gowns to the master of minimalism View Gallery 78 Photos Style evolution: Anushka Sharma From the girl who debuted opposite Shah Rukh Khan in her first film, to a producer in her own right, Anushka Sharma's journey in Bollywood has been one worth following. Known to be fastidious about her privacy, an animal rights activist and a fan of minimalism, Sharma may have spent a little less than a decade in Bollywood but is already one of the highest paid actors in the industry Film career The star debuted in Rab Ne Bana Di Jodi (2008), followed by Badmaash Company (2010), Band Baaja Baaraat (2010), Patiala House (2011), Ladies vs. Ricky Bahl (2011), Jab Tak Hai Jaan (2012) and Matru Ki Bijlee Ka Mandola (2013). She took on lead roles that a made a mark in films like PK (2014) and NH10 (2015). She also starred in films like Bombay Velvet (2015), Dil Dhadakne Do (2015), Sultan (2016), Ae Dil Hai Mushkil (2016), and most recently, Phillauri (2017) and Jab Harry Met Sejal (2017). Currently, Sharma is working on the horror film Pari by her own production house. Style files As a Bollywood newcomer still working on making her mark in the industry, Anushka Sharma spent most of 2012 stepping out in extravagant evening gowns and Indian ethnic wear. Her favourites were embellished Roberto Cavalli floor grazers and Abu Jani-Sandeep Khosla anarkalis. The beauty look to match them all was almost always intensely dark eyes, often coupled with equally intense lips. As 2014 passed, Sharma finally established her personal style: boho chic for lazy days at the movies, and more often than not, tailored separates and vibrant prints when it was time to clean up. One of her best looks that year included her head-to-toe Burberry look at the brand's fashion show. Another highlight was at Vogue Beauty Awards 2015, when Anushka Sharma and Virat Kohli stepped out in public as a couple. The star chose a lemon yellow Gauri & Nainika gown for the occasion. Style evolution As she moved on from those earlier days, Sharma started inching towards cleaner lines and sharper silhouettes. “She is never in excess. For Anushka, she likes to keep things more real in that sense. But if a red-carpet event demands she dress up, she does step out in all her glory. I would say she dresses quite appropriately, given where she is and what she is attending,” said her stylist Allia al Rufai. The star recently tied the knot to her long-time beau Virat Kohli and made a stunning bride in Sabyasachi. column1: Phoebe Philo exits Céline but her legacy will live on
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Why women love the French brand Since joining Céline in late 2008, Phoebe Philo has captured our collective imagination, striking a fine balance between approachable and aspirational. Her work immediately offered an articulate expression of modern luxury, one characterized by sleek, unfussy minimalism. Ramya Giangola, founder of global brand consultancy Gogoluxe and noted ‘Philophile', was struck: “When Phoebe launched the new direction of Céline for Resort 2010, I saw the collection in the brand's temporary showroom in NYC. I was immediately blown away, and the mood in the showroom was palpable. Every single detail—logo, fabrics, ready-to-wear, accessories—was covetable. I was hooked from that first moment.” “Céline is the only show I really watch as a consumer,” says Jo Ellison, fashion editor at the Financial Times. “I'm reviewing it, but in the back of my mind I'm shopping it. Every season there's always something exciting to yearn for in the months before it arrives in store. She has an absolute genius for identifying that thing that makes a collection really sing.” Tricia Smith, executive vice president of women's apparel at Nordstrom, tells a similar tale: “I can't remember the last time I haven't been able to separate my own personal wardrobe considerations from those of the Céline customers we buy for at Nordstrom. There is both a sophistication and edge that appeals to so many generations of women.” Philo's work isn't all sophistication. As Giangola notes, there is a sense of captivating playfulness: “From her porcelain deer earring, to her super chubby, electric pink shearling, to her mismatched red and white boots, I think there is real humour in her aesthetic. You can be high fashion and humorous at the same time and still super desirable.” It's this subtle mélange of energies that animates Philo's designs. Her work is tough, elegant and eccentric, sometimes all at once. It is closer to a personality than a brand image, and this is what gives it its particularly feminine, nuanced strength. “It's not complicated,” says Ellison. “Every season that Phoebe has spoken about her work, and she rarely does anymore, she's talked about her design being about modern femininity, and new perspectives on glamour, and what women want. She has continued to put women and their lives at the heart of her design, without compromising attitude, intelligence, or excitement.” “She has an uncanny ability to interpret the direction of the cultural zeitgeist,” Eugenie Dalland, stylist and publisher of cult art/fashion magazine Riot of Perfume. “I think that there's a steady, albeit slow, development in pop culture of an ideal woman who is mature, and autonomous, and sexy, as opposed to the sexually objectified ideal we've known for so long. She's designing clothes for a strong, opinionated, chic, adult woman, and I think that's an ideal that women of all ages can instantly get behind.” That ideal and approach emerges in all facets of Philo's Céline. In January 2015, the brand unveiled a campaign featuring a portrait of legendary essayist Joan Didion in chunky shades, shot by Juergen Teller. The image revealed a pinpoint understanding of the Céline customer. She's bored of commercial fashion imagery, fed up with being force-fed traditional beauty standards. She has a sense of humour. She's well-read. The photograph went predictably viral. At the time, Céline didn't have an official Instagram account—it does as of this past February—but in the smartphone era, any image has the potential to be digitized, so it's possible to win the game without obviously playing it. This has, in a sense, been Céline's overall business strategy over the past decade: create perfectly resonant collections, and trust that the clothes will find their audience. And it's worked—though the label has eschewed e-commerce thus far, sales have more than tripled during Philo's tenure. Giangola explains why: “The quality is bar none, and the pieces never feel dated. You know that when you buy pieces from the collection, you can wear them forever. It's anti-fast fashion.” This quiet resistance to the ever-quickening pace of the industry is part of the appeal. When Philo joined Céline, it was after a three-year break from fashion to focus on her family life. She is famously reticent, too, press-shy protective of her privacy. The way she has approached her work is arguably as much of an inspiration as the work itself. “I do hope that part of her legacy will be to serve as an example to designers—and to CEOs—that it's important to take a break from creating,” says Dalland. “You must have time in order to generate ideas, hone them, come up with fresh perspectives.” I asked Ellison to suggest an item or two that stand as emblems of Philo's design ethos. She gave me three: the mannish trouser, the oversized roll neck and the ugly shoe. “Minimal, luxurious, and always slightly unexpected,” she explains. That's as apt a summary as you'll find of the universe Philo has created at Céline—one that will continue to enchant even after her exit.” Culture & Living Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Massimo Giorgetti speaks candidly about leaving Pucci
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion “I have found my brand, and I am at home now.” On a blustery winter morning at the Hotel Café Royal in London, Massimo Giorgetti is grinning ear to ear. The strikingly handsome Italian designer, 40, is in town to shoot his Spring 2018 campaign with longtime collaborators Katie Grand and Alasdair McLellan. He's smiling because, after a year of twos—two years as creative director of two brands (Pucci and his own MSGM), two years of weeks split between two cities (Florence and Milan), and two years of helming two different design teams, two collections and two shows—his focus has returned solely to his own brand. In 2015, when Pucci announced that the MSGM founder would replace outgoing designer Peter Dundas, the industry applauded. It was about time a traditional Italian fashion house handed the reins to a young, fun designer popular with the influencer crowd—one who could make a storied luxury brand exciting for a younger generation of customers. But it was not to be a long-term partnership. In April 2017—one year before his three-year contract was set to expire—Pucci and Giorgetti announced that they had agreed to part ways, the latter to refocus on his own label. (At the time of writing, Pucci has not yet named a replacement.) Here, in his first interview since a “mutual termination of contract” with the brand, the designer talks candidly about his time at Pucci, the challenges of being a young designer in Milan and his new MSGM PM collection of eveningwear, launching in January. On Pucci... I feel very lucky, because Pucci for me was an experience. I studied when I arrived in this different world that I didn't know. Luxury, amazing fabrics, prints, also Italian craftsmanship on embroidery, on leather, on accessories, on shoes. For me, it was like going back to school, and I grew up a lot. With the LVMH group there are a lot of meetings, a big business strategy. I understood the power of the product manager, the power of the merchandiser—because the wrong merchandiser can do a lot of damage. When I accepted Pucci, I was younger. It's now three years later, and now I feel completely different to how I did then. On “abandoning” his team at MSGM… When I was at Pucci I better understood what MSGM means to me. It's like if you were to go outside your home and look at it from the outside. I studied my company, but I also studied myself. When I came back 100 per cent to MSGM, I had some problems with my team. They felt like I disappeared and left them alone, because I was working with Pucci. It's really like when you have a boyfriend, or a family, and you leave for a while. At the end of the day, MSGM is my life; it is my family, so I can understand it now, but I didn't realise how it felt to them when I was doing both. On designers who become bigger than their brands… I am happy that MSGM is more famous than me. I prefer to work than to go to the parties, and I can say that I live a normal life. When I started Pucci, I tried to do a different life. But it was not for me, to go to all these parties, to go to Los Angeles. There are some designers that want more, more, more about them and less about the clothes. On making mistakes... Sometimes I made mistakes at Pucci, but in fashion mistakes can be about one collection, or about a strategy. Sometimes you give a lot of power to stylists, a lot of power to photographers, and that can be a problem. Success in fashion goes in waves. After the big success, there comes the natural fall. So “Bravo, bravo, bravo” one minute, and two years later they go, “Bye bye!” On being approached by other brands... I'm still getting offers to go and design for other brands, but nothing could convince me to accept another job. I feel very lucky to have a brand of my own. I realised it is a special thing to work for a brand that is yours, that you created. They could offer me a lot of money; they could offer me anything, but I would say no. Because when you are designing at a house that is not yours, you are like a guest in their home. I have found my brand, and I am at home now. On Milan, and its closed ranks... In the beginning of MSGM I suffered, because in Milan the press said, “Oh, sweatshirts”, and they weren't interested. The big Italian brands have the attitude, “This is our house, our garden,” and they are big, old families. For a young designer it is tough to carve a space. At the beginning the government, the Camera Moda, they didn't help me. Only when I had 200 stores, 300 stores, they said, “Oh my god, MSGM is amazing, it's a success, please enter into the calendar, please do a show.” On his new eveningwear line, MSGM PM In Asia, I discovered they are not so interested in feminine clothes. It's much cooler, denim oversized jackets—oversized everything. In Europe, Italy, America, they want fitted, more feminine. So I realised I have to do this kind of easy cocktail dress, with a little ruffle, a little ruche that exists in every MSGM collection. But I wanted to present it again, as PM—for the Post Meridian time—because I observe the women around me and I know there's a need for real women to dress for dinner, for the theatre, but not for the red carpet. On fashion's flirtation with see-now-buy-now... I do not believe in it, and of that I am sure. I think when you see something—a bag, a dress—and you can immediately have it, you don't give it its full importance. The desire has to start in your heart, in your brain, and then you have to wait. I think fashion has to come back to the original model. My dream is one collection a season. I have to do pre-fall, the main show, capsule collections, and then there are capsules for e-commerce, capsules for department stores, a T-shirt for this person, a plisse skirt for that person. Every week we have special projects, and everyone wants exclusives. Though I do think exclusive pieces for exclusive buyers are important, and an opportunity to have fun. My dream would be one collection per season, and a lot of little projects. On the secret to his success... Now I feel that I am back at home. I am happy, and now I have to get my head down and work. Humility is the secret. And not to say, “Bravo, bravo, wow, wow, wow” to myself. Because that is when you make a mistake. When you think, “I have arrived”—no no. You will never arrive. You are always in an important step; every six months is a step. I am learning, learning, learning all the time in every fitting, every meeting, in every day of my life, and that is the secret. column1: Sonam Kapoor’s best style moments from 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Wardrobe diaries View Gallery 41 Photos Sonam Kapoor’s best style moments from 2017 No matter the occasion she's dressing for, Sonam Kapoor makes sure to turn heads with her wardrobe choices. From walking the runway at Paris Couture Week for designer duo Ralph & Russo, making it to Vogue's annual style list to launching her very own high-street fashion label Rheson with her sister Rhea Kapoor, Sonam Kapoor's list of sartorial achievements have scaled new heights this year. The actor not only made headlines with her red carpet appearances, but also surprised with her everyday wardrobe. The star is known for her love for red carpet gowns and is often seen stepping out in statement numbers at various events. Some of the most outstanding red carpet looks of 2017 seen on the star were the Fouad Sarkis Couture gown for the Vogue Women Of The Year Awards, an ivory Ashi Studio gown, a Ralph & Russo off-shoulder pastel gown for IWC Gala and her recent gold strapless gown by Atelier Zuhra at Filmfare Glamour and Style Awards 2017. Like each year since her debut at the Cannes Film Festival, 2017 also saw her on her annual trip to the French Riviera as a L'Oréal ambassador favouring both Indian and international fashion labels. During her trip, Kapoor was spotted in an iridescent NorBlack NorWhite sari, a blush pink sequinned Elie Saab Couture gown, a custom-made Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla cape, an Anamika Khanna ensemble and a mint sari hybrid by Masaba. While the actor's everyday style is enough to grab everyone's attention, Kapoor made sure to top the style lists with her holiday dressing. Channeling her love for Indian wear, the star went all out in ethnic outfits, cased in point: the high-shine Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla sari and the Anamika Khanna sari she wore while receiving the National Film Award. Kapoor admitted her love for fashion in an interview with Vogue “Nobody [can] love fashion as much as I do. It's just about how you wear it, and that's all that matters." Weather it was with a midi dress and denim combo, or a Rheson sari dress, or an elegant anarkali, Kapoor used every opportunity this year to turn the airport into her personal runway. Shuttling frequently between Mumbai and Delhi while shooting for her upcoming feature Veere Di Wedding, she showed us how to ace on-the-go dressing. And as a bona fide fashion enthusiast, the actor has made sure she put the spotlight on some of the lesser known yet worthy designers including Jacquemus, Nabil Nayal, Mother of Pearl, George Keburia and more. One thing's for sure, there's hardly a dull sartorial moment in Sonam Kapoor's life. Since picking out one standout look is particularly tough choice to make, browse through the gallery of our favourite looks seen on Sonam Kapoor in 2017. Don't let the stress of dressing up come in the way of you enjoying with your friends; instead, dial down the extravagance for a few events and go light this wedding season. A serial baraati knows the right loopholes on the event schedule where you can wear an easy kurta set and not look underdressed. If the night demands some extra shine on your part, go with decadent, embellished anarkalis. Scroll through our edit of the best salwar sets, kurtas and shararas to choose from this wedding season. column1: Kangana Ranaut’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Closet envy View Gallery 148 Photos Kangana You know her to be the ambitious model from Fashion, the romantically confused Tanuja Trivedi from Tanu Weds Manu and the girl on a path of self-discover in Queen. Not unlike her transformations on-screen, Kangana Ranaut's wardrobe undergoes drastic changes based on the star's state of mind. From traditional saris to gowns and trickier trends, there's not a look the actor wouldn't try. “Bohemian, very earthy and moody,” is how she describes it. Film career Ranaut debuted in Bollywood with Gangster (2016). Since then she starred in numerous films like Who Lamhe (2007), Shakalaka Boom Boom (2007), Life in a Metro (2007), Dhaam Dhoom (2008), Fashion (2008), Raaz: The Mystery Continues (2009), Kites (2010), Once Upon a Time in Mumbaai (2010), Tanu Weds Manu (2011), Game (2011), Ready (2011), Double Dhamaal (2011) and Rascals (2011). She has also work in films like Shootout at Wadala (2013), Queen (2013), Krrish 3 (2013), Revolver Rani (2014), Tanu Weds Manu Returns (2015), Katti Batti (2015), Rangoon (2017) and Simran (2017). The actor is currently working on projects like Zindabaad, Jaljeera and Manikarnika: The Queen of Jhansi. Style files During her early days in Bollywood, Ranaut was seen in a series of bright, embellished gowns with flat ironed hair. As she gained her footing in films, the star started experimenting with her style. From cocktail dresses indicative of old-worldly charm to suits and saris, the star tried and tested until she was well versed in designer labels. As the ensembles got more flattering, the hair and make-up relaxed, creating a perfect balance. If Ranaut wasn't bouncing her natural curls around, she was pulling them back in sleek buns. Burberry emerged as one of Ranaut's favourites when it came to red carpet choices; starting with the pastel dress she wore sitting front row at the label's show, followed by a brick-hued suit, lime green summer dress, and several more. For her 25th birthday, Ranaut spent her savings on a Dior dress, meanwhile her sequinned Tom Ford dress became so popular she could never wear it again at risk of accidentally twinning on the red carpet with another star. She is also known to be partial to labels like Valentino, Sabyasachi and Sanjay Garg. Evolution If you had to define Ranaut's style, it would be hard to categorise it under one specific aesthetic. Which is not to say that sometimes, the styling veers towards the extreme and severe. However, the star is never seen without having put thought and effort in her wardrobe choices for the day. Even at the airport where most prefer slouchy, athleisure basics, Ranaut is seen in tailored jackets and drapes. With every passing year, Ranaut leaves the audience with looks to draw inspiration from. Here's a complete look at the star's style evolution. column1: JJ Valaya celebrates 25 years in fashion with Swarovski
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Shine on Celebrating his 25-year milestone and longstanding relationship with Austrian luxury brand Swarovski, veteran designer JJ Valaya is collaborating with the brand for the The Alika Project. Taking his signature Alika jacket one step forward, the designer has created 25 versatile coats using Swarovski stones in colours of gold patina, scarlet red, luminous green and crystal golden shadow. What's more, the designer has collaborated with 24 young designers on a unique project. Drawing inspiration from the original, the designers will be adding the essence of their own brand with ensembles and accessories to go with the jackets with Swarovski detailing. “This year, we decided to take the Alika into new territories, and in creating 25 special editions, each signifying one year of the 25 years of the brand, we decided to invite 24 creative individuals to come on board. Be it fabric, silhouette, technique, craft or even their own spirit, these are those creative minds, who I believe, are successfully managing to interpret a new India in a distinct, modern and beautiful style of their own.” says the designer. "The Alika project is therefore about celebration, and I am humbled to see how these fabulous 24 have created a unique synergy by infusing their distinct signatures with the Alika jacket. Needless to say, I am deeply thankful for their enthusiasm, generosity and graciousness. I wish all of them the very best for an immensely satisfying journey as they go ahead in making India modern a highly covetable style statement.” explains Valaya. The veteran designer will not only design the jackets but will also be photographing the entire campaign for the The Alika Project. The 24 designers and labels creating ensembles for the jacket include Gaurav Jai Gupta, Amrapali, Sumant Jayakrishnan, Rina Singh, Nappa Dori, Suket Dhir, Peter D'Ascoli, Punit Jasuja, Alpana & Neeraj, Tanira Sethi, Aparna Chandra of Nicobar, Payal Pratap Singh, Ekaya, Archana Rao, Péro, Antar Agni, Pernia Qureshi, Gautam Kalra, Swati & Sunaina and more. column1: Payal Singhal opens doors to her first store in New Delhi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Brides take note The past few years have seen New Delhi's Mehrauli district evolve into a melting pot that houses countless ateliers and multi-brand stores established by Indian designers. Payal Singhal adds to the repertoire, as her eponymous label celebrates the launch of their second store in the country, which is housed in the area. The store is will be run in association with Carma, the multi-designer platform. Delhi's fashion set has shown much love and appreciation to the collections doled out by the designer over the years, and it comes as no surprise that she chose the capital as her next stopover. “We are very excited to give them an opportunity to shop the entire Payal Singhal product range under one roof,” says Singhal. Known for seamlessly bridging the gap between the aesthetics of modern day necessities and age-old traditions, this will be the designer's second store in the country, the first being in Mumbai. The interiors of the store have been designed keeping in mind the label's appeal—classic, yet contemporary. An Art Deco theme accentuated with distressed mirror walls, soft gold tones and pink velvet furniture pieces will add to the space along with the designer's signature ethnic wear looks. Since the end of the year is a stipulated season for Indian weddings, the store comes right in time for the bridal party shopping. The brand's future plans include another store in Mumbai by the end of next year, and revamping the brand's e-commerce platform which will offer a wider range of product lines including accessories, kids wear and an upcoming menswear line. Payal Singhal opens doors to public on December 19. H 5/7 Kalkadas Marg, Behind Qutub Minar, Mehrauli, New Delhi Culture & Living People Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How the costumes of Star Wars: The Last Jedi came to be
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Fashion of the future View Gallery 12 Photos Fashion of the future: Inside the costumes of ‘Star Wars: The Last Jedi’ When Disney and Lucasfilm decided to launch a new Star Wars trilogy in 2015, it was up to costume designer Michael Kaplan to figure out how to dress the characters. Kaplan, the man responsible for the BAFTA Film Award-winning costumes in 1982's Blade Runner as well as JJ Abrams's Star Trek reboot, was chosen to costume both The Force Awakens and its new sequel, The Last Jedi. He began by looking back to the original Star Wars films from the late 1970s. “I want to continue the path that has already been set,” Kaplan tells Vogue. “We made a conscious decision to return to the look and feeling of [the original 1977 Star Wars film] A New Hope, when I started on Episode VII with [director] JJ Abrams. It's always thinking about things that are right for Star Wars and that are believable in that world.” It took Kaplan and his team a year and half to conceptualise the looks in 2015's The Force Awakens, mostly because they had to redesign the Empire and Rebel uniforms, as well as the Stormtroopers. The Last Jedi, which follows Rey (Daisy Ridley) as she begins her Jedi training with Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill), took a year to design. It sustains the sparse, utilitarian and—with its notes of Haider Ackermann and Rick Owens—surprisingly of-the-moment aesthetic established in the first film. The latest instalment includes thousands of costumes, which were kept secret during the production. For Rey, Kaplan once again focused on rugged, functional pieces suited to running and fighting, including padded trousers, textured knits and flat-heeled boots, all rendered in earthy tones that camouflage easily against a rocky landscape. “She continues into Episode VIII wearing what she ended the last film in,” he says of Rey's wardrobe in The Last Jedi. “But then she has the accoutrements that are right for the terrain where she's going to be. There [are] parkas and ponchos for the inclement weather—things that keep her protected and dry and warm—and then when she's training she's moving, and it's pared down to a very, very minimal look.” Leia, played by the late Carrie Fisher, also gets a makeover of sorts. As head of the Resistance, which is once again preparing to battle the First Order, Leia needed to appear in charge. “She was very rough and ready in Episode VII,” Kaplan notes. “[Director] Rian Johnson decided with me that he wanted her to look a little more regal, more like a princess. We did a series of different capes for her, which added a bit of authority and regalness to her appearance. I think [Fisher] was very happy with the outcome.” The result is a combination of the daring Princess from the first trilogy, who appears remarkably elegant even in the face of danger, and the impressive war admiral of The Force Awakens. This Leia reveals her authority both in her actions and her garb, but still retains her signature look—and memorable hairstyles. A few new characters emerge in the film, including Laura Dern's Admiral Amilyn Holdo, who arrives in an unusual striking lavender dressgown and lavendermatching hair. “She's in the military and she's an admiral, so I thought she would have been in a uniform, but Rian did not want her in a uniform,” Kaplan explains. “He wanted her to have a much more elegant and feminine look, and he wanted to be aware of Laura's body... she needed to be in something that was a little more form-fitting. I looked back to the work of Madame Grès, the designer from the ‘30s and ‘40s, and the gowns she did, which had inspiration from the classic Greek. We were going to do silver hair, but they thought it might look like she had grey hair, so Rian thought lavender hair would be nice and in keeping with the dress.” One of the film's biggest challenges for Kaplan was a scene involving a casino filled with the wealthy and well-dressed citizens of the Star Wars universe. It's the first time we've ever seen characters appear in evening attire during the franchise, and Kaplan had to do extensive research to find inspiration. He looked to eccentric characters from history, like British poet Edith Sitwell, and integrated their personal style into the clothes. “It was a few hundred extras each in their own individual look,” Kaplan says. “The prerequisite was that it be all black and white, which was what Rian Johnson wanted. That was very exciting and a bit daunting for me. Not only to produce that many fashionable looks with jewellery and gloves, but to bring it into the world of Star Wars and not have it look like a futuristic movie or just a ball in a contemporary movie.” The result is very glamorous and just beyond contemporary, with suits and dresses like you might see at the Met Gala. It's in the voluminous, punk-inspired hairstyles, fantastical jewellery—and, of course, alien faces—that the fantasy elements come into play. Kaplan's favourite look is the Praetorian guard, who has been drastically remodeled from the original trilogy. It was difficult to make the armored pieces functional, the designer notes. “It was one thing to come up with a great-looking silhouette on paper, but they had to actually work and fight and have complete capacity of movement, because they were fighting with big swords and other weapons,” says Kaplan, who has already begun to work on the final film in the trilogy, due in 2019. “It wasn't just having a great-looking costume. They had to actually move and have total visibility through the helmets even though there are no eyes.” He adds, “We have to make sure all the characters are able to do what is called upon for them to do.” Star Wars: The Last Jedi opened in theatres December 15 Culture & Living What's New What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s best style moments from 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From red-carpet glamour to airport dressing View Gallery 24 Photos Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s best style moments from 2017 When Aishwarya Rai Bachchan is not stealing the limelight on red carpets in striking ballgowns, she's keeping it easy in athleisure separates. From twinning with her daughter Aaradhya, to making a statement at award shows, this year, the actor's wardrobe was full of sartorial hits. Safe to say, whenever the actor sets foot on the Cannes red carpet, it's a hot topic for style watchers. In 2017, the actor was seen in the French Riviera in a variety of evening wear dresses—from a vibrant Yanina Couture maxi to strapless beige Mark Bumgarner gown and a Cinderella-esque icy blue Michael Cinco number. Known to be partial to the colour black, the actor attended Vogue Beauty Awards 2017 in a black Nedret Taciroglu number and Vogue Women Of The Year Awards in a dramatic Malan Breton gown. When it comes to festive events, like the Ambani family's Ganpati celebrations, the actor switched it up in anarkalis and elegant saris. The actor was spotted wearing Indian couture labels like Sabyasachi, Manish Malhotra, Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla and Rohit Bal through the year. The actor made also news at the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne (IFFM), when the mother-daughter duo stepped out in custom-made Manish Malhotra ensembles. When not in the spotlight, the star favoured wardrobe essentials like embroidered jackets, trench coats, sweatshirts and midi dresses to airports and dinner dates with her family. Rai Bachchan's stylist, Aastha Sharma, described working with star in a recent interview, “Aishwarya has her own personality, she has been an icon for years, she is always appropriately dressed so it's very easy for me as a stylist. Back home, she favours Indian designers and a more understated sense of style. I don't have to convince her to do anything—if it's an international red-carpet event we go all out because she is representing a brand and herself—it's almost a form of art.” In the last few weeks, Rai Bachchan has had a packed calendar. She attendedthe  Ambanis' dinner in a strapless tuxedo gown by French designer Alexis Mabille, Prernaa Arora's party in Bibhu Mohapatra's bodycon LBD and monochrome polka-dotted separates by Andrew GN for Aaradhya's annual day event at her school. Scroll through our gallery to go through Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's most memorable style moments from 2017. Fashion What's New What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Best red outfits seen on celebrities in 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Too hot to handle View Gallery 27 Photos Best red outfits seen on celebrities in 2017 Passion, celebration, joy, danger—the emotions associated with the colour red fall in a wide spectrum. Most tread with caution when wearing red—it is never easy to balance the bold hue with the right amounts of embellishment, skin bared and accessories. But 2017 has shown us how to embrace the hue with complete abandon. From Alexander McQueen to Fendi, Gucci and Givenchy, head-to-red was the commandment for autumn/winter 2017. Taking cues from the runway, celebrities have been devoted to championing the tricky colour on red carpets. From Alia Bhatt's full skirted glory to Kareena Kapoor Khan's daring choice completed with a plunging neckline, Bollywood stars did not hold back when it came to the colour. Red gowns on the red carpet—a power move or a faux pas? Deepika Padukone tried the look more than once. For the premier of xXx: Return of Xander Cage, the star chose a short embellished red dress by Ashish but for the HT Glamour & Style Awards, the actor chose a satin gown by Gauri & Nainika. On the Cannes 2017 red carpet, Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's made a a mark in a statement Ralph & Russo gown. Anushka Sharma and Vanessa Hudgens were amongst those who tried the red pantsuit trend. Meanwhile, Sonakshi Sinha and Athiya Shetty went with sheer gowns in the fiery colour, and Jacqueline Fernandez and Malaika Arora combined red with ruffles, making for powerful looks. From Ruth Negga's Valentino gown at the Oscars to Anushka Sharma's red sari at her engagement, these are our favourite red looks seen on celebrities in 2017. column1: 23 Bollywood celebrity looks to help you decide your mehandi outfit
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Brides-to-be, take note View Gallery 23 Photos Bollywood celebrity looks to inspire your mehandi outfit As one of the first functions on the wedding itinerary, the mehandi often sets the tone for the revelry to follow. A laid-back event to get the festivities rolling, the mehandi is also the perfect event for brides to the skip the expected ornate route and experiment with their ensembles instead. Curating a winning bridal wardrobe is a mammoth task, so we don't blame you if you're in a fix over your mehandi outfit. Vogue style-stalked our favourite celebrities and their go-to festive looks to put together just the guide you were looking for. Who better than bride of the moment, Anushka Sharma, to take a cue from? The actor who broke the Internet with her recent wedding in Tuscany decided to go bright and boho for her mehandi. A graphic fuchsia pink and Indian orange lehenga with a floral blouse by Sabyasachi Mukherjee was her outfit of choice, and is the ideal choice for the bride on the lookout for a fuss-free, comfortable look. For brides who can't get enough of twirl-friendly creations, lehengas are the obvious way to go. But play with contemporary versions that you wouldn't be able to wear for your other functions like the sangeet or pheras. Get inspired by Alia Bhatt and opt for a modern cropped shirt blouse with a traditional Benarasi or Lucknowi lehenga. Mehandis and cape lehengas are a match made in sartorial heaven—the outfit is trendy, doesn't come in the way of henna application, and allows for easy movement. Let Shilpa Shetty Kundra and Katrina Kaif in their Anamika Khanna lehengas lead the way. A pop-hued lehenga with a fringed blouse minus the dupatta as seen on Sara Ali Khan won't disappoint either. If you're not shy of unconventional silhouettes, then add some drama to your mehandi look by way of drapes. A colour-blocked palazzo sari as seen on Jacqueline Fernandez is sure to score you the title of the coolest bride in town. Mira Rajput Kapoor's tulip pant and asymmetrical cape set is what you need when hosting an intimate mehandi ceremony at home. Don't write off sharara sets either. Turn to Esha Gupta for the ultimate inspiration. As far as mehandi prints are concerned, florals always work like a charm. Follow Jhanvi Kapoor's lead and team a voluminous floral skirt with a sheer blouse. Or do like Kriti Sanon and team an off-shoulder blouse with a geometric print skirt. Mehandis are licence to play with stop-and-stare hues, and no shade is off limits. From pastels to neon, choose one that ties in with your personality and function theme. And if you've decided to forego bridal red for the pheras, wear it for the mehandi instead, by choosing a belted draped creation like the one worn by Deepika Padukone. Factor in practicality as well. Swap the full sleeves for short or elbow-length ones, and keep any dupattas belted, as they are bound to come in the way. If you plan to apply henna on your feet during the function, choose a raised hemline, such as the cropped Anita Dongre anarkali worn by Parineeti Chopra. column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan’s best style moments from 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Bollywood celebrity shows the way View Gallery 50 Photos Kareena Kapoor Khan’s best style moments from 2017 Kareena Kapoor Khan is rarely sets a wrong foot when it comes to her wardrobe. Between jaw-dropping red carpet gowns to relaxed travel separates on the airport, Kapoor Khan's love for all-things-fashion cements her high rank on best dressed lists in the country. From making her way back to a film set after the birth of son to getting back in shape, 2017 was a big one for the actor. After taking a short break after her delivery, Kapoor Khan started shooting for Veere Di Wedding in 2017. With constant travel to the Delhi set and back, the actor showed us just how to nail comfort with style while on the go. Often spotted with baby Taimur and her favourite travel companion, her Hermès Birkin, the actor was on point every time with her airport looks. In her down time, Kapoor Khan was often spotted in understated-yet-impactful separates like denim jacket, leggings, comfy T-shirts and midi dresses. While stepping out for dinner dates with husband Saif Ali Khan or attending parties with her girl gang, the actor dressed up in an array breezy dresses. “I think most of my fans see me as the girl that is casual yet stylish, yet the working woman of today. That, is key and I cater to that—I do. That's why you'll never really see me dressed over-the-top,” she said in an interview. While her everyday style might be relatable, the actor doesn't shy away from pulling out the stops on the red carpet. From a glittering Falguni and Shane Peacock gown for the Zee Cine Awards to the most recent statement-making Rami Al Ali Official number, the actor made some scene stealing appearances in 2017. Her love for Indian ethnic wear, too, stays strong: while attending Diwali parties this year, the actor was spotted in exquisite sharara sets and saris by Tarun Tahiliani, Bloni Atelier by Akshat Bansal and Rimple and Harpreet Narula. The year also saw the actor introduce Pakistani designer Faraz Manan to her ethnic wardrobe. Another highlight from her year was her body transformation. Juggling back-to-back shoots for her upcoming movie and spending quality time with little Taimur, the actor made sure she gave herself as much time, with regular yoga sessions with her trainer to gain strength and muscle tone. She was often spotted after her rigorous workouts in classic leggings, oversized jackets and slogan T-shirts. Flaunting the results of her transformation, Kapoor Khan was recently spotted in elegant bodycon dresses and sheer gowns. From Gucci T-shirts to elegant sharara sets, there's hardly a boring style moment in Kapoor Khan's life. Go through our gallery and check out our favourite looks seen on Kareena Kapoor Khan in 2017. column1: How Star Wars became fashion’s favourite film franchise
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A timeless well of inspiration View Gallery 19 Photos How ‘Star Wars’ became fashion’s favourite film franchise Since the release of Star Wars: A New Hope in 1977, fashion designers have found inspiration in a galaxy far, far away, nostalgically emblazoning the faces of characters like Luke Skywalker and Yoda onto sweatshirts and silk dresses, or, more subtly, replicating the earthy, largely monochrome palette that defined the look of the original film. It's little wonder that A New Hope continues to inspire designers more than 40 years after its release. Because it takes place in the past, director George Lucas and costume designer John Mollo eschewed the neofuturistic look of most sci-fi films of the period, taking their cues from Japanese samurai and vintage military garb for a look that has remained remarkably timeless. “Star Wars was a cultural phenomenon when it was released in 1977,” says Patricia Mears, deputy director of the Museum at FIT in New York. “The sets and costumes were a blend of two distinctly different aesthetics: high tech and deconstructed, apocalyptic. This duality, in a way, presaged the two major trends of 1980s. On the one hand, there was the strong and sharply cut suits that were both highly polished and angular that were being designed by couturier Yves Saint Laurent. And on the other was the rise of deconstruction spearheaded by avant-garde designers, mainly Rei Kawakubo and Yohji Yamamoto.” American Vogue paid tribute the year of A New Hope's release, casting Darth Vader and C-3PO alongside models including Jerry Hall in a fashion spread of fur coats. In 1979, Thierry Mugler showed a collection of metallic gowns, which The New York Times wrote were influenced by "Star Wars syndrome”. The Star Wars prequels of 1999-2005—often looked down upon by Star Wars purists—have had their high fashion moments, too. Around the release of Star Wars: Episode 1—The Phantom Menace, Yves Saint Laurent Beauté unveiled a makeup collection called One Love inspired by Queen Amidala's on-screen look. The collection sold out in two weeks. In recent years, interest from the fashion community has become so keen that Disney (which acquired Lucasfilm in 2012) has actively collaborated with designers including Rodarte, Comme des Garçons, Rag & Bone, Preen and, most recently, Christian Louboutin. To coincide with the release of The Force Awakens in 2015, the company launched Force 4 Fashion, a charitable initiative that asked several designers, including Diane von Furstenberg, Peter Pilotto and Jonathan Anderson, to create capsule looks based on Star Wars, raising money for Child Mind Institute. “We want to bring the world of stories [like Star Wars] to life through world-class products and experiences… in ways you might not expect,” Josh Silverman, executive vice president of licensing at Disney Consumer Products and Interactive Media, says of the collaborations. A Rag & Bone capsule collection, which launched on December 1 to coincide with the upcoming release of Star Wars: The Last Jedi, reflects this idea. According to Rag & Bone co-founder and CEO Marcus Wainwright, the pieces in the collection reference the Star Wars aesthetic first created in 1977, a style sustained in the more recent trilogy by costume designer Michael Kaplan. “The enlightening thing for me, having gone to meet the costume designers and look at the Rogue One stuff, is that we're definitely drawing from the same vein,” Wainwright tells Vogue. “Rag & Bone is a mixture of English tailoring, workwear and American military. We have a big vintage archive at Rag & Bone, which has many of the same pieces they reference. There's timelessness to the Star Wars movies because they're set in the past and they're set in a parallel dimension to ours. It doesn't feel futuristic. It's all drawing on things I think people are inherently familiar with and fashion draws on the same place anyway.” This isn't the first time Rag & Bone—which used to keep an actual Stormtrooper in its New York office—has looked to Star Wars. The slick, technical fabrics and military-inspired garb shown for autumn/winter 2009 directly referenced both the films and samurai. The present decade has seen more Star Wars references on the catwalk than ever before. Maya Hansen's autumn/winter 2013 show, Raf Simons's pre-fall 2015 show for Dior and Mara Hoffman's autumn/winter 2015 all borrowed elements of the original trilogy, including Princess Leia-style hair twists. Perhaps the most famous Star Wars/catwalk moment to date was Rodarte's autumn/winter 2014 collection, which employed large-scale stills from the original trilogy—including a close-up of Yoda and a black dress emblazoned with the Death Star—as part of a five-dress collaboration with Disney. For Rodarte—as for many of its fans and contemporaries—the moment was all about nostalgia. “[Star Wars] are the only films that we can never remember not having seen, and in many ways, they seem to have become a part of who we are,” the Rodarte sisters wrote on StarWars.com at the time. “In a broader sense, they have melded with the collective conscious of our cultural DNA. They are a heartbeat that joins so many people together or a complex nervous system, connecting far off worlds with the very real and universal human experience.” What's New Wellness Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Deepika Padukone’s best style moments from 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Do you have a favourite? View Gallery 56 Photos Deepika Padukone’s best style moments from 2017 Trust Deepika Padukone to make a statement with whatever she wears. While juggling a hectic work schedule both in the country and overseas this year, the actor did not fail to make headlines with her exceptional sartorial choices too. From head-turning gowns on red carpets to acing athleisure on home turf, the actor pushed the envelope on her style quotient even further in 2017. The beginning of 2017 saw Padukone make her Hollywood debut in xXx Return of Xander Cage opposite Vin Diesel. For the promotional tour, the actor stepped out in scene-stealing sequinned gowns and embellished dresses in various places across the globe. At the 70th Cannes Film Festival as one of L'Oréal's global ambassadors, the actor left a mark with her wardrobe choices. Whether it was the red ruffled Johanna Ortiz maxi dress or the custom Brandon Maxwell gown or the diaphanous Marchesa number, the star's trip to the French Riviera was a memorable one. Another eventful occasion for the star was attending the Met Ball in 2017. Padukone stepped out in an understated, yet impactful satin slip gown by Tommy Hilfiger for the big night. In an interview, Padukone's stylist Elizabeth Saltzman revealed “I think she is open to learning and excited so there are no demands, we work on everything together. The one thing I do ask of her and every client I work with is complete honesty and feedback, which I think is important." Describing her personal style, Saltzman added “I think her style is classic with a twist. She can do sportswear really well but I like that she looks great even in travel clothes. Her personal style is little bit bodycon, a little edgy, not funky-edgy, but interesting.” On days when the occasion did not warrant red carpet dressing, the actor switched it up in classic dresses and basic separates by some of her favourite designers, including Label by Ritu Kumar, Ekà, Shift, Nike, and her very own brand All About You by Deepika Padukone. With the jet-setting lifestyle came mastery of the art of airport dressing. The actor was often spotted after flights championing bomber jackets, ripped jeans and tracksuits. While doing promotional rounds for her upcoming period drama Padmavati, the actor worked multiple ethnic outfits, most of them being by her favourite Indian designer, Sabyasachi. column1: Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee’s most stunning real brides
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Real-life bridal dressing inspiration from real women View Gallery 20 Photos Sabyasachi Mukherjee’s most stunning real brides will give you wedding goals It's common knowledge that designer Sabyasachi Mukerjee's eponymous label is one of the most sought-after names when it comes to bridal couture. Brides in India and overseas are happy customers of the designer. Even celebrities can't resist dressing up in Sabyasachi—the popularity of Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma's wedding outfits—is a clear sign of how well-received the designer's work is. From monochrome magic to lush florals and decadent old-world charm, there's something about a Sabyasachi lehenga that makes brides go weak in their knees. The designer's couture 2017 collection was an ode to Rajasthani Royalty. The autumn/winter 2017 couture drop again took you back to vintage treasures. Add to that, Mukherjee also started a jewellery line earlier this year to go with his opulent garments. Over the years, Mukherjee has spoken about his unique formula behind his covetable creations. “When you take something beautiful from the past and you make it wearable for today, it will become a commercial hit. A lot of what I make is inspired by bygone eras. When I'm making clothes, I think of how they can be functional for today's woman. For instance, the pace of life is faster, so if she is wearing a lehenga does it have to weigh a ton and be fashioned out of 60 metres of fabric when it can easily be made from 20? My concerns are about making the garment viable for the pace we live in," he told Vogue. Whether it's the voluminous skirts, longline jackets or the dreamy dupattas, brides seem to glow from within in their Sabyasachi outfits. column1: Best of 2017: 10 most unforgettable runway moments
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Do you remember these In 2017, Vogue editors took in hundreds of shows around the word, from New York to Paris, Copenhagen to Seoul. These are the 10 moments we'll never forget. Naomi Campbell opening Alaïa When your audience has waited six years to see your show, what better way is there than to open and close it with a legendary supermodel, who also happens to be an intimate friend? At Azzedine Alaïa's unexpected show during couture week in July, his last before his passing in November, Campbell took her strides to cheers and applause, wearing a bell-shaped monochrome coat, zip-front ankle boots and hair wrapped in a plastic headdress. The Supers at Versace In honour of her late brother Gianni Versace, who was murdered in Miami Beach 20 years ago, Donatella reunited five of the original supers to close her Versace spring/summer 2018 show. At the finale, curtains drew back, revealing Cindy Crawford, Naomi Campbell, Claudia Schiffer, Carla Bruni-Sarkozy and Helena Christensen wearing chainmail goddess gowns and standing statuesque on white blocks, before making two laps around the runway to George Michael's “Freedom! '90”—the second time arm-in-arm with Donatella herself. Saint Laurent at the Eiffel Tower For his spring/summer 2018 show, designer Anthony Vaccarello sent models down a vast, open-air runway on the Trocadéro in a sexy, decadent mix of leather, sequins and ostrich feathers. Backlit by the sparkling Eiffel Tower, it was a sight that neither editors nor the audience alike—comprising the likes of Courtney Love, Lenny Kravitz, and Chloë Sevigny—will soon forget. It was all the more poignant given the passing of Yves Saint Laurent's partner Pierre Bergé just weeks before. “I really wanted to pay homage to him,” Vaccarello told Vogue after the show. “To Yves Saint Laurent, to the house. Even if it's a cliché, I want to push the cliché so far it's beautiful.” Kaia Gerber's runway debut The eyebrows have it. Just four days after her 16th birthday—and 26 years after her mother's runway debut for Donna Karan—Cindy Crawford's lookalike daughter, Kaia Gerber, took her first steps down the catwalk for Calvin Klein, wearing a diner-inspired uniform of silk Western shirt over a polo neck sweater and mustard-yellow satin trousers. Designer Raf Simons handpicked Gerber for the much-anticipated show—his second for the house. She stepped out fourth but not unnoticed. Smiles of recognition warmed even the front row's coolest customers and knowing nudges rustled the crowd. However fashion moves quickly—and this memorable moment of the future was gone before most iPhones could catch it. Halima Aden walking for Max Mara The Somali-American model Halima Aden was one of the breakout stars of 2017. Hitting runways in New York and Milan, the 20-year-old Vogue Arabia covergirl made a striking, modern figure at Max Mara, modelling the label's signature style of classic camel coat with her hijab for autumn/winter 2017. Witnessing what felt like a distinctly landmark occasion in today's political temperament—and a bold statement of inclusion by Max Mara. Approving eyes followed the model to the end of the runway, some necks even strained, as fingers promptly started to type. Dior in California When Dior set up fashion day camp in California in May, it raised the bar—and several gargantuan tents. Artistic director Maria Grazia Chiuri shuttled guests including Rihanna, Charlize Theron and Demi Moore to her debut Cruise collection show in the dusty Santa Monica Mountains, where scenes from Gone With the Wind and Little House on the Prairie were filmed. Referencing the feminist shamanic healer Vicki Noble and author of Women Who Run With the Wolves, Clarissa Pinkola Estés, the show took place in the Upper Las Virgenes Canyon Open Space Preserve in Calabasas. Dior Sauvage hot air balloons settled and the label's lettering stood out from mountainous backdrop in homage to the infamous Hollywood sign. Campfires burned, drums banged and gold dust woman Solange Knowles later performed to the tune of green juice and vodka. Dries van Noten's 100th show For his 100th collection this March, Dries van Noten pulled from all his past designs. He also pulled in all his best-known faces, casting only women who had walked for his show before. Missy Rayder, Hannelore Knuts, Alek Wek, Delfine Bafort and Tasha Tilberg pulled on our nostalgia strings, wearing jeans and metallic jackets, mannish coats and multi-coloured shirt dresses and jumpers. A sea of phones raised like a modern champagne toast to the show. Catherine Deneuve sat front row, and online the brand's Instagram account hit half a million followers straight after the show. Raf Simons's womenswear debut at Calvin Klein He's a Belgian man in New York. Debuting his first women's wear collection for the label—and also its first dual-gender show—here was the genius behind invigorating turnarounds at both Jil Sander in Milan and Dior in Paris, pitching up to play for one of the biggest names on team America. His audience heaved with A-list fans from Millie Bobby Brown and Brooke Shields, to Julianne Moore and Naomie Harris. They sat in an artwork by Sterling Ruby, while David Bowie's “This is Not America” hauntingly played about them as a new Americana style pioneered before them (both on the catwalk and in the wider country,with Trump's inauguration). Simons instigated a new life into the label and seemed more than satisfied. Taking a run through his myriad of catwalks at the show's finale, he blew kisses with longstanding right-hand man and new creative director Pieter Mulier. Chanel presents around a rocket Chanel's autumn/winter 2017 show was a case of Karl Lagerfeld meets Carl Sagan, with a space-themed show staged in Paris's Grand Palais. Lagerfeld took his audience to infinity and beyond, with silver pearl-encrusted headbands and glitter boots that came back down to earth as a street style favourite. But the piece de resistance was a life-sized Chanel-branded rocket in the middle of the room. At the finale Lagerfeld and a mini mascot took a spin around the foot of the rocket, where smoke bubbled and engines roared. A button was pushed, a recorded countdown began, sparks flew, “Rocket Man” played, and then we actually had lift off. Mario Testino held his camera up, mesmerised, and Cara Delevingne couldn't have clapped any faster. It was thoroughly out of this fashion world. Gigi loses her shoe at Anna Sui It's what fashion fairytales are made of. The not-so-well-heeled but decadently-dressed Gigi Hadid taking a tiptoe tour down the Anna Sui runway after losing her glittering stiletto at the start of her second turn. Her sister, Bella, stepped up to the job of Princess Charming, providing a shoulder for Gigi—who wore an Almost Famous-inspired outfit—to hang on to. In sisterly solidarity, they buoyantly closed the spring/summer 2018 show to the tune of The Beatles' “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds” and ample applause. Bella could sympathise: last September she took a high-heeled fall from grace at Michael Kors. Rihanna closes her show on a motorbike Motocross drivers had spun stunts atop mountains of sparkling pink sand, but when closing her Fenty X Puma spring/summer 2018 show, Rihanna was of course the real star. Most designers opt for a modest bow to finish a show, but instead, the singer-turned-designer channelled her inner girl racer, hanging off the back of a motorbike driven by a helmet-hidden man. With sunglasses on, hair in a topknot and wearing athletica with flare-heeled, racer-striped boots, she was clearly enjoying herself. Royally cruising past the whooping crowd, she blew kisses and playfully stuck out her tongue, before driving off further into her Instagram Live.
