column1: 20 pairs of shoes that are perfect for the wedding season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Best foot forward View Gallery 20 Photos 20 pairs of shoes that are perfect for the wedding season After you're done picking up your outfits for the wedding season ahead, shopping for accessories needs to be next mission to you need to tick off your checklist. Whether you're the bride or a part of the bridal crew, finding the right pair of shoes for each ceremony is crucial. Between running errands for your best mate who is getting married and endless nights of dancing, weddings can take a toll on your feet, especially if your festive footwear is the kind that will leave you with blisters or worse, a twisted ankle. The smart way to survive a wedding is knowing when to alternate between towering stilettos, block heels and flats. If you're hesitant about wearing strappy sandals and will have to be on your feet for longer than four hours, it's best to avoid them because the day is only going to end in discomfort. For smaller events like the mehendi or haldi ceremony, go traditional with a pair of embroidered juttis. If you don't have much of a role to play during the pheras, give your soles some time to recover in a pair of dressy slides. Save the stilettos for the reception, and opt for chunky heels to dance at the sangeet. Given that most wedding wear is bound to be embellished or bear a touch of metallic hues, avoid recycling evening shoes from your party wardrobe for the occasion. A pair of shoes in gold and one in silver are a must have in your arsenal. You can also look at rose gold, pale pinks and glitter shoes for the wedding season. If you really want to take things up a notch and have your Cinderella moment, go for a pair of shocking pink satin slides or something with pearl detailing. column1: Careers in fashion: Raghavendra Rathore on cultivating fashion’s next gen
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A look into his special project Raghavendra Rathore might not be a regular on fashion week schedules, but his presence on the scene is nonetheless felt by way of his quiet dedication to his craft. Known for his refined, minimalistic take on tailoring, a Rathore bandhgala is instantly recognisable in a crowd. Channeling his expertise in another direction, for a while now, Rathore has been working on a special project—the launch of the Gurukul School of Design in Jaipur India. Designed to endow students with a mature sense of vision, business acumen and better communication, Rathore has brought in the best international and Indian educators on board to create a wholesome curriculum for the school. Vogue spoke to the designer about the importance of design education for someone seeking a career in fashion. What made you want to start a design school in India? It was a natural progression, a full circle back to the classroom. Though it was very much a conscious decision I had taken years ago, the time has presented itself now. While studying at Parsons, New York, back in 1994, I worked shifts after school to support myself. That phase and experience somewhere engrained in me an appetite to possibly one day provide a similar opportunity to budding talent back home one day. On a more personal front, I received help from someone who simply told me that the biggest payback would be if I one day could also do a similar thing for someone. The stepping stone was establishing the Raghavendra Rathore Foundation, that works with a cross-section of society under arts, crafts and design, and I think Gurukul School of Design is a formalisation of all these thought processes and experiences, amalgamated into a structure that will allow individuals to become successful entrepreneurs and keep this cycle moving. How important is it to have a fashion education if you want to be a fashion designer? To me, education has always been a little more than just the formal dissemination of information. Especially in design, what one learns in the field is so much more than can be taught—design and aesthetic must be felt and experienced to be understood. I also strongly endorse the school of thought which is multi-dimensional—for example if one trains to be a fashion designer, they should also be taught the ropes of commerce, brand building and finance—an all-encompassing education is important. With established institutions like NIFT, NID and Pearl Academy offering exemplary programs and placement opportunities, what does The Gurukul School of Design offer that sets its students apart from the rest? Many design schools today teach design only from the art and pattern point of view, in other words, students focus on one and only one aspect. The Gurukul School of Design is an all-pervasive, 360-degree approach to the design industry. It's to create an ecosystem, something that is interconnected with a lot of other organisations and inclusive. Once out of school, students tend to run into potholes where holistic solutions and multitasking comes into question. We want to create visionaries and entrepreneurs, not one-track professionals. How is the GSD program designed to help students learn the practicalities of design? From a very strong foundation that deals not only with fashion but with the design world, to a comprehensive curriculum that looks into multiple aspects over and above the sphere of fashion, practicality is something we focus on from the word go. What does design education in India lack? How are you trying to fill that gap? While design education in India is well-equipped, I personally feel it lacks two important factors. The first being, searching for and bringing out the best in students. We have no dearth of talent in the country, it is a matter of the right guidance and exposure, which in today's day is not a bonus but an essential. The second would be discipline. To process a design, one needs to be very disciplined; from being certain about the design structure right up to marketing and selling the final outcome, there needs to be a clear process in place. The traditional Indian teaching methods were built on the foundation of discipline, and at Gurukul School of Design, we aim at reviving the basics, in order to excel. How is the design mentorship program structured? The design mentorship program primarily teaches students how to think in real time, and come to real solutions. How to style and build a brand, coupled with the basic understanding of how to make a design successful and what would lead to its failure. This will be incorporated at Gurukul School of Design through collaborations with industry giants who can mentor the students and help them develop these basics from the beginning, as the inputs provided will in themselves be from a cauldron of immense years of experience and design leadership in their respective fields. How is the entrepreneurial mentorship program structured? The entrepreneurial mentorship program will teach students how to market their ideas, work in tandem with manufacturers, managing the brand and profit making, verbal and presentation skills and idea conceptualising and communication. What do aspiring students need to know about breaking into the fashion industry? Apart from the fashion industry knowledge that they imbibe and the on-ground experience they earn, students inherently need to have a keen sense of what works and what doesn't. In a world of brand and slogan overdose, future designers not only need to comprehend the business of design but understand their customers. From personal experience, staying close to my brand and inhabiting the classic space with the bandhgala, can at times be questionable—but the solution lies in maintaining the equation, but at the same time customising it for the customer in the right proportion. column1: Chanel in Hamburg: Karl Lagerfeld revisits his roots
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Behind this year's Métiers d'Art venue View Gallery 15 Photos Chanel in Hamburg: Karl Lagerfeld revisits his roots The wind in Hamburg is whipping across the water, making bare branches sway on the shore and even the Christmas trees in the streets bend in the stiff breeze. But Karl Lagerfeld feels right at home as he brings Chanel to Germany, his birth country. ‘'I come from the North, near to the Danish border, so I was lucky, I escaped everything,” says the designer about his childhood. “My father had bought the estate because he knew that war would come.'' Lagerfeld left Hamburg for Paris when he was 17 years old—although his age is always a subject of debate. He moved to France in 1952, starting with Pierre Balmain a career rooted in couture that has flourished into this week's exceptional Chanel show, held in the newly built Philharmonic orchestral building. The swooping geometry of the building's architecture is drawn—as is every single one of his fashion designs—by Lagerfeld's own hand, to create the ‘Paris-Hamburg' invitation for today's show. But true to his vision of never looking back, the designer has not devised a collection based on nostalgic memories of the past, as he weaves in the skills of embroiderers, knitters, milliners, jewellers and shoe-makers that the Paris fashion house has nurtured through the new millennium as ‘Métiers d'Art'. Instead, Karl's focus is on the sea and its far horizon as mighty boats come into Hamburg's port, which is now, the designer says, “one of the biggest harbours in Europe which has changed completely the mood and the view.'” “I'm not a person who has nostalgia—just ideas—and the inspiration is container shipping, the geometric look of the containers,” continues Lagerfeld, whose flow of conversation is interspersed with instructions to his team to place a clip “there, at the base of the collar, behind the bow”; to shorten a pair of trousers by half a millimetre; or to alter stitching to smooth a minuscule crease. His aim, as always, is to create a modern ambiance for classic designs and to give a sense of super-high quality to anything from a hand-knit dress to a sailor's cap that is veiled in silken chiffon. Beside him is Amanda Harlech, his inspirational supporter, whose book of misty black and white photographs of the boats and harbour area have a mysterious beauty. Karl says that his decision to come to Hamburg is not to do with his past nor any suggestion that Coco Chanel had a connection with the city, as has been the case in previous places chosen for the shows. Instead, the concept was inspired by the wave-roof building of the new concert hall—still under dispute in the city for its high cost. “I think it's the most interesting new building in Europe in terms of design—Herzog & de Meuron, they are geniuses,” says Lagerfeld of the Swiss architectural duo behind the Elbphilharmonie. Always looking forward is the essence of the Lagerfeld attitude, yet he suggests a faint aftershock from the recent deaths of his two great fashion sparring partners: Azzedine Alaïa and Pierre Bergé, partner to Yves Saint Laurent. “Do you know, in the past three months my two arch-rivals have passed away,” he muses. “Azzedine hated me, even though we never knew each other—I saw him three times only, in Milan. He always disliked me and criticised me for not actually making the clothes myself—although he could not draw like me. Pierre Bergé is another story. Once we were friends—40 years ago. But when he died, my flower shop called and asked if I was sending something. I just said ‘no'. Then she said: ‘we could have just sent a cactus!'” The love of Karl's life suddenly appears: Choupette, the fluffy white Birman cat who has accompanied him (along with a personal maid) on this trip to Hamburg. The models, seamstresses, hair stylists, make-up artists and music-makers all stand still, as though royalty had entered the room. Choupette looks the part. And, like the thousands of books on every kind of subject that Karl keeps in his homes, the cat is here as a very best friend. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: A look back at 2017: The year in fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Do you have favourites? Time, they say, flies fast. Was 2017 the year of unprecedented changes, of inclusivity, collaborations and celebrating milestones? Here's a look at the most standout fashion moments from 2017. [#image: /photos/5ce4338d9cc0c060bdf9df5b]||| ||| Image: Getty Zara opened its largest flagship store in Mumbai near the iconic Flora Fountain. The 50,000sqft property costs a whooping 30 crores a year with a five-year lock in period. This was reportedly the largest overseas space-related transaction made by a high street brand. If you're in town, drop by at the restored vintage space for a quick shopping exercise.   [#image: /photos/5ce4338dc33f5cd6088f1f50]||| ||| Rheson Bollywood's interest in fashion went beyond stars and their personal wardrobes. Sonam Kapoor co-launched high street fashion label Rheson with her producer/stylist sister Rhea Kapoor. Anushka Sharma launched her line Nush, a project Sharma had in the pipeline for a while. Alia Bhatt invested in India's first styling portal StyleCracker, positioning herself as an important player in the celebrity fashion space.   [#image: /photos/5ce4338db40d2671bdd6d487]||| ||| Riccardo Tisci Fashion's very own version of musical chairs continues to keep the audience on its toes with the guesswork. Riccardo Tisci parted ways with Givenchy after spending 12 years with the brand. Burberry released a statement that Christopher Bailey would be in a transitioning role and exit from the brand at the end of 2018. Bailey who has spent no less than 17 years with the luxury British label said that, “it has been a truly inspiring place to work and the decision to leave was not an easy one.” Phoebe Philo of French label Céline will also be making her exit from the label. Meanwhile Natacha Ramsay-Levi, who trained under Nicholas Ghesquière, made her debut at Chloé starting with resort 2018.   [#image: /photos/5ce4338ecc50beca7813ff89]||| ||| Priyanka Chopra and Nick Jonas. Image: Getty The Costume Institute of the Metropolitan Museum of Art honoured Rei Kawakubo with the ‘Rei Kawakubo/Comme des Garçons: Art of the In-Between' exhibit. Kawakubo was the only living designer to be the subject of a retrospective since Yves Saint Laurent. The open-for-interpretation dress code at the Met Ball made way for several interesting looks on the red carpet. Priyanka Chopra made her debut at the event in a dramatic trench dress by Ralph Lauren that earned her meme-level fame on the internet.   [#image: /photos/5ce4338ef55c27c0dda281ad]||| ||| Aishwarya Rai Bachchan. Image: Getty Deepika Padukone, Sonam Kapoor and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan made headlines with their carpet choices in the French Riviera. In tulle gowns and ice princess-worthy dresses embellished to the T, Bollywood stars sent the style watchers in a frenzy with their carefully planned looks from the Cannes Film Festival.   Calling out infringers of intellectual property is a mission for Instagram account Diet Prada. From Gucci's uncredited reference to Dapper Dan's work from the brand's resort 2018 collection to campaigning for the boycott of photographer Terry Richardson who was accused of sexual harassment, the duo behind the internet phenomenon are not ones to mince their words. Let's just say, being featured on the account's feed may not always work in your favour.   [#image: /photos/5ce4338d3bf9b40e29b1d1c5]||| ||| Suneet Varma. Image: Sagar Ahuja/Vogue 2017 marked JJ Valaya's 25th year in Indian fashion as did designer duo Abraham & Thakore. Couturier Suneet Varma completed 30 years in the industry. Not nearly done, the designer commented saying, “I'm very excited about the future. Great runway moments are made when you don't strive to make a statement,” about his milestone moment.   Italian luxury giant Gucci announced that will be joining the fur-free alliance from spring/summer 2018. Despite the brand's growing popularity under the helm of Alessandro Michele, Balenciaga replaced Gucci as the hottest brand in fashion. Virgil Abloh's street fashion inspired label Off-White moved up 31 places to becoming the third most popular brand in fashion.   [#image: /photos/5ce4338e1dc267f61ec7947d]||| ||| Versace 2017 marked the 20th death anniversary of Gianni Versace and the brand payed a tribute to its founder in the most remarkable way possible. Responsible for catapulting the supermodel phenomenon of the '90s, the then Versace girls had a reunion mimicking the Versace runway from the Gianni era. Carla Bruni-Sarkozy, Claudia Schiffer, Naomi Campbell, Cindy Crawford and Helena Christensen walked the runway for Versace spring 2018 giving the audience goosebumps with the wave of nostalgia.   [#image: /photos/5ce4338fb803116cf08f7867]||| ||| Azzedine Alaïa Tunisian-born couturier Azzedine Alaïa, dubbed the ‘King of Cling', died at the of 77. A mentor figure and inspiration to many fashion greats including Naomi Campbell and Alexander Fury, the industry mourned the loss of an icon.   [#image: /photos/5ce4338fa7e6a425158ed87a]||| ||| Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. Image: Rex Features Meghan Markle and Prince Harry's relationship is the internet's newest obsession. What drew more attention than Markle's fashion choices was the ring the Prince designed himself for his fiancé, using diamonds from his late mother's collection. Analysts have put the ring's worth down as invaluable. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Pamela Anderson: sex icon, social activist, lingerie mogul?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Why Pamela Anderson’s lingerie line isn’t like the rest View Gallery 4 Photos Pamela Anderson: sex icon, social activist, lingerie mogul? “We need to get more people in lingerie,” Pamela Anderson says from her seat on the second floor of London's Covent Garden Hotel. “People need to loosen up.” The actress, model and activist is in town to discuss her new co-branded lingerie collection, Pamela Loves Coco de Mer. Despite being often associated with risqué attire, the collaboration marks the first time Anderson, 50, has put her own name on a set of undergarments. And although she's been a longtime fan of the brand, which is known for its edgy yet classy approach to lingerie, it was only a year ago that Anderson connected with Coco der Mer managing director Lucy Litwack, while staying at this very hotel, overlooking the brand's London shop. “I think I have one of everything,” Anderson admits, “maybe two of some things.” “When [Lucy and I] met, it was like a match made in heaven because the brand is so me. We talked about me modelling for the Icon line, but we also talked about doing our own collection.” Inspired by '50s and '60s glamour, the collaboration pays tribute to film stars like Brigitte Bardot. It's meant to be playful, sexy and sophisticated. The bodysuits, which cut high up over the thighs, reference Anderson's iconic red swimsuit from Baywatch. Each item in the collection accentuates a woman's natural curves, which, according to Anderson, means that anyone, of any size, can wear them. “I was waiting for the right time, because I didn't necessarily want to do something very mass market and cheap,” Anderson says of designing lingerie. “I wanted to do something that was elegant and for everybody, but mid-range. Something really good quality. It's a perfect match because the brand is naughty and sexy. I'm a little twisted, and they're a little twisted.” For Anderson, the collection is meant to help women embrace their sexuality. She previously starred in a Rankin-shot short film for the brand around Valentine's Day, as well as in their Icon campaign. “My mother and my aunts always inspired me to be like this and enjoy it,” Anderson says. “I like that I can be a part of doing that for somebody else. But it all starts with yourself and feeling good about yourself. Keeping love alive is going to save the world, really. It's really important to have that kind of spark,” she laughs. The collection feels like a logical next step for Anderson, who has loved lingerie since she was young. When she first arrived in Los Angeles and started working for Playboy, she discovered the possibilities of underwear in the magazine's closet at the urging of the late Hugh Hefner. “I didn't have any clothes hardly,” she admits. “Hef used to tell my kids, ‘Your mom couldn't afford clothes when she got here.'” They had this huge closet and of course lots of lingerie. It was so fun to play in—it was like dress up. Stockings, garters and things I'd never even heard of before I went to Playboy. I want to encourage that.” Anderson has her hand in a lot of pots these days, from fashion to political and social activism, to filmmaking (“I don't really know what I want to be when I grow up,” she jokes). The German filmmaker Werner Herzog, who is known for his documentaries, is currently writing a feature film for her to star in. And Anderson's even considering directing her own film in the near future. She stepped behind the camera to shoot her son Dylan for ODDA magazine and hopes to do more of that soon. But activism remains her main focus, particularly animal rights. She feels hopeful about the progress the fashion industry is making when it comes to environmental concerns and the use of fur, exemplified by the recent Gucci fur ban. Anderson also recently sent American First Lady Melania Trump a fake fur coat and a letter asking her to be a better role model. “That doesn't mean I'm a Trump supporter,” Anderson notes. “I think as First Lady she can be very influential. I was hoping she would never wear fur, which she hasn't since we talked. I'm going to send the same to Kim [Kardashian]. These are the positive ways [to create change]: To send someone a gift and talk about it. You ask them to think about it.” What's New Wellness Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Manish Arora’s larger-than-life art installation in Mumbai is all about love
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Swarovski-studded graffiti walls and glow-in-the-dark facades View Gallery 4 Photos Manish Arora’s larger-than-life art installation is not to be missed If the kaleidoscopic excess of his designs hadn't tipped you off already, Manish Arora isn't one to do things quietly. His larger-than-life imagination finds expression on global runways, with individual outfits becoming instant conversation starters to be explored at length. So, it stands to reason that his idea of ending the year would involve a slew of big-ticket collaborations, from art installations to bejewelled chambers—and is there another international store on the cards? The Paco Rabanne alumni has lent his fashion savvy to the ongoing edition of St+Art India Mumbai 2017, an urban art festival that has so far added to the cityscape with a mural of Mahatma Gandhi at the iconic Churchgate station, and a sprawling exhibition at Sassoon Docks. Joining the milieu, the designer has taken over a landmark building, Jindal Mansion on Pedder Road, with an explosion of colours. Titled ‘All We Need Is Love', the installation involves 2,400 of his personal pieces that were worked on by a team of 35 artisans, who over a period of three months, crafted and mounted the final installation. “I want people to stop and ponder when they look at the installation and for that one minute, feel pure unadulterated love,” he admits, before adding, “In today's social and political environment, it's so important to remember that its love that makes us human and connects us all.” Adding to the sensory invasion is the ‘Ready To Love' mural, brought to life with glittering Swarovski crystals. Arora's penchant for whimsy can be seen in the neon lights silhouetting his handiwork. "‘Ready to Love' was inspired by my vision for a colourful utopia where I wanted to beckon visitors to enter a fantastical world full of emotions. A facade of an Indian temple was juxtaposed with dazzling neon lights, creating a true place of love. Each of the hearts in the room have been handcrafted with various traditional Indian techniques, even as an array of carefully crafted, jewel-adorned heart-fairies soar above. I wanted to leave people with an enchanting sight, a wonderful message, and for them to declare their love at the graffiti wall,” he smiles. And he isn't looking at taking things easy anytime soon. We hear the designer is looking to expand his presence on the map with a boutique in Shanghai, China, and will be joining hands with Designer Parfums to add to the ‘Ready To Love' franchise with an eponymous perfume, slated to launch globally in February 2018, and in India a month later. column1: Here’s what you need to know about Mugler’s new creative director
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet Casey Cadwallader After four years at the helm, David Koma is stepping down from his position at Mugler. His replacement is American designer Casey Cadwallader. Doesn't ring a bell? That's because Cadwallader has spent most of his career behind the scenes. After graduating from Cornell University with a degree in architecture, he worked at TSE, Narciso Rodriguez, Loewe, and J. Mendel before returning to Narciso Rodriguez to become design director for women's ready-to-wear and accessories. In 2015, he was appointed design director of Acne Studios's pre-collections, a position he held until being named creative director of Mugler. It's likely that Cadwallader's Mugler will look markedly different than that of his predecessor. During the tenure of the label's founder, Thierry Mugler, the brand stood for a techno-sexuality, embodied by cinched waists, a haute irreverence, and bold architectural curves. In recent memory, first under Nicola Formichetti and then Koma, Mugler became a mainstay of the after-dark scene, the place to shop for slinky, strong separates for a night out. If Cadwallader's résumé and Instagram page, which is flooded with images of fine art, are any indication, the designer has an architect's precision paired with a softer, more organic feel. “The Clarins Group is very happy to welcome Casey Cadwallader to Mugler,” said Sandrine Groslier, president of the Clarins Fragrance Group, Mugler Fashion and Fragrance, in a release. “His determination and unique sensitivity to Mugler's artistic and experimental heritage will enable us to pursue the renewal of the house in the long term. We are confident that his personal vision and talent will position Mugler among the most sought-after avant-garde fashion brands of today.” This story was previously published on Vogue.com Beauty Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Meghan Markle’s style file: Charting the actor’s fashion graph
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All the workwear inspiration you need View Gallery 39 Photos Style cues to take from Meghan Markle Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's story is a modern fairy tale. The couple met at a party in 2016 and have been caught in a whirlwind romance ever since. So, when Prince Harry finally got down on his knee and popped the question, news of their happily-ever-after spread like wildfire, quickly becoming a topic of interest for everyone following celebrity relationships. Every detail from the engagement ring Prince Harry gave Markle to the clothing choices this newly-engaged couple makes for public appearances has been brushed through with a fine-toothed comb. And while one can't deny Markle's great taste in men, the other thing we can't help but notice is her taste in fashion. Most popularly known for her role in the legal drama Suits, Markle effortlessly channels her character Rachel Zane's refined air off-screen with breezy blouses, midi skirts and neutral pumps to match. She is known for playing favourites, often choosing clothes from American designer Misha Nonoo and unique Canadian labels like LINE, whose white trench coat she paired with a dress from the Italian label Parosh at her first public interview, following the engagement. Whether she's dressed in draped looks or head-to-toe-black, Markle has always turned heads with her choice of clothing. The actor isn't afraid to don a pretty mini like the Alexander McQueen dress she wore at the Hunger Games: Catching Fire premiere in 2012 or the metallic mini she slipped on for the CFDA/ Vogue Fashion Fund Awards in 2015. And while she's traded in sundresses and lace frocks for sleek shirts and tailored trousers, Markle certainly knows how to keep things classy. Markle can often be spotted pairing blazers with matching shorts and sweaters with pencil skirts. Take for instance her outfit at the Invictus Games in Toronto, which happened to be her very first public appearance with her now-fiancé, where she opted for a crisp white shirt with distressed denims to keep things interesting. Whether she's settling for slouchy sophistication or going for something glamorous, Markle's sense of style is sure to keep fans interested as she prepares for her Royal Wedding come May 2018. Until then, scroll through our gallery to catch some of her most stylish moments till date. Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Fendi and Farfetch’s project brings you closer to owning a personalised bag
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Made to order View Gallery 4 Photos Fendi and Farfetch’s exclusive custom project is the next step in online shopping In the spirit of more and more luxury brands renewing the art of craftsmanship through customisation, Fendi and luxury e-commerce website Farfetch launch ‘Customize It', a made-to-order service that gives online shoppers across the globe a chance to personalise their very own Fendi bags. Available exclusively on Fendi.com and Farfetch.com, Customize It allows the buyer to bring their creativity onto the fashion house's offerings with a huge variety of contemporary colour palettes, logo styles and hardware add-ons to pick from. You can play around with 120 possible combinations for the bag and a further 70 for the strap, and include features like coloured leather, wrapped silk twill, conical studs and leather carved flowers. Perfect for those who desire the exclusivity of a custom handbag, skilled artisans from Fendi's Atelier in Florence will bring together each intricate detail of the chosen combination and have the item at your doorstep within 12 weeks. This project, which began last week, comes amidst a wave of digital innovation, including Farfetch's Store of The Future, which uses technology to take fashion to its root, allowing easier access to statement pieces made from scratch based on the customer's personal design. column1: Selena Gomez on going blonde, her Fashion Awards look and Instagram
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Texas-born pop star gets candid View Gallery 3 Photos How Selena Gomez’s Fashion Awards look came together “I haven't been in the space of doing the expected lately,” says Selena Gomez, the Texas-born pop star from her dressing room seat at Coach's Regent Street store. She's talking about going blonde, and, more importantly, her custom-made dress for tonight's Fashion Awards. “It's still in my comfort zone,” she says, “but I've loved being able to explore. A lot has kind of happened in the last year, and I'm enjoying wrapping it up in a way where I just feel it is exciting and fresh.” It is an understatement, of course. 2017 has been a significant year for the 'Bad Liar' singer. Less than a week after winning Billboard's Woman of the Year Award, Gomez also received a life-saving kidney transplant, started and ended a number of high-profile romantic relationships (The Weeknd and, more recently, Justin Bieber,) and released four chart-topping singles in the past twelve months—becoming the most-followed person on Instagram, with 130m followers, in the process. That rebellious streak is evident in her dress choice tonight: a long-sleeved, satin gown inspired by the runway collection, featuring a lace hem, tea rose details and small floral accents on the bodice. It's romantic and nostalgic, but in that “Coach American prairie spirit,” as the company's executive creative director Stuart Vevers put it. Paired with dark, goth-inspired makeup and wet-look hair, Gomez finishes off her “dark romance” ensemble with white lace-up boots. “I always feel like the accessories are the whip cream of an outfit, you know?” she says. “It's really important for me that Selena feels like her best,” explains Vevers, despite it being he who is nominated for an award, Accessories Designer of the Year, tonight. “I want [the dresses] to always to have an ease to them: a sense of movement and freedom. Coach has a down-to-earth approach to luxury, which is different from the traditional European houses,” adds Vevers. “I want to celebrate that ease; that New York City attitude.” This isn't the first time Vevers has created a bespoke look for Gomez—nor is it the first time they've co-designed something (the duo famously created the Selena Grace bag, now sold out worldwide despite having only launched in September). “Working with her is always really fun,” grins Vevers. “It's great sitting down and talking with a smart, creative person who's got a strong point of view.” When it comes to red carpet ensembles (Vevers was behind Gomez's Met Gala and American Music Awards looks earlier this year,) the starting point is always the same. “It's about something I feel strongly about—like a look or an idea; a silhouette or decoration—and then it's that conversation with Selena about how she feels at that moment.” Which begs the question, how does she feel right now? “I feel bold,” she smiles from behind her blonde fringe, “I feel strong, and I feel like me.” Before hitting the red carpet, she spent hours in Coach's Regent Street store, signing autographs and meeting her fans, many of whom queued for hours. “It's one of my favourite parts of my job. This is the moment where we get to celebrate all the work [my team and I] have done, when I get to include [my fans] in my work, and also just say hi and hang out.” Speaking about her record-breaking Instagram following, she call it a “strong connection.” As Gomez says,“It is something that I feel is very personal,” skirting the issue of what she once saw as a toxic environment which led her to relinquish control to her assistant. “I do think it is a great place to make a statement—whatever that statement is.” The clothes she wears are another way to make a statement, too. As is her hair. “The blonde has made me feel a little bolder, and I feel confident. I wake up every morning thinking ‘oh my gosh,' it's just different for me.” Different, it turns out, isn't always a bad thing. Beauty Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How to wear dramatic gowns in your 20s
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you need to have your own red carpet moment Blame it on all the fairytales we've been steadily spoon-fed through our childhood, but gowns will always have an otherworldly charm to them. If you don't remember staring doe-eyed at an ethereal 5-foot-something concoction of tulle and lace when you were eight, you may want to borrow a time machine and redo your childhood. Once you hit your 20s, the possibilities multiply, from full skirted ballgowns to crystal-encrusted trains to sleek silhouettes with risqué cutouts. Now that you have the motive and the means to take this red carpet staple for a spin, allow us to walk through the basics to ensure that you have your very own showstopper moment to keep as a souvenir. Get it right Bear in mind that the 20s provide you with the leeway to test-drive a plethora of non-boring styles, so you're honour-bound to make the most of your sartorial hall pass. That showstopper gown with the bold cutouts you spotted on the runways that you didn't think you had it in you to pull off? Skip the bikini-bods-only disclaimer, and make the dress work for you rather than the other way around. If hitting the gym a few days before makes you feel more confident, do it. That gorgeous gown with the risqué slit you haven't been able to muster up the courage to wear outside the trial room? Slip on the right inner wear, pin everything securely and take it out for a spin. There are no rules to this game–except the ones that we tell you, of course. View Gallery 31 Photos How to wear gowns in your 20s – Celebrities Borrow from the best The 20s mark the formative years of your sartorial sensibilities, and if you're still finding your footing and deciding what your signature style should be, take heart from the A-lister names who have been in your shoes. Alia Bhatt keeps her sprightly girl-next-door persona alive with voluminous princess-gowns and strapless numbers that veer just on the right side of sexy. As Kriti Sanon's career graph acquires an edgy note, you'll find her sporting bolder cutouts and flirty slits. Athiya Shetty, meanwhile, wisely plays up her best assets and ensures that her abs have their moment in the spotlight. Ever the charmer, Disha Patani flits from sheer gowns and plunging necklines to elegant capes and flowy trains. Inner wear is everything For something that won't be seen, you'd be surprised at the veto power that this one wardrobe item holds over your entire look. Peekaboo straps, ill-fitted cups and visible seams can, and will gladly, rain on your parade. Once you've picked the fairy tale gown of your dreams, drop everything and make a beeline for the lingerie counter. Halter necks require certain kind of bras, while a strapless number calls for an entirely different type of corset. Every gown is different, and there's no room for negotiation when it comes to the right inner garments to complement your final look. Accessories can be a deal-breaker Any gown is only as good as the accessories it is paired with. Statement jewellery is all well and good, but you don't want to have too much of a good thing. If you're picking maximalist earrings, take a rain check on the necklace and vice versa. Likewise, when it comes to shoes, you don't want to go too matchy-matchy with your gown, while also hitting the delicate balance between style and comfort. You may want to consider not buying the gown and the accessories in the same session as it's easy to get carried away with the excitement of it all, only to go home and question your purchases. When possible, keep your gown fittings for one day, sleep on it and then finalise your accompanying accessories the next day to ensure that your final look is something that you're absolutely confident about. Silhouette matters You don't need to have the entire lexicon of body types down pat, but ensure that you're familiar with your body type and what works for you to make your designer's job easier. Confidence is 90 per cent of what's requisite for working a gown, and if you're not comfortable, it will definitely show. When you're starting out in your 20s, a gown often tends to be an investment purchase, one that you'll be comfortable carrying off in the long term as well. If you're petite, be on your guard against the oversized trend, as it can easily swamp your frame. If you're lean on the torso, a halter neck is just what you need to play up your assets. Curvy women, let us see those Spanish ruffles and fit-and-flare ballgowns. Like what you've seen so far? Take your pick from the Vogue edit of the most drool-worthy gowns available right now. Keeping with the theme of the awards, the stars turned out in their sartorial best: while Deepika Padukone chose a scarlet gown by Gauri & Nainika, Kareena Kapoor Khan went all-white in a sheer and 3-D floral look by Galia Lahav. Ever a fan of being the belle of the ball, Sonam Kapoor chose a sparkly gold strapless gown by Atelier Zuhra for the evening. Katrina Kaif went with a risqué cut-out number by Jean Paul Gaultier, while Alia Bhatt picked a demure, baby pink floral dress. Kriti Sanon also chose a deep red embellished gown by Zara Umrigar and Sonkashi Sinha went with a steel grey ensemble by Nupur Kanoi. Sridevi made a statement with an embellished gown by Ziad Nakad. The men weren't too far behind—Shahid Kapoor, Prateik Babbar, Harsh Kapoor, Hritik Roshan, Varun Dhavan arrived in dapper suits for the awards ceremony. column1: En Inde and Anavila’s latest collaboration is for fans of the colour black
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Shop your favourites Only a true-blue shopaholic can separate the experience of choosing from a curated selection versus going through the entire inventory of a brand on a website. Mumbai's concept design store, Bungalow 8 will be bringing two design labels with complimenting aesthetics to manifest the concept of ‘foiling'. Sari label Anavila and progressive jewellery label En Inde will be showcasing their latest works along with a special capsule collection featuring the art of foiling. The Indian consumer is no stranger to the use of metal in festive wear. Foiling involves beating metal into thin strips and incorporating these into the body of design. Anavila Misra has juxtaposed metallic yarn against black in her saris for this capsule collection. "It feels good to see how the linen saree has become a wardrobe staple, but of late I have also felt the urge to step back and revisit some of my designs that perhaps deserved more space and attention and I was delighted when Maithili [Ahluwalia] approached me with this idea of distilling it down to black and metal," says the designer. On the other hand, Anupama Sukh Lalwani and Sonal Sood of En Inde have put together a collection for Bungalow 8 exhibiting their signature style in free flowing black and gold threads, leather, stainless steel, gold plated stainless steel and jute. “This capsule collection is a resurrection of the En Inde classics. They express a simple sense of personal luxury. Can something be classic and relevant at the same time? En Inde creations continually addresses this question. For Bungalow 8, I have taken this idea using an ever classic and relevant color, Black and used it with the essential jute and steel to reimagine our classics,” said Lalwani, creative director and founder of En Inde. Looking for occasion wear that stands out in a crowd? Head to Bungalow 8 to get your hands on the exclusive capsule collection along with Anavila and En Inde's latest collections. Foiling by Bungalow 8 will be hosted on December 2 between 12pm-8pm at Bungalow 8, Wankhede Stadium, North Stand E & F Block, D Road, Churchgate, Mumbai Beauty Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 13 bridal lehengas designs that will be big this wedding season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Do you have a favourite? View Gallery 14 Photos Bridal lehengas designs that will be big this wedding season While choosing the perfect bridal lehenga design for your big day, how do you get ahead of the pack to pick the right design for your big day? Brides usually favour more classic silhouettes so as to not look too outlandish on the important occasion. But the right one bears the perfect blend of the designer's signature style with traditional detailing. When choosing a bridal lehenga—be it for your pheras or the reception—pretty much the only thing you must keep in mind is to choose one that will make a statement. For a touch of old-world charm, there's no going wrong with Sabyasachi lehengas. Pair yours with knockout jewellery by the designer to complete the look effortlessly. If your dream wedding looks something out of a fairytale, choose a Tarun Tahiliani lehenga complete with a trailing veil. For a seriously glamorous reception look, there is no doubt a Manish Malhotra lehenga will do justice to the occasion. Embrace the beading, fringing and the general extravagance of bridal lehenga designs by the designer . Anita Dongre lehengas are for the bride who wants to go for a traditional look on her wedding day. Sanjay Garg's kurta-lehenga combination is perfect for the understated bride. From Rahul Mishra's hand-embroidered gossamer number to Varun Bahl's floral extravagance, these are the bridal lehenga designs that will big this wedding season. column1: Twinkle Khanna proves there is no going wrong with a shirtdress
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The modern basic you can’t live without View Gallery 3 Photos Twinkle Khanna proves there is no going wrong with a shirtdress Time and again, the shirtdress has proved to be the saviour in the urban woman's wardrobe. Equal parts formal and comfortable, the cosier cousin of the shift can be worn at a brunch, for an evening out and even to work. Twinkle Khanna, whose sartorial choices remain sensible and perfect for city wear, was seen in a striped shirtdress at an event last evening. Khanna paired hers with a simple pair of black lace-up pumps that complemented her style basic. Staying in the classics category, Khanna's choice of navy and white stripes kept her look elegant while the knotted detail on the front of the dress, made it contemporary. The interior designer and author went with a signature blowout and pink lips. When it came to accessories, she favoured hoops and a gold Bulgari Serpentini watch. You can try Twinkle Khanna's versatile shirtdress for choice this weekend. Dress up the basic with a pair of metallic heels, tasseled earrings and a belt for an evening out. column1: Budget buys: 10 jackets and coats that will help you keep cosy in style
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Winter wardrobe MVPs View Gallery 10 Photos Budget buys: 10 jackets and coats that will help you keep cosy in style With temperatures dipping (finally) and winter fast approaching, it's time to give your wardrobe an annual makeover. Stay cosy this season with the most versatile part of your wardrobe—jackets and coats. From double breasted jackets and velvet ones to faux fur coats, there's something to suit everyone's needs. As you step out for a sun-kissed weekend brunch, opt for a velvet jacket with pearl detailing by H&M or throw on a Zara denim jacket with detailed sleeves. For a night about town, nothing does the trick like an elegant metallic jacket. If you're after a borrowed-from-the-boys vibe, then opt for oversized hooded coat by Monki. Those looking to make a statement with bold colours should style the bright red duster coat by Miss Selfridge with flared denims. The trick lies in balancing the proportions. Invest in knee-high boots and minimal accessories to complete the look. Go through our edit of stylish coats and jackets that will keep you warm this winter season. What's more? column1: 15 designer wedding lehengas, saris and more for minimalist brides
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Subtle does it View Gallery 15 Photos 15 stunning designer outfits that are made for minimalist brides With "less is more" making a comeback, weddings are no longer just about heavily-embellished lehengas and designer saris with sweeping trails. Whether you've envisioned an intimate destination wedding or a private affair with close family members, it's your sartorial choices that will help you channel the vibe you seek. If you're looking to add subtle opulence to your wedding wardrobe, place your bets on simple yet statement making ensembles. Trade the bright coloured sharara sets with nude anarkalis for day ceremonies. You can also look at embroidered jackets with basic twirl-worthy skirts that don't need a dupatta to complete the look. For your cocktail party, pre-draped designer saris can also substitute the traditional six-yard silhouette. Look at labels like Astha Narang and Dheeru and Nikita for a new approach to the traditional bridal sari. The fashion-forward yet minimalist bride can opt for an off-shoulder sari blouse. If you're all about understated elegance, then choose a brocade lehenga and let the fabric do the talking. If you thought minimal dressing is bound to be boring, you're mistaken. Choose from mint green lehengas to those with floral detailing, and of course traditional red numbers. Say goodbye to heavy traditional ensembles and say hello to easy silhouettes. The trick lies in balancing the elements. While most brides are fans of heavy embroidery, stay true to your own style. Ditch the fairy tale gowns and choose from interesting silhouettes. Play with versatile accessories and jewellery that will pop against the neutral tone of your outfits. We tracked down the perfect edit outfits that are sure to please a minimalist bride. Scroll through our slideshow and bookmark your favourites. column1: Looking for a cool sweater? We’ve got 22 options to pick from
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Warm up to comfort and style View Gallery 22 Photos 22 sweaters to keep you warm this winter As we slip into the December chill, statement coats and leather jackets are sure to make a splash, but the sartorial equivalent of the burrito-blanket mood you can't fight off is the quintessential winter sweater. The best qualities of a sweater lie in its comfort and versatility. But, while neutrals such as those by Acne Studios and Burberry are a necessary closet basic, nothing battles those winter blues better than a pop of colour. Brighten up your wardrobe with Raey's royal blue cable-knit sweater and Sies Marjan's fuzzier bright pink one. While sweaters have a tendency to be considered more for their function than form, there's no reason this winter staple can't be a stylish part of your daily wear. When dressing for a wind-beaten day, opt for elements that are lively but low-key like Allude's floral graphics and  Chloé's colourful fluff. Meanwhile, the frosty after-hours warrant a darker shade with detailing like Michael Kors' feathery infusion, Isabel Marant's shimmering threads or Esteban Cortazar's sheer number. The best way to make a statement is by having it plastered across your outfit, so load up on these cheeky slogan sweaters by Gucci and Lingua Franca. But if what you're really looking for is a comfortable knit, invest in quality cashmere pieces like those by Valentino. column1: 31 outfits that you will definitely need this December
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion End of year treats View Gallery 31 Photos 31 outfits that are perfect for an amazing December There is no month on the calendar quite like December. Filled with parties, weddings and Christmas cheer, there is an infectious air of merrymaking that makes you want to dress up every single day. With a loaded social calendar ahead of you, we've got the perfect wardrobe edit to keep you in your party best. Nothing speaks elegance like a dress. Whether it's a short, black, one-shoulder number for a night of dancing or a floral number for a New Year's Eve by the beach, the one-outfit-wonder is a must-have in your closet. We are crushing on fringes, velvet and sparkly looks this season. Jumpsuits make for excellent alternatives if you get bored of dresses. Choose something with lace inserts or a dramatic number with a train. Look to coordinated sets for a different approach to an ensemble. Given the popularity of weddings towards the end of the year, be armed with saris, lehengas and anarkalis that will come handy for events demanding a festive wardrobe. Last but not the least, pair your favourite pair of jeans with a luxe bodysuit for a cheat day. Scroll through our gallery of the perfect ensembles to wear this December. column1: Aditi Rao Hydari makes an anarkali jacket and long skirt set work for a flight
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Florals for the win View Gallery 3 Photos Aditi Rao Hydari show you how to wear an anarkali jacket with a long skirt If there's one thing Aditi Rao Hydari nails every time, it's easy ethnic wear. She was spotted at Mumbai airport yesterday, foregoing the athleisure airport uniform for an ivory anarkali jacket and matching skirt by Rahul Mishra. The hand-embroidered micro florals on the anarkali added a delicateness to the outfit in contrast to the geometric motifs on the border of the skirt. The hints of orange and yellow in her ensemble brightened up the otherwise understated colour palette. As is important for any travel look, comfort was central to Rao Hydari's fuss-free look. Keeping it simple, actor offset the floral ensemble with silver jhumkas, brick brown lips, dewy make-up, naturally blow-dried hair and mascara. Known to update ethnic numbers with a twist, actor's anarkali jacket and skirt set made for a refreshing change from all the athleisure usually spotted at the airport. If you aren't one to go heavy on the bling and are looking to make maximum impact with minimum effort, take cues from actor's recent ensemble and opt for a light anarkali. column1: Mrinalini Chandra’s jewellery collection is perfect for Candy Crush addicts
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Sugar rush View Gallery 7 Photos Mrinalini Chandra’s jewellery collection is perfect for Candy Crush addicts Mrinalini Chandra might refer to her eponymous brand as a small craft-based one, but trend forecasting agency WGSN have clearly put their bets on her. After listing her as the top jewellery designer in Asia, Chandra's work caught the eye of King Digital Entertainment, the company that owns the popular phone game Candy Crush. Candy Crush is expanding on its merchandise in fashion sector, such as the brand's collaboration with Moschino for autumn/winter 2017. Blending Chandra's signature meenakari work with Candy Crush's pop colours and shapes, Mrinalini Chandra will be launching four such capsule collections for the next two years. Starting with a contemporary line of necklaces, bracelets, earrings, brooches and rings inspired by the game, Chandra wanted to offer the first range to wider audience. The second collection has a festive touch to it and will also have kaliras for the alternate bride. The following collection will have menswear accessories lie pins and cufflinks. For jewellery label based between Benaras and Jaipur, producing hand painted jewellery in large quantities would pose a problem. “We created the casts for the jewellery using 3-D printing for the sake of uniformity. The enamelling was done by hand, maintaining the brand's DNA,” the designer tells us. And while the collection was made to suit the taste of the local audience, making something that would be shopped with equal enthusiasm overseas was a challenge. “We went back and forth on the use of gold and perfecting the enamel colours even though they were hand processed, but I am so happy with the final product,” Chandra, nervous but thoroughly pleased with her handiwork. The debut collection of rings, necklaces, bracelets and earrings will be launched in India on Mrinalinichandra.com on November 29, following which it will be made available on Myntra.com. The line will also be showcased world over through various trade fairs. Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why Meghan Markle’s engagement ring is being valued ‘priceless’ by experts
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And other details about the wedding announcement View Gallery 9 Photos Why Meghan Markle’s engagement ring is valued by experts as ‘priceless’ Easily the most popular couple of 2017, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle took their relationship to the next level when the prince went down on one knee with a ring and popped the question to the American actor and humanitarian earlier this month. Not surprisingly, the royal couple has been making headlines ever since the formal announcement by Clarence House earlier this week. The ring in question is unique and thoughtfully-designed by the prince himself and created by Cleave & Company, Queen Elizabeth II's preferred jeweller. Made of diamonds, the centre stone was sourced from Botswana where Prince Harry travelled to while growing up, and also happens to be where he celebrated Markle's 36th birthday. The diamonds surrounding it come from the late Princess Diana's personal jewellery collection, the stones are set in yellow gold, which is Markle's favourite. Given the significance of the diamonds being from Princess Diana's collection, and sentiment surrounding to each of the elements, experts have valued the ring as priceless, according to Money. The happy couple posed for pictures in their first official photo call yesterday, where Markle was seen in green dress and white trench coat by Canadian-based label Line, and a pair of tie-up pumps. It's a given that the Line will be expecting a heavy flow of orders now that a royal has been spotted wearing it. When Kate Middleton opted for a dress by Anita Dongre during her visit to India, the designer spoke about the chaos that followed. “The phone has been ringing non-stop. I have barely been able to work at all. The site crashed and the IT team was up all night fixing it. I guess we went overboard with the Instagram posts but I am such a fan of her style I couldn't help myself. Sold out? I'm beyond sold out and the orders are still pouring in!” she said. Historically, royal weddings lead to much public curiosity and it goes without saying that when Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's takes place in spring 2018, it will be one of the most heavily-reported events seen till date. column1: This pop-up brings together all you need for a destination wedding wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion For brides and their crews View Gallery 6 Photos This exciting pop-up is just what you need to make your destination wedding wardrobe stand out It's wedding season all around, which means you've probably got plans of jet-setting away to some exotic location as part of the celebration. But between clearing out your schedule and filling up your suitcase, knowing what to pack can be tough, especially if you're looking to stand out and make a statement. Luckily, this collaboration has got all your destination wedding demands covered. Luxury concept store Le Mill, fashion designer Surily Goel and jewellery designer Kajal Fabiani have come together to curate ‘Memorable Matches', a two-day trunk show at Pali Hill, Bandra between November 28 and 29. As the name may suggest, ‘Memorable Matches' is all about inspired pairings of Indian outfits with international labels, styled by Vogue India's fashion director and leading celebrity stylist, Anaita Shroff Adajania. Think high-end labels like Saint Laurent, Alexander McQueen, Balmain and Balenciaga mixed with the ethnic elegance of Surily G designs, and topped off with accents by Kajal Fabiani's KAJ Fine Jewellery. The idea is to shake things up and explore refreshing ways to style those wedding staples. Whether its adding the contemporary touch of a crop top to your traditional sari or a jacket to your lehenga, ‘Memorable Matches' not only promises to leave you with a unique and interesting wedding trousseau, but a renewed perspective on styling wedding wear as well. Speaking of the demands of modern customer, Surily Goel says “I have always believed that it's very important for our clients to bring their personality and their style into our garments. Inspired by destination weddings and the growing needs of my clients, the new collection has pieces that can be worn together or separates. Women today are looking for something unusual, and Anaita would help marry my Indian creations with international labels.” Kajal Fabiani agrees, “Destination weddings have become increasingly common and it's important for our clients to have access to pieces that are easily wearable. Due to safety concerns our clients don't want to carry separate jewellery for each occasion.” While attendance at this exclusive pop-up is by appointment only, the special trunk show has been established with the aim of evolving into an annual edition, including a travelling version that caters to other metro cities in India. So, if you're looking to spruce up your vacation wedding wardrobe, this one-of-a-kind event is worth an appointment. Weddings Weddings Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And other incredibly beautiful pieces of jewellery View Gallery 7 Photos Sotheby’s to sell the largest round diamond ever to be offered to auction December is officially the season for shimmer, shine and all things sparkly. Just in time for the holidays, Sotheby's is hosting two auctions, Magnificent Jewels, and Fine Jewels on December 5 and 7, in New York. The Magnificent Jewels auction will display a 5.69-Carat Vivid Blue Diamond Ring (estimated price 12/15 million dollars) and an extremely rare 110.92-Carat Round Diamond (estimated price 4.2/6.2 million dollars), the largest round diamond ever to be offered at a Sotheby's auction. Expect to find a slew of vintage and contemporary pieces like vivid yellow diamond and diamond earrings, elegant sapphire and diamond bracelet by Van Cleef & Arpels, Paris, rare sapphire and diamond ear clips by Harry Winston, an exquisite orangish-pink diamond ring, and more by prominent houses including Tiffany & Co., JAR, and Cartier, along with noteworthy gemstones. If you're looking for impressive coloured stones to match your fashion-forward ensembles, this auction also offers a variety of vibrant rubies, emeralds and sapphires. On the other hand, the Fine Jewels sale will put an end to all your gifting dilemmas as it brings fashionable pieces for every style and occasion at accessible price points. From classic diamond rings to whimsical brooches, here you'll find something for almost everyone on your list this season. column1: The best bridesmaid dresses for all kinds of church weddings
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Instagram perfect View Gallery 9 Photos The best bridesmaid dresses to make a statement in this wedding season – Celebrities While we are all fans of the week-long Bollywood hits-fuelled affair that is the great Indian wedding, church weddings have their own charm. The coordinated bridal party, corsages, the chapel, all make for a picture-perfect setting that will stay in memories for years to come. And of course, one of the most crucial aspects of making the pictures truly memorable is finding the perfect bridesmaids dresses to complement the bride's gown. There are many ways to go about dressing the bride's troupe. You can choose for everyone to wear the same dress, you can look at several styles from one designer's collection or choose a theme and go freestyle with it. What's most important to keep in mind for a church wedding is the overarching vision you have for it and execute it to perfection. Bridesmaid dresses can be based on the bride's choice of gown. If the bride has an elaborate number, bridesmaid dresses can be dressy gowns. Take inspiration from Sonam Kapoor's floor grazing numbers. For a glam bride, bridesmaids can also be dressed in embellished outfits, like Deepika Padukone's Sabyasachi dress. For an intimate wedding look, at Kangana Ranaut's tidy but bold yellow dress. Certain dos and don'ts apply when picking for a bridesmaid's dress. Keeping in mind the somber setting of the church, it's best to avoid anything that's too revealing. Having said that, your bridesmaids don't have to look deathly boring. Draw on trends like ruffles, metallics and sequins for a unique take on bridesmaid dresses. Pastel hues in luxe fabrics might be done over and over again, but there's a reason that the formula works. If your bridesmaids are disputed on one look, choose an umbrella theme like florals or a colour and allow them to pick a dress within the context. column1: Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla on bridal wear, films and the joy of designing
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The stalwarts have spoken View Gallery 17 Photos Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla on bridal wear, films and the joy of designing “We design for ourselves, full stop,” Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla categorically state when asked how they manage to remain relevant even 30 years after they launched their couture label. “Great design isn't made for an audience. Instead, it always finds an appreciative one.” This credo has served the duo well, indeed—they started out in 1986, when designer wear was still an unfamiliar concept, and have eventually played a pioneering role in shaping the Indian fashion industry. While their sensibility has always been rooted in classical elegance, they haven't shied away from embracing the future through the reinvention of technique, craft and silhouette. But at the end of the day, it ultimately boils down to a reverence for beauty, finesse and detail for them. “This informs not just our sensibilities, but also our lifestyle and every single ensemble we put our name to.” Their journey is peppered with several milestones—being the first to use chiffon, georgette and organza; winning the National Award for Costume Design for Devdas; and dressing the likes of Dame Judi Dench and Beyoncé are only a few of the many. Their army of loyalists boasts the likes of Amitabh Bachchan, Jaya Bachchan, Dimple Kapadia, Amrita Singh, Shweta Bachchan Nanda and Sonam Kapoor. But it's not the mere matter of dressing celebrities in their case; the designers have become ones in their own right. As they look back on “30 years of a life fully lived, and a journey packed with adventure, ambition and passion,” the stalwarts speak to Vogue about how they do it (on their own terms). When you started out in 1986, designer wear was still a niche concept. What has the evolution of the brand been like? We didn't define our work or classify it as designer wear. We knew we were passionate about expressing our creativity, and that that creativity was informed by a zealous commitment to the finest. Sans shortcuts or compromise. For any artist, that expression is a continuum. The drive and passion to excel, to set impossible standards, meet them, and then raise the bar higher is key. The evolution of the brand has been a natural result of our own creative progression. Whether it is our work in interior design or adding diffusion and western wear through new labels like ASAL by Abu Sandeep and Khosla Jani, this growth has been fuelled by our relentless ambition to work in new mediums and fulfil new dreams. ASAL by Abu Sandeep is diffusion wear that carries all the hallmarks and sensibilities of our couture but diffused to reach a wider and different demographic. Khosla Jani is our international, western wear label, steeped in romance and carries forth the mystique of Hollywood in its golden era. The idea is to challenge ourselves as artists as well as to expand our own vision and expression. Describe the woman you were designing for back then. How has she changed today? We have never designed for anyone in particular, always for ourselves, and what our own joy and satisfaction dictated. Today's couture client is definitely more exposed, adventurous and open to experimentation. However we also miss the more ‘natural' self-created individualistic sense of style, which wasn't so trend-conscious or prone to clone-like conformity. Rather, it was set by one's own sense of style. We are fortunate that those who appreciate our creativity tend to be men and women who are confident, discerning and prefer to please themselves, rather than fit in or conform to outside rules. We like to think of couture as being something people deserve rather than need. Your label is known for reviving traditional techniques like chikankari, mirror work and zardozi, among others. How do you reinvent these to appeal to the modern Indian woman? We reinvent techniques for our own satisfaction and to follow our own calling. For instance, it was our first trip to Lucknow that ignited our imagination and mission to revive and reinvent chikankari. The modern Indian woman, much like Indian women through the ages, are delighted by beauty, by dressing up, and by celebrating their femininity through their clothes and accessories. It isn't a case of creating something that appeals to them. It's about creating something appealing that they will naturally be drawn to. How have you managed to remain an unwavering favourite with brides over the years? By constantly upping our own game. By digging deep into our own creative reserves and letting the sky be the limit for our own ambition and imagination. By never resting on our laurels or changing our core sensibilities or aesthetics. By setting trends rather than following them. Our madness has its method. Create that which satisfies you, and you will create a market for your work. Cater to a market and its demands, and you will soon run out of both steam and success. It is never enough to draw from the well of one's legacy. One must always push further and leave one's own stamp on the classical. How has the Indian bride evolved in her tastes and preferences, and what is she looking for according to you? Every bride dreams of the perfect wedding, and her ensembles are key to that fantasy. Brides have become more adventurous when it comes to sartorial choices. Weddings have become more cosmopolitan with theme nights that call for western wear. We don't cater to the bridal market. We create bridal couture that reflects our own inspiration and sensibilities. So we created chikan, khadi, and white and beige ensembles. It's all about twisting and breaking traditional rules for us. We have always found that brides who possess a sense of adventure have lapped these up. What is the key to reinventing Indian bridal wear without compromising on its traditional essence? It is a je ne sais quoi that cannot be defined. You have to strike an unquantifiable balance between the reinvention of and reverence for tradition. It is, of course, an art to know what to leave behind and what to retain. If it ain't broke, don't fix it. And if you are going to fix it then make sure it's better than what was broke. We are designers not writers. The art is the statement. Was the launch of your cocktail line a conscious decision to present outfits that cater to pre-wedding functions as well? We don't make conscious decisions. That is the methodology of businessmen. The need to create drives us. It is emotional, not cerebral. We didn't do western wear as part of the herd or to capitalise on a new market demand. When we became enthused and driven to design dresses and gowns, we began designing them and our label, Khosla Jani was born. If it isn't a compulsion, it's just a product, and remains a mediocre one at that. It has to be a mad restlessness and unbridled passion if you're going to excel at your craft. You are also working on the costumes for Veere Di Wedding. How is working on movies different from designing for the runway for you? For us, film is as real as the runway. These aren't just costumes, they are the character's wardrobe. So the same attention to detail, quality, and personal style is given to a film ensemble as we would give to a made-to-measure outfit for a client. The character, her personality, spirit, mood, situation and physical beauty all come into play. So it isn't like designing for the runway, it is designing a custom ensemble for X. There is no compromise on quality whatsoever just because it's for the screen. This is why we work so rarely in cinema, as we can't cut corners. It is against our sensibilities as artists. Rhea Kapoor, who is a trendsetter herself having introduced the concept of celebrity styling and dressing in India, is producing Veere Di Wedding. We have worked closely with her for years to develop looks for Sonam (Kapoor), who is our muse. When Rhea approached us, it was an instant yes, an absolute no-brainer to design for her movie. We love all the girls in the movie (Sonam Kapoor, Kareena Kapoor Khan, Swara Bhaskar and Shikha Talsania), and with Rhea and Ekta Kapoor as producers, it was a delight to collaborate on this project. Rhea sat with our team and us, and we developed looks for each character. It's been a great experience. Fashion Fashion Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How to make sustainable choices when shopping for your wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Navigating ethical fashion While Stella McCartney showed “alter croc”, “alter nappa” and alter everything at Paris Fashion Week, Zara-wearers in Istanbul found hidden notes of protest in their jackets that read “I made this item you are going to buy, but I didn't get paid for it.” Just three years after the Rana Plaza factory tragedy, an H&M factory in Dhaka caught fire due to lack of necessary safety parameters in place. Around the same time, the fast-fashion giant presented its Conscious Exclusive collection made from ocean shoreline plastic waste that typically takes 450 years or more to break down. These paradoxes in the world of fashion are almost impossible to overlook, but between the smoke and mirrors there's a welcome new awareness to herald. No longer is “sustainability” a cloudy myth, avoided or tossed around with little meaning. How? You must be thinking. Here's a definitive guide to help you build a mindful wardrobe where the journey of every piece can be traced back to its beginnings. And where your choices really matter. REUSE, RECYCLE Drop your old clothes in-store at H&M—the store has clothing collection bins tucked away in its corners. In 2015, the high-street giant collected more than 12,000 tons of garments. 12,000 tons = fabric for 60 million T-shirts(!). Home grown Indian labels like Péro and Amit Aggarwal have a minimum waste policy. Rubbished scraps of fabric are either used as patchwork on other garments, made into accessories and bags or upcycled into entire brand-new collections. Amit Aggarwal's label AM.IT used recycled Patola saris to create dresses for its summer/resort 2017 collection, ‘Seamless'. “These saris usually end up being sold as wall-hangings or kitschy upholstery in street markets, which in my opinion is largely underutilising the textile,” said the designer of his upcycling initiative, in a previous interview. KNOW YOUR CLOTHES For all of us who buy most of our wardrobes from fast-fashion brands, there's a way to know what you're spending that Rs 1,890 on. Pressure from keen and loyal shoppers, led to high-street giants assimilating their eco-friendly initiatives with mainstream collections. Racks of Zara's Join Life and Conscious by H&M have been pulled out from the depths of the stores and now bask front and centre. Zara releases an annual sustainability report, while H&M carries out numerous sustainable projects under its head of sustainability, Anna Gedda. “When we engage customers, they realise they are part of the solution and that their opinion matters. We can definitely see a growing interest in more sustainable fashion from our customers,” said Gedda, while spotlighting plans of using only sustainable and organic cotton by 2020. ECO-CHIC COLLABORATIONS Parley for the Oceans, a think tank of creatives and leaders creating awareness about the fragility of the world's rivers, seas and lakes, partnered with Adidas in 2015 to create shoes made from plastic. Now they're going to make a collection of clothes from thread made from plastic. Anita Dongre introduced her sustainable option Grassroot in 2015 in an attempt to revive indigenous crafts of India by surging the skill at grass root level. Partnering with NGOs that work with local artisans around the country, the label mixes its urban aesthetic with hand crafts like chikankari, Warli and katha embroidery. VEGAN Have you heard of pineapple leather? What about bags made of cork? Yep, these are all legit substitutes for leather. And surprisingly, not far from the real thing. You'll be surprised. Grain, a boutique started out of Bandra by designer and illustrator Avinash Bhalerao, serves up bags for him and her in Ahimsa leather. Ahimsa leather is made from recycled skin of dead animals have not been slaughtered. In the celebrity realm, Sonam and Rhea Kapoor's label Rheson, received a PETA Compassionate Business Award for its easy on the pocket animal-friendly bags. CONSCIOUSLY COOL Then, there are labels that are just inherently eco-friendly. Reformation, the Los Angeles based celebrity-approved label, watches its carbon footprint using an in-house RefScale. Their dreamy dresses (seen on Alexa Chung and Taylor Swift) are made in partnership with responsible manufacturing houses. Barcelona brand, Sea2see turns ocean plastic into sunglasses perfect for every summer holiday. For every 10 kilos of plastic brought in from the ocean, one pair of glasses can be made. With more than eight million tons of plastic thrown into our seas each year, these sunglasses are a necessary step to clean up the oceans. Making small but steady differences in all our quotidian closets could finally add up in the larger scheme of things. After all, who doesn't love fashion with a heart? column1: 40-plus designer blouse styles to check out for the wedding season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Your ultimate guide View Gallery 30 Photos The best designer blouses for the wedding season – celebrity Never has there been a better time to curate an Indian ethnic wear wardrobe. Individuality and inventiveness are encouraged and the same ol' isn't your only modus operandi. But as you set out to amass a bevy of designer lehengas, saris, and shararas this wedding season, stop to give the not-so-humble-anymore blouse its due attention as well. Treating it as an afterthought just won't do, as this erstwhile supporting act could very well turn out to be the hero of your look. Vogue shines the spotlight on some must-have designer blouses from our go-to fashion labels and Bollywood celebrities. Versatile favourites like a mirror work blouse (with scallops for added impact) and neutral metallic variants never disappoint, as they can amp up a simple chiffon sari just as easily as they can an embellished lehenga. The same goes for Benarasi and gota blouses that lend themselves well to mixing-and-matching. Turn to Indian fashion designers like Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla, Arpita Mehta, and Anavila Misra for fitting finds. And while traditional blouse styles may be the designated dress code for certain wedding functions, you are bound to be tempted to try on the blouse's reinvented versions for events like the mehandi, sangeet and reception. Don't resist the urge, we insist. Off-shoulder designer blouses remain au courant as ever, particularly with bridesmaids, to give their looks a spot of coquettish charm, and this is just what designers like Masaba, Payal Singhal, and Gaurav Gupta among others offer. Fringes and tassels are another winner this season. Take baby steps with tasselled sleeves or better yet, go all the way for that unrivalled Boomerang from the sangeet after-party. Jani and Khosla, Manish Malhotra, and Ridhi Mehra are some of the names you ought to consider. The focus, though, is largely on the sleeves this time around—from cape sleeves and floor-skimming fringes to ruffles and flouncy bell sleeves; get creative with your arm candies. If it's structure you're after, then jacket blouses, especially by Anita Dongre and Anamika Khanna, will do your bidding. Floor-length jackets or flimsy capes teamed with crop tops complement lehengas and wide-legged trousers while bandi-style cropped designer blouses will pair beautifully with saris. Think beyond Indian fashion designers for your blouse too. Nothing should stop you from clubbing that The Row camisole with a lehenga and diamond choker or replacing the designer blouse that came with your sari with a Zimmerman crop top. Want to wear your newly acquired H&M x Erdem blouse with a floral lehenga skirt? Do it, and add a Sabyasachi belt to the mix for added impact. Or wear your mum's real zari work lehenga with your dad's white shirt and vintage jewellery. Nothing is off-limits. The only restrictions are the ones in your mind.
