column1: What Veere Di Wedding’s designer costumes reveal about the lead characters
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Designer Sandeep Khosla of Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla lets us in on all the inside information Sonam Kapoor and the cast of Veere Di Wedding have been blasting social media with posters of the upcoming rom-com. From the four co-stars—Sonam Kapoor, Kareena Kapoor Khan, Swara Bhaskar and Shikha Talsania—preening in lehengas to dancing in sherwanis, the two looks have already got us placing bets on what can be expected from the film that's set to release in May 2018. Given that producer and stylist Rhea Kapoor and her fashion enthusiast/actor sister Sonam Kapoor have worked together on the project, it's guaranteed to be a visual treat for style watchers. Designer duo Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla have created the costumes for the film and we couldn't help but get on call with them for more insight on the wardrobe (and plot) details. Vogue spoke to one half of the designer duo, Sandeep Khosla, about what went into the making of Veere Di Wedding's costumes. A post shared by sonamkapoor (@sonamkapoor) on Oct 24, 2017 at 2:43am PDT What did you have in mind when setting the tone for the movie via costumes? The brief given to us was that it's a chick flick in a way, but it's also about emancipation of women. Rhea (Kapoor) was very clear that she wanted one look to be men's sherwanis. What inspired you to try a vibrant palette of yellows, greens and tangerines for the first look? The first poster is a bit of a tease—you can see the girls but you can't really see them. The colour palette was our take on the marigold flower, which is also a part of the poster. Tell us about your experience styling the four stars of the film. Any fun instances you encountered along the way? The fittings have been a laugh riot. Going with the character and the mood, we have made some outfits sexier, some more covered. There are some corny clothes also! How have you channeled each character's personality via their clothes? What makes each character special? Each of the girls has a certain personality and Rhea was keen on bringing that in through the costumes. If somebody is a rebel, then it shows in their clothes. What was the biggest challenge you faced as designers while working on Veere Di Wedding? No challenges! The girls have been very supportive. They have really imbibed the vibe of their characters and the clothes and the whole experience of it. From whatever working stills I have seen of the movie—they all seem to be having a blast. Other than Sonam, we had never worked with Kareena, Swara or Shikha before. Kareena was more than happy to experiment different styles. Rhea really had a vision for the film and the thought process has come through. Originally, the plan was to go completely crazy with the fashion element of the film, but we made the brief a little more realistic. What palette have you relied on for this film? As the film is about four girls bonding, we have got them in colour stories in places but otherwise they have independent styles. The clothes are not typical bridal clothes. The second poster of Veere Di Wedding had all four stars looking sharp in co-ordinated sherwanis. Can a bride really step out in a sherwani? Maybe not the bride (laughs). But having your bridesmaids in sherwanis can be a really cool idea. What is your ultimate tip for Indian brides this season? More and more brides are moving away from jadau jewellery and wearing diamonds, and white diamonds with red just looks awkward. We love the idea of fuchsia pink, yellow, pastels and even white for bridal lehengas. column1: Careers in Fashion: Payal Singhal on bringing practicality to bridal wear
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And the one thing she wishes she had done differently Payal Singhal is a quiet powerhouse who has, in the last two decades, set up a fashion label that services the needs of her bridal and occasion wear clientele without straying from its modern, contemporary aesthetic. Singhal's unique use of prints and minimal embellishments has made it a celebrity favourite, with the likes of Sonam Kapoor, Deepika Padukone and Neha Dhupia amongst others, regularly spotted in her creations. Along with maintaining the brand's voice, Singhal's learnings in fashion have included managing business, trusting staff and using self-doubt to her advantage. Vogue spoke to the fashion designer about the most practical advice she would offer to an upcoming designer. What is the distinct identity of a Payal Singhal girl? When I started out, I was purely trying to find clothes for girls like myself who didn't grow up wearing Indian clothes. We were the ‘jeans-and-T-shirt' generation who were raised solely on westernised clothing. There was this clear understanding that you only wore Indian clothes for occasions. I could see that we were uncomfortable with certain aspects of ethnic wear, because we weren't used to it. I wanted to tap into that [idea]. Payal Singhal is really for a woman who relates to western silhouettes. We are more comfortable in them, we can carry them with more elegance, and so even if we're wearing a sari, it has to be easy to wear. Our clothes allow you to move, are not very restrictive and have achievable price points—that is our brand ideology. I'm not saying we are economical—we give good quality products so we have to charge for it—but they're not ridiculously priced. View Gallery 24 Photos Payal Singhal at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2016 Payal Singhal at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2016 At what point did you realise that you didn't want to do heavy lehengas and ornate saris? Actually, it was not a realisation. It was just my own aesthetic: it's what I bring to the table. I do get complaints that I don't use enough colour, for example—I use pale pastels or very muted jewel tones—but it's just my own eye. I always tell my design department that each and every design that comes out of our workshop has to be put to the test of "Would I wear this?". If my answer is no, I'm not putting it out there. Maybe I can't fit into it, maybe I won't be able to carry it off, but that's not the point. The point is if I could fit into it and I could carry it off, would I wear this garment? Only if my answer is yes, does it make the cut. So essentially, you're answering to yourself over the demands of the market? I think so, because eventually as an artist or a designer, that's what you bring to the table: your aesthetic and your understanding of a garment or silhouette. That's what one resonates with. When I started the label, I was 21 and at that point of time there was no one who was making festive clothes for girls my age. Our clientele grew with me and now I have 20-year-old customers, which is the entry point of the label, and also women who are now in their 40s. So, [the aesthetic is] something that I'm banking on because that is why they comeback to us again and again. What did you learn outside of fashion school that still comes handy? I'll be very honest—I went to a design school that stresses on technical details and craft. You don't learn too much of the business side of things there, which I learnt on the job. I think one of the more valuable pieces advice I got was from my own father, who used to run a garment business. He said that you should always know an end use to the product you are making. I think that was something that stayed with me. The collection I showed in my graduation show, it sold off the runway so it's what we do today. We're a very wearable brand. We don't do art for the sake of art, we believe clothes are meant to be worn. I think that is where you have quality as a brand and as a designer. You work with your mother. What is that like? It's very comforting and challenging at the same time. Comforting because you know you always have someone to fall back on, who has your back and is trustworthy so you never feel insecure. It can be very lonely and isolating to work as a single owner. If you have a partner, and especially if they're family, it's great. It is also challenging because if you had a team where you told people what to do and they were just listening to you, it wouldn't be great for your brand but it would be easier for you. But when it's your mother, there is constant contradiction. Luckily, I look after the creative aspect and she looks into the finances, so we don't butt heads on the same topic. What are certain myths that people have about being a designer that you would like to dispel? The biggest myth of course is that it's a very glamorous job. It is absolutely the opposite, 180 degrees the opposite of that. I would say 98 per cent of my time, I'm in a factory where I'm working with skilled labour. At fashion school you learn terms like ‘French seams', that are all thrown out of the window because while explaining it to your tailor you have to call it 'andar bahar', otherwise they don't get it. It's very stressful, it's more business than fashion. As a designer if I had to mark out how much time I spend designing versus the time I spend managing of the business aspects of the label, I would say it would be more like 80/20. It's a big misconception when people think that as a designer all I'm doing is sketching and sourcing and looking at beautiful beads; it's not at all like that. A lot of young designers who join us and leave disappointed in six months. I'm like, what were you expecting? What were you thinking the job is going to be? If you start your own business this is exactly how it's going to be. View Gallery 25 Photos Payal Singhal at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016 Payal Singhal at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016 Other than design, what are some aspects of business that you personally pay attention to? I'm really lucky that I don't look into the finance at all, because my mum and my husband joined the business four years ago. As the creative director, what I personally look into is any communication that leaves the company that has our name on it. So, things like our logo, all our paper products, packaging, any creatives, our biannual in-house magazine, social media, website, shoots, fashion weeks—are all things that I have the final sign-off on. What is your advice to someone who wants to become a bridal wear designer in a saturated market that already has some established big names? I agree and disagree with you on the market. If you look at the landscape of the two big fashion weeks that we have right now in our country, you will notice there are not enough young designers doing Indian wear. Because if you look at the fashion weeks, out of the 60-70 designers that show per season, maybe only 10 Indian wear collections come out. That's why I don't agree that it's a saturated market. There are a lot of smaller players, a lot of non-branded stores doing Indian wear and they're actually making money. The joke we have as Indian designers especially, is that we're not just competing with each other, we're competing with every aunty who sits in her living room, tailoring and making clothes. My first show in a fashion week was in 2007 and now we're 2017. In these 10 years, I've seen several labels that we've shown with in fashion week that don't even exist anymore. We're talking about the top bracket of designers who are going into mainstream stores or opening their own flagship stores who have a substantial amount of business. In that if you notice, there are like 20 designers and that's not enough in a country that is so big. Have there been any failures in your journey? What were your learnings from those? Absolutely, in fact I would say I had one last week. I don't think successes are real successes unless there are failures. As Steve Jobs said—stay hungry, stay foolish. I believe insecurity and self-doubt have been the biggest assets for me as a designer because you know no designer is truly ever happy with their final product. We are the biggest critiques of our own work and when you are that, you will always strive to be better than that. I have had many failures, not one or two. Luckily for me, they are not failed businesses. I showed a collection that maybe I wasn't proud of, or I have had fallouts with certain brands that maybe I regret today. When you're young and passionate and very idealistic, you think that you're going to fight this fight, but as you grow older you realise that maybe in the big picture, it's not worth it. These are small failures and these will set you back, but eventually if you work hard, if you put your head down and do your thing, and you just concentrate on doing good work, you can overcome those failures and low points. And like I said, every week there's a low point and that's good; nothing wrong with that. You to go to sleep miserable but wake up saying, "You know what, it doesn't matter. I'm just going to make a kickass collection because I love what I do". View Gallery 42 Photos Payal Singhal at Lakmé Fashion Week Summer/Resort 2017 Payal Singhal at Lakmé Fashion Week Summer/Resort 2017 Do you hire anyone straight out of college without work experience? A lot! In fact, I prefer it. I feel like they come without any fixed ideas, they are energetic, they're excited to work and I just feel like it's easier for me to work with someone who I can train to understand and think in the way our company functions, than to work with someone who has the experience. Of course, we do have people with other work experience. We have a lot of people who don't just do their internships here, but stay on with us for five, sometimes ten years. I don't look at the portfolios because initially I used to do that and try to find the person who understands the design, and then I stopped doing that because I realised that half the time the portfolios are not so authentic. The greatest of designers don't have great sketching skills and sometimes a great illustration has no design elements to it. The biggest test for a new hire is surviving the first three months. I'm not very fussy when I hire, but I kind of see who I retain. And usually the first three months are a big giveaway. What I really look at is the zest for design, the eagerness to learn, the passion. If you're smart enough, you can learn anything, even how to fly a plane. If you could give one last piece of advice to a young fashion designer, what would it be? I think the only thing that I always encourage young students to do, is something I didn't do and regret. I never worked for another designer, I just did my internship and that was the end of it. I really wish I did because I think that is real learning. A lot of young designers do it now, it's kind of considered a prerequisite. A lot of young designers have put their label out in the past and then where are they today? But you'll see the ones who have actually worked elsewhere, understood where they want to be, found their footing, found their design philosophy and then started their own businesses, are the ones still around. And while I didn't do it, I worked in my parents' business, which was a fashion house. It was a different kind of product but at least I had some practical experience. But essentially that would be my biggest advice to any student wanting to start their own label. column1: Priyanka Chopra’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Mumbai to LA to New York and more View Gallery 125 Photos Complete style evolution of Priyanka Chopra The jet-setting Priyanka Chopra is unstoppable. Film festivals, red carpet screenings, international collaborations, family vacations, fashion weeks—she seems to be making the most of her life at all times. The Miss World-turned-Padma Shri awardee has had one of the most envy-worthy career graphs in Bollywood. Chopra started off early in the Noughties with films like Andaaz (2003), Aitraaz (2004), Bluffmaster ! (2005), Don (2006), Dostana (2008) and Kaminey (2009). It was more challenging roles in films like Barfi (2012) and Mary Kom (2014) that changed the course of her acting career. Her career graph also includes lending her voice to hit singles 'In My City' (2012) and 'Exotic' (2013). But her most recent successes include playing the part of Alex Parrish in the ABC Series Quantico (2015-2018) and Victoria Leeds in Baywatch (2017). Style Files Over her nearly two decade-long career, Chopra's style has evolved, to say the very least. From draped satin dresses to trench coats with OTT trains, the actor has become more experimental in her sartorial ways. The star's stylist Cristina Ehrlich revealed in a recent interview that “Priyanka is incredibly porous and really loves collaboration and depending on the day, she likes to do different things—she loves urban street wear, is inspired by music and model off-duty looks.” Ehrlich also added that, “She is very versatile and will try anything from a pair of men's pants to a pyjama look, to a classic bombshell moment.” Evolution Back in 2010, the star favoured cropped silhouettes and a relaxed travel style. Towards 2013, she ventured in the fitted shift dress territory, trying everything from leather detailing to all-over shimmer. Over the years, Chopra has been a fan of the six-yard drape when it comes to ethnic dressing and has been spotted in several saris. It was in 2015 that Chopra started experimenting with international labels like Self-Portrait, Michael Kors, Ralph Lauren, Prabal Gurung, Sally LaPointe and Altuzarra. With every passing day, the driven star manages to create headlines with her choices, fashion or otherwise, and shows no signs of stopping, at least in the near future. column1: Can you wear bold colours in your 60s?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Or, more the point, why can’t you? The 60s mark new beginnings in multiple ways, none of which gives you an excuse to slack off on your duties towards your wardrobe, no sir. With any luck, your professional and family commitments have lightened, giving you all the time in the world to find a fashion wingman to tide you over the coming decade. If you're looking for takers, we recommend you make fast friends with bold colours. View Gallery 11 Photos Can you wear bold colours in your 60s? Celebrities who wear bold colours The most elegant 60-somethings in showbiz have been flawlessly working this vivid trend. There's no denying Rekha's flair for drama, and she regularly indulges her wild side with a head-to-toe tangerine sari. The ever-graceful Shabana Azmi looked resplendent at a fashion show held for her charity, Mijwan, earlier this year in a vibrant pink sari that made heads turn. Of course, there's no telling Meryl Streep when it comes to acing trends, and setting a couple of her own. The Devil Wears Prada boss woman turned up at the Costume Designer Guild Awards this year in a lust-worthy colour-blocked Valentino number. Fuss-free, attention-grabbing and minimalist: check, check and check. How to wear bold colours in your 60s If done tastefully, everything from a plunging neckline to your favourite sequinned top from your 30s can make the cut. We aren't asking you to dig through your high school relics for neon extensions and glitter heels, but with the right amount of homework, you can give your favourite trends an age-appropriate update. Bold colours are for everyone, and if you're scared to dip your toe in the water, start out with some elegant colour-blocked separates and take it from there. What not to do Rule of thumb: if it hurts your eyes to stare at it for more than two minutes, it doesn't work. But there are plenty of bold hues on the colour wheel, and there's definitely something out there for you. Skip the neon shades so that you don't end up twinning with your niece at her graduation party, and instead look for wardrobe-saviours in the form of peppy tangerine or sunshine yellow. If you've always been happy to try new trends and push the envelope, by all means, experiment with the very best of what the world of match-y fashion has to offer. If you've been a card-carrying minimalist all your life and are looking to shake things up a little, start out small. Add one bold-hued accessory to your monochrome ensemble in the form of a bag or gloves, and watch those heads turn. Once you've gained your footing, upgrade to a vivid jacket or trousers. If you like what you see, play around with multi-tasking separates until you find your rhythm. If you're looking to get in on the trend, here are the pieces you should invest in. column1: How the Haim sisters developed their personal style
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In conversation with the siblings View Gallery 8 Photos Haim Sisters Alana, Danielle and Este—the three sisters who make up the Los Angeles pop rock band Haim—are famous for their hugs. When we meet them and their stylist, Rebecca Grice, at the Amastan hotel in Paris's 8 Arrondissement, they've got one for everyone, publicists and photographer included. Their hugs are warm, confident and genuine—just like the women themselves. Music has been part of Alana, Danielle and Este's lives for as long as they can remember. They grew up performing, Partridge Family-style, with their parents in a cover band called Rockinhaim. Each plays more than one instrument. In the band, Alana, 25, plays guitar, keyboard and percussion; Danielle, 28, is the lead vocalist and guitarist; and Este, 31, is the bassist. They formed Haim in 2007, taking a break for various projects before reforming in 2012. The release of their debut album, 2013's Days Are Gone, catapulted them to international fame. It hit no. 1 in the UK its first week. Stevie Nicks became a mentor. Taylor Swift became a friend. They went, as Danielle recounted in a 2013 interview, from appearing “bottom of the bill at 50-capacity venues [where] no one should up” to playing to sell-out crowds at Glastonbury and Webster Hall in New York. They followed it up with a critically lauded second album, Something To Tell You, this July. But it's not just their catchy lyrics and easy, '90s R&B-inflected sound that have garnered them legions of fans and nabbed the attention of designers like Balenciaga (who lent Danielle a denim jacket for a Saturday Night Live performance in May), Diane von Furstenberg (who brought them to the CFDA Awards in June) and Chanel (who dressed them head-to-toe for Paris Fashion Week). Working with Grice, the trio has developed a modern, polished take on '70s California style that combines vintage band tees and cut-off Levi's for day, slouchy suiting and structured mini-dresses for evening, and always the tumbling, sun-kissed, centre-parted hair that is their signature (and the subject of more than a few Pinterest boards). Discovering vintage For Haim, a love of fashion came early—fuelled by an admiration for '90s grunge icons like Kate Moss, a style-conscious high school (“People in our high school were pretty cool, they wore Dr. Martens in 2004,” says Alana) as well as runway photos on Vogue. “We would always look at collections,” Danielle says. “Obviously we couldn't afford that growing up, but we would go to thrift stores and vintage stores and try to find similar pieces. And it really allowed us to experiment in fashion.” On Sundays, they would wake up at 6am and head down to the dollar sale at Jet Rag. “It's this thing where you have to wake up at like 6 in the morning and you have to wait–” “Basically like The Hunger Games,” says Danielle. “But it's like incredible vintage clothing from around the US and everything is a dollar,” continues Alana. “So for us in high school where we had no money, it was a gold mine.” “Our parents,” Este interjects, “would each give us $10–” “And we would get 10 things!” they say together, laughing. Always, they were on the hunt for T-shirts and denim. “We've always been Levi's girls,” says Danielle. The Pasadena Rose Bowl Flea Market was, and continues to be, another favourite stop. Developing a sense of style As a group, their style is harmonious, yet each sister gravitates towards different silhouettes. Este, the tallest, wears a lot of mini skirts and wrap dresses from Réalisation. Danielle, who long favoured skinny jeans, says she feels most comfortable in trousers and suits. “And I kind of run in between,” says Alana. Above all, the clothes have to perform. “We're constantly playing music,” Alana explains. “I can't walk out of the house in something that I can't play in, because I feel like I'm going to have to pick up a big guitar at any point of time.” “We want to wear things that make us feel like the superhero versions of ourselves,” adds Danielle. “[While] Being on stage, it's so important to feel like your best self, because it brings out the performance.” Although she had two style-conscious older sisters, Alana says it wasn't until sophomore year of high school that she started to develop a sense of style. “There are pictures of me on the internet that I wish would never have surfaced,” she says, citing a gingham-shirt-with-pigtails phase as particularly cringe-worthy. “There were some questionable outfits,” Este admits. “Now,” says Alana, “we know what our bodies look good in, which is I think the hardest thing you can ever learn.” Working with a stylist The trio met Grice, a fellow California Valley girl, on the set of a shoot that was never published, and said they immediately felt like family. They describe their working process as “organic” and “collaborative”, which starts with input from the sisters and often a director. Grice has introduced them to designers like Simone Rocha, Marques'Almeida, and Adam Selman, and also taught them the importance of tailoring. At fittings, they photograph the clothes together and test out their dance moves. Despite the rigorous testing, and a heavy supply of thick, double-sided tape, there are still mishaps. “My pants splitting has happened so many times at this point,” says Este. “You just kind of have to roll with it, you can't stop the show just because my pants split.” The hair The three take a similarly laid-back approach to their enviable hair. “It's really just waking up and telling yourself I'm going to let my hair do whatever it wants to do today,” says Este. “If I do anything to my hair it just rebels against me.” Danielle sleeps with hers in a braid, giving her natural, textured waves. They each swear by Davines All in One Milk shampoo and conditioner, and Oribe Dry Texturizing Spray. “Let it air dry,” Este advises. “We're so lucky because it's always sunny in LA, so we just sit outside.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan’s new mom style, decoded
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Not all superheroes wear a cape View Gallery 29 Photos Kareena Kapoor Khan’s new mom style: decoded Being Kareena Kapoor Khan is not easy. When she isn't honouring her work commitments and shutting down the cynics, she is busy treating the shutterbugs to heartwarming shots of her newborn son, Taimur Ali Khan Pataudi. All while juggling a back-to-back gym and yoga schedule to ensure that she remains in the fittest shape of her life. Feel overwhelmed just reading about her itinerary? We do, too. When she isn't setting new benchmarks for herself, Kapoor Khan can be spotted around town with her glam squad in an array of non-boring looks, with no two styles being repeated twice. You think dressing a baby bump is tricky? Try navigating the in-between figure that most women face post-delivery, and the fresh set of challenges it poses. Not that you'd ever find Khan setting a toe out of line though. From taking the latest Gucci merch, hot off the runways, for a spin to acing casual ethnic looks—yes, even a humble salwar kameez—there's little that this fashion superwoman can't do. If you're looking to get in on her style A-game, bring out your clipboard and prepare to take copious notes. Lesson #1: Smart layering is everything We live in a time when it's impossible to come up with outfit ideas that haven't been rinsed on the runways a million times already, and layering is your cheatsheet to circumventing fashion ennui. Not a fan of match-y fashion? Skip the monochrome blues by introducing some tone-on-tone magic to your wardrobe à la Kapoor Khan in her military separates from Chola. Or throw on a blazer over a tie-and-dye Bloni sari to bring your festive wardrobe into 2017. Lesson #2: There's no such thing as too many prints For her first post-delivery appearance in public, Khan offered up a riot of prints in the form of a flowy maxi dress. For the book launch of her dietician and dear friend, Rujuta Diwekar, the new mom went for the gold with a chevron top and patterned skirt from Missoni, topped off with shoulder-grazing tasselled Valliyan earrings. Lesson #3: Don't knock yourself out to fit in that killer pair stilettos though Kim Kardashian West's feet uncomfortably squeezed into heels make for more than just an interesting headline. No trend is ever worth killing yourself for, and no one understands the importance of comfort more than Kareena Kapoor Khan, who casually got back on her feet post-delivery and returned to her workload in a variety of flip-flops, fringed sandals and cool-girl sneakers. Always put your comfort first, and your body will thank you for it in kind. Lesson #4: Always, but always, play up your best assets Maybe you feel more confident about your arms, or maybe you've got a razor-sharp collarbone that never fails to fetch compliments. It doesn't matter if you're still getting back on the fit wagon after delivering a baby—pick any one body part to highlight and style your entire wardrobe around it. Kapoor Khan beautifully flaunted her toned arms in an off-shoulder gown with slit sleeves from Poem. Likewise, there's no denying the wonders of her sharply tailored tuxedo dress from Ashish N Soni. Lesson #5: Don't stick to what you know Tempting as it may be to sidle towards the labels that you know always make you look good, once you get caught in a fashion rut, there's no coming out. Look to the vivacious new mother for inspiration. Sure, she loves her hot-off-the-runways Gucci stash when making a quick dash to the airport, but she's just as comfortable adding new designers to her repertoire—the 37-year-old made heads turn in a simple but effective salwar kameez from Simar Dugal. Long story short? Throw the rulebook out of the window every once in a while. If you're looking for (yet) more fashion inspiration, flip through our gallery of Kareena Kapoor Khan's new mom style. column1: How to dress for work in your 50s
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The essential edit Often, hitting 50 means reaching a comfortable place in your life, personally and professionally. After achieving a healthy work-life balance, there's no reason for you to give up on playful printed and colourful separates. Gone are those days of cost-per-wear calculation. As you hit your '50s, your wardrobe must already be brimming with timeless classics that you must have collected over the years. As you reach the peak of your work life, make sure you step out in your sartorial best. Adopt classic styles in luxe fabrics to nail dressing at the workplace. Striking a balance between trendy and sophisticated can be a task, but we've got you covered. Here everything you need to get started. Know before you go With the years gone by, your nine-to-five dressing should be the easiest decision of the day. Finally done juggling with multiple checklists, its finally time to take a step back from the responsibilities and create an impact with your stylish wardrobe. View Gallery 8 Photos How to dress for work in your 50s- Celebrities Borrow from the stars If you are looking for some inspiration, then who better than these always-stunning 50-something A listers to guide you through this. From versatile crisp shirts to smart turtle necks, Sridevi's wardrobe has no shortage of classics. Have a work meeting? Pair your pencil skirt with a white button-down or try a formal wrap dress, or style your formal pants with a sleek blouse. Madhuri Dixit, too, serves a masterclass in dressing for work events in colourful pant suits and structured jumpsuits. What not to do With age comes wisdom, and by the time you touch your big five-o, you are fully aware of the dos and don'ts of formal dressing, but just a refresher. One, resist the urge to step inside bodycon dresses, two, steer clear of anything sheer or strappy, and three, keep cropped hemlines for the after hours. What you should do Ditch the structured outfits and opt for effortless and easy pieces that will help you get through the long hour of hectic meetings. While planning your look, make sure to keep the surprise meetings in mind. Make room for sleek accessories and a smart change of footwear for out-of-office meetings and important work lunches. Curate a balanced collection of footwear with some flat mules and classic peep toes for varied work occasions. The formal section of wardrobe should be your best friend by now. Think trousers, striped shirts, midi dresses and relaxed kurtas. Invest in designer bags to amp up your formal look. column1: Phoebe Philo is preparing to leave Céline
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The end of an era? LVMH is interviewing designers to replace Céline creative director Phoebe Philo, sources report. However, the company denies her departure will be taking place any time soon. Philo joined Céline in 2008, turning the label from an underachieving brand into the iconic French label it has become. According to multiple sources, the design team is preparing for Philo's eventual exit from the French fashion powerhouse brand by interviewing designers to take her place for when the impending time comes. Although the brand denies Philo's imminent departure, they too haven't denied that interviews for her replacement have been taking place. “We categorically deny any imminent departure of Phoebe Philo from Céline,” shared a spokesman for LVMH. According to Business of Fashion, “Industry sources said potential replacements for Philo could include former Stella McCartney design director Natasa Cagalj, who is now at Ports 1961 and has a similar aesthetic.” Other proposed names included Michael Rider, design director of Céline ready-to-wear, as well as Ilaria Icardi, the design director at Victoria Beckham who was previously senior design director at YSL and Céline. After ten years of working for the luxury fashion brand, perhaps Philo has decided her era has come to an efficacious finale. Until confirmed, Philo hasn't verbally committed to any permanent decision with regards to concluding her career with Céline just yet. column1: Instagram’s Eva Chen on how social media has changed fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Reinventing the game View Gallery 20 Photos Instagram’s Eva Chen on how social media has changed fashion Sitting front row at the Gucci show in Milan this season was none other than Dapper Dan, the Harlem designer who had incorporated the logos of high-fashion houses, Gucci among them, in his unsanctioned designs during the 1980s. How exactly did a man whose business model was thought to be anathema to the luxury brands of Milan—and whose store was shut down as a result of legal action by one of the brands he hijacked—end up at arguably the city's biggest show 30 years later? Just four months earlier, in June, Gucci creative director Alessandro Michele sent designs resembling Dan's creations down the catwalk during the brand's cruise 2018 show, provoking immediate backlash and accusations of cultural appropriation on social media. Gucci swiftly got in touch with Dan, inviting him to collaborate on a capsule collection and star in the brand's advertising campaigns—and in an unexpected twist, Dan revealed that he would reopen his atelier later this year, with raw materials supplied by Michele. Towards transparency Today, we're in what Eva Chen, director of fashion partnerships at Instagram, calls a “new level of transparency and expectation.” It's no longer prudent to keep quiet in the face of criticism, hoping for the wave of denunciations to blow over. “[Instagram] allows people to raise awareness,” Chen told Vogue over the phone from New York last week, whether that's acknowledging an act of plagiarism that would have otherwise gone unnoticed, or highlighting the injustices present in the industry. When the model casting director James Scully took it to Instagram to call out model abuse during the Balenciaga castings earlier this year, he drew comments from model Joan Smalls to LVMH's Antoine Arnault. This series of events, unfolding on social media, immediately led to the firing of the casting team and undoubtedly played a role in initiating the Kering and LVMH Model Charter unveiled this fashion month. What's more, in raising awareness, users also educate those they are in dialogue with. When designer Marc Jacobs adorned white models with dreadlocks for his spring/summer 2017 show, the Instagram community did its part of starting a conversation about cultural appropriation: this exchange caused the designer to shift his views and acknowledge the insensitive nature of his initial reaction, when he uncharitably compared his actions to women of colour straightening their hair. Changing industry standards Relatedly, in ushering in this new age of transparency, Instagram has, in many ways, transformed the industry's longstanding practices as well. This season, Chen praises the feeling of inclusivity that she witnessed during fashion month. “When I see designers putting models whether they're curvier or differently-abled, or using ‘unconventional' beauties, I think the amazing thing about Instagram is that the community of 800 million strong says, ‘Why should there be a definition of conventional?' Unconventional in one market can and should be conventional in another,” she continued. “I think that global sense of beauty is very much attributed to Instagram.” Transforming fashion shows Before the rise of blogs and social media a decade ago, fashion weeks happened largely behind closed doors. All of that, of course, has radically changed. And no social media platform has played a more significant role in opening doors than Instagram. “What people come to expect on Instagram is not the perfect glossy life. Because of Instagram Stories, they want to see their favourite people and the different aspects of their lives,” Chen said. Today, models, hairstylists and makeup artists regularly offer backstage access via Instagram Stories; brands voluntarily stream shows in their entirety on Live; and fashion editors give their thousands of followers a prime view from the front row. But though Instagram has become an agent of social change, some industry critics have accused the social media platform of transforming fashion month into a circus, where the attention has been diverted away from the garments. At shows, it might seem that brands continuously one-up each other with increasingly lavish sets and grand finales tailored just for Instagram. Recall the Versace moment, Chanel's indoor cliffs and waterfalls, or Saint Laurent's shiny Eiffel Tower behind the runway this past season. Chen, however, doubts all of this can be attributed to Instagram. “I think about the McQueen hologram or the time Marc Jacobs sent a marching band down the runway—all of that happened before Instagram existed,” Chen explained. “I don't think Instagram has necessarily forced the industry to change their shows.” What it does do instead, according to Chen, is make designers more aware of the so-called “ripple effect” of their shows. “If they have one influencer in the audience with 1 million followers, what will that 1 million followers experience?” But even if Instagram doesn't dictate the way fashion shows are produced, it does, in a big way, dictate how we consume fashion content. With the rise of Stories, consumption of fashion week has shifted away from blurry runway images to videos of the catwalk, allowing Instagram to drive traffic to new heights. This season, the social media platform's fashion community, comprising 143 million users, generated 709 million engagements, tripling the numbers from last fashion month, according to Instagram's in-house data team. How to succeed on Instagram Consequently, in democratising fashion, Instagram has rendered the battleground much more competitive. Now that everyone has a voice, how can you make sure yours gets heard? “Know your audience,” Chen said, listing such Instagrammable examples as the LVMH Prize finalist Molly Goddard, whose carefree models danced and skipped down the runway, or fellow Londoner Ashish, known for the vibrant energy at his shows. Of course, armies of top models and majestic stages are perennial favourites amongst the Instagram community, but as Topshop, London Fashion Week's best performing brand, exemplifies, “a lot of the images that did well showed people behind the scenes,” Chen revealed. “A lot of it had to do with the fact that they posted a lot of Instagram Stories, and this great behind-the-scenes narrative they employed,” she continued. “You don't need a cliff. Indoor waterfalls are magnificent if you have that kind of budget. But not everyone needs that.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Jade’s Monica Shah and Karishma Swali on mixing business with family
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A balancing act Mumbai-based couture label Jade by Monica & Karishma has become a go-to for brides in the city for the brand's ability to take vintage heirloom silhouettes and give them a distinctly contemporary appeal without compromising on its traditional essence. Launched by sisters-in-law Monica Shah and Karishma Swali in 2008, the brand was “born out of a fiercely creative spirit and a unique sensibility.” The duo followed up Jade's success with a festive cocktail wear label Innana in 2013, an eclectic diffusion line Amoha in 2016, and a sprawling new flagship store in Mumbai earlier this year. “The idea was to create a space that embraces and envelops you with an inspiring ambience, while celebrating Indian design heritage and reviving the time-honoured legacy of our craftsmanship. We have designed a space that draws you in while encouraging you to discover every nook and corner, all at your own pace,” Shah explains. View Gallery 18 Photos Jade at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016 Jade at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016 So to say that Swali and Shah's venture has grown exponentially in less than a decade would be understatement. And while working with your closest kin has its perks, it is not without its challenges either. The designers demystify the dynamics of working as a duo, and lay out the ground rules for functioning like a well-oiled creative unit. Where did the idea of starting Jade come from? The seeds for the launch of Jade were sown when the Shah and Swali were working with their family-owned export house Chanakya, which Suzy Menkes also famously visited on her recent trip to India. “We both are still very involved with Chanakya. We have an international office in Italy now, and it is still a major source of inspiration for us. We've worked with a lot of internationally acclaimed luxury fashion houses such as Dior, Giorgio Armani, Valentino, Gucci, and Alberta Ferretti among many others for several years now. And Jade is culmination of our learnings from this experience. After having successfully researched and consulted for so long, Karishma and I came up with this idea of launching Jade together,” reminisces Shah. View Gallery 17 Photos Amoh by Jade at Lakmé Fashion Week Summer/Resort 2017 Amoh by Jade at Lakmé Fashion Week Summer/Resort 2017 What is it like to work with a family member? Shah reveals that the two were friends before family ties added another link to their liaison. “We have several common interests, love sharing ideas with each other, and when we set our mind on a goal, we always figure a way to achieve it. We are still friends, which is why we continue to share a very comfortable equation. It's easy for both of us to switch between work and family. We can work together just as easily as we can holiday together. It's rare and we are blessed,” says Shah of their relationship—one that has also heightened the respect they have for each other. How do the two of you work together without conflict? Demarcating their roles, while still working in perfect tandem, is what makes their partnership tick. Swali is in charge of research and couture wear, while Shah heads the brand's design and marketing endeavours. While they take all ownership for their respective areas of expertise, the twosome also keeps the other in the loop so that synergy is never missing from their equation. “Having worked for over 15 years now, we are both experts in our fields, and also respect each other's opinions. We try to get the best out of each other, and any creative difference only helps us reach a stronger output through brainstorming together.” What are the benefits of playing for the same team ? The duo feels that one should play up on individual merits while working towards a common vision when launching a business with a friend or family member. “Our tremendous synergy, complete trust in each other, and a precise goal to work towards has worked for us. The sum of two is greater than two. Focus on each other's strengths and respect each other. It's also very important to give your partner space and value their opinions,” Shah adds about the key ingredient to making it work. column1: Amazon India Fashion Week S/S 2018: Highlights from the grand finale
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Save the best for last View Gallery 12 Photos Inside Amazon India Fashion Week S/S 2018 grand finale show Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018's grand finale featured 'See Now Buy Now' pret collections by some of the most talented designers of the industry. The first half of the finale lineup was presented by designers Ashish N Soni, Pankaj & Nidhi, Rina Dhaka, Krishna Mehta and Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna, who were a part of the instantly shoppable model that made the runway collections available on Amazon.in's Designer Boutique right after the shows. Husband-wife designer duo Pankaj & Nidhi presented a cobalt blue-and-black evening wear collection featuring off-shoulder dresses and easy separates, while Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna stuck to monochromatic wardrobe essentials with asymmetric skirts and jackets. Rina Dhaka played with fuchsia and pink frilled saris and dresses, a collection perfect for evening occasions. While sleek silhouettes in earthy hues featured in Krishna Mehta line-up, smart monochromatic knits formed the basis of Ashish N Soni's finale collection. Who better to bring the 30th edition of Amazon India Fashion Week to a close than veteran designer Suneet Varma, who also marks his third decade in the industry this year. As his label completes 30 years, it was all about celebrating couture for the designer. With 37 versatile outfits, his collection titled 'Garden of Eden' comprised of a fairy tale-worthy line-up. The designer transformed the runway into a spectacle, with synchronised design identities that spoke of glamour and sensuality, playing with sheer and lucid fabrics. The collection of embellished and embroidered garments that ranged from gowns, lehengas, saris and dresses was opulent to say the least. With a line of festive Indian wear, including embellished floor-grazing gowns, fringed saris and voluminous lehengas, the designer stayed true to his aesthetic. Featuring electric blues, reds and nudes, the colour story of the collection was as timeless as the classic silhouettes. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

Among the A-listers who attended the decadent evening was Priyanka Chopra, who was seen in a colour blocked dress and pastel trench from Bottega Veneta's spring 2018 runway collection. column1: Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018: Highlights from Day 4
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A quick recap View Gallery 12 Photos Highlights from day 4 of Amazon India Fashion Week spring / summer 2018 From Shivan & Narresh's Japanese art-inspired separates to Anju Modi's Swadesi line, Day 4 of Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018 came packed with talent. Here's everything you need to know. Shivan & Narresh In keeping with their aesthetic, this season, luxury resort wear label Shivan & Narresh drew from the works of Japanese visual artist Nobuyoshi Araki. The designers have translated Araki's love for florals using their signature skein work. Catering to destination brides, the collection came packed with floral jumpsuits, decadent lehengas, embellished saris and relaxed swimwear separates. The label also extended their capsule line of accessories and footwear to their resort wear collection. Dhruv Kapoor From African tribal patchwork to the costumes worn by Japanese geishas, Dhruv Kapoor's spring/summer collection saw a blend of easy silhouettes and relaxed fabrics. The collection featured striped jumpsuits, embellished dresses and coats, and printed dresses. Models weaved through the ramp in dramatic creations that channelled individuality. The colour palette varied from bright yellows and reds to high shine hues. Anju Modi Adding to the sustainable fashion movement, designer's collection, titled Swadeshi, was yet another one of her thematic tributes to Indian heritage designs. Giving a contemporary spin to basic ethnic separates, the designer played to her strengths with a powerful collection of relaxed tie-and-dye kurtas, saris, flowing capes and asymmetric cuts. Mustard, navy blue, white and red dominated her unconventional colour story for spring/summer. Huemn With the focus on raising awareness about social causes, designers Pranav Mishra and Shyma Shetty of Huemn dedicated their spring/summer 2018 collection to the the wearer who believes in change. Offering a ‘fearless aesthetic' this season to counter the dystopian world today, their fierce line featured easy separates including a mixture of hoodies, over-sized jackets and velvet pant suits, to name a few. In addition to their ready-to-wear-collection, they also presented presenting a lineup of up-cycled denim. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018: Get a closer look at Day 4
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Saris, neoprene and more The fourth day of Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018 saw standout shows by designer labels Shivan & Narresh, Dhruv Kapoor and Anju Modi. Inspired by the works of Japanese visual artist Nobuyoshi Araki, the designers drew from his vivid depiction of florals for this season. The duo described the collection to fit the needs of the destination bride with an envious honeymoon wardrobe. Embellished saris to decadent lehengas, the Shivan & Narresh lineup is bound to draw in the festive shopping crowd. Vogue India Fashion Fund winner Dhruv Kapoor broke away from his severe aesthetic to bring in more relaxed fabrics and silhouettes. The runway saw oversized shirts, lame corsets, glittering dresses and the use of prints. Kapoor introduced a cotton neoprene that could be worn in the heat of the Indian summer. Anju Modi's work is often looked at in the detailed, ethnic occasion wear category that brings to mind images of Deepika Padukone's diaphanous anarkalis from Bajirao Mastani. Taking a 360 degree turn from that, veteran designer Modi chose to instead offer Indian ethnic separates that are relevant in the contemporary context. Modi also brought in conversation the idea of slow fashion and slow living with the collection ‘Swadeshi'. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Amazon India Fashion Week S/S 2018: Abhay Deol plays showstopper on Day 3
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s what you missed Delhi-based designer Payal Pratap, sent out a happiness-inducing line-up of summer separates. The tea-stained runway flanked by hanging terrariums swiftly filled up with pretty go-with-the-flow dresses and laid-back jackets. While Pratap opted for simple silhouettes in handloom cotton khadi and linen, the fresh colour story of petal pink, sunshine yellow and indigo drew from a field of flowers. From embroidered to beaded, florals were the designer's finishing touch of choice. Designer duo David Abraham & Rakesh Thakore, whose label turns 25 this year, delivered yet another a standout collection, #blockblackwhite. The show, which saw a front row filled with industry insiders, decoded the process of creating patterns on surfaces with an uncarved wooden block. Contemporary separates such as jackets and button-downs were seamlessly merged with traditional silhouettes ranging from the six-yard staple to dhoti pants. While the colour palette was mostly monochromatic, it also saw bursts of yellow and striking blue. The day came to a close with Rajesh Pratap Singh's surprise-packed show, which began with FDCI president Sunil Sethi taking the ramp for the designer in a black suit, sporting sunglasses from Indie Eye, a collaborative initiative by his daughter Tanira Sethi and artist Jayanta Roy. Brimming with monochrome and metallic tailored separates, the line-up served up more ways than one to make a statement but the pieces featuring images of Prince, Jimi Hendrix and David Bowie were the stars of the show. The evening also saw contemporary artists Thukral and Tagra walk the ramp for the designer in high-shine jackets. As models weaved through the audience in the designer's standout creations, a dapper Abhay Deol played showstopper. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018: Highlights from Day 3
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A quick recap In case you missed Day 3 of Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018, here's everything you need to know. View Gallery 12 Photos Highlights from day 3 of Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018 Anomaly While Medha Khosla's collection showcased what her label is best known for—fuss-free, wearable separates, this season also saw the designer introduce a hint of handmade. Khosla joined forces with Sally Holkar's WomenWeave to develop a commercially viable cotton fabric for her line-up. Made of three hues (navy blue, white and red) the colour palette was classic. Statement stripes played up the drama on otherwise simple silhouettes. Payal Pratap This season, the Delhi-based designer's collection, Here Comes the Sun, proved that happiness never goes out of style. On a tea-stained runway flanked by hanging terrariums, models walked past in expertly layered, relaxed separates. Think pretty go-with-the-flow summer dress and laid-back jackets. While Pratap opted for simple silhouettes in handloom cotton khadi and linen, the fresh colour story of petal pink, sunshine yellow and indigo took its cues from a field of flowers. Embroidered, printed or beaded, florals, in all their glory, were the designer's finishing touch of choice. Abraham & Thakore Two-and-half decades in, David Abraham and Rakesh Thakore show no signs of slowing down. For spring/summer, the designer duo sent out yet another scene-stealing collection, #blockblackwhite, focused on decoding the process of creating patterns on surfaces with an uncarved wooden block. On the runway, contemporary separates such as jackets and button-downs seamlessly merged with traditional silhouettes ranging from the six-yard staple to dhoti pants. The designers played with a largely monochromatic colour palette with bursts of yellow and striking blue. Rajesh Pratap Singh Count on Rajesh Pratap Singh to bring the day to a memorable close. This season, the designer's eagerly anticipated show was opened by FDCI president Sunil Sethi in an all-black suit, sporting statement sunglasses by Indie Eye, a collaborative initiative by his daughter Tanira Sethi and artist Jayanta Roy. With monochrome and metallic tailored separates quickly filling up the reflective ramp, the line-up served up more ways than one to make a statement but the pieces featuring images of Prince, Jimi Hendrix and David Bowie stole the show. What's more? The evening also saw contemporary artists Thukral and Tagra walk the ramp for the designer in high-shine jackets. As models weaved through the audience in the designer's standout creations, a dapper Abhay Deol played showstopper. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 20+ stunning designer earrings to buy this festive season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get your shine on View Gallery 24 Photos The best designer earrings to wear this Diwali Nothing like the festive season to use as an excuse to shop of more. With the year coming to an end and the spirit of celebration is in the air, it's time get busy shopping for what's ahead. As you gear up for Diwali don't forget to add a touch of sparkle (or more than that) to your festive wardrobe. Earrings are ideal choice to amp-up the shine quotient and there's no reason to not invest in these. The versatility of the events surrounding Diwali—card parties, impromptu dinners and chance encounters mean that you need to have your style game on point at all times. Earrings have a way of highlighting your facial features like no other accessory. Without weighing yourself down in full sets, go for sparkly chandeliers and danglers to get into the spirit of the festivities. Choose from coloured gemstones and solid metal to make your Indian ethnic wear really stand out. Accessories are the best way to distinguish your personal style from others. Given the focus on earrings on the runways this season, the style staple is sure to be the MVP in your arsenal. Use Diwali as a license to splurge and get your hands on those diamond earrings you've had your eyes on for a while. Choose from jhumkas and drop earrings to gold earrings that are anything but boring; look for details like meenakari to add colour to your look. Don't rule out more artistic iterations of earrings—we are talking ear cuffs and more sculptured pieces. Chandbalis are a permanent hit when it comes to earrings, and will definitely prove themselves useful come wedding season. Don't shy away from going over the top with your jewellery choices. Shoulder duster earrings are perfect to pair with an off-shoulder blouse. Feel free to skip on the necklace and add a mang tikka to create a look with recall value. For a versatile take on traditional jewellery, go with Burberry's asymmetrical floral earrings. Wear your hair on side to truly highlight the contrast of your earrings. Minimalists can look at unfussy diamond stuffs or hoops to accessorise their festive looks with. Ellery's two hoops, while contemporary, are not out of the realm of festive accessories. Scroll through our gallery of the best designer earrings to choose from this festive season. column1: Amazon India Fashion Week S/S 2018: Watch all that happened on Day 2
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get the inside scoop From Hemant & Nandita's cult classic-inspired collection to Lovebird's wardrobe of simple and functional separates for the urban woman, day two of Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018 brought together some of the industry's finest. Who doesn't love fashion with a heart? For spring/summer, Ragini Ahuja paid tribute to the calm rebellion of tribes who fled their countries and live as ethnic refugees. Her collection, Clan, came packed with soft, voluminous separates featuring patterns ranging from traditional tribal to contemporary graphics. Playing with sharp contrasts, the designer's shade card combined the the likes of ivory, navy, red and black signifying the strength and survival of the tribes. When it comes to understated elegance, Amrita Khanna and Gursi Singh of Lovebirds seem to have it down pat. This season, the duo catered to the urban woman with a wardrobe of simple and function separates accentuated by their signature, sharp cuts. Broderie anglaise formed the basis of Hemant & Nandita's collection inspired by cult classic Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975). The runways came into full bloom as models walked the ramp in feminine separates in a pretty palette of navy blue and pink. Finishing touches which came in the form of pussy bows and cascading frills put a playful spin on the duo's designs. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you need to know Couldn't make it to Day 2 of Amazon India Fashion Week? We've got you covered: View Gallery 12 Photos Highlights day two of Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018 Ikai by Ragini Ahuja Since her runway debut four years ago, Ragini Ahuja has never ceased to impress. This season, the Vogue India Fashion Fund finalist's collection, Clan, was a tribute to the calm rebellion of the tribes who fled their homeland and live as ethnic refugees. The line-up came packed with soft, voluminous silhouettes, which played with patterns that progressed from tribal motifs to contemporary graphics. With an emphasis on contrasts, the colour story combined ivory, navy, black and red signifying the strength and survival of the tribes. Lovebirds Understated elegance continues to lie at heart of designer duo Amrita Khanna and Gursi Singh's label Lovebirds. Catering to the urban woman, the duo showcased an effortlessly layered line-up of simple and functional separates featuring their signature, statement cuts. Monochrome, dusty pink, navy, slate grey and mustard dominated their unconventional colour story for spring/summer. Hemant & Nandita Nothing says spring quite like florals. The runway came into full bloom as the husband and wife design duo sent out a collection focused on broderie anglaise. The cult film Picnic At Hanging Rock (1975) powered the designers line-up, which featured summer separates in a pretty palette of pale pink and blue. Effortlessly knotted pussy bows and cascading frill put a playful twist on the designs guaranteed to secure the fashion flock's seal of approval. Ashish N Soni Whatever the season, for the veteran designer, whose label turns 25 this year, black never goes out of style. For spring/summer, the designer played to his strengths with a powerful collection of sharply tailored, androgynous separates (jumpsuits, blazer dresses and fierce suits) in the every-reigning hue. Asymmetric cuts, flowing capes and metallic embellishments lent the perfect finishing touch. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Stock up for the coming week View Gallery 10 Photos Budget buys: 10 Kurtas that are perfect for any occasion Whether it's because of its versatile elegance or effortless functionality, a kurta can be the most fuss-free piece in your wardrobe. Go down the ethnic route or channel a contemporary vibe, the all-rounder can transition in any way you chose to style it. Pick from Shibori kurta by Ikai or make a statement in vibrant high-low number by Masaba Gupta. For a small family gathering, invest in Krishna Mehta's tie-and-dye kurta, and while attending a puja step inside striking yellow number by Global Desi. For drinks with friends, give your kurta a fresh spin and pair it with ripped denims. For a more ethnic look, style them with palazzos or sharara; the trick here lies in balancing the proportions. column1: 15 perfect designer lehengas for the Indian bridesmaid
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion For the girl who just wants to twirl View Gallery 15 Photos All the perfect designer lehengas for the Indian bridesmaid As much as you detest your bride-to-be bestie's insufferable micromanaging of the bridal shower or her inability to return your phone calls once she dives into wedding planning, let's be honest. Bridesmaids do have all the fun. Once the bridezilla meltdowns have been dealt with, and the big day finally rolls around, it's all one big party. Being the last one to be ushered out of the cocktail party, shining in the sangeet spotlight, and exchanging coquettish banters with the eligible groomsmen—all eyes are not just on the bride but also her trusty crew. If you're going to be in the limelight, make sure it's for the right reasons. Hearing “I love what you're wearing” at every wedding function never gets old, so call in the cavalry; ie some compliment-friendly lehenga sets. Prints lend themselves beautifully to a bridesmaid's wardrobe, with florals leading the pack. Team a painterly floral skirt with a cape or crop top for the sangeet or mehandi, so that you can dance with carefree abandon. Turn to embellishments for the pheras and reception, but go easy on the ornate embroidery—leave that to the bride and her kin. A sprinkle of sequins or delicate mirror work is a safer bet for you. Or better yet, choose a heritage weave like Benarasi, Patola or Lucknowi styled with a touch of modernity. The easiest way to give your repertoire a flirty update befitting the bride's favourite single girlfriend is with your blouse. Cue off-shoulder blouses, crop tops, and bustiers. Ditch the dupatta in favour of a choli with cape sleeves that renders one unnecessary or nonchalantly throw on a sheer jacket over your blouse. Let the pearl clutching aunties say what they will; itsy-bitsy is not out of the question. Designers such as Gaurav Gupta, Payal Singhal and Arpita Mehta should be your go-tos, while the likes of Ridhi Mehra, Ridhima Bhasin and Saaksha & Kinni are ideal for when your wardrobe budget doesn't rival the bride's. We suggest you save those anarkalis and sharara sets for the pre-wedding soirees. Twirl your way through the main dos in voluminous lehengas that are the last word in comfortable cool. If nothing, do it for the Boomerang video. We tracked down the perfect lehengas to do your bidding. Scroll through our slideshow for the edit. column1: Gucci announces it will be going fur-free
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Italian brand will remove fur from all its collections as of spring/summer 2018 Alessandro Michele's Renaissance aristo woman has long been depicted as one not afraid to raid the 1970s wardrobe vaults—and that includes nicking those Margot Tenenbaum-style fur coats to wear with her tan tights and fluffy loafers. But that's set to change as of this season: Gucci will join the Fur-Free Alliance from spring/summer 2018, CEO Marco Bizzarri announced this evening. Speaking at the 2017 Kering Talk at the London College of Fashion, Bizzarri revealed he had taken the ground-breaking decision to remove fur from all of Gucci's collections, and hoped other luxury brands would follow suit. "We've been talking about it, Alessandro [Michele] and I, for a few months. Technology is now available that means you don't need to use fur. The alternatives are luxurious. There is just no need," Bizzarri told Vogue. The brand currently sells a wide variety of furs, including a mink coat listed on its website for £25,920 as well as a lamb fur coat for £11,340. Gucci's fur-free policy going forward will include mink, coyote, raccoon dog, fox, rabbit, and karakul (otherwise known as Swakara, Persian lamb or astrakhan) and all others species specially bred or caught for fur. Bizzarri went on to reveal that he takes advice from some of the youngest people currently working at Gucci, and recently invited employees under the age of 30 to attend a series of lunches in order to obtain their unique perspective on where the brand was going wrong. "Young kids are more intelligent and more confident than us," he told the talk's host, Eco-Age founder Livia Firth. "Experience can be a prison. To be a leader, we need to learn as well as teach. I asked around 150 young people working for Gucci across the world to tell me three things wrong with Gucci. I was seeing the company from the bottom to the top." He revealed a "shadow committee" of young people had also been set up to mirror the meetings taken by the CEO and senior management. "I wanted to see if they came up with different solutions to us," he explained. "It's important to get a new perspective." "Gucci is so visible, so well-known—we need to use that in a positive way." Marco Bizzarri When asked about the extraordinary financial success of the company—sales were up 48.3 per cent in the first quarter of 2017, and 39.3 in the second—he cited company culture as a major factor. "A journalist came recently to the headquarters and said to me, 'All the people are smiling'," Bizzarri said. "At Gucci it's an incredible team. You have to let people take risks, make a mistake—not twice, but once!—and allow everyone to make a difference. It's all about people." The evening also revealed that Gucci will contribute Euro 1 million as a founding partner of UNICEF's Girls' Empowerment Initiative. Bizzarri suggested that this will help UNICEF reach more than 50,000 girls directly with programmes aimed at empowering them, and indirectly reach 150,000 more. Bizzarri said he hoped Gucci's decision to go fur-free would encourage other high-profile brands to follow suit. "Gucci is so visible, so well-known—we need to use that in a positive way."
