column1: Careers in fashion: Amit Aggarwal on why innovation is key
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion "Know why you’re creating" It's not every day that designers resort to restoring rich vintage Benarasi saris with three-dimensional hand embroideries or reinterpreting zari with art nouveau patterns and intricately embroidered recycled cord, but one wouldn't expect any different from Amit Aggarwal's take on bridal wear. Best-known for making recycled plastics and industrial materials mainstream fashion conversation in India, Aggarwal's winter/festive '17 collection was a testament to his adeptness in bringing an inimitable touch of inventiveness to the use of Indian weaves. While brocade was the highlight of this collection, the true hero was its structured and avant-garde treatment—“a marriage of contrasts”, as Aggarwal likes to define his signature style. A brand that is steeped in “the transformation of architecture, structure and fantasy into fashion”, it has grown from a one-room office to a three-floor studio-cum-factory, a flagship store in Delhi, and retail points in 15 countries including Germany, Panama, United Kingdom, and UAE among others. Aggarwal spoke to Vogue from Paris Fashion Week, where he recently showcased his SS '18 ready-to-wear and couture collections that were fashioned from African textiles with upcycled elements. The beginning Aggarwal's ideas about form and structure began to take shape from a young age as he observed his father working on his engineering projects. He transformed interest to skill at the National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT) in Delhi, after which he apprenticed with Russian couturiers, Seredin and Vasiliev for six months, working as a design assistant and pattern cutter. Aggarwal then worked as a ready-to-wear assistant designer with Tarun Tahiliani before venturing out on his own. A collaboration with Delhi-based apparel design studio, Creative Impex, led to the designer's first independent clothing line called Morphe in 2008. For Aggarwal, this was a validation that, “fearlessness and truthfulness to my beliefs paid off”. Morphe eventually culminated in his eponymous couture label, Amit Aggarwal in 2012 followed by his diffusion label AM.IT in 2015. View Gallery 36 Photos AM.IT by Amit Aggarwal at Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2017 AM.IT by Amit Aggarwal at Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2017 On innovating with upcycling While Aggarwal's vision is not limited to just upcycling or the use of industrial materials, it has always been an indispensable part of his work. Constructing ensembles from amorphous forms is the brand's mainstay. “If it wasn't noticed before, it was only because back in the day, no one in India was looking at fashion as a tool of intellect. In 2008, I used upcycled bottle caps for fine and intricate handwork that were hidden between layers of fabric. Then in 2009, I sourced fabrics woven by chanderi weavers that were turned into structural pieces with plastic polymer and zari.” Since then, Aggarwal has worked with upcycled vintage Patola with recycled polymer detailing, upcycled vintage Benarasi borders, hand block prints, recycled discs, molten recycled plastic, plastic bags, bindi sheets, toy parts and Patola and Benarasi fabrics that were no longer usable as saris. The process “The process begins with the search for the right kind of material that excites, and is ready to be treated differently. It's always a mix of natural and manmade that is the base for creating our textiles. We fuse, melt, embroider and stitch—various processes are utilised to amalgamate opposing elements, for instance, polythene on chanderi. The challenge is to find a new upcycled material every time, and ensuring its availability and consistency. Stitching non-fabric material like fabric is another challenge.” View Gallery 33 Photos Amit Aggarwal at Lakmé Fashion Week Summer/Resort 2017 Amit Aggarwal at Lakmé Fashion Week Summer/Resort 2017 The diffusion line Aggarwal's diffusion label AM.IT, a play on ‘I am it', is a montage of various industrial and cultural design elements from India, and follows the same ideologies as the main line. “AM.IT came about with a growing consciousness that the youth has today. This consciousness can be seen on different levels—be it the roots that we come from or where we would like to take ourselves from there. Even though the pieces are more casual and easy to wear, the ideas of construction are similar to our main line, with the visual contrast being higher.” The milestones Aggarwal recounts the awards received during the beginning of his career, a standing exhibit at the ARKEN Museum of Modern Art in Copenhagen (2012-2013), and a Ted Talk in 2012 as some of the highlights of his journey thus far. The designer considers his ‘Plastic Perfect' collection, blending two utilities of the common Indian man (the polythene and the gamcha), Morphe's moulded collection with thin nylon boning in chiffon, and the Amazon India AW '17 grand finale with upcycled Patolas and Benarasi brocades, as his top three shows, and the bird dress created for the Vogue Fashion Fund as the ensemble he is most proud of. The advice to aspiring designers “Reason why do you want to make what you want to make. Start only when you feel some answers are coming your way. There is no dearth of beautiful clothes in the market. But one should know the reason they want to create. I feel it's especially important to stick to the purest form of your language in your initial years.” View Gallery 30 Photos Amit Aggarwal at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017 Amit Aggarwal at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017 This article is part of our Careers in Fashion series which will get fashion enthusiasts advice, guidance and inspiration from the biggest names in the fashion industry What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Inside H&M’s upcoming designer collaboration with Erdem
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Pet Shop Boys and more The Pet Shop Boys and his mum's school-run outfit formed the starting point for Erdem X H&M. Vogue has the exclusive. [#gallery: /galleries/5ce4380fcc50be17fe14059b]||| ||| “I've never made a hoodie before. It was great to think about what I wanted a hoodie to be,” says Canadian-born, London-based Erdem Moralioğlu excitedly about his latest collaboration with H&M. With this project, Erdem joins the ranks of past collaborators Roberto Cavalli, Karl Lagerfeld, Olivier Rousteing and Rei Kawakubo. “It's a thrill to be able to explore what I do on such a large scale,” he says. Tell us about the inspiration. The Pet Shop Boys' music video ‘Being Boring', imagining a group of young friends invading an English country house. I then thought about my childhood. My sister would wear a fleece with tea dresses, my mum wore my dad's jacket over her shoulders when she drove us to school. I also looked back at my work, re-examining silhouettes and shapes. You've been labelled the ‘Master of Florals'... It comes from my fascination with things that imply femininity, whether it's flowers or fabrics such as lace. I like playing with this language. What's the most surprising element of this collaboration? Designing pieces that were totally new to me. I love the idea of pairing the hoodie with the gowns, like someone might do at the end of a party in the countryside. What are your favourite styles? I love the dresses, especially the jacquard gown or the sun plissé dress. The faux leopard coat has a grosgrain ribbon that can either be tied at the neck or worn as a belt. The grey Harris tweed suit for women came from a fitting where I tried men's tailoring on a woman and loved the way it looked. I wanted it to be a totally versatile collection. Ann-Sofie Johansson, Head Of Design, H&M H&M has collaborated with a number of designers in the past. Can you play favourite? The timing felt right for a collaboration with a British designer known for his romantic style after sassy Balmain and street-smart Kenzo. What surprised you the most about working with Erdem? His creations are about pure beauty, romantic, magical, feminine and powerful at the same time. It is all about the love for the craft and textiles and delicately designed feminine fashion. What are your favourite pieces? The whole collection is very versatile. You can mix the lace blouses or the long dresses with a men's-style blazer over your shoulder. I really like the jacquard suit, the Harris tweed garments or the leopard fake-fur long coat, together with the jewel bag. The collection launches at H&M stores at Ambience Mall and Vasant Kunj in New Delhi and at High Street Phoenix Mall in Mumbai in November. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Apple CEO Tim Cook on the future of fashion and augmented reality
column2:
© Vogue Images Fashion How AR is going to change how you see, use and buy fashion Imagine that you're out to lunch, and in walks a woman wearing a terrific-looking coat. Who designed it? Did she buy it last season, or is it still on sale? Covertly, you give her coat a quick scan on your smartphone, find out it's available on Farfetch, and moments later it's on its way out for delivery. According to Apple CEO Tim Cook, that future may not be far off. In a sit-down interview with Vogue in London on Tuesday, the leader of the world's most valuable technology company said he is betting big on augmented reality (AR), which he believes will transform everything from runway shows to shopping. “I don't think there is any sector or industry that will be untouched by AR,” he said. Fashion shows are particularly ripe for AR intervention, he said: “If you think about a runway show in the fashion world, that's great application of AR because some of these, you want to see the dress all the way around, you do not want to just see the front.” That kind of experience is all the more important now that runway shows are catering to a wider consumer audience watching online, and not just those seated in the front rows, he added. At the end of September, Burberry—always one to take advantage of new technologies—introduced a new AR feature to its flagship iPhone app. It allows users to overlay Burberry-inspired digital illustrations by the artist Danny Sangra onto their camera view, which they can then share with their friends on social media. The feature was built using ARKit, a new toolset from Apple that enables software developers to build AR experiences on iPhones and iPads in an easier way. Unveiled at its annual developers' conference in June, it officially hit the market with the launch of the iPhone and iPad's latest software update, iOS 11, in September. Since Apple rolled out ARKit in September, a number of retailers have begun integrating the technology into their iPhone and iPad apps, giving us a glimpse of online shopping's future. Last month, Ikea and Anthropologie released new versions on their apps that allow customers to see how a new chair or lamp might look in their living rooms—and in the latter's case, even sample different fabrics and colours. “Over time, I think [these features] will be as key as having a website,” Cook said.    [#gallery: /galleries/5ce439f04a30b3869012e5f1]||| |||      
 But these are examples are just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the impact AR will have on fashion and shopping in the long-term, Cook indicated. Over the past few years, technology startups and brands including Rimmel and Gap have launched apps that invite shoppers to “try on” makeup and clothes virtually. But none have been advanced enough to compare to the experience of trying on a beautiful matte foundation or tricky pair of trousers in store. Is that about to change? Cook said he doesn't think the technology will get there “this year”, but he does see a significant role for AR in the online shopping experience—and potential for offline applications, too. It will also take some time before we'll be able to scan and identify other women's coats on our phones, a la the example outlined above. Cook says the company has no plans to build the giant database of clothes, shoes and other goods that would make it possible. But Apple does plan to support companies who might embark on such an endeavour, he said. “We don't have a plan to collect all of these objects, but I know companies who are working on that for their products,” Cook said. “If you think about companies that offer a fair number of shoes, and [if a customer] sees a shoe and goes I want that one, you just want to point and [buy]. That will be a part of the shopping experience of the future, it absolutely will.” One other area where Apple, AR and fashion might intersect? Glasses. For years, tech bloggers have salivated over the promise of AR glasses designed by Apple—ones that would offer greater capabilities than Google's ill-fated Google Glass, and look slicker, too. But the bloggers will have to wait a little longer. “There are rumours and gossip about companies working on that, and we obviously don't talk about what we work on. But today I can tell you that the technology itself doesn't exist to do that in a quality way,” Cook said. “We don't give rats about being first, we want to be best in creating people's experiences. column1: Deepika Padukone’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The actor has a wardrobe worthy of her killer body View Gallery 148 Photos Deepika Padukone’s complete style evolution When she first burst onto the scene in 2007 with Om Shanti Om, then-model Deepika Padukone let her style fall in line with the widely-accepted Bollywood actor stereotype: embellished Indian wear, strong highlights in her hair and dark make-up. Now a global phenomenon cheered on by the the crowds at Cannes and the Met Gala, Deepika Padukone is something of style icon. Instrumental in crafting her identity as a style maven was her role as the party hopping Veronica Malaney from Cocktail (2012). The Sanjay Leela Bhansali heroine went on to star in period dramas like Goliyon Ki Rasleela Ram-Leela (2013), Bajirao Mastani (2015) and now Padmavati (2017) which highlighted the actors ability to transform into characters from an era past. Equally adept in taking on contemporary drama, Padukone is known for films like Tamasha (2015) and Piku (2015). Her role as Serena Unger opposite Vin Diesel in xXx: Return of Xander Cage  (2017) that cemented Padukone as an international sensation. Style files It was in 2011 that the star really came into her own and started picking silhouettes and edgy styles that suited her model good looks and poise. It started with a CUE by Rohit Gandhi and Rahul Khanna one-shoulder metallic dress, a difficult silhouette for anybody without Padukone's athletic arms. The Bollywood actor then discovered the magic of New York-based designer Naeem Khan, repeatedly choosing evening looks from his runway shows. Deepika Padukone spent 2013 shooting and promoting four films without a hair (or red carpet look) out of place. The star was spotted in everything from an Alexander McQueen gown to a Shehla Khan lehenga, Sonaakshi Raaj sari gown and that barely-there Gaurav Gupta gown. Partial to work of designer Sabyasachi Mukerjee, Padukone is known to favour Indian ethnic looks by his label. In 2016 we saw Padukone's love for athliesure. Whenever the star wasn't attending award ceremonies, she favoured sportswear basics like leggings and bombers from airports to shoots. The red Ralph & Russo number worn by the star at the 2016 Filmfare Awards was one of the best received looks seen on the star. 2017 has been one of the best years, sartorially speaking, for the actor. From her pristine white Tommy Hilfiger gown at the Met Ball to the plum tulle Marchesa number, Padukone's been on the global style watch. Evolution Padukone was never one to make a style faux pass but there's a certain identity the star has found for herself balancing athleisure style with all out glamour. Once a fan of saturated hues of reds and royal blues, Padukone now favours a more mature palette of colours. From Gucci pyjama suits to floral saris, there's hardly a boring style moment for this star. Go through our gallery to have a complete look at Deepika Padukone's style evolution. column1: What you can learn from Priyanka Chopra’s airport style
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion There are no rules View Gallery 10 Photos What can you learn from Priyanka Chopra’s airport style? We're pretty sure Priyanka Chopra has got her hands on some Hermione Granger-approved time-turning secrets; how else would you explain the nonchalant ease (and dizzying frequency) with which she hops from Mumbai to Montreal to Amman to LA in a New York minute? With a transcontinental acting career, Chopra's current passport count stands at six, and she has often confessed that she spend at least a couple of days a month, maybe even a full week, on a plane. And boy, does she do it in style. So if you're looking for airport dressing cues, you might as well take them from someone who clocks in more air miles a month than most people do in a year. Jeans and tees don't feature that often in PC's airport wardrobe, though maxi dresses and jumpsuits have become a fixture this year. Of late, the actor has been notably bringing a more resort vibe to her travel repertoire. Need to dash to your private island villa straight from the airport? Do like Chopra and choose a roomy floral maxi that marries tropical chic with on-flight comfort. From striped and floral floor-skimming numbers to strapless and buckled jumpsuits, Chopra often teams her travel go-tos with long duster coats and denim jackets. If you'd rather touch down in joggers but are a staunch believer in standing tall even through long security check queues, Chopra suggests you give your athleisure look a well-heeled update. Though if you're taking a leaf from her book, swap the stilettos for platform heels and throw on a leather jacket for some extra cool girl cred. One look at Chopra's high-flyer staples, and it's evident that ‘never say never' is the only airport-dressing rule you need to adhere to…one that she endorsed quite literally with her bomber jacket as she recently hopped aboard yet another private jet. column1: Dolce & Gabbana to bring an Italian Christmas Market to London
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Puppets included! View Gallery 28 Photos Dolce & Gabbana is building an Italian Christmas Market in London Stefano Gabbana loves Christmas. Every year on the 24th of December, he and Domenico Dolce, his design and business partner of 32 years, stay up until midnight to usher in the holiday. Later, on Christmas Day, the pair host a lunch for 25 or 26—“children, uncles, nephews, brothers, sisters... we mix our families,” Gabbana tells Vogue. There is always a tree, hung with dozens upon dozens of mementoes, the result looking like “total chaos, a flea market.” Everyone is asked to cook a dish—and this being Italy, there is always a meat ravioli—though Gabbana usually cheats and buys something. “I'm not a good cook,” he confesses. “Domenico is very good.” While only a few can enjoy the privilege of dining in famiglia with Dolce and Gabbana, this holiday season, shoppers in London can at least get a little taste. From November 2 until December 28, the designers are setting up an Italian Christmas Market inside the lacquered walls of the luxury department store Harrods. There will be a tree out front, decorated not like a flea market but in gold ribbons and colourful lights. The windows will be designed in the style of a Sicilian puppet theatre, with Dolce and Gabbana appearing in marionette form to introduce passersby to the story of the house. On the fourth floor, visitors will walk into a replica Italian piazza strung with coloured lights. Booths will display a variety of goods, many designed exclusively for the department store, including floral and sequin-embroidered women's evening dresses, festive men's suits in striped lurex and silk shantung, and children's ready-to-wear. Those on the hunt for gifts will find displays full of toys, fragrance, fine jewellery, shoes, handbags and other accessories. Dolce and Gabbana have even engaged a painter to personalise any Sicily bags purchased on site. This is not the first time Harrods has invited a single brand to deck its halls for the holiday. Last year, Burberry installed “A very British fairy-tale” in the store's windows, with items designed just for Harrods available for purchase inside. In 2015, the brand was Samsung. “We put our personal [selves] in everything we do,” Gabbana says of this year's takeover. “For me, Christmas is the tree and the nativity, friends and love and all of the most warming things… and now we are [bringing] it to Harrods.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How to wear long skirts as lehengas this festive season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get the most out of your wardrobe With your social calendar probably brimming with party invites, the upcoming festive season gives you an opportunity to make your mark on the circuit by stepping out in your best ensembles. However, if all-out traditional is not the way you want to go, this Diwali, ditch you basic lehenga and kurta sets for long skirts. Style wisely and the long skirt can be your superhero. It could be a piece you have been hesitant to step inside because of its dramatic nature for everyday looks, but the season presents the perfect opportunity to use it to channel an Indian-contemporary vibe. Look through your wardrobe (or browse through your mom's) and style your long skirts with crop tops or long jackets. Go glam with pleated skirts or channel the '90s in tulle numbers. Opt for skirts with embellished hems that make for the perfect pictures when you're twirling through the night. Turn to bright reds and pinks when you need to amp up your look. Acing a long skirt as a lehenga may not seem like an easy feat, but Bollywood stars have done it quite effortlessly. Wear your long skirt with a crisp white shirt or pair a metallic number with a subtle black blouse as seen on Alia Bhatt. While prepping up for a Diwali party, we recommend going with a printed long skirt like Tamannaah Bhatia's. Or you can play the festive field like Karisma Kapoor by throwing on a jacket over your lehenga-slash-skirt. View Gallery 11 Photos How to wear long skirts as lehengas this festive season -celebs A solid-hued flared skirt, like the Oscar De La Renta number in our edit, will look great with an embellished cropped top. For a more celebratory look, opt for a long, embellished net skirt like the one from Maison Esve, and throw on a stylish tasselled jacket. For a more relaxed ensemble, step out in a tropical print skirt by Manish Arora and bright crop top that will make for a feminine yet effortless sartorial choice. Mix in some antique jewellery to finish the look. If a long night is on the cards (pun intended), try to pick lightweight fabrics like satin and embroidered nets to help you survive the revelry effortlessly. Experiment with blouses and opt for contemporary Indian pieces. Whether it's small evening puja or an extravagant family gathering, the brief here is festive, without being over-the-top glamorous. For such events, choose a skirt with floral embroidery or pair a velvet number with a breezy blouse. Turn on the drama for evening festivities with a sequinned number by Ingie Paris, styled with an embellished cropped top. For a more daring look, choose the shimmery pleated long skirt by Reem Acra and style it with a versatile blouse. column1: Here’s what you can expect from Nappa Dori Warehouse in Delhi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Retail v2.0 Imagine this: spending a leisurely yet enriching day at an aesthetically curated space where you can shop, learn how to customise your own leather belt, browse through design magazines, and then round it up with coffee at an in-house café. And now consider this: this is not a hipster store we're recommending you visit on your next trip to Europe. Gautam Sinha, the man behind homegrown luxury handmade leather brand Nappa Dori, is bringing this idea to the capital city with an experiential retail space monikered Nappa Dori Warehouse. A sprawling 6,000sqft warehouse-turned-concept store in a secluded spot in central Delhi, the brand's latest outpost takes the signature Nappa Dori experience, and amplifies it exponentially. View Gallery 5 Photos Nappa dori “Guys, please be careful, we cannot have that breaking!” we hear Sinha call out to his team as we dial him for a lowdown on the upcoming space. It's a bank holiday weekend, but unsurprisingly, Sinha is busy adding finishing touches to his latest pet project. Ever since its launch in 2010, Nappa Dori has crafted an identity that is steeped in uncompromising design and craftsmanship with leather at the forefront of its repertoire. Whether it's the artisanal quality of its products or the inimitable DNA of their stores, the brand has a strong identity, and this new venture takes it forward. “The idea has been brewing in my head for a long time, but I only started working on it in the last six months. The term ‘concept store' has been used in the wrong context in India for a long time, and we are trying to change that. This is the first truly ‘concept' store in Delhi where it's not just about retail but a bouquet of different element combined together,” Sinha explains who counts Colette and Merci in Paris as his favourite concept stores. What's in store? The open-planned warehouse has a dedicated shopping area that not only offers Nappa Dori bestsellers like trunks, stationery, accessories, and bags, but also complementing brands like menswear by Shift, tailored classics by Bodice, and limited edition sneakers by VegNonVeg. But Sinha feels that the retail landscape is changing and customers are now looking for experiences that go beyond merely buying products. And this is exactly what the space thrives on. So there is also a workspace-cum-library catering to the creative set. This section not only houses design books but also indie magazines like Moniker, Wallpaper, and Kinfolk among others for which Sinha has tied up with Mumbai-based Paper Planes. And should you wish to refuel, Café Dori ensures you don't need to leave the premises. Designed like a greenhouse with large terrariums livening up the vibe, the in-house eatery is fashioned after a European café with a menu of all-day breakfast favourites and easy bites. There is also a dedicated coffee menu (currently Blue Tokai but other Indian and international brews will be added to the mix soon), as Sinha believes that coffee and leather blend well together. Retail goes experiential Rolling out next month is Nappa Dori Warehouse's atelier, where patrons can book master classes to learn crafts like making leather belts and colouring leather. “The Indian leather industry has been neglected for the longest time, and this is an attempt to revive artisanal craft. Moreover, creating your own products establishes an emotional connect with the brand, as well as a sense of ownership and entitlement,” feels Sinha. The on-site master artisan will also be available to customise certain key Nappa Dori products while one browses through the space. Come November, one can also look forward to specially curated events like book readings and movie screenings. “I am also keen to invite brands who speak a language similar to ours to bring their experiences here,” adds Sinha. “We have worked hard to build a brand with a strong recall value over the last seven years. This space was the next logical way forward. The challenge at hand was, how do we change the social fabric of our society when it comes to design? Delhi lacks places that encourage cultural stimulation. So the idea here is to get like-minded people together to brew a culture that is less competitive, and more community-based,” he carries on. The evolution of the Indian design connoisseur But does Sinha think that the Indian customer is truly ready for this experience? “Think about it—cities like Delhi and Mumbai, which are the country's design hubs, don't offer such experiences. So where will design enthusiasts go? We have to aid their evolution as well.” Sinha believes that the popularity of Nappa Dori is a testament to the changing mindset of the Indian customer. “The younger generation is edgier and broad-minded in their retail habits. They are proud to flaunt homemade products, even when travelling abroad. In fact, they would rather carry Indian brands.” The way forward Sinha is already charting his next steps to change the game with similar experiential retail spaces in other cities as well. Mumbai's suburb of Bandra features high on his wishlist. “Nappa Dori is also experimenting with lifestyle products with objects that marry vintage charm with an Indian sensibility. Home products are also in the pipeline,” reveals Sinha. But the real dream is to go international. “It really surprises me that as far as design is concerned, India does not have an identifiable stamp in the key cities of the world. We are content with displaying our products in small corners of big stores. That needs to change with bold step, and I feel Nappa Dori is ready for this leap.” Nappa Dori Warehouse opens doors on October 14. Dhan Mill Compound, Chattarpur, New Delhi. column1: Fila launches The Culture Project with fashion designers and more
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get a closer look at it View Gallery 4 Photos Fila launches The Culture Project with fashion designers and more Athleisure's gleaming role in our everyday lives is evident to all. While they may be divided by profession, millennials are united by the lifestyle athleisure purports, and sportswear brands are tapping in on that. Fila's support for athletes par excellence like Adriano Panatta, Paolo Bertolucci and Björn Borg is well known. Communicating the brand's journey from that to a newer, younger audience requires storytelling from a new perspective. Who better to translate that than young influencers and designers who have made a cross vocational impact on the youth culture? To celebrate Fila's Iconic collection, and to bring it closer to the new consumers, the brand has launched ‘The Culture Project'. The initiative comprises the likes of designers Sanjay Garg, Ruchika Sachdeva, Nimish Shah, Sanchita Ajjampur, Arjun Saluja, Abhishek Paatni, conservational architect Abha Narain Lambah, musical duo Parekh & Singh, producer, screenwriter and director Kiran Rao and photographer Ashish Shah, who have been roped in for the project. The list also includes notable names from the art and design world such as Aman Khanna, Shiva Nallaperumal, Daksha Salam, journalist Chinki Sinha and tennis player Rian Pandole. Their combined narrative has resulted in illustrations, art pieces and fashion experiments that come together under The Culture Project that has been curated by Kshitij Kankaria. Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice spoke about how getting out of her comfort zone was a learning experience. “It was creatively liberating to merge sensibilities with such a paradoxical yet iconic brand. Such collaborations always make me grow as a designer,” she said. Meanwhile Sanjay Garg, best known for his love for handloom saris, spoke about clash of two seemingly opposite aesthetics and the brainchild born from it. “I like to think that my garments are fundamental classics. Take my saris for instance, that I have tried to make more accessible and appealing to a larger audience. Given the pluralism of this generation, I love how a traditional handloom can be paired with a sporty logo tee and still work.” Scroll through the slideshow for a closer look at The Culture Project by Fila. column1: Why do artists collaborate with fashion designers?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As Frieze London kicks off, Vogue investigates Elsa Schiaparelli and Salvador Dali, Yves Saint Laurent and Piet Mondrian - fashion designers have embraced the world of art to create some of their best and most lasting work. Today, the tradition carries on, stronger than ever. So what's in it for artists? As Frieze London kicks off, Vogue investigates. View Gallery 10 Photos Why do artists collaborate with fashion designers? Virgil Abloh debuted his Spring/Summer 2018 menswear collection at Pitti Uomo earlier this year against the backdrop of a Jenny Holzer installation. For the show, Holzer – the American neo-conceptualist renowned for her large-scale installations in public spaces – projected lines of poetry from Anna Świrszczyńska, written during the Warsaw Uprising, alongside texts by writers of Middle Eastern origins, including Syrian-American writer Osama Alomar, behind the runway. The collaboration, the latest in a series of high-profile partnerships between fashion designers and fine artists, was hailed as a poignant reflection on current events – an example of how fashion can reflect the emotions of the world in which it inhabits. But for every Off-White x Jenny Holzer, there are dozens of artist-designer collaborations where artworks are merely xeroxed onto garments, only to be forgotten at the end of the season. “I always think that designers have fetishised artists,” Esben Weile Kjaer, a Danish artist who has collaborated with the designer Anne Sofie Madsen, tells Vogue. Kjaer's assessment is likely correct. But for the artist, who operates in the lofty realm of galleries and exhibitions as opposed to the rails of boutique stores and down catwalks, why accept the invitation to collaborate at all? The obvious answer is, of course, that partnerships like these often allow artists to create and exhibit their work on a greater scale than before. In the past two seasons, Moncler and photographer Annie Leibovitz invited Chinese performance artist Liu Bolin – known in the art world as the Invisible Man for his chameleon-like acts – to create the brand's imagery, where Liu disappears into the glaciers through body painting. It is one of the most memorable campaigns in recent memory. “I am very particular about who I collaborate with, and I was intrigued by the epic quality of this project, and I've always imagined doing a project in such an intense landscape and backdrop, as in Iceland,” says Liu, whose performances double as environmentalist commentary. But beyond the support that brands provide, the rise of artist-designer collaborations is also perhaps indicative of a much broader shift in the worlds of art and fashion, where the boundaries between the two worlds are becoming increasingly porous. Designers are often heralded as artists, while artists are starting to dabble in design: Liu is an excellent case in point. “From Valentino and Jean Paul Gaultier to Guerlain and Ruinart, I have partnered with many fashion and luxury brands over the years…I've always been interested in fashion collaborations, especially at the brink of my newest project: the launch of my own fashion collection, Liu Bolin,” he reveals. Likewise, the artist Sterling Ruby, a longtime collaborator of Raf Simons's across Dior and Calvin Klein, produces his own wardrobe, conceding little distinction between his artwork and his garments. Nevertheless, some artists, including Christophe Chemin, who partnered with Prada for Autumn 2016, are becoming sceptical of the benefits of collaborations, which have become commonplace. “It became such a trend, even though the idea is absolutely not new,” says Chemin. “I think it should happen only if there is a genuine interest from both sides, and a real exchange… Fashion designers don't really need artists to do great collections, and artists are not clothes enhancers.” But what exactly constitutes a real exchange? While it might be hard to explain, Chemin cites The Ritva Man, a London-based knitwear brand from the ‘60s and ‘70s, as an example. Created by Ritva, a Finnish model and painter, and her husband Mike Ross, an American who briefly attended the Royal College of Art, the brand was embedded in the vibrant art scene of London during the period, inviting the likes of Elisabeth Frink, David Hockney, Patrick Hughes and Allen Jones to share designs for the brand's limited-edition Artist Collection. The garments, sold with acrylic cases so that they could be displayed when not worn, were revered as pieces of art in their own right. Although the Ritva brand is no more, some of its hallmarks have survived. There are surely parallels in the ongoing collaborations between designer Jonathan Anderson, creative director of J.W. Anderson and Loewe, and the artist and photographer Ian David Baker, who is known for his male nudes. Their partnership developed naturally out of patronage, and the respect the designer had for the artist. “My work had a resurgence of interest around 2013 and 2014… I had a call from Jonathan who was interested in buying some photo images and drawings… Later in 2014, [Anderson] suggested a meeting at his offices for a collaboration project,” says Baker. “I think he was a bit obsessed with my work. I mentioned that I hoped he thought it was all going to be worth the effort.” Similarly, by regularly inviting artists to collaborate, Rochambeau designers Laurence Chandler and Josh Cooper are, much like the Rosses, inhabitants in the world they tap into. “I met Laurence of Rochambeau in 2013 at the opening of my Lincoln Center exhibition. He's a collector and had bought some work of mine,” recalls Aaron Curry, who collaborated with the brand for their Spring 2018 collection. “I later met Josh, and without trying to sound too Californian, I really liked their energy,” says Curry, who likened the collaborative process to customising Vans sneakers during his youth. In fashion, where clothes are subject to seasonal turnover, the collection with Curry, which features streetwear staples adorned with the artist's psychedelic creations, possesses also that rare sense of permanence, not unlike the sweaters created by The Ritva Man nearly half a century ago earlier. In December, the collection will be displayed to the art world during Art Basel Miami Beach, where Curry is a regular fixture, alongside his other works. Only after will they appear on the sales floors of fashion boutiques around the world. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Amazon India Fashion Week 2018’s finale designer on 30 years of fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Suneet Varma traces the trajectory View Gallery 7 Photos Amazon India Fashion Week finale designer talks about 30 years of fashion Back in 1991 when Suneet Varma debuted a breastplate on the Indian runways, it caused quite the stir in the country. It was only Varma's intention to show the world his version of Botticelli's 'The Birth of Venus' but the designer jokes about the reaction being ‘titillating'. After straying from becoming a sculptor and finding his footing in fashion, Varma started off his career working with Yves Saint Laurent, and after creating his eponymous label, went on to collaborate with the likes of Swarovski and Judith Leiber in the course of his career. As the chosen one to close the Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2018 edition, he is not done yet. “I have a lot of creativity to explore and a lot of things I wish to do. I like to challenge myself as a designer, whether it's through textiles or accessories or different mediums. I'm very excited about the future. Great runway moments are made when you don't strive to make a statement,” he tells us. Taking the Garden of Eden as his reference point—a good foundation to lay ground when one has an imagination as effervescent as Varma's, the designer expresses his intentions with several adjectives. “The glamour and sensuality in this collection comes through the use of sheer and lucid fabrics, the delicate placement of embellishments, the drapes and the unexpected details—and what they reveal or conceal. Couture is like a sixth sense of seduction. It has its own vocabulary and language, like an elaborate braid entwined with history, myth and tradition. It may be modern, whimsical or demure but always magnificent and carefully crafted,” he says. From breastplates to more subtle innuendos, Varma is not afraid to talk about the position of sex in fashion. “I believe fashion is the politest way of speaking about sex. But I like the subtle unspoken word, left to the imagination of the wearer,” he goes on. “I find my clothes come alive on self-assured, sexy and the modern women of today.” Varma's finale show stage will be shared with six others—Ashish N Soni, Krishna Mehta, Pankaj & Nidhi, Rina Dhaka and Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna who will present their ready-to-wear capsule collections for Amazon.in that will be available to the consumers for purchase instantly. Happy to join the pool of talent, Varma discusses the evolution of the industry since its inception in India. “It [The Indian fashion industry] has become much more organised in the retail sector, client expectations, and of course the platform of fashion weeks. The corporates are now eager to align themselves with fashion and designers. The online medium has been a game changer, but I also like the starry-eyed youngsters who enter the industry with big dreams. And that is the magic of our industry.” Check out the slideshow for peek into Suneet Varma's spring/summer 2018 collection for The Amazon.in Grand Finale. column1: The best designer bridal lehengas to choose for your pheras
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Twirl time View Gallery 17 Photos The best designer lehengas to choose for your pheras Bridal lehengas hold a special place in a woman's wardrobe. There is no day bigger in your week-long wedding celebration than the main event itself. Nothing is going to be as important as making the memory of your pheras picture perfect, and sure enough you need a bridal lehenga do that moment complete justice. First off, if you're debating between a sari and a lehenga, the latter, with its full skirt and the possibility of two dupattas is certainly going make a prettier picture. The ideal bridal lehenga isn't too heavy—be warned there is a lot of movement involved during the pheras, and you don't want to be weighed down by your sartorial choices. Choose from blush pink lehengas to those with floral detailing and of course the traditional red bridal lehengas. You can, of course, make an alternative choice and go with a full gold look to make a statement. Don't write off shades of peach when it comes to choosing a lehenga for pheras. Look at labels like Rahul Mishra and Neeta Lulla for a varied approach to the traditional bridal lehenga. Sabyasachi is a label that values tradition over all else. If you plan to go old school on your big day, pick an ornate bridal lehenga by Sabyasachi. Manish Malhotra, meanwhile is a fan of sparkle. Look at Manish Malhotra lehengas if you want to make your debut as a married woman in full glamour. Tarun Tahiliani is a master at balancing sophistication with lightweight couture. If you're all about understated elegance, look no further than a Tarun Tahiliani lehenga. If you're one for minimal embellishments, choose a rich brocade lehenga and let the fabric do all the talking. What's also crucial when choosing a bridal lehenga is picking one with the perfect blouse. Don't hesitate to ask for a custom blouse if you're not fully satisfied with the one that comes as a part of the set. The bold bride can choose an embellished blouse with mesh panels that feels like second skin. Elegance is preferred at the usually-traditional phera ceremony, so avoid sleeveless blouses when it comes your bridal lehenga. You can opt for a heavily-embellished neckline and go easy on the statement neckpieces to avoid feeling overtly decked up on you wedding day. The true test of a bridal lehenga is for it to be able to stand the test of time. Don't fall prey to passing trends and choose a piece that could seem too outlandish in the years to come. Have a clear vision in mind about the kind of bride you want to be and make sure that the message comes through with what you choose to wear on one of the most important days of your life. Make an early appointment with the designer of your choice and pencil in those fittings for your dream look. Scroll through our gallery of the best designer lehengas to choose from for your pheras. column1: Anushka Sharma’s new clothing line is for every girl-on-the-go
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get ready to fill your wardrobe with Nush View Gallery 3 Photos Anushka Sharma Nush launch From actor to producer, Anushka Sharma juggles many hats. And just when you thought she couldn't possibly manage anymore, the star surprised her fans all over the world last evening, announcing the launch of her very own clothing line. “This is something I've been wanting to do for a very long time,” Sharma revealed about the brand, which has aptly been named Nush, one of her nicknames. “Clothes are actually something that we live in, they are a huge part of our lives. Our style is the way we express ourselves, the way we express our mood. I wanted to create a brand that can add that value to someone's life, be a part of that person's life.” A feel-good combination of easy-breezy cuts, vibrant colours, happy prints and low maintenance casuals, Nush channels Sharma's trademark, fuss-free style. If you're a fan, you'll definitely recognise the actor's vibe in the distressed denims, cosy bombers and boho blouses, all made keeping the wearer's comfort in mind. Think floaty dresses in opaque fabrics that don't need layering, jackets featuring lots of pockets, and versatile pieces that aren't a stress to style. “I have personally taken interest in the styles of Nush, so there's a bit of myself in all the outfits,” Sharma tells Vogue before sharing her journey. “I got really emotional before the launch. I was thinking about the time when my mom and I used to go shopping. We didn't have enough, I come from a very regular middle class family, my father's in the army, and I was modelling back then. It was difficult; I needed to have good clothes because I used to have to go for auditions, and my mother used to make sure that I was able to have those things. As a young girl, shopping for clothes that suited my sense of fashion under one roof was a struggle. If we got the right style, the price didn't fit, when we found the right price, it was lacking in style. My father used to get so bored, he'd be sitting outside talking to the guy making bhel puri! When my parents came and joined me today, all those memories came back to me. I thought to myself, I couldn't have imagined at that time that one day I'd have my own clothing line!” Comprising of over 160 pieces, the debut collection of Nush hits Shoppers Stop outlets in India on October 12, and you can also buy pieces online on Myntra. “What you do is really important, and so is who you do it with,” says Sharma. “I want to take this opportunity to thank Suditi Industries (the clothing company behind your new favourite buys).” Can't wait to start shopping? Scroll through our slideshow for a sneak peek at the line, and discover Sharma's style secrets below. On standing her ground "I've gone to my friends' parties wearing pyjamas in the past, and I felt damn cool. So many times, people have made fun of me, saying ‘How can you wear this and come?' and I'm like, ‘So what? I'm feeling damn good in this!' Someone once told me, ‘This is an old season you're wearing.' I said, ‘I don't give a shit. This is what it is and I'm completely okay with it'." On her non-screen style twin "Every role that I've done, there's been a part of me that I've left behind in. My personal style has been reflected in each character because the stylist wants you to wear what you look best in. I would say the character whose style matches mine the most is Farah, from Dil Dhadakne Do, or even Simran from Patiala House. Definitely not Sejal from Jab Harry Met Sejal though. She used to wear a necklace that said ‘Sejal'. I would never wear a necklace with my own name!" On the one trend she'll never get on board with "I don't like wearing tight dresses, I feel very uncomfortable in bodycons. It just doesn't suit me." On the best style advice in her book "If you enjoy wearing clothes, that's one thing. But treating it as a pressure, and trying to find gratification and value for yourself through clothes, that's not good. That's not a good mindset to have. My only advice is wear clothes to feel good. Clothes, or anything else exterior, should not be something you need to add value to yourself. It's not an easy thing to do, but try making little efforts in not letting that be your focal point of your life, the primary reason you do things." On her go-to shopping method "I don't even try clothes on. I know what's going to fit me, and I shop very quickly. I know what I need, and I take it as a huge achievement, that as I'm growing older, I'm becoming faster and faster. There's no ‘what ifs'. Quick, quick, quick!" On Bollywood's best dressed "From Sonam Kapoor to Kangana Ranaut and Jacqueline Fernandez, I think everybody dresses well. Amongst the men, I think Akshay Kumar has a great individual sense of style, Ranbir Kapoor also dresses really well, and Ranveer Singh is a bit on the other side, but it's really good also!" On wardrobe malfunctions "It's sad that people write about wardrobe malfunctions; it's akin to someone falling and you laughing at them. As a human being, if you see someone in distress, would you publish that and say, ‘Look! This person is in distress!' No right? What is that mindset? It really shocks me that anybody would do that. It's highly disrespectful and disgusting. I wouldn't give a damn if someone did that to me. I don't think I'd give it so much attention. But that is why with Nush, we've made an effort to make fabrics thicker, to provide camisoles and slips with the clothes, to make life easier for the wearer." column1: The visible thong and other strange things making a comeback in fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Never say never If Shefali Zariwala's bold wardrobe choices didn't make your parents enforce a ban on the infamous ‘Kaanta Laga' music video, did you really grow up during the Noughties? If fashion's affair last season was with the choker loving decade of the nineties, this spring/summer 2018, designers have pushed the envelope to bring back some of the most shock-inducing trends from the early 2000s. View Gallery 12 Photos The visible thong and other strange things that are making a comeback in fashion Exhibit A: The visible thong Kendall Jenner's shimmery La Perla dress at the Met Ball (one that left very little to the imagination) was an early harbinger of the trend. The runways this season starting with risk loving Becca McCharen-Tran of Chromat made a full dive to the hip-baring blast from the past look. Another veteran in the arts of provocative fashion, Tom Ford himself showed a high-cut bodysuit well over the waist of low slung pants for this runway show this season. New York-based creative studio Linder's take on the extremities-only underwear was to shine the spotlight on them. Their version of the exaggerated high-waisted thong is not for the faint of heart. Bella Hadid of the hip-baring Cannes gown fame is a natural at wearing the trend and was spotted in a mesh bodysuit riding over her track bottoms. Masterfully done in a monochrome, Hadid's sartorial choices are certainly more 2017 than The Simple Life era Paris Hilton. Try it: We are not saying showing off your thong is for everyone. There certainly is a time and place for your underwear to peek out and say hello to your peers. Save the attention-seeking look for the after-hours. Exhibit B: Return of the Crocs Do Crocs have a place in high fashion? Demna Gvasalia at Balenciaga who made blanket bags a thing sure thinks so. Pairing evening dresses with platform Croslite footwear did raise eyebrows but this is not the first time we've seen the phenomenon. London-based Christopher Kane was first to bring Crocs to the runway for autumn/winter 2017. Try it: What does the recurrent presence of the lovingly dismissed shoe mean for the viewers? Wear with a sense of humour is the only styling tip on this one. Exhibit C: Are bum bags the new 'It-bags'? Bum bags are going strong this season as they did with the influx of Gorpcore a few months ago. Spotted at Prada and Gucci, the bum bag is showing no signs of receding from mainstream fashion. Need further proof? Look no further than Kim Kardashian West taking hers out for a spin in the evening. Try it: All things considered, this is probably the most doable of the throwback trend revivals we've seen so far. column1: Sabyasachi Mukherjee and Christian Louboutin kick off their world tour together
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Their new collaboration gets a global stage He's celebrating 25 years of his eponymous label this year and far from scaling things back, Christian Louboutin is raring to go. Case in point: the forthcoming launch of his latest project, a collaboration with Indian haute couture designer - and Bollywood favourite - Sabyasachi Mukherjee. The exclusive collection sees 15 women's styles and four menswear styles created using sarees and ribbons from Mukherjee's atelier archive - cut-offs which have been kept and treasured - making each pair totally original and totally unique. "The way we started to work together was very organic - very Indian, in a way," Louboutin told us. "What happened is that Mukherjee asked me if I could do shoes for his couture fashion shows in India, after we met randomly by accident in his Mumbai store. We started to collaborate, integrating my shoes in his shows and from that it was a natural step for me to do this collection. In his studio, where the embroidery is created, it's basically a type of Ali Baba cave - a profusion of colours, of beads, and of beauty in general. It's unreal, you have a lot of beautiful things which are sort of just put on the side, leftovers of things. I thought, instead of wanting to create something very specific and new, it would be very nice to work around things which are already existing and doing a mosaic of all those little bits and pieces." The art of collaboration - an increasing trend among high-profile designers - is one which Louboutin holds dear. Speaking frankly about the importance of "marrying different points of view", the famed footwear designer believes that's it's "nice to collaborate with people who are concerned with other things". The beauty of working with Mukherjee also gave Louboutin the chance to get hands-on with Indian handcraft, which he calls the best in the world. "The luxuriance of Indian couture is unparalleled, things you see in India you see nowhere else," he enthused. "I wanted the world outside of India to love it as I do." So why, then, wait until now? View Gallery 20 Photos Sabyasachi Mukherjee and Christian Louboutin kick off their world tour together "When you reach some milestone dates like a quarter of a century, you sort of want to look back and see what has been interesting for yourself," he explained. "Basically, when you are a bit successful in your work, you have access to different opportunities, try and experience different things and it's not too dangerous for you. You have a sense that you can go in a new direction and if it doesn't work, or it just isn't interesting, you can just leave it on the side and move onto something else. It's important to have a focus, but at the same time you can have variations and this is what I have found success is good for." While there are myriad reasons for his success, one key reason must be his believe in letting "things go with the flow", as is the fact that the designer is happy to consider all manner of projects and unions that may come his way and recognises that it's important "to accept that something you have never been thinking about could be interesting and to accept that meeting this person or that person can bring you a new wind and could be something which makes you excited". It's a philosophical approach that comes courtesy of his father, a carpenter, who taught a young Louboutin that if he wanted to make beautiful things, he had to go in the direction of the grain, not against it as that's when "you end up having splinters". "If you go in the direction of life, you have to go along with the direction it is taking you but sometimes the grain is not a straight line," he explained. "I allow myself to let things come to me instead of giving to myself a direction that dictates to me. You don't need to programme everything you do, but what does need to be programmed is to be receptive to different possibilities instead of narrowing yourself in one direction and this is how I approach the process for this collaboration." View Gallery 33 Photos 33 times Bollywood chose Sabyasachi wedding wear For Louboutin this means living life with "passion and enthusiasm because, just like love, it's communicated through your enthusiasm and your passion in your work and therefore communicated to people who like your work too." And it shows. Christian Louboutin and Sabyasachi Mukherjee will be travelling to London (Harrod's, October 11), New York (Bergdorf Goodman, October 16-17), Los Angeles (October 19-20), Hong Kong (Lane Crawford, November 1), Shanghai (Art021, November 8-19), Tokyo (Aoyama, November 9), Dubai (Level Shoes) and Paris,  with their collection. column1: Manish Malhotra showcases 85 stunning looks in a runway show in Dubai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Dubai brides, you need to check this out View Gallery 29 Photos Manish Malhotra showcases 85 stunning looks in a runway show in Dubai Manish Malhotra has always spoken about his love for Dubai, the Indian designer who makes regular trips to this city has had a retail presence in the city for a decade now. So when the couturier, who is known for glamorous designs, and whose devotees include Kareena Kapoor Khan, Sridevi and Jacqueline Fernandez, presents a pop-up, he does it in his characteristic flamboyant style. Malhotra held a preview of his flash retail shop with a fashion show on scale that is grand even by Dubai standards. It is his love for high-octane glamour that has made him Bollywood's favoured designer. And he proved that by closing his show with not one but three showstoppers—Kriti Sanon, Sidharth Malhotra and Manish's long-time friend, Karan Johar. 650 of Dubai's fashion set turned up for the event held on Friday night, though there were only 400 seats. As the anchor designer of Design One Dubai which took place this weekend at the Jumeirah Emirates Towers, this show was truly a “Best of Manish Malhotra 2017”. The 85 piece show included pieces from his India Couture Week (ICW) finale presentation in Delhi, 'A Sensual Affair, and his Lakmé Fashion Week finale show 'Tales of Indulgence' which was staged in Mumbai, as well some pieces especially tailored for Dubai. And be it the long trains, the oversized surface ornamentation, blinged-out fringes, and feather details, it was a collection for someone who wants to embrace her inner diva. Yet it seemed cleaner and more contemporary than any of his previous collections. A colour palate that was mostly in greys, silvers, beiges and gold ensured that there was an overall sense of elegance, so it balanced the drama of the embroidery and embellishments. While his cuts had their roots in Indian tradition, they were married with European couture silhouettes. After the show, Malhotra decoded this presentation and said, "It is a complete collection that can be worn in numerous scenarios from weddings to grand gala events. These are drapes that cam be worn in Mumbai or Milan."  It is obvious that he now feels that it is time to expand out of India. The designer did reveal that he would like to open his own flagship store in the city soon. And Dubai can't wait to welcome him. What's New Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This playful pop-up exhibit brings Jaipur to Mumbai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Mark your calendars View Gallery 11 Photos This playful pop up exhibit brings Jaipur to Mumbai A pop up exhibit coinciding with the festive season is not unheard of in the city, so what makes ‘Everyday, Play A Little' different? A collaboration between Baro and Wolf Jaipur, this one cannot be boxed as yet another shopping event. For starters, it has been curated as one-of-a kind experiential show. Srila Chatterjee and Siddharth Sirohi founded Baro as a space focusing on creative expression, design and furniture. Ritu and Surya Singh's Wolf is about bringing together like-minded, passionate individuals to collaborate on artistic pursuits. The two have come together for ‘Everyday, Play A Little' to remind everyone to not get so caught up in life that you forget to enjoy it. Secondly, it shines the spotlight on a collective of designers, artists, game specialists, and installations from Jaipur who have been carefully handpicked for their inimitable aesthetic. And here comes the intriguing clincher—Baro's midtown space has been metamorphosed into a fantasy doll house using scrap and discarded materials, where each room not only narrates whimsical stories from Jaipur and beyond, but also encourages the feeling of curiosity and wonder rather than materialism among the attendees. “Ever since we launched Baro, we have been committed to making a statement about our headspace, which is a mix of great design and originality. We are interested in an equity in society, and in showcasing talent from different places that is not ‘trending' or commonplace,” explains Chatterjee. She roped in Ritu to curate this show with designers from Jaipur who embody the spirit of not just being thoroughly committed to their craft, but also enjoying it. As you stroll through this unconventional exhibit setup, Chatterjee and Singh are sure you'll fall in love with every piece on display, but what they really want you to do is appreciate it and expose yourself to newer concepts and ideas. Carrying on the theme of ‘play', you'll find tops (the first toys ever invented) and design products centred on board games by Priyanka Shah of Shed. Brigitte Singh who is known for her work with traditional textile printing and block printing will be displaying her creations in the form of a classic tea party while Umrao Jewels will be serving up a bling feast on the dining table. Look out for their designs that range from vintage Art Deco and Art Nouveau to Mughal heritage kundan and meena work. Padmini Bika of O'd' Gulabee Jaipur has been collecting a treasure trove of antiques and curios for the past 25 years, and her addition to the exhibit is a selection of old utensils, tiffins, dabbas, barnis, and thalis, all with stories behind them. Textile aficionados will be drawn to Rajasthan Fabric & Arts' display of museum-worthy antique textiles as well as contemporary textile house Satayam's (patron of dying weaves and textile printing) collection. Anjana Nair's ‘Lap of the Artist' will be showcased on seats and chairs while Wolf's series of old photographs finds any interesting form of presentation in memory boxes in dollhouses. And then there is Timmie Kumar, who has created a line of products for Help-in-Suffering that provides a large veterinary hospital, treatment care and succour to suffering animals in Jaipur. Each designer is uniquely different, and that is what ties them together as well. “What is fundamental to us is not just what you do, but also the way you do it. The spirit of an individual's work is as essential to us as the product. Every designer in the showcase shares ideologies similar to us. We wanted to work with people whose thoughts we enjoy, who are special in their work and being, and bring an individualistic quality of whimsy and energy to the exhibit,” explains of Singh. So if you feel all work and no play is dulling your being, make a beeline for this showcase. But don't attend it with the intention of merely filling up your shopping totes, as that would defeat the very purpose. All you need is the intent to have a good time. ‘Everyday, Play A Little' is being held at Baro from October 1 to 11, 2017. Sun Mill Compound, 12, Lower Parel Bridge, Lower Parel, Mumbai What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Inside Rahul Mishra’s technicolour showcase at Paris Fashion Week 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Straight off the runway View Gallery 12 Photos Inside Rahul Mishra’s technicolour showcase at Paris Fashion Week If there was ever a designer to stress on the importance of ‘stop and smell the roses' (or all things nature in his case) it was Rahul Mishra. Now an invariable on the Paris Fashion Week schedule, Mishra's efforts to keep up with the momentum are anything but unnoticed on the international runway. A clear departure from floral motifs save for a few pieces is evident in his spring/summer 2018 collection. Edging towards shirting inspired dresses, flowing skirts, ruffled hems, Mishra's lineup was pure summer and crafted for the international palette. “Imagine driving through a natural park at 300 kilometers per hour. You are surrounded by the most wonderful things but you're moving so fast ahead, all you can see is lines of colours past you,” he explains. From last season's Van Gogh-inspired colour experiment of using five to seven hues per garment, Mishra pushed the envelope to using 70 odd colours in each look—the finish of which is so subtle that the hand embroidery can easily be mistaken for print. A proud father, Mishra's spring/summer 2018 showcase happened to coincide with his two-year-old daughter Aarna's birthday who subconsciously formulated the designer's perspective for the new season. “I wanted to bring to notice how much of our lives are spent looking through four inches of the phone screen. I wonder how spending all this time on the phone might disable Aarna from seeing beauty,” he muses. Showcasing in the homeland as well as internationally while balancing sustainable production is no mean feat but Mishra's enthusiasm is such that it will fuel his strategy for more seasons to come. column1: Careers in fashion: Payal Khandwala on switching careers
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And having a point of view Ever since she launched her eponymous label in 2012, Payal Khandwala has come to be known for her innovative use of colours and textures to craft layered silhouettes that made a statement while still flirting with minimalism. The nuanced attention to detailing and her focus on a refined sense of luxury were what lent Khandwala's creations their dramatic flair, minus an ornate aesthetic. In the years that followed since her fashion debut, Khandwala came to be preferred for her relaxed and free-spirited cuts, especially by the non-conformist connoisseur who did not wish to dress like one in a crowd. Her contribution to the conversation on the contemporary reimagination of the Benarasi weave for the millennial Indian woman also strengthened her standing in the industry. And while Khandwala is a fashion design graduate from SNDT in Mumbai, was under the tutelage of Wendell Rodricks, and won ‘designer of the year' in a nationwide competition held by ShoppersStop in 1994, she did not immediately dive into the industry. In fact, she went on to pursue a BFA in Fine Arts and Illustration from the Parsons School Of Design, New York. During this time, she also worked with designer Sandy Dalal, CFDA's winner of the Perry Ellis Award for menswear in 1997. Khandwala also studied at Metafora, an international workshop for Contemporary Art in Barcelona, in 2005 and exhibited her artworks across Mumbai, Delhi, New York, London, Barcelona, Tokyo and Singapore before fashion came calling. Despite having studied fashion before fine arts, Khandwala decided to explore the latter as she felt that she did not have a design point of view back then. “This is essential in my opinion. Do what you love and believe in it, irrespective of whether it will make you money or not, and do it well. And if you don't have a voice that is unique, then wait till you find it. No point adding to the clutter,” feels Khandwala. “I only started making clothes when I thought there might be other women like myself out there, that might like to wear what I was creating. As long as they are around I'm happy to continue what I'm doing. Happy accidents along the way are always welcome.” Vogue speaks to the designer on how to tread forward when your calling comes serendipitously knocking, on cultivating a distinct voice, and the importance (or lack thereof) of planning in the face of passion. You have an educational background in both fine arts and fashion, and you chose to initially pursue a career in art. What is your advice to someone who wants to jump careers? Oddly enough, I studied fashion before fine arts. But I was young and inexperienced, and would have struggled to decide what I would design and for whom. I had painted since I was a little girl. So I simply followed my instinct and my passion. I knew I would have more control and freedom. Moreover, I was always very comfortable with paint and pencils. Almost two decades later, an opportunity arose to show at fashion week. But the jump for me was more a shift in canvas. However this time, my tryst with fashion was also very different, as I knew the woman I was designing for. I chose to make clothes that I could not find, clothes I wanted to wear, and clothes that represented a new India. This was something that was almost non-existent five years ago in our fashion landscape. So even though it was not strategic, this time around I had complete clarity. View Gallery 42 Photos Payal Khandwala at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016 Payal Khandwala at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016 How easy or difficult was it to make this choice? I'm impulsive by nature and I trust my instincts. So I jumped right into it. I always enjoyed the process of making a garment, the draping, and the textiles… so I knew the journey, regardless of the outcome, would be fun. I was also grateful for the opportunity to launch the label this way and I didn't want to miss it. So for me personally, because I didn't approach it with some long-term plan, the choice was pretty straightforward. As an ex-art student, what were some of your most important learnings during the initial years in the fashion business, given that the skill set required for both careers is starkly different? I did a lot of learning on the job. I studied fashion in the '90s; things—the technology, the Internet, and software programs—had changed so much since then. But I had studied pattern making, sewing, and draping; so that holds me in good stead even now. Most of what I learnt on the job was the business of fashion—the merchandising, stockists, branding, marketing, the excel sheets, data, and so on. For me, that was much harder than the creative part of the job. And I'm still learning. Which skills acquired while working as an artist helped you along the way in the fashion industry? Which were the ones you had to unlearn? It helps tremendously that I can draw. This goes a long way in trying to pen an idea when I design. My training in fine arts equips me robustly to play with colour theory and proportions, composition and line. These, in turn, I feel help give my design process depth and distinction. What I had to unlearn is giving up control. Painting is an insular process, where I'm responsible for the end product because everything is created by me. In fashion, I had to learn to rely on others, to outsource, to train, to trust a team, and to try not to micromanage while still being responsible for my product. This is definitely still a work in progress for me. View Gallery 40 Photos Payal Khandwala at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2016 Payal Khandwala at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2016 How different is the Indian fashion industry from the art industry? In what ways are they similar? I've always been on the periphery of both circles. I didn't study art here so I didn't know many of my contemporaries from my university days. Now that I'm in the fashion industry, I'm still a bit of an outsider because I started so late. I think there are several similarities though. The business aspect of things is a big part of both art and fashion today. This implies small circles of influencers, critics, gallerists, politics and then, there is the commerce of it all. It's not that different from any other industry. It's just a product of the way the world works now. Talent and success are not always related, as marketing is a huge machinery in itself. The one noticeable difference is the trickle-down effect that the Indian film industry and the celebrities have on the fashion industry here. You can draw parallels between the art industry and the stock markets, but perhaps its still not as pervasive. How can one use their learnings in a different industry to their advantage when switching careers? Anything you learn, even when it is from a different discipline, is never in vain. No knowledge goes to waste. If you look at things from a prism that is different from the one you are accustomed to, then it gives you a unique perspective. And this can be your differentiator. Plus everything can inspire and inform you—travel, business, architecture, art, music, or dance. Elements from a different discipline can really enrich your experiences and end product, especially if you are in the creative field. How does one strike a balance between spontaneity and planning when making a mammoth career switch? I enjoy dichotomy in everything. Perhaps it's because I'm a Gemini, but being spontaneous while also being organised comes very naturally to me. In fact, I thrive on it. I can be as impulsive as I can be meticulous. So this is not something I struggle with. Switching to fashion was a huge change. All of a sudden I was working with a team. It was not an insular activity like painting alone in my studio—there were deadlines, it was harder to micromanage, and the hardest part was that I had to let go of control. But I am quite disciplined by nature, so it was easy for me to organise my time. I had to as I had a little daughter and I was a first-time mom when I made the switch. Prioritising my time really helped me, and I allowed myself to be spontaneous within that window. I never had a plan when I started this label. It seemed like a fun project at the time. I wanted to make clothes that I would get to wear once the show was done. If other women liked them, I would have made some more. It was really that simple. But one thing led to another and we found a lot of support from the industry and our customers, so here I am. Moreover, it has grown so organically. I was quite content designing the line from my living room with two racks of samples and my three-year-old daughter hiding behind them! Starting from scratch can never be easy. What advise would you give someone playing the waiting game to get their due in a new industry? First and foremost, be realistic. Assess how good you are in an absolute way, but also in relation to your peers. It's easy to study what others are up to these days. Are you relevant? Are you ahead of the curve? Are your ideas distinct? Are you ready for the hard work, the sweat, and the tears? If you have clarity when it comes to your product, and it is a strong, wholesome product that the industry needs, then all you have to do is hang in there. It will find its audience. You just have to persevere. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All the bridal inspiration you need View Gallery 55 Photos Bollywood in Manish Malhotra “I feel an actress' life is never complete if she doesn't walk for Manish Malhotra once,” said Alia Bhatt, after her very first time walking the runway for the designer in 2014. And she's done it not just once, but twice, her most recent being for his couture 2017 collection. The self-taught designer's journey into fashion started from his modelling days in college. At the age of 19, he worked as a sales boy in a boutique and by 21 he was already designing, during which his learnings from sixth-grade painting classes proved to be useful. “Then I thought to myself, why don't I do movies? I love designing costumes and even if I can bring about a bit of a change, I can make my mark. So with that very clear vision I got into movies. I left modelling because I wanted people to take me seriously as a costume designer.” And Bollywood's love for the couturier is nothing if not obvious. From Bhatt's contemporaries such as Shraddha Kapoor and Kriti Sanon to industry icons including Priyanka Chopra, Kareena Kapoor Khan, Sonakshi Sinha, Madhuri Dixit and Sridevi—every star has had her shining moment in Malhotra over the years. Along with Mira Rajput Kapoor, stars like Preity Zinta and Urmila Matondkar too celebrated their big day in Manish Malhotra creations. Such is the connect of his work to Bollywood, that you can actually trace the evolution of Indian fashion in tandem with Malhotra's work. Starting with Filmfare Award-winning costumes for Urmila Matondkar in Rangeela (1995), to Mohabbatein (2001), Kal Ho Na Ho (2003), Student of the Year (2012), all the way to Ae Dil Hai Mushkil (2016), it's safe to say Malhotra has had the pulse of the era every time. When it comes to ethnic wear too, Manish Malhotra, has been a much-loved name in most Bollywood celebrities' wardrobes. Known for his dramatic flair when it comes to Indian wedding couture, the designer is a popular choice for his sequinned saris, tasseled cape blouses and embellished lehengas. Whatever the A-list festive event, it would be hard not to spot a Manish Malhotra creation.
