column1: Altuzarra’s big moment: What to know ahead of his Paris Fashion Week debut
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion What's next View Gallery 8 Photos Altuzarra explains why he’s bringing his show to Paris When Joseph Altuzarra announced that he would show in Paris instead of at New York Fashion Week this September, he became the latest in a string of American talents to decamp to the French capital. The move to Paris Fashion Week, in many ways, marks a new chapter in Altuzarra's career. The difference between Altuzarra's departure and his peers' is that Paris is both a new land of opportunities and home. “I am as much French as I am American,” he wrote in an e-mail to Vogue. “So although Altuzarra was launched in New York, and we have shown at New York Fashion Week, Paris has been something that we've been thinking about since the beginning.” Born and raised in Paris to a French father and Chinese-American mother, Altuzarra moved to America in 2000 to matriculate at Swarthmore College, a small liberal arts school outside of Philadelphia, where he studied art history. Upon graduation, the young Altuzarra took internships at Marc Jacobs and Proenza Schouler, completed an apprenticeship under patternmaker Nicolas Caito, and worked as Riccardo Tisci's first assistant at Givenchy, back in Paris, before founding his namesake label in New York in 2008. A New York success story Even during the label's infancy, Altuzarra commanded the attention of influential figures, both European and American. The stylist-cum-consultant Vanessa Traina, who has walked for the brand, is a muse and collaborator. Former Vogue Paris editor Carine Roitfeld has championed it from the start. And though conceived as a family operation, in 2013, Kering took a minority stake in Altuzarra, following speculation that the French-American designer was poised to take the helm at Balenciaga from Ghesquière. Today, signatures of the designer's seductive wardrobe include ruffled one-piece dresses, elaborately embellished eveningwear, and a wildly successful range of meticulously crafted accessories, including the beloved saddle and tote bags—all of which work in tandem to accentuate the feminine form in a particularly Altuzarra way. Parisian flavour Though Altuzarra has grown to become one of the faces of New York fashion, the designer's Parisian sensibilities have always shone through his clothes. Even in Altuzarra's debut collection, which premiered during a New York Fashion Week deeply afflicted by the recession, the carefully restrained garments were laden with a suggestive allure. It's a signature approach that has carried into every Altuzarra collection since, from the masculine yet sensual tailoring that transpires every so often on the runway to the erotically charged split hem of his skirts. “The woman that I am designing for continues to be very much the same - she's sexy and confident - while the brand has always been rooted in a sense of French seduction.” What's next As for many buzzy designers based out of New York, the move to Paris Fashion Week is a smart business decision. With the brand's 10-year anniversary coming up, the change certainly helps Altuzarra reposition his brand for the next stage. “From a business perspective, it felt like the right time in terms of reaching a more international audience,” he tells Vogue. Today, the brand is sold in more than 20 countries outside of the U.S. by numerous influential stockists, both online and off. As he approaches the 10-year mark, Altuzarra is still slightly amazed. Establishing his business during the worst financial crisis to plague America since the Great Depression, today's success was unfathomable just a few years ago. “When I started Altuzarra, I had no expectations that it would work,” the designer admits. “I [founded] Altuzarra because I was passionate about fashion, and I thought that if I didn't do it then, I probably would have never done it.” Though such an important milestone warrants celebration, he is, at this moment, still too occupied with his big Paris debut to worry about next year's festivities. column1: Exclusive: Virgil Abloh on Princess Diana and those Versace rumours
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Plus, a sneak peek at his next collection View Gallery 25 Photos Exclusive first look: See Virgil Abloh’s Princess Diana-inspired Spring/Summer 2018 Off-White collection It's a Tuesday afternoon in Paris's Montmartre neighbourhood, some 50 hours before Off-White's spring/summer 2018 show, and Virgil Abloh is looking relaxed. Absent are the usual sounds of a studio on deadline—no shouting, not even the hum of sewing machines. Near the entrance, mannequins in full-skirted evening dresses stand assembled as if in a museum display. Next season's bags and shoes, the latter swathed in plastic and designed in collaboration with Jimmy Choo, are arranged neatly on shelves. From garment rails hang double-breasted blazers and coats, alongside graphic jerseys and cycling shorts, the former emblazoned with “Woman” and “White”. A seamstress hand-stitches the waistband of a pink tulle skirt, while models wait in line for a casting session to begin. “We don't work late here, I don't believe in making fashion in a stressful environment,” Abloh says as he manoeuvres through the mannequins, moodboard in hand. “As you can feel, it's very relaxed.” Abloh sets the board against the wall. On it are 29 photographs of Princess Diana in all states of dress: on a playing field in a T-shirt, baseball cap and jeans; opening a car door in dark slacks and a blazer; ensconced on a red chair at a 1981 exhibition in a floating, off-the-shoulder gown, her head tipped forward sleepily. It's nearly 20 years to the day since Diana died in a car crash only a few kilometres away, and, like a few other designers this season, Abloh had been inspired by the barrage of commemorative photos of her that have surfaced in recent months. In an era where the personas and wardrobes of public figures are tightly managed, Abloh was inspired by the free manner in which Diana experimented with her image in the '80s and '90s. “She was a strong individual who, despite her position, had her own personal taste and it came out through the clothes,” Abloh says, tilting the board. “There is no stylist at play here.” Diana is a departure from muses past—and so too is the resulting collection. First, there are the evening dresses, dyed in lavender, marmalade, and cotton candy pink, with tight, ruched bodices and frothy tulle skirts. (Only the white-ringed zippers and the labels inside assure us these are Off-White.) Cuts and colours are softer and more feminine; trousers have been cropped and slimmed. This time, denim and streetwear, the two cornerstones of the brand, have been toned down considerably.  But fans of the strong-shouldered suiting of Abloh's past two seasons will find plenty more to covet here. This season, Abloh has partnered with Jimmy Choo—a designer Diana patronised—on a collection of Cinderella-inspired shoes, including knee-high stiletto boots wrapped in black tulle and pointed-toe pumps encased in plastic to look like glass. Silk and satin evening bags with jewelled clasps are a clear nod to Diana. So too are a pair of long evening gloves, one black and one red, modelled after a pair she wore to the 1986 America's Cup Ball. “Her personal taste was very out of the way from what she was supposed to wear,” he observes. “It's an inspiration." As Kanye West's closest creative collaborator since the age of 22, Abloh's name became well-known on social media and in streetwear circles long before he launched Off-White in 2014. But he has been in the press with particular frequency lately. First there was the public rift with his design hero, Raf Simons, who, in a GQ Style interview, criticised Abloh as unoriginal. Then there was this summer's announcement that he would be collaborating with Nike, putting his stamp on 10 of their most famous shoes. Most recently, word spread that he would soon be appointed creative director of Versace (which Versace denied, and to which he replied in this interview: “No comment”.) After Off-White was named a finalist in the 2015 LVMH Prize, riffs on the label's designs—to put it generously—began appearing in certain high street stores. But that doesn't bother Abloh. “That's amazing, that's probably the biggest sign of approval, you know? When it is worth somebody generating on it, I take it as a sign of me going in the right direction.” Though Abloh declined to speak about the Versace rumour, he says he does hope to helm a major luxury fashion house one day. “This is sort of my résumé,” he says, gesturing to the mannequins around him. But would he ever give up his other creative endeavours—which also include DJ-ing and furniture design—to focus fully on fashion? “No, one thing informs from another,” he replied. “The consumers aren't just looking at clothes, you have to be inspired.” Off-White c/o Virgil Abloh's spring/summer 2018 show will be held in Paris on September 27, at 9pm local time and live-streamed on Off---white.com   Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

While the India website, Zara.com/in, already existed, now you won't have to visit the store each time you saw something compelling while browsing online, as the brand adds an e-commerce element to the online address. With multiple retail stores all over the country, the brand finally has a digital retail space. Making it easily accessible and consumer-friendly, the new website has multiple payment options like PayPal, all the major credit cards, including Visa, Master Card and American Express and the e-store will deliver nationwide. You can expect the online portal to stock its usual wares of apparel for women, men and children. From formals, to party ensembles to casual denim numbers, the label is known for its on-trend, contemporary separates that are perfect for any occasion. All you have to do now is keep your credit cards ready. column1: Nargis Fakhri’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Charting her sartorial journey View Gallery 58 Photos Nargis Fakhri Style evolution New York-born model and actor, Nargis Fakhri scored a Bollywood launch vehicle—Imtiaz Ali's Rockstar opposite Ranbir Kapoor—that put her in the spotlight from the very beginning. But before making her film debut in 2011, the half-Pakistani, half-Czech actress was a model who had previously appeared on America's Next Top Model as well as featured in the Kingfisher calendar in 2009. Over the past six years, this self-proclaimed global citizen chose to be a part of the industry without getting caught up in the rat race and her subsequent releases included political thriller Madras Cafe (2013), comedy Main Tera Hero (2014); Hollywood action comedy Spy (2015) with Melissa McCarthy, Jason Statham and Jude Law, multi-starrer Housefull 3 (2016), and Banjo (2016). Style files The actor's initial appearances to promote Rockstar included a host of traditional looks, several by Manish Malhotra, which eventually made way for a smattering of fitted minis by the likes of Shivan & Narresh, Namrata Joshipura, Victoria Beckham, and Falguni and Shane Peacock. The dress (largely of the knee-length variety) and heel combination continued to be a go-to for Fakhri, though she did not shun maxis altogether either. 2013 saw her become more inclusive of trousers and jeans, which were often layered with blazers or jackets. Her model frame lent itself well to slinky gowns and her red carpet game was always the right dose of dignified sensuality. But Fakhri's ability to change things up couldn't be underestimated. One minute she could be sashaying down the red carpet in a Cavalli gown with a plunging neckline, and the next, appear in a modest Sabyasachi bandhgala set. The evolution Fakhri's repertoire took a sleeker, more polished turn to coincide with the release of Spy. Cue tailored Osman jumpsuits, Issa separates, Jonathan Simkhai skirts, and Samuel Dougal cape gowns. Prints made way for solid-colours with ensembles that were all about the fit. The aesthetic has largely stuck ever since, and Fakhri gives it a fierce twist every now and then, such as the time she wore an icy blue Monisha Jaising pantsuit at IIFA Madrid. The minis have been replaced by more modest calf-skimming hemlines by labels like Missoni and AM.IT, though Fakhri can still turn up the heat on the red carpet as she did in her décolletage-barring Gauri & Nainika gown at the IIFA Awards this year. If her Instagram account is anything to go, Fakhri is currently enjoying some time off in Los Angeles. Cue holiday-friendly breezy ruffled dresses, off-shoulder numbers, and gladiator flats. Did we mention that the actor has chopped off her tresses into a wob too? As a well-travelled woman of the world, Fakhri never quite allowed herself to be boxed in a style bracket. A nomad at heart by her own confession, the actor always kept her sartorial choices urban and crisp. Though she never vied for that ‘best-dressed' tag, she always appeared to be abundantly at ease in whatever she chose, which is often times an achievement in itself. column1: Manish Malhotra: How to become a fashion designer
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion On resilience, passion and the importance of education View Gallery 2 Photos Careers in fashion: Manish Malhotra on making it big without professional training Manish Malhotra's name is synonymous with Bollywood and Indian fashion. It's not an exaggeration to say that every star, from Kareena Kapoor Khan to Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, Deepika Padukone to Sridevi, is a fan of his work. Which is why it's hard to believe that the model-turned-costume-designer-turned-couturier made a name for himself without any professional training. “I did not go to design school, but I did watch a movie almost every single day,” says the designer who will always cite Bollywood to be his first love. You can trace the evolution of Indian fashion in tandem with Malhotra's work. Starting with Filmfare Award-winning costumes for Urmila Matondkar in Rangeela (1995), to showcasing at the first edition of Lakmé Fashion Week in 2006, to designing theatre costumes for the play 'Mughal-e-Aazam' in 2016, and addressing Harvard students earlier this year, it's safe to say Malhotra has done it all. His notable contribution to Indian cinema by creating iconic looks for films like Pyaar Kiya To Darna Kya (1998), Mohabbatein (2000), Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001), Ae Dil Hai Mushkil (2016) is unmissable. But Malhotra's journey hasn't been without its highs and lows. “The great part about my early days was that I was never jaded by opinions of others," he tells us. "I think I was resilient and that really helped shape my work ethic.” Vogue speaks to the veteran about what went into the making of his expansive legacy. You are one of the rare names in fashion without a background in design education. What was your recipe to success? I am not sure if there is a recipe to success. It has a definite, formulaic connotation to it, which I will never endorse especially because ‘success' is a relative term. To me, anyone who finds their calling and is fortunate enough to pursue and practice it in an ethical and mindful manner, is successful. Do you think having an education in design is absolutely crucial to having career in fashion? I have been fortunate to have a family that works with me and looks into the ancillary functions of the business of fashion. But I am not sure if my label would have been as successful had I been [working on it] solo. I do think that having an education empowers you and anchors your decisions. Having said that, the best education amounts to nothing if you don't have a passion for your work. When starting off a career in design, did you have a vision for yourself? What is your vision for the brand? The vision was to be the best in whatever I did. I know it sounds clichéd; but from a young age I knew that I wanted to leave a legacy behind. It's an abstract vision, but, even today, I find myself asking myself questions to that end all the time. Idea or innovation? A store or an experience? I love to challenge myself and my team constantly—that is the only way to grow! View Gallery 77 Photos Manish Malhotra at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016 Manish Malhotra at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016   How would you describe the industry environment when you first entered fashion? When I started my label 12 years ago, Indian fashion was still fledgling; the industry made clothes and did not tell the stories that went into their making. It was a few years after our economy opened up. People had started traveling more and had so many more options to enrich their lives and lifestyles. We had left the norm of austerity behind and had just started embracing aesthetics that helped us express ourselves. This was a wonderful time for me to take my creativity beyond the silver screen. I was always focused on carving my own niche. I achieved this by presenting the richness of Indian textiles and our centuries-old embroidery techniques in a way that immediately resonated with the modern Indian woman. As far as I knew, I wasn't creating fashion, I was finding and presenting ways that accentuated my clients' personalities. What inspires your work? I derive a lot of inspiration from old-world charm. The beauty of older films, old architecture and so on hold a special place in my mood-boards. This along with a sense of drama and glamour in the detailing sums up the design prism of my label. Films to runway, how did you make the transition? My journey into films was a natural progression of my love for films. I absolutely loved sketching. So, when it was time to focus on a career, I simply made up my mind to bring my two passions together. In retrospect, I think I was fearless to have made this decision—I didn't know anyone in the film industry; I came from a simple Punjabi family in Mumbai. I remember during my first few assignments, I used to keep requesting directors to give me a script in advance. I was categorical that I was not there to go shop for clothes. My work had to add to the story-telling process and if this meant explaining, guiding and supervising tailors till the wee hours of the morning, I would do it. Even today, it is the memory of the hard-work and single-mindedness of my early days in costume design and styling that inspires me. I am proud that I charted my course on my terms. My label was the next chapter in my growth, both personally and in my profession. Up until then, the film's story and the director's vision were key to my work. Launching a label meant that now I was captain of the ship. From devising the creative identity of the label to having a clear business goal, I was part of every detail that defines label Manish Malhotra today. View Gallery 85 Photos Manish Malhotra at India Couture Week 2017 Manish Malhotra at India Couture Week 2017 What do you remember about your first-ever runway show?  My first show in 1999 was an exciting turning point, both personally and professionally. The success of the show boosted my confidence immensely. It was with this show that I realised the nascent potential of Indian fashion and the opportunity it presented to me. From being appreciated for costumes, I could now diversify to conceptualising, designing, creating and presenting my own collections. That show was the genesis of my label. Did you have a mentor? No, but I had—have—so many friends who are my sounding-boards and guides. What are your learnings from being a veteran in the industry? What is your advice to the new crop of designers? I would like to think each of us in the industry have our own niche and space when it comes to our design language, our respective retail experiences, the consumer that we cater to. All these add up to give the brand a personality, which is what eventually resonates in the market and generates business. So, the more clarity one has in what this ‘brand personality' is for them, the better it is. The younger generation has come to understand this really well and I can see them exude this in their work every season. The key is to build a really strong bridge between creativity and commerce. How important is star power for the success of a brand? When you are in India, you just cannot ignore the power of films. A list of the country's most legendary success stories, style icons and opinion-leaders will invariably have a large number of movie stars. What is something you have always wanted to try but still haven't in your career? With my work in films and thanks to my label, I've had the opportunity to travel, meet and work with some inspiring people and constantly learn through my experiences. I am a workaholic and seldom take holidays. As a result, I am completely focused towards working on new milestones for the brand. Be it conceptualising shows, bringing my collections to new consumers across the globe, my work with Mijwan or styling for films, I try to always bring elements never seen or experienced before. If you could change something in your career journey what would it be? Nothing at all. I am 50 years old and I have enjoyed every bit of the journey—the milestones along the way have made it all worthwhile! column1: Claudia Schiffer on why she is glad digital wasn’t a part of her career
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And that iconic Versace runway reunion On Friday night at the conclusion of the Versace show, Donatella honoured the 20th anniversary of her brother's passing with a special tribute moment. Assembled on the stage were five of the supers—each standing on pedestals, swathed in gold lamé, as motionless as statues. Second from the left—between Carla Bruni-Sarkozy and Naomi Campbell—was Claudia Schiffer, who, as a timid girl from the Rhineland, came to the spotlight in the early '90s. Discovered at the age of 17 in a Düsseldorf discotheque, Schiffer's career began in a stroke of pure luck. Growing up as a child, Schiffer was painfully introverted. As the model scout who found her would recall years later, when he first approached Schiffer about a career in modelling, “Claudia did not believe me.” A year later, Schiffer would make her runway debut at Chanel. Of her many shoots over the years, the photos she created with Gianni Versace and Richard Avedon in the early '90s remain to this day some of fashion's most iconic images. As Schiffer recalls, it was Gianni who helped open the door for her and the rest of the supers. “Gianni was one of the frontrunners who changed the fashion show,” Schiffer told Vogue in an interview shortly after the show. “With him, you would find Elton John and Prince in the front row. And shows that were normally only with runway models—and never crossed over with photoshoot models—were suddenly filled with the supermodels that you know today.” In a rare opportunity, the Versace moment also reunited a close group of old friends. Although they've all retired from the world of modelling, and live across the world, Schiffer and the other supers remain close to one another. “We stay in contact through various ways, whether that's Instagram, email or over the phone. And whenever we are in the same place at the same time, we try to hook up, although that sometimes that isn't easy,” Schiffer said. “But I think that bond and connection we share will probably never stop. It feels like a high school reunion whenever I see Cindy again.” Speaking of Crawford, Friday night also marked the first time the supermodel shared a stage with this season's breakout star, her daughter, 16-year-old Kaia Gerber. For Schiffer, who has two girls and a boy of her own, did it ever occur to her that her children might one day strut down the catwalk in their mother's footsteps? “They're much younger than Kaia is, but they have a good understanding of what I do,” Schiffer explained. No strangers to the spotlight themselves, Schiffer and her husband, film director Matthew Vaughn, are naturally protective parents. “We used to live in London, and when [my kids] started school, there was a lot of attention and paparazzi at the gates,” Schiffer continued. “We decided to move to the countryside, where they can have a kind of normal life. We are trying to keep them away from everything for as long as possible until they, one day, voice what they want to do.” “But it's great what [Kaia and Presley] are doing,” Schiffer interjects. “It couldn't be better having Cindy as their mom, looking over them to make sure they are going in the right direction, the right path—protected and secure.” When we move on to discuss the current generation of models, her voice carries the same maternal tone. “I'm so glad, I must say, that digital wasn't a part of our careers in the '90s. Through digital, everything is so much faster. There is so much more expected of a model. You can't just relax. You have to document everything.” Schiffer seems acutely aware of the pressures in today's world of modelling with the advent of social media. “To make a difference and have people remember you [today], you have to do much more than the fashion shoots and show,” she said. “You have to show so many more sides of you as a personality, and maybe even do more things than just fashion.” Not only do today's models have to juggle the demands of social media, they also have more competition from outside the modelling industry. “The industry is so much larger than it was, and you are sharing your platform,” she observed. “Back then, all the covers and campaigns were just us. Now, models are sharing everything with It-girls or actresses and singers.” It might be hard to believe, but for Schiffer, 2017 also marks her 30th year in fashion. In commemoration of the milestone, Rizzoli will release her self-titled book next month. At 47—save for Friday's exception—Schiffer's career has moved far away from the catwalk to focus on Claudia, both the person and the brand. This year, she's launching a capsule collection of shoes with Aquazzura as well as a makeup line, and has served as an executive producer on her husband's film, Kingsman: The Golden Circle. But you won't ever find her backing projects she doesn't believe in, or worse, licensing her name away for an easy paycheque. “I think I've worked hard enough,” Schiffer said. Now, “I'm just doing what I enjoy with the people I like.” View Gallery 16 Photos Claudia Schiffer talks Gianni Versace, Kaia Gerber and staying friends with the supers What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Paris Fashion Week: Your guide to the spring/summer 2018 shows
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All you need to know View Gallery 11 Photos Paris Fashion Week: Your guide to the Spring/Summer 2018 shows Change is afoot at Paris Fashion Week. In a first, the official schedule this season will kick off on Monday night instead of Tuesday, with the Jacquemus show and after-party. New creative directors at four major houses—Chloé, Givenchy, Lanvin and Carven—will make their runway debuts. And the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode is introducing several international designers to its lineup, most notably Thom Browne and Joseph Altuzarra of New York. Read on to see our predictions of the week's highlights. The headliners When it comes to big names, Paris packs a punch like no other. This season marks Maria Grazia Chiuri and Anthony Vacarello's one-year anniversary at Dior and Saint Laurent, respectively. (A tribute will also be in order at Saint Laurent following the passing of co-founder Pierre Bergé earlier this month.) Elsewhere, expectations will be running high at Comme des Garçons, which has attracted a legion of new fans since this year's solo exhibit at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. And while Demna Gvasalia's own label, Vetements, is not showing on the schedule, he will be presenting his radical brand of couture-influenced streetwear at Balenciaga. And not to be missed, of course, is Karl Lagerfeld at Chanel, Phoebe Philo at Céline, Nicolas Ghesquière at Louis Vuitton and Jonathan Anderson at Loewe, who will continue to set the agenda - and dictate our shopping wishlists—for the season to come. 4 debuts to watch British designer Clare Waight Keller, who finished her dreamy six-year-run at Chloé in March, has replaced Riccardo Tisci as Givenchy's artistic director. Although spring/summer 2018 marks her official debut, over the last few months Waight Keller has been dropping hints of what we might expect from her first collection via a series of black-and-white portraits and short films shot by Steven Meisel. It's clear she's ready to embrace a darker, sexier aesthetic that the airy, sun-kissed designs she deployed at Chloé. Count on sharp tailoring—Waight Keller cuts a killer pant. Natacha Ramsay-Levi joined Chloé in April as a relatively unknown talent to the outside world. As creative director of womenswear under Nicolas Ghesquière for 15 years—first at Balenciaga and then Louis Vuitton—she's been esteemed within industry circles for some time. Her work to date has little in common with Chloé's soft, sensual and flou-loving woman. Chloé is ripe for new interpretation and Ramsay-Levi could be the timely appointment in this politically charged era of third-wave feminism. Following the dramatic departure of longtime artistic director Alber Elbaz in 2015, it's no exaggeration to say the future of Lanvin continues to look uncertain. His successor, haute couture designer Bouchra Jarrar, stayed on just 16 months before stepping down down in July. Her replacement, the fifty-nine-year-old French designer Olivier Lapidus, has arrived at Lanvin at a high-pressure time, with sales on the decline after Elbaz's departure. Unlike Jarrar, Lapidus is not widely known in the industry: He worked at Balmain Homme for a year in the mid-'80s and then worked for his father, the designer Ted Lapidus, before setting up his own eponymous “e-couture” brand. As for the rest, we have to wait until Wednesday to see what's in store for France's longest operating couture house. Carven is the fourth storied Parisian label to welcome a new creative director this season. Swiss designer Serge Ruffieux has joined the brand after a nearly 10-year stint at Dior, where he worked as co-artistic director in the period between Raf Simons's departure in October 2015 and Maria Grazia Chiuri's appointment in September 2016. Ruffieux kicked off his new vision with Resort 2018, introducing a new Carven muse who is as streetwise and quirky as she is ladylike. We look forward to seeing more of her on Thursday. Americans in Paris New York-based Joseph Altuzarra and Thom Browne have joined the womenswear calendar this season, proving the cross-Atlantic pull of showing in Paris shows no sign of waning. Following the footsteps of U.S. fashion houses like Proenza Schouler and Rodarte, who showed in Paris during couture in July, and Tommy Hilfiger's recent shows in Las Vegas and London, their appearance adds fuel to the argument that static designer-city ties of old are gradually being replaced by something more fluid. Virgil Abloh's Off-White show also promises to be one of the hottest tickets of the week as the designer continues to clock successes with a recent Nike collaboration and store opening in New York. New names to know Paris is welcoming a wave of new talent this season. Marine Serre, whose skilful cutting and adroit mix of styles and references nabbed her this year's LVMH Prize, will present her Spring/Summer 2018 collection by appointment. column1: Disha Patani’s complete style evolution

Dhoni: The Untold Story in 2016, as well as a music video Befikra with beau Tiger Shroff. Next, she tested international waters with Kung Fu Yoga (2017) that also starred Jackie Chan. Fashion run Though a film and fashion neophyte, there is an undeniable endearing je ne sais quoi about Ms Patani's presence. No wonder then that even in a short span of time, she has become quite the favourite, seen walking the runway at recent fashion weeks on more occasions than one. Distressed jeans, floral minis, slogan tees, denim shorts, and a serious nod to athleisure make up her wardrobe, though the actor's off-duty style is in stark contrast to her red carpet stints where she isn't afraid to dial up the drama. Patani is all about glitter bomb gowns and formal minis, with high shine strapless gowns by Falguni & Shane Peacock emerging as her favourite. There isn't a risqué ensemble that Patani can't pull off with aplomb. A bandeau top with matching satin pants at an award show, a slinky cut-out top with a metallic skirt for Manish Malhotra's birthday celebrations, a Michelle Mason silk slip gown for an event, an ombré sequined barely-there mini at Lakmé Fashion Week, and a daring Nikhil Thampi cut-out gown (sequinned, of course) at Vogue Beauty Awards 2017 are some of her looks that drive this point home. column1: Marni’s Francesco Risso: “Criticism makes you grow”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion What to expect from the fashion house's spring/summer 2018 collection View Gallery 12 Photos Marni’s Francesco Risso: “Criticism makes you grow” One of Francesco Risso's earliest memories of Marni is of falling madly in love with a pair of “the biggest furry gloves” from the brand. “I don't even remember what season they were, but I was obsessed and I'm still kind of obsessed,” said Risso, who replaced Marni's beloved founder and designer, Consuelo Castiglioni, as creative director in October of last year. “It's a good memory because it brings me to the place in myself, of what Marni is.” What Marni is, according to Risso, is a mystery box, the kind you see in cartoons with a big fat question mark painted on top. “Marni is a vortex of extreme influences and playfulness and contradiction and dynamism,” he said. “It's many things. And I think It's the immense number of possibilities that is so exciting.” Risso will be tapping into all of those things this Sunday, when he presents his second women's runway collection for the house in Milan. It's been a bit of a rocky start for the designer. His first main-season collection, which debuted in February of this year, was met with mixed reviews; some critics felt it departed too abruptly from the house's codes, while others said that Castiglioni's shadow prevented the industry from giving him a fair shake. A few pointed out that the collection felt better suited to Prada, where Risso formerly worked as a womenswear designer under Miuccia Prada. Risso, a level-headed creative, took it all to heart. “I think it's good to take care of criticism,” he said. “You always have to personally follow your own path and your own desires but I think it's good to take a look at what people see and adjust to that. When we're presenting collections, we're trying to say something, to communicate something. Criticism is good. It makes you grow. It makes you better.” The designer is feeling good ahead of Sunday's show, despite the fact that, when I speak to him just days before, the clothes have yet to arrive. “We're in the middle of the storm,” he said. “But so far it's been fun.” When I asked when was the last time he got a good night's sleep he said that, despite years of struggling with insomnia, he'd been sleeping every night. “I've surprised even myself,” he said. That lack of angst is a sign, perhaps, that after an iffy debut, Risso is hitting his stride. “The first collection I had been at the company not even three months,” he said. “Now it's much more time and I'm enjoying the Marni reality even more. That's the main difference from last season.” Now that he's settled in with the team, he feels more poised to deliver on the label's distinct blend of oddball intellectualism, while expressing his own unique point of view. “I've been able to work at this company for longer and this is definitely something that makes you more comfortable with the things we're doing,” he said. “The people here understand me more and I understand them more. To me it's always an open dialogue and once you start knowing each other better, you achieve your messages more quickly; they perceive my messages more quickly and I get their messages more quickly. It's as simple as that.” The new effort will explore themes of construction and, in the process, deconstruction. Risso, a film buff, sees the collection as if through a wide-angle lens, zooming in and out on details, and viewing garments from the inside out. It's a search for connection, about finding beauty in how things are made. At the same time, he said, it's “much more than that. It's almost like this girl falls through a bizarre cocktail.” Risso has always been mining the Marni archive. For his first resort collection he said, “some of it was almost like a tribute to the oldest pieces,” reimagined with the help of an artist who designed the prints. Marni's past is a huge influence on the designer. “It's something I go through because I've been following Marni forever,” he said. “Consuelo explored so many diverse things. In that sense she was not necessarily attached to one thing. She was really radical and into changing and trying different things, so that's fun to look back on.” According to Risso, Castiglioni wrote him a note of congratulations shortly after he was appointed. “She's extremely nice in welcoming me here, even her husband too,” he said. The two continue to share letters and cards every now and then. But despite his clear reverence for the former designer, Risso is keen to put his own mark on the label he's loved for so long. “As much as I can try to respect what her fans are attached to, it's not easy because I'm not Consuelo,” he said. “I'm Francesco. And somehow this is now the future; it's not the past. People love her and are attached to her identity, which comes with her head, and her generation. But I come from a different generation and with my different generation I bring different things. But I still care about who the Marni lover is and who she will be. It's a very delicate balance.” It's a tightrope act the whole industry will, no doubt, be watching with rapt attention come Sunday. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Sari lovers cannot miss Gold – The Art of Zari exhibition in New Delhi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Attention textile enthusiasts! View Gallery 6 Photos Sari lovers cannot miss Gold-The Art of Zari exhibition in New Delhi Textile designers Swati Agarwal and Sunaina Jalan behind the label Swati & Sunaina come together with celebrated textile curator Mayank Mansingh Kaul, to exhibit the finest of handwoven gold zari textiles. The exhibition, comprising of pieces from their rich repertoire of work and some rare vintage pieces, makes the exhibit an unmissable event. For Jalan and Agarwal, the explorative journey began with an innocuous wish to buy a few Banarasi saris and the sad realisation at the non-availability of the same, spurred their entry into this world. For the past few years, their label, Swati & Sunaina has been resolute in its commitment to bring to fore the fine craft that has got lost in our memories, including many weaving techniques that have the lost art of gold zari weaving in the forefront. “A sari is an end product of multiple skills including fine craft of zari making, which is completely indigenous as showcased by visuals in this exhibition,” shares Jalan. “Real zari work was a natural progression for our brand when we chose to create textiles that our weaving community had the potential to craft but were not inspired creatively or commercially to engage with,” says Agarwal. The term 'zari' (from the Farsi/ Urdu word ‘zar' meaning gold) is one that is absolutely entrenched in the vocabulary of opulent handwoven saris. Though zari work existed in some form or other among the Mughal workshops in Ahmedabad in the 17th century, its only in Benares that this craft came into its own in the 19th century with complicated weave structures being created with this gold coated thread. Over the years, the fine craft has fallen in the shadows of dubiousness with zari losing its reputation as a symbol of luxury to a garish golden weave executed with cheap synthetic core. Fortunately, all this started to change with the entry of passionate handloom designers armed with an ambition to revive the disappearing craft. Mayank Mansingh Kaul has curated this exhibit to showcase various artistic ways in which silver and gold zari is used through the use of vintage textiles and contemporary saris. “The vintage textiles are sourced from private collections and represent how zari was used in various traditional cultures of the Indian subcontinent,” informs Kaul, “We are also showing a fascinating film on the process of making pure zari. To achieve a hair-like thinness of zari is a purely artisanal method that survives now only in one workshop in the world in Benares, is an art in itself.” On being asked to advise on a sari that is a must-see for any visitor for its artisanal dexterity, Mayank suggests ‘Saffavid', a sari inspired by historical Persian brocades, and ‘Shabnam', which is so translucent that its surface reflects just like water. Gold – The Art of Zari, an exhibition by textile designers Swati Agarwal and Sunaina Jalan, curated by Mayank Mansingh Kaul, will take place at the Bikaner House, New Delhi from September 22 to 27 What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Can you wear cleavage revealing clothes in your 50s?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's how to do it When it comes to sartorial cans or cannots, especially with the dreaded age-word thrown in, it all boils down to tastefulness. If done with dignified elegance, anything goes, and that includes the flaunting of your décolletage. Entering the fifth decade of your life is by no means a warning bell to shroud yourself in yards of fabric and retire your cleavage. When in doubt, turn to members of the style set who get it right. Our favourite Miss Congeniality, Sandra Bullock, does a fine job of leading the way. Borrow from her book and keep it savoury with strapless dresses, sheer bodices, and keyhole detailing. Sridevi presents the ultimate master class in doing décolletage with Indian wear. If you're wearing a revealing blouse, don't attempt a feeble cover-up in a flimsy chiffon or net sari. Instead pick one in a relatively opaque fabric. A sheer dupatta with a low-neck anarkali won't hurt, and a shirt lehenga blouse with an extra button undone can be complemented with a layered necklace. View Gallery 11 Photos Can you show cleavage in your 50s? celebrities But with age comes wisdom—some of which must most definitely be heeded when indulging in a little cleavage show. Vogue issues crucial guidelines for when you find yourself uncertain of how to tread these valleys. DOS AND DON'TS Yes to a dip, no to a plummeting fall If you want to keep your look less “What was she thinking?” and more, “Nicely done,” then give due thought to the depth of your neckline. One that plunges right down to the naval may be taking it too far (quite literally), but tasteful one-or-two-inch cleavage will do you no harm. Factor in the occasion The event in question puts everything in context. What may work for a destination wedding may not fly at your kid's PTA meeting and vice versa. Make sure your cleavage is in tandem with the designated dress code. Go low for night outs, cocktail parties or holidays, by all means. Balance is highly recommended Don't wear a scoop neck top with a mini just to prove a point. Be true to yourself. If we're to be really honest, a look that's all flesh will probably not do you any favours. A peek at your cleavage should always tie in with the rest of your look in an appropriate manner. You may want to balance a deep cowl neck with full sleeves or complement a plunging V-neckline with a necklace. Fit is always sacred when it comes to clothes, and more so here. If your twins are spilling out every time you bend even slightly, then you have a potential wardrobe malfunction on your hands. Support your cleavage with good inner wear Over the years, you've probably made a habit out of never compromising on quality lingerie. That should come handy, because the aesthetic appeal of a cleavage is only as good as the bra under it. Choose one that shapes and lifts your bosom but steer clear of a push up bra because it's likely to give you an unnatural results. Pick ensembles in thick, supportive fabric. Anything too clingy, especially those that conspicuously stretch across your chest, can be left behind in the trial room. Keep it office-friendly If it's not part of your job description, then these are not the assets you are required to bring to the boardroom. Particularly when you're expected to lead by example. Resist the urge to wear your pantsuit blazer minus the shirt or sport a plunging wrap dress that leaves little to the imagination. Did someone say NSFW? column1: Shilpa Shetty Kundra’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Then and now View Gallery 102 Photos Shilpa Shetty Kundra’s complete style evolution 42 going on 22, actor, entrepreneur and fitness enthusiast, Shilpa Shetty Kundra's frozen-in-time looks are envy inspiring. Add to that a physique that can put most millennials to shame and a joie de vivre that's almost infectious, and you'll know why Shetty Kundra continues to remain relevant even 24 years after her Bollywood debut. The actor followed up her 1993 debut Baazigar with the equally popular film Main Khiladi Tu Anari the following year. Though the real turning point in her acting career came with the 2000 hit Dhadkan, her victory in the British reality television series Celebrity Big Brother 5 in 2007 catapulted her to international fame. Her love for the reality TV format continues, as Shetty Kundra has appeared as a judge on a spate of dance shows over the years. But Shetty Kundra has been more active in indulging her entrepreneurial side lately—she is the part owner of the Indian Premier League franchise cricket team Rajasthan Royals with her husband Raj Kundra, co-owns spa chain Iosis, has penned The Great Indian Diet as well as launched her yoga DVD. And then there is her Instagram page—from her ‘Sunday Binge' videos (which even Alia Bhatt claims she keeps track of) to her #ShilpaKaMantra fitness and diet tips, she has firmly secured her place as a fitness influencer. Style files Shilpa Shetty Kundra has the knack of owning just about any look, something she has used to her advantage over the years. After all, not many would have succeeded in pulling off all the bling, daring cutouts and necklines, figure-hugging silhouettes and in-your-face logos that Shetty Kundra did in her earlier days. As far as traditional wear is concerned, the actor has been an unwavering Tarun Tahiliani and Manish Malhotra loyalist from the beginning. She got engaged in a sari by Malhotra, while Tahiliani specially designed her wedding wardrobe in 2009. The evolution The time after her wedding saw a change in her sartorial sensibility. The leopard prints, Hervé Léger bandage dresses and halter blouses made way for tailored separates and an overall polished repertoire. The second decade of the millennium had Shetty Kundra gravitate towards sheath dresses, solid colours, smart blouses, well-fit jeans, blazers and luxe separates (her look in a Meher & Riddhima top with black Pankaj & Nidhi pants particularly stands out). Today, her style is all about power dressing—clean and fuss-free, yet completely capable of turning every head in the room. Now wonder then that she is drawn to pantsuits by the likes of Manika Nanda, Nikhil Thampi and Namrata Joshipura, so often. Being the trendsetter that she is, Shetty Kundra was paving the way with her maternity style way back in 2012 with her pregnancy wardrobe of comfortable and flattering maxi dresses, anarkalis, and kurtas and palazzo sets. Post pregnancy, Shetty Kundra's appearances were punctuated with a spate of sophisticated fashion choices. From head-to-toe white, and chic skirt and blouse pairings to jumpsuits and jeans layered with blazers, motherhood gave the actor's style an exceedingly elegant update. But make no mistake—she still continues to pull out that bold, cutout number for the red carpet every once in a while just to remind everyone what #BodyGoals really look like. Kundra's off-duty looks is all about an ‘I woke up like this' brand of effortlessness. Whether she's grabbing lunch with her family in a blue shift paired with a Goyard bag, catching a flight or movie in cropped denims and a tee, or dining with her friends in a white top, distressed denims and the latest Chanel Gabrielle bag, she does so without breaking the proverbial sweat. The actor's taste in high street brands has evolved from River Island, Whistles, and Reiss, to & Other Stories, Sandro, and Maje, while all those couture lehengas and saris are now balanced by several contemporary pieces by Masaba. One look at her roster of outfits and it's clear that she has mastered the art of mixing high street with luxury labels—such as the time she wore a French Connection top with a jacquard Dolce & Gabbana mini skirt. But Shetty Kundra can pair fancy with fancier with equal ease too. Remember the lace Dolce & Gabbana dress she once wore with a traffic-stopping Bulgari Serpenti necklace? After all, if those rock-sized solitaires and army of Birkins are anything to go by, then Shilpa Shetty Kundra sure knows a thing (or many) about the investment pieces. You'll be hard-pressed to find her without the company of an It-bag—be it a classic Chanel, or a quirky Charlotte Olympia or Anya Hindmarch. column1: Careers in fashion: Anita Dongre on the importance of branding
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion One woman show From Bollywood royalty like Kareena Kapoor Khan, Malaika Arora and Aditi Rao Hydari to the Duchess of Cambridge, Kate Middleton—you're hard pressed to find an A-lister who is not impressed by Anita Dongre's clothes. Anita Dongre's humble beginnings in fashion have, over nearly two decades, culminated into five popular, successful brands: Dongre owns two high street labels—AND and Global Desi—prêt label Grassroot, couture label Anita Dongre and fine jewellery label Pinkcity crafted by Jet Gems. Most recently, Dongre expanded her business overseas by opening two stores in New York. What separates the designer from the rest is her unique instinct that has clearly helped her scale her brand from ready-to-wear to couture and fine jewellery. So when it comes to understanding the value of branding in contemporary Indian fashion, young fashion professionals need look no further than Anita Dongre. We spoke to the powerhouse about running a serious business. How would you describe your signature style? Effortless luxury. Whether it's putting pockets in lehengas, creating a cacophony of prints or reimagining weaves and embroideries from thousands of years ago, I design clothes for the practical but aesthetically inclines of the woman of today. To me, fashion must reflect a woman's holistic persona—her deeply-rooted values and modern sensibilities. The key purpose of fashion is wearability, and comfort is just as important as design aesthetics. What does branding mean? Branding is a promise to the consumer, the finer details that set one brand apart from all others and makes it memorable. When a person walks into any Anita Dongre store in the world, from the welcoming floral fragrance, the Rajasthan-inspired decor, the subtle music, the bespoke services and of course the quality and design of the collections—everything speaks one language to give a complete experience. How do you manage five brands? Each brand was started with a purpose and was built over time. I have invested in developing each one with its unique identity. While AND and Global Desi address the everyday needs of a woman's wardrobe, Anita Dongre bridal couture and Pinkcity jewellery are for special occasions. Grassroot, my most recent brand, is the culmination of my craft-inspired design aesthetic and the fashion-forward philosophy of sustainable practices. It helps to have our headquarters housing all the brands under one roof, in a space that continues to inspire me. Our ergonomically-built workspace is nestled amidst the lush green hills of Navi Mumbai. At what point did you decide to diversify the brand? When I started AND, I wanted to fill the void of affordable and smart western wear for independent women. There was a clear wardrobe need for work and social life. Back then, international high street brands were only available to the frequent fliers who went shopping overseas. As the brand grew, I wanted to address more and more of a woman's wardrobe needs. And finally, Grassroot was born out of the need to bring unique Indian crafts into mainstream fashion. View Gallery 63 Photos Anita Dongre at India Couture Week 2016 Anita Dongre at India Couture Week 2016 What are your learning from managing five brands at once? How do you maintain the balance? I have learned that whether you are managing one brand or five, there is no substitute for hard work. I am very particular about my me-time. I work six days a week from 8am to 6pm but on my time off, I completely switch off from work. I maintain a healthy work-life balance to avoid burning out. I do yoga and eat vegan food, keep my mind constantly working. What is it like to take your business overseas? Opening Anita Dongre Grassroot in New York was a dream come true—the journey has been exciting, overwhelming and filled with gratitude. There has been such an outpouring of love and appreciation from media and the women who walk into our store. What was your journey into fashion? I spent my childhood holidays in Rajasthan. I was intrigued by the crafts, colours and vibe of the people I experienced there before I even knew fashion could be a career option. I would spend whole days designing my own clothes and lac bangles. I think the shopkeepers in Jaipur realised I would be a fashion designer well before I did! It was much later that I decided to study fashion design at SNDT. View Gallery 45 Photos Anita Dongre at Lakmé Fashion Week Summer/Resort 2017 Anita Dongre at Lakmé Fashion Week Summer/Resort 2017 I still remember my first runway show like it was yesterday—the presentation at the end of my course in SNDT. My first design was a one-shouldered jumpsuit that I conceptualised, cut, stitched and even modelled. I was so proud to present my creation to an audience filled with my teachers, mentors and peers. As a fashion student from SNDT with an inherent penchant for business, I felt drawn to this industry. It was a humble start with two sewing machines in the balcony of my Bandra home, making affordable western wear for working women. When starting off a career in design, did you have a vision for yourself? Always. My vision drives me. Of course, my vision keeps reinventing and evolving with time. How important is star power for the success of a brand? Its always nice to have iconic women wear the brand. Stars reach those heights because they are strong, beautiful and opinionated personalities. When they speak a certain language that is in sync with the ethos of the brand, it is an effective influence on people's choices. What were the milestone moments in your journey? In two decades, there have been so many! The very first one was when I showed the self-confidence of being the only woman in the family to work and build her own business. It was an achievement in itself whether I would have found success or not. Today, I am proud that my brands are making global news—from when Kate Middleton wore one of my designs to the launch of Grassroot in New York. View Gallery 54 Photos Anita Dongre at India Couture Week 2017 Anita Dongre at India Couture Week 2017 Did you have a mentor? It is not a person but the essence of the modern indian woman that drives me to create new collections for her. That ideal is both muse and mentor for me. What is something you have always wanted to try but still haven't in your career? Getting into home decor! If you could change something in your career journey what would it be? Nothing at all. Even the mistakes have contributed to bringing me to the point I'm at today. What is your advice to young designers? Work hard, make bold decisions, trust your gut and don't let anyone dim your sparkle. column1: Selena Gomez on partnering with Puma and sharing closets with The Weeknd
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In a candid chat with the singing superstar Selena Gomez has made herself at home—here, in a dimly lit studio loft, filled with Diptyque candles that smell of blackcurrant and roses. “I was totally being moody and just stretching in the bathroom,” she says, welcoming us in with a friendly wave. “I always want to have this kind of bathroom vibe with candles.” It marks the quiet, happy start to her next chapter: Today, Gomez will announce a long-term partnership with Puma, for which she has shot images for the brand's Phenom sneaker launch. It is the first in an ongoing series of projects, as she has been tasked to design product and help direct future campaigns. No doubt Puma hopes Gomez will inject the brand with her trademark authenticity, which has famously drawn more than 127 million Instagram fans. She certainly puts herself into everything she does and everywhere she goes. Take this candlelit studio, for instance. Stacked neatly on a wood coffee table are black and white Polaroids that Gomez had snapped just the night before. “My friend Petra's been teaching me,” she says of Petra Collins, the downtown photographer who directed Gomez's music video “Fetish.” She fans them out, revealing a series of beautifully grainy images—of Petra adjusting the strap on a shoe, of herself and her boyfriend, The Weeknd, linking arms in black tie. It feels intimate in a natural way—a taste of that genuine warmth. Dressed in a black Puma tracksuit (cropped zip-up hoodie, pants cinched at both ankles), she sits down on the couch, tucks her bare feet beneath her, and begins to chat. Congratulations on the collaboration; it's an exciting one.I know—I'm really excited. When it comes to this whole world of fashion—that's what I'm going to call it—I think it's become this collaborative thing where streetwear and fashion blend into one. It's a really beautiful thing because I see girls now feeling sexy in not even necessarily workout clothes, but clothes you could go work out in, then put on a cute pair of shoes and go out after. That's what's so crazy about now. Even just throwing something over a workout pant or just sweats, you kind of feel like you can do whatever you want. What is your personal take on the whole athleisure trend? Is it something you wear often?Every day? [laughs]. I think it's important to feel confident in what you wear. That's all I really care about—I want to make sure anything I put on, I feel good in, because how you're feeling on the outside really does affect how you are on the inside. What do you wear for an actual workout?When I'm at home, it can be very intimate. Maybe just a sports bra and maybe some little spanky kind of cute things. And when I'm out, then it's the typical: something slouchy that feels sexy that I can take off. It's about layering and cute little socks. Socks? What kind of socks?I add little chains to my socks because it adds a little charm, a little sparkle to it. Little anklets, actually. Me and my assistant got a bunch from Japan when I was on tour. I went through this whole phase where I would just wear the anklet around and shower in it. It's effortless. I lose things—for me, it's got to be on me, you know what I mean? Generally speaking, do you put much thought into what you wear out?It depends. I don't like when people feel like they need to put things together or be stressed about that. That's what's really cool about what Puma's been doing lately. It's all these pieces that you know are going to look good together, so it's just kind of throwing this on, throwing that on. I mean, at this point, my boyfriend and I share closets, and [we're] just kind of throwing different ideas around. Sometimes I'll throw on his Puma stuff and just go out with my shoes. I'll just wear that as a little cute date-night dress or something to the movies. You want to feel confident in it. When you start stressing about it and feel you have to create this image . . . you shouldn't feel that way. What pieces do you two share the most?Hoodies. Staple hoodies. So how do you feel about sneakers?They've been so changing my life [laughs]. I actually forgot how to walk in heels, you guys. I've been figuring out the past few events I've gone to, I've forgotten how to walk in heels just a little bit. I'm like Bambi, trying to figure out how to get my legs under. It's the craziest thing because you get so comfortable [in sneakers], and now you can just wear them everywhere. Now that I'm in the city—I'm going to be here for a little while—it's even better. I can walk anywhere, I can put on a cute dress with them. My entire closet is sneakers and cute boots and now a few heels. How many sneakers do you have in rotation right now?Oh gosh. Just in New York? Probably like 20 pairs, but that's not counting [those in] my home in L.A. Now that I'm a part of this [Puma] family, it's nice because I'll get to pick out ones that look good with everything. When you were packing your 20 pairs, did you keep any sort of strategy in mind, or want to pack a specific range of them?Yeah, because you have the sport, where you know you're going to go do something active and want to make sure you feel comfortable. Then there are what I call the untouchables, where someone steps on it and you gasp. Those are the kinds of shoes everyone has, especially guys. I think guys have that on lock. Then you have the ones where you know you're going to walk around and do what you have to do. It also depends on what mood I'm in: the simple high tops, black, white, platforms. It's in my vibe. What about colors? Anything you gravitate toward in particular?I feel my colours are usually primary, sometimes secondary. Look at my sixth-grade arts stuff coming back to me [laughs]. Now I love the little soft colors of red or pink or blue. I'm such a classic person, so when I add a simple taste of colour, I like it to feel not overpowering, for me personally. Do you remember your first pair of sneakers?Oh yes. I think I wanted the shoes with the wheelies at first, remember those? That's what I wanted more than anything. I also don't know what I was doing—it did not work out for me very well. I think I wore them once, I'm not even kidding. I've been working since I was 7, so the earliest memories of me are when I'm on Barney [& Friends], which is so funny. I talked about this the other night, but that style is coming back. I was literally 7, but the way those shoes with the socks that fold over . . . it's so kind of now. Not that I was creepily watching myself on Barney. We were just laughing about how I was on Barney because it becomes a joke amongst friends. But those are my earliest memories. Then getting older, you go through different phases. Would you say you've been in a sneaker phase lately?Yeah. For me, I started just wanting to feel grounded. I took some time off, and I needed to kind of take a moment for myself because all of this has been overwhelming. So I used to just walk around my house barefoot or with socks, and everywhere I would go, I would wear a sneaker from that point on. I've always worn sneakers, but I'd say in the past year, for sure. In terms of workouts and overall wellness, what kind of approach do you take?When it comes to that stuff for me, I love feeling like I'm getting all the stress out. I'm not a very aggressive person; I'm more emotional. So not to be cheesy, but my stretching and all of that really makes me feel like I'm getting stuff out. So I like to do that a lot throughout the day. Sometimes in front of the fireplace, so it just feels warm. Looking ahead at this collaboration, is there anything you feel inspired by right now?I have to be honest, coming to New York has been very inspiring for me because I'm living here for a minute, and I've never lived here. I've come for 10 years for work, but you're here, do a job, and leave. And this is kind of a huge staple city for streetwear—I get so many ideas just walking to get coffee every morning that I wouldn't get in my car in L.A. My friend Petra [Collins] . . . I walk around her area. We went to Queens the other night to have Italian food. And I really like that. This article originally appeared on Vogue.com Beauty What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 25 designer salwar sets to add to your ethnic wear and wedding wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion There's one for every occasion View Gallery 25 Photos The best designer salwars for the festive and wedding season While you may be tempted to spend the better half of the festive and wedding season in dreamy lehengas, it may not always be in tandem with the ethnic wear dress code. Maybe you need something for when you have to dash from the airport to a pre-wedding lunch or are looking for a Diwali party outfit that's glitzy without being OTT. Kurta and salwar sets are just what such occasions call for. Easy to dress up or down depending on the invitation in your mailbox, salwar sets are the very epitome of versatility. Take straight kurta and palazzo sets, for instance. They work well for everything from a Bhai Dooj lunch to a wedding high tea. Turn to sharara sets when you need to amp it up. Be it your distant cousin's sangeet or your own mehandi, this is an ensemble that can work regardless. Choose one with light gota work for when you need to keep it simple, or slip into a sharara set with ornate embroidery and traditional jewellery for ‘belle of the baraat' vibes. A staple in most ethnic wear wardrobes, anarkalis are all about maximum impact with minimum effort. Floor-length versions are incredibly wedding-friendly; even better if it's Lucknowi or Benarasi. Hosting a Diwali extravaganza this season? A cape anarkali or cropped jacket-style one worn with flared palazzos is all you need to catapult into the season's most stylish hostess. If you're a patron of contemporary Indian wear, then experiment with your bottoms. Pair your kurtas with cowl, dhoti or draped pants. Ankle-length churidaars with embellished hems are trending in ethnic wear this season too. Go through our gallery for salwars sets that are perfect for the upcoming festivities. column1: Milan Fashion Week: Your guide to the spring/summer 2018 shows
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you need to know As the third of the four major stops on the fashion month calendar, Milan Fashion Week always feels like a bit of a time out. As a city, it is considerably less frenetic than New York, London or Paris, and its cadence carries over into its fashion scene. Nevertheless, it boasts its fair share of iconic labels and upstart talents. [#image: /photos/5ce43aa09cc0c07adcf9e8c6]||| ||| Gucci; Image: InDigital The heavy-hitters: Gucci and Prada The week's lineup is anchored by Gucci and Prada, two luxury giants currently trending in opposite directions. Gucci's turnaround under creative director Alessandro Michele has been nothing short of miraculous, and as close to an overnight success as you'll ever see in this industry. His brand of maximal, psychedelic bricolage continues to connect worldwide, with sales up an unheard-of 50 percent in the first fiscal quarter of the year, making the Gucci show on September 20, day one of MFW, a must-see. Miuccia Prada is a designer's designer. Her work is subtle and cerebral, expansive in its point-of-view and references. It is politically charged, but never didactic. Expect her spring/summer 2018 collection to be all of the above, presented on 21 September at the Fondazione Prada on a set designed, as always, by architect Rem Koolhaas's firm OMA. It will likely ask a lot of audiences, demanding patient, thoughtful engagement. [#image: /photos/5ce43aa089be3676c07d1326]||| ||| Arthur Arbesser; Image: Getty One to watch: Arthur Arbesser Arthur Arbesser, who shows right after Prada, is an up-and-comer to keep on your radar. The Central Saint Martins graduate and Armani alum was an LVMH Prize finalist in 2015, and though Austrian by birth, his style is quintessentially Milanese. The way he deploys quirky, bold colour blocking and brash patterns recalls the Memphis Group, a post-modern design collective that emerged from Milan in the early '80s. And while his work often springs from similarly esoteric points of reference—Wim Wenders's Wings of Desire or the artist Balthus, for instance—it is eminently wearable. Not one to repeat himself, Arbesser's show is likely to delight. Whatever he shows, it certainly won't be boring. A change-up at Marni? Last February, Francesco Risso showed his first collection as creative director of Marni. He had big shoes to fill—he is the first designer to steward the label since founder Consuelo Castiglioni stepped down after over 22 years at the helm—and the degree to which he departed from the label's codes was jarring for some longtime fans. He replaced subtle gestures with harsh patterning and kitschy furs—a statement, to be sure, but not necessarily a coherent one. Nearly a full year into his tenure, it will be interesting to see if he builds on his first showing or switches things up. [#image: /photos/5ce43a9f1dc2677c80c79d65]||| ||| Jil Sander; Image: Jil Sander The big debut: Jil Sander The most intriguing slot on the calendar belongs to Jil Sander, where a new pair of creative directors—husband-and-wife duo Lucie and Luke Meier—hope to reinvigorate the venerable label. Their combined experience is impressive. Before joining Jil Sander, Lucie did stints at Balenciaga, Louis Vuitton and Dior. Luke served as Supreme's head designer for nearly a decade, and currently heads up directional menswear label OAMC—a job he intends to keep alongside his new role. Together, they seem well-positioned to furnish the label with a directional energy not seen since it was helmed by Raf Simons. The Meiers were appointed in April, and to date have designed the label's 2018 Resort collection. That first offering introduced a mixture of sharp tailoring and utilitarian, military-inspired garb rendered in fabrics that look expensive even on a Macbook screen. Perhaps their first full collection, set to debut Sunday, will add a more conceptual flair to the mix. Here's hoping—a reinvigorated Jil Sander would be a huge lift for Milan Fashion Week. [#image: /photos/5ce43aa0b40d2605c5d6ddda]||| ||| Versace; Image: InDigital Versace: Who's on next? For more than a year, industry pundits have been speculating about who could succeed Donatella Versace as Versace heads towards an initial public offering. Long-rumoured favourite Riccardo Tisci is no longer in the running, and the house has vehemently denied reports that Off-White founder Virgil Abloh is primed to take the reins. Could it be Balmain's Olivier Rousteing? Louis Vuitton's Kim Jones? All eyes will be scanning the room for clues at their show slot on Friday. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Can you wear ripped jeans in your 40s?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s what we found Delicately distressed or artistically slashed, slightly frayed or with busted knees: when it comes to ripped denim, the metre goes from 0 to 100; no stops in between. The OG rebel move has found its way with other everyday basics, but do you need to be hitting the brakes on your obsession with all things frayed after crossing the 40-year mark? Should you be laying your favourite DIY pair to rest, along with neon eyelash extensions and Crocs, and instead, scouting the shopping racks for no-nonsense mom jeans? What will the counter lady even think if you shimmy up with a pair of glued-to-your-skin distressed jeans? Unfortunately, we live in a world where our wardrobes are expected to fall in line with an invisible, arbitrary age limit. And it is in this imperfect world that ripped jeans continue to defiantly flout the rules, finding a home in the closets of everyone from 14 to 40, and well after. Throw on a faded pair for a low-key brunch or slink into a strategically ripped set for a night out in town—there are a million ways of wearing this street style favourite, and few chances of getting it wrong. What more could you ask of a wardrobe staple? Borrow from the stars View Gallery 11 Photos Can you wear ripped jeans in your 40s? celebrities If in doubt about whether ripped denims are really just a ‘young girl' thing, take a seat while the most fashionable names on the Bollywood circuit prove you woefully wrong. Malaika Arora works her favourite distressed pair from nine-to-wine, taking them everywhere from the airport to store launches. Karisma Kapoor takes hers with peekaboo cutouts at the thigh. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan is a fan of taking her jeans out for a spin while travelling, while Shilpa Shetty wears hers to date nights. Get it right Bear in mind, as fuss-free as this trend looks, you don't want the result to appear shabby. Since information is best absorbed when presented as a crisp set of dos and don'ts, here's our guide to helping your put your most distressed foot forward. DO - Opt for scrapes that are located strategically across your hips and the length of your thighs to flash some peekaboo skin without regretting the fact that you skipped your salon appointment. - If in two minds, go in for a statement slash across the knees that works just fine for daywear, and will keep your street style cred in place. - Believe it or not, you can wear your favourite distressed pair to work too. Tuck in a smart formal shirt to counter the casualness of your jeans, and you're golden. - If you're feeling creative, you could even take a pair of scissors and tweezers to an old pair that could do with a makeover. DO NOT - Shop for a pair without testing the hole placement first. Slashes need to go above your knee; anything below could like you threw on a pair of hand-me-downs. - Get overenthusiastic and opt for a completely frayed pair that's coming apart at the seams. There's no written rule set in stone here, but you can allow yourself a safe limit of five rips before venturing into rebel punk rock territory. - Overthink it. When in doubt, throw on a pair of no-fuss white sneakers to cinch the whole look together, and you're ready to roll out the door and take on the day. column1: Pooja Hegde’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Flip through her fashion files View Gallery 51 Photos Pooja Hegde’s complete style evolution Pooja Hegde may have been starring in films down south since 2012, but she made her Bollywood debut only last year. The 2010 Miss Universe India runner-up made her acting debut in Tamil superhero film Mugamoodi in 2012 and forayed into Bollywood with Ashutosh Gowariker's Mohenjo Daro (2016) opposite Hrithik Roshan. While the period drama received a lukewarm box office response, her launch vehicle did manage to create a buzz around the actor. Style diaries Hegde was no stranger to the red carpet before her Bollywood debut, but it was Mohenjo Daro's press launch that really put her in the sartorial spotlight. Hegde chose a custom-made cobalt blue Swapnil Shinde gown for the occasion. As she continued to promote her movie, Hegde was seen in a mix of versatile looks ranging from Philipp Plein bodycons to tailored Osman sheath dresses. It became clear that the actor has a penchant for dresses, particularly of the cold shoulder and off-shoulder variety that emphasis her collarbones. Off-duty, her look is all about comfort. Casual dresses, most often worn with white sneakers, have become something of a uniform with her. Hegde balances these laid-back looks by dialling up the glamour on the red carpet. Her Temperley London gown at the GQ Men Of The Year Awards 2016, a sculpted Gaurav Gupta dress that not many could have pulled off, a semi-sheer Ziad Nakad gown, and a flared Amit Aggarwal dress are cases in point. When not keeping it clean in solid colours, Hegde is drawn to floral and tropical prints, and her appearances in a Zara pantsuit, Andrew Gn column gown, and Sachin & Babi high-low skater dress illustrate this. Her traditional repertoire is all about layering and soft tones such as the Manish Malhotra jacket lehenga and Anita Dongre anarkali jacket set she has been spotted in. The verdict Hegde's lithe frame does make her the perfect clotheshorse for crop tops and riding hemlines. But truth be told, she fares best when she chooses elegant, ladylike dresses such as the Edeline Lee halter midi and Theia off-shoulder ball gown she has been seen in. Only one film old in Bollywood, Pooja Hegde has only started experimenting with her wardrobe and we're looking forward to what's next from the star. Scroll through our gallery for a closer look.
