column1: Why Tommy Hilfiger is bringing his see-now-buy-now show to London
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you need to know View Gallery 22 Photos Tommy Hilfiger explains why he’s bringing his see-now-buy-now show to London Following stops in New York City and Venice Beach, California, Tommy Hilfiger's travelling spectacle of a fashion show, “Tommynow”, will arrive in London on Tuesday just in time to close out Fashion Week. The show, inspired by Hilfiger's love of rock and grunge styles of the '90s, will feature women's and men's looks together for the first time since 2010. It will also unveil the third instalment of Hilfiger's ongoing—and highly successful—collaboration with model and ambassador Gigi Hadid. Plenty of designers have shuffled back and forth in recent memory, switching from city to city in search of a fresh stage; but few, if any, seem to share aspirations as ambitious or as inclusive as Hilfiger, who will host both industry members and as many as 2,000 members of the public at the event. To see these events merely as profligate undertakings, where supermodels with eight-figure Instagram followings parade against a colourful backdrop, is to miss the point entirely. “Tommynow continues to put the consumer at the heart of the event, fusing fashion, pop culture and entertainment, and connecting with our global fans in an authentic way,” Hilfiger told Vogue over e-mail ahead of his show. Last year, for the inaugural Tommynow event, Hilfiger transformed a New York pier into a carnival on the boardwalk, inviting participation from the press and consumers alike. Earlier this year, he rebranded Venice Beach as “Tommyland”, a theme park complete with flamethrowers, food stands and a performance by Fergie for the 3,000 guests in attendance. While some brands have abandoned the see-now-buy-now model in recent months, Hilfiger says it “continu[es] to exceed expectations season after season.” He sees nothing wrong in giving his customers exactly what they want, when and how they want it. “Expectations are constantly changing, and our [show] format fulfils that demand for instant gratification,” he explains. “Every brand is different, and each needs to consider what's best for them.” The London show will mark Hilfiger's third see-now-buy-now event so far, but it will also be the first to take place in Europe, where his business is booming. That the event is being held at the Roundhouse, the legendary concert venue in Camden, is telling—reflective of the ongoing cultural exchange between the designer and the world of music. But picking a stage is just the first of many steps Hilfiger has taken in preparation for this international debut. “We love to break conventions,” he tells Vogue. “Tommynow acts as an incubator for innovation.” In some sense, Hilfiger sees the present moment as being on the course of a trajectory he set himself on several decades prior, when he first started designing clothes. “Our original brand DNA is the starting point of everything we do, and our designs are rooted in classic American cool,” he writes. “It's about celebrating individuality, breaking conventions and keeping the relentless optimistic spirit that I founded the brand on.” Although the Tommy Hilfiger brand might be less established as a cultural institution in some parts of the world when compared to his native America, Hilfiger has sustained his brand's momentum beyond geographical borders, well into the new millennium, with the help of a few stars. In the '90s, Hilfiger's clothes could be seen on the backs of Aaliyah, and Snoop Dogg; today, it's on the likes of A$AP Rocky and Zayn Malik. At the end of the night, his gaze will inevitably shift forward—into the future. “Each season, we continue to select locations and times that complement the collections,” Hilfiger tells Vogue. Though there is no word on where the next Tommynow event will take place after its departure from London, “I'm always dreaming of what we could be doing tomorrow,” he continues. “And as I always say, the best is yet to come.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 25 best designer lehengas for your sangeet
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Bust a move View Gallery 25 Photos 25 of the most dramatic lehengas for your sangeet Whether you've spent most of your adulthood shying away from the dance floor or otherwise, chances that you might channel your inner Bollywood diva during your wedding are pretty high. The sangeet is usually the highlight of a wedding—with great music, choreography and celebration on the charts, nothing quite compares to the liveliness of this pre-wedding event. This is the one evening the couple can have serious fun and the bride needs to be on her A-game when it comes to fashion. Picking a lehenga for your sangeet is easy—you're spoilt for choice, but that doesn't mean you should go ahead and buy the first thing you like. Most Indian ceremonies have specific colour for brides on the day of the wedding. Dressing for the sangeet party though is very much in your control. Look through your trousseau and pick a colour that you wanted to wear to your wedding but weren't sure of. Go glam with fringes and pick lehenga skirts with hems that will twirl with your moves. Try not to pick a base fabric like velvet since it will weigh you down. Wear as much bling as you dare—it's your special day. From celebrity inspiration to the best styles, go through our gallery for the wedding lehengas to choose form for your sangeet. column1: Soha Ali Khan Pataudi’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From headbands to maternity chic View Gallery 64 Photos Complete style evolution of Soha Ali Khan Pataudi The quiet Pataudi sibling, Soha Ali Khan Pataudi, was first seen in Bollywood in the mid-Noughties in films like Dil Maange More!!! (2004), Pyaar Mein Twist (2005), Shaadi No. 1 (2005). Quick to highlight the versatility of her acting talent, Pataudi was applauded for her role in the critically acclaimed Rang De Bastani in 2006. From then on, Pataudi's roster has included wide range of films from Midnight's Children (2012), Mr Joe B. Carvalho (2014) to 31st October (2015). Style files The stars early beginnings in fashion were careful. Most often choosing safe shift dresses and easy jeans, it's clear Pataudi is not one to experiment sartorially, but there is something to be said about the quiet elegance she brings to the environment she is in. Through the years, Pataudi has been a fan of tailored dresses in bold hues. Never one for display of skin, Pataudi was even seen layering shorter hemlines with tights. Favouring modesty with Indian ethnic wear, the star has always chosen high necklines and full-sleeves at events. The star tied the knot to actor Kunal Khemu in 2015, for which she chose looks by designers Sanjay Garg and Sabyasachi. In the recent past, Pataudi's maternity wardrobe has made way for kimono wraps and off-shoulder dresses. Evolution A quick glance at the star's wardrobe will make it clear that Pataudi favours comfort above all else. From floral prints to midi length skirts, the star's style has always been about feminine grace. Occasionally twinning with her better half, the star has made more confident choices with fashion. While the star picked roomy dresses for the day (just like sister-in-law Soha Ali Khan Pataudi is doing currently), she didn't hesitate to spruce things up with Deme by Gabriella maxis and that spiked Philipp Plein gown when it was time to party. While the singer switched up between Dolce & Gabbana maxis and slogan tees, Amal Clooney went the elegant route with with comfortable gowns, Serena Williams dressed her baby bump in a green Versace gown at the Met Gala, and Kate Middleton (who is now expecting her third) went classic in demure coat dresses. column1: London Fashion Week is here: Your guide to the spring/summer 2018 shows
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's what to look out for On Friday, the second—and shortest—of the four major fashion weeks kicks off in London, with its signature draw of fresh talent and unpredictable weather. In recent years, the city has established itself as an international hub for emerging designers, fostering some of the industry's newest stars—largely thanks to the city's strong fashion education system and the nurturing support afforded by incubators like Fashion East. While London's reputation is continuously elevated by its homegrown stars, the city is increasingly becoming attractive destination for more established players, too—something evident in this week's schedule. [#image: /photos/5ce43c67c33f5c7cfd8f2a7f]||| ||| Giorgio Armani; Image: Getty Fashion's godfather returns Coinciding with the opening of the newly renovated Emporio Armani store on Bond Street, Italian legend Giorgio Armani has decided to take his Emporio show to London Fashion Week this month. As the first Armani event to be held in London in over a decade—since his "One Night Only" event in 2006—the decision comes shortly after the company's decision to restructure its lines, consolidating the company's peripheral labels into the three core brands: Giorgio Armani, Emporio Armani and Armani Exchange. “British style has become increasingly free and innovative over the years, which is a good thing,” the designer tells Vogue. “For this reason it is the perfect setting for my Emporio Armani collection.” [#image: /photos/5ce43c673bf9b46892b1dcd6]||| ||| Tommy Hilfiger; Image: Rex Features Tommy Hilfiger hosts a carnival for 2,000 After “Tommy Pier” in New York and “Tommyland” in Venice Beach, Tommy Hilfiger is taking his see-now-buy-now fashion event to London Fashion Week. An extravagant display of force designed for the social media era, Hilfiger's travelling fashion show—which he likens to a “rock-and-roll world tour”—will be descending upon the Roundhouse in Camden Town on Tuesday. This season's collection will combine men's and women's looks for the first time in nearly a decade. As always, the in-season clothes will be made available to purchase shortly after, for instant gratification. [#image: /photos/5ce43c68dc705e9b977ad578]||| ||| Molly Goddard; Image: Getty New names to know Visitors can always count on London for fresh faces, and this season is no exception. Showing on Friday is Richard Malone, included in this autumn's “Items: Is Fashion Modern?” exhibit at New York's Museum of Modern Art. His sculptural, boldly patterned designs incorporate ideas from his upbringing, such as his mother's Argos work uniform, and the clothes he used to wear working on building sites. Another not to be missed is Saturday's show from Molly Goddard, whose masterly use of vivid colour and voluminous tulle wowed the LVMH Prize jury, which named her a finalist in this year's contest. And be sure to watch out for Paris-born Faustine Steinmetz, whose innovative, craft-based designs will be presented on the catwalk for the first time this season, and Estonian Roberta Einer, who will present her inimitable mix of hand embellishment and sporty-feminine silhouettes. Another hot ticket is one-year-old Halpern, the New York disco-laced eveningwear label already stocked at Browns and Bergdorf Goodman. [#image: /photos/5ce43c679cc0c0717df9eb4e]||| ||| Sonam Kapoor in Ralph & Russo. Image: Instagram.com Ralph & Russo launches ready-to-wear In 2014, Ralph & Russo became the first British fashion house in nearly a century to be invited to show haute couture in Paris. Having experienced “monumental growth over the past year,” the brand will be making its foray into the ready-to-wear market; but instead of Paris, the debut will take place Friday in London. “The collection remains true to our core values of quality and craftsmanship—it will provide dynamic ensembles for the modern women, across every aspect of her life,” says creative director Tamara Ralph. [#image: /photos/5ce43c68f55c27816da28cb4]||| ||| Image: Getty The headliner: Burberry Burberry is London's headline act, and this season promises to live up to the hype. This time, Burberry has moved from its regular Monday slot in Soho to a Saturday showing at a brand new venue at Old Sessions House in Clerkenwell. The show will be the first under new chief executive Marco Gobbetti, the former Céline CEO who took over the role from chief creative officer and president Christopher Bailey in July. Now that Bailey has been freed up to focus on design, we're expecting great things. Burberry will host a photographic exhibition co-curated by Bailey, entitled Here We Are, in the show space, focusing on British documentary photographers including Shirley Baker, Ken Russell and Alasdair McLellan. “I knew I wanted it to celebrate a certain strand of British photography that I have always loved—one which documents the many and varied tribes and clans and classes that make up this island of ours," says Bailey. “It's the spirit of those photographs—sometimes ironic, sometimes tender, always truthful—that has guided our September collection.” [#image: /photos/5ce43c68b40d269b2dd6e02b]||| ||| Image: Getty Fiorucci gets a reboot In the 1970s, the Italian label Fiorucci was famous for its high-waisted jeans, maximalist aesthetic and subversive ads. Its Lexington Avenue store was known as the daytime Studio 54, with regulars including Keith Haring, Cher, Calvin Klein and Marc Jacobs. Madonna played her first gig there, and at one point the shop doubled as Andy Warhol's office. On Friday the brand will re-launch in London, with a 4,000-square-foot Soho store complete with basement club. With its signature blend of art, sex, glamour and disco, the timing of Fiorucci's relaunch feels right for now. [#image: /photos/5ce43c673bf9b45329b1dcd5]||| ||| Image: Getty Nicopanda teams up with Amazon Nicola Formichetti's Nicopanda will be making its London Fashion Week debut this month in collaboration with Amazon Fashion—just one of the many ways the online mega-retailer is making its foray into the world of fashion. Catering to the millennial generation, the accessible streetwear-inspired capsule collection, which features hoodies and bomber jackets, will be available in selected locations for delivery in 60 minutes or less. It might just be the fastest straight-from-the-catwalk shopping experience to date. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Careers in fashion: Tarun Tahiliani on the commerce of couture
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And why design is not a licence for self-indulgence View Gallery 3 Photos Careers in fashion: Tarun Tahiliani on the commerce of couture As one of the luminaries of Indian fashion, one who has revolutionised the way we consume couture with his inimitable take on it, it's hard to imagine that Tarun Tahiliani did not always plan to be a designer. Tahiliani studied business management at the prestigious Wharton School of Business, and then worked in his family business before fashion came calling. “The business degree was mainly to keep my father happy,” he admits. “Even then, I took several art and live model-drawing classes in art school. When I returned to India, my father was becoming the chief of naval staff and couldn't continue as a trustee of our family business. So I threw myself into it, developing our division that sold oil field equipment to ONGC. But I soon realised this is not something that I could do all my life.” The idea for Ensemble was born from a discussion with his wife, Sal. The duo decided to launch a fashion store that would promote Indian talent they saw all over the world. This was in 1987. Today, Ensemble is one of the country's leading multi-designer boutiques and is helmed by the designer's sister, Tina Tahiliani-Parikh. As he set up the boutique, Tahiliani decided he wanted to be more than just a retailer. He launched his eponymous label in 1990, and went on to hone his understanding of design techniques at the Fashion Institute of Technology, New York, the following year. In the past 27 years, Tahiliani's namesake brand has catapulted into one of India's most revered fashion houses, reinventing centuries-old traditions with a fresh, contemporary expression. Late stylist Isabella Blow recognised Tahiliani's talent and bestowed him with the title of ‘Karl Lagerfeld of India'. Incidentally, this is the very designer whose success inspires Tahiliani till date. “I look at Karl Lagerfeld, and think, if I could even have half of what he does, I'll be lucky. I don't know how he manages to do what he does.” Not unlike Lagerfeld, Tahiliani himself has succeeded in several diverse markets without ever compromising on his voice. While his bridal wear is heavily sought-after, so are his prêt collections, signature drapes, and digital prints. “Our separates are bestsellers too as they allow women to style them in their own way,” he says. Individuality could easily be Tahiliani's middle name. Whether he's telling it like it is, redefining the traditional sari with his constructed tailoring, or unburdening the quintessentially heavy bridal lehenga, Tahiliani is a champion of always having a distinct signature. It reflects in the kind of woman he designs for too—well-read, with a strong identity and sense of purpose. Designing for the ‘modern Indian woman' has become something of a catchphrase today. It is something more than a few designers claim to do. But this has been at the core of Tahiliani's vision from the very beginning. And not because he wanted to jump onto a bandwagon, but because this is the only ‘kind' of woman he has known all his life. “I grew up surrounded by very modern women who always considered themselves equal to men. My mother was an engineer—in fact, the first female engineer at VJTI, Mumbai. Even though she dabbled with modelling, and dressed in chiffons and pearls, she argued like a man and was ready to take on any challenge that came her way. I've never really known docile women who were content sitting at home, playing housewife, and dressing up. It's not something I have a problem with, but these were just not the kind of women who inhabited my existence,” Tahiliani explains. In this exclusive tell-all with Vogue India, the designer delves deep to discuss the dynamics of Indian couture, marrying creativity with sustainability, and being truly excited by your work every single day. You have an educational background in both business and design. Was this an added advantage when you launched your brand? I suppose all experience and knowledge that one garners helps in the development of a business, but that is not enough. You need to have a vision too. I was always excited by the idea of starting a business, rather than building an existing one, and that's what I eventually ended up doing. But I have only now understood that after a certain point one cannot carry on a business in a wonderfully haphazard manner. My outlook has changed and I now look at the brand equally as a business rather than just an indulgence in what I love. As a result, we have opened wonderful new stores, our shoots have become more exciting, and we have appointed a strong team. The brand is still born from all the techniques we developed and owned over the years, but adding this structure is just something I had to do as my own penance. Today, I do feel that having design and business skills is a definite advantage because I can not only navigate both worlds, but enjoy them as well. What are some of the most important lessons from your initial years in the business? I think the most important learning (although it took me a really long time to learn this) is that being a designer is not a licence to be self-indulgent, and only create things you find beautiful. Your designs must be relevant to the culture you live in and to the body types of the women who wear your clothes if you want to build a business. If you only want to remain in the conceptual space for the sake of art, it's a different story. I am not saying you allow yourself to be caught in the trap of doing it just for the money. Good design can also result in a very good business, which in turn, can further enhance the quality of your design. I am conscious of the fact that I should enjoy going to work every day. Ultimately, it's about striking a fine balance—learning to address the needs of the people while being true to your design aesthetics, delivering on time, and creating clothes that make your customers feel good. How has the Indian couture consumer changed from when you started your brand to now? Couture was restricted to ultra-rich Indians and diamond merchants in the '90s. It was all about embroideries, they did not understand fit and finesse. Today's couture consumer is very aware and well-exposed. They wear everything from Dior and Chanel to Elie Saab. This millennial consumer is also more whimsical. For instance, they worry about Instagram reducing the repeat value of their clothes. They don't want very size-specific outfits that they can't use down the line. They want lightness, and really understand the importance of fit. For instance, a Natasha Poonawalla will never wear Indian couture that doesn't fit as well as the couture pieces she buys from international brands abroad. You have adapted to what's current and relevant while still appealing to a versatile age group. How do you manage to do that? I don't do it consciously; I just work really hard. I'm excited about street fashion, by what I see at the Kumbh [festival], by images of Indian drapes from an earlier time. What I am always conscious about is that my real contribution to fashion should not just be about reinventing embroideries, but in keeping tradition alive. It excites me to give Indian embroideries the lightness of French couture, so that women can really have fun while looking ethereal rather than being bogged down by a 50-kilo outfit. This is the sentiment that drives me and I hope it continues to be relevant. Your focus has been to reinterpret tradition for the modern Indian woman. How do you marry wearability with the often-elaborate nature of couture, especially bridal wear? My biggest challenge has been to make bridal wear more comfortable. Most brides today don't look like themselves. They are trying to be someone they are not, and end up looking like actresses portraying a role. The need is to balance our heritage with our current needs. If you're going to have a DJ and a party, then shouldn't the bride wear something she can dance easily in? Apart from being modern, clothes also need to be comfortable. The same goes with jewellery—it doesn't need to be this huge projection. Wear what you love and that which reflects your personality. View Gallery 59 Photos Tarun Tahiliani at Lakmé Fashion Week Winter/Festive 2016 Tarun Tahiliani at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2016 How do you modernise Indian couture? There is only one way to modernise couture—weight. To be modern, is to be light. To me, Indian couture (mostly associated with bridal wear) is so ridiculously heavy that women wearing it can't have fun. Instead, they end up looking overburdened, dragging themselves around like dead ducks, desperate to change out of it. A cool woman is one who wears an outfit she can have fun in all evening while still looking super glamorous. So we work a lot on construction to make our couture effortless. Even if it's heavy, the outfit should bounce on you, allowing you to glide like a swan. Apart from your flagship stores and Ensemble boutiques, you are available online, and at other multi-designer boutiques sparingly. Is this a conscious strategy? Our retail strategy is centred on concept stores like our outlet in Mehrauli, Delhi—it's a sweeping store with dedicated spaces for our ready-to-wear, occasion wear, menswear, and couture collections. It also carries our accessory and jewellery lines. We have smaller versions of this store in Mumbai and Hyderabad, and are looking at other cities as well. We've had a long-term association with Ensemble because of their understanding of our drapes as well as their respect for our products. Our experience with a lot of other multi-brand outposts, however, has been less than satisfactory. They mix up the merchandise and often stock duplicates of our work, so we don't feel the need to be there. Our current model is to diversify our availability online, and host a series of beautifully staged trunk shows around the world to connect with our global patrons. Indian couture is a populated market. How can a designer starting out in the business ensure longevity? Couture is a very important market, but it may not be for everyone. They are some designers who belong only in couture, others only in prêt, and some who can straddle both worlds. This decision is very personal and there is no right or wrong. When starting out as a couture designer, it is important to create an identity from the very beginning. Cater to your own age group by creating designs for women whose sensibility you understand. View Gallery 57 Photos Tarun Tahiliani at Lakmé Fashion Week Summer/Resort 2017 Tarun Tahiliani at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2017 You have extended your aesthetic to prêt collections as well. Is this an important market for couture designers to explore to maintain sustainability? I love the prêt collections because they keep traditions alive, while also making it wearable. For instance, let's take the tradition of draped clothing that I've see at the Kumbh and on Kathewadi men. Our brand's Indian prêt collections keep this alive with our dhotis, draped saris, cinched T-shirts, kedeo jackets and the use of deconstructed cotton. This is what truly excites me—collections that are young, organic and can be anywhere in the world… pieces that one can individualise. Bridal couture is restricted to Indians, akin to pieces for a costume party. But prêt is not a costume, it is real. But as far as sustainability is concerned, one can be perfectly sustainable doing just bridal wear; you don't need to venture into prêt for it. What is your advice to designers on balancing integrity of design with profitability? Integrity of design will always pay off, but in the long run. Every designer makes mistakes or choices that they have later regretted. Learn from them, understand who you are and what makes you feel secure. It's a part of growing up professionally and personally. Everyone has a unique handprint. You may be stellar at marketing and manipulating markets into believing in your design ideology. But if you want to spend your life as an adventure, doing what you love, you need to do it with integrity. And if you can make that work financially, then you are guaranteed to have a wonderful life. What is the key to succeed in the bridal couture market in India? Designers need to understand that the grandmothers of today are wearing what brides wore two generations ago. And more importantly, there are different strata even within the same bridal market —from the Rajwada look and Bollywood-inspired cocktail wear to qualitative modern Indian glamour. Understand where you belong and focus on that. Never try and be everything to everyone. How much does a celebrity spotted in your design affect sales? A celebrity like Sonam Kapoor in your clothes can affect sales (especially with NRIs), but it has to be a style that people relate to. If it's a generic outfit, no one really cares. There are way too many celebrity sightings these days, so it's not as exciting as it used to be. In fact, customers now come to the store and say they don't want to look like everyone else, but would rather be true to themselves. And you have to agree that's one really cool woman. column1: Diana Penty’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Take inspiration from the urban sophisticate View Gallery 48 Photos Diana Penty’s complete style evolution It was opposite a vivacious Deepika Padukone that Diana Penty made a quiet, assured debut in Cocktail (2012). With her doe eyes, silky tresses and elegant sartorial sensibility, Penty booked a berth in our collective conscience, and hasn't quite vacated the spot ever since. After her big ticket debut, she returned to the big screen a cool four years later, with Happy Bhaag Jayegi (2016). Through the highs and lows that charted in her career, Penty rose through the ranks as a fashionable name you could bet on. Armed with an acute understanding of what worked for her body type, the Cocktail stunner paraded a lush line-up of fitted silhouettes and easy separates that did wonders for her limber frame. As she gears up for the release of her upcoming thriller, Lucknow Central (2017), here's a closer look at her fashion scorecard over the years. Style diaries Penty set foot in Bollywood with a wardrobe dominated by easy layers; a fringed blazer here, a Sabyasachi vest there. Not one to discriminate against the powers of a statement anarkali, she showed up on the premiere night of her big debut in a flowy Anamika Khanna number and to-die-for chandbalis from Amrapali. As her calendar filled up in 2013 with professional commitments, Penty kept pace with her schedule in ruched Amit Aggarwal gowns and co-ordinated separates that made the best of her 5'8” frame. 2014 had her expanding her sartorial boundaries, and she made space in her otherwise-muted colour palette for an eye-popping cerulean blue gown and a forest green Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna maxi. Comeback queen Fans who were pouting when Penty all but dropped off the radar in 2015, however, soon had plenty to rejoice over. The gorgeous 30-year-old took to the limelight again with the release of her sophomore outing, Happy Bhaag Jayegi, leaving her comfort zone safely behind. First up, a mustard, asymmetrical Urvashi Joneja top that she boldly paired with dhoti pants and spiked Louboutin pumps; no sweat. Next came some print-on-print magic in the form of AM:PM separates, and then a raspberry Ridhi Mehra maxi that screams sangeet night. In case you had any doubts about her status as a bona fide style icon, she worked a ruffled Madison On Peddar top with a printed Label Ritu Kumar skirt. If anyone needs us, we'll be busy taking notes on how to work fusion wear before the festive season hits us. The good news just continued from there: 2017 had Penty casually wearing a printed Payal Khandwala number to the airport, and working an H&M suit with bohemian baubles from Aaraa by Avantika. For those days when she couldn't even, she simply slipped into head-to-toe nude separates from Sahil Kochhar. As the 31-year-old well and truly comes into her own, flip back the pages of her style diary in the gallery above. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Careers in fashion: Rahul Mishra on giving local crafts global appeal
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And the power of competitions View Gallery 3 Photos Rahul Mishra talks about taking local craft global Rahul Mishra catapulted into worldwide fame when he made headlines for winning the famed International Woolmark Prize in 2014, after what Mishra calls "accidental success as a Gen Next designer" in 2006. Today, Mishra not only showcases on the official calendar of Paris Fashion Week but also sells his collections through international fashion portals like Modaoperandi.com, Yoox.com, Lyst.com as well as stores like Colette in Paris. Mishra is unwavering in his use of Indian textiles and craft, primarily including fabrics like Chanderi and thread work in his designs that are packaged for an international audience, all while trying to maintain sustainability in production. These days, he is shuttling back and forth between schedules in India and Paris, beaming with success and using his learnings to make a bigger mark globally than ever before. Despite his journey so far, Mishra is keen to absorb all he can with the exposure he is blessed with, calls his company a ‘young brand', and above all, is excited to be creating. Vogue spoke to the designer about taking local Indian craft to an international scale, the power of winning competitions, and his advice to young designers. What was your first ever runway show and what did you learn from it? My first ever runway show was the Gen Next show for Lakmé Fashion Week in 2006 when I was in the second year at NID. I showcased my reversible Kerala handloom collection. It was prescribed by the college, so it was never my idea. There was an excess stock of handloom fabric in Kerala and you had to create a collection to consume the stock and augment the demand of textile. As a designer if I would have known I was showcasing at fashion week, I wouldn't have created it the way I did. I made it more like a classroom project. Luckily, I got a call from Lakmé to showcase it, but I had no team, no tailors, so I couldn't even change it. But it became a success. I remember Sabyasachi [Mukherjee] telling me that it takes a lot of courage to take such a humble fabric and make an entire collection out of it. That project gave me confidence. Without those limitations, I would probably have ended up over-designing my collection. Do you think there is any merit in design students taking up Masters courses? I had already been covered on Style.com at the time I graduated from NID and I could have started my brand back then, but I chose to study further. I would say that as a young designer, you really have to weigh the options of spending or not spending that money, but studying always helps. I got a scholarship to study in Istitiuto Marangoni in Milan. I could do a lot of things other than fashion at NID like photography, graphic design and animation, which is all coming handy right now when I am conceptualising. On the other hand, fashion colleges like Marangoni teach you about trends and street style—they synthesise all that information and bring it to you. One should never treat college in isolation. Fashion cities introduce you to new brands, art and so much more that gets into your subconscious and trains you. The infinite imagery that you surround yourself with helps you. View Gallery 37 Photos Rahul Mishra at India Couture Week 2016 Rahul Mishra at India Couture Week 2016 How would you say winning the International Woolmark Prize impacted your career? FDCI nominated all of us—Pankaj & Nidhi, Amit Aggarwal, Péro, Gaurav Gupta—to enter the competition. We didn't get through the first season we tried. We got nominated again the second time and we won; it was great timing. I was setting up my new company and I won the prize, which I used as a start-up fund for my company. I still remember Franca Sozzani announcing my name and she came backstage and spoke to me. Everybody at the party told me that the prize is a small thing, it just recognises your talent—what you do with it ultimately is important. Do you think international competitions can help a designer? There are different prizes that are known all over the world and many winners, but not all of them show at fashion weeks. Ultimately, it's not about the sensational headlines, it's the attitude. You have to be willing to start from zero each time you begin a collection. The real competition is within yourself. When someone comes to see my show during Paris Fashion Week, I know that they are going to see labels like Valentino, Comme des Garçons—labels that create the greatest products in the world. How is the international press going to react to my collection when it's being viewed alongside brands like Louis Vuitton? I don't have the setup and ambience that they do. I just have my clothes, so in that way, the importance on the body of work is something you cannot compromise on. You can't just refresh old ideas. You are just wasting a slot if you don't have anything to show. How is showing internationally different from showing in India? Backstage culture is very different in Paris as compared to what it is in India. The press and buyers actually come backstage after the show is done to see the garments up close. Clothes look very different on hangers compared to what they do on models under the light. It is really about your attitude and your appetite for learning and your hunger to start from zero every time. View Gallery 40 Photos Rahul Mishra at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017 Rahul Mishra at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017 How does one globalise an indigenous craft? The question you are finding the answer to when you are showcasing at an international scale is how do you stand out. What is uniqueness? Rather than me taking Chanderi out of India, is the craft that is taking us as a brand and making us more recognisable and giving us a signature. You don't need one more brand that's like another existing brand. When you look at a Japanese designer, he is bringing the Japanese ethos into play. You look at Issey Miyake's pleating techniques, Yohji Yamamoto's construction, Sacai's hybrid of Japanese ideas. They all have a clear stamp of being made in Japan. That's one of the recipes [to standing out] when you are looking at international fashion. I remember being mentored by Colin McDowell who once said that it's incredibly difficult to achieve the balance between a strong universal appeal and ethnicity in your product. I don't think it will be wrong to say I have achieved it. How can you modernise a craft that's ages old? All the young brands, including me, have to keep asking ourselves—how can you make something your own? There are a lot elements to designing that you can't even define, that you realise only when you are in the process of creating. Indian craft and embroideries have a lot to do with that. I can't explain the new technique that has come to life when sampling, but you can feel the newness in it and that to me is the secret. Techniques and inspiration always existed but what is it that you make your own? There's no formula, but that is the best way I can explain it. The future or modernity is a moving target, you can't say you have achieved it. Modernity is not always about cutting up neoprene, clashing it and making it into a unique piece. It's probably much more than that. column1: Alessandro Michele on the past and future of fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Hear from the best What is truly original? A language—whether it be verbal, visual or gestural—doesn't develop in a vacuum, but originates from a sort of chemical reaction sparked by something already existing. If authentic, a creative act is in fact born from a theft taken to unforeseen consequences. One steals an attitude from the muse, a colour from nature, and from there one starts inventing. Pupils start their journey from the style of their masters; a vogue simmers when taken to foreign territory, a bit like the alien that Ridley Scott and HR Giger conceived. After all, once again in Godard's words and in an unheard-of yet happy pairing of classic linear thought and postmodern non-linear logic, it is not important where you take things from, but where you take them to. This is even more evident in fashion: the new originates from an incessant, cathartic, superstitious elaboration of the past that stops time, or at least it tries to, through remaking, endlessly. What would the '80s have been without the '40s, and the '70s without the '20s? Even the modernism of the '60s, so inebriated with the future, clearly owes more than a little bit to the brisk lines of the jazz era. Not to mention the creators, who are always amazingly indebted. What would Yves Saint Laurent have invented had he not looked at the Rive Gauche of the protesters or at Mondrian; or Gianni Versace had he not laid his eyes on Greek vases and on Beppe Spadacini's prints; or Walter Albini had he not been intrigued by Benito's drawings and by the sophistications of the Gazette du Bon Ton? “I am brazen. For me, creating means regurgitating, distorting and assembling everything that has passed through me and continues to do so,” says Alessandro Michele, tireless appropriator and Gucci's creative director. Michele is an author, and his language is unequivocal. In a short amount of time, he has triggered a pleasurably decorative shock wave that has turned the Florentine fashion house into the epicentre of a liberated, libertarian and liberating Baroquism. It has become the encyclopaedic temple of narrative and maximalist fashions, which celebrate diversity while freeing their political power in the party-hard superficiality that glorifies outcasts, skanks, queers and beautiful freaks. And it does this through mad collages imbued with the past yet in no way nostalgic, as they are devoid of established hierarchies and orders. As a result, Renaissance and kitsch, Star Trek and Elizabethan theatre, refinement and pop often coexist in the same outfit. With sardonic humour, he calls himself a washing machine that spin-dries everything. He is, indeed, a situationist of pastiche, an inexorable maker and undoer of lavish spatiotemporal twines. His kaleidoscopic world is a catalogue of clichés in which everything goes with everything as long as the clash of irreconcilable opposites is deafening. And this is exactly his way of being original. “Clothes are endless possibilities for meaning, because with every change or different association you are a different person,” he professes. For sure, Alessandro Michele is not the first appropriationist in fashion history and will not be the last. But he is probably the most archaeological and accurate and surely the most derisive, because he plays it hard and risky with pseudo copies that unsettle the moralists while he keeps on elaborating new juxtapositions. “I am almost pornographic in the way I pay homage to what I like and what has influenced me,” he explains, referring to the deliberate literalness of his own citations. The assemblage, instead, is always idiosyncratic, hectic and Dionysian. “I find things, but many things find me, because chance is also imaginative,” he adds, describing his modus operandi made of both chaos and order. “Quoting means rehabilitating, transforming. Denying this means nullifying the very act of creation.” Such crystal clarity leaves no room for doubts, but despite it Alessandro Michele has often been questioned for the very same zest for appropriation which is his own creative trademark, and ended up being the victim par excellence of the anti-appropriation police. “My sources are so evident that, perhaps wrongly, I don't consider captions necessary,” he explains. “For me, reworking the past over and over again is a way not to trivialise the garments and not to obsess over hem lengths. What I am interested in, as a matter of fact, is telling a story and, if someone sees fragments of other stories in it, be my guest. I don't have to justify myself. What is urgent for me is what I want to say.” Michele especially refers to the controversy that spread on Instagram at the end of May for a look in the cruise 2018 collection which refers quite literally to the work of Daniel Day, the tailor who in the '80s in Harlem created a magnificent idea of appropriationist ghetto tailoring with the Dapper Dan atelier, defining the image of the first hip-hop stars from scratch, through the illicit theft of luxury labels' logos. “Maybe I should have said it openly, but to me it was far too obvious,” he explains. Theorising the neo-mannerist wave of the '80s, art critic Achille Bonito Oliva forged the formula “the traitor's ideology”, which is a perfect way to define appropriation as creative practice. It is exactly the way Michele works: he respects his sources by betraying them at will to compose overwhelming symphonies. This includes Cranach's paintings, Walter Albini's and Botticelli's beauties, which, however, don't trigger the politically correct rage of social media censors. “I believe the problem springs from a widespread cultural attitude. Citations have always been a fundamental part of everyone's cultural journey. Today, however, citations are confused with paralysing nostalgia. On the contrary, I believe obsessing over the future is the best way not to live the present.” Here we get to the vital point. Seeing the past as a lively mine full of references and possibilities is a way to bring the present into the limelight. What is fascinating in Alessandro Michele's work is his rewriting of time, akin to a psychedelic trip that frees cognition and knowledge, and that finds the value of today exactly in archaeology. “I grew up with a father who didn't wear a watch and this has permanently marked my relationship with time,” he concludes. “All that inspires me and all that I quote, whether it is one day or four hundred years old, occurs at the same time before my eyes, so it becomes the present. It's my present, my time and it's the only thing that I can and want to describe.” This article was originally published on Vogue.it Fashion Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: In an increasingly casual world, Oscar de la Renta rethinks the formula
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion "It’s very important to have an evolution, not a revolution" Three years after the passing of its founder and namesake, the house of Oscar de la Renta has achieved a delicate parity: courting a new, more casual customer while continuing to outfit the elegant women he dressed for decades. Vogue speaks to co-creative directors Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia, and son-in-law Alex Bolen, about the American fashion house's next chapter. View Gallery 12 Photos Oscar de la Renta keeps it in the family Last February, when Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia presented their first collection as co-creative directors of Oscar de la Renta, they took an impressive first step towards ensuring the brand's legacy. For the duo, it marked a triumphant return to the place that they began their careers in fashion. And for the company, it signalled the beginning of a new chapter after a rudderless few seasons. It is no exaggeration to suggest that Oscar de la Renta was one of the most important figures in 20th century American fashion—and one of its most beloved, too. De la Renta learned his craft through an apprenticeship with Cristóbal Balenciaga, and then worked as a couture assistant at Lanvin. With his own label, founded in 1965, he established a sartorial blueprint for a certain sort of aspirational woman—a woman for whom dressing up was de rigueur, for whom cocktail dresses were more than a once-yearly occasion. His designs, rendered in sumptuous fabrics and vibrant colours and patterns—he favoured floral motifs—were devoted to making women look and feel their best. De la Renta, along with contemporaries like Halston and Bill Blass, proved that American brands could drive trends rather than simply follow them. But times change, and maintaining a legacy is at least as difficult as building one. It requires adapting to a shifting social context—the cocktail dress may have been Oscar's bread and butter, but in an increasingly casual world that no longer calls for them, the label has needed to adjust. It falls, now, to Kim and Garcia to shepherd it into a new era, and update its offerings in a way that remains true to its history. When Oscar de la Renta CEO Alex Bolen refers to Kim and Garcia as part of the family, he is not doling out platitudes. The pair has contributed hugely to the brand since Kim joined in 2003 while in the midst of completing her BFA in Fashion Design at the Pratt Institute. Says Bolen: “Laura and I started working at Oscar de la Renta in the same week. Laura started here as an intern, and I started as, I thought, a consultant who was going to help sell my wife's family's business. But, for both of us, it turned into a much longer engagement.” Garcia joined the company in 2009, as an intern reporting to Kim, after completing a degree in architecture at Notre Dame at his family's behest. Just before de la Renta passed away in October of 2014, British designer Peter Copping was named his successor, and Kim and Garcia—by then design director and senior designer, respectively—left the company shortly thereafter. The designer was deeply concerned with ensuring a smooth transition, fearing the slide into irrelevancy suffered by Blass and Halston after their founders' deaths. He was directly involved in bringing Copping aboard, courting him while he held the position of creative director at Nina Ricci. The hiring looked great on paper—Copping had couture training, which mattered to de la Renta, and the two shared a proclivity for refined, colourful, joyful femininity in their designs. But Copping's tenure at the house lasted just three full ready-to-wear cycles. His resignation was announced abruptly in July of 2016, not quite two years after he joined the company. While Copping was helming Oscar de la Renta, Kim and Garcia were busy building Monse, one of New York's buzziest young labels. Monse's presence was immediately felt when it debuted at New York Fashion Week in September of 2015—the collection they showed, built around playful, sexy reinterpretations of the traditional dress shirt, earned rave reviews. The brand quickly became a fixture on red carpets, worn by such sought-after stars as Sarah Jessica Parker, Selena Gomez and Lupita Nyong'o. These prominent placements were partly the result of relationships with A-list stylists Garcia cultivated during his early years at Oscar de la Renta. And while it appeared to outsiders that Monse emerged from thin air, that, of course, was not the case. The years Kim and Garcia spent under Oscar's tutelage left them amply prepared to launch a label with a strong commercial foundation. Though Monse skews funkier than the ready-to-wear offerings at Oscar de la Renta—it's more adventurous in its fabric selections, more provocative in its cuts, more directional in concept—it shares a focus on wearability that Kim and Garcia picked up from Oscar himself. Says Kim: “In fittings, Oscar always said, ‘What does that dress do for her?' That's something I always keep in mind.” “Oscar always said that it's not fashion until a woman buys it and wears it,” adds Bolen. “I think that Laura and Fernando very much take that to heart.” Bolen is refreshingly candid about his reasons for hiring Copping over Kim and Garcia. “I was not aware of the extent of their maturity,” he admits. But the interlude proved beneficial. “I was not a boss, so to speak, when I was at Oscar,” Garcia explains. “I've learned, since I left and came back, how to manage a team, how to make everyone feel listened to, feel involved in the design, and feel excited every day. The most important thing that you need to run a company is a happy team.” For Kim and Garcia, the challenge of juggling both labels has turned out to be a blessing, an energising challenge that generates free-flowing creative momentum.“You get to switch off your thinking for one type of woman and turn it on for the other,” says Garcia. “The ideas stay—in a positive way—as naive as possible.” While Kim and Garcia wasted no time in adding new categories to the Oscar de la Renta repertoire—denim and suiting, for instance—they are keenly aware that they have a dedicated customer base that mustn't be alienated. Says Garcia: “It's very important to have an evolution, not a revolution, as people say. We're protecting that client who loves the brand and has bought so many clothes throughout the years—decades, for some. If this was a brand that relied on beauty or accessories, sure, it would have been fine to toss the DNA of the ready-to-wear out the window and start fresh with a brand new idea, but it's a brand that's strongest in ready-to-wear, so it has to be protected.” Speaking with Kim and Garcia, it's clear that they feel a sense of responsibility for Oscar de la Renta's legacy—the kind of deep connection that can only develop organically. “They are part of the DNA of this house,” says Bolen. “I think very much about how our organisation is living and breathing every day,” he continues. “The way that we're living and breathing these days feels like we're moving in the right direction. We hadn't really felt that way in a long time.” And home, after all, is not a building, but a feeling. Kim and Garcia have found themselves right back where they belong. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The fashion editor's new book is full of funny anecdotes and more Giovanna Battaglia Engelbert, senior fashion editor at Vogue Japan and a contributing fashion editor to W Magazine, is one the most known faces in the contemporary fashion industry. The editor recently launched her latest book, Gio Graphy: Fun in the Wild World of Fashion (Rizzoli), with a party hosted at Bergdorf Goodman during New York Fashion Week. We spoke to Battaglia Engelbert between car rides to shows about writing, smiling and laugh-crying. Tell us what Gio Graphy is all about? Well my book is a mix of a little bit of everything. column1: Nimrat Kaur on being the new face of Ritu Kumar
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And why it's important to preserve our textile heritage View Gallery 9 Photos Nimrat Kaur is the new face of Ritu Kumar Ritu Kumar's new collection, Urban Gypsy, is as the name suggests, perfect for the urban wanderer. The Bollywood actor who is often seen travelling across the world serves as the perfect muse for this winter/festive 2017 collection that attempts to combine the glamorous sensibility of a sophisticated traveller with down-to-earth comfort. With a unique take on the bohemian trend, expect to find tie-dye kurtas, embellished jackets, tasselled scarves, geometric print kaftans and cold shoulder cut out kurtas in this new collection. Vogue chats with Nimrat Kaur to find out everything about her new association with Ritu Kumar. How do you feel about being the face of Ritu Kumar's latest collection? I feel very privileged to be associated with Ritu Kumar. She's amongst the oldest, first names in fashion. I remember being in school and knowing that there was a label called Ritu Kumar. I grew up in Delhi and I remember Ritu Kumar wasn't just a common name, there was a certain pride people took in owning her clothes. What do you like about her clothing? I adore that the pieces are rooted in the traditional Indian weave, but at the same time there is a lot of modernism to them. There is a beautiful combination of the old and the new. Ritu Kumar uses such exquisite embroidery, Indian motifs and weaves that look so heavily Indian, but the silhouettes and cuts make the clothing contemporary. Ritu Kumar is a champion of reviving Benarasi textiles. What do you feel about the movement towards sustaining Indian crafts and Indian textiles? I think there is nothing more superior than our own weaves, our own cloth and our artists, and the pain-staking detail with which they work. No matter where you go, you just don't see that kind of craftsmanship and that kind of labour of love. For instance, the amount of time it can take to make a Benarasi sari, it is almost like a form of art. It's not just a piece of cloth, it's an heirloom that is passed on from a grandmother to mother to daughter. I feel like her love and passion towards reviving Benarasi textiles is very inspiring. What's your sense of style when it comes to ethnic wear? I love traditional Indian wear. I rarely mix stuff up and do a combination of things. I really love everything that is in its purest form. So, if I wear a sari, I wear it in a way that the sari is supposed to be worn and it's supposed to be draped. What are your thoughts on this new collection? The collection is absolutely exquisite. The construction of these garments is thoughtful and detailed. The fabrics are luscious to touch and designed with contemporary sensibilities. There is a sense of understated glamour, which makes these pieces so appealing. What is your favourite piece from the collection? It's very hard to pick, but if I absolutely had to, it would have to be the noir black dhoti salwar with the intricately worked velvet top. The outfit is so contemporary and versatile yet it has that distinct Ritu Kumar signature. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Gaurav Gupta collaborates with the maker of Deepika Padukone’s Cannes shoes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Exclusively available at Level Shoes, Dubai Dubai has a strong connect with India, being almost a gateway to the rest of the world, especially when it comes to fashion. And now Level Shoes, the 96,000sqft space dedicated to all things footwear located in Dubai Mall, is celebrating the Middle East's love for this country with their fall campaign, 'Dear India'. For this, 16 designers have created shoes exclusively for Level that are inspired by India. Aquazurra, Alberta Ferretti, Malone Soulier, Tod's and Dubai's very own Ingie Paris are among the designers participating. Says Rania Masri, general manager, Level Shoes, “For Dear India, we really are pulling out all the stops. We have an impressive in-store line up of activities, designer talks, the debut of our exclusive collections and a three day in-store festival, all leading up to Diwali.” And this includes a campaign shot at Jaipur's Samode Palace. Home-grown companies like fashion jewellery brand Isharya and footwear label The Soul Sisters will also be part of the special pop-ups at the store. These all lead up to a gala that takes place at the end of October. Among those flying down from India for the special soiree will be Gaurav Gupta, as he has collaborated with New York-based footwear designer Chloe Gosselin on one design for this project. Called, “Opia” the shape of the sunset pink platform sandal is one that Chloe's label is known. The sole and the heel are sprinkled with pearl surface ornamentation from Gaurav Gupta's atelier. It has been a true east-meets-west project as the fabric was cut in Italy, embroidered by hand in India and then assembled again in Italy. Gaurav is a designer who loves for fantastical increases each season, and last couture collection 'Moondust', confirmed that sculptures will always be his muse. French Chloe Gosselin is a former model, and her shoes mix Parisian feminine elegance with a New York girl-about-town vibe. In India, she is best known for the moss green velvet platform sandals that Deepika Padukone wore at Cannes Film Festival this year. Vogue caught up with Gaurav Gupta and Chloe Gosselin to find out more about this pairing. How did this partnership come about? Chloe Gosselin: Level Shoes reached out to me to participate in their project, Dear India, which I was thrilled about because India and specifically the Holi festival is the main inspiration behind my new spring/summer 2018 collection. The team at Level Shoes suggested me and Gaurav come together again for this unique collaboration. Did you know much about each other's work? Gaurav Gupta: Not much. I knew about Chloe's was David Copperfield's partner. Also, I had heard her name because of the shoes that Deepika Padukone had worn at Cannes, but did not know her work so well. Through this collaboration we discovered more about each other, and each other's style of work. So have you actually met each other? GG: Chloe and I have been talking on the phone and been on Skype with each other. We are excited to meet in Dubai and she's already planning a lot of creative things. Your styles are so different, so was it a case of opposites attract? CG: I think Gaurav's work and mine converge in this idea of timeless beauty, but also intricate details and a particular attention to craftsmanship. So it was very easy, in fact, to understand each other. Will India get to see these shoes? GG: As of now, they will be retailed exclusively at Level Shoes at The Dubai Mall. This is the beginning of the collaboration; I'm sure many more things will come out of this. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Gauri Khan’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From bandage dresses to elegant midis View Gallery 47 Photos The complete style evolution of Gauri Khan As superstar Shah Rukh Khan's other half, Gauri Khan is a key member of Bollywood's It-crowd. But don't dismiss her as just another ‘lady who lunches'. When not grabbing eyeballs for her jet-setting lifestyle and Insta-famous girl squad, the interior designer is creating headlines with her star-studded clientele. Khan is behind the dreamy homes of the likes of Karan Johar and Ranbir Kapoor, and also recently extended her aesthetic to the interiors of swanky modern Indian restaurant Arth in Mumbai. Add to that the launch of her new store, Gauri Khan Designs, and her collection of designer Italian lights for Tisva, and there is no stopping this design tour de force. Khan's reputation as one of India's coolest interior designers hasn't kept her entirely away from Tinseltown though. Too reclusive to join her husband in front of the camera, she prefers to don the producer's hat as the co-owner of Red Chillies Entertainment with films like Main Hoon Na, Happy New Year, Chennai Express, and My Name is Khan, among others, to her credit. Style files Sartorially speaking, whenever Khan made an appearance, she did so with the intent of making a splash. Cue in-your-face animal prints (with an acute loyalty for Dolce & Gabbana), logo-bearing accessories (think YSL belts, Chanel bags, and Bottega Veneta Knot clutches), and look-at-me hues. Her love for luxury labels was hard to miss too, as her repertoire was always peppered with designers pieces like Missoni dresses, Alexander McQueen maxis, limited edition Valentino clutches, Hermès scarf tops, and Donna Karan gowns. It's no surprise that she gravitated more towards statement-making brands like Emilio Pucci, Roberto Cavalli, and Versace. Though the brand that has instant recall when you think of Khan is Hervé Léger. Why? Owing to her steady patronage of their bandage dress, but of course. She can safely be dubbed a card-carrying rep of the bodycon brigade, a mania that had gripped all of Bollywood at one point. Strapless dresses and halter tops were other constants. Khan's traditional looks were all about no-holds-barred Bollywood glamour with glittering saris paired with strappy blouses, and was drawn to designers like Monisha Jaising, Tarun Tahiliani, Manish Malhotra, and Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla. Sartorial turnover Once recognised for her singular dramatic style, complete with bronze make-up and big blowouts, Khan toned it down over the years. The bandage dress has now retired and been replaced by elegant midi dresses in mellow prints. Gone are her once-staple OTT prints. They have made way for solid colours and monochrome ensembles, resulting in a look that's more polished and less flamboyant. But that's not to say that Khan has shunned her erstwhile dressing sensibility. She continues to remain loyal to her jeans and top uniform. You will often spot her in folded jeans (a definite favourite) worn with tees and vests, formal cold shoulder blouses, or bohemian tops, topped off with Louboutin heels. column1: Careers in fashion: Masaba Gupta on harnessing the power of youth
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And working even when not View Gallery 3 Photos Masaba Gupta on harnessing the power of youth Masaba Gupta is a bit of a firecracker—she's not afraid to print what's on her mind. What's more is that she's sure of having caught the pulse of the moment and the fact that everything she makes will translate into sales. When asked how can an upcoming designer use the power of youth to their advantage, Gupta is candid in her response: “By being honest,” she simply lays it down. The designer began her journey in 2009 with Lakmé Fashion Week's prized Gen Next spot. She's on the latest Forbes 30 under 30 list, regularly dresses the likes of Kareena Kapoor Khan, Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor, and has no plans to slow down. “I'm never not working. If I am not at work, I am talking to a stylist or an actor or an agent for something or the other,” she says. But how did the 28-year-old achieve all that in less than a decade? Gupta categorises her eponymous brand that's best known for its wild use of colour and eye-grabbing prints under ‘kitsch pop'. “It's independent, easy, forward thinking,” she says. She now boasts three stores in the country and sells online. But her biggest strength lies in understanding and catering to the market several designers have desperately attempted to woo—the youth. “I design for girls like me, I go to the same places to eat drink as these girls and I have the same problems as them, so I am literally living their life and designing for that life,” says. Aside from ready-to-wear, and a fresh dive into festive and occasion wear, Gupta also has a line of accessories that includes diaries with original design sketches, travel pillows, trays, socks and even custom gifting options for weddings. She is smart not alienate the customer that forms her strong fan base. Far be it from Gupta to undermine the power of small fashion goods. “The fact is that there are young girls who can't afford me but they should feel like they own a part of my label anyway. It's just to keep them from being intimidated. Also, print is the easiest thing to translate onto everything, so why not,” she says. From cameras to candies and firecrackers, Gupta has made a mark with her unique sensibility. Vogue spoke to the designer about making it big, getting ripped off and finding her own tune. What was your first ever runway show? What were your learnings from it? That would be my graduation show at my college. My learning was whatever can go wrong, will go wrong anyway; and chances are it will go wrong on your biggest day. When starting off a career in design, did you have a vision for yourself? No, it's more to do with survival each day at that stage because you are still testing waters. At what point did you realise you were going from a known label to one that was recognised all across the country? I was in Lajpat Nagar in Delhi when I saw my fakes at a market. You had one of the first Instagram shows in the country; how did you plan that? We didn't plan it. We had this idea, and my friend Joy Dutta the photographer, who is no more, sat down and said let's make it happen. So, we shot it like a regular show and sat down in real time uploading it—and then the WiFi died for a few minutes. It wasn't planned at all, but it was one of our bestselling collections! You have a large fan base of young girls—how do you create clothes for that audience while also catering to a larger more varied audience? It's a mix, because I have my mum and her friends who also love my clothes and give me feedback. I am a little bit of an old soul and my style is fun, but some days I only wear monochrome with pearls and drink whisky. Rest of the time I am doing shots and downing pizza. That's exactly how I design... a little bit of refinement and a little bit wild and fun. What role does social media play in the growth of brand? Everything today. Sadly, it's very misused. Visibility on social media is of key importance, but it depends from brand to brand. How important is it for you to react to current events, to continue having a dialogue with your audience? I react to what's relevant to me and what I can add to. Like I find that talking about body confidence and just regular girl issues is up my alley, and I know what I say will be heard and maybe even save a life, so I constantly talk about it. But if you ask me to comment about Rahul Gandhi just to join a bandwagon, I won't. View Gallery 35 Photos Masaba Gupta at Lakmé Fashion Week Winter/Festive 2015 Masaba Gupta at Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2015 How important is it to have your own voice and aesthetic reflect on your social media? Ask those 200 designers who think its okay to copy other designers and call it their invention. I think very, very few people have an individual aesthetic. You can and you will get lost if you don't stick out of the crowd because it is the easiest thing to have mistaken identities in fashion. What is your advice to the new crop of designers? Please stop saying you are 'overwhelmed' to be acknowledged and featured in the paper when you've paid yourself for an article on the front page of a newspaper and written the caption yourself. We all know media net exists; I know the cost too. Think ahead, you will have to find a plan beyond the first showcase. View Gallery 36 Photos Masaba at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2016 Masaba at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2016 What are the things you stay away from while using social media? Nothing really… haven't thought about it... but maybe nudity? What are the benefits of having your own store versus selling online? You need people to touch and feel clothes. Also in India, people need the experience and shopping for them is an event. Online is great for the smaller towns where you can't reach sometimes. How much does a celebrity spotted in your design affect sales? There's a huge success rate [when a celebrity sports your design] but it depends who wears it. Sonam, Alia and Shilpa can create an online shopping crisis overnight when they wear us, which is great. Have you ever resisted change? No, but I am not in love with it either. column1: Have you seen the ‘Boys Equals Girls’ T-shirt? Meet the women behind it
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Have you ordered one? View Gallery 12 Photos Why is everyone talking about the Boys Equals Girls t-shirt? The founders of the Unborder Collective—an alternative agency that's talking about issues that are of human interest—have launched their first venture, Mixx, which dedicated to the cause of gender equality. Their hit (and only) fashion product at the moment is a casual white T-shirt bearing the words ‘Boys Equals Girls', and is garnering attention on social media. Ruchika Parab, Janina Frahm and Shruti Singhi and the three women leading the platform that aims to create a safe space for people to discuss their stories tracking issues of gender and identity. “There are a lot people doing great work in the space of gende and sex education at the grass root level, educating and spreading awareness. We don't have the expertise that NGOs do, we can't even begin to compare ourselves with them. With Mixx, we want to spread awareness but we want people to enjoy doing it, and make it fit into people's lifestyles as something of interest to them, we want to package it in a way that is relevant to urban mindset,” says Parab, who wants Mixx to be known as a lifestyle, not an organisation. At the moment, Mixx functions as an e-zine that featured articles like ‘Gender Neutral Parenting', ‘Let's Talk Boys' and ‘Alpa Girl', and sells the aforementioned statement-making T-shirt. "You can show solidarity to the cause just by wearing the T-shirt, it's an easy way to spread the message," says Parab. "We have the T-shirt and the zine, but our next step is to collaborate with artists and have them paint over the T-shirt." Talking about gender binary and rights might be the need of the hour, but it has to be treated with much caution. Parab, Farhm and Singhi are careful to source stories from sincere voices. “You hear of so many instances of violence and discrimination in cities--so how do you provoke thought and discussions around the subject?” Parab further elaborates how Mixx is positioning it's stand on gender equality. In the future, Mixx aims to start on-ground activities by hosting events where photographers, artists, poets can all collaborate to showcase work around the theme of gender equality. column1: Parineeti Chopra’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A complete 180 View Gallery 78 Photos Then and now: The complete style evolution of Parineeti Chopra Manchester Business School graduate Parineeti Chopra harboured ambitions of a career in investment banking in the UK, when the 2009 recession forced her to return to India. A stint in Yash Raj Films' public relations department led to an acting contract, and Chopra made her debut with a supporting role in Ladies vs Ricky Bahl in 2011 alongside Ranveer Singh and Anushka Sharma. Her act garnered her widespread acclaim and her subsequent films like Ishaqzaade, Shuddh Desi Romance, and Hasee Toh Phasee continued to establish Chopra's credibility as a powerhouse performer. The early years While Chopra proved her acting mettle early on, she did not find her fashion footing with ease during the former years of her career. Her debutante style can be dubbed as basic at best—she was mostly seen in shift and sheath dresses, and jeans and tops (often with a blazer) with the odd jumpsuit thrown into the mix. There was also a brief flirtation with midi-length pencil skirts. And while Chopra did move away from her comfort zone on the red carpet with gowns by Gauri & Nainika, Nikhil Thampi, and Rajat Tangri among others, her choices did not exactly have her topping best-dressed lists. A new leaf Chopra went from being known as ‘Priyanka Chopra's cousin' to carving her own identity with the strength of her performances. The same transformation extends to her sartorial aesthetic as well. Chopra took 2015 off to get into shape, and emerged in her fittest form ever later that year. What followed was a newly acquired body confidence, along with a complete style makeover. Chopra also candidly admitted that it was her desire to be able to up her fashion game that inspired her to work on her physique. Chopra 2.0 was quick to embrace a new look. Her second innings in the style department saw her come into her own and create an entirely fresh sartorial identity. From Kanika Goyal pantsuits, Mark Bumgarner gowns and Gauri and Nainika dresses to leather separates and trench dresses, Chopra became more open to versatile silhouettes that flattered her frame. The actor's off-duty style, on the other hand, is more laid-back. A torchbearer for athleisure cool, Chopra is a key member of the gen-next Bollywood pack that is all about comfort, with her uniform of ripped jeans, oversized jumpers, and denim jackets, particularly when travelling. Sneakers by the likes of Gucci, Saint Laurent, and Lacoste are a constant part of her repertoire, as are backpacks in pastel tones. column1: 30+ lehenga options that are perfect for your mehandi event
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Hands-free comfort View Gallery 33 Photos All the best fuss-free lehengas that are perfect for your mehendi If you thought picking a lehengas for your wedding day was a mammoth decision to make, you haven't even gotten to the monster that is the mehandi lehenga. Most brides are fans of floral jewellery when it comes to mehandi, making it particularly tricky to choose a colour palette that complements it. Given that your hands will be wet with henna, your ensemble needs to be one that's as comfortable as it is stunning, making sure that you can actually enjoy the event. There's also the question of whether you want to go with prints or embellishments. Taking all of these variables in consideration, picking a lehenga for your mehandi requires some brainstorming. First, decide whether you want to give the dupatta a skip and look for an alternative option. You can choose from cape blouses or blouses with an attached trail that create the illusion of a dupatta. You can also look at blouses with ruffles and fringe detailing that don't need a dupatta to complete the look. Silk shirts can also substitute the traditional blouse silhouette—simply roll up the sleeves to make room for the henna. If you do choose to go down the dupatta route, make sure it is pinned securely in place. Avoid any designs that might interfere with the mehandi, such as trailing cape sleeves. It's better to stay away heavily-embellished ensembles that will weigh you down. Pastels are the preferred colour palette for this event, but you can also go with monochrome and floral prints to make a statement.
