column1: How the Indian-origin Miss Japan is busting the pageant winner stereotype
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet Priyanka Yoshikawa Think pageant contestants are all beauty, no brains? Miss World Japan Priyanka Yoshikawa has no time for your stereotypes. A quick scroll through Priyanka Yoshikawa's Instagram feed, and you'd be excused for thinking of her as just another twenty-something. The dimpled beauty shares our love-hate relationship with everything from junk food to Doraemon, and isn't beneath a good ol' fashioned mirror selfie. You'd almost write her off as just another enterprising millennial—if it weren't for the regular snaps of the Miss World Japan 2016 sash peppering her feed. But make no mistake; Yoshikawa has a lofty résumé backing up her credentials as a name to watch out for. If her stint at the Miss Japan beauty pageant hadn't worked out as marvellously as it did, the sprightly 23-year-old could have taken her pick from a slew of career options—Yoshikawa is the proud owner of an elephant trainer's license, is passionate about kick-boxing and a self-confessed fitness freak. After being born and raised in California, she then shuffled around the globe, and calls both Kolkata and Japan home. She ultimately went on to enrol for the Miss Japan pageant at the age of 22, but her victory wasn't without strings. Born to an Indian father and a Japanese mother, Yoshikawa's multinational ethnicity attracted the ire of conservative internet trolls. An unfortunate controversy followed her in the wake of her crowning, but she only came out stronger for it and moved on to the Miss World pageant last December, where she placed in the top 20. During a brief visit to India, we caught up with the bubbly beauty queen to talk about what it's like to wear the Miss Japan crown, her multiple charitable efforts and everything in between. Congratulations on becoming the second multiracial person to land the coveted Miss Japan title. In hindsight, what do you make of the controversy that followed? Japan, as a nation, is extremely diverse in ethnicity, which is what made the backlash shocking. But I wasn't the only one; Ariana Miyamoto faced the same naysayers when she won the Miss Universe Japan title in 2015. The issue at hand is that people need to be educated, and taught that we are just as capable of representing Japan and its varied heritage. It is up to us to take the conversation forward and ensure that the small spark of change is kept alive. Who do you count as your inspiration? There's no denying the doors that Priyanka Chopra has opened for the rest of us by shattering conventions and becoming a household name in the West. I also ended up becoming friends with Ariana [Miyamoto] after I won the title last year, and she has been a pillar of support. What's keeping you busy currently? I've recently taken up the mantle as Brand Ambassador for the Eastern Himalayas project with Balipara Foundation, and am excited to be speaking at the forum in November about the inhumane treatment meted out to wild animals. I am also serving as Brand Ambassador for Smile Asia, one of the biggest charities in the continent that helps provide surgical treatment for kids with cleft lips. I hope to raise awareness about this facial deformity as knowledge is sparse about this condition. How do you deal with the stereotypes that come attached with your beauty pageant title? I like to believe that beauty cannot exist without purpose. Good looks can only take you so far; it's the way you conduct yourself and what you're ultimately striving towards that defines your story. What would you say is your purpose? The backlash that I faced after the contest helped me realise that I need to speak up against racial slurs and insults like ‘haffu' (a colloquial Japanese term for multiracial people). And while I did face a lot of ire, I also received an immense outpouring of support and encouraging messages. I hope to be the voice for this positivity. What has been your biggest takeaway from your experience in the Miss Japan pageant? It's very easy to lose yourself in the glamour of it all. The one thing that I learned was to be honest with myself, regardless of what everyone tries to tell you. I was competing with 118 girls, all of whom had an equal shot at winning. I knew my weaknesses and what I should be focusing my training on. At the end of the day, you're also competing with yourself and you need to ensure that you come out as a better, stronger person. column1: Let Deepika Padukone’s traditional Indian looks inspire your festive wear
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion So much to choose from View Gallery 26 Photos Deepika Padukone’s most iconic traditional looks That Deepika Padukone is a bona fide style star is a non-negotiable fact. Whether she's grabbing dinner in Gucci pyjama sets or turning heads at the Met Gala dressed in Tommy Hilfiger, she has made being impeccably put-together an art. By her own admission, Padukone believes that style ought to be an extension of one's personality. Hence it comes as no surprise that the actor has cited the sari as her most favourite garment on multiple occasions, often picking it over a gown. Ever since she made her film debut in 2007, Padukone has never shied away from traditional looks, both on and off the red carpet. Her repertoire is peppered with memorable looks in silhouettes ranging from anarkalis and lehengas to saris. Back in 2012, Padukone was riding the anarkali wave, favouring voluminous creations by Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla, and Rohit Bal. Statement earrings and hair in an updo was her preferred way to sport these. Though saris soon took over as the dominant pick, with the fashionista often being drawn to elegant ivory drapes by Jani-Khosla and Anamika Khanna, though pop-hued saris by designers like Arpita Mehta also made an appearance. 2013 saw Padukone develop a particular penchant for Sabyasachi Mukherjee's elaborate creations, replete with his signature old-world charm. And it's a sartorial partnership that continues till date. An embellished floor-length anarkali for IIFA 2014, cape sari for the Happy New Year music launch, sequinned red and gold sari for IIFA 2015, ivory sharara set for the Bajirao Mastani poster launch, floral silk sari at Lakmé Fashion Week, and a lehenga, bustier and cape set for IIFA 2016 are some of her most standout Sabysachi looks. Most recently, the sworn Sabysachi patron has been seen in a hand-painted floral sari and floor-length pallu from his Udaipur collection, as well as a tissue sari from the designer's Baroda collection. What strikes you most about Padukone's traditional looks is her affinity for timeless, fail-safe ensembles. That's not to say she completely steers clear of experimenting; instead, she does so within reasonable limit. You're most likely to find the style maven in fuss-free Indian silhouettes in a monochrome colour palette—with ivory and beige coming out as winners. What you can also pick up from her is the key to finishing off a traditional look. Let a heavily-embellished outfit take due centre stage by pulling your hair back, keeping the make-up minimal, and adding only one piece of statement jewellery. column1: Priyanka Chopra on when she starred in a skin-lightening cream commercial
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Our September 2017 cover girl talks about leaving India, accepting herself and playing a villain on-screen It is 2.09 pm, and I am running through New York City's La Guardia Airport with a suitcase on my head. An exit sign glows in the distance, and I hurdle children to get to it, whispering, Priyanka Chopra, Priyanka Chopra, like a path-clearing mantra. I have 51 minutes to get to Chopra's Manhattan apartment, and it isn't looking good. Say “Priyanka Chopra” to the average American woman and you might get an ode to her endorsement-worthy hair, a take on what makes her so compulsively watchable as agent Alex Parrish in Quantico, or speculation about whom she is dating. Say her name to the average Indian American woman, like me, and you will get a proud earful about why “our girls” are so beautiful, which of her more than 50 Hindi movies is best, and what her presence as the first Indian lead on a major US network show means for our future. All of which is to say, Chopra is already causing quite a commotion. And now, after her US film debut as villain Victoria Leeds in the action comedy Baywatch, she's bringing some much-needed diversity to Hollywood. She's also starring in A Kid Like Jake alongside Jim Parsons and Claire Danes, and will be producing a sitcom based on the life of Madhuri Dixit. This is a particularly interesting moment for an immigrant to be fronting a TV show and appearing in a quintessentially American movie, a fact not lost on Chopra, who understands how essential seeing a face like hers can be for the millions of Americans who don't fit the blond-haired, blue-eyed Californian ideal. “Kids from all over—not just Indians—come talk to me,” she says. “I met this Dominican girl the other day who said, ‘Everyone tells me that I look like you.' She gave me a hug, and said, ‘You gave me the strength to stand up onstage and give a presentation in school on where I came from.'” My inner teenage girl quakes a little when I hear this story. As someone who grew up seeing almost no one who looked like me on TV, I can't help but feel relieved for the legions of girls and women coming up with Chopra in the mainstream. And it occurs to me, as I cut the taxi line and yell, “Meeting with Priyanka Chopra!” to my South Asian driver (who yells, “Meeting with Priyanka Chopra!” back to me before peeling out), that in some way I have been waiting to see her my whole life. Half an hour later, I'm breathless, sweaty, a little dizzy—but on time—as Chopra walks across her living room toward me, smiling. “Come, come,” she says, pulling me into an embrace that makes all of it worth it. “We're huggers here.” MIRA JACOB: One thing first: You didn't wear the iconic red swimsuit. PRIYANKA CHOPRA: I didn't have to, because I was the antagonist. MJ: Were you sad not to wear it? PC: I'm so glad I didn't have to eat one olive and one, like, almond! No. MJ: How was it playing the villain? PC: I take over the beach. I open up a club. I'm this big-shot billionaire chick who plays hardball in a man's world. And what I love about Victoria [Leeds] is that she's not baselessly evil. She thinks she's just driven. She had the business acumen, but her family business went to her brother, because he was a boy. So she has a point to prove. There's this amazing line in the [script]: Zac [Efron] says, “You're such a bitch!” And I'm like, “If I were a man, you'd call me driven.” MJ: I love the bitch boss in movies. Was it fun to play? PC: Yeah. Victoria goes into an evil territory; not every driven woman is evil. [But] ambition is a word associated with women negatively. “She's too ambitious.” Why is that bad? MJ: You've said your parents treated you and your brother pretty equally. PC: My parents were really progressive. My dad was a surgeon in the Indian Army. My mom is a double MD; she's an ENT/ob-gyn. Go figure. Way to set your kids up for failure, you know? [Laughs] MJ: Overachievers! And you moved to America to live with your aunt at age 12, right? How did that come about? PC: My mom, my brother and I came for summer vacation to be with my aunt and my cousins. I went with my cousin to her school, and it was fascinating. Nobody wore uniforms. You had lockers. What my cousin was studying was really easy. I was like, “Okay, I don't even have to study, and I would get As.” So I had this devious plan in my head. I sat with my mom, and said, “I want to go to school here. Mausi's okay with it.” I shuttled between my aunt and uncle. I lived in Iowa, then New York, Indianapolis and Boston. MJ: Was it a shock to leave India? PC: A huge shock the first year, but I'm adaptable. In India, my dad was in the army, and we'd move every two years. He said, “Every new city, you can decide who you want to be. If you were not good at debate in one school, you can be a dancer in the next one.” MJ: It was like you were auditioning for a new life. So why did you go back to India [in 11th grade]? PC: There was this girl who was a major bully. I think she didn't like me because her boyfriend liked me, or some high-school dynamic. She made my life hell. She used to call me names and would push me against the locker. High school's hard for everybody, and then there's this woman. I asked my mom, “What do you think about me coming back?” She flew down and picked me up. MJ: Did you always get a lot of attention [for your looks]? PC: After 15. MJ: Did you welcome it? PC: Oh, it was great for my ego. Before 15, I had a lot of self-esteem issues. I was very conscious of the colour of my skin. I was very conscious of being, like, a super-gawky, skinny teenager. MJ: You were conscious of your skin colour here, or in India? PC: India, because there you're prettier if you're fairer. MJ: But you're not considered fair? PC: No, dude. I'm, like, dusky. MJ: I'm several shades darker than you, so to me, you're fair. What feelings go with the label “dusky”? PC: A lot of girls with a darker skin hear things like, “Oh, poor thing, she's dark.” In India they advertise skin-lightening creams: “Your skin's gonna get lighter in a week.” I used it [when I was very young]. Then when I was an actor, around my early twenties, I did a commercial for a skin-lightening cream. I was playing that girl with insecurities. And when I saw it, I was like, “Oh shit. What did I do?” I started talking about being proud of the way I looked. I actually like my skin tone. column1: Athiya Shetty’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Elegant to a T View Gallery 70 Photos Athiya Shetty style evolution Second-generation actor Athiya Shetty, daughter of Suniel and Mana Shetty, has had an undeniable patina of pedigreed elegance ever since she stepped foot in the film industry. Shetty made her debut opposite Sooraj Pancholi with Hero in 2015. While she won the Filmfare debut award for her performance, the film received mixed reviews. Her next release—Mubarakan—only came this year. Though 24-year-old Shetty is only two films old, she is already a bonafide style star. Her statuesque frame makes her the ideal model for the latest trends, and her sensibility is poised beyond her years (and no, that's not code for boring). Vogue US called her an It-girl in a recent article on her style, and went on to say, “Shetty has emerged as a fashion star. And she's just as adept at generating buzz with her casual off-duty style as she is on the red carpet.” Considering she can pull off Elie Saab and Topshop with equal (effortless) ease, there's no refuting her sartorial cred. Sartorial debut Shetty chose a Neha Taneja full-skirted midi dress with a floral obi belt for her maiden appearance at Hero's trailer launch. A ruffled yellow Gauri & Nainika gown complemented with berry lips soon followed at Vogue's Beauty Awards. Both these early appearances set the tone—classic with a youthful twist is what you could expect for this debutante's repertoire. Her succeeding ensembles exemplified this signature. Maxi and midi dresses (riding hemlines are clearly not her jam), often with ethnic undertones, by designers like Label Ritu Kumar, Vrisa, and Payal Pratap quickly emerged as a favourite, as did crop tops often worn with palazzos, culottes and midi skirts. Shetty was always inclined towards peppering her style with homegrown touches. So separates by Indian designers ranging from Dev R Nil and Armaan Aiman to Rutu Neeva and Swati Vijaivargie were worn in abundance. Lehengas, particularly in ivory, have been a traditional wear favourite with Shetty. Designs by Sanjay Garg, Anita Dongre, Rohit Bal, Anju Modi, Monisha Jaising, and Vikram Phadnis, among others, won her favour, and she was seen in unconventional blouses from time to time, to elevate the overall impact. It became clear that Shetty's preference was for comfortable, and not overtly tailored, looks. Jeans were a clear winner when it came to her off-duty style, mostly worn with casual tees or sweatshirts. But don't write it off as basic as it sounds—Kenzo and Rodarte were her choices for the latter. And as an athleisure enthusiast, sneakers, backpacks, and bomber jackets were often part of the mix. But when she did yearn for some structure, pantsuits by Shehlaa, Kanika Goyal, and AM:PM did her bidding. Shetty's red carpet game was mostly princess-like with gowns by Elie Saab, Shriya Som and Monique Lhuillier. But she did experiment with a fierce Amanda Wakeley semi-sheer gown and Philipp Plein studded number with a waist cutout. The pastel Rayane Bacha cape jumpsuit Shetty wore for IIFA in 2016 was another unexpected look. Tracing the year thus far Come 2017, Shetty's has turned to a cleaner palette that champions monochrome tones—be it by way of striped separates or polka dotted pantsuits. Adding more crispness to her wardrobe are trusty white shirts that she has been wearing tied-up with embroidered Farah Sanjana cropped jeans or tucked-in with textured ankle-skimming skirts. Crop tops continue to be a must-have, but this year, Shetty has been all about wearing them as part of coordinated sets with roomy pants and matching duster coats. Her love for denims remains intact too, but they have been punctuated with interesting spins. Think two-toned jogger jeans, layered denim dresses by Masaba or drawstring jeans worn with crop tops. As someone who has always had a keen eye for covetable bags (Shetty was carrying the Céline luggage tote and Gucci's Soho leather disco bag long before they became ubiquitous), her latest love is her Bao Bao Issey Miyaki tote. column1: The best bags to pair with your Indian ethnic wear
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Arm candy alert View Gallery 20 Photos The best bags to pair with your Indian wear Whether you're planning ahead for Diwali and wedding season or are trying to sail through ongoing festivities in your traditional best, your ethnic wardrobe is probably demanding all your attention at the moment. And while you're scouring the stores for sharara and lehenga sets or meeting your jeweller to order a pair of statement chandbaalis, don't forget to invest in the right bags to complement your traditional wear either. As an accessory that can make or break your look, form and functionality should be of equal importance when choosing your festive season bags. Box clutches are a popular choice for Indian wear, be it saris, lehengas or cape sets. But pay attention to its size—you may not need to pack the kitchen sink, but a bag that can accommodate a few key essentials (compact, gloss, keys, cardholder) doesn't hurt. After all, what's the point of a minaudière, bejewelled as it may be, when it can't even fit a lipstick, let alone your smartphone and its portable charger? Hand clutches work best for sit-down dinners or festive functions that require minimal movement. You could even consider personalising one with your initials. But look for add-on chain straps for occasions like the mehndi or sangeet where slinging the bag over your shoulder becomes imperative as the event progresses. Oversized envelope or foldover clutches, casually tucked under your arm, add a sense of effortless insouciance to an otherwise traditional look. They will give your dhoti sari or Lucknowi anarkali a cool girl update, while also leaving your hands free to text your bestie about what the other engagement attendees are wearing. For the lady who wants to go all-out traditional with her choice of handbag, a potli is the way to go. But resist the urge to have a matching one made from the remains of your fabric material. Instead, pick a mirror or pearl work number in a versatile colour so that it's easy to pair with several ensembles. Or dig through your mum's collection and pull out her neutral-hued wristlet. Extra props for one with a striking strap as it renders a bracelet unnecessary. If you're feeling experimental, even fasten a bum pack around your lehenga waist belt, and give the dupatta a skip. So while you may or may not have a date for your cousin's cards party, a covetable bag will ensure that you have the chicest plus-one at every festive occasion irrespective. column1: Payal Singhal champions women empowerment with her latest collaboration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Fashion with a heart View Gallery 16 Photos Payal Singhal is championing the cause of women empowerment with her latest collaboration Occasion wear designer Payal Singhal has been keen to partner with a charitable foundation and do her bit for the community for several years now. But she was looking for a platform that allowed her to get involved beyond mere monetary support. The perfect opportunity presented itself when New York-based Megha Desai, president of the Desai Foundation, attended Singhal's festive trunk show in Mumbai last November. “We have known each other for 14 years, from back when I lived in New York. Megha has always been a patron of the brand. The Payal Singhal X Desai Foundation collaboration took shape when we met last year,” explains the designer over a telephonic call. The Desai Foundation is focused on empowering women and children in India and the US through their various community programmes in a bid to elevate their health and livelihood. Singhal chose to associate with the foundation's sewing vocational program that is centred in Valsad, Gujarat. Two signature PS prints—the anaar and mor print, and the chidiya print (these prints were chosen not only for their popularity, but also because they feature a lotus, which is Desai Foundation's logo too)—have been dedicated to this collaboration that has been nine months in the making. The highlight of the association is the first ever line of bags, totes, and make-up bags in these prints that are being created by the women associated with the Desai Foundation's sewing program. “We (Singhal, Desai, and Monica Dogra, who is the face of the collaboration) travelled to the vocational centre in Valsad to brief the women about the project, explain how it would benefit them, as well as conduct lessons in quality control. Megha has flown down a seamstress from America to train them in superior finishing, as these products will be sold internationally.” Other products from Singhal's main lines featuring these two prints such as Indian occasion wear, kids wear, stationery, as well as a newly introduced men's line are also part of the collaboration's roster. A part of the proceeds from the sale of these products from any of their retail points across the world will go towards the foundation. The income from producing the bags will be directed towards the members of the vocational program. “The Payal Singhal X Desai Foundation association is very close to my heart. I've been yearning to create an entity that not only provides women employment and financial independence, but also gives them sense of purpose and adds value to their lives. This is the first step in that direction,” Singhal signs off. The Payal Singhal X Desai Foundation products launch on September 1, 2017 with a preview at the St Regis Mumbai from 11am to 7pm. They will also be available on Payalsinghal.com Fashion Culture & Living Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: First look inside Arket: H&M’s new sister brand everyone is talking about
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Insider eye The time is now. Arket, the newest store to come from the H&M stable, is opening its doors for the first time on London's Regent Street this week - and the wait has been worth it. Finding its aesthetic niche somewhere in between the clean cuts of Cos and the more insouciant prints and silhouettes of & Other Stories, Arket successfully stands apart from its sister brands. No more so than because of its lifestyle and kidswear categories and café offering - a close rival to the clothes for our attention when we had a preview earlier this week (the homewares are French-market-meets-stripped-back-Scandi chic; the mini Arket edit is irresistible; and the coffee is delicious). It has also achieved independence in the atmosphere of its first bricks-and-mortar home. True to its name, which translates from Swedish into "piece of paper", the store design is minimal and fuss-free - industrial even - letting the clothes and the concept take the spotlight with mini explanatory installations informing customers about the bespoke yarn creations and dying techniques adding substance to the style. And what of the style? The timeless and relaxed pieces we saw back at the first press preview in June have been expanded on, creating an extensive edit that particularly specialises in stripes, sweaters and swimwear - not to mention shirting and suiting. It's a welcome addition to the British high-street which is increasingly seducing its shoppers with Scandi style. column1: Sophie Choudry’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion True to her taste View Gallery 83 Photos Sophie Choudry’s complete style evolution Actor, singer, and erstwhile VJ, UK-born Sophie Choudry crooned her way into the music industry in 2000 as a pop singer with all-girl band Sansara, but went solo the very next year. Her stint as a VJ for MTV added to her popularity, as did the chart-toppers she continued to release year after year, albums that were a mix of remixed classics and original numbers. The multilinguist can also sing in French, apart from Hindi and English. The multi-hyphenated entertainer added acting to her job description when she appeared in Pyaar Ke Side Effects in 2006. Ever since, she has been seen in movies like Ishkq in Paris and Once Upon a Time in Mumbai Dobaara. Vogue tracks her style evolution from her first years to now. Style files Choudry has become synonymous with a polished, feminine-meets-urban style sensibility, and it's one she has been true to over the past many years. She found her sartorial comfort zone early on, and continued to experiment, but within tried-and-tested boundaries, ever since. We're yet to see her ‘shake things up', so to speak, but nor are we complaining about it. Choudry has veered towards dresses in a variety of silhouettes from the very start—be it wrap dresses, cowl neck numbers, sheaths, skater, shift dresses or fitted minis. She went through a phase of one-shoulder and strapless styles, which has now evolved into off-shoulder ensembles. Monochrome and solid colours have been definite go-tos for the songstress, and whenever she does sport a print, it is often of the statement, and not subdued, variety. Choudry developed a penchant for lace early on, the love affair still continues in the form of dresses, tops, and blazers. Evolution Not your typical jeans-and-tee girl-next-door, Choudry is more likely to be seen in tailored trousers or culottes with a smart top (even better if it's lace), especially back in the day. Though she has warmed up to denims of late, giving her nod to its laidback charm mostly when travelling. And given her love for monotones, she prefers to stick to similar-coloured pairings. Think Canadian tuxedos, matching blue tops or white-on-white. Crop tops made their way into Choudry's wardrobe around 2015, and she chose to largely wear these with pencil and skater skirts. Her love for crisp, well-turned-out looks also saw her add pantsuits, preferably worn with open button jackets and bustiers, to her repertoire. It's a well-documented fact that Choudry is an unrelenting Manish Malhotra patron, a designer with whom she enjoys a close friendship as well. Though she does wear the occasional SVA or Sukriti & Aakriti outfit, you'll be hard-pressed to find her in traditional wear that's not Malhotra more often than not. From cold shoulder blouses and lehenga sets to floor-length anarkalis by the designers, she is a poster girl for his glamorous designs. This, though, is a clear shift from the more blingy Indian wear that she favoured earlier. When it comes to western wear, you'll always see Choudry wearing the coolest international labels—think Self-Portrait, Whistles, Sandro, Pinko, and Kendall & Kylie among others. Wardrobe staples While Choudry has no qualms about playing favourites when it comes to the silhouettes and styles that flatter her best, the one department where she is always embracing the new is her handbags. Find us an It-bag, and we'll find you Choudry flaunting it. From Bottega Veneta Knots and Alexander McQueen's Knucklebox to Valentino and Stella McCartney studded clutches more recently, she has always nursed a weakness for the most stylish bags on the block. If you follow her on Instagram, you'll know that her personalised Goyard tote is her arm candy of the season. Considering that this lady takes her final touches seriously, an enviable collection of footwear is a given. Peep-toes, pumps and strappy heels by Jimmy Choo, Gianvito Rossi and Christian Louboutin are how she prefers to put her best foot forward. column1: 20 pieces of formal wear to help you build your work wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Power dressing done right View Gallery 20 Photos These are the formals you need in your closet As you progress in your professional career, dressing right for the job becomes more and more important. Not only are you setting an example for your juniors, trying to scale the ranks but also trying to stand out amongst your contemporaries. And when it comes to your wardrobe, there is no substitute for formals that will enhance your personality in the workspace. Given the expected decorum in a formal environment, your work wardrobe is limited to formal blouses, skirts, blazers, kurtas and saris. More often than not, there is no room for denim and relaxed fabrics like jersey. To elevate your office wardrobe, accessories are key. Invest in quality handbags and shoes that will last long. Play with colours and fabric textures where you can't with silhouette and form. Avoid sheer fabrics, laces and embellishment. Stock your wardrobe with soft tailoring, which stays in the formal category of clothing but also offers garments that are not too restrictive to wear all day long. Even though knee lengths are permitted at most workplaces, midi lengths have a more elegant touch to them and are also in trend, so opt for styles that are between calf and ankle length. Keep busy patterns to a minimal; instead, look for stripes, checks. And if you must wear prints, then invest in abstract ones to keep your work look in place. Maintain a colour palette of neutrals and somber deep hues that make for envy-inspiring power dressing. Scroll through our edit of the sharpest formals to invest in right now. column1: How to look stylish when pregnant
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A pregnant Vogue editor's guide Vogue fashion features director Sarah Harris is in the third trimester of her pregnancy - but she's not going to start wearing mumsy empire line maternity wear any time soon. Here, she reveals her tips for dressing a bump without compromising on personal style. Maternity wear. Yuck. I don't think there has ever been a smugger category of clothing. Even the terminology of it repels me. At eight months pregnant, I haven't bought a stitch of it. And I don't intend to. I gave it a shot. I'll admit it was a quick-fire kind of a shot, because I inherently knew that it wouldn't end in success. Desperate for something inexpensive to wear during the recent heatwave – nothing radical, a simple black cotton T-shirt dress was on my agenda – I wandered into the maternity department of a high-street chain and was faced with a disappointing selection of mumsy empire line dresses in polyester and bump-emphasizing frilled peplum tops in another synthetic mix. (Yes, I always look at the composition labels, who wants to wear polyester in 34 degrees?) Composition aside, why do brands think that suddenly, because you happen to be pregnant, your sense of style leaves you completely and utterly? I couldn't get out of there quick enough, hotfooting it over to Selfridges where I bought a Céline dress instead. Roomy enough to conceal a bump with a pleasing stripe of acid yellow, it was a purchase that was akin to paracetamol. I always buy clothes with longevity in mind. The idea of buying something for a three to six-month window feels completely alien to me, hence the aforementioned Céline dress, which I saw on the mannequin and knew there and then that I had to have it. Long-sleeved, sheer, to the floor, black, with a pale neon yellow shoulder, I bought it one size up – I always think Céline looks best a little oversized, and it meant it fit over my bump. I'll get it taken in at a later date if necessary. Now, nearing the end of my third trimester, I've got away with wearing the same Paige jeans I always wear, with the addition of the elastic band trick looped through the button hole to offer a few inches of extension. I've always favoured mannish shirts and so my current stock still fit me. Meanwhile my Catherine Quin ‘Neutra' dress – a black, sheer, long-sleeved, button-through silk maxi, which is an annual summer holiday favourite – has been a lifesaver for the office, layered over a slip. In fact my only ‘pregnancy' purchase has been three pairs of non-maternity but roomy Joseph trousers, all with a sporty drawstring waist: a black silk pair with elasticated ankles, a crease front white cotton pair, and a black tailored tracksuit style. I wear them all with crew neck t-shirts or shirts and my black Givenchy longline tuxedo blazer. N.B. These are the kind of trousers I would buy anyway, regardless of being pregnant, and, because I bought them in my usual size (they sit low on the hips – so below the bump) they're something I will wear afterwards, too. Likewise, a trio of Raquel Allegra's midi-length T-shirt dresses in softest, most comfortable stretch jersey or tie-dye are one size fits all; and a blue and white striped cotton/linen midi length kaftan by Three Graces London is great for now and most likely every summer for the rest of my life. Accessories also help boost things along, earrings specifically. Large gold hoops by Spinelli instantly dress up something informal, and Berenford sunglasses are a newfound favourite. Why splash out on something you'll never wear again, when you can just gently extend your wardrobe? Given that celebrating Ganesh Chaturthi was started during the British rule with an agenda of bringing together masses, the nature of the festivities heavily features social visits. Whether you celebrate the festival at home or not—chances are high that you have to step out to partake in the festivities. Ganesh Chaturthi is taken seriously by those who host it—so it's important you don't show up underdressed for the occasion. Whether it's a silk sharara or a floor-grazing anarkali, make an effort when you go out. If you are hosting, you can extend your wardrobe to include lightly embellished lehengas and capes. column1: How to wear your tracksuit to office and everywhere else
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion 5 ways to elevate athleisure View Gallery 5 Photos 5 Ways to Elevate Your Tracksuit for the Office—And Everywhere Else If you've been sleeping on the tracksuit trend, rest assured there's still plenty of time to try it out—in fact, it might just be here for the long haul. Consider the evidence: The '90s and early '00s are trending everywhere you look; Vetements's track and athleisure pieces are still flying off the shelves (and inspiring copycats); and Juicy Couture's new creative director, Jamie Mizrahi, is already making twisted track skirts and jackets for influential dressers like Katy Perry and Sasha Lane. Valentino even had track suits (and track dresses) in its Resort 2018 show. The tracksuit is so embedded in the current zeitgeist, in fact, that it's easy to forget its divisive, cheap-chic beginnings. Now, it's simply a chill alternative to a T-shirt and jeans—but can you wear it to work? It goes against conventional wisdom, but mixed with the right sleek, architectural (read: nonsporty) pieces in your wardrobe, we think the answer is yes. First, skip the head-to-toe look—that might be a little too chill for 9 to 5—and mix different colours, patterns, and textures instead. For instance, a black track jacket would tone down bubblegum-pink stretch pants, while velvet trousers and calf-hair sandals would upgrade the basic Adidas zip-up. And while there's a time and place for tracksuits with sneakers, it's safe to say that the office isn't it; swap out Vans for a pair of sensible block heels. Above, see more ways to elevate the tracksuit for the office—or just about everywhere else. This article originally appeared on Vogue.com Beauty Culture & Living Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Malaika Arora’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Why we never tire of her View Gallery 94 Photos Style evolution of Malaika Arora Malaika Arora at the age of 43 still looks as she did at the start of her career—there is something to be said about the age-defying beauty. The VJ-turned-actor has had one of the most varied careers among Bollywood stars. Arora was big on television scene when she hosted series like Love Line and Style Check on MTV. No '90s kid will forget Arora from the popular music video ‘Gur Naalo Ishq Mitha'. She made her debut in films with the hit song ‘Chaiyaa Chaiyaa' from the move Dil Se (1998) opposite Shah Rukh Khan. After which, Arora has been spotted in films like Kaante (2002), Kaal (2005), Om Shanti Om (2007), Housefull (2010), Dabangg (2010), Housefull 2 (2012), Happy New Year (2014) and Dolly Ki Doli (2015). The star also one of the three women behind the successful e-commerce platform The Label Life with Bipasha Basu and Sussanne Khan. Always staying true to flattering sartorial choices, Arora sense of style has gone from mass appeal to a more curated one. Style files Arora's hourglass figure looks best in body hugging silhouettes and back in 2010, her style was all about that. From Grecian draped gowns to sheer to draped minidresses, the star was spotted in several party-ready ensembles nearly a decade ago. Her choices only got bolder as time progressed, and she was seen in sheer numbers, plunging necklines and more saturated hues. Not one to resist a flattering lehenga or a sari, whenever the actor stepped out in Indian ethnic, it was always about over-the-top glamour. On the whole, Arora likes her monotone—whether it was a trusty black jumpsuit, a white part dress or a gown. She is also known to favour a well-fitting pair of white jeans and easy shifts for day wear. Over the last few years, Arora's style repertoire has become more inclusive of experimental choices, whether it's a distressed shirt look for the Justin Bieber concert or a white shirtdress at the airport or several athleisure looks. “I am far more experimental compared to what I used to be and I give complete credit to my stylist Maneka Harisinghani who I have been working with for the last couple of years. If it were left to me I wouldn't have tried different things but I am very open to her ideas,” said Arora in a recent interview with Vogue India. Evolution Malaika Arora's breaking away from the girl-in-a-tight-dress mould was the most pivotal moment in the evolution of her style. The star has come a long way from wearing form fitting styles to more relaxed and trendier ones. “Earlier I used to be very impulsive and buy the same pair of shoes in different colours and stuff like that but not anymore. I am pretty organised when it comes to shopping, I know exactly what I want buy,” the star tells us. “Personally, I think I know my body type and what looks good on me so if I think something looks good one me, I just go with it,” she says. Currently Arora is contemplating going with a seriously short haircut, and we can't wait to see what it might look like. column1: Where to find Deepika Padukone-approved jewellery in Bandra, Mumbai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Isharya is opening the doors to its first-ever retail studio View Gallery 15 Photos Where to find Deepika Padukone approved jewellery in Bandra, Mumbai Ask co-founders Gauri and Radhika Tandon what inspired them to finally set down roots, and pat comes the reply; “After years of sitting next to amazing brands at iconic stores worldwide, it's great to have a dedicated space to showcase Isharya exclusively,” explains Gauri. International architect Bill Bensley was roped in to ensure that every inch of the jewellery studio is stamped with their distinct aesthetic, from the marble flooring that's been inlaid with brass detailing in the form of druzy-cut agate semi-precious stones to the wall mirrors that employ hand-cut polki—another Isharya staple. “The way the displays have been styled, it's almost like an installation paying tribute to elements that have been celebrated in our designs over the years,” confesses Gauri while Radhika chimes in, “It was in our family home in Bandra where Isharya's story began, so it made sense for our first studio to be housed here.” You'd think that the label packs in the perfect double whammy with its thriving e-commerce business and the precious real estate that it occupies at international retailers, including Bloomingdale's and Harvey Nichols. But Radhika insists that neither digital nor traditional retail stores can survive without the other, “With the growing numbers on our e-commerce site, we felt that having a brick-and-mortar presence of our own was a necessary step as it allows for the touch-and-feel experience.” If their new milestone wasn't enough, the Tandons are sweetening the deal by launching their new Bombay Deco collection that packs in rose gold plating, a surefire crowd-puller. “You can expect chokers, fun multi-ring sets, glamorous cuffs and decadent earrings with structural designs and old-world opulence reminiscent of the Jazz Era of Bombay,” promises Gauri. Time to make some space in our jewellery kits, yes? Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This pop-up in Kolkata will bring together the best of fashion and homeware
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Commun India’s first ever edition View Gallery 13 Photos Are you attending this talked about pop-up in Kolkata? Kolkata natives find it hard to get Calcutta out of their colloquial. Stylist and creative director Nikhil Mansata is one such ex-resident of the culturally rich capital of West Bengal. Despite Kolkata's deep roots in aesthetics, unfortunately, the residents of the city don't experience much of what happens in the mainland or globally, without travelling. Mansata will be curating a three-day pop-up to highlight some of the best designer fashion and homeware from the country. “These are my personal favourites that I have put together for the first edition of Commun India. The idea is to showcase the new Indian aesthetic and create access to these beautiful things where there isn't,” he says. Mansata's mother, Anita Mansata is a interior designer and growing under her influence made the creative director appreciate the ability of homeware in lighting up spaces. “I think we need to highlight what's happening the homeware space today, it's equally as important,” he says. Commun India's first edition is bound to pleased seasoned travellers and curators, and the selection at the pop-up will offer fashion from labels like Rajesh Pratap Singh, Péro, international labels like Valentino and Balenciaga by Le Mill, homeware and accessories by Bandit Queen, Ranjit Ahuja, Cocoon Fine Rugs, Design Temple, Claymen, Velvet Ribbon and furniture by Anita Mansata. Mansata hopes to extend the pop-up to other cities within the country and internationally. Commun India Edition 01 will take place at The Galaxy, Park Street, Kolkata, between August 22-24. column1: Highlights from the final day of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you need to know View Gallery 16 Photos What happened at the final day of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017 Did the incessant rain leave you stranded at home? Here's what you missed at the final day of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017. Arpita Mehta Who says florals aren't for fall? This season, Arpita Mehta's collection, 'Midnight Muse', came into full bloom with the lotus flower as its central motif. Mehta sent out a lineup of sensuous, east-meets-west separates—lehenga-skirt hybrids, one-shoulder blouses and structured, floor-skimming jackets—which showcased the designer's ability to seamlessly merge the traditional with the contemporary. Navy, forest green and magenta were on Mehta's lush colour palette. Kriti Sanon turned showstopper in an ornate blue lehenga. Amoh by Jade Designer duo Monica Shah and Karishma Swali's had a surprise (or two) in store for their guests. The show began on a musical note with a performance by Ananya Birla, as models discretely seated in the audience made their way to the ramp. Titled 'Aiyana', the collection featured delicately embellished, fuss-free yet statement separates, which we're promptly adding to our festive wardrobes. On the shade card were hues that varied from jewel-toned to vintage. Divya Reddy The Hyderabad-based designer, who made her Lakmé Fashion Week debut in 2015, presented Sage, a collection with a strong focus on contemporary bridal wear. While rich floral embroidery found the perfect backdrop in striking shades of green and pink, Reddy opted for ruffles and exaggerated sleeves to add drama to traditional silhouettes. In an embellished, floor-length jacket, Tapsee Panu played showstopper for the designer. Manish Malhotra For the closing of Lakmé Fashion week, Manish Malhotra gave us just the after party we were looking for. Delivered on a glass runway, the collection, 'Tales of Indulgence', came packed with everything from Studio 54-worthy separates to heavily-embellished gowns guaranteed to find a following in red carpet regulars. Think dresses with sky-high slits and feather-laden skirts. To match his inherently glamorous line for women, the designer also showcased a collection of slick bespoke menswear. The show came to a close with Aditya Roy Kapur taking the ramp, clad in a black suit followed by Jacqueline Fernandez in a sweeping, sheer number.       Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Jacqueline Fernandez closes Manish Malhotra’s show at Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion This is why she was scared before taking the runway Manish Malhotra, besides being a veteran couturier, is a Bollywood favourite. This means that his shows are packed with celebrities, and we not just talking about the showstoppers. Karisma Kapoor, Jhanvi and Khushi Kapoor, Sridevi, Amrita Arora, Sushant Singh Rajput, Karan Johar and more A-listers walked into the show area in glittering cocktail dresses and suits—serving as a teaser for the kind of clothes that we were about to witness. When the designer announced his closing show for Lakmé Fashion Week, he mentioned that this season would be a stark departure from the Indian ethnic aesthetic he is best known for. For winter/festive 2017, he chose to showcase cocktail dresses and bespoke suits; an uncharted territory for the designer. However staying true to his love for all things glamorous, Malhotra swung through with ease. As seen on his celebrity clientele, there's no reason this new vision won't be applauded with just as much enthusiasm as any other Manish Malhotra creation. 'Tales of Indulgence' was about a bolder Manish Malhotra girl who clearly is the life of a party. Fringes, fur, feathers, beading, velvet, sheer panels—Malhotra did not hold back on the elements that elevate a simple dress to red carpet status. Jacqueline Fernandez and Aditya Roy Kapur walked the runway for the designer. Fernandez wore a sheer embroidered gown and despite her confidence, expressed nerves before getting on to the runway. column1: Day 4 at Lakmé Fashion Week: Ranveer Singh at Manish Arora and more
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion An inside look This season, Nachiket Barve finally took the plunge into bridal wear and couldn't have picked a better spot on the schedule than that of the Lakmé Salon Show Stopping Bride. Saiyami Kher played muse for the designer, who drew inspiration from Greek goddesses for his collection. Kher's blouse had ‘Aphrodite' emblazoned on it in Greek and was quite pleased with the ease of movement her look offered. Ujjawal Dubey of Antar-Agni presented ‘Disobedience', a collection of wearable easy separates. Dubey's idea was to create contrasts of lengths, textures and patterns in the same garment to show dual sides of the same piece of clothing. Manish Arora returned to the Lakmé Fashion Week schedule after nearly six years of being away and after 10 years of showing in Paris. The show was set in Palladium Mall, Mumbai, and shoppers stood by to watch the spectacle. Adding to the double din of shoppers and show attendees were fans of Ranveer Singh, who were all too excited to see the star in the front row. Models descended from the escalators wearing Arora's latest ‘Cosmic Love' collection, which was outrageously covered in sparkle and colour in true Manish Arora fashion. It isn't fashion week until the grand logistics of one show creates stories for seasons to come, and Arora's grand showcase was one of them. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights from Day 4 of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Miss no detail View Gallery 20 Photos Highlights from Day 4 of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017 Emerging or established, designers brought their A-game to day 4 of Lakmé Fashion Week. Couldn't make it? Here's everything you need to know. SVA by Sonam and Paras Modi This season, the designers whose creations have swiftly found a spot in nearly every bride's trousseau, unveiled their collection 'Naseem Bagh', for which they turned to Kashmir's magical Chinar leaves for inspiration. Models gracefully took the ramp in ornate, traditional separates featuring a varied colour story ranging from autumnal to midnight hues. Finishing touches came in the form of the label's signature, intricate embroidery and the duo's festive take on a corset. Vaani Kapoor brought the show to a dramatic close in a fiery crimson lehenga. Antar-Agni by Ujjwal Dubey It's hard to believe that Ujjwal Dubey—the Delhi-based designer who has the mastered the sartorial mix of statement and sombre like no other—once wanted to be an engineer. For autumn, the International Woolmark Prize finalist presented another collection with wearability at its core. Titled disobedience, the line packed with architectural yet fuss-free separates played with contrasts (light and heavy, texture and sheen, structure and flow). While black and white were still the designer's hero hues, Dubey also experimented with soft shades like dusty pink. Lakmé Salon Showstopping Bride by Nachiket Barve He has had the fashion world's attention since his debut show as a Gen Next designer, so when Nachiket Barve showcases his foray into bridal wear, you can be sure to find the front row dotted with the industry's finest. Drawing from the legends and qualities of Greek goddesses (Aphrodite, Gaia, Artemis, Athena and Hera), Barve sent out his fierce yet feminine collection, 'Theia', which juxtaposed soft detailing with a toughness and sheen reminiscent of warrior armours. Grecian detailing such as capes, panelled skirts and drapes played up the drama on traditional separates in a colour palette of deep blue, ivory and statement red. Saiyami Kher turned showstopper for the designer in a cascading lehenga. Huemn Project  Did you know that women wear garments only an average of seven times before they throw it away? It was on this alarming note that designers Pranav Mishra and Shyma Shetty began their chill-inducing presentation. For the 10 looks on display, the duo took waste from seven designers and deftly converted them into deconstructed separates. Guests left the room reminded that mindful consumption is key to a future we all want to be part of. Manish Arora When it comes to being the centre of attention, no one does it quite like Manish Arora. This season, the designer turned the ground floor of Mumbai's bustling Palladium Mall into a runway for his show. Arora's collection 'Cosmic Love', which celebrates his 10th anniversary on Parisian catwalks and is inspired by the universe, lit up the mall as models made their way down escalators in his signature vibrant separates replete with celestial bodies and tribal patterns. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Showstoppers, style and more View Gallery 12 Photos Highlights from Day 3 of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017 Bollywood loves fashion and if there was any doubt in that department, you should just see the celebrities who turn up for Lakmé Fashion Week. On Day 3 alone we saw Kalki Koechlin at Nikita Mhaisalkar, Chitrangada Singh at Neha Agarwal, Radhika Apte at Sailesh Singhania, Sarah-Jane Dias at Urvashi Joneja, Preity Zinta at Falguni & Shane Peacock, Esha Gupta at Amit Aggarwal and finally Shraddha Kapoor at Rahul Mishra. Ekà's Rina Singh was looking at unfinished works of art, “infinto aesthetic'' as she describes it, and happened to stumble upon the late Indian artist Amrita Sher-Gil. Singh reimagined a wardrobe for her keeping in mind the various stages of her life and travels. It is not the Ekà way to keep up with what is trending and if Singh isn't up to a show, she's rather not make it to the schedule at all. But yesterday's lineup was so compelling we'd like to see the designer work more frequently. There was a worn-in quality to all the clothes that Singh laboriously tries to add to each one of her products, but given the season directive of "winter festive", the Ekà girl had glammed up in her own way. Singh introduced touches of lace and hints of gold ever so gently throughout the collection. In the favoured palette of dusty rose and beiges, there were whites, blacks, pale blues and jade—Singh's research on artist certainly influenced her own work. Falguni & Shane Peacock showcased their collection along with jewellery designer Farah Khan. The lineup of crystal studded gowns was complemented with even more shine by way of the jeweller's work. A cocktail-ready collection worthy of any red carpet, we are sure to be seeing Falguni & Shane Peacock's work at the award shows this year. Preity Zinta walked out in the end in a strapless ballgown that accentuated her figure. Amit Aggarwal's show this season was presented by Monaco Tourism. While looking for inspiration pertaining to Monaco, Aggarwal ended up drawing parallels to inspiration closer to home. His collection ‘Monaco from the Heart of Kashi' mixed visual narratives from the architecture of Monaco and Benarasi saris. Winter-festive at Amit Aggarwal was shinier than usual, but fans of his work will find something to work with despite the felt, velvet, lurex and gold in large doses. Dia Mirza sat front row while Esha Gupta walked for the designer. Rahul Mishra put Reliance's Project Eve to task by challenging them to produce handloom fabric for mass consumption. While there have been several designer initiatives to work with weaving clusters for their work including Mishra himself, the designer's collaboration with a retail giant is a unique one. Mishra went back to his roots of subtle Chanderi weaves producing a ready-to-wear line that's going to be a sure hit this festive season. On the runway, the clothes were paired with some of Mishra's couture pieces. Shraddha Kapoor walked for the designer in an embroidered lehenga. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights from Sustainable Fashion Day, Day 2 at Lakmé Fashion Week 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get behind the scenes View Gallery 29 Photos Highlights from Sustainable Fashion Day, Day 2 at Lakmé Fashion Week 2017 Over the past few seasons, the sustainable fashion day is finding its lucent vocabulary in a space that is devoid of relevant context. The conversation is pertinent due to myriad reasons, including the huge demographic that subsists on handweaving and surface enhancement handicrafts, the continued environmental damage caused by fashion industry, and then the ever-dwindling heritage of handcrafted textiles. As the day meandered to a close, it managed to add meaning to the fashion quotient and nudge it towards a gentle consciousness. The #CraftIsCool show by Paramparik Karigar Paramparik Karigar is an organisation that has, for the past 20 years, scanned the length and breadth of India to discover artisans and gave them a regular configuration of selling their work in a direct weaver to consumer interface. In this show, five master craftsmen were paired with five young designers to create the collection in a synergic, collaborative spirit. The collections showcased in traditional crafts of dabu, bagh, shibori, bandhani and ajrakh were palette cleansing in their minimal sensibility. Matr Bihar Khadi x Kopal New York Because of Nature Australia Praveen Chauhan started Matr to promote the artisanal communities of Bihar, who were losing their craft of khadi weaving, Today, it works with designers and retail brands to develop customised products in an environmentally-responsible initiative. Two of Matr's collaborations showcased garments made from lovingly handspun and hand-loomed yardage. Ethicus The label shared its organic cotton line in its comfortable, eco-friendly and texturally beautiful avatar in a farm-to-fashion presentation in the form of pleasing saris and garments, in an easy-to-wear vibe. Sunita Shankar Sunita Shankar is an authority on the weaves with the stunning ability to infuse effortlessness in the technically complex handloom textiles. This show was a celebration of her design aesthetic that offered looks comprising bandhani, kantha, Benarasi weaves, Chanderi and bagh prints, all of which come from various parts of the country but were presented in ways that adapt easily into our lifestyle. Akaaro The collection used the textile in fine blend of wool, silk, cotton and metal to create separates for the urban woman. Handwoven pleats in saris, festive lehngas were included as a restrained ode to the festive season. Craftmark by AIACA A Craftmark certification is provided by The All India Artisans and Craftworkers Welfare Association to inform the customer of the fair trade and sustained lifestyles of the artisans involved. The NGOs that provide employment and benefits to women artisans from Nabha (Punjab), Dehradun (Uttarakhand) and Sandur (Karnataka) showcased garments in an interactive format, featuring embroidery techniques like phulkari, patchwork and lambadi. ANAVILA Anavila Misra's show, as an apt finale to the Sustainable Fashion Day, was dedicated to the weaving heritage of our land and pushed the brand's boundaries. The colour black was dominant in the collection of a brand known dearly for its soft pastel shades. The blouses infused a sense of freshness to the ubiquitous sari and excited the audience about dabbling with this beloved drape. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Take a look inside Day 2 of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Sustainable fashion never looked this good The second day of Lakmé Fashion Week was dedicated to the cause of conscious fashion and was aptly titled Sustainable Fashion Day. Starting the day off were emerging designers who have collaborated with artisans of Paramparik Karigar to explore their design identity beyond the usual. Each design label was paired off with a master craftsmen to create work that highlighted laborious crafts of India that with a modern identity that can stand up to the test of time. Bheerulal Chippa and Poochki worked on dabu, Mohammed Yousef and Vineet Rahul on bagh, Aranya Naturals Rouka on shibori, Safraz Khatri and Verandah on ajrakh and Shohel Khatri and The Pot Plant worked on bandhani. Gaurav Jai Gupta's label Akaaro explored Benarasi textiles for winter/festive 2017 with his collection ‘Irreverence'. Innovation came by way of blending silks with merino wool and engineering colours of the silk in the warp and weft to transform with movement. The lineup also saw Chanderi and jamdani fabrics. With a mature colour palette and lineup of understated yet impactful ocassion wear, Gupta's collection was one of the most mature ones the designer has presented so far. Anavila Misra's label Anavila has cemented its identity as the go-to label for handwoven linen saris. Typically, favouring neutrals and pastels, Misra stepped away from what comes naturally to her to explore the usage of the colour black in her collection titled ‘Blur'. column1: Nimrat Kaur’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Charting her style graph View Gallery 44 Photos The complete style evolution of Nimrat Kaur Nimrat Kaur began her journey with theatre, music videos, and commercials. Her acting debut was a role in the English film One Night with the King (2006) though it was Anurag Kashyap-produced Peddlers that marked her foray into Hindi cinema in 2012. Then came Lunchbox in 2013 that really thrust her into the limelight. The film garnered much acclaim, and Kaur's nuanced performance left no room for doubt about her superior acting chops. Despite the attention, Kaur has been fastidious in her choices that followed—she appeared in the fourth season of American TV series Homeland in 2014, and was then seen in Airlift opposite Akshay Kumar in 2016. The early years Kaur's entry into Bollywood was marked by stints at the Cannes Film Festival, and Kaur was mostly seen favouring traditional garb in the beginning. Saris by designers like Sabyasachi, Manish Malhotra, Shehlaa by Shehla Khan, and Atsu won her favour. When not draped in the nine-yard, Kaur often gravitated towards metallic dresses and gowns with a generous helping of sparkle and sequins for the red carpet. Blazers were a recurring part of her wardrobe—and she teamed them with everything from skirts and printed trousers to dresses. The latter, too, has been a sartorial constant for actor. It's hard to miss Kaur's penchant for dresses. From sheath and skater dresses to princess-like flared numbers, she swore by the ‘when in doubt, wear a dress' dictum, whether it was a movie screening or the red carpet. Tracing the change Nimrat Kaur's multiple international red carpet appearances in 2015 led to a gradual elevation in her style sensibilities; though she continued to retain her erstwhile love for dresses. Midi dresses still ruled the roost for her, but there was an inescapable sprinkle of understated glamour that helped add definite polish to her looks. A glittering black Julien Macdonald dress with sheer neckline and sleeve detailing that Kaur wore for the 2015 BAFTA nominees party particularly stood out. The strapless midi dress emerged as another favourite with her, and Kaur was seen picking ones with structured bodices when donning them for formal events. While several of her fashion choices remained in the tried-and-tested territory, Kaur cannot be accused of playing it safe with her choice of gowns. Be it a Georges Hobeika gown with a keyhole neckline and cape sleeves or a full-sleeved Pankaj & Nidhi creation, she wasn't afraid to shake things up in this department. When not spotted in her trusty dresses, the largely reclusive actor changes it up in maxi skirts, jackets, and trousers. Off shoulder crop tops and cold shoulder dresses are the latest addition to her repertoire. Prints (and lots of it)—floral, geometric, polka dots, and painterly—are Kaur's preferred way to add visual appeal to her ensembles. Her fuss-free aesthetic extends to her Indian wear choices too, and monotone ankle-length anarkali and churidar sets often make the cut for her. column1: All the highlights from Day 1 of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Keep up with the runway View Gallery 20 Photos All the highlights from Day 1 of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017 If you see surprisingly well-dressed people hurriedly walking around at the Palladium Mall or St Regis, sacrificing comfort for great-looking shoes and with battery packs in tow—they are probably on their way to Lakmé Fashion Week's winter/festive 2017 edition that is taking place at the hotel. In case you are wondering what's going on there, we take you inside the fashion week. In keeping with their tradition, Day 1 of Lakmé Fashion Week started off with the Gen Next show, which highlights upcoming talent in the country. Sumiran Kabir Sharma's label Anaam debut collection for LFW spoke about Kolkata's red-light district Songachi. In draped suiting and austere silhouettes, Anaam's army demanded recognition, identity and respect. Shenali Sema and Rimzim Lama's label Untitled Co. focused on treatment of textiles displaying pastel looks in plissé and intricate threadwork. Saaksha Parekh and Kinnari Kamat's label Saaksha & Kinni dedicated their premiere show to the grace of 12th century samurai warrior Tomoe Gozen. The collection featured macro florals in sepia offset with embellishments. Akshat Bansal's label Bloni took inspiration from snow-clad mountains, which he translated in monochrome on garments through engineered hand-dyeing processes and embroidery detail. Deepak Pathak based his collection for his label, Integument, on the lives of fishermen. The lineup of soft greys was subtly enhanced by way of detailed tone-on-tone embroidery. Label Ritu Kumar presented their spring/summer 2018 collection in keeping with international timelines. The lineup saw versions of tropical prints, white lacy day dresses, tulle skirts and colour-blocked garments that were perfect for a holiday wardrobe. Disha Patani walked down the runway for the designer in a white corset dress covered in florals. Masaba Gupta delved into occasion and bridal wear this season with her collection ‘Madagascar'. Nowhere near the heavy lehengas favoured by girls on the wedding day, Gupta's brides are about pre-draped sari hybrids in pop hues with matching bum bags. The colour palette stayed true to the label's kitsch-pop DNA with fuschia, bright greens, blues, black and moving into maroon. It's certain Gupta's bridal is for a younger, cooler audience than the median. The biggest highlight of the day was easily Sanjay Garg's presentation of the Lakmé Absolute Grand Opening for winter/festive 2017. Set against the romantic, newly-revived Royal Opera House, Mumbai, the show was a sight for sore eyes. Garg's collection 'Cloud People' explored themes of cupids, unearthly spirits and symbols of hope through the use of chikankari and signature weaves. To go with the theme of cupids, Garg thought of using a choir to provide the perfect background track for the length of the show. From Kiran Rao to Manish Malhotra, the show was well attended and applauded by the audience. Catch the video highlights here: Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: “Do I need to wear Spanx?” and other shapewear questions, answered
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion No more uncomfortable truths View Gallery 6 Photos Do you need to wear Spanx? Time and again we find ourselves falling for clothes that are more trouble fitting into than they are worth. Enter, Spanx. Shapewear has been a part of women's wardrobes all the way since the time Catherine de' Medici, wife of King Henry II of France, enforced a ban on thick waists in 1550, thus introducing the agony-inducing corset. You can look at shapewear in two ways—the not so positive one is that it reinforces the norm that bodies need to look a certain way to be attractive. You can also look at it as a layer you add on to give your clothes a smooth finish. Given that in the current times, no monarch's spouse can dictate the shape of our bodies, wearing shaping undergarments is purely a matter of choice. Say you were to find yourself wanting to wear a white ribbed bodycon dress minus the panty lines, shapewear would make the outcome seamless. However, before you order one online, here's what you should know about the show behind the no-show. What is Spanx? Spanx, same as Xerox, is actually a popular brand that has now become a catch-all for any kind of shapewear. When you are looking for control fit garments—they are not all made by Spanx. Some of the other popular brands that specialise in control wear are Fashion Forms, Fleur du Mal, Wolford, La Perla, Commando and DMondaine. Understand the limitations of shapewear Just like going on a crash diet two days before a major event is not going to result in a drastic makeover, squeezing yourself into a pair of shapewear tights is not going to make you magically fit into a dress that's not your size. The best option out there is to work on maintaining a healthy and balanced lifestyle. Shapewear is out there to assist you in pulling off tricky outfits without hitches, and nothing else. How to buy the correct size of shapewear Sizing for shapewear follows the same rules as shopping for other clothes. If you wear a medium normally, buy control wear that's also medium. The garment is designed to smoothen and bulges that you may have. Like we said before, it's not going to bring you down a size. Control wear is already high in in lycra and spandex content when it comes to fabric composition—meaning things are going to be snug. Anything smaller than your usual size will cause body mass to bulge where the garment ends resulting in rolls that you tried to avoid in the first place. How to wear shapewear Shapewear comes in different styles—they can be bodysuits, long slips, tights, underwear, waist shapers and so on. The garments are meant to be worn as undergarments, so you don't need to wear an additional layer of clothing inside them. Depending on what your needs are, shapewear can be chosen accordingly. For instance, a pencil skirt might require just a pair of tights underneath while a cocktail gown might need a bodysuit. Be mindful of the fabrics you choose—don't pair lace-finished control garments with lighter fabrics like satin. Try the entire look a couple of times before you wear it on the day of the occasion. How to care for shapewear Since shapewear is used as an intimate; maintain it the same way you would care for your undergarments. Given the high stretch content of the garment, avoid throwing it in the wash spin cycle where it could lose form, or worse, shrink. When should you avoid shapewear Kim Kardashian once famously said, “I always pee all over my Spanx, it's a disaster. They aren't crotchless enough.” Dinner dates ending in sleepovers, long nights of drinking and dancing when you might have to use the bathroom more than just once or any occasion where you want to focus on eating are all times you want to give shapewear a ditch and go with something else that makes you feel confident, sexy and less restrictive. Why you shouldn't feel guilty about wearing shapewear There's too much in the world you feel guilty about already, like spending time on Netflix instead of taking up a hobby or reading work mail at family dinners—cheating a little for the sake of fashion doesn't have to be one of them. column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan on what it’s really like being a working mother
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet the muse and face for AND autumn/winter 2017 View Gallery 2 Photos Kareena Kapoor Khan speaks the truth about being a working mom This is not the first time Kareena Kapoor Khan has been the face of AND—Anita Dongre's high street label that specialises in workwear. But is the first time the star is the muse and face of a clothing label after being a mother. Both the designer and the actor have carved successful paths in their own right while experiencing motherhood. “Whether it was during her pregnancy or after she had her baby, her commitment to work never strayed and that's something we wanted to celebrate,” says Dongre, to whom the choice of the face for AND's autumn/winter 2017 campaign was an obvious one. Nothing Kapoor Khan has undergone hasn't been felt by other women in her position, the actor is the first to accept that. Vogue spoke to the Bollywood legend about what has changed and what hasn't. How would you say the women in your life shaped you as a person? My family comes from the film background. My mother, my sister—they've all inspired me. Are there any pieces from the upcoming AND collection that you would love to wear? For sure, because AND always stands for the working woman. I'm a mother now and I'm working so you know the fact is, I represent the woman of today. The clothes are "to go". You kind of wear them, go to work, you go out for cocktails or you go out to a party—you can still look chic in any of them, the whole idea is that it kind of covers the spectrum. And that's the way I think most of my fans see me as the girl that is casual yet stylish, yet the working woman of today. That, is key and I cater to that—I do. That's why you'll never really see me dressed over-the-top. How is life as a working mother? I think it is amazing. After having a good day at work, I am waiting to see your son home. It's quality over quantity. Some can stay at home all day but the idea is to keep the focus going, whatever it is you are doing at the time. If you like what you do at work it's even better. Acting is my passion and if I go to work, I feel like a more enriched mother. Women multitask the best. What is the kind of support new mothers returning to work need? I think new mothers need love and nurturing. You definitely need support from your husband who is working but you have to balance things. You just have to learn to do things. How has motherhood changed you? It is an amazing experience. There's a part of me and Saif in the world and he is my responsibility and I am going to be showing and teaching him new things. We cannot stress more on the importance of feminism in the world. What is the most important thing you will teach Taimur about respecting women? Taimur is going to grow up with a working mom. My sister, his masi is also a working woman. He has my mother to look up to, my mother-in-law who is still working woman. So, he is going to grow up in that atmosphere and learn to respect women in that sense. He also has a wonderful nanny, again another working woman who looks after him so he will be growing up seeing the power of women from as early as seven months old. You have had a long working relationship with Anita Dongre, why do you think her work is relevant today? Accessibility, wearability—there's a lot of amazing designer wear out there that looks wonderful but takes so long to get in and out of. Her clothes can be worn from work to party and you're still in style without the added fuss. Fashion People Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Kriti Sanon’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Then and now View Gallery 63 Photos Style Evolution: Kriti Sanon The ‘beauty with brains' cliché is not a stretch in the case of Bollywood's current blue-eyed girl, Kriti Sanon. The Delhi native, who studied to be an engineer, couldn't resist the lure of the limelight when modelling assignments happened to come her way. After appearing in ads and walking runways, an acting career, as is the norm du jour for many, was the next natural step. Telugu film 1: Nenokkadine (2014) marked her acting debut, and Sanon forayed into Bollywood with Heropanti opposite Tiger Shroff in the same year, though it was being cast alongside Shahrukh Khan, Kajol and Varun Dhawan in Rohit Shetty's Dilwale in 2015 that really singled her out as one to watch out for. While her last release Raabta did not set the cash register ringing, she's already looking ahead to her next release, Bareilly Ki Barfi, with Aayushmann Khurrana and Rajkumar Rao. The early years Sanon's coming out sartorial party was mostly a barrage of bodycon dresses and minis alongside midriff baring crop tops, cut-outs, and bare backs. With a frame as statuesque and lithe as hers, one can understand the draw to aforementioned silhouettes, but this did not lead to a particularly memorable impact in the style department in the initial years. Prints—be it stripes by Dior, caricatures by QuirkBox or florals by Dhruv Kapoor—were a consistent part of her repertoire as was traditional wear by glam pack favourite Manish Malhotra. Sanon's red carpet game, however, was strong from the very beginning. She stood out for her ability to strike a balance between drama and demure with grace; looking just as effortless in a feminine strapless Gauri & Nainika gown as she did in avant-garde numbers by Amit Aggarwal or Georges Chakra Couture. An evolution of style The actor's off-duty style took on a more sophisticated turn mid-2015, coinciding with the release of Dilwale. The figure-hugging ensembles made way for more nuanced, urban choices—think jackets by Sanchita, shift dresses by Osman, and solid-coloured separates by Payal Khandwala. While dresses continued to be a favoured silhouette, Sanon was also seen embracing pantsuits and trouser sets by designers like Namrata Joshipura, Anand Bhushan and Vikram Phadnis among others. Today, Sanon can safely be slotted as a denimphile. From denim overalls with leather patches, ripped denims and high-waist flared trousers to denim jackets worn with slip dresses and twin sets in the fabric; in denim, Sanon most definitely trusts. Her roster of go-tos has now been widened to include oversized sweatshirts, jumpsuits, anti-fit dresses, maxis, and boho chic minis. The actor is unrelenting in her championing of homegrown designers and has been seen in creations by Kanika Goyal, Lola by Suman B, Chola, Sukriti & Aakriti, Rahul Mishra, Doodlage, Hemant & Nandita, and Péro among others. Sanon wears pret by Indian designers as easily as she does high street pieces by brands like H&M, Zara, Bershka, and Global Desi. Scroll through our slideshow for all her looks through the years.
