column1: Manish Arora talks about his return to Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And the one thing he learnt in Paris View Gallery 13 Photos Manish Arora talks about his return to Lakmé Fashion Week after 10 years Amongst many designers and their firsts on the arduous schedule of Lakmé Fashion Week, is the return of Manish Arora to this runway after six years. The designer's decade in Paris was an illustrious one—from shocking the world with his unique technicolor vision to helming Paco Rabanne. As much of an icon globally as he is known in the homeland for his body of work, Arora's return to Lakmé Fashion Week is a cause of celebration. “Paris inspires you, it accepts you as an individual and in that way Paris has influenced my work,” says the designer on his to the airport as we chant over the phone. “But the most important thing of all is that it teaches is you where to stop. There is a fine line between making a statement and going over the top,” he says. In the case of Arora, whose avant-garde clothing is the kind to stop traffic, restraint was perhaps the most important learning of his experience in the French capital. Of course, restraint is a matter of relativity when talking about Arora. His collection ‘Cosmic Love' boasts of celestial bodies, embellishments, optical illusions, Atzec prints and embellishments. “It's still the Manish Arora girl, but she has grown up now. She hasn't lost her sense of humour but she is mature.” he describes the vibe of the line. “We try to do something new with denim each time, as we have this season too. The collection is detailed, it is more believable,” Arora tells us before rushing off to check in. column1: Inside Nachiket Barve’s debut bridal collection for Lakmé Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Woolmark Prize winner wants you to look and feel like a goddess View Gallery 6 Photos Inside Nachiket Barve’s debut bridal collection for Lakmé Fashion Week Winter/Festive ‘17 Nachiket Barve doesn't do things by half measures. So it stands to reason that his premier venture on the bridal circuit would assume mythical proportions—via the famed Greek goddesses Athena, Aphrodite and Artemis, who hold credit for inspiring his debut festive lineup. His collection, titled 'Theia', will be on display at his show, the Lakmé Salon Show Stopping Bride by Nachiket Barve. What does the Woolmark recruit have in store at the upcoming edition of Lakmé Fashion Week winter/festive 2017? For starters, traditional aari embroidery will be juxtaposed with Greek typography, the revered olive wreath is reimagined with zardosi, and Roman goddess Juno's peacock will serve as a motif on voluminous lehengas. As for the beauty look, Sushma Khan, national creative director - makeup, Lakmé Salon, has this to say: "You can expect to see make-up with holographic highlights and prismatic hues, interrupted and coloured graphic liners, dimensional lips with metallic reflects and more.” In between fittings and the usual chaos that precedes a show, we picked his brain on his grand festive debut. What inspired you to take the label in this new direction? I've spent years working with beautiful techniques and textiles, adapting traditional forms of embellishments for a modern audience. Clients have been consciously asking me why I'm not doing traditional wear, which prodded me to think what sort of festive wear I would want to do. Without a doubt, the Nachiket Barve bride is someone who is confident and individualistic and that's the spirit that I've tried to capture in my new offering, Theia. Some would argue that you've already proven your festive chops with the stunning bridal lehenga that you created for your wife in 2013… [laughs] I've been inundated with requests from people who saw the lehenga I made for my wife. When I decided to finally take the plunge, I was very clear about two things: First, I'm obsessed with making clothes comfortable for women. Yes, there is something for the traditional bride, but there is also something for the bride who wants to get married on the beach and dance the night away. Despite all the embellishments, I've strived to make the garments lightweight and fuss-free. Second, I was adamant that my take on festive wear shouldn't just consume closet space. I don't want my clothes to languish in the back of storage trunks and wardrobes. How would you advise women to get the most out of your festive offering? This collection has been directed at real women. They are the ones I see celebrating and regaling in these clothes, which is why I've strived to maximise the versatility of my creations. Take for instance, the Greek typography blouse which comes with a lehenga. It can be easily worn again with palazzos for a cocktail night later. What can we hope to see on the ramp at Lakmé Fashion Week? When I was trying to imagine what a Nachiket Barve bride would look like, [I focused on] the idea that women want to look, and feel, like a goddess on their wedding day. I looked to Greek and Roman mythology, and tried to reimagine those elements in the festive space. You'll find exquisite threadwork, stacked sequins, appliqué and cutwork. Filigree from old Roman textiles has been interpreted as aari embroidery, while the olive wreath serves as the leitmotif in intricate zardosi. How has your time at the International Woolmark Prize shaped the designer that you are today? When you appear on a global platform, it immediately makes you up your game. Whether it is traditional embroidery or prints, it has to challenge the existing parameters and egg you on to create something that hasn't been done before. The Woolmark Prize really helped me stretch my boundaries as a designer. column1: 30 outfit ideas for Janmashtami puja
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ethnic chic View Gallery 30 Photos 30 outfit ideas for Janmashtami pooja August is a month packed with festivities and it is imperative you dress right for the occasion at hand. Not every festive occasion warrants Indian ethnic outfits that involve pulling all the stops. Pujas like that for Janmashtami are important yet smaller in scale, and need an ensemble that honours tradition but is low key. Given that celebrating Janmashtami is most likely going to be confined to limits of your house, you can settle for an anarkali, kurta or a sari. column1: Bipasha Basu’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Look how far we have come View Gallery 82 Photos Bipasha Basu’s complete style evolution On the issue that launched Vogue in India, Bipasha Basu was one of the six women gracing the cover. Basu started her career as a model back in 1996, and as a natural progression, moved on to movies, winning the Filmfare Award for the Best Debut Actress in 2001 for her work in the thriller Ajnabee. While Basu is best known for her work in Bollywood, she has also starred in Tamil, Telugu and English language films. Some her most well-known movies include Raaz (2002), Mere Yaar Ki Shaadi Hai (2002), Jism (2003), Humko Deewana Kar Kayege (2006), Phir Hera Pheri (2006), Omkara (2006), Bachna Ae Haseeno (2008) and Race 2 (2013), amongst others. Today, she is also one of the three women behind the successful e-commerce platform The Label Life. Style files Basu's style choices are the perfect example of highlighting the popular trends in the decade. In 2012, Basu was a fan of short monochrome dresses that accentuated her body. These varied from ruched dresses to more party ready, embellished styles. In 2014, the star picked longer lengths of skirts and dresses in pop hues. Basu's preferred choice of hairstyle remained the open waves on most occasions. In 2016, Basu tied the knot with actor Karan Singh Grover in a Sabyasachi lehenga. The star picked other ensembles by Anita Dongre, Sukriti & Akriti and Arpita Mehta for various other events. Post her wedding, Basu was spotted on many occasions with Grover, but the most iconic image of the duo is in matching red ensembles for the couple's first Valentine's Day after the wedding. Basu and Grover and both fans of the active lifestyle and more often than not spotted on their way to the gym channeling athleisure. Style evolution Indian ethnic dressing has always been a part of Basu's wardrobe. Since 2011, the star is has been seen in saris on the red carpet. Some of our favourite looks seen on the star are the Gaurav Gupta gown she wore to the IIFA Awards this year, the floor grazing Anarkali by Anita Dongre worn earlier in March, and the sheer embellished sari the star wore last week. In the past year, Basu has also taken to a streamlined aesthetic, favouring tailored dresses and jumpsuits, forgoing prints and bold colours. There's no doubt Basu's aesthetic has evolved through the years but the star's enthusiastic experimentation has her fans coming back for more. column1: Sonam Kapoor’s favourite brand is showing their first RTW collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ralph & Russo on its first RTW collection British couture brand Ralph & Russo has shared its excitement about showing its first-ever ready-to-wear collection at London Fashion Week. The brand, headed up by Michael Russo and Tamara Ralph, is usually a regular on the Paris Couture Fashion Week schedule, but will bring its inimitable signature to the capital where it is based come September 15. “With London being a cosmopolitan hub, we couldn't think of a better place to launch our first ready-to-wear offering," said Russo today. "We continue to listen to the demand of our customer and the market, which will continue to fuel the expansion of the R&R product and universe." It's a savvy move from the brand (favoured by Angelina Jolie) which is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year, during which time it has cemented its reputation as one of the hottest tickets in Paris and the worlds of couture and ready-to-wear to merge like never before in customers' wardrobes. A release from the label this afternoon said that its "first RTW collection will remain true to its brand DNA and heritage whilst expressing itself as an independent extension of the Ralph & Russo offering". Praise came from British Fashion Council CEO Caroline Rush today, who said that she was "delighted to welcome Ralph & Russo to the London Fashion Week schedule. The craftsmanship behind their couture collection is a shining example of Britain's artisanal heritage, and I'm excited to see their debut ready to wear collection." The brand will be one of many new faces at the showcase next month, as Giorgio Armani and Tommy Hilfiger are both slated to join proceedings. column1: Manish Malhotra has a surprise for his fans in his latest collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You will love these new additions View Gallery 6 Photos Did you expect this collection from Manish Malhotra? Malhotra's work has been veering to address the needs of cocktail dressing for the last few seasons. And while his focus has been on gowns, the designer will be working on a line of cocktail dresses, saris and bespoke menswear for his latest collection. After showcasing ‘Sensual Affair' for couture 2017, Malhotra's collection for winter/festive 2017 is called ‘Tales of Indulgence'. “As a designer I want to keep adding a lot of diversity to my brand. This collection is going to be a huge amalgamation of silhouettes starting from cocktail dresses to funky saris to lehengas skirts and suits for men. I think it's all changing—the wedding cocktail is more formal. Girls today have a more evolved, diversified aesthetic,” said the designer about introducing a fresh perspective to his body of work. Malhotra described his mood for the collection as “me in my most indulgent form”. You will be sure to spot beaded fringes, threadwork and tailoring at the show. “I have wanted to work on suits for men for the last couple of years, and dresses for women, but I was waiting for the right positioning and the opportunity presented itself with this collection,” he said. The presence of Kareena Kapoor Khan, Malhotra's longtime friend and permanent fixture on the last day of Lakmé Fashion Week, is uncertain. However, the designer did promise a showstopper to close the show with an element of surprise. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 14 Bollywood-approved designer gowns to inspire your wedding look
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Which of these is your favourite? View Gallery 14 Photos 14 celebrity approved designer gowns to inspire your wedding look When it comes to wedding dressing, it's always best to be sure about your choice of outfits. If you are smart, you will probably try on all your outfits with a hair and make-up trial to make sure you achieve the desired results on your big day. Advice will come from far and wide about the best colours to pick from, the best stores to visit and what silhouettes to choose, but the ultimate person whose approval you need is yourself. Cocktail dressing is an important part of your wedding trousseau. Whether it's the reception, drinks night or sangeet that you pick a black-tie dress code for, the gown bears as equal an importance as any other look. Bollywood stars have illustrated the power of the red carpet staple gown time and again. From Sonam Kapoor's sweeping trails to Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's dramatic silhouettes, which celebrity approved gown could be the foundation of your look? Bigger is better Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's show-stopping ice blue gown by Michael Cinco is for the bride who doesn't like to hold back on the drama. There's no doubt all eyes will be on you if you choose to go with a look this powerful. You can also look to Deepika Padukone's Ralph & Russo gown or Sonam Kapoor's textured lavender gown (also by Ralph & Russo) for reference. Since your wedding is probably the only time you will be able to pull off a look so striking, don't think twice before making the choice. Colour power If you aren't a fan of embellishments, make a statement with colour. Priyanka Chopra's red Jason Wu gown and Alia Bhatt's hot pink Sachin and Babi number are perfect examples of understated glamour. You can load up on the accessories to make the ensemble more wedding-appropriate. A solid coloured look in a warm hue will photograph better than a muted tone. Bling is king Embellishments are a fail-safe choice to go with as has been proven time and again. From Sonam Kapoor's gold gown to Sonakshi Sinha's red crystal studded look from the IIFA Awards, embellishments can be the focus of your cocktail look. Tone down on the accessories if your outfit is too busy with other elements. Scroll through our gallery to look for inspiration for celebrity-approved designer gowns for your wedding. column1: Multi-designer store Ensemble has a new address in Mumbai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Credit cards at the ready View Gallery 5 Photos Multi-designer store Ensemble has a new address in Mumbai If you try and trace the origin of the Indian fashion shopping experience as we know it today, chances are, Ensemble will be one of the first names that will come to mind. Ever since it opened doors in 1987, this chain of multi-designer stores has been a frontrunner in championing home-grown designers and Indian craftsmanship. The pioneering endeavour by Tina Tahiliani-Parikh (executive director - Ensemble) had started out with five designers, namely Tarun Tahiliani, Rohit Khosla, Neil Bieff, Amaya, and Abu Jani-Sandeep Khosla, back in the day. Today, the store's repertoire boasts the country's top couturiers stocked alongside burgeoning design talent. After giving their flagship Kala Ghoda store a recent makeover, Ensemble's Bandra boutique that catered to suburban fashionistas for close to a decade, now has a new address. Luckily, the new 4,000-plus sqft store, in a leafy bylane off Linking Road, Santacruz, is not too far from its erstwhile location. “Ensemble has been in Bandra for eight years now. Over the years, Mumbai's suburbs have evolved immensely. We want to offer them the best of Indian fashion, and felt the need to move to a bigger space to do so. This better-appointed store will help us bring the true 'Ensemble experience' to the suburbs,” explains Tahiliani-Parikh. The store will offer a mix Ensemble regulars plus new additions to their designer roster, with a special focus on Indian contemporary fashion. Patrons can look out for contemporary wear by brands like Lovebirds, Antar-Agni and Surily Goel, traditional wear by the likes of Anamika Khanna, Sabyasachi and Jayanti Reddy, as well as an expansive selection of couture and bridal wear. Tahiliani-Parikh, however, is particularly excited about the latest addition of couture by Amit Aggarwal and contemporary wear by Arjun Saluja. A dedicated space for Tarun Tahiliani couture, which was immensely popular at the earlier address, will be retained at the new store as well. “Ensemble and Tarun Tahiliani are moving to their new Santacruz home—housed on four levels, the new store is on the heels of the Lion Gate expansion. As Mumbai moves North, Ensemble follows her growth and continues to provide wonderful sartorial solutions with the new location,” says the designer. Interior designer Vinod Narkar has married an industrial design aesthetic with indigenous elements to give the store a fittingly chic appearance. Think cement floors with exposed beams and lime plaster-covered pillars juxtaposed with a handmade wooden staircase. This retail haven is one that looks as stylish as the collections it stocks. Ensemble Santacruz opens doors on August 11, 2017 Ground Floor, 11 Span Centre, South Avenue Road, (Opposite Ramakrishna Mission), Santacruz (W), Mumbai. column1: This London-based label is introducing India to the world in a new light
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Quiet luxury at its best View Gallery 8 Photos Meet the London based label that will make you India proud London-born label Varana of Indian origins is all about understated luxury. Brainchild of Sujata Keshavan who used to head Ray + Keshavan, and Ravi Prasad, ex-chairman of Himalaya Herbals, the label is only two years old but already has a three-storey flagship in London's Dover Street Market. How did a couple who comes with diverse career paths in advertising design and pharmaceuticals find themselves launching a fashion label? “The idea of a fashion brand was brewing in my mind for about 15 odd years. I always thought we need a luxury brand from India in the world. I saw Shanghai Tang years ago and I thought those guys are from China and they have put together this brand, and we could have one too,” says Keshavan. One of the meanings of Varana (which comes from Varanasi) is river. The brand's logo is a wave, which is the representation of the Asi river. Keshavan and Prasad brainstormed on bringing about a fashion label that is India proud and caters to the global luxury customer. “I connected with Ravi on this at one point and he get got interested in the idea to put together an Ayurveda beauty range along with the clothing line. So, we decided to put together design teams and work on both brands, take it internationally and showcase it in a flagship store,” she further explains. The Varana flagship also houses beauty and gifting products from its sister brand Almora which is led by Prasad. While neither founders come from any expertise in fashion design, the duo has put together a talented team that is overseen under the creative direction of Keshavan. “The brand is very much in my aesthetic. It's kind of structures and silhouettes I like and are done under my creative direction. I have a wonderful team of designers who are specialists in their field. We have textile designers from NID, a knitwear specialist who hails from Japan, our pattern cutter is French and the womenswear designer is from Italy. Our quality control team has people who have worked at Prada and Marni before,” she tells us. Varana's spring/summer 2017 line ‘The Taj Collection' takes elements of architecture from the monument and gives them a contemporary twist. From hand block-printed dresses to custom jacquard inspired by the lattice detailing, much of Varana's design ideology stems from ideation at the fabric. There are jackets woven to resemble kantha embroidery and bandhani, and long staple cotton dresses that have the same texture as silk. Varana is also focusing on creating bringing back the identity of cashmere to India. With plans to expand through luxury retailers both online and through stores like Bergdoff Goodman, Netaporter.com and Matchesfashion.com, Varana is well on its way to living up to its founders' dreams. column1: How China’s largest e-commerce site is leading on the luxury fashion field
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Alibaba has turned the tables around Alibaba, China's largest e-commerce platform, has made major headway in the last week to dispel the notion that it is a facilitator of counterfeit designer goods and solidify its position as a lead player on the international luxury fashion field. Firstly, it announced last week that it has partnered with Kering to work together to stop rogue sellers profiting from illegally selling fakes on its numerous platforms (a major development, considering Kering and Alibaba have been locked in a legal tangle since 2015 when the French fashion conglomerate sued the latter twice for allegedly selling counterfeit versions of items from its stable of fashion houses that includes Gucci, Saint Laurent and Balenciaga). As per a report in the New York Times, the businesses released a joint statement in which they said "that they would establish a task force to share information and work with law enforcement to protect Kering's brands", as well as "make use of Alibaba's technology to seek out fakes". Then, as a part of its "New Retail" plan, last week it created a special luxury pavilion on one of its most popular subsites, Tmall. Before now, luxury brands - while eager to target Chinese consumers who are increasingly investing in luxury at home and online - were hesitant to sell on the platform, which sells everything from food to fashion, as it could potentially be positioned alongside products that they felt were a bad match (like alcohol, pet food or medicine). By creating an environment that allows luxury houses to distance themselves from such brands and potential counterfeiters alike, as well as giving them access to the consumer market, Tmall boasted brands such as Burberry, La Mer, Hugo Boss, Maserati and Guerlain at launch, reports Digiday.com. Now, it has partnered with the Marriot Hotel Group to offer members of its new luxury loyalty programme access to benefits offered by both businesses. “Consumers today, things have completely changed. More and more young consumers not only want to find goods and services, they are searching for a more spiritual side to stuff; they want to go everywhere in the world and have experiences,” Alibaba CEO Daniel Zhang said today, reports WWD. “There has been a lot of discussion about this ‘New Retail' strategy but it all starts with the customers. Ultimately, it's our job to bring new exposure to consumers, whether it's a brand, experiences, services. It's about giving consumers what they want.” It's a far cry from last year when the International Anti-Counterfeiting Coalition (IACC) suspended the membership of Alibaba, one week after brands including Kering-owned Gucci, Michael Kors and Tiffany & Co were said to have departed the coalition as a direct result of its being admitted, saying that they felt it was a part of the problem. At the time, Jennifer Kuperman, head of international corporate affairs at Alibaba Group, said that "the only way to solve the complex, industry-wide issue of counterfeiting is through strong industry collaboration and we believe that intermediaries, like Alibaba, must be an integral part of the solution." The last week's worth of announcements show that working together to help achieve a common goal is a concept that's certainly catching on. column1: Actor Samantha Ruth Prabhu is championing the cause of Indian handlooms
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All about Woven 2017 Samantha Ruth Prabhu is on her way back to Hyderabad from a promotional event in Rajahmundry when we call her this evening. The award-winning South Indian actor, it becomes apparent early on in the conversation, has her hands full. “Apart from my endorsements, I am working on seven Telugu and Tamil films at the moment; the release dates for which are spread between October this year and summer 2018.” While films are an integral part of her being, Prabhu has been dedicating the bulk of her hours to a fashion-centric passion project lately. As Telangana's handloom ambassador, she has joined forces with the state's government to debut Woven—a platform dedicated to championing the cause of Telangana's weavers, honouring their work, and infusing present-day relevance to age-old techniques that are unique to the South Indian state. “I have been travelling across the state for the past few months to understand the problems that plague our weavers at a grass root level. Their skills are unmatched, but it's disheartening that they fear their craft will die with them. We want weavers to get due recognition, and also restore respect for their art. Therein was born the idea for this initiative, and it's a cause I am deeply vested in,” she explains. The event fittingly takes place today, on August 7, 2017, which is also National Handloom Day. Apart from felicitating weavers, a fashion show focused on Telangan fabrics like ikat, mangalagiri, Narayanapeta and Gadwal among others will be a highlight of the event. “We are working with local designers like Preetham Jukalker, Shilpa Reddy, and Shravan Kumar among others, as they are well-versed with these fabrics. Handlooms are often straitjacketed as the older generation's domain. But its contemporary reinterpretation by these young designers will help change this misconception. The collections will not only feature handloom saris but also modern silhouettes. Moreover, this will also help establish a synergy between the designers and weavers, and assist the latter to thrive,” says Prabhu, who will be wearing a double ikat sari by Jukalker for the event. While Prabhu has always been sartorially conscious since she started out as an actor seven years ago, it was a handwoven designer sari she wore two years back that drew her attention to the handloom industry. “As exquisite as the sari was, I was taken aback by its hefty price tag. On the one hand, weavers were committing suicide owing to the lack of sustainability, and on the other, the public was shying away from handlooms because of how expensive it was. It did not fit.” This propelled Prabhu to dig deeper, and use her influence to make the right noise. And while she is not under the illusion of affecting overnight change with Woven, she feels it's a step in the right direction for the industry's rightful revival. “I do believe that we are a deeply caring and responsible generation. If we can modernise these fabrics and make them affordable, a change is bound to follow. It helps that our government is proactive and eager to see this initiative through too.” So are handwoven ensembles a dominant part of Prabhu's personal repertoire? “I am innately drawn to clothes with a story, so handwoven pieces check that box. For instance, I wore a gota skirt and boxy top set by Punit Balana today that was handwoven into a chevron pattern.” Saris are also a constant in Prabhu's wardrobe—it's a drape she feels abundantly feminine and elegant in. Though she prefers to wear them with a twist, and will often throw in a flouncy or boxy blouse to add visual appeal. “I steer clear of anything that is too tight. I need to be at ease in what I wear. Any discomfort manifests into the most awkward expression on my face,” she laughs. Aside from her film commitments and gearing up for the launch of Woven (“I have been involved in every aspect, right down to what goes into the gift bags!”), one can't help but note that even her impending nuptials to actor Naga Chaitanya hasn't slowed her down. “It has been challenging, but I am all about testing my limits and pushing myself. People assumed I would take a step back to focus on my domestic life, but I like to prove such expectations wrong. In fact, this has been one of the busiest phases of my life, and I wouldn't have it any other way,” Prabhu signs off. Fashion Culture & Living Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Sanjay Garg busts common myths about handlooms
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's what you didn't know Sanjay Garg has been an ardent supporter of the handloom since the start of label Raw Mango in 2008. Unlike designers introducing handloom to their vocabulary since the government's active involvement in uplifting the handloom sector, Garg's design philosophy stems from it. For the designer, innovation begins at the loom. On Handloom Day, August 7, Vogue spoke to the designer about changing the perception of the often used, rarely understood word. How would you explain handloom to a layperson? Explaining handloom is like explaining religion, or the idea of India. There is a fact-based explanation and a doctrine-based one, which includes community societal and emotional reasoning. Factually, handloom is a loom operated by hand. Apart from that, it is about culture, community, craft and much more. Both definitions together make handloom so special. How can one identify handloom fabric over machine-made fabric? It is becoming increasingly difficult for people to differentiate between the two. Education, experience and a sense of the tactile qualities make it easier to identify. However, fewer people are taking the time to understand textiles and lack basic knowledge—even the difference between a warp and weft. What are some common misconceptions people have about handlooms? I think the most common misconception is that everything called ‘handloom' is handloom. There is a grey zone between handloom and machine-made. Some handloom fabrics include the use of mechanised processes, what does that make them? People also tend to think it should be much cheaper than it is, but that [kind of fabric] is often either a lower base quality, or more often—made from exploitative wages. Why do you favour using handloom fabrics in your work? To me, all our explorations in design, be it from textile, handloom or interiors come from the same place: to question the use and presence of material, methods, techniques and aesthetics. I do not favour handloom over other fabrics, it's just the expression of my work. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Selena Gomez collaborates with Coach on a new collection of accessories
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Find out more about the pop star playing designer View Gallery 10 Photos Selena Gomez collaborates on a bag with Coach that sends a message Selena Gomez has been working on something special with American luxury brand Coach. After announcing Gomez as the face of Coach's fall advertising campaign, the brand announced a special collection of accessories called ‘Coach x Selena' in collaboration with Selena Gomez. Vogue spoke to the pop star about playing the part of a designer.  Tell us about the experience of designing a bag in collaboration with Coach. What was it like designing with the creative director, Stuart Vevers? The relationship I've created with Stuart is very special. We really bonded from the beginning—we spoke for weeks and weeks before we decided to do something together. He showed me his vision of what he wants Coach to be, what it stands for, and how it's this great American brand. It's really great to have an influence and some control when you're working with a brand. Having control in a situation is something that's important to me, as a woman and as a businessperson. What they represent as a brand is something I can embody. The handbag I've designed has an inspirational message that comes with it. How did you come up with the shape of the bag? I love a bag that is easy, and has room to fit my life! A bag that goes with everything is so important to me—I need to be able to have a bag for months and not change it out. I am always on the move so I literally have everything in there. Can you share what was most important to have in a bag? What makes this the ultimate bag for you? Like most people, I would have to say my phone, just because phones are more than just phones these days. I've really learned to appreciate that craftsmanship and small details of a bag. I think the ultimate bag is something that goes with almost everything and you don't have to even give it a second thought if it goes with your outfit. Was there an inspiration for your Coach collaboration? Who do you envision wearing Selena Gomez for Coach? I really was just inspired by what I was looking for in a bag. It was incredible to work so closely with Stuart. That in itself was beyond inspiring. My hope is that anyone will feel drawn towards the bag. Even with my music it's so interesting to see the diverseness in my audience when I am on tour. That makes me really happy. Tell us about “Selena Red”? How did you find the perfect red? I think everyone has a colour that has some significance, gives you an instant confidence boost. For me, red is both classic and has an edge. I definitely have noticed over the years I tend to wear red often. There are some very personal touches on the bag—can you tell us about the inscription that says “Love yourself first”? I've spoken in the past about how important it is to be true and honest with yourself. I have spoken with my fans about the importance of taking care of yourself. I am so lucky to get to be creative in my life, and work on a variety of projects. But it is very important to make time for yourself, listen to yourself, and be kind to yourself. column1: The ultimate guide to kick-starting your trousseau shopping
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Tackling this tall order “Will you marry me?” may have been music to her ears, but if we are to be really honest, the four words that every bride-in-the-making really wants to hear is, “Let's go trousseau shopping?” For the uninitiated, a trousseau (derived from the French word ‘trousse' meaning bundle or case) refers to the paraphernalia of clothing, linen, and other essentials collected by a bride ahead of her marriage, which was traditionally packed in hope chests. Wealthy Victorians even practised the tradition of displaying trunks loaded with linens, china and clothes as part of the wedding festivities, in an event that was monikered ‘trousseau tea'. Since times immemorial, curating an enviable trousseau has been the first order of business for most brides-to-be; one where she ideally does not want to spare any expense. For instance, when Italian noblewoman Catherine de' Medici married into the French royal family in 1547, the Pope (also her uncle), had to utilise funds originally meant for the fortification of Florence to pay for chests of lace, silks, bed linen, and jewels. American-socialite-turned-Duchess-of-Windsor, Wallis Simpson's trousseau boasted 66 trunks of clothes and accessories by Chanel and Elsa Schiaparelli. Closer home, Maharani Gayatri Devi's wedding trousseau was bursting with sheets from Czechoslovakia, Ferragamo shoes and bags from their factory in Florence, and mousseline de soie nightgowns from Paris. For the modern bride, it is also about balancing this extravagance with a sense of practicality. Yes, the process does start out as all fun and games. But once the rose-tinted glasses come off and the novelty wears off, the realisation dawns that trousseau shopping, is in fact, a bride-to-be's dream come true and biggest nightmare rolled into one. Sure, it's an excuse to go all Blair Waldorf or Cher Horowitz (take your pick) on your credit card, but nothing can quite prepare you for the overwhelming wave that is waiting to wash over you once you enter this sea of infinite options at your disposal. “I thought this was supposed to be fun—shopping has never been such a daunting and dreaded task for me before,” an exasperated soon-to-wed friend recently confided in me. So our guide is the ideal starting point for a bride-in-distress. Ditch the haphazard approach and tread one step at a time to keep any bouts of PTSD (post trousseau shopping disorder) at bay. Draw up a list Physical lists are highly underrated. Just take our word for it, and go old school with this one. Get yourself a personalised wedding planner if it helps. Dedicate separate lists to every area of your trousseau—think clothing, handbags, footwear, jewellery, make-up, bed linen, crockery, and other miscellaneous must-haves. Then move on to meticulously breaking down each list. Your clothing list should be further divided into Indian wear, everyday western wear, occasion wear, honeymoon clothes, swimwear, and so on. Assign a quantity to every last item on your list, but always value quality above all else. Since the list will set the tone for the shopping to follow, practicality should reign supreme. Don't waste check boxes on whimsical items. Take stock of what you already have If your mum is of the quintessential Indian variety, chances are that she started curating your trousseau long before Mr Right even entered the picture—an exquisite Pashmina shawl from her last trip to Gulmarg, an elaborate silver dinner set from Bhattar that she has been adding to for years, a Jim Thompson toiletry set acquired in Bangkok, Murano showpieces from when your favourite aunt went to Italy, and on the list goes. Tick these off (phew!) your list already. Set a budget This is perhaps the most arduous part of the process. No one despises number crunching more than a bride, but it has got to be done. “I'll get married only once,” will seem like a good enough reason for everything from buying an exorbitant exotic skin designer bag to wiping out Harrods' beauty department. The urge to splurge will be stronger than usual; so tap into your very last reserve of self-restraint. We aren't asking you to cut corners, but to exercise sensibility when allocating funds to various aspects of your trousseau. More pragmatic, less pompous is the dictum to swear by. Do your research ‘Being spoilt for choice' does not even begin to describe the sheer volume of options that will be thrown your way. Put on your Sherlock hat and do some serious digging around. Get recommendations from recently married or fashion-savvy friends, use the Internet and social media to compare collections and prices, and conduct a preliminary recce of what stores and bridal exhibitions are offering. This will ensure that you don't end up with impulse purchases you regret later. Create a game plan Now that you're armed with adequate ammo, you can confidently march onto the battlefield. Every item on your checklist should be assigned a deadline, but be strategic when doing so. For instance, sale season is an opportune time to shop for clothes, especially traditional occasion wear. Anything that is made-to-order should be a priority on your timeline. Delivery delays are bound to crop up, so factor that in. Use a trip abroad to stock up on lingerie and international brands (one can't be thankful enough for VAT refunds). If you aren't travelling yourself, identify friends or family members who you can ship certain items to. Aim at wrapping up all your shopping at least a month before the wedding. That way, you still have a buffer period if end up running behind schedule. Now would also be a good time to add finishing touches to your trousseau. Order blouses for all those chiffon and Benarasi saris your grandmother passed on to you, order plastic covers to store your Indian wear in, and have the jeweller polish all your bridal sets. Be open-minded While it helps to have a clear idea of what you want, being rigid will only be counter-productive. Leave room for sweet surprises—be open to brands, styles, silhouettes, and designs you probably never considered before. And while you may fall in love with a certain brand or trend, don't go crazy just yet. There is something to be said about variety, after all. The end game is to create a trousseau that is as versatile and classic as it is up-to-the-minute. Balance is more than a buzzword in this case. column1: Exclusive: The Bachchan-Nanda women in their first ever interview together
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The ladies come together for Vogue India’s August 2017 issue Amitabh Bachchan calling on FaceTime; Jaya comparing photographs of Navya and her at the same age; Shweta making fun of her mother posing, only to realise Navya was doing the same to her... At our cover shoot, one thing was clear—the Bachchan-Nanda women share a bond that's as special as it's normal. Sure, there are disagreements and con­flicts, but there are also memories of Euro Disney, of evenings in pyjamas, and a closeness that can only be shared by mothers and (grand)daughters. JAYA BACHCHAN She's a stickler for discipline, a sentimentalist (she's carefully saved her children's clothes and school badges) and is known to shoot from the hip. Mother of two, and grandmother of three, Jaya Bachchan tells us that even at 69 she's constantly learning When it comes to parenting, Jaya says she hasn't really dispensed a lot of advice to Shweta or Abhishek. “This generation are friends with their children, but I am also always surprised with the liberties they accord them.” At the shoot, Jaya gently prods Navya about her whereabouts of last night. “I worry but Shweta tells me, ‘Mum, she lives alone in New York,'” she says, sighing. “It's going to be even harder when Aradhaya grows up.” While Shweta is wiser with her words than Jaya, Navya, according to Jaya, is quite ‘bindaas'. “She's always been an easy child. She has an opinion, but if you say something to her she never takes offense.” How would she describe their dynamic? “We're all cool women, we're really comfortable with each other. Shweta is always in charge, but Navya will take over soon.” Is there one question she has always wanted to ask her daughter? “Maybe. But I'm scared of her answer.” Jaya pauses to take a mouthful and looks straight at Shweta sitting across the table. “Have I been a good mother?” SHWETA BACHCHAN NANDA Shweta Bachchan Nanda is one cool mom. And for the most part, her children agree. Except, that is, when she's not nagging them to brush their teeth and wash their faces, or punctuating all their text messages History, they say, repeats itself. Many years ago, similar conversations took place between Jaya and Shweta, with Jaya urging Shweta to channel her skills in diplomatic relations or journalism. But Shweta, who married young, choosing family over career, doesn't want Navya to follow in her footsteps. “Only after you become a parent do you understand why your parents say and do the things they do. The instinct to protect suddenly becomes real.” Even now, she says, her parents are the voice of reason in her head. While as a child, her mother was more present in the daily parenting (“my mum was always the bad cop”), Shweta is still her father's daughter (even in their shared physicality), marvelling at his hunger to keep abreast of what's happening, borrowing watches and clothes from his extensive wardrobe (“both my parents are hoarders”), and cooking his favourite pasta. “We never discussed films with him as children, but now he uses me and Abhishek as sounding boards. We spend a lot more time now, and talking about his life and his journey, I see a more vulnerable side... I can pretty much get my way with him.” Her relationship with her father is a lot easier, she says, while with Jaya it's a more complex dynamic. The two intelligent women who don't necessarily mince words, though, enjoy a repartee that indicates a closeness that needn't always be spelled out. NAVYA NAVELI NANDA She loves rajma chawal, her boxer (named Boxer) and Justin Bieber; is close to her brother Agastya; makes rap music playlists for granddad Amitabh; has found a shopping buddy in uncle Abhishek (“the biggest shopaholic in the family”); and wants to take her mother and grandmother on a safari on their next girls trip. Meet Navya Naveli Nanda “I'm actually really proud of my mum, the fact that after so many years she's going out there to make a life for herself.” Wise words from 19-year-old Navya Naveli Nanda, the older child of Shweta and Nikhil Nanda, as her mother takes her position in front of the camera for her second Vogue shoot. Wearing a white tee, track pants and the newest Gucci slides, Navya is waiting for her turn in the spotlight. But let's get the elephant in the room out of the way. The dark-haired beauty will not be following in her famous grandfather's footsteps when it comes to a career in acting. “No way,” says the young teen emphatically, tearing off pieces of her dosa. In a family with a long lineage in films (she's the granddaughter of Amitabh and Jaya Bachchan, and the great-granddaughter of Raj Kapoor on her father's side), it's a natural question, especially in an industry known for its dynasties. Chalk it up to dissuasion on her mother's part (“I really try to tell her about all the cons... I have nothing against the industry—it's who we are—but it's not an easy world to be in,” Shweta tells me) or to being a young girl still finding her calling, but for now the communications major is not looking at either of the family businesses (her father Nikhil is the managing director of Escorts Group). Instead, she is enjoying her current internship at advertising agency Ogilvy & Mather while on break from university in New York. “I love the independence,” she says about life in Manhattan, mornings spent at Soul Cycle, trawling the streets of Soho on Saturdays for cool boutiques, long meals with friends at her favourite restaurant Serafina or going to concerts (“I'm a huge Justin Bieber fan—I literally cried for three hours when I saw him perform!”). Just another teen in the Big City. Read the complete interview in Vogue India's August 2017 issue that hits stands on August 3, 2017 Photographed by Tarun Vishwa. column1: Masaba Gupta to close India Day at London Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And more news from the designer Masaba Gupta and Athiya Shetty at Amazon India Fashion Week Fashion Scout—one of the largest showcases at London Fashion Week will be hosting Masaba Gupta this season. Designers supported by INIDF (International Institute Of Fashion Design) will be under the spotlight on India Day at the showcase where Gupta will present her collection. Continuing on their theme for the season, Madagascar, the designer will present a lineup that is catered to the audience in London. “We realised that the client overseas may not always want bold striking colours that we do a lot of, so decided to work with a classic palette of tans and ochres around this line. You will see a lot of monochrome and we will style our separates in way that is more appealing to the sensibilities there,” said Gupta. The designer also has plans to host a pop-up in London before the showcase to connect to the customer abroad. “We don't want to show just our festive wear for the NRI customer but also reach out to the locals with our aesthetic that is between Indian and Western,” she talks about her strategy to expand the brand. Gupta's shows no signs of resting. Even on a recent holiday in the States, the designer hosted a trunk show in San Jose. “I met three generations of women wearing Masaba and it was interesting to see their take on the label,” she says. The designer strongly believes that travel not only offers a fresh perspective to her design process but also helps in evolving the narrative of the brand. In the next couple of months, Masaba will be hosting a trunk show in Singapore. Gupta will also be showcasing at the upcoming Lakmé Fashion Week, where she will focus on festive dressing further exploring the Madagascar theme. “I have stopped naming my collections for the last few seasons, instead I focus on a mood,” she says. Among the brand's many extensions, Gupta recently introduced a line of accessories that includes diaries with original design sketches, travel pillows, trays, socks and even custom gifting options for weddings. “Despite my trying to keep the price range in an affordable range, the younger girls who follow  our label might find the clothes too expensive to buy which is why introduced a product range that starts at Rs 299 which is a lot more accessible,” she says. column1: Ileana D’Cruz’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Girl-next-door chic View Gallery 53 Photos Style evolution: Ileana D’Cruz While Ileana D'Cruz has been a well-recognised name in the South Indian film industry since 2006, she made her Bollywood debut only in 2012. Her launch vehicle was Anurag Basu's Barfi!, in which she starred alongside Ranbir Kapoor and Priyanka Chopra. She followed up this superlatively successful film with a spate of action/romantic comedies like Phata Poster Nikhla Hero, Main Tera Hero, and Happy Ending, which failed to make a lasting impact on the box-office. Rustom was a redeeming release, and the actor was most recently seen in Mubarakan. Her next release is Baadshao with Ajay Devgn. Whatever the fate of her films, D'Cruz was instantly embraced by audiences early on owing to her endearing demeanour. Her girl-next-door aura extends to her style preferences too. Not overtly experimental or avant-garde, the actor never really vied for a fashionista title. But she has had clarity on works best for her from the very start, and mastered the art of using that to her advantage. Early years Just before her Bollywood debut in 2012, D'Cruz had a brief flirtation with Bollywood's then tried-and-tested go-to, ie, snug bodycon dresses. Agreed that she did give into the temptation, but (thankfully) the affair was short-lived, and better sartorial sense soon prevailed. D'Cruz continued to channel a fuss-free, and laid-back chic vibe thereafter. She did not limit herself to a formulaic set of silhouettes, deciding to go the style chameleon route instead. For the red carpet, she most often chose gowns by international brands like Dior and Dolce & Gabanna. Maxi dresses soon became her staple, though she did shake things up with an assortment of jumpsuits, pencil skirts, and a mixed bag of dresses, ever so often too. Evolution Ileana D'Cruz's knack for bringing a sense of elegance to whatever she sported continued to work in her favour. In 2014, the actor toyed with giving her ensembles a slightly more glamorous update. So out came the bandeau tops, crop tops, bralets, bustiers, thigh-high slits, cutouts, bare backs, and ample décolletage show. Ever since, she has returned to her trusty dresses—mostly shoulder-barring midi and maxi dresses—for appearances in the recent past. D'Cruz is most definitely not a quintessential jeans-and-tee dresser, unless she's pairing her button-down maxi dress with ripped jeans. Coordinated separates—think crop tops with skirts or trousers—are the latest addition to her repertoire. As far as traditional wear goes, D'Cruz is a patron of anarkalis, with the odd lehenga or sari thrown in for good measure. column1: 5 hacks to help you ace festive dressing when you’re short on time
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion For those on the go [#image: /photos/5ce43d3c3bf9b45748b1ddde]||| ||| Image: Ruven Afanador As unwise it is to leave festive dressing in India to last-minute choices, it is extremely easy to do, which can result in last minute chaos. The best way to avoid this is to have a mix of fail-safe pieces in your arsenal that will save you from having a hard time about dressing for the upcoming season of festivities. When it comes to clothing, my go to look is minimal with an eclectic edge. I like to highlight traditional nuances of my outfit while using deconstructed silhouettes to suit my style and vibe. Depending on how you feel, you could wear a highly embellished outfit while keeping the accessories to a minimal, or go bold. Here are pro tips on how to dress for a festive occasion in five minutes flat. Understand the colour wheel Mixing designers and creating an outfit is easy if you keep the principle rule of colour in mind. It may seem overly punctilious, but sticking to three colours is the most beneficial way to a well-formulated look. For example if you have black and white it can be complemented by a touch of bright red. Create a stark contrast of two colours like red and violet or stick to colours that complement each other, such as neutral tones. Wear a cape Capes are not only easy to wear, but they also add a bit of flair to your wardrobe. Pair your cape with a simpler inner outfit such as a top and pants, skirt or long dress. You can go heavy on the accessories to dress up the cape. There's no going wrong with jewel tones Wear bold jewel tones at night, it always adds vibrancy to one's look. Tones of burgundy, jade, sapphire are perfect for evening soirees. Wear an embellished jacket Long line jackets with embroidery and beading add the perfect drama for a more formal affair. Wear them with pants that work effortlessly during the day or night. I recommend the classic cigarette pant for a more formal ensemble. Experiment! Experiment! I tend to mix and match a lot of my clothes to create new outfits and appreciate what already lies in the depths of my closet. Never be scared about being experimental with your clothing. It makes for a more fun life and helps you enjoy the season of celebration more. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Together for the first time Manish Malhotra is a stage at his career where he is only competing against himself. Last evening, the designer closed India Couture Week 2017 with his show, ‘Sensual Affair'. The Wedding Design Company put together the set that included a reflective mirrored flooring and black flowers hanging overhead, nearly mimicking the actual decor for a cocktail reception or a sangeet party. Malhotra's 85 looks on runway took everything you knew about bridal couture in India and put it in a brighter, bolder, magnified perspective. Forget about ensembles with trains the wearer is afraid of being stepped on—Malhotra's version had trains that demanded space—almost as though wearing his clothes would give the wearer their rightful importance on an evening. There were tasseled tops, feather trims, the return of the '90s corset version of a blouse and trailing capes, each design meant to signify liberation and glamour at its best. The front row included the likes of Shweta Nanda Bachchan, Huma Qureshi, Sophie Choudry, Natasha Poonawala and more. Apparently, Ranveer Singh walking the runway for the designer had been on the cards for nearly three years, and finally took place last night. Alia Bhatt, who worked with Manish Malhotra on her very first film, Student of the Year, shares a long-term relationship with him. Models walked in between the lights—the combination of Gupta's vision in two design voices was a powerful one. The designer chose a softer approach to his structured silhouettes for couture 2017. The collection titled ‘Moondust' explored the abstract concepts of sculptures found mythological forests, moondust and moonlight. From conceptual cocktail dresses to lace pant suits, draped gowns and sari gowns, Gupta created every hybrid garment that could be made possible by bringing western and Indian clothing together. Aditi Rao Hydari may have walked the runway for the designer for the first time, but has been wearing Gupta's clothes for years. column1: Inside Rahul Mishra’s stunning couture 2017 collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Light as air When Rahul Mishra thinks of couture, it's clear that he is designing for the needs of the woman wearing it. Proof is in the models, who will gush about how light the garments feel. Bereft of any detailing of Royal India, Mishra's breezy collection stands fresh, evoking elegance and a feeling of lightness that's hard to come by in the Indian couture landscape. This season the designer clashed geometric patterns inspired by Islamic architecture with his usual palette of florals for his collection ‘Parizaad'. Starting with muted somber whites, moving into pastels of icy blues and millennial pink, the line-up went into saturated hues of chrome yellow and royal blue. The silhouettes saw trapeze blouses, long line jackets, anarkalis—styles that women wear without worrying about exposing more skin than they are comfortable with. Mishra balanced the modest options with lehengas, long dresses with sheer panels and sheer saris, giving a wide range of options for the festive shopper. Islamic architectural references called for tessellation often seen on tiles, that Mishra's craftsmen brought about beautifully by way of thread work. For the florals, they employed techniques of traditional Parsi gara embroidery. Despite the density of the embroidery, Mishra's diaphanous clothes offer mobility to the wearer, which instantly translates to grace. The designer aims to expand his sustainable ecosystem of reverse migration by generating more employment opportunities with a collection this heavy on hand work. column1: Marine Serre tells us what’s next for her LVMH Prize-winning label
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The French designer talks to Vogue about what it’s like to win the LVMH Prize at 25 Image: Virgile Guinard On 16 June, the 25-year-old Corrèze-born designer Marine Serre won the LVMH Prize - one of the most prestigious awards for young designers in fashion - pocketing €300,000 and marking her place as fashion's newest darling. She'd been sipping water behind the stage when she heard Rihanna announce her name at the awards ceremony in Paris. “That was a weird moment because I was really not expecting anything,” says Serre, speaking in the 18ème arrondissement apartment-slash-studio she and her team of two moved into a month after winning the Prize. “It was kind of magical.” Serre stands just over five feet tall, with short, cropped hair that frames a sly smile. Her petite frame is hunched over a laptop next to her sister Justine when I arrive, and her demeanour is all business. Hanging on the far wall are the two collections responsible for her win, “15-21” and “Radical Call for Love,” designed during her student days at La Cambre-Mode in Brussels. It was a jury of industry legends had decided her fate, among them Karl Lagerfeld (whose own career launched after winning a design prize in 1954) and Louis Vuitton's Nicolas Ghesquière. Serre, who joined Balenciaga as a design assistant in March, hadn't expected to win. In fact, she didn't think she was established enough to apply to the first place, despite the interest in her graduate collection from such influential stockists at The Broken Arm boutique in Paris and H. Lorenzo in Los Angeles. It was a scout from the French luxury group who asked the designer in January to participate in the competition against 1,200 other hopefuls. “[Our decision] was quite unanimous,” Ghesquiere told Vogue shortly after her name was read. “It was the way she represents dressing today: the sports clothes, the body consciousness, and a kind of romanticism and femininity. It really speaks of [this] generation.” Serre thinks her win bodes well for emerging talent in an industry that is increasingly shaped by the corporate parent companies like LVMH and Kering that financially back the major fashion houses. “That this big and huge company is actually giving a chance to someone like me, who is independent of them…I think it gives a lot of hope to people,” says Serre. “It's hard for a lot of designers today because things move so quickly. I don't want to do it only to make money.” Serre's designs contain multitudes. The two collections she's produced to date deftly combine a range of techniques, silhouettes and fabrics, from lycra and velcro to screen-printed moiré. Much of her genius lies in the details. The tag inside one especially remarkable coat, with an open collar that brings to mind the work of Cristóbal Balenciaga, reads: “Orange Recovery Blanket, Satin Ribbon, Brussels, 2015.” The lapels of another jacket are fastened by small, tear-drop shaped French porcelain doorknobs. Her pairing of colour is masterful, too: The bell sleeves of a tailored camel coat lined in a burnished orange, a kelly green sports top contrasted with a skirt of sky blue. Like that other great alchemist of colour, Raf Simons, Serre doesn't draw. That is because she “never sees things flat,” she says. “It's important for me that you should dress directly and see how it fits on someone real.” While her collars and colour palettes are plenty worthy of admiration, it's Serre's adroit fusion of styles, periods and references - a mish-mash of karakous, kaftans and other 19th-century silhouettes, combined with the materials and cuts of ‘90s sportswear - that makes her work unlike anything else on the runways. It's encapsulated in the crescent moon that appears throughout “Radical Call for Love” - equal parts modern sports logo and Islamic art reference. The moon is also the symbol of the woman, and Serre revels in the plethora of meaning. “It's something for me that is a beautiful form, and then in another way it's referring to a sportswear brand. So it's also just playing with what is fashion today and playing also with branding,” says Serre. “I think it's really beautiful, I'm not making a joke. I have irony, but I also think irony can be serious.” She plans to use the symbol again in her next collection, which she's hoping to debut in January 2018. The initial inspiration for “Radical Call for Love” came from the terrorist attacks in Brussels and Paris between 2015-2016 and Serre's desire to braid the tensions of the East and West into something beautiful - a peace offering of sorts. Serre lived in Marseille and Brussels before moving to Paris in September 2016. All of the clothing and shoes in the lineup - 35 designs in total, three that have been added since its initial debut at La Cambre - are made either in a little atelier in Brussels or in France. One thousand pieces from the collection will be stocked for Autumn/Winter 2017 by Dover Street Market and Opening Ceremony. Isabelle Huppert and Ariana Grande have both been photographed in pieces. Buyers have been watching Serre with keen interest for months. Guillaume Steinmetz, Anaïs Lafarge, and Romain Joste, the three founders of The Broken Arm in Paris, say it's difficult to explain what exactly drew them to the young designer, “because the collection of Marine has generated for us an irrational emotion,” they wrote in an e-mail to Vogue. “Ninety-nine percent of the time another designer who tried to mix this kind of fabric with this kind of colours will do something that is too much, but not with her, she is an equilibrist. You can't really explain or define why you like it. That's exactly what we are looking for, when it's a little bit uncomfortable, not easy to catch.” The next few months will be big ones for the designer, who will leave her role at Balenciaga after its next show and put a team together to start on her next collection. (“Come on, I cannot have two jobs at the same time, it's impossible!” she says with a laugh.) But first, a brief pause. After a year of mounting accolades, press requests and industry acclaim, Serre will take a much-needed holiday in the Pyrenees - with only the open sky and crescent moon for distraction. column1: Nineties’ favourite label Helmut Lang to come back with a new look
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's what to expect Some things you need to know about Helmut Lang: this man exerted total control over fashion in the Nineties. He was one of the first designers to embrace the internet, broadcasting his new show online in 1998. He was responsible for New York Fashion Week moving from the end of the month-long fashion show schedule to the beginning. He was obsessively attentive to detail. He ushered in a decade of minimalism. A generation of fashion editors grew up aspiring to own a black Helmut Lang suit and gold-tipped shoes. Then, in 2005, he quit. Helmut Lang the man now lives as an artist in East Hampton. Helmut Lang the brand, however, is about to get a serious reboot. At its helm is Dazed and Confused's editor-in-chief Isabella Burley, operating under the title “editor-in-residence”. Burley, the chief executive Andrew Rosen outlined in March, will oversee all creative aspects of the brand, and will sign up individual designers to work on solo collections, beginning with Shayne Oliver of Hood By Air. Sounds like a strange set-up? Burley spoke exclusively to Vogue on Wednesday as phase one of the Helmut Lang relaunch got underway. column1: Michael Kors is to buy Jimmy Choo for £900 Million
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you need to know Michael Kors is to buy British luxury shoe and accessory brand Jimmy Choo for £900 million, reports The Guardian. At auction, bids came from a host of competitive international names with the luxury goods brand coming out on top. The US-based business has agreed on a sum of 230p per share, with board directors - who currently own 1.3 per cent - agreeing to the "fair and reasonable" terms of acquisition. Additionally, unless a third party presents an additional offer, this agreement is "final and will not be increased." The founders of Jimmy Choo - Tamara Mellon and Jimmy Choo - are no longer involved with the shoe brand, whose strappy stilettos have reached cult status. In April this year, majority shareholder JAB Luxury placed the business on the market and will sell its six per cent hold to focus on other areas of growth. While changes are being made financially, Pierre Denis, who has run Jimmy Choo since 2012, will remain at the helm with creative director, Sandra Choi, staying in her role also. Choi is expected to gain £2.2 million for her stake in the business, Denis £6.2 million. Speaking of the acquisition, Michael Kors himself described the new partnership as "ideal", while chief executive, John Idol, added: “Jimmy Choo is known worldwide for its glamorous and fashion-forward footwear. The company is a leader in setting fashion trends. Its innovative designs and exceptional craftsmanship resonate with trendsetters globally. We believe that Jimmy Choo is poised for meaningful growth in the future and we are committed to supporting the strong brand equity that Jimmy Choo has built over the last 20 years.” The article was originally published on Vogue.co.uk Fashion What's New What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Anamika Khanna’s couture 2017 line covers every person in the bridal party
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Take a close look View Gallery 27 Photos Anamika Khanna at India Couture Week 2017 Runway shows aren't for every designer's clothes. If you see a model walk a floral Anamika Khanna lehenga all the way up to the head ramp and back in 60 seconds, you'd be hard pressed to distinguish the print from the embroidery, the metallic threadwork from the fabric and the architecture of its drape. Last evening, Anamika Khanna started off India Couture Week 2017 with an installation presentation at The Kila in Seven Style Mile, New Delhi, where attendees got the chance to see the complete collection up close and personal. Visibly relaxed than backstage at a runway show, the designer was interacting with guests who were busy admiring the couture on display. The collection ‘Happily Ever After' offered sartorial solutions for the bride and the bridal party for the events preceding the Indian wedding and the wedding itself. The idea came to Khanna upon browsing an old book someone had written about their wedding, “It struck me then, why don't I just present the whole wedding? Indian weddings and couture go hand-in-hand. Why don't I get in the moods that encapsulate the whole of it?" said the designer. Tracing the welcome lunch, mehendi, cocktail and wedding, the details in the garments were built up to a crescendo that ultimately ended with bridal lehengas. “In each segment, there is the mother of the bride, there is the mother-in-law of the bride, the sister and so on. When we were making the collection, we were like, 'but what will the bride's friends wear?' That's how went through it. You will find that each piece has its own character,” Khanna explains. The jewellery seen along with the clothes was created in collaboration with Birdhichand Ghanshyamdas Jewellers. From pastel long jackets to embellished capes, signature draped trousers to lehengas, each look this season has a purpose. In the ‘cocktail' section of the show, Khanna also introduced organza gowns with unfinished hems, made to mimic feathering, for the ‘western dress code' often demanded at these events. Don't be fooled by the dainty, rose picture the words ‘Happily Ever After' paint; Khanna continues to choose burnished metal finishes in place of shiny brights. Her anthology of draped structures in ethnic wear surpasses any other's work in the country. Amongst black and gold pieces tinged with hints of a tribal aesthetic, the kind a traveller picks up on was one lone, strong pantsuit covered with threadwork. “I don't want them to always wear gowns, I want them to wear pantsuits, that's why!” Khanna offers by way of explanation. The ‘mehendi' and ‘wedding' segments saw a mix of traditional heritage textiles and more embroidery, the combination of which in the hands of Khanna is always breathtaking and never overpowering. “The inside of the garment is embroidered by us but the top of it is a heritage textile. The whole idea behind that was hand-me-downs—brides want to wear their nani's sari too. These are small feelings surrounding weddings that we wanted to encapsulate,” says the designer. At some point Khanna, is brave enough to let go of thought in favour of instinct. Amongst the bridal looks is one embroidered with flowers to such an extent it resembles a fabric. “Flowers are us and each wedding is incomplete without flowers,” she concludes. column1: India shines at International Woolmark Prize’s regional round
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ruchika Sachdeva and Ujjwal Dubey of India move to the finals View Gallery 6 Photos Woolmark Prize It was a double win for India at the regional round for India, Pakistan and the Middle East at the International Woolmark Prize (IWP) held in Dubai last night. Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice (a former Vogue India Fashion Fund Winner) walked away with the women's prize and Ujjwal Dubey's three-year-old label Antar Agni took the men's prize. John Roberts, The Woolmark Company's general manager - Eastern Hemisphere, said, “This region is really known for winning. I think India being hot, understands how to use wool innovatively and being so rich with handcrafts, its designers have such great techniques to work with.” And this win confirms that global fashion is waking up to India's talents—among the previous winners of the International Woolmark Prize have been Rahul Mishra in 2014 and Suket Dhir in 2015 for menswear. Bodice and Antar Agni will now go on to try their hand at being the winners in Florence early next year. As regional winners, they also walk away with a cash prize if AU$70,000 each. The IWP is known to be a door-opener in fashion, with both Yves Saint Laurent and Karl Lagerfeld being previous winners. More recently, Public School and India's very own Rahul Mishra gained the international spotlight after their IWP win. Vogue caught up with both and Ruchika Sachdeva and Ujjwal Dubey minutes after their win: So it has been quite the night for India? Ujjwal Dubey: Yes, both of us (Ruchika and I) are from Delhi. Tell us about the inspiration for the collection, there seems to be a lot of use of drape? UD: It is inspired by Indian nomads. I imagined them looking up to the sky, so you see the midnight blue as well as the air force blue. And the subtle shine in the piece represents the star. I used zari to achieve this. Tell us about the heavy use of layering? Ruchika Sachdeva: I just want to make clothes that women that can wear. I want women to be comfortable and that is the idea. The middle piece may look like a waistcoat but is actually a stitched shawl using a technique known as extra weft. It is so light. And while the wool might come from Australia, how is this garment representative of India? RS: I travelled all over India for this piece—I worked with Raymond on the 150 GSM wool, so that took me to Mumbai. The texturing on jacket is kantha, a stitch that comes from West Bengal. The shawl piece was hand-loomed in Himachal Pradesh's Kullu. For the finishing, I went to Nagpur to use a special anti-bacterial technique so that the clothes are still hygienic after one wear. Many women told me they feel the need to dry clean clothes after one wash just for hygiene reasons. And the dress with its pleats shape is inspired by the costumes of Nautch (dance) girls of the royal courts in 18th century India. One of the judges, Manish Malhotra, mentioned the importance of clothes having adaptability. Do you feel you achieved this? RS: I have always believed that clothes should be not limited to where they come from. And so what do you have planned for the finals? RS: My mind is already ticking, but it will be an extension of what I have presented here. Fashion People Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Inside Rohit Bal’s extravagant couture 2017 show
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion An ode to craftsmanship Veteran couturier Rohit Bal never strays too far from references to his home state of Kashmir. For couture 2017, the designer presented his collection ‘Shahaan-e-Khas' that pays an ode to Mughal craftsmanship. Given Bal's continued exploration of the theme, there were some usual suspects—the floor grazing angarkhas in ecru, embellished velvet jackets in jewel tones and the bridal looks in burgundy. The show took place at Bikaner House, a building with a colonial touch owned by the Rajasthan Government. Filled to maximum capacity for the cocktails preceding the show, guests inched into the show space and started filling up seats well in advance.
