column1: Prince George at 4: How the young royal is reshaping children’s fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue takes a look at the young prince’s enormous selling power View Gallery 33 Photos Prince George at 4: How the young royal is reshaping children’s fashion Prince George made his first mark on the fashion world when he was merely a day old. 7 million people tuned in to watch his parents ferry the third in line to the British throne—wrapped in a snowy, avian-print swaddling blanket—home from St. Mary's Hospital in London on 23 July 2013. The impact was instantaneous. Within hours the blanket, by New York-based Aden + Anais, had been ordered over 10,000 times, its website had crashed, and, once fixed, its visits spiked by nearly 2,000 percent. This was the first iteration of what has been dubbed the “Prince George Effect”, and since then, his continuous ability to deplete the shops of stock has become a national phenomenon. On his first birthday, the Prince toured the Natural History Museum wearing a simple pair of striped denim dungarees by Petit Bateau. They sold out even before the official picture was released. His first Christmas portrait was met with the same response. Sitting on the steps of Kensington Palace in a sleeveless, already-sold-out Cath Kidston tank top patterned with marching royal guards, shoppers spiralled into a festive frenzy, and the store rushed to re-add the knit to its range. Accompanying his parents on their tour of New Zealand in 2014, the Prince modelled a pair of Rachel Riley dungarees, cheerfully adorned with sailing boats. Within moments of the picture appearing online, they sold out in two sizes. The brand was suddenly swamped with international orders, a trend that has continued to the present day—particularly in countries like the US, where interest in the Royal Family runs high. “[Prince George] has certainly led to increased global demand for our collections”, Riley tells Vogue. After his tour of New Zealand, the young prince arrived in neighbouring Australia dressed in a Les Petites Abeilles romper suit that riffed on the nautical theme again. Besotted customers were added to a two-month waiting list. Later that year, he sported a pale-blue sweater with his name emblazoned across the chest. It promptly became a bestseller, racking up 1,200 orders on My1stYears.com in subsequent days. Marcus Tagesson, chief executive of the premium retail site The Luxury Kids Group, says the impact the Prince can have on sales is immediate and tangible: “As with the so-called ‘Kate effect', anything Prince George wears, we will see demand for those items increase quite considerably”. Although Prince George's sell-out skills remain largely unrivalled—except by his sister, Princess Charlotte—he isn't the only high-profile child currently causing a stir in the fashion industry. Harper Beckham, the six-year-old daughter of David and Victoria Beckham, is particularly well put-together, with a rotating wardrobe of Burberry, Chloé and Stella McCartney. Kim Kardashian West and Kanye West's four-year-old daughter, North, has been known to carry a mini Louis Vuitton tote, and, in 2016, mother and daughter attended West's Madison Square Garden concert in matching silver sequinned Vetements dresses. Beyoncé and Jay-Z's five-year-old daughter, Blue Ivy, also seems to have developed a penchant for designer dressing, accompanying her mother to the 2016 Video Music Awards in New York in a Mischka Aoki dress replete with a four-foot tulle train, Giuseppe Zanotti shoes and a tiara. View Gallery 9 Photos Celebrity Children As the sartorial choices of these celebrity children are shared, scrutinised and copied, the childrenswear industry is booming. Back in 1967, Dior led the charge, opening Baby Dior, but it was not until the turn of the millennium that they were joined by a raft of other luxury designers, who spotted the lucrative possibilities of cultivating brand loyalty early. Stella McCartney launched her kids line in 2010, and was followed by the likes of Lanvin, Gucci, Marni and Dolce & Gabbana, who shrunk their sumptuous prints down to pint-size. Over the past five years, growth in the childrenswear market has outstripped both womenswear and menswear, according to Euromonitor research. In the UK, the childrenswear market is set to rise a further 13.2 percent in the next five years, to £6.1 billion. Despite competition from his contemporaries, it was a barely-talking Prince George who was crowned “the world's most influential toddler” by Forbes magazine in 2014, has a clutch of blogs dedicated to his dressing, and according to a study conducted by Brand Finance, is worth roughly £2.3 billion to the British economy. What is it about the Prince George's style that has captured the imagination of parents around the world? His penchant for Peter Pan collars and Start-rite shoes, supplemented by the occasional knee-high sock for a touch of impish, Just William-style charm, don't instinctively chime with the Instagram generation; his stripy cotton T-shirts could be considered no match for Blue Ivy's trails of tulle. The appeal of Prince George's style is that it firmly twists poeticism with pragmatism. It is sweet, but not staid, traditional but not out-of-touch. Its power, just like his mother's, is that it errs reassuringly on the side of normalcy. As Taggeson says, “William and Kate seem to dress George in really great-quality, functional pieces. Many of the brands they favour are at the mid-price point too, meaning attaining their style is much more accessible to parents”.  Take the coat he wore on his first day at Westacre Montessori school in Norfolk. Navy blue and quilted, with corduroy elbow patches and a tartan-lined hood, it was £30, and from John Lewis. After pictures emerged, the store reportedly experienced a 447 percent surge in enquiries for similar items. Sarah Coonan, head of buying for beauty, home and children's at luxury department store Liberty London, notes that Prince George's championing of simple, quintessentially childlike styles has sparked a wider movement across the entire industry, bolstering independent, established brands and the high street rather than high fashion. “I think there is a shifting aesthetic towards something more traditional”, she says. “Prince George has definitely been a factor in this changing aesthetic, particularly in the growth we've seen in terms of classic brands”. “In fact”, she adds, “we frequently have customers ask us if we stock anything he has worn”. column1: Twinkle Khanna’s complete style evolution
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion An account of Mrs Funnybones’ sartorial history View Gallery 29 Photos Twinkle Khanna’s complete style evolution Twinkle Khanna, former actor, now wears many hats including but not limited to interior designer, producer, author and columnist. She is the author of Mrs Funnybones published by Penguin in 2015 and The Legend Of Lakshmi Prasad published by Juggernaut in 2016. She authors weekly blogs for a national daily and in her own words, “firmly believes that nothing in life is sacred except laughter.” Born into a Bollywood family, Khanna chose to follow the footsteps of her parents Dimple Khanna and Rajesh Khanna debuting in the 1995 film Barsaat. After working in films like Dil Tera Diwana (1996), Jab Pyaar Kisise Hota Hai (1998), International Khiladi (1999), Mela (2001) and Jodi No. 1 (2001), Khanna slowly transitioned into the role of a producer. She has co-founded Grazing Goats Pictures, the production company that has churned out films like Tees Maar Khan (2010) and 72 Miles (2013). The multi-hyphenate also co-owns a chain of interior decor stores—The White Window and has designed the homes of Bollywood actors like Tabu, Rani Mukerji and Kareena Kapoor Khan. Style files Fashion was never on the radar for Khanna, who has earned a solid fan following for her satirical brand humour that she unleashes on all things misogynistic and politically ludicrous. We'll admit we're not fans of the peeptoes that could have been abandoned in the early Noughties, but in the recent past, Khanna has been serving some serious style that's caught our radar. Style evolution of Twinkle Khanna Back in 2010, Twinkle Khanna was spotted in Hervé Leger bandage dresses and animal print. Jackets, blouses and easy dresses are staples of the mom-on-the-go's wardrobe. In 2015 she switched to printed trousers and culottes. In 2016, Khanna moved on to ripped denim and experimenting with accessories. In 2017, she was named the L'Oréal Professionnel ambassador and has been seen more often in public. It can be said the Khanna has been more experimental with her style, which has oscillated from a traditional Raw Mango sari to crisp white separates for the airport and a ruffled asymmetric number by Self-Portrait. column1: Your exclusive first look at Shivan & Narresh’s new flagship store
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You may have to plan a vacation just for this View Gallery 5 Photos Your exclusive first look at Shivan & Narresh’s new flagship store We've seen Shivan & Narresh's vintage swimwear in that Wes Anderson-esque pool scene in Life of Pi, and we've applauded them as the first Indian brand to showcase at the Mercedes Benz Fashion Week back in 2011. So it's no surprise that the young entrepreneurs have continued to expand their luxury brand—this time with a gorgeous new flagship store at the DLF Emporio in New Delhi. A reflection of the brand's beach and resort wear, the store was inspired by the sails of a boat, bringing out their signature minimalist design philosophy with shades of elegant ivory and gold. Pops of colour and graphic carpets complement the space's natural lighting and indoor greenery, making it look like something right out of Sex and the City. The cherry on top is that the store itself smells like the wind at that destination wedding you were shopping for. Shivan & Narresh partnered with an Italian perfumery to develop a fragrance for the store that mixes notes of tropical flowers for a scent reminiscent of the Mediterranean coast. Shivan & Narresh, which made its name by becoming the first resort wear brand to do 100 per cent handcrafted and stitch-free swimwear, has always aimed to make it a staple in Indian wardrobes through their ready-to-wear and ‘made to measure' services. In addition to the brand's swimwear classics, the new store will feature accessories and a men's collection as part of its effort to become a leading address for destination wedding, holiday and honeymoon essentials. The Destination Bride line, for instance, will feature their skeinwork skirts and sarees while other resort necessities, like kaftans and pareos, will be readily available. Perhaps most exciting is the store's launch of the brand's second phase of its jewellery collaboration with Crystals from Swarovski, which will help complete your holiday look with its bold bijouterie. If you don't see something you like, fear not, because the store will also offer a service that lets you scan through previous collections, allowing you to shop from the complete range of each season. Shivan & Narresh will open on July 22 at 332A, Second Floor, DLF Emporio, Nelson Mandela Marg, Vasant Kunj, New Delhi Fashion Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This is where to find the world’s most luxurious perfumes in Pune
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Amouage to Nasomatto View Gallery 4 Photos This is where to find the world’s most luxurious perfumes in Pune Pune may not pride itself as first when it comes to most things fashion and luxury, but it does pride itself with India's first luxury perfume store, “Scent Sutra”, that houses some of the world's most exclusive perfume brands—Dali Haute Parfumerie from Paris, Amouage from Oman, and Nasomatto from Italy. Launched by Neha Kedia and Vivek Chidambaram, the duo aims at bridging distances—perfumes that occupy a pride of place at Harrods in London or Harvey Nichols in Dubai or even Printemps in Paris, are now in Pune. Situated in the Nitesh Hub Mall at Koregaon Park, the 425sqft store designed by Kunaal Seolekar, combines French aesthetics, of metal architectural arches, with glass facades and display of tree shelves at the entrance that add to the avant garde experience. Dali Haute Parfumerie There's an unmistakable elegance to the nuances of a Dali—the exceptional way the bottles have designed with several emblems from the Salvador Dali's iconography—the eye, butterfly, hand and watch. So when the celebrated perfumer Alberto Morillas was called on by Dali house to craft fragrances, he wanted to distill the same mix of timelessness and charm into each bottle. Rs 24,000 onwards for 100ml Amouage A luxury perfume house established by the Sultan of Oman, it finds use of choicest of ingredients—silver frankincense, myrrh and rock roses. The women's scents recall the shape of Palace Ruwi Mosque in Muscat while the bottles with men's scents have a shape of Khanjar, the traditional dagger of Oman, both embellished in gold and studded with a Swarovski crystal. When we ask Kedia for her favourite, she points me to Interlude and Epic, “These make use of oudh, which is one of the most expensive perfume ingredients in the world”, she explains. Rs 17,000 onwards for 100ml Nasomatto “I want my perfumes to have an intelligence of their own, not just be slaves to my meaning, ” says Alessandro Gualtieri, the nose behind Nasomatto perfumes. The bottles are packaged beautifully and finished off with a wooden cap. It's also worth noting that some of the fragrances—Absinth, Baraonda, Black Afgano, Blamage and Hindu Grass, are unisex. We fell for Narcotic that has top notes of white floral, tuberose that makes it perfect to wear during the day. Rs 10,000 onwards for 30ml Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Longchamp opens its second store in India
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Details this way View Gallery 5 Photos Longchamp open its second store in India From creating the world's first leather-clad smoking pipes to designing the iconic La Pliage bag, it's evident that Longchamp's story is anything but ordinary. The next chapter? A sprawling space in Mumbai. As the storied French house opens the doors to its second store in the country, Vogue sits down with artistic director Sophie Delafontaine on everything from the latest collection to the biggest challenge she faced bringing the label to Mumbai. What prompted you to bring Longchamp to Mumbai? The idea was to build something very strong in India. We feel really confident about the development the label can make in the country. After the store in Delhi last year, we chose Mumbai because while they are both big cities, the type of consumer is different. Tell us about the latest collection in store and the inspiration behind it? For the latest collection, I worked around the art of being a woman which isn't always easy. Today's woman is multifaceted. Sometimes she's a business woman, sometimes she wants to be a cool mom and sometimes she just wants to feel sexy. I wanted to capture all these roles. Our new line Mademoiselle Longchamp represents the many faces of the Longchamp woman. You can carry it in many different ways for different occasion. Did you customise the products to cater to the country? I don't generally cater to a country but to a type of woman instead. I don't care about the nationality or age, it's more a question of spirit. I design for women who are very dynamic, active and self-confident. They are fashionable but not fashion victims. The limited-edition bags are not focused on the Indian woman but are a tribute to India. I've customised them based on how I see the country. If I could have added the fragrance of fresh flowers, I would have. What's the one thing in the store every woman should own? I think every woman should own the Le Pliage bag. It's great because you can use it when you travel, when you play a sport or when you go to work. It's timeless, chic and elegant. Also, I like small bags because sometimes all you need is your iPhone and credit card. What was the biggest challenge you faced when setting up a store in Mumbai? Firstly, the biggest challenge was to find the right partner in India. We are very happy to be working with Radha Kapoor. Secondly, we wanted to let people here know that we have arrived and to make sure they discover our collection, our craftsmanship and our know-how.  That's really why I am here today, to try to explain what Longchamp is. How has the brand evolved over the years? Nearly 70 years ago when my grandfather started, it was just a tobacco stall. He used to cover smoking pipes with leather. He then introduced leather goods for men and luggage. It was only in the '80s when my father joined the company that he started making bags for women. In the '90s he created the Le Pliage. I arrived in the early 2000s and in 2006 we developed the ready-to-wear and eventually shoes. I think we have created a real international luxury brand, which has stayed within the family. At the end of the year, we are going to launch our first eye-wear collection. Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: What anyone buying their first diamonds should know
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We asked an expert View Gallery 4 Photos What anyone buying their first diamond should know Forevermark is a big name in the world of gems. The company is best known for ethically-sourced high quality diamonds. We spoke to Federica Imperiali, head of new product development at Forevermark about investments, trends and the personality of those who wear diamonds. What makes Forevermark diamonds better than the rest? Less than one per cent of the world's diamonds may be eligible to become Forevermark diamonds. In addition to being some of the most beautiful diamonds in the world, they are also responsibly sourced. The promise is given in the unique inscription number on each of them. The inscription is really the assurance that the diamonds are rare, beautiful and of course as I told you, responsibly sourced. What are the biggest trends in jewellery for the upcoming season? For the autumn/winter season we have two main trends, one is declaration. Declaration is all about the power of communication of the jewellery. You will see transformable jewellery as well as pieces that can have a message. The second one is Geo Deco, which is about nature and geometry. How do you determine these trends? Well, the forecasting is a long process for us, it takes about one year and we actually go through different areas, from exhibitions to fashion, cinema, social media and social phenomena. Then we create a big wall on which we put all that we feel is meaningful for us as a brand. We group them and we define the key four trends for the coming season. As you know, being a diamond brand means we should not use trends like in fashion, just to last for a season. We need to be able to create jewellery that is eternal because it may last forever. It is more about the story you're telling than about the creation. What is a good investment to make in jewellery? Diamonds. How would you direct someone who is buying their first diamond? If it is the first diamond, I would say go for a classic. A classic means something that's able to survive over time and can is suitable for a variety of looks and occasions. What are three key jewellery pieces one must own? Stud earrings for sure, and a ring set that is meaningful to you. A diamond is one of the most powerful stones in term of emotional association, so you really need to find the reason and the insight that brings you to make the purchase. It should be something that you can link to, an emotional moment or a memory that should be always with you. It could be on a ring or a pendant, but important is the emotion you associate with it. What are aspirational pieces to aim for to invest in? If it is about the neck area, I would say a two-lined choker; if it is earrings, then I would say chandelier earrings that you can wear with a formal dress or even with a jeans and white T-shirt, and of course a cocktail ring that may be used transversally, among looks and occasion. According to you, how does jewellery describe a personality? Jewellery describes a personality in the way it interacts with the woman who is wearing it. The way you mix and match your outfit, your personality and your approach to jewellery define you as a person. Beauty Fashion What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Is fashion becoming more accepting of the awkward?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion School of uncool View Gallery 15 Photos Is fashion becoming more accepting of the awkward? If you walk into the closest outlet of a fast fashion brand, you'd be hard-pressed to find clothing that's not asymmetric or unfinished, that doesn't give you flashbacks, and last but not least, raise the question—how is this worn? Who took fashion and turned it upside down? In the last few years, runway fashion went through major changes. The spirit of the underground made its way to the mainstream, making room for those who stand left of centre. Alessandro Michele's appointment at Gucci in 2015 ushered in an era of vintage glam and granny chic. Also in 2015, Demna Gvasalia brought the Vetements aesthetic to Balenciaga, erasing any notions of propriety from the luxury house. Virgil Abloh, ex-creative director to Kanye West's label, launched Off-White in 2014, which was name-dropped by every style influencer. Known for his sports-meets-street style, Abloh's dress for Liu Wen this Met Ball had skirt made out of ripped denim. The only thing common between these three distinct yet hugely successful labels is that they're offering the option of being anything but sexy to the luxury customer. You didn't have to be in a bodycon dress on the red carpet any longer. Shirts could do whatever they damned well pleased and nerdy glasses encrusted with rhinestones became a fashion statement. Taking cues from what was on the runway, A-listers started pulling off ‘awkward' style with some grace. Surprisingly, Bollywood stars, whose carefully edited public looks yield commercial appeal, also fell for this. From Katrina Kaif's louche Monse shirt to Priyanka Chopra's oversized, slashed suit, Athiya Shetty's layered Bibhu Mohapatra ensemble and Sonam Kapoor's oversized Chloé coordinates—celebrity style is steadily inching in this direction. Pulling off awkward fashion is also about how a piece is worn. Kendall Jenner's Gorpcore revival is not for the faint of heart. The combination of cropped velour pants, a nylon bag, plastic mules and blazer worn with a sheer bra seen on Kim Kardashian West is for an advanced experimentalist. Our only word of advice while trying out the trend—confidence is key. Fashion What's New What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Style evolution: Aditi Rao Hydari
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Of ripped jeans and lehengas View Gallery 82 Photos Style evolution: Aditi Rao Hydari Aditi Rao Hydari is as popular in Tamil cinema as she is in Bollywood. Having worked with the likes of Farhan Akhtar, Katrina Kaif, Tabu and Amitabh Bachchan, Rao Hydari's career has evolved in the past decade. The same came be said of her sartorial aesthetic, which has come a long way from rosettes and sequinned gowns to ripped boyfriend jeans and tasteful Indian ethnic wear. Screen time The Hyderabadi native first appeared on screen in 2006 in the Tamil film Srigaram. She won her first Screen Award in the Best Supporting Actress category for the 2011 romantic thriller Yeh Saali Zindagi directed by Sudhir Mishra. In the same year, she starred alongside Ranbir Kapoor and Nargis Fakhri in Rockstar. In 2013, she played a lead role in Murder 3 and another supporting role in the film Khoobsurat (2014) with Sonam Kapoor and Fawad Khan and. 2016 was another important year in the actor's career, having starred with Amitabh Bachchan and Farhan Akhtar in Wazir and in Fitoor with Tabu and Katrina Kaif. The star is currently shooting for Sanjay Leela Bhansali's period drama Padmavati along with Deepika Padukone, Ranveer Singh and Shahid Kapoor. Early years Back in 2013, Aditi Rao Hydari was a fan of bold colours, platform peep toes and the occasional all-over sequinned dress. The star slowly transitioned on to skater silhouettes, choosing cocktail dresses in solid tones. Evolution Sophistication on the red carpet came by way of streamlined looks and clean make-up towards the later half of 2015. In the course of her sartorial evolution, the star was seen favouring Indian wear, which she pulled off with easy grace and continues to, even now. In the recent years, Rao Hydari's downtime style has featured ripped boyfriend denim, easy shorts and athleisure. While Indian silhouettes continue a place of prominence in her wardrobe, her red carpet style is often seen on best dressed lists. Here's a closer look at Aditi Rao Hydari's style evolution. column1: Shaadi by Marriott is a dream luxury wedding collaboration for brides-to-be
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Save the date View Gallery 2 Photos Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla join hands for ‘Shaadi by Marriott’ In an age where wedding planning can dangerously extend itself month after month, it's a blessing when luxury hotels like Marriott step in to save the day. Elevating the experience to the next level is one of the most exciting collaborations of the wedding season. Design duo Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla are tying the knot with hospitality chain Marriott International for a unique event, ‘Shaadi by Marriott'. The bridal event will feature a showcase of the designers' five wedding-ready segments, for each of festivities leading up to the big day, namely, the cocktail, mehendi, haldi, sangeet and of course, the shaadi. From fabrics like organza to duchess satin, the elegant wedding collection infuses a soft Parisian touch with glamour for a range of creations inspired by the ebbs and flows of nature. The silhouettes oscillate between Indian and Western designs, allowing brides-to-be the luxury of a diverse range of looks for each event. Considering the grandeur that accompanies Indian weddings, the event aims to bring brides-to-be a form of wedding preparation that sees them through every step of the way, from finalising catering to that special sangeet lehenga. “At Marriott, it is our endeavour to create a wedding experience that is superlative in its offerings, be it great food, fabulous venue settings, decor and above all, unparalleled service levels,” said Khushnooma Kapadia, director of marketing for South Asia for Marriott International Inc. The glamorous event is sure to put Marriott on the map as a keystone of wedding planning in India—a position that requires, as Kapadia mentioned, “a promise of faith, trust, quality and value.” ‘Shaadi by Marriott' will be held on July 21 at JW Marriot, New Delhi Aerocity, 8pm onwards Fashion Weddings Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Winter wear essentials you should start investing in
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Bundle up Winter dressing can prove to be a tricky job. While we are all for celebrating the joy of layering after a long monsoon, what are the right pieces of winter wear to look for? What is the right time to invest in a coat? How many do you really need every season?  You can stock up on winter wear through the year if you know what to invest in. Get a head start by shopping for the right pieces. Coats are obviously the most important investment to make when it comes to winter wear for women. There is no point in skimping out on buying a coat; allocate the larger part of your budget for this. Typically, you need two coats for the season—one that can be worn to work, one that can be worn after hours. Buy the one you need for work first, you can shop for the casual/party coat once the season begins. It's advisable to buy something well-tailored and fitted that goes with pretty much everything. For the weekend and after hours, choose styles with prints and colour. The sweater too, like the coat, can be an expensive buy if you are fussy about materials. If winter in your city doesn't warrant a coat, limit shopping for winter wear to a luxurious sweater. Try and avoid done to death greys and blacks. Look for softer tones of caramel and ecru. Look for detailing that will make the piece more up to date with trends like lace and wide sleeves. Work will require you to be dressed in something sharp and formal for special occasions. Unfortunately, you can't always be seen in something too loud or colourful in the corporate space so look for distinguishing details again that will make your look more unique. Place your bets on power shoulders and military detailing for some statement making winter wear shopping. You may have noticed; a snug fitting outfit is better at avoiding a chill than something roomier. Look or winter dresses that are structured without being too tight for a workday. Fabrics like heavy crepe and tweed or anything with a wool blend is bound to keep you warm without having to layer indoors. After maintain a distance from your beloved denim through the length of the rainy season it's back to reinstate denim in your winter wardrobe. From skinny black jeans with lace up detailing from Zayn x Versus to bubblegum pink jeans by Isabel Marant Étoile, the winter style guide for jeans is only about breaking the norm. column1: Tarun Tahiliani doesn’t want you weighed down by your wedding lehenga
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We speak with him exclusively on his new couture collection View Gallery 6 Photos Tarun Tahiliani doesn’t want you weighed down by your wedding lehenga Indian bridal couture is designed for the bride who demands a larger than life expression on her big day. The combination of rich fabrics, heavy embroidery and serious jewellery adds a few kilos to your person that eventually tend to drag you down on the day of the wedding. But veteran designer Tarun Tahiliani does not think that needs to be the norm. “Couture around the world is known as much for feathery lightness as well as the gravity defining construction—this is where our new couture began, as we thought deeply of lightness so Indian brides can enjoy their wedding and dance in their clothes. That is how we have evolved—by creating a new vocabulary of design. Our clothes need to embody the spirit of our cultural legacy, which has to be updated for the global, peripatetic customer,” says Tahiliani describing his upcoming collection. This season, the designer's presentation titled ‘Tarakanna' draws from the night sky. Tahiliani has worked with Swarovski crystals to give life to his expression that upholds the theme of celestial elegance and lightness. column1: Natacha Ramsay-Levi on what we can expect from her Chloé
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As the new girl at Chloé, Natacha Ramsay-Levi is set to inject the maison with a fresh dose of streetwise Parisian attitude Natacha Ramsay-Levi has been at Chloé for all of six weeks when we meet on a Friday afternoon in May, in Paris. Thunderstorms are forecast, and in the plush confines of La Réserve, a grand hotel in the 8th arrondissement, the air is close. But as other diners fan their faces and implore waiters for iced water, Ramsay-Levi remains unruffled. “Chloé for me feels super natural,” she shrugs, settling into a velvet sofa. “I was very ready for the position.” She has come straight from the Vogue shoot in the cavernous Chloé Maison, an ambitious five-floor renovation project 30 seconds from the brand's Avenue Percier headquarters. Its endless Haussmann-style rooms are soon to be filled with an archive, an exhibition and events space, VIP fitting rooms and a press showroom, and parts will be open to the public, including the exhibition of Guy Bourdin's photography for Chloé, which runs until September 3. It's fitting that the new creative director should arrive just as the paint is drying. But if the scale of this project is to be expected of a brand with such blue-chip French fashion credentials and commercial clout as Chloé (this year it will open 12 stores, including a new London flagship), the appointment of Ramsay-Levi is a little more surprising. When her predecessor Clare Waight Keller announced in January she would be leaving after six years at the helm, Ramsay-Levi – a relative unknown – was not the obvious candidate. A devotee of Nicolas Ghesquière, she rose through the ranks to become his design deputy at Balenciaga and then Louis Vuitton over a 15-year period. Hertaste for hard-edged, futuristic androgyny was, on paper, at odds with Chloé's soft-focus, bohemian flou. We order coffee and tiny cubes of chocolate arrive alongside. Natacha is wearing a white T-shirt, a black ruffled Balenciaga skirt (“old, by Nicolas”) and cowboy-style Louis Vuitton boots. She looks simultaneously younger and older than the brooding photographs that accompanied the news announcing her appointment in March: younger, because she is all smiles and no make-up; older, because she has presence informed by typical French candour. She has spent the past few weeks getting to know her team, scouring the archive, adjusting to a fast-paced schedule (“meetings and meetings and meetings”), and beginning in earnest to design her debut collection. Nothing so far has surprised her. “Surprise would not be the good word,” she smiles, the first of many corrections she will make to my questions over the course of our meeting. “It was exactly what they told me, you know. At Chloé, everybody is luminous, joyful, people get along very well together… I need to be in a position where I feel we are all working in the same team, building the same thing. I like to be super open about what I do.” Super open, and super precise. Ramsay-Levi knows where she is going with the 65-year-old brand, exuding the preternatural self-confidence that first endeared the 37-year-old to Chloé president Geoffroy de La Bourdonnaye when they met. “She understood Chloé straight away. She was very compelling,” recalls de La Bourdonnaye. “Chloé is always about freedom. It is very democratic, it does not impose. It is always of the moment, and Natacha understands that.” Her relative youth is another plus point. “I met Gaby Aghion, the founder of Chloé, many times, and Gaby always said to me that youth is very important. What Natacha has is the savoir-faire of the couture atelier, and the savoir-être of the cool young person.” Ramsay-Levi's vision for Chloé is pragmatic. She is keen to emphasise the invitations to personality that the Chloé girl has always been able to seize upon, and frequently returns to its impressive roster of designers – spanning Karl Lagerfeld, Stella McCartney and Phoebe Philo, among others. “It's a house that is about joy, it's about naturalness, easiness, it's about femininity. It's something between maybe the street, the urban style, that has something very easy, and also the sophistication.” She pauses for breath. “Every woman can recognise herself with Chloé. You can really take it and make it personal.” Tellingly, she doesn't see the brand as bohemian – that's not her style. She will undoubtedly give it back some streetwise boyishness for her first show in September, perhaps pairing those classic floaty lace confections with some tomboy suiting – but she shies from the idea of power. She prefers the term strength. “When I think about Chloé, I think about very delicate blouses, something that is pretty sophisticated.” Questions of how her futuristic design principles will evolve to incorporate Chloé's lightness of spirit are immediately dismissed: “I am not doing Natacha's brand, I am doing Chloé's brand. The bags have to stay Chloé, the clothes have to stay Chloé.” Store interiors will also remain in their current guise, though she admits the show location will no longer be the Grand Palais. What key pieces will she focus on for her first collection? “It's kind of a cliché to even say them,” she sighs. “Of course it's the blouse, it's the pants, it's the cape, it's the long dress, the mousseline, the lace – Chloé is very diverse. But I think what is more important than picking up the pieces – it's about the attitude.” She leans back into the dark green sofa. “It's the way you take this DNA and make it talk with the present. And you mix it. And you make it modern. Add a bit of audacity.” Ramsay-Levi is Paris personified. Born and raised in the city, she originally wanted to be a historian, but spent more time during her history degree wrapping fabrics around her body and making clothes for a “super naive” collection with a friend. “One day I realised I was going in the wrong direction for myself and I wanted to be creative. I wanted to dare. So I changed,” she says, simply. Her parents had their reservations about fashion but she enrolled at Studio Berçot fashion school nevertheless. She set her sights on Balenciaga, then helmed by Nicolas Ghesquière, and begged for an internship. Before long she had ingratiated herself with the tiny team by making coffee, and quickly clicked with Ghesquière. She describes her time there as “a love affair”. She has hardly left his side for 15 years: when he left Balenciaga, where he eventually appointed her creative director, he took her to Louis Vuitton to work on prêt-à-porter. “He taught me everything… When I arrived [at Balenciaga] I was obsessed already with what he was doing. I felt it was so strong, I really wanted to be that woman. I thought it was the coolest thing ever,” she enthuses. His influence will undoubtedly inform her work at Chloé. “I always think about him, nearly every day,” she smiles bashfully. A topic she returns to continually is his skill in mixing: “He can mix high-end fashion with something that is very pop, very easy to understand.” She switches off from fashion via family. She lives in central Paris, and is fiercely private about her life outside work. She has a four-year-old son, Balthus, with Olivier Zahm, the provocative founder of Purple magazine, who once publicised their painful break-up on his website. The couple are no longer together, and she is raising his 12-year-old daughter from a previous relationship. “It's the most important thing, spending time with the kids. You forget everything – you don't have a choice.” Ramsay-Levi has the unabashed confidence of someone who runs with a cool crowd and is attuned to success. She doesn't do self-doubt. “I have always been like that in my life. Timings are always good.” Of her career at Chloé, she doesn't foresee any challenges. “The idea of ‘challenge', it's the idea of climbing a mountain,” she frowns. “I don't feel I am climbing a mountain. I feel I am just walking strongly on a path that I love. So, no, I think the question is... I hope everybody will like it and want to wear it. I think that's the only question.”  This article was originally published on Vogue.co.uk What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Sabyasachi Mukherjee just announced his first ever jewellery collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer talks about his venture in an exclusive chat with Vogue Sabyasachi Mukherjee has been single-mindedly persistent in his efforts to resurrect a bygone era of craftsmanship and has only encountered success in these endeavours. Having forsaken the typical couture week schedule over the last few seasons, Mukherjee chooses to drop his complete collections all at one go via Instagram lately, sending his loyal followers into a frenzy. This season, outdoing its own game, the label will be announcing its first ever jewellery line. “I am starting my jewellery business with the same principle with which I started by clothing business. We have been successful with what we do because we have been able to find a gap in the market that others did not see and bought relevance back to these things,” said the designer, whose thought and aesthetic is deep-rooted in old-world Kolkata, or Calcutta, as he prefers calling the city. “I grew up in Calcutta. Calcutta injects a sense of aesthetic into your soul, and things that are seen as unique in other cities are a way of life here. Subconsciously, this way of life has shaped my design identity. It was almost frightening; this city does that to you,” he says. Mukherjee's earliest memory of jewellery was rummaging through his mother and grandmother's closets for treasure. “Their taste was simply exquisite. Perhaps, this is why I feel disappointed, where has all the art gone? Perhaps it was this question that pushed me to find the answer and hence the genesis of my jewellery line. When women wear my clothes, I invariably expect them to pair it with that kind of jewellery,” he concludes. column1: How to get Game of Thrones style for season 7
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Channel Game of Thrones' fashion in the real world View Gallery 16 Photos How to Get Game of Thrones Style for the Season Seven Premiere Game of Thrones finally returns. The show's seventh and penultimate season will at last set the stage for the series' climax, as the few remaining contenders battle among themselves (and against a far greater threat) to rule from the Iron Throne. Looking back, it is impossible to overstate the impact GOT has had for the past six years—not only on pop culture, but on fashion in particular. Note the medieval grandeur and witchy romance that has flitted across the runways since 2011. Designers have always loved the opulence of high fantasy, and there is plenty of that in Westeros, if you ignore the heads on pikes. Then there is the cult of Daenerys Targaryen, whose empowered khaleesi struck a serious chord. Yet on its most basic level, Game of Thrones is simply entertaining, and working a bit of Westeros into your own wardrobe should be more fun than anything else. Why not reach for a dramatic black cashmere shawl draped with fur, then double it up with a leather breastplate of a dress? It's just the thing for brooding about climate change (just take it from Jon). A high-necked Dries Van Noten blazer is better suited for Lannister plotting—even better when topped with a chain-link choker—while a Daenerys-style white draped-sleeve gown from Roland Mouret says, “Yes, I am the hero.” If a queenly floor-length frock feels a bit much, one might instead take a page from Arya's Braavosi playbook and slip into cropped linen trousers and a comparatively breezy ruff neck, or celebrate the series in even subtler ways—a Gucci wolf head ring, the Dornish swagger of a leather Zana Bayne harness, or simply a head of perfectly styled, ice- and fire-resistant curls. column1: Anita Dongre’s latest couture collection tells a beautiful tale of sacrifice
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Exclusive first look at the 'Tree of Love' View Gallery 7 Photos Anita Dongre’s latest couture collection tells a beautiful tale of sacrifice Anita Dongre is consistently drawing from the heritage of Rajasthan for her eponymous couture label. This season, the designer narrates the tale of the Tree of Love, an ominous one of sacrifice and morals. The Kherjarli village in the Jodhpur district gets its name from the ‘khejri' trees popular in the region, considered sacred by the Bishnoi tribe that inhabits the village. Legend has it that Maharajah Abhay Singh of Jodhpur ordered the trees to be chopped down, and in trying to save them, several Bishnois sacrificed their lives. Dongre pays homage to these trees by way of her couture collection where the tree is a recurring motif. Dongre's ethical fashion vertical Grassroot works in association with several NGOs across the country and the designer has carried some of those principles into the new line. “The range sees western influences with glorious gowns in tulle and silk, long-sleeved hand-embroidered jackets finished off with an obi belt, frilly skirts in organza and tulle, floor-length embellished tabards, short embellished kurtas and hand-embroidered dresses. The clear winner, however, is the floor-length jacket hand embroidered by the women artisans of SEWA (Self Employed Women's Association),” said the designer. column1: Shantanu & Nikhil’s couture 2017 collection is not your usual wedding wear
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s why View Gallery 26 Photos Shantanu & Nikhil’s new approach to couture will make you rethink what you know about Shantanu and Nikhil Mehra got a head start at couture week this year by making a solo presentation almost a week ahead of the main schedule. Set against the colonial backdrop of The Imperial Hotel in Janpath, the venue for the Shantanu & Nikhil show was the same hotel where Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, Lord Mountbatten, Mahatma Gandhi and Mohammad Ali Jinnah discussed the Partition of India. The label has previously invoked themes of strength and discipline in its body of work, through presentations like ‘The Cabinet Mission' and ‘The Mutiny'. This time, the label's collection was titled ‘The Regiment', which the designers described as a salute to those who protect our country. The designers laid down their expression of couture, drawing inspiration from the uniforms of the Indian Air Force, Navy and Army. Aestheticised band jackets, camo saris and gowns, bandhgalas with braided detailing and pleated jackets formed the lineup. “Modesty is very Shantanu & Nikhil because less is always more for us, we believe in minimalism, which is very difficult to carry forward in couture, so it's almost as though we need to disrupt ourselves. We go beyond the skill of the artisans, beyond the hand embroideries into structure and silhouettes,” the designers commented after the show. By using drapes often seen in womenswear on men's kurtas, and adopting jacket construction reserved for menswear for womenswear, the designers are opening a dialogue about the democratisation of fashion between the sexes by way of their work. In the context of Indian couture, which is spoken about in the same breath as bridal couture, Shantanu & Nikhil carves a spot for minimalism and structure. “It's a very functional take on occasion wear. It's not necessarily catering to the bride, but it is for the friends of the bride and the attendees,” said Shantanu Mehra on their positioning. column1: Vero Moda champions the cause of sustainable fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Equal parts cool and conscious View Gallery 16 Photos Vero Moda champions the cause of sustainable fashion Just by the nature of its operations, fashion can take a toll on the environment. Fast fashion has been criticised for its contribution to global warming, waste disposal hazards, and the alarming working conditions of the employees manufacturing the clothes. Given the heat brands face on the matter, creating a conscious fashion industry is the need of the hour. 'Aware' is Vero Moda's first step towards bridging this gap between fast fashion and a more sustainable world. Equal parts cool and conscious, this standalone collection is packed with covetable staples made from four eco-friendly materials, namely, tencel, recycled polyester, recycled cotton and organic cotton, that reduce the load on natural resources used during production. Vogue catches up with Malene Malling, creative director at Vero Moda, at their headquarters in Denmark, who tells us everything she envisions for the Danish womenswear brand. How has the label evolved since it started? Vero Moda has been on a very interesting journey since it was launched 30 years ago. We try to keep our clothing on trend, with good quality that is accessible at a great price. Take us through the Aware collection and the inspiration behind it. It's hard to ignore the impact the fashion industry has on the planet and the environmental challenges we face. Aware rethinks wardrobe staples and the classics in a sustainable way. Every item in this collection has a Scandi-chic touch of elegant modernity. Besides, it complements the current Vero Moda collections and is also easy to style with your existing wardrobe. How are you changing your offering to cater to a larger audience that doesn't only include millennials? I believe that great taste doesn't come with an age tag. I am inspired by super cool, young girls and sophisticated and stylish elderly women alike. For me, great taste and great style is not about age. It is about knowing what suits you, dressing according to your mood, and being a little adventurous. What, according to you, are some of the biggest trends of the season? Strong denim, slip dresses, beautiful colours, pyjama suits—but then I find the feminine, masculine dialogue forever interesting. Have you customised your products to suit the tastes of the Indian audience? If yes, how? I think of India as a cool, fashion-forward place so I haven't changed it for the Indian market. Just like the collection hasn't been changed for Paris. It is an international collection with a lot of pretty pastels and reds that look beautiful in the stunning India light. How important is social media to high street brands? Used in the right way, social media can be hugely influential. It can inspire as well as inform. And it can keep a constant dialogue going with your customers. Aside from having Vero Moda on Instagram, I have just launched MM/VM on Instagram, because it is a great way of showing cool girls wearing our clothes. Real women with life experience and attitude who are beautiful, but also so much more than that. How do you think online shopping is changing the current fashion scene?  It is giving power to the consumer, because it means that you [the consumer] can show fashion houses what you actually want, and not be so dependent on someone having bought a particular style for their store. It is making the current fashion scene exiting, fresh. And more daring. However, I also love entering a well-edited shop where the owner clearly gets what the customer wants. Where do you envision your label in the next 10 years? It will be the most interesting fashion brand on high street. Are there any collaborations in the pipeline? We have lots of really exciting new stuff going on at Vero Moda all the time. One of the amazing things about the fashion industry is that it doesn't stand still, that it keeps evolving. However, other than that, my second MM/VM collection is coming out in October. The Aware collection will be available starting October 2017 at select Vero Moda stores in the country What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Would you be okay with your man carrying a tote bag?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Let’s talk about men and their tote bags Man bags aren't a new thing. They've been everywhere for a while—remember Joey from Friends? There's an entire episode of that show from 1999 dedicated to the goofball's newfound love for a simple black purse. (”At first, I thought it just looked good, but it's practical too,” he said. “Check it out! It's got compartments for all your stuff! Your wallet! Your keys! Your address book!”) Now, the man bag is no longer a novelty: Also known as a “murse,” it's worn under the arms and across the chest, in forms ranging from satchels to messenger bags. Proponents have included a buff David Beckham, a cool A$AP Rocky, and a hip Pharrell. The latest incarnation of the man bag? The “mote”—a men's tote bag. Just a few weeks ago, Balenciaga's dadcore-themed Spring 2018 men's show included slews of tote bags in sleek leather, and a can't-miss-it lime green raffia piece. Louis Vuitton showed a monogrammed version, while J.W.Anderson had large knit totes. The piece also made cameos on the street during men's fashion week: Many showgoers wore the tote in cloth form, clutching the formless carryalls in their hairy hands or slinging them over strong shoulders. But despite their ubiquity on the street, tote bags seem to carry some baggage, especially those dime-a-dozen, cheaply made cloth ones, which function as a lazy substitute for a briefcase or a computer bag. On a man, in my opinion, it's a cringeworthy accessory that suggests he's as formless and bland as the bag itself. And even men seem to understand this. A male friend who works in tech has long been conflicted about his tote-carrying ways, noting that it made him “feel like a ninny, and has a frequency with which it gets tangled on my arm.” Photographer Daniel Arnold also shared some choice words. “Hate and wear. It makes me look like a babysitter, which I can say because I have been a major babysitter,” he emailed. ”Part of it is that, at least in my life, tote bags are always freebies. You never pick out a tote bag that you like. They're always advertisements for whoever gave them to you, which adds to the shame of wearing them.” Women seem to agree. In a recent Facebook poll I conducted, one friend felt forced to defend her tote-carrying boyfriend's manliness: “He carries snacks! Like apple, dried fruit, almonds, duh!” she wrote, adding: “My boyfriend is very masculine, I swear!” Vogue.com fashion writer Brooke Bobb sees the genre as “a pseudo-intellectual thing,” explaining that she frequently spots men with bookstore totes. (True, the item does remind me of a some dorky guy bent over like a right angle carrying textbooks back from his master's-in-philosophy class.) Still, men who tote are everywhere, and in light of the item's recent runway resurgence, I did some soul-searching to come to terms with them. Part of my aversion may stem from the idea that men should be low-maintenance, and that a bag—any bag—indicates otherwise. After all, what on earth could they be carrying? They have pockets for their necessities—there should only be two, right?—keys and a wallet. And they can stuff those into their pockets without a care about bulking up their silhouette. But then I remember that this is 2017, a time when busy people need iPads, lunches, books, charging cords, and yes, snacks. (All those Balenciaga dads have to carry diapers and bottles in something.) And not every guy wants to be weighed down by all the pockets, hardware, and general bulk of a backpack or briefcase. As for the mote's manliness factor, even that may be changing: Just look to the 6'4", 220-pound basketball star Dwyane Wade, who, alongside his purse-carrying wife Gabrielle Union, recently was spotted carrying Thom Browne's “Hector” tote bag, an actual leather bag in the shape of a dog. What was he carrying in there? Who knows. But his barrel-chested message for men who tote seems to be to simply tote with confidence—and perhaps invest in a leather version while you're at it. column1: Iconic store Colette Paris has shocked all by closing its doors for good
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The end of an era Instagram.com/colette “As all good things must come to an end, after 20 wonderful years, Colette should be closing its doors on Dec 20 of this year,” the store said in a statement this morning, reports WWD. “Until our last day, nothing will change. Colette will continue to renew itself each week with exclusive collaborations and offerings, also available on our website Colette.fr.” The three-story space, located on Rue Saint-Honoré, is one of the top shopping destinations for editors and style aficionados alike in the city, thanks to its mix of the latest brands, contemporary collections and exclusive capsule edits with more niche and quirky items including books, souvenirs and filming equipment and - of course - its legendary café.   Founded in 1997 by Colette Roussaux - who lived above the retail space with her daughter Sarah Andelman, the current creative director of the store - the 8,000-square-foot space has played host to the hottest merchandise available and cemented its reputation for spotting the next-big-thing 10 times over. “It's the only shop where I go because they have things no one else has," Karl Lagerfeld told the Business of Fashion last year. "I buy watches, telephones, jewellery there - everything really. They have invented a formula that you can't copy easily, because there is only one Colette and her and Sarah are 200 per cent involved." Toutes les bonnes choses ont une fin. Après vingt années exceptionnelles, colette devrait définitivement fermer ses portes le 20 décembre prochain. Colette Roussaux arrive à l'âge où il est temps de prendre son temps ; or, colette ne peut exister sans Colette. Des échanges ont lieu avec Saint Laurent et nous serions fiers qu'une Marque aussi prestigieuse, avec qui nous avons régulièrement collaboré au fil des années, reprenne notre adresse. Nous sommes ravis du grand intérêt que Saint Laurent a montré dans ce projet, ce qui pourrait constituer une très belle opportunité pour nos salariés. Jusqu'au dernier jour, rien ne changera. colette continuera de se renouveler toutes les semaines comme d'habitude, avec une sélection unique et de nombreuses collaborations, également disponibles sur notre site colette.fr Nous vous remercions pour votre confiance, et à bientôt chez colette, jusqu'au 20 décembre! #colette BREAKING NEWS As all good things must come to an end, after twenty wonderful years, colette should be closing its doors on December 20th of this year. Colette Roussaux has reached the time when she would like to take her time; and colette cannot exist without Colette. Negotiations are under way with Saint Laurent and we would be proud to have a Brand with such a history, with whom we have frequently collaborated, taking over our address. We are happy of the serious interest expressed by Saint Laurent in this project, and it could also represent a very good opportunity for our employees. Until our last day, nothing will change. colette will continue to renew itself each week with exclusive collaborations and offerings, also available on our website colette.fr We thank you for your support and see you soon at colette--until December 20th! column1: What to wear for a run in the rain
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Invincible you If you're serious about running, there's nothing more frustrating than skipping a session in the week owing to bad weather. It's obvious that the rain outside will cause some chaos in your regimen, either retiring you to the treadmill or not running at all. One can argue about the downside of spending too much time on the treadmill, which can cause unnecessary impact to your knees and lower back. The good news is that you can continue your endurance training while it drizzles outside without getting soaked, at the cost of making a few necessary changes in your wardrobe. Here's how: Avoid layers Avoid layering when it comes to clothing. Wet clothes tend to get heavy as they retain moisture. Wear fewer layers when you go for a run. Swap a jersey top in favour of a rash guard that is quick drying. Prevent chafing Running shorts might not be the best choice of garment in the rains as they might cause chafing against wet skin. Either choose leggings or look for performance shorts with inbuilt tights for the run. Waterproof when you can It's best to wear a lightweight jacket if the weather outside is cold. Invest in a waterproof shell jacket that will keep your torso dry through the rain. Don't carry accessories in the rain While a host of fitness accessories are waterproof or water resistant, it's best to avoid carrying any of these in the rain. Rain reduces visibility and it is advisable to focus on the task at hand and to avoid any slips and falls. Pick the right kind of shoes You may have noticed that your regular running shoe might not have the best grip against wet terrain. Choose a pair of kicks that offers better traction and support—for this we advise you to read the product description carefully before shopping. Dry your shoes after the rain As soon as you are back from the run, air your shoes to get all the moisture out. You can also stuff them with newspaper so that they retain the shape. Change your clothes Don't waste time hanging around in your running gear post workout. Dry yourself to avoid any possible chances of falling sick in wet clothing. Treat problem areas Friction against certain areas like the waistband and bra straps is sure to make your skin raw. Use Vaseline beforehand to prevent unnecessary irritation during the run. Wear a cap A waterproof cap with a brim will improve chances of visibility when running in rain. Brace yourself from the elements by making the small change. column1: 7 things to know about Lanvin’s new artistic director Olivier Lapidus
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From who he is to what to expect He has just been appointed as artistic director at Lanvin, replacing Bouchra Jarrar in the role, but how much do we know about Oliver Lapidus? Here's an introduction to the man in charge of one of France's most prominent fashion houses. Early Fashion History One of three children, 59-year-old Olivier Lapidus is the son of the famed French designer Edmond Lapidus and his wife Jeanne. Edmond – himself the son of a Russian tailor - was known as Ted. Widely considered to be one of the originators of unisex fashion, Ted established his eponymous fashion house in 1958 and it became popular with a group of the most influential figures of the Sixties and Seventies, including Brigitte Bardot, Françoise Hardy, Alain Delon, Twiggy and John Lennon. In 1989, Olivier took over the design direction of the house and continued its haute couture collections for another 11 years, before calling couture to a halt and focusing the label's efforts on accessories and fragrances. Fashion Credentials Before joining his father's brand, Olivier was artistic director of Balmain Homme from 1985 to 1986, following which he enjoyed a three-year stint in Japan where he created collections for the Miki Group. Following his decade-long tenure at his father's house (1989 to 2000), he moved to Beijing for three years, designing various ranges of objects, furniture, luminous materials, and glassware for lifestyle brands, before returning to France in 2003 where he continued to collaborate with fellow fashion houses. In 2010, he launched Lapidus Vintage, a capsule collection inspired by the archives of his family's fashion house and in 2013 he was tapped to design the interior décor for Hotel Felicien in Paris. The Unconventional Designer At 59 years of age, father of two Lapidus may be older than both his predecessors at Lanvin - Alber Elbaz, 56, and Bouchra Jarra, 46 – but his approach is considered to be a permanently innovative one. French publication Le Monde, credits the designer with “advocating a marriage between haute couture, crafts and industrial research laboratories”, in the Nineties, conceiving dresses with “solar panels, fruit fibres or dust of precious stones”.  While ahead of his time, his vision is one that has attracted criticism, according to the designer himself. "From 89, I was often mistreated and criticised by journalists who did not understand my approach," he told Luxe Magazine in 2007. His Own-Name Label Over the last four years, he has concentrated his efforts on his own fashion house, Creation Olivier Lapidus, which he describes as “an e-couture house” predominantly based on the web. Speaking to Vogue.com following his appointment at Lanvin, he revealed that he will be maintaining his eponymous label simultaneously with his new role: “My house will remain quite exclusive - there's no problem in doing small collections of eight pieces in parallel with my work at Lanvin. My little maison is high tech and experimental.” His brother and sister, Thomas and Eloise, also continued the family profession and work together on Bobo House, a contemporary ready-to-wear label that merges “the femininity of the iconic French woman with the casual charm of the classic California girl”, according to its website. What We Can Expect “When we began discussions, Lanvin was interested by my Internet approach,” said Lapidus. “New technologies can be very pertinent for the oldest couture house in France. Clearly there is something innovative to tap there in terms of positioning and communications.” Despite his contemporary approach, his heart is devoted to preserving the art of couture. “My DNA is couture. I see the value in Jeanne Lanvin; I want to speak to the person she is and mine her DNA. I want to explore techniques and detail and give the brand meaning. We must get back to the fundamentals. There's a story to tell at Lanvin. In all modesty, I'd like to say that I'm going to do Jeanne by the book.” On The Record Lapidis has given many interviews over the years, keen to promote and explain his modernist vision and how he believes fashion and lifestyle should be fused. About the designers that inspire him the most, he told Achica last year: “Jacobsen, Le Corbusier, Jasper Morrison, Patricia Urquiola, Charles Eames, Gio Ponti, Fujita,  Ron Arad, Jonathan Ive, Zanuso, Eileen Gray, Andrée and Sophie Putman, Jean Prouvé, and of course Zaha Hadid who disappeared much too early,  Starck of course and many others”. Of his influences he said: “Creating is also a kind of automatic writing; I'm influenced by some images from the Seventies of my parents in the family workshop and a kind of ‘lost paradise mood' that is evoked by certain pictures: an armchair in silver and orange, a shop in Plexiglas and metal”. And of the most exciting project he has worked on since the start of his career, he responded: “My two kids”. All Eyes On September Despite only being officially appointed this week, Lapidus is expected to turn around his first collection for the house in just over two months, ready to show at Paris Fashion Week in September (“I'll be spending my vacation at Lanvin!” he joked to Vogue.com yesterday). At just 24, Athiya Shetty has made a name for herself with roles in Hindi films and an engaging presence on social media. When she isn't starring in action dramas or musical comedies, Shetty is sharing her distinctive personal style with fans on Instagram. Switching from sumptuous embroidered saris one day to flirty minidresses from Coach the next, Shetty's wardrobe merges traditional pieces with fresh-from-the-runway finds. A second generation actor—her father is '90s Bollywood action star, Sunil—Shetty stepped into the family business with her role in 2015's romantic drama Hero. With photo calls, talk show appearances, and awards shows to attend, Shetty has brought her A-game. column1: Why are we still obsessed with white sneakers?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A trend that may be on its way to becoming a classic View Gallery 17 Photos White Sneakers When athleisure came into being late in 2015, the fashion world breathed a collective sigh of relief. Suddenly what you normally wore to the gym was classified as mainstream fashion. Sneakers had the same importance as a towering stiletto in the wardrobes of so many style influencers, you couldn't help but be relieved to enjoy fashion with comfort for once. Of all the styles that came into prominence—the varsity jacket, visible sports bra, track pants, sneakers are easily the largest segment of products that spawned off collaborations, revivals and sell out sales. But if we had to narrow down to the most seen of all sneakers—it was the simple white ones that were ubiquitous by a wide margin. Major brands are reworking styles that worked for them to offer a new batch season after season. It's perhaps the democracy of the sneaker that volumes find comfort in. Airport travel, yoga class, late night coffee, sequins, dresses—sneakers just fit in and even though we've seen them for nearly four seasons now—there's no sign of retiring the trusty white shoe. Bollywood stars are happy to switch to comfort between events and some wore them to make public appearances too. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and Aaradhya Bachchan pull off mommy-and-me style with matching kicks. Anushka Sharma wore hers with culottes and Alia Bhatt was recently seen wearing a pair with ripped jeans and sweatshirt. Katrina Kaif and Athiya Shetty were happy to take the athleisure favourite to events. Meanwhile, Malaika Arora Khan and Kangana Ranaut deemed them to be the perfect choice of footwear between workouts. With a fresh new batch of squeaky clean sneakers that have been released by major luxury players like Gucci, Burberry, Prada and Balenciaga, we have proof that the white sneaker is well on its way to graduating to a style staple, if not a modern classic, in the near future. column1: Aspiring fashion designers can now study couture at house of Saint Laurent
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Learn from the best Learning from some of the best designers in the world might be out of reach for many blossoming fashion students, but now thanks to YSL, a dream job in couture might just be a reality. As part of a new program launched by the French fashion house, students will now be able to study in a six-month course at Saint Laurent, focusing on innovation and sustainability. A partnership with Institut Français de la Mode and the École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne — two Paris-based fashion schools — the courses will allow students an inside look into the YSL head offices and creative departments. “Preserving our heritage while evolving and being very relevant in our epoch is a pillar of our strategy, and investing in talents is an imperative condition to build on our success even further,” president and CEO of Saint Laurent, Francesca Bellettini, told WWD. The mentorship-like program aims to instill the importance of sustainability in its participants, and is part of Saint Laurent's parent group Kering's wider focus on “future-proofing” fashion. The courses are already open for applications for a September start, and will allow students to present their work to a panel which will include representatives from Saint Laurent. Couture in your sights? Might want to get yourself to Paris, stat. This article originally appeared on Vogue.com.au Fashion Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Olivier Lapidus is Bouchra Jarrar’s Lanvin successor
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion He has been tasked with turning the stalwart into a "French Michael Kors" Following the news that Bouchra Jarrar is to step down as creative director of Lanvin after two collections, it is being reported that Olivier Lapidus will now take on the role. According to Business of Fashion, the designer -- who has previously held roles at Balmain Homme as well as running Maison Lapidus alongside his father, Ted -- started at the French headquarters on Monday and has been tasked with turning the stalwart into a "French Michael Kors." The appointment of Lapidus is not the only change expected for Lanvin. Following news of a 23 per cent drop in revenue in 2016, the title also reports that the company will be moving on from its Boissy d'Anglas HQ - the original location of Jeanne Lanvin's atelier - and instead taking a premises in a more suburban area of north west Paris. The change is being dubbed "the end of an era" for the independent brand which has already seen major change within the last few years. In October 2015, Alber Elbaz - the designer that placed Lanvin as a contemporary fashion house - left his creative director position acrimoniously. In January, it was reported that advisory firm Long Term Partners had been appointed to help the house reduce costs. Vogue has reached out to Lanvin for confirmation. column1: Why you need to consider rain boots this monsoon
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Best boot forward View Gallery 6 Photos Why you need to consider rain boots this monsoon The most uninspiring part about the monsoon—and it sure catches up after the initial Instagrams of coffee mugs against grey windows—is the feeling of constant wetness surrounding you. Whether you step out to go to work or for a run, the trees are dripping, the road is never dry and the need to avoid coming in contact with water is heightened. If you're the kind of person who cannot stand getting your feet wet, you might consider making an extra effort to swap between two pairs of shoes. Wellington boots, or wellies as they are popularly referred to, were worn by Arthur Wellesley, the first Duke of Wellington. These became an official part of hunting gear for the British aristocracy and their functionality caught on. Modern day royals like Kate Middleton and Margot Robbie also see the sense in wearing the boots to protect themselves from the elements. Potholes, public transport and puddles pepper the urban landscape—the process of leaving a dry space feels like making a magnanimous effort. Wellies seem like the thing in this muddy, unpredictable environment that will keep your pedicure intact. Here's how you can get on to the drier side of things. *Look for a sturdy pair of boots in a neutral colour like grey or khaki that will go with most outfits. Avoid lurid patterns and colours if you plan to wear these to work. *Always wear your wellies with a pair of socks inside to avoid blisters. *Wear tapered pants that can be tucked inside your boots for a streamlined look. *Keep a couple of pairs of normal sandals at your workplace that you can change into once you arrive at the office. *Clean your boots from time to time. The exterior is bound to get soiled so take time to wipe your shoes down. You can choose from a buffing spray or a silicone sponge to keep the appearance intact. *Air your wellies. Rubber boots should ideally be cleaned by drying them off with baby powder or simply air them. column1: #SuzyCouture: Dolce & Gabbana Alta Sartoria—The end of the business suit?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Dolce & Gabbana’s sartorial style for men, shown in Sicily’s Palermo, offers a glittering variety of formal and casual wear Swapping local dress for the international business suit has been the mark of a man who has made it – for nearly a century. Even in India or the Middle East, where a globally recognised men's dress code, appropriate to the climate and local customs, still exists, men travelling abroad for work have almost always adopted universal tailoring. The exception is for formal meetings held on home territory—take President Trump's recent visit to Saudi Arabia, for which political figures in the Kingdom wore their traditional clothing. But is this supposition of global businessmen in suits still accurate? Watching Dolce & Gabbana's presentation of Alta Sartoria—meaning “high-level formal wear” in Italian—you can see how the world is changing. This weekend, the models walking by the Duomo (or cathedral) in Monreale, in the hills above Palermo, sometimes wore suits, but the garments were more likely to be created with shimmering silvered scales than with plain, woven fabrics. Then there were the robes—swishing around the piazza where an orchestra played classical music as the audience walked over Persian rugs to be seated on red velvet divans with a gilded flourish. Rather than divide the collection into formal and smart casual, the ensembles were all put together with high-level handwork and could range from a simple T-shirt embroidered with “Monreale” to magnificent patterns replicating the Moorish and Byzantine decorated pillars in the cathedral cloisters, where Domenico and Stefano hosted a sit-down dinner. Both designers are passionate about their couture project and Domenico waxed lyrical about the importance of human connections in a fashion world of mighty brands. “Fashion is not marketing; it is not about money, money, money. Fashion is love,” said the designer as he toured the long tables seating more than 300 clients. He went on to talk about his admiration for the independence of Giorgio Armani and Gianni Versace, saying, “Mr Versace was at his office door at six o'clock every day. This is love.” Translating that passion into their vision of fashion lead to the creation of a Dolce & Gabbana handbook for the show. “Each garment, like every mosaic at Monreale, embodies a constant quest for perfection in beauty and artisanal excellence,” read one description of the duo's work. And that connection with religious faith included coats, jackets and tops with Christian iconography on the back. The concept was that the cathedral, with its Arabian tiles and Baroque decoration, was a starting point in Dolce & Gabbana's thinking process of Sicily's long heritage of absorbing different cultures. And that idea was integral to this section of the four-part weekend of shows that included menswear, womenswear and jewellery for both sexes. Significantly, this menswear made-to-order collection for the international super-rich is targeting clients of different cultures. An African guest, wearing a robe rather than a suit, chased after a model in a more decorative version of his own outfit and ordered one for himself—along with the red velvet shoes with gilded pom-poms. The wife of a Chinese client chose for her husband a casual zippered jacket with dense geometric embroideries creating black-on-white squares and angular patterns. There will surely be a catfight for the impeccably-cut suit smothered in roses and another highly decorative outfit with silver glitter flowers. Or, marginally less showy, wine-red irises embroidered on the back of a jacket with matching silken trousers or palm trees decorating the back of beige trousers. Other tailoring, following the body shape with a curve, was more classic and therefore more predictable in a men's collection. Since the new millennium, men's wardrobes have opened up to unexpected colours, fabrics and styles. But that has been in ready-to-wear, not at the height of bespoke tailoring. Yet male style has, indeed, been here before. Inside Monreale Cathedral, a room was dedicated to religious robes—a garden of blooms embroidered on silk, pink lace sleeves and layers of glossy colour. Some of those decorative religious “uniforms”—such as the silver flower patterns on pink lace—had inspired Domenico and Stefano, and replicas could be spotted in the show. For all their skills at plain tailoring, the duo has found a way of getting under the skin of a global generation not so in love with the plain grey office suit.
