column1: Why this chic bodysuit is perfect for your corporate office
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And for others who prefer modest fashion View Gallery 6 Photos Why This Chic Bodysuit Is a Hit Among Orthodox Jews and Corporate Warriors Have you ever tucked your shirt into your underwear to keep it from sprawling out of the waistband? If so, you aren't alone. This is one of the many wardrobe confessions that Tamar Daniel discovered when creating her label Tuxe. Daniel, a former designer for Topshop, built her entire business around the bodysuit, reforming the polarising garment into a chicly engineered item. “People had bodysuit PTSD from the '90s because they had snaps that were really uncomfortable or snaps that opened,” said Daniel, alluding to the sometimes carelessly placed fasteners on naughties-era bodysuits. “Or they left them with these hideous panty lines.” Her decision to transform the wardrobe staple happened during the 2008 crisis while Daniel and her friends were on the hunt for new positions. “We were all going out to interview again and I noticed that there was a return to more tucked-in dressing and suit dressing,” she says. “I thought that this would be a good moment to make something that would be about tucking in.” Daniel's first creation was a classic white button-up bodysuit, a hit among among women in the corporate world. To make the piece less conspicuous, she replaced the traditional snaps with a bra hook and eye (“It stays shut so you aren't worrying if it is going to pop open”), moved that placement higher up on the pelvic bone (“So you aren't sitting on the snap, which is a pet peeve of many previous bodysuit wearers”), and made it laser cut with a bonded edge (“It doesn't have VPL”). Since then, Daniel has expanded her bodysuit offerings, which include minimalist pieces like a black sleeveless cashmere turtleneck or a silk slip-like tank. On the more outré side, meanwhile, there's one piece with frilled shoulders or another shimmery one made out of Lurex. The prices typically range from about $80 for a plain sleeveless number and can go anywhere up to $312 for a silk dress-shirt version. So far, the label is currently stocked in Bloomingdale's and Nordstrom as well as e-commerce outlets like Moda Operandi. Along with office professionals, the label has also found a niche among religious communities that follow modesty guidelines in clothing, including Orthodox Jewish and Muslim women. (Modest Jewish fashion designers and bloggers including The Frock and Fabologie's Adi Heyman have both collaborated with Tuxe.) For religious women, Tuxe's bodysuits have become trend-enabling pieces that provide more coverage and are used for layering. “They say, ‘I want to wear the slip dress that everyone is wearing but we don't show that much skin. Can you suggest a piece that will disappear under the dress, to supplement a trend and make it accessible for me?' ” says Daniel. The next step for Daniel's bodysuits comes with applying more tech aspects. Her latest creation is a featherweight, copper-infused fabric that repels sweat and odour. “[This piece] is about removing distractions like sweat marks under their arms and wrinkles,” says Daniel. “Based on the feedback from women in the office setting, in the hospital, courtroom, or working hard out of their home all day, I think it is important to bring them an additional level of comfort. We want to make sure they are feeling their most confident.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.com Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Here’s the designer closing London Fashion Week this September
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And it’s not just your basic show American fashion house Tommy Hilfiger has just announced that it will be closing London Fashion Week's Fall 2017 edition with a TommyNow experiential runway event. The London show, which will be held at the city's Roundhouse music venue on Tuesday, September 19, will be the third of its kind. The first, a Fall 2016 show called, ‘Tommy Pier' took place in New York, while the second, Spring 2017's ‘Tommy Land' was held in Los Angeles. The Fall 2017 presentation will mark the first time the brand showcases men's clothing from Hilfiger Edition, the label's premium line, on a runway. Another milestone to keep in mind: This will be the first Tommy Hilfiger show since 2010 to showcase clothing for both genders on one runway. What else will you spot at the show? Think the coolest creations from the Fall 2017 TommyxGigi line, and women's wear from Hilfiger Edition as well. “My vision for TommyNow was to create a global platform that could bring our shows to audiences around the globe like a rock-and-roll world tour,” says Hilfiger. “It's about celebrating the connection between fashion and pop culture with experiences, performances and inspiring interactions that are designed around our consumers. We look forward to celebrating the rebellious spirit and star studded glamour of rock-and-roll in London for Fall 2017.” Can't wait to shop your favourite pieces from the show? The upcoming collection follows Tommy Hilfiger's ‘See Now, Buy Now' format, making the clothing available instantly across 70 countries. What's not to love? Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Demna Gvasalia, CFDA International Award Winner, on being true to yourself
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion “Keep in touch with yourself, enjoy being human” Few designers have made a fashion impact faster than Demna Gvasalia. Five years ago nobody in the business knew his name. Now, on Monday, June 5, the CFDA will present him with its International Award for his influential work at Vetements and Balenciaga, the artistic directorship of which he assumed with a smashing womenswear debut for Fall 2016. Not bad for a teenage refugee from Communist Georgia. It helps that he's had the resourceful support of his business-minded younger brother Guram. From the beginning, their secret has been to follow their intuition. In turn, shoppers connected on a gut level with Demna's oversize hoodies, floral tea dresses, and sculptural suiting, and reconstructed jeans. On a phone call from Zurich, Switzerland, where the Gvasalia brothers have relocated Vetements's headquarters, Demna discussed his newfound meditation practice, his decision to close his social media accounts, and why, though he may qualify for the term, he rejects the label “disruptor.” Demna, how do you feel about your CFDA International Designer of the Year award, and being recognized by the American fashion industry?I'm very flattered, honored, and motivated by it, but I'm already having anxiety attacks! When I was a kid in kindergarten, I was always the one running away from having to perform in front of people. When was the first time you came to America?I was a student in 2003. I'd won an IFF (International Fragrances and Flavors) project when I was at Antwerp Academy. We were brought to New York in 2003. You know, Linda Loppa, your professor, told me she didn't really need to teach you at Antwerp. Fast forward to now—here you are, famous, being celebrated one of the most influential designers in the world, for what you've achieved at Vetements and at Balenciaga.But five years ago, people didn't know my name. I started Vetements with my brother Guram on December 12, 2013. That really shows how fast the industry is now— and how brutal it can be, too. You can have a fast success, but you know, you can really have a fast failure too. Vetements has shaken it up by coming from behind the scenes, apparently from nowhere. You've changed the seasons you show in, produced a collection that was only collaborations with other brands, constantly operate in two-way communication with young fans all over the world – all these serial actions have earned you the label of fashion “disruptor.” How do you respond to that?It's on my list of words I hate. “Cool” is another one. I don't feel I'm against the system. Whatever we do, it's not against the system-- it's for Vetements. Whatever decisions we make, we do it for our brand. People confuse that with being disruptive. You've recently moved your entire Vetements operation to Zurich: a piece of news which has taken the industry aback. Why have you taken the decision to remove yourselves from Paris? It's a bit of 180-degree turn away from everything you were telling me about when I interviewed you for Vogue a year ago-- the parties in the suburbs, taking your whole team off to Berlin on a Friday night.We've completely changed the lifestyle from the clubby Parisian way—I've just turned 36, and there comes a time… (laughs) We did it right after the last show. The most important reason is to regain our creative freedom. A lot of people have said we've done it because of taxes. I'm not going to lie— that is part of it. But what we are doing is setting up a sort of laboratory, to concentrate more on product, and think long term. At Vetements, it's always a constant brainstorm. I want to work more on concepts. I'd like to work with people in Silicon Valley. For everyone to be geographically detached from Paris, for some of the time helps with this. But you have to be present in Paris too, of course. Since stepping up to being artistic director at Balenciaga, you've had all the success of overhauling the women's and men's collections, the image, and the stores, in double-quick time. How do you manage it?I programmed my brain. When I'm at Balenciaga, I can almost forget I'm at Vetements. I have my right-hand Martina who I worked with when we were at Margiela; she completely understands. But yes: time management is the most complex thing, aside from team management. The fact that I worked as part of teams for many years at Margiela and Louis Vuitton really helps me. I can imagine being in their place. There's a lot of psychological complexity involved. You have to be kind of a shrink; to be able to work with people's characters, understand their ambitions. It's a really hard job that people do in fashion. But it's always difficult for designers to concentrate on driving two brands. Notoriously, the relentless pressure often breaks creative people—and not just them. I've seen a lot of people beginning to walk away, or wishing they could.With Balenciaga at the beginning, I said, “I don't work Saturdays or Sundays.” I thought maybe people would think I was lazy or a diva. But this is absolutely normal in the world. What really matters is keeping sane and happy. Fashion doesn't need to turn you into this person who never sees friends. I hate it that this industry has this reputation for being nasty and vicious, because there are so many nice people in it, and sometimes the higher they are the more humble they'll be. So, to be able to say no is important. Other than my work, being with my boyfriend is the priority. (laughs) I definitely have a very healthy lifestyle now. In order to function, to be lucid. I do spend a lot of time alone, meditating—until I did, I never knew how many successful people do it. Demna Gvasalia has discovered mindfulness! How did that start?Funnily enough, on the web. Sitting watching a candle on a screen (laughs). I have zero patience, that's the bad thing about me. I have so many thoughts I cannot stop, but learning that you can ignore them, like clouds passing, that's amazing. When you're going through days when there's no gap between meetings, I've learned ten minutes [of meditating] is enough. I sit in a room, and I come out feeling fine again. Nature gave us this mental ability. I wish all our parents had known about it, and taught us. It's keeping me sane and happy. How does this jibe with having to be conscious of everything that's going on in fashion in this time of social media, when we're all constantly staring at our phones?It's a jail. I'm closing my accounts. Spending time in clean, healthy Switzerland surely helps with this?I've started running, which is really interesting. You start noticing things you'd never see. Then ideas come when you're not thinking about it. You can't force the unconscious. Let's go back to the very beginning of Vetements. You've been so methodically successful together, it's easy to suspect that you and Guram must have hatched a teen master-plan for how this would turn out?We didn't sit down before! I didn't visualize any of it. At the beginning, it was a side project to calm me down creatively. I thought it would be a small, niche brand to be honest. I was so scared. I only had negative information; all the things every designer has on their mind—you'll be bankrupt, all that. But Guram and I kind of go for things. When he saw the collection, he said, “You have to have your own brand. There are people who will want this.” He always believed in that. So, if I understand you, the plan is to live in the moment, while spending time thinking logically about constructing the future?I keep saying to Guram, whatever happens, we must enjoy this. I'm really enjoying what I do at Vetements and Balenciaga more than ever. Guram gets excited working on Excel spreadsheets, managing the business and the Vetements team, figuring out what the mistakes are. That is his creativity. The most important thing is that we both follow our gut. The clothes are the goal. And we can take trips to the mountains or the lakes, have a yoga class. Then we have a family evening every week, with his husband and my boyfriend, watching some terrible thing on TV and eating melted cheese with potato chips. I like this idea of a normal life being the new avant garde! There are so many young people who hang on your every word and move. What you say is influential. What advice would you give young designers?The advice is to keep in touch with yourself. To enjoy being human. And what will you be telling the great and the good of the fashion industry when you take to the CFDA Awards on Monday?The same. column1: Forget normcore. It’s time you acquainted yourself with gorpcore
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Say what? View Gallery 6 Photos It’s time to acquaint yourself with Gorpcore Gorp, a word used by hikers to refer to trail mix (Good Old Raisins and Peanuts), is about to influence your wardrobes very shortly. If you look up gorpcore, Urban Dictionary's understanding of the term's semantics goes thusly: “fashion design that is influenced by outdoors style, such as fleece jackets, fanny packs, windbreakers, puffy jackets, parkas, and hiking boots. rich people go glamping (glamourous camping) and wear gorpcore clothes.” Long story short, the average puffer jacket and bum bags—clothes you struggle to look attractive in on a hiking weekend—are about to be mixed with the kind you wear to feel like a street style celebrity. Insouciance is key when sporting gorpcore—so what if you thought wearing hiking boots in the city is normal? Brands known for making famously functional clothing like North Face, Patagonia and Birkenstock will be in focus. “These clothes are paired with painter pants, Vans, Hawaiian shirts, and Dickies because head-to-toe outdoorwear would be too literal, of course—it has to be thrown off to communicate the wearer is in on the joke. The outfit isn't designer, but it is fashion, in the way that any aesthetic executed with intentionality—ever insistent and dissonant—can become ‘a look',” explains Jason Chen of The Cut. Inarguably, gorpcore will strike the male population harder as the spring 2017 runways have predicted. Demna Gvasalia of Vetements and Balenciaga is already ahead of the game; the popularity of Balenciaga's puffer jacket is a clear indication that gorpcore, along with normcore, is here to stay. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion This could be your chance Over the years Lakmé Fashion Week has earned a rep for spotlighting fresh talent. Last year, the fashion week made history with Anjali Lama, the first transgender model to walk down the Indian runway. Prior to this model auditions have been held in Assam to encourage inclusivity. This season, an international talent scout will be present at the model auditions and will offer the winner an international modelling contract with IMG Models. “Lakmé Fashion Week is truly a hotbed for new talent in India. We will be looking for all that an IMG Model embodies: an inimitable personality, spirit, and the willingness to work hard,” said Jeni Rose, vice president, IMG models. Recently, with Indian models like Pooja Mor, Bhumika Arora and Radhika Nair receiving recognition on the international runways, global scouts are certainly interested in the mainland right now. At the moment, the auditions are only open to female models. column1: Ranveer Singh on the time Amitabh Bachchan did not approve of his outfit
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Are you surprised? In an industry that often demands conforming, Ranveer Singh's eccentric style is refreshing. Singh tells us how his unique spin on fashion is actually just an extension of his personality and recalls the one time he knew he had gone too far (courtesy Mr Bachchan). View Gallery 4 Photos Ranveer Singh on why dressing crazy is actually good When Band Baaja Baaraat (2010) happened, stardom hit me head-on. Suddenly, I was in the limelight without the tools to cope with the attention. And when you are unsure, your guard goes up. A part of that measured response was to dress conventionally, perhaps in keeping with how I thought a rising leading man in films should be dressing. But I was not comfortable with what I was wearing, or what I was saying. This was to continue through that initial phase of stardom. The change, the empowerment, ultimately came from the validation I got for my performances. THE TURNING POINT The turning point came in 2013. It was the year I got critical acclaim for Lootera and commercial acclaim for Goliyon Ki Rasleela Ram-Leela. People recognised that I was good at what I did. As I gained confidence, I began to do and say what I wanted. And I began to wear what I wanted to wear. I didn't create a new sartorial identity for myself; I just freed myself of judgement. In school and adolescence, I was known for my outrageous fashion. I was the first to sport baggy jeans and show off the top of my briefs as a fashion statement, the first to wear sports jerseys, use styling gel, wear chunky silver jewellery. It's how I have always been. People in my school WhatsApp group are hardly surprised; they say it's good to know I haven't changed. If there's a rack of 10 suits and one that's a riot of colours, that's what will attract me—I invariably go for what's unique. I have to credit my stylist Nitasha Gaurav; I've learnt so much from her. She's opened up a new dimension of fashion for me. I remember it began when I went on Anupama Chopra's show in an Ermenegildo Zegna suit, Kolhapuri chappals, a fedora and retro facial hair. I remember thinking that after a long time I looked and felt like the guy I lost somewhere along the way. FREEDOM TO STYLE My style reflects how I've freed myself of judgement. That's a very big part of it. The argument for or against—the judgement—is going to happen either way. So I decided that I might as well do what I want. These days, with the proliferation of technology, and social media in particular, everybody has an opinion. So I do what I feel like. I guess you could draw a parallel between my fashion choices and my films. I wear something because I want to wear it. I am not filtering my expression. Fashion is the most honest form of expression. Good, bad, ugly, like it or dislike it, agree or disagree, I am just being true. So if people call it attention-seeking, maybe I am like that. (I prefer to describe my style as whimsical and individualistic, though.) I love the post-apocalyptic look. I always wanted to dress that way and I finally found a kindred spirit in the Bulgarian brand Demobaza. It's as if the designers peeked into my soul and tried to search for what I wanted to wear and made just that. I have dedicated cupboards for Demobaza, Jack & Jones and Adidas. Between these three, I get by most days. THE GOALKEEPER SYNDROME The outfits people consider outlandish don't seem that way to me. But there was one that I thought was truly ghastly. I was clean-shaven and had light hair for my look in Kill Dill (2014). I wore a patterned suit to a TV show taping. But the look didn't translate well under the set's warm lights. I left home feeling like a million bucks but the reactions on set were less than positive. I went upto Mr Bachchan and asked him how I looked. He said, “Son, you look like a plant.” I am a bit far-out, but my craziest look is yet to come. I think Lady Gaga is outrageous and I love her, but I am not that crazy. The way actor Daniel Day Lewis makes me feel like the craft of acting is limitless, in the same vein Lady Gaga makes me feel expression is limitless. I dress according to my mood and instinct. And I don't always expect to be photographed. For every post-apocalyptic outfit I wear, I also have very normal clothes. I call it the goalkeeper syndrome: he makes nine good saves and no one comments but it's the one he misses that's remembered. column1: Sanjay Garg set to exhibit his collection in London

His forte lies in manipulation of textiles, and after close to eight years of designing, Garg has a set of formulas that work well in his favour. This summer he will be exhibiting some of his work at the Asia House in London. As a precursor to the exhibition, the designer will be in conversation with Rosemary Crill, former senior curator at the Victoria & Albert Museum. “Just as any conversation, the idea is to be open. Raw Mango has a strong client base in London and Garg is also looking forward to interacting with the old and the new audience. “Our efforts tend to be focused on creating a conversation first, and trusting the rest will follow,” he said. column1: All the trends that will be big this holiday season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Which of these will you wear? The term ‘cruise fashion' was conceived out of necessity. Back in the day, sophisticated travellers would request couture houses to create special collections during holiday season which would be shipped from Paris to New York on cruises. This information was shared by way of short videos before the Dior show took place in Los Angeles. Cruise or resort presentations are hosted by luxury houses in a manner where no expenses are spared. Typically, select media is flown to exotic locations or the mood is recreated to allow the viewers to fully soak in the vision of the creative head. Karl Lagerfeld at Chanel and Alessandro Michele at Gucci thought of Ancient Greece, Maria Grazia Chiuri looked into Christian Dior's archives to discover the Paleolithic Lascaux cave paintings while Nicolas Ghesquière of Louis Vuitton worked with Kansai Yamamoto himself. After a five-year hiatus, Prada returned to schedule with a collection that referenced the house's spring 2008 collection along with its signature use of nylon, sherbet hues and embellishments. Designers explored notions of identity this season. Some like Pierpaolo Piccioli of Valentino showed an interesting mix of Italian craftsmanship and hip-hop. Along with classes in fashion history, trends like knife pleats, fringes edges, lace, gold and patched fabric emerged strong. Scroll through our resort 2018 report to find out more. column1: Sonam Kapoor: “Nobody can love fashion as much as I do”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The National Award winner talks films and fashion It's the second time in our 10-year history that Sonam Kapoor leads the way for our annual style list. For the recent National Award winner, fashion and film have always gone hand in hand. Vogue talks to her about her love for Russian and Middle Eastern couture and why she will never reveal her favourite vintage stores. STYLE AND SCREEN Few can argue with the fact that Kapoor is unequivocally comfortable in her own skin. Industry insiders will tell you that the one thing the Kapoor family has in spades is complete self-assurance. So when it came to critics who dismissed her as a “fashion plate” and predicted that her success would last only till the red carpet, the National Film Award she received for Neerja is testament to her self-belief. “Films without fashion and fashion without films don't work,” she says about this now-exhausting debate, naming her style icons—Audrey Hepburn, Grace Kelly and Cate Blanchett—all serious actors and fashion favourites. “Both are visual mediums. It's not only about dialogue and acting; I should appeal to the audience,” Kapoor says, citing the example of Neerja (2016), where a uniform defined her character. Even for Aisha (2010), Khoobsurat (2014) and Delhi-6 (2009), fashion played an important role, pushing her to embrace her character's state of mind. Not surprisingly, she has immense respect for the role of a costume designer, previously dismissed as the darzi on film sets. Kapoor belongs to the social media generation and is a strong believer in the power of image. It's the stylist who adds the layers a character needs, taking into account the political and social context of the time, she explains. Looking back at how fashion in films has evolved, you'd be forgiven if you thought of the previous decades as a bit of a fail, but not for Kapoor. For her, Sridevi's chiffon sari in Mr India (1987) was a fashion breakthrough, as was Madhuri Dixit's look in Tezaab (1988). “It's just about how you wear it, and that's all that matters,” she says. Currently, Kapoor is filming with Radhika Apte. “Fashion and style are about who you are as a person; you need to be individualistic,” she says. And Apte's distinct personality, according to Kapoor, makes her very stylish, her other favourite being Kalki Koechlin. “Although,” Kapoor admits with a giggle, “Nobody [can] love fashion as much as I do.” Read the complete interview in Vogue India's June 2017 issue that hits stands on June 2, 2017 Photographed by: Signe Vilstrup. column1: Gucci rewrites history in Florence’s Pitti Palace
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Six things to know Gucci's Alessandro Michele is as much a historian as he is a creative director. For Gucci's Resort 2018 show, Michele brought the brand back to its home in Florence, imbuing his collection with heritage, irreverence, and some kitschy charm. Here are the six things to know about the 115-look show. View Gallery 54 Photos Gucci Rewrites History in Florence’s Pitti Palace The SettingFlorence's Pitti Palace was the backdrop for Gucci's Resort 2018 show. Filled with Renaissance art, the palace was decorated with stools printed with "Bacchus' Song,” a poem by Lorenzo de' Medici. The show took place throughout seven rooms of the palace with a harpist was stationed in every room. The most surprising detail? That models walked on a runway roped off by velvet rope. VIPs only! The CelebsLongtime Gucci muse and Alessandro Michele's BFF Jared Leto was the first star to turn heads at the Gucci Resort 2018 show. Wearing a pink coat, bee print shirt, and yellow trousers, Leto gave Michele himself a run for his money as best dressed today. Others stars in the front row included Beth Ditto, Kirsten Dunst, Dev Hynes, Dakota Johnson, and Soko. The Historical SpiritGolden laurel wreaths, Latin verses, and cithara-embellished headbands were some of the historically minded elements of Michele's collection. There were also gilded animal heads, and detailed dragon and tiger embroideries. The Faux-Real PiecesThroughout his career at Gucci, Michele has played on knockoff culture, and this season he did it in myriad ways. Michele began with a series of slogan tees that read “Guccify Yourself” and “Guccification” that lead to “Guccy” beaded gowns and entire suits made in Gucci's monogram print. The piece de resistance of Michele's ode to copycat culture was Look 33, a take on a famous photo of a woman in a faux Louis Vuitton jacket made by uptown legend Dapper Dan. The Body EmbellishmentMichele's love of glitz doesn't end at clothing and accessories. Models at this season's had their bodies embellished with pearl trimming and their fingertips dipped in black ink. The Non-Traditional ModelsQuirky boys and girls are the bread and butter of Gucci's runway cast, but this season, Michele accented his lineup with several musicians. Dirt Hand's Arun Roberts, Savages's Jehnny Beth, and Shock Machine's James Righton were some of the famous musicians that took a turn. column1: 7 sweet, feminine ways to wear summer’s top sportswear trend
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Athleisure doesn’t have to mean health goth View Gallery 7 Photos Athleisure Doesn’t Have to Mean Health Goth: 7 Sweet, Feminine Takes on Summer Sportswear How to get into the sportswear look without appearing as though you've just left the gym? Try injecting a dose of sugar into your athleisure. A noughties favorite, spearheaded by labels like BabyPhat and Jennifer Lopez's now-defunct Sweetface, the pastel-athletics look is still as cool as it was back in the 2000s. And it's making a comeback on today's runways, too: Rihanna's candy-hued Fenty x Puma line and Gucci's floral tracksuits have infused the often hard-edged category with a little tenderness. To nail the trend, focus on wearing athletic pieces in soft colors like pink and lavender. Dress up the theme for a day on the town with a Zara purple zip-up with a Marie Antoinette ruffle (Sneakers are always a must, too, but also keep the colors saccharine). To add some date-night appeal to a workout ensemble, try a lacy tank and skirt set by Alexander Wang finished off with a pair of black Balenciaga kicks that sport a slice of bubblegum pink. Really looking to make a statement? A pale pink ruched Alessandra Rich tracksuit with a rhinestone zipper pull is less warm-up than the main event. column1: Martin Margiela’s time at Hermès is an important part of fashion history
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Understanding the sense of an object View Gallery 6 Photos Martin Margiela’s time at Hermès is an important part of fashion history A surprise train ride across Europe, a nearly 8km walking tour of a city, and a mesmerising performance and exhibit that illustrated the function of fashion (or the sense of an object)—all in a day with Hermès. Its 7.15am on a Monday morning in Paris, and the Gare du Nord is understandably crowded as travellers hurry to catch their trains across France and Europe. Standing apart from the maddening crowd, were a group for whom their final destination was not so clear. Two hundred and fifty journalists from across the world had congregated on the platform to be whisked away to a surprise destination, as a part of Hermès 2017 theme: Le sens de l'objet (The meaning of an object). After a two-hour ride and some petit déjeuner, we arrived in Antwerp. The Belgian city is the home of the original Antwerp Six, the group of legendary designers who graduated from Antwerp's Royal Academy of Fine Arts, who were known for their avant-garde style. Often mistakenly included with them is Martin Margiela (who served as creative director of Hermès from 1997-2003, and whose work was being celebrated at the MoMu Museum, just a few miles from the station) and a few years later, the house's current artistic director Nadège Vanhee-Cybulski, who also attended the same institution. A tram ride later we're at the waterfront warehouse St Felix Pakhuis where in silence we ascend a narrow spiral staircase to a cavernous room where Studio Olivier Saillard has choreographed a performance. Hermès models from Margiela's time, dressed in monochrome tights and leotards, literally interpret the show notes across different seasons, describing seminal looks and leaving it to the guests to visualise. Post a lunch of local cheese, bread and fresh fish in the sun dappled courtyard, our group proceeds on a walking tour across the cobbled stones of the city for dessert, coffee and some incredible fashion history at the MoMu museum. 'Margiela, The Hermès Years', designed in collaboration with the reclusive designer, showcases just how far reaching Margiela's influence is. From oversized sleeves to cape jackets, the classic white shirt to multi-tasking clothes, Margiela's designs are an integral of the fashion vocabulary 20 years later. Inflections of his work can be seen on the runways even today. And that is clearly the sense of an object, for it to go beyond time and space. Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How IBM has predicted the future of Indian fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Bet you’ve never heard of something like this before View Gallery 3 Photos How IBM has predicted the future of Indian fashion Trends have come and gone year after year every season, but if you thought their appearances and disappearances were just chance, you couldn't be more wrong. Looking back just within India and its most influential pop culture platform, Bollywood, it's easy to see some patterns: while the biggest films in the '80s (think Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak, Tezaab and Maine Pyaar Kiya) featured a palette of black olive, liquorice and camouflage green, the '90s leaned heavily on raisin black, navy blue and light grey. But how does one determine what's going to be trending next season? Making the business of fashion predictions a touch easier, American multinational IBM lent their latest technology, IBM Watson (named after the company's founder Thomas J Watson), to Indian designer duo Falguni & Shane Peacock, for their brand new collection centred around the theme of ‘Future of Bollywood Fashion'. A type of next-generation cognitive computing (meaning ‘simulation of human thought processes in a computerised model'), IBM Watson searches through large pieces of data for patterns and insights, learning as it goes. “We first started by getting Watson to understand fashion better,” says Sriram Raghavan, director of IBM's India Research Labs. “Originally we were looking to make people's retail experience better, whether it's shopping, online retail, providing conversational shopping experiences, image-matching, let people upload images and choose styles… But we realised these same building blocks can also be used in the design process. Watson understands colours, styles and silhouettes in a very significant way.” For this particular project, the technology, which runs on IBM Cloud, first analysed about 6,00,000 historical fashion runway images from London, New York, Milan and Paris Fashion Weeks held over the past decade. It then proceeded to analyse close to 5,000 images of Bollywood stars (“everything from screenshots to posters and pictures from social media,” says Raghavan) from the '70s, '80s, '90s and 2000s. The two pieces of research came together to spotlight exactly which trends worked during different periods of time in history, and which ones are going to be the most popular in the near future. Simply put in Raghavan's words, “Watson lets you travel visually over space and time.” The result: Clothing that's ahead of its time, created using a logical, left-brain perspective rather than the usual right-brain method. “We always talk about Watson assisting professional services… nurses, doctors, teachers. This here is Watson assisting a creative process. What we are doing for a fashion designer today is no different to what we can do for a doctor. People don't think of diagnosis as a creative task, they view it as a specialised task. But if you're talking about augmenting the process with data and insights, the parallel does hold. The system empowers the designer.” For fashion enthusiasts all over the world, IBM Watson could in the future serve as an effective time-saver, letting full collections be manufactured in a much shorter period. The technology has also been used in everything from suggesting innovative food and flavour combinations, to identifying skin cancers, investment analysis, and wealth management. “We're still just scratching the surface!” Raghavan smiles. column1: Bella Hadid on how her Nike campaign has placed her in a league of her own
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The model talks about her job, favourite workout and what beauty means to her Bella Hadid might only be 20 years old but her fashion CV already boasts some of the industry's biggest names. The latest, however sings more in tune with her personal style history than others that have come before it. The California girl is the latest to join the Nike family (although Bella has already fronted Riccardo Tisci's collection for the brand), starring in the sportswear giant's Beautiful x Powerful campaign and is the first non-athlete to step into these storied sneakers. “Growing up, Nike was pretty much all that I wore,” Bella told us on the set of the all-action shoot. “I think my love for Nike properly started at the beginning of high school and I would only wear my Air Force Ones. I had them in every single colour, they were my favourite thing. That was where my obsession grew from and now I'm here on the set!” It makes for quite the tale. “What is so amazing about Nike, is that they always choose powerful women and I'm one of the first models to do the campaign,” she explained. "I feel really lucky to be able to shoot this after so many amazing people.” The decision by the brand marks a big moment in Bella's career. Her flexibility to go from wearing vintage Galliano on the red carpet to then skateboarding in a Nike campaign, proves an ability that isn't all that common within the fashion industry. In fact, Bella herself isn't so sure that there is anyone booking as diverse jobs as she is right now. "It is kind of rare to be able to do all of that and it's really cool to be able to do a variety of things. I don't really know anyone who has done this”. However, she's taking it all in her stride. “I'm just going with the flow and my agent Anne knows a lot about all of this stuff. She's been working in the business for a long time so she's the one I ask for advice. We're just kind of going with it! Hoping for the best.” While high-fashion shoots often call for models like Bella to use their posing intuition to best portray the beauty of the clothes they're wearing, this shoot was a different process altogether. "This exact shoot is an old-school homage to the original Cortez shoe. I think the best part about today is just to being able to have fun and be active. Usually, it's very 'Stand there and show off the clothes'. Right now, it's more ‘You have to get dirty in a pair of Nikes, you have to be able to work and run and do fun stuff.' That's what's making today so fun.” Starring alongside Bella in the Beautiful x Powerful collection is athlete Elaine Thompson – Jamaica's two-time Olympic gold medal athletics star, who also happens to be just 24. “I think that's what is so amazing about this brand is that they always portray a beautiful strong woman," Bella confesses. “Everybody before me - and Elaine - have been the most incredible, powerful athletes.” If the campaign is all about being beautiful and powerful, what do these words mean to Bella? "I think that beauty comes from within and when it comes to the other, I think Serena Williams is one of the most powerful and strong women on the inside and out. She is so kind and sweet. I think that she is genuinely one of the greatest women.” Hectic schedules, constant travelling between time zones and living with a chronic illness (Lymes disease), how does Bella make this hectic – albeit exciting – lifestyle work for her? “To go to sleep I always have meditation music and that keeps my brain focused and then unfocused. If I don't take the time for myself then I'm constantly thinking about work and it overwhelms me. I like to find even just an hour in a day to just have me time and just sit and think. I love to write.” When it comes to incorporating fitness into her daily routine, Bella's approach is one that most of us will totally be able to relate to. "I haven't had a lot of time to be able to work out recently. If I have a day off I like to be dedicated and go with my trainer to do stuff that I enjoy doing. I just like to have fun when I work out. I don't really like doing it and if I'm going hard I want to be able to go hard for two hours and be done with it or just kind of mess around. I love boxing and I love doing that slidey thing? See - I don't know what any of it is actually called! It's just really fun.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Wellness Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Meet the women behind the popular Indian bridal couture label, Jade
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Twice as good View Gallery 10 Photos Meet the women behind luxury Indian label Jade Sisters-in-law Monica Shah and Karishma Swali have been running the label Jade for nearly a decade. Over the course of time, Jade has evolved into two lines—couture label Jade and a younger diffusion line—Amoh by Jade. The design house recently embarked on their tenth year in fashion with a fresh, sprawling new address on Mumbai's Peddar Road. But what went into the making of a successful brand that's constantly striving for more? Inception Shah discovered her love for draping at the critically-acclaimed Central Saint Martins art school in London while Swali honed her skills in design at the National Institute of Fashion Technology. “We found our calling in fashion early and have been successfully researching and consulting for internationally acclaimed luxury fashion brands for two decades,” says Shah, who also cites this grounding to be instrumental in creating their own brand. “There was the yearning to chart a different course. Jade (founded in 2008) is the culmination of this yearning. Our experience in international fashion helped us experiment. Our range of handcrafted vegan Italian leather shoes is one such accomplishments that we're very proud of,” she says. Dual forces As two distinct creative entities heading a womenswear label, their roles are distinctly cut out. Shah is in charge of their signature fabric developments, while Swali looks after the styling, communications and in-store visual merchandising. Shah, who is also a certified architect and interior designer, took over the responsibility of designing the 3,500sqft store. “The space has been conceived in keeping with Jade's DNA of taking inspiration from India's heritage and reinventing the use of age-old techniques to make them relevant for today's brides. We wanted to give the artefacts at the store their due as installations, rather than being integrated as a part of the interiors, lending to a feel of walking through an art gallery. This complements our couture collections, also intricately embroidered using age-old techniques,” says Shah. Manifestation The nuances of creativity, space and time have been a cause for intrigue for Shah, who always wondered why a certain craft is born and thrives over centuries only in a specific region. Talking about the premise behind designing the space she adds, “This fascination played an important role in outlining the concept when Karishma and I set out to design the space that was to be Jade's concept flagship. Handcrafted heritage objects of art of varied origins, each with a unique history of its own have found their way to our store.” Preserving tradition has always been at the heart of the label, which takes inspiration from sculpture, colours, patterns and motifs of Indian arts. “As you transverse through the space you are greeted with installations wherein Jade creations have been juxtaposed against handcrafted heritage art. The installations and our flagship are our tribute to India's long tradition of hand-craftsmanship and we hope you enjoy the journey they take you on, discovering India's heritage,” Shah offers. column1: Inside Anna Sui’s solo exhibition in London
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s your first look View Gallery 11 Photos Inside Anna Sui’s solo exhibition in London Today, London's Fashion and Textile Museum will open its doors to “The World of Anna Sui”, the first retrospective dedicated to an American fashion designer. Sui, 52, is one of fashion's great independent success stories. Born in Detroit, her dreamy, romantic-bohemian creations were propelled to fame in the early '90s by her close relationships with Parsons classmate, photographer Steven Meisel, as well as supermodels Naomi Campbell and Christy Turlington, who starred in her runway debut in '91. (They affectionately referred to her as “Super Sui”.) Today, Sui runs a multi-million-dollar fashion empire spanning ready-to-wear, shoes, fragrance and even home goods, which is stocked in more than 300 stores in 35 countries. In 2009, she was recognised by the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) with a Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award. Sui was busily adjusting a pastel pixie-cut wig when we are arrived at the museum for a preview earlier this week. Wearing the same rich tones as the mannequins surrounding her, she nearly blended in. “It's mind-blowing,” she said, moving between displays of Mongolian-inspired knitwear and jewel-toned biker boots. “It's the first time I've seen many of these outfits since the initial show[s].” While Sui is a product of Manhattan's Garment District, London feels like just the place to celebrate her history. British iconography has played a role in Sui's vision for her lines since she began designing. “When I first heard about London—about The Beatles and The Rolling Stones—it seemed like such a faraway place,” she recalled. “Those impressions stuck with me, and you can see it all reflected in my work." Given fashion's current obsession with all things '90s, there couldn't be a better moment to revisit Sui's contribution to the industry. “Anna Sui's work is particularly significant now because there is a resurgence of interest in late 20th-century fashion, which directly or indirectly reference Anna Sui, and make the show timely,” observed the museum's curator, Dennis Nothdruft. At a time when American designer brands, from Bibhu Mohapatra to Suno, are facing bankruptcy, Sui's staying power is all the more remarkable. According to Kolb, it's her willingness to innovate, combined with her authenticity, that has allowed her to survive and to thrive over the decades. “While the elements around Anna might have changed, she hasn't.” The World Of Anna Sui is on view at the Fashion and Textiles Museum from May 26 to October 1, 2017 Culture & Living Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How Netflix’s hit show ‘The Get Down’ trickled up to the runways
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All the way to Valentino's resort 2018 collection This week, Pierpaolo Piccioli gave Valentino fans a lot to get excited about. His resort '18 outing, shown here in New York, featured plenty of his beloved ethereal gowns and Zandra Rhodes prints, but it also revisited the house's more streetwise, sporty signatures—including sneakers, army jackets, and denim. This time, there was a groovy twist: In a preview with Vogue's Nicole Phelps, Piccioli said he's been watching a lot of The Get Down, Netflix's popular series about the rise of hip-hop culture in the Bronx of the 1970s. The varsity jackets, sporty knits, and tracksuits you've seen on TV made several cameos in the collection, but Piccioli also captured the fresh, freewheeling mood of the '70s in New York. Chances are he isn't the only designer who's tuned into The Get Down, and we have a feeling you'll see more vibes of this kind in upcoming collections. Here, get a head start with a few of the parallels we've drawn between The Get Down's stylish cast and Piccioli's new lineup. View Gallery 4 Photos The Classic Tracksuits The Classic Tracksuits We lost count of the tracksuits in The Get Down, but they're always refreshingly no-frills in red, black, or kelly green with classic ticking stripes. Even when characters aren't wearing a tracksuit, though, they're often in a sporty ribbed knit or T-shirt with exposed seams and color-blocking. Piccioli's version of the tracksuit came in hammered silk, and he also designed a few track-inspired dresses with drawstring waists and hoods. View Gallery 4 Photos The Fatigue Jackets The Fatigue Jackets Jaden Smith's character, Dizzee, is a graffiti artist with a thing for statement jackets—he wears a denim one covered in buttons (it was tradition for graffiti artists to customize their own jean jackets in the '70s) and lots of embroidered, embellished army jackets. At the time, army jackets were relatively new on the street; they were designed for soldiers in the Vietnam war, but Alpha Industries began producing them for the commercial market in the '70s, too. Piccioli's take on the classic look ranged from sequined parkas to an army green dress covered in sky blue embroidery. View Gallery 3 Photos The Custom Varsity Jackets The Custom Varsity Jackets In the beginning of The Get Down's second season, the rappers perform in matching red varsity jackets with their group's name, “The Get Down Brothers,” on the back. Piccioli's varsity jackets in jersey and brightly colored leather came with similar cursive “Valentino” embroidery, so those of us without musical talent can at least feel like we're part of Piccoli's squad. View Gallery 4 Photos The Floral Frocks The Floral Frocks Mylene, Yolanda, and Regina's wardrobes in The Get Down are the stuff of a vintage lover's dreams. The matching floral, flutter-sleeve dresses they wear for a group performance capture the bohemian spirit we all associate with the '70s. Piccioli's whisper-sheer floral dresses were inspired by archival Valentino numbers, but had the same dreamy vibe. column1: Which emoji was a fashion favourite on the Cannes 2017 red carpet?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The dancing girl definitely had her moment View Gallery 12 Photos Which emoji was a fashion favourite on the Cannes 2017 red carpet? If Coco Chanel was right when she said, “Fashion has to do with (…) the way we live, and what is happening,” then #SayItWithAnEmoji is easily the most fitting hashtag to describe the social media-obsessed times we live in. Texting has replaced talking; and if it's not on Instagram, it didn't really happen. So when your smartphone is always your number one accessory, its influence is bound to seep into your sartorial choices. Case in point: The Cannes 2017 red carpet. Any WhatsApp addict will vouch for the fact that the film festival's red carpet was, but in fact, simply a parade of their favourite emojis. And the dancing girl, with her red ruffled dress and ‘let's get this party started' vibe, was the one with maximum followers. A word to the wise: unabashed joie de vivre is a non-negotiable when sporting this look. Deepika Padukone's stylist Elizabeth Saltzman cited it as her “favourite emoji” when she posted a Boomerang of the actor having some fun in her dancing girl-inspired look. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan too went that extra mile as she twirled and pirouetted in her take on the emoji while Bella Hadid reinterpreted it with her signature cool girl “you can't sit with us” sensibility. Then there was Sonam Kapoor owning every bit of her custom Anamika Khanna look that instantly conjured up images of the French fries emoji. Is it a coincidence that the next collection of her clothing brand Rheson too shines the spotlight on the same emoticon? Sure, Kendall Jenner's Giambattista Valli Couture ensemble was playful. But did you also notice the look bearing an uncanny resemblance to that ice cream emoji? The topknot definitely contributed to the overall visual. We also spotted Rihanna looking just as cool (if not more) as the sunglass-clad smiley; Fan Bingbing, as pristine as a snowflake emoji, and Emily Ratajkowski twinning with the dancing girls in black leotards. Safe to say, words could fail you, but a trusty emoji never would. Fashion Fashion What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why Cristóbal Balenciaga was ahead of his time, nearly 100 years ago
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s revisiting the legacy View Gallery 11 Photos Why Cristóbal Balenciaga was ahead of times, nearly a 100 years ago When Cristóbal Balenciaga closed his fashion house in 1968, the socialite Mona von Bismarck was devastated. “Mona didn't come out of her room for three days,” recalled Diana Vreeland in D.V ., her memoir. “It was the end of a certain part of her life.” Bismarck's reaction was eccentric, yes, but the fabled episode neatly sums up the strength of feeling in fashion circles towards this quiet giant of haute couture. Despite shunning all publicity, choosing “monsters” as his models, and shocking the clients and press with provocative silhouettes, the enigmatic Balenciaga was and continues to be revered as the designer's designer. Cecil Beaton described him as “fashion's Picasso”. A survey of the Spanish fashion designer's career at London's Victoria & Albert Museum opens Saturday. The exhibition is a visual feast for fashion nerds. Uncompromising and exacting, graceful and awkward, Balenciaga's creations are poised on a line where fashion turns into something else. The striking modernity of his work is evident from the start. The first thing visitors encounter is a 1961 chartreuse silk gazar dress-cape. Evocative of an elegant caterpillar, it could easily be mistaken for Comme des Garçons. “The dress is a fantastic distillation of his ideas and it shows his abstraction of the body—it's strikingly modern,” observed Cassie Davies-Strodder, the exhibition's curator. Born in a small fishing village in the Basque region of Spain in 1895, Balenciaga began training as a tailor in Madrid at age 12. He established a successful career as a designer in Spain and in 1937 he moved his business to Paris. The V&A exhibition focuses on the designer's work in the 1950s and 1960s. “These decades mark a critical point in Balenciaga's career where he is significantly departing from what other people are doing,” said Davies-Strodder. The shapely simplicity of Balenciaga's garments is deceptive, but the exhibition shows “exploded” versions of garments created by X-ray artist Nick Veasey. The images reveal a level of technical mastery imperceptible to the naked eye. Balenciaga's training as a tailor meant he was a hands-on worker and ingenious pattern-cutter, but it is the pure originality of his designs that has ensured his legacy. The sack, the babydoll and the balloon dress were just a few of his innovations. “These were actually very shocking at the time because they completely eliminate the waist,” said Davies-Strodder. “They are from a time when Dior's New Look was still dominating the fashion landscape, so people thought they were revolting.” On paper the designer and Balenciaga's current creative director, Demna Gvasalia, are poles apart. The former was a high society darling; the latter is a streetwise provocateur. But the parallels between the two men in the exhibition are hard to ignore. “I think they have a similar attitude to the fashion system and the press, and aren't afraid to challenge norms,” said Davies-Strodder. “They also have a similar approach to the body. Demna approaches the body in 360-degree way… he has that technical confidence in cutting and assembling that you see in Balenciaga's work.” And like Gvasalia, Balenciaga shocked the Paris salons of the 1950s with his choice of unconventional models, often of diverse ages, shapes and sizes. “The fashion press called them monsters,” said Davies-Strodder. “He taught them to walk in this really haughty way so they didn't make eye contact and stomped down the catwalk.” Balenciaga's knack for anticipating—and shaping—the zeitgeist is made plain in the final section of the exhibition. His influence is seen in garments by protégés Oscar de la Renta and Paco Rabanne right through to present-day trailblazers like JW Anderson, Molly Goddard and, of course, Gvasalia. “The reverence contemporary designers have for Balenciaga is like no one else,” said Davies-Strodder. “He had such a clear vision that he elevated dressmaking to the realm of art.” 'Balenciaga: Shaping Fashion' is on view at the Victoria & Albert Museum from May 27, 2017 until February 18, 2018; Vam.ac.uk/balenciaga Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Here’s how Chanel played a key role in the Cannes hit ‘Okja’
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A must-watch Okja may be the most controversial film to debut at Cannes this year. Directed by Bong Joon-ho of The Host and Snowpiercer fame, the Korean-American production is being distributed by Netflix, a fact that has led to criticism by some who worry about the streaming giant muscling its way into cinema's most prestigious festival. Yet by early accounts, the film is a marvel—a humanistic coming-of-age tale with a strong political message—that drew a four-minute standing ovation as the credits rolled, thanks in part to its clever costuming. The movie stars young actress Ahn Seo-hyun and Okja, the titular CGI “super-pig” she lovingly raises on Korean farmland, until the Mirando Corporation returns to “harvest” its genetically engineered swine. Tilda Swinton, who first collaborated with Bong in 2013's Snowpiercer, plays Lucy Mirando, a corporate heiress with an image to project, and for one of the film's pivotal scenes, she conjures a compelling costar—a couture Chanel gown. Tilda Swinton in a Chanel Resort 2017 jacket with director Bong Joon-ho Image: Jae-Hyeok Lee / Netflix “I immediately saw my character in Okja as adoring Chanel,” Swinton says. Before shooting began, her mind drifted back to the house's Resort 2016 show, held in Seoul and filled with sartorial nods to the hanbok, the country's traditional dress. “So for the scene where the businesswoman presents the awards for the super pig competition she initiated, I remembered the pink hanbok that caught my eye at the Cruise show,” she adds. “I thought it would be perfect for this powerful businesswoman and her desire to pay tribute to Korea as the winning country at this event.” When model Ji Hye Park closed Chanel's Paris-Seoul show in Karl Lagerfeld's reimagined hanbok, it struck the right chord—floating layers of pink silk and chiffon, the dangling goreum ribbon redone as a tight velvet bow. Custom-made for Swinton, as seen in the images below, the dress accomplished a lot in a few strokes. It conveyed her character's extravagant wealth and worked as an elegant reference to Korean culture that doesn't read as costume, despite Mirando's less than noble intentions. Subtler still is the matching twinset worn by Ahn—instead of Swinton's fine silks, Ahn's is done in humble cotton and linen, conveying the vast distance between them. It's a perfectly executed film-fashion moment, courtesy of Swinton and the house of Chanel. column1: Priyanka Chopra attends Baywatch screening: “This is outfit four today!”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Serious fashion View Gallery 11 Photos Zac Efron, Priyanka Chopra, and More Make a Splash at a Screening of Baywatch When the Cinema Society hosted a screening of Baywatch on Monday at the Landmark Sunshine Cinema, the inclement weather felt like a far cry from the clear skies and high temps associated with the show. Leave it to actress Priyanka Chopra, though, to take a little rain and run with it (and no, not in that Baywatch brand of slow motion). “This is outfit four today!” she said, tallying up her multiple quick-changes. She spent the morning in Derek Lam, the afternoon in Ralph Lauren, and was now in a sequined Roberto Cavalli minidress. “Because I play the villain, I want my clothes to have a point of view, not just be a pretty outfit,” Chopra said of her press tour wardrobe. “And because it's Baywatch, I wanted to channel a little bit of summer fun, too.” Indeed, Chopra and her female castmates all seemed to be having fun with serious fashion: Kelly Rohrbach chose a Prabal Gurung suit and Ilfenesh Hadera wore a menswear-inspired Mugler blazer as a makeshift dress. But while Rohrbach and Hadera spend much of their screen time in swimwear, Chopra relies on accessories to make a splash. “My character goes to a beach in heels and someone has to pull out a stool for her to stand on—she's too diva-esque for the sand!” she said with a laugh. “It's so absurd and yet so fabulous and that's what I love about her.” Perhaps just as unexpected is the emphasis the film places on female empowerment. “We really wanted to flip the genre on its head and go against the expectation where you have these super-athletic guys next to these beautiful women,” explained producer Beau Flynn. “The girls are super badass and like the guys, they're avengers on the beach.” Once it came time for the after-party at Mr. Purple, the rain had subsided, and guests were transported to the shores of Los Angeles, thanks to on-theme Svedka cocktails with the names Beach Blast, Lifeguard's Libation, and Bikini Bombshell. Even Baywatch babes can benefit from a night off. This article originally appeared on Vogue.com What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Tracksuits anyone? Pierpaolo Piccioli presented his Resort 2018 collection for Valentino in New York City today, marking the brand's second pre-collection show in the Big Apple. On the runway, Piccioli picked up a sporty thread inspired by the NYC streets, showing tracksuits, zip-ups, and sleek, cut-out dresses. Here, four talking points from the show. Track Is BackCan athleisure be pretty? That seemed to be the question on the catwalk. Piccioli took sport-inspired details like exposed seams and snaps and applied them to Valentino's signautre midi-dress silhouette. There were plenty of proper track suits and varsity jackets too, done in very sporty shades of astroturf green and cardinal red. Zandra Rhodes's Prints ContinuePiccioli's first solo collection for Valentino was based on a print collaboration with iconic designer Zandra Rhodes. Her work was seen again in the Resort collection on dresses and patterned jackets. Not Your Normal FootwearThe era of the proper pump is over. Today, Valentino put two shoe styles classically considered bad taste on the catwalk. The first? Thin white socks worn with heeled sandals, echoing the thin sock-and-sandal combo Kendall Jenner wore at the Cannes Film Festival earlier this week. The second: Flip flops. The feathered thong sandals were worn with trousers and minidresses on the runway, proving that the beachy shoe is truly making a comeback. Piccioli Expands with Unexpected MaterialsThink Valentino, and you think thin laces and silks. Those were on the runway today alongside more surprising fabrications like denim and a dress made entirely of vertical sequin paillettes. column1: Your first look at Paul Andrew’s debut collection for Ferragamo
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion #AmoFerragamo View Gallery 12 Photos Your first look at Paul Andrew’s debut collection for Ferragamo New-York based British designer Paul Andrew has announced the first ever footwear director at the house of Salvatore Ferragamo. Andrew cut his teeth at labels like Alexander McQueen, Narciso Rodriguez and Donna Karan, and is one of the most celebrated footwear designers of contemporary fashion. His first collection for Salvatore Ferragamo is inspired by the founder's dedication to his craft. “My concept for the collection was simply to highlight the fundamentals that made Salvatore such a profound and groundbreaking presence in his field and to express those values through designs that are relevant to a new generation of strong, discerning women,” says Andrew. The line sees signature design details that are associated with brand like ‘F' wedge, the traditional use of black and gold reimagined for the modern times. To mark the launch of the pre-fall and fall 2017 lines, the brand will be launching a multi-sensory digital series #AmoFerragamo that captures the essence of the collection linking the past and present of the brand. Nicole Warne, Julia Restoin Roitfeld, Lee Sung Kyung and others, will star in their own chapter of the series: “Shoe La La”, “Shoe It”, “Shoe Me”, “Alphabet Yourself”, “How To”, and “Dance, Dance, Dance”. Scroll through our slideshow to have a complete look at the collection. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Queen Rania of Jordan conquers Cannes in Givenchy Haute Couture
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion She attended Naomi Campbell’s Fashion for Relief gala While the Cannes Film Festival red carpets are heating up, this weekend saw Queen Rania Al-Abdullah of Jordan smoulder at Naomi Campbell's Fashion for Relief gala in a custom Givenchy Haute Couture dress. The piece by Riccardo Tisci is only the latest example of Queen Rania's striking style. When meeting Melania Trump at the White House in April, Queen Rania opted for Haider Ackermann's sixties-inspired, strongly tailored suit while earlier this fall saw her coordinate in shades of red with Queen Letizia of Spain. And today's approach was similar with the royal reworking a wardrobe favourite, the shirtdress, but giving it a high-fashion spin with natty design details. The Tisci-designed piece made its runway debut during fall/winter 2016, but Queen Rania gave it new life here, amping up the one-note effect with tonally coordinated satin pumps and a ladylike box clutch. A fishnet slip with lace trim acted as the ideal underpinning, providing a contrast in texture and length, while hand-embroidered silk ribbons on the bodice and sleeves lent a sculptural element to the effortlessly elegant evening look. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Sari on the go [#image: /photos/5ce4480d4a30b386a812f769]||| ||| Image: Rex Sonam Kapoor always seems to be having the time of her life—did you catch the star at Cannes, sitting on a swing wearing Snapchat glasses in what looked like the most comfortable sari we've seen in a while? Snap-happy and swinging 🕶#LifeAtCannes A post shared by VOGUE India (@vogueindia) on May 22, 2017 at 5:51am PDT Kapoor's three-piece mint sari was a custom look created by designer Masaba Gupta, which includes a blouse, cropped pants and a half jacket that converts into a pallu. “We were looking at something in nude tones by Rhea [Kapoor] who does thorough planning of each outfit, [and she] suggested a mint might look better in the daylight. We made the look in a day and a half,” said Gupta. The designer worked with a self-striped neoprene fabric and tone-on-tone sequins to create an understated yet striking ensemble. Orders for the look have already starting piling in but Gupta won't be making more of the saris anytime soon. “It's a little unfair to put a look that was customised for someone on sale right after they wear it. I am going to give it a break of a month until I start producing,” said the designer. Gupta will be introducing the silhouette in her festive collection, which will be out in August. “Everyone has destination weddings these days and people want to wear something that looks good but is easy to move around in, so it makes perfect sense to offer that to the customers. We are going to make sure the price range is also affordable,” said Gupta. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Women’s Work: Being Female Before Feminism
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How fashion artists, from Elsa Schiaparelli to Rei Kawakubo, expressed their gender battle with wit I'm in #Paris taking another look at 'Women's Work?' Hidden upstairs in the Musée des Arts Decorative'. The question mark tells the story: a witty questioning A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 22, 2017 at 5:40am PDT There are no Dior T-shirts announcing “We should all be feminists”. No grainy movies showing women marching for the right to vote. The breakthrough of trousers into the female closet is not recorded. Yet “Women's Work?” (“Travaux de Dames?”), the current exhibition at the Musée des Arts Decoratifs in Paris (until the 17th of September 2017), takes a look both sharp and sly at the evolving role of women in the applied arts. That encompasses everything from ceramics to clothes, fashion to photography, and drawing to design. Does this look contemporary - or what? Sonia Delaunay design from 1920's at 'Travaux des Dames?' At Musee des arts Decoratifs in Paris A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 22, 2017 at 5:54am PDT This discreet exhibition, tucked away on the museum's upper floor, is also designed to show the powerful role that the museum itself has played in supporting women in these fields – although its purpose is to express the artistic freedom that ultimately developed from a modest beginning. For example, a picture from 1895 of two women, one sewing, the other pointing at the words “Arts by Women” later leads to Kristin McKirdy's ceramic sculptures of 2016. [#image: /photos/5ce445041dc2678618c7aa92]||| ||| Kristin McKirdy: Ceramic sculpture in enamelled earthenware, 2016 Image: Copyright Les Arts Décoratifs, Paris/Jean Tholance It is interesting to see a museum presentation that is focused on no particular artist or designer. An ever-increasing number of exhibitions today concentrate on a single figure, such as “Balenciaga: Shaping Fashion”, opening this week at London's Victoria and Albert Museum (complementing another Balenciaga show in Paris); or Dior's 70th birthday show (“Christian Dior: Couturier du rêve”) opening on the 5th of July in this very museum of decorative arts. Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons: Two-piece ensemble in synthetic leather from the "18th-Century Punk" collection. A retrospective of Rei Kawakubo's work, "Art of the In-Between", is currently on show at the Costume Institute of the Metropolitan Museum of Art (until 4th September 2017 ) Image: Copyright And Courtesy Of Comme Des Garçons Yet the heroines stand out in this exhibition: Here are Sonia Delaunay and Elsa Schiaparelli, the former such a powerful contributor to the geometric patterns of the early 20th century, while “Schiap's” trompe l'oeil sweaters from the 1920s, with their pretend collars and bows, are utterly wearable today. Yet they were significant in introducing the simplicity and freedom of the sweater to the world of women nearly a century ago.[#image: /photos/5ce445044a30b344fa12f39f]||| ||| Elsa Schiaparelli: Sweater in wool and jacquard knit with trompe-l'œil knotted scarf motif, January 1928 collection Image: Copyright Les Arts Décoratifs, Paris/Jean Tholance Delaunay was a pluralist artist who wanted to bring down the barriers between major and miner art and also deplored the concept that “decorative” arts could not be taken seriously. The furniture on display from her personal dining room, especially the cabinets in sycamore, face off the Jazz Age geometry of her print blouses.[#image: /photos/5ce445049cc0c08e21f9f5ce]||| ||| Sonia Delaunay: Dining-room chair in wood, toile with wool embroidery, and velvet, circa 1923 Image: Copyright Les Arts Décoratifs, Paris/Jean Tholance Then there are the patterns created in l'Atelier Martine, set up by Paul Poiret in 1911 after a visit to Berlin and Vienna to understand the work of Josef Hoffmann, where the object was to marry fine and applied art. L'Atelier Martine for Paul Poiret: Wallpaper with repeated floral motif for the Desfossé and Karth company, 1919 Image: Copyright Les Arts Décoratifs, Paris I was constantly surprised by this quirky little exhibition – not so much by the baby-pink fake leather outfit from Comme des Garçons, cut away with straps and openings to reveal flesh, but by the fact that in the 1980s Rei Kawakubo designed furniture for her boutiques to blend with her aesthetic vision of East meets West. Did YOU know that Rei Kawakubo designed East/West furniture for her Comme stores back in the '80's/'90's? At Paris Musee des Arts Deco at 'Women's Work?' exhibition A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 22, 2017 at 5:51am PDT The exhibitions opens with “Travaux de Dames?” printed on a washcloth – something I saw as an ironic view of women artists being metaphorically chained to the kitchen. Add to that another unlikely reflection: a dining table with a series of silver cutlery shaped into animals and plants. The next surprise is a carved wooden bust, spiky with pins, looking like some contribution to an African ritual, but in fact designed by artist Janine Janet in 1959 as one of three bustiers for the windows of the Balenciaga boutique on Avenue George V. Janine Janet: "The Queen", sculpture in wood with metal nails, designed for the windows of the Balenciaga boutique in Paris, 1959 Image: Copyright Les Arts Décoratifs, Paris/Jean Tholance Within the interconnecting areas, I was drawn to the fashion elements, such as the patterned fabric from Paul Poiret's Atelier Martine, or Schiap's mad hats, which we have seen many times before, but which suggest in their elegant wit the spirit of the 1920s and 30s. In a spirit of collaboration, Schiap's designs were photographed by Horst P. Horst – not least a sweater with circular patches with deliberate holes – suggesting an early outing for Comme des Garçons knits – known fondly as the “Gruyère cheese sweater”.[#image: /photos/5ce44505cc50beae2414152d]||| ||| Elsa Schiaparelli in collaboration with Salvador Dali: Illustration for the "Skeleton" dress, A/W Haute Couture 1937, ink and gouache on paper Image: Copyright Les Arts Décoratifs, Paris/Jean Tholance The collaborations between female and male artists announce from the start of the 20th century that applied art was no longer geared towards “women's work”. Even Schiap's whimsical suede gloves with lace finger nail decoration were more than a lighthearted joke and were linked to the Surrealists through the designer's collaboration with Salvador Dali. It seems that creative women of the 1930s were already working in tandem with artistic men. Who designed the fingernail gloves? Elsa Schiaparelli of course with Salvador Dali. At 'women's Work?' exhibition in #paris. The irony is in that question mark A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 22, 2017 at 5:43am PDT By the time Niki de Saint Phalle's colourful creations appeared in the 1960s, when her “Nanas” were political and feminist, women were definitely artists in their own right. Niki de Saint-Phalle: political, feminist, radical painter and sculptor. This 'goddess of light' created in Polyester. At 'Travaux des Femmes?' at Paris Musée des Arts Deco A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 22, 2017 at 6:21am PDT I liked the wit that keeps this exhibition on the light side, such as the jewellery by Monika Brugger interpreting the theme of the sewing thimble, while the finale displays a troupe of powerful female artists under the banner, “Did you say women?” Jacomijn Van der Donk: "Hands" necklace in oxidised silver lace, 1994 Image: Copyright Les Arts Décoratifs, Paris/Jean Tholance The show is small, but thought-provoking. And hats off (especially Schiap's shoe hat!) to curatorial assistants Raphael Bille and Karine Lacquement, who look at women's work without making an aggressive feminist statement. “Travaux de Dames?” is at Le Musée des Arts Decoratifs, Paris, until 17th September 2017 (www.lesartsdecoratifs.fr) View Gallery 10 Photos Women’s Work: Being Female Before Feminism This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Culture & Living Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s stylist talks about that giant Michael Cinco gown
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And the logistics of putting together a look like that Aishwarya Rai Bachchan went to Cannes, hit the red carpet like a pro, had a mother-daughter style moment and she is back. Each year the actor travels to the French Riviera to represent L'Oréal as a global ambassador and her sartorial choices on the red carpet become talking points for days after. We spoke Rai Bachchan's stylist Aastha Sharma about creating these conversation starters. View Gallery 7 Photos Aishwarya Rai Bachchan’s stylist talks about that giant Michael Cinco gown Aishwarya Rai Bachchan is something of a legend at Cannes, the French press loves her—tell us what is like to be there? Cannes as a festival is so exciting, it's one of the most sought out red carpets all over the world and just to witness it—it's a different ballgame altogether. The people attending it, the organisers, the fans who are standing there waiting to see a glimpse of their favourite stars, the energy is so positive. It's one place where art and cinema come together. It's a lot of hard work that goes into the hair, make-up, clothing when someone like Aishwarya is attending an event of that magnitude. We worked on the styling almost four to five months in advance. It takes time because it has to be perfect, but it's a fun process. There is serious work happening but we try to be as creative as we can. The Michael Cinco look was one of the biggest, most dramatic looks we saw on the red carpet this year, what made you choose that particular dress? When I saw Michael Cinco's collection in March, I knew I wanted to pick this look for her. Michael was really helpful in keeping the look exclusive, we didn't want it to be released before she wore it to Cannes. How it looks in pictures and how it translates on a person are two different things. But when Aishwarya tried it on, it was a perfect match. I can't imagine anyone else wearing it. It's a big outfit but only she could carry it off with such poise and elegance. It could have gone very wrong, but she pulled it off. Tell us about the second red carpet look. We had worked with Ralph & Russo in 2015 when she had first worn something by them and it was well appreciated, so I was looking forward to working with them again. The aim was to have two separate looks that stand out in their own right. Wearing red on the red carpet is a challenge but it worked out. Aaradhya had her own style moment this year, tell us a little about that. Gauri & Nainika were very helpful in working on Aaradhya's look. She is a little princess of a girl but she is very grown-up, she travels to Cannes with her mom often so she also understands what is happening. We thought, why not go all out with her look too? That moment they walked together was just perfect. Aishwarya's style otherwise is very understated, but at Cannes we see a very different side of her. How do you balance both sides? Aishwarya has her own personality, she has been an icon for years, she is always appropriately dressed so it's very easy for me as a stylist. I don't have to convince her to do anything—if it's an international red carpet event we go all out because she is representing a brand and herself—it's almost a form of art. Back home, she favours Indian designers and a more understated sense of style. Going back to the Michael Cinco dress, was it difficult to manage behind the scenes? The dress came in a big bag, it had a room of its own. When you are working on something that will make an impact, you don't think about how you will take care of that dress or details like that. You're so involved in creating that perfect moment everything else just falls into place. Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast
