column1: Have you seen Manish Arora’s playful Middle Eastern collaboration?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer ties up with popular brand Riva View Gallery 6 Photos Your first look at Riva x Manish Arora Manish Arora knows the power of a collaboration. In his 20-year career he has worked with over 50 brands, including MAC and My Little Pony. For his latest venture, he's tied up with Middle Eastern fashion brand Riva. One of the region's most-loved fast fashion brands, Riva is known to fuse modesty with modernity. “Working with a brand is like a marriage, and I found it easy to merge my brand aesthetic with that of Riva,” says the designer. The man who calls himself a darzi (tailor), is one of India's most recognised names on the global fashion scene. The former creative director of Paco Rabanne divides his time between Delhi and Paris. But when it comes to his work, be it through a reference to Indian artist Bharti Kher's swirls, or his use of the oversized paisley—you can never forget that Manish comes from India. His collection for Riva finds flowing dresses, cape-style abayas and military-inspired jackets. “I think both India and the Middle East have same approach to embellishment. It is about the ‘more is more' philosophy,” says Arora, which probably explains why Riva looked to an Indian designer for their first designer collaboration. “I think I am international thanks to the fact I never forget to be Indian. By that I mean Indian culture is always a part of what I do,” the designer adds. In the last few months, Arora has been in Middle East more than once—he was most recently in Oman speaking at the Condé Nast International Luxury Conference on 'Mindful Luxury' and prior to that was in Bahrain and Beirut. He counts Elie Saab as one his closest friends. “There is no such thing as western and ethnic fashion anymore,” he says. Which is why Arora made sure that while the Riva collection was tailored to respect the culture of the Middle East, it is also something women can wear in Milan, Mumbai or Muscat. Arora has been very conscious about the pricing, starting with a tag of DHS 250 (approximately Rs 4,400). “I want this to be a collection that is truly accessible.” And while the collection is exclusively available in retail store at Riva's Dubai Mall store, you can buy in online in most countries (including India) on Sivvi.com. RivaXManishArora is available at Riva, Dubai Mall and on Sivvi.com Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Kate Moss launches jewellery collaboration with Brazilian designer
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion "It’s my drug of choice." "I love jewellery," Kate Moss enthuses, "I can't walk past a jewellery shop without seeing something I love." Jewels have been the main ingredient in the style mix of Kate Moss ever since she was a child - "I would always hunt at Christmas for the smallest box and hope there was a piece of jewellery inside." In 1997 she told Vogue, "It's my drug of choice." Although we've seen Kate's design aesthetic in the fashion arena, in spite of her obsession, we have never seen it in jewels. Until now. Next week, her first limited-edition jewellery collection launches, in collaboration with Brazilian designer Ara Vartanian. The pair first met in Sao Paolo years ago, when Kate visited Vartanian's store to commission a tanzanite ring, but it wasn't until last year that the idea for the collection of 18-karat gold, diamond and Brazilian gemstone rings, pendants, earrings and buckles materialised. "Ara always wore this pendant and he explained to me it was an amulet," Moss says, "which brings good energy." Vartanian gave her the leather necklace with seven diamonds facing the front, and five amethysts on the inside, touching the skin for protection. "When we spoke about working together I said I wanted to make more jewellery like that," Moss continues, "Pieces that have meaning and that you can wear every day." This was followed by an invitation into Moss's London closet. "Every time afterwards that I visited London I'd spend time in her wardrobe to get ideas of what she likes," laughs Vartanian. Clothes, fabrics, and textures are what Moss wanted him to see, he says, as well as two particular antiques: a Russian Twenties cigarette case and pair of matching gold cuffs studded with rubies. "We use a lot of red garnet in the collection," says Vartanian, "because it's Kate's birthstone." As well as garnet she also loves amethyst. "I find them more organic, I feel they're a bit more spiritual. There's something earthy about them," she says. The gems are set into Vartanian's designs of diamond moons and stars, combined with Moss's sense of stylish freedom and asymmetry, two glistening on one ear, worn with a simple garnet stone on the other. The pair bonded over the story of St George, patron saint of England, slaying the dragon which comes to life on a pendant, with a eye embroidered with black diamonds on the back for protection. This led to them explore other medieval symbols, such as sickle moons, shields and mounted swords as motifs. "Kate wears jewellery in a very free way," says Vartanian. "She just throws it on." This spirit is demonstrated in the campaign, shot by Fenton Bailey in the grounds of Moss's Cotswolds home, where the jewellery twinkles as happily on models Elfie Reigate and Anna Lee Gardner, as it does on the boys, Luka Isaac and Louis Baines. "But these pieces aren't about fashion," insists Vartanian. "The stones and attitude give them a powerful energy, they are forever." And what does Moss hope is in one of the small boxes she opens from the collection? "I love the moon rings, and the pendulum necklace." column1: Elizabeth Saltzman on styling Deepika Padukone for Cannes 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And why she is one of the hardest working talents in the industry Deepika Padukone is no longer a Bollywood star, the term ‘crossover actor' is far more accurate to describe her in this current phase of her career. Since 2016, when she was on Vanity Fair's list of Hollywood's Next Generation stars, she's been to the Oscars after-party, the Met Ball, and now she's at the 70th Cannes Film Festival as one of L'Oréal's global ambassadors. Padukone's quietly graceful sartorial choices have always made their way to best-dressed lists. When she's on international turf, the star's wardrobe is entrusted to one of Hollywood's leading stylists—Elizabeth Saltzman, whose clientele includes the likes of Gwyneth Paltrow, Uma Thurman and Saoirse Ronan. Saltzman is a senior professional in the industry, with over 30 years of experience in fashion. This year at Cannes, she is working exclusively with the homegrown, now global talent. Some quick math will reveal Saltzman's start in fashion predates Padukone's toddler years. We called her up in the French Riviera minutes after Padukone stepped out on the red carpet in that Marchesa dress, to chat with her about the business of creating one of the most-talked-about looks this year and transforming an Indian actor's style to appeal to a larger audience. The Cannes red carpet is one of the most-watched events in the world. Given that this will be Deepika's L'Oréal debut, what do you have in mind to create an impact? We were discussing it and the big conversation was to have elegance, glamour and fun. She wanted [her style] to be different than what she's done; which is hard because she has done so many amazing things. It's a whole different set of rules between countries for fashion, which I think is interesting. How would you say you have influenced Deepika's look? I read the comments on her Instagram [on the picture of her in the white Tommy Hilfiger dress at the Met Gala] and I learnt that the Indian market doesn't want to see her in a slip dress, they want to see her as they know her. You have to figure out between the two worlds. We try not to read too much into that [the comments] but go with what is best for Deepika, and it's interesting because it is so important not to lose a single fan in life. They have such faith and they are so loyal. I was hired by the American team and the message I received was that they wanted her to be seen a bit differently than she has been. We opened the eyes of the world to her beauty, elegance and talent to other countries. While she is by far one of the biggest stars in the world, but that doesn't mean people know her films outside of India, because not all of them play in other countries. So when I got the job, I was so excited to work with her. She is so elegant, I mean truly one of the most elegant bodies and brains I have worked with and then there's the naughtiness, the dimples, the fun and flirtation! A post shared by Deepika Padukone (@deepikapadukone) on May 3, 2017 at 3:47am PDT What has been your experience styling her? Everything looks good on her—that's fun. I like big hair and I love bold colours, but you also don't want to age her. She is really the most beautiful when she is wearing her track pants with no make-up on and just a beautiful brow and that smile, and you just sit there thinking wow! Then she comes in with her hair done and you're like that's even more amazing. And then she puts on the dress and it almost takes away from the elegance. It's amazing to work with someone so beautiful that clothes actually don't add to it. The only other person who I have encountered is like that Christy Turlington. Today I introduced her to some of the designers she hadn't met before and they were shocked by her beauty. And these are the people who work with Gisele [Bündchen] and everybody, and they were speechless. What can we expect from her second look? I can't tell you much except that it is one colour, sexy and glamorous. What is one thing Deepika demands when planning her look? I think she is open to learning and excited so there are no demands, we work on everything together. The one thing I do ask of her and every client I work with is complete honesty and feedback, which I think is important. You have to be comfortable in what you choose because if you don't feel good, you don't look good. I think Deepika listens to her fans and respects them, most of all she just wants peace of mind and happiness. I think she wants to feel good, even last night she was working out at gym instead of partying. She is dedicated to her craft. When you've flown in from India and your stylist says go go go and your bed says stay stay stay so you meet halfway and then you go go go @deepikapadukone A post shared by Elizabeth Saltzman (@elizabethsaltzman) on Feb 25, 2017 at 10:37pm PST Is there a colour you prefer to see her in? I like her in almost any colour. Because of her beautiful skin, honestly, you can work with any colour. I do particularly like her in green, pinks and whites. I have no favourites, but I stay away from black for red carpets. I think she deserves more than that. You have been working with Deepika for a while now, what's her personal style like? I think her style is classic with a twist. She can do sportswear really well but I like that she looks great even in travel clothes. Her personal style is little bit bodycon, a little edgy, not funky-edgy, but interesting. Before last night, before make up and hair, in a fitting, that moment when a woman feels so good in a dream dress that you know it's hers 🔥💥💘💘💘💘@deepikapadukone x @moniquelhuillier #oscars #vanityfair #goodnight A post shared by Elizabeth Saltzman (@elizabethsaltzman) on Feb 27, 2017 at 4:19am PST How many suitcases of clothing have you shipped over to Cannes? People get robbed in Cannes often, so I rolled both of Deepika's red carpet looks and put them in my own carry on suitcase. I am not going to take a chance with that! Plus, clothes get held behind with customs and it's just not worth the stress. We did two fittings—in New York and in London—so we have edited it down to just what we need. That makes it five suitcases. The way my team and I pack is that every look down to the shoes and jewellery is put in one bag with a picture of the person wearing it. "It's a little naughty this dress because even though you are showing nothing, you are showing everything," says Elizabeth Saltzman (@elizabethsaltzman) who is styling @DeepikaPadukone at #Cannes2017. "We put this dress on hold the minute the @marchesafashion show was over. The colours are extraordinary, not just the rich plum but also the green. The morning after the Met Ball, @georginachapmanmarchesa Chapman, Deepika Padukone and I did a quick fitting. It has a wow factor that is important for Cannes. The dress is not too much, it's not too little, it's not overpowering, she can get in and out of the car, she can have fun in it, she is so excited to be here." A post shared by VOGUE India (@vogueindia) on May 17, 2017 at 10:47am PDT What are you looking forward to most this year at Cannes? We want to all go jump in the ocean and have our first swim. That's what I am most looking forward to, jumping in the ocean like a child. I am also looking forward to this pair of earrings we might be using for the second look. We or may or may not use it, but details like that make my job exciting. What makes you work in the industry year after year? We know it's an important business, but we also know we are not saving lives, so it is important to have fun. I love my job and I love that I get to see all of this talent. I am so blessed, but it wasn't just luck. I worked so hard to make it happen. No-one leaves the office later than I do. I put in the work because I care. Sometimes I am packing and unpacking, and I wonder why this can't happen automatically! If they can invent cellphones, why can't they invent something to do the packing? I was raised by loving parents who supported me but they also taught me work ethic—and those are two different things. The reason I like working with Deepika is that she works hard because she cares [about her work], and I respect that Here's a look at the star's journey in Cannes: Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The only kind of Manolo Blahniks Carrie Bradshaw would be wearing today
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Cue Vetements x Manolo Blahnik View Gallery 9 Photos The only kind of Manolo Blahniks Carrie Bradshaw would be Boots have been around for a while, reincarnating at various lengths and heel sizes. Everybody from Andy Sachs in The Devil Wears Prada (“Are you wearing the Chan-” “The Chanel boots? Yeah I am.”) to Madonna have been an ardent wearer of the style. Fast forward to SS '17, the label that everyone loves name dropping—Vetements—collaborates with Manolo Blahnik, and together they spawn a whimsical take on the shoe style that could double as pants. The waist-high boots starred in the spring 2017 runway show at Paris and presented an overall surreal silhouette that paid an ode to Manolo's craft, manifesting itself into these shoes of the future. It was a showcase that saw Vetements collaborating with 18 other labels, including Juicy Couture, Dr. Martens, Reebok, Comme des Garçons and more, but it was the jewel-toned boots that caught everyone's attention in the departmental store. The waist-high boots are a towering incarnation of the satin pedestals Blahnik has been providing in the form of footwear. Naturally, the likes of Rihanna, Kendall Jenner and Vetements' stylist Lotta Volkova have displayed their love for the piece with unique styling. Rihanna chose to flaunt orange boots and match it with the same shade of a floor length outerwear. Others seen in these were Kim Kardashian West, Kendall Jenner, and Lily Aldridge who wore the thigh-high, skin tight version of the boots to the Met Gala. The boots question today's fashion psyche—is a Vetements product undeniably Vetements if it defies convention and compels you to think whether it is wearable or affordable in real life? The answer is defined by the lasting effect that this label seems to have on its consumers who relish every runway piece introduced by the label (the DHL T-shirt, Champion hoodie, Thrasher sweatshirt). Validating this ideology is virtual retail giant Net-a-Porter, which made the boots exclusively accessible on their website since February. In some ways, the Vetements x Manolo Blahnik boots are a requiem of the past, revolutionised by the style curators of today. Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How to pull off absurdly yellow sunglasses like a supermodel
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Question: What do Bella Hadid, Adwoah Aboah, and Hunter S. Thompson have in common? Answer: yellow-lens sunglasses Yes, the gonzo style staple (famously sported by Johnny Depp as Raoul Duke in the 1998 film of Thompson's freak-out novel, Fear And Loathing In Las Vegas) is having a moment. So, how do you pull them off as well as Bella? Firstly, make an effort to keep the rest of your look super-groomed (leave the bucket hat at home). This translates as a vampish lip and sleek, pulled-back hair. Put the extra effort in - you want the glasses to be the singular 'off' detail about an otherwise regular look, which means forget about the psychedelic band tee and do sharp black tailoring instead. Our final rule? You can and should wear yellow sunglasses from dawn till way after dusk. Plus, the beauty of tinted lenses is that (even in fashion circles where it's acceptable to wear sunglasses indoors) you can wear them inside and out. column1: 6 stylish ways to wear mesh this season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It's surprisingly versatile View Gallery 6 Photos 6 Stylish Ways to Wear Mesh This Season If you weren't obsessed with Madonna in the '80s or you didn't spend part of your youth dressed as a punk, wearing mesh might seem like an alien concept. It's an intimidating fabric, to say the least—after all, it's almost totally transparent. But mesh is actually quite versatile; it's not always about being overtly sexy in a see-through top and bra, or playing the part of Goth rocker in fishnet leggings. If styled properly, mesh can make for a useful layering piece. For instance, a bell-sleeve mesh top can add edge to preppy stripes, boot-cut jeans, and slick loafers. The material can also go from punk to pretty when worn underneath a soft slip dress or with a flouncy pink skirt and floral-print tee. Sportier mesh, meanwhile, works well with track pants and a velour tank on top. Above, six of the coolest ways to mess around with mesh this season. column1: What Bella Hadid learnt about fashion by working with Chrome Hearts
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We found out View Gallery 6 Photos What Bella Hadid learnt about fashion by working with Chrome Hearts One of the biggest events this season during Paris Fashion Week was the launch party for Bella Hadid's collaboration with Los Angeles-based accessories label Chrome Hearts. The collection will retail at Selfridges Oxford Street in London. Vogue caught up with the supermodel on playing designer. How did the collection come about? The whole collection is very much my style, and very much Chrome Hearts but a lot more modern. The collection came about as a result of a very long friendship that me and Jesse Jo Stark (the designer) have. I have learned a lot from Jesse and the Starks (owners), not only on the design process but also what it takes to get to the final product. We have all grown together. Do you have a favourite piece from the collection? The leopard print bondage coat—it's my little baby. It has gone through a lot of production. What was the biggest challenge? Not being able to be there all the time. I work a lot in Europe and New York and they are in Los Angeles and we would Skype a lot. Jesse instinctively knew what I would want and like, so made it a lot easier. Also timing was very difficult, we had about six months with production to make it all work. What were your references when working on the line? I got a lot a lot of inspiration from Chrome Hearts itself, particularly their '80s and '90s archives. Mostly '90s street style-inspired but elevated to the Chrome Hearts level, which is so iconic. I want people to feel badass when they wear it. Will there be another collection? We really want to do shoes and jewellery and the next thing will be eyewear. Culture & Living Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Here’s a look at Off-White’s latest street-friendly collaboration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You even have a chance to win a piece View Gallery 15 Photos Off-White collaborates exclusively with this luxury e-retailer on a collection Virgil Abloh, who rose to underground stardom as Kanye West's art director, is high on the list of cool designers in contemporary fashion. Ever since the launch of his fashion label Off-White, his aesthetic has favoured by the influencer crowd—from Beyoncé and Jay Z to the Kardashians. The designer is joining forces with luxury e-retailer Mytheresa.com for the launch of a capsule collection (that will be sold exclusively on Mytheresa.com) titled ‘Cut Here'. Abloh is not your traditional designer—with degrees in engineering and architecture and exposure to rap culture, his meteoric rise in fashion has caused some disapproval, most notably from Raf Simons. ‘Cut Here' embraces street culture and allows audience to participate in conversation with the makers of Off-White. One of the key pieces from the line, a khaki mac, has the alphabets A, B, C and D written at different levels and viewers are asked to regram or a post a picture of it stating their preferred length. “The idea is that the garment is labeled with a series of marks. People can chime in with their opinion on where the garment should be cut. I take in the suggestions, but ultimately will make the final decision,” said Abloh. In the age of post normcore, separates like the T-shirt combined with an exposed corset make winning Saturday night looks. Scroll through our gallery to see the complete collection. column1: Which bag trend will you try this spring?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion What kind of bag lady are you? View Gallery 19 Photos Which Bag Trend Will You Try This Spring? What do Balenciaga, Loewe and Fendi have in common? Stylistically, virtually nothing—but when it comes to baggage, these houses are part of a growing trend of pushing accessories to extreme proportions. This season, look to opposite ends of the size and scale spectrum—from bottomless totes at Marni and Balenciaga (because there's big, and there's big) to itty-bitty clutches at Fendi and Louis Vuitton—for your bag du jour. Next, it's time to ask yourself the hard-hitting question: What kind of bag lady are you? Like to cart a day-and-night's worth of stuff around? Sonia Rykiel's floppy canvas satchel and Hayward's extra-large silk-brocade sac promise to withstand the weight of the world—dry cleaning, gym clothes, and a daily read, say—on your arm. In search of a statement-making, super-size style that does the talking? The grandiose graphic embroidery on Gucci's Modern Future tote is so mesmerising that, even despite its heft, you won't want to put it down. (Don't worry: Drawstrings let your shoulders share the burden.) Maybe you're of the less-is-more mindset, in which case a discreet and chic Chloé wristlet holds a certain appeal for those looking to go hands-free. The shape is curious, but the attitude is cool. And if you're a die-hard packrat but live for a good challenge, take note: The mythical quest to squeeze all your stuff (and your iPhone 7) into a bag small enough to cup in the palm of your hand will always be with us. But as any wise woman will tell you: In bags, as in life, love conquers all. And what's not to love about Alexander Wang's furry micro bucket bag—or Altuzarra's python and cherry-printed pouch? What they lack in space, they more than make up for in personality. Even better? Exercising restraint by downsizing to a dainty number can be highly liberating. And if you've weighed the options but still can't commit (or simply can't get enough), carry two bags in tandem. Test your strength as you let a Céline cabas carryall and Chanel camera case comingle on your arm for an over-the-top look that's sure to send spirits soaring and heads turning. column1: Louis Vuitton taps into Japanese culture for resort 2018
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion 6 things to know about the show Last year it was the Niterói Contemporary Art Museum in Brazil's Rio de Janeiro. This year, Louis Vuitton set its sights on Kyoto, Japan for its Resort destination show, choosing the Miho Museum for the site of its spectacular presentation. There, models crossed a suspension bridge wearing Nicolas Ghesquière's latest in leopard spots, studded leathers, and sequin-adorned sheer fabrics. The LocaleVuitton chose Kyoto's Miho Museum as the site for its Resort 2018 show. The spectacular space was designed by I. M. Pei in 1997 to house textile heiress Mihoko Koyama's art collection. The space consists of several buildings connected through tunnels and walkways that cut into the mountains cape. The CelebritiesIsabelle Huppert, Sophie Turner, Riley Keough, and Laura Harrier numbered among Louis Vuitton's celebrities perched in the front row. The ModelsJapanese actress Rila Fukushima opened the show, followed by a parade of LV favorites include Kiki Willems, Marte Mei van Haaster, Natalie Westling, and Fernanda Ly. The Make-upEchoing the glam, artful makeup of Vuitton's Resort 2016 show in Palm Springs, Pat McGrath created faces with bold brushstrokes of violet and shocking pink colors. The painterly strokes resembled Kabuki makeup, giving some of the models a heightened sense of drama. For the rest, it was thick-drawn cat-eyes and little else. The CollabJapanese designer Kansai Yamamoto, seated in LV's front row in a bright red suit, created samurai faces and other traditional Japanese designs for Ghesquière's sequin dresses and leather bags. The SleeveLeather studded cap sleeves were a focal point of Ghesquière's Resort collection, followed by soft blouson pouf sleeves that appeared on blouses and oversize suit jackets worn on the runway sans pants by Mica Argañaraz. column1: These experts are willing to answer all your questions regarding your career
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Industry advice from the wise Harmeet Bajaj, apart from being a designer, stylist, choreographer, product developer, and columnist, also takes a keen interest in education. “Around this time of the year, I get a lot of queries about career choices,” she says—one can only imagine why. “I have been planning to start a school of fashion but while that falls in place, Suneet (Varma), Kanika (Singhal) and I thought of coming up with a workshop that would help guide students,” she says, explaining the premise of Platform Masterclass—a career guidance workshop led by the best in the business. The workshop will take place at The Hauz Khas Social in New Delhi over a span of two days. Each of the industry experts will speak to the audience for an hour, followed by another hour-long open session for questions. Students and young professionals can look forward to interacting with heavyweights in the contemporary Indian fashion landscape like designers Manish Arora, Rahul Mishra, fashion critic Shefalee Vasudev and Vivek Ramabhadran, vice president for Asia South Region for Swarovski Professional, at the sessions. Over the course of two days, the masterclass aims to cover areas of fashion design, buying and merchandising, PR and Communication, E-Commerce and Brand Building at the end of which, applicants will be asked to take an aptitude test to help gauge a direction for themselves. The Platform Masterclass will take place on May 25 and 26 at Hauz Khas Village, New Delhi. Application fee is Rs 25,000. column1: Gucci’s new tongue-in-cheek collection is for anyone who loves graphic art
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And you can buy it right now View Gallery 13 Photos Gucci’s new tongue-in-cheek collection is for anyone who loves graphic art Alessandro Michele in his role as creative director at Gucci is ushering an era of collaborating with street artists and illustrators. After working with names like Trouble Andrew and Jayde Fish, Michele has invited illustrator Angelica Hicks to work on a line of T-shirts. Hicks likes to illustrate puns. She has authored Tongue in Chic: The Fabulous Fashion World of Angelica Hicks and the bio on her website featured her in a trucker hat saying ‘Make America Chic Again' (here's looking disapprovingly at you, Trump). Her collection with Gucci touches on politics, board games, inclusivity and some really silly puns. For an added touch of exclusivity, only 100 units of each of the eleven T-shirt designs have been produced. Michele wants to you treat each one as a piece of art and they come bearing unique serial numbers. To celebrate this collaboration, two art walls in New York and Milan will feature Hicks' designs. Gucci owes its success to influencer marketing and Michele's knack of tapping the millennial audience. T-shirts encouraging the United Kingdom to show some ‘team spirit', referencing the Church's opposition to homosexuality, are bound to strike a note with the vocal youth. column1: LVMH reveals more details about new luxury shopping site
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It'll sell more than 150 brands Following its announcement in March that it would be launching its first multi-brand e-commerce platform, LVMH has revealed more details about the ambitious - and highly anticipated - launch. The new site for Le Bon Marché - the luxury department store that the French conglomerate owns - will be called 24Sevres.com, after its Paris address (24 rue de Sèvres) and will be open for business in the second week of June. It will initially focus on womenswear; ship to 75 countries; offer exclusives from 68 brands for the launch; and will sell more than 150 brands, approximately 30 of which will be LVMH-owned, including Dior and Louis Vuitton, marking the first time that the two brands will be available in a multi-brand online platform. “Our clients are highly sophisticated and always in search of creativity and innovation," said Bernard Arnault, chairman and CEO of LVMH. "With the launch of 24 Sèvres, we are offering them a truly differentiated online experience built on our unique expertise at Le Bon Marché in Paris. Shopping at Le Bon Marché is a special and unmissable experience for both local and international clienteles. With 24 Sèvres, our clients can now enjoy this unique feeling every day and night, worldwide.” It will also be a hub for moving image and innovative visual merchandising (such as on-the-spot, video styling consultations), rather than focus on editorial content, as with many competitors including Net-a-Porter, Style.com, and Matchesfashion.com, Farfetch.com. For chief digital officer Ian Rogers (for whom 24 Sèvres is his first major project for LVMH since he was headhunted from Apple 18 months ago), this is a key point of difference. "The move toward social-media platforms like Instagram and Snapchat comes hand-in-hand with the rise of the internet as a more visual medium and of mobile domination," he told The New York Times "If you look at our site, we lean far further toward visually-led merchandising than the more editorial skew of our competitors." As for joining said online luxury competitors, Rogers is confident that with the move by many brands towards omnichannel experiences (a much debated topic at this year's Condé Nast International Luxury Conference), the time is perfect to strike. "We don't want to be early adopters. We have been before and we paid the price for that," he said, referring to LVMH's former venture into e-commerce with eLuxury.com which closed in 2009. "When it comes to the internet specifically there isn't necessarily a reward for being first. There is, however, currently a major focus on omnichannel and experience, and we are moving from a mass culture to a mass of niches. If there is quality in what you do, you're not threatened. Timing-wise, this is exactly where LVMH wants to be." This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk   Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Tommy Hilfiger confirms yet another collection with Gigi Hadid
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Hilfiger keeps Hadid on the books Tommy Hilfiger has announced that Gigi Hadid is to design another two collections for their collaborative label, Tommy X Gigi, making their union more of a permanent fixture rather than a two-season fling. “Gigi is a force in the fashion industry and the ultimate Tommy Girl,” said Tommy Hilfiger today. “Her positive, down-to-earth energy, and cool, effortless style continue to captivate her audiences around the world. I have loved designing the Tommy X Gigi collections with her and I look forward to continuing our partnership for another year." Hadid first debuted her designs for the brand for autumn/winter 2016 last September, and showed her second collection for spring/summer 2017 in February in LA as a part of the brand's see-now, buy-now structure which it has called Tommy Now. Contracted to the brand, Hadid traversed the globe, popping up in multiple cities to promote the collections which were available to purchase immediately. “The Tommy X Gigi collaborative collections and our Tommy Now see-now, buy-now global runway platform are driving the strong momentum behind Tommy Hilfiger Womenswear,” said Daniel Grieder, CEO of Tommy Hilfiger Global and its owner, PVH Europe, who added that "the results continue to exceed expectations in every area of our business - from engagement with new audiences to increases in social media and press visibility to double digit sales growth for two consecutive seasons". For her part, Hadid is understandably happy to continue to flex her creative muscle in addition to owning the catwalk and multiple campaigns. “It has been a dream come true to work with Tommy Hilfiger, a brand that I genuinely love and have been a fan of my entire life,” she enthused. “Collaborating with Tommy has been inspiring and an amazing introduction to the world of design. column1: Roberto Cavalli appoints creative director
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's how thing will change Roberto Cavalli has appointed Paul Surridge as its creative director, following Peter Dundas's departure from the role last October. British designer Surridge studied at Central Saint Martins, before moving on to work at Calvin Klein in the Nineties, Burberry (under Christopher Bailey) and Jil Sander (under Raf Simons) in the Noughties, and most recently Z Zegna, where he was creative director and Acne Studios, where he acted as a creative consultant. His new role will see him take responsibility for "all of the group's brands and for all creative functions", a statement confirmed this morning, with his first outing for the brand slated to take place during the spring/summer 2018 showcase at Milan Fashion Week this September. “I am honoured and proud to carry forward the legacy of this extraordinary Italian house," said Surridge today. "This is a unique opportunity to contribute a new chapter to the Roberto Cavalli universe, which positively celebrates the beauty, sensuality and power of women. It is my intention to show the passion I share for the codes and vision on which Roberto Cavalli built his brand while celebrating the excellence of Italian craftsmanship." There has been plenty of upheaval at the Italian fashion house over the last year. Following his appointment as creative director in March 2015, Peter Dundas departed after 19 months in the role, shortly after CEO Gian Giacomo Ferraris joined from Versace. The brand released a statement shortly after, announcing that it would be undergoing a significant restructure - including redundancies - news of which was met with upset and the threat of action from employees. The company reached an agreement with its employees last December. “I have worked with Paul, and I had the opportunity to appreciate his creative talent as well as his managerial abilities," said Ferraris today. "Paul has a 360-degree vision on brands and branding. He is passionate, mature and an amazing team player. We all believe that he is the ideal candidate to complete our management team and contribute to implementing the ambitious development plans for Roberto Cavalli, which we have agreed with our stakeholders." This article previously appeared on Vogue.co.uk. Weddings What's New What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Shirts may be everywhere, but the stars wear this brand
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet Caroline Constas Shirting is as ubiquitous in 2017 as blue denim – with pieces from the catwalk to the high street making their way into virtually every wardrobe – but one designer still secures endless support from the stars: Caroline Constas. The New York-based Canadian designer often sees her pieces worn by celebrities from Sarah Jessica Parker and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley to Chrissy Teigen and Rita Ora – as well as Insta influencers galore, so what makes them so special? We caught up with the designer behind the brand to find out. Tell us about the your brand? Caroline Constas is a lifestyle brand which caters to the cosmopolitan woman. I have always loved the saying, “Style is not what you wear but how you live” this is exactly what we are all about. There is an intellectual side to the brand; a philanthropic one in addition to the destination-bound attitude. It is truly a brand which complements the lifestyle of our worldly customer. Describe the Caroline Constas woman in three words. She is sensual, sophisticated and cosmopolitan. Your collection is destination focused, perfect for a woman who travels widely, but what are your tips for travelling with shirts? How should we pack, unpack, and wear them? Absolutely! When it comes to packing I actually prefer rolling over folding, it keeps the clothing from wrinkling and also takes up less space. The wonderful thing about the shirting fabric that I work with is that it is made from a very high-quality cotton, and thus is an easy fabric to care for and is quite ideal for travel. It can be hand washed, air dried and worn without needing to be pressed or steamed. You've dressed many stars, whose interpretation of your brand did you really enjoy? I loved how Sarah Jessica Parker wore one of my dresses with a political safety pin on Jimmy Fallon. The pin stands against hate and was a socio-political statement that I honored and supported. I have quite a passion for current affairs and politics so that moment really resonated with me, I felt very touched to be a part of it. You have a background working with retailers as well as being trained in design, how does the marriage of the two help you? It is how I was able to break into the market! I started my company very organically, with just $10,000 in 2013. I wasn't able to hire staff, I was a one-woman show with an idea and some confidence that I could build something that would be advantageous to retailers. My advantage was that I knew the buyers and some editors and I wasn't afraid to pick up the phone and put myself out there. Shirts are everywhere this season, from the catwalk to the high street, what makes yours so popular? Besides the emotional factor that a customer might have when they see one of my styles, I think that the brand really has an identity. Customers appreciate that and when they find a label that is consistent, there is a loyalty that is formed. Who would be your dream CC woman? Cleopatra if I could have it all. I would also love to dress the Duchess of Cambridge, I think she has lovely taste. What is next for the brand? We have a stockist list that I am very honored by and proud of. Nurturing those relationships and growing together will always be our number one priority. We will also be expanding categories. We just launched knits for autumn/winter 2017 and I plan to launch two more categories in 2018 that are destination-oriented. We have also just re-launched the website, which I am extremely excited about. There is a disruptive element to it which I think that our customer will find exciting. The website will be a large point of growth in 2018. column1: Here’s why the Prada backpack is the greatest travel It-bag of all time
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A money-making hit that no one saw coming Yesterday, Prada staged its stand-alone Cruise show at the Fondazione Prada's Osservatorio in Milan. While most major labels like Chanel, Dior, and Louis Vuitton have adopted the “go big or go home” motto when it comes to showing Resort collections, the Italian house helmed by Miuccia Prada has shied away from the holiday-inspired season, recently including a small amount of it within the Spring men's lineup, shown in June. That's not to say that Mrs. Prada is turned off by travel. In fact, Prada was a leather goods and luggage company first, and much of the designer's work borrows from the idea of wandering, like the “vagabond” women who walked in her Fall 2016 show or the Spring 2017 menswear collection full of backpack-strapped lads on a mission to, well, anywhere. The backpack, of course, is itself an iconic symbol for Prada. It represents the designer's nomadic, exploratory sensibilities but also her understanding of the importance of utility in fashion. When Prada released its original nylon backpack in 1984, people went nuts. It was a money-making hit that no one saw coming—an impressive amount of hype for a plain black nylon sack. Decorated only with that iconic triangular logo, the backpack made label lovers rethink their Hermès bags and quilted Chanel double Cs. As Mrs. Prada told The New Yorker in a 1990 interview: “I want always to mix the industrial way of doing things, with the patrimonio of the past, with the artisanal tradition.” Who knew that a backpack could go so deep? Today, the Prada backpack is as prized a possession as it was back in the late '80s and early '90s. This writer happily still has hers: a large two-pocket Vela in black that can go from home to the gym to the office to a plane ride far away. It's the most comforting thing in my closet. I use it almost every single day and I'd like to think that Mrs. Prada would be proud. It's a little bit of everything: simple, durable, useful, fashionable, sophisticated, covetable. It's a travel bag by definition, but a style totem in spirit. The enduringly cool Prada backpack taught me what fashion-meets-function actually means and, in turn, just how “It” a bag can be. column1: Here’s why Bebe should try to stage a comeback in 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In defense of the ’90s brand that made crystal logo tees cool The year was 2001. It was the summer before freshman year of high school, and I was attending a weeklong program called “study skills,” aimed at easing kids into the rigorous curriculum of a college prep institution—one helmed by Jesuits, no less. I walked in looking like a backup dancer on the “Spice Up Your Life” video. My classmates were all dressed in freshly pressed white polo shirts and Abercrombie & Fitch jeans, while I made my first impression in turquoise track pants and a scoop-neck logo T-shirt with the word Bebe scrawled in crystals across my nonexistent chest. Today one of my best friends, who I met for the first time at study skills, still mocks me endlessly for said ensemble. I argue, though, that she was the one who came up to me first and asked to hang out. I stand my ground that it must have been the eye-catching Bebe. It was my first lesson in fashion peacocking. I was an unabashed devotee to the store back in the late '90s and early '00s. Bebe struck a chord among tweens and teens looking for platform heels and low-slung bellbottoms à la Britney Spears. Plus, it was an easy sell to the parents who were skeptical of overspending—or spending at all—on a sequined snakeskin-print tank for their 14-year-old. Alas, the glory days of Bebe are long gone and the retailer is flailing. A few weeks ago it announced that it'd be shuttering all of its brick-and-mortar stores, around 168 in the U.S. and Canada. Its goal is to close each door by the end of the month but maintain an e-commerce platform in an effort to sidestep filing for bankruptcy. How far the mighty have fallen. Bebe is just one of several early aughts–era retailers that are struggling or completely defunct, chief among them being BCBG, Wet Seal, and Abercrombie & Fitch. Though it's probably far-fetched to think that a Wet Seal or an Abercrombie can make a strong comeback today, Bebe could and should make a play. After all, we're living in a time where nostalgia rules in fashion, and logomania, both of the high and low kind, is as popular as ever. Bebe was a sexy brand that celebrated influencers and famous faces of the day, like Rose McGowan, Rebecca Romijn, Mischa Barton, and even the Kardashian sisters. In 2017, couldn't they appeal to the new guard of Jenner and Hadid sisters who have brought other '90s trends back from the dead? Recently, Gap successfully launched a capsule collection comprised of its most popular '90s denim and produced a commercial that recalled the iconic singing and dancing ads from that era. Last year, Guess Jeans released a similar capsule that included old school jean jackets and logo tees, modeled by Hailey Baldwin in the style of the original Guess Jeans bombshell Claudia Schiffer. Sex sells, but so does sentimentality. Bebe might not currently have the cash to hire a Kendall or a Kylie to pose for its billboards, but we're quite sure either girl would be happy to rock a thrift store crystal tee in an Instagram selfie. It makes no difference that they were toddlers when the brand was at its prime. I wish I still had my original Bebe tee. I also wish I still had some of my old Bebe staples, like those striped crop tops and trashy-cool printed slip dresses. I'd wear it all again—maybe not the full look that sparked a lifelong friendship that day at study skills, but certainly bits and pieces. In this writer's opinion, those little crystal letters still have something worth paying attention to. This article originally appeared on Vogue.com Beauty Fashion What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Rei Kawakubo: “In general, I am always angry”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Costume Institute at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York is honouring the creator of Comme des Garçons – and the result is powerful, artistic and emotional Katy Perry performing at the Met Ball THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 1, 2017 at 11:29pm PDT Katy Perry, her sexy silver bodysuit flashing flesh, sang her heart out – enough to shake the dust off the ancient Egyptian statues at New York's Metropolitan Museum. While the star-studded audience swayed to the music, Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons, the subject of this year's exhibition at the Costume Institute, sat still and silent. What was the 74-year-old Japanese designer thinking as Rihanna flaunted a Comme outfit strewn with three-dimensional flowers? She competed on the red carpet stairway with Madonna in camouflage-patterned Moschino, Julianne Moore in feathery Calvin Klein, Kim Kardashian in a sexy white Vivienne Westwood dress and Kylie Jenner in a lacy Versace dress, while Donatella herself was in a shiny gold sheath with hair dyed to match. Rihanna says it with 🌺 at the Met Ball in her homage to Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garcons THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 1, 2017 at 11:11pm PDT Donatella goes for GOLD. (And that includes her HAIR. THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 2, 2017 at 12:02am PDT “In general, I am always angry,” Rei Kawakubo told me a few weeks before, as we sat in her Paris showroom on the Place Vendôme – she a tiny, tense figure, her face hidden under a clothes brush of a fringe. “I wasn't particularly angry at the time of the punk collections,” she continued, “but ‘Dress Meets Body' came out of anger – not something specific, but a more abstract anger at the unfairness and contradiction in the world.” The inscrutable Rei Kawakubo and her husband and business partner Adrian Joffe with Carla Sozzani at the Met Ball gala evening THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 1, 2017 at 10:57pm PDT The designer, who has been at the helm of Comme des Garçons for nearly half a century, was referring to her Spring/Summer 1997 collection of clothes with contortions and protuberances. It was immediately dubbed ‘Lumps and Bumps' and was seen as a reference to tumours and a belief that clothes could be, even must be, more than something merely to cover the body. Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Body Meets Dress - Dress Meets Body" collection, Spring/Summer 1997. The collection was nicknamed "Lumps and Bumps" by Kawakubo's detractors Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art “From the very beginning, her search was always to look for something new – and in the natural process of time passing, that became harder and harder, so inevitably clothes became more than just clothes,” explained Adrian Joffe, Kawakubo's husband of 25 years and the CEO of Comme des Garçons and Dover Street Market. 'The Art of the In-Between' is the definition of the current Rei Kawakubo exhibition. It is the first fashion exhibition the Met has dedicated to a living designer since Yves Saint Laurent, in 1983. Although not a retrospective, meaning an A to Z view of Kawakubo's past four decades, curator Andrew Bolton has a clear vision of his subject. He positions the designer not in the context of fashion's development through the 1980s – when there was a dramatic split between an orgy of gorgeousness on the one hand, and the simple lines of Japanese and Belgian designers on the other – but in Kawakubo's native Japan. Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "18th-Century Punk" collection, Autumn/Winter 2016–17, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art The show titles – those few words that Comme offers for each collection – echo Zen philosophy and especially “Mu”, which Bolton says “roughly translates as ‘emptiness'”. This also links to “Ma”, meaning the gap, pause, or space between, hence Bolton's title: “The Art of the In-Between”. The curator's displays reveal a face-off between fashion and anti-fashion; the high and low; then and now, and many more of Kawakubo's designer-isms. With Andrew Bolton at New York's #metropolitanmuseum THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 1, 2017 at 11:26pm PDT But to the museum visitor, the effect is primarily visual and emotional. It starts with the famous lumps and bumps, in coloured checks, with a film (the only one in the exhibition) of choreographer Merce Cunningham showing the clothes on dancers in motion. “It was only when I was here alone that I felt the emotion and what we have achieved,” Bolton said, looking out at displays of clothes framed by white squares or rounded structures that hold red punk tartan, fitted black jackets, or pretty, girly dresses. The eye is also drawn upwards to white wedding dresses and black garments in the blinking brightness of a neon installation by lighting designer and visual artist Thierry Dreyfus. Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Not Making Clothing" collection, Spring/Summer 2014 Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art But all this seems not so much Japanese as a reflection of the world, from the tiny, red baby outfit to the all-black lace, suggesting mourning. Bodies covered in parcels of white cotton tied with bows, with black hair shielding the face, have a label that reads “Life/Loss”. I asked Kawakubo whether she felt that her creativity was rooted in her Japanese identity and if she could ever envisage working outside Japan – perhaps in Paris, where she has shown her collections since 1981? Her emphatic response surprised me. Comme at its most mathematical - at the Met museum THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 2, 2017 at 12:00am PDT “I have no consciousness on a day-to-day basis of being Japanese,” she said, “and yes, I could work somewhere else – it doesn't have to be Japan.” Whatever way you look at the exhibition, it is about a visionary blurring the distinction between art and fashion and pushing the boundaries of design. This applies as much to the extraordinary headpieces as to the clothes. Grace Coddington with Comme's long term, inventive hair stylist Julian d'Ys - remembering the day when they dressed Lady Gaga as a witch and put her in an oven! THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 1, 2017 at 11:17pm PDT At the exhibition opening, hair stylist Julien d'Ys, creator of wigs and hair wonders for Comme, chatted with Vogue editor Grace Coddington, recalling the moment when they dressed Lady Gaga as a witch. The exhibition itself is full of examples of his hair craft: punk peaks rising above red velvet dresses, or a fuzz of scarlet curls contrasting with animalistic garments in furry deep pile or feathers. Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Blue Witch" collection, Spring/Summer 2016, courtesy of Comme des Garçons. Kawakubo frequently collaborates with hair stylist Julien d'Ys on headpieces and hairstyles for her collections, as shown here. Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art “Every time is the same: there is always a surprise that pulls at my creativity until something comes into my brain,” said d'Ys, referring to the time when Kawakubo demanded “No hair”. His response was to wrap strands of hair into individual pieces of plastic. At the Met Ball, few even tried to make hair the focus, unless you count Thandie Newton's bunch of country garden flowers or the long locks of Gucci's Creative Director, Alessandro Michele. But Alessandro Michele doesn't seem to notice that he has Kendall Jenner displaying almost all - right behind him. THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 1, 2017 at 11:57pm PDT As the exhibition proves, there have been different phases in the development of Comme collections, each one beginning with a rupture that Joffe says expresses “the torture and the hell of making something new”. I asked specifically about ‘White Drama' – a powerful vision from Spring/Summer 2012 in which all-white clothes led the show through the rituals of birth, marriage, and death from a lacy christening gown to wide papal sleeves. Kawakubo explained that it was “nothing to do with sadness as part of the starting point”. “It was not a conscious decision to make a sad collection,” she said, “but it is totally understandable that people have that reaction because it comes from a very sad place.” I did not see the early Comme work as sad, although the models were almost entirely dressed in black, as they were in Yohji Yamamoto's shows and the audience's own clothes. Passers-by who saw us gathering around some obscure show location would whisper, “Who is the funeral for?” Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Blood and Roses" collection, Spring/Summer 2015, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art The effect of the pieces selected by Burton for the Met show is very different. The overall impression is of colour, especially the vivid scarlet splashed like blood stains on white dresses or shaped as big whisks of red roses. Or a delicious display of 18th-century punk from Autumn/Winter 2016 – all rose patterns and elegant, courtly frills, as if the designer had switched the 1970s with the 1790s. Eighteenth century PUNK. When Rei Kawakubo turned 1970 into 1790... THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 2, 2017 at 12:07am PDT Many of the clothes – for example from the lumpy ‘Body Meets Dress - Dress Meets Body' collection – look more elegant in the museum than they did on their original outing. Other clothes that I remember first seeing in raw and drab spaces – the cellar of a Paris bank, filled with water pipes, comes to mind – take on a different perspective in the Met setting. The accompanying exhibition catalogue goes even further to impress beauty on tortured shapes, and includes the work of sensitive photographers such as Craig McDean, Inez & Vinoodh, and Paolo Roversi. The Comme history is given a quirky prettiness in the catalogue, while my memory of the actual shows is of a much harder and tougher aesthetic. The absence of videos of the original presentations is a great loss. Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Cubisme" collection, Spring/Summer 2007, courtesy of Comme des Garçons. Photographed by frequent Comme collaborator, Craig McDean Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art It is interesting to ask Kawakubo how she feels about this uncharacteristic looking back to the past. According to a conversation with Bolton that is published in the catalogue, the designer compared her recent work to “outsider art”. This “schism or big change”, as Joffe described it to me, started with the Spring/Summer 2014 collection, called ‘Not Making Clothes'. The dramatic direction here was to exchange recognisable materials for what looked like garbage re-cycled into clothing. The most recent Comme show in March had models walking across a pale pink space in felted creations that resembled stuffing, rubber, duct tape and carpet underlay moulded onto the body. Only the Comme des Garçons x NikeLab sneakers seemed to have any connection with the reality of modern clothing. Comme des Garcons. Rei says that fabric is all 'non fabric' - no wovens, no fashion fabrics A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 4, 2017 at 2:40pm PST This rupture had a dramatic response from even the most vaguely fashion-conscious general public, as I saw when I posted on Instagram a video clip of two models in the show – and had one million responses. That figure has now gone up to more than twelve million, many of the comments derogatory or downright nasty.While Joffe was astounded by the figures drawn by a company that was until recently “very selective, very secretive” – and under most people's radar, Kawakubo herself had an interesting reaction. “Let's hope the turnover goes up as much,” she said. Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Cubisme" collection, Spring/Summer 2007, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art Kawakubo's status as an artist – so successfully illustrated by curator Bolton – has to be viewed alongside her business acumen, which is intensified by Joffe's skill as an exceptional retailer, especially with the Dover Street Market stores. Equally important is the fact that over her long career, Kawakubo has created space for other designers in her business, including her nurturing of Junya Watanabe, who entered the company as a pattern cutter and was given his own label in 1992. Other protégés are Chitose Abe and Junichi Abe, who went on to found their own brands, Sacai and Kolor. Kei Ninomiya's Noir is another example of Comme's support of others. Whether for Comme or for her mentees, Kawakubo says that every show she has given over the past 40 years has been designed to create a sale. Certainly her elegant, subtle designs for menswear have legions of loyal fans all over the world, who return season after season for the clever and highly wearable cuts. “Because I see the collection first, sometimes I have panic attacks, thinking ‘What are we going to sell?'” Joffe admits. “But this time I was almost blown away by the way she interpreted the show into a collection.” Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "The Infinity of Tailoring" collection, Autumn/Winter 2013–14, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art At our meeting in Paris, Kawakubo led me towards the sales floor, where the “Who would ever wear those clothes?” mantra has an instant response. From the woolly tangle that I had interpreted from the front row as a horse blanket put though a washing machine, emerged tailored coats and jackets, knits and tailoring – clothes in the Comme spirit interpreted from the deliberate oddities on the runway. Who makes these interpretations? A team of designers? The store manager? The answer is, of course, Kawakubo herself, who draws each outfit and creates them with her two pattern makers. The “outsider artist” is in fact an astute fashion designer and business woman. Blood red as a pivotal colour for Rei Kawakubo at Comme des Garcons THE REAL REI: Read my story about the Met Ball. Link in bio. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on May 1, 2017 at 11:13pm PDT Nothing of this is to be found in the Met exhibition. That is understandable perhaps, as Bolton wants to focus on the designer as artist. But my unstinted admiration of the designer's ethic and aesthetic is that the two fit together. And I would like to have seen a reference, even an explanation, to visitors about how these extraordinary creations can turn into a buck. So is “artist” or “craftsperson” the definition of Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons? Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Blue Witch" collection, Spring/Summer 2016, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art I asked Thierry Dreyfus, who has created the lighting for the Comme shows for the last decade, whether he considered Kawakubo to be an artist or a fashion designer – or an artist who expresses herself through clothes? This was his reply: “When Alberto Giacometti was asked if he was an artist, he answered, ‘I am a sculptor'. Picasso was asked the same question and he replied, ‘I am a painter'. Rei is a poet, working freely on the human form.” ‘Rei Kawakubo/Comme des Garçons: The Art of the In-Between' is at the Costume Institute of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, from 4th May to 4th September Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Body Meets Dress - Dress Meets Body" collection, Spring/Summer 1997 Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Body Meets Dress–Dress Meets Body" collection, Spring/Summer 1997, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Body Meets Dress–Dress Meets Body" collection, Spring/Summer 1997, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Blue Witch" collection, Spring/Summer 2016 Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "18th-Century Punk" collection, Autumn/Winter 2016–17, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Cubisme" collection, Spring/Summer 2007, courtesy of Comme des Garçons Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art Rei Kawakubo for Comme des Garçons, "Ceremony of Separation" collection, Autumn/Winter 2015–2016 Image: © Paolo Roversi; Courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Isha Ambani walked the Met Gala 2017 red carpet in Dior couture
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And we can't get over how pretty she looked The First Monday of May comes with its fair share of excitement. Every year, the Met Gala, fashion's most fabulous party with the likes of Rihanna, Blake Lively and Kendall Jenner in attendance, celebrates New York's Metropolitan Museum latest exhibit and this year it honours Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons. And when Anna Wintour is the host, you know the guests pull out all the stops, sartorially speaking. This year, while Priyanka Chopra and Deepika Padukone made their presence felt, we spotted Isha Ambani marking her debut at the gala as well. View Gallery 4 Photos Isha Ambani’s debut at the Met Gala was all kinds of fabulous Ambani, kept things elegant and feminine in a dress from Maria Grazia Chiuri's first couture collection for  Dior. She styled it beautifully with a clutch from the brand's latest collection, minimal hair and make-up. The young entrepreneur arrived at the gala with close friends, Natalia Vodianova and Diane von Furstenberg and was spotted hanging out with Emma Roberts. Fashion Fashion Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How has our on-flight wardrobe evolved over the years?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Where comfort and decorum meet Growing up, my father had a strict dress code for when we travelled. No jeans, no track pants and no leggings. Believe it or not, my sister and I were always in dresses or trousers and we also always carried a pair of pyjamas to change into on flights. Suffice it to say, it was a different era when travel was glamorous, and men and women dressed up on flights. Sadly, things have changed now. While my father still always flies in a suit, we've gone more casual. But still some of his lessons remained. Till date, I have yet to wear trackpants or shorts on a plane. Now, on most flights you'll catch me in Topshop leggings with a DKNY cosy, or in the softest jumpsuits from Uniqlo that look great with a denim shirt and easy-to-slip-off ballerinas. In my carry on: Monisha Jaising's monogrammed scarf, a change of clothes and a loaded Kindle. As summer travel heats up, I decided to poll the Vogue staffers to ask them how they stay chic on long haul flights. Here's their airport style decoded. column1: This is what went into Priyanka Chopra’s epic Met Gala entrance
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Includes: two assistants, one bus, and a Jonas Brother View Gallery 9 Photos This is what went into Priyanka Chopra’s epic Met Gala entrance “I will probably faint, but it's so cool,” said first-time Met Gala attendee Priyanka Chopra of the custom Ralph Lauren look she wore to the event on Monday. The Indian actress was a newbie at Golden Globes this year too, where she donned a head-turning custom piece by the American brand—a glittering gold dress with a plunging neckline that recalled a Studio 54 kind of glamour. Chopra and Lauren had more classic reference points in mind for the Museum's annual ball this past Monday and used the classic elegance of Katharine Hepburn as a jumping-off point. The resulting trench coat was given an avant-garde twist thanks to a dramatic train which required four hands to get out of the lobby of her hotel. But Chopra didn't let her train stop her from dancing the night away. The floor-sweeping trench cleverly converted into a minidress for Katy Perry's Boom Boom Bash and Rihanna's epic late-night party. Here, a behind-the-scenes peek inside her big red carpet moment. column1: Which Bollywood star’s sunglasses should you steal this summer?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Update your collection with these celebrity-approved picks View Gallery 32 Photos Which Bollywood star’s sunglasses should you steal this summer? With the summer at its strongest right now, it's a great time to invest in a pair of sunglasses. But which ones should you be putting your money on? Pick your ideal pair from Bollywood's list of favourites. Basic black For the girl who loves classics, nothing will do (or last) as well as a reliable pair of black shades. Pair yours with a flouncy skirt like Sonam Kapoor, use it by the pool like Karisma Kapoor, or match with a jet black ensemble as Katrina Kaif and Bipasha Basu have. This is one accessory that will never fail you. Crazy colours When it comes to sartorial experiments, Kareena Kapoor Khan and Alia Bhatt are always up to the challenge. While the former recently stepped out sporting icy blue sunnies, the latter opted for a shaded yellow-meets-green pair. Want to go even bolder? Try Shilpa Shetty Kundra's favourite red, or even pink like Parineeti Chopra. Reflective A little bling goes a long way. Just ask Sridevi and Sonakshi Sinha! Both stars updated their classic aviators with mirrored lenses while on vacation. While the former picked a tint of gold, the latter went with a striking silver pair, similar to Malaika Arora's. Fun frames Think your sunglass collection includes every pair worth having? Wrong! Change things up this summer with experimental details. Play with Perspex and patterns like Anushka Sharma and Esha Gupta respectively, follow in Deepika Padukone's footsteps with a matte frame, and try on unexpected shapes. The possibilities are never-ending. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Nirav Modi expands business eastwards with a new store in Beijing
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion China, are you ready for this? View Gallery 5 Photos Nirav modi Recognising the value of the market in China, haute diamantaire Nirav Modi has opened a new boutique in Beijing. Previously, Nirav Modi has marked its presence internationally by opening standalone store in New York, London and Hong Kong. The boutique in Beijing is set inside the The Peninsula Beijing hotel. “The Chinese customer is changing the face of luxury retail industry all over the world. They are sophisticated luxury buyers, with an eye for detail and craftsmanship. The boutique in Beijing is our first one in China and we have more boutique launches in China planned over the next few years,” Modi says of his plans. Seen on the likes of Kate Winslet, Taraji P Henson, Sonam Kapoor and Priyanka Chopra, celebrities are no strangers to the Nirav Modi label. Golden glass, mother of pearl, brushed silver and rose gold tones accentuate the interiors of the store, which also has VIP rooms for its clientele. column1: Inside Chanel’s spectacular ancient Greece-themed resort 2018 show
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Have you seen the set yet? Under Karl Lagerfeld, Chanel has made a habit of taking its Cruise collections on the road to fabulous destinations, from Cuba to Seoul, and drawing inspiration from the local culture and style. But if Lagerfeld can stage a rocket launch in the Grand Palais, as he did for Fall 2017, maybe he can also conjure the spirits of international style right at home in Paris. That he did today with a collection called “La Modernité de l'Antiquité” that raised ancient Greece from the past. Ionic columns rose in the Grand Palais, while a Greek sunset served as a painted backdrop. While you wait for Luke Leitch's review, get the five things you need to know about Chanel Resort 2018 here. The inspirationIn Coco Chanel's Rue Cambon apartment, a bust of Venus sat on the mantle. That served as Lagerfeld's jumping-off point this season, with the designer saying, “The criteria of beauty in ancient, then classical, Greece still hold true. There have never been more beautiful representations of women. Or more beautiful columns. The entire Renaissance, in fact, was based on antiquity. It is really about the youth of the world in all its power and unpredictability.“ The column shoesForget stiletto or block heels. Lagerfeld's take on Greek style comes complete with Ionic column–heeled gladiator sandals. If history has taught us anything, it's that Ionic columns are quite sturdy. The pottery dressesRed-and-black-figure-painted pottery was one of the most popular ways ancient Greeks depicted the human body in two dimensions. Lagerfeld reworked the motifs in column dresses with rows and rows of illustrations evoking the Greek originals. The modelsLagerfeld's many muses came out today. Vogue cover star Vittoria Ceretti opened the show, followed by Kiki Willems, Binx Walton, Lindsey Wixson, Amanda Sanchez, and Arizona Muse. As always, Lagerfeld took his bow with his youngest model, Hudson Kroenig. The GoddessesIf a breezy, wide silhouette defined the beginning of the presentation, the final looks were pure Venus. Bias-draped gowns in pale pink and cream with gold embellishments closed the show, worn by models with golden headbands and nymph-like waves. column1: Veteran Met Gala photographers reveal what really happens on the red carpet
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Wardrobe malfunctions, the craziest parts of the night and more View Gallery 9 Photos Confessions of a Met Gala Photographer New York based photographers Sherly Rabbani and Josephine Solimene have been working as professional photographers in the fashion and entertainment industry for over 17 years. As the photo agency Rabbani and Solimene, they have shot for many publications, including Vogue and Glamour. They have been shooting the Met Gala for over 15 years and swear it gets better every year. Here, Rabbani shares the juiciest secrets from behind the lens at fashion's biggest night. Most memorable/hilarious red carpet moments from this year's red carpet? Sean Combs laying down on the red carpet while Ciara posed for photos. The other funniest part of the night was when Katie Holmes and Zac Posen didn't pose for us, so all the photographers started chanting “Katie and Zac please turn back, Katie and Zac please turn back!” and finally they did. How do you get celebrities' attention on the red carpet? There are a couple of ways to get celebrities to pay attention to you on the red carpet. The first and best way is to scream their name like crazy. The second way is to make amazing eye contact with them and have a conversation with them about a movie they're doing, or something detailed and special you know about them. That connection helps a lot because they stand for you longer and give you better moments to photograph. Another way is by knowing their manager or the PR. If you know them or have a connection with them, they'll always bring the celebrity right to you no matter what. Who gave you the best reaction? The person who gave us the best reaction has to be Katy Perry. When Katy Perry shows up to the Met Gala, she walks slowly and makes sure every photographer gets their shot. She makes amazing eye contact with each and every photographer. I personally got the best reaction last night from Madonna. She has to be one of my all-time favourite performers and when I saw her, I told her I love her and she yelled back “I love you too!”, so that made my night. Which celebrity caused the most commotion in the photographers' pit when walking tonight's red carpet? That would have to be a tie between Rihanna and Beyoncé. The reason why they always get the most amazing moment on the red carpet is because they wear the most beautiful dresses. They go all out when they attend the Met Gala. Two other celebrities that caused a lot of commotion, in particular last night, I would have to say were Paris Jackson and Frances Bean Cobain. These two girls had fathers who are legends in the music world and having a them attend an event like this was very cool and special. Of course, having Celine Dion at this event for the first time was very, very amazing as well. Any wardrobe malfunctions you witnessed? The Met Gala always has malfunctions on the red carpet. Like when Beyoncé dropped her wedding ring on the floor and Jay Z went down on one knee to pick it up for her as if he was asking her to get married again. This year we didn't have anything like that but we did have a major make-up malfunction when Frances Bean Cobain kissed Courtney Love on the face and left lipstick marks all over her chin. Whose look was the most shocking to see on the red carpet? The most shocking people that show up on the red carpet are usually the ones that have just started dating and making their red carpet debuts together like Selena Gomez and The Weeknd or Jennifer Lopez and A-Rod. Other than that, it's really not shocking to see anyone show up on the red carpet because the Met Gala is seriously like the Oscars and anyone who is anyone shows up. I am never shocked by the celebrities that attend. The most shocking look to see on the red carpet would probably have to be Katy Perry and her Galliano dress, with the red veil covering her face. What is usually the most chaotic part of the night? The most chaotic part of the night is always when they have multiple celebrities on the red carpet at the same time. When this happens, it becomes a very hard to focus and take your time with one celebrity. It becomes very hard to shoot Jennifer Lopez when Gwyneth Paltrow is on the other side and you don't want to miss a shot because both shots are super important. What goes into shooting a larger-than-life outfit, like Rihanna's yellow outfit from last year? Two things. The first one being that the celebrity is wearing a magnificent dress, usually with a train. The second part is making sure that no other talent is on the red carpet at the same time. A clear shot is what makes a beautiful moment. Having a clear shot with no one else in the photo can produce an iconic fashion moment. Who is your all-time favourite celebrity to shoot and why? Our favourite celebrities to shoot at the Met Gala have to be Beyoncé, Rihanna, and Sarah Jessica Parker. They take the fashion to a whole other level. They try to make sure they stick with the theme in the best way they can and they give us the best shots of the night, always. Fashion Fashion People © 2019 Condé Nast
