column1: Mario Testino, world-renowned photographer, actually wanted to be a priest
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And everything you ever wanted to know about him Visceral and often voyeuristic, iconic lensman Mario Testino's hard-bodied portraits have made him fashion world royalty. Vogue India editor Priya Tanna meets the ace photographer in Jaipur to discuss how he finds beauty in everything. His photographs do not speak a thousand words to me. Not even when a bare-bodied Kate Moss is staring at me for the umpteenth time, invoking a provocation only she can. Not even when it is an image of the late Princess Diana, dazzling with her cheekbones and chutzpah in a one-shoulder gown, immortalised in my mind forever. Words cannot legitimise the impact of his work. Mario Testino's images sizzle with a heady sensuality that is guaranteed to create a stir. And this unique vision has secured his singular position in the fashion firmament—as the su􏰫per hero of fashion and celebrity photography. Possessing the dual superpowers of being a creative genius whose three-decade-long career has also earned him much commercial success, his significance is unparalleled􏰝. He is royalty at front rows, on speed dial with stars and designers alike, and, if you were to visit his Wikipedia profile, his career highlights and achievements alone will take you days to scope out. It quotes: “Alongside his practice as a photographer, Testino has also worked as a creative director, guest editor, museum founder, art collector/collaborator and entrepreneur.” It really doesn't get more multi-hyphenate than this. I have followed Testino's work closely for years now—in particular, the Gisele Bündchen images, those daring campaigns for Gucci in its Tom Ford days, and the entire Diana portfolio. Up until now, our paths have only crossed socially. But over the years, I have sporadically reached out to him to shoot for Vogue India, and it's taken a full decade for this to happen. It took an entire army of well-heeled organisers, months of negotiations and countless emails to set this partnership in motion. So when I meet him at our cover shoot in Rajasthan at the Sujan Rajmahal Palace, it is with the trepidation of being stonewalled into a monologue.􏰝 Instead, I find in him a warm, honest and 􏰛funny raconteur who speaks from his heart and offers incredible insights into a life less ordinary. Here are excerpts from our chat. Priya Tanna: Mario, is this your first time in India? Mario Testino: I came 20 years ago to Jaipur. It is one thing to see India as a tourist and another thing to see it with someone who lives here. This time, with the Vogue team, it was very exciting. To be honest, I didn't want to come back to Jaipur; I wanted to go to Mumbai and Delhi. I've realised that I'm an urban tourist and I thrive on cultural cities and social communication. I like to meet people, to see what people are doing, business, art...but my editors wanted to go to Rajasthan. And I'm glad I came; the city is beautiful. PT: So far, how have you managed to capture Indian culture? MT: To me it is very interesting to delve into a culture and immerse myself in it to try and understand the things that work in that country. I recently worked with Katrina [Kaif], and my team did the hair, make-up and styling in our specific way.􏰝 Then I went out with her in the eve􏰫ning and thought these are two different women—how she styled herself and how we perceived her. I want to see how the public will react to our pictures of Katrina. Will they be able to relate, will they like what we did—you know what I mean? I am not trying to change your culture; I am trying to get what you can give me and bring what I can give you. PT: People transform differently under each lens. From the time you started to now, how have you evolved as a photographer? MT: It is inevitable to evolve because we learn from every new place that we go. So, what I do here will influence me in a way, so I try to keep my eyes open and fresh. My work has changed a lot. When I started, I used to look at things from far away but now I look at things closely. I am more into the woman today than I was before. PT: I read that you wanted to become a priest. And now your photography is known for its incredible sexuality. How did you go from there to there? MT: I don't think I went from there to there; I just inhabit all these different worlds. The years when I wanted to be a priest were because of my involvement with social work. There's something in me that likes giving and helping. Now I apply it in a different way. I work with [model] Natalia Vodianova's Naked Heart Foundation. We recently set up Teresita Parque [a playground for underprivileged children], named in memory of my mother Teresa, who passed away last year. This is my way of giving today. In between, I was in the period of deriving pleasure from beauty, excesses and the body. I am obsessed with sexuality because I find that some people are particularly gifted when it comes to bodies. I don't know if it's a search for my ideals or an exploration. PT: The in-between phase reminds me of the time you had pink hair and wore lilac terrycloth jumpsuits. What happend to that man? MT: I used to be a model in my earlier years, but now the stress of deciding what to wear in the morning is the last thing on my mind. Now, I wake up and think about my photographs and about what I'm going to do. The photograph seems to be the end of what I love. I like defining the story, deciding the clothes, casting and working with editors. The entire process of storytelling—that's what attracts me. You have been very generous to invite me to edit your magazine. It's like giving someone your baby. It􏰇's interesting to try and define the identity o􏰛f a country through Vogue. Vogue is all over the world, but each one has its own identity. PT: Do you define yourself as a fashion photographer today? MT: I see myself as many things. A fashion photographer, a portrait photographer, a businessman, a museum founder, an agency founder, a creative director, a philanthropist. I think people today have to fill many roles to survive􏰝 I am more interested in the person than the clothes. column1: Inside Mario Testino’s cover shoot with Kendall Jenner for Vogue India
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The new Jenner-ation NY-Jaipur-Shanghai… Just 72 hours in the life of supermodel and Insta-star Kendall Jenner. If those frequent-flier miles don't make you dizzy, stomach this: over 75 million Instagram followers, 14 Vogue covers, around 85 runway shows [at the time of the interview], contracts with Victoria's Secret, Estée Lauder and Calvin Klein, a fashion line with her sister and a burgeoning photography career. Did I mention she's only 21? Hers is, clearly, the face the fashion industry is betting on. Jenner's meteoric rise (in an early season of Keeping Up With The Kardashians, the shy teenager showed her mother a flipbook of pictures she shot of herself, and declared to their nearly 5 million viewers, “I want to model”) is, of course, a result of talent, hard work and dedication on the young beauty's part, but it's also a reflection of the social culture in which we are currently living. For those who've been living under a rock, Jenner is part of the Kardashian-Jenner mega empire presided over by matriarch and momager Kris and includes children from her first marriage to Robert Kardashian (OJ Simpson's close friend and lawyer, famously immortalised in the recent Netflix show)—Kourtney, Kim, Khloé and Robert—and daughters from her second marriage to Olympian Bruce Jenner (now known as Caitlyn), Kendall and Kylie. Keeping up? With numerous fashion and beauty brands, video games, makeover shows, books and more endorsements than you can imagine under their belt, they've made a business of living their lives. And those lives—messy, chaotic and in all their glory—are showcased on prime time, in Snapchat filters and updated constantly through their very popular apps. Confession: In case you hadn't guessed already, I know my Kardashian (in fact, in the office I am called Parkashian—it even says so on my coffee cup). So when I heard that Jenner was going to be in India to shoot our May cover with Mario Testino, I flew to Jaipur to get an insight into a person I felt I already knew. “HI, I'M KENDALL” It's 7.30am at the Samode Palace and it's hard not to notice the 5ft10in beauty sitting in the breakfast room. Not that Jenner is doing anything to attract attention to herself (she is rather subdued in a grey tee and a fringed leather jacket, her hair pulled back into her famous top knot) but because, even at this unearthly hour, and despite the few hours of sleep she got last night, she looks every bit the glamazon I stalk on Instagram. The next time I see Jenner is over another meal—lunch. She's spent the morning shooting with Testino (“He has such a young personality and I love working with him. This will probably be my most memorable shoot with him, because I flew all the way down to India for it,” she says sweetly) and is ready to tuck into her plate of pasta, white rice and potato wedges. A supermodel who eats carbs—I mean, that's just the holy grail. “I get asked that all the time!” she drawls, when I comment on her plate and ask her how she maintains that incredible body. “I don't know… My father's genes, I guess. I also can't tolerate any amount of spice, and I know you love it here,” she says by way of explanation. We're sitting out on the verandah in the afternoon sun and Jenner is casual and relaxed in her white bathrobe, distracted by a stray cat swirling around her bare feet. Later that afternoon, I catch her clicking pictures of said feline. column1: Of course, you can wear leggings as pants. Here’s how
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Work it View Gallery 14 Photos Yes, You Can Wear Leggings as Pants—Here’s How Leggings have long been designated for running on treadmills or lounging around. In fact, the stretchy bottom is considered so off-duty that it has frequently landed people in hot water when spotted outside a relaxed setting—particularly when worn as pants. Leggings have been controversially banned from some schools, and just last month, two young women were denied entry on a United Airlines flight because their spandex didn't fit the carrier's dress code for “buddy passes” awarded to family and friends of employees. But compared to those less-than-favourable cameos in the news, leggings are having a rather chic moment on the runway. For Spring 2017, Max Mara went with all-over botanical print athleisure, pairing a track jacket with some eye-catching leaf leggings, while Stella McCartney showed a more out-on-the-town look with a red lace dress. For a cool compromise between gym and cocktail hour, look no further than Giambattista Valli's Fall 2017 collection, which chose black Nike spandex to go with a frilled blouse. Yoga lovers can rework their flared versions for every day, too: At Paco Rabanne, for Spring 2017, the low-slung sun salutation–favourite received a moody rocker–meets–Bella Hadid makeover, thanks to a cropped sleeveless hoodie. If you're looking to take the fashion legging outside of the gym—or dare to board a plane in it—Vogue associate market editor Alexandra Gurvitch suggests that you keep the proportions in mind. “Shows like Balenciaga and Stella McCartney gave me full permission to wear leggings to places other than to the gym,” she explains. “I am obsessed with the slim silhouette and tend to wear a fuller top to counterbalance them.” Here, the best legging looks to take safely and chicly onto the street and all places beyond. column1: Meet the American designer whose pieces are handmade by Indian artisans
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Championing sustainable fashion View Gallery 5 Photos Anaak’s Luxurious, Artisan-Made Collections Are as Sustainable as It Gets Designer: Marissa Maximo Label: Anaak Instagram: @anaakcollection Location: Philadelphia—but spends half of the year working with artisans in India and Bolivia Education: Rhode Island School of Design Why it should be on your radar: Anaak is the rare fashion label that's elegant, beautifully made, easy to wear, and sustainable, too—from organic fabrics to the women artisan groups Marissa Maximo employs around the world. Everything is made by hand with natural dyes, and Maximo hopes to empower women by giving them work and keeping their traditional crafts alive in an age of fast fashion. It's truly global: Maximo's passport got a lot of stamps in the early 2000s. As the director of artwork and colour at Anthropologie, she travelled to India, Taiwan, China, Indonesia, and South America to develop the brand's prints by hand—“before everyone used computers,” she says with a laugh. The job introduced her to other cultures and crafts, and as fashion became increasingly hectic in the following years—Maximo also worked for Urban Outfitters during the recession—she felt she wasn't making a positive impact. “The fast calendar just got really fast,” she says. “At Anthropologie, we had four seasons, then we had six, and then 12, and the disposal of it all was really disheartening. I wanted to make things that matter to the people who wear them.” So she started Anaak in 2015 as the polar opposite to all of that: Natural, organic clothes that harm the earth as little as possible and are socially impactful, too. Most of the pieces are handmade in small batches by women artisan groups in India; see Fall '17's chikankari dress, which features slices of fabric cut and hand-stitched like 3-D embroidery, and the block-printed silks with natural dyes. Every season, Maximo explores new fabrics and finishes: “If there's a technique I'm interested in, I basically travel to that area and work with the artisans,” she says. “I'll base my collection off what they're doing, as opposed to coming in with a preconceived idea of what it will look like. So I usually design on the road.” Also new for Fall '17: chunky hand-knitted Alpaca sweaters made by artisans in the Andes mountains of Bolivia. Slow and steady wins the race: Because artisan-made products take much longer to produce, Maximo says it's difficult to work on a strict fashion calendar. But instead of scrapping the system and doing it her way, she simply works even further ahead. “I try to work a year in advance to develop fabrics,” she says. “That's been the challenge. I was trained to work so fast and move through ideas so quickly, so it's been a lesson to work on the DNA of Anaak and take the customer through slowly. With fast brands, there's no DNA—you're just reacting to trends.” Fashion first, sustainability second: “Our success has been about product, not any kind of advertising or branding,” Maximo says. There's a good chance some of her customers don't know that Anaak's clothes are made by artisans, but they still love the way they look and feel. On the other hand, there are probably lots of women who have been searching for something like Anaak—clothes that are elegant, simple, and effortless but also good for the earth and socially conscious. Now, they can stop searching. Where to find it: Anaak is mainly stocked in specialty boutiques, including Bird Brooklyn and 180 in New York and Ron Herman in Los Angeles. You can find more information at AnaakCollection.com. This article originally appeared on Vogue.com Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: You can now travel the world alongside Mario Testino
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Hop on Mario Testino may have started his career before social media exploded, but that wasn't going to be a hurdle in his track record. “I am always quick to jump. I find people debate too much whether to do or not. I am surrounded by young people, and they are always pushing me into the zeitgeist,” he talks of his approach to digital media. With over three million followers on Instagram, he is one of the most followed photographers from an older generation—and he is owning a space otherwise ruled by millennials. Social media, he says, is crucial for a photographer. “It's terribly important as it communicates what we want to say directly, truthfully and immediately,” he says. He has regularly taken over several Vogue Instagram handles to curate a unique selection of imagery for its followers. The biggest perk of being a photographer is the travel that comes with it. Last year, Testino launched his video platform MiraMira.tv to take his viewers with him as travels the world for fashion. The photographer works with a team of extraordinary filmmakers who capture the essence of the space. Given the scale of talent he is usually surrounded with, Testino has access to some of the most interesting personalities in the fashion industry. ‘Mira mira' translates to ‘look look' in Spanish—it's almost as though he wants you to open your eyes to sights you didn't have access to. “I travel so much for work both and pleasure. So if I am going to New York for the Met, we work on content around that. When going to India we looked at all the themes I was doing for the issue and then the Mira Mira team picked apart these themes from many different angles,” he says. Until the footage of Testino's time in India arrives, from behind-the-scenes footage to interviews take a look at the photographers journeys on the website and his Instagram handle. column1: How the latest Met Exhibit will influence fashion trends in 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion With Proof From “Manus x Machina” and “China: Through the Looking Glass” Christopher Kane's high-tech, 3-D sequined flowers from Fall 2017. Photo: Alessandro Garofalo / Indigital.tv Anticipation for Monday's Met Gala and the exhibit it's honoring, “Rei Kawakubo/Comme des Garçons: Art of the In-Between,” has reached a fever pitch. It's CDG central here at Vogue, and you can bet we'll be first in line when the exhibit opens to the public on May 4. But before we immerse ourselves in decades of Kawakubo's work, we're taking a minute to consider how last year's exhibit, “Manus x Machina: Fashion in an Age of Technology,” is still influencing fashion today—and what that means for “Art of the In-Between.” The focus of “Manus x Machina” was the history of hand-crafted couture and its relationship with technology—two schools of fashion often perceived as polar opposites. The Met made the case that high-tech embellishments and 3-D printing aren't threatening the dignity of couture; instead, today's designers are bringing the two worlds together (see: Chanel, Prada, Dior). Interestingly enough, lots of designers explored this concept on the Fall '17 runways, too. Among the season's biggest trends were two that mirrored the scope of “Manus x Machina”: On the one hand, there was an embrace of hand-crafted, grounded clothing (akin to the “Manus” section) and, on the other, there were plenty of futuristic and forward-thinking garments (similar to “Machina”). The common denominator? Both groups had mind-blowing details and were uncompromisingly beautiful. Alexander McQueen's hand-embroidered, unraveling tapestry dresses for Fall 2017. Photo: Alessandro Garofalo / Indigital.tv Consider the unraveling tweeds and hand-embroideries at Alexander McQueen, inspired by the ribbons tied around Clootie trees to symbolize wishes. Those were firmly in “Manus” territory, along with the crafty-chic dresses at Loewe, Maison Margiela's dreamy patchworks, and Valentino's hand-stitched lace dresses. Then there were the giant, intricately sequined flowers at Christopher Kane, which looked like they'd been plucked from a 3-D cartoon garden—“Machina” all the way. On that note, Karl Lagerfeld continued to explore technology at Chanel, where he showed classic tweed suits in dense, futuristic fabrics and embellishments, while at Gucci, Alessandro Michele mixed the natural and unnatural with floral and avian prints covered in thick, glittering computer-made embellishments. This particular jacket from Look 2 might have weighed a lot, and probably took weeks to finish. Chanel's signature tweeds got a futuristic spin for Fall 2017 with dense, sparkling embellishments. Photo: Alessandro Garofalo / Indigital.tv Fashion fans might be tempted to pick a side: Are you more of a “Manus” girl, gravitating towards those McQueen dresses? Or is a pixelated Christopher Kane frock more your speed? Some will say it's simply a coincidence that these opposing themes were Fall's biggest takeaways. But considering how influential the Met's exhibits have been in the past, it isn't such a stretch to think these designers may have drawn inspiration from “Manus x Machina.” Remember when Chinese blouses, floral and dragon prints, and silk kimonos were all the rage? That was just after “China: Through the Looking Glass” became the Costume Institute's most-visited exhibition ever. The timing was uncanny, and we're still seeing Eastern motifs on the street and the runway (see: Gucci Fall 2017 and Prada Spring 2017, below). Prada's take on Chinese pajamas for Spring 2017, complete with marabou feathers. Photo: Alessandro Garofalo / Indigital.tv With that in mind, we're already speculating how “Art of the In-Between” might affect the zeitgeist. Will designers walk away with the urge to study Kawakubo's work even further? Will they see her work and feel inspired to get a little more experimental and avant-garde? Perhaps that's just what we need right now. In the past few seasons, many of us have wondered what happened to fantastical, transporting, out-of-this-world fashion, and no designer could kick-start a new era of creativity quite like Kawakubo. Watch this space to see how “Art of the In-Between” translates onto the runways for Spring '18 and Fall '18, and stay tuned for our complete coverage of the red carpet on Monday. column1: Met Gala 101: Everything you wanted to know but didn’t know who to ask
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here are all the details The 2017 Met Gala is set for tonight, and as the world waits to see what celebrities will be wearing, it's worth refreshing your memory before the red carpet is rolled out. The Met Gala, of course, is the fashion-world equivalent of the Oscars—the night when models, designers, and Hollywood stars convene in the year's most over-the-top looks. As one of the first personalities to greet the stars as they step onto the 150-foot-long red carpet and a regular there since 1974, larger-than-life Vogue Contributing Editor André Leon Talley knows a thing or two about the grand annual affair. And so who better to turn to for a primer on the storied occasion than the man himself? From the event's origins to the best Met Gala dress of all time, ALT explains everything you need to know ahead of fashion's biggest night. What is the Met Gala? The Met Gala is the Super Bowl of fashion. On the first Monday in May, everyone who is anyone comes to the Metropolitan Museum of Art for the annual fundraising gala celebrating the Costume Institute's magnificent new exhibition on a changing theme. It all started in 1946, and over the decades has become a grand affair—the party of the year. The one other constant is the red carpet fashion. There is nothing quite like it, and it is vital and exciting to be a part of that. What is this year's theme? The phenomenal Japanese designer Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons. The exhibition will showcase 150 of Kawakubo's most extraordinary designs dating as far back as the early 1980s. It's a showcase of fashion as told through the lens of our contemporary culture, and should not be missed. Who gets invited? The world's best achievers in all the spheres, of music, film, Broadway, fashion, and music, as well as simple supernova personalities. The list changes each year. My favourite guest was Diana Ross, also in a full-length dress of exotic feathers. Which bird was it, I am not sure: guinea hen, turkey, or some exotic bird. It was strapless and full-skirted. What is the dress code? Dress codes vary. If you are Kanye West and Kim, you come in your own matching Balmain silver jacket and dress. If you are Beyoncé, you wear something that's a big statement. This year, I want to see if Bette Midler might take the night off from Hello, Dolly! to come up the red carpet. Last year, she wore Marc Jacobs. As a Met Gala regular, do you have a favourite memory from over the years? My favourite memory is when Cher joined the gospel choir from a local church in Harlem one year when the Met was held in December. And also, I was there when she descended the escalator in her brilliant Bob Mackie sequin see-through jumpsuit, way ahead of her time, in 1974. What do you think is the best Met Gala red carpet dress of all time? Rihanna's yellow Guo Pei cape edged in fur, with train bearers, from 2015. column1: Mario Testino on one of the most important projects of his life
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s where it began View Gallery 8 Photos Mario Testino on one of the most important projects of his life Peruvian photographer Mario Testino is a favourite in fashion's hall of fame. While the camera captures his imagination, Testino is also a lover of the fine arts. After making a name for himself on the international landscape, the photographer worked on creating an environment that connected Peru to the world by way of art, thus founding MATE - Museo Mario Testino in 2012. MATE not only hosts a permanent collection of Testino's work, but also that of visiting artists. The photographer talks about his work with MATE with Vogue. “I wanted to be part of the cultural scene happening in my country, Peru, and help with the push for urban tourism there. I felt it was important to show my love for endangered historical monuments like the building MATE is housed in, as people don't value them and would rather have modern buildings. I also realised that I have the access and the contacts that could help open doors to artists from Peru, and that my country in general could take advantage of these possibilities. I wanted to give back to my country, where I started my visual education. "We try to vary them between photographic work with photographers who have changed the way we look at that art form—and foreign contemporary artists that can feed the local scene with their ideas and experiences. We have a residence program in London where we send a Peruvian artist to spend six weeks living at the Delfina Foundation, in London. Here they get exposed to the British art scene, then they come back and do a show in MATE, using everything they experienced. We also have other shows that we feel can open the eyes of local art consumers about the freedom in art. This year we are doing a show of Graciela Iturbide, as part of our Masters of Photography series. We then have Alan Poma, as the last artist to visit the Delfina Foundation. There is also a show of Chris Levine's work, he's a contemporary artist who works with light. Finally Miguel Andrade, a Peruvian artist, that has done an installation at MATE. We also have letters of MATE in the entrance of the museum that are reinterpreted by Peruvian artists. At present, we have Ishmael Randall and coming up will be Christian Bendayan.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Mario Testino talks about the Gucci campaign that raised eyebrows
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The power of an image View Gallery 11 Photos Mario Testino talks about the Gucci campaign that raised eyebrows While you may be familiar with Mario Testino's editorial photography, you may not be as fluent with his commercial work. In his decades-long career, the Testino lens has transformed the perception of many brands with his images. The supermodel + famous photographer combo has led to lifelong partnerships, and in case of Mario Testino, these have been with the likes of Kate Moss, Lily Aldridge and Amber Valetta. Naturally, a striking image is the combination of great talents coming together to give the audience something they haven't yet seen. One of the most memorable campaigns for the Peruvian photographer was the subversive Gucci campaign with French stylist Carine Roitfeld that changed the boundaries of advertising. “This helped me identify the power of advertising; not as a subdued version of editorial—but as a place for stronger imagery that is liberated from editorial,” he says. Elaborating on the pivotal moment in his career, he says, “I particularly liked the period doing Gucci in the '90s with Tom Ford [the brand's creative director at that point] who used to push me, rather than control, me on the strength of these images. He was not afraid—and perhaps I had the preconceived notion that I had to be careful rather than daring.” Aside from the Gucci campaign, Testino also worked with Cara Delevingne and Kate Moss together for Burberry, Kiera Knightley for Chanel and Madonna for Versace. column1: Here are the Indian nominees for the 2017/18 International Woolmark Prize
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All you need to know View Gallery 6 Photos Here are the Indian nominees for the 2017/18 International Woolmark Prize The International Woolmark Prize has put India in the limelight many times in the past. Rahul Mishra won it in 2014, charting his way through Paris Fashion Week shortly after, followed by menswear designer Suket Dhir in 2016, who now stocks around the world at Saks Fifth Avenue, David Jones, L'Eclaireur and Isetan. This year, making the cut from India are womenswear designers Bodice by Ruchika Sachdeva, Dhruv Kapoor, Péro by Aneeth Arora, Hemang Agrawal and menswear designer Ujjwal Dubey of Antar-Agni. The prize previously won by legendary designers Karl Lagerfeld and Yves Saint Laurent in 1954 is judged by industry stalwarts, including Bouchra Jarrar of Lanvin, Victoria Beckham, Dame Natalie Massenet of the British Fashion Council, and online retail giant Farfetch.com, Stefano Tonchi, editor-in-chief of W magazine and Imran Amed of The Business of Fashion. This year, the prize money has increased to AU$2,00,000 for the final winners, and AU$70,000 for the regional winners to go towards creating their final collections. All winners will receive a trophy made by artist Jonathan Zawada using recycled shoreline plastic. Moreover, the finalist with the most unique yarn or fabric will be presented with AU$1,00,000 and commercial opportunities as part of a new addition Innovation Award. Vogue spoke to the designers on being nominated for the prize. Dhruv Kapoor: “Being nominated itself has opened multiple doors. I personally feel the Innovation Award is a great addition as it is always a challenge to strike a balance between creative exploration and commercial viability. Now there is something for both.” Ruchika Sachdeva: “I feel honoured to be nominated. Clothing is a very saturated industry and it has become extremely important to bring something new and relevant to the table. Indian design is broadly stereotyped, which unfortunately limits us as designers. It is an incredible opportunity to present the contrary to the world, while staying true to our Indian roots and core values of the brand.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why fashion seems to be warming up to an older audience
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It’s not what you think View Gallery 5 Photos Why fashion seems to be warming up to an older audience Fashion has always favoured the youth—almost everything you see on the runway is flattering to those under 40. From youth-defying serums to glorifying adolescence, the industry has received criticism for not addressing ageing in a healthy way, rather, offering solutions to fight it. Age has been inversely proportional to relevance—until now. Older women started appearing in the conversations of current and critically received labels over two years ago. Joan Didion, an octogenarian American author, posed for Céline's spring 2015 campaign, while Donatella Versace (61) and Julia Roberts (49) starred in Givenchy's autumn/winter 2015 campaign. In an article titled “Fashion's Two-Faced Relationship With Age”, Vanessa Friedman at The New York Times called out the polarity between image versus appeal: “Here's the disconnect: On the one hand, fashion pays endless aesthetic homage to youth; on the other, it remains firmly in the thrall, and power, of the mature.” When a brand that once put a 17-year-old Kate Moss in its most memorable campaigns now makes a statement by including 73-year-old Lauren Hutton in their most recent one, it's not just the message it is sending out that has changed. A large fashion conglomerate like Calvin Klein is not one to create an advertising campaign without concrete research about its elements. The carefully calculated move on the part of the label, and others like it, comes from a market survey that reveals that fashion, despite popular culture and social media suggesting otherwise, is actually being consumed by an older audience. Wooing the new (older) age bracket is just makes sense for the business. According to a report by Nielsen, Baby Boomers (people born roughly between 1946 and 1964, currently falling in the 53-to-71 age bracket) control 70 per cent of the disposable income in the United States, making them the most valued generation for marketing at the moment. And it doesn't take rocket science to figure out that those without educational loans and mortgages to pay off are more likely to spend on luxury products than those with. Conversations about inclusivity in the fashion industry will only broaden with this move. Are we going to see more women flaunting wrinkles and silver hair on billboards and runways in the future? The statistics point in the direction of fortune for those who are willing to adapt to the formerly sidelined market. As Anna Wintour, editor in chief, Vogue US, stated in a recent interview with BoF on the future of fashion business, “Change has to be what we breathe.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 6 ways to ensure that you’re shopping mindfully
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Fashion revolution Who made the clothes you're wearing right now? It's a simple enough question. But four years on from the Rana Plaza disaster, it's more important than ever that we keep asking it. This week marks the anniversary of the collapse of the Bangladesh factory complex that killed 1,138 garment workers and injured a further 2,500 in one of the worst industrial tragedies in history. In four years the Bangladeshi government, clothing companies, and labour unions have made some progress towards improving workers' rights. 38 people have been charged with murder – although none have been convicted. [#image: /photos/5ce446953bf9b413fcb1e908]||| ||| Image: Getty   But just a few months ago, in January, protests erupted in Bangladesh over low pay at dozens of garment factories in Bangladesh. Scores of protesters have been arrested, and over 1,500 have lost or been suspended from their jobs, though that number is probably far higher, as a recent investigation by the New York Times found. Conditions in the factories remain desolate. The minimum wage in Bangladesh – 32 cents an hour – is still frighteningly low, indeed the lowest minimum wage in the world. Garment workers earn £44 a month, which is nowhere near a living wage. And Bangladesh's largest factory owner lobby has said it will not enter into new wage negotiations until 2018. It's easy to feel powerless when faced with these statistics. Fashion's supply chains are incredibly complicated beasts that require hours of unravelling – from farm to factory to store, from zips to buttons to beading, it's never clear under what conditions they came into being. Often brands don't own factories outright – so garment production is subcontracted out, making it difficult to hold people to account. As Jenny Holdcroft, Assistant General Secretary at IndustriALL Global Union, told a panel at Fashion Question Time, held in the House of Commons on Monday: “Companies are getting the benefit of workers' labour without shouldering the responsibility of being their employer.” But it's also easy to start asking questions. In the spirit of transparency, this week also marks Fashion Revolution Week, an ethical initiative whose current focus is #WhoMadeMyClothes, a campaign which encourages consumers to demand greater transparency in the fashion supply chain. Here are six ways to get involved with Fashion Revolution Week, and shop mindfully in the process. 1 Take a picture of your label Snap a label selfie, post it on Instagram or Twitter, tag the brand, and ask them #WhoMadeMyClothes. During Fashion Revolution Week last year, the hashtag reached 129 million people through 70,000 posts on Twitter and Instagram. 2 Be more curious – there's an app for that Looking at your label can tell you where your clothes were stitched together – but it doesn't tell you where the cotton, for instance, was grown, where the fibre was spun into yarn, where the yarn was woven into fabric, where the fabric was dyed, or where the buttons, zips, beads and stitching came from. Start investigating how your clothes really came into being. Apps such as Ethical Barcode and Buycott allow you to scan the barcode of a garment whilst you're out shopping, so you can then find out the social or environmental impact of the products. 3 Jump at the chance to go to a designer's studio Fashion Revolution Week's Open Studio initiative, on all this week, includes Christopher Raeburn opening up his space in the old Burberry factory in Hackney. Join him on Saturday, April 29, for a workshop stitching and personalising your own tote bags. Take a studio tour with Blackhorse Lane Ateliers. Learn how to crochet or make a jacket patch with Katie Jones. Or try lino printing with young London brand Kepler. For more information click here. 4 Go schwopping or organise a #Haulternative Organise an evening where you swap clothes with your friends, go hunting for gems in charity shops (#haulternative) or go Schwopping – Marks & Spencer and H&M both offer clothes donation services, whereby you drop your clothes off at stores in exchange for a voucher. The cut and sew team at Iris Textiles, a textile mill operating since 1956, recently launched a new eco-textiles project named "The New Denim Project" creating upcycled natural fabrics using pre-consumer denim waste, saving 20,000 litres of water for each kilogram of upcycled material in the process. 5 Write to your policymakers With a General Election around the corner, there's no better time to write, call, tweet your local politicians and tell them what you want to know about your clothing, and why it's so important that we protect the people and the environment on which the fashion industry depends. 6 Watch this film Haven't seen The True Cost? A fashion documentary that traces fashion from slum to runway, and asks questions at every turn, it's a must-watch. Also published this week is Fashion Revolution's Loved Clothes Last film - a three minute short directed by Balthazar Klarwein, who has worked with Mario Testino. column1: The Met Gala 2017 theme: everything you need to know
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get updated before the event Are you ready for the first Monday in May? While many will enjoy the bank holiday, for America and fashion-enthusiasts alike it is an entirely different thing: it is the Met Gala. This year's theme, for both the Metropolitan Museum of Art's annual Costume Institute exhibition and 2017 Met Gala, is Rei Kawakubo/Comme des Garçons. First predicted by Suzy Menkes during Paris Fashion Week (following the presence of both Anna Wintour, editor-in-chief of American Vogue, and Andrew Bolton, curator of the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute, at the Comme des Garçons show), Rei Kawakubo will be the first living designer since Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 to be the sole subject of the Met's blockbuster fashion exhibit. "Rei Kawakubo is one of the most important and influential designers of the past 40 years," Bolton commented to Vogue.com. "By inviting us to rethink fashion as a site of constant creation, recreation, and hybridity, she has defined the aesthetics of our time." As the exhibition prepares to open on May 4, plenty of celebrities will be preparing to hit the red carpet on May 1. Kawakubo will act as honorary chair alongside Katy Perry, Pharrell Williams - who launched a fragrance in collaboration with Comme des Garçons in 2014 - and Anna Wintour. column1: Three designers making the summer breezier through this collaboration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Perfect for the season View Gallery 4 Photos Three designers making the summer breezier through this collaboration Summer often comes with a catch-22. On the one hand there is that holiday state of mind. But then there is the weather that makes leaving the confines of an air-conditioned room an unwelcome thought. And as far as your summer wardrobe is concerned, airy ensembles become the flavour of the season. The Liva Crème fabric by the Aditya Birla Group, which is equal parts breathable, luxurious and soft, might just fit the bill. The Group unveiled a range of new collections from brands like Allen Solly, Van Heusen, Shoppers Stop, Biba, Pantaloons, Imara, Crimson Club and more, to mark the launch of this fabric, also roping in three designers to interpret it in their signature styles. The showcase saw brand ambassador Kangana Ranaut walk the ramp. Nikhil Thampi collaborated with Allen Solly for a modern work wear collection that does not lack an element of whimsy. “The entire collection has a very ‘desk-to-date' vibe and the idea was to create a line that allows women to add a dash of fun to their office wardrobe. The collection is replete with separates that allows one to transition from am to pm with effortless class,” explains the designer. He advises some serious mixing and matching with these pieces—beige culottes paired with a rust blouse, a rust jacket with a blue dress or straight pants with a leather appliqué sleeveless blouse. Shivan and Narresh's collection for Van Heusen marries the fabric's fluidity with the duo's signature art-focused design sensibility. American artist Robert Motherwell serves as the inspiration for this range, which is bursting with statement pieces to take one from work to play. “We have worked with a classic colour palette with hints of bright tones and eclectic prints in a bouquet of silhouettes,” they say. The fluid summer trench in deep tones of navy is one of their favourite picks from the line. “This separate will quickly become a staple—you can wear it over a breezy day summer look or with a belted maxi for an evening affair. Our relaxed maxi dress in a bold seri print is another must-have from the collection,” the designers declare. Karishma Shahani Khan of the label Ka-Sha turned to collages by artist Ben Lewis Giles for her collaborative collection for Haute Curry by Shoppers Stop. The result is an easy-to-wear collection that balances Indian and western inspirations. “The collection is very print heavy and mainly focuses on traditional Indian flowers like marigold and lotus. The idea was to create separates that encourage mixing and matching,” the designer tells us about the line that is high on versatile dresses, crop top and skirt sets, tunics, trousers and light summer jackets. The signature tassels from Khan's line remains a mainstay here as well. “When you're collaborating with a high street brand, it's important to strike a synergy between your design aesthetic and the audience the label is catering to. So while the collection should resonate with what you are best known for, it has to be more about the new set of shoppers you're trying to reach out to,” she signs off. Biba and Vajor.com predicted a white summer with breezy Indian staples like flared palazzos, printed kurtas and maxi skirts. Layering with scarves, dupattas and light jackets was a mainstay. The Izabela London and Akkriti collection for Pantaloons was high on prints like floral, abstract and Aztec, as well as chirpy summer-friendly hues, making it perfect for your next vacation. column1: Is the sari really a practical choice for the summer?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We asked the expert View Gallery 9 Photos Is the sari really a practical choice for the summer? Sanjay Garg's clientele is not one that needs to be sold the concept of buying saris; they have already bought it and they keep coming for more. In what was once Bombay Electric, racks Garg's saris and blouses. They are neatly piled one on top of the other—the effect of which reminds you of walking into a highly organised, colour-coded stationery store. Raw Mango was Garg's first label which started in 2008 and focused on the Chanderi weave. “I am not one to pick something up and leave it after each season, I still work with what I started from,” says the designer. The label distances itself from categorising collections under ‘summer' or ‘winter'. “In the Indian fashion context, it is quite laughable given the temperature is high around the year in most parts of the country. There was always the question—what do I wear in summer? And while I can't tell someone to wear or not wear a brocade based on weather, I turned to Chanderi tissue saris where the weft is silk and metal and warp is cotton,” he says. Juggling several women vying for his attention as they pick saris, Garg offers advice on tonality, pairing blouses that you would have never considered otherwise. Such is his confident study in the nuances of the yardage and where every different weave emerges from, that it is hard for him to be threatened by those imitating his minimalist design. Neither garishly shiny nor stiff, Garg's innovation for this season is at the loom level, some pieces so sheer you could see through them. Techniques matter when there is little scope for innovation in an unstitched garment. Finding the right balance of yarns can take between 8-10 months. “When we talk about seasons in fashion, we are borrowing a vocabulary from the west. It's not that this particular handloom fabric is not good for fashion, in fact it is the other way round, maybe fashion is not good for handloom, where it is difficult to churn out fabric to meet orders.” The designer strongly believes that fashion needs to be seen from an anthropological view. “The lungi is one of the most evolved garments for our weather. The sari used to be worn without a petticoat, which was a British influence. You didn't have a blouse, or if you did it had many versions—it was friendlier for our climatic conditions then. I'm not against westernisation, all I am saying is that the sense of where you come from needs to be retained.” Garg tries to explain that the evolving trajectory of the sari may have made the sari impractical for the conditions we live in. Addressing the larger topic of the widespread movement towards including saris in everyday life, Garg strongly feels that the measurement of the influence is limited to just two cities—Mumbai and Delhi. “I think we have a very narrow perspective, it's not a change in large numbers. We have a limited audience in small fashion circles that and the influence on those cannot be counted as a change.” Fashion Fashion What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How South Asian women in London are reclaiming the bindi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Embracing their heritage [#image: /photos/5ce44972b40d26e826d6f086]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/simisear_ Simran Randhawa's striking selfies are one of the main draws to her popular South Asian-influenced Instagram, @simisear_. Randhawa, born in London to a Punjabi family, takes wearing a bindi to a bejewelled level, either by placing gilded bits in a line down her forehead or by tracing her brow bone with glinting dots. Though the traditional piece is now synonymous with the 21-year-old's Indo-West look, she only began wearing a bindi a few years ago. The decision to finally embrace it “very much comes from my own apprehension [about] wearing Indian clothes outside of the house when I was younger,” says Randhawa, who rejected her cultural heritage as a teenager while trying to fit into her English friend group. “It was a tense battle for me.” The bindi is a decorative mark worn between the eyes or in the middle of the forehead by Hindu women. The term hails from the Sanskrit word bindu meaning “drop” or “spot” and comes in different forms that can be jewellery or a small red circle made from vermillion powder. Its meaning varies as well: At times, the bindi is considered to have religious significance and is worn during prayer; it can also dictate marital status. Further West, however, the distinctive mark has a long history of cultural appropriation. Gwen Stefani often wore the bejewelled piece during her late-'90s No Doubt years; Selena Gomez, along with other concert-goers, sported a bindi during Coachella in 2014. But for Randhawa, now living in a Brexit-era England, the bindi has always symbolised a struggle. “I don't think it is cool for it to be trendy. I think [the] bindi is a very hot topic. Especially, for South Asians in the diaspora.” [#image: /photos/5ce44972b40d26687ad6f088]||| ||| Image: Instagram.com/fixated_f Randhawa, currently a student at the University of Bristol and the assistant politics editor for Gal-dem, is a part of a small group of women of South Asian heritage in England who have been redefining the appearance of the bindi and reclaiming their culture by wearing the traditional piece with their everyday London looks. 21-year-old Amisha Acharya, a cosmetic studies undergraduate who hails from a Nepali-Hindu family, wore bindis as a child, stopped, and then recently started wearing them again. “It was [around the time that] Kendall Jenner wore a bindi to Coachella, and High Street stores started selling them for ridiculous prices. I realised later I wasn't the only one [who] felt uncomfortable. I saw so many beautiful South Asians turn to social media as a platform to reclaim our culture,” writes Acharya of her decision. “It's a part of my identity and where I come from. column1: The how and why of LVMH’s Christian Dior acquisition
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It's €13 billion deal LVMH has announced that it is to integrate the entire Christian Dior label into the luxury group. The news may seem confusing to many – who believed the French conglomerate already controlled Dior along with fellow design houses including Céline, Givenchy and Fendi – but in actual fact Christian Dior SE is the main holding company of LVMH, which in turn controls the other brands. Any confusion is forgivable since Bernard Arnault, the chairman and chief executive of LVMH, is also the chairman and majority shareholder of Dior. As well as streamlining the business and simplifying its structure for the market's benefit, the move will also allow "the strengthening of LVMH's fashion and leather goods division thanks to the acquisition of Christian Dior Couture, one of the most iconic brands worldwide", Arnault explained. The €13 billion deal will be made through "a simplified public offer by the Arnault family group for Christian Dior shares — that it does not currently hold — and take form of a primary offer consisting of €172 per share in cash and 0.192 Hermès International shares for each Christian Dior share, and would be completed by two secondary offers, in cash and in Hermès shares respectively", LVMH said in a statement, reports the BoF. The brand expects the deal - which will unite Christian Dior make-up and perfume, haute couture, leather, men's and women's ready-to-wear and shoes businesses under one roof - to reach completion at the end of May or early June. column1: Remembering the legacy of Martand ‘Mapu’ Singh
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In memoriam... Martand Singh, better known as Mapu, usually found draped in ahmisa silk shawls extolling the virtues of hand-woven textiles, realised the need to conserve handlooms back in the late 1960s. He spoke of khadi as his voyage of self-realisation; could spend days delighting in the essence of the sari that according to him began on a loom, and yet he never allowed the nostalgia of India's craft heritage to interfere with his dynamic vision for reviving, conserving and making relevant these near-forgotten arts. Renowned for his nuanced textile exhibits and research, and for founding the conservation body Indian National Trust for Art and Culture Heritage (INTACH), the erstwhile Rajput prince and conservationist from Kapurthala passed away on April 25, at the age of 70. Already embedded in our shared cultural consciousness, Singh's prodigious achievements and tireless pursuit of conserving India's heritage of textiles is now his legacy. Which joins a rich lineage established by his mentor, the late and now legendary cultural activist Pupul Jayakar (who was quoted by Malvika Singh in her seminar ‘Tapestry Of Life') as having said that, “My living heritage is manifested in Mapu. He is carrying forward what I was able to initiate…” From Ritu Kumar to Rajesh Pratap Singh who credits him as the man he learnt the virtues of indigenous textiles from and Rohit Bal who recognises him as the man who led him to discover the glorious weaves of Benares—Singh's heritage has seamlessly merged with the contemporary. India's reigning fashion community remain indebted to Singh, for sharing with them the knowledge and authenticity of textiles, through heritage, history and culture. Tarun Tahiliani remembers him as an inspiring presence in his life and work: “His reservoir of knowledge and willingness to share has laid the foundations for so many of us. I remember when we were starting Ensemble, me and Sal [Sailaja Tahiliani, his wife] with my firstborn Anand still in his crib, went to see him and he gave me the book on The Costumes of Royal India, that documented the exhibit he had put together with Diana Vreeland in 1985 in Tokyo and at the Metropolitan Museum in New York—it was an early pre-curser to the big Met Gala that has become an annual star-studded event. Going on many years later, when I started my couture exhibitions, even before couture week, they were styled on what I had learnt from the great legacy that he had made accessible to me. No one straddled the love of khadi and couture of royal India with an equal passion. We've lost a national treasure.” And Suneet Varma recalls his friend and guide, “It's an immeasurable loss. He was the kindest, most compassionate, wonderful man I knew and how fortunate I am that he guided me every step of the way from the beginning to now. My world will never be the same without him.” In an interview in 2014, when talking about the current state of the handloom industry, Singh said, “Believe me, although we have come a long way, we still have a long way to go.” And here's hoping Singh's life's work, and his legacy of conserving India's grand heritage of crafts and textiles, carries on. It may not seem like it now, but buying fine jewellery is a brilliant move—even if you have to sacrifice a few late-night deliveries to make it happen. column1: Is sloppy dressing the new proper?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Toeing the line View Gallery 11 Photos Is louche the new proper? After nearly two whole seasons of reliving the '90s, you may have noticed that despite the throwback love for the bygone era—we look nothing like the women from the decade. Far from the clean, streamlined looks of Jennifer Aniston and Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, the present approach to reviving the decade has been original in the way we are styling the resurrected. Spring runways saw jagged hems, ruched seamlines and oversizing to comical proportions. The new appeal in yet another decade reexamined lies in how a garment is worn. Jackets draped across in all sense of impracticality have made way to shrobing on the streets. The impracticality of the Spanx lifestyle is not lost on anyone—the days of bodycon fashion are numbered, although the Kardashians regularly make a case for it with their car-to-event-and-back routines. The Indian runway too loves the one-size fits all take on clothing. After all, roomy cotton silhouettes in 40-degree weather are forgiving. Does the rise of shabby-chic mean the decline of sexy fashion? Balenciaga's dresses with no daring slits and Off-White's collarbone on display styles will beg to differ. Arguably critically lauded labels like JW Anderson and Preen by Thornton Bregazzi are in on the new era of dressing. column1: Rhea Kapoor shares her tips on buying precious jewellery
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Her tips are such gems When it comes to fashion, celebrity stylist Rhea Kapoor is a dictator of taste. Not only is she known for curating sister Sonam Kapoor's winning (and fashion-forward) repertoire, but also for her minimalistic-meets-androgynous personal style. A self-confessed jewellery connoisseur, Kapoor has collaborated with diamond boutique Zoya to launch their ‘Diamonds of Eve' collection. The line of brilliant-cut diamonds embellished with South Sea pearls, rubies, sapphires and emeralds is equal parts flirty and versatile, and Kapoor has shared her recommendations on sporting them in a special Style Digest video series for the brand. Vogue caught up with the stylist du jour and had her part with ace jewellery advice. What are must-have jewellery pieces for the millennial Indian woman? Stick to classics with individualistic design elements when investing in jewellery. Diamond or coloured stone (such as emeralds or yellow stones) studs pair well with just about everything, and can be worn throughout the day. A delicate piece of jewellery, such as a day-to-night necklace (this could be a slim diamond choker or a gemstone pendant) is another essential. So is a tennis bracelet. What are the most important aspects to consider when buying precious jewellery? Don't compromise on craftsmanship or quality. You should know what you are buying—look out for ethical stones and be very clear about the quality you are paying for. Don't hesitate in asking for a certificate of purity. At the end of the day, jewellery is an investment, and you want it to pay off later in life. What are your jewellery shopping habits like? I am not an impulsive shopper, especially not when purchasing fine jewellery. A lot of research is required when you're investing that kind of money. I believe in buying jewellery that is timeless, and can eventually be passed down as family heirlooms. I usually end up picking pieces that are unusual but don't lack a touch of heritage either. Diamonds vs gold vs coloured stones? I am completely partial to emeralds; there is something about them that is luxurious yet cool, and I am drawn to their intense colour. I also love gold jewellery, but when it features a contemporary twist, though I don't mind temple jewellery either. And who doesn't love diamonds? It's really hard to play favourites here. What was your first precious jewellery buy? And which is your most prized jewellery possession? My first precious jewellery buy was emerald stones. I saved up to buy them and my mother helped me design them into drop earrings. My most prized piece of jewellery is the solitaire pendant I wear every single day. I never take if off. Whose jewellery collection would you want to raid? Indira Devi's, who had a statement Cartier diamond necklace that she once wore with a plain chiffon sari. The Maharaja of Patiala or the Nizam of Hyderabad's jewellery collection would be worth raiding too. Decode the perfect jewellery for: Brunch: Delicate jewellery that doesn't wear you down such as pearls, subtle gold or platinum. Date night: A memorable piece that draws attention to your face and neck. Jewellery can be really sexy when it sits well and complements you and your skin colour. Wedding: Choose a one-of-a-kind, spectacular piece and build your entire look around it. The focus should be on one piece only. It's about quality and not quantity in this case. Family celebrations: I like borrowing jewellery from my mum (jewellery designer Sunita Kapoor) and sister (Sonam Kapoor) and mixing it with my pieces. I steer towards sentimental pieces that have been in the family for years for family gatherings. There are certain pieces that you can only wear when your sister or cousin is getting married—so bring those out! We tend to go all out during Diwali festivities as well. Work meeting: Stick to your everyday jewellery, but add one piece that makes you feel special, like a bracelet. For a formal dinner meeting, add a bold ring, but nothing fussy that will constrict you. For an evening work event, you could wear a no-fuss statement piece like individualistic earrings. column1: Calvin Klein’s new campaign is breaking a big underwear model stereotype
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Age no bar Following the launch of Calvin Klein's men's underwear campaign starring the lead actors of the Academy Award–winning Moonlight, the brand has released its women's underwear campaign shot by Sofia Coppola. The grainy black-and-white videos celebrate women ages 18 to 73, each handpicked by Coppola for the series. The director's longtime muse Kirsten Dunst appears, as does Rashida Jones, Nathalie Love, up-and-coming actress Laura Harrier, Maya Thurman-Hawke (the daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman), and Chase Sui Wonders (niece of Coppola's friend, the designer Anna Sui). The true star of the campaign, however, is the inimitable Lauren Hutton, who at 73, makes showing off her skivvies look like a piece of cake. No surprise there—she is a modelling legend after all—but the choice of Calvin Klein to cast women of all ages and ethnicities to model underwear is worthy of reflection. Think back to other Calvin Klein brand ads created in the '80s and '90s, and you'll remember the teenaged Brooke Shields whispering about nothing coming between her and her Calvins, or the teenaged Kate Moss pressed, topless, against a butch and bulky Marky Mark. The Moss campaign, seen alongside other early-'90s advertising and fashion shows, put an image of youthful sexiness at the fore of American culture. The images were so shocking at the time for their depictions of waifish, adolescent beauty they were accused of promoting “heroin chic” aesthetics and condemned by President Bill Clinton in 1995 and again in 1997. Today's campaign marks another shift for the brand since coming under the direction of Raf Simons last year. Yes, the slim, youthful models you'd associate with CK and Simons remain—but mostly in the brand's ready-to-wear advertising and runway shows. In other arenas, Calvin Klein is taking a more pointed stance to include people of different cultures, age demographics, and ethnicities in its campaigns, providing a more inclusive look at American culture. And with advertising billboards plastered throughout major cities—and ad spots on New York's Taxi TV and on cable networks—the brand's outlook on sexiness is being served to a massive audience. That's the good news. Oh, and there's also a new tagline for fans to learn: “Calvin Klein, or nothing at all.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.com What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Your first look at the Outhouse flagship in Mumbai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You’ve never seen jewellery like this View Gallery 11 Photos Your first look at the Outhouse flagship in Mumbai Ever since we heard the Delhi-based costume jewellery label Outhouse would be opening their flagship store in Mumbai, we've been patiently waiting to see what it looks like. After numerous delays with construction, sisters Kaabia and Sasha Grewal have finally set a date for the launch. It goes without saying that the Vogue India Fashion Fund 2015 winners for accessories have untiringly worked towards ensuring the Outhouse store in Mumbai offers a retail experience unlike any other. We spoke to the designer duo, and here's what transpired. Outhouse has been available with e-retailers for a while, what made you want to launch an independent store? Kaabia Grewal: We have always believed in giving an authentic Outhouse experience to our clients. The soul of the brand stands for design, innovation, craftsmanship, affordable luxury and a passion for jewellery, which we communicate to our clientele through our flagships. Each of our stores offers a unique experience, which ultimately relates to Outhouse as a youthful, sophisticated and passionate entity. Another motivation was the fact that we create lines catering to various needs and occasions, which can be showcased in entirety at our store. We have recently launched Outhouse Couture and a bridal line. Everything together, from the moment you walk in and feel the energy around, try the pieces on, to the blush pink box that encases them is an important part of the Outhouse experience, which is something you can only get at our flagship boutiques. What is the thought behind this store? Sasha Grewal: The Mumbai store has been a very special project, because even though we aren't from the city, we have always felt a very strong bond with it that gave rise to the concept of the store. It is our ode to the city of Mumbai and its culture. We decided to go the minimal route with a design language that speaks Mumbai, and at the same time can adapt to and complement our creations without being overbearing. The character of the store owes itself to the materials chosen in the making. Our signature brand colours—salmon pink, grey and accents of brass—are juxtaposed on oakwood and wicker weave—an element that was key in colonial Indian architecture. The Terrazzo flooring, a recurring trend of the '90s, makes a comeback in the store and was especially created in salmon peach with white chips to lend a synchronised ambience to it. A small private enclosure serves as the Outhouse Couture Room for private one-on-one interactions, gives the customer the luxurious Outhouse experience through a bespoke service to help them pick the right pieces. What makes shopping at the Outhouse store a unique experience? SG: At Outhouse, our customers are everything and we try our best to keep them happy with the whole process, whether it be a customer who wants help picking the right piece or after-sales services. Attention to detail is not limited just to the piece, but making sure that the experience of being an Outhouse woman starts from the moment you walk into the store. How has the brand evolved over the years? KG: We started off in 2012 with a young, edgy and glamorous vibe, but over the years, Outhouse has grown and evolved into something more sophisticated, while keeping the youth in it alive. As a brand, it is based on five central tight knit values of innovation, luxury, craftsmanship, design and expression. Our products have become more innovative each year, so much so that we have a separate section for ‘Outhouse Innovations', which are unique, inimitable and stylish. Our latest collection, ‘Imago', has been a breakthrough–it's a level up from anything we've done before and it's only going to get better. Winning the Vogue Fashion Fund in 2015 gave us a real push and invaluable exposure that helped us make some wonderful changes in our working system to get better at what we do. Being featured in the Forbes 30 under 30 list last year has been the best thing offered to us in 2016. It gave us an acknowledgment that we are on the right path, growing and improving each day. Today, we pride ourselves on being a dynamic, vibrant and eccentric brand. Outhouse thrives on constantly pushing the envelope of design, redefining how fashion jewellery is perceived; every piece aims to be a work of art and a conversation starter. We have come a long way in monitoring internal growth and are looking to expand even further in the coming years with more sale points and international shows. column1: Have you seen Sabyasachi’s stunning new collaboration with Forevermark?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Let that sink in Sabyasachi Mukherjee, designer, is a man of many talents. Alongside his critically acclaimed, commercially successful eponymous label, he runs an art foundation, co-hosts a TV show, lends his talents to home decor and shoe design and has now collaborated on collection of fine jewellery with Forevermark diamonds. Mukherjee's work forces you to you travel the fourth dimension when you look at the pieces. We spoke to the designer about his love for all things vintage, handcrafted and the art of enamelling. View Gallery 7 Photos Have you seen Sabyasachi’s stunning new collaboration with Forevermark? The collection is reminiscent of Art Deco and Victorian influences, what did you have in mind? It's a mix of both—it also has Bengal craftsmanship that is married into Italian renaissance. It has a very strong Art Deco vibe, the earrings specially. Because you see, the earrings for me are the fashion component of the collection, while the rings are classic. Also, because the diamonds are larger pieces—we are playing between 1 carat and 10 carats—you don't make disposable jewellery out of such expensive diamonds. I wanted to play with a little bit of Italian baroque, French Renaissance and old Indian craftsmanship—the smaller pieces are great engagement rings and the bigger pieces are better cocktail rings. But the idea was that they are carefully positioned in such a way that there is always a price point for everybody. Forevermark works with diamonds and you used enamelling to introduce colour to the pieces. What made you chose that as a surface finish? You see enamelling is a very old tradition of jewellery. When I started working on the line, I said that I don't want to make machine-made jewellery. I wanted people to know that this jewellery has been handcrafted. You know today, machines can replicate a lot of things hands can do, but there are genres that machines still can't replicate, enamelling is one of them. Where do you look for inspiration? A lot of my research comes from Etsy.com. One of my favourite places to go jewellery shopping is this bridge on Florence called Ponte Vecchio, where you have a lot of old jewellery stores, cranky Italian men selling beautiful vintage jewellery in crumbling velvet boxes. So, I wanted the jewellery to feel like it was vintage, [pieces] that you could find from perhaps those really old vintage sites or flea markets but also it is precious. How did you work with the materials at hand? I think today people like to have a lot more fun with precious jewellery. They do not want precious jewellery to be stereotyped. It is no longer only about a single row of diamonds or a single solitaire, it is also about how you use large stones, how you use precious material and play with them. And I think the great trick is to bring certain amount of personality into diamonds, otherwise diamonds can become really—I won't say hostile—but I would probably use the word intimidating. To me, it's like wearing couture with sneakers. When you start using things like enamel and filigree with diamonds, it gives a little bit of playfulness and little bit of a slightly more lived in, comforting feel that softens the whole aura of the gems. Which is one of the reasons we have played with different colours of gold; so there was rose gold, yellow gold, white gold, we had yellow diamonds and white diamonds that were put together. What happens then is you don't get a diamond that is very white and cold, but you get a one that has a warmer glow, which looks beautiful next to Indian skin. column1: The fool-proof way to stretch out new shoes (without the blisters and pain)
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Never be uncomfortable ever again Couldn't it be wonderful if you could avoid the rubbing and blistering of new shoes? Royal couturier Stewart Parvin has spoken about how HRH Queen Elizabeth II sidesteps that issue: “The shoes have to be immediately comfortable,” he told the Evening Standard. “She does get someone to wear them. The Queen can never say ‘I'm uncomfortable, I can't walk any more.' She has the right to have someone wear them in.” While we may not have someone whose sole job it is to break in our shoes, there are ways it can be done without shredding your feet to pieces. Read on for Vogue's top tips: Wear them in a little at a time The impulse to just wear new shoes out straightaway is sometimes too much to ignore, but if you can fight the temptation (and you should) wear them around the house first – in thick socks, if possible - and begin the wearing-in process. Spoon straps and backs Using the back of a spoon, furiously work it into the heel or anywhere a pair of shoes are rubbing. It is essentially mimicking the effect of your foot, but it will make those strappy, tighter places softened up before wearing. Blast on the hairdryer Wearing multiple pairs of socks and the shoes in question, hold a hairdryer up to the parts of the shoe that are tightest whilst flexing or moving your feet. This will help stretch them. Just be sure to let the shoes cool with your feet still in them. Invest in shoe stretchers Less useful for heels, but flats can easily be stretched using metal or wooden stretchers. Try Amazon for a range of styles. Some will even come with a shoe stretch spray that can help the process along. Just be prepared to put the stretchers in and let them sit tight for a while. Stuff them with newspaper Crumple up newspaper, wet it slightly – note: it must not be soaked through, otherwise it will damage the inner sole – let it dry and remove before wearing. Go to the professionals Take a cue from the Queen and enlist a professional. Vogue's go-to shoe repair specialist is The Restory, and they provide a breaking-in service. Just be sure to allow at least three days for them to work their magic. This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Marchesa designer Georgina Chapman is a huge fan of this Indian celebrity
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Her own following includes the likes of Selena Gomez and Chrissy Teigen From helming a label that quickly became a red carpet go-to, to making regular appearances on best-dressed lists, Georgina Chapman has always been on our radar. As one-half of the duo behind New York-based powerhouse Marchesa visits India, she tells Vogue everything from the Bollywood actor she would like to dress to why the country holds a special place in her heart. View Gallery 6 Photos This celebrity favourite designer just visited India Take us through your latest collection and the inspiration behind it?  The Marchesa autumn/winter '17-18 collection was inspired by the grandiose of imperial China. The exquisite intricacies of the empire greatly influenced our choice of colour, embroidery and textiles. Marchesa is a regular at the Oscars and Golden Globes, what's the one red carpet rule you swear by? My recommendation to anyone walking the red carpet is that a dress should never impose, it should complement its wearer. Don't let seasonal trends dictate your look and pick a silhouette that is figure flattering! You've dressed almost every A-list celebrity, what has been your most memorable experience? Keren [Craig] and I have had the incredible honour of dressing so many talented women for the red carpet. Every time someone wears our designs it is such a thrill! Watching Sandra Bullock accept her Academy Award in 2010 wearing Marchesa was exhilarating and one of the most rewarding moments! Also, Renee Zellweger wearing a red sari-inspired dress to the Bridget Jones's Diary premiere in 2004 (Marchesa's first big red carpet moment) is a wonderful memory, which will always stay with me. Is there a Bollywood actor that you would like to dress? Priyanka Chopra. She is so elegant and I am a huge fan of her films! How would you describe the Marchesa muse?  Marchesa Luisa Casati is our muse. She was so daring and dramatic in the way she dresses. A living work of art! In school, I trained as a costume designer, so I design through that lens and my work caters to the modern-day woman. Of course, I tend to veer towards the dramatic and that's how the label embodies Luisa Casati's spirit. What's the one thing you've enjoyed most during your stay here? What was on your itinerary? During my time in India, I focused on visiting Magic Bus programs, particularly in Mankhurd and Bombay Port Trust. I wanted to get a better idea of the ongoing challenges so that we can raise more awareness and funding for the charity in the USA. Other than that, I did a bit of shopping of course and bought some jewellery and gifts for my family. Your extensive work with Magic Bus has helped countless children, what inspires you? Magic Bus, a non-profit, helps children grow up equipped with the life skills, knowledge and education to move out of poverty. I've been fortunate enough to support the community of Mankhurd in eastern Mumbai since 2014. My work with the organisation allows me to give back to the families and communities that have contributed to the success of Marchesa. We do a lot of our embroideries in India and I am constantly inspired by the rich culture and the colours, it has had a huge influence on many of our collections. You named your daughter India. The country clearly holds a special place your heart, when did the love affair begin? I've been fascinated with the country since a young age, as my mother's side of the family lived in India for several generations and my grandmother was born here. I've travelled here many times throughout my life. Keren and I were actually travelling in India together in 2003 when we decided to start Marchesa!
