column1: A history of the Met Gala in 60 Seconds, narrated by Vogue’s Hamish Bowles
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you ever wanted to know On the fashion calendar, few dates are as important as the first Monday in May. That's when the annual fundraising gala for the Costume Institute at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, known simply as the party of the year, is held. So what is the Met Gala? And why all the hype? It all starts with a major exhibition on a changing theme that showcases the museum's extraordinary holdings. These displays have run the gamut theme-wise—from historical periods to genres to individual design innovators (Paul Poiret, Alexander McQueen, and Miuccia Prada). This year's honoree is the Japanese designer Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons, and the show, named “Rei Kawakubo/Comme des Garçons: Art of the In-Between,” will showcase 150 of her womenswear creations dating from the early 1980s. All the exhibitions serve to place fashion—old and new—within the context of contemporary culture. “Over the years,” observes Hamish Bowles, Vogue's International Editor at Large, “the gala has become a reflection of our changing culture.” In fact, the Met Gala is the hottest ticket in town. Often dubbed the “Fashion Oscars,” with a m-a-j-o-r red carpet, the event is, in Bowles's words, “an ever more glamorous arena for high fashion.” (The many-stepped entrance allows for trains to display at full impact, too.) Among the sartorial highlights have been Kate Moss's 2009 arrival in a draped lamé minidress accessorized with a shimmering turban, à la Gloria Swanson. Then there was the time when Sarah Jessica Parker and Alexander McQueen wore matching tartans to the Anglomania show. Rihanna's voluminous yolk-yellow Guo Pei gown launched a thousand memes in 2015; the next year, on the heels of her groundbreaking Lemonade release, Beyoncé Knowles arrived solo, and, yes, slayed it in a beaded latex Givenchy Haute Couture dress. The antithesis of a come-as-you-are party, the Met Gala is an A-list bash that serves, says Bowles, “to establish and confirm fashion trends, through both the exhibitions themselves and the sartorial choices of the guests.” Here, the editor tells the history of the Met Gala in 60 seconds flat. column1: Farfetch Announces Store of The Future
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Last week at the Condé Nast International Luxury Conference, Farfetch founder José Neves spoke about his vision for a future retail experience, where advancements in technology (including virtual reality) would start to free up time and can help make the consumer experience more human. This morning, the retail entrepreneur revealed that he is putting plans into motion, unveiling Farfetch's Store of the Future - an augmented retail solution that "links the online and offline worlds, using data to enhance the retail experience". "Physical retail accounts for 93 per cent of sales today, and even with online growing at fast speed, it will account for 80 per cent by 2025," Neves explained today. "Retailers need a way to collect information about their customers while they are browsing in-store, just as they collect data from online searches. The Store of the Future aims at providing the in-store experience of the future by giving visibility to retailers on what is happening in the store. It's the offline cookie that closes the loop, between a great online presence and a complete omni-channel offering and, finally, in-store technology which augments the experience of customers in store and overall." At the CNI Conference, Neves said that employing new technology - including virtual reality, emotion-scanning software, and innovative payment options - can "be a positive force for fashion as it can be transformative in a very informative way”. Today, he reiterated those words. "The next stage in the evolution of the fashion industry is the connected store, which uses technology to enhance the luxury retail experience to become even more customer centric," he said. "Farfetch is at the crossroads of luxury and technology and is well placed to understand its needs and deliver a tailored solution." The tailored solution element is crucial for Farfetch. Being a multi-brand platform, the brand is intent on making sure that the Store of the Future technologies will be able to create bespoke experiences for each brand in each city and each store. "Whatever in-store digital tools, technology or services each brand or store uses, the key value is in the data that will drive personalised meaningful customer experiences, and on the business side a significant competitive advantage." read a press release this morning. The first fashion businesses that will see the Store of the Future technologies deployed will be Browns, which Farfetch bought in 2015, and Thom Browne. “As we open stores in key capitals around the world and develop a strong direct-to-consumer, omni-channel business, we believe the connected store to be a great opportunity to enhance our in-store customer experience," said the American fashion house's CEO, Rodrigo Bazan. We are very excited to have been chosen by Farfetch, and look forward to starting the global roll out of this new service from the New York store.” For Farfetch-owned Browns, the introduction of the technology chimes with its plan "to re-establish Browns as the coolest boutique in the world", according to CEO Holli Rogers. "One of the most important factors in making this happen is to stay completely in tune with the ever changing lifestyle needs of our customers and to keep pushing our product assortment and innovating," said Rogers. "Deploying the digital innovations that make up Store of the Future facilitates us to take big steps towards this longer term vision. Implementing these innovations within our stores will fundamentally allow our customers to enjoy a bespoke and effortless experience that harmonises the best parts of boutique shopping with the speed and convenience of e-tail. column1: A young Missoni celebrates plus-size women with her new collaboration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion “I wanted to give this community an elevated and beautiful product that was designed especially for them" View Gallery 10 Photos A Young Missoni Steps Into the Spotlight With a New Plus-Size Collaboration As a young member of the Missoni dynasty, Teresa Maccapani Missoni has been immersed in the world of fashion since birth. And though she's more muse than designer for the family house (her mother, Angela, is creative director), when approached with the opportunity to collaborate with Eloquii—a brand dedicated to larger sizes—she found the challenge too intriguing to resist. Speaking from Milan, where she's celebrating the birth of her first child, Zeno, Missoni admits to being drawn in by the possibility of providing a traditionally underserved market with a fresh set of choices. “I wanted to give this community an elevated and beautiful product that was designed especially for them,” she says. A regular on street style blogs thanks to her colorful, pattern-filled wardrobe, Missoni sought to bring the carefree glamour of her personal look to the 24-piece collection. “I wear a lot of maxi styles and comfortable, free-flowing silhouettes,” says Missoni. She looked to her Mediterranean upbringing and love of the seaside for inspiration for the line, which sports whimsical touches like embroidered blue fish swimming across a skirt and on-trend details like ombré and eyelets. Naturally, it wouldn't be a Missoni collection without prints, but for this collaboration, she chose to steer clear of the ubiquitous zigzag, instead creating drawings of coral and a blue paisley with sketches of mermaids mixed in. “It was pivotal for me to not only focus on the prints and shapes but [also] on the quality of the textiles, especially in the summer,” she continues. “I knew I wanted to use natural fibers alongside embellished details and beautiful patterns.” These high-end touches serve to separate Missoni's capsule from typical plus-size fare. Though there's been a recent uptick of established designers lending their talents to lines with larger sizes, the market mostly remains geared toward fast fashion and basics. Keeping things luxurious while staying within Eloquii's contemporary price point was key for Missoni. And while the final pieces, with their bold color and eye-catching add-ons, may require a bit of daring on the part of the wearer, Missoni wouldn't want it any other way: “I wanted my collection to inspire women to feel confident, powerful, and—above all—to give them lots of options.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.com Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Guess which New York-based label just opened a store in Delhi
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Keep your credit cards at the ready View Gallery 8 Photos Guess which New York-based label just opened a store in Delhi? We've done our homework and have a long shopping list ready, just as Kate Spade New York opens two stores in New Delhi this month (the first is at DLF Emporio on April 13). Deborah Lloyd, the label's chief creative officer gives us a peek into the spring/summer collection, and picks out pieces that give her the feeling of being on a permanent vacay. In fact, Lloyd's inspiration for the collection was a trip she took to Morocco, resulting in a line of flirty, feminine pieces with touches of whimsy, where elements as diverse as roses and camels make an appearance. “Spring was about the roses—the gorgeous rose dresses mixed with lace, in soft colours like pink, were inspired by Moroccan roses,” says Lloyd. She lets the softer tones of blush and pink play out in the beginning of the season, and gravitates towards yellow and blue as the summer progresses. “The saffron yellow just jumped out to me in Morocco. It really cut through and spoke to me this season. Then, towards the end of summer, the blues I saw at Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé's Jardin Majorelle in Marrakech were exquisite—that incredible, intense blue. These gorgeous, clean colours helped me formulate the collection.” Among her favourite pieces are the woven wicker camel bag, tassel earrings in a rainbow of shades, and denim juxtaposed with rose prints. And true to the brand, there's always a hint of playfulness: “The Embroidered Camel Coat is a play on a classic camel coat—it's a really cute coat with pom pom details,” she says. Lloyd might be looking eastward again for inspiration. “I'm so excited about opening in India and coming to visit someday—it's been on my list so many times. It's a country I can't believe I haven't yet done a collection inspired by.” Weddings Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This celebrity-approved shoe label just launched its first kids’ collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Olivia Palermo, Emma Watson and Rihanna are fans View Gallery 9 Photos This celebrity-approved shoe label just launched its first kids’ collection In six short years, Colombian Egardo Osorio along with Ricardo D'Almeida Figueiredo, his partner (in business and in life) have built a tidy little shoe business. Osorio is the creative director and co-founder of Aquazzura the Italian shoe brand famous for tie-ups, fringes and pom-poms, there is a sense of fun to everything this label does.  A favourite with Olivia Palermo, Emma Watson and Rihanna, Net-a-Porter and Matches Fashion nearly always sell out of his collection within a few weeks of arrival. Aquazzura is not just about red carpet shoes and is also the working woman's go-to label, being one of the few high-end shoe brands that believes in including a wide variety of flat and block heels in their collections. Which means his collections have all the right elements required for a collection of “mini-me” shoes. “This is first season for our mini-me shoes. The inspiration came from our clients, who were posting pictures of their daughter in similar shoes to their Aquazzuras and sending them to us,” says Osorio. The designer, who has previously worked with Salvatore Ferragamo and Roberto Cavalli, has always believed in listening and learning from his clients. “Interestingly many of our clients where telling us they learnt of our brand through their teenage daughters.” They are about 20 styles which have been translated into “mini-me” shoes, with most stores carrying about 15 different styles. In each region, Aquazzura has chosen one store to carry the collection. In London it is Harrods, in New York, Bergdorf Goodman and in the Middle East, Dubai is his chosen city. The brand just launched the collection at Level Shoes at the Dubai Mall. “We choose the more playful and classic designs,” Osorio says, so naturally his there is a pom-pom sneaker and also, the popular 'Wild' sandal with a fringing detail. With sizes starting at 21 and going up to 35, this line will also fit women with petite feet. Osorio says, “These shoes are like keep sakes, something you can pass on to the next generation,” With most daughters wanting to dress like their mom, the whole mini-me trend Osorio is a natural progression for fashion. And boys need not feel left out, as next on his agenda is range of shoes for men, and he hopes to follow that up with a line for boys. Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: If you are unsure of wearing ruffles, you should read this
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Drawing the line between pretty and tough View Gallery 15 Photos If you are unsure of wearing ruffles, you should read this Ruffles, like lace and florals are traditionally attributed to the romantic shopper. While you might not picture yourself particularly as the daisy weaving, day-dreaming sort, florals, prints lace and ruffles have their own appeal—and no amount of stereotyping should stand in the way of trying a trend. Unlike Scarlett O'Hara's full-skirted debutante glory, spring/summer 2017's ruffles are an edgier lot. They come inserted in a slash on a top, asymmetric on trouser legs and even surrounding a leather miniskirt. In a nutshell, the trick to wearing the trend in a grown-up way is to pick pieces in which the balance of ruffles on either side does not coincide. You can wear them in the day by way of day dresses and striped skirts. For the after-hours, try Rosie Assoulin's daring one-shoulder top, or Facetasm's flared trousers. JW Anderson's pastel ankle boots will require some balancing of proportion in the outfit you are wearing but are definitely worth a try. For a knockout option, try A.W.A.K.E.'s midi skirt that goes best with a plain white T-shirt. Our edit of the coolest ruffled pieces for the skeptics will definitely change your mind about the trend. column1: A new exhibition puts the focus on Martin Margiela’s Hermès years
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A retrospective show about the reclusive Belgian designer is on view in Antwerp View Gallery 10 Photos A new exhibition puts the focus on Martin Margiela’s Hermes years Martin Margiela, who lived in Antwerp as a student while attending The Royal Academy of Fine Arts, returns to the ModeMuseum (MoMu) with a show dedicated to his time and lasting influence as the artistic director for women's ready-to-wear for Hermès. This show, titled Margiela: The Hermès Years, highlights 12 collections spearheaded by Margiela between 1997 and 2003 (although the 118 individual pieces from the exhibition span his entire career between 1988 and 2008), and marks the 20 years since he took the designing helm at Hermès. He is often described as press phobic, and the avant-garde designer's appointment as artistic director was puzzling to the fashion world at the time. Margiela presented his collections on women of different ages and body types, and his fashion was harmonised with the wearer instead of being forced onto her body. For the most part, Margiela wanted his body of work to speak for itself, with several runway shows and photoshoots rendering models anonymous, veiled or with strips across their eyes: nothing that would distract from the garments. The exhibition spans the breadth of an entire floor at MoMu, with several walls painted the characteristic Hermès orange interspersed with mannequins adorned in his designs, photographs and videos. Director of the museum, and curator of this show, Kaat Dabo explains that the exhibition is divided in two worlds—on one side the work Martin did for Maison Martin Margiela in white, and on the other side the orange, featuring the work he did when he was working for Hermès. The two worlds exist in collusion with each other and one very important aspect of the exhibit was the visual part; by working with these two colours you immediately create a distinction between his worlds. His primary focus was on exquisite and exceptional tailoring—each stitch, seam and finishing. He borrowed from men's wear with suits in fine wool and cashmere, and promoted sleek, unadorned silhouettes, brought to life gloves made in the softest kid skin and worn under structured capes, refrained from drawing excessive attention to the waistline countering power dressing of the 1980s, and emphasised an open back over décolletage. His flirtation with cashmere lead to the creation of seamless sweaters for Hermès (much unlike his own label, which emphasised seams and stitches) and was inspired by the lining of a glove. Margiela managed to take from accessories to garments seamlessly creating a whole new piece that was never before done. As Dabo describes, he was a fountain of creativity: his work for the Maison and for Hermès continues to influence the work of many contemporary designers. During Paris Fashion Week for autumn/winter 2016-2017, the international press described Martin Margiela—who retreated from the fashion world more than eight years ago—as the "true protagonist" of fashion week. Even though he's been away from fashion for almost a decade, his lasting influence on the fashion scape, from couture to high street fashion is indisputable. The lust-worthy garments part of this exhibition could easily translate into the lines of contemporary labels like Vetements, Max Mara, Celine, Helmut Lang and several others. “Margiela's vision, concepts and ideas, prove to be still relevant and a source of inspiration for many in the fashion world. I think all designers that have resisted fashion as spectacle or glamour and sought for a more realistic alternative, have sooner or later turned to him for inspiration,” Dabo states. Putting this show together, however, was not as seamless. “Showcasing garments in an exhibition is very challenging, we wanted to bring the silhouettes to life and with Hermès, Martin wanted to create a timeless wardrobe for women (and in the process resisting giving into trends, Dabo points out). Many of the garments he designed could be worn in different ways, that's why we created a video where models that Martin used in his Hermès shows are wearing the garments in the different ways they could be worn or combined; for example, the trench coat that can be worn in three different ways. You cannot show these details and layers on a mannequin doll,” Dabo explains. Margiela himself was involved in every step of putting this show together, from the hang of the show, to the staying of the mannequins and designing catalogues and materials that accompanied it. It is likely in part preserving a legacy, but also a mark of a perfectionist par excellence. Belgium, and specifically Antwerp, was propelled to the international fashion scene courtesy of the Antwerp Six: Walter van Beirendonck, Marina Yee, Dirk Van Saene, Ann Demeulemeester, Dries Van Noten, and Dirk Bikkembergs. Although Margiela is not part of this group, he is often associated with this group. This show in particular celebrates a particular period on Margiela's career, with a larger show celebrating his genius on the calendar for Paris next year. “Margiela: The Hermès Years” is on view at the ModeMuseum Province Antwerpen until August 27, 2017 Fashion Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Louis Vuitton’s latest collaboration is one for art history fans
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Masters collection View Gallery 7 Photos Louis Vuitton launches collaboration with Jeff Koons Louis Vuitton has today unveiled its latest venture into the art world - a new line of bags and accessories that they have created with Jeff Koons, marking the first stage of its collaboration with the artist. The Masters collection features imagery from Koons's Gazing Ball series of paintings - large-scale hand-painted reproductions of masterpieces - on a range of the fashion house's most popular products. Recreations of the most famous works by some of the Old Masters - Da Vinci, Titian, Rubens, Fragonard and Van Gogh - have been transposed onto the canvas of bags such as as the Speedy, the Keepall and the Neverfull with the names of the artists emblazoned across them. Speaking to us about the collaboration, Koons - one of the most recognised figures in the contemporary art world and whose Balloon Dog (Orange) became the most expensive piece by a living artist when it sold for $58.4 million at Christie's in New York in 2013 - said: "What's wonderful about working with Louis Vuitton is that there really aren't parameters. When they come and speak to you about a project, everybody already has an understanding of what the possibilities are to create something special. We both had the same objective: we wanted to make something that really uses material, texture and colour to communicate and create something desirable. So there was tremendous freedom." The artist has reconfigured the brand's monogram to bear his initials, the first time in the fashion house's history that it has allowed its famous logo to be reshaped. Each bag also features a tag of the inflatable rabbit, which is a recognisable feature in Koons's work and, inside, a biography and portrait of the Master whose work has been recreated. The Masters collection lands on April 28. This article was originally published on Vogue.co.uk. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Pippa Middleton’s wedding: everything we know so far
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From bridesmaid to bride With Pippa Middleton's wedding to her hedge fund manager fiancée James Matthews scheduled for mere weeks away, we've put together every confirmed detail about the impending nuptials. The date The couple will tie the knot on May 20, 2017. The ceremony location The wedding ceremony is said to be an intimate moment taking place in her family's village church of St Mark's in Englefield, Berkshire. Berkshire is located about an hour out of London and is where Pippa and Kate's parents, Carole Middleton and Michael Middleton live. St Mark's Resident priest Rev Nick Wynne-Jones will officiate the ceremony, a spokeswoman at the church has told The Telegraph. The reception location The reception will also be an intimate affair, held in the Middleton's back garden. According to E!, the family home is an-acre Georgian Grade II-listed manor home. The Bachelorette party It happened back in March: Pippa chose to go skiing with sister Kate Middleton and close friends at the French resort Meribel. Pippa picked the ski destination as her choice of getaway and as this source cited to The Sun, it was a small yet super luxe getaway: “Pippa loves skiing, so it was her first choice for a hen weekend. They stayed in a really exclusive catered chalet with maids and chef, who ensured that they were totally spoilt. The owners also wanted to impress their royal guests, so the girls were showered with gifts. They were given Swatch watches, Ugg slippers, leather-bound notebooks, and bespoke fragrances. It was a very small, private party, and they had an amazing time.” The wedding party The Middleton's 27-year-old brother James Middleton is set to join Pippa's fiancé's three siblings to form the groomsmen, according to E!. There is no confirmation yet as to who will join Pippa. Prince George and Princess Charlotte are going to be taking on the roles of pageboy and bridesmaid respectively. The role of Kate Middleton Back in November of last year, royal author, Judy Wade weighed in on the nuptials saying Kate will most likely not be playing any formal part in the wedding, as it would detract from her sister. Kate's name has been omitted from a list of official duties for the wedding released by Kensington Palace, which details Prince George and Princess Charlotte's roles. Royal experts are suggesting she will still play a smaller role, perhaps by giving a reading during the ceremony. The guests The couple has settled on 150 guests. Prince Harry is definitely attending and is likely to have a plus one, meaning he will bring along girlfriend Meghan Markle. However, the couple may want to avoid the press around this and politely suggest Markle not attend. The dress Giles Deacon is the favorite after he was spotted meeting Pippa and her mother last November. “I can never really comment on rumours,” he told Hello!. “Until things are confirmed it's just rumors.” Royal experts have also picked Jenny Packham and Victoria Beckham as favourites to dress Pippa. column1: Forget kurtas, the shirtdress is your new summer staple
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The perennial power of the shirtdress Shirting has long been the backbone of my wardrobe – shirts with jeans, shirts with black trousers – mannish, non-decorative styles in classic white, blue, and banker stripes by designers like Céline, Valentino, Palmer//Harding (joint winners of this year's BFC/Vogue Designer Fashion Fund prize) and newcomer, Monographie, complete with irresistible tortoiseshell buttons. But as spring blooms, the shirtdress has become "the thing"; and it's easy to see why. This extension of the shirt, sans trousers, is smart and chic and has the power to take you everywhere from the office to after-work drinks and all with the ease of it looking like something you've borrowed from your boyfriend. (On that note, to prevent it resembling an excuse-me-but-I-just-got-out-of-bed look ensure yours is crisp and not creased and furnish with jewellery - an armful of gold bangles, say - or a man's watch). In other good news, there's a shirtdress for every woman, from androgynous types to feminine souls – just dial up (or down) the flourish. Image: Indigital Where to look? Favourites include Raey's short sleeved black style, Balenciaga's blue striped version with button-back "tails", Loewe's with sash-tied waist, Palmer//Harding's tobacco-striped offering with asymmetric hemline and Sonia Rykiel's mustard mini with balloon sleeves. Image: Indigital Of course, until pins are lightly sun-kissed (the shirtdress shouldn't be attempted with tights – it's just all wrong) no one actually said you had to lose the trousers. Last week, LA-based designer, Rosetta Getty instagrammed a picture of herself wearing her maxi white cotton shirtdress over a pair of indigo jeans, neatly tucked into the waistband or otherwise scooped back so it only looked like a shirtdress from behind with its dramatic cotton poplin train. Now there's a way to make an entrance – and exit. This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

Emily Ratajkowski and Ileana D'Cruz make a case for all-white bikinis and the latter also for a ruffled top. Leave it to Lisa Haydon to rock a bikini atop a water cycle raft whilst joyfully pregnant. Insta-queen Kim Kardashian West rocks her full hips in her high-cut bikini bottom, paired with a white T-shirt. Bella Hadid demonstrates the power of the ultimate lace-up suit in her post. column1: You can now have Louis Vuitton luggage like no-one else’s
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How to travel luxuriously View Gallery 8 Photos You can now have Louis Vuitton luggage like no-one else’s French luxury fashion house Louis Vuitton started out as a malletier back in 1845. While the brand prides in keeping up with matters of current interest, it also loves drawing from its heritage. Synonymous with luxury, Louis Vuitton has always offered various customisation services to add deft touches to the consumer experience. After hot stamping, bespoke handbag creation and Mon Monogram, LV now offers hand painting on trunks. You can request the brand's skilled atelier to create a custom design on your favourite piece of luggage—and it's not restricted to initials. You don't even need to purchase a new trunk to avail of the customisation service, the brand is happy to show love to its older friends. The art of trunk making is revered skill at Louis Vuitton—varying grades of wood, stitching, use of leather, edging—processes that are executed by hand—are done with alarming uniformity to maintain an exacting standard across the product range. It's not just the LV monogram on the outside that makes a trunk a coveted piece of luxury, it is also the detailing in the craftsmanship. Of course, with the personalisation service, you can make yours truly unique. Louis Vuitton's personalisation service is available on request at flagship stores Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Are we looking at the end of seasons at fashion weeks?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Unscrambling the calendar The once-static format of runway shows is now seeing major transformations in the way fashion is consumed. We now have the ‘see now, buy now model', the convergence of men's and women's collections, and the Insta-show. All of these have emerged from a growing restlessness amongst consumers, whose need for instant gratification remains insatiable. This recent seismic drift leaves us in the audience a little confused: what is it that we are seeing on the runway, and which season should we attribute the said shows to? Christopher Bailey was one of the first to action the ‘see now, buy now' model at Burberry, reworking the backend operations to start even earlier than before. According to Business of Fashion, in the new format, Burberry's shows will be ‘seasonless' and only the name of the month in which the collection was released would be used as markers. Michael Kors, Tommy Hilfiger, Rebecca Minkoff and Tom Ford were other early adopters of the movement. Axis tilt There are two schools of thought in India. Designers like Tarun Tahiliani and Abraham & Thakore have successfully launched their shoppable runway modules to the point of showing current season at Amazon India Fashion Week which follows international timelines. Abraham & Thakore who work with handwoven textiles are staggering the complete collection through the season owing to challenges in production. “There is the obvious struggle with handloom fabrics, sometimes we get as little as just 15 meters of fabric a week because it takes time produce, but we are working several handloom centres across the country to have our collections available in the store as soon as we show them,” says David Abraham. Meanwhile, the younger crop is following international timelines and often showcase collections that are a season ahead, ready for buyers to peruse. Labels like Rara Avis by Sonal Verma and Lovebirds work nearly a year in advance to keep things fresh with international buyers. “Sometimes the design innovation starts with fabrics, meaning we need to work with mills to make sure fabrics are ready in time. We have worked even a year and a half in advance at times,” says Verma. At Lovebirds, the creative process for what's ahead is always in motion. “We make sure samples are ready for two seasons ahead of the current one,” says Gursi Singh of Lovebirds. As Lisa Aiken, fashion director at Netaporter.com says in her interview with Vogue.com.au, “Seasons are becoming less and less relevant as customers no longer think in these terms. What the customers are looking for is fashion that also has longevity, she wants to be able to pick key pieces that she can style for now and for later. We pay a lot of attention to ensure our buy balances continuity and fashion so that there is newness as well as permanency, especially as we are a global retailer.” Binary wars Changes on the runway are not limited to timelines. An important marker in the current changes is also the common showcase of men's and women's looks at the same show, where typically both have their dedicated fashion weeks. Alessandro Michele at Gucci and Miuccia Prada at Prada started showing women's looks at men's shows during the autumn/winter 2017 shows, setting into motion a domino effect of inspiring more brands to join the co-ed format, including D2Squared, Dolce & Gabbana and Vetements. “At Vetements, it really works. It's this street thing. You don't see streets where there are just girls walking. It brings it more to reality,” Demna Gvasalia told The New York Times Style Magazine. Follow for likes The brick and mortar concept has evolved to make room for online shopping, and now, is moving to social media. Translation: you can be a designer from any corner of the world and be accessible to practically anyone, shipping permitting. Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee has reduced the number of shows to presenting just one annual spectacle a year. He has till date launched three successful collections on Instagram, taking a step away from runway shows, which were until now was the way to connect the consumer to the product. “I personally believe that big conversation pieces of design houses should reach out to customers and fans worldwide. Doing a show on Instagram does not mean we will shortchange the exuberance, [but] we are able to connect across Indian diaspora and present a direct point of view by reaching our customer directly,” said the designer. Mukherjee's model eliminates the runway to a great extent, but in no way reduces the brand's standing in the context of fashion. Two roads diverged "Any industry tent-poled by old guards is going to resist disruption; fashion, potentially more so," believes Hilary Milnes of Glossy.co. There is no formula that works for all. Some have embraced the changes, some found out that it didn't make sense for them commercially, and others are evolving as they go along. Tom Ford's business thrived initially when he showed in-season, but there was a downside to the new modus operandi, calling for Ford to scrap the model. “The store shipping schedule doesn't align with the fashion show schedule,” he told WWD, going on to say that he lost a month of selling in stores. Dhruv Kapoor, on the other hand, finds the idea of seasons being redundant in India. “When we showcase at Lakmé Fashion Week, which follows the in-season format, we are a season ahead. Amazon India Fashion Week follows international timelines, so for that we are showing the right collection. Recently we have had requests from buyers demanding autumn/winter collections before summer is over, because the customers want new styles,” he says. Meanwhile, resort wear designers Shivan Bhatia and Narresh Kukreja have been timing shows to coincide with wedding season—an important sector for Indian fashion. “The idea of seasons is slowly blurring—there is consumption of all kinds of fashion at all points of the year. Apart from this our connoisseurs are honeymooning round the year, which makes our category timeless and classic,” says Kukreja. This makes sense, especially since a large part of the revenue that forms India's fashion economy comes from the bridal market. Weddings will go on, and brides will need to be dressed, come hail or shine—or the season on the runway. Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How does the world economy affect your skirt’s hemline?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Skirt lengths, it’s said, rise and fall with the financial markets. So what should we make of today’s zigzagging hemlines? View Gallery 10 Photos The Highs And Lows Of Zigzag Hanky Hemlines In the world of quack economic theories, the Hemline Index is up there with the Pizza Principle (a slice of New York's thin-crust always matches the cost of a subway ride) and the Cockroach Theory (trouble comes not in single spies, but in battalions). The adage goes that skirt lengths rise and fall with the stock market. Skirts were short in the prosperous Twenties and Sixties; in the impoverished Thirties, hems fell. The theory comes apart, however, during the war years, when despite national penury skirts were shorter than they had been before. Then there was the recession of the early Nineties, when skirts were long – not to mention the fact that it's deeply unfeminist to hold women's skirts to account for the health of the FTSE. And yet. Was it mere coincidence that fashion designers, in their post-Brexit, pre-Trump malaise, fashioned hemlines that zigzagged wildly in the s/s 2017 collections they showed in September? As I write, the weak pound continues to depreciate and inflation continues to rise. America is yo-yoing into a world of wilful mendacity punctuated by the news that Donald Trump spent more money on branded hats than on polling – and still won. The world at large – the Middle East, Africa… hell, even Iceland – is in a state of unprecedented flux. Flick over to the catwalks, then, and designers start to look spookily clairvoyant: hemlines across the board – at Louis Vuitton, Chloé, Marni, Preen by Thornton Bregazzi, Proenza Schouler, Rodarte, Sacai – are helter-skelter this season. “We were thinking about the breakdown of society after Brexit,” confirms Thea Bregazzi, on the subject of designing Preen's spring collection with her husband Justin Thornton in the wake of a national identity crisis. (The full effect of the foundering was presumably rammed home by Samantha Cameron wearing a Preen dress to watch her husband tender his resignation as prime minister on the morning of June 24 – the dress being a “silver lining”, as Bregazzi puts it.) Preen's response was dresses with hems that rose and fell with the sharpness of points on an approval-rating chart: lopsided chiffons ruffled across knees at 45-degree angles in sugary blues and yellows, edges left to fray and “decay”; others featured pointed shards of white sequins that hovered around the calf. It was an extreme version of the scarf hem that has gently persisted in Preen's collections for the past few years: it lends its dresses an easy, fluid nonchalance that belies their black-tie formality. The fluid effect was more controlled at Loewe, where Jonathan Anderson showed dresses and skirts with handkerchief hemlines in linen, cotton and burlap. His now established fit-and-flare silhouette undulated stylishly: some trailed yards of rough-edged linen, others comprised choppy fringed layers of wool that frothed at the ankle. Earlier in the month, at his eponymous JW Anderson show in London, the Northern Irish designer had adopted an even more deliberate approach: ombré minidresses swooped and dipped, cut straight and then allowed to spiral into longer S shapes at the hips – not forgetting a dress constructed entirely out of white Irish linen handkerchiefs, cleverly laid on top of one another. Their simplicity appealed to Anderson. “I was in the South of France this summer and found these handkerchiefs in a flea market. I liked the purity behind them,” he says. Hemlines have always had an emotional resonance Hemlines have always had an emotional resonance. In the Twenties, when “skirts crept upwards like the mercury column on a midsummer's day,” as Cecil Beaton put it, women in short skirts were banned from church. When Monsieur Dior took his revenge on ugly wartime clothes and plunged hems to ankle-skimming length in 1947, savage fights broke out in Paris as early New Look adopters had their full-skirted dresses ripped from their backs by other women who merely saw a frivolous waste of material. The mini ruled the Sixties, but as the Seventies loomed it was all about midi- and maxi lengths. In 1968, Women's Wear Daily banned miniskirts from the office, explaining in a memo: “We all know minis are dead.” Still, that didn't stop national groups in America boycotting midis as sexist, a capitalist conspiracy designed to force women to cover up. Sure enough, by the mid-Seventies, retailers were lopping lengths off their midis in desperate attempts to sell them as minis. But back to 2017: is the zigzag an all-inclusive hem? Yes, says Yasmin Sewell, Style.com's fashion director, who favours fluted styles. “There's something about an uneven hem that feels easy to wear, and more flattering because it doesn't just cut you off in one place,” she says, citing Proenza Schouler and Esteban Cortazar as key purveyors of the look for spring. “I'll be wearing this with a lot of length, quite oversized, so that the only bits you can see are my ankles and my neck.” Sewell is wise to focus on the slimmest parts of the body: the danger with uneven hems is that their occasional fussiness can prove swamping. Keep volumes slim and simple on top to emphasise the fluidity of the cut below, make use of sculptural, mismatched earrings and bangles to punctuate wrists and necks, and seek out belts that cinch in the waist to break up the silhouette. Make sure you catch the behind-view, too: undulating hems can expose areas one might rather keep under wraps, such as the backs of knees. And as for shoes? You need a proper high heel. Think of it as doing your bit for the FTSE.  This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #CNILux: Welcome to Vogue Arabia
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion HH Deena Aljuhani Abdulaziz, editor-in-chief of Vogue Arabia, shares her views on the Middle Eastern consumer One of the most memorable sessions at the Condé Nast International Luxury Conferences was in 2015, when Angelica Cheung, editor-in-chief of Vogue China, lifted the lid on the modern Chinese consumer's nuances, spending habits and demands for more recognition from the luxury conglomerates. Fast-forward two years and the woman in charge of the most recent addition to the global Vogue portfolio, HH Deena Aljuhani Abdulaziz, mirrored her sentiment. “We stand at the apex of a new Vogue; it represents a new apex for the brand and the region respectively,” said Deena Aljuhani Abdulaziz, editor-in-chief of Vogue Arabia, which launched online in October 2016 and published its first print issue in March 2017. Abdulaziz, who is credited with the publication's authenticity and dynamism, has a past in the luxury retail sector with the phenomenally successful boutique D'NA, and knows better than most what women in the region want and how they want to connect. [#image: /photos/5ce448ca1dc267eb02c7af7c]||| ||| Delegates at the CNI Luxury Conference in Oman gather at the Condé Nast newsstand. Image: Indigital.tv “Arabs don't lose their sense of self, it's instinctive. We want the Arab woman to feel heard, and to feel connected to her blend of luxury no matter where she is,” said Abdulaziz. “The Arab woman is not meek and confused about what she wants: she is your utmost discerning client, the hand behind the next generation, the heart of the household, respected in communities, and renowned for the care she applies to her sartorial choices.” “Make no mistake, the Arab customer knows luxury,” she continued. “Couture sensibilities are an inherent part of our culture. The silk roads, the world's most striking fabrics, and intricate embroidery have been the founding staples of the Arab wardrobe since the beginning of time. Speaking to the Arab woman is not that different to how you address women everywhere. column1: #CNILux: Ingie Chalhoub in Conversation With Suzy Menkes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The President & Managing Director of the Etoile Group and Creative Director of INGIE Paris shares her insights on the luxury industry in the Arab world Ingie Chalhoub describes how she became the leading luxury retailer in the Arab world to Suzy Menkes at the CNI Luxury Conference in Oman Image: Indigital.tv Following the talk by HH Deena Aljuhani Abdulaziz, Editor-in-Chief of Vogue Arabia, came further insights into the luxury markets from Ingie Chalhoub, President and Managing Director of the Etoile Group and Creative Director of her eponymous label, INGIE. Chalhoub is in an excellent position to define her female clients given her specialism in bringing brands such as Chanel, Ralph Lauren, and Anya Hindmarch to the Gulf region. However, Chalhoub does have a poignant perspective on making it a success and the perseverance required. “It was just after the Gulf War and I had the business with my mother and husband - stocking Chanel and all the other labels - that we started in Kuwait. It was all about educating people about what Chanel is and what luxury is,” she recalled. “During the Iraq War we lost everything, as well as the business, but my husband said to me, ‘You have to keep going to the shows, to be seen.' So I kept going to the shows and seeing beautiful things, even though everything was not okay in my country. With encouragement, we saw that there was a future in Dubai and the people that believed in me and saw what I was trying to do stayed with me.” With #ingiechalhube and Jonathan Newhouse before the opening dinner at #muscatnationalmuseum for the #cnilux conference @cniluxury @ingieparis A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Apr 4, 2017 at 8:27pm PDT But, said Chalhoub, while times have changed and exposure is easier, the basic premise behind getting your business off the ground is the same here as it is all over the world. “I believe that the new generation has more power than we had at the time. We needed to have financial support to do our first store and marketing. Today you can go global by Instagram and using all the digital tools. This new generation needs to know that there will be setbacks, but you need to work hard from the heart,” she concluded. “When you believe in something, you have to continue and not give up on your dreams.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #CNILux: Alber Elbaz Philosophical About Lanvin Exit
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion At the CNI Luxury Conference in Oman, the designer references his highly publicised departure from the maison Suzy Menkes with Alber Elbaz at the opening ceremony for the CNI Luxury Conference in Muscat, Oman Image: Indigital.tv Alber Elbaz struck a philosophical note about his departure from French fashion house Lanvin this morning at the Condé Nast International Conference, as he delivered a heartfelt speech about the importance of designers in an age of increasing autonomy. “Without designers there are not going to be dreams, and without dreams there is no fashion, and without dreams, there are no perfumes. When we designers create, we must first start with a dream and intuition. Marketing comes later, not before – I repeat: marketing comes later, not before. column1: #CNILux: Meet the Real Manish Arora
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The celebrated Indian designer explains the secret of his success Manish Arora with Suzy on the first day of the Condé Nast International Conference in Oman Image: Indigital.tv Manish Arora was in an honest mood at the first day of the Condé Nast International Luxury Conference in Oman. Charting his trajectory from unknown dreamer in India to a star of London Fashion Week, the designer told Suzy Menkes, “It was tough, but I did it.” “I come from nowhere; I come from a family where I think my mother still doesn't understand what I do,” he laughed. “In the history of my family, I am the first one ever to do anything. When I arrived in London for Fashion Week, I didn't realise what a fashion PR was, what a stylist was – or anything else, indeed, that I needed for a show!” No one who saw his joyous catwalk creations would realise this initial inexperience, as the young designer always had confidence in his ability and upbringing. With Manish Arora in Oman at the 'Mindful Luxury' conference event. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Apr 5, 2017 at 12:20pm PDT “When you are honest about what you do, people like you and come to you,” he smiled. “You have to make your own drive. You have to make what you want. If people don't like it, there will be others that do. I am what I am. Indians are born strong; we get stuff done. You may be broke, but you will do it. It takes a lot of courage.” This self-reliance also informs Arora's marketing approach, the designer explained, especially when it comes to the red carpet. “As much as I love India, I think the Bollywood red carpet is overrated,” he disclosed. “It's a marketing strategy; they're not wearing what they're wearing because they want to. I dressed people, but they came to me because of what I had.” There's confidence and creativity in equal measure for Manish Arora today, and long may it continue. column1: Balmain sets its sights on your casual wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion "We want to put more denims, we want to bring more jersey in the collection" Balmain has enlisted a new CEO to replace 17-year veteran Emmanuel Diemoz. Massimo Piombini, whose appointment takes immediate effect, aims to take the company's aesthetic to an even broader audience. Fans of the brand may wonder how it might be possible to reach any wider than £5,000 dresses and an H&M collaboration, but the new regime sees the brand entering the most casual areas of your wardrobe - including the denim it used to be famous for during Christophe Decarnin's tenure - as well as your partywear. “We want to rethink casual luxury. We want to put more denims, we want to bring more jersey in the collection, knitwear - something more casual, but still keeping it couture and luxury,” creative director Olivier Rousteing told WWD. “You know the Balmain customer for being really rock n roll or hip-hop style or pop star, but I think we're going to open Balmain to different kinds of ages, different kinds of men, and this is really important. I'm known for the superstar Balmain, but I think now it's time for Balmain to show another aspect, and this is what excites me.” As well as helping Rousteing bring more “fragility” and “romanticism” to the usually unapologetically fierce and powerful Balmain woman, Piombini - who has previously held executive positions at Valentino and Gucci – is overhauling the company's retail structure, as well as focusing on the growth of the brand's new accessories. “For us, it's not difficult to open stores, but it's more difficult to make stores work, so to make stores work we need the proper concept, the proper retail format, the proper retail culture overall. And this is something that Olivier and I will build together for Balmain's future,” Piombini said. “There is a great opportunity in the market. Balmain is one of the best hidden secrets, because it's not developed at full potential yet, and so with the support of Olivier and a structure that we have and that we are going to reinforce, I think we're going to have a great future.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How drawing dresses can get you a career in fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From someone who knows The name Megan Hess isn't exactly a new one. With collaborations with everyone from Prada and Dior to Sex in the City, Hess has become somewhat of an iconic fashion artist, the best at what she does. Currently living in Melbourne, Hess initially worked in advertising in London before realising it was illustration which really stole her heart, at first working on small commissions before making it her career. “As my clients got bigger and better I was able to be a little more selective and just work on briefs that I knew had a great creative opportunity. Then in 2006 I got a call in the middle of the night from Candace Bushnell's publisher asking if I would illustrate the cover of Sex and The City. This really was my big break,” she tells us. Since then, the collaborations haven't stopped coming. From animating for Prada to sketching live for Dior Couture, Hess has made a life doing what she loves. But what's her favourite project to date? “Most recently I have worked with Fendi in Rome to create an illustrated campaign for their spring summer 2017 collection. It has probably been the most fun I've ever had working on a project - I created an imaginary Fendi Palace with magical couture scenes in every room, Fendi carriages with white horses and signature Fendi girls floating high above the sky, all wearing Karls creations! It's the kind of project that I live for!” Now, Hess has come out with a new range of coffee cups, each with a signature illustration on them. “My new collection of coffee cups is inspired by my Monday Coffee girl sketches - every Monday I love to create new sketches of chic girls wearing designer ensembles caring their signature takeaway coffee cup. I always think we all need a little extra boost on a Monday morning so that's why I started sketching them.” So why coffee cups? It's the perfect pick-me-up, Hess says - something we'd definitely agree on. “It is the perfect accessory to carry your morning cup of coffee on the go! If you get take away coffee you can save a paper cup and just get this one filled up which I think is great - it also makes your coffee a little more personal to have your own special cup.” Coffee aside, Hess's favourite designer is classic and timeless, just like her art. “I do always come back to Chanel. I've always been very inspired by Coco Chanel and her story as a woman - it is the history of a brand that makes you fall in love with it.” Art, fashion and coffee - can you name a more perfect combination? According to BoF, J.Crew women's head of design Somsack Sikhounmuong will take on the role of chief design officer effective immediately and any other teams reporting to Lyons will now report to Drexler. Lyons first joined the brand in 1990, becoming president in 2010, though she is considered the face of the brand. “It has been beyond my wildest dreams to work with such an amazing team of people at such an incredible brand and alongside Mickey — one of retail's most talented visionaries,” Lyons said in a statement to BoF. "I am excited about the next chapter for J.Crew as well as the opportunity for other creative leaders within the organisation to step up and take on new responsibilities. Having spent the better part of my life with J.Crew, I feel an immense pride and love for everyone at the company.” Lyons did not comment on what her next move will be. column1: Tell your boyfriend to download this app to learn your ring size
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s how to accurately capture a ring size in secret If you've been with your partner a while and things are going well, it may feel like an engagement is on the cards. Whether you want to push things along or just want him to be prepared for that day when he steps foot in the jeweler, a ring sizer app is your answer. There is a plethora of these types of apps on both the iTunes App store and Android for free, and they are often associated with a diamond jeweler – clever. The premise is that you place your ring onto a circle on the app, and then pinch the circle until it fills and aligns with your ring, but doesn't peep through on the edges, meaning you have captured the ring size accurately. You can then take the ring off, screenshot this (or export if the app has that function), take into a jeweler, and voila. Any potential rings can be tested for size on this circle. Look for the free apps like ones called Ring Sizer, Gemporia Ring Sizer or Ring Sizer from Jason Withers, which all do the job. Make sure you opt for one with a coloured circle so it's easy to see when it spills over the edge. Then you can go ahead and download the Tiffany & Co. Ring Finder app to find 'the one' and you're sorted. Congratulations in advance, bride-to-be. This article originally appeared on Vogue.com.au Weddings Wellness Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Martin Margiela’s first authorised biography is finally out
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The book to own View Gallery 12 Photos Martin Margiela’s first authorized biography is finally out There are designers who make clothes that are loved and there are those that make concepts that question clothing; and when you talk about the greats in fashion history, Martin Margiela is a name that cannot be missed for the latter. The throne in the contradictarian hall of fame belongs to this Belgian designer, whose body of work could be summarised as one dedicated to the idea of upturning what is ‘proper'. In the early '90s when designers like Tom Ford and John Galliano offered spectacles of luxury, Maison Martin Margiela held shows in Salvation Army stores featuring hair wigs and dry cleaning bags. The display of his unique vision prompted the late Jean-Louis Dumas, head of the Hermès family and CEO of the company, to appoint him as the artistic director of Hermès between 1997-2003. What must have been the most reaction-garnering move on part of the French luxury house turned out to be a commercially successful and a seminal partnership for both entities. Margiela lent his avant-garde vision for a brand whose design language emerges from equestrian life, which will be documented in Margiela: The Hermès Years a book by Lannnoo Publishers of Belgium. Martin Margiela is fashion's man with no face. He was never available for comments, there is all but one photo of the designer, which has never been verified. This the first biography of the designer that has been authorised by the man himself, making it eagerly awaited. The book accompanies the ongoing exhibition at MoMu. column1: The Sri Lankan designers Mumbai shoppers need to watch out for
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Mark your calendars View Gallery 5 Photos The Sri Lankan designers Mumbai shoppers need to watch out for Fashion entrepreneur Maithili Ahluwalia's stay at Shanth Fernando's Paradise Road The Villa Bentota in Sri Lanka in 2009 left an indelible impression on her. She so was inspired by the aesthete's attention to detail that she felt compelled to reach out to his daughter, Annika Fernando. A designer, curator and connoisseur, Fernando is the founder of her fashion concept and lifestyle store in Colombo, PR, under her father's realm but in her own unique voice. An attempt to put Sri Lankan design on the global fashion map, Fernando's aesthetic of marrying the local with a global vocabulary struck home with Ahluwalia, whose much-loved concept store in Mumbai, Bungalow 8, is built on the same premise. The two fashion forces are bringing a slice of Sri Lanka to the city with a special showcase of celebrated designers from the island nation. The mood is decidedly bohemian and travel-friendly with its smorgasbord of breezy and tropical styles. “We, at Bungalow 8 share a lexicon with PR, even though our ways of exploring it are similar yet different," says Ahluwalia. "These works will also perhaps subvert some misconceptions about Sri Lankan fashion. The integrity and individuality of the fashion voices are authentic, and a departure from the sameness of noise is increasingly being seen in fashion today. The discerning customer, who is looking to be surprised and see something different, won't be disappointed,” she explains, mentioning Sonali Dharmwardena's interpretation of batik through today's lens as one of her favourites from the current repertoire of designers. On offer is a collection of classic silhouettes in tropical colours by Samaadhi Weerasinghe's ready-to-wear brand Anuk; dumbara weaving, batik, and a handloom collection by KT Brown (where every dress is made from a single piece of fabric minimising the seams); and beeralu lace and vintage maxis by Kûr by Kasuni Rathnasuriya. One should look out for neutral cocktail wear by Touché by Heidy Rampinelli and Catherine Obrenovic. Also on display will be a summer and swimwear line by Fernando's own label Maus and a jewellery collection inspired by Kandyan dancers by her sister and gallerist Saskia Fernando's brand Papillon du thé. LaPard by Dinushi Pamanuwa will be showcasing a collection inspired by geometric patterns, created on the surface of fabrics that are brought to life through a wax-resistant dyeing technique. Her growing Indian customer base initially surprised Fernando. “I now appreciate that they find relief in our Sri Lankan sense of design despite coming from a country with such a developed fashion design and retail market. Maithili's own love for our island, and her long appreciation of my family's design aesthetic makes this the perfect platform to create an experience to transport the Mumbai shopper,” signs off Fernando. The PR pop-up will held at Bungalow 8 on March 31, 2017 (5pm to 9pm) and April 1-2, 2017 (11am to 8pm) People Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 5 things to know about Fashion Forward Dubai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Style files Fashion Forward Dubai (FFWD), the definitive platform for fashion for this region, wrapped up on Saturday at the Hai, in Dubai Design District. Despite the unexpected rain, shows carried on. This is the ninth season, and it is the closest the Middle East has to a fashion week. Thirty-eight designers participated, ranging from debut designers to Dubai's couture maestros Michael Cinco and Amato. Here are five highlights from this Middle Eastern fashion platform: The fashion talks are where the real networking is done. They are “must attends” for anyone who is in the industry and there are often long queues to enter the hall. Ethienne Cochet, general manager Who's Next and Premier Class in Paris, and Janet Wong, founder of Miami's resort trade show, Cabana, opened the talks. The apex body of the industry, the Dubai Design and Fashion Council (DDFC), presented a talk on “See Now, Buy Now”. The art of digital storytelling was addressed by Daniel Couthino CEO of Nowness, the global video platform owned by luxury conglomerate LVMH. Samsung presented a talk on “E-Commerce: How to Jump on to the Online Bandwagon” where speakers included London College of Fashion's expert on the subject, Paul McGregor. Acile Sleiman, industry head-retail, ecommerce and online, Google MENA, spoke on “Data is the New Black: Technology and Fashion.” The designer to know is Beirut's Hussein Bazaza who presented on day one. The first winner of the region's DDFC/Vogue Arabia's Fashion Prize, he has worked with both ModaOperandi.com and Farfetch.com on capsule collections. Queen Rania of Jordan and Jacqueline Fernandez have worn his label. He made his debut 2012 and collection after collection he has proved to be a consistent. His inspirations usually come from nature. He combines texture with colour that has a feel of the darker side. His Fall/Winter collection was called “Akane”. This is a red deep dye from the rubia plant and can also means “Angry Child.” Motifs of tigers and water dragons added a real feel fierceness and power to the collection. Men need not look further than Emperor. This Dubai-based label started by the three Iranian brothers, Babak, Farhan and Haman Golkar. It is one of Dubai's pioneering local labels and at FFWD, their catwalk show was presented by Reebok. This was athleisure that mixed urban street style details with regal attire. Decadence got injected with fitness through this collection. With DJ Pepstar playing in the background, you really felt you were at an underground nightclub. And the Golkar brothers are planning to open a store in London's Westfield next. It was also FFWD first “See Now Buy Now” catwalk presentation. If you are looking for an Abaya that feels at home in London, Paris or New York, then the Saudi Arabian label Ghudfah is for you. They made their FFWD debut on Saturday, with a clean collection in black and white interspersed with a few blush pieces. Everything was presented in sets so each abaya came with its own inners. Pajamas details and printed linings gave them a real feel of au courant chic. What is a fashion week without the after-parties? The shows at FFWD usually end at around 11pm, and since the event is held at Dubai Design District, most of the after parties are right on site. The home-grown fashion industry is still young in this region, and a small and close-knit community. The street style at FFWD is sometimes better than what is on the ramp, so you will spot some incredible fashion at the after-parties. As we all known Dubai is a city that just loves to dress up! column1: Introducing Arket: H&M’s New Label
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It opens this fall H&M has seen lucrative success with its additional brands, including Cos, & Other Stories, Monki, Weekday and Cheap Monday, and it will be hoping that the new name in its portfolio, Arket, will do the same. The brand - which will launch online in early autumn to coincide with the opening of its first flagship on London's Regent Street (conveniently sandwiched in between H&M and Cos) - "will offer a broad yet selected range of essentials for men, women and children, as well as a smaller, curated assortment for the home", CEO Karl-Johan Persson explains in H&M's three-month financial report, which was released today. "The overall direction and focus is quality in simple, timeless and functional designs," he continued. "There will be products in a broad price range, however in a slightly higher price segment than H&M with emphasis on materials, function and fit." Adding that the in-house collections would be supported by "a selection of external brands", Persson revealed that Arket - which means "sheet of paper" in Swedish and relates to the brand's fresh start with the new label - is opting for more of a lifestyle approach than we have seen from other H&M brands, with Arket stores including a café where space permits. "The café will be based on the New Nordic Kitchen and its vision of quality ingredients and healthy living," he explained. Following the launch in the capital (in the space formerly occupied by Banana Republic), stores will open in Brussels, Copenhagen and Munich. "Starting this project, a little bit over two years ago, we did quite extensive research and what we clearly saw was a broad customer base out there who are looking for classic, quality products in an environment that should be both simple and inspiring, but also putting our own fantastic design together with complementary brands," Lars Axelsson, Arket's managing director, told BoF this morning. "Today the customer is very busy. They are looking for convenience, but also a place that they can really enjoy." column1: How to avoid common mistakes when buying uncut diamonds
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Shop smart Ramesh Narang, director, Hazoorilal Legacy, educates us about acquiring the best of the coveted stone. View Gallery 3 Photos The most common mistakes to avoid when buying uncut diamonds How to collect “It is very important to understand that uncut diamonds are slices of real diamonds. Clients typically feel that uncut means glass, and are therefore unable to understand the pricing behind certain pieces. Always purchase from a reputed source. At Hazoorilal Legacy we have been specialising in uncuts since the brand's inception in 1952.” How to avoid mistakes “There are different variations in uncut diamonds. The traditional styles have a wax filling, which allows detailed enamelling work to be engraved on the reverse of the pieces. Hazoorilal Legacy is famous for this, as it allows you to relive the Mughal style and genre of jewellery. However, one should be aware that there are some jewellers that take advantage of this by weighing the wax component in the gold weight. This makes the piece heavier, without the minute and intricate signature craftsmanship.” How to mix and match “Uncut diamonds can be teamed with precious gemstones like sapphires, rubies and emeralds. The contrasting colours elevate the regal look for a more precious combination and add value.” Beauty Beauty Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Kriti Sanon on why she would prefer dating someone from the industry
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion “A boyfriend will have to understand my profession” She may be new to the limelight but Sanon already knows how to walk the personal and professional tightrope. There have been errant rumours about romancing a co-star, but she remains exasperatingly tight-lipped and caves in only to say that any relationship, platonic or not, is organic. “You can't plan a relationship. You connect with people or you don't. I'm single, honestly. But I'm okay dating someone from the industry—a boyfriend would have to understand my profession and it's not an easy one to understand unless you're a part of it,” she explains. Voluble about her opinions and carving out her own path, she refused to take the ensemble film and small-part offers, until the perfect debut beckoned. No wonder her industry muse is world dominator Priyanka Chopra. “PC is fearless, secure in where she is and what she's doing—and she's always been like that. She's never come across as fragile and is so inspiring.” Sanon may have imbibed PC's fearlessness but she won't mistake that for foolhardiness. She seems honest in her answers, but her responses are always measured and restrained. The reason we haven't heard much about her is because she's adept at keeping you at an arm's length while making you believe that she's sharing everything. She acknowledges it too: “It's easy for an actor's personal life to overshadow his/her work and I hate that. So it's better to say things that won't get you into trouble. You cannot be fake but there are questions I cannot truly answer—and often as I'm giving a diplomatic answer I'll be thinking, ‘What the hell am I saying! It's so clichéd.'” CALL OF THE WILD As the questions get personal, she takes longer to reply. “Thanks to acting, I'm constantly learning things about myself—I like to argue, and I question everything, even on set with my directors. It's my nature to be logical.” It's a trait that her academic upbringing has nurtured. “I can be annoyingly rigid with my opinions but I'm trying to be flexible,” she adds. It's easy to see that Sanon is still figuring herself out, analysing her in-flux nature and choices. She may have jumped into Bollywood but the person I'm talking to isn't the naïve girl who began her modelling career on a lark. She's more introspective, focused and less insecure than her years would suggest, as if getting closer to self-actualisation. Sanon might have started out as an unassuming debutante in the film jungle but she's here to quietly conquer this adopted kingdom. column1: Is India’s fashion community respectful of choices?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Celebrating individuality At the recently concluded Amazon India Fashion Week, I noticed several boys dressed in women's clothing—I wouldn't dare to assign them as transgender—after all, their wardrobe choices don't define what they identify as. In a city like Delhi where women still find themselves unable to move around without fearing the worst, it was something out of the ordinary to see these boys dressed the way they were, casually going about their own business. On the other hand, to think that respecting people's choices, whether in what they wear or who they love, is even a point of debate in 2017, is a shame. However, hate crimes against minorities happen at an alarming frequency, and as fellow humans, raising more awareness about their rights is everyone's duty. In Time magazine's latest report on gender binary Katy Steinmetz mentions, “These aspects of identity—the sense of being a man or a woman, for instance, and whom one is drawn to physically or romantically—are distinct. But they are related, and together, they're undergoing a sea change, an increasing number of people say they aren't one or the other but perhaps neither or maybe both.” Celebrity hair and make-up artist Elton Fernandez openly identifies as gay and is a proud member of the LGBT community. As I carefully construct questions with the right choice of words to ask if he agrees with me, that the fashion community more accepting of people with different choices, there's a sigh followed by an affirmative. “I would say the entertainment industry is more accepting towards the members of the LGBT community—but that's a small, small number of people as compared to the world out there,” he says. Finding work in the entertainment industry might be easier than elsewhere, but that isn't to say that it is always so. “There is a such a thing as ‘gay shame' within the community. If someone in a position of power is not out of the closet, they are likely to be hateful of those who are, and more bound to ‘draw attention' by being the way they are.” Fernandez's team of artists includes members of the LGBTQ+ community, who are grateful to be working with someone who treats their choices with sensitivity. Anjali Lama, rejected as a model in Nepal, made headlines as the first transgender model to walk the runway in India at this year's Lakmé Fashion Week. Hari Nef, who identifies as transgender and refers to herself as an “accidental activist” is something of a fashion royal today. Belgian model Hanna Gaby Odiele recently came out as intersex. Transgender, gender fluid, intersex, pansexual, genderqueer, asexual, aromantic; I am still learning about pronouns and technicalities, and every insight is educational. Back in the 1930's when Katherine Hepburn, Marlene Dietrich and Greta Garbo wore pants like men, Movie Classic magazine ran opinion polls to gauge how people perceived it and if it was 'right' of them to co-opt men's garments. What was once a rallying point for women's rights movements, now, is a non-issue—I for one haven't worn in a skirt in months. We are told suits equate to power dressing and shirts must be borrowed from the boyfriend. Conditioning over the years has made us accepting of women wearing masculine clothing, the reverse, though is still uncomfortable to many. “I feel like every passing generation is more tolerant, and challenging notions about gender and clothing through their work,” designer-turned-model Dhruv Kapoor remarks. Labels like Lovebirds, Antar-Agni, DRVV and Rishta by Arjun Saluja have been making gender-neutral clothing for several seasons. Kapoor frequently wears his own clothing on and off the runway. “I would like to say that the fashion community is something of a safe space for people like me, and that only comes from a place of exposure and education. Popular media loves to make caricatures of gay men, rarely showing a human side—how will someone relate to a person like that?” Kapoor asks. There are of course times when the errant buyer chooses not to interact with Kapoor, judging him by his getup. “By and large I haven't experienced hatred so far, and I feel like I was able to come into my own due to the support I received.” The designer walked for label Huemn, whose autumn/winter 2017 collection was preceded by a campaign honouring human choices. Members of the LGBTQ+ community are subject to discrimination in the most basic walks of life—from finding a landlord that will agree to lease a home to them to wearing what they please—tougher struggles than what others face. It's natural to fear the unknown, but take a moment to pause and understand the person who chooses to stand out in the crowd and if you can't, simply let them be. As for the fashion community, for a group of people that love passing judgments on aesthetics, it is one that is accepting of differences and respectful of individualistic choices. Long story short, we might hate that skirt on you if it's a bad look, and we'll gladly recommend another skirt that's better suited, but we won't stand in the way of you wanting to be in a skirt.
