column1: Fashioning Chatsworth With Personality and Grandeur
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Cavendish family and their stately home are the subjects of an exhibition of fashionable clothes and historic objects with a characterful, aristocratic twist Laura Burlington looked down at the long sweep of intricate white lace laid out for display at Chatsworth, the grandest of English stately homes, and saw the baby christening gown as the start of it all. When she married into the Cavendish family and had her first child, her mother-in-law, Amanda, the present Duchess of Devonshire, suggested she explore the box room. And there, among the elegant storage, was a parcel containing the christening gown, passed down the generations. “From the cradle to the grave,” Lady Burlington said, showing me rooms at Chatsworth displaying family wedding dresses (including Helmut Lang's silk slip from 1999 for Stella Tennant, one of the Cavendish/Devonshire brood, who made her career as a model). The next room had a drastic switch of mood and colour with entirely black dresses displayed against sombre, dark panels. “House Style” is an exceptional exhibition, which lives up to its theme of “Five Centuries of Fashion at Chatsworth”. It is also the subject of a new book by Laura Burlington and Hamish Bowles that showcases the ultra-grand, historic building and the colourful characters that lived there. At Chatsworth, it is all melded into a show of high style. Some enchanted evening - at Chatsworth. 'House Style, five centuries of fashion' is on display from 25 March until October 22. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 22, 2017 at 8:16am PDT Hamish Bowles, Editor-at-Large of American Vogue, who curated the exhibition with Laura Burlington, explained his lifelong fascination with British historical grandeur. “It's a house of wonders and treasures,” said Hamish, explaining that his childhood family holidays in rain-swept Yorkshire introduced him to costume museums and stately homes. “From that moment on, I realised the story-telling power of clothes and the potency of these objects that can tell us so much about the wearer, the times they lived in, and the spaces they inhabited,” he explained. The world of interiors and fashion at Chatsworth is intimately related to the Devonshire family, past and present. The set-design duo of Patrick Kinmonth and Antonio Manfreda, who created the exhibition, chose to celebrate both the intimate world of an aristocratic family and how their lives – and clothes – fit into society over 500 years. The grandeur was not hard to find. As the current Duke of Devonshire stood on the plush red entrance stairway to welcome guests, it was easy to imagine that nothing much had changed since the 18th-century, when the estate's original house – built in the 1560s and whose ruins remain on the hills above Chatsworth - was redesigned. (Even if the roof is currently under tarpaulins for repairs.) How do you present fashionable clothes – including 21st-century designs by Alexander McQueen and Christopher Kane – in a historic building in a meaningful way? “When I saw the costumes for the Duchess of Devonshire's ball, I thought this show CAN be theatre,” Patrick Kinmonth said. “We can go there and we will have the resources to do it properly.” “It is such a fabulous collection of things that we patched together,” he continued, “and it goes in both directions, from clothes through to the person who has worn them. But it also oscillates from a collection of books or paintings to the costumes. We were so lucky to be able to do things in both directions. It gave me the cue to do each room differently.” The recreation of the Devonshire Fancy Dress Ball of 1897 reveals a vision of an entire society based on nobility. Weaving history through the rooms, Hamish explained the significance of a 2007 gown by Vivienne Westwood, with a floral pattern that is a precise remaking of a portrait of Queen Elizabeth I by Bess of Hardwick, a notable figure in Elizabethan society and part of the Chatsworth set. With dimmed lighting to protect the clothes and some arcane commentary written by Kinmonth in flourishing pen and ink, there is a great deal to take in. Some enchanted evening - at Chatsworth. 'House Style, five centuries of fashion' is on display from 25 March until October 22. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 22, 2017 at 8:16am PDT But even if you are not well versed in the intricacies of English aristocratic history, the famous Mitford Sisters, and Adele Astaire - Fred Astaire's elder sister, the exhibition scores on visual impact alone. There is a change of pace in each room and Antonio Manfreda told me how much priceless furniture he had been allowed to move from other rooms in Chatsworth House to make a home for the exhibition. This was not meant to be disruptive, but rather the opposite. For example, a sofa in the perfect shade of pale green that happened to match a gown by John Galliano for Dior was placed in the adjoining corridor. Hats, some of them theatrical pieces by milliner Stephen Jones, were used throughout, often co-ordinated with portraits of hat-wearing members of the family. Hamish and super milliner Stephen Jones talk hats at the Chatsworth exhibition of five centuries of style. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 22, 2017 at 8:07am PDT “The Duke was Chairman of Royal Ascot (the society horse-racing event) for decades so the Duchess was obliged to wear fabulous new hats each season,” Hamish explained. “All the ritualistic moments in the life of a family like this – weddings, christenings, funerals, and Ascot – need hats, and the ladies have really responded.” Stella Tennant from the Cavendish clan and a famous model, with milliner Stephen Jones. Stella's exquisite taste in clothes is shown in the Chatsworth exhibition and its Rizzoli book. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 22, 2017 at 1:17pm PDT The introduction of contemporary style – a Christopher Kane pleated dress that mirrors the library shelves behind – or outfits by Erdem or Gucci – the exhibition's main sponsor – bring the exhibition up to date. Book ends at Chatsworth. Christopher Kane organza dress from 2014 in the library. Exhibition dates: 25 March to 22 October 2017. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 22, 2017 at 8:18am PDT Yet, inevitably, it is also pitched as a romantic memory of a by-gone era. I envisage visitors shuffling through the vast dining room, where a sound installation reproduces the chit-chat of high society on loud speakers, transported by the lavish environment so far from the crowded, often violent and frightening world of today. Ah, the stately homes of England! Designed for the high and mighty, and now powered by the people and the entry tickets they buy. “House Style” is a beautiful and fascinating re-imagining of a vanished world. It has been created with such a delicate mix of drama and elegance that you can almost believe - while the two-hour tour lasts - that the fairy tale is real. "House Style" is on display at Chatsworth from 25th March to 22nd October 2017 (www.chatsworth.org). column1: Did you spot this piece of Indian craftsmanship in ‘Beauty and the Beast’?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s why it is special If you haven't seen the live action remake of Beauty and the Beast, you are missing out on a marvel of production. Remakes of Disney classics are laden with expectations and this one does not disappoint. The costumes for Emma Watson's character Belle were created by a team of experts led by the critically acclaimed Jacquelien Durran, who has worked on period costume dramas like Atonement, Pride and Prejudice and Anna Karenina in the past. Sinéad O'Sullivan of The Costume Directory worked as an assistant costume designer on the project who recently uploaded two posts evoking emotions of India pride. According to one of the posts, the floral bodice worn by Belle was hand embroidered by two artisans—Kasam and Juma in Bhuj, Gujarat. The second post talks about sourcing of fabrics from India and Nepal for the red cape look worn by the actor in the film. The Costume Directory is known for ensuring ethical sourcing of costumes for the UK screen arts. Watson has always championed eco fashion and one can only imagine her being appreciative of the thought and effort gone into the making of the costumes, with sustainability at the core. Here's what Sinead had to say in the posts. Belle's bodice from @Beautyandthebeast was beautifully hand embroidered by artisan brothers Kasam and Juma in Bhuj, Western India. They used a technique called "Aari work" which is a very fine chain stitch traditional to the Kutch area of Gujarat. This style lent itself very nicely to this eighteenth century French floral design. Costume designed by Jacqueline Durran, photo credit: Simon Marks @dyptsimonmarks #beautyandthebeast #costume #whomademyclothes #disney #artisan #bhuj A post shared by Sinéad O'Sullivan (@thecostumedirectory) on Mar 17, 2017 at 9:44am PDT @beautyandthebeast is out today! I was an assistant designer to Jacqueline Durran on the job, which had a costume team of almost 100 people. As a team, we tried to source ethical, fair-trade and sustainable fabrics wherever possible. For Belle's "red cape look" in particular we decided to challenge ourselves to see how difficult it would be to create a costume that was head to toe fair-trade, organic and sustainable, but which didn't compromise Jacqueline's design. We contacted Eco Age, who provided us with a set of criteria which we could adhere to. All of the production was done in our in-house workshops, and the whole costume team got involved in the challenge. This specific costume required 12 different fabrics to make her cape, jacket, blouse, bodice, skirts and bloomers, with trims and ties, and we ensured that each element was certified organic and fair-trade. Our dyeing team took on the challenge of using natural and low impact dyes, and printing with traditional wood blocks, which the set carpenters helped make in the construction department, from redundant bits of the set. Some of the fabrics and trims used were vintage, including the cape which was made from hand-woven Scottish Jacob's wool, that was then over-dyed using madder. The fabric for the jacket was made using a hand-woven linen found on E-bay, which was actually a lady in manchester's school project from the 1960's. The rest of the fabrics were sourced from fairtrade co-operatives in India and Nepal. #whomademyclothes #whomademycostume #ethicalcostume #ootd #jacquelinedurran #fairtrade #behindthescenes #beautyandthebeast #artisan #organic #naturaldyes #vintage #disney #sustainable @beautyandthebeast A post shared by Sinéad O'Sullivan (@thecostumedirectory) on Mar 17, 2017 at 9:15am PDT What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Designers across the globe help you nail the new rules of power dressing
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Mean business Your button-down can be four sizes larger. Your khakis can come ruched. Going by the spring shows, there's more than one route to fabulous power dressing. “Intimate technology” was how Karl Lagerfeld described the theme of the Chanel spring/summer 2017 show. Set in ‘Data Center Chanel', and centred on the woman who sees all, does all, the collection saw the coming together of tweed and lingerie. But the tweed was softer, more personal—the shoulders became rounded, the lapels wider, the fabric itself woven with rubber strands and vinyl strips. Pendant necklaces simulated ID badges. “New materials and a wardrobe that is not classic at all,” said Lagerfeld. The bastion of power dressing, thus, subverted the classics in a way the times demand. With the noticeable shift towards wardrobing pieces—those beautiful building blocks of our daily lives that impress season after season as opposed to more fleeting fashions—tailoring is finding a wider fan base, where even a kid in South Korea can line up to buy a blue striped button-down (thank you, Demna Gvasalia). And workwear, tailoring's most enduring canvas, is all set for play. Yes, we want our pinstriped suits, our blue men's shirts and our khaki trousers. And we can't do without our black blazers either. But we also bore easily. The spring/summer 2017 shows, though, assured us there's some time before we get there. Through clever manipulation, exquisite craftsmanship and an inherent respect for the classics, when it came to power dressing, this was a season of the best-ever versions of familiar friends. After all, we're not just working in our workwear. View Gallery 5 Photos Designers across the globe on how to nail power dressing Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 5 ways you can wear your leggings outside of the gym
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Don't reserve Lycra pants for spinning - luxury leggings are the unlikely trouser hit of the new season We'd  all thought leggings had been relegated to a sartorial no-go zone. But thanks to Balenciaga, Gucci, and Céline, cinching Lycra has never been so appealing. A flash of second-skin spandex beneath a calf-grazing dress is the ultimate style trick to wear now, instantly adding a modern edge. Note: It's worth spending the money on a plush pair that flatters, and conceals any (ahem) underwear issues. Leggings are in fact surprisingly edgy and adaptable. A pop of crimson Lycra streamlines an asymmetric floral dress - ideal for women who ordinarily swerve prettified prints - or dare to switch out roomy tailored trousers for a pristine black legging, and team with an angular blazer (as seen at Versace), or oversized varsity sweater. The point is to tap into the laid-back grace of an off-duty ballerina or early Nineties supermodel. Lastly, lose the trainers (the athleisure moment has been and gone) and replace with a kitten heel slingback. Not only is this the shoe of the season, and the fastest shortcut to the Eighties style references that are inspiring now, but the pointed toe will instantly flatter non-supermodel legs. column1: Why flats are replacing heels as the new favourite shoes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion As heels go down, the imagination soars upwards – designers are making high fashion out of flatter shoes Another aspect of the Roger Vivier 'dancing shoe' story in an installation by Jean-Paul Goude with music by Sam Spiegeleisen. Does it make you want to dance - or just BUY the shoes?!?! A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 19, 2017 at 2:44pm PDT The perilous stiletto is not going out of fashion any time soon. At six months pregnant, Amal Clooney is teetering around in high heels that pitch her taller than her movie star husband. And the Duchess of Cambridge showed up at last week's St Patrick's Day celebrations in Gianvito Rossi high-heeled pumps to match her Catherine Walker coat. Yet pin heels are being challenged by a wide choice of more practical shoes that appeared in the latest round of collections. Here's some news for women who want to take fashion in their stride. Roger Vivier: Ottomania Otto woman - an inspiration of 19th century Ottoman hangings for Roger Vivier collection A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 19, 2017 at 3:07pm PDT The knock-out audio-visual installation by Jean-Paul Goude set feet tapping before a single shoe had been put on display. The wall panels of moving figures were an uplifting example of how an imaginative artist can create a lasting fashion image for the digital world. For those who could drag their eyes away from the all-singing, all-dancing figures, there was a wide selection of low-heeled shoes from Creative Director Bruno Frisoni. It is all about the Podium Square heel on boots from Roger Vivier A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 19, 2017 at 2:49pm PDT But if flats once seemed designed just for striding or for Plain Janes, today's offering is different, including exotic shoes called “Ottowoman”, inspired by exotic Ottoman wall hangings; fur-trimmed mules; and bold blooms on flat slippers. High octane glamour for velvet slipper from Roger Vivier A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 19, 2017 at 3:09pm PDT A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 19, 2017 at 2:49pm PDT For a little more uplift, there was the podium-square bootie, with a hint of the famous Vivier silhouette worn by French actress Catherine Deneuve in the 1960s. For full sensuality, feathers floated and waved over sexy high heels. But the plumes also decorated knee-high boots and floaty sandals, proving that allure can be presented in all kinds of footwear. Decorative feathers on BOOTS from Roger Vivier A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 19, 2017 at 3:11pm PDT Hermès: All in the details And yes, HERMES do some lighter, fancier and decorative shoes too for winter 2017 A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 11, 2017 at 8:32am PST Over the last few seasons, Hermès has been presenting shoes and bags as separate collections. (Don't ask me why they don't include their incomparable scarves.) The Hermès handbag has cast its powerful spell since the days of the Kelly, but there are now some interesting elaborations, for example bags with a multiple choice of colourful, woven detachable straps, or even a pattern of the straps printed on a woven bag. Swinging shoulder straps and fancy decoration at Hermes A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 11, 2017 at 8:27am PST The shoes have been quite a revelation: ankle boots with stolid square heels or with front lacing that would require a lady's maid to do them up. Sports shoes include upgraded leather or suede sneakers complete with simple slip-ons. Shoe heaven? Loafers in bottle-green suede with a bold, gold “H” for Hermès as decoration. For those feeling sartorially chatty without a cause will find themselves spoilt for choice with runway inspiration. Ashish would like you to know that “Your wish is my command” and Jeremy Scott wants you to “Just say Moschi no”. Also spotted were messages like “Be your own hero” at Haider Ackermann, “Time is money” at Vetements and plain old “Love” at Givenchy. House of Holland's reboot of their signature slogan tees (“Let's breed Bella Hadid”, “Let's get obscene Cara Delevingne”, and “I'm yours for a tenner Kendall Jenner” are a few) are a must for the millennial celeb devotee. column1: Burberry hires new design director From Dior
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Meet Sabrina Bonesi Christopher Bailey is well aware of Burberry's strengths – with almost 40 per cent of its revenue coming from accessories – and so, ahead of a summer of executive movement, he's shoring up that area; hiring an accessories specialist from the Dior fold. Sabrina Bonesi will become design director of leather goods and shoes - a new role, WWD reports – and will oversee the bags, shoes and accessories for both the men's and women's collections. Bonesi is not the only new girl in team Burberry this year; just over a month ago the company recruited one of Net-a-Porter's co-founders, Claudia Plant, also in to a newly created role. Plant will serve as senior vice president, brand experience: a role that will see her work to “bring fashion and products to life for customers, and help to establish a strong editorial voice that will support brand and product initiatives”. Bailey, who is currently both CEO and chief creative officer of the British house, will welcome new CEO Marco Gobbetti in July. Bailey will then become president, as well as retaining his chief creative officer role overseeing his new hires alongside the existing team – a set-up that he is convinced will work well for the brand. “I will focus more specifically on design, the products, creativity, architecture, marketing, communication, experiences,” Bailey said when Gobbetti's accession was announced. “He will focus more on the operational side, finance, retail and merchandising. I see this really as two pieces working together. We will jointly lead all the strategies and people.” This story was originally published on Vogue.co.uk Mode Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Tom Ford stops see-now, buy-now model
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Is the business model really sustainable? Tom Ford has announced his decision to abandon the see-now, buy-now model he adopted with his eponymous fashion house last February, confirming that he will return to New York Fashion Week this September to show his spring/summer 2018 collection on the official schedule. The designer, one of many who decided to try out the new format with the view to shorten the timespan between clothes being shown on the catwalk and being available to purchase, explained that while he had been optimistic about the new structure, ultimately "the store shipping schedule doesn't align with the fashion show schedule", reports WWD. He added that last September (his first outing as a see-now, buy-now brand) he "lost a month of selling" because he held back on putting the autumn/winter 2016 collection on the shop floor until after it had been seen on the catwalk (it had been ready since mid-August). He also revealed that while "business boomed" immediately after the show (as is the intention with see-now, buy-now brands), the initial buzz did not make up for the coverage he lost from long-lead press. The news comes in the same week that fellow see-now, buy-now business Thakoon announced that it was abandoning the model, although in that case operations are halting entirely for the time being. A spokesperson for the brand mirrored Ford's reasoning, saying that the label had "recognised that the business model is ahead of the current retail environment", confirming that it is "taking a pause and an eventual restructure". With two major advocates of the model now calling it quits, questions will be asked about how sustainable the model - which caused ructions around the industry, as well as much comment and speculation - is. column1: 2 mega designers close Amazon India Fashion Week 2017 with a grand finale
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The best for the last Tarun Tahiliani and Amit Aggarwal once worked together in Tahiliani's designer studio. After nearly 15 years, the mentor and his student came together to take the stage at the Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017 grand finale. What followed was the work of two designers who had evolved into their distinct styles yet crossed paths. If Tarun Tahiliani was the disciplined master couturier, Amit Aggarwal was the prodigy who was destined to shine in a spotlight of his own. Aggarwal played his strengths—sustainable solutions, structural balance, sculpting while Tahiliani focused on creating highly stylised ready to wear pieces that highlighted his deft hand at draping. With upcycled patola saris (Aggarwal) and motifs inspired by Mughal motifs (Tahiliani) the collection took many courses. The designers transformed the runway into the Amazon forest to put together a spectacle with synchronised design identities that spoke of respect and the humble-yet-profound give and take of learnings. As Tahiliani put it across succinctly, "there's a lot of respect here." What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights from Day 4 of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The final day View Gallery 9 Photos Highlights from Day 3 of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017 In case you couldn't make it to Day 4 of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017, here's everything you need to know. Ilk  With their latest collection, designers Shikha Grover and Vinita Adhikari once again proved that laid-back elegance lies at the heart of their Delhi-based label. From the six-yard staple to fuss-free dresses, the duo presented a line-up of simple silhouettes in seasonal shades such as emerald green, navy blue, deep purple and black. Dainty floral embroidery accentuated the dark hues. H&M Conscious exclusive collection The last day of Amazon India Fashion Week also saw a sundowner, which celebrated H&M's Conscious Exclusive collection. In its sixth edition, the line included everything from basics to red carpet-worthy pieces featuring recycled materials. The star of the collection was a powder pink gown made using Bionic yarn—a product of shoreline waste. Organic cotton and recycled polyester were some of the other materials used.  "With each collection, we want to experiment and find fabrics that are environment-friendly," explains Elin Ästrom, sustainability manager of H&M India. The collection will be available in 160 stores worldwide starting April 20th. Amazon India presents Tarun Tahiliani and Amit Aggarwal At this season's grand finale, veteran designer Tarun Tahiliani and protégé Amit Aggarwal presented their interpretations of Amazon's "Fresh New Look" concept with 80 looks on a runway that doubled as an enchanted forest for the evening. While Aggarwal's collection focused on upcycled Benarasi brocades and Patola saris staying true to his label's philosophy of catering to the environmentally conscious woman, for Tahiliani, Mughal armory-inspired art formed the basis of his ready-to-wear line of relatable yet glamorous modern ethnic separates divided into eight categories (Polka, Kashuti, Chikankari, Mondrian Damask, Renaissance Stripes, Constructed Drapes, Golden Weave and Hussar). A common colour story of rich jewel tones brought the two collections together. column1: Alia Bhatt hits the runway on Day 3 of Amazon India Fashion Week 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Catch all the excitement Maybelline New York ambassador Alia Bhatt walked down the runway for Namrata Joshipura on Day 3 of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017. Based on the sponsor's brief of a New York-inspired collection, Joshipura drew references from the Netflix mini-series, The Get Down. From street style-inspired sweatshirts to OG hip-hop dollar pendants all the way to dramatic evening gowns, the designer captured the essence of a New Yorker's dressing choices. Banking on the popularity of the one-off embellished Stan Smiths she created for Adidas, Joshipura introduced a line of embellished sneakers this season. Luxury resort wear and lifestyle designers Shivan & Narresh drew inspiration from Austrian artist Egon Schiele. The label, which is popular with the party loving, wedding hopping crowd has more cocktail saris, velvetrene designer lehengas and skein work detailing for the season. The designers also introduced the acorn and Schiele prints with the collection. Anju Modi's autumn/winter 2017 collection ‘Neelambar' was inspired by the night sky. The veteran designer is best know for her light, layered, embellished ethnic wear and drew from her strengths this season. She worked with a version of the jamdani weave, also known as neelambari, from parts of northern India that uses silver zari in the body of the fabric. After having dressed the likes of Deepika Padukone and Priyanka Chopra for period dramas, Modi's work has captured the imagination of the fashion consumer and this season's offering only adds to that. column1: Highlights from Day 3 of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get on board Missed day 3 of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017? Here's everything you need to know: View Gallery 20 Photos Highlights from Day 3 of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017 [KA][SHA] by Karishma Shahani Khan Black and grey aren't the hues in charge this winter and Karishma Shahani Khan's collection is testament to that fact. Breaking the sartorial status quo, the designer sent out an inherently happy line-up packed with mood-elevating colours. Silhouettes ranged from trench coats to flowy dresses infused with bold patterns and vibrant tassels, which added an element of playfulness. Anju Modi Blue was the colour of the season for designer Anju Modi whose collection, Neelambar, drew inspiration from the inky midnight sky. Models walked the ramp in timeless traditional separates featuring architecture-inspired detailing. Ivory, gold and deep purple were some of the other hues on the designer's shade card. Shoes from Needledust and bold, sculpted accessories by Roma Narsinghani lent the perfect finishing touch. Shivan & Narresh If you have a destination wedding on the cards, your suitcase is incomplete without an ensemble (or two) from the Delhi-based duo's eponymous label. The designers, who have always taken inspiration from the art world, turned to renowned expressionist Egon Schiele for their latest collection—The Egon Series. A strong colour story ranging from jewel to neutral tones, drew from Schiele's early works, which presents nature in an Art Nouveau style. This season also saw the designers showcase two new elements—the flute lehenga (a new silhouette which follows the lines of a Bordeaux goblet) and Velvetrene (a fabric innovation that adds structure and volume to velvet). A lakeside Viennese celebration made for the ideal backdrop, highlighting the opulent skein work. Namrata Joshipura The Big Apple was central to Namrata Joshipura's collection, the Get Down, presented in collaboration with Maybelline New York. In a room flanked with graffitied walls, the designer delivered a line-up which graduated from sporty separates in lush fabrics to red carpet-worthy gowns. Finishing touches came in the form of dramatic fringe and lustrous sequins. Maybelline New York's ambassador Alia Bhatt brought the show to a close in a scene-stealing emerald jumpsuit. Schulen Fernandes for Wendell Rodricks Keeping in line with Wendell Rodricks' geometric philosophy, Schulen Fernandes' second collection for the designer was an ode to the rose in a cubist avatar. Fernandes filled the runway with structured yet voluminous silhouettes in elegant fabrics. Think layered organza, silk and lush pashmina wool. While fiery reds aptly dominated the colour palette, the designer also experimented with cooler hues like pale blue and teal green. Rose gold and silver accents were used to play up the drama. column1: Highlights from Day 2 of Amazon India Fashion Week A/W 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From beat boxing to gorillas View Gallery 20 Photos Highlights day 2 AIFW AW 2017 If the first day of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017 was about celebrating Indian heritage, the second day was about celebrating the modernity that fresh talent represents. Vogue India Fashion Fund 2017 winner Huemn presented its latest collection that spoke about the right of choice and the liberation that comes from it. Safe to say Huemn as a label has grown stronger with every passing season, which was evident from its energy-packed runway presentation. For autumn winter 2017 the brand highlighted some of the strongest elements it has come to include in its vocabulary—gorillas, athleisure detailing, and recently, florals. The brand launched its line of denim and rainwear with the show. Designers Hemant Lalwani and Nandita Raipurani of label Hemant & Nandita have always succeeded in keeping up with the season's trends. For their autumn/winter 2017 collection, the designers brought in details such as asymmetric ruffled hemlines, corset belts and dresses worn over trousers. While the brand may fall short on adding a story to the collection, it makes up in creating clothes relevant in the present context with a healthy balance of commercially and editorially appealing garments. Patine is a label you associate with elegant Indian ethnic wear. However in a spirit of disruption, the brand showcased modern western separates that were targeted at a younger clientele. The collection titled ‘Eclectic Folklore' drew from the idea of a travelling gypsy. Embroidered biker jackets were paired with track pants and longline jackets with ripped jeans—not unlike what you see in street style. Pankaj & Nidhi's ‘Telefunk' was an ode to monochrome. The label showed its prowess in surface manipulation with this collection highlighting it with details like leather applique, paillettes and fringes. The designers drew from static screen television patterns to play on the contrast of visual proportions for the evening wear collection. Péro's autumn/winter 2017 collection was inspired by designer Aneeth Arora's travelogues. Without restricting herself to one particular region, she chose elements of how people dressed in some parts of China and Latin America and translated the same for a collection to dress what she calls the ‘Péro tribe'. Models skipped and jumped in dreads to the live sounds of the djembe, saxophone and beat boxing at the Kulu hut in the National Crafts Museum. Fashion Weddings Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Jade opens its newest boutique in the city of nizams
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here's a peek View Gallery 8 Photos Jade hyderabad Succulent grains of rice blended with rich spices—decadent biryani. Associations with the infamous Koh-i-noor and endless jewellery stores. Ancient monuments, steeped in history. And of course, the grandeur associated with the nawabi lifestyle—Hyderabad is synonymous with regal grandeur and a brazen taste for luxury. It's no surprise then that designers Monica Shah and Karishma Swali of JADE decided that it was time their luxe designs found a permanent home in the city. The founders hosted an intimate launch preview in Hyderabad on March 15 at their newly minted Banjara Hills boutique. Between models outfitted in the best of Jade, twirling around in the 3,000sqft old-world-styled store and sublime clothing displays, interspersed with silver accents, Tanjore paintings and accessories evoking a vintage look and feel, shoppers and socialites mingled over endless food and drink as an intoxicating scent of flowers wafted through the space. The collection in store, is inspired by the worship and mythological love stories depicted in the form of Mithila art (Madhubani paintings). Using heirloom fabrics and a palette of colours that includes rich hues like Prussian blue, Persian rose and auburn to bring their designs to life, they've created a range that even distinct non-brides would be intrigued by. What grown woman doesn't enjoy floating around in clothes fit for a queen? And for authentic bridezillas, the by-appointment-only Jade Couture Bridal Studio promises the services of fashion consultants who'll work with demanding brides on fulfilling their every whim. All this, within a spaced that houses antiques from Shah and Swali's private collections. Taking the bridal dream one step further, the store offers a customised trousseau packaging service, which includes trousseau trunks, shoes, bags and silverware. From outfits perfect for the bride and wedding party, to lighter creations, to even simpler silhouettes for every day special occasions, the store offers more than just wedding wear. So if you're flying through the city or call it home—here's another reason to get excited about shopping this summer. column1: Clare Waight Keller confirmed at Givenchy
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The new artistic director takes over from Ricardo Tisci in May Givenchy has announced Clare Waight Keller as its new artistic director, effective from May 2. Waight Keller, who departed her creative director position at Chloé earlier this month, replaces Riccardo Tisci who announced his departure in January. The brand announced the news this afternoon on its Instagram account accompanied by an image of Waight Keller shot by Steven Meisel, prior to which it posted a quote which read: “True elegance comes with a natural gesture, an attitude in simplicity”, as well as an image of the brand's founder, Hubert de Givenchy. In her new role, Waight Keller will be responsible for the house's women's and men's ready-to-wear and accessories collections, as well as haute couture. "Hubert de Givenchy's confident style has always been an inspiration and I am very grateful for the opportunity to be a part of this legendary house's history," said Waight Keller today. "I look forward to working with the teams and writing a new chapter in this beautiful story." Waight Keller is the second high-profile female hire for the LVMH group in the last year, following the appointment of Maria Grazia Chiuri at Dior. Today, the conglomerate's chairman and CEO, Bernard Arnault, revealed that he is very happy that she has joined the ranks. "I believe her widespread expertise and vision will allow Givenchy to enter the next phase of its unique path," he said. "I am very much looking forward to her contribution to the maison's continued success." His sentiments were echoed by Philippe Fortunato, CEO of Givenchy, who said: "The teams join me in warmly welcoming Clare Waight Keller into the Givenchy family. I am very excited to see Clare bring her singular sense of elegance and modernity to Givenchy. By exploring our maison's 65-year heritage and the outstanding savoir-faire of its ateliers, I am convinced Clare will help Givenchy reach its full potential." Speculation has been rife as to who would take up the reins at the house founded in 1952, with Off/White's Virgil Abloh the favourite to have been tapped for the role. Rumour also had it that Waight Keller would return to her native England, rather than take up a role at another French fashion house. The industry will be eager to see the vision that Waight Keller, who is known for her feminine bohemian-inspired designs, materialises at Givenchy, a brand that Tisci took in an edgy and darkly romantic direction during his 12-year tenure. Tisci, meanwhile, is mooted for a role at Versace, alongside Donatella Versace, although nothing has been confirmed at this point. Back at Chloé, the brand's president, Geoffroy de la Bourdonnaye, announced that Natacha Ramsay-Levi would take over from Waight Keller last week, effective from April 3. column1: A shoe designer shares his rules for choosing the perfect party heels
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Gianvito Rossi’s top 5 tips View Gallery 12 Photos A shoe designer shares his rules for choosing the perfect party heels A decade ago Gianvito Rossi started his eponymous shoe label, which is now a firm red carpet favourite. He was in Dubai recently to celebrate this landmark with the opening of his first store in the Middle East at Dubai's Level Shoes, where we asked him to share some of tips on choosing a red carpet shoe: “I started this label because I had a story to tell. Ten years ago shoes had become heavy as it was all about the platform, and I believe in the lightness of shoes, so my first shoe was the Gianvito, a classic pointed stiletto pump.” And if in doubt this should be every girl's go-to shoe for any occasion. “A shoe is an accessory but it is not a piece of jewellery, it should not overwhelm. When you are on a red carpet it is not about the dress or the shoe, it is about the woman.” Which is why he believes his Portfino sandals (which have been worn by Miranda Kerr, Alexa Chung and Eva Longoria) and Plexi shoe (a firm favourite with Kim Kardashian West) are so popular; they are very elegant yet subtle. “Do not let width of the heel worry you,” he says. It is all about balance according to Rossi, the heel must be placed right in the centre of the heel so that it maintains balance. Which is why he chooses to pay attention to engineering and proportion. His heels have an average diameter of nine millimetres, making then very slim, but he says this does not take away from the comfort. For an important day event, he suggests the Gianvito in red satin. “Satin is the new fabric of this season. And wearing satin in the day is unexpected, it surprises.” Rossi does not believe that women need to wear high heels all the time. “I design a line of sneakers for a reason, they are a necessity.” So when not on the red carpet, the designer believes everyone should rest their feet in a pair of flats or sneakers. column1: Vogue India’s first ever runway show at Amazon India Fashion Week 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Featuring saris created by 60 designers It's a game of numbers for Vogue India—the magazine is in its 10th year, and to celebrate the decade of fashion in India, curated a special show titled Sari 24/7, showcasing the works of 60 leading designers. Fashion director Anaita Shroff Adajania described the concept behind the initiative as, “Each of the leading India's best designers creating one-of-a-kind saris and going with the mood of what the sari means to them. What we are really celebrating is the democracy of the sari today.” The process of creating a sari came naturally to some designers, while others took it up as a challenge—Dhruv Kapoor's skirt sari with a corset, Huemn's parka-inspired silhouette and Rajesh Pratap Singh's hooded and gloved sari were sure-fire firsts. column1: This iconic Indian designer just completed 45 years in fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion This is how she plans to celebrate the sartorial milestone View Gallery 13 Photos Pallavi Jaikishan completed 45 years in fashion There's little that veteran designer Pallavi Jaikishan hasn't achieved. Since her lifestyle store's inception in the 1970's, Jaikishan's designs have made it to major department stores (Saks Fifth Avenue, Lord and Taylor and Bergdoff Goodman) and found followers in the country's A-listers including the likes of Natasha Poonawala, Queenie Singh and Prerna Goel. As the designer gears up to celebrate 45 years in business with a grand show featuring her classic designs, she talks to Vogue about everything from her inspiration to her plans for the future. What has been the biggest takeaway from your 45 years in the fashion industry? 45 years in couture has been a very enriching experience and a wonderful journey for me. What's been amazing is the different kinds of women I've met of various ages—the apprehensive bride, the excited bridesmaids, the supportive mums and even the wilful girls know who exactly what they want. Many of them have turned into good friends. Some call me and request for slight alterations or a new blouse to wear with their wedding lehenga (made 20 years ago) so they can wear it for their sons or daughter's weddings. It feels lovely to be able to create heirlooms that women cherish. Sometimes we get asked to design for three or four generations when there's a wedding in the family. So much trust and respect truly touches a chord and makes me proud. How has your work changed over the years? My work is classic without too many changes in the workmanship and textiles. Maybe silhouettes change as trends change, but a Pallavi Jaikishan design is always a classic without adhering to fad and of the moment fetishes. If you had to pick one thing that has been a constant source of inspiration, what would it be? My travels! I'm an ardent fan of bazaars, marketplaces, museums and galleries. My travels inspire [me] to create. What's the one piece of advice you would give emerging designers? Stay focused on your strengths and don't try to please everyone. Know your clients, cherish relationships, respect people's time and don't look for shortcuts! What do you have planned for the future? We will continue to take part in leading fashion weeks and merge younger silhouettes with our classic crafts, so that more young women can don our designs. I also hope to start working on my book on fashion, lifestyle and entertainment. column1: Highlights from Day 1 of Amazon India Fashion Week 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The week kicks off View Gallery 15 Photos AIFW AW 17 Highlights day 1 The first day of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017 started out addressing the buzzword sweeping the nation—handloom. Debates have questioned the relevance of the sector in fashion and those working towards transforming into sustainable businesses have only pushed back. In celebration of our 10th year anniversary, Vogue India curated its first ever show, named Sari 24/7. Here's what you missed from the opening day: Maheshwar's pride, The Handloom School worked with nine designers for a show supported by luxury retailer Good Earth. For over nine months, designers worked with weavers and textile designers from The Handloom School—a taskforce headed by Sally Holkar. The main objective of the show was to open a dialogue between designers and handloom weavers. Labels Akaaro by Gaurav Jai Gupta, Antar Agni, Ekà, Good Earth, Neeru Kumar, Nicobar, Rajesh Pratap Singh, Rohit Bal and Péro were seen on the runway. Just before the show, Good Earth hosted a panel to start a conversation about the handloom sector and its current state in India. Sally Holkar, Uzramma of the Malkha Marketing Trust, Anita Lal founder Good Earth and designers Sanjay Garg and Gaurav Gupta were speakers at the talk moderated by Shefalee Vasudev, fashion and style editor, Mint. From the role that women play in weaving, to the possibility of a green supply chain of production, the aesthetics of luxury fashion, the faltering lack of glamour associated with handloom textiles to grassroot-level difficulties involved in mass production—each speaker raised awareness about the many challenges of bringing handloom into a fashion consumer's wardrobe. Designers David Abraham and Rakesh Thakore of Abraham & Thakore worked on a workwear collection to offer alternative separates in Indian silhouettes that are office friendly. The collection of striped saris, straight-cut kurtas and robe jackets was their spring/summer 2017 collection, which is available in stores now. The designers have worked with various handloom clusters over the country for the fabric. Sixty designers came together to support Vogue India's Sari 24/7 show, that celebrated the Indian drape. Whilst rooted in tradition, the sari is ubiquitous in a fashion lover's closet. From Bodice's austere reinvented small border sari to Rohit Bal's decadent black one, complete with a floral bolero, to Abu Jani Sandeep Kosla's fringed look, each model walked out in a sari made to inspire you take your drape game up a few notches. Monica Dogra performed live on runway flanked by models on either side. White balloons were a part of the decor, apt for the sense air of celebration in the air. column1: “I’m a feminist and an idealist, but I’m not morally right in every way”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Firebrand Anushka Sharma on the obsession with correctness View Gallery 7 Photos Why our March covergirl Anushka Sharma is not afraid to embrace the Anushka Sharma is having a good day. In fact, she's been having a few good years now! She's sprawled along the L-curve of her couch, her hair is up, her denims are relaxed, her family is next door and her almond-milk cappuccino is just strong enough. For Sharma, perfection is in the details. Her sea-facing apartment in Mumbai is flooded with the subtle glow of the evening sun and soft growls from her three-year-old Labrador, Dude, fill the living room. I catch her right after a meeting with her brother and now business partner Karnesh, where the duo have just outlined a rough two-year plan for their production company, Clean Slate Films. When I ask for details, she shakes her head firmly, but her broad almost cheeky grin confirms a few hidden aces, at the very least. As we settle into a steady stream of banter, she lets slip the little don't-care moments that epitomise her as an actor: “One day Karan Johar was making fun of my [last-season] bag and I told him, I don't give a f**k. It does its job and I'm going to use it,” she laughs, her sentences typically accelerated. “I'm not an extravagant person. But I'll be honest; people send me free stuff, so I'm very fortunate.” In an industry that prefers to speak in banal platitudes, Sharma's is a voice that stands out. She's frank and forthright about problems at work, embraces awkwardness with open arms and narrates her anecdotes with disarming candour. It makes getting to know her wholly enjoyable. She's all that Most of Sharma's on-screen journey has played out like a gratifying '90s blockbuster. Meet-cutes with Bollywood's best-loved men (Ranveer, Ranbir and all the leading Khans), emotional breakdowns in picturesque locations (Jab Tak Hai Jaan), viral wedding anthems (Band Baaja Baaraat) and some pretty gruesome post-interval violence (NH10). I remember first watching the Yash Raj debutante as the affable Taani Sahni in Rab Ne Bana Di Jodi (2008)—capable and ingenuous but not blindingly charismatic—and I was nervous for her. We all know how embarrassingly brief the life cycle of a Bollywood newbie can be: a swell of interest, a flashy entry and then a quiet retreat to anonymity. But with each new release, Sharma has only dug her heels further in. She managed this while disobeying two of the industry's golden rules: don't take an early hiatus (she waited two years for her sophomore film) and show face at industry parties. I ask Sharma what it would take to get her to attend one, and she flinches at the thought. “Just…no. By now people have accepted that I'm anti-social and not stand-offish. This is not just the case with industry friends, I've always been this way.” Even then, big-ticket filmmakers won't stop calling. Two of Sharma's films—Sultan and Ae Dil Hai Mushkil—crossed the 100-crore mark last year, and she's now wrapping up Imtiaz Ali's tentatively titled The Ring as well as a cameo for Raju Hirani's biopic of Sanjay Dutt. Then there's her other day job: of bringing brave, unsullied talent to the spotlight. Sharma the producer waxes eloquent on the creative payback of her new role. “We had some writers here a few weeks ago, everyone was pitching stories, and in that moment I remember thinking, this is just the best thing. A script comes to an actor in the absolute last stage; as a producer, it comes to you first,” she says. This rare privilege has meant having to learn generosity and trusting in her instinct for good cinema. “Actors are very selfish, so I had to suddenly change the way I was looking at a film. After the success of [our first production] NH10, I've become more confident and more courageous with the films that we do. We just want to push unique concepts.” One example is this month's off-kilter rom-com Phillauri, Sharma's second production, which also stars Suraj Sharma and Diljit Dosanjh, and is directed by first-timer Anshai Lal. Sharma plays a friendly ghost who resides on a tree in Phillaur, a village in Punjab, and ends up in an awkward marriage with a manglik NRI. It's far more accessible than NH10, she says, but not without its novelties. “I was hanging from a harness and floating for most of the film, which was uncomfortable, but technically it's really exciting. I bet you've never seen a ghost like this on screen, and not just in India.” I'm with her Sharma isn't afraid of the F-word—a vocal feminist, she has spoken against gender bias, persisting with tedious conversation even when people grew tired of listening. She's refused decorative roles from star directors, rallied for equal pay (and equal treatment on set), and called out contemporary male actors, most of them her friends, for not being good sports. In a 2005 interview with Anupama Chopra for Film Companion, she said, “If I'm doing a film in which my role is going to be a bit longer than the [lead] guy's I know for a fact that none of the guys are going to do it...” The optimist in her, however, makes it a point to acknowledge little victories. “Girls aren't reducing themselves to any role. They look at a script and say, ‘What am I doing in this film?' That's the way I've been with my career from the start.” And yet, last year, Sharma drew flak for playing two weak-willed women. Decriers found Ae Dil Hai Mushkil's Alizeh unrealistic; outwardly cool but then maddeningly lenient with a callous lover. Even Sultan's Arafa was deemed regressive, a wrestler whose grit and ambition fades too quickly with her pregnancy and the subsequent death of her child. Sharma reasoned in interviews for a while, and then, the day after Meryl Streep's viral Golden Globes speech this January, posted a fervent, if slightly discursive, rebuttal on Instagram. It takes only a passing reference for Sharma to spring forward and elaborate. “When Streep said ‘an actor's only job is to enter the lives of people who are different from us and let you feel what that feels like', I felt this urge to express myself. In our country, everyone wants to see things they are comfortable with and people whose values are like theirs. [By doing that] you're denying my right to be a better actor because you're telling me I have to limit myself, [that] I can only play certain characters and that's it; girls like Alizeh don't exist. Of course, girls like Alizeh exist.” I imagine it must be frustrating to celebrate the recent acceptance of strong female characters on one hand, and equally, become entrapped by them. The sexually liberated, morally upright woman is multiplying, which is great news for NH10's Mira, but what happens to the problematic women, the unreasonable women, the women who constantly drive you up the wall? Let's lose the obsession with the correctness, Sharma says. “Either you have to uphold these moralistic values, or you're some floozy chick who's perfect for a guy. It's either end of the spectrum. I believe in characters that lie in between. I'm well brought-up, I'm a feminist and an idealist, but I'm not morally right in every way.” Centre of balance If that is true, it's not from lack of trying. Sharma says her big aspiration for 2017 is to become a better person. It won't make great interview copy, she warns, and is apologetic for it, but that's all she's got on her checklist for the year—be kinder to animals, more patient with people and less scathing on Koffee With Karan. Her career will continue to hurtle forward, freestyle. “Setting professional goals is actually limiting. You're not as productive as you are when you just do the work required for that day. I realise now that experience makes you more confident than anything else,” she says. Sharma wears her celebrity status lightly by limiting extravagance, converting her savings into safe investments and putting the excess to good use. Recently, she bought a plot of land outside of Mumbai, and a part of it will house Sharma's beloved pet project: a shelter and rehab centre for sick and ageing animals. She continues with grim certitude, “Whatever dissatisfaction I used to feel when I was younger, before I had the money and fame, I still feel that now. It's like Jim Carrey said, ‘Everybody should get rich and famous, and do everything they ever dreamed of so they can see that it's not the answer.'” Double-fried food is not the answer either, I checked. So what is? She raises her hand for me to notice the tiny rudraksh beads circling her wrist. “Spirituality is my life. It's a path that I follow, a path that I believe in. I have a guru in Haridwar and…” she pauses, perhaps fearing she's blundered with the admission. (Last December, she was photographed visiting an ashram in Haridwar with boyfriend Virat Kohli, and engagement rumours were rife until Kohli shot them down on Twitter.) But it's just the vulnerability of conceding to faith in a hyper-rational world. “Sometimes it feels a little awkward to talk about it because it can be difficult to explain. The thing is, I was always trying to find…something. Even when I was 14 or 15, my friends were out doing other things, and I was looking at Art of Living courses.” This quietude feels entirely new. I sense we're only just getting to know Sharma the woman—braver in cinema, impervious to chatter off-screen and silently widening the scope of her life. Before I leave, she offers me some meditation advice. It doesn't require storage for an app, or even the effort of an upright spine, just an awareness of breath. “People fuss too much about posture and chanting. It's not an exercise. You're already calm inside—you just need to reach there.” And once you do, she says, the view is breathtaking. column1: Jil Sander’s creative director departs
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Rodolfo Paglialunga moves on from the brand after a three-year stint Jil Sander creative director Rodolfo Paglialunga has exited his position, the brand has confirmed this morning. Paglialunga had been at the helm of the fashion house for three years and showed his last collection for the house at Milan Fashion Week last month. "We decided to terminate our professional journey with Rodolfo Paglialunga together with the designer himself," said CEO Alessandra Bettari. "We want to deeply thank Paglialunga for his great job at Jil Sander and the respect he paid to the brand's DNA." Paglialunga took over the reins from the label's eponymous founder herself in 2014, who had returned to the label after a nine-year hiatus in 2012 (during which time Raf Simons enjoyed nearly a decade of success in the creative director chair). After only a year in the role, she departed the brand for the third time in 2013, leaving the position unfilled until Paglialunga - formerly womenswear design director at Prada and creative director at Vionnet - made his debut for spring/summer 2015. Paglialunga - whose next move is unknown, but will no doubt be the subject of speculation given the number of top positions yet to be filled at houses including Roberto Cavalli and Givenchy - said this morning: "It was a great pleasure to collaborate with everyone in Jil Sander and to give my contribution in the brand's history and legacy." column1: Exclusive: Tomas Maier on Bottega Veneta’s 50th anniversary
column2:
© Vogue Images Fashion Why he favours a quiet approach to luxury fashion Few reach the levels of craftsmanship that Bottega Veneta has mastered. On the 50th anniversary of the Italian luxury label, we spoke to creative director Tomas Maier about what he's learnt in his 15 years at its helm. One of the most Instagram-worthy moments of the spring/summer 2017 shows had to be when 73-year-old model, actor and ageless beauty Lauren Hutton walked out on the runway arm in arm with present-day It girl Gigi Hadid. Talk about a casting coup, and also the fact that this occurred on the runway of Bottega Veneta, fashion's quietest luxury brand. Even for the German-born designer and creative head Tomas Maier—a strong believer in subtle sophistication and the standalone quality of workmanship that this Made in Italy label is so renowned for—this was a break from habit. So what made Bottega's otherwise discreet creative director indulge fashion watchers in a moment like that? REEL CALLING This year is a double celebration—15 years for Maier at the helm and the 50th anniversary of Bottega Veneta. Maier dedicated the occasion to the Bottega Veneta Atelier by reinventing 15 iconic handbags from the archives for a capsule collection. “All the bags showcase the extraordinary skills of our artisans, who are the heart of our brand. These spanned many designs, including a re-edition of the famous red clutch carried by Lauren Hutton in the 1980s movie American Gigolo,” he says. The ‘Lauren' in question was first seen on screen in the cult classic in which a young Richard Gere seduces Hutton—its hue signifying both the owner's passion and position of power. So, in short, this was no marketing gimmick but Maier's well-thought-out ode to beauty across ages. And Lauren Hutton is an integral part of the Bottega Veneta history. “Actually, both women, as well as many others who walked on our runway, such Eva Herzigová, Adriana Lima and Karen Elson, represent the idea of beauty at every age,” says Maier. WHAT'S IN A BAG? To me luxury is deeply personal and private,” says Maier. The Bottega Veneta ateliers are located in a resorted villa in Montebello Vicentino in northern Italy, where secrets of the house are safeguarded. Over the years, many an icon has emerged from here, like the Knot, the classic intrecciato weave that has now become synonymous with the brand's vocabulary. Whether it's the Settantuno (‘seventy-one' as it was launched in the year), or the Bas- ket launched the year Maier took over the reins at Bottega Veneta or two versions of the Knot clutch, the handbags revisit memories woven into the brand's timeline. “Our goal is to create items that represent everything Bottega Veneta should be: they transcend seasons, and they are unique,” Maier explains.
When he started out as creative director back in 2001, the concept of archiving did not exist in the company. “Today, we have archives that comprise almost everything that was ever created since 1966, including sketches, bags and prototypes.” The Knot, whose design Maier calls a “treasure in its minimalism and compactness,” remains his favourite discovery. Despite Bottega Veneta's no-logo approach, almost a conservative one in the current times, the company has seen a rapid rise under Maier, and he is unequivocal in his decision to not follow trends. “At Bottega Veneta we create a lifestyle and value the importance of craftsmanship and research for new techniques and materials, which have very specific timings that need to be respected and that can't be betrayed.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

I was looking at my old journals while I was there and that's where the idea for the new season came from,” she says. Arora dislikes being questioned about the similarities between her two points of inspiration. “I found visual overlaps in two cultures and I thought of ways to enhance their signature styles. She stays true to her notes—weaving stripes in Kulu and adding oriental tassels to hand-knitted caps. “I was keen to use colour in the collection since winter for us is usually a darker colour palette,” Arora adds. Typical of her nature to tie all loose ends, the show will take place at the Kulu Hut in the National Crafts Museum, completing the full circle of her vision. column1: 5 important things to remember the next time you’re buying diamonds
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Need to know Every diamond has its own personality. Sachin Jain, India president, Forevermark, summarises the art of purchasing the perfect stone: 1 “Diamonds occur naturally in all colours of the rainbow. Generally, the rarest diamonds are colourless. Polished diamonds are graded from ‘colourless' to ‘light colour. Forevermark inscribes diamonds from D to L as well as fancy colours.” 2 “The carat is a measure of weight. A diamond can appear larger, or smaller, than its actual weight, depending on its cut. Your diamond may actually have a higher carat weight than a bigger-looking diamond with a more shallow cut. Forevermark inscribes diamonds from 0.10 carat and upwards.” 3 “The cut refers to the shape of the diamond. Round, princess, oval, marquise, pear and emerald are some of the most familiar cuts. It also affects the sparkle of a polished diamond and is expressed in terms of the brilliance, fire and scintillation of a diamond. Forevermark cuts are only certified ‘very good' or ‘excellent'.” 4 “In terms of clarity, nature ensures that every diamond is as unique as the person who wears it. Naturally-occurring features, known as inclusions, provide a special fingerprint within the diamond.” 5 “Every Forevermark diamond can be tracked along its journey from the mine to the finger. They all have a unique identification number inscribed on the table of the stone to assure it is genuine, untreated and responsibly sourced. Given this rigorous selection criteria, less than 1 per cent of the world's diamonds can become Forevermark-certified.” Here are some pieces to add to your shopping list: View Gallery 4 Photos How to buy the perfect diamond   What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: These women prove that you can mix business with friendship
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How to make the equation work There's nothing quite like doing business with your girlfriends, swear these creative entrepreneurs. Wearing shades of the season's hottest hue, over champagne and small plates at Mumbai's dining hotspot The Clearing House, we got them to spill how they are all true partners in crime. [#image: /photos/5ce4500cb8031121b08f9c58]||| ||| Nandita Mahtani, Dolly Sidhwani, Bhavana Pandey, directors, Love Genration Personal connect: They share a love for all things fashion, often making it to the same best-dressed lists, but there's more to this friendship than just a good sense of style, Nandita Mahtani, Dolly Sidhwani and Bhavana Pandey share an enviable camaraderie. Fashion collaboration: After years of talking about it, the trio finally launched their prêt-a-porter label, Love Genration, in 2015. The first collection debuted at Who's Next in Paris. “We want to make Love Genration a world-class high-street brand made in India itself,” says Mahtani. While Mahtani looks after design, Sidhwani and Pandey (who doubles up as their model for fittings) are in charge of production and marketing respectively. “Our collections are very mindful of Indian sensibilities and yet adhere to international trends and forecasts,” says Sidhwani. The price points (the clothes range between Rs 900-Rs 3,500) and ramp-to-rack availability are also big draws. And there's one more USP, says Pandey: “We are our biggest clients and, because our personal styles and body structures are quite different, our collections have a good mix.” Currently available online at Amazon, Myntra and Koovs as well as at Shoppers Stop, Love Genration will soon have a store of its own. Style files: While Sidhwani is the most adventurous among the three, Pandey's style is a mix of classic and sexy. For Mahtani, comfort is key. “There's rarely been a day we've not liked what the other is wearing,” says Mahtani. [#image: /photos/5ce4500c1dc2675309c7b84c]||| ||| Queenie Singh, jewellery designer and Rhea Pillai, spiritual teacher and fashion designer Personal connect: Queenie Singh and Rhea Pillai have been best friends for over 25 years. “Through work, then kids and now work again, our bond has only gotten stronger,” says Pillai, as Singh adds, “Rhea is synonymous with spirituality and teaching, yet she's so glamorous and beautiful….” Fashion collaboration: Last year, after much persuasion from Singh, Pillai launched her label, Temple House, which brought together two parts of her life—Art of Living and fashion. She launched her first collection of ‘temple' saris in collaboration with Jewels by Queenie. “Queenie's jewellery is glamorous and contemporary, but she also makes incredible Indian pieces. It's the same with my designs, which is why this collaboration has worked so well,” says Pillai. Q & R—a title they are keen on for this partnership (it's not official just yet)—has already made its debut at several well-known exhibitions in the country so far, the focus being more on traditional wear. Plans are now on to tap into the international market, specifically London, Los Angeles and New York, through exclusive trunk shows. Singh, whose jewellery has been worn by the likes of Kim Kardashian West, Lindsay Lohan and Paris Hilton in the past, has already made her mark globally. Pillai's next step is to design Western wear, shirts being first on her list. “Ours is high end luxury—I work with only real gold and premium diamonds and Rhea works with authentic fabrics sourced from across India,” says Singh. Style files: “There's nothing casual about Queenie,” says Pillai. “She'll look ultra glamorous even in a simple pair of jeans. I admire how focused she is on looking the best she can,” says Pillai, who now has her eyes set on the Dragon ring designed by Singh. “It's made of yellow gold, with diamonds and Baroque pearls,” she adds. Singh, who owns several saris from Temple House, says she likes Pillai's personal style, which is classic and timeless. “She won't get swayed by trends,” she adds. [#image: /photos/5ce4500c9cc0c02bfdfa03fa]||| ||| Payal Singhal, fashion designer and Shaheen Abbas, jewellery designer Personal connect: Payal Singhal and Shaheen Abbas were admirers of each other's work long before they became friends. When they did start meeting each other socially around six years ago, they got on like a house on fire. “We realised how similar we were as people—we share the same values,” says Singhal. “We can talk about anything and everything—from work to husbands and kids,” adds Abbas. Fashion collaboration: Last December, the duo co-hosted a star-studded festive pop-up of their individually designed collections (Singhal's Paakiza and Abbas's Chand Taara) in Mumbai. Abbas's cocktail jewellery blended seamlessly with Singhal's signature styles, translating into big sales for both designers. “Both our collections can go from day to night, Indian to Western, and are multitasking—like my drop-waist kurta that can be worn as a dress and her chokers that can double up as tennis bracelets. We've both pushed boundaries to create some really unique contemporary pieces,” says Singhal, adding that they plan to collaborate professionally a lot more in the future. Style files: Singhal says Abbas's modern-day spin is what makes her stand out from the crowd. And Abbas loves the way the couturier carries off her drop-crotch dhotis. “Her clothes make a statement without trying too hard.” Photographed by Neville Sukhia and Styled by Priyanka Parkash Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Understanding the mind of Rei Kawakubo with the idea of “in-betweeness”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Embracing the power of duality View Gallery 5 Photos Understanding the mind of Rei Kawakubo with the idea of “in-betweeness” Comme des Garçons, despite its Japanese origins (Komu de Gyaruson is how the name is pronounced in Japanese), is very much a household name in France. Founded by the enigmatic Rei Kawakubo, the brand sent shockwaves through the Paris circuit in the 1970s with its radical approach to fashion. Much has been said about fashion's ‘contrarian', and more will try to find a point of view on her body of work after the exhibition opens doors to public on May 1. After Yves Saint Laurent, Rei Kawakubo is the only living designer to be the subject of a monographic exhibition at the Costume Institute of the Metropolitan Museum of Art titled ‘Rei Kawakubo/Comme des Garçons: Art of the In-Between'. Head curator at the Costume Institute, Andrew Bolton, who has been working with the subject of the exhibition for the last few months offers insight into her psyche. “When we started working with Rei, she didn't want to do a retrospective,” he says. “It would have been easier to do it historically, but neither of us wanted it to be that way, so I thought we should use the pieces that give an understanding of her work, sort of contextualise it in a way that allows people the freedom of authority in a way—so this idea of space and in-betweeness was a good way to do it, to create an avenue for people to talk about it.” Condensing the critically-acclaimed brand's identity to one singular adjective would be doing injustice to its many faces. On the runway it remains fiercely conceptual, in the stores it is surprisingly approachable, and to those who put it on a pedestal—a web of intellectual fashion consumers—Comme des Garçons will always be a purist brand that can only be looked up to.  The search for newness Notorious for maintaining her silence through the decades, Kawakubo arrives without any noise for the press presentation of the exhibition. She is only seen in the spotlight during a photo-op towards the end of the preview and ushered out swiftly after, with husband and CEO, Comme des Garçons, Adrien Joffe, never leaving her side. In 1979 Kawakubo explained the vision for her brand to the New York Times, “I felt I should be doing something more directional, more powerful ... [so] I decided to start from zero, from nothing, to do things that have not been done before, things with a strong image.” Thus began her search for ‘newness', the only commandment she followed through the years, using her craft to challenge conventional notions of beauty and aesthetics. “The exhibition at The Metropolitan Museum in May will examine eight recurring aesthetic expressions of “in-betweenness” in Rei's collections: fashion/anti-fashion; design/not design; model/multiple; then/now; high/low; self/other; object/subject; and clothes/not clothes. In her work, Rei breaks down the false walls between these dualisms, exposing their artificiality and arbitrariness,” said Bolton. In circles Of the handful interviews the designer has agreed to, the one stands out as the most accurate understanding of her thought process was with fashion journalist Susannah Frankel, who asked the designer to explain her collection 'Body Meets Dress—Dress Meets Body'. Kawakubo simply drew a circle on a scrap of paper and disappeared. “The circle in Buddhism means enlightenment actually, but she was referring to the idea of mu (emptiness) and ma (space). It was nice because what she was doing was inviting you to be in this space. She'd rather no-one interpret her work but just experience it, which to me was an invitation,” says Bolton in awe of Kawakubo's genius. After having sent his selections for the catalogue, the curator flew down to Tokyo to see the archives in person. Despite everything Bolton has seen before, he confesses to being blown away by the full force of the body of work of an artist. “Walking into a room full of those pieces that you either see in photographs or on Vogue.com or on the runway, and to see them all in one room—that to me was rather extraordinary because you are overwhelmed by this woman's creativity,” he says. Despite Kawakubo's highly conceptual stream of thought, CDG, as the brand is known on the streets, remains highly successful commercially. “Rei is an enigma, since her artistic practice remains legible and assertive, even in the context of its commerciality. Ultimately, it's within this elastic zone between fashion/commerce that Rei's ‘art of the in-between' occupies and most powerfully expresses itself,” Bolton concludes. column1: What to expect from Amazon India Fashion Week’s autumn/winter 2017 finale
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In conversation with the two talents View Gallery 4 Photos What to expect from Amazon India Fashion Week’s autumn/winter 2017 finale The news is out that Tarun Tahiliani and Amit Aggarwal will be sharing space at the grand finale of Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017. Aggarwal, who spent the early years of his career honing his skills at Tarun Tahiliani's design studio, will again be working with his mentor for the collection. Tahiliani, a veteran in the Indian fashion industry, is best known for his drapes and couture. Amit Aggarwal on the other hand veers to a sculpted conceptual look with his labels Amit Aggarwal and AM.IT. “It's been nearly a decade since we worked together and we have both evolved into different design voices. The collection is not meant to be a copy of what we used to do—God forbid if that happens!” said Tahiliani. Both the designers are working on Amazon's campaign for the season—Fresh New Look. Tahiliani's work will interpret the theme in spirit than taking it literally. “The Fresh New Look for us is simplified evening wear. It's not something for the bride or her close family but it is something a guest could wear to a wedding,” said the designer. Aggarwal, meanwhile, will show traditional textiles in a light. “We are upcycling patola and Benarasi saris in our silhouettes for new-age brides who want to wear heirloom pieces on their big day but not how it is usually done,” he explains. The show will feature 70 looks highlighting techniques such as latticing, ruching, fluting used in variations by both design houses in the same colour scheme. “Indians must rule their fashion moment—not become overtly traditional or western, and find a middle ground,” said Tahiliani describing the overarching theme for the finale. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Featuring Manish Malhotra, Anita Dongre and more As Vogue India completes 10 successful years in 2017, what better way to celebrate the milestone than by empowering our country's strongest style staple? Amazon India Fashion Week's upcoming season, autumn/winter 2017, brings the perfect platform to host Vogue's ‘Sari 24/7', a collection featuring different versions of the nine-yard favourite by 50 of India's most prolific labels including Manish Malhotra, Raw Mango, Abraham & Thakore, Rahul Mishra, Suneet Varma, Bodice, Huemn, Rara Avis, Payal Singhal, Anita Dongre, Nikasha, Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla and Kallol Datta. "Vogue India has always celebrated the best of fashion, and for us, that begins with the most symbolic and timeless piece of clothing, the sari," says Vogue India editor, Priya Tanna. "Our intent was matched by the enthusiasm of 50 designers who have each created a unique sari for this special show." "The 'Sari 24/7' show is a project close to my heart, especially because it brings together India's best designers," says Anaita Shroff Adajania. "It's a milestone event for us, and our way of putting the spotlight on our favourite garment." In the words of president of FDCI, Sunil Sethi, "As the bible of fashion, Vogue India celebrates its tenth anniversary, the AIFW runway will light up with a special show. The ‘Vogue Sari 24/7' will bring sari-torial splendour to the stage, with the unmatched elegance of traditional drapes. column1: LVMH’s big plans includes an e-commerce site and an art museum
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Under the mantle of Bon Marché It is proving to be a big week for French conglomerate LVMH, which yesterday announced its plans to open a new art museum on the outskirts of Paris (building on the success of the Fondation Louis Vuitton), coinciding with reports that it would be launching its own e-commerce platform under the mantle of Bon Marché - the multi-brand French department store it has owned since 1984. Regarding the first announcement, LVMH owner Bernard Arnault revealed the plans to renovate the Musee National des Arts et Traditions Populaires in Paris in the presence of French president Francois Hollande, mayor of Paris Anne Hidalgo, French ecology minister Segolene Royal, and architect Frank Gehry, who designed the Fondation Louis Vuitton and has been employed to mastermind the new cultural landmark. The new space will have "an arts and crafts focus, featuring a concert hall and workshops for a 50-year concession granted to Arnault by the City of Paris", reports the BoF, and is slated to cost €158 million. Concerning its first foray into the multi-brand e-commerce landscape, the Bon Marché site - which will launch in May - will not only sell products from all 70 LVMH-owned brands, but products from additional labels that don't belong in its stable, reports The Financial Times. It is the first major digital initiative to come from the brand since its chief digital officer, Ian Rogers, arrived from Apple in 2015. Now, to the delight of Mumbai's fashion-conscious elite, the designer's vibrant, handwoven creations have found a new home in one of the city's most iconic buildings.
