column1: #SuzyPFW Louis Vuitton: A Sensational Setting
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Marble statues at the Louvre Museum were an overwhelming background for Vuitton’s Creative Director Nicolas Ghesquière Neptune, with rippling muscles, was stabbing a dying horse. A nymph was stretched out on a plinth, every part of her beautiful body exposed - except for a drape of cloth around the loins. Below that sculpture, a wild boar was being heroically slain in a scene from classical Greek mythology. The setting for the Louis Vuitton show in the Louvre's home of classic statuary in the Cour Marly was, in that overused fashion phrase, truly awesome. The audience felt a sense of privilege to be there, among these historical creations of such beauty and eternal elegance. The classic revival of the 17th and 18th centuries produced exceptionally fine work. And we fashion folk were alone in the often overcrowded museum, at night, in the sculpture court, with spotlights trained on the white marble. Image: Indigital “For me, it is truly a dream come true,” said Louis Vuitton Creative Director Nicolas Ghesquière, speaking after the last model had walked a series of marble stairwells in front of an audience that included Michelle Williams, Isabelle Huppert, and the timeless Catherine Deneuve. Image: Indigital So what do you do as a fashion creative when faced with art that has marked history? The designer's decision seemed to be: business as usual. There were no draped dresses such as those of Madame Grès, so memorably displayed in the Paris sculpture museum, the Musée Bourdelle (“Couture at Work”, 2011). Nor were there riffs on the creamy greys of stone or the off-whites of marble that captured the timelessness of beauty – although there were silken dresses. They were new for Vuitton, especially one in sky blue, cut in strips on the bias so that it slithered across the body. But otherwise, there was Ghesquière's random mix of a black leather coat with satin, a familiar studded leather jacket with blue silk trousers standing in for jeans, and fluffy snowballs of fur down the front of a jacket. In fact, fur played a larger part than usual in the Vuitton repertoire, although it was more often pieced together like a puzzle or even in blue shearling dyed a denim-blue. Image: Indigital Ghesquière's casual stance with high quality fabrics and exceptional craftsmanship is the essence of his work for Vuitton. Whereas the brand's signature bags were classic, often worn slipped across the wrist, the clothes were more experimental, as when squares of what looked like glitter leather appeared in patches on a white top. The only link between accessories and clothes seemed to be the extraordinary handwork. Image: Indigital Did the designer miss a moment in not aligning his work more closely with the exceptional surroundings? In the movie world, they say never to work with dogs or children. Timeless art comes into the same category with fashion, which is essentially transient. So the designer was surely wise to leave the art alone - even if those sculptures did rather steal the Vuitton show. column1: #SuzyPFW: Hermès – Pattern Is Back
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion With a flourish of print and richness of colour, designer Nadège Vanhee-Cybulski changed the pace at the illustrious house Time was that Hermès was known primarily for its patterned scarves and neckties - unless you were buying a saddle or other horsey elements on which the French house was founded. Nadège was the first female designer at the house in 20 years when she was appointed in 2015, and had kept to muted shades in fine fabrics to express the upscale, double-face-cashmere spirit of the house. Vulgarity, in this populist era, is unknown at Hermès. Image: Indigital So it was good to see Nadège's increasing confidence in taking prints of keys (the kind that go with historic country houses) and elegant gloves to give an edgy modernity to graceful clothes. Both patterns date from the Sixties and the names of the three designers were scrupulously noted in the programme. Image: Indigital "That's coming from the archives" Nadège said backstage, referring to the prints. "What is the beauty of the house is that there is such a massive collaboration with different illustrators and (there are) stacks and stacks of sketches and they were so eclectic. There's a connection but beyond that I just felt that I really wanted to bring something unexpected." Image: Indigital The patterns joined another crucial element that is helping Hermès to move forward in its own smooth, slow-paced way: colour. The show began with long, elegantly cut coats - Nadège called them "horse blanket" drapes. Those outfits opened to show a brighter side: a pink lining and orange hose or a red lining and soft pink trousers. Some of the colouring was subtle, as in a faint squiggle pattern on navy blue, but the designer had definitely moved away from minimalist style. Image: Indigital Since the bags and shoes were shown separately earlier in the week, Nadège had the opportunity to enhance the fashion offering, which has sometimes looked like an adjunct to accessories. This time, the extras were defined as that: a wide belt here, a woolly hat there, discreet bags and some horsey-looking necklaces and other classic pieces in rose gold. Leather aprons were transformed into clothing. Image: Indigital The designer, now in her fifth season at Hermès, is moving forward quietly but firmly towards a position that menswear, created by a different long-term designer, reached some time ago. The clothes have to be appealing, perfectly made, but above all relevant to women of today. Nadège is approaching that goal. column1: #SuzyPFW: Stella McCartney Goes Country
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer reflects on a very British style in a deliberately downsized show that had a big impact With George Michael's 'Faith' blasting out on the soundtrack and the models dancing and singing, Stella McCartney's show finished on a vibrant note. But the overall mood was literally about downsizing, as the designer had moved the set to the underground area of her usual venue, the Paris Opera, reducing the size of her audience from major to minor. Image: Indigital The mood had also shifted, from urban woman dressing for a crazy busy modern life, to an equestrian world of the past when women wore fitted jackets, long coats, sand beige knits - and might own a skittish pony. That appeared as a bold horse print on a mid-calf skirt. Image: Indigital Individually, there were strong pieces and some of these easy winter-in-the-country clothes could have been separated out for city sportswear. But definitely not the silken headscarf - an accessory that was presumably meant as a jokey take on Queen Elizabeth II's out of town style. Image: Indigital "A lot of inspiration at the beginning of the show was about being British and the precision of that side of Britain - then trying to question it, disrupt it and dismantle it," Stella explained. Stella Mccartney brings her horsey British show to an ending with George Michael's 'Faith'. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 6, 2017 at 2:33am PST The designer went on to say how much the silhouette and female attitudes have changed since earlier times, now that "women had taken ownership of their sexuality" and that looking back to the era of pre-empowerment of women gave her story a new slant. Image: Indigital Although that sounded a familiar line from female designers this season, Stella uniquely has followed her fervent desire never to use animal products. The result is now so sophisticated and stylish that McCartney's strong attitude has helped change the once general view that eco fashion was a contradiction in terms. column1: #SuzyPFW: Valentino – We Are All Romantics
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion With exquisite workmanship and Victoriana melded with pop, Pierpaolo Piccioli had a new vision of romance for the digital era Prudishness and pop - can the two really meld together? Yes! If the Victorian-style cape is in a vivid, sugary, postmodern pink and the dress underneath a colourful geometric pattern, recalling the Memphis era. At Valentino, the 1880s met the 1980s with sensational results as designer Pierpaolo Piccioli dismissed the feminist vibe that has reverberated through the Autumn/Winter 2017 season yet created a collection that was respectful to, and joyful for, women. Image: Indigital Just looking at the designer's four moodboards was a history lesson, as Pierpaolo whizzed me through dark Victorian carved birds, bright Memphis furniture, coral with a religious connection to Medusa - so much from the past crammed into one collection. Image: Indigital Yet on the runway, the result was far from overloaded, as the history of coral was subsumed into the necklaces all the models wore and the deflated Victorian silhouette - long and high waisted, but slim where a crinoline once was, seemed perfectly acceptable as a romantic vision of the 21st century. Image: Indigital "I wanted to add deepness and romanticism to the modernity of the shapes, so these are absolutely items that you can wear separately - a white shirt or the skirt with your own sweater," said Pierpaolo. "I think fashion is made for dreams, but sometimes you want a dream that is daywear." http://www.vogue.co.uk/article/suzy-menkes-paris-autumn-winter-2017-valentino The Valentino studios are at the heart of the matter, apparently finding it as easy to toss off a tailored coat with a mid-calf hemline nudging Victoriana bootees, as it is to make a soft, light dress to flow underneath. The detail and delicacy of the dresses seemed like an extension of the haute couture, but the designer was eager to point out that the clothes came from the Italian factory dedicated to Valentino. Image: Indigital Whether it is so easy visually to mix a sorbet pink top with tiny ruffles down the arms that flowed into a cherry ripe panelled skirt, the result was surprisingly calm. Even the dresses patterned with Memphis pop blended in with the plainer, pleated versions. And just when you thought that the show's high romance was over blown, the designer would slip in a black top over a pair of sloppy velvet trousers or calm a Memphis patterned dress with a tailored coat. A severe black jacket could be worn with anything already in the closet from an LBD to blue jeans. Like the tailored coats, it kept ripe femininity in check. Image: Indigital "For me it is important to keep the lightness, otherwise it doesn't feel confident and if you don't feel that you don't feel beautiful," said Pierpaolo. "I think if you feel confident you can even be able to show your sensibility and really feel stronger." With Pierpaolo by the Valentino mood board A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 6, 2017 at 12:02am PST However you rated the clothes - too fancy, too froufrou, too historical - there is no denying that Pierpaolo has created a vision that is respectful to women and which makes them beautiful. In a churning political universe, Valentino offers a small, still voice of calm. This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why you need to know about Ruth Negga
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The actor who swept all the award nominations this year Ethiopian-Irish actor Ruth Negga shot to fame this year with her powerful performance in Loving, a historical drama based on the true story of Richard and Mildred Loving, a couple fighting laws that prohibited interracial marriage in Virginia, US. With a long string of award nominations (including a BAFTA, Golden Globe and an Oscar), this year has seen Negga in many stunning red carpet appearances. We chat with her about her personal style, inspirations and the role that has put her in the spotlight. Your role as Mildred Loving in Loving speaks to many modern women. It sends a message that love is colourless and borderless, and many argue that Mildred Loving was not afraid of fighting for what she believed in. How much do you personally identify with Mildred Loving? I think I identify most with Mildred's concrete belief that no one has the right to legislate on who you choose to love in such discriminatory ways. And that equal rights for all should be non-negotiable. Her tenacity, her refusal to be quieted, made her all the more radiant to me. As someone who has been on the covers of many magazines, you're clearly having an influence on fashion and with your work in film, are likely to become a role model. How do you feel about this responsibility? It's always special to collaborate with a magazine and their team of incredible artists, but what's been notable for me to be a part of is the shift of fashion publications to increasingly reflect who our wider society is. That people look at newsstands and see not a homogenised uniform look, but a varied and all-embracing array of people. I am glad to be part of that. You convey a confidence on screen and on the red carpet. Where does that come from and does that influence the clothing and jewellery? Thank you. I'm fortunate to be surrounded by a talented and artistic styling, hair and make-up team who are extremely collaborative. The most important thing is that you go out feeling confident about what you are wearing and how you look and feel.  That imports an inner confidence that I think really translates. How has your unique background and upbringing influenced your personal style? I grew up in a lot of different places so I feel that I've maybe absorbed those varied experiences and cultures. It's often been said that if one has had a peripatetic childhood that one develops a chameleon quality, and a nature that is often quite distinct. I think perhaps that's why I like to experiment with different styles and play with image. When it comes to the red carpet, it seems like you and your stylist are a match made in heaven as you've landed on numerous best-dressed lists. Tell us about your process of working together and how you come up with your looks. Luckily my excellent publicist Bryna Rifkin has an extraordinary ability to pair and match people's energies, spirit and tastes in a super complementary way. That's how I met Karla Welch. Karla possesses an intuitive talent for identifying someone's style and their likes and dislikes in a really organic way. It's about people reading. She has a unique, artistic eye and her bona fide love of fashion and style is infectious and exhilarating. We are also unafraid to be super honest with one another, so there is a mutual trust there that is key. Everyone loved the Fred Leighton cuff you wore to the Golden Globes—are you drawn to vintage-inspired jewellery? Yes, I feel I have a very old-fashioned “period” look… I often feel that vintage is what suits me best. I have always been fascinated by old Hollywood.... from Metropolis, silent era through to the vibrancy of Dorothy Dandridge in Carmen. The cuff featured an amazing 25.5 carat Gemfields ruby. What do rubies mean to you? Dorothy's ruby slippers [from the Wizard of Oz], always. The flashing beauty of those shoes is indelible in the memory. Tell us about your everyday style, in both fashion and jewellery. To be honest it varies so much.  I'm in sweats a lot right now as they are easiest to slip on for those early morning production pick-ups as I'm currently filming. But I would say to look at my wardrobe you see a lot of black and deep bottle greens and oxblood reds. I really love a classic French look with a Gothic twist. So my jewellery choices reflect that. My favourite piece at the moment is a pair of lion head clip-on earrings with dangly bits.   Fashion Culture & Living Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Fancy a handbag inspired by ‘Beauty and the Beast’?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Fairy tale vibes View Gallery 7 Photos Fancy a handbag inspired by ‘Beauty and the Beast’? Disney's Beauty and the Beast is decidedly one of the most anticipated releases this summer, especially with Emma Watson's feminist reinterpretation of Belle. If the fairy tale brings back memories of bedtime story sessions with your mom, or if you simply just love a happy ending, then you might want to extend this sprinkle of magic to your wardrobe as well with Disney India and Hidesign's collection of bags and wallets. Called ‘Enchanted', the idea for the collection stemmed from Disney India's wish to extend the storytelling experience they offer their patrons. Partnering with a hallowed local brand was the way to go, which is where Hidesign came in. Founded in 1978, the homegrown luxury leather brand is renowned for its focus on heritage, craftsmanship and ecological values. With Hidesign mirroring the classic and understated tone of the story, the match was perfect. It was the aesthetic fabulosity of the imagery and visuals of Beauty and the Beast that first struck Dilip Kapur when Disney India approached him with the idea for this collection. What followed is this collaboration (a first of its kind for Hidesign) that is classic yet contemporary, and trendy yet timeless. Fantasy, naturally, serves as the key theme for the line. “We did not really go into the psychology or emotions of the characters with the collection. The treatment was more visual—after all, it's the beauty that attracts us. The creative process began with us receiving imagery related to the story from Disney, and then merging that with quintessentially Hidesign shapes and colours. The idea was to take what's iconic about Beauty and the Beast and translate it into this collection, while also staying true to our brand values. The end result is classic, cool, and fashion-forward but at the same time, very sophisticated,” explains Kapur. The 30-piece collection, which was in the work for nine months, features a range of leather and canvas handbags and wallets, all crafted in the brand's Pondicherry factory. Versatile and age agnostic, you'll find a plethora of styles, such as totes, satchels, slings, backpacks and structured handbags in a colour palette of red, black, midnight blue, brown and white. The enduring rose motif from the story has been incorporated by way of leather appliqué, patchwork and etching, exuding an overall polished appeal. Though, the collection doesn't lack a dose of fun either—quirky patches such as Mrs Potts and her son Chip, and a broken heart to symbolise Beast, do the needful. “My two favourites from the collection include the red patchwork unlined leather tote and the black mini version of our signature ‘Virgin' bag with a red rose appliqué on it. These two bags would look great on Emma Watson too!” signs off Kapur. The Hidesign Beauty and the Beast collection in available in stores and on Hidesign.com Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #SuzyPFW: Christian Dior – Join The Feminist Navy!
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Maria Grazia Chiudi's second RTW collection With even Rihanna wearing a fetching beret and the celebrity front row bathed in a blue light, it seemed that everyone at the Christian Dior show should have been singing along to 'In the Navy.' Image: Indigital For navy blue was everywhere on the smart tailored clothes worn with that forceful feminist stride which reflects the spirit of the new female designer at the illustrious house founded by Monsieur Christian Dior. After sending out, in her first season, jousting models in fencing inspired clothes and T-shirts with a 'We Should All Be Feminists' message that has resonated around the world, Maria Grazia Chiuri took her feisty female attitude further. Rihanna: off to join the DIOR ARMY! A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 3, 2017 at 7:01am PST “I am generation black!" announced the designer. "And I decided that the only colour that could compete with black was blue." “I believe that colour is a sign of society and a very good reference and blue is also the colour of uniform," the designer continued. "If there is something that speaks about equality, it's uniform. You can propose different pieces that can be used as a private uniform. It is a strange word, because you can have military uniform, working uniform, even jeans - everybody builds up a personal uniform." Image: Indigital So out marched Dior's fashion army - first a feisty woman in soft, sash jacket and trousers, her bag, with its metallic strap, slung across her body. Next out on drill was a navy dress, the fabric light and crisp. Flat boots, or occasionally court shoes, accompanied this line-up of fashion uniforms that featured the slogan 'J'ADIOR', meaning 'I love Dior', on waistbands. It's a war for the navy (blue) at Dior A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 3, 2017 at 12:49pm PST The executives at LVMH, the luxury conglomerate behind Dior, must adore Maria Grazia. Because after all the dramas and complexities with previous male designers, Raf Simons and John Galliano, here is a creative who does what it says on the tin. She creates comprehensive, wearable and surely sellable clothes. Add to the parade of cashmere coats and silken pleated skirts, a line-up of blue jeans, and you had an entire wardrobe in one. The fact that it was also in one colour made the show a bit one note. But there will, of course, be other colours in store. Image: Indigital Maria Grazia explained the backstory, how she had searched the archives and found in 1947, just after the war, references to capes and even what now looks like the base of a jumpsuit. She then mixed all these elements together to make an acceptable wardrobe for Autumn/Winter 2017. The revival of women's marches stoked by the defeat of Hillary Clinton and the criticism of President Trump's attitude towards women, has played into the long held feelings of Maria Grazia. But when handling a couture house, where even ready-to-wear comes at a price, the designer cannot live only on a current enthusiasm for her personal attitude. The clothes themselves had to live up to a perceived value. If you removed the berets and the storyline, there were some fine pieces such as a skirt in semi-transparent tulle, worn with a hefty navy sweater, and the same material used for a long dress where a galaxy of star crystals covered the long skirt. Rihanna, the military coat and beret from Stephen Jones at Dior with design director Maria Grazia Chiuri A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 3, 2017 at 7:15am PST I would like to have heard more about Christian Dior's sister Catherine, who joined the French Resistance and was imprisoned by the Nazis in a German concentration camp. That story would have given the army angle more depth. That period of his sister's suffering was when Dior started playing with Tarot cards - a subject which Maria Grazia picked on for patterns on skirts. They look like becoming an icon of the brand. Image: Indigital At this point, I would give Maria Grazia seven out of 10 for her attractive but predictable clothes. But 10 out of 10 for her feminist attitude and the way she has perked up the maison, produced wearable work and taken on a powerful attitude regarding women's equality that will not leave any of her customers feeling the blues. column1: #SuzyPFW: Haider Ackermann – Draining Off The Colour
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer limited himself to just four colours. And however lovely, the show lacked a heartbeat 'Wild Is The Wind' by Nina Simone filled the space devoted to the Haider Ackermann show, where the designer's slow pace, in his past shows, had the effect of inducing a hypnotic trance in thrall to colour. Image: Indigital Out came a black coat, a black suit, a white top and furry white trousers – graceful bodies walking one at a time. Image: Indigital Then suddenly, a gilded line – like the one that was traced on the invitation – appeared crossing the black like a tiny, shining rivulet. As the pace quickened, the placement of golden rills became denser until they criss-crossed a jacket with sketchy regularity. Image: Indigital But even with insertions of white, as puffy sleeves and swaddled legs, to face off against all the darkness, there was still no soft or hard colour. Then finally – finally! – a bright sapphire shade of blue came out to break the absence of colour. Image: Indigital Image: Indigital Lovely as the show was in that way of Haider's – cutting trousers close to the body and jackets tight and tidy, I had to go backstage after the roar of applause and ask a simple question: when you are one of the finest colourists in fashion today – why reduce yourself to just four shades? Image: Indigital “I wanted to do something unexpected – to challenge myself,” said the designer. “Colour is always attractive, but I just wanted the show to be very sober, very calm. There's enough happening outside so I just wanted to have something very serene.” Wild is the Wind - Nina Simone as the opening of Haider Ackermann's black and white collection, crosses with gold thread and purple A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 4, 2017 at 11:12am PST So, Haider gave himself the chance – or indeed, the challenge – of making a statement restrained to black and white. He did it beautifully – but the heart of his show missed a beat. The power of black. The texture of white. column1: Rahul Mishra’s latest collection is an ode to pointillism
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s everything you need to know about it View Gallery 30 Photos Rahul Mishra Rahul Mishra's autumn/winter 2017-18 collection is proof that designers never really stop thinking. After his last season's showcase in Paris, the designer was on the lookout for a restaurant that might be serving late at night and stumbled up on the Centre Pompidou. “It happened to be White Night [an all-night art festival] and miraculously, the museum was open. I stayed back for six hours and looked at the paintings. After that I set out a really difficult task for my artisans to recreate pointillism on garments with thread and needle,” the designer explained the premise of the new collection. It is unlike Mishra to play with colour; not that he is averse to a few supportive additions of pastels in his Indian ethnic silhouettes, but stark primary hues alongside somber suiting fabrics was a first for him. Embracing a marriage of pointillism and impressionism, Mishra set out to perfect the raised thick layering of paint through embroidery. Mishra spoke highly of his craftsmen who work with the designer's reverse-migration model of ethical production, “To me it felt like working with 500 artists. I might be the brain working them, but they are my hands.” This season, the designer went with cool girl cold shoulders, ruffles, dresses worn over shirts and sweatshirts over skirts—all separates laboured over for more hours than your average ready to wear garment. The chase for perfection didn't stop at an aesthetic level; Mishra went beyond what meets the eye to get rid of the weight of such embroidery. True to his word, he crushes the embroidered surface of his jacket like it were made of jersey. “We worked on a technique and got rid of the entire fabric underneath. Clothes should feel like they can be worn and not just stared at,” he says. With every passing showcase at the French capital, Mishra seems to grow out of his comfort zone to evolve. It is not unlike a designer hailing from India to brag about the prolificacy of their atelier. But where most don't know to stop, Mishra uses a restraining hand, allowing fabric and cut to play their own part in the garment. “Another important aspect for me was to communicate emotion. I wanted to draw in the melancholia of Van Gogh's sunflowers,” he refers to a dress in the line-up. “When you look at his [Van Gogh's] work, despite the sunlight and the flowers, there is an undertone of sadness to it. I wanted to draw out the beauty of those contrasts in my work,” he says. Mishra may have lost his wallet in the frenzy of putting together a show, but he is deeply content as he calls back home to update his wife about the details. He waits with his small contingent of taskmasters from India including friend and designer Gaurav Jai Gupta, until every last bag is loaded, thanking the staff at the Palais de Tokyo after the guests have left. Ever humble, he says, “I am lucky to have a team that has confidence in my thought process and executes it. One might say, why the colour; but if I don't challenge myself, how will I grow?” Weddings What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: 5 successful women in fashion tell us how they made it to the top
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion #GirlBoss The female boss is often stereotyped in popular culture as the ice queen with unreasonable demands, one who has little regard for those who she rules over. Your experiences in real life may or may not relate to this skewed portrait of the strong working woman, but the truth of the matter is that women have historically had a tough draw, struggling to be seen in the same light as their male counterparts. We spoke to five women who have scaled the heights of the ecosystem, survived it all and lived to tell the tale. Signe Vilstrup, photographer “At 14 years, I started photographing my girlfriends with my dad's old SLR camera. At 18, I got my first job at a commercial photo studio. It really was a man's world, I was the only girl between 30 men, including my male boss... I struggled for three hard years to find my place in the hierarchy, not being a technique enthusiast like all the guys, and not as physically strong. I got bullied quite a bit. I thought this was not for me. “It was a big defeat, but I quit and replaced my dream for a job as a booking assistant at a model agency—photocopying and passing the phone on to more important bookers. In retrospect, that turned out to be a wise decision. I didn't know much about fashion or the industry, but I quickly got a great insight and I was so fortunate to have a female boss who gave me the big push. She encouraged me to do test shoots with new models. I was hesitant in the beginning—I didn't have a big camera or equipment. But my boss helped me overcome my inhibitions and just like that I started shooting again. “Soon I got my first professional assignment with the jewellery company Pandora, and from there it took off quickly. Today I work with magazines like Vogue and Vanity Fair and clients such as Giorgio Armani and Swarovski. In the early 2000s I was one of few female photographers and there was a demand for my feminine expression in photography. Being a woman in what was until then, a man's world, I guess I was in the right place at the right moment. “In the recent past, there has been an overwhelming change in the field of fashion photography, which now has a significant amount of influence on the worldwide fashion industry—it has evolved to be an admired art form and taken as a respectable career. Many women have entered the field and are respected artists with lucrative profits. With visual overload from social media every second, it is easy to become desensitised to the power of the still photograph. But for me, flipping through a magazine in its printed form, being overwhelmed and inspired by the visual impression, is still such a treat. Shooting for Vogue India especially, I really get to fulfil my need to create universes and dreams, with colour and storytelling." Priya Tanna, editor Vogue India “It happened organically, there was no real plan. As a kid who was drawn to anything that has an element of aesthetics to it, I found myself drawn to magazines at the age of 10. That was the time when international titles were not available here, so you relied on relatives visiting from abroad, or for a trip. I used to pore over American Vogue and was particularly in love with clothes by Oscar de la Renta and Bill Blass. One of my fondest memories was going to Italy on holiday with my parents at age 12. I was fascinated by the Versace store, and ended up taking pictures of the store—I was so drawn to the show windows. “My first job was reporting on fashion at the Afternoon Despatch & Courier, but as it is well known, a big part of my career was not dedicated to fashion. [After my first job] I went into a period when I had nothing to do with the industry, but the interest in fashion never left me. In my case, I can truly say that fashion found me, I didn't go looking for fashion. Eleven years back when I was headhunted for the job, my affair with this world became legit. “When I took on the position, I was the youngest editor of Vogue. I think good work speaks for itself, if it is impactful, then you are a person of value to your company. That is what I have built myself to be—a person of value, not as man or a woman. “It's never easy to balance motherhood with a career. It is difficult with the jobs that we do, to go home to be the parents we want to be. I wouldn't be in this room if I didn't have amazing caregivers who do my job when I am not around. It also takes mindfulness; you have to draw lines. The most incredible thing about being a woman is that we can multitask, which is what makes us heroes. There are people who like micro jobs, I get my adrenalin rush from doing many things at once, and that's what has kept me going." Anju Modi, designer “Whenever I look back on my journey, about how I started and how far I've come, there are many stories and memories that make me realise what passion and drive can make you achieve. My love for the craft often had me travelling to the farthest corners and remotest villages, untouched and disconnected with the main cities and towns. This was at a time when technology wasn't at my disposal, there was no Google Maps or navigation devices or even mobile phones for me to carry around, but the determined person that I am, I was not going to let logistics keep me from exploring these treasure troves of textile knowledge and craftsmanship. “One such instance was when I as traveling alone in a taxi to Hyderabad. We were some 450 kilometres away from the city and roads weren't as busy as they are today. The cab driver stopped the car in the middle of nowhere and said that there is some issue in the engine—in that moment it would've been very natural to feel panicked, but I found the bravado to tell the driver to stay outside, and that I would lock the car and sleep inside till we find help next morning. I cannot say whether there was any malicious intent or not, but the car started in 15 minutes and we were back on track with the journey. My biggest learning after that incident was that I would never succumb to weakness in a time when I am being tested—I would rather always find the strength in spirit and courage to face the situation head on. “I have always believed that smooth sails never made a skilled sailor—because it is our struggles, our hurdles and a sense of defiance to the norm, a passion to sail, to weather that storm instead of sitting it out, that shape us and make us who we are. It has most definitely made me who I am today, as a person and as a designer.” Marielou Phillips, head public relations and press - global, Chanel India Pvt Ltd “I started modelling in the early days of fashion in India, when designers like Tarun Tahiliani and James Ferreira were just shaping the scene. I was discovered by Yves Saint Laurent in 1993 and I went on to work in Paris after that. I ran into Karl Lagerfeld at the airport in Rome. During that time, I walked for all the luxury powerhouse labels—Givenchy, Armani, Chanel… I have some incredible memories from those years. Eventually, I quit modelling but I was offered work with Karl Lagerfeld at the Chanel design studio. My job was to liaise between Karl and the atelier, and I worked on footwear and swimsuit lines. When I heard that Chanel would be opening in India, I asked for the communications position. “If you would have asked me then about how I saw my career shaping up, I wouldn't have seen this. It wasn't easy moving to a new country so early—new language, new food; it was quite a challenge, but I have always embraced challenges. Without trusting myself, having faith in me, I wouldn't have had the experiences that I did. How many people can say they met Mr Givenchy himself?” Tina Tahiliani Parikh, executive director Ensemble “My first brush with fashion was when I attended the first Ensemble show at the Taj. I was still a student at Stanford and was leaving that night to do my thesis research, ironically which involve interviewing the weavers in Maheshwar. My hair still stands on end when I remember that Phillip Glass music starting and Shyamolie Verma walking out in an ankle length plait with a draped Tarun Tahiliani skirt on. I guess I should have known at that time that this would be what I would come to love. “I started my career as an investment banker in San Francisco, never dreaming that I had a single creative bone in my body. When I returned to India, I thought I was taking care of Ensemble for a year whilst Tarun completed his degree at FIT. During the course of that one year, I was exposed to Rohit Khosla's incredible styling, Rohit Bal's embroidered bolero jackets, Asha Sarabhai's bandhani abhas, Shahab Durazi's incredible tailoring and Tarun's textured Bhagalpurs. I visited the Calico museum of textiles and travelled in India and realised what my country was about with its art and craft. I was sold. When Tarun came back he told me he did not want to be in retail and I told him I never wanted to be a banker again.” What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #SuzyPFW: Manish Arora – A Decade Of Bringing India To Paris
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer reached for the stars as his intergalactic patterns took him from Aztec prints to outer space. Manish Arora was full of joy backstage after his show. In fact, you might say that he was flying high - but not just because his theme of the season was reaching up to the cosmos. He was celebrating 10 years showing his collections in Paris and also being presented last month to Queen Elizabeth II in London as part of an Anglo-Indian event. Image: Indigital So there were many reasons to celebrate with wavy lines and a galaxy of stars or moons. Try that same intergalactic print on a multi-coloured padded coat - and note that even the handbags were moon-shaped as they glistened with colour. Manish Arora - Cosmic Love for his TENTH anniversary A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 2, 2017 at 4:46am PST For the last few seasons, the designer had been camping it up in small shows in his Paris office with a dog dyed blue to match the clothing and other jokey larks. This was the right moment to come back to a full show at the Grand Palais where the Indian workmanship was given the space to shine. Image: Indigital That was a literal vision of a sporty India with a sweat tops made of silk patterned with stars and space stations. Add to that three dimensional decoration in fringes of vivid colours forming a feathery necklet. Manish Arora - off to the Cosmos A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 2, 2017 at 7:17am PST Manish had not lost his sense of fun. The crochet squares that have been in fashion at least since the folksy Seventies were shown here as digitalised patterns on a silken dress, while men's turbans were re-established in a whimsical way as scarfs morphing into hats. Image: Indigital There is an elegance to Indian clothes, and the designer caught that regal touch in a velvet dress with a Paisley curve illuminated with Swarovski crystal. And with so many designers today embracing pattern and print only via digital means, the authenticity of this designer's Aztec prints was impressive. Image: Indigital Manish called the visual journey from India to outer space “Cosmic Love". Write that in a rainbow of colours. column1: Here’s why this Manish Malhotra show is unlike any other
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Marking his sixth year with Mijwan For the last six years, Manish Malhotra has been working with the Mijwan Welfare Society NGO. Set up by the late Kaifi Azmi, the institution works towards the empowerment of women and female children through education and employment generation. About 300 craftswomen work at the embroidery centre to create the chikankari that is seen on Malhotra's garments. “Mijwan to me is a microcosm of what India has to offer the world. I see this not as an act of charity, but a win-win situation for both. The girls get a means of livelihood by which they can negotiate a better position for themselves in a patriarchal society,” says the designer. Throughout the year, Malhotra uses and modifies embroidery from the Mijwan Welfare Society in his work. “My father believed that India's remarkable economic progress can only be meaningful if it reaches rural India. After suffering from a paralytic stroke, he gave up the comforts of Mumbai and settled in Mijwan, a village frozen in time,” Shabana Azmi spoke of her father. “I once asked him, 'don't you get frustrated when change doesn't occur at the pace you want it to?' To which he replied, 'when you are working for change, you should build into that expectation the possibility that the change might not happen in your lifetime. But you must have the conviction that if you carry on working with dedication then the change is bound to occur–even if it happens after you,'” said Azmi. Kaifi Azmi's godchild, Namrata Goyal, who looks after the workings of the NGO spoke about the transformation in village of Mijwan due to the efforts taken. “Today, every girl child in Mijwan wants to either be an entrepreneur, computer engineer or supermodel.” The Mijwan summer 2017 show will take place on March 5. column1: #SuzyPFW: Saint Laurent’s Sexual Charge
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Anthony Vaccarello picks YSL influence from the brash 1980s Leather moulded into a shoulder piece set at an angle or another draped leather dress with one shoulder opening to reveal the inside of a shearling sleeve – everything screamed about the 1980s at the Saint Laurent show. Image: Indigital The only small change over 30 years seemed to be the boots in squishy leather that sent them in rivulets from knee to sole. Image: Indigital This Amazonian sexiness from designer Anthony Vaccarello, in his second round at the house, did not include a stand off with soft dresses and droopy cardigans, as seen in Hedi Slimane's tenure, that ended in 2016. Although there was slushy velvet and malleable leather as a contrast to the aggressive sculpturing that fitted with Slimane's final angry show in 2016. Image: Indigital We were sitting (although I was actually sheltering under an umbrella in the rain) in the bones of a triumphant new building for the brand. Its steel bones were the background to a show where the spirit could not get much harder. If anything, the men's collection, shown as a centre piece, was slightly more gentle. Image: Indigital A final orgy of Swarovski crystals added royal blue to the black, white and silver round up. Saint Laurent: silver moment A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 28, 2017 at 1:55pm PST As an ode to the 1980s and to a narrow slither of the broad YSL legacy, it was not a bad show. In terms of keeping on side the edgy rock ‘n' roll generation who don't know the history of Monsieur Saint Laurent, Vacarello followed smartly in the stomping footsteps of Hedi's angry kids brigade, but now tramping in high heels. Saint Laurent: stomping out A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 28, 2017 at 2:10pm PST But where was the French connection? Yves Saint Laurent was the essence of francophilia. Although himself an outsider from the Maghreb region, he embraced – and reformed – French elegance in a youthful way. Vacarello, born in Belgium to Italian parents, is having none of that bourgeois perfection. He is part of a current quasi-feminist push for deliberate vulgarity. In fact, the line up of models, dressed in their ultra-sexy clothes as if parading to the I'm Too Sexy chant from Right Said Fred in 1991, was a reminder of Christophe Decarnin at Balmain in 2005. That was the beginning of this in-your-face sexiness for the new millennium. Image: Indigital But vulgarity is surely not the perfect fit for Saint Laurent. Time for Vacarello to move his considerable cutting and draping talent out of the dark and into the daylight hours. Saint Laurent. column1: #SuzyPFW: Maison Margiela – From Runway To Reality
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion John Galliano creates a wearable collection with imaginative flourishes and intriguing rear views. It takes time!” exclaimed Renzo Rosso. “This is the first time in three years that it has come together.” Maison Margiela. Intriguing rear view from John Galliano A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 1, 2017 at 4:18am PST The executive and brand owner was referring to the fact that Maison Margiela had finally found in the work of John Galliano, its creative director, a collection that could move from powering the runway to sales reality. Image: Indigital The audience applauded this collection that flagged up all the Galliano ideas such as windows – small, neat ones – on the body and threads wafting from a tailored blazer. That concept not only offered a sophisticated version of the undone – a familiar story from the designer; but also introduced colour in the most subtle way. Image: Indigital More importantly, the idea of the unfinished or the partly destroyed was controlled in a masterful way with a small, neat square of cloth scissored out at the front; while at the back the open spaces were rampant: a grid that alternately revealed and concealed flesh; sometimes an open window on the body with a single strip of cloth down the spine; and finally, the fabric reduced to strings from knees to hem. Image: Indigital Galliano talked in his show notes about breaking wardrobe classics down to their core as he had done in his previous ‘Artisanal' collection. But this time, he had put the pieces back together again. Image: Indigital It is frustrating not to be able to talk face-to-face with the designer, when he sends out such an excellent show, for the notes sounded like some corporate statement about an art installation. They read: “Iconography is founded in collective emotions created by the memories which unite us and give us hope.” Image: Indigital Of course, the real ‘collective memory' here is the exceptional work Galliano has produced over the years for his own line and for Christian Dior. And in this show, when the designer spoke through the clothes, rather than in stilted words, the effect was powerful. Image: Indigital Galliano cited the varsity jacket and the trench coat among many other key starting points. But after the opening note of a classic beige coat, other tailored clothes came out in diverse fabrics from wool to denim. Add an image of Marilyn Monroe making a ghostly appearance among other blown-up prints; plus some checks and dots; and a little nudity under a cover-up of fleshy stretch fabric. In resume, it was everything that Galliano loves – in moderation. Maison Margiela powered by John Galliano A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Mar 1, 2017 at 4:16am PST This was a fine moment for the designer, rehabilitated from his past; but also a great step forward for Margiela. With the original Martin Margiela putting his seminal work on display at the MoMu museum in Antwerp at the end of March, Galliano has given the founding designer the pleasure of seeing his spirit living on in a pure and passionate way. column1: The new heel is one you can actually dance in
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Happy feet, indeed View Gallery 9 Photos Are chunky heels the new stilettoes? Remember the cringe-worthy moment when you had to muster all your inner grace while entering a bar to maintain your balance (and dignity) in those too-high pencil heels? The ones that your mom warned you against buying in the first place. We've all been there. Despite the glamour they promise, maintaining poise when strutting in stilettos is a not a walk in the park for everyone. Cue, the rise of ‘sensible heels', with the chunky version racing ahead as a clear winner. If you're one who prefers a strong #ShoeGame but without compromising on practicality, this sturdy block heel trend is for you. In fact, the chunkier, the better. A constant on spring/summer '17 runways, it made many an aching soles heave a sigh of relief. Turns out, there are multiple shoe styles that this heel is compatible with. They were spotted on booties at Hermès and Alexander McQueen while Vivienne Westwood added them to platform Mary Janes (worn with socks). The trend made its way to Carven's snakeskin mules and strappy heels, while Mugler was all about the low chunky shoe and Missoni favoured low crossover sandals. If you're looking for the ideal dancing partners, then Dolce & Gabbana's take on the style has your name all over it—think blocky heels with carved rosettes, slogans, and fringes. And if you, like most of the fashion world, is swooning over all things Gucci, then their loafers with pearl and crystal embellishments won't disappoint. Suede, satin, and velvet renditions are have a definite moment as well. If one is to believe that giving a girl the right shoes can let her conquer the world, then turns out, we are in luck. With this on-trend style firmly secured on our feet, we can (phew!) do so with utmost comfort too. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Natalie Massenet Joins Farfetch
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From founding Net-a-porter to her new role Natalie Massenet has announced that she is joining Farfetch as non-executive co-chairman. The fashion industry has been speculating about Massenet's next move for some time in the wake of her exit from Net-a-Porter, which she founded in 2000, following its merger with Yoox. Ever the digital pioneer, she made the announcement today via her Instagram account. "Over the past 18 months my entrepreneurial drive, and passion for how innovation in technology can transform the future of luxury remains undiminished," she wrote. "In 1999 when I first thought about selling fashion online, the world was just waking up to the possibility. Today we expect access to everything, anytime, anywhere. The tech and logistics platforms that power the best ecommerce today have new decentralised business models. If I were starting an ecommerce company today, I would do it very differently." Her role at Farfetch will see her work alongside executive co-chairman, founder and CEO José Neves, who she called "the best of our entrepreneurs; a brilliant mind, a visionary leader and a gentleman". The pair have experience of working alongside each other at the British Fashion Council, of which Massenet is chairman and Neves an executive. "I have been a fan since he founded Farfetch in 2008, admiring how José and his team have forged their own path in luxury e-commerce. Farfetch aggregates the most beautiful fashion curated by the world's best boutiques and designer stores with the widest selection of styles into one easy-to-shop and brilliantly conceived API-enabled platform. A simple idea that is staggeringly difficult to execute that Farfetch has cracked!!" "I have, since Net-A-Porter launched, been a huge admirer of Natalie, she really is the undisputed pioneer, paving the way for the rest of us by demonstrating that not only could luxury be sold online but also that the internet would eventually become the primary way consumers engage with brands, globally," said Neves today. Massenet's new position will also see her reunited with her former long-term Net-a-Porter colleague Holli Rogers, who is CEO of Browns Fashion, which Farfetch bought last year. "It's no coincidence that all the most successful companies - Facebook, Amazon and Apple - are also API-enabled platforms," continued Massenet. "Farfetch is an example of the 'collaborative economy' when businesses historically seen as competitors work together to offer the best possible customer experience and support the world's luxury fashion brands. It is a truly global business (over 750 designers and boutiques partners delivering to 190 countries, same day delivery in nine cities, translated into nine languages) and growing fast. Over the last year trading has grown by 70 per cent, with the most recent investment valuing the company at over $1 billion. In my new non-exec role, I look forward to further realising Farfetch's potential, developing its global brand and strengthening its fashion industry partnerships." column1: Tarun Tahiliani and Amit Aggarwal come together yet again
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Collaborating at Amazon India Fashion Week autumn/winter 2017 Following their mentor-protégé act for the finale show last season, Amazon India Fashion Week has called upon designers Tarun Tahiliani and Amit Aggarwal to close the autumn/winter 2017 showcase. The theme for the collection will centre on the ‘Fresh New Look' campaign by Amazon. As for what to expect from the coming together of the unparalleled design aesthetic of the designers, here's an interview from our archives that best describes the dynamics between the two. In almost a quarter of a century, master innovator Tarun Tahiliani has revolutionised the way Indian women approach clothes. It's hard to imagine now, when Indian fashion is so acceptable and designers so celebrated, that there was a time when fancy aunties wouldn't even dream of plonking down vast sums of money on traditional attire. He forced the swish set to migrate from the corner darzi and adopt an evolved approach to dressing. And those who recall the late '80s, when Tahiliani and his sister Tina started India's first fashion boutique, Ensemble, will also remember the excitement it generated. Two decades later, Ensemble is still a must-shop destination. For years, Tahiliani's studio has been a haven for young, upcoming designers, who have the privilege of working under him before subsequently embarking on their own lines. Raakesh Agarvwal, Rakha & Rabani, Narendra Kumar and Vineet Bahl are just a few of the talents who've had the benefit of Tahiliani's tutelage. When Vogue asked the master to pick a designer he thought could fashion a brand and sustain a legacy, someone who had the potential to fill Tahiliani's size-10 shoes, he thought long and hard before coming up with a choice few would fault: Amit Aggarwal. “I made an effort to go to his shows and I saw beautiful clothes. He is someone I would anoint based on many dimensions,” says Tahiliani. “How someone designs is one thing, but how do you treat your workers? How do you treat people around you? I've always liked and respected his work. He always has a twist which is original. His clothes are really well crafted and thought out. And importantly, there is great integrity to his work, which is important. Amit has taken the techniques he's learned and made them fresh and new.” Aggarwal says he was “shocked” when Tahiliani picked him. “I got this call in the morning, and I heard that deep voice on the other end of the phone, and I thought, ‘Oh god, what have I done wrong?' When Tahiliani told me about this Vogue piece, I almost choked on my cornflakes!” says the designer. Aggarwal's label, Morphe, was launched in 2007 [he has since left Morphe and launched his eponymous label and AM.IT], and is much loved by magazine editors and fashion insiders across the country. A low-key but much sought-after brand, Aggarwal's spring/summer 2009 show was considered one of the ten best debut shows of the year by Vogue. Initially inspired by the San Francisco Bay Area's collection of jellyfish, Aggarwal says that he found the amorphous creatures beautiful. “They transcend all forms. The woman I want to dress should similarly not be stereotypical. She shouldn't take herself so seriously. She should morph. I am always changing my look, and I work with what inspires me.” Speaking of his fashion philosophy, Aggarwal says, “As a creative person, I have a responsibility not only to the field I work in but also to myself. Unless I create something that challenges me, I don't enjoy it. I get easily bored. I am inspired by the mechanics of nature, of its architectural forms. I love to create structure out of drapes. If it's a moving drape and you can freeze that, it's what my work signifies.” Tahiliani and his nominee share a healthy camaraderie, although it was apparent from their interaction at the photo shoot that Aggarwal looks upon the legendary designer as a guru. Aggarwal is shy, quiet, restrained, clearly less at ease at a photo shoot than his ex-boss. Yet it's apparent that the two have a good rapport, and are very fond of each other, in the way, say, a master and his pupil could be. It's a relationship that's been built over more than a decade. In 1998, Tahiliani was a judge at the National Institute of Fashion Technology's graduate show, which included Aggarwal's works. Needless to say, the young designer swept the show, winning four awards. A year later, Aggarwal began working with Tahiliani. “One of the big advantages of working with Tarun was learning what fashion is really all about. Tarun's clothes are approachable and beautiful and that's an aesthetic I got from him,” says Aggarwal, who spent three years working with the icon. Aggarwal, who was selected but passed up the opportunity for graduate study at London's prestigious Central Saint Martins, recalls the intensity of working under Tahiliani: “I came from an alien world. Tarun was extremely patient. We were poles apart. It's like Viktor & Rolf compared to Armani! That whole lifestyle, the whole essence of luxury is what I derived from him. No school or college could have given me that. After working with him, I'm a combination of my old self and an upgraded one.” This interview is excerpted from Vogue India's October 2010 issue. column1: What is Shrobing? And how do you do it?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here is everything you need to know about the shrobing, the Frow's favourite street style trend this season View Gallery 11 Photos What Is Shrobing? And How Do You Do it? We can thank Demna Gvasalia for our obsession with artful, off-shoulder styling. His debut autumn/winter 2016 show for Balenciaga showcased an upscale anorak (look 8 to be precise), which was cut and styled to be worn peeled-down off the shoulders. The contrast of wearing ordinary outerwear as though it was an exotic opera coat was startlingly modern, and the trend for 'shrobing' (i.e. shoulder-robing) was born. "I think there's always appeal in a look that appears nonchalant and ‘thrown on' which is what this is (similar thing with the shirt half tucked in, half tucked out) although, of course, it takes a lot more prepping than if you just put your coat on properly," says Vogue's fashion features director, Sarah Harris. "I also like that it has a sort of Fifties couture element to it – if you're applying it to something like a trench coat – the way those necklines were pushed back which in turn made the neck look longer." Fast forward to 2017's February fashion month, and it seems the only way to wear that new-season pinstriped shirt, puffer, or track top, is yanked downwards - the neckline skimming the décolletage, and revealing the back of the neck. There are a few rules to note in order to pull off a successful shrobe. "It doesn't work with every coat, the fabric has to be fairly fluid, you can't take a tailored wool coat and shrobe it, it just looks wrong," advises Harris. Be prepared to go hands-free: There's no shoulder left to hang a handbag on, so it's about going it alone with an iPhone and credit card and making the most of utility pockets. Shrobing also demands an assortment of plush polo necks to drive away the cold - the tighter the better to keep the neck looking elongated rather than swaddled. Our advice? Move quickly. There's the danger of the shrobing trend reaching saturation point - "in the same way that propping coats over shoulders became so ubiquitous a few seasons ago," warns Harris. "We might all have to actually start wearing a coat properly, with arms fed through sleeves and fitted on the shoulders. Actually, in NY I saw someone tie a coat around her neck using the sleeves, like a scarf. A scarf coat. A scoat. Maybe that will catch on." column1: Remembering Franca Sozzani
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The moving celebration of her life and work View Gallery 9 Photos Remembering Franca Sozzani As Milan Fashion Week closed, the final event was a spectacular farewell to the much-admired and adored Franca Sozzani, editorial director of Vogue Italia, who died in December. Franca was, in several ways, the human embodiment of Milan fashion and the memorial organised by Jonathan Newhouse, Carlo Capasa of the Camera Nazionale della Moda and the city's mayor Giuseppe Sala which took place in the prestigious Duomo was a fittingly momentous tribute. After a lunch hosted by her son Francesco Carrozzini, niece Sara Maino and sister Carla Sozzani, the restaurant guests walked together in a large group across the Piazza del Duomo, crowded with sightseers, pigeons and lines of security to the side door of the cathedral, where they were joined by hundreds of stylists, designers, models and friends. Rarely has there been such a gathering of the leading players in the fashion world of the past 30 years. Franca was an editor whose Vogue was known for its adventurous fashion photography and many of those who had grown their careers in its pages joined the enormous crowd filing into the great cathedral – Mario Sorrenti, Peter Lindbergh, Tim Walker, Paolo Roversi, Mario Testino to name a few. They were joined by a roll-call of the most famous designers in the fashion universe. Stella McCartney arrived with Kate Moss, both beautifully veiled, Phoebe Philo, Victoria Beckham, Burberry's Christopher Bailey and Alexander McQueen's Sarah Burton flew the British flag. A navy pea-coated Giorgio Armani and a tiny Donatella Versace led the many Italians who included Maria Grazia Chiuri, now at Dior, and Valentino Garavani with his partner Giancarlo Giammetti. Despite the fame of the crowd and the grandeur of the surroundings this was first and foremost a tribute to Francesco's mother. During his moving speech at lunch he made it clear how very close they were and what a good job she had done at providing him support while encouraging his independence, he also announced that the documentary he had made about her, Chaos and Creation, had just been nominated for a major Italian film award. Then he, along with his cousin Sara, both did readings at the service, which was a Catholic mass of an intensity and purpose that well suited the woman it commemorated. As the voices of the Duomo's choir soared high into the buttressed ceilings you could only think that the ceremony would have met even Franca's very high standards. column1: #SuzyMFW: Dolce & Gabbana – Fashion For All
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Stefano and Domenico celebrated diversity as young and old walked in a joyful family-centred show Striding boldly, stepping shyly, toddling or folded in parents' arms - everyone - mothers, daughters, sons and fathers - was a part of the Dolce & Gabbana show. [#image: /photos/5ce44fa33bf9b4c2b7b1f47b]||| ||| Image: Indigital As Pamela Anderson and Christie Brinkley applauded their kids on the runway and heartthrob Austin Mahone crooned, the event took on a folksy fashion feeling. It was as though Domenico Dolce and Stefano Gabbana - who by the end of the show joined their models drinking Champagne on the catwalk - were celebrating dressing "real" women (admittedly, these included a British royal and children of rock stars). All stars st the Dolce&Gabbana show A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 26, 2017 at 6:50am PST The design duo also handed out a gift to Instagrammers with a projection of each person taking part, famous or unknown, posted above the catwalk. What Dolce & Gabbana pulled off was no great shakes for fashion. Most of the clothes were reruns on familiar territory. That meant curvaceous dresses in black lace (for her) and silvered dressing robes (for him). As well as all kinds of animal embellishments from big cats (leopard prints or the animal as embroidery) to cute cats, Stefano's passion. [#image: /photos/5ce44fa3cc50be8a38142249]||| ||| Image: Indigital Although the invitation had suggested a space age theme, that idea was buried in the overall melee of the company's classics. But there was a red plastic coat worn over a scarlet patterned dress and with a space warrior's helmet. And a long-sleeved dress printed with an astronaut space-walking in a flower-strewn galaxy. [#image: /photos/5ce44fa3ba773d8a000b6520]||| ||| Image: Indigital But forget the clothes as a design statement. The designers, with their lighthearted fun and games, pulled off something exceptional: making diversity - of body shape, skin colour and ethnicity - seem natural and desirable. Dolce & Gabbana's line up of 'real' ( and really famous) people A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 26, 2017 at 6:25am PST Surrounded by their "family", as if in a hammy version of a fashion wedding, it was impossible to get a clear answer from the boys as to how they had pulled this show off. Had the Dellal family - former model Andrea Dellal and her daughters, shoe designer Charlotte Olympia and face of Chanel Alice, been individually fitted with their outfits? [#image: /photos/5ce44fa34a30b376b213010d]||| ||| Image: Indigital Had Rafferty Law (son of Jude) been hopping over to the Milan studio to be measured for his suit with unicorns embroidered onto the pockets? When had vlogger Marcus Butler been fitted for his white suit in-between postings to his 3.7 million Instagram fans? [#image: /photos/5ce44fa3b40d2605fed6f81b]||| ||| Image: Indigital This embrace of those who wear their clothes comes from deep roots. Since the D&G range of lower priced clothes was closed and Alta Moda - or high fashion - put in its place, Dolce & Gabbana has become touchy feely with their clients. [#image: /photos/5ce44fa41dc267a32fc7b7b5]||| ||| Image: Indigital This new foray into private lives seemed like an extension of the client events. Stefano's enthusiasm for posting on Instagram to reach his 901,000 followers (and counting), combined with Domenico's ability to play personal tailor to their clients, has placed them in a unique position in the fashion world. And for once, after years of putting a token dark skinned model on the runway and, more recently, a single plus-sized silhouette, Dolce & Gabbana brought the reality of diversity to the catwalk. And made it Fun! Fun! FUN! This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Culture & Living Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Séverine Merle joins Céline as the new CEO
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion She's the third female CEO at LVMH Céline has confirmed the appointment of Séverine Merle as its new CEO, making her the third female CEO in the LVMH stable of brands. She replaces Marco Gobbetti, who left the house last year to take up the same position at Burberry. Merle joins the house from another of LVMH's labels, menswear brand Berluti, where she is currently executive vice president, reports WWD. When she takes up her new position on April 1, she will report to Pierre-Yves Roussel, chairman and CEO of LVMH Fashion Group, who has been filling the breach at Céline since Gobbetti's departure. Merle has plenty of experience with the inner workings of LVMH brands, having previously worked at Kenzo and Louis Vuitton. “We see this as a smooth transition building on the project and continuing the momentum of the brand,” Roussel said of Merle's appointment. “Séverine represents a good fit with the culture of the brand.” Also new for the brand is its decision to launch e-commerce under Merle's watchful eye. Having held out until now, the brand is said to be introducing the retail platform later this year. “We believe it's important that we show the breadth and depth of the collection,” Roussel continued. “We want to be very product focused. It's always been the motto of creative director Phoebe Philo since the very beginning.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #SuzyMFW: Giorgio Armani and Emporio Armani – From Darkness To Light
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Giorgio Armani closed Milan Fashion Week with a playfully graceful show and plaudits for dressing male and female stars for the Oscars Armani: Lightness and sophistication Giorgio Armani was standing in a crowd of models at the end of his show explaining why he thought his outfits had such a success at the Oscars - not just his long term male fans like Leonardo DiCaprio and Denzel Washington, but also the female surprises. Nicole Kidman and French actress Isabelle Huppert both appeared in pale, shimmery, slender dresses while Viola Davis accepted her Oscar for Best Supporting Actress in a red Armani Privé gown. They all got the red carpet thumbs up. [#image: /photos/5ce4506fb40d2681a2d6f954]||| ||| Image: Indigital "Lightness and sophistication," said Armani - and that was pretty much the essence of this Autumn/Winter 2017 collection that closed the Milan season. Giorgio Armani talked about the lightness and sophisticated of his collection - and winning dresses for Nicole Kidman and Isabelle Hupert at the controversial Oscars. Armani appears st the far end of this video. A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 27, 2017 at 2:34am PST There was a sporty feel about the daytime clothes, which included, among the tailoring, jackets that had a fleeting look of a fleece because of the velvet surface. But the real surprise were what appeared to be long skirts that morphed into trousers at the back. They went with the flow of a softer, gentler Armani collection. [#image: /photos/5ce4506eba773d5c980b6637]||| ||| Image: Indigital The designer was in a playful mood with small trilby hats perched on each head, patterns of little dogs and vivid colour on velour. The clothes popped in scarlet and royal blue or grass green. [#image: /photos/5ce4506f9cc0c066c7fa046b]||| ||| Image: Indigital This sweet gentility merged into evening dresses, rather few by Armani standards - but with convincing combinations of abstract patterns in beading teamed with more of the velvet trousers. [#image: /photos/5ce4506fba773d20eb0b663b]||| ||| Image: Indigital Slender dresses, worked with the elegance of Armani Privé couture outfits, were all striking in a good way. They seemed to enhance the wearer, rather than shouting for attention. No wonder that the designer has become known at the Academy Awards for grace. Emporio Armani's wide range While the Giorgio Armani show was clear and well lit, what does it say about the Armani empire that social media seems to have drawn a blank when it came to over 100 outfits in the Emporio Armani collection? There were visual treasures, from checked black and white coats with a trickle of scarlet ribbon to sporty wide-legged trousers printed like a chessboard. So why was there a universal laying down of smartphones in this graphic show? [#image: /photos/5ce4506fb40d26aa6cd6f94e]||| ||| Image: Indigital Whether through fear of copyists or from the vagaries of fashion show lighting, the entire show – with its sporty energy and textures that saw plastic and fluffy jackets facing off against each other – was digitally unfriendly. Seen from the audience through a smartphone screen, the image was a ghostly white. [#image: /photos/5ce4506f9cc0c08b2dfa046f]||| ||| Image: Indigital Many designers today are frustrated that their front rows are filled with editors lifting up their phones when they are the privileged few who see the clothes with their own eyes. [#image: /photos/5ce4506fb40d263d90d6f951]||| ||| Image: Indigital As one of the guilty snappers, I would agree that there should be a balance between editors absorbing the textures, detail and mood of the live spectacles to which they've been invited and recording it as an aide-mémoire – just like we used to sketch and take notes back in the old days – as well as to share with the wider public. [#image: /photos/5ce4506fb40d2645cdd6f94f]||| ||| Image: Indigital Our Instagram age may have turned fashion into a sport of celebrity posturing at times, but digital access has also unpeeled the exclusivity of fashion - which can only be a good thing. column1: #SuzyMFW: Versace – Glamorous Power Dressing
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Donatella Versace wore her heart on her sleeve for another Milan fashion show with strong women at its core Donatella Versace can claim to be in the forefront of the second - or is it third? - round of fashion addressing the subject of strong women. And, indeed, dressing those who support the cause. The process has taken a long time since the Seventies, when women supposedly burned their bras to protest against sexual stereotypes (although there is no evidence that this ever actually happened). Messages from Donatella A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 24, 2017 at 10:32am PST The Eighties, when ultra-broad shoulders and trouser suits for work announced the shattering of the glass ceiling and women breaking into the boardroom, was more obviously a fashion era when evolving wardrobes announced societal change. It could be said broadly that Angela Merkel and Hillary Clinton were destined to underscore their political positions by wearing masculine clothes. All those fashion statements had faded by the new millennium. But another round had already appeared before the current political situation, when President Trump's attitudes towards women have caused concern on various levels and has brought many thoughtful women back into an arena of protest. On Friday, Miuccia Prada made a deliberate, and even dramatic, statement about female sexuality and women's position in what is still a masculine dominated world. She talked a good deal after the show about how she saw the situation. I sat down with Donatella before the Versace show, wondering whether this forceful designer - who already has three seasons of strong women looks behind her - would expand on Miuccia's questioning about role models. Best friends: Naomi and Donatella A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 24, 2017 at 10:14am PST Donatella tore herself away from a conversation with her good friend, the model Naomi Campbell and announced: "I changed and the collection is for a different type of woman." The designer wore her heart on her sleeve with the word "equality" in bold white letters on black. These were subsequently followed in the show with the words "courage", "loyalty", "love", "unity" and "strength" printed in various places, including headbands, dresses, scarves and a top. "It's not the same collection - it's for a different kind of woman," Donatella said. "I try to think as a woman with strength, coming together like in a time of war, every side. We are living in a very difficult time right now. Scary. I don't know what the future is going to be." But for her collection, Donatella knew what she wanted: "Normal looking clothes, but with more fluidity for the body to move. She plays with proportion, but she's strong." "Empowering women – everyone says the same thing now - but this has been a few years in my mind," she continued. "I've been talking to very intelligent women. In America and the rest of the world. We are strong and if we get together, we can do something." As the show started with dark tailoring, perhaps with a white shirt crossed with the word "love" at the hem, I could see the Versace thought process. This sexually confident woman was happy to show flesh in a split skirt dress or a waistcoat cropped at the midriff. And she walked out boldly in a dress where "loyalty" - the words swivelled round - appeared from neck to mid-calf hem. It was a bold statement, spelled out almost entirely in black and white, with yellow and orange joining the parade. A couple of puffer jackets reached a new level of casual and ergonomic dressing for Versace. But a revolution of women's attitudes? I don't think so. The ending showed evening clothes with leg splits for marching out in high heeled shoes. The slender golden dress seemed just the thing for the red carpet. But not, perhaps, for Red Square. column1: Sabyasachi just dropped his spring 2017 couture collection on Instagram
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And it is everything you expect it to be Sabyasachi Mukherjee, with his curated old-world aesthetic that we have all come to find endearingly charming, somehow manages to pack a punch every season. There are never-before seen versions of florals, the intricate embroidery is more interesting than when you last saw it and brides simply can't get enough of the design label. Just as we were settling into the long weekend, Sabyasachi Mukherjee dropped his entire spring couture 2017 collection through an Instagram show. ‘The Udaipur Collection' is, as the name suggests, inspired by Rajasthani royalty. There are references to maharanis, palaces, stately luncheons, rose gardens, gulaal, The Sheesh Mahal and more. But what moves an ingenious designer like Mukherjee look at such a derivative inspiration? “Whether the maharanis in their French chiffon with European flora and fauna print, the maharajas in their quiet arrogance, the exuberant interiors of their majestic palaces, their culture, traditions of clothing, their often eclectic tastes in luxury, all of those notions and insinuations come to life with my creative liberty in the Udaipur collection, says the designer. "While there is global exposure to these iconic people, they are also extremely insular and proud of who they are and where they come from. And the existence of that feral dichotomy to me is the essence of empowered luxury." column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Following the obsession Emojis are an essential part of every millennial's life. Let's face it—throwing in a couple of hearts and flowers, or flying money and pizza slices is crucial to conversations in the virtual realm. Scribes amongst us would've been surprised, shocked even, when Oxford Dictionaries chose the ‘Face With Tears of Joy' emoji as its word of the year for 2015. The whiz-kid behind the phenomenon, Shigetaka Kurita, designed them for Japanese mobile communication company NTT Docomo in 1999. And recently, Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), New York acquired the original 176 characters for an exhibition, establishing Kurita's emojis in the hall of modern-art fame. It's no wonder then, fashion brands and designers have taken to the trend—brands sure do know how to win themselves a million likes.
