column1: #SuzyLFW: The explosion of London’s fashion millennials
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion How young designers, hovering around 30, are building a new tier of British creativity THE FASHION EAST COLLECTIVE Mimi Wade: Old Hollywood Meets Young London Mimi Wade, 25, a Central Saint Martins graduate in her third season with Fashion East, played with an undone version of Hollywood glamour, where Dial 'M' For Murder Mimi is embroidered on a skirt, alongside a stitched-on dragon and a lace-trimmed hem. Appliquéd hearts, pie-crust necklines and visible frilly underthings did not look girly – more a statement from a strong and sexually aware woman who can make a feather boa look hardcore.   Asai Ta: A Couture-esque Mash-Up Asai Ta, 29, a British designer of Asian origin, has already won an award for his modern embroidery techniques and is another Central Saint Martins graduate. He made the most of the runway space at London's Tate Modern museum. Like his fellow designers, he focuses on ‘anti-perfectionism'. The result is a sense that young designers – almost all trained at Central Saint Martins – are creating a new and, of course different, version of John Galliano's make-do madness.   Matty Bovan: Back To The Future Matty Bovan, 26, was inspired by pagan folklore – hence perhaps the miniature papier-mâché matchstick huts of a small village were created as a backdrop. As with all the Fashion East performers, diversity in models, ethnicity and natural shape was paramount. The designer also played with strong colour and a tribal vibe. His choice of bold colours, like mixes of pink and orange, gave a suggestion of far-flung places as seen in a sci-fi movie. And the patterns were created with such energy and verve that the mini show might have been a distant mediaeval parade – but transferred to London's melting pot of cultures.   Huishan Zhang: A New Sophistication An historic British building and a sophisticated collection of decorative designs from lace to pearls: Huishan Zhang, 34, has come a long way since the Chinese national started showing his clothes in London. For his first runway collection, he focused on the intricate embellishments done in China, but also included diagonal patterns, tunic dresses and full midi skirts – all expanding the designer's range from evening wear. That category had also moved fast forward from lacy dresses to more casual designs like a pleated tunic and trousers. There was nothing to suggest that Huishan Zhang is changing the face of fashion, but to create appealing modern clothes with intricate detail is already an achievement.   Alice Archer: Flower Power Embroidery, bold but decorative, is the calling card of Alice Archer, 30, who gives craft work a sophisticated edge. The conventional big, flat roses that were stitched into the skirt of her own dress competed with a tailored coat, where hollyhocks climbed up the front panels or bright blooms decorated a satin robe. New this season was a special technique of using the embroidery so it appeared to be washed out – a smart idea at a time when the concept of fading beauty has a poignancy and grace.   Michael Halpern: Disco Couture Quick! Reach for the sunglasses! Michael Halpern, 29, is bringing on the bling. With the showmanship of a player in Tinsel Town, a background in his native New York and a training at Central Saint Martins, the designer sent out a glitter gulch of made-in-England sparkle. The vivid colours and the slightly undone or unfinished feel suggested party clothes with an edge. And a 1970s vibe added a touch of perversity to what otherwise might have been seen as just another party parade. column1: Warp ’n Weft hits a milestone, celebrates with images of strong, influential women
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The iconic institution turns 20 View Gallery 8 Photos Warp ’n Weft hits a milestone, celebrates with seminal women Warp 'n Weft is one of the country's oldest labels that takes pride in celebrating Benarasi craftsmanship; and has held fort at Marine Lines for the last two decades. As the store and brand turn 20, founder Sagrika Rai plans to expand the store by taking up a larger space in the same location. Rai's plans of furthering the brand still has very much to do with what she loves and knows best. The new space will serve as a place to exhibit the weaves. “I wanted to start this space exactly the way I started my life in this city—soaking up everything I saw, touched and felt,” she says. “I wanted an interior that would lend an emotional and sensory appeal to the visitor and would not overpower the weaves.” She works on nostalgia to create a unique experience for her consumers, bringing in antiques from her grandfather's collection to give an authentic feel of Benares with chandeliers, buggy lamps and a metallic shiva linga. The store will also have a lounge upstairs for customers to bond with the founder over chai. “Many of the store's clients have over time become my closest confidants,” says Rai. On pricing the exquisite weaves, she says, “If I promote an art form, I cannot do so by bringing it to a price ticket that is unaffordable. The most exquisite saris in the store will be acceptable and affordable, and at the same time reflect the artist's caliber.” Warp 'n Weft will also be launching the first ever line of ready to wear collection this season. What started in 1997 along with a makeshift nursery for Rai's daughter is now seeing the fruits of her labour. To mark the moment, Warp 'n Weft has shot with strong women who exemplify with the brand's identity. We spoke to founder about hitting the milestone. How does it feel to have started something that has withstood the test of time? Benares, along with its famed brocade and silk weaves, have occupied a key position in the landscape of handloom in the Indian subcontinent. Delve into the alcoves of tradition and artistry, and you'll realise that Benarasi has been the preferred fabric of the royals. The predilection for the craft and the passion for making it acceptable has been my driving force all along. When I look back, I lose count of the years spent doing so, but take ahead with me an exalted credibility with not just customers but also my weavers. It's a high that comes with gratitude. How did the idea of the photoshoot come about?  My association with the women who walk into our space sees an equation beyond the world of weaves. We connect because we think alike and hold similar ideas of appreciating and encouraging art. When the digital world did not exist, my customers would bring back pictures to share of their special moments and stories to tell of how they stood apart from the crowd and pulled compliments on their woven rhapsody. These are women who are proud champions of the Indian weave and were happy to wear it. This photoshoot helps us reach out to audiences to educate them not only about the different weaves from Benares but also how this craft can be worn in a contemporary and stylish way, without losing its ethos and relevance. How would you say the Warp 'n Weft customer evolved? Warp 'n Weft Women are real people who aren't easily swayed by hollow glamour. When I started Warp 'n Weft, it was predominantly the pristine whites and beiges in silken resham work. Then came the play of subtle metallics in silver and gold with nude tones. Today we boastfully bring the vibrant palette of gulaabi (rose), naarangi (orange), sindhuri (red), jamuni (purple) and so on to the lives of our customer. I had to first enter their hearts and now all elements Benarasi rule their mind. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #SuzyLFW: Mary Katrantzou and Peter Pilotto – art and craft
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion To print or not to print, that is the question for designers who have made pattern part of their fashion identities Mary Katrantzou: Fantasia "It felt the right time to bring a lot of things together and be able to think about the collection in a different way - and be brave," said Mary Katrantzou, who was focusing mainly on film noir, the mid-century movies whose heroines had strict Forties silhouettes and, as their name suggested, leaned towards black and other dark shades like purple or inky blue. But it is hard to imagine Mary separated for long from the colours, patterns and wild digital prints of her earlier days. So the other movie in her sight line was Fantasia, the 1940 Disney animation that was a meld of various film concepts with a pioneering stereophonic sound. Backstage, after the show with its lush, dark velvet colours (that were quiet by Mary's standards), the designer spilled out her message. "I was looking into magic kingdoms and that took me to Fantasia," she said. "The first time I saw it, I was so inspired by the way the music came together." She was also galvanised by the interplay of male and female, with garments that mixed tailoring with embellishment and masculine fabrics with florals. More inspirations piled on including the work of the artist MC Escher with an exploration of geometric and naturalistic forms. Long show notes are not always helpful, and I found the classical music played by the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra a clearer representation of how Mary, the founding mother of wild digital printing, was thinking in 2017. There was no sense of the cartoonish part of the film. And the designer who once made clothes that appeared to animate china plates back in 2012, had reduced her crockery decoration to small prints that might be teamed with checks. This was an apparently deliberate way of playing down the flowers, which were very much reduced in size and impact. The result of mixing geometry and nature could literally be called keeping flowers in check. The show was charming in many ways and colourful with its fluffy yellow collars or pink furry sleeves. But something has been lost in the translation from big and bold blooms to today's more timid, if graceful, patterns. Peter Pilotto: Art for fashion's sake I was lead to the 'art table' at the Peter Pilotto show, plonking myself down on a mushroom shaped stool by furniture designer Martino Gamper and surrounded by a crowd of makers, painters, movers and shakers. What a great start and statement of intent from Peter Pilotto and Christopher de Vos, who are enthusiastically in favour of art for fashion's sake. The venue alone, with leafy trees living up to the name Palm Court in the Waldorf Hotel, suggested an artistic glamour, only compounded by patterned rugs and paintings. But the design duo had the sense to make their clothes artistic but totally wearable, as in tweedy padded coats and sweaters inspired by Nazca quilting from Peru (de Vos is half-Peruvian). According to the show notes, there were as many layers as there are in a hand-worked rug - embroideries, scribbled velvet, cross hatch tweed and metallic weaving. The duo had a word for these effects: "decorative utility". And that did not mean much more than the very good sense of making fashion, however decorative, wearable. In the case of this autumn/winter 2017 collection, that meant the clothes also had the advantages of looking right for a cold climate. Padded outerwear has moved a long way from the ubiquitous puffer jacket, with giant embroidered patch pockets in wintry rust and green laid over a blue and white surface. Peter Pilotto in action A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 21, 2017 at 11:05am PST Such a collection really required an ever-vanishing list to understand the many techniques and fabrics. But one of the charms of this label is that the designers do not take themselves too solemnly, offering a twist of powder pink velvet over red military trousers as well as the more complex pieces. Significantly, among the many patches of quilting and sweaters with colourful squares, there was hardly a flower in sight. It seems that blooms, apart from an abstract, artistic kind, are wilting in imaginative fashion. This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #SuzyLFW: Marques’Almeida – celebrating diversity
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Portuguese design duo captured the raw, youthful and multiculturalism of London 'I Wish I Knew How It Would Feel To Be Free' - Nina Simone's soul song played through at the end of the Marques'Almeida show that effectively closed London Fashion Week. 'I Wish I Knew how it Would Feel to be Free.' Nina Simone's voice at the close of the Marques/Almeida show A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 21, 2017 at 7:12am PST Models with afro hair walked the runway at the Old Truman Brewery on London's multi-cultural Brick Lane and the mannish, forceful freedom of the geometrically patterned clothes all suggested the current, modern layers of this ancient city. While not perfect as a show, it was an exceptional presentation expressing the raw spirit of the area and its designers - even if Marta Marques and Paulo Almeida are Portuguese in origin. That offered another wry reflection on Brexit, their adopted country's voted departure from the EU and the uncertain future for fledgling designers, like this pair, to attend British fashion schools. The winners of the first LVMH Young Fashion Designer Prize in 2015 have moved on from the shredded denim that seemed to be their fashion calling card. Although Paulo explained backstage that denim still featured "a little bit, ribbed and brush stroked". But mainly the story was of geometric checks and stripes, made in big shapes and worn with confident bluster. With the opening outfit a red and black striped oversize jacket, (with a suggestion of hot brand Vetements), worn over slim black and white striped trousers, the designers made a strong statement. And that continued with giant sleeves and with a zippered sweater, its striped top opening to bare the shoulders. Black and white stripes and checks were followed by large polka dots, always giving the impression that everything was designed with a compass or a set square. "The whole thing with graphics is mainly from Malick Sidibé photographs," said Marta, referring to the Mali-born photographer whose black and white pictures from the Sixties and Seventies are being shown at London's Somerset House. They were also the inspiration of Antonio Mara's show in Milan in September 2016. For Paulo, the lure was the colour blocking and graphic effects, but for Marta there was a further story. "I think it is a time to speak about diversity - it makes sense," she said. "Sidibé's photography was all about youth in the Fifties and Sixties celebrating in their best clothes and best earrings. It made sense for us to do it now with all those different girls in our casting." The duo admitted to a sense of mixed references between the photographs, Nina Simone and the song 'By Ourselves' from artist Blood Orange, which features lyrics paying tribute to hip hop star Missy Elliott as an inspiration to black women. Marques\Almeida: fashioning the Ashlee Haze Missy Elliott Poem 'For Coloured Girls'. 'I will tell you that right now There are millions of black girls just waiting To see someone who looks like them .....' A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 21, 2017 at 7:03am PST This is why fashion people from across the world come to London. And the fact that Marques'Almeida have moved forward, producing tailoring and bold mixes of checks and frills, shows how fruitful it was for them to win the LVMH award that will have another voting panel at work this month in Paris to unearth more burgeoning talent. column1: Have you seen Emma Watson’s new Instagram account?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Why you need to check it out Emma Watson is a savvy social-media user. Not only does she use it to drum up followers of her book club and her work on the gender-equality initiative He For She (in her capacity as a UN global goodwill ambassador), just last week she was seen on an iPad in Grand Central Station New York - in the capable hands of Derek Blasberg - offering commuters advice for $2 as a part of an unknown project. Now, she has turned to the medium to keep her fans up to date with every look from her promotional tour for Beauty and the Beast by launching a dedicated account, The Press Tour. Today was a brilliant day of interviews, press conferences and photoshoots for @beautyandthebeast in France. We snuck out of the junket and onto the roof of the hotel to capture these shots against the beautiful Paris skyline. Custom @louisvuitton dress designed by @nicolasghesquiere. The dress fabric is Newlife recycled polyester, created from used plastic bottles. These are sourced, mechanically processed and spun into yarns in Italy, with a fully traceable supply chain. This saves energy and reduces CO2 emissions compared to creating brand new polyester fibre. The arm band was created in a carbon-neutral mill. Dress validated by @ecoage #ecoloves A post shared by The Press Tour (@the_press_tour) on Feb 20, 2017 at 2:16pm PST The actress has already put up four posts to the account, which is clearly intended to raise awareness of the sustainability of her tour wardrobe. In her first post, she wore a Stella McCartney coat and highlighted the designer's ethical approach. "Coat is from @stellamccartney, the world's first luxury brand that is committed to producing products that do not use leather, skins, feathers or fur," she informed. "Instead, Stella has spent years developing ways of using materials such as regenerated cashmere, recycled fabrics, organic cotton and forest-friendly fabrics." About to set off on day one of the @beautyandthebeast press tour with Team Watson... Hello Paris! Bonjour! I've started a new Instagram called @the_press_tour so you can follow our journey. I hope you enjoy seeing what goes on behind the scenes. It takes a village! Love, Emma A post shared by Emma Watson (@emmawatson) on Feb 19, 2017 at 8:05am PST While Watson is the first high-profile star to create an account solely intended for her red-carpet choices, she's not the first celebrity to take control of the coverage that comes with global fame. Over the weekend, David Beckham shared multiple images of his family skiing holiday in Whistler, Canada, telling his followers: "Don't usually post so many but it's so beautiful up here, plus having a special time so before anyone else sells pictures of the family I wanted you guys to see them first." column1: Burberry continues to forge ahead in the digital sphere
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The brand showcased its latest menswear and womenswear collections Christopher Bailey, the passionate and articulate chief creative and chief executive Officer of Burberry, has steered Britain's only truly global luxury brand through some choppy waters recently. But their third quarter results published in January showed comparable sales up 40 per cent and their joyous relief is much deserved. Taking into account the seismic shifts within the brand over the last three years - first the decision to fold its three separate fashion lines into one, then fully moving to a see-now, buy-now model last September - tonight's show of their February 2017 men and womenwear collection, hosted again at Burberry Maker's House in Soho, was the perfect moment to celebrate their colossal strength and success. Bailey has always enriched the house's history with British creative talent old and new, while also forging ahead in the digital sphere and tonight was no different. Young Brit Anna Calvi sang in the new collection, to a front row lined with celebrities - including Naomi Campbell, Penélope Cruz and Suki Waterhouse - while the British sculptor Henry Moore and his studio was the inspiration for looks that embraced the rustic romance of the English countryside and artisan lifestyle. Delicate broderie anglaise dresses, blue artist studio smock tops and overalls, crisp white dress shirting and striped T-shirts, and warm cream one-shoulder Aran knits were all paired with thick cream shearling overcoats and trenches with ruffles spiralling around sleeves. The menswear was a simpler mirror to the women's, with many super desirable pieces the girls with a more androgynous leaning will certainly want to shop. The finale included a dazzling collection of couture capes, of feathers, beading and lace, which are made-to-order and will be travelling around the world as part of an exhibition. From tomorrow they join the exhibition of over 40 Moore sculptures which opens to the public at the Maker's House. The collection itself went on sale just as the show's live stream ended. "This little island is intensely creative and the world is inspired by that," said Bailey. A loud 'hear, hear' to that! column1: India bags International Fashion Showcase Country Award
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The country’s most promising designers created an award-winning sustainable fashion exhibition View Gallery 5 Photos India bags International Fashion Showcase Country Award India's debut at the International Fashion Showcase (IFS) was a victorious one. Every year during London Fashion Week, IFS celebrates emerging talent from across the world through a series of specially-commissioned and curated fashion installations. This year, in association with Lakmé Fashion Week and IMG Reliance, five emerging designers—Ujjawal Dubey of Antar-Agni, Ragini Ahuja of Ikai, Karishma Shahani Khan of [KA][SHA], Priyanka Lama of PELLA and Alan Alexander Kaleekal of Kaleekal—showcased their work at the iconic Somerset House. The exhibition titled ‘Indian Pastoralists', which drew from the multi-faceted lifestyles of India's nomadic pastoral communities, bagged the International Fashion Showcase Country Award. Karishma Shahani Khan, [KA][SHA] The London College of Fashion graduate's work was inspired by Rabaris—pastoral nomads predominantly found in Kutch, India. “My first interaction with Rabari craft was through a project I did with their community as a student. The Rabaris have always fascinated me with their layers, colours and techniques,” explains Shahani Khan. Fabrics such as cotton and mashru, characteristic of the community, formed the basis of her creations. While the colour palette varied from jet black to bright blue, the surface textures included traditional techniques of tie and dye, thread embroidery, mirror work and appliqué. Kaleekal by Alan Alexander Kaleekal Based in the Nilgiri hills of southern India, the Toda community is known for their shawls accentuated with heavy hand embroidery and intricate geometric patterns. Kaleekal's exhibit presented three shawls handwoven in Pashmina wool, Tussar silk and cashmere, featuring Toda embroidery reinterpreted over 60 days by local artisans. Ragini Ahuja, Ikai Ragini Ahuja's work took its cues from the Drokpa community's cultural exuberance. “Their eclectic sense of dressing as well as their fanatical attachment to purity is what inspired me to work with them,” says Ahuja. The designer showcased a present-day version of the sheep skin cape, a handwoven Himalayan silk wool jacket appliquéd with sheep nappa leather. Finishing touches came in the form of tonal flowers and lustrous silver beads. Priyanka Ella Lorena Lama, PELLA The highland communities of Lachen and Lachung served as inspiration for the Bangalore-based designer's exhibit, which focused on indigenous Eri silk, yarn waste and patterns developed from a single block of fabric. Ujjawal Dubey, Antar-Agni High slits that ease travels and raw edges that represent affinity for nature, Ujjawal Dubey's creations incorporated the distinct layering and draping styles of the Van Gujjars. The fabric used was a custom weave of handwoven cotton and khadi with heavy weight warp and slubs in black and beige. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #SuzyLFW: Erdem – A Flow Of Turkish And Scottish Blood
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer tracks his two grandmothers' roots from the Ottoman Empire to Scotland What! No fancy set conjuring up a distant and lost world? No objects, floating curtains nor back story - just a trellis of what might be Arabian patterning painted as a barely visible pattern on the white wall? [#image: /photos/5ce44b4ab80311db2e8f95c8]||| ||| Image: Indigital That turned out to be key to Erdem's story. "It was important to strip the set back for this collection - which is quite a personal one - the story of my two grandmothers and their improbable meeting," the designer explained. [#image: /photos/5ce44b4a9cc0c03a91f9fdb0]||| ||| Image: Indigital "It's about two women - one from my mum's side, married to my great grandfather who was in the Royal Scots Regiment and died in World War One; and on my father's side a background in Turkey, near the Syrian border. I wanted to imagine what would have happened to those women had they met." Erdem: the subtle colours worked in lace A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 20, 2017 at 6:54am PST Without that knowledge, gleaned before the show, I would not have understood half of what I saw - the Ottoman effect on pure white cotton; roses re-embroidered with Turkish miniatures; striped cotton dresses and military jackets. [#image: /photos/5ce44b4a9cc0c03921f9fdae]||| ||| Image: Indigital Erdem is a deep thinker with a poetic aesthetic. The little booklet that he produces for each collection was on this occasion showing contrasting images - photographs of his British grandmother in her Twenties satin robe and his Turkish grandmother in layers of soft, sheer robes in black against a white horse. Then there was grandfather in Highland army uniform and his grandmother again, but in more overtly Turkish dress with tiny embroidered flowers in a white robe edged in mosaic tile-blue. "It was also the idea of something quite simple and pure, but related to something very precious," said Erdem, whose work is typically rich, but delicate. [#image: /photos/5ce44b4bcc50be0eae141cf0]||| ||| Image: Indigital On the runway the dresses , which dominated the show, seemed mainly for late afternoon onwards, although there were some trouser suits and marginally daytime dresses, both using the mix of flowers and Islamic shapes. A cut-out teardrop at the breast gave out a perfume of sensuality. [#image: /photos/5ce44b4ab80311180c8f95ca]||| ||| Image: Indigital Night came speedily - but beautifully, occasionally with a dramatic mix of garden trees and flowers, others calmer, as in a mustard yellow velvet dress with flower print in devoré, (burnt out patterns) lined in cotton. [#image: /photos/5ce44b4b4a30b3269312fb3a]||| ||| Image: Indigital The collection only occasionally slipped towards a cinematic idea of Middle Eastern decoration. The rest of this fine show was gentle and moving - a designer paying tribute to his heritage in a subtle and meaningful way. column1: The millennial celebrity guide to cool designer labels
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The crusaders of street fashion View Gallery 11 Photos What are millennials wearing It's hard to describe the wardrobe sensibilities of a millennial without sounding trite—a mix of old and new labels put together with great care, to look thoughtfully dressed yet nonchalant. The influential gang of these Insta celebrities seem to have an understanding that these images will be disseminated to the millions of their followers. There are polaroid photographs, street style shots that may or may not have been staged, and then the very direct mirror selfie. There's the obvious favouritism towards jeans, the staple casual—sweatshirt and bombers galore, but each image conveys the style influencer's solidarity with design labels. The new generation is less about ball gowns and more about earning street cred. French design collective Vetements is a favourite with everyone from Gigi Hadid to Kendall Jenner and Sarah Snyder. Sports brands that until now were never regarded in the same category as high fashion, like Champion and North Face, find themselves reincarnated as must-haves. Does that mean that the days of old-school fashion houses are numbered? Not in the least. Designers like Alessandro Michele at Gucci, Stuart Vevers at Coach and Nicolas Ghesquière at Louis Vuitton have found fans in the new FROWers. That is to say, Selena Gomez, Chiara Ferragni and Tavi Gevinson have been instrumental in bringing the luxe closer to an audience that they "hang out with" on a daily basis. In comparison, smaller labels like MISBHV and Revice might be one-post wonders, but are certainly labels to watch out for, given the patronage they receive. Then there are brands like Supreme and Calvin Klein, whose DNA always lends more to the wearer's cred, no matter how famous they are to begin with. Naturally, these items of clothing are the first to be sold out on websites. Here are some of the most memorable millennial celebrity-fashion pairings we have spotted on social media. column1: #SuzyLFW: Simone Rocha’s Call To Arms
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer reflected the current political battles in an exceptional collection that showed women diffusing anger with flowers. Why red flowers?” I asked Simone Rocha, referring to the blood red blooms embroidered on dresses or even socks. [#image: /photos/5ce44d8a65bc1a463d7017d0]||| ||| Image: Indigital “It was taken from the colour of anger – but I was trying to do it in a peaceful way, through flowers,” said Simone backstage, standing with models of different ages, some definitely of an older generation. [#image: /photos/5ce44d8a1dc267a3f2c7b54c]||| ||| Image: Indigital “It's really mixing red and pink with the idea of foliage, so it starts off all green, goes through black and then I've added masculinity in the tailoring,” explained the designer. “I've played with the idea of masculinity and femininity, including the way we have cast the show, inclusive of different types of women.” Suzy with Simone Rocha backstage. @simonetocha_ Read my review. Link in bio A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 18, 2017 at 4:01pm PST Words cannot describe the beauty and the strength of this collection which seemed to catch the global vibe of anger but turned swords into ploughshares in the most mindful way. Off with the frills representing the girlish innocence of Simone's previous collections. Goodbye to Irish farmland for escapes and escapades. Farewell to the Church and its pious little dresses. You could envisage this sober new woman in her dark fur saying farewell to her husband, maybe to her entire family, as she joined the marching band. A call to arms. Simone Rocha was thinking 'armour, camouflage, foliage. READ MY STORY. link in bio A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 18, 2017 at 3:54pm PST Not that there was anything elegiac or mournful about the Simone Rocha collection. The reverse was true. The women seemed purposeful and their clothes as intricately put together as in previous presentations. [#image: /photos/5ce44d8aba773d0fec0b6262]||| ||| Image: Indigital The show opened with a belted coat and skirt in the brown of a muddy battlefield, but lush in its thick velvet. The designs moved on to khaki, and then black, but these military coats were feminised by a curving cut around the broad belts. Then came the flowers: primroses smothering dark tulle that was strapped and belted with leather. [#image: /photos/5ce44d8b1dc267c65ac7b54e]||| ||| Image: Indigital “It was my interpretation of armour as a kind of camouflage and how it can be done through foliage,” Simone said. “So I've embedded all these nuances into the fabrication, like the organza with embroidered flowers.” Simone Rocha: 'protection, feminine, famine'. Read my story. Link in bio A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 18, 2017 at 3:55pm PST Those arriving for the show in the grand surroundings of a royal palace found a sheet of paper with a few key lines. They were laid out like a poem with these words: “armour, camouflage, foliage, peace, peace of mind.” There were more lists of words: “protection, feminine, famine,” and “archivists, dirt and grit.” It is rare to find a designer who can express poetry through words, rather than clothes. But Simone Rocha's skill was to do both: to live up to these evocative phrases in what she made. The most significant expression was that against every drab background, there was always hope: a dull black coat, but smothered with black embroidery; an all-embracing black fur – but with a fluffy white fur sash. The blood red flowers bloomed not only as embroidery on dresses, but also as big floral crystals on a fur stole. [#image: /photos/5ce44d8bb803117fe88f98e1]||| ||| Image: Indigital In some ways this was the most ‘masculine' show Simone has ever done in terms of the cut and sobriety of the clothes. But not really, because even if her women might dress for a battle, you could feel that the fight was to sustain female strength. Simone has benefited as a woman and as a designer from the support of her close-knit family, who were with her last week in Manhattan for the opening of her first American store. She has fought for her success. But the power of this collection lies in that she was designing to show that women could find a way to lay down their arms. column1: Rejoice, retro-philes: The polka dot is making a comeback
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Spot the trend The polka dot has had an enduring love affair with fashion. One look at its timeline is proof enough—it first captured popular imagination when Disney introduced Minnie Mouse wearing a red polka dot dress and matching bow in 1928; then came Christian Dior's ‘New Look'. Marilyn Monroe pretty much became synonymous with the polka dotted bikini after she was photographed in one in 1951. And then there was the brown and white polka dot dress Julia Roberts made us fall in love with in Pretty Woman. The polka dot has been one of those trends that though not stealing the spotlight at all times, has faithfully lingered in the background. And as designers continue to revisit the past for inspiration season after season, it's only fitting that it has made a comeback as one of the key resort 2017 trends. The pattern evokes a sense of nostalgia, instantly conjuring beachside imagery—think a polka-dotted high-waist bikini (complete with heart-shaped sunglasses) on a sunny day, with a Coca-Cola bottle in one hand. And while designers this season have retained some semblance of this old-school charm, they haven't entirely shied away from an au courant update either. So cut to 2017, and the happy-go-lucky print has been largely reimagined in a monochrome palette on tea length dresses, ruffles, pleats and cinched silhouettes. But it's not all prim and proper. Add a dot of risqué to your maxi dress for date night with a thigh-high slit as seen at Calvin Klein, midriff cut-outs à la Carolina Herrera or turn to cold shoulder tops as advocated by Monse. If all-round polished if your sartorial mantra, then a belted midi dress with bell sleeves as shown at Rosetta Getty or a Gucci-approved ruffled dress will be perfect for everything from a family gathering to an after work dinner. Not over chokers yet? Take your cue from Michael Kors, and team your drop-waist pleated polka dot dress with a matching skinny scarf tied around your neck. But if you're on the lookout for something more androgynous, turn to Emporio Armani for inspiration. Those flared trousers with oversized polka dots are just what you need to ace that casual Friday look. Turns out Marc Jacobs was right all along when he said, “I don't think there is ever a wrong time for a polka dot.” Check out all the runway inspiration in our slideshow: View Gallery 15 Photos The polka dot is making a comeback What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #SuzyLFW: JW Anderson – A Fashion Odyssey
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer offered powerful, yet seemingly disparate, clothes that deliberately disrupted conventions As models walked purposefully through the narrow walls, often in complex outfits, it was more or less impossible to take everything in at the JW Anderson show. Here was a simply beautiful dress with a gilded pattern and nothing complicated but different length sleeves. Or a dress with white pleated bib like something carved in alabaster – except that it swayed gently across the body. Image: Indigital Yet there were as many ideas from Jonathan Anderson as there were complex additions: purses hanging from a neck piece on a pin-striped dress that was cut on the bias with skirt folds flowing every which way. When the designer carried off his fashion flourishes they could be stellar, like a skirt with twin inserts of silver and gilt paired with a leather jacket cropped only just below bare breasts. Image: Indigital The more you tried to capture the moment, the harder it seemed: drapes here, flowers there and then a flutter of ostrich feathers. Yes, opposites attract – especially if you are Jonathan Anderson with enough ideas to design all this and the Loewe brand too. As the show came towards its end with an absolute winner – an olive green silk dress that seemed to have been poured in a thin stream over the body – I was determined to go backstage. Image: Indigital But I did not feel much the wiser when I had found the designer, who was wearing the runway olive green colour as a zippered jacket with torn jeans. Words tumbled out as he tried to explain his thought process. “It's the idea of building up layers – and there are kind of couture edges that can be warped and disrupted – like the feathers,” he said. “You know that things shouldn't really work but they kind of make it. Like dropping the waistline to compensate for not having a heel.” Image: Indigital Jonathan went on to pick out some specific clashes, like brocade that faced off against a completely different material like leather. He also talked about the insertion of pockets, giving a 'utilitarian' look even to fur. Image: Indigital So, was all this planned as disruptive and off-key? “No, it's not awkward – except in the combination of fabrics – the idea that you try to devalue it through the process,” he said. “So you get the skirt which becomes more like streetwear. Then you up it with leather to make it more for daytime. I like this idea where the look became a bit Dickensian. And I just wanted to explore something that was reduced to an extent. The idea of the silhouette as if it was an incline drawing it upwards – and then it fades out.” Image: Indigital Once Jonathan started talking about “one utopia – the idea of a style odyssey” he completely lost me, as my mind clicked through the clothes which were so appealing in many ways: the clever cuts, the intriguing fabrics and the colours facing off black and white. And then the designer said one short sentence which defined the entire presentation with is subtle shaping and sudden baring of flesh: “It's this idea throughout the show of a style odyssey where you show different parts of a woman to make her sensuous,” Jonathan said. Aaaah! Got it! Jonathan Anderson. READ MY STORY. column1: #SuzyNYFW: Marc Jacobs – Nostalgia For Hip Hop Era
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer is inspired by a '"poignant and pivotal cultural moment”. Nostalgia for bling? Really? There was Marc Jacobs running with a bold gold necklace clanking over his sweater as he dashed down an improvised runway. It was, in fact, two single lines of chairs leading across the vast, empty back lot of The Lexington Armory. Image: Indigital The models were exceptionally tidy hip-hoppers, compared to the baggy trousers and oversize hoodie tops of their predecessors. Instead they wore well-fitting zipped tops or elegantly cut checkered jackets that seemed to belong more to Seventies punk than the street outfits of 20 years ago. Image: Indigital Heads were covered in rounded caps while fur trimmings at the collar suggested a well-off bunch. And after the show, as the models lounged in the street by a vehicle blaring out deafening music, they seemed utterly laid back. But maybe that was because they were occupied with devices that no-one envisaged back in the hip hop days. Or should that be "daze"? RESPECT! Marc Jacobs goes back to the Hip Hop years A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 16, 2017 at 12:02pm PST A documentary called Hip Hop Evolution had inspired this show, Marc. He referred to "the poignant and pivotal cultural movement that reshaped and redefined the landscape of music, which gave way to a whole new language of style". Image: Indigital That was an introduction to the tidy clothes that he described as "my presentation of the well-studied dressing up of casual sportswear". Image: Indigital It is weird to think of Marc himself, who lived through that period of wild music and attitude, looking back with nostalgia to the not so distant past. There he goes! Marc Jacobs with rapper bling at the end of his 3.7 minute show! A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 16, 2017 at 12:09pm PST The collection had some fine pieces, especially in the tailoring, that looked very marketable. And cranberry suede - or was it velvet? - looked classy as it shot by. Image: Indigital But given Marc's track record of fashion daring and controversy, this vision of street style, seen through rose tinted spectacles, seemed rather tame. column1: How to nail power dressing for every kind of job
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Nine-to-fives have never looked better They say “dress for the job you want, not the one you have” and it's true—never has it hurt someone to be well-turned-out at all times. Aesthetics matter, and being sharply dressed at your workplace seems to have a positive effect on your progress graph. But each profession has its own understanding of what counts as appropriate work wear. Lawyers seem to live in a permanent wardrobe of monochrome, corporate dressing, though open to colours, stays in close quarters with sharp tailoring. For the creative folk, rules are lot more relaxed—jeans are perfectly normal to be worn to client meetings. Regardless of what your job description entails, leaving a mark on your peers is possible by way of your ensemble. No matter how liberal a work place, stick to day-dressing. Leave lace and velvet for the after-hours. It is best to avoid embellishment of all sorts—no need to turn into an ornament just because a dress fits well. Invest in statement accessories in neutral colours. Don't forget to keep up with trends—just because you work a standard nine-to-five doesn't mean you forget the fashion girl inside you. column1: #SuzyNYFW: Michael Kors – Marshalling The Military
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The designer sent out a collection of sharp tailoring and utilitarian hardwear with a military touch In this moment of transition and political confusion that has made New York Fashion Week seem almost irrelevant, few designers have hit the right note. But Michael Kors did just that - and not only because a live orchestra was telling us hopefully that 'Sweet Dreams Are Made Of This'. Day to night - and back again - at Michael Kors A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 15, 2017 at 8:37am PST The designer used all those clichés of tough and tender, with solid camel tailoring set against bands of sparkling fringe, and bare flesh facing off against winter cover-up. This was made more meaningful - and modern - by a deliberate mix of work wear and party pieces, rather than the traditional day-through-night presentation. "You gotta have some glamour," said Kors backstage with his friend Blake Lively who was wearing the designer's flower-smothered dress that seemed to belong to a different - and sweeter - American era. Seeet dreams are made of this ... Blake Lively with Michael Kors A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 15, 2017 at 7:57am PST A faultless mix of what the designer described as "sharp tailoring, utilitarian hardware and military strength" came with more fanciful evening pieces in molten metals and liquid lamé. That decoration kept a hint of the military from daytime looks to evening wear. It was as though Kors had perceived in advance the storms rolling over Washington DC and the new administration and made this collection purposeful, rather than escapist. Three quarters of the show, which included the men's collection, was played out in fifty shades of camel and grey. Only towards the end did the designer pour in wine red, mostly a very dark burgundy. The rest of the day clothes were as utilitarian as they could be when using the finest fabrics and matching the colour of fur to the cloth. Even the high heeled shoes or boots were made for walking - or perhaps striding - while slit skirts were made for movement. You could tick off the wardrobe list: knits in camel, matching hose and suede boots, the same concept in severe tweed or in a more playful animal print fabric. "Urban luxury" was another phrase that Kors used, meaning that the same uptown looks were carried through to the evening outfits when the surfaces or fringes sparkled. With the demise of other uptown brands - whose new designers are bringing them literally and metaphorically downtown, in the case of Oscar de la Renta for example - the Michael Kors look stands alone. But far from trotting out the familiar off-to-the-Hamptons Waspy cashmere and casual trousers, there was a meaty feel to this collection - marshalling the fashion military in a city - and a country - facing a tough moment in history. column1: #SuzyNYFW: Coach 1941 – Prairie Grit
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion With moon boots stomping over a dusty, tumbleweed strewn path past a rickety wooden house, Coach had shifted from prairie to Badlands - and it worked Over the last three years, designer Stuart Vevers has been creating a full-on fashion statement for the handbag brand, and his British eye on America's Wild West is creating a convincing fashion universe. Image: Indigital The boots were key in the Autumn/Winter 2017 show, because the whimsical patterns of cherries and flowers on hefty shapes were symbolic of the entire collection. Cherry picking of a pattern here, a tufted flower there, or even a bird sewn on pearls on a leather jacket, created the tough-and-tender meld that is working for Coach. Vevers calls it a "hybrid world". Image: Indigital "I think our approach on craft is really important - it's an American approach, less precious, either with a playful quality or in a more elemental way, leaving the edges of the shearling raw," said the designer. He quoted Tatum O'Neal as Addie Loggins in the 1973 film Paper Moon, and explained the "tomboy references were turned into embroideries and floral prints". Coach in action A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 15, 2017 at 6:46am PST Mix the hippy spirit of the Seventies with hip hop from the Eighties, and the message was still clear - hefty coat shapes in shearling with bold flowers as decoration, or slim, light dresses with miniature florals. Image: Indigital The personalising of both clothes and accessories is all part of the Vevers concept of a young woman exploring and customising the pieces "and making them her own". Image: Indigital Nostalgia is included in the fashion plot - military jackets as worn on Eighties music tours, but so much fresher and cleaner. Or the ubiquitous furry jackets, but all in shearling - not granny's beat-up, cast off furs. And whereas the originals might have been hefty and heavy, here everything was light and easy. At Coach, Stuart Vever talks bags A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 15, 2017 at 6:38am PST Although the clothes make a strong statement on the runway, Vevers admits the "vast majority" of the business is accessories, since the clothing has existed for only the last three years. Image: Indigital But the handbags with bunch-of-flowers embroideries and the walking-on-the-moon boots all offer a young shopper a price point to start buying. This is in the Coach tradition of making the purse a graduation gift. Image: Indigital But the vision is now so much larger and more international - and to add to the company's global reach, Coach opens its first store in Italy's fashion capital Milan next week. column1: #SuzyNYFW: Monse Precedes Oscar de la Renta
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia’s deconstructionism was the overture for their debut in charge of American high society’s favourite house Monse: A Personal Vision In all the many cases of passing the fashion baton, this must have been the weirdest takeover by a backroom pair of designers. After Oscar de la Renta's death in 2014 and a brief replacement by international designer Peter Copping, the historic company looked for talent in its in-house team. The story is complex, but it has ended up with Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia as Creative Directors at de la Renta, but also maintaining their own personal brand, Monse – as it is named. This is not so strange to high fashion: in Paris John Galliano, for example, kept his own line while working for Dior. But to my knowledge, there has never been a display of a designer's work at the same time as the offering of the brand where they're employed. And in this case, the personal collection came first! To emphasise the divide, the Hilton sisters, Nicky (now Rothschild) and Paris, posed by the flimsy curtains, one wearing an outfit from Monse; the other in Oscar. Hilton sisters Paris and Nicky at the Monce/ Oscar de la Renta show A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 13, 2017 at 4:31pm PST I would describe the Monse offering as experimental couture – starting with a widely ruffled white top worn with narrow pants. That was followed by a tailored grey herringbone coat with cutaway shoulders and then the look was roughed up with big, furry, off-kilter tops, falling off one shoulder or in a tangled mix of fabrics. This all looked like a deconstructed version of Oscar's couture perfection and, as such, had possibility. Striking pieces included colourful paillettes giving gleam and sheen to simple evening dresses. Homage At Oscar de la Renta Then, after a malfunction left the swish of the curtains half closed, came the Oscar collection. It started with streamlined black outfits, such as narrow trousers and a wide-shouldered top cinched in by a gilded rose buckle belt. But then came elegant, if very familiar, coats and jackets that looked like the couturier's archives on speed. That was because of bright mixes of orange, red, shocking pink and royal blue. Surely women who still wear these uptown outfits would choose a classic, not a vivid or lurid shade? The black tops with narrow pants or little black dresses seemed more convincing – but they were not designed with the same experience of cutting on the bias. Each time a dress passed by, I saw the tell-tale line of a seam stitched in silk or velvet. Is it such a sewing sin not to make everything in the old-school way? Not necessarily. But it did not look as though the duo was experimenting, instead rather playing homage in a caricaturist way. It was their choice to send out a strapless evening dress with a bell-shaped skirt that looked very like ‘Oscar' in his heyday. So let's look at this show as an homage for their debut season. Hopefully, there will be some new developments for next season. column1: #SuzyNYFW: Tory Burch – A Tomboy’s Valentine
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Katharine Hepburn and a childhood in Philadelphia inspire a tomboy approach. “My home town!” said Tory Burch, as she talked about Katharine Hepburn in the movie Philadelphia Story – while greeting backstage her faithful client and famous Chinese actress, Li Bingbing. Li Bingbing and Tory Burch: HAPPY VALENTINE's day 💜❤️💙💚💛 A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 14, 2017 at 6:59am PST That film from 1940 was the designer's inspiration because of what she described as “tomboy chic, outdoor glamour and a confident femininity.” All that seemed a perfect fit for Tory, who knows how to make a big bow flop over a silk shirt and to tie a mini version to feminise a shoe. Tory Burch in motion A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 14, 2017 at 12:07pm PST   This gentle masculine/feminine game is the designer's calling card. But this season she added a dollop of sweetness – and not just in the Valentine's day books of love poems or the heart-patterned cups of hot chocolate printed with the words ‘love conquers all.'   There were soft colours like a blush pink coat, identified by a new logo with ‘TB' in gold lettering. While colourful floral patterns came in Tory's favourite lupin flower blue. But this look faced off with the more sporty pieces, including a country cardigan worn like a comfort blanket and masculine checked trousers. For evening, there was yet another code: gilded or mother-of-pearl patterns. It is still hard to know just what the Tory Burch brand stands for. It is very much a personal manifestation of its founder. But the way that she radiates her vision from clothing to interior design, from china to homewear, create a style universe to which other women can relate. column1: Manish Malhotra’s Harvard speech will inspire you to fight for your dreams
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get ready for this emotional rollercoaster Manish Malhotra, who turned 50 last year, was amongst the esteemed guest speakers at the India Conference 2017 in Harvard Business School. In his speech, he describes how against consistent opposition from his parents who disapproved of his “tailoring” career and resistance from a film industry set in its ways, he followed his heart and passion to reach where he is today. Read on for a full transcript of his speech as narrated at the conference. Thank you, Harvard, for inviting me here because it somewhere assures a person who is not educated, who hasn't come to Harvard, who hasn't studied at all. I haven't even studied design, and so this evening, being with all of you really means a lot to me, so thank you! Being here and [speaking] on the topic of inspired stories—many years ago, before many of you were even born, I was being inspired in the movie theatres in Mumbai. My entire childhood was in the film theatres. I have to give it to my mother, who encouraged me and never stopped me from watching a film. I would tell her, “I don't like your sari, there's something wrong with it. I like that actress' sari”. And she would be like, “what's wrong with you? Okay, you go and see a film again”. So she truly encouraged me, and my cousins are sitting here, they know for a fact that whenever we met for family dinners I would be, “Hurry up, we need to go and see this film”. Image: Tarun Vishwa So my entire childhood was movies, movies and movies. I was fascinated by (their) colour, by the clothes, the music. I used to look at Yash Chopra's films and wonder, “Will I ever go to a five-star hotel and have a meal?”. When I saw a song from a film called Trishul where they are playing golf, doing yoga, romancing, and they had big parties in that film—I always thought, would I ever be over there? Go for such parties, meet film stars; would I have this kind of lifestyle? Would I make a noise in this world, in this entire big world? So with those dreams I came into college. When I was in college I started watching English films, so it was always movies for me. The only good thing I did in school (because I was a real bad student) was that I enrolled myself into a drawing class and that's where I learnt painting, I learnt drawing, sketching and I was fascinated with it and kept getting better and better. When I was in college, one day someone offered me this modelling assignment and I was like, “I can model? Are you sure?” So, they said, “you can”, and I was very excited with that and I started modelling. At the age of 19 I told my father, “I haven't even been abroad, I want to see the world. Otherwise how will I make something out of my life?” So he was like, “you are modelling, save your money and then go if you want to”. That's when I worked really hard as a model and I used to take up every assignment. I used to not meet my friends, I used to be shooting every second day, taking every assignment that came to me so I could travel abroad. In those days, I managed to save some Rs 90,000 and I went to Singapore and Bangkok for the first time, really proud that I could do this on my own. When I came back I was so excited that I [had] travelled abroad. [That encouraged me to enroll] in Air India, I wanted to be a purser. And when the questions came to me at the exam… all the general knowledge questions… I absolutely failed because all I knew was movies. Image: Tarun Vishwa Thereafter, I took up a job at a boutique as a sales boy. My parents were absolutely horrified, they were like, “What are you doing? You are going to become a tailor, why are you a sales boy? Why don't you join your father's air conditioning business?” I was like, “No, I'm going to be a film director”. So, they said, “Why not a film actor?” Every Punjabi mother feels her son is the best looking and he can become a hero, so every profession comes down to movies and you should become an actor. I was in this boutique and I was a sales boy but I took it on and I used to sit with the tailor. I used to learn about cuts. I was very curious. I used to ask questions. I used to meet with the clients. I used to sketch all day long. I used to dress up the mannequin. And that's the year, which is about 1988, when the fashion movement in India was just starting. Ensemble was opening and there were a lot of designers who had come out with their collections. Image: Tarun Vishwa So, I was very fascinated with that and I wanted to assist Yash Chopra and I didn't know him. …I was like, “How will I become a film director?” and my parents went on with “become an actor, become an actor” and I was like, “No I want to be a designer” and they were like, “that means a tailor”. I was like, “No, I want to be a designer”, so I kept two machines in my house, I had two tailors in my bedroom. I started with taking orders for salwaar kameez and my mother was horrified. She was like I can't believe I'm going to tell my friends that my son takes salwaar kameez orders, come and give him orders. I was like no, there is something better [coming] out of this. I met a photographer who took me to meet Sridevi, who at that time was a huge star. This is in 1990. I had just done a song for Juhi Chawla in the movie Swarg and I thought to myself films are great to start because no designer was touching movies. They were all looking down on (films) because [in the] late '80s, it was a complete decline of fashion and films. I thought to myself, if I can make a change here I'll be able to make a name. Since I don't have the money to go abroad and study fashion, and I neither wanted to go to NIFT in Delhi because I didn't want to stay with my relatives in Delhi, I said, let me start working on films. Here I was at 23, leaving modelling completely to my mother's unhappiness, and starting working in movies. Since I could sketch so fast, all the actors started giving me a lot of work and it was two-three years of running around the producers. My father said, “What are you doing? You are going to lose money and whatever you made out of your modelling career.” I was determined [that] I didn't want to work for the air conditioning business. I [asked myself] what is the USP that I can give to my work, and I came with this concept of styling. I was the first designer who came up with this concept in Hindi movies. I started with, “What is going to be your make-up and what is going to be your hair?” All the make-up artists used to be like, “why is this costume designer interfering in our make-up and hair?” I asked a director… I remember, I was with Raveena Tandon and a director—we were listening to some script and he was telling [me to] make some western clothes for her. Like “something sexy”. I looked at him and I said, “What is her look and what is the story of the film? What is she playing?” And he looks at Raveena and he's like, “How dare he ask me the story of the film?” I was like, “I'm just asking you for the character!” In those days they didn't really flesh out a character. Either she's a glamorous girl, she's an Indian girl, she will wear salwaar kameez in these scenes or she will wear western clothes. I happened to meet younger directors like Aditya Chopra, Karan Johar, Ram Gopal Verma—so many of them. And (then) came Rangeela and Raja Hindustani. And the ‘makeover' happened. [It was] not that planned, yet all of us wanted to do something fabulous, wanted to work and change the way films looked and in 1995. Filmfare Awards for the first time ever gave a Costume Designer Award and that was to me for the film Rangeela. From there, it all started. From a person (who had) not travelled at all, I was on a flight every week to Switzerland. If you all remember, if you all were born in the '90s—chiffon sari in the snow! While the heroes were in mufflers and trench coat, the heroines were in the itsy-bitsy blouses, which I was tacking there in the snow. Image: Arsh Sayed I was in and out of Switzerland. I was in London shopping. I was in New York shopping. But, I have to say (to) all of you here, that I think the best education has been travel—learning, imbibing, watching people, watching different cultures. You know seeing fashion, seeing everything around has been the biggest education for me. And while I was interested, of course, and I thought that was my life. My dream was fulfilled and I was going to be a costume designer (for films) all my life. I was already working with the best of directors, producers, actresses and actors. Then came the very prestigious Birla family couple—Yash and Avanti Birla who offered me a retail store and I was like “retail?!” I was a costume designer and that's how I started my store and came into retail. Then I moved on to launch my new label, which was in the year 2006, and two-three years went balancing, you know, movies and my own label. This was when for the first time I introduced the concept of a show-stopper. Fashion critics criticised me [saying] all my fashion shows had a very impressive film industry front row, which was not really a norm in fashion in those days, neither was a showstopper. But, after 11 years today, actors are paid to be showstoppers and everybody looks at having a good front row. So that was the fashion and trend that I started, and work went on. I was busy, day by day doing more and more work. I love to work I don't like Sundays. I wake up every morning at 6am and I dream what am I going to do next. Image: Abhay Singh I'm a visualiser. Sometimes [the] manifestations are personal, sometimes they are professional. But, all those goals always (lead to) work. You have to work hard, you know, like when Madhavan spoke about dreaming—for all your dreams to be fulfilled you have to work and I love to work. When the label moved ahead and we started a big store in Delhi—I was the first designer, who started a 9,500sqft store—it changed how my company worked. My positioning in the fashion industry became more serious and we became one of the first Rs 100 crore independent company in fashion design. Today, when I'm asked to look at 2030, I look at India (and) I look at Indian fashion to be on par with international fashion. I hopefully see a lot of investors coming and investing in Indian designers. We have everything: we have culture, tradition, we have texture, textile. We have great craftsmen. I run an NGO with actor Shabana Azmi. We had 40 women working (there) and now we have 280 women who come to our institute. (They) work and (create) beautiful chikankari work in a small village called Mijwan. I want to take a lot of handloom and weaves from Benaras, Mijwan (and present them) internationally. I think a lot of Indian designers will be out there by 2030. Indian fashion and Indian textile are going to be up there [internationally] and we all will be celebrating it. column1: #SuzyNYFW: Proenza Schouler – On The Move
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The American duo is moving presentations to Paris to homogenise the different offerings Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez were the darling buds of New York fashion when they launched their brand near the turn of the millennium. They have kept their freshness and enthusiasm for the rare and the raw. But this season was the last of the duo's shows in America before they move lock, stock and hand woven, laced-leather dress to Paris. "We are trying to switch the calendar up a bit - there are too many collections," said Jack, explaining the show "into which we pour our heart and soul'' was only on display for a scant six weeks. Meanwhile, as I tried to grasp whether what I had seen was mostly leather or included some plastic, Lazaro bear-hugged Raf Simons, who has moved in the opposite direction across the pond. The Belgian designer has come via Paris couture to take on the role of chief creative officer at Calvin Klein in New York. Models backstage at Proenza Schouler just have fun ... A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 13, 2017 at 11:18am PST The show might have been expected to be a dashing last hurrah, but between the weird lighting and the criss-cross runways, it was hard to tell if the pair had moved far outside their comfort zone. Proenza Schouler shows are always about craft, with the techniques and effects becoming more sophisticated each season. This time, wrapping was on the agenda: a cream top that caressed female curves with the effect of a marble sculpture. That classic piece was worn with a pair of trousers fastened deliberately askew. Proenza Schouler in action A post shared by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 13, 2017 at 11:03am PST Other dresses were as if bandaged across the body, creating slithers of other materials and colours and sometimes an opening to reveal flesh at the midriff or hipline. To match the drape and shape of the outfits, sandals were tied on with ribbons binding toes and ankles. The Proenza pair seem recently to be stuck in the same position - able to make clothes with intriguing effects, like the swirls and rivulets of fabric. Yet at the same time not really inventing a singular look that stamps their name on the clothes as effectively as "Proenza" was printed on a shearling, plastic-covered zipper jacket. Maybe the competitive Paris arena will oblige them to up their game. But in the meantime, there were many fine pieces in this show, from a perfectly simple grey woollen jacket to a navy double breasted coat - both garments illuminated with fluffy white shearling collars and silver trousers. I quizzed Jack about the fabrics and he explained that to get "an industrial vibe", they had "plasticised" shearling coats and given "guipure lace a plasticised coating". Lazaro explained that they were energised by New York, especially the recent events. "The last few weeks in New York have been so awesome with everything going on in the street here," he said, referring to the protests against President Trump. "We want to give America some love before we move to Europe," he said. This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Think wearing yellow is tricky? Take cues from these celebrities
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Sunny side up View Gallery 18 Photos Think wearing yellow is tricky? Take cues from these celebrities Whether it's in an effort to beat those winter blues or in a quest to find some cheer in the gloomy state of world affairs, sunny yellow has displayed a serious rise in popularity of late. It (tap) danced its way into our hearts when Emma Stone wore a sundress in the hue in La La Land, while the spate of celebrities favouring it on the red carpet has only strengthened its case. Associated with optimism, joy and positivity, your wardrobe will surely be happy for this addition. The prime concern, though, surrounding the colour is that it often tends to be overwhelming. So Vogue rounds up some celebrity inspiration on how to style it just right. First up, let's dispel the myth that cheery yellow is not an evening-friendly colour. A look at Deepika Padukone in that one-shouldered Ralph Lauren gown and you'll know why. With the addition of glamorous make-up, this is a look you can easily sport to your next cocktail party. But if you would rather go strapless with your gown, then add a necklace to the mix like Reese Witherspoon did at the Golden Globes this year. Channel Natalie Portman's pared-down aesthetic with a statement-sleeved maxi dress for Sunday brunch, or go all girl boss like Priyanka Chopra in a matching vest and pants. But if head-to-toe yellow has you running for the hills, then easy does it. Introduce the colour in moderate doses. A printed dress with splashes of yellow as seen on Parineeti Chopra is a safe (yet stylish) bet. As is a yellow duster thrown over jumpsuits and dresses alike, as advocated by Alia Bhatt. column1: 8 women talk about what it’s really like to be a millennial
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Life in the age of the smartphone This hashtag loving, emoji-using generation may seem narcissistic and obsessed with instant gratification, but the millennials and Gen Z are heralding a new world order—and a cooler, kinder one at that.   For starters, we have an entirely new vocabulary to describe them and what they do. They are digital natives who work in the gig economy, never having known a world without smartphones and viral connectivity. In the US alone, they are the largest generation, swiftly dethroning the Baby Boomers. And world over, each country's social currency and pop-cultural soft power is defined by this brat-pack generation, powerful in its digital universe of common ideals and egalitarianism. This generation's world view has been defined by global events experienced in real time, opinions synchronised by Instagram hashtags and Twitter handles, making their parents' generation wonder if they are indeed not millennials but Martians. Technology is embedded in their lives and has become the guiding force in the way they toggle between the digital and real worlds. Jobs? That's “so like, yesterday,” they will tell you. They do gigs, floating from one job to another, as they cross-pollinate ideas and mash up creative and professional disciplines. They live the ultimate hybrid and hyphenated lives. Constant connectivity and sharing of information and opinions on social media have allowed for a level of cultural integration never seen before. No matter which country you go to, millennials and Gen Z seem to look the same. They are tech-savvy, liberal, educated and opinionated. They are also politically progressive and deeply engaged in social issues of our times. Yet they are particularly individualistic, defining their personality in clothes and styles that make them stand out and stand up for a world of diversity and acceptance, whether you are gender-proud or gender-fluid, fashion victim or fashion activist. One of the most impactful consequences of this global connectivity is that they have a deep sense of individual worth and a singular voice, allowing them to meander through life with a strong sense of social empathy and a desire to change the world. To throw a little light into their complex world, we invited eight young peeps to ask them what sets them apart, and if their online chatter translates to offline impact. column1: #SuzyNYFW: At Calvin Klein, Raf Simons Puts America First
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The Belgian designer reveals his first vision of men’s and women's clothes for the iconic U.S. house This is not America,' announced David Bowie on the soundtrack. But oh, yes – it was! Almost every piece of the Calvin Klein collection, reconfigured and relaunched by Raf Simons, was an ode to the country where the Belgian designer now lives. There were dark blue skinny jeans – not quite as tight as Calvin's original sexpot denims from the 1980s – with ideas from the Big Country including cowboy shirts and early settlers' quilting. All this was reinforced by an installation of hanging fringes, flags and sheets of denim produced as a stage set by Los Angeles-based artist Sterling Ruby, who had previously collaborated with Simons. Brooke Shields:'nothing comes between me and ... Raf Simons at Calvin Klein! Lauren Hutton as stylish front row partner. #Calvin show. #gwynethpaltrow #calvinklein @calvinklein #ck A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 10, 2017 at 8:09am PST One of those dangling decorations included a bra – which I deciphered as a reference to the worldwide success of Calvin Klein underwear and to the infamous claim by a young Brooke Shields in 1980: ‘You want to know what comes between me and my Calvins? Nothing.' The actress sat front row, proving that beauty is eternal, while other celebrities were generous in their praise for this autumn/winter 2017 show that effectively kicked off the new international season. ‘Brilliant,' said Gwyneth Paltrow, wearing a classic tailored camel coat that was very Calvin – and very different from the experimental fabrics produced by designer Francisco Costa, who took over from Calvin Klein in 2003. BRILLIANT! said Gwyneth Paltrow as she left the Calvin Klein show wearing the streamlined look of Raf Simons at his first #Calvin show. #gwynethpaltrow #calvinklein @calvinklein #ck A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 10, 2017 at 7:59am PST I loved it- I nearly cried, said Julianne Moore of the Calvin Klein show by Raf Simons. 'As a show, it was very commercial - but it is hard to make clothes mean something - and I think he did.' #Calvin show. #gwynethpaltrow #calvinklein @calvinklein #ck A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 10, 2017 at 8:03am PST Julianne Moore said of Raf's show, ‘I loved it – I nearly cried. As a show, it was very commercial. But it is hard to make clothes mean something – and I think he did.' This was a fine and interesting show that gave promise of much more. But Simons has to decide whether he wants to follow his skill as a masculine tailor, which he showed both with male and female examples in the show. This first attempt seemed – as it should have done – to be an homage to Calvin Klein in the years his style was defined as ‘Calvin Clean,' with streamlined camel coats and a sense of a rangy, uptown American woman. But that was then, when Calvin was a design lion in the 1980s, before grunge and the ugly aesthetic and other fashion disruptions. Simons brought the Calvin cut into the new millennium with plastic encasing tailored coats and dresses; it was sometimes streamlined and glamorous, but often reminiscent of Helmut Lang, especially when wafting feathers were trapped inside the transparent plastic. Backstage, I asked about the focus on America, while Raf was introducing his team, including creative director, and formerly long-time assistant, Pieter Mulier, who took a joint bow with the designer at the end of the show. ‘I've always been thinking of America,' Raf said. ‘Now is the moment to focus on it. Energy and youth! You have to think about youth now, they are the future.' Colour was one of those prongs of youthfulness. Bright colour-blocking appeared from the deep blue shirt shown with ruby red trousers at the start, to shades of yellow, orange and of purple – say in the arms of knitted sleeves, while the front was of barely veiled transparency. Shoes with see-through fronts and wings at the back of the ankle seemed more convincing. The sexuality of the original Calvin Klein is undisputed. After his explosively successful launch of skin-tight jeans in 1978 he announced, ‘Jeans are sex – the tighter they are, the better they sell.'  The Raf Simons version of semi-nudity and plastic transparency seemed more forced, especially with cropped tops designed to rise up to expose the curve of the lower bust. The fact that the show took place in the garment district headquarters of Calvin Klein shows the commitment of the vast company to its high fashion, the seed bed of its identity. While in the recent past, the shows had seemed almost irrelevant to the progress of image and sales. Now Raf and Pieter Mulier hold a strategic position to direct all the CK products including the high-earning fragrance and underwear. This would seem an impossible task to achieve in the first six months, but it has the promise of a wide commercial platform. In this collection, the Raf Simons menswear – always his strength – looked good and so did the streamlined tailoring for women, such as a trouser suit in Prince of Wales check with a modern shaping and a purposeful attitude. This concept of a female closet may not be new. But in this era of female force in America, when a disappointed community of women has given an aggressive response to their new President, the idea of the tailored suit, so beloved by Hillary Clinton, is not a foolish offering. Yet the Raf Simons period, like that of President Trump, is just beginning in America. And after this reasonably successful start, time will tell whether this designer ‘gets' the dis-United States and can re-create a fashion empire for Calvin Klein.
