column1: #SuzyNYFW: Alexander Wang’s ‘Night of Treason’
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A rebellious collection, clashing together strong women and street power, shakes up a Harlem theatre As the women stomped out – along the metallic, intersecting tracks and under the theatre's majestic but crumbling dome – their legs announced in white letters on black hose: ‘No after party.' In the even more decrepit back stage area, Alexander Wang's sweat top had the same message, as he hugged Zoë Kravitz, Mexican model of the moment Issa Lish and glitter toothed Harlem-native, rapper ASAP Ferg. WOW FOR WANG - and his empowered women. With Zoe Kravitz A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 11, 2017 at 7:55pm PST   WOW FOR WANG! And his STREET POWER. Alexander with rapper ASAP Ferg A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 11, 2017 at 7:53pm PST ‘Power – street power!' said Wang, surrounded by a group of scowling models in their crystal-edged coats, black mesh tops and stretch skirts hung with metallic shards. Striding down the runway, the effect was of anger and rage; of powerful women who were dangerous with it. These ideas were not so new for an Alexander Wang collection: the pent-up rage, the ‘don't mess with me' attitude and the sporty black outfits worked in varied depths of colour from sleek leather to semi-sheer hose. Tailoring in Prince of Wales check gave a mannish angle to these female cohorts and showed the designer balancing street style with outfits for the office.   Yet there was something different about the scene enacted under the peeling cupola of Harlem's Hamilton Theater. Let's call it post-Trump attitude. There is no doubt that a wide swathe of women feels enraged and let down by the result of the US election. Even if Wang only amped up the anger coming from his familiar vision of strong women, it gave the clothes a new twist. ‘No After party' surely suggested that there might be no reason to celebrate Punk was, after all, born in England three decades ago out of politics, with Margaret Thatcher's United Kingdom divided into an ‘Us' and an enraged ‘Them.' New for Wang was the broad-shouldered tailoring of the 1980s, although that probably reflected Vetements and that brand's take on Martin Margiela. These references are in the current fashion air. So are the touches of the American west: fringed twin breast pockets, studs and rhinestone cowboy decoration. They gave a freshness to street looks. The fashion statement was clear – even if the clothes had been removed from the spectacle of the venue, with its full-on rap music and the all-standing crowd dividing their attention between bags with heavy metal handles, studded boots and the flaking paint crumbling like powdery confetti from the majestic dome. For all the business-like tailoring, including coats and jackets, always drawn from a wide shoulder line with lapels ending, 1980s-style, at the stomach, there was a plethora of party gear. That included plunging cleavage, leather boots rising to the thighs and that ‘No After Party' message crawling up the sheer black hose. A statement from the designer or a reference to the day the United States changed its political allegiance? And what was this T-shirt message ‘Night of Treason'? A tribute to the current punk band as 1970s revivalists? Or a red-hot memory of the moment America voted against a female president? Sometimes fashion speaks louder than words – even when it's competing for attention with decibels of heavy sound. column1: #SuzyNYFW: Victoria Beckham – Empowering Women
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A stronger identity was offered by covering the body, colouring the clothes and drawing on British heritage fabrics Freedom, confidence, power – strength, reality, and identity.' Who expressed these words to define her work? Victoria Beckham. In a collection that pushed forward her aim to make clothes that are winners for women, the designer showed a new confidence in linking her looks to her native Britain – using heritage fabrics, thick knits and even tartan – but styled with her own international experience of the requirements of a streamlined wardrobe in mind. The result was based on tailoring ‘light' – literally when a chiffon or georgette skirt swing mid-calf below a smart flannel jacket. Or when a vivid red dress that covered the body from neck to calf was teamed with over-the-knee boots with a light wedge. There were even flat pointed toe shoes with a hint of a punk winkle picker to them – and this from a woman who once relied on perilous high heels. How tall is the high VB boot? A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 12, 2017 at 12:01pm PST ‘I feel that I've been talking about empowering women for so many years and never was there a time when that was more relevant with what's going on in the world,' said the designer. ‘For me and my customer, what I believe is that she wants to feel secure and comfortable. For me, it was also looking at my heritage: you can see we've got heritage fabrics here in the houndstooth and tartan. British – but with a global outlook.' Victoria was referring to a camel trouser suit or a grey swing coat with bulbous sleeves and also to a more unexpected insertion: abstract patterns in bright colours inspired by a visit to the paintings of Paul Nash in London's Tate Britain – the first time I can remember a Victoria Beckham show referencing art. But each season, it seems that Victoria's vision grows a little. And like all women designers she absorbs her life changes into her collections. One strategic move for her company must be the highly successful make-up collaboration with Estée Lauder: the cue to a square handbag looking like a vanity case. Did the Victoria Beckham collection with its rich, soft colours and lean shapes alter the face of modern fashion? Not in any major way. But the designer is clearly sensing the changing attitudes of women and linking that to her collections. And the fact that there was not a single outfit aimed expressly at the evening – meaning that you would have to get back from work to change – was significant from a designer who once relied on celebrity status. David Beckham and family come to cheer on the Victoria Beckham show. A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 12, 2017 at 8:00am PST The softly, softly approach to moving forward is good for brand Beckham. And so is the sense that there are family values rooted within Team Beckham – Brooklyn, Romeo, Cruz and their sister Harper were sitting with dad David Beckham in the front row. Brooklyn was focused on his camera, after a period of studying photography in New York. Those who want to study the skills of this next Beckham generation will be able to buy Brooklyn's book of images, titled What I See and published by Penguin, in May. column1: Iconic artisan jeweller Fabergé comes to India
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Here’s more about the legendary brand View Gallery 6 Photos Iconic artisan jeweller Fabergé comes to India You've probably come across Fabergé eggs in heist movies where one inevitably gets stolen. If you are lucky, you may have seen a couple in museums. What's the fuss about a decorated egg? As the artisan jewellers behind those fabled eggs come to India, here's a quick recap of its history. A Fabergé egg is perhaps one of the most valuable collectibles in the world. Legend goes, Tsar Alexander III of Russia commissioned Peter Carl Fabergé to create a special Easter egg for his wife Empress Maria Feodorovna. Instead of your average chocolate variety, this was made from precious metals and gemstones, thus starting the tradition of gifting meticulously crafted eggs as opulent tokens of appreciation. Fifty such eggs were commissioned by the Russian Empire, which later came to be called ‘Imperial Fabergé Eggs' and only 43 of them have survived. Since the times of Maharajas, India has always held a place of interest for Fabergé. In 1903, Maharaja Sir Pratab Singh Bahadur of Jammu and Kashmir commissioned a crystal stamp holder by Fabergé. The Maharaja of Bikaner gifted a presentation box by the iconic jeweller to Queen Mary in 1937. “Fabergé strikes a deep chord with the customs and cultures of India. The rarity inherent in reflecting individual expressions of inspiration and style, echoes deeply cherished Indian traditions,” said Sean Gilberston, CEO, Fabergé. Today the brand works with Gemfields—the world's leading supplier of ethically-sourced gemstones—to create it luxury products, which now also include jewellery and watches. Fabergé will be bringing the objects d'art, jewellery and timepieces to India. Available to view on request and by appointment only, via Gemfields. column1: This Indian company is embellishing garments for Gucci and Margiela
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Discreetly but proudly, Mumbai wears the halo of haute couture A tide of workers heading home in this crowded Indian city, cars honking, trucks painted as vividly as the colours of the saris, cows wandering past makeshift stalls, and then – POW! – a serpent wrapped round a tiger fighting for its life. A tiger? In Mumbai? I am facing a wall of birds, butterflies, flowers, and jungle creatures from which I immediately recognise the tiger embroidered on the back of my own Gucci coat. So I have traced my @Gucci tiger to Mumbai - and the #Chanakya family-owned embroidery business that Alessandro Michele loves. #suzyinmumbai @vogueindia. To read the story I have written - link in Bio A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 6, 2017 at 2:24am PST   “My father, Vinod Maganlal Shah, started the business in 1984 to bring the finest craftsmanship to the world – and we have been working with fashion houses in Italy for a long time,” says Managing Director Karishma Swali who, with her sister-in-law Monica Shah and Karishma's brother Nehal Vinod Shah, is now running the teams of hand-embroiderers for the family company, Chanakya.   Don't miss my story about Karishma Swali and Monica Shah and how their Indian family company #Chanakya creates couture embroidery for designers across the world. suzyinmumbai @vogueindia. To read the story I have written - LINK IN BIO A video posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 6, 2017 at 2:00am PST   “I think what brought all of us here is wanting to keep the arts alive,” says Karishma as she showed me treasured historic pieces with real gold thread from the era of Moguls and Maharajahs; and then displayed Chanakya's resolutely modern handwork. That included embroidery worked into three-dimensional pieces from re-cycled tins, foam mattresses, and even DVDs cut in to fine strips. The rubber, silicone, and industrial materials re-appear as high fashion in the collections of Maison Margiela or Gucci's “Go Green” collections (which are part of its parent company Kering's Science Based Targets Initiative to reduce its greenhouse emissions).   Garbage drink cans re-cycled as embroidery by Monica Shah at #Chanakya in Mumbai. #suzyinmumbai @vogueindia A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 6, 2017 at 4:47am PST “We have always been passionate about ‘Go Green', so we used different recycled materials – for example, Coke cans that we flattened and cut up – and Moschino produced a huge collection all with recycled materials,” Monica says. “Margiela does it with passion – they make sure they have it season after season. They hound us!” Since the two women have their own brand, Jade – using the family's people skills to create fashionable clothes and serve the vast Indian wedding market – they understand the demands of international high fashion and have built relationships with leading designers – going back more than two decades in the case of Maria Grazia Chiuri, now the Artistic Director of Christian Dior. Maria Grazia of @Dior and previously #Valentino met the Indian family of #Chanakya nearly 30 years ago when she worked on the #Fendi 'baguette'. #suzyinmumbai @vogueindia @fendi #dior READ MY STORY. LINK IN BIO. A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 6, 2017 at 4:26am PST On the table I see a book on the first fashion “It” bag – the Fendi “Baguette”, which debuted in 1997, devised by Silvia Fendi and the then-unknown Maria Grazia, who had started her fashion career at Fendi in 1989 in the accessories department. “I started working with India 28 years ago,” the Dior designer said when I asked her about the Chanakya connection, and she recalled her first meeting with the family and its founder, Nehal Vinod Shah, when she was 25 yeas old. Plastic fantastic as re-cycled embroidered fabric from #Chanakya in Mumbai. #suzyinmumbai @vogueindia READ MY STORY. Link in BIO A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 6, 2017 at 4:48am PST “They are so special because they are such a good image of India – they love the handwork and they care about recycling. They work hard to study, to understand European culture,” Maria Grazia continued, adding that the family's Jain religion was another source of interest to her. “I'm sure you have sat in the studios where the men are and they don't look like they are overworked – they look quite happy.” I had indeed visited the handwork “factory” where the embroiderers are all male, which is the tradition in India. Although I promised not to reveal anything about the new collections, I watched the embroiderers, who sit at floor benches, working on pieces for Gucci's Alessandro Michele and other mostly Italian designers such as Alberta Ferretti. Sewing bead embroideries for Alberta Ferretti. #suzyinmumbai @vogueindia READ MY STORY. Link in bio A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 6, 2017 at 4:34am PST Embroiderers at work in Mumbai. This is traditionally the world of the Indian male - but #Chanakya want to start a school to train women. #suzyinmumbai @vogueindia A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 6, 2017 at 4:32am PST One team of workers, who all wear a uniform of white shirts, had their fingers on tiny, translucent beads that were laid out in patterns with thread across black chiffon. “The embroiderers work entirely by hand with the most sophisticated techniques, and over the years I have learnt to trust them implicitly,” said Ferretti, who explained that Chanakya was the principal embroidery supplier to her parent company Aeffe for more than 20 years. “They understand my requests, which are always very specific and precise, and more often than not they come back with embroideries that exceed my original expectations,” the designer explained. “Chanakya has such a natural sense of colour and a talent for use of materials, which shines through their exquisite creations. I feel it must be an innate part of their rich culture.” The family-owned Indian company has built more than a relationship with Italian designers. It has an office and showroom in Bologna, which includes some displays of heritage garments to give a visual understanding of the subcontinent's rich and rare history in lavishly embellished clothing. There is also a display area in New York, where Ralph Lauren and Tory Burch have shown interest. Where did those @Gucci embroiderers for Alessandro Michele and Jared Leto come from? From hand workers for #Chanakya in Mumbai. #suzyinmumbai @vogueindia #Gucci #jaredleto. Read my story! LINK IN BIO A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 6, 2017 at 2:02am PST But what about the future? Europe once had an exceptional embroidery tradition, as evidenced by Opus Anglicanum - the extraordinary mediaeval embroidery exhibition held recently at the Victoria & Albert Museum in London, as well as many other historical embroidery displays across the world. The noble heritage of Indian embellishment in a historic private collection of #Chanakya in #Mumbai. #suzyinmumbai @vogueindia READ MY STORY. Link in bio. A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Feb 6, 2017 at 4:54am PST   The Chanakya family is thinking about how to support embroidery in India, and will found a school either in Bengal – where most of their embroiderers come from – or in the village of Kutch in their ancestral home of Gujarat, in western India, where craftsmen have not received much exposure to international design. “So far, embroiderers are all men,” Karishma says, “but women are now ready to start, not only from their homes, but also officially. I am excited to do something where kids can get an education, but we also get embroidery. Sadly, we have a lot of grandfathers and fathers, but their sons are moving on to computers and technology. The artisanry is getting lost. So we are determined to do something by 2018.” “You will not believe how fashion-forward the village women are – their patterns, colours, and designs you could use today,” Karishma reveals. “And they won't think twice before telling you if things work – saying a colour is not a good idea and sticking to aubergine and orange! If you gain their respect and they see you are there for them, they are incredibly open and happy to learn new techniques.” And just in case Chanakya is short of new recruits, Karishma's 10-year-old daughter is already on-message. She comes each Saturday and helps teach the children of the embroiderers to make their own handwork – the ultimate example of Indian family companies keeping the flag flying. column1: New York Fashion Week 2017: CFDA to support Planned Parenthood
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Sartorial solidarity The Council of Fashion Designers of America have announced they will be supporting Planned Parenthood in the United States. The CFDA hope to raise awareness of President Trump's executive order which will defund the organisation. Capitalising on the increased attention the fashion industry is awarded during New York Fashion Week, the CFDA will distribute pins that read "Fashion Stands with Planned Parenthood" — meaning we can expect to see many of them on the front row and street style set, come next week. There are also hopes the pins will also generate talk on social media using the hashtag #IStandWithPP. In a press release, CFDA board member Tracy Reese said "by creating a visually engaging and fashionable pin, we hope to create an organic social media movement promoting awareness and education.” Each pin will be accompanied by a card that explains how people can get involved and facts demonstrating the importance of Planned Parenthood. "We know that so many people stand with Planned Parenthood — including designers and entertainers — because they and their loved ones have relied on Planned Parenthood for health care, including life-saving care like cancer screenings, birth control, STI testing and treatment and sex education,” Reese said. “Planned Parenthood is often the only option for this type of care in under served communities." Over 40 labels have already signed on to participate in the initiative include DVF, Carolina Herrera, Proenza Schouler, Narciso Rodriguez and Prabal Gurung. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Style lessons to swear by Whether it's her superlative acting chops, endearing Instagram feed, or ability to take a joke, there is no denying that our February cover girl, Alia Bhatt, knows how to make things work for her. Over the past couple of years, not only has she carved her niche in the industry, but has found her fashion voice too—youthful, breezy and experimental from time to time, but always effortless. One look at Bhatt's repertoire, and you know that dresses are a mainstay in her wardrobe. Her Instagram bio describes her as ‘moody'. Let's just say her choice of dresses is too. We've decoded Bhatt's aesthetic. [#gallery: /galleries/5ce44ab31739e7b5162fe839]||| ||| The right occasion From outbound flights and red carpet appearances to swanky fashion parties and movie promotions, Bhatt demonstrates that it's never a bad time to wear a dress. The trick lies in styling it right. A solid-coloured maxi button-down dress with a backpack and sneakers will keep you comfortable as you hop on a flight, and a sequinned blazer dress is guaranteed to get you the spotlight at a glamorous do. Silhouettes, cuts and hues Yet again, nothing is off-limits for our cover girl. The idea is to give every style a go and find the ones that work best for you. The actor has been spotted in a versatile range of silhouettes like shift, sheath, anti-fit, drop waist, and fit-and-flare among others. Not one to restrict herself to a particular end of the spectrum, Bhatt believes in having her fun with colours. You will spot her in siren red and bottle green as often as blush pink and pristine white. Black and blue are the darker tones she is drawn to. Standing out in your dress How does one stand out in a room full of dress-clad ladies? Bhatt's stylebook shows that it's by picking a dress that boasts one ingenious element. Drop waists and tulip hemlines, knife pleats, dramatic ruffled sleeves, a slogan, a smart print—a cutesy cat, floral or graphic—appliqué work, and texture play such as lace overlay over pinstripes have her vote. Styling tricks Just like her demeanour, the actress prefers fuss-free styling when it comes to her dresses. Loose waves and dewy make-up never disappoint. The footwear, however, needs to be a conversation-starter—think tan brogues, metallic sneakers, pop coloured pumps, and even mismatched heels. Jewellery is optional. Formal vs casual According to Bhatt, shift and sheath dresses in fun colours and playful prints are a no-brainer when you're aiming for a youthful vibe. An androgynous blazer dress or strapless number with sleek hair and smoky eyes works best after hours, while formal occasions call for voluminous, thigh-grazing fit-and-flare dresses. After all, it's never a bad idea to channel your inner princess. Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The making of Veena Reddy’s dramatic sangeet gown
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Designer Gaurav Gupta breaks it down View Gallery 6 Photos The making of Veena Reddy’s dramatic sangeet gown Keshav and Veena Reddy's grand wedding was certainly to be one of the most lavish social events of 2017. The sangeet alone was attended by the likes of Shilpa Shetty Kundra, Manish Malhotra, Sooraj Pancholi and Raveena Tandon, and featured a performance by Ranveer Singh. For the event, Veena Reddy wore a stunning crimson gown designed by Gaurav Gupta. The family met with Gupta at his Kala Ghoda store where it was decided that Reddy's look for the evening had to make a statement. “I took out what I love the most from my sculpted collections as a reference and then scribbled this abstract shape,” said the designer of his futuristic creation. “The bodycon fit flatters her figure and the abstract waves at the bottom form a fantastical sculpture. It is one of my favourites now!” Reddy accessorised the look with a diamond-and-emerald necklace and earrings. Naturally, Keshav matched his bowtie to the colour of her gown for a hint of coordination. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: You need to watch out for Fendi’s cool new digital platform
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Attention all millennials View Gallery 6 Photos You need to watch out for Fendi’s cool new digital platform Italian luxury brand Fendi draws from its craftsmanship deep rooted in heritage, but it's not stuck in the past. Their newest campaign, ‘F is for Fendi', aims at creating an online community for and by millennials to create a network of like-minded people. The brand will roll out this campaign at on-ground events followed by an app, which will bring members of the community closer. Fendi will work towards highlighting underground artists and musical talent through the campaign. The different communities within the larger group are named Freaks, Fulgore, Faces, Freedom and Fearless, and will span fashion, travel and influencers. column1: Kareena Kapoor Khan back on the Lakmé Fashion Week runway for Anita Dongre
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Details from the grand finale Last time Kareena Kapoor Khan walked for the Lakmé Fashion Week finale, she was expecting her first child. Her next appearance on the runway comes barely two months after her delivery, closing for Anita Dongre's finale show last evening. Anita Dongre and Kareena Kapoor Khan are proof that women can balance groundbreaking careers with a fulfilled family life—and they're inspiring women through their example. Kapoor Khan, a multiple award-winning actor, breezed through endorsements, runway shows and TV appearances throughout her pregnancy. On the other hand, Dongre is one of the few women at the top of the business, and presenting the grand finale at Lakmé Fashion Week was an honour long overdue for the designer. Bearing in mind Lakmé's theme of liquid gold, Dongre's collection was titled ‘Alchemy'. The 60-piece collection focused on the chanderi fabric laced in the designer's signature gota patti work in silhouettes both contemporary and ethnic. Dongre's vision of gold wasn't an overpoweringly gilded deduction of the theme, but closer in resemblance to the glow emitted from the metal. The elaborate show was staged at the amphitheatre at Bandra Fort, a venue close to the designer's heart. Dongre only altered the setting by adding a touch of green to the environment, as simple glass votives hung from trees. Kapoor Khan is the face of Anita Dongre's high street workwear label AND, and it's safe to say that the two women in the spotlight yesterday already share a strong relationship. The designer's son Yash Dongre now works with her and the two women have exchanged notes about raising children without losing the focus on their careers. Last night was a clear example that working women can have their cake and it eat it too. In all, the show left us hoping to see more women in deserving positions of power in the future. column1: Highlights from Day 5 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The best for the last There is such a thing as fashion fatigue and those who attend fashion week religiously commonly suffer from it. Naturally the last day is greeted with euphoria and there's always the spectacle of the finale to look forward to. Here's what you missed from Day 5 of Lakmé Fashion Week. View Gallery 7 Photos Highlights from Day 5 of Lakmé Fashion Week Divya Reddy Malaika Arora Khan walked the runway for Divya Reddy. The actor chose a chartreuse and red lehenga from Reddy's ‘Shahibzadi' collection. Khan's Instagram handle proves she is fashion junkie and spoke about Lakmé Fashion Week being an important platform that supports emerging talent. You can watch the video below. Gaurang Shah Gaurang Shah may not have shown on Textile Day, but that doesn't affect his status as one of the country's most leading designers championing the cause of textile revival. This season Shah focused on muslin—the most basic of fabrics often used to create toiles in designer workshops. Parsi gara embroidery and chikankari was used extensively through the line. The collection also included fabrics like kota, muga silk and organza. Shah's prowess lies in his knowledge of materials and how seamlessly he moves from the use of one to another, which came through this season. Tabu walked the runway for the designer. Anita Dongre Anita Dongre closed summer/resort 2017 with a grand finale show. The collection titled ‘Alchemy' drew inspiration from the glistening deserts of Rajasthan. Dongre used her signature gota patti work on lightweight fabrics on contemporary silhouettes. This was the first time the designer presented a finale collection at Lakmé Fashion Week. The venue was the amphitheater in the Bandra Fort, and the decor was minimal yet elegant. New mum Kareena Kapoor Khan walked down the runway in a white dress highlighted with gold embroidery, paired with a long jacket. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How to wear fuchsia this season no matter what your budget
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Go bright or go home As working theories of how to wear colour go, Barbara Cartland had a diverting one. Strong people like strong colour, beige people like beige, and no Englishwoman should wear beige or brown because it makes her look like a baked potato, the romantic novelist told The Observer in 1983. She, naturally, stuck to “Cartland pink” for most of her life, a shocking shade she wore head-to-toe – painted lips included. Take her as your muse for spring – vivid pink is enough to send shock waves through anyone's winter wardrobe malaise. From Valentino's body-swamping fuchsia cape-dress (styled with red tights and shoes) to Ralph Lauren Collection's tactile multi-pink proposition, to Balenciaga's shrink-wrapped boots and shocking pink combo – brazen and head-to-toe is best. And for everyone else there's Miu Miu's divine velvet shoulder-bag. Shop Vogue's edit of the best fuchsia pieces to buy immediately. column1: You need to keep a watch out for Nimish Shah’s collaboration with SpiceJet
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A whole lot of red Dressing for the airport has been a big focus for celebrities of late. Kareena Kapoor Khan, Kangana Ranaut, Sonam Kapoor and Jacqueline Fernandes have all championed travel wardrobes that marry utility and comfort with style, with the former two often spotted in Shift by Nimish Shah. View Gallery 4 Photos You need to keep a watch out for Nimish Shah’s collaboration with SpiceJet The Mumbai-based designer has now taken airport style to next the level, and has designed a collection for SpiceJet's crew. Shah was first approached by the airline a year ago, and after months of presentations and fittings, the uniforms were finalised: short shift dresses, sling bags and box heels for women from the cabin crew, and three-piece suits with a red waistcoat, white shirt and lace up oxford shoes for the men. On ground, women staffers will be seen in a button-back blouse in white and red polka dots paired with mini skirt suits. Shah's brief was very precise—the look has to “bring back the oomph factor, making aviation visually aspirational again,” he says. SpiceJet has “a very young enterprising vibe across the company and I had to take that forward,” he tells us. Aside from the design aspect, the designer had to also keep the functionality of the uniforms in mind. “For me, the maintenance of the uniform was key, they were wearing three-piece suits until now. Moving to a shift dress did the trick, along with easy-to-iron fabrics.” The biggest challenge however, was the brand's colour scheme, “There is very little that matches with red that has already not been done before and they were very clear about no caricature elements like hats, scarves and belts,” Shah explains. The end results are uniforms inspired by modern minimalism that are fuss-free and utilitarian. Debojo Maharishi, chief marketing officer, SpiceJet Limited, says of the new range, “[they have been] meticulously designed to amplify the brand values of SpiceJet while giving a more contemporary look in line with the global standards.” And Shah agrees. “This project was a grand undertaking, not least because of the pride associated with it but also [because it was] highlighting the ambassadors of the brand.” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights from Day 4 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A night of many returns The fourth day of Lakmé Fashion Week saw Nupur Kanoi and Savio Jon back on the schedule, while Padma Lakshmi retuned to the runway to walk for close friend Tarun Tahiliani. Here are our favourite shows from the day and all the action you missed. View Gallery 15 Photos Highlights from Day 4 of LFW Rara Avis by Sonal Verma Vogue India Fashion Fund finalist Sonal Verma of label Rara Avis was one of the few designers whose collection this season instantly spelled out summer/resort fashion. Verma's fresh palette of pastels was accented with bold red and cerulean tones. Wide-legged trousers, paperback waist skirts, oversized jackets and handful of evening dresses formed the line-up, which was clearly aimed at the modern traveller. Light embellishments were spotted on some of the layered ensembles in motifs of seashells and cacti, which brought obvious visuals of summer to mind. Verma's collections are never without the use of leather and this season was punctuated with soft suede belts, necklaces and tassels—subtle but effective detailing which puts Verma ahead of the pack. Nupur Kanoi Nupur Kanoi's name may have been missing on the fashion week line-up for a few seasons, but there was no mistaking the words ‘strong show' being used to describe her presentation, ‘Lost and Found in Africa', right after the show ended. Her collection was inspired by the body tattooing and piercing rituals from Africa that were depicted by way of tie-dye and embellishments. One half of Kanoi's line-up focused on tie-dye on ombre backdrops, creating an optical illusion, while the second half focused on embellishments on grey. Aside from functionality, what makes a garment wearable is the feel good factor it offers. Sexy sells—a fact that is not lost on Kanoi. Outhouse Jewellery designers Sasha and Kaabia Grewal of Outhouse narrated the transformation of the caterpillar into the butterfly in their collection ‘Imago'. The designers spoke about the cathartic process of growing up, battling changes and struggles that eventually define our adult identities metaphorically by way of the butterfly. Outhouse has been leading the fashion jewellery market in India for the last few years and is careful to create as many ready-to-wear pieces each season as the more theatrical ones. Savio Jon Goa-based designer Savio Jon Fernandes returned to the runway with his label Savio Jon after several years. Fernandes is not one to be moved by passing trends; in fact he refused to refer to his collection as a collection, but rather chose to describe it as a "wardrobe". The designer used buttons from the 1930s that are no longer in production, batiks collected over the years, raffia, signature layered architectural silhouettes, light quilting as part of the collection. Will he be a part of regular fashion weeks to come? One will never know, but you sure can count on it being standout show when he chooses to. Tarun Tahiliani Tarun Tahiliani is so ahead of the season cycle, that the garments that were shown on the ramp last night were already in the stores. The entire collection is bound to stagger through the rest of the spring/summer season but all of the pieces are already available to pre-order. Tahiliani spoke of returning to some of the label's quintessential basics like draping and florals in this collection. The ready-to-wear separates were no doubt aimed at a premium buyer who can appreciate the fine detailing in tone-on-tone ivory, the luxury of an anarkali that doesn't weigh you down and recognise that lehengas worn with shirts doesn't take away from the dressiness of ethnic wear. Author, chef and actress Padma Lakshmi returned to the runway nearly after a decade and both opened and closed the show for Tahilani. The designer said that Lakshmi wasn't the muse for the collection, but rather someone who embodied the spirit of it. International Woolmark Prize Regional winners of last year's International Woolmark Prize—Nachiket Barve and Zubair and Renni Kirmani of Bounipun announced this year's contenders today. Aneeth Arora of Péro, Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice, Ujjawal Dubey of Antar Agni and Nitin Chawla of Theorem will be participating in the International Woolmark Prize competition this year. column1: Padma Lakshmi returns to the runway at Lakmé Fashion Week S/R 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Can’t miss this Author, chef and actor Padma Lakshmi returned to the runway after nearly after a decade and both opened and closed the show for Tarun Tahilani. The designer elaborated on his choice of showstopper saying that Lakshmi wasn't the muse for the collection, but rather someone who embodied the spirit of it. Goa-based designer Savio Jon Fernandes of label Savio Jon also made a fashion week comeback after several years. Fernandes is not one to be moved by passing trends; in fact he refused to refer to his collection as a collection, but rather chose to describe it as a "wardrobe". Jewellery designers Sasha and Kaabia Grewal of Outhouse narrated the transformation of the caterpillar into the butterfly in their collection ‘Imago' with which they launched their couture line. The designers spoke about the cathartic process of growing up, battling changes and struggles that eventually define our adult identities metaphorically by way of the butterfly. column1: Highlights from Day 3 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Everything you need to know View Gallery 18 Photos LFW Day 3 Highlights From Falguni and Shane Peacock's glamorous return to the runway to Payal Singhal's murder mystery-inspired collection, here's what you missed on Day 3 of Lakmé Fashion Week. Chola Flouncy frill, dramatic layers, over-sized pussybows—Sohaya Misra's line-up came packed with old-school charm. While the designer stayed true to her fluid aesthetic, her collection, which found its inspiration in geometric lines and old Moroccan tiles, also saw bold, structured silhouettes. Singer Anushka Manchanda walked the ramp as showstopper. Amoh by Jade Monica Shah and Karishma Swali's collection ‘Amaat' (Sanskrit for boundless qualities) was designed keeping in mind the fast-paced millennial woman. With the likes of capes, corsets and off-the-shoulder blouses featuring intricate embroidery, the duo managed to strike the perfect balance between traditional and contemporary. Coral, crimson and ivory made for a striking colour palette. SVA by Paras and Sonam Modi The charm of celebrated dancer Noor was the inspiration for designers Sonam and Paras Modi this season. Their inherently regal line featured a slew of traditional silhouettes in hues like burnt rose and burl wood. Rich silk and satin added to the decadence of the designs. Nimrat Kaur brought the show to a close in an ornate red and gold lehenga. Payal Singhal Payal Singhal's collection ‘Lady M', took its cues from Agatha Christie's murder mystery Death on the Nile. Chandeliers and the soundtrack of La La Land set the mood for elaborate creations inspired by the high society glamour of the late 1930s. Singhal's signature silhouettes and embroidery put an unexpected spin on designs otherwise characteristic of the period. When it came to colours, the designer experimented with deep hues like midnight blue as well as soft shades like rose and ivory. Label by Ritu Kumar Who says military-inspired fashion is just about muted hues and chunky army boots? Case in point: Label by Ritu Kumar's latest collection ‘Maharaja Pop'. At the show, models marched down the ramp clad in everything from high-shine cargo pants to vibrant, embroidered army jackets. Vaani Kapoor played showstopper in a sheer bodysuit and floral bomber jacket. Falguni Shane Peacock The closing act for the day was by designers Falguni and Shane Peacock, who returned to the runway after a six-year hiatus. The duo turned up the heat with their risqué cocktail collection ‘Rebel' made of sheer unitards, curve-hugging dresses and bodysuits. Finishing touches came in the form of dazzling crystal work and feather detailing. Bipasha Basu concluded the show in a floor-sweeping gown. Fashion Fashion Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Bipasha Basu and Vaani Kapoor at Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Catch them in our video recap The third day of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2017 saw a host of celebrities walking the runways for designers. Falguni and Shane Peacock returned to the Indian runway after six years with their collection ‘Rebel'. Bipasha Basu, who was the show stopper found her caped gown equal parts glamorous and edgy. Payal Singhal's Art Deco-inspired collection took elements from the era and used them in contemporary Indian silhouettes. Diana Penty walked for the designer in a blush and gold embroidered lehenga and blouse. Label by Ritu Kumar's ‘Maharaja Pop' collection was again a contemporary version of costumes of royal India. Vaani Kapoor, who closed the show for the label spoke about the wearability of the garments and how they appeal to a wide age group. Amoh by Jade's collection was called ‘Amaat', which means infinite possibilities. Swara Bhaskar walked for the label.   Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights from Day 2 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Inside Sustainable Fashion and Textile Day View Gallery 29 Photos Day 2 highlights The Sustainable Fashion and Textile Day at Lakmé Fashion Week continued strengthening its alignment with style that is contextual to this land. If there was a time when this event was far removed from the real concerns and challenges of the common people's sartorial choices, well, that time is over. The narrative now is that of inclusion, in a space where the daunting unease over tonnes of fashion waste, concerns of weavers in handloom industry or the delicate issue of norms of beauty have become mainstream talking points. The ‘Reincarnations' show was an attempt to tackle fashion's dubious distinction of being the second largest polluting industry after oil. Designers Shubhi Sachan of Jambudweep and Smriti Dixit, the label Wandering Whites, and initiatives I was a Sari and The Stitching Project—all working with upcycling—showcased myriad ways in which non-biodegradable landfill waste can be repurposed back into our lives as things of beauty. The humble khadi was shown in highly luxurious form by Sailesh Singhania with real zari and intricate, whimsically woven squirrels, deer, cranes and birds. House of Milk delved in the concept of wellness with non-toxic fabric treated in soothing Ayurvedic herbs. The line was in white with clever cuts that would suit all body shapes. Galang Gabaan from Odisha featured easy to wear separates, made with hand-spun cotton in natural dyes in timeless stripes/checks, and elusive saris made by the Santhal tribe. Indigene continues on sustainable style with a Boro-inspired line to create lovely surface textures with buttons, strips and trims from leftover fabric. Handwoven sari found love again in Naushad Ali's line that efficiently uses the 5.5-metre yardage to create garments with folds, drapes and stitched details. It's easy to get overwhelmed by textile and its techniques, but Padmaja infuses playful joy in her line through soothing pastels, easy to wear cuts and amazing textile woven by Women Weaves. Sanjukta Dutta continued on her path of making the mekhela chador a part of the festive wear of the country rather than being just the ceremonial garment of a state. The saris showcased traditional weaving patterns in celebratory colours; Preity Zinta closed the show in a bright red, black and gold number. Playing with deep contrasts and various types of hand-weaving from all over India, Amrich created his adorable, sustainable, wearable line. The synergy of the designer and the artisan in Sayantan Sarkar's show was palpable. He inspired weavers who had left their craft and taken up construction labour jobs to re-embrace their 1,500 abandoned looms in Coochbehar. The garments are nurturing in their yellows as the rising sun of the Bengal. To add value to the weavers' craft is second nature to Soham Dave's design sensibility. Yarns were experimented on and Chanderi was hand-printed with ajrakh for his line. He maintained his signature of fuss free garments made with an eye on creating charming details. Kutch has been a nurturing place for myriad forms of weaving, printing, dying and embroidery. The expansive Artisans of Kutch Show created a flavourful line-up that showcased the region's many facets. Shrujan has brought back countless forgotten patterns of embroidery into existence and gives employment to thousands of women. In its many innovate approaches, one of note is the ‘Shrujan Bus' which would travel from village to village with framed pieces of fabric with traditional embroidery. The creations were a joy to see on the ramp. The Khatri community has been the keeper of ajrakh for over nine generations. Noted master craftsman Sufiyan Khatri showcased his heritage craft in garments made with intricate techniques. Kala cotton does not need litres of water but is tough to drape. Craftsman Chaman Siju took on this challenge to showcase pretty versions of these eco-friendly saris, woven in charming patterns. Judy Frater, founder and director of Somaiya Kala Vidya, has mentored a generation of artisans to help them realise the greatness of their inherent craft. The garments showcased on the runway were created by the empowered students of this school. The Sustainable Man show by Péro, Rajesh Pratap Singh and Abraham & Thakore showcased options for Indian men who wish to align with the ethos of sustainability and yet want to retain a quirky, fun style. Péro proposes light garments crafted with khadi, adorably detailed to combine sporty with tailored. ‘Recycle' was the dominant message in Rajesh Pratap Singh's chic garments, woven with yarns made out of bottles and damaged cloth. The concept of pre-owned is not finding too many takers, but post this show, worn would be seen as pre-loved and would connect better with the man who is open to experimentation. Abraham & Thakore repurposed garment production waste and gave direction on ways to stylishly recycle and upcycle. The easy tailoring made for cool dressing inside out. The real people on the ramp for this show added to the realness of the garments, making the statement that sustainable fashion is an option that can be adopted by all. column1: Priyanka Chopra talks about her most prized piece of jewellery
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The new face of Nirav Modi on memories, fashion and future plans Crossover stardom, it seems, is not just limited to the stars. In just a few years, Nirav Modi's eponymous Indian jewellery brand has seen international success in New York, London and Macau. Seeing how global domination in on their agenda, getting Priyanka Chopra on board to be the face of the jewellery label seems like the obvious choice. For the brand's latest advertising campaign, Chopra stars in a timely commercial (Valentine's Day's almost here) with Sidharth Malhotra. The video sees Malhotra struggling to pull off the perfect proposal for Chopra, who, coincidentally, has just resolved to stop saying yes—of course, some hilarity and feels ensue. There's big and then there's Priyanka Chopra's big level of success. In the last couple of years, the actor has not let the ball drop on a single count, both internationally and on the home front. Vogue spoke to the actor on her association with jewellery, an ever-evolving sense of style, and scaling new heights. You have been representing India on a global scale for a while now, as has the Nirav Modi label. How did the conversation for the campaign come about? Thank you for the compliment. I'm very happy to be associated with the brand. Nirav and I are share a fierce pride in our heritage and are united by the idea of bringing that heritage to the global forefront. How would you define ‘India Modern'? It is all around us—be it the world of business, entertainment, technology, social change. There is a whole new India emerging that's more confident, more in step with the globe. Our demographic is our strength, majority being below the age of 35 who are driven to affect change and are increasingly getting involved in things that will bring about that change. Modern India does not mean that we were ever backward, it just means we are more connected globally than ever before. Does jewellery hold sentimental value for you? Is there a piece that you treasure? Yes, it most definitely does. There is something about having a piece handed down generations or owning a piece that was crafted specifically for you. I have this charm necklace, which is extremely special to me because it belonged to my father, whom I lost to cancer almost four years ago. At the beginning of his health battle (in 2005), my mom bought him this solid-gold chain with a single charm—an emerald (which, as per astrology, can positively affect your health). Over the next eight years, my family collected healing charms from around the world to add to this chain. My dad hated wearing it—probably because of how heavy it became. When we lost him, the chain with all its charms was given to me and I've worn it pretty much every day since then. As someone who's almost never home, the chain makes me feel like I'm connected to my family and my world, wherever I go. If you could gift your mother a piece of jewellery from Nirav Modi's latest collection, what would it be? The ‘Embrace' bangles—I love the ingenious mechanism they have. My mom is very eclectic in what she wears and these bangles can be worn with pretty much everything. Not only are they elegant, but they're also a little playful, which is like my mom in many ways. You recently accessorised the Sally LaPointe ensemble at the People's Choice Awards with jewellery by Nirav Modi. How would you describe the look? The Sally LaPointe ensemble was a very feminine outfit… very light, which brought a touch of spring to a cold January. I accessorised the dress with the Nirav Modi ‘Jasmine' ear studs and ‘Embrace' rings, which I stacked up, one on top of the other. I love the versatility of these rings and the fact that I could wear them with on the red carpet as easily as I could wear them with my jeans and a simple top. The ear studs are so delicate, lightweight, and fuss-free—I like the design of the asymmetrical petals as they add a sense of unpredictability to the piece. Speaking of style, how do you think yours has evolved? Quite dramatically! I think I experiment far more now, than I did before. Over the years, I began to understand what suits me and stopped following fashion trends blindly. That understanding helps me carry what I am wearing with confidence. I have also come to enjoy the process, so prepping and being on the red carpet is so much more fun now. What are the projects you will be working on in 2017? There is lots happening this year. Quantico season two is just back from the winter break and shoot for the same is in full swing. Baywatch releases this summer on May 26. Promotions will be across the globe so yes, more travelling. What has also been a very exciting journey is setting up and working on my production house Purple Pebble Pictures. It has been a huge learning curve and so exciting to interact and support the immense talent we have across India. Post the first three regional films, we have three more lined up for release as well as three children's films, which will also release this year. More are in the discussion stage. As for Hindi films, I am currently working through what interests me. More on that soon.   What's New Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Riccardo Tisci exits Givenchy after 12 years with the fashion house
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Fashion world's game of musical chairs continues Riccardo Tisci has left his role at Givenchy after 12 years at the helm. His departure was confirmed today by the house, who told WWD that his final collections have already been shown - during menswear and couture weeks in Paris. “The chapter Riccardo Tisci has written with the house of Givenchy over the last 12 years represents an incredible vision to sustain its continuous success, and I would like to warmly thank him for his core contribution to the house's development," Bernard Arnault, chairman and chief executive officer of Givenchy owner LVMH, said today. Despite the seemingly hasty exit - which will not see him take a bow at the ready-to-wear shows next month, and the forthcoming autumn/winter 2017 collection be completed by the studio team - the parting has been described as "mutual and amicable" and was effective on the expiry of his contract on January 31. Speculation has been swirling for several months that Tisci is being lined up to take the helm at Versace. The designer is firm friends with Donatella Versace, even enlisting her for a Givenchy ad campaign, and his dark but sexy aesthetic is seen as a perfect fit for Versace. While speculation over Tisci's next move is nothing new, the chatter over who should fill his shoes will now begin. A raft of high-profile recent designer departures - Peter Dundas, Hedi Slimane, Clare Waight Keller and Peter Copping - could find themselves linked with the role, while Balmain's Olivier Rousteing is already being mooted for a move. Tisci is the go-to red-carpet designer for a diverse collection of stars - from Kim Kardashian West, whose wedding dress he created, and Beyoncé Knowles, to Madonna and Meryl Streep. His unarguable skill, as well as his celebrity pull, make him a desirable appointment for any house, but he may be subject to a non-compete clause meaning his next move may not come for a while. column1: Chloé confirms creative director Clare Waight Keller’s departure
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Moving on after six years with the label French fashion house Chloé has confirmed that its current creative director, Clare Waight Keller, will be leaving her position on March 31, after the brand's forthcoming autumn/winter 2017 show at Paris Fashion Week. "Clare has been a remarkable partner at Chloé over the past six years,” Chloé's president, Geoffroy De La Bourdonnaye, said today. "She helped rejuvenate the legacy of Gaby Aghion, the first ever Chloé girl, by infusing a cool and easy breeze into the Chloé wardrobe, effortlessly mixing graceful and feminine flou with a free-wheeling and boyish take on tailoring. Clare has a unique talent in directing a large studio of strong creatives. I would like to personally thank Clare for her loyalty and dedication to Chloé." Rumours first surfaced about Waight Keller's exit from the brand - which is said to be a mutual decision between the designer and management - towards the end of 2016, but it was earlier this month that her successor was mooted as Natacha Ramsay Levi. Currently womenswear designer at Louis Vuitton, Ramsay Levi is expected to be officially announced as Chloé's new helmer imminently, although the brand did not comment on its future designer today. “After six extraordinary years at Chloé I would like to thank Geoffroy and all my colleagues for their enormous efforts over the past years,” said Waight Keller, who took the Chloé reins in May 2011 from Hannah MacGibbon, who had been artistic director since 2008. “Working for this maison has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my career. Chloé is a brand with values close to my heart and I have truly enjoyed working with some of the best talents in the industry. I feel privileged to have worked for a maison with such a heritage and I am very proud of all that has been achieved.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Koovs just announced its next big designer collaboration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Mark your calendars for February 16 View Gallery 3 Photos Koovs just announced its next big designer collaborations With a spot in the Merriam Webster dictionary and almost every It girl's wardrobe, it's clear that athleisure is here to stay. The latest designer to join the movement? Masaba Mantena. In collaboration with online store Koovs.com, Mantena has designed a 32-piece capsule collection featuring athleisure staples that strike the perfect balance between fashion and function. Think curve-hugging bodysuits, bold crop tops and fashion's favourite, the bomber jacket. Vogue gets the first look and chats with her about her new collection. Tell us about your collection and the inspiration behind it. Masaba x Koovs aims to make activewear a fun and high-energy experience, bringing together high fashion and functional clothing. The line embodies signature Masaba prints providing the body-conscious youth activewear that can easily transcend from day to night. How would you describe your personal style? How does the collection fit into your wardrobe? My personal style is laid-back and easygoing. The collection fits into my everyday wardrobe because I love to work out, and that's the first thing I do as soon as I wake up. I've always preferred comfort over luxury on a day-to-day basis. I can step out in these pieces right after a workout by pairing them with my favourite sneakers or throwing on a tailored shirt over my tracks. What are some of your favourite pieces? The bodysuit and the chocolate slippers. But, I also adore the printed skorts and the jackets from the line. What kind of woman did you have in mind when you were designing the collection? The collection is aimed at the healthy, fashionable youth who want to blur the lines between active wear and their everyday wardrobe. It also targets those women who aren't obsessed with diet and fads and have the perfect balance between fitness and indulgence. If you had three words to describe the collection, what would they be? Relaxed, bold, round-the-clock. Masaba x Koovs launches on February 16, 2016 on Koovs.in Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights from Day 1 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Details this way View Gallery 18 Photos Highlights from Day 1 of Lakmé Fashion Week summer/resort 2017 Missed Day 1 of Lakmé Fashion Week? Here's everything you need to know: Gen Next The Gen Next show has given the country some of its finest designers and this season, which saw five emerging labels, was no exception. While Pallavi Singh of ARCVSH and Soumodeep Datta celebrated traditional crafts, Kolkata-based Nakita Singh's collection ‘Outline', inspired by the technique of sketch, featured linen and khadi creations heightened by brilliant strokes and surface design. Resham Karmchandani and Sanya Suri of The Pot Plant presented a line-up of comfort-driven, fuss-free clothing with floral motifs, adding an element of playfulness. For Ishanee Mukherjee and Anirudh Chawla of Poochki, a label that takes its name from the duo's pet manx cat, creating awareness about animal conservation was on the agenda. Fauna-inspired prints on sheer, muted fabrics put a whimsical spin on airy silhouettes. Antar-Agni Ujjawal Dubey's collection ‘Free and Nothing' is what summer dreams are made of. With an emphasis on draping and asymmetry, the designer delivered a dreamy line of laid-back staples. White, beige and navy blue were on his shade card. Eká by Rina Singh Cotton duster coats, midi dresses over linen pants, and roomy culottes paired with boxy basics—you can always count on Rina Singh to teach you a thing or two about effortless summer layering. This season, watercolour florals and gingham gave her collection a romantic, vintage feel. The colour palette varied from fail-safe white to bold pink. Dev R Nil The designers' return to Lakmé Fashion Week after a nine-year hiatus, was a triumphant one. Titled the Valley of Missing Flowers, their collection took its inspiration from the juxtaposition of beauty and conflict characteristic of war-torn zones across the world. Painterly blooms dotting delicate, sheer fabrics represented the fragile beauty often seen in such regions. AM.IT by Amit Aggarwal Who doesn't love fashion with a heart? In his collection ‘Seamless', Amit Aggarwal, whose label AM.IT focuses on upcycling, gave old, un-claimable pieces of patola saris a new lease on life by turning them into contemporary, red carpet-worthy silhouettes. Earth tones of traditional patola saris were contrasted with glamorous, high shine hues for added drama. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Accessories label Mansur Gavriel ventures into ready-to-wear this year
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Pieces to pair with your bucket bag New York-based brand Mansur Gavriel has announced it will debut its first ready-to-wear collection. Well-loved for its leather bucket bags, the brand is expanding from accessories into clothing, with the first collection to be unveiled this September at New York Fashion Week. “Creatively, we were always ready,” co-founder Rachel Mansur told Business of Fashion. “We had such fast growth with the bags that we felt that we needed to be operationally prepared. Now the time is right.” Moving forward, the brand will adopt a ‘see now, buy now' model where the collection will be available for purchase immediately. Founded by Rachel Mansur and Floriana Gavriel in 2012, the brand has reached somewhat of a cult following, taking out the Accessories Designer of the Year Award at the 2016 CFDA Awards. column1: Fail-proof footwear buying tips no shop owner will share with you
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion No 3: Never buy shoes thinking they will stretch Five perfect shoe tips: New-season shoes are a smart way to update anything existing in your wardrobe. Wear shoes inside for at least 30 to 45 minutes before wearing them outside. Walk on different surfaces at home, from carpet to harder flooring such as wood or marble (but be careful not to scratch the soles. If in doubt, lightly cover them with masking tape). If unbearable, return. Never buy shoes thinking they will stretch. Never wear brand-new pointed-toe shoes without taking them to a cobbler to fix a metal plate under the toe. They will last exponentially longer. When it comes to daily shoe choices, check the weather. Don't wear leather-soled shoes in the rain; wet pavements will destroy them in an instant. column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Hint: Katy Perry, Fergie, Kylie Jenner and JLo have worn it REBEL MODE #fashionfever #rebelmode #wildchild #falgunishanepeacock #lakmefashionweek #keepcalmandrocktheworld A photo posted by falgunipeacock (@falgunipeacock) on Jan 19, 2017 at 11:25pm PST Kylie Jenner wore a matador jacket by the duo for a campaign shoot while JLo and Fergie favour their body suits for stage performances. It is no secret that husband-wife designer duo Falguni and Shane Peacock, who enjoy avid patronage on home ground and international shores, are synonymous with unadulterated cocktail glamour. The designers are bringing their signature flair to the Lakmé Fashion Week runway after six years this season. We caught up with them ahead of their show on Friday, February 3, 2017. On returning to Lakmé Fashion Week after six years We were busy with multiple fashion weeks abroad, including New York Fashion Week. Hence it was difficult for us to show in India. That being said, it's always great to put up a show in our homeland. LFW is a great platform and we are equally excited about the Jio Gardens venue. Our decision to participate was last-minute but we can't wait to unveil this specially curated line. On the S/R 2017 collection The collection ‘Rebel' is inspired by the metaphysical world coupled with playfulness. It is a balance between our mixed expressions and every ensemble is bold, modern and decadent. The collection has elements of the galaxy and stars, used predominately in our appliqué work. Delicate crystal embellishments, feathers, sequins and sheer panels capture the radiance and sparkle of the universe while the colour palette boasts tones of blue, sliver, wine, black and champagne gold. Sheer fabrics like organza, luxe net, and exotic lace have been used with bold crystal appliqué with a dash of intricate sequin embroideries. We love using sumptuous feathers dipped in a plethora of colours and have played up this feature in the limited edition pieces of this collection. The silhouettes range from gowns and body suits to minis and jumpsuits. Structure has been fused with fluidity, and the techniques used are such that they don't overwhelm the bold silhouette of the outfits. Defining this rebel: Every woman has a rebel in her, the idea of which changes through different stages of her life. This collection is for these edgy and independent women who make a statement with their thoughts, attires and mindsets. And even though rebellious, this millennial woman has a penchant for tasteful elegance and offbeat looks that are not necessarily over the top. Celebrity muse We would love to dress up Sonam Kapoor in a signature cape gown from this collection as she carries our gowns beautifully. An independent modern woman, who has created a niche not only in the film industry but also in the fashion world, she epitomises the very strong and witty fashionista this collection has been made for. On achieving red carpet glam The sensibilities of the Vogue woman has evolved over time and she is more fashion-aware and open to experimentation. The idea is to dress up by dressing down. The key to a red carpet-ready look is to add glamour in an elegant manner. Keep it simple and classy. Steer clear of overloading yourself in layers of old-school fabrics that will weigh you down. column1: Inside Dolce & Gabbana’s latest couture outing Alta Moda
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion One night of couture in Milan View Gallery 19 Photos Inside Dolce & Gabbana’s latest couture outing Alta Moda There is nothing quite like the Dolce & Gabbana Alta Moda experience. When Stefano Gabbana and Domenico Dolce conceived the idea of hosting a series of shows in their Italian homeland - to demonstrate their vision of women and men's couture and jewellery to an audience primarily of clients rather than press and buyers - I was one of the people who thought they were pretty misguided in this ambition. Who would want to fly to Italy for one brand's shows when there was the whole razzamatazz of the long-established Paris couture already in existence? Well, wrong. Now in its fifth year, the Alta Moda has grown clientele and sales, and the duo have more than proved that their idea has legs, and long, expensively clad ones at that. Last night in Milan, the series of warehouses where all the industry behind the sets, costumes and rehearsals for the hugely prestigious performances of La Scala takes place, became instead the set for the latest show. Guests were guided through a series of workrooms where the tables were ready for the next day's stitching, rails of costumes either completed or being constructed lined room after room, and through an atmospheric billowing smoke could be seen the vast wooden carpentry involved. Room after room, metal walkway after metal walkway, it was a journey into the heart of La Scala except what we finally reached was something entirely different – the heart of Dolceland. A space lit by a thousand candles accompanied by several thousand crimson roses, and where figures in operatic costume mingled with the invited guests who themselves were in costumes equally fantastic and mainly purchased from an Alta Moda collection. The divide between the show to come and the cocktail party was slim, and in this it was a replica of the way couture originally functioned. It was not, like the last week in Paris, a time where designers of all kinds could utilise the presence of a large number of industry folk to show pre-collections, presentations, early ready-to-wear and a little couture. The week used to be a focal point where women who could afford to buy couture and who appreciated the whole notion of not only the skills but the lifestyle that accompanied it would gather twice a year in Paris and lunch, party, mix and mingle in a series of events designed to allow them to wear the expensive and bespoke clothes. My neighbours for this show, which took place next to the opening cocktail party, were a Paraguayan couple, she a pretty blonde woman in full-length gold lace Dolce & Gabbana right down to her gold sandals and he in matching gold brocade tux from the Alta Sartoria collection. They, like many others in the audience, come to meet their fellow devotees as much as to see the collections. The occasion has come to feel like a gathering of a wildly international club, the membership of which extends far outside Europe and America. And it provides a great venue to actually wear the clothes, for where else would your fellows be adorned with pearl headdresses and velvet capes, and wearing corsets and embroidered jackets, or in head-to-toe sequins finished off with fur opera coats? A few classic black cocktail dresses appeared, their simplicity ramped up several notches paired with an extraordinary theatrical headdress, but in the main this collection was for the woman who had no desire to meld in with a general crowd. If there was any link it was in the roses that could be found everywhere, in sequins, prints, needlepoint and appliqué. They appeared on a beautiful midnight velvet cap-sleeved dress (one of the more sober items on show) and on a yellow plaid skirt. They found their way onto furs and velvets, satins and tapestry. As the final cyclamen outfits wound their way back up the long staircase at the end of the catwalk, Stefano and Domenico arrived to take their bow, but also to join in with the audience and chat and pose for pictures in a mark of the sociability of this occasion. Dinner later was in yet another vast warehouse space, allowing us to see en route the small maquettes used for decades of designing the operas, like really wonderful miniature theatres of childhood. A fairytale woodland of illuminated trees as table decorations continued the party feel of the occasion and as I left, the dancing had begun, the nightclub was taking off and the guests who had come to Milan to indulge in a few days of Dolce festivities were ready to boogie into the night. column1: #SuzyCouture Galliano And Margiela: An Increasingly Comfortable Fit
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion In black and scarlet The wonky, pieced together wooden doors at the end of the runway were the backdrop for Maison Margiela. But the way John Galliano developed his long-held belief in the beauty of the unfinished and undone was the designer's own. [#image: /photos/5ce4509aba773deb1d0b666b]||| ||| Image: InDigital Add some discreet references to his past and some contemporary statements of protest and this seemed like a confident step forward in melding Galliano's own vision and that of the original Martin Margiela, who gave up his role in the house in 2009. [#image: /photos/5ce4509acc50be78fc14239c]||| ||| Image: InDigital From Galliano's opening outfits of flamboyant deconstruction, to the silk that filtered in and out of the designs, there was a sense of control, even elegance. Maison Margiela, with its vivid reds but controlled shapes, seemed to be facing in the right direction. [#image: /photos/5ce4509ab8031124c48f9d10]||| ||| Image: InDigital "This collection is about adding filters, but as much about removing them and sharing as about connecting with a community, becoming part of a union and relating through mutual emotions rooted in memories," Galliano said in one of his opaque comments. The words cannot be challenged or explained as the designer no longer comes out at the end of his shows nor discusses his work. Maison Margiela - by John Galliano A video posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Jan 25, 2017 at 2:02am PST However, there was clarity in this spring/summer 2017 artisanal approach, with some dresses beautifully cut and finished. But more were only half done, carrying an emotional tie to Galliano's past. Those links became literal in the strands holding a garment together. [#image: /photos/5ce4509b3bf9b4d949b1f5e0]||| ||| Image: InDigital There were also painted, printed or embroidered words, vague and incomplete, as if the designer had gone back to his roots in the unfinished and undone. [#image: /photos/5ce4509a3bf9b4bf37b1f5de]||| ||| Image: InDigital Perhaps the most beautiful piece was a tall South American-style felt hat above an all-white coat that was swathed in sheer black chiffon decorated with a face. This seemed like couture as theatre, but also as absolute elegance. [#image: /photos/5ce4509bb40d261cf5d6f98a]||| ||| Image: InDigital I would have liked to have seen some overt references to Martin Margiela, particularly with the Belgian designer's upcoming exhibition about his design years at Hermès that opens at the end of March at the ModeMuseum in Antwerp. [#image: /photos/5ce4509b1dc2675f7cc7b906]||| ||| Image: InDigital Yet this Paris show definitely seemed like a step forward for Galliano at Margiela, hovering between reality and dream with a fine balance between heritage and the new. column1: #SuzyCouture Valentino: Such Stuff As Dreams Are Made On
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Greek myths, Shakespearean references and superb handwork I have always thought that beauty is eternal and fashion transient. But the Valentino show stood out in Paris couture week for its light-handed grace, wistful elegance, purity and poetry. Photo: InDigital Pleats cascading across the body suggested an ancient column shivering to life. And designer Pierpaolo Piccioli said that in a turning world, with no time to dream, he wanted to give a sense of eternity. Photo: InDigital His mission was written in a statement he hung above the models' entrance, laid out like a poem reading: "You are living in a dream. Keep walking in your dream. Feel your dream and breathe your dream." BRAVO for VALENTINO and designer Pierpaolo Piccioli. Most beautiful and poetic show of the Paris haute couture weeek. A video posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Jan 25, 2017 at 10:02pm PST As the ethereal young women walked through the different rooms, there was a pale palette of faded greens and pinks, with the occasional splash of red. Studying the dense programme notes, all the outfits were named after mythical Grecian figures from Daphne and Eurydice to Eros and Zeus. Photo: InDigital This was an important collection for Pierpaolo - his first couture since Maria Grazia Chiuri, his design partner of 25 years, left for Dior and who shown her couture collection earlier in the week. Photo: InDigital But the "dreamer" of the two presented a powerful collection that was as strong in spirit as it was in execution. It opened with a minute's silence in memory of Franca Sozzani, editor in chief of Italian Vogue who died in December.   Backstage Valentino - those feather light pleats in detail A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Jan 25, 2017 at 10:06pm PST Why the pleats? Not since Mariano Fortuny invented the poetry of pleating a century ago have vertical lines been used to such effect. But realising the importance of designing for today's woman, Pierpaolo's straight lines were loose and free. They might open as an ankle length tunic over trousers, or as an infinity of vertical silken braids. Photo: InDigital Visible flowers were some of the masterly effects: fat, flat white roses, requiring 2,000 stitches, or macrame flowers adding no bulk to the airy outfits. Valentino chiffon hand-made romantic roses A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Jan 25, 2017 at 10:24pm PST Then there were the poetic colours, inspired by the symbolist paintings of Odilon Redon, that brought in shades of white from ivory to putty and so many other painterly constructs. Photo: InDigital The hypnotic effects of the simple, vertical lines intensified with craftsmanship ended in a prolonged roar of applause as Pierpaolo took his bow and kissed his wife. [#image: /photos/5ce451ffb40d260fb4d6fb8a]||| ||| Photo: InDigital Should the designer have included some more obviously "practical" clothes for work and play as founder Valentino, sitting front row, might have done in his time? To quote William Shakespeare: "To sleep, perchance to dream". Photo: InDigital Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Anita Dongre on what to expect from her Lakmé Fashion Week grand finale
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Is it fashion week yet? View Gallery 6 Photos Anita Dongre tells us what to expect from the grand finale The news of Anita Dongre closing this season of Lakmé Fashion Week obviously raised curiosity. The first question, of course, was: where would the show take place? Grand finales are, by virtue of name alone, grand to say the least. Live orchestras, thousands of handcrafted origami cranes suspended from ceilings, and in some cases, last-minute venue changes—the closing shows have a history of being memorable. This is the first time Dongre will be closing Lakmé Fashion Week, and though the bar is set pretty high, she plans to deliver a stunning show at the Bandra Fort. Though an unconventional choice for some, she tells us why the venue is close to her heart. “I'm born and brought up a Bandra girl, I've been visiting the Fort since I was a child and it's a lovely heritage structure—I have been wanting to show at the amphitheater since a long time.” Dongre's summer/resort 2017 collection titled ‘Alchemy' reflects the essence of Lakmé's latest beauty range, which centres around the theme of liquid gold. “Our collection is inspired by the glistening sun-kissed sands of Rajasthan. It will also show influences from the state's unique flora and fauna,” said the designer. Anita Dongre might be a Bandra girl, but she hasn't forgotten her Jaipuri roots. The brand's signature gota patti work no doubt will feature in this collection. “We will be showcasing over 60 looks on the runway in contemporary silhouettes for the modern, young Indian woman,” she said. Far be it from Kareena Kapoor Khan to miss the evening. The Lakmé Absolute brand ambassador, also the face of Anita Dongre's label AND (and new mum to Taimur Ali Khan Pataudi) will be there to model the closing look of the season. Alchemy by Anita Dongre will close Lakmé Fashion Week's Summer Resort 2017 on February 5, 9pm at Bandra Fort, Mumbai. Watch this space for more updates. column1: Can you wear sporty stripes to a formal event?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Tackling the resort trend Deepika Padukone recently wore a striped green and black dress from Prabal Gurung's resort 2017 collection for her xXx: The return of Xander Cage promotions. A blend of sporty mesh fabric in colour blocked stripes with a figure-flattering cut, the dress hit the sweet spot between casual and formal. This further stirred the ultimate conundrum—does sports luxe make the cut for formal occasions? Sporty stripes aren't exactly what you see on workout gear; rather they evoke a spirit of activity without pounding on the obvious. Under the growing influence of athleisure, the frenzy around all things adrenalin-inducing is bound to show up in every sartorial void. The sporty stripes we spotted on the runways this season reminded us of '70s-style ribbed knits, dresses that bore a striking resemblance to vests, and technicolor lines. Alia Bhatt's striped ensemble was interjected with florals, still staying in the sporty category with its elasticated waistband. Athiya Shetty styled her monochrome striped T-shirt with a pair of silver sneakers, while Alexa Chung's sweater reminded us of vintage tennis apparel. The joy of resort fashion is the flexibility that comes with the transitory season—wear your stripes to brunch or dinner. With the right selection of accessories, you are faux pas free.
