column1: How fashion foretold the populist Trump shoot-out
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion From Kim Kardashian’s exhibitionism to Vetements’ celebration of ordinary people Kim Kardashian's exhibitionism and Vetements' celebration of ordinary people both pre-empted seismic shifts on the world stage. Forget designer influentials. Donald Trump has had a mighty influence on global fashion. How? Why? Read my story. Link in bio. A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Jan 3, 2017 at 3:55am PST Two opposing ideologies vie for attention. Dedicated supporters believe fervently in one, single vision. Ultimately, half a century of the old order is upturned. A new era dawns. We're talking about the Trump-Clinton stand-off and the UK's “Brexit” - right? Wrong! This is about fashion: How the people's choice up-ended taste, timing and fame - and all of this before politics even began to mirror the same populist trends. I see fashion's polarisation as happening around two years ago. On one side was Balmain, where an in-your-face, brash-and-flash couture was heartily disapproved of by the fashion establishment. But the bold and sexy style of Creative Director Olivier Rousteing was adored by his A-list audience, led by Kim Kardashian, who embraced the glitter and glamour. Speaking to the people. The sexy side of fashion from Olivier Rousteing of Balmain - who has made Kim Kardashian one of the pinnacles of the rage for change- reflecting wider history. Read my story- link in bio A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Jan 3, 2017 at 2:34am PST Let's see this fashion movement as a precursor to Donald Trump's up-turning of America's presidential race, with his lewd comments, sexy wife and rabble-rousing. To some, a Kardashian backside might seem as distasteful as a Trump rant. But millions love Kim's look as much as they gave the thumbs-down to the Hillary Clinton trouser suit. But something else - even more populist and unsettling - was going on in fashion. The people are speaking. The Vetements non-fashion style is the most powerful look to reflect the global urge for change. Read my story- link in bio A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Jan 3, 2017 at 2:33am PST Demna Gvasalia and his brother Guram, whose migration from Georgia in the former Soviet Union eventually led them to Paris, caused a different kind of shake-up: a “non-style” revolution they called “Vetements”, meaning “clothes”. Instead of fashion as we understand it, the defining pieces were resolutely plain: hoodies, puffer coats, and jeans, albeit meticulously worked. [#image: /photos/5ce452b84a30b367b013058d]||| ||| A signature look from Vetements, backstage at the Autumn/Winter 2016-17 presentation Credit: Pierre-Ange Carlotti In retrospect, this new brand, which also challenged the timing of shows and the distribution of the collections, can be seen as a fashion mirror-image of a world-wide people's revolt, from Britain's Brexit to Italy's Beppe Grillo, whose day job is on stage as a clown. [#image: /photos/5ce452b73bf9b459f1b1f91e]||| ||| Italian comedian-turned-politician Beppe-Grillo, founder of the "Movimento 5 Stelle" (Five Star Movement), performs at Unipol Arena in Bologna (10th April, 2014) Credit: Getty The Vetements collective was launched in 2014, before global politics started heaving with change. But now that Demna has been made Creative Director of Balenciaga, whose founder Cristóbal was the epitome of grandeur, the graffiti is on the wall. An haute couture house has been taken over by an agent of street populism. [#image: /photos/5ce452b89cc0c0012efa07e6]||| ||| Demna Gvasalia's first show for Balenciaga, Autumn/Winter 2016 ready-to-wear, included this hiking jacket cut with a Balenciaga twist Credit: InDigital With people demanding to “see now, buy now” and brands as mighty as Burberry and Tommy Hilfiger responding to their cries, it seems like populism is winning. Not to mention the effect of Instagram, where Rousteing has 4.1 million followers to Trump's 4.5. But why be surprised by fashion as the harbinger of history? It has always been so. [#image: /photos/5ce452b8b40d265180d6fca0]||| ||| The Barbican's current exhibition, "The Vulgar: Fashion Redefined", explores the history of good taste in fashion through the centuries (until 5th February, 2017) Credits: Michael Bowles, Getty In the early 1960s, Mary Quant ramped up her hemlines to start the rise of the “mini-skirt” - right before the contraceptive pill became available to all women. Twenty years on, in the 1980s designers celebrated in advance the shattering of the boardroom's glass ceiling by swapping Flower Child dresses for mighty padded shoulders on female trouser suits. [#image: /photos/5ce452b8ba773d83620b6945]||| ||| British fashion designer Mary Quant making final adjustments to a zip-up mini-dress on a fashion model in her London design studio, January 1967 Credit: Getty Reeling back through history, Marie Antoinette threw off rigid, royal clothes, replaced in 1783 by portraits of her dressed with Rococo sweetness - six years before the French monarchy was overthrown. [#image: /photos/5ce452b91dc267a303c7bc22]||| ||| Detail of a portrait of Marie-Antoinette, by Elisabeth Louise Vigée Le Brun (1788) Credit: Getty Other theories, pooh-poohed by financial experts, have the rise and fall of hemlines linked to the ups and downs of Wall Street. So is there a traceable link between fashion and politics? In this new millennium, the designers themselves are now bitterly divided. Playing fashion feminist - like Clinton to Trump or “Remain” to “Leave” - are key houses such as Valentino, presenting powerful, cover-up clothes with long sleeves and hemlines. [#image: /photos/5ce452b9b8031105858fa020]||| ||| Nicole Kidman wearing Valentino for the premiere of "Queen Of The Desert" at the 2015 Berlin International Film Festival Credit: Getty Significantly, when Maria Grazia Chiuri, one half of the long-term Valentino duo, left for Dior, she brought to that august house a T-shirt printed with the words: “We Should All Be Feminists” [#image: /photos/5ce452b9b40d26d94ad6fca8]||| ||| The Victoria's Secret "Angels" creating a frenzy at the 2016 show Credit: First View On the other side are an increasing number of hyper-flashy, sexist brands, such as Victoria's Secret and its rowdy, revealing lingerie spectaculars or the loud looks of German designer Phillipp Plein and his display of rhinestone-cowboy decorated denim. How fashion foretold the Trump shoot out and was ahead of political change. On the sexy populist side of fashion. Philipp Plein and Paris Hilton. Read my story- link in bio. A photo posted by Suzy Menkes (@suzymenkesvogue) on Jan 3, 2017 at 2:32am PST Two ideologies and two audiences competing for the triumph of one belief. Sounds familiar? Fashion and politics: It's all one. column1: The cool new ways Bollywood is styling the classic white shirt
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Update this wardrobe staple View Gallery 11 Photos The cool new ways Bollywood is styling the classic white shirt Considering that the classic white shirt is the very definition of a wardrobe MVP today, it's hard to imagine that it created quite the scandal when it made its first appearance back in 1793. Worn by queen Marie Antoinette under a muslin dress for a portrait, it was considered against royal etiquette, far from the de rigueur status the shirt enjoys today. Over the years, the white shirt has witnessed a transformation—what was considered a symbol of wealth in the 19th century as those who didn't work wore it, was given a (then) revolutionary androgynous spin by Coco Chanel in the '20s. Celebrities such as Audrey Hepburn, Lauren Bacall and Katherine Hepburn to Julia Roberts and Gwyneth Paltrow, have done their bit to make it even more iconic. The one-piece wonder continues to intrigue the current Bollywood set too. Want to take your white shirt from office to cocktail party? Let Sonam Kapoor lead the way—swap those pinstriped trousers for a formal silk maxi skirt and a statement necklace to boot. If it's a sangeet you're attending, you can team your white shirt with a lehenga just as easily. Her sister, Rhea Kapoor, shows us how to give the shirt serious cool girl cred. A crisp white with exaggerated shoulders and light stripes, worn with high-waist trousers is just what you need for Saturday night drinks with your girls. What works in this staple's favour is that it serves as a blank canvas for your sartorial sensibilities, in tune with the occasion in question. For instance, you can wear it with patchwork denim shorts and combat boots like Alia Bhatt for a music festival or with a feminine midi skirt à la Soha Ali Khan to meet the boyfriend's parents. If you're looking to add to your ever-increasing collection of white shirts, turn to one in its new-age avatar—the high-low knotted version seen on Malaika Arora Khan or the deconstructed one worn by Vaani Kapoor—are great options. Safe to say, the classic white shirt is anything but basic. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why this piece of jewellery makes a case for being worn twice
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Sunita Shekhawat weighs in Sunita Shekhawat tells me she's the coolest mom her daughter could have asked for—she might be a traditionalist in her aesthetic, but her approach to life is not behind times. The jewellery designer of her eponymous label has carved a space for herself in India's luxury bridal market with her distinct line of meenakari jewellery. When Shekhawat started with her line, her thought was to offer her customer more than the next jewellery designer. “It comes from my middle-class upbringing. My father was in the Air Force and we always looked at the value of a purchase before it was bought,” she says. Meenakari, by way of design creates reversible jewellery. One of the biggest reasons behind the success of her label is that all of her neckpieces can be worn both ways because of the enameling at the back which is a work of art in itself. If you see the campaigns by the brand, it's evident that the jewellery can be worn outside of the festive context. “When we offer custom solutions to the bridal party, we take everything into account—the length of the customer's neck, the size of the ears, the shape of their face and then help them decide whether they should opt for a big earrings or layered necklaces and so on,” she says. The lotus is a constant leitmotif in her designs. “We pick polki that's shaped like teardrops, to get the shape of the petals right. Detail to the smallest of things is what creates a designer piece. The extra is what takes it from ordinary to extraordinary,” she explains. Watch what goes into the making of the jewellery. Fashion Fashion Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How competitions like Wool Runway are changing the face of fashion
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion India’s got talent Designer Troy Costa and Vaani Kapoor felicitate winners of the Wool Runway. Left to right: winner Ankit Kajla, second runner-up Miloni Kothari, Arti Gudal of The Woolmark Company, second runner-up Apoorva Wadhwa and first runner-up Kavya Doultani. Great talents have emerged from the International Woolmark Prize competition held every year by the Woolmark Company. Legends like Yves Saint Laurent, Karl Lagerfeld and recently closer to home Rahul Mishra and Suket Dhir were brought to a global platform by way of the prestigious prize. This year, in order to scope out even fresher talent, the company launched the first-ever Wool Runway competition. Students from leading design schools in India, namely the National Institute of Fashion Design, National Institute of Design and Pearl Academy were invited to work with Merino wool and were mentored by Gautam Vazirani, fashion curator IMG Reliance. The jury for the competition included the likes of Sudhanshu Pokhriyal, president, Raymond Limited; John Roberts, general manager - Eastern Hemisphere, The Woolmark Company, Karunesh Vohra, creative director, Louis Philippe and Simon Carter, Kapil Batus, founder and creative director, WhiteBoard and designer Payal Khandwala. Ankita Kajla of NIFT Bangalore took home the winning prize, followed by first runner-up Kavya Doultani of Pearl Academy, Jaipur and second runners-up Apoorva Wadhwa of Pearl Academy, Noida and Miloni Kothari. Vogue spoke to the winner and jury members of the first leg of Wool Runway about the contribution of talent competitions to the future of the industry. How does a competition like Wool Runway help grow design talent in the country? Karunesh Vohra: It identifies and showcases talent and gives students a chance to go through the rigour of the process. A lot of young designers will come out and showcase their talent. As a practicing, established member of the design community what is the first piece of advice you would give to a student of fashion? Sudhanshu Pokhriyal: I would say that a student should look at the commercial aspect of fashion. Their success depends on their ability to marry commercial aptitude with design. I think it's very rare to see that, but if you can get that right, then the sky is the limit. What was your biggest takeaway from Wool Runway? Ankit Kajla: I would say it's the kind of exposure I've got. The Wool Runway mentors saw the bigger picture here and didn't adhere to the typical classroom approach. I received constructive criticism from the judges that boosted my confidence. Vaani Kapoor along with the judges was present at the awards ceremony to felicitate the winners. column1: Vogue India’s editor Priya Tanna remembers Franca Sozzani
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion "She did it all and made it look good, easy, and effortlessly glamorous" You hear of people being spoken of as living legends in fashion, their names followed by monikers such as “force of fashion” or “formidable” or “the genius behind those Meisel shots”—and when this happens way before you meet them, you mark your first encounter with trepidation. I met the woman behind the monikers first in Milan at a cocktail evening to mark my first outing as the newly-appointed editor of the Indian edition of Vogue. It was always easy to seek Franca Sozzani out from the rest. If it wasn't her trademark Botticelli curls and bright, piercing eyes, then it was by the attendees who so devotedly flocked her—designers, retailers and photographers in the room all magnetically gravitated towards her. That first meeting was brief but it was warm and pleasant. I was respectful, she encouraging. Over the last decade, I met Franca at fashion weeks or at the dinners hosted by Condé Nast International's chairman and chief executive Jonathan Newhouse. And although our exchanges did not progress beyond a smile or the occasional hug, between us, there was an ease that came from belonging to the same tribe of Vogue editors. It took an editors' conference in Berlin and one lazy lunch in Dubai for us to move past pleasantries. In Berlin, we found ourselves on the same team in a breakout session. Even if it was for a few hours, it felt like I was hanging out with the coolest girl in the room. We met a year later at an event hosted by Italian Vogue in Dubai. That same evening at a glittering charity ball she played hostess to international celebrities, local industrialists and designers. She used the occasion to speak about her two passions—supporting young designers and giving to eradicate world hunger. Her energy amazed me. Through both these interactions, what stayed with me was her approach to all that she did. Anna Wintour remembers her as “the hardest-working person she has known” and indeed, she was a tireless worker, a real doer; a woman with strong opinions and even stronger beliefs. She had the hunger and passion of a novice, which she wore with the experience of a veteran. With her, Italian Vogue turned fashion editorials into dramatic and provocative works of art. And her gusto at embracing the digital era of publishing made her a truly multimedia editor. At the helm of Italy's most prominent fashion magazine for 28 years, she became known for working with photographers such as Bruce Weber and Steven Meisel, creating talking-point visuals that often provoked debate. Alex Kuruvilla, the managing director of Condé Nast India, often used Franca as a great example of an editor who stayed true to Vogue and yet carried her brand into the age of omni-channel publishing. She did it all and made it look good, easy, and effortlessly glamorous. Only two months ago, a documentary made by her son, Francesco Carrozzini, Franca: Chaos and Creation, was screened as part of the Jio MAMI Mumbai Film Festival in Mumbai. (For those who didn't have a chance to see it, it will be released in early 2017.) Thank you Franca, for inspiring us to do more and be more. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: The celebrity-approved skirt style for the party season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Pleats please View Gallery 15 Photos The celebrity-approved skirt style for the party season You probably called it back in February when Beyoncé wore a monogrammed version of this skirt by Gucci as the opening outfit for her Formation video. Come September, Paper magazine dropped its web-exclusive cover featuring Deepika Padukone in another version of said skirt. In fact, all year-round celebrities have been sporting this style from front-rows and red carpets to their off-duty jaunts, leaving no doubts about its fabulousness. And if you're the style devotee you claim you are, you'd know by now that we are expounding the (many) merits of the knife-pleated midi skirt. If you haven't already given the trend a go yet, the party season is the ideal time to remedy the situation — especially when everyone else around is more likely to go the ‘riding hemline' route. A metallic version of the skirt (liquid gold or gleaming silver, we'll let you take your pick) is a no-brainer for the parties galore that December calls for. Wear yours with a lace Victorian blouse like Huma Qureshi or a camisole top as seen on Sonali Bendre. Can't imagine blending into the sea of red, green and white at that Christmas Eve bash? Ask yourself "what would Beyoncé do?" and then slip into a pink and white pleated skirt with a jewel-encrusted jumper and leather jacket to match. But if it's a Christmas brunch you're headed for, we recommend going preppy à la Frieda Pinto. Agreed that the knife pleat midi has a certain Miss Goody Two-shoes quality, but that doesn't mean you can't mix it up for some cool cred. Take a cue from Alia Bhatt and pair it with a military jacket and metallic plimsolls for a slay-ready look that doesn't try too hard. Or you can play the field like Jacqueline Fernandez by throwing on an oversized varsity jacket and high top sneakers to your pleated skirt and crop top combination. The fluid ease of the knife pleats skirt's movement makes it a winner in the aesthetic department. It's forgiving fit and no-ironing-required silhouette don't hurt either. And then imagine how great you'll look carelessly swirling in it at that big party this weekend (as your bestie diligently captures the moment for Instagram). Sold already? column1: Jonathan Newhouse writes a heartfelt tribute to Franca Sozzani
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Condé Nast mourns the loss of an icon Image: Paolo Ferrari This is the saddest news I have ever had to report to you. Franca Sozzani, the Editor of Italian Vogue for 28 years, died today in Milan after a year-long illness with her son Francesco by her side. It is an incalculable loss for Vogue and for the fashion world along with the many people around the world whose lives she touched -- readers, photographers, journalists, fashion designers and professionals, and people around the world whom she met through her role at the United Nations. Franca was one of the greatest Editors who ever made a magazine. She was by far the most talented, influential and important person within the Condé Nast International organisation. She made Italian Vogue a powerful and influential voice in the worlds of fashion and photography by publishing ground-breaking photography and journalism. In doing so she expanded Vogue beyond what had been the traditional model of a fashion magazine and often courted controversy by doing so. The greatest fashion photographers looked to Franca as the creative leader who would give them the freedom and the scope to produce their best work and they did so, month after month. Those who had the good luck to know and work with Franca loved, respected and admired her. She demanded the highest level of performance from those around her, and they gave it. Like all great editors she had an understanding of the business realities, and her grasp of these realities enabled her to drive Vogue to the highest levels. As an editor she was focused, demanding, open to ideas and experiment and extremely tough, especially with herself. She never stopped pushing contributors and the people around her to do more and better. As a human being she was honest, funny, warm and possessed a sense of irony and humility. While Italian Vogue and L'Uomo Vogue were the focus of her professional life, she also had been Editorial Director of Condé Nast Italy since 1994. In recent years she also served as the Ambassador to Fashion for the United Nations, a mission which took her around the world to bring support to the fashion world and the people behind it in places like Africa, Asia and regions beyond the usual fashion venues. In her UN role she also joined the fight against hunger in poor countries and helped raise awareness of the issue along with money. She carried out these activities with deep commitment and energy. On a personal level I had the great privilege to work with Franca since 1989, and it was a collaboration which animated my professional life. I loved and admired her, and I will miss her terribly. The fashion world in mourning. My thoughts and prayers go out to her son Francesco, her sister Carla, her niece Sara and all of us who knew her and were touched by her. We are heartbroken. Jonathan Newhouse 22nd December 2016 Fashion Fashion Wellness © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Would  you wear head to toe yellow?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Choosing colour will make you happier "Couldn't we all use a little sunshine right now?" Vogue UK's contributing fashion editor Francesca Burns said to me a few weeks ago when we were discussing spring's yellow trend after the biannual Vogue Trends Talk. That was a week that brought an icy cold snap, which made the prospect of being outside for more than five minutes highly unappealing. She's right though, with the festive period looming, we could all use some sunshine. But she was also wearing head to toe inky black when she said that. View Gallery 15 Photos Trend Test: Head To Toe Yellow This is the thing about full look, fearless colour - which was all over the spring/summer catwalks at Chloe, Valentino, Emilio Pucci, and Chanel - to go from browsing an eye-popping suit (in an ideal world: Gucci's fuchsia tailoring) to actually wearing it to a party, on the tube or to the office takes a leap of faith, something more than style advice alone. We've grown so used to wearing the darkest colours in a wardrobe as a means to blending in within the sea of black clothes that have defined the dress code of the last three decades. Dark clothes provide a security blanket. A well-cut black dress? Chic. The same in cobalt blue? Brave. Austere fashion has become the norm on the street, prevailing over a risk taking colour palette. It's not been the done thing to sport head to toe colour for fear of looking ridiculous and out of place, like a children's TV presenter in a boardroom. But, brace yourself - there is a change coming. Colour feels good, it engages positive feelings that are contagious, and come February it will be all over the high street thanks to those catwalk cues. Unlike previous seasons where we looked to accessories to add a 'pop' of colour, for 2017 it's about a full immersion. The look I've been trend testing at work this week comprised a banana yellow Jacquemus sweater dress with oversized quarter-back-style shoulders (purchased on a whim from Ssense) and mango-hued opaque tights. (I'm hooked on wearing a rainbow of tights at the moment as a means to reviving last season's party dresses). Which sounds ridiculous (OK, the shoulders might not yet be for everyone) but you'll have to give me a minute here. I felt brighter wearing it: my hair colour popped; the lazy purple-ish eye pencil I haphazardly scrawl on each morning felt considered. Yes, I added a thick black belt and slouchy black Isabel Marant boots for polish - but, otherwise I was in it up to my neck. Literally. There were the second glances, a steady stream of "wow"s, and a lot of "I could never wear that". Which isn't true. Saturated shades - particularly this punchy shade of daffodil - invite onlookers to presume a degree of confidence, which feels very now. Wearing fortifying yellow on a misty winter morning in London is an instant mood lifter. It may create only an illusion of self-assurance, but sometimes that's enough. column1: How to wear metallics like a celebrity this party season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Light up the party View Gallery 17 Photos These celebrities show us how to wear metallic this December As you prep your party season wardrobe, we'll tell you this: your millennial ‘belle of the ball' (or should we say, bar?) look will be quite incomplete without a generous helping of high-shine pieces. A merrymaking staple, you can always count on trusty metallics to ensure that your fashionista title remains intact as you dance your way through the parties galore. The style set has already RSVP'd to this trend. Follow our guide to follow suit. Red carpet allure If you have a cocktail party (or many) on your calendar this month, channel your inner movie star for a red carpet worthy look. Drama, the celebrities dictate, is the way to go. Swap a same ol' jumpsuit for a dramatic one like Jacqueline Fernandez . If you wish to tone down the metallic presence, but not the glamour, take a cue from Katrina Kaif and opt for an ombre gold and sheer gown. Stop and stare glam The best table at the swankiest club in town? Dress like the ultimate it-girl as you prepare for a bubbly-filled night. This is not the time to play coy. Instead, turn up the sex appeal. Kendall Jenner's glittering silver halter neck mini with a plunging neckline has New Year's Eve blowout bash written all over it. Sridevi's daughters prove that a sequinned mini teamed with neutral accessories is a fail-safe choice. Pick one with a tulip hemline and belt detailing like Khushi Kapoor. Man up Metallics are just the lustrous update your androgynous outfits need for a party-friendly vibe this month. Team a well-fitted blazer with golden trousers like Aditi Rao Hydari for a boss-lady-meets-party-girl flair. Alia Bhatt's dull gold sequinned blazer dress, topped off with smokey eyes and sleek hair, is tailor-made for the fierce dresser. Sophistication in simplicity By its very nature, metallic ensembles are designed to put you in the limelight. Maximum impact with minimum effort, if you may. Hence, keeping it simple is a good way to go. Heads will turn anyway. Pernia Qureshi's liquid metallic drop waist midi is perfect for a girls' night out, whereas Freida Pinto gives us a master class in dressing for a sit down dinner. Colour me metallic Gold and silver are the most widely favoured metallic tones. But that doesn't mean you should shy away from vivid hues altogether. Spruce your look by injecting some (metallic) colour to it — a jewel green mini as seen on Natasha Poonawalla for a Christmas Eve party or a pink sequinned gown for a ‘more is more' repertoire. Bella Hadid took to Instagram overnight to announce she is now a fashion designer, having created a collection for US clothing and jewellery label Chrome Hearts. “So damn excited!” Bella wrote on Instagram, posting the below picture of herself wearing a T-shirt printed with the letter B in the brand's signature font. “You have no idea what's coming! My new collection with @chromeheartsofficial designed by me, shot by my angel mother @laurielynnstark.”  “I CANT [sic] wait for you all to see what we've made! Follow @chromeheartsxbella for more #chromeheartsxbella coming soon soon soon...” Bella is a fan of the streetwear brand, having been snapped in their clothes plenty of times, with the brand posting on their Instagram grid when she's spotted in their pieces. She is also close friends with the brand's creators. Judging by the brand's design aesthetic, the collection will include T-shirts, hoodies and leather pieces. The brand has created a dedicated Instagram account for the collaboration @chromeheartsxbella, and while there is only one picture at this stage, more will be dropping soon soon soon. column1: This fashion brand truly believes that charity begins at home
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Ritu Kumar x Magic Bus What is the greater impact of a trade? What is the ultimate outcome of a dedicated lifetime to making ends meet? In an attempt to tackle these questions, Amrish Kumar, CEO at Ritu Kumar wanted to give back to the workers at the various factories employed by the mammoth brand started by his mother, Ritu Kumar. On meeting with Mathew Spacie, founder of the charitable organization Magic Bus, the two started working on what would become the film-led Artly program. Vogue spoke to Amrish Kumar and Spacie about their plans of a better tomorrow. How did the ‘Artly' program come into being? AK: “I bumped into Matthew couple of years ago at a gala and he spoke about the quality of life which stuck with me and since then I visited some of the projects they have in Delhi. The natural intention was to look at the areas where the migrant population end up in the textile trade. Where do they live? What kind of opportunities exist for their children? So we identified two communities—Tuglakhabada and Govindpuri in Delhi. The other place we wanted to do this was in Kolkata where the company has a base. A lot of the skill set in that area is dying due to lack of patronage and opportunities of trade just pass by. It was important to us that this was an area we work with. For Magic Bus this was a challenge since it's an area that they have not worked at in the past. One of the significant things that has come out of this is they have admirably managed to put this together and they are now running a community program in Uluberia outside Kolkata. What is the program like? AK: The next step for us was to figure out, ‘how do you enhance other parts of a child's life?'. Here you look within—what are the things that you hold dear as a child? For me that was the exposure to art, the idea of liberal arts, film and I wanted to work on a similar program. Therefore, the film project came into the picture and we developed a program to introduce films. How does Magic Bus plan to expand the program with Ritu Kumar? MS: A lot of the work we do is about relevance and engagement. It could be film, sport, drama or song but what's absolutely critical is that a young person feels engaged. The reason that a lot of programs fail is because a lot of children aren't interested in participating and the key to that is to find interesting ways to deliver the point. It's about creating an activity that can deliver a message. We are focusing now on three things—getting children in school, getting good jobs and the third is not getting married. Everything we do in the country with 400,000 children is to reach to those three outcomes. What we are doing with Ritu Kumar is applying the same framework but specifically to community that operates in the textile trade. These are children who come from a community where trades are passed down from generations. While they are introduced to a whole new world, how do you think this impacts their careers in the next couple of decades? MS: We are not going to go into a community and say you are doing anything wrong. The worst thing we can do is to make judgements on current practice. Our objective is to make young people aware of their own abilities, their potential, ensure they have a purpose and then provide them the opportunity structure so that they can have that choice, that control to be successful. If I could get away with it, I would have our core impact as happiness! Because it is all about that. It's about the quality of life. I'll be very honest with you, getting a kid in school and getting him a job is a very small part of being. The point of Magic Bus is to make sure that a young person is not forced to do just one thing because they don't have another choice. We have to be careful with aspiration, and young India has stacks of that which can sometimes be pointed in the wrong direction. I sense of realism, of connect with the outside world is paramount to success. How will Ritu Kumar be involved in the program? AK: What's important to us is to do more than write a check and I think this is why it has taken us time to come up with the plan. What we are also doing is get people who work within Ritu Kumar to come to the field once in while so that they themselves become ambassadors of the program in whichever way they wish. Mathew and I are going to spend time together and figure out a way for the two birds to fly together. MS: Ritu Kumar has already started employing some of the recipients of the program. And leading by example has an immense ripple effect across the community. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

Fashion consultant and stylist Nikhil D is all set to host ‘Lady Pow' this month, a pop-up at Lifaafa in Bandra. The pop-up holds a line of vintage pieces from sporty separates to cocktail-ready dresses, tennis skirts and pussy-bow blouses. She mentioned how she wanted to get rid of everything she was hoarding, including some items that were impulsive buys she had barely worn, if never.” The pop-up will also host a round of story-sharing with plum cake, cutlets and port wine to share. column1: Tracing the evolution of the Benarasi weave over centuries
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Tracing threads View Gallery 5 Photos How has the vintage Benarasi weave evolved over centuries This could be the scene from a period film though occurring in a weavers' guild in Benares just over thirty years back. Floor mattresses lined three sides of the tranquil room with the client sitting, elbow rested on a bolster, in anticipation of the pleasing textiles that he would peruse soon. A few feet away from him sat bade sahib (the head of this weaver-traders guild), in crisp white kurta and wide legged pyjama with legs neatly tucked under him. This head-weaver's erect frame exuded an innate dignity and composure with no visible anxiousness about the sales. Polite enquiries were made on the well-being of elders while, unhurriedly, bade sahib unwrapped a small bundle of ‘paan' and graciously offered it to the client who, with an equally elegant gesture of thanks, took one and tucked it into his cheek. As the first rectangular box of sari was opened, the murmurs decease into deferent silence. The business of the day could now commence. Soon musical words like phekwa, karua and kallabatu filled the conversation where price was rarely mentioned as both parties exchanged comments on technique, colour and craftsmanship. This was no seller peddling his wares. This was an artist proud of his artisanal lineage with a deep empathy, understanding and love for his craft that has been honed over centuries. The survival of the handwoven heritage of Benares that finds mention in Rig Veda written in 2000 BC, is a miraculous phenomenon due to, perhaps, its capability to absorb techniques, ideas and styles with gleeful curiosity. The Vedas mention silk gold cloth worn by Gods and woven cotton yardage that also finds reference in Mahabharat and Ramayan. When Buddha imparted his auspicious preaching, Benares and its weaving techniques were already deemed ‘ancient.' As a young prince renouncing his throne, Gautam Buddha gave up opulent silk robes and took to humble cotton ones of a monk and was cremated, wrapped in fine woven muslin. The connect of the weavers with Buddhism stays till date as they continue to weave brocades in Tibetan motifs. The intricate jamawar shawls of Kashmir inspired the weavers to introduce those shades and patterns to silk and jamawar saris, with a dense field of paisleys, were born. With the coming of Islam, weavers were up for more artistic challenges. Mashru, a mixed fabric of cotton and silk, was discovered as wearing pure silk is prohibited by Islam. Religious injunctions also forbade wearing animal or human figures so the pattern artist—naqshaband  created pleasing geometric and floral themes to cater to the Islamic nobility. To assuage their Hindu patrons, dupattas and saris with holy inscriptions or dohas from Ramayana or from weaver-poet Kabir were woven. Occasionally, socially progressive thinking found expression, as was showcased on Maharani of Baroda's sari that read – “If God is everywhere then who is untouchable.” The East India Company glutted our market with its machine made fabric while blocking Benarasi textile exports to Europe and almost killed this craft.  The weavers were impoverished but somewhere held on to their resilient artistic spirit, sustaining themselves on the Indian bridal demands. The changing landscape with influx of foreign lifestyle impelled the weavers to reflect foreign objects like gramophone, motor cars, a ship with buntings or a vase with roses. English wall paper patterns were adapted into brocade weaving. The short-lived days of friendship with China inspired the weavers. The demand by the women of independent India for a flattering silhouette has led to woven saris that more lissome and easier to drape than before. Just like the city of its nurture, the weavers continue to adopt, adapt and assimilate, carrying on their looms the perennial favorite motifs like marigold, mango and shikaargah, cultural symbolism like lotus and elephants while merrily meandering through the trend bound pastel colors and motifs like owls and Cinderella's carriage. With the passage of time, the elegant bade sahibs have gone missing unable to survive the onslaught of power looms, unfair whole sellers, shameless plagiarism and fraudulent dealings. In the cacophony of our modern life, the delicate duets of experimentation among artists like the dyers, pattern makers, loom setters and weavers have become faint. The centuries old thriving laboratory of design – Benares – awaits the revival of enthusiastic and daring artists who interpreted and immortalized the beauty of our land. column1: Why the statement coat is the most valuable piece in your wardrobe
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Big, bold, and glamourous enough for night as well as day View Gallery 13 Photos The New Statement Coat Forget what anyone has ever told you about the evening coat. It's now a category of your wardrobe that is null and void, or rather has simply segued into daylight hours. It's the same nonsense about a day perfume and a night perfume: your fragrance is your fragrance, and if it is chosen well, you can make the transition from day to night without having to reach for a second scent. Now, it's the same with coats – and the more out-there they are in their colour, texture, silhouette and decoration, the better. Few are more decorated than those at Erdem. Ankle-skimming skirted coats in Prince of Wales check were embroidered with rich floral displays; flocked-velvet styles had shoulder seams and lapels embellished with crystals and pearls; and fit-and-flare brocade versions came double-breasted in an ad hoc selection of jewelled buttons. (Tip for turning last season's tame black coat into this season's statement-maker: load the lapels with crystal brooches – apply the flower-arranging rule that odd numbers work best, and try groupings of three or five.) Miu Miu, too, went the rich and opulent route: noble tapestries trimmed in black velvet had something of the dowager about them (until, that is, one arrived on Gigi Hadid and looked sizzling with heels and bare legs). But you don't have to be Gigi Hadid – nor, for that matter, Theresa May. Now there's a woman who can navigate her way around a loud coat with apparent ease. From graphic and abstract to retina-burning brights, or with placement colour block, she's worn them all, and mostly succeeded. But there's one shade she can't wear: white. A coat thereof would suit the British PM perfectly, but the connotations would never wash among her critics because the woman in a white coat doesn't do anything. She can't. Brave the British weather? No way. Address the public? Forget it. Leaf through a newspaper? Not unless there's a steaming towel to hand – the type that's proffered from a pair of tongs in first-class cabins. White coats are reserved for a special breed, one that flits through life magically repelling dirt and grime. She will find her fix at Chanel, Dior and Giambattista Valli. When it comes to shape, go big or go home. But if you're the type prone to coffee spillages and other mishaps – go wipe-clean. Black oil-slick numbers were a theme at Loewe, where Jonathan Anderson opted for roomy and sweeping; at Miu Miu, where belted long-and-lean styles had a flicker of retro; and at Proenza Schouler, where Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez pimped theirs with contrast stitching and a shearling collar. This brings us neatly to the subject of fuzz – another factor featuring high on the statement-coat agenda. Yes, Preen's pink Mongolian-fur style was particularly pretty, but several designers decided on a murky, swampy green – the exact hue, in fact, of Sesame Street's Oscar the Grouch. Christopher Bailey presented Burberry's in fox fur; at Nina Ricci it arrived in shiny goatskin; while at Rochas it was shearling. When it comes to shape, go big or go home. Puffed-up coats are giving a whole new meaning to the term “duvet days”, meaning that now you can pretty much leave the house with your bedclothes on your back. Sounds good, doesn't it? Stella McCartney favoured deflated down styles, while Chanel showed quilted padded versions in palest pink – with matching handbags. But no one cemented the renaissance of padding better than Balenciaga's Demna Gvasalia (let's get the pronunciation correct, since you're going to be hearing his name a lot: it's Deem-nah Vas-ah-lia – the G is silent), who sent out a red oversize quilted jacket that was worn shrugged off Julia Nobis's shoulders. Interestingly, it was partnered with a crystal turtleneck, black dress trousers and jewelled stilettos, which makes this topper a choice that points to a whole other kind of statement – the coat that's an anti-statement statement. This is an idea that extends to the return of the all-weather anorak, too, even though at Balenciaga those Helly Hansen-style zip-ups were actually inspired by opera coats discovered in the archives of the storied Spanish house; this was made evident by the attention paid to how they were worn – with yanked-back open necklines and collars swept firmly up. It may be an anorak but it's styled as though it's a grand couture piece made in expensive duchesse satin. While over at Dior, smart double-breasted coats were skewed, draped from one shoulder to look as if they had been tossed on in a hurry. And therein is the directive on how to wear your coat this season: the more outstanding the coat, the more nonchalance required; conversely, the more casual the coat, the more important the demeanour. column1: British Fashion Awards 2016: The winners announced
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Congratulations are in order Handpicked from an impressive selection of nominees, the winners of the most significant event in the British fashion calendar have been announced. Awarded at the Royal Albert Hall on the night of December 5, the winners were joined by over four thousand guests, with names such as Naomi Campbell, Alexa Chung, and Kate Moss among them. The ceremony saw a range of both international and home-grown British talent take home an array of prestigious titles, with Gigi Hadid crowned International Model of the year, Alexander McQueen awarded best British Brand, and Jaden and Willow Smith equally named the New Fashion Icons of 2016. The British Fashion Awards have been subject to significant change in 2016, having been rebranded as the Fashion Awards by the British Fashion Council in an effort to celebrate fashion on an international scale. The event will serve as an annual fundraising gala for the British Fashion Council Education Foundation to aid in raising funds for scholarships to allow the best talent in fashion to attend leading schools globally. "As a global industry, we should make a commitment to support talented people from all backgrounds to fulfil their dreams and access the best universities in the world," says BFC chairman, Natalie Massenet. "Over the next 10 years, our ambition is to raise and invest £10 million to support young people in this goal. London is seen as the capital for the most creative new talent in the world that provides talent and energy for the global fashion industry." As expected, the event also took a more glamourous approach than years passed. "We aspire to create an event that is like a mix of the Academy Awards and the Met Ball, on a global scale," Massenet told Business of Fashion. "It's going to be the most sweeping, beautiful, magical, sparkly, twinkly, elegant red carpet you've ever seen." See the full list of winners below. column1: Akaaro redefines the Indian handloom story, this time in Australia
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Gaurav Jai Gupta’s adventures down south View Gallery 6 Photos Akaaro redefines the Indian handloom story, this time in Australia About six years ago, Gaurav Jai Gupta's Akaaro began very quietly, as part of a studio collective in the capital that included various designer-makers including furniture and ceramic artists. Gupta didn't start off with the usual star collection at some fashion week or the other; his relationship with fashion began, quite literally, on the loom. A trained weaver, the loom still stands at the centre of his now solo and still-under-renovation studio that doubles up as a design laboratory of sorts. For the first few years, Akaaro remained introspective, offering hushed narratives that boldly innovated with handlooms to create new and original textiles. He began with scarves, and went on to expand his collection to include saris and tunics, and today the forms get bolder each season. Gradually, the Woolmark shortlisted brand seems to have stepped out of its quietude and into the limelight—from memorable runway performances to rave reviews at recent fashion weeks, Akaaro has become the go-to brand for the cognoscenti. Recently, Gupta, supported by the Australian Consulate General in Mumbai, headed to Australia to represent and promote not just his own brand, but also the new and innovative direction that Indian fashion seems to be headed in. But the handloom story being told by Akaaro isn't within the revivalist tradition that veterans of Indian fashion like Ritu Kumar and Sabyasachi have brought to the forefront, he explains, “I am a weaver, I know what it takes to create textiles. And while I understand the need to preserve history, I also believe you have to be progressive to stay relevant. I think a more sustainable future for handwoven textiles lies in constant design interventions.” Dislocating from the mainstream narrative around handlooms came very organically for Gupta; his entire practice is based on the idea of creating original textiles and is a true reflection of his academically inclined bent of mind and abstract idea of design. In Australia, Gupta spent days interacting with contemporary designers like Dion Lee and Virginia Martin of Búl, engaging in a panel on the “Happiness of Handloom”, interacting with faculty from the Fashion Design Studio, previewing his S/S '17 collection, and of course, brainstorming with the Woolmark team. Apart from exchanging notes on contemporary design, market trends and techniques, Gupta's main goal was to shift the perception of India as a manufacturing centre and emphasise the design innovations that are also part of the conversation here, “India is a fashion-strong country, and we don't talk enough about that. Handloom is definitely the buzzword, but that is because it's our real story, our base and it's also where the best innovations are taking place—we need to push this dialogue ahead. I've also begun conversations on collaborating on capsule collections and retail opportunities. I'm excited about what might lie ahead.” Culture & Living Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Maxwell Osborne And Dao-Yi Chow Out At DKNY
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Lots of changes happened at the brand DKNY creative directors Maxwell Osborne and Dao-Yi Chow will leave the label at the end of the year and return their joint focus to their own brand, Public School. The news comes shortly after the sale of DKNY and its parent company Donna Karan International (DKI) from Kering to G-III Apparel Group for $650 million in July. "Given the company sale and subsequent change in strategies, we have decided to step down and focus on our own business Public School," said the pair - who have been with DKNY since April 2015 - in a statement, reports WWD. "It's been an unbelievable experience to work side by side with the wonderful people at DKNY, especially our amazing design team and atelier. We wish the company success in the future." In addition to Osborne and Chow, CEO Caroline Brown will also leave her role as 2016 comes to a close. “As Donna Karan International transitions to new ownership and therefore new directions, I have decided it is the right time to step down and explore new opportunities,” said Brown, who would have marked two years in her role in January. “This decision accompanies much appreciation and admiration for all of the talented teams here, our founder Donna Karan and our creative directors Dao-Yi Chow and Maxwell Osborne. I know the company rests in good hands under the new leadership of G-III for the next stage of its development." Donna Karan, who remained on as a close advisor the brand after she departed officially in 2015, said yesterday: “The people of Donna Karan have my heart. Together, as a family, we created and built two brands — Donna Karan and DKNY — that I will always be thankful and proud bear my name. I want to send everyone at the company my love and thanks for their enormous energy, passion, creativity and dedication, and good wishes as this new chapter begins." While the search for a new CEO and creative directors commences, the company will be managed by Morris Goldfarb, chairman and CEO of G-III Apparel Group, who emphasised the importance of Karan's involvement with the brand moving forward. “I've spoken to Donna several times. We don't know what direction that will take," he said when asked about the possibility of Karan making a return, reports WWD. “Clearly this is an important name to Donna as it is to us. She's interested clearly on how we've positioned it, how we protect her name, her DNA. Donna is extremely talented and I respect everything she's done." column1: The way Indians buy fashion is changing. Here’s how
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Industry experts weigh in on the shift The average Indian fashion consumer today takes as many cues from an international supermodel as from Bollywood celebrities, contributes annually the booming wedding industry, and finds answers to their wardrobe needs online. To make an impact on the buyer, a designer today has more boxes to tick than ever—celebrity approval, instant availability of the product and transparency in means of production. The economy of fashion is balanced on the dual scales of vanity and practicality. While the selling point is based on utopian aspirations, increasing uncertainty has the consumer grounding their choices in reality. Designers and buyers, therefore, have had to evolve their business modules to adapt. We spoke to the key players in the industry about the new moves. Money talks Veteran designer Tarun Tahiliani believes that the increase in spending power has been the decisive factor in changing the consumer's mentality. “This has meant a more exacting customer in terms of fit, finish and quality of product, as the new Indian has become increasingly aware of global standards of quality,” he says. According to Tahiliani, weddings still remain the crux of the fashion business here. “Indian bridal wear is a niche market in the sense that only Indians and the Indian diaspora across the world have an interest in buying [from that segment]. Nonetheless, it probably accounts for 70 per cent of an Indian designer's repertoire. Indians spend much more on their wedding wear than the rest of world,” says Tahiliani. Instant gratification “The industry is in transition. The ‘See Now, Buy Now' model is becoming more and more prevalent because of the internet and social media,” says Tina Tahiliani Parikh, executive director of the multi-brand store, Ensemble. “It is a well-known fact that a lot of top fashion houses world over are rethinking their strategies in light of this. They are also more aware of the fact that fast fashion brands put trends from the runway onto racks much faster than couture brands,” she says. Designer Manish Malhotra, one of the biggest names in the industry, has invested in e-commerce heavily over the last couple of years. While a vast majority of his clientele frequent the designer's boutiques for their couture needs, his designs are available on several e-commerce platforms as well. “Our strategy so far has been to strike a balance between both worlds. Our newest collections can be found on shelves in-store and online just a couple of days after a show,” he says. Ground rules While many labels are adapting to ensure they have online retail presence, expectations from the shopping experience when buying luxury are not quite the same as with ready-to-wear, primarily due to stark difference in prices. Malhotra believes that, “The beauty of retail today lies in its dichotomy. On one hand, we have brick and mortar—where I talk to my clients, let them touch and feel an outfit, try it on, and then purchase it. And then we have e-commerce, where the physical retail experience is simulated to bridge geographical gaps.” Make it bigger Anita Dongre's business includes her main line Anita Dongre, Global Desi, AND, Grassroot by Anita Dongre and jewellery brand Pink City crafted by Jet Gems. In her coterie of labels that include accessible mall staple stores, NGO collaborations and bridal go-tos, Dongre's unique model targets consumers of varying ages and income brackets. Focus on social media has always been important to her brand, but her learning curve was when the Duchess of Cambridge was spotted in a dress by her label and the overnight demand for it was such that brand's website crashed from the excessive orders. “We have a lot of customers come in with pictures of celebrities demanding the same [garment]. It's not that there is a dearth of the fashion conscious, but the response an outfit has when worn by a celebrity is incomparable,” says the designer. Simple, but significant “I think consumers are more thoughtful and considered in making buying choices, be it what they wear, or for that matter what they eat,” says Maithili Ahluwalia, owner, CEO and creative director of Bungalow 8. Anita Dongre's label Grassroot by Anita Dongre is consciously focusing on ethical means of production. “There is a definite demand for ethical fashion, but we still have a long way to go for this to be a mass shift,” says Dongre. column1: Tom Ford on dressing Melania Trump: “She’s not necessarily my image.”
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Another designer weighs in The impending Trump Presidency has already touched the energy, infrastructure and banking industries, to name a few. And unsurprisingly the world of fashion is also involve in potential ramifications and outcomes of the next president of the United States. In the days post election, Michelle Obama favourite Sophie Theallet penned an open letter saying she would not be dressing the First Lady-to-be. Following her comments, all-American designer Tommy Hilfiger said he would be proud to dress both Melania and Ivanka Trump firmly stating that dressing the first family is not a matter of politics. Today more debate on the matter has been provided by yet another Tom, this time creative director Tom Ford whose namesake label is a staple on many red carpets. "She's not necessarily my image," Ford said on American talk show, The View. Ford was very open about his allegiance during the election declaring he was "sad and disappointed" when democratic candidate Hillary Clinton lost the electoral vote. The designer also went on to say that he didn't think his haute couture approach is relatable to everybody. When asked about whether or not he has dressed current First Lady Michelle Obama Ford said he had dressed FLOTUS for her meeting with Queen Elizabeth II earlier this year. "And that, I thought, was appropriate. I live in London so that made sense, and it was an honour." This article originally appeared on Vogue.com.au Fashion Beauty Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Love Vaani Kapoor’s Parisian look in ‘Befikre’? Get it now!
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Our favourite fashion picks + advice from her stylist Back in 2013, Vaani Kapoor made her big Bollywood entry as the kurta-clad girl next door for Shuddh Desi Romance. But if that's what you're expecting from her character in Befikre, you're in for a big surprise. This time around, Kapoor takes over the screen opposite Ranveer Singh as Shyra, a free-spirited wild child with a wardrobe to match. “This was my first time dressing a Bollywood star and my first time working on a film,” her Paris-based stylist Natalie Yuksel tells Vogue. “The experience was totally different and on a much larger scale. A fashion shoot takes a few weeks; this project took me seven months! It has definitely been one of my career highlights so far.” Want to know more about Kapoor's Befikre vibe? We asked Yuksel to break it down for us. Tell us a little bit about Vaani Kapoor's look in Befikre Vaani has three main looks in this film, each one showing her character's evolution. The first is much more daring and rebellious: dip-dyed orange hair, rings on each finger, skimpier outfits. The second is where we see her as a typical Parisian with an emphasis on sharp stylish combinations with an element of comfort. There was more emphasis on denim, sneakers and loose fitting T-shirts. The third look is where we see her as a woman. Her wardrobe becomes more feminine and sleek, chunky boots are replaced by stiletto heels. Name five separates a Bollywood fan would need to channel Kapoor's on-screen look in reality 1. A well-cut pair of jeans, preferably the 'mom jeans' style 2. A well-cut white T-shirt 3. A beige trench 4. A black leather jacket 5. A pair of minimal sneakers in white or black From all of Kapoor's looks in the movie, which one is your absolute favourite? Gosh, it's impossible for me to pick just one! I'll tell you my favourites from each section of the film. In look one, I loved the 'unavailable' tight black dress she wore during a scene where she has dinner on the boat. In look two, I loved the white cable knit jumper and cognac orange A-line skirt from her supermarket scene. And in look three, my favourite was the red satin dress where Shyra dances the tango with Dharam; she looked spectacular. Also I must say I really loved all of her St Tropez looks. How do you think Kapoor's ensembles in the movie complement her character in the film? I think the looks were crucial for this. Her character evolves so much during the film and this evolution is really highlighted through the styling. The idea of having three different looks was something that came quite spontaneously upon reading the script. It become evident that Shyra's personal journey should be accompanied by the changes in style. Like Vaani Kapoor's style from the movie? column1: Meet the Indian débutante who attended the prestigious Le Bal in Paris
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Jayati Modi’s diaries Remember Shamira from Gippi? Jayati Modi, who featured in Karan Johar's film back 2013, was recently introduced at the iconic Bal des Débutantes in Paris. Modi, who spends her time travelling (she was recently part of a Semester at Sea), or attending summer school in New York and the occasional walk down the runway, was thrilled to bits to have been a part of Le Bal. Vogue spoke to the young deb about the big night. View Gallery 4 Photos Meet the Indian débutante who attended the prestigious Le Bal in Paris What was your experience like? What did you expect and did the evening live up to your expectations? The whole experience was surreal—it was a magical weekend to say the least. It was an incredible weekend and I met the most extraordinary group of people, many of whom I became very close to! Tell us about the dress you picked for the evening. I wore a three-piece Vivienne Westwood gown, in shades of orange and pink. I loved it because it was different, not the typical dress you'd imagine for a ball, and yet it was regal in its own way. What was the grooming process like? On the evening before the Bal, we had a waltz rehearsal. I went in really nervous, but it turned out to be a lot of fun. We spent a lot of time having our hair and make-up done as our days were filled with photoshoots. What is your favourite thing about Paris? I love the charm and quaintness of European cities. Paris in particular is even more special, with its unique mix of art, culture, fashion and people. It has a little something for everyone. Fashion Weddings Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Exclusive: Deepika Padukone reveals the secret to her super-fit body
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We chat with her on the set of her NIKEiD shoot A photoshoot with Bharat Sikka and a quick change (high-waist tights, fitted tank top, structured jacket and trainers) later, she sits down with Vogue India for an exclusive interview. On the concept of NIKEiD As a sporting family, a visit to a Nike store was a must whenever we travelled abroad. I'd see a lot of people walk in and create their customised shoes, so I am extremely excited that NIKEiD is finally launching in India. It's not just for sports enthusiasts. It allows you to add a personal touch and has a fashion angle as well, ideal for people with a strong sense of identity. Moreover, it's one more thing to encourage people towards fitness and a healthier lifestyle. On her NIKEiD shoe My shoe features the number five, as it is really close to my heart. Not only is it my birth date, but also the day I was born as an athlete. I prefer versatile shoes that I can wear with several outfits. I also don't like an overdose of colour. Keeping that in mind, I've kept my NIKEiD subtle, with just the right amount of colour to make it pop. The foundation is black and white with a hint of blue and green to add flair. Anaita (Shroff Adajania), whose instincts I absolutely trust, helped me design the shoe, and nudged me to add certain elements to it too. So, my NIKEiD shoe is my reflection with a sprinkle of inputs from the fashion guru! On athleisure I tend to steer towards comfort dressing for my off-duty looks. It helps that athletic wear is considered cool today, and that there are so many options to choose from. It doesn't look like you simply walked out in your gym wear anymore. You'll mostly find me in sneakers when I'm not dressing specifically for an event, shoot or endorsement. On her Nike favourites The high-waist tights are a definite favourite and I find them extremely comfortable to work out in. They suit the Indian body type really well too. I have the Nike Free Trainers in every possible colour—soon I'm going to need a separate cupboard just for them! On her fitness regime When I'm in Mumbai, I largely follow a combination of Pilates and functional training. But my regime also depends on where I am, how much time I have to work out and whether I'm training for something specific. But I do make sure to pack in some form of exercise even when I'm travelling or pressed for time—even if it's just a 10-minute walk on a treadmill and some stretching. While this doesn't compensate for a full-blown workout, it helps with the blood circulation and makes me feel alive. On sport and the three Ds (dedication, determination, and discipline) Sport has played a big role in instilling these qualities in me, and have been passed on to me from a sportsman (father, Prakash Padukone) himself. I've also learnt this from my mother who has had a very disciplined childhood and life. These qualities were ingrained in my sister and me from a young age. Since we were athletes, we were raised in a very disciplined manner. Every minute of our lives—from the time we slept and woke up to our practise and study schedules—were accounted for and we rarely went off-track. These qualities are a part of me now and I realise the value it has added to my life. We are not in an easy profession and are faced with constant challenges, negativity and speculation. I feel these qualities help the mind too—they make you a better person, allow you to deal with situations more effectively and stay focused. On the Indian woman's changing relationship with fitness I cross Worli Sea Face on my way to the gym every morning, and have been doing so for years. Earlier, I would mostly see men exercising there. But over the years, it makes me extremely happy to see the number of women has increased as well. Culturally, Indian women have always been made to feel like just homemakers. Even when fitness became a fad in the country, it was mostly men who embraced it. But I see that changing now. Whether they're going to the gym, playing a sport, or just brisk walking, women are giving physical fitness due importance in their own ways today. On making fitness a lifestyle I would say don't follow fads or fitness trends. No one understands your body better than you do. So listen to it and tailor your food and exercise regime accordingly. Yes, there will be times when you will have to push yourself out of bed, but understand that being physically active makes a huge difference to your mind and body and keeps you mentally fit too. In all honesty, fitness is a complete lifestyle change. It's not just about how many hours you spend in the gym. Be mindful of the food that you eat, the hours you sleep, the amount you hydrate yourself, and the environment you surround yourself with. These wholesome changes will make all the difference. column1: Gucci and Burberry’s digital footprint now leads fashion industry
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Thanks to Snapchat and Instagram In the age of e-commerce fashion houses are no longer relying on a facade of exclusivity, with many brands boosting their numbers by investing in their 'Digital IQ'. Research firm L2 releases an annual list of brands leading the digital market in fashion and this year's list bears little resemblance to that of 2015. Famed for their trench coats and Oscar-worthy Christmas campaigns Burberry has always lead the fashion pack being one of the first luxury houses to foray in e-commerce and consumer engagement. However, this year the British-based company has come off second best to Alessandro Michele's Gucci. With the benchmark for digital performance sitting at 85 for luxury brands, Burberry and Gucci are well ahead of the game with scores of 144 and 145, respectively. The 2016 round up also marks the first time Gucci has earned a place in L2's top five - this year joined by Burberry, Coach, Ralph Lauren and Tory Burch. When crunching the numbers L2 takes into account a label's e-commerce, search visibility, social media interaction and mobile aptitude. According to the research company, Gucci's success this year can be credited to the brand's innovative content integration features and their visibility on third party sites like Net-a-Porter. Additionally, the Italian label's social media engagement doubled over the past 12 months with the introduction of celebrity-endorsed social media initiatives as well as artist collaborations and behind-the-scenes content via Snapchat and Instagram. Since welcoming Michele as well as new CEO Marco Bizzari, Gucci further overhauled their online presence through the relaunch of its e-commerce in October. column1: Pirelli’s 2017 calendar features our favourite women with zero make-up
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Shot by ace photographer Peter Lindberg View Gallery 10 Photos Pirelli’s 2017 Calendar Girls Pirelli has revealed the first images from its 2017 calendar - shot this year by Peter Lindberg - of Robin Wright, Julianne Moore, Uma Thurman and Nicole Kidman. The actresses' images have all the hallmarks of Lindbergh's work - stripped back, natural and beautiful - and continue in a similar portraiture vein to last year's calendar, which was photographed by Annie Leibovitz. Lindbergh chose to give the work the title "Emotional" to emphasise how the idea behind his photos was “to create a calendar not around perfect bodies, but on sensitivity and emotion, stripping down to the very soul of the sitters, who thus become more nude than naked,” said the brand today. It marks the third time that he has shot the famous compilation, having been responsible for the 1996 and 2002 editions. Joining the four stars who were revealed today are Jessica Chastain, Penelope Cruz, Rooney Mara, Helen Mirren, Lupita Nyong'o, Charlotte Rampling, Lea Seydoux, Alicia Vikander, Kate Winslet, Zhang Ziyi and Anastasia Ignatova, professor of Political Theory at the Moscow State University of International Relations. The subjects were shot this year, between May and June in locations including Berlin, Los Angeles, New York, London and the beach at Le Touquet, France. “My aim was to portray women in a different way and I did it by calling in actresses who've played an important role in my life, getting as close as possible to them to take my photos," explained Lindbergh. "As an artist, I feel I'm responsible for freeing women from the idea of eternal youth and perfection. The ideal of perfect beauty promoted by society is something that simply can't be attained.” This article originally appeared on Vogue.co.uk What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Are you ready for the hottest show of the year? The Victoria's Secret show will, as we predicted, be missing two of its most prominent figures, as Angels Candice Swanepoel and Behati Prinsloo confirm that they will sit this one out. The twosome told their Instagram followers this weekend that they wouldn't travel to Paris with the rest of the Victoria's Secret line-up after all. The show would have been the tenth Victoria's Secret outing for both models, but both confirmed that they will be back on the catwalk for next year's show. “To the girls and crew, good luck in Paris, me and Dusty Rose will be cheering,” Prinsloo said. “Love you all, have fun in Paris and see you next year!” Meanwhile Swanepoel echoed her sentiments a few hours later: “Good luck in Paris beautiful ladies! So sad to be missing this show! No doubt it will be magical. So hard for me to disappoint the people that always root for me, I wish I was there making you all proud. In their absence, the rest of the Angels were on hand to give advice to the new starters. “Take a breath and try to enjoy the moment,” Josephine Skriver said, while Romee Strijd advised them to “really embrace” the experience, despite their nerves. column1: Neeta Lulla designs for a Bollywood-themed musical in Dubai
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A class act View Gallery 4 Photos Neeta Lulla designs for a Bollywood-themed musical in Dubai There is no denying that Bollywood is akin to a religion to Indians. Testimony to the fact is the opening of world's first Bollywood-inspired theme park: Bollywood Parks Dubai by Dubai Parks and Resorts (Middle East's largest integrated theme park destination). Apart from rides, activities and restaurants that pay homage to some of the biggest Bollywood movies, another crowd-puller promises to be the mega musical Jaan e Jigar, which will be unveiled on December 1, 2016. A highly-anticipated part of the park's entertainment roster, this Bollywood-inspired fairy tale themed musical with over 10 songs promises to be fittingly larger than life. A magnum opus of this scale demanded an experienced designer and stylist to get the look just right. Enter Neeta Lulla. The designer, who has been associated with blockbusters like Chandni, Lamhe, Khuda Gawah, Devdas and Jodha Akbar among several others through the course of her illustrious career, was a natural fit. “A production of this magnitude demands time and I have been working on it for close to a year. I have worked on costumes not only for the lead dancers, but for the entire crew, rounding it up to around 1,200 costumes!” says the designer. Lulla described the costumes for certain characters—a delicate, floral-heavy look for Gulpari, the princess of the forest; and an edgy serpentine-inspired wardrobe for Marjaani, the anti-heroine—as some of her favourites. “Working on costumes for characters like Nashooq, who is half man-half hyena and Jharna, the pirate chieftain's daughter, were most challenging,” she adds. Ask her about the experience, and Lulla is quick to point out the difference between designing for films and for stage. “A lot of factors have to be taken into consideration when designing for live stage shows. The costumes need to be easy and quick to change. Comfort plays a big role, and one also needs to take into consideration that the costumes should not hurt the accompanying dancers during the performances. The fabrics used should be long-lasting but also equally glamorous. Finishing touches like jewellery and footwear need to play dual roles—aid the overall look but not hamper the dancers' ease and movement either,” the designer explains. The designer strongly believes in the influence Bollywood has on fashion. “Fashion has always been influenced by films. Movies are larger than live and bring dreams alive on screen.
