column1: What will Deepika Padukone’s look be like as ‘Rani Padmavati’?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion We asked the costume designers themselves We now know that couture designers Rimple & Harpeet Narula have been chosen to dress the star-studded cast of Sanjay Leela Bhansali's upcoming period drama—Rani Padmavati. Rumour has it, the famously tight-lipped director has constructed tents around the production site to avoid any images being leaked on the internet. Curiosity got the better of us and Vogue got into conversation with Harpeet Narula about the costume designing of one of the most talked about films in recent history. What are the challenges involved in creating costumes for a period drama like Rani Padmavati? Since it is a period piece, we had to be extra careful when it came to maintaining the authenticity of the costumes. Bearing that in mind, we did intensive research on the period by going through old travellers' accounts from that era as well as regular visits to the Calico and Jaipur museums to get the touch-feel-look right. Most of the actual samples of antique textiles and costumes from that period are dispersed all over the world in various museums and archives, so our love for travel and museums also came in handy when we had to collate all the information required during the research process. Even then, physical samples of such textiles are few and far in between, so we had to refer to a lot of miniature paintings, murals and frescoes to get the nuances of the styling as close to how they used to be. As there were no man-made fabrics at that time, nor was sericulture prevalent in the subcontinent, we have avoided using silk or other Chinese substitutes and only used organic cottons, along with traditional techniques such as block printing and ‘varq ka kaam' that were popular then. Apart from getting these cultural and period references right, we had to come up with signature looks for all three main characters that would define their personas and set them apart in the eyes of the audience. देवी स्थापना के शुभ अवसर पर मिलिए रानी पद्मावती से #Padmavati @FilmPadmavati A post shared by Deepika Padukone (@deepikapadukone) on Sep 20, 2017 at 5:54pm PDT What was the brief given to you by Sanjay Leela Bhansali? Besides having a great eye for detail, Mr Bhansali is a great story teller. During the initial stages of the project, him and his team took us through the script in order to understand the flow of the narrative and truly understand each character, because the garments have to reflect each of their personalities. From a design perspective, it was very interesting since various cultures come together through the course of the story—the Sinhalese princess who becomes a Rajput queen, the Afghan invader who becomes the Sultan of Delhi. The elements used show how every region leaves its stamp on the textiles and costumes, and how one motif can have different meanings given the region and the culture. For example, the paisley can represent both a date sapling in Islamic iconography or a raw mango (keri) in Hindu traditions. Of all the looks, which was the most iconic? Interestingly, we asked Mr Bhansali during the initial script readings which outfit would he consider the most important and iconic, and all he said to us was that between the three main characters, we would need to come up with over a hundred-plus looks and that each look has to be equally important as it would define that particular moment of the storyline, so we had to give our best to each. Given the scale of production, elaborate detailing and wear-tear during intense sequences such as the battle scenes, we had to come up with replicas of almost all the looks, which in itself was quite challenging since we used actual antique textiles mixed with newer fabrics, and getting backups was quite the task. However, it is not the designer nor the film-maker who makes a look iconic but the audience that eventually does so by referring to it over the years. To call one's current work iconic would be getting too big for your boots. View Gallery 11 Photos What Deepika Padukone looks like in Rani Padmavati A post shared by Deepika Padukone (@deepikapadukone) on Sep 20, 2017 at 6:14pm PDT So far, whose character are you most drawn to? We have had our phases when it comes to a favourite character with each look test. Deepika (Padukone), Shahid (Kapoor) and Ranveer (Singh) are truly dedicated to their craft and the moment they don a costume they leave behind the actor and become the character, imbibing Mr Bhansali's vision, and it's very difficult to pick a favourite. What would you say is the highlight we need to look out for? Keeping aside the scale and production of the project, we feel that the way Mr Bhansali stays true to his craft, working in a pure zone, not using any gimmicks and making his story, the characters and their intertwined destinies; the true hero of the project will be the thing to look out for and what the audience will take back home with them. While Padukone's look in the period drama is a closely-guarded secret (for now) the fact that she carries off ethnic silhouettes with stunning grace, is not. Here's a look at some of the star's most beautiful Indian looks yet. View Gallery 11 Photos What Deepika Padukone looks like in Rani Padmavati What's New Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Thinking of adopting a furry friend? This is where you should be this weekend
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Find your match at World For All’s Adoptathon 2016 View Gallery 8 Photos Adoptathon Eyes like melting pools of honey that you'd want to lose yourself in; soft-warm furry bodies to snuggle up to when you're feeling lonely—and they don't talk your ear off, like pesky humans tend to. Yes, we're talking about god's greatest creations—puppies and kittens. It's a documented fact that bringing an animal into your home can change your life—and theirs too. Mumbai is home to innumerable strays who spend their lives fighting the harsh streets of the Maximum City, fending for themselves. And often, they don't succeed. Many organisations work tirelessly to help stray animals, providing medical aid and shelter. World For All Animal Care & Adoptions (WFA), a Mumbai-based animal welfare NGO is one of them, and has been uniting lonely dogs and cats with aspiring animal-parents for five years now with Adoptathon, Asia's largest adoption camp. At Adoptathon 2016, you can choose from 150 breeds of Indian puppies and kittens (all between two and six months) to add to your family—if you're ready to put in the hours and effort that they need. If you're wary or haven't adopted before, WFA will be on hand post-adoption to help the new parents through the journey. They've also partnered with veterinaries, behaviourists and adoption counsellors and a set up stalls with brands like Raw Pressery, The Label Life, Pedigree, Bollywoof Barkery (baked goodies for your furry friends) and more, to ensure your weekend is as fun as it is furry. And to entice you further, Vogue hung out with a few of the adoptees, gave them some Louboutins and Choos to play with (naturally) and discovered for ourselves, the real meaning of pet therapy—and this weekend, you should too. Adoptathon will take place in Bandra West on November 26 and 27 between 11am and 7pm. St Theresa Boys High School Ground, St Theresa Road, Bandra (W), Mumbai. column1: This is how your favourite celebrities are wearing the ’90s cool-kid patches
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Bringing quirky back View Gallery 9 Photos This is how your favourite celebrities are wearing the ’90s cool-kid patches We bet our vintage Versace and Calvin Klein that your present wardrobe is a testament to fashion's rekindled romance with the '90s. And your nostalgic selection of chokers, crop tops, pompoms and slogan tees is all good, but the style set has already moved on to another favourite from the decade—the embroidered patch. An emblem (quite literally) of one's individuality, this DIY-friendly trend was, and still is, preferred for its knack to give any look a quirky and youthful spin. Bollywood's pack of young style icons has wasted no time in warming up to this trend that is a throwback to their childhood, with Alia Bhatt leading the way. Bhatt has been spotted in appliqué patches on her jackets, crop tops and shorts on several occasions. We love her combination of retro denim shorts, a white shirt, and booties—perfect for a music festival. There is no denying that denim and patches make for a winning team. Kangana Ranaut and Anushka Sharma demonstrate the merits of a patchwork denim jacket—a staple that can be styled with ripped jeans and jersey dresses with equal ease. You can also take a leaf from Jacqueline Fernandez's book and break the monotony of a denim-on-denim look with a denim duster jacket featuring whimsical patches. Bored of your same ol' jeans? Update them with some playful add-ons as seen on Amy Jackson. Esha Gupta gives us a master class in balancing girl boss with cool girl. Follow her lead and team a pencil skirt with a patchwork shirt for a job interview or lunch meeting. Parineeti Chopra shows how one can save a formal look from falling into a boring trap. Simply sew on some patches to your double-breasted blazer and you're good to go! And trust Mira Rajput in a patchwork shirt, to give us the ultimate lesson in post-maternity chic. A true demonstration of the trend's versatility, turns out, you really can sport this one as you fancy. Fashion Beauty What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: This London-based Indian designer is proud to be an immigrant
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And unafraid to wear it on his sleeve Ashish Gupta of the fashion brand Ashish took the bow at his spring/summer 2017 show in a T-shirt emblazoned with the word ‘Immigrant'. The London-based Indian-origin designer, in the light of recent political changes, wants to make the term ‘Immigrant' free of its alienating subtext. His spring/summer 2017 show itself was Gupta's ode to Indian culture. But what caught the eye of the masses was the designer's sartorial speak. Recently, retail giant Brown's announced that they will be stocking a line of the ‘Immigrant' T-shirts along with Ashish's diffusion range like T'aint by Ashish. Vogue speaks to the designer about what inspired his bold move. The word ‘Immigrant' has a heavy context, given the current global socio-political climate. What made you have it on your sweatshirt? There is a wave of racism and xenophobia sweeping the world and we cannot let it win. I think the whole political system has and continues to be so disrespectful towards immigrants. Despite the fact that we contribute so much to the economy and culture, we pay taxes, create new jobs, set up businesses, bring different experiences and skills. So why does this word have such a negative connotation, why are we always described as a burden that needs to be 'controlled'? How can laws uphold our equality and freedom when the people making those laws play on one group's fears about another group? I am tired of hearing ‘we are tolerant of other cultures'. I will not be tolerated as if I am something unpleasant that refuses to go away. I would like to be embraced, welcomed, treated equally. The language must change. Brexit and the US election have exposed the racism that has consistently been denied to have existed, and it is more important than ever that we educate people about the fact that we are all human beings and we are all equal, regardless of where we come from or what are beliefs are; whether we are men, woman, trans, gay, or straight. What was the response you received from people when they saw you wearing it? I was overwhelmed—it was good to know that there are so many people that supported me and that message. I was so touched to know that I had made people feel proud of their heritage. So many sent me their stories, one person said how her family's store was vandalised with the word 'immigrant' when she was growing up and they had to clean up all the graffiti; another said how much she was bullied while growing up in Sweden and how the show made her feel so proud of her Indian heritage. It's so sad that people are bullied or treated like second class citizens because they are from another country or culture. There is only one race, and it's the human race. T'aint by Ashish is aimed at a younger, bolder, more creative audience. What can we expect from this collection? I started T'aint as a personal project. I want it to be project that gives me the freedom to explore things like sexual freedom, LGBT rights, gender and race issues. It is a project that I hope will become a platform for visual dialogues about important issues like this. T'aint by Ashish is available at Brownsfashion.com Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Franca Sozzani honoured with fashion award
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Italian Vogue editor-in-chief recognised Franca Sozzani will be awarded the Swarovski Fashion Award For Positive Change at this year's Fashion Awards, set to take place on December 5 at the Royal Albert Hall. The newly created award "recognises individuals who promote the welfare of others by the generous donation of their resources in order to achieve change and positive impact to good causes", according to the British Fashion Council. The Italian Vogue editor-in-chief has been chosen as its first recipient as a result of "her commitment to diversity and for utilising her position and influence to positively impact the wider world", in her role as global ambassador against hunger for the UN World Food Program; her work with Convivo to eradicate AIDS; and her work with the European Institute of Oncology where she is committed to diagnosing and preventing oncological disease. “Words cannot express the huge deal of admiration and respect I have for Franca and her work," said BFC chairman Natalie Massenet. "She exemplifies those qualities this award has been created to honour, and her tireless commitment to the causes she cares so passionately about is a great example to us all. The positive impact she has had on the fashion and global communities will be felt for generations to come." column1: Chatsworth House to host its largest exhibition to date
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion House Style: Five Centuries Of Fashion At Chatsworth will open next spring View Gallery 4 Photos House Style: Five Centuries of Fashion at Chatsworth The residence of the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire, a frequent location for film sets and home to an extensive private art and sculpture archive, Chatsworth House is one of the most stylish stately homes in the country, and next year it is opening its doors to its largest exhibition to date. House Style: Five Centuries Of Fashion At Chatsworth - curated by American Vogue's international editor-at-large Hamish Bowles - will open at the Derbyshire estate next spring, showcasing the history of fashion in the Devonshire Collection. Notable names from the last 500 years will be at the centre of the exhibition, including the 18th century "Empress of Fashion” Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire; Adele Astaire, sister and dance partner of Fred Astaire; two of the infamous Mitford sisters - Deborah Devonshire and Nancy Mitford; Stella Tennant, who was photographed with her grandmother, the 11th Duchess, at Chatsworth for Vogue; and John F Kennedy's sister Kathleen "Kick" Kennedy. The stories of these captivating women will be brought to life through a comprehensive exploration of their clothing and accessories. Ordered by themes such as Coronation Dress, The Devonshire House Ball, The Georgiana Effect, Country Living, and Entertaining At Chatsworth, the exhibition's highlight pieces will range from Jean-Phillipe Worth and Christian Dior couture and items from Gucci, Erdem, Alexander McQueen and Vetements, to livery and uniforms at Chatsworth across the ages, as well as 19th-century fancy-dress costumes and the family's coronation and wedding gowns. Of curating the extensive exhibition, Bowles said this morning: "Chatsworth is a real treasure house and the characters of generations of Cavendish family members who have peopled its rooms and gardens and landscapes is revealed as vividly through their choice of clothing and adornments, as through the canvases and lenses of the great artists and photographers who have memorialised them through the centuries." "In House Style," he continued, "we hope to bring these compelling and fascinating people and the very different worlds they inhabited to life, through the clothes and the jewels that they wore.” House Style: Five Centuries Of Fashion At Chatsworth will run from March 25 to October 22 2017. column1: This traditional wedding staple is making a huge comeback
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It’s also celebrity approved View Gallery 16 Photos This traditional wedding staple is making a huge comeback Gone are the days when your kurtas and anarkalis solely revolved around the churidaar. With the undeniable return of historical traditional silhouettes, the sharara has captured our imagination (and wardrobes) like never before. A dramatically flared trouser typically worn with jackets, anarkalis and kurtis, the sharara was brought to Indian shores by the Mughals, and was heavily favoured by the women of their royal household. Its recent reappearance on the silver screen—Deepika Padukone in Bajirao Mastani, Anushka Sharma in Sultan, Madhuri Dixit-Nene in Dedh Ishqiya and Pernia Qureshi in Jaanisaar, to name a few—can be touted as a big reason for its renewed popularity. Off-screen celebrity approval too has sealed the sharara's status as a traditional wear MVP. With the wedding season upon us, it's just the silhouette you need stand out at a baraat or during a sangeet performance. Sharara sets in pastel hues, particularly ivory, are a unanimous favourite. Opt for a heavily-embroidered piece with a short kurta like Sridevi for an engagement or reception party. If you wish to go casual in the same colour, an ankle-length one paired with a kurta embellished with light gota work, as seen on Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, is an easy winner. You could also channel your inner begum like Kareena Kapoor Khan, in a black and gold set, statement chand balis and kohl-heavy eyes for a sangeet. Another celebrity-approved way to sport your sharara set is with a scalloped dupatta, as demonstrated by Bachchan, Juhi Chawla and Sophie Choudry. Think long kurtas are the only options you can pair your sharara with? Allow Nargis Fakhri in a thigh-grazing short kurta and Karisma Kapoor in an asymmetrical jacket, to change your mind. If you're going short with your kurta, remember to opt for an ornate, statement-making sharara for maximum impact. Fashion Wellness Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Who inspired Stella McCartney’s debut menswear line?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion "Tailoring is something that has always been in the DNA of our brand" At a star-studded party to launch her debut menswear line - alongside a presentation of her spring 2017 womenswear collection - Stella McCartney made her mark (literally, her name glittered in big, bold lettering in every room) on a venue very familiar to her family - Abbey Road Studios. We caught up with the designer to discuss the motivations and inspirations behind her latest venture. Browse her first menswear collection below. View Gallery 20 Photos Who Inspired Stella’s Debut Menswear Line? Who or what was the inspiration behind your first menswear collection? There was so much inspiration behind the collection. I of course looked to the men in my life, my husband, my father, my friends. I also thought of great men of the world, people who have had an impact, like artists and musicians. We really drew inspiration from London as well, in particular it's musical history; we wanted that feeling and spirit. What do you love about the way the men in your life wear clothes? I really admire honesty in wearing clothes, whether it be a man or a woman, and I always notice that quality in the men in my life. But I don't really feel that as a house we will approach that honesty and that spirit differently for men than we do women. I think the most important thing in wearing clothes is being yourself, being effortless, being true to yourself and not trying to be anyone else for the sake of fashion; not compromising who you are and your beliefs for style. I love that my husband has a more controlled side to how he wears clothes, but then he can also be more casual and sporty, and I find that that way of having a juxtaposition is something that I really use in both my womenswear and my menswear. What menswear staples do you regularly buy/wear/borrow? I trained at Saville Row and tailoring is something that has always been in the DNA of our brand. Why is now the right time for the brand to introduce the category? I don't really think there is ever a “right time” to launch anything. It's something we'd been talking about for a long time and something I really wanted to do, and I felt like as a brand we were ready to take on that challenge. I'm very happy with where we are with the womenswear and I felt like it was time for the Stella woman to have a complement; the Stella man. Why did you decide to throw a fabulous event rather than show at menswear fashion week? As a house we really don't take ourselves too seriously. We're not approaching this in a conventional manner; we don't want to do it in the same way as everyone else. We're starting something new and we wanted to do it in a new way, because this is like nothing we've ever done before. What is your favourite piece in the collection? I would have to say that my favourite piece is the silk shirt with the two swallows on it. It's very similar to a shirt that my dad used to own and I absolutely loved when I was growing up. I did the exact blouse in womenswear as well because when I was younger I actually thought it was my mum's, but when I realised it was my dad's I felt like I just had to include it in the menswear. It's a very nostalgic piece for me. I am also very enthusiastic about the non-leather sneakers. They are, of course, a sustainably sourced vegan material, and the shoes have turned out so beautifully. I don't find that an emphasis on sustainability is evident in men's fashion, so it was crucial to me to include that in my collection and bring that part of me into the realm of men's fashion. How does the menswear marry with your womenswear? I think the two complement each other very well. I always try to have some humour in my designs, and a versatility in all of the pieces. I want someone of any age and from any walk of life to be able to come to me and find something that suits them, and that is something I strongly believe in for both the menswear and womenswear. column1: What the world can expect from Melania Trump
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion She has a nigh on impossible sartorial act to follow as FLOTUS, where Michelle Obama’s stunning smart-casual style reigned supreme View Gallery 6 Photos What We Can Expect From Melania Trump? Donald Trump's victory speech on Tuesday evening, which sealed an astonishing win over Hillary Clinton, was stunning in many aspects. Moderate sentiment, conciliatory tones, an appeal for unity: all were unexpected hints that Mr. Trump would undergo a gracious reimagining even as he remoulded the presidency in his own image. Fashion-watchers, however, were less shocked. Melania Trump, the 46-year-old third wife of the Republican president elect, has been undergoing a subtle transformation, sartorially-speaking, for several months. Melania has sought, over the course of the campaign, to elevate her style. The thigh-split dresses have been replaced by more demure shift dresses from Michael Kors. Low-cut necklines have been superseded by high-necked jumpsuits. She may have even taken tips from Ivanka Trump, who is so expert at dressing for the political occasion that she simultaneously managed to introduce her father as the Republican nominee for president in July and ensure that the pale pink, knee-length sheath number she was wearing from her own fashion line subsequently sold out at Macy's and Nordstrom. (“Shop Ivanka's look from her #RNC speech,” read the tweet, with a link to her dress.) Melania wears clothes her way, and according to her own agenda. Why else would she don a white silk Ralph Lauren jumpsuit for her husband's victory speech: a clear reference to the white Ralph Lauren pant suits Hillary Clinton wore at critical moments in her campaign, for the Democratic National Convention in July, and at the third presidential debate, and which spawned a hashtag #wearwhitetovote? Of course, white is a familiar choice for Melania. She has always favoured the kinds of pale pastels, whites and creams that indicate there's a limousine round every corner, and a dry-cleaning bill comprising figures to rival the GDP of a small European country (Slovenia, for instance – where Melania was born). But choosing to wear a designer, a colour and a style so closely aligned to the image of her husband's rival cannot be coincidence. That's not to say she's curbed the sexiness altogether. A former model, Melania ploughs the trophy wife furrow with more attention to detail than most. Witness the closely fitted, white Roksanda Margot dress she wore in July, with salon-fresh hair and sky-high nude courts (presumably to offset the fact of its being from Net-A-Porter's bridal range). Or the Emilia Wickstead pink crepe top and white high-waisted skirt she chose to deliver a speech in Pennsylvania on the campaign trail, which enhanced her pin-up proportions. Mrs. Trump knows that her image must square with the affluence people have come to expect from her husband. Ergo, her accessories are an expert exercise in ticking the boxes of prosperity. There's the Hermès Birkin and Chanel quilted handbags (in those hyper-feminine blush and cream colours), the car-to-carpet Louboutins, the emerald-cut Graff wedding ring, all topped off with freshly blow-dried hair, Colgate white teeth and the dewy, age-defying complexion. And while this high-maintenance image will prevail when Melania enters the White House, it will be interesting to see whether she seeks to temper it with more affordable brands, as Michelle Obama did (she paid “homage” to her predecessor in a much-derided speech, after all). Obama worked this strategy to impressive effect, careful to mix lower-priced brands such as J Crew into her FLOTUS wardrobe. Melania will presumably stick to the labels she loves and purchases for herself from Net-A-Porter – Dolce & Gabbana, Roksanda, Balmain, Michael Kors – but she may well fall for a Self Portrait dress, or even debut styles from Ivanka's affordably-priced eponymous range. She would be wise to favour predominantly American designers, and to respect the sartorial codes set out by the Duchess of Cambridge and Obama, who both are careful to convey deference with their clothes, wearing Italian designers when visiting Italy, for instance. Melania understands the calculated effect her wardrobe plays, make no mistake. I must admit I choked when she wore the fuchsia Gucci pussybow blouse in the aftermath of the tape scandal which threatened to derail her husband's campaign. Was it an attempt at humour? Maybe, but then again, maybe she just likes fuchsia. Whatever the conclusion, Melanie will be bold in her fashion choices. In 2000, she told the New York Times she would be “very traditional – like Betty Ford or Jackie Kennedy” should her husband ever become president. This is going to be interesting. column1: Christian Louboutin and Sabyasachi Mukherjee just made your dreams come true
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Two good Christian Louboutin and Sabyasachi Mukherjee's collaboration wasn't just a fleeting association; as the designers gear up for a second coming of their accessories line, Vogue India finds out what it means for you. View Gallery 3 Photos Christian Louboutin and Sabyasachi Mukherjee just made your dreams come true Few men have understood what women want in their wardrobes than shoe maverick Christian Louboutin and the bride whisperer Sabyasachi Mukherjee. In this age of global fashion, that the paths of a designer from Kolkata would cross with one from Paris was not entirely out of the realm of possibility; especially as Louboutin often travels to Chennai to work with Lesage, the renowned embroidery house, and their flagship stores are a 10-minute distance away from each other in south Mumbai. "Christian visited my Mumbai store and we both realised we are very similar people who built our businesses independently. We hit it off as people first and the collaboration happened organically," said Mukherjee. Looking twice When audiences were first introduced to Christian Louboutin X Sabyasachi shoes at Sabyasachi Mukherjee's couture 2015 show 'Bater', shoefies were snapped before the show started and models in vertiginous heels couldn't hide their glee of being the first ones to try out the dangerously wicked shoes. On November 12, the designers are set to showcase their second collection which will also include handbags and Louboutin assures, “nothing is better than a work in progress.” While the obvious connect one makes on seeing the two names on the label is of bridal accessories, Mukherjee and Louboutin clarify that the line isn't just restricted to that. Mukherjee explains the personality this season, "Our last collection was gothic and mostly comprised of black, gold and metallic. The spirit of this collection is hipster meets steam punk meets whimsical baroque". Up close, you will notice the choice materials used to manifest their vision are as diverse as cork, leather, raffia, pony hair and different kinds of embroidery sourced from all over India. A certain vintage loving rebel personality will instinctively be drawn to the collection. Meeting wants “We worked with flats combined with very high heels. The very high heels are also very ornamented, but still allowing for the shape and posture to be highlighted,” says Loubutin whose signature red soles are coveted by women all over the world. “As long as we both stay committed to make beautiful products the market should continue to grow organically for the collection,” says Mukherjee. The Christian Louboutin X Sabyasachi collection will be available at Christian Louboutin stores in Delhi and Mumbai. column1: CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund Winners Named
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A fashion focused vote On the eve of a historic election, another vote took place in the US earlier this week - the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund 2016. And, at the award ceremony's 13th annual gala, Laura Vassar and Kristopher Brock of Brock Collection were named this year's recipients by keynote speaker Michael Kors. The husband-and-wife design duo - who met while studying at Parsons School of Design in New York and founded their elegant womenswear label in 2013 - will receive the $400,000 prize, while this year's runners up, Stirling Barrett of Krewe du Optic and Adam Selman, will be awarded $150,000 each. In being awarded the prize, Vassar and Brock follow the likes of Jonathan Simkhai, Aurora James of Brother Vellies and Rio Uribe of Gypsy sporty - who were last year's recipients - and previous winners such as Dao-Yi Chow and Maxwell Osborne of Public School, Joseph Altuzarra, and Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez for Proenza Schouler. column1: How to wear Benarasi weaves like a celebrity this wedding season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Your look book for the upcoming months View Gallery 10 Photos Wear celebrity-approved Benarasi looks this wedding season You probably already know that November is all about the Benarasi weave for Vogue India. Essentially brocade work using silk and gold threads, this regal fabric, named after the city it is made in, was termed so by British merchant Ralph Fitch in the 16th century. Heavily favoured by everyone from the Mughals to present-day royalty, Benarasi weaves represent the glorious history of Indian textile art. Stately and statement making, they always make an impact without the supplementary assistance of any other frills. It is no surprise then that designers today are bringing it back in a big way—breathing contemporary relevance to this age-old fabric, but without diluting its essence. So if you're looking to add guaranteed opulence to your wedding season wardrobe, place your bets on a Benarasi number. Need some inspiration? Let these celebrities lead the way. Giving their woven pieces a modern update is bound to be the prime concern on a millennial serial wedding attendee's mind. Malaika Arora Khan has the perfect solution. Team your Benarasi lehenga with an off-shoulder cape blouse and a statement necklace for a mehendi or sangeet. Or do like Neha Dhupia and team your crisp Benarasi trouser or lehenga with a tucked-in shirt blouse. Just what you need when you know that the engagement party is bound to shift to a bar after hours. Benarasi and black is a divine combination, as demonstrated by Sonam Kapoor and Natasha Poonawalla. Poonawalla's look is ideal for the woman who believes in ‘more is more'. A Benarasi lehenga with a heavily embellished border and ornate jewellery can be easily recreated for your brother's sangeet, or perhaps even your own. Take a cue from her and add another heritage weave—a chikankari dupatta—to the mix. Kapoor's look is more fitting when you're looking to dress it down. Marry comfort and style with an ankle-grazing Benarasi skirt and crop top. Wear it for a wedding party where you plan to dance the night away. But if you're looking to sport this time-honoured weave in all its traditional glory, look no further than Jacqueline Fernandez. A classic zari sari (raid your grandmother's wardrobe for one) will do the trick. Add temple jewellery and gajras in your hair for the perfect finishing touch. Vogue talks to fashion director Anaita Shroff Adajania about dressing Alia Bhatt in the poetic feature, working with a female director and styling a film that is not hyper-trendy. One girl many faces “Alia as an actor is extremely giving. She takes on whatever persona you give her and it is extremely gratifying working with her. I think we have had fun with this character without needing it to stand out for the fashion choices. A lot of young girls will be able to identify with her—she likes fashion, she has fun with it, but it is not the be-all and end-all of her life.” Business as usual “She plays the part of a young girl living in Mumbai, so I wanted her character to be very real. We have kept the look close to how young people dress today and more importantly, how people have their own style and don't dress in one particular manner every day. You can see a lot of light, easy layering—there's almost an unkempt, causal approach to how she dresses but there's also this girly-ness in her.” Second glance “As the film evolves you see her softer side. The character Alia plays has many layers and those, from a fashion perspective, was very interesting to me because her sense of style moves with the way her emotions move. There a lot of moments in the film where she is just at home, and it was nice to portray those realistically, the accessories are also minimal and I hope everyone enjoys it.” Girl power “Working with a female director was extremely fun. The luxury fashion label teases its upcoming 25th anniversary in 2017, with their first exhibition in Australia. The recently launched Viktor&Rolf: Fashion Artists at the National Gallery of Victoria explores Viktor & Rolf's radical practice of wearable art. The exhibition examines the unique grammar of their body of work that trades trend for concept and brings together master craftsmanship with quixotic design even as their runway shows merge performance art and fashion seamlessly. Curated by Thierry-Maxime Loriot (curator of the path-breaking exhibition The Fashion World of Jean Paul Gaultier) the exhibition showcases over 40 of their most iconic works curated from their haute couture, ready-to-wear and various fashion installations over the years. Along with a large display of 21 dolls (handmade by a Belgian doll maker) dressed in miniaturised versions of emblematic garments from their key collections. And also includes specially commissioned installations to celebrate the maverick design duo. ‘Viktor & Rolf: Fashion Artists' opened at the National Gallery of Victoria, Australia on October 21, 2016, and continues till 26 February 2017. column1: How this filmmaker explored the grim side of the fashion industry
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The true cost of fashion As one of the world's biggest garment-manufacturing hubs, the small country of Bangladesh has rattled the fashion industry. Film director Andrew Morgan travels to Dhaka to document the story of the factory workers. View Gallery 9 Photos Why this eye-opening documentary about fashion is a must-watch As India's eastern neighbour, Bangladesh is often seen as a farming and fishing country, with its fertile soils and plentiful waterways feeding the Bay of Bengal. It also happens to be home to a US$26-billion clothing industry that accounts for 80 per cent of the nation's exports, ranking just behind China as the world's largest apparel manufacturer supplying to Western countries. “I still remember the sea of patterns and colours in the saris worn by the crowds of garment workers at rush hour in Dhaka,” muses Andrew Morgan, the film director behind the 2015 documentary The True Cost. Based on the 2013 Rana Plaza tragedy, where a deteriorating eight-storeyed building housing several garment factories linked to supplying retail giants like H&M, Walmart, Primark and Mango collapsed, killing 1,138 people and injuring over 2,500. Like the 29-year-old American cinematographer, the world was stunned. With a far lower minimum wage (one third of China), it plays a key role in the fast-fashion supply chain. But if cheap clothing comes at human cost, what really becomes the price of fashion? You don't have a fashion background. What lead you to create The True Cost? The day after I wrapped shooting After The End, I was getting coffee when I was instantly drawn to a photograph on the cover of a newspaper. It was an image of two boys, close in age to my own two boys, standing in front of a wall of missing-people signs. I had to pick it up immediately. It turned out to be the story of the Rana Plaza collapse. I remember standing there and thinking how it's possible that an industry this powerful is doing business in a way that leads to the loss and lessening of human rights. And then, on a more personal level, I thought how it was possible that I never stopped to think about where my clothes come from. That really left me with a very humbling, chilling feeling. Why did you pick film as a medium to convey this story? Telling a story through film is the most compelling thing in the world. It's really like falling in love. I have to personally be fascinated, curious and dying to find answers to the questions. The more I looked at this topic, the more I found that it touched all the things I really cared about: women's issues (most of the garment workers are female), human rights and the environment. I also wanted the film to be uncomfortably close; I wanted the visuals to cut through the worlds that we like to keep separate. While doing the research, what numbers really stood out to you? The fashion industry is an almost US$3-trillion global industry, with 80 billion new garments made every year. That is a 400 per cent increase in the last two decades. When you read Vogue, or observe fashion, you typically look at it through a creative lens as something beautiful. But on the business side the numbers are staggering. It's also the most labour-dependent industry on earth. We employ the poorest of the working poor and I've never read about them, I've never heard them speak, I've never heard their story. It's like they are invisible. What made the story of Shima, a garment worker in your film, so powerful? I was looking for a key character that could represent and speak on behalf of the female garment workers. Shima had a boldness, a toughness, a resilience. She was a mother too. Before her responses were even translated to me, I knew she was the one, and she would be an honest portrayal. What was the most emotional scene to film for you? The scene that gripped me was when Shima went to the village of Borishal to drop her daughter off. As a parent it was just heartbreaking. She told me that this might be my life, my fate, but I don't want my daughter to work in a garment factory like me. I remember crying my eyes out that night, just wanting to go home to my kids. It just does something to you; it moves it out of the abstract. What was your overall experience in Bangladesh like? There is something about the whole spirit of the country—there's a distinct purity to it and a certain courage that emanates from people. Everyone was always so friendly and welcomed us into their homes. We would be walking with expensive equipment through slums and dark areas at night, amongst so much poverty, but we never once felt unsafe. Safia Minney, founder and CEO of People Tree, took me to the Swallows Development Society in Thanapara village, which was an incredible fair-trade production community. What challenges did you face while trying to film in the garment factories? At times it was like robbing a bank, because the guards had guns. Sometimes we had to go in through the back door, stall and distract, just to get the inside shots. What changes would you like to see taking place for the garment workers in Bangladesh? I want to see a more organised representation of workers' voices that extend all the way up the supply chain. There should be proper unions in place. The Rana Plaza collapse was a horrific example because the garment workers had pointed out the cracks and structural flaws in the building earlier, but their voices were not heard. What about the flip side of the coin? Bangladesh's garment industry provides 4 million jobs. Isn't this a path out of poverty? I think it is possible in 2016 to create beautiful products that are market-ready, to employ people in dignified ways, and still make a profit. I don't just think that, I know that. There are no excuses to justify inhumane behaviour. With these profits why should their wage be negligible? The year after the Rana Plaza collapse was the most profitable of all time for the fashion industry. How did that make you feel? I was in Bangladesh when I read that chilling number. The line between empowerment and exploitation is thin, and looking at those dollar signs and the level of poverty in Bangladesh is really tough. I wasn't naïve enough to think that Rana Plaza would bring the industry to its knees, but I hoped for more change in the country. What do you think will be the future of fast fashion? Fast fashion takes us in the opposite direction of where we need to be. I hope it will become outdated, irrelevant and obsolete. We are the first generation to grow up in a world where we can directly see the impact of our actions. We know the cost of our consumption. The views expressed in this article are solely of the filmmaker. Culture & Living Culture & Living Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Watch it now View Gallery 6 Photos You can’t miss the modern-day retelling of the Burberry story To celebrate 160 years of the iconic British brand, award-winning director Asif Kapadia and Academy Award-nominated screenwriter Matt Charman have come together to create Burberry's latest new short film, The Tale of Thomas Burberry, which recounts the story of founder Thomas Burberry. The film highlights milestone moments that amounted to the label's illustrious history. “The aim was to make a trailer for a film that we haven't actually made,” says Kapadia. “So to bring together all these epic moments of life, death, birth, love and relationships, and to go through time and to have various characters that would appear and reappear—it was about finding these epic movie moments that would then make the trailer.” Starting from the conception of the weatherproof gabardine fabric, to making trench coats for the soldiers during the First World War to kitting pilots and explorers—Thomas Burberry's vision was ahead of its times and made a revolutionary impact in combating climatic conditions. “We feel very proud to be sharing The Tale of Thomas Burberry this Christmas—his spirit and his vision are still at the heart of everything we do at Burberry today,” said Christopher Bailey, Burberry chief creative and chief executive officer. Starring Domhnall Gleeson, Sienna Miller, Dominic West and Lily James, the short captures the essence of what goes on in a creator's mind. Watch it here. column1: Exclusive: This homegrown label worn by Beyoncé is set to launch in India
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Are you ready for Khosla Jani? Forerunners of Indian couture, designer duo Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla are trailblazers who are constantly seeking to break new ground and deliver well beyond the realms of what is expected from them. And while they have always had a bevy of loyalists both on Indian and foreign shores, this year saw them catapult into particular favourites on the international scene. Remember when Beyoncé created ripples wearing a hand-embroidered and embellished dress, and a floor-length gota, bead and multi-coloured resham and appliqué work coat by the designers in Coldplay's 'Hymn For The Weekend' video? Or when Gwen Stefani chose a red taffeta gown by the duo for her Grammy Awards performance this year? Turns out, the international western couture label worn by these celebrities (and also seen on Dame Judi Dench, Carrie Underwood, Giuliana Rancic and Kesha), called Khosla Jani, is all set to officially launch in India. The veterans plan on unveiling the very first collection from the label, ‘Enchanted', with a fashion presentation on November 4, 2016. This new addition to their repertoire is the designers' “reimagining and reinventing our own creativity for new audiences and geographies.” Vogue India catches up with one half of the duo, Sandeep Khosla, in an exclusive interview ahead of this launch. Vogue India: Tell us about the Khosla Jani label and its key aesthetic. Sandeep Khosla: Khosla Jani is our newest label. It is, quite simply, us letting our imagination find new expression in the form of silhouettes that are fluid and transcend geographical and cultural borders. Instead, they are an amalgam of diverse lands, influences and eras. It is ultimate couture. We didn't dabble in western wear for years because we weren't interested in doing things half-heartedly or merely being part of the herd. It had to be on our own time and at our own pace. The aesthetic of the label is decidedly Abu Sandeep. It is craftsmanship at its most meticulous, using myriad techniques, embellishments and finishes with cutting-edge tailoring. The mission is to invent a new aesthetic through couture that represents the best of all worlds but is straight out of India. Vogue India: Why did you to choose to launch it internationally first, and then bring it to India?  SK: It wasn't a calculated or conscious decision. When we created the first 12 ensembles, a few stylists and stars in London and Los Angeles who were keen to wear them, instantly approached us. It took off in an entirely organic manner, which has been our story since the beginning. We create and are blessed to always find people who love what we do. Khosla Jani is beyond haute couture. It is about time, labour, ideas and intensive research, and it needed to be perfect before we could also launch it in India. Vogue India: What are the silhouettes one can expect from this label? What are the key pieces from the 'Enchanted' collection? SK: The silhouettes are myriad and range from classic gowns to little black and non-black dresses. This is what we like to call ‘the art of brevity'. There is architectural and structured volume in some as well as use of fluid and free fabrics in other pieces. We let ourselves run wild with this collection, as creativity must if it is to manifest fully. The red carpet gowns are deeply inspired by the '30s and '40s, which in our eyes, was the most magical era of Hollywood. Then comes ‘Illusion', which is essayed entirely in black and white satin appliqué and sequins. The ‘Masai' lines are our ode to its source—Africa. We are mad about tribal art and culture. It begins with multi-hued ensembles and then moves on to ton sur ton, skin-tone pieces. Vogue India: Do you have a favourite? SK: Every line in the collection is treasured and cherished. But if we have to play favourites, then it is the ‘Mehjabeen' line. In our beloved white, it features the most divinely delicate hand shadow work. This is ultimate expression luxe and whispers power. Vogue India: How would you describe the typical Khosla Jani muse? SK: There is nothing typical about the Khosla Jani woman or muse. She stands her own ground and is not shy of standing apart. Unbound by convention, she makes her own rules and breaks them too. Khosla Jani celebrates the spirit of the free and unfettered, utterly fabulous woman. It's grown-up, fierce and fierily glamorous. Think dead sexy and dead stylish. Vogue India: The line has found patronage among several international celebrities. Who would you like to see it on in Bollywood? SK: We don't design with anyone in mind. We design clothes that celebrate our passion for ultimate style and beauty. They always find their way to women who demand the same for themselves.   Culture & Living Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Manish Malhotra talks about Anushka Sharma’s lehenga from ‘Ae Dil Hai Mushkil’
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion More from him on styling the leading ladies View Gallery 12 Photos Manish Malhotra talks about Anushka Sharma’s lehenga from ‘Ae dil Hai Mushkil’ The year is not up yet but it is safe to say, Karan Johar's Ae Dil Hai Mushkil is one of the knockout films of 2016. The tumultuous love between the characters will certainly elicit some tears, but the fashion loving audience will not be able to take their eyes off the styling of the leading ladies. Vogue chats with designer and stylist Manish Malhotra about putting together the looks for Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and Anushka Sharma. Vogue India: How did you dress Sharma and Rai Bachchan's characters differently? Manish Malhotra: For Aishwarya, who plays an independent, contemporary woman living in Vienna, I have styled her in long coats and casual V-neck tops in colours, making it all a relaxed look as the film is set in winters. It was great seeing Ash in a chic and casual avatar, as she is already so beautiful and carries off any look with utmost ease. I had always wanted to try this look on her and luckily, Karan's film came along. Styling Anushka's character particularly has been a fun yet challenging experience for me. Anushka plays a character from Lucknow, and we wanted to give her a graceful, feminine look that a modern Muslim girl would opt for. We have blended traditional and contemporary details throughout the movie. You will see Anushka teaming long chikan and thread work kurtas with ripped jeans through many of her scenes. Vogue India: How did Sharma's bridal lehenga come about? MM: For her bridal look, we kept in mind the cultural direction giving her a long-trail dupatta with bold accents of red, interplayed with muted hues of salmon, pink and peach. While the former is the traditional highlight, the modernity comes through in the interesting play of colours. The thread work on the outfit gives it a certain old-world charm, reminiscent of Lucknow's noble past. I've kept the jewellery minimal, so that it subtly accents the whole look. Vogue India: There is a lot of focus on outerwear. What were your references while dressing the lead actresses? MM: My style has always been opulent and grand, yet staying true to the nature of the character being portrayed, I went with dressing the cast in a perfect blend of international and Indian accents, so that our audience both loves and relates to the pieces. Since the greater part of the film is set in winters, and keeping in mind the premise of the movie and the characters, majority of our garments were sourced from shopping districts and high-end luxury brands in the UK, Paris and India. Layering, playing with colours and textures has been quite fun for this film and I am glad the response has been phenomenal so far. Vogue India: What are some of your favourite looks from the movie? MM: I love all the looks from the film, but my favourite is Anushka's bridal outfit. It's one of my most glamorous pieces. I also like the kurta with ripped jeans look that Anushka carries off so effortlessly. Ash's character is chic and casual, which I love as well because it's something I've always wanted her to be seen in. What's New Weddings Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: India’s finest designers come together to help the families of Uri martyrs
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Bid to make a difference View Gallery 6 Photos India’s finest designers come together to help the families of Uri martyrs Fashion and philanthropy no longer make strange bedfellows and blogger Pallavi Datta's initiative firmly establishes that. With the support of Axis Mutual Fund, Datta has organised an online auction to raise funds for the orphaned families of Uri martyrs. “Fashion has the ability to lead change, especially in India, with our opulent repertoire of sustainable choices like natural dyes, hand-spun, and handwoven natural fibres,” explains Datta. The auction, which will be open for 24 hours, focuses on handwoven creations by ace designers from across the country. When asked about the importance of keeping the Indian handloom industry alive, Datta answered, “handloom gives employment to our villages and stops urban migration, it empowers women, and gives them the freedom to nurture their families, it has a happy impact on our environment, and above all it nourishes the spirit of an artist who is given the freedom to explore his creative calling.” The impressive list of designers includes the likes of Rahul Mishra, Eká, Péro, Anavila, Payal Khandwala, Purvi Patel, Gaurang Shah, Raw Mango and Antar Agni. “One of my favourites is a dupatta from revivalist Purvi Patel. It comes adorned with forgotten embroidery patterns, done with a fine point needle. The work is so fine it's reminiscent of a ray of light,” she adds. Proceeds from the auction will be invested by Axis Mutual Funds in tailor-made schemes to ensure the long-term well-being of the families The auction will take place on 27th October at xstok.com Culture & Living Fashion Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Priyanka Chopra and Prabal Gurung on making it big in America
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Vogue listens in as the designer and actor talk cross-border love It's a cause of pride when your country's people make waves beyond its borders. But when they take things to the next level, commanding popular culture and international consciousness in an unprecedented fashion, well, that's a game changer. That's just what Priyanka Chopra, Quantico star, Baywatch villain, and cover girl of every major magazine on American newsstands, from Time to W magazine, has done. And for Nepalese designer Prabal Gurung, the trajectory has been just as sharp. Since launching his label in New York just seven years ago, he's dressed every A-lister on the Hollywood circuit, from Jennifer Lawrence to Anne Hathaway. And in the wake of the Nepal earthquake, he rallied his famous friends to raise thousands of dollars for disaster relief in his home country. Vogue chats with the two superstars flying the flag for our subcontinent. Vogue India:What do you think it is about each other that has made both of you such crossover successes? Prabal Gurung: Besides the obvious fact that she's beautiful and talented, I think it's her grit and determination. She's a superstar, there's no denying it, but there's a level of humanity to her that's so incredibly endearing. When you meet her, you can't help but be impressed with her professionalism and what she's achieved but at the same time there's a vulnerability to her that I personally find attractive. That comes across when she's performing. The generosity, the grit, the talent, the beauty… I remember when I first saw her face on posters. I was like, ‘does India have any idea what's happening here?' The scale of her success is insane. Priyanka Chopra: What I love about Prabal is that it's not about his ethnicity or where he's from. When you see his clothes, you don't know he's from Nepal, you don't know he's lived in India, you don't know anything about him except for the fact that he makes clothes that stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the biggest and best designers in the world. And then you realise he's from the subcontinent and you're like ‘oh yeah, homeboy, represent!' PG: When I started out, I didn't want to be known as an ‘ethnic' designer. PC: Because then people will put you in a box. I'm an Indian actor, no one knew me in mainstream America before Quantico. Even then, I had to stand my ground and say ‘listen, I'm used to being the face on a poster and if you're not going to give me that, see ya, I don't need it.' You do it on your own terms or you don't do it at all. PG: That's what I love about her. She's defied every norm. PC: I don't believe in norms. When I went to high school in America, I didn't see anybody who looked like me on television. But it didn't matter. I loved Buffy, she was my icon at that point and I was like ‘yeah, I want to grow up and be Buffy!' As I grew older, I realised how important it is for girls who look like me, or immigrants who come to America, to know that we also have opportunities in global entertainment. I hope to be able to pave the way where people look at global talent differently, can see that it has the capability to carry a show on its shoulders. Even with my choice of films here—I didn't want to be the girl who stands behind the boy. I take on the entire squad of Baywatch. In fact, my character was written for a man! He was called Victor, and it became Victoria. I chose to be the antagonist for my first movie role here because it's so much fun to do things a little to the left. Then it's your own. I'm not a me-too person, I don't want to walk a path that's been walked before. Vogue India: This issue is all about celebrating the subcontinent. What's one cross-border collaboration you'd love to see? PC: I think I'm seeing it at the moment, with what I'm doing and what Prabal has done. What Prabal has done for fashion, for people from South Asia, is massive. It changed the idea people had about South Asian fashion just being about ethnic clothes. He made it mainstream and that's a win. What I've done with my show, going to 216 territories around the world, that's a win. That's what I'd like to see more of. I hope what he and I are doing paves the way for more international talent to come in and enjoy the kind of mainstream success that we have seen. PG: I couldn't have said it better. She and I have been able to challenge the preconceived notion of what people who look like us can do in popular culture. I have a six-year-old niece and when she grows up, I want her to be able to see a face on the cover of a fashion magazine that is familiar to her, someone she can see herself in. Vogue India: Your favourite spots on the Indian subcontinent? PC: Goa, Goa, Goa! Goan fish curry… oh man. I have two houses in Goa, one's a farmhouse and one's a city house, and we go there just to chill and vegetate—and eat! I also love Manali. It's so beautiful and the food is great. Oh, and Kerala—it really is God's paradise. PG: I love Bombay. I lived there for two years. In Nepal, one of my favourite things to do when I go back is go trekking in the mountains. I like to go by myself, with just one guide. That really grounds me. Every time I come back, I feel more refreshed. column1: These dresses are perfect vacation wear
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Cecile D’ascoli’s new collection hits all the right spots   Striking a balance between style and comfort is no mean feat, especially on vacation. Cecile D'ascoli's new collection ticks all the right boxes with vibrant, boho-chic separates, perfect for anyone with a glamorous getaway around the corner. D'ascoli talks to Vogue about her creations, the inspiration, and her favourite destinations to unwind. Can you tell us a little bit about your collection and the inspiration behind it? This collection is called “Silk Road - Modern Vagabonds” to express how I feel about my eclectic life living between Europe, where I was born and raised, and India. The ancient silk road was an international space that transmitted ideas and mixed cultures, spreading wisdom and mixing diverse aesthetics. I love this idea and so I worked with the Talianna Studio in Delhi to develop a mix of strong patterns that reflect both Eastern European, Persian, and Indian handicrafts colored for today's modern woman. ‘Vagabond' is a reference to a particular bohemian sensibility that I feel strongly about, typified by a casual, easygoing attitude reflected in the silhouettes. What sets this collection apart? My collections are always made up of easygoing dresses and tops, and until now I have mostly used handwoven cottons in natural colours. This collection is all in printed silk so it is a big departure for me, and captures the mood of the moment; the prints are a celebration of decorative arts. Your pieces are ideal for a vacation, what's your favourite holiday destination? I spend summers at my home near the sea in the southwest of France, and I often holiday in Goa in the winter. This collection is meant to be global and is for the lady who travels easily from Morocco or Miami to Gstaad or St Barts. Who, according to you, is the one woman that captures the essence of the collection? Janis Joplin, Talitha Getty and Sienna Miller are all icons of boho-chic but I think that this collection can help anyone make a statement of stylish, carefree creativity. What's next for your label? I am exploring applying some of this same sensibility in handwoven cotton. The colour palette will probably be a bit more muted, which lends itself to cotton as opposed to the silk, which takes saturated colours so beautifully. The collection is available at Le Mill, Mumbai and Vayu, Delhi What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Why people can’t stop talking about that Kenzo x H&M party
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Freestyle dancing, celebrities and the black market Another highly-anticipated merger between the Swedish super chain H&M and French luxury label Kenzo, was previewed at a Manhattan Pier as the fashion fraternity skipped the presidential debate to see the new designs by Carol Lim and Humberto Leon instead. Layered animal prints, saturated colours, eclectic graphics and the iconic tiger logo were remixed for mass production, with a wild jungle display on stage. Here are the top five highlights of the evening: View Gallery 34 Photos People can’t stop talking about that Kenzo X H&M party The show It was all about freedom of expression on the catwalk, as models bounded from all four sides of the square runway, breaking into choreographed and freestyle dance while dressed in the colourful garb. French photographer Jean-Paul Goude directed the performance that included a bright yellow marching band, a string quartet, beat boxers and dramatic choreography by Ryan Heffington. The after party As the lights dimmed into a red haze with a shower of confetti, the event space transformed into night club and fully functional pop-up shop. After some retail therapy, guests lounged on animal print bean bags as servers passed around truffle popcorn, fried chicken in takeout boxes, Kenzo's signature cocktail of grapefruit vodka and a concert by rapper Ice Cube. The crowd A mix of talent was invited to the front row showcasing key pieces from the collection. Elizabeth Olson wore the pajama set, while Chloë Sevigny opted for a frilly folk dress. British musician Charli XCX flew in while Chance the Rapper, Rosaria Dawson and Lupita Nyong walked the red carpet. Familiar faces from the advertising campaign, Suboi and Iman were spotted in the crowds too. The clothes Without losing the DNA of Japanese designer Kenzo Takada, who founded his label in 1970, the team delved into the archives resurrecting reversible jackets with embroidery, quirky oriental platform flip flops, frilly silhouettes with ruffle trims and kimono elements. Key pieces include a leather jacket with pink faux fur trim and a high neck layered dress, the most expensive in the lineup at $549. The black market As with last year's highly sought after Balmain partnership, hot items from the line are already reselling at incredible rates, sometimes even five times the price tag, on trade sites like eBay. Coats are going for over $500, gloves for $199, and men's $34.99 T-shirts have been significantly hiked up. If you want your hands on some of the loot ahead the rest of the flock, be ready to shell out some serious cash, before it hits stores on November 3. Fashion Fashion What's New © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Payal Pratap on why she is a champion of wearable clothes
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And why her evolved garments are not commonplace Payal Pratap's eponymous brand, much like the designer, is unique and unpretentious. Her clothes are for women who appreciate style, yet are not slaves to passing trends. Sachin Soni (who has photographed backstage for designers like Rajesh Pratap Singh, Gaurav Jai Gupta and Aneeth Arora) shows us a peek into the backstage via his images that detail the painstaking work that goes on behind the scenes. View Gallery 20 Photos Payal Pratap on why she is a champion of wearable clothes The designer talks about the details that went into her spring/summer 2017 collection ‘A Twist in my Sobriety'. “I had started with a very colourful collection in July. I lost my father mid-August and everyone in the family was in and out of hospitals all of that month. After that I really got back to work in September and started over from scratch. I decided to use monotones, not too much colour; it was just the space that I was in at that time." Colour story "I chose something minimal, classic—there was a deep burgundy, a beautiful blue and beige. I played around with muted embroidery, nothing too in-your-face. I was working on craft stitches and embroidery stitch details and this came out like an extension of the cross stitch but in a new way. I played around with modern motifs of the chintz rose and worked it into the surface ornamentation of the fabrics. We used cotton linens and khadis—breathable fabrics for the summer." Fabric details "I like working on fabric from scratch and the was surface ornamentation was in the form of embroidery on it. We did the art work and then got the fabrics embroidered. It was like a myriad of stitches on octagons that were assembled to form a fabric. Each octagon had a different stitch pattern, I think I just got sucked into that whole thing of exploring thread stitches." Borrowing from the neighbours "Orientalism comes from the Indian subcontinent. Like the classic band collar that we have been using from our garments, like the bandhgalas, and the Chinese band collar are both the same thing. It wasn't a conscious effort to work on Oriental influences but the collection saw wrap jackets, dropped shoulders, garments without armholes—a more relaxed silhouette that I wanted to work with." A question of fit "I wouldn't call my collection anti-fit, it was a more semi-fit breathable collection that a wearer would be comfortable in. I think fashion is a seeing a movement where more and more people are going towards comfort. I associate myself quite loudly with wearable clothes, but on the ramp I like to style it in a different way that looks worthy of a show. I think it is very important for you to present your collection in a certain way for it to look delicious on the ramp." Backstage "I was clear that I wanted the hair to be gelled and tied into this interesting knot with thread that you normally use to treat fabric with. For the make-up, I wanted the girls to look like rustic beauties. I wanted the skin to have a natural glow on their eyelids and cheeks, just mascara, bushy eyebrows and highlight the lips. I didn't want a messy look at all." Individuality matters "Being the way I am, I just wanted to work on slight twists. Even though the silhouettes looks wearable, I think there was a lot of thought that went into each piece like the asymmetric hemlines, draped skirts, pants, the sari dress. There was an evolution in each style—it would be a wearable pair of pants but you still won't be able to look for it in Zara.” Sachin Soni is a photographer, he was backstage to shoot Payal Pratap's spring/summer 2017 show at Amazon India Fashion Week. column1: Why rural India never fails to inspire Rajesh Pratap Singh’s work
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion And why it will never be kitschy Rajesh Pratap Singh is a man of few words. He isn't the biggest fan of the camera. Given a choice, he would avoid an interview entirely, but the tremendous amount of thought that goes in his work begs for storytelling. At the recently concluded Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2017, the designer put together a collection of men's and women's garments that was inspired by the sartorial sensibilities of rural India. Sachin Soni (who has previously photographed backstage for designers like Payal Pratap, Gaurav Jai Gupta and Aneeth Arora) shows us a peek via his photographs -- the beautifully shot black and white images reflect only an essence of the madness that goes on backstage: from last minute fittings to make-up touches and a rush to get on stage. View Gallery 20 Photos Why rural India never fails to inspire Rajesh Pratap Singh’s work Why does the narrative of rural India capture your imagination? These are the things we are working on continuously, or influences we take from our environment—how people are dressing up in India or how they are mixing up elements in their own way, so that is a constant. Was there a conscious effort on your part to include more elements of menswear in the womenswear than you normally do? I use a lot of tailored clothing for women. For me, it works the other way round. I know the trend is to put men in women's clothing, but for me it's always been the reverse. Again, it's a cliché, but I think a lot of masculine clothing works beautifully for women so it was an extension of that. [In this collection] Bandhgalas and jackets were worn with dhotis. If you see present day Rajasthan, you will see World War II uniform jackets worn with dhotis. I love those silhouettes—hand-me-down Salvation Army jackets paired with bottoms that are more comfortable. I just find that kind of confidence missing anywhere else. It's very Indian and at the same time, they can be worn anywhere else. I love seeing the interesting mix of elements. You put a lot of effort into creating new textiles in Neemrana, Rajasthan, why is that? Because I love it. Anybody who is vaguely interested in textiles would understand what is going on and we love doing that. How it is made is sometimes more important than the surface treatment and that's our method of doing. I know it's easy to just print an asymmetric ikat, but that is not the way we want to approach it. How much time goes into the development of textiles over designing? Which of these happens faster for you? No, no. I'm very slow. I waste a lot of time and more and more so on textiles. Once you have the fabric, making the garment is not that difficult. The weight of the fabric helps you do that. If it's a heavy weight, you know whether you want to cut it on a bias or you want to cut it straight. Do you want to make it into a jacket or do you want to drape it. Your show music clearly also ties in with your thought process. What made you choose Leonard Cohen this time? You know you don't need a reason for Cohen.  I felt his voice, music and lyrics would do justice to the show. He creates that atmosphere; his voice is super special for a men's show with that much severity. Maybe the next Nobel for literature goes to him (laughs). It's a cliché but the lines between menswear and womenswear are blurred now. In fact, I wanted to open the show with a girl to the opening track, ‘I'm Your Man', but the directive was eight women's looks and 17 men's, so that wasn't really possible. What was the idea behind the white stripe for the make-up? Again the thought came through the black and white optic concept and we wanted to carry it through with the stripe. The idea was to split the face into two and then it became more and more graphic, and Ambika (Pillai) who is excellent just took over. Were any of the accessories custom-created? The accessories were custom-created, but the stylist Nikhil D used a lot of the jewellery on the boots, which looked great. Do you have a muse or an idea of a muse in mind when you are working on your garments? Words like inspiration and muse are heavy. It's not as if you have a new person every six months. It's a feeling, for men's shows it's always the person you encounter in smaller places, it's not influenced by evening klutz. It is more about what's on the street or in the desert, in rural India. I find those way more interesting and people more confident with what they wear rather than in the nightclubs and metros. I find more honesty there. That idea can be can be a muse. I find purity in design references in that. And it's not kitsch India—it is not what tourists see India, it is not the imagery of Gods or Bollywood posters. Do you travel to these places to observe people better? No it's not like that. I don't have to travel to these places. I like going to these places, I was born in a place like that (Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan). Sachin Soni is a photographer, he was backstage to shoot Rajesh Pratap Singh's spring/summer 2017 show at Amazon India Fashion Week. Fashion What's New Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Ekaya Leela’s new line is just perfect for the upcoming festive season
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Shop away View Gallery 10 Photos Ekaya Leela’s new line is just perfect for the upcoming festive season Sari brand Ekaya has earned a place of prominence in the India fashion lexicon with its exquisitely crafted, handwoven textiles woven in Benares. Over the years, CEO Palak Shah has collaborated on capsule lines with designers including Archana Rao, Anupama Dayal and Abraham & Thakore. Recently, Ekaya made its foray into ready-to-wear with sister brand ‘Ekaya Leela' that focuses on a younger audience. Harmeet Bajaj, the creative director for Ekaya Leela, is helping you prep for the party season with their new festive line Inaayat, which is based on the Hyderabadi royal aesthetic. “‘Inaayat' means blessing, which I thought was apt for the upcoming celebrations,” explains Bajaj. “The thought behind the line was to offer clothing that could be worn for an auspicious occasion, something that speaks of a quiet elegance,” she further elaborates. To CEO Palak Shah, chosing Harmeet Bajaj to lead Ekaya Leela was a no-brainer. “She wears so many hats—stylist, choreographer, product developer, columnist. There are very few people who have her level of experience,” she says. Bajaj kept in mind what Ekaya speaks for—the weaves and highlighted the fabric by adding minimal embroidery that ‘uplifts the look and look and feel'. The motifs are primarily geometric and inspired by architecture. “I understand the customer for this line is niche, but I wanted to create a line for a confident girl who doesn't need too many elements for a festive look. It is understated, and the wearer, not the dress, is the topic of conversation,” says the designer. What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Tired of your regular lehenga-choli? Arpita Mehta’s line is perfect for you
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Black is back View Gallery 2 Photos Arpita Mehta festive 2016 looks Arpita Mehta's eponymous label is best known for its flattering take on Indian ethnic wear. “I not only make clothes for the bride but also her BFF, sister, the bridesmaids,” the designer explains the demographics of her clientele. Unlike the pop fuchsias and vivid oranges one often associates with the Arpita Mehta label, this winter/festive 2016 season is about neutrals. “I understand black and cream are not traditional choices for this season but the line is for young girls who don't pay too much attention to that kind of thing anyway,” she says. The campaign, shot by photographer Arjun Mark, features supermodels Sheetal Mallar, Ujjwala Raut and Tamara Moss. “I wanted to work with these iconic women who have such strong individual personal style of their own,” says Mehta.  The common motif in the line is that of the wild gingko leaf, which the designer has interpreted by way of prints and embroidery. The separates include bodysuits worn with lehengas, palazzos, capes—anything that's not a skirt and crop top combination, which the designer accurately explains as to have been explored to its fullest. “Bodysuits allow more sensuous cuts because of the way they are constructed and allow so much ease to the wearer,” she adds. Mirrorwork, cutdana embroidery and threadwork add the shocking contrast to the base, making the collection perfect for almost any occasion. The Arpita Mehta winter/festive 2016 collection is available to order now. Arpita Mehta Studio, 4A, Sheetal Apartments, Juhu road, opposite Chandan Cinema, Mumbai.
