column1: Do you know all the different ways of draping a sari?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion This film series might be of help Recently the panda was moved from the endangered category to vulnerable on the Red List of Threatened Species—a massive win for wildlife preservation. The sari may not be an endangered species (yet) but it has definitely lost its standing as the leading garment of choice. But rather than sit back and let the fast-disappearing art of draping pass us by, Malika Verma-Kashyap of Border&Fall (a digital publication and creative agency) decided to do something about this. Her agency along with three filmmakers, including Qaushik Mukherjee (better known as ‘Q'), Pooja Kaul and New York-based Bon Duke, decided to create “the first complete digital anthology on how to drape India's sari in 84 ways through three short films on the sari's past, present and future”. The films will be a mix of personal and cultural history, Kaul explains, “We have memories of our mothers and grandmothers wearing their saris in the morning, of lying under our mother's pallu, and now we have the challenge of taking it into the future, of re-imagining it, of maybe even loosening it from the ties of memory. There is a sense of a battle for the sari, which makes the project important." The project titled, 'The Sari: A How To Drape Film Series' is part of a crowdfunding campaign that calls for public participation and support to contribute to documenting this cultural icon. So if you've been silently championing the sari, now's the time to make yourself heard. If the sheer joy of being part of an exciting archiving process isn't enough, they've developed a rewards program that includes saris from Anavila, Rahul Mishra and Raw Mango, dinners with fashion elite in New York and New Delhi, and associate producer credits on the films. With leading sartorial experts including sari expert Rta Kapur Chisti, designer Rashmi Varma, art director Deep Kailey onboard as contributors and an advisory board that consists of Sunitha Kumar Emmart (Founder GallerySKE), Vogue's Bandana Tewari and Sanjay Garg of Raw Mango—the project is all set to not only recall the saris' long cultural trajectory but also keep the art of draping relevant and modern. To contribute and for more information log on to Kickstarter.com. Watch the series on Borderandfall.com What's New Fashion Culture & Living © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Check out these celebrities looking flawless in red
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion You won’t be able to take your eyes off of them View Gallery 17 Photos Check out these celebrities looking flawless in red The Oxford Dictionary defines the colour red as, “(….) as of blood, fire, or rubies.” The siren hue has many associations. It is the colour of love, passion, seduction and festivity. It is also the colour of anger, danger and violence. In fashion, red is all about making a bold sartorial statement. It is about saying “all eyes on me” without the aid of any other frills. This guaranteed head-turning quality is also probably what makes the colour such a hot favourite with celebrities. A traffic-stopping red gown, in varied fearless avatars, is the new norm du jour on the red carpet. Cases in point: a thigh-high slit for Deepika Padukone, bold cutouts for Katrina Kaif, a twirl-friendly version for Priyanka Chopra and dramatic ruffles for Waluscha De Sousa. Plenty of inspiration for those looking to channel similar glamour at the next cocktail party on their calendar. Alternatively, you could skip the gown and slip into a bloodshot pantsuit instead like Gigi Hadid. Top it off with the accessory of the moment, the choker. Turn up the heat on date night like bad gal RiRi and go all out in a slinky red slip dress with a plunging neckline and bare-all slits. If you have your heart set on the colour for the festive/wedding season, take a cue from Kaif and opt for a contemporary palazzo sari in the tone or go-all out in a red and gold embroidered lehenga and crop top set like Padukone. column1: The homecoming of Alpana and Neeraj at JJ Valaya’s Amazon India Fashion Week finale
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion All you need to know about the AIFW grand finale from last night View Gallery 60 Photos JJ Valaya & Alpana Neeraj (Guru Shishya) at Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2017 The grand finale this season for Amazon India Fashion Week 2017 continued the theme of  ‘India Modern Festive'. The highlight was the way the show was presented, taking inspiration from the ‘Guru-Shishya' (teacher-student) philosophy and co-conceptualised by veteran designer JJ Valaya and his former assistants Alpana Mittal and Neeraj Chauhan. The label Alpana Neeraj is best known for its architectural, sculpted and, for the lack of a better word, 'dramatic' ensembles. The designers and now partners in real life started their professional careers as designers under the mentorship of JJ Valaya. “Alpana is undoubtedly the best illustrator in the country, it all starts on the paper,” Valaya said of his student with pride after the show ended. For the show, the designers worked on a line, which Valaya edited. “For me it was very important to help take it to the next level, from colours to the set, to the audiovisuals, the background score—the complete presentation,” he said. The collection of jewel-toned garments that ranged from gowns to lehengas and dresses was opulent to say the least. The exaggerated constructions of the garments themselves were certainly an aspirational representation of ‘India Modern Festive' rather than a practical one. The joy of retracing the start of what turned out to be a very successful journey was certainly a moment of pure joy for both the mentor and the students. Fashion Fashion Beauty © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Highlights from day 4 of Amazon India Fashion Week spring / summer 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A quick recap View Gallery 15 Photos Day 4 highlights of Amazon India Fashion Week From Masaba Gupta's New York-inspired pieces to Amit Agarwal's nostalgic line, day 4 of Amazon India Fashion Week spring / summer 2017 came packed with talent. Here's everything you need to know. Hemant & Nandita Revamping the era of Victorian romance was on the agenda for the designer duo. Summery silhouettes in bright hues formed the basis of the collection. While ruffles and high necklines added to the old-school charm, shoulder and back cut outs gave it a contemporary appeal. Not So Serious by Pallavi Mohan This season, the designer stuck to her guns with a romantic collection titled ‘Sweet Nectar'. Drawing inspiration from the honeybee, voluminous layers of tulle in feminine hues mimicked the hive and the complexity of its chambers. Relaxed silhouettes came adorned with quilled floral applique, reminiscent of the circular movements of a bee. AM.IT by Amit Aggarwal Glitter-filled balloons and losing an eye of a bedtime teddy bear were some of the childhood memories that lead to Amit Aggarwal's dreamy collection ‘icloud'. Models weaved through the audience in dramatic creations featuring glitter and sequin waste, recycled doll eyes, music discs and pom-poms. Soft shades such as salmon, lemon, powder blue and ivory were on the designer's shade card. Pankaj & Nidhi Pankaj and Nidhi explored new territory with their collection ‘Chromatique', which took its cues from the Summer Exhibition held at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts.  Mesh textures and painterly prints came together making for an unusual but eclectic combination. The colour palette was varied ranging from pastels to high shine hues. Masaba Iconic locations from the Big Apple served as the perfect backdrop for Masaba Gupta's collection, which was an ode to the diverse culture of the city. With a line of progressive Indian wear including peek-a-boo bustiers, bell bottoms and over-sized shirts, the designer stayed true to her aesthetic. While monochrome dominated the palette, the runway also saw a slew of vibrant ensembles in shades of red, pink and electric blue. Athiya Shetty walked the ramp as showstopper. column1: Everything you need to know from Day 3 of Amazon Fashion Week S/S 2017
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Get on board Missed day 3 of Amazon Fashion Week spring /summer 2017? Scroll through our highlights to catch up on all the action: View Gallery 24 Photos Day 3 highlights of Amazon India Fashion Week Huemn An ode to the feral confidence of today's influencers, 'go bold or go home' sums up the motto of Huemn's collection. Their fierce line featured the likes of power suits and athleisure staples with an updated retro feel. This season also saw the launch of a capsule line of clutches and bags. Ikai by Ragini Ahuja Using bohemian artwork and punk detailing, the designer gave relaxed Indian silhouettes a new lease of life. The collection came packed with long line silhouettes including summer jackets, shirts and maxi dresses in neutral hues. Ashima Leena Titled ‘Romance of the Florals', Ashima Leena's collection drew inspiration from the elements of nature. Models sporting beach hats and oversized sunglasses made their way down the runway in feminine creations adorned with flowers and delicate lace. Silhouettes ranged from fuss-free separates to the quintessential sari. Siddartha Tytler Siddartha Tytler never fails to bring a heavy dose of glamour to the runway. From curve-skimming gowns to structured suits, his collection saw a slew of red carpet-worthy pieces. The colour palette ranged from striking gold to subdued shades of silver. Anupamaa by Anupama Dayal If you have a beach vacation on the calendar, don't forget to pack in one of Anupamaa Dayal's creations. Summery dresses and lights layers formed the basis of the designer's collection this season. Vibrant pom-pom detailing added an element of playfulness to classic holiday hues. Sanchita Taking its cues from a surrealistic tropical garden, Sanchita's collection presented boudoir-inspired fashion at its eccentric best. Models walked the ramp in pyjama sets, camisoles and robes dotted with bugs. The line also featured an unusual cactus print, the inspiration for which was found in National Geographic's Instagram handle. Laid-back silhouettes were offset with embellished waist belts. Gauri and Nainika With dramatic ruffles and cascading layers of tulle taking over the runway, the duo's inherently romantic collection is guaranteed to be a hit with fashion A-listers. While feminine tones such as red and hot pink were the focus of the collection, the designer's shade card also had classics like black and white. Leather harnesses designed by New York-based accessory designer Zana Bayne and pinstripes gave the soft silhouettes a tough edge. Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna The designers proved that no matter the season, black and grey will always be key players. Team them with asymmetrical silhouettes and high shine detailing and you have an evening wear collection worthy of Studio 54. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Ekà’s slow take on garments will remind you what luxury truly means
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Be kind, unwind View Gallery 9 Photos Eka Rina Singh of Ekà is a champion of slow fashion. Her garments are the opposite of trendy or sexy, but you will often find models backstage exclaiming how soft and cozy they are and how the luxury of being in such a thing is pure joy. Singh's sentiments behind her clothing come from the thought that attention to perfecting the basic purpose of clothing is paramount, and not what sells it. In an age of instant gratification, Singh's unhurried approach in the garment business is a radical one. For spring/summer 2017, she was looking at watercolour renditions of flowers and prints from vintage wallpaper. “Checks and stripes come naturally to me, and for the floral motifs we thought of using block prints,” she says. Each of the colour ways for the flowers are made using different blocks. “The process of printing every petal was almost like painting,” Singh explains. The tactile aspect of the collection, which is the primary draw in Ekà clothing, is dominated by handwoven linen, khadi and cotton silk. Delicate tone-on-tone embroidery is added subtly in the crochet of slips and tea towel-inspired motifs. “Once the garment is created it has such a polished feel, I usually have it laundered for a lived-in feel. I don't like the unfamiliarity of a new garment and I think a softer, lived-in feel is what speaks most to my customers,” says the designer. The garments also follow a one-size-fits-all, inclusive philosophy. As for not showing on the runway this season, Singh has a pure thought. “I don't know if I my clothes belong to the ramp or not. If our treatments are different, why should the way we show our work be the same as everyone? We are looking at arriving at a newer forms of presentation.” Singh has another thought, “By virtue of being a part of smaller group of designers who follow the slow fashion movement, our clothes offer a different unpretentious luxury that one day I hope is mainstream.”   Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Short saris and khadi on Day 2 of Amazon India Fashion Week S/S17
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Cool kid fashion View Gallery 16 Photos Day 2 highlights of Amazon India Fashion Week The second day of Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2017 saw collections from designers that are responding to the evolving landscape of customers by way of modifying their craft. Here's a quick recap of the standout collections from day two: Tarun Tahiliani decided to give the shows a skip and instead have a private presentation of his spring/summer 2017 collection. Tahiliani has put thought in providing comfort to the modern bride, offering lighter pieces for various occasions without compromising on the glam factor. The line ‘Chashme Shahi' explores lightweight silks printed with hand-painted motifs of flowers that are perfect for occasion wear in the summer. (Take image from our own Insta) Gaurav Jai Gupta of Akaaro blended filaments of stainless steel with silk creating saris and separates of different weights. Gupta worked with a primarily jewel-toned palette, the effect of which was muted because of the metallic-sheer visual quality of the fabrics used. Anavila Misra of label Anavila was in the mood to make the sari more utilitarian for everyday wear. “I really wanted to add pockets to the sari,” said Misra. The designer shortened the traditional six yards to a shorter drape, exposing the petticoat to which she added pockets for functionality. The designer also worked on creating textures with linen, finer details, which might be lost from a distance but are the core of the Anavila aesthetic that her loyal fans so deeply admire. David Abraham and Rakesh Thakore of Abraham & Thakore wanted to take khadi out of the “politically correct” space it has belonged to in our country. The duo treated the handloom fabric with carefree abandon, coating it with metallic foil, using negative cutwork on the surface and adding logos in Devnagri script. Even the totes that were handed out to the press had logos of high fashion brands loosely basing the calligraphy on scripts from fabrics found near places of worship. “Aren't they the new mantras anyway?” said Abraham laughingly. Payal Pratap's offering for this season was remastering what comes naturally to her. Starting with soft pyjama set separates to grown-up ladylike dresses, Pratap's clothes are made for a mature audience. Going back to the drawing board, the designer was drawn to cross stitch embroidery. The subtle variations in the ivory fabrics and floral motifs on jackets and dresses were all custom embroidered. Rajesh Pratap Singh said he often goes back to the sartorial landscape of rural India and that was the inspiration behind this season's collection. The womenswear in particular continued on the ‘school uniforms of rural India' stream of thought. Pratap's version of it is obviously entirely modern, a study in proportions and balance of silhouettes and textures. column1: This story of two Indian designers chasing their dream is pure inspiration
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Do the work you love and love what you do View Gallery 17 Photos Gopi Vaid Nestled in the Municipal Industrial Estate of Lower Parel lies the Gopi Vaid studio, workshop and design lab. The label Gopi Vaid by Arnaz and Gopi follows the quiet, non-advertorial, non-PR-led way of business. It is old school in that sense, and if you have heard of them, it's probably owing to a friend's recommendation or having spotted them at Design One or Aza. The label is best known for its range of kurtas and tunics which is also exported, and takes requests for customised bridal wear. As Gopi Vaid by Arnaz and Gopi opens its first standalone store in Kala Ghoda this month, we traced their journey from its inception to now. CROSSING PATHS The creative force behind the label—co-founders and designers Gopi Vaid and Arnaz Soonawalla met each other in school. Soonawalla went on to become a gold-medalist ENT while Vaid studied to be a lawyer and businesswoman. The two reconnected after their weddings and Soonawalla learnt the Vaid had been harbouring a dream of starting her own label someday. “I said let's go ahead, the label all yours, I don't know how long I will be able to work on it but let's get this going,” says Soonawalla. STARTING POINT Vaid's family has always been a patron of the arts. “I grew up in a bungalow where all the artisans worked on the ground floor, and mummy was so dynamic in the way she thought—she used to work from nine-to-nine, and as children that had a huge impact for us,” she says. The influence is hard to miss—besides her own eventual foray into the creative arts, her sister Radhi Parekh started the Artisans' gallery in Kala Ghoda that supports indigenous crafts of India. Many of the craftsmen at the Gopi Vaid studio hail from the same families of karigars that once worked in Vaid's mother's atelier. “All the workers are really members of the family. Their creativity is important, there's a lot of give and take. It's always a fusion of what Arnaaz and I think with the karigars. Our staff has a very strong identity,” says Vaid. BALANCING ACT How do you go from friends to work partners? Most business people would discourage the idea of working with someone who is so close to you personally, yet for this label, it is the core philosophy on which its functioning rests. Vaid veers towards the bold, glamorous aesthetic while Soonawalla prefers are quieter take on the garment. “We balance each other out,” says Vaid. Customisation is the key at the studio. “Everything just evolves. When a client walks in, you can immediately tell if somebody can take a richer look, somebody has a more subdued personality so you swap with a different colour. I think a garment should ultimately be in tune with the person wearing it—it can be a little elaborate, it can be something you never imagined yourself to be in, but someone has to visualise it for you,” explains Soonawalla. IN STORE The duo is excited to own space in the heritage district of Kala Ghoda, the area that is increasingly gaining popularity as the design district of Mumbai. The label will stock a mix of their export line with the local line. The idea is for the customer to experience a new range of garments each time they visit the store. “We don't want to take away the customer that comes to Aza. What will be available at the store, is going to be something that you can wear without thinking too much and will be available at an affordable price tag,” says Vaid. “We don't want to stock heavier pieces in the store because we won't always be present there to customise them. For that, the clients will have to come to the factory,” says Soonawalla, further cementing that some things will never change at Gopi Vaid, and that's just how the founders want it to be. Gopi Vaid by Arnaz and Gopi will open doors on October 15. 49 Kala Ghoda, behind Rhythm House, Mumbai.  Tel: 022-24914864 Studio address: Gopi Vaid by Arnaz and Gopi, 98 Municipal Industrial Estate, Opposite Lady Ratan Towers, Lower Worli. column1: Get to know Sri Lanka’s leading design family
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Creativity is in their DNA View Gallery 14 Photos Get to know Sri Lanka’s leading design family For a new visitor to Sri Lanka, it would seem (and not incorrectly so) that Udayshanth Fernando's distinct stamp is all over Colombo. After all, the harbour city's chicest guidebook-worthy spots are all a part of Fernando's nearly three-decade-strong empire. Let's take a look at his portfolio—there's the flagship home store Paradise Road (which started the entire journey) and its adjoining café; the lush 10-suite hotel Tintagel; the Geoffrey Bawa-designed The Gallery Café; the concept store PR, founded by his older daughter, Annika; the Saskia Fernando Art Gallery started by his younger daughter; and, further south of the city, another Bawa property, The Villa Bentota. It's a unique situation where, in a city of approximately 800,000 residents, a family of four has made it their life's purpose to bring a distinct style of living that many believe has become synonymous with a modern Sri Lankan aesthetic. For nearly 30 years, the Fernandos have been considered arbiters of taste, with their fingers in many proverbial pies—starting with home, and moving to food, hospitality, art and fashion. All due respect to Aristotle, who famously said “the whole is greater than the sum of its parts,” but when it comes to the Fernandos' family business, each entity, while singular on its own, is also deeply connected. Saskia's art gallery is on the floor above Annika's store, PR; Saskia designs jewellery that she stocks at PR; till very recently Shanth used a table at The Gallery Café as his personal office (“For the longest time my nephew, Annika's son, thought that was his grandfather's home,” Saskia says, laughing); and their mother, the German-born, Dutch-Danish-Austrian Angelika, is responsible for the food, especially the 38 desserts The Gallery Café offers. “It's a thread,” Shanth tells me. “It's all about design, and once you meet my daughters you'll see they have a very keen, clear taste. It's timeless. No gimmicks.” In this family, the boundaries between work and pleasure have dissolved—what binds them is an aesthetic, native pride, an overriding passion, and an incredible work ethic. “I've babysat the girls in art galleries,” says Shanth. “Our dinner table conversations have always revolved around design, and for us living well and good design is a religion.” STARTING FROM SCRATCH With its beautiful sea-facing promenade, wide roads and rich colonial heritage, Colombo is a Bombay we are all nostalgic for. It was 29 years ago, on a business trip, that Shanth, who had been living in Australia and New Zealand, saw the incredible potential in the country of his roots. “I've always worked with circumstances. I saw there was a lack of a singular, sophisticated identity.” So indigenous bright colours were replaced with neutrals and a monochrome palette (“When many people think of Shanth Fernando, they think of black and white”); fussy swirls and curls were replaced with straightforward stripes and squares; batik was reinvented in geometric patterns; and, in the case of Tintagel, a former private home that Shanth converted to a hotel that has Prince Charles's seal of approval, an eclecticism emerged—a neutral canvas brought to life by colourful objets d'art. “I bought chandeliers from Baccarat in Paris, Dutch antiques, Spanish sofas. I transformed a colonial heritage building into something completely unexpected.” What resonates is a complete disregard for trends, whether it comes to his wardrobe or his work (“I have a collection of 20-year-old Issey Miyake shirts that I wear even today”), an obsession with art (three floors of his new home hold 300 pieces of art) and an insistence on a Sri Lankan connect. It's this cultural pride that connects him to the star architect Geoffrey Bawa, who was known for his brand of tropical modernism. “I remember seeing my black and white cushions at his residence,” Shanth remembers fondly. “He became a very good acquaintance. We have a continuity in style, and that's why he trusted me to be true to his aesthetic. There's a patina to his work, and we've tried to honour that.” OF LOVE AND LEGACY Respect comes up a great deal in my conversations with the incredibly attractive, unfailingly polite, multi-hyphenate Annika and Saskia Fernando, Shanth's two daughters. Thirty-seven-year-old Annika is a mother of one, an interior designer and the owner of the city's first fashion concept store, PR, which stocks Indian and Sri Lankan designers alongside her own self-designed label, Maus. The label was named after the German term of endearment used by their mother, and also as an homage to her work. (“She's the backbone. She's a strong personality, a silent power, and an incredible cook.”) Her younger sister, 34-year-old Saskia, has established herself as one of the country's foremost gallerists and experts on contemporary art, and is also a jewellery designer with her semi-precious label Papillon du Thé. It's over a long lunch of fresh fish and salad at Colombo's popular Café Francais that I discover how deeply ingrained their father's philosophy is. The sisters, who share an office, started out with divergent interests—Annika studying chemistry and medicine (her father's dream) and Saskia commerce and hospitality before exploring her twin passions of art and jewellery—ending up right where they were destined to belong. “It's always been a part of my life,” says Annika. “We never had child-friendly holidays. We were taken to beautiful cities to look at architecture and art. I remember hating it…” Saskia chimes in, laughing, “It was a bit torturous, because you know my father is such an eccentric, creative person. But it gets instilled in you, and that knowledge is a part of our education.” Their father “threw them into the deep end” expecting them to “find themselves,” so holidays were spent working. “I realised that I was running the art side of The Gallery Café, so I had a conversation with my father,” says Saskia about switching fields. There's been no silver spoon. Annika spent her savings to start PR. “Paradise Road is my father's baby, so we had to find ways to complement the brand but still be independent. PR is my interpretation. We work incredibly hard, something we have seen with our parents.” The sisters are incredibly close, with a common love for clean lines and minimalism, but with their own stamp. Annika leans towards androgyny, while Saskia tends to add more bohemian and feminine detailing to her looks. “We've often bought the same thing without realising it but worn it completely differently,” says Saskia. Has there been no generational conflict? How do they resolve creative differences? Saskia laughs. “It's not a very structured company. We're involved in everything but we're sensitive about each other's spaces. Yes, there is criticism and we do get irritated, especially if we don't agree. I think it's a very unique relationship when two sisters can actually work on one project and I admire that, but our roles have always been completely defined.” AGENTS OF CHANGE Despite the years of strife, which severely curtailed tourism in Sri Lanka, the Fernandos have never veered away from their design ideologies. “My father's motto has always been ‘You just stick through it and mind your own business.' So I really stick strong. Consistency is the hardest thing to maintain; it's not something you can buy alone, you have to feel it,” Annika says. A defined aesthetic aside, value is an important factor. “I find I'm picking designers where I can explain the value and who have a strong identity. I only stock what's relevant to the climate, and I choose pieces that I like. Maus was initially started to set the aesthetic of the store and fill my racks, and it's now become the brand that pays the bills,” says Annika. That's not to say they haven't faced their share of obstacles, especially in changing the proclivities of the local market. “There is a preference for the decorative, and our pieces tend to be more modern, abstract and conceptual,” says Saskia about the art hanging in homes. “But it's changing with the younger collectors. We've also introduced different platforms for educating and consulting on the art market, so it's a work in progress.” Saskia, represents 22 contemporary artists, including Rajni Perera, Priyantha Udagedara and Nadia Haji Omar. The girls are unanimous in one thought—they are living their dreams. Saskia counts the independent relationships that she's built in the industry as her biggest source of pride, while for Annika it's the potential she sees in Maus, which just launched swimwear, to become the country's leading high-street brand. Clearly, their father's personal passion has become their life's goals. “My son took his first steps at Villa Bentota… this is our family's work,” says Annika. Going back to their father, I ask Shanth which word would best describe his life so far. Serendipity, perhaps? “Versatility. From retail to restaurants, hotels to a gallery. If I wasn't versatile, how could I do it all?” Hair and make-up: Dilhara, Chalana/Ramani Fernando Salons Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Love Chanderi? Don’t miss these images from Amazon India Fashion Week
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Highlights from day 1 View Gallery 51 Photos Opening Show at Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2017 The opening show for Amazon India Fashion Week S/S 2017 ‘The Road To Chanderi' highlighted the weave from Madhya Pradesh. Sixteen designers were given the brief to create garments using Chanderi while working within a colour palette of gold and white or jewel tones. Jyotiraditya Scindia, part of the former royal family of Gwalior and member of Indian Parliament, was present for the show. Here's everything you need to know about it. The Chanderi town of Madhya Pradesh, where the Chanderi saris are woven, has long received patronage from royalty as part of a nationwide tradition, through which local arts were aided and promoted with pride by the rulers. The Scindia family continues to do so for the weavers in Chanderi. Designer Sanjay Garg of sari label Raw Mango, who started his label working on Chanderi saris, spoke highly of the work of the Scindias who have empowered weavers in Madhya Pradesh, not only by promoting them but by ensuring adequate water and electricity to help them work in humane conditions. Jyotiraditya Scindia's note at the end of the show advised buyers to shop wisely, “In Chanderi we only use handlooms, and fabrics are registered through a Geographical Indication. Please shop wise and ensure that the money you spend falls in the hands of the rightful owners, those who create these fabrics.” Anita Dongre showcased her diffusion line Grassroot by Anita Dongre, through which she works with indigenous craftspeople, and the collection made a case for the versatility of the fabric. The Chanderi sari is woven with cotton and silk yarns, making it the perfect choice for the tropical Indian humidity and happened to be Dongre's fabric of choice for spring/summer 2017. Aditi Rao Hydari closed the show by walking the runway for Raw Mango, and could not stop gushing about how the fabric felt like a cloud against her skin. The actor wore a black and gold lehenga by designer Sanjay Garg. Ruchika Sachdeva of Bodice highlighted the three qualities of the fabric—the sheerness, the shine and the lightness of the weave, which she translated in her own modern, minimalist aesthetic. Of the designers that showed, Payal Pratap, Péro by Aneeth Arora, Atsu by Atsu Sekhose, Akaaro by Gaurav Jai Gupta, Ikai by Ragini Ahuja, Grassroot by Anita Dongre, Bodice by Ruchika Sachdeva and Raw Mango had distinct looks that stood out. column1: Why Péro is not on the Amazon India Fashion Week S/S 2017 schedule
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Fans of the label will not be disappointed The Péro show is noticeably missing on the Amazon India Fashion Week spring/summer 2017 schedule. This of course is genius on the part of the brand's creative director Aneeth Arora. Péro recently moved its headquarters to a new venue, and Arora wanted to bring the crowd to the new location. “We always challenge ourselves to transport the audience to our world. If you go to see, the size constrains of the ramp are the same for everyone, but we work hard on transforming it. This season we wanted everyone to see what our own working space is like,” says Arora. The studio, workshop and store are all under the same roof at the new location. It is very green and Arora has been conscious of making sure the store emits very little waste. Because the space is rented, she was unable to install solar panels but that is definitely on the cards, she assures us. Péro will run a live installation on all days of Amazon India Fashion Week, where customers can come and interact with the karigars who are in process of making garments and even meet the designer. And in good news for those aren't in the city and don't want to miss the show—the showcase will take place on Instagram and Facebook on October 15 at 8.00 pm. This season, it was the work of painter and botanist Pierre-Joseph Redouté that caught Arora's eye. Redouté was the court artist for Marie Antoinette, often known as the Raphael of Flowers. Drawing references from his illustrations of the garden at the Château de Malmaison, Arora has worked detail into her garments by mirroring the artwork through embroidery. “We have used satin stitches to replicate the brushwork,” she says. The focus this season was on using the striped Mashru textile that was traditionally woven for the Muslim community who were forbidden to use silk. The weave of the fabric is such that the cotton warp is closer to the skin than the silk weft. Keeping an overall vintage look in mind, the clothes this season bear tulle and hand-crocheted lace details. Arora has also used floral prints and kora linen to balance the colour palette. One of the key reasons Péro clothes are popular amongst fashion enthusiasts despite not being hyper trendy or even favourable choices for occasion wear is the level of meticulousness with which Arora attempts to fully materialise her vision. This season's press kit will include a cross-stitch pattern with an embroidery ring and tile coasters bearing floral designs (Arora recently collaborated with FCML on a collection of tiles). It will also include hand-crocheted floral brooches created by Afghani refugees. Tune in to the Péro show on October 15 at 8:00 pm from any part of the world, or if you happen to be in town, drop by at the store between October 12-16 to meet the designer and browse through the special exhibit. But first, check out the slideshow for a little teaser of what's in store for you. View Gallery 12 Photos Pero Péro, 231 Patparganj Industrial Area, New Delhi. column1: Are celebrities bringing back the tracksuit?
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Life comes a full circle View Gallery 15 Photos Are celebrities bringing back the tracksuit? Whether the revival of the tracksuit makes you roll your eyes or dust off that Von Dutch buried at the back of your closet, brace for impact, for it's here to stay. If you're wondering why the athletic basic assumes the pride of a conversational topic, here's a jog down memory lane for you. The tracksuit became the symbol of unapologetic luxury for the jet-setting crew in the early 2000's. Paris Hilton owned them by the dozen and Jennifer Lopez wore them to proclaim that she's real. Amy Poehler, mother to sorority queen Regina George offered unsolicited ‘cool mom' advice in her pink Juicy Couture number in Mean Girls. What goes up must come down, and as tracksuits lost their rhinestones, their status as the ultimate couldn't-care-less rich girl vibe soon went south. That's until recently, when the athleisure trend brought it back into our lives—high-street to designer wear, their presence now is unmissable. Gucci and Chloé were the first to brave a tracksuit down the runway, embroidered and colour blocked to perfection for spring/summer 2016. Tommy Hilfiger's floral take on it at his resort 2017 showcase was more lounge appropriate. If you walk into the nearest Zara, you're likely to find a budget-friendly version too. The celebrities clearly can't get enough: Kim Kardashian and Bella Hadid styled theirs with sultry tops, while Cara Delevingne and Margot Robbie got matching satin ones with their names emblazoned on the jacket. Rihanna, who must have the last word on things, took a bow at her recent Fenty x Puma collection launch in a blush number, complete with a trail. Want in on the trend? column1: #SuzyPFW Chanel: Intimate Technology
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Karl Lagerfeld gets tangled up in computer wires View Gallery 19 Photos #SuzyPFW Chanel: Intimate Technology The sunlit arch of the Grand Palais (venue for the Chanel spring/summer 2017 show) looked down on a line-up of hefty clicking, whirring computers with snarls of multi-coloured twisting wires at their base. This gigantic techno data centre (that did nothing to boost the feeble signal of an audience clutching their smartphones) formed the backdrop for the line-up of guests. The mighty machines followed the audience's benches into what seemed like techno infinity. Karl Lagerfeld had already thought up another of his 'bons mots' or smart expressions. "Intimate technology", the designer said, referring to the Chanel tweed outfits that inevitably kicked off the show, their short, thick skirts opening with front and rear vertical zippers to reveal pink chiffon underwear. The girly effect of this lingerie seemed like an outmoded "oh la la!" vision of womankind in 2016. But then almost everything was wrong about this start-up. If the models were supposed to be a futuristic tech group (and the first two came out as robotic, space age figures in helmets and padded mittens), shouldn't these smart women have been wearing techno fabrics and the kind of clothes that suit hot desking and 20 hour work shifts? Instead they had on boring old baseball caps. Karl was the first couturier to understand the concept of fashionable sneakers, yet his spring/summer 2017 footwear was only punched sandals with straps wrapping the ankles and ballet flats. But far more than the minutiae of the accessories, there was no sense of the powerful beauty of technology in the blurry-check suits, a striped puffer jacket with a snow drift of chiffon on the sleeves, or in tweeds illuminated with crystals. We all know, of course, that the intangible 'cloud' that contains the content of our electronic devices is a string of wires and grinding computers—probably something like what appeared on the Chanel stage. But we want to believe in something more poetic: the 'cloud' as heavenly, out there and up there, looking after the collections of our lives in digital words and images. It was that magic that was missing in this Chanel show, although Karl gave it some vivid touches like tabs of shocking pink or chilly crystal for bold necklaces. There were also some techno patterned dresses—bright, light and colourful—and no doubt in subtle texture and careful construction—totally different from the digital prints in the windows of every high street shop. For the Chanel store windows there was plenty of stuff to rock the clients: flashy colour for plaid jackets and cute plastic-looking box bags in bright pink. But this show, for all its fine clothes, looked like a gimmick to keep up with a shifting world. And there is more beauty in the smooth metallic oblong device held in the palm of the hand than in the fancy clothes on Chanel's clicking and flashing stage. column1: Why Radhika Apte prefers this accessory to diamonds
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion It’s about time you got one of these It's not every day you hear a woman say she prefers timepieces to jewellery, but Radhika Apte has never been one to follow the crowds. “I never wear diamonds!” the star confessed to us at the opening of Swatch's very first corporate store in Mumbai's Phoenix Marketcity on October 4. “I usually like very subtle jewellery. It has to be very delicate, and should merge with what I'm wearing.” And what about when she's in the mood to stand out? “When I want to make a statement, I do so with a watch. I don't have to wear anything else, just this. For me, a watch does make a statement. It conveys style. I'd prefer to wear a watch over a piece of jewellery any day.” Wondering where Apte's obsession with the accessory stems from? “I don't have a huge collection [of watches], but my love for them began in my childhood. My father is a doctor, and he used to get a lot of watches as gifts, but he never wore them. And so I started wearing his watches. My collection includes lots of his old pieces.” What makes the Swiss watch label's new space more exciting than others is that it houses its latest pieces from both, its fall/winter 2016 collection, and the Sistem51 Irony line, and will continue to bring in the brand's newest creations the same time they launch worldwide. Before you stop by, take a cue from Apte's style file. “It's cool to be androgynous,” she says, “And the kind of the designs Swatch has come up with, you can just put them together and create a look effortlessly. If I were going out at night, I'd probably pick one of the metallic pieces. And for day, maybe one of the white strapped designs that feature a pop of colour in the dial. They're so bright and fun!” Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Jacqueline Fernandez tells us why she’s in love with this designer label
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Understated yet impactful couture Ankur and Priyanka Modi's label AM:PM is an established name in pret fashion. Constant requests to create one-off festive garments pushed the designers to consider the possibility of working on a couture line. After eight months of ideation, the first collection ‘Zivar' emerged, just in time for the festive season. “The initial thought was how to do festive wear, keeping in mind the key ingredients of AM:PM—the same understated simplicity, same colour palette and the effortlessness,” says Priyanka Modi, creative director, AM:PM. The brand's primary motive was to work on a line that the AM:PM customer could relate to. “Most people are used to a certain amount of bling when it comes to occasion wear, but you can't lose your USP,” she adds. The inspiration for the collection stems from the ancient Persian craft of bidri ware. Modi roughly explains the process as that of inlay work of sheets of silver on a blackened alloy. The colour palette of ‘Zivar' is primarily monochromatic but also uses hues of mint and scarlet. Details of the embellishments are translated by way of threadwork, mukaish, zardozi stitches, pearls and subtle 3D highlights. “Women today are more practical; they want to simply look effective. It is about creating versatility in those silhouettes,” explains Modi when describing the thought behind the pieces, each of which has been worked on with a view to be worn as a separate. The brand chose Jacqueline Fernandez as the face of their meticulously detailed couture line. Fernandez described the collection as a, “beautiful take on incorporating modern details in traditional silhouettes”. She further stated that on a personal level, her choice in festive wear is something that's impactful but not necessarily over the top. “Their stuff is amazing and I'm just hoping I can elevate that,” she said. Watch the making of the autumn/winter 2016 couture campaign here. The AM:PM couture collection will be available at all AM:PM stores October 15 onwards Fashion Fashion Weddings © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: #SuzyPFW Céline: It’s A Woman’s World
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Designer Phoebe Philo reflected the calm and the chaos of modern life. View Gallery 15 Photos #SuzyPFW Céline: It’s A Woman’s World That woman with the raffia straw bra over a white dress with its hemline dipped in blue ink—is she crazy? But here she is again, looking sleek and absolutely normal in her pale plaid pant suit, its waist cut away to let a belt slip through. So there it is: the dichotomy of modern women's lives at Céline. Even if the models had been stark naked in the rush to get up, make breakfast, stuff their tablet into a bag, drop the kids off at school and make it to work on time—designer Phoebe Philo would still have got her message across. It cried out from the planning of the set, where the models walked purposefully in different directions, as if following a map of organised chaos. The only thing that stayed constant as the figures criss-crossed the space were the shoes and the bags, always perfectly selected even if a neat, square hard bag and soft white sandals were teamed with a white dress that looked as though a maverick artist had painted ink splodges on a woman's intimate areas from breasts to thighs. Phoebe's innate understanding of a modern women's multiple roles could probably be summed up by the fact that she had two daughters discreetly placed beside a pillar on the set, tidy in blue jeans with highly decorated shoes. Who knows if they give their mother fashion advice—or inspire her just by being there? This Céline collection was notable for its harmony of the essential and the whimsical: the first embodied by a smart jacket, the other by what looked like a fraying white table napkin absent-mindedly left tucked into the bodice. Was this Céline collection an ode to women's crazy busy lives? If so, Phoebe Philo turned it into an art form with a display of quiet and bright colours in perfect harmony. It seems that the chaos theory of fashion can become a thing of beauty—if left in the right artistic hands. This article previously appeared on Vogue.co.uk Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: How fashion is lending its support to World Animal Day
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Standing up for our furry friends View Gallery 8 Photos World Animal Day Artist Bina Aziz has always been an ardent animal lover. A trip to the Masai Mara safari in Kenya last year not only gave her the subject for her next collection of paintings, but also moved her to take a concrete step against animal cruelty. She garnered support from her friends and fellow animal lovers, fashion designer Amy Billimoria; and Gautam Ghanasingh, CEO and creative director of jewellery brand Ghanasingh BE TRUE; to use their work in raising a voice and taking a step towards change. The result is their thought-provoking initiative—an event being held on World Animal Day, on October 4, 2016—where the three will use their craft and expertise to draw attention to the brutality against our furry friends. “It's heart-breaking to hear of ghastly stories about animal abuse on a daily basis. Our endeavour is about three like-minded professionals who are committed to this cause that is close to our hearts. It's about celebrating human relationships, and our bond with the animal kingdom,” explains Aziz. The artist has curated a special jewellery collection for Ghanasingh BE TRUE for the event. “It symbolises the magnificence of nature while also showcasing the brand's craftsmanship skills. The collection uses unique patterns and designs with a focus on modernism to highlight the atrocities against endangered species. This is our way of giving back to the society,” explains Ghanasingh. Billimoria, on the other hand, has created a clothing collection inspired by Aziz's paintings. “This is a contemporary range of separates with appliqué detailing, layering, laser cuts, cording and varied embroidery techniques to create interesting surface textures. Wearing animal-inspired clothing without harming them is the basis of my collection,” the designer explains. The trio will donate a part of the proceeds from the event to Probably Paradise Trust by Roxanne Davur, that shelters more than 200 animals in need of attention. “Roxanne has devoted her entire life to the welfare and protection of India's animals. We felt that our aid could help her do so much more,” says Aziz, signing off. Fashion Fashion Fashion © 2019 Condé Nast

column1: Everything you ever wanted to know about bras
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion But didn’t know who to ask View Gallery 13 Photos Everything you ever wanted to ask about bras Marks & Spencer's reputation as one of the best makers of innerwear is undisputed. As the iconic British label turns 90 this year, Vogue catches up with Julia Mercer, the lingerie fit expert at Marks & Spencer, about everything there is to know about intimates. Is there such a thing as a ‘perfect bra'? Yes and no, as the ‘perfect bra' is a very individual thing. What is perfect for one woman is not perfect for another. It's is important to get fitted correctly and to work with the fitter to find a bra that best suits your needs. I do feel confident that within our wide range, we have the perfect bra for every woman, given the size, style, colour and price range that our brand offers. What are the most common mistakes women make while picking bras? The biggest mistake is not wearing the right size. If I can give women one piece of advice, it is to get fitted. A well-fitting bra will help your posture, give you confidence in your outerwear and even make you look slimmer, besides being supremely comfortable. I would recommend that women get measured every six to twelve months. Your breast shape can change from gaining or losing weight, therefore it is imperative that you are fitted by a fully-trained bra-fit expert to ensure you are wearing the right size. Talk to the fitter about what you want and how you want the bra to feel; what you will be wearing the bra with, shapes you prefer. If it's a sports bra, then tell her what sports you play so she can suggest the impact level. The more information you provide the better, so the fitter can help you choose the perfect style. Additionally, I always say that if you're prepping for a special occasion, bring your outfit in for the fitting and we can help you find the right bra for your outfit. Marks & Spencer has created lingerie for different needs. Of all the products made, which of them have been the most challenging from the design perspective? Lingerie is a really specialised product, and due to the nature of the craftsmanship and technical aspects of the development process, many bras incorporate over 40 individual components, so it's always a huge challenge to develop a new bra. One of the most recent examples I can think of is our Extra High Impact Sports Bra. Sports bras for high impact games are very technically challenging [to create] and it is key to work out where the impact is, how to minimise it, how to ensure perfect comfort and also how to develop something that looks attractive. With this bra, our technical team worked with Japanese scientists who were experimenting with cutting edge avatar technology to develop hi-tech air bags for the car industry! Utilising this research, we identified the key points of impact, and built the bra from there. It's an amazing product and allows women to exercise in comfort. We always seek feedback on our lingerie from customers and the comments from customers about this bra are glowing. The bra has certainly changed its form over the decades. How does Marks & Spencer contribute to innovating it further? It's all about constant research and identifying customer needs. We're always talking and listening to our customers, looking at trend forecasts, analysing changing lifestyles as well as working with fabric suppliers to make sure we are ahead of the trends. This helps us to always be at the forefront of lingerie innovation. Sometimes it not just about how the lingerie feels, it might be about how it makes our customers lives easier. One of our really popular innovations has been the introduction of all our 100 per cent silk lingerie and sleepwear, made with machine-washable silk. This continues to be well-received by customers even though it was introduced some time ago. Innovation therefore comes in many forms, but we are always looking for the next new thing. column1: Everything you need to know about Maria Grazia Chiuri’s debut collection
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion A first in fashion history View Gallery 12 Photos Everything you need to know about Maria Grazia Chiuri’s debut collection The first-ever female creative director in Dior's 70-year history couldn't have made a more fitting debut. Maria Grazia Chiuri's collection at Paris Fashion Week came packed with girl power. While the ramp saw a slew of pretty-meets-powerful ensembles, the highlight of the show was the unusual combination of a slogan T-shirt that read, “we should all be feminists” with a semi-sheer tulle skirt and sneakers. Models walked the ramp to Beyoncé's iconic single 'Flawless', which features Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's TEDx talk about feminism. In addition to Adichie, the show's front row found itself dotted with stars including Rihanna and Kate Moss. Chiuri's endeavour didn't go unnoticed amongst the fashion crew. “Even if you had been living under a rock these past months, it was easy to sense the new direction at Dior's S/S '17 show,” says Vogue India's editor, Priya Tanna. “Young and fun, the tulle, the sporty jackets and the whimsical astrology motifs flirted with femininity. The collection, which was ready to show in only six weeks, defied our expectancies and gave a strong signal for the times to come for the brand. Is it old Dior in a new bottle, or is it a new bottle with hints of old Dior? Time will tell, but for now, the newly-appointed creative director Maria Grazia Chiuri has our undivided attention, appreciation and intrigue.” “There was so much anticipation for Maria Grazia Chiuri's first collection for Dior, and she shone,” says Vogue India's fashion director Anaita Shroff Adajania. “Her collection seamlessly brought together elements of the house's illustrious past and her distinctive taste. Ballet tulle dresses sparkled down the runway with fine narrative embroidery, toughened by street style-esque leather elements. It's a cool new dawn for Dior, let's welcome Dior's new street cred.” Before Chiuri skipped over to Dior, she was part of the famous Valentino duo, alongside Pierpaolo Piccioli. This year, Paris Fashion Week also saw Piccioli's first show as sole creative director. The collection was inherently romantic, with reds and pinks dominating the shade card. column1: #SuzyPFW Valentino’s Garden Of Earthly Delights
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion This major success for Pierpaolo Piccioli, left alone after his partner's departure to Dior, was helped by a collaboration with Zandra Rhodes View Gallery 15 Photos #SuzyPFW Valentino’s Garden Of Earthly Delights The fragility of the dresses, the sweetness of the faces, the gentle spirit of the Valentino show won over the audience before more than a handful of outfits had hit the runway. Yet the test was tough for Pierpaolo Piccioli as to how he would fair now that his design partner of more than two decades had departed. Maria Grazia Chiuri left the Italian house earlier this year for French Christian Dior and made an acceptable start with her first show on Friday. Pierpaolo showed his strength as the romantic of the pair. For Valentino spring/summer 2017, he used a winning blend of historicism, Italian technique and the country's distant past, to make a collection that was clear in its message and simple in its vision. Pierpaolo wanted women to look beautiful. And he had found an unlikely spiritual partner—Zandra Rhodes—the British designer whose hand-drawn patterns have been a perpetual inspiration in fashion since they first appeared in the 1970s. But instead of screen-grabbing some of the unique illustrations, Pierpaolo went to London and asked Zandra to create something new for Valentino. His dream—a new version of the Hieronymus Bosch painting The Garden of Earthly Delights—incorporating the Bosch art which he loves so deeply, with clothes for today. “The idea of the Bosch painting was because I was seeking out that idea from the past," said the designer, who had on his mood board the original art work—Zandra's interpretations and pictures of her in the 1970s with bright fuchsia hair, an invention of the Punk period when to dye your hair pink really was shocking. The result was historic and modern in equal measures, as a black dress appeared with bright pink inserts that looked like spears, as a prelude to the skirt's wider pinstripes. Then came other dresses, mostly ankle length, but fresh and summery—not at this stage precious evening pieces. The total looks were rather more relaxed than at recent Valentino shows which had an almost religious undertone; there was even a casual white shirt with velvet patterned trousers and a leather jacket shrugged on for this season. I asked the designer, who showed in the same grand building as previously, how he had coped with being left at Valentino as sole designer. "The initial philosophy is that you have to forget your past, but I think this season I have to go inside myself—I have to understand my idea of beauty," said Pierpaolo. "I'm Italian," he continued, "and even if my idea of beauty comes from other countries, it's generally from the same moment of the late Middle Ages, because there was an evolution of culture. "I think of Bosch and The Garden Of Earthly Delights not as a Renaissance painting, but before this time, from the Middle Ages." So the designer, loving the delicacy of the painting, its fantastic imagery and detailed landscapes, asked Zandra to interpret Bosch in a new print, but still in the traditional way of Italian handcraft, not as digital prints. It is important that Valentino, its Italian roots planted so long ago by the founder, keep the balance between global success and its historic and artistic Italian past. That showed in each dress. These were elements seen in previous collections that Pierpaolo was now re-drawing as his own. Except that he had chosen Zandra to collaborate on a pattern on a pink georgette dress or one in yellow, lightly printed from bodice to floor. I picked up a pattern of cacti and palm trees on a shorter dress and some prints that looked like black markings straight off the drawing board. Why a Renaissance of Zandra Rhodes at age 76, even if her artistic skills have been present in fashion for 40 years? Pierpaolo explained how he needed someone who could re-think the concept of treating and over-dyeing fabrics to soften bright colours physically and visually. After all this preparation, the show was a hit, with the audience cheering the designer's first show as a singleton. With Giancarlo Giammetti, Valentino's partner joining in the applause, I asked Zandra how she felt. "For me it was wonderful when Pierpaolo flew over with his team," she said. "He showed me the Hieronymus Bosch book and asked me to do interpretations that were then sent to Como (Italy's silk centre) and the embroiderers. He totally followed me and my drawings and I was so honoured to be on the storyboard. I hope I can work with Valentino again." But Zandra has not come out of retirement just for this work. She still designs across the globe and has a unique collection of 10 archive looks currently on sale online at Matches [Matchesfashion.com]. column1: #SuzyPFW Balenciaga: Fetishising The Past
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion Designer Demna Gvasalia brought the haute down from its heights View Gallery 15 Photos #SuzyPFW Balenciaga: Fetishising The Past Can Cristóbal and Spandex be spoken in the same breath? One is to be whispered in awe as the first name of hallowed Spanish designer Balenciaga; the other is a synthetic fabric that is body-hugging, super stretchy and exuding a certain brash vulgarity. They were both at the peak of invention in the same year: 1958. But does designer Demna Gvasalia really want to sexualise an icon of haute couture and a designer who marked the course of fashion history? Why not? It made for a bright, bold show in which the undercurrent of sexuality brought the haute down from its heights. Instead of grandeur and grace, there was a streamlined collection that still applied the brand's codes, from architectural shapes to prints of flowers. It also had its elegant side with pleated blouses and diamanté brooches. "Not sexy—sensual," said Demna backstage, although he was wearing a sweatshirt with SPANDEX written on the front. And his show notes suggested that today's designer saw something that lay behind the fashion sculptures of the past. That sparkling circular brooch was borrowed from the Balenciaga archives and might indeed, as Demna imagined, have been held in Cristóbal's own hand "as he pinned it to the breasts of his original models". Fetishistic thoughts indeed. Here is an intriguing designer who seems to be able to think through the VIP of his collections. No! Not those front row stars, but Visually, Intellectually and Practically. So the show could be seen on those three levels—visually there were the vivid colours, bright enough to bring life to a simple skirt or a pair of the stretch trousers. And the bags—so vast that they were a statement all of their own with big buckets of red, orange, royal blue or florals. All the bags had the effect of having a feminine spirit from the 1950s given a bold new masculine stance. Intellectually, there seemed to be various thought processes—the wide-shouldered trench coats as a continuation of Demna's debut Balenciaga display of sporty puffer jackets; femininity resuscitated as shapely blouses in mannish shirt materials; and the flowers that were part of both Cristóbal's oeuvre and of Vetements, Demna's other day job. And the practical side at Balenciaga? Much of the above, producing clothes that seem wearable and 'normal' give or take the fetishistic vision of crochet mesh, not only as the partner to a prim lace skirt, but also as hosiery that looked like it was growing on the legs. Demna's notes added "the thrill of fetishism" to latex capes, although I would have judged them more as the plastic ponchos on sale on the street during rain storms. By the time that George Michael's Careless Whisper filled the thin, tented rooms, where Salma Hayek sat with her husband François-Henri Pinault, Balenciaga's owner, there is only one conclusion—the executive made a very smart choice in Demna. With so many empty chairs in the carousel of couture houses, this designer has the guts and the smarts to give Balenciaga a new turn on Fortune's wheel. column1: #SuzyPFW Balmain: Moving To The Country
column2: © Vogue Images Fashion The fashion army built by Olivier Rousteing is taking a gentler route through nature View Gallery 15 Photos #SuzyPFW Balmain: Moving To The Country Only Olivier's friend Kim Kardashian, in a dress with the body coverage of a fishing net, and her extended family gave a hint of the seductive gowns that would later glitter their path down the catwalk. "I love hardwear - I am addicted to it," said Kim backstage with her sister Kourtney Kardashian in a bower of greenery, as hot model Gigi Hadid, former French First Lady Carla Bruni and the ever glamorous Giancarlo Giammetti, milled around them. Balmain is making waves - partly for the sum Qatar investment Mayhoola offered to take on the house, which is no doubt hoping to create the same success as with Valentino - the company's other big fashion name. There is also a latent criticism of Olivier himself and the shake-up he has given to the once staid French couture house - whether that is based on envy or a dislike of his feisty approach. But like a new day dawning, something had changed at Balmain. It was a kinder, gentler and more nature based view of fashion. After the first clothes, the colours inspired by the green tropical plantation heated up to a fiery shade. But the earlier outfits cascaded down the body softly. Only later came hefty belts, double slit skirts letting legs out up to the thigh, and a shade of blue brighter than any tropical sky. As red took over, Olivier started his game of more-flesh-than-dress. But this sexuality was counterbalanced by craftsmanship and by coloured coverups. The show was assured yet fresh. But just when you thought that this 80-strong collection was coming to a crescendo, out came metallic outfits, Gianni Versace 1980s style, glittering like an entire galaxy of stars had fallen from the skies onto these quivering bodies. What to make of the drama of Balmain's presentation? Firstly, this in-your-face sexy glamour is working, and secondly, that Olivier Rousteing is pushing in a new direction. His nature trail may be long, and its destination distant, but full marks for trying to take a new direction.
